docs.title: C, C++ Systems Engineering Learning Path
docs.text:
A 12-week curriculum that takes a working C programmer to production-depth knowledge of C, modern C++17, concurrency, debugging, Linux, databases and distributed systems, built around one real project: a multithreaded TCP key-value server.

Every module follows the same shape: plain words first, then the real mechanism, complete code, what happens under the hood, how it fails in production, exercises, and interview questions.

Start here: the 12-week plan Set up your machine

docs.title: The courses
docs.text:
• Environment Setup

    WSL, GCC 13, CMake, gdb, Valgrind and sanitizers working on day one.

    From complexity to B+trees, graphs and DP, plus a 10-week interview problem plan.

    Threads, mutexes, condition variables, atomics and the memory model, thread pools, Win32.

    13 modules ·

    Open

  • Memory, Debugging & RCA

    Process memory, malloc internals, gdb, core dumps, WinDbg, sanitizers, writing an RCA.

    13 modules ·

    Open

  • Linux, Toolchain & DevOps

    The linker, GCC flags, CMake, GoogleTest, Git, Docker, CI, systems calls.

    12 modules ·

    Open

  • Database Internals

    Pages, B-trees, WAL, MVCC, EXPLAIN, PL/pgSQL, Berkeley DB, YugabyteDB, Redis.

    14 modules ·

    Open

    TCP, sockets, epoll, RPC, HTTP, consistency, Raft, sharding, system design.

    14 modules ·

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
1. Follow the week-by-week table in Start here. Study three or four courses in parallel, one module per sitting.
  2. Type the code yourself. Every program is linked to GitHub and builds with -Wall -Wextra -Werror on GCC 13.
  3. Press Mark as done at the top of a module when you can say its recap out loud without looking. Your progress is saved in this browser only.
  4. Use the search box (press /) to find any topic across all courses.

docs.title: START HERE — The 12-week plan to a C, C++ systems job by December 2026
docs.text: Written for: Shakir, 2.5 years of production C, moving to a senior-level C, C++ systems role. Dates: Week 1 starts Tuesday 2026-10-06. Weeks run Tuesday to Monday. Week 12 ends Monday 2026-12-28. Rule of the plan: every line on the resume must be backed by something you have built, debugged or can explain at whiteboard depth. Nothing on the resume is allowed to stay a "keyword".

docs.title: 1. How this folder is organised
docs.text:
LEARNING_PATH/
  00_START_HERE.md                      <- this file: the plan and the schedule
  _STYLE_GUIDE.md                       <- how every course is written (you can ignore it)
  01_Environment_Setup/                 <- 1 evening. Do this first.
  12_C_Programming/                     <- C to senior depth: pointers, UB, POSIX (16 modules)
  02_Modern_CPP/                        <- C++17 for a C programmer          (14 modules)
  03_Data_Structures_Algorithms/        <- DSA to interview level            (16 modules)
  04_Concurrency/                       <- threads, locks, atomics, pools    (13 modules)
  05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/              <- gdb, WinDbg, cores, Valgrind, RCA (13 modules)
  06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps/            <- Linux, GCC, CMake, Git, Docker, CI(12 modules)
  07_Databases_Internals/               <- PostgreSQL, YugabyteDB, BDB, Redis(14 modules)
  08_Networking_Distributed/            <- sockets, TCP, epoll, RPC, Raft    (14 modules)
  09_OOP_Design_Patterns_Architecture/  <- OOP, patterns, LLD interviews     (12 modules)
  10_Capstone_Projects/                 <- build tcpkv step by step (+ minidb)
  11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search/         <- question banks, stories, applications, negotiation
                                           (private: kept out of the public site and repo)

Every course has the same shape:

  • README.md — syllabus, hours, "you are done when you can..." checklist.
  • 01_*.md ... NN_*.md — modules. Each module: plain words -> real thing -> code -> under the hood -> in production -> exercises -> interview questions -> recap. Study one module per sitting.
  • code/ — complete programs. Build them on WSL with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread.
  • EXERCISES.md and INTERVIEW_QA.md — all exercises and interview questions in one place.

docs.title: 2. How to study (read this once, then trust it)
docs.text:
1. Read the module, then type the code yourself. Do not copy-paste. Typing is where it sticks.
  2. Break the code on purpose. Remove a std::move, drop a lock, overflow a buffer. Watch what gdb / ASan / TSan says. This is how production debugging skill is built.
  3. Say the recap out loud at the end of every module as if an interviewer asked. If you cannot say it without looking, you are not done.
  4. One notebook file: keep MY_NOTES.md in this folder. After every module write 5 lines: what surprised me, what I would say in an interview, what I still do not get.
  5. Parallel tracks, not serial. You study 3 to 4 courses at once (see the schedule). Each gets a fixed slot. Do not "finish C++ first and then start concurrency" — the project needs both at once.
  6. The project is the spine. Every week the tcpkv repo must have commits. The courses exist to make the project good and to make you able to defend every line of it.

docs.title: 3. Daily schedule (full-time job, about 3 h weekdays, 8 h weekend days)
docs.text:
Slot Weekday Weekend 06:00 - 07:00 DSA: 1 problem fully (think, code, test, write the pattern down) DSA: 2 problems + 1 review Lunch (20 min) Read one INTERVIEW_QA.md section, say answers in your head — 20:00 - 21:00 Course module (the week's "primary" course) Course modules (primary + secondary), 3 h 21:00 - 22:00 Project: tcpkv step of the week, commit Project: 3 h, commit, CI green — — Sunday 18:00: 1 h weekly review (11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search/12_weekly_checklists.md)

Weekly total: about 31 hours. Over 12 weeks: about 370 hours. That is enough if you do not skip days. If you miss a day, do not "catch up" by doubling; just continue. Consistency beats intensity.

docs.title: 4. The 12-week schedule

Not earlier (resume would 404), not later (December offers need November interviews).

Keep 2 to 3 processes alive in parallel. 11 Dec 15 - 21 Review Gap-filling only — Offers, negotiation, closing. 12 Dec 22 - 28 Light — — Accept. Resignation plan. First-90-days plan.

This table is the single schedule for the whole curriculum. The week-by-week tables in 11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search add interview-practice and application detail on top of it. Where they mention the project, the step numbers here and in 10_Capstone_Projects win.

The project runs ahead of the theory on purpose. Each tcpkv step guide starts with a "Read first" list. When it names a module scheduled for a later week, read only that module's sections 1 and 2 now (plain words and the real thing, about 30 minutes) and do the full module in its scheduled week. Example: step 08 in week 4 needs 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA module 08 on sanitizers, which is scheduled for week 6.

Starting late? If you begin after 2026-10-06, do not move December. Merge the missed week into the next ones using the cut list below, and protect week 5: tcpkv public and applications started by Monday 2026-11-09.

docs.title: If you fall behind, cut in this order
docs.text:
1. minidb (second project) — drop entirely. tcpkv alone is enough.
  2. 08_Networking modules 11-13 (Raft, sharding, HA) — read the recaps only.
  3. 09_OOP_Design modules 07-08, 12 — skip.
  4. 03 DSA modules 15 (tries/bits) — skip. Never cut: tcpkv, 02_Modern_CPP, 04_Concurrency, 05 modules 01-06, 07 modules 03-06, daily DSA.

docs.title: 5. Which course backs which resume line
docs.text: Resume line Course that makes it true C++17, STL, RAII, smart pointers, templates, OOP, memory & ownership 02_Modern_CPP, 09_OOP_Design C (language), multithreaded server-side C, memory corruption investigation 12_C_Programming Data structures & algorithms 03_Data_Structures_Algorithms Multithreading & concurrency; thread synchronisation layer; pooled request model 04_Concurrency Crash dump & core dump analysis, memory corruption, leaks, RCA 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA Linux, GCC, CMake, GDB, Git, Docker, CI/CD 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps PostgreSQL, YugabyteDB, Berkeley DB, Redis, internals, indexing, transactions, PL/pgSQL 07_Databases_Internals Sockets, TCP/IP, RPC, HTTP, distributed SQL, sharding, replication, HA 08_Networking_Distributed tcpkv project (every word of both bullets) 10_Capstone_Projects Performance optimisation 02/12, 04/10, 07/06, 07/14

docs.title: 6. Definition of "senior-level understanding" used throughout
docs.text:
For each topic you should be able to do all four:

  1. Explain it to a junior in plain words (the "In plain words" sections).
  2. Explain what happens under the hood (compiler, OS, kernel, storage engine).
  3. Write it from scratch (the code/ examples and the project).
  4. Debug it when it breaks in production (the "In production" sections and course 05).

Interviewers for 2 to 4 years of experience test 1 and 3 always, 2 often, 4 for systems roles. This plan targets all four.

docs.title: 7. Before you start (tonight)
docs.text:
1. Open 01_Environment_Setup/README.md and do the two modules. About 2 hours.
  2. Create MY_NOTES.md here.
  3. Create a private GitHub repo tcpkv now (make it public at week 5 when it is green).
  4. Put the daily schedule in your phone calendar with alarms.
  5. Read 11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search/README.md once so you know where this is going.

docs.title: 01. Environment Setup — one evening, then never think about it again
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours total. Prerequisites: none.

docs.title: Why this course exists
docs.text:
Your Windows toolchain is MinGW GCC 6.3 from 2016. It does not support most of C++17 (no std::optional, no std::string_view, no std::filesystem, no std::shared_mutex, broken threads). Everything on your resume says Linux, GCC, CMake, GDB. You already have the answer installed: WSL Ubuntu 24.04 with GCC 13.3, Clang 18, CMake 3.28, Ninja, GDB 15, Valgrind 3.22, Docker, Python 3.12 and the PostgreSQL 16 client. Checked on 2026-10-03; nothing to install.

From now on all C and C++ in this curriculum is built and run inside WSL, edited from VS Code on Windows through the Remote-WSL extension. Windows-only topics (WinDbg, MSVC, Win32 threads) stay on Windows and are covered in their own modules.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: # Module Time 01 VS Code + WSL development loop 1 h 02 Verify the toolchain: build, test, debug, sanitize 1 h

docs.title: You are done when you can
docs.text:
• Open a folder that lives in /home/shakir/... in VS Code with the green "WSL: Ubuntu-24.04" badge.
  • Build code/hello.cpp with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread and run it.
  • Build the tiny CMake project in code/cmake_hello/ with Ninja and run its test with ctest.
  • Hit a breakpoint in VS Code inside WSL, and separately in plain gdb in the terminal.
  • Run a program under Valgrind and under AddressSanitizer and read both reports.
  • Say in one sentence why the code must live in the Linux filesystem, not under /mnt/d.

docs.title: Resume lines this course backs up
docs.text: "Linux, GCC, CMake, GDB" in Platforms & Tools, and "Building modern C++17 systems projects on Linux".

docs.title: 1. VS Code + WSL development loop
docs.text: Time: ~1 hour Prerequisites: none

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
WSL2 is a real Linux kernel running inside a lightweight virtual machine on your Windows laptop. Ubuntu 24.04 is installed in it, with your user shakir. You edit files with VS Code on Windows, but the compiler, debugger and your program all run inside Linux. VS Code's Remote-WSL extension makes this feel like one machine: the editor window is Windows, everything else is Linux.

Analogy: a Windows laptop with a Linux server sitting under the desk, connected by a very fast cable. VS Code is the screen and keyboard, Linux does the work.

docs.title: 2.1 Two filesystems, one rule
docs.text:
Path seen from Linux What it is Speed for builds /home/shakir/... Linux's own ext4 disk (a virtual disk file on Windows) Fast /mnt/c/..., /mnt/d/... Your Windows drives, mounted through a 9P network protocol 5x to 20x slower, file watching unreliable

Rule: project code lives under /home/shakir. From Windows you can still see it in Explorer at \\wsl$\Ubuntu-24.04\home\shakir\. Your D:\Cpp_DSA folder stays where it is for notes and this curriculum; when a module says "build this", copy or create the code under ~/dev/... in Linux.

docs.title: 2.2 Memory
docs.text: Your C:\Users\msi1\.wslconfig gives WSL 3 GB RAM, 4 processors, 2 GB swap. That is enough for all C++ work and for a local PostgreSQL. It is not enough to run a YugabyteDB Docker node comfortably (it wants about 2 GB on its own). When you reach 07_Databases_Internals module 11, temporarily change memory=3GB to memory=5GB, run wsl --shutdown in PowerShell, and change it back afterwards. Everything else in this curriculum works at 3 GB.

docs.title: 2.3 Install the VS Code side (Windows)
docs.text:
1. VS Code -> Extensions -> install WSL (publisher Microsoft, id ms-vscode-remote.remote-wsl).
  2. Press Ctrl+Shift+P -> "WSL: Connect to WSL using Distro..." -> Ubuntu-24.04. A new window opens with a green badge bottom-left: WSL: Ubuntu-24.04.
  3. In that window, install these extensions into WSL (the Install button will say "Install in WSL: Ubuntu-24.04"):
    • C/C++ (ms-vscode.cpptools) — IntelliSense and the gdb debugger UI.
    • CMake Tools (ms-vscode.cmake-tools) — configure/build/test from the status bar.
    • clangd (llvm-vs-code-extensions.vscode-clangd) — optional, better diagnostics. If you install it, disable cpptools IntelliSense ("C_Cpp.intelliSenseEngine": "disabled").

docs.title: 2.4 Prepare Linux
docs.text:
Open the VS Code terminal (it is a Linux bash now) and run:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y build-essential cmake ninja-build gdb valgrind \
    clang clang-tidy clang-format lldb git curl netcat-openbsd strace ltrace linux-tools-common \
    python3-pip postgresql-client libpq-dev libdb-dev libgtest-dev
mkdir -p ~/dev && cd ~/dev
git config --global user.name "MD Shakir Khan"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"   # the email on your GitHub account
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

libdb-dev is Berkeley DB (for 07_Databases_Internals module 10). libpq-dev is the PostgreSQL client library. netcat-openbsd gives you nc for talking to tcpkv by hand.

Add to the end of ~/.bashrc (then source ~/.bashrc):

# C++17 quick build: cb hello.cpp  -> ./hello
cb() { g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -g -O0 "$1" -o "${1%.*}" && echo "built ${1%.*}"; }
# Same but with AddressSanitizer + UBSan
cbs() { g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -g -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer "$1" -o "${1%.*}_asan" && echo "built ${1%.*}_asan"; }
# ThreadSanitizer
cbt() { g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -g -O1 -fsanitize=thread "$1" -o "${1%.*}_tsan" && echo "built ${1%.*}_tsan"; }
export ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1:strict_string_checks=1
ulimit -c unlimited   # allow core dumps (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA)

docs.title: 2.5 Open a project folder
docs.text:
mkdir -p ~/dev/scratch && cd ~/dev/scratch && code .

code . from inside WSL opens that Linux folder in a Remote-WSL window. Always open folders this way, or via File -> Open Folder in a WSL window (the file dialog then shows Linux paths).

docs.title: 2.6 Minimal .vscode for single-file experiments
docs.text:
Create ~/dev/scratch/.vscode/tasks.json:

{
  "version": "2.0.0",
  "tasks": [
    {
      "label": "g++ build active file (C++17, warnings as errors)",
      "type": "shell",
      "command": "g++",
      "args": ["-std=c++17", "-Wall", "-Wextra", "-Werror", "-pthread", "-g", "-O0",
               "${file}", "-o", "${fileDirname}/${fileBasenameNoExtension}"],
      "group": { "kind": "build", "isDefault": true },
      "problemMatcher": ["$gcc"]
    }
  ]
}

and ~/dev/scratch/.vscode/launch.json:

{
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "gdb: active file",
      "type": "cppdbg",
      "request": "launch",
      "program": "${fileDirname}/${fileBasenameNoExtension}",
      "cwd": "${fileDirname}",
      "MIMode": "gdb",
      "preLaunchTask": "g++ build active file (C++17, warnings as errors)",
      "setupCommands": [
        { "text": "-enable-pretty-printing", "ignoreFailures": true }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Now Ctrl+Shift+B builds the open file and F5 builds and debugs it with breakpoints. For real projects you will use CMake Tools instead (next module and 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps/04).

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: Nothing to write yet; module 02 has the verification programs.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
• WSL2 runs a Microsoft-built Linux kernel in a Hyper-V utility VM. Your processes are real Linux processes with real pids, real ptrace (so gdb works fully), real epoll, real core dumps.
  • /mnt/c is served by a 9P file server running in the Windows side; every stat() is a network round trip. That is why builds there are slow and why inotify-based file watching misses events.
  • The VS Code Remote-WSL extension installs a small Node.js server inside Linux (~/.vscode-server). The Windows UI talks to it over a local socket. Extensions marked "workspace" run in Linux, "UI" extensions run in Windows. That is why you install C/C++ into WSL.
  • Memory given to WSL shows up in Windows as vmmem / Vmmem WSL. autoMemoryReclaim=gradual in your .wslconfig returns idle pages to Windows.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text: Most C++ backend jobs you will interview for build and run on Linux servers, usually Ubuntu or RHEL, in Docker containers, in CI. Being fluent in a Linux shell, gdb and the GCC toolchain is assumed at the senior level. Your Windows/MSVC experience is a plus, not a substitute. Interviewers notice candidates who cannot type ls -la, grep -rn, or explain what ulimit -c does.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy. Open ~/dev/scratch in a WSL window. Confirm the green badge. Done when a screenshot shows WSL: Ubuntu-24.04 bottom-left.
  2. Easy. Run time (for i in $(seq 1 200); do stat /home/shakir > /dev/null; done) and the same with /mnt/c/Users/msi1. Done when you can state the ratio.
  3. Medium. Create a file from Windows Explorer at \\wsl$\Ubuntu-24.04\home\shakir\dev\scratch\x.txt and cat it from Linux. Then touch a file in Linux and find it from Explorer. Done when both work.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between WSL1 and WSL2? WSL1 translated Linux syscalls to Windows calls; WSL2 runs a real Linux kernel in a lightweight VM, so system call compatibility is complete (ptrace, epoll, Docker all work) at the cost of slower cross-filesystem access.

Q: Why are builds slow under /mnt/c? Files are served over the 9P protocol from Windows; every metadata call is an inter-VM round trip, and compilers do thousands of them.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• All C and C++ work happens in WSL Ubuntu 24.04 with GCC 13. MinGW 6.3 is retired.
  • Code lives in /home/shakir/dev, never under /mnt/d.
  • VS Code connects through Remote-WSL; install C/C++ and CMake Tools into WSL.
  • cb, cbs, cbt shell functions give you normal, ASan and TSan builds in one word.
  • ulimit -c unlimited is set so core dumps are possible later.
  • Raise WSL memory to 5 GB only when running YugabyteDB in Docker.

docs.title: 2. Verify the toolchain: build, test, debug, sanitize
docs.text: Time: ~1 hour Prerequisites: 01_vscode_wsl_dev_loop

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text: Before learning anything, prove that every tool you will rely on actually works on your machine: the compiler with C++17, CMake with Ninja and a unit test, gdb with breakpoints, Valgrind and AddressSanitizer catching a real bug. Each check takes minutes. Finding out in week 4 that Valgrind was broken would cost you a weekend.

docs.title: 2. The real thing
docs.text:
Copy the code/ folder of this course into Linux first:

mkdir -p ~/dev/setup && cp -r /mnt/d/Cpp_DSA/LEARNING_PATH/01_Environment_Setup/code/* ~/dev/setup/
cd ~/dev/setup

docs.title: Check 1: C++17 compiles
docs.text:
cb hello.cpp && ./hello

Expected output ends with C++ standard: 201703 and all C++17 checks passed. If the compiler reports 201703 you are on C++17; GCC 13 defaults to C++17 anyway, but we always pass -std explicitly so the project builds the same on every machine and in CI.

docs.title: Check 2: CMake + Ninja + a test
docs.text:
cd ~/dev/setup/cmake_hello
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
./build/greeter_app

Expected: 100% tests passed. This is the exact shape of the tcpkv build.

docs.title: Check 3: gdb in the terminal
docs.text:
cd ~/dev/setup && cb hello.cpp
gdb -q ./hello
(gdb) break main
(gdb) run
(gdb) next
(gdb) next
(gdb) info locals
(gdb) print words
(gdb) continue
(gdb) quit

print words should show the vector contents thanks to the STL pretty printers that ship with Ubuntu's gdb. If you see raw pointers instead, add source /usr/share/gcc/python/libstdcxx/v6/printers.py style setup as described in 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/05.

docs.title: Check 4: gdb inside VS Code
docs.text: Open ~/dev/setup in a WSL window, open hello.cpp, click in the gutter next to the first line inside main to set a breakpoint, press F5. The debugger should stop there and show locals.

docs.title: Check 5: Valgrind and AddressSanitizer find the same bug
docs.text:
buggy.cpp reads one past the end of a heap array and leaks a buffer.

cb buggy.cpp && valgrind --leak-check=full ./buggy

Look for Invalid read of size 4 and definitely lost: 40 bytes in 1 blocks.

cbs buggy.cpp && ./buggy_asan

Look for heap-buffer-overflow with the exact line number, then after the program exits, LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks. ASan is faster (about 2x slowdown) but needs a rebuild; Valgrind is slower (20x to 50x) but runs on any binary. You will use both in 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA.

docs.title: Check 6: ThreadSanitizer finds a data race
docs.text:
cbt race.cpp && ./race_tsan

If instead you see FATAL: ThreadSanitizer: unexpected memory mapping, that is not your code. Ubuntu 24.04's kernel randomises memory addresses with 32 bits of entropy, and the TSan runtime in GCC 13 only understands up to 28 bits. It fails at random, so it may work once and crash the next run. Fix it once per WSL boot:

sudo sysctl -w vm.mmap_rnd_bits=28
# make it permanent:
echo 'vm.mmap_rnd_bits=28' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-tsan.conf

Or, without sudo, run one command with randomisation off: setarch $(uname -m) -R ./race_tsan. The tcpkv CI workflow applies the same sysctl before its TSan job.

Look for WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race. Then open race.cpp, uncomment the std::lock_guard line, rebuild, rerun: the warning disappears. That is the whole idea of 04_Concurrency in one minute.

docs.title: Check 7: a core dump
docs.text:
cb crash.cpp
ulimit -c unlimited
./crash            # prints "Segmentation fault (core dumped)"
ls core*           # Ubuntu 24.04 may route cores through apport; if no file appears:
cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern

If core_pattern starts with |/usr/share/apport/apport, set a plain pattern for development:

sudo sysctl -w kernel.core_pattern=core.%e.%p
./crash && gdb -q ./crash core.crash.*    # inside gdb: bt

bt should show the crash inside write_through_null. Core dumps are the subject of 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/06; this check only proves your machine can produce them.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
All files are in code/:

File Purpose hello.cpp Uses std::optional, std::string_view, structured bindings, if constexpr, std::shared_mutex, std::filesystem so a pre-C++17 compiler fails loudly. buggy.cpp Heap overflow read + leak for Valgrind/ASan. race.cpp Two threads incrementing an int for TSan. crash.cpp Null pointer write for the core dump check. cmake_hello/ CMakeLists.txt, a tiny library, an app and a GoogleTest test fetched with FetchContent.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
• -Wall -Wextra -Werror: warnings become errors. Production C++ teams do this because a warning ignored today is a crash dump next quarter. The tcpkv resume bullet claims exactly this.
  • -g emits DWARF debug information into the ELF file; gdb maps addresses back to lines with it. -O0 disables optimisation so variables are not kept only in registers and stepping is faithful.
  • ASan works by instrumenting every load and store at compile time and keeping "shadow memory" (1 byte of shadow per 8 bytes of application memory) that records which bytes are addressable. It also surrounds heap allocations with poisoned red zones; reading one past the end hits a red zone. Valgrind instead runs the unmodified binary on a synthetic CPU and tracks validity bits for every byte, which is why it is slower and needs no rebuild.
  • TSan records, for every memory location, which threads accessed it and under which locks (a vector-clock algorithm). Two accesses with at least one write and no happens-before edge is a race. Memory cost is about 5x to 10x, so keep test inputs small.
  • A core dump is the process's memory image plus register state written by the kernel on a fatal signal. ulimit -c is the size limit (0 disables); kernel.core_pattern decides the filename or the program that receives it on a pipe.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text: The exact commands in this module are what a CI pipeline runs on every commit for a serious C++ service: a -Werror build, unit tests through ctest, one ASan+UBSan job and often one TSan job. At your current job the equivalent on Windows is a /W4 /WX MSVC build plus Application Verifier and PageHeap. Being able to say "I run ASan and TSan in CI and Valgrind before every release" is a senior-level answer to "how do you keep a C++ server stable".

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy. Make hello.cpp fail: change -std=c++17 to -std=c++11 in the cb function temporarily and read the first error. Done when you can say which C++17 feature it rejected.
  2. Easy. In buggy.cpp, fix the overflow but keep the leak; confirm ASan now reports only the leak. Then fix the leak with std::vector; confirm a clean run.
  3. Medium. In cmake_hello, add a second test that fails on purpose, run ctest, read the failure output, fix it. Done when you can explain --output-on-failure.
  4. Medium. Build race.cpp without TSan and run it 20 times in a loop. Count how often the final value is wrong. Then explain why TSan reports the race every time even when the result happens to be right.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does -Werror do and why do teams use it? Treats every warning as a compile error, so the build fails until the code is clean. It prevents warning accumulation and catches real bugs (unused results, sign conversions, missing returns).

Q: ASan vs Valgrind: when would you pick which? ASan during development and CI: fast, precise line numbers, needs a rebuild. Valgrind when you cannot rebuild (third-party binary), need uninitialised-value tracking (memcheck), or want cache/profiling tools (cachegrind, callgrind).

Q: Why is -O0 -g used for debugging and -O2 -g for production symbols? At -O0 every variable has a memory slot and lines map one-to-one, so stepping is faithful. At -O2 the compiler inlines, reorders and keeps values in registers, so frames and locals can be "optimized out"; but production runs -O2, so production cores are read with -O2 -g symbols.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Seven checks: C++17 compile, CMake+ctest, gdb terminal, gdb in VS Code, Valgrind, ASan, TSan, core dump.
  • -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread is the default flag set for the whole curriculum.
  • ASan: compile-time instrumentation, shadow memory, fast. Valgrind: binary instrumentation, slow, no rebuild.
  • TSan proves a race exists even when the output looks right.
  • Core dumps need ulimit -c unlimited and a plain core_pattern on Ubuntu.

docs.title: 02_Modern_CPP — Modern C++17 for a C programmer, to senior depth
What this course covers
docs.text:
You have written production C for 2.5 years: a Berkeley DB to YugabyteDB migration engine, a multithreaded RPC-over-TCP application server, crash-dump analysis. You know what the stack is, what malloc does, and what happens when someone forgets a free on the third error path. What you do not have yet is fluency in the language that most C++ systems teams write every day: C++17 with RAII, value semantics, move semantics, smart pointers, the STL, templates and virtual dispatch.

This course takes you from "C with classes" to "I can design an ownership model for a server, write it in idiomatic C++17, and explain to an interviewer what the compiler generates for every line."

Every module starts from something you already do in C and shows the C++ way of saying the same thing more safely. Then it goes under the hood: object layout, vtables, the shared_ptr control block, vector reallocation, exception landing pads, name mangling, what -O2 does to undefined behaviour. That second half is what separates a mid-level answer from a senior one.

The thread running through the course is ownership. Who owns this resource? When is it released? Can it be copied, moved, shared, or only borrowed? If you can answer those four questions for every object in a design, you can write C++ that does not leak, does not double-free, and does not crash at 3 AM.

docs.title: Why it is on the resume
docs.text:
This course backs the language half of your resume. These exact phrases depend on it:

  • "C++17"
  • "STL, RAII, smart pointers, templates, OOP, memory & ownership design, performance optimisation"
  • tcpkv: "RAII socket and file-descriptor wrappers and move-only connection handles"
  • tcpkv: "shared_mutex" (the C++17 type itself is introduced in module 13; the full readers-writers treatment is in 04_Concurrency/04_shared_mutex_and_readers_writers.md)

Interviewers for C++ systems roles open almost every loop with a language round. The questions are predictable: what a vtable looks like, what std::move actually does, why vector copies instead of moves when your move constructor is not noexcept, what lives in a shared_ptr control block, which iterators a push_back invalidates, what the exception-safety guarantees are, and what the difference is between C and C++ for a programmer like you. Every one of those is answered here to the depth where you can derive the answer instead of reciting it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• C at a professional level: pointers, structs, malloc/free, function pointers, header/source split, the build and link model. You have this.
  • 01_Environment_Setup done: WSL Ubuntu 24.04 with g++ --version reporting GCC 13, and VS Code connected to WSL.
  • Nothing else. No prior C++ beyond the arrays and binary search you are doing now.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
# File Topic Hours 01 01_from_c_to_cpp.md References, namespaces, overloading and name mangling, const, auto, nullptr, enum class, extern "C", the build model 2 02 02_classes_constructors_destructors.md Object lifetime, construction/destruction order, initialiser lists, special member functions, explicit, = default, = delete 2.5 03 03_raii_the_core_idea.md RAII, file and socket-fd wrappers, scope guards, stack unwinding, landing pads 2.5 04 04_value_semantics_copy_move.md Value categories, rvalue references, std::move, rule of five, copy elision and NRVO, parameter-passing choices, move-only handles 3 05 05_smart_pointers_and_ownership.md unique_ptr with custom deleters, shared_ptr control block, weak_ptr, cycles, enable_shared_from_this, ownership graphs 3 06 06_stl_containers_deep_dive.md vector growth, map vs unordered_map, node vs contiguous, iterator invalidation, custom keys and hashes 3 07 07_stl_algorithms_lambdas_iterators.md Algorithms, erase-remove, strict weak ordering, lambdas and closures, std::function cost, iterator categories 2.5 08 08_templates_and_generic_programming.md Function and class templates, deduction, specialisation, traits, SFINAE, variadic templates, if constexpr 3 09 09_oop_inheritance_virtual.md Inheritance, virtual functions, vtable and vptr layout, virtual destructors, override/final, interfaces vs composition 3 10 10_error_handling_exceptions_optional_expected.md Exceptions, exception-safety guarantees, noexcept, optional, variant, error_code, expected-style results 3 11 11_const_constexpr_and_compile_time.md const correctness, constexpr functions and tables, static_assert, compile-time UB detection 2 12 12_memory_model_layout_and_performance.md Layout, padding, alignment, cache lines, false sharing, stack vs heap, arenas and pmr, benchmarking, what -O2 does, UB 3.5 13 13_cpp17_features_tour.md Structured bindings, if with initialiser, string_view, optional/variant/any, filesystem, parallel algorithms, folds, CTAD, attributes, shared_mutex 2 14 14_writing_production_cpp.md Project layout, headers, ODR, warning flags, sanitizers, clang-format/tidy, Core Guidelines, code review, library API design 2.5

Total: about 37.5 hours. At 4 to 5 hours a week alongside the other courses, this is 8 to 9 weeks.

Order: 01 to 05 are the core and must be done in order; everything else in C++ builds on RAII, move semantics and ownership. 06 to 08 come next in order. 09, 10 and 11 can be done in any order after that. 12 is the hardest and the most "senior" module; budget a second pass. 13 is a short tour best done after 06 to 11. 14 ties everything together and leads straight into the tcpkv capstone.

docs.title: Supporting files
docs.text:
• code/ — 28 complete programs plus kv_store.hpp. Each module names the files it uses. Files are named mNN_short_name.cpp, where NN is the module number.
  • EXERCISES.md — every exercise from every module's "Try it" section, with difficulty and a hint.
  • INTERVIEW_QA.md — 38 questions from basic to senior, with model answers.

docs.title: How to build the code
docs.text:
Build inside WSL, from a copy in the Linux filesystem (not under /mnt/d; see 01_Environment_Setup for why). Every C++ file compiles cleanly with:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 m04_move_only_handle.cpp -o m04_move_only_handle
./m04_move_only_handle

To build everything at once:

cd code
for f in m*.cpp; do
    g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 "$f" -o "${f%.cpp}" || echo "FAILED: $f"
done

Useful variants while studying:

# Catch memory and UB bugs (modules 03 to 06, 12)
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -g -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined file.cpp -o file

# Checked STL: aborts on invalid iterators and bad comparators (modules 06, 07)
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -g -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG file.cpp -o file

# See what the compiler generated (modules 03, 09, 11, 12)
g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -S -masm=intel file.cpp -o file.s

# Show copies and moves that elision would hide (module 04)
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fno-elide-constructors m04_copy_elision_nrvo.cpp -o elide

m12_* benchmarks only mean something at -O2 or higher. m14_library_api_demo.cpp includes kv_store.hpp, so build it from inside code/.

docs.title: Suggested order with the other courses
docs.text:
• Do modules 01 to 05 here before 04_Concurrency/03_mutexes_lock_guard_unique_lock.md: a lock_guard is just RAII, and you should recognise it as such.
  • Module 06 pairs with 03_Data_Structures_Algorithms: learn the STL container first, then implement its data structure from scratch there.
  • Module 09 is the language half; 09_OOP_Design_Patterns_Architecture is the design half.
  • Module 12 pairs with 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA (heap internals, sanitizers) and 04_Concurrency/10_cache_lines_false_sharing_performance.md.
  • Module 14 leads into 10_Capstone_Projects/tcpkv, steps 01 and 02.

docs.title: You are done when you can...
docs.text:
• Explain, without notes, the four things that change when a C programmer moves to C++: references, overloading and mangling, constructors/destructors, and the type system being stricter (no implicit void* conversion). Call a C library from C++ with extern "C".
  • State the construction and destruction order of a class with bases and members, and explain why a destructor is not called for an object whose constructor threw.
  • Write a move-only RAII wrapper for a file descriptor (or FILE*, or a socket) from memory, with the move constructor, move assignment and destructor all correct and noexcept.
  • Say what std::move really is (a cast to an rvalue reference, nothing more), when a named rvalue reference is an lvalue, and when the compiler elides a copy entirely.
  • Apply the rule of zero, and when that is not possible, the rule of five, and justify which one a given class needs.
  • Draw the memory layout of make_shared<T>() vs shared_ptr<T>(new T), name what lives in the control block, and explain why weak_ptr keeps the block alive but not the object.
  • Design the ownership graph for a small server (listener, connections, worker pool, shared store) and assign value, unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr or reference to every edge.
  • Explain vector growth, why it copies elements whose move constructor is not noexcept, and list which operations invalidate iterators for vector, map and unordered_map.
  • Pick between map, unordered_map and a sorted vector for a given workload and explain the choice in terms of cache lines and node allocation.
  • Replace raw loops with STL algorithms and lambdas, and explain what a lambda compiles into and what std::function costs.
  • Write a class template, a variadic function template, and a type trait, and read a long template error down to the "required from here" line that points at your code.
  • Draw an object with a vptr and its vtable, explain how a virtual call compiles, why a base class needs a virtual destructor, and when final lets the compiler devirtualise.
  • Name the three exception-safety guarantees, show the copy-and-swap route to the strong one, and choose between exceptions, optional, error_code and an expected-style type for a given API.
  • Explain padding and alignment, reorder a struct to shrink it, show false sharing in a benchmark, and name four kinds of undefined behaviour the optimiser exploits.
  • Use the C++17 features that matter in production (string_view, optional, variant, structured bindings, if initialisers, filesystem, shared_mutex, [[nodiscard]]) and name the lifetime trap of string_view.
  • Lay out a C++ library with a clean public header, build it warning-free with sanitizers, and explain what the One Definition Rule forbids.

docs.text:
• "C++17"
  • "STL, RAII, smart pointers, templates, OOP, memory & ownership design, performance optimisation"
  • tcpkv: "RAII socket and file-descriptor wrappers and move-only connection handles" (modules 03, 04, 05 and 14; built for real in 10_Capstone_Projects/tcpkv/02_step_raii_fd_and_socket.md)

docs.title: 1. From C to C++: what actually changes
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: none (solid C assumed)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
C++ started as "C with classes" and it still compiles with the same toolchain, links with the same linker, and produces the same kind of ELF binary you already debug. You do not throw away anything you know about the stack, pointers, malloc, or how main is reached. What changes is the set of tools the language gives you for saying what you mean: a reference instead of a pointer that "must not be null", a namespace instead of a bank_ prefix on every function, a function name that can be reused for different parameter types, and a compiler that enforces const instead of politely ignoring it.

Think of it like moving from a plain text editor to one with a type checker. The file format is the same, the keyboard is the same, but a whole category of mistakes is now caught before you run anything.

This module is a tour of the small-but-everywhere changes. Each later module takes one big idea (RAII, move semantics, templates, virtual dispatch) and goes deep.

docs.title: 2.1 References
docs.text:
A reference is an alias for an existing object. Under the hood it is almost always implemented as a pointer, but the language rules are different:

Pointer T* Reference T& Can be null yes no (binding to null is undefined behaviour) Can be re-seated to another object yes no, bound once at initialisation Syntax at the call site f(&x) f(x) Syntax inside the function p->field, *p r.field, r Arithmetic yes no 
void deposit(Account& a, long long paise);        // "I will modify the caller's Account"
long long balance(const Account& a);              // "I will only read it, and I will not copy it"

Rule of thumb: pass by const T& when the object is bigger than a pointer and you only read it; pass by T& when you modify it; pass by value for small things (int, double, small structs); use a pointer only when "no object" is a legal input.

docs.title: 2.2 Namespaces
docs.text:
namespace tcpkv {
    struct Connection { /* ... */ };
    void serve(Connection&);
}
tcpkv::Connection c;
using tcpkv::serve;    // import one name

using namespace std; in a header is a well-known mistake: it dumps hundreds of names into every file that includes the header and causes silent ambiguities later. In a .cpp file it is tolerable; in a header it is a code-review rejection.

docs.title: 2.3 Function overloading
docs.text:
Several functions may share a name if their parameter lists differ. The compiler chooses at compile time by matching argument types (overload resolution). The return type does not take part.

int    twice(int);
double twice(double);
twice(21);     // int version
twice(1.5);    // double version
twice('a');    // int version: char promotes to int

Overload resolution has precise ranking rules (exact match > promotion > conversion > user-defined conversion). You rarely need the details, but you must know that an ambiguous call is a compile error, not a silent pick.

docs.title: 2.4 const correctness
docs.text:
In C, const is advisory. In C++ it is a type property the compiler enforces through member functions:

class Account {
public:
    long long balance() const;      // promise: does not modify *this. Callable on a const Account.
    void deposit(long long);        // not const: cannot be called on a const Account.
};

A function taking const Account& can only call const member functions. This propagates: once you accept const& in your API, callers can pass temporaries and read-only data, and you cannot accidentally mutate.

docs.title: 2.5 auto, range-for, uniform initialisation
docs.text:
auto it = container.begin();          // type deduced from the initialiser (compile time, no cost)
for (const auto& x : container) ...   // iterates begin() to end(); works for arrays, vectors, maps, your own types
int x{5};                             // brace init: refuses narrowing. int y{3.7}; is an error.
std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};          // initialiser list
Account a{"ACC-1", 100};              // aggregate / constructor call

auto deduces a value type by default (it drops const and &). Write auto& or const auto& when you want a reference. auto x = v[0]; copies.

docs.title: 2.6 nullptr and enum class
docs.text:
NULL in C is ((void*)0) or plain 0. In C++ 0 converts to any pointer, so f(NULL) with overloads f(int) and f(char*) calls the wrong one. nullptr has type std::nullptr_t and only converts to pointers.

enum class gives scoped, strongly typed enumerators: no implicit conversion to int, no name clashes between Status::Ok and Result::Ok, and the underlying type can be fixed (enum class Op : std::uint8_t { ... }), which matters for wire formats.

docs.title: 2.7 iostream vs printf
docs.text: std::cout << x is type-safe (no %d vs long mismatch) and extensible (you overload operator<< for your types). printf is terser, usually faster, and format strings are checked by GCC with -Wformat. Both are fine. In production servers you will mostly use a logging library anyway. One trap: std::endl flushes the stream every time. Use '\n' unless you actually need a flush.

docs.title: 2.8 How a C++ program is built
docs.text:
Exactly like C: preprocess -> compile each translation unit to an object file -> link.

g++ -std=c++17 -c a.cpp -o a.o
g++ -std=c++17 -c b.cpp -o b.o
g++ a.o b.o -o prog           # g++ as the driver adds -lstdc++ automatically; gcc would not

Differences you will notice:

  • Name mangling. Because of overloading and namespaces, the symbol for int area(int) is _Z4areai, not area. nm -C or c++filt demangle.
  • extern "C". Disables mangling for a declaration so C code (or dlsym) can find the symbol. Every C header you include from C++ is wrapped in #ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { #endif.
  • Templates and inline functions in headers produce the same code in several object files; the linker is allowed to merge them (see 14_writing_production_cpp.md on the ODR).
  • The standard library is libstdc++ on GCC. ldd ./prog shows it.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m01_c_vs_cpp_basics.cpp exercises every item above in one small program. The key parts:

namespace bank {
    struct Account { std::string id; long long balance_paise; };
    void deposit(Account& a, long long paise) { a.balance_paise += paise; }   // reference: same object
    long long balance(const Account& a) { return a.balance_paise; }          // const&: read-only view
}

int         twice(int x)                { return 2 * x; }      // three overloads, chosen at compile time
double      twice(double x)             { return 2.0 * x; }
std::string twice(const std::string& s) { return s + s; }

enum class Status { Ok, Timeout, Refused };

int main() {
    bank::Account acc{"ACC-001", 0};
    bank::deposit(acc, 50000);
    std::vector<int> v{3, 1, 4, 1, 5};
    for (int& x : v) x *= 10;                      // by reference: modifies in place
    auto total = 0LL;
    for (auto x : v) total += x;
    int* p = nullptr;
    Status s = Status::Timeout;
    std::cout << static_cast<int>(s) << '\n';      // explicit, never implicit
}

code/m01_extern_c_mangling.cpp shows mangling and C linkage:

int    area(int side)    { return side * side; }           // symbol: _Z4areai
double area(double side) { return side * side; }           // symbol: _Z4aread
extern "C" int c_area(int side) { return side * side; }    // symbol: c_area

#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif
int legacy_checksum(const char* data, int len);            // how every C header does it
#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif

Build and inspect on WSL:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread m01_extern_c_mangling.cpp -o mangling
nm mangling | grep -E 'area|checksum'       # _Z4areai, _Z4aread, c_area, legacy_checksum
nm -C mangling | grep -E 'area|checksum'    # area(int), area(double), c_area, legacy_checksum
echo _Z4areai | c++filt                     # area(int)

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
References are pointers without the syntax. void f(int& r) compiles to the same machine code as void f(int* p). The compiler knows r is never null, so it can drop null checks and sometimes keep the referenced value in a register. A reference member in a class takes sizeof(void*) bytes. Binding a reference to a dangling object is undefined behaviour exactly like dereferencing a freed pointer.

Overload resolution is compile-time only. After it picks a candidate the call is a direct call instruction, same as C. There is no runtime dispatch (that is what virtual is for, module 09).

Mangled names encode the signature. _Z prefix, then 4area (length-prefixed name), then parameter type codes (i = int, d = double, PKc = pointer to const char, RSt6vectorIiE = reference to std::vector<int>). Namespaces appear as N...E nesting. This is the Itanium C++ ABI, shared by GCC and Clang on Linux; MSVC uses a different scheme (?area@@YAHH@Z), which is why you cannot link MSVC and MinGW C++ object files together, while plain C objects link fine.

extern "C" changes linkage, not calling convention. On x86-64 Linux both C and C++ use the System V ABI, so a C function and a C++ function with the same signature are called identically. extern "C" only suppresses mangling. You cannot overload an extern "C" function (two functions would need the same symbol).

enum class has a fixed size. Default underlying type is int; with : std::uint8_t it is one byte and can be memcpy'd into a wire header. Plain enum has an implementation-defined underlying type unless you fix it.

Brace initialisation and narrowing. int x{3.7} is a compile error because the standard forbids narrowing conversions in list-initialisation. This is the one place where C++ is stricter than C about implicit conversions by default; everywhere else (int x = 3.7;) it still truncates silently.

auto and decltype are compile-time. auto never adds runtime cost. It can hide an expensive copy though: auto row = table[i]; copies the row; const auto& row = table[i]; does not.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Mixing C and C++ in one binary is normal. Your existing C libraries (the Berkeley DB layer, the RPC marshalling code) can be linked into a C++ server as long as their headers carry extern "C". Compile C files with gcc or g++ -x c, link with g++.
  • extern "C" and callbacks. When a C API wants a function pointer (qsort, pthread_create, signal), pass an extern "C" function or a non-capturing lambda converted to a function pointer. Never pass a member function pointer.
  • Shared libraries and the ABI. A .so built with GCC 13 exposes mangled names; a client built with the same compiler finds them. Mixing libstdc++ versions is usually fine on Linux because libstdc++ keeps backward ABI compatibility, but mixing -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0 and =1 builds is not (you will see std::__cxx11::basic_string in the undefined-symbol error).
  • const as documentation. In code review, a member function that could be const but is not is a smell: it tells readers "this might mutate" when it does not, and it blocks callers who hold a const&.
  • 3 AM debugging. A crash in std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>::_M_assign is not a bug in the standard library. It is almost always a dangling reference or a buffer overrun somewhere else that corrupted the string's internals. Build with -fsanitize=address,undefined and run again; this is the C++ equivalent of running your C code under Application Verifier.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Write swap_values(int& a, int& b) using references, then write the C version with pointers. Done when both compile and you can explain why the reference version cannot be called with nullptr.
  2. (easy) Build m01_extern_c_mangling.cpp, run nm with and without -C, and write down the mangled name of a function std::string greet(const std::string&, int) you add. Done when you can read PKc, i, and RK fragments.
  3. (medium) Take any 100-line C file you own, rename it .cpp, and compile it with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror. Fix every error. Done when it compiles and you have a list of the three most common differences you hit (expect: implicit void* conversions, new/class as identifiers, missing casts on malloc).
  4. (medium) Write a C header legacy.h with a function, compile its implementation with gcc -c, and call it from a C++ main.cpp with proper extern "C" guards. Done when g++ main.cpp legacy.o links and runs.
  5. (hard) Create overloads void log(int), void log(long), void log(double), void log(const char*). Call log(NULL), log(0), log('x'), log(3.0f), log(nullptr) and predict which one is chosen before compiling. Done when every prediction matches and you can explain the one that is ambiguous or does not compile.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a reference and a pointer? A reference is an alias bound once to an existing object; it cannot be null, cannot be re-seated, and has no arithmetic. A pointer is a value that may be null and may be reassigned. Both usually compile to the same machine code; the difference is in what the compiler will let you write.

Q: Why does C++ mangle names and what does extern "C" do? Overloading and namespaces mean many functions can share a source-level name, so the linker symbol must encode the full signature. extern "C" tells the compiler to emit the plain, unmangled symbol so C code and dlsym can find it. It does not change the calling convention on Linux x86-64.

Q: Can you overload a function on return type alone? No. Overload resolution only looks at the arguments. Two functions that differ only in return type are a redefinition error.

Q: What does enum class give you over a plain enum? Scoped names (no clashes), no implicit conversion to int, and a fixed underlying type you can choose. The price is writing static_cast<int>(e) when you really want the number.

Q: auto x = vec[i]; versus auto& x = vec[i];: what is the difference? The first copies the element into x; the second makes x an alias for the element inside the vector. For int the copy is free; for std::string or a large struct it is an allocation and a memcpy. auto always deduces a value type unless you add &.

Q: Why is using namespace std; in a header considered wrong? It injects every standard name into every translation unit that includes the header, so a later addition to the standard library (or to the user's code) can silently change which function an unqualified call resolves to, or make it ambiguous.

Q: How would you call a C library compiled with gcc from a C++ program? Include its header, which must declare its functions inside extern "C" { } (guarded by #ifdef __cplusplus). Compile the C sources with the C compiler, compile the C++ sources with g++, and link everything with g++ so libstdc++ is pulled in.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• C++ uses the same compile-and-link pipeline as C; the differences are mangled symbols, extern "C", and libstdc++ linked in by the g++ driver.
  • A reference is a non-null, non-reseatable alias; prefer const T& for read-only parameters.
  • Overloading is resolved at compile time by argument types; return type does not participate.
  • const member functions are enforced by the compiler and are part of your API contract.
  • auto deduces a value type; add & or const& to avoid copies.
  • Brace initialisation forbids narrowing; nullptr is a typed null; enum class is scoped and typed.
  • Range-for works for any type with begin()/end().
  • std::endl flushes; use '\n'.
  • Mangled names follow the Itanium ABI on Linux; c++filt and nm -C decode them.

docs.title: 2. Classes, constructors and destructors: object lifetime
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 01_from_c_to_cpp.md

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
In C a struct is a bag of bytes. You memset it, fill it, and remember to clean up whatever it points to. In C++ a class is a bag of bytes plus two guaranteed hooks: a constructor that runs exactly once when the object comes into existence, and a destructor that runs exactly once when it goes out of existence. Everything in modern C++ (RAII, smart pointers, lock guards, move semantics) is built on the promise that those two hooks always run, in a defined order, no matter how the scope is left.

Analogy: a hotel room. Check-in (constructor) always happens before you can use the room; check-out (destructor) always happens when you leave, even if you leave through the fire exit (an exception). The hotel, not the guest, guarantees the room is cleaned.

docs.title: 2.1 Lifetime
docs.text:
An object's lifetime begins when its constructor finishes and ends when its destructor starts. Where the object lives decides when that happens:

Storage Constructed Destroyed Local (automatic) when the declaration is reached when the enclosing block exits (any way) Global / namespace-scope before main starts (within one TU, in declaration order) after main returns, reverse order static local first time the declaration is reached (thread-safe since C++11) after main, reverse order of construction Member as part of the enclosing object's construction as part of its destruction Heap (new) at the new expression at the matching delete (or never, if you forget) Temporary at the expression at the end of the full expression (the ;)

docs.title: 2.2 Construction order (fixed by the standard)
docs.text:
For Derived d;:

  1. Base class constructors (in the order bases are listed).
  2. Members of Derived, in declaration order (not initialiser-list order).
  3. The body of Derived::Derived().

Destruction is the exact reverse: body of ~Derived, members in reverse declaration order, then bases. GCC's -Wreorder warns when your initialiser list is written in a different order than the declarations, because the written order is misleading.

docs.title: 2.3 Member initialiser lists
docs.text:
class Account {
    const std::string id_;   // const member: must be initialised, cannot be assigned
    long long balance_;
public:
    Account(std::string id, long long b) : id_(std::move(id)), balance_(b) {}   // initialise directly
};

Assigning in the body (id_ = id;) would first default-construct id_ and then assign: two operations instead of one, and impossible for const members, reference members, and types without a default constructor. Always use the initialiser list. Default member initialisers (long long balance_ = 0;) are the second tool; the initialiser list overrides them.

docs.title: 2.4 The special member functions
docs.text:
Six functions the compiler can write for you:

struct T {
    T();                        // default constructor
    ~T();                       // destructor
    T(const T&);                // copy constructor
    T& operator=(const T&);     // copy assignment
    T(T&&);                     // move constructor        (module 04)
    T& operator=(T&&);          // move assignment         (module 04)
};

The generated versions are memberwise: copy each member, move each member, destroy each member. That is exactly right when the class owns no raw resource, and exactly wrong when it does (two objects would both free the same pointer).

docs.title: 2.5 explicit, = default, = delete
docs.text:
• explicit T(int) stops T t = 5; and f(5) where f takes a T. Single-argument constructors should be explicit unless the conversion is genuinely intended (like std::string from const char*).
  • T() = default; asks for the compiler-generated version. Needed when another constructor you wrote suppressed it. Also documents intent.
  • T(const T&) = delete; removes a function. Calling it is a compile error with a clear message. This is how you make a type non-copyable.

docs.title: 2.6 Rule of zero / three / five (preview)
docs.text:
• Rule of zero: if your class owns no raw resource (it holds std::string, std::vector, std::unique_ptr, ints), write no special members. The generated ones are correct.
  • Rule of three (C++98): if you write any of destructor / copy ctor / copy assignment, you almost certainly need all three, because you are managing a resource.
  • Rule of five (C++11): add move ctor and move assignment to the three, or copies will be used where moves were possible. Module 04 does this in full.

Aim for rule of zero. Write rule-of-five classes only in thin wrappers around raw resources (file descriptors, FILE*, C library handles), then compose everything else out of those.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m02_ctor_dtor_order.cpp prints the order of every construction and destruction:

struct Tracer {
    std::string name;
    explicit Tracer(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) { std::cout << "  construct " << name << '\n'; }
    ~Tracer() { std::cout << "  destroy   " << name << '\n'; }
};

struct Base {
    Tracer t{"Base::t"};
    Base()  { std::cout << "  Base() body\n"; }      // body runs after all members exist
    ~Base() { std::cout << "  ~Base() body\n"; }     // body runs before members die
};

struct Derived : Base {
    Tracer a{"Derived::a"};   // constructed in declaration order ...
    Tracer b{"Derived::b"};   // ... regardless of initialiser-list order
    Derived()  { std::cout << "  Derived() body\n"; }
    ~Derived() { std::cout << "  ~Derived() body\n"; }
};

Expected output for the Derived d; block:

construct Base::t
Base() body
construct Derived::a
construct Derived::b
Derived() body
d alive, sizeof=...
~Derived() body
destroy   Derived::b
destroy   Derived::a
~Base() body
destroy   Base::t

code/m02_explicit_default_delete.cpp shows the keywords:

class Meters {
public:
    explicit Meters(double v) : value_(v) {}   // print(3.5) will not compile; print(Meters{3.5}) will
    double value() const { return value_; }
private:
    double value_;
};

class Connection {                              // rule of five: owns an fd
public:
    explicit Connection(int fd) : fd_(fd) {}
    ~Connection() { reset(); }
    Connection(const Connection&) = delete;             // copying = double close: make it impossible
    Connection& operator=(const Connection&) = delete;
    Connection(Connection&& o) noexcept : fd_(std::exchange(o.fd_, -1)) {}
    Connection& operator=(Connection&& o) noexcept { if (this != &o) { reset(); fd_ = std::exchange(o.fd_, -1); } return *this; }
private:
    void reset() noexcept { if (fd_ != -1) { /* ::close(fd_) */ fd_ = -1; } }
    int fd_;
};

struct Point { int x = 0; int y = 0; };         // rule of zero: nothing to write

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
A constructor is an ordinary function with a hidden this parameter. Account a("X", 5); compiles to: reserve sizeof(Account) bytes on the stack, then call Account::Account(&a, "X", 5). There is no allocation unless a member allocates. The destructor is called by the compiler at the closing brace: it emits call Account::~Account(&a) on every exit path, including the hidden paths created by exceptions (landing pads in the .gcc_except_table section, see 03_raii_the_core_idea.md).

Members are constructed by the constructor itself. The member initialiser list is compiled into the constructor's prologue: constructor calls for each member in declaration order, then the body. If a member's constructor throws, the members already constructed are destroyed in reverse order and the exception continues; the containing object's destructor does not run because the object never finished being born. This is why a constructor that acquired two resources manually (two raw fopen calls) leaks the first when the second fails, and why wrapping each resource in its own object (rule of zero on the outside) fixes it.

Trivial types. If a class has no user-provided constructors/destructor, no virtual functions, and all members are trivial, the compiler-generated special members are trivial: copy is a memcpy, destruction is a no-op, and std::vector<T> can memmove elements when it grows. std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T> tells you. Adding an empty user-written destructor ~T() {} makes the type non-trivial and silently disables those optimisations; ~T() = default; does not.

Static local initialisation is thread-safe. static Logger& get() { static Logger l; return l; } compiles to a guard variable plus __cxa_guard_acquire/__cxa_guard_release; the first thread constructs, others block. This is the modern singleton. Static destruction order across translation units is unspecified, which is the "static initialisation order fiasco": do not let one global's constructor use another global from a different file.

sizeof an object. It is the sum of members plus padding (module 12) plus 8 bytes for a vptr if the class has any virtual function (module 09). Member functions, constructors and destructors add nothing to the object: they are code, not data. An empty class has sizeof == 1 so that two objects always have distinct addresses.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The leak you keep fixing in C (a function that returns early and forgets free) is structurally impossible for a member of a class with a correct destructor. Module 03 turns this into a design principle.
  • Two-phase init is a smell. A class with init() that must be called after the constructor invites the bug of using it before init(). Do the acquisition in the constructor; if it can fail, throw or use a factory function returning std::optional<T> (module 10).
  • Never call virtual functions from a constructor or destructor expecting the derived override: during Base::Base() the object is a Base, the vptr points to Base's table. The call goes to the base version (or std::terminate on a pure virtual).
  • Static objects in a shared library run their constructors at dlopen time and destructors at dlclose / process exit. A banking server that exit()s from a worker thread while another thread still uses a static object will crash in the destructor. Prefer std::quick_exit or structured shutdown.
  • -Wreorder, -Wuninitialized, -Weffc++ catch init-order and missing-init bugs at compile time. The first two are in -Wall.
  • 3 AM debugging. A crash dump showing a destructor called twice on the same address means a class with a raw pointer member was copied (rule of three violated). Grep for classes that define a destructor but not a copy constructor; -Wdeprecated-copy-dtor (not in -Wall) finds them.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Compile and run m02_ctor_dtor_order.cpp. Before running, write the expected output on paper. Done when your prediction matches line for line.
  2. (easy) Add a third Tracer c to Derived and initialise it in the initialiser list before a. Observe the -Wreorder error, then fix it. Done when you can state the rule in one sentence.
  3. (medium) Write class Temperature with an explicit constructor from double in Celsius and a static Temperature from_fahrenheit(double) factory. Show that Temperature t = 36.6; fails and Temperature t{36.6}; works. Done when both facts are demonstrated by a compile error and a run.
  4. (medium) Write a class holding two Tracer members where the second member's constructor throws (add a bool fail parameter). Observe which destructors run. Done when you can explain why the outer object's destructor is not called.
  5. (hard) Implement a Singleton using a function-local static. Compile with g++ -S -O2 -std=c++17 and find the __cxa_guard_acquire call in the assembly. Done when you can point at the guard variable and explain why a second call skips the lock.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: In what order are base classes, members and the constructor body executed? Bases first (in declaration order), then members in declaration order, then the body. Destruction is the exact reverse. The initialiser-list order has no effect, which is why -Wreorder exists.

Q: Why use a member initialiser list instead of assigning in the constructor body? Initialisation constructs the member directly with the right value; assignment default-constructs first and then assigns, doing two operations. const members, references and types without a default constructor can only be initialised in the list.

Q: What does explicit prevent? Implicit conversions through that constructor: T t = 5;, f(5) where f(T), and return 5; from a function returning T. Direct initialisation T t(5) and T{5} still work.

Q: What is the rule of zero? If a class owns no raw resource, declare none of the special member functions: the compiler-generated copy, move and destructor are correct. Put resource management in small dedicated wrapper types and compose.

Q: What happens if a constructor throws halfway through? Members already constructed are destroyed in reverse order, the exception propagates, and the object's destructor does not run because the object never existed. Any resource acquired manually in the body before the throw leaks unless it is held by a member with its own destructor.

Q: Why does adding ~T() {} slow down std::vector<T>? A user-provided destructor makes T non-trivially-destructible and (for the implicit copy) prevents the vector from treating elements as raw bytes. Element relocation becomes a loop of copy/move constructor plus destructor calls instead of one memmove. ~T() = default; keeps the type trivial.

Q: Is a function-local static thread-safe to initialise? Yes since C++11. The compiler emits a guard and uses __cxa_guard_acquire; concurrent first callers block until the one constructing finishes. It is the standard way to write a lazy singleton.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Constructors and destructors run exactly once per object, on every exit path; this is the foundation of RAII.
  • Order: bases, then members in declaration order, then body; destruction reverses it.
  • Use member initialiser lists; const and reference members require them.
  • Six special members; the compiler generates memberwise versions.
  • Rule of zero by default; rule of five only in thin resource wrappers.
  • explicit on single-argument constructors; = default to restore; = delete to forbid.
  • A user-provided destructor makes a type non-trivial; prefer = default.
  • Function-local statics are thread-safe lazy singletons; cross-TU global init order is unspecified.
  • An object that throws from its constructor never gets a destructor call.

docs.title: 3. RAII: the core idea of C++
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 02_classes_constructors_destructors.md

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
RAII stands for "Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation", which is a terrible name for a simple idea: tie every resource to the lifetime of an object. Acquire the resource in the constructor. Release it in the destructor. Because the destructor runs automatically when the object goes out of scope (module 02), the resource is released automatically, on every path, including the paths you forgot about.

A resource is anything you must give back: heap memory, a file descriptor, a socket, a mutex lock, a database cursor, a reference count, a temporary directory. In C you track each one by hand and write goto cleanup ladders. In C++ you wrap each one once, in a small class, and never think about it again.

Analogy: a library book with an automatic return date. You do not remember to return it; it returns itself when you leave the building. You cannot forget, and you cannot return it twice.

docs.title: 2.1 The C problem
docs.text:
int process(const char* path) {
    FILE* f = fopen(path, "r");
    if (!f) return -1;
    char* buf = malloc(4096);
    if (!buf) { fclose(f); return -1; }            /* path 1 */
    if (read_header(f, buf) != 0) { free(buf); fclose(f); return -1; }   /* path 2 */
    if (validate(buf) != 0)        { free(buf); fclose(f); return -1; }   /* path 3 */
    /* ... every new early return needs the same two lines ... */
    free(buf);
    fclose(f);
    return 0;
}

Every exit path must release everything acquired so far, in reverse order. Add a third resource and the number of cleanup lines grows with the number of exits. Miss one and you leak; release twice and you crash. Your Berkeley DB migration engine almost certainly has functions shaped like this.

docs.title: 2.2 The C++ solution
docs.text:
int process(const char* path) {
    FileHandle f(path, "r");            // throws if fopen fails
    std::vector<char> buf(4096);        // owns its memory
    if (read_header(f.get(), buf.data()) != 0) return -1;   // f and buf released automatically
    if (validate(buf.data()) != 0) return -1;              // same
    return 0;
}                                       // same

Three exits, zero cleanup lines. Add a fourth resource: still zero cleanup lines. The compiler generates the release calls, in the right order (reverse of acquisition), on every path.

docs.title: 2.3 The three rules of an RAII class
docs.text:
1. Acquire in the constructor. If acquisition fails, throw (or make the object represent "empty" and give it an explicit operator bool). An object that exists must be usable.
  2. Release in the destructor. The destructor must not throw and must handle the "moved-from" or "empty" state (releasing nothing).
  3. Decide copy semantics. Either delete copy (one owner: unique_ptr-like), implement deep copy (value-like: std::string), or share with reference counting (shared_ptr-like). The default memberwise copy is wrong for raw handles. Always make the choice explicit.

docs.title: 2.4 Exceptions and stack unwinding
docs.text:
When an exception is thrown, the runtime walks back up the call stack ("unwinds") looking for a matching catch. For every stack frame it passes, it runs the destructors of all fully constructed local objects in reverse order. That is the mechanism that makes RAII complete: a return, a break, falling off the end, and a throw all lead to the same destructor calls.

main()
 └ handle_request()         Guard g1;   <- ~g1 runs third
    └ parse()               Buffer b;   <- ~b  runs second
       └ read_field()       Lock  l;    <- ~l  runs first
             throw ParseError{...};

Without RAII, a thrown exception would skip your manual cleanup code entirely. This is why "exceptions vs error codes" (module 10) is not really a choice in C++: once you use any library that throws (and the standard library does, on allocation failure), only RAII keeps the program correct.

docs.title: 2.5 RAII beyond memory and files
docs.text: Resource Standard RAII type heap object std::unique_ptr<T>, std::shared_ptr<T> (module 05) array of T std::vector<T> string std::string mutex lock std::lock_guard, std::unique_lock, std::shared_lock (04_Concurrency) thread that must be joined std::jthread (C++20) or your own wrapper file stream std::ifstream / std::ofstream C FILE*, fd, socket, library handle write a 20-line wrapper, or unique_ptr with a custom deleter "undo this on exit" a scope guard (exercise 4)

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m03_file_handle_raii.cpp is fopen/fclose done properly:

class FileHandle {
public:
    FileHandle(const char* path, const char* mode) : f_(std::fopen(path, mode)) {
        if (!f_) throw std::system_error(errno, std::generic_category(), std::string("fopen ") + path);
    }
    ~FileHandle() { if (f_) std::fclose(f_); }                  // runs on every exit path
    FileHandle(const FileHandle&) = delete;                      // one owner
    FileHandle& operator=(const FileHandle&) = delete;
    FileHandle(FileHandle&& o) noexcept : f_(o.f_) { o.f_ = nullptr; }   // ownership transfer
    FileHandle& operator=(FileHandle&& o) noexcept {
        if (this != &o) { if (f_) std::fclose(f_); f_ = o.f_; o.f_ = nullptr; }
        return *this;
    }
    std::FILE* get() const noexcept { return f_; }              // hand the raw handle to C APIs
private:
    std::FILE* f_;
};

void write_report(const char* path, bool fail_midway) {
    FileHandle out(path, "w");
    std::fputs("header\n", out.get());
    if (fail_midway) throw std::runtime_error("disk quota exceeded (simulated)");
    std::fputs("body\n", out.get());
}   // fclose happens here on both paths

code/m03_socket_fd_raii.cpp is the pattern tcpkv uses for every socket, a move-only fd owner:

class SocketFd {
public:
    SocketFd() noexcept = default;
    explicit SocketFd(int fd) noexcept : fd_(fd) {}
    ~SocketFd() { reset(); }
    SocketFd(const SocketFd&) = delete;
    SocketFd& operator=(const SocketFd&) = delete;
    SocketFd(SocketFd&& o) noexcept : fd_(std::exchange(o.fd_, -1)) {}
    SocketFd& operator=(SocketFd&& o) noexcept { if (this != &o) { reset(); fd_ = std::exchange(o.fd_, -1); } return *this; }
    int  get() const noexcept   { return fd_; }
    bool valid() const noexcept { return fd_ >= 0; }
    int  release() noexcept     { return std::exchange(fd_, -1); }  // opt out: give the fd back to manual code
    void reset(int fd = -1) noexcept { if (fd_ >= 0) ::close(fd_); fd_ = fd; }
private:
    int fd_ = -1;
};

SocketFd make_listener(std::uint16_t port) {
    SocketFd s(::socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0));
    if (!s.valid()) throw std::system_error(errno, std::generic_category(), "socket");
    // ... setsockopt, bind, listen; each failure throws and s closes itself ...
    return s;     // ownership travels to the caller
}

Note the std::exchange(o.fd_, -1) idiom: read the old value and store the new one in one line. It is the standard way to write "steal and empty the source".

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Zero-cost exceptions. GCC implements exceptions with tables, not with code on the normal path. For each function, the compiler emits an entry in .eh_frame (how to restore registers and find the caller's frame) and .gcc_except_table (which destructors to call for which range of instructions, and which catch clauses apply). On the happy path there is no check, no flag, no extra instruction: a function with RAII objects runs as fast as the C version without cleanup code. When throw executes:

  1. __cxa_allocate_exception gets memory for the exception object (heap, with a small emergency pool for bad_alloc), the object is copied/moved there.
  2. __cxa_throw calls _Unwind_RaiseException (libgcc). Phase 1 ("search"): walk frames using .eh_frame, ask each frame's personality routine (__gxx_personality_v0) whether it has a matching handler. If none, std::terminate.
  3. Phase 2 ("cleanup"): walk again; for each frame, jump to its landing pad, a block of code the compiler generated that runs the destructors of live locals and then calls _Unwind_Resume.
  4. At the handler frame, control enters the catch block. __cxa_begin_catch / __cxa_end_catch manage the exception object's lifetime.

Costs: a throw is expensive (microseconds: two stack walks, table lookups, often a lock inside the unwinder for dl_iterate_phdr). Exceptions are for exceptional paths, not for control flow in a hot loop.

Landing pads are why destructors matter even without try. A function with no try block still has landing pads if it has objects with non-trivial destructors; the pads run the destructors and resume unwinding. A function whose locals are all trivial has no landing pad and the unwinder skips straight through it.

noexcept on destructors. Destructors are implicitly noexcept. If one throws during unwinding (two exceptions in flight), std::terminate is called. This is why ~FileHandle ignores fclose's return value: there is no good way to report it. If flush errors matter, offer an explicit close() method that can throw, and let the destructor be the fallback.

Why -fno-exceptions is not a free lunch. Some embedded teams disable exceptions. Then new failing calls std::abort, constructors cannot report failure, and you are back to two-phase init. For a Linux server, keep exceptions on and use them for genuinely exceptional failures.

Static vs dynamic cost of RAII. The destructor call at scope end is a direct call (or inlined). A std::lock_guard compiles to the same pthread_mutex_lock/pthread_mutex_unlock pair you would write by hand; look at g++ -O2 -S output to confirm there is nothing else.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Your C leak bugs, classified. Early-return leaks, error-path double-frees, "forgot to close the cursor on the exception path", lock not released when a function bails out: all are the same bug class, and all vanish when each resource lives in an object. In code review, a raw fopen, malloc, socket, pthread_mutex_lock outside a wrapper's constructor is a finding.
  • Ownership transfer across layers. make_listener returns a SocketFd by value: the caller now owns it, and the function cannot "forget" to hand it over. In C the same function returns an int and the documentation has to say who closes it.
