  • Interfacing with C APIs that take ownership. Use release() to hand the raw handle to code that will close it itself (e.g. passing an fd to epoll plus a struct that owns it). Document every release() call site; they are the only places the compiler stops protecting you.
  • The destructor-order guarantee is a tool. Declare the lock guard after the object it protects, and a logger before the things that log, so they die in the right order.
  • 3 AM debugging. lsof -p <pid> shows thousands of open fds climbing over hours: some code path gets an fd from accept() and stores it as int. Fix: SocketFd conn(::accept(...)) at the one place the fd is born; the leak is then impossible rather than merely fixed.
  • Valgrind / ASan after RAII. Leaks found by valgrind --leak-check=full in RAII code almost always point to a release() without a matching manual close, or to a shared_ptr cycle (module 05).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m03_file_handle_raii.cpp. Add a third exit path (return early when the path contains "skip"). Done when you can show that fclose still runs without touching the function body.
  2. (easy) Write class DirHandle wrapping opendir/closedir with the same shape as FileHandle. Done when it is move-only, non-copyable, and lists the entries of /tmp.
  3. (medium) Rewrite the C process() function from section 2.1 in C++ with RAII. Count the lines before and after. Done when the C++ version has zero explicit cleanup calls.
  4. (medium) Write a generic ScopeGuard that takes a lambda in its constructor and calls it in its destructor, with a dismiss() method. Use it to roll back a partially applied change (map.erase(key) if a later step fails). Done when the rollback runs on throw and is skipped after dismiss().
  5. (hard) Run m03_socket_fd_raii.cpp under strace -e trace=socket,bind,listen,close and confirm exactly one close per socket. Then add a bug (a copy of the fd into a second int that is also closed) and observe EBADF. Done when you can explain which line the kernel rejected and why SocketFd makes the bug unwritable.
  6. (hard) Compile m03_file_handle_raii.cpp with g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -S and locate the landing pad for write_report (look for .LLSDA, _Unwind_Resume, and the fclose call reached only from the pad). Done when you can point at the normal-path code and show it contains no exception checks.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is RAII in one sentence? Bind each resource to the lifetime of an object: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor, so the compiler releases it on every exit path, including exceptions.

Q: Why is RAII more than "remember to call cleanup"? Because the destructor call is generated by the compiler at every scope exit, including the hidden exits created by exceptions. Manual cleanup code is skipped by a throw; destructors are not.

Q: What happens to local objects when an exception propagates through a function? Stack unwinding runs the destructors of all fully constructed locals in reverse construction order, via compiler-generated landing pads, then continues unwinding to the next frame.

Q: Why should a destructor never throw? If an exception is already propagating and a destructor throws a second one, the runtime calls std::terminate. Destructors are implicitly noexcept; report cleanup failures through an explicit close() method instead.

Q: How much does exception support cost on the non-throwing path with GCC? Essentially nothing: GCC uses table-based ("zero-cost") unwinding. The tables live in .eh_frame and .gcc_except_table and are consulted only when a throw happens. The throw itself costs microseconds (two stack walks), so exceptions should not be used for routine control flow.

Q: What are the three decisions every RAII class must make? How to acquire (constructor, and what to do on failure), how to release (destructor, handling the empty state), and what copying means (deleted, deep copy, or shared). Leaving copy as the default is the classic double-free bug.

Q: You get an int fd from accept(). How do you prevent fd leaks in a server? Wrap it immediately in a move-only owner (SocketFd conn(::accept(...))) at the point of creation. Pass the owner by value when transferring ownership, by reference when lending it, and call release() only where a C API takes over ownership.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• RAII: constructor acquires, destructor releases; the compiler calls the destructor on every path.
  • The destructor runs for return, break, end of scope, and during exception unwinding.
  • An RAII class must define copy semantics explicitly: delete, deep copy, or share.
  • Destructors must not throw and must tolerate an empty/moved-from state.
  • std::exchange(member, empty_value) is the idiom for "steal and empty".
  • GCC exceptions are zero-cost on the happy path, expensive when thrown; use them for exceptional cases.
  • Landing pads in .gcc_except_table run destructors during unwinding.
  • Standard RAII types already exist for memory, strings, locks and streams; write wrappers only for raw C handles.
  • In review, any raw resource acquisition outside a wrapper's constructor is a finding.

docs.title: 4. Value semantics: copy, move, and the rule of five
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
In C, a = b for structs copies the bytes. If the struct holds a pointer, both copies now point at the same memory and you have to decide by convention who frees it. C++ lets a type define what copying means: std::string a = b; makes an independent deep copy. That is value semantics: objects behave like integers, independent after copy.

Deep copying is expensive when the source is about to die anyway, like a function's return value or a temporary. Move semantics (C++11) adds a second operation: instead of copying the contents, steal them, leaving the source empty but valid. Moving a std::vector of a million elements copies three pointers.

Analogy: copying a house means building an identical second house. Moving a house means handing over the keys: the first owner is left with nothing, but nothing was rebuilt.

docs.title: 2.1 Value categories: lvalue and rvalue
docs.text:
An lvalue is an expression that names an object that persists: a variable, *p, arr[i], a function returning T&. An rvalue is a temporary or something about to expire: f() returning by value, T{}, a + b, or std::move(x).

The compiler uses the category to pick between copy and move:

std::string a = b;              // b is an lvalue  -> copy constructor
std::string c = make_name();    // rvalue          -> move constructor (or elided entirely)
std::string d = std::move(a);   // std::move casts a to an rvalue -> move constructor; a is now moved-from

std::move does not move anything. It is a cast: static_cast<T&&>(x). It says "you may treat this as a temporary". The move happens in whatever constructor or assignment receives it.

docs.title: 2.2 Rvalue references
docs.text:
T&& binds to rvalues only. It is how you write an overload that receives temporaries:

void push(const std::string& s);   // called for lvalues: must copy
void push(std::string&& s);        // called for rvalues: may steal from s

Inside the second function, s itself is an lvalue (it has a name), so to actually move its contents you write std::move(s) again. Forgetting that is the most common move-semantics bug: a T&& parameter that is copied.

docs.title: 2.3 The rule of five, written correctly
docs.text:
class Buffer {
    char* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
public:
    Buffer() noexcept = default;
    explicit Buffer(std::size_t n);
    ~Buffer() { std::free(data_); }                                  // 1: release

    Buffer(const Buffer& o);                                         // 2: deep copy (allocate + memcpy)
    Buffer(Buffer&& o) noexcept                                      // 3: steal
        : data_(std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr)), size_(std::exchange(o.size_, 0)) {}

    Buffer& operator=(Buffer o) noexcept { swap(*this, o); return *this; }   // 4 and 5 together: copy-and-swap
    friend void swap(Buffer& a, Buffer& b) noexcept { std::swap(a.data_, b.data_); std::swap(a.size_, b.size_); }
};

Key points:

  • Move operations must be noexcept. std::vector only moves elements during reallocation if the move constructor is noexcept; otherwise it copies, to preserve the strong exception guarantee. A non-noexcept move constructor silently makes your type slow in containers.
  • Moved-from state must be valid. The destructor will run on the source. free(nullptr) is fine; fclose(nullptr) is not. Reset handles to their empty value.
  • Copy-and-swap gives one assignment operator for both lvalues and rvalues (the parameter is copy-constructed or move-constructed depending on the argument), handles self-assignment, and is strongly exception-safe: if the copy throws, *this is untouched.
  • Declaring any of the five suppresses the implicit move operations. Declaring a move suppresses implicit copies. Write all five or none (rule of zero).

docs.title: 2.4 Copy elision and NRVO
docs.text: C++17 guarantees that T x = T(...) and return T(...) (a prvalue) construct the object directly in its final location: zero copies, zero moves, even if the type is not movable. For a named local (T t; ...; return t;) the compiler is allowed to elide (NRVO) and GCC does it at every optimisation level when there is a single return object; otherwise it falls back to a move. Writing return std::move(t); is wrong: it disables NRVO and forces a move. GCC warns with -Wpessimizing-move.

docs.title: 2.5 Choosing parameter types
docs.text:
You want to Take Why read, not copy const T& no copy, binds to everything modify the caller's object T& keep a copy ("sink": store into a member, push into a container) T by value, then std::move into place 1 copy for lvalues, 0 for rvalues, one overload steal specifically from temporaries T&& plus a const T& overload only when the by-value version's extra move matters small trivially copyable (int, double, string_view, pointers) T by value cheaper than a reference forward anything to another function T&& in a template + std::forward<T>(x) perfect forwarding

Return by value. Returning const T& to a local is a dangling reference; returning T&& almost never makes sense.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m04_move_only_handle.cpp contains UniqueFd (move-only) and Buffer (full rule of five, as above). The part that shows the noexcept rule and moved-from state:

std::vector<UniqueFd> fds;
fds.push_back(UniqueFd(3));         // rvalue: moved in
UniqueFd f(4);
fds.push_back(std::move(f));        // f is now moved-from: valid, holds -1
// fds.push_back(f);                // error: copy constructor is deleted
fds.emplace_back(5);                // constructed in place
// vector grows by MOVING elements only because UniqueFd(UniqueFd&&) is noexcept
std::vector<UniqueFd> moved = std::move(fds);   // O(1): three pointers change hands; fds is empty

code/m04_copy_elision_nrvo.cpp uses a Loud type whose special members print, so you can see exactly what happens. Build it twice, once with -fno-elide-constructors, and compare:

Loud make_prvalue() { return Loud("prvalue"); }   // C++17: guaranteed elision, prints only "ctor"
Loud make_nrvo()    { Loud l("nrvo"); l.tag += "!"; return l; }   // NRVO: "ctor" only on GCC; MOVE if disabled
Loud make_no_nrvo(bool flag) { Loud a("a"), b("b"); if (flag) return a; return b; }   // two candidates: MOVE

void by_value(Loud l);         // COPY for lvalue arguments, MOVE for rvalues
void by_cref(const Loud& l);   // nothing
void by_rref(Loud&& l);        // nothing at the call; the move happens inside when you std::move(l)

struct Person {
    std::string name;
    explicit Person(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) {}   // sink parameter
};
Person p1(n);              // 1 copy into the parameter, 1 cheap move into the member
Person p2(std::move(n));   // 0 copies

Expected highlights of the output:

-- prvalue (guaranteed elision)
ctor  prvalue
-- nrvo
ctor  nrvo
-- no nrvo possible
ctor  a
ctor  b
MOVE  a
-- by_value(lvalue): COPY
COPY  prvalue

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
A move is a shallow copy plus a reset. For std::vector, the move constructor copies three pointers (begin, end, capacity end) and nulls the source's. For std::string with libstdc++'s small-string optimisation, a short string (15 chars or fewer) lives inside the object, so moving it is copying 32 bytes; only long strings move by pointer steal. Moving is not free, it is just cheap.

Why noexcept matters to std::vector. On reallocation the vector must relocate N elements into the new buffer. If relocation can throw halfway, some elements have been moved out of the old buffer and the vector cannot restore the old state: the strong exception guarantee is lost. So std::vector uses std::move_if_noexcept: it moves when the move constructor is noexcept, and copies otherwise. Check with static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>).

Moved-from state in the standard library. The standard says "valid but unspecified" for most types. Practically, libstdc++ leaves a moved-from std::string empty and a moved-from std::vector empty, but code relying on that is non-portable. std::unique_ptr is guaranteed null after a move. The safe operations on any moved-from object: assign to it, destroy it, or call functions with no preconditions (size(), empty(), clear()).

Copy elision mechanics. Without elision, Loud x = make_prvalue(); would construct a temporary in the callee's frame and then move it to x. With elision, the caller passes the address of x as a hidden first argument (the return slot) and the callee constructs directly there. This is why returning large objects by value is free in modern C++ and why "return by output parameter" is a C-era habit to drop.

Implicit moves on return. return local; treats local as an rvalue first (so a move is tried), then as an lvalue. Writing std::move there is redundant at best (GCC: -Wredundant-move) and harmful when it blocks NRVO (-Wpessimizing-move, in -Wall).

Self-move. x = std::move(x) is legal and must leave x valid. Copy-and-swap handles it (result: x ends up empty). Hand-written move assignment needs if (this != &o) or must be written so the order of operations is safe. GCC 13's -Wself-move flags the obvious cases.

Perfect forwarding. In template <class T> void f(T&& x), T&& is a forwarding reference: T deduces to U& for lvalues and U for rvalues, and reference collapsing (U& && -> U&) makes x an lvalue or rvalue reference accordingly. std::forward<T>(x) restores the original category when passing x on. This is how emplace_back and make_unique avoid copies.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Move-only handle types make ownership transfer explicit in function signatures. In tcpkv, a Connection is move-only: passing it to a worker thread by value is the hand-off, and the compiler stops two threads from both owning it.
  • Hidden copies are the most common performance bug in C++ written by C programmers. for (auto conn : connections) copies every element. std::string s = view; allocates. Passing std::vector by value to a function that only reads it copies the whole thing. Build with -Wall -Wextra and watch for -Wrange-loop-construct (in -Wall since GCC 11).
  • std::move on a const object silently copies. const T&& cannot bind to a move constructor taking T&&, so the copy constructor is chosen. No warning. Grep for std::move( on const locals and on members accessed through const methods.
  • Returning std::move(member) from a getter destroys the object's state for the next caller. A move-out should be a named, documented operation (take_result()), never a getter.
  • Benchmark before adding T&& overloads. The by-value sink costs one extra move over the const&/&& pair. For a std::string that is 32 bytes of copying. Add the overloads only when profiling shows it matters.
  • 3 AM debugging. A use-after-move: an object is moved into a container inside a loop and then used after the loop. Symptoms: empty strings, null pointers, "impossible" states. clang-tidy's bugprone-use-after-move catches most cases statically; enable it in CI (module 14).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m04_copy_elision_nrvo.cpp with and without -fno-elide-constructors. Count the MOVE and COPY lines in each. Done when you can explain every difference.
  2. (easy) Change UniqueFd's move constructor to drop noexcept, then add a static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<UniqueFd>). Done when you see it fail and can explain what std::vector would do differently.
  3. (medium) Write class Matrix (owning double*, rows, cols) with the full rule of five using copy-and-swap. Verify with a Loud-style print that Matrix m = a * b; performs zero copies. Done when the output shows only constructions and moves.
  4. (medium) Write void set_name(std::string) (sink) and the pair set_name(const std::string&) / set_name(std::string&&). Call each with an lvalue, an rvalue, and a string literal, and count copies and moves. Done when you have a table of 6 cells and can say when the two-overload version is worth it.
  5. (hard) Write a template <class... Args> T& emplace(Args&&... args) for a tiny fixed-capacity container using perfect forwarding and placement new. Verify with Loud that emplace("x") constructs exactly once. Done when emplace(std::move(loud)) prints one MOVE and emplace(loud) prints one COPY.
  6. (hard) Find the bug: a function takes std::string&& s and does names.push_back(s);. Fix it, then explain why the original compiles without warning. Done when you can state the rule "a named rvalue reference is an lvalue".

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does std::move do? Nothing at run time. It is a cast to an rvalue reference (static_cast<T&&>). The move actually happens in the move constructor or move assignment that receives the result. Applied to a const object it silently results in a copy.

Q: What state is an object in after being moved from? Valid but unspecified for most standard types: it can be destroyed or assigned to, and functions without preconditions (size, clear) are safe. std::unique_ptr is guaranteed null. Your own types should reset handles so the destructor is a no-op.

Q: Why must move constructors be noexcept? Containers like std::vector relocate elements during reallocation. If the move could throw midway, the old buffer would be partially destroyed and the strong exception guarantee lost, so the vector falls back to copying unless the move is noexcept. A non-noexcept move makes your type slower without any warning.

Q: Explain copy-and-swap. Write assignment as T& operator=(T other) { swap(*this, other); return *this; }. The parameter is constructed by copy or move depending on the argument, so one function serves both. The swap is noexcept, so if the copy throws nothing has changed (strong guarantee), and self-assignment is handled because the copy is made before anything is modified.

Q: What is guaranteed copy elision in C++17? Initialising an object from a prvalue (T x = T(...), return T(...)) constructs it directly in place with no copy or move, and it works even for non-movable types. NRVO (returning a named local) remains optional but is done by GCC when there is a single return object.

Q: Should you write return std::move(local);? No. return local; already tries a move, and std::move prevents NRVO, so it is strictly worse. GCC flags it with -Wpessimizing-move / -Wredundant-move.

Q: How do you pass a parameter you intend to store? Take it by value and std::move it into place. Lvalue callers pay one copy (unavoidable), rvalue callers pay one cheap move, and there is a single overload to maintain. Add const& / && overloads only if profiling shows the extra move matters.

Q: What is a forwarding reference? T&& where T is a deduced template parameter. It binds to both lvalues and rvalues, deducing T as U& or U, and std::forward<T>(x) passes the argument on with its original value category. This is how emplace_back constructs elements in place with zero copies.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Lvalues name persistent objects; rvalues are temporaries or std::moved objects.
  • std::move is a cast; the move happens in the receiving constructor/assignment.
  • Move = steal the guts and reset the source; the source must remain destructible.
  • Move operations must be noexcept, or std::vector will copy instead.
  • Rule of five: destructor, copy ctor, copy assign, move ctor, move assign; copy-and-swap merges the last two safely.
  • C++17 guarantees elision for prvalues; NRVO is optional but GCC does it; never return std::move(x).
  • Parameter rules: const T& to read, T by value to sink, T&& + std::forward to forward.
  • A named T&& parameter is an lvalue inside the function; std::move it to actually move.
  • std::move on const copies silently; use-after-move is caught by clang-tidy, not the compiler.

docs.title: 5. Smart pointers and ownership design
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A raw pointer answers "where is the object?" but not "who deletes it?". In your C code that second question is answered by a comment, a naming convention, or the arena allocator's contract. A smart pointer answers it in the type: std::unique_ptr<T> means "I am the single owner and I will delete it"; std::shared_ptr<T> means "we jointly own it; the last one out deletes it"; a raw T* or T& then means, by convention, "I am only looking, someone else owns it".

Analogy: a car. unique_ptr is the title deed: exactly one person holds it, and it can be handed over. shared_ptr is a car-share where the car is scrapped when the last member leaves. weak_ptr is knowing the car's number plate: you can check whether it still exists and borrow it if so, but you do not keep it alive. A raw pointer is a passenger: enjoys the ride, never owns anything.

docs.title: 2.1 std::unique_ptr<T, Deleter>
docs.text:
• Owns exactly one object (or array with unique_ptr<T[]>). Move-only. Destructor calls the deleter.
  • std::make_unique<T>(args...) constructs the object and the pointer in one step. Prefer it over unique_ptr<T>(new T(...)): exception-safe in expressions with several allocations, and no new in your code.
  • get() gives the raw pointer for non-owning use (passing to a C API). release() gives up ownership and returns the raw pointer. reset(p) deletes the current object and takes p.
  • Custom deleters make it the universal wrapper for C APIs:
struct FileCloser { void operator()(std::FILE* f) const noexcept { if (f) std::fclose(f); } };
using FilePtr = std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser>;          // sizeof == sizeof(FILE*)

using ZctxPtr = std::unique_ptr<zctx, void (*)(zctx*)>;          // sizeof == 2 pointers
ZctxPtr z(zctx_new(6), &zctx_free);

A stateless functor deleter costs nothing (empty base optimisation). A function-pointer deleter costs one extra pointer in the object.

docs.title: 2.2 std::shared_ptr<T>
docs.text:
• Shared ownership through a control block holding a strong count, a weak count, the deleter, and (with make_shared) the object itself.
  • Copying increments the strong count atomically; destroying decrements; when it hits zero the object is destroyed; when the weak count also hits zero the control block is freed.
  • std::make_shared<T>(args...) does one allocation for control block and object together. shared_ptr<T>(new T) does two, and leaks T if the control block allocation throws.
  • sizeof(shared_ptr) == 2 * sizeof(void*): a pointer to the object and a pointer to the control block. The object pointer can differ from what the control block manages (aliasing constructor, shared_ptr<Base> from shared_ptr<Derived>).
  • Thread safety: the reference count is atomic, so copying shared_ptrs to the same object from several threads is safe. Access to the pointed-to object is not synchronised, and concurrent modification of the same shared_ptr variable is a data race.

docs.title: 2.3 std::weak_ptr<T>
docs.text:
A non-owning observer of a shared_ptr-managed object. lock() returns a shared_ptr (null if the object is gone). expired() is a cheaper check but racy: by the time you act, it may have died. Two uses:

  • Breaking cycles. Parent owns child (shared_ptr), child refers back to parent (weak_ptr). With two shared_ptrs neither count ever reaches zero and both leak.
  • Caches and observers. A cache holds weak_ptrs so it never keeps an object alive on its own.

docs.title: 2.4 Ownership design
docs.text:
Decide, for every object in the system, exactly one of:

Ownership Type to use Typical case Single owner, lifetime = scope plain member / local object (no pointer at all) most objects Single owner, polymorphic or optional or heap-sized std::unique_ptr<T> a Logger behind an interface, a 1 MB buffer Single owner, transferable across threads/queues std::unique_ptr<T> moved into the queue request objects in a worker pool Several owners with unrelated lifetimes std::shared_ptr<T> a config snapshot read by many threads while being replaced Observer that must not extend lifetime std::weak_ptr<T> caches, back-pointers, callbacks that might outlive the target Non-owning access, owner guaranteed alive T& or T* (nullable) function parameters, iteration

shared_ptr is not the default. It is for genuinely shared, non-hierarchical lifetime. Most C++ codebases that overuse it end up with unclear ownership, cycles, and atomic traffic in hot loops. Start with values and unique_ptr; introduce shared_ptr only when you can name the second owner.

docs.title: 2.5 Mapping to your arena allocator
docs.text: Your C arena with "explicit ownership contracts" is exactly this discipline done by hand: the arena is the single owner of every block, callers get non-owning pointers, and the lifetime ends when the arena resets. In C++ that design still exists (module 12, std::pmr), and the vocabulary types make the contract checkable: a function taking T* is documented as non-owning; one taking std::unique_ptr<T> takes ownership; one returning std::unique_ptr<T> gives it.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m05_unique_ptr_c_api.cpp wraps three kinds of C resources:

if (FilePtr f = open_file("/tmp/m05_demo.txt", "w")) {   // contextual bool: non-null?
    std::fputs("hello\n", f.get());                       // raw pointer to the C API
}                                                          // fclose here

MallocPtr<char> buf(static_cast<char*>(std::malloc(64)));  // deleter calls free

ZctxPtr z(zctx_new(6), &zctx_free);
ZctxPtr z2 = std::move(z);        // z is null now
zctx* raw = z2.release();         // hand ownership back to C; z2 will not free
zctx_free(raw);

auto arr = std::make_unique<int[]>(8);   // delete[] on destruction

code/m05_shared_weak_ptr.cpp shows the counts changing, a cache that does not keep objects alive, and a parent/child cycle broken with weak_ptr:

auto s1 = std::make_shared<Session>("shakir");   // one allocation: control block + Session
{ std::shared_ptr<Session> s2 = s1; }            // use_count 1 -> 2 -> 1 (two atomic ops)

class SessionCache {
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::weak_ptr<Session>> cache_;
public:
    std::shared_ptr<Session> get(const std::string& id) {
        auto it = cache_.find(id);
        return it == cache_.end() ? nullptr : it->second.lock();   // null if the session died
    }
};

struct Node {
    std::shared_ptr<Node> child;    // owning edge
    std::weak_ptr<Node> parent;     // back edge: weak, or both nodes leak
};

Expected: ~Session(shakir) prints as soon as s1.reset() runs even though the cache still holds a weak_ptr, and both ~Node lines print at the end of the block.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
unique_ptr is a zero-overhead abstraction. sizeof(std::unique_ptr<T>) == sizeof(T*) with a stateless deleter; operator-> and operator* inline to a load; the destructor inlines to if (p) delete p;. The one real cost is at the ABI boundary: on x86-64, a unique_ptr is passed to a function in memory (because it has a non-trivial destructor), not in a register like a raw pointer. Measurable only in very hot code.

The shared_ptr control block (libstdc++, _Sp_counted_base) contains a vptr (the control block is polymorphic so it can hold different deleters and allocators), an int strong count (_M_use_count), and an int weak count (_M_weak_count). With make_shared, the T object is embedded directly after it in the same allocation (_Sp_counted_ptr_inplace). Typical size: 16 bytes of header plus the object. shared_ptr<T>(new T) instead allocates T separately and a smaller control block that stores the pointer: two allocations, two cache lines.

Atomic reference counting cost. Every copy and destroy of a shared_ptr is a lock xadd (or lock dec) on the control block's count. On x86 that is a full barrier, roughly 20 cycles uncontended and far more if another core recently touched the same line (the count is a shared write hotspot). libstdc++ skips the atomic instructions when the program has not linked libpthread (__gthread_active_p()), which is why a single-threaded benchmark can look faster than the server. Passing shared_ptr by value through five layers of calls does five increments and five decrements for no reason; pass const shared_ptr<T>& or, better, T& when the callee does not need to own.

Why make_shared can delay freeing memory. Because object and control block share one allocation, the memory cannot be returned until the weak count also reaches zero. A long-lived weak_ptr to a large object keeps the object's bytes allocated (though destroyed) until the weak_ptr dies. For large objects observed by long-lived weak pointers, shared_ptr<T>(new T) is the better choice.

weak_ptr::lock() is a CAS loop. It must increment the strong count only if it is non-zero, so it reads the count, checks, and does a compare-and-swap; retries on contention. expired() is a plain load and is only a hint.

enable_shared_from_this. A class that must produce a shared_ptr to itself from inside a member function (typical in async callbacks: self = shared_from_this() captured in the lambda) derives from std::enable_shared_from_this<T>, which stores a weak_ptr to the control block that make_shared fills in. Calling shared_from_this() on an object not owned by a shared_ptr throws std::bad_weak_ptr.

Custom deleter type erasure. shared_ptr<T> has one type regardless of deleter (the deleter lives in the control block); unique_ptr<T, D> has the deleter in its type. That is why shared_ptr is convenient for plugin-style APIs and unique_ptr is the tool for zero-overhead wrappers.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Hot paths and shared_ptr. A request handler that copies a shared_ptr<Config> per request is one atomic RMW per request; per field access it would be a disaster. Pattern: take a copy once at the top of the request (or hold a const Config& if the owner is guaranteed to outlive the call), then use references.
  • Config hot-reload is the textbook shared_ptr use: readers hold shared_ptr<const Config> for the duration of a request; the reloader builds a new Config and atomically swaps the pointer (std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> in C++20, or a mutex-protected pointer in C++17). Old readers finish on the old snapshot; it is freed when the last one lets go.
  • Cycles are silent leaks. A Session holding a shared_ptr<Connection> whose callback captures shared_ptr<Session> never frees. Valgrind reports "still reachable", not "lost". Rule: callbacks capture weak_ptr and lock() when invoked, or capture a raw pointer with a documented lifetime.
  • Never delete what a smart pointer owns; never wrap the same raw pointer twice. shared_ptr<T> a(p); shared_ptr<T> b(p); creates two control blocks and a double free. Always copy the shared_ptr, never the raw pointer, to add an owner.
  • Interop with C callbacks. void* user_data in a C API is where ownership gets lost. Pass handle.get() and keep the owner alive in a known scope, or pass handle.release() and document which C callback frees it.
  • 3 AM debugging. ASan reports "heap-use-after-free" on an object held through a raw pointer: some unique_ptr owner was destroyed while an observer kept the raw pointer. Fix the design (the observer should hold a weak_ptr, or the owner must outlive the observer), not the symptom.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Write a unique_ptr alias for DIR* (opendir/closedir) with a stateless deleter and assert sizeof equals one pointer. Done when it lists /tmp and the static_assert holds.
  2. (easy) In m05_shared_weak_ptr.cpp, change Node::parent to shared_ptr and run under valgrind --leak-check=full. Done when you can read the report and identify the cycle.
  3. (medium) Implement class Connection : std::enable_shared_from_this<Connection> with an async_read(std::function<void()> on_done) that stores a lambda capturing shared_from_this(). Show that the connection survives until the callback runs. Done when the destructor prints after the callback, not before.
  4. (medium) Write a tiny SharedPtr<T> with an int strong count (non-atomic), copy/move/destroy, and use_count(). Then make the count std::atomic<int> and benchmark copying in a loop from one thread vs four threads sharing one object. Done when you can report the ratio and explain it.
  5. (hard) Design the ownership for a tcpkv-style server: Server owns listening SocketFd, accepts into Connection objects, each handled by a worker from a pool, with a shared KvStore. Draw the ownership graph and assign a type (value / unique_ptr / shared_ptr / weak_ptr / reference) to every edge. Done when no edge is shared_ptr without a named second owner and no cycle exists.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When would you choose unique_ptr over shared_ptr? By default. unique_ptr expresses single ownership, costs the same as a raw pointer, and can be moved to transfer ownership. shared_ptr is for genuinely shared lifetime where no single owner can be named, and costs two pointers plus atomic reference counting on every copy.

Q: What is in a shared_ptr control block, and why does make_shared matter? A strong count, a weak count, the deleter (and allocator), and with make_shared the object itself. make_shared does one allocation instead of two and cannot leak the object if the second allocation fails. The downside: the object's memory is held until all weak_ptrs are gone too.

Q: Is shared_ptr thread-safe? The reference count is atomic, so copying and destroying different shared_ptr instances pointing to the same object from several threads is safe. The managed object itself is not protected, and two threads writing the same shared_ptr variable is a data race.

Q: What problem does weak_ptr solve? Observing a shared object without extending its lifetime: it breaks ownership cycles (parent/child) and lets caches or callbacks check whether the object still exists via lock(), which returns a shared_ptr or null.

Q: How do you wrap a C API handle in a smart pointer? std::unique_ptr<Handle, Deleter> where Deleter is a stateless functor calling the C free function. The result is the size of a raw pointer and inlines to the same code. A function-pointer deleter also works but adds a pointer of storage.

Q: What does a raw pointer mean in a modern C++ codebase? Non-owning, nullable access to an object someone else owns. References mean non-owning, non-null. Owning raw pointers (new without a smart pointer) should not appear outside of allocator internals.

Q: Why is passing shared_ptr by value through many layers a performance problem? Each copy and destroy is an atomic read-modify-write on the control block, a full memory barrier on x86 and a contended cache line if several threads share the object. Pass const shared_ptr& or a plain T& when the callee does not need to participate in ownership.

Q: What happens if you construct two shared_ptrs from the same raw pointer? Two independent control blocks each believe they own the object; the second to die double-frees it. Always copy an existing shared_ptr to add an owner, or use shared_from_this().

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Ownership belongs in the type: unique_ptr = single owner, shared_ptr = shared, weak_ptr = observer, raw pointer/reference = non-owning.
  • unique_ptr costs nothing over a raw pointer with a stateless deleter; use custom deleters for C APIs.
  • make_unique / make_shared instead of new; make_shared does one allocation.
  • shared_ptr copies are atomic RMWs; pass by const& or T& in hot paths.
  • weak_ptr breaks cycles and backs caches; lock() is a CAS loop, expired() is only a hint.
  • Two shared_ptrs from one raw pointer is a double free; cycles are silent leaks.
  • enable_shared_from_this for async callbacks that must keep the object alive.
  • Start with values and unique_ptr; justify every shared_ptr with a named second owner.
  • Your C arena "ownership contracts" are the same discipline; C++ makes them checkable types.

docs.title: 6. STL containers deep dive
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 04, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
The standard library gives you the data structures you kept re-writing in C: a growable array (vector), a double-ended queue (deque), a linked list (list), a balanced tree (map, set), and a hash table (unordered_map, unordered_set). Each one is a template, so it works for any element type, and each one owns its elements (RAII), so you never free them by hand.

The real skill is not knowing that map exists. It is knowing what each container does to memory, which operations invalidate your pointers and iterators, and why vector wins most benchmarks even when the textbook says list should. This module is about the mechanics behind the interface.

Analogy: vector is a bookshelf (books side by side, fast to scan, painful to insert in the middle); list is a treasure hunt (each clue points to the next, easy to insert a clue, slow to reach the tenth); map is a library catalogue sorted by title; unordered_map is a coat check with numbered hooks.

docs.title: 2.1 std::vector<T>: the default container
docs.text:
Contiguous array on the heap, three pointers in the object (begin, end, capacity_end).

  • size() = elements, capacity() = allocated slots. push_back is amortised O(1): when size == capacity, it allocates a bigger block (libstdc++: doubles; MSVC: 1.5x), moves (or copies) all elements over, frees the old block.
  • Reallocation invalidates everything: every pointer, reference and iterator into the old buffer.
  • reserve(n) allocates up front; shrink_to_fit() is a request; clear() keeps capacity.
  • insert/erase in the middle shift elements: O(n). Iterators at or after the point are invalidated (erase returns the next valid one).
  • emplace_back(args...) constructs in place; push_back(T&&) moves in.
  • std::vector<bool> is a bit-packed specialisation: operator[] returns a proxy, not bool&. Use std::vector<char> or std::bitset when you need real references.
  • data() gives the raw T* for C APIs.

docs.title: 2.2 std::array<T, N>
docs.text: A C array with a container interface. Size fixed at compile time, lives wherever you declare it (stack or inside another object), no heap, zero overhead. Use it instead of T arr[N] to get size(), bounds-checked at(), iterators, and copy semantics.

docs.title: 2.3 std::deque<T>
docs.text: Blocks of fixed size (libstdc++: 512 bytes per block) indexed by a small array of block pointers. O(1) push_front and push_back, O(1) indexing with two dereferences, and pointers/references stay valid on push/pop at either end (iterators do not). Good as a FIFO queue; std::queue uses it by default.

docs.title: 2.4 std::list<T> and std::forward_list<T>
docs.text: Doubly (or singly) linked nodes, one heap allocation per element. O(1) insert/erase anywhere given an iterator, and insert/erase never invalidate other iterators. The price: each node is sizeof(T) + 16 bytes plus allocator overhead, traversal is a pointer chase with a cache miss per node, and there is no indexing. It is rarely the fastest choice; it is the right choice when iterator stability matters (an intrusive LRU list, a registry where handles must stay valid).

docs.title: 2.5 std::string and std::string_view
docs.text:
std::string is std::vector<char> plus a null terminator and the small-string optimisation (SSO): libstdc++ stores up to 15 characters inside the 32-byte object with no heap allocation. Beyond that, heap. c_str() is always null-terminated.

std::string_view (C++17) is a (const char*, size_t) pair: a non-owning view of any character range. Pass it instead of const std::string& so callers with a literal, a char*, or a substring do not allocate. It does not own and is not null-terminated; never let it outlive the string it views and never pass .data() to a C API expecting a C string (module 13).

docs.title: 2.6 std::map<K, V> and std::set<K>
docs.text:
Red-black trees: self-balancing binary search trees with O(log n) find/insert/erase, elements sorted by K's operator< (or a comparator). Each element is a separately allocated node (libstdc++: 32 bytes of header: colour, parent, left, right pointers; then the pair<const K, V>).

  • Iterators and references are never invalidated by insert, and by erase only for the erased element.
  • operator[] inserts a default-constructed value if the key is absent (and needs V to be default-constructible). Use find, count, at, or try_emplace when you do not want that.
  • lower_bound/upper_bound/equal_range give O(log n) range queries: the reason to pick map over unordered_map.
  • multimap/multiset allow duplicates.

docs.title: 2.7 std::unordered_map<K, V> and std::unordered_set<K>
docs.text:
Hash tables with separate chaining: an array of buckets, each a singly linked list of nodes. Average O(1) find/insert/erase, worst case O(n) when many keys collide.

  • load_factor() = size() / bucket_count(). When it would exceed max_load_factor() (default 1.0) on insert, the table rehashes: allocates more buckets (libstdc++ picks the next prime) and re-links every node.
  • Rehash invalidates all iterators but not pointers/references to elements (the nodes themselves do not move).
  • reserve(n) sizes the bucket array for n elements with no rehash on the way.
  • Iteration order is unspecified and changes after rehash. Never depend on it.
  • You need std::hash<K> and operator== for K. For your own key type, specialise std::hash or pass a hasher type.
  • No heterogeneous lookup in C++17: find with a string_view key forces a std::string construction. (C++20 adds is_transparent support.)

docs.title: 2.8 Which container?
docs.text:
Need sorted order or range queries?           -> map / set
Need stable iterators across inserts?         -> list, or map/unordered_map (node-based)
Need O(1) at both ends?                       -> deque
Fixed size known at compile time?             -> array
Key lookup, no ordering needed?               -> unordered_map (reserve it!)
Everything else, especially < 10k elements    -> vector (sorted vector + binary search beats map
                                                 for read-mostly data)

Measure before deviating from vector. Linear scan over 100 contiguous ints is faster than a hash lookup; a sorted vector<pair<K,V>> with lower_bound is usually faster than map for read-heavy tables because of cache locality.

docs.title: 2.9 Iterator invalidation summary
docs.text: Container insert / push erase vector all, if reallocation; else at/after the point at/after the point deque all iterators; pointers/refs survive if at the ends all, except at the ends only the erased list, forward_list none only the erased map, set none only the erased unordered_map/set all iterators if rehash; pointers/refs never only the erased string like vector like vector

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m06_vector_growth.cpp prints every reallocation and shows the safe erase/insert idioms:

std::vector<int> v;
std::size_t last_cap = v.capacity();
for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) {
    v.push_back(i);
    if (v.capacity() != last_cap) {               // 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 on libstdc++
        std::cout << "size=" << v.size() << " capacity " << last_cap << " -> " << v.capacity() << '\n';
        last_cap = v.capacity();
    }
}

for (auto it = nums.begin(); it != nums.end();) {   // erase while iterating: use the returned iterator
    if (*it < 0) it = nums.erase(it);
    else ++it;
}

code/m06_map_vs_unordered.cpp shows ordering, operator[] inserting, and rehash points:

int z = ordered["zulu"];       // inserts "zulu" -> 0 silently; size grows
if (auto it = hashed.find("zulu"); it == hashed.end()) std::cout << "find() does not insert\n";

std::unordered_map<int, int> h;
for (int i = 0; i < 2000; ++i) {
    h[i] = i;
    if (h.bucket_count() != last_buckets) { /* print rehash: 1 -> 13 -> 29 -> 59 -> 127 -> 257 -> 541 -> 1109 -> 2357 */ }
}
std::unordered_map<int, int> pre;
pre.reserve(2000);              // bucket array sized once; no rehash during the inserts

auto lb = ordered.lower_bound("c");   // only ordered containers can do this

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why vector beats list even for "list-friendly" workloads. A modern core fetches 64-byte cache lines and prefetches sequential ones. Walking a vector<int> touches one new line every 16 elements and the prefetcher stays ahead; walking a list<int> touches a new, unpredictable line every element: a cache miss (roughly 100 ns from DRAM, typical) per node. Inserting in the middle of a vector of 10,000 ints memmoves on average 20 KB, which takes about the same time as a handful of cache misses. Bjarne Stroustrup's often-cited benchmark shows vector winning insert/erase-in-the-middle up to around 100k small elements. m12_bench_basics.cpp lets you measure it.

Growth factor and amortisation. Doubling gives amortised O(1) push_back: total copies for n pushes are n + n/2 + n/4 + ... < 2n. A growth factor of 1.5 wastes less memory and lets the allocator reuse freed blocks (1 + 1.5 < 1.5^2 so old blocks can be coalesced for the next one); 2.0 never can. libstdc++ chose 2 for simplicity and speed.

Exception safety during reallocation. vector uses std::move_if_noexcept: if T's move constructor is noexcept, elements are moved; otherwise copied, so that if a copy throws the old buffer is intact (module 04). For trivially copyable T it is a memcpy/memmove.

Allocator and operator new. By default every container allocates through std::allocator<T>, which calls ::operator new, which calls malloc. glibc malloc adds a 16-byte header per block and rounds up to 16 bytes, so a list<int> node (24 bytes of data) costs 32 or 48 bytes. A million map nodes is about 64 MB of allocator traffic and a million small malloc calls. Module 12 shows how std::pmr and arenas remove that.

Red-black tree invariants. Every node is red or black; root is black; red nodes have black children; every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes. This bounds height at 2*log2(n+1), so find is at most about 40 comparisons for a million elements. Insert and erase do O(1) rotations amortised. libstdc++ also keeps a header node with leftmost/rightmost cached, so begin() and rbegin() are O(1).

Hash table layout (libstdc++). A single forward list of all nodes plus a bucket array of pointers into that list ("before-begin" pointers). Iteration walks the single list, so iterating an unordered_map is as fast as a forward_list, independent of bucket count. Each node stores the cached hash when the hash is not fast to recompute (it does for std::string keys), making rehash cheap: no re-hashing of strings, just re-linking. Bucket counts are primes to spread poor hashes.

Hash quality and DoS. std::hash<int> is the identity on libstdc++. Keys that are multiples of the bucket count all collide. For attacker-controlled keys (HTTP headers, JSON fields) use a seeded hash or a different container; a hash-flooding attack turns O(1) into O(n) per lookup.

std::string SSO layout (libstdc++, new ABI). 8-byte pointer, 8-byte size, 16-byte union of either capacity or the inline buffer (15 chars + null). Moving a long string steals the pointer; moving a short string copies the 16 bytes and the pointer is re-pointed into the destination. So a "moved" short string is a full copy and the source stays valid and unchanged.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Reserve when you know the size. Reading 100k rows into a vector without reserve performs about 17 reallocations and moves 200k elements. reserve(row_count) makes it one allocation. The same applies to unordered_map::reserve and std::string::reserve.
  • The iterator-invalidation bug. for (auto& x : v) if (cond) v.push_back(...) is UB on reallocation and may "work" for months. ASan catches it (heap-use-after-free on the old buffer). -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG builds also abort with a clear message; use it in your test builds.
  • map::operator[] in a read path silently fills the map with default entries and holds a write lock where a read lock would do. Use find.
  • Keys that outlive views. A std::unordered_map<std::string_view, V> whose keys point into a request buffer that is reused is a dangling-view bug that shows as corrupted keys.
  • Erasing from unordered_map while iterating is fine with it = m.erase(it); erasing a different element invalidates only that element's iterator. Inserting while iterating may rehash and invalidate everything.
  • Memory never comes back. vector::clear() keeps the capacity; a vector that once held a 100 MB batch holds 100 MB forever. Use v = {} or the swap-with-empty idiom (std::vector<T>().swap(v)) to actually release.
  • 3 AM debugging. A server grows to 8 GB RSS over a week. pmap/heaptrack shows the growth is in std::_Rb_tree_node allocations: a std::map used as a cache with no eviction. Or in _Hashtable buckets: an unordered_map with max_load_factor lowered to 0.1 "for speed" and 10x the memory. Know what the mangled container internals look like in a heap profile.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m06_vector_growth.cpp. Change the element type to a struct with a non-noexcept move constructor that prints, and observe that growth now copies. Done when you see COPY lines at every reallocation and can state the rule.
  2. (easy) Write a program that inserts 1M ints into std::set and into a std::vector that is then sorted. Time both, then time 1M find/binary_search lookups. Done when you have numbers and an explanation involving cache lines.
  3. (medium) Implement struct AccountKey { std::string branch; int number; } as a key for std::unordered_map (write operator== and a std::hash specialisation combining both fields) and for std::map (write operator<). Done when both containers compile and find the same entries.
  4. (medium) Write an LRU cache with std::list<std::pair<K,V>> plus std::unordered_map<K, list::iterator>. Explain why the iterator stored in the map stays valid when you splice the node to the front. Done when get promotes and put evicts correctly in a test.
  5. (hard) Build with -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG and write three deliberate invalidation bugs (vector push during range-for, map iterator used after erase, unordered_map iterator used after rehash). Done when each one aborts with a diagnostic you can explain, and you have run the same binary under ASan to compare the reports.
  6. (hard) Benchmark std::map<int,int> vs a sorted std::vector<std::pair<int,int>> with lower_bound for 1k, 100k and 10M elements, read-only lookups. Done when you can state the crossover point on your machine and explain it with node size and cache misses.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What happens inside std::vector::push_back when size equals capacity? It allocates a new buffer (twice the capacity on libstdc++), moves the existing elements if T's move constructor is noexcept (otherwise copies), constructs the new element, destroys the old elements and frees the old buffer. All iterators, pointers and references into the old buffer are invalidated.

Q: Which containers keep pointers to elements valid across insertions? Node-based ones: list, forward_list, map, set, unordered_map, unordered_set (pointers and references survive rehash; iterators do not). deque keeps pointers valid for push/pop at the ends only. vector and string invalidate on reallocation.

Q: Why is std::vector often faster than std::list even for insertions in the middle? Memory locality. The vector's elements share cache lines and the prefetcher streams them, so shifting thousands of small elements costs less than the cache misses of walking the list to the insertion point. list wins only with very large elements or when iterator stability is required.

Q: What is the load factor and what happens on rehash? size() / bucket_count(). When an insert would push it over max_load_factor() (1.0 by default), the table allocates a larger prime-sized bucket array and relinks every node. Iterators are invalidated; element pointers and references are not, because the nodes do not move. reserve(n) avoids rehashes.

Q: What is wrong with if (map[key] == x) in a read path? operator[] inserts a default-constructed value when the key is missing, so the lookup mutates the map, needs a write lock under concurrency, and leaves junk entries behind. Use find or count.

Q: std::map vs std::unordered_map: when do you pick the tree? When you need ordered iteration or range queries (lower_bound), when keys have no good hash, when worst-case latency matters more than average (no rehash spikes, no hash flooding), or when you need iterators that survive inserts. Otherwise the hash table is usually faster for point lookups.

Q: What is the small-string optimisation? std::string keeps short contents (15 bytes on libstdc++) inside the object instead of the heap, so short strings cost no allocation. Consequence: moving a short string copies bytes rather than stealing a pointer, and sizeof(std::string) is 32 even when empty.

Q: How do you erase elements while iterating a vector? Either it = v.erase(it) in a manual loop (never ++it after erase), or the erase-remove idiom v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred), v.end()), which is O(n) instead of O(n^2).

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• vector is the default; it is contiguous, cache-friendly, and reallocation invalidates everything.
  • reserve when the size is known; clear keeps capacity; shrink_to_fit is only a hint.
  • Node containers (list, map, unordered_map) keep element addresses stable; vector/deque do not.
  • map = red-black tree, O(log n), sorted, range queries; unordered_map = chained hash table, O(1) average, rehash on load factor, no ordering.
  • operator[] inserts; use find for lookups.
  • string has SSO (15 chars); string_view is non-owning and not null-terminated.
  • Every container allocates through operator new/malloc; node containers pay per element.
  • Know the invalidation table; -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG and ASan catch violations.
  • Measure: sorted vector + lower_bound frequently beats map for read-mostly data.

docs.title: 7. STL algorithms, lambdas and iterators
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 06

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Most loops you write in C do one of a few things: find something, count something, copy with a transformation, remove matching elements, sort, sum. <algorithm> and <numeric> already contain these loops, written once, tested for decades, and specialised for every container through iterators. Your job becomes saying what you want (std::count_if(begin, end, is_overdue)) instead of how to loop.

The missing piece in C was a cheap way to pass "the condition" to such a function. Function pointers work but cannot carry state. A lambda is an anonymous function object that can capture local variables, so the condition can be written right where it is used.

Analogy: qsort with a comparator function is the C version. Lambdas and templates make the comparator inline, type-safe, and able to see your local variables, and the compiler inlines the whole thing so it runs as fast as a hand-written loop.

docs.title: 2.1 Iterators
docs.text:
An iterator is a generalised pointer: *it gives the element, ++it advances, it != end tests. Raw pointers are iterators for arrays. Containers expose begin()/end(); end() is one past the last element and must not be dereferenced.

Iterator categories decide which algorithms are available and how fast they are:

Category Can do Examples Input / Output read (or write) once, forward only istream_iterator, back_inserter Forward multi-pass, ++ forward_list, unordered_map Bidirectional plus -- list, map, set Random access plus it + n, it[n], it1 - it2, < in O(1) vector, deque, array, string, pointers

std::sort requires random access (so you cannot std::sort a list; use list::sort). std::lower_bound works on forward iterators but is only O(log n) with random access. std::distance(a, b) is O(1) for random access and O(n) otherwise.

docs.title: 2.2 The algorithms you will use every week
docs.text:
// searching
std::find(b, e, value);  std::find_if(b, e, pred);  std::count_if(b, e, pred);
std::any_of / all_of / none_of(b, e, pred);
std::lower_bound(b, e, value);   // sorted range: first element >= value
std::upper_bound(b, e, value);   // sorted range: first element >  value
std::binary_search(b, e, value); // sorted range: bool
std::min_element / max_element / minmax_element(b, e [, cmp]);

// ordering
std::sort(b, e [, cmp]);          // O(n log n), not stable (introsort)
std::stable_sort(b, e [, cmp]);   // keeps relative order of equal elements, may allocate
std::partial_sort(b, mid, e);     // top-k
std::nth_element(b, nth, e);      // O(n) median / k-th
std::partition / stable_partition(b, e, pred);
std::reverse(b, e);  std::rotate(b, mid, e);  std::unique(b, e);   // unique: on sorted, then erase

// modifying / copying
std::copy / copy_if(b, e, out);  std::transform(b, e, out, f);  std::fill(b, e, v);  std::iota(b, e, start);
std::remove / remove_if(b, e, pred);   // returns new logical end; MUST be followed by erase
std::swap_ranges;  std::move(b, e, out);   // the three-argument std::move moves elements

// numeric
std::accumulate(b, e, init [, op]);    // type of init is the accumulator type
std::reduce (C++17, parallel-friendly), std::inner_product, std::partial_sum, std::adjacent_difference

Erase-remove idiom. std::remove_if cannot change the container's size (it only sees iterators), so it shifts survivors to the front and returns the new logical end. You then call v.erase(new_end, v.end()). C++20 adds std::erase_if(v, pred) to do both.

Comparators must be strict weak orderings. cmp(a, a) must be false; if cmp(a, b) then !cmp(b, a); transitive. Using <= instead of < is UB in std::sort and crashes libstdc++ with out-of-bounds reads. The same comparator must be used for sorting and for lower_bound.

docs.title: 2.3 Lambdas
docs.text:
[captures](parameters) specifiers -> return_type { body }
  • [x] capture by copy (at creation time), [&x] by reference, [=]/[&] capture everything used by copy/reference, [this] the enclosing object pointer, [n = expr] init-capture (C++14; also how you move something into a lambda: [p = std::move(ptr)]).
  • Captured-by-copy variables are const inside the body unless the lambda is mutable.
  • auto parameters make a generic lambda (its operator() is a template).
  • Return type is deduced; write -> T when branches disagree or you return a braced list.
  • A lambda with no captures converts to a plain function pointer, so it can be passed to C APIs (qsort, pthread_create, signal).

A lambda is sugar for a struct with an operator(): the captures are its members, so sizeof(lambda) equals the size of its captures (1 for none). The compiler sees the exact type, so calls through a template parameter are inlined.

docs.title: 2.4 std::function
docs.text: A type-erased wrapper that can hold any callable with a given signature: lambda, function pointer, functor, std::bind result. Use it when you must store heterogeneous callables (a handler table, a callback member). Costs: 32 bytes on libstdc++, a heap allocation if the callable does not fit the internal 16-byte buffer, and one indirect call per invocation (no inlining). Do not use it as a parameter type when a template parameter would do.

docs.title: 2.5 Projections and ranges (preview)
docs.text: C++20 ranges (std::ranges::sort(v, {}, &Txn::amount)) remove the begin()/end() boilerplate and add projections and lazy views. Not available in C++17; know they exist for interviews.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m07_algorithms_lambdas.cpp runs through the daily toolkit on a vector of transactions:

std::sort(txns.begin(), txns.end(), [](const Txn& a, const Txn& b) {
    if (a.priority != b.priority) return a.priority > b.priority;   // strict: never true for equal elements
    return a.account < b.account;
});

txns.erase(std::remove_if(txns.begin(), txns.end(),
                          [](const Txn& t) { return t.paise == 0; }),
           txns.end());                                              // erase-remove

long long total = std::accumulate(txns.begin(), txns.end(), 0LL,    // 0LL, not 0: accumulator type
                                  [](long long acc, const Txn& t) { return acc + t.paise; });

std::transform(txns.begin(), txns.end(), std::back_inserter(labels),
               [](const Txn& t) { return t.account + "/" + std::to_string(t.paise); });

auto lb = std::lower_bound(sorted.begin(), sorted.end(), 20);       // first >= 20
auto ub = std::upper_bound(sorted.begin(), sorted.end(), 20);       // first >  20
auto mid = std::partition(txns.begin(), txns.end(), [](const Txn& t) { return t.paise > 0; });

code/m07_lambdas_std_function.cpp shows captures and the cost model:

auto by_value = [threshold](int x) { return x > threshold; };   // copies threshold now
auto by_ref   = [&hits](int x) { if (x > 5) ++hits; };          // hits must outlive the lambda
auto counter  = [n = 0]() mutable { return ++n; };              // init-capture + mutable: owns state
auto generic  = [](auto a, auto b) { return a + b; };           // template operator()

template <class F> void apply_template(const std::vector<int>& v, F f);                        // inlined
void apply_function(const std::vector<int>& v, const std::function<void(int)>& f);             // indirect

std::cout << sizeof(by_value) << ' ' << sizeof(by_ref) << ' ' << sizeof(empty) << ' '
          << sizeof(std::function<void(int)>);     // 4 8 1 32 on x86-64 libstdc++

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Templates make algorithms free. std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), cmp) instantiates a sort specialised for vector<Txn>::iterator and the exact lambda type. The comparator call is a direct call to a known function and is inlined; the result is the same machine code as a hand-written quicksort for that struct. qsort in C calls through a function pointer per comparison and cannot inline, which is why std::sort typically beats qsort by 2x or more on small element types.

std::sort is introsort. Quicksort with median-of-three pivots, switching to heapsort if recursion depth exceeds 2*log2(n) (guaranteeing O(n log n) worst case), and finishing with insertion sort on partitions of 16 or fewer elements. std::stable_sort is a merge sort that tries to allocate a temporary buffer (falls back to an in-place O(n log^2 n) version if allocation fails).

Lambda object layout. [threshold](int x) {...} compiles to struct __lambda { int threshold; bool operator()(int x) const { ... } };. [&hits] stores int* hits. [this] stores a pointer. Capturing a large object by value copies it into the lambda, so a lambda capturing a std::vector by value is as expensive to copy as the vector. Each lambda expression has a unique, unnameable type, so two lambdas with identical text are different types.

Generic lambdas are templates: [](auto a, auto b) has template <class T, class U> auto operator()(T a, U b) const. Each distinct argument type pair instantiates a new operator().

std::function internals (libstdc++). 32 bytes: a 16-byte local storage union, a pointer to the invoker function, and a pointer to the manager function (copy/destroy/type query). Callables up to 16 bytes that are nothrow-move-constructible are stored inline; larger ones are heap-allocated. A call does: load invoker pointer, indirect call, which then calls the stored callable. Branch prediction usually handles it, but there is no inlining across the boundary and no vectorisation of the surrounding loop.

Dangling captures. A lambda capturing by reference stores a pointer; if it is called after the referenced variable's scope ends, it dereferences freed stack. [=] can also dangle: capturing this by copy copies the pointer, not the object. In asynchronous code (threads, callbacks, timers) default to capturing by value or by shared_ptr/weak_ptr, and capture by reference only when the lambda is consumed before the enclosing scope ends (e.g. passed to std::sort).

back_inserter and output iterators. std::back_inserter(v) returns an iterator whose *it = x calls v.push_back(x). Algorithms can grow the destination this way, at the usual amortised cost. For known sizes, v.resize(n) first and write with a normal iterator avoids the reallocation checks.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Replace raw loops in review. A for loop that computes a sum, finds an element, or filters is a candidate for an algorithm. The algorithm version states intent, has no off-by-one errors, and is easier to make parallel later.
  • Sorting with a bad comparator is a classic latent crash: works for years on small inputs, then a particular dataset makes std::sort read past the end. Rules: use <, never <=; compare all fields in a fixed order; std::tie(a.x, a.y) < std::tie(b.x, b.y) is the idiom for lexicographic comparison.
  • std::function in a request handler table is fine (one indirect call per request). In a per-byte parser loop it is not; use a template parameter or a plain function pointer.
  • Callbacks that outlive their captures are the most common crash in asynchronous C++ servers: a timer lambda captures [&conn] and fires after the connection is closed. Capture a weak_ptr and lock() it, or a shared_ptr when the callback must keep the object alive.
  • Ranges of std::string_view and std::sort. Sorting a vector of views is cheap (16 bytes per element, no string copies); sorting a vector of std::string moves 32-byte objects and may be memory-bound. Choose the element type with the algorithm's data movement in mind.
  • 3 AM debugging. A stack trace inside std::__introsort_loop or std::__unguarded_partition with a segfault means a non-strict comparator or a comparator that reads uninitialised fields. Check the comparator before suspecting the library.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Rewrite three raw loops from your own code (sum, find-first, remove-matching) using accumulate, find_if, and erase-remove. Done when the outputs are identical and the loops are gone.
  2. (easy) Write a comparator with <= instead of < and sort 1000 equal elements under -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG or ASan. Done when you have seen the failure and can explain strict weak ordering.
  3. (medium) Implement top_k(const std::vector<Txn>&, size_t k) three ways: full sort, partial_sort, and nth_element + sort of the prefix. Time them for n = 1M, k = 10. Done when you can rank them and explain why.
  4. (medium) Write a std::vector<std::function<void(Event&)>> handler registry and a template dispatch(Handlers&, Event&) alternative using a std::tuple of lambdas. Measure the per-call cost of each with 100M dispatches. Done when you have numbers and a recommendation for when each fits.
  5. (hard) Implement a word-frequency counter: read a file into a string, split into std::string_view tokens without copying, count with unordered_map<string_view, int>, then produce the top 20 using partial_sort on a vector of pairs. Done when it runs on a 100 MB file in under a few seconds and makes no per-word std::string allocations (verify with ltrace -e malloc or a counting allocator).
  6. (hard) Write a generic template <class It, class Pred> It stable_partition_copy_free(It, It, Pred) that works on bidirectional iterators, and use static_assert with std::iterator_traits to reject forward iterators. Done when list works, forward_list fails to compile with your message, and vector works.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the erase-remove idiom and why is it needed? std::remove_if only sees iterators, so it cannot resize the container; it moves the survivors to the front and returns the new logical end. container.erase(new_end, end()) then drops the tail. Forgetting the erase leaves stale elements at the back.

Q: What are the requirements on a comparator passed to std::sort? A strict weak ordering: irreflexive (cmp(a,a) is false), asymmetric, transitive, and with transitive equivalence. Using <= violates irreflexivity and is undefined behaviour; libstdc++ can read out of bounds and crash.

Q: How does a lambda differ from a function pointer? A lambda is an object of a unique class with an operator(); it can capture state and the compiler knows its exact type, so calls through templates inline. A function pointer carries no state and is called indirectly. A capture-less lambda converts to a function pointer.

Q: When should you use std::function? When you need to store or pass callables of different types through one non-template interface: callback members, handler tables, plugin hooks. Avoid it as a parameter type in hot or generic code; a template parameter is zero-cost.

Q: What does std::function cost? 32 bytes on libstdc++; a heap allocation if the stored callable exceeds the 16-byte inline buffer; an indirect call per invocation that cannot be inlined. Copying it copies (or clones) the stored callable.

Q: Why can you not std::sort a std::list? std::sort needs random-access iterators (it + n, it1 - it2). std::list iterators are only bidirectional. Use list::sort(), a merge sort that relinks nodes.

Q: What is the difference between std::lower_bound and std::find on a sorted vector? Both find an element, but lower_bound is a binary search, O(log n), and requires sorted input, returning the first element not less than the value. find is a linear scan, O(n), works on any range, and returns the first equal element.

Q: What is wrong with auto f = [&x]{...}; returned from a function? x is a local; the lambda stores a pointer to it, and after the function returns calling the lambda dereferences a dead stack slot (undefined behaviour). Capture by value, or by a smart pointer when the lambda will run asynchronously.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Iterators generalise pointers; categories (input, forward, bidirectional, random access) decide which algorithms work and how fast.
  • Know the daily set: find_if, count_if, any_of, sort, stable_sort, lower_bound, partition, transform, accumulate, remove_if + erase.
  • Comparators must be strict weak orderings; use <, never <=; std::tie for lexicographic.
  • A lambda is a struct with operator(); its size is its captures; capture-less lambdas convert to function pointers.
  • [x] copies now, [&x] stores a pointer, [n = expr] init-captures (and moves), mutable lets by-copy captures change.
  • Template parameters inline the callable; std::function type-erases with an indirect call and possible heap allocation.
  • Reference captures in asynchronous code dangle; capture by value or shared_ptr/weak_ptr.
  • std::sort is introsort; std::stable_sort is merge sort with a buffer.
  • accumulate's initial value sets the accumulator type: write 0LL or 0.0.

docs.title: 8. Templates and generic programming
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 06, 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
In C, a generic container means void* and casts (losing type safety), or a macro that stamps out code per type (losing debuggability). A template is a recipe the compiler follows to generate a real, fully typed function or class for each set of types you use it with. std::vector<int> and std::vector<std::string> are two different classes, both generated from one recipe, each as fast as if you had written it by hand for that type.

The cost is that templates are compiled where they are used, not where they are written, so the recipe must be visible (in a header) and errors show up at the use site, often with long messages. Learning to read those messages, and to constrain templates so the messages get shorter, is most of the skill.

Analogy: a template is a cookie cutter. vector<int> and vector<string> are two different cookies from the same cutter. The cutter itself is not a cookie; you cannot eat std::vector.

docs.title: 2.1 Function templates and deduction
docs.text:
template <class T>
T max_of(T a, T b) { return (b < a) ? a : b; }

max_of(3, 7);          // T deduced as int
max_of(2.5, 1.5);      // T deduced as double
max_of(3, 2.5);        // error: conflicting deductions (int vs double)
max_of<double>(3, 2.5);// explicit: fine

Deduction happens from the arguments only (never from the return type). Deduction does not perform conversions except trivial ones (array-to-pointer, adding const), which is why 3 and 2.5 conflict.

docs.title: 2.2 Class templates and non-type parameters
docs.text:
template <class T, std::size_t N>
class RingBuffer { T buf_[N]{}; /* ... */ };

RingBuffer<int, 4> a;    // a distinct type from RingBuffer<int, 8>

Non-type parameters (integers, pointers, enums; also auto in C++17) make the value part of the type, so the compiler can unroll and allocate statically. std::array<T, N> is the canonical example.

C++17 class template argument deduction (CTAD) lets you write std::pair p{1, 2.5} and std::lock_guard g(mutex) without the angle brackets (module 13).

docs.title: 2.3 Instantiation and the header-only rule
docs.text:
A template is not compiled until it is instantiated with concrete arguments. At that point the compiler needs the full definition, in the same translation unit. Hence templates live in headers. Each translation unit that uses vector<int>::push_back generates its own copy; the linker merges identical copies (they are "weak"/COMDAT symbols, module 14 on the ODR). Only the member functions actually used are instantiated, so std::vector<T> for a T without operator< compiles fine as long as you never call sort on it.

Explicit instantiation (template class RingBuffer<int, 4>; in one .cpp, with extern template in the header) can move the code into one object file to speed up builds.

docs.title: 2.4 Two-phase lookup
docs.text:
A template is checked twice. At definition the compiler parses it and resolves every name that does not depend on a template parameter. At instantiation it resolves the dependent names (item.size() where item's type depends on T). Consequences:

  • Typos in non-dependent code are caught even if the template is never used.
  • Calling a member of a dependent base class requires this->member or Base<T>::member, because the compiler cannot look into a base whose definition depends on T during phase one.
  • typename is required before dependent type names: typename Container::value_type x;.

docs.title: 2.5 Specialisation
docs.text:
Full specialisation replaces the template for one exact set of arguments:

template <> const char* max_of<const char*>(const char* a, const char* b) { return std::strcmp(b, a) < 0 ? a : b; }

Partial specialisation (class templates only) replaces it for a pattern:

template <class T> struct Describe     { static const char* kind() { return "value"; } };
template <class T> struct Describe<T*> { static const char* kind() { return "pointer"; } };

Function templates cannot be partially specialised; overload them instead.

docs.title: 2.6 Variadic templates and fold expressions
docs.text:
template <class... Ts>
void log_line(const Ts&... parts) { (std::cout << ... << parts) << '\n'; }   // C++17 fold

template <class... Ts> auto sum_all(Ts... xs) { return (xs + ... + 0); }

Ts... is a parameter pack; sizeof...(Ts) counts it; parts... expands it. Before C++17 you peeled one argument per recursive call with a base-case overload; a fold expression applies an operator across the pack in one line. std::make_unique, emplace_back, std::tuple and std::variant are all variadic templates.

docs.title: 2.7 SFINAE, if constexpr, type traits
docs.text:
Type traits (<type_traits>) are compile-time predicates and transformers: std::is_integral_v<T>, std::is_same_v<A, B>, std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>, std::remove_reference_t<T>, std::decay_t<T>, std::conditional_t<cond, A, B>.

SFINAE ("Substitution Failure Is Not An Error"): when substituting deduced types into a function template's signature produces an invalid type, that candidate is silently dropped from overload resolution instead of causing an error. std::enable_if_t<cond, int> = 0 as a dummy template parameter is the classic way to enable a template only for some types; std::void_t<decltype(expr)> detects whether an expression is valid.

if constexpr (C++17) is the readable replacement for most SFINAE tricks inside a function body: the branch not taken is discarded and never instantiated, so it may contain code that would not compile for the current T.

Concepts (C++20 preview). template <std::integral T> T twice(T x); states the requirement directly, gives readable errors ("constraints not satisfied: T does not satisfy integral"), and replaces most enable_if. Know the syntax for interviews; use enable_if or static_assert in C++17.

docs.title: 2.8 Compile-time cost
docs.text: Every distinct instantiation is parsed, checked and code-generated. Heavy template libraries (Boost.Spirit, Eigen) make a .cpp take seconds to minutes. Mitigations: include less, use explicit instantiation for hot templates, keep template bodies small and delegate to non-template helpers, use -ftime-report or Clang's -ftime-trace to find the cost.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m08_templates_basics.cpp covers deduction, specialisation, two-phase lookup, and SFINAE:

template <class T> T max_of(T a, T b) { return (b < a) ? a : b; }
template <> const char* max_of<const char*>(const char* a, const char* b) { return (std::strcmp(b, a) < 0) ? a : b; }

template <class T, std::size_t N> class RingBuffer { /* push/pop; T buf_[N]{}; */ };
static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<RingBuffer<int, 4>>);   // no owned resources: memcpy-able

template <class Container>
std::size_t total_size(const Container& c) {
    std::size_t n = 0;
    for (const auto& item : c) n += item.size();   // dependent: checked only at instantiation
    return n;
}

// SFINAE: drops out when T has no .c_str(); the long long overload is then the only candidate
template <class T, class = std::void_t<decltype(std::declval<const T&>().c_str())>>
std::size_t text_len(const T& t) { return std::strlen(t.c_str()); }
std::size_t text_len(long long v) { return std::to_string(v).size(); }

code/m08_variadic_if_constexpr.cpp covers packs, folds, if constexpr, traits and enable_if:

template <class T>
std::string to_text(const T& v) {
    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, std::string>)   return v;
    else if constexpr (std::is_arithmetic_v<T>)     return std::to_string(v);
    else if constexpr (std::is_pointer_v<T>)        return v ? to_text(*v) : std::string("null");
    else static_assert(sizeof(T) == 0, "to_text: unsupported type");   // only fires if reached
}
