template <class T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_integral_v<T>, int> = 0>
T twice(T x) { return 2 * x; }      // twice(1.5) -> "no matching function"

Try to_text(std::vector<int>{}) and read the error: it names the static_assert message and the instantiation chain. Then try twice(1.5) and read that error: "no matching function... candidate template ignored: requirement ... was not satisfied" (wording varies by GCC version).

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Instantiation produces real functions with mangled names. max_of<int> becomes _Z6max_ofIiET_S0_S0_. nm -C shows int max_of<int>(int, int). Each instantiation is a weak symbol placed in its own COMDAT section (.text._Z6max_ofIiET_S0_S0_); the linker keeps one copy and discards the rest. This is why identical template code in 50 object files does not bloat the final binary, but does bloat compile time and object file size.

Why templates cannot be "compiled once" like C functions. The compiler needs the concrete type to know the size of T, which operator< to call, whether the copy is a memcpy or a constructor call. Without the type there is no code to emit. C++20 modules reduce parsing cost by storing a pre-parsed form, but instantiation still happens per use.

Template code bloat is real and bounded. std::vector<int*> and std::vector<char*> generate separate code even though the machine code would be identical. libstdc++ mitigates in places by having vector<T*> forward to a vector<void*> implementation (the "hoisting" technique). In your own templates, move type-independent work into a non-template base or helper and keep the template layer thin.

Dependent names and this->. In template <class T> struct Derived : Base<T> { void f() { helper(); } }, helper is looked up in phase one, cannot be found (Base is not examined because a specialisation might remove it), and the compiler assumes a free function; the error says "there are no arguments to 'helper' that depend on a template parameter". Writing this->helper() defers lookup to phase two.

SFINAE only applies in the immediate context. A substitution failure inside the function body is a hard error, not a dropped candidate. That is why enable_if goes in the signature (return type or a template parameter), and why if constexpr inside the body is a different tool: it discards a branch, it does not remove an overload.

if constexpr and discarded statements. Inside a template, a discarded branch is not instantiated, so it may reference members T does not have. Outside a template (or in a non-dependent branch), both branches are still checked, and static_assert(false) fires unconditionally; hence the sizeof(T) == 0 idiom to make it dependent.

Type traits are implemented with specialisation and compiler intrinsics. std::is_pointer<T> is false_type with a partial specialisation is_pointer<T*> : true_type. Traits like is_trivially_copyable need information only the compiler has and map to builtins (__is_trivially_copyable(T)).

Templates vs virtual functions. Both achieve polymorphism. Templates resolve at compile time: zero call overhead, inlining, but a separate instantiation per type and a header-only interface. Virtual functions resolve at run time: one implementation, binary-compatible interface, an indirect call. Module 09 covers the second; use templates when the type set is known at compile time and performance matters, virtuals when the set is open (plugins) or when compile time and binary boundaries matter.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Error messages. Read from the top: the first "required from here" line is your code; everything below is the instantiation stack. static_assert with a message at the top of a template turns a 200-line error into one line. Clang's errors are shorter than GCC's; using both compilers in CI helps.
  • Header hygiene. A template in a header that includes <regex> or <iostream> adds seconds to every TU that includes it. Keep template headers minimal, forward-declare where you can, and move non-template code into .cpp files.
  • Explicit instantiation for build speed. If Serializer<Message> is used in 80 files, declare extern template class Serializer<Message>; in the header and template class Serializer<Message>; in one .cpp. The 80 files now only need the declaration.
  • Templates in library ABIs. A template in a public header is compiled into every client; changing its body is an ABI break for them. Libraries that promise ABI stability keep templates thin and forward to non-template, exported functions.
  • When not to template. If only one type is ever used, a template is slower to compile, harder to debug (template frames in gdb are long), and gives nothing. Write the concrete type. Generalise when the second type arrives.
  • 3 AM debugging. gdb shows frames like std::__detail::_Map_base<...>::operator[] 400 characters wide. set print demangle on, set print asm-demangle on, and frame function <short name> help; so does building with -Og -g for a debuggable optimised binary.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Write template <class T> void print_all(const std::vector<T>&) and call it with int, std::string, and a type without operator<<. Read the full error for the last and find the "required from here" line. Done when you can point at your own line in the error.
  2. (easy) Add static_assert(std::is_arithmetic_v<T>, "T must be a number") at the top of max_of and re-run the failing call. Done when the error is one readable line.
  3. (medium) Implement template <class T, std::size_t N> class StaticVector (fixed capacity, no heap, push_back/pop_back/operator[]/size) with placement new into an aligned byte array and correct destruction of only the live elements. Done when it holds std::strings without leaking under Valgrind and sizeof(StaticVector<int, 8>) is 8*4 + sizeof(size_t).
  4. (medium) Write a template <class T> constexpr bool has_size_v trait using std::void_t that is true for std::vector and std::string and false for int. Then write the same with if constexpr inside a function. Done when both pass identical static_asserts.
  5. (hard) Write a variadic template <class... Fs> auto compose(Fs... fs) that returns a lambda applying the functions right-to-left. Done when compose(f, g, h)(x) == f(g(h(x))) for lambdas of mixed types, and compose() returns identity.
  6. (hard) Compile a file that uses std::map<std::string, std::vector<int>> with g++ -std=c++17 -ftime-report and read the time per phase. Then add extern template for a template of your own used across five .cpp files and measure total build time before/after. Done when you can quantify the saving.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why do templates have to be in header files? The compiler generates code for a template only when it sees a use with concrete types, and it needs the full definition at that point in the same translation unit. Splitting declaration and definition across files works only with explicit instantiation of every type you will ever use.

Q: What is two-phase lookup? Templates are checked at definition for everything not depending on a template parameter, and at instantiation for dependent names. It catches typos early, and it is why you write this->member for members of a dependent base class and typename before dependent type names.

Q: What is SFINAE? If substituting deduced template arguments into a function template's signature produces an invalid type or expression, the template is removed from overload resolution instead of causing a compile error. It enables enable_if-style constraints and detection idioms. C++20 concepts replace most uses with clearer syntax.

Q: Difference between if constexpr and a normal if inside a template? A normal if compiles both branches for every instantiation; if constexpr discards the untaken branch at compile time so it can contain code invalid for the current type. The condition must be a constant expression.

Q: What is a fold expression? A C++17 way to apply a binary operator across a parameter pack: (xs + ... + 0) or (std::cout << ... << args). It replaces recursive variadic templates with a base-case overload.

Q: How do templates affect binary size and compile time? Each distinct instantiation is compiled separately in every translation unit that uses it; the linker deduplicates identical weak symbols, so binary size grows with the number of distinct instantiations while compile time grows with the number of uses. Explicit instantiation and thin template layers over non-template code mitigate both.

Q: Templates or virtual functions for polymorphism? Templates when the set of types is known at compile time and you want inlining and zero call overhead; virtual functions when the set is open (plugins, runtime configuration) or when you need a stable binary interface. Templates trade compile time and header exposure for speed.

Q: Can you partially specialise a function template? No. Only class templates support partial specialisation. For functions, write overloads; the more specialised overload wins by the normal rules.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A template is a recipe; each set of arguments instantiates a separate, fully typed function or class.
  • Deduction works from arguments only and does not convert; conflicting deductions are errors.
  • Templates live in headers because instantiation needs the definition; the linker merges duplicates.
  • Two-phase lookup: non-dependent names checked at definition, dependent at instantiation; this-> and typename for dependent names.
  • Full specialisation for exact types; partial specialisation for patterns (classes only).
  • Variadic templates + fold expressions handle any number of arguments.
  • SFINAE removes candidates in the signature; if constexpr discards branches in the body; static_assert gives readable errors; C++20 concepts replace enable_if.
  • Type traits answer compile-time questions about types.
  • Compile time and code size scale with instantiations; keep templates thin and use explicit instantiation for hot ones.

docs.title: 9. OOP: inheritance, virtual functions and what a vtable really is
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
In your C server you probably have a struct of function pointers somewhere: struct handler_ops { int (*open)(void*); int (*read)(void*, ...); void (*close)(void*); }, and every "driver" fills in its own functions. That is object-oriented programming, done by hand. C++ virtual functions are the same idea with the compiler maintaining the table of function pointers for you, guaranteeing it is filled in correctly, and giving you a syntax (obj->read()) that hides the indirection.

Inheritance lets one class extend another. Virtual functions let the caller work with the base type while the derived type's code runs. That combination is runtime polymorphism: one interface, many implementations, chosen when the program runs. The cost is one pointer per object and one indirect call per virtual invocation, and the benefit is that new implementations can be added without touching the callers.

Analogy: a power socket (the base-class interface). Any appliance (derived class) that fits the socket works, and the wall does not care which appliance it is.

docs.title: 2.1 Inheritance basics
docs.text:
class Shape {                       // base
public:
    virtual ~Shape() = default;
    virtual double area() const = 0;          // pure virtual: no body here, Shape is abstract
    virtual const char* name() const { return "shape"; }   // virtual with a default
    int id = 0;
};
class Circle final : public Shape { // derived; 'final' forbids further derivation
public:
    explicit Circle(double r) : r_(r) {}
    double area() const override { return 3.14159 * r_ * r_; }   // override: compiler checks it really overrides
    const char* name() const override { return "circle"; }
private:
    double r_;
};
  • public inheritance means "is-a": a Circle can be used wherever a Shape& or Shape* is expected.
  • A pure virtual function (= 0) makes the class abstract: it cannot be instantiated, only derived from. A class with only pure virtuals and a virtual destructor is an interface.
  • override turns a silent mistake (wrong signature, so you hid instead of overrode) into a compile error. Always write it.
  • final on a class or function stops further overriding and lets the compiler devirtualise calls.

docs.title: 2.2 Dispatch: static vs dynamic
docs.text:
Circle c(1.0);
Shape& s = c;
s.area();         // dynamic dispatch: Circle::area, chosen at run time via vtable
s.Shape::name();  // qualified call: static, skips the vtable
c.area();         // the compiler knows c is a Circle (final): direct call, inlinable

The static type is what the compiler sees (Shape&); the dynamic type is what the object actually is (Circle). Non-virtual functions dispatch on the static type; virtual functions on the dynamic type. Dispatch only happens through a reference or pointer; a Shape object by value is just a Shape.

docs.title: 2.3 Virtual destructors
docs.text:
Shape* p = new Circle(1.0);
delete p;      // calls ~Circle only if ~Shape is virtual. Otherwise: undefined behaviour (usually a leak of r_ ... and worse)

Rule: a class with any virtual function needs a virtual destructor (or a protected non-virtual one if deletion through the base is forbidden). std::unique_ptr<Shape> and std::shared_ptr<Shape> call delete on a Shape*, so the same rule applies when they hold derived objects (shared_ptr is the exception: it captures the deleter at construction, so it works even without a virtual destructor, but do not rely on that).

docs.title: 2.4 Object slicing
docs.text:
void f(Shape s);     // takes by VALUE (does not even compile for an abstract Shape)
void g(Animal a);    // compiles if Animal is concrete
g(dog);              // copies ONLY the Animal part: the Dog's data is cut off, and a.sound() is Animal's

Passing or assigning a derived object by value into a base type copies only the base subobject. The copy's vptr is the base's. Always pass polymorphic objects by reference or pointer, and consider deleting the copy operations of base classes to make slicing impossible.

docs.title: 2.5 Composition over inheritance
docs.text:
Inheritance is the tightest coupling in the language: the derived class depends on the base's implementation details and cannot be changed independently. Prefer composition: Server has a std::unique_ptr<Logger> injected from outside, rather than is a ConsoleLogger. Inherit only from abstract interfaces, and only when you need runtime substitution.

The Non-Virtual Interface (NVI) idiom: public non-virtual run() enforces the protocol (lock, log, time) and calls a private virtual do_run() that derived classes implement. Callers cannot bypass the protocol; implementers cannot break it.

docs.title: 2.6 When NOT to use virtual
docs.text:
• The set of types is closed and known at compile time: use templates (module 08) or std::variant
    • std::visit (module 10). Zero indirection, inlinable.
  • The call is on a hot inner loop with a tiny body (get_x()): the indirect call and lost inlining cost more than the work. Hoist the dispatch out of the loop ("one virtual call per batch").
  • Value types (Point, Money, Timestamp): no virtual functions, no inheritance. They should be trivially copyable.
  • You are tempted to inherit for code reuse only: a free function or a member object is simpler.

docs.title: 2.7 Multiple inheritance and RTTI (briefly)
docs.text: Multiple inheritance is used mainly to implement several interfaces. Avoid inheriting from more than one class with data. dynamic_cast<Derived*>(base_ptr) checks the dynamic type at run time (null if wrong) using RTTI; typeid(*p) names it. Frequent dynamic_cast means the design is missing a virtual function. -fno-rtti removes both and shrinks binaries; dynamic_cast then fails to compile.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m09_vtable_demo.cpp makes the hidden machinery visible:

struct Plain { int a; int b; };                 // sizeof 8: no vptr

class Shape { public: virtual ~Shape() = default; virtual double area() const = 0;
              virtual const char* name() const { return "shape"; } int id = 0; };   // sizeof 16: vptr + int + padding

std::uintptr_t read_vptr(const Shape& s) {      // the vptr is the first 8 bytes on the Itanium ABI
    std::uintptr_t v = 0;
    std::memcpy(&v, &s, sizeof v);              // memcpy: no strict-aliasing violation
    return v;
}
// c1 and c2 (both Circle) print the same vptr; sq (Square) prints a different one.

std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> shapes;     // dynamic dispatch through the base pointer
for (const auto& s : shapes) std::cout << s->name() << " area=" << s->area() << '\n';

Shape& ref = c1;
ref.name();          // "circle" via vtable
ref.Shape::name();   // "shape": qualified call, no vtable

void slice(Animal a);          // by value: prints "..." for a Dog
void no_slice(const Animal& a);// by reference: prints "woof"

Run g++ -std=c++17 -fdump-lang-class m09_vtable_demo.cpp and open the generated .class file: it prints every class layout and vtable (Vtable for Circle, slots with offsets).

code/m09_interfaces_composition.cpp shows a pure interface, injection, a template alternative and NVI:

class Logger { public: virtual ~Logger() = default; virtual void log(const std::string&) = 0; };

class Server {
public:
    explicit Server(std::unique_ptr<Logger> logger) : logger_(std::move(logger)) {}   // injected, owned
    void handle(const std::string& req) { logger_->log("handled " + req); ++handled_; }
private:
    std::unique_ptr<Logger> logger_;
    int handled_ = 0;
};

template <class Codec> std::string encode_with(const Codec& codec, const std::string& payload) {
    return codec.encode(payload);      // static polymorphism: no vtable, inlinable
}

class Task {                            // NVI
public:
    virtual ~Task() = default;
    void run() { std::cout << "begin\n"; do_run(); std::cout << "end\n"; }
private:
    virtual void do_run() = 0;
};

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
The vtable. For every class with at least one virtual function the compiler emits one read-only table per class (in .rodata, symbol _ZTV5Shape = "vtable for Shape"). On the Itanium ABI it looks like:

_ZTV6Circle:
    [-2]  offset-to-top        (0 for the primary base; non-zero for secondary bases in multiple inheritance)
    [-1]  pointer to typeinfo  (_ZTI6Circle, used by dynamic_cast and typeid)
    [ 0]  Circle::~Circle()           (complete object destructor)
    [ 1]  Circle::~Circle()           (deleting destructor: runs ~Circle then operator delete)
    [ 2]  Circle::area()
    [ 3]  Circle::name()

Slots are in declaration order of the base's virtual functions; a derived class's new virtuals are appended. Square does not override name(), so _ZTV6Square[3] holds the address of Shape::name. The two destructor entries exist because delete p needs a version that also frees memory, while a stack object or a base subobject needs one that does not.

The vptr. Each polymorphic object starts (on this ABI) with a hidden pointer to its class's vtable, pointing at slot 0 (so negative indices reach the typeinfo). Hence sizeof(Shape) == 16: 8 for the vptr, 4 for id, 4 padding. The constructor writes the vptr: Shape::Shape stores &_ZTV5Shape[2], then Circle::Circle overwrites it with &_ZTV6Circle[2]. That is why a virtual call inside Shape's constructor goes to Shape's version: at that moment the vptr still points at Shape's table.

A virtual call compiles to three instructions:

mov   rax, [rdi]          ; load vptr from the object (rdi = this)
call  [rax + 16]          ; load slot 2 (area) and call it  (8 bytes per slot)

versus one call for a non-virtual function. The real cost is not the two loads (the vtable is hot in L1); it is that the compiler cannot inline across the indirect call, and the branch predictor must guess the target. Modern CPUs predict a stable target well; a loop alternating between two implementations mispredicts. Devirtualisation: when the compiler can prove the dynamic type (final class, object constructed in the same function, -fdevirtualize with LTO, or speculative devirtualisation guarded by a vptr comparison), it emits a direct call and can inline.

Why pointer adjustments happen in multiple inheritance. With class D : public A, public B, a B* to a D points into the middle of the object (at the B subobject, which has its own vptr). Converting D* to B* adds an offset; a virtual function of B overridden in D is reached via a "thunk" that subtracts the offset before jumping to D's code. The offset-to-top slot lets dynamic_cast<void*> find the start of the complete object.

Virtual destructors in the vtable are why delete base_ptr works. delete p with a virtual destructor calls slot 1 (the deleting destructor), which knows the complete object's size and runs operator delete with the right pointer. Without virtual, delete p calls Shape::~Shape directly and operator delete(p) with the size of Shape; the derived members are never destroyed and the allocator may be told the wrong size (undefined behaviour, often silently "works").

Pure virtual slots hold __cxa_pure_virtual, which prints "pure virtual method called" and aborts. You see that message when a destructor or constructor calls a pure virtual function, or when an object is used after its destructor has started.

RTTI uses the typeinfo pointer at slot -1: typeid(*p) loads it; dynamic_cast walks the typeinfo graph (__dynamic_cast in libstdc++), which for deep hierarchies costs tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, far more than a virtual call.

Virtual functions and std::function/std::variant. All three are runtime dispatch. Virtual: one pointer per object, open set of types, binary-compatible. std::variant + visit: closed set of types known at compile time, no heap, no vptr, a jump table over the index. std::function: dispatch on the callable rather than the object. Pick by whether the type set is open or closed.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Your handler_ops struct is a hand-rolled vtable. The difference in C++ is that the compiler checks every slot is filled (a missing override on an abstract class is a compile error), that the right destructor runs, and that nobody mutates the table at run time.
  • Interfaces at module boundaries, templates inside. A pure virtual Storage interface lets you swap a real Berkeley DB backend for an in-memory fake in tests; inside the backend, use templates and values for speed. One virtual call per request is noise next to a syscall.
  • ABI stability. Adding a virtual function to a class in a shared library changes the vtable layout; every client compiled against the old header calls the wrong slot. Append new virtuals at the end and only in major versions, or keep the hierarchy out of the public ABI (pimpl).
  • Never call virtuals from constructors/destructors expecting the override. During construction the object's dynamic type is the class whose constructor is running.
  • Object slicing in containers. std::vector<Shape> cannot even hold derived objects (and does not compile for an abstract Shape); std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> is the pattern. A std::vector<Animal> filled from Dogs compiles and silently slices.
  • 3 AM debugging. "pure virtual method called / terminate called without an active exception": a virtual call during construction/destruction, or a use-after-free where the vptr was overwritten by the allocator's freelist pointer. In gdb, p *obj shows _vptr.Shape = 0x...; info symbol on that value tells you which class's vtable it is (or that it is garbage). A vptr that points into the heap rather than .rodata means the object is dead.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m09_vtable_demo.cpp with -fdump-lang-class and read the Vtable for Circle section. Done when you can name what is in each slot and explain why there are two destructor entries.
  2. (easy) Remove virtual from ~Shape and compile with -Wall -Wextra. Find the -Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor warning (make delete explicit if needed). Done when you can explain what would go wrong at run time.
  3. (medium) Rewrite a C-style struct ops { int (*open)(void*); ... } plus void* ctx pair as an abstract Device interface with two implementations. Done when the C++ version has no void* and the test can inject a fake.
  4. (medium) Write a tight loop calling shape->area() 100M times on a vector containing (a) only Circles, (b) alternating Circle/Square. Time both with -O2. Then replace the vector of pointers with a std::variant<Circle, Square> and std::visit. Done when you can report three numbers and explain the branch predictor's role.
  5. (hard) Implement a tiny plugin system: extern "C" Plugin* create() in a .so returning a class derived from an abstract Plugin, loaded with dlopen/dlsym. Done when the main program calls virtual functions on an object whose class it never saw at compile time, and you can explain why extern "C" is needed only for create.
  6. (hard) Using g++ -O2 -S, compile a function that calls a virtual function on a final class object and on a non-final one. Done when you can show the direct call in the first and the mov rax,[rdi]; call [rax+N] sequence in the second.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How are virtual functions implemented? Each class with virtual functions has a static table of function pointers (the vtable); each object holds a hidden pointer to its class's table (the vptr), written by the constructor. A virtual call loads the vptr, loads the slot for that function, and calls through it. Overriding replaces the slot in the derived class's table.

Q: Why must a base class destructor be virtual? So that delete through a base pointer (including inside unique_ptr<Base>) dispatches to the derived destructor. Without it, only the base destructor runs and derived members are never destroyed; the behaviour is undefined.

Q: What is object slicing? Copying a derived object into a base-type object (by-value parameter, assignment, container of base) copies only the base subobject. The derived data and the derived vptr are lost. Pass polymorphic types by reference or pointer.

Q: What does override do and why use it? It makes the compiler verify that the function really overrides a base virtual with the same signature. Without it, a mismatched signature silently creates a new, unrelated function and the base version keeps being called.

Q: What is the runtime cost of a virtual call? Two dependent loads and an indirect call, usually a few cycles when predicted. The larger cost is lost inlining and optimisation across the call, and branch mispredictions when the target alternates. Devirtualisation (final, LTO) removes it where the type can be proven.

Q: What happens if you call a virtual function in a constructor? It dispatches to the version for the class whose constructor is currently running, because the vptr points to that class's table at that moment. Calling a pure virtual there aborts with "pure virtual method called".

Q: When would you prefer std::variant to a class hierarchy? When the set of alternatives is closed and known at compile time: variant stores values inline (no heap, no vptr), std::visit dispatches with a jump table and the compiler checks every case is handled. Hierarchies win when the set is open (plugins) or when binary compatibility matters.

Q: What is the NVI idiom? A public non-virtual function that implements the fixed protocol (pre/post conditions, locking, logging) and calls a private virtual hook that derived classes override. It separates "what the interface promises" from "what the implementation customises".

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Virtual = runtime dispatch via a per-class vtable and a per-object vptr; cost is one pointer per object and an indirect call.
  • Vtable slots: offset-to-top, typeinfo, two destructors, then virtuals in declaration order.
  • Always override; use final to enable devirtualisation; always a virtual destructor on a polymorphic base.
  • Dispatch happens through references and pointers only; by-value copies slice.
  • Virtual calls in constructors/destructors go to the class being constructed/destroyed.
  • Inherit from interfaces, compose everything else; NVI keeps the protocol in the base.
  • Use templates or std::variant for closed type sets and hot loops; virtuals for open sets and binary boundaries.
  • Adding a virtual function changes the vtable layout: an ABI break for shared libraries.
  • "pure virtual method called" and a vptr pointing into the heap are the signatures of lifetime bugs.

docs.title: 10. Error handling: exceptions, optional, variant, error_code
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
In C you return an int, set errno, or hand back NULL, and every caller must check. Forgetting a check is silent. C++ gives you four tools and you will use all of them: exceptions for failures that the immediate caller cannot handle and that should unwind to a recovery point; std::optional for "there might be no value" (a lookup miss); std::variant / a result type for "either a value or a structured error" that the caller must handle right here; and std::error_code for carrying C-style numeric errors (errno, library codes) without allocation or unwinding.

The skill is not learning the syntax. It is deciding, per function, which kind of failure it has and picking the matching tool, then making the chosen behaviour a policy for the whole server rather than a per-function mood.

Analogy: optional is an empty mailbox (normal, check it). error_code is a form letter saying why (cheap, routine). An exception is the fire alarm: everybody drops what they are doing and goes to the designated exit. You do not pull the fire alarm because the mailbox is empty.

docs.title: 2.1 Exceptions
docs.text:
struct ParseError : std::runtime_error {
    int line;
    ParseError(const std::string& what, int l) : std::runtime_error(what), line(l) {}
};

try {
    parse(input);
} catch (const ParseError& e) {      // catch by const reference: no slicing, no copy
    log(e.line, e.what());
} catch (const std::exception& e) {  // most general LAST
    log(e.what());
}
  • Throw by value, catch by const&. Derive from std::exception (usually std::runtime_error or std::logic_error) so generic handlers can log what().
  • throw; inside a handler rethrows the current exception without copying.
  • An exception escaping main or a thread function calls std::terminate. Wrap every thread body in a try/catch that logs and decides.
  • Exceptions are for errors the caller cannot reasonably handle at the call site: resource exhaustion, broken invariants, I/O failures deep in a call chain, constructor failures. Not for expected outcomes (key not found, EOF, invalid user input in a parser's normal operation).

docs.title: 2.2 Exception safety guarantees
docs.text:
Every function you write provides one of these, and your API documentation should say which:

Guarantee Meaning How to achieve Nothrow (noexcept) never throws only call nothrow operations; swap, move, destructors, integer math Strong if it throws, state is exactly as before (transactional) do all throwing work on the side, then commit with nothrow operations (copy-and-swap) Basic if it throws, state is valid but unspecified; no leaks RAII for every resource None may leak or corrupt unacceptable

RAII (module 03) gives the basic guarantee almost for free. The strong guarantee costs a copy or a careful ordering: "throwing operations first, committing operations last". The standard library documents its guarantees: vector::push_back is strong; vector::insert of a range is basic (unless the element type's move is noexcept, when it becomes strong).

docs.title: 2.3 noexcept
docs.text: A promise that the function does not throw; if it does, std::terminate is called immediately (no unwinding). Mark: destructors (implicit), move constructors and move assignment (module 04: needed for vector to move), swap, simple getters, and anything you want callers to be able to rely on. Do not mark functions that allocate or call unknown code. noexcept(expr) queries whether an expression can throw, so templates can propagate the property.

docs.title: 2.4 std::optional<T>
docs.text: A T or nothing, stored inline (no heap). has_value(), *opt, opt->member, value() (throws bad_optional_access if empty), value_or(default). Use it for lookups and parsers where "absent" is a normal result. sizeof(optional<T>) is sizeof(T) plus a bool plus padding.

docs.title: 2.5 std::variant<Ts...> and std::visit
docs.text: A type-safe tagged union: holds exactly one of the alternatives, knows which (index()), and std::visit(visitor, v) calls the visitor's overload for the held type, checked at compile time (missing an alternative is an error). A Result = std::variant<Value, Error> type forces the caller to handle both. C++23 adds std::expected<T, E> for exactly this; in C++17 either write a small Expected class or use variant.

docs.title: 2.6 std::error_code and std::error_condition
docs.text:
A (int value, const error_category&) pair, 16 bytes, trivially copyable, no allocation. The category supplies message() and maps codes to portable std::errc conditions (so ec == std::errc::timed_out works whether the code came from errno or from your own category). std::system_error is the exception that carries an error_code, bridging the two worlds: throw it from a constructor when socket() fails, return an error_code from a hot-path send().

Define your own category for a library (class KvCategory : public std::error_category) so callers can compare against your enum without string matching.

docs.title: 2.7 An error-handling policy for a server
docs.text:
1. Programming errors (null where non-null promised, index out of range, broken invariant): assert in debug, and in release either std::terminate via a checked helper or a logged exception. Do not try to continue; the state is unknown.
  2. Resource failures (out of memory, cannot open listening socket, config file missing): exceptions. Caught at the top of the component (connection handler, startup), logged, and the component is torn down and restarted or the process exits cleanly.
  3. Expected operational errors (client sent garbage, key not found, peer closed connection, EAGAIN): return values. optional for absent, error_code or a result variant for "why". These are the normal paths of a server and must not unwind.
  4. Boundaries: C callbacks, thread entry points, destructors, noexcept functions must never let an exception escape. catch (...) at those boundaries, log, convert.
  5. Logging: log once, at the point where the error is handled, with context. Do not log at every level of the stack; that is what the exception's message and the error_code carry up for you.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m10_exceptions_safety.cpp demonstrates the guarantees and unwinding:

void add_basic(long long amount)  { total_ += amount; entries_.push_back(amount); }  // basic: inconsistent on throw
void add_strong(long long amount) { entries_.push_back(amount); total_ += amount; }  // strong: throw-first, commit-last

void replace_all(const std::vector<long long>& fresh) {
    std::vector<long long> copy(fresh);   // may throw; *this untouched
    long long sum = 0; for (long long v : copy) sum += v;
    entries_.swap(copy);                  // noexcept commit
    total_ = sum;
}

long long parse_amount(const std::string& s, int line) {
    try { /* std::stoll ... */ }
    catch (const std::invalid_argument&) { throw ParseError("not a number: '" + s + "'", line); }   // translate
    catch (const std::out_of_range&)     { throw ParseError("out of range: '" + s + "'", line); }
}

struct Guard { const char* name; ~Guard() { std::cout << "  unwinding through " << name << '\n'; } };
void level3(const std::string& s) { Guard g{"level3"}; parse_amount(s, 3); }   // prints as the stack unwinds

code/m10_optional_variant_error_code.cpp shows the non-throwing tools:

std::optional<int> parse_port(std::string_view s);             // nullopt for "", "80a", "99999"
std::error_code open_device(std::string_view name);            // {} on success; errno wrapped on failure
if (ec == std::errc::device_or_resource_busy) retry();         // portable comparison

using Result = std::variant<long long, Error>;
template <class... Fs> struct overloaded : Fs... { using Fs::operator()...; };
template <class... Fs> overloaded(Fs...) -> overloaded<Fs...>;

std::visit(overloaded{
    [](long long bal)   { std::cout << "balance=" << bal << '\n'; },
    [](const Error& e)  { std::cout << "error: " << e.code.message() << " (" << e.context << ")\n"; },
}, lookup_balance(db, acct));

using Message = std::variant<Get, Put, Del>;                   // a protocol message without a hand-written tag
if (auto* g = std::get_if<Get>(&msg)) use(g->key);             // null if the wrong alternative

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Throw cost, measured in mechanism. throw X{} calls __cxa_allocate_exception (heap, with an emergency pool for bad_alloc), copy-constructs X there, then __cxa_throw, which runs the two-phase unwinder from libgcc (module 03 section 4). Phase 1 walks frames reading .eh_frame and calling the personality routine to find a handler; phase 2 walks again running landing pads. Each frame costs a lookup in the unwind tables (binary search over FDEs, cached by dl_iterate_phdr, which takes a lock in older glibc, a real contention point in multithreaded servers that throw a lot). Typical: 1 to 10 microseconds per throw, proportional to stack depth. A return std::error_code is a register move. At 1% throw rate on a 100k req/s server that is still fine; at 50% it is not.

No cost when not thrown. The normal path has no checks. try blocks are free. The tables take space in the binary (.eh_frame, .gcc_except_table), typically 5 to 15% of text size.

noexcept and code generation. A noexcept function needs no landing pads for its own cleanup (the compiler may still emit a call to std::terminate guard), and callers can skip generating cleanup paths around it. In std::vector, std::is_nothrow_move_constructible picks move over copy. Violating noexcept calls std::terminate directly; the stack is not unwound (destructors do not run), which matters for anything that flushes in a destructor.

std::optional layout. A union of T and nothing, plus a bool engaged; sizeof(optional<int>) == 8, sizeof(optional<std::string>) == 40. No dynamic allocation ever. Returning optional<T> by value is subject to the same elision rules as T.

std::variant layout and visit. Storage for the largest alternative plus an index (unsigned char for up to 255 alternatives, aligned up). std::visit with one variant generates a table of function pointers indexed by index() (or a switch for small counts in newer libstdc++), so dispatch is a bounds check and an indirect jump: comparable to a virtual call but with no heap and no vptr. A variant can become valueless_by_exception if a type-changing assignment throws midway; check valueless_by_exception() only if your alternatives have throwing move constructors.

std::error_code is a C-compatible value. Two words, trivially copyable, returned in registers. The category is a pointer to a singleton with virtual functions (message(), equivalent()), so comparison with an errc calls through the category: cheap, but not free; do it on the error path only.

Exception objects and what(). std::runtime_error stores its message in a reference-counted string (libstdc++ __cow_string) so copying the exception does not allocate and what() cannot throw. Your own exception types should avoid members whose copy constructor can throw; the copy performed by throw would then throw inside a throw, terminating the program.

Thread boundaries. An exception does not cross threads. std::thread with an escaping exception terminates the whole process. std::async/std::promise capture it (std::exception_ptr) and rethrow in get(); this is how you move an error from a worker to the thread that cares.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Pick per layer, not per mood. Constructors and startup: throw. Request-handling hot path: return optional/error_code/result. Component tops (connection loop, thread entry): catch, log with context, recover or exit. Write this down in the project's README and enforce in review.
  • The catch (...) {} that swallows turns an out-of-memory into a silent data loss. If you catch broadly, log the what() (via catch (const std::exception&) first) and re-throw or terminate anything you cannot identify.
  • Destructors that can fail (flush, close with pending writes, commit) need an explicit close()/commit() that can throw, with the destructor as a best-effort fallback that logs. std::fstream works this way: the destructor closes silently; call flush() and check if you care.
  • Error codes and [[nodiscard]]. A function returning std::error_code or bool should be [[nodiscard]] (module 13) so the compiler enforces the check your C callers kept forgetting.
  • Map C errors at the boundary. Wrap errno into std::error_code(errno, std::generic_category()) the moment it is produced; downstream code then compares against std::errc names instead of magic numbers, and message() gives the strerror text for logs.
  • Banking semantics. A multi-step balance update needs the strong guarantee: compute everything, then commit with nothrow operations, or hold a transaction object whose destructor rolls back unless commit() was called (the ScopeGuard from module 03). Your PL/pgSQL BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN block is the same shape.
  • 3 AM debugging. terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::system_error' what(): Resource temporarily unavailable: a noexcept function or thread body let an exception escape. Core dump shows __cxa_throw at the top; walk down to the first frame of your code. catch throw in gdb breaks at every throw.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m10_exceptions_safety.cpp. Swap the two lines in add_strong and write a test with a custom allocator that throws on the 3rd allocation. Done when you can show total() disagreeing with the entries after the throw.
  2. (easy) Write std::optional<Account> find_account(std::string_view id) over a std::vector and use it with if (auto a = find_account("X")), value_or, and ->. Done when there is no sentinel value anywhere.
  3. (medium) Define enum class KvErr { KeyNotFound = 1, TooLarge, Readonly }, a KvCategory : std::error_category, make_error_code(KvErr), and the is_error_code_enum specialisation. Done when std::error_code ec = KvErr::TooLarge; compiles and ec.message() prints your text.
  4. (medium) Implement template <class T, class E> class Expected with has_value(), value(), error(), and a map(f) method, built on std::variant<T, E>. Done when a chain of three map calls short-circuits on the first error in a test.
  5. (hard) Benchmark parse_port returning optional<int> vs a version that throws on invalid input, over 10M inputs where 0%, 1%, 50% are invalid. Done when you have a table and can state where the crossover is and why.
  6. (hard) Write a thread pool worker loop that catches exceptions from tasks, stores them in a std::exception_ptr inside a per-task result, and rethrows them in the caller's get(). Done when a task throwing ParseError is caught as ParseError in the submitting thread with its line intact.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Exceptions or error codes? Exceptions for failures the immediate caller cannot handle and that should unwind to a recovery point (resource exhaustion, constructor failure, broken invariants); return values (optional, error_code, result types) for expected outcomes on normal paths (lookup miss, bad input, EAGAIN). The decision should be a project-wide policy per layer, not per function.

Q: Name the exception safety guarantees. Nothrow (never throws, noexcept), strong (on throw, state unchanged, transactional), basic (on throw, state valid and nothing leaked), and none. RAII gives basic; "throwing work first, nothrow commit last" or copy-and-swap gives strong.

Q: What does noexcept do and when should you use it? It promises the function will not throw; if one escapes, std::terminate is called without unwinding. Use it on destructors, move operations, swap, and simple non-allocating functions. It lets std::vector move instead of copy and lets the compiler drop cleanup paths.

Q: Why catch by const&? Catching by value copies the exception (possibly throwing again) and slices derived exceptions down to the base type, losing information. A const reference binds to the exception object the runtime allocated, with its full dynamic type.

Q: What happens if an exception leaves a destructor during unwinding? Two exceptions would be in flight; the runtime calls std::terminate. Destructors are implicitly noexcept, so the terminate happens at the destructor even outside unwinding. Provide an explicit close() for failures that matter.

Q: What is std::optional for, and what does it cost? Representing "a value or nothing" without sentinels or heap allocation: a union of T and a bool flag, stored inline. value() throws on empty; *, -> and value_or do not check.

Q: How does std::visit on a std::variant work? The variant stores the active alternative's index; visit dispatches on it through a generated table or switch to the visitor's matching overload. The compiler checks that the visitor handles every alternative, so adding a type to the variant breaks every visitor that forgot it: a feature.

Q: What is std::error_code and when is it better than an exception? A 16-byte value: an integer plus a pointer to a category that gives it meaning and a message. No allocation, no unwinding, trivially returned in registers. Right for hot paths, C API boundaries (wrap errno immediately), and libraries that must not throw. std::system_error carries one when you do need to throw.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Four tools: exceptions (unwind to a recovery point), optional (absent value), variant/result (value or structured error, handled here), error_code (cheap numeric error with a category).
  • Throw by value, catch by const&, derive from std::exception, most specific handler first.
  • Guarantees: nothrow, strong, basic, none; RAII gives basic, "throw first, commit last" gives strong.
  • noexcept on destructors, moves, swap; violating it terminates without unwinding.
  • Throwing costs microseconds (two stack walks); not throwing costs nothing.
  • optional and variant are inline, no heap; visit is a checked jump table.
  • Wrap errno into error_code at the boundary; compare with std::errc names.
  • Policy per layer: constructors/startup throw, hot paths return, component tops catch and log once.
  • Exceptions never cross thread or C boundaries; use exception_ptr or convert.

docs.title: 11. const, constexpr and compile-time programming
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: 08

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
C has two ways to make a constant: #define SIZE 256 (textual, untyped, invisible to the debugger) and const int size = 256; (typed, but in C not usable as an array bound at file scope and sometimes not folded). C++ fixes this with constexpr: a typed constant that the compiler must be able to evaluate at compile time, and which you can use anywhere a literal can go. More importantly, constexpr applies to functions: the same code that runs at run time can be executed by the compiler to build lookup tables, validate configuration, or check invariants before the program ever starts.

Analogy: const is a sign that says "do not touch". constexpr is a vending machine built into the compiler: feed it constants and it hands you the answer baked into the binary.

docs.title: 2.1 const: immutability
docs.text:
const means "cannot be modified through this name". It is about access, not about when the value is known: const int n = std::rand(); is fine. Uses:

  • Variables: const int max_retries = 5; (internal linkage by default at namespace scope in C++).
  • Pointers and references: const T* (pointee const), T* const (pointer const), const T&.
  • Member functions: long long balance() const; promises not to modify *this (module 01).
  • mutable members may be modified inside const member functions (caches, mutexes).
  • const_cast removes const; modifying an object that was defined const through it is undefined behaviour.

docs.title: 2.2 constexpr variables
docs.text:
constexpr int seconds_per_day = 60 * 60 * 24;     // must be a constant expression; implies const
constexpr double pi = 3.141592653589793;
int table[seconds_per_day / 3600];                 // usable as an array bound, template argument, case label

The initialiser is evaluated at compile time or the program does not compile. constexpr on a variable also implies const and (since C++17) inline for static data members.

docs.title: 2.3 constexpr functions
docs.text:
constexpr std::uint32_t crc32_entry(std::uint32_t i) {
    std::uint32_t c = i;
    for (int k = 0; k < 8; ++k) c = (c & 1u) ? (0xEDB88320u ^ (c >> 1)) : (c >> 1);
    return c;
}
static_assert(crc32_entry(1) == 0x77073096u);     // evaluated by the compiler
std::uint32_t x = crc32_entry(user_input);         // same function, evaluated at run time

A constexpr function can be evaluated at compile time when all its arguments are constants and the context requires a constant (array bound, static_assert, constexpr variable, template argument). Otherwise it is an ordinary function. Since C++14 the body may contain loops, local variables, if, multiple statements. Not allowed (C++17): try, goto, static locals, uninitialised variables, calls to non-constexpr functions, dynamic allocation (C++20 relaxes some of these), reinterpret_cast, and undefined behaviour (the compiler must diagnose UB during constant evaluation, which makes constexpr a UB detector).

docs.title: 2.4 Literal types
docs.text:
A type usable in constant expressions: scalars, references, arrays of literal types, and classes with a constexpr constructor (or an aggregate), a trivial destructor, and literal-type members. std::array, std::pair, std::string_view, std::optional of a literal type are literal types; std::string and std::vector are not in C++17 (they allocate).

struct Version {
    int major, minor, patch;
    constexpr bool operator<(const Version& o) const { /* ... */ }
    constexpr int packed() const { return major * 10000 + minor * 100 + patch; }
};
constexpr Version kMinSupported{1, 4, 0};
static_assert(kMinSupported < Version{2, 0, 0});

docs.title: 2.5 static_assert
docs.text: A compile-time assertion with a message. Use it to pin down ABI assumptions (sizeof(Header) == 12), type properties (std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>), and the results of constexpr computations (unit tests that run inside the compiler). A failing static_assert is a build error, which is the cheapest possible time to find a bug.

docs.title: 2.6 Inline variables (C++17)
docs.text:
inline constexpr std::array<std::uint32_t, 256> kCrcTable = make_crc_table();   // in a header

Before C++17, a non-const or class-type variable defined in a header produced "multiple definition" link errors, so people wrote extern declarations plus one .cpp definition, or function-local statics. inline on a variable means "every translation unit may define this; the linker keeps one". static constexpr data members are implicitly inline, so they no longer need an out-of-class definition.

docs.title: 2.7 Compile-time tables
docs.text: The pattern: a constexpr function returns a std::array filled by a loop; assign it to an inline constexpr variable; use it. The compiler emits the finished table into .rodata. Zero start-up cost, no "init on first use" race, and static_assert can verify entries. CRC tables, sine tables, enum-to-string tables, state-machine transition tables, protocol opcode tables all fit.

docs.title: 2.8 if constexpr and constexpr lambdas
docs.text: if constexpr (module 08) selects code at compile time. Lambdas are implicitly constexpr in C++17 when they can be, so constexpr auto sq = [](int x) { return x * x; }; static_assert(sq(3) == 9); works.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m11_constexpr_tables.cpp builds a CRC-32 table at compile time and verifies it:

constexpr std::array<std::uint32_t, 256> make_crc_table() {
    std::array<std::uint32_t, 256> t{};
    for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < 256; ++i) t[i] = crc32_table_entry(i);
    return t;
}
inline constexpr auto kCrcTable = make_crc_table();              // 1 KiB in .rodata, computed by g++

constexpr std::uint32_t crc32(std::string_view data) {
    std::uint32_t c = 0xFFFFFFFFu;
    for (unsigned char ch : data) c = kCrcTable[(c ^ ch) & 0xFFu] ^ (c >> 8);
    return c ^ 0xFFFFFFFFu;
}
static_assert(crc32("123456789") == 0xCBF43926u);                 // the standard CRC-32 check value

constexpr Version kMinSupported{1, 4, 0};                          // literal type
static_assert(Version{1, 5, 2}.packed() == 10502);

const int     runtime_const = std::rand();      // const: read-only, value known at run time
constexpr int compile_const = 60 * 60 * 24;     // constexpr: value known at compile time

constexpr std::string_view op_name(Op op) { switch (op) { /* ... */ } }
static_assert(op_name(Op::Put) == "PUT");

Verify the table is really precomputed: g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -S m11_constexpr_tables.cpp and look for kCrcTable in .rodata as 256 .long values, with no loop that fills it at start-up. Then objdump -d the binary and confirm crc32("123456789") in main became a single constant load (mov esi, 0xcbf43926).

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Constant evaluation is an interpreter inside the compiler. GCC's constexpr evaluator walks the function's tree representation, tracking the values of every variable, following loops and branches. It has limits (-fconstexpr-loop-limit, default 262144 iterations; -fconstexpr-ops-limit, 33 million operations) to stop infinite compile times. The evaluation must be deterministic: no reading uninitialised memory, no out-of-bounds, no signed overflow, no reinterpret_cast. Any UB is a hard error with a message pointing at the operation, which is why pushing code into constexpr tests is a cheap way to find UB.

When is a constexpr function evaluated at compile time? Only when the result is required to be a constant: constexpr variable initialisers, static_assert, array bounds, template non-type arguments, case labels, if constexpr conditions, enumerator values. In int x = f(3); the compiler may fold it (and at -O2 it will for simple cases), but it is not required to. To force evaluation use constexpr auto v = f(3); and then use v.

.rodata and relocations. A constexpr table of integers lands in .rodata, shared between processes (the page is file-backed and read-only). A table of pointers (const char* names) needs load-time relocations unless the binary is non-PIE or the strings are placed relative; std::string_view tables have the same issue because they contain a pointer. Still constant-initialised, but the dynamic loader touches those pages at start-up (.data.rel.ro).

Constant initialisation vs dynamic initialisation. A global whose initialiser is a constant expression is constant-initialised: the bytes are in the binary, no code runs at start-up, and it is usable from any other global's constructor without ordering problems (no "static initialisation order fiasco"). A global initialised by a non-constexpr call runs code at start-up in an unspecified order across translation units. constexpr globals are always safe; const globals might not be. C++20 adds constinit to demand constant initialisation without implying const.

inline variables and the linker. An inline variable is emitted as a weak symbol in a COMDAT section in every translation unit that uses it (exactly like inline functions and template instantiations); the linker keeps one copy. Address identity is preserved: &kCrcTable is the same in every TU. Before C++17, static const in a header gave each TU its own copy with different addresses.

const and the optimiser. const int n = 5; at local scope lets the compiler fold n because it sees the initialiser. const int& n or const int* p gives the optimiser nothing: the object behind the reference may be modified by someone else (it is "const through this view", not "immutable"). Only constexpr or a const object with a visible constant initialiser is truly foldable. const on a by-value parameter (void f(const int x)) is purely local documentation.

constexpr and ODR. A constexpr function is implicitly inline, so defining it in a header is fine and expected.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Replace #define constants. constexpr int kMaxConnections = 1024; is typed, scoped, visible to the debugger, and still folds. #define only remains for conditional compilation and include guards.
  • Protocol constants and wire formats. static_assert(sizeof(WireHeader) == 7) next to the #pragma pack struct (module 12) makes a silent layout change a build error. The same for enum values that are part of the protocol: static_assert(static_cast<int>(Op::Del) == 2).
  • Lookup tables at zero start-up cost. A banking server that spends 200 ms at start-up building tables (character classes, checksum tables, holiday calendars for the next decade) can have most of them computed by the compiler instead, which also removes the "was it initialised yet?" race.
  • constexpr as unit tests. static_assert(parse_amount("12.50") == 1250) runs on every build, on every developer machine, with no test harness and no flakiness. Keep the heavy tests in a real framework; use static_assert for invariants of pure functions.
  • Compile-time cost. A constexpr loop of 10 million iterations takes seconds per translation unit on every build. Keep compile-time work small (tables of a few KB), or precompute offline and check it in.
  • 3 AM debugging. A value that "cannot change" changed: someone const_casted a const object or wrote through a pointer. If the object was constexpr/const-defined, the compiler may have folded reads of it, so the code reads the old value in one place and the new one in another. Modifying a defined-const object is UB; find the cast.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m11_constexpr_tables.cpp with -O2 -S. Find kCrcTable in .rodata and the constant 0xcbf43926 in main. Done when you can show both in the assembly.
  2. (easy) Write constexpr int days_in_month(int month, bool leap) and static_assert every month. Then deliberately introduce an out-of-bounds array read and observe the compile-time UB diagnostic. Done when you can quote the error.
  3. (medium) Write a constexpr enum-to-string table for a 6-value enum class as std::array<std::string_view, 6> with static_asserts that every entry is non-empty and that table[static_cast<int>(E::Last)] is correct. Done when adding a 7th enumerator breaks the build.
  4. (medium) Implement constexpr std::array<int, 1000> primes() using a sieve, and time the compile with and without it (time g++ ...). Then raise to 100,000 and read the -fconstexpr-loop-limit / ops-limit error. Done when you can explain the trade-off.
  5. (hard) Write a constexpr state-machine transition table for a tiny protocol parser (states: Start, Key, Sep, Value, Done; inputs: letter, colon, newline, other) and a constexpr bool accepts(std::string_view) that walks it. static_assert five inputs. Done when the same function parses runtime input and the table is in .rodata.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between const and constexpr? const means the object cannot be modified through this name; the value may be computed at run time. constexpr means the value must be a compile-time constant, usable as array bounds, template arguments and in static_assert. constexpr implies const; the reverse is false.

Q: When is a constexpr function evaluated at compile time? When it is called with constant arguments in a context that requires a constant expression (constexpr variable, static_assert, array bound, template argument, case label). Elsewhere it is a normal function, though the optimiser may still fold it.

Q: What can a constexpr function not do in C++17? Allocate, use static or thread-local locals, try/catch, goto, reinterpret_cast, call non-constexpr functions, leave variables uninitialised, or perform undefined behaviour (which is diagnosed as an error during constant evaluation).

Q: What is a literal type? A type whose values can exist in constant expressions: scalars, references, arrays of literal types, and classes with a constexpr constructor or aggregate initialisation, a trivial destructor, and literal-type members. std::array qualifies; std::string does not (in C++17).

Q: What problem do inline variables solve? Defining a variable in a header without "multiple definition" link errors: each translation unit emits a weak definition and the linker keeps one, with a single address program-wide. It replaces extern declarations plus a .cpp definition for constants and makes static constexpr members definition-free.

Q: Why are constexpr globals immune to the static initialisation order fiasco? They are constant-initialised: their bytes are in the binary and no constructor runs at start-up, so any other global's constructor can read them regardless of translation-unit order.

Q: Does const int& x help the optimiser? No. const on a reference or pointer only restricts what you can do through it; the referenced object may change through other paths, so the compiler must reload it. Only a const or constexpr object with a visible constant initialiser is foldable.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• const = read-only access; constexpr = compile-time constant (implies const).
  • constexpr functions run at compile time when the context requires a constant, else at run time; same source for both.
  • Constant evaluation diagnoses undefined behaviour: constexpr tests find UB.
  • Literal types: constexpr constructor, trivial destructor, literal members; std::array yes, std::string no (C++17).
  • static_assert is a free, always-on unit test for invariants and ABI assumptions.
  • inline variables (C++17) allow header-defined constants with one address; static constexpr members are implicitly inline.
  • Compile-time tables: constexpr function returning std::array, assigned to an inline constexpr variable, landing in .rodata.
  • Constant initialisation is free and order-safe; dynamic initialisation of globals is not.
  • const through references and pointers gives the optimiser nothing.

docs.title: 12. Memory layout, allocation and performance
docs.text: Time: ~3.5 hours Prerequisites: 05, 06

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A program's speed is mostly decided by how it touches memory, not by how many instructions it executes. A core can do several additions per nanosecond but waits around 100 ns for a value that is not in cache. So the questions that matter are: how are my objects laid out (padding, alignment, size), where do they live (stack vs heap), how often do I allocate, and do my hot loops walk memory in a cache-friendly order. You already know most of this from C; this module shows how the C++ features map onto it and adds the parts C programmers often skip: cache lines, false sharing, small buffer optimisation, PMR allocators, benchmarking honestly, and undefined behaviour as a performance contract.

Analogy: a warehouse. Items on the shelf next to the one you are holding are free to grab (cache line). Walking to another aisle costs seconds (cache miss). Ordering from the supplier costs days (heap allocation plus page fault). Layout and allocation policy decide which of these your loop does.

docs.title: 2.1 Object layout, alignment, padding
docs.text:
Every type has sizeof and alignof. A member must sit at an offset that is a multiple of its alignment, so the compiler inserts padding; the struct's size is rounded up to a multiple of its own alignment (the largest member's) so arrays stay aligned.

struct Bad  { char tag; double amount; int id; char flag; };   // 1+7pad, 8, 4, 1+3pad = 24 bytes
struct Good { double amount; int id; char tag; char flag; };   // 8, 4, 1, 1, 2pad     = 16 bytes

Sort members by alignment descending to remove padding. alignas(64) over-aligns (one object per cache line); #pragma pack(1) removes padding for wire formats at the cost of misaligned access (use memcpy in and out). offsetof and static_assert pin the layout. std::is_standard_layout_v<T> tells you the layout is C-compatible; a vptr (module 09) adds 8 bytes at the front.

docs.title: 2.2 Cache lines and false sharing
docs.text: Memory moves between cores and caches in 64-byte lines. Reading one int pulls its whole line into L1; the next 15 ints are then free. Two variables in the same line that are written by two different cores force the line to bounce between the cores' caches on every write: false sharing. It looks like a lock without a lock. Fix: alignas(64) the per-thread fields so each gets its own line. Full treatment in 04_Concurrency; m12_false_sharing_bench.cpp shows the effect.

docs.title: 2.3 Stack vs heap
docs.text:
Stack allocation is a subtraction from rsp: free, cache-hot, and freed automatically. Heap allocation (new, malloc) costs tens to hundreds of nanoseconds (glibc malloc fast path with a thread cache is around 20 ns, typical; a fresh page from the kernel is far more), takes a lock or a per-thread arena, scatters your data, and must be freed. Modern C++ hides heap use inside vector, string, unique_ptr, std::function, so you must know which operations allocate:

Allocates Does not std::vector growth, std::string > 15 chars, std::map/unordered_map node per element, make_unique/make_shared, std::function with a large callable, std::any, std::stringstream std::array, std::optional, std::variant, std::string_view, std::pair/tuple, small std::string (SSO), lambdas, std::function with a small callable, std::span (C++20)

docs.title: 2.4 Allocation patterns
docs.text:
• Reserve once. v.reserve(n), m.reserve(n), s.reserve(n).
  • Reuse buffers. Keep a std::vector<char> member and clear() it per request instead of allocating a new one; capacity is retained.
  • Arena / bump allocators. One large block; allocation is a pointer increment; "free" is resetting the pointer at the end of a request. Your C arena with ownership contracts. In C++17 the standard version is std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource plus std::pmr::vector, std::pmr::string.
  • Pools. Fixed-size blocks in a free list for objects of one type (connections, messages): std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource / synchronized_pool_resource.
  • Small buffer optimisation (SBO). Store small payloads inline, spill to the heap only when large. std::string does it (15 bytes), std::function (16 bytes), many small_vector implementations.

docs.title: 2.5 Benchmarking basics
docs.text:
1. Use std::chrono::steady_clock, never system_clock (it jumps).
  2. Build with -O2 (or whatever production uses). -O0 numbers are meaningless.
  3. Warm up, repeat, take the minimum or median, not the mean.
  4. Make the result observable (print it, write to a volatile, or use a benchmark library's DoNotOptimize) or the optimiser deletes the work.
  5. Benchmark the realistic size and access pattern: a 1k-element test fits in L1 and says nothing about a 100 MB table.
  6. Use perf stat -e cache-misses,instructions,cycles ./bench to see why, not just how long. Google Benchmark is the standard library for serious micro-benchmarks.

docs.title: 2.6 What -O2 does
docs.text: Inlining (the enabler for everything else), constant folding and propagation, dead code elimination, loop-invariant code motion, strength reduction, common subexpression elimination, register allocation, instruction scheduling, auto-vectorisation (SSE/AVX for simple loops), devirtualisation when provable, and tail-call elimination. -O3 adds more aggressive inlining and loop transforms; -Os optimises for size; -march=native enables the CPU's full instruction set (but the binary then runs only on that CPU class); -flto optimises across translation units. The optimiser assumes your program has no undefined behaviour; that assumption is what makes the next section matter.

docs.title: 2.7 Undefined behaviour and why it matters
docs.text:
Undefined behaviour (UB): the standard imposes no requirements. The compiler may assume it never happens and optimise accordingly, so the program may do anything, including "work" until the next compiler upgrade. Categories you will hit:

UB Example What the optimiser does with it Signed integer overflow int x = INT_MAX; x + 1 assumes x + 1 > x always; removes overflow checks like if (x + 1 < x) Out-of-bounds access arr[n] assumes the index is in range; may remove a later bounds check Dereferencing null / dangling *p after delete p, returning int& to a local assumes p non-null; reorders or deletes checks Strict aliasing violation *(float*)&int_value assumes an int* and float* never alias; may reorder loads/stores across them Data race two threads write a non-atomic int assumes single-threaded view; hoists loads out of loops (spin loop never exits) Uninitialised read int x; if (x) ... may treat x as any value, both branches "taken" Shift by >= width or negative 1 << 32 on 32-bit int arbitrary Modifying a const object, violating noexcept-adjacent rules, misaligned access through pointer

Tools: -fsanitize=undefined (UBSan) reports most of these at run time, -fsanitize=address (ASan) catches memory errors, -fsanitize=thread (TSan) catches data races, -Wall -Wextra plus -Wstrict-aliasing -Wshadow -Wconversion catch some at compile time. Use std::memcpy for type punning (the compiler turns it into a register move), unsigned or __builtin_add_overflow for wrap-around arithmetic, std::launder and std::bit_cast (C++20) where needed.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m12_padding_alignment.cpp prints sizes, alignments and offsets:

struct Bad  { char tag; double amount; int id; char flag; };   // sizeof 24
struct Good { double amount; int id; char tag; char flag; };   // sizeof 16
struct alignas(64) CacheLineBox { int counter; };              // sizeof 64, alignof 64
#pragma pack(push, 1)
struct WireHeader { std::uint8_t type; std::uint32_t length; std::uint16_t flags; };   // sizeof 7 (12 unpacked)
#pragma pack(pop)
std::cout << offsetof(Bad, amount) << ' ' << offsetof(Bad, flag) << '\n';   // 8 20
static_assert(sizeof(Good) % alignof(Good) == 0);

code/m12_arena_pmr.cpp is your C arena in C++, then the std::pmr version:

class Arena {
    void* allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t align) {
        std::size_t aligned = (used_ + align - 1) & ~(align - 1);   // round up
        if (aligned + n > cap_) throw std::bad_alloc();
        used_ = aligned + n;
        return buf_ + aligned;                                      // no header, no free list, no lock
    }
    template <class T, class... Args> T* make(Args&&... args) {
        return new (allocate(sizeof(T), alignof(T))) T(std::forward<Args>(args)...);   // placement new
    }
    void reset() noexcept { used_ = 0; }                            // O(1) free-all (trivially destructible T only)
};

std::byte stack_buf[2048];
std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource pool(stack_buf, sizeof stack_buf, &upstream);
std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string> names(&pool);   // every allocation (vector + each string) comes from the pool

The CountingResource in the file shows the number of heap calls: with the pool, zero until the 2 KB buffer is exhausted; without it, one per vector growth plus one per long string.

code/m12_false_sharing_bench.cpp (build with -O2) and code/m12_bench_basics.cpp (vector vs list, linear vs binary search, best-of-N timing) give you numbers from your own machine:

struct Adjacent { std::atomic<std::uint64_t> a{0}; std::atomic<std::uint64_t> b{0}; };            // one line
struct Padded { alignas(64) std::atomic<std::uint64_t> a{0}; alignas(64) std::atomic<std::uint64_t> b{0}; };  // two lines
// two threads, each hammering its own counter: expect Adjacent to be several times slower (typical: 3x to 10x)

template <class F> double time_ms(F&& f, int reps = 5) {   // best-of-N
    double best = 1e300;
    for (int r = 0; r < reps; ++r) { auto t0 = steady_clock::now(); f(); best = std::min(best, elapsed_ms(t0)); }
    return best;
}
std::uint64_t sink = 0;   // every result feeds 'sink', which is printed: the optimiser cannot delete the work

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why alignment exists. Loads of a naturally aligned 8-byte value are one memory transaction. A misaligned 8-byte load that crosses a cache line is two transactions and, on x86, is legal but slower; on ARM it may fault or be emulated. Atomic operations require alignment: a misaligned std::atomic<uint64_t> is not atomic. SIMD loads (movaps) fault on misalignment. The ABI's alignment rules exist so the compiler can emit the fast instructions without checks.

The cache hierarchy (typical x86-64 server, 2020s). L1d 32 to 48 KB per core, around 4 cycles; L2 1 to 2 MB per core, around 14 cycles; L3 tens of MB shared, around 40 to 70 cycles; DRAM 70 to 100+ ns. A pointer chase that misses to DRAM costs as much as roughly 300 simple instructions. The hardware prefetcher detects sequential and strided access and hides latency; it cannot follow a linked list. This is the whole argument for vector over list and for structure-of-arrays layouts in hot loops.

False sharing in the coherence protocol. Caches keep lines in states (MESI: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid). A write requires the line in Modified state on that core; any other core's copy is invalidated. Two cores writing different bytes of one line ping-pong the line through the interconnect on every write (tens of ns each). Padding to 64 bytes makes them independent. Reads alone do not cause it (Shared state is fine); one writer plus many readers of the same line does.

What malloc does (glibc ptmalloc). Per-thread cache (tcache) of recently freed small blocks (fast path: pop from a singly linked list, no lock); then per-arena bins with a mutex; then brk/mmap from the kernel for new memory (page faults on first touch, zeroing by the kernel). Each block has a 16-byte header and is rounded up to 16 bytes; a new int costs 32 bytes. Freed memory is coalesced but rarely returned to the OS (fragmentation keeps RSS high). Many small allocations from many threads contend on arenas; that is where arenas, pools and jemalloc/tcmalloc (drop-in via LD_PRELOAD) win.

std::pmr design. std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T> holds a memory_resource* and forwards allocate/deallocate through two virtual calls. The container type does not change with the resource (unlike classic allocators, where std::vector<T, MyAlloc> is a different type), so a function can accept std::pmr::vector<int>& regardless of where its memory comes from. monotonic_buffer_resource never frees individually (deallocate is a no-op), grows by asking its upstream for geometrically larger chunks, and releases everything in release()/destructor. The pool resources keep free lists per size class. All of them chain to an upstream (default new_delete_resource()), so a pool can sit on top of an arena on top of malloc.

Small buffer optimisation mechanics. A union of an inline buffer and a (pointer, capacity) pair, plus a discriminator (often folded into the capacity or size field). Access checks the discriminator; moves of the inline case copy bytes; moves of the heap case steal the pointer. std::string's 15-byte buffer and std::function's 16-byte buffer are both "the object's own storage reinterpreted". sizeof goes up, allocations go down. Right for types that are usually small.

How UB enables optimisation. for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) a[i] = b[i] + 1; is vectorised only because the compiler may assume a and b do not alias when their types differ (strict aliasing), the loop counter does not overflow (signed overflow UB lets it use 64-bit induction variables), and the indices are in bounds. Replace int i with unsigned i and some loops get slower because wrap-around is defined and must be honoured. UB is the contract that lets the compiler stop proving things.

The two aliasing escape hatches. char, unsigned char and std::byte may alias anything, so byte-wise access is always legal. std::memcpy between objects of different types is the sanctioned type pun; GCC compiles an 8-byte memcpy to a single mov. The union trick is legal in C, UB in C++ (though GCC documents it as supported).

Stack size. The main thread's stack is typically 8 MB (ulimit -s); other threads default to 8 MB on glibc but are configurable. A 1 MB std::array on the stack in a deep recursion is a segfault with no diagnostic other than SIGSEGV at a sub rsp or a push. Large buffers belong in a vector (heap) or a static.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Measure RSS, not just speed. A std::map<int, int> with 10M entries is about 640 MB (64-byte nodes); a sorted std::vector<std::pair<int,int>> is 80 MB. In a banking server where the cache of account summaries dominates memory, layout is capacity planning.
  • Per-request arenas. Allocate everything for one RPC from a monotonic_buffer_resource created at request start and released at the end: one allocation per request instead of hundreds, no fragmentation, no per-object frees, and a natural leak guard. This is the design you already use in C.
  • -O2 -g always. Debug builds (-O0) are 5 to 20x slower and behave differently (no UB "surprises"). Ship -O2 with debug symbols (-g), strip them into a separate file (objcopy --only-keep-debug), and symbolise core dumps with it.
  • Sanitiser builds in CI. ASan + UBSan on the test suite catches the bugs that only show in production under -O2. TSan on the concurrency tests. The cost (2 to 3x slower tests) is nothing next to a corrupted ledger.
  • -Wall -Wextra -Werror plus -Wconversion -Wshadow at the start of a project, not later. Adding them to a 200k-line codebase afterwards produces thousands of warnings nobody fixes.
  • Beware "optimisations" without a profile. perf record -g ./server then perf report shows where time goes. The usual winners: an unexpected allocation in a hot loop (std::string temporaries from +), a std::map where a vector would do, a shared_ptr copy per call, false sharing on a counter, and std::endl flushing a log on every line.
  • 3 AM debugging. A function "returns garbage only in release builds": UB. Classic causes: reading an uninitialised member (constructor forgot it), signed overflow in a hash or a timer calculation, returning a reference to a local, strict-aliasing punning of a network buffer. Rebuild with -fsanitize=undefined,address -O1 -g, re-run the failing input, read the first report.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m12_padding_alignment.cpp. Reorder Bad to minimise size by hand before running, predict the offsets, run. Done when predictions match and you have added a static_assert on sizeof(Good).
  2. (easy) Build and run m12_false_sharing_bench.cpp with -O2. Change the padding to 32 bytes and observe. Done when you can state your CPU's line size from the experiment and from getconf LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE.
