  3. (medium) Extend Arena with a destroy_all() that runs destructors for non-trivial objects (keep a small vector of (void*, void(*)(void*)) finalisers). Done when a std::string allocated in the arena is destroyed correctly under Valgrind.
  4. (medium) Run m12_bench_basics.cpp at -O0, -O2, -O3 -march=native, and with perf stat -e cache-misses. Done when you have a table of times and cache misses and can explain the vector/list ratio with them.
  5. (medium) Write a SmallVector<T, N> with inline storage for N elements and heap beyond it (SBO). Done when sizeof(SmallVector<int, 8>) is as expected, moves of the inline case copy and of the heap case steal, and a Loud-style element type shows the right number of moves.
  6. (hard) Write three functions containing (a) a signed overflow check if (x + 1 < x), (b) a null check after a dereference, (c) a float read through an int*. Compile at -O2 with -S and show how the optimiser removed or changed each. Then run under UBSan. Done when you can explain, for each, which assumption the compiler made.
  7. (hard) Replace the allocator of a std::unordered_map<int, std::string> with std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource and benchmark 1M inserts and erases against the default. Done when you have numbers for time and peak RSS (/usr/bin/time -v) and a recommendation.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why does struct { char; double; int; char; } occupy 24 bytes? Each member must be aligned to its own alignment (8 for double, 4 for int), so the compiler inserts 7 bytes after the first char and 3 at the end so that arrays of the struct keep every double 8-byte aligned. Reordering members by descending alignment gives 16 bytes.

Q: What is false sharing and how do you fix it? Two cores writing different variables that happen to share a 64-byte cache line force the line to bounce between their caches on every write, serialising them as if they held a lock. Fix by placing the variables in different lines with alignas(64) or padding, or by giving each thread its own counter and summing at the end.

Q: Which standard library operations allocate? vector/string growth beyond capacity (strings over 15 chars), every node of map/set/ unordered_map/list, make_unique/make_shared, std::function holding a callable larger than 16 bytes, std::any, stringstream. array, optional, variant, string_view, pair, tuple and lambdas do not.

Q: What does an arena allocator buy you and what does it cost? Allocation becomes a pointer bump (no lock, no header, no free list), objects are contiguous and cache-friendly, and freeing is O(1) for the whole arena. The cost: no individual frees (memory is held until reset), destructors must be run manually for non-trivial types, and sizing must be chosen. The C++17 standard version is std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource.

Q: Why is undefined behaviour a performance feature and a danger at once? The optimiser assumes UB never happens, which lets it drop bounds and overflow checks, keep values in registers, reorder memory accesses, and vectorise loops. The same assumption means that if UB does happen the program's behaviour has no relation to the source: checks vanish, branches invert, and the bug appears only at -O2. Sanitisers exist to find UB before the optimiser exploits it.

Q: How do you legally reinterpret the bytes of a float as an int? std::memcpy(&i, &f, sizeof i), which GCC compiles to a single register move. Casting the pointer (*(int*)&f) violates strict aliasing and is UB. C++20 adds std::bit_cast.

Q: What is the small buffer optimisation? Storing small payloads inside the object itself and using the heap only when the payload exceeds a threshold: std::string keeps up to 15 characters inline, std::function keeps callables up to 16 bytes. It trades a larger sizeof and a branch per access for zero allocations in the common case.

Q: How do you benchmark a function honestly? Build with production flags (-O2), use steady_clock, warm up, repeat and take the minimum or median, make the result observable so the optimiser cannot remove the work, use realistic data sizes, and check perf stat counters (cache misses, instructions) to understand the result rather than just report it.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Members are padded to their alignment; order by descending alignment; alignas and #pragma pack for lines and wire formats; static_assert the layout.
  • 64-byte cache lines; sequential access is prefetched, pointer chasing is not; false sharing is two writers in one line.
  • Stack is free; heap costs tens of ns plus scattering; know which standard types allocate.
  • Reserve, reuse, arena (std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource), pool, SBO.
  • -O2 assumes no UB; UB categories: signed overflow, out of bounds, dangling/null, strict aliasing, data races, uninitialised reads.
  • memcpy for type punning; char/std::byte alias anything.
  • ASan, UBSan, TSan in CI; -O2 -g in production with separate debug symbols.
  • Benchmark: -O2, steady_clock, best-of-N, observable results, realistic sizes, perf stat.
  • Layout decides memory footprint as much as speed: node containers cost 32 to 64 bytes per element.

docs.title: 13. C++17 features tour
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: 06 to 11

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
C++11 was the big change (move semantics, lambdas, smart pointers, auto, threads). C++14 polished it. C++17 is a collection of medium-sized conveniences that make daily code shorter and safer: unpacking a pair into two names, declaring a variable inside an if, passing strings without copying, saying "this function's result must not be ignored", deducing template arguments from constructor calls. Plus a few new library types (optional, variant, any, string_view, filesystem) and std::shared_mutex, the reader-writer lock your tcpkv store uses.

This module is the checklist: each feature, what it replaces, the one trap. You have met several already; here they are collected so you can say "C++17" on a resume and mean every item.

docs.title: 2.1 Structured bindings
docs.text:
auto [it, inserted] = map.insert({key, value});      // replaces std::pair<iterator,bool> r = ...; r.first; r.second
for (const auto& [name, age] : ages) ...             // unpack map entries
auto [count, mean] = compute(v);                     // any struct with public members, std::tuple, std::array, C array

The names are aliases into a hidden copy (or reference, with auto&/const auto&) of the whole object. You cannot skip a field or nest them; unused names do not warn.

docs.title: 2.2 if / switch with initialiser
docs.text:
if (auto it = m.find(k); it != m.end()) use(*it); else miss();    // 'it' scoped to the if/else
if (std::lock_guard lock(mu); !queue.empty()) pop();              // lock scoped to the statement
switch (auto op = next_op(); op) { ... }

Replaces a variable declared on the line before whose scope leaks to the end of the block.

docs.title: 2.3 std::string_view
docs.text: A (const char*, size_t) pair. Take it as a parameter wherever you used to take const std::string& and only read: callers with literals, char*, std::string, or substrings pay nothing. remove_prefix, substr (O(1), no copy), find, comparison operators all work. Traps: not null-terminated (do not pass .data() to C APIs expecting a C string); does not own (never store a view to a temporary or to a buffer that will be reused); std::string s = sv; is an explicit copy by design.

docs.title: 2.4 std::optional, std::variant, std::any
docs.text: Covered in module 10. optional<T>: maybe a T, inline. variant<Ts...>: exactly one of several types, inline, std::visit. any: any copyable type, type-erased, heap for large payloads, any_cast checks at run time. Use variant when the set of types is known; any is for genuinely open-ended plugin data and is rare in good code.

docs.title: 2.5 std::filesystem
docs.text: Portable paths and file operations: fs::path with / joining, exists, file_size, create_directories, remove_all, directory_iterator, recursive_directory_iterator, temp_directory_path, rename, last_write_time. Every operation has a throwing overload and an std::error_code& overload. GCC 9+ needs no extra library; GCC 8 needed -lstdc++fs.

docs.title: 2.6 Parallel algorithms
docs.text: std::sort(std::execution::par, b, e), also par_unseq, seq, for most algorithms plus std::reduce, std::transform_reduce, std::exclusive_scan. On GCC the implementation is Intel TBB: #include <execution> and link with -ltbb (apt install libtbb-dev). Your callable must be thread-safe and must not throw (an exception in a parallel algorithm calls std::terminate). Speed-ups appear for large inputs with real work per element; a 10k-element sort is faster serial.

docs.title: 2.7 Fold expressions and variadic improvements
docs.text: (args + ...), (std::cout << ... << args), ((xs > 0) && ...) (module 08). Also if constexpr, and auto as a non-type template parameter.

docs.title: 2.8 Inline variables
docs.text: inline constexpr int kVersion = 3; in a header: one object across all translation units (module 11). static constexpr members no longer need an out-of-class definition.

docs.title: 2.9 Attributes: [[nodiscard]], [[maybe_unused]], [[fallthrough]]
docs.text:
• [[nodiscard]] on a function (or a type): discarding the return value is a warning, an error with -Werror. Put it on anything returning an error code, a bool success flag, a handle, or a value whose computation is the only effect (empty(), size()).
  • [[maybe_unused]] silences unused-variable/parameter warnings for things used only under #ifdef or in assert.
  • [[fallthrough]]; documents an intentional case fall-through so -Wimplicit-fallthrough stays quiet.

docs.title: 2.10 Class template argument deduction (CTAD)
docs.text: std::pair p{1, 2.5};, std::vector v{1, 2, 3};, std::lock_guard lock(mu);, std::shared_lock lock(rw_mutex);, std::tuple t{1, 'c', "s"};. Deduction follows constructor parameters or explicit deduction guides (module 10's overloaded uses one). Trap: std::vector v{other_vector}; deduces vector<int> (copy), not vector<vector<int>>.

docs.title: 2.11 std::byte
docs.text: An enum class over unsigned char with only bitwise operators: raw memory that cannot be accidentally added or printed as a character. std::to_integer<int>(b) converts explicitly. Use it for buffers and arena storage (std::byte buf[4096]); it aliases anything like char.

docs.title: 2.12 std::shared_mutex and std::scoped_lock
docs.text: std::shared_mutex (C++17; shared_timed_mutex was C++14): many threads may hold it in shared mode (std::shared_lock), or one in exclusive mode (std::unique_lock). Right for read-mostly data (configuration, a key-value cache) where readers outnumber writers heavily. std::scoped_lock locks several mutexes at once in a deadlock-free order. Both are covered in depth in 04_Concurrency/03_mutexes_lock_guard_unique_lock.md; here you get the shape of the tcpkv store.

docs.title: 2.13 Smaller items
docs.text: Guaranteed copy elision (module 04), std::size/std::data/std::empty free functions, std::clamp, std::gcd/std::lcm, std::apply, std::invoke, std::not_fn, std::as_const, std::uncaught_exceptions, __has_include, hexadecimal floating literals, u8 character literals, static_assert without a message, nested namespaces namespace a::b::c {}, std::map::try_emplace and insert_or_assign, extract/merge of map nodes, std::sample, std::launder, std::aligned_alloc, std::hardware_destructive_interference_size, removal of auto_ptr, random_shuffle, trigraphs, register and dynamic exception specifications.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m13_cpp17_tour.cpp touches every language-level item:

inline constexpr int kProtocolVersion = 3;

auto [count, mean] = compute({1.0, 2.0, 6.0});
for (const auto& [name, age] : ages) ...
if (auto [it, inserted] = ages.insert({"ann", 99}); !inserted) ...
if (auto it = ages.find("bob"); it != ages.end()) ... else ...

std::string_view trim(std::string_view s) {              // O(1) slicing, no allocation
    while (!s.empty() && s.front() == ' ') s.remove_prefix(1);
    while (!s.empty() && s.back() == ' ') s.remove_suffix(1);
    return s;
}

std::pair p{1, 2.5};  std::vector words{std::string("a"), std::string("b")};  std::tuple t{1, 'c', "txt"};
template <class... Ts> constexpr bool all_positive(Ts... xs) { return ((xs > 0) && ...); }

[[nodiscard]] bool try_reserve(std::vector<int>& v, std::size_t n);
[[maybe_unused]] bool ok = try_reserve(buf, 2'000'000);  assert(!ok);

std::any a = 42;  a = std::string("now a string");  std::any_cast<std::string>(&a);
std::byte b{0x0F};  b <<= 4;  std::to_integer<int>(b);

fs::path dir = fs::temp_directory_path() / "m13_demo";
fs::create_directories(dir);
for (const auto& entry : fs::directory_iterator(dir)) entry.path().filename(), entry.file_size();
fs::remove_all(dir);

code/m13_shared_mutex_cache.cpp is the read-mostly store:

class KvStore {
public:
    std::optional<std::string> get(const std::string& key) const {
        std::shared_lock lock(mu_);              // readers run concurrently
        auto it = map_.find(key);
        return it == map_.end() ? std::nullopt : std::optional<std::string>(it->second);   // copy out under the lock
    }
    void put(const std::string& key, std::string value) {
        std::unique_lock lock(mu_);              // exclusive
        map_[key] = std::move(value);
    }
private:
    mutable std::shared_mutex mu_;               // mutable: const get() may lock
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string> map_;
};

Four reader threads and one writer run against it; the program prints the hit count and the final state. Note mutable on the mutex and that get returns a copy, never a reference into the map.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Structured bindings are not variables. auto [a, b] = f(); creates a hidden object e of the returned type and makes a and b names for e.first/e.second (or get<0>(e), get<1>(e) for tuple-like types, or the members in order for aggregates). There is no copy of a and b individually; decltype(a) is the member's declared type, even though a behaves like a reference. With auto& the hidden object is a reference and no copy happens at all.

std::string_view ABI. Two words, passed in registers (rdi, rsi) on x86-64, trivially copyable; const std::string& is one pointer but requires a std::string object to exist (a literal argument creates a temporary with a heap allocation if longer than 15 bytes). string_view::substr is pointer arithmetic; std::string::substr allocates.

std::variant vs union vs inheritance. variant is a union with an index byte and compiler-generated copy/move/destroy that switch on the index. Storage is max(sizeof(Ts...)) rounded to max(alignof(Ts...)) plus the index. No heap, no vptr.

std::any storage. libstdc++ stores types that fit in a pointer-sized buffer and are nothrow-movable inline; everything else is heap-allocated. Each any holds a pointer to a static manager function per stored type (effectively a hand-rolled vtable), which is how any_cast checks the type via typeid comparison.

std::shared_mutex on Linux is pthread_rwlock_t (56 bytes, vs 40 for std::mutex). Taking a shared lock is an atomic increment of a reader count when no writer holds or waits; a writer waits for readers to drain. glibc's rwlock prefers readers by default (PTHREAD_RWLOCK_PREFER_READER_NP), which can starve writers under constant read load; the writer-preferring variant exists but std::shared_mutex does not expose it. Uncontended shared lock/unlock is slower than a plain mutex (more atomic operations), so a shared mutex only wins when critical sections are long enough or readers numerous enough that parallel readers pay for the extra cost. Measure. For very short reads a plain std::mutex or a lock-free snapshot (shared_ptr<const Config> swap) is often faster.

CTAD mechanics. The compiler synthesises a set of function templates from the class's constructors (and from explicit deduction guides), performs overload resolution on them with the constructor arguments, and uses the deduced class template arguments. That is why std::vector v{other}; picks the copy constructor's deduction (vector) rather than the initializer-list constructor.

[[nodiscard]] codegen. None; it is purely a compile-time diagnostic. The same is true for all attributes here. [[fallthrough]] suppresses a warning; [[maybe_unused]] suppresses another.

std::filesystem and errors. The throwing overloads throw std::filesystem::filesystem_error (derived from std::system_error) carrying both paths and the error_code. The error_code& overloads never throw and are the right choice in servers (fs::remove(path, ec)). Path operations are string manipulation and never touch the disk; exists, file_size etc. are stat calls.

Parallel algorithms and TBB. libstdc++ delegates to Intel's PSTL on top of TBB's task scheduler (work-stealing thread pool, one worker per hardware thread). par_unseq additionally allows vectorisation within a thread, which forbids anything that could deadlock across lanes (no locks in the callable). Without -ltbb the link fails with undefined tbb:: symbols.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• [[nodiscard]] everywhere a C programmer forgets to check. On error_code-returning functions, bool try_*, release(), factory functions returning handles. With -Werror the compiler enforces the check that code review used to miss.
  • string_view parameters, std::string members. Accept views at the API, store strings. A member string_view is a lifetime bug waiting for a reused buffer. In a parser, views into the request buffer are fine within the request's processing; anything that outlives it must copy.
  • Structured bindings in map loops remove the .first/.second noise that hides bugs (it->second.second). Name the parts.
  • shared_mutex for config and caches, not for everything. In tcpkv the store is read-mostly, so readers in parallel is a real win; a mostly-written structure under a shared_mutex is slower than under a std::mutex. Profile with perf and look at pthread_rwlock_* time.
  • std::filesystem in servers. Use the error_code overloads; a missing directory is a normal condition, not an exception. fs::rename is atomic within a filesystem (the write-temp-then-rename pattern for crash-safe config updates).
  • Parallel algorithms are a tool for batch jobs, not for request paths: the TBB pool competes with your own thread pool for cores and adds tail latency. Use them in offline tooling (report generation, migration jobs) where throughput is all that matters.
  • 3 AM debugging. A std::string_view printing garbage or crashing in operator<<: dangling view. gdb shows a _M_str pointer into freed heap. Search for views stored in members or captured by lambdas that outlive the string. ASan reports it as heap-use-after-free with the allocation and free stacks.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m13_cpp17_tour.cpp. Remove the [[maybe_unused]] and build with -DNDEBUG. Then remove the if (!try_reserve(...)) check. Done when you have seen both warnings become errors and can explain each.
  2. (easy) Rewrite a function of yours taking const std::string& to take std::string_view, and call it with a literal, a std::string, and a substring. Count allocations with a counting operator new. Done when the view version allocates zero times.
  3. (medium) Write a config_reload(const fs::path&) that writes to path + ".tmp", fsyncs, and fs::renames over the original, using error_code overloads throughout. Done when killing the process at any point leaves either the old or the new file intact, never a partial one.
  4. (medium) Benchmark m13_shared_mutex_cache.cpp with std::shared_mutex vs std::mutex for reader:writer ratios 100:1, 10:1, 1:1 and critical sections of 100 ns and 10 us (add a spin). Done when you have a table and can say where shared_mutex wins on your machine.
  5. (hard) Install libtbb-dev and sort a std::vector<std::uint64_t> of 1M, 10M and 100M elements with std::sort vs std::sort(std::execution::par, ...). Done when you have the speed-ups and perf stat shows the number of threads used; explain the 1M result.
  6. (hard) Implement template <class... Ts> class TypeMap using a std::tuple<std::optional<Ts>...> with get<T>()/set<T>() via fold expressions and if constexpr, and a visit_all(f) that calls f on each present value. Done when static_asserts verify it is constexpr-constructible and a test covers an empty map.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What are structured bindings and what can you bind? A declaration auto [a, b] = expr; that names the parts of a pair, tuple, std::array, C array, or struct with all-public members. The names alias the members of a hidden object (copy, or reference with auto&); you cannot skip or nest.

Q: std::string_view versus const std::string&: when and why? Use string_view for read-only string parameters: it is two words passed in registers, accepts literals and char* without constructing a std::string, and slices in O(1). Keep const std::string& (or std::string) when you need a null-terminated C string or will store the value. Never store a view that may outlive its source.

Q: What does [[nodiscard]] do? Marks a function (or type) whose return value must not be silently discarded; ignoring it produces a compiler warning, an error with -Werror. It has no runtime effect. Use it on error codes, success flags, handles and pure computations.

Q: What is CTAD? Class template argument deduction: the compiler deduces a class template's arguments from the constructor arguments, so std::pair p{1, 2.5} and std::lock_guard lock(mu) need no angle brackets. Deduction uses the constructors and any user-written deduction guides.

Q: How does std::shared_mutex differ from std::mutex, and when does it help? It allows many concurrent shared (read) holders or one exclusive (write) holder. On Linux it is a pthread_rwlock_t. It helps when reads greatly outnumber writes and critical sections are long enough to amortise its higher per-lock cost; for very short sections a plain mutex is often faster. Readers can starve writers with glibc's default policy.

Q: Why does std::vector v{other_vector}; not create a vector of vectors? CTAD prefers the copy-constructor deduction over the initializer-list constructor when the braced list holds a single element of the same template. Write std::vector<std::vector<int>> v{other}; or std::vector v{other, other2}; to get the nested type.

Q: What do you need to use parallel algorithms on GCC? #include <execution>, an execution policy argument (std::execution::par), and linking against Intel TBB (-ltbb). The callable must be thread-safe and must not throw.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Structured bindings and if-initialisers tighten scope and remove .first/.second noise.
  • string_view for read-only string parameters; never store a view beyond its source's lifetime.
  • optional, variant, any: inline, inline, type-erased; prefer variant over any.
  • filesystem: use the error_code overloads in servers; rename is atomic.
  • Parallel algorithms need -ltbb on GCC and are for batch work.
  • Fold expressions, if constexpr, inline variables, CTAD, std::byte.
  • [[nodiscard]] turns forgotten checks into compile errors; [[maybe_unused]], [[fallthrough]] document intent.
  • std::shared_mutex = pthread_rwlock_t; wins only for read-mostly, long-enough critical sections; see 04_Concurrency for the full treatment.
  • Guaranteed copy elision, try_emplace, insert_or_assign, node extract/merge, std::clamp, std::apply, nested namespaces.

docs.title: 14. Writing production C++
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: all previous modules

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Knowing the language is half the job. The other half is the set of habits that make a C++ codebase survive five years and twenty engineers: how files are split, how the build is configured so the compiler finds bugs for you, how formatting and static analysis are automated so review time goes to design, what a reviewer looks for, and how an API is shaped so it is hard to misuse. This module collects those habits and ends with the API-design rules the tcpkv project will apply.

Analogy: a kitchen. The recipes are the language; the mise en place, labelled containers, sharp knives and a cleaning routine are what let the kitchen serve 300 covers a night without anyone getting hurt.

docs.title: 2.1 Project structure
docs.text:
tcpkv/
  CMakeLists.txt
  include/tcpkv/        public headers, one per public class or concept: kv_store.hpp, socket_fd.hpp
  src/                  implementation .cpp files, private headers
  tests/                one test file per header; a tiny main or Catch2/GoogleTest
  bench/                micro-benchmarks (Google Benchmark)
  tools/                clang-format, clang-tidy configs, scripts
  third_party/          vendored or FetchContent dependencies

Public headers live under a namespace-named directory so includes read #include <tcpkv/kv_store.hpp> and cannot collide with other libraries. Everything in a public header is API; everything else is free to change.

docs.title: 2.2 Headers vs sources
docs.text:
• A header declares; a source defines. Exceptions: templates, inline/constexpr functions, and class definitions (which are declarations of the type, with inline member function bodies allowed).
  • Every header must be self-contained: it includes what it uses and compiles on its own (g++ -fsyntax-only header.hpp or a per-header test). Never rely on the includer having included something first.
  • Include order in a .cpp: its own header first (proves self-containment), then project headers, then third-party, then standard library. Alphabetical within groups; clang-format does it.
  • Forward-declare (class Connection;) instead of including when you only need a pointer or reference. It cuts compile time and coupling.
  • Include guards. #pragma once is supported by every compiler you will use and is simpler than #ifndef TCPKV_KV_STORE_HPP. Either is fine; pick one for the project.
  • Minimise what a header exposes: private implementation details go in the .cpp or behind a pimpl (std::unique_ptr<Impl> impl_;) when ABI stability or compile-time isolation matters.

docs.title: 2.3 The One Definition Rule (ODR)
docs.text:
• A non-inline function or variable must be defined exactly once in the whole program. Two definitions = linker error ("multiple definition").
  • A class, inline function, template, or inline variable may be defined in several translation units, but every definition must be token-for-token identical with the same meaning. If they differ (same class name, different members, in two .cpp files; a header whose content depends on a macro that differs between TUs), the program is ill-formed with no diagnostic required: the linker picks one at random and the other TU reads garbage.
  • Anonymous namespaces (namespace { ... }) or static give internal linkage: safe to define the same name differently in different .cpp files.
  • Practical ODR hygiene: no #define that changes a header's layout (NDEBUG affecting struct members is the classic), no using namespace in headers, unique names for helper types in .cpp files (anonymous namespace), same compiler flags for every TU in a binary (-std, -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG, -fno-rtti).

docs.title: 2.4 Build flags that find bugs
docs.text:
-std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic
-Wshadow -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion -Wnon-virtual-dtor -Wold-style-cast -Wcast-align
-Wunused -Woverloaded-virtual -Wnull-dereference -Wdouble-promotion -Wformat=2 -Wimplicit-fallthrough
Debug:   -O0 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer   (and -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG for container checks)
Release: -O2 -g -DNDEBUG   (symbols split out with objcopy)
Thread tests: -fsanitize=thread (separate build; incompatible with ASan)

-Werror from day one. Warnings that are tolerated become warnings that are ignored.

docs.title: 2.5 clang-format and clang-tidy
docs.text:
• clang-format fixes layout mechanically. Commit a .clang-format (start from BasedOnStyle: Google or LLVM, set ColumnLimit, IndentWidth), run it in a pre-commit hook or CI check. Formatting never appears in review again.
  • clang-tidy is the static analyser. A reasonable .clang-tidy enables bugprone-*, performance-*, modernize-*, readability-*, cppcoreguidelines-* minus a few noisy ones. Key checks: bugprone-use-after-move, bugprone-dangling-handle (string_view), performance-unnecessary-copy-initialization, performance-for-range-copy, modernize-use-nullptr, cppcoreguidelines-owning-memory, misc-non-private-member-variables-in-classes. Run on changed files in CI (clang-tidy -p build/ file.cpp with a compile_commands.json from CMake).
  • cppcheck and include-what-you-use are useful extras; sanitisers (module 12) cover the runtime side.

docs.title: 2.6 C++ Core Guidelines highlights
docs.text:
The Core Guidelines (Stroustrup, Sutter; isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines) are long; these are the rules that matter most for your kind of code:

  • P.4 Ideally, a program should be statically type safe. ES.46 Avoid narrowing conversions.
  • R.1 Manage resources automatically using RAII. R.3 A raw pointer is non-owning. R.11 Avoid calling new and delete explicitly. R.20/21 Prefer unique_ptr over shared_ptr unless ownership is shared.
  • C.20 If you can avoid defining default operations, do (rule of zero). C.21 If you define any, define all (rule of five). C.35 A base class destructor should be public and virtual, or protected and non-virtual. C.46 explicit for single-argument constructors. C.128 Virtual functions specify exactly one of virtual, override, final.
  • F.15/F.16 Pass cheap types by value, others by const&. F.20 Return outputs by value. F.21 Return multiple values as a struct or tuple. F.43 Never return a pointer/reference to a local.
  • E.2/E.3 Throw to signal that a function cannot perform its task; use exceptions for errors only. E.6 Use RAII to prevent leaks. E.12 noexcept when throwing is impossible or unacceptable.
  • ES.20 Always initialise an object. ES.23 Prefer {} initialisation. ES.50 Do not cast away const. ES.100/101 Do not mix signed and unsigned arithmetic.
  • CP.1 Assume your code will run as part of a multithreaded program. CP.20 Use RAII, never plain lock()/unlock(). CP.21 Use std::lock or std::scoped_lock to acquire multiple mutexes.
  • SF.7 Do not write using namespace at global scope in a header. SF.8 Use include guards. SF.11 Header files should be self-contained.
  • Con.1/Con.4 By default, make objects immutable; use const to define objects whose values do not change.

docs.title: 2.7 Code review checklist
docs.text:
Ownership and lifetime

  • Every raw pointer: non-owning and the owner outlives it? Every new: inside a smart pointer? Every release(): documented hand-off?
  • References/views (string_view, span, iterators) stored in members or captured in lambdas: does the source outlive them?
  • Rule of zero or full rule of five; moves noexcept; moved-from state valid.

Correctness

  • override on every override; virtual destructor on polymorphic bases.
  • Comparators are strict weak orderings; std::tie for multi-field.
  • Containers: iterator invalidation across the loop body? operator[] on a map in a read path?
  • Signed/unsigned mixing, narrowing, uninitialised members, order of member initialisers.
  • Exceptions: what guarantee does this function give? noexcept only where true. Destructors do not throw.
  • Thread safety: which mutex protects this member? Is it stated in a comment next to the member?

API

  • explicit single-arg constructors; [[nodiscard]] on results that must be checked; const wherever possible.
  • Parameters: string_view/const& to read, by value to sink, pointer only when nullable.
  • No bool parameters that make call sites unreadable (send(data, true, false)): use an enum class.

Hygiene

  • Header self-contained, no using namespace in headers, no macros where constexpr/inline works.
  • Names say what things are; comments say why, not what.
  • Tests exist for the new behaviour and for the failure path.

docs.title: 2.8 Reading cppreference
docs.text: cppreference.com is the reference, not a tutorial. For any function: read the signature (which overloads, const, noexcept), the parameters and return value, then the complexity, the exceptions section (what guarantee), the iterator invalidation notes for containers, and the "since C++NN" markers so you do not use a C++20 feature in a C++17 build. The example at the bottom is compilable; paste it to verify behaviour. For library headers, the top-level page per header lists what it provides. For the language, the pages on value categories, lifetime, and undefined behaviour are worth reading once in full.

docs.title: 2.9 API design for a library (what tcpkv needs)
docs.text:
1. Make ownership visible in signatures. Factory returns std::unique_ptr<Connection> or a move-only value; functions borrowing take Connection&; nothing takes or returns an owning raw pointer.
  2. Make misuse a compile error. explicit constructors; deleted copy on identity types; [[nodiscard]] on error codes and handles; enum class for options; strong typedefs (struct Port { std::uint16_t value; }) instead of bare integers where they could be swapped.
  3. Make the common case the default. Sensible defaults in constructors; the simplest call does the right thing; advanced knobs behind an options struct, not a 9-parameter function.
  4. Choose the error-reporting style per layer (module 10) and state it in the header comment. tcpkv: constructors throw std::system_error; get/put/erase return values; nothing on the request path throws for client errors.
  5. Return copies or values from shared state, never references into a container another thread may mutate (the KvStore::get rule).
  6. Keep the ABI surface small. Public headers expose the minimum; pimpl for anything that may change its members; no std:: types across a C ABI (if tcpkv ever exposes a C API, it is extern "C" with opaque handles and plain types).
  7. Thread-safety contract in the header. "All public member functions are safe to call concurrently" or "externally synchronised" per class, next to the class comment.
  8. Document complexity and allocation. get is O(1) average and allocates one std::string for the returned copy; put may rehash.
  9. Test the API from the outside. A test that uses only the public header catches leaks of implementation details and verifies the header is self-contained.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/kv_store.hpp is a public header written to these rules, and code/m14_library_api_demo.cpp plays the role of both kv_store.cpp (implementation) and main.cpp (a user) in one file so the example builds with one command:

// kv_store.hpp
#pragma once
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <unordered_map>

namespace tcpkv {
class KvStore {
public:
    KvStore() = default;
    explicit KvStore(std::size_t expected_keys);          // explicit: 'KvStore s = 100;' must not compile

    KvStore(const KvStore&) = delete;                     // identity type: copying is a bug, so it is an error
    KvStore& operator=(const KvStore&) = delete;
    KvStore(KvStore&&) noexcept = default;                // but moving is fine and cheap
    KvStore& operator=(KvStore&&) noexcept = default;
    ~KvStore() = default;

    [[nodiscard]] std::optional<std::string> get(std::string_view key) const;   // copy out, never a reference in
    bool put(std::string_view key, std::string value);                          // sink parameter for the value
    [[nodiscard]] bool erase(std::string_view key);                             // the caller must look at the answer
    [[nodiscard]] bool contains(std::string_view key) const;
    [[nodiscard]] std::size_t size() const noexcept { return map_.size(); }
    void clear() noexcept { map_.clear(); }
private:
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string> map_;
};
}  // namespace tcpkv

// what would be kv_store.cpp
std::optional<std::string> KvStore::get(std::string_view key) const {
    auto it = map_.find(std::string(key));    // C++17 cost: materialise a key; C++20 heterogeneous lookup removes it
    if (it == map_.end()) return std::nullopt;
    return it->second;
}
bool KvStore::put(std::string_view key, std::string value) {
    auto [it, inserted] = map_.insert_or_assign(std::string(key), std::move(value));
    return inserted;
}

// what would be main.cpp
// store.erase("acct:1");                  // error under -Werror: [[nodiscard]] value ignored
bool erased = store.erase("acct:1");
tcpkv::KvStore moved = std::move(store);   // allowed
// tcpkv::KvStore copy = moved;            // error: deleted
static_assert(!std::is_copy_constructible_v<tcpkv::KvStore>);
static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<tcpkv::KvStore>);

Try to misuse the API (copy it, ignore erase's result, construct from a bare integer) and read the three compile errors. That is the API doing the reviewer's job.

A minimal CMakeLists.txt for the layout in 2.1:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(tcpkv CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)            # compile_commands.json for clang-tidy

add_library(tcpkv src/kv_store.cpp src/socket_fd.cpp)
target_include_directories(tcpkv PUBLIC include)
target_compile_options(tcpkv PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wnon-virtual-dtor)
find_package(Threads REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(tcpkv PUBLIC Threads::Threads)

add_executable(tcpkv_server src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(tcpkv_server PRIVATE tcpkv)

enable_testing()
add_executable(kv_store_test tests/kv_store_test.cpp)
target_link_libraries(kv_store_test PRIVATE tcpkv)
add_test(NAME kv_store COMMAND kv_store_test)

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What the linker does with inline and template definitions. Each TU emits inline functions, template instantiations, inline variables and vtables as weak symbols in COMDAT groups (sections named .text._Z..., with .section ... ,"axG",@progbits,<name>,comdat). The linker keeps the first group with a given name and discards the rest. It does not compare contents: if two TUs produced different code for the same symbol (an ODR violation), one TU's callers silently run the other's code. -Wodr with -flto is the only compile-time check; otherwise it shows as "impossible" behaviour.

Why a header-only change rebuilds everything. Each .cpp is preprocessed into one giant TU containing every included header, and make/ninja rebuild a TU when any of its dependencies' timestamps change (dependencies are tracked with -MMD). Touching a header included by 300 files costs 300 compilations. Forward declarations, pimpl, and smaller headers are compile-time engineering. Precompiled headers and C++20 modules attack the same problem.

#pragma once vs guards. Guards are pure preprocessor; the compiler still opens and tokenises the file to find the #endif on later includes (GCC optimises this away when it recognises the guard pattern). #pragma once lets the compiler skip the file by identity (inode/path), which is why it is not in the standard: file identity is not portable in theory. In practice both are fine.

Symbol visibility. By default every non-static symbol in a shared library is exported, making the .so large and every type part of the ABI. -fvisibility=hidden plus __attribute__((visibility("default"))) (or a TCPKV_API macro) on the public API shrinks the export table, speeds up loading, and lets the compiler optimise internal calls as if they were static. It is the Linux equivalent of __declspec(dllexport) on Windows.

-Werror and compiler upgrades. New GCC versions add warnings to -Wall; a -Werror build can break on a compiler upgrade without any code change. Pin the compiler version in CI and bump it deliberately, fixing the new warnings in the same change.

clang-tidy's model. It runs the Clang front end on each TU using the exact flags from compile_commands.json, builds the AST, and matches checks against it. It therefore sees templates only as instantiated in that TU and sees macros expanded. It is slow (seconds per file); run it on the diff in CI and on the whole tree nightly.

Sanitiser interaction with the ODR. ASan has an ODR-violation detector for global variables with the same name in different TUs (detect_odr_violation=2); it fires at start-up and is one of the few runtime checks for the problem.

Debug symbols and -g. DWARF debug info can be several times the size of the code. -g does not change the generated machine code at any -O level; build release with -O2 -g, then objcopy --only-keep-debug server server.debug; strip --strip-debug server; objcopy --add-gnu-debuglink=server.debug server. gdb finds the .debug file by the link (and by build-id in /usr/lib/debug). You get symbolised core dumps from production without shipping symbols.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Day one checklist for tcpkv (or any new C++ project): -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror, a .clang-format, a .clang-tidy, a sanitiser CI job, a test target, compile_commands.json, and a README section titled "Error handling policy" and "Thread-safety conventions". It takes an hour and saves weeks.
  • The header is the contract. When reviewing, read the header first and ask: can I misuse this? If a reviewer needs to read the .cpp to know who owns a pointer or whether a function throws, the header is incomplete.
  • Review for lifetime first. Most severe C++ bugs are lifetime bugs (dangling reference, use after move, iterator invalidation, view outliving its string). Logic bugs are caught by tests; lifetime bugs often are not, so reviewers should spend their attention there.
  • Fix warnings at the source, never with casts. A -Wsign-conversion warning on v[i] with int i is fixed by making i a std::size_t, not by static_cast<size_t>(i) at the use site.
  • Treat clang-tidy findings as bugs until proven otherwise. NOLINT with a reason is acceptable; bare NOLINT is a review finding.
  • Keep the build reproducible. Same compiler, same flags, same standard library for every TU; pinned third-party versions; no "works on my machine" -D flags. ODR violations and ABI mismatches come from inconsistency, not from the language.
  • 3 AM debugging. "Impossible" crash in code that has not changed: check whether all objects were built with the same flags after a header changed (stale object files, two definitions of a struct with different #ifdefs). nm -C the objects and compare the symbol list; -Wodr -flto on a clean build usually names the culprit.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Split m14_library_api_demo.cpp into kv_store.cpp and main.cpp, build with the CMakeLists.txt above, and run clang-tidy -p build src/kv_store.cpp. Done when the build is warning-free and you have read every tidy finding.
  2. (easy) Create an ODR violation on purpose: define struct Config { int a; }; in one .cpp and struct Config { int a; int b; }; in another, each with a function that constructs and prints it, both non-inline. Link and run. Done when you can explain the (lack of) diagnostic and have seen -flto -Wodr catch it.
  3. (medium) Add a SocketFd (module 03) header to the tcpkv layout, write a test that uses only the public header, and add -fvisibility=hidden with a TCPKV_API macro. Done when nm -D libtcpkv.so lists only the intended symbols.
  4. (medium) Take any 200-line C++ file you have written during this course, run clang-tidy with bugprone-*,performance-*,modernize-*,readability-*, and fix every finding without NOLINT. Done when it is clean and you can name the three most common findings.
  5. (hard) Write the public header for tcpkv's Connection class (move-only, owns a SocketFd, read_message() returning std::optional<Message> or an error_code, write(std::string_view) returning error_code), with the thread-safety contract and error policy in comments. Have someone (or a later you) try to misuse it from a test. Done when every misuse you can think of is a compile error or a documented behaviour.
  6. (hard) Set up a GitHub Actions (or local script) pipeline: clang-format check, build with -Werror, tests under ASan+UBSan, tests under TSan, clang-tidy on the diff. Done when a deliberate use-after-move and a deliberate data race each fail the pipeline with a readable report.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the One Definition Rule? Every non-inline function and variable must be defined exactly once in the program (the linker enforces this). Classes, templates, inline functions and inline variables may be defined in many translation units but every definition must be identical; if not, the program is ill-formed with no diagnostic required, and the linker silently picks one definition.

Q: What makes a header self-contained and why does it matter? It includes everything it uses and compiles on its own. Otherwise it works only when included after some other header, which breaks when include order changes and hides the real dependency graph. The "own header first" include order in .cpp files tests it on every build.

Q: #pragma once or include guards? Both prevent double inclusion. #pragma once is non-standard but universally supported and uses file identity; guards are standard but need a unique macro per file. Pick one per project; the choice is not worth a debate.

Q: How do you keep a shared library's ABI stable? Hide implementation behind a pimpl or opaque handle, do not expose standard-library types or templates across the boundary, only append virtual functions (or avoid virtual in the ABI), use -fvisibility=hidden with an explicit export macro, and never change the layout of exported structs without a version bump.

Q: What do you look for first in a C++ code review? Lifetime and ownership: who owns each pointer, do references/views outlive their source, use after move, iterator invalidation, thread-safety of shared members. Then the API shape (can it be misused?), then exception guarantees, then style, which should already be automated.

Q: What is the role of clang-tidy versus the compiler's warnings? Compiler warnings catch local, syntactic issues quickly. clang-tidy does deeper, slower semantic analysis on the AST: use after move, dangling string_view, unnecessary copies, modernisation, Core Guidelines rules. Run warnings on every build and tidy on the diff in CI.

Q: How do you ship optimised binaries but still debug core dumps? Build with -O2 -g, split the DWARF info into a separate file with objcopy --only-keep-debug, strip the binary, add a .gnu_debuglink, and keep the debug file by build-id. gdb loads it when analysing the core.

Q: Name five Core Guidelines rules you apply every day. Manage resources with RAII (R.1); a raw pointer is non-owning (R.3); rule of zero or rule of five (C.20/C.21); explicit single-argument constructors (C.46); virtual functions specify exactly one of virtual/override/final (C.128); return outputs by value (F.20); never return a reference to a local (F.43); use RAII for locks (CP.20).

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Layout: include/<project>/ public headers, src/, tests/, bench/; headers declare, sources define.
  • Headers self-contained, own header first, forward-declare where possible, #pragma once or guards.
  • ODR: one definition for non-inline entities; identical definitions for inline/templates/classes; violations are undiagnosed. Same flags for every TU.
  • -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror plus -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wnon-virtual-dtor; sanitisers in CI; -O2 -g with split debug info in release.
  • clang-format removes style from review; clang-tidy finds use-after-move, dangling views, copies.
  • Review lifetime first, then API misuse, then guarantees; style is automated.
  • Core Guidelines: RAII, non-owning raw pointers, rule of zero/five, explicit, override, return by value.
  • cppreference: read signature, complexity, exceptions, invalidation, "since C++NN".
  • API design: ownership in signatures, misuse as compile error, defaults for the common case, stated error policy and thread-safety contract, copies out of shared state, small ABI surface.

docs.title: 02_Modern_CPP — All exercises
docs.text:
Every exercise from the "Try it" section of all 14 modules, in one place. The module file has the full wording and the exact "done when" condition; this list gives the short version plus a hint.

Build everything in WSL with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread unless the exercise says otherwise. Do the easy ones the same day you read the module. Do at least one medium per module. Pick the hard ones that match the job you want: the ownership, invalidation, vtable and performance ones come up most in interviews.

Difficulty count: 28 easy, 29 medium, 24 hard (81 total).

docs.title: 01. From C to C++ (01_from_c_to_cpp.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) swap_values(int&, int&) with references, plus the C pointer version.
    • Hint: a reference must bind to an object at initialisation, so there is no nullptr to pass. Try swap_values(*p, *q) with a null p and note that the UB moves to the caller's dereference.
  2. (easy) Build m01_extern_c_mangling.cpp, run nm with and without -C, and decode the mangled name of std::string greet(const std::string&, int).
    • Hint: R = reference, K = const, P = pointer, i = int, c = char. std::string shows up as a long NSt7__cxx1112basic_string... chunk; c++filt confirms your reading.
  3. (medium) Rename a 100-line C file to .cpp and fix every error under -Werror.
    • Hint: malloc needs static_cast<T*>, identifiers named new/class/this must be renamed, and string literals are const char*, not char*.
  4. (medium) C header + gcc -c object, called from C++ with extern "C" guards.
    • Hint: wrap the declarations in #ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { #endif in the header itself, not in main.cpp, so every C++ includer gets it for free.
  5. (hard) Predict which log overload is chosen for NULL, 0, 'x', 3.0f, nullptr.
    • Hint: GCC defines NULL as __null, an integer zero with the width of a pointer, so on 64-bit Linux log(NULL) picks long, not const char* (other compilers differ). 3.0f is a float-to-double promotion; 'x' promotes to int; only nullptr reaches const char*.

docs.title: 02. Classes, constructors and destructors (02_classes_constructors_destructors.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) Predict the output of m02_ctor_dtor_order.cpp on paper, then run it.
    • Hint: bases first, then members in declaration order, then the constructor body. Destruction is the exact reverse.
  2. (easy) Add Tracer c to Derived and list it first in the initialiser list; see -Wreorder.
    • Hint: members are initialised in declaration order, never in initialiser-list order.
  3. (medium) Temperature with an explicit constructor and a from_fahrenheit factory.
    • Hint: explicit blocks copy-initialisation (T t = 36.6;) but not direct-initialisation (T t{36.6};). A named static factory documents the unit at the call site.
  4. (medium) A class whose second member's constructor throws; observe which destructors run.
    • Hint: only fully constructed subobjects are destroyed. The outer object's lifetime never began, so its destructor does not run. This is why each resource needs its own RAII member.
  5. (hard) Function-local static singleton; find __cxa_guard_acquire in -O2 -S output.
    • Hint: look for a byte-sized guard variable tested with a plain load before the call. Once it is set, later calls take the fast path and never reach the lock.

docs.title: 03. RAII (03_raii_the_core_idea.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) Add an early-return path to m03_file_handle_raii.cpp; show fclose still runs.
    • Hint: put a printf in the destructor. Every path that leaves the scope runs it.
  2. (easy) DirHandle wrapping opendir/closedir, move-only, listing /tmp.
    • Hint: copy FileHandle's shape exactly: delete copy, write move ctor/assign that null the source, and check for null in the destructor.
  3. (medium) Rewrite the C process() from section 2.1 with RAII; count lines before and after.
    • Hint: each goto cleanup label becomes one RAII local. Declare them in acquisition order so the reverse-order destruction matches what the C code did by hand.
  4. (medium) Generic ScopeGuard with dismiss(), used to roll back map.erase(key).
    • Hint: template <class F> class ScopeGuard { F f_; bool active_ = true; ... }. Make the destructor noexcept and call f_() only while active_. Call dismiss() after the last step succeeds.
  5. (hard) strace -e trace=socket,bind,listen,close on m03_socket_fd_raii.cpp, then add a double-close bug and see EBADF.
    • Hint: the second close on the same number fails because the kernel already freed that fd slot. In a threaded server the slot may have been reused, so the "harmless" bug closes someone else's socket.
  6. (hard) Find the landing pad for write_report in -O2 -S output.
    • Hint: search for _Unwind_Resume. The block just before it calls fclose; the normal path reaches fclose separately and has no flag checks. The .gcc_except_table maps call sites to pads.

docs.title: 04. Value semantics, copy and move (04_value_semantics_copy_move.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m04_copy_elision_nrvo.cpp with and without -fno-elide-constructors.
    • Hint: in C++17, prvalue elision is mandatory and the flag cannot disable it; only NRVO and the move from a named local appear when you pass the flag.
  2. (easy) Drop noexcept from UniqueFd's move constructor and static_assert it.
    • Hint: vector uses std::move_if_noexcept during reallocation. A move-only type is still moved (there is no copy to fall back on), but the strong guarantee is lost.
  3. (medium) Matrix with rule of five and copy-and-swap; zero copies in Matrix m = a * b;.
    • Hint: operator* returns a prvalue, so m is constructed in place. Write Matrix& operator=(Matrix other) noexcept { swap(other); return *this; } to get both assignments at once.
  4. (medium) Sink set_name(std::string) vs the const&/&& overload pair; 6-cell table.
    • Hint: the sink version costs one extra move in every case. The pair wins only when moves are expensive or the function is very hot; a std::string move is a few pointer stores.
  5. (hard) Fixed-capacity container with template <class... Args> T& emplace(Args&&...).
    • Hint: ::new (static_cast<void*>(slot)) T(std::forward<Args>(args)...). Without std::forward every argument is an lvalue and you get a COPY where you expected a MOVE.
  6. (hard) Fix void f(std::string&& s) { names.push_back(s); }.
    • Hint: s has a name, so it is an lvalue and push_back(const T&) is chosen. Use std::move(s). The compiler is right not to warn: the code is valid, just slower.

docs.title: 05. Smart pointers and ownership (05_smart_pointers_and_ownership.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) unique_ptr alias for DIR* with a stateless deleter; static_assert on sizeof.
    • Hint: struct DirCloser { void operator()(DIR* d) const noexcept { closedir(d); } };. An empty deleter takes no space thanks to the empty-base optimisation. A function pointer deleter doubles the size.
  2. (easy) Make Node::parent a shared_ptr and run under valgrind --leak-check=full.
    • Hint: the report shows "definitely lost" for the root block and "indirectly lost" for the children. The cycle keeps every strong count at 1 or more after main's pointer dies.
  3. (medium) Connection : enable_shared_from_this with an async callback that keeps it alive.
    • Hint: capture self = shared_from_this() in the lambda. The object must already be owned by a shared_ptr (create it with make_shared), or shared_from_this throws bad_weak_ptr.
  4. (medium) Toy SharedPtr<T> with a plain then an atomic count; benchmark 1 vs 4 threads.
    • Hint: the atomic increment is a lock xadd. From four threads the cache line holding the count bounces between cores, so it is much slower per copy than the single-thread case.
  5. (hard) Ownership graph for a tcpkv-style server, with a type on every edge.
    • Hint: Server owns the listener by value, the pool by value, and the store by value. Workers receive the store by reference. A connection is a unique_ptr moved into the task. shared_ptr only appears if a connection truly has two owners (for example, async I/O plus a registry).

docs.title: 06. STL containers (06_stl_containers_deep_dive.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) Element type with a non-noexcept move in m06_vector_growth.cpp; see copies.
    • Hint: the rule is "move if nothrow-movable or not copyable, else copy", so that a throw half-way through reallocation leaves the old buffer intact.
  2. (easy) 1M ints in std::set vs a sorted vector; time inserts and lookups.
    • Hint: each set node is a separate allocation of roughly 40 bytes (typical on 64-bit libstdc++), so every step of a lookup is a likely cache miss. Binary search on a vector touches far fewer lines.
  3. (medium) AccountKey { branch, number } as a key for unordered_map and map.
    • Hint: specialise std::hash<AccountKey> in namespace std and combine with h1 ^ (h2 + 0x9e3779b9 + (h1 << 6) + (h1 >> 2)). For map, std::tie(a.branch, a.number) < std::tie(...).
  4. (medium) LRU cache with std::list plus unordered_map<K, list::iterator>.
    • Hint: list::splice relinks the node without copying or destroying it, so every iterator to it stays valid. Evict from back() and erase the map entry using the key stored in the node.
  5. (hard) Three deliberate invalidation bugs under -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG and then ASan.
    • Hint: the debug STL reports "attempt to dereference a singular iterator" at the bad line. ASan only reports if freed memory is actually touched, so the vector case is the one it catches best.
  6. (hard) std::map vs sorted vector<pair> + lower_bound at 1k, 100k, 10M.
    • Hint: at 1k both fit in L1/L2 and differ little. As size grows the map's pointer chasing costs a cache miss per level while the vector's top levels stay hot. Report what you measure, not what you expect.

docs.title: 07. STL algorithms, lambdas, iterators (07_stl_algorithms_lambdas_iterators.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) Replace sum, find-first and remove-matching loops with algorithms.
    • Hint: std::accumulate needs <numeric> and an initial value of the right type (0LL, not 0, for paise). Remove-matching is v.erase(std::remove_if(...), v.end()).
  2. (easy) <= comparator on 1000 equal elements, under -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG or ASan.
    • Hint: strict weak ordering requires comp(a, a) == false. With <= the unguarded inner loop of introsort can run past the end of the array.
  3. (medium) top_k with sort, partial_sort, nth_element + sort of the prefix.
    • Hint: full sort is O(n log n); partial_sort is O(n log k) with a heap; nth_element is O(n) average and then sorting k items is trivial. Expect nth_element to win for k = 10.
  4. (medium) vector<std::function> handler registry vs a std::tuple of lambdas.
    • Hint: std::function is an indirect call that the optimiser usually cannot inline. The tuple version, walked with std::apply and a fold, gives the compiler every concrete type to inline.
  5. (hard) Zero-copy word-frequency counter with string_view keys and partial_sort.
    • Hint: keep the whole file in one std::string that outlives the map, or every key dangles. Call reserve on the map to avoid rehash churn.
  6. (hard) Bidirectional-only algorithm that rejects forward iterators via iterator_traits.
    • Hint: static_assert(std::is_base_of_v<std::bidirectional_iterator_tag, typename std::iterator_traits<It>::iterator_category>, "needs bidirectional"). Random-access tags derive from bidirectional, so vector passes.

docs.title: 08. Templates (08_templates_and_generic_programming.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) print_all with a type that has no operator<<; find "required from here".
    • Hint: read the error bottom-up. The first "required from here" line that names your own file is the call to fix.
  2. (easy) static_assert(std::is_arithmetic_v<T>, ...) at the top of max_of.
    • Hint: the assertion fires before the body is instantiated, so the long cascade disappears.
  3. (medium) StaticVector<T, N> with placement new into aligned storage.
    • Hint: alignas(T) std::byte buf_[N * sizeof(T)];, construct with placement new, destroy with std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(...))->~T() only for indices below size_.
  4. (medium) has_size_v with std::void_t, then the same check with if constexpr.
    • Hint: primary template : std::false_type; specialisation on std::void_t<decltype(std::declval<T&>().size())> : std::true_type.
  5. (hard) Variadic compose(fs...) applying right-to-left; compose() is identity.
    • Hint: recurse: compose(f, rest...) returns [=](auto x) { return f(compose(rest...)(x)); }. The base case is a lambda that returns its argument unchanged.
  6. (hard) -ftime-report on a heavy file, then extern template across five .cpp files.
    • Hint: put extern template class Foo<int>; in the header and one template class Foo<int>; in exactly one .cpp. Measure total wall time with a clean build each time.

docs.title: 09. OOP, inheritance, virtual (09_oop_inheritance_virtual.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) -fdump-lang-class on m09_vtable_demo.cpp; read Vtable for Circle.
    • Hint: slot 0 is offset-to-top, slot 1 is the typeinfo pointer, then the function entries. The two destructor entries are the "complete object" destructor and the "deleting" destructor.
  2. (easy) Remove virtual from ~Shape; find -Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor.
    • Hint: delete base_ptr then calls only ~Shape, so the derived part is never destroyed. It is UB formally, and in practice it leaks whatever the derived class owns.
  3. (medium) C struct ops + void* ctx rewritten as an abstract Device interface.
    • Hint: the function pointer table becomes the vtable and ctx becomes the derived class's members. Tests inject a FakeDevice through a Device& parameter.
  4. (medium) 100M shape->area() calls: uniform, alternating, and std::variant + std::visit.
    • Hint: uniform types let the indirect-branch predictor hit every time. Alternating may still predict well on modern CPUs; measure. variant keeps objects contiguous and lets the compiler inline.
  5. (hard) Plugin .so with extern "C" Plugin* create(), loaded by dlopen/dlsym.
    • Hint: dlsym looks up a plain string, so the factory must not be mangled. Virtual calls need no symbol lookup at all: they go through the vptr stored in the object. Link the host with -ldl on older glibc.
  6. (hard) -O2 -S on calls through a final class vs a non-final one.
    • Hint: with final, the compiler knows the dynamic type exactly and emits a direct call (or inlines it). Without it you see a load of the vptr then call QWORD PTR [rax+N].

docs.title: 10. Error handling (10_error_handling_exceptions_optional_expected.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) Swap the two lines in add_strong and throw on the 3rd allocation.
    • Hint: if the total is updated before the push that can throw, a failed push leaves the total wrong. Do the throwing step first, then the non-throwing commit.
  2. (easy) std::optional<Account> find_account(std::string_view) with no sentinel values.
    • Hint: if (auto a = find_account("X")) { use(a->balance); }. value_or needs a full default Account, so it suits small types best.
  3. (medium) KvErr enum, KvCategory, make_error_code, and is_error_code_enum.
    • Hint: specialise std::is_error_code_enum<KvErr> : std::true_type in namespace std, and put make_error_code in the same namespace as KvErr so argument-dependent lookup finds it.
  4. (medium) Expected<T, E> on std::variant<T, E> with a short-circuiting map.
    • Hint: map(f) returns Expected<decltype(f(value())), E>; if this holds an error, return that error without calling f. Make sure T and E are distinct types, or the variant is ambiguous.
  5. (hard) optional<int> vs throwing parse_port at 0%, 1%, 50% invalid input.
    • Hint: the throwing version is free on the happy path and costs on the order of a microsecond per throw (typical), because unwinding walks tables and allocates the exception object.
  6. (hard) Thread-pool worker that captures task exceptions into std::exception_ptr.
    • Hint: catch (...) { result.ex = std::current_exception(); } in the worker, and if (ex) std::rethrow_exception(ex); in get(). The original dynamic type and its members survive.

docs.title: 11. const and constexpr (11_const_constexpr_and_compile_time.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) Find kCrcTable in .rodata and 0xcbf43926 in main.
    • Hint: search the .s file for .section .rodata. GCC prints 32-bit immediates as signed decimals, so 0xcbf43926 appears as $-873187034, not in hex.
  2. (easy) constexpr days_in_month with static_assert per month, then an out-of-bounds read.
    • Hint: UB is forbidden in constant evaluation, so the compiler must reject it; the message says something like "array subscript value is outside the bounds".
  3. (medium) constexpr std::array<std::string_view, 6> enum-to-string table.
    • Hint: add a Count or Last enumerator and static_assert(table.size() == size_t(E::Count)). Adding a value without a name then breaks the build.
  4. (medium) constexpr sieve producing 1000 primes; time the compile, then push to 100,000.
    • Hint: GCC caps constexpr loops (-fconstexpr-loop-limit, default 262144) and total operations (-fconstexpr-ops-limit). Compile-time work moves cost from every run to every build.
  5. (hard) constexpr state-machine table and constexpr bool accepts(std::string_view).
    • Hint: constexpr State table[5][4] = {...}; indexed by [state][input_class(c)]. The same function used at runtime reads the same .rodata table.

docs.title: 12. Memory layout and performance (12_memory_model_layout_and_performance.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) Reorder Bad by hand in m12_padding_alignment.cpp; predict offsets; add static_assert.
    • Hint: sort members from largest alignment to smallest. Size is rounded up to the largest alignment.
  2. (easy) Change padding to 32 bytes in m12_false_sharing_bench.cpp.
    • Hint: two counters 32 bytes apart can still share a 64-byte line, so the slowdown returns. Note that adjacent-line prefetch on some Intel CPUs can make 64 behave worse than 128.
  3. (medium) Arena::destroy_all() with a list of finalisers for non-trivial objects.
    • Hint: store {ptr, [](void* p) { static_cast<T*>(p)->~T(); }} when !std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>. Run finalisers in reverse order of creation.
  4. (medium) m12_bench_basics.cpp at -O0, -O2, -O3 -march=native, and under perf stat.
    • Hint: perf stat -e cache-misses,instructions,cycles ./bench. The list's cache-miss count explains its time much better than its instruction count does.
  5. (medium) SmallVector<T, N> with inline storage and heap spill.
    • Hint: a move of the inline case must move each element (the buffer lives inside the object). A move of the heap case steals the pointer and resets the source to inline mode.
  6. (hard) Signed overflow check, null check after dereference, float read through int*.
    • Hint: the optimiser assumes UB never happens: x + 1 < x becomes false, the null check is deleted because the earlier dereference "proved" non-null, and strict aliasing lets it reorder the load. -fsanitize=undefined reports the first; -fsanitize=null the second.
  7. (hard) std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource for an unordered_map<int, std::string>.
    • Hint: use std::pmr::unordered_map<int, std::pmr::string> so the strings use the pool too. Check peak RSS with /usr/bin/time -v: pools often trade lower time for higher peak memory.

docs.title: 13. C++17 features tour (13_cpp17_features_tour.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) Remove [[maybe_unused]] and build with -DNDEBUG; drop the try_reserve check.
    • Hint: under -DNDEBUG the assert vanishes, the variable becomes unused, and -Werror fails. Ignoring a [[nodiscard]] result triggers -Wunused-result.
  2. (easy) const std::string& to std::string_view; count allocations with a counting operator new.
    • Hint: replace global operator new(std::size_t) to increment a counter. Literals longer than the SSO buffer (15 chars in libstdc++) allocate when passed as const std::string&.
  3. (medium) Crash-safe config_reload via .tmp + fsync + fs::rename.
    • Hint: rename is atomic on the same filesystem. fs:: has no fsync, so open with open(), write, fsync(fd), close, then rename. For full durability also fsync the directory.
  4. (medium) shared_mutex vs mutex across reader:writer ratios and critical-section lengths.
    • Hint: with a 100 ns critical section the shared lock's extra atomic work often loses. With a 10 us critical section and many readers, parallel reading wins. See 04_Concurrency module 04.
  5. (hard) std::sort vs std::sort(std::execution::par, ...) with TBB at 1M, 10M, 100M.
    • Hint: link with -ltbb. At 1M the thread start-up and merge overhead eats most of the gain.
  6. (hard) TypeMap<Ts...> on std::tuple<std::optional<Ts>...> with fold-based visit_all.
    • Hint: std::get<std::optional<T>>(tuple_) selects by type, so all Ts must be distinct. visit_all: std::apply([&](auto&... o) { ((o ? f(*o) : void()), ...); }, tuple_);.

docs.title: 14. Writing production C++ (14_writing_production_cpp.md)
docs.text:
1. (easy) Split m14_library_api_demo.cpp into kv_store.cpp + main.cpp; build with CMake; run clang-tidy.
    • Hint: set CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON so clang-tidy -p build can find the flags.
  2. (easy) Two different struct Config definitions in two .cpp files.
    • Hint: this is an ODR violation, "ill-formed, no diagnostic required". The linker never sees types, so it links silently. -flto -Wodr compares type layouts at link time and catches it.
  3. (medium) SocketFd header in the tcpkv layout, test via public header, -fvisibility=hidden.
    • Hint: #define TCPKV_API __attribute__((visibility("default"))) on exported classes and functions only. Then nm -D --defined-only libtcpkv.so | c++filt should be short.
  4. (medium) Run clang-tidy (bugprone-*,performance-*,modernize-*,readability-*) on a 200-line file.
    • Hint: expect modernize-use-auto, performance-unnecessary-value-param, and readability-magic-numbers to dominate. Fix the cause, never add NOLINT.
  5. (hard) Public header for tcpkv's move-only Connection with documented contracts.
    • Hint: delete copy, [[nodiscard]] on every result, return std::optional<Message> plus an std::error_code& out-parameter or a small result struct. State in a comment which methods are safe to call from two threads (likely none).
  6. (hard) CI pipeline: clang-format, -Werror, ASan+UBSan, TSan, clang-tidy on the diff.
    • Hint: TSan and ASan cannot be combined in one binary; build twice. bugprone-use-after-move catches the use-after-move statically; TSan catches the data race at run time.

docs.title: 02_Modern_CPP — Interview questions and model answers
docs.text:
38 questions, ordered from basic to senior. Answer out loud, then compare. A good answer is short, precise, and ends with a consequence ("so in production you...") when there is one. The module that covers each question is in brackets.

Levels: Q1 to Q10 basic, Q11 to Q24 intermediate, Q25 to Q38 senior.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
Q1. You are a C programmer. What are the most important differences when you move to C++? [01]

C++ adds constructors and destructors, which make RAII possible: cleanup is tied to scope instead of to every error path. It adds references, overloading (and therefore name mangling), namespaces, templates, and a stricter type system (no implicit void* to T* conversion). The standard library gives you containers, strings and smart pointers so you rarely manage memory by hand. The compile and link model, the stack, the heap and the ABI concepts are the same, so C debugging skills carry over directly.

Q2. What is the difference between a pointer and a reference? [01]

A reference is an alias that must be bound to an object at initialisation and cannot be re-seated or null. A pointer is an object holding an address; it can be null, reassigned, and used in arithmetic. Under the hood a reference is usually implemented as a pointer. Use a reference for "must exist, will not change what it refers to" parameters, a pointer (or std::optional<std::reference_wrapper>) when "nothing" is a valid value.

Q3. What is name mangling and why does extern "C" exist? [01]

Because C++ allows overloading, the compiler encodes the parameter types (and namespace) into the symbol name, for example _Z7depositR7Accountx. C has no overloading and uses the plain name. extern "C" tells the C++ compiler to use C linkage (no mangling) so a C++ program can call a C library, or expose functions to C or to dlsym. Wrap C headers in #ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" {.

Q4. In what order are members and bases constructed and destroyed? [02]

Virtual bases first, then direct bases in declaration order, then members in declaration order, then the constructor body. The order in the member-initialiser list does not matter; GCC warns with -Wreorder if it differs. Destruction is the exact reverse. If a constructor throws, only the already-constructed bases and members are destroyed, and the object's own destructor does not run.

Q5. What does explicit do on a constructor? [02]

It forbids the constructor from being used for implicit conversions and copy-initialisation, so Temperature t = 36.6; and passing 36.6 to a Temperature parameter both fail to compile, while Temperature t{36.6}; works. Single-argument constructors should be explicit by default; it stops silent conversions such as an int turning into a buffer of that size.

Q6. What is RAII? [03]

Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation: a resource (memory, file, socket, lock, transaction) is acquired in a constructor and released in the destructor of an object with automatic lifetime. Because destructors run on every exit from a scope, including return, break and exceptions, cleanup cannot be forgotten. It replaces the C pattern of goto cleanup and makes exception-safe code possible. std::lock_guard, std::unique_ptr and std::fstream are all RAII types.

Q7. What are the special member functions, and what are the rules of zero, three and five? [02, 04]

Default constructor, destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment. Rule of five: if you write any of destructor, copy or move operations, you probably need to think about all five, because you are managing a resource by hand. Rule of three is the pre-C++11 version. Rule of zero: prefer composing classes from members that already manage themselves (std::string, std::vector, std::unique_ptr) so you write none of them and the compiler-generated ones are correct.

Q8. What does const on a member function mean? [01, 11]

It means the function does not modify the observable state of the object; inside it, this is a pointer to const. You can call only const member functions on a const object or through a const&. mutable members (for example a cache or a mutex) are exempt. In production, const-correctness is also a thread-safety signal: the standard library assumes const operations are safe to call concurrently.

Q9. std::vector vs std::list: which do you default to and why? [06]

std::vector, almost always. It is contiguous, so iteration is cache-friendly and the hardware prefetcher helps, while every std::list node is a separate heap allocation reached by a pointer chase. Even middle insertions are often faster on a vector for small-to-medium sizes because moving contiguous memory is cheap. Use list only when you need stable iterators across insertions and erasures or O(1) splice, such as an LRU cache.

Q10. What is a lambda, and what does it compile into? [07]

A lambda is an unnamed function object. The compiler generates a unique class whose data members are the captures and whose operator() is the body. Capture by value copies into members; capture by reference stores references, which dangle if the lambda outlives the scope. Because each lambda has its own type, passing it to a template lets the compiler inline the call, unlike a function pointer.

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
Q11. What are lvalues and rvalues, and what is an rvalue reference? [04]

An lvalue has an identity you can take the address of (a named variable); an rvalue is a temporary or a value about to expire. T&& is a reference that binds only to rvalues, which lets an overload know "nobody else will look at this object again, so I may steal its resources". Precisely, C++17 has lvalues, xvalues and prvalues; xvalues (such as the result of std::move(x)) and prvalues together are rvalues.

Q12. What does std::move actually do? [04]

Nothing at run time. It is a static_cast<T&&> that turns an lvalue into an xvalue so that overload resolution picks the move constructor or move assignment. The move itself is done by those functions. If the type has no move constructor, the copy constructor is chosen instead, silently. And std::move on a const object yields const T&&, which binds to the copy constructor, so it copies.

Q13. A function takes std::string&& s and does v.push_back(s);. What is wrong? [04]

s has a name, so the expression s is an lvalue even though its type is an rvalue reference. push_back(const std::string&) is chosen and the string is copied. Write v.push_back(std::move(s));. In templates with forwarding references (T&& where T is deduced), use std::forward<T>(s) instead so lvalue arguments are still copied.

Q14. What state is a moved-from object in? [04]

For standard library types, "valid but unspecified": you may destroy it, assign to it, and call functions without preconditions such as clear() or size(), but you must not assume its value. For your own types you choose the guarantee; for resource handles the convention is to leave the source empty (fd = -1, pointer = null) so its destructor does nothing. Using a moved-from object's value is a logic bug, and clang-tidy's bugprone-use-after-move catches many cases.

Q15. What is copy elision, and what changed in C++17? [04]

Copy elision lets the compiler construct a returned object directly in the caller's storage, so no copy or move happens. Since C++17 it is mandatory for prvalues: T x = T{}; and return T{}; construct in place, and the type need not even be copyable or movable. NRVO (returning a named local) is still optional but done by GCC and Clang in practice. Writing return std::move(local); defeats NRVO and is a pessimisation.

Q16. How should a function take a std::string parameter? [04, 13]

Read-only and not stored: std::string_view (or const std::string& if you need a null-terminated c_str()). Stored into a member ("sink"): take std::string by value and std::move it into place; callers passing rvalues pay one move, lvalues pay one copy plus one move. The const& plus && overload pair saves that one move but doubles the code; use it only on hot paths.

Q17. When do you use unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr, or a raw pointer? [05]

unique_ptr for single ownership; it is the default, and costs the same as a raw pointer with a stateless deleter. shared_ptr only when there are genuinely several owners whose lifetimes you cannot order. weak_ptr for observers that must not keep the object alive and to break cycles. A raw pointer or reference for non-owning access when the owner provably outlives the user. In code review, every shared_ptr should be able to name its second owner.

Q18. How do you wrap a C API handle such as FILE* or sqlite3* in a smart pointer? [05]
