Use std::unique_ptr<T, Deleter> with a custom deleter, ideally a stateless struct: struct FileCloser { void operator()(FILE* f) const noexcept { std::fclose(f); } }; and using FilePtr = std::unique_ptr<FILE, FileCloser>;. A stateless deleter adds no size thanks to the empty-base optimisation; a function-pointer deleter doubles the size. For an int file descriptor, which is not a pointer, write a small move-only class instead.

Q19. What does vector::push_back cost, and when does it invalidate iterators? [06]

Amortised O(1). When size() == capacity(), the vector allocates a larger buffer (libstdc++ doubles; MSVC grows by 1.5x), moves or copies every element across, and frees the old buffer. That invalidates every iterator, pointer and reference into the vector. Without reallocation only end() is invalidated. If you know the size, reserve() first; and never hold a pointer into a vector across a push_back unless capacity is guaranteed.

Q20. Why does std::vector copy your elements during reallocation instead of moving them? [04, 06]

Because your move constructor is not noexcept. vector gives the strong exception guarantee on push_back: if reallocation fails half-way, the original contents must be intact. Moving destructively and then throwing would lose data, so it uses std::move_if_noexcept, which copies when the move might throw and a copy exists. Mark move operations noexcept (they almost never need to throw) and check with static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>).

Q21. Iterator invalidation rules for map and unordered_map? [06]

std::map is a node-based red-black tree: insertion invalidates nothing, erase invalidates only iterators to the erased element. std::unordered_map is a bucket array of node chains: erase invalidates only the erased element, insertion invalidates iterators (not pointers or references to elements) if it triggers a rehash. Use reserve() to prevent rehashes, and use the iterator returned by erase when erasing inside a loop.

Q22. std::map vs std::unordered_map: how do you choose? [06]

map gives ordered iteration, range queries (lower_bound) and guaranteed O(log n), but each lookup chases about log2(n) pointers through separate nodes. unordered_map gives average O(1) with a single hash and usually one or two cache misses, but no ordering, worst-case O(n) with a bad hash, and rehash spikes. For read-mostly data that is built once, a sorted vector with binary search often beats both because it is contiguous.

Q23. Why must templates usually be defined in headers? [08]

A template is not code; it is a recipe. The compiler generates code only when it sees the template used with concrete types, and it needs the full definition at that point in that translation unit. If the definition lives in a .cpp, other translation units cannot instantiate it and you get undefined-symbol link errors. The exception is explicit instantiation (template class Foo<int>;) paired with extern template declarations, which also cuts build time.

Q24. What is SFINAE, and what does if constexpr replace? [08, 13]

Substitution Failure Is Not An Error: if substituting template arguments into a declaration produces invalid code, that overload is silently removed from the candidate set rather than causing an error. It is used with std::enable_if and std::void_t to select overloads by type properties. C++17's if constexpr discards the untaken branch at compile time inside one function, which replaces most SFINAE overload sets with readable code. C++20 concepts replace most of the rest.

docs.title: Senior
docs.text:
Q25. Describe the memory layout of an object with virtual functions, and how a virtual call compiles. [09]

Each polymorphic object carries a hidden vptr, typically at offset 0 under the Itanium ABI used by GCC and Clang, pointing into its class's vtable in .rodata. The vtable holds offset-to-top, a typeinfo pointer, then one function pointer per virtual function in declaration order, with derived overrides replacing base entries. A call p->area() compiles to: load the vptr from *p, load the slot at a fixed offset, indirect call. The constructor sets the vptr, which is why a virtual call inside a base constructor dispatches to the base version.

Q26. Why does a polymorphic base class need a virtual destructor? [09]

delete base_ptr; on an object of derived type, through a base with a non-virtual destructor, is undefined behaviour. In practice only the base destructor runs, so the derived class's members (strings, buffers, sockets) leak, and the deleting destructor may free with the wrong size. With a virtual destructor, the vtable's deleting-destructor slot dispatches to the most-derived destructor. Rule: public and virtual, or protected and non-virtual. shared_ptr created with make_shared<Derived> captures the right deleter, but do not rely on that.

Q27. What is object slicing? [09]

Copying a derived object into a base object by value copies only the base subobject; the derived members are dropped and the vptr is the base's, so virtual calls go to base versions. It happens with Base b = derived;, by-value parameters, and std::vector<Base>. Prevent it by passing polymorphic types by reference or pointer, storing std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Base>>, and deleting or protecting the base's copy operations.

Q28. What does final buy you beyond documentation? [09]

It lets the compiler devirtualise. When the static type is a final class, or a final virtual function, the dynamic type is known exactly, so the indirect call becomes a direct call that can be inlined. That removes the vtable load and the indirect branch, and, more importantly, enables inlining and further optimisation of the caller. GCC's -Wsuggest-final-types points to candidates.

Q29. What is in a shared_ptr control block, and what does make_shared change? [05]

A shared_ptr is two pointers: one to the object, one to a control block holding the strong count, the weak count, the deleter and the allocator (type-erased). Counts are atomic, so copying a shared_ptr across threads costs a locked instruction on a shared cache line. shared_ptr<T>(new T) makes two allocations; make_shared<T>() makes one block containing both, which is faster and more cache-friendly. The catch: with make_shared the object's memory cannot be freed until the last weak_ptr is gone, because it shares the allocation with the control block (the object is still destroyed when the strong count hits zero).

Q30. Is shared_ptr thread-safe? [05]

The control block is: different threads may copy and destroy different shared_ptr instances that share one object, and the count stays correct. The pointee is not protected at all; concurrent access to the object needs its own synchronisation. And one shared_ptr instance is not safe to read and write from two threads at once; for that you need std::atomic_load/atomic_store on it in C++17 or std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> in C++20, or a mutex.

Q31. How do you create a reference cycle with shared_ptr, and how do you fix it? [05]

A parent holding shared_ptr to children while each child holds shared_ptr to its parent: when the last external owner goes, every strong count is still at least 1, so nothing is freed. Valgrind reports the blocks as definitely and indirectly lost. Fix it by making the back edge a weak_ptr (lock it to use it) or a raw pointer when the parent provably outlives the children. The design rule is that ownership must form a tree or a DAG, never a cycle.

Q32. What are the exception-safety guarantees? [10]

No-throw: the operation never fails (destructors, swaps, moves, noexcept functions). Strong: if it throws, state is exactly as before, like a transaction. Basic: if it throws, no resources leak and all invariants hold, but the state may have changed. No guarantee: anything can happen. The usual route to the strong guarantee is "do all throwing work on a copy, then commit with a non-throwing swap", which is copy-and-swap. Destructors must not throw; since C++11 they are noexcept by default and a throw calls std::terminate.

Q33. What happens at run time when an exception is thrown, and what does it cost? [03, 10]

GCC and Clang use the zero-cost table-based model: the normal path has no checks, and per-function unwind tables plus .gcc_except_table describe what to clean up. A throw allocates the exception object (__cxa_allocate_exception), then the unwinder walks the stack twice, first to find a handler, then to run landing pads that call destructors, and finally enters the catch. That costs on the order of microseconds per throw (typical), so exceptions suit rare failures, not control flow or per-request expected errors like "key not found".

Q34. How do you choose between exceptions, std::optional, std::error_code and an expected type? [10]

Exceptions for rare, cannot-continue failures far from where they can be handled (out of memory, corrupt configuration at start-up); they keep the happy path clean. std::optional when absence is normal and needs no explanation (find). std::error_code, or an expected-style variant<T, Error>, when failure is a normal outcome the caller must handle and you need the reason, especially on hot paths, across a C ABI, or in code built with -fno-exceptions. In a server, never let an exception escape a thread function: catch at the request boundary, log, and return an error response.

Q35. Name the main categories of undefined behaviour, and why the optimiser makes them dangerous. [12]

Memory: out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, double free, null dereference, uninitialised reads. Arithmetic: signed overflow, shift by negative or by at least the bit width, division by zero. Type: strict-aliasing violations, calling through the wrong function type, misaligned access. Lifetime and concurrency: dangling references, data races, modifying a const object. The compiler assumes UB never happens and optimises on that assumption, so if (x + 1 < x) is deleted and a null check after a dereference is removed. The bug therefore appears only at -O2 and far from its cause; catch it with -fsanitize=address,undefined and TSan.

Q36. What is padding, and how does layout affect performance? [12]

Each type has an alignment; the compiler inserts padding so every member is aligned and the struct size is a multiple of its largest alignment. {char; double; char;} is 24 bytes, reordered {double; char; char;} is 16. Smaller structs mean more objects per 64-byte cache line and fewer misses. False sharing is the opposite trap: two threads writing different variables on the same line make the line bounce between cores; separate hot per-thread data with alignas(64).

Q37. Which C++17 features do you actually use in production, and what is the trap in string_view? [13]

Structured bindings (for (auto& [k, v] : map)), if (auto it = m.find(k); it != m.end()), std::optional, std::variant with std::visit, std::string_view, std::filesystem, std::shared_mutex for read-mostly data, [[nodiscard]], if constexpr, fold expressions, inline variables and CTAD. The string_view trap is lifetime: it does not own its characters, so returning a view of a local string, or storing a view of a temporary, leaves it dangling. It is also not null-terminated, so never pass sv.data() to a C API that expects a C string.

Q38. Design the ownership for a TCP server: listener, connections, worker pool, shared store. [05, 14]

The Server owns the listening socket as a move-only SocketFd by value, the thread pool by value, and the store by value, so destruction order is declared order reversed: declare the store before the pool so workers are joined before the store dies. Each accepted connection is a move-only Connection holding a SocketFd, moved into the task that serves it, so exactly one owner closes each fd. Workers get the store by reference; the store guards its map with a std::shared_mutex (shared_lock for reads, unique_lock for writes). shared_ptr appears only if a connection genuinely has two owners, such as async I/O plus a registry, with the registry holding weak_ptr. This is exactly the tcpkv design in 10_Capstone_Projects/tcpkv.

docs.title: 03. Data Structures and Algorithms — DSA in C++17, from arrays to interview-ready
What this course covers
docs.text:
You already wrote array.cpp, lowArray.cpp and orderedArray.cpp: a fixed-size array with linear search, delete-by-shifting, and a binary search on a sorted array. That is the floor. This course starts one step above it and ends with you able to:

  • analyse any loop or recursion for time and space cost, and explain why the constant factors (cache misses, branch misprediction) sometimes matter more than the Big-O;
  • implement from memory, without looking anything up: a hash map, a singly and doubly linked list, an LRU cache, a ring buffer, a binary search tree, an AVL rotation, a B+tree with range scan, a binary heap, a trie, union-find, BFS/DFS/Dijkstra, and the standard dynamic-programming tables;
  • pass a 45-minute LeetCode-medium coding round for a C++ systems role: talk while you code, pick the right pattern in two minutes, write it bug-free in fifteen, test it in five;
  • connect each structure to the systems you have worked on: B-trees to Berkeley DB and PostgreSQL indexes, hash tables to connection lookups in your RPC server, ring buffers to socket I/O, heaps to timer wheels and schedulers, external merge sort to ORDER BY.

Everything is C++17 on WSL Ubuntu 24.04 (g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread). The code files never use using namespace std;. Module 01 explains why.

docs.title: Why this is on the resume
docs.text:
The resume says "Data structures & algorithms", "B-tree cursor traversal", "indexing", and "hashing". Those are not decorative. A Berkeley DB -> YugabyteDB migration engine walks B-tree pages with a cursor; a core-banking application server hashes session ids and account numbers to find state in O(1); PostgreSQL indexes are B+trees. An interviewer who reads those lines will ask you to implement or explain them. This course makes sure you can.

The second reason is the coding round. Every C++ systems role you will apply to in the next 12 weeks screens with one or two 45-minute problem-solving rounds. They are LeetCode-medium style: arrays, hashing, linked lists, trees, graphs, DP. Module 16 turns the first 15 modules into a 10-week practice schedule.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• C at a professional level (pointers, structs, malloc/free, function pointers). You have this.
  • C++ basics: classes, constructors, references, std::vector, std::string. You have most of this. Where a module uses something newer (std::unique_ptr, std::optional, structured bindings, lambdas, std::string_view), it explains it in one paragraph at the point of use.
  • Ability to compile and run a C++ file on WSL: g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread file.cpp -o file && ./file.

Study the modules in order; each one assumes the previous ones. If you are short on time, the minimum path for the coding round is 01, 02, 04, 05, 06, 09, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16. The minimum path for the "B-tree cursor traversal / indexing" resume line is 01, 09, 10, 11.

Study this course in parallel with the Modern C++ course. Module 05 here uses std::unique_ptr; if that is unfamiliar, read the smart-pointer module there first.

docs.title: You are done when you can...

  • Explain why iterating a std::vector is often 10x faster than iterating a std::list of the same size even though both are O(n).

docs.title: 01. Complexity and how to think
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: none

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
When you wrote array.cpp, deleting the number 9 meant finding it (a loop) and then shifting everything after it one cell left (another loop). If the array had 10 elements that was fast. If it had 10 million, the shift alone would be 10 million copies. "Complexity" is the habit of asking, before you run anything: how does the amount of work grow when the input grows?

Big-O notation is the shorthand for the answer. O(n) means "work grows in proportion to the input size n". O(1) means "work does not grow at all". O(n^2) means "double the input, four times the work". It deliberately ignores constants: whether a loop does 3 or 30 operations per element, both are O(n), because for large n the shape of the curve matters more than its slope. Think of it like describing a journey: "it is a flight" versus "it is a drive" tells you more about a 3000 km trip than the exact speed of the car.

The senior twist is that constants do matter once you are in production. Two O(n) algorithms can differ by 50x because one walks memory in order and the other jumps around. Big-O picks the algorithm; cache behaviour picks the implementation. This module teaches both habits.

docs.title: 2.1 Definitions
docs.text:
• n — the size of the input: array length, string length, number of nodes, number of bits in a number (for arithmetic algorithms).
  • T(n) — the number of "basic operations" (comparisons, assignments, memory reads) the algorithm performs on an input of size n, in the worst case unless stated otherwise.
  • O(f(n)) — "T(n) is eventually at most c * f(n) for some constant c". An upper bound. Formally: T(n) is O(f(n)) if there exist c > 0 and n0 such that T(n) <= c * f(n) for all n >= n0.
  • Omega(f(n)) — a lower bound. Theta(f(n)) — both; the tight bound. Interviewers say "Big-O" when they mean Theta almost always. Use the same convention.
  • Worst / average / best case — three different functions. Quicksort is O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst. Say which one you mean.
  • Space complexity — extra memory beyond the input. Recursion depth counts, because each frame lives on the stack.

docs.title: 2.2 Rules for counting
docs.text:
1. Sequential statements add. O(n) + O(n) = O(n); O(n) + O(n^2) = O(n^2). Keep the dominant term.
  2. Nested loops multiply. A loop of n inside a loop of n is O(n^2). A loop of n inside a loop of m is O(n * m) — do not collapse to n^2 unless n == m.
  3. Drop constants and lower-order terms. 3n^2 + 20n + 7 is O(n^2).
  4. Logarithms appear when you halve. A loop where i *= 2 or n /= 2 each step runs log2(n) times. Binary search is the canonical example: each step throws away half.
  5. Base of the logarithm does not matter. log2(n) and log10(n) differ by a constant factor.
  6. Recursion: write the recurrence, then solve it.
    • T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) -> O(log n) (binary search)
    • T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) -> O(n log n) (merge sort)
    • T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) -> O(n) (linear recursion)
    • T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) -> O(n^2) (e.g. naive selection sort written recursively)
    • T(n) = 2T(n-1) + O(1) -> O(2^n) (naive Fibonacci) The Master Theorem covers T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(n^d): compare d with log_b(a). If d < log_b(a) the answer is O(n^(log_b a)); if equal, O(n^d log n); if greater, O(n^d). You rarely need it in interviews beyond the three common cases above.

docs.title: 2.3 Worked examples
docs.text:
// Example A: O(n). One pass.
int sum = 0;
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) sum += v[i];

// Example B: O(n^2). Inner loop runs n, n-1, n-2, ... 1 times. Sum = n(n-1)/2.
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i)
    for (std::size_t j = i + 1; j < n; ++j)
        if (v[i] == v[j]) ++dups;

// Example C: O(n log n). Outer loop n times, inner loop log n times.
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i)
    for (std::size_t k = 1; k < n; k *= 2) work();

// Example D: O(n). Looks nested but the inner pointer never goes backwards.
// Total moves of j across the whole run <= n. This is the two-pointer pattern (module 02).
std::size_t j = 0;
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    while (j < n && v[j] < v[i] + k) ++j;
}

// Example E: O(sqrt(n)). Loop until i*i exceeds n.
for (long i = 2; i * i <= n; ++i) if (n % i == 0) return false;

Example D is the one beginners get wrong. The question to ask for any nested loop is not "how many loops are there" but "how many times does the inner body execute in total".

docs.title: 2.4 Amortised cost
docs.text:
Amortised analysis answers: "if I do a sequence of m operations, what is the average cost per operation, even if some individual operations are expensive?" This is not the same as average case (which is about random inputs). Amortised is about the worst-case sequence.

The classic example is std::vector::push_back. Most pushes write one element: O(1). When capacity is full, the vector allocates a bigger block, copies all n elements, frees the old block: O(n). If capacity doubles each time, how much copying happens across n pushes?

push #       1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9 ... 16  17 ...
capacity     1  2  4  4  8  8  8  8 16 ... 16  32
copies on    0  1  2  0  4  0  0  0  8 ...  0  16
   growth

Total copies for n pushes = 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2 < n. So n pushes cost at most n + n = 2n element writes. Divide by n: 2 per push, amortised O(1). The general formula with growth factor g: the geometric series 1 + 1/g + 1/g^2 + ... sums to g/(g-1). For g = 2 that is 2; for g = 1.5 it is 3. So 1.5x growth copies more in total (3n vs 2n) but wastes less memory (at most 50% slack vs 100%). libstdc++ uses 2x; MSVC uses 1.5x. Both are amortised O(1).

What breaks it: growing by a constant (capacity += 100). Then growth happens every 100 pushes and copies n elements each time: total ~ n^2 / 200, amortised O(n) per push. That is why you never write a "grow by fixed step" dynamic array.

The accounting view: charge every push 3 "coins". It spends 1 to write itself and banks 2. When a growth of size n happens, the n/2 elements pushed since the last growth have banked n coins between them — enough to pay for copying all n elements. The bank never goes negative, so the amortised cost is 3 = O(1).

docs.title: 2.5 Space
docs.text:
Count what you allocate beyond the input:

  • A few scalars: O(1).
  • An array of size n (prefix sums, visited flags, a hash set of all elements): O(n).
  • A 2D table n by m (edit distance): O(n * m).
  • Recursion depth d: O(d) stack frames. Depth-first search on a path graph of n nodes recurses n deep: O(n) stack. Merge sort recurses log n deep: O(log n) stack plus O(n) temp buffer.

In interviews, "in-place" means O(1) extra space, and the input may be modified.

docs.title: 2.6 Common complexity table
docs.text:
Complexity Name Example n = 10^6 ops (typical) O(1) constant array index, hash lookup (average), stack push 1 O(log n) logarithmic binary search, balanced BST op, heap push/pop ~20 O(n) linear single pass, linear search, BFS on a path 10^6 O(n log n) linearithmic merge sort, heapsort, sort then sweep ~2 * 10^7 O(n^2) quadratic nested loops, bubble/insertion/selection sort, naive pair search 10^12 (too slow) O(n^3) cubic Floyd-Warshall, naive matrix multiply only for n <= ~500 O(2^n) exponential subsets, naive recursion with two branches only for n <= ~25 O(n!) factorial permutations only for n <= ~11

Rule of thumb for a coding round (one CPU, ~1 second, typical judge): about 10^8 simple operations. So n = 10^5 rules out O(n^2) (10^10) and demands O(n log n) or better. n = 10^3 allows O(n^2). n = 20 allows O(2^n). Read the constraints in the problem statement first; they tell you the target complexity before you think about the algorithm.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m01_vector_growth.cpp prints the capacity after each push so you can see the doubling, counts the total number of element copies, and compares three ways to build an array of n integers: push_back with no reserve, push_back after reserve(n), and grow-by-constant (a hand-written array that grows by 1024 each time). It also times a row-major versus a column-major sweep of a 2D array to show the cache effect.

Key part:

// Watch capacity change. Each change is a reallocation: allocate, copy, free.
std::vector<int> v;
std::size_t last_cap = 0;
long long copies = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) {
    v.push_back(i);
    if (v.capacity() != last_cap) {
        copies += static_cast<long long>(v.size() - 1);   // elements moved on this growth
        std::printf("size=%4zu capacity=%4zu\n", v.size(), v.capacity());
        last_cap = v.capacity();
    }
}
std::printf("total element copies: %lld (n=1000, bound 2n=2000)\n", copies);

On libstdc++ you will see 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 1024: exact doubling. Total copies = 1023 < 2n.

Why the course never writes using namespace std;: in a 50-line homework file it is harmless. In a header, or any file that is included or grown over years, it pulls every name from std into the global scope. std::size, std::data, std::count, std::distance, std::begin — all collide with names you are likely to have in a server codebase. Writing std:: costs five characters and tells the reader exactly where the name comes from. All code files in this course use the std:: prefix.

docs.title: 4.1 Why Big-O lies: the memory hierarchy
docs.text:
A modern CPU core executes a simple instruction in well under a nanosecond. Reading a value from main memory (DRAM) takes roughly 60 to 100 ns (typical for a desktop; see Intel/AMD optimisation manuals for exact figures). That is a factor of 100 or more. To hide it, the CPU has caches: L1 (about 32 to 48 KB per core, ~4 cycles), L2 (hundreds of KB to a few MB, ~12 cycles), L3 (tens of MB shared, ~40 cycles). Data moves between memory and cache in cache lines of 64 bytes.

Consequences:

  • When you read v[i], the CPU fetches 64 bytes, i.e. 16 ints. Reading v[i+1] next is almost free. Sequential access is cheap; the hardware prefetcher also notices the pattern and fetches ahead.
  • A linked list node lives wherever new put it. Following next is a fresh cache miss each time. Walking a list of n nodes is O(n) in Big-O and O(n) cache misses in practice; walking a vector of n ints is O(n) in Big-O and O(n/16) cache misses.
  • This is why "vector beats list for almost everything, including inserting in the middle for sizes up to a few thousand" is a true statement that surprises people who only know Big-O. Shifting 1000 ints (4 KB, 64 cache lines, sequential) is faster than one pointer chase that misses L3.

The 2D sweep in m01_vector_growth.cpp demonstrates it: row-major (inner loop walks contiguous memory) is typically 5 to 10x faster than column-major (inner loop jumps by a full row each step) on a 4096 x 4096 int matrix, with the same O(n^2) count.

docs.title: 4.2 Branch prediction
docs.text: The CPU guesses which way an if will go and starts executing early. A wrong guess costs ~15 to 20 cycles (pipeline flush). A loop over random data with if (v[i] > 128) sum += v[i] is much slower than the same loop over sorted data, because sorted data makes the branch predictable. Same Big-O, different wall-clock. Interviewers for systems roles like to ask "why would sorting the input first make this loop faster?" — this is the answer.

docs.title: 4.3 Allocation cost
docs.text: new and malloc are not O(1) in the way a comparison is. They take a lock or hit a thread-local cache, search a free list, possibly call mmap/brk. A data structure that allocates per element (list, std::map, std::unordered_map nodes) pays this per insert. A vector pays it log n times total. When you say "O(1) insert" for a list, add "plus one allocation" in your head.

docs.title: 4.4 Big-O of library calls
docs.text:
Memorise these, because you will build on them:

Call Complexity std::vector::push_back, pop_back, operator[] O(1) amortised / O(1) / O(1) std::vector::insert or erase at position p O(n - p) std::sort O(n log n) worst case (introsort, module 08) std::lower_bound on random-access range O(log n) std::unordered_map find/insert/erase O(1) average, O(n) worst (all keys in one bucket) std::map find/insert/erase O(log n) std::priority_queue push/pop/top O(log n) / O(log n) / O(1) std::string::operator+= O(1) amortised per char std::list::splice O(1) std::deque::push_front/back O(1) amortised

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The 3 AM version of O(n^2): a request handler that, for each of n open sessions, scans the list of n sessions to find duplicates. Works fine in testing with 50 sessions. In production with 20 000 sessions it is 400 million comparisons per request. CPU goes to 100%, latency climbs, the pager goes off. The fix is a hash set (module 04) and the symptom to recognise is "it got slower as the system got busier, non-linearly".
  • Hidden O(n) inside a loop: std::vector::erase(v.begin()) inside a for loop over the vector is O(n^2). std::string s; for (...) s = s + c; is O(n^2) because s + c builds a new string each time (use +=). std::find inside a loop is O(n^2). These are the three most common accidental quadratics in C++ code review.
  • Reserve when you know the size. If you are reading 1 million rows from a database cursor into a vector, v.reserve(count) avoids ~20 reallocations and the copying that goes with them. Not asymptotically important; measurably important.
  • Your Berkeley DB migration engine: reading a B-tree sequentially via cursor is O(n) with excellent locality (leaf pages are contiguous and linked, module 11). Doing a point lookup per key instead would be O(n log n) with a random page read each time. Same output, 100x slower on a cold cache. Knowing the access pattern of the structure is what tells you which to use.
  • Measure before you believe. Big-O gets you to the right algorithm. After that, a profiler (perf on Linux, see the Linux systems course) tells you where the time actually goes, and it is usually cache misses or allocations, not instruction count.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) For each snippet below, write the Big-O time. Done when you have an answer and a one-line justification for each. 
    for (i = 0; i < n; ++i) for (j = 0; j < 10; ++j) f();            // (a)
for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 3) f();                                   // (b)
for (i = 0; i < n; ++i) for (j = i; j < n; ++j) f();             // (c)
for (i = 0; i < n; ++i) for (j = 1; j < i; j *= 2) f();          // (d)
void r(int n) { if (n <= 1) return; r(n/2); r(n/2); f(); }       // (e)
  2. (easy) Compile and run code/m01_vector_growth.cpp. Note the capacity sequence. Change the growth of the hand-written array from +1024 to x2 and observe the copy count. Done when your copy count for n = 1 000 000 is below 2n.
  3. (medium) Prove that growth factor 1.5 gives amortised copy cost at most 3 per push. Write the geometric series and sum it. Done when you can do it on paper in 5 minutes.
  4. (medium) In m01_vector_growth.cpp, change the matrix size to 1024 x 1024 and then to 8192 x 8192. Record row-major vs column-major times. Explain why the ratio changes with size (hint: at which size does one row stop fitting in L1? in L2?). Done when you can explain the ratio in terms of cache sizes on your machine (lscpu prints them).
  5. (hard) Write a function that takes a sorted std::vector<int> and a target and counts pairs (i < j) with v[i] + v[j] == target, in O(n). Then write the O(n^2) version. Time both at n = 100 000. Done when the O(n) version finishes in under 1 ms and you can state why the inner pointer in your O(n) version never moves backwards.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between O, Theta and Omega? O is an upper bound, Omega a lower bound, Theta is both. Interviewers usually say O and mean Theta. If an algorithm is O(n^2) worst case but O(n) best case, say "O(n^2) worst, O(n) best".

Q: push_back is O(1) amortised. Explain. Most pushes write one slot. On a full buffer the vector doubles capacity and copies n elements. Total copies across n pushes form a geometric series 1 + 2 + 4 + ... < 2n, so the average per push is bounded by a constant. Growing by a fixed amount instead would make the total quadratic.

Q: Two algorithms are both O(n). Can one be 50x faster? Yes. Big-O hides constants. Sequential memory access (vector) hits cache; pointer chasing (linked list) misses cache on every node. Branch predictability and allocation count also matter. Big-O chooses the algorithm family; the memory access pattern chooses the speed.

Q: What is the complexity of this nested loop? (shows two-pointer code) O(n). The inner loop's index never resets; across the entire outer loop it moves at most n times in total. Count total executions of the inner body, not the nesting depth.

Q: How do you analyse a recursive function? Write the recurrence: how many sub-calls, on what size, plus how much work outside the calls. Solve it with the standard cases: halving with constant work is O(log n), two halves with linear merge is O(n log n), two branches reducing by one is O(2^n).

Q: What is the space complexity of recursive DFS? O(depth of recursion) for the stack plus whatever you allocate (visited set: O(V)). On a path graph the depth is O(V), which can overflow a default 8 MB stack at around 100 000 frames.

Q: n = 10^5 in the problem constraints. What complexity do you aim for? O(n log n) or O(n). O(n^2) is 10^10 operations, too slow for a one-second limit.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Big-O describes how work grows with input size; it drops constants and lower-order terms.
  • Sequential code adds, nested loops multiply, halving gives log, two-branch recursion gives 2^n.
  • For nested loops count total executions of the inner body; two-pointer loops are O(n).
  • Amortised cost is the average over a worst-case sequence; vector doubling gives amortised O(1) push with at most 2n copies; constant-step growth gives O(n) per push.
  • Space counts extra memory plus recursion depth.
  • n = 10^5 means O(n log n); n = 10^3 allows O(n^2); n = 20 allows O(2^n).
  • Cache lines are 64 bytes; sequential access is ~100x cheaper than pointer chasing; this is why vector beats list in practice at small and medium sizes.
  • Branch misprediction and allocation are the other two hidden constants.
  • The three accidental quadratics: erase in a loop, s = s + c, find in a loop.
  • Big-O picks the algorithm; profiling picks the implementation.

docs.title: 02. Arrays, vectors and two pointers
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 01

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
An array is a row of boxes in memory, all the same size, side by side. Box i is at start + i * sizeof(element). That one multiplication is why indexing is O(1) and why arrays are the fastest structure a CPU knows: the next element is literally the next address.

std::vector is the array you should use in C++. It owns a heap block, remembers how many boxes are in use (size()) and how many are allocated (capacity()), and grows itself. Your LowArray class in lowArray.cpp wrapped a vector and then re-did by hand what the vector already does (resize, shift on delete). From this module on, you use std::vector directly and spend your effort on the algorithms.

The algorithms in this module share one idea: walk the array with more than one index at a time, and never walk backwards. Two pointers, sliding window and prefix sums all turn an O(n^2) "for every i, for every j" into an O(n) single pass. These three patterns alone solve roughly a quarter of all array interview questions.

docs.title: 2.1 std::vector essentials
docs.text:
std::vector<int> v;            // empty, size 0, capacity 0
v.reserve(100);                // capacity >= 100, size still 0. No elements constructed.
v.resize(10);                  // size 10, elements value-initialised (0 for int)
v.push_back(5);                // size 11, amortised O(1)
v.emplace_back(5);             // same, constructs in place (matters for non-trivial types)
v[3] = 7;                      // no bounds check. UB if 3 >= size().
v.at(3) = 7;                   // bounds-checked, throws std::out_of_range
v.front(); v.back();           // first / last element (UB if empty)
v.pop_back();                  // O(1), removes last
v.insert(v.begin() + i, x);    // O(n - i): shifts tail right
v.erase(v.begin() + i);        // O(n - i): shifts tail left. Same as your delete loop.
v.erase(v.begin() + i, v.begin() + j);  // erase range [i, j)
v.clear();                     // size 0, capacity unchanged
v.shrink_to_fit();             // request capacity == size (non-binding)
v.data();                      // int* to the contiguous buffer. Pass to C APIs.
v.empty(); v.size();           // size() returns std::size_t (unsigned!)

Half-open ranges: [begin, end) everywhere in the standard library. end() points one past the last element. erase(first, last) removes last - first elements. Get used to this; it makes "empty range" and "length = end - begin" fall out naturally and is the convention you will use for your own binary search bounds in module 09.

Iterator invalidation. After push_back that reallocates, or any insert/erase, every iterator, pointer and reference into the vector may be dangling. The classic bug:

for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it)
    if (*it % 2 == 0) v.erase(it);          // UB: it is invalid after erase

Correct forms:

for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); )
    if (*it % 2 == 0) it = v.erase(it);     // erase returns the next valid iterator
    else ++it;
// Better, O(n) instead of O(n^2):
v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int x) { return x % 2 == 0; }), v.end());

The erase-remove idiom (second form) is the two-pointer pattern in disguise: remove_if keeps a write index that only advances for kept elements, then erase chops the tail once.

Signed/unsigned. v.size() is std::size_t. v.size() - 1 when size is 0 wraps to

  1. for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) warns under -Wextra (sign compare) and fails under -Werror. Either loop with std::size_t, or take int n = static_cast<int>(v.size()); once at the top and use int throughout. In problem code this course does the latter, because many loops need to go down to -1 or compare with i - 1.

docs.title: 2.2 Pattern 1: two pointers
docs.text:
Two indices move through the array, each only in one direction. Total movement <= 2n, so O(n).

  • Opposite ends (l = 0, r = n-1, move towards each other): sorted two-sum, container with most water, reverse in place, palindrome check, 3-sum inner loop.
  • Same direction, slow/fast (write trails read): remove duplicates, remove element, move zeroes, partition. The write index marks the boundary of the "good" prefix.
  • Two arrays (i in A, j in B): merge two sorted arrays, intersection of sorted arrays.

The invariant you state out loud in an interview: "everything before write is the finished output; everything between write and read is garbage I will overwrite; everything from read on is unprocessed."

docs.title: 2.3 Pattern 2: sliding window
docs.text:
A contiguous subarray [l, r] grows at the right and shrinks at the left. Each index moves at most n times: O(n). Use it when the question says "contiguous subarray/substring" and "longest / shortest / count with property P", where P is monotone: if a window violates P, every larger window containing it also violates P (or the reverse). Sum >= k with non-negative numbers is monotone. "At most k distinct" is monotone. "Sum equals exactly k with negatives" is not — use prefix sums + hash for that.

Fixed window (size k): add v[r], remove v[r-k], one pass. Variable window: for r: add v[r]; while (window invalid) remove v[l++]; record answer.

docs.title: 2.4 Pattern 3: prefix sums
docs.text: P[0] = 0, P[i] = v[0] + ... + v[i-1]. Then sum(v[i..j)) = P[j] - P[i] in O(1) after O(n) build. Use for: many range-sum queries, "count subarrays with sum == k" (store seen prefix sums in a hash map), "subarray sum divisible by k" (prefix sums mod k), 2D range sums (2D prefix table). Works for any invertible operation: sum, XOR, product without zeros.

docs.title: 2.5 Pattern 4: in-place deletion
docs.text:
Your array.cpp shifted elements one cell left after finding the key. For deleting many elements that is O(n^2). The slow/fast two-pointer does all deletions in one O(n) pass:

read ->  [3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 5]
write    keep if != 0: write 3, write 1, write 5  -> [3,1,5,_,_,_], new size = 3

If order does not matter, swap the deleted element with the last one and pop_back: O(1).

docs.title: 2.6 Pattern 5: Kadane's algorithm
docs.text: Maximum sum of a contiguous subarray. The idea: at each index decide "extend the best subarray ending at i-1, or start fresh at i". cur = max(v[i], cur + v[i]), best = max(best, cur). It is a one-dimensional dynamic programme (module 14) with O(1) state. Generalises to maximum product (track min and max because negatives flip), circular arrays (total - minimum subarray), and "best time to buy and sell stock" (differences).

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: Files: code/m02_vector_basics.cpp (vector API, invalidation, erase-remove), code/m02_two_pointers.cpp (problems 1 to 4), code/m02_sliding_window.cpp (problems 5, 6), code/m02_prefix_sums_kadane.cpp (problems 7, 8). Each has a small check() harness so you can add your own cases. Below, every problem: statement, reasoning, solution, complexity.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Two Sum on a sorted array
docs.text:
Given a sorted array and a target, return indices of two numbers that add to target.

Reasoning: brute force is O(n^2). Sorted order means if v[l] + v[r] < target, the only way to increase the sum is to move l right (moving r left can only decrease it). Symmetric for > target. Each step eliminates one index for good.

std::pair<int, int> two_sum_sorted(const std::vector<int>& v, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = static_cast<int>(v.size()) - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        long long s = static_cast<long long>(v[l]) + v[r];  // avoid int overflow
        if (s == target) return {l, r};
        if (s < target) ++l; else --r;
    }
    return {-1, -1};
}
O(n) time, O(1) space. Unsorted input: use a hash map (module 04) — O(n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place
docs.text:
Return the new length; the first k elements must be the unique values in order.

Reasoning: because it is sorted, duplicates are adjacent. Keep write as the end of the unique prefix. For each read, if v[read] != v[write-1], copy it in.

int remove_duplicates(std::vector<int>& v) {
    if (v.empty()) return 0;
    int write = 1;
    for (int read = 1; read < static_cast<int>(v.size()); ++read)
        if (v[read] != v[write - 1]) v[write++] = v[read];
    return write;
}
O(n), O(1). The invariant: v[0..write) is strictly increasing and equals the unique values seen so far.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Move zeroes to the end, preserving order of non-zeroes
docs.text:
Reasoning: same slow/fast pattern. Write non-zeroes forward, then fill the tail with zeroes. Or swap-in-place so the zeroes bubble right (fewer writes when few zeroes).

void move_zeroes(std::vector<int>& v) {
    int write = 0;
    for (int read = 0; read < static_cast<int>(v.size()); ++read)
        if (v[read] != 0) std::swap(v[write++], v[read]);  // swap is a no-op when write == read
}
O(n), O(1). Note that the swap version does at most n swaps and keeps relative order.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Container with most water
docs.text:
h[i] is a wall height. Pick two walls so that the water between them (width x min height) is maximal.

Reasoning: start with the widest container l = 0, r = n-1. The area is limited by the shorter wall. Moving the taller wall inward can never help (width shrinks, height is still capped by the shorter one). So move the shorter one. Every step discards one wall that cannot be part of a better answer.

long long max_area(const std::vector<int>& h) {
    int l = 0, r = static_cast<int>(h.size()) - 1;
    long long best = 0;
    while (l < r) {
        long long area = static_cast<long long>(r - l) * std::min(h[l], h[r]);
        best = std::max(best, area);
        if (h[l] < h[r]) ++l; else --r;
    }
    return best;
}
O(n), O(1). The proof-by-elimination argument is what the interviewer wants to hear.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Minimum size subarray with sum >= target (positive integers)
docs.text:
Reasoning: positives make sum monotone in window size. Grow r until sum >= target, then shrink l while it stays >= target, recording the length.

int min_subarray_len(int target, const std::vector<int>& v) {
    int n = static_cast<int>(v.size()), l = 0, best = n + 1;
    long long sum = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < n; ++r) {
        sum += v[r];
        while (sum >= target) {          // shrink while still valid
            best = std::min(best, r - l + 1);
            sum -= v[l++];
        }
    }
    return best == n + 1 ? 0 : best;
}
O(n): l and r each move at most n times. O(1) space. If the array had negatives this breaks (shrinking could make the sum larger) — then you need prefix sums + a monotonic deque (module 06).

docs.title: Problem 6 — Longest subarray of 1s after flipping at most k zeroes
docs.text:
Reasoning: a window is valid if it contains <= k zeroes. That is monotone. Track zero count.

int longest_ones(const std::vector<int>& v, int k) {
    int l = 0, zeros = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < static_cast<int>(v.size()); ++r) {
        if (v[r] == 0) ++zeros;
        while (zeros > k) if (v[l++] == 0) --zeros;
        best = std::max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
O(n), O(1). The template "add right, while invalid drop left, record" is worth memorising verbatim; it solves "longest substring with at most k distinct", "fruit into baskets", "longest repeating character replacement" with only the validity test changed.

docs.title: Problem 7 — Count subarrays with sum exactly k (integers may be negative)
docs.text:
Reasoning: sliding window fails with negatives. sum(i..j) = P[j+1] - P[i] = k means for each j we need the number of earlier prefix sums equal to P[j+1] - k. A hash map from prefix sum to count gives that in O(1).

int subarray_sum_equals_k(const std::vector<int>& v, int k) {
    std::unordered_map<long long, int> seen;   // prefix sum -> how many times seen
    seen[0] = 1;                                // empty prefix
    long long prefix = 0;
    int count = 0;
    for (int x : v) {
        prefix += x;
        auto it = seen.find(prefix - k);
        if (it != seen.end()) count += it->second;
        ++seen[prefix];
    }
    return count;
}
O(n) time, O(n) space. Same skeleton solves "longest subarray with sum k" (store first index instead of count) and "subarray sums divisible by k" (store prefix % k, normalised to non-negative).

docs.title: Problem 8 — Maximum subarray sum (Kadane)
docs.text:
long long max_subarray(const std::vector<int>& v) {
    long long cur = v[0], best = v[0];
    for (std::size_t i = 1; i < v.size(); ++i) {
        cur = std::max<long long>(v[i], cur + v[i]);  // extend or restart
        best = std::max(best, cur);
    }
    return best;
}
O(n), O(1). Why it works: the best subarray ending at i either is just v[i] or extends the best one ending at i-1. If cur ever goes negative, it is worth dropping, because any future subarray would be better off without it. To return the indices, record start when you restart and (start, i) when best updates.

docs.title: Also in the code files
docs.text:
• Merge two sorted arrays into the first one, which has room at the end: fill from the back so nothing is overwritten (m02_two_pointers.cpp).
  • Rotate array by k using three reversals (m02_two_pointers.cpp).
  • Range-sum queries with a prefix array (m02_prefix_sums_kadane.cpp).
  • Best time to buy and sell stock as Kadane on differences (m02_prefix_sums_kadane.cpp).

docs.title: 4.1 What std::vector<int> actually is
docs.text:
Three pointers: begin, end (one past last used), end_of_storage (one past allocated). sizeof(std::vector<int>) is 24 bytes on 64-bit libstdc++. size() is end - begin, capacity() is end_of_storage - begin. push_back with spare capacity is: construct at *end, increment end. That inlines to roughly three instructions plus the store — which is why push_back into a reserved vector is as fast as writing to a C array.

Reallocation calls operator new for the new block, move-constructs (or copies, if the type's move constructor is not noexcept) each element into it, destroys the old elements, frees the old block. For trivially copyable types like int the move loop becomes a memcpy. For std::string it moves 32-byte objects (three pointers plus SSO buffer, module 03). For a type with a throwing move constructor the vector falls back to copying to keep the strong exception guarantee — mark your move constructors noexcept.

docs.title: 4.2 Why v[i] has no bounds check
docs.text: operator[] compiles to one load with a computed address. at() adds a compare and a branch. In a hot loop that branch is nearly free (predicted), but the standard chose to leave the choice to you. Under -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS libstdc++ adds a check to operator[] as well; turn it on in debug builds. Out-of-range operator[] is undefined behaviour: in practice it reads the next heap object, which is how you get the "works in debug, corrupt in release" bug.

docs.title: 4.3 Why two pointers is fast beyond Big-O
docs.text: Both indices move forward. Every memory access is to a cache line already fetched or the next one. The hardware prefetcher sees two sequential streams and keeps both fed. Branch prediction works well because the "move l or move r" decision is often locally consistent. A two-pointer pass over 10^7 ints finishes in a few milliseconds; the equivalent hash-map solution, also O(n), is typically 10 to 30x slower because each lookup is a random access.

docs.title: 4.4 std::array, C arrays, and spans
docs.text: std::array<int, N> is a C array with a size and iterators, no heap. Use it for fixed small buffers (a 256-entry character count, a 4-entry direction table). A raw int arr[100] like in your array.cpp decays to int* when passed to a function and loses its length; std::array does not. C++20 has std::span for "pointer plus length" views; in C++17 pass (const int* data, std::size_t n) or a const std::vector<int>&.

docs.title: 4.5 Growth factor, memory and the allocator
docs.text: With 2x growth the peak memory during reallocation is old + new = 3n elements. With 1.5x it is 2.5n and freed blocks can be coalesced and reused by the allocator more often (because the sum of previous sizes exceeds the next size: 1 + 1.5 > 2.25). That is Folly's and MSVC's argument for 1.5. libstdc++ chose 2 for fewer reallocations. For your server, if a vector holds hundreds of MB, reserve once from a known upper bound and the growth factor stops mattering.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Request buffers. The receive buffer in a TCP server is a vector of bytes that grows as partial reads arrive. Without reserve to the expected message size, a 64 KB message arriving in 1 KB chunks causes about 6 reallocations and copies — on every request. Reserve.
  • Compacting a list of active connections. Removing closed connections from a vector one at a time with erase is O(n^2) per sweep. Use remove_if + erase (one pass), or swap with back and pop_back if order does not matter.
  • Sliding window in monitoring. "Requests in the last 60 seconds" is a sliding window over a time-ordered array of timestamps. Keep l at the oldest timestamp still inside the window. This is also how rate limiters are implemented.
  • Prefix sums in reporting. "Sum of transactions between day i and day j" over a year of daily totals: build the prefix array once, answer any range in O(1). Databases do the same thing with materialised running totals when queries are heavy and writes are light.
  • Kadane in anomaly detection. The maximum-sum window of (latency - baseline) finds the worst sustained degradation period in a metrics series.
  • Debugging story. A vector of Session* was iterated while a callback inside the loop called push_back on the same vector. Reallocation moved the buffer; the loop's iterator pointed into freed memory. Symptom: random crash under load, never in test. Fix: iterate by index with the size snapshotted, or collect new sessions into a separate vector and append after the loop. Iterator invalidation is the vector's one sharp edge; respect it.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Rewrite your array.cpp using std::vector<int>: build from the arrivals list, search with std::find, delete with erase. Done when it compiles under -Wall -Wextra -Werror with no using namespace std.
  2. (easy) Squares of a sorted array (may contain negatives) in sorted order, O(n). Hint: two pointers from both ends, fill the output from the back. Done when [-4,-1,0,3,10] -> [0,1,9,16,100].
  3. (medium) Longest subarray with at most two distinct values ("fruit into baskets"). Use the variable-window template with a count map of size <= 3. Done when [1,2,1,2,3] -> 4 and [1,2,3,2,2] -> 4.
  4. (medium) Product of array except self, O(n), no division. Hint: prefix products from the left into the output, then a running suffix product from the right. Done when [1,2,3,4] -> [24,12,8,6] and [0,1] -> [1,0].
  5. (medium) Three Sum: all unique triplets summing to zero. Sort, fix i, two-pointer the rest, skip duplicates. O(n^2). Done when [-1,0,1,2,-1,-4] -> {[-1,-1,2],[-1,0,1]} with no duplicate triplets.
  6. (hard) Maximum sum circular subarray. Hint: answer is max(Kadane(v), total - min subarray), with a special case when all elements are negative. Done when [5,-3,5] -> 10 and [-3,-2,-3] -> -2.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why is std::vector preferred over std::list even for frequent middle insertion? Contiguous memory gives cache locality and prefetching; shifting a few thousand elements with memmove is faster than one cache-missing pointer chase. Lists win only when elements are huge and non-movable, or when you hold iterators that must survive insertions elsewhere.

Q: What does reserve do and when do you call it? Allocates capacity without constructing elements, so subsequent push_backs do not reallocate. Call it when you know the final size or a good upper bound, e.g. reading n rows from a query. It does not change size().

Q: What invalidates vector iterators? Any reallocation (push_back past capacity, insert, reserve to a larger value) invalidates all. erase/insert invalidate iterators at and after the position even without reallocation. pop_back invalidates only the end iterator and the erased element's.

Q: How do you turn an O(n^2) pair search into O(n)? If sorted: two pointers from both ends, moving the one that must move. If unsorted: one pass with a hash set of seen values. If it is about contiguous ranges: sliding window (monotone property) or prefix sums with a hash map (exact sums, negatives).

Q: When does sliding window fail and what replaces it? When the property is not monotone in window size, e.g. "sum == k" with negative numbers. Replace with prefix sums and a hash map keyed by prefix value.

Q: Explain Kadane's algorithm and why it is correct. Maintain the best sum of a subarray ending at i: cur = max(v[i], cur + v[i]). If the running sum turns negative, any later subarray does better without it, so restarting is safe. The answer is the max over all i. O(n), O(1).

Q: for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) fails to compile with -Werror. Why? size() returns unsigned size_t; comparing with signed int triggers -Wsign-compare. Either use size_t for i or cast size() to int once.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• std::vector is three pointers; push_back is amortised O(1); insert/erase at i is O(n-i).
  • Ranges are half-open [begin, end); size() is unsigned — cast once or loop with size_t.
  • Reallocation invalidates all iterators; erase returns the next valid one; prefer erase-remove.
  • Two pointers: opposite ends on sorted data, slow/fast for in-place filtering, one per array for merging.
  • Sliding window: "add right, while invalid drop left, record"; needs a monotone property.
  • Prefix sums: sum(i..j) = P[j+1] - P[i]; with a hash map handles exact sums and negatives.
  • In-place deletion of many elements is one slow/fast pass, not repeated shifting.
  • Kadane: extend or restart; O(n) max subarray; generalises to products and circular arrays.
  • Sequential access patterns are 10 to 30x faster than hash lookups at the same Big-O.
  • Reserve receive buffers; never push_back to a vector you are iterating.

docs.title: 03. Strings
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
In C a string is a char* that ends at the first zero byte. You know the consequences: strlen is O(n), you carry a separate length when you care about speed, and every buffer is a potential overflow. std::string fixes this by storing the length, owning its memory and growing like a vector. Think of it as std::vector<char> that also guarantees a trailing '\0' so you can hand c_str() to any C API.

Most string interview problems are array problems in disguise: two pointers for palindromes and reversals, sliding window for "longest substring with property", a 26-entry or 256-entry count array instead of a hash map. What is specific to strings is parsing (turning text into numbers and tokens safely), hashing (comparing many substrings cheaply) and pattern matching (finding a needle in a haystack faster than O(n*m)).

The one new tool this module adds is std::string_view: a pointer plus a length that does not own anything. It lets you slice and pass strings around without copying, which is what you would do with const char*, size_t in C — but with a real type that knows its bounds.

docs.title: 2.1 std::string essentials
docs.text:
std::string s = "hello";          // copies the literal into s
s.size(); s.length();             // same thing, O(1), std::size_t
s[1]; s.at(1);                    // unchecked / checked
s += " world";                    // amortised O(1) per char (vector-like growth)
s + "!"                           // creates a NEW string: O(n). Avoid in loops.
s.substr(pos, len)                // copies: O(len)
s.find("wor")                     // std::string::npos if absent; O(n*m) naive, fine in practice
s.compare(t); s == t; s < t       // lexicographic, byte-wise
s.c_str(); s.data()               // const char* (data() non-const since C++17), '\0'-terminated
s.push_back('x'); s.pop_back(); s.back(); s.front()
s.insert(pos, "x"); s.erase(pos, len)   // O(n), shifts like vector
std::to_string(42); std::stoi("42"); std::stoll("9000000000")
std::getline(std::cin, s);        // read a line

Strings are mutable, contiguous, and '\0'-terminated (guaranteed since C++11). s.size() does not count the terminator. s[s.size()] is '\0' and reading it is defined; writing it is not.

docs.title: 2.2 std::string_view (C++17)
docs.text:
std::string_view sv = s;               // no copy, points into s
sv.substr(2, 3);                       // O(1): a new view, not a new string
sv.remove_prefix(1); sv.remove_suffix(1);
sv.find('x'); sv.starts_with(...)      // starts_with is C++20; in C++17 use sv.substr(0,n) == prefix
std::string owned(sv);                 // explicit copy when you need ownership

Rules:

  • A string_view is not '\0'-terminated. Never pass sv.data() to a C function that expects a C string.
  • It dangles the moment the underlying string is destroyed or reallocated. Do not store a string_view as a member unless you control the lifetime of the source. Do not return a view of a local std::string.
  • Take std::string_view as a function parameter when you only read: it accepts std::string, const char* and literals without a copy. Take const std::string& when you need c_str(); take std::string by value when you will store it.

docs.title: 2.3 Characters, bytes, and the 256-table trick
docs.text:
char is a byte, signed on x86 GCC. 'a' is 97. c - 'a' maps lowercase letters to 0..25. Before indexing any table with a char, cast: static_cast<unsigned char>(c) — otherwise a byte above 127 indexes with a negative number. For "letters only" problems a std::array<int, 26> replaces a hash map and is 10x faster. For arbitrary bytes use std::array<int, 256>.

Unicode: std::string is a sequence of bytes. In UTF-8, "é" is two bytes and size() says 2. Reversing a UTF-8 string byte by byte breaks it. Interview problems are ASCII unless stated; say "assuming ASCII" out loud when you reverse or count characters.

<cctype>: std::isdigit, std::isalpha, std::isspace, std::tolower. They take an int that must be in unsigned char range or EOF — cast first.

docs.title: 2.4 Parsing safely
docs.text:
std::stoi throws std::invalid_argument on garbage and std::out_of_range on overflow. atoi returns 0 on garbage and has undefined behaviour on overflow — the same behaviour you know from C. For hand-written parsing (the "string to integer" interview problem), the rules are: skip whitespace, read an optional sign, accumulate digits, check overflow before multiplying:

if (result > (INT_MAX - digit) / 10) return sign == 1 ? INT_MAX : INT_MIN;  // would overflow
result = result * 10 + digit;

Tokenising: a loop with find_first_not_of(delims, pos) and find_first_of(delims, start) over a string_view splits without allocating per token. std::istringstream with >> is simpler and fine when performance does not matter.

docs.title: 2.5 Hashing strings
docs.text:
A hash function maps a string to an integer so that equal strings give equal hashes and different strings usually give different hashes. std::hash<std::string> (libstdc++ uses MurmurHash2 on 64-bit) is what std::unordered_map<std::string, ...> uses. It reads every byte: O(length). It is not cryptographic and not stable across platforms or versions — never persist it or send it over the wire.

Polynomial rolling hash. For algorithm problems you want to hash every substring of length m in O(1) each. Treat the string as a number in base B modulo a prime M:

H(s[0..m)) = s[0]*B^(m-1) + s[1]*B^(m-2) + ... + s[m-1]   (mod M)
H(s[i+1..i+m+1)) = (H(s[i..i+m)) - s[i]*B^(m-1)) * B + s[i+m]   (mod M)

Slide the window: remove the leading character's contribution, shift, add the new one. All O(1). Typical constants: B = 131 or 31, M = 1e9+7 or 2^61-1. Collisions are possible (probability about 1/M per comparison), so either verify a hash match by comparing the actual substrings, or use two independent moduli. This is Rabin-Karp string search: O(n + m) expected.

docs.title: 2.6 KMP: the idea
docs.text:
Naive search for pattern P (length m) in text T (length n) restarts at i+1 after a mismatch: O(nm) worst case (e.g. T = "aaaa...a", P = "aaab"). KMP observes that when a mismatch happens after matching k characters, you already know what those k characters are — they are P[0..k). The longest proper prefix of P[0..k) that is also a suffix of it tells you how far to slide without missing a match. Precompute that for every k into the failure table* f[k] in O(m). Then the text pointer never moves backwards: O(n + m) total.

P = "ababc"
f = [0,0,1,2,0]   f[k] = length of longest proper prefix of P[0..k] that is also its suffix

Mismatch at P[4]='c' after matching "abab" -> f[3] = 2 -> continue comparing at P[2] without re-reading text. Interviews ask you to explain the idea; writing KMP bug-free from memory is rare. The failure-table build is itself a KMP of P against P, which is the elegant part.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: Files: code/m03_string_basics.cpp (SSO demonstration, string_view usage and dangers, tokenising), code/m03_string_problems.cpp (classic problems), code/m03_kmp_rabin_karp.cpp (rolling hash search and KMP with failure table).

docs.title: SSO demonstration
docs.text:
std::string s;
const char* before = s.data();
s = "short";                         // fits in the internal buffer: data() unchanged
std::printf("%s\n", s.data() == before ? "inline" : "heap");
s = "this string is longer than fifteen chars";
std::printf("%s\n", s.data() == before ? "inline" : "heap");   // heap
std::printf("sizeof(std::string) = %zu\n", sizeof(std::string));  // 32 on libstdc++

docs.title: Classic problems in m03_string_problems.cpp
docs.text:
1. Valid palindrome (alphanumerics only, case-insensitive) — two pointers from both ends, skip non-alphanumerics. O(n), O(1).
  2. Reverse words in place — reverse the whole string, then reverse each word. O(n), O(1).
  3. Valid anagram — 26-entry count array: +1 for s, -1 for t, all must be zero. O(n), O(1).
  4. Longest substring without repeating characters — sliding window with a 256-entry last-seen index. O(n), O(1).
  5. String to integer (atoi) — whitespace, sign, digits, overflow clamp. O(n).
  6. Longest palindromic substring — expand around each centre (2n-1 centres). O(n^2), O(1). Mention Manacher's O(n) exists; nobody expects you to write it.
  7. Group anagrams — key = sorted word (or 26-count string), hash map of vectors. O(n * k log k).
  8. Split by delimiter without allocating tokens — string_view tokeniser.

Each is in the file with a check() call; key parts:

// 4. longest substring without repeating characters
int longest_unique_substring(std::string_view s) {
    std::array<int, 256> last{};      // last index + 1 where each byte was seen; 0 = never
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < static_cast<int>(s.size()); ++r) {
        unsigned char c = static_cast<unsigned char>(s[static_cast<std::size_t>(r)]);
        l = std::max(l, last[c]);     // jump l past the previous occurrence, never backwards
        last[c] = r + 1;
        best = std::max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}

The std::max(l, last[c]) line is the whole trick: a window is invalid only if the previous occurrence of c is inside it, and l must never move left.

docs.title: 4.1 Small String Optimisation (SSO)
docs.text:
A heap allocation per string would make short strings — most strings — slow. libstdc++'s std::string is 32 bytes: a pointer, a size, and a 16-byte union that is either the capacity (heap mode) or an inline buffer of 15 chars plus '\0' (inline mode). Strings up to 15 bytes live entirely inside the object: no new, no cache miss to reach the characters, and copying the string is copying 32 bytes. MSVC's layout also gives 15 chars inline; libc++ (Clang on macOS) packs it differently and gets 22.

Consequences you should be able to state:

  • std::move of a short string copies 32 bytes; of a long string it steals the pointer. Both are O(1).
  • data() changes when a string crosses the 15-char boundary — any pointer you took is dead.
  • A std::vector<std::string> of short strings has good locality; of long strings it is a vector of pointers in disguise, one cache miss per string to read the text.
  • sizeof(std::string) == 32 versus sizeof(std::string_view) == 16. Passing a view is two registers.

docs.title: 4.2 Growth and reserve
docs.text: Like vector: += doubles capacity on overflow (libstdc++ grows to max(2*cap, needed)). Building a 1 MB string with += does about 17 reallocations. Call reserve when you know the size, e.g. when serialising a message of known length in your RPC server.

docs.title: 4.3 Why s = s + c in a loop is O(n^2)
docs.text: s + c constructs a brand-new string of size n+1 and copies n chars. Then assignment moves it into s. Across n iterations that is 1 + 2 + ... + n = O(n^2) copies. s += c appends in place: amortised O(1). Same for s = s.substr(1) in a loop (O(n) per call). Use indices or a string_view to "consume" a string instead of making smaller copies.

docs.title: 4.4 std::string::find and strstr
docs.text: libstdc++'s find for a multi-character needle is a straightforward scan using memchr for the first character then memcmp — worst case O(nm) but with hardware-accelerated inner loops that make it faster than KMP for realistic text. glibc's strstr uses the Two-Way algorithm (O(n+m) worst case). Takeaway: in production, use the library. In an interview, know why naive is O(nm) and what KMP/Rabin-Karp do about it.

docs.title: 4.5 Hash quality and DoS
docs.text: If an attacker can choose keys, they can pick thousands that collide under a known hash and turn every unordered_map lookup into O(n). This happened to several web frameworks around 2011 ("hash flooding"). Defences: randomised per-process seed (SipHash in Python, Rust), switching to a tree when a bucket grows too long (Java 8 HashMap). libstdc++ does neither. If your server hashes untrusted strings (account numbers from the network are untrusted), know this. Module 04 covers the table side.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Message parsing in the RPC server. A fixed-format message header ("LEN=00120;TYPE=TXN;") should be parsed with string_view slices and a hand-written digit loop with overflow checks, not atoi on strtok output. strtok is not thread-safe (static state), which matters in your multithreaded server; strtok_r or string_view tokenising are.
  • Logging. std::string line = a + ", " + b + ", " + c; creates temporaries. Fine at 1 kHz. At 100 kHz, reserve and += or std::snprintf into a stack buffer. Measure first.
  • Case-insensitive comparison. Do not lowercase both strings (two allocations). Compare with std::tolower on each char pair, or use a locale-free custom comparator.
  • Account numbers as keys. A 16-digit account number stored as std::string takes 32 bytes in the object (fits SSO) and hashes in ~16 byte reads. Storing it as std::uint64_t takes 8 bytes and hashes in one multiply. When a map has 10 million entries this is 240 MB. Choose the key type on purpose.
  • War story. A log-parsing tool read 2 GB of text with std::getline and did tokens.push_back(line.substr(a, b - a)) for every field. Profile: 70% of time in malloc/free. Switching tokens to std::string_view into the line (which outlived the processing of its tokens) made it 6x faster with no algorithmic change.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Write bool is_palindrome(std::string_view) ignoring non-alphanumerics and case. Done when "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" is true and "race a car" is false.
  2. (easy) Write std::vector<std::string_view> split(std::string_view s, char delim) that skips empty tokens. Done when ",a,,b," gives ["a","b"] and no std::string is created.
  3. (medium) Implement my_atoi with overflow clamping. Done when " -91283472332" gives INT_MIN, "4193 with words" gives 4193, "words 987" gives 0.
  4. (medium) Longest repeating character replacement: longest substring that can be made all one letter by changing at most k letters. Hint: window is valid when length - maxFrequencyInWindow <= k; you never need to decrease the max. Done when ("AABABBA", 1) -> 4.
  5. (hard) Implement Rabin-Karp with two moduli and verify a match with memcmp. Count occurrences of a pattern in a 10 MB random string of 'a'..'d' and compare the time with std::string::find in a loop. Done when both counts agree and you can explain which is faster and why.
  6. (hard) Write the KMP failure table and search, test on "aaaaab" in "aaaaaaaaab" and on "abcabd" in "abcabcabd". Done when both find the correct index and you can explain the value of every failure-table entry for "abcabd".

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is SSO and why does it matter? Small String Optimisation stores short strings (15 chars on libstdc++) inside the 32-byte object, avoiding heap allocation. Most strings are short, so this removes most allocations and gives cache locality. It also means data() moves when a string grows past the threshold.

Q: std::string vs std::string_view — when do you use which? View for read-only parameters and slicing without copies; it is 16 bytes and non-owning. String when you need ownership, mutation or a '\0'-terminated buffer. Never store a view beyond the lifetime of its source.

Q: Why is s = s + ch in a loop quadratic and what is the fix? Each + builds a new string of the current length, so total copies are 1+2+...+n. Use +=, which appends in place with amortised O(1) per character, or reserve first.

Q: How would you check if two strings are anagrams? Count characters: +1 for one string, -1 for the other, in a 26-entry (or 256-entry) array; all counts must end at zero. O(n) time, O(1) space. Sorting both and comparing is O(n log n).

Q: Explain rolling hash and what it is used for. Treat the string as a base-B number mod a prime. Sliding one character right updates the hash in O(1): subtract the outgoing char times B^(m-1), multiply by B, add the incoming char. Used in Rabin-Karp search, duplicate-substring detection, and plagiarism checks. Verify matches or use two moduli because collisions are possible.

Q: What is the idea of KMP? On a mismatch after matching k pattern characters, use the precomputed longest proper prefix-suffix length of P[0..k) to shift the pattern without rewinding the text pointer. Preprocessing O(m), search O(n). The text pointer never goes back.

Q: Why cast char to unsigned char before indexing a table or calling isdigit? char is signed on x86 GCC; bytes above 127 become negative, which indexes before the table start (undefined behaviour) and is outside the range <cctype> functions accept.

Q: How does hash flooding work and how do you defend against it? An attacker sends many keys that collide under the known hash, degrading unordered_map to O(n) per operation. Defences: a per-process random seed in the hash, limiting input size, or a structure that degrades gracefully (tree-backed buckets).

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• std::string is a growable, contiguous, '\0'-terminated byte array; size() is O(1).
  • SSO keeps up to 15 chars inline on libstdc++; sizeof(std::string) is 32; crossing the threshold reallocates and moves data().
  • string_view is pointer + length, 16 bytes, non-owning, not '\0'-terminated; use for read-only parameters and O(1) slicing; never let it outlive its source.
  • += is amortised O(1); s + c in a loop is O(n^2); substr copies.
  • Cast char to unsigned char before table indexing or <cctype>.
  • Letters-only problems: 26-entry array beats a hash map.
  • Rolling hash: O(1) per slide; verify matches or double the modulus.
  • KMP: failure table from the pattern, text pointer never rewinds, O(n + m).
  • Hashes from std::hash are not stable across builds; never persist them.
  • Parse untrusted text with explicit overflow checks; strtok is not thread-safe.

docs.title: 04. Hashing and hash tables
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Your array.cpp finds the number 7 by looking at every box until it sees a 7. Your orderedArray.cpp does better by keeping the boxes sorted and halving. A hash table does something that sounds like cheating: it computes, from the value itself, which box to look in. "7? That goes in box 7 mod 10 = box 7." One arithmetic step, one memory read. O(1).

The catch is collisions: 7 and 17 both want box 7. Every hash table design is an answer to "what do we do when two keys want the same box". Chaining hangs a short linked list off the box. Open addressing walks to the next free box. Both work; they have very different cache behaviour, and knowing why is a senior-level distinction.

Think of a coat check. The attendant hashes your ticket number to a hook. If two coats land on one hook, chaining means they hang together on that hook; open addressing means the second coat goes on the next empty hook and the attendant knows to keep looking. Either way, you get your coat in roughly constant time as long as there are enough hooks for the coats — that ratio is the load factor, and keeping it low is what keeps the "roughly constant" honest.

docs.title: 2.1 Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Hash function h(key) -> integer. Deterministic. Should spread keys uniformly.
  • Bucket (slot): one position in the table array of size m. index = h(key) % m.
  • Collision: two different keys map to the same index.
  • Load factor alpha = n / m: number of stored elements per bucket on average.
  • Rehash: allocate a bigger table (typically 2x), reinsert every element. O(n), but amortised O(1) per insert by the same argument as vector growth.

docs.title: 2.2 Chaining (separate chaining)
docs.text:
Each bucket is the head of a linked list of entries (key, value, next). Lookup: hash, walk the chain comparing keys. Expected chain length is alpha. With alpha <= 1 that is O(1) expected. Worst case: all keys in one bucket, O(n).

buckets[0] -> (16,"p") -> (32,"q") -> null
buckets[1] -> null
buckets[2] -> (18,"r") -> null
buckets[3] -> (3,"s") -> (11,"t") -> (19,"u") -> null    <- hash % 8
...

Pros: simple; deletion is trivial; tolerates alpha > 1; pointers/iterators to elements stay valid across rehash (the node moves between buckets, it is not copied). Cons: one allocation per element; each chain hop is a cache miss; memory overhead of a next pointer per entry. std::unordered_map is specified such that only chaining satisfies its guarantees (stable references, bucket_count(), max_load_factor() default 1.0).

docs.title: 2.3 Open addressing
docs.text:
All entries live in the table array itself. On collision, probe other slots in a fixed order until a free one is found.

  • Linear probing: slots i, i+1, i+2, ... Best cache behaviour (probes stay in one or two cache lines). Suffers from primary clustering: runs of occupied slots grow and merge.
  • Quadratic probing: i, i+1, i+4, i+9, ... Less clustering, slightly worse locality.
  • Double hashing: i, i+h2(k), i+2*h2(k), ... Best distribution, worst locality.

Deletion cannot simply empty a slot: a later key that probed past it would become unreachable. Use a tombstone marker ("deleted, keep probing"), and count tombstones toward the load factor so a table full of tombstones still rehashes. Alternatively, backward-shift deletion (move later entries in the cluster back) avoids tombstones at the cost of a more complex delete; Robin Hood hashing uses this.

Load factor must stay well below 1 (typically rehash at 0.5 to 0.875). Expected probes for a successful search under linear probing ~ (1 + 1/(1-alpha)) / 2: at alpha = 0.5 about 1.5, at alpha = 0.9 about 5.5. Beyond that it degrades sharply.

Pros: no per-element allocation, one contiguous array, excellent cache behaviour, 2 to 5x faster than chaining in practice for small keys. Cons: rehash invalidates all references; needs tombstones or backward shift; sensitive to a bad hash function (clustering).

Modern high-performance tables (Google's absl::flat_hash_map, Facebook's F14) are open addressing with SIMD-accelerated probing over groups of 16 control bytes. If an interviewer asks "how would you make unordered_map faster", that is the answer.

docs.title: 2.4 Hash functions for the table
docs.text:
For integers: std::hash<int> on libstdc++ is the identity. That is fine when the table size is a prime (libstdc++ uses a prime bucket count) and keys are arbitrary; it is terrible with power-of-two table sizes and keys that share low bits (e.g. all multiples of 8 — pointers, aligned addresses). For your own open-addressing table with power-of-two size, mix the bits first: a multiply by a large odd constant and a shift (Fibonacci hashing: (k * 11400714819323198485ULL) >> (64 - log2(m))), or splitmix64.

For strings: std::hash<std::string> (MurmurHash2 on libstdc++), FNV-1a (tiny to write), or the polynomial hash from module 03. For composite keys (pair, struct): combine member hashes with seed ^= h(member) + 0x9e3779b9 + (seed << 6) + (seed >> 2) (Boost's hash_combine) and specialise std::hash<YourType> or pass a hasher as a template argument.

docs.title: 2.5 std::unordered_map and std::unordered_set pitfalls
docs.text:
std::unordered_map<std::string, int> m;
m["key"];              // INSERTS a default-constructed 0 if absent. Use find() to test membership.
m.count("key");        // 0 or 1; cheap membership test
auto it = m.find("k"); // end() if absent; no insert
m.try_emplace("k", 5); // insert only if absent; does not construct value if present (C++17)
m.insert_or_assign("k", 5);
m.erase("k");
