m.reserve(n);          // pre-size buckets for n elements: avoids rehashes
m.load_factor(); m.bucket_count(); m.max_load_factor(0.7f);
for (auto& [k, v] : m) ...   // iteration order is unspecified and changes after rehash

Pitfalls to know:

  1. operator[] inserts. In a loop that checks membership this silently grows the map.
  2. Iteration order is unspecified. Code that depends on it breaks on rehash or a different library. Tests that print a map and compare output are flaky by construction.
  3. Iterating is slow: it walks bucket by bucket through a node list; each node is a cache miss. std::unordered_map with 1M entries iterates ~10x slower than a vector of pairs.
  4. Erasing during iteration: it = m.erase(it) is fine; anything else is UB.
  5. Rehash invalidates iterators but not pointers/references to elements (chaining).
  6. No std::hash for std::pair or your structs: provide one.
  7. The worst case is O(n). If the keys come from an attacker, see module 03 hash flooding.
  8. max_load_factor default is 1.0; libstdc++ rehashes when size exceeds bucket_count. Lowering it trades memory for shorter chains.

When to use std::map instead: you need sorted iteration, range queries, lower_bound, or predictable worst-case O(log n). When to use a sorted std::vector instead: the data is built once and queried many times (binary search, best cache behaviour, smallest memory).

docs.title: 2.6 Designing with hashes: the three questions
docs.text:
1. What is the key? Exactly the thing you want O(1) lookup on. Normalise it (sorted string for anagrams, prefix % k for divisibility, (x, y) packed into one int64).
  2. What is the value? Count, first index, last index, list of indices, a node pointer (module 05 LRU).
  3. What do I look up? target - x, prefix - k, x - 1 and x + 1, pattern -> canonical form.

Most hash-map interview problems are solved by answering those three questions out loud.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: Files: code/m04_hash_map_chaining.cpp (a complete chained hash map with resize, templated on key/value with a hasher), code/m04_hash_map_open_addressing.cpp (linear probing with tombstones and Fibonacci hashing), code/m04_hash_problems.cpp (the six problems).

docs.title: Your own chained hash map (key parts)
docs.text:
template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>>
class HashMap {
    struct Node { K key; V value; Node* next; };
    std::vector<Node*> buckets_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    Hash hash_;

    std::size_t index_of(const K& k) const { return hash_(k) % buckets_.size(); }

    void rehash(std::size_t new_bucket_count) {
        std::vector<Node*> nb(new_bucket_count, nullptr);
        for (Node* head : buckets_)            // move every node; no reallocation of nodes
            while (head) {
                Node* next = head->next;
                std::size_t i = hash_(head->key) % new_bucket_count;
                head->next = nb[i]; nb[i] = head;   // push front into the new bucket
                head = next;
            }
        buckets_.swap(nb);
    }
public:
    V* find(const K& k) {
        for (Node* p = buckets_[index_of(k)]; p; p = p->next)
            if (p->key == k) return &p->value;
        return nullptr;
    }
    bool insert(const K& k, const V& v) {      // returns false if key existed (value updated)
        if (V* existing = find(k)) { *existing = v; return false; }
        if (size_ + 1 > buckets_.size() * MAX_LOAD) rehash(buckets_.size() * 2);
        std::size_t i = index_of(k);
        buckets_[i] = new Node{k, v, buckets_[i]};
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }
    bool erase(const K& k) {
        Node** pp = &buckets_[index_of(k)];     // pointer-to-pointer: no special case for head
        while (*pp) {
            if ((*pp)->key == k) { Node* dead = *pp; *pp = dead->next; delete dead; --size_; return true; }
            pp = &(*pp)->next;
        }
        return false;
    }
};

The Node** trick in erase is the same one you use in C to unlink from a singly linked list without a "previous" variable. The full file adds a destructor, move semantics, operator[] and iteration.

docs.title: Open addressing with linear probing (key parts)
docs.text:
enum class State : std::uint8_t { Empty, Full, Tombstone };
struct Slot { K key; V value; State state = State::Empty; };
std::vector<Slot> slots_;              // size is a power of two
std::size_t mask_;                     // slots_.size() - 1

std::size_t probe_start(const K& k) const {
    std::uint64_t h = hash_(k) * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15ULL;   // Fibonacci mixing
    return static_cast<std::size_t>(h >> (64 - log2_size_)); // take the HIGH bits
}
V* find(const K& k) {
    for (std::size_t i = probe_start(k);; i = (i + 1) & mask_) {
        if (slots_[i].state == State::Empty) return nullptr;       // hit a hole: not here
        if (slots_[i].state == State::Full && slots_[i].key == k) return &slots_[i].value;
        // Tombstone or other key: keep probing
    }
}

docs.title: The six problems (m04_hash_problems.cpp)
docs.text:
1. Two Sum (unsorted) — map value -> index; for each x look up target - x before inserting x (handles x + x == target with distinct indices). O(n), O(n).
  2. Longest consecutive sequence — put all values in a set; for each x that has no x - 1 (it is a run start), count upward. Each value is visited O(1) times amortised. O(n).
  3. Group anagrams — key = 26-count encoded as a string (avoids sorting). O(total chars).
  4. First unique character — count array of 256, then second pass. O(n), O(1).
  5. Top-k frequent elements — count map, then bucket by frequency (array of vectors indexed by count) and read from the top. O(n). The heap version (module 12) is O(n log k).
  6. LRU cache is in module 05 (it needs a list); here instead: contains duplicate within k — sliding window set of the last k values. O(n), O(k).

docs.title: 4.1 libstdc++ unordered_map layout
docs.text:
A singly linked list of all nodes, plus a bucket array of pointers into that list. Each bucket pointer points to the node before the first node of that bucket (so insertion into a bucket can splice without a second pointer). Each node holds the key-value pair, a next pointer, and (for keys whose hash is not "fast", e.g. strings) a cached hash code so rehash does not recompute it. Node size for <int,int>: 16 bytes payload + 8 next = 24, rounded up by malloc to 32. Bucket count is the next prime above size / max_load_factor. Iteration walks the single node list — so it is O(n) regardless of bucket count, but every step is a pointer chase.

Rehash: new bucket array of the next prime size, walk the node list, relink. Nodes are not reallocated, which is why references stay valid.

docs.title: 4.2 The cost of a lookup, in cache misses
docs.text:
Chained unordered_map<int,int>: hash (free for int) -> read bucket pointer (miss 1) -> read node (miss 2) -> compare -> done. Two dependent cache misses ~ 200 ns on a cold cache.

Linear-probing flat_hash_map<int,int>: hash with mixing (~2 ns) -> read slot (miss 1) -> compare; a second probe is usually in the same cache line. One miss ~ 100 ns.

A sorted vector<int> of 1M entries: binary search touches ~20 cache lines, but the first ~10 are the same lines every time and stay in L1/L2. Measured on typical hardware the three are within 2 to 3x of each other for point lookups at 1M elements; the flat table wins, the chained table loses. For 1000 elements the sorted vector often wins outright.

docs.title: 4.3 Why prime bucket counts
docs.text: With index = h % m, if m is a power of two the index is just the low bits of h. Keys that differ only in high bits (multiples of 1024, pointers to 64-byte-aligned objects) all collide. A prime m makes every bit of h matter. The cost is an integer division (~20 to 40 cycles) on every operation. Power-of-two tables avoid the division (h & (m-1)) but must mix the hash first — that is the Fibonacci multiply in the open-addressing file.

docs.title: 4.4 Amortised resize and latency spikes
docs.text: Doubling on load factor gives amortised O(1) but a single insert can take O(n) when it triggers the rehash. For a 10M-entry map that is tens of milliseconds — a latency spike your monitoring will see. Mitigations: reserve to the expected size at startup; incremental rehash (keep old and new tables, move a few buckets per operation — Redis does this); or accept the spike and do it off the hot path.

docs.title: 4.5 Database hashing
docs.text: PostgreSQL hash indexes (reliable since version 10) bucket keys by hash(key) % nbuckets and grow by linear hashing: buckets split one at a time rather than all at once, so there is no O(n) rehash. Hash joins build an in-memory hash table on the smaller relation and probe it with the larger one; when it does not fit in work_mem it partitions both sides to disk ("grace hash join"). Berkeley DB's DB_HASH access method uses extended linear hashing for the same reason. Your unordered_map and these are the same idea at different scales; the database ones care about not stalling for a full rehash.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Session lookup in the RPC server. Session id -> Session*. unordered_map is right. Reserve to the max connection count at startup so no rehash happens under load. Guard it with a mutex or shard it by id % nshards with one mutex per shard (see 04_Concurrency); the shard index is itself a hash.
  • Pointer keys. unordered_map<Connection*, ...>: the identity hash on an 8- or 16-byte aligned pointer with a prime bucket count is fine; with a power-of-two custom table it is a disaster (every pointer ends in 000 or 0000). Mix the bits.
  • Account numbers. Store as std::uint64_t, not std::string. 8 bytes vs 32, one multiply vs 16 byte reads, and no SSO edge cases.
  • Memory. Each unordered_map<int,int> entry costs ~32 bytes of node plus ~8 bytes of bucket pointer: 40 bytes for 8 bytes of data. 10M entries = 400 MB. A flat table at 0.5 load costs 16 bytes per entry. A sorted vector costs 8. Choose consciously.
  • Debugging a slow map. Symptoms: lookups take microseconds, CPU in _M_find_before_node. Check load_factor() and the chain lengths (bucket_size(i) for a sample of buckets). If a few buckets are huge, the hash is bad for your key distribution — e.g. hashing only the first 8 bytes of a key that always starts with the same prefix.
  • War story (typical). A cache keyed by std::string request path was iterated every second to expire entries; with 2M entries the sweep took 300 ms and stalled request handling. Fix: keep a separate time-ordered structure (a list, module 05) for expiry so the sweep touches only what is expiring, and never iterate the hash map on the hot path.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Using std::unordered_map, count word frequencies in a text file and print the 10 most frequent. Done when it runs on a 10 MB file in under a second and never uses operator[] for lookups that should not insert.
  2. (easy) Write struct Point { int x, y; } with a std::hash<Point> specialisation using hash_combine, and store 1M random points in an unordered_set<Point>. Done when bucket_count() and load_factor() printed after insertion look healthy (load <= 1).
  3. (medium) Add operator[], a destructor, move constructor and size() to the chained HashMap in m04_hash_map_chaining.cpp if you cover them yourself without reading the file, then compare with the file. Done when the file's test harness passes with your version.
  4. (medium) Implement "subarray sums divisible by k" using prefix sums mod k and a count map. Done when ([4,5,0,-2,-3,1], 5) -> 7. Handle negative remainders.
  5. (hard) Add backward-shift deletion to the linear-probing table (no tombstones). Done when 1M random insert/erase operations produce the same contents as a std::unordered_map mirror, and find never reads a tombstone state because there are none.
  6. (hard) Benchmark point lookups at n = 1 000, 100 000, 10 000 000 for: std::unordered_map, your open-addressing map, and std::lower_bound on a sorted vector. Done when you have a table of ns/lookup and can explain each crossover in terms of cache lines touched.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does a hash table achieve O(1) lookup? Compute an index from the key with a hash function and go straight to that bucket. With a good hash and bounded load factor, the expected number of keys examined is constant. Worst case is O(n) when many keys collide.

Q: Chaining vs open addressing — trade-offs? Chaining: one node per element, simple deletion, tolerates load > 1, stable references, poor cache locality. Open addressing: everything in one array, excellent locality, no per-element allocation, needs tombstones or backward shift for delete, must keep load below ~0.8, rehash invalidates everything. Flat tables are faster for small keys; std::unordered_map is chained because the standard requires reference stability.

Q: What is load factor and what happens when it grows? Elements per bucket, n/m. For chaining, expected chain length is the load factor. For open addressing, expected probes grow as 1/(1-alpha) and explode near 1. Tables rehash to a bigger array when a threshold is crossed; that is O(n) once and amortised O(1).

Q: Why does m[key] in a membership check cause bugs? operator[] inserts a default-constructed value when the key is absent. The map grows, memory leaks logically, and later count()/iteration see phantom entries. Use find or count.

Q: Why is iterating an unordered_map slow? Elements are individually allocated nodes linked in a list; each step is a pointer chase to an unpredictable address, i.e. a cache miss. Order is also unspecified. If you iterate a lot, keep a vector alongside or use a flat table.

Q: How would you hash a struct with two ints? Specialise std::hash (or pass a hasher functor): combine the member hashes with seed ^= h(x) + 0x9e3779b9 + (seed << 6) + (seed >> 2), or pack both into a 64-bit value and mix it. Never just XOR them — (a, b) and (b, a) would collide.

Q: An attacker controls the keys. What can go wrong? Hash flooding: chosen collisions push every operation to O(n). Mitigate with a keyed/seeded hash per process, by bounding input, or by using a structure with guaranteed bounds (std::map) for untrusted keys.

Q: How does PostgreSQL avoid an O(n) rehash on its hash index? Linear hashing: it splits one bucket at a time as the index grows, keeping two active hash-range sizes, so growth is spread across inserts instead of stalling on one.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A hash table turns the key into a bucket index; collisions are the whole design problem.
  • Chaining: list per bucket, stable references, cache-unfriendly; this is std::unordered_map.
  • Open addressing: probe sequence in one array, cache-friendly, needs tombstones or backward shift, keep load factor below ~0.8; this is absl::flat_hash_map.
  • Load factor alpha = n/m; rehash doubles the table; amortised O(1) but a single insert can stall — reserve at startup.
  • Prime bucket counts tolerate a weak hash; power-of-two tables need bit mixing first.
  • operator[] inserts; iteration order is unspecified and iteration is slow; provide std::hash for your own key types with hash_combine.
  • Three design questions: what is the key, what is the value, what do I look up.
  • Two cache misses per chained lookup versus one for a flat table; sorted vector can win at small n.
  • Databases use linear hashing to grow without a stop-the-world rehash.
  • Untrusted keys mean hash flooding is possible; know the mitigation.

docs.title: 05. Linked lists
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
An array keeps its elements side by side; to insert in the middle you shift everything after it. A linked list keeps each element in its own box anywhere in memory, and each box stores the address of the next one. Inserting in the middle is now two pointer writes, no shifting. The price: to reach box number 500 you must follow 500 pointers, because there is no formula for "where is element i".

You have written this in C: struct node { int val; struct node* next; } with malloc and free, and you have debugged the use-after-free and the forgotten free that go with it. C++ gives you std::unique_ptr so the "who deletes this" question has a compile-time answer, and std::list / std::forward_list so you rarely write a list yourself in production.

So why a whole module? Three reasons. Interviews love lists because a pointer bug shows immediately and the problems (reverse, cycle, merge, nth from end) test whether you can hold an invariant in your head. The LRU cache — a doubly linked list glued to a hash map — is the single most-asked design problem for systems roles and appears in every cache, buffer pool and connection manager you will ever read. And intrusive lists (the node lives inside the object) are everywhere in kernels, databases and your RPC server's queues.

docs.title: 2.1 Singly linked list
docs.text:
head -> [3 | *] -> [7 | *] -> [1 | *] -> nullptr
Operation Cost Note push_front O(1) new node, point at old head, head = new push_back O(1) with tail pointer, else O(n) insert after node p O(1) n->next = p->next; p->next = n; delete after node p O(1) dead = p->next; p->next = dead->next; delete dead; delete node p itself O(n) need the predecessor; or O(1) if you copy the next node into p find by value / index O(n) reverse O(n) three pointers

The order of the two pointer writes on insert matters: set the new node's next first, or you lose the rest of the list. On delete, save next before freeing.

docs.title: 2.2 Doubly linked list
docs.text: Each node also has prev. Deleting a node given only its pointer is O(1): p->prev->next = p->next; p->next->prev = p->prev;. Costs one more pointer per node. This is what std::list is, and what the LRU cache needs.

docs.title: 2.3 The dummy head (sentinel)
docs.text: Many list bugs are special cases for "the list is empty" or "the node to delete is the head". A sentinel node that always exists, holds no value, and sits before the first real node removes those cases: there is always a predecessor. In a circular doubly linked list the sentinel also serves as the tail marker: head->prev is the last element and the list is empty when head->next == head. std::list is implemented this way. In interview code, ListNode dummy(0); dummy.next = head; ListNode* prev = &dummy; is the idiom; return dummy.next at the end.

docs.title: 2.4 Ownership: unique_ptr versus raw pointers
docs.text:
std::unique_ptr<T> is a pointer that deletes what it points to when it goes out of scope, cannot be copied, and can be moved. For a list, struct Node { int val; std::unique_ptr<Node> next; } means: the list owns its nodes, destroying the head destroys the chain, and there is no way to leak or double-free. Traversal uses raw pointers obtained with .get(): raw pointers observe, unique_ptr owns. That split is the whole rule.

Two caveats:

  1. Recursive destruction. Destroying the head destroys next, which destroys its next, ... recursively. A list of 1M nodes overflows the stack. Write an explicit destructor that pops nodes iteratively (while (head) head = std::move(head->next);), which is what the code file does.
  2. Doubly linked with unique_ptr: next owns, prev is a raw back-pointer. Two owning pointers to the same node would double-free.

In interview problems the ListNode is almost always given as a raw-pointer struct, and you do not free anything. Use raw pointers there, say "in production I would use unique_ptr or std::list", and move on. The code file m05_list_problems.cpp follows that convention and frees the test lists in a helper.

docs.title: 2.5 Classic problems and their invariants
docs.text:
Reverse (iterative): prev = nullptr; while (cur) { next = cur->next; cur->next = prev; prev = cur; cur = next; } return prev;. Invariant: prev heads the reversed prefix, cur heads the unprocessed suffix. Recursive: reverse the rest, then head->next->next = head; head->next = nullptr; — O(n) stack, do not use for long lists.

Middle node: slow moves one, fast moves two; when fast hits the end slow is at the middle (the second middle for even length).

Cycle detection (Floyd): slow +1, fast +2. If there is a cycle, fast laps slow and they meet; if not, fast hits nullptr. Why they must meet: once both are inside the cycle the gap shrinks by exactly 1 per step, so it reaches 0 within one cycle length. To find the cycle start: after they meet, reset one pointer to head and advance both by 1; they meet at the start. Proof: let the distance head -> start be a, start -> meeting point be b, cycle length L. Slow travelled a + b; fast travelled 2(a + b) = a + b + kL, so a + b = kL, so a = kL - b: walking a from head lands exactly where walking a from the meeting point does, i.e. the start.

Merge two sorted lists: dummy head, tail pointer; take the smaller head each time; attach the leftover. O(n + m), O(1), no allocation.

Remove nth from end: two pointers n apart; when the lead hits the end, the trailer's next is the node to remove. Use the dummy so removing the head is not special.

Palindrome: find middle, reverse the second half in place, compare, (optionally restore). O(n), O(1).

Reorder L0 Ln L1 Ln-1 ...: middle, reverse second half, interleave. Combines three primitives — a good test of whether you can compose.

docs.title: 2.6 LRU cache
docs.text:
Least Recently Used: a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the entry unused for the longest time. Needed: O(1) get, O(1) put, O(1) "move to front", O(1) "evict from back".

  • A doubly linked list in recency order (front = most recent). Move-to-front and pop-back are O(1) given a node pointer.
  • A hash map key -> node pointer, so that get finds the node in O(1).
map: {k1 -> n1, k2 -> n2, k3 -> n3}
list: [sentinel] <-> n2(k2) <-> n1(k1) <-> n3(k3) <-> [sentinel]
                     most recent              least recent
get(k1): map lookup -> n1; unlink n1; insert after sentinel. list: n1 n2 n3
put(k4) at capacity 3: evict back (n3): map.erase(k3), unlink n3; insert n4 at front.

With std::list and std::unordered_map<K, std::list<...>::iterator>, list::splice does move-to-front in O(1) without allocating. The code file has both that version and a hand-rolled node version, because interviewers sometimes ask for it without the library.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: Files: code/m05_singly_list.cpp (owning list with unique_ptr, iterative destructor, push/pop/insert/erase/reverse/find, iteration), code/m05_list_problems.cpp (raw-pointer ListNode problems: reverse both ways, middle, Floyd cycle + start, merge, nth from end, palindrome, reorder, remove duplicates), code/m05_lru_cache.cpp (LRU with std::list + unordered_map, and a hand-rolled doubly linked version).

docs.title: Owning singly linked list (key parts)
docs.text:
class SinglyList {
    struct Node { int val; std::unique_ptr<Node> next; };
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
    Node* tail_ = nullptr;          // observer: the last node, owned via the chain
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
public:
    ~SinglyList() { while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next); }  // iterative: no deep recursion

    void push_front(int v) {
        auto n = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{v, std::move(head_)});  // steal old head into n->next
        if (!tail_) tail_ = n.get();
        head_ = std::move(n);
        ++size_;
    }
    void push_back(int v) {
        auto n = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{v, nullptr});
        Node* raw = n.get();
        if (tail_) tail_->next = std::move(n); else head_ = std::move(n);
        tail_ = raw;
        ++size_;
    }
    bool erase_first(int v) {
        // Pointer-to-unique_ptr walk: `link` is the owner slot that leads to the current node,
        // so unlinking the head is no special case (same trick as Node** in C).
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &head_;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
        while (*link) {
            if ((*link)->val == v) {
                if (link->get() == tail_) tail_ = prev;
                *link = std::move((*link)->next);   // old node is destroyed here
                --size_;
                return true;
            }
            prev = link->get();
            link = &(*link)->next;
        }
        return false;
    }
    void reverse() {
        std::unique_ptr<Node> prev, cur = std::move(head_);
        tail_ = cur.get();
        while (cur) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> next = std::move(cur->next);
            cur->next = std::move(prev);
            prev = std::move(cur);
            cur = std::move(next);
        }
        head_ = std::move(prev);
    }
};

docs.title: LRU with the standard library (key parts)
docs.text:
class LRUCache {
    using Entry = std::pair<int, int>;                       // key, value
    std::size_t cap_;
    std::list<Entry> order_;                                 // front = most recently used
    std::unordered_map<int, std::list<Entry>::iterator> pos_;
public:
    explicit LRUCache(std::size_t capacity) : cap_(capacity) {}
    std::optional<int> get(int key) {
        auto it = pos_.find(key);
        if (it == pos_.end()) return std::nullopt;
        order_.splice(order_.begin(), order_, it->second);   // O(1) move-to-front, iterator stays valid
        return it->second->second;
    }
    void put(int key, int value) {
        auto it = pos_.find(key);
        if (it != pos_.end()) {
            it->second->second = value;
            order_.splice(order_.begin(), order_, it->second);
            return;
        }
        if (order_.size() == cap_) {                          // evict least recently used
            pos_.erase(order_.back().first);
            order_.pop_back();
        }
        order_.emplace_front(key, value);
        pos_[key] = order_.begin();
    }
};

std::optional<int> (C++17) is "either an int or nothing"; it replaces returning -1 as a sentinel. splice relinks the node without invalidating the iterator stored in the map — that is the property that makes std::list the right container here, and the reason std::vector cannot do this job.

docs.title: 4.1 Memory layout and why lists are slow
docs.text:
Each new Node goes through malloc: for a 16-byte node (int + pointer, padded) glibc hands out a 32-byte chunk (16 bytes header-adjacent overhead and alignment), from whatever free region it has. Consecutive allocations are often adjacent when the heap is fresh, so a freshly built list happens to be sequential and benchmarks well. After hours of mixed allocate/free in a server, nodes are scattered: each next is a cache miss (~100 ns). A 1M-node traversal is ~100 ms; the same 1M ints in a vector traverse in ~1 ms.

std::list<int> node on libstdc++: prev + next + int + padding = 24 bytes, allocated as 32. So 4 bytes of payload cost 32 bytes of memory plus the allocator's bookkeeping. This is why "use a list for O(1) middle insertion" is usually wrong advice: the vector's memmove of a few KB beats a cache miss, and the vector uses 8x less memory.

docs.title: 4.2 When lists are right
docs.text:
• You hold pointers/iterators to elements that must stay valid while other elements are inserted or removed (vector invalidates; list never does). The LRU cache is exactly this.
  • You splice ranges between lists in O(1) (std::list::splice): moving a connection from the "idle" list to the "active" list without copying.
  • Elements are large or non-movable.
  • Intrusive lists: the next/prev fields live inside the object itself (Linux kernel struct list_head, Boost.Intrusive). No separate node allocation, the object can be in several lists at once, and removing it from all of them is O(1) given the object. Your RPC server's per-connection structure almost certainly sits in an intrusive list of active connections and another of pending timers.

docs.title: 4.3 unique_ptr codegen
docs.text: std::unique_ptr<Node> is one pointer: sizeof == 8. Move is a pointer copy plus nulling the source. Destruction is if (p) delete p;. With optimisation on, a unique_ptr-based list compiles to the same machine code as raw pointers, plus the destructor calls the compiler inserts at scope exit — which are the ones you would have forgotten.

docs.title: 4.4 Floyd's algorithm correctness, once more
docs.text: With slow at position s and fast at position 2s (steps since start), both inside a cycle of length L after at most a steps (a = distance to the cycle): the gap (2s - s) mod L = s mod L hits 0 when s is a multiple of L, i.e. within L more steps. Total steps <= a + L <= n. So the algorithm is O(n) with two pointers of state: this is why it beats the "hash set of visited nodes" solution, which is also O(n) but needs O(n) memory.

docs.title: 4.5 LRU in real caches
docs.text: A true LRU with one global list has a problem under concurrency: every get writes to the list (move-to-front), so a read-heavy cache serialises on one lock. Real systems approximate: PostgreSQL's buffer pool uses a clock sweep (a usage counter per page, a hand that decrements and evicts at zero); Linux uses two lists (active/inactive) with promotion on second access; CPUs use pseudo-LRU bits. Memcached uses a segmented LRU with per-slab locks. Berkeley DB's mpool uses an LRU-ish priority with a buffer-count-based clock. When an interviewer asks "how would you make this LRU thread-safe", the answer is "shard it by key hash, one lock and one list per shard, and accept that eviction is approximate across shards".

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Connection management. A doubly linked list of idle connections ordered by last activity, plus a map from socket fd to node, is the LRU cache with a different name. Idle timeout sweep: pop from the back while now - last_used > timeout. O(k) for k expired connections, not O(n).
  • Free lists. Your memory pool keeps freed blocks on a singly linked list threaded through the blocks themselves (the first 8 bytes of a free block hold the next pointer). O(1) allocate and free, no metadata. This is how malloc's small-size bins work.
  • Timer queues. A sorted doubly linked list of timers works when timers are mostly added at the end (same timeout value). For arbitrary timeouts use a heap (module 12) or a timer wheel.
  • Debugging a corrupted list at 3 AM. Symptom: a traversal spins forever (accidental cycle) or crashes on a wild pointer. In a crash dump, walk the list by hand with a counter; if it exceeds the known size you have a cycle. Common causes: a node freed while still linked (use-after-free), a node inserted into two lists with one set of link fields, or a next write done before saving the old next. A debug build that poisons freed nodes (memset(0xDD)) makes the crash happen at the bug, not later.
  • Lock-free stacks and queues (Treiber stack, Michael-Scott queue) are linked lists with compare-and-swap on the head pointer; see 04_Concurrency for the ABA problem that makes them hard.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Reverse a singly linked list in place with raw pointers, then with unique_ptr. Done when 1->2->3->4 becomes 4->3->2->1 and valgrind (or -fsanitize=address) reports no leaks.
  2. (easy) Delete all nodes with a given value in one pass using the dummy-head idiom. Done when [1,2,6,3,4,5,6], 6 -> [1,2,3,4,5] and [7,7,7], 7 -> [].
  3. (medium) Detect a cycle and return the index of the node where it starts. Build a test list where the tail points to node 2. Done when you can write the a = kL - b proof on paper.
  4. (medium) Merge k sorted lists two at a time (O(nk)) and then with a heap (O(n log k), module 12). Done when both give identical output on three lists of 1000 random sorted ints.
  5. (hard) Implement LRUCache by hand with your own doubly linked nodes and std::unordered_map<int, Node*>, no std::list. Done when the test sequence in m05_lru_cache.cpp passes against both implementations and put on an existing key updates the value and recency.
  6. (hard) Make the LRU cache thread-safe with N shards (key % N), each with its own mutex, list and map. Done when 8 threads doing 1M mixed operations produce no data race under -fsanitize=thread and total capacity is still respected per shard.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Array vs linked list — when do you use a list? When you need stable pointers to elements across insertions elsewhere, O(1) splicing, or O(1) removal of an element you already hold a pointer to (LRU, intrusive queues). For everything else a vector is faster because of cache locality and lower memory overhead.

Q: Reverse a linked list. Three pointers: prev, cur, next. Save next, point cur->next at prev, advance both. Return prev. O(n) time, O(1) space. The recursive version is O(n) stack.

Q: How do you detect a cycle, and find where it starts? Floyd: slow +1, fast +2 — they meet if and only if there is a cycle, in O(n) with O(1) space. To find the start, move one pointer to the head and advance both by one; they meet at the cycle entry because the head-to-entry distance equals the meeting-point-to-entry distance modulo the cycle length.

Q: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. Doubly linked list in recency order plus a hash map from key to list node. get: map lookup, move node to front. put: if present update and move to front; else if full, remove the back node and its map entry; insert at front and in the map. With std::list use splice so iterators stay valid.

Q: Why not use a vector for the LRU recency order? Move-to-front in a vector is O(n) (shift), and it invalidates the indices stored in the map. The list gives O(1) unlink/relink and stable node addresses.

Q: What is a sentinel/dummy head and why use it? A node that always exists before the first element so that insert/delete at the head is not a special case. It eliminates the "if (head == nullptr)" and "if (node == head)" branches that cause most list bugs.

Q: What goes wrong with unique_ptr<Node> next on a very long list? The destructor is recursive — each node's destructor destroys the next — so a list of ~100k nodes overflows the stack. Write an iterative destructor that pops the head repeatedly.

Q: Why does std::list::splice matter for the LRU cache? It relinks a node to a new position in O(1) without allocating or copying and without invalidating iterators to it, so the map's stored iterator remains correct after move-to-front.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A list trades O(1) index access for O(1) insert/delete at a known node; every next is a potential cache miss.
  • Set the new node's next before linking it in; save next before freeing.
  • Dummy head removes empty-list and delete-head special cases.
  • unique_ptr for ownership, raw pointers for observation; write the destructor iteratively.
  • Reverse: prev/cur/next. Middle: slow/fast. Cycle: Floyd, meet then reset to head for the start.
  • Merge: dummy + tail, take the smaller head. Nth from end: two pointers n apart.
  • LRU = doubly linked list (recency) + hash map (key -> node); splice keeps iterators valid.
  • std::list<int> costs ~32 bytes per 4-byte element; vector costs 4.
  • Intrusive lists (links inside the object) are how kernels and servers queue things.
  • Real caches approximate LRU (clock sweep, segmented LRU) to avoid a global lock.

docs.title: 06. Stacks, queues and deques
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A stack is a pile of plates: you add to the top and take from the top. Last in, first out (LIFO). A queue is a line at a bank counter: join at the back, served from the front. First in, first out (FIFO). A deque ("deck", double-ended queue) lets you add and remove at both ends. All three are restricted containers: they deliberately offer fewer operations than an array so that every operation is O(1) and the usage pattern is obvious.

You already use a stack without naming it: every function call pushes a frame, every return pops one. Your RPC server uses a queue: requests arrive at the back, worker threads take from the front. The receive buffer on a socket is a ring buffer — a queue of bytes in a fixed array that wraps around.

The interview value is in two patterns built on top: the monotonic stack (a stack kept sorted so that "next greater element" questions become O(n)) and the monotonic deque (sliding window maximum in O(n)). Both look like magic the first time and are mechanical once you see the invariant.

docs.title: 2.1 Stack
docs.text:
Operations: push, pop, top, empty, size. All O(1). Implement on a std::vector: push_back, pop_back, back(). std::stack<T> is an adapter over std::deque<T> by default; std::stack<T, std::vector<T>> uses a vector. The adapter exists to hide random access so the code states its intent.

Where stacks appear: function calls, expression evaluation (operators and operands), undo history, bracket matching, DFS (iterative), backtracking, parsing (shift-reduce), the "recently opened" set in a monotonic-stack problem.

docs.title: 2.2 Queue
docs.text:
Operations: push (back), pop (front), front, back, empty, size. On a vector, pop_front is O(n) — wrong container. Options:

  • std::deque<T> (what std::queue<T> uses): O(1) both ends.
  • Two stacks: push onto in; to pop, if out is empty move everything from in to out (reversing order), then pop out. Each element is moved at most once, so amortised O(1). This is the classic "implement a queue with stacks" question, and it is also how functional languages implement persistent queues.
  • Ring buffer (circular buffer): a fixed array with head and tail indices that wrap modulo capacity. O(1) both ends, zero allocation after construction, cache-friendly. The structure behind socket buffers, audio buffers, log rings, lock-free SPSC queues.

docs.title: 2.3 Deque
docs.text: std::deque<T>: O(1) push/pop at both ends, O(1) random access, iterators invalidated by insertion at either end (but references are not invalidated by push at the ends — a quirk worth knowing). Implemented as a vector of fixed-size blocks (512 bytes per block on libstdc++) plus a map array of block pointers. Random access is two indirections. Growing at either end allocates a new block; no element is copied. Use it when you need a queue with indexing, or a stack that must not reallocate (block addresses are stable).

docs.title: 2.4 Ring buffer in detail
docs.text:
capacity 8, head=2 (read), tail=6 (write), size=4
index:  0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
        . . A B C D . .
            ^head   ^tail
push(E): buf[6]=E; tail=(6+1)%8=7
push(F): buf[7]=F; tail=0          <- wrapped
pop(): return buf[2]=A; head=3

Design decisions:

  1. Full vs empty: with only head and tail, head == tail is ambiguous. Either keep a count, or sacrifice one slot (full when (tail+1)%cap == head), or use monotonically increasing 64-bit head/tail counters and index with % cap (then size = tail - head, never ambiguous, and the counters serve as sequence numbers — this is what high-performance queues do).
  2. Power-of-two capacity turns % cap into & (cap-1): a division becomes an AND. Worth it in a hot path; irrelevant otherwise.
  3. Overwrite or reject when full? A log ring overwrites the oldest (you want recent history). A network buffer rejects (backpressure). Make it an explicit policy.
  4. Contiguous reads: readv/writev or two memcpy calls when the data wraps. Some implementations mirror the buffer with mmap so the wrap is invisible ("magic ring buffer").

docs.title: 2.5 Monotonic stack
docs.text:
A stack whose elements are kept in sorted order (increasing or decreasing from bottom to top) by popping anything that would violate the order before pushing. Each element is pushed once and popped at most once: O(n) total.

Use it for: next greater/smaller element to the left or right, daily temperatures ("days until a warmer day"), largest rectangle in a histogram, trapping rain water, stock span, removing k digits to make the smallest number, and "previous smaller" boundaries generally.

Template (next greater element to the right):

for i in 0..n-1:
    while stack not empty and v[stack.top] < v[i]:
        answer[stack.top] = i        # v[i] is the first greater element for stack.top
        pop
    push i
remaining indices on the stack have no greater element to the right

The stack holds indices of elements still waiting for their answer, in decreasing value order from bottom to top. When a larger value arrives it resolves everyone smaller.

docs.title: 2.6 Monotonic deque: sliding window maximum
docs.text: Maintain a deque of indices with decreasing values. For each new i: pop from the back while v[back] <= v[i] (those can never be the max while i is in the window); push i; pop from the front if it has left the window; v[front] is the current maximum. O(n). The brute force is O(nk); a heap gives O(n log k). This is the structure for "max over the last k samples" in monitoring.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: Files: code/m06_stack_queue.cpp (vector-backed stack, two-stack queue, min-stack, valid parentheses, evaluate RPN), code/m06_ring_buffer.cpp (templated ring buffer with counters, power-of-two mask, overwrite/reject policies, test), code/m06_monotonic_stack.cpp (next greater element, daily temperatures, largest rectangle, sliding window maximum).

docs.title: Problem 1 — Valid parentheses
docs.text:
Push openers; on a closer, the top must be the matching opener. Empty at the end.

bool valid_parens(std::string_view s) {
    std::vector<char> st;
    for (char c : s) {
        if (c == '(' || c == '[' || c == '{') { st.push_back(c); continue; }
        if (st.empty()) return false;
        char open = st.back(); st.pop_back();
        if ((c == ')' && open != '(') || (c == ']' && open != '[') || (c == '}' && open != '{')) return false;
    }
    return st.empty();
}
O(n), O(n).

docs.title: Problem 2 — Min stack: push, pop, top, get_min all O(1)
docs.text:
Keep a second stack of "minimum so far". Push min(x, mins.back()) with every push; pop both.

void push(int x) { data.push_back(x); mins.push_back(mins.empty() ? x : std::min(x, mins.back())); }
void pop() { data.pop_back(); mins.pop_back(); }
int get_min() const { return mins.back(); }
Why it works: the minimum of the stack after popping is exactly the minimum of the elements below, which mins recorded at the time they were pushed.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
docs.text:
Push numbers; on an operator pop two (right operand first), apply, push the result.

int eval_rpn(const std::vector<std::string>& tokens) {
    std::vector<long long> st;
    for (const std::string& t : tokens) {
        if (t == "+" || t == "-" || t == "*" || t == "/") {
            long long b = st.back(); st.pop_back();
            long long a = st.back(); st.pop_back();
            st.push_back(t == "+" ? a + b : t == "-" ? a - b : t == "*" ? a * b : a / b);
        } else st.push_back(std::stoll(t));
    }
    return static_cast<int>(st.back());
}
This is how a stack machine (the JVM, Forth, PostScript, the bytecode of many interpreters) executes. Infix to RPN conversion is the shunting-yard algorithm, another stack.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Daily temperatures
docs.text:
answer[i] = number of days until a warmer temperature, or 0. Monotonic decreasing stack of indices.

std::vector<int> daily_temperatures(const std::vector<int>& t) {
    std::vector<int> ans(t.size(), 0), st;
    for (int i = 0; i < static_cast<int>(t.size()); ++i) {
        while (!st.empty() && t[st.back()] < t[i]) { ans[st.back()] = i - st.back(); st.pop_back(); }
        st.push_back(i);
    }
    return ans;
}
O(n): each index is pushed once and popped at most once.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Largest rectangle in a histogram
docs.text:
For each bar, the widest rectangle with that bar's height extends left to the previous shorter bar and right to the next shorter bar. A monotonic increasing stack finds both boundaries in one pass: when a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar on the stack has found its right boundary (the current index) and its left boundary (the new stack top).

long long largest_rectangle(const std::vector<int>& h) {
    std::vector<int> st;        // indices with increasing heights
    long long best = 0;
    int n = static_cast<int>(h.size());
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i) {
        int cur = (i == n) ? 0 : h[i];        // sentinel 0 flushes the stack at the end
        while (!st.empty() && h[st.back()] >= cur) {
            int height = h[st.back()]; st.pop_back();
            int left = st.empty() ? -1 : st.back();
            best = std::max(best, static_cast<long long>(height) * (i - left - 1));
        }
        st.push_back(i);
    }
    return best;
}
O(n). The sentinel at i == n is the trick that avoids a second loop. This is the hardest stack problem commonly asked; "maximal rectangle in a binary matrix" reduces to it row by row.

docs.title: Problem 6 — Sliding window maximum
docs.text:
std::vector<int> max_sliding_window(const std::vector<int>& v, int k) {
    std::deque<int> dq;                     // indices, values decreasing front to back
    std::vector<int> out;
    for (int i = 0; i < static_cast<int>(v.size()); ++i) {
        while (!dq.empty() && v[dq.back()] <= v[i]) dq.pop_back();   // dominated: never the max again
        dq.push_back(i);
        if (dq.front() <= i - k) dq.pop_front();                      // left the window
        if (i >= k - 1) out.push_back(v[dq.front()]);
    }
    return out;
}
O(n), O(k).

docs.title: 4.1 The call stack is a stack
docs.text: Each call pushes a frame: return address, saved registers, locals. rsp is the stack pointer and moves down on x86-64. The default thread stack is 8 MB on Linux (ulimit -s), 1 MB on Windows. A recursive DFS on a 1M-node path, or the recursive list destructor from module 05, exceeds it: SIGSEGV with a stack address, which in a core dump looks like a crash in a tiny function with an enormous backtrace. Converting recursion to an explicit std::vector stack moves the frames to the heap, where the limit is memory. Module 07 does this conversion.

docs.title: 4.2 std::deque layout
docs.text: libstdc++: a "map" (array of pointers) to fixed-size chunks of 512 bytes (so 128 ints or 64 pointers per chunk), plus start/finish iterators that each hold (current, first, last, node). push_back with room in the last chunk: one store and an increment. Without room: allocate a chunk (no copying of elements), possibly grow the map (copying pointers only). Random access: compute chunk index and offset — two loads. Iteration crosses chunk boundaries with a branch per element, which is why std::sort on a deque is slower than on a vector. Rule: deque for queues, vector for everything else.

docs.title: 4.3 Ring buffer and the hardware
docs.text: A ring buffer of 4096 bytes is 64 cache lines. A producer writing at tail and a consumer reading at head touch different lines most of the time — until they get close, when they share a line and false sharing makes both slow (each write invalidates the other core's copy). Lock-free single-producer single-consumer queues pad head and tail to separate cache lines (alignas(64)) for this reason, and read the other side's index only when necessary (cache the last-seen value). The Linux kernel's kfifo, DPDK's rte_ring, and the LMAX Disruptor are all ring buffers with these tricks. See 04_Concurrency for the memory ordering needed to make it correct without a mutex.

docs.title: 4.4 Why monotonic stack is O(n) — amortised, again
docs.text: The inner while looks nested, but each index enters the stack once and leaves once. Sum of all inner-loop iterations <= n. Same argument as module 01's two-pointer and vector growth: count total work, not loop depth. If you are asked for the complexity and say O(n^2), you lose the problem even with correct code.

docs.title: 4.5 std::stack and std::queue adapters
docs.text: They hold a container member and forward: push -> push_back, pop -> pop_front (queue) or pop_back (stack). They have no iterators, deliberately. pop() returns void because returning the value by copy and then popping would not be exception-safe if the copy threw after the pop (the "Sutter pop problem"); so you write x = q.front(); q.pop();. Under optimisation the adapters cost nothing.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Request queue between acceptor and workers. A std::deque<Request> guarded by a mutex and a condition variable is the simplest correct design (04_Concurrency). When it is the bottleneck, a bounded ring buffer per worker with lock-free SPSC semantics replaces it. The bound is important: an unbounded queue hides overload until memory runs out.
  • Socket receive buffer. Bytes arrive in arbitrary chunks; the parser consumes whole messages. A ring buffer lets recv write at tail and the parser read at head without ever shifting data. Your server's "partial message" handling is exactly this problem.
  • Undo/redo and transaction logs. Undo is a stack; redo is a second stack; a new action clears redo. A database's undo log for a transaction is a stack of before-images popped on rollback.
  • Expression evaluation in PL/pgSQL or rules engines. Shunting-yard to RPN once at parse time, then a stack machine per evaluation.
  • Flow-control debugging. A queue whose depth grows without bound is the first signal of a consumer that fell behind. Export queue depth as a metric; alert on it. A ring buffer that overwrites silently is a data-loss bug waiting to be found in an audit.
  • 3 AM story (typical). Latency spikes every few minutes; CPU normal. Queue depth metric shows a sawtooth: the consumer thread blocks on a slow downstream call while holding the queue mutex, producers pile up, then it drains. Fix: never block on I/O while holding the queue lock; take the item out, release, then call.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Implement MinStack and test with the sequence push 3, push 5, get_min, push 2, push 1, get_min, pop, get_min, pop, get_min. Done when you get 3, 1, 2, 3.
  2. (easy) Implement a queue with two stacks and prove to yourself (write it down) that n operations cost O(n) total. Done when 1M mixed push/pop operations run in well under a second.
  3. (medium) Extend RingBuffer<T> in m06_ring_buffer.cpp with peek(i) (i-th element from the front) and read_contiguous() returning up to two (pointer, length) spans suitable for writev. Done when a wrapped buffer returns two spans whose lengths sum to size().
  4. (medium) Trapping rain water with a monotonic stack. Done when [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] -> 6; then re-solve it with two pointers and compare.
  5. (hard) Maximal rectangle of 1s in a binary matrix via "largest rectangle in histogram" per row. Done when the 4x5 LeetCode example gives 6 and you can state the O(rows * cols).
  6. (hard) Build a single-producer single-consumer lock-free ring buffer with std::atomic<std::size_t> head and tail and alignas(64) padding. Done when a producer and a consumer thread exchange 100M integers without loss or duplication under -fsanitize=thread (04_Concurrency explains acquire/release ordering).

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Implement a queue using two stacks and give the complexity. Push onto in. To pop or peek, if out is empty, move all of in onto out (reverses order), then use out.top(). Each element is moved from in to out once, so n operations cost O(n): amortised O(1) per operation, O(n) worst case for a single pop.

Q: What is a ring buffer and where is it used? A fixed-size array used as a queue with head/tail indices that wrap modulo the capacity. O(1) push/pop, no allocation, cache-friendly. Used for socket and audio buffers, log rings, and lock-free SPSC queues. Full-vs-empty is disambiguated with a count, a spare slot, or monotonically increasing counters.

Q: Explain the monotonic stack and its complexity. A stack kept sorted by popping violating elements before each push. Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so a pass is O(n) despite the nested loop. Solves next-greater, daily temperatures, histogram rectangle, rain water.

Q: How do you get the sliding window maximum in O(n)? A deque of indices with decreasing values. For each element, pop smaller-or-equal values from the back (they can never be the max again), push the index, drop the front if it left the window; the front is the maximum.

Q: Why does std::stack::pop() return void? Returning the popped value by copy could throw after the element was removed, losing it. The standard separates top() and pop() so each is exception-safe.

Q: How does std::deque give O(1) at both ends and O(1) indexing? It is an array of pointers to fixed-size blocks. Pushing at either end fills a block or allocates a new one without moving elements; indexing computes block and offset with two loads. References stay valid on end pushes; iterators do not.

Q: When does recursion need to be converted to an explicit stack? When depth can reach tens of thousands (deep DFS, long lists, degenerate trees): the thread stack (8 MB default on Linux) overflows. An explicit std::vector of frames lives on the heap.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Stack: LIFO, std::vector with push_back/pop_back/back. Queue: FIFO, std::deque or ring buffer.
  • Two-stack queue: amortised O(1), each element moved once.
  • Ring buffer: fixed array, head/tail wrap; disambiguate full/empty with a count or 64-bit counters; power-of-two capacity for & mask; decide overwrite vs reject.
  • std::deque is blocks plus a pointer map; O(1) ends, O(1) index via two loads.
  • Monotonic stack: pop violators, push; each index in and out once; O(n). Next greater, daily temperatures, histogram rectangle (with a sentinel), rain water.
  • Monotonic deque: sliding window maximum in O(n).
  • Min stack: parallel stack of running minimums.
  • RPN evaluation is a stack machine; shunting-yard converts infix to RPN.
  • The call stack is a stack with an 8 MB limit; deep recursion becomes an explicit stack.
  • Pad producer and consumer indices to separate cache lines in a concurrent ring buffer.

docs.title: 07. Recursion and backtracking
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 06

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Recursion is a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem, and stopping when the problem is small enough to answer directly. You know the mechanics from C: each call gets its own frame on the stack with its own locals; return pops it. What trips people up is not the mechanics but the trust: you have to write the function assuming the recursive call already works, and only make sure of two things — the base case is right, and every call moves toward it.

Backtracking is recursion used as a search: build a candidate solution one choice at a time, and when a choice cannot lead to a valid solution, undo it ("back track") and try the next one. Think of walking a maze with a piece of chalk: at every fork you mark a path, walk it, and if it dead-ends you walk back to the fork and take the next one. Permutations, subsets, N-queens, Sudoku and "all combinations that sum to k" are all backtracking.

Memoisation is the trick that turns exponential recursion into polynomial time when subproblems repeat: write the answer down the first time, look it up afterwards. It is the bridge to dynamic programming (module 14).

docs.title: 2.1 Anatomy of a recursive function
docs.text:
R solve(State s) {
    if (base_case(s)) return direct_answer(s);        // 1. stop
    R sub = solve(smaller(s));                        // 2. trust the smaller call
    return combine(s, sub);                           // 3. build the answer from it
}

Rules that prevent 90% of bugs:

  • Write the base case first. Test it alone.
  • Every recursive call must strictly reduce something (size, index, remaining budget).
  • Decide what the function returns versus what it accumulates in a parameter passed by reference. Mixing the two in one function is the usual source of confusion.
  • Think about the depth: it is the space complexity and, past ~100k frames, a crash.

docs.title: 2.2 Call stack mechanics
docs.text: On x86-64 Linux, a call pushes the return address (8 bytes), the callee saves rbp and any callee-saved registers it uses, then subtracts space for locals. A frame for int f(int n) with one local is around 32 to 48 bytes; with a std::string local or an array it is far more. The default main-thread stack is 8 MB (ulimit -s), secondary threads get 8 MB by default on glibc (2 MB on some systems, 1 MB on Windows). So a plain recursive function overflows at roughly 100 000 to 200 000 frames, less if frames are big. Tail-call optimisation (compiler turns return f(n-1) into a jump) exists at -O2 but is not guaranteed in C++ — do not depend on it. When depth can be large, convert to an explicit stack (section 2.6).

docs.title: 2.3 Classic recursions and their shapes
docs.text:
Problem Recurrence Time Depth factorial, sum of list T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) O(n) n binary search T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) O(log n) log n merge sort T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) O(n log n) log n naive Fibonacci T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) O(phi^n) ~ O(1.618^n) n subsets of n items 2^n leaves, O(n) each to copy O(n 2^n) n permutations of n n! leaves O(n n!) n tower of Hanoi T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 O(2^n) n

The Fibonacci row is why memoisation exists: the recursion tree has 2^n nodes but only n distinct arguments.

docs.title: 2.4 Backtracking template
docs.text:
void backtrack(State& state, Path& path, Results& out) {
    if (is_solution(state)) { out.push_back(path); return; }
    for (Choice c : candidates(state)) {
        if (!valid(c, state)) continue;      // prune: do not even recurse
        apply(c, state, path);               // choose
        backtrack(state, path, out);         // explore
        undo(c, state, path);                // un-choose: restore EXACTLY the previous state
    }
}

Three things make or break it:

  1. Choose / explore / un-choose must be symmetric. If apply pushes and sets a flag, undo pops and clears the flag. The state after undo must be bit-for-bit what it was before apply.
  2. Pruning (valid) is where the speed is. N-queens without pruning tries n^n placements; with column/diagonal checks it visits a tiny fraction.
  3. Avoid duplicates by construction, not by filtering at the end: for subsets, only consider candidates with index > the last chosen index; for combinations with repeated values, sort first and skip v[i] == v[i-1] when i > start.

Complexity is "number of nodes in the search tree times work per node". Say it that way.

docs.title: 2.5 The three canonical problems
docs.text:
Subsets (power set). At each index decide include/exclude. 2^n leaves.

void subsets(const std::vector<int>& v, std::size_t i, std::vector<int>& cur,
             std::vector<std::vector<int>>& out) {
    if (i == v.size()) { out.push_back(cur); return; }
    subsets(v, i + 1, cur, out);                 // exclude v[i]
    cur.push_back(v[i]);                         // include v[i]
    subsets(v, i + 1, cur, out);
    cur.pop_back();                              // undo
}

Alternative "for-loop" form, which is what you use for combinations and k-subsets:

void subsets2(const std::vector<int>& v, std::size_t start, std::vector<int>& cur, Out& out) {
    out.push_back(cur);                          // every prefix is a subset
    for (std::size_t i = start; i < v.size(); ++i) {
        cur.push_back(v[i]);
        subsets2(v, i + 1, cur, out);            // i + 1: only later elements, no duplicates
        cur.pop_back();
    }
}

Permutations. Choose which unused element goes in position pos. Swap-based in-place version: swap v[pos] with each v[i], i >= pos, recurse on pos + 1, swap back. n! leaves, O(n) to copy each: O(n * n!).

void permute(std::vector<int>& v, std::size_t pos, Out& out) {
    if (pos == v.size()) { out.push_back(v); return; }
    for (std::size_t i = pos; i < v.size(); ++i) {
        std::swap(v[pos], v[i]);                 // choose v[i] for position pos
        permute(v, pos + 1, out);
        std::swap(v[pos], v[i]);                 // un-choose
    }
}

N-queens. Place one queen per row. Track used columns and the two diagonal families: row - col (constant on "\" diagonals) and row + col (constant on "/" diagonals). A placement is valid if none of the three is taken. Three boolean arrays make the check O(1).

void queens(int row, int n, std::vector<int>& col_of, std::vector<char>& cols,
            std::vector<char>& d1, std::vector<char>& d2, int& count) {
    if (row == n) { ++count; return; }
    for (int c = 0; c < n; ++c) {
        int a = row - c + n - 1, b = row + c;              // shift a to be non-negative
        if (cols[c] || d1[a] || d2[b]) continue;           // prune
        cols[c] = d1[a] = d2[b] = 1; col_of[row] = c;
        queens(row + 1, n, col_of, cols, d1, d2, count);
        cols[c] = d1[a] = d2[b] = 0;                       // undo
    }
}

n = 8 gives 92 solutions; n = 12 gives 14 200. Without the diagonal arrays you would scan all previous rows for each placement — O(n) per check instead of O(1).

docs.title: 2.6 Recursion to explicit stack
docs.text:
Any recursion can be made iterative by pushing what the frame holds onto a std::vector. The mechanical translation: a struct with the parameters and a "where was I" marker; a loop that pops, does the work, pushes continuations. In practice you rarely need the general form; you need the two common cases:

  • Tree/graph DFS: push the root; loop: pop node, process, push children. (Module 10, 13.)
  • Tail recursion (return f(smaller)): becomes a while loop directly.

Do this when depth may exceed ~10^4 to 10^5, or in production code where a stack overflow is an unacceptable failure mode.

docs.title: 2.7 Memoisation
docs.text:
Cache results keyed by the arguments. For integer arguments a std::vector<long long> with a sentinel; for composite arguments a std::unordered_map or a 2D vector.

long long fib(int n, std::vector<long long>& memo) {
    if (n < 2) return n;
    if (memo[n] != -1) return memo[n];
    return memo[n] = fib(n - 1, memo) + fib(n - 2, memo);
}

O(n) instead of O(1.6^n). When to memoise: the recursion has overlapping subproblems (the same arguments recur) and optimal substructure (the answer for the whole is built from answers for parts). When the subproblems are all distinct (permutations, subsets), memoisation buys nothing — the search tree really is that big. Module 14 turns memoised recursion into bottom-up tables.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Files: code/m07_backtracking.cpp (subsets both forms, permutations with and without duplicates, combination sum, N-queens count and boards, letter combinations of a phone number, word search in a grid), code/m07_memo_fib.cpp (naive vs memoised vs iterative Fibonacci with timing and call counts, climbing stairs, grid paths with memo, and the recursion-to-explicit-stack conversion of a tree DFS).

Highlights from m07_backtracking.cpp:

// Combination sum: unlimited reuse of candidates; pass `start` = i (not i+1) to allow reuse,
// and sort so that we can break (not continue) when a candidate exceeds the remaining target.
void combination_sum(const std::vector<int>& c, int start, int remaining,
                     std::vector<int>& cur, std::vector<std::vector<int>>& out) {
    if (remaining == 0) { out.push_back(cur); return; }
    for (int i = start; i < static_cast<int>(c.size()); ++i) {
        if (c[i] > remaining) break;              // sorted: everything after is bigger too
        cur.push_back(c[i]);
        combination_sum(c, i, remaining - c[i], cur, out);
        cur.pop_back();
    }
}

// Permutations with duplicate values: sort, and at each position only use the FIRST unused
// copy of a value. The `used[i-1]` test is the standard duplicate guard.
if (used[i] || (i > 0 && v[i] == v[i-1] && !used[i-1])) continue;

Highlights from m07_memo_fib.cpp:

// Naive: counts calls so you can see the explosion. fib(30) makes 2.7 million calls.
long long fib_naive(int n, long long& calls) {
    ++calls;
    return n < 2 ? n : fib_naive(n - 1, calls) + fib_naive(n - 2, calls);
}
// Memoised: 2n-1 calls.
// Iterative: two variables, O(1) space, the bottom-up version from module 14.

docs.title: 4.1 What a frame costs
docs.text: g++ -O2 inlines small leaf functions and converts simple tail recursion to loops, so fib_iterative and a tail-recursive sum compile to the same code. But any function that makes two recursive calls (Fibonacci, merge sort, tree traversal) cannot be a loop without an explicit stack, and the compiler will not invent one. For those, the cost per call is: call (push return address, ~1 cycle but a branch), prologue (save registers, adjust rsp), the work, epilogue, ret (a predicted indirect branch; return-address prediction is good unless recursion is deep). Roughly 5 to 15 cycles overhead per call. A backtracking search that makes 10^8 calls spends ~1 second in call overhead alone. Iterative versions of hot inner recursions pay off; for depth-20 searches it does not matter.

docs.title: 4.2 Stack overflow in a crash dump
docs.text: The symptom is SIGSEGV with a faulting address just below the stack's guard page, and a backtrace with thousands of identical frames. gdb: bt -10 shows the bottom. In WinDbg !analyze -v reports STACK_OVERFLOW and kb shows the repetition. Causes in production code: unbounded recursion on malicious input (a JSON parser given 100 000 nested [), a recursive destructor on a long list, mutual recursion between two callbacks. Defence: depth limits on recursive parsers, iterative destructors, explicit stacks for DFS.

docs.title: 4.3 Why memoisation changes the complexity class
docs.text: The recursion tree for fib(n) has ~1.6^n nodes but only n+1 distinct labels. Memoisation makes each distinct label compute once, so the total work is (number of distinct states) x (work per state excluding recursive calls). This "states x transitions" formula is how you compute DP complexity in module 14, and it is the same number for memoised top-down and tabulated bottom-up.

docs.title: 4.4 Backtracking and pruning in real engines
docs.text: A SQL query planner choosing a join order for 10 tables faces 10! orderings; PostgreSQL's standard planner does dynamic programming over subsets (2^10 states) with pruning, and switches to a genetic algorithm (GEQO) above 12 tables. SAT solvers are backtracking with clever pruning (unit propagation, clause learning). Regular expression engines that backtrack (PCRE, Java's) can hit exponential time on pathological patterns — the reason RE2 and Rust's regex use automata instead. If you ever see a regex take seconds, that is backtracking without memoisation.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Recursive descent parsers for message formats and config files: each grammar rule is a function that calls the functions for its sub-rules. Clean, but put a depth counter in and fail at, say, 1000 to defend against nested-bracket attacks.
  • Directory walking, tree serialisation, dependency resolution are recursions over trees and DAGs. For DAGs, memoise ("visited") or you re-walk shared subtrees exponentially.
  • Retry with backtracking in distributed transactions: try a plan, on conflict undo and try the next. Same choose/explore/undo shape; the undo is the hard part to get right there too.
  • Debugging a backtracking bug. The state after undo is not identical to the state before apply: a counter not decremented, a flag not cleared, a vector not popped because an early return skipped the cleanup line. Put the cleanup in an RAII guard (a small struct whose destructor undoes) or structure the code so undo cannot be skipped. In an interview, walk through one apply/undo pair out loud.
  • Memoisation as caching in a server: a function price(account, date) called a million times a day with 10 000 distinct arguments is a memoisation opportunity, with the extra questions production adds: invalidation, bounded size (LRU, module 05) and thread-safety.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Write recursive sum, max, and reverse on a std::vector<int> by index. Then write the loop versions. Done when you can state the recurrence and depth for each.
  2. (easy) Generate all binary strings of length n. Done when n = 3 prints 8 strings in lexicographic order and you can say why the order comes out that way.
  3. (medium) Combinations of k out of n (C(n,k) results) using the for-loop subset template with start. Add the prune "if remaining slots > remaining candidates, return". Done when C(20,10) runs instantly and the count is 184 756.
  4. (medium) Generate all valid parentheses strings for n pairs. Hint: track open and close counts; you may add ( if open < n, ) if close < open. Done when n = 3 gives 5 strings.
  5. (hard) Sudoku solver with backtracking and the "fewest candidates first" heuristic for cell order. Done when it solves a hard puzzle from any newspaper in under 100 ms and you can report how many placements it tried with and without the heuristic.
  6. (hard) Convert the recursive subsets function to an iterative one with an explicit stack of (index, cur_size) frames. Done when both produce identical output for n = 15 and the iterative version handles n = 10 000 with a single subset request without overflowing (generate lazily — do not store 2^10000 results).

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do you approach writing a recursive function? Define what it returns for a given input, write the base case, make the recursive call on a strictly smaller input, trust its result and combine. Check the depth for stack safety.

Q: Permutations vs subsets — what is the structure of each search tree? Subsets: depth n, two branches per level (include/exclude), 2^n leaves. Permutations: depth n, n-i branches at level i, n! leaves. Both are O(n) work per leaf to copy out the answer, so O(n 2^n) and O(n n!).

Q: How does N-queens prune? One queen per row by construction; before placing in column c, O(1) checks on three boolean arrays: column c, diagonal row-c, anti-diagonal row+c. Any conflict skips the recursive call. This cuts the search from n^n to a tiny fraction.

Q: How do you avoid duplicate results in combination problems with repeated values? Sort the input and, within one level of the loop, skip a value equal to the previous value (i > start && v[i] == v[i-1]). For permutations use !used[i-1] so only the first unused copy is chosen at each position.

Q: When does memoisation help and when does it not? It helps when the same subproblem arguments recur (Fibonacci, grid paths, edit distance): exponential becomes polynomial. It does not help when every call has distinct arguments (enumerating all permutations): the output itself is exponential.

Q: What is the space complexity of recursive backtracking? O(depth) frames plus the current path; for subsets and permutations that is O(n), not counting the output.

Q: Your recursive function crashes with SIGSEGV on large input. Why and what do you do? Stack overflow: each frame uses stack space and the default stack is 8 MB. Convert to an iterative version with an explicit heap-allocated stack, or bound the depth, or (rarely) enlarge the thread stack when creating the thread.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Recursion: base case first, strictly smaller call, trust and combine; depth = space.
  • Default stack is 8 MB; ~10^5 frames overflow it; convert deep recursion to an explicit stack.
  • Backtracking = choose, explore, un-choose; undo must restore the exact prior state.
  • Pruning is where speed comes from; duplicates are avoided by construction (start index, sorted skip, used[i-1]).
  • Subsets: include/exclude or for-loop with start; 2^n leaves.
  • Permutations: swap in place; n! leaves. Combination sum: pass i to reuse, i+1 otherwise.
  • N-queens: one per row; column and two diagonal arrays give O(1) validity checks.
  • Memoise when subproblems overlap; complexity becomes (distinct states) x (work per state).
  • Naive Fibonacci is O(1.6^n); memoised is O(n); iterative is O(n) time, O(1) space.
  • Depth-limit recursive parsers; backtracking regex engines are exponential on bad input.

docs.title: 08. Sorting
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Sorting puts things in order so that everything after it gets easier: binary search works, duplicates sit next to each other, the smallest k are at the front, two sorted lists merge in one pass. Your orderedArray.cpp kept the array sorted by inserting each new element in its place — that is insertion sort, one element at a time, and it is O(n^2) for n elements because each insertion may shift everything.

The O(n log n) sorts beat that by dividing the work. Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half (recursively), and merges — always O(n log n), needs a scratch buffer, and is stable (equal elements keep their order). Quicksort picks a pivot, moves smaller elements left and larger right, and recurses on both sides — O(n log n) on average, in place, fastest in practice, but O(n^2) if the pivots are bad. Heapsort uses the heap from module 12 to pull out the minimum n times — O(n log n) always, in place, but slower because it jumps around memory.

std::sort combines all three (introsort): quicksort for speed, heapsort when quicksort starts degrading, insertion sort for the tiny pieces at the end. A senior engineer can explain why each piece is there. And a database engineer knows one more: when the data does not fit in memory, you sort runs that do fit and merge them from disk — external merge sort, which is what ORDER BY and index builds do.

docs.title: 2.1 The comparison sorts
docs.text:
Insertion sort. For i from 1 to n-1, take v[i] and shift it left past every larger element. The prefix v[0..i) is always sorted. Worst case O(n^2) (reverse order), best case O(n) (already sorted), adaptive (fast on nearly-sorted data), stable, in place. For n <= ~16 it is the fastest sort there is, which is why every library sort finishes with it.

Selection sort. For i from 0 to n-1, find the minimum of v[i..n) and swap it into v[i]. Always O(n^2) comparisons, exactly n-1 swaps (minimum possible), not stable in the usual swap form. Only useful when swaps are extremely expensive compared to comparisons.

Merge sort. Split, recurse, merge with a scratch buffer. 

T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n), always.
Space O(n) scratch. Stable (take from the left half on ties). Sequential access: cache-friendly.
Bottom-up variant: merge runs of 1, then 2, then 4, ... No recursion. Used for linked lists (no random access needed; std::list::sort is a merge sort) and for external sorting.

Quicksort. Choose a pivot, partition so that elements < pivot are left and > pivot are right, recurse on both sides. 

Average: T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + O(n) -> O(n log n), about 1.39 n log2 n comparisons on average.
Worst: pivot is always min or max -> T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) -> O(n^2). Happens on sorted or
       reverse-sorted input with first/last-element pivot, or on all-equal input with Lomuto.
Space: O(log n) stack if you recurse on the smaller side first and loop on the larger.
Not stable. In place.

Partition schemes:

  • Lomuto: pivot at the end; i marks the boundary of the "< pivot" region; scan j, swap v[j] into position when v[j] < pivot; finally swap pivot into v[i]. Simple, ~3x more swaps than Hoare, degrades to O(n^2) on many equal keys (all go to one side).
  • Hoare: two indices moving inward from both ends, swapping out-of-place pairs; stops when they cross. Fewer swaps, handles equal keys well (they get split between sides). Returns a split point, not the pivot's final index — the recursion is [lo, p] and [p+1, hi].
  • Three-way (Dutch national flag): partitions into < pivot, == pivot, > pivot and recurses only on the outer two. Linear time on all-equal input. Used when many duplicates are expected.

Pivot choice:

  • First or last element: O(n^2) on sorted input. Never do this.
  • Random: expected O(n log n) on any input; an adversary cannot pick a bad input in advance.
  • Median of three (first, middle, last): cheap, good on sorted/reverse data, what most libraries use. Median-of-medians gives a guaranteed O(n log n) but the constant is too high for practice.

Heapsort. Build a max-heap in O(n) (module 12), then repeatedly swap the root to the end and sift down: n times O(log n). Always O(n log n), in place, O(1) extra space, not stable. Slower than quicksort by about 2x in practice because the sift-down jumps across the array (poor locality) and branches unpredictably. Its guarantee is its value.

docs.title: 2.2 std::sort: introsort
docs.text:
libstdc++'s std::sort (and MSVC's, and libc++'s) is introspective sort (Musser, 1997):

  1. Quicksort with median-of-three pivot (libstdc++ uses the median of first+1, middle, last-1 moved to first, then Hoare-style unguarded partition).
  2. Track the recursion depth. If it exceeds 2 * floor(log2(n)), the input is behaving adversarially: switch that sub-range to heapsort. This caps the worst case at O(n log n).
  3. Stop recursing when a sub-range has <= 16 elements (_S_threshold). After the quicksort phase, run one insertion sort over the whole array: every element is within 16 positions of its final place, so it is O(n) total.

Result: O(n log n) worst case guaranteed (since C++11 the standard requires it), quicksort's speed on average, insertion sort's speed on the small pieces. It is not stable.

std::stable_sort is a merge sort (with an in-place fallback if the buffer allocation fails: O(n log^2 n)). std::partial_sort(first, middle, last) is a heap-based selection of the smallest middle - first elements in sorted order: O(n log k). std::nth_element is quickselect: O(n) average, puts the k-th element in place with smaller before and larger after — the right tool for "find the median" or "top k, order irrelevant".

docs.title: 2.3 Stability
docs.text: A sort is stable if elements that compare equal keep their input order. It matters when you sort by one key after another: sort transactions by time, then stable-sort by account, and each account's transactions remain time-ordered. Stable: insertion, merge, counting, radix (LSD), std::stable_sort. Not stable: selection (swap form), quicksort, heapsort, std::sort. To make any sort stable, append the original index to the key as a tiebreaker.

docs.title: 2.4 Lower bound and non-comparison sorts
docs.text:
Any sort that only compares elements needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case: there are n! orderings, each comparison halves the possibilities, log2(n!) ~ n log2 n. To beat it you need to look at the keys themselves.

Counting sort. Keys are integers in [0, k). Count occurrences, prefix-sum the counts to get starting positions, place each element. O(n + k) time and space, stable if you place in input order from the back. Perfect for bytes, small enums, bucket indices.

Radix sort (LSD). Sort by the least significant digit (byte) with a stable counting sort, then the next digit, ... For 32-bit keys with 8-bit digits: 4 passes of O(n + 256). O(n * d) total with d = number of digits. Beats std::sort on large arrays of integers by 2 to 4x. Not comparison-based, so it cannot take an arbitrary comparator; works for integers, fixed floats (with a sign-bit flip), fixed-length strings.

Bucket sort. Distribute into buckets by range, sort each bucket, concatenate. O(n) when the data is uniformly distributed; degenerates when it is not.

docs.title: 2.5 External merge sort (databases)
docs.text:
When n elements do not fit in memory of size M:
