  1. Run generation: read M elements, sort in memory (std::sort), write a sorted run to disk. Repeat: n/M runs. Replacement selection with a heap produces runs of ~2M on average from a buffer of M.
  2. Merge: open k runs, keep the head of each in a min-heap (module 12), repeatedly pop the minimum and write it, refill from that run. k-way merge is O(n log k) comparisons and one sequential read of all runs. If k is too large for the available buffers, merge in multiple passes (each pass reads and writes everything once).

I/O cost: 2 x (number of passes) x n. With a 1 GB sort buffer and 100 GB of data, run generation makes 100 runs; a 100-way merge finishes in one more pass. Total I/O: 4 x 100 GB. Making the buffer bigger reduces the number of runs; making the fan-in bigger reduces the passes. PostgreSQL's work_mem controls the buffer; when a sort exceeds it the planner's EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Sort Method: external merge Disk: NNN kB. Index build (CREATE INDEX) on a B-tree sorts the keys this way and then builds the tree bottom-up from the sorted stream (module 11). maintenance_work_mem is the buffer for that.

docs.title: 2.6 Choosing
docs.text: Situation Use General, in memory, any type std::sort Need stability std::stable_sort (or sort pairs with index) Only the k smallest in order std::partial_sort k-th element or median, order irrelevant std::nth_element Integers, n large, speed critical LSD radix sort Keys in a small range counting sort Linked list merge sort (std::list::sort) Nearly sorted insertion sort, or std::sort (handles it fine) Does not fit in memory external merge sort Streaming, need sorted output continuously heap (priority queue)

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Files: code/m08_sorting.cpp (insertion, selection, merge top-down and bottom-up, quicksort with Lomuto / Hoare / three-way partition and median-of-three, heapsort, counting sort, LSD radix sort; all tested against std::sort; timing on 1M ints; a demonstration of quicksort's worst case with a bad pivot), code/m08_external_merge.cpp (simulated external sort: splits a large vector into runs of size M, sorts each, and k-way merges with a heap, counting "I/O" operations).

Key parts:

// Hoare partition: returns j such that [lo, j] <= pivot <= [j+1, hi]. Both sides non-empty.
int partition_hoare(std::vector<int>& v, int lo, int hi) {
    int pivot = v[lo + (hi - lo) / 2];
    int i = lo - 1, j = hi + 1;
    while (true) {
        do { ++i; } while (v[i] < pivot);     // stop at >= pivot: equal keys get split
        do { --j; } while (v[j] > pivot);
        if (i >= j) return j;
        std::swap(v[i], v[j]);
    }
}
void quicksort_hoare(std::vector<int>& v, int lo, int hi) {
    while (lo < hi) {
        int p = partition_hoare(v, lo, hi);
        // Recurse on the smaller half, loop on the larger: stack depth stays O(log n).
        if (p - lo < hi - p) { quicksort_hoare(v, lo, p); lo = p + 1; }
        else                 { quicksort_hoare(v, p + 1, hi); hi = p; }
    }
}

// LSD radix sort on unsigned 32-bit keys, 4 passes of 8 bits, stable counting sort per pass.
void radix_sort(std::vector<std::uint32_t>& v) {
    std::vector<std::uint32_t> tmp(v.size());
    for (int shift = 0; shift < 32; shift += 8) {
        std::array<std::size_t, 257> count{};
        for (std::uint32_t x : v) ++count[((x >> shift) & 0xFF) + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < 256; ++i) count[i + 1] += count[i];   // prefix sum = start positions
        for (std::uint32_t x : v) tmp[count[(x >> shift) & 0xFF]++] = x;   // stable placement
        v.swap(tmp);
    }
}

// Heapsort: build max-heap bottom-up, then extract max n times.
void sift_down(std::vector<int>& v, int i, int n) {
    while (true) {
        int largest = i, l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
        if (l < n && v[l] > v[largest]) largest = l;
        if (r < n && v[r] > v[largest]) largest = r;
        if (largest == i) return;
        std::swap(v[i], v[largest]);
        i = largest;
    }
}
void heapsort(std::vector<int>& v) {
    int n = static_cast<int>(v.size());
    for (int i = n / 2 - 1; i >= 0; --i) sift_down(v, i, n);         // O(n) build
    for (int end = n - 1; end > 0; --end) { std::swap(v[0], v[end]); sift_down(v, 0, end); }
}

docs.title: 4.1 Why quicksort beats mergesort and heapsort in practice
docs.text: All three are O(n log n). Quicksort's partition is a tight loop over contiguous memory with one comparison per element and a predictable access pattern — the prefetcher keeps up, and it needs no extra buffer, so it uses half the memory bandwidth of merge sort. Heapsort's sift-down touches 2i+1, 4i+3, ... — stride doubling, a new cache line each step past the first few levels. Mergesort writes every element to the scratch buffer and back at each of log n levels: 2x the memory traffic. Measured on 1M random ints (typical): std::sort ~70 ms, std::stable_sort ~90 ms, heapsort ~150 ms, radix sort ~20 ms. Run m08_sorting.cpp for your numbers.

docs.title: 4.2 Branch misprediction in sorting
docs.text: Each comparison in quicksort is a branch that is unpredictable on random data (50/50). That is roughly 1.39 n log2 n mispredictions at 15 to 20 cycles each — a large fraction of the total time. Tricks that remove branches: branchless partition (write both candidates, select with a conditional move), block partitioning (BlockQuicksort), and pattern-defeating quicksort (pdqsort, which is also what Rust's sort_unstable and recent libc++ std::sort use). Radix sort has no data-dependent branches at all, which is a second reason it is fast.

docs.title: 4.3 The 16-element threshold
docs.text: Below ~16 elements, the O(n^2) of insertion sort is maybe 100 comparisons, all on one or two cache lines, with a loop that the branch predictor learns quickly. The recursive overhead of quicksort (function calls, pivot selection, partition bookkeeping) costs more than that. The exact threshold is tuned empirically; libstdc++ uses 16, libc++ uses 6 for trivially copyable types and 30 otherwise.

docs.title: 4.4 Introsort's depth limit, exactly
docs.text: libstdc++: __introsort_loop(first, last, depth_limit = 2 * __lg(n)). Each recursion level decrements depth_limit; at 0 it calls __partial_sort(first, last, last) which is a heapsort of that range. On random data the depth stays around log2(n) + a bit, so heapsort is never triggered. On the "median-of-three killer" sequence (a crafted input) it would be triggered and performance degrades to heapsort's constant — still O(n log n). Since C++11 the standard guarantees std::sort is O(n log n) worst case; before, it allowed O(n^2).

docs.title: 4.5 Sorting in PostgreSQL
docs.text: tuplesort.c: starts with an in-memory quicksort (actually a specialised introsort variant), switches to external merge when work_mem is exceeded, using replacement selection (historically) or just quicksorted runs (since PG 10, because larger runs from replacement selection did not pay for the heap's cache misses) and a k-way merge with a heap of tape heads. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows Sort Method: quicksort Memory: NNNkB or external merge Disk: NNNkB. Berkeley DB does not sort; its B-tree keeps keys ordered on insert — the bulk-load path in your migration engine benefited from pre-sorted input because sequential inserts into a B-tree hit the same leaf page repeatedly (module 11).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Sorting before bulk insert. Loading 100M rows into a B-tree index with random keys does a random page write per row. Sorting first makes consecutive inserts hit the same leaf: 100x fewer page writes. Your Berkeley DB -> YugabyteDB migration almost certainly read in key order for this reason; if it did not, that is the first optimisation to mention.
  • ORDER BY with LIMIT. PostgreSQL uses a bounded heap (top-k, module 12) instead of a full sort when LIMIT k is small: O(n log k) and O(k) memory. In your own code, std::partial_sort or std::nth_element is the equivalent — do not sort 10M rows to show the top 100.
  • Stability bugs. A report sorted by amount shows transactions of equal amount in a different order every run because std::sort is unstable and the input order varies. If the display order matters, add a tiebreaker (timestamp, id) to the comparator. This is a frequent "flaky test" cause.
  • Comparator bugs. A comparator that is not a strict weak ordering (<= instead of <, or inconsistent with equality) makes std::sort read out of bounds — a real crash, not just a wrong order, because the unguarded partition relies on the pivot stopping the scan. Rule: comp(a, a) must be false; comp(a, b) && comp(b, c) implies comp(a, c).
  • Sorting pointers vs sorting objects. Sorting a vector of 1 KB records moves 1 KB per swap. Sort a vector of indices or pointers instead, then permute once (or just read through the index). std::sort on 64-byte or smaller elements is fine to do directly.
  • 3 AM story (typical). A nightly batch took 6 hours instead of 1. EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query showed external merge Disk: 48 GB where it used to say quicksort Memory. The data grew past work_mem. Fix: raise work_mem for that session, or add an index so the sort disappears. Knowing what "external merge" means is the difference between a 10-minute and a 2-day investigation.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Rewrite your orderedArray.cpp insert as an insertion sort over a whole std::vector<int>, then count comparisons and shifts on sorted, reverse-sorted and random input of 1000 elements. Done when you can explain why the sorted case is O(n).
  2. (easy) Implement merge sort for std::vector<int> with a single scratch buffer allocated once (not per recursion). Done when it matches std::sort on 1M random ints and you can state its time, space and stability.
  3. (medium) Make quicksort go quadratic: use the first element as pivot and feed it a sorted array of 100 000 elements. Time it. Then switch to median-of-three and time again. Done when you have both numbers and the recursion did not overflow the stack (recurse on the smaller side).
  4. (medium) Implement three-way partition quicksort and test on an array of 1M elements that are all the same value, then on one with 10 distinct values. Compare with Lomuto. Done when Lomuto is visibly quadratic on the all-equal input and three-way is linear.
  5. (hard) Implement nth_element via quickselect and use it to find the median of 10M random ints; compare the time with a full std::sort. Done when quickselect is at least 3x faster and you can explain the expected O(n) via the geometric series of partition sizes.
  6. (hard) Extend m08_external_merge.cpp to a two-pass merge when the number of runs exceeds the fan-in (e.g. 100 runs, fan-in 10). Count total "block reads" and "block writes". Done when the count equals 2 x n x (number of passes) and you can explain what work_mem controls in PostgreSQL.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does std::sort work? Introsort: quicksort with median-of-three pivots; if recursion depth exceeds 2 log2 n, that range switches to heapsort (guaranteeing O(n log n)); ranges of 16 or fewer are left for a final insertion sort pass. Not stable. std::stable_sort is merge sort.

Q: Quicksort's worst case — when and how to avoid it? O(n^2) when every pivot is an extreme element: sorted input with first/last pivot, or many equal keys with Lomuto partition. Avoid with median-of-three or random pivots, Hoare or three-way partition for duplicates, and a depth limit falling back to heapsort (introsort).

Q: Merge sort vs quicksort? Merge: always O(n log n), stable, O(n) extra space, sequential access, good for lists and external sorting. Quick: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst (mitigated), in place, not stable, fastest in practice because of locality and no buffer traffic.

Q: What is stability and when does it matter? Equal elements keep their input order. Matters for multi-key sorts (sort by time, then stable by account) and for deterministic output. std::sort is not stable; add a tiebreaker or use std::stable_sort.

Q: Can you sort faster than O(n log n)? Not with comparisons alone (information-theoretic lower bound: log2(n!) comparisons). With key structure, yes: counting sort O(n + k), radix sort O(n * digits), bucket sort O(n) on uniform data.

Q: How would you sort 100 GB of data with 1 GB of RAM? External merge sort: read 1 GB chunks, sort each in memory, write ~100 sorted runs; then k-way merge the runs with a min-heap of run heads, streaming output to disk. Two passes over the data; more if the fan-in is limited by buffer memory.

Q: How do you find the median of a large array quickly? std::nth_element (quickselect): partition around a pivot, recurse only into the side containing position n/2. Expected O(n), worst O(n^2) with bad pivots (median-of-medians fixes it in theory). No full sort needed.

Q: Why does a bad comparator crash std::sort instead of just mis-sorting? The partition loop is unguarded: it relies on the pivot element to stop the scan. A comparator that returns true for equal elements (<=) lets the scan run past the pivot and off the end of the array.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Insertion sort: O(n^2) worst, O(n) nearly-sorted, stable; fastest for n <= 16.
  • Merge sort: O(n log n) always, stable, O(n) buffer, sequential; lists and external sorting.
  • Quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst; median-of-three or random pivot; Hoare or three-way partition for duplicates; recurse on the smaller side for O(log n) stack.
  • Heapsort: O(n log n) always, in place, not stable, ~2x slower (locality).
  • Introsort = quicksort + depth-limit fallback to heapsort + final insertion sort; std::sort.
  • std::stable_sort is merge sort; partial_sort for top-k in order; nth_element for median/top-k unordered.
  • Comparison sorts need Omega(n log n); counting and radix sort beat it using key structure.
  • External merge sort: sorted runs of memory size, then k-way merge with a heap; passes x 2n I/O.
  • Comparators must be strict weak orderings or std::sort reads out of bounds.
  • Sort keys before bulk-loading a B-tree; use top-k instead of a full sort for LIMIT.

docs.title: 09. Binary search and ordered data
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 08

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
You wrote binary search in orderedArray.cpp: look at the middle, throw away the half that cannot contain the key, repeat. Twenty steps find anything in a million sorted items. This module is about everything that idea can do beyond "is the key here": find the first place a key could go, the last, count how many equal keys exist, find the smallest value that satisfies a condition even when there is no array at all ("search on the answer"), and — the connection to your resume — find the right child pointer inside a B-tree page.

The reason binary search deserves a module is that most people get it subtly wrong. Off-by-one on the bounds, infinite loops when mid rounds the wrong way, overflow in (lo + hi) / 2. Knuth noted that the first bug-free binary search appeared 16 years after the first published one. The fix is not more care; it is a single template you memorise, with one invariant you can state in a sentence, and never deviate from.

docs.title: 2.1 The one template: lower_bound
docs.text:
Find the first index i in a sorted range such that v[i] >= target (or n if none). This is std::lower_bound. Use half-open bounds [lo, hi):

std::size_t lower_bound(const std::vector<int>& v, int target) {
    std::size_t lo = 0, hi = v.size();          // answer is in [lo, hi]; hi == n means "not found"
    while (lo < hi) {
        std::size_t mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;   // no overflow; rounds down so mid < hi
        if (v[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;      // mid is too small: answer is strictly after it
        else hi = mid;                          // v[mid] >= target: mid might be the answer
    }
    return lo;
}

Invariant to say aloud: "everything before lo is < target; everything from hi on is >= target." The loop ends when lo == hi, the boundary. It cannot loop forever because mid < hi always (rounding down) so hi = mid shrinks, and lo = mid + 1 > mid >= lo grows.

Every other variant is this template with a different predicate or a +1:

Want Code first index with v[i] >= t lower_bound(t) first index with v[i] > t (upper_bound) same loop, condition v[mid] <= t -> lo = mid + 1 does t exist i = lower_bound(t); i < n && v[i] == t first occurrence of t lower_bound(t) (check it equals t) last occurrence of t upper_bound(t) - 1 (check) count of t upper_bound(t) - lower_bound(t) insert position keeping sorted lower_bound(t) (before equals) or upper_bound(t) (after) largest v[i] <= t upper_bound(t) - 1 smallest v[i] >= t lower_bound(t)

std::lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), t), std::upper_bound, std::equal_range (both at once), std::binary_search (bool) do all of this. Know them, use them in production, and be able to write the loop by hand in an interview.

docs.title: 2.2 Search on a predicate (the general form)
docs.text:
Binary search does not need an array. It needs a monotone predicate P(x) over an ordered domain: false, false, ..., false, true, true, ..., true. It finds the first x where P(x) is true. The array version is P(i) = (v[i] >= target). Other domains:

  • Search on the answer. "Minimum capacity so that the tasks fit in d days": P(cap) = can we finish in d days with capacity cap? is monotone (more capacity never hurts). Binary search cap in [max(task), sum(tasks)], each check O(n). Total O(n log(sum)). Same shape: Koko eating bananas, split array largest sum, minimum days to make bouquets, allocate minimum pages, sqrt(x) to integer precision.
  • Bisection on reals. Root of a continuous function f with f(lo) < 0 < f(hi): halve the interval 50 to 60 times for double precision. Used for solving equations without a closed form (interest rate from payments — an actual banking calculation).
  • Lower bound of the first "bad" version (git bisect): P(version) = is broken.

The template is unchanged; only P and the domain differ:

// first x in [lo, hi) with P(x) true, or hi if none; P must be monotone false->true
long long first_true(long long lo, long long hi, const std::function<bool(long long)>& P) {
    while (lo < hi) {
        long long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (P(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}

docs.title: 2.3 Rotated sorted array
docs.text: [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] is sorted then rotated. At any mid, at least one of [lo, mid] and [mid, hi] is properly sorted (the one that does not contain the rotation point). Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half (plain comparison with its ends); if yes go there, else go to the other half. O(log n). Finding the minimum (the rotation point): P(i) = v[i] <= v[last] is monotone — binary search for its first true. With duplicates the problem degrades to O(n) in the worst case because v[lo] == v[mid] == v[hi] gives no information.

docs.title: 2.4 2D and other shapes
docs.text:
• Row-sorted matrix where each row starts after the previous ends: treat it as one array of rows * cols, index (mid / cols, mid % cols).
  • Matrix sorted by rows and by columns independently: start top-right, go left if too big, down if too small — O(rows + cols), a two-pointer "staircase" not a binary search.
  • Peak element: P(i) = v[i] > v[i+1] is not globally monotone, but binary search still finds a peak because moving toward the larger neighbour always has a peak ahead.
  • Median of two sorted arrays in O(log(min(m, n))): binary search the partition point in the smaller array. The classic hard one; know the idea (partition both so left halves have the right size and maxLeft <= minRight), do not expect to derive it under pressure.

docs.title: 2.5 Binary search inside a B-tree node
docs.text:
A B-tree page (module 11) holds a sorted array of up to a few hundred keys and the child pointers between them. Descending the tree means: in this page, find the child whose key range contains the search key. That is exactly upper_bound(keys, target): the index of the first key > target is the index of the child to follow (child i holds keys in [key[i-1], key[i])). For a leaf, lower_bound tells you whether the key exists and where a cursor should start a range scan. PostgreSQL's _bt_binsrch is this loop with a twist: it remembers the result of the search on the previous page to skip comparisons when inserting sorted data. With 300 keys per page, each page costs 8 to 9 comparisons; a 4-level tree costs ~35 comparisons total — and 4 page reads, which dominate.

Why not a linear scan inside the page? For keys that fit a cache line (integers), a linear scan of 16 keys is about as fast as 4 branchy comparisons and vectorises; for 300 keys or for string keys, binary search wins. Some engines (e.g. in-memory tries like ART, or "Eytzinger layout" arrays) reorder keys so that binary search's memory accesses become sequential.

docs.title: 2.6 std::map, std::set and sorted vectors
docs.text:
std::map<K, V> and std::set<K> are red-black trees (module 11): O(log n) insert/find/erase, sorted iteration, lower_bound/upper_bound members, stable iterators. Per element: a node of 32 bytes + payload, one allocation, a cache miss per level (~log2 n misses per lookup).

A sorted std::vector with std::lower_bound has the same O(log n) lookup with far better constants (contiguous, half the cache misses, 8x less memory) but O(n) insert. Use it when the data is built once or rarely changes (configuration tables, static lookup tables, a snapshot sorted once per batch). Boost's flat_map and C++23's std::flat_map are this pattern packaged. Rule: std::map for heavy interleaved insert and lookup; sorted vector for build-then-query; unordered_map when order and range queries are not needed.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m09_binary_search.cpp — hand-written lower_bound/upper_bound, first/last occurrence and count, first_true on a predicate, integer square root, search on answer (ship capacity / Koko bananas), rotated array search and minimum, peak element, 2D matrix search, bisection on a real function (loan interest rate), and a benchmark of std::map::find versus std::lower_bound on a sorted vector at 1M entries. All with asserts.

Key parts beyond the template above:

// Search on answer: minimum ship capacity to send all packages within `days` days.
int ship_within_days(const std::vector<int>& w, int days) {
    auto feasible = [&](long long cap) {
        int used = 1; long long load = 0;
        for (int x : w) {
            if (load + x > cap) { ++used; load = 0; }
            load += x;
        }
        return used <= days;
    };
    long long lo = *std::max_element(w.begin(), w.end());        // must fit the heaviest item
    long long hi = std::accumulate(w.begin(), w.end(), 0LL);     // one day for everything
    while (lo < hi) {
        long long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (feasible(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return static_cast<int>(lo);
}

// Rotated array search: one half is always sorted; decide if target is inside that half.
int search_rotated(const std::vector<int>& v, int t) {
    int lo = 0, hi = static_cast<int>(v.size()) - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {                                   // closed bounds here: we test v[mid] == t
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (v[mid] == t) return mid;
        if (v[lo] <= v[mid]) {                           // left half sorted
            if (v[lo] <= t && t < v[mid]) hi = mid - 1; else lo = mid + 1;
        } else {                                         // right half sorted
            if (v[mid] < t && t <= v[hi]) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

Note the closed-interval form here (lo <= hi, hi = mid - 1): it is natural when you test for equality at mid and can discard mid from both sides. The half-open form is natural when you are looking for a boundary. Pick the one that matches the question, and know why.

docs.title: 4.1 Overflow and the famous bug
docs.text: int mid = (lo + hi) / 2 overflows when lo + hi > INT_MAX, i.e. arrays over ~1 billion elements or when hi is INT_MAX in a search-on-answer. Java's Arrays.binarySearch had this bug for nine years. lo + (hi - lo) / 2 cannot overflow when lo <= hi. With std::size_t the sum cannot be negative but can still wrap past 2^64 in theory; the subtraction form is correct everywhere. Make it a habit.

docs.title: 4.2 Branches, cache lines and the cost of a comparison
docs.text: Each iteration of binary search is a data-dependent branch that is unpredictable (50/50 on random queries): ~15 cycles of misprediction per step. For 20 steps that is ~300 cycles, already more than the comparisons. std::lower_bound in libstdc++ is written to let the compiler produce a conditional move (cmov) for the lo/hi update instead of a branch — a "branchless binary search" — and gains 2x on large arrays. The first few probes (middle, quarters) are the same for every query and stay in L1; the last ~log2(n) - 10 probes are scattered and each costs a cache miss (~100 ns) on arrays larger than L2. So a binary search over 16M ints costs ~10 cache misses ~ 1 us, dominated by memory, not by the 24 comparisons. Prefetching both possible next probes (__builtin_prefetch) hides some of it.

docs.title: 4.3 Why B-trees exist (a preview)
docs.text: If a binary search over 16M keys costs 10 cache misses, and a disk page read costs 100 us or more, you want each memory access (or each disk read) to eliminate as much of the search space as possible. A B-tree node with 300 keys eliminates 299/300 of the remaining keys per page read, versus 1/2 per probe for binary search. That turns 24 probes into 3 or 4 page reads — and within each page you binary search anyway. Binary search is the inner loop of every ordered index.

docs.title: 4.4 Interpolation and exponential search
docs.text: If keys are uniformly distributed, interpolation search guesses mid proportionally (lo + (t - v[lo]) * (hi - lo) / (v[hi] - v[lo])) and takes O(log log n) probes on average, O(n) worst case. Exponential (galloping) search probes 1, 2, 4, 8, ... from the start to bracket the target, then binary searches within the bracket: O(log i) where i is the answer's position — the right tool when the answer is likely near the beginning, and what merge algorithms (Timsort) use when one run is much longer than the other.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Time-series lookup. Log records sorted by timestamp in a vector: "first record after T" is lower_bound; "records between T1 and T2" is [lower_bound(T1), lower_bound(T2)). This is the pattern for any append-only, time-ordered buffer, including WAL segment indexes.
  • Rate tables and tiers. Interest rate tiers by balance, fee schedules by amount: a sorted vector of thresholds and upper_bound(amount) - 1 gives the tier in O(log n). Do not write the if-else ladder.
  • Capacity planning via search on answer. "Smallest thread pool that keeps p99 under 50 ms" is a monotone predicate over pool size, evaluated by load test. Binary search needs 5 or 6 runs instead of 40.
  • Version bisection. When a regression appears between release 1.40 and 1.72, git bisect finds the commit in ~5 builds. Same with configuration changes in a deployment history.
  • Debug story (typical). A lookup table of fee thresholds returned the wrong tier for amounts exactly equal to a threshold. The code used a hand-written search with v[mid] < target in one branch and <= in another — a hybrid of lower_bound and upper_bound. Equal values fell on the wrong side. The fix was to delete the hand-written loop and call std::upper_bound, and the lesson was to decide "where do equal keys go" before writing anything.
  • Sorted vector vs map in the hot path. A std::map<int, Handler*> with 200 entries was looked up per message. Replacing it with a sorted std::vector<std::pair<int, Handler*>> and lower_bound removed ~8 cache misses per lookup — measurable at 200k messages per second. Build-once tables should be vectors.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Implement lower_bound and upper_bound by hand and test against the standard library on 1000 random arrays with duplicates. Done when every result matches, including targets below the minimum and above the maximum.
  2. (easy) Count occurrences of t in a sorted array in O(log n). Done when [1,2,2,2,3], 2 -> 3 and [1,3], 2 -> 0.
  3. (medium) Integer square root: largest r with r*r <= x for x up to 10^18. Done when isqrt(10^18) == 10^9 and isqrt(2^63 - 1) returns the right value without overflow (use mid <= x / mid rather than mid * mid <= x).
  4. (medium) Koko eating bananas: minimum eating speed to finish all piles within h hours. Done when [3,6,7,11], 8 -> 4 and [30,11,23,4,20], 5 -> 30.
  5. (hard) Find minimum in a rotated sorted array with duplicates. Done when [2,2,2,0,1] -> 0, [1,1,1] -> 1, and you can explain why the worst case is O(n).
  6. (hard) Implement a B-tree-style node search: given a node with sorted keys k[0..m) and children c[0..m], return the child index to descend into for target t (child i holds keys in [k[i-1], k[i])). Then write the leaf version that returns the position for a cursor to start a >= t range scan. Done when you reuse the same lower_bound/upper_bound function for both and can say which one and why.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Write binary search without bugs. Half-open [lo, hi), mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, if (v[mid] < t) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid;, loop while lo < hi, return lo. State the invariant: before lo everything is less than t, from hi on everything is at least t. Check v[lo] == t for existence.

Q: lower_bound vs upper_bound? lower_bound is the first element >= t; upper_bound is the first element > t. Between them lie all elements equal to t; their difference is the count. Insert at upper_bound to keep stability.

Q: What is "binary search on the answer"? When the answer is a number and "is x feasible" is monotone (feasible for x implies feasible for all larger x), binary search x over its range, evaluating feasibility with a linear check. O(n log(range)). Examples: minimum ship capacity, Koko bananas, split array largest sum.

Q: How do you search a rotated sorted array in O(log n)? At mid, one of the two halves is sorted (compare v[lo] and v[mid]). If the target lies within that sorted half's range, search it; otherwise search the other half. With duplicates the worst case degrades to O(n).

Q: Why lo + (hi - lo) / 2 instead of (lo + hi) / 2? The sum can overflow when the indices are large (or when searching on a value range up to INT_MAX). The difference form never exceeds hi.

Q: How is binary search used inside a B-tree? Each node holds sorted separator keys; upper_bound of the target among them gives the child index to descend; in a leaf, lower_bound gives the slot where the key is or where a range scan starts. Node fan-out of hundreds means a few page reads replace dozens of probes.

Q: Sorted vector with lower_bound versus std::map — when each? Sorted vector: build once, query many; smaller memory, fewer cache misses, O(n) insert. std::map: interleaved inserts and lookups, stable iterators, O(log n) everything with a cache miss per level.

Q: Why is std::lower_bound faster than a textbook loop on large arrays? It is written so the compiler emits conditional moves rather than branches, avoiding ~15 cycles of misprediction per step, and its access pattern keeps the first probes in L1.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• One template: half-open [lo, hi), mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, move lo past "too small", move hi onto "could be the answer"; return lo.
  • lower_bound: first >= t. upper_bound: first > t. Count = difference. Last occurrence = upper_bound - 1.
  • Any monotone predicate over an ordered domain is binary-searchable: search on the answer, bisection on reals, version bisection.
  • Rotated arrays: one half is sorted; check whether the target lies inside it.
  • Peak finding works by always moving toward the larger neighbour.
  • Closed bounds (lo <= hi) when testing equality at mid; half-open when finding a boundary.
  • Each late probe on a big array is a cache miss; branchless search and B-tree fan-out exist to cut those.
  • B-tree descent is upper_bound on the node's keys; leaf positioning is lower_bound.
  • Sorted vector beats std::map for build-once tables; std::map for interleaved updates.
  • Decide where equal keys go before writing the loop.

docs.title: 10. Trees and binary search trees
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 05, 07, 09

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A tree is a linked structure where each node points to children instead of to one "next". A file system is a tree: directories contain directories and files. An organisation chart is a tree. The expression (a + b) * c is a tree with * at the top. Trees are how you represent anything hierarchical, and how you search ordered data while still inserting quickly.

A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree (at most two children) with one rule: every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key, every key in its right subtree is larger. That rule makes search a walk: compare, go left or right, repeat. If the tree is "bushy" (balanced), the walk is log2(n) steps — the same as binary search — but inserting a new key is also just a walk plus one pointer write, with no shifting. Your sorted array could search in O(log n) but had to shift on insert; a linked list could insert in O(1) but had to scan to search. The BST does both in O(log n), if it stays balanced.

The "if" is the whole story of modules 10 and 11. A BST built from keys arriving in sorted order is a linked list in disguise: every node has only a right child, height n, O(n) search. Module 11 fixes that with self-balancing trees and then with the B-tree, which is what disks and databases need.

docs.title: 2.1 Terminology
docs.text:
• Root: the top node. Leaf: a node with no children. Internal node: has children.
  • Parent / child / sibling / ancestor / descendant: as in a family tree.
  • Depth of a node: edges from the root to it. Height of a tree: max depth (a single node has height 0; the empty tree is -1 by convention, or 0 if you count nodes).
  • Subtree rooted at x: x and all its descendants.
  • Binary tree: each node has at most two children, called left and right.
  • Full: every node has 0 or 2 children. Complete: all levels full except possibly the last, which is filled left to right (this is the heap shape, module 12). Perfect: all levels full; n = 2^(h+1) - 1. Balanced: height is O(log n) — different structures use different exact definitions (AVL: child heights differ by at most 1).
  • Degenerate: every node has one child; effectively a linked list.
  • BST property: for every node, all keys in the left subtree < key < all keys in the right subtree. Note "all keys in the subtree", not just the immediate child — that distinction is the bug in most "validate BST" attempts.

docs.title: 2.2 Traversals
docs.text:
Visiting every node exactly once, in some order. Four orders matter:

Traversal Order Use Pre-order node, left, right copy / serialise a tree; prefix expression In-order left, node, right BST: yields keys in sorted order Post-order left, right, node delete a tree (children before parent); evaluate expression; compute heights Level-order (BFS) by depth, left to right shortest path in unweighted tree; printing by level; serialising with structure

The first three are depth-first (DFS) and are naturally recursive. Each is O(n) time, O(h) space for the recursion stack (h = height; O(n) worst case on a degenerate tree).

Iterative in-order uses an explicit stack: push all left descendants, pop and visit, move to the right child, repeat. Iterative pre-order: push root; pop, visit, push right then left (so left is processed first). Iterative post-order is awkward; the trick is "pre-order with children pushed left-then-right, then reverse the output". Level-order uses a queue; to get levels as separate lists, process the queue in batches of its current size.

Morris traversal does in-order in O(1) extra space by temporarily rewiring right pointers (threading). Know it exists; it comes up as a "can you do it without a stack" follow-up.

docs.title: 2.3 BST operations
docs.text:
Search: while (node && node->key != k) node = k < node->key ? left : right. O(h).

Insert: search for the key; when you fall off the tree, attach the new node there. Keys always become leaves. O(h). Duplicates: reject, count, or put them consistently to one side.

Minimum / maximum: leftmost / rightmost node. O(h).

Successor (next key in sorted order): if the node has a right subtree, the minimum of it; else the nearest ancestor of which the node is in the left subtree. This is how a cursor moves to "next key" in an ordered tree (and why std::map::iterator::operator++ is amortised O(1) but O(h) worst case).

Delete — three cases:

  1. Leaf: unlink it.
  2. One child: replace the node with its child.
  3. Two children: find the in-order successor (minimum of the right subtree, which has no left child), copy its key into this node, then delete the successor from the right subtree (which is case 1 or 2). Using the predecessor (max of left subtree) is symmetric. O(h).

With std::unique_ptr<Node> the "replace node with child" step is *link = std::move((*link)->right) where link is the owning pointer that leads to the node — the same pointer-to-owner walk as the linked list in module 05.

Height: 1 + max(height(left), height(right)), post-order. Size: 1 + size(left) + size(right). Balanced check: compute heights bottom-up and return -1 as soon as a node's children differ by more than 1 — O(n) in one pass instead of O(n^2) with a naive height-at-every-node.

docs.title: 2.4 Classic problems
docs.text:
Validate BST. Wrong: check left->key < key < right->key at each node. That accepts [5, [1, null, 6], 8] where 6 is in 5's left subtree. Right: pass down a (lo, hi) range each node's key must lie in; the left child gets (lo, key), the right gets (key, hi). Or do an in-order traversal and check it is strictly increasing. O(n).

Lowest common ancestor (LCA). In a BST: walk from the root; if both keys are smaller go left, if both larger go right, else the current node is the LCA. O(h). In a general binary tree: recurse; if a subtree returns both targets found (or one found below each child), the current node is the LCA. O(n).

Serialise / deserialise. Pre-order with explicit null markers ("5 3 # # 8 # #") reconstructs uniquely. For a BST you can skip the null markers: pre-order plus the BST property suffices (rebuild with the (lo, hi) range technique). Level-order with nulls is what LeetCode uses for its examples.

k-th smallest. In-order traversal, stop at the k-th visit. O(h + k). With a size field in each node it is O(h) — this is an order-statistic tree.

Build from sorted array. Middle element is the root; recurse on halves. Produces a perfectly balanced BST in O(n). This is also how a B-tree is bulk-loaded from sorted data (module 11).

Diameter. Longest path between any two nodes = max over nodes of (height(left) + height(right) + 2). One post-order pass. Path sum, invert, symmetric, same tree, max depth, count nodes — all one recursive pass each; they are the warm-up problems interviewers use to check you can write a recursion cleanly.

docs.title: 2.5 Why an unbalanced BST is bad
docs.text: Insert 1, 2, 3, ..., n in order: each key is larger than everything so far, goes to the far right. Height n - 1. Search is O(n). Insert is O(n). You have built a linked list with extra pointers. Random insertion order gives expected height ~ 2.99 log2(n) — fine on average, but "random" is not something you can rely on in production: timestamps, sequence numbers and sorted batch loads are the common case and they are the worst case. That is why no production system uses a plain BST; std::map is a red-black tree, databases use B-trees, and both guarantee O(log n) by rebalancing.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Files: code/m10_bst.cpp (BST with unique_ptr: insert, search, min/max, delete with all three cases, height, size, in-order to vector, validate, LCA, k-th smallest, build from sorted array, serialise/deserialise pre-order with null markers; an experiment that inserts sorted vs shuffled keys and prints the height), code/m10_tree_traversals.cpp (recursive and iterative pre/in/post-order, level-order with levels, Morris in-order, max depth, diameter, invert, same-tree, path sum, LCA in a general binary tree, on a raw-pointer TreeNode as problem sites define it).

Key parts of m10_bst.cpp:

struct Node {
    int key;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> left, right;
};

// Owning-pointer walk: `link` is the unique_ptr that leads to the current node. Insert
// attaches at the first null link; delete rewires through the same link.
void insert(int key) {
    std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
    while (*link) {
        if (key == (*link)->key) return;                 // no duplicates
        link = key < (*link)->key ? &(*link)->left : &(*link)->right;
    }
    *link = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{key, nullptr, nullptr});
    ++size_;
}

bool erase(int key) {
    std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
    while (*link && (*link)->key != key)
        link = key < (*link)->key ? &(*link)->left : &(*link)->right;
    if (!*link) return false;
    Node* n = link->get();
    if (n->left && n->right) {
        // Two children: find the successor (leftmost of right subtree), steal its key,
        // then delete the successor node, which has at most one (right) child.
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* succ = &n->right;
        while ((*succ)->left) succ = &(*succ)->left;
        n->key = (*succ)->key;
        *succ = std::move((*succ)->right);
    } else {
        // Zero or one child: replace the node by its only child (or null).
        *link = std::move(n->left ? n->left : n->right);
    }
    --size_;
    return true;
}

// Validate with ranges. Using long long bounds avoids the INT_MIN/INT_MAX edge cases.
bool valid(const Node* n, long long lo, long long hi) {
    if (!n) return true;
    if (n->key <= lo || n->key >= hi) return false;
    return valid(n->left.get(), lo, n->key) && valid(n->right.get(), n->key, hi);
}

// Height and balance in one post-order pass: -1 means "unbalanced somewhere below".
int balanced_height(const Node* n) {
    if (!n) return 0;
    int l = balanced_height(n->left.get());  if (l < 0) return -1;
    int r = balanced_height(n->right.get()); if (r < 0) return -1;
    if (std::abs(l - r) > 1) return -1;
    return 1 + std::max(l, r);
}

Key parts of m10_tree_traversals.cpp:

// Iterative in-order: push the left spine, pop-visit, go right.
std::vector<int> inorder_iter(TreeNode* root) {
    std::vector<int> out; std::vector<TreeNode*> st;
    TreeNode* cur = root;
    while (cur || !st.empty()) {
        while (cur) { st.push_back(cur); cur = cur->left; }
        cur = st.back(); st.pop_back();
        out.push_back(cur->val);
        cur = cur->right;
    }
    return out;
}
// Level order, one vector per level: process the queue in batches of its current size.
std::vector<std::vector<int>> level_order(TreeNode* root) {
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> out;
    std::deque<TreeNode*> q;
    if (root) q.push_back(root);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        std::size_t width = q.size();
        out.emplace_back();
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < width; ++i) {
            TreeNode* n = q.front(); q.pop_front();
            out.back().push_back(n->val);
            if (n->left) q.push_back(n->left);
            if (n->right) q.push_back(n->right);
        }
    }
    return out;
}

docs.title: 4.1 Node layout and cache behaviour
docs.text: A BST node with an int key and two unique_ptr children is 24 bytes (4 + 4 padding + 8 + 8); std::map<int,int>'s red-black node is 48 bytes (colour + 3 pointers + key + value + padding). Each node is a separate allocation, so a search of depth 20 touches 20 cache lines at unpredictable addresses: ~20 cache misses, ~2 us on a cold cache for a 1M-entry map. Compare binary search on a sorted vector: the first 10 probes are shared by all queries and stay cached; ~10 misses. Compare a B-tree node of 4 KB holding 500 keys: 3 misses to reach the leaf (plus the binary search within each node, which is in-cache). This is the memory-hierarchy argument for B-trees even in RAM, and it is why std::map is rarely the fastest choice.

docs.title: 4.2 Recursion depth and the degenerate tree
docs.text: Recursive traversal of a degenerate tree with 10^6 nodes recurses 10^6 deep: stack overflow. Any production tree code must either guarantee balance (then depth is ~2 log2 n ~ 40) or use iterative traversal. Deleting a unique_ptr-based tree is recursive by default (the destructor chain) — same hazard as the linked list in module 05. The code file deletes iteratively with a post-order stack.

docs.title: 4.3 Expected height of a random BST
docs.text: Inserting n distinct keys in uniformly random order gives expected height about 4.311 ln n ~ 2.99 log2 n, and expected average node depth about 1.39 log2 n (the same 1.39 as quicksort's comparison count — the BST built by insertion order and the recursion tree of quicksort on that order are the same tree). "Random order" is a model; real key streams are sorted far more often than random, so you rebalance.

docs.title: 4.4 Threaded trees and parent pointers
docs.text: std::map nodes store a parent pointer so ++iterator can find the successor without a stack: go to the right subtree's minimum, or climb until you come from a left child. Across a full in-order traversal every edge is crossed exactly twice, so n increments cost O(n) total: amortised O(1) per step, O(h) worst case for a single step. A cursor in a B-tree leaf chain (module 11) does better: next key is pos + 1 in the same page, or follow one sibling pointer.

docs.title: 4.5 Trees in the systems you know
docs.text: PostgreSQL's planner builds an expression tree for every WHERE clause and evaluates it by post-order walk (children first). The query plan itself is a tree of plan nodes executed by pulling tuples from the root (Volcano model). Your RPC server's message schema is a tree. JSON, XML and ASN.1 parsers produce trees. Directory walkers are pre-order DFS. Compilers' ASTs are trees walked in post-order to generate code. When you say "tree traversal" in an interview, having two of these examples ready makes the answer concrete.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Never ship a plain BST. Use std::map/std::set (red-black), a sorted vector, or a B-tree library. The plain BST is a teaching tool and an interview topic.
  • Iterative deletes and traversals for anything that might be deep. A recursive destructor on a degenerate tree is a crash at shutdown — the worst time, because it hides real errors and corrupts the exit code.
  • Validate on load. If you persist a tree (or an index) and read it back, validate the ordering invariant with an in-order walk before trusting it. PostgreSQL's amcheck extension does exactly this for B-tree indexes (bt_index_check) and finds corrupted indexes that would otherwise return wrong query results silently.
  • Expression trees in rules engines. Fee and limit rules in banking systems are often expression trees evaluated per transaction. Post-order evaluation with short-circuit AND/OR is the standard; a stack machine (module 06) is the optimised version.
  • Debug story (typical). A cache keyed by timestamp used a hand-written BST "because it was simple". Keys arrived in increasing order. After a week the tree had height ~500 000 and each lookup took milliseconds; a thread pool of 32 was saturated doing lookups. Replacing it with std::map (same interface, O(log n) guaranteed) fixed it in one line. The lesson is not "use std::map"; it is "sorted input is the normal case, and a plain BST is O(n) on it".

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Write recursive pre-, in- and post-order on the TreeNode type and run them on the tree [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, 6]. Done when the outputs are 1 2 4 5 3 6, 4 2 5 1 3 6, 4 5 2 6 3 1.
  2. (easy) Maximum depth, count of nodes, count of leaves, sum of all values — each as a one-function recursion. Done when all four work on an empty tree too.
  3. (medium) Delete from a BST handling all three cases; after each delete, verify the in-order sequence is still sorted and has one fewer element. Done when 10 000 random inserts followed by 5000 random deletes leave a valid BST (use the validator).
  4. (medium) Serialise a binary tree in pre-order with # for null, deserialise it, and check the round trip reproduces the same structure (compare with same_tree). Done when a tree with 1000 random nodes round-trips.
  5. (hard) k-th smallest in a BST in O(h) per query by storing subtree sizes in each node and maintaining them on insert and delete. Done when 1000 random queries agree with the in-order list.
  6. (hard) Measure it: insert 1, 2, ..., 100 000 into your BST in sorted order and time 1000 searches; then insert the same keys shuffled and time again; then do both with std::map. Done when you have four numbers and can explain each (expect the sorted BST to be ~1000x slower than the others, and std::map to be the same for both orders).

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What makes a binary tree a BST? For every node, all keys in its left subtree are less than its key and all keys in its right subtree are greater. "All keys in the subtree", not only the direct children.

Q: In-order traversal of a BST gives what? Why? The keys in sorted order: everything smaller (left subtree) is visited before the node, everything larger (right subtree) after, recursively.

Q: How do you delete a node with two children? Replace its key with its in-order successor's key (the minimum of the right subtree), then delete that successor node, which has at most one child. The predecessor works symmetrically.

Q: How do you validate a BST correctly? Pass an allowed range (lo, hi) down: the left child must be in (lo, key), the right in (key, hi). Checking only immediate children misses violations deeper in the subtree. Alternatively check that an in-order traversal is strictly increasing.

Q: What is the time complexity of BST search, and what is the catch? O(h) where h is the height. Balanced: O(log n). Degenerate (sorted insertion): O(n). Plain BSTs do not control h, which is why real systems use self-balancing trees or B-trees.

Q: How do you find the LCA of two nodes? BST: walk from the root; go left if both keys are smaller, right if both larger, otherwise the current node is the LCA. General tree: post-order recursion returning which targets were found below; the first node that sees both is the LCA.

Q: How would you traverse a tree without recursion? With an explicit stack for DFS (push left spine for in-order; push right then left for pre-order) or a queue for BFS. Needed when the tree may be deep enough to overflow the call stack.

Q: Why does std::map iterate in O(n) total if each ++ can be O(log n)? Each tree edge is traversed exactly twice over a full in-order walk (down and back up), so n increments do O(n) work in total — amortised O(1) per step even though one step can climb O(h).

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Tree terms: root, leaf, depth, height, balanced, complete, degenerate.
  • Pre-order (serialise), in-order (sorted for BST), post-order (delete, heights), level-order (BFS).
  • DFS is O(n) time, O(h) stack; iterative versions use an explicit stack; level-order uses a queue.
  • BST search/insert/min/max/successor are O(h); delete has three cases, two-children uses the successor.
  • Validate with (lo, hi) ranges or an in-order strictness check — never with child-only comparisons.
  • LCA in a BST is a root-to-split walk; in a general tree a post-order recursion.
  • Height and balance in one post-order pass with a -1 sentinel.
  • Sorted insertion makes a plain BST a linked list: O(n). Random order gives ~3 log2 n height.
  • Each tree level is a cache miss; B-trees and sorted vectors touch fewer lines than std::map.
  • Never ship a plain BST; use std::map, a sorted vector, or a B-tree; traverse and destroy iteratively when depth is not guaranteed.

docs.title: 11. Balanced trees, B-trees and disk
docs.text: Time: ~6 hours Prerequisites: 09, 10

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Module 10 ended with the problem: a BST is only fast if it is balanced, and real key streams (sequence numbers, timestamps, sorted batch loads) make it a linked list. Self-balancing trees fix this by doing a little extra work on every insert and delete — a rotation, which is a local re-wiring of three nodes that lowers one side and raises the other — so the height stays within a constant factor of log2(n). AVL trees keep the two subtrees of every node within one level of each other. Red-black trees use a looser rule that needs fewer rotations; that is what std::map is.

The B-tree answers a different question: what if each step down the tree costs not a nanosecond but a disk read of 100 microseconds, or at least a cache miss of 100 nanoseconds? Then you want each step to eliminate as much as possible. A B-tree node is a whole disk page holding hundreds of keys; one page read narrows the search by a factor of hundreds instead of two. A billion keys fit in a tree of height 3 or 4. Every relational database index you have ever used — PostgreSQL's CREATE INDEX, Berkeley DB's DB_BTREE, SQLite, MySQL InnoDB — is a B-tree variant called a B+tree, where all the data sits in the leaves and the leaves are chained together so that a cursor can walk a range without going back up.

Your resume says "B-tree cursor traversal" and "indexing". The migration engine you worked on opened a Berkeley DB cursor and walked it with DB_NEXT: that is a leaf-chain traversal. This module gives you the vocabulary and the mechanics to explain exactly what happened underneath, and an in-memory B+tree you can write from memory.

docs.title: 2.1 Rotations
docs.text:
A rotation changes the shape of a BST without changing its in-order sequence.

Right rotation at y            Left rotation at x
      y                x              x                    y
     / \              / \            / \                  / \
    x   C    ->      A   y          A   y      ->        x   C
   / \                  / \            / \              / \
  A   B                B   C          B   C            A   B

In-order is A x B y C before and after. Right rotation makes x the parent of y; x's old right subtree B becomes y's left. Three pointer writes (plus parent pointers if you keep them). O(1). With unique_ptr the rotation is a sequence of std::moves on the owning links:

// right rotation: `link` owns y; afterwards it owns x.
std::unique_ptr<Node> y = std::move(link);
std::unique_ptr<Node> x = std::move(y->left);
y->left = std::move(x->right);     // B moves under y
x->right = std::move(y);           // y goes under x
link = std::move(x);

docs.title: 2.2 AVL trees
docs.text:
Invariant: for every node, |height(left) - height(right)| <= 1. Store the height in each node. Guarantees height < 1.4405 log2(n + 2): a 1M-node AVL tree has height at most 28.

Insert: BST insert, then walk back up updating heights. At the first node whose balance factor (height(left) - height(right)) becomes +2 or -2, fix with one or two rotations. Four cases:

Case Shape Fix Left-Left left child is left-heavy right rotation at the node Right-Right right child is right-heavy left rotation at the node Left-Right left child is right-heavy left rotation at the left child, then right rotation at the node Right-Left right child is left-heavy right rotation at the right child, then left rotation at the node

After the fix the subtree height is what it was before the insert, so no ancestor needs further rebalancing: insert does at most 2 rotations. Delete may need a rotation at every level on the way up: O(log n) rotations worst case, still O(log n) total.

AVL is stricter than red-black: shorter trees (faster lookups), more rotations on update. Use when lookups dominate.

docs.title: 2.3 Red-black trees
docs.text:
Each node is red or black. Invariants:

  1. Root is black.
  2. Red nodes have black children (no two reds in a row).
  3. Every path from a node to its null leaves has the same number of black nodes (the black height).

Consequence: the longest path (alternating red and black) is at most twice the shortest (all black), so height <= 2 log2(n + 1). A 1M-node red-black tree has height at most 40 (typically ~20 to 22).

Insert: colour the new node red (never violates 3). If the parent is red, violation of 2; fix with recolouring (if the uncle is red: recolour parent, uncle, grandparent and move up) or one or two rotations (if the uncle is black). Amortised O(1) recolourings and at most 2 rotations. Delete has more cases (6 in the textbook) but also at most 3 rotations.

Why std::map, Java's TreeMap, the Linux CFS scheduler and epoll's timer tree use red-black and not AVL: fewer rotations per update (each rotation is pointer writes to several cache lines, which matters under concurrent modification), and insert/delete with at most a constant number of rotations. A red-black tree is isomorphic to a 2-3-4 tree (a B-tree with 2 to 4 children per node): a black node with its red children is one 2-3-4 node. That is the conceptual bridge to the B-tree.

Know the invariants and the height bound, and be able to describe the insert fix-up in words. Nobody expects you to write red-black delete from memory; everyone expects you to know what std::map is and why it is O(log n).

docs.title: 2.4 B-trees
docs.text:
A B-tree of order m (or "minimum degree" t, with m = 2t) is a search tree where:

  • every node has at most m - 1 keys and m children;
  • every non-root node has at least ceil(m/2) - 1 keys (nodes are at least half full);
  • the root has at least 1 key (unless the tree is empty);
  • all leaves are at the same depth (the tree is perfectly height-balanced);
  • within a node, keys are sorted, and child i holds keys strictly between key[i-1] and key[i].

Height h satisfies n >= 2 (m/2)^h - 1, so h <= log_(m/2)((n+1)/2). With m = 500 and n = 10^9: h <= log_250(5 x 10^8) ~ 3.6. Four levels. With the root and the next level cached (they are hot), a point lookup costs 2 disk reads.

Search: in each node, binary search the keys (module 09): upper_bound gives the child index. Descend. O(log_m n) nodes, O(log2 m) comparisons each: O(log2 n) comparisons total, same as a BST, but O(log_m n) page reads.

Insert: descend to the leaf, insert in sorted position. If the leaf now has m keys (overflow), split: the median key moves up into the parent, the keys left of it stay, the keys right of it form a new sibling. The parent gains one key and one child; if it overflows, split it too, possibly up to the root. A root split is the only way the tree grows taller — and it grows at the top, which is why all leaves stay at the same depth.

Delete: remove the key from the leaf. If the leaf falls below the minimum (underflow), either borrow a key from a sibling through the parent (rotation at the B-tree level), or if the sibling is also at minimum, merge with it and pull the separator key down from the parent. Parent underflow propagates up. If the root ends with zero keys, its single child becomes the root: the tree shrinks at the top.

In the original B-tree (Bayer & McCreight, 1972) values are stored in every node alongside keys, including internal nodes.

docs.title: 2.5 B+trees
docs.text:
The variant every database uses. Differences from the B-tree:

  1. Internal nodes hold only separator keys and child pointers. No values. So an internal node of 8 KB holds many more separators -> higher fan-out -> shorter tree.
  2. All key/value pairs live in the leaves. Every key appears in a leaf; a separator in an internal node is a copy (or a shortened form — see suffix truncation) that only guides the search.
  3. Leaves are linked left-to-right (and usually right-to-left). A range scan descends once to the first leaf and then walks siblings. No parent revisits.

Leaf split in a B+tree: the new right leaf gets the upper half; the first key of the right leaf is copied up as the separator (the key itself stays in the leaf). Internal split: the median separator moves up (it is not needed in the children, since it only guides).

Internal:            [ 20 | 40 ]
                    /     |     \
Leaves:   [5 10 15] -> [20 25 30] -> [40 45 50 55]  -> null
          values      values         values

Search for 25: 25 >= 20 and < 40 -> middle child -> binary search in leaf -> found. Range scan [12, 47): descend for 12 -> first leaf, lower_bound = position of 15 -> emit 15; follow next -> emit 20 25 30 -> follow next -> emit 40 45; stop at 50 >= 47.

docs.title: 2.6 Page size and fan-out arithmetic
docs.text:
Pages are 8 KB in PostgreSQL (BLCKSZ), 4 KB default in Berkeley DB (configurable to 64 KB), 16 KB in InnoDB, 4 KB in SQLite by default. A page holds a header, an array of item pointers ("line pointers", 4 bytes each in PostgreSQL), the items themselves, and a "special space" at the end for sibling pointers and flags.

PostgreSQL B-tree leaf item for an 8-byte integer key: 8-byte IndexTupleData header (6-byte heap TID + 2 bytes info) + 8-byte key = 16 bytes, aligned to 8 -> 16 bytes, plus a 4-byte line pointer = 20 bytes. Page usable space ~8 KB - 24 header - 16 special ~ 8150 bytes -> about 400 items per leaf at 100% fill; with the default leaf fill factor of 90% at build time, ~360. Internal pages hold the same tuple shape (the TID field repurposed as the child block number), so fan-out is also ~400. So:

Rows Leaf pages Height (levels incl. root) 10^5 ~280 2 10^7 ~28 000 3 10^9 ~2 800 000 4

Index size for 10^9 bigint keys: ~2.8M pages x 8 KB ~ 22 GB. The root and the ~400 level-2 pages (3 MB) stay in the buffer pool permanently; a point lookup on a cold leaf is 1 to 2 random I/Os. These are the numbers to have in your head when someone asks "how big is the index and how many reads is a lookup".

Wider keys (text, UUID) mean fewer items per page, lower fan-out, taller trees, and — for random UUIDs — inserts spread over every leaf, so no page stays hot in cache. That is why "UUID v4 primary keys are bad for B-tree indexes" is a thing, and why time-ordered UUIDs (v7) exist.

docs.title: 2.7 Cursor traversal
docs.text:
A cursor is a position in the leaf chain: (leaf page, slot index). Operations:

  • seek(key) / DB_SET_RANGE: descend from the root, lower_bound in the leaf; the cursor sits on the first key >= key.
  • next() / DB_NEXT: slot + 1; if past the end of the page, follow the right sibling pointer and go to slot 0. Amortised O(1) per step; O(n / fan-out) page reads for a full scan.
  • prev() / DB_PREV: symmetric with the left sibling pointer.
  • first() / DB_FIRST: descend always-left; last() / DB_LAST: always-right.
  • get(key) / DB_SET: seek and check equality.

Your migration engine: cursor->get(cursor, &key, &data, DB_FIRST) then a loop of DB_NEXT until DB_NOTFOUND. Underneath: one root-to-leaf descent, then a walk of the leaf chain reading each leaf page once, in key order. That is the most efficient way to read a whole B-tree — sequential leaf pages, no repeated descents — and it is why the migration read in key order "for free" and why bulk-loading the destination in that same order was cheap (sequential inserts hit the rightmost leaf, which stays in cache).

What makes cursors hard in a real engine: the tree changes under the cursor. A concurrent insert splits the leaf the cursor is on; the cursor's slot index is now wrong. Solutions: remember the key rather than the slot and re-seek after a change (PostgreSQL does this when it has to drop its pin on the page); or pin the page so it cannot be split until the cursor moves on (Berkeley DB keeps the page locked/pinned while the cursor is positioned on it, which is why a cursor left open in your code blocks writers — a real operational hazard).

docs.title: 2.8 Concurrency: latch coupling and B-link trees
docs.text:
Readers and writers in the same tree at the same time:

  • Latch coupling (lock crabbing): take a read latch on a child before releasing the parent. Writers take write latches top-down pessimistically (if a child might split) or optimistically (read latches down, write latch on the leaf only, restart if a split is needed).
  • B-link tree (Lehman & Yao, 1981): each node has a right-sibling pointer and a high key (upper bound of what it may contain). A reader that arrives at a node and finds its key is greater than the high key simply moves right — the node was split and the key moved to the new sibling. No latch coupling needed for readers; splits are done right-then-up so a concurrent reader always finds a consistent path. PostgreSQL's nbtree is a B-link tree; the "move right" logic in _bt_moveright is exactly this. Every leaf page stores its high key as the first item.

You do not implement this in an interview. You mention it when asked "how do databases allow concurrent reads and writes to an index".

docs.title: 2.9 Engineering refinements you should be able to name
docs.text:
• Fill factor: leave pages 10% empty at build so the first inserts do not split.
  • Rightmost-leaf fast path: sequential inserts always go to the rightmost leaf; PostgreSQL caches that page and skips the descent when the key is larger than its high key.
  • Suffix truncation: internal separators need only be long enough to separate the two children: between "smith" and "stevens" the separator "sn" suffices. Smaller separators -> higher fan-out.
  • Prefix compression: keys in a leaf share a prefix; store it once.
  • Deduplication (PostgreSQL 13+): a leaf item with many TIDs for one key value instead of one item per TID.
  • Bulk loading: sort the data (module 08 external merge sort), fill leaves left-to-right at the fill factor, build internal levels bottom-up. O(n) after the sort, perfectly packed. This is CREATE INDEX and Berkeley DB's DB_BULK loading.
  • Bottom-up deletion / vacuum: deleted keys are first marked dead, physically removed later when the page needs space, so a delete does not immediately cause merges.
  • Siblings are not always merged on underflow: PostgreSQL never merges; it deletes a page only when it becomes completely empty (and leaves a tombstone until no scan can still be pointing at it). Underflow merging is textbook; "delete empty pages lazily" is practice.

docs.title: 2.10 Why not a hash index?
docs.text: Hash: O(1) point lookup, no range scans, no ordering, no prefix matches, rehash cost, poor locality for sequential keys. B+tree: O(log n) with tiny constants, range scans, ORDER BY for free, prefix and LIKE 'abc%' matches, min/max in O(log n), excellent locality for sequential keys. In PostgreSQL a B-tree index is the default for a reason; hash indexes are for equality-only on wide keys. The same reasoning applies in memory: std::map (ordered) versus std::unordered_map (not).

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: Files: code/m11_avl.cpp (AVL tree with unique_ptr, insert and erase with all four rotation cases, height field maintenance, invariant validation, differential test against std::set, height bound check), code/m11_bplus_tree.cpp (in-memory B+tree templated on key, value and max keys per node: search, insert with leaf and internal splits, erase with borrow and merge, range scan, a Cursor class with seek/next/valid, invariant validator, differential test against std::map with random operations, and a printout of the tree shape for a small fan-out so you can see splits happen).

docs.title: B+tree node and insert (key parts)
docs.text:
template <typename K, typename V, std::size_t kMaxKeys = 4>
class BPlusTree {
    struct Node {
        bool leaf;
        std::vector<K> keys;                              // sorted
        std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> children;     // internal: keys.size() + 1
        std::vector<V> values;                            // leaf: keys.size()
        Node* next = nullptr;                             // leaf chain (right sibling)
    };
    struct Split { K separator; std::unique_ptr<Node> right; };   // result of an overflow

    std::optional<Split> insert_rec(Node* n, const K& key, const V& value, bool& inserted) {
        if (n->leaf) {
            auto pos = std::lower_bound(n->keys.begin(), n->keys.end(), key);
            std::size_t i = pos - n->keys.begin();
            if (pos != n->keys.end() && *pos == key) { n->values[i] = value; inserted = false; return std::nullopt; }
            n->keys.insert(pos, key);
            n->values.insert(n->values.begin() + i, value);
            inserted = true;
            if (n->keys.size() <= kMaxKeys) return std::nullopt;
            return split_leaf(n);
        }
        std::size_t i = std::upper_bound(n->keys.begin(), n->keys.end(), key) - n->keys.begin();  // child index
        auto s = insert_rec(n->children[i].get(), key, value, inserted);
        if (!s) return std::nullopt;
        n->keys.insert(n->keys.begin() + i, std::move(s->separator));     // new separator at i
        n->children.insert(n->children.begin() + i + 1, std::move(s->right));
        if (n->keys.size() <= kMaxKeys) return std::nullopt;
        return split_internal(n);
    }

    Split split_leaf(Node* n) {
        std::size_t mid = n->keys.size() / 2;
        auto right = std::make_unique<Node>(); right->leaf = true;
        right->keys.assign(n->keys.begin() + mid, n->keys.end());
        right->values.assign(n->values.begin() + mid, n->values.end());
        n->keys.resize(mid); n->values.resize(mid);
        right->next = n->next; n->next = right.get();                     // link into the chain
        return {right->keys.front(), std::move(right)};                   // COPY first key up
    }
    Split split_internal(Node* n) {
        std::size_t mid = n->keys.size() / 2;
        K sep = n->keys[mid];                                             // MOVES up: not kept below
        auto right = std::make_unique<Node>(); right->leaf = false;
        right->keys.assign(n->keys.begin() + mid + 1, n->keys.end());
        for (std::size_t j = mid + 1; j < n->children.size(); ++j) right->children.push_back(std::move(n->children[j]));
        n->keys.resize(mid); n->children.resize(mid + 1);
        return {sep, std::move(right)};
    }

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
class Cursor {
    const Node* leaf_ = nullptr; std::size_t pos_ = 0;
public:
    bool valid() const { return leaf_ && pos_ < leaf_->keys.size(); }
    const K& key() const { return leaf_->keys[pos_]; }
    const V& value() const { return leaf_->values[pos_]; }
    void next() {                                   // DB_NEXT
        if (!valid()) return;
        if (++pos_ >= leaf_->keys.size()) { leaf_ = leaf_->next; pos_ = 0; }   // hop to the sibling
    }
};
Cursor seek(const K& key) const {                   // DB_SET_RANGE: first key >= key
    const Node* n = root_.get();
    while (!n->leaf) n = n->children[std::upper_bound(n->keys.begin(), n->keys.end(), key) - n->keys.begin()].get();
    std::size_t pos = std::lower_bound(n->keys.begin(), n->keys.end(), key) - n->keys.begin();
    Cursor c(n, pos);
    if (pos == n->keys.size()) c.next();            // landed past the end of this leaf
    return c;
}

A range scan [lo, hi) is for (auto c = t.seek(lo); c.valid() && c.key() < hi; c.next()).

docs.title: 4.1 A PostgreSQL B-tree page, byte by byte
docs.text:
offset 0    PageHeaderData (24 bytes): LSN of last WAL record that touched the page, checksum,
            flags, pd_lower (end of line pointer array), pd_upper (start of item data),
            pd_special (start of special space)
offset 24   ItemIdData[] line pointers, 4 bytes each: (offset, flags, length). Items are
            addressed by line pointer number, so items can move within the page without
            changing their identity.
   ...      free space
pd_upper    IndexTuples packed from the end backwards. Each: ItemPointerData t_tid (6 bytes:
            block number + offset -> heap row, or child block for internal pages), t_info
            (2 bytes: size + flags), then the key datum(s), aligned.
pd_special  BTPageOpaqueData (16 bytes): btpo_prev, btpo_next (sibling block numbers),
            btpo_level (0 = leaf), btpo_flags (leaf/root/half-dead/...), btpo_cycleid.

The high key (first item on every non-rightmost page) is the upper bound of the page's key range: a reader checks it to decide whether to move right (B-link). Search within a page is binary search over the line pointer array (_bt_binsrch), comparing keys via the operator class's comparison function — so a text index costs a strcoll per comparison, which is why collation choice affects index speed.

docs.title: 4.2 Buffer pool and I/O
docs.text: Pages live on disk and are cached in a buffer pool (shared_buffers, Berkeley DB DB_ENV->set_cachesize). A lookup descends through pages that are usually cached (root, level 2) to a leaf that may not be: one random read, 100 us on SSD, 10 ms on spinning disk. A range scan reads consecutive leaves; if the index was built in one go they are physically sequential and the OS read-ahead helps; after years of splits they are scattered — "index fragmentation", fixed by REINDEX. Modifications are written to the WAL first (so a split is atomic across crashes), then the dirty page is written back later by the checkpointer. A split touches 3 pages (left, right, parent) and logs all three.

docs.title: 4.3 Why B+trees beat binary trees in RAM too
docs.text: A std::map with 10^7 entries: ~23 levels, each a cache miss on a 48-byte node: ~23 misses per lookup. A B+tree with 64-byte nodes holding 7 keys (one cache line each): log_7(10^7) ~ 8 levels, 8 misses. With 4 KB nodes: 3 levels, but each node's binary search touches ~log2(500) ~ 9 lines, several of which are prefetchable; ~12 misses. Measured, in-memory B+trees (Google's absl::btree_map, which uses 256-byte nodes) are 2 to 4x faster than std::map for lookups and use half the memory. absl::btree_map is a drop-in replacement for std::map except that iterators are invalidated by insert/erase (keys move within nodes). If an interviewer asks "how would you speed up std::map", this is the answer, with the iterator caveat.

docs.title: 4.4 Split cost and the "sequential insert" hot spot
docs.text: Sequential keys (auto-increment ids, timestamps) always insert into the rightmost leaf. Good: that leaf is always cached; only one leaf is being written; bulk inserts are almost O(1) each. Bad: that one page is a contention point under many concurrent writers (every writer wants the write latch on the same page) — the "rightmost leaf hot spot". PostgreSQL's fast path helps the latency; some systems (e.g. Oracle's reverse-key indexes) scatter inserts on purpose, trading range-scan locality for write concurrency. Random keys (UUID v4) have the opposite profile: no hot spot, but every insert touches a random leaf (cache miss, possible disk read, random write), and leaf pages end up ~70% full on average because splits happen everywhere.

docs.title: 4.5 Berkeley DB specifics you can speak to
docs.text: DB_BTREE access method, default page size 4 KB (or the filesystem block size), configurable with DB->set_pagesize up to 64 KB. Keys and data are both stored in leaf pages (B+tree); overflow pages hold items larger than a quarter of a page. Internal pages store the first key of each child (no suffix truncation by default). Duplicates go in on-page duplicate sets or off-page duplicate trees (DB_DUP, DB_DUPSORT). DB->set_bt_compare installs a comparison function — your migration engine would have had to match the exact comparison semantics to read keys in the right order, or ordering would differ from the source. Cursors (DB->cursor, DBC->get with DB_FIRST/DB_NEXT/DB_SET_RANGE) hold a page lock while positioned, so an open cursor blocks concurrent writers to that page; DB_READ_COMMITTED degree-2 isolation releases locks as the cursor moves. Statistics (DB->stat) report the tree height (bt_levels), page fill, and overflow pages — the first things to check when a Berkeley DB store is slow.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Choosing the key order. A composite index on (account_id, txn_date) supports WHERE account_id = ? AND txn_date BETWEEN ? AND ? as one range scan on the leaf chain. (txn_date, account_id) does not — the account rows are scattered across the date range. "Equality columns first, then the range column" is the rule, and it falls directly out of how the leaf chain is ordered.
  • Covering indexes. If the index leaf contains every column the query needs (INCLUDE in PostgreSQL), the scan never touches the heap: index-only scan. The leaf chain is the result set.
  • Index bloat. Deletes leave dead items; splits leave half-empty pages. An index that was 2 GB at build grows to 6 GB over a year of churn with the same row count. pgstattuple or bt_index_check to measure; REINDEX CONCURRENTLY to rebuild. Watch for it when "the same query got slower and nothing changed".
  • Monitoring a B-tree store. Height (should be stable), pages per level, average fill, cache hit ratio on the buffer pool, number of splits per second (a sudden rise means a new insert pattern), long-held cursors (blocking writers).
  • Migration lesson. Reading a source B-tree with a cursor in key order and inserting into a destination in that order is the optimal pattern for both sides: sequential leaf reads on the source, rightmost-leaf appends on the destination. If the destination has a different key order (different comparator, different collation, or a distributed system that hashes the key like YugabyteDB does by default for its primary index), the inserts become random and throughput can drop 10x. When you describe your migration engine, this is the detail that shows you understood what you were doing: key order, cursor semantics, and batch size versus lock hold time.
  • 3 AM story (typical). Writes stall every few seconds. The buffer pool is full of dirty index pages; the checkpointer is writing them out and the WAL volume is 5x normal. Cause: a new feature inserts UUID v4 keys into a large index, so every insert dirties a random leaf page. Fix: switch to a time-ordered key (UUID v7, or a bigint sequence), or move the UUID to a non-indexed column with a hash index for equality. Understanding "random key = random leaf = random I/O" is what gets you from symptom to cause.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Draw by hand the B+tree with max 3 keys per node after inserting 1..10 in order. Then after inserting 10..1 in reverse order. Done when both drawings have all leaves at the same depth and you can point to each separator's origin (which split copied it up).
  2. (easy) Compute the fan-out and height for an index on a 16-byte UUID key with 8 KB pages and 10^9 rows, using the PostgreSQL item layout from section 2.6. Done when you have items per page, leaf page count, height, and approximate index size in GB.
  3. (medium) In m11_avl.cpp, insert 1..1 000 000 in order and print the height. Compare with the bound 1.44 log2(n + 2). Then count rotations performed. Done when you can explain why sorted insertion into an AVL tree produces the minimum possible number of rotations per insert (about 1 every other insert).
