docs.text: Counting problems explode fast: the number of ways can exceed 2^63 for modest inputs. Interviews often say "return the answer modulo 10^9 + 7". Apply the modulus at every addition (dp[x] = (dp[x] + dp[x - c]) % MOD), keep values in int64_t so that one addition of two values below MOD never overflows, and remember that % of a negative number is negative in C++.

docs.title: 4.6 DP in systems you know
docs.text:
• Query optimisers: PostgreSQL's standard join planner is a DP over subsets of relations (System R style): the best plan for joining {A, B, C} is built from the best plans for its subsets. That is bitmask DP, exponential in the number of tables, which is why PostgreSQL switches to the genetic optimiser (GEQO) at geqo_threshold (12 by default) relations.
  • diff and version control: edit distance / LCS on lines (Myers' algorithm in git and GNU diff).
  • TCP and networking: not DP, but the Viterbi algorithm in modems and Wi-Fi decoders is DP over a trellis (best path through states over time).
  • Fuzzy matching of customer names in banking KYC and deduplication: Levenshtein (or Jaro-Winkler) distance between names, usually with a cut-off so the DP can stop early when the minimum in a row exceeds the threshold.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Fuzzy name matching with a threshold. "Is RAJESH KUMAR the same person as RAJESH KUMMAR?" Full Levenshtein over millions of pairs is O(n m) each. With a threshold k, only cells within k of the diagonal can matter (banded DP: O(k n)), and you stop as soon as every cell in a row exceeds k. Index first (trigram index, pg_trgm in PostgreSQL) to get candidates, then run the DP only on those.
  • Fee and limit optimisation. "Split a payment across instruments to minimise fees under a daily limit" is a knapsack variant. Amounts in paise make the capacity huge; scale the amounts (e.g. to rupees) when the precision allows, or switch to a different formulation. Pseudo-polynomial complexity bites when the capacity is a currency amount.
  • Pitfall: the hidden O(n) in a transition. s.substr(j, i - j) inside a word-break loop allocates and copies; the "O(n^2)" DP becomes O(n^3) with allocations. Use std::string_view for lookups (C++20 heterogeneous lookup in unordered_set, or a trie — module 15).
  • Pitfall: -1 as "not computed" when -1 is a legal answer. Use std::optional, a separate bool computed[], or a sentinel outside the answer range.
  • Pitfall: answer is not dp[n-1]. For "ending at i" states (LIS, maximum subarray), the answer is the max over all i.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Min cost climbing stairs: cost[i] to step on stair i, you may start at 0 or 1 and climb 1 or 2. Write all four rungs. Done when [10,15,20] -> 15 and [1,100,1,1,1,100,1,1,100,1] -> 6, and all rungs agree on 1000 random inputs of length <= 20.
  2. (easy) Maximum subarray (Kadane) restated as DP: dp[i] = best sum ending at i. Done when you can explain why Kadane is a rolled DP and the answer is a max over i.
  3. (medium) Longest palindromic substring with the interval DP dp[i][j], then with "expand around centre". Done when "babad" -> "bab" or "aba", "cbbd" -> "bb", and you can state O(n^2) time for both and O(n^2) vs O(1) space.
  4. (medium) Target sum: assign + or - to each number to reach target; count the ways. Done when [1,1,1,1,1], 3 -> 5 and you can show the reduction to subset sum (sum + target) / 2, including the parity and negative checks.
  5. (hard) Edit distance with a threshold k: return the distance if <= k, otherwise -1, in O(k * n) time using a band around the diagonal and early exit. Done when it agrees with the full DP on 10 000 random pairs of length <= 50 for k = 3.
  6. (hard) Russian doll envelopes ([w, h] pairs, nest strictly in both dimensions): reduce to LIS in O(n log n). Done when [[5,4],[6,4],[6,7],[2,3]] -> 3 and you can explain why sorting by width ascending and height descending for equal widths is required.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do you recognise that a problem is DP? It asks for a count, an optimum or feasibility; choices are made step by step and constrain later choices; the plain recursion recomputes the same subproblems (overlapping subproblems); and the best answer is built from best answers to smaller inputs (optimal substructure). A greedy counterexample is a strong hint.

Q: Memoisation vs tabulation? Memoisation keeps the recursion and caches results: easy to derive, computes only reachable states, but has call overhead and a recursion-depth limit. Tabulation fills a table in dependency order: no recursion, predictable memory access, and enables rolling arrays. Same time complexity.

Q: Why does the 0/1 knapsack one-row loop go downward? dp[c - w] must still hold the value from before this item was considered; iterating capacity downward guarantees that, so each item is used at most once. Iterating upward reads values that already include the current item, which gives the unbounded knapsack.

Q: Coin change: why does loop order change "combinations" into "permutations"? With coins in the outer loop, each amount is built by adding coins in a fixed coin order, so each multiset is counted once. With amounts in the outer loop, every coin can be the last one added at every amount, so different orders are counted separately.

Q: Give the LCS and edit distance recurrences and complexities. LCS: match -> dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Edit distance: match -> dp[i-1][j-1], else 1 + min(delete, insert, replace) with base cases i and j. Both O(n m) time; O(min(n, m)) space for the value with two rows.

Q: How does LIS in O(n log n) work? Maintain tails[k], the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1; it stays sorted. For each element, binary-search the first tail >= it and replace it, or append. The size of tails is the LIS length; reconstructing the sequence needs predecessor links.

Q: Is the knapsack DP polynomial? No, pseudo-polynomial: O(n C) is polynomial in the numeric value of C but exponential in its bit length. Knapsack is NP-hard; the DP is practical only when C is small enough to index an array.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• DP = recursion + remembering answers; needs optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.
  • Recognise it: count / min-max / feasible, step-by-step choices, greedy fails.
  • Ladder: state in one sentence -> recurrence + base cases -> memo -> table -> roll.
  • Time = number of states x work per state.
  • Climbing stairs, house robber, decode ways: dp[i] from dp[i-1], dp[i-2].
  • Coin change: min = 1 + min dp[x-c]; ways = coins outer (combinations) vs amounts outer (permutations).
  • 0/1 knapsack: one row, capacity downward; upward = unbounded. Pseudo-polynomial.
  • LCS and edit distance: dp[i][j] on prefixes, O(n m), two rows for the value.
  • LIS: O(n^2) "ending at i", or O(n log n) with tails + lower_bound.
  • Array beats hash map for memo; fill in memory order; watch overflow and use % MOD.

docs.title: 15. Tries and bit manipulation
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 04, 14

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A trie (say "try", from retrieval) is a tree for strings where each edge is one character. To store "app" and "apple" you walk a, p, p from the root, mark the node "a word ends here", then continue l, e and mark again. Words that share a prefix share the path. It is the structure behind the autocomplete box on your phone: type "ban", walk three edges, and every word below that node is a suggestion. A hash set can tell you "is bank a word?" just as fast, but it cannot answer "which words start with ban?" without scanning everything. A trie answers both in time proportional to the length of the word, no matter how many words are stored.

Bit manipulation is using the individual bits of an integer as data. A 64-bit integer is 64 yes/no flags you can test, set and combine in a single CPU instruction. You already do this in C with flag masks (O_RDONLY | O_CREAT) and permission bits. Interviews ask a small, fixed set of tricks: is this a power of two, count the set bits, find the number that appears once, list all subsets. Systems interviews go one step further: bitsets for "which of 10 million ids have I seen", bitmaps in allocators and databases, and why x & (x - 1) is everywhere.

The two topics meet in the binary trie: a trie over the bits of integers, which finds the maximum XOR of two numbers and is how IP routing tables do longest-prefix match.

docs.title: 2.1 Trie structure
docs.text:
insert: app, apple, ape, bank

            (root)
           /      \
          a        b
          |        |
          p        a
         / \       |
        e*  p*     n
            |      |
            l      k*
            |
            e*          * = a word ends here

Each node has:

  • children: one slot per possible next character. Options: a fixed array of 26 pointers (fastest, 208 bytes of pointers per node on 64-bit), a sorted small vector of (char, child) pairs, or a hash map (sparse, slow constant).
  • an end marker: bool is_end, or a counter end (how many copies of the word end here — needed for multiset semantics and for deletion).
  • optionally pass: how many words pass through this node — gives "count words with this prefix" in O(prefix length).

Operations, L = length of the word or prefix:

Operation Time Notes insert(w) O(L) creates at most L nodes search(w) O(L) walk, then check the end marker starts_with(p) O(L) walk only count_prefix(p) O(L) needs pass counts erase(w) O(L) decrement counts; free branches whose pass hits 0 autocomplete(p, k) O(L + size of the output subtree visited) DFS below the prefix node, children in order gives lexicographic output

Memory: O(total characters x alphabet size) for array children in the worst case. 100 000 English words average ~9 letters; with no sharing that is 900 000 nodes x ~216 bytes = ~190 MB. Real sharing helps a lot, but array-of-26 tries are memory-hungry. That is the main trade-off to state in an interview.

docs.title: 2.2 Trie vs hash set vs sorted array
docs.text:
Need Hash set Sorted vector + binary search Trie Exact lookup O(L) average O(L log n) O(L) All words with prefix p O(n L) scan O(L log n) to find the range, then output O(L) to find, then output Count with prefix O(n L) two binary searches: O(L log n) O(L) with pass Memory low lowest high Ordered iteration no yes yes (DFS)

The sorted vector is underrated: lower_bound(p) and lower_bound(p + '\x7f') (or a "prefix successor") bound the range of words with prefix p, and the data is a contiguous array. If the dictionary is static, a sorted array often beats a pointer trie on real hardware. The trie wins when the set changes, when you need per-node data (counts, "best suggestion below here"), or when you walk the text character by character against many patterns at once (word search II, replace words, Aho-Corasick).

docs.title: 2.3 Prefix problems that want a trie
docs.text:
• Implement trie / prefix tree: insert, search, starts_with.
  • Replace words: replace each word by its shortest root in a dictionary — walk the word in the trie and stop at the first end marker.
  • Word search II: find all dictionary words in a letter grid. Put the dictionary in a trie and DFS the grid walking the trie in parallel; prune when the current path is not a prefix. Searching each word separately is far slower.
  • Autocomplete / search suggestions: prefix walk, then DFS for the first k words. Store the top suggestions at each node if queries dominate.
  • Longest common prefix: walk from the root while the node has exactly one child and is not an end. (Without a trie: sort, compare only the first and last words.)
  • Maximum XOR of two numbers: binary trie (2.7).

docs.title: 2.4 Bit operations you must know cold
docs.text:
On unsigned integers (always do bit work on unsigned types — see 4.1):

Expression Meaning Example (x = 0b101100) (x >> i) & 1 test bit i bit 2 -> 1 x \| (1u << i) set bit i x & ~(1u << i) clear bit i x ^ (1u << i) toggle bit i x & (x - 1) clear the lowest set bit 0b101000 x & -x (or x & (~x + 1)) isolate the lowest set bit 0b000100 x != 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0 x is a power of two x \| (x + 1) set the lowest clear bit 0b101101 (x & mask) == mask all bits of mask set

XOR facts: a ^ a = 0, a ^ 0 = a, XOR is commutative and associative. So XOR-ing a list in which every value appears twice except one leaves that one ("single number"). XOR-ing 0..n with the array leaves the missing number.

Counting set bits (popcount):

  • loop over 32 bits: O(32);
  • Kernighan: for (; x; x &= x - 1) ++c; — O(number of set bits);
  • __builtin_popcount / __builtin_popcountll (GCC, Clang), std::bitset<N>::count(), or std::popcount in C++20 — a single POPCNT instruction when compiled with -mpopcnt or -march=native, a table/bit-twiddling sequence otherwise.

Related builtins: __builtin_ctz (count trailing zeros = index of the lowest set bit), __builtin_clz (count leading zeros; 31 - clz(x) = floor(log2 x)). Both are undefined for x == 0 — check first. C++20 gives std::countr_zero, std::countl_zero, std::bit_width, std::has_single_bit, which are defined for 0.

docs.title: 2.5 Subsets as masks
docs.text:
n items, mask from 0 to 2^n - 1: bit i set means item i is in the subset. This replaces the backtracking subset generator of module 07 for n <= ~20.

for (std::uint32_t mask = 0; mask < (1u << n); ++mask)
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        if (mask & (1u << i)) { /* item i is in this subset */ }

All submasks of m: for (s = m; ; s = (s - 1) & m) { ...; if (s == 0) break; }. Iterating submasks of every mask costs 3^n in total, not 4^n — a known bound worth quoting.

Bitmask DP: state = (set of items used so far, last item). Travelling salesman over n cities: dp[mask][v] = cheapest path from city 0 visiting exactly mask, ending at v; O(2^n n^2). n = 16 is about 16 million states x 16 — fine; n = 30 is hopeless.

Gray code: g(i) = i ^ (i >> 1); consecutive values differ in one bit. Used in rotary encoders and to enumerate subsets by toggling one element at a time.

docs.title: 2.6 Bitsets
docs.text:
std::bitset<N> is N bits packed into machine words with a fixed compile-time N: set, reset, test, count, &, |, ^, <<, >>, any, none. Operations on whole bitsets work a word (64 bits) at a time, so intersecting two sets of 1 million flags is ~15 600 word ANDs.

For a runtime size, std::vector<bool> is a specialised, bit-packed vector — but its operator[] returns a proxy object, not a bool&, so auto& b = v[i] does not compile and it is not a real container. Many codebases avoid it; use std::vector<char> when you want bytes, or a small hand-written dynamic bitset (in m15_bit_tricks.cpp) when you want bits and word-level operations. boost::dynamic_bitset exists too.

Classic uses: Sieve of Eratosthenes (one bit per number), "seen" sets over dense integer ids, Bloom filters (k hash functions setting k bits; false positives, no false negatives), allocation bitmaps (which pages/blocks/slots are free — find the first zero bit with ctz(~word)), and subset DP where the DP row itself is a bitset (dp |= dp << w solves subset sum for all sums at once, 64 sums per instruction).

docs.title: 2.7 Binary trie: maximum XOR of two numbers
docs.text: Insert every number's bits from bit 31 down to bit 0 into a trie with two children per node. For a query x, walk from the top bit and at each level try to go to the child with the opposite bit (that bit of the XOR becomes 1); if it does not exist, take the same bit. A 1 in bit k outweighs all lower bits combined (2^k > 2^k - 1), so greedy from the top is optimal. O(32 n) total. The same structure, keyed by IP address bits, is a routing table's longest-prefix match (production routers use compressed variants — Patricia/radix tries).

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Files:

  • code/m15_trie.cpp — a 26-way pointer trie with insert, search, starts_with, count_prefix, erase (frees unused branches) and lexicographic autocomplete; an index-based trie with all nodes in one std::vector; longest common prefix; replace words; maximum XOR with a binary trie; a 20 000-operation differential test against std::multiset<std::string>.
  • code/m15_bit_tricks.cpp — test/set/clear/toggle, lowest set bit, power of two, three popcounts, counting bits 0..n, single number I and II, missing number, reverse bits, subset masks, submask enumeration, Gray code, a std::bitset sieve, a dynamic bitset with count, &= and next, and bitmask-DP TSP.

docs.title: 3.1 Trie with counts (key parts)
docs.text:
class Trie {
    struct Node {
        std::array<std::unique_ptr<Node>, 26> next{};
        int pass = 0;                     // words passing through this node
        int end = 0;                      // words ending here
    };
    Node root_;
public:
    void insert(std::string_view w) {
        Node* n = &root_;
        ++n->pass;
        for (char ch : w) {
            auto& child = n->next[ch - 'a'];
            if (!child) child = std::make_unique<Node>();
            n = child.get();
            ++n->pass;
        }
        ++n->end;
    }
    bool erase(std::string_view w) {
        if (!search(w)) return false;
        Node* n = &root_;
        --n->pass;
        for (char ch : w) {
            auto& child = n->next[ch - 'a'];
            if (--child->pass == 0) { child.reset(); return true; }   // frees the whole branch
            n = child.get();
        }
        --n->end;
        return true;
    }
    // search / starts_with / count_prefix all use the same walk(prefix) helper.
};

docs.title: 3.2 Index trie: one allocation, 4-byte links
docs.text:
class IndexTrie {
    struct Node { std::array<std::int32_t, 26> next{}; bool end = false; };
    std::vector<Node> nodes_{1};                   // node 0 = root; 0 also means "no child"
public:
    void insert(std::string_view w) {
        std::int32_t n = 0;
        for (char ch : w) {
            std::int32_t c = nodes_[n].next[ch - 'a'];
            if (c == 0) {
                c = static_cast<std::int32_t>(nodes_.size());
                nodes_.emplace_back();             // may reallocate: do not hold a Node& across this
                nodes_[n].next[ch - 'a'] = c;
            }
            n = c;
        }
        nodes_[n].end = true;
    }
};

The comment on emplace_back is the bug everyone writes once: Node& cur = nodes_[n]; then nodes_.emplace_back() reallocates and cur dangles. Indices survive reallocation; references and pointers do not.

docs.title: 3.3 Bit tricks (key parts)
docs.text:
constexpr std::uint32_t clear_lowest(std::uint32_t x) { return x & (x - 1); }
constexpr bool is_pow2(std::uint64_t x) { return x != 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0; }

int popcount_kernighan(std::uint32_t x) { int c = 0; for (; x; x &= x - 1) ++c; return c; }

std::vector<int> count_bits(int n) {               // a one-line DP
    std::vector<int> b(n + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) b[i] = b[i >> 1] + (i & 1);
    return b;
}

int single_number(const std::vector<int>& a) { int x = 0; for (int v : a) x ^= v; return x; }

int single_number_ii(const std::vector<int>& a) {  // others appear three times
    std::uint32_t result = 0;
    for (int b = 0; b < 32; ++b) {
        int cnt = 0;
        for (int v : a) cnt += static_cast<int>((static_cast<std::uint32_t>(v) >> b) & 1u);
        if (cnt % 3) result |= (1u << b);
    }
    return static_cast<int>(result);
}

docs.title: 3.4 Maximum XOR (key parts)
docs.text:
std::uint32_t best = 0;
for (each x after the first) {
    std::int32_t n = 0; std::uint32_t cur = 0;
    for (int b = 31; b >= 0; --b) {
        int want = static_cast<int>(((x >> b) & 1u) ^ 1u);       // the opposite bit
        if (t[n][want] != 0) { cur |= (1u << b); n = t[n][want]; }
        else n = t[n][want ^ 1];
    }
    best = std::max(best, cur);
    add(x);
}

docs.title: 4.1 Signed shifts and undefined behaviour
docs.text:
In C++17: left-shifting a negative value, or shifting a 1 into or past the sign bit of a signed type, is undefined behaviour; right-shifting a negative value is implementation-defined (GCC does an arithmetic shift). Shifting by >= the width of the type is undefined for any type: 1u << 32 is UB, and on x86 the hardware masks the count to 5 bits, so it often yields 1, not 0 — a classic silent bug. 1 << 31 with an int is UB in C++17. Rules: use unsigned types (std::uint32_t, std::uint64_t), write 1u or std::uint64_t{1}, and never shift by a count that might equal the width. C++20 defines signed integers as two's complement and makes more of this well-defined, but the shift-count rule remains.

Your C background helps here: these are the same rules as C. -fsanitize=undefined catches bad shifts at run time.

docs.title: 4.2 What the compiler does with bit idioms
docs.text: GCC and Clang recognise idioms: x & (x - 1) compiles to BLSR with BMI1 (-mbmi/-march=haswell or newer), x & -x to BLSI, __builtin_ctz to TZCNT/BSF, popcount to POPCNT. Without -march, the default x86-64 baseline has no POPCNT, so __builtin_popcount becomes a library call or a ~12-instruction bit-twiddling sequence. For bit-heavy hot loops, compile with -march=native (or a known minimum like x86-64-v2, which includes POPCNT) and check the assembly on Compiler Explorer.

docs.title: 4.3 Trie memory and cache behaviour
docs.text:
A pointer trie touches one new node per character, and each node is a separate allocation somewhere on the heap: one likely cache miss per character on a cold trie. Lookup of a 10-character word in a large trie is ~10 misses — often slower than hashing the 10 bytes and taking one or two misses in a hash table. Ways production systems fix this:

  • Index trie / arena: nodes in one vector, 4-byte indices instead of 8-byte pointers (IndexTrie above). Nodes created together sit together.
  • Radix (Patricia) tree: collapse chains of single-child nodes into one edge labelled with a string. The Linux kernel uses radix trees (now the XArray) for the page cache index; routing tables use compressed tries for longest-prefix match.
  • Adaptive radix tree (ART): nodes of size 4, 16, 48 or 256 chosen by fan-out; used in main-memory databases (HyPer, DuckDB's indexes).
  • Double-array tries and FSTs (finite state transducers): read-only, extremely compact — Lucene stores its term dictionary as an FST.
  • Sorted array + binary search for static dictionaries (2.2).

docs.title: 4.4 Bitmaps in the systems you know
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL: the visibility map and free space map are per-page bitmaps/maps; a bitmap heap scan (EXPLAIN: Bitmap Index Scan -> Bitmap Heap Scan) builds a bitmap of matching pages from one or more indexes, ANDs/ORs them (BitmapAnd, BitmapOr), and then reads the heap in physical order. The null bitmap in each tuple header has one bit per nullable column.
  • File systems: ext4 tracks free blocks and inodes with bitmaps; finding a free block is "find first zero bit".
  • Linux: cpumask_t is a bitset of CPUs; find_first_bit / find_next_bit use ctz per word — exactly DynBitset::next in the code.
  • Bloom filters: LSM-tree databases (RocksDB, Cassandra, YugabyteDB's DocDB which is built on RocksDB) keep a Bloom filter per SSTable so a point lookup skips files that certainly do not contain the key. Your YugabyteDB target uses this on every read.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Dedup of ids in a batch. "Which of the 10 million account numbers appeared in today's file?" If ids are dense (or can be mapped to dense ranks), a bitset of 10 million bits is 1.25 MB and fits in L2/L3 cache; std::unordered_set<int> of the same is hundreds of MB and orders of magnitude slower. Counting the overlap of two days is popcount(a & b).
  • Flags in protocol headers. Your RPC protocol probably has a flags byte. Define the bits as constexpr std::uint8_t kCompressed = 1u << 0; etc., test with &, never with == (other bits may be set), and document reserved bits as must-be-zero so future versions can use them.
  • Endianness. Bit tricks are on values, not on bytes, so they are endian-independent; the moment you memcpy an integer into a network buffer, convert with htonl/htobe64. Mixing the two is a classic interop bug between a Windows client and a Linux server — both little endian, so it hides until something big-endian appears or someone byte-swaps twice.
  • Autocomplete for account search. A teller types the first digits of an account number or letters of a name: a trie or a sorted array of keys with lower_bound gives the candidates. For a database-backed version, a B+tree index (module 11) already supports prefix queries via LIKE 'abc%' with the text_pattern_ops operator class in PostgreSQL.
  • Pitfall: std::bitset<10000000> on the stack. 1.25 MB on a 1 MB Windows thread stack crashes. Make it static, a member of a heap-allocated object, or use a vector-backed bitset.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Implement is_pow2, popcount_kernighan, lowest_set and clear_lowest and check them against std::bitset<32>::count() on 10^6 random values. Done when all agree and you can say what x & (x - 1) does in one sentence.
  2. (easy) Implement the 26-way trie with insert, search, starts_with without looking at the code. Done when insert("apple"); search("app") == false; starts_with("app") == true; insert("app"); search("app") == true.
  3. (medium) Search suggestions: given a product list and a search word, return after each typed character up to three lexicographically smallest products with that prefix. Solve it with a trie and again with a sorted vector and lower_bound. Done when both agree on the LeetCode example (mobile, mouse, moneypot, monitor, mousepad, query mouse).
  4. (medium) Single number III: two numbers appear once, every other twice; find both in O(n) time and O(1) space. Done when [1,2,1,3,2,5] -> {3,5} and you can explain why diff & -diff splits the array into two groups.
  5. (hard) Word search II: find all dictionary words in a letter grid using a trie-guided DFS, removing words from the trie as they are found and pruning empty branches. Done when a 12 x 12 grid with a 10 000-word dictionary runs in under 100 ms and the result equals searching each word separately.
  6. (hard) Subset sum with a bitset: std::bitset<100001> dp; dp[0] = 1; for x: dp |= dp << x;. Done when it agrees with the boolean knapsack from module 14 on random inputs and you can explain the 64x speed-up.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When would you use a trie instead of a hash set? When you need prefix queries (autocomplete, count with prefix, shortest root), ordered iteration, or to match many patterns while walking text once. A hash set is better for exact lookups only: less memory and fewer cache misses. For a static dictionary, a sorted array with binary search also handles prefix ranges well.

Q: What are the time and space costs of a trie? Insert, search and prefix walk are O(L) in the word length, independent of how many words are stored. Space is O(total characters x alphabet) with array children, which is large; maps or sorted child lists, radix compression, or index-based arenas reduce it.

Q: What does x & (x - 1) do, and where is it used? It clears the lowest set bit, because subtracting 1 flips that bit and all zeros below it. Uses: power-of-two test (x && !(x & (x - 1))), Kernighan's popcount, and iterating set bits of a mask.

Q: Find the number that appears once when every other appears twice. XOR all of them: pairs cancel because a ^ a = 0, and XOR is associative and commutative. O(n) time, O(1) space. For "every other appears three times", count each bit position mod 3.

Q: Why should bit manipulation use unsigned types in C++? Shifting into or out of the sign bit of a signed integer is undefined or implementation-defined in C++17, and >> on negative values is arithmetic in practice. Unsigned arithmetic is fully defined (modulo 2^N). Shifting by the type width or more is undefined for both.

Q: How do you find the maximum XOR of any two numbers in an array? Insert numbers bit by bit from the top into a binary trie; for each number walk greedily toward the opposite bit at every level. A high bit outweighs all lower bits, so greedy is optimal. O(32 n) time.

Q: What is a bitset good for and what does std::vector<bool> get wrong? Dense sets of small integers: one bit per element and set operations a word at a time — sieves, seen-sets, allocation bitmaps, Bloom filters, subset-sum DP. std::vector<bool> is bit-packed but returns a proxy instead of bool&, so it does not behave like a normal container; prefer std::bitset, std::vector<char>, or a dedicated dynamic bitset.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Trie: one edge per character, end marker per node; insert/search/prefix in O(L).
  • pass counts give count-with-prefix; end counts give multiset semantics and safe erase.
  • Trie vs hash vs sorted array: prefix queries vs memory vs cache behaviour.
  • Index-based tries (one vector, int32 links) beat pointer tries; never hold a reference across emplace_back.
  • x & (x - 1) clears the lowest bit; x & -x isolates it; power of two = one bit set.
  • Popcount: Kernighan, __builtin_popcount, std::bitset::count; compile with -march for POPCNT.
  • XOR cancels pairs: single number, missing number.
  • Masks enumerate subsets (n <= 20); bitmask DP is O(2^n x n^2).
  • Unsigned types for bit work; never shift by >= the width.
  • Bitsets: 64 flags per word; PostgreSQL bitmap scans, ext4 free maps, Bloom filters.

docs.title: 16. Interview coding playbook
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours to read, then ~6 hours a week of practice for 10 weeks Prerequisites: 01-15 (the schedule tells you which module each week depends on)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A coding interview is not a test of whether you can solve the problem. It is a 45-minute sample of what working with you is like. The interviewer watches how you understand a vague request, how you choose an approach, how you write code someone else can read, and how you check your own work. A candidate who silently produces a perfect answer in 20 minutes often scores lower than one who talks through a clean, tested solution in 35, because the interviewer had nothing to write in the feedback form.

So you need two things: a method you run every time, the same way a pilot runs a checklist, and pattern recognition, so that within two minutes of reading a problem you know which of about fifteen standard shapes it is. This module gives you the method (six steps), the script for talking while you code, a cheat sheet that maps problem signals to patterns, a 10-week practice schedule from 2026-10-06 to 2026-12-14 aligned with modules 02-15, a fixed 45-minute practice block, and a procedure for when you are stuck.

You already have an advantage most candidates lack: production C. You think about memory, ownership, edge cases and failure. The playbook makes sure the interviewer sees that.

docs.title: 2.1 The six-step method
docs.text:
Budget for a 45-minute round with one medium problem (the clock starts after introductions, so you usually have ~40 minutes):

Step Minutes What you do What you say 1. Clarify 0-4 Restate the problem. Ask about input size, value ranges, duplicates, empty input, sortedness, what to return when there is no answer, whether input may be modified. "Let me restate to be sure... Can n be zero? Can values be negative? Is the array sorted?" 2. Examples 4-7 Write one normal example and one or two edge cases in a comment block. Work the normal one by hand. "For [2,7,11,15], target 9, the answer is indices 0 and 1. Edge case: no pair, I will return an empty vector." 3. Brute force 7-10 State the obvious solution and its complexity. Do not code it unless asked or stuck. "Brute force: every pair, O(n^2) time, O(1) space. With n up to 10^5 that is 10^10 — too slow." 4. Optimise 10-15 Find the bottleneck in the brute force and name the pattern that removes it. State the final complexity. Get agreement before coding. "The inner loop searches for target - x. A hash map makes that O(1), so O(n) time, O(n) space. Shall I code that?" 5. Code 15-32 Write clean, compilable C++. Narrate intent, not syntax. Helper functions with good names. "I iterate once; for each value I check whether its complement was seen, then record the value." 6. Test 32-40 Trace your example through the code line by line, with variable values. Then the edge cases. Fix bugs calmly. State final complexity. "i=0: x=2, need 7, not in map, store 2->0. i=1: x=7, need 2, found at 0, return {0,1}."

The last 5 minutes are for the interviewer's follow-ups ("what if the data does not fit in memory?", "what if it is a stream?") and your questions.

Rules that make the method work:

  • Never start coding before step 4 is agreed. Coding the wrong approach for 15 minutes is the most common way to fail a round you could have passed.
  • Size the input before choosing the algorithm. n <= 20: exponential is fine (2^n backtracking, bitmask). n <= 10^3: O(n^2) fine. n <= 10^5-10^6: you need O(n log n) or O(n). n up to 10^9 or more: O(log n) or math. A modern CPU does roughly 10^8-10^9 simple operations per second; that is the arithmetic behind these limits.
  • Write the test cases before the code (step 2). They catch misunderstandings early and you reuse them in step 6.
  • Trace, do not reread. Reading your code you see what you meant; tracing with concrete values you see what you wrote.

docs.title: 2.2 Talking while coding
docs.text:
Silence is the enemy, but so is narrating syntax ("now I write for int i equals zero..."). Narrate decisions and invariants:

  • Why this structure: "I use unordered_map<int,int> from value to index because I need O(1) lookup by value."
  • The invariant: "Everything left of slow is already deduplicated." "The window [left, right] always has at most k distinct characters."
  • Edge cases as you pass them: "If the list is empty, head is null and the loop does not run, so we return null — fine."
  • Trade-offs you are skipping: "I take the string by const&; a string_view would also work."
  • Explicit TODOs instead of silent gaps: "I will assume valid input here and come back to validation if we have time."

When you need to think, say so: "Let me think for thirty seconds about the boundary condition." Then think. Interviewers accept silence that has been announced.

When the interviewer gives a hint, take it, say thanks, and say what it changes: "Right, if it is sorted I can use two pointers instead of the map, which brings space to O(1)."

C++-specific habits that read as senior:

  • const& for input containers, return by value (move/NRVO make it free).
  • std::size_t or explicit casts for sizes; mention signed/unsigned when comparing.
  • auto [a, b] = ... structured bindings, range-for, std::vector::reserve when the size is known.
  • Say the complexity of the STL calls you use: std::sort O(n log n), unordered_map average O(1) worst O(n), std::map O(log n), std::priority_queue push/pop O(log n), lower_bound on a vector O(log n) — but on a std::set use the member set.lower_bound, not the free function (which is O(n) on non-random-access iterators).
  • No using namespace std; and no #include <bits/stdc++.h> in an interview for a C++ role; some interviewers read it as competitive-programming habits.
  • Overflow: mention int vs int64_t when sums or products can be large; mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2.

docs.title: 2.3 Pattern cheat sheet
docs.text:
Read the problem, find the signal, pick the pattern. Module numbers point at the full treatment.

Signal in the problem Pattern Typical complexity Module Sorted array, find pair/triplet with a sum; remove duplicates in place; palindrome Two pointers O(n) 02 Longest/shortest contiguous subarray or
