docs.title: 2.4 The 10-week problem schedule
docs.text:
Weeks run Tuesday to Monday starting Tuesday 2026-10-06, the same weeks as ../00_START_HERE.md. Each week has a pattern focus aligned with the course modules you study in parallel, and 10-12 problems: the first half warm-up level (easy or easy-medium), the rest medium, one stretch problem. Names are the standard LeetCode titles so you can find them. Re-solve every problem you fail on day +3 and day +10 (see 2.5).

Week 1 — 2026-10-06 to 10-12. Arrays, two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums (modules 01, 02). Two Sum; Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock; Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array; Squares of a Sorted Array; Two Sum II (sorted input); Container With Most Water; 3Sum; Maximum Subarray; Product of Array Except Self; Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters; Minimum Size Subarray Sum. Stretch: Trapping Rain Water.

Week 2 — 10-13 to 10-19. Hashing and strings (modules 03, 04). Valid Anagram; Contains Duplicate; Valid Palindrome; Group Anagrams; Top K Frequent Elements; Longest Consecutive Sequence; Subarray Sum Equals K; Longest Repeating Character Replacement; Permutation in String; String to Integer (atoi); Encode and Decode Strings. Stretch: Minimum Window Substring.

Week 3 — 10-20 to 10-26. Linked lists, stacks, queues (modules 05, 06). Reverse Linked List; Merge Two Sorted Lists; Linked List Cycle; Middle of the Linked List; Remove Nth Node From End of List; Reorder List; Valid Parentheses; Min Stack; Implement Queue using Stacks; Daily Temperatures; Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation; LRU Cache. Stretch: Largest Rectangle in Histogram.

Week 4 — 10-27 to 11-02. Recursion, backtracking, sorting, intervals (modules 07, 08). Subsets; Permutations; Combination Sum; Generate Parentheses; Letter Combinations of a Phone Number; Word Search; Merge Intervals; Insert Interval; Non-overlapping Intervals; Sort Colors; Kth Largest Element in an Array (quickselect). Stretch: N-Queens.

Week 5 — 11-03 to 11-09. Binary search and heaps (modules 09, 12). Binary Search; Search Insert Position; Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array; Search in Rotated Sorted Array; Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array; Koko Eating Bananas; Time Based Key-Value Store; K Closest Points to Origin; Last Stone Weight; Merge k Sorted Lists; Task Scheduler. Stretch: Find Median from Data Stream.

Week 6 — 11-10 to 11-16. Trees and BSTs (modules 10, 11). Maximum Depth of Binary Tree; Invert Binary Tree; Same Tree; Subtree of Another Tree; Binary Tree Level Order Traversal; Binary Tree Right Side View; Validate Binary Search Tree; Kth Smallest Element in a BST; Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST; Diameter of Binary Tree; Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal. Stretch: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.

Week 7 — 11-17 to 11-23. Graphs (module 13). Flood Fill; Number of Islands; Max Area of Island; Rotting Oranges; Clone Graph; Course Schedule; Course Schedule II; Pacific Atlantic Water Flow; Number of Provinces; Redundant Connection; Network Delay Time. Stretch: Word Ladder.

Week 8 — 11-24 to 11-30. Dynamic programming I: 1D (module 14). Climbing Stairs; Min Cost Climbing Stairs; House Robber; House Robber II; Coin Change; Coin Change II; Decode Ways; Word Break; Longest Increasing Subsequence; Maximum Product Subarray; Partition Equal Subset Sum. Stretch: Russian Doll Envelopes.

Week 9 — 12-01 to 12-07. DP II (2D) plus tries and bits (modules 14, 15). Unique Paths; Minimum Path Sum; Longest Common Subsequence; Edit Distance; Longest Palindromic Substring; Target Sum; Implement Trie (Prefix Tree); Design Add and Search Words Data Structure; Single Number; Counting Bits; Missing Number. Stretch: Word Search II.

Week 10 — 12-08 to 12-14. Mixed timed mocks. No new pattern. Four full mock rounds of two problems each (one medium, one medium-hard) under a 45-minute timer, chosen at random from weeks 1-9 problems you have not re-solved recently, plus these new mixed ones: Meeting Rooms II; Cheapest Flights Within K Stops; Accounts Merge; Design Hit Counter; Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums; Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix; Snapshot Array; Alien Dictionary. If possible do at least two mocks with another person (a friend, a peer-interview site) — talking to a real listener is a different skill from talking to yourself.

Weekly rhythm (about 6 hours): five weekday 45-minute blocks (one new problem each plus review), and one weekend session of three blocks (two new problems and one re-solve). Read the matching module on the weekend before the week starts.

docs.title: 2.5 The 45-minute practice block
docs.text:
Practise exactly like the real thing, or the practice does not transfer.

00:00  Timer on. Read the problem once. Write the clarifying questions you would ask
       as comments, and answer them from the problem statement / constraints.
00:04  Examples: one normal, two edge cases, in a comment.
00:07  Brute force + complexity, one line in a comment.
00:10  Optimised approach + complexity in two lines. Name the pattern.
00:15  Code. Out loud (yes, alone at your desk). No autocomplete, no compiling yet.
00:32  Trace your example by hand. Then compile and run the tests.
00:40  Fix. Submit.
00:42  Log it (below). Stop at 00:45 whatever the state.

If you are not done at 00:45, read a good solution, close it, and write it from memory the same day. Then it goes into the re-solve queue.

The log is a plain file, one line per attempt:

date        problem                       pattern          result   time  note
2026-10-07  Longest Substring Without...  sliding window   solved   28m   forgot to shrink with while
2026-10-08  Product of Array Except Self  prefix products  hint     45m   missed the two-pass idea

Re-solve queue: anything marked hint or failed comes back on day +3 and day +10. A problem is "owned" when you solve it cold in under 25 minutes, twice. By week 10 the log tells you exactly which patterns are weak; spend the mock week on those.

Write each solution in a local file with a tiny test harness (section 3) and compile it with the course flags. Platform judges hide your compiler warnings; your interviewer will not.

docs.title: 2.6 When you are stuck
docs.text:
Use this ladder in order. Say each step out loud in a real interview.

  1. Re-read the constraints. n tells you the target complexity (2.1). "Sorted", "distinct", "positive", "at most k" are hints you skipped.
  2. Do a small example by hand, slowly, and watch what you do. Your hands often perform the algorithm before your head names it.
  3. Write the brute force and ask: what is it recomputing? What is it searching for in the inner loop? Repeated work -> memo/DP or prefix sums; searching -> hash map, binary search or heap; scanning a window -> sliding window.
  4. Walk the cheat sheet (2.3) top to bottom and ask "could this be X?" for each row.
  5. Change the problem: solve it for sorted input, for k = 1, for a tree that is a list, for n = 2. Then generalise.
  6. Think backwards from the answer: "if I knew the answer for the first n-1 elements, how would I get it for n?" — that is a DP or an inductive invariant.
  7. Ask for a hint after ~5 minutes of no progress, framed with what you have: "I have an O(n^2) approach using X; I suspect the bottleneck is Y; is the direction of using a heap reasonable?" A specific question costs you very little; ten minutes of silence costs you the round.
  8. If time is short, code the brute force cleanly and test it. A correct, clean O(n^2) with a clear explanation of how to improve it beats a broken O(n).

When you have a bug in step 6 and cannot see it: re-trace with the smallest failing input, print (or say) the variables at each loop iteration, and check the usual suspects — off-by-one in loop bounds, the empty input, int overflow, a reference to a vector element across a push_back, a missing break, modifying a container while iterating it.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
No new program file for this module: every pattern's reference code is in code/m02_* to code/m15_*. What you need is a practice template. Save this as practice.cpp (outside the course folder), copy it for every problem, and compile with the course flags. The check helper prints the failing case instead of only aborting, which saves time in a 45-minute block.

// practice.cpp — copy per problem.
// Build: g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fsanitize=address,undefined practice.cpp -o p && ./p

#include <algorithm>
#include <cassert>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

// Clarify:   n in [2, 1e5], values may be negative, exactly one answer?  -> return {} if none
// Examples:  [2,7,11,15], 9 -> {0,1}     [3,3], 6 -> {0,1}     [1,2], 7 -> {}
// Brute:     all pairs, O(n^2) time, O(1) space
// Optimised: hash map value -> index, O(n) time, O(n) space

std::vector<int> solve(const std::vector<int>& a, int target) {
    std::unordered_map<int, int> seen;                   // value -> index
    seen.reserve(a.size());
    for (int i = 0; i < static_cast<int>(a.size()); ++i) {
        auto it = seen.find(target - a[i]);
        if (it != seen.end()) return {it->second, i};
        seen.emplace(a[i], i);                           // emplace keeps the FIRST index of a duplicate
    }
    return {};
}

std::vector<int> brute(const std::vector<int>& a, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < static_cast<int>(a.size()); ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < static_cast<int>(a.size()); ++j)
            if (a[i] + a[j] == target) return {i, j};
    return {};
}

template <typename T>
void check(const T& got, const T& want, const char* what) {
    if (got == want) return;
    std::cerr << "FAIL: " << what << '\n';
    std::abort();
}

int main() {
    check(solve({2, 7, 11, 15}, 9), std::vector<int>{0, 1}, "example 1");
    check(solve({3, 3}, 6), std::vector<int>{0, 1}, "duplicates");
    check(solve({1, 2}, 7), std::vector<int>{}, "no answer");

    // Differential test against the brute force on small random inputs: the fastest way to
    // find the bug you cannot see. Compare only "found / not found" plus validity when the
    // problem allows several correct answers.
    std::mt19937 rng(1);
    for (int t = 0; t < 10000; ++t) {
        std::vector<int> a(2 + rng() % 8);
        for (int& x : a) x = static_cast<int>(rng() % 21) - 10;
        int target = static_cast<int>(rng() % 21) - 10;
        auto s = solve(a, target), b = brute(a, target);
        check(s.empty(), b.empty(), "found vs not found");
        if (!s.empty()) check(a[s[0]] + a[s[1]], target, "valid pair");
    }
    std::cout << "ok\n";
}

Two habits this template builds: writing the clarify/examples/brute/optimised notes before code (steps 1-4 of the method), and keeping a brute-force oracle for differential testing, exactly as the course's code files do.

docs.title: 4.1 What the interviewer writes down
docs.text:
Most companies use a rubric with four or five dimensions, scored separately. The names vary; the content is stable:

  • Problem solving: did you clarify, consider alternatives, reach an efficient approach with little help, and justify complexity?
  • Coding: is the code correct, readable, idiomatic for the language, with sensible names and structure? Did you handle edge cases?
  • Verification: did you test without being asked, find your own bugs, and reason about correctness?
  • Communication: could the interviewer follow your thinking throughout? Did you respond well to hints?
  • (for senior and systems roles) Depth: can you discuss memory layout, concurrency, scale, and production trade-offs when the follow-up comes?

The six steps map one-to-one onto these. Steps 1-4 are problem solving, step 5 is coding, step 6 is verification, and talking throughout is communication. The "Under the hood" sections of modules 01-15 are your material for depth.

docs.title: 4.2 Follow-ups for C++ systems roles
docs.text:
After the algorithm works, expect one of these. Prepare a two-sentence answer for each:

  • "What if the input does not fit in memory?" External sort and k-way merge (modules 08, 12), streaming with bounded state (top-k heap), partition by hash and process each part (04).
  • "What if it is a stream?" Sliding windows, heaps, reservoir sampling, count-min sketch.
  • "Make it thread-safe." Mutex around the structure, then sharding by key (module 05, LRU), then read-mostly structures; name the contention point. See 04_Concurrency.
  • "What is the cache behaviour?" Contiguous vs node-based (vector vs list, open addressing vs chaining, B+tree vs BST, CSR vs adjacency lists).
  • "What happens with 10^9 elements?" int overflow, size_t indices, memory footprint per element, recursion depth.
  • "How would you test this in production code?" Unit tests on edge cases, differential tests against a brute-force oracle, sanitizers, fuzzing.

docs.title: 4.3 Why practising out loud matters
docs.text: Explaining while you code uses working memory; so does holding the algorithm in your head. The first few times you do both, your coding speed drops noticeably and you make bugs you would not make silently. That cost goes away with practice — but only with practice out loud. This is the main reason silent LeetCode grinding transfers poorly to interviews, and why the practice block insists on narration even when alone.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
The playbook's habits are the same habits that make a good production engineer, which is the point you want the interviewer to notice.

  • Clarify = requirements. "Can the account number be empty? Can amounts be negative (reversals)?" is the same question you ask before writing a migration step. Mention a real example when it fits: "In our core-banking server, a reversal is a negative amount, so I would not assume non-negative input without asking."
  • Brute force first = a correct baseline. In the BDB -> YugabyteDB migration, the first version that is obviously correct (row by row) is the oracle for the fast batched version. Same as the differential test in the practice template.
  • Test = reconciliation. Row counts and checksums after a migration are step 6 at scale.
  • Stories for the behavioural part. Prepare three, each two minutes, in situation -> action -> result form, each with a data-structure or algorithm angle: a performance bug you fixed (an O(n^2) loop, a lock held too long, a missing index), a crash you debugged from a dump (stack overflow from recursion is a good one), and a design decision with a trade-off (hash vs B-tree lookup, ring buffer for socket I/O).
  • Pitfall: over-engineering in the interview. Templates, custom allocators and class hierarchies for a 30-line function cost time and read as poor judgement. Write a function. Mention the production version in one sentence.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run the practice template as given. Then break solve on purpose (use operator[] instead of emplace, which overwrites the first index of a duplicate) and see whether the tests catch it. Done when you understand which test would catch it and add one if none does.
  2. (easy) Write the pattern cheat sheet (2.3) from memory on one page. Done when you can fill in at least 20 of the 27 rows with signal, pattern and complexity in 15 minutes.
  3. (medium) Do three 45-minute blocks on week 1 problems out loud while recording audio on your phone. Listen back. Done when you have written down three things you said that were noise ("so, um, now I...") and three decisions you did not say aloud but should have.
  4. (medium) Take one problem you solved and answer the systems follow-ups in 4.2 for it in writing, two sentences each. Done when each answer names a concrete technique and a module.
  5. (hard) Week 10 mock: two problems, 45 minutes, with another person as interviewer using the rubric in 4.1. Done when you have their scores on each dimension and one concrete thing to change for the next mock.
  6. (hard) Keep the practice log for all ten weeks. Done when on 2026-12-14 the log has at least 110 entries, every hint/failed entry has two re-solve entries, and you can name your two weakest patterns with evidence from the log.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
These are meta-questions interviewers actually ask, plus the ones you should be ready to answer about your own process.

Q: How do you approach a problem you have never seen? Clarify inputs and edge cases, work examples by hand, state a brute force and its complexity, find the bottleneck and the pattern that removes it, agree on the approach, code it while explaining, then trace tests. I size the input first because it tells me the complexity I need.

Q: Your solution is O(n^2). Can you do better? Name what the inner loop does — searching, recomputing, or scanning a window — and replace it with a hash map, prefix sums/DP, binary search or heap, or a sliding window. State the new time and space, and the trade-off (usually memory for time).

Q: How do you test your code? A normal case traced by hand, then edge cases: empty, single element, all equal, negatives, maximum size (overflow, recursion depth), no answer. Off the whiteboard: differential tests against a brute-force oracle and sanitizers.

Q: What would you change for production? Input validation and error handling, int64_t where values can grow, iterative instead of recursive for deep inputs, reserve and avoid needless copies, thread-safety if shared, and tests. Name the one that matters most for this problem.

Q: What do you do when you are stuck? Re-read constraints, do a tiny example by hand, write the brute force and ask what it repeats, try simpler versions of the problem, and ask a specific question if I am still stuck after a few minutes, explaining what I have.

Q: Why C++ for this interview? It is the language of the role and my strongest after C; it gives me the standard containers and algorithms with known complexities, and I can reason about memory layout and cost precisely — which is the part of the follow-up discussion I enjoy most.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Six steps: clarify, examples, brute force, optimise (agree before coding), code, test.
  • Budget: ~15 minutes to an agreed approach, ~17 to code, ~8 to test.
  • Input size picks the complexity: 20 -> exponential, 10^3 -> n^2, 10^5-10^6 -> n log n or n.
  • Narrate decisions and invariants, not syntax; announce thinking pauses.
  • Pattern cheat sheet: signal -> pattern -> complexity -> module.
  • Schedule: 10 weeks from 2026-10-06, one pattern family per week, mocks in week 10.
  • Practice in 45-minute blocks, out loud, logged; re-solve misses on day +3 and +10.
  • Stuck ladder: constraints, small example, brute force bottleneck, cheat sheet, simplify, backwards, specific hint request, clean brute force.
  • Keep a brute-force oracle and differential tests, as in production.

docs.title: Exercises — 03. Data Structures and Algorithms
docs.text:
Every exercise from modules 01-16 in one place. The full "done when" criteria are in each module's section 6; this list gives the difficulty and a hint you can read after you have been stuck for 10 minutes. Build everything with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread on WSL, and add -fsanitize=address,undefined while developing.

Suggested use: do every easy exercise, at least four of the six per module overall, and the hard ones for modules 04, 05, 11, 12 and 13 — those back up resume lines directly.

docs.title: 01. Complexity and how to think
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 1.1 Big-O of five snippets (a)-(e) easy (a) the inner 10 is a constant; (b) count how many times you can multiply by 3 before reaching n; (c) sum of n + (n-1) + ... ; (d) inner loop runs log i times; (e) write T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 and expand the tree. 1.2 Run m01_vector_growth.cpp, switch +1024 growth to x2, count copies easy With doubling, the copies form the series n/2 + n/4 + ... < n. With a fixed increment, each regrowth copies everything so far: quadratic. 1.3 Prove growth factor 1.5 gives amortised copy cost <= 3 per push medium At the last growth you copy at most n elements; the earlier growths copy n/1.5, n/1.5^2, ...; sum the geometric series 1 / (1 - 1/1.5) = 3. 1.4 Row-major vs column-major at 1024^2 and 8192^2 medium A 1024-int row is 4 KB; an 8192-int row is 32 KB. Compare those with your L1d (often 32-48 KB) and L2 from lscpu; column-major touches one new cache line per element once rows stop fitting. 1.5 Count pairs summing to target in a sorted vector, O(n) and O(n^2) hard Two pointers from both ends; when the sum is too big move right left, too small move left right. With duplicates, count runs of equal values and multiply (or use n*(n-1)/2 when both pointers hit the same value).

docs.title: 02. Arrays, vectors, two pointers
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 2.1 Rewrite array.cpp with std::vector<int> easy std::find returns an iterator; compare with end(). erase(it) shifts for you. 2.2 Squares of a sorted array, O(n) easy The largest square is at one of the two ends. Fill the output from the back. 2.3 Longest subarray with at most two distinct values medium Variable window: grow right, update a count map; while the map has more than 2 keys, shrink left and erase keys whose count hits 0. 2.4 Product of array except self, no division medium Pass 1: out[i] = product of everything left of i. Pass 2 from the right with a running suffix product multiplied in. 2.5 Three Sum, unique triplets medium Sort; for each i skip a[i] == a[i-1]; two pointers on the rest; after a hit, skip equal values on both sides. 2.6 Maximum sum circular subarray hard Either the best subarray does not wrap (Kadane) or it wraps (total minus the minimum subarray). If all are negative, the second formula gives 0 (empty) — return the Kadane answer.

docs.title: 03. Strings
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 3.1 is_palindrome(std::string_view) ignoring non-alphanumerics and case easy Two pointers; skip with std::isalnum(static_cast<unsigned char>(c)); compare with std::tolower. The cast matters for chars above 127. 3.2 split into string_views, skipping empty tokens easy Use find(delim, start); substr on a string_view returns a string_view (no allocation). 3.3 my_atoi with clamping medium Skip spaces, read sign, then digits; before r = r*10 + d check r > (INT_MAX - d) / 10. 3.4 Longest repeating character replacement medium Window valid while len - maxFreq <= k. maxFreq only needs to grow: a stale max can only keep the window the same size, never report a wrong larger answer. 3.5 Rabin-Karp with two moduli, compare to std::string::find hard Rolling hash: remove s[i] * base^(m-1), multiply by base, add the new char; keep everything in uint64_t mod a prime < 2^31 to avoid overflow. Verify each hit with memcmp. 3.6 KMP failure table and search hard fail[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of p[0..i] that is also a suffix. For "abcabd": 0 0 0 1 2 0. On mismatch, fall back to fail[j-1], never move the text pointer back.

docs.title: 04. Hashing and hash tables
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 4.1 Word frequencies, top 10, 10 MB file easy ++counts[word] is fine for counting; use find for read-only lookups. Top 10 with std::partial_sort or a heap of size 10 (module 12). 4.2 std::hash<Point> with hash_combine, 1M points easy seed ^= h + 0x9e3779b9 + (seed << 6) + (seed >> 2). Specialise std::hash in namespace std and provide operator==. 4.3 Add operator[], destructor, move ctor, size() to the chained map medium operator[] = find or insert a default value and return a reference. The move constructor steals the bucket vector and leaves the source empty but valid. 4.4 Subarray sums divisible by k medium Count prefix sums by ((sum % k) + k) % k; each earlier prefix with the same remainder forms a valid subarray. Start with count[0] = 1. 4.5 Backward-shift deletion in linear probing hard After emptying slot i, scan forward; move an element at j back into i if its home slot is not cyclically in (i, j]. Stop at the first empty slot. 4.6 Benchmark lookups: unordered_map, open addressing, sorted vector hard Use random keys and random query order; prevent the optimiser from deleting work by summing results. Explain crossovers with cache lines touched per lookup vs data size vs L2/L3 size.

docs.title: 05. Linked lists
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 5.1 Reverse a list, raw pointers and unique_ptr easy Three variables: prev, cur, next. With unique_ptr, move cur->next out first, then move prev into cur->next. 5.2 Remove all nodes with a value, one pass, dummy head easy Node dummy{0, head}; Node* p = &dummy; while (p->next) if (p->next->val == v) unlink else p = p->next; — do not advance after unlinking. 5.3 Cycle start index medium Floyd: after slow and fast meet, restart one pointer at head; move both one step; they meet at the cycle start (a = kL - b). 5.4 Merge k sorted lists pairwise and with a heap medium Pairwise in rounds (1+2, 3+4, ...) is O(n log k) too; merging one-by-one into an accumulator is O(nk). The heap holds (value, list index). 5.5 Hand-made LRU with your own doubly linked nodes hard Sentinel head and tail nodes remove all null checks. get = unlink + push front; put on a full cache evicts tail->prev and erases it from the map. 5.6 Sharded thread-safe LRU hard std::array<Shard, N>, each with its own std::mutex, list and map; pick the shard by hash(key) % N; never hold two shard locks at once.

docs.title: 06. Stacks, queues, deques
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 6.1 MinStack easy Push (value, min so far) pairs, or keep a second stack of minimums. 6.2 Queue with two stacks, prove O(n) total easy Pop from out; when out is empty, move everything from in. Each element is moved at most once: amortised O(1). 6.3 RingBuffer::peek(i) and read_contiguous() medium Index (head + i) & mask (or % cap). Two spans: [head, min(head + size, cap)) and the wrapped part from 0. 6.4 Trapping rain water, stack then two pointers medium Stack of indices with decreasing heights; on a taller bar pop the bottom and add (min(left, right) - bottom) * width. Two pointers: move the side with the smaller max. 6.5 Maximal rectangle of 1s hard Build a histogram per row (h[c] = row[c] ? h[c] + 1 : 0), then run largest-rectangle-in-histogram on each. 6.6 Lock-free SPSC ring buffer hard Producer writes the slot then stores tail with release; consumer loads tail with acquire before reading. Put head and tail on separate 64-byte cache lines.

docs.title: 07. Recursion and backtracking
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 7.1 Recursive sum, max, reverse by index easy sum(i) = v[i] + sum(i + 1); reverse swaps v[i] and v[n-1-i] and recurses on i + 1 until the middle. Depth n or n/2. 7.2 All binary strings of length n easy Choose '0' first, then '1', recursing on the next position; the order is lexicographic because '0' < '1' at every level. 7.3 Combinations C(n, k) with pruning medium Loop i from start to n - (k - cur.size()) — the upper bound is the prune. 7.4 Valid parentheses for n pairs medium Add ( if open < n; add ) if close < open. Base case when the length is 2n. 7.5 Sudoku with fewest-candidates-first hard Keep row/column/box bitmasks; candidates = ~(row \| col \| box) & 0x1FF; pick the empty cell with the smallest popcount (module 15). 7.6 Iterative subsets with an explicit stack, lazily hard A subset of n items is an n-bit decision path; generate lazily with an iterator-like object holding the stack of (index, included?) frames rather than storing results.

docs.title: 08. Sorting
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 8.1 Insertion sort, count comparisons and shifts easy On sorted input the inner loop stops after one comparison: n - 1 comparisons, 0 shifts. 8.2 Merge sort with one scratch buffer easy Allocate the buffer once in a wrapper and pass it down; merge into the buffer, copy back (or alternate roles per level). Use <= when taking from the left to stay stable. 8.3 Make quicksort quadratic, then fix it medium First-element pivot on sorted input splits n into 0 and n - 1. Recurse on the smaller side and loop on the larger to keep stack depth O(log n). 8.4 Three-way partition quicksort medium Dutch national flag: lt, i, gt; elements equal to the pivot stay in the middle and are never recursed on. 8.5 Quickselect median of 10M ints hard Recurse (or loop) only into the side containing k; random pivot; expected work n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = 2n. 8.6 Two-pass external merge with fan-in limit hard Merge runs in groups of fan_in into longer runs, then merge those. Every pass reads and writes every block once.

docs.title: 09. Binary search and ordered data
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 9.1 Hand-written lower_bound / upper_bound easy Half-open [lo, hi); lower_bound moves lo = mid + 1 when a[mid] < t, upper_bound when a[mid] <= t. Return lo. 9.2 Count occurrences in O(log n) easy upper_bound - lower_bound. 9.3 Integer square root up to 10^18 medium Search on answer in [0, min(x, 2^32)]; test mid <= x / mid to avoid overflow. 9.4 Koko eating bananas medium Search the speed in [1, max pile]; hours at speed s = sum of (p + s - 1) / s; find the first s with hours <= h. 9.5 Minimum in rotated sorted array with duplicates hard Compare a[mid] with a[hi]: greater -> go right, smaller -> go left (keep mid), equal -> --hi (this is the O(n) worst case). 9.6 B-tree node child index and leaf cursor start hard Child to descend = upper_bound(keys, t) index (keys equal to a separator live in the right child under the stated convention); leaf start for >= t = lower_bound.

docs.title: 10. Trees and BST
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 10.1 Pre-, in-, post-order on a sample tree easy Only the position of "visit" changes relative to the two recursive calls. 10.2 Max depth, node count, leaf count, sum easy Each is combine(f(left), f(right)) with a base case for null that returns 0. 10.3 BST delete, all three cases, validate medium Two children: copy the in-order successor's key (leftmost of the right subtree) into the node, then delete the successor from the right subtree. 10.4 Serialise / deserialise in pre-order with # medium Deserialise with a shared index into the token list: read a token, # -> null, else make the node and recurse left then right. 10.5 k-th smallest with subtree sizes hard size(left) == k - 1 -> this node; smaller -> go right with k - size(left) - 1; larger -> go left. Update sizes on the way down only if the insert/delete will succeed. 10.6 Sorted vs shuffled insert, BST vs std::map hard Sorted inserts make your BST a list: height n, so each search is O(n). Recursive insert will overflow the stack at 100 000 — use an iterative insert.

docs.title: 11. Balanced trees, B-trees and disk
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 11.1 Draw a B+tree (max 3 keys) after inserting 1..10 and 10..1 easy Leaf split: copy the first key of the new right leaf up; internal split: move the middle key up. Sequential inserts leave half-full leaves behind. 11.2 Fan-out, height and size for a UUID index easy Index tuple = 8-byte header + 16-byte key, plus a 4-byte line pointer, rounded to 8-byte alignment; divide usable page space by that. Height = ceil(log_fanout(leaf pages)) + 1. 11.3 AVL height and rotation count for sorted inserts medium Compare height with 1.44 log2(n + 2). Sorted inserts always unbalance the right spine in the same way; count single rotations. 11.4 prev() on the B+tree cursor medium Maintain prev in split_leaf (new right leaf's prev = old leaf; old right neighbour's prev = new leaf) and in merges. 11.5 Bulk loading from_sorted hard Pack leaves left to right to the fill factor, chain them, then build each internal level from the first key of each child until one node remains. 11.6 Simulated B-link search hard Split: create the right node with the high key, link it, then update the parent. A search that finds key > high_key follows the right link instead of failing.

docs.title: 12. Heaps and priority queues
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 12.1 Max-heap push/pop/top vs std::priority_queue; build vs n pushes easy Build = sift down from n/2 - 1 to 0. Compare at every pop with the reference. 12.2 k-th largest with a heap and with nth_element easy Min-heap of size k; answer = top. nth_element(v.begin(), v.begin() + k - 1, v.end(), std::greater<>()). 12.3 Median of a data stream medium Max-heap low half, min-heap high half; push into low, move low's top to high, rebalance so low has the extra element. 12.4 k closest points to the origin medium Max-heap of size k by squared distance (no sqrt); pop when it exceeds k, so the farthest of the current best k leaves. 12.5 Indexed heap with decrease_key and erase hard Maintain pos[id] on every swap — write one swap_nodes(i, j) helper that updates both. erase(i): swap with last, pop, then sift the moved element up or down. 12.6 Timer queue: lazy deletion vs indexed heap hard Lazy: store (deadline, conn, version); skip pops whose version is not the connection's current version. Track the max heap size to see the lazy version's growth.

docs.title: 13. Graphs: BFS, DFS and friends
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 13.1 Adjacency list and CSR, BFS on both easy CSR: count degrees into offsets[u+1], prefix-sum them, then fill targets using a copy of offsets as write cursors. 13.2 Flood fill, recursive and iterative; crash the recursive one easy If the new colour equals the old, return immediately (otherwise infinite loop). Iterative: std::vector<std::pair<int,int>> as a stack, recolour on push. 13.3 Minimum number of semesters (parallel course schedule) medium Kahn's algorithm processed layer by layer: each layer is one semester. If not every course is output, return -1. 13.4 Cheapest flights within k stops medium Bellman-Ford for k + 1 rounds; each round relaxes from a copy of the previous round's array so a path cannot use more than one extra edge per round. 13.5 Strongly connected components for deadlock cycles hard Kosaraju: DFS finish order on the graph, then DFS on the reversed graph in reverse finish order; each tree is an SCC. Tarjan: one DFS with index, lowlink and an on-stack flag. 13.6 Bidirectional word ladder hard Keep two frontier sets; always expand the smaller one; stop when a generated word is in the other frontier.

docs.title: 14. Dynamic programming
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 14.1 Min cost climbing stairs, all four rungs easy dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]); answer min(dp[n-1], dp[n-2]). Or define dp[i] = cost to reach step i (top is step n). 14.2 Kadane as DP easy dp[i] = max(a[i], dp[i-1] + a[i]) — either start fresh at i or extend. Rolling it into one variable gives Kadane. 14.3 Longest palindromic substring, DP and expand-around-centre medium dp[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] && (j - i < 2 \|\| dp[i+1][j-1]), filled by increasing length. Centres: 2n - 1 (each char and each gap). 14.4 Target sum (count +/- assignments) medium P - N = target and P + N = sum, so P = (sum + target) / 2. If that is odd or negative, the answer is 0. Count subsets summing to P with a downward 1D loop. 14.5 Edit distance with threshold k in O(k n) hard Only cells with abs(i - j) <= k can hold a value <= k; compute that band per row and stop when the row minimum exceeds k. If abs(n - m) > k, return -1 immediately. 14.6 Russian doll envelopes via LIS hard Sort by width ascending, and by height descending for equal widths, so two envelopes with the same width cannot both be in the increasing sequence; then LIS on heights with lower_bound.

docs.title: 15. Tries and bit manipulation
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 15.1 is_pow2, Kernighan popcount, lowest set bit, clear lowest easy Subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 and every 0 below it; AND with the original keeps everything above. 15.2 26-way trie from memory easy Node = std::array<std::unique_ptr<Node>, 26> + bool end. search and starts_with share one walk helper and differ only in checking end. 15.3 Search suggestions, trie and sorted vector medium Sorted vector: for each prefix, lower_bound(prefix) and take up to three entries that still start with the prefix. The start position only moves right as the prefix grows. 15.4 Single number III medium XOR everything to get a ^ b; its lowest set bit differs between a and b; partition the numbers by that bit and XOR each group. 15.5 Word search II with trie pruning hard DFS from each cell carrying the trie node; when you find a word, record it and clear its end flag; on the way back, delete child nodes that became empty so later searches skip them. 15.6 Subset sum with std::bitset shifts hard dp \|= dp << x adds x to every reachable sum at once, 64 sums per machine word. Answer: dp[target].

docs.title: 16. Interview coding playbook
docs.text: # Exercise Level Hint 16.1 Run the practice template; break it on purpose easy seen[a[i]] = i overwrites the first index of a duplicate; the [3,3] test still passes because the complement is found before the overwrite — think about which input would expose it, or decide it is harmless and say why. 16.2 Pattern cheat sheet from memory easy Group the rows by data structure (array, hash, list, stack, tree, heap, graph, DP, trie/bits) and rebuild each group. 16.3 Three recorded out-loud blocks medium Listen for silences longer than 20 seconds and for syntax narration; replace both with "the invariant is..." or "I am choosing X because...". 16.4 Systems follow-ups for one problem medium Use section 4.2's list: memory, stream, threads, cache, scale, testing. Each answer: technique + module reference. 16.5 Mock with a real interviewer and the rubric hard Give the interviewer the rubric from 4.1 before you start; ask for one score per dimension, not an overall impression. 16.6 Ten-week practice log hard Keep it in one text file you open every day; the re-solve dates (+3, +10) are written when you log the miss, so the schedule is never in your head.

docs.title: Interview questions — 03. Data Structures and Algorithms
docs.text: 40 questions with model answers, ordered from basic to senior. Say each answer out loud in under a minute. The module in brackets has the full explanation.

docs.title: Basics: complexity and arrays
docs.text:
1. What does O(n) actually mean? [01] An upper bound on how the cost grows with input size, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms: there is a constant c such that the cost is at most c * n for large n. It says nothing about the constant, so an O(n) algorithm with bad memory access can lose to an O(n log n) one at realistic sizes. Big-Theta is the tight bound; in interviews "O" is used loosely to mean the tight one.

2. What is amortised complexity? Use std::vector::push_back as the example. [01, 02] Amortised cost is the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations, not a probability. push_back is usually O(1) but occasionally reallocates and copies all n elements. With geometric growth (factor 2 in libstdc++, 1.5 in MSVC), the total copies over n pushes are n/2 + n/4 + ... < n, so the total is O(n) and each push is amortised O(1). A fixed increment (+1000) would make the total O(n^2).

3. Why do 1.5x and 2x growth factors both work, and why might 1.5x be preferred? [01] Any factor > 1 gives a geometric series, hence amortised O(1); a bigger factor means fewer copies but more wasted capacity. With factor < ~1.618 (the golden ratio), the sum of previously freed blocks can eventually be large enough to hold the next allocation, so an allocator can reuse that memory; with 2x it never can. That is the usual argument for 1.5x.

4. When does std::vector invalidate iterators, pointers and references? [02] Any reallocation (a push_back/insert/reserve that exceeds capacity) invalidates all of them. Without reallocation, insert and erase invalidate everything at or after the point of change. reserve up front and indices instead of pointers avoid the bug.

5. Two pointers vs sliding window — what is the difference? [02] Two pointers usually start at opposite ends of a sorted array and move toward each other based on a comparison (pair sum, palindrome). A sliding window has both pointers moving in the same direction, maintaining a contiguous range that satisfies a property, and works when the property is monotone (shrinking the window can only fix a violation). Both are O(n) because each pointer moves at most n times.

6. What is small string optimisation? [03] std::string stores short strings (up to 15 chars in libstdc++, 22 in libc++) inside the object itself instead of on the heap, so creating and copying them does not allocate. Longer strings allocate. It makes std::string 32 bytes in libstdc++ and means moving a short string is a copy.

docs.title: Hashing
docs.text:
7. How does std::unordered_map work internally? [04] An array of buckets; each element is a heap-allocated node in a singly linked list. libstdc++ links all nodes in one list and each bucket points to the node before its first element, which makes iteration O(n) and erase O(1). Lookup hashes the key, takes it modulo the bucket count (a prime in libstdc++), and walks that bucket's chain comparing keys. When size / bucket_count exceeds max_load_factor (1.0 by default) it rehashes into about twice as many buckets.

8. Chaining vs open addressing? [04] Chaining stores colliding elements in per-bucket lists: simple, tolerates load factor > 1, stable element addresses, but a pointer chase and an allocation per element. Open addressing stores elements in the array itself and probes (linear, quadratic, Robin Hood) on collision: no per-element allocation and far better cache behaviour, but needs load factor well below 1, tombstones or backward-shift for delete, and moves elements on rehash. Fast modern hash maps (Abseil's flat_hash_map, Folly's F14) are open addressing.

9. What is the worst case of a hash table and how can it be triggered? [04] O(n) per operation, when many keys land in the same bucket. It happens with a weak hash or an adversary who knows the hash function (hash-flooding attacks on web servers). Defences: a seeded, strong hash (SipHash), or capping chain length and switching to a tree (Java 8 HashMap converts long buckets to red-black trees).

10. Why does std::unordered_map iteration and lookup lose to a sorted vector at some sizes? [04, 09] Each node is a separate allocation, so lookup is hash + bucket array read + at least one pointer chase to a random address, and iteration follows pointers all over the heap. A sorted vector is contiguous; binary search touches log n cache lines but the first few levels stay cached, and iteration is sequential. For small or read-mostly data the vector often wins; for large data with frequent inserts the hash map wins.

docs.title: Linked lists, stacks, queues
docs.text:
11. When would you use a linked list over a vector? [05] When you need O(1) insertion and removal in the middle given a pointer to the node and stable element addresses — an LRU cache's recency list, intrusive lists in kernels, free lists in allocators. For almost everything else a vector wins because traversal is sequential and the prefetcher hides memory latency; a list costs a cache miss per node.

12. How do you detect a cycle in a linked list and find its start? [05] Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves one step, fast two; they meet inside the cycle if there is one. Then reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle start, because the distance from the head to the start equals the distance from the meeting point to the start modulo the cycle length. O(n) time, O(1) space.

13. Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. [05] A doubly linked list ordered by recency plus a hash map from key to list node. get looks up the node, moves it to the front, returns the value. put updates and moves an existing node, or inserts at the front and, if over capacity, evicts the tail and erases its key from the map. In C++, std::list plus unordered_map<Key, list::iterator> with splice for the move.

14. What is a ring buffer and where is it used? [06] A fixed-size array with head and tail indices that wrap around, giving an O(1) FIFO with no allocation. Using a power-of-two capacity lets you wrap with a mask instead of a modulo. Used for socket send/receive buffers, logging, audio, and lock-free single-producer single-consumer queues between threads.

15. What is a monotonic stack and what does it solve? [06] A stack kept in increasing or decreasing order: before pushing, pop everything that violates the order. Each element is pushed and popped once, so it is O(n) total. It answers "next greater or smaller element" for every position in one pass: daily temperatures, largest rectangle in a histogram, trapping rain water.

docs.title: Sorting and searching
docs.text:
16. What does std::sort actually do? [08] Introsort: quicksort with median-of-three pivots; if the recursion depth exceeds about 2 log2 n it switches that range to heapsort, guaranteeing O(n log n) worst case; and ranges below 16 elements are left unsorted and finished with one insertion-sort pass at the end. It is not stable; use std::stable_sort (merge sort, O(n) extra memory, O(n log^2 n) if it cannot allocate) when equal elements must keep their order.

17. Why is quicksort usually faster than merge sort and heapsort in practice? [08] Partitioning scans memory sequentially in place, so it is cache-friendly and has a small inner loop; merge sort needs an extra buffer and copies; heapsort jumps around the array (children at 2i) and has poor locality. The cost is a worst case of O(n^2) for bad pivots, which introsort removes.

18. What is a stable sort and when does it matter? [08] Stable means equal keys keep their original relative order. It matters when you sort by multiple keys in passes (sort by time, then stable-sort by account, and each account's entries stay in time order) and when the displayed order must be deterministic.

19. How do you sort data that does not fit in memory? [08] External merge sort: read chunks that fit in memory, sort each and write it as a run, then merge the runs with a k-way merge using a min-heap of run heads, streaming input and output in large blocks. Cost is about 2 * N * (number of passes) block I/Os; with enough fan-in it is two passes. This is what PostgreSQL does when a sort exceeds work_mem.

20. Write lower_bound without off-by-one errors — what is the invariant? [09] Use a half-open range [lo, hi) with the invariant "everything before lo is < target, everything at or after hi is >= target". While lo < hi, take mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if a[mid] < t set lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid. Return lo. upper_bound is the same with <=.

21. What is "binary search on the answer"? [09] When the question is "the minimum x such that condition(x) is true" and the condition is monotone (false, false, ..., true, true), binary-search x over its range and evaluate the condition at each mid. Examples: minimum eating speed, minimum ship capacity, integer square root. Cost: O(log range * cost of checking).

docs.title: Trees
docs.text:
22. Why does an unbalanced BST degrade to O(n), and what do balanced trees do about it? [10, 11] A BST's operations cost O(height); inserting sorted keys makes every new node the right child of the previous one, so height is n and the tree is a linked list. Balanced trees (AVL, red-black) detect imbalance after insert or delete and fix it with O(1) rotations per level, keeping height O(log n).

23. AVL vs red-black tree? [11] AVL keeps subtree heights within 1, so it is more strictly balanced (height <= 1.44 log2 n), giving slightly faster lookups but more rotations on updates. Red-black allows height up to 2 log2(n + 1) but needs at most two rotations per insert and three per delete, so updates are cheaper. std::map and std::set use red-black trees; so does the Linux CFS scheduler.

24. B+tree vs binary search tree — why do databases use B+trees? [11] A B+tree node is a whole page (8 KB in PostgreSQL) holding hundreds of keys, so the fan-out is in the hundreds and a billion keys need only 3-4 levels — 3-4 page reads instead of ~30 for a binary tree, which matters when each level is a disk read or cache miss. All values live in leaves, and leaves are linked, so a range scan is one descent plus a sequential walk. Splits and merges keep it balanced with all leaves at the same depth.

25. B-tree vs B+tree? [11] A B-tree stores values in internal nodes too, so some lookups end early, but internal nodes hold fewer keys (lower fan-out) and range scans must move up and down the tree. A B+tree keeps only separator keys in internal nodes (higher fan-out, shallower) and all records in a linked leaf level, which makes range scans and cursors simple. Databases and file systems almost always use B+trees.

26. What does "B-tree cursor traversal" mean in practice? [11] A cursor is a position in the leaf level: it remembers the current leaf page and slot. Positioning does one root-to-leaf descent (binary search inside each page); next moves to the next slot and follows the right-sibling link at the end of a page, without going back up the tree. Berkeley DB's DBC->get(DB_SET_RANGE) then DB_NEXT, and PostgreSQL's index scans, work this way; concurrent splits are handled with latch coupling or B-link right-links.

27. Why are B+trees good even in RAM? [11] Memory latency to DRAM is about 100 ns, so a tree's cost is dominated by cache misses per level. A binary tree of 10^7 nodes has ~23 levels, each a likely miss; a B+tree with 64-256-byte nodes has a handful of levels, each node read as a few adjacent cache lines that the prefetcher fetches together. That is why in-memory databases and absl::btree_map beat std::map.

docs.title: Heaps
docs.text:
28. What is a binary heap and what are its complexities? [12] A complete binary tree stored in an array (children of i at 2i+1 and 2i+2) where each parent is

= its children (max-heap). top is O(1); push sifts up and pop sifts down, both O(log n); building from n elements bottom-up is O(n). It is not sorted — only the root is guaranteed extreme.

29. Why is building a heap O(n)? [12] Sift down from the last internal node to the root. A node at height h moves at most h levels, and there are about n / 2^(h+1) nodes at height h; summing h * n / 2^(h+1) over all h converges to n. Most nodes are near the bottom and barely move.

30. How do you find the top k of a large stream? [12] Keep a min-heap of size k: for each element, if it is larger than the heap's minimum, replace the minimum. O(n log k) time, O(k) memory, single pass. If all data is in memory and order does not matter, std::nth_element gives O(n) average.

31. How would you implement timers for 50 000 connections in an event loop? [12] A min-heap keyed by deadline: the loop's poll timeout is top.deadline - now, and on wake it pops every expired timer. Resetting a timer on activity is done with lazy deletion (push a new entry, skip stale ones by version) or an indexed heap with decrease-key. For millions of coarse timers, a hierarchical timer wheel gives O(1) insert and cancel; the Linux kernel uses wheels.

docs.title: Graphs
docs.text:
32. BFS vs DFS — properties and uses? [13] Both visit every vertex and edge once: O(V + E). BFS uses a queue, explores by distance, and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; mark vertices when enqueued. DFS uses recursion or a stack and is the tool for reachability, cycle detection, topological sort and connected components; deep graphs need an explicit stack to avoid stack overflow.

33. How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph, and how is that used in databases? [13] DFS with three colours: white unvisited, grey on the current path, black finished; an edge to a grey vertex is a back edge, so there is a cycle. Alternatively, Kahn's topological sort fails to output every vertex. Databases detect deadlocks this way: PostgreSQL and Berkeley DB build a waits-for graph of transactions and search it for a cycle, then abort a victim.

34. Explain Dijkstra's algorithm and its limits. [13] Repeatedly take the unfinished vertex with the smallest tentative distance from a min-heap, finalise it, and relax its outgoing edges. With a binary heap it is O((V + E) log V); with lazy deletion the heap holds up to E entries. It requires non-negative weights, because it assumes a finalised distance cannot be improved later; with negative edges use Bellman-Ford (O(V E)), which also detects negative cycles.

35. What is union-find and why is it "almost constant time"? [13] A forest stored as a parent array: find follows parents to the root, unite links one root under another. Union by size keeps trees O(log n) tall, and path compression points every visited node at the root; together m operations cost O(m alpha(n)), where the inverse Ackermann function alpha is at most 4 for any realistic n. It is used for Kruskal's MST, dynamic connectivity, and grouping records that share identifiers.

docs.title: Dynamic programming, tries, bits
docs.text:
36. How do you recognise a DP problem, and how do you build the solution? [14] Signals: it asks for a count, a minimum/maximum or feasibility; choices are made step by step and restrict later choices; a greedy rule has a counterexample; and the brute-force recursion repeats subproblems. Build it as a ladder: define the state in one sentence, write the recurrence and base cases as a recursion, memoise it, convert to a table filled in dependency order, then keep only the rows the recurrence reads.

37. Explain 0/1 knapsack and why the one-row version iterates capacity downward. [14] dp[c] = best value with capacity c; for each item, dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - w] + v). Going downward means dp[c - w] still holds the value without the current item, so each item is used at most once; going upward lets the item be reused, which is the unbounded knapsack. It is O(n C): pseudo-polynomial, because C is a number, not an input size.

38. Give the edit distance recurrence and one production use. [14] dp[i][j] = edits to turn the first i chars of a into the first j of b; on a match take dp[i-1][j-1], otherwise 1 + the min of delete dp[i-1][j], insert dp[i][j-1] and replace dp[i-1][j-1]; base cases are i and j. O(n m) time, two rows of space for the value. It is used for fuzzy matching of customer names in deduplication and KYC, usually banded to a threshold k so it costs O(k n).

39. When is a trie better than a hash table, and what does it cost? [15] When you need prefix operations — autocomplete, count words with a prefix, shortest matching root — or many patterns matched in one pass over text. Lookups are O(L) in the key length regardless of the number of keys. The cost is memory (an array-of-26 node is over 200 bytes) and a cache miss per character; radix trees, index-based arenas or a sorted array mitigate it.

docs.title: Senior: cache effects and putting it together
docs.text: 40. Two O(n) loops — one over a std::vector<int>, one over a std::list<int> of the same size — differ by 10x or more. Explain. [01, 02, 05] The vector is contiguous: one 64-byte cache line holds 16 ints, and the hardware prefetcher detects the sequential pattern and loads lines before they are needed, so the loop runs at memory bandwidth. Each list node is a separate heap allocation, often scattered, and the next address is only known after loading the current node, so every step can be a full DRAM latency (~100 ns, typical) that the prefetcher cannot hide. Big-O counts operations, not cache misses; data layout — contiguous arrays, structure of arrays, B+trees over BSTs, open addressing over chaining, CSR over adjacency lists — is how you win the constant factor in systems code.

docs.title: 04_Concurrency — Multithreading and concurrency, C++17 and Win32, to production depth
What this course covers
docs.text:
You already run threads in production. Your application server creates Win32 threads, guards shared tables with CRITICAL_SECTION, waits on Events and Mutex handles, and serves loan-origination requests through a pooled request model. What you have not done yet is any of that in C++, and you have never had to explain why it works: what a data race really is, what the compiler and the CPU are allowed to reorder, what "acquire" and "release" mean, or how to prove a thread-pool shutdown cannot lose a task.

This course takes you from "I use locks and it has not crashed" to "I can design, explain and debug a concurrent server, in C++17 on Linux and in C on Win32, and I can defend every decision in a senior interview."

Every Win32 primitive you use today is mapped to its C++17 standard-library and POSIX equivalent, so you can describe your existing work in portable terms and write the same designs in modern C++.

docs.title: Why it is on the resume
docs.text:
Three resume items depend on it directly:

  • "multithreaded application server handling transactional loan-origination requests"
  • "thread synchronisation layer — mutexes, critical sections, wait objects and a pooled request model"
  • tcpkv: "fixed thread pool ... store guarded by shared_mutex"

and two more depend on it indirectly: "in-memory caching" (a cache shared by many threads is a concurrency problem first and a data-structure problem second) and "concurrency faults" (which you cannot debug without a model of what the hardware is doing).

Interviewers for senior C++ roles ask about this topic in nearly every loop. The questions are predictable: data races, mutex vs atomic, condition-variable predicate loops, memory orders, deadlock diagnosis, thread-pool design, false sharing. This course covers every one of them to the depth where you can derive the answer rather than recite it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• C at a professional level (you have this).
  • C++ basics: classes, RAII destructors, templates at the "I can read std::vector<T>" level, lambdas. If [&](int x) { return x + n; } looks foreign, do the first modules of 02_Modern_CPP first and come back.
  • WSL Ubuntu 24.04 with g++ --version reporting GCC 13. Every C++ file in code/ compiles with:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 file.cpp -o file
  • For ThreadSanitizer (modules 02 and 12): add -fsanitize=thread -g -O1.
  • Win32 .c examples are Windows-only. Build them with MSVC (cl /W4 file.c) or MinGW GCC (gcc -Wall file.c). They are reference material for module 13, not the main track.

docs.title: You are done when you can...
docs.text:
• State precisely what a data race is (two accesses, at least one write, not atomic, not ordered by happens-before) and explain why the standard makes it undefined behaviour rather than "unspecified value".
  • Write a producer-consumer queue with std::mutex and std::condition_variable, and explain from first principles why the wait must be in a predicate loop.
  • Explain acquire and release in the "message passing" model, and say what seq_cst adds that acquire/release does not.
  • Write a fixed-size thread pool whose shutdown provably drains every submitted task, and whose tasks can throw without killing a worker.
  • Look at the stacks of eight blocked threads in gdb or WinDbg and name the two that are deadlocked and the lock order that caused it.
  • Explain why std::shared_mutex can be slower than std::mutex and when that happens.
  • Explain false sharing with a drawing of two cache lines and say what alignas(64) fixes.
  • Describe your Win32 synchronisation layer entirely in portable terms: CRITICAL_SECTION is a non-recursive-in-spirit mutex with a spin phase, SRWLOCK is a shared_mutex, an auto-reset Event is roughly a binary semaphore, WaitForMultipleObjects has no direct std equivalent.
  • Design the locking for a master-table cache that is read by 200 threads and refreshed every five minutes, using an immutable snapshot and one atomic pointer swap.
  • Explain the ABA problem and why a Treiber stack needs tagged pointers or hazard pointers.

docs.title: 01. Processes, threads and the OS
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: none

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A process is a running program with its own private memory. A thread is one line of execution inside that process. All threads in a process see the same memory, the same open files, the same heap. Each thread has only three things of its own: a stack, a set of CPU registers (including the program counter), and a small block of bookkeeping the kernel keeps for scheduling it.

Analogy: a process is a kitchen. Threads are cooks. Every cook can reach every shelf and every pan (shared memory). Each cook has their own hands and their own notepad (registers and stack). The restaurant manager (the OS scheduler) decides which cook is standing at the stove at any moment, and when the manager swaps one cook for another, the outgoing cook has to write down exactly what they were doing (save registers) and the incoming cook has to read their own notes back (restore registers). That swap is a context switch, and it is not free.

You already create threads with CreateThread on Windows. This module shows you what the kernel does when you call it, what the POSIX and C++17 versions look like, and how to decide how many cooks the kitchen should have.

docs.title: 2.1 What the kernel keeps per thread
docs.text:
On both Linux and Windows the kernel has a structure per thread. Windows calls it the ETHREAD / KTHREAD pair (the user-mode shadow is the TEB, Thread Environment Block); Linux calls it task_struct (Linux does not distinguish processes from threads at this level; a thread is a task that shares its address space with other tasks). Textbooks call it the TCB, Thread Control Block.

It contains, at minimum:

+---------------------------------------------+
| thread id                                   |
| state: running / ready / blocked / ...      |
| saved registers (when not running)          |
|   - program counter (RIP)                   |
|   - stack pointer (RSP)                     |
|   - general purpose regs, flags, FP/SIMD    |
| pointer to kernel stack (for syscalls)      |
| pointer to user stack base and size         |
| scheduling info: priority, time slice used, |
|   which CPU it last ran on (affinity, cache)|
| pending signals / APCs                      |
| pointer to the owning process (mm / EPROCESS)|
| thread-local storage block pointer          |
+---------------------------------------------+

The process holds what is shared: the page tables (address space), the file descriptor / handle table, the heap, environment, signal handlers, and the list of threads.

docs.title: 2.2 Two stacks per thread
docs.text:
Each thread has a user stack (typical default: 8 MB on Linux, from ulimit -s; 1 MB on Windows, from the PE header or CreateThread parameter) and a kernel stack (small, typically 16 KB on x86-64 Linux). When the thread makes a system call or takes an interrupt, the CPU switches to the kernel stack. The user stack is only reserved virtual address space at first; pages are committed as the thread actually touches them.

This matters for "how many threads": 10,000 threads with 8 MB stacks reserve 80 GB of virtual address space. That is fine on 64-bit for reservation, but each thread touches at least one page, and the kernel structures per thread are not free either.

docs.title: 2.3 Scheduling and the context switch
docs.text:
The scheduler picks which runnable thread gets each CPU. Linux uses CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) by default, which tracks virtual runtime per task and picks the one that has had the least. Windows uses a priority-based preemptive scheduler with 32 priority levels and dynamic boosts (e.g. a thread woken from a wait gets a temporary boost).

A context switch happens when the CPU moves from one thread to another. The steps:

  1. Something triggers it: the timer interrupt says the time slice is over, the thread blocks on I/O or a lock, or a higher-priority thread becomes runnable.
  2. Kernel saves the current thread's registers into its TCB.
  3. Scheduler picks the next thread.
  4. If the next thread belongs to a different process, the kernel loads a new page-table root (CR3 on x86). This flushes or tags the TLB, which is the expensive part. Switching between threads of the same process skips this.
  5. Kernel restores the next thread's registers and returns to user mode.

Cost: the direct cost is on the order of 1 to 2 microseconds on modern x86 Linux (typical, measured with tools such as lmbench lat_ctx; your numbers will differ). The indirect cost is larger and harder to see: the new thread's working set is not in L1/L2 cache, so it runs slower for a while. This is why a thread that blocks on a lock for 200 ns is worse off than one that spins for 200 ns: blocking means two context switches plus cold caches.

docs.title: 2.4 User threads vs kernel threads
docs.text:
• Kernel threads (1:1): every thread you create is known to the kernel and scheduled by it. This is what pthreads on Linux (NPTL), Win32 threads, and std::thread all use. Blocking one thread in a syscall does not block the others.
  • User threads (M:N or N:1): a library multiplexes many user-level "threads" onto fewer kernel threads. Go goroutines, Windows fibers, and most coroutine schedulers are examples. Switching is cheap (no kernel entry) but if one blocks in a syscall, the kernel thread under it blocks too unless the runtime intercepts the call.

For this course, "thread" means kernel thread. Coroutines come up in 08_Networking.

docs.title: 2.5 The three APIs side by side
docs.text:
Operation Win32 POSIX (pthread) C++17 std::thread create CreateThread(NULL, stack, fn, arg, 0, &id) pthread_create(&t, NULL, fn, arg) std::thread t(fn, args...) entry signature DWORD WINAPI fn(LPVOID) void* fn(void*) any callable, any args wait for finish WaitForSingleObject(h, INFINITE) then CloseHandle(h) pthread_join(t, &ret) t.join() fire and forget CloseHandle(h) immediately pthread_detach(t) t.detach() current id GetCurrentThreadId() pthread_self() std::this_thread::get_id() sleep Sleep(ms) nanosleep / usleep std::this_thread::sleep_for(10ms) yield SwitchToThread() sched_yield() std::this_thread::yield() return value thread exit code via GetExitCodeThread void* from fn use std::future (module 09) hardware threads GetSystemInfo sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN) std::thread::hardware_concurrency()

Two things that will feel different coming from Win32:

  1. A std::thread must be joined or detached before it is destroyed. If a std::thread object that is still joinable goes out of scope, the destructor calls std::terminate(). There is no silent "handle leak" equivalent of forgetting CloseHandle. This is deliberate: the committee decided a crash is better than a thread you forgot about writing to a destroyed object. C++20 adds std::jthread which joins in its destructor; in C++17 you write a small RAII wrapper (shown below).
  2. Arguments are copied into the thread by value unless you wrap them with std::ref. The C habit of passing &local_struct and hoping the thread reads it before the function returns is still possible (pass a pointer) but no longer the default.

On Linux, std::thread is a thin wrapper over pthread_create, which is a thin wrapper over the clone() syscall with flags CLONE_VM | CLONE_FS | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD and more: "make a new task that shares my memory, files and signal handlers". On Windows, MSVC's std::thread calls _beginthreadex, which calls CreateThread after setting up the CRT's per-thread state.

docs.title: 2.6 Thread-local storage
docs.text:
Sometimes you want a global that is separate per thread: an error code (errno is exactly this), a per-thread RNG, a per-thread scratch buffer, a per-thread log prefix.

Win32 POSIX C++11 __declspec(thread) int x; __thread int x; (GCC) thread_local int x; TlsAlloc / TlsSetValue / TlsGetValue pthread_key_create / pthread_setspecific (not needed; thread_local covers it)

thread_local works on any type, including types with constructors and destructors. The object is constructed the first time that thread touches it (or at thread start for trivially constructible types) and destroyed when the thread exits. Under the hood each thread's TLS block is reached through a segment register (%fs on x86-64 Linux, %gs TEB on Windows) so access costs one extra indirection, not a lock.

docs.title: 2.7 How many threads?
docs.text:
Rules that hold up in practice:

  • CPU-bound work: as many threads as hardware threads (hardware_concurrency()), sometimes one fewer to leave room for the OS and the main thread. More than that only adds context switches and cache thrashing.
  • Blocking I/O-bound work (your RPC server waiting on the database): more threads than cores, because most of them are asleep most of the time. A starting estimate is cores * (1 + wait_time / compute_time); for a request that spends 20 ms waiting on YugabyteDB and 1 ms computing, that is 21 threads per core. In practice you cap it (64, 128, 256) and measure, because the database has its own connection limit and every extra thread is a stack and a scheduler entry.
  • Never one thread per request without a cap. A burst of 10,000 requests must not become 10,000 threads. That is the whole reason your server has a pooled request model; module 09 builds one.
  • Measure. Thread count is a tuning knob, so read it from config, not a #define.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m01_threads_basics.cpp

#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <chrono>

// A tiny RAII wrapper so a thread can never be destroyed while joinable.
// C++20 has std::jthread; in C++17 we write this ourselves.
class joining_thread {
    std::thread t_;
public:
    template <class F, class... Args>
    explicit joining_thread(F&& f, Args&&... args)
        : t_(std::forward<F>(f), std::forward<Args>(args)...) {}
    ~joining_thread() { if (t_.joinable()) t_.join(); }   // WHY: never terminate() by accident
    joining_thread(const joining_thread&) = delete;        // threads are move-only
    joining_thread& operator=(const joining_thread&) = delete;
    joining_thread(joining_thread&&) = default;
    joining_thread& operator=(joining_thread&&) = default;
    std::thread& get() { return t_; }
};

// thread_local: one instance per thread, constructed on first use in that thread.
thread_local int call_count = 0;

std::mutex cout_mtx;   // std::cout itself will not interleave characters, but lines can; serialize.

void worker(int id, int iterations) {
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; ++i) ++call_count;   // no race: call_count is per-thread
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(cout_mtx);
    std::cout << "worker " << id << " os-tid " << std::this_thread::get_id()
              << " local count " << call_count << '\n';
}

int main() {
    unsigned hw = std::thread::hardware_concurrency();   // 0 means "unknown"
    std::cout << "hardware threads: " << hw << '\n';

    // 1. Create and join. Arguments are copied into the new thread.
    std::vector<joining_thread> pool;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) pool.emplace_back(worker, i, 1000 * (i + 1));
    pool.clear();   // joins all four; destructors run here

    // 2. Pass by reference on purpose with std::ref. Without it, the thread gets a copy of
    //    'total' and the main thread never sees the result.
    long total = 0;
    std::thread t([](long& out) {
        for (int i = 1; i <= 100; ++i) out += i;
    }, std::ref(total));
    t.join();
    std::cout << "sum via ref: " << total << '\n';   // 5050

    // 3. Detach: fire and forget. The thread must not touch anything that main might destroy.
    //    Here it only uses its own stack and a copy of a value, which is the only safe pattern.
    std::thread bg([](int v) {
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(10));
        (void)v;   // pretend to do work
    }, 42);
    bg.detach();
    // main could exit before bg finishes; the process ends and bg is killed. Acceptable only
    // because bg owns nothing.

    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(20));
    std::cout << "main thread local count: " << call_count << '\n';   // 0: never incremented here
    return 0;
}

Build and run on WSL:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 m01_threads_basics.cpp -o m01 && ./m01

The equivalent in C with Win32 and in C with pthreads is in module 13 and in code/m13_win32_threads.c.

docs.title: What std::thread t(f, a, b) does on Linux with libstdc++
docs.text:
1. Packs f, a, b (decay-copied) into a heap-allocated state object.
  2. Calls pthread_create(&handle, nullptr, execute_native_thread_routine, state).
  3. glibc's pthread_create allocates the stack with mmap (anonymous, with a guard page at the bottom marked PROT_NONE so overflow faults instead of corrupting the neighbour), sets up the TLS block and the struct pthread descriptor at the top of that stack, then calls clone() with the CLONE_THREAD family of flags.
  4. The kernel creates a new task_struct, copies the parent's register state, points the new task's stack pointer at the mmap'd region, marks it runnable and returns the new TID.
  5. The new task is picked by the scheduler, lands in start_thread, which calls your f(a, b). When f returns, the wrapper runs TLS destructors and calls the exit syscall for that thread (exit, not exit_group; exit_group would kill the whole process).

join() calls pthread_join, which does a futex wait on the thread's TID field until the kernel clears it on thread exit (the CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID flag arranges this). Module 03 explains futex.

docs.title: Stack guard pages and overflow
docs.text: The guard page explains a crash signature you will recognise: a thread with deep recursion or a large local array dies with SIGSEGV and the faulting address is just below the thread's stack. On Windows the same event produces STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW (0xC00000FD). Fix: smaller frames, heap allocation, or a larger stack (pthread_attr_setstacksize; CreateThread stack parameter; std::thread has no portable way, which is one of its real gaps).

docs.title: Why too many threads hurt even when idle
docs.text: Each thread costs: the TCB (several KB), kernel stack (16 KB), at least one committed user-stack page (4 KB) plus the TLS block, an entry in scheduler run-queues or wait-queues, and a slot in every lock's wait list it touches. Idle threads cost nothing in CPU but they still pay the cold-cache penalty when they wake, and 5,000 of them make thread apply all bt in gdb an afternoon's reading.

docs.title: Thread exit and resources
docs.text: On Linux, a thread's resources (kernel stack, task_struct) are released when it is joined or if it was detached. A thread that exits and is never joined is a "zombie thread" until the process ends. On Windows, the thread object persists until every handle to it is closed, which is why you must CloseHandle even after WaitForSingleObject returns. std::thread::join() does both the wait and the release in one call.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Your server's startup. Your Win32 server creates N worker threads at startup, each blocking on a wait object for work. In C++17 terms that is a std::vector<std::thread> plus a std::condition_variable. Module 09 writes it. The portable description of your design is "fixed-size pool of kernel threads, blocking work queue".
  • Thread naming. Give threads names: pthread_setname_np(pthread_self(), "worker-3") on Linux, SetThreadDescription on Windows 10+. Then thread apply all bt and Process Explorer show "worker-3" instead of a TID. This is the single cheapest debugging investment in a multithreaded server.
  • Detached threads and shutdown. A detached thread that touches a global std::map while main returns and static destructors run is a use-after-free that happens only at shutdown and only sometimes. Rule: in a server, never detach. Keep every thread's handle and join all of them in a known order at shutdown.
  • Thread count from config. You will be asked "how did you size the pool?" The senior answer: started at 2x cores because requests are mostly database-bound, measured throughput and p99 latency under load, found the knee, and set it with headroom. The junior answer is "32, it seemed fine".
  • 3 AM symptom: CPU at 100% with throughput falling. Often too many runnable threads thrashing caches, or a spin-wait that should be a blocking wait. top -H (Linux) or Process Explorer threads tab (Windows) shows which threads are burning CPU.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Compile and run m01_threads_basics.cpp. Change the number of workers to 100 and observe that output lines never interleave mid-line because of cout_mtx. Remove the lock and run several times; find one interleaved line. Done when you have seen the interleaving.
  2. (easy) Write a program that prints std::thread::hardware_concurrency() and, on Linux, also reads /proc/self/status after creating 50 threads and reports the Threads: line. Done when the number is 51.
  3. (medium) Remove the joining_thread wrapper and let a joinable std::thread go out of scope. Run it; observe terminate called without an active exception. Then write a one-line explanation of why the committee chose terminate over detach. Done when the explanation mentions dangling references.
  4. (medium) Measure thread creation cost: create and join 10,000 threads one after another with std::chrono::steady_clock. Report microseconds per create+join. Then compare with the time to push 10,000 items through a single reused thread via a queue (you may use the queue from module 05 after you reach it). Done when you have both numbers and a sentence on what they imply for a request server.
  5. (hard) Write a thread_local struct with a constructor and destructor that print the thread id. Create three threads that each touch it. Verify construction happens once per thread and destruction happens at thread exit, not at program exit. Done when the output shows three constructions and three destructions before main prints "exiting".

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a process and a thread? A process owns an address space, file handles, and at least one thread. Threads inside a process share all of that and own only their stack, registers and scheduling state. Creating a thread is cheaper than a process and communication is through shared memory instead of IPC, but one thread's bug can corrupt every other thread's data.

Q: What does a context switch cost, and why? Directly, saving and restoring registers plus the scheduler's decision, on the order of a microsecond on modern x86 (typical). Indirectly and usually larger, the incoming thread's data and code are not in L1/L2 cache and, if it is a different process, the TLB has been flushed. That is why spinning briefly can beat blocking for very short critical sections.

Q: What happens if a std::thread is destroyed while still joinable? std::terminate() is called. The standard chose this over implicit detach because a detached thread holding references to the destroyed scope is a use-after-free waiting to happen. You must call join() or detach() first; in practice wrap the thread in an RAII type that joins.

Q: How is std::thread implemented on Linux? It calls pthread_create, which mmaps a stack with a guard page, sets up TLS, and issues the clone() syscall with flags that share the address space, file table and signal handlers. The kernel makes a new task_struct; Linux does not have a separate "thread" object, just tasks that share resources.

Q: How many threads should a server use? CPU-bound: one per hardware thread.
