Blocking-I/O-bound: more, roughly cores times (1 + wait/compute), capped and measured, because beyond the knee you only add context switches, memory and lock contention. Never unbounded, never one per request without a cap.

Q: What is thread_local and how is it accessed? A storage duration where each thread gets its own instance, constructed on first use in that thread and destroyed at thread exit. Access goes through a per-thread base register (%fs on x86-64 Linux) plus an offset, so it is a memory load with one extra indirection, not a lock or a hash lookup. errno is the classic example.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A thread owns a stack, registers and a kernel control block; everything else is shared with the process.
  • Context switch cost is roughly a microsecond directly and more indirectly through cold caches.
  • pthreads, Win32 threads and std::thread are all 1:1 kernel threads; std::thread wraps pthread_create on Linux and _beginthreadex on Windows.
  • A joinable std::thread going out of scope calls std::terminate; wrap it in an RAII joiner.
  • std::thread copies its arguments; use std::ref or pointers to share deliberately.
  • Each thread has a user stack with a guard page and a small kernel stack; overflow gives SIGSEGV just below the stack or STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW on Windows.
  • thread_local replaces __declspec(thread) and TlsAlloc, works with constructors, and costs one segment-relative load.
  • Size thread pools by measurement; CPU-bound means one per core, I/O-bound means more but always capped.
  • Name your threads. Never detach in a server.

docs.title: 02. Data races and why they are undefined behaviour
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 01

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A data race is two threads touching the same memory at the same time, where at least one of them is writing, and nothing forces one to happen before the other. In C and C++ that is not "you get one of the two values". It is undefined behaviour: the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, and it generates code on that assumption. Programs with data races can print impossible values, loop forever, skip code, or work perfectly for three years and fail the week after a compiler upgrade.

Analogy: two clerks updating the same paper ledger line without talking. One reads 100, the other reads 100, both add 10 and both write 110. You lost an update. That is the easy case. The hard case is that the clerks are allowed to use shorthand, write digits in any order they like, and copy the ledger to a scratch pad and never look at the original again, all because the ledger rules promise that nobody else will touch the line while they hold it. When that promise is broken you do not get a slightly wrong number; you get a line that nobody wrote.

You have avoided most races at work by wrapping shared state in CRITICAL_SECTION. This module explains what you were protecting against, so that you can spot the ones that are not wrapped.

docs.title: 2.1 The precise definition
docs.text:
The C++ standard (intro.races) says two expression evaluations conflict if one modifies a memory location and the other reads or modifies the same location. A program has a data race if it contains two conflicting actions in different threads, at least one of which is not atomic, and neither happens before the other. Any such execution is undefined behaviour.

Three parts to remember:

  1. Conflict: same memory location, at least one write. Two reads never race.
  2. Not both atomic: operations on std::atomic<T> are excluded. Two atomic writes to the same variable from two threads are a race in the English sense but not in the standard's sense; the result is one of the two values, well defined.
  3. No happens-before: if something orders them (a mutex unlock then lock, a thread join, an atomic release then acquire), there is no race. Module 07 defines happens-before properly. For now: a mutex makes the unlock happen before the next lock, so everything inside the critical section is ordered.

"Memory location" means a scalar object or a maximal sequence of adjacent bit-fields. Two different int members of the same struct are different memory locations: writing s.a in one thread and s.b in another is not a race (it may be slow; see module 10 on false sharing). Two bit-fields in the same word usually are the same memory location.

docs.title: 2.2 Why undefined and not "unspecified value"
docs.text:
Because every optimising compiler already assumes single-threaded semantics for non-atomic variables, and the committee chose to legalise what compilers do rather than forbid optimisation. Concretely the compiler may:

  • Keep a variable in a register across a loop. while (!done) {} with a plain bool done becomes if (!done) for(;;); because nothing in this thread writes done. GCC does this at -O2. The thread spins forever even after another thread sets done = true.
  • Reorder loads and stores to different addresses when the single-threaded result is the same. x = 1; flag = true; can be emitted as flag = true; x = 1;.
  • Invent loads and stores. A compiler may read a variable twice where you wrote one read, or speculatively write a value and write it back if a branch is not taken. Each of these is harmless single-threaded and catastrophic if another thread is watching.
  • Assume a race-free program is deadlock-free when hoisting a lock... and so on. The list is long and grows with every compiler release.

Making races UB means the compiler never has to reason about them. Making them "unspecified value" would forbid all of the above and cost measurable performance on every program, including the single-threaded ones. Java made the other choice (races produce some observed value, with strict rules); the cost shows up in what the JIT may not do.

docs.title: 2.3 Torn reads and writes
docs.text:
Even without the compiler doing anything clever, the hardware may not write your value in one piece. A torn access is one where a reader sees half of an old value and half of a new one.

  • A naturally aligned 1, 2, 4 or 8 byte access on x86-64 is single-copy atomic in hardware. You will not see a torn int.
  • An 8-byte access that crosses a cache-line boundary (misaligned) can tear on x86. It will tear on ARM.
  • A 16-byte struct { int64_t balance; int64_t version; } written with two 8-byte stores can always be seen half-written by another core. A reader may see new balance with old version.
  • A long double, a __int128, a std::string (pointer + size + capacity): all torn.

Hardware atomicity is not language atomicity. The compiler can still split an 8-byte store into two 4-byte stores if it wants to, and it sometimes does for constants (two mov dword with immediates instead of one mov qword through a register). Only std::atomic guarantees "all or nothing".

docs.title: 2.4 Compiler reordering
docs.text:
int data = 0;
bool ready = false;

// thread A                 // thread B
data = 42;                  while (!ready) {}
ready = true;               std::cout << data;   // may print 0

Three separate reasons B can print 0:

  1. Compiler keeps ready in a register in B: infinite loop (not 0, but also not 42).
  2. Compiler swaps the two stores in A because they are to different addresses and single-threaded semantics do not care.
  3. Even if the compiler emits them in order, the CPU can make them visible in another order (next section).

The fix is one of: a mutex around both sides, or std::atomic<bool> ready with release/acquire (module 07). volatile does not fix it; it stops reason 1 and sometimes reason 2 but never reason 3, and it does not create happens-before so the program is still UB.

docs.title: 2.5 CPU reordering
docs.text:
A modern core executes out of order and buffers stores. On x86-64 the rule (the TSO model, Total Store Order) is: stores can be delayed in a store buffer and become visible to other cores later than subsequent loads from this core execute. Loads are not reordered with other loads, stores are not reordered with other stores. So on x86 the example above is actually safe at the hardware level once the compiler is prevented from reordering; ready cannot become visible before data.

On ARM and POWER, stores to different addresses may become visible in any order and loads may be satisfied out of order. The example genuinely prints 0 on a phone. Code that "works" on your x86 laptop because of TSO is still UB and will fail the day it is built for an ARM server (AWS Graviton, Apple silicon, Ampere).

The classic demonstration is store buffering:

x = y = 0 initially
thread A:  x = 1;  r1 = y;
thread B:  y = 1;  r2 = x;

Can r1 == 0 && r2 == 0? In a sequentially consistent world, no: one of the stores happened first and the other thread's load must see it. On real x86 hardware, yes, routinely: both stores sit in their store buffers while both loads read the old 0 from cache. Module 07 shows the same test with atomics and memory orders.

docs.title: 2.6 "It worked on my machine"
docs.text:
Races are timing-dependent. Things that hide a race:

  • Debug builds (-O0): the compiler does not keep values in registers, so reason 1 above disappears. The race is still there.
  • Single-core VM or a heavily loaded machine: threads rarely run truly simultaneously.
  • Adding printf for debugging: the I/O takes a lock and tens of microseconds, which serialises the threads. The race disappears while you are looking at it and returns in production.
  • x86 TSO hiding the CPU-reordering class of bugs.
  • Small test data: a race on a hash table with 10 entries hits the same bucket rarely.

Things that expose it: -O2, many cores, ARM, running for hours, and ThreadSanitizer.

docs.title: 2.7 ThreadSanitizer in one paragraph
docs.text:
TSan (-fsanitize=thread) instruments every memory access and every synchronisation call. It keeps, per 8-byte memory word, a small history of recent accesses tagged with thread id and a vector clock. When a new access conflicts with a recorded one and the vector clocks say neither happened before the other, it reports a race with both stack traces. It finds races that did not actually produce a wrong result on this run, because it checks the ordering rules, not the outcome. Cost: 5x to 15x slowdown and 5x to 10x memory (typical, from the LLVM documentation). Module 12 goes deep; for now just run it.

g++ -std=c++17 -g -O1 -fsanitize=thread -pthread m02_race_demo.cpp -o race && ./race

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m02_race_demo.cpp

#include <thread>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <atomic>
#include <cstdint>

// Demo 1: lost updates. Two threads increment a plain int. Expected 2,000,000; you will get less.
int plain_counter = 0;

void bump_plain(int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) ++plain_counter;   // load, add, store: three steps, interleavable
}

// Demo 2: tearing. A 16-byte record written as two 8-byte halves. Reader checks invariant a == b.
struct Record { std::int64_t a; std::int64_t b; };
Record rec{0, 0};
std::atomic<bool> stop{false};

void writer_tear() {
    std::int64_t v = 0;
    while (!stop.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
        ++v;
        rec.a = v;        // WHY two separate stores: this is what any struct assignment compiles to
        rec.b = v;        // reader may observe a == v, b == v-1
    }
}

long reader_tear() {
    long torn = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 5'000'000; ++i) {
        Record snapshot = rec;         // plain copy: itself racy; this is the demo
        if (snapshot.a != snapshot.b) ++torn;
    }
    return torn;
}

int main() {
    // Demo 1
    std::thread t1(bump_plain, 1'000'000);
    std::thread t2(bump_plain, 1'000'000);
    t1.join(); t2.join();
    std::cout << "plain counter: " << plain_counter << " (expected 2000000)\n";

    // Demo 2
    std::thread w(writer_tear);
    long torn = reader_tear();
    stop.store(true, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    w.join();
    std::cout << "torn reads observed: " << torn << '\n';

    // Both demos are undefined behaviour on purpose. Compile with -fsanitize=thread and it will
    // report both races with the two stacks involved. That is the point of this file.
    return 0;
}

What you will see at -O2 on a multi-core WSL: the counter is well short of 2,000,000 and the torn count is non-zero. At -O0 the counter is still short. With -fsanitize=thread, TSan prints WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race for both, naming bump_plain and writer_tear/reader_tear.

Note the use of std::atomic<bool> stop. That one is correct: the loop termination flag must be atomic or the compiler may hoist the load out of the loop (reason 1 in 2.4). The racy parts are only the ones the comments mark.

docs.title: What ++plain_counter compiles to
docs.text:
At -O2, GCC emits for the loop body something like:

    add  DWORD PTR plain_counter[rip], 1

A single instruction. It is still not atomic: the CPU performs it as load, add, store internally, and another core can store between the load and the store. x86 provides the lock prefix to make it atomic (lock add), which is what std::atomic<int>::fetch_add compiles to. The lock prefix asserts exclusive ownership of the cache line for the duration of the read-modify-write. Without it, two cores do read 100 / read 100 / write 101 / write 101.

Often GCC does better than that for the loop: it notices nothing else in the function touches plain_counter, so it keeps the running total in a register and stores once at the end:

    mov  eax, DWORD PTR plain_counter[rip]
    add  eax, 1000000
    mov  DWORD PTR plain_counter[rip], eax

Now the "race window" is the whole function. One thread's million increments can be entirely overwritten by the other's. This is why the measured counter can be exactly 1,000,000. The compiler is allowed to do this precisely because the race is UB.

docs.title: Store buffers and cache coherence, briefly
docs.text: Each core has a store buffer: a FIFO of stores that have executed but not yet reached L1 cache. A store drains when the core gets the cache line in exclusive state (MESI, module 10). Loads from the same core check the store buffer first (store-to-load forwarding), so the core sees its own stores immediately, but other cores see them only after the drain. That gap is the CPU reordering of 2.5. An mfence instruction (or any lock-prefixed instruction) waits for the store buffer to drain; that is what seq_cst stores cost on x86 and what release stores do not.

docs.title: Why volatile is not the answer
docs.text: volatile tells the compiler every access is an observable side effect: do not elide, do not reorder with other volatile accesses, do not cache in a register. It was designed for memory mapped hardware registers. It says nothing about the CPU (no fences), nothing about atomicity (a volatile 16-byte struct still tears), and nothing about ordering with non-volatile accesses (the data = 42 store can still move after ready = true). MSVC on x86 historically added acquire/release semantics to volatile as an extension (/volatile:ms), which is why Win32 code you have seen gets away with it. Portable C++ does not. Use std::atomic.

docs.title: What TSan actually tracks
docs.text: For every 8-byte memory word TSan keeps a shadow of 4 slots (configurable), each recording (thread id, epoch, address offset and size, is_write). Each thread has a vector clock: its own epoch and the latest epoch it has synchronised with from every other thread. mutex.unlock publishes the thread's clock into the mutex; mutex.lock merges the mutex's clock into the locker. An access races with a shadow slot if it conflicts, is from a different thread, and the current thread's clock for the other thread is older than the recorded epoch. This is why TSan has no false positives when all synchronisation uses primitives it knows (pthread, std::atomic, std::mutex) and why it reports races that happened to produce the right value this time.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The counter you never locked. Statistics counters (requests_served++) in your server are the most common unprotected shared write in C servers. They look harmless. With the compiler optimisation above, a worker can overwrite another's hundred increments. Fix: std::atomic<long> with memory_order_relaxed, or per-thread counters summed on read (module 10).
  • The flag you never made atomic. volatile BOOL g_shutdown polled by workers. On MSVC x86 it works because of the /volatile:ms extension. Port it to GCC on ARM and the workers never stop. Portable fix: std::atomic<bool>.
  • The struct copied under no lock. Reading a config struct that another thread updates "rarely" is a torn read waiting for the day the update lands mid-copy. In a loan server, interest rate 7.25 with the old rounding mode is the kind of fault that reaches the customer. Fix: immutable snapshot swapped through an atomic pointer (module 11).
  • Heisenbugs. If adding logging makes a bug disappear, assume a race until proven otherwise. Do not ship the logging as the fix.
  • Make TSan a CI job. Build the test suite with -fsanitize=thread and run it nightly. It is the cheapest way to find these before customers do. If your production build is Windows-only, the test suite still runs on WSL; races in portable code are the same on both.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m02_race_demo.cpp at -O0 and -O2 and run each five times. Record the counter values. Done when you can explain why -O2 sometimes gives exactly 1,000,000.
  2. (easy) Build with -fsanitize=thread and read the report. Identify the two stack traces, the "previous write" and the "current read", and the thread creation sites. Done when you can point to the line number of both accesses.
  3. (medium) Write the while (!ready) {} spin with a plain bool ready and a second thread that sleeps 100 ms then sets it. Build at -O2. Observe it hangs. Look at the assembly (g++ -O2 -S) and find the loop that never reloads ready. Then change to std::atomic<bool> and confirm it terminates. Done when you have both assembly snippets side by side.
  4. (medium) Write the store-buffering litmus test from 2.5 with two threads, a start barrier (spin on an atomic counter so both start together), and run it 1,000,000 times counting how often r1 == 0 && r2 == 0. Done when you have seen a non-zero count on x86 with plain ints or relaxed atomics, and a zero count with seq_cst atomics (come back after module 07 if needed).
  5. (hard) Take a piece of C from your server (or write a 100-line stand-in) that has a statistics struct updated by workers under no lock. List every memory location, classify each access as read or write, and mark each pair that conflicts with no happens-before. Rewrite with the minimum synchronisation needed. Done when TSan is quiet on the rewrite.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Define a data race. Two accesses to the same memory location from different threads, at least one a write, at least one non-atomic, with no happens-before relationship between them. Any program containing one has undefined behaviour. Two reads are not a race, and two atomic operations are not a race.

Q: Why is a data race undefined behaviour rather than just an unpredictable value? Because optimising compilers assume single-threaded semantics for non-atomic variables: they hoist loads out of loops, keep variables in registers, reorder independent stores, and invent temporary stores. Defining a race result would forbid those optimisations everywhere. UB lets the compiler ignore the possibility, and puts the burden on the programmer to use atomics or locks.

Q: Can int x tear on x86-64? An aligned 4-byte int does not tear at the hardware level. But a struct of two ints, a misaligned int, a 16-byte value, or a value the compiler chooses to write in two halves all can. Hardware atomicity for a particular size is not a language guarantee; only std::atomic is.

Q: Why doesn't volatile fix a race? It prevents the compiler from eliding or caching the access and from reordering it with other volatile accesses. It adds no CPU fence, no atomicity for multi-word types, and no ordering with non-volatile accesses, and the standard still calls the program UB. MSVC's /volatile:ms adds acquire/release on x86 as an extension, which is why Win32 code sometimes gets away with it.

Q: Explain store buffering and why r1 == r2 == 0 can happen. Each core buffers its stores before they reach cache. Thread A stores x = 1 into its buffer and loads y, which is still 0 in cache. Thread B does the mirror image. Both loads complete before either store drains. Sequential consistency forbids this; real x86 permits it. A full fence or seq_cst atomics prevents it.

Q: How does ThreadSanitizer find a race that did not produce a wrong answer? It tracks happens-before with vector clocks and keeps a per-word history of recent accesses. It reports when two accesses conflict and the clocks prove neither is ordered before the other, regardless of what values resulted. So it finds the bug in the ordering, not the symptom.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Data race = conflicting accesses, different threads, at least one non-atomic, no happens-before. Result: undefined behaviour.
  • Compilers assume no races and will hoist, register-cache, reorder and invent accesses.
  • CPUs reorder too: x86 delays stores behind loads (TSO); ARM reorders almost everything.
  • Torn reads happen for anything the hardware cannot write in one piece, including every multi-word struct.
  • volatile is for hardware registers, not for threads.
  • "Works on my machine" usually means x86 TSO plus luck plus -O0.
  • std::atomic<bool> for flags, mutex or atomics for everything shared, immutable snapshots for rarely-changing config.
  • Run the test suite under -fsanitize=thread; it reports ordering violations, not just wrong values.

docs.title: 03. Mutexes: lock_guard, unique_lock, scoped_lock
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A mutex (mutual exclusion) is a token that only one thread can hold at a time. A thread that wants to touch shared data takes the token, does its work, and gives the token back. A thread that finds the token taken waits. That is all a mutex does. Everything else in this module is about how to take and give back the token without ever forgetting, how to hold two tokens without two threads each waiting for the other's, and what the operating system does while a thread waits.

You already do this with EnterCriticalSection / LeaveCriticalSection. The C++ difference is that you almost never call lock and unlock by hand. You create a small object whose constructor locks and whose destructor unlocks, so that leaving the scope by return, break, or exception always releases the mutex. This is RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation) applied to locks, and it eliminates the single most common bug in C lock code: the early return that skips the LeaveCriticalSection.

docs.title: 2.1 The mutex types in <mutex> and <shared_mutex>
docs.text:
Type Recursive? Timed? Shared? Win32 nearest std::mutex no no no CRITICAL_SECTION (but CS is recursive), SRWLOCK exclusive std::timed_mutex no yes no WaitForSingleObject(hMutex, ms) std::recursive_mutex yes no no CRITICAL_SECTION, Win32 Mutex handle std::recursive_timed_mutex yes yes no Win32 Mutex with timeout std::shared_mutex (C++17) no no yes SRWLOCK std::shared_timed_mutex (C++14) no yes yes none

Operations on all of them: lock(), try_lock(), unlock(). Timed ones add try_lock_for(duration) and try_lock_until(time_point). Shared ones add lock_shared() etc. (module 04).

Rules the standard imposes:

  • unlock() must be called by the thread that locked. Unlocking from another thread is UB.
  • Locking a non-recursive mutex you already hold is UB (in practice: deadlock on Linux, or an exception / assertion in debug builds).
  • Destroying a locked mutex is UB.
  • std::mutex is neither copyable nor movable. A class containing one is not copyable unless you write the copy yourself (and lock both sides while copying).

docs.title: 2.2 The lock wrappers
docs.text:
std::lock_guard<M> — the default. Locks in the constructor, unlocks in the destructor, nothing else. No member functions. Cannot be moved. Use it for 90% of critical sections.

{
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);   // locked here
    shared_value += 1;
}                                        // unlocked here, even if += threw

std::unique_lock<M> — a movable lock that can be unlocked and re-locked, can defer locking, can adopt an already-held lock, and can try or time out. It is slightly larger (holds a bool owns flag) and slightly slower. You need it when:

  • a std::condition_variable must unlock and re-lock around the wait (module 05);
  • you need to release the lock early in the middle of a function;
  • you want to transfer lock ownership out of a function (return it);
  • you want try_lock or a timeout.
std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m, std::defer_lock);   // not locked yet
if (lk.try_lock_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(50))) {  // only for timed_mutex
    ...
}
lk.unlock();          // early release
...
lk.lock();            // re-acquire

std::scoped_lock<M...> (C++17) — locks one or more mutexes at once with a deadlock-avoiding algorithm, unlocks all in the destructor. With one mutex it is identical to lock_guard. With two or more it replaces the C++11 idiom std::lock(m1, m2); lock_guard a(m1, adopt_lock); ....

void transfer(Account& from, Account& to, long amount) {
    std::scoped_lock lk(from.m, to.m);   // any order of arguments: never deadlocks against
    from.balance -= amount;              // another transfer(to, from, ...)
    to.balance   += amount;
}

With C++17 class template argument deduction you write std::scoped_lock lk(a, b); without the template arguments. Prefer scoped_lock over lock_guard in new code; it does everything lock_guard does and also handles the multi-lock case.

docs.title: 2.3 How std::lock avoids deadlock
docs.text: std::lock(m1, m2, ...) (used by scoped_lock) locks the first mutex, then try_locks the rest. If any try_lock fails, it unlocks everything it holds, yields, and starts again with the one that failed as the first to lock(). This is "lock one, try the rest, back off". It cannot deadlock because at no point does a thread hold one mutex while blocking on another. It can livelock in theory under extreme contention; libstdc++ rotates the starting mutex to avoid that in practice. For two mutexes a fixed global order (module 06) is cheaper; scoped_lock is for when you cannot know the order statically (two Account objects chosen at runtime).

docs.title: 2.4 recursive_mutex and why to avoid it
docs.text:
A recursive mutex lets the same thread lock it again while already holding it; it counts depth and only the matching number of unlocks release it. CRITICAL_SECTION and the Win32 Mutex handle are both recursive, which is why you may never have thought about this.

Why it is a design smell:

  1. It hides the fact that a function is called both with and without the lock held. The invariant "this data is consistent when the mutex is unlocked" becomes "consistent when the depth is zero", and a function at depth 2 may see state that a function at depth 1 left half-updated.
  2. It makes it impossible to use with condition_variable correctly: the wait releases one level, and the outer levels still hold the lock, so the notifier can never acquire it.
  3. It costs a thread-id compare on every lock.

The fix is almost always two functions: a public foo() that takes the lock and calls a private foo_locked() that assumes it. Convention: suffix _locked or _unlocked and a comment saying which mutex must be held. This also documents the lock discipline for the next reader.

docs.title: 2.5 Timed mutexes
docs.text: try_lock_for is for "I would rather fail this request than block the thread forever". In a request server that is a legitimate design: a worker that cannot get the cache lock within 50 ms returns a "retry later" error instead of becoming one of the 64 stuck threads at 3 AM. Combine with a counter of how often it times out; a rising count is your early warning of a lock convoy.

docs.title: 2.6 Granularity
docs.text:
Coarse-grained: one mutex for the whole store. Simple, correct, serialises everything. Fine-grained: one mutex per bucket, per account, per table. More parallelism, more mutexes, more chances of deadlock, more memory (a std::mutex is 40 bytes on x86-64 Linux glibc; a SRWLOCK is pointer-sized; a CRITICAL_SECTION is 40 bytes on 64-bit Windows).

Rules of thumb:

  • Start coarse. Measure. Split only the mutex that shows contention.
  • Hold a lock for as short a time as possible: compute outside, lock, copy or swap, unlock.
  • Never hold a lock across a blocking call you do not control: disk I/O, a database round trip, a network send, malloc of large size, or a call into code that might take another lock. This is the rule that your 3 AM deadlock will have broken.
  • Never hold a lock while calling a user-supplied callback.

docs.title: 2.7 Mapping to what you already use
docs.text:
Win32 C++17 Note InitializeCriticalSection(&cs) std::mutex m; constructor does it InitializeCriticalSectionAndSpinCount(&cs, 4000) std::mutex glibc mutex does not spin by default; PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP does EnterCriticalSection(&cs) m.lock() or lock_guard CS is recursive, std::mutex is not TryEnterCriticalSection(&cs) m.try_lock() LeaveCriticalSection(&cs) m.unlock() or scope exit DeleteCriticalSection(&cs) destructor CreateMutex(NULL, FALSE, NULL) std::recursive_timed_mutex roughly Win32 Mutex is a kernel object: cross-process, waitable with WFMO, 1 µs per lock WaitForSingleObject(hMutex, 100) try_lock_for(100ms) ReleaseMutex(hMutex) unlock() abandoned mutex (WAIT_ABANDONED) no equivalent a thread dying while holding a std::mutex is UB; the kernel Mutex detects it

The important conceptual shift: CRITICAL_SECTION is a user-mode spin-then-block lock inside one process; the Win32 Mutex handle is a kernel object that costs a syscall every time. You have probably been told "use CRITICAL_SECTION unless you need cross-process". std::mutex is the CRITICAL_SECTION of C++, and it is implemented the same way: user-mode fast path, kernel wait on contention. The kernel wait mechanism on Linux is the futex.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m03_mutex_counter.cpp

#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
#include <map>
#include <string>

// A thread-safe counter map: the smallest realistic "store guarded by a mutex".
class CounterMap {
    mutable std::mutex m_;              // mutable: const readers must still lock
    std::map<std::string, long> data_;  // GUARDED_BY(m_)
public:
    void increment(const std::string& key, long by = 1) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m_);      // RAII: unlocked on every exit path
        data_[key] += by;
    }
    long get(const std::string& key) const {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m_);
        auto it = data_.find(key);
        return it == data_.end() ? 0 : it->second;
    }
    // Snapshot copy: hold the lock only for the copy, never while the caller iterates.
    std::map<std::string, long> snapshot() const {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m_);
        return data_;
    }
};

// Two accounts, two mutexes, lock both without deadlock regardless of argument order.
struct Account {
    std::mutex m;
    long balance = 0;
    explicit Account(long b) : balance(b) {}
};

void transfer(Account& from, Account& to, long amount) {
    std::scoped_lock lk(from.m, to.m);   // WHY: std::lock algorithm; transfer(a,b) and
    from.balance -= amount;              // transfer(b,a) in parallel cannot deadlock
    to.balance   += amount;
}

// unique_lock: release early so the slow part runs unlocked.
std::mutex log_mtx;
std::vector<std::string> log_lines;

void log_and_do_slow_work(const std::string& msg) {
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(log_mtx);
    log_lines.push_back(msg);
    lk.unlock();                                   // WHY: the sleep below must not hold the lock
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::microseconds(50));
}

int main() {
    CounterMap counters;
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < 8; ++t) {
        ts.emplace_back([&counters, t] {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) counters.increment(t % 2 ? "odd" : "even");
        });
    }
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::cout << "odd=" << counters.get("odd") << " even=" << counters.get("even") << '\n';
    // 400000 and 400000, every time.

    Account a(1000), b(1000);
    std::thread t1([&] { for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i) transfer(a, b, 1); });
    std::thread t2([&] { for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i) transfer(b, a, 1); });
    t1.join(); t2.join();
    std::cout << "a=" << a.balance << " b=" << b.balance << " sum=" << a.balance + b.balance << '\n';

    std::vector<std::thread> loggers;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i)
        loggers.emplace_back([i] { for (int k = 0; k < 100; ++k) log_and_do_slow_work("t" + std::to_string(i)); });
    for (auto& t : loggers) t.join();
    std::cout << "log lines: " << log_lines.size() << '\n';   // 400
    return 0;
}

The // GUARDED_BY(m_) comment is a convention worth adopting: it tells the reader which mutex protects which field. Clang's thread-safety analysis can check it mechanically if you use the real attributes (__attribute__((guarded_by(m_)))), which is worth knowing exists even if you build with GCC.

docs.title: What std::mutex::lock() does on Linux (glibc, x86-64)
docs.text:
std::mutex wraps a pthread_mutex_t. The default (PTHREAD_MUTEX_NORMAL) lock path:

  1. Fast path, user mode. Atomic compare-and-swap on the 32-bit lock word: 0 (unlocked) to 1 (locked, no waiters). One lock cmpxchg instruction, roughly 20 ns uncontended (typical, depends on whether the cache line is local). No syscall. This is why uncontended mutexes are cheap and why "I replaced the mutex with an atomic for speed" rarely helps.
  2. Contended path. CAS failed. Set the word to 2 (locked, waiters present) with an atomic exchange, then call the futex(addr, FUTEX_WAIT, 2) syscall. The kernel checks that *addr is still 2 (if not, the lock was released in between and it returns immediately: this check is what prevents a lost wakeup) and then puts the thread to sleep on a hash bucket keyed by the address.
  3. Unlock. Atomic exchange the word to 0. If the old value was 2 (there were waiters), call futex(addr, FUTEX_WAKE, 1) to wake one. If the old value was 1, nobody is waiting, no syscall. So an uncontended lock/unlock pair is two atomic instructions and zero syscalls.

A futex ("fast userspace mutex") is just that: a kernel wait queue addressed by a user-space memory address, with an atomic "sleep only if the value is still X" check. It is the primitive under every glibc lock, condition variable, semaphore and pthread_join. Windows has the same thing since Windows 8: WaitOnAddress / WakeByAddressSingle, and SRWLOCK and CRITICAL_SECTION (on recent Windows) are built on it.

docs.title: What CRITICAL_SECTION does
docs.text: The same shape: an InterlockedCompareExchange on LockCount for the fast path. On contention, optionally spin SpinCount times re-trying the CAS (useful on multi-core because the owner is probably about to release), then wait on an auto-reset Event (older Windows) or via a keyed event / WaitOnAddress (newer). RecursionCount and OwningThread implement the recursion. The SpinCount is why InitializeCriticalSectionAndSpinCount exists; glibc's default mutex does not spin, PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP does, and std::mutex gives you no knob (one of its gaps).

docs.title: Why lock_guard has no runtime cost
docs.text: The constructor and destructor are inline; after optimisation the only instructions left are the lock() and unlock() calls. The "cost" of RAII is zero; what you gain is that the unlock is emitted on every return path and in the exception-unwinding landing pad, which the compiler generates for you.

docs.title: The cost of contention is not the lock, it is the sleep
docs.text: An uncontended lock is tens of nanoseconds. A contended lock that has to futex-wait costs two context switches (sleep, wake) plus a cold cache on return: tens of microseconds. A lock that is contended 1% of the time at 1 µs each and uncontended 99% at 20 ns spends over 80% of its total lock time in the 1%. This is why reducing hold time matters more than reducing lock count.

docs.title: Lock convoys
docs.text: If many threads block on a mutex and the owner releases it, the kernel wakes one waiter, but a running thread may grab the mutex before the woken one is scheduled (glibc mutexes are not fair). The woken thread goes back to sleep; another context switch wasted. Under heavy contention this cascades into a convoy where throughput falls below single-threaded. Symptom: many threads in futex_wait, CPU not saturated, throughput poor. Fix: shorter critical sections, or sharding the lock, or a different structure (module 10 and 11).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Your LeaveCriticalSection bugs are gone. Every C critical section that has an early return or a goto cleanup is a place where a forgotten unlock hung the server. RAII removes the class of bug. When you describe your synchronisation layer in interviews, say that moving it to C++ would make the unlock structural rather than disciplinary.
  • The mutex must have the same lifetime as the data. A std::mutex that is a member of the class it protects is destroyed with the class. If another thread is still inside lock(), that is UB. The usual cause: a connection object deleted by the acceptor thread while a worker is still finishing its request. Fix: shared_ptr ownership or an explicit "drain before destroy" protocol (module 09 shutdown).
  • Lock across the database call. The classic mistake: lock the cache mutex, miss, query YugabyteDB (20 ms), fill the cache, unlock. Every other request on the server now waits 20 ms behind the miss. Fix: unlock, query, re-lock, insert (and accept that two threads might both miss and both insert; last write wins and that is fine for a cache).
  • recursive_mutex as a porting crutch. When porting CRITICAL_SECTION code, the temptation is std::recursive_mutex everywhere because CS was recursive. Resist; find the re-entrant calls (they are the ones that would deadlock with std::mutex) and split them into foo() / foo_locked(). Each one you find is a place where the old code's invariants were weaker than anyone thought.
  • Timed locks as a circuit breaker. A worker that times out on a lock, logs the lock name, the thread id and the owner (if you record it), and fails the request, turns a silent hang into a diagnosable event.
  • 3 AM symptom: all 64 workers show futex_wait (Linux) or WaitForSingleObject inside RtlEnterCriticalSection (Windows) in their stacks. One of them holds the lock and is blocked on something else. Module 06 and 12 show how to find that one.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run m03_mutex_counter.cpp. Remove the lock_guard from increment and confirm the totals are wrong. Put it back. Done when totals are 400000 both ways.
  2. (easy) Replace std::scoped_lock lk(from.m, to.m) with two sequential lock_guards in argument order. Run the transfer test. It will probably deadlock (hang). Attach gdb (gdb -p PID, thread apply all bt) and find both threads inside lock. Done when you have the two stacks and can say which thread holds which mutex.
  3. (medium) Write a foo() that locks m and calls bar(), which also locks m. With std::mutex this hangs. Fix it the right way: bar_locked() that assumes the lock. Then write one paragraph on why std::recursive_mutex would have been the wrong fix. Done when the paragraph mentions invariants at intermediate depth.
  4. (medium) Measure uncontended lock cost: 10 million lock_guard acquisitions on one thread, timed with steady_clock. Then measure contended: two threads, each doing 10 million, same mutex. Report ns per lock in both cases. Done when you can explain the ratio in terms of futex calls and context switches.
  5. (hard) Implement class ConfigStore with get(key) and reload(path) where reload reads a file (slow). Version A holds the mutex during the file read. Version B reads the file into a local map first, then swaps under the lock. Run 8 reader threads and 1 reloader; measure reader p99 latency (keep a vector of per-call durations, sort, take index 0.99 * n). Done when version B's p99 is at least an order of magnitude lower and you can explain why.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between lock_guard, unique_lock and scoped_lock? lock_guard locks in the constructor and unlocks in the destructor, nothing else, zero overhead. unique_lock adds deferred locking, manual unlock and relock, try and timed lock, move, and is required by condition_variable::wait. scoped_lock (C++17) locks any number of mutexes with the deadlock-avoiding std::lock algorithm and should be the default for new code.

Q: How does std::lock or scoped_lock avoid deadlock with multiple mutexes? It locks the first, then try_locks the rest. If any fails it releases everything, yields, and retries starting with the one that failed. A thread never blocks while holding another of the set, so the hold-and-wait condition for deadlock is never met.

Q: Why avoid recursive_mutex? Recursion hides that a function is reached both with and without the lock, so the invariant "consistent when unlocked" weakens to "consistent at depth zero" and inner calls may see partial state. It also cannot be used correctly with condition variables and costs an owner check per lock. Split into f() and f_locked() instead.

Q: What is a futex? A Linux syscall providing a kernel wait queue keyed by a user-space address, with an atomic check "sleep only if *addr still equals this value". It lets a mutex take and release the lock in user space with a CAS and only enter the kernel when a thread must actually sleep or be woken. Windows has WaitOnAddress as the equivalent.

Q: How does std::mutex compare with CRITICAL_SECTION and with a Win32 Mutex handle? std::mutex and CRITICAL_SECTION are both intra-process locks with a user-mode atomic fast path and a kernel wait on contention; the differences are that CRITICAL_SECTION is recursive and can spin. A Win32 Mutex handle is a kernel object: every acquire is a syscall, it works across processes, it can be waited on with WaitForMultipleObjects, and it reports abandonment.

Q: What is a lock convoy? A pattern where a mutex is released and a waiter is woken, but a running thread grabs the mutex first, so the woken thread sleeps again. Each handoff wastes context switches; throughput can fall below single-threaded. It appears as many threads blocked in the lock with low CPU use. Shorter critical sections and sharding are the fixes.

Q: Should a mutex ever be held across a database call? No. The hold time becomes the database latency, and every other thread that needs the mutex waits that long. Fetch outside the lock, then lock briefly to insert or swap. Accept duplicate work on a miss rather than serialising all requests behind one.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A mutex gives one thread at a time exclusive access; std::mutex is the C++ CRITICAL_SECTION minus recursion.
  • Always lock through an RAII wrapper; the unlock then runs on every return and on exceptions.
  • lock_guard for simple scopes, unique_lock for condition variables and early unlock, scoped_lock for multiple mutexes and as the default in C++17.
  • std::lock avoids deadlock by lock-one, try-the-rest, back off.
  • Avoid recursive_mutex; split functions into locked and unlocked versions.
  • Timed locks turn hangs into diagnosable failures.
  • Uncontended lock: one CAS, ~20 ns. Contended: futex syscall, context switch, cold cache, microseconds. Hold time is what matters.
  • Never hold a lock across I/O, a database call, or a callback.
  • Futex: kernel wait queue by address with an atomic value check; WaitOnAddress on Windows.
  • Document which mutex guards which field; GUARDED_BY comments at minimum.

docs.title: 04. shared_mutex and readers-writers
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Most shared data in a server is read far more often than it is written. A master table of branch codes is read on every request and refreshed once an hour. With a plain mutex, two threads that only want to read the table still take turns, even though neither would disturb the other. A reader-writer lock fixes that: any number of readers may hold it at once, but a writer needs it alone. std::shared_mutex is the C++17 name; SRWLOCK is the Win32 name you have seen; pthread_rwlock_t is the POSIX one.

Analogy: a museum room. Any number of visitors can be inside looking at the paintings. When the curator wants to rehang a painting, everyone must leave and nobody may enter until the curator is done. The guard at the door counts visitors in and out and holds newcomers back when the curator is waiting.

The catch, which this module spends half its time on, is that the guard's counting is itself a shared write. For very short reads, the cost of counting readers in and out can exceed the cost of a plain mutex, and a plain mutex wins. "Use shared_mutex for read-mostly data" is the beginner rule. "Measure, because the reader count is contended too" is the senior one.

docs.title: 2.1 The API
docs.text:
#include <shared_mutex>

std::shared_mutex m;

// writer: exclusive
{ std::unique_lock<std::shared_mutex> lk(m);  /* or std::lock_guard, or std::scoped_lock */ }

// reader: shared
{ std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lk(m); }

Member functions: lock / try_lock / unlock (exclusive) and lock_shared / try_lock_shared / unlock_shared (shared). std::shared_lock is the RAII wrapper for the shared side; it has the same interface as unique_lock (defer, try, move, unlock early). std::shared_timed_mutex (C++14) adds try_lock_for and try_lock_shared_for; std::shared_mutex (C++17) drops the timed operations and is usually a thinner wrapper over the platform primitive.

Rules:

  • A thread holding a shared lock must not request the exclusive lock (UB; deadlock in practice). There is no standard "upgrade" operation. If you need read-then-maybe-write, release the shared lock, take the exclusive lock, and re-check the condition, because another writer may have run in between.
  • A thread holding the exclusive lock may not take the shared lock either.
  • Same single-owner rules as std::mutex: unlock from the locking thread, no recursion.

docs.title: 2.2 Mapping
docs.text:
Win32 POSIX C++17 SRWLOCK srw = SRWLOCK_INIT; pthread_rwlock_t std::shared_mutex m; AcquireSRWLockExclusive(&srw) pthread_rwlock_wrlock m.lock() / unique_lock ReleaseSRWLockExclusive(&srw) pthread_rwlock_unlock m.unlock() AcquireSRWLockShared(&srw) pthread_rwlock_rdlock m.lock_shared() / shared_lock ReleaseSRWLockShared(&srw) pthread_rwlock_unlock m.unlock_shared() TryAcquireSRWLockExclusive pthread_rwlock_trywrlock m.try_lock()

SRWLOCK is pointer-sized, non-recursive, cannot be upgraded, and is faster than CRITICAL_SECTION even in exclusive-only use on modern Windows. If you have a CRITICAL_SECTION protecting read-mostly data, SRWLOCK is the drop-in improvement, and std::shared_mutex is how you describe it portably.

docs.title: 2.3 Reader-writer trade-offs
docs.text:
When shared_mutex helps:

  • Read sections are long relative to the lock overhead (say, a std::map lookup with string compares, or walking a few hundred entries), and
  • readers greatly outnumber writers, and
  • there are enough cores that readers actually run in parallel.

When a plain std::mutex is as fast or faster:

  • Read sections are tiny (a single integer load, an unordered_map lookup on a small key). The shared lock still does an atomic increment on acquire and an atomic decrement on release; both hit the same cache line from every reading core. That cache line bounces between cores exactly as a mutex's lock word would. You pay the contention cost without the exclusivity benefit.
  • Low core count. Two readers on two cores gain little; the bookkeeping dominates.
  • Writers are frequent. Every writer must wait for all readers to drain, and readers arriving during that drain must wait too, so under write pressure a rwlock behaves like a mutex with extra steps.

Measured on typical x86-64 Linux hardware, the crossover is on the order of a few hundred nanoseconds of read work: below that a mutex wins, above it shared_mutex wins (this is the kind of number you must re-measure on your own machine; see exercise 4). For a cache of immutable snapshots (module 11) you can eliminate the reader lock entirely, which beats both.

docs.title: 2.4 Writer starvation and fairness
docs.text:
If readers arrive continuously, a naive rwlock that admits any reader whenever no writer holds the lock will never let a writer in: the reader count never reaches zero. That is writer starvation. Implementations handle it in one of two ways:

  • Writer preference: once a writer is waiting, new readers block even though current readers are still inside. The writer gets in as soon as current readers drain. glibc's pthread_rwlock can be configured for this (PTHREAD_RWLOCK_PREFER_WRITER_NONRECURSIVE_NP); its default prefers readers. libstdc++'s std::shared_mutex on Linux wraps pthread_rwlock_t with default attributes, so by default it is reader-preferring and can starve writers. SRWLOCK on Windows does not document a policy but behaves roughly fair in practice.
  • Fair / FIFO: readers and writers are queued in arrival order; a batch of adjacent readers runs together. Fair, no starvation, slightly lower reader throughput.

Practical consequence: in a server with a steady stream of reads, a writer on a default libstdc++ shared_mutex may wait seconds. If the writer is your five-minute master-table refresh, the data goes stale. Know your implementation's policy or design around it (snapshot swap, module 11).

docs.title: 2.5 The tcpkv store design
docs.text:
Your tcpkv project: a TCP key-value server, fixed thread pool, store guarded by shared_mutex. The portable, defensible design:

class Store {
    mutable std::shared_mutex m_;
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string> map_;   // GUARDED_BY(m_)
public:
    std::optional<std::string> get(const std::string& k) const {
        std::shared_lock lk(m_);              // many GETs in parallel
        auto it = map_.find(k);
        if (it == map_.end()) return std::nullopt;
        return it->second;                    // copy out while holding the lock
    }
    void set(std::string k, std::string v) {
        std::unique_lock lk(m_);              // SET excludes everyone
        map_[std::move(k)] = std::move(v);
    }
    bool del(const std::string& k) {
        std::unique_lock lk(m_);
        return map_.erase(k) > 0;
    }
};

Why get returns a copy and not a reference or pointer: the moment the shared lock is released, a set may rehash the map and invalidate every reference into it. Returning const std::string& from a function that releases the lock on return is a use-after-free that only shows under load. Returning std::optional<std::string> (a copy) is correct and the copy is cheap compared to the TCP write that follows.

Why std::optional and not an empty string: an empty string is a valid value. The protocol must distinguish "key absent" from "key present with empty value".

What to say when asked "why shared_mutex here?": GETs dominate in a KV workload, the read section is a hash lookup plus a string copy (hundreds of ns), and the pool has 8 threads on 8 cores, so parallel reads are real. What to say when asked "what would you do next?": shard the map into 16 or 64 buckets each with its own shared_mutex keyed by hash(key) % N, which cuts contention on both reads and writes, and consider making the read path lock-free with an atomic snapshot if writes are rare.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m04_shared_mutex_map.cpp

#include <shared_mutex>
#include <mutex>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <string>
#include <optional>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include <atomic>
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>

class Store {
    mutable std::shared_mutex m_;
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string> map_;   // GUARDED_BY(m_)
public:
    std::optional<std::string> get(const std::string& k) const {
        std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lk(m_);
        auto it = map_.find(k);
        if (it == map_.end()) return std::nullopt;
        return it->second;                 // WHY copy: references die when lk is released
    }
    void set(std::string k, std::string v) {
        std::unique_lock<std::shared_mutex> lk(m_);
        map_[std::move(k)] = std::move(v);
    }
    bool del(const std::string& k) {
        std::unique_lock<std::shared_mutex> lk(m_);
        return map_.erase(k) > 0;
    }
    std::size_t size() const {
        std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lk(m_);
        return map_.size();
    }
};

// A sharded variant: N independent stores, chosen by hash. Same interface.
template <std::size_t N>
class ShardedStore {
    Store shards_[N];
    static std::size_t idx(const std::string& k) { return std::hash<std::string>{}(k) % N; }
public:
    std::optional<std::string> get(const std::string& k) const { return shards_[idx(k)].get(k); }
    void set(std::string k, std::string v) {
        std::size_t i = idx(k);                 // compute before moving k
        shards_[i].set(std::move(k), std::move(v));
    }
    bool del(const std::string& k) { return shards_[idx(k)].del(k); }
};

template <class S>
double run_benchmark(S& store, int readers, int writers, std::chrono::milliseconds dur) {
    std::atomic<bool> stop{false};
    std::atomic<long> ops{0};
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) store.set("key" + std::to_string(i), "value");

    for (int r = 0; r < readers; ++r)
        ts.emplace_back([&] {
            long local = 0;
            while (!stop.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
                for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) { (void)store.get("key" + std::to_string(i % 1000)); ++local; }
            }
            ops.fetch_add(local, std::memory_order_relaxed);   // WHY: one atomic add per thread, not per op
        });
    for (int w = 0; w < writers; ++w)
        ts.emplace_back([&] {
            long local = 0;
            while (!stop.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
                store.set("key" + std::to_string(local % 1000), "v2"); ++local;
            }
            ops.fetch_add(local, std::memory_order_relaxed);
        });

    std::this_thread::sleep_for(dur);
    stop.store(true);
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    return static_cast<double>(ops.load()) / dur.count() / 1000.0;   // million ops per second
}

int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono_literals;
    Store s;
    ShardedStore<16> sh;
    std::cout << "shared_mutex, 8 readers 0 writers: " << run_benchmark(s, 8, 0, 500ms) << " Mops/s\n";
    std::cout << "shared_mutex, 8 readers 2 writers: " << run_benchmark(s, 8, 2, 500ms) << " Mops/s\n";
    std::cout << "sharded x16,  8 readers 2 writers: " << run_benchmark(sh, 8, 2, 500ms) << " Mops/s\n";

    // Correctness smoke test
    Store c;
    c.set("a", "");
    std::cout << "present-empty: " << (c.get("a").has_value() ? "yes" : "no")
              << ", absent: " << (c.get("zz").has_value() ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';
    return 0;
}

Note the benchmark constructs a std::string key per lookup; that allocation is part of the "read work" and makes the read section long enough for shared_mutex to pay off. Exercise 4 asks you to remove it and watch the result flip.

docs.title: glibc pthread_rwlock_t layout and the shared fast path
docs.text:
The lock holds a 32-bit __readers word with the reader count in the upper bits and two flag bits: "writer present" and "writers waiting / phase". rdlock does a CAS loop: read the word, if no writer flag, CAS in count + 1. unlock (shared) does an atomic fetch_sub. Every reader thus performs two atomic read-modify-writes on one cache line. On a 2-socket machine the line travels across the interconnect for each; that is 100 ns or more per operation (typical). A std::mutex lock/unlock is also two atomics on one line, which is why for tiny read sections they cost the same and the mutex, with less logic, often wins.

The writer: sets the writer flag with a CAS when the count is zero, otherwise futex-waits on the word. Readers that see the writer flag futex-wait on a separate word. The reader/writer-preference policy decides whether a reader arriving while a writer waits (not holds) increments the count or blocks.

docs.title: Why SRWLOCK is fast
docs.text: It is a single pointer-sized word. The low bits are flags (locked, waiting, multiple shared holders) and the rest is either the shared count or a pointer to a wait block chain on the waiters' stacks. Acquire is one InterlockedCompareExchange; release likewise. Waiters block via keyed events (a kernel object addressed by a key, the Windows futex ancestor). No allocation, no kernel object creation, which is why it can be statically initialised (SRWLOCK_INIT) and why Windows's own CONDITION_VARIABLE is designed to pair with it.

docs.title: Reader scalability ceiling
docs.text: Even with no writers, N readers on N cores do not get N times throughput from a single shared_mutex, because the reader count line is contended. The ceiling is set by the cache coherence latency of that one line. To scale reads linearly you must stop writing shared memory on the read path: sharding (each core mostly touches its own shard's lock), per-core reader counts (the "big reader lock" design from the Linux kernel, brlock), or no lock at all with immutable snapshots and RCU (module 11).

docs.title: Upgrade and the lost-update race
docs.text:
Because there is no upgrade, this pattern is wrong:

{ std::shared_lock lk(m); if (map.count(k)) return map[k]; }
{ std::unique_lock lk(m); map[k] = compute(); return map[k]; }   // another thread may have inserted

It is not a data race (every access is locked) but it is a logic race: two threads miss, both compute, both insert. For a cache that is acceptable. For "insert if absent, else fail" it is a bug: use try_emplace under the exclusive lock and check the returned bool. Boost offers upgrade_lock which reserves the right to upgrade; the standard does not, because supporting upgrade cheaply constrains the implementation.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Master tables. Your core-banking server's product codes, branch lists, interest matrices: read on every request, refreshed by a scheduled job. This is the textbook SRWLOCK / shared_mutex use. If you still have them under CRITICAL_SECTION, switching to SRWLOCK is a one-day change with a measurable p99 gain under concurrent load. The next step beyond that is the snapshot swap in module 11, which removes the reader lock entirely.
  • Writer starvation in the wild. A refresh thread that logs "refresh took 14 s" while the table is 100 entries: it was waiting for a gap in readers that never came. Fix: snapshot swap (writer builds the new table unlocked, then takes the exclusive lock for a single pointer assignment) so the exclusive section is nanoseconds and readers barely notice.
  • Holding a shared lock across a call-out. A reader that takes the shared lock and then calls into code that eventually tries the exclusive lock on the same mutex (a lazy-fill in a getter) deadlocks itself, and because it is a reader, every writer behind it is stuck too. The _locked naming convention from module 03 is how you spot this in review.
  • Returning references. A const T& get(key) on a shared_mutex-guarded map is the most common serious bug in KV stores written by people who have just learned shared_lock. It is a use-after-free that passes every single-threaded test.
  • 3 AM symptom: throughput drops to near zero, all worker stacks show pthread_rwlock_rdlock or AcquireSRWLockShared. A writer holds the lock and is doing something slow inside it (the refresh job calling the database under the exclusive lock). Find the one thread in wrlock's critical section and look at what it is waiting on.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run m04_shared_mutex_map.cpp. Note the three throughput numbers. Done when the sharded store beats the single store with writers present.
  2. (easy) Change get to return const std::string* pointing into the map. Run with -fsanitize=address and 8 readers plus 2 writers that del and re-set. Done when ASan reports a heap-use-after-free and you can explain the lifetime problem in one sentence.
  3. (medium) Replace std::shared_mutex with std::mutex (and shared_lock with lock_guard) in Store. Re-run the 8-reader / 0-writer benchmark. Done when you have both numbers and a sentence on which won and why.
  4. (medium) Make the read section tiny: pre-build the 1000 key strings in a vector and look them up by index so there is no per-lookup allocation. Re-run shared_mutex vs mutex. Done when you have found the point where the plain mutex is as fast or faster, or can explain why on your machine it never is.
  5. (hard) Demonstrate writer starvation on libstdc++: 8 readers in a tight loop of shared_lock, one writer that measures how long unique_lock takes to acquire. Report max wait over 10 seconds. Then implement a small fair rwlock (mutex + condition_variable + counts + "writer waiting" flag that blocks new readers) and show the writer's max wait drops. Done when both numbers are recorded and your rwlock passes TSan.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When is shared_mutex faster than mutex, and when is it not? Faster when read sections are long enough (hundreds of nanoseconds or more) that running them in parallel outweighs the cost of the atomic reader-count increment and decrement, readers dominate, and there are enough cores. Not faster, often slower, when reads are a few instructions, because the reader count is a contended cache line just like a mutex's lock word, or when writes are frequent and keep draining readers.

Q: What is writer starvation and how do implementations avoid it? With continuous readers, a reader-preferring rwlock never reaches a zero reader count and a writer waits indefinitely. Writer-preferring locks block new readers once a writer is waiting; fair locks queue in arrival order. glibc defaults to reader preference, so libstdc++ shared_mutex can starve writers unless the writer's exclusive section is kept to a pointer swap.

Q: Can you upgrade a shared lock to exclusive? Not with std::shared_mutex; attempting to lock exclusively while holding shared is UB. Release the shared lock, acquire exclusive, and re-check the condition because another writer may have intervened. Boost's upgrade_lock provides a reservation mechanism; the standard omitted it.

Q: Why must get on a shared_mutex-guarded map return a copy? A reference or pointer into the map is valid only while the lock is held. After get returns and releases the shared lock, a writer may erase or rehash and the caller holds a dangling reference. Copying under the lock (or returning a shared_ptr to an immutable value) is the only safe interface.

Q: Describe the tcpkv store and what you would do to scale it. An unordered_map behind a shared_mutex; GET takes a shared lock and copies the value out, SET and DEL take exclusive. To scale: shard by key hash into N independent maps each with its own lock, so both readers and writers of different shards do not contend; beyond that, make reads lock-free with immutable snapshots if writes are rare.

Q: What is SRWLOCK and how does it relate to shared_mutex? Windows's slim reader-writer lock: a pointer-sized, non-recursive, non-upgradable lock with shared and exclusive modes, acquired with one interlocked operation and waited on via keyed events. It is the direct equivalent of std::shared_mutex and faster than CRITICAL_SECTION even in exclusive-only use.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• shared_mutex: many readers or one writer. shared_lock for readers, unique_lock or scoped_lock for writers.
  • Direct equivalents: SRWLOCK on Windows, pthread_rwlock_t on POSIX.
  • The reader count is a contended atomic; tiny read sections are no faster than with a mutex.
  • Writer starvation is real under reader preference, which is libstdc++'s default on Linux.
  • No upgrade; release, re-acquire exclusive, re-check.
  • Never return references into locked data; copy under the lock.
  • Shard to scale both reads and writes; snapshot swap to make reads lock-free.
  • Keep the exclusive section to a swap; build the new state outside the lock.

docs.title: 05. Condition variables and wait objects
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A mutex lets you protect data. It does not let you wait for the data to change. A worker thread that wants the next request from a queue must either check the queue in a loop (burning CPU) or sleep until someone tells it there is work. A condition variable is the "tell it" mechanism: a thread goes to sleep on the condition variable, releasing the mutex while it sleeps; another thread changes the data and signals the condition variable; the sleeper wakes up, re-takes the mutex, and checks the data.

Analogy: a restaurant pass. Cooks (producers) put plates on the pass and ring a bell. Waiters (consumers) wait near the bell. A waiter who hears the bell walks over, but checks that there is actually a plate before picking one up, because another waiter may have been faster, or the bell may have been rung by mistake. That check-after-wake is the predicate loop, and it is the single most important rule in this module.

You have done this on Win32 with an Event handle and WaitForSingleObject. Events and condition variables solve the same problem differently, and the differences explain a class of bugs (lost wakeups) that your Win32 code may have hit without anyone knowing why.

docs.title: 2.1 The API
docs.text:
#include <condition_variable>

std::mutex m;
std::condition_variable cv;
std::deque<Request> queue;   // GUARDED_BY(m)
bool shutting_down = false;  // GUARDED_BY(m)

// consumer
std::optional<Request> pop() {
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);
    cv.wait(lk, [&] { return !queue.empty() || shutting_down; });   // predicate loop
    if (queue.empty()) return std::nullopt;                           // shutting down, drained
    Request r = std::move(queue.front());
    queue.pop_front();
    return r;
}

// producer
void push(Request r) {
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);
        queue.push_back(std::move(r));
    }                      // unlock before notify: the woken thread can take the lock immediately
    cv.notify_one();
}

Members of std::condition_variable:

  • wait(unique_lock&): atomically release the mutex and block; on wake, re-acquire the mutex before returning. The mutex must be held when calling.
  • wait(unique_lock&, Predicate p): equivalent to while (!p()) wait(lk);. Always use this form.
  • wait_for(lk, duration[, pred]), wait_until(lk, time_point[, pred]): timed variants. Return std::cv_status::timeout or no_timeout, or with a predicate, the predicate's value.
  • notify_one(): wake at least one waiter (if any). notify_all(): wake all waiters.

std::condition_variable works only with std::unique_lock<std::mutex>. If you need a different lock type, std::condition_variable_any works with anything that has lock()/unlock() at some cost in size and speed.

docs.title: 2.2 Why the predicate loop: three derivations
docs.text:
You must call wait in a loop that re-checks the condition. Here is why, three independent times. Any one of them is sufficient.

Reason 1: spurious wakeups. The standard permits wait to return without any notify. This is not laziness; it is because the underlying futex wait can be interrupted (a signal delivered to the thread, EINTR) and because efficient implementations on some platforms cannot distinguish "woken by notify" from "woken by the kernel for its own reasons" without an extra round trip. The POSIX standard permits the same for pthread_cond_wait. Windows SleepConditionVariableCS also documents spurious wakeups. So a thread may wake with the queue still empty.

Reason 2: stolen wakeups. Producer pushes one item and calls notify_one. Waiter A is woken. Before A re-acquires the mutex, thread C (which was never waiting) calls pop, takes the mutex, finds the item, and takes it. A now acquires the mutex and finds the queue empty. Without the loop, A pops from an empty queue.

Reason 3: notify_all with a condition that is true for one. Producer pushes one item and calls notify_all (perhaps it does not know how many it pushed). Five waiters wake. One gets the item. Four must go back to sleep. Without the loop, four threads pop from an empty queue.

The predicate form cv.wait(lk, pred) encodes the loop so you cannot forget it. The condition must be checked under the mutex, which is why wait re-acquires before returning and why the predicate runs with the lock held.

docs.title: 2.3 Lost wakeups
docs.text:
The opposite failure: a notify that nobody hears. This happens when the waiter checks the condition, finds it false, and then goes to sleep, with a gap in between during which the producer sets the condition and notifies. The notify finds no waiters and is dropped (condition variables have no memory). The waiter then sleeps forever.

consumer                              producer
lock m
check queue: empty
unlock m             <- gap
                                      lock m; push; unlock m; notify_one()  -- nobody waiting
wait on cv           <- sleeps forever

The condition variable API prevents this by making "release the mutex and start waiting" one atomic step inside wait. Because the consumer holds the mutex from the check until the moment the wait registers it, the producer cannot push in the gap: it is blocked on the mutex. When it does push and notify, the consumer is already registered as a waiter.

This is the rule: the condition must be modified under the same mutex that the waiter holds when checking it. If a producer sets shutting_down = true without the lock and then notifies, a lost wakeup is possible. Even if the variable is std::atomic<bool>, you still need to take the mutex (and release it) around the write to close the gap. "Atomic flag plus condition variable" is a classic bug.

docs.title: 2.4 notify_one vs notify_all
docs.text:
• notify_one when exactly one waiter can make progress from this change (one item pushed, one consumer should take it). Cheaper: wakes one thread.
  • notify_all when the change may let several waiters proceed (shutdown flag, "queue is no longer full" with several producers blocked, a state transition that different waiters care about for different reasons). Also the safe default when waiters have different predicates on the same condition variable: notify_one might wake a waiter whose predicate is still false while the one whose predicate is now true stays asleep. That waiter re-checks, sleeps again, and the intended waiter never wakes: a lost wakeup in disguise.

Rule: one condition variable per condition. A bounded queue has "not empty" (consumers wait) and "not full" (producers wait); give each its own condition variable so notify_one is always correct.

docs.title: 2.5 Notify with or without the lock held
docs.text: Both are correct. Notifying after unlocking lets the woken thread acquire the mutex immediately instead of waking, failing to acquire, and sleeping again (a wasted context switch). glibc has an optimisation (wait morphing was removed; current glibc simply requeues) that makes the difference small. Notify-after-unlock is the convention; notify-while-locked is required only when the condition variable itself may be destroyed by the woken thread (rare: a one-shot "done" signal where the waiter deletes the object).

docs.title: 2.6 Mapping to Win32
docs.text:
Concept Win32 C++17 condition variable CONDITION_VARIABLE (Vista+) with SleepConditionVariableCS / SleepConditionVariableSRW, WakeConditionVariable, WakeAllConditionVariable std::condition_variable manual-reset event CreateEvent(NULL, TRUE, FALSE, NULL); SetEvent leaves it set until ResetEvent no direct equivalent; mutex + bool + condition_variable or std::future<void> for one-shot auto-reset event CreateEvent(NULL, FALSE, ...); SetEvent wakes exactly one waiter and resets roughly a binary semaphore: mutex + int count + condition_variable wait for any of N WaitForMultipleObjects(n, handles, FALSE, timeout) none; one condition variable with a composite predicate, or a single queue of events wait for all of N WaitForMultipleObjects(n, handles, TRUE, ...) none; a counter of completed tasks under a mutex plus a condition variable, or N futures joined in sequence

The crucial difference: an Event has state (set or not set); a condition variable does not. SetEvent on a manual-reset event with no waiter is remembered; a later WaitForSingleObject returns immediately. notify_one with no waiter is forgotten. This is why Event-based code does not need the "modify under the mutex" rule for simple one-shot signals, and why condition variable code does. But it is also why Event-based code has its own classic bug: an auto-reset Event that is set twice before the waiter runs wakes it only once; the second signal is lost. A condition variable plus a counter does not have this problem because the state lives in the counter you control.

Since Vista, Windows has CONDITION_VARIABLE, which is the same thing as std::condition_variable (same spurious wakeups, same predicate-loop requirement, pairs with CRITICAL_SECTION or SRWLOCK). If your server still uses Events for producer-consumer, CONDITION_VARIABLE with SRWLOCK is the modern Win32 replacement, and module 13 shows it.

WaitForMultipleObjects has no standard C++ equivalent. The portable designs are: (a) one queue that all event sources push into, with one condition variable (what an actor's mailbox is, module 11); (b) a select/epoll/poll loop for I/O events (08_Networking); (c) std::future and when_any from the Concurrency TS, not standard in C++17.

docs.title: 2.7 Timed waits and the deadline pattern
docs.text: Use wait_until with an absolute deadline, not wait_for with a relative duration, when looping: a wait_for(100ms) inside a predicate loop that wakes spuriously at 99 ms waits another 100 ms, so the total timeout stretches. wait_until(deadline, pred) handles this correctly and returns false if the deadline passed with the predicate still false.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m05_producer_consumer.cpp

#include <condition_variable>
#include <mutex>
#include <deque>
#include <optional>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
#include <atomic>

// Bounded blocking queue. Two condition variables: one per condition.
template <class T>
class BoundedQueue {
    std::mutex m_;
    std::condition_variable not_empty_;   // consumers wait here
    std::condition_variable not_full_;    // producers wait here
    std::deque<T> q_;                     // GUARDED_BY(m_)
    const std::size_t cap_;
    bool closed_ = false;                 // GUARDED_BY(m_)
public:
    explicit BoundedQueue(std::size_t cap) : cap_(cap) {}

    // Blocks while full. Returns false if the queue was closed (item not enqueued).
    bool push(T item) {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m_);
        not_full_.wait(lk, [&] { return q_.size() < cap_ || closed_; });   // WHY loop: spurious/stolen
        if (closed_) return false;
        q_.push_back(std::move(item));
        lk.unlock();                 // WHY unlock first: the woken consumer can lock without a bounce
        not_empty_.notify_one();     // WHY one: exactly one consumer can proceed per item
        return true;
    }

    // Blocks while empty. Returns nullopt only when closed AND drained.
    std::optional<T> pop() {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m_);
        not_empty_.wait(lk, [&] { return !q_.empty() || closed_; });
        if (q_.empty()) return std::nullopt;        // closed and nothing left
        T item = std::move(q_.front());
        q_.pop_front();
        lk.unlock();
        not_full_.notify_one();
        return item;
    }

    // Timed pop: returns nullopt on timeout or on closed-and-drained.
    template <class Rep, class Period>
    std::optional<T> pop_for(std::chrono::duration<Rep, Period> d) {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m_);
        auto deadline = std::chrono::steady_clock::now() + d;   // WHY absolute: loop does not stretch
        if (!not_empty_.wait_until(lk, deadline, [&] { return !q_.empty() || closed_; })) return std::nullopt;
        if (q_.empty()) return std::nullopt;
        T item = std::move(q_.front());
        q_.pop_front();
        lk.unlock();
        not_full_.notify_one();
        return item;
    }

    // Close: no more pushes accepted; consumers drain what remains and then get nullopt.
    void close() {
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m_);   // WHY under the lock: closes the lost-wakeup gap
            closed_ = true;
        }
        not_empty_.notify_all();   // WHY all: every blocked consumer must re-check and exit
        not_full_.notify_all();    // every blocked producer must learn it will fail
    }
};

int main() {
    BoundedQueue<int> q(8);
    std::atomic<long> consumed_sum{0};
    std::atomic<int> consumed_count{0};

    const int producers = 3, consumers = 4, per_producer = 10000;

    std::vector<std::thread> cs;
    for (int c = 0; c < consumers; ++c)
        cs.emplace_back([&] {
            while (auto v = q.pop()) {               // loop ends on nullopt: closed and drained
                consumed_sum.fetch_add(*v, std::memory_order_relaxed);
                consumed_count.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
            }
        });

    std::vector<std::thread> ps;
    for (int p = 0; p < producers; ++p)
        ps.emplace_back([&, p] {
            for (int i = 0; i < per_producer; ++i) q.push(p * per_producer + i);
        });

    for (auto& t : ps) t.join();   // all items are in the queue or already consumed
    q.close();                     // consumers drain and exit
    for (auto& t : cs) t.join();

    long n = static_cast<long>(producers) * per_producer;
    long expected = n * (n - 1) / 2;   // sum of 0..n-1
    std::cout << "consumed " << consumed_count.load() << " items, sum " << consumed_sum.load()
              << " (expected " << n << ", " << expected << ")\n";

    // Timed pop on an empty, open queue
    BoundedQueue<int> empty(1);
    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto r = empty.pop_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(50));
    auto ms = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - t0).count();
    std::cout << "timed pop: " << (r ? "got value" : "timeout") << " after ~" << ms << " ms\n";
    return 0;
}

The shutdown protocol here is the one you will reuse in the thread pool (module 09): producers finish, close() flips a flag under the mutex and wakes everyone, consumers drain until the queue is empty and closed. No task is lost because pop returns nullopt only when both are true.

docs.title: wait as an atomic release-and-sleep
docs.text:
glibc's pthread_cond_wait:
