  1. Read the condition variable's sequence counter (__wseq), which counts signals issued.
  2. Unlock the mutex.
  3. futex(&cond->__g_signals, FUTEX_WAIT, expected_value). The kernel compares the word against expected_value atomically with enqueuing the thread. If a notify happened between step 1 and step 3, the word has changed, the futex call returns immediately, and no wakeup is lost. This is the mechanism that makes "check then sleep" atomic from the producer's point of view.
  4. On return (notified, spurious, or EINTR), re-lock the mutex with the normal mutex path (which may itself block if the notifier still holds it).
  5. Return to the caller, who re-checks the predicate.

glibc's implementation since 2.25 uses two "groups" of waiters to guarantee that a signal wakes a thread that was waiting before the signal, not one that arrived after (this was a correctness fix; the previous design could effectively steal a signal). The details are intricate; what you need is: notify increments a counter and does FUTEX_WAKE; wait sleeps on a futex only if the counter has not changed since it checked.

docs.title: Why wait needs unique_lock and not lock_guard
docs.text: wait must call unlock() and lock() on the lock object. lock_guard has neither member. This is a compile-time enforcement that the mutex is the kind that can be released mid-scope.

docs.title: Spurious wakeups are not a bug in your platform
docs.text: On Linux, futex returns EINTR when a signal is delivered; glibc returns from wait rather than restarting the futex, because restarting would require re-reading state under the lock anyway. Requiring the caller to loop is cheaper than requiring the library to guarantee no false returns. Windows SleepConditionVariableCS is documented the same way. Any design that requires "exactly one wake per notify" is fighting the primitive and will lose.

docs.title: Thundering herd
docs.text: notify_all on a condition variable with 64 waiters wakes 64 threads that then all try to take one mutex. 63 of them block again on the mutex. That is 64 context switches to deliver one item. glibc used to "morph" the condvar wait into a mutex wait inside the kernel (FUTEX_CMP_REQUEUE) to avoid this; current versions still use requeue in pthread_cond_broadcast. Even so, prefer notify_one when one waiter suffices, and prefer per-condition condition variables.

docs.title: Condition variable vs semaphore
docs.text: A counting semaphore (C++20 std::counting_semaphore, Win32 CreateSemaphore, POSIX sem_t) has state: a count. release increments; acquire blocks until the count is positive then decrements. It does not need a mutex or a predicate loop for the simple "N items available" case, and a release with no waiter is remembered. In C++17 you build one from mutex, condition variable and an int (exercise 3). A condition variable is the more general primitive because the predicate can be anything.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The pooled request model. Your server's "worker waits for request" is exactly pop() above. If it is built on an auto-reset Event, it has the two-signals-one-wake hazard: two requests enqueued in quick succession, one SetEvent coalesced, one worker woken, one request sits in the queue until the next signal. It is invisible under load (the next request arrives within milliseconds) and a mystery under light load (the last request of the day waits until morning). The fix on Win32 is a semaphore (count = items) or CONDITION_VARIABLE with a predicate loop; the fix in C++ is the queue above.
  • Shutdown that hangs. Workers blocked in wait and main joined them without ever notifying. Rule: every wait must have a shutdown predicate (|| closed_) and shutdown must set the flag under the mutex and notify_all.
  • Shutdown that loses work. closed_ checked before the queue in pop: if (closed_) return nullopt; ahead of if (!q_.empty()). Items pushed just before close are abandoned. The order in the code above (queue first, then closed) is deliberate. Interviewers ask about this; module 09 makes it the central design point of the thread pool.
  • Missing the lock on the flag. std::atomic<bool> stop; ... stop = true; cv.notify_all(); with a waiter checking stop in its predicate. The waiter reads stop == false, the setter sets it and notifies, the waiter then calls the internal wait: lost wakeup. Taking and releasing the mutex around stop = true (even for an atomic) is required.
  • 3 AM symptom: one worker's stack shows pthread_cond_wait while the queue has items. Either someone pushed without notifying (missing notify_one on a rarely used code path) or the predicate is wrong. Dump the queue size and the waiter count; if size > 0 and waiters > 0, the notify is missing.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run m05_producer_consumer.cpp. Replace not_empty_.wait(lk, pred) with the non-predicate not_empty_.wait(lk) and if (q_.empty()) return nullopt; after it. Run with 4 consumers; observe lost items or early exits. Done when you can name which of the three derivations caused the failure you observed.
  2. (easy) Move closed_ = true outside the lock_guard in close(). Run 50 times with a tiny queue and many consumers. It may or may not hang (lost wakeup). Add a 1 ms sleep between the predicate check and the futex wait if you want to force it (you cannot easily from outside; instead reason it through and write the interleaving). Done when the interleaving is written down with line numbers.
  3. (medium) Implement class Semaphore { void acquire(); void release(); } with mutex, condition variable and an int. Then implement a Win32-style auto-reset event on top of it (release only if count is 0, so repeated signals coalesce) and a manual-reset event (a bool plus notify_all). Done when a test shows the auto-reset version losing the second of two back-to-back signals while the semaphore does not.
  4. (medium) Add a size() and a waiting_consumers counter to BoundedQueue and a dump() that prints both. Deliberately remove the notify_one from push and show that dump() after the producers finish prints size > 0, waiters > 0. Done when you have the diagnostic output.
  5. (hard) Implement a WaitForMultipleObjects-style "wait for any" in C++17: a class EventSet where N sources each call signal(i) and one waiter calls int wait_any() which returns the index of a signalled source and clears it. One mutex, one condition variable, a std::bitset. Then explain why this design does not need notify_all and under what change it would. Done when a test with 8 sources and 1 waiter receives every signal exactly once.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why must condition_variable::wait be called in a loop that re-checks the condition? Three reasons: the standard permits spurious wakeups (the futex can return on a signal), a non-waiting thread can take the mutex and consume the state between the notify and the waiter's re-acquire (stolen wakeup), and notify_all wakes threads whose condition may be true for only one of them. The predicate overload encodes the loop.

Q: What is a lost wakeup and how does the condition variable API prevent it? A notify issued while no thread is waiting is dropped; if a waiter checked the condition just before and sleeps just after, it sleeps forever. The API prevents it by making "release the mutex and register as a waiter" atomic inside wait, so the producer cannot modify the condition in the gap as long as it modifies the condition under the same mutex.

Q: Why does the shared flag need to be modified under the mutex even if it is std::atomic? Because atomicity of the flag is not the problem; the problem is the window between the waiter's predicate check and its entry into the kernel wait. Holding the mutex while setting the flag means the setter cannot run inside that window. Without it the notify can fire before the waiter is registered.

Q: When do you use notify_all instead of notify_one? When more than one waiter may be able to proceed (shutdown, a batch insert, "not full" with several producers), or when waiters on the same condition variable have different predicates so a single wakeup might go to the wrong one. Prefer one condition variable per condition so notify_one is usually correct.

Q: How does a Win32 Event differ from a condition variable? An Event has state: a set that nobody is waiting for is remembered, and a manual-reset Event stays set. A condition variable has no state; a notify with no waiter is lost, so the state must live in your own variables under a mutex. An auto-reset Event coalesces two sets into one wake, which a counter-based condition variable design does not.

Q: What is the C++17 equivalent of WaitForMultipleObjects? There is none in the standard library. Portable designs route all events into one queue with one condition variable (an actor mailbox), use a composite predicate over several flags under one mutex, or use the OS I/O multiplexer (epoll, poll) for file-descriptor events.

Q: Describe a correct shutdown for a blocking queue. Set a closed flag under the queue's mutex, then notify_all on every condition variable. Consumers' predicate is "not empty or closed"; after waking they take an item if one exists and return "no more" only when the queue is empty and closed. Producers see closed and fail their push. This drains every item that was enqueued before close.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A condition variable lets a thread sleep until shared state changes; the mutex protects the state, the condition variable signals the change.
  • wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps; it re-acquires before returning.
  • Always wait in a predicate loop: spurious wakeups, stolen wakeups, and notify_all all require it. Use cv.wait(lk, pred).
  • Modify the condition under the mutex, even if it is atomic, or you risk a lost wakeup.
  • One condition variable per condition; notify_one for one-item changes, notify_all for shutdown and batch changes.
  • Unlock before notify (convention), use wait_until with a deadline in loops.
  • Events have state and coalesce signals; condition variables have no state. Win32 has CONDITION_VARIABLE since Vista; use it.
  • WaitForMultipleObjects has no std equivalent; use a single queue or epoll.
  • Shutdown: flag under the lock, notify_all, consumers drain then exit.

docs.title: 06. Deadlocks, livelocks and starvation
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 03, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A deadlock is two or more threads each waiting for something another one of them holds, forever. Thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2; thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1. Neither will ever release what it holds because neither will ever finish. The server stops accepting requests, CPU drops to zero, and nothing in the log says why.

Analogy: two cars meet on a one-lane bridge from opposite ends. Each waits for the other to back up. Both are being perfectly reasonable and nobody moves. A livelock is when both back up, both try again at the same moment, meet again, back up again, forever: lots of motion, no progress. Starvation is when the bridge has a priority rule and one car is always told to wait because a higher-priority car keeps arriving.

You have almost certainly seen a deadlock in your server: the one where every worker is "stuck" and the only fix was a restart. This module gives you the theory to prevent them, the discipline (a lock order document) to keep them prevented as the code grows, and the technique to find the culprit in a crash dump in minutes rather than hours.

docs.title: 2.1 The four necessary conditions (Coffman, 1971)
docs.text:
A deadlock can occur only if all four hold at once:

  1. Mutual exclusion: a resource can be held by one thread at a time. (Every mutex.)
  2. Hold and wait: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another.
  3. No preemption: a resource cannot be forcibly taken from its holder.
  4. Circular wait: a cycle of threads each waiting for a resource held by the next.

Break any one and deadlock is impossible. In practice:

  • (1) cannot be broken for a mutex; it is the point. You can reduce it with lock-free structures (module 08) or immutable data.
  • (2) is broken by acquiring all locks at once (std::scoped_lock, std::lock) or by never holding a lock while blocking on another (try_lock and back off).
  • (3) is broken by timeouts: try_lock_for gives up and releases what it holds. The lock is not preempted but the thread voluntarily releases.
  • (4) is broken by lock ordering: if every thread acquires locks in the same global order, a cycle cannot form. This is the standard production answer.

docs.title: 2.2 Lock ordering
docs.text:
Assign every mutex in the program a rank. A thread may acquire a mutex only if its rank is greater than every mutex the thread currently holds. Then a thread holding rank 3 can never wait for rank 1, and a thread holding rank 1 that wants rank 3 may wait for the first thread, but the first thread is never waiting for the second. No cycle.

Two variants:

  • Static order: a document (section 2.7) listing mutexes by rank. Enforced by code review and by a debug-build checker (section 2.3).
  • Dynamic order by address: when two locks are of the same kind and chosen at runtime (two Account objects), order by std::less<void*> on their addresses, or by a stable id. Or just use std::scoped_lock, which does not need an order.

docs.title: 2.3 Lock hierarchies with a runtime checker
docs.text:
A hierarchical mutex records, in a thread_local variable, the rank of the most recently acquired lock. On lock(), if the new mutex's rank is not greater than the current thread-local value, throw or abort. On unlock(), restore the previous value. In debug builds this turns a potential deadlock into an immediate, deterministic failure at the first wrong-order acquisition, even if the second thread needed for the actual deadlock never runs.

class hierarchical_mutex {
    std::mutex m_;
    const unsigned rank_;
    unsigned prev_rank_ = 0;
    static thread_local unsigned this_thread_rank;   // 0 = holding nothing; higher = outer
    void check() const {
        if (this_thread_rank != 0 && rank_ >= this_thread_rank)
            throw std::logic_error("lock hierarchy violated");
    }
    void update() { prev_rank_ = this_thread_rank; this_thread_rank = rank_; }
public:
    explicit hierarchical_mutex(unsigned rank) : rank_(rank) {}
    void lock()   { check(); m_.lock(); update(); }
    void unlock() { this_thread_rank = prev_rank_; m_.unlock(); }
    bool try_lock() { check(); if (!m_.try_lock()) return false; update(); return true; }
};
thread_local unsigned hierarchical_mutex::this_thread_rank = 0;   // but see the file for the
                                                                 // "ULONG_MAX means nothing held" variant

(Here lower rank is acquired later: hold 1000, may take 500, may not take 2000. The code file uses the convention "may only take a lower rank than you hold"; either is fine if documented.)

Clang's -Wthread-safety with ACQUIRED_BEFORE / ACQUIRED_AFTER attributes checks a static order at compile time. Valgrind's helgrind detects inconsistent lock orders at runtime without any code changes (module 12).

docs.title: 2.4 try_lock and back-off
docs.text:
When you cannot impose an order (two subsystems that each think they own the top rank), the fallback is:

for (;;) {
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> la(a);
    if (b.try_lock()) { /* have both */ ... b.unlock(); return; }
    la.unlock();
    std::this_thread::yield();   // or sleep_for a random few microseconds
}

This breaks hold-and-wait: the thread never blocks while holding. It risks livelock: two threads each take their first lock, each fail try_lock on the second, each release, each retry at the same instant, forever. Randomised back-off (sleep for a random 1 to 50 µs) makes the collision probability drop each round. std::lock does this internally, which is why scoped_lock is the better tool whenever both mutexes are known at the same call site.

docs.title: 2.5 Livelock and starvation
docs.text:
Livelock: threads are running, not blocked, but make no progress because they keep undoing each other. Symptoms: 100% CPU, zero throughput. Causes: try-lock loops without back-off, two threads each retrying a CAS that the other keeps invalidating, two protocol peers each waiting for the other to speak first with identical timeouts.

Starvation: a thread that is runnable and would make progress never gets the resource. Causes: a reader-preferring rwlock with continuous readers (module 04), an unfair mutex where a busy thread keeps re-acquiring before woken waiters get scheduled (lock convoy, module 03), a scheduler priority gap where a high-priority spinner never yields.

docs.title: 2.6 Priority inversion
docs.text:
A low-priority thread L holds a mutex. A high-priority thread H blocks on it. A medium-priority thread M, which needs no lock, becomes runnable and preempts L. Now H waits on L, L waits for CPU behind M. H is effectively running at M's priority: inverted. The Mars Pathfinder lander (1997) rebooted repeatedly from exactly this until a priority-inheritance flag was turned on remotely.

Fixes: priority inheritance (the mutex temporarily raises L to H's priority while H waits; PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT on Linux, automatic for Win32 kernel Mutex objects through the balance set manager's boosts, not available for CRITICAL_SECTION), priority ceiling (every lock has a ceiling priority; the holder runs at it), or simply do not use thread priorities in a server. Most request servers run every worker at the same priority precisely to avoid this class of problem. If you have a real-time thread (audio, trading), give it a lock-free path.

docs.title: 2.7 A lock order document for a server
docs.text:
Every multithreaded server of any size should have one. It fits on a page:

LOCK ORDER (acquire top to bottom; never acquire a higher line while holding a lower one)

 10  g_shutdown_mtx          process lifecycle flag; held for microseconds
 20  ConnectionTable::mtx    accept thread inserts; workers look up by fd
 30  Session::mtx            per-session; one at a time; never two sessions at once
 40  Cache::mtx (shared)     master-table cache; readers shared, refresh exclusive
 50  Metrics::mtx            counters; leaf lock; never call out while holding
 60  Logger::mtx             leaf lock; held only for the write(2); never call out

RULES

 - A "leaf" lock is one under which no other lock is taken and no callback is invoked.
 - Locks 50 and 60 are leaf locks. Anything that logs while holding 20..40 is fine because 60 > 40.
 - Never take any lock while holding a DB connection's lock (DB pool lock is 25) except 50, 60.
 - Two Session locks are never held together. Cross-session work goes through a message.
 - Any new mutex must be added here with a rank before merge.
 - Debug builds use hierarchical_mutex and will abort on violation.

The things that make it work: numbers with gaps (insert later), the leaf-lock concept (so logging and metrics can be called from anywhere), an explicit "never" for same-rank pairs, and a merge gate. Interviewers asking "how do you prevent deadlocks in a large codebase" want to hear this, not "I am careful".

docs.title: 2.8 Detecting a deadlock in a crash dump or a live process
docs.text:
Deadlocked processes do not crash; they hang. Capture a dump (Windows: Task Manager "Create dump file", or procdump -ma pid; Linux: gcore pid, or attach with gdb -p pid). Then:

gdb:

(gdb) thread apply all bt

WinDbg:

0:000> ~*k           ; stack of every thread
0:000> !locks        ; CRITICAL_SECTIONs that are currently owned, with owner thread id
0:000> !cs -l        ; locked critical sections with details

Procedure:

  1. Find every thread whose top frames are a wait: futex_wait, __lll_lock_wait, pthread_mutex_lock, pthread_cond_wait; on Windows NtWaitForSingleObject, RtlpWaitOnCriticalSection, RtlEnterCriticalSection, NtWaitForAlertByThreadId (SRWLOCK).
  2. For each, note which mutex it is waiting on. In gdb, go up to the frame that called lock() and print the mutex's address (frame 3, p &m_ or info locals). In WinDbg, the argument to RtlEnterCriticalSection is the CRITICAL_SECTION address, and !cs ADDR prints its owner thread.
  3. For each mutex, find who holds it. glibc pthread_mutex_t stores the owner's TID in __data.__owner (p *(pthread_mutex_t*)ADDR). WinDbg's !locks lists owners directly.
  4. Draw the graph: thread -> waiting on mutex -> held by thread -> waiting on mutex -> ... A cycle is your deadlock. Two threads is common; three or four happens.
  5. Read down each deadlocked thread's stack to find the application frames that took the first lock and are now trying the second. Those two code paths acquire in opposite orders. That is the bug and the fix is to make them agree with the lock order document.

If every waiting thread's mutex is held by a thread that is not waiting on a mutex but is in a recv, read, or database call: not a deadlock, but a lock held across I/O (module 03 rule). Same symptom, different fix.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m06_deadlock_demo.cpp

#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
#include <atomic>
#include <string>
#include <stdexcept>

struct Account {
    std::mutex m;
    long balance;
    std::string name;
    Account(std::string n, long b) : balance(b), name(std::move(n)) {}
};

// BROKEN: acquires in argument order. transfer(a,b) and transfer(b,a) in parallel will deadlock.
void transfer_broken(Account& from, Account& to, long amt) {
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> l1(from.m);
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::microseconds(10));   // WHY: widen the window so it reliably hangs
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> l2(to.m);
    from.balance -= amt; to.balance += amt;
}

// FIX 1: scoped_lock locks both with the std::lock algorithm; argument order is irrelevant.
void transfer_scoped(Account& from, Account& to, long amt) {
    std::scoped_lock lk(from.m, to.m);
    from.balance -= amt; to.balance += amt;
}

// FIX 2: a global order by address. Equivalent guarantee, shows the principle explicitly.
void transfer_ordered(Account& from, Account& to, long amt) {
    Account* first = &from; Account* second = &to;
    if (std::less<Account*>{}(second, first)) std::swap(first, second);   // WHY std::less: defined for unrelated pointers
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> l1(first->m);
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> l2(second->m);
    from.balance -= amt; to.balance += amt;
}

// FIX 3: try_lock with back-off. Breaks hold-and-wait; needs randomised sleep to avoid livelock.
void transfer_trylock(Account& from, Account& to, long amt) {
    for (int attempt = 0;; ++attempt) {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> l1(from.m);
        if (to.m.try_lock()) {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> l2(to.m, std::adopt_lock);
            from.balance -= amt; to.balance += amt;
            return;
        }
        l1.unlock();
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::microseconds(1 + (attempt * 7) % 13));   // crude jitter
    }
}

// A hierarchical mutex: debug-time enforcement of a lock order. Convention here: you may only
// acquire a mutex with a rank LOWER than the lowest you currently hold.
class hierarchical_mutex {
    std::mutex m_;
    const unsigned long rank_;
    unsigned long prev_ = 0;
    static thread_local unsigned long this_thread_lowest;   // ULONG_MAX = holding nothing
    void check() const {
        if (rank_ >= this_thread_lowest)
            throw std::logic_error("lock order violation: rank " + std::to_string(rank_) +
                                   " while holding " + std::to_string(this_thread_lowest));
    }
public:
    explicit hierarchical_mutex(unsigned long rank) : rank_(rank) {}
    void lock()   { check(); m_.lock(); prev_ = this_thread_lowest; this_thread_lowest = rank_; }
    void unlock() { this_thread_lowest = prev_; m_.unlock(); }
    bool try_lock() { check(); if (!m_.try_lock()) return false; prev_ = this_thread_lowest; this_thread_lowest = rank_; return true; }
};
thread_local unsigned long hierarchical_mutex::this_thread_lowest = ~0UL;

hierarchical_mutex high(10000), low(5000);

void correct_order()  { std::lock_guard<hierarchical_mutex> a(high); std::lock_guard<hierarchical_mutex> b(low); }
void wrong_order()    { std::lock_guard<hierarchical_mutex> b(low);  std::lock_guard<hierarchical_mutex> a(high); }

template <class F>
void run_pair(const char* label, F transfer, bool expect_hang) {
    Account a("A", 1000), b("B", 1000);
    std::atomic<bool> done{false};
    std::thread t1([&] { for (int i = 0; i < 2000; ++i) transfer(a, b, 1); });
    std::thread t2([&] { for (int i = 0; i < 2000; ++i) transfer(b, a, 1); });
    std::thread watchdog([&] {
        for (int i = 0; i < 300 && !done.load(); ++i) std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(10));
        if (!done.load()) {
            std::cout << label << ": DEADLOCKED (watchdog fired after 3 s). Attach gdb now, or ctrl-C.\n";
            if (expect_hang) std::_Exit(0);   // WHY _Exit: joining the deadlocked threads is impossible
        }
    });
    t1.join(); t2.join();
    done.store(true);
    watchdog.join();
    std::cout << label << ": ok, sum=" << a.balance + b.balance << '\n';
}

int main(int argc, char**) {
    run_pair("scoped_lock ", transfer_scoped, false);
    run_pair("ordered     ", transfer_ordered, false);
    run_pair("try_lock    ", transfer_trylock, false);

    correct_order();
    try { wrong_order(); } catch (const std::logic_error& e) { std::cout << "hierarchy caught: " << e.what() << '\n'; }

    if (argc > 1) {   // ./m06 hang  -> demonstrate the real deadlock for gdb practice
        std::cout << "running the broken version; this will hang...\n";
        run_pair("broken      ", transfer_broken, true);
    }
    return 0;
}

Run ./m06 for the fixes and ./m06 hang to produce a real deadlock. While it hangs, from another WSL terminal: gdb -p $(pgrep m06) then thread apply all bt. You will see two threads inside __lll_lock_wait under transfer_broken, each having passed the first lock_guard. That is the exercise in section 6.

docs.title: What a blocked thread looks like
docs.text: In Linux, a thread in futex_wait is in state S (interruptible sleep) in /proc/PID/task/TID/ stat, consuming no CPU. cat /proc/PID/task/TID/wchan shows futex_wait_queue. The scheduler has removed it from the run queue and placed it on the futex hash bucket's wait list. It will never be considered for scheduling until a FUTEX_WAKE on that address or a signal. That is why a deadlocked process shows 0% CPU and why kill -SEGV (to force a core dump) still works: signals interrupt the futex wait.

docs.title: Reading the owner out of a glibc mutex
docs.text:
(gdb) frame 4                   # the frame inside your code that called lock()
(gdb) p *(pthread_mutex_t*)&m_
$1 = {__data = {__lock = 2, __count = 0, __owner = 12345, ...}}

__lock = 2 means locked with waiters, __owner is the kernel TID (what info threads shows as LWP 12345). This is only populated for default and error-checking mutexes, which is what std::mutex uses on glibc. Match __owner to info threads and you have the holder.

docs.title: Why deadlock detection is not in the mutex
docs.text: PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK detects self-deadlock (locking what you hold) and returns EDEADLK. General cycle detection across threads would require every lock to record its waiters in a shared graph and run cycle detection on each blocking acquire: a global lock on every lock operation. Databases do this (PostgreSQL's deadlock detector runs when a lock wait exceeds deadlock_timeout, default 1 s, and aborts one transaction) because transaction locks are already expensive and rollback is possible. Mutexes cannot roll back. So detection is left to debug tools (helgrind, the hierarchical mutex) and to the human with a dump.

docs.title: std::lock's algorithm, precisely
docs.text: libstdc++ locks m1, then tries m2 ... mn in order with try_lock. On failure at mk it unlocks everything, then rotates so mk is the first to be fully lock()ed next round. Because the thread blocks on at most one mutex at a time while holding nothing else, hold-and-wait is never satisfied. The rotation reduces livelock: the mutex that was contended becomes the one we wait on, which is also the one most likely to be released soon.

docs.title: Watchdogs
docs.text: A production server should detect its own hang. A watchdog thread increments a heartbeat counter; each worker touches a per-worker "last progress" timestamp when it finishes a request; the watchdog checks that at least one worker progressed in the last N seconds while the queue is non-empty. If not: log every thread's state, dump the lock-owner table (if you record owners), write a core (abort() on Linux produces one with ulimit -c unlimited; MiniDumpWriteDump on Windows), and exit so the supervisor restarts. Thirty minutes of downtime become thirty seconds, and you get a dump to analyse in the morning.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The accept-thread / worker deadlock. Accept thread holds ConnectionTable::mtx to insert a new session and calls Session::init(), which takes Session::mtx. A worker holds Session::mtx to finish a request and calls ConnectionTable::remove() on close, which takes ConnectionTable::mtx. Order: 20 then 30 vs 30 then 20. The fix after the lock order document exists is obvious: remove() must be called after Session::mtx is released. Before the document exists, it is a week of "it hangs sometimes".
  • The logger that locks. Logger has a mutex. Someone adds a log line inside the cache's exclusive section. Someone else adds a cache lookup inside the logger (to print the current user). Deadlock across two unrelated subsystems. Rule: leaf locks never call out.
  • Database lock plus process mutex. Worker A holds a process mutex and waits for a database row lock. Worker B holds that row lock (in its own transaction) and waits for the process mutex. The database's deadlock detector does not see the process mutex, so it never fires. Rule: never hold a process lock across a database call (module 03).
  • The deadlock that is not one. All workers blocked on a mutex held by a thread that is blocked in recv() from a client that went silent. No cycle, but the same symptom. Fix: socket timeouts, and never hold the lock across the recv.
  • Timeouts as a last line. If a lock acquisition in a request path takes a timed lock and logs the lock name and holder on timeout, the first deadlock in production produces a log line that names both sides. Cheap insurance.
  • 3 AM procedure. Capture a dump before restarting. Always. The restart fixes the symptom; the dump is the only evidence. procdump -ma or gcore, then restart, then analyse in the morning with section 2.8.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m06_deadlock_demo.cpp, run ./m06, then ./m06 hang. Attach gdb and run thread apply all bt. Identify the two threads in __lll_lock_wait, the frame in transfer_broken for each, and which Account each holds. Done when you have written the cycle: "T1 holds A waits B; T2 holds B waits A".
  2. (easy) In gdb, print the owner field of the mutex each deadlocked thread is waiting on and match it to info threads. Done when the TIDs match your cycle.
  3. (medium) Write a three-thread deadlock: T1 takes A then B, T2 takes B then C, T3 takes C then A. Produce the hang, dump the stacks, and draw the three-node cycle. Then fix it with the lock order document approach by assigning ranks. Done when the fixed version runs 10,000 iterations without hanging.
  4. (medium) Remove the jitter sleep from transfer_trylock and replace it with a bare yield. Run with two threads on two cores pinned (taskset -c 0,1 ./m06). Measure throughput versus the jittered version. Done when you can show the livelock-prone version is slower or stalls, and explain why randomisation helps.
  5. (hard) Write the lock order document for a server you know (your real one, anonymised, or tcpkv extended with a connection table, a metrics block and a logger). Assign ranks, mark leaf locks, list every "never" pair. Then implement hierarchical_mutex for all of them in a debug build and write a test that violates the order and is caught. Done when the document is one page and the test fails deterministically.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What are the four conditions for deadlock and which do you break in practice? Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. In practice you break circular wait with a global lock order, or hold-and-wait with std::scoped_lock / std::lock or try-lock with back-off, or no-preemption with timed locks that give up and release.

Q: How do you prevent deadlocks in a large codebase? A lock order document: every mutex has a rank, locks are taken in increasing rank only, leaf locks never call out, and adding a mutex requires adding it to the document. Enforce in debug builds with a hierarchical mutex that aborts on the first out-of-order acquisition, and run helgrind in CI. Also never hold a lock across I/O or a callback.

Q: How do you diagnose a deadlock from a crash dump? Get every thread's stack (thread apply all bt, ~*k). Find threads blocked in a lock wait and which mutex each is waiting on. Find each mutex's owner (__owner in glibc's pthread_mutex_t, !locks in WinDbg). Draw thread -> mutex -> owner -> mutex; a cycle is the deadlock. The application frames above the waits show the two code paths that acquire in opposite orders.

Q: What is the difference between deadlock, livelock and starvation? Deadlock: threads blocked forever in a cycle, zero CPU. Livelock: threads running but undoing each other's progress, full CPU, zero throughput, typically try-lock loops without back-off. Starvation: a runnable thread never gets the resource because the policy always favours others, e.g. reader-preferring rwlocks or unfair mutexes.

Q: What is priority inversion and how is it solved? A high-priority thread waits on a lock held by a low-priority thread that is preempted by a medium-priority thread, so the high-priority thread effectively runs at medium priority. Solutions: priority inheritance (holder temporarily inherits the waiter's priority; PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT), priority ceiling, or avoiding thread priorities in servers altogether.

Q: Why does std::scoped_lock with two mutexes not deadlock, and when would you still use an explicit lock order instead? It uses std::lock: lock one, try the rest, release all and retry on failure, so it never blocks while holding another of the set. You still use an explicit order when the two locks are acquired at different call sites or in different functions, where no single scoped_lock can see both.

Q: A hung server shows all workers waiting on one mutex, and the owner is in a recv call. Is that a deadlock? No; there is no cycle. It is a lock held across blocking I/O. The owner will proceed when the peer sends or the socket times out. The fix is to never hold the lock across the call and to put a timeout on the socket. The diagnosis technique is the same: find the owner and see what it is waiting for.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait, all at once.
  • Lock ordering breaks circular wait and is the standard production prevention.
  • std::scoped_lock / std::lock break hold-and-wait for locks acquired at one site.
  • try-lock with randomised back-off breaks hold-and-wait at the cost of livelock risk.
  • Timed locks break no-preemption and turn hangs into logged failures.
  • A hierarchical mutex turns order violations into deterministic debug-build failures.
  • Write and maintain a one-page lock order document with ranks and leaf locks.
  • Diagnose from a dump: all stacks, who waits on what, who owns what, find the cycle.
  • Priority inversion: avoid thread priorities in servers or use priority inheritance.
  • Always capture a dump before restarting a hung server.

docs.title: 07. Atomics and the memory model
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
An atomic variable is one that every thread sees as a single, indivisible value: no torn reads, no lost updates on increment, and, critically, a way to say "when you see this value, you are also guaranteed to see everything I wrote before I stored it". That last part is the memory model, and it is the part most engineers get wrong.

The mental model that works is message passing. Think of a store with release semantics as sealing an envelope: everything the sender wrote before sealing goes into the envelope. A load with acquire semantics that reads that value is opening the envelope: everything in it is now visible to the reader. Nothing is promised about writes that happened after the seal, and nothing is promised to a reader who did not open the envelope. Relaxed atomics are postcards with no envelope: the value arrives intact, but nothing else is promised about what else you can see. Sequentially consistent atomics are envelopes that are also stamped by a single global post office so everyone agrees on the order all envelopes were sent.

You have used InterlockedIncrement and InterlockedCompareExchange. On Windows x86 those are full barriers (seq_cst). This module explains what you were getting for free, what it costs on ARM, and how to ask for exactly as much ordering as you need.

docs.title: 2.1 std::atomic<T>
docs.text:
#include <atomic>
std::atomic<int>   counter{0};
std::atomic<bool>  ready{false};
std::atomic<Node*> head{nullptr};

T must be trivially copyable. Operations:

Operation Meaning load(order) / operator T read store(v, order) / operator= write exchange(v, order) write, return old compare_exchange_weak(expected&, desired, ...) CAS, may fail spuriously compare_exchange_strong(expected&, desired, ...) CAS, fails only if value differs fetch_add / fetch_sub / fetch_and / fetch_or / fetch_xor read-modify-write, return old (integral and pointer types) operator++ / -- / += ... same, seq_cst is_lock_free() / is_always_lock_free does this use a hardware instruction or a hidden lock?

is_lock_free() is true for 1, 2, 4, 8 byte types on x86-64 and usually for 16-byte with -mcx16 (cmpxchg16b). For a 24-byte struct it is false: libatomic implements it with a hidden mutex (a hash of spinlocks keyed by address). A non-lock-free atomic is still correct, just not usable in signal handlers or where you were promised no blocking. static_assert(std::atomic<T>:: is_always_lock_free) when you depend on it.

docs.title: 2.2 Compare-and-swap
docs.text:
bool compare_exchange_strong(T& expected, T desired,
                             memory_order success, memory_order failure);

Atomically: if the current value equals expected, write desired and return true. Otherwise write the current value into expected and return false. This is the universal building block; every lock-free structure is a CAS loop:

int old = counter.load();
while (!counter.compare_exchange_weak(old, old * 2)) {
    // old has been updated to the current value; loop recomputes desired
}

compare_exchange_weak may return false even when the value equals expected (on LL/SC architectures like ARM, the store-conditional can fail because of an unrelated cache event). Use weak inside a loop (it is the natural fit and cheaper on ARM), strong when a spurious failure would make you take a wrong branch and you are not looping.

On x86 both compile to lock cmpxchg. On ARMv8 weak is ldaxr / stlxr once; strong is the same in a retry loop.

docs.title: 2.3 The six memory orders
docs.text:
enum class memory_order {
    relaxed, consume, acquire, release, acq_rel, seq_cst
};

Forget consume; no compiler implements it as specified (they promote it to acquire) and it is being redesigned. The five that matter:

Order Used on Promise relaxed any atomicity only. No ordering with other memory accesses. release store, RMW every write before this store (in this thread) is visible to a thread that acquire-loads the stored value. "Seal the envelope." acquire load, RMW every read or write after this load (in this thread) sees what the releasing thread wrote before its store. "Open the envelope." acq_rel RMW both: the RMW is an acquire for the load half and a release for the store half. For passing the envelope along a chain. seq_cst any acquire and/or release, plus a single total order of all seq_cst operations that every thread agrees on. Default.

The precise rule, which you should be able to state in an interview:

If thread A performs a release store to atomic x and thread B performs an acquire load of x that reads the value A stored (or a later value in x's modification order written by a release sequence), then A's release synchronizes-with B's acquire, and everything sequenced-before the release in A happens-before everything sequenced-after the acquire in B.

"Sequenced before" is the within-thread program order. "Happens before" is the cross-thread guarantee. A write that happens-before a read is visible to that read. That is the whole memory model in one sentence; the rest is consequences.

docs.title: 2.4 The canonical example: publish a result
docs.text:
int data = 0;                         // plain, non-atomic
std::atomic<bool> ready{false};

// producer                                   // consumer
data = 42;                                    while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}
ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release); assert(data == 42);   // guaranteed

Why it is correct: data = 42 is sequenced-before the release store. The acquire load reads true, which the release stored, so the release synchronizes-with the acquire. Therefore data = 42 happens-before assert(data == 42). The compiler may not move data = 42 below the release store, nor the data read above the acquire load, and it must emit whatever CPU instructions make the hardware honour that.

With relaxed on both, there is no synchronizes-with. The assert can fail: the compiler may reorder, or the CPU may (on ARM). The program is not a data race on ready (it is atomic) but it is a data race on data, because the write and read of data are unordered. Relaxed atomics do not create happens-before.

docs.title: 2.5 Relaxed: when it is enough
docs.text:
Relaxed guarantees: the operation is atomic, and all threads agree on the modification order of that one variable (you never see a counter go 5, 7, 6). That is exactly what a statistics counter needs:

requests_total.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);   // nobody reads other data based on this

Also enough for: a "stop" flag where the consumer only needs to eventually see it and does not read other data based on it; a sequence number generator; a reference count increment (you already hold a reference, so you are not publishing anything).

Not enough for: any flag that says "the data is ready", any pointer that is published for others to dereference, a reference count decrement that leads to delete (the deleter must see every write from every other previous owner: fetch_sub(1, acq_rel) or release plus an acquire fence before the delete; this is what shared_ptr does).

docs.title: 2.6 What seq_cst adds
docs.text:
Acquire/release gives you pairwise agreement: A and B agree about A's envelope. It does not give you a global order of unrelated envelopes. The store-buffering test from module 02:

std::atomic<int> x{0}, y{0};
// thread 1                              // thread 2
x.store(1, release);                     y.store(1, release);
int r1 = y.load(acquire);                int r2 = x.load(acquire);
// can r1 == 0 && r2 == 0?  With acquire/release: YES.  With seq_cst: NO.

With acquire/release each thread's store and load are to different variables and nothing synchronizes (no load read the other's store), so no happens-before edge exists and both can read

  1. With seq_cst, all four operations are in one total order; whichever store is first in it is visible to the other thread's load. Dekker's and Peterson's mutual exclusion algorithms depend on this, which is why they fail with acquire/release.

Rule: use seq_cst (the default) unless you have measured a cost and can write down the acquire/release argument for why the weaker order is correct. On x86 the only extra cost of seq_cst is on stores (an mfence or xchg instead of a plain mov); loads are free either way. On ARM both loads and stores pay.

docs.title: 2.7 Fences
docs.text:
std::atomic_thread_fence(order) is a standalone barrier. A release fence followed (later in program order) by a relaxed store makes that store act as a release; a relaxed load followed by an acquire fence makes that load act as an acquire. Use case: you have many relaxed operations and want one barrier instead of one per operation:

// producer: fill 1000 slots relaxed, then one fence, then publish
for (...) slot[i].store(v, relaxed);
std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_release);
published.store(true, std::memory_order_relaxed);

// consumer
while (!published.load(relaxed)) {}
std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire);
// all slot[i] visible

std::atomic_signal_fence is the compiler-only barrier (no CPU instruction) for ordering with a signal handler on the same thread. The old asm volatile("" ::: "memory") is the GCC equivalent.

docs.title: 2.8 Why volatile is not atomic
docs.text: Covered in module 02; the one-line version: volatile constrains the compiler's treatment of that variable's accesses and nothing else. No atomicity for multi-word types, no CPU fence, no ordering with other variables, no happens-before. MSVC's /volatile:ms extension gives acquire/release on x86 and ARM, which is why old Win32 code with volatile LONG flags works on MSVC and breaks on GCC. Replace with std::atomic.

docs.title: 2.9 x86 vs ARM
docs.text:
x86-64 (TSO) ARMv8 (weakly ordered) relaxed load / store mov ldr / str acquire load mov (free) ldar release store mov (free) stlr seq_cst load mov (free) ldar seq_cst store xchg or mov; mfence (expensive) stlr (+ dmb on some compilers) fetch_add any order lock xadd (full barrier always) ldxr/stxr loop or ldadd (ARMv8.1) with ordering flags CAS any order lock cmpxchg (full barrier) ldaxr/stlxr loop or cas full fence mfence dmb ish

Consequences: on x86 every RMW is already a full barrier so memory orders on fetch_add change nothing in the generated code; the only place you see a difference is seq_cst stores. On ARM every order choice changes the code and the cost. Code that is subtly wrong (relaxed where acquire was needed) passes on x86 and fails on ARM. Test on ARM if you can (a Raspberry Pi, an AWS Graviton instance, Apple silicon).

docs.title: 2.10 Mapping to Win32 Interlocked
docs.text:
Win32 C++ InterlockedIncrement(&v) v.fetch_add(1) + 1 (seq_cst) InterlockedExchange(&v, x) v.exchange(x) InterlockedCompareExchange(&v, desired, expected) v.compare_exchange_strong(expected, desired) (note argument order differs; Win32 returns the old value, C++ returns bool and updates expected) InterlockedExchangeAdd fetch_add InterlockedOr / And fetch_or / fetch_and InterlockedIncrementAcquire / Release fetch_add(1, acquire / release) InterlockedIncrementNoFence fetch_add(1, relaxed) MemoryBarrier() atomic_thread_fence(seq_cst) _ReadWriteBarrier() atomic_signal_fence(seq_cst) (compiler only) volatile with /volatile:ms acquire load / release store

All un-suffixed Interlocked functions are full barriers. The Acquire, Release and NoFence suffixed variants exist for ARM Windows where the difference matters.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m07_atomic_counter_orders.cpp — counter correctness and the cost of each order.

#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>

template <class F>
double time_ms(F f) {
    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    f();
    return std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - t0).count();
}

std::atomic<long> counter{0};

void bump(std::memory_order mo, int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) counter.fetch_add(1, mo);   // WHY: on x86 all orders emit lock xadd
}

std::atomic<long> seq_store_target{0};
void seq_stores(std::memory_order mo, int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) seq_store_target.store(i, mo);   // WHY: here x86 differs: mov vs xchg
}

int main() {
    const int threads = 4, per = 2'000'000;
    for (auto mo : {std::memory_order_relaxed, std::memory_order_acq_rel, std::memory_order_seq_cst}) {
        counter.store(0);
        double ms = time_ms([&] {
            std::vector<std::thread> ts;
            for (int t = 0; t < threads; ++t) ts.emplace_back(bump, mo, per);
            for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
        });
        std::cout << "fetch_add order " << static_cast<int>(mo) << ": counter=" << counter.load()
                  << " (expected " << static_cast<long>(threads) * per << ") " << ms << " ms\n";
    }
    for (auto mo : {std::memory_order_relaxed, std::memory_order_release, std::memory_order_seq_cst}) {
        double ms = time_ms([&] { seq_stores(mo, 50'000'000); });
        std::cout << "single-thread store order " << static_cast<int>(mo) << ": " << ms << " ms\n";
    }
    static_assert(std::atomic<long>::is_always_lock_free, "need lock-free long");
    struct Big { long a, b, c; };
    std::atomic<Big> big{};
    std::cout << "atomic<24-byte struct> lock free: " << (big.is_lock_free() ? "yes" : "no") << '\n';
    return 0;
}

File: code/m07_message_passing.cpp — the publish pattern, and the store-buffering litmus test showing acquire/release vs seq_cst.

#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <cassert>

// Part 1: publish non-atomic data through an atomic flag with release/acquire.
struct Payload { int a; int b; long c; };
Payload payload{};                       // plain data, written by producer before publish
std::atomic<bool> ready{false};

void producer() {
    payload = Payload{1, 2, 3};                           // sequenced-before the release store
    ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);        // seal the envelope
}
void consumer(long& out) {
    while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}    // open the envelope
    out = payload.a + payload.b + payload.c;             // guaranteed 6; no data race
}

// Part 2: store buffering. Count how often both threads read 0.
template <std::memory_order StoreMO, std::memory_order LoadMO>
long store_buffering(int iterations) {
    long both_zero = 0;
    for (int it = 0; it < iterations; ++it) {
        std::atomic<int> x{0}, y{0};
        std::atomic<int> start{0};
        int r1 = -1, r2 = -1;
        std::thread t1([&] {
            start.fetch_add(1); while (start.load() < 2) {}     // WHY barrier: both start together
            x.store(1, StoreMO);
            r1 = y.load(LoadMO);
        });
        std::thread t2([&] {
            start.fetch_add(1); while (start.load() < 2) {}
            y.store(1, StoreMO);
            r2 = x.load(LoadMO);
        });
        t1.join(); t2.join();
        if (r1 == 0 && r2 == 0) ++both_zero;
    }
    return both_zero;
}

int main() {
    long sum = 0;
    std::thread c(consumer, std::ref(sum));
    std::thread p(producer);
    p.join(); c.join();
    std::cout << "published sum: " << sum << '\n';
    assert(sum == 6);

    const int iters = 20000;   // thread creation dominates; keep modest
    std::cout << "store-buffering (release/acquire): both-zero " 
              << store_buffering<std::memory_order_release, std::memory_order_acquire>(iters)
              << " / " << iters << "  (non-zero is legal and happens on x86)\n";
    std::cout << "store-buffering (seq_cst):         both-zero "
              << store_buffering<std::memory_order_seq_cst, std::memory_order_seq_cst>(iters)
              << " / " << iters << "  (must be 0)\n";
    return 0;
}

The first number is often small but non-zero on a multi-core x86 (you need the two stores to be in flight at the same moment). Thread creation per iteration makes the window narrow; exercise 3 asks you to improve the harness. The second number is always 0.

docs.title: What the compiler emits (x86-64, GCC 13, -O2)
docs.text:
ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);  // mov BYTE PTR ready[rip], 1
ready.store(true, std::memory_order_seq_cst);  // mov eax,1 ; xchg al, BYTE PTR ready[rip]
ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire);         // movzx eax, BYTE PTR ready[rip]
counter.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);   // lock add QWORD PTR counter[rip], 1

The release store is a plain mov because x86 TSO already forbids a store from passing an earlier store or load. The compiler's job on x86 is mostly to not reorder across the atomic; the hardware does the rest. The seq_cst store needs xchg (which is implicitly locked and therefore a full fence) to prevent a later load from being satisfied before this store leaves the store buffer: the store-buffering case.

On ARMv8 the same four lines are stlr, stlr, ldar, and an ldaxr/add/stlxr loop (or ldadd on v8.1). Every ordering decision becomes an instruction choice.

docs.title: Cache coherence makes atomics possible
docs.text: All modern multi-core CPUs are cache coherent: at any instant, a given cache line has one agreed value across all cores (MESI protocol, module 10). Coherence is why a relaxed store is eventually seen by every other core and why all cores agree on the modification order of a single variable. What coherence does not give you is ordering between different cache lines. Core A may see line X's new value before line Y's new value while core B sees the reverse. Memory orders are about cross-line ordering; coherence alone handles single-variable atomicity.

docs.title: The store buffer and the invalidation queue
docs.text: Two hardware structures cause reordering. The store buffer holds stores waiting for cache-line ownership; later loads from the same core can complete before earlier stores drain (store-load reordering, allowed on x86). The invalidation queue on each core holds "your copy of line L is stale" messages that the core acknowledges before processing; a load can hit a stale line still in cache (allowed on ARM/POWER, not x86). A release store on ARM (stlr) waits for prior stores to drain; an acquire load (ldar) processes the invalidation queue before loading. On x86 the hardware does both implicitly for ordinary loads and stores, which is why only the store-load case needs mfence/xchg.

docs.title: lock prefix cost
docs.text: A lock-prefixed instruction must obtain the line in Exclusive state, perform the RMW with the line pinned, and (because it is a full fence) drain the store buffer. Uncontended, on a line already in L1: roughly 20 cycles (typical). Contended across cores: the line bounces, 100+ ns per operation (typical), and throughput falls as you add cores. That is why fetch_add on one shared counter from 16 threads is slower than from 1 thread, and why module 10 uses per-thread counters.

docs.title: Modification order and release sequences
docs.text: Each atomic variable has a single modification order all threads agree on. If A release-stores value 1, and then B does a relaxed fetch_add producing 2, and C acquire-loads 2, C still synchronizes with A's release: the RMW extends A's release sequence. This is what makes a reference count work: the thread that decrements to zero acquires the releases of all previous decrementers, not just the last one.

docs.title: Why the standard, not the hardware, is the contract
docs.text: Writing to the hardware model ("x86 is TSO, so relaxed is fine for this flag") is wrong even if the generated code would be right, because the compiler is bound only by the standard. A relaxed store gives the compiler permission to move data = 42 below it. GCC does this. The hardware never gets a chance to save you.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Statistics counters. Replace g_requests++ with std::atomic<long> and fetch_add(1, relaxed). Correct, portable, and cheap when read rarely. If 32 workers hammer it, it becomes a contended line; module 10 fixes that with per-thread counters.
  • Shutdown flag. std::atomic<bool> stop. Workers load(relaxed) in their loop condition is fine if they only exit on it. If they also read "final config" or "drain target" that the stopper wrote just before setting the flag, it must be release/acquire. When unsure, use the default seq_cst; a shutdown flag is read once per loop and the cost is irrelevant.
  • Published pointers. A config or cache snapshot swapped by ptr.store(new_table, release) and read by ptr.load(acquire). The acquire is not optional: without it the reader may see the pointer but not the table's contents (on ARM) or the compiler may hoist reads of the table above the load. Module 11 builds this.
  • Double-checked locking. The textbook broken pattern becomes correct with an acquire load on the fast path and a release store after construction, or you use std::call_once which does it for you (module 11).
  • Porting volatile LONG Win32 flags. Each one is a bug on GCC. Audit, replace with std::atomic, choose the order by asking "does anyone read other data based on this value?" If yes, release/acquire. If no, relaxed.
  • 3 AM symptom: a flag-based handshake works on the x86 build and the consumer reads garbage on the new ARM box. Nine times out of ten a relaxed store that should have been release. TSan (which understands memory orders) reports this on x86 even though x86 hides it at runtime.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run m07_atomic_counter_orders.cpp. Confirm all three orders give the correct count. Compare the store timings: relaxed and release should be similar, seq_cst slower. Dump the assembly (-S) and find the xchg. Done when you can point to it.
  2. (easy) In m07_message_passing.cpp, change the producer's store to relaxed and the consumer's load to relaxed. Build with -fsanitize=thread. TSan reports a data race on payload. Restore release/acquire; TSan is silent. Done when you can explain why TSan considers the relaxed version a race even though x86 would run it correctly.
  3. (medium) Improve the store-buffering harness: two long-lived threads with a shared atomic "round" counter, each iteration both threads spin until the round increments, then do their store/load, then signal completion. Run 10 million rounds. Report the both-zero count for relaxed, release/acquire, and seq_cst. Done when relaxed and acq/rel show non-zero and seq_cst shows exactly zero.
  4. (medium) Implement a reference-counted struct Shared { std::atomic<int> refs; Payload p; } with acquire_ref() (relaxed increment) and release_ref() (decrement; if it hits zero, delete). Choose the memory order for the decrement and write a comment deriving why acq_rel (or release plus an acquire fence) is necessary and relaxed is not. Done when the comment mentions "the deleter must see every other thread's writes to p".
  5. (hard) Write Peterson's mutual-exclusion algorithm for two threads with atomics. Use seq_cst and verify two threads incrementing a plain shared counter 1 million times each give exactly 2 million. Then change to release/acquire and observe (on x86 you may need many runs, on ARM it fails quickly) that mutual exclusion breaks. Explain in terms of the store-buffering test which reorder breaks it. Done when the explanation names the two stores and two loads involved.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Explain acquire and release. A release store seals everything the storing thread wrote before it into the stored value; an acquire load that reads that value unseals it, so everything the storer did before the release is visible to the loader after the acquire. Formally the release synchronizes-with the acquire and sequenced-before plus synchronizes-with gives happens-before. Nothing is promised to threads that do not load the value, and relaxed operations do not create this edge.

Q: What does seq_cst add over acquire/release? A single total order over all seq_cst operations that every thread agrees on. Acquire/release only orders the pair that actually communicated; two threads each storing to their own flag and loading the other's can both read the old value. Under seq_cst one store is first in the global order and the other thread's load must see it. Dekker's and Peterson's algorithms need this.

Q: When is memory_order_relaxed correct? When you need atomicity and nothing else: a statistics counter nobody makes decisions from, a sequence generator, a reference count increment where you already own a reference, a stop flag checked in a loop where no other data is read based on it. The moment another thread reads other memory because it saw the value, you need release on the writer and acquire on the reader.

Q: Why does std::shared_ptr use acq_rel (or release plus acquire fence) on the decrement? The thread whose decrement reaches zero deletes the object and must see every write every other owner made to it before releasing their reference. Each decrement releases that thread's writes; the final decrement must acquire all of them. Relaxed would allow the deleter to free memory that another core's writes have not yet reached.

Q: What is the difference between compare_exchange_weak and strong? Weak may fail spuriously, returning false even when the value matched, because on LL/SC architectures the store-conditional can fail for reasons unrelated to the value. Use weak in a retry loop (natural fit, cheaper on ARM), strong when a false failure would send you down a wrong path and you are not looping. On x86 both are lock cmpxchg.

Q: Why is volatile not a substitute for std::atomic? It only constrains the compiler's handling of that variable's accesses: no elision, no caching in registers, no reordering with other volatiles. It gives no atomicity for multi-word types, emits no CPU fences, imposes no order relative to non-volatile accesses, and creates no happens-before, so the program is still UB under the standard. MSVC's /volatile:ms adds acquire/release as an extension, which is why some Win32 code gets away with it.

Q: Why does the same memory-order bug pass on x86 and fail on ARM? x86 is TSO: hardware never reorders stores with stores or loads with loads, so acquire loads and release stores are plain movs and relaxed code often behaves as if it were acquire/release. ARM reorders almost everything unless told not to, so a missing ldar/stlr lets the hardware expose the reorder. The compiler can reorder on both, so even on x86 the relaxed version is a real bug that happens to be hidden most of the time.

Q: What does lock xadd cost and why does a shared counter get slower with more threads? The lock prefix requires the core to hold the cache line in Exclusive state for the duration and acts as a full fence. Uncontended on a local line it is tens of cycles; contended, the line migrates between cores on every increment at 100 ns or more each, so total throughput drops as cores are added. Per-thread counters that are summed on read avoid the shared line.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• std::atomic<T>: indivisible load, store, exchange, CAS, fetch-ops; is_lock_free tells you whether it is a hardware instruction or a hidden lock.
  • Release store + acquire load that reads it = synchronizes-with; sequenced-before plus that = happens-before; happens-before means visible.
  • Relaxed is atomicity only, no ordering; fine for counters and simple flags, wrong for publishing data.
  • seq_cst adds a single global order; needed when two threads each write their own flag and read the other's. It is the safe default.
  • acq_rel for read-modify-write that passes ownership along a chain; shared_ptr's decrement.
  • Fences let one barrier cover many relaxed operations.
  • volatile is not atomic; MSVC's extension is why Win32 code sometimes survives.
  • x86: acquire/release are free, seq_cst stores cost an xchg, RMWs are always full barriers. ARM: every order choice is a different instruction.
  • Interlocked* are seq_cst; Acquire/Release/NoFence suffixes map to the C++ orders.
  • The compiler is bound by the standard, not by your CPU; write to the standard.

docs.title: 08. Lock-free basics
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A lock-free data structure is one where threads coordinate using atomic instructions instead of mutexes, and where at least one thread is always guaranteed to make progress no matter what the others are doing. If a thread holding a mutex gets descheduled, everyone waiting on that mutex stalls. If a thread in the middle of a lock-free operation gets descheduled, the others simply retry and succeed. That is the appeal.

Analogy: a whiteboard where anyone may write, but the rule is "copy the current number, compute the new number, and write it back only if the board still shows the number you copied; otherwise start over". Nobody holds a pen exclusively, so nobody can walk away with it. But if two people keep colliding, both keep restarting, and if someone erases a number and writes the same number back while you were computing, your check passes even though the world changed under you. That last problem is called ABA and it is why lock-free code is hard.

The honest senior position: lock-free structures are rarely needed in a request server, they are easy to get subtly wrong, and a well-designed mutex-based structure with short critical sections is usually as fast. Learn the three classics (spinlock, SPSC ring, Treiber stack) so you can recognise them, reason about them, and explain why you chose not to use them.

docs.title: 2.1 Progress guarantees
docs.text:
• Blocking: a thread may wait indefinitely for another (mutexes).
  • Obstruction-free: a thread completes if it runs alone long enough.
  • Lock-free: at least one thread completes in a bounded number of steps system-wide. Some thread always makes progress; an individual thread may starve.
  • Wait-free: every thread completes in a bounded number of steps. The strongest; rare and usually expensive.

A CAS loop is lock-free: if your CAS fails, it is because someone else's succeeded. A spinlock is not lock-free (the holder can be descheduled and everyone spins); it is a blocking lock that happens to wait by spinning.

docs.title: 2.2 Spinlock
docs.text:
class Spinlock {
    std::atomic<bool> locked_{false};
public:
    void lock() {
        for (;;) {
            if (!locked_.exchange(true, std::memory_order_acquire)) return;   // got it
            while (locked_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) { /* pause */ }     // spin on a load
        }
    }
    void unlock() { locked_.store(false, std::memory_order_release); }
};

Memory orders: acquire on the successful exchange (so the critical section cannot start before we own the lock, and sees the previous owner's writes), release on unlock (so our writes are visible to the next acquirer). The inner loop spins on a load, not on exchange: an exchange is a write that steals the cache line from the holder every iteration and slows the unlock; a load lets the line sit in Shared state on every spinner until the unlock invalidates it. That is the test-and-test-and-set pattern.

The pause: _mm_pause() on x86 (#include <immintrin.h>) or __builtin_ia32_pause(), which tells the CPU to back off the spin loop for a few tens of cycles and avoids a memory-order violation pipeline flush on exit. On ARM use __asm__ volatile("yield"). After some number of spins (hundreds), fall back to std::this_thread::yield() or a real futex wait: a spinner on a single-core VM holding the CPU while the lock owner waits for the CPU is a livelock.

When a spinlock is right: critical sections of a few dozen instructions, known-low contention, and more cores than threads (so the holder is never descheduled mid-section). Kernel code, and very little else. The glibc adaptive mutex spins briefly then sleeps and is almost always the better choice in user space.

docs.title: 2.3 SPSC ring buffer
docs.text:
Single producer, single consumer. Because each index is written by exactly one thread, no CAS is needed; two atomic indices and release/acquire pairs are enough. This is the one lock-free structure worth memorising because it is genuinely simple and genuinely useful (log pipelines, audio, network packet hand-off between an I/O thread and a worker).

template <class T, std::size_t N>   // N power of two
class SpscRing {
    static_assert((N & (N - 1)) == 0, "N must be a power of two");
    alignas(64) std::atomic<std::size_t> head_{0};   // written by consumer, read by producer
    alignas(64) std::atomic<std::size_t> tail_{0};   // written by producer, read by consumer
    alignas(64) T buf_[N];
public:
    bool push(const T& v) {
        std::size_t t = tail_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);        // own index: relaxed
        std::size_t h = head_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);        // see consumer's pops
        if (t - h == N) return false;                                 // full
        buf_[t & (N - 1)] = v;
        tail_.store(t + 1, std::memory_order_release);                // publish the slot
        return true;
    }
    bool pop(T& out) {
        std::size_t h = head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        std::size_t t = tail_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);        // see producer's pushes
        if (h == t) return false;                                     // empty
        out = buf_[h & (N - 1)];
        head_.store(h + 1, std::memory_order_release);                // free the slot
        return true;
    }
};

Why it is correct: the producer writes buf_[t] before the release store of tail_ = t+1. The consumer's acquire load of tail_ that sees t+1 therefore sees buf_[t]. Symmetrically the consumer's release of head_ after reading the slot tells the producer the slot is free to overwrite. Indices are monotonic size_t that wrap naturally; t - h is the occupancy even across wraparound because unsigned subtraction is modular.

The alignas(64) puts each index on its own cache line so the producer's writes to tail_ do not invalidate the consumer's head_ line (false sharing, module 10). A common refinement is to cache the other side's index locally and only re-load it when the cached value says full or empty, cutting the cross-core traffic further.

docs.title: 2.4 Treiber stack and the ABA problem
docs.text:
A lock-free stack: push and pop by CAS on the head pointer.

template <class T>
class TreiberStack {
    struct Node { T value; Node* next; };
    std::atomic<Node*> head_{nullptr};
public:
    void push(T v) {
        Node* n = new Node{std::move(v), nullptr};
        n->next = head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        while (!head_.compare_exchange_weak(n->next, n,
                   std::memory_order_release, std::memory_order_relaxed)) {}
    }
    bool pop(T& out) {
        Node* old = head_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
        while (old && !head_.compare_exchange_weak(old, old->next,          // <-- reads old->next
                   std::memory_order_acquire, std::memory_order_acquire)) {}
        if (!old) return false;
        out = std::move(old->value);
        delete old;                                                          // <-- the problem
        return true;
    }
};

Two bugs hide in pop, and they are the whole lesson.

Bug 1: use-after-free. Thread A loads old = head (node X) and is about to read old->next. Thread B pops X and deletes it. A now reads freed memory. A mutex-based stack cannot have this problem because B could not pop while A held the lock. Lock-free structures have no critical section, so a node may be freed while another thread still holds a pointer to it. This is the memory reclamation problem and it is the real difficulty of lock-free programming.

Bug 2: ABA. Thread A loads old = X, reads old->next = Y. Thread B pops X, pops Y, pushes a new node that happens to be allocated at X's old address (allocators reuse hot addresses eagerly). Head is X again (same address, different node) and its next is now Z, not Y. A's CAS compares head to X, succeeds, and sets head to Y, which is freed. The stack is corrupt. The CAS checked the value of the pointer; it could not know the identity behind it changed and came back.

Fixes:

  • Tagged pointers / version counters. Pack a 16-bit counter into the unused high bits of the pointer (x86-64 user-space addresses use 47 bits) or use a 128-bit CAS (cmpxchg16b) on a {pointer, counter} pair. Every successful CAS increments the counter, so X-then-X-again has different tags. Fixes ABA; does not fix use-after-free.
  • Never free. Keep nodes in a free list owned by the stack; recycled, never returned to the allocator. Memory never becomes invalid, so the dereference in bug 1 reads stale-but-valid memory, and the tag fixes ABA. Common in fixed-size pools.
  • Hazard pointers. Each thread publishes "I am currently looking at node P" in a per-thread slot before dereferencing it, and re-checks that head is still P after publishing. A thread that wants to free a node first scans all hazard slots; if any thread has it marked, the free is deferred to a retire list and retried later. Bounded memory, lock-free, and the standard answer in interviews. C++26 is adding std::hazard_pointer.
  • Epoch-based reclamation / RCU. Threads announce when they enter and leave a "read epoch"; freed nodes are queued and only released when every thread has passed through a quiescent state. Cheaper per access than hazard pointers; higher memory latency. Module 11 uses the idea with shared_ptr.
  • shared_ptr with atomic operations. std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> (C++20) or the C++17 free functions std::atomic_load(&sp) give you reference counting instead of manual reclamation. Not lock-free in most implementations (a hidden spinlock) but correct and simple.

The code file includes the broken version (for TSan/ASan to flag) and a tagged, never-free version that is correct for a fixed pool.

docs.title: 2.5 MPMC queues: a warning
docs.text: A multi-producer, multi-consumer lock-free queue is where most engineers should stop. The well-known designs (Michael-Scott queue, Vyukov's bounded MPMC, LMAX Disruptor) each run to hundreds of lines with subtle invariants and all need a reclamation scheme or a fixed ring. In a request server, a std::mutex plus std::deque plus std::condition_variable queue handles hundreds of thousands of items per second and blocks consumers properly when idle. Lock-free queues spin or sleep-poll when empty, which is wrong for a thread pool. Use a library (moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue, boost::lockfree, folly) if you truly need one; do not write it.

docs.title: 2.6 When lock-free is not worth it
docs.text:
• Your critical section is more than a few dozen instructions. A CAS loop over a large update re-does the work on every collision.
  • You need to block when empty (every work queue). Lock-free gives you "return false"; you still need a condition variable or a futex to sleep, at which point the lock-free part bought little.
  • You cannot afford to get it wrong, and you cannot test on ARM. Lock-free bugs are the hardest class to reproduce.
  • Contention is low. An uncontended mutex is two atomics; a CAS loop is at least one. The gain is nil.
  • The structure needs delete. See bug 1.

When it is worth it: a single hot counter or flag (that is just std::atomic), SPSC hand-off between two specific threads, a spinlock in a tight kernel-style section, and a published immutable snapshot (module 11). Those four cover almost every legitimate use in a server.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m08_spinlock.cpp

#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
#include <mutex>
#if defined(__x86_64__) || defined(__i386__)
#include <immintrin.h>
static inline void cpu_relax() { _mm_pause(); }
#else
static inline void cpu_relax() { std::this_thread::yield(); }
#endif

class Spinlock {
    std::atomic<bool> locked_{false};
public:
    void lock() {
        for (int spins = 0;; ++spins) {
            if (!locked_.exchange(true, std::memory_order_acquire)) return;
            // Test-and-test-and-set: spin on a read so the line stays Shared across spinners.
            while (locked_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
                if (spins < 100) cpu_relax();                 // WHY: short back-off, holder is likely active
                else std::this_thread::yield();               // WHY: let a descheduled holder run
            }
        }
    }
    void unlock() { locked_.store(false, std::memory_order_release); }
    bool try_lock() { return !locked_.exchange(true, std::memory_order_acquire); }
};

template <class Lock>
double bench(const char* name, int threads, int iters) {
    Lock lk;
    long shared = 0;
    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < threads; ++t)
        ts.emplace_back([&] {
            for (int i = 0; i < iters; ++i) { std::lock_guard<Lock> g(lk); ++shared; }
        });
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    double ms = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - t0).count();
    std::cout << name << " threads=" << threads << " total=" << shared
              << " (expected " << static_cast<long>(threads) * iters << ") " << ms << " ms\n";
    return ms;
}

int main() {
    for (int t : {1, 2, 4, 8}) {
        bench<Spinlock>("spinlock  ", t, 1'000'000);
        bench<std::mutex>("std::mutex", t, 1'000'000);
    }
    return 0;
}

File: code/m08_spsc_ring.cpp — the ring buffer above with a throughput test and a checksum.

File: code/m08_treiber_stack.cpp — the naive stack (compile with -DBROKEN to see ASan/TSan catch it) and a tagged-pointer, pooled-node version that is correct.

Key part of the tagged version:

struct TaggedPtr { std::uint32_t index; std::uint32_t tag; };   // index into a fixed node pool
std::atomic<std::uint64_t> head_;   // packed TaggedPtr; 8 bytes, always lock-free

bool pop(T& out) {
    std::uint64_t old = head_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
    for (;;) {
        TaggedPtr h = unpack(old);
        if (h.index == NIL) return false;
        std::uint32_t next = pool_[h.index].next;            // WHY safe: pool memory is never freed
        TaggedPtr nh{next, h.tag + 1};                       // WHY tag+1: defeats ABA
        if (head_.compare_exchange_weak(old, pack(nh), std::memory_order_acq_rel,
                                        std::memory_order_acquire)) {
            out = std::move(pool_[h.index].value);
            free_node(h.index);                              // onto a second Treiber free-list
            return true;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Why test-and-test-and-set matters
docs.text: With N spinners doing exchange in a loop, every iteration on every core requests the line in Exclusive state. The line ping-pongs N ways; the holder's unlock store has to fight for it. With spin-on-load, after the first miss every spinner has the line in Shared state and spins entirely in its own L1. The holder's unlock invalidates all copies once; spinners miss once, reload, see false, and one wins the next exchange. Coherence traffic drops from O(N) per iteration to O(N) per unlock.

docs.title: Why _mm_pause
