docs.text: Tight spin loops on Intel trigger a pipeline flush when the loop exits because of speculative loads past the branch; pause hints the CPU to delay (tens to ~140 cycles depending on microarchitecture, per Intel's optimisation manual) and reduces power and the flush penalty. It also gives the sibling hyperthread the core. It is a hint; without it the spinlock is still correct.

docs.title: CAS loop fairness
docs.text: compare_exchange has no queue. Under contention the core that most recently touched the line tends to win the next CAS (the line is in its cache), so one thread can starve while others proceed. Lock-free is not fair. Ticket locks and MCS/CLH queue locks fix fairness for spinlocks; they are the standard answer to "how would you make a fair spinlock" and are worth reading about after this module.

docs.title: 128-bit CAS and is_lock_free
docs.text: std::atomic<TaggedPtr> where TaggedPtr is 16 bytes is lock-free on x86-64 only if compiled with -mcx16 (and GCC still may route it through libatomic for ABI reasons). That is why the code packs index and tag into 64 bits: a 32-bit index into a pool plus a 32-bit tag fits in one always-lock-free word. On ARMv8.1 there is casp for 128 bits; on older ARM you use ldxp/stxp.

docs.title: Hazard pointers, concretely
docs.text: Each thread owns K slots (usually 1 or 2) in a global array of std::atomic<void*>. To dereference node P: slot.store(P, seq_cst); if (head.load() != P) retry;. The re-check closes the window where P was freed between the load and the publish. To free node Q: push it onto the thread's private retire list; when the list exceeds a threshold R, scan all slots (O(threads * K)) and free the retired nodes not present in any slot. Amortised cost per retire is O(threads*K / R). Memory overhead is bounded by threads * K * R unreclaimed nodes. The seq_cst store on every read is the hot-path cost that RCU avoids.

docs.title: Why a mutex often wins
docs.text: An uncontended std::mutex lock+unlock is two atomic RMWs on one line, roughly 40 ns total (typical). A CAS loop for a stack push is one CAS when uncontended, roughly 20 ns. Under contention the mutex serialises (threads sleep, no wasted work) while the CAS loop wastes the losers' work and burns cache bandwidth. For critical sections longer than roughly 100 ns the mutex pulls ahead under contention. Lock-free wins only when the operation is tiny and you cannot tolerate a descheduled holder blocking others (real-time, signal handlers, kernel paths).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Spinlocks in user space are a bug until proven otherwise. The classic failure: a container limited to 1 CPU, a spinlock holder descheduled, 7 spinners burning the CPU the holder needs. Throughput near zero, CPU at 100%. If you inherit one, add a spin limit and yield, or replace with std::mutex.
  • SPSC for logging. A worker pushes log records into a per-worker SPSC ring; a single logger thread drains all rings and writes. Workers never block on disk, the logger never takes a lock. This is the right use of lock-free in a server, and moodycamel::ReaderWriterQueue is a battle-tested implementation if you do not want to own the code.
  • The "lock-free for performance" rewrite that got slower. Someone replaces a std::mutex protected std::vector<Order> with a hand-rolled lock-free list. It is faster in the single-thread microbenchmark and slower under 16-thread load because the CAS loop collides and the structure's traversal is cache-hostile. Always benchmark under realistic contention before and after.
  • ABA at 3 AM. A corrupted free list in a custom allocator after days of uptime. The signature is a crash in the allocator with a node pointing to itself or to a freed block, with no reproducer. If the allocator uses a CAS'd head pointer without a tag, you have found it.
  • Memory reclamation is the question. When an interviewer asks about a lock-free stack, the senior answer leads with "the push is easy; the pop is the problem because of reclamation and ABA, and here is how hazard pointers solve it". The junior answer writes the CAS loop and stops.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run m08_spinlock.cpp. Compare spinlock vs mutex at 1, 2, 4, 8 threads. Then run with taskset -c 0 (one core). Done when you have seen the spinlock's single-core collapse and can explain it.
  2. (easy) Build m08_spsc_ring.cpp, run, confirm the checksum. Change tail_.store(..., release) to relaxed and run under TSan. Done when TSan reports the race on buf_.
  3. (medium) Build m08_treiber_stack.cpp with -DBROKEN -fsanitize=address and run with 4 threads pushing and popping. Done when ASan reports heap-use-after-free in pop, and you have written the interleaving (which thread deleted what while which thread held it).
  4. (medium) Add local caching of the other side's index to SpscRing (producer caches head_ and only reloads when it believes the ring is full; consumer symmetric). Measure throughput before and after with perf stat -e cache-misses if available. Done when the number of acquire loads per operation drops and you can explain why it is still correct.
  5. (hard) Implement hazard pointers for the Treiber stack with real new/delete: one slot per thread, a per-thread retire list, scan at 2x thread count retired. Verify with ASan and TSan under 8 threads for 10 million operations. Done when both sanitizers are silent and you can state the memory bound.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does lock-free mean, precisely? At least one thread completes its operation in a bounded number of steps regardless of what other threads do, including being descheduled. Wait-free is stronger: every thread completes in bounded steps. A spinlock is not lock-free; a descheduled holder blocks everyone.

Q: Explain the ABA problem. A CAS checks that a location still holds the value you read, but a value can be changed and changed back. In a lock-free stack, a thread reads head X and X's next Y; another thread pops X and Y and pushes a new node at X's recycled address; the first thread's CAS sees X, succeeds, and installs Y, which is freed. Fixes: a version tag alongside the pointer so X-again has a new tag, or reclamation schemes that prevent the address from being reused while anyone holds it.

Q: Why is memory reclamation the hard part of lock-free structures? There is no critical section, so a thread may hold a pointer to a node while another thread frees it. The freeing thread must know nobody is looking. Hazard pointers have readers publish what they hold and freers defer nodes that are published; epoch/RCU schemes defer until every thread passes a quiescent point; or you never free and recycle from a pool.

Q: How does an SPSC ring buffer work without a CAS? Each index has exactly one writer. The producer writes the slot then release-stores the tail; the consumer acquire-loads the tail, so it sees the slot. The consumer reads the slot then release-stores the head; the producer acquire-loads the head, so it knows the slot is free. Monotonic unsigned indices with power-of-two masking handle wraparound, and each index lives on its own cache line.

Q: Why spin on a load rather than on an exchange? An exchange is a write and pulls the cache line into Exclusive state on the spinning core every iteration, stealing it from other spinners and from the holder trying to unlock. Spinning on a load leaves the line Shared in every spinner's cache until the unlock invalidates it once. This is test-and-test-and-set.

Q: When would you choose a mutex over a lock-free structure? Almost always in a server: when the critical section is more than a few dozen instructions, when consumers need to block on empty, when the structure needs to free memory, when contention is low so the mutex is uncontended anyway, or when you cannot test on weakly ordered hardware. Lock-free is for tiny operations where a descheduled holder is unacceptable.

Q: What is a hazard pointer? A per-thread published pointer saying "I am reading this node". Before dereferencing, a reader stores the pointer in its slot and re-validates that the node is still reachable. A thread retiring a node checks all slots and defers freeing any node that is published. It bounds unreclaimed memory to threads times slots times the scan threshold and is lock-free.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Lock-free: some thread always progresses; wait-free: every thread does. Spinlocks are neither.
  • Spinlock: exchange to acquire, spin on a load, pause, yield after a limit, release to unlock. Rarely right in user space.
  • SPSC ring: two single-writer indices, release on publish, acquire on observe, indices on separate cache lines. The one lock-free structure worth owning.
  • Treiber stack: CAS on head. Pop has use-after-free and ABA. Both come from the absence of a critical section.
  • ABA fixes: tags or never-free pools. Reclamation fixes: hazard pointers, epochs/RCU, reference counting.
  • 64-bit packed index+tag is always lock-free; 128-bit CAS needs -mcx16 and may not be.
  • MPMC lock-free queues: use a library or a mutex, do not write one.
  • Under contention a CAS loop wastes losers' work; a mutex serialises cleanly. Benchmark under real contention.
  • In interviews, lead with reclamation and ABA, not with the CAS loop.

docs.title: 09. Thread pools and task queues
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 03, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A thread pool is a fixed set of worker threads that sit waiting on a queue of tasks. Anyone who has work to do puts a task in the queue and, optionally, keeps a ticket (a future) to collect the result later. A worker takes the next task, runs it, and goes back to the queue. Threads are created once at startup, not per request, so a burst of ten thousand requests becomes ten thousand queue entries handled by thirty-two threads, not ten thousand threads fighting for eight cores.

This is the "pooled request model" of your application server, described in portable terms. The Win32 version uses CreateThread for the workers, a CRITICAL_SECTION around a linked list of requests, and an Event or Semaphore to wake workers. The C++17 version uses std::thread, std::deque, std::mutex and std::condition_variable, and adds two things C makes painful: a typed result that travels back to the submitter (std::future<T>) and exceptions that cross the thread boundary intact instead of becoming a return code that someone forgets to check.

The design question interviewers ask is always the same: how do you shut it down without losing a task and without hanging? This module answers it with a protocol you can prove correct.

docs.title: 2.1 Futures and promises
docs.text:
A std::promise<T> is the writing end; its std::future<T> is the reading end. The producer calls promise.set_value(v) or promise.set_exception(ptr); the consumer calls future.get(), which blocks until one of those has happened, then returns v or rethrows the exception. get() may be called once. future.wait_for(d) returns std::future_status::ready, timeout, or deferred.

std::promise<int> p;
std::future<int> f = p.get_future();
std::thread t([&p] { p.set_value(compute()); });   // or p.set_exception(std::current_exception())
int result = f.get();                                // blocks; rethrows if set_exception
t.join();

A std::packaged_task<R(Args...)> wraps a callable and a promise: calling the task runs the callable and stores its return value, or the exception it threw, into the promise. That is exactly the wrapper a thread pool needs: the worker calls task(), and whatever happens is delivered to the submitter's future. A worker never sees the exception; it cannot be killed by one.

std::shared_future<T> is a copyable future; many threads may get() it (each gets a copy of the value). Use it to broadcast a one-shot result (a "config loaded" signal, for instance).

Mapping to Win32: a future is a manual-reset Event plus a result slot plus an exception slot. You have built this by hand with a struct Request { HANDLE done; int rc; ... }. std::future is that struct with the lifetime problems solved.

docs.title: 2.2 std::async and why not to build a server on it
docs.text:
auto f = std::async(std::launch::async, work, arg);   // runs on a new thread, now
auto g = std::async(std::launch::deferred, work, arg);  // runs on the calling thread at g.get()
auto h = std::async(work, arg);                          // implementation chooses; usually async

Pitfalls:

  1. The future's destructor blocks. A future returned by std::async with launch::async waits for the thread in its destructor. std::async(std::launch::async, f); with the result discarded is therefore synchronous: the temporary future is destroyed at the semicolon and blocks until f finishes. This surprises everyone once.
  2. No pool. Every launch::async call creates a new thread (libstdc++) or uses a system pool (MSVC). Ten thousand calls is ten thousand threads on Linux. There is no bound and no queue.
  3. Default policy is unspecified. Without a policy, the call may be deferred and never run until get(), which with a wait_for loop means you poll forever on a deferred status.
  4. No cancellation, no priorities, no affinity.

std::async is fine for a one-off "do this in the background and give me the answer" in a tool. For a server, write or use a pool.

docs.title: 2.3 The fixed pool: design
docs.text:
submit(f, args...)
                            |
                            v   (lock m_; push; unlock; not_empty_.notify_one)
   +----------------------------------------------------------+
   |  deque<function<void()>>  tasks_     GUARDED_BY(m_)       |   bounded by max_queue_
   +----------------------------------------------------------+
        ^           ^           ^           ^
        |           |           |           |     (wait not_empty_ with predicate
    worker 0    worker 1    worker 2    worker 3       closed_ || !tasks_.empty())

Components:

  • std::vector<std::thread> workers_: created in the constructor, joined in shutdown().
  • std::deque<std::function<void()>> tasks_: type-erased tasks. std::function requires a copyable callable, and std::packaged_task is move-only, so each task is wrapped in a std::shared_ptr<std::packaged_task<R()>> captured by a copyable lambda.
  • std::mutex m_, std::condition_variable not_empty_ (workers wait), std::condition_variable not_full_ (submitters wait when the queue is at its bound).
  • bool closed_ under m_: no more submissions; workers drain and exit.

submit:

template <class F, class... Args>
auto submit(F&& f, Args&&... args)
    -> std::future<std::invoke_result_t<std::decay_t<F>, std::decay_t<Args>...>>
{
    using R = std::invoke_result_t<std::decay_t<F>, std::decay_t<Args>...>;
    auto task = std::make_shared<std::packaged_task<R()>>(
        std::bind(std::forward<F>(f), std::forward<Args>(args)...));
    std::future<R> fut = task->get_future();
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m_);
        not_full_.wait(lk, [&] { return closed_ || max_queue_ == 0 || tasks_.size() < max_queue_; });
        if (closed_) throw std::runtime_error("ThreadPool: submit after shutdown");
        tasks_.emplace_back([task] { (*task)(); });
    }
    not_empty_.notify_one();
    return fut;
}

Worker loop:

void worker_loop() {
    for (;;) {
        std::function<void()> task;
        {
            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m_);
            not_empty_.wait(lk, [&] { return closed_ || !tasks_.empty(); });
            if (tasks_.empty()) return;            // closed AND drained: the only exit
            task = std::move(tasks_.front());
            tasks_.pop_front();
        }
        not_full_.notify_one();                    // a submitter may be waiting on the bound
        task();                                    // packaged_task: exceptions go to the future
    }
}

docs.title: 2.4 Shutdown without lost tasks: the proof
docs.text:
void shutdown() {
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m_);
        if (closed_) return;
        closed_ = true;
    }
    not_empty_.notify_all();
    not_full_.notify_all();
    for (auto& w : workers_) if (w.joinable()) w.join();
}

Claim: every task that was successfully submitted before shutdown() returned is executed.

  1. A successful submit pushes the task into tasks_ under m_ while closed_ == false. closed_ is set under the same mutex, so the push and the close are totally ordered: every submitted task is in the deque at the moment closed_ becomes true.
  2. A worker exits only when it observes, under m_, tasks_.empty(). Since tasks are only removed by workers executing them, a worker observing an empty deque means every task has been taken by some worker.
  3. A worker that has taken a task executes it before returning to the loop; join() waits for the worker to return from worker_loop; therefore join() returning means that worker's task ran.
  4. notify_all after setting closed_ under the mutex wakes every waiting worker (no lost wakeup, module 05). A worker that is running a task will finish it and re-enter the loop, see closed_ or more tasks, and either take one or exit.
  5. Therefore after all joins, the deque is empty and every task that was in it has been executed.

The subtle part is the order in the predicate's consumer: check tasks_.empty() first, exit only if empty. The broken version if (closed_) return; before draining loses every task that was queued when shutdown began. Interviewers probe exactly this.

shutdown_now(), for the "abandon everything" case: set closed_, swap tasks_ with an empty deque under the mutex (the abandoned packaged_tasks are destroyed, which sets a std::future_error with broken_promise on every outstanding future so submitters do not hang), notify_all, join.

The destructor calls shutdown(). A pool destroyed with tasks still queued drains them. If you do not want that, call shutdown_now() first.

docs.title: 2.5 Exceptions crossing threads
docs.text:
std::packaged_task catches whatever the callable throws and stores it via promise.set_exception(std::current_exception()). The submitter's future.get() rethrows it on the submitter's thread with the original type. The worker thread is unaffected. Without this (a raw std::function<void()> that throws), the exception propagates out of worker_loop, out of the thread's entry function, and std::terminate() kills the whole process. A try/catch (...) in the worker loop as a last line of defence is reasonable; logging and continuing is the right policy for a server, because one bad request must not take down the other 63 workers.

std::exception_ptr is the type-erased handle: std::current_exception() inside a catch gives you one; std::rethrow_exception(p) throws it again anywhere. It is how you move an exception from a Win32 thread's DWORD rc world into a typed C++ error on the caller.

docs.title: 2.6 Backpressure
docs.text:
An unbounded queue turns a burst into unbounded memory growth and unbounded latency: the 10,000th request waits for 9,999 others. Bounding the queue forces a decision at submit time:

  • Block the submitter (the code above): the accept thread stops reading from sockets, TCP receive buffers fill, clients see slow connects. Simple, self-regulating, and what a C server with a fixed-size request array does implicitly.
  • Reject: try_submit returns false or throws; the caller returns "503 busy" immediately. Better latency for everyone who does get in. Required when the submitter is itself an I/O loop that must not block (module 11).
  • Shed load by priority: drop old items, or low-priority items. Needs a priority queue and a policy; rarely worth it below very high scale.

Whatever you choose, expose pending() as a metric. Queue depth over time is the single best health signal a pooled server has: rising depth means you are falling behind before latency alarms fire.

docs.title: 2.7 Sizing and variations
docs.text:
• Thread count from module 01: cores for CPU-bound, more for I/O-bound, from config.
  • One global queue is simplest and balances load perfectly. Per-thread queues with work stealing (each worker pops from its own deque, steals from others when empty) cut contention on the queue mutex at high task rates (millions per second) at the cost of complexity. A request server doing thousands of requests per second does not need it.
  • Task size: a task should be tens of microseconds or more; below that the queue overhead (lock, notify, context switch) dominates. Batch tiny tasks.
  • Never block a worker waiting on a future from the same pool: with all workers blocked waiting for tasks that are stuck behind them in the queue, the pool deadlocks. Rule: a task may submit to its own pool but must not wait on the result. Use continuations, a separate pool, or run the dependent work inline.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Files: code/m09_thread_pool.hpp (the pool), code/m09_thread_pool_demo.cpp (results, exceptions, backpressure, shutdown drain count), code/m09_async_pitfall.cpp (the blocking destructor and the deferred policy).

The header's public interface:

class ThreadPool {
public:
    explicit ThreadPool(std::size_t threads, std::size_t max_queue = 0);   // 0 = unbounded
    ~ThreadPool();                                   // calls shutdown(): drains, then joins

    template <class F, class... Args>
    auto submit(F&& f, Args&&... args)
        -> std::future<std::invoke_result_t<std::decay_t<F>, std::decay_t<Args>...>>;

    void shutdown();        // graceful: refuse new work, run everything queued, join
    void shutdown_now();    // abandon queued work (futures get broken_promise), join
    std::size_t pending() const;
    long completed() const;
    std::size_t size() const { return workers_.size(); }
private:
    void worker_loop(std::size_t index);
    ...
};

Demo excerpt:

ThreadPool pool(4, /*max_queue=*/16);

// 1. Results come back typed.
std::vector<std::future<long>> futs;
for (long i = 0; i < 100; ++i) futs.push_back(pool.submit([i] { return i * i; }));
long sum = 0; for (auto& f : futs) sum += f.get();           // 328350

// 2. Exceptions cross the thread boundary; the worker survives.
auto bad = pool.submit([] () -> int { throw std::runtime_error("bad request"); });
try { bad.get(); } catch (const std::runtime_error& e) { std::cout << "caught: " << e.what() << '\n'; }
auto good = pool.submit([] { return 7; });                   // same workers, still alive
assert(good.get() == 7);

// 3. Backpressure: with max_queue 16 and 4 slow workers, the 21st submit blocks.
// 4. Shutdown drains: submit 1000 quick tasks then destroy the pool; completed() == 1000 + earlier.

docs.title: What a std::future is
docs.text: std::future<T> holds a shared_ptr to a heap-allocated shared state: a storage slot for T or an exception_ptr, a ready flag, and a wait mechanism (libstdc++ uses an atomic plus a futex via __atomic_futex_unsigned; before that, a mutex and condition variable). set_value constructs the result, sets the flag with release semantics, and futex-wakes waiters. get() acquire-loads the flag, futex-waits if not ready, then moves the result out. Allocation: one per promise/future pair. That is cheap compared with a request but not free, which is why latency-critical pools sometimes use a custom task type without futures.

docs.title: packaged_task and type erasure
docs.text: std::packaged_task<R()> stores the callable in a type-erased buffer (small-buffer optimised, heap otherwise) plus a shared state. Our pool then wraps that in a std::function<void()>, which is a second type-erasure layer and possibly a second allocation. A production pool with a hot path typically defines its own UniqueFunction (move-only std::function) to remove one layer. C++23 adds std::move_only_function for this reason.

docs.title: Why the task runs outside the lock
docs.text: task() is called after lk is released. If it were called under m_, the pool would be single-threaded (one task at a time) and any task that submits to the pool would self-deadlock. This is the module 03 rule, "never hold a lock across a call-out", in its purest form.

docs.title: Wakeup cost and batching
docs.text: Each submit does lock, push, unlock, notify_one. If a worker is sleeping in futex_wait, notify_one is a FUTEX_WAKE syscall (about 1 µs) plus the woken thread's context switch and cache warm-up (several µs). At 100,000 submits per second that is a measurable fraction of a core. Optimisation when it matters: keep a count of idle workers and skip notify_one when zero are idle (they will find the task on their next loop), or submit in batches with one notify.

docs.title: Thread exit during shutdown
docs.text: join() on each worker in sequence is fine because every worker has already been told to exit; joining them serially just waits for the slowest. A worker still executing a 30-second task delays shutdown by 30 seconds. If that is unacceptable, tasks must be cancellable: check a std::atomic<bool> stop token periodically (C++20 formalises this as std::stop_token). You cannot kill a thread safely from outside; TerminateThread and pthread_cancel leave locks held and heap corrupted. Never use them in a server.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Your pooled request model, described portably. "Fixed pool of N worker threads created at startup. Acceptor thread reads a request from the socket and pushes it onto a bounded queue protected by a mutex; workers block on a condition variable. Each request carries a completion handle so the acceptor can reply. Shutdown closes the queue, drains in-flight work, then joins." This sentence is what the interviewer wants, and every element maps to a line in m09_thread_pool.hpp.
  • The blocking std::async destructor. std::async(std::launch::async, send_audit_log, rec); in a request handler, result discarded. It looks asynchronous. It is a synchronous call with the overhead of a thread creation. Found in code review by anyone who has read this module; found in production by a latency graph.
  • Worker self-deadlock. A task calls pool.submit(sub_task).get(). Under light load it works (a free worker runs sub_task). Under full load all N workers are inside tasks that are each waiting for a sub_task that is queued behind them. The server hangs with an empty CPU and a full queue. Rule: never get() inside a task on the same pool.
  • Lost tasks at shutdown. The C version checked a g_shutdown flag at the top of the worker loop and returned. Requests that arrived in the last 50 ms before shutdown were in the queue and never processed; the client got no response and retried against the new instance, double posting a loan disbursement. This is why the drain order matters.
  • Exceptions killing workers. A std::function<void()> task that throws in a pool without packaged_task or a catch (...) calls std::terminate. One malformed request takes down the server. Always wrap.
  • 3 AM symptom: queue depth climbing, CPU low, all workers in recv or a database call. The pool is sized for compute and the work is I/O. Raise the thread count or (module 11) move the I/O waiting onto an event loop.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m09_thread_pool_demo.cpp with the header and run it. Confirm the sum, the caught exception, and that completed() equals the number submitted after the pool is destroyed. Done when all three match.
  2. (easy) Build and run m09_async_pitfall.cpp. Measure the elapsed time around the discarded-future std::async call. Done when you have shown it is sequential.
  3. (medium) Break the shutdown: change the worker's exit test to if (closed_) return; before taking a task. Submit 1,000 tasks that each sleep 1 ms, then destroy the pool immediately. Print completed(). Done when you have observed lost tasks and restored the correct order.
  4. (medium) Add bool try_submit(F&&) that returns false instead of blocking when the queue is full, and a pending() sampler thread that prints queue depth every 100 ms during a burst of 10,000 submits. Done when the depth graph (just numbers) shows the bound being hit and the rejection count is non-zero.
  5. (hard) Reproduce the self-deadlock: 4 workers, each task submits a sub-task and calls get() on it; submit 8 outer tasks. Observe the hang, dump stacks with gdb, and explain why every worker is in futex_wait inside future::get. Then fix it two ways: (a) run the sub-task inline if the caller is a pool worker (thread_local bool in_pool), (b) use a second pool. Done when both fixes complete and you can state the rule.
  6. (hard) Implement a cooperative cancellation: ThreadPool holds a std::atomic<bool> stop_requested_; tasks receive a const std::atomic<bool>& and check it. shutdown_now() sets it before swapping out the queue. A long-running task (loop of 100 x 10 ms sleeps) must exit within 20 ms of shutdown_now(). Done when the measured shutdown time is under 50 ms.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Design a thread pool. What are the components? A fixed vector of worker threads, a queue of type-erased tasks guarded by a mutex, a condition variable workers wait on with the predicate "closed or queue not empty", and a closed flag for shutdown. submit wraps the callable in a packaged_task, pushes a copyable lambda holding it, notifies one worker, and returns the future. Workers pop under the lock, run the task outside the lock, and loop. Optionally a bound on the queue with a second condition variable for backpressure.

Q: How do you shut a thread pool down without losing tasks or hanging? Set closed under the queue mutex, notify_all, join every worker. Workers exit only when the queue is empty and closed, checked under the mutex, so every task pushed before close is popped and run. The notify under the mutex prevents a lost wakeup. The join waits for in-flight tasks. Checking closed before draining is the classic bug; it abandons queued work.

Q: How do exceptions cross from a worker to the submitter? std::packaged_task catches anything the callable throws and stores an exception_ptr in the shared state. The submitter's future.get() rethrows it on the calling thread with the original type. The worker thread never sees it. Without this wrapper an exception escapes the thread entry function and std::terminate kills the process.

Q: What is wrong with std::async in a server? The future's destructor blocks for launch::async, so a discarded result makes the call synchronous. Each call creates a new thread with no bound or queue. The default policy may be deferred, which never runs until get(). No cancellation. It is for one-off background work, not for request handling.

Q: What is backpressure and how do you implement it in a pool? Limiting queued work so a burst does not become unbounded memory and latency. Bound the deque; submit either blocks on a "not full" condition variable (self-regulating, pushes back to TCP) or returns failure so the caller can reply "busy" immediately. Expose queue depth as a metric; it is the earliest signal of overload.

Q: Why must a task never wait on a future from the same pool? If all workers are inside tasks that are blocked waiting for sub-tasks queued behind them, no worker is free to run those sub-tasks and the pool deadlocks with an idle CPU. Run dependent work inline, use continuations, or a separate pool.

Q: Why does the worker release the lock before running the task? Holding the lock would serialise all tasks and make any task that submits to the pool self-deadlock. The lock protects only the queue; the task is a call-out and must run unlocked.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A pool: fixed threads, mutex-guarded task deque, condition variable, closed flag.
  • packaged_task + future: typed results and exceptions cross threads; workers survive throws.
  • submit wraps in shared_ptr<packaged_task> because std::function needs copyable.
  • Shutdown: close under the lock, notify_all, workers drain until empty-and-closed, join. Check empty before closed.
  • shutdown_now swaps the queue out; abandoned futures get broken_promise.
  • Bound the queue; block or reject; publish depth.
  • std::async: blocking destructor, no pool, unspecified default policy. Not for servers.
  • Never get() on the same pool inside a task; never hold the queue lock while running a task.
  • Cancellation is cooperative; never terminate a thread from outside.
  • Your Win32 pooled request model is this design with Events for futures and a CS for the queue.

docs.title: 10. Cache lines, false sharing and performance
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Your CPU does not read memory one byte or one integer at a time. It reads 64-byte blocks called cache lines, and it keeps copies of recently used lines in small, fast caches next to each core. When two cores both have a copy of the same line and one of them writes to it, the other core's copy is thrown away and must be fetched again. That is correct behaviour (both cores always agree on the value) but it is slow: a fetch from another core's cache costs tens of nanoseconds, a hundred times more than a hit in your own L1.

False sharing is when two threads write to different variables that happen to sit in the same 64-byte line. Neither thread cares about the other's variable, but the hardware does not know that; it bounces the line between the cores on every write. Two per-thread counters declared next to each other can run ten times slower than they would with 64 bytes of padding between them.

Analogy: two clerks each keep their own tally on the same sheet of paper. Only one can hold the sheet at a time. They spend all day passing the sheet back and forth even though they never read each other's numbers. Give each clerk their own sheet and the problem vanishes. This module teaches you to recognise the shared sheet, measure it, and separate the sheets with alignas(64).

docs.title: 2.1 Cache hierarchy in numbers
docs.text:
Typical figures for a modern x86-64 server core (the shape matters more than the exact values; measure your own machine):

Level Size Latency Shared by L1 data 32 to 48 KB ~4 cycles (~1 ns) one core L2 1 to 2 MB ~14 cycles (~4 ns) one core L3 30+ MB ~40 to 70 cycles (~15 to 25 ns) all cores on the socket another core's L1/L2 (coherence miss) ~40 to 100 ns DRAM ~80 to 120 ns another socket's memory (NUMA) ~150 to 250 ns

The unit of transfer between every level is the 64-byte line. std::hardware_destructive_ interference_size (C++17, <new>) is the standard's name for "how far apart to put things to avoid false sharing"; on GCC x86-64 it is 64. Some recent Intel cores prefetch pairs of lines (128-byte "spatial prefetcher"), so 128-byte separation is sometimes used for the hottest data.

docs.title: 2.2 MESI in plain words
docs.text:
Every cache line in every core's cache is in one of four states:

  • Modified: this core has the only copy and it is dirty (newer than memory).
  • Exclusive: this core has the only copy and it matches memory.
  • Shared: this core has a copy, other cores may too, all match memory. Read-only.
  • Invalid: this core's copy is stale; must re-fetch before use.

Rules: to write, a core needs the line in M or E. If it is in S, it must broadcast an "invalidate" to every other core holding it (they go to I) and wait for acknowledgements, then it moves to M. If it is in I, it must first fetch the line ("read for ownership"). To read, S is enough; if the line is in I, fetch it from whoever has it (another core's cache or memory) and enter S.

That is the whole protocol at the level you need. The consequence: a line that is written by one core and read or written by another goes S -> I -> (fetch) -> S -> I -> ... on every alternation. Each transition is a coherence message across the on-chip network. A line that is only read stays S in every cache forever at L1 speed. A line that is written by one core and never touched by another stays M in that core's cache at L1 speed. The expensive case is exactly one: shared and written.

docs.title: 2.3 False sharing
docs.text:
struct Counters {
    long thread0_count;   // offset 0
    long thread1_count;   // offset 8   <- same 64-byte line as thread0_count
    long thread2_count;   // offset 16
    long thread3_count;   // offset 24
};

Four threads each incrementing their own counter: no data race (different memory locations), yet every increment invalidates the other three cores' copies. Measured slowdown versus padded counters is commonly 5x to 20x (typical; the benchmark in section 3 gives your number).

Fix:

struct alignas(64) PaddedCounter { long count; };   // sizeof == 64; each in its own line
PaddedCounter counters[4];

alignas(64) on the struct makes its size a multiple of 64 and its address 64-aligned, so consecutive array elements are on different lines. Alternatively pad explicitly: long count; char pad[64 - sizeof(long)];. C++17 also offers std::hardware_destructive_interference_size, but GCC 12 and later warn when you use it (-Winterference-size) because its value can change with -march/-mtune flags and silently give different struct layouts in different translation units. Under -Werror that warning is a build failure, so most production code simply writes 64.

Where false sharing hides:

  • Per-thread counters or flags in an array or a struct (the classic).
  • A mutex next to the data it protects when other threads read that data without the lock: not usual with a mutex, but an std::atomic<bool> stop flag sitting next to a hot counter is.
  • The head and tail of a queue (module 08's SPSC ring aligns them for this reason).
  • std::vector<std::atomic<int>> indexed by thread id.
  • Struct members where one is hot-written by one thread and another is hot-read by many.
  • Heap objects allocated back to back by different threads (allocators like jemalloc/tcmalloc use per-thread arenas partly for this reason).

docs.title: 2.4 True sharing
docs.text:
One counter incremented by all threads is true sharing: everyone writes the same variable. Padding cannot help. The fix is structural: per-thread (or per-core) counters, each on its own line, summed when read. Reads become O(threads) but writes stop contending. This is the "striped counter" or LongAdder pattern, and it is how every serious metrics library works.

class StripedCounter {
    struct alignas(64) Slot { std::atomic<long> v{0}; };
    std::vector<Slot> slots_;
public:
    explicit StripedCounter(std::size_t n) : slots_(n) {}
    void add(std::size_t tid, long d) { slots_[tid % slots_.size()].v.fetch_add(d, std::memory_order_relaxed); }
    long read() const { long s = 0; for (auto& x : slots_) s += x.v.load(std::memory_order_relaxed); return s; }
};

The read is not a consistent snapshot (slots may change while summing); for a metric that is fine. For an exact total you need a lock or a quiescent point.

docs.title: 2.5 Amdahl's law
docs.text:
If fraction s of a job is inherently serial and 1 - s is perfectly parallel, the speedup on N processors is

speedup(N) = 1 / (s + (1 - s) / N)

With s = 0.05 (5% serial), 8 cores give 5.9x, 64 cores give 14.5x, infinite cores give 20x. The serial fraction caps you. In a server, the serial fraction is whatever runs under one global lock: the queue mutex, the logger, the connection table. Every nanosecond under a global lock is in s. This is why "the lock is only held for a microsecond" matters when there are a million requests per second: that is one full second of serial time per second, s = 1, speedup 1.

Gustafson's counterpoint: as you add cores you usually also add work (more clients), so the parallel part grows and the serial part becomes a smaller fraction. True for throughput, not for the latency of a single request.

docs.title: 2.6 How to benchmark concurrency honestly
docs.text:
• Warm up. The first iterations pay for page faults, cold caches, thread creation, CPU frequency ramp. Run for a second before timing.
  • Steady state. Time a fixed duration (not a fixed count) and count operations, so slow configurations do not take forever and the measurement window is the same.
  • Pin threads (taskset, pthread_setaffinity_np, SetThreadAffinityMask) when measuring cache effects, so the OS does not migrate threads mid-run and smear the result. Report whether you pinned.
  • Repeat and report the distribution (min, median, p99), not one number. Variance between runs is itself a finding.
  • Control the machine. No browser, no indexer. On WSL, remember the host is also running.
  • Measure the right thing. Throughput (ops/s) and latency (time per op, percentiles) are different and often move in opposite directions. A server cares about p99 latency under a target throughput.
  • Use counters when available. perf stat -e cache-misses,L1-dcache-load-misses on Linux (not always available under WSL). On Windows, VTune or xperf.
  • Beware the compiler. A loop whose result is unused is deleted. Accumulate into a volatile sink or return the result from main.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m10_false_sharing.cpp

#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
#include <new>
#include <cstddef>

// The standard name would be std::hardware_destructive_interference_size, but GCC 12+ warns
// (-Winterference-size) that its value can differ between compiler flags, which breaks -Werror
// and can silently change struct layout across translation units. Production code pins 64,
// the cache line size on every current x86-64 and most ARM server cores. See code/m10_false_sharing.cpp.
constexpr std::size_t kLine = 64;

struct Packed  { std::atomic<long> v{0}; };                       // 8 bytes: 8 per line
struct alignas(kLine) Padded { std::atomic<long> v{0}; };         // one per line

template <class Slot>
double run(const char* label, int threads, std::chrono::milliseconds dur) {
    std::vector<Slot> slots(threads);
    std::atomic<bool> stop{false};
    std::vector<long> local(threads);
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < threads; ++t)
        ts.emplace_back([&, t] {
            long n = 0;
            while (!stop.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
                slots[t].v.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);   // WHY relaxed: pure counter
                ++n;
            }
            local[t] = n;
        });
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(dur);
    stop.store(true);
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    long total = 0; for (long n : local) total += n;
    double mops = static_cast<double>(total) / dur.count() / 1000.0;
    std::cout << label << " threads=" << threads << " sizeof(slot)=" << sizeof(Slot)
              << " : " << mops << " M increments/s\n";
    return mops;
}

// True sharing: all threads hit one counter.
double run_shared(int threads, std::chrono::milliseconds dur) {
    alignas(kLine) std::atomic<long> one{0};
    std::atomic<bool> stop{false};
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < threads; ++t)
        ts.emplace_back([&] { while (!stop.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) one.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed); });
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(dur);
    stop.store(true);
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    double mops = static_cast<double>(one.load()) / dur.count() / 1000.0;
    std::cout << "true-shared threads=" << threads << " : " << mops << " M increments/s\n";
    return mops;
}

int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono_literals;
    std::cout << "cache line assumed: " << kLine << " bytes\n";
    for (int t : {1, 2, 4, 8}) {
        run<Packed>("packed (false sharing)", t, 500ms);
        run<Padded>("padded (no sharing)   ", t, 500ms);
        run_shared(t, 500ms);
        std::cout << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Expected shape (your numbers will differ): padded scales nearly linearly with threads; packed is flat or falls as threads are added; true-shared falls hardest. The stop flag is read by every thread but written once, so it stays in S state everywhere and does not interfere.

docs.title: Coherence traffic for one false-shared increment
docs.text:
Core 0 does lock add [line+0], 1; core 1 does lock add [line+8], 1. Sequence on a MESI machine with both lines initially S:

  1. Core 0 sends invalidate for the line; core 1 acknowledges, marks I. Core 0 -> M, performs add.
  2. Core 1 needs the line: sends read-for-ownership. Core 0 must write back (or forward) its M copy and go to I. Core 1 -> M, performs add.
  3. Repeat.

Each step is a round trip on the ring/mesh interconnect: ~40 to 100 ns. An L1-resident increment is ~1 ns. Hence the order-of-magnitude penalty.

Real Intel cores use MESIF (F = Forward, to designate which sharer answers a request) and AMD uses MOESI (O = Owned, dirty but shared). The extra states reduce memory traffic; the S/I bouncing is the same.

docs.title: Why lock-prefixed RMW is worse than a plain store under sharing
docs.text: A plain store can retire into the store buffer and the core moves on; the coherence miss is paid asynchronously (until the buffer fills). A lock add must hold the line and complete before subsequent instructions retire (it is a full fence), so the core stalls for the entire round trip. Relaxed fetch_add on x86 is still lock xadd; the memory order does not help here. Only restructuring (per-thread slots) does.

docs.title: Store-buffer and prefetcher interactions
docs.text: Adjacent-line prefetching on Intel can pull in the neighbouring 64-byte line, so two padded variables on adjacent lines can still interfere slightly. That is the origin of 128-byte padding advice. Measure before paying double the memory.

docs.title: NUMA
docs.text: On a two-socket machine, memory is attached to one socket or the other. A thread on socket 1 writing to a line homed on socket 0 pays an extra hop. False sharing across sockets is roughly twice as bad as within a socket. numactl --hardware shows the topology; numactl --cpunodebind --membind pins. For a single-socket developer box this does not apply; for a production server it may, and "first touch" allocation (memory is homed where the thread that first writes it runs) is the rule to know.

docs.title: Measuring with hardware counters
docs.text: perf stat -e L1-dcache-load-misses,LLC-load-misses,instructions,cycles ./m10 shows miss counts; the false-shared run has orders of magnitude more LLC misses for the same instruction count. perf c2c (cache-to-cache) identifies false-shared lines by address in a real program. Intel VTune's "memory access" analysis does the same on Windows. If your WSL kernel lacks perf, run the binary on a native Linux box or reason from the timing.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Per-worker stats in an array. struct WorkerStats { long requests; long errors; } stats[64]; updated by each worker: 16 bytes per worker, four workers per line, false sharing on every request. Pad to 64 bytes. This is a ten-minute change with a measurable throughput gain at high request rates, and a good story for "a performance fix you made".
  • The global request counter. InterlockedIncrement(&g_requests) on every request from 64 workers is true sharing. At 10,000 requests per second nobody notices. At 1,000,000 the counter is a bottleneck. Striped counter.
  • The mutex and its data. A std::mutex (40 bytes) followed by the data it protects shares a line with it. That is fine and even good: the lock acquirer will need the data next. Padding between a lock and its data is a common mis-optimisation.
  • Measuring on the wrong machine. A 4-core laptop shows a 2x false-sharing penalty; the 32-core production box shows 15x. Scaling bugs appear with cores. Test on the biggest box you can get before concluding "it's fine".
  • Amdahl in a loan server. If every request takes a global "audit sequence number" lock for 2 µs, at 10,000 req/s the serial fraction is 2%; at 100,000 it is 20% and the box cannot scale past 5x no matter how many cores. Replace with per-thread sequence ranges or an atomic fetch_add (which is still true sharing but ~50 ns instead of a mutex's microsecond).
  • 3 AM symptom: throughput falls when you add workers. Almost always true or false sharing on a hot line, or a lock convoy. perf c2c or VTune finds the line; the fix is padding or striping.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run m10_false_sharing.cpp. Record the three series. Done when you have the ratio padded/packed at your maximum thread count.
  2. (easy) Change alignas(kLine) to alignas(32) and alignas(128). Done when you can explain the 32 result (two slots per line) and whether 128 differs from 64 on your CPU.
  3. (medium) Implement StripedCounter from 2.4 and compare add throughput against a single std::atomic<long> at 1, 4, 8 threads. Then measure read() cost. Done when you can state the trade-off in numbers.
  4. (medium) Pin threads with pthread_setaffinity_np (one per core) and re-run the benchmark. Compare variance across 5 runs pinned vs unpinned. Done when you have both variances.
  5. (hard) Take the ThreadPool from module 09 and add per-worker statistics (tasks run, total task time). Implement them packed and padded, drive the pool with 1,000,000 ten-nanosecond tasks, and measure throughput both ways. Then compute the serial fraction implied by the queue mutex using Amdahl: measure single-thread throughput and 8-thread throughput, solve for s. Done when you have s and a sentence on what dominates it.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is false sharing? Two threads writing to different variables that share a 64-byte cache line. The coherence protocol invalidates the line in the other core on every write even though the data is logically independent, so each access becomes a cross-core transfer of tens of nanoseconds instead of an L1 hit. Fix by placing hot per-thread data on separate lines with alignas(64) or padding.

Q: Explain MESI briefly. Each cached line is Modified (sole dirty copy), Exclusive (sole clean copy), Shared (clean, possibly in other caches), or Invalid. Writing requires M or E, so a writer invalidates all other copies first. Reading requires at least S. Lines that are read-only or written by a single core are fast; lines written by one core and touched by another bounce and are slow.

Q: How do you fix a hot shared counter? Stripe it: one slot per thread (or per core), each on its own cache line, updated with a relaxed atomic add; sum the slots on read. Writes stop contending; reads become O(threads) and are not an instantaneous snapshot, which is acceptable for metrics.

Q: What does Amdahl's law say about a global lock? Speedup is bounded by 1 over the serial fraction; time spent under a global lock is serial. A lock held for 2 µs per request is 2% serial at 10,000 req/s and 20% at 100,000, capping speedup at 5x. Shrink or shard anything held under a global lock on the hot path.

Q: Why does memory_order_relaxed not help a contended fetch_add? On x86 every atomic RMW is a lock-prefixed instruction, which is a full fence and must own the cache line regardless of the C++ order. The cost is the line transfer, not the ordering. Only restructuring to avoid the shared line helps.

Q: How would you benchmark a concurrent data structure honestly? Warm up, run for a fixed duration at steady state and count operations, pin threads, repeat and report a distribution, measure both throughput and latency percentiles, prevent the compiler from deleting the work, use hardware counters to confirm the mechanism, and test on a machine with as many cores as production.

Q: Is it a problem that a mutex shares a cache line with the data it protects? Usually not; the thread that acquires the lock will immediately need the data, so having both in one line saves a miss. Padding between a lock and its data is a common mistake. The problem is a hot-written variable sharing a line with data that other threads read without the lock.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Memory moves in 64-byte lines; L1 hit ~1 ns, cross-core transfer ~40 to 100 ns.
  • MESI: writing needs exclusive ownership and invalidates other copies; shared-and-written lines bounce.
  • False sharing: independent variables on one line. Fix with alignas(64) / padding.
  • True sharing: one variable, many writers. Fix with striped per-thread slots summed on read.
  • std::hardware_destructive_interference_size is the standard's name for the padding size, but GCC warns on it; pin 64 in practice.
  • lock-prefixed RMWs stall on the transfer; relaxed ordering does not help.
  • Amdahl: serial fraction caps speedup; global locks are serial fraction.
  • Benchmark at steady state, pinned, repeated, with percentiles, on a big machine.
  • Throughput falling as threads are added means sharing or a convoy; perf c2c finds the line.

docs.title: 11. Concurrency patterns for servers
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 04, 05, 07, 09

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
The primitives from modules 03 to 09 are bricks. This module is about the buildings: the handful of shapes that every production server takes, and how to choose between them. How do you map connections to threads? How do you let two hundred threads read a master table that changes every five minutes without a lock on every read? How do you initialise a shared object exactly once when ten threads ask for it at the same moment? How do you hand out database connections to workers without exhausting the database?

Analogy: a bank branch. Thread-per-connection is one teller per customer, hired when the customer walks in and fired when they leave. A thread pool is a fixed number of tellers and a queue. An event loop is one very fast teller who never waits: when a customer needs a form fetched from the back office, the teller takes the next customer and comes back when the form arrives. Each shape is right for a different branch.

Your server is the pool shape. Your master-table cache is the immutable-snapshot shape. Your database connections are the pool-of-resources shape. This module names them, shows their portable C++17 form, and tells you what to say when asked why you chose each.

docs.title: 2.1 Mapping connections to threads
docs.text:
Thread per connection. Accept, spawn a thread, that thread does blocking reads and writes for the life of the connection. Simple code: the handler reads like a single-threaded program. Cost: one thread (stack, kernel structures, context switches) per connection, unbounded, and mostly asleep. Fine to around a few hundred connections. Falls over at thousands.

Thread pool with blocking I/O (your server). Acceptor thread accepts and reads a request, pushes it to the pool; a worker processes it (including the database call) and writes the reply. Bounded threads, good for request/response protocols where each request is short and connections are many but mostly idle. Weakness: a worker blocked on a slow database call is a worker not serving anyone; sizing is a guess (module 01). Still the right default for a transactional backend with a few hundred to a few thousand connections.

Event loop (reactor). One thread (or one per core) calls epoll_wait (Linux), kqueue (BSD), or an I/O completion port (Windows) on thousands of sockets at once. When a socket is readable it reads without blocking, parses, and either replies immediately or hands CPU-heavy or blocking work to a pool. No thread ever blocks on a socket. Handles 100,000 connections on one box. Cost: the handler is a state machine, not a straight-line program; any blocking call in the loop stalls every connection. nginx, Redis, Node.js and every modern proxy are this shape. 08_Networking builds one.

Hybrid (the modern default). N event-loop threads (one per core) for all I/O plus a separate pool for blocking work (database calls, disk). Requests move between them via queues. This is what you would build if you rewrote your server today, and it is the answer to "how would you scale it to 50,000 connections".

Decision table:

Connections Request type Shape < 500, long-lived anything thread per connection is acceptable 500 to 5,000 short request/response, blocking DB pool (your server) > 5,000 or mostly idle anything event loop + pool for blocking work any CPU-bound compute per request pool sized to cores

docs.title: 2.2 Actors and message passing
docs.text:
An actor is a thread (or a task on a pool) that owns some state exclusively and communicates only through a queue of messages. Nobody else touches its state, so it needs no locks. The queue is a BoundedQueue<Message> from module 05 and the thread is while (auto m = inbox.pop()) handle(*m);. This is what a "logger thread", a "stats aggregator thread", a "connection manager thread" each are. Benefits: no shared-state races, no lock ordering because there are no locks, each actor is testable alone. Costs: every interaction is a copy or a move into a queue, latency of one queue hop per interaction, and a request that needs state from three actors becomes three messages and a correlation id.

Rule of thumb: state that is owned by one logical component and mutated frequently is a good actor. State that many components read and few write is a snapshot (next section). State that many components mutate is a lock, sharded if hot.

docs.title: 2.3 Immutable snapshots and read-copy-update
docs.text:
Your master-table cache: product codes, branch tables, rate matrices. Read on every request by every worker. Refreshed every five minutes by one thread. The reads vastly outnumber the writes and the data is small enough to copy.

Design: the cache holds a single std::shared_ptr<const Table>. Readers atomically load the pointer, use the table, and drop the pointer. The refresher builds a brand-new Table off to the side (unlocked, as slow as it likes), then atomically swaps the pointer. Readers who already hold the old pointer keep using the old table; when the last of them drops it, the shared_ptr deletes it. New readers get the new table. No reader ever blocks, no reader ever sees a half-updated table, and the writer's critical section is one pointer store.

class SnapshotCache {
    std::shared_ptr<const Table> current_;   // accessed only via the atomic free functions
public:
    std::shared_ptr<const Table> get() const {
        return std::atomic_load_explicit(&current_, std::memory_order_acquire);   // C++17 form
    }
    void publish(std::shared_ptr<const Table> next) {
        std::atomic_store_explicit(&current_, std::move(next), std::memory_order_release);
    }
};

C++17 provides std::atomic_load / std::atomic_store free functions overloaded for std::shared_ptr. C++20 replaces them with std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>. The acquire on load and release on store are the module 07 publish pattern: the reader who sees the new pointer sees the fully built table behind it.

Why not std::shared_mutex? Because even a shared lock is two atomic RMWs on one line per read (module 04); with 200 readers that line is hot. The snapshot read is one atomic RMW (the shared_ptr copy increments the control block's count) plus one at release. Still a shared line, but with no writer ever excluding readers, no starvation, and a refresh that never blocks a request. To eliminate even that count traffic, use RCU proper.

RCU (read-copy-update), the Linux kernel's version: readers mark "I am reading" with a per-CPU, cache-local operation (no shared line at all) and the writer, after swapping the pointer, waits for a "grace period": a point at which every CPU has passed through a quiescent state since the swap, guaranteeing no reader can still hold the old pointer. Then it frees the old copy. In user space, liburcu implements it; a simpler approach that captures most of the benefit is epoch-based reclamation: a global epoch counter, each reader records the current epoch on entry in its own padded slot, the writer retires old tables tagged with the epoch and frees them when every reader's recorded epoch is past it. shared_ptr swapping is "RCU with reference counting as the grace period" and is the pragmatic choice unless you are at millions of reads per second.

Costs and constraints of snapshots: the whole table is copied on every refresh (fine for megabytes every five minutes, wrong for a gigabyte every second); there is a window where two copies live; a reader that holds a snapshot for a long time holds the old memory. For a cache with frequent small updates (a session table), this is the wrong shape and a sharded shared_mutex map is right.

docs.title: 2.4 Double-checked locking and std::call_once
docs.text:
The problem: initialise a shared object lazily, once, on first use, from any thread, cheaply after the first time. The naive double-checked pattern:

Table* instance = nullptr;   // plain pointer: BROKEN
std::mutex m;
Table* get() {
    if (!instance) {                       // unsynchronised read: data race with the write below
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);
        if (!instance) instance = new Table();   // the compiler/CPU may publish the pointer
    }                                             // before the Table's constructor completes
    return instance;
}

Two bugs: the first read is a data race (UB), and even if it were atomic, a relaxed read could see the pointer before the pointed-to object's fields. Correct versions:

// 1. Atomic pointer with acquire/release.
std::atomic<Table*> instance{nullptr};
Table* get() {
    Table* p = instance.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
    if (!p) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);
        p = instance.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);   // under the lock: ordered by the mutex
        if (!p) { p = new Table(); instance.store(p, std::memory_order_release); }
    }
    return p;
}

// 2. std::call_once: the standard does the above for you.
std::once_flag flag;
Table* instance2 = nullptr;
Table* get2() {
    std::call_once(flag, [] { instance2 = new Table(); });   // exactly once; others block until done
    return instance2;                                        // call_once provides the happens-before
}

// 3. Function-local static (C++11 "magic static"): the compiler emits the call_once for you.
Table& get3() {
    static Table t;    // thread-safe initialisation guaranteed by [stmt.dcl]; one guard check after
    return t;
}

Use 3 when the object can be a static with a fixed lifetime (most singletons). Use 2 when the initialisation needs arguments or the storage is a member. Use 1 only when you need to replace the pointer later as well (then it is the snapshot pattern). If the initialiser throws inside call_once, the flag stays unset and the next caller retries; a thrown exception from a magic static's constructor does the same.

Win32 equivalent: InitOnceExecuteOnce with an INIT_ONCE structure (Vista+), which is exactly call_once.

docs.title: 2.5 Connection pools
docs.text:
A database allows a limited number of connections, and opening one costs a TCP handshake, TLS, and authentication (milliseconds). A pool of pre-opened connections handed out to workers is a resource pool: a bounded set, a mutex, a condition variable to wait when all are out, and an RAII handle that returns the connection on destruction.

class ConnectionPool {
    std::mutex m_;
    std::condition_variable available_;
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Conn>> idle_;   // GUARDED_BY(m_)
public:
    class Lease {   // RAII: returns the connection to the pool in its destructor
        ConnectionPool* pool_; std::unique_ptr<Conn> c_;
    public:
        Lease(ConnectionPool* p, std::unique_ptr<Conn> c) : pool_(p), c_(std::move(c)) {}
        ~Lease() { if (c_) pool_->give_back(std::move(c_)); }
        Lease(Lease&&) = default;
        Lease(const Lease&) = delete;
        Conn& operator*() { return *c_; }
    };
    Lease acquire(std::chrono::milliseconds timeout) {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m_);
        if (!available_.wait_for(lk, timeout, [&] { return !idle_.empty(); }))
            throw std::runtime_error("connection pool exhausted");   // WHY throw: fail fast, do not hang
        auto c = std::move(idle_.back()); idle_.pop_back();
        return Lease(this, std::move(c));
    }
private:
    void give_back(std::unique_ptr<Conn> c) {
        { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m_); idle_.push_back(std::move(c)); }
        available_.notify_one();
    }
};

Production additions: health check on give-back (discard a connection whose last query failed with a connection error), maximum age (recycle connections older than an hour to pick up DNS and failover changes), a timeout on acquire that is shorter than the client's request timeout, and metrics for in-use count and wait time. Pool size: at most the database's limit divided by the number of server instances, and often fewer; a database is rarely faster with 200 connections than with 32.

Rule interaction with module 06: never hold a process mutex while holding a connection (lock order puts the DB pool below everything but leaf locks), and never hold a connection while waiting for a pool lease (two leases per worker with a pool smaller than 2 x workers deadlocks).

docs.title: 2.6 Choosing
docs.text: Problem Shape many connections, short requests, blocking DB acceptor + pool (module 09) 10,000+ connections event loop + pool state owned by one component, mutated often actor with a queue read-mostly data, periodic refresh immutable snapshot, atomic shared_ptr swap read-mostly, frequent small updates sharded shared_mutex map lazy one-time initialisation magic static or call_once limited external resources RAII-leased pool with timeout hot counter striped per-thread atomics (module 10)

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m11_call_once_singleton.cpp — the three correct forms and a stress test that proves exactly one construction under 16 threads.

File: code/m11_rcu_snapshot_cache.cpp — the snapshot cache with 8 readers and 1 refresher, verifying every reader always sees a consistent table (a checksum stored in the table matches its contents), while the refresher's publish never blocks.

Key part of the snapshot cache:

struct Table {
    std::vector<long> rates;
    long checksum;                                  // consistency witness: sum of rates
    explicit Table(long version) : rates(1024), checksum(0) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < rates.size(); ++i) { rates[i] = version * 1000 + static_cast<long>(i); checksum += rates[i]; }
    }
};

class SnapshotCache {
    std::shared_ptr<const Table> cur_;
public:
    explicit SnapshotCache(std::shared_ptr<const Table> t) : cur_(std::move(t)) {}
    std::shared_ptr<const Table> get() const {
        return std::atomic_load_explicit(&cur_, std::memory_order_acquire);   // WHY acquire: see the table's contents
    }
    void publish(std::shared_ptr<const Table> next) {
        std::atomic_store_explicit(&cur_, std::move(next), std::memory_order_release);
    }
};

// reader
auto t = cache.get();              // one atomic refcount increment; no lock
long s = 0; for (long r : t->rates) s += r;
if (s != t->checksum) ++inconsistent;   // never happens
// t goes out of scope: refcount decrement; last holder frees the old table

// refresher
auto next = std::make_shared<const Table>(version++);   // slow build, unlocked
cache.publish(std::move(next));                          // one pointer swap: sub-microsecond median

docs.title: std::atomic_load(&shared_ptr) is usually not lock-free
docs.text: libstdc++ implements the shared_ptr atomic free functions with a small table of spinlocks keyed by the address of the shared_ptr object (_Sp_locker). The load takes the spinlock, copies the two pointers (object and control block), increments the control block's count, releases. So a "lock-free" snapshot read is actually a spinlock hold of a few nanoseconds plus one lock xadd. This is still far better than shared_mutex under heavy reads (the spinlock is held for ~4 instructions, never across anything slow) but it is not zero shared-line traffic. Two shared lines are written per read: the spinlock word and the control block count. Epoch-based RCU brings that to zero. C++20's std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> is implemented similarly in libstdc++; some implementations use a 128-bit CAS.

docs.title: Why the release/acquire pair matters even with shared_ptr
docs.text: make_shared<const Table>(v) runs the constructor, then the publish stores the pointer. Without release on the store the compiler may reorder the table's field writes after the pointer store (it cannot see that another thread will read through the pointer). Without acquire on the load, the reader on ARM may see the pointer and stale table contents. The shared_ptr control block's own atomics are about the count, not about your data. You need the explicit orders (or seq_cst).

docs.title: Magic static implementation
docs.text:
static Table t;

compiles to a 64-bit guard variable, an inline check of its first byte (acquire load; "already initialised" fast path, one instruction), and on the slow path a call to __cxa_guard_acquire, which takes a mutex (glibc uses a futex-based lock per guard), re-checks, runs the constructor, calls __cxa_guard_release (sets the byte with release semantics, wakes waiters). If the constructor throws, __cxa_guard_abort resets the guard so the next caller tries again. Recursive initialisation (the constructor calls get3()) deadlocks or throws; the standard says it is UB.

docs.title: std::call_once implementation
docs.text: libstdc++'s call_once historically wrapped pthread_once, which has a well-known limitation: an exception thrown from the initialiser could leave the once-control in a bad state on some versions. Since GCC 11 libstdc++ uses its own futex-based implementation to handle exceptions correctly per the standard. If you see std::call_once in a crash on an old toolchain, that is the history. For new code on GCC 13, both magic statics and call_once are correct.

docs.title: Grace periods in the kernel's RCU
docs.text: Classic RCU readers do rcu_read_lock(), which merely disables preemption (so no shared memory is written at all). The writer does synchronize_rcu(), which waits until every CPU has context switched at least once (a quiescent state); since readers cannot be preempted inside a read-side section, a context switch on every CPU proves no reader from before the swap is still running. Read cost: zero. Write cost: milliseconds of waiting. User-space liburcu approximates this with per-thread counters and a signal-based or periodic quiescent-state announcement. This is the end state of "readers must not write shared memory"; the shared_ptr snapshot is the 90% solution at 1% of the complexity.

docs.title: Why actors avoid the lock-order problem
docs.text: An actor never holds its own state's "lock" (it has none) while waiting for another actor; it sends a message and continues or returns to its queue. Hold-and-wait (module 06) cannot occur. The failure mode instead is a full mailbox: actor A's queue is bounded, A is blocked sending to B, B is blocked sending to A. That is a distributed deadlock across queues, and the fix is the same as for locks: an ordering (A never blocks sending to B if B may block sending to A) or unbounded mailboxes with a drop policy.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Describing your server. "Acceptor thread, fixed worker pool, bounded request queue, blocking database calls in the worker. Master tables in an immutable snapshot cache refreshed on a timer thread. Database connections leased from a pool with a timeout. Statistics in per-worker striped counters." Every noun in that sentence is a module in this course, and that is the description that gets you to the system-design round.
  • The refresh that locked the world. A master-table refresh under the table's CRITICAL_ SECTION took 400 ms (it re-queried the database inside the lock). Every request during those 400 ms waited. Snapshot swap: build the new table from the query result first, then swap. The exclusive section shrinks from 400 ms to one pointer swap: under a microsecond typically, a few hundred microseconds to milliseconds in the worst case when more threads than cores fight over the library's internal spinlock (see exercise 2).
  • The cache that returned references. const Rate& lookup(code) into a map that the refresh replaced. Dangling reference once per refresh under load. A snapshot shared_ptr held by the request for its lifetime makes this structurally impossible: the request's table cannot be freed while the request holds the pointer.
  • Lazy init that double-constructed. A connection-string parser called from two threads at startup, both saw nullptr, both constructed, one leaked and the other's construction raced with the first's use. Magic static.
  • Pool exhaustion as a hang. A worker that leaked a lease (forgot to return the connection on an error path) eventually drained the pool; every subsequent request blocked forever on acquire. RAII lease plus an acquire timeout turns a silent hang into a logged "pool exhausted" error with a stack.
  • 3 AM symptom: latency spike every five minutes. Timer-driven refresh under a lock. Snapshot swap fixes it, and the graph flattening is a satisfying before/after for your portfolio.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run m11_call_once_singleton.cpp. Confirm "constructed: 1" for each of the three forms under 16 threads. Then write the broken double-checked version with a plain pointer and run it under TSan. Done when TSan reports the race.
  2. (easy) Build and run m11_rcu_snapshot_cache.cpp twice: ./m11_rcu_snapshot_cache 3 and ./m11_rcu_snapshot_cache 8. Confirm zero inconsistent reads both times. Compare the publish median and p99. On a 4-core laptop (measured on WSL, GCC 13) the median stays below a microsecond, but with 8 readers p99 jumps to milliseconds because readers outnumber cores and contend on libstdc++'s internal spinlock. Done when you can explain why the tail grows and the median does not.
  3. (medium) Replace the snapshot cache with a std::shared_mutex-guarded table that the refresher rebuilds in place under the exclusive lock (the slow way). Measure reader p99 latency with and without the refresher running. Compare to the snapshot version. Done when you have the two p99 numbers and the ratio.
  4. (medium) Implement the ConnectionPool from 2.5 with a fake Conn that sleeps 1 ms per "query". 16 workers, pool of 4, acquire timeout 50 ms. Count successful queries and timeouts over 2 seconds. Then leak one lease on purpose and watch the pool degrade. Done when the leak is visible in the in-use metric.
  5. (hard) Build a two-actor system: a Parser actor that receives raw strings, parses them to Order structs, and sends them to an Accountant actor that keeps per-account balances and answers Query messages by replying through a std::promise. Both have bounded mailboxes. Drive it with 4 producer threads. Then make the mailboxes small (2) and construct a mailbox-deadlock between the actors; explain it in terms of hold-and-wait. Done when both the working system and the deliberate deadlock are demonstrated.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Thread per connection, thread pool, or event loop? Thread per connection is simplest and fine below a few hundred connections. A pool bounds threads and suits short request/response with blocking back-end calls at thousands of connections. An event loop handles tens of thousands of mostly idle connections on a few threads but requires non-blocking handlers; the modern default is event loops for I/O plus a pool for blocking work.

Q: How do you share a read-mostly table with hundreds of threads without a lock on every read? Hold it behind an atomically swapped shared_ptr<const Table>. Readers acquire-load the pointer and use that immutable snapshot; the refresher builds a new table off to the side and release-stores the pointer. Readers never block or see partial state; the old table is freed when the last reader drops it. Real RCU goes further by making the read side write no shared memory at all.

Q: Why is classic double-checked locking broken, and what is the fix? The unlocked first read of a plain pointer is a data race, and even if atomic, without acquire it may observe the pointer before the object's fields on weakly ordered hardware (or because the compiler reordered the constructor's stores). Fix: std::atomic with acquire on the fast-path load and release on the store, or std::call_once, or a function-local static, which the compiler implements with exactly that protocol.

Q: How does a function-local static achieve thread-safe initialisation? The compiler emits a guard variable, an inline acquire check on the fast path, and on the slow path __cxa_guard_acquire, which takes a lock, re-checks, runs the constructor, and releases with a release store. Exactly one thread constructs; others block until it is done; a throwing constructor resets the guard so the next call retries.

Q: Design a database connection pool. A bounded set of pre-opened connections behind a mutex and a condition variable. acquire waits with a timeout and throws on exhaustion rather than hanging; it returns an RAII lease that gives the connection back on destruction so error paths cannot leak. Add health checks on return, a maximum connection age, in-use and wait-time metrics, and size it below the database's limit.

Q: What is an actor and when would you use one? A component that owns its state exclusively and interacts only through a message queue, so it needs no locks and cannot participate in a lock-order deadlock. Use it for state owned by one logical component and mutated frequently, such as a logger, a stats aggregator, or a connection manager. The cost is a queue hop per interaction and bounded mailboxes that can deadlock each other if two actors block sending to one another.

Q: Is std::atomic_load on a shared_ptr lock-free? Usually not; libstdc++ uses a small table of spinlocks keyed by the shared_ptr's address, so the load is a few nanoseconds of spinlock plus an atomic count increment. It is still far cheaper under heavy reads than a shared_mutex and never blocks readers for the duration of a refresh.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Connection shapes: thread-per-connection (small), pool (your server), event loop + pool (large).
  • Actors own state and communicate by queue; no locks, no lock order, but mailbox deadlocks exist.
  • Read-mostly, periodically refreshed data: immutable snapshot behind an atomically swapped shared_ptr<const T> with release/acquire. Refresh becomes a pointer store.
  • RCU is the same idea with a grace period instead of reference counting; liburcu or epochs when reference counts are too hot.
  • Lazy init: magic static first, call_once second, atomic pointer with acquire/release only when you also need replacement.
  • Connection pools: bounded, RAII lease, acquire timeout, health check, max age, metrics.
  • Never hold a process lock across a leased connection; never take two leases per worker.
  • shared_ptr atomic functions are spinlock-backed in libstdc++; still much better than a reader-writer lock under heavy reads.
  • Describe your server in these nouns: acceptor, pool, bounded queue, snapshot cache, connection pool, striped counters.

docs.title: 12. Debugging concurrency bugs
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 06, 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Concurrency bugs are the worst class of bug because they do not reproduce. The code is correct almost all the time; it fails when two threads hit a two-instruction window at the same moment, which happens once a day in production and never on your laptop.
