docs.title: 2.2 Threads
docs.text:
#include <windows.h>
#include <process.h>

unsigned __stdcall worker(void* arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;
    /* ... */
    return 0;
}

HANDLE h = (HANDLE)_beginthreadex(NULL, 0, worker, &id, 0, NULL);
WaitForSingleObject(h, INFINITE);
CloseHandle(h);

_beginthreadex versus CreateThread: the CRT (errno, strtok state, locale, C++ exception state) is per-thread and _beginthreadex initialises it; CreateThread from C code that uses the CRT historically leaked that state. MSVC's std::thread uses _beginthreadex.

GetExitCodeThread retrieves the return value after the thread ends. In C++ terms that is the future (module 09).

docs.title: 2.3 CRITICAL_SECTION
docs.text:
CRITICAL_SECTION cs;
InitializeCriticalSectionAndSpinCount(&cs, 4000);   /* spin ~4000 iterations before blocking */
EnterCriticalSection(&cs);
/* ... */
LeaveCriticalSection(&cs);
DeleteCriticalSection(&cs);

Structure (RTL_CRITICAL_SECTION): LockCount (encoded: locked bit, waiters count, wake flag), RecursionCount, OwningThread, LockSemaphore (the kernel wait object, allocated lazily on first contention), SpinCount. Fast path: InterlockedCompareExchange on LockCount. Contended: spin SpinCount times, then wait on the lazily created event / keyed event. Recursive: the owner re-entering increments RecursionCount.

Portable description: "a recursive user-mode mutex with an adaptive spin before blocking". C++ equivalent for most uses: std::mutex after you have removed the recursive entries (module 03). !locks and !cs in WinDbg resolve owners because OwningThread is recorded; this is the one diagnostic advantage CS has over SRWLOCK.

docs.title: 2.4 SRWLOCK
docs.text:
SRWLOCK lock = SRWLOCK_INIT;
AcquireSRWLockShared(&lock);    ReleaseSRWLockShared(&lock);
AcquireSRWLockExclusive(&lock); ReleaseSRWLockExclusive(&lock);
TryAcquireSRWLockExclusive(&lock);   /* Win7+ */

One pointer-sized word. No recursion (re-acquiring exclusive from the owner deadlocks; acquiring shared while holding shared is permitted but undefined if a writer is waiting, so do not). No upgrade. Faster than CS even for exclusive-only use because there is no recursion check and no lazily allocated kernel object. Portable description: std::shared_mutex. If your server has CRITICAL_SECTIONs around read-mostly data, converting to SRWLOCK is the single easiest measurable win.

docs.title: 2.5 CONDITION_VARIABLE
docs.text:
CONDITION_VARIABLE cv;   InitializeConditionVariable(&cv);
SRWLOCK lock = SRWLOCK_INIT;

/* consumer */
AcquireSRWLockExclusive(&lock);
while (queue_empty(&q) && !closed)                             /* predicate loop, same as C++ */
    SleepConditionVariableSRW(&cv, &lock, INFINITE, 0);        /* releases lock, waits, re-acquires */
/* ... */
ReleaseSRWLockExclusive(&lock);

/* producer */
AcquireSRWLockExclusive(&lock);
push(&q, item);
ReleaseSRWLockExclusive(&lock);
WakeConditionVariable(&cv);

SleepConditionVariableCS pairs with a CRITICAL_SECTION; SleepConditionVariableSRW with an SRWLOCK (the last argument CONDITION_VARIABLE_LOCKMODE_SHARED lets a shared holder wait). The documentation states that spurious wakeups occur and the condition must be re-checked. Everything in module 05 applies unchanged. If you still use Events for producer-consumer, this is the replacement.

docs.title: 2.6 Events and Semaphores
docs.text:
HANDLE evManual = CreateEvent(NULL, TRUE,  FALSE, NULL);   /* manual-reset, initially not set */
HANDLE evAuto   = CreateEvent(NULL, FALSE, FALSE, NULL);   /* auto-reset */
SetEvent(ev); ResetEvent(ev); PulseEvent(ev) /* deprecated; unreliable */;
WaitForSingleObject(ev, timeout_ms);                       /* WAIT_OBJECT_0, WAIT_TIMEOUT, WAIT_FAILED */

HANDLE sem = CreateSemaphore(NULL, initial, maximum, NULL);
ReleaseSemaphore(sem, 1, NULL);                            /* count += 1 */
WaitForSingleObject(sem, INFINITE);                        /* count -= 1 when > 0 */

Events are kernel objects: every SetEvent and every wait is a syscall (~1 µs typical), which is why a request queue signalled per item with an Event is slower than a CONDITION_VARIABLE that only enters the kernel when a thread is actually asleep. They are also cross-process and waitable in groups, which condition variables are not.

Semantics to describe portably:

  • Manual-reset event = a latch. C++: std::promise<void> / std::shared_future<void> for one shot; mutex + bool + condition_variable with notify_all for resettable.
  • Auto-reset event = a binary semaphore with coalescing. C++: mutex + bool + condition_variable with notify_one. Note the coalescing hazard (module 05): two SetEvents before a wait is one wake.
  • Semaphore = a counting semaphore. C++20: std::counting_semaphore. C++17: mutex + int + condition_variable.

docs.title: 2.7 WaitForMultipleObjects
docs.text:
HANDLE h[3] = { hShutdownEvent, hWorkSemaphore, hTimer };
DWORD r = WaitForMultipleObjects(3, h, FALSE /* any */, INFINITE);
switch (r) {
case WAIT_OBJECT_0 + 0: /* shutdown */ break;
case WAIT_OBJECT_0 + 1: /* work */     break;
case WAIT_OBJECT_0 + 2: /* timer */    break;
case WAIT_FAILED: /* GetLastError() */ break;
}

Limit MAXIMUM_WAIT_OBJECTS = 64. With bWaitAll = FALSE and several objects signalled, the lowest index is returned (so put the shutdown event first; this is why your shutdown is responsive). WAIT_ABANDONED_0 + i means a mutex handle whose owner died.

No standard C++ equivalent. Portable rewrites:

  • "Wait for shutdown or work" = one condition variable with predicate closed || !queue.empty() (module 05). This covers 90% of WFMO use in request servers.
  • "Wait for any of N heterogeneous events" = an actor mailbox: each source pushes a tagged message into one queue (module 11).
  • "Wait for all of N tasks" = N futures joined, or a counter plus condition variable (a latch; std::latch in C++20).
  • "Wait for socket or event" = epoll with an eventfd for the non-socket signal (08_Networking).

docs.title: 2.8 Interlocked
docs.text:
LONG v = 0;
InterlockedIncrement(&v);                                    /* returns new value */
LONG old = InterlockedCompareExchange(&v, 10 /*desired*/, 5 /*expected*/);   /* returns old */
if (old == 5) { /* swapped */ }
InterlockedExchangePointer(&p, newp);
MemoryBarrier();

All un-suffixed forms are full barriers (seq_cst) on every architecture. Acquire / Release / NoFence suffixed variants exist for ARM64; on x86 they compile to the same lock instruction. volatile LONG with /volatile:ms gives acquire loads and release stores, which is why many Win32 flags "work"; under /volatile:iso (the default on ARM64) they do not. Portable: std::atomic<long>.

Mapping the CAS convention: Win32 returns the old value and you compare it yourself; C++ returns bool and writes the current value into your expected variable on failure. Both express the same loop.

docs.title: 2.9 Thread pool API (Vista+)
docs.text:
PTP_POOL pool = CreateThreadpool(NULL);
SetThreadpoolThreadMaximum(pool, 8);
SetThreadpoolThreadMinimum(pool, 2);
TP_CALLBACK_ENVIRON env; InitializeThreadpoolEnvironment(&env); SetThreadpoolCallbackPool(&env, pool);

VOID CALLBACK work_cb(PTP_CALLBACK_INSTANCE inst, PVOID ctx, PTP_WORK work) { /* ... */ }
PTP_WORK work = CreateThreadpoolWork(work_cb, ctx, &env);
SubmitThreadpoolWork(work);                        /* may be submitted many times */
WaitForThreadpoolWorkCallbacks(work, FALSE);       /* wait for outstanding callbacks */
CloseThreadpoolWork(work);
CloseThreadpool(pool);

Also CreateThreadpoolTimer, CreateThreadpoolWait (wait on a handle and run a callback: this is how you get "wait for N > 64 objects"), CreateThreadpoolIo (IOCP integration), and cleanup groups. There is no result/future; you build completion signalling yourself. It is a solid, well-tested pool and the right default for new Windows code; module 09's pool is what it looks like inside. The legacy QueueUserWorkItem is the older API with less control.

docs.title: 2.10 I/O completion ports in one paragraph
docs.text: An IOCP is a kernel queue of completed asynchronous I/O operations. You associate handles (sockets, files) with the port, issue overlapped operations (WSARecv with an OVERLAPPED), and a small number of threads (usually one per core) block in GetQueuedCompletionStatus, which returns one completion at a time. The kernel also limits how many threads it wakes concurrently to the port's concurrency value, so you get an event loop that is automatically multi-threaded. This is the Windows equivalent of an epoll + pool design, and the natural shape for a Windows server that must handle more connections than threads. PostQueuedCompletionStatus lets you inject your own messages, which is how you integrate a request queue with the same loop. 08_Networking covers the Linux side; the concepts are identical, the readiness-vs-completion distinction is the main difference (epoll tells you a socket can be read; IOCP tells you a read has completed).

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
File: code/m13_win32_threads.c (Windows-only) — _beginthreadex, a CRITICAL_SECTION-guarded counter, an auto-reset Event based request queue showing the coalescing hazard, and a Semaphore based version that does not have it.

File: code/m13_win32_srwlock_condvar.c (Windows-only) — the module 05 producer-consumer queue in C with SRWLOCK and CONDITION_VARIABLE, with the same close-and-drain shutdown protocol, plus a WaitForMultipleObjects shutdown-or-work example and InitOnceExecuteOnce.

Key fragment of the condition-variable queue in C:

typedef struct {
    SRWLOCK lock;
    CONDITION_VARIABLE not_empty;
    CONDITION_VARIABLE not_full;
    int buf[64]; size_t head, tail, count;
    BOOL closed;
} Queue;

BOOL queue_pop(Queue* q, int* out) {
    AcquireSRWLockExclusive(&q->lock);
    while (q->count == 0 && !q->closed)                       /* predicate loop */
        SleepConditionVariableSRW(&q->not_empty, &q->lock, INFINITE, 0);
    if (q->count == 0) { ReleaseSRWLockExclusive(&q->lock); return FALSE; }   /* closed and drained */
    *out = q->buf[q->head]; q->head = (q->head + 1) % 64; q->count--;
    ReleaseSRWLockExclusive(&q->lock);
    WakeConditionVariable(&q->not_full);
    return TRUE;
}

Compare line by line with BoundedQueue::pop in m05_producer_consumer.cpp. They are the same program.

docs.title: Kernel objects vs user-mode primitives
docs.text: Win32 has two families. Kernel objects (Mutex, Event, Semaphore, WaitableTimer, Thread, Process, File) are referenced by HANDLE, live in the kernel's object manager, are securable and nameable, can be shared across processes, and are waited on through NtWaitForSingleObject / NtWaitForMultipleObjects. Every operation is a syscall and a kernel dispatcher lock. User-mode primitives (CRITICAL_SECTION, SRWLOCK, CONDITION_VARIABLE, INIT_ONCE, Interlocked) do their fast path with an interlocked instruction in user space and enter the kernel only to block, via keyed events (historically) or NtWaitForAlertByThreadId / WaitOnAddress (Windows 8+). This is the same split as glibc's futex-based primitives vs System V semaphores on Linux. The rule "use CRITICAL_SECTION unless you need cross-process or WFMO" is the rule "use the user-mode primitive unless you need a kernel feature".

docs.title: Keyed events and WaitOnAddress
docs.text: Before Windows 8, user-mode primitives blocked on a single global keyed event object: a wait is keyed by an address, and a wake releases the waiter with that key. That is a futex without the value check. Windows 8 added WaitOnAddress(addr, compare, size, timeout): block only if *addr still equals *compare, which is exactly FUTEX_WAIT. WakeByAddressSingle/All are FUTEX_WAKE. Modern CRITICAL_SECTION and SRWLOCK use these. If you ever write your own primitive on Windows, WaitOnAddress is the building block, just as futex is on Linux.

docs.title: Dispatcher objects and the wait block
docs.text: When a thread waits on a kernel object, the kernel allocates a wait block linking the thread to the object's wait list, marks the thread Waiting, and the scheduler picks another thread. SetEvent walks the wait list, satisfies the waits, and makes the threads ready, with a priority boost (EVENT_INCREMENT, +1) so that a thread woken for I/O or an event gets scheduled promptly. WFMO with bWaitAll = TRUE allocates one wait block per object and the thread becomes ready only when all are signalled. The 64-object limit is because the wait blocks are allocated in a fixed array in the thread's kernel structure.

docs.title: Priority boosts and your server
docs.text: Windows boosts a thread's priority when it wakes from a wait (so a worker just handed a request runs soon) and decays it over a few quanta. This mostly helps a request server. It also means a thread that never waits (a spin loop) never gets boosted and can be starved by threads that do. On Linux CFS the analogous effect is that a sleeping task accumulates less virtual runtime and is favoured when it wakes. Either way: block, do not spin, in a user-space server.

docs.title: Why SRWLOCK does not record its owner
docs.text: Recording the owner costs a store on every acquire and makes the structure larger than a pointer. SRWLOCK's design goal was a single word for both modes. The cost shows up in debugging: WinDbg's !locks cannot tell you who holds an SRWLOCK. If your server is SRWLOCK-heavy, keep a debug-build owner field next to each lock, written after acquire and cleared before release, so a dump can resolve it.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Describing the synchronisation layer. "Per-connection state is behind a user-mode mutex with a spin phase (CRITICAL_SECTION). Master tables are behind a reader-writer lock (SRWLOCK). The request queue is a bounded buffer with a condition variable (or, if it still uses Events, say: signalled with an auto-reset event, which we bounded with a semaphore to avoid coalesced wakeups). Shutdown is a manual-reset event placed first in every WaitForMultipleObjects so workers exit promptly. Counters use Interlocked operations, which are sequentially consistent on x86." Every phrase is now precise and portable.
  • Converting Events to CONDITION_VARIABLE. The migration is mechanical: the Event becomes a CONDITION_VARIABLE plus the predicate it stood for (queue non-empty, shutdown requested), the WaitForSingleObject becomes the predicate loop with SleepConditionVariableSRW, the SetEvent becomes "modify state under the lock, then Wake". The coalescing bug disappears. The syscall per item disappears.
  • CS to SRWLOCK. Find the CRITICAL_SECTIONs around read-mostly data, confirm no recursive entries (debug: assert RecursionCount == 1 after each Enter, or temporarily switch to a checker), convert. Measure p99 under concurrent load before and after.
  • TerminateThread. If the codebase has it, it is a latent heap corruption. Replace with a cooperative stop flag checked by the thread. This is a good "what would you fix first" answer.
  • Dumps and SRWLOCK. Because !locks cannot resolve SRWLOCK owners, a hang analysis on an SRWLOCK-heavy server needs your own owner tracking. Add it in debug builds now.
  • 3 AM on Windows. procdump -ma PID, open in WinDbg, !analyze -v -hang, ~*k, !locks. Same procedure as module 12, same wait-for graph. WAIT_ABANDONED in a log means a thread died holding a kernel Mutex; find the crash that killed it.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build m13_win32_threads.c with MSVC or MinGW and run it. Observe the auto-reset Event version losing a wake when two SetEvents coalesce and the Semaphore version not. Done when you can explain the difference in terms of state.
  2. (easy) Build and run m13_win32_srwlock_condvar.c. Put it side by side with m05_producer_consumer.cpp and annotate each line with its equivalent. Done when every line has a partner.
  3. (medium) Write a table of every synchronisation primitive your real server uses (count them: how many CRITICAL_SECTIONs, Events, Semaphores, Mutex handles, SRWLOCKs) and, for each, the C++17 equivalent and whether a conversion would change behaviour (recursion, coalescing, cross-process). Done when the table is complete and you have identified the one conversion with the best payoff.
  4. (medium) Implement WaitOnAddress-based spinlock-then-block mutex in C on Windows (fast path interlocked, slow path WaitOnAddress, unlock WakeByAddressSingle). Compare its uncontended cost to CRITICAL_SECTION. Done when both numbers are recorded and the design maps to glibc's futex mutex in your explanation.
  5. (hard) Rewrite the module 09 thread pool using the Vista thread pool API (CreateThreadpoolWork), adding your own completion signalling with a per-task manual-reset Event or a counter plus CONDITION_VARIABLE so that a submitter can wait for a result. Then write a paragraph comparing it with m09_thread_pool.hpp: what the OS pool does for you and what it does not (futures, exceptions, bounded queue). Done when both run the same workload and the paragraph is written.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Describe the synchronisation in your Windows server in portable terms. A user-mode recursive mutex with an adaptive spin phase (CRITICAL_SECTION) for per-connection state; a reader-writer lock (SRWLOCK) for read-mostly master tables; a bounded request queue with a condition variable (or event plus semaphore) for the pooled workers; a manual-reset shutdown latch checked first in every multi-object wait; sequentially consistent atomic counters (Interlocked). The C++17 names are std::mutex, std::shared_mutex, std::condition_variable, a promise/future or flag-under-mutex, and std::atomic.

Q: What is the difference between a CRITICAL_SECTION and a Win32 Mutex handle? A CRITICAL_SECTION is a user-mode lock: interlocked fast path, optional spin, kernel wait only on contention, intra-process only, recursive, records its owner. A Mutex handle is a kernel object: every acquire is a syscall, works across processes, can be waited on with other handles via WaitForMultipleObjects, has a timeout on acquire, and reports abandonment if the owner dies.

Q: How does a Win32 Event differ from a condition variable, and which is the C++ equivalent? An Event is a kernel object with state: a set with no waiter persists, and an auto-reset Event coalesces multiple sets into one wake. A condition variable is stateless and must be paired with a predicate under a mutex. C++ has only the condition variable; an Event is modelled as a flag or count under a mutex with a condition variable, or std::promise<void> for a one-shot latch. Windows also has CONDITION_VARIABLE, which is the same as the C++ one.

Q: What does WaitForMultipleObjects do and what is the portable replacement? Blocks until any (or all) of up to 64 kernel objects are signalled, returning the lowest signalled index. No standard C++ equivalent. Portable designs: one condition variable with a composite predicate (shutdown or work), a single tagged message queue for heterogeneous events, a latch or joined futures for wait-all, and epoll with an eventfd for sockets plus signals.

Q: Are Interlocked operations the same as std::atomic? Un-suffixed Interlocked functions are atomic read-modify-writes with full barrier (seq_cst) semantics. std::atomic defaults to seq_cst and offers weaker orders; Win32 added Acquire, Release and NoFence suffixes for ARM64 to match. The CAS convention differs: Win32 returns the old value, C++ returns a bool and updates expected.

Q: What is WaitOnAddress? Windows 8's futex: block the calling thread only if the value at an address still equals a comparand, and wake with WakeByAddressSingle/All. It is the building block under modern CRITICAL_SECTION, SRWLOCK and CONDITION_VARIABLE, exactly as futex(2) is under glibc's mutex and condition variable.

Q: What is an I/O completion port? A kernel queue of completed overlapped I/O operations on associated handles, drained by a bounded set of threads blocked in GetQueuedCompletionStatus, with the kernel limiting concurrent active threads to a configured value. It is the Windows event loop and the counterpart of epoll plus a pool on Linux, with completion semantics rather than readiness semantics.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Two families: kernel objects (handles, syscalls, cross-process, WFMO) and user-mode primitives (interlocked fast path, block only on contention). Same split as System V vs futex on Linux.
  • CRITICAL_SECTION = recursive spinning std::mutex; SRWLOCK = std::shared_mutex; CONDITION_VARIABLE = std::condition_variable; INIT_ONCE = std::call_once.
  • Events have state and coalesce; condition variables do not. Model an Event as flag + mutex + cv.
  • Semaphore = counting semaphore; C++20 has it, C++17 builds it from mutex + int + cv.
  • WaitForMultipleObjects has no standard equivalent; use composite predicates, one queue, latches, or epoll.
  • Interlocked = seq_cst atomics; CAS return convention differs from C++.
  • WaitOnAddress is the Windows futex.
  • Vista thread pool is a fine default on Windows; it lacks futures and bounded queues.
  • IOCP = completion-based event loop, the Windows epoll-plus-pool.
  • SRWLOCK does not record owners; add debug owner tracking for dump analysis.
  • Never TerminateThread.

docs.title: 04_Concurrency — all exercises
docs.text:
Every exercise from section 6 ("Try it") of modules 01 to 13, in one place, with a difficulty and a hint. The full "done when" condition is in the module; it is repeated here in short form so you can tick exercises off without opening the module.

How to use this file:

  • Do every easy exercise as you finish each module. They take 10 to 30 minutes.
  • Do at least two medium exercises per module. They are where the understanding sticks.
  • Pick the hard exercises that match your resume story (thread pool, deadlock RCA, lock-free, Win32 mapping). Each one is a talking point in an interview.
  • Build everything with code/build.sh on WSL Ubuntu 24.04. TSan builds land in code/build/tsan/.

TSan note for WSL Ubuntu 24.04: if a TSan binary dies immediately with FATAL: ThreadSanitizer: unexpected memory mapping, the kernel's ASLR entropy is higher than TSan expects. Run it as setarch $(uname -m) -R ./build/tsan/prog, or once per boot sudo sysctl vm.mmap_rnd_bits=28. This is an environment issue, not a bug in your code.

Legend: E = easy, M = medium, H = hard.

docs.title: Module 01 — Processes, threads and the OS (01_processes_threads_and_the_os.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 1.1 E Run m01_threads_basics.cpp with 100 workers; remove the cout_mtx lock and find an interleaved line. std::cout << a << b is several separate calls; another thread can write between any two of them. Run 5 to 10 times. 1.2 E Print hardware_concurrency(); after creating 50 threads read Threads: from /proc/self/status. Done when it says 51. Keep the 50 threads blocked (on a latch or a sleep) while you read the file, or they may have exited already. 1.3 M Let a joinable std::thread go out of scope; observe terminate. Explain why the committee chose terminate over detach. Think about a lambda capturing a local by reference: implicit detach would leave a thread reading a dead stack frame. 1.4 M Time 10,000 create+join cycles vs pushing 10,000 items through one reused thread via a queue. Use steady_clock, divide by 10,000. Creation costs a clone syscall, a stack mmap and scheduler work; a queue push costs a lock and a notify. 1.5 H thread_local struct with printing ctor and dtor; three threads; show 3 constructions and 3 destructions before main prints "exiting". Construction happens on first use in each thread, not at thread start. Destruction runs during thread exit, so join before printing "exiting".

docs.title: Module 02 — Data races and why they are UB (02_data_races_and_why_they_are_ub.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 2.1 E Build m02_race_demo.cpp at -O0 and -O2, run 5 times each, explain why -O2 sometimes prints exactly 1,000,000. At -O2 the compiler may hoist the counter into a register and store once at the end, so the threads' updates do not interleave; one thread's final store overwrites the other's. 2.2 E Build with -fsanitize=thread; find "previous write", "current read" and thread creation sites. Read the report top-down: two stacks, then "Location is global ...", then "Thread T1 created at". Look for your file name, skip libstdc++ frames. 2.3 M while (!ready) {} with plain bool at -O2 hangs; find the non-reloading loop in g++ -O2 -S; fix with std::atomic<bool>. Look for a jmp to itself (.L3: jmp .L3). The compiler may assume no other thread writes a non-atomic, so it loads ready once. 2.4 M Store-buffering litmus test, 1,000,000 runs with a start barrier; count r1 == 0 && r2 == 0. Use an atomic counter both threads increment then spin on until it reaches 2. The reorder comes from the store buffer; only seq_cst (an mfence or xchg on x86) forbids it. 2.5 H Audit a stats struct updated by workers with no lock; mark every conflicting pair without happens-before; rewrite minimally; TSan quiet. Per-field: is it written by more than one thread? Read by a reporter thread? Pure counters become relaxed atomics; fields that must be consistent together need one mutex or a snapshot.

docs.title: Module 03 — Mutexes, lock_guard, unique_lock (03_mutexes_lock_guard_unique_lock.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 3.1 E Remove the lock_guard in m03_mutex_counter.cpp's increment; see wrong totals; restore. Same lost-update mechanism as module 02. Run several times; the loss varies. 3.2 E Replace scoped_lock(from.m, to.m) with two sequential lock_guards; hang; gdb -p PID, thread apply all bt. Look for two threads in __lll_lock_wait (or futex_wait). Go up to your transfer frame in each and print which account it locked first. 3.3 M foo() locks m and calls bar() which also locks m; fix with bar_locked(); paragraph on why recursive_mutex is wrong. When bar runs inside foo, foo's invariant may be half-updated. A recursive mutex lets bar see that broken state silently. 3.4 M Uncontended vs contended lock cost: 10 million lock_guard on one thread vs two threads. Uncontended is one atomic CAS plus one atomic store (typically tens of ns or less). Contended adds futex syscalls and context switches; count them with strace -c -f. 3.5 H ConfigStore: version A reads the file under the lock, version B reads into a local map then swaps. Measure reader p99. Store each get() duration in a per-thread vector, merge, sort, take index 0.99 * n. B's critical section is a pointer swap; A's is file I/O.

docs.title: Module 04 — shared_mutex and readers-writers (04_shared_mutex_and_readers_writers.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 4.1 E Run m04_shared_mutex_map.cpp; note the three throughputs; sharded beats single with writers. Sharding divides contention by the shard count because unrelated keys stop sharing a lock. 4.2 E Make get return const std::string* into the map; ASan with 8 readers and 2 writers doing del and set. The pointer outlives the shared_lock; a writer erases the node; the reader dereferences freed memory. Return by value or by shared_ptr. 4.3 M Replace shared_mutex with plain mutex; rerun 8 readers, 0 writers. shared_lock still does an atomic RMW on one shared counter, so readers bounce one cache line. With tiny critical sections a plain mutex can win. 4.4 M Pre-build keys so the read section has no allocation; find where plain mutex matches or beats shared_mutex. The shorter the critical section, the more the lock's own cost dominates. shared_mutex only pays off when readers hold it long enough to overlap. 4.5 H Show writer starvation with 8 tight readers; build a fair rwlock (writer-waiting flag blocks new readers); compare max writer wait. Fields: readers, writer_active, writers_waiting, one mutex, two condition variables. Readers wait while writer_active || writers_waiting > 0. Verify with TSan.

docs.title: Module 05 — Condition variables and wait objects (05_condition_variables_and_wait_objects.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 5.1 E Replace wait(lk, pred) with bare wait(lk) plus if (q_.empty()) return nullopt;; 4 consumers; observe failures. Name the cause: spurious wakeup, stolen wakeup (another consumer took the item first) or wake for close. Each makes an empty queue look like "closed". 5.2 E Move closed_ = true outside the lock in close(); write the lost-wakeup interleaving with line numbers. Consumer checks predicate (false) -> producer sets flag and notifies -> consumer blocks. The notify hit nobody. The lock makes "check and block" atomic relative to the setter. 5.3 M Semaphore from mutex + cv + int; auto-reset event on top (coalescing) and manual-reset event (bool + notify_all). Show the auto-reset event losing the second of two back-to-back signals. Auto-reset: if (count == 0) count = 1; in signal. Two signals with no wait in between leave count at 1. Compare with code/m13_win32_threads.c. 5.4 M Add size(), waiting_consumers and dump(); remove notify_one from push; show size > 0, waiters > 0. Increment waiting_consumers before the wait and decrement after, both under the lock. That pair of numbers is the signature of a lost notify in a production dump. 5.5 H EventSet wait-for-any with one mutex, one cv, a std::bitset; 8 sources, 1 waiter; every signal received once. Explain why notify_one suffices. wait_any waits for bits.any(), finds the lowest set bit, clears it. With one waiter notify_one is enough; with several waiters waiting for different subsets you need notify_all.

docs.title: Module 06 — Deadlocks, livelocks, starvation (06_deadlocks_livelocks_starvation.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 6.1 E ./m06_deadlock_demo hang; gdb thread apply all bt; write "T1 holds A waits B; T2 holds B waits A". In each transfer_broken frame, print from.name and print to.name. The thread waits on to; it holds from. 6.2 E In gdb, print the owner of the mutex each thread waits on and match to info threads. frame N into the lock call, then print to.m._M_mutex.__data.__owner: that is the LWP id shown in info threads. 6.3 M Three-thread cycle A->B, B->C, C->A; dump stacks; draw the cycle; fix with ranks; 10,000 iterations clean. Give A=30, B=20, C=10 and require descending acquisition. T3 then takes A before C, which breaks the cycle. 6.4 M Replace the try-lock jitter with a bare yield; pin to 2 cores; compare throughput. Without randomness both threads retry in lock-step and keep colliding (livelock). Random back-off desynchronises them, like Ethernet's exponential back-off. 6.5 H Write a one-page lock order document for a real or stand-in server; enforce with hierarchical_mutex in debug; test that a violation is caught. List every lock, give ranks with gaps (10, 20, 30), mark leaf locks (logger, metrics). The test should take two locks in the wrong order and expect the throw or abort.

docs.title: Module 07 — Atomics and the memory model (07_atomics_and_the_memory_model.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 7.1 E Run m07_atomic_counter_orders.cpp; compare store timings; find the xchg in the -S output. A seq_cst store compiles to xchg (implicitly locked, a full barrier) on x86; relaxed and release stores are a plain mov. 7.2 E Make m07_message_passing.cpp relaxed on both sides; TSan reports a race on payload; restore acquire/release. TSan checks the C++ model, not x86. Relaxed creates no happens-before, so the payload accesses are unordered by the language even if the hardware happens to keep them in order. 7.3 M Long-lived store-buffering harness with a round counter, 10 million rounds; both-zero count per order. acq/rel does not forbid store-load reordering; only seq_cst does. Expect relaxed and acq/rel non-zero, seq_cst exactly zero. 7.4 M Refcount with relaxed increment; choose and justify the decrement order. Every thread's writes to p must happen-before the delete. Release on each decrement publishes them; acquire on the one that hits zero receives them. Hence acq_rel, or release plus an acquire fence. 7.5 H Peterson's lock with atomics; seq_cst gives exactly 2,000,000; release/acquire breaks it. Name the reorder. Each thread stores flag[me] then loads flag[other]: store-then-load to different addresses, which is the store-buffering pattern. Both can read false and both enter.

docs.title: Module 08 — Lock-free basics (08_lock_free_basics.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 8.1 E m08_spinlock.cpp vs mutex at 1, 2, 4, 8 threads; then taskset -c 0. On one core a spinner burns its whole time slice while the holder is descheduled; a mutex sleeps and lets the holder run. 8.2 E m08_spsc_ring.cpp: change tail_ store to relaxed; TSan reports the race on buf_. The release store on tail_ is what publishes the slot write. Without it the consumer's read of buf_ has no happens-before. 8.3 M m08_treiber_stack.cpp with -DBROKEN -fsanitize=address, 4 threads; write the use-after-free interleaving. T1 loads head and reads head->next; meanwhile T2 pops the same node and deletes it. T1's read touches freed memory. That gap is what hazard pointers close. 8.4 M Cache the other side's index in SpscRing; measure before and after. The producer only reloads head_ (acquire) when its cached copy says "full". A stale cached value is always conservative, so correctness holds. 8.5 H Hazard pointers for the Treiber stack; 8 threads, 10 million ops; ASan and TSan silent; state the memory bound. Publish the hazard with seq_cst (or a fence) then re-check head before using the node. Bound: at most H + R unreclaimed nodes, where H is the hazard count and R is the scan threshold.

docs.title: Module 09 — Thread pools and task queues (09_thread_pools_and_task_queues.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 9.1 E Run m09_thread_pool_demo.cpp; confirm sum, caught exception, and completed() equals submitted. The exception is delivered through the packaged_task's future. get() rethrows it on the caller's thread. 9.2 E Run m09_async_pitfall.cpp; show the discarded-future std::async call is sequential. Three 200 ms jobs take about 600 ms because each temporary future's destructor joins. Keeping the futures in a vector gives about 200 ms. 9.3 M Break shutdown with if (closed_) return; before taking a task; 1,000 tasks of 1 ms; destroy immediately; see lost tasks; restore. The correct exit is "closed AND queue empty". Checking only closed exits with work still queued. 9.4 M try_submit returning false when full, plus a sampler printing queue depth every 100 ms during a 10,000-submit burst. try_submit is submit with the not_full_ wait replaced by if (q_.size() >= max_queue_) return false; under the same lock. 9.5 H Self-deadlock: 4 workers, each task submits a sub-task and calls get(); 8 outer tasks. Fix with inline execution and with a second pool. All 4 workers block in future::get; the sub-tasks sit in the queue with no free worker. thread_local bool in_pool set in worker_loop lets submit run inline. 9.6 H Cooperative cancellation via std::atomic<bool> stop_requested_; a 100 x 10 ms task exits within 20 ms of shutdown_now(). Check the flag between each 10 ms step with a relaxed load (the join after shutdown gives the ordering you need). Measure from shutdown_now() to the end of join.

docs.title: Module 10 — Cache lines, false sharing, performance (10_cache_lines_false_sharing_performance.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 10.1 E Run m10_false_sharing.cpp; record packed, padded, true-shared; padded/packed ratio at max threads. Close other programs. On WSL the Windows host shares the CPU, so run 3 times and take the median. 10.2 E Try alignas(32) and alignas(128); explain 32 and whether 128 differs. 32 puts two slots per 64-byte line, so pairs of threads still fight. 128 can help on Intel because the adjacent-line prefetcher pulls lines in pairs. 10.3 M StripedCounter vs one std::atomic<long> at 1, 4, 8 threads; then measure read() cost. Writes go to the thread's own padded stripe (index by a hashed thread id). read() sums all stripes, so reads get slower as writes get faster. 10.4 M Pin threads with pthread_setaffinity_np; variance across 5 runs pinned vs unpinned. Use cpu_set_t, CPU_ZERO, CPU_SET(t % ncpu). Report min, median and max of each set of 5 runs. 10.5 H Per-worker stats in the module 09 pool, packed vs padded; 1,000,000 tiny tasks; solve Amdahl for s. speedup = 1 / (s + (1 - s) / N); solve s = (N / speedup - 1) / (N - 1). Expect the queue mutex, not the stats, to dominate s.

docs.title: Module 11 — Concurrency patterns for servers (11_concurrency_patterns_for_servers.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 11.1 E Run m11_call_once_singleton.cpp ("constructed: 1" for all three forms); write the broken plain-pointer DCLP and catch it with TSan. Copy form 1 and change std::atomic<Table*> to Table*. TSan reports the unlocked first read racing with the write under the mutex. 11.2 E Run m11_rcu_snapshot_cache.cpp; zero inconsistent reads; note the publish time. If you have fewer than 9 hardware threads, also run ./m11_rcu_snapshot_cache 3. The median publish is the honest number; the tail includes scheduling. 11.3 M Replace the snapshot with a shared_mutex table rebuilt in place under the exclusive lock; compare reader p99 with and without the refresher. Rebuilding in place makes every reader wait for the whole build. The snapshot version's p99 should barely move when the refresher runs. 11.4 M ConnectionPool with fake 1 ms Conn: 16 workers, pool of 4, 50 ms acquire timeout; count successes and timeouts; leak a lease. Lease = RAII object whose destructor returns the connection. Leak by new-ing a lease and never deleting it; the in-use metric stays one higher forever. 11.5 H Parser and Accountant actors with bounded mailboxes, replies via std::promise; then mailboxes of 2 to build a mailbox deadlock. Deadlock: Parser blocks sending to a full Accountant mailbox while Accountant blocks replying into a full Parser mailbox. Each holds its own thread (the resource) and waits for the other.

docs.title: Module 12 — Debugging concurrency bugs (12_debugging_concurrency_bugs.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 12.1 E m12_tsan_demo under TSan: race, order, wakeup. One-line fix for each. Fixes: lock (or atomic) on hits; one global order for m_cache/m_conn; set ready under wm. If TSan dies with "unexpected memory mapping", use setarch $(uname -m) -R. 12.2 E ASan build, uaf mode; find the freeing stack and the using stack; state the ownership fix. ASan prints three stacks: the bad access, "freed by thread T0 here", "previously allocated by". Fix with shared_ptr or by joining the worker before delete. 12.3 M Run m06_deadlock_demo hang under valgrind --tool=helgrind; compare with TSan's lock-order-inversion. Both report the inversion from the lock graph before the actual hang. helgrind is slower but needs no rebuild. Kill the program once the report appears. 12.4 M Add RACE_POINT to m05_producer_consumer.cpp between predicate check and wait; remove the lock around closed_ = true; hang every run. Inline while (!pred) { RACE_POINT("gap"); cv.wait(lk); }. m12_tsan_demo.cpp's wakeup mode is a worked example; build with -DRACE_POINTS. 12.5 H gcore the hung m06_deadlock_demo; from the core alone find both threads, each mutex's __owner, and write the wait-for graph; repeat for a 3-lock cycle. gdb ./m06_deadlock_demo core.PID, info threads, thread N, bt, frame K, print *mutex_ptr. Owner is an LWP id; map it with info threads. 12.6 H Per-thread ring-buffer event log plus a sigaction crash handler that dumps every thread's ring. Register each ring in a fixed-size global array at thread start (no allocation in the handler). In the handler use write(2, ...), not printf; only async-signal-safe calls.

docs.title: Module 13 — Win32 concurrency reference (13_win32_concurrency_reference.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Hint 13.1 E Build and run m13_win32_threads.c; see the auto-reset Event lose a wake and the Semaphore not. An Event is one bit: signalled or not. A Semaphore is a count. Two SetEvent calls with no waiter in between set the same bit twice. 13.2 E Run m13_win32_srwlock_condvar.c; annotate it line by line against m05_producer_consumer.cpp. AcquireSRWLockExclusive = unique_lock, SleepConditionVariableSRW in a while = cv.wait(lk, pred), WakeAllConditionVariable = notify_all. 13.3 M Inventory every primitive in your real server; give the C++17 equivalent and whether conversion changes behaviour. Watch for three behaviour changes: recursion (CRITICAL_SECTION allows it, std::mutex does not), coalescing (Events), and cross-process (named kernel objects). 13.4 M WaitOnAddress-based spin-then-block mutex; compare uncontended cost with CRITICAL_SECTION. Use three states: 0 unlocked, 1 locked, 2 locked with waiters. Unlock only calls WakeByAddressSingle if the old state was 2. This is exactly the glibc futex mutex design. 13.5 H Module 09 pool on the Vista thread pool (CreateThreadpoolWork) with your own completion signalling; compare with m09_thread_pool.hpp. The OS pool gives you thread management and sizing. It does not give futures, exception transport or a bounded queue; you build those with a per-task struct plus SRWLOCK and CONDITION_VARIABLE.

docs.title: Suggested order if you are short of time
docs.text:
1. All E exercises in modules 02, 03, 05, 06, 07 (the core of every concurrency interview).
  2. 5.3 (semaphore and events: maps directly to your Win32 work), 6.3, 7.4, 9.3, 9.5.
  3. One H per interview story: 6.5 (lock order document), 9.5 (pool self-deadlock), 12.5 (deadlock from a core), 13.5 (Win32 pool vs std pool).

docs.title: 04_Concurrency — interview questions and model answers
docs.text:
38 questions, ordered from basic to senior. Each answer is what you would say out loud in 30 to 60 seconds. The module that covers the topic in depth is given in brackets. Where your Win32 background gives you a better answer, the answer uses it: interviewers like hearing that you have shipped this in production, in any dialect.

Practise by covering the answer, saying yours aloud, then comparing. If yours is longer than the model answer, cut it.

docs.title: Part A — Foundations
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a process and a thread? [01] A process owns an address space, handles and at least one thread; a thread is a schedulable execution context (registers, stack, thread-local storage) inside a process. Threads in one process share all memory, so communication is cheap and bugs are shared too: one thread's wild write or crash takes down the whole process. On Linux both are task_structs created by clone with different sharing flags; on Windows they are distinct kernel objects (CreateProcess vs CreateThread).

2. What does std::thread's destructor do if the thread is still joinable, and why? [01] It calls std::terminate. The alternatives were worse: an implicit join could hang silently in a destructor during exception unwinding, and an implicit detach would leave a thread running with references to stack variables that no longer exist. So you must join() or detach() explicitly, or use an RAII wrapper (C++20 std::jthread joins in its destructor).

3. What is a data race, and why is it undefined behaviour rather than just "a wrong value"? [02] A data race is two accesses to the same memory location from different threads, at least one a write, at least one non-atomic, with no happens-before relation between them. The standard makes it UB so the compiler may assume single-threaded semantics for ordinary variables: it can keep values in registers, merge or delete loads and stores, and reorder them. So a racy while (!flag) loop can become an infinite loop, and a racy struct copy can tear. "It is only a counter" is not a defence; the compiler is allowed to break any code that races.

4. Define happens-before in one or two sentences. [02, 07] A happens-before B means A's effects are guaranteed visible to B. It is built from sequenced-before within one thread plus synchronises-with edges between threads (unlock then lock of the same mutex, release store read by an acquire load, thread creation, join), closed transitively. If two conflicting accesses are not ordered by happens-before, you have a data race.

5. Why is volatile not a substitute for std::atomic? [02, 07] volatile only tells the compiler each access must actually happen, for memory-mapped I/O and signal handlers. It does not make a read-modify-write atomic (v++ is still load, add, store), it creates no happens-before between threads, and it emits no CPU barriers. A volatile flag used to publish data is still a data race in C++. MSVC's /volatile:ms gives volatile acquire/release semantics as a vendor extension, which is why some Windows code gets away with it; portable code cannot.

docs.title: Part B — Mutexes and locking
docs.text:
6. Why use std::lock_guard or std::unique_lock instead of calling lock() and unlock()? [03] RAII guarantees the unlock on every exit path, including early returns and exceptions. A manual unlock() that is skipped by a throw leaves the mutex locked forever and the next locker hangs, which is the classic "worked for months, then deadlocked after a rare error" bug. It is the C++ answer to the goto cleanup pattern you write in C.

7. When do you need unique_lock rather than lock_guard? [03, 05] When the lock must be released and reacquired, deferred, tried, timed or moved: condition variable waits (which unlock and relock internally), try_to_lock, defer_lock with std::lock, and unlocking early before a slow call. lock_guard is a zero-overhead scope lock and should be the default; scoped_lock is the default when you need several mutexes at once.

8. What does an uncontended std::mutex lock cost, and what happens when it is contended? [03] On Linux, glibc's mutex is futex-based: an uncontended lock is one atomic compare-and-swap in user space and the unlock is one atomic store or exchange, typically tens of nanoseconds or less. Under contention the loser may spin briefly, then calls futex(FUTEX_WAIT) and sleeps in the kernel; the unlocker sees the "waiters" state and calls futex(FUTEX_WAKE). So the cost of contention is syscalls and context switches (microseconds), not the lock instruction itself. A CRITICAL_SECTION works the same way with a spin count and a kernel event (or keyed event) as the slow path.

9. Mutex vs spinlock vs futex: what is each, and when would you choose a spinlock? [03, 08] A spinlock busy-waits on an atomic flag; it never sleeps. A futex is the Linux kernel primitive "sleep if this word still equals X / wake N sleepers on this word", which lets a mutex stay in user space when uncontended and sleep when contended. A std::mutex is built on the futex (or on WaitOnAddress/keyed events on Windows). Choose a spinlock only when critical sections are a few dozen instructions, threads are not oversubscribed (ideally pinned), and you cannot afford a syscall; for example in a kernel or a real-time core. In general server code a spinlock is a mistake: if the holder is descheduled, every waiter burns its whole time slice.

10. Why is std::recursive_mutex usually a design smell? [03] Recursion means a function that already holds the lock calls another that takes it again, so the inner function may run while the outer one has the invariant half-updated. The recursive mutex hides that by not deadlocking. The clean design is a public locking function plus a private _locked helper that assumes the caller holds the lock. CRITICAL_SECTION is recursive by default, so this is a real migration hazard when porting Win32 code to std::mutex: code that "worked" will now self-deadlock.

11. When does std::shared_mutex beat std::mutex, and when does it lose? [04] It wins when reads are frequent, long enough to overlap usefully, and writes are rare. It loses when critical sections are tiny: every lock_shared still does an atomic RMW on one shared counter, so readers bounce a cache line between cores and you pay more than a plain mutex while gaining no parallelism. It can also starve writers depending on the implementation. Measure; and for read-mostly data refreshed periodically, an immutable snapshot swap usually beats both.

docs.title: Part C — Condition variables and waiting
docs.text:
12. Why must you wait on a condition variable in a loop with a predicate? [05] Three reasons. Spurious wakeups: the implementation may return from wait with no notify. Stolen wakeups: between the notify and your reacquiring the mutex, another thread may consume the item. Multi-purpose notifies: one condition variable may signal several state changes (item available, or shutdown). So the wake only means "re-check", and cv.wait(lk, pred) is exactly while (!pred()) cv.wait(lk);.

13. What is a lost wakeup and how does the mutex prevent it? [05, 12] A lost wakeup is a notify that arrives when nobody is waiting yet, after the waiter has checked the predicate (false) but before it has blocked. The waiter then sleeps forever. It is prevented by modifying the shared state under the same mutex the waiter holds while it checks and blocks: then the setter cannot run between "check" and "block", because wait releases the mutex atomically with going to sleep. Setting the flag outside the mutex, even if the flag is atomic, reopens the window.

14. Should you call notify_one while holding the lock or after releasing it? [05] Both are correct as long as the state change was made under the lock. Notifying after unlock avoids "hurry up and wait", where the woken thread immediately blocks on the mutex the notifier still holds; glibc mitigates this but unlocking first is still a good default. Notifying under the lock is required in one case: when the waiter might destroy the condition variable as soon as it sees the state change.

15. Map Win32 Events and Semaphores to the standard library. What has no direct equivalent? [05, 13] A Semaphore is a counting semaphore: C++20 std::counting_semaphore, or mutex + int + condition variable in C++17. A manual-reset Event is a boolean plus notify_all. An auto-reset Event has no direct equivalent: it is a binary semaphore that saturates at one, so two SetEvent calls with no waiter in between merge into one wake. That coalescing is a common source of "stuck request" bugs; in C++ you express the real condition as a predicate on the queue state, which cannot coalesce.

docs.title: Part D — Deadlock and liveness
docs.text:
16. What are the four conditions for deadlock, and which one do you usually break? [06] Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait (the Coffman conditions). All four must hold. In practice you break circular wait with a global lock order: every thread acquires locks in the same ranked order, so no cycle can form. You break hold-and-wait with std::scoped_lock over all needed mutexes at once, or with try-lock and back-off.

17. How does std::scoped_lock(a, b) avoid deadlock? [06] It uses the std::lock algorithm: lock one mutex, try-lock the others, and if any try fails, release everything and retry starting with the one that failed. It never holds one lock while blocking on another, so it breaks hold-and-wait for that acquisition, regardless of argument order. It only helps when you know all the locks up front; it cannot fix a lock taken inside a callback later.

18. What is livelock, and how is it different from deadlock? [06] In livelock threads are running and changing state but making no progress, typically two threads that each back off and retry in lock-step forever. CPU is high, throughput is zero. In deadlock the threads are blocked and CPU is zero. Livelock is fixed by randomised or exponential back-off, which desynchronises the retries, or by deterministic ordering so retries are unnecessary.

19. You get a hung server. Walk me through reading the deadlock from the thread stacks. [06, 12] First capture state without restarting: gcore PID on Linux, procdump -ma on Windows, and check per-thread CPU (all zero means blocked, not spinning). Dump all stacks (thread apply all bt, or ~*k in WinDbg). Classify each thread by its top frames: in __lll_lock_wait/futex_wait or RtlpWaitOnCriticalSection means waiting for a lock. For each waiter, find which lock it wants (the frame's argument) and who owns it (__owner in a glibc mutex, !cs or !locks in WinDbg gives OwningThread). Draw the wait-for graph; a cycle is a deadlock: "T7 holds cache, waits conn; T12 holds conn, waits cache". No cycle with the owner in recv or a DB call means a lock held across I/O.

20. What is priority inversion and how is it handled? [06] A high-priority thread waits for a lock held by a low-priority thread, which in turn is preempted by a medium-priority thread, so the high-priority thread effectively runs at low priority. Fixes are priority inheritance (the holder temporarily inherits the waiter's priority, as in PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT mutexes) or priority ceiling. Windows mitigates it by randomly boosting starved threads. It matters most in real-time systems.

docs.title: Part E — Atomics and the memory model
docs.text:
21. Explain acquire and release correctly. [07] A release store makes every write the thread did before it visible to any thread whose acquire load reads that stored value (or a later value in the release sequence); that read creates a synchronises-with edge. Acquire also prevents later reads and writes in the acquiring thread from moving before the load; release prevents earlier ones from moving after the store. They are one-way barriers that pair up: release alone, or acquire alone, guarantees nothing to another thread. The classic use is publishing data: fill a buffer, release-store ready = true; the consumer acquire-loads ready and then reads the buffer safely.

22. What does seq_cst add over acquire/release, and what does it cost? [07] seq_cst adds a single total order over all seq_cst operations that every thread agrees on. That forbids the store-then-load reordering that acquire/release allows, which algorithms like Peterson's lock and Dekker-style flags need. On x86, loads are plain mov in every order, but a seq_cst store compiles to xchg (or mov plus mfence), a full barrier that drains the store buffer and typically costs tens of cycles. On ARM it costs barriers or ldar/stlr pairs on both sides. It is the default because it is easiest to reason about; relax only on hot paths with a written proof.

23. When is memory_order_relaxed correct? [07] When only the atomicity of that one variable matters and nothing else is published through it: a statistics counter, a sequence-number generator, a "stop" flag where the thread join provides the ordering for any data. It is wrong whenever another thread will use the value to decide that some other memory is ready to read. Relaxed operations on one variable still have a single modification order, so a counter never loses increments.

24. Why does shared_ptr's reference count decrement need acq_rel, while the increment can be relaxed? [07] The increment only needs atomicity: you already hold a reference, so the object cannot die. The decrement that reaches zero runs the destructor, and the destructor must see every write that every other owner made to the object before dropping its reference. Release on each decrement publishes those writes; acquire on the decrement that hits zero receives them. Relaxed decrements could let the deleter free memory while another thread's earlier writes to it are still unordered with the delete.

25. What does compare_exchange_weak do, and why prefer it in a loop over _strong? [07, 08] It atomically compares the variable with expected and, if equal, writes desired; if not, it writes the current value into expected and returns false. The weak form may also fail spuriously even when the values are equal, because on LL/SC architectures (ARM, POWER) a cache-line event can break the reservation. Inside a retry loop that is harmless and the weak form compiles to tighter code; use strong when a spurious failure would make you do expensive work or take a wrong branch.

docs.title: Part F — Lock-free
docs.text:
26. What is the ABA problem? [08] A CAS-based algorithm reads A, gets delayed, and meanwhile another thread changes the value to B and back to A; the CAS succeeds because the value matches, but the world has changed. In a Treiber stack: thread 1 reads head = A and A->next = B, thread 2 pops A, pops B, pushes A back; thread 1's CAS(head, A, B) succeeds and installs B, which is no longer in the stack. Fixes are a version tag next to the pointer (double-width CAS), or safe memory reclamation so a node cannot be reused while anyone might still hold it.

27. Why is memory reclamation the hard part of lock-free data structures? [08] A thread that has read a node's address may dereference it at any later point, and there is no lock telling the popper that it is safe to delete. Freeing too early is a use-after-free; never freeing is a leak. Solutions: hazard pointers (each thread publishes the pointers it is using; reclaimers skip those), epoch-based reclamation (free only after all threads have passed a quiescent point), or reference counting. Garbage-collected languages get this for free, which is why lock-free is so much easier in Java.

28. Lock-free vs wait-free vs obstruction-free? [08] Lock-free: at any time, some thread makes progress, so the system never stalls even if one thread is suspended, but an individual thread may retry forever. Wait-free: every thread completes in a bounded number of its own steps. Obstruction-free: a thread makes progress if it runs alone. A spinlock is none of these: if the holder is suspended, nobody progresses. Lock-free is not automatically faster; under contention a CAS loop can be slower than a good mutex.

29. Describe a single-producer single-consumer ring buffer and its memory orders. [08] A fixed array with a head written only by the consumer and a tail written only by the producer, each on its own cache line. The producer writes the slot, then release-stores tail; the consumer acquire-loads tail, reads the slot, then release-stores head; the producer acquire-loads head to check for space. Each side reads its own index relaxed. No CAS is needed because each index has exactly one writer. Caching the other side's index locally cuts cross-core traffic further.

docs.title: Part G — Thread pools and server design
docs.text:
30. Design a thread pool. [09] A fixed vector of workers, a queue of type-erased tasks guarded by a mutex, a condition variable that workers wait on with the predicate "closed or queue not empty", and a closed flag. submit wraps the callable in a std::packaged_task, pushes it, notifies one worker and returns the future; exceptions travel through the future instead of killing the worker. Workers pop under the lock and run the task outside the lock. A bounded queue with a second condition variable gives backpressure so a burst cannot exhaust memory.

31. How do you shut a thread pool down without losing tasks or hanging? [09] Set closed = true under the queue mutex, then notify_all. Workers exit only when the queue is closed AND empty, so everything already submitted is still run (graceful drain); submit after close throws or returns an error. Then join every worker. The common bug is checking only closed in the worker, which drops queued tasks; the other is setting the flag without the lock, which can lose the wake-up and hang the join. If you need a fast stop, provide a separate shutdown_now() that swaps out the queue and lets the abandoned futures report broken_promise.

32. Why should a task never block on a future from its own pool? [09] If every worker runs a task that waits for a sub-task, and the sub-tasks are queued behind them, no worker is free to run the sub-tasks: the pool deadlocks with all threads in future::get. Fixes: run the sub-task inline when the caller is already a worker, use a separate pool for the dependent work, or use continuations instead of blocking waits.

33. What is wrong with building a server on std::async? [09] With launch::async, libstdc++ creates a new thread per call, so there is no bound and no queue. The returned future's destructor blocks until the task finishes, so a discarded result makes the call synchronous. With the default policy the task may be deferred and never run until get(). There is no cancellation or priority. It is fine for a one-off background computation in a tool, not for request handling.

34. How do you serve a read-mostly table (rates, configuration) to many threads with near-zero reader cost? [11] Make the table immutable and publish it through an atomic shared_ptr (RCU-style snapshot). A reader atomically loads the pointer, uses its own snapshot for as long as it likes, and drops it. The refresher builds a complete new table off to the side and atomically swaps the pointer with release; old snapshots die when their last reader finishes. Readers never wait for a rebuild and never see a half-built table. In libstdc++ the atomic shared_ptr operations use a small internal lock pool, so it is "short lock, never held across anything slow", not truly lock-free; true RCU or epochs get the read side to zero shared writes.

35. What is the safe way to do lazy one-time initialisation? [11] First choice: a function-local static; since C++11 the compiler emits a thread-safe guard with an acquire-load fast path. Second: std::call_once with a std::once_flag when initialisation needs arguments or the storage is a member. Hand-written double-checked locking is correct only with an atomic pointer, acquire on the fast-path load and release on the publishing store; with a plain pointer it is a data race. If the initialiser throws, both standard forms leave the flag unset and the next caller retries. Win32's equivalent is InitOnceExecuteOnce.

docs.title: Part H — Performance and debugging
docs.text:
36. What is false sharing and how do you find and fix it? [10] Two threads write different variables that sit in the same 64-byte cache line. The coherence protocol (MESI) must give the writing core exclusive ownership of the whole line, so the line ping-pongs between cores and each write costs a cross-core transfer instead of an L1 hit. Symptom: per-thread counters that scale negatively with thread count. Find it with perf c2c on Linux or VTune; fix with alignas(64) per-thread slots, padding, or accumulating locally and publishing rarely. True sharing (everyone updating one counter) needs a different fix: striping or batching.

37. How do you find a data race you cannot reproduce? [12] Build with ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread -g -O1) and run the tests and a stress test: TSan tracks happens-before with vector clocks and reports unordered conflicting accesses even if the bad interleaving did not occur on this run, with both stacks. Run it in CI and treat reports as failures. For deterministic reproduction, add race points (sleeps at named windows enabled by an environment variable) to widen the suspected window. A debugger is weak for races because stopping threads changes the timing.

38. Your Windows server uses CRITICAL_SECTION, SRWLOCK, Events and Semaphores. How would you explain it, and what changes moving to C++17? [13] In standard terms: a user-mode mutex with a spin phase, a reader-writer lock, condition signalling and a counting semaphore. Mapping: CRITICAL_SECTION to std::mutex (but it is recursive, std::mutex is not), SRWLOCK to std::shared_mutex, CONDITION_VARIABLE to std::condition_variable, Semaphore to C++20 std::counting_semaphore or mutex+int+cv, InitOnceExecuteOnce to std::call_once, Interlocked* to std::atomic (Interlocked ops are full barriers, like seq_cst). Three things do not map directly: auto-reset Event coalescing, WaitForMultipleObjects (replace with one composite predicate or one queue), and named cross-process kernel objects. Debugging also changes: !locks/!cs in WinDbg become __owner in gdb, and an SRWLOCK records no owner at all, so a SRWLOCK-heavy server needs its own owner tracking in debug builds.

docs.title: 05. Memory, crash dumps, debuggers and root cause analysis
What this course covers
docs.text:
This course is about what happens when a C or C++ program goes wrong at runtime and how you find out why. It starts with how a process is laid out in memory, moves through the stack, the heap and the catalogue of memory bugs, then teaches the tools: gdb and core dumps on Linux, WinDbg and crash dumps on Windows, Valgrind and the sanitizers. It ends with the human side of the job: triaging a production incident at 3 AM and writing a root cause analysis (RCA) that a bank's engineering leadership will accept.

You already debug Windows crash dumps with WinDbg at a working level. This course takes that to expert level (heap internals, PageHeap, Application Verifier, reading a dump without !analyze) and adds the Linux side from zero: gdb, core dumps, Valgrind, AddressSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer. Every Linux example targets g++ -std=c++17 on WSL Ubuntu 24.04 (GCC 13).

docs.title: Why it is on the resume
docs.text: Core-banking software runs for months without restart, handles money, and is supported under SLAs. A crash is a client incident with a clock on it. The engineer who can take a dump, find the faulting instruction, trace it back to the line that corrupted the heap three hours earlier, fix it, and write a document that explains all of that to a non-engineer is the person a vendor keeps. Interviewers for senior C, C++ roles probe this hard: "What does free(): invalid pointer mean?", "How do you debug a crash you cannot reproduce?", "Walk me through a core dump."

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Solid C (pointers, malloc/free, structs). You have this.
  • Beginner C++ (classes, new/delete, std::vector, std::string). Enough to read the examples.
  • Module 10 assumes you have done at least the mutex and condition variable modules of 04_Concurrency.
  • WSL Ubuntu 24.04 with: sudo apt install build-essential gdb valgrind heaptrack binutils elfutils. Optional: clang (for libFuzzer in module 13), systemd-coredump.
  • Windows: WinDbg (from the Microsoft Store, "WinDbg" / formerly WinDbg Preview), Sysinternals ProcDump and VMMap, Windows SDK Debugging Tools for gflags.exe, umdh.exe, appverif.exe.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:

Total: about 44 hours of study plus exercises. Done in parallel with other courses this is 4 to 5 weeks at 10 hours a week.

Supporting files:

  • code/ - deliberately broken programs (null deref, stack overflow, heap overflow, use-after-free, double free, uninitialised read, leak, data race, deadlock) plus the worked core-dump example, a crash handler, and fixed versions. code/build_debug.sh builds every variant (debug, optimised, ASan, TSan, UBSan) and runs Valgrind. code/gdb_cheatsheet.md is the one-page gdb reference with WinDbg equivalents. code/gdbinit.sample is a starter .gdbinit.
  • EXERCISES.md - every exercise in one place with difficulty and hints.
  • INTERVIEW_QA.md - 36 interview questions with model answers, basic to senior.

docs.title: Suggested order
docs.text: Do 01 to 04 first; they are theory and you need them to interpret anything a debugger shows you. Then 05 and 06 (gdb and cores) on WSL with the programs in code/. Then 07 to consolidate your WinDbg knowledge against the gdb vocabulary you just learned. Then 08 and 09 (tools). Then 10 after you have done the concurrency course modules on mutexes and condition variables. Finish with 11 to 13, which are about process and prevention and are best read with a real incident from your own work in mind.

docs.title: You are done when you can...
docs.text:
• Explain what a pointer value means in terms of page tables, and why dereferencing 0x10 faults but dereferencing a freed heap block usually does not.
  • Draw an x86-64 stack frame from memory and explain how gdb or WinDbg walks it, with and without frame pointers.
  • Explain the glibc chunk header, tcache, fastbins and why free(): invalid next size means "somebody wrote past the end of the previous allocation, possibly hours ago".
  • Take a core dump you have never seen, with the matching binary, and within 15 minutes state the signal, the faulting address, the faulting instruction, the source line, and whether it is a null dereference, a wild pointer, a stack overflow or heap corruption.
  • Do the same with a Windows minidump in WinDbg without relying on !analyze -v alone.
  • Choose between Valgrind, ASan, TSan and UBSan for a given situation and explain the cost of each.
  • Distinguish a leak from legitimate growth from fragmentation using RSS data and a heap profiler, on Linux and Windows.
  • Read a deadlock dump: identify every waiting thread, the lock it waits for and who holds it.
  • Run the first 15 minutes of a Sev-1 incident on a banking server without losing forensic evidence or the client's confidence.
  • Write an RCA that separates trigger from root cause, includes evidence, and proposes verifiable prevention.
  • Set up a build with warnings-as-errors, hardening flags and sanitizer CI jobs, and explain what each flag protects against.

docs.title: 01. Process memory layout
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: none

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Every running program believes it owns the whole computer's memory, from address 0 up to some enormous number. It does not. The operating system gives each process a private map, called the virtual address space, and the CPU translates every address the program uses into a real physical location using that map. If the program touches an address that is not on its map, the CPU raises a fault and the OS kills the process. That is a segmentation fault on Linux and an access violation on Windows.

Think of the address space as a very long street where each house number is an address. Most of the street is empty land. The program's code lives in one block of houses, its global variables in the next, the heap grows upward from there, shared libraries are placed somewhere in the middle, and the stack hangs from the top and grows downward. A pointer is just a house number. Dereferencing it means walking to that house. If there is no house there, you fall in a hole.

Almost every crash you will ever debug comes down to one question: which part of this map was the bad pointer pointing at, and how did it get that value? So you need to know the map cold.

docs.title: 2.1 Virtual memory, pages and page tables
docs.text:
• The CPU works in pages, normally 4 KiB. The OS maps virtual pages to physical frames through page tables. x86-64 uses a 4-level tree (PML4, PDPT, PD, PT); each level is indexed by 9 bits of the address and the final 12 bits are the offset within the page.
  • Only 48 bits of a 64-bit address are used on current x86-64 (57 with 5-level paging, rare). Linux gives user space the lower half: 0x0000_0000_0000_0000 to 0x0000_7FFF_FFFF_FFFF (128 TiB). Kernel addresses start with 0xFFFF_8.... A user pointer that looks like 0xFFFF... or 0x0000_8000_... is garbage; it can never be valid.
  • Each page table entry carries permission bits: present, writable, user, no-execute. A page can be readable but not writable (code, string literals) or not present at all.
  • The TLB caches translations. A page fault happens when the entry is not present or the access violates permissions. The kernel then decides:
    • minor fault: the page is legitimately part of the process but not yet backed (first touch of a heap page, copy-on-write after fork) -> allocate a frame, continue silently.
    • major fault: the page must be read from disk (file-backed mapping, swap) -> slow, continue.
    • invalid: the address is not in any mapping, or the permission is wrong -> SIGSEGV (Linux) / STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION 0xC0000005 (Windows).
  • This is why freed heap memory can be read without a crash: the page is still mapped. The allocator gave the bytes back to its own pool, not to the OS. And why *(int*)0 = 1 always crashes: the first page (and on Linux the first 64 KiB, mmap_min_addr) is never mapped.

docs.title: 2.2 The regions of a Linux process (low to high)
docs.text:
0x0000_0000_0000_0000  +----------------------------+
                       |  unmapped (null page etc.) |  <- any access here faults
0x0000_5555_5555_4000  +----------------------------+  (PIE binaries load around 0x5555...)
                       |  .text    r-x  code        |
                       |  .rodata  r--  literals    |
                       |  .data    rw-  initialised globals
                       |  .bss     rw-  zero-init globals (no bytes in the file)
                       +----------------------------+
                       |  [heap]   rw-  brk area, grows UP  (glibc main arena)
                       +----------------------------+
                       |            ...  huge gap  ...
                       +----------------------------+
0x0000_7FFF_F7xx_xxxx  |  mmap region, grows DOWN:  |
                       |   - large malloc blocks (>= 128 KiB default)
                       |   - thread stacks (8 MiB each, with guard page)
                       |   - secondary malloc arenas (64 MiB reservations)
                       |   - shared libraries (libc.so.6, libstdc++.so.6, ld-linux)
                       |   - file mappings (mmap of data files)
                       +----------------------------+
                       |  [stack]  rw-  main thread, grows DOWN, 8 MiB limit (ulimit -s)
                       |  [vvar] [vdso]  kernel-provided pages (gettimeofday etc.)
0x0000_7FFF_FFFF_F000  +----------------------------+
                       |  [vsyscall] (legacy, at 0xFFFF_FFFF_FF60_0000)

Facts you will use when reading a dump:

Region How it is created Permissions What lives there Typical bad-pointer symptom .text loaded from ELF r-x machine code writing to it: SIGSEGV with si_code=SEGV_ACCERR; jumping into data: SIGSEGV or SIGILL .rodata loaded from ELF r-- string literals, const tables strcpy into a literal -> SIGSEGV on write .data / .bss loaded / zero-filled rw- globals, statics overflow of a global array quietly corrupts the next global [heap] brk/sbrk grown by glibc rw- small/medium malloc blocks UAF reads stale data; overflow corrupts the next block; crash later in free() mmap mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS) rw- big malloc blocks, thread stacks, arenas reading just past a big block: SIGSEGV immediately (next page often unmapped) shared libs mmap of .so by ld.so r-x / r-- / rw- libc code and data a crash with pc inside libc usually means your argument was bad, not libc [stack] kernel at exec rw- locals, return addresses overflow -> SIGSEGV just below the mapping; overwrite return address -> crash at ret with garbage pc

docs.title: 2.3 /proc/<pid>/maps
docs.text:
The kernel's own list of every mapping. Each line:

address range             perms offset   dev   inode    pathname
5555_5555_4000-5555_5555_5000 r--p 00000000 08:10 1234 /home/me/prog     <- ELF header, .rodata part
5555_5555_5000-5555_5555_6000 r-xp 00001000 08:10 1234 /home/me/prog     <- .text
5555_5555_6000-5555_5555_7000 r--p 00002000 08:10 1234 /home/me/prog     <- .rodata, .eh_frame
5555_5555_7000-5555_5555_8000 r--p 00002000 08:10 1234 /home/me/prog     <- .data.rel.ro (RELRO)
5555_5555_8000-5555_5555_9000 rw-p 00003000 08:10 1234 /home/me/prog     <- .data, .bss
5555_5555_9000-5555_5557_a000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0    [heap]
7fff_f7c0_0000-7fff_f7c2_8000 r--p 00000000 08:10 5678 /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6
7fff_f7c2_8000-7fff_f7db_0000 r-xp 00028000 08:10 5678 /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6
...
7fff_fffd_e000-7fff_ffff_f000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0    [stack]
  • perms: r read, w write, x execute, p private (copy-on-write) or s shared.
  • offset: offset into the file for file-backed mappings.
  • No pathname and inode 0: anonymous memory (heap, mmap'd malloc, thread stacks).
  • pmap -x PID gives the same with RSS per mapping. cat /proc/PID/smaps adds per-mapping detail (Rss, Pss, Private_Dirty, Swap). /proc/PID/status summarises: VmSize (virtual), VmRSS (resident), VmHWM (peak RSS), VmData, VmStk.

In gdb the equivalent is info proc mappings, which also works on a core dump (gdb reads the NT_FILE note). When you have a faulting address, this is the first table you compare it with.

docs.title: 2.4 ASLR and PIE
docs.text:
ASLR (address space layout randomisation) shifts the base of the stack, the heap, the mmap area and, for PIE (position independent executable) binaries, the program itself, on every run. /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space is 2 on Ubuntu (everything randomised). Ubuntu's gcc produces PIE by default (-pie), hence program addresses like 0x5555_5555_xxxx under gdb and 0x5Xxx_xxxx_xxxx in production.

Consequences for debugging:

  • Addresses in a crash log from production will not match addresses on your machine. You need the offset within the module (address minus module base), which is what addr2line -e prog 0xOFFSET and info symbol want. Core dumps carry the mappings so gdb does this for you.
  • gdb turns ASLR off by default (set disable-randomization on) so runs repeat. A bug that depends on layout (uninitialised pointer that happens to be valid) can vanish under gdb. Use set disable-randomization off to debug with production-like randomisation.
  • ASLR is a mitigation, not a fix: it makes exploitation of memory bugs harder, it does not make the bugs go away.

docs.title: 2.5 What a pointer really is
docs.text:
A pointer is an integer. The hardware does not know what type it points to; the type is a compile-time fiction that tells the compiler how many bytes to load and how to interpret them. acct->balance where balance is at offset 16 compiles to mov rax, [rdi + 0x10]. If rdi is 0, the CPU tries to read address 0x10, the page at 0 is unmapped, the fault address reported to you is 0x10. Small fault addresses are null pointers plus a field offset. Learn to recognise them: 0x0, 0x8, 0x10, 0x18, 0x40 ... are all "null + offset".

Other recognisable values:

Fault address looks like Probable meaning 0x0 to 0xFFF null pointer + field/array offset 0x7FFF_xxxx_xxxx just below [stack] stack overflow (guard page) 0x5555_... or 0x55xx_... but unmapped pointer into the program's area that was freed/unmapped, or an offset computed wrongly 0x4141_4141_4141_4141, 0x2020_2020... pointer overwritten by ASCII data ("AAAA", spaces): a string overflow 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF -1 used as pointer (an error return that was not checked) 0xdead_beef, 0xcdcd_cdcd, 0xdddd_dddd debug fill patterns (see module 10 for the Windows table) an address that IS mapped but pc is in free/malloc heap metadata corruption (module 03)

docs.title: 2.6 Stack growth and stack overflow
docs.text:
• The main thread's stack is a mapping near the top of user space with a soft limit (ulimit -s, 8 MiB on Ubuntu). The kernel grows it on demand downward until the limit. Below the limit is a gap; touching it is a fault.
  • Thread stacks (pthreads, std::thread) are mmap'd by glibc, default size from ulimit -s (so also 8 MiB; override with pthread_attr_setstacksize). Each has a guard page (PROT_NONE) at its low end. Running into it is an immediate SIGSEGV with a fault address just below the thread's stack mapping.
  • Each call pushes a return address and usually allocates a frame. 4 KiB of locals per frame means about 2000 frames fit in 8 MiB. A bt with thousands of identical frames plus a fault address next to a stack mapping is a stack overflow. Causes: unbounded recursion, huge local arrays (char buf[1 << 20]), alloca in a loop, deep recursion in a parser on malicious input.
  • A large local array is not the only way to blow the stack: std::array<char, 1<<20> or a big struct by value does it too, and in a thread with a reduced stack size (some servers use 256 KiB per worker to allow thousands of threads) it happens much sooner.
