  • Windows: the exception is STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW 0xC00000FD. The default thread stack is 1 MiB (linker /STACK, or CreateThread parameter), eight times smaller than Linux. Code that runs on Linux can overflow on Windows.

docs.title: 2.7 How Windows differs
docs.text:
Concept Linux Windows Address space view /proc/PID/maps, pmap VMMap (Sysinternals), !address in WinDbg, VirtualQuery API User space size (x64) 128 TiB 128 TB (Windows 8.1+), 8 TB earlier Executable image ELF, PIE at 0x5555... PE, /DYNAMICBASE relocates it; images at 0x7FF6.../0x7FF7... Default heap glibc [heap] via brk + mmap arenas NT heap via HeapAlloc on top of VirtualAlloc; several heaps per process (process heap, CRT heap, private heaps) Reserve vs commit mmap is reserve+commit lazily (overcommit) explicit: MEM_RESERVE then MEM_COMMIT; stack is reserved 1 MiB, committed page by page Thread stack 8 MiB default, guard page 1 MiB default, guard page, STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW Shared libraries .so via ld.so, LD_LIBRARY_PATH .dll via loader, search order, KnownDLLs ASLR randomize_va_space, PIE /DYNAMICBASE, /HIGHENTROPYVA, system-wide "mandatory ASLR" option Null page first 64 KiB unmapped (mmap_min_addr) first 64 KiB reserved and never mapped Big allocations mmap directly (>= 128 KiB) VirtualAlloc directly for >= ~512 KiB (heap's VirtualMemoryThreshold)

VMMap shows you the same picture as /proc/PID/maps but with Windows categories: Image, Mapped File, Shareable, Heap, Managed Heap, Stack, Private Data, Page Table, Unusable, Free. "Private Data" is roughly Linux anonymous mmap. The "Committed" column is what counts against the system commit limit; "Working Set" is roughly RSS.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m01_memory_layout.c prints the address of one object of each kind and then dumps /proc/self/maps so you can match them. Key part:

extern char etext, edata, end;          /* linker-provided end-of-section markers      */
static int        g_bss_counter;        /* .bss: zero-initialised, costs no file bytes */
static int        g_data_counter = 42;  /* .data                                       */
static const char g_rodata_text[] = "hello";   /* .rodata: writing here faults        */

char *small_heap = malloc(100);         /* brk heap (main arena)                        */
char *big_heap   = malloc(1 << 20);     /* 1 MiB >= mmap threshold -> its own mapping   */
void *anon_map   = mmap(NULL, 4096, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
int   stack_local = 7;

Build and run:

cd code && mkdir -p build
gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -g -O0 -o build/m01_memory_layout m01_memory_layout.c
./build/m01_memory_layout
./build/m01_memory_layout        # run again: every address moved (ASLR)
gdb -batch -ex run ./build/m01_memory_layout | head -20   # under gdb: stable addresses

Check three things in the output:

  1. text < rodata < data < bss < heap, all close together, all starting 0x5....
  2. malloc(1 MiB) is not near malloc(100); it is up at 0x7f... next to libc, because it was served by mmap not brk.
  3. The stack local is the highest address, and the [stack] line in the maps dump contains it.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Demand paging and overcommit. malloc(1 << 30) for 1 GiB returns almost instantly and RSS does not move. glibc called mmap, the kernel recorded a mapping and did nothing else. Pages become real only when first written (minor fault, zero-filled frame). With the default vm.overcommit_memory=0 the kernel lets processes map more than physical RAM + swap; when the pages are actually touched and memory runs out, the OOM killer kills a process (often not the one at fault). dmesg | grep -i oom is the first check when a server "disappeared" with no core.

Copy-on-write after fork. fork duplicates the page tables, not the pages, and marks them read-only. The first write by either process faults and the kernel copies that one page. A multi-GB server that forks a helper pays only for the pages the child dirties. This is also why RSS of parent and child double-count shared pages; use PSS (smaps) for honest accounting.

RSS vs VSZ. Virtual size is how much is mapped; RSS is how many of those pages are resident. Monitoring VSZ for leaks is meaningless (glibc reserves 64 MiB per arena); monitoring RSS is better but still confused by freed-but-not-returned memory (module 09).

Huge pages. With Transparent Huge Pages (/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled) the kernel may back a 2 MiB-aligned region with a single 2 MiB page. Fewer TLB misses, but a 4-byte heap allocation can pin 2 MiB of RSS. Databases often disable THP for that reason.

Why the gap matters. Pointer arithmetic that goes a little past a buffer stays inside the same page most of the time, so the hardware says nothing. Only when the pointer crosses into an unmapped page do you get a fault. Faults are the exception; silent corruption is the rule. Tools like ASan exist to turn silent corruption into loud faults (module 08).

Windows reserve/commit. On Windows, VirtualAlloc(MEM_RESERVE) claims address space and MEM_COMMIT charges it against the commit limit (RAM + pagefile). The stack is reserved in full (1 MiB) and committed one page at a time by the guard-page mechanism: touching the guard page raises a guard exception, the OS commits the page and moves the guard down. Running out of reservation gives STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW. There is no overcommit; HeapAlloc fails with NULL when commit is exhausted, which means Windows servers sometimes fail allocations where Linux servers would have been OOM-killed later.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Read si_addr before anything else. A crash report with "SIGSEGV at address 0x18" is a null dereference of a field at offset 24, and you can often find the struct from that alone. "SIGSEGV at 0x7ffd1234000" next to the stack is an overflow. "SIGSEGV at 0x41414141" is a string that overwrote a pointer. Five seconds of thought before you even open gdb.
  • Thread stacks in a 500-thread RPC server. 500 x 8 MiB = 4 GiB of virtual reservation, but only touched pages count toward RSS. People reduce stack size to allow more threads and then hit stack overflows in deep recursion (JSON parsers, regex engines, recursive descent) that the developer machine never saw. Decide stack size deliberately; log it at startup.
  • Big static buffers in .bss are free until touched. A 256 MiB .bss array costs nothing in the binary or in RSS until used. Fine. But put it in .data (initialised to non-zero) and the binary is 256 MiB on disk.
  • mlockall, huge pages and RSS alarms. Monitoring that alarms on RSS will fire on normal warm-up. Alarm on RSS trend over hours, not absolute value (module 09).
  • Mapping a file for a migration engine. mmap of a 10 GiB data file shows 10 GiB of VSZ and a growing RSS as pages are read; it is reclaimable (page cache), not a leak. smaps shows it as file-backed Rss with zero Anonymous.
  • Windows: VMMap on a leaking server. Snapshot, wait, snapshot, compare. If "Heap" grows: !heap -s (module 09). If "Private Data" grows: someone is calling VirtualAlloc directly or the heap is using large blocks. If "Image" grows: DLLs being loaded repeatedly without unload (plugin systems do this).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - map the program. Build and run m01_memory_layout. In the maps dump, find the line containing each printed address and write down the region name. Done when you can explain why malloc(1 MiB) landed where it did.
  2. Easy - fault addresses. Write a 10-line program that dereferences (int*)0x10, (int*)0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF and a pointer 1 past the end of a malloc(4096) block. Run each under gdb -batch -ex run -ex 'p $_siginfo._sifields._sigfault.si_addr'. Done when you have three fault addresses and an explanation of each (and have noticed that the third one may not fault at all).
  3. Medium - find the guard page. Start m04_stack_overflow, let it crash under gdb, then run info proc mappings and locate the [stack] line. Compute si_addr - stack_start. Done when you can state how far below the mapping the fault was and why.
  4. Medium - ASLR on and off. Run m01_memory_layout five times outside gdb and five times inside gdb. Then setarch x86_64 -R ./build/m01_memory_layout (disables ASLR for one run). Done when you can explain the three sets of results and the security trade-off.
  5. Hard - thread stacks. Write a program that starts 4 threads, each printing the address of a local variable and pthread_getattr_np stack size/base, then sleeps. From another shell, dump /proc/PID/maps and identify each thread's stack mapping and its guard page (the ---p mapping right below). Done when you can point at all four stacks and say what happens if a thread uses 9 MiB.
  6. Hard - Windows comparison. Run any small program on Windows, open it in VMMap, and map every VMMap category to a line in the Linux maps output. Done when you can explain "Committed" vs "Working Set" vs "Private" to a colleague in two sentences each.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between virtual and physical memory, and why does a process never see physical addresses? A: Each process has a private virtual address space; the CPU translates virtual to physical through per-process page tables maintained by the OS. This isolates processes (one cannot address another's memory), lets the OS lazily back pages on demand, share read-only pages (libraries) between processes and swap. The program only ever sees virtual addresses.

Q: Why does dereferencing a null pointer crash but dereferencing a freed pointer often does not? A: The page at address 0 is never mapped, so the hardware faults. Freed heap memory stays mapped: the allocator returns it to its own free lists, not to the OS. The read succeeds and returns whatever the allocator or a later allocation left there. That is why use-after-free is silent corruption rather than a crash, and why tools like ASan quarantine freed memory.

Q: What does a fault address of 0x10 tell you? A: Almost certainly a null pointer plus a field offset of 16: code did p->field with p == nullptr where field is 16 bytes into the struct. Look at the faulting instruction (mov ... [rdi+0x10]) and the type of the register's variable to confirm.

Q: How would you recognise a stack overflow from a core dump? A: The signal is SIGSEGV with a fault address just below the [stack] mapping (or a thread's stack mapping, next to a ---p guard page), the stack pointer is near that address, and the backtrace is very deep with repeating frames or shows a frame with a huge local array. On Windows the exception code is 0xC00000FD.

Q: Where do malloc(100) and malloc(10 MiB) come from and why does it matter? A: Small requests are carved from the arena heap (brk area for the main arena); large ones (above the mmap threshold, 128 KiB by default) get their own mmap mapping. It matters for debugging because overflow past an mmap'd block often hits an unmapped page and faults immediately, while overflow past a small block silently corrupts the neighbouring chunk. It matters for memory accounting because free of an mmap'd block returns memory to the OS at once, while small frees do not.

Q: What does ASLR change for a debugger? A: Addresses differ on every run, so you must work in module-relative offsets when matching production logs to your build. gdb disables ASLR by default for reproducibility, which can hide layout-dependent bugs; set disable-randomization off restores it.

Q: How do Windows reserve and commit differ from Linux mmap? A: Windows separates reserving address space from committing backing store, and commit is charged against RAM plus pagefile with no overcommit, so allocation fails deterministically when commit is exhausted. Linux mmap reserves and (with overcommit) promises memory it may not have; pages are backed on first touch and the OOM killer resolves shortages after the fact.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A process sees a private 128 TiB virtual address space; the CPU translates through page tables in 4 KiB pages; unmapped or wrong-permission access is SIGSEGV / 0xC0000005.
  • Regions low to high: text, rodata, data, bss, heap (brk), big gap, mmap area (big mallocs, thread stacks, libraries), main stack, vdso.
  • /proc/PID/maps, pmap -x, info proc mappings (gdb), VMMap and !address (Windows) show the regions. Compare every bad address against them.
  • A pointer is an integer. Small fault addresses are null plus offset. ASCII-looking addresses are string overflows. Addresses just below a stack mapping are stack overflow.
  • Freed memory stays mapped, so UAF rarely faults; it corrupts.
  • ASLR randomises bases each run; gdb turns it off by default; work in module offsets.
  • Main stack 8 MiB (Linux) vs 1 MiB (Windows); thread stacks have a guard page.
  • RSS counts touched pages; VSZ counts mapped bytes; neither alone proves a leak.

docs.title: 02. Stack frames and calling conventions
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
When one function calls another, the CPU needs to remember where to come back to, and the callee needs space for its local variables. Both go on the stack. Each active function has a slice of the stack called its frame. The frames are stacked like plates: the function running now is on top, main is at the bottom. A backtrace is simply a walk down the plates, reading the "come back here" address written on each one.

The rules for how arguments are passed, which registers a function may trash and how the frame is shaped are called the calling convention. Linux and Windows use different ones on x86-64, and you need both because you debug on both. The debugger relies on these rules plus extra information the compiler leaves behind (DWARF on Linux, PDB files on Windows) to rebuild the backtrace and show you variables. When the compiler optimises, some frames and variables disappear; knowing why stops you from distrusting a correct backtrace or trusting a wrong one.

docs.title: 2.1 What a frame holds (x86-64, frame pointer kept)
docs.text:
higher addresses
        |  caller's locals ...                      |
        |  arg 7, arg 8 ... (only if > 6 int args)  |  <- pushed by caller, SysV
        |  return address                           |  <- pushed by `call`
rbp --> |  saved rbp (caller's frame pointer)       |  <- pushed by `push rbp` in prologue
        |  callee-saved registers (rbx, r12-r15)    |
        |  local variables                          |
        |  spill slots (temporaries)                |
        |  outgoing args for the next call          |
rsp --> |  (red zone: 128 bytes below rsp, SysV only, leaf functions may use without moving rsp)
lower addresses

Prologue and epilogue the compiler emits at -O0:

push   rbp              ; save caller's frame pointer
mov    rbp, rsp         ; this frame's base
sub    rsp, 0x40        ; room for locals (kept 16-byte aligned)
...
leave                   ; mov rsp, rbp ; pop rbp
ret                     ; pop rip  <- jumps to the return address

So with frame pointers the frames form a linked list: [rbp] is the previous rbp, [rbp+8] is the return address into the caller. A debugger (or backtrace()) can walk this list with no other information. That is exactly what x/2xg $rbp in gdb shows you.

docs.title: 2.2 x86-64 System V ABI (Linux, macOS, BSD)
docs.text:
Item Rule Integer/pointer args rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9; the 7th onward on the stack Floating args xmm0-xmm7 Return value rax (and rdx for 128-bit); floats in xmm0; large structs via hidden pointer in rdi Callee-saved (preserved) rbx, rbp, r12, r13, r14, r15 Caller-saved (clobbered) rax, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi, r8-r11, all xmm Stack alignment rsp is 16-byte aligned before call (so rsp+8 aligned at function entry) Red zone 128 bytes below rsp usable by leaf functions without adjusting rsp this pointer first integer argument (rdi) Variadic al holds the number of vector registers used

Debugging consequence: at a breakpoint at function entry, rdi is this or the first argument, rsi the second. Once the function has run a few instructions those registers may have been reused. At -O0 the compiler stores the arguments to the frame immediately, which is why info args always works at -O0 and sometimes fails at -O2.

docs.title: 2.3 Windows x64 calling convention
docs.text:
Item Rule Integer/pointer args rcx, rdx, r8, r9; the 5th onward on the stack Floating args xmm0-xmm3 (position-based: 2nd arg in xmm1 even if 1st was int) Return value rax; floats xmm0; structs > 8 bytes via hidden pointer in rcx Callee-saved rbx, rbp, rdi, rsi, r12-r15, xmm6-xmm15 Caller-saved rax, rcx, rdx, r8-r11, xmm0-xmm5 Shadow space (home space) caller reserves 32 bytes above the return address for the callee to spill rcx, rdx, r8, r9 Red zone none Stack alignment 16 bytes at call this pointer rcx Unwinding mandatory unwind metadata in .pdata/.xdata (RUNTIME_FUNCTION, UNWIND_INFO) for every non-leaf function

Debugging consequence: in WinDbg kb shows "child-SP, RetAddr, Args to Child" but on x64 the first four args were in registers; the values kb prints are whatever is in the home space, which is only meaningful if the callee spilled them there (debug builds do, release builds often do not). kv adds the calling-convention column. Trust dv (locals via symbols) over kb.

docs.title: 2.4 How a debugger reconstructs the backtrace
docs.text:
There are three methods, in order of reliability:

  1. Unwind tables (.eh_frame / .debug_frame CFI on Linux; .pdata/.xdata on Windows). For every code address they describe where the return address and saved registers are, relative to the current rsp or rbp. GCC emits .eh_frame by default even without -g because C++ exceptions need it. This is what gdb uses. It works with -fomit-frame-pointer.
  2. Frame pointer chain ([rbp] -> [rbp] -> ...). Fast, needs no tables, used by backtrace() fallbacks, perf, many profilers. Breaks when any function in the chain was built with -fomit-frame-pointer (the default at -O1 and above in GCC) - those frames are skipped or garbage follows.
  3. Heuristic stack scanning. Look at every 8-byte word on the stack and ask "does this point into a code region just after a call instruction?" WinDbg does this when unwind info is missing ("Stack unwind information not available. Following frames may be wrong."); gdb's x/40ag $rsp lets you do it by hand. Produces false frames from stale return addresses that were never overwritten.

When you see ?? () frames in gdb or 0x00000000 frames in WinDbg, one of these methods ran out: a module without unwind info (hand-written asm, JIT code, a stripped third-party library), or the stack itself is corrupted (a buffer overflow wrote over the saved rbp/return address).

docs.title: 2.5 Why optimised builds have missing frames
docs.text:
Optimisation Effect on the backtrace Inlining (-O2, inline, small functions) The callee has no frame at all. With DWARF DW_TAG_inlined_subroutine gdb synthesises an "inlined frame" (#1 0x... in level3 (...) at file.cpp:30 with no real rbp), so the frame appears but has no separate stack memory, and finish behaves oddly. Without debug info the function simply vanishes from bt. Tail-call optimisation (-O2: jmp instead of call; ret) The caller's frame is reused by the callee; the caller disappears. bt shows the callee's caller's caller. Marked by gdb as [tail call frame] when DWARF 5 call-site info is present. Frame pointer omission (-O1+) rbp is a general register; frame-pointer walkers fail; CFI-based unwinders are fine. -fno-omit-frame-pointer costs ~1% and makes perf and crash handlers reliable. Ubuntu 24.04 builds its packages with frame pointers for this reason. Register allocation / dead store Locals live in registers or are gone: <optimized out>. Arguments may be unrecoverable once the register is reused. -Og keeps more. Identical code folding, cloning (func.part.0, func.constprop.1, func.isra.2) Names in bt have suffixes: .part = outlined part, .constprop = specialised for a constant argument, .isra = scalar replacement of aggregates, .cold = unlikely path moved out of line. They are your function. -fomit-frame-pointer + no CFI (asm, some JITs) Unwinding stops; ?? frames.

Rule of thumb for production: build with -O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer, ship the binary stripped, keep the debug info separately (next section). You lose almost no speed and gain correct backtraces from both the debugger and the in-process crash handler.

docs.title: 2.6 Debug info: DWARF and PDB
docs.text:
DWARF (Linux, ELF) is stored in sections of the object itself:

Section Contents .debug_info types, variables, functions, their locations (register/stack offset) and inlining tree .debug_line address -> file:line mapping (what list, bt and addr2line use) .debug_frame / .eh_frame call frame information for unwinding .debug_str, .debug_abbrev, .debug_aranges, .debug_loclists strings, abbreviations, lookup tables, location lists for variables that move between registers .symtab ELF symbol table (function names and addresses) - this is not DWARF; strip removes it; .dynsym stays

Flags: -g (DWARF 5 on GCC 13), -g3 adds macro definitions, -gsplit-dwarf writes .dwo files to shrink objects, -gz compresses. Debug info does not change the generated code; -g -O2 is the same machine code as -O2. Anyone who says "debug info slows it down" is confusing -g with -O0.

Separate debug files (how distributions and sensible teams ship):

g++ -O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -o server server.cpp
objcopy --only-keep-debug server server.debug     # extract debug info
strip --strip-debug --strip-unneeded server       # ship this (keeps .dynsym)
objcopy --add-gnu-debuglink=server.debug server   # tell gdb where to look
readelf -n server | grep 'Build ID'               # same build-id in both files

gdb finds server.debug via the .gnu_debuglink section (same directory, .debug/ subdirectory, or /usr/lib/debug/), or via the build-id: /usr/lib/debug/.build-id/ab/cdef....debug. The build-id is a hash of the code; a mismatched debug file is rejected. Archive the .debug file for every build you ship, keyed by build-id. A core from a client is useless without it.

debuginfod: a server that hands out debug files by build-id. Ubuntu runs one (https://debuginfod.ubuntu.com); gdb 15 asks to enable it on first run. For your own builds you can run debuginfod -F /path/to/debugfiles internally. For libc symbols on Ubuntu you can also install libc6-dbg.

PDB (Windows): debug info is always in a separate .pdb file produced by cl /Zi and link /DEBUG. The executable stores the PDB's path, GUID and age; the debugger loads only a PDB with a matching GUID (.symopt+ 0x40 forces a mismatch, dangerous but occasionally useful). /DEBUG:FULL vs /DEBUG:FASTLINK matters: fastlink PDBs reference object files and are useless on another machine. Public vs private symbols: a public PDB (stripped with /PDBSTRIPPED) has function names but no locals/types; private PDBs have everything. Microsoft's symbol server provides public PDBs for Windows DLLs. Your release pipeline should symstore add every PDB into your own symbol store so .sympath can find them by GUID (module 07).

docs.title: 2.7 Reading a frame by hand in gdb
docs.text:
(gdb) info frame
Stack level 0, frame at 0x7fffffffe0d0:
 rip = 0x555555555189 in level3 (m02_backtrace_frames.cpp:33); saved rip = 0x5555555551e6
 called by frame at 0x7fffffffe100
 source language c++.
 Arglist at 0x7fffffffe0c0, args: c=6
 Locals at 0x7fffffffe0c0, Previous frame's sp is 0x7fffffffe0d0
 Saved registers:
  rbp at 0x7fffffffe0c0, rip at 0x7fffffffe0c8

"frame at" is the canonical frame address (CFA): the value of rsp before the call. "saved rip" is the return address, stored 8 bytes below the CFA. "rbp at" tells you where the caller's rbp is saved. x/2xg 0x7fffffffe0c0 prints both. Do this once with the example program and the stack stops being abstract.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m02_backtrace_frames.cpp has four nested functions, each printing the address of a local so you can see the stack grow downward, and level3 calls glibc's backtrace() so you see an in-process unwind next to gdb's.

__attribute__((noinline)) static long level3(long c)
{
    volatile long local3 = c * 3;        // volatile forces a stack slot even at -O2
    std::printf("level3: &local3 = %p\n", (void *)&local3);
    print_native_backtrace();            // backtrace() + backtrace_symbols_fd()
    return local3 + 1;
}
static long level2(long b) { long local2 = b * 2; ...; return level3(local2) + 1; }
static long level1(long a) { long local1 = a + 1; ...; return level2(local1) + 1; }

Build both ways and compare:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -g -O0 -fno-omit-frame-pointer -o build/m02_frames_O0 m02_backtrace_frames.cpp
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -g -O2 -o build/m02_frames_O2 m02_backtrace_frames.cpp

gdb -q ./build/m02_frames_O0
(gdb) b level3
(gdb) run
(gdb) bt
#0  level3 (c=6) at m02_backtrace_frames.cpp:33
#1  0x... in level2 (b=3) at m02_backtrace_frames.cpp:41
#2  0x... in level1 (a=2) at m02_backtrace_frames.cpp:48
#3  0x... in main (argc=1) at m02_backtrace_frames.cpp:55
(gdb) info frame
(gdb) x/2xg $rbp          # saved rbp, then return address == "saved rip" above
(gdb) p/x *(long*)($rbp+8) # the return address, by hand
(gdb) info symbol *(long*)($rbp+8)   # "level2 + 42 in section .text"
(gdb) up
(gdb) info locals          # local2
(gdb) finish               # "Run till exit from #0 ..." then "Value returned is $1 = 19"

Now the -O2 binary: level1 and level2 are inlined into main; gdb still shows them as frames thanks to DWARF but info frame for them says "inlined into frame 3", local2 may be <optimized out>, and backtrace() output (which uses unwind tables, not DWARF) shows only level3 and main.

Also look at the raw unwind data once, so it is not magic:

readelf --debug-dump=frames-interp build/m02_frames_O2 | head -60   # CFI rows: CFA = rsp+16, rip at cfa-8 ...
objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn build/m02_frames_O0 | grep -A12 '<_ZL6level3l>:'   # prologue: push rbp / mov rbp,rsp
addr2line -f -i -e build/m02_frames_O2 0x1189   # address -> function + inlined chain + file:line

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
call and ret are the whole mechanism. call target pushes the address of the next instruction and jumps. ret pops into rip. Nothing else is architectural. Frames, frame pointers and calling conventions are conventions between compilers. This is why overwriting the return address (stack buffer overflow) hijacks control flow: ret happily jumps wherever the corrupted word says. Stack protector (-fstack-protector-strong, MSVC /GS) puts a random canary between locals and the return address and checks it before ret; a mismatch calls __stack_chk_fail (SIGABRT, " stack smashing detected ") or on Windows raises STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN 0xC0000409 via __fastfail. A crash in __stack_chk_fail is therefore a diagnosis, not a mystery: a local array in the function that was about to return overflowed.

CFI is a state machine. .eh_frame encodes, for each instruction address range, rules like "CFA = rsp + 16; return address at CFA - 8; rbx saved at CFA - 24". The unwinder executes these rules frame by frame. readelf --debug-dump=frames-interp shows the table. Hand-written assembly without .cfi_* directives has no rows, and unwinding stops there. This is why a crash inside an optimised memcpy from libc still unwinds fine (glibc's asm has CFI) but a crash inside a JIT-generated buffer does not.

Shadow stack / CET. Modern CPUs (Intel CET, -fcf-protection) keep a hardware shadow stack of return addresses; ret compares the two and faults on mismatch (SIGSEGV with si_code SEGV_CPERR on Linux 6.6+, enabled per-process). Windows 11 exposes this as "Hardware-enforced Stack Protection". It turns a return-address overwrite into an immediate, precise fault.

Red zone and signal handlers. The SysV red zone lets leaf functions use 128 bytes below rsp without moving it. The kernel knows this and skips 128 bytes before pushing the signal frame. A crash handler that corrupts the red zone (hand-written asm) corrupts the interrupted function's temporaries.

Variadic functions and al. On SysV the caller sets al to the number of vector registers used. printf with a double argument but %d format reads rsi instead of xmm0 and prints garbage; -Wformat catches it. Across the Windows x64 boundary, floating varargs are duplicated in the integer register too, which is why printf("%d", 1.5) prints different garbage on each OS.

Windows x64 unwinding is table-only. There is no frame-pointer chain requirement; the UNWIND_INFO for each function lists prologue operations (UWOP_PUSH_NONVOL, UWOP_ALLOC_SMALL, UWOP_SET_FPREG). RtlVirtualUnwind interprets them. A function with wrong or missing unwind info (hand-written asm without .pdata) breaks exceptions and stack walks; kv shows "(FPO: ...)" markers and .fnent address dumps the entry for a function. This is also why SEH works on x64 without any runtime cost on the non-exceptional path.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The frame you crash in is often not the frame at fault. pc in memcpy, strlen, free, std::__cxx11::basic_string::_M_assign means your code passed a bad pointer or size. Walk up (up, .frame) to the first frame in your own code and inspect its arguments.
  • "Following frames may be wrong" in WinDbg, or ?? in gdb, right after a frame with a char buf[N] local: the stack was overwritten. The frames above it are untrustworthy; the function with the buffer is the suspect.
  • Mismatched symbols lie confidently. A PDB from a different build or a debug file with a different build-id produces a backtrace with plausible-looking but wrong function names. gdb warns about build-id mismatch; WinDbg marks modules with *** WARNING: Unable to verify checksum or loads nothing. Always check lm / info sharedlibrary first. Keep every shipped build's debug info; a client core for a build whose symbols you deleted is a lost week.
  • Optimised backtraces in your crash handler. backtrace() uses the unwind tables (good) but backtrace_symbols_fd needs -rdynamic or .symtab to print names; stripped binaries print prog(+0x1234). Log the offsets anyway; addr2line -e prog.debug 0x1234 recovers everything later. Log the build-id at startup so you know which .debug to use.
  • -O2 -g is the correct production build. Not -O0 (slow), not -O2 without -g (undebuggable). The debug info goes in a separate file. Shakir's server should ship like this if it does not already; it is the single biggest improvement to post-crash diagnosis.
  • Windows: kb arguments are unreliable on x64. Ask for locals with dv in each frame, or read registers at the time of the call with .frame /r. In release builds dv often shows <value unavailable>; then you read the disassembly and registers (module 07).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - read a frame. With m02_frames_O0 stopped in level3, use info frame, x/2xg $rbp and info symbol to show that [rbp+8] is the return address into level2. Done when you can draw the three frames with real addresses from your run.
  2. Easy - registers at entry. break level3, run, p $rdi, p c. Then ni a few times and watch p $rdi change while p c stays. Done when you can explain where c lives after the prologue (info address c).
  3. Medium - inlining. With m02_frames_O2, break level3, run, bt, info frame in frame 1 and 2. Compare with backtrace() output printed by the program. Done when you can explain why they differ.
  4. Medium - separate debug file. Build m04_null_deref with -O2 -g, run objcopy --only-keep-debug, strip, --add-gnu-debuglink. Run gdb on the stripped binary (a) with the .debug file present and (b) renamed away. Done when bt shows source lines in (a) and only addresses in (b), and you can state the build-id of both files.
  5. Hard - stack scan by hand. Crash m04_null_deref ACC-9999 under gdb, then without using bt use x/40ag $rsp and info symbol on each plausible word to reconstruct the call chain. Done when your manual chain matches bt.
  6. Hard - Windows x64. Build a 3-level program with MSVC /O2 /Zi, break in the innermost function in WinDbg, run kv, .frame /r 1, dv, .fnent @rip, and dps @rsp L20. Done when you can identify the shadow space and the return address in the raw dump.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is in a stack frame? A: The return address pushed by call, usually the saved frame pointer of the caller, saved callee-preserved registers, the function's locals and spill slots, and space for outgoing arguments to callees. With frame pointers the frames form a linked list through the saved rbp values.

Q: How does gdb produce a backtrace when the compiler omitted frame pointers? A: From the call frame information in .eh_frame/.debug_frame: for each code address range it records how to compute the previous frame's stack pointer and where the return address and saved registers are. GCC always emits it because C++ exceptions need it. Without it (assembly without CFI directives, JIT code) unwinding stops and you see ?? frames.

Q: Name the argument registers for SysV and for Windows x64, and one practical difference. A: SysV: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9; Windows: rcx, rdx, r8, r9 plus a 32-byte shadow space reserved by the caller. Practical difference: Windows has no red zone and requires unwind metadata for every non-leaf function, so stack walking is table-driven; SysV leaf functions may use 128 bytes below rsp without adjusting it.

Q: Why does an optimised backtrace show fewer frames than the source suggests? A: Inlining removes callee frames (gdb can still show them as inlined frames if DWARF describes them), tail-call optimisation replaces call/ret with jmp so the caller's frame disappears, and functions may be split into .part/.cold clones. Variables shown as <optimized out> lived in registers that were reused or were eliminated entirely.

Q: Does -g make the program slower? A: No. -g adds DWARF sections and does not change code generation; -O2 -g is byte-identical code to -O2. Slowness comes from -O0. The right production build is -O2 -g with the debug info split into a separate file via objcopy --only-keep-debug and matched by build-id.

Q: How does WinDbg know which PDB to load, and what happens with the wrong one? A: The executable's debug directory stores the PDB path, GUID and age; the debugger looks the GUID up in the symbol path (local folders and symbol servers). A PDB with a different GUID is refused unless you force it with .symopt+ 0x40, in which case the names it shows will be wrong while looking plausible.

Q: What does a crash inside __stack_chk_fail or exception code 0xC0000409 tell you? A: The stack protector detected that a canary between locals and the return address was overwritten when a function was about to return. Some local buffer in that function (or one it inlined) overflowed. On Windows 0xC0000409 is also used for other fail-fast conditions; check the subcode in the exception parameters.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• call pushes the return address, ret pops it; everything else about frames is convention.
  • With frame pointers: [rbp] = caller's rbp, [rbp+8] = return address, a linked list.
  • SysV args: rdi rsi rdx rcx r8 r9; Win64 args: rcx rdx r8 r9 + 32-byte shadow space.
  • Callee-saved SysV: rbx rbp r12-r15; Win64 adds rdi rsi xmm6-15.
  • Debuggers unwind with CFI (.eh_frame / .pdata), fall back to frame pointers, then to stack scanning; ?? frames mean the chain broke or the stack is corrupt.
  • Inlining, tail calls and register allocation make frames and variables vanish at -O2; -fno-omit-frame-pointer and -Og help.
  • DWARF lives in .debug_* sections; split it out with objcopy --only-keep-debug and match by build-id; PDBs are always separate and matched by GUID.
  • Ship -O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer, strip the binary, archive the debug file. Always.

docs.title: 03. The heap: malloc internals
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 01

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
The heap is the pool of memory you ask for with malloc/new and give back with free/delete. The allocator is the library code that manages that pool. It is not the kernel; it is malloc inside the C library. The kernel gives the allocator big slabs of pages; the allocator chops them into the small pieces your program asks for and remembers which pieces are free so it can reuse them.

To remember all that, the allocator keeps bookkeeping data right next to your blocks: a little header just before each block saying how big it is, and when a block is free it reuses the first few bytes of your old data to link it into a list of free blocks. That is the single most important fact in this whole course. Your data and the allocator's bookkeeping are interleaved. So if you write one byte past the end of your array, you are not scribbling on empty space, you are scribbling on the size field of the next block. The allocator will not notice until much later, when it tries to use that corrupted size. That is why heap bugs crash far from where they happen, often in an innocent free or malloc called by code that did nothing wrong.

Understanding the layout turns a baffling "crash in malloc" into a specific sentence: "something wrote N bytes past a block of about this size, some time before this free." That sentence is most of an RCA.

docs.title: 2. The real thing (glibc ptmalloc2)
docs.text: glibc's allocator is ptmalloc2, derived from Doug Lea's dlmalloc. The following is x86-64, glibc 2.35-2.39 (Ubuntu 22.04/24.04).

docs.title: 2.1 The chunk
docs.text:
Everything the allocator hands out is a chunk. The pointer you get points just past the chunk header.

         +-------------------+  <- chunk start (16-byte aligned)
 -16     | prev_size         |  8 bytes: size of previous chunk, ONLY valid if prev is free
 -8      | size        |A|M|P|  8 bytes: this chunk's size (incl header), low 3 bits are flags
  0      | user data...      |  <- malloc returns THIS address
         | ...               |
         | (prev_size of next chunk can overlap the last 8 bytes of our data if next is in use)
         +-------------------+
  • Flags in the low 3 bits of size (sizes are always multiples of 16, so the bits are free):
    • P (PREV_INUSE, 0x1): the previous chunk is in use. If clear, prev_size is valid and the previous chunk can be coalesced with this one.
    • M (IS_MMAPPED, 0x2): this chunk came from mmap (a large request), not an arena.
    • A (NON_MAIN_ARENA, 0x4): this chunk belongs to a secondary arena, not the main one.
  • Minimum chunk size is 32 bytes; sizes round up so the usable size is a multiple of 16. The header steals 8 bytes, but because the prev_size of the next chunk can be borrowed when this chunk is in use, malloc(24) fits in a 32-byte chunk (size field 0x21 = 32 | P). malloc(25) needs 48 (0x31). This off-by-one in your head matters when reading a dump.

code/m03_chunk_inspect.c prints exactly this for several sizes. Run it before reading on.

docs.title: 2.2 Free lists: bins
docs.text:
When you free a chunk it is not returned to the OS; it goes on a free list ("bin") so the next malloc can reuse it fast. ptmalloc has several, fastest first:

Bin What it holds Policy Coalesce? tcache (per-thread, glibc 2.26+) up to 7 chunks per size class, sizes 32..1040 bytes LIFO singly-linked, no locking no fastbins small chunks (<= 160 bytes default), per size LIFO singly-linked, lock held no (deferred) unsorted bin recently freed/split chunks, mixed sizes FIFO, a staging area on the way through small bins exact sizes < 1024 bytes doubly-linked, FIFO per size yes large bins size ranges >= 1024 bytes doubly-linked, sorted yes top chunk the one big free chunk at the end of the arena split from / returned to grows via brk/mmap

A malloc checks tcache, then fastbins, then the unsorted/small/large bins, then splits the top chunk, then asks the kernel for more (sbrk/brk for the main arena, mmap for others). A free pushes to tcache if there is room, else fastbin for small sizes, else coalesces with free neighbours and goes to the unsorted bin.

tcache is why so many things changed since 2.26. It is per-thread and lock-free, so most small alloc/free pairs never touch a lock. It is also singly linked through the first 8 bytes of the freed user data (the next pointer) with the next 8 bytes as a key used to detect double frees. Two consequences you will see in dumps:

  1. After free(p), p[0..7] is a pointer (to the next tcache entry, or 0) and p[8..15] is the tcache key (a per-arena random value). A use-after-free that reads the first 8 bytes of a freed object gets a pointer-looking value or 0, not your old data. Recognise it.
  2. glibc 2.32+ stores that next pointer safe-linked: stored = (address_of_next_field >> 12) XOR next. So a freed chunk's first word looks like a shifted-and-xored pointer, not a clean heap address. m03_chunk_inspect.c prints this.

docs.title: 2.3 Arenas and threads
docs.text:
• The main arena uses the brk heap (the [heap] mapping). It is one contiguous region grown with sbrk.
  • Secondary arenas are created when threads contend on the main arena's lock. Each is a 64 MiB mmap reservation (committed lazily). A thread sticks to an arena. Default max arenas is 8 * number_of_cores (MALLOC_ARENA_MAX overrides). This is why a multithreaded server's RSS can be threads * arena_working_set, and why MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 is a common tuning knob for memory-constrained servers at the cost of lock contention.
  • Large requests (>= M_MMAP_THRESHOLD, 128 KiB default, auto-tuned upward) bypass arenas and get a dedicated mmap. free on them calls munmap, returning memory to the OS immediately. That is the one case where memory shrinks right away.

docs.title: 2.4 How corruption is detected (the glibc messages)
docs.text:
glibc does cheap consistency checks and aborts with a message when they fail. Memorise these; each maps to a bug class:

Message What glibc noticed Likely cause free(): invalid pointer pointer not 16-aligned, or outside any arena freeing a non-heap pointer, a stack/global address, or an interior pointer free(): invalid size size field not a sane multiple of 16, or absurd the size field was overwritten (overflow of the previous chunk) free(): invalid next size (fast/normal) the next chunk's size field is insane overflow past the end of the chunk being freed, corrupting the neighbour's header malloc(): corrupted top size the top chunk's size was overwritten overflow of the last allocated chunk free(): double free detected in tcache 2 tcache key matches -> already in this tcache double free of a tcache-sized chunk malloc(): memory corruption (fast) / corrupted unsorted chunks a bin's linked list is inconsistent overflow into a free chunk's fd/bk pointers, or a UAF write malloc_consolidate(): ... corruption found while merging fastbins overflow, surfaced later during consolidation munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer freeing an mmapped chunk whose header is wrong overflow of a large block, or freeing a realloc-moved pointer

The lesson repeated: the message names the symptom location (a free/malloc operating on a chunk), not the bug location (whoever wrote past a buffer earlier). "invalid next size" literally means "the chunk after the one I'm freeing has a corrupted header", i.e. someone overflowed the chunk being freed. Tools in module 08 find the write; glibc only finds the aftermath.

docs.title: 2.5 Fragmentation
docs.text:
Two kinds:

  • External fragmentation: free memory exists but is split into pieces too small for the next request, so the allocator grows the heap instead of reusing. Classic cause: a long-lived small allocation sitting at a high address keeps the top chunk from shrinking, and a sea of freed small chunks cannot satisfy a medium request. m09_growth_not_leak.cpp reproduces it.
  • Internal fragmentation: rounding up. malloc(17) uses a 32-byte chunk; 15 bytes wasted. Millions of small allocations waste a lot. malloc_usable_size(p) tells you the real size.

Fragmentation is not a leak: the bytes are free, the allocator just cannot give them back. Leak tools report nothing. You diagnose it with malloc_stats()/mallinfo2() (in-use bytes much less than system bytes) and fix it with arena allocators, size-class pooling, or periodic malloc_trim(0) (module 09).

docs.title: 2.6 The Windows heap and the LFH
docs.text:
Windows has its own allocator, unrelated to glibc. Several heaps per process: the process heap (GetProcessHeap), the CRT heap (what C++ new/malloc use, which is the process heap on modern CRTs), and any private heaps (HeapCreate).

  • The classic NT heap keeps free lists and a header per block. The header is encoded (XORed with a per-heap random key) since Windows Vista, so a naive overflow of the next block's header produces a detectably invalid decode and a heap corruption fast-fail.
  • The Low Fragmentation Heap (LFH) is a front-end, on by default since Vista, that serves small blocks (<= 16 KiB) from per-size-class subsegments of fixed-size buckets, like a slab allocator. It cuts fragmentation and (incidentally) changes corruption behaviour: an overflow lands in the next bucket of the same size class, which is often another live block.
  • Heap corruption on Windows is reported as a fail-fast: exception code STATUS_HEAP_CORRUPTION 0xC0000374, usually raised by RtlReportCriticalFailure -> __fastfail at the moment the heap manager notices an inconsistency (on free, allocate or a background validation). Like glibc, this is the aftermath, not the bug. The tool that finds the actual write is PageHeap/Application Verifier (module 07): it puts each allocation on its own page with an unmapped guard page right after, so the overflowing write faults immediately with the exact call stack.
Concept glibc ptmalloc Windows NT heap Per-thread fast path tcache LFH per-processor affinity, lookaside (older) Header 8-byte size+flags, plaintext encoded (XOR key) 8/16-byte header Corruption signal abort() with a message, SIGABRT fail-fast 0xC0000374 Large blocks mmap, freed to OS on free VirtualAlloc, freed to OS on HeapFree Return to OS malloc_trim, munmap of large HeapFree decommits, HeapCompact "Find the write" tool ASan, Valgrind PageHeap / Application Verifier Free-fill pattern none by default (tcache next/key) 0xFEEEFEEE freed, 0xBAADF00D uninit (debug CRT), 0xABABABAB/0xCDCDCDCD guard/no-mans-land

docs.title: 2.7 Why arena / pool allocators avoid all of this
docs.text:
Shakir's Berkeley-DB-to-YugabyteDB migration engine is exactly the kind of code that benefits from an arena (a.k.a. region or bump) allocator. The idea: for a phase of work with a clear lifetime (processing one batch, one record, one request), allocate a big block once and hand out pieces by just bumping a pointer; free nothing individually; at the end of the phase, free (or reset) the whole block in one call.

typedef struct { char *base, *cur, *end; } Arena;
void  arena_init(Arena *a, size_t n){ a->base=a->cur=malloc(n); a->end=a->base+n; }
void *arena_alloc(Arena *a, size_t n){ n=(n+15)&~15u;              /* align */
                                       if (a->cur+n > a->end) return NULL;   /* or grow */
                                       void *p=a->cur; a->cur+=n; return p; }
void  arena_reset(Arena *a){ a->cur=a->base; }   /* "free" everything, O(1) */
void  arena_free (Arena *a){ free(a->base); }

Why it is safer and faster:

  • No per-object free, so no double free, no use-after-free within the phase (lifetimes are tied to the arena, not tracked per object), no free-list metadata to corrupt.
  • No fragmentation within a phase: allocation is a pointer bump.
  • Fast: no locks, no bin search, cache-friendly sequential layout.
  • Trade-offs: you cannot free individual objects early (so a long phase holding many dead objects wastes memory), and a buffer overflow still corrupts the next object in the arena (it just will not corrupt allocator metadata or crash free). Pair it with guard regions or ASan during testing.

This is the standard pattern in databases (PostgreSQL's MemoryContext is a hierarchical arena; you write PL/pgSQL on top of it), compilers, and request-scoped server code. When an interviewer asks "how would you make a hot allocation path safe and fast", arenas are the senior answer.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m03_chunk_inspect.c reads the chunk header (the 8 bytes before the returned pointer) for several allocation sizes and shows the free-chunk contents after free. It deliberately reads outside the allocation to show you the metadata, so do not run it under ASan (ASan would correctly flag the header read). Key output to understand:

malloc(24)  a  size_field=0x21   chunk=32   PREV_INUSE
malloc(24)  b  size_field=0x21   chunk=32   PREV_INUSE
malloc(25)  c  size_field=0x31   chunk=48   PREV_INUSE
malloc(100) d  size_field=0x71   chunk=112  PREV_INUSE
malloc(1MiB) e size_field=...    IS_MMAPPED
b - a = 32 bytes                       # consecutive same-size chunks are one chunk apart
a[0..7] after free:  <safe-linked ptr> # tcache next pointer overwrote your first 8 bytes
a[8..15] after free: <tcache key>
malloc(24) again -> same address as b  # tcache is LIFO

Build and run:

gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -g -O0 -o build/m03_chunk_inspect m03_chunk_inspect.c
./build/m03_chunk_inspect

To watch bins change live in gdb, use the pwndbg or gef extension (heap, bins, vis commands) if you can install one; plain gdb works too:

(gdb) p main_arena                 # with libc debug symbols installed (libc6-dbg)
(gdb) p main_arena.top
(gdb) x/4xg <chunk address>

The heap-overflow program code/m04_heap_overflow.cpp (module 04) shows the corruption side: an off-by-one write that trips free(): invalid next size or is caught cleanly by ASan.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why free(): invalid next size points backward in time. When you free(p), glibc reads the size field of p to find the next chunk at p + size, then reads that chunk's size to decide whether to coalesce. If someone overflowed p earlier, they wrote past p's user data into the next chunk's header, so the next size is garbage and the check fails. The write happened whenever the overflow ran; the detection happens now, at free. Between the two, the program ran normally. This temporal gap is the entire reason heap bugs are hard and why you need a tool that traps the write itself.

tcache poisoning and the security angle. Because the tcache next pointer lives in freed user data, an attacker with a use-after-free or overflow can overwrite it to make malloc return an arbitrary address ("tcache poisoning"). Safe-linking (the >> 12 XOR) and the alignment check added in 2.32 raise the bar. You do not exploit this, but you will read CVEs and hardening notes that reference it, and it explains why freed-chunk contents look mangled.

fastbins defer coalescing. Fastbin chunks keep PREV_INUSE set even though they are free, so neighbours do not coalesce them. This speeds the common case but means a double free into a fastbin is only caught by a shallow "is the top of the fastbin the same chunk" check (easily bypassed historically). malloc_consolidate later flushes fastbins into the unsorted bin and does the real coalescing; corruption written into a fastbin chunk often surfaces there, hence malloc_consolidate(): ... messages far from the bug.

Alignment and memalign. malloc guarantees 16-byte alignment on x86-64 (enough for any scalar and max_align_t). posix_memalign/aligned_alloc/new with over-aligned types create chunks with padding and a special header so free can find the real chunk start. Freeing a pointer that is not a chunk start (e.g. the aligned pointer handed back by a naive manual alignment) gives free(): invalid pointer.

malloc_trim and MADV_DONTNEED. glibc can return free pages in the middle of the heap to the OS with madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) (the pages fault back in zeroed if touched again), not only trim the top. This is why RSS can drop sharply after malloc_trim(0) even when the heap's top chunk has not moved. The automatic trimming threshold is M_TRIM_THRESHOLD (128 KiB of contiguous free top).

Environment tunables worth knowing. MALLOC_ARENA_MAX, MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_, MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_, MALLOC_TOP_PAD_, MALLOC_PERTURB_ (fills alloc/free with a byte to expose uninitialised-use and UAF bugs cheaply), MALLOC_CHECK_=3 (enables extra consistency checks and aborts with a report; a poor-man's debug malloc). GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.* is the modern interface. MALLOC_PERTURB_=165 in a test environment turns many silent UAF/uninit bugs into obvious garbage-value failures for almost no cost.

jemalloc / tcmalloc. Servers often LD_PRELOAD a different allocator for lower fragmentation and better multithread scaling. They have their own metadata layout, their own corruption reports (<jemalloc>: Invalid chunk ...) and their own profiling (jeprof, tcmalloc's pprof). If Shakir's server links one, the glibc messages above do not apply; know which allocator you are running (ldd the binary, check LD_PRELOAD).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• "Crash in free / malloc / _int_malloc" in a core is almost never a bug in glibc. It is your code having corrupted a chunk earlier. Read the glibc abort message (it is on stderr and often in the log): it names which check failed, which tells you overflow vs double-free vs wild pointer. Then reproduce under ASan (module 08) to catch the actual write.
  • Intermittent heap corruption that moves around is the signature of an overflow whose victim depends on allocation order, which depends on timing and input. It will "move" when you add logging (you changed the allocation pattern). Do not chase the moving symptom; trap the write with ASan/PageHeap.
  • RSS climbs then plateaus, no leak reported: fragmentation or arena growth, not a leak. Check malloc_stats() in-use vs system bytes; try MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 and a periodic malloc_trim(0) on an idle tick. Measure before and after (module 09).
  • Multithreaded server using more memory than expected: per-thread arenas. Each worker thread may hold a 64 MiB arena's worth of working set. Cap arenas or use a thread pool with fewer, long-lived threads.
  • Migration engine war story shape: a bump/arena allocator for per-record scratch turns a class of free-ordering bugs into non-bugs and speeds the hot loop. But a single overflow inside the arena silently corrupts the next record's fields and shows up as wrong data in Yugabyte, not a crash. That is worse for a bank than a crash. Run the migration under ASan in CI and keep guard bytes between arena objects in debug builds.
  • Windows: 0xC0000374 in a dump. Heap corruption fail-fast. !heap -p -a <address> and !heap -s (module 07) give the heap state; to find the writer, re-run under PageHeap (gflags /p /enable yourapp.exe /full) or Application Verifier, which fault at the overflowing write with the allocating and faulting stacks.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - chunk sizes. Run m03_chunk_inspect. For malloc(1), malloc(16), malloc(17), malloc(24), malloc(40), predict the chunk size and size field before running, then verify. Done when all five predictions are right and you can state the formula.
  2. Easy - tcache LIFO. Modify the program to malloc three 24-byte blocks a,b,c, free them in order a,b,c, then malloc three more and record the addresses. Done when you can explain the order they come back in (c,b,a) from the tcache LIFO rule.
  3. Medium - read the abort message. Build m04_heap_overflow (no ASan), run it with several n values until it aborts, and capture the exact glibc message. Done when you can say which check failed and translate it into "a write of about X bytes past a ~Y-byte block".
  4. Medium - perturb. Run m04_uninit_read (module 04) normally, then with MALLOC_PERTURB_=165 ./build/.... Done when you can explain why the "flags" value became a consistent nonzero pattern and how that would help you spot the bug in testing.
  5. Hard - fragmentation vs leak. Run m09_growth_not_leak and read its malloc_stats() output. Then run it under Valgrind --leak-check=full. Done when you can explain why Valgrind reports zero leaks while RSS was high, and what malloc_trim(0) changed.
  6. Hard - arena allocator. Implement the Arena above, use it to allocate 100000 small records in a loop, and compare the time and peak RSS against the same loop using malloc/ free per record. Then deliberately overflow one arena object by one byte and observe that free/exit does not crash (unlike the malloc version) but a neighbouring record's field is wrong. Done when you can state the safety trade-off of arenas in one sentence.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is stored in a glibc malloc chunk header and why does it matter for debugging? A: Eight bytes of size with three low flag bits (PREV_INUSE, IS_MMAPPED, NON_MAIN_ARENA), and a prev_size field used only when the previous chunk is free. It matters because the header sits immediately before your data, so a buffer overflow corrupts the next chunk's header, and the allocator only notices later during free/malloc - the crash is far from the bug.

Q: Why does heap corruption usually crash far away from the actual bug? A: The bad write corrupts allocator metadata (a size field or a free-list pointer) but the program keeps running normally until the allocator next touches that metadata - a later free or malloc of a neighbouring chunk - which is where it aborts. The time and code distance between the write and the detection is why these are hard and why you need a tool that traps the write itself.

Q: What is the tcache and how did it change what you see in a freed block? A: A per-thread, lock-free cache of up to 7 recently freed chunks per small size class (glibc 2.26+). It links chunks through the first 8 bytes of the freed user data and stores a key in the next 8 for double-free detection, and since 2.32 the next pointer is "safe-linked" (shifted and XORed). So a use-after-free that reads a freed small block sees a pointer-looking value or 0, not the old contents.

Q: What does free(): invalid next size mean? A: When freeing a chunk, glibc read the size field of the physically next chunk and found it insane. That means something overwrote the next chunk's header, i.e. the chunk being freed was overflowed earlier. It is a heap buffer overflow, detected at free time.

Q: How is the Windows heap different, and how do you find a heap overflow on each platform? A: Windows has multiple heaps, encoded headers, and a Low Fragmentation Heap front-end serving fixed-size buckets; corruption is reported as fail-fast 0xC0000374. glibc uses plaintext headers, tcache/bins, and aborts with a text message. To find the actual overflowing write, use ASan or Valgrind on Linux and PageHeap/Application Verifier on Windows - all of them trap the write at the moment it happens instead of at the later allocator operation.

Q: When would you use an arena allocator and what does it not protect against? A: For request- or phase-scoped work with a common lifetime - request handlers, per-record migration scratch, parsers - where you allocate many objects and free them all at once. It removes per-object free bugs (double free, UAF within the phase) and fragmentation, and is fast and lock-free. It does not stop a buffer overflow from corrupting the next object in the arena; it just stops that corruption from crashing the allocator, which can be worse because it turns a crash into silent data corruption.

Q: Your multithreaded server uses far more memory than the sum of live objects. No leak is reported. What is going on? A: Most likely per-thread arenas (glibc creates up to 8*cores of them) each holding working set, plus fragmentation and freed-but-not-returned memory. Confirm with malloc_stats() (system bytes >> in-use bytes) and /proc/PID/smaps; mitigate with MALLOC_ARENA_MAX, fewer long-lived threads, periodic malloc_trim(0), or a different allocator (jemalloc/tcmalloc).

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• malloc hands out chunks; each has an 8-byte size+flags header right before your pointer; data and metadata are interleaved.
  • size low bits: PREV_INUSE, IS_MMAPPED, NON_MAIN_ARENA. Min chunk 32 bytes, sizes multiples of 16; malloc(24) -> 32-byte chunk.
  • Free lists fastest-first: tcache (per-thread, 7/size), fastbins, unsorted, small, large, top.
  • Freed small blocks hold a safe-linked tcache next pointer and key in their first 16 bytes - recognise it in a UAF.
  • glibc abort messages name the symptom (a chunk operation); the bug is an earlier overflow, double free or wild pointer. "invalid next size" = overflow past the freed chunk.
  • Secondary arenas (64 MiB each, up to 8*cores) explain multithread memory use; big allocations use mmap and return to the OS on free.
  • Windows: multiple heaps, encoded headers, LFH buckets, fail-fast 0xC0000374; find the write with PageHeap/AppVerifier (Linux: ASan/Valgrind).
  • Arena allocators remove per-object free bugs and fragmentation and are fast, but an overflow inside an arena silently corrupts the next object - test them under ASan.

docs.title: 04. The catalogue of memory bugs
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
There is a fixed, small list of ways C and C++ programs go wrong with memory. Every crash dump you will ever read is one of these, or a combination. If you know the list by heart - what each one looks like in the source, what symptom it produces in production, and which tool catches it - then reading a dump becomes a matching exercise instead of a fishing expedition.

This module is the catalogue. One entry per bug class: a minimal reproduction, the typical production symptom, how it shows up in a debugger, and which tool finds it fastest. The code files in code/ are the full versions with build and debug notes in the comments; this module is the reference card you keep next to the dump.

docs.title: 2. The real thing
docs.text:
A compact index first; details follow.

Bug One-line cause Crashes? Best tool Buffer overflow (heap) write past end of a heap block later, in free/malloc ASan, Valgrind, PageHeap Buffer overflow (stack) write past end of a local array at ret (canary) or garbage ASan, -fstack-protector, /GS Off-by-one loop bound <= instead of < often silent, sometimes as above ASan, -fsanitize=bounds, .at() Uninitialised read use a variable/field never set nondeterministic behaviour Valgrind, MSan, -Wmaybe-uninitialized Use-after-free use memory after free/delete silent corruption, sometimes crash ASan, Valgrind Double free free the same block twice abort in free, or later UAF ASan, Valgrind, glibc Dangling pointer/reference pointer outlives its target like UAF ASan, -Wdangling-pointer Stack-use-after-return return address of a local garbage reads/writes ASan (detect_stack_use_after_return) Invalid iterator use an iterator after container mutates silent or crash _GLIBCXX_DEBUG, ASan Memory leak lose the last pointer to a block growth, eventual OOM LSan, Valgrind, heaptrack Type confusion reinterpret memory as the wrong type garbage, crash on vtable UBSan (vptr), review Integer overflow -> bad size size arithmetic wraps tiny alloc then overflow UBSan, -ftrapv, review Null dereference deref a null pointer immediate crash at small addr any; obvious in dump

docs.title: 2.1 Buffer overflow (heap and stack)
docs.text:
Cause. Writing more bytes than the buffer holds. Heap version corrupts the next chunk's header (module 03); stack version corrupts the saved frame pointer and return address.

char *p = malloc(16);
strcpy(p, "this string is longer than sixteen bytes");   // heap overflow
char buf[16];
gets(buf);                                                 // stack overflow (gets: never use)

Symptom. Heap: a crash later in free/malloc with a glibc free(): invalid next size message, or ASan heap-buffer-overflow. Stack: " stack smashing detected " + SIGABRT (if the canary caught it), or SIGSEGV at ret with a garbage pc (the return address was overwritten), or on Windows 0xC0000409 STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN. code/m04_heap_overflow.cpp.

In the dump. Stack overflow into the return address: bt shows ?? frames or a top frame with a pc that is not in any function; the overflowed buffer's function is the one just below. Heap: pc in _int_free; walk up to your free call; the chunk being freed is the overflowed one or its neighbour.

docs.title: 2.2 Off-by-one
docs.text:
Cause. The most common overflow: for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) a[i] = ... writes a[n], one past a length-n array. Or malloc(strlen(s)) forgetting the NUL terminator's byte.

int *a = new int[n];
for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i) a[i] = i;   // writes a[n], one past the end

Symptom. Usually silent: one element over often lands in padding or the next chunk's unused space and nothing happens, until the input size or allocation pattern changes. Then it becomes a heap overflow. The "works on my machine, fails at the client" bug. code/m04_heap_overflow.cpp is an off-by-one.

Tool. ASan catches it at the write. std::vector::at() or -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS turns it into a clean std::out_of_range or assertion. With compile-time-known bounds, GCC -Warray-bounds (in -Wall at -O2) catches some.

docs.title: 2.3 Uninitialised read
docs.text:
Cause. Reading a variable, struct field, or heap block before writing it. Its value is whatever was in that memory. For locals the compiler may leave a register; for heap, whatever the allocator last left (often another object's old data - information disclosure risk).

Record *r = new Record;   // no initialiser: members indeterminate
r->id = 7;                // but r->flags never set
if (r->flags & 1) ...     // reads garbage

Symptom. Nondeterministic: different behaviour run to run, works in debug (zeroed by luck or by MALLOC_PERTURB_) fails in release, or the reverse. Security: leaked stale data. code/m04_uninit_read.cpp.

Tool. Valgrind memcheck is the tool (--track-origins=yes tells you where the uninitialised value came from). ASan does not catch uninitialised reads; MemorySanitizer (MSan, clang only) does. For locals, -Wmaybe-uninitialized / -Wuninitialized (better at -O2) catch many at compile time. MALLOC_PERTURB_=N makes them reproducible.

docs.title: 2.4 Use-after-free and dangling pointers/references
docs.text:
Cause. Keeping and using a pointer (or reference, or iterator) after the object it points to has been freed/deleted/gone out of scope. "Dangling" is the pointer; "use-after-free" is the act.

Session *s = table[id];
table.erase(id);          // deletes the Session
audit(s);                 // s now dangles -> use-after-free

const std::string &ref = make_name();   // binds to a temporary that dies at the semicolon
use(ref);                               // dangling reference

Symptom. Usually silent corruption, because freed memory stays mapped (module 01): you read stale data or, worse, data belonging to a different object that reused the block, so one feature's bug corrupts another feature's data. Sometimes a crash when the freed block's first bytes (now a tcache pointer) are dereferenced. code/m04_use_after_free.cpp.

Tool. ASan is ideal: it quarantines freed memory and reports heap-use-after-free with three stacks (use, free, allocation). Valgrind too. -Wdangling-pointer (GCC 12+, in -Wall) and -Wreturn-local-addr catch the easy cases at compile time. The real fix is ownership discipline: unique_ptr/shared_ptr, or ids instead of raw pointers (module 13).

docs.title: 2.5 Double free
docs.text:
Cause. Two owners both free the same block, or one path frees then an error path frees again.

free(r->payload);   // handler frees it
free(r->payload);   // caller also frees it

Symptom. free(): double free detected in tcache 2 + SIGABRT, if the block is still in the tcache. If it was reallocated in between, the second free destroys a live object and you get a UAF elsewhere - no double-free message, a mystery corruption instead. code/m04_double_free.cpp.

Tool. ASan (attempting double-free with both free stacks + alloc stack), Valgrind, glibc's own check. Fix: set the pointer to nullptr after free (defensive), or use RAII so there is one owner.

docs.title: 2.6 Stack-use-after-return
docs.text:
Cause. Returning the address of a local, or storing it somewhere that outlives the function.

const char *name() { char buf[32]; sprintf(buf, "acc-%d", id); return buf; }  // returns dangling
int *p;
void set() { int local = 5; p = &local; }   // p dangles after set() returns

Symptom. The memory is reused by the next function call, so reads return garbage and writes corrupt the next call's frame. Highly timing/layout dependent. code/m04_stack_overflow.cpp is the recursion kind; the return-address kind is the snippet above.

Tool. ASan with detect_stack_use_after_return=1 (default on recent versions) reports stack-use-after-return with the function and variable. -Wreturn-local-addr / -Wdangling-pointer catch the direct forms at compile time.

docs.title: 2.7 Invalid iterator / reference into a container
docs.text:
Cause. Mutating a container while holding an iterator, pointer or reference into it. vector push_back/resize reallocates and moves elements; erase invalidates iterators at and after the point; unordered_map rehash invalidates iterators (but not references to elements).

for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it)
    if (*it == x) v.erase(it);    // erase invalidates it; ++it is UB

Symptom. Skipped elements, duplicates, or a crash reading freed vector storage. Depends on reallocation, so it may hide until the container grows past its capacity. code/m04_invalid_iterator.cpp.

Tool. -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG (libstdc++ debug mode) turns it into a clear abort at the point of misuse ("attempt to increment a singular iterator"); ASan catches the reallocation UAF. The erase/remove idiom (v.erase(std::remove_if(...), v.end())) and re-fetching iterators from erase's return value are the fixes.

docs.title: 2.8 Memory leak
docs.text:
Cause. Losing the last pointer to an allocation without freeing it: an early return that skips delete, an exception between new and delete, overwriting a pointer, a container of raw pointers cleared without deleting, or reference cycles with shared_ptr.

void handle() {
    Request *r = new Request;
    if (!valid(r)) return;    // leak on the error path
    delete r;
}

Symptom. Slow RSS growth over hours/days, eventual OOM kill or allocation failure. Not a crash at the leak site. code/m09_leak.cpp (covered fully in module 09).

Tool. LeakSanitizer (free with ASan), Valgrind --leak-check=full, heaptrack/massif for growth over time. Fix: RAII (unique_ptr), and for cycles weak_ptr.

docs.title: 2.9 Type confusion
docs.text:
Cause. Interpreting memory as a type it is not: a bad reinterpret_cast, a union read through the wrong member, a downcast to the wrong derived type (static_cast where dynamic_cast was needed), deserialising into the wrong struct.

struct A { virtual void f(); };
struct B : A { int extra; };
A *a = new A;
B *b = static_cast<B*>(a);   // a is not a B
b->extra = 1;                // writes past A; b->f() via a wrong vtable later

Symptom. Garbage field values, or a crash on a virtual call because the vtable pointer is read from the wrong offset and jumped through. A pc that is 0 or points into data after a virtual call is a classic sign.

Tool. UBSan -fsanitize=vptr catches bad polymorphic casts at the point of use; -Wall catches some; dynamic_cast + checking for null is the safe pattern. Strict-aliasing violations are a related UB class (-fsanitize=alignment, -Wstrict-aliasing).

docs.title: 2.10 Integer overflow leading to a bad size
docs.text:
Cause. Size or index arithmetic that wraps, producing a too-small allocation or a negative value used as an unsigned size.

int bytes = count * elem_size;        // count * elem_size overflows int -> small/negative
char *p = malloc(bytes);              // tiny allocation
memset(p, 0, count * elem_size);      // writes the intended (huge) size -> overflow

Symptom. A heap overflow whose size depends on input; often reachable from untrusted data, so a security issue (CVE-shaped). code/m04_integer_overflow_size.cpp.

Tool. UBSan -fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow catches signed wrap; unsigned wrap is defined so use -fsanitize=unsigned-integer-overflow deliberately or check with __builtin_mul_overflow. Compute sizes in size_t, validate against a maximum, use std::vector/std::span. -Wconversion/-Wsign-conversion flag the risky narrowings.

docs.title: 2.11 Null dereference
docs.text:
Cause. Dereferencing a pointer that is null because a lookup/allocation failed and the result was not checked.

Account *a = find(id);   // returns nullptr when not found
a->balance -= fee;       // crash when a == nullptr

Symptom. Immediate SIGSEGV at a small fault address (null + field offset). The easiest bug to diagnose from a dump (module 06). code/m04_null_deref.cpp.

Tool. Obvious in any debugger. Prevent with checks, std::optional, references where null is impossible, and -fsanitize=null (part of UBSan) to catch it precisely with a message.

docs.title: 2.12 Combinations
docs.text: Real bugs combine: an integer overflow produces a small buffer (bug 10) that then overflows (bug 1); a use-after-free (bug 4) reallocates the block as a different type, producing type confusion (bug 9); a data race (module 10) frees an object twice (bug 5) or leaves a pointer dangling (bug 4). The catalogue is the vocabulary; the skill is naming the combination from the evidence.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Each bug has a self-contained program in code/, with build and debug notes in the header comment. They are the module-04 reproductions:

File Bug Default behaviour m04_null_deref.cpp null dereference SIGSEGV at 0x10 with ACC-9999 m04_stack_overflow.cpp unbounded recursion (and the SUAR note) SIGSEGV near the stack guard m04_heap_overflow.cpp off-by-one heap write abort in free or ASan heap-buffer-overflow m04_use_after_free.cpp use-after-free silent wrong output or ASan heap-use-after-free m04_double_free.cpp double free SIGABRT "double free detected in tcache 2" m04_uninit_read.cpp uninitialised heap read nondeterministic; Valgrind catches it m04_invalid_iterator.cpp erase-while-iterating + ref across realloc garbage/crash; _GLIBCXX_DEBUG aborts m04_integer_overflow_size.cpp size wrap then overflow UBSan signed-overflow report

Build them all (none with -Werror, since they are intentionally buggy) and run the sanitizer suite:

cd code
./build_debug.sh debug       # -g -O0 versions in build/
./build_debug.sh asan        # ASan versions
./build_debug.sh run-asan    # run each and show the first 25 lines of the report
./build_debug.sh run-valgrind

Example: the use-after-free under ASan gives you the three stacks that make it a five-minute fix:

==12345==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x... at pc 0x...
READ of size 8 at 0x... thread T0
    #0 audit_session(Session const*) m04_use_after_free.cpp:52
    #1 main m04_use_after_free.cpp:66
0x... is located 8 bytes inside of 48-byte region [...,...)
freed by thread T0 here:
    #0 operator delete(void*)
    #1 close_session(long) m04_use_after_free.cpp:39
previously allocated by thread T0 here:
    #0 operator new(unsigned long)
    #1 open_session(long, char const*) m04_use_after_free.cpp:30

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why each class has the symptom it has comes straight from modules 01 and 03:

  • Overflows corrupt whatever is physically adjacent. Stack: saved registers and the return address (control-flow hijack, canary catches it). Heap: the next chunk's header (allocator aborts later) or the next object's fields (silent data corruption). Globals: the next global.
  • UAF and double-free are silent because freed memory stays mapped and the allocator reuses the bytes for its free-list metadata (the tcache pointer you saw in module 03) or for a later allocation. Reading sees a pointer or another object; writing corrupts them.
  • Uninitialised reads are nondeterministic because the value is literally leftover memory; it changes with allocation history, ASLR, and what ran before.
  • Integer-overflow-to-small-buffer is dangerous because the two halves (the wrap and the overflow) are in different statements and the size often comes from untrusted input, making it a remote memory-corruption primitive.

Undefined behaviour is the common thread. Every bug here is UB in the language standard, which is why the compiler is allowed to do surprising things: delete a null check after a dereference (because UB means the pointer "cannot" be null), assume a signed add does not overflow and optimise a bounds check away, or reorder around a use-after-free. This is why a bug can appear only at -O2: the optimiser exploited a UB assumption. -fsanitize=undefined exists precisely to make these assumptions observable. The senior mindset: a warning or sanitizer finding about UB is a real bug even if the program "works today", because the next compiler version may compile it differently.

Exploitability. Overflows, UAF and type confusion are not just crashes; they are the raw material of exploits (control-flow hijack via overwritten return address or vtable, heap grooming via tcache poisoning). For a banking vendor this elevates a "stability bug" to a "security vulnerability" with disclosure obligations. Treat memory-safety findings as security findings.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Match the symptom to the class before touching a debugger. SIGSEGV at 0x10: null deref. SIGABRT with a glibc message: heap corruption or double free (read the message). SIGSEGV with pc garbage and ?? frames: stack overflow of a return address. Nondeterministic wrong answers: uninitialised read or data race. Steady RSS growth: leak. This triage (module 11) is faster than opening the core.
  • The "works here, fails there" bugs are the catalogue's uninitialised reads, off-by-ones and races. They depend on memory contents, allocation order and timing, which differ between the developer laptop and the client's production box. Reproduce under ASan/Valgrind/TSan rather than on the developer machine.
  • Banking data corruption is worse than a crash. A UAF or overflow that silently changes a balance and does not crash is the nightmare scenario: wrong numbers, no alarm. This is the argument for running the whole test suite under sanitizers in CI, and for arena allocators with guard bytes in the migration engine.
  • Your C background is a double edge. C has no RAII, no bounds-checked containers, manual ownership - every bug in this catalogue is easy to write. Moving the new C++ code to std::vector/std::string/smart pointers removes whole classes (module 13). The existing C server benefits most from sanitizer CI and defensive asserts.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - classify by symptom. For each of these, name the bug class without running anything: "SIGABRT, free(): invalid next size"; "SIGSEGV at 0x0"; "balance sometimes wrong, never crashes"; "RSS up 2 GB over a week"; "crash at ret, pc = 0x4141414141414141". Done when all five are named with one-line reasoning.
  2. Easy - run the suite. Run ./build_debug.sh run-asan and for each program write the one line of the report that names the bug. Done when you have eight lines.
  3. Medium - ASan vs Valgrind vs nothing. Run m04_uninit_read three ways: plain, under ASan, under Valgrind. Done when you can explain why only Valgrind reports it.
