  4. Medium - make the off-by-one bite reliably. Modify m04_heap_overflow so it reliably aborts (hint: allocate, free a neighbour, allocate again to control layout; or just run with a size that makes the stray write hit a header). Done when it aborts every run and you can name the glibc message.
  5. Hard - combination bug. Write a program that combines an integer overflow and a heap overflow (size wrap producing a small buffer, then a copy of the intended size). Catch it with UBSan and separately with ASan. Done when you can show both tools' reports and explain which half each caught.
  6. Hard - turn a crash into silent corruption. Take m04_double_free, insert an allocation of the same size between the two frees so the second free destroys a live object instead of aborting. Show that the program now produces wrong output with no error. Done when you can explain why the glibc double-free check no longer fires.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Give the catalogue of memory bug classes. A: Buffer overflow (heap/stack), off-by-one, uninitialised read, use-after-free, double free, dangling pointer/reference, stack-use-after-return, invalid iterator, memory leak, type confusion, integer-overflow-to-bad-size, and null dereference. Each is undefined behaviour and maps to a specific production symptom and a best-fit tool.

Q: Which of these does AddressSanitizer NOT catch, and what do you use instead? A: ASan does not catch uninitialised reads (use Valgrind memcheck, or MemorySanitizer on clang), and it does not catch most integer-overflow or type-confusion UB (use UBSan). ASan is for spatial (overflow) and temporal (UAF, double free, leak) memory errors.

Q: Why is use-after-free more dangerous than a null dereference? A: A null dereference crashes immediately and deterministically at a recognisable address, so it is easy to find and it fails safe. A use-after-free usually does not crash - freed memory is still mapped and may be reused by another object - so it silently corrupts data, can leak or alter sensitive values, and is exploitable for control-flow hijack. It fails dangerously and is hard to reproduce.

Q: How can an integer overflow become a buffer overflow? A: If a size is computed with count * element_size in a type too small, the multiplication wraps to a small value, malloc returns a tiny buffer, and a subsequent copy or loop writes the intended (large) number of bytes past it. Because the count often comes from untrusted input, this is a remotely triggerable memory-corruption primitive. Fix: compute in size_t, use __builtin_mul_overflow, and cap sizes.

Q: Why does a bug sometimes appear only in an optimised build? A: The optimiser is allowed to assume the program has no undefined behaviour, so it may remove a null check after a dereference, assume a signed add does not overflow, or reorder around a use-after-free - exposing a latent bug that the unoptimised build happened to tolerate. The bug was always there; -O2 just stopped hiding it. Build with -O2 -Wall and sanitizers to surface these.

Q: A balance is occasionally wrong but the service never crashes. Which classes are in play? A: Silent-corruption classes: use-after-free writing through a reused block, a heap/stack overflow into a neighbouring object's fields, an uninitialised read, or a data race producing a lost update. Reproduce under ASan (overflow/UAF), Valgrind (uninitialised) and TSan (race); whichever fires names the class.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• There is a fixed catalogue of memory bugs; every dump is one or a combination of them.
  • Overflows corrupt adjacent memory: stack -> return address (canary/0xC0000409), heap -> next chunk header (later free abort) or next object (silent corruption).
  • UAF, double free and dangling pointers are usually silent because freed memory stays mapped; ASan quarantines freed memory and gives use/free/alloc stacks.
  • Uninitialised reads are nondeterministic; Valgrind (not ASan) catches them; MSan on clang too.
  • Integer-overflow-to-small-buffer is a security-grade overflow; compute sizes in size_t.
  • Null deref is the easy one: immediate SIGSEGV at a small address.
  • Tool fit: ASan = spatial+temporal memory errors + leaks; Valgrind = those + uninitialised; UBSan = integer/type/alignment UB; _GLIBCXX_DEBUG = iterator misuse; LSan/heaptrack = leaks.
  • Every entry is undefined behaviour, so the optimiser can make it appear only at -O2; treat UB findings as real bugs and as potential security vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 05. gdb from zero to fluent
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02; code/gdb_cheatsheet.md open beside you

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
gdb is the Linux debugger. It does what WinDbg does for you on Windows: run a program under control, stop it where you say, show you variables, registers and the stack, and open crash dumps. The commands are different and the interface is a terminal, but the concepts map one to one. Because you already think in WinDbg, every command in this module is given next to its WinDbg equivalent so you learn by translation rather than from zero.

The goal is fluency: not knowing every command, but being able to sit at a crashed or hanging process and get to the answer without looking things up. That comes from doing the exercises in this module with the programs in code/, not from reading.

docs.title: 2.1 Building for debugging
docs.text:
Build Flags Use Debug -g -O0 -fno-omit-frame-pointer stepping line by line; every variable visible; 3-10x slower Debug-optimised -g -Og optimised but keeps debuggability; good default for dev Production -g -O2 -fno-omit-frame-pointer what you ship; <optimized out> appears; backtraces fine Macros too -g3 p SOME_MACRO works

-g never changes code; -O0 does (module 02). Debug the production build when the bug only shows there. Debug -O0 when you need to step and inspect.

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -pthread -g -O0 -o build/m04_null_deref m04_null_deref.cpp

docs.title: 2.2 Starting and running
docs.text:
gdb ./prog                       # load binary
gdb --args ./prog arg1 arg2      # with arguments
gdb -p 12345                     # attach to a running process
gdb ./prog core.12345            # open a core dump (module 06)
gdb -q -batch -ex run -ex bt --args ./prog arg   # scripted: run, print bt, exit

(gdb) run            # r   : start (stops at breakpoints or signals)
(gdb) start          #      : run and break at main
(gdb) set args a b   #      : change arguments
(gdb) continue       # c    : WinDbg g
(gdb) kill
(gdb) quit           # q

Everything accepts unique prefixes (b, c, n, s, p, bt, i r). Enter repeats the last command (press Enter to keep stepping). Tab completes symbols. help cmd and apropos word.

docs.title: 2.3 Breakpoints
docs.text:
(gdb) break main                      # b main           WinDbg: bp prog!main
(gdb) break m04_null_deref.cpp:52     # file:line
(gdb) break apply_fee if fee > 20     # conditional
(gdb) tbreak process_request          # one-shot
(gdb) break Account::deposit          # C++ method; use tab completion for templates/overloads
(gdb) rbreak ^handle_                 # regex: every function starting with handle_
(gdb) info breakpoints                # i b            WinDbg: bl
(gdb) delete 2 / disable 2 / enable 2 #                WinDbg: bc / bd / be
(gdb) condition 2 id == 7             # add/change condition
(gdb) ignore 2 100                    # skip first 100 hits
(gdb) commands 2                      # run these each time bp 2 hits
> silent
> printf "fee=%ld\n", fee
> continue
> end

Breakpoints in shared libraries not yet loaded: set breakpoint pending on (in the sample .gdbinit). Breakpoints work by writing an int3 (0xCC) byte at the address; gdb hides this from you and single-steps over the original instruction when continuing.

docs.title: 2.4 Stepping
docs.text:
gdb Meaning WinDbg next / n next source line, step over calls p step / s next source line, step into calls t nexti / ni, stepi / si one machine instruction p/t in asm mode finish run until the current function returns, print the return value gu until / u like next but does not go backwards in loops - advance 60 run to line 60 g \file:60`` return force the current function to return now (dangerous) -

step into a function without debug info (libc) steps over it unless you set step-mode on. display/i $pc shows the next instruction after every step; display x shows x every stop.

docs.title: 2.5 The stack
docs.text:
(gdb) bt                       # backtrace            WinDbg: k
(gdb) bt full                  # with locals          WinDbg: kP + dv
(gdb) bt 5   /  bt -5          # innermost 5 / outermost 5
(gdb) frame 2   / f 2          # select frame         WinDbg: .frame 2
(gdb) up / down                # move one frame
(gdb) info frame               # CFA, saved rip, saved regs (module 02)
(gdb) info locals              #                      WinDbg: dv
(gdb) info args

Frame 0 is where the program stopped. Variables and list are relative to the selected frame. In a crash, go up until you reach your own code, then inspect arguments.

docs.title: 2.6 Looking at data
docs.text:
(gdb) print acct               # p acct      -> (Account *) 0x0
(gdb) p *acct                  # dereference (fails if 0x0: "Cannot access memory at address 0x0")
(gdb) p acct->balance
(gdb) p/x acct->balance        # hex;  /d /u /o /t (binary) /c /a (address+symbol) /s
(gdb) p g_ledger               # std::vector with pretty printer: "std::vector of length 3, ... = {{...}}"
(gdb) p g_ledger[1]            # operator[] works with the libstdc++ xmethods
(gdb) p g_ledger._M_impl._M_start[1]      # raw access when printers are absent
(gdb) p arr[0]@5               # five elements starting at arr[0]
(gdb) p sizeof(Account)  /  p offsetof(Account, balance)   # offsetof may need: p &((Account*)0)->balance
(gdb) p $rip  /  p/x $rax  /  info registers   # registers    WinDbg: r
(gdb) p $_siginfo              # signal details after a crash
(gdb) p $_siginfo._sifields._sigfault.si_addr   # the faulting address
(gdb) ptype acct               # type definition       WinDbg: dt Account
(gdb) whatis g_ledger          # just the type name
(gdb) x/16xg $rsp              # examine 16 giant (8-byte) words in hex at rsp     WinDbg: dq @rsp L10
(gdb) x/s acct->id             # as string                                          WinDbg: da
(gdb) x/8i $pc                 # 8 instructions                                     WinDbg: u @rip L8
(gdb) x/4xw 0x7ffff7dd1000     # 4 words (4-byte)
(gdb) set var acct->balance = 0           # modify                                  WinDbg: ed
(gdb) call std::printf("%s\n", acct->id)  # call a function in the inferior
(gdb) info symbol 0x555555555189          # which function is this address in     WinDbg: ln
(gdb) info address apply_fee              # where is this symbol
(gdb) info line *0x555555555189           # address -> source line
(gdb) list apply_fee  /  list 40,60  /  list   # show source
(gdb) disassemble /s             # current function with source interleaved        WinDbg: uf

x format letters: x hex, d decimal, u unsigned, s string, i instruction, a address, c char. Size letters: b byte, h 2, w 4, g 8. x/16xg = 16 x 8-byte hex. Memorise this one and x/s, x/Ni.

set print pretty on makes structs readable; it is in the sample .gdbinit.

docs.title: 2.7 Watchpoints (data breakpoints)
docs.text:
The most powerful tool for "who changed this value":

(gdb) watch g_total                        # stop whenever g_total is written (hardware, 4 available)
(gdb) watch -l acct->balance               # -l: watch the ADDRESS, even after acct goes out of scope
(gdb) watch *(long*)0x5555555592a0         # by address
(gdb) rwatch x  /  awatch x                # on read / on read-or-write
(gdb) watch x if x > 1000                  # conditional

x86-64 has 4 debug registers, each watching up to 8 bytes. Larger regions or more watchpoints fall back to software watchpoints (single-stepping everything, thousands of times slower). When it triggers, gdb prints old and new value and stops at the instruction after the write; bt shows who did it. This is how you find "something is corrupting this field": watch the field's address (watch -l) and continue until it fires with an unexpected stack.

WinDbg equivalent: ba w8 <address>.

docs.title: 2.8 Exceptions and signals
docs.text:
(gdb) catch throw                 # stop when any C++ exception is thrown (even if caught later)
(gdb) catch throw std::out_of_range    # specific type (gdb 9+)
(gdb) catch catch                 # stop at the catch
(gdb) catch syscall write         # stop on a system call
(gdb) catch fork  /  catch exec
(gdb) info signals                # table of signals and whether gdb stops
(gdb) handle SIGPIPE nostop noprint pass   # servers: SIGPIPE on closed sockets is normal
(gdb) handle SIGUSR1 nostop noprint pass
(gdb) signal SIGINT               # deliver a signal to the program and continue

catch throw is how you find where an exception that "came from somewhere" is thrown; bt at that point shows the thrower. WinDbg: sxe eh (break on first-chance C++ exception, code e06d7363).

docs.title: 2.9 Threads
docs.text:
(gdb) info threads                # list: Id, Target Id (LWP = kernel tid), Frame   WinDbg: ~
(gdb) thread 3                    # switch                                          WinDbg: ~3s
(gdb) thread apply all bt         # every thread's stack                            WinDbg: ~*k
(gdb) thread apply all bt full    # with locals
(gdb) thread apply 2 3 bt 5
(gdb) thread name worker-1        # label the current thread
(gdb) set scheduler-locking on    # only the current thread runs when you step
(gdb) set non-stop on             # other threads keep running while one is stopped (before run)

The LWP number in info threads is the kernel thread id (gettid()), the same number you see in top -H, in /proc/PID/task/, in pthread_mutex_t.__data.__owner (module 10) and in your logs if you log gettid(). Log it.

Default behaviour (all-stop): when one thread hits a breakpoint, all threads stop. Stepping one thread lets the others run unless scheduler-locking is on.

docs.title: 2.10 Attaching to a running process
docs.text:
./build/m10_deadlock &            # hangs
gdb -p $(pgrep m10_deadlock)      # attach; the process freezes while attached
(gdb) thread apply all bt
(gdb) detach                      # let it continue

ptrace permissions. Ubuntu (and WSL) ship Yama with /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope = 1: you may only attach to your own descendant processes. To attach to an arbitrary process you own: sudo gdb -p PID, or temporarily echo 0 | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope, or give gdb the capability (sudo setcap cap_sys_ptrace=eip $(which gdb)). In containers you need --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE. "ptrace: Operation not permitted" is this, not a gdb bug.

Attaching stops the process; in production that means requests stall. For a live server prefer gcore PID (seconds of pause, then the process continues) and analyse the core offline (module 06). WinDbg's equivalent is non-invasive attach or ProcDump.

docs.title: 2.11 TUI and the environment
docs.text:
gdb -tui ./prog            # or Ctrl-x a inside gdb to toggle
(gdb) layout src           # source + command
(gdb) layout split         # source + asm + command
(gdb) layout regs          # add registers
(gdb) focus cmd            # Ctrl-x o cycles focus; arrow keys scroll the focused window
(gdb) refresh              # Ctrl-l when the screen is garbled
(gdb) winheight src 20

For a graphical experience with the same engine: VS Code's C++ extension on WSL drives gdb ("MIMode": "gdb"), or gdb -ex 'py import gdb' ... with the gdb-dashboard script, or the pwndbg/gef extensions that add heap and context views. Learn the raw commands first; the UIs all break down to them.

docs.title: 2.12 .gdbinit
docs.text:
code/gdbinit.sample is a working starter; cp it to ~/.gdbinit. Highlights:

set pagination off          # long bt without prompts
set print pretty on
set history save on
set disassembly-flavor intel
handle SIGPIPE nostop noprint pass
set debuginfod enabled on   # fetch libc/libstdc++ debug info by build-id automatically
define crashinfo ... end    # custom commands: signal, fault address, pc, instructions, bt

A project-local .gdbinit in the current directory is loaded too, if listed in add-auto-load-safe-path. Teams keep one with set substitute-path, directory, and project macros (define dump_request).

docs.title: 2.13 STL pretty printers
docs.text:
Without them p vec shows _M_impl._M_start and friends. Ubuntu auto-loads libstdc++'s Python printers for the system libstdc++ (info pretty-printer lists them). With them:

(gdb) p g_ledger
$1 = std::vector of length 3, capacity 3 = {{id = "ACC-1\000\000\000\000\000\000", balance = 1000, pending = 0}, ...}
(gdb) p name           -> "shakir"
(gdb) p mp             -> std::map with 2 elements = {[1] = "a", [2] = "b"}
(gdb) p up             -> std::unique_ptr<Session> = {get() = 0x5555555592a0}
(gdb) p sp             -> std::shared_ptr<Session> (use count 2, weak count 0) = {get() = 0x...}
(gdb) p *sp            # dereference works
(gdb) p/r g_ledger     # /r: raw, bypass printers
(gdb) p g_ledger.size()   # calls the function (needs -O0 or non-inlined); printers make this unnecessary

For a core from another machine with a different libstdc++, load the printers manually (the commented block in gdbinit.sample). Write your own printer for project types in 30 lines of Python when you find yourself doing p *(Account*)0x... for the tenth time.

docs.title: 2.14 Reverse debugging (know that it exists)
docs.text:
(gdb) record full         # start recording after a breakpoint; everything after is replayable
(gdb) continue            # ... crash ...
(gdb) reverse-step  /  reverse-next  /  reverse-continue  /  reverse-finish
(gdb) record stop

record full is 1000x slower and limited (no AVX in some versions), fine for a short window. rr (rr record ./prog, rr replay) records whole runs with ~2x overhead and gives you reverse execution and deterministic replay of races; it is the single best tool for Heisenbugs on native Linux. It needs hardware performance counters, which WSL2 does not expose, so plan to use it on a Linux box or VM with PMU passthrough.

docs.title: 2.15 Scripting
docs.text:
gdb -q -batch -ex 'run' -ex 'bt' -ex 'info registers rip' --args ./build/m04_null_deref ACC-9999 2>&1 | tee crash.txt
gdb -q -batch -ex 'thread apply all bt' -p $(pgrep server) > stacks.txt    # poor man's profiler
gdb -q -batch -x commands.gdb ./prog core

The Python API (python print(gdb.parse_and_eval("g_total")), gdb.selected_frame(), gdb.lookup_type) lets you automate dump analysis: walk a linked list, dump every request in a table, check invariants over all threads. A 50-line script that prints your server's internal state from a core is worth building once.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Use the module-04 programs. Session 1: a null dereference, start to finish.

cd code && ./build_debug.sh debug
gdb -q --args ./build/m04_null_deref_debug ACC-9999
(gdb) run
Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
0x0000555555555281 in apply_fee (acct=0x0, fee=25) at m04_null_deref.cpp:52
52          acct->balance -= fee;
(gdb) p acct                        -> (Account *) 0x0
(gdb) p $_siginfo._sifields._sigfault.si_addr   -> (void *) 0x10
(gdb) x/i $pc                       -> mov rax, QWORD PTR [rax+0x10]     (reading acct->balance)
(gdb) bt
#0  apply_fee (acct=0x0, fee=25) at m04_null_deref.cpp:52
#1  process_request (id="ACC-9999") at m04_null_deref.cpp:60
#2  main (argc=2, argv=...) at m04_null_deref.cpp:66
(gdb) up
(gdb) list                          # see: Account *acct = find_account(id);  no null check
(gdb) p id                          -> "ACC-9999"
(gdb) p g_ledger                    # it is not in the ledger

Session 2: who modifies a value (watchpoint).

gdb -q ./build/m04_use_after_free_debug
(gdb) break audit_session
(gdb) run
(gdb) p *s                          # garbage or tcache pointer in id, since s was freed
(gdb) # now find the free: restart and watch the object
(gdb) start
(gdb) break open_session
(gdb) c
(gdb) finish                        # returns the Session*; "Value returned is $1 = (Session *) 0x5555555592a0"
(gdb) watch -l ((Session*)$1)->id   # watch the ADDRESS of the id field
(gdb) c                             # fires inside _int_free / tcache_put: glibc wrote the tcache next pointer
(gdb) bt                            # ... close_session <- main : there is your free

Session 3: threads and a hang.

./build/m10_deadlock_debug & sleep 1
gdb -q -p $!           # if "Operation not permitted": sudo gdb -p, or see 2.10
(gdb) info threads
(gdb) thread apply all bt
(gdb) thread 2
(gdb) frame 4          # the frame in transfer_a_to_b
(gdb) p g_connections_mtx._M_mutex.__data.__owner    # LWP of the holder: compare with info threads
(gdb) detach; q
kill %1

Session 4: C++ exceptions.

gdb -q ./build/m13_raii_fix_debug
(gdb) catch throw
(gdb) run
Catchpoint 1 (exception thrown), __cxxabiv1::__cxa_throw ...
(gdb) bt            # allocate_table <- main : the std::length_error thrower
(gdb) up 2 ; info locals

Do all four. Then do them again without looking at this file.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
ptrace. gdb controls the inferior with the ptrace syscall: PTRACE_ATTACH, PTRACE_PEEKDATA/POKEDATA to read/write memory, PTRACE_GETREGS, PTRACE_SINGLESTEP, PTRACE_CONT. The traced process stops on every signal and the tracer is told first; this is why gdb sees the SIGSEGV before the process dies and why handle SIGPIPE nostop matters (each delivery is a round trip into gdb). ptrace is slow (one syscall per word for memory reads in old gdb; process_vm_readv now), which is why software watchpoints and record crawl.

Breakpoints. gdb writes 0xCC (int3) over the first byte of the instruction. Hitting it raises SIGTRAP; gdb restores the byte, backs rip up by one, reports to you; on continue it single-steps the original instruction, re-inserts 0xCC, continues. Consequences: breakpoints in shared code (a library mapped in another process) do not affect the other process because of copy-on-write; a breakpoint inside a signal handler that runs on a corrupted stack can hang things; and x/i $pc in a core never shows 0xCC because cores are not from under gdb.

Hardware watchpoints. DR0-DR3 hold addresses, DR7 holds length/type; the CPU traps after the access completes (hence gdb stops at the next instruction). Four slots system-wide per thread context; the kernel virtualises them per process. A watch on a 16-byte struct uses two slots.

<optimized out>. DWARF location lists say where a variable is for each address range; if the current pc is in a range where the value is in no register or memory (dead, or folded into another value), gdb says so. It is honest, not broken. -Og and -fno-omit-frame-pointer reduce it; -fvar-tracking-assignments (default with -g -O2) improves it.

Disabling ASLR. gdb starts the inferior with personality(ADDR_NO_RANDOMIZE), which is why addresses repeat between runs. set disable-randomization off restores production behaviour - use it when a bug depends on layout.

Why finish can print the wrong value. It reads rax/xmm0 per the ABI. For a struct returned via hidden pointer or a type gdb cannot infer, it shows garbage or nothing. p $rax after finish is the raw answer.

debuginfod. gdb hashes each loaded module's build-id and asks the server for the matching debug file and source. First run on a new libc downloads ~100 MB into ~/.cache/debuginfod_client. It is what lets you see __GI_raise with line numbers in a backtrace through libc without installing libc6-dbg.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Attaching freezes the process. On a live banking server that is an outage. Prefer gcore (brief pause) or let the crash handler produce a core, then debug offline. Attach only to a process that is already hung or to a canary instance.
  • Poor man's profiler. for i in 1..10: gdb -batch -ex 'thread apply all bt' -p PID with a second between samples, then sort the stacks. Shows what a slow server is doing without any profiler installed. Each sample pauses the process for tens of milliseconds.
  • Scripted first-look. Keep a crash.gdb with crashinfo, thread apply all bt, info sharedlibrary, info proc mappings, and run it on every core before a human looks: gdb -batch -x crash.gdb ./server core > first_look.txt. Attach the output to the ticket.
  • Symbols on the production box. You will not have debug info there. Copy the core and the exact binary (and libc) to your machine where the .debug file lives (module 06). Never debug on the client's box longer than it takes to copy the core.
  • Watchpoints for "who corrupts this field" work on a reproduction, not on a core. If the corruption is reproducible under load, a watchpoint on the field's address plus commands that print bt and continue logs every writer without stopping the test.
  • Signals your server uses. A server that uses SIGUSR1 for log rotation or SIGPIPE on disconnects will "stop" constantly under gdb until you handle ... nostop noprint pass. Put it in the project .gdbinit.
  • WinDbg habit translation. !analyze -v -> there is no equivalent; crashinfo + bt is it. dt -> p * and ptype. dv -> info locals. ~*k -> thread apply all bt. .frame -> frame. dps @rsp -> x/40ag $rsp. The cheat sheet has the full table.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - the null deref. Do Session 1 and write down: signal, fault address, faulting instruction, the frame in your code, the line, the fix. Done when it takes under 3 minutes.
  2. Easy - stepping. start m02_backtrace_frames_debug, step into level1, level2, level3, finish out of each, reading the return values. Done when you can predict each Value returned before finish prints it.
  3. Medium - watchpoint hunt. Do Session 2 and identify the exact glibc function that overwrote the freed object's first bytes. Then repeat with watch -l on balance instead. Done when you can explain why one fires inside glibc and the other does not fire at all.
  4. Medium - attach and deadlock. Do Session 3; produce a two-line statement "thread A (LWP x) holds M1 and waits for M2; thread B (LWP y) holds M2 and waits for M1". Done when the LWP numbers are the real ones from your run.
  5. Hard - a pretty printer. Write a Python pretty printer for Account (from m06_crash_example.cpp) that prints ACC-1: 1000 (pending 0), register it from .gdbinit, and show p g_ledger using it. Done when p g_ledger prints a clean one-line-per-account list.
  6. Hard - scripted triage. Write crash.gdb that prints the crashinfo, all thread stacks, shared libraries and mappings, and run it in batch mode against a core from m06_crash_example. Done when a colleague could read first_look.txt and name the bug class.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do you find what is writing garbage into a field? A: A hardware watchpoint on the field's address: watch -l obj->field, continue, and when it fires bt shows the writer. If the writes are frequent, add commands to print the stack and continue so you get a log of all writers. On Windows the equivalent is ba w8 address.

Q: What is the difference between next, step and finish? A: next executes one source line stepping over calls; step enters called functions that have debug info; finish runs until the current function returns and prints the return value. ni and si are the instruction-level versions.

Q: Why might info locals show <optimized out> and what do you do? A: In optimised code the variable lives in a register that was reused or was eliminated; DWARF location lists tell gdb it has no value at this pc. Move to a different line where it is live, read the register or memory it was derived from via disassembly, or rebuild with -Og/-O0 if the bug reproduces there.

Q: You run gdb -p PID and get "Operation not permitted". Why? A: Yama's ptrace_scope (1 on Ubuntu) restricts attaching to descendant processes. Use sudo, set ptrace_scope to 0 temporarily, grant cap_sys_ptrace, or in Docker add SYS_PTRACE. Also check you own the process and it is not already traced.

Q: How do you stop at the point where a C++ exception is thrown? A: catch throw (optionally with a type) sets a catchpoint on __cxa_throw; when it fires, bt shows the throwing frame and you can inspect its locals before unwinding destroys them. catch catch stops at the handler instead.

Q: Why does attaching gdb to a production server need care? A: ptrace stops the whole process while attached; requests stall and timeouts fire. Reading memory and stepping is slow. Prefer gcore for a snapshot or a crash-produced core, and analyse offline with the matching debug symbols. Attach live only for a process that is already hung.

Q: What does gdb do differently from a plain run that can hide bugs? A: It disables ASLR (disable-randomization on) so layout-dependent bugs may vanish; it changes timing (races may not reproduce); breakpoints and stepping serialise threads; and the environment differs (LINES, COLUMNS are set). set disable-randomization off and running outside gdb with a core dump are the countermeasures.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Build -g -O0 to step, -g -O2 -fno-omit-frame-pointer to match production; -g is free.
  • run, b, c, n, s, finish, bt, frame, info locals, p, x/16xg, x/s, x/8i $pc, info registers, p $_siginfo - the core twenty commands.
  • watch -l addr finds who writes a value; 4 hardware slots; commands logs without stopping.
  • catch throw finds where an exception is thrown; handle SIG nostop noprint pass silences signals the program uses normally.
  • info threads (LWP = kernel tid), thread N, thread apply all bt; set scheduler-locking on.
  • gdb -p PID needs ptrace permission (Yama ptrace_scope); attaching freezes the process - prefer gcore in production.
  • .gdbinit: pagination off, pretty on, history, debuginfod, custom defines; STL pretty printers make p vec readable.
  • record/rr give reverse execution; rr needs perf counters (not in WSL2).
  • Script it: gdb -batch -x crash.gdb ./bin core for a first look at every core.

docs.title: 06. Core dumps on Linux
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A core dump is a snapshot of a process at the moment it died: its memory, its registers, the signal that killed it, which files were mapped where. The kernel writes it when a process gets a fatal signal like SIGSEGV or SIGABRT, if the system is configured to allow it. You load the core into gdb together with the same binary that produced it, and gdb shows you the program frozen at the instant of death: the backtrace of every thread, every variable, every byte of the heap.

It is the Linux equivalent of a Windows full user-mode dump. The main differences are in how you get one (ulimit and core_pattern instead of WER and ProcDump), how you make sure the symbols match (build-id instead of PDB GUID) and how you read it (gdb instead of WinDbg). This module walks the whole path and ends with a worked example you can reproduce on WSL in ten minutes.

docs.title: 2.1 Getting the kernel to write a core
docs.text:
Three things must be true:

  1. The core size limit is not zero. ulimit -c shows it; ulimit -c unlimited sets it for the current shell and its children. It is a per-process resource limit (RLIMIT_CORE), inherited across fork/exec. Make it permanent:
    • for login shells: /etc/security/limits.conf -> * soft core unlimited
    • for a systemd service: LimitCORE=infinity in the unit's [Service] section
    • from inside the program: setrlimit(RLIMIT_CORE, {RLIM_INFINITY, RLIM_INFINITY}) at startup (your server should do this; it removes a whole class of "no core was produced" incidents)
  2. The process is dumpable. Set-uid programs, programs that changed credentials, and those that called prctl(PR_SET_DUMPABLE, 0) do not dump unless /proc/sys/fs/suid_dumpable allows. Processes being ptraced by another debugger do not dump to the kernel.
  3. core_pattern points somewhere useful. /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern says where and how:
cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern
# Ubuntu desktop default:
|/usr/share/apport/apport -p%p -s%s -c%c -d%d -P%P -u%u -g%g -- %E
# Fedora/Arch/most servers with systemd:
|/usr/lib/systemd/systemd-coredump %P %u %g %s %t %c %h
# A plain file pattern:
/var/crash/core.%e.%p.%t

A leading | means the kernel pipes the core into that program instead of writing a file. On WSL and minimal containers the apport pipe target often is not running, so the core silently disappears. Set a file pattern:

sudo sysctl -w kernel.core_pattern='/tmp/core.%e.%p.%t'     # until reboot
echo 'kernel.core_pattern=/tmp/core.%e.%p.%t' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/60-core.conf   # persistent
sudo sysctl -w kernel.core_uses_pid=1

Pattern specifiers: %e executable name (15 chars), %E full path with ! for /, %p pid, %P pid in the initial namespace, %t UNIX time, %s signal number, %u/%g uid/gid, %h hostname, %c core size limit. core_pattern is global, not per container: inside Docker the host's pattern applies and a | handler runs on the host. Many "no core in the container" tickets end here.

Core size is also shaped by /proc/PID/coredump_filter (bitmask: 0x01 anonymous private, 0x02 anonymous shared, 0x04 file-backed private, 0x08 file-backed shared, 0x10 ELF headers, 0x20 huge pages private, ..., default 0x33). Servers with a 20 GiB cache that must dump quickly set MADV_DONTDUMP on the cache with madvise, or lower the filter. A full-memory core of a big process takes minutes and the process is frozen the whole time.

docs.title: 2.2 systemd-coredump and coredumpctl
docs.text:
When core_pattern pipes to systemd-coredump (the common server setup, and Ubuntu 24.04 if you install systemd-coredump), cores are compressed into /var/lib/systemd/coredump/ and metadata goes to the journal:

coredumpctl list                      # TIME PID UID GID SIG COREFILE EXE SIZE
coredumpctl info 12345                # signal, command line, stack (if gdb installed), build-id, timestamp
coredumpctl debug 12345               # opens gdb on it with the right binary
coredumpctl dump 12345 -o core.12345  # extract to a file to copy elsewhere
journalctl -t systemd-coredump        # the log entries

Config: /etc/systemd/coredump.conf (Storage=external, Compress=yes, ProcessSizeMax=, ExternalSizeMax=, MaxUse=). If a core is "truncated" or missing, ProcessSizeMax (defaults in the low GiB) is the usual reason. WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 runs systemd by default (/etc/wsl.conf [boot] systemd=true), but systemd-coredump may not be installed; cat core_pattern tells you which world you are in.

docs.title: 2.3 Getting a core from a live process
docs.text: gcore PID (part of gdb) attaches, writes a core, detaches. The process pauses for the duration (seconds for a few hundred MB). From inside gdb: generate-core-file. This is the equivalent of ProcDump -ma and is the right tool for a hang, a leak snapshot, or "capture evidence before we restart it" (module 11). Needs ptrace permission (module 05).

docs.title: 2.4 What is inside a core
docs.text:
A core is an ELF file of type CORE with a PT_LOAD segment for each memory mapping that was dumped and a PT_NOTE segment with notes:

Note Contents NT_PRSTATUS (one per thread) registers, pid/tid, pending signals, the signal that stopped the thread NT_PRPSINFO process name, state, uid, command line (truncated) NT_SIGINFO the siginfo_t: signal, si_code, fault address NT_AUXV auxiliary vector (program entry, page size, platform) NT_FILE the list of file-backed mappings: address ranges and paths - how gdb knows which libc to load NT_FPREGSET, NT_X86_XSTATE floating point / vector registers 
file core.12345                  # "ELF 64-bit LSB core file, x86-64, ... from './m06_crash_example', real uid: ..."
readelf -n core.12345 | less     # the notes, including NT_FILE mappings
readelf -l core.12345 | head -40 # the LOAD segments (which memory was dumped)
eu-readelf -n core.12345         # elfutils version, nicer NT_FILE output

What is not in a core: the binary's code pages (file-backed, excluded by default filter - gdb reads them from the binary you supply), the shared libraries' code, and anything the filter excluded. This is why you must give gdb the same binary and libraries.

docs.title: 2.5 Loading a core with the right binary and libraries
docs.text:
gdb ./m06_crash_example core.12345
# or
gdb -q -c core.12345 ./m06_crash_example
# or, if you forgot the binary:
gdb -c core.12345          # gdb reads NT_FILE/NT_PRPSINFO and tries to find the executable
(gdb) file ./m06_crash_example

Matching rules:

  • The binary must be the exact build. gdb checks the build-id (readelf -n prog | grep Build) against the note in the core and warns warning: core file may not match specified executable file. A mismatched binary gives a plausible, wrong backtrace. Treat the warning as fatal.
  • The core references libraries by path (NT_FILE). If you are on a different machine, those paths point at your libc, which differs. Either copy the originals into a sysroot and tell gdb, or install the matching packages:
(gdb) set sysroot /tmp/client-root       # contains lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 etc. copied from the client box
(gdb) set solib-search-path /tmp/client-libs
(gdb) set debug-file-directory /tmp/client-debug:/usr/lib/debug
(gdb) info sharedlibrary                 # "(*)" = no debug info; "No" in Syms Read = library not found
(gdb) set debuginfod enabled on          # fetch matching libc debug info by build-id (Ubuntu's server has it)

Collect from the client box, every time: the core, the binary, ldd binary output, and copies of each listed library. A tar of those four things is "a complete core". Script it (module 11).

Debug info for your own binary: the separate .debug file (module 02) in the same directory, in .debug/, or under /usr/lib/debug/.build-id/xx/yyyy.debug, or symbol-file server.debug. Without it you get function names (from .dynsym) but no lines or locals; with it, everything.

docs.title: 2.6 Reading a crash from a core: the fixed procedure
docs.text:
Do these in order, every time, before forming a theory:

(gdb) info inferiors / info program     # pid, "terminated with signal SIGSEGV"
(gdb) p $_siginfo                       # si_signo, si_code, si_addr
(gdb) p $_siginfo._sifields._sigfault.si_addr
(gdb) bt                                # the crashing thread (gdb selects it)
(gdb) info registers                    # rip, rsp, rbp, and the register the instruction used
(gdb) x/i $pc                           # the faulting instruction
(gdb) x/8i $pc-16                       # a little context (may misalign; use disassemble instead)
(gdb) disassemble /s                    # whole function with source
(gdb) frame N  (first frame in your code) ; info locals ; info args ; p *ptr
(gdb) info proc mappings                # which region is si_addr in?
(gdb) info sharedlibrary                # are the symbols right?
(gdb) thread apply all bt               # what were the other threads doing? (races, deadlocks)

si_code for SIGSEGV: SEGV_MAPERR (1) = address not mapped at all; SEGV_ACCERR (2) = mapped but wrong permission (write to read-only, execute data). For SIGBUS: BUS_ADRALN = misaligned access (SSE instruction on unaligned data), BUS_ADRERR = mmap'd file region past EOF. For SIGABRT the si_addr is meaningless; look at the glibc message in stderr/logs and the frame above abort. For SIGFPE: FPE_INTDIV = integer divide by zero (idiv).

Mapping the instruction back to source: bt and disassemble /s do it when debug info is present. Without debug info: note pc, find the module base in info proc mappings, compute the offset, and addr2line -f -i -e prog.debug 0xOFFSET on your machine with the debug file. For a PIE binary gdb already does the relocation; for addr2line you need the file offset.

docs.title: 2.7 Reading the faulting instruction
docs.text:
=> 0x555555555291 <post_entry+17>:  sub    QWORD PTR [rdi+0xc],rax

Read it as: "subtract rax from the 8-byte value at rdi+12". Then p/x $rdi. If rdi is 0, si_addr is 0xc: null pointer, field at offset 12. If rdi is 0x5555555592a0 and that address is not in any mapping, it is a stale pointer into freed/unmapped memory. If rdi is 0x4141414141414141, something overwrote the pointer with ASCII. The instruction plus the register value plus the mapping table is the diagnosis; the backtrace tells you who.

Common instruction shapes:

Instruction Meaning mov rax,[rdi+0x10] / mov [rdi+0x10],rax field read/write through pointer in rdi mov eax,[rax+rdx*4] array index: base rax, index rdx, 4-byte elements call [rax+0x8] / call rax virtual call through vtable (rax = vtable); garbage rax = type confusion/UAF rep movsb / inside memcpy bulk copy; look at rsi, rdi, rcx (src, dst, count) ret with bad pc after return address overwritten: stack overflow in the function that just returned ud2 __builtin_trap, std::unreachable, or the compiler proving UB movaps [rsp+..],xmm0 -> SIGSEGV misaligned stack (ABI violation, often from asm or wrong calling convention)

docs.title: 3. Code: the worked example
docs.text:
code/m06_crash_example.cpp processes a batch of ledger entries. It pre-resolves account pointers into a vector, then processes an entry that removes an account from the ledger (std::vector::erase), shifting the remaining elements and leaving the pre-resolved pointers stale; one entry also names an account that does not exist (lookup returned null). Build it optimised, like production:

cd code
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -pthread -g -O2 -fno-omit-frame-pointer -o build/m06_crash_example m06_crash_example.cpp
ulimit -c unlimited
cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern          # if it starts with '|' and you are on WSL, set a file pattern (2.1)
./build/m06_crash_example
processing 5 entries
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
ls -la /tmp/core.* core*                   # wherever your pattern put it

Now the analysis session. Addresses will differ on your machine; the shape will not.

$ gdb -q ./build/m06_crash_example /tmp/core.m06_crash_examp.4242.1759500000
Reading symbols from ./build/m06_crash_example...
[New LWP 4242]
Core was generated by `./build/m06_crash_example'.
Program terminated with signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
#0  0x000055d0c2a4a2f1 in post_entry (acct=0x0, e=...) at m06_crash_example.cpp:58
58          if (e.kind == 'D') acct->balance -= e.amount;

Step 1 - the signal and address:

(gdb) p $_siginfo.si_signo
$1 = 11
(gdb) p $_siginfo.si_code
$2 = 1                                    <- SEGV_MAPERR: not mapped at all
(gdb) p $_siginfo._sifields._sigfault.si_addr
$3 = (void *) 0xc                         <- 12 = offsetof(Account, balance)  (id is char[12])

Twelve is the offset of balance after a 12-byte id. Null pointer plus field offset. We already know the class.

Step 2 - instruction and registers:

(gdb) x/i $pc
=> 0x55d0c2a4a2f1 <post_entry+17>:  sub    QWORD PTR [rdi+0xc],rax
(gdb) p/x $rdi
$4 = 0x0
(gdb) p/x $rax
$5 = 0x5                                  <- e.amount == 5 : this is the "D ACC-9 5" entry

Step 3 - the stack:

(gdb) bt
#0  0x000055d0c2a4a2f1 in post_entry (acct=0x0, e=...) at m06_crash_example.cpp:58
#1  0x000055d0c2a4a5b8 in process_batch (batch=std::vector of length 5, capacity 8 = {...}) at m06_crash_example.cpp:92
#2  0x000055d0c2a49f1c in main (argc=<optimized out>, argv=<optimized out>) at m06_crash_example.cpp:118
(gdb) frame 1
(gdb) p i
$6 = 4
(gdb) p batch[4]
$7 = {kind = 68 'D', id = "ACC-9\000\000\000\000\000\000", amount = 5}
(gdb) p resolved
$8 = std::vector of length 5, capacity 5 = {0x55d0c3e5e2c0, 0x55d0c3e5e2d8, 0x55d0c3e5e2c0, 0x55d0c3e5e2f0, 0x0}
(gdb) p g_ledger
$9 = std::vector of length 2, capacity 3 = {{id = "ACC-2", balance = 2050, pending = 0}, {id = "ACC-3", balance = 3000, pending = 0}}

Two findings from one p: resolved[4] is null (ACC-9 never existed - lookup returned nullptr and nobody checked), and resolved[3] is 0x...2f0, which is one past the end of the current 2-element ledger: the pointer that was resolved to ACC-3 before the X ACC-1 entry shifted the vector. Entry 3 (D ACC-3 20) therefore wrote into a dead slot and the ledger shows ACC-3 still at 3000 instead of 2980. The null is the trigger; the stale-pointer design is the root cause (module 12 makes this distinction formal).

Step 4 - confirm the stale pointer:

(gdb) p *(Account*)0x55d0c3e5e2f0
$10 = {id = "ACC-3", balance = 2980, pending = 0}   <- the old element slot, written after erase shifted it
(gdb) p &g_ledger._M_impl._M_start[2]
$11 = (Account *) 0x55d0c3e5e2f0                      <- indeed one past _M_finish
(gdb) info proc mappings                             <- the address is in [heap]; mapped, so no fault on the stale write

Step 5 - the other threads (thread apply all bt; here there is one) and the libraries (info sharedlibrary: everything resolved, no (*) on our binary). Done. Total time with practice: under ten minutes. The write-up for the RCA: signal, address, instruction, frame, the two pointers, the design flaw, the fix (resolve at use time, or keep ids not pointers, and check lookup results) and the prevention (-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS would not catch this; ASan in CI would catch the stale write as heap-buffer-overflow past _M_finish... only if the vector had reallocated; a std::vector is a contiguous buffer so a review rule "no raw pointers into a container that is mutated in the same scope" is the real prevention).

Compare with the -O0 build: argc and argv are no longer <optimized out>, and i is visible in frame 1 at every line. In the -O2 core, batch was still printable because gdb had the DWARF location for it; e printed as ... because it was passed by reference and the reference register had been reused. That is normal optimised-core reading.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
How the kernel writes the core. On a fatal signal with SIG_DFL action and a core-dumping disposition, do_coredump() in the kernel: checks RLIMIT_CORE and dumpability, formats core_pattern, either opens the file or spawns the pipe program with the core on its stdin, then walks the VMAs and writes those selected by coredump_filter, plus the notes, as an ELF file. All threads are stopped first (the process is in a "coredumping" state and does not run again). For a pipe handler the kernel waits for it to exit (core_pipe_limit caps concurrent handlers). A 30 GiB process with a full filter takes minutes; during that time the process is frozen and your service is down. Deciding the filter and the cache MADV_DONTDUMP is a design decision for a banking server.

Why gdb needs the binary. Code pages are file-backed and not dumped (filter bit 0x04 off by default), so gdb reads .text from the file to disassemble and to find .eh_frame for unwinding. It also needs .symtab/DWARF for names. The build-id in the binary's .note.gnu.build-id and in the core's NT_FILE/mapped ELF header is how gdb detects a mismatch. Same for each shared library: NT_FILE says /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 was at 0x7f..., and gdb opens that path (under sysroot) to get its code and symbols.

Why thread apply all bt matters even for a single-thread-looking crash. The crashing thread is the victim; in a race the culprit is another thread that freed or modified the object. Its stack at the moment of the dump often shows it inside the mutating function (module 10).

Core files and ASLR. The core records where everything was in that run. Symbol resolution uses the mapped addresses from NT_FILE, so ASLR is not a problem for gdb. It is a problem for humans comparing addresses between runs; use info symbol to turn addresses into function+offset, which is stable.

gcore vs crash cores. gcore uses ptrace to read the memory and writes the same ELF format; registers are captured from the stopped state; there is no NT_SIGINFO fault address because nothing faulted. A gcore of a hung server gives you all thread stacks and the heap - enough for deadlock and leak analysis (modules 09, 10).

Minidumps on Linux. Google Breakpad/Crashpad produce small Windows-format minidumps from Linux processes (stacks + selected memory), convertible with minidump-2-core. Useful when full cores are too big to ship; you lose heap contents.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Make sure cores can happen before you need one. setrlimit(RLIMIT_CORE) in main, a file-based core_pattern (or systemd-coredump with a big ProcessSizeMax) on every server, LimitCORE=infinity in the unit file, disk space on the core partition, and a test: kill -SEGV a test instance and check the core appears. Most "we have no dump of the incident" stories are a missing one of these.
  • Ship the complete core. Core + exact binary + ldd output + the listed libraries + /proc/PID/maps if you have it + the last 10k log lines. Name them by the incident id. The analyst usually is not on the client's box.
  • Keep every shipped build's debug file, keyed by build-id, forever. A core without symbols is a guess. This is the Linux equivalent of your PDB symbol store.
  • A truncated core (gdb: "warning: core file is truncated" / backtraces end in ??) comes from ulimit -c being a number not unlimited, systemd ProcessSizeMax, or the disk filling. Check ls -la size against expected RSS.
  • Sensitive data. A core of a banking server contains customer data, keys, PANs, in plain text. Treat core files as confidential artefacts: encrypt in transit, restrict access, delete after the RCA, and say so in your incident procedure. Some clients will not let a core leave their network; then you debug on their jump host with your symbols copied in.
  • SIGABRT cores: the top frames are raise/abort/__libc_message/malloc_printerr (glibc heap check) or __GI___assert_fail (a failed assert) or std::terminate (uncaught exception). Go up to the first frame in your code; for std::terminate, p $_siginfo is useless but frame with __cxa_throw in it lets you p *exception_object - or find the exception type via info symbol on the __cxa_exception type_info pointer.
  • Hang cores (from gcore): no fault; start with thread apply all bt, look for the pattern (module 10): all threads in futex_wait = deadlock or starvation; one thread spinning with others waiting = lock holder stuck; threads in read/poll = waiting on the network.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - make a core happen. Configure ulimit -c, check core_pattern, crash m04_null_deref ACC-9999, find the core, file it, readelf -n it. Done when you can point at the NT_SIGINFO and NT_FILE notes.
  2. Easy - the procedure. Open the core from (1) and run the fixed procedure of 2.6 in order. Done when you have written the signal, si_code, si_addr, instruction, register, frame, line and bug class on one line.
  3. Medium - the worked example cold. Delete batch.txt, build m06_crash_example at -O2, produce the core, and reproduce the analysis in section 3 without reading section 3. Done when you have found both the null and the stale pointer and can explain the stale one in terms of erase shifting elements.
  4. Medium - wrong binary. Change one character in a printf string of m06_crash_example, rebuild, and open the old core with the new binary. Done when you can show gdb's warning and one thing in the backtrace that is wrong or suspicious because of the mismatch.
  5. Hard - another machine. Copy a core and binary from WSL to a different Linux (a VM, a Docker container with a different distro, or just a different directory simulating a different libc path), and make gdb load the correct libc using set sysroot. Done when info sharedlibrary shows the copied libc and bt goes through __libc_start_main with symbols.
  6. Hard - gcore of a hang. Run m10_deadlock, gcore it, open the core, and determine both lock owners from __owner fields and info threads. Done when your two-line deadlock statement is backed by the core, not a live attach.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: A client says the server crashed but there is no core file. What do you check? A: In order: ulimit -c / RLIMIT_CORE for the service (systemd LimitCORE), whether core_pattern is a pipe to a handler that is not running or a path that does not exist or is full, whether the process was dumpable (setuid, PR_SET_DUMPABLE), coredump_filter and systemd ProcessSizeMax for truncation, and dmesg for an OOM kill (which produces no core). Then I fix the configuration and prove it with a kill -SEGV test.

Q: What do you need alongside a core to analyse it, and why? A: The exact binary that produced it (same build-id - code pages are not in the core and gdb needs .eh_frame and symbols from the file), its separate debug info, and the shared libraries at the paths recorded in the core's NT_FILE note (or a sysroot copy of them). A mismatched binary gives a confident, wrong backtrace.

Q: What is the first thing you look at in a core, and what does it tell you? A: $_siginfo: the signal and the fault address. A small address means null plus offset; an address next to a stack mapping means stack overflow; SIGABRT means an assertion, uncaught exception or allocator check - look at the glibc message and the frame above abort. Then the faulting instruction and the register it dereferenced, then bt.

Q: Explain si_code SEGV_MAPERR vs SEGV_ACCERR. A: MAPERR: the address is not mapped at all - null, stale, or wild pointer. ACCERR: the address is mapped but the access violated permissions - writing to .rodata or code, executing data, or hitting a PROT_NONE guard page. ACCERR on a write to a string literal is a classic.

Q: How do you take a core of a live, hung server without killing it? A: gcore PID (or ProcDump -ma on Windows): it attaches with ptrace, writes the memory and registers to an ELF core, and detaches; the process pauses for seconds and continues. Needs ptrace permission. Then thread apply all bt offline shows what every thread was waiting on.

Q: How do you read an optimised core where variables are <optimized out>? A: Use what is there: the faulting instruction and registers give the dereferenced pointer and offset; DWARF often keeps function arguments and some locals; callers' frames may hold the value in a visible variable; the heap object itself can be printed by casting its address. -O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer keeps enough in practice. Rebuild at -O0 only to reproduce, never to analyse the original core.

Q: What are the risks of core dumps in a banking environment? A: They contain customer data and secrets in clear text, so they must be treated as confidential artefacts: access controlled, encrypted in transit, retained only as long as the RCA needs, and sometimes analysed only inside the client's network. Also, writing a multi-GB core freezes the process for minutes - a design decision between forensic completeness and availability.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A core needs ulimit -c unlimited (or LimitCORE=infinity/setrlimit), a dumpable process, and a core_pattern that works; | means a pipe handler, which is host-global even in Docker.
  • coredumpctl list/info/debug/dump for systemd-coredump systems; gcore PID for a live snapshot.
  • A core holds dumped memory segments plus notes: NT_PRSTATUS (registers per thread), NT_SIGINFO (signal + fault address), NT_FILE (mappings). Code pages are not in it.
  • Load with the exact same binary (build-id) and the same libraries (set sysroot); add the .debug file for lines and locals; info sharedlibrary to verify.
  • Fixed procedure: $_siginfo -> bt -> info registers -> x/i $pc -> frame in your code -> info locals/p *ptr -> info proc mappings -> thread apply all bt.
  • Fault address small = null+offset; near stack = overflow; mapped-but-faulting = ACCERR permission; SIGABRT = read the glibc/assert message.
  • The worked example: null from an unchecked lookup (trigger) and stale pointers after vector::erase (root cause) found from one core in ten minutes.
  • Ship core + binary + libraries + debug file together; keep debug files forever; treat cores as confidential.

docs.title: 07. WinDbg and Windows crash dumps
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03, 05, 06 (you will map every command to gdb)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
You already use WinDbg. This module is about using it the way a senior engineer does: knowing what !analyze -v did so you can do it by hand when it is wrong, reading an optimised stack when the symbols are partial, knowing which dump type you need before the incident, and - the big one - turning a heap corruption fail-fast into the exact line that overflowed, using PageHeap and Application Verifier. Every command is paired with its gdb equivalent so the two debuggers become one skill in your head.

Vocabulary note: Windows people say "bug check" for a kernel crash (blue screen, !analyze on a kernel dump) and "exception code" for a user-mode crash. The codes you meet in a user-mode server crash (0xC0000005, 0xC0000374, 0xC0000409, 0xC00000FD) are NTSTATUS exception codes, not bug check codes. Interviewers notice the distinction.

docs.title: 2.1 Dump types
docs.text:
Type How made Contains Use Minidump (MiniDumpNormal) WER default, MiniDumpWriteDump thread stacks, registers, module list, exception record; no heap crash location and stack only; tiny (hundreds of KB) Minidump with data segments / handles / unloaded modules MiniDumpWithDataSegs, ...WithHandleData, ...WithUnloadedModules plus globals, handle table more context for little size Full user-mode dump (MiniDumpWithFullMemory) ProcDump -ma, Task Manager "Create dump file", WER DumpType=2 everything mapped in the process: heaps, stacks, images heap corruption, leaks, UAF, deadlocks - what you want for an RCA Kernel / complete memory dump system crash kernel memory drivers, BSOD; not this course

"Full dump" in Windows speech means full user-mode dump (.dmp, same size as the process's committed memory). It is the equivalent of a Linux core with the default filter. A minidump is roughly a Breakpad minidump: stacks without heap. If a client sends you a 400 KB .dmp for a heap corruption, you will get the stack and nothing else; ask for a full dump next time and configure WER so it happens automatically.

docs.title: 2.2 Capturing a dump
docs.text:
WER LocalDumps (the config every production Windows server should have):

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps\YourServer.exe
    DumpFolder   REG_EXPAND_SZ  D:\dumps
    DumpType     REG_DWORD      2          (0 custom, 1 minidump, 2 full)
    DumpCount    REG_DWORD      10

Any unhandled exception in YourServer.exe then writes YourServer.exe.<pid>.dmp without a debugger installed. This is the Windows core_pattern.

ProcDump (Sysinternals; the gcore/ulimit swiss army knife):

procdump -accepteula -ma -e -x D:\dumps YourServer.exe args    # launch, full dump on unhandled exception
procdump -ma -e 1 -f "" <pid>                                  # dump on FIRST-chance exceptions (all), useful for swallowed ones
procdump -ma -e 1 -f C0000005 <pid>                            # first-chance access violations only
procdump -ma -t <pid>                                          # dump at process termination
procdump -ma -h <pid>                                          # dump when a window hangs (GUI)
procdump -ma -c 90 -s 10 -n 3 <pid>                            # 3 dumps when CPU > 90% for 10 s (spinning thread)
procdump -ma -m 4000 <pid>                                     # dump when committed memory exceeds 4000 MB (leak)
procdump -ma <pid>                                             # snapshot NOW (hang, like gcore)
procdump -ma -w YourServer.exe                                 # wait for the process to start, then attach

Task Manager > right-click process > "Create dump file" writes a full dump to %TEMP%. Fine for a one-off hang. Note: a 32-bit process dumped from 64-bit Task Manager produces a dump that needs .effmach x86 or !wow64exts.sw; use the 32-bit Task Manager (SysWOW64\taskmgr.exe) or ProcDump instead.

From code: SetUnhandledExceptionFilter + MiniDumpWriteDump (dbghelp) to write your own dump, ideally from a watchdog process rather than the crashing one (the crashing process's heap may be the corrupted thing). This is the Windows twin of code/m11_crash_handler.cpp.

From the debugger: .dump /ma D:\dumps\now.dmp while attached.

docs.title: 2.3 Symbols
docs.text:
.sympath srv*C:\Symbols*https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols   # Microsoft public symbols, cached locally
.sympath+ \\build\symbols\YourServer                                   # your own symbol store (symstore.exe add ...)
.sympath+ D:\builds\2026.10.03\pdb                                     # a plain folder of PDBs
.symfix                                                                # shortcut for the MS symbol server
.reload /f                                                             # force load for all modules
.reload /f YourServer.exe                                              # just one
lm                                                                     # module list: "(pdb symbols)" good, "(export symbols)" bad, "(deferred)" not loaded yet
lmvm YourServer                                                        # verbose: PDB path, GUID, timestamp, checksum
!sym noisy                                                             # show every symbol lookup and why it failed
.symopt+ 0x40                                                          # SYMOPT_LOAD_ANYTHING: accept mismatched PDB (last resort; names may be wrong)
!lmi YourServer                                                        # image info incl. debug directory
.srcpath D:\src;srv*                                                   # source paths; srv* = source server if PDBs are source-indexed

Environment variable _NT_SYMBOL_PATH sets the default. Every shipped build's PDB must be in your symbol store (symstore add /r /f D:\build\*.pdb /s \\build\symbols /t YourServer /v 2026.10.03). Private PDBs have locals and types; public (stripped) PDBs only names. Keep the private ones internally.

gdb mapping: .sympath = set debug-file-directory / debuginfod; lm = info sharedlibrary; .reload = sharedlibrary; !sym noisy = set verbose on; lmvm = readelf -n build-id.

docs.title: 2.4 !analyze -v and what it actually does
docs.text:
!analyze -v reads the exception record stored in the dump, switches to that thread's exception context, walks the stack, applies heuristics (known bad patterns, heap corruption signatures, stack overflow, CLR frames) and prints:

FAULTING_IP:            YourServer!post_entry+11  ... sub qword ptr [rdi+0Ch],rax
EXCEPTION_RECORD:       ExceptionCode: c0000005 (Access violation)
                        ExceptionAddress, NumberParameters: 2
                        Parameter[0]: 0000000000000001       <- 0 read, 1 write, 8 execute (DEP)
                        Parameter[1]: 000000000000000c       <- the address   (= gdb si_addr)
                        Attempt to write to address 000000000000000c
CONTEXT:                the registers at the exception     (= gdb info registers)
PROCESS_NAME / ERROR_CODE / EXCEPTION_CODE_STR: c0000005
STACK_TEXT:             the walked stack                   (= gdb bt)
SYMBOL_NAME / MODULE_NAME / IMAGE_NAME
FAILURE_BUCKET_ID:      INVALID_POINTER_WRITE_c0000005_YourServer.exe!post_entry

The FAILURE_BUCKET_ID is how WER groups crashes; two dumps with the same bucket are the same bug - very useful for "is this the same crash as last month" (module 11). What !analyze gets wrong: heap corruption (it points at the heap manager, not your code), stack corruption (the walk is garbage), second-chance exceptions where the first-chance context was more informative, and wrong-thread cases (it analyses the excepting thread; the culprit may be another). So learn the manual steps:

.ecxr                  # switch to the Exception Context Record (registers at the fault); like landing in gdb frame 0
.exr -1                # the exception record: code, address, parameters   (= p $_siginfo)
.cxr                   # back to the current (non-exception) context
.lastevent             # what stopped the debugger
r                      # registers (after .ecxr)                             (= info registers)
u @rip                 # disassemble at rip                                  (= x/8i $pc)
ub @rip                # disassemble backwards
k                      # stack                                               (= bt)
kv                     # with FPO/calling convention info
kb                     # with first 3 "args" - unreliable on x64 (module 02)
kp / kP                # with parameters from private symbols
kn                     # with frame numbers (needed for .frame)
kL                     # no source lines
~*k                    # all threads                                         (= thread apply all bt)
~*kb
~#s                    # switch to the thread that raised the exception      (gdb lands on it)
~3s                    # switch to thread 3                                  (= thread 3)
~~[1a2c]s              # switch by OS thread id (hex)
.frame 2               # select frame 2                                      (= frame 2)
.frame /r 2            # with the registers as they were in that frame
dv                     # locals and args                                     (= info locals / info args)
dv /t /v               # with types and addresses
dt Account 0x...       # dump typed memory                                   (= p *(Account*)0x...)
dt -r Account 0x...    # recursive
dt YourServer!g_ledger # a global
dq @rsp L20            # 20 quadwords at rsp                                 (= x/20xg $rsp)
dps @rsp L40           # quadwords with symbol lookup - stack scan           (= x/40ag $rsp)
dpp / dpu              # pointer to pointer / pointer to unicode
da / du 0x...          # ASCII / Unicode string                              (= x/s)
dd / dw / db           # dwords / words / bytes
!address 0x...         # which region (heap, stack, image, free)             (= info proc mappings)
!address -summary      # memory usage by type (like VMMap)
ln 0x...               # nearest symbol                                      (= info symbol)
x YourServer!g_*       # list symbols matching                                (= info variables / info functions)
!error c0000374        # decode an NTSTATUS/Win32 code
!gle                   # GetLastError for the current thread
!teb / !peb            # thread/process environment blocks (stack limits, env, cmdline)
!runaway               # CPU time per thread (find the spinner)
!uniqstack             # all threads, duplicates collapsed (deadlock overview)
!findstack YourServer!LockTable 2   # threads whose stack contains that symbol
!handle 0 f            # handle table (handle leaks)
s -d 0 L?0x7fffffffffff 41414141    # search memory for a pattern (slow on full dumps; scope it)

Exception code parameters for an access violation: Parameter[0] = 0 read, 1 write, 8 execute (DEP violation: jumping into data - a smashed return address or vtable); Parameter[1] = the address. Exactly si_code/si_addr.

docs.title: 2.5 Reading the stack when symbols are partial
docs.text:
With only public symbols for Windows DLLs and private ones for your module, a typical stack:

 # Child-SP          RetAddr               Call Site
00 000000e3`6f5ff2c0 00007ff6`9a4b1e58     YourServer!post_entry+0x11 [D:\src\ledger.cpp @ 58]
01 000000e3`6f5ff2f0 00007ff6`9a4b22a3     YourServer!process_batch+0x1b8 [D:\src\ledger.cpp @ 92]
02 000000e3`6f5ff3a0 00007ff6`9a4c0f2c     YourServer!main+0x9c
03 000000e3`6f5ff3f0 00007ffd`b2a17374     YourServer!__scrt_common_main_seh+0x10c
04 000000e3`6f5ff430 00007ffd`b3fdcc91     KERNEL32!BaseThreadInitThunk+0x14
05 000000e3`6f5ff460 00000000`00000000     ntdll!RtlUserThreadStart+0x21

Child-SP is the stack pointer in that frame; the difference between consecutive values is the frame size (0x30 for frame 0). RetAddr is the return address into the caller. Red flags: 0x00000000 or a tiny RetAddr in the middle; a frame YourServer+0x1234 without a function name (symbols not loaded for your module - fix symbols before anything else); *** Stack trace for last set context - .thread/.cxr resets it; and "Stack unwind information not available. Following frames may be wrong." - the walk is now heuristic; verify with dps @rsp.

When dv shows <value unavailable> in release builds, do what module 02 taught: .frame /r N for the registers at that frame, u the function, see which register/stack slot holds the variable at the faulting instruction, read it with dq/dt.

docs.title: 2.6 Common exception codes and what they mean
docs.text:
Code Name What to do 0xC0000005 STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION .exr -1: read/write/execute + address. Small address: null+offset. Execute: smashed return address or vtable. Address inside heap but process still has it mapped: stale pointer (full dump: !heap -p -a tells you if the block is free). 0xC0000374 STATUS_HEAP_CORRUPTION Fail-fast from the heap manager (ntdll!RtlReportCriticalFailure -> RtlpHeapHandleError). The stack shows where corruption was detected, not where it happened. !heap -s, !heap -p -a <addr> on the parameter / the block being freed. To find the writer: PageHeap or AppVerifier (2.8). 0xC0000409 STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN Historically /GS cookie failure (__report_gsfailure): a local buffer overflowed. Since Windows 8 it is also the generic __fastfail code; the first exception parameter is the FAST_FAIL subcode: 2 = stack cookie, 3 = corrupt LIST_ENTRY, 4 = incorrect stack, 5 = invalid argument, 7 = fatal app exit (abort()), 8 = range check, 10 = control flow guard check (CFG) failure... Decode it before saying "buffer overrun". 0xC00000FD STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW ~#k shows thousands of frames or a huge local; !teb gives stack base/limit; compare @rsp. Default thread stack is 1 MiB. 0xC0000008 STATUS_INVALID_HANDLE closed/garbage handle; !handle; enable AppVerifier Handles 0xC000001D STATUS_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION ud2/garbage code: jumped into data or __fastfail on older OS 0xC0000094 STATUS_INTEGER_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO idiv by zero; .ecxr and read the divisor register 0xC000008C STATUS_ARRAY_BOUNDS_EXCEEDED rare; /RTC or checked indexer 0xE06D7363 C++ exception (msc) .exr -1: parameters include the thrown object and its type; !analyze -v decodes std::exception::what() often. First-chance means thrown, second-chance means uncaught. 0x80000003 STATUS_BREAKPOINT DebugBreak(), __debugbreak, int 3 in code, or the CRT abort() path in debug 0x80000004 STATUS_SINGLE_STEP trace flag; debugger artefact 0xC0000017 STATUS_NO_MEMORY commit exhausted; !address -summary, !heap -s

!error 0xc0000374 prints the name. sx lists exception handling settings; sxe c0000374 breaks when it happens in a live session.

docs.title: 2.7 Heap commands
docs.text:
With a full dump:

!heap -s                     # summary of every heap: handle, reserved, committed, virtual blocks, free, LFH on/off
!heap -s -h 0000012ab4c00000   # one heap
!heap -stat -h <heap>        # allocation size histogram for that heap: which sizes dominate (leak hunting, module 09)
!heap -flt s 0x40            # list every busy block of size 0x40 (after -stat points at a size)
!heap -p -a 0x0000012ab4c53a20   # which block contains this address: heap, entry, user ptr, size, state (busy/free) and, if +ust was enabled, the ALLOCATING STACK
!heap -p -all                # every block with page-heap info (slow)
!heap -x 0x...               # search heaps for a block containing the address
!heap -l                     # leak detection: busy blocks with no reference anywhere (slow, heuristic)
!heap -h <heap> -v           # validate; reports where the walk breaks = corruption location
!heap -i <addr>              # detailed info on a heap entry (segment, flags, size, unused bytes)

Reading !heap -p -a output after a 0xC0000374:

    address 0000012ab4c53a20 found in
    _HEAP @ 12ab4c00000
              HEAP_ENTRY Size Prev Flags            UserPtr UserSize - state
        0000012ab4c53a00 0004 0000  [00]   0000012ab4c53a10    00030 - (busy)
        ...

Size is in 16-byte units (0004 = 64 bytes). A UserSize of 0x30 (48) in a 64-byte entry means your request was 48 bytes. If the entry's Flags or Prev are inconsistent with the neighbour, that neighbour's header was overwritten: an overflow of the block before it (just like glibc's "invalid next size"). The gdb/glibc equivalent is reading the chunk header by hand (module 03).

With user-mode stack trace database on (gflags /i YourServer.exe +ust), !heap -p -a also prints the stack that allocated the block. That answers "whose block is this" instantly.

docs.title: 2.8 Finding the heap corruption at the source: PageHeap and Application Verifier
docs.text:
This is the Windows answer to ASan. The heap manager detects corruption later; PageHeap makes the overflowing write itself fault.

Full PageHeap (gflags, from Debugging Tools for Windows):

gflags /p /enable YourServer.exe /full      # every allocation on its own page(s), followed by an inaccessible guard page
gflags /p /enable YourServer.exe            # "normal" page heap: fill patterns + checks on free (cheaper, catches on free)
gflags /p /disable YourServer.exe
gflags /i YourServer.exe +ust               # user-mode stack trace DB: allocation stacks for !heap -p -a and UMDH
gflags /p                                   # show current settings

With /full, a write one byte past a block hits the guard page -> 0xC0000005 at the exact instruction, with the full stack, and !heap -p -a <addr> shows the block, its size and the allocating stack. Cost: memory use rises hugely (every allocation takes at least a page plus a guard page) and speed drops; use it on a test instance or a reproduction, not production. Settings live in the registry (HKLM\...\Image File Execution Options\YourServer.exe) and apply to the next process start.

Application Verifier (appverif.exe): a broader runtime checker. Enable for your exe: Basics > Heaps (this is PageHeap with extra checks), Handles (invalid/closed handle use), Locks (critical section misuse: deleting a held lock, unlock by non-owner, lock order?), Memory (VirtualFree misuse, stack overflow pre-check), TLS, Exceptions (first-chance access violations). Run the process under WinDbg; AppVerifier breaks with a verifier stop (!avrf shows details): stop code, description, and the stacks. Example stop: Heap: Corrupted heap block... Heap block overrun with the block, the allocation stack and the current stack. Verifier stops are the single best heap-bug input to an RCA: they name the allocation site and the corrupting site.

Comparison for the brief: PageHeap ~ ASan for the heap (no stack/global coverage); AppVerifier Locks ~ a subset of TSan deadlock checks plus lock-API misuse; UMDH ~ heaptrack/LSan (module 09).

docs.title: 2.9 Locks and deadlocks
docs.text:
!locks                       # every critical section with a non-zero lock count: address, owner thread id, recursion, waiters
!locks -v                    # include uncontended
!cs -l -o                    # list locked critical sections with owner stacks (needs +ust or symbols)
!cs 0x...                    # one critical section
dt ntdll!_RTL_CRITICAL_SECTION 0x...   # OwningThread, LockCount, RecursionCount
~~[<OwningThread>]s ; k      # jump to the owner and see what it is waiting on
!runaway                     # a thread with huge user time while others wait: spinning holder
!uniqstack                   # collapse duplicate waiting stacks; the odd one out is often the culprit

SRW locks (SRWLOCK, std::shared_mutex on MSVC) and std::mutex (MSVC implements it on SRWLOCK) do not record an owner thread; !locks cannot show them. You infer the owner from ~*k: whoever is inside the protected region (not in RtlAcquireSRWLockExclusive) holds it. Waiters sit in ntdll!NtWaitForAlertByThreadId. Module 10 covers the reasoning.

docs.title: 2.10 Command map (WinDbg -> gdb)
docs.text: WinDbg gdb Notes !analyze -v crashinfo macro + bt + info registers no equivalent; do the steps .ecxr / .exr -1 automatic / p $_siginfo fault address: Parameter[1] / si_addr k, kn, kv, kp bt, bt full, info frame kb args unreliable on x64 ~*k thread apply all bt ~Ns, ~#s, ~~[tid]s thread N, (auto), thread find LWP .frame N / .frame /r N frame N / info frame + info registers dv, dv /t /v info locals, info args, ptype dt Type addr / dt -r p *(Type*)addr with set print pretty on dq/dd/dw/db addr L n x/ngx, x/nwx, x/nhx, x/nbx addr dps @rsp L40 x/40ag $rsp stack scan da / du x/s / x/ws u, ub, uf x/8i $pc, disassemble /s r, r rax info registers, p $rax ba w8 addr watch -l *(long*)addr hardware data breakpoint bp mod!func, bl, bc break func, info b, delete g, p, t, gu continue, next(i), step(i), finish sxe eh catch throw lm, lmvm, .reload info sharedlibrary, readelf -n, sharedlibrary .sympath set debug-file-directory, debuginfod, set sysroot !address / !address -summary info proc mappings / pmap -x !heap -s / -stat / -p -a malloc_stats(), heaptrack, x/4xg ptr-16 glibc has no !heap !locks, !cs p mutex.__data.__owner !runaway top -H -p PID !handle ls -la /proc/PID/fd .dump /ma file generate-core-file / gcore ProcDump -ma -e ulimit -c unlimited + core_pattern gflags /full PageHeap, AppVerifier ASan, Valgrind UMDH heaptrack, massif, LSan module 09

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
The programs in code/ are g++/Linux. All of them except the ones that use execinfo.h, /proc, malloc.h and sigaction (m01, m02, m03, m09_growth, m11) compile unchanged with MSVC (cl /std:c++17 /W4 /Zi /EHsc /Od file.cpp). Use them to practise WinDbg on the same bugs you debugged with gdb:

cl /std:c++17 /W4 /Zi /EHsc /Od /Fe:m04_null_deref.exe m04_null_deref.cpp
windbg m04_null_deref.exe ACC-9999        # or: WinDbg > Launch executable (advanced) with arguments
0:000> g
(1a2c.3f10): Access violation - code c0000005 (first chance)
0:000> .exr -1
    ExceptionCode: c0000005 (Access violation)
    Parameter[0]: 0000000000000000       <- read
    Parameter[1]: 0000000000000010       <- offset of balance: null + 0x10, same as gdb
0:000> k
0:000> dv                                 <- acct = 0x0000000000000000
0:000> u @rip L1                          <- mov rax,qword ptr [rcx+10h]   (rcx: Win64 first argument!)

Note the register: SysV passes acct in rdi; Win64 in rcx. Same bug, same offset, different register - that is module 02 made concrete.

Heap overflow with PageHeap:

cl /std:c++17 /W4 /Zi /EHsc /Od /Fe:m04_heap_overflow.exe m04_heap_overflow.cpp
gflags /p /enable m04_heap_overflow.exe /full
gflags /i m04_heap_overflow.exe +ust
windbg m04_heap_overflow.exe 10
0:000> g
Access violation - code c0000005 (first chance)        <- at the stray write, not at delete[]
0:000> k                                                <- fill_totals is frame 0
0:000> .exr -1                                          <- Parameter[1] = address one past the 40-byte block
0:000> !heap -p -a <Parameter[1] - 4>                   <- the block, UserSize 0x28, and the allocating stack (operator new[] <- main)
gflags /p /disable m04_heap_overflow.exe

Without PageHeap the same program either runs "fine" or dies in delete[] with 0xC0000374 and a stack in ntdll!RtlReportCriticalFailure - exactly the "far from the bug" symptom.

Deadlock: build m10_deadlock.cpp with MSVC (std::mutex is an SRWLOCK underneath), run, attach with WinDbg, ~*k, and identify the two waiters in NtWaitForAlertByThreadId and what each holds by reading the frames of transfer_a_to_b/transfer_b_to_a (!locks will show nothing for SRW locks - that is the lesson).
