Then rebuild using CRITICAL_SECTION and see !locks name the owners.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
First-chance and second-chance exceptions. When an exception is raised, the debugger is notified first (first chance); if no handler catches it the debugger gets it again (second chance) and then the process dies. WER dumps are second-chance; ProcDump -e 1 catches first chance, which matters when code swallows exceptions with a catch-all and continues in a bad state. Structured Exception Handling on x64 is table-driven (.pdata/.xdata, module 02): the OS walks the stack with RtlVirtualUnwind to find handlers; a corrupted stack makes unwinding fail and the process is terminated with the original exception reported as unhandled.

Why 0xC0000374 looks like a crash in ntdll. The heap manager validates headers on allocate/free (and RtlValidateHeap on demand). On an inconsistency it calls RtlpLogHeapFailure which records the failure type (corrupted header, double free, invalid address), the heap and the block, and then RtlReportCriticalFailure raises the fail-fast 0xC0000374 with that information in the exception parameters. The encoded header (XOR with a per-heap key) is what makes most overflows detectable; without it a few overwritten bytes could go unnoticed much longer. !analyze -v on such a dump often prints HEAP_CORRUPTION_ACTIONABLE_ BlockNotBusy_DOUBLEFREE or similar, which is the failure type decoded.

Why PageHeap works. With /full, RtlAllocateHeap is redirected to RtlpDebugPageHeap allocators which place each user block at the end of a page so the next byte is in a PAGE_NOACCESS guard page; freed blocks are decommitted (so UAF faults too) and kept out of reuse for a while; fill patterns (0xC0 / 0xF0) detect uninitialised use and underflow on free. The cost is one+ page per allocation, hence the memory blow-up. /full is ASan's redzone+quarantine implemented with MMU pages instead of shadow memory - precise, but 4 KiB granularity per block instead of 8 bytes.

Fill patterns you will see in Windows dumps (the equivalent of module 03's tcache pointers):

Pattern Who writes it Meaning 0xCDCDCDCD debug CRT malloc/new allocated, never written (uninitialised heap) 0xDDDDDDDD debug CRT free/delete freed heap memory (use-after-free if you see it in a live object) 0xFDFDFDFD debug CRT guard bytes ("no man's land") around a block; overwritten = overflow 0xCCCCCCCC /RTC or /Zi debug stack init uninitialised stack variable 0xFEEEFEEE NT heap on free (when a debugger is attached / heap tail checking) freed block 0xBAADF00D NT heap with debug flags on allocate uninitialised heap 0xABABABAB NT heap guard bytes after a block (HeapAlloc debug) 0xC0C0C0C0 / 0xF0F0F0F0 PageHeap uninitialised / freed under page heap

A pointer equal to one of these, or a field full of one, is a diagnosis by itself.

Symbol server internals. The debugger computes <pdbname>/<GUID><age>/<pdbname> and asks each path in .sympath in order; srv* caches downloads. .reload /f refuses a PDB whose GUID mismatches the executable's debug directory entry - the same guarantee as the ELF build-id. A PDB "matches" only the exact link; rebuilding from the same source produces a different GUID, which is why you archive PDBs rather than rebuilding them later.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Configure WER LocalDumps with DumpType=2 on every Windows server you support. A minidump of a heap corruption is an unsolvable ticket. Put the dump folder on a disk with space and rotate with DumpCount.
  • Do not trust !analyze -v for 0xC0000374/0xC0000409. It tells you the detector, not the bug. Collect the dump for the record, then reproduce under PageHeap/AppVerifier in a test environment to get the writer's stack. If it cannot be reproduced, !heap -p -a with +ust enabled in production (moderate overhead) at least tells you whose block was corrupted, which narrows the suspects to code that writes near that block type.
  • +ust in production is acceptable overhead for many servers (allocation stacks captured per allocation; memory grows); full PageHeap is not. Know which switch you are flipping on a bank's box and document it in the change record.
  • The excepting thread is not always the guilty one. ~*k every time. Another worker inside the same object's mutating method, or inside HeapFree for the block the excepting thread is using, is the real story (module 10).
  • 32-bit vs 64-bit confusion costs hours: a 32-bit process dumped by a 64-bit tool shows wow64 frames and nonsense until !wow64exts.sw/.effmach x86. Check vertarget and lm first.
  • Shakir's current practice to upgrade: keep a per-release PDB store (symstore), enable LocalDumps full dumps at every client, run the regression suite with PageHeap and AppVerifier (Heaps, Handles, Locks) once per release, and write the FAILURE_BUCKET_ID into every incident ticket so recurrence is searchable.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - manual analyze. Open any 0xC0000005 dump (make one with m04_null_deref.exe under ProcDump -e). Without !analyze, use .ecxr, .exr -1, k, u @rip L1, dv to state read/write, address, instruction, register, frame and line. Done when it matches !analyze -v afterwards.
  2. Easy - symbol hygiene. Deliberately point .sympath at an empty folder, .reload /f, lm, k. Then fix the path, .reload /f, lm, k. Done when you can describe three differences in lm and k output between the two states.
  3. Medium - PageHeap. Follow the heap overflow walkthrough in section 3. Done when you have the faulting stack, the !heap -p -a block info and the allocating stack from +ust.
  4. Medium - fail-fast subcode. Build a program that calls abort() and one that overflows a stack buffer under /GS. Dump both (0xC0000409), run .exr -1 and decode the first parameter. Done when you can explain why both are 0xC0000409 and how you told them apart.
  5. Hard - deadlock, two ways. Build m10_deadlock.cpp with MSVC (std::mutex), hang it, attach, and identify owners from ~*k alone. Then rewrite with CRITICAL_SECTION and use !locks and ~~[tid]s. Done when both analyses name the same two threads and the same lock order inversion.
  6. Hard - AppVerifier stop. Run m04_use_after_free.exe under AppVerifier (Heaps) in WinDbg. Done when you can quote the verifier stop code and description, and show both the allocation stack and the faulting stack.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a minidump and a full user-mode dump, and which do you want for heap corruption? A: A minidump has thread stacks, registers, module list and the exception record but no heap memory; a full dump (MiniDumpWithFullMemory) has everything the process had mapped. Heap corruption, use-after-free and leak analysis need the heap, so you need a full dump; configure WER LocalDumps DumpType=2 or ProcDump -ma.

Q: !analyze -v says the crash is in ntdll!RtlReportCriticalFailure with code 0xC0000374. Is ntdll broken? A: No. 0xC0000374 is the heap manager's fail-fast when it detects a corrupted block during an allocate or free. The stack shows where the corruption was detected, not where it was caused. Use !heap -p -a to identify the block, then find the writer with PageHeap (gflags /p /enable app /full) or Application Verifier, which make the overflowing write itself fault.

Q: What does exception code 0xC0000409 mean? A: Historically a /GS stack cookie failure - a local buffer overran into the return address. On Windows 8 and later it is the generic __fastfail code; the first exception parameter is the FAST_FAIL subcode (2 = stack cookie, 7 = fatal app exit from abort(), 10 = Control Flow Guard failure, etc.). You decode the subcode before concluding "buffer overrun".

Q: How does PageHeap find a heap overflow that the normal heap only detects later? A: Full PageHeap places every allocation at the end of its own page with an inaccessible guard page after it, so a write one byte past the block raises an access violation at that instruction with the full stack; freed blocks are decommitted so use-after-free faults too. It trades large memory and speed overhead for precise detection - the Windows analogue of AddressSanitizer.

Q: How do you find the owner of a lock in a deadlock dump? A: For critical sections, !locks or !cs -l -o lists each held section with its owning thread id; ~~[tid]s then k shows what the owner is waiting on, and you follow the cycle. For SRW locks and MSVC std::mutex no owner is recorded, so I read ~*k: threads blocked in NtWaitForAlertByThreadId are waiters, and the thread executing inside the protected region holds the lock.

Q: How do symbols get matched, and what happens if you force a mismatched PDB? A: The executable's debug directory stores the PDB GUID and age; the debugger requests pdbname/GUIDage/pdbname from each symbol path and refuses a GUID mismatch. Forcing with .symopt+ 0x40 loads it anyway and you get plausible but wrong function names and line numbers. That is why PDBs for every shipped build are archived in a symbol store.

Q: Name the WinDbg equivalents of bt, info locals, p $_siginfo, thread apply all bt, watch -l, and info proc mappings. A: k (or kn/kv), dv, .exr -1 (after .ecxr), ~*k, ba w8 <addr>, and !address.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Minidump = stacks only; full dump = everything. Configure WER LocalDumps DumpType=2; use ProcDump -ma -e / -t / -c / -m / plain for exceptions, exit, CPU, memory, snapshot.
  • Symbols: .sympath srv*cache*MS-server + your own symstore; lm must say (pdb symbols) for your module; GUID match is mandatory; archive PDBs.
  • !analyze -v = .ecxr + .exr -1 + k + heuristics + FAILURE_BUCKET_ID; learn to do it manually and distrust it for heap/stack corruption.
  • .exr -1 Parameter[0] read/write/execute, Parameter[1] address = gdb si_code/si_addr.
  • Codes: C0000005 AV, C0000374 heap corruption (detector, not cause), C0000409 fast-fail (decode subcode), C00000FD stack overflow, E06D7363 C++ exception.
  • !heap -s, -stat, -flt, -p -a (++ust for alloc stacks); !locks/!cs for critical sections; ~*k for SRW locks; !runaway, !uniqstack, !address.
  • PageHeap (gflags /p /enable app /full) and Application Verifier trap the corrupting write at the source: the Windows ASan.
  • Win64 passes the first argument in rcx (SysV: rdi); same bug, same offset, different register.

docs.title: 08. Valgrind and the sanitizers
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 03, 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Debuggers show you the aftermath. Valgrind and the sanitizers catch the bug at the moment it happens: the exact instruction that wrote past a buffer, read a freed block, used an uninitialised value, raced another thread or overflowed an integer - with the stack trace of that moment and often the stacks of the allocation and the free as well. They turn the "crash far from the bug" problem of module 03 into "here is the line".

They do it in two different ways. Valgrind runs your unmodified binary on a software CPU that checks every memory access; nothing to rebuild, but 20 to 50 times slower. The sanitizers are compiler features: you rebuild with a flag and the compiler inserts checks into the code; 2 to 3 times slower for ASan, fast enough to run your whole test suite under them every night. A senior engineer knows which to reach for, how to read each report in ten seconds, and what each one cannot see.

docs.title: 2.1 Valgrind memcheck
docs.text:
sudo apt install valgrind
g++ -std=c++17 -g -O0 -o prog prog.cpp          # -g for line numbers; -O0 for exact lines; -O1 ok
valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all --track-origins=yes --num-callers=30 \
         --error-exitcode=99 ./prog args

Memcheck runs the program on Valgrind's synthetic CPU (dynamic binary instrumentation via the VEX IR) and keeps shadow state for every byte: an A bit (addressable?) and eight V bits (are these bits defined?). Every load/store is checked against A bits; every use of a value in a way that affects behaviour (branch, syscall argument, address) is checked against V bits. Heap blocks get red zones around them and freed blocks are quarantined (not reused for a while) so UAF is caught. It intercepts malloc/free/new/delete with its own versions.

Report types and what they mean:

Report line Meaning Bug class Invalid read of size 8 / Invalid write of size 4 access to a non-addressable byte overflow, UAF, wild pointer Address 0x... is 0 bytes after a block of size 40 alloc'd just past the end of a heap block, with its alloc stack heap overflow / off-by-one Address 0x... is 8 bytes inside a block of size 48 free'd inside a freed block, with the free stack and alloc stack use-after-free Address 0x... is not stack'd, malloc'd or (recently) free'd nowhere Valgrind knows null+offset, wild pointer, stale pointer to long-freed memory Address 0x... is on thread 1's stack with N bytes below stack pointer stack misuse stack-use-after-return, bad alloca Invalid free() / delete / delete[] / realloc() pointer is not the start of a live block double free, freeing interior/stack pointer Mismatched free() / delete / delete [] new[] freed with delete, or malloc with delete mismatched allocator Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s) a branch used undefined bits uninitialised read Use of uninitialised value of size 8 undefined value used as an address or in a syscall uninitialised pointer Syscall param write(buf) points to uninitialised byte(s) sending undefined memory out uninit; information leak Source and destination overlap in memcpy(...) memcpy with overlap (UB; use memmove) Uninitialised value was created by a heap allocation / stack allocation origin (with --track-origins=yes) points you at the malloc/local

Leak summary categories:

Category Meaning Action definitely lost no pointer to the block anywhere a real leak; fix indirectly lost only reachable from a definitely-lost block (children of a leaked tree) fixed by fixing the parent possibly lost only an interior pointer points to it usually a leak unless you use interior pointers deliberately still reachable a pointer exists at exit (globals, caches) not a leak by Valgrind's definition; may still be unbounded growth (module 09) suppressed matched a suppression file ignore

Useful switches: --xtree-leak=yes (leak sites as a callgrind tree), --gen-suppressions=all (print suppression entries for noisy third-party code; collect into --suppressions=file), --vgdb=yes --vgdb-error=0 (attach gdb to the valgrind'd process at the first error: gdb then target remote | vgdb), --trace-children=yes, --log-file=vg.%p.txt, --xml=yes for CI parsing, --malloc-fill=0xAA --free-fill=0xBB, --redzone-size=256 (catch bigger overruns), --undef-value-errors=no (speed when you only want addressability).

Limits: ~20-50x slowdown and 2x memory (the Valgrind manual's own figures for memcheck); no detection of stack or global buffer overflows (there are no red zones around stack arrays - ASan does this); only one thread runs at a time (races are hidden; use helgrind); does not work with ASan-instrumented binaries; some SIMD instructions unsupported in old versions. Works on WSL2.

docs.title: 2.2 Helgrind and DRD
docs.text:
valgrind --tool=helgrind ./prog          # data races, lock order violations, pthread API misuse
valgrind --tool=drd --check-stack-var=yes ./prog   # similar, different algorithm, lower memory

Helgrind tracks every lock/unlock/create/join to build a happens-before relation (vector clocks) and reports accesses to the same address from two threads with no ordering:

==1234== Possible data race during write of size 8 at 0x4A4C040 by thread #3
==1234== Locks held: none
==1234==    at 0x109234: worker(int) (m10_data_race.cpp:30)
==1234== This conflicts with a previous write of size 8 by thread #2
==1234== Locks held: none
==1234==    at 0x109234: worker(int) (m10_data_race.cpp:30)
==1234==  Address 0x4A4C040 is 0 bytes inside data symbol "g_total"

It also reports Thread #1: lock order "0x... before 0x..." violated with both acquisition stacks - a potential deadlock found on a run that did not deadlock. Costs ~100x; use TSan when you can rebuild, helgrind when you cannot (third-party binary, no source). Both understand pthreads and C++11 threads (which are pthreads underneath); custom spinlocks and lock-free code produce false positives unless annotated.

docs.title: 2.3 Cachegrind and Callgrind (intro)
docs.text:
valgrind --tool=cachegrind ./prog  && cg_annotate cachegrind.out.<pid>
valgrind --tool=callgrind ./prog   && callgrind_annotate callgrind.out.<pid>   # or kcachegrind GUI

Cachegrind simulates I1/D1/LL caches and counts instructions and misses per line; Callgrind adds the call graph and inclusive costs. Deterministic, so two runs compare exactly - good for "did my change reduce cache misses in the hot loop". Not for wall-clock profiling (perf is), and 50x slow. Mentioned here so you know the names; it is not a debugging tool.

docs.title: 2.4 AddressSanitizer (ASan)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -g -O1 -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer -o prog_asan prog.cpp
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1:halt_on_error=1:abort_on_error=1 ./prog_asan

The compiler inserts a check before every load/store: it looks up the shadow byte for the address (shadow = (addr >> 3) + 0x7fff8000 on x86-64 Linux; one shadow byte per 8 bytes of memory) and traps if the shadow says the bytes are poisoned. The ASan runtime replaces malloc: every block gets poisoned redzones before and after, freed blocks go into a quarantine (256 MB by default) poisoned as "freed", stack frames get redzones around each local, globals get redzones after them. The result: overflows, underflows, UAF and double free are caught at the access, with stacks for the access, the allocation and the free.

A report, annotated:

==4242==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x602000000038 at pc 0x55e9... bp 0x7ffd... sp 0x7ffd...
WRITE of size 4 at 0x602000000038 thread T0                         <- what: a 4-byte write
    #0 0x55e9... in fill_totals(int*, int) m04_heap_overflow.cpp:27  <- where: your line
    #1 0x55e9... in main m04_heap_overflow.cpp:36
0x602000000038 is located 0 bytes after 40-byte region [0x602000000010,0x602000000038)   <- which block, how far past
allocated by thread T0 here:                                        <- who allocated it
    #0 0x7f... in operator new[](unsigned long)
    #1 0x55e9... in main m04_heap_overflow.cpp:33
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow m04_heap_overflow.cpp:27 in fill_totals(int*, int)
Shadow bytes around the buggy address:
  0x0c047fff8000: fa fa 00 00 00 00 00[fa]fa fa ...                  <- [fa] = the shadow byte hit: heap redzone
Shadow byte legend (one shadow byte represents 8 application bytes):
  Addressable:           00
  Partially addressable: 01 02 03 04 05 06 07
  Heap left redzone:       fa
  Freed heap region:       fd
  Stack left redzone:      f1
  Stack mid redzone:       f2
  Stack right redzone:     f3
  Stack after return:      f5
  Stack use after scope:   f8
  Global redzone:          f9

Error names you will meet: heap-buffer-overflow, stack-buffer-overflow, global-buffer-overflow, heap-use-after-free, stack-use-after-return, stack-use-after-scope, double-free, attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed (bad free), alloc-dealloc-mismatch (new[]/delete), memcpy-param-overlap, negative-size-param, container-overflow (writing into a vector's unused capacity when libstdc++ annotations are on), SEGV on unknown address (ASan caught a plain segfault; it adds "Hint: address points to the zero page" for null derefs), stack-overflow.

ASAN_OPTIONS worth knowing: detect_leaks=1 (LSan; on by default on Linux x86-64), halt_on_error=0 (keep going after the first error, needs -fsanitize-recover=address), abort_on_error=1 (SIGABRT so you get a core), detect_stack_use_after_return=1, strict_string_checks=1, check_initialization_order=1, symbolize=1, log_path=/tmp/asan, malloc_context_size=30, quarantine_size_mb=, print_stats=1, handle_segv=0 (let your own handler run), allocator_may_return_null=1. __asan_poison_memory_region and ASAN_DEFAULT_OPTIONS via __asan_default_options() for custom allocators (arena allocators! poison the free part of your arena so ASan sees overflows inside it).

Cost (from the ASan paper and GCC/LLVM docs, typical): ~2x CPU, ~2-3x memory (shadow + redzones

  • quarantine). Fast enough for CI and for a canary test instance; not for production.

Cannot: detect uninitialised reads (that is MSan, clang-only); see overflows that stay inside a block (writing field B through a pointer to field A); detect races; be combined with Valgrind or TSan in the same binary. Uninstrumented libraries (a vendor .so built without ASan) are not checked inside, but their mallocs are still tracked.

docs.title: 2.5 LeakSanitizer (LSan)
docs.text:
Part of ASan; runs at exit and reports blocks not reachable from roots (globals, stacks, registers, TLS):

==4242==ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks
Direct leak of 32000 byte(s) in 250 object(s) allocated from:
    #0 0x7f... in operator new(unsigned long)
    #1 0x55... in handle_request(int) m09_leak.cpp:33
Indirect leak of 16000 byte(s) in 250 object(s) allocated from: ...   <- the std::string buffers owned by the leaked Requests
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 48000 byte(s) leaked in 500 allocation(s).

Standalone, without ASan's overhead: -fsanitize=leak. Runtime check on demand in a long-running server: #include <sanitizer/lsan_interface.h> and call __lsan_do_recoverable_leak_check() from an admin command - it reports leaks accumulated so far without exiting. Suppressions: LSAN_OPTIONS=suppressions=lsan.supp with lines like leak:libcrypto. "Direct" vs "indirect" is the same idea as Valgrind's definitely vs indirectly lost. LSan has no "still reachable" category; growth in live containers is invisible to it (module 09).

docs.title: 2.6 UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -g -O1 -fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all -o prog_ubsan prog.cpp
UBSAN_OPTIONS=print_stacktrace=1 ./prog_ubsan
m04_integer_overflow_size.cpp:27:21: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 1073741824 * 4 cannot be represented in type 'int'

Checks inserted for: signed integer overflow, division by zero, shift exponent out of range or shifting into the sign bit, null pointer dereference (-fsanitize=null), misaligned access (alignment), out-of-bounds index on arrays with a known bound (bounds), vptr (clang: wrong dynamic type via dynamic_cast-style checks), return (falling off a non-void function), vla-bound, float-cast-overflow (not in the default group), enum/bool invalid values, unreachable, pointer-overflow, nonnull-attribute, object-size. Unsigned wrap is not UB, so -fsanitize=unsigned-integer-overflow exists only in clang and is opt-in.

Cost: small (tens of percent), no shadow memory; it combines with ASan or TSan. Default behaviour is to print and continue; -fno-sanitize-recover=all makes the first error fatal, which is what you want in CI. It is the cheapest sanitizer and the one most people forget. Every "appears only at -O2" bug (module 04) is a UBSan candidate.

docs.title: 2.7 ThreadSanitizer (TSan)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -g -O1 -fsanitize=thread -fno-omit-frame-pointer -pthread -o prog_tsan prog.cpp
TSAN_OPTIONS=second_deadlock_stack=1:detect_deadlocks=1:halt_on_error=0 ./prog_tsan

TSan instruments every memory access and every synchronisation operation (mutexes, atomics, thread create/join, condition variables) and keeps, per 8-byte word, the last few accesses with their thread and vector clock. Two accesses to the same location, at least one a write, not ordered by the happens-before relation = a data race, reported with both stacks:

WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=4242)
  Write of size 8 at 0x55e9c2c0a0c0 by thread T2:
    #0 worker(int) m10_data_race.cpp:30
  Previous write of size 8 at 0x55e9c2c0a0c0 by thread T1:
    #0 worker(int) m10_data_race.cpp:30
  Location is global 'g_total' of size 8 at 0x55e9c2c0a0c0
  Thread T2 (tid=4245, running) created by main thread at:
    #0 pthread_create
    #1 std::thread::_M_start_thread
    #2 main m10_data_race.cpp:41
SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: data race m10_data_race.cpp:30 in worker(int)

Also reports: lock-order-inversion (potential deadlock) with detect_deadlocks=1 (both acquisition orders, even if the run did not deadlock - run m10_deadlock_tsan), thread leak, destroy of a locked mutex, double lock of a mutex, unlock of an unlocked mutex, signal-unsafe call inside of a signal, data race on vptr (destructor racing a virtual call).

Cost (LLVM docs, typical): 5-15x CPU, 5-10x memory. Not combinable with ASan. Needs all code instrumented to see all races: an uninstrumented library's internal races are invisible, and its synchronisation may be misunderstood (false positives) unless it uses pthread/atomics TSan intercepts. Races that never execute in the test run are not found - TSan finds races in the paths you exercise, so coverage matters; it does not need the race to manifest, only both accesses to run unordered.

If you see FATAL: ThreadSanitizer: unexpected memory mapping on a new kernel, run under setarch $(uname -m) -R ./prog_tsan (disables ASLR for that run) or update the toolchain.

docs.title: 2.8 MemorySanitizer (mention)
docs.text: clang++ -fsanitize=memory finds uninitialised reads like Valgrind, at ~3x instead of 30x, but requires everything including libstdc++ to be instrumented (otherwise false positives), so in practice it means a clang build of your whole dependency tree. On GCC you use Valgrind for this.

docs.title: 2.9 Build flags table
docs.text:
Tool Compile/link flags Runtime env Slowdown (typical) Memory Combine with Valgrind memcheck none needed; -g for lines, -O0/-O1 for accuracy valgrind --leak-check=full --track-origins=yes 20-50x 2x nothing instrumented Helgrind / DRD none; -g valgrind --tool=helgrind 50-100x high - ASan (+LSan) -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -O1 ASAN_OPTIONS=... ~2x 2-3x UBSan LSan alone -fsanitize=leak -g LSAN_OPTIONS=... ~1x small ASan built-in, UBSan UBSan -fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all -g UBSAN_OPTIONS=print_stacktrace=1 1.1-1.5x none ASan or TSan TSan -fsanitize=thread -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -O1 -pthread TSAN_OPTIONS=detect_deadlocks=1 5-15x 5-10x UBSan MSan (clang) -fsanitize=memory -fsanitize-memory-track-origins MSAN_OPTIONS=... ~3x 2x UBSan libstdc++ debug -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG (ABI change) / -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS (no ABI change) - small small any glibc checks none; MALLOC_CHECK_=3, MALLOC_PERTURB_=165 env vars ~1x none any

Always -g. Prefer -O1 for sanitizers: -O0 can hide some bugs the optimiser would expose and is slow; -O2 inlines so much that line numbers get fuzzy. -fno-omit-frame-pointer makes the fast stack unwinder in the sanitizer runtime reliable. For CI, build three variants: ASan+UBSan, TSan+UBSan, plain -O2 -Wall -Werror.

docs.title: 2.10 Choosing
docs.text:
Situation Reach for You can rebuild, want overflow/UAF/double-free/leaks, want it fast enough for the full test suite ASan (+LSan, +UBSan) Suspected uninitialised read, GCC toolchain Valgrind memcheck --track-origins=yes Cannot rebuild (vendor binary, production build, no source) Valgrind Nondeterministic wrong results, multithreaded TSan (rebuild) or helgrind (no rebuild) Deadlock that will not reproduce TSan detect_deadlocks=1 on the test suite "Only fails at -O2" / weird arithmetic / bad casts UBSan Memory grows over days, no leak reported heaptrack / massif (module 09), not a sanitizer Which line is slow / cache misses Cachegrind / perf, not a debugger Windows PageHeap/AppVerifier (ASan-like), MSVC /fsanitize=address (ASan exists in MSVC 2019 16.9+), UMDH (leaks), no TSan

ASan beats Valgrind when: you own the build, you need stack/global overflow detection, you need speed, or the program is large. Valgrind beats ASan when: you cannot rebuild, you need uninitialised-value detection on GCC, or you need to check a binary exactly as shipped.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Everything is driven by code/build_debug.sh:

cd code
./build_debug.sh all            # debug, opt, asan, tsan, ubsan variants of every program
./build_debug.sh run-asan       # heap overflow, UAF, double free, leak, stack overflow, null deref, ...
./build_debug.sh run-valgrind   # memcheck on the -O0 builds, helgrind on the race
./build_debug.sh run-tsan       # the data race and the lock-order inversion
./build_debug.sh run-ubsan      # the integer overflow

The exact flags live in flags_for() in that script - the same table as 2.9. Run each and read the first 25 lines of every report until the format is boring. Specific things to confirm:

  • m04_uninit_read: ASan silent, Valgrind Conditional jump ... depends on uninitialised value(s) with the origin created by a heap allocation at make_record.
  • m04_heap_overflow: ASan WRITE of size 4 ... 0 bytes after 40-byte region; Valgrind Invalid write of size 4 ... 0 bytes after a block of size 40 alloc'd.
  • m04_use_after_free: both tools give use, free and alloc stacks.
  • m09_leak: LSan direct + indirect leaks; Valgrind definitely + indirectly lost with matching byte counts.
  • m10_data_race: TSan names g_total and both threads; helgrind same with different wording.
  • m10_deadlock under TSan: lock-order-inversion (potential deadlock) within seconds, no hang needed.
  • m04_integer_overflow_size 1073741824 under UBSan: signed integer overflow.

Also try: MALLOC_PERTURB_=165 ./build/m04_uninit_read_debug (glibc fills allocations with 0xA5; the garbage becomes a recognisable pattern) and -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG on m04_invalid_iterator (immediate abort with "attempt to increment a singular iterator").

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Shadow memory arithmetic. ASan maps 8 application bytes to 1 shadow byte: value 0 = all 8 addressable, k in 1..7 = first k bytes addressable, negative = poisoned with a reason code (fa heap redzone, fd freed, f1-f3 stack redzones, f5 after-return, f8 after-scope, f9 global redzone). The check for an 8-byte access is if (*(addr>>3 + offset)) report(); for smaller accesses it compares the low 3 bits of the address against k. The shadow region (1/8th of the address space) is reserved at startup with mmap(MAP_NORESERVE), which is why ASan processes show ~20 TB of virtual size in top. This is also why ASan cannot catch an overflow that lands in another addressable byte (inside the same block or in an adjacent live block with no redzone between them in a custom allocator): the shadow says "fine".

Why ASan needs its own allocator. Redzones must surround every block and freed memory must not be reused immediately. The ASan allocator uses size classes, puts redzones (16 bytes minimum, larger for big blocks) around each block, records the allocation stack in the block's header, and moves freed blocks through a FIFO quarantine of quarantine_size_mb. UAF detection is only as good as the quarantine: a program that churns gigabytes between the free and the use can evict the block, after which the use is seen as a valid access to a new block. Increase the quarantine when hunting a long-gap UAF.

Stack-use-after-return requires the compiler to allocate frames with address-taken locals on a fake stack (heap-allocated per thread) so that after return the memory stays poisoned instead of being reused by the next call. That is why it is a runtime option with a compile-time component and why it costs more.

Valgrind's V bits are per bit, not per byte. This lets it be precise about partially initialised values (bitfields, struct padding copied with memcpy) and defer complaints until the undefined bits actually influence a decision. That deferral is why the report points at a branch rather than the load, and why --track-origins=yes is needed to find the allocation. It is also why Valgrind is slow: every arithmetic instruction propagates V bits.

TSan's happens-before. Each thread has a vector clock; each synchronisation object stores the clock at release; an acquire merges it. Each 8-byte word's shadow holds up to 4 recent accesses (thread id, epoch, size, write?). A new access races with a stored one if their clocks are not ordered. Consequence: TSan has no false positives for pthread/atomic-based code (if it reports a race, two accesses really were unordered), but "unordered" is defined by the synchronisation TSan can see; a hand-rolled spinlock using volatile is invisible and reports false races - and is also a real bug under the C++ memory model (04_Concurrency).

UBSan is mostly branches. Each check is a compare-and-branch to a runtime handler, inserted where the front-end knows the operation can be UB. That is why it is cheap and why it finds only what the compiler could instrument - no shadow, no heap tracking.

Why not run sanitizers in production? Memory (2-10x), speed, and the attack surface of the runtime (the sanitizer runtime is not hardened; ASAN_OPTIONS is an environment variable). Some companies run a small fraction of production traffic through sanitized canaries; banks rarely can. The production equivalents are hardening flags (_FORTIFY_SOURCE, stack protector, CFG - module 13), not sanitizers.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Sanitizers belong in CI, not in debugging emergencies. The time to find a heap overflow is the night before the release, in the ASan job, not in a client's dump. Three nightly jobs (ASan+UBSan, TSan+UBSan, Valgrind on the slow integration tests) catch most of the catalogue before a bank sees it. This is the single highest-leverage practice in this course for Shakir's server.
  • Reproduction-first triage. When a dump says heap corruption, do not stare at it for hours. Build the ASan variant, run the request mix that preceded the crash (from logs, module 11), and let ASan name the line. Return to the dump to confirm the same block type/size is involved.
  • Valgrind for the thing you cannot rebuild. A vendor library, a stripped production binary the client insists on reproducing with, a Python/Java process embedding your C code: Valgrind runs it as is. Budget for the slowdown (timeouts fire; raise them or stub out time checks).
  • Suppressions are a maintained artefact. Third-party noise (OpenSSL uninitialised-value tricks, leaks in dlopen) will drown the signal; keep valgrind.supp/lsan.supp in the repo and review it when you upgrade dependencies.
  • Sanitizer output in the RCA. An ASan report with the three stacks is the strongest possible evidence of root cause; paste it (module 12). It converts "we believe" into "we observed".
  • Windows parity. MSVC has /fsanitize=address since VS 2019 16.9 (no LSan/TSan/UBSan); PageHeap/AppVerifier for the rest; UMDH for leaks. If the Windows build is the production one, run the ASan job on the Linux build of the same code anyway - most bugs are platform-neutral and the Linux job is cheaper.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - run them all. ./build_debug.sh all && ./build_debug.sh run-asan run-valgrind run-tsan run-ubsan. For each program, write the tool, the error name and the line number. Done when you have a 10-row table.
  2. Easy - read the shadow. From the m04_heap_overflow ASan report, find the [fa] in the shadow dump and explain each shadow byte on that line (00, fa, and the partial byte if any). Done when you can compute the block's start address from the shadow line.
  3. Medium - who sees what. Make a table of the 8 module-04 programs x {ASan, Valgrind, UBSan, TSan} with "catches / misses / n.a." and run every cell. Done when every cell has been observed, not guessed.
  4. Medium - quarantine eviction. Modify m04_use_after_free to allocate and free 300 MB of junk between the free and the use. Run under ASan with default and with quarantine_size_mb=1024. Done when you can show the report disappear and reappear and explain why.
  5. Hard - annotate an arena. Write a bump allocator (module 03), use it for 100 small objects, overflow one by 1 byte. Show ASan is silent. Then add __asan_poison_memory_region on the unused tail after each allocation (include <sanitizer/asan_interface.h>, guard with #ifdef __SANITIZE_ADDRESS__). Done when ASan reports the overflow with your allocator's stack.
  6. Hard - CI script. Write a ci_sanitize.sh that builds the ASan+UBSan and TSan+UBSan variants of m13_raii_fix.cpp and m13_fuzz_target.cpp (plain build), runs them with halt_on_error=1, and exits non-zero on any report, printing only the SUMMARY: lines. Done when it passes on the clean programs and fails when you point it at a buggy one.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: ASan or Valgrind - when do you pick which? A: ASan when I can rebuild: it is 2x slow instead of 30x, catches stack and global overflows that Valgrind cannot, and runs in CI on the whole suite. Valgrind when I cannot rebuild (vendor or production binary) or when I need uninitialised-value detection on a GCC toolchain, since ASan does not detect that and MemorySanitizer is clang-only and needs everything instrumented.

Q: How does AddressSanitizer detect a heap buffer overflow? A: Its allocator surrounds each block with poisoned redzones and the compiler inserts a check before each load/store that reads the shadow byte for the address (one shadow byte per 8 bytes; addr>>3 + offset). An access to a redzone byte sees a poisoned shadow value and the runtime reports the access stack plus the block's allocation stack. Freed blocks are quarantined and poisoned so use-after-free is caught the same way.

Q: What does "Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s)" mean and how do you find the cause? A: Valgrind tracked definedness per bit and saw a branch whose outcome depends on bits that were never written. The report points at the branch; --track-origins=yes adds where the undefined memory was allocated (heap block or stack frame), which is the variable that was never initialised.

Q: What can ThreadSanitizer find that a debugger cannot, and what are its limits? A: It finds data races and lock-order inversions on any run where both accesses execute unordered, even if the race did not produce a visible failure, with both stacks. Limits: 5-15x slowdown, cannot combine with ASan, needs all code instrumented (uninstrumented libraries hide races or cause false reports), and it only sees paths the test exercised.

Q: Explain definitely lost, indirectly lost, possibly lost and still reachable. A: Definitely lost: no pointer to the block exists - a true leak. Indirectly lost: reachable only from a definitely lost block (children of a leaked structure). Possibly lost: only an interior pointer references it. Still reachable: a pointer exists at exit (globals, caches) so Valgrind does not call it a leak, though it may still be unbounded growth.

Q: Why run UBSan if the program "works"? A: Undefined behaviour lets the optimiser assume things that break code later: a null check removed after a dereference, an overflow check folded away, a bounds check skipped. UBSan makes the UB visible at low cost (tens of percent), combines with ASan or TSan, and finds the class of bugs that appear only at -O2 or after a compiler upgrade.

Q: What is the Windows equivalent of ASan? A: Full PageHeap (gflags /p /enable app /full) and Application Verifier's Heaps checks: each allocation gets a guard page so overflow and use-after-free fault at the access, with the allocation stack available via !heap -p -a. MSVC also ships a real /fsanitize=address since VS 2019 16.9. There is no TSan on MSVC; UMDH covers leaks.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Valgrind: no rebuild, 20-50x slower, catches heap overflow/UAF/double free/leaks and uninitialised reads; misses stack/global overflow; helgrind/DRD for races; cachegrind for cache profiling.
  • ASan: rebuild with -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -O1; ~2x; shadow bytes + redzones + quarantine; catches heap/stack/global overflow, UAF, double free, bad free, use-after-return/scope; LSan included; misses uninitialised reads.
  • UBSan: -fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all; cheap; integer/shift/null/alignment/ bounds/vptr UB; combine with everything.
  • TSan: -fsanitize=thread; 5-15x; data races and lock-order inversions with both stacks; not with ASan; needs all code instrumented.
  • Read reports top-down: error name -> access stack -> block location/alloc stack -> free stack -> SUMMARY line. Paste them into the RCA.
  • Leak categories: definitely / indirectly / possibly lost, still reachable; LSan direct / indirect.
  • Run ASan+UBSan and TSan+UBSan in CI nightly; use Valgrind for what you cannot rebuild; PageHeap/AppVerifier//fsanitize=address/UMDH on Windows.
  • Sanitizers are for test and reproduction, not production; hardening flags are for production.

docs.title: 09. Leaks and memory growth
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 08

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
"The server's memory keeps going up" is the most common long-running-process ticket and the most misdiagnosed. People say "leak", but memory grows for three different reasons that need three different fixes: a leak (memory nobody can reach any more and nobody will free), growth (memory that is reachable and in use - a cache, a table, a queue that is legitimately or illegitimately bigger than planned) and fragmentation (memory the allocator holds but cannot reuse or return). Leak tools find only the first. A cache without an eviction policy is not a leak to Valgrind, but it will still take the server down on day 40.

So the job has two halves. First, measure what kind of growth you have: resident memory over time, and inside it, live bytes versus allocator overhead. Second, find the allocation site that accounts for the growth, which is what heap profilers do: they record a stack trace for every allocation and show you which stacks own the most bytes that are still alive. This module does both on Linux (heaptrack, massif, LSan) and on Windows (UMDH, !heap), and ends with the C++ specific traps: smart pointer cycles and containers that never shrink.

docs.title: 2.1 Three kinds of growth
docs.text:
Kind Reachable? Will it ever be freed? Tool that sees it Fix Leak no no LSan, Valgrind (definitely lost), heaptrack "leaked" RAII / fix the missing free Growth (unbounded live data) yes only if the program decides to heaptrack/massif/UMDH: large and growing live stacks; Valgrind "still reachable" eviction policy, size cap, erase when done Fragmentation / allocator retention n/a (free) it is already free malloc_stats: system >> in-use; !heap -s committed >> busy malloc_trim, arena cap, pooling, different allocator

A fourth that looks like memory growth but is not heap: thread count (each thread's stack and arena), file descriptors / handles (not memory, but "resource leak"), and mapped files (page cache attributed to the process). Check these first; they are a ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l, ls /proc/PID/task | wc -l, !handle, away.

docs.title: 2.2 Measuring: RSS over time, and what is inside
docs.text:
# resident set, every 10 s, forever; graph it later
while sleep 10; do echo "$(date +%s) $(ps -o rss= -p $PID)"; done >> rss.log
# or one shot with more detail
grep -E 'VmRSS|VmHWM|VmSize|VmData|VmStk|Threads' /proc/$PID/status
cat /proc/$PID/smaps_rollup                # Rss, Pss, Anonymous, Private_Dirty totals
pmap -x $PID | sort -k3 -n | tail -20      # biggest mappings by RSS: [heap]? anon (arenas)? a file?

Interpretation:

  • RSS rises then plateaus: warm-up (caches filling, arenas reaching steady state). Normal. Alarm thresholds must sit above the plateau.
  • RSS rises linearly with requests, never falls: leak or unbounded growth. Proportional to traffic is the tell.
  • RSS rises in steps and stays: fragmentation or arena growth under thread churn; or periodic big jobs whose freed memory is retained.
  • [heap] grows: main-arena allocations (single-threaded or main thread). Anonymous 64 MiB-aligned mappings grow: per-thread arenas. A file mapping grows: page cache, not your bug.

Inside the process (glibc):

#include <malloc.h>
malloc_stats();                 /* to stderr: "system bytes" (from OS) vs "in use bytes" (live) per arena */
struct mallinfo2 mi = mallinfo2();  /* mi.uordblks = in use, mi.fordblks = free in bins, mi.hblkhd = mmapped, mi.arena = brk size */
malloc_info(0, stdout);         /* XML with per-arena, per-bin detail */

Expose these on an admin endpoint or log them hourly. "In use" climbing = leak/growth; "system" climbing while "in use" is flat = fragmentation/retention. That one comparison decides which half of this module you are in. code/m09_growth_not_leak.cpp prints exactly this.

Windows equivalents: Performance Monitor counters Process\Private Bytes (committed private memory, closest to "heap grew"), Process\Working Set (RSS), Process\Handle Count, Process\Thread Count; !heap -s in a dump for committed vs busy per heap; VMMap for the categorisation.

docs.title: 2.3 Allocator retention and fragmentation (glibc)
docs.text:
Reasons freed memory does not come back:

  • Small chunks go to bins, not to the OS (module 03). Only the top of an arena is trimmed, and only when the free top exceeds M_TRIM_THRESHOLD (128 KiB). One live 64-byte block near the top pins everything below it.
  • Each thread arena retains its own free lists. 100 worker threads, each with a 20 MB working set at some point, keep 2 GB even when idle.
  • std::vector, std::string, std::unordered_map keep capacity after clear().
  • realloc growth patterns leave holes.

Remedies, in order of how often they are the right answer:

  1. Fix unbounded containers first (2.6); fragmentation is often a symptom of churn in huge containers.
  2. MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 (or mallopt(M_ARENA_MAX, 2)) for servers with many threads and modest allocation rate. Measure contention before and after.
  3. Call malloc_trim(0) on an idle tick (every few minutes). Cheap; returns whole free pages with MADV_DONTNEED. m09_growth_not_leak.cpp shows the effect.
  4. Pool or arena-allocate the hot, same-size, same-lifetime objects (requests, records).
  5. Switch allocator (LD_PRELOAD=libjemalloc.so.2); jemalloc's size classes and background purging reduce retention and give malloc_stats_print() with much better diagnostics.

docs.title: 2.4 Leak hunting tools
docs.text:
LeakSanitizer (build with ASan or -fsanitize=leak): at exit, every unreachable block with its allocation stack (module 08). For a server that never exits cleanly, add an admin command that calls __lsan_do_recoverable_leak_check(); or make shutdown clean (SIGTERM handler that frees and exits) so the exit report is meaningful. Noise: still reachable globals are not reported; singletons are fine.

heaptrack (the best Linux heap profiler for this job):

sudo apt install heaptrack heaptrack-gui
heaptrack ./server args                 # or: heaptrack -p PID  (attach to a running process, via LD_PRELOAD injection - needs ptrace)
# ... run the workload, stop the server or ^C heaptrack ...
heaptrack_print heaptrack.server.4242.zst | less
heaptrack --analyze heaptrack.server.4242.zst      # GUI: flame graph, "Allocations", "Temporary", "Leaked", "Peak" tabs, consumption over time

It records every malloc/free/new/delete with a stack trace (via libunwind, cheap) and compresses the stream. The report sections: peak heap memory consumption with the stacks that held it, leaked (never freed by the end of the trace - includes still-reachable growth, which is what you want for a server), most calls to allocation functions, most temporary allocations (malloc immediately followed by free - a performance smell). The GUI's "Consumed" graph over time lets you see which stacks are responsible for the slope. Overhead is modest (roughly 1.5-3x on allocation-heavy code; it depends on stack depth) - it has been run in staging for hours.

Valgrind massif:

valgrind --tool=massif --time-unit=B --detailed-freq=1 --max-snapshots=200 ./prog
ms_print massif.out.<pid> | less           # ASCII graph of heap size over time + per-snapshot allocation trees
valgrind --tool=massif --pages-as-heap=yes ./prog   # count mmap too (arenas, big blocks)

Massif gives heap snapshots over time with the allocation tree at each peak. Slower than heaptrack (Valgrind overhead) and cannot attach to a running process, but needs no install beyond valgrind and is precise about --pages-as-heap (total mapped memory, not just malloc).

Valgrind memcheck --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all at exit: definitely/indirectly lost for leaks; still reachable with big counts and the stack points at growth.

gdb on a core: when you only have a dump of the bloated process and no profiler was running, you can still find the growth: info proc mappings to see which region is big; if [heap], walk it by hand (x/4xg on chunk headers, or a Python script that walks from the arena start, reading size fields) and histogram the sizes; a dominant size class points at one struct type. Then x/16xg a few blocks of that size to recognise the type (vtable pointer, string lengths). This is slow and manual; the Windows side has it built in (!heap -stat).

docs.title: 2.5 Windows: UMDH and !heap
docs.text:
UMDH (User-Mode Dump Heap, Debugging Tools for Windows) is heaptrack by snapshots:

gflags /i YourServer.exe +ust                  # enable stack-trace DB for the process (next start)
set _NT_SYMBOL_PATH=srv*C:\Symbols*https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols;D:\pdb
umdh -p:<pid> -f:snap1.txt                     # snapshot 1: every allocation stack with counts and bytes
... let it run / drive load ...
umdh -p:<pid> -f:snap2.txt
umdh snap1.txt snap2.txt -f:diff.txt           # the DIFF: stacks whose byte count increased, sorted

diff.txt lines like + 4194304 ( 4259840 - 65536) 65536 allocs BackTrace7A3B followed by the stack: 64 K more allocations of 64 bytes from this stack between snapshots. That is your growth site, whether leak or unbounded container. Requires +ust (allocation stacks captured), symbols, and the process to be alive. Overhead of +ust is acceptable in many production servers.

In a full dump (!heap):

!heap -s                                 # per heap: Committed vs Virt vs Free; the heap whose committed bytes are huge
!heap -stat -h <heap>                    # size histogram: "size 0x40: 1,200,000 blocks = 76 MB"  <- the dominant size class
!heap -flt s 0x40                        # list blocks of that size (take a few addresses)
dt YourServer!Session <UserPtr>          # does it look like a Session? vtable? strings?
!heap -p -a <UserPtr>                    # with +ust: the allocation stack  <- the site
!heap -l                                 # heuristic leak detection: busy blocks with no pointer to them (slow)

The -stat -> -flt -> recognise -> -p -a chain is the Windows "walk the heap by hand" and it is faster than the Linux manual version. Do it on two dumps taken an hour apart and compare the histograms: the class that grew is the culprit.

Also: !address -summary (is it even heap? or VirtualAlloc'd private data, or mapped files?), !handle 0 0 counts (handle leak), ~ thread count.

docs.title: 2.6 C++-specific causes
docs.text:
• Containers that only grow: std::map<SessionId, Session> where erase happens on a path that is skipped on error; std::unordered_map keyed by request id "for correlation"; a std::vector<LogEntry> ring that was never made a ring; a std::deque queue with a consumer that fell behind. The fix is a policy: max size, TTL, LRU eviction; and a metric for the size.
  • clear() keeps capacity: vector::clear() leaves capacity() unchanged; shrink_to_fit() or swap with an empty vector releases it. A per-request std::vector member that once held 10 MB holds 10 MB forever. Same for std::string. unordered_map keeps its bucket array.
  • shared_ptr cycles: A holds shared_ptr<B>, B holds shared_ptr<A>; use counts never reach zero. Parent/child, observer/subject, node/graph structures. LSan reports these as leaks (unreachable from roots). Fix: one direction becomes weak_ptr (child -> parent, observer -> subject). p sp in gdb shows use count; a use count that never drops below 1 after the owner released is the sign.
  • Lambdas capturing shared_ptr by value stored in callbacks/timers/std::function members of the same object: a cycle through the closure. Capture weak_ptr and lock inside.
  • std::thread detached with captured state, or threads never joined: each keeps its stack and arena.
  • Exceptions between new and delete: not a leak if you use unique_ptr; a leak with raw new. Also new[] / delete mismatch (ASan alloc-dealloc-mismatch).
  • Static/global caches ("still reachable"): intentional, but they need bounds.
  • C-style ownership in the migration engine: a record struct with char *name freed on the success path but not on continue in the loop - the m09_leak.cpp shape. In C the cure is goto cleanup discipline or arenas (module 03); in C++ it is RAII.

docs.title: 2.7 Hunting a leak in a long-running server: the procedure
docs.text:
1. Confirm it is heap. smaps_rollup / pmap / !address -summary: anonymous heap growing, not threads, fds, mapped files.
  2. Confirm live bytes grow. malloc_stats in-use (or !heap -s busy) climbing. If only system/committed climbs, it is retention: go to 2.3.
  3. Correlate with traffic. Does it grow per request, per session, per minute, per batch? Which request type? Logs with request ids (module 11) answer this; it halves the suspects.
  4. Profile in staging with the same traffic: heaptrack (Linux) or UMDH diff (Windows). Look at the top growing stacks. Nine times out of ten you now have the line.
  5. If only production shows it: +ust + UMDH on the production box in a maintenance window; or heaptrack -p attach for 10 minutes; or two full dumps an hour apart and the !heap -stat / heap-walk comparison; or gcore twice and compare with a Python heap walker.
  6. Classify: leak (fix the free / RAII), growth (add a bound/eviction), retention (trim / arena cap / allocator).
  7. Verify: same workload, RSS flat after warm-up, in use flat, heaptrack "leaked" near zero. Put the metric on a dashboard so recurrence is visible (module 12's verification section).

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m09_leak.cpp: a request loop that leaks on the error path (every 4th request). Build and run three ways:

./build_debug.sh debug asan
./build/m09_leak_asan 1000
# ==ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks
# Direct leak of 32000 byte(s) in 250 object(s) allocated from: #1 handle_request m09_leak.cpp:33
# Indirect leak of 16250 byte(s) in 250 object(s) ...                    <- the std::string buffers
valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all ./build/m09_leak_debug 1000
#    definitely lost: 32,000 bytes in 250 blocks / indirectly lost: 16,250 bytes in 250 blocks
heaptrack ./build/m09_leak_debug 100000 && heaptrack_print heaptrack.m09_leak_debug.*.zst | sed -n '/MEMORY LEAKED/,/^$/p'

Note that LSan's direct+indirect equals Valgrind's definitely+indirectly: a Request (direct) owning a std::string buffer (indirect). Fixing the one missing delete (or using unique_ptr, as m13_raii_fix.cpp does) removes both.

code/m09_growth_not_leak.cpp: 3 million 64-byte blocks, then free 99.9% of them, then malloc_trim(0). Typical output shape (your numbers will differ):

start                        VmRSS =      3 MiB
after 3M x 64B malloc        VmRSS =    230 MiB
after freeing 99.9%          VmRSS =    230 MiB      <- free() returned nothing to the OS
after malloc_trim(0)         VmRSS =     20 MiB      <- most pages given back; 3000 live blocks pin ~3000 pages
malloc_stats(): system bytes = ..., in use bytes = ~200 KB

Run it under Valgrind or LSan: zero leaks. That is the whole lesson in one screen: RSS high, in-use tiny, no leak. Then try MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_=0 ./build/m09_growth_debug and see how the "after freeing" line changes.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why RSS does not fall on free. free puts the chunk in a bin; the page it lives on stays resident because other chunks on the same page may be live and because munmap/madvise per small free would be far slower than the free itself. glibc trims only the top (sbrk negative or munmap of a secondary heap's tail) when it exceeds the trim threshold, and malloc_trim additionally scans for whole free pages and madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)s them. MADV_DONTNEED drops the physical pages; the virtual range stays mapped; a later touch faults in a zero page. That is why RSS falls but VSZ does not.

How LSan decides "unreachable". At the check, it stops all threads, takes the root set (globals in writable sections of all modules, every thread's stack and registers, TLS), and does a conservative mark from them: any aligned word that looks like a pointer into a live allocation marks that allocation, recursively. Anything unmarked is a leak; a leak pointed to only by other leaks is "indirect". Conservative scanning means an integer that happens to equal a block's address hides a leak (rare), and pointers stored XORed or in unusual places cause false positives.

heaptrack's trick. It LD_PRELOADs a library that interposes malloc/free/etc., records each with a stack trace captured by libunwind, deduplicates traces into ids, and streams (trace_id, size, ptr) events to a compressor. Replaying the stream tells you at any instant which trace ids own which bytes. "Leaked" is simply "allocated, not freed by end of trace", so it includes still-reachable growth - exactly what you want for a server.

Why UMDH needs +ust. The NT heap by default stores no allocation stacks. +ust makes RtlAllocateHeap capture a stack (via RtlCaptureStackBackTrace) into a per-process stack trace database and store its index in the block header. UMDH reads that database; so does !heap -p -a. Without +ust you can histogram sizes but cannot see who allocated.

shared_ptr cycles and the mark-sweep contrast. Reference counting cannot collect cycles; garbage-collected runtimes can. LSan's mark from roots is a tracing collector's reachability analysis, which is why it sees the cycle as a leak. weak_ptr breaks the cycle by making one edge non-owning: the control block keeps a weak count so lock() can fail safely after the object is gone.

Heap walking in a core. glibc's main_arena (in libc's .data; needs libc symbols) has top and the bins; the main heap starts at the [heap] mapping start; chunks are contiguous: next = chunk + (size & ~7). A 60-line Python gdb script can walk it, bucket sizes and print the first 32 bytes of samples from the dominant bucket. Windows' !heap -stat is this script, shipped.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Instrument before you need it. Log mallinfo2().uordblks, RSS, thread count and fd count every few minutes, and the sizes of your big containers (sessions, caches, queues). Most leak investigations become "look at the graph" when these exist, and the RCA's verification section becomes a screenshot.
  • Set the alarm on slope, not level. RSS 6 GB is fine if it has been 6 GB for a month. +50 MB per hour for six hours is not, even at 2 GB.
  • Distinguish before you fix. Adding malloc_trim to a server with a real leak hides the symptom for a while and costs CPU; adding a cache bound to a server with fragmentation does nothing. The in use vs system comparison is five minutes and settles it.
  • Restarts are a mitigation, not a fix. Banks run month-long processes; a nightly restart "to clear memory" is sometimes accepted operationally but must be documented as a known issue with a tracked fix, never as the resolution in an RCA (module 12).
  • Session tables in RPC servers. A client that disconnects uncleanly (TCP RST, crash) leaves a session entry if cleanup only runs on a graceful close. Timeouts and periodic sweeps are not optional. Shakir's multithreaded RPC-over-TCP server is the textbook case: count sessions, compare to connections, alarm on divergence.
  • Windows specifics. Private Bytes is the counter to trend. UMDH diffs with +ust are routine in a maintenance window. Beware the CRT debug heap in debug builds (_CrtDumpMemoryLeaks reports leaks at exit for the debug CRT, useful in tests) - not available in release.
  • Third-party and driver leaks. Database client libraries (connection handles, prepared statements not finalised), TLS contexts, compression streams. The profiler stack will end in the library's allocation with your call above it - the fix is usually a missing *_free call on an error path in your code.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - three tools, one leak. Run m09_leak under LSan, Valgrind and heaptrack. Done when you can show that all three attribute the same bytes to handle_request and explain direct/indirect vs definitely/indirectly.
  2. Easy - growth vs leak. Run m09_growth_not_leak, then run it under LSan. Done when you can write the three RSS numbers and the in use bytes number on one line and name the kind of growth.
  3. Medium - RSS trend script. Write a shell script that samples RSS, VmHWM, thread count and fd count of a PID every 5 seconds to a CSV, run it against m09_leak 10000000 (slow it down with a small usleep if needed) and plot or eyeball the slope. Done when you can state bytes leaked per request from the slope alone and compare it with LSan's total.
  4. Medium - fix it two ways. Fix m09_leak with (a) a delete on the error path and (b) std::unique_ptr. Introduce a throw in validate and show that only (b) still does not leak. Done when LSan is clean for (b) with the throw and dirty for (a).
  5. Hard - shared_ptr cycle. Write a Node with std::shared_ptr<Node> next and make a two-node cycle that goes out of scope. Show the leak with LSan, inspect use count in gdb, fix with weak_ptr. Done when LSan is clean and you can explain why reference counting cannot collect cycles.
  6. Hard - heap histogram from a core. Run m09_leak 200000 under gdb, break at the end, gcore, and write a gdb Python script that walks the main heap from the [heap] start, histograms chunk sizes and prints the top 3 size classes with the first 32 bytes of a sample chunk. Done when the dominant class matches sizeof(Request) rounded to a chunk size.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: RSS grows steadily but Valgrind and LSan report no leaks. What are the possibilities? A: Unbounded but reachable growth (a container, cache or queue without a bound - "still reachable" to Valgrind), allocator retention/fragmentation (freed memory kept in bins and arenas, visible as malloc_stats system bytes far above in-use bytes), thread or handle growth, or mapped-file page cache. I distinguish them with malloc_stats/mallinfo2, smaps, thread and fd counts, and a heap profiler that shows live bytes per stack over time.

Q: How do you find the allocation site responsible for growth in a running Linux server? A: heaptrack attached to the process (or run under it in staging with the same traffic): it records a stack per allocation and reports the stacks owning the most still-live bytes and the growth over time. Alternatives: massif, LSan's recoverable leak check from an admin command, or two gcores and a heap-walking script.

Q: What is UMDH and how do you use it? A: Windows' user-mode heap snapshot tool. Enable the stack trace database for the process (gflags /i app.exe +ust), take umdh -p:PID -f:snap1.txt, let the growth happen, take a second snapshot, then umdh snap1 snap2 diffs them and lists the allocation stacks whose byte counts increased - the growth sites. Needs symbols and a live process.

Q: Why does free not return memory to the OS, and how can you make it? A: Small chunks go into the allocator's bins for reuse; the OS only gets memory back when the top of an arena exceeds the trim threshold or a large mmapped block is freed. malloc_trim(0) scans for whole free pages and madvises them away; capping arenas (MALLOC_ARENA_MAX) limits per-thread retention; pooling same-size objects or switching to jemalloc reduces fragmentation. Measure in-use vs system bytes first to confirm retention is the problem.

Q: How can std::shared_ptr leak? A: Through reference cycles: two objects owning each other via shared_ptr never reach a zero count. Also via lambdas that capture a shared_ptr to the object that stores the lambda. The fix is to make the back edge a weak_ptr and lock() it when needed. LSan detects the cycle as unreachable; p sp in gdb shows a use count that never drops.

Q: A std::vector member of a long-lived object once held 100 MB and now holds 10 elements. How much memory does it use? A: Still about 100 MB: clear() and erase do not reduce capacity. Call shrink_to_fit() or swap with an empty vector to release it. The same applies to std::string and to the bucket arrays of unordered containers.

Q: What do you log in a server so leak investigations are short? A: Periodic RSS, mallinfo2 in-use and system bytes, thread count, fd/handle count, and the sizes of every major container (sessions, caches, queues), plus request counts by type with request ids so growth can be correlated to traffic. With those, most investigations start from a graph that already names the suspect.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Three kinds of growth: leak (unreachable), growth (reachable, unbounded), retention/ fragmentation (free but held). Leak tools see only the first.
  • First measure: RSS trend; then malloc_stats/mallinfo2 in-use vs system (Windows: !heap -s, Private Bytes). In-use flat + system rising = retention; both rising = leak/growth.
  • Check threads, fds/handles and mapped files before blaming the heap.
  • Linux tools: LSan (exit or __lsan_do_recoverable_leak_check), heaptrack (attach or run; live bytes per stack over time), massif, Valgrind leak kinds, manual heap walk in gdb.
  • Windows tools: UMDH snapshots + diff with +ust; !heap -s / -stat / -flt / -p -a; !address -summary; VMMap; Private Bytes counter.
  • Retention remedies: malloc_trim(0) on idle, MALLOC_ARENA_MAX, pooling/arenas, jemalloc.
  • C++ traps: containers without bounds, clear() keeps capacity, shared_ptr cycles (use weak_ptr), capturing lambdas, unjoined threads, raw new on exception paths.
  • Instrument by design: log memory stats and container sizes; alarm on slope; verify the fix with the same graph.

docs.title: 10. Concurrency crashes and Heisenbugs
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 04, 06, 08; 04_Concurrency modules on mutexes, condition variables and module 12 of that course (debugging concurrent code)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A Heisenbug is a bug that changes or disappears when you look at it. Almost all of them are concurrency bugs: two threads touch the same data without agreeing on an order, and whether the program breaks depends on which thread got there first by a few nanoseconds. Attach a debugger, add a printf, run on a different machine, and the timing changes and the bug hides.

Concurrency bugs do not have their own crash signature. They cause the ordinary memory bugs of module 04 - a use-after-free because thread B deleted what thread A was reading, a corrupted container because two threads inserted at once, a lost update because both read-modify-wrote - or they cause a hang when threads wait for each other forever. So the debugging skill is: look at an ordinary-looking crash or hang, recognise the fingerprints that say "another thread did this", and then switch tools from "find the bad line" to "find the missing ordering". This module is the fingerprints, the dump-reading procedure for deadlocks, and how to make the bug reproduce on purpose.

docs.title: 2.1 Crash signatures of data races
docs.text:
A race rarely crashes at the racing instruction. It corrupts something, and the crash comes later, in the thread that trusted the corrupted thing. The fingerprints:

What the dump shows What probably happened Crash inside a container's internals (std::_Rb_tree_insert_and_rebalance, _Hashtable::_M_insert, std::vector::_M_realloc_insert, std::deque iterator math) with a garbage pointer two threads mutated the container without a lock (or one read while another mutated: find racing insert is enough for unordered_map rehash) UAF-shaped crash (tcache pointer / 0xDDDDDDDD / 0xFEEEFEEE in the object) in a thread that did not free anything another thread freed the object: lifetime race; shared object with unclear ownership, or a callback after shutdown Crash in a virtual call with a bad vtable pointer (call [rax+8] with garbage rax) object destroyed by another thread while this one was about to call a method on it Counter/total wrong but no crash; checksum mismatch; "impossible" state assertion lost update: unsynchronised read-modify-write (++, +=, if (!x) x = ...) Crash only under load / only with N cores / only on the client's 32-core box / never under gdb or Valgrind timing-dependent -> race; Valgrind serialises threads so races vanish under it Same corruption, different crash site every time a race that corrupts a shared structure; which thread trips over it varies Crash in a thread's stack frame whose locals look "half-updated" (one field new, one old) torn read/write of a multi-word value (a 16-byte struct, a std::string, a double on 32-bit) thread apply all bt shows two threads inside the same non-reentrant method of the same object that is the race, caught in the act; compare the this pointers Crash in a signal handler, or malloc deadlock with one thread in the handler async-signal-unsafe call in a handler (module 11); technically a race between the handler and the interrupted code

The decisive move in a core: thread apply all bt and look at every thread, not just the one that crashed. Then for the crashing object, ask "who else could have a pointer to this?" and look for that thread. In a race, the other thread is often in the same function or in a destructor / erase / close for the same object at the moment of the dump. p $_siginfo and the registers tell you what broke; the other threads tell you who.

docs.title: 2.2 Deadlock dumps
docs.text:
A deadlock is two or more threads each waiting for a lock the other holds. The dump is static - nothing is moving - which makes it the one concurrency bug that a core proves outright.

Linux procedure (gdb on a gcore of the hung process):

(gdb) thread apply all bt 12

Every blocked thread shows __futex_abstimed_wait_common / ___pthread_mutex_lock / __lll_lock_wait (mutex), or pthread_cond_wait (condition variable), or __GI___poll / read (I/O), or pthread_rwlock_rdlock/wrlock. Collect the ones waiting on mutexes.

For each, go to the frame that owns the std::lock_guard / calls lock() and print the mutex:

(gdb) thread 3
(gdb) frame 4                        # the frame in transfer_a_to_b
(gdb) p g_connections_mtx
$1 = {<std::__mutex_base> = {_M_mutex = {__data = {__lock = 2, __count = 0, __owner = 4243,
      __nusers = 1, __kind = 0, __spins = 0, __elision = 0, __list = {__prev = 0x0, __next = 0x0}}, ...

__lock = 2 means locked with waiters, __owner = 4243 is the kernel thread id (LWP) of the holder. (__lock = 1 = locked, no waiters; __lock = 0 = free.) Now:

(gdb) info threads
  Id   Target Id                                     Frame
  1    Thread 0x7f... (LWP 4241) "m10_deadlock"      ... pthread_join
  2    Thread 0x7f... (LWP 4242) "m10_deadlock"      __futex_abstimed_wait_common ...   <- waits for connections_mtx

* 3    Thread 0x7f... (LWP 4243) "m10_deadlock"      __futex_abstimed_wait_common ...   <- waits for sessions_mtx
(gdb) thread 2 ; frame 4 ; p g_sessions_mtx.__data.__owner      ->  4242? no: 4243...

Build the table:

Thread (LWP) Holds Waits for Held by 4242 g_sessions_mtx g_connections_mtx 4243 4243 g_connections_mtx g_sessions_mtx 4242

A cycle. That is the deadlock, proven. The fix is a lock order (always sessions before connections) or std::scoped_lock(m1, m2); the RCA says which code path acquired in the wrong order and since which change.

Variations:

  • Self-deadlock: __owner equals the waiting thread's own LWP. A non-recursive mutex locked twice on one thread (a callback re-entering, or a method calling another method of the same object that also locks). One-thread cycle.
  • Lock held by a dead thread: __owner is an LWP not in info threads. A thread exited (or was cancelled) while holding the mutex; or the lock is in shared memory and another process holds it. PTHREAD_MUTEX_ROBUST exists for the cross-process case.
  • Condition variable "deadlock": everyone in pthread_cond_wait, nobody holds the mutex. Not a lock cycle: a lost wakeup (signal before wait with no predicate re-check) or a predicate that can never become true. Check the predicate variables in the frame.
  • Starvation / livelock: threads not blocked but never progressing (spinning on a CAS, retrying). top -H shows CPU; gcore twice a minute apart and compare the frames.
  • Blocked on I/O that will never complete: read on a socket whose peer is gone with no timeout; connect to a dead DB. Looks like a hang; not a lock bug; fix with timeouts.

Windows procedure: ~*k (or !uniqstack to collapse identical waiters), waiters sit in ntdll!NtWaitForAlertByThreadId (SRW locks / std::mutex), RtlpWaitOnCriticalSection (critical sections), NtWaitForSingleObject (events, mutex objects). For critical sections, !locks lists OwningThread per held section; ~~[tid]s jumps to it; k shows what it is waiting on; follow the cycle. For SRW locks no owner is stored: the holder is the thread that is inside the protected code, not inside a wait; the frame with the lock_guard tells you which lock. !runaway to spot a spinner.

docs.title: 2.3 Stack traces that lie
docs.text:
Concurrency dumps punish literal reading:

  • The crashing thread is the victim. It dereferenced what another thread freed. Its stack is correct and innocent. The culprit's stack is in another thread, and only if that thread is still near the scene; often it has moved on and its stack shows the next request. Then you need the object's history (ASan's free stack, or your own trace buffer), not the dump.
  • Inlined and optimised frames (module 02) make "two threads in the same function" look like "two threads in the caller". info frame and disassemble to confirm what was executing.
  • <signal handler called> frames: the code below the marker was interrupted asynchronously; its locals may be mid-update.
  • Stale frames after a corrupted stack (??, "following frames may be wrong"): if the race overflowed a stack buffer, the trace past that frame is fiction.
  • Thread names and ids: info threads ids are gdb's numbering (1..N by discovery), not the LWP; logs and __owner use the LWP. Mixing them up is a classic wrong-thread conclusion.
  • Under TSan/ASan the stack is right but the timing is different: the race TSan reports may not be the one that crashed in production; it is still a real race. Fix all of them.
  • The thread that "holds" a lock per __owner may have been pre-empted inside a 3-instruction critical section: holding a lock in a dump is not evidence of a long hold, just a snapshot. Two gcores show whether anything moved.

docs.title: 2.4 Reproducing on purpose
docs.text:
A race needs a specific interleaving. Make interleavings more likely and more varied:

Technique How Effect More cores than threads run on a big box; taskset -c 0-15 true parallelism of the racing threads Fewer cores than threads taskset -c 0 ./prog forces pre-emption at arbitrary points; exposes lost-wakeup and ordering assumptions Background load stress-ng --cpu 8 --io 2 --vm 2 --timeout 10m alongside random pre-emption and cache pressure Loop the test for i in $(seq 1000); do ./test || break; done rare interleavings eventually occur Sleep/yield injection std::this_thread::yield() or usleep(rand()%100) at suspected points (behind a #ifdef RACE_TEST) widens the window of the suspected race Randomised scheduling rr record --chaos (native Linux), or setarch -R + taskset combos explores schedules deliberately TSan -fsanitize=thread on the test suite finds the race from any run that executes both accesses; no manifestation needed Barrier-start start all workers on a std::latch/barrier so they race from the first instruction removes thread start-up skew that hides races Hostile allocator MALLOC_PERTURB_=165, ASan quarantine turns UAF-by-race into a loud failure

Order of attempts in practice: TSan first (cheapest, most reliable), then stress + loop with the test that resembles the production traffic, then sleep injection at the suspected window to confirm the mechanism, then the fix verified by the same TSan run and stress loop.

docs.title: 2.5 Diagnostics that do not change the timing too much
docs.text:
Adding printf to a race often cures it: printf takes the stdio lock, does a syscall, and serialises the threads. The rules for observing without disturbing:

  • Per-thread in-memory ring buffers (a "flight recorder"): each thread appends fixed-size records (timestamp, event id, two integers) to its own array with a relaxed atomic index. No locks, no syscalls, ~20 ns per event. On crash, the buffers are in the core dump, and you read them with p trace_buf[thread] or a Python script. This is how production databases and trading systems debug races.
  • Timestamps: rdtsc (__rdtsc()), or std::chrono::steady_clock (vDSO, no syscall). Never gettimeofday through a lock or time() with formatting in the hot path.
  • Atomic counters (std::atomic<uint64_t> with fetch_add(1, memory_order_relaxed)) for "how many times did we enter path X" - cheap, no ordering, no timing impact worth mentioning.
  • Log after the fact: record in the ring, dump the ring from the crash handler (module 11) using write(2) only.
  • Kernel tracing: perf trace, strace -f -tt (slows a lot), ltrace, bpftrace uprobes on your functions (bpftrace -e 'uprobe:/path/server:close_session { printf("%d %s\n", tid, ustack) }')
    • observes without recompiling, overhead per probe in the microsecond range.
  • Windows: ETW (TraceLoggingWrite, xperf/WPA) is the ring-buffer approach built into the OS; OutputDebugString is a lock+syscall and perturbs like printf.
  • Assertions on invariants (assert(owner_tid == gettid()) inside a critical section; assert(refcount > 0) before use) crash at the race instead of later; cheap enough to leave in release builds as ALWAYS_ASSERT for the critical ones (module 13).

What does change timing and should be avoided while hunting: printf/std::cout, mutex- protected log calls in the hot path, strace, running under Valgrind (serialises threads), and breakpoints.

docs.title: 2.6 Fixing versus papering over
docs.text: A race fix is one of: add the missing synchronisation (mutex, atomic with the right ordering), remove the sharing (per-thread data, message passing, immutable snapshots), or fix the lifetime (owner-controlled destruction, shared_ptr/weak_ptr, "stop then join then destroy"). A deadlock fix is one of: a global lock order (documented and asserted), std::scoped_lock for multi-lock acquisition, try_lock with back-off, or lock splitting/removal. "Added a sleep", "retry on failure", "made the mutex recursive" are not fixes; they change the odds. An RCA must say which of the real categories the fix is (module 12). The design side is in 04_Concurrency.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m10_data_race.cpp: two threads increment a global and mutate a std::map without a lock.

./build_debug.sh debug tsan
./build/m10_data_race_debug          # "expected 2000000 got 1737422 (map size 97)" - or a crash in _Rb_tree
./build/m10_data_race_tsan 2>&1 | head -40
# WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race ... Write of size 8 ... by thread T2 ... Previous write ... by thread T1
#   Location is global 'g_total' of size 8
