# then a second report for the map node pointers

Watch the plain binary crash occasionally in the red-black tree code: that is signature #1 of 2.1. Run taskset -c 0 ./build/m10_data_race_debug and note how the lost-update count changes (fewer cores -> different interleavings).

code/m10_deadlock.cpp: lock-order inversion.

./build/m10_deadlock_debug &  PID=$!
sleep 2; gcore -o /tmp/hang $PID; kill $PID
gdb -q ./build/m10_deadlock_debug /tmp/hang.$PID
(gdb) thread apply all bt 8
(gdb) thread 2 ; frame 5 ; p g_connections_mtx.__data.__owner ; p g_sessions_mtx.__data.__owner
(gdb) info threads

Fill in the Holds / Waits-for / Held-by table from section 2.2 with your real LWPs. Then:

TSAN_OPTIONS=detect_deadlocks=1:second_deadlock_stack=1 timeout 10 ./build/m10_deadlock_tsan 2>&1 | head -50
# WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: lock-order-inversion (potential deadlock)
#   Cycle in lock order graph: M1 (0x...) => M2 (0x...) => M1
#   Mutex M2 acquired here while holding mutex M1 in thread T1: ... transfer_a_to_b
#   Mutex M1 acquired here while holding mutex M2 in thread T2: ... transfer_b_to_a

TSan finds the inversion even on a run where the deadlock did not happen. That is why it belongs in CI.

Diagnostic ring buffer sketch (to put in your own server; not a separate file):

struct TraceRec { uint64_t tsc; uint32_t ev; uint32_t a; uint64_t b; };
struct ThreadTrace { TraceRec rec[4096]; std::atomic<uint32_t> idx{0}; };
inline thread_local ThreadTrace *t_trace = nullptr;          // assigned from a global table at thread start
inline void trace(uint32_t ev, uint32_t a, uint64_t b) {
    if (!t_trace) return;
    uint32_t i = t_trace->idx.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed) & 4095;
    t_trace->rec[i] = { __rdtsc(), ev, a, b };                // ~20 ns, no lock, no syscall
}
// in gdb on the core:  p g_traces[3].rec[(g_traces[3].idx-1)&4095]   or a 20-line Python dump sorted by tsc

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why races corrupt containers. std::map::insert rebalances a red-black tree through several pointer writes; unordered_map::insert may rehash, allocating a new bucket array and relinking every node; vector::push_back may reallocate and move. A second thread reading or writing midway sees a tree with a node linked from two parents, a bucket array half-populated, or a dangling pointer into the old vector buffer. The standard's guarantee is: concurrent const operations on the same container are fine; any non-const operation requires exclusive access. find concurrent with insert is a data race and UB, not "mostly safe".

Why a lost update happens even on x86. g_total += 1 compiles to mov rax,[g]; add rax,1; mov [g],rax (or add [g],1, which is still not atomic across cores without lock). Two cores can both load 5, both store 6. The cache coherence protocol keeps each store coherent; it does not make the read-modify-write sequence atomic. lock add / std::atomic::fetch_add does. The C++ memory model says the plain version is UB, so the compiler may also keep g_total in a register for the whole loop (it does at -O2: look at the asm), making the lost-update count enormous.

futex and __owner. glibc mutexes are a 32-bit word in user space: uncontended lock is a single cmpxchg (0 -> 1); on contention the word becomes 2 and the thread sleeps in the kernel with futex(FUTEX_WAIT); unlock stores 0 and, if the word was 2, calls futex(FUTEX_WAKE). __owner is written after acquiring, for debugging and for error-checking/recursive mutex types. That is why a core shows __lock = 2, __owner = <tid>, and why a mutex "held by a dead thread" stays locked forever: nothing in the kernel knows about user-space mutex ownership (unlike Windows mutex objects, which are abandoned on thread exit and report WAIT_ABANDONED).

Why TSan does not need the race to manifest. It computes happens-before from the synchronisation it observes; two unordered accesses are reported regardless of whether, in that run, they actually overlapped in time. This is strictly more powerful than stress testing for the paths the test executes. Its blind spot is paths not executed and synchronisation it cannot see (custom spinlocks without atomics - which are also UB).

Signal handlers as a concurrency problem. A handler runs on the interrupted thread between any two instructions. Calling malloc, printf, or taking a mutex inside it can deadlock (the interrupted code may hold that same lock) or corrupt (the allocator was mid-operation). Only async-signal-safe functions (write, _exit, sigaction, ...) are allowed; code/m11_crash_handler.cpp follows those rules and module 11 explains them.

Memory ordering and "it works on x86". x86 is strongly ordered (stores are not reordered with other stores, loads not with loads), so many ordering bugs are invisible on x86 and appear on ARM (phones, Graviton, Apple silicon). A bank migrating to ARM servers can surface years-old races. The C++ model (memory_order_*) is the only portable contract - 04_Concurrency.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Dumps for hangs are routine, not exceptional. A gcore/ProcDump of a hung server before restarting it is non-negotiable (module 11); a deadlock is proven by a dump and guessed without one. Train the operations team to take it.
  • Two dumps a minute apart distinguish deadlock (nothing moved), livelock/starvation (same threads, different frames), and slow progress (everything moved).
  • Lock order as documentation and as a check. Write the global lock order down (module 13's review checklist). In debug builds, assert it: a thread-local stack of held lock ranks and an assert that a new lock's rank is higher. Cheap, finds inversions before TSan does.
  • Lifetime races in RPC servers: a connection is closed by the reader thread (peer went away) while a worker is still writing a response to it; a session is expired by the sweeper thread while a request on it is mid-flight. The dump: worker crashed in send/write on a freed connection object, and the sweeper/reader thread's stack shows close/erase for that id a moment ago. The fix is ownership: refcount the connection (shared_ptr), or "mark closed, let the last user destroy".
  • Thread pools and callbacks after shutdown: a timer fires into an object already destroyed during shutdown. Dump: crash during exit, with __run_exit_handlers on one thread and a worker in a callback on another. Fix: stop timers and join workers before destroying what they use.
  • Windows specifics: std::mutex on MSVC is an SRW lock - no owner in the dump, infer from stacks; CRITICAL_SECTION has !locks; the Windows kernel mutex object reports WAIT_ABANDONED if the owner dies, pthreads do not. Also WaitForMultipleObjects deadlocks through the loader lock (DllMain) are a Windows-only classic: a thread inside DllMain waiting for a thread that needs the loader lock. !locks shows ntdll!LdrpLoaderLock.
  • Never close a concurrency RCA with "could not reproduce, added a retry". Either TSan/stress reproduces it and the fix is one of the real categories, or the RCA states the evidence, the most likely mechanism, the mitigation and the detection added to catch the next occurrence with more data (ring buffer, asserts) - and stays open.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - see the race. Run m10_data_race_debug ten times and record the totals; then under taskset -c 0; then under TSan. Done when you can explain the three sets of results.
  2. Easy - the deadlock table. Do the gcore walkthrough in section 3 and produce the Holds / Waits-for / Held-by table with real LWPs. Done when __owner values match info threads.
  3. Medium - victim and culprit. Write a program where thread A deletes a shared object after 1 ms and thread B calls a virtual method on it in a loop. Crash it, take the core, and from thread apply all bt identify both threads and the evidence that A freed it (A's frame, the tcache pointer where the vtable was). Done when the evidence is listed without using ASan; then confirm with ASan.
  4. Medium - sleep injection. Make m10_data_race race only rarely (e.g. increment every 1000th iteration), confirm it is hard to see, then inject std::this_thread::yield() between the load and the store (split g_total += 1 into two statements with a yield) and show it fails every run. Done when you can state why the yield widens the window.
  5. Hard - ring buffer in the core. Add the trace ring from section 3 to m10_data_race, record (ev=1, a=tid, b=i) around the map insert, crash it (or abort() on a wrong total), and in gdb print the last 10 records of each thread sorted by tsc. Done when the interleaving around the failure is visible from the core.
  6. Hard - lock-rank assertion. Implement a debug-only lock rank checker (thread-local vector of ranks, assert on acquisition out of order) and wrap the two mutexes of m10_deadlock. Done when the program aborts with a clear message at the first inverted acquisition, before it has a chance to deadlock.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do you recognise that a crash was caused by a data race rather than a plain memory bug? A: The crash is in a shared structure (container internals, a shared object with a garbage vtable or a freed-pattern), it depends on load or core count, vanishes under Valgrind or a debugger, and thread apply all bt shows another thread in a mutating operation on the same object (erase, close, destructor) at the time of the dump. The crashing thread is the victim; the other thread is the suspect; TSan on the same test confirms.

Q: Walk me through diagnosing a deadlock from a core dump. A: thread apply all bt (or ~*k) to find threads blocked in mutex waits; for each, select the frame holding the lock guard and print the mutex: __owner is the LWP of the holder and __lock = 2 means contended; map LWPs with info threads; build a holds/waits-for table and find the cycle. On Windows, !locks gives critical section owners; for SRW locks infer the holder from the thread executing inside the protected region.

Q: Why does adding a printf make a race disappear, and what do you do instead? A: printf takes the stdio lock and performs a syscall, serialising the threads and widening or closing the race window. Use per-thread lock-free ring buffers with rdtsc timestamps and relaxed atomic indices, read them from the core after the crash, or use kernel tracing (bpftrace, ETW) which observes without recompiling and with microsecond overhead.

Q: What does ThreadSanitizer report that stress testing cannot? A: TSan reports any pair of unordered conflicting accesses that executed, whether or not they overlapped in time in that run - it derives ordering from the synchronisation it observes (happens-before via vector clocks). Stress testing needs the bad interleaving to actually occur and to produce a visible failure. TSan also reports lock-order inversions as potential deadlocks from a run that never hung.

Q: How do you reproduce a race that only happens at the client? A: Run the TSan build of the test closest to the client's traffic; run the plain build in a loop under stress-ng with more and with fewer cores than threads (taskset); inject yields at the suspected window to confirm the mechanism; use a hostile allocator (MALLOC_PERTURB_, ASan) so a lifetime race fails loudly. If none reproduces, add a ring buffer and invariant asserts to the production build so the next occurrence captures the interleaving.

Q: A pthread_mutex_t in a core shows __owner equal to a thread id that no longer exists. What happened? A: A thread exited (or was cancelled) while holding the mutex, so it is locked forever - pthread mutexes have no kernel-side ownership and are not released on thread death (unlike Windows mutex objects, which report WAIT_ABANDONED). Every later locker blocks. The fix is RAII locking so the unlock cannot be skipped, and not letting threads die with locks held; PTHREAD_MUTEX_ROBUST for the cross-process case.

Q: What are legitimate fixes for a race and a deadlock, and what are not? A: Race: add correct synchronisation (mutex, atomic with proper ordering), eliminate the sharing (thread-local, message passing, immutable snapshots), or fix the lifetime (owner-controlled destruction, shared_ptr/weak_ptr). Deadlock: a documented and asserted global lock order, std::scoped_lock for multiple locks, try_lock with back-off, or removing a lock. Not fixes: sleeps, retries, making the mutex recursive, or "could not reproduce".

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Races cause ordinary memory bugs (UAF, corrupted containers, lost updates); recognise them by the container-internals crash, the freed-pattern object, load dependence, and another thread mid-mutation in thread apply all bt.
  • The crashing thread is the victim; look at every thread; match this pointers.
  • Deadlock from a core: find mutex waiters, print the mutex, __owner = holder's LWP, __lock = 2 = contended, build holds/waits-for, find the cycle. Windows: !locks for critical sections, stack inference for SRW/std::mutex.
  • Variants: self-deadlock (__owner == self), dead owner, lost wakeup (all in cond_wait), livelock (take two dumps), I/O without timeout.
  • Stacks lie: inlining, signal frames, corrupted stacks, gdb ids vs LWPs, culprit moved on.
  • Reproduce: TSan first; then loop + stress-ng + taskset; yield injection to confirm; hostile allocator for lifetime races.
  • Observe without perturbing: per-thread lock-free ring buffers with rdtsc, atomic counters, bpftrace/ETW, invariant asserts; never printf in the window.
  • Real fixes: synchronisation, no sharing, or ownership; lock order, scoped_lock, try_lock. Sleeps and retries are not fixes.

docs.title: 11. Production incident triage
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 06, 07, 09, 10

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
An incident is the period between "something is wrong in production" and "it is fixed and we understand why". Triage is the first part of it: deciding how bad it is, stopping the damage, and collecting enough evidence that you can find the cause later. Debugging is what you do afterwards, calmly, with the evidence on your desk.

The analogy is an emergency room. The doctor at the door does not start surgery. They check breathing and bleeding, decide who is most urgent, stabilise the patient, and draw blood before giving drugs that would change the test results. A server is the same. The dump, the logs and the metrics are the blood sample. Restart the process first and the sample is gone; the client is back up, but you will never know why it fell over, and it will fall over again next Tuesday.

The skill this module teaches is doing the first 15 minutes in the right order, every time, at 3 AM, with a bank's operations manager on the phone. Most of it is decided before the incident: what the server logs, whether dumps are configured, whether there is a feature flag to switch the broken path off, and whether operations knows how to take a dump without calling you.

docs.title: 2.1 The first 15 minutes, in order
docs.text:
The order matters more than speed. Each step takes a minute or two; skipping one costs days.

Minute Action Why in this order 0-2 Acknowledge in the incident channel / to the client contact. "Investigating, next update at HH:MM." Open an incident log (a text file with timestamps is enough). The client's first fear is silence. The log becomes the RCA timeline. 2-4 Scope: what is broken, for whom, since when. One branch or all? One API or all? Errors, hangs or wrong results? Decides severity and whether this is your component at all. 4-6 Classify severity (2.2) and escalate if Sev-1. Severity decides who wakes up and how often you report. 6-10 Capture evidence while the faulty state still exists: dump of the hung or looping process, logs around the start time, metrics snapshot, config and build version. After the restart the state is gone. A hung process is the evidence. 10-13 Stop the bleeding: restart, fail over, roll back, switch a feature flag off, block one bad input. Pick the smallest action that restores service (2.4). Mitigation before root cause. The client cares about the service first. 13-15 Verify recovery with a real signal (transactions succeeding, error rate back to baseline), then send the second update. "We restarted it" is not recovery. Success rate is.

After minute 15 the incident becomes an investigation: you work on the evidence copy, not on the production box, and you keep sending updates on the agreed cadence until it is resolved.

docs.title: 2.2 Severity classification
docs.text:
Severity is about business impact, not technical interest. A beautiful heap corruption in a nightly report job is lower severity than a boring config typo that stops UPI payments.

A typical four-level scheme (the exact names and response times come from the support contract with the client, so read yours):

Sev Meaning Example in core banking Typical response 1 Critical business function down or money at risk, no workaround Fund transfer service crashing in a loop; wrong balances being posted Immediate, all hands, updates every 30 min, client leadership informed 2 Major function degraded, workaround exists or partial outage One branch cluster down, others serving; latency 10x but completing Within an hour, updates every 1-2 hours 3 Minor function affected, low business impact Statement PDF generation failing for some accounts; retry works Next business day 4 Cosmetic, question, or no current impact Log message wrong; a single crash that self-recovered Planned release

Three rules that matter more than the table:

  • Data integrity beats availability. A service that is up but posting wrong amounts is worse than a service that is down. If you suspect wrong results, the mitigation may be to stop the service. Say so explicitly to the client.
  • Severity can go up or down. Re-evaluate at every update. Downgrading after mitigation is normal; say why.
  • Repeated low-severity crashes are a high-severity problem. A process that crashes once a day and auto-restarts is "only Sev-3" until the day it crashes during end-of-day batch.

docs.title: 2.3 Capturing evidence
docs.text:
What to capture depends on the failure mode. Do the capture as a script that operations can run, not a sequence of commands typed by a tired person (code/m11_collect_evidence.sh).

Failure mode Capture on Linux Capture on Windows Crashed The core (coredumpctl dump PID -o file or from core_pattern), the exact binary, its .debug file, the shared libraries (NT_FILE list), logs The .dmp from WER LocalDumps or ProcDump -e, the exe, the PDBs, logs Hung / deadlocked gcore -o hang PID twice, 30-60 s apart, then logs, then restart procdump -ma PID twice, or Task Manager "Create dump file" High CPU / spinning gcore twice plus top -H -p PID (per-thread CPU) and perf top -p PID for 10 s ProcDump -c 90 -s 10 -n 2 (dump when CPU > 90% for 10 s), Process Explorer thread view Memory growth RSS history from metrics, /proc/PID/smaps_rollup, one gcore (big, but valuable), heaptrack attach if allowed Two procdump -ma hours apart for !heap -s comparison, UMDH snapshots if +ust is on Wrong results Logs with request ids for the affected transactions, the input data, the DB rows; the process may be fine Same

Always also capture: build version and build id (readelf -n binary | grep Build), the deployed config, the host (uname -a, distro, glibc version), the time window, and what changed recently (deploys, config pushes, OS patches, traffic). "What changed?" answers more incidents than any debugger.

Two dumps of a hang. One dump of a hung process tells you where every thread is. Two dumps a minute apart tell you whether anything is moving: identical stacks mean deadlock; same threads in different frames mean livelock or a very slow loop; everything different means it is just slow (module 10).

Dump size and data protection. A full dump of a banking server contains customer data: account numbers, names, maybe card data and session tokens. Treat it like production data. It stays inside the client's environment or moves through the approved secure channel, is stored encrypted, has access control, and is deleted when the investigation closes. Never attach a dump to an email or a public ticket. If the contract does not allow dumps to leave the client site, you analyse on their jump host. Know this before the incident.

docs.title: 2.4 Stopping the bleeding: restart versus keep for forensics
docs.text:
This is the central decision. It is a trade-off between service and evidence, and the answer is almost always "both, in that order, within two minutes".

            is the process still alive and in the faulty state?
                     |                         |
                    yes                        no (crashed)
                     |                         |
     take dump(s) NOW (60-120 s)       is the core / .dmp there?  -> if not, fix dump config
                     |                         |                     as part of the incident
     is there a standby / other node?  restart (supervisor already did?)
           |                 |                 |
          yes               no                 is it crash-looping?
           |                 |                 |              |
   fail over first,    restart after          no             yes -> roll back / flag off /
   then keep the bad    the dump              done                  block the bad input
   node isolated for
   live debugging

Mitigation options from smallest blast radius to largest:

  1. Block the bad input. If one malformed message or one account triggers the crash, reject it at the edge (a deny-list, a validation rule). The service stays up for everyone else.
  2. Switch off a feature flag. If the crash is in a new code path, turn it off. This is why new paths should ship behind flags (2.7).
  3. Fail over to the standby node, leaving the faulty node isolated. Best of both worlds: the service is restored and the evidence is still running.
  4. Restart the process. Loses in-memory state; check that in-flight transactions are either completed or safely rolled back (idempotency, 2.7).
  5. Roll back the last deployment. Effective if the incident started with a deploy; costs the new features.
  6. Stop the service. Correct when results are wrong and money is at risk.

When the client pushes to "just restart it, now", the answer is: "Yes. I need 90 seconds to take a memory snapshot first, otherwise we cannot find the cause and it will happen again." In a banking context this is almost always accepted if you say it calmly and the 90 seconds are real. Having the capture as a one-line script is what makes it 90 seconds.

When you do not wait: when every second of the faulty state is posting wrong money, or a crash loop restarts faster than you can type (then the cores are being written anyway, check the core_pattern and disk space).

docs.title: 2.5 Communication cadence with a bank client
docs.text:
The bank's operations and IT leadership have their own escalation chain and their own regulator. Your updates are what they forward upwards. Make them easy to forward.

Rules:

  • Fixed cadence, announced in advance. "Next update at 03:30." Then update at 03:30 even if there is no news. "No change; still analysing the dump; next update 04:00" is a valid update. Silence is what turns a Sev-2 into an escalation to your CEO.
  • One voice. One person (the incident commander or the support lead) talks to the client. Engineers feed facts to that person. Five engineers posting guesses in the client's channel destroys confidence.
  • Facts, actions, next time. Every update has: current status, what we know, what we are doing, what we need from you, next update time.
  • Separate fact from hypothesis. "The process crashed at 02:41 with an access violation" is fact. "We believe it is related to yesterday's release" is a hypothesis; label it.
  • Never promise a root cause time. Promise the next update time. "Root cause by 10:00" is a promise you cannot keep; "preliminary findings by 10:00" you can.
  • No blame, no internal names. Not "the developer forgot a lock". "A defect in the session handling code."

A template update:

[Update 3 - 03:30 IST] Fund Transfer Service - Sev-1

Status:       Service restored at 03:12 IST via restart of APP-NODE-2. Transactions succeeding
              at normal rate since 03:14 (monitoring confirms).
Impact:       Between 02:41 and 03:12 IST fund transfer requests on APP-NODE-2 failed. Node 1
              continued serving. Approx. count of affected requests will be confirmed from logs.
Known so far: The service process terminated unexpectedly at 02:41. A memory dump was captured
              before restart and is under analysis.
Doing now:    Analysing the dump; checking logs for the request pattern before the failure.
Need from you: Confirmation that no batch job was started on APP-NODE-2 around 02:30.
Next update:  04:30 IST, or earlier if status changes.

After resolution: a short closure note the same day ("resolved, monitoring, RCA by "), then the formal RCA within the contractual window (module 12). Typical contracts ask for a preliminary RCA within 24-72 hours and a final one within 5-10 business days; check yours.

docs.title: 2.6 What a server should log by design
docs.text:
You cannot add logs during an incident. Whatever the server logs today is all you will have. Design the logging for the 3 AM reader.

Every log line carries:

Field Example Why Timestamp, UTC or with offset, millisecond or microsecond resolution 2026-10-12T02:41:07.318+05:30 Correlate with other systems; order events within a second Level ERROR Filter Process id and thread id (kernel tid, not the pthread_t) pid=4120 tid=4187 Match a log line to a thread in the core (info threads shows LWP) Request id / correlation id req=7f3a2c19-... Follow one transaction across threads, processes and services Component / module comp=xfer Find the area Event name, stable evt=xfer.debit.failed Grep and count without parsing prose Key fields acct=XXXX1234 amt=5000 err=DB_TIMEOUT The facts, masked where needed Build version at startup and in the crash handler Match the dump to the binary

Structured logs. Write key=value pairs or one JSON object per line, not free text. Free text like "Failed to debit account 1234 because timeout" cannot be counted or joined reliably. A structured line can (one line in the file; wrapped here to fit):

ts=2026-10-12T02:41:07.318+05:30 lvl=ERROR pid=4120 tid=4187 req=7f3a2c19 comp=xfer
  evt=xfer.debit.failed acct=XXXX1234 amt_paise=500000 err=DB_TIMEOUT latency_ms=5003 build=4.12.3

What else to log:

  • Startup: build version and id, config hash, host, glibc version, limits (ulimit -c!), thread pool sizes. Half the RCAs start with "which version was running?".
  • Request boundaries: start and end of every request with duration and result. These two lines alone let you find the last request a crashed thread was handling (start without end).
  • State transitions: connection open/close, session create/expire, failover, config reload.
  • Resource gauges every minute: RSS, heap in use (from mallinfo2), thread count, fd count, queue depths, pool usage. These turn "memory growth" into a slope you can read (module 09).
  • The crash itself: a crash handler that writes the signal, fault address, build, thread id, current request id and a backtrace to stderr, then re-raises so the core is still written (section 3).

What never to log: full card numbers, PINs, passwords, CVV, OTPs, full session tokens. Mask account numbers to the last 4 digits unless the client's policy says otherwise. Logs are copied to more places than dumps; a leak through logs is a reportable data breach for the bank.

Cost and volume. Logging is I/O. Use asynchronous logging (a queue and a writer thread) so a slow disk does not block request threads; bound the queue and count dropped lines rather than blocking. Keep DEBUG off in production but switchable at runtime per component, without restart.

docs.title: 2.7 Log correlation
docs.text:
Correlation is joining events from different sources into one timeline.

  • Request id propagation. Generate an id at the edge (or accept the client's), put it in a thread-local when a worker picks up the request, include it in every log line, pass it to downstream calls (RPC header, DB application_name or a comment in the SQL), and return it to the caller in error responses. Then "customer complaint about transfer at 10:42" becomes one grep.
  • Thread id to core. The crash handler prints the tid; info threads in gdb shows LWP; ~ in WinDbg shows Id: pid.tid. The log lines with that tid just before the crash are the request that killed the process.
  • Clock alignment. All servers on NTP/chrony. A 3-second skew between the app server and the DB server makes a timeline lie. Note the timezone in every timestamp.
  • Across a restart. Log a "process start, previous exit reason" line. On Linux, systemctl status / journalctl -u svc show code=dumped, status=11/SEGV; on Windows the Application event log has event 1000 (Application Error) with the faulting module and offset. Correlate with the dump timestamp.

A one-liner that answers "what was each thread doing just before the crash":

# last request each thread started but never finished, before 02:41:07
awk '$0 < "ts=2026-10-12T02:41:08"' app.log | grep -E 'evt=req\.(start|end)' |
  awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++){split($i,kv,"="); f[kv[1]]=kv[2]}
        if (f["evt"]=="req.start") open[f["tid"]]=f["req"]; else delete open[f["tid"]]}
       END {for (t in open) print "tid", t, "was handling", open[t]}'

docs.title: 2.8 Feature flags and safe restarts
docs.text:
Feature flags are runtime switches that turn a code path on or off without a deploy. For incident response they are the cheapest mitigation there is. Rules that make them useful:

  • New risky paths (a new parser, a new caching layer, a new batch algorithm) ship behind a flag, default off, enabled gradually.
  • The flag is read at a safe point (per request), not once at startup, so flipping it does not need a restart.
  • The old path stays working until the new one has been on for a full business cycle (month-end included, for a bank).
  • Flags are removed once the new path is proven. A server with 200 permanent flags has 2^200 configurations nobody has tested.

Safe restarts mean a restart cannot corrupt data or lose money:

  • Idempotent operations. Every money-moving request has a unique transaction reference; repeating it is detected and returns the original result instead of posting twice. Then a client retry after a crash is safe.
  • Transactions own the truth. The DB transaction commits or it does not; in-memory state can be rebuilt from the DB on startup. If a crash mid-request can leave "debited but not credited", that is a design bug, and the RCA should say so.
  • Graceful shutdown path: stop accepting, drain in-flight requests with a timeout, then exit. The supervisor (systemd Restart=on-failure, a Windows service recovery action) restarts crashed processes; add a restart limit (StartLimitBurst) so a crash loop stops and alerts instead of spinning silently and filling the disk with cores.
  • Rolling restarts across nodes, one at a time, with health checks between them.

docs.title: 2.9 Postmortem culture
docs.text:
A postmortem is the meeting and document after the incident where you work out what happened and what to change. The RCA you send the bank (module 12) is its external, formal form.

  • Blameless. The question is "how did our system allow this?", not "who did this?". People hide facts from a blame meeting; you need the facts. A missing lock is a review-process gap and a missing TSan job, not a stupid developer.
  • Timeline first, from evidence. Logs, dump timestamps, chat history. Not memory.
  • Action items are owned, dated and verifiable. "Improve testing" is not an action item. "Add TSan CI job for the session module - owner: Shakir - by 2026-10-30 - done when the job runs on every merge request" is.
  • Track them to closure. Most organisations are good at writing action items and bad at finishing them. Review open items weekly.
  • Look for repeats. Group incidents by stack signature (!analyze bucket, or a hash of the top 5 frames). Three incidents with the same signature in a quarter means the previous RCAs fixed symptoms.

docs.title: 3.1 A crash handler that preserves the core
docs.text:
code/m11_crash_handler.cpp installs a handler for SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, SIGBUS, SIGFPE and SIGILL that prints the signal, fault address, build id, kernel thread id, current request id and a backtrace, then re-raises the signal with the default action so the kernel still writes the core.

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -g -O1 -fno-omit-frame-pointer -rdynamic \
    -o build/m11_crash_handler m11_crash_handler.cpp
ulimit -c unlimited
./build/m11_crash_handler
# *** FATAL signal 11 (SIGSEGV) fault addr 0x0000000000000010
# build  = 2026.10.03-rel-1
# thread = 12345  request = REQ-00042
# backtrace:
# ./build/m11_crash_handler(+0x...) ...
# Segmentation fault (core dumped)

The key parts and why they look like that:

static thread_local char t_request_id[32] = "none";   // set by the dispatcher per request

static void crash_handler(int sig, siginfo_t *info, void *)
{
    write_str("\n*** FATAL signal "); write_dec(sig);  // write(2) only: printf takes a lock
    ...
    write_str("  request = "); write_str(t_request_id); // the log-correlation key
    void *frames[64];
    int n = backtrace(frames, 64);
    backtrace_symbols_fd(frames, n, 2);                 // writes to fd 2 without malloc
    signal(sig, SIG_DFL);                               // restore default action...
    raise(sig);                                         // ...so the kernel writes the core
}

static void install_crash_handler()
{
    static char altstack[64 * 1024];                    // stack overflow needs its own stack
    stack_t ss{}; ss.ss_sp = altstack; ss.ss_size = sizeof altstack;
    sigaltstack(&ss, nullptr);
    void *warm[4]; backtrace(warm, 4);                  // first call may malloc: do it now
    struct sigaction sa{};
    sa.sa_sigaction = crash_handler;
    sa.sa_flags = SA_SIGINFO | SA_ONSTACK | SA_RESETHAND;
    ...
}

Why each rule exists:

  • Async-signal-safe calls only. The handler runs on the crashed thread, in the middle of whatever it was doing. If it crashed inside malloc (heap corruption, module 03), the arena lock is held; calling malloc or printf (which may allocate and takes the stdio lock) from the handler deadlocks the process. Now you have a hang instead of a crash, and no core. The POSIX list of safe functions is in man 7 signal-safety: write, _exit, sigaction, raise, and not much more. Hence hand-written number formatting.
  • sigaltstack + SA_ONSTACK. For a stack overflow the faulting thread has no stack left; without an alternate stack the handler itself faults and the kernel kills the process. (The alternate stack is per thread; a real server installs one in each thread it creates.)
  • Warm up backtrace(). glibc's backtrace loads libgcc_s via dlopen on first use, which allocates. Calling it once at startup moves that out of the handler.
  • Re-raise with SIG_DFL. If the handler just returned or called _exit, there would be no core. SA_RESETHAND plus raise gives the default action, which is "terminate and dump".
  • The request id is a thread_local char array, not a std::string: reading it from the handler must not touch the heap.

On Windows the equivalent is a vectored exception handler or SetUnhandledExceptionFilter that writes a short line and calls MiniDumpWriteDump from a separate watchdog process or thread (writing a dump from the crashed thread itself is unreliable for the same reasons). In practice WER LocalDumps or ProcDump -e is simpler and more robust; configure them (module 07).

docs.title: 3.2 Evidence collection script
docs.text:
code/m11_collect_evidence.sh is the script operations runs at minute 6. It takes a PID (hung process) or a core path (crashed process) and produces one tarball with everything module 06 says a "complete core" needs.

sudo ./m11_collect_evidence.sh --pid 4120 --log /var/log/app/app.log --out /secure/incidents
# [collect] gcore 1 of 2 ...
# [collect] waiting 30 s for second gcore (hang analysis needs two)
# [collect] gcore 2 of 2 ...
# [collect] per-thread CPU, limits, maps, fds, binary, debug link, shared libs, last 20000 log lines
# [collect] wrote /secure/incidents/inc-20261012T024312-pid4120.tar.gz (sha256 ...)

Read the script once: it is mostly a checklist turned into commands. It records the SHA-256 of the tarball so the RCA can say which evidence was analysed (chain of custody).

docs.title: 3.3 A structured log line in C++
docs.text:
Not a separate file; the core of a logger you would add to your server. It shows the fields from 2.6 and the thread-local request id shared with the crash handler.

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <ctime>
#include <sys/syscall.h>
#include <unistd.h>

thread_local char t_request_id[32] = "none";          // same variable the crash handler reads

inline long current_tid() { return static_cast<long>(syscall(SYS_gettid)); }

// One line, key=value, UTC with microseconds. In a real server this formats into a buffer and
// pushes it to an async writer thread; snprintf + one fwrite keeps lines from interleaving.
inline void log_event(const char *lvl, const char *comp, const char *evt, const char *kv)
{
    using namespace std::chrono;
    auto now = system_clock::now();
    auto us  = duration_cast<microseconds>(now.time_since_epoch()).count() % 1000000;
    std::time_t t = system_clock::to_time_t(now);
    std::tm tm{};
    gmtime_r(&t, &tm);                                  // reentrant; gmtime is not thread-safe
    char line[512];
    int n = std::snprintf(line, sizeof line,
        "ts=%04d-%02d-%02dT%02d:%02d:%02d.%06ldZ lvl=%s pid=%d tid=%ld req=%s comp=%s evt=%s %s\n",
        tm.tm_year + 1900, tm.tm_mon + 1, tm.tm_mday, tm.tm_hour, tm.tm_min, tm.tm_sec,
        static_cast<long>(us), lvl, static_cast<int>(getpid()), current_tid(), t_request_id,
        comp, evt, kv);
    if (n > 0) std::fwrite(line, 1, static_cast<size_t>(n) < sizeof line ? static_cast<size_t>(n)
                                                                          : sizeof line - 1, stderr);
}

// usage at a request boundary:
//   std::snprintf(t_request_id, sizeof t_request_id, "%s", req.id);
//   log_event("INFO", "xfer", "req.start", "acct=XXXX1234 amt_paise=500000");

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What the kernel does when a process crashes. The faulting instruction raises a CPU exception; the kernel's page-fault handler finds no valid mapping and queues SIGSEGV to the thread. If a handler is installed, the kernel builds a signal frame on the (alternate) stack and resumes the thread in the handler. When the default action runs, the kernel calls do_coredump: it checks RLIMIT_CORE (ulimit -c), the dumpable flag (prctl(PR_SET_DUMPABLE), cleared by setuid transitions), then either writes the file named by core_pattern or, if the pattern starts with |, pipes the core to a user-space program (systemd-coredump, apport). Only then does the process die and its parent (systemd) get SIGCHLD with "dumped core". So a misconfigured core_pattern, a full disk, ulimit -c 0 in the service unit (LimitCORE= in systemd) or a setuid binary each silently produce no core. Check these at startup and log them.

Why gcore pauses the service. gcore attaches with ptrace, which stops all threads, then reads every writable mapping through /proc/PID/mem and writes the ELF core. For a 20 GB process that is tens of seconds of a frozen server (disk speed bound). Health checks may fail and a load balancer may take the node out - which is fine during a hang, but plan for it. On Windows procdump -r uses process reflection (clones the process and dumps the clone) to cut the pause.

Windows Error Reporting. On an unhandled exception, kernel32!UnhandledExceptionFilter hands the process to WER (WerFault.exe), which suspends it and, if HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\ Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps is configured (DumpType=2 for full), writes the dump. The Application event log entry (Event ID 1000) records the faulting module, its version and the offset - enough to correlate without opening the dump. A service with "recovery: restart" in the SCM restarts after WER finishes.

Log ordering across threads is not causal order. Two threads that log within the same microsecond can appear in either order; with an async logger, the queue order is the enqueue order, which is not the order the events happened. Within one thread, order is reliable. Across threads, only synchronisation (a lock both took, a message passed) establishes order. That is why the request id plus tid matter more than the timestamp.

syscall(SYS_gettid) versus pthread_self(). pthread_self() returns the address of the thread's struct pthread (its TCB) in user space; it is what gdb shows as Thread 0x7f.... The kernel tid (LWP) is what top -H, /proc/PID/task/, perf and the crash handler use. Log the kernel tid; it is the one that joins logs, top and the core. (glibc 2.30+ has gettid().)

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Test the dump path before you need it. After every deployment or OS patch, on a staging box with the same config, kill -SEGV a test process (or the real one in a maintenance window) and confirm the core appears with the right size and opens in gdb with symbols. Dump configuration silently breaks: a systemd unit file update resets LimitCORE, a disk cleanup cron deletes /var/lib/systemd/coredump, someone sets DumpType=1 (minidump) to save space.
  • Store symbols for every release. The .debug files / PDBs for every build that ever reached a client, indexed by build id, kept for the life of the support contract. A dump without matching symbols costs a day; a dump of a build whose symbols were deleted is nearly useless.
  • The 3 AM checklist is printed. At 3 AM nobody remembers procdump -ma. Keep a one-page runbook per service: where the logs are, how to take a dump, how to fail over, how to flip the flags, who to call.
  • Watch for the restart that hides the problem. A supervisor that silently restarts a crashing process makes availability look fine while the system crashes 40 times a day. Alert on restarts, not only on downtime.
  • Disk full during the incident. Cores of a big process can fill /var and take down logging and the DB on the same box. Put cores on a separate volume with a quota and a retention policy.
  • Banking specifics. End-of-day and month-end batches are the high-risk windows; freeze deploys around them. Regulators may require incident reporting within hours for customer-facing outages; your RCA timeline will be used in that report, so the timestamps must be exact and the timezone stated.
  • War story pattern. The crash is in the overnight interest calculation; operations restarts it three times before calling anyone; each restart partially re-runs the batch. The incident is now a data reconciliation incident, much bigger than the crash. The fix in the runbook: "batch job crashes - do not restart - take the core - call the on-call engineer". Restarts are not always safe; the runbook must say which ones are.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - core configuration audit. On WSL, write down the current values of ulimit -c, /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern, and (if systemd) coredumpctl list. Crash m11_crash_handler and find the core. Done when you have the crash handler output and a core that opens in gdb with bt matching the handler's backtrace.
  2. Easy - write the update. For a fictional incident ("balance enquiry API returning errors for 20% of requests since 10:05"), write update 1 (minute 2) and update 2 (minute 15, after a restart of one node fixed it) using the template in 2.5. Done when each update has status, impact, known facts, actions, a request to the client and the next update time, and no hypothesis is stated as fact.
  3. Medium - collect evidence from a hang. Run m10_deadlock_debug and run m11_collect_evidence.sh --pid <PID> against it. Open both cores from the tarball. Done when you can show the two cores have identical stacks for the deadlocked threads (proving deadlock, not slowness) and the tarball contains binary, libs and logs.
  4. Medium - structured logging. Add the log_event function from 3.3 and a thread_local request id to m10_data_race.cpp (each thread logs req.start and req.end around its loop). Done when you can grep the output by tid= and by req= and the tid matches info threads LWP in a core of the program.
  5. Hard - find the killer request. Extend exercise 4: give each of 1000 simulated requests an id, make request number 637 trigger a null dereference, install the crash handler. Using only the log file and the core (not the source), identify the request id that crashed the process and the thread that ran it. Done when the awk one-liner in 2.7 (adapted) prints that request id and it matches the crash handler's request = line.
  6. Hard - runbook. Write a one-page runbook for a service you know from work (anonymised): severity rules, dump capture on Windows and Linux, failover, feature flags, who to call, update template. Done when someone who has never seen the service could take a correct dump and send a correct first update from the page alone.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: A production server is hung. The client wants it restarted now. What do you do? A: Agree to the restart and ask for 60-120 seconds first: take two dumps (gcore or procdump -ma) about 30-60 seconds apart, grab logs and per-thread CPU, then restart or fail over. The dumps prove whether it is a deadlock (identical stacks) or slowness, and without them the root cause is guesswork and the hang will recur. If a standby node exists, fail over first and keep the hung node isolated for analysis.

Q: How do you decide incident severity? A: By business impact, not technical complexity: which function is affected, how many users or transactions, whether money or data integrity is at risk, and whether a workaround exists. Wrong results outrank unavailability. Severity is re-evaluated at every update and repeated "self-healing" crashes are escalated because they will eventually hit a critical window.

Q: What should every log line in a multithreaded server contain? A: A precise timestamp with timezone, level, pid, kernel thread id, request or correlation id, component, a stable event name and key fields in structured form, with sensitive data masked. The thread id joins the log to a thread in the core; the request id joins events across threads and services; the event name makes logs countable.

Q: Why must a crash handler only call async-signal-safe functions? A: The handler interrupts the faulting thread at an arbitrary point, possibly inside malloc or printf with their internal locks held or their data structures half-updated. Calling them again deadlocks or corrupts further, and a deadlocked crash handler means no core at all. So the handler uses write, preformatted buffers and backtrace_symbols_fd, runs on an alternate stack, and re-raises the signal with the default action so the core is still written.

Q: How do you correlate a core dump with application logs? A: The crash handler (or the last log lines) gives the kernel tid and request id; info threads in gdb shows the LWP of each thread, so the faulting thread's LWP finds its log lines; the request-start-without-request-end line for that tid is the request that was running. Timestamps from the core file, journalctl or the Windows event log 1000 entry align the rest, assuming NTP is working.

Q: What makes a restart "safe" in a payment system? A: Every money-moving operation is idempotent through a unique transaction reference, the database transaction is the source of truth so partial in-memory state is discarded harmlessly, and the restart drains in-flight work or relies on the DB to roll back incomplete transactions. A supervisor restarts on failure with a burst limit so a crash loop stops and alerts.

Q: What is a blameless postmortem and why does it matter? A: A review that asks how the system allowed the failure rather than who caused it. People share the uncomfortable facts (the skipped review, the ignored warning) only when they are not punished for them, and those facts are exactly where the prevention lies. Its outputs are an evidence-based timeline and owned, dated, verifiable action items that are tracked to closure.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• The first 15 minutes: acknowledge, scope, classify, capture, mitigate, verify - in that order.
  • Severity is business impact; data integrity outranks availability; re-evaluate every update.
  • Capture before restart: two dumps for a hang, the core plus binary plus symbols plus libs for a crash, logs and "what changed" for everything. Script it.
  • Dumps contain customer data: secure channel, encrypted, access-controlled, deleted after.
  • Mitigate with the smallest blast radius: block input, flag off, fail over, restart, roll back, stop.
  • Client communication: one voice, fixed cadence, facts separate from hypotheses, never promise a root-cause time.
  • Log by design: timestamp with zone, pid, kernel tid, request id, stable event name, structured fields, masked data; request start and end; startup build info; resource gauges.
  • Crash handler: async-signal-safe only, alternate stack, warm backtrace, print request id and tid, re-raise so the core survives.
  • Safe restarts need idempotency, DB-owned truth, graceful drain and a restart burst limit.
  • Postmortems are blameless, evidence-based and produce owned, dated, verifiable actions.

docs.title: 12. Writing a formal RCA
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 06, 07, 10, 11

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A root cause analysis (RCA) is the document that explains, after an incident, what happened, why it happened, and what you have done so it cannot happen again. For a bank, it is also a contract artefact: the support agreement usually requires one within a fixed time, the bank's IT risk team reviews it, and parts of it may go into their report to the regulator.

Think of an aircraft accident report. It does not say "the plane crashed because it hit the ground". It says the pilot descended because the altimeter read wrong, because a sensor was iced, because the heater had failed, because the maintenance check did not include the heater. Each step has evidence. The fix is not "tell pilots to be careful"; it is "add the heater to the checklist and add an alarm". A good software RCA has the same shape: a chain of evidence from the symptom to the defect, from the defect to the process gap that let it ship, and fixes for both.

The hard part is not the writing. It is being honest about what you proved and what you only believe, separating the thing that happened that night (the trigger) from the thing that was wrong all along (the root cause), and writing it so a bank's operations head and its chief architect both come away trusting your team more than before the incident.

docs.title: 2.1 The structure
docs.text:
Every RCA in this course uses this structure. Most banks and vendors use a variant of it; if the client has a template, use theirs and map these sections onto it.

# Section What goes in Length 0 Header Incident id, title, severity, service, environment, dates, author, reviewers, version, status (preliminary/final) table 1 Executive summary What happened, impact, root cause, fix, in plain words. A reader who stops here knows everything important. 4-8 sentences 2 Impact Who and what was affected, duration, counts, financial and data impact, SLA impact table + few lines 3 Timeline Timestamped events from first symptom to resolution, with sources table 4 Root cause The defect, the mechanism from defect to failure, the evidence 1-2 pages 5 Trigger Why it happened that day a paragraph 6 Contributing factors Conditions that made it possible, worse or slower to fix bullets 7 5-whys The causal chain from symptom to process gap numbered list 8 Resolution / fix Immediate mitigation and permanent fix, with versions bullets 9 Preventive actions Owned, dated actions for the process gaps table 10 Verification How you proved the fix works and how you will know it holds bullets 11 Appendix Evidence excerpts: stacks, log lines, tool output, references as needed

docs.title: 2.2 Trigger versus root cause
docs.text:
This is the distinction that separates a senior RCA from a junior one.

  • Trigger: the event or condition that made the latent problem visible at that moment. A traffic spike, a particular input, a config change, a month-end batch, an OS patch.
  • Root cause: the defect or design flaw that made the system fail when triggered. Remove the root cause and the trigger becomes harmless. Remove only the trigger and the system fails again on the next one.
Wrong (trigger presented as root cause) Right "Root cause: unusually high load at month-end." Trigger: month-end load. Root cause: a race in session expiry that needs two concurrent requests on the same session; it only becomes likely at high load. "Root cause: a malformed message from the partner bank." Trigger: a 13-character account id. Root cause: the parser writes one byte past a 12-byte buffer and does not validate field lengths. "Root cause: the server ran out of memory." That is a symptom. Root cause: a cache with no eviction bound. "Root cause: human error during deployment." Root cause: a deployment step that can be done wrong without any check failing. The fix is the check.

A useful test: "If this condition happens again tomorrow, will the system now survive?" If the answer depends on the condition not happening, you have described the trigger.

There can be more than one root cause (a defect plus a missing safeguard). And there is often a second level: the technical root cause (the bug) and the process root cause (why review, tests and tools did not catch it). A good RCA names both and fixes both.

docs.title: 2.3 Evidence
docs.text:
Every claim in the root-cause section is one of:

  • Proven: you have direct evidence - a stack from the dump, a log line, a reproduction that fails before the fix and passes after, a tool report (ASan, TSan, !heap -p -a).
  • Inferred: it follows from proven facts by reasoning you can state.
  • Hypothesis: consistent with the evidence but not proven.

Label them. "The dump shows" (proven), "therefore" (inferred), "we believe" (hypothesis). An RCA whose root cause is a hypothesis is a preliminary RCA; say so, say what evidence would confirm it, and say what detection you added to get that evidence next time (module 10's ring buffer, asserts, PageHeap on one node). Never present a hypothesis as proven to close an incident faster: if it is wrong, the incident recurs and the next RCA starts with zero credibility.

Put raw evidence in the appendix (stacks, log excerpts, tool reports, trimmed to the relevant lines) and reference it from the body: "(Appendix A.2)".

docs.title: 2.4 5-whys
docs.text:
The 5-whys is a way to walk from the symptom to the process gap by asking "why?" repeatedly. Five is a guideline, not a rule; stop when the next answer is outside your control or is a process you can change.

Rules that make it work:

  • Each answer must be supported by evidence or be clearly a process statement.
  • Follow the most important branch; note other branches as contributing factors.
  • Do not stop at the bug. "Why did the bug exist?" leads to "why did review not catch it?" and "why did tests not catch it?". That is where prevention lives.
  • Never end at a person. "Because the developer made a mistake" is always followed by "why did the system let a mistake reach production?".

docs.title: 2.5 Tone for a banking client
docs.text:
• Factual, calm, precise. No adjectives that judge ("unfortunately", "silly", "minor glitch"). Numbers with units and timestamps with timezone.
  • Own it. "A defect in our session handling code" - not "an unexpected condition", not "a third-party library" unless you proved it.
  • No blame, no names. Internal names never appear. Teams can appear as roles ("vendor support", "bank operations").
  • No excessive apology, no defensiveness. One sentence acknowledging impact is right; three paragraphs read as evasive.
  • Explain technical terms once, in plain words. The operations head must follow the summary; the architect must find the mechanism precise. Put the plain version in the summary and the precise version in section 4.
  • Commit only to what you control. Dates for your actions; "recommend" for the bank's.
  • Be explicit about data. Banks care first whether any transaction was lost, duplicated or posted wrongly. State it, and state how you verified it (reconciliation query, count).
  • Same terms everywhere. If the summary says "fund transfer service", the timeline does not switch to "FT module" and "xferd".

docs.title: 2.6 Preventive actions that actually prevent
docs.text:
A preventive action is good when it is specific, owned, dated and verifiable:

Weak Strong Improve code review. Add "every buffer write is bounded by the destination size" to the review checklist for parser code; owner: dev lead; by 2026-11-15; done when the checklist is in the merge-request template. Add more testing. Add a libFuzzer target for the ISO 8583 parser running 30 minutes nightly; owner: Shakir; by 2026-11-30; done when the job runs and its first week's results are reviewed. Monitor memory. Alert when RSS of the service grows more than 200 MB in 6 hours; owner: support lead; by 2026-10-25.

Classify actions by what they do: eliminate the bug class (RAII, bounded types), detect it earlier (sanitizers in CI, fuzzing, static analysis), contain it (input validation, flags, restart limits), diagnose faster (logging, dump config). Module 13 is the catalogue.

docs.title: 2.7 Verification
docs.text:
"We fixed it" needs proof, in two parts:

  • The fix fixes it. A reproduction (test, fuzz input, stress run) that fails on the old build and passes on the new one. Sanitizer runs clean. For races: TSan clean, stress test passes N iterations that previously failed within M.
  • The fix holds in production. A metric or log signal you will watch, for how long, and what value means success: "zero occurrences of event sess.uaf_guard and zero crashes over 30 days including month-end".

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: There is no program for this module. The "code" is the two complete RCAs below. They are illustrative: the bank, the system, the people, the numbers and the timestamps are invented for teaching, though the bug mechanisms are real and match the programs in code/. Use them as templates. Copy the structure, not the facts.

docs.title: 3.1 Example RCA 1: heap memory corruption
docs.text:
ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE - fictional bank, system and data, written as a template.

Root Cause Analysis - INC-2026-0917: Payment Gateway Adapter process terminations

Field Value Incident id INC-2026-0917 Client Example Bank Ltd. (fictional) Service Payment Gateway Adapter (PGA), version 4.12.3 Environment Production, data centre DC1, nodes PGA-1 and PGA-2 (Linux, RHEL 8) Severity Sev-2 (degraded; partial outage with automatic retry) Incident window 2026-09-17 11:02 IST to 2026-09-17 14:40 IST (mitigated); permanent fix 2026-09-21 Document status Final, version 1.1 (preliminary v1.0 issued 2026-09-18) Prepared by Vendor product support, core engineering Reviewed by Vendor engineering head; bank IT application owner

1. Executive summary

On 17 September 2026, between 11:02 and 14:40 IST, the Payment Gateway Adapter process terminated unexpectedly 14 times across two nodes. Each termination interrupted in-flight requests for a few seconds until the process restarted automatically. 312 payment requests failed and were retried successfully by the upstream channel; no transaction was lost, duplicated or posted with a wrong amount (verified by reconciliation, section 2).

The root cause is a defect in the PGA's message parser: when a beneficiary reference field is longer than 35 characters, the parser writes past the end of a memory buffer, corrupting the memory allocator's internal data. The process then terminates later, when the allocator detects the corruption. The defect has existed since version 4.10.0 (released March 2026); it was triggered on 17 September when a partner bank began sending a longer reference format.

Service was restored at 14:40 IST by rejecting over-length references at the input boundary. The permanent fix (version 4.12.4) bounds the copy and validates every field length; it was deployed on 21 September. We are adding fuzz testing and memory-error detection to our build pipeline to find this class of defect before release.

2. Impact

Item Value Source Duration of impact 3 h 38 min (11:02 - 14:40 IST) PGA logs, monitoring Process terminations 14 (PGA-1: 8, PGA-2: 6) systemd journal, core files Failed requests 312 payment requests returned a connection error to the channel PGA access log, channel logs Requests retried successfully 312 of 312, by the channel's automatic retry Channel logs, transaction reference match Lost / duplicated / mis-posted transactions None Reconciliation query on 17 Sep, 18:00 IST: all 312 references posted exactly once, amounts match Customer-visible effect Payment confirmation delayed by up to 40 s for affected customers Channel latency report Data exposure None - SLA Availability for the day 98.7% against 99.5% target Monitoring

3. Timeline (all times IST, 2026-09-17 unless stated)

Time Event Source 2026-03-12 Version 4.10.0 released, containing the defective parser change Release notes 10:30 Partner bank switches to extended beneficiary reference format (up to 40 characters) Partner bank change notice, received after the incident 11:02 First PGA termination on PGA-1, SIGABRT, core written journal, core file 11:02 - 12:10 6 further terminations, auto-restarted by systemd journal 12:14 Monitoring alert: PGA restart count > 5 per hour Alerting system 12:20 Vendor support acknowledges, Sev-3 opened Ticket 12:45 Severity raised to Sev-2 (terminations continuing on both nodes) Ticket 12:50 Bank operations and vendor bridge call opened; updates every hour agreed Bridge notes 13:05 Three core files and binaries collected with evidence script Evidence log, SHA-256 recorded 13:40 Core analysis: all cores abort inside the memory allocator with heap-corruption messages; the faulting stacks differ Analysis notes (Appendix A.1) 14:05 Log correlation: every termination preceded within 2 s by a request with a reference longer than 35 characters PGA logs (Appendix A.2) 14:20 Reproduced in test with a 40-character reference under AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow in parse_beneficiary Test log (Appendix A.3) 14:35 Mitigation deployed: input rule rejects references > 35 characters with a business error; partner bank informed Change record CHG-5521 14:40 Last termination before mitigation took effect; none since journal 15:30 Service declared stable; Sev-2 downgraded to Sev-3 pending permanent fix Ticket 18:00 Reconciliation confirms no lost, duplicated or mis-posted transactions Reconciliation report 09-18 17:00 Preliminary RCA (v1.0) issued - 09-21 01:00 Version 4.12.4 deployed in the maintenance window; input rule removed after verification Change record CHG-5530 10-21 30-day observation ends with zero terminations; incident closed Monitoring

4. Root cause

4.1 The defect. parse_beneficiary() copies the beneficiary reference into a 36-byte field of the PaymentMessage structure (35 characters plus terminator). The copy loop is bounded by the length of the input field, not the destination:

// version 4.10.0 - 4.12.3
for (size_t i = 0; i < field.len; ++i)      // field.len comes from the wire
    msg->beneficiary_ref[i] = field.data[i];
msg->beneficiary_ref[field.len] = '\0';

For a 40-character reference this writes 4 characters and a terminator (5 bytes) past the end of beneficiary_ref. PaymentMessage is allocated on the heap and beneficiary_ref is its last member, so the excess bytes overwrite the allocator's header of the next heap block.

4.2 Why the process terminated later and in different places. The glibc allocator stores the size of each block in a header just before it. The overwritten header is not checked when it is written; it is checked when that neighbouring block is freed or merged. That happens in whatever code next frees memory near the corrupted block - often in a different thread, milliseconds to seconds later. The allocator then detects an impossible size and stops the process deliberately (malloc(): invalid next size, free(): invalid next size (fast)). This is why the 14 core files show 5 different stacks, none of them in the parser (Appendix A.1). Heap corruption typically presents this way: the crash site shows where the damage was found, not where it was done.

4.3 Evidence chain.

  1. Proven - all 14 terminations are SIGABRT raised by glibc's heap consistency checks (core files, p $_siginfo, abort messages in the journal). Appendix A.1.
  2. Proven - in all 14 cases, the same thread (matching kernel thread id) processed a request with a beneficiary reference of 36-40 characters between 0.1 and 1.8 seconds before the termination; no termination occurred without such a request. Appendix A.2.
  3. Proven - in 3 analysed cores, the heap block adjacent to a PaymentMessage contains the ASCII tail of a beneficiary reference where the allocator header should be (x/8xg on the block). Appendix A.1.
  4. Proven - the test build with AddressSanitizer reports heap-buffer-overflow ... WRITE of size 1 ... in parse_beneficiary payment_parser.cpp:212 for a 40-character reference, located 0 bytes after the 168-byte PaymentMessage region. Appendix A.3.
  5. Proven - with version 4.12.4, the same test and 10 million fuzzed messages produce no sanitizer reports (section 10).

5. Trigger

At 10:30 IST on 17 September a partner bank began sending beneficiary references of up to 40 characters, permitted by its updated message specification. References longer than 35 characters had not appeared in production before that day (checked against 90 days of logs). The trigger is the new input; the root cause is the parser's failure to bound its copy and validate field length.

6. Contributing factors

  • No input validation at the gateway boundary for field lengths; the parser trusted the wire.
  • The parser change in 4.10.0 was reviewed, but the review checklist had no item for bounded copies, and unit tests used only valid-length references.
  • Memory-error detection (AddressSanitizer) and fuzz testing were not part of the release pipeline.
  • The restart alert threshold (5 per hour) delayed engagement by 72 minutes after the first termination.
  • The partner bank's format change was not communicated to the vendor in advance.

7. 5-whys

  1. Why did requests fail? The PGA process terminated 14 times.
  2. Why did it terminate? The memory allocator detected corrupted heap metadata and aborted.
  3. Why was the heap metadata corrupted? parse_beneficiary wrote up to 5 bytes past a 36-byte field for references longer than 35 characters.
  4. Why did the parser write past the field? The copy was bounded by the input length, not the destination size, and field lengths were not validated against the specification.
  5. Why did this reach production? Tests covered only valid-length inputs, review had no bounded-copy check, and the pipeline had no fuzzing or AddressSanitizer stage that would have found it in seconds.

8. Resolution

  • Mitigation (17 Sep, 14:35): input rule at the gateway rejects beneficiary references longer than 35 characters with business error PGA-422, so the partner bank's system receives a clear rejection instead of a dropped connection. Partner bank informed at 14:50.
  • Permanent fix (version 4.12.4, 21 Sep): the parser validates every field against the maximum length in the specification and rejects the message if exceeded; copies use a bounded helper that cannot exceed the destination size; beneficiary_ref changed to a fixed-capacity string type with checked assignment. All 23 other fields of the parser reviewed for the same pattern; 2 further unbounded copies found and fixed (not yet triggered).
  • Extended format: support for 40-character references is scheduled for version 4.13 as a planned change, with the partner bank's specification.

9. Preventive actions

# Action Type Owner Due Status P1 Add libFuzzer targets for all wire-format parsers; run 30 min per target nightly; crashes block release Detect Vendor core engineering 2026-10-31 In progress P2 Add AddressSanitizer + UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer build and full regression run to CI for every merge Detect Vendor build team 2026-10-15 Done P3 Add "every copy bounded by destination size; every wire field length validated" to the parser review checklist Eliminate Vendor dev lead 2026-09-30 Done P4 Replace raw char[] fields in message structures with a bounded string type across the PGA Eliminate Vendor core engineering 2026-12-15 Planned P5 Lower restart alert threshold to 2 per 10 minutes and page on-call Diagnose Bank operations (recommended) 2026-10-05 Done P6 Agree notice period for partner message format changes Contain Bank integration team (recommended) 2026-10-31 Open

10. Verification

  • The reproduction test (40-character reference) fails under AddressSanitizer on 4.12.3 and passes on 4.12.4. Added to the regression suite as test_beneficiary_ref_overlength.
  • 10 million fuzzer-generated messages on 4.12.4 with AddressSanitizer: no reports.
  • Production: zero terminations from 21 Sep to 21 Oct, including month-end. Watched via restart count and the new pga.field_rejected counter (14 over-length references rejected cleanly during the period, all from the same partner, before their 4.13 switch).

Appendix A - Evidence (excerpts)

A.1 Core analysis, core 1 of 14 (PGA-1, 11:02:41):

Program terminated with signal SIGABRT, Aborted.
(gdb) p $_siginfo.si_signo
$1 = 6
(gdb) bt 8
#0  __pthread_kill_implementation (...) at pthread_kill.c:44
#1  raise (sig=6) at ../sysdeps/posix/raise.c:26
#2  abort () at abort.c:79
#3  __libc_message (fmt="%s\n") at ../sysdeps/posix/libc_fatal.c:150
#4  malloc_printerr (str="free(): invalid next size (fast)") at malloc.c:5664
#5  _int_free (...) at malloc.c:4472
#6  AuditRecord::~AuditRecord () at audit.cpp:58
#7  AuditQueue::flush () at audit.cpp:131
(gdb) x/6xg 0x7f2c4c012a40          # chunk following PaymentMessage at 0x7f2c4c0129a0
0x7f2c4c012a40: 0x0000000000003334  0x0000000000000000   <- "43" ASCII where size field expected

A.2 Log correlation (PGA-1; same kernel thread id 48213 in log and core):

ts=2026-09-17T11:02:40.912+05:30 lvl=INFO tid=48213 req=a91f... evt=req.start src=PARTNER-B ref_len=40
ts=2026-09-17T11:02:41.004+05:30 lvl=INFO tid=48213 req=a91f... evt=req.end result=OK
(process terminated 11:02:41.337, journal: code=dumped status=6/ABRT)

A.3 AddressSanitizer reproduction (test build of 4.12.3):

==9124==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x60e000000128
WRITE of size 1 at 0x60e000000128 thread T0
    #0 parse_beneficiary(...) payment_parser.cpp:212
    #1 parse_payment(...) payment_parser.cpp:388
0x60e000000128 is located 0 bytes after 168-byte region [0x60e000000080,0x60e000000128)
allocated by thread T0 here:
    #0 operator new(unsigned long)
    #1 PaymentMessage::create() payment_message.cpp:41

docs.title: 3.2 Example RCA 2: deadlock
docs.text:
ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE - fictional bank, system and data, written as a template.

Root Cause Analysis - INC-2026-1003: Core Banking Application Server unresponsive

Field Value Incident id INC-2026-1003 Client Example Bank Ltd. (fictional) Service Core Banking Application Server (CBAS), version 7.3.1, RPC-over-TCP Environment Production, node CBAS-APP-3 (Windows Server 2022) Severity Sev-1 (all branch transactions on one cluster blocked) Incident window 2026-10-03 18:47 IST to 2026-10-03 19:21 IST Document status Final, version 1.0 Prepared by Vendor product support, core engineering Reviewed by Vendor engineering head; bank IT head of applications

1. Executive summary

On 3 October 2026 between 18:47 and 19:21 IST, the core banking application server on node CBAS-APP-3 stopped responding. Branch users connected to that node (61 branches in the western region) could not complete transactions for 34 minutes; other nodes were unaffected. The server was restarted at 19:19 after a memory snapshot was taken, and service resumed at 19:21. No transaction was lost, duplicated or posted wrongly; transactions in progress at 18:47 were rolled back by the database and were re-entered by the branches.

The root cause is a deadlock: two internal locks in the server could be taken in opposite orders by two different operations - the end-of-day cash position update and the session timeout sweeper. When both ran at the same moment on the same branch session, each waited for the other forever, and all later requests queued behind them. The defect was introduced in version 7.3.0 (August 2026). It was triggered on 3 October by an extended end-of-day window that overlapped the sweeper's schedule. The fix (version 7.3.2) enforces a single lock order; it was deployed on 6 October.

2. Impact

Item Value Source Duration 34 min (18:47 - 19:21 IST) Server logs, monitoring Affected 61 branches (western region cluster), approx. 420 branch users Session table in dump, connection logs Requests not processed 1,874 requests timed out at the branch client Branch client logs aggregated by bank operations Transactions in progress at 18:47 37, rolled back by the database (not committed) DB logs Lost / duplicated / mis-posted transactions None Reconciliation 3 Oct 21:00 IST: 37 rolled-back references re-entered once each; no orphan postings Internet / mobile banking Not affected (served by other nodes) Monitoring SLA Sev-1 response met (acknowledged in 6 min); availability breach for the western cluster for the day Contract report

3. Timeline (all times IST, 2026-10-03 unless stated)

Time Event Source 2026-08-14 Version 7.3.0 released; adds locking of the session object during cash position update Release notes 18:30 End-of-day cash position job started, 30 min later than usual (bank-requested extension) Job scheduler log 18:47:12 Session sweeper starts its 15-minute cycle Server log evt=sweep.start 18:47:12 Last completed request on CBAS-APP-3; request queue starts growing Server log, queue-depth metric 18:49 Branch helpdesk receives first "transaction hanging" calls Bank helpdesk 18:52 Monitoring alert: CBAS-APP-3 queue depth > 500, zero completions Alerting 18:58 Vendor on-call acknowledges, Sev-1 declared; bridge opened; updates every 30 min Ticket 19:04 CPU near 0% on the process, threads alive: hang, not overload Performance monitor 19:08 Two full memory dumps taken 60 s apart with procdump -ma Evidence log, SHA-256 recorded 19:12 First dump analysed: 2 worker threads waiting on each other's lock; 46 workers waiting behind them Analysis (Appendix B.1) 19:15 Second dump: identical stacks for all blocked threads - deadlock confirmed Analysis 19:19 Process restarted; branch connections redistributed Change record EMG-2210 19:21 Transactions completing normally; queue depth zero Monitoring 19:30 Update to bank: service restored, cause identified as internal deadlock, fix in progress Bridge notes 21:00 Reconciliation complete: no lost, duplicated or mis-posted transactions Reconciliation report 10-04 16:00 Reproduced in test with stress harness; ThreadSanitizer reports lock-order inversion on 7.3.1 Test log (Appendix B.3) 10-06 02:00 Version 7.3.2 deployed to all nodes Change record CHG-5588 11-05 30-day observation (including month-end) complete, no recurrence; incident closed Monitoring

4. Root cause

4.1 The defect. The server protects two pieces of shared state with two locks:

  • cash_lock - protects the branch cash position table.
  • session_lock (per branch session) - protects the session object.

Version 7.3.0 changed the cash position update so that, while holding cash_lock, it also takes the branch's session_lock to stamp the session with the new position. The session sweeper, which already existed, takes session_lock and then, for sessions with open cash drawers, takes cash_lock to release the drawer:

Cash position update (thread A)        Session sweeper (thread B)
  lock(cash_lock)                        lock(session_lock[branch 0417])
  ...                                    ...
  lock(session_lock[branch 0417])  <-->  lock(cash_lock)
  waits forever for B                    waits forever for A

If both run for the same branch session at the same moment, each holds the lock the other needs. Neither can proceed and neither ever releases. This is a lock-order inversion deadlock. All further requests that need cash_lock (every cash transaction) or that branch's session queue behind them, and within about a minute every worker thread is blocked.

4.2 Evidence chain.

  1. Proven - process CPU near 0% with all threads alive, and two dumps 60 s apart show identical stacks for every blocked thread: nothing was progressing (Appendix B.1, B.2). This rules out an overload or slow database.
  2. Proven - !locks shows cash_lock (a critical section) owned by thread 0x1a2c, which is waiting in EnterCriticalSection for session_lock of branch session 0417, owned by thread 0x2f40. Thread 0x2f40 is waiting for cash_lock. That is a cycle (Appendix B.1).
  3. Proven - thread 0x1a2c's stack is in CashPosition::apply; thread 0x2f40's stack is in SessionSweeper::expire. Their call paths take the locks in opposite orders (source review of 7.3.1, cited lines in Appendix B.1).
  4. Proven - 46 other worker threads are waiting on cash_lock (!locks contention list), explaining the total loss of service.
  5. Proven - in test, a stress harness running both operations against one session deadlocks within 3 minutes on 7.3.1; ThreadSanitizer (Linux test build) reports lock-order-inversion (potential deadlock) naming the same two functions, even on runs that did not hang. On 7.3.2: no deadlock in 8 hours and no TSan report (Appendix B.3, section 10).

5. Trigger

The sweeper and the cash position update had never run at the same time in production: the update normally finishes by 18:30 and the sweeper's cycles were at 18:32 and 18:47. On 3 October the bank extended the end-of-day window by 30 minutes, so the cash position update ran from 18:30 and overlapped the 18:47 sweep. The overlap made the deadlock possible; it occurred when both reached branch session 0417 at the same moment. The extension is the trigger; the opposite lock order is the root cause. Without a fix, any overlap - for example on a slow month-end - could cause it again.

6. Contributing factors

  • No documented global lock order existed, so the 7.3.0 change could not be checked against one.
  • Concurrency tests ran the cash update and the sweeper separately, never together.
  • ThreadSanitizer was not part of CI (the Windows production build has no TSan; the Linux test build supports it but was not run under it).
  • The server had no lock-wait watchdog; a hang was detected by queue-depth alert after 5 minutes and diagnosed only by dump.
  • Restart procedure was correct (dumps taken first), which made the 30-minute diagnosis possible.

7. 5-whys
