  1. Why did branches lose service? All worker threads on CBAS-APP-3 were blocked.
  2. Why were they blocked? They waited for cash_lock, held by a thread that was itself blocked.
  3. Why was that thread blocked forever? It waited for a session lock held by the sweeper, which waited for cash_lock: a lock-order cycle.
  4. Why could the locks be taken in opposite orders? The 7.3.0 change added a nested lock without a defined global lock order to check against.
  5. Why was it not caught before release? No documented lock order, no test running both operations concurrently, and no ThreadSanitizer stage, which would have reported the inversion from a single non-hanging run.

8. Resolution

  • Mitigation (3 Oct): dumps captured, process restarted at 19:19. Until the fix, the sweeper schedule was moved to avoid the end-of-day window (configuration change, 3 Oct 22:00).
  • Permanent fix (version 7.3.2, 6 Oct): the cash position update no longer takes session_lock while holding cash_lock; it records the session stamp after releasing cash_lock. A global lock order (session before cash) is documented and enforced in debug and test builds by a lock- rank checker that fails immediately on an out-of-order acquisition. The sweeper's schedule restored.
  • All 14 other code paths that take two or more locks reviewed against the new order; one more latent inversion found (report generation versus branch close) and fixed in 7.3.2.

9. Preventive actions

# Action Type Owner Due Status P1 Document the global lock order in the architecture guide; review checklist item "new nested lock respects the order" Eliminate Vendor architect 2026-10-20 Done P2 Lock-rank checker enabled in all debug and test builds Detect Vendor core engineering 2026-10-06 Done (in 7.3.2) P3 ThreadSanitizer stage in CI on the Linux test build for the concurrency test suite Detect Vendor build team 2026-10-31 In progress P4 Concurrency test that runs all scheduled jobs against live sessions simultaneously Detect Vendor QA 2026-11-15 Planned P5 Lock-wait watchdog: log thread ids and lock names when a lock wait exceeds 10 s; alert Diagnose Vendor core engineering 2026-11-30 Planned P6 Alert on "zero completed requests for 60 s while queue > 0" Diagnose Bank operations (recommended) 2026-10-15 Done

10. Verification

  • Stress harness: 7.3.1 deadlocks within 3 minutes (5 of 5 runs); 7.3.2 runs 8 hours without deadlock (3 runs).
  • ThreadSanitizer: lock-order-inversion report on 7.3.1; clean on 7.3.2 for the full concurrency suite.
  • Lock-rank checker: deliberately reverting the fix in a test build makes the checker abort at the first out-of-order acquisition with both lock names, on every run.
  • Production: no hang and zero lock-watchdog events from 6 Oct to 5 Nov, including month-end (31 Oct) with the original sweeper schedule.

Appendix B - Evidence (excerpts)

B.1 Dump 1 (19:08:22), WinDbg:

0:000> !locks
CritSec cbas!g_cash_lock+0 at 00007ff6`4a2c1e40
WaiterWoken        No
LockCount          47
RecursionCount     1
OwningThread       1a2c
EntryCount         0
ContentionCount    2f
*** Locked

CritSec +2d81f3a8 at 000001d3`2d81f3a8          (Session 0417 session_lock)
LockCount          1
RecursionCount     1
OwningThread       2f40
*** Locked

0:000> ~~[1a2c]s ; k 6
 # Child-SP          RetAddr           Call Site
00 0000003c`9a6ff1a8 00007ffc`1e2d5c6e ntdll!NtWaitForAlertByThreadId+0x14
01 0000003c`9a6ff1b0 00007ffc`1e2a1a3b ntdll!RtlpWaitOnCriticalSection+0x1ee
02 0000003c`9a6ff2b0 00007ffc`1e2a1860 ntdll!RtlpEnterCriticalSectionContended+0x1cb
03 0000003c`9a6ff310 00007ff6`4a1b33c2 ntdll!RtlEnterCriticalSection+0x40
04 0000003c`9a6ff340 00007ff6`4a1b2a17 cbas!Session::lock+0x12 [session.cpp @ 88]
05 0000003c`9a6ff370 00007ff6`4a19e450 cbas!CashPosition::apply+0x1a7 [cash_position.cpp @ 214]

0:000> ~~[2f40]s ; k 6
 ...
03 0000003c`9b0ff0f0 00007ff6`4a19e9c1 ntdll!RtlEnterCriticalSection+0x40
04 0000003c`9b0ff120 00007ff6`4a1c0f22 cbas!CashDrawer::release+0x31 [cash_drawer.cpp @ 57]
05 0000003c`9b0ff160 00007ff6`4a1c0b10 cbas!SessionSweeper::expire+0xd2 [sweeper.cpp @ 143]

Holds / waits-for:

Thread Holds Waits for Held by 0x1a2c (CashPosition::apply) g_cash_lock session_lock 0417 0x2f40 0x2f40 (SessionSweeper::expire) session_lock 0417 g_cash_lock 0x1a2c 46 workers - g_cash_lock 0x1a2c

B.2 Dump 2 (19:09:23): ~*k output for threads 0x1a2c, 0x2f40 and the 46 workers identical to dump 1 frame for frame; !locks ContentionCount unchanged.

B.3 ThreadSanitizer, Linux test build of 7.3.1, stress harness:

WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: lock-order-inversion (potential deadlock) (pid=30117)
  Cycle in lock order graph: M1 (0x7b0c00000040) => M2 (0x7b1000001a80) => M1
  Mutex M2 acquired here while holding mutex M1 in thread T3:
    #1 Session::lock() session.cpp:88
    #2 CashPosition::apply(...) cash_position.cpp:214
  Mutex M1 acquired here while holding mutex M2 in thread T7:
    #1 CashDrawer::release(...) cash_drawer.cpp:57
    #2 SessionSweeper::expire(...) sweeper.cpp:143

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What a bank does with your RCA. The application owner reads the summary and impact; IT risk checks that the root cause is distinguished from the trigger and that preventive actions are owned and dated; the architecture team reads section 4 for whether the explanation is technically credible; audit later checks that the actions were closed. Regulators in many jurisdictions expect banks to report significant IT incidents and to show root-cause analysis and remediation; your document is the source for that. Write as if each section will be read by a different, sceptical person - because it will.

Causal models beyond 5-whys. 5-whys is linear; real incidents are usually a combination of conditions (a defect, a missing check, a trigger, slow detection). Two tools seniors use:

  • Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram: branches for code, design, process, testing, environment, people/communication; list causes on each. Good for finding contributing factors.
  • Fault tree / "necessary and sufficient": list the conditions that were all necessary (remove any one and the incident does not happen). Each necessary condition is a place a preventive action can break the chain. In RCA 2: the opposite lock order (defect), the overlap (trigger), the same session at the same moment (timing), no watchdog (slow detection). Breaking the first prevents every future occurrence; breaking the second only this one.

Why "proven" is a high bar for memory corruption. The crash site is not the bug site (module 03), so the dump alone rarely proves the cause. The chain usually needs: the dump showing what was corrupted (header bytes, freed-pattern), correlation showing which input preceded it, and a reproduction under ASan/PageHeap showing which line wrote it. Two of the three give a strong inference; all three give proof. Say which you have.

Why "proven" is achievable for deadlocks. A deadlock is a static state; the dump shows every thread, every lock owner and the cycle. Two dumps prove that nothing moves. That is why the deadlock RCA can state the root cause as proven within an hour, while a heap-corruption RCA often needs a reproduction first.

Preliminary versus final. Issue a preliminary RCA when the contract requires it, even if the root cause is not yet proven: impact, timeline, mitigation, current hypothesis clearly labelled, and what you are doing to confirm it. The final RCA replaces it; keep a version history so the reader can see what changed and why.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Start the RCA during the incident. The incident log of module 11 (timestamped actions and observations) becomes section 3 almost unchanged. Reconstructing a timeline from memory a week later is unreliable and slow.
  • Have someone who did not work the incident review it. The reviewer checks: can the summary be understood without the rest; is every root-cause claim backed by appendix evidence; is the trigger separated; does each preventive action have owner, date and a "done when".
  • The "could not reproduce" RCA. Sometimes you cannot prove the root cause. The honest version: evidence gathered, most likely mechanism with its supporting evidence, what else was ruled out and how, mitigation in place, diagnostics added so the next occurrence will be conclusive, and the RCA stays open. Banks accept this far more readily than a confident wrong answer that fails a month later.
  • Repeat incidents. Before writing, search previous RCAs for the same stack signature or component. If this is a recurrence, say so in the summary and explain why the previous fix did not hold. Hiding it is found out in the client's quarterly review.
  • Third-party causes. If the bug is in a library, OS or database, prove it (a minimal reproduction, the vendor's bug id). Even then, the RCA usually has a part you own: why your system was exposed, why there was no containment.
  • What you leave out. Internal blame, speculation not labelled as such, customer personal data (mask account numbers in evidence), and full dumps (reference them by id and hash; they stay in the secure store).
  • Shakir's context. For Extrieve-style deployments at HDFC Bank or Kotak Mahindra Bank, the bank usually has its own RCA template and review board. Map this module's sections onto their template; the content requirements are the same. Keep the WinDbg excerpts short (the 6 lines that prove it, not 200 lines of !analyze -v).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - trigger or root cause. For each, label trigger, root cause or symptom, and rewrite the wrong ones: "server ran out of file descriptors"; "a new partner sent an empty amount field"; "connections were not closed on the error path"; "Windows patch Tuesday"; "an unordered_map was modified by two threads without a lock". Done when each has a label and a one-line justification using the "will it survive tomorrow" test.
  2. Easy - critique a summary. Rewrite this summary for a bank: "Due to an unexpected issue the xferd module crashed several times. The developer has fixed it. Root cause was high load. We apologise for any inconvenience caused and regret the same." Done when the rewrite states what failed, impact with numbers, the root cause, trigger, fix and data integrity in under 8 sentences.
  3. Medium - RCA from the course's deadlock. Run m10_deadlock, take two gcores (module 11 evidence script), and write sections 4 (root cause with evidence chain), 5, 7 and 10 of an RCA for it, with your real LWPs and stacks in an appendix. Done when every claim in section 4 is labelled proven, inferred or hypothesis and points to an appendix item.
  4. Medium - RCA from the heap overflow. Using m04_heap_overflow (no ASan core plus an ASan reproduction), write a complete RCA following RCA 1 as a template, inventing a plausible trigger. Done when a reviewer can find the root cause, the trigger and three preventive actions that are specific, owned, dated and verifiable.
  5. Hard - the unprovable one. Write a preliminary RCA for m10_data_race as if you had only one core showing a crash in _Rb_tree_insert_and_rebalance and no reproduction yet. Done when the document makes no unproven claim as fact, lists what was ruled out, and names the diagnostic you added to make the next occurrence conclusive.
  6. Hard - your own incident. Take a real incident from your work (anonymise the bank, people and numbers) and rewrite its RCA in this structure. Done when you can present it in 5 minutes in an interview, including the trigger-versus-root-cause distinction and one preventive action that would have stopped it.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between the trigger and the root cause? A: The trigger is the event that exposed the problem at that time - a traffic spike, an unusual input, a schedule overlap. The root cause is the defect that made the system fail under that event; removing it makes the trigger harmless. Test: if the trigger recurs tomorrow, will the system survive? If not, you have only described the trigger.

Q: Walk me through the structure of an RCA you would send a bank. A: Header, executive summary in plain words, impact with numbers and data-integrity statement, timestamped timeline with sources, root cause with a labelled evidence chain, trigger, contributing factors, 5-whys down to the process gap, resolution (mitigation and permanent fix), owned and dated preventive actions, verification of the fix and of its holding in production, and an appendix of evidence excerpts.

Q: How do you write an RCA when you could not prove the root cause? A: Issue it as preliminary: state the evidence, the most likely mechanism labelled as a hypothesis, what was ruled out and how, the mitigation in place, and the diagnostics added so the next occurrence is conclusive. Keep it open with a review date. A confident wrong root cause costs far more credibility when the incident recurs.

Q: What makes a preventive action good? A: It is specific, owned, dated and verifiable, and it addresses the process gap, not only the bug: eliminating the bug class, detecting it earlier, containing it or diagnosing it faster. "Add a libFuzzer target for the parser to nightly CI by 30 Nov, owner X, done when it runs" is an action; "improve testing" is not.

Q: Why does a heap-corruption RCA usually need a reproduction while a deadlock RCA does not? A: The heap corruption is detected later, in other code, so the dump shows where the damage was found, not who did it; you need correlation plus an ASan or PageHeap reproduction to prove the writing line. A deadlock is a frozen state: the dump shows every waiter, every owner and the cycle, and two dumps prove nothing is moving.

Q: What tone do you use with a banking client? A: Factual, calm and owning: precise numbers and timestamps with timezone, "a defect in our code", no internal names or blame, one sentence of acknowledgement rather than repeated apology, plain words in the summary and precision in the technical section, and an explicit statement about whether any transaction was lost, duplicated or mis-posted and how that was verified.

Q: How far should the 5-whys go? A: Past the bug, to the process that let it ship: why review, tests and tooling did not catch it. Stop when the next answer is outside your control or is a process you can change. Never end at a person; "a developer made a mistake" is always followed by "why did the system allow it to reach production?".

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• An RCA: header, summary, impact, timeline, root cause with evidence, trigger, contributing factors, 5-whys, resolution, preventive actions, verification, appendix.
  • The trigger is why it happened that day; the root cause is why the system could fail at all. Test: will it survive the trigger tomorrow?
  • Label every claim as proven, inferred or hypothesis; evidence goes in the appendix.
  • Technical root cause plus process root cause: the bug and why it shipped.
  • Banking tone: factual, owning, blameless, numbers and timezones, explicit data-integrity statement, plain summary.
  • Preventive actions are specific, owned, dated, verifiable; classify as eliminate, detect, contain, diagnose.
  • Verification has two parts: the fix fixes it (fails before, passes after) and the fix holds (a metric over a period including high-risk windows).
  • Heap corruption RCAs need correlation plus reproduction; deadlock RCAs are proven by two dumps.
  • Preliminary RCAs are honest about uncertainty and add diagnostics; they stay open.

docs.title: 13. Defensive design to prevent the bugs
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 04, 08, 12

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Modules 01 to 12 taught you to find memory bugs after they have hurt someone. This module is about making them impossible, or at least making them fail loudly in your test lab instead of quietly at a bank. It is the "preventive actions" column of every RCA, turned into habits.

The analogy is a building. You can hire excellent firefighters (debuggers, dumps, RCAs). You can also build with fire-resistant materials (RAII, bounded types), install smoke detectors that go off early (assertions, sanitizers in CI), run fire drills with random fires (fuzzing), have an inspector check the plans (static analysis, code review), and fit fire doors that stop a fire spreading (hardening flags that turn an exploit into a clean crash). Each layer catches what the others miss. None of them is enough alone.

The order matters for cost: a bug made impossible by the type system costs nothing; a bug caught by a compiler warning costs a minute; by a sanitizer in CI, an hour; by a fuzzer, a day; in production, an incident, a dump, an RCA, and the client's trust.

docs.title: 2.1 RAII: make ownership impossible to get wrong
docs.text:
RAII ("Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation") means: every resource (memory, file, socket, lock, DB connection) is owned by an object whose destructor releases it. When the object goes out of scope - by normal return, early return or exception - the resource is released exactly once.

What it eliminates, from module 04's catalogue:

Bug class RAII tool Why it cannot happen any more Leak on early return / exception std::unique_ptr, containers, std::lock_guard Destructors run on every exit path Double free std::unique_ptr (move-only) Exactly one owner; moving transfers it Use after free (single-thread) Ownership in one place; others hold ids or weak_ptr Nobody keeps a raw pointer past the owner's lifetime Lifetime races (multi-thread) std::shared_ptr captured by each user, or owner joins users before destroying The object lives while anyone uses it Lock not released std::lock_guard, std::scoped_lock, std::unique_lock Unlock in the destructor Deadlock from inconsistent order of two locks std::scoped_lock(a, b) Acquires both with a deadlock-avoidance algorithm

Rules that make RAII work in practice:

  • No naked new/delete or malloc/free in application code. Use std::make_unique, std::make_shared, std::vector, std::string. A raw new is a code-review finding.
  • One owner. Decide who owns every object. Everyone else gets a reference valid for one call, or an id they look up again (code/m13_raii_fix.cpp, SessionTable).
  • Wrap C resources once. For a C API (FILE*, a socket fd, a DB handle from a C library) write a small wrapper or use unique_ptr with a custom deleter:
struct FileCloser { void operator()(std::FILE *f) const noexcept { if (f) std::fclose(f); } };
using FilePtr = std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser>;
FilePtr f{std::fopen("ledger.csv", "r")};      // closed on every exit path
  • shared_ptr is for shared ownership, not for "I could not decide". It costs an atomic refcount and makes lifetime harder to reason about. Cycles leak (module 09); break them with weak_ptr.
  • For C code (much of your existing code): the equivalent discipline is a single cleanup path (goto cleanup; with every resource initialised to NULL at the top and released once at the bottom), and ownership comments on every pointer parameter (/* borrowed */, /* takes ownership */).

docs.title: 2.2 Bounds-checked access
docs.text:
Out-of-bounds writes are the most dangerous bug class: they corrupt the heap (module 03) and are the basis of most memory-safety exploits.

  • Use types that know their size. std::vector, std::array, std::string, std::span (C++20) or gsl::span, std::string_view. A char* plus a separate length is two things that can disagree.
  • .at() where an index comes from input. Throws std::out_of_range instead of corrupting. Use [] in hot loops where the bound is the container's own size().
  • Hardened standard library in debug and test (and often in production). -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS (libstdc++) makes operator[], front(), back(), iterator dereferences and more check their preconditions and abort. MSVC: _ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL=2 (debug default) or _CONTAINER_DEBUG_LEVEL=1. The cost of _GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS is usually small (a compare and branch per access); measure before deciding to drop it from production.
  • Range-for and algorithms over index arithmetic. for (auto &x : v) cannot go out of bounds; for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i) can.
  • Validate lengths at the boundary. Every length field from the wire is checked against the protocol maximum and the destination size before any copy. The parser in RCA 1 of module 12 and code/m13_fuzz_target.cpp both trusted the wire.
  • C string functions: never strcpy, strcat, sprintf, gets. Use snprintf and check the result; prefer std::string. strncpy does not always terminate; it is not the safe version people think.
  • Integer sizes: sizes are size_t; check multiplications before allocating (if (count > SIZE_MAX / elem) fail;) - m04_integer_overflow_size.cpp and allocate_table in m13_raii_fix.cpp.

docs.title: 2.3 Assertions and contracts
docs.text:
An assertion states something that must be true if the program is correct. If it is false, the program has a bug, and the safest thing is to stop now, close to the cause, rather than continue and crash far away (module 03's "found, not done" problem).

  • Preconditions at function entry (arguments in range, pointer non-null, lock held), postconditions before return, invariants of a class at the end of each public method (balance == sum(entries), size <= capacity).
  • assert() is compiled out with -DNDEBUG, which most release builds define. Keep it for checks that are expensive or purely for development.
  • For checks that guard money or memory safety, use an always-on assertion that logs and aborts in production too (so you get a core and a clear message instead of corrupted data):
// Always-on check: stays in release builds. Aborting with a core beats posting a wrong balance.
#define ALWAYS_ASSERT(cond, msg)                                                   \
    do {                                                                           \
        if (!(cond)) [[unlikely]] {                                                \
            std::fprintf(stderr, "ASSERT FAILED %s:%d %s: %s\n",                   \
                         __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond, msg);                          \
            std::abort();                                                          \
        }                                                                          \
    } while (0)

(Macro line continuations are backslashes on preprocessor lines, which is fine; the rule in this course is only that a // comment line must never end with one, because the next line would silently become part of the comment.)

  • Assertions are not error handling. Bad input is expected and gets an error response. A broken invariant is a bug and gets an abort. Asserting on user input turns a malformed message into a denial of service.
  • Contracts in C++: C++26 adds contract assertions (pre, post, contract_assert). Until your compiler and codebase use them, the macros above and [[nodiscard]] on functions whose return value must be checked (error codes, try_lock) give most of the benefit.
  • Debug-only structural checks are a form of assertion too: the lock-rank checker from module 10 (abort on out-of-order acquisition), canary fields in structs (uint32_t magic = 0xC0FFEE11; checked on every access, set to 0xDEADDEAD in the destructor) that catch use-after-free and overwrites close to the cause.

docs.title: 2.4 Fuzzing with libFuzzer
docs.text:
Fuzzing feeds a function millions of automatically generated inputs and watches for crashes, hangs and sanitizer reports. Coverage-guided fuzzers (libFuzzer, AFL++) keep inputs that reach new code and mutate them further, so they find their way through parsers that random input never gets past.

A libFuzzer target is one function:

extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const uint8_t *data, size_t size)
{
    Request r{};
    parse_request(data, size, r);      // must not crash, leak, hang or trigger UB for ANY input
    return 0;
}

code/m13_fuzz_target.cpp contains a request parser with a deliberate off-by-one and this target. Built with clang++ -fsanitize=fuzzer,address,undefined, it finds the bug in seconds (section 3).

What to fuzz in a banking server: every parser of external input (ISO 8583, ISO 20022 XML, fixed- width files from partners, your RPC wire format, config files), decoders (base64, compression), and anything with length fields. What makes a good target:

  • Deterministic and fast: no network, no disk, no global state carried between calls (or reset it). Thousands of executions per second.
  • Sanitizers on: a fuzzer without ASan finds only crashes; with ASan and UBSan it finds the silent overflow that would have corrupted the heap.
  • A seed corpus: a handful of real (anonymised) valid messages in corpus/ gives the fuzzer a head start.
  • Dictionaries (-dict=) of protocol tokens help with text formats.
  • Regression: every crash input found becomes a unit test. CI runs the target for a few minutes on every change and for longer nightly; tools like OSS-Fuzz / ClusterFuzzLite run them continuously.

GCC has no libFuzzer; on Linux use clang for fuzz builds. On Windows, MSVC supports /fsanitize=fuzzer alongside /fsanitize=address (VS 2022).

docs.title: 2.5 Static analysis
docs.text:
Static analysers read the source without running it and report likely bugs: null dereferences on some path, leaks on an error path, use after move, uninitialised variables, buffer overruns with known sizes, lock misuse.

Tool Platform Run as Strengths Compiler warnings all -Wall -Wextra ..., /W4 Cheapest, fastest, always on clang-tidy Linux, Windows clang-tidy -p build/ file.cpp with compile_commands.json Modernisation (modernize-*), C++ Core Guidelines (cppcoreguidelines-*), bug patterns (bugprone-*), Clang Static Analyzer path checks (clang-analyzer-*) cppcheck Linux, Windows cppcheck --enable=warning,performance,portability --inconclusive --project=compile_commands.json Works on C and C++ without a full compile; good at buffer, leak and null checks in C code MSVC /analyze Windows cl /analyze or "Run Code Analysis" in Visual Studio Path-sensitive checks; with SAL annotations (_In_reads_(n), _Out_writes_(n)) it checks buffer sizes across calls - very relevant for C and Win32 code Clang Static Analyzer Linux scan-build make Deep inter-procedural path analysis

Practical adoption on an existing codebase:

  • Generate compile_commands.json (CMake: -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON; make: bear -- make).
  • Start with a small, high-value check set (bugprone-*, clang-analyzer-*, cppcoreguidelines-owning-memory is noisy on legacy code - add later).
  • Baseline: record today's findings and fail CI only on new findings in changed files. A wall of 4,000 old warnings gets ignored; zero new warnings per change is enforceable.
  • Suppressions are local and justified (// NOLINT(bugprone-xyz): reason), never global.

docs.title: 2.6 Warnings as errors
docs.text:
Compiler warnings are free static analysis. Many memory bugs of module 04 are warnings first: uninitialised variables (-Wmaybe-uninitialized), sign/size confusion (-Wsign-compare, -Wconversion), format string mismatches (-Wformat), returning a reference to a local (-Wreturn-local-addr), missing return, fall-through in switch.

A recommended GCC/Clang set for new code (the one m13_raii_fix.cpp builds clean with):

-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror
-Wshadow -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion -Wnon-virtual-dtor -Wold-style-cast
-Wcast-align -Wnull-dereference -Wdouble-promotion -Wformat=2 -Wimplicit-fallthrough

MSVC: /W4 /WX /permissive- and consider /w14640 (thread-unsafe static init) and /we4715 (not all paths return).

Rules: -Werror in CI and developer builds always; for third-party headers use -isystem so their warnings do not fail your build; on a legacy codebase, turn on warnings one at a time and fix them module by module. Compiler upgrades add warnings; budget for them.

docs.title: 2.7 Hardening flags
docs.text:
Hardening flags do not remove bugs. They turn a silent corruption or an exploitable overflow into an immediate, diagnosable crash, and make exploitation harder. For a bank that is a security requirement as much as a reliability one.

Flag Compiler What it does Cost -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 (or =3, GCC 12+) GCC/Clang, needs -O1+ Replaces memcpy, strcpy, sprintf, read... with checked versions when the destination size is known at compile time (=3 also when known at runtime via __builtin_dynamic_object_size); aborts with *** buffer overflow detected *** Very low -fstack-protector-strong GCC/Clang Canary between locals and the return address in functions with arrays or address-taken locals; checked before return: *** stack smashing detected *** Low /GS MSVC (default on) Same idea; failure is 0xC0000409 (module 07) Low -fstack-clash-protection GCC/Clang Probes each page when growing the stack by large amounts so a huge alloca/VLA cannot jump over the guard page Low -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS libstdc++ Bounds and precondition checks in containers (2.2) Low to moderate -fPIE -pie, -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now, -Wl,-z,noexecstack GCC/Clang + ld Full ASLR for the executable; read-only GOT after startup; non-executable stack Very low -fcf-protection=full GCC/Clang x86 Intel CET: indirect branch tracking and shadow stack (when CPU and kernel support it) Low /guard:cf (CFG) MSVC + linker Control Flow Guard: indirect calls checked against a bitmap of valid targets; a corrupted function pointer or vtable becomes a fail-fast 0xC0000409 instead of a jump to attacker data Low /DYNAMICBASE, /HIGHENTROPYVA, /NXCOMPAT MSVC linker (defaults) ASLR, 64-bit high-entropy ASLR, DEP None /CETCOMPAT MSVC linker Hardware shadow stack on supported Windows and CPUs Low

The Ubuntu 24.04 GCC enables several of these by default (_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 at -O1+, -fstack-protector-strong, -fstack-clash-protection, PIE, -fcf-protection). Check with gcc -Q --help=common or checksec --file=binary; do not assume your production build environment matches your laptop. Pass them explicitly in the build system.

Relationship to dumps: a hardening abort produces a better core than the corruption it prevented. *** buffer overflow detected *** from __chk_fail has the guilty memcpy caller on the stack; the unhardened version would have crashed in malloc an hour later.

docs.title: 2.8 A memory-safety code review checklist
docs.text:
Print this and use it for every change to C or C++ code in a server. Each line is a bug class from this course.

Ownership and lifetime

  • Every allocation has exactly one owner; no naked new/delete/malloc/free outside a wrapper.
  • No raw pointer or reference is stored beyond the call that received it (ids or weak_ptr instead).
  • Objects used by other threads, timers or callbacks outlive them (or are shared_ptr captured); shutdown stops and joins users before destroying.
  • No reference, pointer or iterator into a container is used after an insert, erase or push_back that may invalidate it (m04_invalid_iterator).
  • No std::string_view / std::span outlives the data it views.

Bounds and sizes

  • Every copy is bounded by the destination size; every wire length is validated against the spec maximum and the destination.
  • Sizes are size_t; multiplication and addition of sizes checked for overflow before allocation.
  • No strcpy/strcat/sprintf/gets; snprintf results checked; strncpy termination handled.
  • Loops use < with the container's own size, or range-for.

Initialisation

  • Every variable and member initialised at declaration (int x = 0;, default member initialisers, T obj{};).
  • Struct copied to the wire or disk is zero-initialised (no padding leaks).

Errors and early exits

  • Every error path releases what the success path releases (RAII makes this automatic).
  • Return values of [[nodiscard]] functions, system calls and snprintf are checked.
  • Exceptions cannot escape destructors, thread functions or C callbacks.

Concurrency

  • Every shared mutable variable is protected by a named lock or is std::atomic; the comment says which lock.
  • New nested lock acquisitions follow the documented global lock order; multiple locks taken with std::scoped_lock.
  • No blocking call (I/O, DB, RPC, sleep) while holding a lock that request threads need.
  • Condition variable waits use a predicate loop.
  • Signal handlers call only async-signal-safe functions (module 11).

Observability

  • New error paths log with request id and a stable event name.
  • Invariants that protect money or memory safety use an always-on assertion.

Tests

  • New parsing code has a fuzz target; new concurrent code runs under TSan in CI; the change passes the ASan+UBSan suite.

docs.title: 3.1 The fixed versions: code/m13_raii_fix.cpp
docs.text:
This file rewrites the bugs of m04_use_after_free, m04_heap_overflow, m09_leak and m06_crash_example the defensive way. It builds clean with the strict warning set and the hardening flags, and every sanitizer run is clean:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion -pthread \
    -g -O2 -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS -fstack-protector-strong -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 \
    -o build/m13_raii_fix m13_raii_fix.cpp
./build/m13_raii_fix
# audit: session 1 no longer exists
# audit: 2 other 100
# sum 4500
# accepted 750/1000, nothing leaked
# rejected: table too large
# fee applied: 975
./build_debug.sh asan && ./build/m13_raii_fix_asan     # no report
valgrind --leak-check=full ./build/m13_raii_fix_debug   # "All heap blocks were freed"

The key patterns, one per bug class:

// Use-after-free -> one owner; callers keep ids, not pointers.
class SessionTable {
    std::unordered_map<long, std::unique_ptr<Session>> sessions_;
public:
    void close(long id) { sessions_.erase(id); }            // unique_ptr deletes; nothing dangles
    const Session *find(long id) const;                     // valid for this call only; may be null
};

// Heap overflow -> the container is the bound; .at() throws instead of corrupting.
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < totals.size(); ++i) totals.at(i) = static_cast<int>(i) * 100;

// Leak on early return -> the resource dies with the scope.
auto r = std::make_unique<Request>(Request{id, std::string(64, 'x')});
if (r->id % 4 == 0) return false;                           // freed here too

// Size overflow -> policy limit checked before the multiplication.
if (count > kMax) throw std::length_error("table too large");

Exercise 1 below asks you to break each one back and watch which layer (warning, hardened library, sanitizer) catches it.

docs.title: 3.2 Fuzzing: code/m13_fuzz_target.cpp
docs.text:
The parser copies an account id into char account[12] with a wrong bound check (j > sizeof out.account instead of j + 1 >= sizeof out.account). For an account id of 12 characters it writes the terminator to account[12], one past the end of the array; for a longer one it writes a character to account[12] before the check rejects the input. The plain build runs four hand-written inputs and looks fine.

There is a lesson hidden in this file. account is a member of struct Request { char kind; char account[12]; long amount; }. Offset 13 (account[12]) is padding inside the same struct, before amount at offset 16. AddressSanitizer works at the granularity of whole allocations: the write is still inside the 24-byte Request object, so ASan sees nothing wrong. Most people expect an ASan heap-buffer-overflow here; predicting that it will not appear, and saying why, is a good interview answer. What catches it is UBSan's -fsanitize=bounds check (included in clang's -fsanitize=undefined), which knows the array type is char[12] and checks the index. UBSan only prints by default and carries on, so make it fatal for the fuzzer:

sudo apt install clang          # once; libFuzzer ships with clang
clang++ -std=c++17 -g -O1 -fsanitize=fuzzer,address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all -DFUZZING \
    -o build/m13_fuzz m13_fuzz_target.cpp
mkdir -p corpus && printf 'D:ACC-1:100\n' > corpus/seed1
./build/m13_fuzz corpus -max_len=256 -timeout=5
# INFO: Seed: 2344653046
# INFO:        1 files found in corpus
# m13_fuzz_target.cpp:35:9: runtime error: index 12 out of bounds for type 'char[12]'
# SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior m13_fuzz_target.cpp:35:9
# MS: 1 InsertRepeatedBytes-; base unit: ...
# artifact_prefix='./'; Test unit written to ./crash-661bf4dbc4c7659ddff3685176cb9050b56159d0
./build/m13_fuzz crash-<sha1>   # reproduces deterministically: this file becomes a unit test

That is real output from clang 18 on Ubuntu 24.04: one mutation of the seed (MS: 1) was enough.

A second lesson from the same file. Build the plain program with g++ -O0 and with g++ -O2 and run the four samples. At -O0 the over-long D:ACCOUNT-TOO-LONG-1:1 is rejected as bad. At -O2 it is accepted as ok with account=ACCOUNT-TOO-LON - 15 characters in a 12-byte array. The write account[j] with j == 12 is undefined behaviour, so GCC may assume it never happens, conclude that j > 12 is always false, and delete the check. The program now overflows into amount and beyond, silently, and only in the optimised build - which is the one you ship. This is why "it works in debug" proves nothing about memory bugs, and why UBSan belongs in CI.

If the same field were the last member of a heap object - as in RCA 1 of module 12 - the write would leave the allocation and ASan would report heap-buffer-overflow. If it were followed directly by another member with no padding, it would silently overwrite that member and only UBSan bounds checking, _FORTIFY_SOURCE (for library copies) or a review would catch it. Defence in layers, in one struct.

Fix the bound to j + 1 >= sizeof out.account, rebuild, and run the fuzzer for 10 minutes: no report.

docs.title: 3.3 Static analysis on the course code
docs.text:
sudo apt install clang-tidy cppcheck
cd code
clang-tidy m04_use_after_free.cpp m04_double_free.cpp m09_leak.cpp \
    -checks='-*,clang-analyzer-*,bugprone-*,cppcoreguidelines-owning-memory' -- -std=c++17
# Typical findings (exact wording and which ones fire depend on the clang-tidy version):
#   [clang-analyzer-cplusplus.NewDelete]       use of memory after it is freed
#   [clang-analyzer-unix.Malloc]               attempt to free released memory
#   [clang-analyzer-cplusplus.NewDeleteLeaks]  potential leak of memory
#   [cppcoreguidelines-owning-memory]          raw new/delete outside an owner type
# Whether the analyzer follows the pointer across functions decides whether it finds the bug.
cppcheck --enable=warning --inconclusive m04_*.cpp m09_leak.cpp
clang-tidy m13_raii_fix.cpp -checks='-*,clang-analyzer-*,bugprone-*' -- -std=c++17   # clean

Note what static analysis finds (single-function, single-thread ownership errors) and what it does not (races, overflows whose size depends on runtime input across many functions). That gap is why you also need sanitizers and fuzzing.

docs.title: 3.4 The CI build matrix
docs.text:
This is the build matrix the preventive actions of module 12 ask for, as a shell sketch (module 08's exercise 6 builds it out):

STRICT="-std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion -pthread"
HARDEN="-O2 -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS -fstack-protector-strong \
        -fstack-clash-protection -fcf-protection=full -fPIE -pie -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now"
g++ $STRICT $HARDEN                                   -o out/release   src.cpp   # what ships
g++ $STRICT -g -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -o out/asan src.cpp
g++ $STRICT -g -O1 -fsanitize=thread                  -o out/tsan     src.cpp
clang++ -std=c++17 -g -O1 -fsanitize=fuzzer,address,undefined -DFUZZING -o out/fuzz fuzz.cpp
# test stage: run the suite on release, asan, tsan with halt_on_error=1; fuzz for 5 min;
# clang-tidy on changed files; any finding fails the merge request.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
How _FORTIFY_SOURCE works. glibc's headers, when _FORTIFY_SOURCE > 0 and optimisation is on, redirect memcpy(d, s, n) to __memcpy_chk(d, s, n, __builtin_object_size(d, 0)). The compiler substitutes the size of d if it can see it (a local array, a struct member, a malloc with a constant size); if it cannot, the size is (size_t)-1 and the check is a no-op. =3 uses __builtin_dynamic_object_size, which can also track sizes known only at runtime (e.g. malloc(n) with n a variable), catching more. On failure __chk_fail prints *** buffer overflow detected *** and aborts. That is why it needs -O1 or higher: object-size tracking happens in the optimiser.

How the stack protector works. At function entry the compiler loads a random canary from thread-local storage (fs:0x28 on x86-64 Linux) and stores it between the local arrays and the saved registers/return address; before ret it compares and calls __stack_chk_fail on mismatch. A linear overflow of a local array must overwrite the canary before it reaches the return address. -strong instruments every function with a local array or an address-taken local (a middle ground between -fstack-protector, which only covers char arrays of 8+ bytes, and -all). It does not catch overflows that skip the canary (an indexed write buf[i] with a wild i) or overflows of heap objects.

How CFG works. The linker emits a bitmap of valid indirect-call targets (function entry points). Every indirect call is preceded by a call to _guard_check_icall / __guard_dispatch_icall_fptr, which looks the target up in the bitmap, provided by the OS loader. A corrupted function pointer or vtable entry that points into the middle of a function or into data fails the check and the process fail-fasts with 0xC0000409 (subcode FAST_FAIL_GUARD_ICALL_ CHECK_FAILURE). In a dump this looks different from the access violation you would otherwise get

  • module 07 shows how to decode the subcode. Intel CET's indirect branch tracking (endbr64 instructions at valid targets) is the hardware version on Linux.

How libFuzzer finds the bug so fast. -fsanitize=fuzzer adds SanitizerCoverage: a callback or counter at every edge of the control-flow graph, plus comparison tracing (__sanitizer_cov_ trace_cmp) that records operands of == and switch. When an input reaches a new edge, it is kept in the corpus. Comparison tracing lets the fuzzer see "the code compared byte 1 with ':'" and insert ':' there, so it gets through the format checks in a handful of iterations instead of random luck. Then it mutates the account field length upward until ASan reports.

Why static analysis has false positives and negatives. Path-sensitive analysers explore paths symbolically and must cut off (loop unrolling bounds, inter-procedural depth, unknown library behaviour). Cutting off loses real bugs (false negatives); approximating unknown values as "anything" reports paths that cannot happen (false positives). SAL annotations on Windows and [[gnu::nonnull]], [[nodiscard]], ownership types (unique_ptr, gsl::owner<T*>) in C++ give the analyser facts it cannot infer, which reduces both.

Assertions and the optimiser. assert(p != nullptr) before *p documents the precondition; in release (NDEBUG) it disappears. An always-on check followed by abort() (a noreturn function) lets the optimiser assume the condition after the check, which can make later code faster. The dangerous variant is __builtin_unreachable() / [[assume]] used as an assertion: if the condition is false, behaviour is undefined, and the optimiser may delete your safety checks. Never use assume-style hints for conditions that depend on input.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Legacy C code is where your bank servers live. You will not rewrite it in C++ with RAII. The realistic path: warnings on and fixed module by module; -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE and stack protector in the release build (often a zero-code-change win); ASan in the test environment; fuzz targets for the parsers that take external input; clang-tidy/cppcheck//analyze with a baseline so new code is clean; RAII-style wrappers for every new C++ component.
  • Hardening changes the crash signature. After enabling _FORTIFY_SOURCE or CFG, some old "random" crashes turn into *** buffer overflow detected *** or 0xC0000409. That is the flag working: it has turned a heap-corruption investigation into a one-line fix. Tell operations to expect it, and treat the first such crash as a gift.
  • ASan in a staging environment. An ASan build of the whole server in a staging environment that replays production traffic (anonymised) finds bugs no unit test reaches. Memory cost is about 2-3x and CPU about 2x (typical figures from the ASan documentation); a staging box can afford it.
  • Release builds keep some checks on. _GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS, always-on asserts for money invariants, and the stack protector cost little. Turning them off for "performance" without a profile showing they matter trades a cheap abort-with-core for an expensive corruption incident.
  • Review checklists rot if they are long and generic. Keep the checklist in the merge-request template, and add a line every time an RCA finds a class of bug the checklist did not cover. The checklist then becomes the memory of every incident.
  • Measure the layers. In RCAs, record which layer should have caught the bug and why it did not. After a year, the pattern tells you where to invest (e.g. "6 of 9 incidents were parsing bugs: fuzzing first").

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - break it back. In a copy of m13_raii_fix.cpp, reintroduce one bug at a time: [] with i <= size() instead of .at(); a raw new with an early return; a raw Session* kept after close. For each, record which layer catches it: strict warnings, _GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS, ASan, LSan, or none. Done when you have a 3-row table with an observed (not guessed) answer per cell.
  2. Easy - checksec. Build m04_heap_overflow.cpp twice: with no flags and with the HARDEN set from 3.4. Run checksec --file= (from the checksec package) or readelf -lW/-d on both. Done when you can point at PIE, RELRO, canary, NX and FORTIFY in the output and say which flag produced each.
  3. Medium - fuzz and fix. Build and run the fuzzer from 3.2, save the crash input, turn it into a unit test in the plain build, fix the bound, re-run the fuzzer for 10 minutes. Done when the crash input passes, the fuzzer runs clean, and you can explain why the plain build's four samples did not show the bug.
  4. Medium - FORTIFY in action. Write a 10-line program that strcpys argv[1] into the char buf[16] member of a struct allocated with new (taking it from argv avoids a compile-time -Wstringop-overflow error). Run it with a 20-character argument. Build with -O2 with -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE and again with -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2. Done when one build prints *** buffer overflow detected *** and you can show __strcpy_chk in objdump -d and bt of the core.
  5. Hard - static analysis baseline. Run clang-tidy and cppcheck on every file in code/. Make a table of which tool found which deliberate bug and which bugs no static tool found. Then write a script that fails only if the finding count increases relative to a saved baseline. Done when adding a new strcpy to any file makes the script fail and nothing else does.
  6. Hard - fuzz a real parser. Write a fuzz target for a parser you have written or used (an RPC message decoder, a fixed-width record reader, a config parser), with a seed corpus of three valid inputs. Run it for an hour with ASan and UBSan. Done when you have either a found bug with a reproduction test, or the coverage report (-print_final_stats=1, or -fprofile-instr-generate with llvm-cov) showing which branches the fuzzer reached and which it did not.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does RAII prevent memory bugs? A: It ties every resource to an object whose destructor releases it, so release happens exactly once on every exit path, including early returns and exceptions. That eliminates leaks on error paths, double frees (one owner via unique_ptr), unreleased locks (lock_guard), and with clear ownership and ids instead of stored raw pointers, most single-threaded use-after-free.

Q: What does _FORTIFY_SOURCE do and what are its limits? A: It redirects functions like memcpy, strcpy and sprintf to checked variants that know the destination size from __builtin_object_size and abort on overflow. It only works with optimisation on and only when the compiler can determine the destination size (=3 extends this to some runtime sizes); it does not check hand-written loops or indexed writes.

Q: What is fuzzing and why does it find bugs unit tests miss? A: Fuzzing runs a function on millions of generated inputs and reports crashes, hangs and sanitizer errors. Coverage-guided fuzzers keep inputs that reach new code and mutate them, and comparison tracing lets them satisfy format checks, so they explore edge cases (over-length fields, empty values, odd encodings) that people do not think to write tests for. With ASan on, they find silent overflows, not just crashes.

Q: Assertion versus error handling - when do you use which? A: Error handling is for conditions that can legitimately happen: bad input, network failure, a full disk; they get an error response and a log line. Assertions are for conditions that can only be false if the program has a bug - a broken invariant; the safest response is to stop with a core close to the cause. Asserting on input turns a malformed message into a denial of service.

Q: What hardening flags do you put on a production C++ build on Linux and on Windows? A: Linux: -O2 -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 -fstack-protector-strong -fstack-clash-protection -fcf-protection=full -fPIE -pie -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,-z,noexecstack, often -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS. Windows: /GS, /guard:cf, /DYNAMICBASE /HIGHENTROPYVA /NXCOMPAT, and /CETCOMPAT where supported. They turn overflows and control-flow hijacks into immediate, clean aborts.

Q: How do you introduce static analysis on a large legacy codebase? A: Generate a compilation database, start with a small set of high-signal checks, record a baseline of existing findings, and fail CI only on new findings in changed code. Fix old findings opportunistically, module by module, and make suppressions local with a reason. This keeps the signal high and avoids a wall of warnings everyone ignores.

Q: What is on your memory-safety code review checklist? A: Single ownership and no naked new/delete; no stored raw pointers or iterators across invalidating operations; every copy bounded by destination size and every wire length validated; size arithmetic overflow-checked; everything initialised; error paths release resources; shared state protected by a named lock with a global lock order; signal handlers async-signal-safe; new parsers fuzzed and new concurrent code run under TSan.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Defence in layers: types that make bugs impossible, warnings, assertions, sanitizers, fuzzing, static analysis, hardening, review. Earlier layers are cheaper.
  • RAII: one owner, destructors release, no naked new/delete; ids or weak_ptr instead of stored raw pointers; scoped_lock for multiple locks.
  • Bounds: sized types, .at() for input-derived indexes, _GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS, validate lengths at the boundary, never strcpy/sprintf, overflow-check size arithmetic.
  • Assertions are for bugs, error handling for input; always-on asserts for money and memory invariants; never assume-style hints on input-dependent conditions.
  • libFuzzer + ASan + UBSan on every parser of external input; crash inputs become unit tests.
  • Static analysis (clang-tidy, cppcheck, MSVC /analyze with SAL) with a baseline; warnings as errors with a strict set.
  • Hardening: _FORTIFY_SOURCE, stack protector, stack clash protection, PIE/RELRO/NX, CET; MSVC /GS, CFG, ASLR, DEP, CET. They turn silent corruption into clean, diagnosable aborts.
  • The review checklist is the memory of every incident: add a line after every RCA.

docs.title: 05. Memory Debugging and RCA - all exercises
docs.text:
Every exercise from modules 01 to 13 in one place. The full wording and the "done when" criterion are in each module's section 6; this file gives a one-line summary, the difficulty and a hint. Build everything in WSL Ubuntu 24.04 with code/build_debug.sh unless the exercise says Windows.

Suggested path if short on time: do every easy one, then the medium ones in modules 04, 06, 07, 08, 10 and 12, then pick two hard ones that match your work (for example 07.5 and 12.6).

Difficulty totals: 26 easy, 26 medium, 26 hard.

docs.title: Module 01 - Process memory layout
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 1.1 Map the program: match each address printed by m01_memory_layout to its line in the maps dump. easy Compare the address against the start-end range of each line; large malloc goes to an anonymous mmap region, not [heap] (threshold is 128 KiB by default). 1.2 Fault addresses: dereference 0x10, 0xFFFF...FF and one past a malloc(4096) block; record si_addr. easy The third one usually does not fault: the page after the block is still mapped heap. Faults happen at page granularity, not object granularity. 1.3 Find the guard page: crash m04_stack_overflow, compute si_addr - stack_start. medium info proc mappings gives the [stack] start; the fault is just below it, in the guard gap the kernel keeps under the stack. 1.4 ASLR on and off: run m01_memory_layout outside gdb, inside gdb, and under setarch -R. medium gdb disables ASLR by default (set disable-randomization on); that is why addresses repeat inside gdb. 1.5 Thread stacks: 4 threads print local addresses and pthread_getattr_np info; find each stack and guard in maps. hard Thread stacks are anonymous rw-p mappings of 8 MiB (default ulimit -s) with a ---p guard page just below; 9 MiB of use hits the guard and segfaults. 1.6 Windows comparison: map every VMMap category to a Linux maps line. hard Committed = backed by RAM or pagefile; Working Set = currently resident (like RSS); Private = not shareable (like anonymous mappings).

docs.title: Module 02 - Stack frames and calling conventions
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 2.1 Read a frame: show [rbp+8] is the return address into level2. easy x/2xg $rbp shows saved rbp then return address; info symbol on the second word names the caller. 2.2 Registers at entry: watch $rdi change while p c stays. easy At -O0 the prologue spills rdi to the stack; info address c shows an rbp offset. 2.3 Inlining: compare gdb bt with backtrace() output in m02_frames_O2. medium gdb uses DWARF inline info to show inlined frames; backtrace() only sees real return addresses. 2.4 Separate debug file: objcopy --only-keep-debug, strip, --add-gnu-debuglink. medium readelf -n shows the same build id in both files; gdb matches by build id or debuglink. 2.5 Stack scan by hand: rebuild the call chain from x/40ag $rsp without bt. hard Look for words that info symbol resolves into .text just after a call instruction; those are return addresses. Ignore pointers into data. 2.6 Windows x64: kv, .frame /r 1, dv, .fnent @rip, dps @rsp L20 in an MSVC /O2 build. hard The 32 bytes above the return address belong to the callee's shadow space (home area for rcx, rdx, r8, r9); .fnent shows the unwind info that replaces frame pointers.

docs.title: Module 03 - The heap and malloc internals
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 3.1 Chunk sizes: predict chunk size for malloc(1/16/17/24/40). easy Chunk = max(32, round_up(request + 8, 16)) on x86-64; the size field also has the low bit PREV_INUSE set. 3.2 tcache LIFO: free a, b, c then malloc three times. easy tcache is a singly linked stack per size class: last freed, first returned (c, b, a). 3.3 Read the abort message of m04_heap_overflow and translate it. medium invalid next size means the next chunk's size field was overwritten: your write went past the end of the block into the next header. 3.4 Perturb: run m04_uninit_read with MALLOC_PERTURB_=165. medium glibc fills freed and newly allocated memory with the byte (and its complement), so uninitialised reads give a consistent recognisable value. 3.5 Fragmentation vs leak: m09_growth_not_leak with malloc_stats() and Valgrind. hard Valgrind counts unreachable blocks; freed memory that glibc keeps in its bins is not a leak but still counts in RSS until malloc_trim. 3.6 Arena allocator: compare speed/RSS to malloc; overflow one record by a byte. hard No headers between arena objects means no glibc checks fire: corruption becomes silent data damage in the neighbour.

docs.title: Module 04 - The catalogue of memory bugs
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 4.1 Classify five symptoms without running anything. easy Heap overflow; null deref; race or uninitialised read; leak or unbounded growth; stack buffer overflow over the return address. 4.2 Run the suite: ./build_debug.sh run-asan, one report line per program. easy The first ERROR: AddressSanitizer: line names the class; the #0 frame below it names the line. 4.3 ASan vs Valgrind vs nothing on m04_uninit_read. medium ASan does not track initialisation (that is MSan, clang only); Valgrind Memcheck tracks definedness bit by bit. 4.4 Make the off-by-one in m04_heap_overflow abort every run. medium Control the layout: allocate the victim, then a neighbour of the same size class, so the stray byte hits the neighbour's size field. 4.5 Combination bug: integer overflow producing a small buffer, then a full-size copy. hard UBSan catches signed overflow (not unsigned wrap unless -fsanitize=unsigned-integer-overflow in clang); ASan catches the copy. 4.6 Turn a double free into silent corruption. hard Insert a same-size malloc between the frees: it takes the chunk out of tcache, so the second free releases a live object and the double-free check sees nothing.

docs.title: Module 05 - gdb from zero to fluent
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 5.1 Null deref in under 3 minutes: signal, address, instruction, frame, line, fix. easy run, bt, p $_siginfo._sifields._sigfault.si_addr, x/i $pc, frame N, list. 5.2 Stepping: predict each Value returned before finish prints it. easy Read the function body before finish; step enters, next steps over, finish returns. 5.3 Watchpoint hunt on the freed object. medium A hardware watchpoint on freed memory fires inside free because tcache writes its next pointer and key into the first 16 bytes; watch -l balance may never fire if that field is not overwritten. 5.4 Attach and deadlock statement with real LWPs. medium thread apply all bt, then in each waiting thread print the mutex: __owner is the holder's LWP. 5.5 Python pretty printer for Account. hard Subclass nothing: a class with to_string(), a lookup function matching str(val.type.strip_typedefs()), gdb.pretty_printers.append(...) from .gdbinit. 5.6 Scripted triage crash.gdb in batch mode. hard gdb -batch -x crash.gdb binary core > first_look.txt; include info registers, x/i $pc, thread apply all bt full, info sharedlibrary, info proc mappings.

docs.title: Module 06 - Core dumps on Linux
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 6.1 Make a core happen and find NT_SIGINFO and NT_FILE notes. easy WSL may pipe cores to apport or nothing; set core_pattern to a file path; readelf -n core lists the notes. 6.2 Run the fixed procedure of section 2.6 on that core and write one line. easy Signal, si_code (1 = SEGV_MAPERR, 2 = SEGV_ACCERR), si_addr, x/i $pc, the register in the instruction, frame, line, class. 6.3 Analyse m06_crash_example at -O2 cold. medium Two bugs: the null and the stale pointer; the stale pointer is a reference into a vector taken before an erase shifted the elements. 6.4 Wrong binary: open an old core with a rebuilt binary. medium gdb warns about build-id mismatch (or not at all for the main binary on old versions); line numbers and local values are the first things that lie. 6.5 Analyse on another machine with set sysroot. hard Copy the libraries listed in info sharedlibrary (or the NT_FILE note) into a directory tree mirroring their absolute paths; set sysroot before loading the core. 6.6 gcore a hang of m10_deadlock and name both owners from the core. hard Same as 5.4 but from a static file; map __owner LWPs to gdb thread numbers with info threads.

docs.title: Module 07 - WinDbg and Windows crash dumps
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 7.1 Manual analyse of a 0xC0000005 dump without !analyze. easy .ecxr switches to the exception context; .exr -1 parameter 0 is 0 = read, 1 = write, 8 = DEP; parameter 1 is the address. 7.2 Symbol hygiene: bad .sympath vs good. easy With bad symbols lm shows (export symbols) or (deferred), k shows module+0xoffset and frames may be wrong. !sym noisy shows the search. 7.3 PageHeap walkthrough: faulting stack, !heap -p -a, allocation stack. medium gflags /p /enable app.exe /full places a guard page after each block; +ust must also be on for the allocation stack. 7.4 Fail-fast subcode: abort() vs /GS overflow, both 0xC0000409. medium .exr -1 parameter 0 is the FAST_FAIL_* code: 7 is FAST_FAIL_FATAL_APP_EXIT (abort), 2 is FAST_FAIL_STACK_COOKIE_CHECK_FAILURE. 7.5 Deadlock two ways: std::mutex (SRW) from ~*k, then CRITICAL_SECTION with !locks. hard SRW locks have no owner field: infer the holder from which thread is inside the protected function; !locks shows OwningThread for critical sections. 7.6 AppVerifier Heaps stop on m04_use_after_free.exe. hard Enable Heaps in appverif.exe, run under WinDbg; the verifier break shows the stop code; !avrf and !heap -p -a <addr> give the stacks.

docs.title: Module 08 - Valgrind and sanitizers
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 8.1 Run every tool on every program; 10-row table. easy ./build_debug.sh all then the four run-* targets; take the first error line of each. 8.2 Read the ASan shadow line around [fa]. easy Shadow address = (addr >> 3) + 0x7fff8000; 00 = 8 addressable bytes, 0N = first N addressable, fa = heap redzone. 8.3 Catch matrix: 8 programs x 4 tools, all observed. medium TSan and ASan cannot be combined in one build; expect "n.a." for TSan on single-threaded programs. 8.4 Quarantine eviction hides the UAF. medium ASan keeps freed memory in a 256 MB quarantine by default; churn more than that and the block is reused, so the access is "valid". 8.5 Poison a bump allocator for ASan. hard ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION(tail, len) after each allocation, unpoison the returned bytes; ASan then reports use-after-poison. 8.6 ci_sanitize.sh that fails on any report. hard ASAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=1, -fno-sanitize-recover=all for UBSan, check $? per run, grep SUMMARY: the logs.

docs.title: Module 09 - Leaks and memory growth
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 9.1 Same leak in LSan, Valgrind and heaptrack. easy Direct = the leaked block itself; indirect = blocks reachable only from a leaked block. Valgrind calls them "definitely" and "indirectly lost". 9.2 Growth vs leak on m09_growth_not_leak. easy LSan reports nothing because everything is still reachable (or freed); RSS stays up because of retention or fragmentation. 9.3 RSS trend script to CSV; derive bytes per request. medium Read VmRSS and VmHWM from /proc/PID/status, ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l; slope = delta RSS / delta requests. 9.4 Fix the leak with delete and with unique_ptr; add a throw. medium The delete on the error path does not run when an exception propagates; the unique_ptr destructor does. 9.5 shared_ptr cycle; fix with weak_ptr. hard Each node keeps the other's count at 1 after both outer pointers die; p node.use_count() or p node._M_refcount in gdb. 9.6 Heap histogram from a core with gdb Python. hard Start at the [heap] mapping start, read the size field at +8, mask the low 3 bits, step by size until the top chunk; count sizes in a dict.

docs.title: Module 10 - Concurrency crashes and Heisenbugs
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 10.1 See the race: plain x10, taskset -c 0, TSan. easy One core still interleaves via preemption but much less often; TSan reports the race even when the total is right. 10.2 Deadlock table with real LWPs from a gcore. easy p g_connections_mtx.__data.__owner, info threads; holds / waits-for / held-by for each thread. 10.3 Victim and culprit: delete in thread A, virtual call in thread B. medium The vtable pointer slot holds the tcache next pointer after free; thread A's stack (or its log) shows the delete. 10.4 Sleep injection: make a rare race fail every run with a yield. medium Split g_total += 1 into load, yield, store; the yield gives the other thread time to run between the read and the write. 10.5 Ring buffer in the core; print the last 10 records per thread sorted by tsc. hard Make the trace table a global so gdb can find it; a small gdb Python script reads each ring and sorts. 10.6 Debug-only lock-rank checker that aborts on inversion. hard thread_local std::vector<int> of held ranks; on lock, assert the new rank is greater than back(); pop on unlock.

docs.title: Module 11 - Production incident triage
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 11.1 Core configuration audit and a core from m11_crash_handler. easy Build with -rdynamic so backtrace_symbols_fd prints names; ulimit -c unlimited in the same shell. 11.2 Write updates 1 and 2 for a fictional balance-enquiry incident. easy Use the 2.5 template; label anything not proven "we believe"; give the next update time. 11.3 Collect evidence from m10_deadlock with m11_collect_evidence.sh. medium Compare thread apply all bt of core1 and core2: identical stacks for the blocked threads prove a deadlock. 11.4 Add structured logging and a request id to m10_data_race. medium Copy log_event from 3.3; set t_request_id at the top of each thread function; compare tid= with LWPs. 11.5 Find the killer request from log plus core only. hard Log req.start and req.end; the request with a start and no end on the crashing tid is the one; the crash handler's request = line confirms. 11.6 One-page runbook for a service you know. hard Test it on a colleague: if they need to ask you anything to take a dump or send an update, add it to the page.

docs.title: Module 12 - Writing a formal RCA
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 12.1 Label five statements trigger, root cause or symptom. easy Ask "if this happens again tomorrow, will the system survive?"; fd exhaustion is a symptom, unclosed connections is a root cause. 12.2 Rewrite a bad executive summary. easy What failed, when, impact with numbers, root cause in plain words, trigger, fix, data integrity statement; drop the double apology. 12.3 RCA sections 4, 5, 7, 10 for m10_deadlock with real evidence. medium Follow RCA 2; the appendix is your gdb output trimmed to the lines that prove the cycle. 12.4 Complete RCA for m04_heap_overflow. medium Follow RCA 1; you need three evidence types: the abort in the core, a correlation with an input, an ASan reproduction. 12.5 Preliminary RCA for m10_data_race with one core and no reproduction. hard Every mechanism statement says "we believe"; list what you ruled out; the action is a TSan run and a ring buffer or invariant assert in production. 12.6 Rewrite one of your own incidents in this structure. hard Anonymise everything; rehearse the 5-minute version aloud; lead with trigger vs root cause.

docs.title: Module 13 - Defensive design
docs.text: # Exercise Difficulty Hint 13.1 Break m13_raii_fix back, one bug at a time; record which layer catches each. easy i <= size() with [] is caught by _GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS and ASan; the raw new with early return by LSan; the stored raw pointer by ASan (UAF). 13.2 checksec an unhardened and a hardened build. easy Ubuntu's GCC already enables several flags by default; build with -fno-stack-protector -no-pie -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE for a true "before". 13.3 Fuzz m13_fuzz_target, turn the crash into a test, fix, re-fuzz. medium ASan alone misses it (the write lands in struct padding); use -fsanitize=fuzzer,address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all. 13.4 FORTIFY in action: strcpy from argv[1] into a 16-byte member. medium Needs -O1 or higher; objdump -d shows a call to __strcpy_chk; the core's bt shows __chk_fail. 13.5 Static analysis baseline script. hard Store clang-tidy ... | grep -c warning: per file in a file; fail if any count increases. 13.6 Fuzz a real parser for an hour with a seed corpus. hard Make the target deterministic (no globals carried between calls); -print_final_stats=1 and -print_coverage=1 show what was reached.

docs.title: 05. Memory Debugging and RCA - interview questions
docs.text: 36 questions with model answers, ordered from basic to senior. Answers are what you would say aloud: 2 to 6 sentences. The module that covers each topic in depth is in brackets.

docs.title: Part A - Memory fundamentals
docs.text:
1. What is virtual memory, and what does a pointer value actually mean? [01] Every process sees its own private address space; a pointer is an address in that space, not in physical RAM. The CPU's MMU translates it through page tables (4 KiB pages on x86-64) to a physical frame, and the kernel fills those tables lazily. If no valid mapping exists, or the access violates the page's permissions, the CPU faults and the kernel sends SIGSEGV (Linux) or raises an access violation 0xC0000005 (Windows).

2. Describe the memory layout of a Linux process. [01] From low to high addresses: the executable's text (code), read-only data, data and BSS; the heap growing up from just after BSS (brk); a large region of mmaps for shared libraries, large allocations, thread stacks and file mappings; and the main thread's stack at the top growing down, with a guard gap below it. ASLR randomises the base of each region. /proc/PID/maps shows all of it; VMMap is the Windows equivalent.

3. Why does dereferencing 0x10 crash, but dereferencing a freed heap pointer usually does not? [01, 04] Page zero and the pages around it are never mapped, so any access near null faults at once - 0x10 is a null struct pointer plus a field offset. Freed heap memory usually stays mapped: the allocator keeps the pages and reuses them, so a read returns stale or recycled data and a write silently corrupts whoever owns the block now. That is why use-after-free is so much worse than a null dereference.

4. What is in a stack frame on x86-64? [02] The return address pushed by call, optionally the saved caller's rbp (frame pointer), saved callee-saved registers, local variables, and space for outgoing arguments beyond the first six in registers (SysV) or four (Win64, which also reserves 32 bytes of shadow space for the callee). Arguments arrive in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9 on Linux and rcx, rdx, r8, r9 on Windows; the return value is in rax.

5. How does a debugger produce a backtrace when frame pointers are omitted? [02] It uses unwind tables: DWARF CFI in .eh_frame on Linux, and .pdata/.xdata unwind info on Windows x64. For each return address, the table says how to compute the caller's stack pointer and where the return address and saved registers are, so the unwinder walks frame by frame without rbp. If the stack is corrupted or the code has no unwind info, the walk goes wrong and you must scan the stack manually for plausible return addresses.

6. What does a glibc malloc chunk look like? [03] Each chunk has an 8-byte header before the user pointer holding its size, with the low three bits as flags (PREV_INUSE, IS_MMAPPED, NON_MAIN_ARENA); the 8 bytes before that hold the previous chunk's size when the previous chunk is free. Chunks are 16-byte aligned with a 32-byte minimum. When free, the user area holds list pointers: fd/bk in the bins, or the tcache next pointer and a key used to detect double frees.

7. What are tcache, fastbins, and arenas? [03] The tcache is a small per-thread LIFO cache per size class (7 entries by default) that serves most small allocations with no locking. Fastbins are per-arena singly linked lists for small sizes that are not coalesced immediately. Arenas are independent heaps (the main one plus extra ones created for threads under contention), each with its own lock, so threads do not all serialise on one allocator lock.

8. Why does heap corruption crash far from the bug? [03] The allocator does not check its metadata when you write past a block; it checks it later, when it next touches the neighbouring chunk - a free, a coalesce, a malloc from that bin. That can be milliseconds or hours later, on another thread, in unrelated code. So the crash site shows where the damage was found, not where it was done, and messages like free(): invalid next size tell you "someone wrote past the end of the previous block", not who.

9. Name the main memory bug classes and their typical symptoms. [04] Null dereference (SIGSEGV at a small address), stack overflow (fault just below the stack mapping, deep recursion in bt), buffer overflow (heap: allocator aborts later; stack: stack smashing detected or a garbage return address), use-after-free (garbage or freed-pattern values, crash in a virtual call), double free (double free detected in tcache), uninitialised read (nondeterministic values), leak (steady RSS growth), integer overflow in sizes (tiny buffer, big copy), iterator invalidation (UAF into a reallocated container), and data races (wrong totals, corrupted containers).

docs.title: Part B - Tools
docs.text:
10. What do you do first with a core dump you have never seen? [06] Check the binary matches (build id), load it with symbols, then: the signal and si_code (p $_siginfo), the fault address, the faulting instruction (x/i $pc) and the register it used, bt for the crashing thread, thread apply all bt for the rest, then the locals of the frames in my code. From the address and instruction I classify it - null, wild pointer, stack overflow, heap corruption abort - before forming any theory.

11. What must you have to analyse a core on another machine? [06] The core, the exact binary that produced it (same build id), its debug symbols, and the exact shared libraries it had loaded (listed in the core's NT_FILE note), because libc and others differ between distributions. In gdb you set sysroot to a directory mirroring the library paths and set debug-file-directory for the symbols. Without matching libraries, stacks through libc are wrong.

12. Why might a crashing process produce no core? [06, 11] ulimit -c 0 (often LimitCORE in the systemd unit), a core_pattern pointing at a missing directory or a pipe handler that discards it, a full disk, a setuid or otherwise non-dumpable process, or a crash handler that never re-raises the signal or deadlocks. Test the dump path after every deployment.

13. What does !analyze -v do, and why should you not rely on it alone? [07] It finds the exception record, switches to the faulting context, walks the stack with symbols and applies heuristics to name a faulting module and a bucket id for grouping. It is a good first look but it blames whoever touched the corrupted memory, which for heap corruption is the victim, and it can be misled by bad symbols. I confirm with .ecxr, .exr -1, k, u @rip and dv myself.

14. Give the WinDbg commands you use most and their gdb equivalents. [07] ~*k = thread apply all bt; .ecxr and .exr -1 = p $_siginfo plus the signal frame; k = bt; dv = info locals; dt Type addr = p *(Type*)addr; u @rip = x/10i $pc; lm = info sharedlibrary; !heap -p -a addr (with PageHeap) has no direct gdb equivalent - ASan's report or heaptrack fill that role; !locks = printing each mutex's __owner and matching LWPs with info threads.

15. What do !heap -s, !heap -p -a and PageHeap give you? [07, 09] !heap -s summarises every heap's committed and reserved size, used for growth and fragmentation. With PageHeap (gflags /p /enable app.exe /full), each allocation sits against a no-access page, so an overflow faults at the faulting instruction instead of corrupting silently, and !heap -p -a addr shows the block and, with +ust, the stack that allocated it. It turns a "crash far away" into a crash at the bug.

16. ASan or Valgrind - which do you use when? [08] ASan needs a rebuild, runs at about 2x slowdown, and catches heap, stack and global overflows, use-after-free, double free and leaks with allocation and free stacks. Valgrind Memcheck needs no rebuild but runs 20-50x slower (typical figures from their docs), catches heap errors and uninitialised reads (which ASan does not) but not stack or global overflows. I use ASan in CI and staging, Valgrind for a binary I cannot rebuild or for uninitialised-value bugs.

17. What do TSan and UBSan catch, and what are their limits? [08] TSan detects data races and lock-order inversions from happens-before tracking, even when the race did not manifest in that run; it costs 5-15x CPU and lots of memory and cannot be combined with ASan. UBSan catches undefined behaviour such as signed overflow, bad shifts, misaligned access and out-of-bounds array indexes with known bounds, at low cost. Both only see code paths the test executes.

docs.title: Part C - Leaks, growth and concurrency
docs.text:
18. How do you tell a leak from legitimate growth from fragmentation? [09] A leak is memory no longer reachable that was never freed: LSan or Valgrind report it and RSS grows proportionally to requests forever. Growth is reachable memory that keeps increasing - an unbounded cache or queue - which leak checkers do not report but a heap profiler (heaptrack, massif, UMDH) attributes to an allocation site. Fragmentation is freed memory the allocator cannot return: heap in-use bytes (mallinfo2) are flat while RSS is high, and malloc_trim or a different allocator changes it.

19. How do you hunt a leak in a server that runs for months? [09] Plot RSS against request count from metrics to get bytes per request and which request types correlate. Reproduce in staging with LSan or heaptrack attached, or on Windows take UMDH snapshots hours apart with +ust and diff them. Two production dumps compared with !heap -s or a chunk histogram show which size class grows; the dominant size often identifies the structure.

20. How do you recognise a race from a crash dump? [10] The crash is in shared structure internals (red-black tree rebalance, hashtable insert) or in an object with a freed-pattern or garbage vtable in a thread that freed nothing; it depends on load or core count and vanishes under Valgrind or a debugger. thread apply all bt often shows another thread mutating, erasing or destroying the same object - compare this pointers. The crashing thread is the victim; TSan on the same scenario confirms the culprit.

21. Walk me through diagnosing a deadlock from a dump. [10] Take two dumps a minute apart; identical stacks mean nothing is moving. List the threads blocked in lock waits (__lll_lock_wait, RtlEnterCriticalSection). On Linux print each mutex: __owner is the holder's LWP and __lock = 2 means contended; on Windows !locks gives the owning thread of each critical section, while SRW locks need inference from which thread is inside the protected code. Build a holds / waits-for table and find the cycle.

22. Why does adding a printf make a race disappear? [10] printf takes the stdio lock and makes a syscall, which serialises the threads and changes timing by microseconds, closing the race window. Instead, record events into per-thread lock-free ring buffers with timestamps and read them from the core after a crash, use TSan, or use kernel tracing (bpftrace, ETW) that does not change the code path.

23. What are real fixes for races and deadlocks, and what are not? [10, 13] Real: correct synchronisation (a mutex or atomics with proper ordering), removing sharing (thread-local data, message passing, immutable snapshots), fixing lifetime (shared_ptr, owners that join users before destroying), a documented and asserted lock order, std::scoped_lock for multiple locks.
