Not fixes: sleeps, retries, recursive mutexes, or "could not reproduce, closed".

docs.title: Part D - Incidents and RCA
docs.text:
24. A server is hung and the client wants it restarted now. What do you do? [11] Say yes, and ask for 60-120 seconds first to take two dumps 30-60 seconds apart, plus logs and per-thread CPU, with a prepared script. Then restart, or fail over first if there is a standby and keep the hung node for analysis. Without the dumps the root cause is guesswork and the hang will recur.

25. What are the first 15 minutes of a Sev-1? [11] Acknowledge with a next-update time and start an incident log; scope what is broken, for whom and since when; classify severity and escalate; capture evidence while the faulty state exists; apply the smallest mitigation that restores service (block input, flag off, fail over, restart, roll back); verify recovery with real success metrics and send the second update.

26. What should a server log so incidents can be diagnosed? [11] Structured lines with a precise timestamp and timezone, level, pid, kernel thread id, request id, component, a stable event name and key fields; request start and end with duration and result; build version and config at startup; periodic resource gauges (RSS, heap in use, threads, fds, queue depths). Sensitive data masked. The thread id joins a log line to a thread in the core; the request id joins events across threads and services.

27. What can a crash handler safely do? [11] Only async-signal-safe things: write preformatted text, the fault address, thread id and request id, backtrace_symbols_fd (after warming backtrace up at startup), on an alternate signal stack so stack overflows are handled. Then restore the default action and re-raise so the kernel still writes the core. Calling malloc or printf there can deadlock on locks the crashed code held and lose the core entirely.

28. How do you communicate with a bank during an incident? [11] One voice to the client, updates on a fixed announced cadence even when there is no news, and each update with status, impact, known facts, actions, what we need from them and the next update time. Facts are kept separate from hypotheses, no root-cause time is promised, no internal names or blame, and data integrity is addressed explicitly.

29. What is the difference between a trigger and a root cause? [12] The trigger is what exposed the problem at that moment - a traffic spike, an unusual input, a schedule overlap. The root cause is the defect that made the system fail under it; removing it makes the trigger harmless. The test is whether the system will survive the same trigger tomorrow. "High load at month-end" is a trigger; "a race in session expiry that needs two concurrent requests on one session" is a root cause.

30. What sections does a formal RCA contain? [12] Header, executive summary in plain language, impact with numbers and a data-integrity statement, a timestamped timeline with sources, root cause with an evidence chain where each claim is labelled proven, inferred or hypothesis, trigger, contributing factors, 5-whys down to the process gap, resolution (mitigation and permanent fix), owned and dated preventive actions, verification, and an appendix with evidence excerpts.

31. How do you use 5-whys without it becoming blame or guesswork? [12] Each answer must be backed by evidence or be a clear process statement, and you follow the most important branch while noting others as contributing factors. You go past the bug to why review, tests and tools did not catch it, and you never stop at a person: "a developer made a mistake" is always followed by "why could the mistake reach production?".

32. How do you write an RCA when you could not prove the root cause? [12] Issue it as preliminary: evidence collected, the most likely mechanism clearly labelled as a hypothesis, what was ruled out and how, the mitigation in place, and the diagnostics added so the next occurrence is conclusive (ring buffers, invariant asserts, PageHeap on one node). It stays open with a review date. A confident wrong answer that fails a month later costs far more trust.

docs.title: Part E - Prevention and senior judgement
docs.text:
33. Which defences would you put into a C++ server's build and CI, and why? [13] Warnings as errors with a strict set; ASan+UBSan and TSan builds running the full test suite; libFuzzer targets on every parser of external input; clang-tidy or /analyze with a baseline so new code is clean; hardening in the release build (_FORTIFY_SOURCE, stack protector, stack clash protection, PIE/RELRO/NX, CET; on Windows /GS, CFG, ASLR, DEP). Each catches a different class earlier, and hardening turns silent corruption into a clean, diagnosable abort.

34. How does RAII change the memory bugs you see? [13] Destructors release every resource exactly once on every exit path, so leaks on error paths, double frees and unreleased locks largely disappear. With a single owner (unique_ptr, containers) and ids or weak_ptr instead of stored raw pointers, most single-threaded use-after-free goes too. What remains is lifetime across threads, iterator invalidation and logic errors, which is where review and TSan focus.

35. You find a fix for a crash but cannot reproduce it. Do you ship it? [10, 12] I ship it if the evidence supports the mechanism and the fix is low risk, but I do not call the incident root-caused. The RCA says what is proven and what is inferred, the fix ships with detection - an assertion or counter on the suspected path, a ring buffer, or a sanitizer build in staging replaying traffic - and the incident stays open for an observation period that includes the high-risk windows. If the detector fires, I have the proof; if the crash recurs without it firing, my theory was wrong.

36. Tell me about a hard production crash you root-caused. [all] Use the RCA structure as the story: impact and constraints in one sentence; the evidence you captured and why (the dump before the restart); what the dump showed and why the obvious reading was wrong (heap corruption found far from the bug); how you narrowed it (log correlation by request and thread id, a reproduction under ASan or PageHeap); the root cause versus the trigger; the fix and the preventive action you added to the process. End with a number that shows it held, such as zero recurrences over a quarter.

docs.title: 06. Linux, GCC, CMake, Git, Docker and CI/CD for a Windows C programmer
What this course covers
docs.text:
You have spent 2.5 years shipping production C on Windows with Visual Studio, MSBuild and WinDbg. Almost every C and C++ job you will interview for in late 2026 assumes you can do the same work on Linux: build with GCC or Clang, describe the build with CMake, test with GoogleTest, keep history in Git, ship in a Docker image and let a CI pipeline prove every commit still builds and passes.

This course takes you from "I have WSL installed" to "I can set up a Linux C++ project from an empty directory, with CMake, tests, sanitizers, a multi-stage Dockerfile and a green CI badge, and I can explain what every line does". Every module ends with commands you type into WSL Ubuntu 24.04.

The running example is tcpkv, a small TCP key-value server in C++17 that you also build in 08_Networking. Here it is the thing we build, test, containerise and ship. The code/ folder contains a complete CMake skeleton for it that you can copy into your own repository.

docs.title: Why it is on the resume
docs.text:
• "Linux, GCC, CMake, GDB, Git, Docker, CI/CD (Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions)" is a tool list. Interviewers probe tool lists. "Tell me how a shared library is found at run time" or "what does PRIVATE mean in target_link_libraries" are routine screening questions.
  • "Builds clean under -Wall -Wextra -Werror with CMake; GoogleTest suite" is a claim about a project. You must be able to show the CMakeLists.txt and explain why it is structured that way.
  • Your Windows background is an asset only if you can compare it with Linux precisely: .lib/.dll vs .a/.so, MSBuild vs CMake+Ninja, WinDbg vs GDB, /W4 /WX vs -Wall -Werror.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• C at a professional level (you have this).
  • Basic C++17 syntax (classes, std::string, std::vector). You are learning this in parallel; the C++ in this course is deliberately plain.
  • WSL Ubuntu 24.04 installed. Verify: open a terminal and run wsl -l -v; it should show Ubuntu-24.04 with VERSION 2.
  • Nothing else. Module 01 installs every tool used later.

docs.title: First 10 minutes: set up the toolchain
docs.text:
Open Ubuntu (Start menu -> Ubuntu 24.04) and run:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y build-essential gdb cmake ninja-build git clang clang-tidy clang-format \
    valgrind strace ltrace linux-tools-generic htop lsof tcpdump python3 python3-pip \
    pkg-config curl wget unzip tree hyperfine
gcc --version      # expect 13.x
g++ --version
cmake --version    # expect 3.28.x on Ubuntu 24.04
git --version

Docker Desktop for Windows with the WSL2 backend is covered in module 08; install it when you get there.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
# File Topic Hours 01 01_linux_for_a_windows_developer.md WSL2, shell, filesystem, permissions, processes, pipes, grep/sed/awk, apt, ssh 3 02 02_how_a_cpp_program_is_built.md Preprocess, compile, assemble, link; ELF, symbols, static and shared libraries, the dynamic loader 3 03 03_gcc_and_clang_flags_that_matter.md Optimisation, debug info, warnings, sanitizers, defines, include and library paths; MSVC equivalents 2 04 04_make_and_cmake_from_scratch.md Make, then CMake targets, visibility, build types, presets, Ninja, FetchContent, install; tcpkv layout 3 05 05_testing_with_googletest_and_ctest.md GoogleTest, fixtures, parameterised tests, death tests, gMock, ctest, sanitizers in tests 2.5 06 06_git_properly.md Object model, branching, rebase, conflicts, bisect, reflog, PR workflow, semver, GitHub profile 3 07 07_debugging_and_profiling_tools_on_linux.md gdb quick ref, strace, ltrace, perf, callgrind, /proc, lsof, ss, tcpdump, hyperfine 2.5 08 08_docker_for_cpp.md Images, containers, multi-stage builds, layers, volumes, networking, compose with PostgreSQL and Redis 3 09 09_ci_cd_github_actions_and_azure_devops.md GitHub Actions matrix build, sanitizers, Valgrind, caching, badges; azure-pipelines.yml; secrets 2.5 10 10_scripting_bash_and_a_little_python.md Bash for build/test/deploy, traps, load generation; a Python socket client for tcpkv 2 11 11_linux_systems_programming_essentials.md Syscalls, file I/O, mmap, signals, fork/exec, pipes, epoll preview, errno, systemd, ulimit, OOM 3 12 12_windows_toolchain_reference.md MSVC, MSBuild, vcpkg, VS debugger, WinDbg Preview, ProcDump, dumpbin; Windows vs Linux side by side 2

Total: about 31 hours. Suggested pace: two modules a week alongside the other courses, so about six weeks. Modules 01-04 are the foundation and should be done in order. 05-09 can be reordered. Do 10-12 when you have a real repository to apply them to.

docs.title: Suggested order relative to the other courses
docs.text:
• Do 01 and 02 before starting any C++ course that asks you to compile on WSL.
  • Do 04 and 05 before you write the tcpkv code in 08_Networking, so that the project starts with CMake and tests from the first commit.
  • Do 07 together with 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA; that course owns the deep GDB material.
  • Do 08 and 09 once tcpkv builds and passes tests locally.

docs.title: You are done when you can...
docs.text:
• Explain what WSL2 is (a real Linux kernel in a lightweight VM) and why code under /mnt/c is slow.
  • Draw the four build stages and name the tool and file type at each step.
  • Read an "undefined reference to foo" error and state the three possible causes.
  • Explain the difference between .a and .so, what -fPIC is for, and how ld.so finds a library.
  • Write a CMakeLists.txt for an executable plus a library plus GoogleTest, from memory, with correct PUBLIC/PRIVATE/INTERFACE visibility, and explain why that visibility matters.
  • Configure and build with cmake --preset and Ninja, and produce compile_commands.json.
  • Write a GoogleTest fixture and a parameterised test, run it under ASan via ctest.
  • Explain Git's object model, the difference between merge and rebase, and recover a lost commit with reflog.
  • Read strace -f -tt output for a server accepting a connection and name each syscall.
  • Record a perf profile and read the report.
  • Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a C++ server that produces an image under 100 MB.
  • Write a GitHub Actions workflow with a gcc/clang matrix, -Werror, ctest, an ASan job and a cache step.
  • Write a bash script with set -euo pipefail and a trap, and explain each flag.
  • Write a systemd unit for tcpkv with Restart=on-failure and read its logs with journalctl.
  • Compare MSVC/MSBuild/WinDbg with GCC/CMake/GDB precisely, in two minutes, in an interview.

docs.title: Resume line this course backs up
docs.text:
• "Linux, GCC, CMake, GDB, Git, Docker, CI/CD (Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions)"
  • "Windows (Win32, MSVC, Visual Studio, MSBuild, WinDbg)"
  • tcpkv: "Builds clean under -Wall -Wextra -Werror with CMake; GoogleTest suite"

Each of these phrases is a promise. By the end of the course you will be able to demonstrate each one live, on your own laptop, in under five minutes.

docs.title: 01. Linux for a Windows developer
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: none

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Linux is an operating system kernel plus a set of small programs that each do one job. Windows gives you one big integrated environment (Explorer, Visual Studio, the registry, services.msc). Linux gives you a toolbox: a shell to type in, hundreds of tiny commands, and a convention that everything is a file and text is the universal interface. Once you learn to chain those tiny commands together, you will do in one line what used to take a PowerShell script.

WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux, version 2) is a real Linux kernel running inside a lightweight virtual machine managed by Windows. It is not an emulator and not a compatibility layer. When you type g++ in your Ubuntu terminal, a real Linux process runs on a real Linux kernel and the output binary is a real Linux ELF executable. The only "magic" is that Windows and Linux can see each other's files and that the VM starts in under a second.

Analogy: think of WSL2 as a second PC under your desk that shares your monitor and your C: drive over a very fast network share. Anything you do on "that PC" is real Linux. Anything you do across the share is slower.

docs.title: 2.1 WSL2 mental model
docs.text:
+---------------------------- Windows 11 ---------------------------------+
|  Explorer, Visual Studio, Docker Desktop, VS Code                         |
|                                                                          |
|  +------------------ Lightweight utility VM (Hyper-V) -----------------+ |
|  |  Real Linux kernel (Microsoft-built, e.g. 5.15 / 6.6)               | |
|  |  Ubuntu 24.04 userland: bash, apt, gcc, cmake, systemd (optional)   | |
|  |  Linux filesystem: ext4 inside a .vhdx file on your C: drive        | |
|  |     /home/shakir/...   <- FAST: native ext4                         | |
|  |     /mnt/c/Users/...   <- SLOW: 9P network filesystem to Windows    | |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------------------+ |
|  \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-24.04\home\shakir  <- Windows view of Linux FS  |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Three rules that follow from this picture:

  1. Keep source code in the Linux filesystem (/home/<you>/...). Compiling a project under /mnt/c/ is routinely 5-20x slower (typical, from Microsoft's own WSL documentation and common experience) because every stat() and open() crosses the 9P file-protocol boundary. git status on a large repo under /mnt/c can take seconds instead of milliseconds.
  2. Edit from Windows if you like. Open the folder in VS Code with the "WSL" extension, or browse \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-24.04\home\... in Explorer. The editor talks to the Linux side; the compiler runs natively.
  3. Networking: WSL2 has its own IP (ip addr show eth0), but localhost is forwarded both ways by default. A server listening on port 7000 in WSL is reachable from Windows at localhost:7000. The reverse (Linux reaching a Windows service) uses the Windows host IP from /etc/resolv.conf (nameserver line) or $(hostname).local.

Useful WSL commands from PowerShell:

wsl -l -v                 # list distros and WSL version
wsl --shutdown            # stop the VM (frees RAM, resets networking)
wsl -d Ubuntu-24.04       # start a shell
wsl --update              # update the kernel

Memory: WSL2 grows to 50% of host RAM by default. Cap it in C:\Users\<you>\.wslconfig:

[wsl2]
memory=8GB
processors=6
swap=2GB

docs.title: 2.2 The shell
docs.text:
Your default shell is bash. The prompt shakir@LAPTOP:~$ shows user, host, current directory (~ is your home, /home/shakir). Core moves:

Action Command Where am I pwd List ls -la (-l long, -a include dotfiles, -h human sizes, -t by time) Change dir cd dir, cd .., cd - (previous), cd (home) Make dir mkdir -p a/b/c (-p creates parents, no error if exists) Copy / move / delete cp -r src dst, mv a b, rm -rf dir (no recycle bin: it is gone) Show file cat f, less f (q to quit, / to search), head -n 20 f, tail -f log (follow) Find text grep -rn "pattern" src/ Find files find . -name "*.cpp" Help man ls, ls --help, tldr ls (after sudo apt install tldr) History history, Ctrl-R (reverse search), !! (last command), sudo !! Tab completion Tab completes files, commands, and (with bash-completion) subcommands

Quoting: single quotes '...' are literal; double quotes "..." expand $VAR and $(cmd). * and ? are globs expanded by the shell before the program sees them. rm *.o is expanded by bash into rm a.o b.o c.o; the program rm never sees the star.

docs.title: 2.3 Filesystem layout
docs.text:
There are no drive letters. One tree rooted at /.

/            root of everything
/home/shakir your home directory ($HOME, ~)
/etc         system configuration (text files): /etc/passwd, /etc/hosts, /etc/ssh/
/bin, /usr/bin      programs (ls, gcc, cmake). On Ubuntu 24.04 /bin is a symlink to /usr/bin
/usr/lib, /lib      shared libraries (.so). /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libstdc++.so.6
/usr/include        system headers (stdio.h, c++/13/vector)
/usr/local          things you install by hand (make install) - keeps apt and you separate
/opt                third-party bundles (/opt/microsoft/...)
/var                variable data: /var/log (logs), /var/lib (databases), /var/run
/tmp                scratch, cleared on reboot
/proc               virtual: kernel and process info as files (/proc/1234/status)
/sys                virtual: devices and kernel parameters
/dev                devices: /dev/null, /dev/zero, /dev/urandom, /dev/sda
/mnt/c              your Windows C: drive (WSL only)

Paths use /. Case-sensitive: Main.cpp and main.cpp are different files. Hidden files start with . (.bashrc, .git/). Extensions are convention only; the kernel decides executability by a permission bit, not by .exe.

Important Windows difference: a file that is open can be deleted or replaced on Linux. The inode stays alive until the last descriptor closes. This is why you can upgrade a running server's binary and why rm of a log file does not free disk until the process closes it (see lsof in module 07).

docs.title: 2.4 Users, groups, permissions
docs.text:
Every file has an owner, a group, and nine permission bits: read/write/execute for owner/group/others.

$ ls -l tcpkv
-rwxr-xr-x 1 shakir shakir 48216 Oct  3 10:12 tcpkv
 ^^^ ^^^ ^^^
 |   |   +-- others: r-x (read, execute)
 |   +------ group:  r-x
 +---------- owner:  rwx
first char: - regular file, d directory, l symlink, c/b device, p pipe, s socket

chmod changes bits: chmod +x build.sh (add execute for all), chmod 644 file (rw-r--r--), chmod 755 dir (rwxr-xr-x). Octal: r=4, w=2, x=1. chown shakir:shakir file changes owner. For a directory, x means "may enter", r means "may list", w means "may create/delete entries".

root is the administrator (uid 0). You are not root. sudo cmd runs one command as root; your password is cached for 15 minutes. Never run your normal shell as root; one typo in rm -rf and the VM is gone. Services should run as a dedicated non-root user (module 11, systemd User=).

Windows ACLs are richer; Linux also has ACLs (setfacl) but almost nobody uses them for dev work. There is no "Run as administrator" dialog: sudo is the equivalent.

docs.title: 2.5 Processes
docs.text:
A process has a PID, a parent PID, a user, a state, and open file descriptors. PID 1 is init (systemd on Ubuntu; in WSL it is a small init unless you enable systemd in /etc/wsl.conf).

ps aux                 # all processes, BSD style
ps -ef                 # all processes, with parent PID
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd -p 1234
pgrep -a tcpkv         # find PIDs by name
top                    # live view; press 1 for per-core, M sort by memory, P by CPU, q quit
htop                   # nicer top; F5 tree view, F9 kill
kill 1234              # sends SIGTERM (15): "please exit"
kill -9 1234           # SIGKILL: kernel removes it, no cleanup, no core dump
kill -INT 1234         # SIGINT, same as Ctrl-C
killall tcpkv          # by name
nohup ./server &       # run in background, survive terminal close
jobs; fg; bg; Ctrl-Z   # job control inside one shell

Signals are the Linux equivalent of Windows console control events plus structured exceptions in one mechanism. The ones you will meet:

Signal Number Default action When SIGINT 2 terminate Ctrl-C SIGTERM 15 terminate kill, systemd stop; your server should handle this gracefully SIGKILL 9 terminate, cannot be caught kill -9, OOM killer SIGSEGV 11 core dump invalid memory access (your access violation) SIGABRT 6 core dump abort(), failed assert, uncaught C++ exception SIGPIPE 13 terminate write to a socket/pipe whose reader closed. Servers ignore it. SIGHUP 1 terminate terminal closed; daemons reuse it for "reload config" SIGCHLD 17 ignore a child exited

Exit status: echo $? after a command. 0 is success. 1-125 program-defined. 128+N means killed by signal N (139 = 128+11 = SIGSEGV). Shell scripts and CI depend on this.

docs.title: 2.6 File descriptors, redirection, pipes
docs.text:
Every process starts with three open file descriptors (small integers indexing the kernel's open-file table): 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr. Redirection rewires them before the program runs:

cmd > out.txt          # stdout to file (truncate)
cmd >> out.txt         # append
cmd 2> err.txt         # stderr to file
cmd > all.txt 2>&1     # both to one file (order matters: redirect 1 first, then point 2 at 1)
cmd &> all.txt         # bash shorthand for the above
cmd < input.txt        # stdin from file
cmd > /dev/null 2>&1   # discard everything
cmd1 | cmd2            # stdout of cmd1 becomes stdin of cmd2 (a kernel pipe buffer, 64 KiB)
cmd1 |& cmd2           # pipe both stdout and stderr
cmd | tee log.txt      # write to file and also pass through

Why 2>&1 order matters: redirections are applied left to right, and 2>&1 means "make fd 2 a copy of what fd 1 is right now". cmd 2>&1 > f sends stderr to the terminal and stdout to f.

Here-doc and here-string:

cat > config.ini <<'EOF'
port=7000
EOF
grep port <<< "port=7000"

docs.title: 2.7 The text-processing toolbox
docs.text:
These five commands cover 90% of daily log and code work.

grep — find lines matching a pattern.

grep -rn "TODO" src/                 # recursive, show line numbers
grep -rni "error" /var/log/syslog    # case-insensitive
grep -E "fail(ed|ure)" log           # extended regex
grep -v "^#" config | grep -v "^$"   # -v inverts: strip comments and blank lines
grep -c "GET" access.log             # count matching lines
grep -l "include <thread>" -r .      # list files only
grep -A3 -B1 "segfault" log          # 3 lines after, 1 before
grep -rn --include="*.cpp" "mutex" . # restrict by glob

find — walk a tree and select files by attributes.

find . -name "*.o" -delete
find src -type f -name "*.cpp" | wc -l
find . -type f -size +10M
find . -mmin -30                     # modified in last 30 minutes
find . -name "*.cpp" -exec clang-format -i {} \;
find . -name "*.cpp" -print0 | xargs -0 grep -l "pthread"   # safe with spaces in names

xargs — turn stdin lines into command arguments.

pgrep tcpkv | xargs kill
find . -name "*.log" | xargs rm -f
cat hosts.txt | xargs -I{} ssh {} uptime      # -I{} substitutes each line
find . -name "*.cpp" | xargs -P 8 -n 1 g++ -c  # -P parallel, -n args per invocation

sed — stream editor; substitutions.

sed 's/foo/bar/' file                # first occurrence per line, print to stdout
sed 's/foo/bar/g' file               # all occurrences
sed -i 's/\bint32\b/std::int32_t/g' *.cpp   # -i edit in place
sed -n '10,20p' file                 # print lines 10-20
sed '/^#/d' file                     # delete comment lines
sed -E 's/([0-9]+)ms/\1 ms/g' log    # -E extended regex with capture groups

awk — a tiny language for column-oriented text. Fields are $1 $2 ..., $0 is the line, NF field count, NR line number.

awk '{print $1}' access.log                       # first column
awk -F: '{print $1, $7}' /etc/passwd              # -F sets separator
awk '$9 >= 500 {count++} END {print count}' access.log   # count 5xx responses
awk '{sum += $3} END {print sum/NR}' latencies.txt       # average of column 3
ps aux | awk '$3 > 50.0 {print $2, $11}'                # PIDs using >50% CPU
awk '/ERROR/ && !/timeout/' app.log                      # pattern logic

Also: sort (-n numeric, -k2 by column 2, -u unique, -r reverse), uniq -c (count duplicates; input must be sorted), cut -d, -f2 (column by delimiter), wc -l, tr a-z A-Z, diff -u a b, head, tail, tee, column -t.

A real pipeline: top 10 IPs by request count from an access log.

awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10

docs.title: 2.8 Environment variables and PATH
docs.text:
Environment variables are inherited by child processes. PATH is a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches for commands, left to right.

echo $PATH                       # /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:...
which g++                        # /usr/bin/g++ - first match in PATH
type cd                          # cd is a shell builtin
export CC=gcc CXX=g++            # export: visible to children
MY_VAR=1 ./prog                  # set only for that one command
env | sort                       # show all
unset MY_VAR

Persistent settings go in ~/.bashrc (run for every interactive shell) or ~/.profile (login shells). After editing: source ~/.bashrc. Example additions:

export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
export CMAKE_GENERATOR=Ninja
export EDITOR=vim
alias ll='ls -lah'
alias gs='git status'

Difference from Windows: there is no registry; there is no system-wide "Environment Variables" dialog that updates running programs. A variable set in one shell does not appear in another.

docs.title: 2.9 Package management with apt
docs.text:
apt is the Ubuntu package manager (think winget/chocolatey with a central, signed repository).

sudo apt update                       # refresh package index (does not install anything)
sudo apt install -y gdb               # install
sudo apt remove gdb                   # remove (keep config); purge removes config too
apt search ninja                      # search
apt show cmake                        # details, version
apt list --installed | grep clang
dpkg -L cmake | head                  # which files a package installed
dpkg -S /usr/bin/g++                  # which package owns a file
sudo apt autoremove                   # remove orphaned dependencies

Dev packages end in -dev and contain headers and link-time .so symlinks: libpq-dev (PostgreSQL client), libssl-dev, libhiredis-dev. The runtime package (libpq5) has only the shared object. A Docker runtime image needs only the runtime package (module 08).

docs.title: 2.10 SSH keys
docs.text:
SSH (Secure Shell) gives you a remote shell and is how Git talks to GitHub without passwords.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "rajaman.ar3@gmail.com"      # accept defaults; set a passphrase
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub                             # paste this into GitHub -> Settings -> SSH keys
ssh -T git@github.com                                 # "Hi <user>! You've successfully authenticated"
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" && ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519   # cache passphrase for this session
ssh user@host                                         # remote shell
scp file user@host:/path/                             # copy over ssh
ssh -L 5432:localhost:5432 user@host                  # port forward local 5432 -> remote 5432

~/.ssh/config saves typing:

Host prod
    HostName 10.0.0.5
    User deploy
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Permissions matter: chmod 700 ~/.ssh; chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. SSH refuses keys that are world-readable.

docs.title: 2.11 Windows concept -> Linux concept
docs.text: Windows Linux Notes C:\Users\you /home/you (~) C:\Program Files /usr/bin, /usr/lib, /opt programs and libs split by type, not by vendor C:\Windows\System32 /usr/lib, /lib %TEMP% /tmp Registry text files in /etc, ~/.config Services (services.msc) systemd units (systemctl) module 11 Event Viewer journalctl, /var/log Task Manager top, htop, ps taskkill /PID n /F kill -9 n dir, type, copy, del ls, cat, cp, rm where cmd which cmd findstr grep set VAR=x export VAR=x %PATH% with ; $PATH with : .exe no extension; execute bit .dll / .lib .so / .a module 02 .pdb DWARF sections inside the ELF (-g) module 03 cl.exe, link.exe g++, ld (via g++) MSBuild, .sln, .vcxproj CMake, CMakeLists.txt, Ninja or Make module 04 WinDbg, Visual Studio debugger gdb, lldb module 07, 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA Process Monitor strace, ltrace module 07 PerfView, VTune perf, valgrind --tool=callgrind module 07 Dependency Walker, dumpbin /DEPENDENTS ldd, readelf -d module 02 dumpbin /SYMBOLS nm, objdump -t module 02 Access violation (0xC0000005) SIGSEGV Minidump .dmp core file (core, coredumpctl) 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA CreateProcess fork + exec module 11 WaitForSingleObject(hProcess) waitpid HANDLE file descriptor (int) CloseHandle close IOCP epoll 08_Networking CreateThread pthread_create / std::thread 04_Concurrency Critical section pthread_mutex_t / std::mutex GetLastError() errno module 11 Administrator root via sudo \r\n line endings \n git config core.autocrlf input on WSL Backslash paths, case-insensitive forward slash, case-sensitive Winget / Chocolatey apt PowerShell bash (or zsh, fish) module 10 Scheduled Tasks cron, systemd timers vcpkg / NuGet vcpkg, Conan, or apt install lib*-dev module 12

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
No C++ in this module; the "code" is shell. Create a scratch project and exercise the tools.

mkdir -p ~/scratch/m01 && cd ~/scratch/m01
cat > hello.cpp <<'EOF'
#include <cstdio>
int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    std::printf("args=%d\n", argc);     // prints to fd 1
    std::fprintf(stderr, "to stderr\n"); // prints to fd 2
    return argc > 1 ? 3 : 0;            // exit status visible with $?
}
EOF
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -o hello hello.cpp
./hello; echo "status=$?"
./hello x y; echo "status=$?"
./hello > out.txt 2> err.txt; cat out.txt; cat err.txt
./hello 2>&1 | grep stderr            # only stderr line, because the pipe carries both
ls -l hello                            # note the x bits
chmod -x hello; ./hello                # "Permission denied": the bit, not the extension, decides
chmod +x hello

Watch a process and its file descriptors:

sleep 300 &                            # background job, prints its PID
PID=$!
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd -p $PID
ls -l /proc/$PID/fd                    # 0,1,2 point at your terminal (/dev/pts/N)
cat /proc/$PID/status | head -12
kill $PID; wait $PID; echo "status=$?"  # 143 = 128 + 15 (SIGTERM)

Log analysis pipeline on synthetic data:

for i in $(seq 1 1000); do
  echo "$((RANDOM % 5 + 1)).example.com GET /api/$((RANDOM % 7)) $((RANDOM % 3 == 0 ? 500 : 200)) $((RANDOM % 900 + 10))ms"
done > access.log
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
awk '$4 == 500' access.log | wc -l
sed -E 's/([0-9]+)ms$/\1/' access.log | awk '{s += $5} END {printf "avg %.1f ms\n", s/NR}'

See code/m10_bash_patterns.sh for the scripting side (module 10).

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Everything is a file descriptor. The shell implements cmd > out.txt with three syscalls: fork() to create a child, in the child open("out.txt", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC) then dup2(fd, 1) to make descriptor 1 refer to that file, then execve("cmd", ...). The program never knows; it just writes to fd 1. A pipe is the same trick with pipe(fds) creating a kernel buffer, dup2(fds[1], 1) in the writer and dup2(fds[0], 0) in the reader. Module 11 shows the C.

Permission bits are checked at open(), not at read(). Once you hold a descriptor, changing the file's mode does not revoke it. This is why a server can open a privileged port or file as root and then drop privileges with setuid().

Signals are delivered on return to user space. The kernel sets a bit in the target's pending mask; the next time that thread transitions kernel -> user (syscall return, interrupt return), the kernel runs the handler on the thread's stack. That is why a thread blocked in read() wakes up with EINTR, and why signal handlers must be async-signal-safe (module 11).

/proc is a filesystem interface to the kernel. cat /proc/1234/maps is how gdb, perf and top learn memory layout; /proc/1234/fd is how lsof works. Reading /proc/meminfo costs one syscall and a few microseconds; no API to learn.

WSL2 file performance. The Linux ext4 filesystem lives in a .vhdx file; the Linux kernel drives it with its own page cache and inode cache, so stat() is a few hundred nanoseconds. For /mnt/c, each metadata operation becomes a 9P request to a Windows-side server (Plan 9 protocol over a VM socket), context switch included; measured latencies are in the tens to hundreds of microseconds. A cmake configure that stats thousands of files feels it immediately.

apt and shared libraries. apt install libpq-dev places /usr/include/postgresql/libpq-fe.h and the symlink /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libpq.so -> libpq.so.5. The link editor needs the unversioned name; the dynamic loader at run time needs the versioned soname libpq.so.5. This split is why a runtime image needs only libpq5 (module 02, module 08).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Logs are text, and the toolbox is the log viewer. On an incident you will do journalctl -u tcpkv --since "10 min ago" | grep -c ERROR and tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "txn=4471" long before you open any GUI. Learn grep -A/-B, awk sums, and sort | uniq -c to reflex level.
  • Exit codes are the contract. CI treats a non-zero exit as failure. A test runner that prints "FAILED" but returns 0 is a silent green build. set -e in scripts (module 10) exists because of this.
  • kill -9 loses data. A banking server with an in-flight transaction needs SIGTERM, a handler that stops accepting, drains, flushes, and exits 0. systemd gives 90 seconds by default (TimeoutStopSec), then sends SIGKILL. Design for it (module 11).
  • Disk full with no big files. A deleted-but-open log file still consumes space. lsof +L1 lists them; restarting the writer frees the space. Classic 3 AM page.
  • Line endings. A bash script written in Notepad has \r\n; bash reports /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter. Fix with sed -i 's/\r$//' script.sh or dos2unix, and set git config --global core.autocrlf input so Git normalises on commit.
  • Mapping to your current work: your RPC server on Windows runs as a service, logs to files and you read dumps in WinDbg. On Linux the same server is a systemd unit, logs to journald, and dumps to a core file read by gdb. The engineering is identical; only the tool names change. Interviewers like hearing that comparison.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Create ~/projects in the Linux filesystem. Time ls -R /usr/include | wc -l and then time the same on /mnt/c/Windows/System32 with time. Done when you can state the ratio and explain why the second is slower.
  2. (easy) Write a one-line pipeline that prints the five largest files under /usr/lib with human-readable sizes. Done when it runs and you can explain each stage. Hint: find -type f, du -h, sort -rh, head.
  3. (medium) Start sleep 1000 &, then from a second terminal find its PID with pgrep, inspect /proc/<pid>/status, /proc/<pid>/fd, and /proc/<pid>/maps. Send SIGTERM and verify the exit status is 143 in the first terminal. Done when you can explain the 143.
  4. (medium) Given /etc/passwd, print only usernames whose login shell is /bin/bash, sorted, using awk and sort. Then do it again with grep and cut. Done when both give identical output.
  5. (hard) Write a pipeline that, given a file of lines <timestamp> <latency_ms>, prints the p50, p95 and p99 latency. Done when it works on 10,000 random lines and you can explain how you computed the percentile index. Hint: sort -n, awk with NR and int(), or collect into an array and index in END.
  6. (hard) Set up an SSH key, add it to GitHub, clone one of your repos over SSH into ~/projects, and set core.autocrlf input. Done when ssh -T git@github.com greets you and git status is clean after a git clone.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is WSL2 and how does it differ from WSL1? WSL2 runs a real Linux kernel in a lightweight Hyper-V VM; syscalls hit a genuine kernel, so Docker, perf and strace work. WSL1 translated Linux syscalls to NT calls in a compatibility layer; faster for /mnt/c file access, but incomplete. For C++ development WSL2 is the right choice, with sources kept in the Linux filesystem.

Q: Explain 2>&1 and why cmd 2>&1 > f behaves differently from cmd > f 2>&1. Redirections apply left to right. 2>&1 copies the current target of fd 1 into fd 2. In cmd > f 2>&1, fd 1 is already the file, so stderr follows it. In cmd 2>&1 > f, fd 2 copies the terminal first, then fd 1 moves to the file; stderr stays on the terminal.

Q: What does exit status 139 mean? 128 + 11: the process was killed by signal 11, SIGSEGV. 134 is SIGABRT (128+6), 137 is SIGKILL (128+9), often the OOM killer in containers.

Q: Difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL? SIGTERM can be caught: the process gets a chance to flush, close sockets and exit cleanly. SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored; the kernel tears the process down immediately. systemd and Docker send SIGTERM, wait a grace period, then SIGKILL.

Q: Why can you delete a file that a process has open on Linux but not on Windows? Linux separates the directory entry (name) from the inode (data). unlink removes the name; the inode lives until the link count and open-descriptor count both reach zero. Windows by default takes a sharing lock on open files. Consequence: on Linux a deleted log can still eat disk space.

Q: How does the shell find the program when you type g++? It walks $PATH left to right and executes the first directory containing an executable named g++. which g++ shows the winner. Builtins (cd, export) are handled by the shell and never searched.

Q: What is the difference between libpq-dev and libpq5? libpq5 is the runtime: the versioned shared object libpq.so.5. libpq-dev adds headers and the unversioned libpq.so symlink the linker needs. Build images need -dev; runtime images need only the runtime package.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• WSL2 is a real Linux kernel in a lightweight VM. Keep code under /home, not /mnt/c.
  • One tree rooted at /; /etc config, /usr/bin programs, /usr/lib libraries, /var/log logs, /proc kernel view, /tmp scratch.
  • Permissions are nine bits (rwx for owner/group/others) plus owner and group; execute bit decides what runs, not the extension.
  • sudo for one privileged command; never a root shell.
  • Processes: ps, top, htop, kill sends SIGTERM by default; kill -9 is SIGKILL.
  • Exit status 0 is success; 128+N means killed by signal N.
  • fd 0/1/2 are stdin/stdout/stderr; >, 2>, 2>&1, | rewire them before the program starts.
  • grep, find, xargs, sed, awk, sort | uniq -c are the daily log and code toolbox.
  • $PATH is searched left to right; persistent environment goes in ~/.bashrc.
  • apt install for tools; -dev packages for headers; ssh-keygen -t ed25519 for GitHub.

docs.title: 02. How a C++ program is built
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
When you press Build in Visual Studio, four separate programs run behind the button: a preprocessor that pastes headers and expands macros, a compiler that turns one .cpp file into assembly, an assembler that turns assembly into an object file, and a linker that glues all object files and libraries into one executable. On Linux you can see and run each of those four steps yourself. Once you can, "undefined reference", "multiple definition", "cannot open shared object file" and "symbol lookup error" stop being mysteries and become specific failures of a specific step.

Analogy: building a book from chapters written by different authors. Preprocessing is each author pasting in their boilerplate. Compiling is each chapter being typeset independently; references to other chapters are left as "see page ???". Linking is the editor binding all chapters together and filling in the real page numbers. A static library is a set of pre-typeset chapters you can bind in. A shared library is a separate volume on the shelf that the book says "go read volume X page 42"; the reader (the dynamic loader) fetches it when you open the book.

docs.title: 2.1 The four stages
docs.text:
main.cpp ---> [cpp: preprocess] ---> main.ii  (pure C++ text, no #, headers pasted in)
 main.ii  ---> [cc1plus: compile] ---> main.s   (x86-64 assembly for THIS file only)
 main.s   ---> [as: assemble]     ---> main.o   (ELF relocatable object: machine code + symbols + relocations)
 main.o + util.o + libfoo.a + libc.so ---> [ld: link] ---> a.out (ELF executable)

g++ is a driver: it decides which of these to run based on file extensions and flags, and calls cc1plus, as, collect2/ld for you. Watch it: g++ -v main.cpp. Stop after each stage:

g++ -E main.cpp -o main.ii     # preprocess only
g++ -S main.cpp -o main.s      # compile to assembly
g++ -c main.cpp -o main.o      # compile + assemble, do not link
g++ main.o util.o -o prog      # link only
g++ -save-temps main.cpp       # keep .ii .s .o

Preprocess: #include is textual paste; #define is textual replace; #if is textual removal. After this step there is no notion of "header". A 30-line main.cpp that includes <iostream> becomes roughly 30,000 lines (g++ -E main.cpp | wc -l). This is why compile times are dominated by headers and why forward declarations and precompiled headers matter.

Compile: parse, semantic analysis, optimisation, code generation, for one translation unit (TU) at a time. The compiler sees one .ii and nothing else. Any function it calls that is not defined in this TU becomes an undefined symbol with a relocation: "call to foo, address to be filled in". Any function it defines becomes a defined symbol.

Assemble: text assembly to machine code in an ELF relocatable object. Still per TU.

Link: take all .o files and libraries, merge same-named sections (.text with .text, .data with .data), build a symbol table, resolve every undefined symbol to exactly one definition, apply relocations (patch the addresses), write an executable.

docs.title: 2.2 Object files and ELF
docs.text:
ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) is the container for .o, .so, executables and core dumps on Linux. Windows' PE/COFF is the equivalent. Key sections:

Section Contents Windows name .text machine code .text .rodata string literals, const tables .rdata .data initialised globals/statics .data .bss zero-initialised globals (no bytes in file, only a size) .bss .symtab symbol table (name, address, size, type, binding) COFF symbol table .rela.text relocations: patch-me-here entries relocations .debug_* DWARF debug info (with -g) .pdb (separate file) .dynamic, .dynsym, .dynstr dynamic linking info (in .so and executables) import/export tables .init_array constructors to run before main (global C++ objects) .CRT$XCU

Tools to look inside:

file prog                         # "ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked ..."
nm main.o                         # symbols: T defined text, U undefined, D data, B bss, W weak
nm -C main.o                      # -C demangles C++ names
nm -D libfoo.so                   # dynamic (exported) symbols only
objdump -d main.o                 # disassemble
objdump -t main.o                 # symbol table
objdump -r main.o                 # relocations
readelf -h prog                   # ELF header: type, entry point
readelf -S prog                   # section headers
readelf -s prog | grep FUNC       # symbol table
readelf -d prog                   # dynamic section: NEEDED libs, RPATH/RUNPATH, SONAME
readelf -l prog                   # program headers (segments the loader maps)
size prog                         # text/data/bss totals
strings -n 8 prog | less          # printable strings
c++filt _ZN5tcpkv5Store3getERKNSt7__cxx1112basic_stringIcSt11char_traitsIcESaIcEEE   # demangle one

nm letters you will read daily:

T  defined function in .text (global)      t  same, local (static) to this TU
U  undefined: needed from elsewhere
D  defined initialised data                 B  defined zero-init data (.bss)
R  read-only data                           W  weak symbol (inline functions, templates)
V  weak object                              i  indirect function (ifunc)

docs.title: 2.3 Name mangling
docs.text:
C++ allows overloading, namespaces and templates, so the linker-visible symbol must encode the full signature. int tcpkv::Store::get(const std::string&) becomes _ZN5tcpkv5Store3getERKNSt7__cxx1112basic_stringIcSt11char_traitsIcESaIcEEE under the Itanium ABI used by GCC and Clang. MSVC uses a different scheme (?get@Store@tcpkv@@QEAAH...), which is one reason you cannot link MSVC objects with GCC objects.

Practical consequence: "undefined reference to foo(int)" vs a definition of foo(long) is a mangling mismatch, not a missing file. extern "C" turns mangling off, which is how C libraries export stable names and how a C++ library exposes a C API.

docs.title: 2.4 Symbols: strong, weak, local
docs.text:
• Strong (global) defined: a normal function or variable definition. Two strong definitions of the same name in two objects is a link error: "multiple definition of foo".
  • Weak: inline functions, template instantiations, inline variables, functions with __attribute__((weak)). The linker keeps one copy and silently discards the rest. This is how the same std::vector<int>::push_back instantiated in ten TUs becomes one function.
  • Local (static): static functions and anonymous-namespace entities. Invisible to other objects. Cannot collide.
  • Undefined: referenced, not defined here. Must be resolved by exactly one strong (or weak) definition somewhere in the link, or the link fails.

docs.title: 2.5 Static libraries: .a
docs.text:
A static library is an archive of .o files with an index. Nothing more. ar creates it.

g++ -c mathlib.cpp -o mathlib.o
ar rcs libmathlib.a mathlib.o          # r insert, c create, s index
ar t libmathlib.a                      # list members
nm libmathlib.a                        # symbols per member
g++ main.o -L. -lmathlib -o prog       # -L search dir, -lmathlib means libmathlib.a (or .so)

How the linker uses it: it walks the command line left to right, keeping a list of currently undefined symbols. When it meets an archive, it pulls in only the members that define a currently undefined symbol, then re-scans those members for new undefineds. Members that nothing needs are dropped. This has two consequences:

  1. Order matters. g++ -lmathlib main.o fails: when the linker reaches libmathlib.a, nothing is undefined yet, so it takes nothing; then main.o adds undefineds that are never satisfied. Libraries go after the objects that use them, and a library that depends on another library goes before it (-lA -lB if A uses B).
  2. The code is copied into your executable. No run-time dependency. Bigger binary. Update the library, relink every consumer.

Windows: .lib produced by lib.exe is the same idea (COFF archive). The MSVC linker is more forgiving about order because it does iterative resolution over all inputs by default.

docs.title: 2.6 Shared libraries: .so
docs.text:
A shared object is a complete ELF file with code and a dynamic symbol table, loaded at run time by the dynamic loader and mapped into the process. One copy of libstdc++.so.6 on disk serves every C++ program on the machine, and its pages are shared in RAM.

g++ -fPIC -c mathlib.cpp -o mathlib.o
g++ -shared -o libmathlib.so.1.0.0 mathlib.o -Wl,-soname,libmathlib.so.1
ln -s libmathlib.so.1.0.0 libmathlib.so.1       # soname: what consumers record
ln -s libmathlib.so.1 libmathlib.so              # dev name: what -lmathlib finds
g++ main.o -L. -lmathlib -o prog
./prog
# ./prog: error while loading shared libraries: libmathlib.so.1: cannot open shared object file

That error is the most common first contact with the dynamic loader. The link succeeded; the run failed because at run time ld.so could not find libmathlib.so.1.

-fPIC: Position-Independent Code. A shared library is mapped at a different address in every process (ASLR), so its code cannot contain absolute addresses. -fPIC makes the compiler emit RIP-relative addressing and go through the GOT (Global Offset Table) for globals and the PLT (Procedure Linkage Table) for function calls. Without -fPIC, ld refuses: "relocation R_X86_64_32 against .rodata can not be used when making a shared object; recompile with -fPIC". On x86-64, cost is small (one indirection for cross-library calls). Executables on Ubuntu are PIE (position-independent executables) by default too.

Soname and versioning. libmathlib.so.1 is the soname; the "1" is the ABI version. Consumers record the soname in their NEEDED entry (readelf -d prog). You can ship libmathlib.so.1.0.1 with bug fixes and all consumers pick it up after updating the symlink; a breaking ABI change becomes libmathlib.so.2 and old binaries keep working with the old file.

Windows comparison: a .dll plus an import .lib. On Linux you link directly against the .so; there is no import library. Windows exports nothing by default (__declspec(dllexport)); GCC exports everything by default. Hide symbols with -fvisibility=hidden and __attribute__((visibility("default"))) on the public API; this shrinks the dynamic symbol table and speeds up loading.

docs.title: 2.7 How the dynamic loader finds libraries
docs.text:
The program's PT_INTERP names the loader: /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2. The kernel maps the executable and the loader; the loader then resolves every NEEDED entry in this order:

  1. DT_RPATH baked into the executable (deprecated, but honoured if there is no RUNPATH).
  2. LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable (colon-separated).
  3. DT_RUNPATH baked into the executable (-Wl,-rpath,... with modern ld sets RUNPATH).
  4. /etc/ld.so.cache, built by ldconfig from /etc/ld.so.conf.d/*.
  5. /lib, /usr/lib (and the multiarch dirs).

Special token: $ORIGIN means "the directory of the executable itself", so -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN/../lib' lets you ship a relocatable tree bin/prog + lib/libfoo.so.

ldd ./prog                         # what will be loaded and from where ("not found" is the bug)
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./prog           # quick fix for testing; never in production configs
g++ main.o -L. -lmathlib -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN' -o prog    # permanent fix: RUNPATH
readelf -d prog | grep -E 'NEEDED|RUNPATH|RPATH'
LD_DEBUG=libs ./prog               # trace the search
sudo ldconfig                      # rebuild cache after installing a lib to /usr/local/lib

Windows search order for comparison: application directory, System32, the PATH variable. LD_LIBRARY_PATH is the PATH of DLL loading; RUNPATH is the application-directory rule made explicit and relocatable.

Lazy binding. Function calls into a shared library go through the PLT. The first call jumps to the resolver, which looks up the symbol and patches the GOT entry; later calls go straight through. LD_BIND_NOW=1 resolves everything at startup (what -Wl,-z,now does permanently; used by hardened builds). A symbol that is missing in a lazily bound program only fails when first called: "symbol lookup error: undefined symbol: foo". That is a run-time undefined reference.

docs.title: 2.8 Reading "undefined reference to"
docs.text:
/usr/bin/ld: main.o: in function `main':
main.cpp:(.text+0x1a): undefined reference to `mathlib::add(int, int)'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

Translate: while linking, object main.o, inside function main, there is a call to a symbol mathlib::add(int,int) and no input provided a definition. Three causes, in order of frequency:

  1. You did not link the object or library that defines it. Forgot mathlib.o, forgot -lmathlib, or forgot target_link_libraries in CMake. Fix: add it.
  2. Order. The library appeared before the object that uses it (static libs). Fix: move the library after, or use -Wl,--start-group ... --end-group for circular static deps.
  3. Signature mismatch. Declared int add(int, int) in the header but defined long add(long, long) in the .cpp; or the header was C++ but the definition compiled as C without extern "C"; or the definition is static/anonymous-namespace and so invisible. Fix: nm -C mathlib.o | grep add and compare exactly.

A fourth, for shared libs: the library is linked but the symbol is hidden (-fvisibility=hidden) or the .so was built from a different version of the header.

Also common: undefined reference to 'pthread_create' means add -pthread; undefined reference to 'std::__cxx11::basic_string...' with a prebuilt library means a _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI mismatch between your build and the library's build; undefined reference to 'vtable for Foo' means you declared a virtual function and never defined it (usually the first non-inline virtual, often the destructor).

docs.title: 2.9 Multiple definitions and ODR
docs.text:
The One Definition Rule: every non-inline function and variable must have exactly one definition in the whole program; every class, inline function and template may be defined in many TUs as long as every definition is token-for-token identical.

Link-time symptom of a broken ODR: multiple definition of 'counter'; util.o:(.bss+0x0): first defined here. Cause: a variable or non-inline function defined in a header that is included by two TUs. Fix: declare extern int counter; in the header, define once in a .cpp; or inline int counter = 0; (C++17 inline variable); or mark the function inline or static.

The dangerous ODR violation is the silent one: two TUs define struct Config with different members (because one was compiled with -DDEBUG_FIELDS and the other not), or two TUs define the same inline function differently. The linker keeps one weak copy at random and the program misbehaves. No error. Sanitizers do not catch it. -Wodr with LTO catches some cases. This is a senior-level "why does it crash only in release" root cause (see 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA).

docs.title: 2.10 Link-time optimisation (LTO)
docs.text: Normally the compiler optimises one TU at a time, so a tiny function in util.cpp cannot be inlined into main.cpp. With -flto the compiler emits its intermediate representation (GIMPLE for GCC) into the object files instead of final machine code; the linker calls back into the compiler to optimise the whole program at once, then generates code. Gains: cross-TU inlining, dead code removal, devirtualisation, and -Wodr warnings. Costs: link time and memory; harder debugging. Enable in CMake with set_property(TARGET tcpkv PROPERTY INTERPROCEDURAL_OPTIMIZATION ON). MSVC equivalent: /GL + /LTCG.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: All examples are in code/m02_*. Each directory has a build.sh that runs the exact commands.

docs.title: 3.1 Static library (code/m02_static_lib/)
docs.text:
// mathlib.h
#pragma once
namespace mathlib {
int add(int a, int b);
int mul(int a, int b);
}

// mathlib.cpp
#include "mathlib.h"
namespace mathlib {
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
int mul(int a, int b) { return a * b; }
}

// main.cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include "mathlib.h"
int main() {
    std::printf("%d %d\n", mathlib::add(2, 3), mathlib::mul(4, 5));
    return 0;
}

# build.sh (key lines)
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c mathlib.cpp -o mathlib.o
ar rcs libmathlib.a mathlib.o
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c main.cpp -o main.o
nm -C main.o                 # U mathlib::add(int,int)  -- undefined here
nm -C libmathlib.a           # T mathlib::add(int,int)  -- defined here
g++ main.o -L. -lmathlib -o prog_static      # correct order
./prog_static
g++ -L. -lmathlib main.o -o prog_wrong 2>&1 | head -3   # wrong order: undefined reference

docs.title: 3.2 Shared library (code/m02_shared_lib/)
docs.text:
Same sources, different build:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fPIC -c mathlib.cpp -o mathlib.o
g++ -shared -Wl,-soname,libmathlib.so.1 -o libmathlib.so.1.0.0 mathlib.o
ln -sf libmathlib.so.1.0.0 libmathlib.so.1
ln -sf libmathlib.so.1 libmathlib.so
g++ -std=c++17 -c main.cpp -o main.o
g++ main.o -L. -lmathlib -o prog_norpath
./prog_norpath || true                        # fails: cannot open shared object file
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./prog_norpath              # works: env var search
g++ main.o -L. -lmathlib -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN' -o prog_rpath
./prog_rpath                                  # works: RUNPATH baked in
ldd ./prog_rpath                              # shows libmathlib.so.1 => ./libmathlib.so.1
readelf -d prog_rpath | grep -E 'NEEDED|RUNPATH'
nm -D libmathlib.so | grep -i add             # exported symbol

docs.title: 3.3 Undefined reference, three ways (code/m02_undefined_ref/)
docs.text:
// util.h
#pragma once
int helper(int x);
// util.cpp
#include "util.h"
int helper(int x) { return x * 2; }
// main.cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include "util.h"
int main() { std::printf("%d\n", helper(21)); return 0; }

g++ -c main.cpp && g++ -c util.cpp
g++ main.o -o prog             # 1: forgot util.o -> undefined reference to `helper(int)'
g++ main.o util.o -o prog && ./prog          # fixed
# 2: signature mismatch. util_long.cpp defines long helper(long)
g++ -c util_long.cpp && g++ main.o util_long.o -o prog   # undefined reference: mangled names differ
nm -C main.o | grep helper; nm -C util_long.o | grep helper   # compare: helper(int) vs helper(long)
# 3: C vs C++ mangling. util_c.c defines helper without extern "C"
gcc -c util_c.c && g++ main.o util_c.o -o prog           # undefined: main wants _Z6helperi, util_c has helper

docs.title: 3.4 ODR violation (code/m02_odr_violation/)
docs.text:
// bad_header.h: a definition in a header (the bug)
#pragma once
int g_counter = 0;             // every TU that includes this DEFINES g_counter
// a.cpp and b.cpp both include bad_header.h

g++ -c a.cpp && g++ -c b.cpp
g++ a.o b.o -o prog   # multiple definition of `g_counter'; b.o:(.bss+0x0): first defined here
# fix 1: header says extern int g_counter; a.cpp defines it
# fix 2 (C++17): inline int g_counter = 0;

The directory also has silent_odr/ where two TUs define struct Config with different layouts behind a macro. It links without error and prints garbage. Run it, then run it with -flto -Wodr and read the warning.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What main.o really contains for mathlib::add(2,3). The compiler emits call <placeholder> with a relocation entry R_X86_64_PLT32 _ZN7mathlib3addEii - 4 at that offset. objdump -dr main.o shows it. The linker computes the final address of add, subtracts the address of the instruction, and writes the 32-bit displacement. For a static link that is the whole story. For a shared library the call goes to a PLT stub instead, and the GOT slot the stub reads is filled at load time (or first call).

Why the linker is single pass over archives. ld is designed around streaming inputs; it keeps an undefined-symbol set and resolves as it goes. This is cheap and predictable but imposes the ordering rule. --start-group/--end-group makes it loop over a set until no new symbols are resolved. MSVC's link.exe and lld effectively do that for all inputs by default, which is why Windows developers rarely meet the ordering problem.

The dynamic loader is user-space code. execve maps the executable's PT_LOAD segments and the interpreter named in PT_INTERP, then jumps to the interpreter's entry. ld.so reads .dynamic, walks NEEDED, mmaps each library (strace ./prog shows the openat + mmap pairs), applies relocations, runs each library's .init_array (C++ global constructors), then jumps to _start in the executable, which calls __libc_start_main, which calls main. Startup time is dominated by this: a program linked against 50 shared libraries pays 50 file opens and thousands of relocations before main. -Wl,-z,now moves lazy PLT resolution to startup; prelinking and static linking remove it.

Copy relocations and why -fPIC is slower on 32-bit but not on x86-64. x86-64 has RIP-relative addressing, so position-independent code to access local data costs nothing extra. Only accesses to symbols that might be interposed (globals from other libraries) go through the GOT. On 32-bit x86 there was no PC-relative addressing, so -fPIC had to dedicate a register (ebx) to the GOT base, costing one of only six general-purpose registers. That history is why older texts call PIC "slow".

Symbol interposition. Because the loader resolves a symbol to the first definition in load order, LD_PRELOAD=./mymalloc.so ./prog replaces malloc for the whole process. This is how valgrind-free leak checkers, libasan, jemalloc and tcmalloc hook in. It is also a security reason that LD_PRELOAD and LD_LIBRARY_PATH are ignored for setuid binaries.

Where .bss goes. Zero-initialised data has no bytes in the file; the ELF program header records p_memsz > p_filesz, and the kernel maps anonymous zero pages for the difference. A 100 MB static array costs nothing on disk and nothing in RAM until touched (demand paging).

Startup of C++ globals across TUs runs in link order within one object file and in an unspecified order across TUs: the "static initialisation order fiasco". The fix is a function-local static (Meyers singleton), which the compiler guards with a thread-safe once-flag.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• "Works on my machine, fails on the server: cannot open shared object file." The dev box has libfoo-dev installed; the server does not. ldd ./tcpkv on the server shows not found. Fixes, from quick to right: LD_LIBRARY_PATH (quick), ldconfig after installing the runtime package, $ORIGIN RUNPATH for relocatable deploys, or static linking of that one library.
  • Static vs shared for a server binary. Static (-static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc at minimum, or fully -static with musl) gives a single file that runs on any kernel-compatible Linux and is what a slim Docker image wants (module 08). Shared gets security updates to libssl without a rebuild and shares pages across processes. Most servers: dynamic against glibc, static for everything else they own.
  • ABI breaks. Upgrading a vendor .so from .1.0.0 to .1.1.0 with a changed struct layout but the same soname corrupts memory silently. The soname contract is your defence; demand it in vendor conversations.
  • Link order in Makefiles. LDLIBS must be after objects; CMake orders this correctly from the target dependency graph, which is one argument for CMake over hand-written Makefiles.
  • Your Berkeley DB to YugabyteDB migration engine links libdb and libpq. On Linux you would ship it with readelf -d showing NEEDED libdb-5.3.so, libpq.so.5 and a RUNPATH; or statically link libdb (BSD licence allows it) and keep libpq dynamic to pick up TLS fixes. Being able to say that is senior-level.
  • Symbol stripping. Release binaries are stripped (or built with -s) to remove .symtab and DWARF; keep an unstripped copy or a separate .debug file (objcopy --only-keep-debug) so you can still symbolise cores. This is the Linux version of archiving .pdb files (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run g++ -E hello.cpp | wc -l on a hello-world with <iostream>, then with <cstdio>. Done when you have both counts and can explain why the preprocessor output is so much larger than the source.
  2. (easy) Build code/m02_static_lib with build.sh. Run nm -C on main.o, libmathlib.a and prog_static. Done when you can point at the U becoming a T.
  3. (medium) Build code/m02_shared_lib. Make prog_norpath work three different ways (LD_LIBRARY_PATH, copy the .so to /usr/local/lib + ldconfig, relink with $ORIGIN). Done when ldd shows a resolved path in all three cases and you can rank them for production use.
  4. (medium) Reproduce all three undefined-reference cases in code/m02_undefined_ref and, for each, write one sentence stating how nm -C output told you which case it was.
  5. (hard) Write libplugin.so exporting extern "C" const char* plugin_name(), and a host program that dlopens it and calls dlsym. Build with -fvisibility=hidden and show with nm -D that only plugin_name is exported. Done when ./host ./libplugin.so prints the name and nm -D lists one symbol of yours.
  6. (hard) Compile code/m02_odr_violation/silent_odr normally (links fine, prints garbage), then with -flto -Wodr and read the warning. Then fix it properly. Done when you can explain why the linker could not catch the first version.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Walk me through what happens when you run g++ main.cpp util.cpp -o prog. The driver preprocesses each file (headers pasted, macros expanded), compiles each to assembly, assembles each to an ELF relocatable object with symbols and relocations, then invokes ld with both objects plus crt1.o, libstdc++, libc to resolve every undefined symbol and patch addresses, producing a PIE executable with an interpreter entry pointing at ld-linux.

Q: Static library vs shared library: what is the difference and when do you pick each? A .a is an archive of object files copied into the executable at link time; no run-time dependency, bigger binary, relink to update. A .so is loaded by ld.so at run time, shared across processes, updatable independently, needs -fPIC and a resolvable path. Static for self-contained deploys and tiny containers; shared for system libraries that need security patches and for plugins.

Q: What does -fPIC do and why do shared libraries need it? It makes the compiler emit position-independent code: RIP-relative data access and indirect calls/loads through the GOT and PLT, so the library can be mapped at any address in any process without relocating its code pages. Without it, the code would contain absolute addresses and the pages could not be shared.

Q: The program links fine but fails at start with "cannot open shared object file". What do you do? ldd ./prog to see which NEEDED library is not found. Then decide: install the runtime package and run ldconfig, set RUNPATH with $ORIGIN for a relocatable tree, or as a test LD_LIBRARY_PATH. The search order is RPATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, RUNPATH, ld.so.cache, /lib and /usr/lib.

Q: Why does g++ -lfoo main.o fail but g++ main.o -lfoo works? ld scans inputs left to right, pulling from an archive only members that satisfy currently undefined symbols. Before main.o is read nothing is undefined, so libfoo.a contributes nothing. Objects first, then libraries, dependents before dependencies.

Q: What is an ODR violation and how does it manifest? Two definitions of one entity that must be unique, or non-identical definitions of an inline entity. The first fails at link time with "multiple definition". The second links silently; the linker keeps one weak copy, and you get crashes or wrong results that depend on link order. -flto -Wodr finds some cases; discipline with headers finds the rest.

Q: What is name mangling and why does extern "C" exist? Mangling encodes namespace, class and parameter types into the symbol name so overloads can coexist at the linker level. extern "C" disables it so a C compiler, or another C++ compiler with a different mangling scheme, can call the function by its plain name.

Q: What is LTO? Link-time optimisation: the compiler emits IR instead of machine code into objects, and the linker runs whole-program optimisation (cross-TU inlining, dead-code elimination, devirtualisation) before code generation. -flto in GCC/Clang, /GL /LTCG in MSVC. Costs link time and memory.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Four stages: preprocess (text), compile (one TU to assembly), assemble (ELF .o), link (merge, resolve, relocate).
  • The compiler sees one TU; everything it calls but does not define is an undefined symbol U with a relocation.
  • nm -C, objdump -dr, readelf -d, ldd are the tools; learn to read T, U, W.
  • Static .a is an archive copied in; link order matters; objects before libraries.
  • Shared .so needs -fPIC, has a soname, and is found at run time by RPATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, RUNPATH, cache, defaults.
  • $ORIGIN RUNPATH is the relocatable-deploy answer; LD_LIBRARY_PATH is for testing only.
  • "undefined reference": missing input, wrong order, or signature/mangling mismatch. nm -C tells you which.
  • "multiple definition": a non-inline definition in a header; use extern, inline, or static.
  • Silent ODR violations link fine and crash later; -flto -Wodr is the best automated catch.
  • LTO lets the linker optimise across TUs; -flto / INTERPROCEDURAL_OPTIMIZATION.

docs.title: 03. GCC and Clang flags that matter
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: 02

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A compiler flag is an instruction to the compiler about how to build, not what to build. "Optimise for speed", "keep debug information", "treat this warning as an error", "insert memory checks into every load and store". In Visual Studio you set these through project property pages and MSBuild writes /O2 /Zi /W4 into the command line for you. On Linux you write the flags yourself, or CMake writes them from a few properties. Either way, a senior engineer knows what each flag does and what it costs.

There are roughly fifteen flags you will use every day and another ten you reach for when something is wrong. This module is that list, with what each does under the hood and the MSVC name next to it.

docs.title: 2.1 Language standard: -std=
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 ...     # the standard this curriculum targets
g++ -std=c++20 ...     # GCC 13 supports most of C++20; modules partially
g++ -std=gnu++17 ...   # GCC default if you say nothing: C++17 plus GNU extensions
gcc -std=c11 ...       # for C

Always set it explicitly. The default changes between compiler versions (GCC 6 defaulted to gnu++14, GCC 11+ to gnu++17), and gnu++ enables extensions like variable-length arrays and statement expressions that MSVC will reject. -pedantic or -Wpedantic warns on extensions. MSVC: /std:c++17, plus /permissive- for standards conformance and /Zc:__cplusplus so the __cplusplus macro reports the truth.

docs.title: 2.2 Optimisation: -O0 to -O3, -Os, -Og
docs.text:
Flag Meaning Use -O0 no optimisation; every variable lives in memory; straightforward code default; debugging -O1 basic: constant folding, dead code, simple register allocation rarely -O2 most optimisations that do not trade size for speed: inlining of small functions, loop invariant motion, vectorisation (GCC 12+), scheduling release default -O3 -O2 plus aggressive inlining, loop unrolling, more vectorisation hot numerical code; measure -Os optimise for size embedded, cold code -Og optimise, but keep debugging experience good debug builds that are too slow at -O0 -Ofast -O3 plus -ffast-math: breaks IEEE semantics avoid unless you know why

What -O2 changes about your view of the program: variables are in registers or gone entirely, functions are inlined so stack traces skip frames, loops are reordered, and reads of a non-volatile variable can be hoisted out of a loop. The classic "my busy-wait loop never sees the flag change" is the compiler legitimately caching a load because you did not use std::atomic (04_Concurrency). -O2 can also expose undefined behaviour that -O0 hid: signed overflow, uninitialised reads, strict aliasing.

MSVC: /Od (none), /O1 (size), /O2 (speed), /Ox. Visual Studio Debug config is /Od, Release is /O2.

docs.title: 2.3 Debug information: -g
docs.text:
g++ -g ...            # DWARF debug info in the object file (default level 2)
g++ -g3 ...           # plus macro definitions
g++ -O2 -g ...        # optimised AND debuggable: what production builds should be
g++ -ggdb ...         # GDB-specific extensions

-g does not change the generated machine code. It adds .debug_* sections that map addresses to source lines, describe variable locations, and encode types. The sections make the file larger (often 5-10x, typical) but they are not loaded into memory at run time. Production rule: always build with -O2 -g, then strip --only-keep-debug into a separate file (or objcopy) so you can symbolise core dumps from the field. This is the Linux equivalent of generating .pdb with /Zi and archiving it: MSVC puts debug info in a separate .pdb; GCC puts it inside the ELF until you split it out.

-fno-omit-frame-pointer: keep rbp as a frame pointer. -O2 omits it to free a register, which makes stack unwinding depend on DWARF .eh_frame data. Frame pointers make perf and in-process backtraces cheap and reliable. Cost is around 1% (typical); Fedora and Ubuntu now build their distributions with it. Use it in any build you will profile.

docs.title: 2.4 Warnings
docs.text:
-Wall           # the "common" set: unused variables, uninitialised, sign-compare, return-type...
-Wextra         # more: unused parameters, missing field initialisers, implicit fallthrough
-Wpedantic      # ISO compliance: warns on GNU extensions
-Werror         # every warning is an error: the build fails
-Wshadow        # a local hides another local or a member; classic source of wrong-variable bugs
-Wconversion    # implicit conversions that may lose value (int -> short, double -> int)
-Wsign-conversion  # signed <-> unsigned implicit conversions (part of -Wconversion in C++)
-Wold-style-cast   # C-style casts in C++
-Wnon-virtual-dtor # class with virtual functions but non-virtual destructor
-Woverloaded-virtual  # a derived function hides a base virtual overload
-Wnull-dereference
-Wdouble-promotion    # float promoted to double silently
-Wformat=2            # printf format string checks, including non-literal formats
-Wimplicit-fallthrough  # switch case falls through without [[fallthrough]]
-Wduplicated-cond -Wduplicated-branches -Wlogical-op   # GCC only
-Wuseless-cast        # GCC only
-Wno-unused-parameter # -Wno-X disables X. Use sparingly and with a comment
-Werror=return-type   # make one specific warning an error

A good baseline for a new project:

-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion -Wnon-virtual-dtor
-Wold-style-cast -Wcast-align -Wunused -Woverloaded-virtual -Wnull-dereference
-Wdouble-promotion -Wformat=2 -Wimplicit-fallthrough -Werror

Why -Werror on a project you own: a warning that is ignored on Monday is 400 warnings by Friday and the one real bug is invisible among them. Why not -Werror for code you distribute as source: a new compiler version adds new warnings and breaks every downstream build. CMake convention: turn -Werror on for CI and developers, off for packagers (an option like TCPKV_WERROR).

What -Wall does not include that you might expect: -Wshadow, -Wconversion, -Wold-style-cast. -Wall is "warnings that are almost always right"; the rest need judgement.

Suppressing one warning at one site:

#pragma GCC diagnostic push
#pragma GCC diagnostic ignored "-Wunused-parameter"
void legacy_callback(int unused_handle) { }
#pragma GCC diagnostic pop

Or [[maybe_unused]], (void)param;, or omitting the parameter name. Prefer those.

docs.title: 2.5 Sanitizers: -fsanitize=
docs.text:
Sanitizers are compiler-inserted run-time checks. The compiler instruments every memory access, every arithmetic operation, or every synchronisation, and links a run-time library that reports violations with a stack trace. They are the single most effective bug-finding tool you have. Full treatment in 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA; the flags:

-fsanitize=address              # ASan: heap/stack/global overflow, use-after-free, use-after-return,
                                #       double free, leaks (LSan included on Linux). ~2x slowdown, ~3x memory
-fsanitize=undefined            # UBSan: signed overflow, misaligned access, null deref, bad shifts,
                                #       out-of-bounds on known arrays, invalid enum/bool. ~1.2x slowdown
-fsanitize=address,undefined    # the usual pair for tests
-fsanitize=thread               # TSan: data races, lock-order inversions. ~5-15x slowdown. NOT combinable with ASan
-fsanitize=leak                 # LSan alone
-fsanitize=memory               # MSan: uninitialised reads. Clang only, needs all libs instrumented
-fno-sanitize-recover=all       # abort on first UBSan report instead of continuing
-fsanitize-address-use-after-scope
-fno-omit-frame-pointer -g      # ALWAYS pair with sanitizers for readable stack traces

Run-time options via environment: ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1:halt_on_error=1:abort_on_error=1, UBSAN_OPTIONS=print_stacktrace=1, TSAN_OPTIONS=second_deadlock_stack=1.

Rules: the sanitizer flag must be given at both compile and link time. Do not mix sanitized and non-sanitized objects of the same library. Build type for sanitizers: -O1 -g is the sweet spot (fast enough, traces accurate). CMake: a separate preset or build directory (module 04).

MSVC: /fsanitize=address since VS 2019 16.9; no UBSan or TSan. Say that in interviews.

docs.title: 2.6 Target architecture: -march, -mtune
docs.text:
-march=x86-64        # baseline: SSE2 only (default on x86-64 Linux)
-march=x86-64-v2     # +SSE4.2, POPCNT  (every x86 since ~2009)
-march=x86-64-v3     # +AVX2, BMI, FMA  (Haswell 2013+; RHEL 10 baseline)
-march=native        # whatever THIS machine supports. Binary may crash with SIGILL elsewhere
-mtune=generic       # scheduling tuning only, no new instructions

The trap: -march=native in CI produces a binary that uses AVX-512 on the build runner and dies with "Illegal instruction" on the customer's older server. For distributed binaries use a named level. For Docker images that run on your own fleet, -march=x86-64-v3 is a reasonable choice. MSVC: /arch:AVX2.

docs.title: 2.7 Preprocessor, include and link paths
docs.text:
-DNDEBUG                  # define NDEBUG: disables assert(). CMake Release adds this automatically
-DTCPKV_VERSION=\"1.2.0\" # define with a value
-DLOG_LEVEL=2
-UNDEBUG                  # undefine
-I include/               # add header search dir (for #include "x.h" and <x.h>)
-isystem /opt/foo/include # like -I but warnings in those headers are suppressed (third-party)
-iquote dir               # only for #include "x.h"
-L lib/                   # add library search dir for the linker
-lfoo                     # link libfoo.so or libfoo.a (searched -L dirs then system dirs)
-l:libfoo.a               # link exactly this file name
