-pthread                  # compile: define _REENTRANT; link: -lpthread. Use this, not -lpthread
-static                   # fully static executable (needs static libc; glibc static has caveats)
-static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc   # static C++ runtime only; glibc stays dynamic. Good for deploy
-shared                   # produce a shared library
-fPIC                     # position independent code (module 02)
-fvisibility=hidden       # export nothing from a .so unless marked
-Wl,<opt>                 # pass <opt> to the linker: -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN' -Wl,--as-needed -Wl,-z,now
-fuse-ld=lld              # use LLVM's linker (faster than bfd); or -fuse-ld=mold
-rdynamic                 # export all symbols from an executable (for backtrace() symbol names, dlopen plugins)

-I vs -isystem matters once -Werror is on: you do not want a warning inside Boost or GoogleTest headers to fail your build. CMake's SYSTEM keyword on target_include_directories emits -isystem.

Why -pthread and not -lpthread: on old glibc -pthread also set preprocessor macros that selected thread-safe variants; on glibc 2.34+ (Ubuntu 22.04 and newer) libpthread is merged into libc and both spellings work, but -pthread remains the portable, correct one. CMake: find_package(Threads REQUIRED) and link Threads::Threads.

docs.title: 2.8 Other flags you will see
docs.text:
-fno-exceptions -fno-rtti    # embedded / game code; breaks much of the standard library
-fstack-protector-strong     # canaries against stack smashing (Ubuntu default)
-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2          # checked versions of memcpy/sprintf (needs -O1+; Ubuntu default)
-fPIE -pie                   # position-independent executable for ASLR (Ubuntu default)
-fstack-usage                # emit .su files with per-function stack sizes (embedded, deep recursion)
-ftime-report                # where compile time goes
-ftime-trace                 # Clang: Chrome-trace JSON of compile time per header/function
-H                           # print the include tree as it is processed
-M / -MM / -MMD -MF x.d      # emit Makefile dependency rules (how build systems know header deps)
-fdiagnostics-color=always   # colour in CI logs
-fmax-errors=5               # stop after 5 errors
-x c++                       # treat input as C++ regardless of extension
-###                         # print the commands the driver would run, without running
-v                           # verbose: show include paths and subprocess commands
-print-search-dirs           # where the driver looks for libs
-Q --help=warnings           # list warnings and whether enabled

docs.title: 2.9 Clang differences
docs.text:
Clang accepts almost all GCC flags. Differences that matter:

  • -Weverything (Clang only) enables literally every warning; use it once to discover warnings, never in a build.
  • Error messages are often clearer, with fix-it hints.
  • -ftime-trace and -fsanitize=memory are Clang only.
  • clang-tidy and clang-format come from the same front end and read compile_commands.json.
  • Default C++ standard library on Linux is still libstdc++ (GCC's); -stdlib=libc++ switches.

CI best practice: build with both. Each catches warnings the other misses (module 09).

docs.title: 2.10 MSVC equivalents
docs.text:
Purpose GCC / Clang MSVC Standard -std=c++17 /std:c++17 /permissive- /Zc:__cplusplus No optimisation -O0 /Od Optimise speed -O2 /O2 Optimise size -Os /O1 Debug info -g (inside ELF) /Zi (separate .pdb), /Z7 (in .obj) Warnings -Wall -Wextra /W4 (/Wall is MSVC's "everything", noisy) Warnings as errors -Werror /WX Specific warning off -Wno-unused-parameter /wd4100 Pedantic -Wpedantic /permissive- Define -DNAME=1 /DNAME=1 Include path -I dir /I dir System include -isystem dir /external:I dir /external:W0 Library path -L dir /LIBPATH:dir (linker) Link library -lfoo foo.lib on command line, or #pragma comment(lib,"foo") Compile only -c /c Output -o x /Fe:x.exe, /Fo:x.obj Preprocess only -E /E, /P Assembly listing -S /FA Position independent -fPIC not needed; PE relocations are always present Shared library -shared /LD (/DLL to linker) Static C++ runtime -static-libstdc++ /MT (debug /MTd) Dynamic C++ runtime default /MD (debug /MDd) Threads -pthread default (CRT is always multithreaded now) Exceptions default on /EHsc (must be explicit) RTTI off -fno-rtti /GR- LTO -flto /GL + linker /LTCG ASan -fsanitize=address /fsanitize=address UBSan, TSan -fsanitize=undefined,thread none Stack protector -fstack-protector-strong /GS (default on) Frame pointer -fno-omit-frame-pointer /Oy- Target ISA -march=x86-64-v3 /arch:AVX2 Parallel build build system (make -j, Ninja) /MP Precompiled header -include pch.h with .gch /Yc /Yu Show commands -v, -### /showIncludes, verbose MSBuild output

The /MD vs /MT choice has no exact Linux analogue because glibc is almost always dynamic; the closest is -static-libstdc++ (statically link the C++ standard library only). The Windows "mismatched runtime library" link error (LNK2038) has no Linux equivalent because there is one glibc.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Keep a flags file and use it in every shell experiment:

# ~/.cxxflags  - source it or paste into scripts
export CXXFLAGS_DEBUG="-std=c++17 -O0 -g3 -fno-omit-frame-pointer -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion -Werror"
export CXXFLAGS_RELEASE="-std=c++17 -O2 -g -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wextra -Werror"
export CXXFLAGS_ASAN="-std=c++17 -O1 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all"

Watch optimisation levels change code. code/m03_flags_demo.cpp:

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

// A loop the optimiser can turn into a closed-form expression at -O2.
std::uint64_t sum_to(std::uint64_t n) {
    std::uint64_t s = 0;
    for (std::uint64_t i = 1; i <= n; ++i) s += i;
    return s;
}

// Shadowing bug that -Wshadow catches: the inner 'total' hides the outer one.
int shadow_demo(int x) {
    int total = 0;
    if (x > 0) {
        int total = x * 2;     // -Wshadow: declaration shadows a previous local
        (void)total;
    }
    return total;              // always 0: the bug
}

// Narrowing that -Wconversion catches.
short narrow(int v) { return static_cast<short>(v); }   // explicit cast: no warning

int main() {
    std::printf("%llu\n", static_cast<unsigned long long>(sum_to(100000)));
    std::printf("%d %d\n", shadow_demo(5), narrow(70000));
    return 0;
}

g++ -std=c++17 -O0 -S -o - code/m03_flags_demo.cpp | grep -A20 '_Z6sum_tom:' | head -30   # a loop
g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -S -o - code/m03_flags_demo.cpp | grep -A20 '_Z6sum_tom:' | head -30   # multiply, no loop
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -c code/m03_flags_demo.cpp          # compiles: -Wall misses -Wshadow
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Wshadow -c code/m03_flags_demo.cpp # warning: declaration of 'total' shadows
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Wshadow -Werror -c code/m03_flags_demo.cpp; echo "status=$?"  # 1

Sanitizer in action, code/m03_asan_demo.cpp:

#include <vector>
int main(int argc, char**) {
    std::vector<int> v(4);
    int idx = argc + 3;        // 4 when run with no args: one past the end
    v[idx] = 1;                // heap-buffer-overflow: ASan reports with line numbers
    return v[0];
}

g++ -std=c++17 -O1 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fsanitize=address,undefined code/m03_asan_demo.cpp -o asan_demo
./asan_demo
# ==12345==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x...
#   WRITE of size 4 at ... thread T0
#     #0 0x... in main code/m03_asan_demo.cpp:5
#   0x... is located 0 bytes after 16-byte region [...]
#   allocated by thread T0 here: ... operator new ... std::vector ...

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What -O2 actually does to your code. GCC runs around 200 passes; the ones you notice: inlining (small functions disappear, call overhead gone, more optimisation across the former boundary), SROA (structs split into scalars that live in registers), GVN/PRE (duplicate computations removed), loop-invariant code motion, strength reduction (i*4 becomes p+=4), induction-variable elimination (the sum_to loop becomes n*(n+1)/2), dead-store elimination, tail-call optimisation, and auto-vectorisation (GCC 12+ at -O2, with a cost model that is more aggressive at -O3). Every one of these is legal only because the standard says what is observable behaviour: values in non-volatile variables between sequence points are not. If your program relies on something that is not observable behaviour, -O2 will "break" it.

Why UB matters more at -O2. The optimiser assumes UB does not happen and uses that as a fact. if (p == nullptr) return; *p = 1; after an earlier *p dereference: the check is removed because p was already dereferenced, so it "cannot" be null. Signed overflow: for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i) with n == INT_MAX becomes an infinite loop at -O2 because i <= n is folded to true. UBSan exists to catch exactly the cases the optimiser exploits.

How -g coexists with -O2. DWARF location lists describe where a variable lives at each instruction range: in rax from 0x401000 to 0x401020, in rbx after, "optimized out" where it has no home. -Og and -fvar-tracking-assignments improve the coverage. GDB printing <optimized out> is this mechanism being honest, not a bug.

How ASan works. Every 8 bytes of application memory has one shadow byte at (addr >> 3) + offset. The compiler inserts a shadow check before each load/store; the run time poisons redzones around allocations and quarantines freed memory so use-after-free is detected rather than recycled. Cost: 2x CPU, 3x memory. Interceptors replace malloc, memcpy, strcpy etc. via symbol interposition (module 02). TSan uses a different shadow: a per-8-byte history of the last four accesses (thread, epoch, size, write-bit) plus vector clocks per thread to detect unordered access. That is why it is so much slower and why it finds real races deterministically.

What -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 does. Where the compiler knows the destination size at compile time (char buf[64]; strcpy(buf, src)), glibc's __builtin___strcpy_chk replaces the call and aborts on overflow. Ubuntu enables it by default at -O1+. It is a cheap partial ASan for production.

Why -march=native is a deployment bug. The compiler emits vpaddd ymm... (AVX2) or AVX-512 instructions. A CPU without the feature raises #UD, the kernel delivers SIGILL, and the process dies with exit 132 before main if a constructor used the instruction. Function multi-versioning (__attribute__((target_clones("avx2","default")))) is the correct way to get native speed on a portable binary.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The build that CI runs must be the build you debug. -O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer everywhere, debug info split and archived with the build ID (readelf -n prog | grep Build.ID). When a core comes in from the field you match it by build ID. Same discipline as archiving .pdb files per release.
  • Warnings as errors in CI, not in distributed source. An option in CMake (module 04) that is ON in presets and in ci.yml. New GCC releases add warnings; you want to know, not to break downstream packagers.
  • Sanitizer builds are a separate pipeline job, not a developer afterthought (module 09). An ASan run of the test suite on every PR catches most memory bugs before review.
  • A 3 AM story: release build works, debug build works, release build with one more log line crashes. Root cause: a stack buffer overflow of exactly one byte, invisible at -O0 because padding absorbed it, invisible with the old layout because the overwritten byte was unused; the log line changed stack layout. ASan found it in 30 seconds. Lesson: run sanitizers before you theorise.
  • Flag hygiene for your banking server: -Wconversion on a codebase that mixes int, size_t, uint32_t from network protocols will produce hundreds of warnings. Enable it on new files first (CMake can set per-target compile options), fix as you touch code.
  • MSVC-isms to drop when porting to GCC: #pragma once is fine (both support it), __int64 becomes std::int64_t, _stricmp becomes strcasecmp, __declspec(dllexport) becomes __attribute__((visibility("default"))) behind a macro, /EHsc is default, #pragma comment(lib) does not exist: libraries go in the build system.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Compile code/m03_flags_demo.cpp at -O0 and -O2 with -S and diff the assembly for sum_to. Done when you can state in one sentence what the optimiser did.
  2. (easy) Build a hello world with -g and without; compare sizes with ls -l and size. Run readelf -S and list the sections that appeared. Done when you can explain why size shows no difference but ls -l does.
  3. (medium) Take one of your existing C files, compile it with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wconversion. Count warnings per category with grep -o '\[-W[a-z-]*\]' | sort | uniq -c. Fix the -Wshadow ones. Done when the shadow count is zero and you can justify each -Wconversion warning as either a real bug or a benign cast.
  4. (medium) Build code/m03_asan_demo.cpp with and without ASan. Without, run it ten times and note the behaviour. With, read the report and identify the allocation site line. Done when you can explain why the non-ASan version did not crash.
  5. (hard) Write a program that triggers signed-integer overflow in a loop condition such that -O0 terminates and -O2 loops forever. Confirm with timeout 2 ./prog; echo $?. Then build with -fsanitize=undefined and read the report. Done when you can explain which assumption the optimiser made.
  6. (hard) Build hello world with -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc, then fully -static. Compare ldd output and sizes. Copy the fully static binary to a scratch Docker container (docker run --rm -v $PWD:/w scratch /w/hello will not work because scratch has no shell; use FROM scratch + COPY + ENTRYPOINT). Done when it runs in an image with zero other files.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between -O2 and -O3, and which do you ship? -O3 adds aggressive inlining, loop unrolling and more vectorisation on top of -O2. It often grows code size and sometimes slows down branchy code through cache pressure. Ship -O2 -g by default and move specific hot translation units to -O3 only after measuring.

Q: Does -g slow down the program? No. It adds DWARF sections that describe the code; the machine code is identical. It increases file size and link time. Production builds should always carry debug info, split into a separate file if size matters.

Q: Why -Wall -Wextra -Werror? What does -Wall miss? -Wall covers the warnings that are nearly always bugs; -Wextra adds more; -Werror keeps the count at zero so new warnings are visible. -Wall omits -Wshadow, -Wconversion, -Wold-style-cast and others that need judgement, so I add them explicitly.

Q: Explain how AddressSanitizer works and what it costs. The compiler instruments each memory access to check a shadow byte that records whether the 8-byte granule is addressable; the run time surrounds allocations with poisoned redzones and quarantines freed blocks. Catches overflow, use-after-free, double free and leaks. Roughly 2x CPU and 3x memory, so it runs in tests and CI, not production.

Q: What does -fPIC have to do with -shared? Shared libraries are mapped at arbitrary addresses, so their code must not embed absolute addresses. -fPIC compiles with GOT/PLT indirection and RIP-relative access so the linker can produce a .so without text relocations.

Q: What is the MSVC equivalent of -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -g? /W4 /WX /O2 /Zi. Note /Wall on MSVC is far noisier than GCC's -Wall; /W4 is the practical maximum. /Zi writes a separate .pdb rather than embedding debug info.

Q: Why should you not use -march=native in CI builds? It targets the build machine's CPU features; the binary can contain AVX-512 instructions that raise SIGILL on an older production CPU. Use a named baseline like x86-64-v3, or function multi-versioning.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Always set -std=c++17 explicitly; defaults change between compiler versions.
  • -O0 debug, -O2 -g release, -O3 after measuring, -Og when debug is too slow.
  • -g costs nothing at run time; always ship with it and split the debug info.
  • -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wconversion -Werror is a sane baseline; -Werror on in CI, optional for packagers.
  • -fsanitize=address,undefined at -O1 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer on every PR; TSan separately.
  • -march=native is for your own machine only.
  • -D, -I, -isystem, -L, -l, -pthread, -Wl, cover defines, paths, libraries and linker options.
  • -static-libstdc++ for self-contained deploys; full -static for scratch containers.
  • MSVC: /W4 /WX /O2 /Zi /MD /std:c++17 /permissive- /EHsc; /fsanitize=address only.
  • Sanitizer flags go at both compile and link; never mix sanitized and unsanitized builds of one library.

docs.title: 04. Make and CMake from scratch
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A build system answers two questions: "which commands build this project?" and "which of those commands need to run again after I change one file?". MSBuild answers both for you from a .vcxproj. On Linux the traditional answer is Make: a file of rules "to make X from Y, run Z", and Make runs only the rules whose inputs are newer than their outputs.

CMake is one level up. It does not build anything. It reads CMakeLists.txt, a description of your targets (executables, libraries) and the relationships between them, and generates a native build file: a Makefile, a Ninja file, a Visual Studio solution, an Xcode project. One description, every platform. For your resume line "Builds clean under -Wall -Wextra -Werror with CMake", you need to be able to write a CMakeLists.txt that a reviewer would accept: targets with correct visibility, no global flag soup, tests wired in, presets for one-command builds.

Analogy: a Makefile is a recipe card. CMake is the cookbook author who writes the recipe card in whatever format your kitchen uses.

docs.title: 2.1 Why build systems exist
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -c protocol.cpp -o protocol.o
g++ -std=c++17 -c store.cpp -o store.o
g++ -std=c++17 -c main.cpp -o main.o
g++ protocol.o store.o main.o -o tcpkv

Four commands. Change store.cpp and only two need to re-run. Change store.hpp and three do (every TU that includes it). With 300 files this is unmanageable by hand, and the header dependency tracking is the hard part. A build system records the dependency graph and does minimal rebuilds.

docs.title: 2.2 Make in ten lines
docs.text:
code/Makefile:

CXX      := g++
CXXFLAGS := -std=c++17 -O2 -g -Wall -Wextra -Werror -MMD -MP
LDFLAGS  :=
LDLIBS   := -pthread
SRCS     := $(wildcard src/*.cpp)
OBJS     := $(SRCS:src/%.cpp=build/%.o)

tcpkv: $(OBJS)
    $(CXX) $(LDFLAGS) $^ -o $@ $(LDLIBS)

build/%.o: src/%.cpp | build
    $(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -Iinclude -c $< -o $@

build:
    mkdir -p build

-include $(OBJS:.o=.d)

.PHONY: clean
clean:
    rm -rf build tcpkv

Line by line:

  • VAR := value assigns. $(VAR) expands. := evaluates now; = evaluates at use (recursive).
  • $(wildcard src/*.cpp) lists sources. $(SRCS:src/%.cpp=build/%.o) rewrites each path: src/store.cpp -> build/store.o.
  • A rule is target: prerequisites then a tab-indented recipe. Spaces instead of a tab is the classic "missing separator" error.
  • Make rebuilds a target if any prerequisite is newer than the target (by mtime) or the target does not exist.
  • $@ is the target, $< the first prerequisite, $^ all prerequisites.
  • build/%.o: src/%.cpp is a pattern rule; % matches the stem.
  • | build is an order-only prerequisite: build/ must exist, but its mtime changing does not trigger rebuilds (directory mtimes change whenever a file inside is created).
  • -MMD -MP tells g++ to write build/store.d containing build/store.o: src/store.cpp include/tcpkv/store.hpp ...; -include pulls those in so header changes trigger rebuilds. Without this, editing a header rebuilds nothing. That is the single most common bug in hand-written Makefiles.
  • .PHONY marks targets that are not files, so make clean works even if a file named clean exists.
  • make -j8 runs 8 recipes in parallel wherever the graph allows.

Run: make, make -j$(nproc), make clean, make -n (dry run: print commands), make -B (force rebuild), make V=1 if the Makefile honours it, make -p (print the database).

Make is fine for a 20-file project and for learning. It is painful at scale: no portable way to find libraries, no built-in test runner, no out-of-source build by default, platform conditionals by hand, and link order mistakes are yours to make.

docs.title: 2.3 CMake: the model
docs.text:
CMake's vocabulary:

  • Target: something that gets built (add_executable, add_library) or an abstraction (INTERFACE library, imported target like Threads::Threads).
  • Property: a setting attached to a target: include directories, compile definitions, compile options, link libraries, C++ standard.
  • Usage requirement: a property that a target exports to whatever links against it. This is the idea that makes modern CMake work: a library says "to use me you need these include dirs and these defines", and consumers inherit them automatically.
  • Generator: the native build tool CMake writes files for: Ninja, Unix Makefiles, Visual Studio 17 2022.
  • Configure (CMake runs, writes build files into the build dir) then build (the generator tool runs the compiler). CMake is not involved in the second step except to re-run itself if a CMakeLists.txt changed.
CMakeLists.txt  --[cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja]-->  build/build.ninja, build/CMakeCache.txt
                --[cmake --build build]----------->  ninja runs g++ ... -> build/tcpkv
                --[ctest --test-dir build]-------->  runs registered tests

docs.title: 2.4 Minimal executable
docs.text:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)       # policy baseline; 3.22 ships with Ubuntu 22.04, 3.28 with 24.04
project(hello VERSION 0.1.0 LANGUAGES CXX) # no C: do not enable languages you do not use
add_executable(hello main.cpp)
target_compile_features(hello PUBLIC cxx_std_17)

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
cmake --build build
./build/hello

-S source dir, -B build dir. Out-of-source: everything CMake generates goes into build/; your source tree stays clean; rm -rf build is a full clean; you can have build-debug/, build-asan/, build-release/ side by side from one source tree. Never run cmake . in the source directory.

docs.title: 2.5 A library and an executable with correct visibility
docs.text:
add_library(tcpkv_core src/protocol.cpp src/store.cpp)     # STATIC by default (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS flips it)
add_library(tcpkv::core ALIAS tcpkv_core)                 # namespaced alias: consumers use tcpkv::core

target_include_directories(tcpkv_core
    PUBLIC  $<BUILD_INTERFACE:${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include>
            $<INSTALL_INTERFACE:include>
    PRIVATE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src)
target_compile_features(tcpkv_core PUBLIC cxx_std_17)
target_compile_definitions(tcpkv_core PRIVATE TCPKV_INTERNAL=1)

find_package(Threads REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(tcpkv_core PUBLIC Threads::Threads)

add_executable(tcpkv src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(tcpkv PRIVATE tcpkv::core)

PUBLIC / PRIVATE / INTERFACE decide who sees a requirement:

Keyword Applied to the target itself Propagated to consumers Use when PRIVATE yes no needed only to build this target's own sources PUBLIC yes yes appears in this target's public headers, so consumers need it too INTERFACE no yes header-only libraries; or requirement only consumers need

Rule of thumb: ask "does my public header #include it or use its types?" If yes, PUBLIC. If only my .cpp files use it, PRIVATE. The include/ directory is PUBLIC because consumers must find tcpkv/store.hpp. src/ is PRIVATE because internal headers are not for consumers. Threads::Threads is PUBLIC here because store.hpp has a std::mutex member, so any consumer compiles code that touches pthread types.

Why this matters: with correct visibility, target_link_libraries(tcpkv PRIVATE tcpkv::core) is the only line the executable needs. Include paths, -pthread, the C++17 requirement all arrive transitively. Get it wrong (everything PRIVATE) and the executable fails to find headers; get it wrong the other way (everything PUBLIC) and every consumer inherits your internal junk, and your build graph becomes a hairball where touching one define rebuilds the world.

Generator expressions $<...> are evaluated at generate time, per configuration. $<BUILD_INTERFACE:...> is used when building in this tree, $<INSTALL_INTERFACE:...> when a consumer uses the installed package. $<$<CONFIG:Debug>:-O0> applies only in Debug. $<$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:GNU>:-Wduplicated-cond> only for GCC.

docs.title: 2.6 Compiler flags the right way
docs.text:
Do not write set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS "-Wall ..."). That is a global string that affects every target including third-party code pulled in by FetchContent, and it concatenates badly. Attach options to targets, through a helper function so the list is defined once:

# cmake/CompilerWarnings.cmake
function(tcpkv_set_warnings target)
    set(gcc_clang_warnings
        -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion
        -Wnon-virtual-dtor -Wold-style-cast -Wcast-align -Wunused
        -Woverloaded-virtual -Wnull-dereference -Wdouble-promotion
        -Wformat=2 -Wimplicit-fallthrough)
    set(gcc_only_warnings
        -Wduplicated-cond -Wduplicated-branches -Wlogical-op -Wuseless-cast)
    set(msvc_warnings /W4 /permissive- /w14640 /w14265 /w14062)

    target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE
        $<$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:GNU,Clang,AppleClang>:${gcc_clang_warnings}>
        $<$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:GNU>:${gcc_only_warnings}>
        $<$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:MSVC>:${msvc_warnings}>)

    if(TCPKV_WERROR)
        target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE
            $<$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:GNU,Clang,AppleClang>:-Werror>
            $<$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:MSVC>:/WX>)
    endif()
endfunction()

Warnings are PRIVATE: they are about how I compile, not a usage requirement. If they were PUBLIC, consumers of your library would be forced to compile with your -Werror.

Options:

option(TCPKV_WERROR      "Treat warnings as errors" ON)
option(TCPKV_BUILD_TESTS "Build unit tests" ON)
set(TCPKV_SANITIZE "" CACHE STRING "Sanitizer list, e.g. address,undefined or thread")

option() creates a boolean cache variable; -DTCPKV_WERROR=OFF on the command line overrides it. Cache variables live in build/CMakeCache.txt and persist between configure runs; that is why "I changed the flag and nothing happened" usually means "the cache still has the old value" and cmake -D... or deleting the cache fixes it.

Sanitizers as a target option:

function(tcpkv_set_sanitizers target)
    if(TCPKV_SANITIZE)
        target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE -fsanitize=${TCPKV_SANITIZE} -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g)
        target_link_options(${target}    PRIVATE -fsanitize=${TCPKV_SANITIZE})
    endif()
endfunction()

docs.title: 2.7 Build types
docs.text:
CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE for single-config generators (Ninja, Make): Debug (-g), Release (-O3 -DNDEBUG), RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g -DNDEBUG), MinSizeRel (-Os -DNDEBUG). If you set nothing, you get no flags at all: not Debug, just empty. Always set one. RelWithDebInfo is what you ship (module 03). For multi-config generators (Visual Studio) the type is chosen at build time: cmake --build build --config Release.

Defaulting it:

if(NOT CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE AND NOT CMAKE_CONFIGURATION_TYPES)
    set(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE RelWithDebInfo CACHE STRING "Build type" FORCE)
endif()

docs.title: 2.8 Generator choice: Ninja
docs.text:
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake -S . -B build -G "Unix Makefiles"
cmake -S . -B build -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64    # on Windows
export CMAKE_GENERATOR=Ninja                              # make Ninja the default

Ninja is a small, fast build executor designed to be generated, not written. It starts faster than Make on large trees (it loads one file instead of recursively running make in subdirectories), it is parallel by default (-j = cores + 2), it only prints output of failed commands, and it tracks header dependencies natively via the compiler's -MD output. There is no reason to use the Makefile generator for new work. ninja -C build -v shows full commands; ninja -C build -t commands tcpkv prints the commands for one target; ninja -C build -d explain says why things rebuilt.

docs.title: 2.9 compile_commands.json
docs.text:
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)

or -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON. Writes build/compile_commands.json: one entry per TU with the exact command line. clangd (VS Code C++ IntelliSense via the clangd extension), clang-tidy and include-what-you-use read it to know your flags and include paths. Symlink it to the source root: ln -sf build/compile_commands.json . so tools find it. This is how a Linux editor gets the same accuracy Visual Studio gets from the .vcxproj.

docs.title: 2.10 Presets: one command to configure
docs.text:
CMakePresets.json lives next to CMakeLists.txt, is committed, and records configure/build/test recipes so nobody types twenty -D flags. CI uses the same presets as developers.

{
  "version": 6,
  "configurePresets": [
    {
      "name": "base", "hidden": true, "generator": "Ninja",
      "binaryDir": "${sourceDir}/build/${presetName}",
      "cacheVariables": { "CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS": "ON", "TCPKV_WERROR": "ON" }
    },
    { "name": "debug",   "inherits": "base", "cacheVariables": { "CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE": "Debug" } },
    { "name": "release", "inherits": "base", "cacheVariables": { "CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE": "RelWithDebInfo" } },
    { "name": "asan",    "inherits": "debug", "cacheVariables": { "TCPKV_SANITIZE": "address,undefined" } },
    { "name": "tsan",    "inherits": "debug", "cacheVariables": { "TCPKV_SANITIZE": "thread" } },
    { "name": "clang",   "inherits": "debug", "cacheVariables": { "CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER": "clang++" } }
  ],
  "buildPresets": [
    { "name": "debug",   "configurePreset": "debug" },
    { "name": "release", "configurePreset": "release" },
    { "name": "asan",    "configurePreset": "asan" }
  ],
  "testPresets": [
    { "name": "debug", "configurePreset": "debug", "output": { "outputOnFailure": true } },
    { "name": "asan",  "configurePreset": "asan",  "output": { "outputOnFailure": true },
      "environment": { "ASAN_OPTIONS": "detect_leaks=1:halt_on_error=1", "UBSAN_OPTIONS": "print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1" } }
  ]
}

cmake --preset asan          # configure into build/asan
cmake --build --preset asan  # build
ctest --preset asan          # test
cmake --list-presets         # what is available

CMakeUserPresets.json is the gitignored personal overlay (your local compiler path, your -j count).

docs.title: 2.11 Finding packages
docs.text:
Two mechanisms.

find_package looks for something already installed: a FooConfig.cmake shipped by the package (config mode), or a FindFoo.cmake module shipped with CMake (module mode). It defines imported targets you link against:

find_package(Threads REQUIRED)             # module: Threads::Threads
find_package(OpenSSL REQUIRED)             # module: OpenSSL::SSL OpenSSL::Crypto
find_package(PostgreSQL REQUIRED)          # module: PostgreSQL::PostgreSQL (libpq)
find_package(fmt CONFIG REQUIRED)          # config: fmt::fmt  (after apt install libfmt-dev)
find_package(GTest CONFIG)                 # config: GTest::gtest GTest::gtest_main GTest::gmock
target_link_libraries(tcpkv PRIVATE OpenSSL::SSL PostgreSQL::PostgreSQL)

Where it looks: CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, /usr/lib/cmake/<Pkg>, /usr/local/lib/cmake/<Pkg>, <Pkg>_DIR. With vcpkg: -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=.../vcpkg.cmake makes find_package see vcpkg ports (module 12). pkg_check_modules(HIREDIS REQUIRED IMPORTED_TARGET hiredis) via find_package(PkgConfig) handles libraries that ship only a .pc file.

FetchContent downloads and builds a dependency as part of your build. Right for test frameworks and small header libraries; wrong for OpenSSL.

include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(googletest
    GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/google/googletest.git
    GIT_TAG        v1.15.2
    GIT_SHALLOW    TRUE)
set(gtest_force_shared_crt ON CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)   # MSVC: match /MD
set(INSTALL_GTEST OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(googletest)
# now targets GTest::gtest, GTest::gtest_main, GTest::gmock exist

Pin a tag, never main. The download happens at configure time into build/_deps/. CI caches that directory (module 09). Prefer find_package(GTest) first and fall back to FetchContent so a system install is used when present:

find_package(GTest CONFIG QUIET)
if(NOT GTest_FOUND)
    # FetchContent block above
endif()

docs.title: 2.12 Tests with ctest
docs.text:
# top level
if(TCPKV_BUILD_TESTS)
    enable_testing()
    add_subdirectory(tests)
endif()

# tests/CMakeLists.txt
add_executable(tcpkv_tests test_protocol.cpp test_store.cpp)
target_link_libraries(tcpkv_tests PRIVATE tcpkv::core GTest::gtest_main GTest::gmock)
tcpkv_set_warnings(tcpkv_tests)
tcpkv_set_sanitizers(tcpkv_tests)
include(GoogleTest)
gtest_discover_tests(tcpkv_tests)       # one ctest entry per TEST(), discovered after build

ctest --test-dir build/debug --output-on-failure -j8. Module 05 covers the test side.

docs.title: 2.13 Install rules
docs.text:
include(GNUInstallDirs)                                       # CMAKE_INSTALL_BINDIR = bin, LIBDIR = lib, etc.
install(TARGETS tcpkv RUNTIME DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_BINDIR})
install(TARGETS tcpkv_core EXPORT tcpkvTargets
        ARCHIVE DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR}
        LIBRARY DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR})
install(DIRECTORY include/ DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_INCLUDEDIR})
install(EXPORT tcpkvTargets NAMESPACE tcpkv:: DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR}/cmake/tcpkv)
install(FILES deploy/tcpkv.service DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR}/systemd/system)

cmake --install build/release --prefix /opt/tcpkv       # or DESTDIR=/tmp/stage cmake --install ...

install(EXPORT) is what makes your library consumable by find_package(tcpkv) in someone else's project. The multi-stage Dockerfile (module 08) uses cmake --install to copy only the runtime into the final image.

docs.title: 2.14 Things to know when reading other people's CMake
docs.text:
• ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR} / ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}: this directory's source and build dir. ${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR}: the nearest project() dir. ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}: the top.
  • add_subdirectory(dir) processes dir/CMakeLists.txt; variables are scoped (child sees parent's, changes do not propagate up without PARENT_SCOPE), targets are global.
  • file(GLOB ...) for sources is discouraged: CMake does not re-run when a file appears, so a new .cpp is silently not built until you reconfigure. List sources explicitly, or use file(GLOB_RECURSE ... CONFIGURE_DEPENDS ...) and accept the configure-time cost.
  • message(STATUS "..."), message(FATAL_ERROR "..."). cmake --trace-expand when lost.
  • cmake -LH build lists cache variables with help. ccmake build is a TUI for them.
  • set_target_properties(t PROPERTIES CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF) makes -std=c++17 instead of gnu++17. Set CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF globally at the top for the same effect.
  • Old style you will still see: include_directories(), link_libraries(), add_definitions(), set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS ...). These are directory-scoped globals. Read them, do not write them.
  • Policies: cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22) sets behaviour to 3.22 rules. Warnings like "Policy CMP0135 is not set" mean a newer CMake changed a default; add cmake_policy(SET CMP0135 NEW).

docs.title: 2.15 tcpkv laid out fully
docs.text:
tcpkv/
  CMakeLists.txt              root: project, options, library, executable, tests, install
  CMakePresets.json           debug / release / asan / tsan / clang presets
  cmake/CompilerWarnings.cmake   tcpkv_set_warnings(), tcpkv_set_sanitizers()
  include/tcpkv/protocol.hpp  public headers (PUBLIC include dir)
  include/tcpkv/store.hpp
  src/protocol.cpp            library sources
  src/store.cpp
  src/main.cpp                executable: socket loop, uses the library
  tests/CMakeLists.txt        GoogleTest via find_package or FetchContent, gtest_discover_tests
  tests/test_protocol.cpp
  tests/test_store.cpp
  scripts/build.sh            cmake --preset wrappers (module 10)
  scripts/run_tests.sh
  Dockerfile                  multi-stage (module 08)
  .github/workflows/ci.yml    (module 09)
  .gitignore                  build/, CMakeUserPresets.json, compile_commands.json

The complete files are in code/tcpkv/. Root CMakeLists.txt in full:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(tcpkv VERSION 0.1.0 DESCRIPTION "TCP key-value server" LANGUAGES CXX)

list(APPEND CMAKE_MODULE_PATH "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/cmake")
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)

option(TCPKV_WERROR      "Treat warnings as errors" ON)
option(TCPKV_BUILD_TESTS "Build unit tests" ON)
set(TCPKV_SANITIZE "" CACHE STRING "Sanitizer list, e.g. address,undefined or thread")

if(NOT CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE AND NOT CMAKE_CONFIGURATION_TYPES)
    set(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE RelWithDebInfo CACHE STRING "Build type" FORCE)
endif()

include(CompilerWarnings)
find_package(Threads REQUIRED)

add_library(tcpkv_core src/protocol.cpp src/store.cpp)
add_library(tcpkv::core ALIAS tcpkv_core)
target_include_directories(tcpkv_core
    PUBLIC  $<BUILD_INTERFACE:${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include>
            $<INSTALL_INTERFACE:include>)
target_compile_features(tcpkv_core PUBLIC cxx_std_17)
target_link_libraries(tcpkv_core PUBLIC Threads::Threads)
target_compile_definitions(tcpkv_core PUBLIC TCPKV_VERSION="${PROJECT_VERSION}")
tcpkv_set_warnings(tcpkv_core)
tcpkv_set_sanitizers(tcpkv_core)

add_executable(tcpkv src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(tcpkv PRIVATE tcpkv::core)
tcpkv_set_warnings(tcpkv)
tcpkv_set_sanitizers(tcpkv)

if(TCPKV_BUILD_TESTS)
    enable_testing()
    add_subdirectory(tests)
endif()

include(GNUInstallDirs)
install(TARGETS tcpkv RUNTIME DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_BINDIR})
install(FILES deploy/tcpkv.service DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR}/systemd/system)

Day-to-day commands:

cd ~/projects/tcpkv
cmake --preset debug && cmake --build --preset debug && ctest --preset debug
cmake --preset asan  && cmake --build --preset asan  && ctest --preset asan
cmake --preset release && cmake --build --preset release
./build/release/tcpkv 7000

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
• code/Makefile: the ten-line Makefile above, with comments. Copy it beside a src/ and include/ directory and run make -j.
  • code/tcpkv/CMakeLists.txt, code/tcpkv/cmake/CompilerWarnings.cmake, code/tcpkv/CMakePresets.json, code/tcpkv/tests/CMakeLists.txt: the complete project.
  • The source files include/tcpkv/*.hpp, src/*.cpp, tests/*.cpp are introduced in module 05 but are present in code/tcpkv/ now so the project configures and builds.

The key part of tests/CMakeLists.txt:

find_package(GTest CONFIG QUIET)
if(NOT GTest_FOUND)
    include(FetchContent)
    FetchContent_Declare(googletest
        GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/google/googletest.git
        GIT_TAG        v1.15.2
        GIT_SHALLOW    TRUE)
    set(gtest_force_shared_crt ON CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
    set(INSTALL_GTEST OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
    FetchContent_MakeAvailable(googletest)
endif()

add_executable(tcpkv_tests test_protocol.cpp test_store.cpp)
target_link_libraries(tcpkv_tests PRIVATE tcpkv::core GTest::gtest_main GTest::gmock)
tcpkv_set_warnings(tcpkv_tests)
tcpkv_set_sanitizers(tcpkv_tests)

include(GoogleTest)
gtest_discover_tests(tcpkv_tests DISCOVERY_TIMEOUT 30)

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What configure actually does. CMake runs a scripting-language interpreter over CMakeLists.txt, builds an in-memory graph of targets and properties, evaluates generator expressions per configuration, resolves transitive usage requirements (walking INTERFACE_* properties of every linked target, depth-first, de-duplicating), then the generator writes build.ninja. It also probes the compiler on the first run (the "Check for working CXX compiler" lines): it compiles tiny test programs to learn the compiler ID, version, supported features, and caches the answers in CMakeCache.txt and CMakeFiles/. That is why the first configure is slow and later ones are fast, and why switching compilers requires a fresh build directory.

How transitive linking becomes a command line. target_link_libraries(tcpkv PRIVATE tcpkv::core) with tcpkv_core having PUBLIC Threads::Threads produces g++ ... main.cpp.o -o tcpkv libtcpkv_core.a -pthread. CMake orders libraries by the dependency graph so the static-library ordering rule from module 02 is satisfied automatically. For PUBLIC include dirs it emits -I/home/.../include on tcpkv's compile lines without you naming it. The INTERFACE_LINK_LIBRARIES property on tcpkv_core is the thing being read.

How Ninja decides what to rebuild. For each edge it compares the mtime of outputs against inputs and the recorded command hash in .ninja_log; if the command line changed (you added a flag), it rebuilds even if sources did not. Header dependencies come from -MD -MF depfiles the compiler writes during the compile, parsed into .ninja_deps (a binary cache) so the next run loads them instantly. Make re-reads every .d file as text on every run; on a 5,000-file tree that is noticeable.

Why file(GLOB) is a trap. The glob is evaluated at configure time and the result baked into build.ninja. Ninja does not know the glob exists. A new .cpp is invisible until something triggers a reconfigure. CONFIGURE_DEPENDS adds a check that re-globs on every build and reconfigures if the set changed; it costs a directory scan per build.

Cache semantics. set(VAR value CACHE TYPE "doc") sets a cache entry only if it does not already exist; FORCE overrides. option() is the same. A normal set(VAR value) creates a normal variable that shadows the cache variable in that scope, which is the source of a class of "why does my -D have no effect" questions: a set() later in the file overrides the command line. Since policy CMP0077 (3.13), option() does not override a normal variable set by the parent, which is what lets you set(INSTALL_GTEST OFF) before FetchContent_MakeAvailable.

Config-mode find_package internals. fmtConfig.cmake is a CMake script that creates IMPORTED targets with IMPORTED_LOCATION and INTERFACE_INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES. Linking an imported target is identical to linking an in-tree target from the consumer's perspective. This is the mechanism install(EXPORT) generates for your own library.

MSBuild comparison. A .vcxproj is per-project; a .sln ties them together with GUIDs; ProjectReference is roughly target_link_libraries but include paths do not propagate (you repeat AdditionalIncludeDirectories or use property sheets). CMake's usage requirements are the feature MSBuild lacks. CMake can generate a .sln from the same CMakeLists.txt, which is how cross-platform teams work: one CMake, Visual Studio on Windows, Ninja on Linux (module 12).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• One CMakeLists.txt, three build directories. build/debug for daily work, build/asan for running tests before a PR, build/release for perf measurements and the Docker image. The presets make this cmake --preset X. Developers who type raw -D flags drift from CI.
  • -Werror toggle. TCPKV_WERROR ON by default and in CI; a packager building with GCC 15 can pass -DTCPKV_WERROR=OFF instead of patching your files.
  • Pin dependency versions. GIT_TAG v1.15.2, not main. Reproducible builds are a security and debugging requirement. Record the exact compiler too (Docker image tag, module 08).
  • Compile times. ninja -C build -d stats, ClangBuildAnalyzer with -ftime-trace, and ccache (-DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER=ccache) are the tools. A 40-minute build becomes 4 with ccache in CI (module 09).
  • Install, do not copy. The Dockerfile runs cmake --install build --prefix /opt/tcpkv; the runtime stage copies /opt/tcpkv. Install rules are the contract of what ships.
  • Mapping to your work. Your RPC server probably has a .sln with a dozen projects and property sheets for common flags. The CMake equivalent is one root CMakeLists.txt, one add_subdirectory per component, a cmake/ folder with the shared functions, and no flags in individual targets beyond what is specific to them. Being able to sketch that migration is a strong interview answer.
  • 3 AM: "the build is green but the binary is stale". Someone ran cmake --build after editing a header that only a file(GLOB)-collected source includes, and the glob did not see a renamed file. Fix the glob, then add CONFIGURE_DEPENDS or list files explicitly.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Copy code/Makefile next to a src/ with two .cpp files and an include/ header. Run make, touch the header, run make again. Done when the header edit rebuilds both objects and you can show the .d file that made it happen.
  2. (easy) Configure code/tcpkv with cmake --preset debug, build, and run ninja -C build/debug -t commands tcpkv | tail -3. Done when you can point at -I.../include, -pthread, -std=c++17 in the command and name the CMake line responsible for each.
  3. (medium) Change target_link_libraries(tcpkv_core PUBLIC Threads::Threads) to PRIVATE, reconfigure and build. Observe whether tcpkv still links and explain why or why not (hint: store.hpp holds a std::mutex; glibc 2.34+ merged libpthread). Then change the include directory from PUBLIC to PRIVATE and read the resulting error. Restore both. Done when you can state the rule for choosing visibility in one sentence.
  4. (medium) Add a clang preset that sets CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER to clang++. Build with it. Fix any warnings Clang finds that GCC did not. Done when both presets build with -Werror.
  5. (hard) Add a second library tcpkv_net in src/net/ with its own include/tcpkv/net/ header and make tcpkv depend on it; tcpkv_net must depend on tcpkv_core. Verify the transitive include dirs arrive at tcpkv without you adding them. Done when ninja -t commands tcpkv shows the include path exactly once.
  6. (hard) Add install(EXPORT ...) rules, run cmake --install build/release --prefix /tmp/tcpkv-install, then create a separate consumer project with find_package(tcpkv CONFIG REQUIRED) and target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE tcpkv::core), configured with -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/tmp/tcpkv-install. Done when the consumer builds and runs.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between CMake and Make? Make is a build executor: it runs rules whose inputs are newer than their outputs. CMake is a build-system generator: from one platform-independent description of targets it produces Makefiles, Ninja files or Visual Studio solutions. CMake also handles finding libraries, tests, installation and packaging.

Q: Explain PUBLIC, PRIVATE and INTERFACE in target_link_libraries. They control propagation of usage requirements. PRIVATE: the dependency is used only to build this target. PUBLIC: used to build this target and propagated to consumers, because it appears in public headers. INTERFACE: not used by this target itself but consumers need it, as with header-only libraries. Correct visibility means a consumer links one target and inherits everything it needs.

Q: Why is set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS "-Wall") considered bad practice? It is a global string applied to every target in the directory and below, including third-party code, and it cannot be scoped or expressed per configuration cleanly. target_compile_options with PRIVATE scope and generator expressions attaches flags to the targets that should have them.

Q: What is an out-of-source build and why does it matter? Build artefacts go in a separate directory from the sources. The tree stays clean, several configurations (debug, asan, release) coexist, and cleaning is rm -rf build. In-source builds pollute the tree and make a full clean impossible to do safely.

Q: How does CMake know to rebuild when a header changes? It does not; the generator does. CMake emits rules with depfile support; the compiler writes -MD dependency files during compilation listing every header included; Ninja (or Make via -include) reads them on the next build. That is why the first build must happen before header dependencies are known.

Q: find_package vs FetchContent: when do you use each? find_package consumes an installed library through its config file or a find module and is right for system dependencies like OpenSSL or libpq. FetchContent downloads and builds a dependency as part of your tree, pinned to a tag, and is right for test frameworks and small libraries where you want an exact version regardless of what the system has.

Q: What are presets for? CMakePresets.json records named configure/build/test recipes (generator, build dir, cache variables, environment) so developers and CI run the identical cmake --preset asan instead of long ad-hoc command lines. Hidden base presets and inheritance avoid repetition.

Q: What does gtest_discover_tests do differently from add_test? add_test registers one ctest entry that runs the whole test binary. gtest_discover_tests runs the binary with --gtest_list_tests after it is built and registers one ctest entry per test case, so ctest -j parallelises across tests and failures are reported per test name.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Build systems exist for minimal rebuilds; header dependency tracking is the hard part (-MMD).
  • Make: target: prereqs + tab-indented recipe; $@ $< $^; pattern rules; .PHONY; -include *.d.
  • CMake generates native build files; configure then build; Ninja is the generator to use.
  • Everything is a target with properties; usage requirements propagate via PUBLIC/INTERFACE.
  • PRIVATE for implementation needs, PUBLIC when it is in your public headers, INTERFACE for header-only.
  • Warnings and sanitizers are PRIVATE compile options attached by a helper function, never global flags.
  • Always set CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE; RelWithDebInfo is what you ship.
  • Out-of-source builds, one directory per configuration, driven by CMakePresets.json.
  • CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON feeds clangd and clang-tidy.
  • find_package for installed libs, FetchContent with a pinned tag for GoogleTest; install() defines what ships.

docs.title: 05. Testing with GoogleTest and ctest
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A unit test is a small program that calls one piece of your code with known inputs and checks the outputs. Hundreds of them run in a second. They are the difference between "I think the parser handles CRLF" and "the parser handles CRLF, here is the test, it has run 4,000 times in CI". When you refactor the store from one mutex to sharded locks, the tests tell you in two seconds whether you broke anything.

GoogleTest is the de facto C++ unit test framework: macros that define tests, assertions that compare values and print both sides on failure, fixtures for shared setup, and a runner. gMock, in the same package, creates fake implementations of interfaces so you can test code that talks to a database or socket without a database or socket. ctest is CMake's test driver: it knows about every test, runs them in parallel, and gives CI a single pass/fail exit code.

Analogy: your banking server's acceptance environment runs end-to-end scenarios overnight. Unit tests are the two-second version that runs every time you save: they do not replace the overnight run, they make it rarely fail.

docs.title: 2.1 What to test, and what not
docs.text:
Test pure logic with many edge cases: the protocol parser (every malformed line), the store (overwrite, delete-missing, empty value, large value), any serialisation, any arithmetic with boundaries. These are cheap, deterministic, and where the bugs are.

Test behaviour, not implementation: assert that get after set returns the value, not that the hash map has one bucket occupied. Tests that mirror the implementation break on every refactor and catch nothing.

Do not unit test the socket accept loop with real sockets in the same binary as the parser tests. That is an integration test: slower, flaky under load, needs ports. Keep it separate (a ctest with a label integration, run less often) or drive it from the Python client (module 10).

Design for testability: the reason parse_command takes a string_view and returns a struct, instead of reading from a socket and writing to one, is so the test can call it directly. Functions that do I/O should be thin wrappers around functions that do not.

docs.title: 2.2 GoogleTest basics
docs.text:
#include <gtest/gtest.h>

TEST(SuiteName, TestName) {            // SuiteName groups related tests; both are identifiers
    EXPECT_EQ(2 + 2, 4);               // on failure: records, prints both values, CONTINUES
    ASSERT_TRUE(ptr != nullptr);       // on failure: records and RETURNS from this test function
    EXPECT_EQ(ptr->x, 1);              // safe: we would not be here if ptr were null
}

EXPECT vs ASSERT: EXPECT_* lets one test report several failures, which is what you want when checking five fields of a result. ASSERT_* stops the test when continuing would crash or be meaningless (null pointer, empty optional, failed parse). ASSERT_* works by return, so it can only be used in functions returning void; in a helper that returns a value, use EXPECT or restructure.

Assertion families:

Assertion Checks EXPECT_TRUE(c), EXPECT_FALSE(c) boolean EXPECT_EQ(a,b), NE, LT, LE, GT, GE ==, !=, <, ... with both values printed EXPECT_STREQ(a,b), STRNE, STRCASEEQ C strings by content (EQ on char* compares pointers) EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ, DOUBLE_EQ, NEAR(a,b,eps) floating point within 4 ULPs / tolerance EXPECT_THROW(stmt, Type), ANY_THROW, NO_THROW exceptions EXPECT_THAT(value, matcher) gMock matchers: Eq, HasSubstr, ElementsAre, Contains, SizeIs, AllOf... EXPECT_DEATH(stmt, regex) statement kills the process (assert, abort) with matching stderr FAIL(), ADD_FAILURE(), SUCCEED() explicit

Every assertion accepts a streamed message: ASSERT_TRUE(r.ok()) << "parse error: " << r.error;. On failure the output is:

tests/test_protocol.cpp:31: Failure
Expected equality of these values:
  r.command->key
    Which is: "user:42"
  "user:43"

Both expressions and both values. This is why EXPECT_EQ(a, b) beats EXPECT_TRUE(a == b). Custom types need operator<< or a PrintTo overload to print nicely; otherwise you get bytes.

docs.title: 2.3 Fixtures
docs.text:
A fixture is a class deriving from ::testing::Test; each TEST_F gets a fresh instance. SetUp() runs before the body, TearDown() after (also on failure). Use the constructor and destructor for things that cannot fail; use SetUp/TearDown when you need assertions in them.

class StoreTest : public ::testing::Test {
protected:
    void SetUp() override { store_.set("a", "1"); store_.set("b", "2"); }
    tcpkv::Store store_;
};
TEST_F(StoreTest, DelReturnsTrueOnlyWhenKeyExisted) {
    EXPECT_TRUE(store_.del("a"));
    EXPECT_FALSE(store_.del("a"));
}

Isolation per test is the point: a test cannot pass because of what a previous test left behind, and --gtest_shuffle can run them in random order to prove it. Expensive shared state (a database connection) goes in static void SetUpTestSuite() / TearDownTestSuite(), once per suite.

docs.title: 2.4 Parameterised tests
docs.text:
When the same check applies to many inputs, write it once and feed a table:

class ParseCommandRejects : public ::testing::TestWithParam<BadInput> {};
TEST_P(ParseCommandRejects, ReturnsExpectedError) {
    const BadInput& in = GetParam();
    const auto r = parse_command(in.line);
    EXPECT_FALSE(r.ok());
    EXPECT_EQ(r.error, in.expected_error);
}
INSTANTIATE_TEST_SUITE_P(MalformedLines, ParseCommandRejects,
    ::testing::Values(BadInput{"", "empty command"}, BadInput{"FLY", "unknown command"}, ...));

Each value becomes its own test: MalformedLines/ParseCommandRejects.ReturnsExpectedError/3. A failure names the index and, with an operator<< on the param type, prints the input. Generators: Values(...), ValuesIn(container), Range(begin, end, step), Bool(), Combine(g1, g2) for a cross product. Typed tests (TYPED_TEST) run the same body against several types, useful for testing a template against int, std::string, a custom type.

docs.title: 2.5 Death tests
docs.text:
A death test asserts that code terminates the process: a failed assert, an abort(), a std::terminate from noexcept. Use them to verify precondition checks fire.

TEST(StoreDeathTest, NullBufferAborts) {
    EXPECT_DEATH(copy_into(nullptr, 10), "buffer must not be null");
}

Mechanism: GoogleTest forks; the child runs the statement; the parent checks the child died and that stderr matched the regex. Name the suite *DeathTest so GoogleTest runs them first (before threads exist; forking a multithreaded process is unsafe, see module 11). Under --gtest_death_test_style=threadsafe the child re-executes the binary to run only that test, which is slower but safe with threads. Death tests do not work under some sanitizers' leak detection without ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 in the child; the tcpkv asan preset sets halt_on_error which is compatible.

docs.title: 2.6 Running tests
docs.text:
./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests                       # all
./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests --gtest_filter='ParseCommand.*'       # suite
./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests --gtest_filter='*Reject*:-*Length*'   # include : exclude
./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests --gtest_repeat=100 --gtest_shuffle    # flakiness hunt
./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests --gtest_break_on_failure              # SIGTRAP into gdb
./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests --gtest_list_tests
./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests --gtest_output=xml:report.xml         # JUnit XML for CI
gdb --args ./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests --gtest_filter='StoreTest.Del*' --gtest_break_on_failure

docs.title: 2.7 gMock introduction
docs.text:
A mock is a generated implementation of an interface where the test says which calls to expect, what to return, and how many times. It lets you test a class that depends on something slow, external or non-deterministic (disk, network, clock, random, PostgreSQL).

class WriteAheadLog {
public:
    virtual ~WriteAheadLog() = default;
    virtual bool append(std::string_view key, std::string_view value) = 0;
    virtual void sync() = 0;
};
class MockWal : public WriteAheadLog {
public:
    MOCK_METHOD(bool, append, (std::string_view, std::string_view), (override));
    MOCK_METHOD(void, sync, (), (override));
};

TEST(PersistentStore, FailedLogAppendLeavesStoreUnchanged) {
    StrictMock<MockWal> wal;                              // unexpected calls fail the test
    PersistentStore ps(wal);
    EXPECT_CALL(wal, append(_, _)).WillOnce(Return(false));
    EXPECT_FALSE(ps.set("k", "v"));
    EXPECT_FALSE(ps.get("k").has_value());
}

Vocabulary: EXPECT_CALL(mock, method(matchers)) with .Times(n), .WillOnce(action), .WillRepeatedly(action), .InSequence(seq). Matchers: _ (anything), Eq(v), Gt(v), HasSubstr(s), Pointee(m). Actions: Return(v), ReturnRef(r), Throw(e), Invoke(fn), SaveArg<N>(&var). NiceMock ignores unexpected calls, StrictMock fails on them, plain mock warns. ON_CALL sets a default behaviour without expecting the call.

When not to mock: do not mock the thing under test; do not mock value types; do not mock std::unordered_map. Mock at architectural boundaries (I/O, time, external services). Mocks need a virtual interface or a template parameter; that is a design cost, paid only where testing needs it. Full example: code/tcpkv/tests/test_gmock_example.cpp.

docs.title: 2.8 ctest integration
docs.text:
enable_testing()                        # top-level CMakeLists.txt
include(GoogleTest)
gtest_discover_tests(tcpkv_tests DISCOVERY_TIMEOUT 30 PROPERTIES LABELS "unit")

gtest_discover_tests runs the binary with --gtest_list_tests after build and writes one ctest entry per test. Then:

ctest --test-dir build/debug                      # run all; one line per test
ctest --test-dir build/debug -j8 --output-on-failure
ctest --test-dir build/debug -R 'StoreTest'       # regex on test name
ctest --test-dir build/debug -L unit              # by label
ctest --test-dir build/debug --rerun-failed
ctest --test-dir build/debug -N                   # list without running
ctest --preset asan                               # with the preset's environment (ASAN_OPTIONS)

ctest exits non-zero if any test failed. That exit code is what CI consumes. For integration tests that need a running server, add_test(NAME integration COMMAND python3 scripts/tcpkv_client.py --selftest) with set_tests_properties(integration PROPERTIES LABELS integration FIXTURES_REQUIRED server) and a fixture test that starts the server; or simply run it as a separate CI step.

docs.title: 2.9 Sanitizers in tests
docs.text:
The test binary is the ideal sanitizer host: it exercises the code with many inputs, it is already in CI, and it runs for seconds. The tcpkv presets asan and tsan build the library and the tests with the sanitizer (both must be instrumented), and the test presets set ASAN_OPTIONS so a report fails the run:

cmake --preset asan && cmake --build --preset asan && ctest --preset asan
cmake --preset tsan && cmake --build --preset tsan && ctest --preset tsan -R Concurrency

Under TSan, StoreConcurrency.ReadersAndWritersOnSameKeySeeOnlyValidValues becomes a proof that Store has no data race. Remove the lock_guard from Store::get and run it: TSan prints the two stacks (the write in set, the read in get) and the test fails. A test that passes without TSan and fails with it is exactly what the TSan job in CI is for (module 09).

docs.title: 2.10 Test naming and organisation
docs.text:
• One test file per production file: src/protocol.cpp -> tests/test_protocol.cpp.
  • Suite = the unit (ParseCommand, StoreTest), test = behaviour under a condition: GetReturnsNulloptForMissingKey, TrailingCarriageReturnIsStripped. The ctest output then reads as a specification.
  • Arrange, act, assert: set up inputs, call once, check. A test that calls three functions and asserts after each is three tests.
  • One concept per test; several EXPECTs on the fields of one result are fine.
  • No logic in tests (loops, conditionals). If you need a loop, you want a parameterised test.
  • Tests are production code: same warnings, same sanitizers, same review.

docs.title: 2.11 What to test in a server like tcpkv
docs.text:
Layer Test type Examples Protocol parser unit, parameterised every verb, CRLF, limits, every malformed shape, round trip Store unit, fixture, TSan set/get/del/clear, overwrite, empty value, concurrency Connection handler unit with injected fake socket, or integration partial lines across recv, pipelined commands in one recv, oversize line disconnect Server lifecycle integration (Python client) start, PING, SET/GET, SIGTERM drains, exit 0 Persistence (future) gMock for the log, integration with a temp dir append-before-store, fsync on checkpoint, recovery

The connection handler in main.cpp reads from a file descriptor. To unit test the line-splitting logic, factor it into a class that takes bytes and emits lines (LineReader::feed(string_view) -> vector<string>), test that, and let serve_client call it. That refactor is exercise 5.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
• code/tcpkv/tests/test_protocol.cpp: plain tests, two parameterised suites, formatter tests.
  • code/tcpkv/tests/test_store.cpp: fixture, concurrency tests meant for TSan.
  • code/tcpkv/tests/test_gmock_example.cpp: interface, mock, StrictMock, EXPECT_CALL.
  • code/tcpkv/tests/CMakeLists.txt: find_package(GTest) with FetchContent fallback, gtest_discover_tests.

Run the whole cycle:

cd code/tcpkv
cmake --preset debug && cmake --build --preset debug && ctest --preset debug
# expect: 100% tests passed, N tests
./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests --gtest_filter='MalformedLines/*' --gtest_brief=1
cmake --preset asan && cmake --build --preset asan && ctest --preset asan
cmake --preset tsan && cmake --build --preset tsan && ctest --preset tsan -R Concurrency

Break something on purpose and watch it fail:

sed -i 's/if (!s.empty() \&\& s.back() == .\\r.) s.remove_suffix(1);/\/\/ removed/' src/protocol.cpp
cmake --build --preset debug && ctest --preset debug     # TrailingCarriageReturnIsStripped fails
git checkout src/protocol.cpp

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
How TEST works. The macro expands to a class SuiteName_TestName_Test deriving from ::testing::Test with a TestBody() override, plus a static TestInfo* initialised by calling MakeAndRegisterTestInfo(...) at static-initialisation time. That registration is why tests in a static library are silently dropped: the linker does not pull an archive member that nothing references (module 02). Rule: tests are compiled directly into the test executable, or linked with --whole-archive, or use object libraries.

gtest_main is a library containing int main(int argc, char** argv) { InitGoogleTest(&argc, argv); return RUN_ALL_TESTS(); }. RUN_ALL_TESTS iterates registered suites, for each test constructs the fixture, runs SetUp, TestBody, TearDown, destroys it, and collects results. Return value is 0 iff all passed. If you need your own main (global environment, custom flags), link GTest::gtest instead.

Why EXPECT prints both expressions. EXPECT_EQ(a, b) expands to a call to EqHelper::Compare("a", "b", a, b) with the stringified expressions, so the failure message can show the source text and the runtime values. The comparison is done with operator== on the deduced types; mixing signed/unsigned can trigger -Wsign-compare inside the template, which is why EXPECT_EQ(v.size(), 2u) and not 2.

Death tests fork. In "fast" style the child continues from the fork point inside the test body, so any threads, locks or buffered output in the parent are duplicated or lost. In "threadsafe" style the child execs the test binary with a filter for that one test, replaying up to the death statement. That is why DeathTest suites run first and why you should not have threads alive before them.

gtest_discover_tests has a build-time cost. It adds a POST_BUILD step running the binary; if the binary needs a display, a device or a long static init, discovery can fail or time out (DISCOVERY_TIMEOUT). DISCOVERY_MODE PRE_TEST defers discovery to ctest run time.

Sanitizers and GoogleTest. ASan's leak checker runs at process exit, after RUN_ALL_TESTS returned; a leak therefore fails the binary, and ctest sees the non-zero exit even though every test printed [ OK ]. That is correct behaviour and a reason to read the whole log. TSan needs -fsanitize=thread on gtest itself too; FetchContent-built gtest inherits your flags only if you set them globally or through CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS for the fetched target, which is why the presets set TCPKV_SANITIZE and the sanitizer helper applies to your targets; gtest's own code is not instrumented, which is fine because TSan instruments the code where the race happens (yours). For ASan, uninstrumented gtest means ASan cannot see overflows inside gtest, which you do not care about.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Tests are what make -Werror and refactoring affordable. Without them, every warning fix is a risk; with them, you fix 200 warnings in an afternoon and know nothing broke.
  • Flaky tests destroy trust. A test that fails 1 in 50 runs is ignored, then a real failure is ignored. Hunt flakes with --gtest_repeat=1000 --gtest_shuffle and TSan. Common causes: shared static state, time-based assertions, real sockets with fixed ports, thread scheduling assumptions.
  • Test the error paths. Production code is 30% happy path and 70% error handling; most test suites are the inverse. Every return fail(...) in the parser has a test. Every errno branch in the server should be reachable from a test with an injected fake descriptor.
  • Regression tests for every bug. When a core dump leads to a root cause (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA), the fix commit includes a test that fails before and passes after. The test is the durable record of the incident.
  • In your banking server: the RPC message codec and the transaction state machine are pure logic and should have hundreds of unit tests. The Berkeley DB adapter should be behind an interface so the migration logic can be tested with a mock, including the "DB returns DB_LOCK_DEADLOCK on the third call" path that only ever happens in production at month-end.
  • 3 AM: CI is green but production corrupts a record. The test suite had EXPECT_TRUE(result == expected) on a struct with a buggy operator== that ignored one field. Lesson: test the comparison operators too, and prefer field-by-field EXPECT_EQ for important types.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Add a test for SET with a key containing : and - characters (valid) and one with a tab (invalid). Done when both pass and you can show them in ctest -N output.
  2. (easy) Run the suite with --gtest_shuffle --gtest_repeat=50. Then introduce a static variable shared between two tests so one depends on the other, and show that shuffle catches it. Revert. Done when you can explain why per-test fixture instances matter.
  3. (medium) Write a death test: add void Store::require_key(std::string_view key) that abort()s with a message on an empty key, call it from set, and assert with EXPECT_DEATH. Done when the test passes in the debug preset. Then decide whether aborting is the right production behaviour for a server and write your answer in a comment.
  4. (medium) Remove the lock_guard from Store::get, build the tsan preset and run ctest --preset tsan -R Concurrency. Read the report: identify the two stacks and the two threads. Restore the lock. Done when you can describe the report format from memory.
  5. (hard) Extract a LineReader class from serve_client: std::vector<std::string> feed(std::string_view bytes) returning complete lines and keeping the partial tail, with an overflow flag when the tail exceeds kMaxLineLength. Write tests for: a line split across three feeds, two lines in one feed, CRLF, and overflow. Make serve_client use it. Done when all tests pass under asan and the server still works with nc localhost 7000.
  6. (hard) Add an integration test: add_test(NAME integration COMMAND python3 ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/scripts/tcpkv_client.py --selftest --port 7123) using ctest FIXTURES_SETUP/FIXTURES_CLEANUP tests that start and stop the server binary. Label it integration and make ctest -L unit skip it. Done when ctest -L integration passes and ctest -L unit finishes in under two seconds.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: EXPECT vs ASSERT in GoogleTest? EXPECT_* records a failure and continues, so one run reports every broken field. ASSERT_* records and returns from the test function, for cases where continuing would dereference null or otherwise make the rest meaningless. ASSERT only works in void functions because it uses return.

Q: What is a fixture and why does GoogleTest create a new one per test? A class with shared setup and members used by several TEST_Fs. A fresh instance per test guarantees isolation: no test can depend on another's leftovers, so tests can run in any order or in parallel, and a failure points at one test's own logic.

Q: When would you use a parameterised test? When one behaviour must hold for many inputs: a parser against a table of malformed lines. One body, a table of values, each value reported as its own test with its index and printed input. It replaces a loop in a test, which would stop at the first failure and hide the rest.

Q: What is a mock and where does it belong? A generated implementation of an interface where the test specifies expected calls, return values and call counts. It belongs at architectural boundaries, such as disk, network, clock, external services, so the unit under test can be exercised without them. Mocking value types or the unit under test is a smell.

Q: How do sanitizers fit into a test strategy? Build the library and the tests with -fsanitize=address,undefined in one configuration and thread in another; run the same suite under each in CI. The suite already exercises edge cases, so sanitizers turn it into a memory-safety and race detector at no extra test-writing cost.

Q: Why might tests placed in a static library never run? GoogleTest registers tests via static initialisers. The linker only pulls archive members that resolve an undefined symbol; nothing references the test objects, so they are dropped and their initialisers never run. Compile tests into the executable, or use --whole-archive.

Q: How does ctest relate to GoogleTest? GoogleTest is the framework inside the test binary. ctest is CMake's runner that knows about test binaries, runs them in parallel with timeouts, labels and filters, and returns one exit code. gtest_discover_tests bridges them by registering each GoogleTest case as a ctest entry.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Test pure logic exhaustively (parser, store); keep I/O behind thin wrappers so it can be injected or integration-tested.
  • TEST, TEST_F (fixture, fresh per test), TEST_P (parameterised table), EXPECT_DEATH.
  • EXPECT continues, ASSERT returns; stream a message with <<.
  • EXPECT_EQ(a, b) prints both sides; give custom types an operator<<.
  • gMock: interface + MOCK_METHOD + EXPECT_CALL(...).Times/WillOnce; StrictMock for exactness.
  • gtest_discover_tests gives one ctest entry per case; ctest --preset X -j --output-on-failure.
  • Run the same suite under asan and tsan presets; the sanitizer failures are real bugs.
  • Name tests as specification sentences; one behaviour per test; no logic in tests.
  • Tests in static libraries vanish at link; compile them into the executable.
  • Every bug fix ships with a regression test.

docs.title: 06. Git properly
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Git is a content-addressed database of snapshots with a graph of pointers on top. Every commit is a complete snapshot of your tree (stored efficiently), named by the SHA-1 of its contents, pointing at its parent(s). A branch is a movable sticky note with a commit's name on it. HEAD is a sticky note saying which branch you are on. Once you see Git this way, every command is "move a sticky note", "make a new snapshot", or "show me the graph", and nothing is scary: a commit that exists is almost impossible to lose.

You use Git already. This module is about using it the way a senior engineer at a company with code review does: small commits with good messages, rebase to keep history readable, bisect to find the commit that broke things, reflog to recover from mistakes, and a GitHub profile that makes a hiring manager stop scrolling.

Analogy: a commit is a save point in a game. A branch is a label on a save point that moves forward as you keep playing. Rebasing is replaying your last five moves on top of someone else's save. Reflog is the list of every save point your console ever pointed at, even ones you "deleted".

docs.title: 2.1 The object model
docs.text:
Four object types live in .git/objects/, each named by the SHA-1 of its content:

blob    file contents (no name, no mode)
tree    a directory: list of (mode, type, hash, name) entries pointing at blobs and trees
commit  tree hash + parent hash(es) + author + committer + message
tag     (annotated) a named, signed pointer at a commit with a message

                 refs/heads/main --> commit c3
                                       |  tree t3
                                       |  parent c2
                                       v
   c1 <------- c2 <------- c3           t3 ---> blob "store.cpp v3"
                                           ---> tree src/ ---> blob "main.cpp"
   HEAD --> refs/heads/main

Because a commit's hash covers its tree and its parent's hash, changing anything anywhere in history changes every hash after it. That is why "rewriting history" means creating new commits, never editing old ones, and why a hash is a tamper-evident identifier.

git cat-file -p HEAD           # the commit object: tree, parent, author, message
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}    # the tree: mode type hash name
git cat-file -t <hash>         # type of any object
git rev-parse HEAD             # the full hash HEAD points at
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate   # the picture above, from the real repo

Same content means same hash: a file copied to ten directories is stored once. Git stores loose objects zlib-compressed, then periodically packs them into .git/objects/pack/*.pack with delta compression (git gc).

docs.title: 2.2 The three areas
docs.text:
working tree  --git add-->  index (staging area)  --git commit-->  HEAD (repository)
     ^                            |                                   |
     +------- git restore --------+------ git restore --staged -------+
  • Working tree: the files you edit.
  • Index: the exact snapshot the next commit will contain. git add -p stages hunks interactively so one editing session can become two clean commits.
  • HEAD: the current commit.
git status                     # working tree vs index vs HEAD
git diff                       # working tree vs index (unstaged changes)
git diff --staged              # index vs HEAD (what the commit will contain)
git add -p                     # stage hunk by hunk: y/n/s(split)/e(edit)
git restore file               # discard working-tree change (DESTRUCTIVE, no undo)
git restore --staged file      # unstage, keep the edit
git commit -v                  # editor shows the diff below the message
git commit --amend --no-edit   # fold staged changes into the last commit (local only)

docs.title: 2.3 Branching
docs.text:
A branch is a 41-byte file .git/refs/heads/<name> containing a commit hash. Creating one is free.

git switch -c feature/parser-crlf        # create and switch (replaces `checkout -b`)
git switch main
git branch -vv                           # local branches with upstream and ahead/behind
git branch -d feature/x                  # delete merged branch; -D forces
git push -u origin feature/parser-crlf   # publish and set upstream
git fetch --prune                        # update remote-tracking refs, drop deleted remote branches

origin/main is a remote-tracking branch: your last-known position of main on the server. git fetch updates it; git pull is fetch + merge (or + rebase with pull.rebase=true, which you want).

docs.title: 2.4 Merge vs rebase
docs.text:
Two ways to bring main's new commits into your feature branch:

Before:          A---B---C  main
                  \
                   D---E    feature

Merge:           A---B---C-------  main
                  \       \
                   D---E---M        feature   (M has two parents; history shows the fork)

Rebase:          A---B---C          main
                          \
                           D'--E'   feature   (D and E REPLAYED on C: new hashes, linear history)

git switch feature
git merge main                    # creates merge commit M
git rebase main                   # rewrites D,E as D',E' on top of C
git rebase -i main                # interactive: reorder, squash, reword, drop (see 2.6)
git push --force-with-lease       # after rebasing a branch you already pushed
