Rule: rebase your own unpublished or personal-branch commits to keep them clean; merge (or squash-merge) into shared branches; never rebase a branch others have based work on because their commits point at the old hashes. --force-with-lease refuses to overwrite if someone pushed to the branch since your last fetch; plain --force does not check. Always --force-with-lease.

Fast-forward: if main has not moved since you branched, merging your branch just moves the main pointer forward; no merge commit. git merge --no-ff forces a merge commit (some teams want the "bubble" to show feature boundaries); --ff-only refuses unless fast-forward is possible.

Squash merge (GitHub "Squash and merge"): all feature commits become one commit on main. Clean main, but the feature branch's individual commits are gone from main's history. Good default for small PRs; bad when the PR is a series of meaningful steps.

docs.title: 2.5 Resolving conflicts
docs.text:
A conflict happens when both sides changed the same lines. Git stops and marks the file:

<<<<<<< HEAD
    if (!s.empty() && s.back() == '\r') s.remove_suffix(1);
=======
    while (!s.empty() && (s.back() == '\r' || s.back() == '\n')) s.remove_suffix(1);
>>>>>>> feature/strip-all

git status                         # "both modified: src/protocol.cpp"
git diff                           # shows conflict hunks with both sides
# edit the file: keep one side, the other, or write the combination; delete the markers
git add src/protocol.cpp           # marks resolved
git merge --continue               # or: git rebase --continue
git merge --abort                  # or: git rebase --abort   -> back to before you started
git checkout --ours file / --theirs file   # take one side wholesale (careful: in a rebase,
                                           # "ours" is the branch being rebased ONTO)
git mergetool                      # launches configured tool (meld, vimdiff, VS Code)

During a rebase, conflicts can occur once per replayed commit; fix, git add, git rebase --continue, repeat. Enable git config --global rerere.enabled true and Git remembers how you resolved a conflict and reapplies it if the same conflict appears again (common during long rebases).

Reduce conflicts: small PRs, rebase often, do not reformat whole files in the same commit as a logic change, agree on .clang-format so formatting is never a diff.

docs.title: 2.6 Interactive rebase (described, no editor needed)
docs.text:
git rebase -i <base> opens an editor with one line per commit, oldest first:

pick a1b2c3 Add CRLF stripping to parser
pick d4e5f6 fix typo
pick 789abc Add tests for CRLF

You change the verb at the start of each line: pick keep, reword keep but edit message, edit stop to amend, squash meld into previous keeping both messages, fixup meld into previous discarding this message, drop delete, and reordering lines reorders commits. Then save; Git replays accordingly.

To do this without an interactive editor (scripts, CI, or just preference):

# squash the last 3 commits into one with a new message
git reset --soft HEAD~3 && git commit -m "Add CRLF handling to parser with tests"

# fixup workflow: commit small fixes marked for a target commit, then autosquash
git commit --fixup=a1b2c3                 # message "fixup! Add CRLF stripping to parser"
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash main   # applies all fixup! lines, no editor

# reword the last commit
git commit --amend -m "New message"

# drop a commit in the middle
git rebase --onto <commit-before-bad> <bad-commit>   # replays everything after bad onto before

GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true makes the "editor" a no-op that accepts the generated todo list; with --autosquash that list already has fixup! commits moved and marked. This is the technique to know for interviews: "I use --fixup and --autosquash to keep PR history clean".

docs.title: 2.7 Finding the breaking commit: bisect
docs.text:
Tests passed at v1.2.0, fail on main, 60 commits in between. Binary search:

git bisect start
git bisect bad                  # current commit is bad
git bisect good v1.2.0          # this tag was good
# Git checks out the midpoint. Build and test. Then:
git bisect good    # or
git bisect bad
# ~6 steps for 60 commits. At the end: "<hash> is the first bad commit"
git bisect reset                # back to where you were

Automated: git bisect run ./scripts/bisect_test.sh where the script exits 0 for good, 1-124 or 126-127 for bad, 125 for "cannot test this commit, skip". Example script:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
cmake --preset debug >/dev/null && cmake --build --preset debug >/dev/null || exit 125
ctest --preset debug -R 'ParseCommand.TrailingCarriageReturnIsStripped' >/dev/null

Bisect is why small, buildable commits matter: a commit that does not compile is a hole in the search space.

docs.title: 2.8 Stash, reflog, and getting out of trouble
docs.text:
git stash                       # shelve working tree + index; tree becomes clean
git stash -u                    # include untracked files
git stash list; git stash show -p stash@{0}
git stash pop                   # reapply and drop (conflicts possible)
git stash apply                 # reapply and keep

Reflog records every position HEAD and each branch has had, for 90 days by default. This is the undo button for almost everything.

git reflog                      # HEAD@{0}: commit: ..., HEAD@{1}: rebase: ..., HEAD@{2}: reset: ...
git reflog show feature/x       # per branch

Recovery recipes:

Mistake Fix git reset --hard lost commits git reflog, find the hash before the reset, git reset --hard <hash> or git branch rescue <hash> Deleted a branch git reflog shows its last commit; git branch name <hash> Rebase went wrong git reflog, git reset --hard HEAD@{n} where n is before the rebase started; or git rebase --abort if still in progress Amended the wrong commit git reflog, the pre-amend commit is HEAD@{1}; git reset --soft HEAD@{1} Committed to main instead of a branch git branch feature, git reset --hard origin/main, git switch feature Committed a secret rotate the secret first; then git filter-repo (not filter-branch) to remove it from history; force-push; everyone re-clones Detached HEAD with commits git switch -c save-me

git fsck --lost-found finds dangling commits not in any reflog. Objects are only deleted by git gc when unreachable and older than the reflog expiry; in practice, a commit you made this month is recoverable.

docs.title: 2.9 .gitignore, attributes, config
docs.text:
# .gitignore for a CMake C++ project
build/
build-*/
cmake-build-*/
CMakeUserPresets.json
compile_commands.json
.cache/            # clangd
*.o
*.a
*.so
*.so.*
core
core.*
*.log
.vscode/
.idea/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env

Rules: patterns are relative to the .gitignore's directory; a trailing / means directory only; !pattern re-includes; ** matches across directories. A file already tracked is not affected by .gitignore: git rm --cached file untracks it. Global ignores (editor swap files) go in ~/.config/git/ignore, not in every project.

.gitattributes for line endings and diff behaviour:

* text=auto eol=lf
*.sh text eol=lf
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.png binary

eol=lf for shell scripts is important: a script with CRLF fails with bad interpreter (module 01).

Config worth setting once:

git config --global user.name "Shakir ..."
git config --global user.email "rajaman.ar3@gmail.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global pull.rebase true
git config --global push.default current
git config --global push.autoSetupRemote true
git config --global fetch.prune true
git config --global rerere.enabled true
git config --global core.autocrlf input       # on WSL/Linux: convert CRLF to LF on commit
git config --global diff.algorithm histogram   # better diffs for moved blocks
git config --global merge.conflictstyle zdiff3 # shows the common ancestor in conflict hunks
git config --global rebase.autosquash true
git config --global rebase.autostash true
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate --all"
git config --global alias.st "status -sb"

docs.title: 2.10 Commit messages
docs.text:
Strip trailing CR in protocol parser

Windows clients and `nc -C` send CRLF. The parser treated "PING\r" as an
unknown command. Strip a single trailing '\r' before tokenising.

Only one CR is stripped on purpose: "PING\r\r" is still malformed.

Fixes #42
  • Subject: imperative mood ("Add", "Fix", "Strip"), 50 characters or so, no trailing period. It completes the sentence "If applied, this commit will ...".
  • Blank line, then body wrapped at 72: why, not what (the diff shows what). What was wrong, why this fix, what alternatives were rejected, side effects.
  • Reference issues. Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, docs:, refactor:, test:, ci:, build:, perf:, chore:) is a common prefix scheme that lets tools generate changelogs and compute the next version; use it if the project does.
  • One logical change per commit. "Fix parser and update CI and rename variable" is three commits.

docs.title: 2.11 Pull request workflow
docs.text:
git switch main && git pull
git switch -c fix/parser-crlf
# ... work, commit in small steps ...
cmake --preset asan && cmake --build --preset asan && ctest --preset asan    # before pushing
git push -u origin fix/parser-crlf
gh pr create --fill --base main           # GitHub CLI; or use the web UI
# review comments -> fix -> git commit --fixup=<hash> -> rebase --autosquash -> push --force-with-lease
gh pr checks; gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch

A good PR: under ~400 changed lines (reviewers lose accuracy beyond that, typical finding from code-review studies), one purpose, description states the problem, the approach, how it was tested, and anything the reviewer should look at first. Screenshots or log excerpts where relevant. Draft PRs for early feedback. Link the issue.

docs.title: 2.12 Code review etiquette
docs.text:
As author: respond to every comment (fix, or explain why not); do not take it personally; make the reviewer's job easy with a clear description and small diffs; never force-push during an active review without saying so (comments lose their anchor).

As reviewer: review within a working day; comment on the code, not the person ("this loop re-locks per iteration" not "you re-lock per iteration"); distinguish blocking issues from nits (prefix nit:); ask questions when unsure; approve when it is better than what exists, not when it is perfect; praise good things, briefly. Look for: correctness, error paths, tests, naming, concurrency, resource ownership. Do not bikeshed formatting if clang-format exists.

docs.title: 2.13 Protecting main
docs.text:
In GitHub: Settings -> Branches -> Add rule for main: require a pull request before merging, require 1 approval, require status checks to pass (your CI jobs, module 09), require branches to be up to date, require linear history (forces squash or rebase merges), do not allow force pushes, do not allow deletions. Optionally require signed commits. CODEOWNERS file assigns reviewers by path. Azure DevOps has the same under Branch Policies.

Result: nothing reaches main without building clean under -Werror, passing tests, passing ASan, and a human reading it. That sentence is a strong interview answer.

docs.title: 2.14 Tags and semantic versioning
docs.text:
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "tcpkv 1.2.0: CRLF support, TSan-clean store"   # annotated: has author, date, message
git tag v1.2.0-rc1                                                     # lightweight: just a pointer
git push origin v1.2.0        # tags are not pushed by default; --tags pushes all
git describe --tags           # v1.2.0-3-g1a2b3c4: 3 commits after v1.2.0 at hash 1a2b3c4
git tag -l 'v1.*'

Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: PATCH for bug fixes with no API change, MINOR for backward-compatible additions, MAJOR for breaking changes. Pre-release -rc1, build metadata +build.5. For a library this is a contract about source and ABI compatibility (module 02 soname: the soname major usually tracks the MAJOR). For a server it tells operators whether an upgrade needs a config migration. CMake's project(tcpkv VERSION 0.1.0) should come from the tag: git describe in a configure step, or a release script that updates both.

Release flow: tag on main, CI builds artefacts for the tag (module 09), GitHub Release with changelog, Docker image tagged tcpkv:1.2.0 and tcpkv:1.2 (module 08).

docs.title: 2.15 Making a GitHub profile look strong
docs.text:
Hiring managers spend about a minute. Make it count:

  • Profile README (<username>/<username> repo): two lines about what you do (C on Windows for core banking, 2.5 years; learning Linux C++ systems programming), three links to your best repos, your email. No wall of badges.
  • Pin 4-6 repos, each with: a one-paragraph README describing what it is and why, a build badge that is green, a "Build and run" section with exact commands, a short architecture note, and tests visible in the tree. tcpkv is the showcase: README, CI badge, cmake --preset, Dockerfile, a diagram of the connection model.
  • Commit history that looks like work: regular commits over weeks with real messages beat one 10,000-line "initial commit". Reviewers click into commits.
  • Topics and description set on each repo so they are searchable.
  • Issues and PRs on your own repos: open an issue for the next feature, close it with a PR. Shows process.
  • A LICENSE file (MIT is fine) so the code is usable.
  • No secrets, no build/ committed, no 500 MB binaries. A .gitignore that works is itself a signal.
  • Contributing a small fix to a well-known project (documentation counts) and linking the merged PR is worth more than another toy repo.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
No C++ in this module. Build a repository for code/tcpkv and practise the graph:

cp -r code/tcpkv ~/projects/tcpkv && cd ~/projects/tcpkv
git init -b main
cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
build/
CMakeUserPresets.json
compile_commands.json
.cache/
EOF
git add . && git commit -m "Initial tcpkv skeleton: CMake, library, server, GoogleTest"
git lg

# a feature branch with three commits, then clean them up without an editor
git switch -c feature/strip-all-eol
echo "// change 1" >> src/protocol.cpp && git commit -am "Strip all trailing EOL chars"
echo "// typo"     >> src/protocol.cpp && git commit -am "fix typo"
echo "// tests"    >> tests/test_protocol.cpp && git commit -am "Add EOL tests"
git commit --allow-empty --fixup=HEAD~2        # mark a fixup for the first commit
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash main
git lg                                          # fixup folded in; three commits remain

# simulate main moving, then rebase and resolve a conflict
git switch main
echo "// main change" >> src/protocol.cpp && git commit -am "Main: tweak protocol"
git switch feature/strip-all-eol
git rebase main                                 # CONFLICT in src/protocol.cpp
git diff                                        # read the <<<< ==== >>>> hunk (zdiff3 shows base too)
# edit src/protocol.cpp to keep both lines, then:
git add src/protocol.cpp && GIT_EDITOR=true git rebase --continue
git lg

# break something and recover with reflog
git reset --hard HEAD~2                         # "lost" two commits
git reflog | head -5
git reset --hard 'HEAD@{1}'                     # back
git lg

# bisect practice
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do echo "// c$i" >> src/store.cpp; git commit -qam "step $i"; done
echo "BUG" >> src/store.cpp && git commit -qam "step 9 introduces BUG"
for i in 10 11 12; do echo "// c$i" >> src/store.cpp; git commit -qam "step $i"; done
git bisect start HEAD HEAD~12
git bisect run sh -c '! grep -q BUG src/store.cpp'   # exit 0 (good) when BUG absent
git bisect reset

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Content addressing. git hash-object file computes sha1("blob " + size + "\0" + content). .git/objects/ab/cdef... is that object zlib-compressed. Trees hash their entries, commits hash their tree and parents. The whole history is a Merkle DAG; a single hash authenticates everything reachable from it. Git is migrating to SHA-256 (git init --object-format=sha256), but SHA-1 with collision detection remains the default in 2026.

Packfiles and deltas. Loose objects are full copies. git gc (run automatically) writes a packfile where similar objects (versions of the same file) are stored as deltas against a base, plus an .idx for lookup. This is why a repository with 10,000 versions of a 1 MB file can be 50 MB. Clones transfer packs; --depth 1 requests only the tips (CI does this, module 09).

What rebase actually does. For each commit to replay, Git computes the diff from that commit's parent to the commit, applies it onto the new base with a three-way merge (base = original parent, ours = new base, theirs = the commit), and creates a new commit object with the new parent and the same author/message. New hash every time, even if the content is identical, because the parent changed. Rerere stores (conflict-hunk-hash -> resolution) in .git/rr-cache.

Index format. .git/index is a binary file listing every tracked path with its blob hash, mode, size and mtime/ctime. git status compares stat data first and hashes content only for files whose stat changed, which is why it is fast and why touching 10,000 files makes the next git status slow once. On WSL /mnt/c, every stat is a 9P round trip; another reason to keep repos in the Linux filesystem (module 01). core.fsmonitor=true uses a daemon to avoid the stats.

Refs and reflog. A ref is a file (or a line in .git/packed-refs). Updating a ref appends to .git/logs/<ref>: old hash, new hash, who, when, why. That log is the reflog. gc.reflogExpire is 90 days (30 for unreachable entries). Objects reachable only from the reflog survive gc until the entry expires. This is the entire basis of "Git never loses committed work".

Merge strategies. Default ort (since 2.34) replaced recursive: it finds the merge base(s), does a three-way merge per path with rename detection, and handles criss-cross merges by merging the bases first. -X ours/-X theirs choose a side for conflicts only; -s ours ignores the other side entirely. zdiff3 conflict style shows the base version between the two sides, which turns "which one is right?" into "what did each side change?".

Why SHA-1 commits still matter for security. Signed tags (git tag -s) and signed commits (commit.gpgsign, or SSH signing with gpg.format=ssh) sign the hash; because the hash covers the whole reachable history, a signed tag authenticates every ancestor. Release pipelines verify git verify-tag.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• History is documentation that cannot go stale. Six months from now, git log -S 'remove_suffix' --oneline src/protocol.cpp and git blame -w -C on a line will tell you why a decision was made, if the commit message said why. Write for that reader.
  • Small commits are a debugging tool. git bisect run ctest finds a regression in minutes only if each commit builds. Squash fixups; do not squash meaningful steps.
  • Never force-push shared branches. --force-with-lease protects against overwriting a colleague; branch protection protects main. If you must rewrite shared history (a leaked secret), announce it, use git filter-repo, and have everyone re-clone.
  • Secrets: rotate first, rewrite second. A key that was ever pushed to a public repo is compromised regardless of history rewriting (mirrors, caches). Prevent with a pre-commit hook or gitleaks in CI (module 09).
  • Large binaries (test fixtures, dumps) go in Git LFS or an artifact store, not the repo. A 200 MB core dump committed once is downloaded by every clone forever.
  • Your current environment: if your employer uses Azure DevOps Repos or TFVC, the PR workflow, branch policies and azure-pipelines.yml (module 09) are the same ideas with different buttons. Being able to say "we used feature branches with required reviewers and build validation policies" maps one to one onto GitHub's protected branches.
  • 3 AM: production broke after a deploy; 40 commits went out. git log v1.2.0..v1.3.0 --oneline -- src/store/ narrows to the subsystem in seconds; git bisect run with the failing integration test finds the commit while you make coffee. Then git revert <hash> (a new commit that undoes it: safe on shared branches) ships the fix, and the real fix follows in daylight.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) In any repo, run git cat-file -p HEAD, then git cat-file -p on its tree hash, then on one blob hash. Done when you can draw the commit -> tree -> blob chain for one file.
  2. (easy) Set every config line from section 2.9. Make a change to a tracked file, stage half of its hunks with git add -p, and commit; then commit the rest. Done when git log -p shows two commits touching the same file with different hunks.
  3. (medium) Create three commits on a branch, mark the second as a fixup of the first using --fixup, and fold it in with GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash. Done when git lg shows two commits and git show of the first contains both changes.
  4. (medium) Produce a conflict by editing the same line on main and a branch, rebase the branch with merge.conflictstyle=zdiff3, and resolve it. Then git reset --hard the branch to before the rebase using reflog. Done when you can explain each of the three regions in the zdiff3 hunk.
  5. (hard) Write scripts/bisect_test.sh for tcpkv that configures, builds (exit 125 on build failure) and runs one ctest. Introduce a bug in Store::del ten commits ago (use a loop of trivial commits), then git bisect run it. Done when bisect names the right commit without you building anything by hand.
  6. (hard) Set up the tcpkv GitHub repository: README with build badge placeholder, LICENSE, .gitignore, .gitattributes, branch protection on main requiring the CI check from module 09, a v0.1.0 annotated tag pushed, and the repo pinned on your profile. Done when a PR you open cannot be merged until CI passes.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Explain Git's object model. Blobs hold file contents, trees hold directory listings pointing at blobs and subtrees, commits point at one tree and their parent commit(s) with author and message, tags name a commit. Every object is named by the SHA-1 of its content, so history is a Merkle DAG: one hash authenticates all ancestors, and identical content is stored once.

Q: Merge vs rebase: when do you use which? Merge preserves the true history with a merge commit and is safe on shared branches. Rebase replays my commits onto the new base, producing linear history with new hashes, and is right for my own feature branch before review. Never rebase commits others have built on; after rebasing a pushed branch, use --force-with-lease.

Q: You ran git reset --hard and lost a day's commits. What now? git reflog lists every position HEAD had, including the commit before the reset. git reset --hard HEAD@{1} or git branch rescue <hash> restores it. Committed objects are only garbage collected after the reflog entry expires, 90 days by default.

Q: How does git bisect work and what does it require? Binary search over the commit range between a known good and a known bad commit; log2(n) steps. git bisect run <script> automates it using the script's exit code: 0 good, non-zero bad, 125 skip. It requires every commit to build, which is why I keep commits small and never commit broken intermediate states.

Q: What is a fast-forward merge? When the target branch has no commits the source lacks, Git moves the target pointer to the source's tip without creating a merge commit. --ff-only enforces it, which some teams use to keep main linear together with rebase-before-merge.

Q: How do you keep a PR's history clean without an interactive editor? Commit review fixes with git commit --fixup=<target>, then GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash main, which folds every fixup into its target automatically. For squashing the last N commits, git reset --soft HEAD~N and one new commit.

Q: What does semantic versioning promise? MAJOR changes may break compatibility, MINOR adds features compatibly, PATCH fixes bugs with no interface change. For a C or C++ library the MAJOR usually matches the shared library soname so the dynamic loader enforces the contract.

Q: What should a commit message contain? An imperative subject under about 50 characters that completes "this commit will ...", a blank line, and a body explaining why the change was made, what alternatives were rejected and any side effects. The diff shows what changed; the message must preserve the reasoning.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Objects: blob, tree, commit, tag; content-addressed by SHA-1; a branch is a pointer, HEAD points at a branch.
  • Working tree -> index (add -p) -> commit; diff vs diff --staged.
  • Merge keeps the fork; rebase replays with new hashes; never rebase shared history; --force-with-lease.
  • Conflicts: edit, remove markers, add, --continue; --abort to bail; zdiff3 and rerere help.
  • --fixup + --autosquash with GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true cleans history without an editor.
  • git bisect run script finds the breaking commit automatically; needs buildable commits.
  • Reflog is the undo for reset, rebase, amend and deleted branches.
  • .gitignore for build/, .gitattributes for eol=lf on scripts, core.autocrlf input on WSL.
  • Subject imperative and short, body explains why; one logical change per commit; small PRs.
  • Protect main: PR required, review required, CI required, no force push; tag releases with semver.

docs.title: 07. Debugging and profiling tools on Linux
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03; tcpkv built with the release and debug presets

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
On Windows you have WinDbg for crashes, Process Monitor for "what files and registry keys is it touching", PerfView for "where is the time going", and Resource Monitor for "which process holds that port". Linux has one or two small tools for each of those questions, and they are all on the command line, scriptable, and installed with one apt command. This module is a tour of the toolbox with the five commands per tool that you will actually use, and a worked example on tcpkv.

The key mental shift: on Linux the kernel exposes almost everything as text under /proc and through tracing hooks (ptrace, perf_event_open, tracepoints). The tools are thin wrappers over those. When a tool is missing, cat /proc/<pid>/... often answers the question directly.

Analogy: Process Monitor is a security camera in the hallway between your program and the OS. strace is the same camera. perf is a stopwatch that clicks 1,000 times a second and writes down which line of code was running. valgrind runs your program inside a slow-motion simulator that checks every memory access.

docs.title: 2.1 Which tool for which question
docs.text: Question Tool Why did it crash? Where? What were the variables? gdb (live or core), sanitizers What syscalls is it making? Why is it hanging? What file did it fail to open? strace Which library functions is it calling? ltrace Where is CPU time going? perf record / perf report, flame graphs Exact instruction and cache counts, call graph with costs valgrind --tool=callgrind + kcachegrind Memory errors ASan (fast), valgrind --tool=memcheck (no rebuild) What is the process doing right now (memory, threads, fds)? /proc/<pid>/, top, htop, pidstat Who has this file or port open? lsof, ss What is on the wire? tcpdump, Wireshark How long does it take? time, hyperfine, perf stat What is the system doing (disk, net, CPU)? vmstat 1, iostat -x 1, sar, dstat

docs.title: 2.2 gdb quick reference
docs.text:
Full coverage, including core dumps, multithreaded debugging and Python scripting, is in 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA. The essentials:

gdb ./build/debug/tcpkv                       # start
gdb --args ./build/debug/tcpkv 7001           # with program arguments
gdb -p $(pgrep tcpkv)                         # attach to a running process (needs ptrace permission)
gdb ./build/release/tcpkv core.1234           # post-mortem on a core file
gdb -batch -ex 'thread apply all bt' -p PID   # non-interactive: dump all stacks and exit

Inside gdb:

(gdb) break tcpkv::parse_command          # b: break at function; b protocol.cpp:62; b main if argc > 1
(gdb) run                                 # r
(gdb) next / step / finish / continue     # n: over, s: into, fin: to return, c
(gdb) backtrace                           # bt; bt full shows locals in every frame
(gdb) frame 2                             # f 2: select frame; up / down
(gdb) print line                          # p: any expression; p *this; p store.map_.size(); p/x val
(gdb) info locals / info args / info registers
(gdb) watch g_stop                        # hardware watchpoint: stop when value changes
(gdb) info threads / thread 3 / thread apply all bt
(gdb) x/16xb ptr                          # examine memory: 16 hex bytes
(gdb) list                                # source around current line
(gdb) display var                         # auto-print on each stop
(gdb) set var port = 7001                 # modify
(gdb) catch throw                         # break on C++ exception throw
(gdb) handle SIGPIPE nostop noprint       # do not stop on this signal
(gdb) tui enable                          # split-screen source view (Ctrl-x a)

Enable core dumps once: ulimit -c unlimited and check /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern (on Ubuntu it is often piped to apport or systemd-coredump; coredumpctl list and coredumpctl gdb <pid> read them). Attaching requires ptrace_scope permission: echo 0 | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope on a dev box, or run gdb with sudo.

docs.title: 2.3 strace: the syscall camera
docs.text:
strace uses ptrace to stop the process at every syscall entry and exit and print the call, arguments and return value. It answers "what is the program asking the kernel to do".

strace ./build/release/tcpkv 7001                 # trace from start; Ctrl-C to stop
strace -f -p $(pgrep tcpkv)                       # attach; -f follows threads and children
strace -f -tt -T -o trace.log ./tcpkv 7001        # -tt timestamps, -T time spent in each call, -o to file
strace -e trace=network ./tcpkv 7001              # only socket calls; also: file, process, memory, signal, desc
strace -e trace=openat,connect -f ./prog          # specific syscalls
strace -c ./prog                                  # summary: count, time, errors per syscall
strace -s 256 ...                                 # show 256 bytes of string args instead of 32
strace -y ...                                     # print the path behind each fd: 3<socket:[12345]>
strace -k ...                                     # stack trace per syscall (slow, superb for "who opened this")

Reading tcpkv accepting a connection and serving SET k v then GET k:

[pid 4123] 10:21:03.112 poll([{fd=3, events=POLLIN}], 1, 500) = 1 ([{fd=3, revents=POLLIN}]) <0.084>
[pid 4123] 10:21:03.112 accept4(3, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(51234), sin_addr=inet_addr("127.0.0.1")}, [16], SOCK_CLOEXEC) = 4 <0.000021>
[pid 4123] 10:21:03.112 setsockopt(4, SOL_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, [1], 4) = 0 <0.000008>
[pid 4123] 10:21:03.112 write(2, "2026-10-03T10:21:03 INFO  accepted 127.0.0.1:51234\n", 52) = 52 <0.000019>
[pid 4123] 10:21:03.113 clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|..., stack=0x7f...}, 88) = 4130 <0.000061>
[pid 4130] 10:21:03.113 recvfrom(4, "SET k v\n", 4096, 0, NULL, NULL) = 8 <0.512>
[pid 4130] 10:21:03.625 sendto(4, "OK\n", 3, MSG_NOSIGNAL, NULL, 0) = 3 <0.000024>
[pid 4130] 10:21:03.625 recvfrom(4, "GET k\n", 4096, 0, NULL, NULL) = 6 <1.203>
[pid 4130] 10:21:04.829 sendto(4, "VALUE v\n", 8, MSG_NOSIGNAL, NULL, 0) = 8 <0.000019>
[pid 4130] 10:21:04.829 recvfrom(4, "", 4096, 0, NULL, NULL) = 0 <2.001>
[pid 4130] 10:21:06.830 close(4) = 0 <0.000011>

Reading it: pid 4123 is the main thread in poll with the 500 ms timeout; accept4 returns fd 4; clone3 with CLONE_THREAD is std::thread starting; the new thread 4130 blocks in recvfrom (recv is recvfrom with null address) for 0.5 s waiting for the client to type; = 8 bytes received; sendto with MSG_NOSIGNAL; recvfrom returning 0 is EOF (client closed); close. Every <time> is wall time inside the syscall, so a server "doing nothing" shows big numbers on blocking calls and that is normal; a server "doing nothing" with tiny numbers in a tight loop is a busy-wait bug.

Typical finds: openat(..., "/etc/app.conf") = -1 ENOENT (wrong path), connect(...) = -1 ECONNREFUSED (nothing listening), futex(...) forever (deadlock: now use gdb to see who holds the lock), write(1, ...) = -1 EPIPE, thousands of stat calls (library probing paths), mmap/munmap churn (allocator thrash), EAGAIN loops (non-blocking fd polled wrongly).

Cost: strace stops the process twice per syscall; a syscall-heavy program can run 10-100x slower (typical). Never leave it attached to a production server; use perf trace or bpftrace there.

docs.title: 2.4 ltrace: library calls
docs.text:
ltrace ./prog                             # calls into shared libraries: malloc, strlen, SSL_read...
ltrace -e 'malloc+free' ./prog            # filter
ltrace -c ./prog                          # summary
ltrace -S ./prog                          # include syscalls

Works through the PLT (module 02), so it only sees calls that cross a shared-library boundary; -static-libstdc++ or inlined calls are invisible. Useful for "how many times does it call malloc per request" and for seeing what a closed-source library does.

docs.title: 2.5 perf: sampling profiler
docs.text:
perf reads hardware performance counters and samples the instruction pointer (and optionally the stack) at a fixed rate. It needs the kernel package linux-tools-$(uname -r) or linux-tools-generic; on WSL2 the Microsoft kernel does not ship a matching perf, so install linux-tools-generic and run the binary directly from /usr/lib/linux-tools/*/perf, or build perf from the WSL2 kernel source. Hardware counters may be unavailable in the VM (software clock sampling still works with -e cpu-clock).

# permissions for non-root sampling
echo 1 | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/perf_event_paranoid
echo 0 | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/kptr_restrict

perf stat ./build/release/tcpkv_tests                 # counters: cycles, instructions, IPC, branch-misses, cache-misses
perf stat -e task-clock,context-switches,page-faults ./prog

perf record -g ./build/release/tcpkv 7001            # -g: call graphs via frame pointers (build with -fno-omit-frame-pointer)
perf record -g -p $(pgrep tcpkv) -- sleep 30          # attach for 30 s while load_test.sh runs
perf record --call-graph dwarf -F 999 -p PID -- sleep 10   # unwinding via DWARF when no frame pointers; bigger files
perf report                                           # TUI: % per symbol; Enter expands callers/callees
perf report --stdio --no-children | head -50          # text; --no-children = self time
perf annotate tcpkv::Store::get                       # per-instruction hot spots with source
perf top                                              # live, system-wide
perf trace                                            # strace-like, far lower overhead

Reading perf report --no-children on tcpkv under load (illustrative shape):

# Overhead  Command  Shared Object       Symbol
    24.1%   tcpkv    libc.so.6           [.] __memmove_avx_unaligned_erms
    18.7%   tcpkv    [kernel.kallsyms]   [k] _raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore
    11.2%   tcpkv    libc.so.6           [.] malloc
     9.8%   tcpkv    tcpkv               [.] std::_Hash_bytes
     7.4%   tcpkv    libc.so.6           [.] pthread_mutex_lock
     5.1%   tcpkv    tcpkv               [.] tcpkv::parse_command

Interpretation: memmove and malloc at the top means string copying dominates (we copy the key into a std::string for every lookup because C++17 unordered_map has no heterogeneous lookup, module 05 noted it). _raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore in the kernel is the socket send/recv path. pthread_mutex_lock at 7% says the single store mutex is contended; perf report -g and expanding it shows the callers. This is how you decide what to optimise: measure, then act on the top entry.

Flame graphs turn the call-graph samples into one SVG where width is time and depth is stack:

git clone https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph ~/FlameGraph
perf record -g -p $(pgrep tcpkv) -- sleep 20
perf script | ~/FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl | ~/FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > tcpkv.svg
# open tcpkv.svg in a browser (from Windows: \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-24.04\home\...\tcpkv.svg)

Read a flame graph bottom-up: main at the bottom, wide plateaus at the top are where CPU is actually spent (leaf functions). Click to zoom. Colours are random unless you use --color=java-style palettes. Off-CPU flame graphs (time spent blocked) need perf sched or eBPF tools; see 08_Networking for latency analysis.

docs.title: 2.6 valgrind: memcheck and callgrind
docs.text:
Valgrind runs the binary on a synthetic CPU, instrumenting every instruction. 20-50x slower (typical), no rebuild needed, works on any binary with symbols.

valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all --track-origins=yes ./build/debug/tcpkv_tests
#   --track-origins: where did the uninitialised value come from
#   exit code: use --error-exitcode=1 so CI fails on errors (module 09)
valgrind --tool=callgrind --dump-instr=yes --collect-jumps=yes ./build/release/tcpkv_tests
callgrind_annotate callgrind.out.<pid> | head -40          # text: inclusive/self cost per function
kcachegrind callgrind.out.<pid>                             # GUI (apt install kcachegrind); works over WSLg
valgrind --tool=massif ./prog && ms_print massif.out.<pid>  # heap profile over time
valgrind --tool=helgrind ./prog                             # race detector (TSan is usually better)

Memcheck vs ASan: ASan is 10x faster and catches stack/global overflows that memcheck misses; memcheck catches uninitialised reads (MSan territory, Clang only) and needs no rebuild. CI runs both (module 09). Callgrind vs perf: callgrind counts instructions exactly and gives precise call graphs regardless of sampling noise, but its "time" is simulated and ignores cache/memory stalls unless you enable --cache-sim=yes; perf measures reality including stalls. Use perf first; callgrind when you need exact counts or the program is too short to sample.

docs.title: 2.7 /proc: the process as a directory
docs.text:
P=$(pgrep tcpkv)
cat /proc/$P/status            # State, Threads, VmRSS (resident), VmSize, voluntary_ctxt_switches
cat /proc/$P/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '
ls -l /proc/$P/fd              # every open descriptor and what it points to
ls /proc/$P/task               # one directory per thread (TIDs)
cat /proc/$P/task/*/comm       # thread names (set with pthread_setname_np)
cat /proc/$P/maps              # memory map: code, heap, each .so, stacks, [vdso]
cat /proc/$P/smaps_rollup      # Rss, Pss (proportional), Shared, Private, Swap
cat /proc/$P/limits            # ulimits in effect (open files!)
cat /proc/$P/stack             # kernel stack: where is it blocked (root)
cat /proc/$P/wchan             # kernel function it is waiting in
cat /proc/$P/io                # bytes read/written
cat /proc/$P/environ | tr '\0' '\n'
cat /proc/$P/sched             # scheduler stats
cat /proc/meminfo /proc/loadavg /proc/cpuinfo
cat /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn   # kernel tunables; writable via sysctl

VmRSS is what top calls RES. For "is it leaking", watch VmRSS over time while load runs: watch -n1 grep VmRSS /proc/$P/status. Pss is the honest number when many processes share libraries.

docs.title: 2.8 lsof, ss: who holds what
docs.text:
lsof -p $(pgrep tcpkv)                    # all fds of a process: files, sockets, pipes, libraries mapped
lsof -i :7000                             # who is listening on / connected to port 7000
lsof -i TCP -s TCP:ESTABLISHED            # established TCP connections, all processes
lsof +L1                                  # open files that were deleted (disk space mystery, module 01)
lsof /var/log/tcpkv.log                   # who has this file open
lsof -u shakir                            # everything a user has open

ss -tlnp                                  # TCP listening sockets with PIDs (replaces netstat -tlnp)
ss -tanp | grep 7000                      # all TCP sockets on 7000 with state
ss -s                                     # summary: sockets by state (how many TIME_WAIT?)
ss -ti dst :7000                          # per-connection TCP internals: rtt, cwnd, retrans
ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l
ss -xlp                                   # unix domain sockets

ss reads netlink, netstat reads /proc/net/tcp; ss is faster and shows more. -p needs root to see other users' processes. "Address already in use" on restart: ss -tanp | grep :7000 shows either the old process still alive or sockets in TIME_WAIT (which SO_REUSEADDR handles, module 11, 08_Networking).

docs.title: 2.9 tcpdump: what is on the wire
docs.text:
Introduction only; 08_Networking goes deep.

sudo tcpdump -i lo -nn port 7000                       # -nn: no name resolution. Watch the handshake and data
sudo tcpdump -i lo -nn -A port 7000                    # -A: print payload as ASCII (text protocols)
sudo tcpdump -i lo -nn -X port 7000                    # hex + ASCII
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn -w capture.pcap port 7000      # write pcap; open in Wireshark on Windows
sudo tcpdump -i lo -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-fin|tcp-rst) != 0'   # connection events only
sudo tcpdump -i lo -nn -c 20 'host 127.0.0.1 and port 7000'              # stop after 20 packets

A SET/GET exchange:

10:30:01.000 IP 127.0.0.1.51234 > 127.0.0.1.7000: Flags [S], seq 1, win 65495, options [mss 65495,...]
10:30:01.000 IP 127.0.0.1.7000 > 127.0.0.1.51234: Flags [S.], seq 2, ack 2, ...
10:30:01.000 IP 127.0.0.1.51234 > 127.0.0.1.7000: Flags [.], ack 1
10:30:01.500 IP 127.0.0.1.51234 > 127.0.0.1.7000: Flags [P.], seq 1:9, ack 1, length 8        <- "SET k v\n"
10:30:01.500 IP 127.0.0.1.7000 > 127.0.0.1.51234: Flags [P.], seq 1:4, ack 9, length 3        <- "OK\n"
10:30:03.000 IP 127.0.0.1.51234 > 127.0.0.1.7000: Flags [F.], seq 9, ack 4                    <- client close
10:30:03.000 IP 127.0.0.1.7000 > 127.0.0.1.51234: Flags [F.], seq 4, ack 10

[S] SYN, [S.] SYN-ACK, [.] ACK, [P.] PSH+ACK (data), [F.] FIN, [R] RST. Seeing [R] from the server right after [S] means nothing is listening; a [P.] with no reply means the server received it and is not answering (now strace or gdb the server).

docs.title: 2.10 time, hyperfine, perf stat: how long
docs.text:
time ./build/release/tcpkv_tests            # real (wall), user (CPU in user space), sys (CPU in kernel)
/usr/bin/time -v ./prog                     # GNU time: max RSS, page faults, context switches, I/O
hyperfine --warmup 3 './build/release/tcpkv_tests' './build/debug/tcpkv_tests'   # statistics, comparison
hyperfine -N --runs 50 './parser_bench 100000'                                   # -N: no shell overhead
perf stat -r 10 ./prog                       # 10 runs with mean and stddev of counters

real >> user + sys means waiting (I/O, sleep, locks, network). sys high means syscall-heavy (small reads, lock contention through futex). user high means compute: profile with perf. hyperfine does warmup, many runs, outlier detection and side-by-side comparison; it is the right tool for "is this change faster" because single time runs are noise.

docs.title: 2.11 Worked example: profile tcpkv under load
docs.text:
cmake --preset release && cmake --build --preset release          # -O2 -g; add -fno-omit-frame-pointer in the preset for perf
./build/release/tcpkv 7001 &  SERVER=$!
./scripts/load_test.sh 7001 8 20000 &                              # 8 clients, 20k ops each (module 10)
perf record -g -p $SERVER -o perf.data -- sleep 15
perf report -i perf.data --no-children --stdio | head -30
perf script -i perf.data | ~/FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl | ~/FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > tcpkv.svg
strace -c -f -p $SERVER -o strace_summary.txt & sleep 5; kill %2   # syscall mix during load
cat strace_summary.txt
ss -tan | grep -c 7001                                              # how many connections
cat /proc/$SERVER/status | grep -E 'Threads|VmRSS'
kill $SERVER

Expected findings on the thread-per-connection design: recvfrom/sendto dominate syscalls, one pair per command (no batching); pthread_mutex_lock visible in perf under 8 clients; string allocation in parse_command and Store::get. Each finding maps to a known fix (buffered writes, pipelining, sharded locks, string_view keys with heterogeneous lookup in C++20), and the tools tell you which one matters first.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
No new source. The tools apply to code/tcpkv and to anything else. For a deliberately slow program to profile, use the tests binary (tcpkv_tests with --gtest_repeat=200 on the StoreConcurrency suite) or the load generator in code/tcpkv/scripts/load_test.sh.

A gdb command file for non-interactive stack dumps of a hung server (code/tcpkv/scripts/ is a good home; inline here):

# dump_stacks.gdb  - usage: gdb -batch -x dump_stacks.gdb -p $(pgrep tcpkv)
set pagination off
set print thread-events off
info threads
thread apply all bt 15
detach
quit

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
ptrace. strace, ltrace and gdb all use the ptrace(2) syscall. The tracer attaches (PTRACE_ATTACH or PTRACE_SEIZE); the kernel then stops the tracee at the requested events (each syscall entry/exit for PTRACE_SYSCALL, breakpoints via int3 for gdb) and wakes the tracer with waitpid. The tracer reads registers and memory with PTRACE_GETREGS / process_vm_readv. Each stop is two context switches, which is the overhead. Yama's ptrace_scope=1 (Ubuntu default) only allows tracing your own descendants, hence the permission step for attaching.

How gdb breakpoints work. gdb writes the byte 0xCC (int3) over the first byte of the target instruction. Executing it raises SIGTRAP, the kernel stops the tracee, gdb restores the original byte, rewinds the instruction pointer by one, lets you poke around, then single-steps the original instruction and re-inserts 0xCC. Hardware watchpoints use debug registers DR0-DR3 (four on x86) so watch var costs nothing until the write happens; software watchpoints single-step everything and are thousands of times slower.

perf sampling. perf_event_open(2) asks the kernel to program a PMU counter (cycles) to overflow every N events, or a hrtimer for cpu-clock. On overflow an NMI/interrupt fires; the kernel records the IP, PID, TID, timestamp and, with -g, walks the user stack following frame pointers (rbp chain) into a ring buffer mapped into perf's address space. Without frame pointers (-O2 default) the chain is broken after the first frame, which is why -fno-omit-frame-pointer (module 03) or --call-graph dwarf (copies a chunk of stack per sample and unwinds offline) is needed. perf_event_paranoid gates access: 2 = own processes without kernel samples, 1 = plus kernel, -1 = everything.

Symbolisation. perf and gdb map addresses to names using .symtab and DWARF (-g) from the binary and from the shared libraries listed in /proc/<pid>/maps. Stripped binaries show hex addresses; debuginfod can fetch symbols for distribution packages (export DEBUGINFOD_URLS="https://debuginfod.ubuntu.com"). Build IDs (readelf -n) match a binary to its separate debug file.

Valgrind's engine. Valgrind disassembles machine code into its own IR (VEX), instruments it (memcheck adds shadow bits: 1 "addressable" bit per byte and 8 "defined" bits per byte, so it tracks uninitialised values bit-precisely through arithmetic), JIT-compiles back to machine code and runs it. It replaces malloc/free with its own allocator that adds redzones and delays reuse. Because every instruction is translated, system calls are intercepted and their argument memory checked too. The 20-50x cost is the translation plus shadow bookkeeping.

/proc is a kernel filesystem. Reading /proc/PID/status calls into fs/proc/ which formats task_struct fields on the fly; there is no file on disk. That is why it is always current and costs microseconds. smaps walks the process's VMAs and page tables to count resident and shared pages, which is expensive for a large process (hundreds of ms); smaps_rollup is the cheaper sum.

TIME_WAIT and ss. After the side that closes first sends its FIN and receives the final ACK, the kernel keeps the socket in TIME_WAIT for 60 s (Linux, tcp_fin_timeout is for FIN_WAIT_2; TIME_WAIT is fixed at 2*MSL = 60 s) to absorb stray packets. A load test that opens and closes 20,000 connections leaves 20,000 TIME_WAIT entries visible in ss -s; SO_REUSEADDR lets the server rebind, and clients exhaust ephemeral ports (ip_local_port_range) if they churn connections.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The order of operations in an incident: (1) ss/lsof: is it listening, how many connections; (2) /proc/PID/status: threads, RSS, state; (3) strace -f -p for 5 seconds: is it doing anything, what is it blocked on; (4) gdb -batch -ex 'thread apply all bt' -p: where exactly is every thread; (5) perf record -p if it is CPU-bound. That sequence takes two minutes and answers 90% of "the server is slow/hung" pages.
  • Attaching gdb stops the process. On a production server with a 30-second health check that gets you restarted mid-investigation. Use gdb -batch for a snapshot (sub-second), or gcore PID to write a core without killing it and analyse offline.
  • strace on production can make a syscall-heavy server miss its latency SLO while attached. Attach for seconds, not minutes, or use perf trace / eBPF (bpftrace, strace-like opensnoop, tcpconnect) which have far lower overhead.
  • Keep symbols. perf report showing [unknown] and gdb showing ?? means stripped binaries without separate debug files. The build pipeline (module 09) must archive them by build ID.
  • Mapping to WinDbg: !analyze -v roughly equals gdb core + bt full + reading the faulting instruction with x/i $pc; ~*k is thread apply all bt; !locks has no direct equivalent (inspect pthread_mutex_t owner field or use TSan/helgrind); lm is info sharedlibrary; .ecxr for the exception context is automatic when gdb loads a core.
  • 3 AM: server at 100% CPU, no requests being served. perf top shows pthread_mutex_lock and __lll_lock_wait dominating: a lock convoy. gdb -batch thread apply all bt shows 200 threads waiting on the store mutex and one thread inside malloc under the lock, which is itself waiting on the allocator's arena lock held by a thread blocked writing to a dead socket. Fix: do not hold the store lock while doing I/O or allocation that can block. Tools found it in ten minutes; without them it is a guess.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run strace -f -tt -T -e trace=network ./build/debug/tcpkv 7001 and connect with nc localhost 7001, send PING, SET a 1, GET a, close. Done when you can name every syscall in the trace and explain the = 0 from recvfrom.
  2. (easy) Run ltrace -c ./build/debug/tcpkv_tests --gtest_filter='StoreTest.*'. Done when you can state how many malloc calls the Store tests make and which test causes most of them (hint: --gtest_filter one at a time).
  3. (medium) Add -fno-omit-frame-pointer to the release preset, rebuild, run the server under perf record -g while load_test.sh runs, and produce a flame graph. Done when you can name the top three self-time symbols and propose one change for each.
  4. (medium) Run valgrind --tool=callgrind on tcpkv_tests --gtest_filter='ParseCommand.*' and open the output in callgrind_annotate. Compare the inclusive cost of parse_command against std::string construction. Done when you can quantify what fraction of the parser's instructions are allocation.
  5. (hard) Simulate a deadlock: add a second mutex to Store and acquire the two in opposite orders in set and del. Run the concurrency test until it hangs (or use timeout). Attach gdb, thread apply all bt, identify the two threads and the two locks; then confirm with cat /proc/PID/task/*/wchan. Then build with the tsan preset and read the lock-order inversion report. Done when you can show both diagnoses.
  6. (hard) Capture a tcpkv session with tcpdump -w, open the pcap in Wireshark on Windows, and follow the TCP stream. Then produce the same view with tcpdump -A only. Done when you can point at the SYN, SYN-ACK, the PSH carrying SET, and the FIN exchange in both.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: A Linux server process is hung. Walk me through your investigation. Confirm with ss -tlnp that it still listens and cat /proc/PID/status for state and thread count. strace -f -p PID for a few seconds to see whether threads are in futex, recvfrom or spinning. gdb -batch -ex 'thread apply all bt' -p PID to get every stack without a long stop. If futex everywhere, read the stacks for the lock owner; if CPU-bound, perf record -p.

Q: What is the difference between strace and ltrace? strace traces system calls (the kernel boundary) via ptrace; ltrace traces calls into shared libraries via the PLT. strace tells you what the program asks the OS; ltrace tells you which library functions it calls, such as malloc counts or SSL calls, but misses statically linked or inlined code.

Q: How does perf find where time goes, and why do you build with frame pointers? It programs a hardware counter or timer to interrupt at a fixed rate and records the instruction pointer and stack at each interrupt. Aggregating samples gives the time distribution. Stack capture follows the rbp chain, which -O2 removes; -fno-omit-frame-pointer restores it for about 1% cost, or --call-graph dwarf unwinds offline at higher recording cost.

Q: Valgrind memcheck vs AddressSanitizer? ASan is compiled in, roughly 2x slowdown, catches heap, stack and global overflows, use-after-free, leaks. Memcheck needs no rebuild, is 20-50x slower, misses stack overflows but tracks uninitialised values bit-precisely and checks syscall arguments. Use ASan during development and CI; memcheck for third-party binaries and uninitialised-value hunts.

Q: What does real 2.0s user 0.1s sys 0.1s tell you? The program spent 1.8 seconds waiting: I/O, sleeping, blocked on locks or the network. CPU profiling will not help; look at syscalls (strace -T), lock contention or the remote side.

Q: How do you find which process owns a port? ss -tlnp 'sport = :7000' or lsof -i :7000. Both read kernel socket tables and map inodes to processes through /proc/*/fd.

Q: How does a gdb breakpoint work? gdb overwrites the first byte of the instruction with int3 (0xCC). Hitting it raises SIGTRAP, the kernel stops the ptraced process, gdb restores the byte and rewinds the PC. To continue it single-steps the original instruction and re-arms the breakpoint. Hardware watchpoints use CPU debug registers so they are free until triggered.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• gdb for crashes and stacks: bt, thread apply all bt, p, watch, -batch for snapshots, cores via coredumpctl.
  • strace shows syscalls with -f -tt -T -y; read blocked time, errors (ENOENT, ECONNREFUSED) and = 0 EOFs.
  • ltrace shows library calls through the PLT; -c for counts.
  • perf: stat for counters, record -g + report --no-children for hot spots, perf script to flame graphs; needs frame pointers.
  • valgrind memcheck without rebuild, callgrind for exact instruction counts, massif for heap over time.
  • /proc/PID/{status,fd,maps,smaps_rollup,limits,task} answers most "what is it doing" questions for free.
  • lsof -i :port, lsof +L1, ss -tlnp, ss -s, ss -ti for files, ports and TCP state.
  • tcpdump -i lo -nn -A port N: SYN, SYN-ACK, PSH data, FIN; RST means nothing listening.
  • time splits wall/user/sys; hyperfine for honest comparisons; perf stat -r.
  • Incident order: ss -> /proc -> strace -> gdb -batch -> perf. Keep symbols so every tool can name functions.

docs.title: 08. Docker for C++
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 04; tcpkv builds locally

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A container is a normal Linux process that the kernel has been told to lie to: it sees its own filesystem (from an image), its own process list, its own network interface and hostname, and it can be limited in CPU and memory. It is not a virtual machine; there is no second kernel. It starts in milliseconds because starting it is just starting a process with some namespaces set up.

An image is a read-only filesystem snapshot built in layers from a recipe called a Dockerfile. "Run the image" means: stack the layers, add a writable layer on top, start the process inside. The win for C++ is reproducibility: the exact compiler, exact library versions and exact runtime environment are pinned in text, built once, and run identically on your WSL, your colleague's Mac, the CI runner and the production server. "Works on my machine" becomes "works in this image".

Analogy: an image is a sealed shipping container with the application and everything it needs packed inside; the host is the ship. The ship does not care what is inside; the container does not care which ship it is on.

docs.title: 2.1 Install on Windows with the WSL2 backend
docs.text:
Install Docker Desktop for Windows, enable "Use the WSL 2 based engine", and in Settings -> Resources -> WSL Integration enable Ubuntu-24.04. Then inside your Ubuntu terminal:

docker version            # Client and Server sections; Server runs in Docker Desktop's own WSL distro
docker run --rm hello-world
docker run --rm -it ubuntu:24.04 bash   # a throwaway Ubuntu shell; exit to destroy

Alternative without Docker Desktop: install Docker Engine directly in WSL Ubuntu (apt install docker.io, sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, enable systemd in /etc/wsl.conf). Either way the commands below are identical.

docs.title: 2.2 Images, containers, registries
docs.text:
Dockerfile --docker build--> image (layers, immutable, tagged tcpkv:0.1.0)
image --docker run--> container (running process + writable layer)
image --docker push--> registry (Docker Hub, ghcr.io, Azure Container Registry)

docker build -t tcpkv:dev .                 # build from ./Dockerfile; -t tags it
docker images                               # local images with sizes
docker run --rm -p 7000:7000 tcpkv:dev      # run; --rm deletes the container on exit; -p host:container port
docker run -d --name kv -p 7000:7000 tcpkv:dev   # detached, named
docker ps; docker ps -a                     # running; all including exited
docker logs -f kv                           # stdout/stderr of the main process
docker exec -it kv sh                       # shell inside a running container
docker stop kv                              # SIGTERM, 10 s grace, then SIGKILL
docker rm kv; docker rmi tcpkv:dev
docker inspect kv | less                    # everything: IP, mounts, env, state
docker stats                                # live CPU/mem per container
docker system df; docker system prune       # disk usage; delete stopped containers, dangling images, build cache
docker tag tcpkv:dev ghcr.io/<user>/tcpkv:0.1.0 && docker push ghcr.io/<user>/tcpkv:0.1.0

A container's PID 1 is your process. When it exits, the container exits. docker stop sends SIGTERM to PID 1: tcpkv's handler (module 11) drains and exits 0; a program that ignores SIGTERM gets SIGKILL after 10 seconds and loses in-flight work. Exit code 137 in docker ps -a is 128+9: SIGKILL, often the memory limit (OOM) or the stop timeout.

docs.title: 2.3 Dockerfile for a C++ build: multi-stage
docs.text:
A naive Dockerfile installs gcc and cmake, copies the source, builds, and runs. The image is 1.5 GB and contains the compiler, your source, and your build tree. Multi-stage builds fix this: one stage builds, a second minimal stage copies only the installed binary.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
# ---------- Stage 1: build ----------
FROM ubuntu:24.04 AS build
ARG DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        build-essential cmake ninja-build git ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /src
# Copy only what the configure step needs first so the dependency download layer is cached
COPY CMakeLists.txt CMakePresets.json ./
COPY cmake/ cmake/
COPY tests/CMakeLists.txt tests/
# Then the rest (changes here do not invalidate the layers above)
COPY include/ include/
COPY src/ src/
COPY tests/ tests/
COPY deploy/ deploy/
RUN cmake --preset release -DTCPKV_BUILD_TESTS=ON \
    && cmake --build --preset release \
    && ctest --preset release \
    && cmake --install build/release --prefix /opt/tcpkv --strip

# ---------- Stage 2: runtime ----------
FROM ubuntu:24.04 AS runtime
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        libstdc++6 ca-certificates tini \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \
    && groupadd --system tcpkv && useradd --system --gid tcpkv --no-create-home tcpkv
COPY --from=build /opt/tcpkv/bin/tcpkv /usr/local/bin/tcpkv
USER tcpkv
EXPOSE 7000
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/tini", "--", "/usr/local/bin/tcpkv"]
CMD ["7000"]

Line by line:

  • FROM ubuntu:24.04 AS build: base image and stage name. Pin a digest (ubuntu:24.04@sha256:...) for byte-exact reproducibility in production.
  • apt-get not apt (stable CLI), --no-install-recommends (smaller), rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* in the same RUN (the layer is what is committed; deleting in a later layer does not shrink the image).
  • WORKDIR creates and enters the directory.
  • COPY order is about cache: Docker reuses a layer if the instruction and the copied files are unchanged. Put slow, rarely changing steps first. Here configure (which fetches GoogleTest) depends only on CMake files, so editing src/store.cpp does not re-download anything.
  • The build RUN runs tests inside the build: an image is never produced from code that fails tests.
  • cmake --install ... --strip installs the stripped binary to /opt/tcpkv. Keep the unstripped one as a CI artifact (module 09) for symbolising cores.
  • Stage 2 starts from a clean ubuntu:24.04 with only the runtime library libstdc++6 (ldd tcpkv tells you what else you need: for libpq, libpq5; module 02).
  • tini is a tiny init that forwards signals and reaps zombies, because PID 1 in a container has special signal semantics (section 4).
  • useradd --system + USER tcpkv: the server does not run as root. A container escape from a root process is root on the host's kernel namespace; from an unprivileged user it is far less.
  • COPY --from=build: pulls one file out of the build stage. Nothing else from stage 1 ships.
  • ENTRYPOINT is the executable; CMD is the default arguments, overridable: docker run tcpkv:dev 7001.
  • EXPOSE is documentation (and used by -P); it does not publish the port. -p does.

Result: build stage ~1.2 GB (cached locally, never shipped), runtime image ~80-100 MB (typical for Ubuntu base + libstdc++). Going smaller: debian:12-slim base (~75 MB total), alpine with a musl static build (~10 MB), or gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12 (~25 MB, no shell, has libstdc++) or FROM scratch with a fully static binary (~2 MB). Trade-off: no shell means docker exec sh does not work; debug with an ephemeral debug container instead (section 2.8).

docker build -t tcpkv:0.1.0 .
docker build --target build -t tcpkv:build .      # stop after stage 1 (for running tests/gdb in it)
docker build --no-cache ...                        # ignore cache
docker build --progress=plain ...                  # full output of each RUN
docker history tcpkv:0.1.0                         # layer sizes: where did the MB go
docker run --rm -p 7000:7000 tcpkv:0.1.0 && nc localhost 7000

docs.title: 2.4 Layers and the cache
docs.text:
Each instruction creates a layer: a tarball of filesystem changes plus metadata. Layers are content-addressed and shared between images (ten images from ubuntu:24.04 share the base). An image is a manifest listing layers. The cache rule: a layer is reused if its parent layer is the same and the instruction is the same; for COPY/ADD, also if the checksum of the copied files is the same. The first changed instruction invalidates everything below it.

Consequences:

  • COPY . . as the first instruction destroys caching: any edit anywhere rebuilds everything.
  • A .dockerignore excludes build/, .git/, editor files so they neither invalidate the cache nor bloat the context sent to the daemon.
  • RUN apt-get update alone in a layer is a trap: it caches an old package index forever; always combine with the install in one RUN.
  • BuildKit cache mounts keep a package cache across builds without putting it in a layer: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt apt-get ..., and for ccache RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.ccache cmake --build ....

docs.title: 2.5 Volumes and bind mounts
docs.text:
Container filesystems are ephemeral: docker rm deletes the writable layer. Persistent data lives in volumes.

docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16      # named volume (managed by Docker)
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src -w /src tcpkv:build cmake --preset debug   # bind mount: host dir into container
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src:ro ...                                      # read-only
docker volume ls; docker volume inspect pgdata; docker volume rm pgdata

Bind mounts from the WSL Linux filesystem are fast; from /mnt/c they are slow (module 01). The "build inside a container, edit on the host" workflow is a bind mount of your source into the build-stage image: same compiler as CI, your editor on the host.

docs.title: 2.6 Networking basics
docs.text:
Each container gets its own network namespace with a virtual interface. By default all containers join the bridge network and can reach the internet via NAT. Ports are not reachable from the host unless published with -p.

docker network create kvnet
docker run -d --name redis --network kvnet redis:7
docker run -d --name kv --network kvnet -p 7000:7000 tcpkv:0.1.0
docker exec -it kv sh -c 'getent hosts redis'      # Docker's DNS resolves container names on user networks
docker network inspect kvnet

-p 7000:7000 is host:container; -p 127.0.0.1:7000:7000 binds only to loopback on the host. On a user-defined network, containers reach each other by name (redis:6379); on the default bridge they cannot (legacy --link). --network host removes the namespace (Linux only; in Docker Desktop it means the Docker VM's host). Inside a container, localhost is the container itself, never the host; use host.docker.internal from Docker Desktop to reach the Windows host.

docs.title: 2.7 docker compose: tcpkv + PostgreSQL + Redis
docs.text:
Compose describes several containers, their networks and volumes in one YAML file and starts them together. This is how you run a realistic local environment: your server plus the database and cache it will talk to in 07_Databases_Internals and 08_Networking.

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  tcpkv:
    build:
      context: .
      target: runtime
    image: tcpkv:dev
    ports: ["7000:7000"]
    environment:
      TCPKV_PG_DSN: "postgresql://tcpkv:tcpkv@postgres:5432/tcpkv"
      TCPKV_REDIS_URL: "redis://redis:6379/0"
    depends_on:
      postgres: { condition: service_healthy }
      redis:    { condition: service_healthy }
    restart: unless-stopped
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits: { memory: 256M, cpus: "1.0" }

  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: tcpkv
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: tcpkv
      POSTGRES_DB: tcpkv
    volumes:

      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./deploy/initdb:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:5432:5432"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U tcpkv -d tcpkv"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
    volumes: ["redisdata:/data"]
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:6379:6379"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  pgdata:
  redisdata:

docker compose up -d --build        # build tcpkv, start all three, in dependency order with health waits
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f tcpkv
docker compose exec postgres psql -U tcpkv -d tcpkv -c '\dt'
docker compose exec redis redis-cli ping
echo PING | nc localhost 7000
docker compose stop tcpkv; docker compose start tcpkv
docker compose down                 # stop and remove containers and network; volumes survive
docker compose down -v              # also delete volumes (data gone)

depends_on with condition: service_healthy makes compose wait for the health check, which avoids the classic "server starts before the database and crashes once". restart: unless-stopped is the Docker equivalent of systemd Restart=always (module 11). The environment variables are how configuration gets in; the server reads them with getenv. Secrets (real passwords) do not go in the compose file: use env_file: .env (gitignored) or Docker secrets.

docs.title: 2.8 Debugging inside a container
docs.text:
docker exec -it kv sh                                     # if the image has a shell
docker exec -it kv cat /proc/1/status                     # PID 1 is tcpkv
docker top kv                                             # processes, with host PIDs
docker logs --since 10m kv
docker inspect --format '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' kv
docker run --rm -it --pid=container:kv --network container:kv --cap-add SYS_PTRACE \
    tcpkv:build bash                                      # debug container sharing kv's PID and net namespaces
# inside: apt-get install -y gdb strace; strace -f -p 1; gdb -p 1
docker cp kv:/tmp/core.1 ./core.1                         # copy a file out
docker run --rm -it --cap-add SYS_PTRACE --security-opt seccomp=unconfined -p 7000:7000 tcpkv:dev

--cap-add SYS_PTRACE is required for gdb/strace inside a container because Docker drops that capability by default; seccomp=unconfined is needed for some ptrace operations on older kernels. Core dumps inside containers go where the host's core_pattern says; with systemd-coredump on the host they land in the host's journal. For a reproducible debug setup, run the build stage with your source bind-mounted and gdb installed.

Distroless/scratch images have no shell: the --pid=container: debug-sidecar pattern above is the answer; Kubernetes calls this an ephemeral debug container.

docs.title: 2.9 Image size and hygiene checklist
docs.text:
• Multi-stage; runtime stage from a slim base; copy only installed artefacts.
  • --no-install-recommends; clean apt lists in the same layer; no build tools in runtime.
  • .dockerignore with build/, .git/, *.md, editor directories.
  • Non-root USER; read-only root filesystem where possible (docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp).
  • Pin base image tags (and digests for production); rebuild regularly for security patches.
  • HEALTHCHECK so orchestrators know when it is really up: HEALTHCHECK CMD sh -c 'printf "PING\n" | nc -w1 localhost 7000 | grep -q PONG'.
  • Labels: LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/<user>/tcpkv and org.opencontainers.image.version.
  • Scan: docker scout cves tcpkv:0.1.0 or trivy image tcpkv:0.1.0.
  • docker history and dive (apt install dive or the GitHub release) to find fat layers.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
• code/tcpkv/Dockerfile: the multi-stage build above, with comments and a HEALTHCHECK.
  • code/tcpkv/.dockerignore.
  • code/tcpkv/docker-compose.yml: tcpkv + PostgreSQL 16 + Redis 7 with health checks and volumes.
  • code/tcpkv/deploy/initdb/001_schema.sql: a table created on first PostgreSQL start, so the compose stack is useful for 07_Databases_Internals.

Run it:

cd code/tcpkv
docker build -t tcpkv:dev .
docker images tcpkv:dev                                  # check the size
docker run --rm -d --name kv -p 7000:7000 tcpkv:dev
printf 'SET a 1\nGET a\nQUIT\n' | nc -q1 localhost 7000  # OK / VALUE 1
docker logs kv
docker stop kv                                           # watch "shutting down" in the logs: SIGTERM handled
docker compose up -d --build && docker compose ps && docker compose down

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Namespaces and cgroups. docker run asks the daemon (via containerd and runc) to clone() a process with CLONE_NEWPID (own PID numbering: your process is PID 1), CLONE_NEWNET (own interfaces and port space), CLONE_NEWNS (own mount table), CLONE_NEWUTS (hostname), CLONE_NEWIPC, and optionally CLONE_NEWUSER. It then pivot_roots into the assembled image filesystem and execves your entrypoint. cgroups v2 limit CPU (cpu.max), memory (memory.max), PIDs and I/O. ls -la /proc/self/ns/ inside and outside a container shows different inode numbers for each namespace. There is no hypervisor; uname -r inside the container is the host kernel. On Docker Desktop the "host" is the WSL2 utility VM's kernel.

Overlay filesystem. Image layers are directories under /var/lib/docker/overlay2/. OverlayFS mounts them as lower (read-only) layers with one upper (writable) layer for the container. Reading a file finds the topmost layer containing it; writing copies the file up to the upper layer first (copy-on-write), which is why writing to a big file inside a container is slow the first time and why container writes should go to volumes.

PID 1 semantics. In a PID namespace, PID 1 gets special treatment: signals with default dispositions are not delivered to it unless it installed a handler (so a naive program ignores docker stop's SIGTERM and gets SIGKILLed after 10 s), and it must reap orphaned children or they stay as zombies. tini (or docker run --init) is a 10 KB init that forwards signals to your process and reaps zombies. tcpkv installs a SIGTERM handler, so it would work without tini; the init is still good practice for anything that spawns subprocesses.

Memory limits and the OOM killer. --memory 256m sets memory.max on the container's cgroup. When the cgroup's usage hits the limit and reclaim fails, the kernel's OOM killer selects a process in that cgroup (by oom_score) and SIGKILLs it: exit 137, OOMKilled: true in docker inspect. The JVM-style "the container has 256 MB but the process saw 64 GB" problem applies to C++ too if you size caches from sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES): read /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max instead (module 11).

Image format. An image is an OCI manifest (JSON) listing a config blob (env, entrypoint, labels) and layer blobs (tar+gzip or zstd), each addressed by sha256 digest. docker pull fetches only layers you do not already have. A registry is an HTTP server for these blobs. This is why layer ordering also affects push/pull time: a changed base layer means re-uploading everything above it.

Networking. The default bridge is a Linux bridge docker0; each container gets a veth pair with one end in the container namespace and one on the bridge; iptables/nftables NAT rules implement -p by DNAT from the host port to the container IP. User-defined networks add an embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 inside containers that resolves service names. ss -tlnp on the host shows docker-proxy or the kernel rule holding the published port.

Build reproducibility. The same Dockerfile produces different images on different days because apt-get update fetches the current index and FROM ubuntu:24.04 is a moving tag. For reproducibility pin the base digest, pin package versions (cmake=3.28.3-1build7) or use a snapshot mirror, and record the resulting image digest in the release. A multi-stage build with tests inside ensures the shipped binary passed tests in exactly the shipped environment.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Dev/CI/prod parity. The build stage image doubles as the CI build environment (module 09: container: tcpkv-build or docker build --target build). Compiler versions can no longer drift between a laptop and the pipeline.
  • Logs go to stdout/stderr. No log files inside containers (they vanish with the container and fill the writable layer). docker logs, journald, or a log shipper collects stdout. tcpkv already logs to stderr for this reason.
  • Graceful stop. docker stop gives 10 s (--stop-timeout / compose stop_grace_period). A banking server draining transactions may need 60 s; set it, and make the server honour SIGTERM promptly (module 11).
  • Configuration via environment variables, secrets via files. TCPKV_PORT, TCPKV_PG_DSN in the environment; passwords mounted as files (/run/secrets/pg_password) so they do not appear in docker inspect or ps.
  • Health checks let orchestrators restart a hung server. A health check that only checks the port is listening misses a deadlocked server; have it do a real PING.
  • Resource limits are not optional. Without --memory, one leaking container takes the host down. With it, the container is OOM-killed and restarted: an incident, not an outage.
  • Your Windows context. Windows containers exist but are rare for this kind of work; the Linux container story is one of the strongest arguments for porting a server to Linux. Being able to say "I would containerise the RPC server with a multi-stage build, non-root user, health check and a 30 s stop grace, and run it with a memory limit" is the answer interviewers want.
  • 3 AM: the container restarts every 40 seconds. docker inspect shows OOMKilled: true. docker stats during startup shows memory climbing to the 256 MB limit while loading a 300 MB cache file. The limit was set from a guess; the fix is sizing the limit from measured RSS plus headroom and reading the cgroup limit in the program to size caches. Second most common: exit 137 with OOMKilled: false is the stop timeout, which means SIGTERM is not being handled.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build code/tcpkv with docker build -t tcpkv:dev . and docker history tcpkv:dev. Done when you can name the three largest layers and say which Dockerfile line produced each.
  2. (easy) Run the container, connect with nc, then docker stop it and read the logs. Done when you see the "shutting down" line and docker inspect shows exit code 0. Then comment out the sigaction lines in main.cpp, rebuild, repeat, and observe exit 137 after 10 seconds.
  3. (medium) Change the runtime stage to debian:12-slim and then to gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12. Compare image sizes with docker images. For distroless, attach a debug sidecar with --pid=container: and run strace -p 1. Done when you have three sizes and have run strace against the distroless container.
  4. (medium) Add a HEALTHCHECK that sends PING and expects PONG. Start the container, watch docker ps show (healthy). Then make the server hang (add a sleep(1000) in serve_client, or stop it with docker kill -s STOP) and watch it go (unhealthy). Done when you can explain what an orchestrator would do with that state.
  5. (hard) Bring up the compose stack, connect to PostgreSQL with psql from the host and to Redis with redis-cli, and verify depends_on ordering by docker compose logs timestamps. Then add a --memory 64M limit to the tcpkv service and run load_test.sh with large values until it is OOM-killed. Done when docker inspect shows OOMKilled: true and you can explain exit code 137.
  6. (hard) Produce a fully static tcpkv (-static, or -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc plus a FROM gcr.io/distroless/static base) and ship it in a FROM scratch image. Compare size with the Ubuntu-based image. Done when the scratch image runs and answers PING, and you can list what you gave up (no shell, no TLS roots, glibc static caveats around getaddrinfo).
