docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Container vs virtual machine? A VM runs a full guest kernel on a hypervisor; a container is a host process isolated by kernel namespaces (PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user) and limited by cgroups, sharing the host kernel. Containers start in milliseconds and cost almost nothing; VMs give stronger isolation and can run a different OS.

Q: Why a multi-stage Dockerfile for C++? The build needs gcc, cmake and headers, around a gigabyte; the runtime needs the binary and libstdc++. A build stage compiles and runs tests, and the runtime stage copies only the installed binary onto a slim base, giving a small image with a minimal attack surface and no source or tools.

Q: How does Docker's layer cache work and how do you order a Dockerfile for it? Each instruction produces a layer reused when the instruction, its parent and any copied files are unchanged; the first change invalidates everything after it. Put slow, stable steps first: package installation, then build-system files, then sources. Clean up inside the same RUN because later deletions do not shrink earlier layers.

Q: What happens on docker stop? SIGTERM to PID 1 inside the container, a grace period of 10 seconds by default, then SIGKILL. PID 1 only receives SIGTERM if it installed a handler; otherwise it is killed and exits 137. Servers must handle SIGTERM and drain within the grace period; tini or --init helps when the process spawns children.

Q: Why run as a non-root user in the container? Root inside a container is root in the kernel's eyes for anything that escapes the namespace, such as a kernel vulnerability or an over-privileged mount. A dedicated system user limits the damage. It also catches code that assumes it can write anywhere.

Q: How do containers on the same compose stack find each other? Compose creates a user-defined bridge network; Docker's embedded DNS resolves each service name to its container IP. tcpkv connects to postgres:5432 and redis:6379 by name. localhost inside a container is that container only.

Q: Where does a container's data go when it is removed? The writable layer is deleted with the container. Persistent data belongs in named volumes or bind mounts; databases in compose use named volumes that survive docker compose down and are removed only with down -v.

Q: A container exits with code 137. What do you check? 137 is 128+9, SIGKILL. docker inspect OOMKilled tells whether the cgroup memory limit was hit; if false, the stop grace period expired because the process did not exit on SIGTERM. Fix the memory sizing or the signal handling accordingly.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Image = layers from a Dockerfile; container = process with namespaces and cgroups over an overlay filesystem; no second kernel.
  • Multi-stage: build stage with gcc/cmake runs tests and cmake --install; runtime stage copies the binary onto a slim base.
  • Cache order: apt first, CMake files, then sources; clean in the same RUN; .dockerignore build/ and .git/.
  • Non-root USER, tini or --init, HEALTHCHECK with a real protocol check, pinned bases, labels.
  • docker stop = SIGTERM, grace, SIGKILL; 137 = SIGKILL (OOM or timeout); handle SIGTERM.
  • Volumes for data; bind mounts for source during development; /mnt/c is slow.
  • User-defined networks give DNS by service name; -p host:container publishes ports.
  • compose: services, depends_on with health conditions, named volumes, env for config, files for secrets.
  • Debug with exec, --pid=container: sidecars, --cap-add SYS_PTRACE; cores follow the host's core_pattern.
  • Size: Ubuntu+libstdc++ ~90 MB, distroless ~25 MB, scratch+static ~2 MB; trade shell and TLS roots for size.

docs.title: 09. CI/CD with GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 04, 05, 06, 08

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Continuous Integration means: every time anyone pushes code, a machine you do not control checks out that exact commit on a clean system, builds it with the project's flags, runs every test, and reports pass or fail next to the commit. Nobody has to remember to run the tests. Nobody can say "it builds on my machine". Continuous Delivery/Deployment extends that: if the checks pass, the machine also produces the release artefact (a binary, a Docker image) and optionally deploys it.

For your resume, CI is where "Builds clean under -Wall -Wextra -Werror with CMake; GoogleTest suite" becomes verifiable: a green badge on the README, and a workflow file anyone can read. GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines are the two systems you list. They are the same idea with different YAML dialects: a trigger, one or more jobs, each job a sequence of steps run on a fresh virtual machine or container.

Analogy: CI is a very patient junior engineer who, on every commit, re-does the full build and test from scratch, exactly as documented, and refuses to let anyone merge until it is green.

docs.title: 2.1 Anatomy of a pipeline
docs.text:
trigger (push, pull_request, tag, schedule, manual)
  -> workflow / pipeline
       -> job A (runs on an Ubuntu VM)      -> job B (parallel)      -> job C (needs: A, B)
            step 1: checkout                    ...                       build Docker image
            step 2: install deps                                          push on tag
            step 3: cmake --preset ...
            step 4: ctest
            step 5: upload artifacts

Jobs run in parallel on separate machines unless they declare dependencies. Each job starts from a clean image; anything you need (compilers beyond the preinstalled ones, libraries) you install in steps or by running the job inside a container. A matrix expands one job definition into several (gcc and clang, Debug and Release). Artifacts are files uploaded from a job and downloadable later or by other jobs. Caches persist directories between runs keyed by a hash (dependency downloads, ccache). Secrets are encrypted variables exposed only to steps that need them. Status checks are the results branch protection waits for (module 06).

docs.title: 2.2 A complete GitHub Actions workflow for tcpkv
docs.text:
.github/workflows/ci.yml (full file in code/tcpkv/.github/workflows/ci.yml):

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ['v*']
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

env:
  CMAKE_GENERATOR: Ninja

jobs:
  build-test:
    name: ${{ matrix.compiler }} / ${{ matrix.build_type }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        compiler: [gcc, clang]
        build_type: [Debug, RelWithDebInfo]
        include:

          - compiler: gcc
            cc: gcc-13
            cxx: g++-13
          - compiler: clang
            cc: clang-18
            cxx: clang++-18
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4


      - name: Install toolchain
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ninja-build ${{ matrix.cc }} ${{ matrix.cxx }} ccache


      - name: Cache ccache and FetchContent
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: |
            ~/.cache/ccache
            build/ci/_deps
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-${{ matrix.compiler }}-${{ matrix.build_type }}-${{ hashFiles('CMakeLists.txt', 'CMakePresets.json', 'tests/CMakeLists.txt') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-${{ matrix.compiler }}-${{ matrix.build_type }}-


      - name: Configure
        run: >
          cmake -S . -B build/ci -G Ninja
          -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=${{ matrix.build_type }}
          -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=${{ matrix.cc }}
          -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=${{ matrix.cxx }}
          -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER=ccache
          -DTCPKV_WERROR=ON


      - name: Build
        run: cmake --build build/ci --parallel


      - name: Test
        run: ctest --test-dir build/ci --output-on-failure --parallel 4 --output-junit junit.xml


      - name: Upload test results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: junit-${{ matrix.compiler }}-${{ matrix.build_type }}
          path: build/ci/junit.xml


      - name: Upload binary with symbols
        if: matrix.compiler == 'gcc' && matrix.build_type == 'RelWithDebInfo'
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: tcpkv-linux-x86_64-unstripped
          path: build/ci/tcpkv
          retention-days: 30

  sanitizers:
    name: ${{ matrix.preset }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        preset: [asan, tsan]
    steps:

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ninja-build
      - run: cmake --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}
      - run: cmake --build --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}
      - run: ctest --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

  valgrind:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ninja-build valgrind
      - run: cmake --preset debug -DTCPKV_WERROR=ON
      - run: cmake --build --preset debug
      - name: memcheck
        run: >
          valgrind --error-exitcode=1 --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=definite
          --track-origins=yes ./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests --gtest_filter='-*Concurrency*'

  docker:
    needs: [build-test, sanitizers]
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - name: Build (and push on main or tag)
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          push: ${{ github.event_name != 'pull_request' }}
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.ref_name }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

What each part does:

  • on: run for pushes to main and version tags, for every PR targeting main, and by hand.
  • concurrency with cancel-in-progress: pushing again to a PR cancels the stale run. Saves minutes.
  • build-test matrix: 2 compilers x 2 build types = 4 jobs in parallel. fail-fast: false so a Clang failure does not cancel the GCC job; you want to see all failures at once. include adds per-compiler variables.
  • ubuntu-24.04 runners come with gcc-13, clang-18, cmake 3.28+, Python, Docker preinstalled. Pin the OS version rather than ubuntu-latest so a runner upgrade does not break you mid-sprint.
  • actions/cache: the key includes a hash of the build files; restore-keys falls back to the latest cache for this compiler when the key misses. ccache turns a 3-minute compile into 20 seconds for small diffs (typical).
  • Configure explicitly rather than with a preset here, because the matrix drives compiler and build type; the sanitizer jobs use presets because the preset is the configuration.
  • ctest --output-junit gives a report CI systems can render per test.
  • if: always() uploads test results even when tests failed, which is when you need them.
  • The unstripped RelWithDebInfo binary is archived for 30 days: match a production core to its build by commit SHA (module 07 build IDs).
  • sanitizers: the exact presets developers use (cmake --preset asan), so CI and laptops agree.
  • valgrind: a second memory checker with a different detection model (module 07). The concurrency tests are excluded because they take minutes under Valgrind; a nightly job runs them.
  • docker: needs makes it wait for build and sanitizer jobs. On PRs it only builds (proves the Dockerfile works); on main and tags it pushes to GitHub Container Registry with the commit SHA and the branch or tag name. GITHUB_TOKEN is an automatic secret scoped to this repo; permissions: packages: write grants it push rights. type=gha cache stores Docker layers between runs.

docs.title: 2.3 Badges
docs.text:
In README.md:

[![CI](https://github.com/<user>/tcpkv/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/<user>/tcpkv/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

The badge reflects the latest run on main. A red badge on a pinned repo is worse than no badge: fix or remove. Add a license badge and, if you publish images, a GHCR link. Do not add twelve.

docs.title: 2.4 Branch protection with required checks
docs.text: Settings -> Branches -> main -> Require status checks: pick gcc / Debug, gcc / RelWithDebInfo, clang / Debug, clang / RelWithDebInfo, asan, tsan, valgrind. Now a PR shows a "Merging is blocked" banner until they pass. Pair with "Require branches to be up to date" so the tests ran against the merge result, not a stale base.

docs.title: 2.5 The Azure DevOps equivalent
docs.text:
azure-pipelines.yml (full file in code/tcpkv/azure-pipelines.yml):

trigger:
  branches: { include: [main] }
  tags:     { include: ['v*'] }
pr:
  branches: { include: [main] }

variables:
  CMAKE_GENERATOR: Ninja

stages:

- stage: Build
  jobs:
  - job: BuildTest
    displayName: Build and test
    pool: { vmImage: 'ubuntu-24.04' }
    strategy:
      matrix:
        gcc_debug:     { CC: gcc-13,   CXX: g++-13,     BUILD_TYPE: Debug }
        gcc_release:   { CC: gcc-13,   CXX: g++-13,     BUILD_TYPE: RelWithDebInfo }
        clang_debug:   { CC: clang-18, CXX: clang++-18, BUILD_TYPE: Debug }
        clang_release: { CC: clang-18, CXX: clang++-18, BUILD_TYPE: RelWithDebInfo }
    steps:
    - checkout: self
    - script: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ninja-build ccache $(CC) $(CXX)
      displayName: Install toolchain
    - task: Cache@2
      inputs:
        key: 'ccache | "$(Agent.OS)" | $(CC) | $(BUILD_TYPE) | CMakeLists.txt | CMakePresets.json'
        restoreKeys: 'ccache | "$(Agent.OS)" | $(CC) | $(BUILD_TYPE)'
        path: $(Pipeline.Workspace)/ccache
      displayName: Cache ccache
    - script: >
        cmake -S . -B build/ci -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=$(BUILD_TYPE)
        -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=$(CC) -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=$(CXX)
        -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER=ccache -DTCPKV_WERROR=ON
      displayName: Configure
      env: { CCACHE_DIR: $(Pipeline.Workspace)/ccache }
    - script: cmake --build build/ci --parallel
      displayName: Build
      env: { CCACHE_DIR: $(Pipeline.Workspace)/ccache }
    - script: ctest --test-dir build/ci --output-on-failure --parallel 4 --output-junit $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/junit.xml
      displayName: Test
    - task: PublishTestResults@2
      condition: always()
      inputs: { testResultsFormat: JUnit, testResultsFiles: '$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/junit.xml', testRunTitle: '$(CC) $(BUILD_TYPE)' }
    - task: PublishPipelineArtifact@1
      condition: and(succeeded(), eq(variables['CC'], 'gcc-13'), eq(variables['BUILD_TYPE'], 'RelWithDebInfo'))
      inputs: { targetPath: build/ci/tcpkv, artifact: tcpkv-linux-x86_64-unstripped }


  - job: Sanitizers
    pool: { vmImage: 'ubuntu-24.04' }
    strategy:
      matrix:
        asan: { PRESET: asan }
        tsan: { PRESET: tsan }
    steps:
    - checkout: self
    - script: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ninja-build
    - script: cmake --preset $(PRESET) && cmake --build --preset $(PRESET) && ctest --preset $(PRESET)
      displayName: $(PRESET)


- stage: Package
  dependsOn: Build
  condition: and(succeeded(), ne(variables['Build.Reason'], 'PullRequest'))
  jobs:
  - job: Docker
    pool: { vmImage: 'ubuntu-24.04' }
    steps:
    - checkout: self
    - task: Docker@2
      displayName: Build and push image
      inputs:
        containerRegistry: 'acr-service-connection'     # a Service Connection configured in Project Settings
        repository: tcpkv
        command: buildAndPush
        Dockerfile: Dockerfile
        tags: |
          $(Build.SourceVersion)
          $(Build.SourceBranchName)

Mapping between the two:

Concept GitHub Actions Azure Pipelines File .github/workflows/*.yml azure-pipelines.yml (any name, selected in UI) Trigger on: push/pull_request trigger: / pr: Grouping jobs: (optionally reusable workflows) stages: -> jobs: -> steps: Machine runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 pool: vmImage: ubuntu-24.04 Matrix strategy.matrix with lists strategy.matrix with named configurations Shell step run: script: / bash: Reusable step uses: org/action@v4 task: Name@2 Variables ${{ matrix.x }}, ${{ env.X }}, $X in shell $(X) Secrets ${{ secrets.NAME }}; repo/org settings Variable groups, Key Vault; $(NAME) marked secret Artifacts actions/upload-artifact PublishPipelineArtifact@1 Cache actions/cache Cache@2 Test report upload JUnit; third-party renderers PublishTestResults@2 (native rendering) Dependencies needs: dependsOn: Conditions if: condition: Registry login docker/login-action with token Service Connection Branch rules Branch protection + required checks Branch policies + build validation Self-hosted self-hosted runners self-hosted agents in pools

Azure's stages are a first-class concept with approvals and environments (deploy to staging, manual approval, deploy to production); GitHub has environments with required reviewers for the same purpose.

docs.title: 2.6 Artifacts, secrets and safety
docs.text:
Artifacts are files produced by a run: test reports, unstripped binaries, coverage, logs. They expire (90 days default on GitHub, configurable). Release binaries attached to a GitHub Release (softprops/action-gh-release or gh release upload) are permanent.

Secrets are encrypted at rest, injected as environment variables or expressions only into the steps that reference them, and masked in logs. Rules: never echo a secret (masking is best-effort); never put secrets in the repo, in Dockerfiles (ARG/ENV end up in image history) or in compose.yml; for PRs from forks, secrets are not available by design (a malicious PR could exfiltrate them), which is why the Docker job above only pushes when the event is not a PR. GITHUB_TOKEN is per-run and expires with it. Use OIDC federation to cloud providers instead of long-lived cloud keys when deploying.

Supply chain: pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA (actions/checkout@<sha>) in security-sensitive repos; @v4 is a moving tag. Dependabot can keep them updated.

docs.title: 2.7 Making CI fast and useful
docs.text:
• concurrency cancellation; shallow clones (fetch-depth: 1 is the checkout default).
  • ccache or sccache; cache _deps; Docker layer caching with type=gha.
  • Split long jobs: unit tests on every PR, Valgrind on the concurrency suite nightly (on: schedule: cron: '0 3 * * *').
  • fail-fast: false and if: always() for uploads: see every failure in one run.
  • Enforce formatting: a job that runs clang-format --dry-run --Werror on changed files, and clang-tidy with compile_commands.json. Formatting disputes end.
  • Report flaky tests, do not retry them silently. A retry step hides real races.
  • Keep the pipeline under 10 minutes for PRs. Beyond that people stop waiting and start merging with "CI is slow, I'll fix it later".
  • Reproduce CI locally: act runs GitHub workflows in Docker; or simply run the same cmake --preset commands, which is why presets matter.

docs.title: 2.8 Continuous deployment
docs.text: Once the image is pushed, deployment is: the target pulls ghcr.io/<user>/tcpkv:<tag> and restarts. Options from simple to industrial: an SSH step that runs docker compose pull && docker compose up -d on a VM; a systemd unit with ExecStartPre=docker pull (module 11); Kubernetes with a Deployment manifest updated by the pipeline; Azure Container Apps / App Service with continuous deployment from ACR. Add an environment: production with required reviewers so a human approves the step. Rollback is redeploying the previous tag, which is why every image is tagged with its commit SHA.

docs.title: 2.9 Talking about CI in interviews
docs.text:
Have a two-minute story:

"On tcpkv I set up GitHub Actions with a gcc and clang matrix across Debug and RelWithDebInfo, -Werror on, ctest with JUnit output, separate ASan+UBSan and TSan jobs using the same CMake presets developers use locally, a Valgrind memcheck job, ccache and FetchContent caching, and a Docker job that builds the multi-stage image and pushes to GHCR on main and tags. Branch protection requires all of those before merge. The unstripped RelWithDebInfo binary is archived per commit for symbolising cores. I wrote the equivalent azure-pipelines.yml with stages, a matrix and a Docker task to an ACR service connection."

Then be ready for follow-ups: why both compilers (different warnings and UB detection), why sanitizers in CI rather than locally (they always run, on every PR, on a clean machine), what you do about flaky tests (fix or quarantine with a label, never retry), how long the pipeline takes and how you keep it fast (cache, cancellation, splitting nightly jobs), how secrets are handled (repo secrets, not available to fork PRs, OIDC for cloud).

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
• code/tcpkv/.github/workflows/ci.yml: the complete workflow.
  • code/tcpkv/azure-pipelines.yml: the complete Azure equivalent.
  • code/tcpkv/scripts/build.sh and run_tests.sh (module 10): the pipeline calls the same commands a developer runs, so a CI failure is reproducible with one command locally.

Validate locally before pushing:

# YAML syntax
python3 -c 'import yaml,sys; yaml.safe_load(open(".github/workflows/ci.yml")); print("ok")'
# the exact steps of the gcc/Debug job
cmake -S . -B build/ci -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=g++-13 -DTCPKV_WERROR=ON
cmake --build build/ci --parallel && ctest --test-dir build/ci --output-on-failure
# the sanitizer job
cmake --preset asan && cmake --build --preset asan && ctest --preset asan
# the GitHub CLI shows runs and logs without a browser
gh run list; gh run watch; gh run view --log-failed

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What a runner is. A GitHub-hosted runner is a fresh VM (2 vCPU, 7 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD for the standard Linux runner; numbers from GitHub's documentation) created from an image with hundreds of preinstalled tools, destroyed after the job. The runner agent polls GitHub for jobs, receives the job definition, executes steps in order, streams logs back, and uploads artifacts. uses: actions are Git repositories checked out into the runner and executed as JavaScript (Node) or as a Docker container or as composite steps; run: steps spawn bash -e {0} by default on Linux, so a failing command fails the step. Azure agents work the same way; the vmImage pool is Microsoft-hosted, or you register your own machines.

Why caches are keyed by hash. The cache action tars the listed paths and stores them under the key. On restore, an exact key hit gives the tarball; restore-keys prefixes give the most recent partial match. Cache entries are immutable once saved: if the key exists, nothing is saved, which is why the key must change when the inputs change (hashFiles(...)). ccache's own hashing of compiler, flags and preprocessed source means a stale ccache directory is harmless, so the prefix fallback is safe.

Status checks and the merge queue. Each job reports a check run with a name to the commit's check suite through the Checks API; branch protection lists check names. Renaming a job breaks the protection rule silently (the old name never reports, so merging is blocked forever) and is a classic trap. GitHub's merge queue re-runs required checks on the speculative merge commit so main never gets a combination that was not tested.

Containers as job environments. container: ghcr.io/<user>/tcpkv-build:latest runs all steps of a job inside that image: your exact compiler, no apt steps, faster, and identical to the Dockerfile build stage. Service containers (services: postgres: image: postgres:16) start side-car containers reachable by hostname for integration tests, the CI version of compose.

Secrets masking works by registering the secret value with the log processor, which replaces occurrences with ***. Encoding the value (base64, splitting across lines) defeats it. The real protections are that secrets are not exposed to fork PRs and that the token is short-lived. OIDC tokens are JWTs signed by GitHub with claims about repo and branch, which the cloud provider trusts instead of a stored key.

Docker layer cache in CI. Without cache-from, every CI Docker build starts from zero. The type=gha backend exports layer blobs to GitHub's cache service using BuildKit's cache manifests; mode=max exports intermediate stages (the build stage) too. A code change then rebuilds only the layers below the COPY src/ line, exactly as locally.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• CI is the executable definition of "done". If a quality rule is not enforced in CI, it does not exist. -Werror, tests, sanitizers, formatting, license headers: all enforced or all optional.
  • Match CI to production. Build the release artefact in CI from the tagged commit, record the image digest, deploy that digest. Never build on the production machine; never deploy something CI did not build.
  • Pipelines fail for environmental reasons (network, runner image update, flaky third-party download). Pin runner OS versions, pin action versions, mirror or vendor dependencies, and retry downloads (not tests).
  • Nightly jobs catch what PR jobs cannot afford: full Valgrind, long TSan runs, fuzzing, -O3 -march=native builds, a build against the latest compiler to see tomorrow's warnings.
  • Your Azure DevOps experience is directly relevant. If your employer builds the RPC server with MSBuild in an Azure Pipeline, the structure (trigger, agent pool, VSBuild@1 or MSBuild@1 task, VSTest@2, publish artifact) is what section 2.5 shows with Linux tasks. Say that in interviews: you have seen pipelines for a real product and can write them for Linux.
  • 3 AM: the release pipeline is green but production crashes at startup with "cannot open shared object file". The CI build job and the Docker runtime stage drifted: someone added libpq to the build but not to the runtime image, and the tests ran in the build stage where the library exists. Fix: run the smoke test (PING) against the final image in the Docker job, not against the build stage. The HEALTHCHECK plus a docker run step in CI would have caught it.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Push code/tcpkv to a new GitHub repository with the workflow. Done when all jobs are green and the badge in the README renders. Record how long the pipeline took.
  2. (easy) Open a PR that introduces an unused variable. Done when the PR is blocked by the -Werror failure and you can find the error line in the job log with gh run view --log-failed.
  3. (medium) Add a format job that runs clang-format --dry-run --Werror over src include tests and a tidy job that runs clang-tidy with -p build/ci. Add a .clang-format and a .clang-tidy. Done when both pass on main and fail on a deliberately misformatted PR.
  4. (medium) Add a smoke test step to the docker job: run the built image, send PING with nc, assert PONG, and stop it. Done when the step fails if you break the runtime stage (remove libstdc++6) and passes otherwise.
  5. (hard) Add a nightly workflow on a cron schedule running the full Valgrind suite including concurrency tests, plus a build with -O3 -flto. Add a release job that, on a v* tag, creates a GitHub Release with the stripped binary and the unstripped symbols archive attached, and tags the Docker image latest and <semver>. Done when pushing v0.1.0 produces a release page with two assets and docker pull ghcr.io/<user>/tcpkv:0.1.0 works.
  6. (hard) Port the complete workflow to Azure DevOps: create a free organisation and project, connect the GitHub repo, add the azure-pipelines.yml, create a Container Registry service connection (or skip the push with a condition), and get the stages green. Done when PublishTestResults shows per-test results in the Azure UI and you can explain two differences between the YAML dialects from memory.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is CI and what does your pipeline do? CI builds and tests every commit on a clean machine so integration problems surface immediately. Mine runs a gcc/clang x Debug/RelWithDebInfo matrix with -Werror, ctest with JUnit output, ASan+UBSan and TSan jobs via CMake presets, a Valgrind job, caches with ccache, archives the symbolised binary, and builds and pushes a multi-stage Docker image on main and tags. Branch protection requires all of it before merge.

Q: Why build with both GCC and Clang? They diagnose different things: different warnings, different UB exploitation, different standard-library implementations if you switch to libc++. Code that compiles cleanly under both is more portable and has fewer latent bugs, and you get MSan and better -ftime-trace from Clang.

Q: Why run sanitizers in CI if developers can run them locally? Because "can" is not "do". CI runs them on every PR, on a clean machine, with the same preset, and blocks the merge. A sanitizer finding in CI is attached to the exact commit; locally it is a terminal nobody saw.

Q: How do you handle secrets in a pipeline? Stored as encrypted repository or organisation secrets, exposed only to steps that reference them, masked in logs, unavailable to pull requests from forks. Prefer short-lived tokens: GITHUB_TOKEN for the registry, OIDC federation for cloud providers instead of stored keys. Never bake secrets into Docker images or print them.

Q: What is a matrix build? One job definition expanded over combinations of variables (compiler, build type, OS) into parallel jobs. fail-fast: false keeps the others running when one fails so all problems are visible in one run.

Q: How do you keep CI fast? Cancel superseded runs, cache compiler output with ccache and dependency downloads by content hash, cache Docker layers, run expensive suites nightly instead of per PR, and parallelise with a matrix and ctest -j. Target under ten minutes for PR feedback.

Q: GitHub Actions vs Azure Pipelines: main differences? Same model: triggers, jobs on hosted or self-hosted machines, steps of scripts and reusable tasks, matrices, artifacts, caches, secrets. Azure has first-class stages with approvals and environments and native test-result rendering; GitHub has a larger marketplace of actions, environments with reviewers, and tighter integration with PRs and GHCR. Syntax differs: ${{ }} vs $( ), uses: vs task:, needs: vs dependsOn:.

Q: A CI job passes but the deployed container crashes. How do you prevent that class of bug? Test the artefact you ship: run the final image in the pipeline and execute a smoke test against it; add a HEALTHCHECK; build the runtime stage's dependency list from ldd of the binary; deploy by image digest so what was tested is what runs.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• CI: every commit built and tested on a clean machine; results block merging via required checks.
  • Workflow = triggers + jobs (parallel VMs) + steps; matrix expands jobs; needs/dependsOn orders them.
  • tcpkv pipeline: gcc/clang x Debug/RelWithDebInfo with -Werror, ctest JUnit, asan/tsan presets, Valgrind, ccache cache, symbol artifact, Docker build and push.
  • Pin runner OS and action versions; fail-fast: false; if: always() for result uploads; cancel superseded runs.
  • Caches keyed by content hash with prefix fallbacks; Docker layer cache with type=gha.
  • Secrets: encrypted, masked, not available to fork PRs; GITHUB_TOKEN and OIDC over long-lived keys.
  • Azure Pipelines: trigger/pr, stages -> jobs -> steps, $(VAR), task:, Cache@2, PublishTestResults@2, service connections.
  • Badges on the README; branch protection requires the named checks; renaming a job breaks the rule.
  • Smoke-test the final image in CI; deploy by digest; nightly jobs for slow checks.
  • Two-minute interview story ready, with follow-up answers on compilers, sanitizers, flakes, speed, secrets.

docs.title: 10. Scripting: bash for build, test and deploy, and a little Python
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: 01, 04, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A script is a text file of commands you would otherwise type. On Windows you used .bat files or PowerShell for the same job: "build, copy the DLLs, run the tests, zip the output". On Linux the default scripting language is bash, the same shell you type into. Every CI step, Docker RUN line and deployment hook in this course is a small bash program.

Bash is very good at one thing: gluing other programs together (run cmake, pipe into grep, check the exit code, start a server in the background, kill it at the end). It is bad at everything else: arithmetic beyond integers, data structures, string parsing, error handling. The senior skill is knowing where the line is. Write bash that fails loudly and cleans up after itself; switch to Python the moment you need real logic, real data or a real protocol.

Analogy: bash is the wiring in a building. It connects the appliances (compilers, servers, test runners) and it must be safe: a bad connection should trip the breaker (set -e), not smoulder. You do not build the appliances out of wiring. When you need an appliance, you use Python.

docs.title: 2.1 The first three lines of every script
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# what this script does, how to call it, what it exits with
set -euo pipefail
  • #!/usr/bin/env bash (the shebang): when you run ./build.sh, the kernel reads the first two bytes #!, and executes the named interpreter with the script path as an argument. /usr/bin/env bash finds bash on PATH (works on macOS and NixOS too). #!/bin/sh is a different, smaller language (dash on Ubuntu): no arrays, no [[ ]], no pipefail before POSIX 2024. If you use bash features, say bash.
  • chmod +x build.sh sets the execute bit. Without it: Permission denied. Git records the bit (git update-index --chmod=+x from Windows).
  • Line endings. A script saved with CRLF fails with /usr/bin/env: 'bash\r': No such file or directory. The \r became part of the interpreter name. Fix with .gitattributes (*.sh text eol=lf, module 06) and dos2unix.

The three set options:

Option Meaning What it prevents -e (errexit) exit when any command returns non-zero a failed cmake followed by "tests passed" -u (nounset) expanding an unset variable is an error rm -r "$BUILD_DIR/" with BUILD_DIR unset becomes rm -r / -o pipefail a pipeline's status is the last non-zero stage ctest \| tee log returning tee's 0 when ctest failed

set -e has well-known holes, and you must know them for interviews:

  • A command whose status is tested never triggers it: in if cmd, cmd || x, cmd && x, ! cmd, while cmd. That is deliberate: you are handling the failure.
  • local x=$(cmd) and export x=$(cmd): the status is that of local/export, which succeeded. Declare first, assign second.
  • ((count++)) returns status 1 when the expression evaluates to 0, so it kills the script on the first increment from zero. Write count=$((count + 1)).
  • Inside a function called from an if (or ||), set -e is disabled for the whole function body.
  • Command substitution in older bash did not inherit -e; bash 5.0+ has shopt -s inherit_errexit.

set -e is a safety net, not error handling. For anything that may legitimately fail, test it explicitly.

docs.title: 2.2 Variables, quoting, arrays
docs.text:
name="tcpkv"                   # no spaces around '='
echo "$name"                   # always double-quote expansions
echo "${name}_tests"           # braces when followed by name characters
port="${1:-7000}"              # first argument, default 7000
: "${BUILD_TYPE:=Debug}"       # set to Debug if unset or empty
dir="$(dirname "$0")"          # command substitution; quotes nest inside $( )
n=$((3 * 4 + 1))               # integer arithmetic only
args=(--preset debug -j 8)     # array
cmake "${args[@]}"             # each element one argument, spaces preserved

Why quoting matters. An unquoted $var undergoes word splitting (on spaces, tabs, newlines) and glob expansion (* becomes file names). rm $file with file="my report.txt" deletes my and report.txt. Quote every expansion unless you specifically want splitting. "$@" expands to all arguments, each one quoted: the correct way to forward arguments.

[[ ... ]] is bash's test command: [[ -f path ]] file exists, -d directory, -x executable, -z "$s" empty string, -n "$s" non-empty, == glob match, =~ regex match. Numbers compare with (( a < b )). Prefer [[ ]] over [ ]: no word splitting inside, && and || work.

docs.title: 2.3 Functions, return values, output
docs.text:
log() { printf '%s %s\n' "$(date +%T)" "$*" >&2; }   # logs to stderr
die() { log "ERROR: $*"; exit 1; }

count_lines() {
    local file="$1"                     # 'local' or it leaks into the caller
    [[ -r "$file" ]] || return 1        # status: 0 success, 1-255 failure
    wc -l < "$file"                     # "return" data by printing it
}
n="$(count_lines access.log)" || die "cannot read access.log"

Functions return a status code (0 to 255), like a process. Data comes out on stdout and is captured with $( ). Keep logs on stderr (>&2) so result="$(myfunc)" gets only data.

docs.title: 2.4 Loops and reading input
docs.text:
for f in src/*.cpp; do clang-format -i "$f"; done        # glob; use shopt -s nullglob for "no match = no loop"
for ((i = 1; i <= 8; i++)); do ...; done                  # C-style
while IFS= read -r line; do echo "[$line]"; done < cmds.txt   # line by line, exactly
some_cmd | while read -r a b rest; do ...; done            # split fields; runs in a subshell!

IFS= read -r: IFS= keeps leading and trailing spaces, -r keeps backslashes. The pipe form runs the loop in a subshell, so variables set inside are gone afterwards; redirect from a file or use process substitution done < <(some_cmd) when you need them.

docs.title: 2.5 Exit codes and traps
docs.text:
Every process exits with a status 0 to 255. 0 is success. Conventions that matter:

Status Meaning 1 generic failure 2 usage error (bash builtins, most CLI tools) 124 timeout killed the command 125 git bisect run: skip this commit 126 found but not executable 127 command not found 128 + N killed by signal N: 130 = SIGINT (Ctrl-C), 137 = SIGKILL (OOM killer, docker kill), 143 = SIGTERM

$? is the status of the last command. PIPESTATUS[@] holds each stage of the last pipeline.

A trap runs code when the shell receives a signal or exits:

WORKDIR="$(mktemp -d)"
cleanup() {
    local rc=$?                         # read first: anything else overwrites it
    kill $(jobs -p) 2>/dev/null || true # stop background servers we started
    rm -r -- "$WORKDIR"
    exit "$rc"                          # preserve the original status
}
trap cleanup EXIT                       # runs on normal exit, on set -e failure, on 'exit N'
trap 'exit 130' INT                     # Ctrl-C -> exit -> EXIT trap runs once
trap 'exit 143' TERM                    # docker stop / CI cancel -> same
trap 'log "failed at line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND"' ERR    # with set -E, also inside functions

EXIT is the one to remember: it is bash's finally. Converting INT and TERM into exit makes cleanup run exactly once with the right status. SIGKILL cannot be trapped by anything.

docs.title: 2.6 Background jobs, wait, timeout
docs.text:
./build/debug/tcpkv 7123 > server.log 2>&1 &   # '&' runs in the background
SERVER_PID=$!                                   # PID of the last background job
for i in 1 2 3; do worker "$i" & pids+=($!); done
for p in "${pids[@]}"; do wait "$p" || failed=$((failed + 1)); done   # wait PID returns its status
timeout 30 ./long_test || echo "status $?"      # 124 if it ran out of time
kill -0 "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null               # "is it still alive?" without sending a signal

docs.title: 2.7 The tcpkv scripts
docs.text:
Four bash scripts live in code/tcpkv/scripts/. They are the commands CI runs, so any red pipeline reproduces locally with one command.

Script Does build.sh [--clean] [preset] cmake --preset + cmake --build --preset; links compile_commands.json to the root run_tests.sh [preset] [ctest args] build, ctest --preset, then start a server on a free port, run the Python self-test and a short load burst, stop the server via trap load_test.sh [port] [clients] [ops] [value_bytes] N parallel pipelined clients through nc, counts replies, reports throughput, fails on any missing or ERROR reply bisect_test.sh [gtest filter] the git bisect run script from module 06: exit 125 on build failure

docs.title: 2.8 When to switch to Python
docs.text:
Switch when any of these is true:

  • You need a data structure beyond a flat list: maps, nested records, JSON, CSV with quoting.
  • You need floating point (latency percentiles, averages).
  • You are parsing a protocol or a structured format (sockets, HTTP, JSON, YAML).
  • You need real error handling: retry this, catch that, clean up those three things in order.
  • The script is over about 100 lines, or has more than two levels of nested if/loops.
  • It must run on Windows too.

Keep bash when the script is a sequence of commands with exit-code checks: build, test, package, deploy hooks, Docker RUN lines, CI steps. A useful rule many teams use: bash for orchestration, Python for logic.

Python's standard library covers what you need without pip: socket, subprocess, argparse, json, threading, time, statistics, pathlib. Ubuntu 24.04 ships Python 3.12.

docs.title: 2.9 Python driving tcpkv over a socket
docs.text:
code/tcpkv/scripts/tcpkv_client.py is a small client library plus four modes:

python3 scripts/tcpkv_client.py SET greeting hello world      # one command, prints the reply
python3 scripts/tcpkv_client.py --port 7123 --wait 5 --selftest   # assertions, exit 0/1
python3 scripts/tcpkv_client.py --bench 20000 --value-size 100    # p50/p95/p99 latency
python3 scripts/tcpkv_client.py --repl                            # interactive

The self-test checks basic commands, error replies, CRLF tolerance, a 64 KiB value, pipelined requests, a request split across two TCP segments, eight concurrent clients and QUIT. It is what run_tests.sh and the ctest integration test (module 05, exercise 6) run.

docs.title: 3.1 code/m10_bash_patterns.sh
docs.text:
Every pattern from section 2 in one runnable file: set -euo pipefail, IFS, readonly constants, logging to stderr, getopts, mktemp + trap cleanup EXIT, an ERR trap with line numbers, functions with local, quoting and arrays, the four set -e gotchas, PIPESTATUS, background jobs with wait, timeout, a retry function with exponential backoff, here-documents.

chmod +x m10_bash_patterns.sh
./m10_bash_patterns.sh          # run all demos
./m10_bash_patterns.sh -v       # with set -x and a PS4 showing file:line:function
shellcheck m10_bash_patterns.sh # sudo apt install shellcheck

The retry helper, which you will copy into many scripts:

# Retry DOWNLOADS and connections, never tests (a flaky test is a bug to fix).
retry() {
    local attempts="$1"; shift
    local delay=1 n
    for ((n = 1; n <= attempts; n++)); do
        if "$@"; then return 0; fi
        log "attempt $n/$attempts failed: $*; sleeping ${delay}s"
        sleep "$delay"
        delay=$((delay * 2))
    done
    return 1
}
retry 5 curl -fsSL -o deps.tar.gz "$URL"

docs.title: 3.2 code/tcpkv/scripts/run_tests.sh (the integration part)
docs.text:
# Pick a free port by asking the kernel for one (bind to port 0), so parallel CI jobs never collide.
PORT="$(python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); print(s.getsockname()[1]); s.close()')"
SERVER_PID=""

stop_server() {
    local rc=$?
    if [[ -n "$SERVER_PID" ]] && kill -0 "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
        kill -TERM "$SERVER_PID"                       # graceful: tcpkv drains and exits 0
        for _ in $(seq 50); do kill -0 "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || break; sleep 0.1; done
        kill -KILL "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true   # same policy as systemd TimeoutStopSec
        wait "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
    fi
    if ((rc != 0)) && [[ -f "$SERVER_LOG" ]]; then tail -n 20 "$SERVER_LOG" >&2; fi
    exit "$rc"
}
trap stop_server EXIT

"$BUILD_DIR/tcpkv" "$PORT" >"$SERVER_LOG" 2>&1 &
SERVER_PID=$!
python3 "$ROOT/scripts/tcpkv_client.py" --port "$PORT" --wait 5 --selftest
"$ROOT/scripts/load_test.sh" "$PORT" 4 2000

Points worth saying in an interview: the free-port trick avoids collisions between parallel CI jobs (there is a tiny race between closing the probe socket and the server binding, acceptable for tests); --wait polls instead of sleep 1 (fast when the server is fast, robust when it is slow); the trap prints the server log only on failure, which is when you need it.

docs.title: 3.3 code/tcpkv/scripts/load_test.sh (the generator)
docs.text:
# awk is far faster than a bash loop for 100k lines. srand(client) makes runs reproducible.
for ((c = 1; c <= CLIENTS; c++)); do
    awk -v c="$c" -v n="$OPS" -v vb="$VALUE_BYTES" 'BEGIN {
        srand(c)
        val = ""; for (j = 0; j < vb; j++) val = val "x"
        for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            k = "c" c "_k" int(rand() * 1000)
            r = rand()
            if      (r < 0.30) print "SET " k " " val
            else if (r < 0.90) print "GET " k
            else               print "DEL " k
        }
    }' > "$WORKDIR/req_$c.txt"
done

start_ns=$(date +%s%N)
for ((c = 1; c <= CLIENTS; c++)); do
    # -N: send FIN after the last request; the server answers, sees EOF, closes; nc exits.
    nc -N -w 30 "$HOST" "$PORT" < "$WORKDIR/req_$c.txt" > "$WORKDIR/resp_$c.txt" &
    pids+=("$!")
done
for p in "${pids[@]}"; do wait "$p" || failed=$((failed + 1)); done

Then it counts reply lines per client (wc -l) and ERROR lines (grep -c ... || true, because grep -c exits 1 when the count is zero), prints one summary line and fails unless every request got a reply. Usage from module 07: ./scripts/load_test.sh 7001 8 20000 & while perf record runs. Usage from module 08: ./scripts/load_test.sh 7000 4 50000 65000 to grow memory until the container's limit is hit.

What this measures, honestly: throughput for pipelined requests (each client sends all its requests without waiting). That is the server's best case. It says nothing about per-request latency, which is what users feel. For latency, use the Python benchmark.

docs.title: 3.4 code/tcpkv/scripts/tcpkv_client.py
docs.text:
The core of the client:

class TcpkvClient:
    def __init__(self, host: str, port: int, timeout: float = 5.0) -> None:
        # Timeout applies to connect() and every later recv()/send(). No timeout = a hung server hangs us.
        self.sock = socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=timeout)
        self.sock.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_NODELAY, 1)
        # readline() over a buffered reader handles a reply split across TCP segments.
        self.reader = self.sock.makefile("rb")

    def request(self, line: str) -> str:
        self.sock.sendall(line.encode() + b"\n")      # sendall loops over partial sends
        raw = self.reader.readline(MAX_VALUE + 64)
        if not raw:
            raise TcpkvError("server closed the connection")
        return raw[:-1].decode(errors="replace")

    def get(self, key: str) -> Optional[str]:
        reply = self.request(f"GET {key}")
        if reply == "NOT_FOUND":
            return None
        if reply.startswith("VALUE "):
            return reply[len("VALUE "):]
        raise TcpkvError(f"GET {key}: unexpected reply {reply!r}")

The latency benchmark sends requests one at a time and records each round trip with time.perf_counter_ns(), then sorts and reads percentiles:

lat_us.sort()
def pct(p: float) -> float:
    return lat_us[min(len(lat_us) - 1, int(p / 100.0 * len(lat_us)))]
print(f"p50={pct(50):.0f} p95={pct(95):.0f} p99={pct(99):.0f} us")

Note that Python's own overhead (tens of microseconds per request, typical) is included in the number. For tcpkv on loopback that overhead can dominate; for comparing two server versions with the same client it is fine. A C++ client or a tool like memtier_benchmark removes it.

Run everything:

cd ~/projects/tcpkv
chmod +x scripts/*.sh scripts/*.py
scripts/run_tests.sh                       # debug: unit + integration
scripts/run_tests.sh asan                  # the same under ASan + UBSan
./build/debug/tcpkv 7000 &
scripts/load_test.sh 7000 8 20000
python3 scripts/tcpkv_client.py --bench 20000
kill %1

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
How bash runs a command. For cmake --build build, bash parses the line, performs expansions in a fixed order (brace, tilde, parameter and arithmetic and command substitution, word splitting, glob), then searches PATH (with a hash cache, hash -r clears it), fork()s, and in the child applies redirections with open + dup2 and calls execve. The parent waitpids for the child unless the command ends in &. Builtins (cd, export, read, [[) run inside the shell process; that is why cd cannot be an external program. strace -f -e trace=execve,clone,dup2 bash -c 'ls | wc -l' shows all of it (module 11 covers fork and exec).

Pipelines are concurrent. a | b | c creates two pipes and three processes at once; data flows through 64 KiB kernel buffers (default Linux pipe capacity). When c exits early (head), the next write by b gets SIGPIPE and b dies with status 141. With pipefail that 141 fails the pipeline: yes | head -1 under set -o pipefail returns 141. That is the one place pipefail surprises people; || true or set +o pipefail locally is the fix.

Subshells. ( ... ), $( ... ), every stage of a pipeline except (with shopt -s lastpipe) the last, and & jobs run in a forked copy of the shell. Variable changes inside never reach the parent. Traps are reset in subshells unless set -E (for ERR) is used.

Signals and background jobs. A non-interactive script's background jobs ignore SIGINT and SIGQUIT. When the terminal sends Ctrl-C to the foreground process group, the script gets it but its & children do not, which is why scripts without a cleanup trap leave servers running. While bash is waiting for a foreground child, it does not run trap handlers until the child exits; with wait (a builtin) the trap runs immediately. That is why long-running scripts use cmd & wait $! when they need responsive signal handling.

$(date +%s%N) and timing. Each $( ) is a fork + exec, about a millisecond (typical); a bash loop doing 100,000 of them takes minutes. That is why the load generator uses one awk process to write 20,000 lines in milliseconds. In bash 5, $EPOCHREALTIME gives microsecond time without forking.

Python's socket layer. socket.create_connection is getaddrinfo + socket + connect with SO_ options; settimeout puts the fd in non-blocking mode internally and uses poll to implement the timeout, so strace shows poll before every recvfrom. makefile("rb") wraps the socket in a BufferedReader which issues recv of 8 KiB (typical buffer size) and serves readline from the buffer. The GIL is released during blocking socket calls, so eight threads of I/O-bound clients do overlap, which is why the concurrency part of the self-test is meaningful.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Every CI step is a bash script. GitHub Actions runs run: blocks with bash -e {0} by default, which has -e but not -o pipefail. ctest | tee log.txt in a run: step passes when tests fail. Add shell: bash (which GitHub runs as bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail {0}) or put the logic in scripts/*.sh with its own set -euo pipefail.
  • The deploy script that deleted the wrong directory. A classic incident pattern: rm -rf "$PREFIX/$APP_DIR" with both variables unset on one host. set -u turns it into an error. Also use ${VAR:?message} for variables that must be set: rm -r -- "${INSTALL_DIR:?}".
  • Leaked background processes. A test script that starts a server and fails before kill leaves the port bound; the next CI run on a self-hosted agent fails with "Address already in use". trap cleanup EXIT plus kill $(jobs -p) prevents it.
  • Hangs. A script waiting on a dead server waits forever and burns CI minutes until the 6-hour job limit (GitHub default). Put timeout on anything that talks to the network, and timeouts on every socket in Python.
  • Your Windows background. The equivalent of a .bat that ignores %ERRORLEVEL% is a bash script without set -e. If your current team's build scripts are PowerShell, the same rules apply: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop', check $LASTEXITCODE after native commands, try/finally for cleanup. Say so in interviews: you know the failure modes, not just the syntax.
  • ShellCheck in CI. shellcheck scripts/*.sh finds unquoted variables, local x=$(cmd), unused variables, and portability issues. Add it as a CI job next to clang-format.
  • 3 AM: the nightly backup script reported success for a week while writing empty files. It ran pg_dump ... | gzip > backup.gz; pg_dump failed on authentication after a password rotation, gzip happily compressed zero bytes and returned 0. No pipefail. The fix is one line; the lesson is to verify outputs (size, gzip -t, a test restore), not just exit codes.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run code/m10_bash_patterns.sh and then with -v. Then run shellcheck on it and on a script of your own. Done when you can explain every line of the -v trace prefix and fix every ShellCheck warning in your script.
  2. (easy) Write hello.sh with CRLF line endings (save it from Notepad on /mnt/c), run it in WSL, read the error, fix it with dos2unix, and add a .gitattributes rule that prevents it. Done when you can explain why the error message mentions bash\r.
  3. (medium) Demonstrate each set -e hole from section 2.1 in a tiny script: the if, the local x=$(false), the ((x++)), and a function called from ||. Done when the script prints which ones did and did not abort, and you can say how to fix each.
  4. (medium) Run scripts/run_tests.sh and then press Ctrl-C during the integration part. Done when pgrep tcpkv shows no leftover server, and you can explain the order in which the INT trap and the EXIT trap ran.
  5. (medium) Extend tcpkv_client.py with --mix get=60,set=30,del=10 --threads 8 --seconds 10 that runs a closed-loop workload and prints throughput and p50/p99 latency per operation type. Done when it runs against the release build and its throughput is within the same order of magnitude as load_test.sh (it will be lower; explain why).
  6. (hard) Add the ctest integration test from module 05 exercise 6 using this client: a FIXTURES_SETUP test that starts the server with a small wrapper script, the --selftest test, and a FIXTURES_CLEANUP test that stops it. Done when ctest --preset debug -L integration passes, and a deliberately broken Store::del makes it fail with a readable message.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does set -euo pipefail do and why use it? -e exits on the first failing command, -u makes unset variables an error, -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails rather than only the last. Together they turn silent failures (a build that failed followed by "deploy OK", an rm with an empty variable, cmd | tee hiding cmd's failure) into immediate, visible exits.

Q: When does set -e not stop the script? When the failing command's status is being tested: in an if or while condition, on the left of && or ||, after !, and anywhere inside a function called from such a context. Also local x=$(cmd) because the status is local's, and ((x++)) evaluating to 0 kills the script unexpectedly. It is a net, not a substitute for explicit checks.

Q: How do you make sure a script cleans up temporary files and background processes? mktemp -d for the directory, a cleanup function registered with trap cleanup EXIT that saves $?, kills $(jobs -p), removes the directory, and exits with the saved status; plus trap 'exit 130' INT and trap 'exit 143' TERM so signals take the same path. Nothing handles SIGKILL, so temp dirs live under a location that is cleaned anyway.

Q: What do exit codes 127, 137 and 143 mean? 127: command not found. 137 = 128 + 9: killed by SIGKILL, typically the OOM killer or docker kill/a stop timeout. 143 = 128 + 15: terminated by SIGTERM, typically a normal docker stop or systemctl stop of a program with no handler.

Q: Why quote "$var"? Unquoted expansions are word-split on IFS and glob-expanded, so a value with spaces becomes several arguments and a * becomes file names. Quoting passes the value as exactly one argument; "$@" forwards all arguments intact.

Q: When would you write a script in Python instead of bash? When it needs data structures, floating point, structured formats (JSON, CSV, a socket protocol), non-trivial error handling, or grows past roughly a hundred lines. Bash stays for orchestration: running tools in sequence and checking exit codes.

Q: How did you load-test tcpkv? A bash generator writes per-client request files with awk and streams them through parallel nc connections, verifying that every request got a reply and none was an error; that gives pipelined throughput. A Python client measures per-request round-trip latency percentiles on one connection. I ran the server under perf record while the generator ran to find the hot spots.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• First lines: #!/usr/bin/env bash, a usage comment, set -euo pipefail; LF line endings, chmod +x.
  • Quote every expansion; "$@" forwards arguments; arrays for argument lists; [[ ]] and (( )).
  • set -e holes: tested commands, local x=$(...), ((x++)), functions called from if/||.
  • Functions return status; data on stdout; logs on stderr; local everything.
  • trap cleanup EXIT is bash's finally; map INT/TERM to exit 130/exit 143; read $? first.
  • Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 fail, 2 usage, 124 timeout, 125 bisect skip, 127 not found, 128+N signal N.
  • &, $!, wait PID, kill -0, timeout; never leave a server running after a script.
  • Retry downloads, never tests; put timeout on network operations.
  • Switch to Python for data, floats, protocols, real error handling, or more than ~100 lines.
  • tcpkv: build.sh, run_tests.sh (unit + live integration), load_test.sh (pipelined throughput), tcpkv_client.py (self-test, latency).

docs.title: 11. Linux systems programming essentials
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 07; C at a professional level

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Your program cannot touch the disk, the network or another process directly. Only the kernel can. When your code needs any of that, it asks the kernel through a system call (syscall): a numbered request like "open this file", "read 4096 bytes from descriptor 5", "create a process". On Windows you called CreateFileW, ReadFile, CreateProcessW, WaitForSingleObject; those are Win32 API functions in kernel32.dll that eventually make Nt* system calls. On Linux the C library (glibc) gives you thin wrappers, open, read, fork, waitpid, that are almost one-to-one with the kernel's syscalls.

This module is the Linux half of what you already know from Win32: files and handles become files and file descriptors, GetLastError() becomes errno, CreateProcess becomes fork + exec, console control handlers become signals, services become systemd units, and the "out of memory" you have seen as a failed malloc becomes the OOM killer. Knowing these lets you read strace output, write a server that shuts down cleanly, and run it as a proper service.

Analogy: the kernel is a bank vault and syscalls are the teller window. You fill in a numbered form (syscall number plus arguments), slide it through, and get back a result or an error code. glibc is the friendly clerk who fills in the form for you; sometimes the clerk does extra work first (buffering in printf, caching in malloc) before going to the window.

docs.title: 2.1 Syscalls vs library calls
docs.text:
your code       printf("x=%d\n", x)       fopen/fread           malloc(64)
                     |                         |                     |
glibc           formats into a buffer;     FILE* buffer;         carves from an arena;
                write() when full/newline  read() in 4 KiB+      brk()/mmap() only when it grows
                     |                         |                     |
kernel          write(1, buf, n)           read(fd, buf, 4096)   brk / mmap
  • A syscall crosses into the kernel: the CPU switches privilege level (syscall instruction on x86-64), the kernel does the work, and returns. Cost: on the order of 100 ns for a trivial one on modern hardware (typical; more with mitigations for CPU vulnerabilities), plus whatever the work costs.
  • A library call may make zero, one or many syscalls. printf usually makes none until its buffer flushes. malloc usually makes none.
  • man 2 read documents the syscall wrapper; man 3 printf documents the library function. Section 2 vs section 3 is the distinction.
  • strace shows syscalls only; ltrace shows library calls (module 07).

Every syscall reports failure the same way: the wrapper returns -1 (or MAP_FAILED, or NULL for some library functions) and sets the thread-local variable errno to a positive code (ENOENT, EINTR, EAGAIN, ...). Some newer interfaces (pthreads) return the error code directly and do not touch errno.

docs.title: 2.2 errno discipline
docs.text:
int fd = open(path, O_RDONLY | O_CLOEXEC);
if (fd < 0) {                         // 1. check the RETURN VALUE, never errno alone
    int e = errno;                    // 2. copy errno immediately: the next call may overwrite it
    log_error("open %s: %s", path, strerror(e));
    if (e == ENOENT) ...              // 3. branch on specific codes you can handle
}

Rules:

  • errno is only meaningful right after a call that reported failure. Successful calls may leave garbage in it.
  • It is per-thread (glibc defines errno as (*__errno_location())), so threads do not clobber each other.
  • Any call in between, including printf and free, may change it. Save it first.
  • Signal handlers must save and restore it (section 2.6).
  • strerror is not thread-safe in old glibc; strerror_r or %m in printf are. In C++, std::system_error(errno, std::generic_category(), "open") carries it as an exception.
  • Windows mapping: errno is GetLastError(), strerror is FormatMessage, and like GetLastError it is valid only right after the failing call.

The codes you must recognise on sight:

errno Meaning Typical response EINTR a signal interrupted a blocking call retry the call EAGAIN / EWOULDBLOCK non-blocking fd has no data or no space wait for readiness (epoll) ENOENT no such file or directory configuration error EACCES / EPERM permission denied / operation not permitted user, mode, capabilities, SELinux/AppArmor EMFILE this process hit its fd limit (ulimit -n) raise the limit; find the leak ENFILE the whole system hit its fd limit fs.file-max ENOSPC disk full (or inodes exhausted) df -h, df -i EPIPE wrote to a pipe/socket whose reader closed close the connection (ignore SIGPIPE) ECONNRESET peer reset the TCP connection close the connection EADDRINUSE port already bound another instance; SO_REUSEADDR for TIME_WAIT ENOMEM kernel could not allocate rare from malloc on Linux (overcommit); real for mmap with limits

docs.title: 2.3 File I/O: open, read, write, fsync, close
docs.text:
int fd = open("data.log", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_APPEND | O_CLOEXEC, 0644);
ssize_t n = write(fd, buf, len);     // may write fewer than len bytes: loop
fsync(fd);                           // wait until the device has it
close(fd);                           // can fail too: check it
  • A file descriptor is a small integer indexing the process's table of open files. 0, 1, 2 are stdin, stdout, stderr. Sockets, pipes, timers, epoll instances and devices are all fds: "everything is a file" means one set of calls (read, write, close, poll) works on all of them.
  • open flags: O_RDONLY/O_WRONLY/O_RDWR, O_CREAT (with a mode), O_TRUNC, O_APPEND (every write goes to the end, atomically for each write on local filesystems), O_EXCL (with O_CREAT: fail if it exists; the safe way to create lock files), O_CLOEXEC (close in the child after exec; always set it), O_NONBLOCK, O_DIRECT (bypass the page cache; databases).
  • Short reads and writes are normal. read returns fewer bytes than asked at end of file, on pipes and sockets, and when a signal arrives. read returning 0 means end of file (or the peer closed a socket). Every serious codebase has a write_all loop; tcpkv's is send_all in src/main.cpp.
  • write is not durable. It copies into the kernel's page cache and returns. The kernel writes dirty pages back later (seconds, typically). If the machine loses power before that, the data is gone, even though write succeeded. fsync(fd) blocks until the data and metadata are on stable storage; fdatasync skips non-essential metadata (timestamps). Creating a file also needs an fsync of the directory to make the directory entry durable.
  • The atomic-replace pattern (configs, snapshots): write file.tmp, fsync(tmp), rename("file.tmp", "file"), fsync(dirfd). rename within one filesystem is atomic: a reader sees the old file or the new one, never half of each.
  • Windows mapping: CreateFileW = open, ReadFile/WriteFile = read/write, FlushFileBuffers = fsync, CloseHandle = close, MoveFileExW(MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING) = rename, FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING = O_DIRECT.

docs.title: 2.4 mmap
docs.text:
mmap maps a file (or anonymous zeroed memory) into your address space. Reading the memory reads the file; no read calls, no copy into a user buffer.

void *p = mmap(NULL, len, PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0);   // file-backed, read-only
void *a = mmap(NULL, 1 << 20, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
               MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);         // 1 MiB of zeroed memory
munmap(p, len);
  • MAP_SHARED: writes go to the file (and other processes mapping it see them); msync flushes them like fsync. MAP_PRIVATE: copy-on-write; your writes are private.
  • Pages load lazily on first touch (a page fault). madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL / MADV_WILLNEED) tunes read-ahead.
  • Uses: fast read-only access to large files (search indexes, .so loading: the dynamic loader mmaps every shared library), shared memory between processes, and big allocations (glibc malloc uses mmap for blocks over 128 KiB by default).
  • Pitfalls: an I/O error on a mapped file arrives as SIGBUS, not as an error code; a file that shrinks under you gives SIGBUS on access past the end; you cannot mmap length 0. Databases that use mmap for their main data (LMDB does; PostgreSQL does not) trade control over write ordering for simplicity.
  • Windows mapping: CreateFileMapping + MapViewOfFile = mmap; VirtualAlloc = anonymous mmap.

docs.title: 2.5 Processes: fork, exec, wait, pipes
docs.text:
Linux splits "start a program" into two calls:

fork()   -> duplicates the calling process. Returns 0 in the child, child's PID in the parent.
            Memory is shared copy-on-write, so it is cheap. File descriptors are duplicated.
exec*()  -> replaces the current program image with a new one. Same PID, same fds (except
            O_CLOEXEC ones). Returns only on failure.
waitpid()-> parent collects the child's exit status. Until then the child is a zombie.

int pfd[2];
pipe2(pfd, O_CLOEXEC);                 // pfd[0] read end, pfd[1] write end
pid_t pid = fork();
if (pid == 0) {                         // child
    dup2(pfd[1], STDOUT_FILENO);        // child's stdout now goes into the pipe
    execlp("uname", "uname", "-srm", (char *)NULL);
    _exit(127);                         // exec failed; _exit, not exit (no atexit, no stdio flush)
}
close(pfd[1]);                          // parent: close the write end or read never sees EOF
/* read(pfd[0], ...) until 0 */
int status;
waitpid(pid, &status, 0);
if (WIFEXITED(status))   printf("exit %d\n", WEXITSTATUS(status));
if (WIFSIGNALED(status)) printf("signal %d\n", WTERMSIG(status));

Why two calls instead of one CreateProcess? Between fork and exec the child can rearrange its own environment with ordinary calls: redirect fds with dup2, change directory, drop privileges, set limits. That is how the shell implements cmd > file 2>&1 | other. The cost is that fork in a multithreaded process is dangerous: only the calling thread exists in the child, and any mutex another thread held (inside malloc, inside your logger) stays locked forever. Between fork and exec in a threaded program, call only async-signal-safe functions. posix_spawn (one call, like CreateProcess) avoids the problem and is faster for large processes; glibc implements it with clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_VFORK).

Pipes are one-way kernel buffers (64 KiB by default) between two fds. A reader blocks when empty; a writer blocks when full; reading after all writers closed gives EOF (0); writing after all readers closed gives SIGPIPE (and EPIPE if SIGPIPE is ignored).

Zombies and orphans. A child that exited but was not waitpided is a zombie (Z in ps): it holds only a PID and its exit status. A parent that never reaps leaks PIDs. If the parent dies first, the child is re-parented to PID 1 (or a subreaper), which reaps it. In a container, your program may be PID 1, which is why the tcpkv image uses tini (module 08).

docs.title: 2.6 Signals and async-signal safety
docs.text:
A signal is an asynchronous notification delivered to a process: the kernel interrupts whatever a thread was doing and runs your handler on its stack.

Signal Number Default Typical source SIGINT 2 terminate Ctrl-C SIGTERM 15 terminate kill PID, systemctl stop, docker stop SIGKILL 9 terminate, cannot be caught kill -9, OOM killer, stop timeout SIGSEGV 11 core dump invalid memory access SIGABRT 6 core dump abort(), failed assert, sanitizers SIGBUS 7 core dump I/O error on mmap, misaligned access on some CPUs SIGPIPE 13 terminate write to closed pipe/socket SIGCHLD 17 ignore a child changed state SIGHUP 1 terminate terminal closed; by convention "reload config" for daemons SIGUSR1/2 10/12 terminate application-defined (dump stats, rotate logs) SIGSTOP/SIGCONT 19/18 stop/continue, cannot be caught kill -STOP, Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP

Install handlers with sigaction, not signal (whose semantics vary):

struct sigaction sa = {0};
sa.sa_handler = on_signal;
sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);         // signals blocked while the handler runs (plus this one)
sa.sa_flags = SA_RESTART;         // auto-restart some interrupted syscalls; omit to get EINTR
sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL);

Async-signal safety. The handler can run between any two instructions of your program, including in the middle of malloc while it holds the heap lock, or in the middle of printf while it holds the FILE lock. If the handler calls malloc or printf, it may deadlock or corrupt the heap. Only functions listed in man 7 signal-safety may be called: write, read, _exit, kill, sigaction, signal-related functions, open, close and a few dozen more. Not printf, malloc, free, syslog, pthread_mutex_lock, exit, or anything in C++ that may allocate or lock (including std::cout and std::string construction).

Three safe patterns:

  1. Set a flag. volatile sig_atomic_t g_stop = 1; in the handler; the main loop checks it. This is what tcpkv's main.cpp does. The main loop must wake up to see it: use a poll timeout or install the handler without SA_RESTART so blocking calls return EINTR.
  2. Self-pipe. The handler writes one byte to a non-blocking pipe; the event loop polls the read end along with everything else and handles the signal in normal context. m11_syscalls.c signals does this.
  3. signalfd (Linux only): block the signals with sigprocmask (in every thread: do it before creating threads) and read them from an fd in the event loop. No handler at all.

In multithreaded programs, a process-directed signal is delivered to any thread that does not block it. The robust design is: block signals in all threads, and have one thread receive them via sigwait or signalfd.

EINTR: a blocking call (read, accept, poll, nanosleep) interrupted by a handled signal fails with EINTR. Retry it in a loop, or treat it as "check your flags". SA_RESTART makes the kernel restart many of them transparently, but never poll, epoll_wait, select or nanosleep.

Windows mapping: SetConsoleCtrlHandler handles Ctrl-C and close events on a new thread, which is why Windows handlers can do more. Service stop requests arrive through the SCM handler. Linux handlers interrupt an existing thread, hence the strict rules.

docs.title: 2.7 Timers
docs.text:
Mechanism Use clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) measuring durations; never jumps when NTP or an admin sets the clock clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) wall-clock timestamps for logs; can jump backwards nanosleep / std::this_thread::sleep_for simple delays timerfd_create a timer that is a file descriptor: put it in poll/epoll beside sockets poll/epoll_wait timeout argument the event loop's own "next deadline" alarm, setitimer, timer_create signal-based timers; avoid in new code (signal-safety rules again)

Event-driven servers keep their timeouts (idle connections, request deadlines) in a min-heap or a timer wheel and pass "time until the earliest deadline" to epoll_wait. timerfd is the simple version. std::chrono::steady_clock is CLOCK_MONOTONIC in C++. Windows mapping: QueryPerformanceCounter = CLOCK_MONOTONIC; waitable timers = timerfd.

docs.title: 2.8 epoll preview
docs.text:
tcpkv uses one thread per connection. That stops scaling at a few thousand connections (each thread has a stack, typically 8 MiB reserved, and context switches cost). The alternative is one thread watching many sockets and acting only on the ready ones:

int ep = epoll_create1(EPOLL_CLOEXEC);
struct epoll_event ev = { .events = EPOLLIN, .data.fd = listen_fd };
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, listen_fd, &ev);        // register interest once
for (;;) {
    int n = epoll_wait(ep, events, 64, timeout_ms);  // sleep until something is ready
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        if (events[i].data.fd == listen_fd) accept_all_pending();   // accept4(... SOCK_NONBLOCK)
        else                                 handle_readable(events[i].data.fd);
    }
}
  • select/poll pass the whole fd list on every call: O(n) per wait. epoll keeps the interest list in the kernel and returns only ready fds: cost proportional to activity.
  • Level-triggered (default): reported on every epoll_wait while the condition holds. Easy. Edge-triggered (EPOLLET): reported once per change; you must read until EAGAIN or you will never hear about the leftover data. Faster, easier to get wrong.
  • All fds must be non-blocking: a blocking read in an event loop stalls every client.
  • Writes: when write returns EAGAIN or a short count, keep the rest in a per-connection buffer, add EPOLLOUT, and continue when writable.
  • Windows mapping: I/O Completion Ports are completion-based (the kernel does the read and tells you it finished); epoll is readiness-based (the kernel says you can read now without blocking). Linux's completion-based interface is io_uring.

code/m11_epoll_preview.c is a complete level-triggered echo server. The full event loop with output buffers, timers and edge-triggered mode is 08_Networking_Distributed/06_nonblocking_io_epoll_event_loops.md.

docs.title: 2.9 Resource limits: ulimit
docs.text:
Every process has soft and hard limits (getrlimit/setrlimit), inherited by children.

ulimit -a                 # all soft limits of this shell
ulimit -n                 # open files: often 1024 soft (Ubuntu default)
ulimit -Hn                # hard limit: the ceiling a non-root process may raise the soft limit to
ulimit -n 65536           # raise for this shell and its children
ulimit -c unlimited       # allow core dumps (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/06_core_dumps_on_linux.md)
cat /proc/$(pgrep -n tcpkv)/limits    # the limits of a RUNNING process
prlimit --pid PID --nofile=65536:65536  # change them on a live process

The one that bites servers is RLIMIT_NOFILE. One TCP connection is one fd. With a soft limit of 1024, the 1021st client makes accept fail with EMFILE. Raise it where the process is started: LimitNOFILE= in the systemd unit, --ulimit nofile= for Docker, /etc/security/limits.conf for login sessions (it does not apply to systemd services). Other useful ones: RLIMIT_CORE (core size), RLIMIT_AS (address space: makes malloc return NULL, good for testing out-of-memory paths), RLIMIT_NPROC (processes/threads per user), RLIMIT_STACK (main thread stack, 8 MiB default).

docs.title: 2.10 Memory overcommit and the OOM killer
docs.text:
Linux by default overcommits: malloc(1 GiB) succeeds even if there is not 1 GiB free, because memory is only allocated when pages are first touched. If the system then runs out of RAM and swap while processes touch their pages, the kernel cannot fail a malloc that already succeeded. It picks a victim process and sends it SIGKILL. That is the OOM killer.

  • Victim choice: the process with the highest oom_score (/proc/PID/oom_score), roughly its share of memory, adjusted by oom_score_adj (-1000 = never kill, +1000 = kill first). systemd's OOMScoreAdjust= sets it for a service.
  • Evidence: the process vanishes with exit status 137 (128 + 9); dmesg or journalctl -k shows Out of memory: Killed process 1234 (tcpkv) total-vm:... anon-rss:.... There is no core dump and no log line from your program: SIGKILL cannot be caught.
  • cgroup limits (Docker --memory, systemd MemoryMax=, Kubernetes limits) give each group its own OOM: the kernel kills inside the group that exceeded its limit, not a random process on the host. docker inspect then shows OOMKilled: true (module 08).
  • vm.overcommit_memory: 0 heuristic (default), 1 always, 2 strict accounting (then malloc can really return NULL). Databases sometimes recommend 2.
  • Windows mapping: Windows commits memory at allocation time against the commit limit (RAM + page file), so VirtualAlloc/malloc fails up front and there is no OOM killer. That is a real difference to mention in interviews.

docs.title: 2.11 systemd: running a server as a service
docs.text:
systemd is PID 1 on Ubuntu: it starts services at boot, supervises them, restarts them, collects their output in the journal, and puts each one in a cgroup. A unit file describes one service. The tcpkv unit, code/tcpkv/deploy/tcpkv.service (abridged):

[Unit]
Description=tcpkv TCP key-value server
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target
StartLimitIntervalSec=60          # crash-loop guard: more than 5 starts in 60 s -> failed
StartLimitBurst=5

[Service]
Type=exec                         # foreground process; "started" once exec succeeded
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/tcpkv 7000
User=tcpkv
Group=tcpkv
Restart=on-failure                # restart on crash or non-zero exit, not on clean stop
RestartSec=2
KillSignal=SIGTERM
TimeoutStopSec=30                 # SIGTERM, wait 30 s, then SIGKILL
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
LimitNOFILE=65536                 # ulimit -n for the service
LimitCORE=infinity
MemoryMax=512M                    # cgroup memory cap: OOM inside this service only
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict              # whole filesystem read-only for this service
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target        # 'enable' hooks it into normal boot

The commands:

sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin tcpkv
sudo cp deploy/tcpkv.service /etc/systemd/system/
