sudo systemctl daemon-reload            # after ANY unit file edit
sudo systemctl enable --now tcpkv       # start now and at boot
systemctl status tcpkv                  # active?, PID, memory, CPU, last 10 log lines
journalctl -u tcpkv -f                  # follow logs
journalctl -u tcpkv -b -p warning       # this boot, warnings and worse
journalctl -u tcpkv --since "2026-10-12 03:00" --until "03:15"
systemctl show tcpkv -p NRestarts,ExecMainStatus,Result
sudo systemctl edit tcpkv               # drop-in override without editing the original
systemd-analyze security tcpkv          # exposure score for the sandboxing options

Restart policies:

Restart= Restarts when no (default) never on-failure non-zero exit, killed by a signal (except clean stop signals), timeout, watchdog on-abnormal signal, timeout, watchdog; not on non-zero exit always any exit, even exit 0 (but not after systemctl stop)

on-failure is right for a server whose clean exit means "someone asked me to stop". Docker's restart: unless-stopped is the equivalent of Restart=always (module 08).

Logging. Under systemd, a service writes plain lines to stdout/stderr and journald stores them with timestamp, unit, PID and priority. No log files, no rotation code, no syslog() needed. Prefix a line with <3> to mark it as error priority (sd-daemon(3)), or use sd_journal_send for structured fields. tcpkv's log_line writing to stderr is exactly right.

Type= matters: simple/exec for programs that stay in the foreground (all modern servers), forking for old-style daemons that double-fork and write a PID file (do not write new ones), notify for programs that call sd_notify("READY=1") when they are really ready to serve, which lets dependent units wait for real readiness. Windows mapping: a systemd unit is a Windows service registration (sc create), Restart= is the Recovery tab, journald is the Event Log, User= is "Log on as".

WSL note: Ubuntu 24.04 on WSL runs systemd by default. If systemctl reports "System has not been booted with systemd", put [boot] and systemd=true in /etc/wsl.conf and run wsl --shutdown.

docs.title: 2.12 strace as your syscall microscope
docs.text:
Module 07 introduced strace. Here it is the tool that makes this module concrete:

strace -f ./m11_syscalls spawn                  # clone, execve in the child, pipe2, dup2, wait4
strace -e trace=openat,read,write,fsync,close ./m11_syscalls fileio /tmp/a.txt
strace -e trace=%signal,poll,timerfd_settime ./m11_syscalls signals   # then kill -TERM it
strace -c ./m11_syscalls mmap /etc/services     # count: compare with reading the file in a loop
strace -f -e trace=epoll_wait,accept4,read,write ./epoll_echo 7100
strace -f -tt -T -p $(pgrep -n tcpkv)           # what is the live server doing, with timings

Reading a line: openat(AT_FDCWD, "/tmp/a.txt", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC|O_CLOEXEC, 0644) = 3 is the call, its decoded arguments and the result. A failure looks like = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory). <0.000021> with -T is the time spent inside the call. Note that glibc's open is the openat syscall, and fork is clone; the wrapper names and the syscall names differ.

docs.title: 3.1 code/m11_syscalls.c
docs.text:
Four demos in one C file, every return value checked:

gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -g m11_syscalls.c -o m11_syscalls
./m11_syscalls fileio /tmp/m11.txt     # open/write/fsync/close, read back, ENOENT demo
./m11_syscalls mmap /etc/services      # map a file and count lines without read()
./m11_syscalls spawn                   # pipe2 + fork + dup2 + execlp + waitpid
./m11_syscalls signals                 # self-pipe + timerfd + poll; Ctrl-C or kill -TERM PID

The heart of the signals demo:

static int g_sigpipe_w = -1;            /* write end of the self-pipe */

/* write() is async-signal-safe; printf, malloc and mutexes are not.

 * Save and restore errno because the interrupted code may be about to read it. */
static void on_signal(int signo) {
    const int saved = errno;
    const unsigned char b = (unsigned char)signo;
    ssize_t ignored = write(g_sigpipe_w, &b, 1);
    (void)ignored;
    errno = saved;
}

/* main loop: one poll() over the self-pipe and a timerfd */
struct pollfd pfds[2] = {{.fd = sp[0], .events = POLLIN}, {.fd = tfd, .events = POLLIN}};
for (;;) {
    const int pr = poll(pfds, 2, -1);
    if (pr < 0) {
        if (errno == EINTR) continue;   /* the self-pipe will tell us which signal */
        die("poll");
    }
    if (pfds[0].revents & POLLIN) { /* read the signal number; now printf and cleanup are fine */ }
    if (pfds[1].revents & POLLIN) { /* read a uint64_t expiration count from the timerfd */ }
}

The file I/O demo shows a detail people get wrong: printf output is buffered in user space and write(STDOUT_FILENO, ...) is not, so mixing them reorders output unless you fflush(stdout) first. The same buffering is why a child created by fork without a flush prints the parent's pending output twice, and why the child must leave with _exit, not exit.

docs.title: 3.2 code/m11_epoll_preview.c
docs.text:
gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -g m11_epoll_preview.c -o epoll_echo
./epoll_echo 7100 &
for i in 1 2 3; do (echo "hello $i"; sleep 1) | nc localhost 7100 & done; wait
kill -INT %1

The accept path drains every pending connection, because one readiness event can stand for many:

if (fd == lfd) {
    for (;;) {
        const int cfd = accept4(lfd, NULL, NULL, SOCK_NONBLOCK | SOCK_CLOEXEC);
        if (cfd < 0) {
            if (errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK) break;   /* none left */
            if (errno == EINTR) continue;
            perror("accept4");                                   /* EMFILE: log, keep serving */
            break;
        }
        struct epoll_event cev = { .events = EPOLLIN | EPOLLRDHUP, .data.fd = cfd };
        epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, cfd, &cev);
    }
}

docs.title: 3.3 code/tcpkv/src/main.cpp revisited
docs.text: Read tcpkv's main now with this module's vocabulary: signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) plus MSG_NOSIGNAL (get EPIPE, do not die); sigaction without SA_RESTART for SIGTERM/SIGINT and a volatile std::sig_atomic_t flag (pattern 1); poll with a 500 ms timeout so the flag is noticed even if the signal went to another thread; SOCK_CLOEXEC on every socket; accept4 failures such as EMFILE logged without exiting; a bounded drain on shutdown so TimeoutStopSec=30 and docker stop's 10 seconds are never reached.

docs.title: 3.4 code/tcpkv/deploy/tcpkv.service
docs.text:
The full unit with comments. CMake installs it (install(FILES deploy/tcpkv.service ...), module 04). Try it on WSL:

cmake --preset release && cmake --build --preset release
sudo cmake --install build/release --prefix /usr/local --strip
sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin tcpkv
sudo cp deploy/tcpkv.service /etc/systemd/system/ && sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now tcpkv
printf 'PING\n' | nc -N localhost 7000                 # PONG
sudo kill -SEGV $(systemctl show -p MainPID --value tcpkv)   # simulate a crash
sleep 3; systemctl status tcpkv                          # restarted; NRestarts=1
journalctl -u tcpkv -n 20

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What a syscall instruction does. On x86-64, glibc's read wrapper puts the syscall number (0 for read) in rax and arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9, then executes syscall. The CPU switches to ring 0 and jumps to the kernel's entry point, which saves registers, looks up sys_call_table[rax], runs ksys_read, and returns with the result in rax. A negative value between -4095 and -1 is an error; the wrapper negates it into errno and returns -1. Some calls (clock_gettime, gettimeofday, getcpu) never enter the kernel: the vDSO is a small shared library the kernel maps into every process that reads the time from a shared page. That is why strace does not show clock_gettime and why it costs tens of nanoseconds (typical).

The fd table. Each process has a table of pointers to open file descriptions (struct file in the kernel), which hold the file offset and status flags and point to the inode. dup2 and fork copy pointers, so parent and child share the offset: if both write to an inherited fd without O_APPEND, their writes interleave at one shared position. open twice creates two descriptions with independent offsets. O_CLOEXEC is a flag on the fd-table slot, not the description. Closing the last fd referring to a description releases it; for a socket, that sends FIN.

Page cache and writeback. read and write go through the page cache: 4 KiB pages of file content kept in otherwise free RAM. write marks pages dirty; the flusher threads write them after dirty_expire_centisecs (30 s default) or when dirty memory exceeds dirty_background_ratio (10 % default); a writer that produces data faster than the disk absorbs it is throttled in write itself. fsync forces writeback of that file and issues a cache-flush command to the device. fsyncgate (2018): PostgreSQL discovered that after a writeback error, Linux could mark the pages clean and a retried fsync returned success while the data was lost. The fix in PostgreSQL was to treat an fsync failure as fatal (PANIC and recover from the WAL). Lesson: an fsync error is not retryable.

fork and copy-on-write. fork copies the page tables, not the pages, and marks every writable page read-only in both processes. The first write by either side triggers a page fault; the kernel copies that one page and makes it writable. A 10 GiB process can fork in milliseconds, but copying its page tables is still proportional to its size, and a parent that keeps writing after fork doubles its memory gradually. Redis's background save relies on exactly this behaviour.

Signal delivery. When a signal is sent, the kernel sets a bit in the target's pending set. On the next return from kernel to user mode (after a syscall, an interrupt or a reschedule), it checks for pending unblocked signals and, for a caught signal, builds a signal frame on the user stack (saved registers, siginfo), points the instruction pointer at the handler and returns to user mode. When the handler returns, it lands in a small trampoline that calls rt_sigreturn, which restores the saved registers. If the thread was blocked in an interruptible syscall, the syscall is aborted with EINTR or restarted per SA_RESTART. Standard signals do not queue: two SIGCHLDs before you handle one become one, which is why a SIGCHLD handler must loop waitpid(-1, ..., WNOHANG) until it returns 0.

epoll internals. epoll_ctl(ADD) inserts the fd into a red-black tree in the epoll instance and registers a callback on the fd's wait queue. When the socket receives data, the network stack wakes its wait queue; the callback appends the item to the epoll ready list and wakes threads in epoll_wait. epoll_wait copies out ready items; for level-triggered items it puts them back on the list if still ready. That is why epoll_wait is O(ready) and not O(registered). The interest is registered on the open file description, not the fd number: closing an fd whose description is still referenced elsewhere (a dup or a forked child) leaves the registration alive and produces events for an fd you no longer have, a classic bug.

systemd and cgroups. Every unit gets its own cgroup under /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/ tcpkv.service/. MemoryMax= writes memory.max, TasksMax= writes pids.max, CPU options write cpu.max. Because systemd tracks the service by cgroup and not by PID, it finds and kills every process the service forked on stop, which PID files never could. KillMode=mixed sends SIGTERM to the main process and SIGKILL to the rest after the timeout. The journal reads the service's stdout/stderr from a socket systemd connected to fds 1 and 2 before exec, so it knows which unit each line came from. systemd-cgls shows the tree; systemd-cgtop shows usage.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The fd leak. The server works for days, then every new connection fails and logs show accept: Too many open files. ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l sits at exactly the LimitNOFILE value; ls -l /proc/PID/fd shows thousands of sockets in CLOSE_WAIT (ss -tanp): the code path for one error forgot to close. Raising the limit buys time; RAII (a C++ unique_fd class, or std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter) fixes it. Your C server's goto cleanup discipline is the C version of the same thing.
  • Missing fsync. A service acknowledged writes after write() only. A host reboot lost the last 30 seconds of "committed" data. In the banking context this is the difference between the WAL being durable and not; it is why PostgreSQL's synchronous_commit and fsync settings exist. Ask "where is the fsync?" in every design review of something that persists data.
  • Logging from a signal handler. A crash handler that calls printf or the logging library to print a stack trace works in testing and deadlocks in production when the crash happens inside malloc. Write a minimal message with write(2, ...), then let the core dump carry the details (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/06_core_dumps_on_linux.md).
  • Fork in a threaded server. Calling system() or popen() from a multithreaded server to run a helper script occasionally hangs the child forever (a lock held by another thread at fork time), and doubles RSS momentarily for large processes. Use posix_spawn, or a small helper process started early, before any threads exist.
  • Silent OOM kills. The service restarts every few hours with no error in its logs. systemctl status shows status=9/KILL, journalctl -k | grep -i oom shows the kill, and systemctl show -p MemoryMax shows the cap. Find the growth with heap profiling (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/09_leaks_and_memory_growth.md), not by raising the limit.
  • SIGPIPE killed the server. A client disconnects mid-response, the next send raises SIGPIPE, the process dies with status 141 and no log line. Ignore SIGPIPE at startup and use MSG_NOSIGNAL; every network server on Linux does this. On Windows the equivalent failure just returns WSAECONNRESET, so this one surprises Windows developers.
  • Restart loops. Restart=always with RestartSec=100ms and a configuration error produces thousands of restarts per minute, floods the journal, and hides the first error. Use on-failure, a RestartSec of seconds, and StartLimitBurst so the unit ends up failed and alerts fire.
  • 3 AM: after a deploy, systemctl restart tcpkv takes exactly 30 seconds and then the service starts. The new code blocks SIGTERM by accident (a library called sigprocmask in its init) so the stop always runs into TimeoutStopSec and SIGKILL. grep Sig /proc/PID/status shows SigBlk with bit 15 set (decode the hex mask). Every restart was dropping in-flight requests.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run each m11_syscalls demo under strace -f. Done when you can name the syscall behind the glibc wrappers open (openat), fork (clone) and waitpid (wait4), and explain why clock_gettime does not appear in any trace.
  2. (easy) Run ulimit -n 64 in a shell, start ./build/debug/tcpkv 7000 from it, and open 100 connections with a small Python loop. Done when the server log shows accept: Too many open files, the server keeps serving existing clients, and cat /proc/PID/limits confirms the limit.
  3. (medium) Remove the fsync from the fileio demo and measure both versions writing 10,000 small records with hyperfine. Then write the atomic-replace version (tmp, fsync, rename, fsync of the directory). Done when you can state the cost of fsync on your disk and explain why the directory needs its own fsync.
  4. (medium) Write mini_shell.c that reads a command line, splits on spaces, supports one | and one > file, and runs it with fork, pipe, dup2, execvp and waitpid, printing the exit status or signal. Done when ls -l | wc -l and echo hi > /tmp/x work, no zombies remain (ps -o stat), and strace -f shows the expected dup2 calls.
  5. (medium) Install tcpkv as a systemd service on WSL with the unit from deploy/. Kill it with SIGSEGV three times, then six times within a minute. Done when you can show NRestarts from systemctl show, the unit in failed state after the burst limit, and the relevant journal lines, and you can explain StartLimitBurst.
  6. (hard) Turn m11_epoll_preview.c into a tcpkv server: non-blocking sockets, a per-connection input buffer split into lines, a per-connection output buffer flushed on EPOLLOUT, the existing C++ parse_command and Store, and a signalfd for SIGTERM. Done when scripts/tcpkv_client.py --selftest and scripts/load_test.sh 7000 64 5000 pass against it, and strace -c shows one thread doing all the work.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a system call and a library function? A system call transfers control to the kernel through a CPU instruction to do something only the kernel can do (I/O, process creation, memory mapping). A library function runs in user space and may make zero or more syscalls: printf buffers and calls write occasionally, malloc calls brk or mmap only when its arenas grow. strace shows the former, ltrace the latter.

Q: Does write() returning success mean the data is on disk? No. It means the kernel copied it into the page cache. It reaches the device later through writeback. For durability call fsync (or fdatasync) on the file, and fsync the directory after creating or renaming files. Treat an fsync error as fatal for that data, because the kernel may have dropped the dirty pages.

Q: What can you safely do in a signal handler? Only async-signal-safe operations: set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, write to a pipe or eventfd, _exit. No malloc, printf, locks or C++ that might allocate, because the handler may have interrupted the same code holding the same lock. Save and restore errno. Do the real work in normal context via a flag, the self-pipe trick, or signalfd.

Q: Explain fork and exec. Why are they separate? fork duplicates the process with copy-on-write memory and duplicated fds; exec replaces the program image in the current process. Separating them lets the child set up its environment (redirect fds, change directory, drop privileges) with ordinary calls before running the new program, which is how shells implement redirection and pipes. In multithreaded programs only async-signal-safe calls are allowed between them; posix_spawn is the safer single call.

Q: What is EINTR and how do you handle it? A blocking syscall interrupted by a caught signal returns -1 with errno == EINTR. Retry the call in a loop, or use the interruption to check a shutdown flag. SA_RESTART restarts many calls automatically but never poll, epoll_wait or select.

Q: Why is epoll more scalable than select or poll? select and poll pass the full fd set on every call and the kernel scans it, so each wait is O(n) in watched fds. epoll registers interest once in a kernel object and maintains a ready list filled by callbacks, so epoll_wait costs O(ready). Level-triggered reports while data remains; edge-triggered reports changes only and requires draining to EAGAIN.

Q: A process disappeared with exit code 137 and no logs. What happened? It received SIGKILL (128 + 9), most often from the OOM killer (system or cgroup limit) or a stop timeout escalating from SIGTERM. Check journalctl -k or dmesg for "Out of memory: Killed process", docker inspect for OOMKilled, or systemctl status for the stop timeout. SIGKILL cannot be caught, so the program never logs it.

Q: How do you run a C++ server as a service on Linux? A systemd unit: ExecStart in the foreground, a dedicated User=, Restart=on-failure with a RestartSec and start-limit burst, TimeoutStopSec matching the graceful-drain time, LimitNOFILE for connections, MemoryMax for a cgroup cap, sandboxing options, logs to stdout/stderr collected by journald and read with journalctl -u. The server handles SIGTERM by draining and exiting 0.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Syscalls enter the kernel (man 2); library calls may or may not make syscalls (man 3). strace sees syscalls.
  • Check the return value, then copy errno immediately; know EINTR, EAGAIN, EMFILE, EPIPE, ENOSPC on sight.
  • read/write can be short: loop. write is not durable: fsync the file and the directory; rename is atomic.
  • mmap maps files or anonymous memory; lazy page faults; I/O errors arrive as SIGBUS.
  • fork (copy-on-write) + exec + waitpid; close unused pipe ends; _exit in the child; posix_spawn in threaded programs.
  • Signal handlers: only async-signal-safe calls; flag, self-pipe or signalfd; save errno; ignore SIGPIPE.
  • Timers: CLOCK_MONOTONIC for durations, timerfd or the epoll timeout for event loops.
  • epoll: register once, wait returns ready fds; non-blocking fds; level vs edge triggered.
  • ulimit -n caps connections; set LimitNOFILE in the unit; /proc/PID/limits shows the live values.
  • Overcommit plus OOM killer: SIGKILL, exit 137, evidence in journalctl -k; cgroup limits contain it.
  • systemd unit: Type=exec, User=, Restart=on-failure, TimeoutStopSec, LimitNOFILE, MemoryMax, journald logs.

docs.title: 12. Windows toolchain reference: MSVC, MSBuild, vcpkg, WinDbg, and Linux side by side
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03, 04, 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
You already use most of these tools at work. This module does two things. First, it fills the gaps: the parts of the Windows toolchain people use daily without knowing what is underneath (what /MD really selects, why LNK2038 happens, how a PDB is matched to a crash dump). Second, it lines everything up against the Linux tools from modules 01 to 11, one row per concept, so that in an interview you can answer "how would you do X on Linux?" by saying "on Windows I did it with Y; on Linux it is Z, and here is the one way they differ".

That comparison is your selling point. Many Linux C++ candidates have never seen a crash dump from a customer machine; many Windows developers have never written a CMakeLists.txt. You will be able to talk about both precisely.

Analogy: two cities with the same services under different names. Both have a post office, a hospital and a bank. If you know where each is in one city and the name it goes by in the other, you can work in either one.

docs.title: 2.1 The pieces of the MSVC toolchain
docs.text:
Piece File Linux equivalent Compiler driver cl.exe g++ / clang++ Linker link.exe ld (GNU ld, gold, lld, mold), usually called through g++ Static library tool lib.exe ar Binary inspector dumpbin.exe (= link /dump) objdump, readelf, nm, ldd Name demangler undname.exe c++filt Build engine MSBuild (.sln, .vcxproj) Make, Ninja Meta-build CMake (also generates .sln) CMake Package manager vcpkg, NuGet, Conan vcpkg, Conan, apt install lib*-dev Platform headers and libs Windows SDK (windows.h, kernel32.lib) glibc headers, /usr/include, /usr/lib C runtime UCRT (ucrtbase.dll) + vcruntime140.dll glibc (libc.so.6) C++ standard library MSVC STL (msvcp140.dll) libstdc++ (libstdc++.so.6) or libc++ Debugger Visual Studio debugger, WinDbg GDB, LLDB Debug info .pdb files, separate from the binary DWARF sections inside the ELF, or split .debug files

The compiler is not on PATH by default. The Developer Command Prompt (or vcvars64.bat, or Enter-VsDevShell in PowerShell) sets PATH, INCLUDE, LIB and LIBPATH to the right MSVC and SDK versions. CI tasks and CMake's Visual Studio generator do this for you. On Linux the compiler is simply in /usr/bin.

docs.title: 2.2 cl.exe flags against GCC flags
docs.text:
Purpose MSVC GCC / Clang Standard /std:c++17 -std=c++17 Strict conformance /permissive- (on by default in new VS projects) default; -pedantic Correct __cplusplus /Zc:__cplusplus always correct Exceptions /EHsc on by default No optimisation /Od -O0 Optimise /O2 (speed), /O1 (size) -O2, -Os Whole program / LTO /GL + /LTCG -flto Debug info /Zi (PDB), /Z7 (in .obj) -g Linker debug info /DEBUG (/DEBUG:FULL) part of -g Warnings /W4 -Wall -Wextra All warnings /Wall (very noisy) Clang -Weverything Warnings as errors /WX -Werror Static analysis /analyze clang-tidy, -fanalyzer (GCC) Define /DNAME=1 -DNAME=1 Include dir /I path -I path AddressSanitizer /fsanitize=address (VS 2019 16.9+) -fsanitize=address UBSan, TSan, MSan not available in MSVC -fsanitize=undefined,thread,memory Stack protector /GS (default on) -fstack-protector-strong Control-flow guard /guard:cf -fcf-protection Source charset /utf-8 UTF-8 by default Parallel compile /MP make -j, Ninja (default parallel) Remove unused code /OPT:REF /OPT:ICF (linker) -ffunction-sections -Wl,--gc-sections, --icf (lld/gold)

The runtime library switch has no direct GCC counterpart and is the source of most MSVC link errors:

Flag Meaning CMake CMAKE_MSVC_RUNTIME_LIBRARY /MD release CRT and STL as DLLs MultiThreadedDLL (CMake default) /MDd debug CRT as DLLs (checked iterators, debug heap) MultiThreadedDebugDLL /MT release CRT linked statically into the module MultiThreaded /MTd debug CRT statically MultiThreadedDebug

Every object file and static library linked into one module must use the same choice. Mixing gives LNK2038: mismatch detected for 'RuntimeLibrary' or for '_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL' (Debug and Release objects mixed). On Linux there is one glibc and one libstdc++ for the whole process, so this class of error does not exist; the nearest equivalent is mixing _GLIBCXX_DEBUG and normal objects, or the libstdc++ dual ABI (_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI).

docs.title: 2.3 Libraries: .lib, .dll and the import library
docs.text:
Concept Windows Linux Object file .obj (COFF) .o (ELF) Static library .lib (archive of .obj) .a (archive of .o) Shared library .dll .so What you link against the import library .lib that comes with the DLL the .so itself Executable format PE/COFF (.exe) ELF (no extension) Exported by default nothing: __declspec(dllexport) or a .def file everything with default visibility; -fvisibility=hidden to opt out Run-time search app directory, system directories, PATH (simplified) RPATH/RUNPATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, ld.so.cache, /lib, /usr/lib Embedded search path none (use app directory, SetDllDirectory, side-by-side manifests) -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN/../lib' Load at run time LoadLibraryW / GetProcAddress / FreeLibrary dlopen / dlsym / dlclose List dependencies dumpbin /dependents app.exe, Dependencies tool ldd app, readelf -d app List exports dumpbin /exports x.dll nm -D --defined-only x.so Position independent DLLs are relocated (ASLR) using a relocation table -fPIC required for .so

The portable export macro every cross-platform library has:

// include/tcpkv/export.hpp - CMake's GenerateExportHeader produces the same thing for you.
#pragma once
#if defined(_WIN32)
#  if defined(TCPKV_BUILDING_DLL)
#    define TCPKV_API __declspec(dllexport)   // compiling the DLL itself
#  else
#    define TCPKV_API __declspec(dllimport)   // compiling a consumer of the DLL
#  endif
#else
#  define TCPKV_API __attribute__((visibility("default")))   // with -fvisibility=hidden
#endif

class TCPKV_API Store { /* ... */ };

Link errors, translated:

MSVC GNU ld Meaning LNK2019: unresolved external symbol "int __cdecl add(int,int)" (?add@@YAHHH@Z) referenced in function main undefined reference to 'add(int, int)' declared, used, never defined in what you linked LNK2001: unresolved external symbol same same, reference not inside a function (e.g. a vtable or data) LNK2005: "x" already defined in a.obj multiple definition of 'x' ODR violation the linker can see (module 02) LNK1104: cannot open file 'foo.lib' cannot find -lfoo library path or name wrong LNK2038: mismatch detected for 'RuntimeLibrary' (no equivalent) /MT and /MD objects mixed LNK4098: defaultlib 'LIBCMT' conflicts with use of other libs (no equivalent) two CRTs requested; same root cause

The three causes of an unresolved symbol are the same on both platforms: the definition is missing from the link, the names differ (C vs C++ linkage, a different signature, __cdecl vs __stdcall on 32-bit), or, for Windows only, the function is in a DLL that does not export it. dumpbin /symbols foo.obj and undname play the role of nm -C.

docs.title: 2.4 MSBuild and CMake on Windows
docs.text:
MSBuild reads XML project files: a .sln lists .vcxproj projects; each .vcxproj lists sources and per-configuration settings (Debug|x64, Release|x64), usually inheriting from .props property sheets. From a Developer prompt:

msbuild tcpkv.sln -p:Configuration=Release -p:Platform=x64 -m -v:minimal
msbuild tcpkv.vcxproj -t:Rebuild -p:Configuration=Debug -p:Platform=x64

In Azure Pipelines, the VSBuild@1 or MSBuild@1 task runs the same command and VSTest@2 runs tests (module 09).

CMake on Windows has two families of generators:

:: Visual Studio generator: multi-config. Produces a .sln you can open; config chosen at build time.
cmake -S . -B build -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64
cmake --build build --config Release --parallel
ctest --test-dir build -C Release --output-on-failure

:: Ninja + MSVC: single-config, faster, the same commands as Linux. Run from a Developer prompt.
cmake -S . -B build/ninja -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
cmake --build build/ninja

Visual Studio's "Open Folder" reads CMakePresets.json directly, so the presets from module 04 work on Windows with a few extra entries:

{
  "name": "windows-msvc",
  "displayName": "MSVC x64 (Ninja)",
  "inherits": "base",
  "condition": { "type": "equals", "lhs": "${hostSystemName}", "rhs": "Windows" },
  "architecture": { "value": "x64", "strategy": "external" },
  "cacheVariables": {
    "CMAKE_C_COMPILER": "cl",
    "CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER": "cl",
    "CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE": "Debug",
    "CMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE": "$env{VCPKG_ROOT}/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake"
  }
}

Portable CMake for both compilers keeps compiler-specific flags behind generator expressions, as cmake/CompilerWarnings.cmake in tcpkv does:

target_compile_options(tcpkv_core PRIVATE
    $<$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:MSVC>:/W4 /WX /permissive- /Zc:__cplusplus /utf-8>
    $<$<NOT:$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:MSVC>>:-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror>)
set_property(TARGET tcpkv_core PROPERTY
    MSVC_RUNTIME_LIBRARY "MultiThreaded$<$<CONFIG:Debug>:Debug>DLL")   # /MD or /MDd

tcpkv itself uses POSIX sockets and would need a Winsock port to build on Windows: WSAStartup once, SOCKET (an unsigned handle, compare with INVALID_SOCKET not < 0), closesocket instead of close, WSAGetLastError() instead of errno, ioctlsocket(FIONBIO) instead of fcntl, no SIGPIPE (send returns WSAECONNRESET), and ws2_32.lib in the link. That is a good exercise (section 6).

docs.title: 2.5 vcpkg
docs.text:
vcpkg is Microsoft's source-based C and C++ package manager. It works on Windows, Linux and macOS, and integrates with CMake through a toolchain file.

Manifest mode (recommended): a vcpkg.json in the project root declares dependencies, and CMake installs them during configure into build/vcpkg_installed.

{
  "name": "tcpkv",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "dependencies": [ "gtest", "fmt", "libpq", "hiredis" ],
  "builtin-baseline": "<commit sha of the vcpkg registry, pins every port version>"
}

git clone https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg.git ~/vcpkg && ~/vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh   # .bat on Windows
export VCPKG_ROOT=~/vcpkg
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=$VCPKG_ROOT/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake

find_package(fmt CONFIG REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(tcpkv_core PRIVATE fmt::fmt)

Triplets name the target platform and linkage: x64-windows (DLLs, /MD), x64-windows-static (static libs, /MT), x64-windows-static-md (static libs, /MD), x64-linux (static by default). Choose with -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=.... Pick the triplet that matches your runtime library choice or you are back at LNK2038.

Binary caching stores built packages (locally under %LOCALAPPDATA%\vcpkg\archives or ~/.cache/vcpkg/archives, or in NuGet feeds / cloud storage) keyed by a hash of the port, its dependencies, the triplet and the compiler. In CI, caching that directory turns a 20-minute dependency build into seconds.

Classic mode (vcpkg install fmt:x64-windows into a global tree) is what older projects use; it cannot pin versions per project. Conan is the other major choice: binary packages, a Python recipe language, more flexible, more to learn. On Linux, apt install libfmt-dev is the third choice, fine for tools, poor for reproducible builds (versions follow the distro).

docs.title: 2.6 Visual Studio debugger: the features worth knowing
docs.text:
• Conditional breakpoints: right-click a breakpoint, Conditions: key == "acct42" or hit count >= 1000. GDB: break store.cpp:40 if ..., ignore.
  • Tracepoints (Actions: "Log a message", continue execution): Store::set key={key} tid=$TID. printf debugging without rebuilding. GDB: dprintf.
  • Data breakpoints (Debug > New Breakpoint > Data Breakpoint): break when 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes at an address change. Uses CPU debug registers, so at most four (x86-64). The tool for "who is corrupting this field". GDB: watch -l.
  • Threads, Parallel Stacks, Parallel Watch windows: all threads' stacks merged into a graph; freeze and thaw threads to force an interleaving. GDB: info threads, thread apply all bt, set scheduler-locking on.
  • Exception Settings (Ctrl+Alt+E): break on first-chance C++ exceptions or Win32 exceptions such as 0xC0000005 access violation, before any handler runs. GDB: catch throw, handle SIGSEGV stop.
  • Watch format specifiers: value,x (hex), ptr,10 (show a pointer as a 10-element array), str,s8 (UTF-8 string), var,! (raw, bypass visualizers). GDB: p/x, p *ptr@10.
  • Natvis files (.natvis) define how your types display in the debugger; GDB's equivalent is Python pretty-printers.
  • Symbols: Tools > Options > Debugging > Symbols. Add the Microsoft symbol server and your own symbol store. "Just My Code" hides library frames; turn it off when a crash is inside the CRT.
  • Diagnostic Tools: CPU usage, memory snapshots with diffing (heap growth between two points). Linux: perf, heaptrack, Massif (module 07).
  • Open a dump file: File > Open > a .dmp, then "Debug with Native Only". Set the symbol and source paths first. Linux: gdb ./tcpkv core.1234.
  • Attach to Process (Ctrl+Alt+P), including remote debugging with msvsmon.exe. Linux: gdb -p PID, gdbserver. Visual Studio can also debug Linux processes over SSH and WSL with its CMake support, which is worth knowing if you keep the IDE.

docs.title: 2.7 WinDbg (WinDbg Preview, now just "WinDbg")
docs.text:
The modern WinDbg from the Microsoft Store or winget install Microsoft.WinDbg has the same engine as classic WinDbg with a better UI, a data-model command dx, JavaScript extensions and Time Travel Debugging. The deep material, including dump analysis walkthroughs, is in 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/07_windbg_and_windows_crash_dumps.md. Command reference with GDB equivalents:

Task WinDbg GDB Use Microsoft public symbols .symfix then .reload debuginfod (set debuginfod enabled on) Add own symbols .sympath+ C:\build\pdb set debug-file-directory, symbol-file Automatic triage !analyze -v (none built in; bt + reading) Switch to the exception context .ecxr (core already stops at the signal) Show exception record .exr -1 p $_siginfo Current stack k, kb, kp (with params), kn (frame numbers) bt, bt full All threads' stacks ~*k thread apply all bt Switch thread ~3s thread 3 Select frame, locals .frame 2, dv frame 2, info locals Display a type dt tcpkv!Store 0x1234 ptype, p *(Store*)0x1234 Loaded modules lm, lmvm tcpkv info sharedlibrary Critical sections / locks !locks, !cs -l info threads + p mutex (__owner field) Heap state !heap -s, !heap -p -a ADDR (with page heap) ASan, Valgrind, malloc_info Memory map !address -summary info proc mappings, /proc/PID/maps CPU time per thread !runaway top -H -p PID Write a dump .dump /ma C:\dumps\x.dmp gcore PID / generate-core-file Record and replay Time Travel Debugging (TTD) rr record / rr replay, GDB record

Page heap (gflags /p /enable tcpkv.exe /full, or Application Verifier) puts every allocation at the end of a page followed by a guard page, so a heap overrun faults at the offending instruction instead of corrupting memory silently. It is the Windows ancestor of what ASan does with redzones.

docs.title: 2.8 ProcDump and Windows Error Reporting
docs.text:
ProcDump (Sysinternals) writes dumps of a running process when a condition triggers:

procdump -accepteula -ma -e tcpkv.exe C:\dumps            :: full dump on unhandled exception
procdump -ma -e 1 -f C0000005 tcpkv.exe C:\dumps          :: on first-chance access violation
procdump -ma -h tcpkv.exe C:\dumps                        :: hung window (GUI apps)
procdump -ma -c 90 -s 10 -n 3 tcpkv.exe C:\dumps          :: CPU >= 90 % for 10 s, 3 dumps
procdump -ma -m 2048 tcpkv.exe C:\dumps                   :: commit memory >= 2048 MB
procdump -ma -w tcpkv.exe C:\dumps                        :: wait for the process to start
procdump -ma -i C:\dumps                                  :: install as the system post-mortem debugger

For a service on a customer machine, the zero-install alternative is WER LocalDumps: registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps\tcpkv.exe with DumpFolder, DumpCount and DumpType = 2 (full). Every crash then leaves a .dmp.

Linux equivalents: ulimit -c unlimited plus /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern, or systemd-coredump with coredumpctl list / coredumpctl gdb; gcore PID for a dump of a live process. The "dump when CPU is high" trigger has no standard tool; a script with top -b and gcore does it, and perf record is usually the better answer for CPU problems anyway.

docs.title: 2.9 dumpbin and the rest of the inspection kit
docs.text:
dumpbin /dependents tcpkv.exe        :: DLLs it imports                     (ldd, readelf -d)
dumpbin /imports tcpkv.exe           :: every imported function            (nm -D --undefined-only)
dumpbin /exports tcpkv_core.dll      :: exported functions                 (nm -D --defined-only)
dumpbin /headers tcpkv.exe           :: PE headers, machine, subsystem, debug directory with PDB path (readelf -h -l)
dumpbin /symbols store.obj           :: COFF symbol table of an object     (nm store.o)
dumpbin /linkermember tcpkv_core.lib :: symbols indexed in a static library (nm -s libx.a)
dumpbin /disasm /section:.text x.obj :: disassembly                        (objdump -d)
dumpbin /pdbpath tcpkv.exe           :: which PDB the binary expects       (readelf -n: build-id)
undname ?add@@YAHHH@Z                :: int __cdecl add(int,int)           (c++filt _Z3addii)

Other tools and their Linux counterparts:

Windows Linux Use Dependencies (lucasg), Dependency Walker ldd, lddtree DLL / .so resolution Process Explorer htop, /proc, lsof processes, handles, loaded modules handle.exe, Resource Monitor lsof -p PID, ls -l /proc/PID/fd open files and sockets Process Monitor strace, inotifywait, fatrace file, registry, process activity TCPView, netstat -ano ss -tanp sockets per process ETW, WPR + WPA, PerfView perf, bpftrace, flame graphs CPU and system tracing Application Verifier, page heap ASan, Valgrind heap and handle misuse Event Viewer journalctl system and service logs Services (sc.exe, services.msc) systemctl service management Task Manager top, htop overview

docs.title: 2.10 The interview table
docs.text:
The one-page comparison to know cold:
