docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
No new files in code/; the examples are inline because they need a Windows machine. To try the Windows side of tcpkv's build:

  1. Install Visual Studio 2022 Community with the "Desktop development with C++" workload (it includes CMake, Ninja, vcpkg and the Windows SDK).
  2. Open a "Developer PowerShell for VS 2022" in a clone of your tcpkv repository on the Windows filesystem (not \\wsl$: builds over the 9P bridge are slow, the same reason module 01 gave for /mnt/c in the other direction).
  3. Build the protocol library and tests only (the server needs the Winsock port):
cmake -S . -B build/vs -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64
cmake --build build/vs --config Debug --target tcpkv_tests
ctest --test-dir build/vs -C Debug --output-on-failure
dumpbin /dependents build\vs\tests\Debug\tcpkv_tests.exe     # expect MSVCP140D.dll, VCRUNTIME140D.dll, ucrtbased.dll

The TCPKV_WERROR option in tcpkv's cmake/CompilerWarnings.cmake already maps to /WX for MSVC, and the warning set to /W4 /permissive-. MSVC and GCC do not flag exactly the same constructs, so expect some warnings GCC did not give (C4267 size_t to int, C4996 "unsafe" CRT functions, for example). Fixing them is exercise 2.

A minimal Winsock initialisation for the port, showing the differences in one place:

#ifdef _WIN32
#  define WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN
#  include <winsock2.h>
#  include <ws2tcpip.h>
#  pragma comment(lib, "ws2_32.lib")         // or target_link_libraries(... ws2_32)
using socket_t = SOCKET;                       // unsigned: never compare with < 0
constexpr socket_t kInvalidSocket = INVALID_SOCKET;
inline int last_socket_error() { return WSAGetLastError(); }
inline void close_socket(socket_t s) { closesocket(s); }
struct WinsockInit {                           // RAII: one per process, before any socket call
    WinsockInit() { WSADATA d; if (WSAStartup(MAKEWORD(2, 2), &d) != 0) std::abort(); }
    ~WinsockInit() { WSACleanup(); }
};
#else
#  include <sys/socket.h>
#  include <unistd.h>
#  include <cerrno>
using socket_t = int;
constexpr socket_t kInvalidSocket = -1;
inline int last_socket_error() { return errno; }
inline void close_socket(socket_t s) { ::close(s); }
struct WinsockInit {};                         // nothing to do on POSIX
#endif

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
PE vs ELF loading. A PE image has an import directory: for each DLL, a list of functions, and an Import Address Table (IAT) the loader fills with addresses at load time (all at once, unless delay-loaded). Calls go through call [IAT slot]. ELF uses the GOT (global offset table) for data and function addresses and the PLT (procedure linkage table) stubs for calls, traditionally resolved lazily on first call; -Wl,-z,now (full RELRO) resolves at load time like Windows. Both then make the table read-only. ELF symbol lookup is by name across all loaded objects in order (symbol interposition: LD_PRELOAD can replace malloc for the whole process). Windows lookup is two-level: each import names the DLL it comes from, so two DLLs can export the same name without conflict and there is no global interposition.

Default visibility and its consequences. Because ELF exports everything by default and resolves by global name, an .so built without -fvisibility=hidden has a huge dynamic symbol table, slower loading, and calls to its own exported functions go through the PLT (they could be interposed). Windows DLLs export only what is marked, so this problem does not arise; the cost is the dllexport/dllimport macro dance.

One heap or many. With /MT, each DLL and the EXE carry their own copy of the CRT, each with its own heap. Memory allocated by malloc in one module and freed by free in another goes to the wrong heap: corruption or a debug assertion. The same applies to FILE* and to std::string crossing DLL boundaries. The rules on Windows: free memory in the module that allocated it, or use /MD everywhere, or pass only C types across DLL boundaries. On Linux one libc.so.6 serves the whole process and the problem does not exist (unless you statically link libstdc++ into several .so files, which recreates a milder version of it).

PDB vs DWARF matching. The linker writes a CodeView debug directory entry (RSDS) into the PE containing the PDB's GUID, an age, and the PDB path. The debugger only loads a PDB whose GUID and age match exactly; that is why you must archive the PDB of every shipped build (a symbol store, symstore.exe add, served over HTTP). Linux's equivalent is the build-id note (readelf -n), a hash of the binary's contents; GDB finds separate debug files by build-id under /usr/lib/debug/.build-id/ or through a debuginfod server. CI archiving the unstripped binary per commit (module 09) is the low-tech version.

SEH vs signals. A Windows access violation is a structured exception: the kernel builds an exception record and context, and user-mode dispatch walks registered handlers (table-based on x64, from the .pdata section), which __try/__except and C++ catch(...) with /EHa can catch, first chance then second chance. A Linux SIGSEGV is a signal delivered to a handler with a ucontext_t; C++ exceptions are a separate mechanism (Itanium ABI unwinding with .eh_frame) and cannot catch it. Both end with a dump/core if unhandled. "Catching" access violations to keep a server running is a bad idea on both: the process state is unknown.

LLP64 vs LP64. Windows kept long at 32 bits on 64-bit platforms for source compatibility with Win32 structs; Linux made long 64-bit. Code that stores a pointer or a size_t in a long works on Linux and truncates on Windows; code that assumes long is 32-bit for a file format works on Windows and breaks on Linux. Use int64_t, uint32_t, size_t, intptr_t.

Calling conventions matter when reading crash dumps without full symbols: on Windows x64 the first four integer arguments are in RCX, RDX, R8, R9, and the caller reserves 32 bytes of shadow space; on Linux x86-64 (System V) the first six are in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9, and leaf functions may use a 128-byte red zone below RSP. Knowing this lets you recover a this pointer from a register in a release-build dump on either platform.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Your experience, framed. "Our core-banking application server is built with MSBuild in Azure Pipelines, crashes at customer sites arrive as WER or ProcDump dumps, and I analyse them in WinDbg with our symbol store." Then: "On Linux the same pipeline is CMake and Ninja in GitHub Actions, crashes are cores collected by systemd-coredump, and I analyse them in GDB with the archived unstripped binary or debuginfod." That pair of sentences answers half the Linux questions an interviewer will ask a Windows developer.
  • Missing redistributable. A build that runs on every developer machine fails on a clean server with "VCRUNTIME140.dll was not found". Developer machines have Visual Studio. Ship the VC++ redistributable with the installer, or use /MT for a self-contained exe. The Linux version is the "cannot open shared object file" from module 09's 3 AM story: same root cause, different runtime.
  • Symbols you did not keep. A customer sends a dump from build 4.2.17; nobody archived its PDB. Rebuilding the same source does not help: the new PDB has a different GUID. You are reduced to reading raw assembly and register values. Every release pipeline must publish PDBs (or unstripped ELF / .debug files) to a symbol store keyed by build, automatically.
  • Porting pitfalls in mixed teams. long size, wchar_t size, path separators and drive letters, case-insensitive file names (an #include "Store.hpp" that works on Windows fails on Linux), CRLF in shell scripts, SOCKET vs int, closesocket, missing SIGPIPE handling when code moves from Windows to Linux, localtime_s vs localtime_r, _stricmp vs strcasecmp. CI on both platforms catches them on the commit that introduces them.
  • ASan on MSVC is real and useful but narrower: no UBSan, TSan or LeakSanitizer in MSVC, and it requires matching runtime libraries. Teams with Windows-only code often keep a Linux or clang-cl CI job just to get the other sanitizers.
  • 3 AM: the Windows service hangs at a customer. Before restarting it, take procdump -ma tcpkv.exe (it does not kill the process), then restart. In WinDbg, ~*k shows 40 threads blocked in RtlEnterCriticalSection; !locks names the owning thread, whose stack is inside a logging call waiting on another lock held by thread 12: a lock-order inversion. On Linux the identical procedure is gcore PID (or gdb -batch -x scripts/dump_stacks.gdb -p PID), systemctl restart, then thread apply all bt and the mutex __owner field.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) On Windows, build any small C++ program in a Developer prompt with cl /std:c++17 /W4 /EHsc /Zi /O2 hello.cpp, then run dumpbin /headers, /dependents and /pdbpath on it. On WSL, do the same with g++ -O2 -g and readelf -h, ldd, readelf -n. Done when you have a two-column table of what each command told you.
  2. (medium) Build tcpkv's tcpkv_core and tcpkv_tests with the Visual Studio generator as in section 3, at /W4 /WX. Fix every warning in a way that also compiles cleanly with GCC -Werror. Done when both platforms build the tests with warnings as errors and all tests pass.
  3. (medium) Reproduce LNK2038: build a static library with /MT and an executable with /MD that links it. Then fix it by aligning CMAKE_MSVC_RUNTIME_LIBRARY. Done when you can explain why Linux has no equivalent error.
  4. (medium) Add a vcpkg.json with fmt to a copy of tcpkv, configure with the vcpkg toolchain file on both Windows and WSL, and use fmt::format in log_line. Done when both builds succeed from a clean checkout and you can name the triplet used on each.
  5. (hard) Port src/main.cpp to Windows using the socket_t shim from section 3: Winsock init, closesocket, WSAGetLastError, SetConsoleCtrlHandler for Ctrl-C instead of sigaction. Done when the same scripts/tcpkv_client.py --selftest (run from Windows Python) passes against the Windows build and the Linux build.
  6. (hard) Crash the Windows build deliberately (null dereference on a CRASH command), capture a dump with procdump -ma -e, open it in WinDbg, and run .symfix; .reload; !analyze -v; .ecxr; kp. Then do the equivalent on WSL with coredumpctl gdb. Done when you have both stack traces pointing at the same source line and can list each command's counterpart.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does linking against a DLL differ from linking against a shared object? On Windows you link against an import library (.lib) that tells the linker which DLL exports each symbol; at run time the loader fills the Import Address Table. Only explicitly exported symbols (__declspec(dllexport) or a .def file) are visible. On Linux you link against the .so itself, everything with default visibility is exported, calls go through PLT/GOT, and the loader searches rpath, LD_LIBRARY_PATH and the cache instead of the application directory.

Q: What does LNK2038 "mismatch detected for RuntimeLibrary" mean? Objects compiled with different C runtime options (/MT vs /MD, or Debug vs Release) are being linked into one module. Each choice selects a different CRT and STL build with different object layouts and heaps. Fix by using one runtime library for everything, in CMake with CMAKE_MSVC_RUNTIME_LIBRARY, and choosing the matching vcpkg triplet.

Q: What are /MD and /MT and which do you ship? /MD links the CRT and STL as DLLs shared by all modules (one heap, requires the VC++ redistributable on the target); /MT links them statically into each module (self-contained, but each DLL gets its own heap, so memory and CRT objects must not cross DLL boundaries). For a product with several DLLs, /MD plus a redistributable is the usual choice; for a single tool exe, /MT.

Q: How do you get a crash dump from a production Windows service, and the Linux equivalent? Configure WER LocalDumps in the registry for the exe, or run ProcDump with -ma -e; for a hang, take procdump -ma on demand. Analyse in WinDbg with the archived PDB: !analyze -v, .ecxr, kp, ~*k. On Linux: ulimit -c/LimitCORE plus systemd-coredump or core_pattern, gcore for live processes, and GDB with the unstripped binary or debuginfod.

Q: Why might code that works on Windows break on Linux (or the reverse) even with the same compiler family? Data model (long is 32-bit on Windows, 64-bit on Linux), wchar_t size, file-name case sensitivity, path separators, line endings, default symbol visibility, SIGPIPE on socket writes, different socket handle types and error retrieval, and APIs with _s/_r variants. Fixed-width integer types, CI on both platforms and portable wrappers catch these.

Q: What is vcpkg manifest mode and what is a triplet? Manifest mode declares a project's dependencies in vcpkg.json and pins versions with a builtin-baseline; CMake's vcpkg toolchain file installs them per project at configure time. A triplet names the target architecture, OS and linkage (x64-windows, x64-windows-static, x64-linux), and must match the runtime-library choice of the project.

Q: Compare WinDbg and GDB for a hang. Both attach to a live process or open a dump. WinDbg: ~*k for all stacks, !locks to find critical-section owners, !runaway for CPU per thread. GDB: thread apply all bt, the mutex's __owner field for the owning thread's LWP, top -H for CPU per thread. The diagnosis is identical: find who holds the lock everyone waits for and what it is waiting for.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• MSVC = cl + link + lib + MSBuild; Linux = g++ + ld + ar + Make/Ninja; CMake drives both.
  • /W4 /WX /permissive- /EHsc /std:c++17 is the MSVC mirror of -Wall -Wextra -Werror -std=c++17.
  • /MD vs /MT must match across a module; LNK2038 is the symptom; Linux has one runtime per process.
  • DLLs export nothing by default and link through import libraries; .so exports everything and links directly.
  • LNK2019/LNK2001 = undefined reference; LNK2005 = multiple definition; dumpbin/undname = nm/c++filt.
  • vcpkg manifest mode + toolchain file + matching triplet; cache binaries in CI.
  • VS debugger: conditional breakpoints, tracepoints, data breakpoints, Parallel Stacks, exception settings.
  • WinDbg: .symfix; .reload; !analyze -v; .ecxr; kp; ~*k; !locks; ProcDump -ma -e; WER LocalDumps.
  • PDB matched by GUID + age, ELF debug info by build-id: archive symbols for every shipped build.
  • LLP64 vs LP64, wchar_t 2 vs 4 bytes, SEH vs signals, IOCP vs epoll: the differences interviewers probe.

docs.title: 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps: all exercises
docs.text:
Every exercise from the twelve modules in one place. The full wording, including the exact "done when" condition, is in section 6 of each module; this file adds a hint for each one. Do the easy ones as you read the module, the medium ones the same week, and pick at least two hard ones per module. The hard ones are what you show in interviews.

Difficulty: E easy (under 30 minutes), M medium (1 to 2 hours), H hard (half a day or more).

Suggested minimum path if time is short: 01.3, 02.4, 02.6, 03.4, 04.3, 04.6, 05.4, 05.6, 06.4, 06.5, 07.1, 07.5, 08.2, 08.5, 09.1, 09.4, 10.4, 11.5, 11.6, 12.6.

docs.title: 01. Linux for a Windows developer
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 1.1 E Time ls -R on /usr/include vs /mnt/c/Windows/System32; explain the ratio. Prefix with time; run each twice so caches are warm. /mnt/c goes through the 9P file-sharing protocol to Windows, every stat is a round trip. 1.2 E One pipeline printing the five largest files under /usr/lib, human-readable. find /usr/lib -type f -exec du -h {} + \| sort -rh \| head -5. Explain why -exec ... + beats \;. 1.3 M sleep 1000 &; inspect /proc/PID/status, fd, maps; SIGTERM it; explain exit 143. pgrep -n sleep; ls -l /proc/PID/fd; after kill PID, wait %1; echo $?. 143 = 128 + 15. 1.4 M Usernames with /bin/bash shell from /etc/passwd, with awk+sort and with grep+cut. awk -F: '$7=="/bin/bash"{print $1}'; grep ':/bin/bash$' \| cut -d: -f1. Diff the two outputs with diff <(...) <(...). 1.5 H p50/p95/p99 from a file of <timestamp> <latency_ms> lines. Generate data with awk 'BEGIN{srand(); for(i=0;i<10000;i++) print i, int(rand()*100)}'. Sort numerically on field 2, load into an awk array, index at int(p*NR) (clamp to at least 1). 1.6 H SSH key, GitHub, clone over SSH into ~/projects, core.autocrlf input. ssh-keygen -t ed25519, paste ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub into GitHub settings; ssh -T git@github.com. Clone into the Linux filesystem, not /mnt/c.

docs.title: 02. How a C++ program is built
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 2.1 E g++ -E line counts for <iostream> vs <cstdio>. g++ -std=c++17 -E hello.cpp \| wc -l. The difference is every header <iostream> pulls in transitively: templates, locales, strings. 2.2 E Build m02_static_lib, find the U that becomes T with nm -C. Run build.sh; compare nm -C main.o \| grep add and nm -C prog_static \| grep add. 2.3 M Make prog_norpath run three ways; rank them for production. LD_LIBRARY_PATH=.; sudo cp libmathlib.so /usr/local/lib && sudo ldconfig; relink with -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN' (single quotes so the shell does not eat $ORIGIN). 2.4 M Reproduce the three undefined-reference cases in m02_undefined_ref; diagnose each from nm -C. Missing object: symbol absent everywhere. C vs C++ linkage: nm shows add in one file and add(int, int) in the other (use nm without -C to see _Z3addii). Signature mismatch: two different mangled names. 2.5 H libplugin.so with one exported extern "C" function, loaded via dlopen/dlsym; -fvisibility=hidden. Mark the function __attribute__((visibility("default"))); link the host with -ldl (not needed on glibc 2.34+, harmless). nm -D --defined-only libplugin.so. 2.6 H silent_odr links and misbehaves; -flto -Wodr reports it; fix it. The linker only sees symbol names, not class layouts, so two different struct Config definitions with the same name both "link". The fix is one shared header.

docs.title: 03. GCC and Clang flags that matter
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 3.1 E -S at -O0 vs -O2, diff the assembly for sum_to. Add -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables -masm=intel for readable output; look for a loop that disappeared (closed-form or vectorised). 3.2 E Hello world with and without -g: ls -l, size, readelf -S. size counts only loadable sections (text, data, bss); .debug_* sections are in the file but never loaded. 3.3 M Compile your own C with -Wshadow -Wconversion etc., count warnings per category, fix shadows. 2>&1 \| grep -o '\[-W[a-z-]*\]' \| sort \| uniq -c \| sort -rn. Rename the inner variable; do not silence with casts. 3.4 M m03_asan_demo.cpp with and without ASan; find the allocation site. Without ASan the overrun lands in malloc padding or another chunk, so nothing visible happens. ASan's report has three stacks: the bad access, the allocation, and (for use-after-free) the free. 3.5 H Signed overflow in a loop condition: terminates at -O0, infinite at -O2; then UBSan. for (int i = 1; i > 0; i *= 2) or i += big. The optimiser assumes signed overflow never happens, so i > 0 is "always true". timeout 2 ./prog; echo $? gives 124. 3.6 H -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc, then fully -static; run in a FROM scratch image. Dockerfile: FROM scratch, COPY hello /hello, ENTRYPOINT ["/hello"]. ldd on the fully static binary says "not a dynamic executable".

docs.title: 04. Make and CMake from scratch
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 4.1 E code/Makefile: header edit rebuilds both objects; show the .d file. The -MMD -MP flags write build/foo.d; -include $(DEPS) pulls them in. cat one. 4.2 E ninja -C build/debug -t commands tcpkv; map -I, -pthread, -std=c++17 to CMake lines. target_include_directories(... PUBLIC ...), Threads::Threads, CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD + CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF. 4.3 M Flip Threads::Threads and the include dir from PUBLIC to PRIVATE; explain what breaks. glibc 2.34 moved pthread into libc, so the link may still succeed; the include change breaks main.cpp at compile time. Rule: PUBLIC if it appears in your headers, PRIVATE if only in your .cpp. 4.4 M A clang preset; fix what Clang warns about. The preset exists in the shipped CMakePresets.json; build it with cmake --preset clang && cmake --build --preset clang. Clang often adds -Wshorten-64-to-32-style findings. 4.5 H Second library tcpkv_net depending on tcpkv_core; tcpkv depends on tcpkv_net. target_link_libraries(tcpkv_net PUBLIC tcpkv::core); tcpkv links only tcpkv_net; check ninja -t commands tcpkv \| grep -o '\-I[^ ]*' \| sort \| uniq -c. 4.6 H install(EXPORT), install to /tmp/tcpkv-install, consume with find_package(tcpkv CONFIG). You need a tcpkvConfig.cmake that include()s the exported targets file; configure_package_config_file + write_basic_package_version_file from CMakePackageConfigHelpers.

docs.title: 05. Testing with GoogleTest and ctest
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 5.1 E SET with : and - in the key passes; a tab in the key fails. Add to the parameterised MalformedLines table for the tab case; check ctest -N \| grep -i tab. 5.2 E --gtest_shuffle --gtest_repeat=50; a shared static makes order matter. Put static int counter in the test file, increment in test A, assert in test B. Shuffle exposes it within a few repeats; --gtest_random_seed=N reproduces. 5.3 M Store::require_key aborts on empty key; EXPECT_DEATH. Death tests fork; name the suite *DeathTest so they run first. Matcher is a regex on stderr. 5.4 M Remove the lock in Store::get; read the TSan report. cmake --preset tsan && cmake --build --preset tsan && ctest --preset tsan -R Concurrency. The report shows "Write of size ... by thread T2" and "Previous read ... by thread T1" with both stacks. 5.5 H Extract a LineReader with tests for split lines, CRLF and overflow. Keep the buffer and a start offset; feed appends, scans for \n, returns complete lines, erases the consumed prefix. Test overflow at exactly kMaxLineLength and one byte more. 5.6 H ctest integration test with FIXTURES_SETUP/FIXTURES_CLEANUP and the Python client. Setup test: a script that starts tcpkv on 7123 in the background and writes its PID to a file; cleanup test: kill $(cat pidfile); main test: tcpkv_client.py --selftest --port 7123 --wait 5. Label all three integration.

docs.title: 06. Git properly
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 6.1 E git cat-file -p from commit to tree to blob. git cat-file -p HEAD, copy the tree hash, git cat-file -p <tree>, copy a blob hash. git cat-file -t prints the type. 6.2 E Stage half a file's hunks with git add -p; two commits on one file. In add -p, s splits a hunk, e edits it by hand. 6.3 M --fixup plus rebase -i --autosquash non-interactively. git commit --fixup=<sha-of-first>; GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash <base>. 6.4 M Conflict with zdiff3, resolve, then undo the whole rebase via reflog. git config merge.conflictstyle zdiff3. The middle region is the common ancestor. Undo: git reflog, find the entry before rebase (start), git reset --hard HEAD@{n}. 6.5 H scripts/bisect_test.sh + git bisect run on a planted bug. The finished script is in code/tcpkv/scripts/bisect_test.sh; copy it outside the repo first so old commits can run it. Plant the bug with git commit in a loop of trivial changes before and after. 6.6 H tcpkv GitHub repo with LICENSE, .gitattributes, branch protection, v0.1.0 tag, pinned. git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "..." && git push origin v0.1.0. Required checks only appear in the protection settings after the workflow has run once.

docs.title: 07. Debugging and profiling tools on Linux
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 7.1 E strace -f -tt -T -e trace=network on tcpkv with an nc session. Expect socket, setsockopt, bind, listen, accept4, recvfrom, sendto. recvfrom(...) = 0 is the client's FIN: orderly shutdown. 7.2 E ltrace -c on the Store tests; count malloc calls. ltrace only sees calls through the PLT, so static or inlined calls are invisible; filter with -e malloc+free. 7.3 M Flame graph of tcpkv under load_test.sh. Add -fno-omit-frame-pointer to the release preset; perf record -g -p $(pgrep -n tcpkv) -- sleep 15 while scripts/load_test.sh 7000 8 20000 runs; Brendan Gregg's FlameGraph scripts render the SVG. 7.4 M callgrind on ParseCommand.*; allocation share of the parser. valgrind --tool=callgrind ./build/debug/tests/tcpkv_tests --gtest_filter='ParseCommand.*'; callgrind_annotate --inclusive=yes callgrind.out.*; compare parse_command inclusive with operator new under it. 7.5 H Lock-order deadlock: gdb thread apply all bt, /proc/PID/task/*/wchan, TSan report. gdb -batch -x scripts/dump_stacks.gdb -p PID dumps all stacks non-interactively. In each blocked thread, p mutex shows __owner = the LWP holding it. 7.6 H tcpdump -w a tcpkv session, read in Wireshark and with tcpdump -A. sudo tcpdump -i lo -w kv.pcap port 7000; copy to /mnt/c/... for Windows Wireshark; tcpdump -r kv.pcap -A for the text view. Flags: [S], [S.], [P.], [F.].

docs.title: 08. Docker for C++
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 8.1 E docker build and docker history; name the three largest layers. docker history --no-trunc --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' tcpkv:dev. The apt layers dominate. 8.2 E docker stop shows exit 0; without sigaction, exit 137 after 10 s. docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' tcpkv. With tini as PID 1, tini forwards SIGTERM and the unhandled default action kills tcpkv at once (143). You see 137 after 10 s when tcpkv itself is PID 1 (--entrypoint /usr/local/bin/tcpkv): the kernel does not apply default "terminate" actions to a namespace's PID 1, so Docker times out and sends SIGKILL. Try both. 8.3 M Runtime stage on debian:12-slim and distroless; strace via a sidecar. docker run --rm -it --pid=container:tcpkv --cap-add SYS_PTRACE ubuntu:24.04 then apt install strace; strace -p 1. 8.4 M HEALTHCHECK goes (healthy), then (unhealthy) after docker kill -s STOP. The shipped Dockerfile already has the healthcheck; docker ps shows the state; docker inspect -f '{{json .State.Health}}' shows the probe log. 8.5 H Compose stack; psql and redis-cli from the host; OOM-kill tcpkv with large values. psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U tcpkv; set the compose memory limit to 64M; scripts/load_test.sh 7000 4 50000 65000; docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' tcpkv. 8.6 H Fully static tcpkv in a FROM scratch image. -static with glibc warns about getaddrinfo (it needs NSS modules at run time); tcpkv only binds to an IP, so it works. Remove the nc-based healthcheck: scratch has no shell.

docs.title: 09. CI/CD with GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 9.1 E Push tcpkv with the workflow; all green; badge renders. The workflow is code/tcpkv/.github/workflows/ci.yml; the badge URL needs your user name and the workflow file name. 9.2 E A PR with an unused variable is blocked by -Werror. gh pr create, then gh run view --log-failed and search for -Werror=unused-variable. 9.3 M format and tidy jobs with .clang-format and .clang-tidy. clang-format --dry-run --Werror $(git ls-files '*.cpp' '*.hpp'); clang-tidy -p build/ci src/*.cpp. Configure first so compile_commands.json exists. 9.4 M Smoke-test the built image in the docker job. Build with load: true in build-push-action, then docker run -d -p 7000:7000, loop on printf 'PING\n' \| nc -N localhost 7000 \| grep -q PONG with a timeout, docker rm -f. 9.5 H Nightly workflow (full Valgrind, -O3 -flto) and a tag-triggered release with two assets. on: schedule: - cron: '0 3 * * *'; release job if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v'); gh release create "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" tcpkv tcpkv.debug.tar.gz; docker/metadata-action generates semver tags. 9.6 H Port the workflow to Azure DevOps; JUnit results visible in the UI. The file is code/tcpkv/azure-pipelines.yml; a free Azure DevOps organisation includes Microsoft-hosted minutes for public projects (check current limits). Gate the Docker stage on a variable if you have no registry.

docs.title: 10. Scripting: bash and a little Python
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 10.1 E Run m10_bash_patterns.sh with -v; ShellCheck it and one of your own scripts. sudo apt install shellcheck. The PS4 variable defines the -x prefix: file, line, function. 10.2 E A CRLF script fails with bash\r; fix with dos2unix; prevent with .gitattributes. file hello.sh reports "with CRLF line terminators"; cat -A shows ^M$. Rule: *.sh text eol=lf. 10.3 M Demonstrate each set -e hole (if, local x=$(false), ((x++)), function under \|\|). Put an echo "still running" after each; the ones that print are holes. Fix: separate declaration from assignment, x=$((x+1)), explicit checks inside functions. 10.4 M Ctrl-C during run_tests.sh leaves no server behind. The INT trap calls exit 130, which runs the EXIT trap (stop_server) once. Check with pgrep -a tcpkv. 10.5 M tcpkv_client.py --mix ... --threads 8 --seconds 10 closed-loop benchmark. One TcpkvClient per thread; random.choices with weights for the op type; per-op latency lists merged at the end. It is slower than load_test.sh because every request waits for its reply (no pipelining) and Python adds overhead per call. 10.6 H ctest integration fixture using the Python client. Same as 5.6. Write a small scripts/start_server.sh and register it with add_test(NAME start_server COMMAND ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/scripts/start_server.sh $<TARGET_FILE:tcpkv> 7123) so ctest passes the real binary path via a generator expression.

docs.title: 11. Linux systems programming essentials
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 11.1 E Each m11_syscalls demo under strace -f; name the syscalls behind open, fork, waitpid. openat, clone (or clone3), wait4. clock_gettime runs in the vDSO without entering the kernel. 11.2 E ulimit -n 64, start tcpkv, open 100 connections; see EMFILE. Python: socks = [socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 7000)) for _ in range(100)] in a try block. cat /proc/$(pgrep -n tcpkv)/limits. 11.3 M Measure the cost of fsync; write the atomic-replace version. hyperfine './w_nosync' './w_sync'. Directory fsync: int d = open(".", O_RDONLY \| O_DIRECTORY); fsync(d);. WSL's virtual disk makes absolute numbers unrepresentative; compare ratios. 11.4 M mini_shell.c with one pipe and one > redirect. Fork twice for a pipeline; in each child dup2 the right pipe end then close both ends; the parent closes both ends and waits for both children. Forgetting a close makes wc wait forever. 11.5 M tcpkv as a systemd service; crash it; exceed StartLimitBurst. sudo kill -SEGV $(systemctl show -p MainPID --value tcpkv). After the burst: systemctl status says start-limit-hit; sudo systemctl reset-failed tcpkv clears it. 11.6 H epoll-based tcpkv server in one thread with output buffers and signalfd. Start from m11_epoll_preview.c (rename to .cpp, or link a C file with the C++ core through a small extern "C" layer). Per connection: std::string in, out; enable EPOLLOUT only while out is non-empty. See 08_Networking_Distributed/06_nonblocking_io_epoll_event_loops.md.

docs.title: 12. Windows toolchain reference
docs.text: # Lvl Exercise Hint 12.1 E cl build plus dumpbin /headers /dependents /pdbpath; the same with g++, readelf, ldd. Use the "Developer PowerShell for VS 2022" so cl and dumpbin are on PATH. 12.2 M tcpkv core and tests under MSVC /W4 /WX; fix warnings portably. Configure with -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 and build only tcpkv_tests. Prefer static_cast and correct types (std::size_t) over #pragma warning(disable). 12.3 M Reproduce and fix LNK2038 (/MT library, /MD exe). set_property(TARGET lib PROPERTY MSVC_RUNTIME_LIBRARY MultiThreaded) on one target only reproduces it; set CMAKE_MSVC_RUNTIME_LIBRARY once at the top to fix it. 12.4 M vcpkg.json with fmt, built on Windows and WSL. Pass -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=$VCPKG_ROOT/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake before the first configure (it cannot be added to an existing cache). Triplets: x64-windows and x64-linux. 12.5 H Port main.cpp to Winsock with the socket_t shim; same Python self-test passes on both. Replace poll with WSAPoll, accept4 with accept, MSG_NOSIGNAL with 0, localtime_r with localtime_s (argument order differs). SetConsoleCtrlHandler runs on its own thread: set an std::atomic<bool>. 12.6 H Crash dump on both platforms: ProcDump + WinDbg, coredumpctl + GDB. WinDbg: .symfix; .sympath+ <dir with your pdb>; .reload; !analyze -v; .ecxr; kp. Linux: coredumpctl list, coredumpctl gdb tcpkv, bt full.

docs.title: 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps: interview questions and model answers
docs.text: 38 questions, ordered from screening level to senior level. Answer out loud, then compare. A good answer is 2 to 6 sentences, uses the precise term, and ends with a practical consequence. Where a module covers the topic in depth, it is named in brackets.

docs.title: Part 1. Building C and C++ on Linux
docs.text:
1. What are the stages of building a C++ program, and what does each produce? [02] Preprocessing (cpp, part of g++ -E) expands #include and macros into a translation unit. Compilation (cc1plus) turns it into assembly; assembly (as) turns that into a relocatable object file (.o, ELF) with a symbol table and relocations. Linking (ld, driven by g++) combines objects and libraries, resolves every undefined symbol to a definition, applies relocations and writes an executable or shared library. -E, -S and -c stop after each of the first three stages.

2. What does the linker actually do? [02] It reads the symbol tables of all inputs, matches every undefined reference (U in nm) with exactly one definition, lays out the sections into segments, assigns final addresses, and patches each relocation with the resolved address. For static libraries it pulls in only the archive members that resolve a currently undefined symbol, scanning left to right, which is why library order on the command line matters with GNU ld. For shared libraries it records a NEEDED entry and leaves the final binding to the dynamic loader at run time.

3. Static library vs shared library: differences and trade-offs? [02] A static library (.a) is an archive of object files; the needed members are copied into the executable at link time, so the binary is self-contained and has no run-time lookup cost, but every binary carries its own copy and a security fix requires relinking everything. A shared library (.so) is loaded once by ld.so and mapped into every process that uses it: smaller binaries, shared memory pages, updates without relinking, at the cost of run-time resolution, version compatibility (ABI, sonames) and "cannot open shared object file" failures in deployment.

4. You get "undefined reference to foo". What are the possible causes? [02] Three families: the definition is not in the link at all (a missing .cpp, a missing -lfoo, or a library listed before the object that needs it); the names do not match (C vs C++ linkage, a missing extern "C", a different signature or namespace, so the mangled names differ); or the symbol exists but is not visible (hidden visibility, a template never instantiated, an inline or static function defined only in another file). nm -C on the objects and libraries tells you which: absent, present under another mangled name, or present but local (t instead of T).

5. What is the One Definition Rule, and why can violations go undetected? [02] The ODR says every non-inline function and variable has exactly one definition in the program, and every class, inline function or template defined in several translation units must be defined identically (token for token, with the same meaning). Duplicate strong symbols give "multiple definition" link errors, but differing class definitions with the same name (two struct Config in two .cpp files, or a header compiled with different macros) produce no error, because the linker only sees symbol names, not layouts. The program then reads the wrong offsets at run time; -flto -Wodr and ASan's ODR checks can catch some cases.

6. What is -fPIC and why do shared libraries need it? [02] Position-independent code addresses its global data and external functions through the GOT and PLT (and PC-relative addressing) instead of absolute addresses, so the same code pages work wherever the loader maps the library and can be shared between processes. Without it, the loader would have to patch text relocations in the code itself, which makes the pages private per process and is refused on x86-64 for most relocation types. Executables are PIE (position-independent) by default on Ubuntu for ASLR.

7. How does the dynamic loader find a shared library at run time? [02] ld.so reads the executable's NEEDED entries and searches, in order: DT_RPATH (if no RUNPATH), LD_LIBRARY_PATH, DT_RUNPATH, the /etc/ld.so.cache built by ldconfig, then the default directories /lib and /usr/lib (and their multiarch subdirectories). ldd shows the result and LD_DEBUG=libs traces the search. In production, prefer installing to a standard path with ldconfig or an $ORIGIN-relative rpath over LD_LIBRARY_PATH.

8. What do -O0, -O1, -O2, -O3, -Os and -Og mean? Which do you ship? [03] -O0 does no optimisation (fast compile, debuggable, slow); -O1 basic optimisations; -O2 nearly all optimisations that do not trade size for speed, the usual release level; -O3 adds aggressive inlining, loop transformations and more vectorisation, which may or may not be faster; -Os optimises for size; -Og optimises without hurting debugging. Ship -O2 -g (CMake's RelWithDebInfo) with symbols archived, and adopt -O3 or LTO only when a benchmark shows a gain.

9. Why build with -g in release builds? [03, 07] Debug info does not change the generated code; it only adds .debug_* sections that are never loaded at run time. Shipping a stripped binary and archiving the unstripped one (or a split .debug file matched by build-id) lets you symbolise production cores and perf profiles with exact file and line numbers. Without it, a release-build crash gives you raw addresses.

10. What are sanitizers, and which ones would you run in CI? [03, 05] Compiler instrumentation that detects bugs at run time: AddressSanitizer (out-of-bounds, use-after-free, double free, leaks via LeakSanitizer; about 2x slowdown, typical), UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (signed overflow, invalid shifts, misaligned access, null dereference), ThreadSanitizer (data races, lock-order inversions; 5 to 15x slowdown, typical) and MemorySanitizer (uninitialised reads, Clang only). ASan and TSan cannot be combined, so CI runs an ASan+UBSan job and a separate TSan job over the whole test suite, with halt_on_error so findings fail the build.

11. What does -Wall -Wextra -Werror give you, and what is the risk of -Werror? [03] -Wall and -Wextra enable the warnings that usually indicate bugs (unused variables, sign comparisons, missing returns, implicit fallthrough); -Werror makes the build fail on any of them, so warnings cannot accumulate. The risk is that a new compiler version adds warnings and breaks the build for packagers and users; the standard answer is -Werror on in CI and for developers, and an option to turn it off (tcpkv's TCPKV_WERROR, the no-werror preset).

docs.title: Part 2. CMake and testing
docs.text:
12. What do PUBLIC, PRIVATE and INTERFACE mean in target_link_libraries and friends? [04] They define which usage requirements (include directories, compile definitions, options, linked libraries) apply to the target itself and which propagate to targets that link to it. PRIVATE: used to build this target only. INTERFACE: not used for this target, only for consumers (header-only libraries). PUBLIC: both. The rule: if a dependency appears in your public headers it is PUBLIC; if only in your .cpp files it is PRIVATE. Wrong visibility either leaks dependencies to every consumer or breaks their compilation with missing headers.

13. Why "modern CMake" with targets instead of setting global variables like CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS and include_directories? [04] Global settings apply to every target in the directory and below, cannot express which consumer needs what, and do not travel with an installed package. Target-based commands attach requirements to the target and propagate them through the dependency graph, so target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE tcpkv::core) brings the right include paths, definitions, C++ standard and -pthread automatically, both in the build tree and through find_package after installation.

14. What are CMake presets and why use them? [04, 09] CMakePresets.json names complete configurations (generator, build directory, build type, cache variables such as sanitizers) and matching build and test presets, checked into the repository. cmake --preset asan && cmake --build --preset asan && ctest --preset asan is then the same command for every developer, every IDE and CI. Personal tweaks go in the gitignored CMakeUserPresets.json.

15. How do you structure tests for a networked server so most of them are fast and deterministic? [05] Keep the logic in pure, I/O-free units (the protocol parser, the store) and test them with GoogleTest directly: fixtures for setup, parameterised tests for input tables, death tests for aborts, gMock for dependencies behind interfaces. Run them under sanitizers. Keep a smaller set of integration tests that start the real binary on a free port and drive it through a client, labelled separately (ctest -L integration) so the unit suite stays under a few seconds.

docs.title: Part 3. Git
docs.text:
16. Merge vs rebase: what is the difference and when do you use each? [06] Merge creates a new commit with two parents that joins the histories, preserving exactly what happened. Rebase replays your commits one by one on top of another base, creating new commits with new hashes and a linear history. Rebase your own unpublished feature branch onto main to keep it current and clean; never rebase commits others have based work on; integrate into main by merge or squash-merge according to the team's convention.

17. You ran git reset --hard and lost commits. How do you get them back? [06] git reflog lists every position HEAD (and each branch) has had, including commits no branch points to any more. Find the entry before the reset, then git reset --hard HEAD@{n} or git branch rescue <sha>. Unreachable commits survive until garbage collection prunes them (reflog entries expire after 90 days by default, 30 for unreachable ones), so recovery is almost always possible for recent mistakes.

18. How does git bisect work, and how do you automate it? [06] It binary-searches the history between a known good and a known bad commit: Git checks out the midpoint, you mark it good or bad, and it halves the range, finding the first bad commit in about log2(N) steps. git bisect run ./script.sh automates it: exit 0 means good, 1 to 124 or 126 to 127 bad, 125 skip (does not build). The script should build in a separate directory and use timeout so a hang counts as bad.

19. What is a Git commit, physically? [06] An object in .git/objects addressed by the hash of its content: it records a tree (a snapshot of the directory, itself made of trees and blobs), zero or more parent commit hashes, author, committer and message. Branches and tags are just references to commit hashes. Because the hash covers the parents, changing any old commit changes every hash after it, which is why rebasing rewrites history.

docs.title: Part 4. Debugging, profiling and scripting
docs.text:
20. What do strace and perf each tell you, and when do you reach for which? [07] strace intercepts system calls with ptrace, showing every syscall, its arguments, result and (with -T) time spent: the tool for "what is it doing with files, sockets and processes" and "why does it fail with EACCES or hang in futex". It slows the target heavily. perf samples the CPU (stack traces at a frequency) with low overhead and shows where CPU time goes, per function, as a report or flame graph. Hang or error: strace first. Slow while busy: perf. Slow while idle (waiting): strace -c, off-CPU analysis, or gdb stacks.

21. A process is at 100 % CPU in production. What do you do? [07] Find the thread: top -H -p PID (or ps -L). Sample it: perf top -p PID or perf record -g -p PID -- sleep 30 then perf report, which names the hot functions. If it is a spin or an infinite loop, gdb -p PID (or a batch stack dump) on that thread shows where. Capture evidence before restarting, compare with a known-good build, and reproduce under the same load with a profiler attached.

22. What does set -euo pipefail do in a bash script? [10] -e exits on the first failing command, -u makes expanding an unset variable an error, and -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails instead of only the last. Together they turn silent failures into immediate exits, for example ctest | tee log passing after failed tests, or rm -r "$DIR/" running with an empty variable. It has holes (commands in if, ||, &&, local x=$(cmd)), so critical steps still need explicit checks, and a trap cleanup EXIT handles cleanup.

docs.title: Part 5. Linux systems programming
docs.text:
23. What is the difference between a system call and a library call? [11] A system call switches the CPU to kernel mode to request a service only the kernel can provide (I/O, memory mapping, process creation); a library call runs in user space and may make zero or several syscalls. printf buffers and calls write occasionally; malloc serves most requests from its arenas and calls brk or mmap only to grow. Failures are reported through a return value plus errno, which must be read immediately after the failing call.

24. What happens when you send SIGTERM to a process, and how should a server handle it? [11, 08] The kernel marks the signal pending; on the next return to user mode it runs the installed handler or applies the default action (terminate). A server should install a handler with sigaction that only sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag (or writes to a self-pipe, or use signalfd), let the main loop notice it, stop accepting, drain in-flight requests within a bounded time and exit 0. systemd and Docker send SIGTERM and follow with SIGKILL after a timeout (TimeoutStopSec, 10 s for docker stop), so the drain must finish within that window.

25. Why can you not call printf or malloc in a signal handler? [11] The handler can interrupt the program in the middle of any function, including malloc or printf while they hold internal locks or have data structures half-updated. Calling them again from the handler can deadlock on the same lock or corrupt the heap. Only async-signal-safe functions listed in signal-safety(7) (such as write, _exit, sigaction) are allowed, and the handler must save and restore errno.

26. Explain fork and exec and the danger of fork in a multithreaded program. [11] fork creates a child that is a copy of the parent with copy-on-write memory and duplicated file descriptors; exec replaces the process image with a new program. The split lets the child set up redirections and privileges before exec. In a multithreaded parent, only the forking thread exists in the child, and locks held by other threads at that moment stay locked forever, so the child may deadlock in malloc or a logger; between fork and exec it must call only async-signal-safe functions, or the program should use posix_spawn.

27. Does write() guarantee the data is on disk? How do you make a write durable? [11] No. write returns once the data is in the kernel's page cache; writeback happens later. Durability requires fsync (or fdatasync) on the file, plus fsync on the directory after creating or renaming a file. For atomic replacement: write a temp file, fsync it, rename over the target, fsync the directory. Treat an fsync failure as fatal for that data: after a writeback error the kernel may have discarded the dirty pages, so retrying can report success falsely.

28. Why is epoll more scalable than select/poll for many connections? [11] select and poll pass the full list of fds on every call and the kernel scans all of them, so each wait costs O(n). epoll registers interest once in a kernel object; readiness callbacks put fds on a ready list, and epoll_wait returns only those, so the cost is proportional to activity. It needs non-blocking fds; level-triggered mode re-reports while data remains, edge-triggered mode reports transitions and requires reading until EAGAIN.

29. A service keeps disappearing with exit code 137 and nothing in its logs. What is happening? [08, 11] 137 is 128 + 9: SIGKILL, which cannot be caught, so the program never logs. The usual sender is the OOM killer, system-wide or because the service's cgroup hit its memory limit (MemoryMax=, Docker --memory), or a stop timeout escalating from SIGTERM. Confirm with journalctl -k | grep -i oom, docker inspect (OOMKilled: true) or systemctl status; then find the memory growth with a heap profiler instead of raising the limit.

30. How do you run a C++ server as a production service on Linux with systemd? [11] Write a unit with ExecStart running the binary in the foreground (Type=exec or notify), a dedicated unprivileged User=, Restart=on-failure with RestartSec and a start-limit burst, TimeoutStopSec matched to the graceful drain, LimitNOFILE sized for connections, MemoryMax for a cgroup cap, and sandboxing (NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=strict, PrivateTmp). Logs go to stdout/stderr and are read with journalctl -u. systemctl daemon-reload after edits, enable --now to start it and at boot.

docs.title: Part 6. Docker and CI/CD
docs.text:
31. What is a Docker image layer, and how does layer caching affect your Dockerfile? [08] Each filesystem-changing instruction (RUN, COPY, ADD) produces a read-only layer, a tarball of the changes, stacked with an overlay filesystem; the container adds one writable layer on top. The builder reuses a cached layer as long as the instruction and its inputs (for COPY, the file checksums) are unchanged, and rebuilds every layer after the first change. So order instructions from least to most frequently changing: system packages, then build files and dependency fetches, then sources. Files deleted in a later layer still occupy space in the earlier one.

32. What is a multi-stage build and why use it for C++? [08] A Dockerfile with several FROM stages, where later stages copy only selected artefacts from earlier ones with COPY --from=. For C++, the build stage has the compiler, CMake and headers and runs the tests; the runtime stage starts from a small base, installs only runtime libraries and copies the stripped binary. The result is an image without compilers or sources: smaller, faster to pull, smaller attack surface, and the tests ran in the exact environment of the shipped binary.

33. Why does PID 1 matter inside a container? [08, 11] The process with PID 1 in a namespace gets no default signal actions from the kernel: a SIGTERM without an installed handler is ignored, so docker stop waits 10 seconds and sends SIGKILL. PID 1 also inherits orphaned processes and must reap them, or zombies accumulate. Either the server installs SIGTERM handling and never forks, or a tiny init such as tini (or docker run --init) runs as PID 1, forwards signals and reaps children.

34. How would you design a CI pipeline for a C++ service? [09] Trigger on every PR and on main and tags; cancel superseded runs. A matrix of compilers (GCC, Clang) and build types with -Werror, running the full test suite with JUnit output; separate sanitizer jobs (ASan+UBSan, TSan) using the same CMake presets developers use; formatting and clang-tidy checks; ccache and dependency caches keyed by content hash. Then build the Docker image, smoke-test that exact image, and push it tagged with the commit SHA only from main or tags. Archive debug symbols per build, require all checks via branch protection, keep PR feedback under about ten minutes and move slow suites (Valgrind, long fuzzing) to nightly jobs.

35. How do you handle secrets in CI and in containers? [08, 09] Store them in the CI system's encrypted secrets (repository, organisation, or a vault such as Key Vault), expose them only to the steps that need them, and rely on them being masked and unavailable to fork PRs. Prefer short-lived credentials: the per-run GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC federation to cloud providers. Never put secrets in the repository, in Dockerfile ARG/ENV (they persist in image history) or in compose files; inject them at run time through environment files, Docker secrets or the orchestrator.

docs.title: Part 7. Senior-level and cross-platform
docs.text:
36. Compare the Windows and Linux toolchains for C++ in two minutes. [12] MSVC cl/link with MSBuild versus GCC or Clang with Make or Ninja, both drivable by CMake. /W4 /WX maps to -Wall -Wextra -Werror; /O2 /Zi to -O2 -g. Windows has PE images, .lib and .dll with import libraries and nothing exported by default, separate PDBs matched by GUID, and a per-module CRT choice (/MD vs /MT); Linux has ELF, .a and .so with everything exported by default, DWARF matched by build-id, and one libc per process. Debugging is WinDbg or Visual Studio on dumps versus GDB on cores; tracing is ETW/Process Monitor versus perf/strace; services are SCM versus systemd; Windows commits memory up front while Linux overcommits and has an OOM killer.

37. A release build crashes in production but the debug build never does. How do you approach it? [03, 05, 07] Optimisation exposes undefined behaviour the debug build hides (uninitialised variables, signed overflow, out-of-bounds, data races, strict-aliasing violations) or changes timing. Get the core dump and the matching unstripped binary, read the stack and registers in GDB; rebuild the release configuration with -g and run the tests and a load test under ASan+UBSan and TSan; compile with more warnings (-Wall -Wextra -Wconversion) and with both GCC and Clang. If it reproduces only in one place, git bisect with the release preset narrows it to a commit.

38. Where do the "it works on my machine" failures come from, and how does your setup prevent them? [04, 08, 09] From differences in compiler version and flags, library versions, environment variables, file system behaviour (case, line endings), and undeclared dependencies installed on the developer machine. The prevention is to define everything in the repository: CMake presets for flags, pinned dependencies (FetchContent tags, vcpkg baselines), .gitattributes for line endings, a Docker build stage that is the reference environment, and CI that builds from a clean checkout on every commit and tests the exact image that ships.

docs.title: 07. Databases from the storage engine up: PostgreSQL, YugabyteDB, Berkeley DB, Redis
What this course covers
docs.text:
You have used databases from the application side for 2.5 years: you wrote a Berkeley DB to YugabyteDB migration engine in C, you write PL/pgSQL, you have fixed a slow login path on a multi-node cluster. This course goes one level down. By the end you can explain what the database engine does with every statement you send it: how a page looks on disk, how a B-tree index is walked, how MVCC decides which row version you see, how WAL survives a power cut, how the planner picks a plan and why it sometimes picks the wrong one, and what changes when the "database" is actually a Raft-replicated cluster of RocksDB instances pretending to be PostgreSQL.

The hands-on database is PostgreSQL 16 on WSL Ubuntu 24.04 (installed with apt). The distributed parts use the YugabyteDB docker image. Caching uses Redis in docker. Berkeley DB examples use libdb-dev from apt and compile with gcc ... -ldb.

docs.title: Why it is on the resume
docs.text:
Resume lines this course backs up (quoted exactly):

  • "PostgreSQL, YugabyteDB, Berkeley DB, Oracle, SQL Server, Redis; database internals, storage engines, key-value stores, indexing, query optimisation, transactions, caching"
  • "PL/pgSQL"
  • Migration-engine bullets: B-tree cursor traversal, record-to-relational mapping, data-parity regression suite, zero-downtime cutover
  • Stored-procedure bullets: PL/pgSQL layer, login-latency bottleneck from full-table scans, execution plans, composite and covering indexes on a multi-node cluster

An interviewer who sees "database internals" on a resume will ask you to explain MVCC, read an EXPLAIN plan, design an index, and walk through a migration. Each of those gets a full module here.

docs.text:
• C at a working level (you have it). C++17 basics for module 12's engine skeleton (see 02_Modern_CPP if you need a refresher on RAII, std::vector, std::optional).
  • Comfortable in a Linux shell on WSL.

docs.title: You are done when you can...
docs.text:
• Draw the layers of PostgreSQL from the wire protocol to the disk and say what each one owns.
  • Describe an 8 KB heap page byte by byte: header, line pointers, tuples, special space.
  • Explain why a B+tree index with 3 levels can find one row in 400 million with 4 page reads.
  • Choose the column order of a composite index from a WHERE clause and justify it.
  • Explain what happens between COMMIT returning and the data being on disk, including WAL, fsync, checkpoints and full-page writes.
  • Given a row's xmin, xmax and a snapshot, say whether a transaction sees it and why.
  • Name the five classic anomalies and which isolation level in PostgreSQL stops each.
  • Read an EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) plan top to bottom and point at the problem node.
  • Write a PL/pgSQL procedure with exception handling, and say when logic belongs in the database.
  • Write the Berkeley DB C code to open an environment, insert, iterate with a cursor, and commit a transaction, from memory.
  • Explain how YugabyteDB turns a PostgreSQL row into DocDB keys and why hash sharding changes index design.
  • Present a zero-downtime KV-to-relational migration with parity verification, and defend each decision.
  • Explain cache-aside, the stampede problem, and why a Redis lock is not a correctness guarantee.
  • Say honestly what differs between PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server on isolation defaults and MVCC.

docs.title: How to study
docs.text: Read section 1 and 2 of a module, then type (not paste) the SQL in section 3 into psql and watch the output. Section 4 is the interview material: read it twice. Do at least the easy and medium exercises. Finish with the module's interview questions out loud.

docs.title: 1. What a database actually does
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: none

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A database management system (DBMS) is a program that takes a question written in a language (SQL, or a get(key) call) and turns it into reads and writes of bytes on disk, while promising three things the file system never promised you: your data is still correct after a crash, many users can work at the same time without corrupting each other, and you can ask for data by its meaning rather than by its byte offset.

Think of a bank branch. You walk up to a counter (the client protocol), say what you want in plain language (the parser), the clerk decides how to do it fastest (the planner), does it (the executor), going to the right filing cabinet (access methods), using the folders already on his desk if he has them (buffer manager), and before closing a drawer he writes a line in a bound ledger that cannot be torn out (the write-ahead log). If the building loses power, the ledger is replayed and the cabinets are repaired. Every serious database, from SQLite to Oracle, has these pieces. They differ in how the pieces are split and tuned.

The second idea of this module: a database can be a library linked into your program (Berkeley DB, SQLite, RocksDB) or a server process you talk to over a socket (PostgreSQL, Oracle, Redis). Same layers, very different operational consequences.

docs.title: 2.1 The layers
docs.text:
client  ---- TCP / Unix socket, frontend/backend protocol v3 ----> backend process
                                                                        |
      +-----------------------------------------------------------------+
      |  1. Protocol handler     parses messages: Query, Parse, Bind, Execute, Sync
      |  2. Parser (gram.y)      SQL text -> raw parse tree  (syntax only)
      |  3. Analyzer             raw tree -> Query tree: resolves names, types, catalogs
      |  4. Rewriter             applies rules and views (view -> its SELECT)
      |  5. Planner/optimizer    Query -> Plan tree: scans, joins, sorts, costs
      |  6. Executor             walks the Plan tree, pulls tuples node to node
      |  7. Access methods       heap AM (tables), index AMs: btree, hash, gin, gist, brin
      |  8. Buffer manager       shared_buffers: 8 KB pages in RAM, pin/unpin, eviction
      |  9. Storage manager      files on disk: base/<dboid>/<relfilenode>, 1 GB segments
      | 10. WAL                  every page change logged first; fsync on commit
      | 11. Lock manager         heavyweight locks (tables), row locks (in tuple headers),
      |                          lightweight locks (in-memory structures), spinlocks
      | 12. Transaction manager  xid assignment, commit log (pg_xact), snapshots
      +-----------------------------------------------------------------

One-line definitions:

  • Protocol: the byte format of messages between client and server. PostgreSQL uses its own "frontend/backend protocol version 3"; libpq, JDBC and psycopg all speak it.
  • Parse tree: the SQL statement as a tree of nodes (SelectStmt, ColumnRef, ...) with no knowledge of whether tables exist.
  • Query tree: the parse tree after name resolution; every column is now (table oid, attnum, type).
  • Plan tree: a tree of executable nodes (SeqScan, IndexScan, HashJoin, Sort, Aggregate...).
  • Access method (AM): the code that knows the layout of one kind of on-disk structure.
  • Buffer manager: the cache of disk pages in shared memory; every page read or written goes through it.
  • WAL (write-ahead log): an append-only record of changes, written and flushed before the changed data page is allowed to reach disk.

docs.title: 2.2 Relational vs key-value
docs.text:
A key-value store gives you put(key, value), get(key), delete(key) and usually an ordered cursor (seek(key), next()). The value is opaque bytes. All interpretation is in your program. Berkeley DB, LevelDB, RocksDB, Redis (with richer value types) are key-value stores.

A relational database stores typed rows in tables, enforces constraints, and lets you ask declarative questions (WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY) that the engine decides how to execute. PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, YugabyteDB (YSQL) are relational.

The relational engine is a key-value store plus four things: a schema (types and constraints), a query language, a planner, and secondary indexes maintained for you. YugabyteDB makes this literal: its SQL layer is PostgreSQL's parser, planner and executor, and its storage layer is a key-value store (DocDB on RocksDB). You spent two years moving data from the first kind to the second kind; the rest of this course explains both ends.

Key-value (Berkeley DB) Relational (PostgreSQL) Unit of storage key bytes -> value bytes typed row in a table Who knows the record layout your C structs the catalog (pg_attribute) Secondary access paths you build them (secondary DBs) CREATE INDEX Query cursor->get(DB_SET_RANGE) loops declarative SQL, planner decides Constraints your code PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, UNIQUE Concurrency page or record locks, you choose MVCC plus row locks, automatic Deployment library in your process server process, network protocol

docs.title: 2.3 Library vs server
docs.text:
Berkeley DB is a C library. db_create(), db->open() happen inside your process. The buffer pool (the "mpool") is a shared-memory region mapped into every process that opens the same environment. There is no SQL, no network, no separate server process to start. Crash recovery is your responsibility: you call DB_ENV->open() with DB_RECOVER. Consequences:

  • Lowest possible latency: a get is a function call and a few memory reads. No syscall unless the page is not in the mpool.
  • No separate failure domain: if your process corrupts memory, it can corrupt the database's in-memory pages. If your process dies holding locks, another process must run recovery.
  • One machine only. Replication exists (Berkeley DB HA) but is rarely used.
  • Schema is in your head and your C headers. Nobody can run an ad-hoc report.

PostgreSQL is a server. The postmaster process listens on a socket, forks one backend process per connection, and all backends share one shared_buffers region. Consequences:

  • Every statement crosses a socket: a round trip costs tens of microseconds on localhost, hundreds across a network, milliseconds across a region. This dominates the design of application code (batching, fewer round trips, stored procedures).
  • The server survives client crashes. Locks held by a dead connection are released when the backend notices the socket closed.
  • Many languages and tools can read the same data. Schema is in the catalog.
  • Process-per-connection means connections are expensive (several MB each, fork cost); hence connection poolers (module 14).

docs.title: 2.4 A request's path from SQL text to disk pages
docs.text:
Take this statement, sent from a C program using libpq:

SELECT customer_id, status FROM loan_applications WHERE application_no = 'LA-2024-000123';
  1. Client: libpq builds a Query message (simple protocol) or Parse/Bind/Execute (extended protocol, used by PQexecParams and prepared statements), writes it to the socket.
  2. Backend reads the message in PostgresMain(), calls exec_simple_query().
  3. Parser: raw_parser() runs the flex lexer and bison grammar, returns a SelectStmt. Syntax errors stop here ("syntax error at or near").
  4. Analyzer: parse_analyze() looks up loan_applications in pg_class (via the relcache, a per-backend cache of catalog rows), resolves application_no to attribute number 2 of type text, checks the literal can be coerced to text. "column does not exist" stops here.
  5. Rewriter: no views or rules here, so the Query passes through unchanged.
  6. Planner: pg_plan_query() looks at pg_statistic for application_no. If there is a unique index, it estimates 1 row and chooses an Index Scan. If not, it estimates the selectivity from n_distinct and may still pick a Seq Scan of the whole heap. Output: a PlannedStmt with a plan tree.
  7. Executor: ExecutorStart() builds executor state, ExecutorRun() calls the top node's ExecProcNode(), which pulls tuples from its child (the Volcano / iterator model). The Index Scan node calls the btree AM: btgettuple().
  8. Access method: btree descends from the root page to a leaf page, comparing the key. Each page it needs is requested from the buffer manager with ReadBuffer(). The leaf holds an index tuple containing the heap TID (block number, item offset) of the row.
  9. Buffer manager: ReadBuffer() hashes (relfilenode, fork, block) into the shared buffer lookup table. If the page is in shared_buffers, it is pinned and returned. If not, a victim buffer is chosen (clock-sweep), written out if dirty, and the page is read with pread() from the file base/<db>/<relfilenode>. The OS page cache may serve it without touching the disk.
  10. Heap AM: heap_fetch() reads the tuple at that TID, checks visibility using the tuple's xmin/xmax against the transaction's snapshot (module 05). Visible: the tuple is projected to (customer_id, status) and sent back as a DataRow message. Not visible: the index scan asks for the next matching entry.
  11. Client: libpq collects DataRows into a PGresult; CommandComplete and ReadyForQuery end the exchange.

For an UPDATE the path is the same until step 10, then: a new tuple version is written to a heap page (the old one gets xmax set), a WAL record describing the change is appended to the WAL buffers, indexes are updated if an indexed column changed, and at COMMIT the WAL is flushed with fdatasync(). The dirty heap page stays in shared_buffers and is written later by the checkpointer or background writer. Module 04 covers why this order is safe.

docs.title: 2.5 Where the time goes
docs.text:
Typical costs on a 2020s server, for scale (orders of magnitude, from standard latency tables):

Step Typical cost Socket round trip, localhost 20 to 50 us Socket round trip, same data centre 100 to 500 us Parse + analyze + plan a simple statement 50 to 200 us Buffer manager hit (page in shared_buffers) under 1 us Page read from OS page cache a few us Page read from NVMe SSD 50 to 100 us Page read from spinning disk 5 to 10 ms fsync of WAL to SSD 0.5 to 2 ms (device dependent)

Two lessons that will repeat through the course: avoid round trips (batch, use set-based SQL), and avoid disk reads (indexes that fit in memory, good shared_buffers). A seq scan of a 10 GB table is slow not because of CPU but because of 1.3 million page reads.

docs.title: 3.1 Talking to the server at the protocol level
docs.text:
code/m01_libpq_hello.c connects with libpq, runs one parameterised query with the extended protocol, and prints the plan the server chose. Build: gcc m01_libpq_hello.c -o hello -lpq.

/* Extended protocol: Parse/Bind/Execute. The server plans once per call with the

 * real parameter value, so it can use the statistics for that value. */
const char *params[1] = { "LA-2024-000123" };
PGresult *res = PQexecParams(conn,
    "SELECT customer_id, status FROM loan_applications WHERE application_no = $1",
    1, NULL, params, NULL, NULL, 0 /* text results */);
if (PQresultStatus(res) != PGRES_TUPLES_OK) {
    fprintf(stderr, "query failed: %s", PQerrorMessage(conn));   /* server-side error text */
}

docs.title: 3.2 Watch the layers from psql
docs.text:
-- the parser alone: a syntax error never touches the catalog
SELEC 1;
-- ERROR:  syntax error at or near "SELEC"

-- the analyzer: valid syntax, unknown relation
SELECT * FROM no_such_table;
-- ERROR:  relation "no_such_table" does not exist

-- the planner's choice and the executor's actual work
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT customer_id, status FROM loan_applications WHERE application_no = 'LA-2024-000123';

-- the storage manager: where the file is
SELECT pg_relation_filepath('loan_applications');          -- base/16384/16432
SELECT pg_relation_size('loan_applications') / 8192 AS pages;

-- the buffer manager: how many of its pages are in shared_buffers right now
SELECT count(*) FROM pg_buffercache b
JOIN pg_class c ON b.relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode(c.oid)
WHERE c.relname = 'loan_applications';

-- the lock manager: what this session holds mid-transaction
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM loan_applications WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT locktype, mode, granted FROM pg_locks WHERE pid = pg_backend_pid();
ROLLBACK;

docs.title: 3.3 Trace one statement through the C source (reading exercise)
docs.text:
If you clone postgres from git (branch REL_16_STABLE), the path above is literally:

src/backend/tcop/postgres.c        PostgresMain -> exec_simple_query
src/backend/parser/gram.y          grammar
src/backend/parser/analyze.c       transformStmt
src/backend/optimizer/plan/planner.c   standard_planner
src/backend/executor/execMain.c    ExecutorRun
src/backend/executor/nodeIndexscan.c   IndexNext
src/backend/access/nbtree/nbtsearch.c  _bt_search, _bt_first
src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c    ReadBuffer_common
src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c       heap_fetch, heap_update
src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c      XLogInsert, XLogFlush

You do not need to read it all. Open bufmgr.c and find ReadBuffer_common; read the comment block. That one function is the boundary between "memory" and "disk" for the whole system.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Process model. PostgreSQL forks a backend per connection. Backends share memory through a System V or mmap shared segment created by the postmaster: shared_buffers, the lock tables, the WAL buffers, the commit log cache, the proc array (one entry per backend holding its current xid and snapshot information). There are also background processes: checkpointer, background writer, WAL writer, autovacuum launcher and workers, stats collector (replaced by shared memory stats in 15+), archiver, logical replication workers. ps aux | grep postgres shows all of them.

Why not threads? Historical, plus isolation: a crash in one backend cannot scribble over another backend's private memory; the postmaster notices the death and restarts everything to be safe (because shared memory may be inconsistent). The cost is heavier connections and no shared per-connection caches (each backend has its own relcache, plan cache, catalog cache). A threaded model has been discussed for years; as of PostgreSQL 16 it is still processes.

Memory contexts. All backend allocations go through palloc() into hierarchical memory contexts (MemoryContext). A query runs in a context that is reset when the query ends, so there is no per-allocation free. This is the same arena idea as the per-batch arena you used in your migration engine: free everything at once at a known boundary. work_mem is the budget per sort or hash node before spilling to disk; it is a soft target, not a hard cap on the backend.

Catalog as tables. The schema itself lives in tables: pg_class (relations), pg_attribute (columns), pg_index, pg_proc (functions), pg_type, pg_statistic. CREATE TABLE is mostly inserts into these. Each backend caches catalog rows (syscache, relcache) and the caches are invalidated through shared invalidation messages when DDL commits. That is why a DROP TABLE in one session takes an AccessExclusiveLock: it must wait for everyone's cached knowledge to be safely discarded.

The iterator (Volcano) model. Every plan node implements ExecProcNode() returning one tuple or NULL. A Hash Join node calls its inner child until exhausted (building the hash table), then calls its outer child one tuple at a time and probes. The entire plan is pull driven from the top. PostgreSQL 10+ adds JIT compilation of expressions with LLVM for large queries, but the per-node structure remains. This matters when you read EXPLAIN (module 06): "loops" and "actual rows" are counts of these per-node calls.

Where Berkeley DB differs internally. Berkeley DB has the same bottom layers (mpool = buffer manager, log = WAL, lock = lock manager, txn = transaction manager) and the access methods (BTREE, HASH, QUEUE, RECNO), but no parser, planner or executor. Your C code is the executor. Opening a cursor and calling DB_NEXT in a loop is you writing an Index Scan by hand. That is exactly what "B-tree cursor traversal" on your resume means, and why module 10 revisits it.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• "The database is slow" is almost never one layer. The first question is which layer: network (round trips, connection setup), planning (bad plan, no index), execution (large sort, many loops), storage (page reads from disk), locks (waiting on another transaction). pg_stat_activity.wait_event_type tells you if a backend is waiting on Lock, IO, LWLock or Client. Start there.
  • Connection count. Each PostgreSQL connection is a process with its own caches. 500 idle connections cost several GB and make every catalog invalidation more expensive. Your RPC application server should hold a small pool (tens, not hundreds) and multiplex. Module 14.
  • Round trips kill. A login path that does 12 single-row SELECTs across a network does 12 round trips. On a multi-node YugabyteDB cluster each may also hop to another node. Folding them into one PL/pgSQL function call or one set-based statement is often a 10x win before any index is touched. Module 07 and 08.
  • A library database is in your blast radius. With Berkeley DB a segfault in your server could leave the environment needing recovery; a hung process could hold page locks forever (db_deadlock, DB_ENV->lock_detect). Moving to a server database trades latency for a clean failure boundary. Say this when asked "why did you migrate?".
  • 3 AM: "all connections are stuck". SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, query FROM pg_stat_activity will usually show them all waiting on Lock behind one session holding an AccessExclusiveLock from a DDL that is itself blocked behind a long transaction. pg_blocking_pids(pid) gives you the chain. Module 05 and 14.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Install PostgreSQL 16 on WSL per the README, create the loans database, load code/m09_schema.sql and code/m09_seed.sql. Done when \dt lists the tables and SELECT count(*) FROM loan_applications returns a number.
  2. (easy) Run the five psql snippets from section 3.2. Done when you can say which layer produced each error or result.
  3. (medium) Run ps -o pid,ppid,cmd -C postgres (or ps aux | grep postgres). Identify the postmaster, checkpointer, background writer, WAL writer, autovacuum launcher and your own backend. Open a second psql and watch a new backend appear. Done when you can name each.
  4. (medium) Build and run code/m01_libpq_hello.c. Change it to run the same query 1000 times in a loop and time it with clock_gettime. Then wrap the loop in one transaction (BEGIN/COMMIT). Done when you can explain the time difference (hint: nothing, it is read-only; now change it to an UPDATE and compare: per-statement commit vs one commit).
  5. (hard) Draw, on paper, the path of an UPDATE loan_applications SET status = 'APPROVED' WHERE id = 42 through all 12 layers, including which pages are touched (heap page, every index on the table whose key changed, WAL), and when each byte reaches durable storage. Done when your drawing matches what modules 02 to 05 say (come back and check).

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Walk me through what happens when I send a SELECT to PostgreSQL. A: The client sends a protocol message over the socket. The backend parses it into a parse tree, the analyzer resolves names and types against the catalog, the rewriter expands views, the planner uses statistics to produce a plan tree, and the executor pulls tuples through that tree. Scan nodes call access methods (heap or index), which fetch pages through the buffer manager; a miss goes to the storage manager and pread(). Each tuple is checked for visibility against the transaction's snapshot before being returned.

Q: What is the difference between a key-value store and a relational database? A: A key-value store maps opaque key bytes to opaque value bytes and lets you look up or scan by key; your program interprets everything. A relational database adds a typed schema with constraints, a declarative query language, a planner that chooses access paths, and secondary indexes maintained automatically. Internally a relational database is often a key-value store plus those layers; YugabyteDB makes this explicit with PostgreSQL's query layer over RocksDB.

Q: Why is Berkeley DB a library and PostgreSQL a server? What does that change? A: Berkeley DB links into your process; a get is a function call with no network, so latency is minimal, but your process shares a failure domain with the data, only one machine can host it, and there is no SQL for ad-hoc access. PostgreSQL runs as separate processes behind a socket; every statement pays a round trip, but the server survives client crashes, enforces schema centrally, and serves many clients and tools.

Q: Why does PostgreSQL use a process per connection and what does it cost? A: Historical design plus fault isolation: a backend crash cannot corrupt another backend's private memory. The cost is that each connection is a process with several MB of private caches and fork startup, so thousands of connections are expensive and a connection pooler is standard.

Q: Where would you look first if "the database is slow"?
