A: pg_stat_activity for what sessions are doing and what they wait on (Lock, IO, LWLock, Client), then pg_stat_statements for the statements consuming the most total time, then EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the top offender. That tells me whether the problem is network round trips, a bad plan, disk reads, or lock contention, which are fixed in different ways.

Q: What is the buffer manager and why does every layer go through it? A: It is the shared cache of 8 KB disk pages in shared_buffers. Every access method asks it for a page by (relation, fork, block number); it pins the page if present or evicts a victim and reads it from disk if not. Centralising this gives one consistent view of each page, allows dirty pages to be written lazily by the checkpointer, and lets WAL rules be enforced in one place.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A DBMS is layers: protocol, parser, analyzer, rewriter, planner, executor, access methods, buffer manager, storage, WAL, locks, transactions.
  • The planner decides how; the executor pulls tuples one node at a time (Volcano model).
  • All page access goes through the buffer manager; a miss is a pread() on a 1 GB segment file.
  • Writes go to WAL first, fsync on commit; data pages are written later by the checkpointer.
  • Key-value store: opaque bytes, you are the executor. Relational: schema, SQL, planner, indexes.
  • Library database (Berkeley DB): function-call latency, shared failure domain, one machine.
  • Server database (PostgreSQL): round trips, clean isolation, many clients, process per connection.
  • Round trips and disk page reads are the two costs that dominate application performance.
  • Catalog is tables; backends cache it; DDL invalidates caches and needs strong locks.
  • Memory contexts are arenas: allocate freely, free all at once at a boundary.

docs.title: 2. Storage engines: pages and heap files
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A database never reads or writes "a row". It reads and writes pages: fixed-size blocks, 8 KB in PostgreSQL, that are the unit of I/O between disk and memory. A table is a file (or a few files) made of these pages laid end to end. Rows are packed into the pages; an index entry points at a row by saying "page 1234, slot 7".

The analogy is a filing cabinet with fixed-size drawers. You never pull one sheet out of the cabinet; you pull a whole drawer onto your desk, find the sheet, maybe change it, and later push the drawer back. Your desk is the buffer pool: it holds a limited number of drawers, and when it is full you have to put one back (eviction) before pulling out another. If a drawer on your desk has been written on (dirty), it must be put back carefully (written to disk) and not just dropped.

Everything in later modules depends on this picture. An index is fast because it reads 3 or 4 pages instead of 100,000. VACUUM exists because deleted rows still occupy page space. WAL exists because a crash in the middle of pushing a drawer back leaves a half-written drawer.

docs.title: 2.1 Files on disk
docs.text:
$PGDATA/
  base/<database oid>/<relfilenode>          main fork, data pages, 1 GB segments: 16432, 16432.1, 16432.2 ...
  base/<database oid>/<relfilenode>_fsm      free space map fork
  base/<database oid>/<relfilenode>_vm       visibility map fork
  base/<database oid>/<relfilenode>_init     unlogged table init fork
  pg_wal/                                    WAL segments, 16 MB each by default
  pg_xact/                                   commit status of every transaction (2 bits per xid)
  global/                                    shared catalogs (pg_database, pg_authid ...)

SELECT pg_relation_filepath('loan_applications') gives the path. A table over 1 GB is split into numbered segment files so that file-size limits and backup tools never see huge files. Each index is its own relation with its own files.

docs.title: 2.2 The 8 KB heap page (slotted page)
docs.text:
offset 0
 +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 | PageHeaderData (24 bytes)                                                |
 |  pd_lsn (8)       LSN of the last WAL record that touched this page      |
 |  pd_checksum (2)  page checksum, if enabled at initdb                    |
 |  pd_flags (2)     PD_HAS_FREE_LINES, PD_PAGE_FULL, PD_ALL_VISIBLE        |
 |  pd_lower (2)     end of line pointer array                              |
 |  pd_upper (2)     start of tuple data                                    |
 |  pd_special (2)   start of special space (8192 for heap: none)           |
 |  pd_pagesize_version (2), pd_prune_xid (4)                               |
 +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 | ItemIdData[1] ItemIdData[2] ItemIdData[3] ...   4 bytes each             |
 |  lp_off:15  lp_flags:2 (UNUSED/NORMAL/REDIRECT/DEAD)  lp_len:15          |
 +------------------------------ pd_lower ----------------------------------+
 |                                                                          |
 |                      free space (grows down and up)                      |
 |                                                                          |
 +------------------------------ pd_upper ----------------------------------+
 | tuple 3 | tuple 2 | tuple 1 |   tuples are added from the END backwards  |
 +------------------------------ pd_special --------------------------------+
 | special space: empty for heap pages; btree pages keep sibling pointers   |
 +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+ offset 8192

Why slotted? A tuple's address (its TID, "tuple identifier" = block number + line pointer index, e.g. (1234,7)) must stay stable so indexes can point at it, but tuples have variable length and get moved when the page is compacted. The line pointer array is the indirection: indexes point at slot 7, slot 7 points at wherever the bytes currently are. Compaction (page pruning) rewrites lp_off values without touching any index.

Line pointer flags matter for module 03 and 05: LP_DEAD marks a slot whose tuple is gone and can be reused after VACUUM; LP_REDIRECT is how HOT update chains are shortened.

docs.title: 2.3 The heap tuple
docs.text:
HeapTupleHeaderData (23 bytes, padded to 24)
   t_xmin (4)       xid that inserted this version
   t_xmax (4)       xid that deleted/updated it, or 0 (also used for row locks)
   t_cid (4)        command id within the inserting transaction (or t_xvac)
   t_ctid (6)       TID of this tuple, or of the NEWER version if updated
   t_infomask2 (2)  number of attributes + HOT flags
   t_infomask (2)   HAS_NULL, HAS_VARWIDTH, XMIN_COMMITTED, XMIN_INVALID, XMAX_COMMITTED,
                    XMAX_INVALID, XMAX_IS_MULTI, UPDATED, HOT_UPDATED, HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE ...
   t_hoff (1)       offset of user data (header + null bitmap, MAXALIGNed to 8)
 null bitmap        1 bit per attribute, only if HAS_NULL
 user data          columns in declaration order, each aligned per its type ('c','s','i','d')

Every row carries 24 bytes of header plus alignment padding. A table with columns (id int8, flag bool, amount int8) wastes 7 bytes after flag because int8 needs 8-byte alignment. Reordering to (id int8, amount int8, flag bool) saves 7 bytes per row. For a 100 million row table that is 700 MB. This is the "column tetris" trick, and it is the same alignment rule you know from C structs.

Variable-length columns (text, bytea, numeric, jsonb) start with a varlena header: 1 byte for short values under 127 bytes, 4 bytes otherwise, with bits saying whether the value is compressed or stored externally (TOAST).

docs.title: 2.4 TOAST: rows bigger than a page
docs.text:
A tuple must fit in one page. "The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique" handles big values. When a tuple would exceed about 2 KB (TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD, 2040 bytes), the engine tries, in order, for each toastable column from largest to smallest: compress it (pglz by default, lz4 if default_toast_compression = lz4), then if still too big move it out of line into the table's TOAST table (pg_toast.pg_toast_<oid>) in chunks of about 2000 bytes, leaving an 18-byte pointer in the main tuple. Per-column storage strategies:

Strategy Compress Out of line Default for PLAIN no no fixed-width types MAIN yes only as last resort EXTENDED yes yes most varlena types (text, bytea, jsonb) EXTERNAL no yes set it for big values you substring often

Consequences: SELECT * on a table with a 50 KB jsonb column fetches from the TOAST table on every row (an index lookup into the toast index per chunk). SELECT id, status does not touch TOAST at all. This is one concrete reason SELECT * is an anti-pattern (module 07).

docs.title: 2.5 Free space map and visibility map
docs.text:
FSM (_fsm fork): for each heap page, one byte recording roughly how much free space it has (in 1/256ths of a page, so 32-byte granularity), organised as a binary tree over pages so that "find me a page with at least 300 bytes free" is a tree descent, not a scan. INSERT consults it; VACUUM updates it.

VM (_vm fork): two bits per heap page: all-visible (every tuple on the page is visible to every current and future transaction, nothing to vacuum) and all-frozen (no xid on the page can ever wrap around). Two users:

  1. VACUUM skips all-visible pages: this is why vacuuming a mostly-static 100 GB table is cheap.
  2. Index-only scans (module 03) can trust the index entry for a page marked all-visible and skip the heap fetch; for other pages they must visit the heap to check visibility. The "Heap Fetches" line in EXPLAIN counts those visits.

Any write to a page clears its VM bits.

docs.title: 2.6 How a sequential scan reads a table
docs.text:
Seq Scan calls heap_getnextslot(), which asks the buffer manager for block 0, 1, 2, ... in order. On each page it walks the line pointers, skips LP_UNUSED/LP_DEAD, and checks each tuple's visibility against the snapshot. Three details make this faster than naive:

  • Page-at-a-time visibility: on first touch of a page the scan computes visibility for all tuples on it under one buffer lock, then releases the lock and returns tuples from a local array.
  • Ring buffer: a scan of a table larger than a quarter of shared_buffers uses a small private ring of buffers (256 KB) so it does not evict the entire working set of other queries. Yes: a big seq scan deliberately does not cache the table.
  • Synchronised scans: a second seq scan of the same big table starts where the first one currently is, so both share the pages being read.
  • The OS does read-ahead on the sequential file reads, which is why seq_page_cost (1.0) is set four times cheaper than random_page_cost (4.0) in the planner's cost model.

docs.title: 2.7 Row store vs column store
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores a row's columns together on one page (row store, N-ary storage model). Good when you read whole rows by key (OLTP: your login path, a loan application screen). A column store stores each column in its own file or block run (Parquet, ClickHouse, Citus columnar, Oracle In-Memory, SQL Server columnstore indexes). Good when you aggregate one or two columns across millions of rows: you read only those columns, and runs of similar values compress 10x or better. Bad for point lookups and single-row updates, which must touch every column's structure. PostgreSQL core has no column store; extensions and separate analytic databases fill that role. Answer "row store, optimised for OLTP" when asked how PostgreSQL stores data.

docs.title: 2.8 The buffer pool
docs.text:
shared_buffers is an array of 8 KB slots (default 128 MB; typical production 25% of RAM) plus a parallel array of BufferDesc headers (tag = relation+fork+block, state bits: dirty, valid, pin count, usage count, I/O in progress) and a shared hash table from tag to slot.

Pin: a backend that is reading a page increments the pin count; the page cannot be evicted while pinned. Content lock: a lightweight lock on the page, shared for reads, exclusive for modifications. Pins are held for the duration of use; content locks for microseconds.

Replacement: clock sweep. A hand moves around the slot array. Each slot has a usage count (0 to 5, incremented on each pin). When looking for a victim, the hand decrements the count of each slot it passes and takes the first slot with count 0 and pin count 0. This approximates LRU without the lock contention of a true LRU list. Dirty victims are written out (pwrite) before reuse; the background writer tries to keep some clean buffers ahead of the hand so backends rarely have to write.

Two caches, not one: PostgreSQL's shared_buffers sits on top of the OS page cache. A "read" that misses shared_buffers often hits the OS cache and costs microseconds, not a disk seek. EXPLAIN's shared hit versus read cannot distinguish OS cache from disk; track_io_timing can (module 06).

docs.title: 2.9 fsync and durability
docs.text:
A write() syscall puts bytes in the OS page cache; the disk has them only after fsync() / fdatasync(), and even then the drive's own write cache must be flushed (the kernel sends a cache flush command; cheap consumer SSDs sometimes lie). PostgreSQL's rules:

  • WAL is fdatasynced (default wal_sync_method on Linux) before COMMIT returns, when synchronous_commit = on.
  • Data pages are written whenever evicted or at checkpoint, and all files touched since the last checkpoint are fsynced at the end of the checkpoint. Between checkpoints data pages on disk are stale; WAL is the source of truth (module 04).
  • If fsync() ever fails, PostgreSQL 12+ PANICs and restarts, replaying WAL. This was the outcome of the 2018 "fsyncgate" discussion: Linux may drop dirty pages after reporting an fsync error, so retrying is unsafe; crash recovery from WAL is the only correct response.
  • fsync = off is a benchmark-only setting; a power loss can corrupt the cluster.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m02_page_inspect.sql walks through all of this with the pageinspect extension.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;

-- 1. Where is the table and how big in pages?
SELECT pg_relation_filepath('loan_applications'),
       pg_relation_size('loan_applications') / 8192 AS main_pages,
       pg_relation_size('loan_applications', 'fsm') / 8192 AS fsm_pages,
       pg_relation_size('loan_applications', 'vm')  / 8192 AS vm_pages;

-- 2. The header of page 0. pd_lower/pd_upper tell you how full it is.
SELECT * FROM page_header(get_raw_page('loan_applications', 0));

-- 3. Every line pointer and tuple header on page 0.
--    lp_off/lp_len: where the bytes are. t_xmin/t_xmax: MVCC (module 05).
--    t_ctid pointing elsewhere means "this version was updated, newer one is there".
SELECT lp, lp_off, lp_len, lp_flags, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid, t_hoff,
       (t_infomask & 1) <> 0 AS has_null,
       (t_infomask & 16384) <> 0 AS hot_updated,
       (t_infomask2 & 32768) <> 0 AS heap_only
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('loan_applications', 0));

-- 4. Watch an UPDATE create a new version on the same page (HOT) or elsewhere.
UPDATE loan_applications SET status = 'UNDER_REVIEW' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('loan_applications', 0))
WHERE lp <= 3;

-- 5. TOAST: which table holds the big values and how many chunks
SELECT reltoastrelid::regclass FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'documents';
SELECT chunk_id, count(*) AS chunks, sum(length(chunk_data)) AS bytes
FROM pg_toast.pg_toast_<oid>   -- substitute the oid printed above
GROUP BY chunk_id LIMIT 5;

-- 6. Alignment padding: compare the row size of two column orders
CREATE TABLE pad_bad  (a int8, b bool, c int8, d bool, e int8);
CREATE TABLE pad_good (a int8, c int8, e int8, b bool, d bool);
INSERT INTO pad_bad  SELECT g, true, g, false, g FROM generate_series(1, 100000) g;
INSERT INTO pad_good SELECT g, g, g, true, false FROM generate_series(1, 100000) g;
SELECT pg_relation_size('pad_bad') AS bad, pg_relation_size('pad_good') AS good;
-- bad is noticeably larger: 7 bytes of padding after each bool before the next int8

-- 7. The buffer pool: what fraction of the table is cached, and usage counts
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_buffercache;
SELECT c.relname, count(*) AS buffers, sum(CASE WHEN isdirty THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS dirty,
       round(avg(usagecount), 2) AS avg_usage
FROM pg_buffercache b
JOIN pg_class c ON b.relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode(c.oid)
WHERE c.relname IN ('loan_applications', 'customers')
GROUP BY c.relname;

-- 8. Free space map: how much room each page claims to have
SELECT blkno, avail FROM pg_freespace('loan_applications') ORDER BY blkno LIMIT 10;

-- 9. Visibility map bits
SELECT blkno, all_visible, all_frozen FROM pg_visibility('loan_applications') LIMIT 10;

Expected observation for step 4: the old tuple's t_xmax becomes your transaction id and its t_ctid points at the new slot; the new tuple has t_xmin equal to that same id. The old version stays until VACUUM. That is MVCC made visible (module 05).

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why 8 KB. It is a compile-time constant (BLCKSZ). It must be a multiple of the OS page (4 KB) and of the disk sector (512 B or 4 KB). 8 KB means one page write is two OS pages, which is not atomic on most storage: a crash can leave a page half old, half new (a torn page). WAL full-page writes exist for this (module 04). Larger pages give better sequential read efficiency and more fan-out in B-trees; smaller pages waste less on point updates. 8 KB is a 30-year-old compromise that still works.

pd_lsn is the hinge between storage and WAL. When a page is modified, the LSN of the WAL record describing the change is stamped into pd_lsn. The buffer manager will not write a dirty page to disk until WAL up to pd_lsn has been flushed (XLogFlush(pd_lsn) in FlushBuffer()). That one rule is write-ahead logging. Hint-bit updates (setting XMIN_COMMITTED after checking pg_xact) are the exception: they are not WAL-logged unless checksums are on, because losing them only costs a re-check.

Page pruning (opportunistic). When a backend reads a page whose pd_prune_xid is older than the oldest running transaction, and the page is nearly full, heap_page_prune() removes dead tuple versions and compacts the page without VACUUM, in the reader's process. This is why a hot table can have many updates per second without exploding: single-page vacuum, done by whoever is holding the page anyway. It cannot remove the line pointers themselves (indexes may still point at them), so it marks them LP_DEAD; only VACUUM, which also cleans the indexes, can set them back to LP_UNUSED.

Buffer header spinlocks and partitions. The buffer mapping hash table is split into 128 partitions, each with its own lightweight lock, so that lookups for different pages rarely contend. Each buffer's state (pin count, usage count, flags) is packed into one 32-bit atomic and updated with compare-and-swap; the spinlock is taken only for complex transitions. This is the standard pattern from 04_Concurrency applied to a cache: partition the lock, use atomics for the hot path.

What read really costs. On a buffer miss the backend calls smgrread() -> mdread() -> pread() on the segment file. If the OS page cache has it, this is a memory copy (a few us). If not, a real device read. With effective_io_concurrency > 0, Bitmap Heap Scans issue posix_fadvise(WILLNEED) for upcoming pages so the kernel prefetches. PostgreSQL 16 and earlier do not use asynchronous I/O (io_uring work landed later), so a single backend's reads are synchronous: one outstanding read at a time. That is why a big index range scan on cold data is latency-bound, and why keeping the working set in memory matters so much.

Checksums. Off by default before 18 (initdb --data-checksums turns them on); when on, every page carries a CRC-style checksum verified on read, which detects storage-level corruption (bit rot, bad firmware) rather than silently returning garbage. Turn them on in production unless CPU is genuinely the constraint.

Berkeley DB pages. Berkeley DB uses the same slotted-page design (its B-tree leaf pages have an index array growing down and items growing up), a configurable page size (512 B to 64 KB, default often 4 KB), and the same "mpool" buffer manager with pin counts and LRU-ish eviction, also mapped as shared memory across processes. When your migration engine opened a cursor and walked DB_NEXT, the library was doing exactly these page fetches via its mpool. The record you got back was an opaque DBT holding your packed struct; PostgreSQL's equivalent is the tuple with a header the engine understands. That is the whole difference between "key-value" and "relational" at the page level.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Bloat. Every UPDATE writes a new tuple; every DELETE leaves the old one. If VACUUM cannot keep up (long transactions block it, or autovacuum is throttled), tables and indexes grow with dead space, scans read more pages for the same rows, and the buffer pool holds garbage. pgstattuple('loan_applications') reports dead_tuple_percent and free_percent. Module 05 and 14 cover tuning.
  • Column order. Put fixed-width 8-byte columns first, then 4-byte, then 2-byte, then booleans, then variable-length. Free space, zero risk, do it at design time. (You cannot reorder an existing table without rewriting it.)
  • Wide JSON blobs in the main table punish every SELECT *. Keep documents in a separate table joined on demand, or at least never select them in list queries.
  • shared_buffers vs OS cache. Setting shared_buffers to 80% of RAM starves the OS cache and makes double-buffering worse. 25% is the common starting point; measure buffer hit ratio (pg_stat_database.blks_hit / (blks_hit + blks_read)) and adjust.
  • "Disk full" at 3 AM. Usually pg_wal growing because archiving failed or a replication slot is holding WAL, or a runaway table rewrite. Check pg_replication_slots, pg_stat_archiver, and du -sh $PGDATA/*. Never delete WAL files by hand.
  • Checksum failures in the log mean a hardware or filesystem problem. Restore the page from a replica or backup; do not zero_damaged_pages unless you have accepted data loss.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run code/m02_page_inspect.sql steps 1 to 3 against loan_applications. Done when you can point at pd_lower, pd_upper and say how many bytes are free on page 0.
  2. (easy) Run step 6 (alignment). Done when you have the two sizes and can explain the difference in bytes per row from alignment rules.
  3. (medium) Insert 200,000 rows into a scratch table with a 3 KB text column. Compare pg_relation_size of the main table and of its TOAST table. Change the column to STORAGE EXTERNAL, rewrite the table (VACUUM FULL) and compare again. Done when you can explain where each byte lives.
  4. (medium) Run a SELECT count(*) on a table larger than shared_buffers / 4 with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) twice. Note that shared read stays high on the second run. Done when you can explain the ring buffer behaviour.
  5. (hard) With pageinspect, update one row 5 times in separate transactions without VACUUM. Dump heap_page_items after each. Then run VACUUM loan_applications and dump again. Done when you can describe the chain of t_ctid pointers, the LP_DEAD/LP_REDIRECT line pointers, and what VACUUM removed.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Describe the layout of a PostgreSQL heap page. A: An 8 KB block with a 24-byte header (LSN, checksum, flags, pd_lower, pd_upper, pd_special), then an array of 4-byte line pointers growing downward from the header, free space in the middle, and tuples growing upward from the end. Indexes point at (block, line pointer), so tuples can be moved within the page during compaction without touching indexes.

Q: What is a TID and why is it indirect? A: A tuple identifier is (block number, line pointer index). It is what index entries store. The line pointer holds the actual byte offset, so compaction can move the tuple and only update the line pointer, keeping all index entries valid.

Q: What is TOAST? A: The mechanism for column values too big for one page. When a tuple exceeds about 2 KB, large variable-length columns are compressed and, if still too big, stored out of line in a TOAST table in roughly 2 KB chunks, with a pointer left in the main tuple. Reading a toasted column means extra index lookups into the TOAST table, so avoid selecting large columns you do not need.

Q: What does the visibility map do? A: Two bits per heap page: all-visible and all-frozen. VACUUM skips all-visible pages, which makes vacuuming large static tables cheap, and index-only scans can skip the heap fetch for pages marked all-visible. Any modification clears the bits.

Q: How does the buffer pool decide what to evict? A: Clock sweep: a hand walks the buffer array, decrementing each buffer's usage count (0 to 5), and takes the first unpinned buffer with count 0. Dirty victims are written out first, after making sure WAL up to the page's LSN is flushed. The background writer keeps clean buffers available so backends rarely wait on that write.

Q: Is data on disk after COMMIT returns? A: The WAL record is, because COMMIT fdatasyncs WAL with synchronous_commit = on. The data pages are not; they stay dirty in shared buffers and reach disk on eviction or at the next checkpoint. Crash recovery replays WAL from the last checkpoint to rebuild them.

Q: Why does column order in CREATE TABLE affect table size? A: Each type has an alignment requirement (int8 needs 8 bytes, int4 needs 4, bool 1) and the engine inserts padding exactly as a C compiler does for structs. Declaring 8-byte columns first, then 4, then 2, then 1-byte, then variable-length minimises padding.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Tables are files of 8 KB slotted pages; rows never move between pages without a new TID.
  • Page = 24-byte header, line pointer array growing down, tuples growing up, optional special space.
  • Tuple = 24-byte header (xmin, xmax, ctid, infomask) + null bitmap + aligned columns.
  • Alignment padding is real; order columns by descending alignment.
  • TOAST compresses and moves big values out of line; SELECT * pays for them.
  • FSM finds pages with room; VM lets VACUUM and index-only scans skip pages.
  • Seq scan reads pages in order, uses a ring buffer for big tables, relies on OS read-ahead.
  • Row store (PostgreSQL) for OLTP; column store for analytics.
  • Buffer pool: pin, content lock, clock-sweep eviction, background writer, double caching with the OS.
  • pd_lsn ties pages to WAL: no dirty page hits disk before its WAL does. fsync failure = PANIC.

docs.title: 3. B-tree indexes in depth
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
An index is a second, smaller, sorted copy of some columns, with a pointer from each entry back to the row it came from. Because it is sorted, you can find an entry by halving the search space repeatedly instead of reading everything. Because it is stored as a tree of pages where each page holds hundreds of entries, three or four page reads find one row among hundreds of millions.

The analogy: a printed phone book is a B-tree index on (surname, first name). You open it roughly in the middle, see "M", jump forward, see "Ra", jump to the right page, scan a few lines. Four looks instead of reading 2000 pages. But notice: the phone book is useless if you know only the first name. Column order in a composite index is exactly this problem, and it is the heart of the "login path doing full scans" story on your resume.

Every index you add speeds up some reads and slows down every write to that table, because the sorted copy must be maintained. Senior engineers know both halves.

docs.title: 2.1 Structure on disk
docs.text:
PostgreSQL's default index type is a B+tree (all data in leaves, internal pages hold only separators), of the Lehman and Yao variant: every page has a pointer to its right sibling and a high key (an upper bound on what the page may contain), which lets readers cope with a concurrent page split without locking the whole tree.

 block 0: meta page  (root block number, tree height, version)

                  +--------------------------+
 level 2 (root)   |  k1 | k2 | k3 | ... hk   |          internal: (separator key, child block)
                  +--+-----+-----+-----------+
                     |     |     |
          +----------+     |     +-----------+
          v                v                 v
 level 1  +---------+ <-> +---------+ <-> +---------+   siblings linked left/right
          | ... hk  |     | ... hk  |     | ... hk  |
          +--+--+---+     +--+--+---+     +---------+
             |  |            |  |
 level 0     v  v            v  v
 (leaves)  +--------------+ <-> +--------------+ <-> ...   leaf: (key, heap TID) in key order
           | k,tid k,tid  |     | k,tid k,tid  |
           +--------------+     +--------------+

Each index page is 8 KB with the same slotted layout as a heap page; the special space at the end holds BTPageOpaqueData: left and right sibling block numbers, level, flags (leaf, root, deleted, half-dead). An index tuple is an 8-byte header (6-byte heap TID + 2 bytes of length/flags) followed by the key columns, aligned. For a bigint key that is 16 bytes, so a leaf page holds about 400 entries (fewer with the 10% default free space). Since PostgreSQL 13, duplicate keys in a leaf are stored once with a posting list of TIDs (deduplication), which shrinks indexes on low-cardinality columns a lot.

Fan-out and height. If a page holds roughly 400 entries, a tree of height 3 (root, one internal level, leaves) addresses 400 x 400 x 400 = 64 million entries; height 4 reaches 25 billion. A lookup reads one page per level plus the heap page: 4 or 5 page reads for a row in a 400-million-row table. The root and the first internal level are almost always in shared_buffers, so in practice a point lookup costs 1 or 2 real I/Os. This is the number to quote in interviews.

Search. _bt_search() starts at the root, binary-searches the separator keys on each page to pick the child, descends to a leaf, then binary-searches within the leaf for the first matching entry. A range scan then walks right along the sibling pointers reading leaves in order: this is why ORDER BY indexed_col can be satisfied with no sort.

docs.title: 2.2 Page splits
docs.text:
A leaf is full; a new key must go in. The leaf is split into two: by default roughly 50/50 by space, except when inserting at the rightmost end (ascending keys such as a bigserial or a timestamp), where the split leaves the old page full and starts a fresh right page (the "fillfactor" split, 90% by default). A new separator key is inserted into the parent; if the parent is full, it splits too, and so on up; splitting the root adds a level. Splits are WAL-logged as one atomic record. Costs: a split copies half a page, writes two index pages and one parent page, and leaves two half-empty pages, which is one source of index bloat.

Random keys (UUID v4, hashes) split everywhere in the tree and keep every leaf around 50 to 75% full; monotonically increasing keys append to the right edge and keep leaves near 90% full with fewer splits. This is a real reason to prefer bigint identity keys or time-ordered UUIDs (v7) over random UUIDs for high-insert tables.

docs.title: 2.3 Scan types the planner can choose
docs.text:
Scan What it does When Index Scan descend, then for each matching entry fetch the heap tuple immediately few rows, or ORDER BY needs index order Index Only Scan like Index Scan but skips the heap fetch when the VM says the page is all-visible all needed columns are in the index Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan collect all matching TIDs into a bitmap sorted by page, then read heap pages in physical order many rows (hundreds to a few %), or combining several indexes with AND/OR Seq Scan read the whole heap large fraction of rows, or no usable index

The Bitmap scan exists because fetching 50,000 heap tuples in index order means 50,000 random page reads with repeats; sorting the TIDs by page first turns that into one sequential-ish pass. When the bitmap would exceed work_mem it becomes lossy: it remembers only pages, not tuples, and every tuple on those pages is rechecked ("Recheck Cond" in EXPLAIN).

docs.title: 2.4 Covering indexes and INCLUDE
docs.text:
An index covers a query when every column the query needs is in the index, so the heap need not be touched (given all-visible pages). Two ways:

-- key columns only: all are searchable and sorted
CREATE INDEX ON users (login_code, branch_code, status);

-- INCLUDE (PostgreSQL 11+): payload columns stored in leaf tuples only,
-- not part of the key: narrower internal pages, cannot be searched/sorted on,
-- but allows UNIQUE on (login_code, branch_code) while still covering status.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (login_code, branch_code) INCLUDE (status, password_hash);

Check with EXPLAIN: Index Only Scan ... Heap Fetches: 0. If Heap Fetches is high, the table needs a VACUUM to set visibility map bits. Covering indexes trade index size and write cost for avoiding a heap read per row, which is a big win for hot point lookups like a login check.

docs.title: 2.5 Composite index column order: the rules
docs.text:
An index on (a, b, c) is sorted by a, then b within equal a, then c. It can efficiently serve a condition on a leftmost prefix: a; a, b; a, b, c. It cannot efficiently serve b alone or b, c (PostgreSQL 16 would have to scan the whole index; skip scan arrived in 18). Rules, in priority order:

  1. Equality columns first. Columns compared with = in the WHERE clause go leftmost. Among them, put the most selective first only if you also need prefix queries on it; otherwise order does not matter much for a full-match lookup.
  2. Then one range column. <, >, BETWEEN, LIKE 'abc%'. After a range condition, the remaining index columns cannot narrow the scan (they are not sorted within the range), only filter rows that are already read.
  3. Then ORDER BY columns, in the same direction, so the sort disappears.
  4. Then INCLUDE what you merely need to output.

Example: WHERE branch_code = $1 AND status = 'ACTIVE' AND created_at > $2 ORDER BY created_at wants (branch_code, status, created_at). An index (created_at, branch_code, status) would scan every row after $2 and filter: often ten to a hundred times more pages.

docs.title: 2.6 Selectivity and when the planner refuses the index
docs.text:
Selectivity is the fraction of rows a condition matches. An index lookup costs roughly (tree height + matching leaf pages + one random heap read per matching row). A seq scan costs (number of heap pages, sequentially). With random_page_cost = 4 and seq_page_cost = 1, once a condition matches more than a few percent of rows, random heap fetches cost more than reading everything. The planner then correctly picks Seq Scan or Bitmap Heap Scan even though an index exists. An index on a boolean or a status column with 3 values is rarely used on its own; a partial index (WHERE status = 'PENDING') on the rare value is the right tool.

The planner's estimate comes from pg_statistic (module 06): n_distinct, most common values and their frequencies, a histogram. Stale statistics give wrong selectivity and wrong plans.

docs.title: 2.7 The login path that did full scans
docs.text:
Your resume says the login latency bottleneck came from full-table scans, because the tables were keyed by business codes rather than surrogate IDs. Here is the mechanism, so you can explain it precisely.

The user table came from a Berkeley DB layout where the record key was a packed business code (say branch_code || user_code). In the relational schema it got a surrogate id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, and the business codes became ordinary columns. The login procedure, ported from the old record-lookup logic, queried:

SELECT id, password_hash, status, failed_attempts
FROM app_users
WHERE user_code = $1 AND branch_code = $2;

With a primary key on id only, the planner has no index on (user_code, branch_code), so it does a Seq Scan of the whole table on every login, plus similar scans on the role and branch tables it joined. On a single node with a small table this is a few milliseconds and nobody notices. On a multi-node YugabyteDB cluster the table is hash-sharded across nodes, so a sequential scan fans out to every tablet on every node and merges, and the latency is tens to hundreds of milliseconds per statement, times the number of statements in the login path.

The fix was a unique composite index on the natural key with INCLUDE for the columns the login needs, so the lookup is an index-only point read on exactly one tablet:

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX app_users_login_idx
    ON app_users (branch_code, user_code)
    INCLUDE (password_hash, status, failed_attempts);

Note the order: both are equality columns, so either order serves the login; branch_code first also serves "all users in a branch" queries. Module 06 walks the EXPLAIN plans before and after; module 11 explains what hash sharding does to this index on YugabyteDB.

Second part of the same story: implicit casts. If user_code is varchar and the application bound the parameter as bigint, the condition becomes user_code::bigint = $1 or user_code = $1::text depending on the driver; the first form cannot use a varchar index at all. Always bind parameters with the column's type (module 07).

docs.title: 2.8 Other index types, briefly
docs.text:
Type Structure Use it for Not for Hash hash buckets of TIDs equality on long values where a B-tree would be wide; WAL-logged since 10 ranges, ordering, multi-column GIN inverted index: each element/token -> posting list of TIDs jsonb @>, arrays @>/&&, full-text @@, trigram LIKE '%x%' point lookups on scalars; slower updates (uses a pending list) GiST balanced tree of bounding predicates (generalised search tree) geometry, ranges (&&), nearest-neighbour ORDER BY <->, exclusion constraints plain equality SP-GiST space-partitioned tree (quad tree, k-d tree, radix tree) points, IP ranges, text prefixes general use BRIN per block range (default 128 pages) min/max summary huge append-only tables where the column correlates with physical order (timestamps) random data; it is tiny but lossy

B-tree handles 95% of OLTP needs. Mention the others by name and one use case each.

docs.title: 2.9 Index bloat and HOT updates
docs.text:
Bloat. Deleting a row leaves its index entries until VACUUM removes them; even then the space stays in half-empty pages, because a B-tree page is only recycled when completely empty. Indexes on columns that are updated often, or on tables with heavy churn, grow to several times their ideal size. Measure with pgstatindex('idx_name'): avg_leaf_density under 50% and a large leaf_fragmentation say rebuild. Rebuild online with REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL 12+). PostgreSQL 14 added bottom-up index deletion: before splitting a page, the B-tree tries to remove entries that point at dead heap tuples, which greatly reduces bloat from non-HOT updates.

HOT (heap-only tuple) updates. An UPDATE normally creates a new heap tuple and a new entry in every index on the table, because the new tuple has a new TID. If (a) no indexed column changed and (b) the new tuple fits on the same heap page, PostgreSQL skips the index updates: the new tuple is marked HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE, the old one HOT_UPDATED, and the old tuple's t_ctid points at the new one. Index entries still point at the old slot; readers follow the chain within the page. When the old version dies, pruning turns its line pointer into LP_REDIRECT straight to the live version. Result: updating last_login_at on a user row costs one heap page write and zero index writes, as long as last_login_at is not indexed and the page has room.

Two design consequences: do not index columns that change on every update unless you must; and set a lower fillfactor (e.g. 80) on hot update tables so pages keep room for new versions. Watch n_tup_hot_upd / n_tup_upd in pg_stat_user_tables.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m03_index_demos.sql builds a 2 million row user table and demonstrates each idea.

-- A user table shaped like the login story: surrogate PK, business codes as columns
CREATE TABLE app_users (
    id              bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    branch_code     text    NOT NULL,
    user_code       text    NOT NULL,
    password_hash   text    NOT NULL,
    status          text    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
    failed_attempts int     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    last_login_at   timestamptz,
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
INSERT INTO app_users (branch_code, user_code, password_hash, status)
SELECT 'BR' || lpad((g % 500)::text, 4, '0'),            -- 500 branches
       'U'  || lpad(g::text, 8, '0'),
       md5(g::text),
       CASE WHEN g % 50 = 0 THEN 'LOCKED' ELSE 'ACTIVE' END
FROM generate_series(1, 2000000) g;
ANALYZE app_users;

-- 1. Before: Seq Scan. Note "Rows Removed by Filter" and the buffer count.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, password_hash, status FROM app_users
WHERE user_code = 'U00123456' AND branch_code = 'BR0456';

-- 2. The fix: unique composite index on the natural key, covering the login columns.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX app_users_login_idx
    ON app_users (branch_code, user_code) INCLUDE (password_hash, status, failed_attempts);
VACUUM app_users;   -- set visibility map bits so the index-only scan skips the heap

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT password_hash, status FROM app_users
WHERE user_code = 'U00123456' AND branch_code = 'BR0456';
-- expect: Index Only Scan using app_users_login_idx ... Heap Fetches: 0, Buffers: shared hit=4

-- 3. Leftmost prefix: branch alone uses the index; user_code alone cannot.
EXPLAIN SELECT count(*) FROM app_users WHERE branch_code = 'BR0456';     -- index
EXPLAIN SELECT count(*) FROM app_users WHERE user_code  = 'U00123456';   -- seq scan (or parallel seq scan)

-- 4. Tree height and fan-out
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;
SELECT * FROM bt_metap('app_users_login_idx');           -- "level" = height - 1
SELECT type, live_items, avg_item_size, free_size
FROM bt_page_stats('app_users_login_idx', (SELECT root FROM bt_metap('app_users_login_idx')));

-- 5. Selectivity: the planner ignores an index on a low-cardinality column...
CREATE INDEX app_users_status_idx ON app_users (status);
EXPLAIN SELECT count(*) FROM app_users WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';   -- 98% of rows: seq scan
EXPLAIN SELECT count(*) FROM app_users WHERE status = 'LOCKED';   -- 2%: bitmap or index scan
-- ... and a partial index is the right tool for the rare value
DROP INDEX app_users_status_idx;
CREATE INDEX app_users_locked_idx ON app_users (branch_code) WHERE status = 'LOCKED';

-- 6. Implicit cast breaks the index
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE user_code = 123456;                   -- ERROR or cast of column
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE user_code::bigint = 123456;           -- seq scan, cannot use idx
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE branch_code = 'BR0456' AND user_code = 'U' || lpad('123456', 8, '0');  -- fine

-- 7. HOT updates: an update that does not touch indexed columns
SELECT n_tup_upd, n_tup_hot_upd FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'app_users';
UPDATE app_users SET last_login_at = now() WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 1000;
SELECT n_tup_upd, n_tup_hot_upd FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'app_users';
-- hot_upd should rise by ~1000. Now update an indexed column:
UPDATE app_users SET status = 'LOCKED' WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 1000;
SELECT n_tup_upd, n_tup_hot_upd FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'app_users';
-- hot_upd does not rise: status is in the INCLUDE list, so every index got a new entry

-- 8. Bloat measurement and online rebuild
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;
SELECT avg_leaf_density, leaf_fragmentation FROM pgstatindex('app_users_login_idx');
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY app_users_login_idx;

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Concurrency without tree locks (Lehman and Yao). A reader descending the tree holds a shared lock on one page at a time and releases it before locking the child ("lock coupling" is not used going down). If a split happens in between, the reader may land on a page whose high key is less than its search key; it then follows the right-sibling link until it finds the right page. The high key and right link make this safe. Writers hold an exclusive lock on the leaf while inserting, and on the parent only while inserting the new separator. The result: readers never block on the root, and the tree scales to many cores. Berkeley DB's B-tree, by comparison, uses page-level locks held for the transaction's duration in transactional mode, which is one reason it deadlocks more often under concurrent writers (module 10).

Index entries and MVCC. Index tuples have no xmin/xmax. An index entry exists for every heap tuple version that was ever indexed, visible or not. That is why an Index Scan must fetch the heap tuple (to check visibility) unless the visibility map says the whole page is visible, and why dead heap tuples leave dead index entries behind until VACUUM. The LP_DEAD hint bit in index pages (set by a scan that found the heap tuple dead) lets later inserts skip over or remove those entries cheaply ("simple index deletion").

Unique indexes and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. Uniqueness is checked at insert time by searching the leaf for the same key and checking the visibility of each matching heap tuple. If a matching tuple was inserted by an uncommitted transaction, the inserter waits for that transaction (this is the "waits on another session's insert" you can see in pg_locks as a transaction-id lock). ON CONFLICT uses speculative insertion: insert the heap tuple, try to insert the index entry, and if a conflict appears, super-delete the heap tuple and take the alternative path.

Deduplication and posting lists (13+). When a leaf page is about to split, the engine first tries to merge duplicate keys into one entry with a sorted TID list. For an index on status with 3 values this cuts the index to a fraction of its size and makes bitmap scans faster. It is off for unique indexes except as a bloat control for non-HOT updates.

Suffix truncation (12+). Internal pages store only as much of a key as is needed to separate children, so an index on (branch_code, user_code) has small internal tuples and high fan-out even if leaf tuples are wide. The heap TID is treated as a tiebreaker column so that duplicates are stored in TID order, which makes VACUUM's deletion of entries efficient.

Why a B-tree and not a hash by default. Hash indexes are O(1) for equality but cannot do ranges, prefix matches, sorts, or multi-column prefix use, and they do not shrink. A B-tree does equality in 3 to 4 page reads anyway, nearly all from cache. The constant factor difference is negligible; the flexibility is not.

Collation. text comparisons under a non-C collation (en_US.UTF-8) use strcoll, which is slow and which does not let LIKE 'abc%' use a plain B-tree (the ordering is not bytewise). Use COLLATE "C" on code-like columns, or create the index with text_pattern_ops. Also, glibc collation changes between OS versions have corrupted indexes after upgrades (the sort order changed under the index); PostgreSQL 15+ tracks collation versions and warns.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Index every foreign key column that you join or delete through; PostgreSQL does not do it for you (unlike Oracle's recommendation and SQL Server, which also do not; MySQL InnoDB does). A DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1 without an index on loan_applications.customer_id seq-scans the child table for the FK check, under a lock.
  • Unused indexes cost writes. pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 since the last stats reset on a production system means the index only costs you. Drop it (after checking replicas, where reads may differ).
  • Duplicate and redundant indexes: (a) is redundant with (a, b) for lookups on a. Review before adding.
  • CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in production, always: the plain form takes a SHARE lock that blocks writes for the duration. CONCURRENTLY does two table scans and waits for existing transactions; it can leave an INVALID index if interrupted, which you must drop and retry.
  • Index-only scans need VACUUM. A fresh bulk load has no VM bits set; the first queries do heap fetches for every row and look slow. Run VACUUM (not FULL) after a bulk load.
  • The 3 AM version: "login is slow since the deployment". pg_stat_statements shows the login SELECT with mean_exec_time up 50x and shared_blks_read huge; EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan; the deployment added a column to the query that is not in the covering index, or changed a parameter type so the index no longer matches. Fix the query or the index; ANALYZE.
  • On YugabyteDB the same mistakes cost far more because scans fan out across nodes (module 11).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run code/m03_index_demos.sql steps 1 to 3. Done when you have both EXPLAIN outputs saved and can read Buffers: shared hit for each.
  2. (easy) With bt_metap, find the height of app_users_login_idx and app_users_pkey. Done when you can compute the approximate fan-out from live_items on the root.
  3. (medium) Write three queries that need indexes on loan_applications: by (customer_id), by (status, submitted_at) for a work queue sorted by submitted_at, and by application_no. Design the minimum set of indexes, create them, and show with EXPLAIN that each query uses an index with no Sort node. Done when all three plans are index-driven.
  4. (medium) Measure HOT: update a non-indexed column 100,000 times on app_users with fillfactor 100 vs a copy with fillfactor = 80. Compare n_tup_hot_upd and pg_relation_size. Done when you can state the HOT ratio for each.
  5. (hard) Create a table with a random uuid primary key and one with a bigint identity key, insert 2 million rows into each, and compare index size (pg_relation_size), avg_leaf_density from pgstatindex, and insert time. Done when you can explain the difference in terms of page splits at the right edge versus everywhere.
  6. (hard) Reproduce the implicit-cast problem: with user_code text, bind a bigint parameter from the libpq program in module 01 (paramTypes[0] = 20). Observe the error or the plan, then fix the binding. Done when you can explain which side of the comparison gets cast and why that disables the index.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does a B-tree index find a row, and how many page reads does it take? A: Start at the root, binary-search the separator keys to choose a child, repeat down to a leaf, binary-search the leaf for the key, read the heap TID, fetch the heap page. Height is 3 or 4 for tables up to billions of rows because each 8 KB page holds hundreds of entries, so a point lookup is 4 or 5 page reads, of which the upper levels are nearly always cached.

Q: What is a covering index and what is INCLUDE for? A: A covering index contains every column a query needs, so the executor can answer from the index alone without visiting the heap (an Index Only Scan, if the visibility map says the pages are all-visible). INCLUDE adds payload columns to leaf entries without making them part of the key, which keeps the key unique and the internal pages narrow.

Q: How do you order columns in a composite index? A: Equality predicates first, then at most one range predicate, then ORDER BY columns in the same direction, then INCLUDE columns for output. The index can only use a leftmost prefix of its columns to narrow the scan; columns after a range predicate only filter.

Q: Why did your login query do a full table scan? A: The table carried a surrogate primary key, but the login looked up by the natural key (branch code plus user code) that had no index, so every login was a sequential scan, which on a hash-sharded YugabyteDB cluster fans out to every node. A unique composite index on the natural key with INCLUDE for the needed columns turned it into a single-tablet index-only point read.

Q: Why does the planner sometimes ignore an index? A: Because the estimated selectivity is low: when a condition matches more than a few percent of rows, one random heap read per matching row costs more than scanning the table sequentially. That is correct behaviour. Fix the query, use a partial index on the rare value, or update statistics if the estimate is wrong.

Q: What is a HOT update? A: An update where no indexed column changed and the new tuple fits on the same heap page. The engine skips all index insertions; the old tuple's ctid points to the new version and readers follow the chain within the page. It makes updates of non-indexed columns far cheaper and is a reason not to index columns that change on every write, and to leave fillfactor headroom.

Q: What causes index bloat and how do you fix it? A: Deletes and non-HOT updates leave dead entries; page splits leave half-empty pages; B-tree pages are only recycled when empty. Measure with pgstatindex (leaf density), rebuild online with REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, and reduce the cause: fewer indexed volatile columns, HOT-friendly fillfactor, timely VACUUM.

Q: When would you use GIN, GiST or BRIN instead of B-tree? A: GIN for containment and membership on composite values: jsonb, arrays, full-text, trigram search. GiST for spatial and range overlap, nearest neighbour, and exclusion constraints. BRIN for very large append-only tables where the column correlates with physical order, such as timestamps, where a tiny lossy summary per block range is enough.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• B+tree: meta page, root, internal separators, linked leaves holding (key, heap TID).
  • Fan-out of hundreds gives height 3 to 4 for billions of rows; point lookup is 4 or 5 page reads.
  • Splits are 50/50 except at the right edge; random keys bloat, sequential keys pack.
  • Scan types: Index, Index Only (needs VM), Bitmap (many rows, sorted by page), Seq.
  • Composite order: equality, one range, ORDER BY, INCLUDE. Leftmost prefix only.
  • Low selectivity means the planner is right to skip the index; partial indexes for rare values.
  • The login full scan: natural key not indexed; fix = unique composite covering index.
  • Implicit casts on the column side disable indexes; bind the right type.
  • HOT updates skip index maintenance when no indexed column changes and the page has room.
  • Index entries have no MVCC info; dead entries wait for VACUUM; rebuild bloat with REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.

docs.title: 4. Write-ahead logging and crash recovery
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A database must survive the power going out in the middle of a write. Writing the changed page directly is not safe: a page write is not atomic, and a transaction usually touches several pages, so a crash can leave half of them changed. The solution every serious database uses is to first append a description of the change to a log file, force that log to disk, and only then (lazily, whenever convenient) write the pages. After a crash, the log is replayed from the last known-good point and the pages are repaired. This is write-ahead logging (WAL).

The analogy is the bound ledger in a bank branch: before any clerk changes a customer's folder, the change is written in the ledger in pen. The folders may be updated later in a batch. If the building floods, the folders are reconstructed from the ledger. The ledger is append-only, so writing to it is fast (the pen never jumps around the page), and it is the one thing that is never allowed to be lost.

WAL buys three things at once: durability (commit means "it is in the ledger"), fast writes (one sequential append instead of many random page writes per commit), and, as a bonus, replication (ship the ledger to another building and replay it there).

docs.title: 2.1 The WAL stream and LSNs
docs.text:
WAL is one logical byte stream, append-only, cut into segment files of 16 MB in $PGDATA/pg_wal/ named like 000000010000000000000042 (timeline, high 32 bits, segment number). A position in the stream is a Log Sequence Number (LSN): a 64-bit byte offset, printed as two hex halves, e.g. 0/1A2B3C40. pg_current_wal_lsn() shows where the stream currently ends; pg_lsn is a SQL type you can subtract to get bytes.

Every WAL record has a header (total length, transaction id, LSN of the previous record, resource manager id, CRC) plus zero or more block references (which relation and block this record modifies, optionally carrying a full copy of the page) and record-specific data. Resource managers are the code modules that know how to replay their records: Heap, Heap2, Btree, Hash, Gin, Gist, Transaction, XLOG (checkpoints), Storage (file create/truncate), and so on.

 a committed UPDATE of one indexed column, as WAL records:
   Heap   UPDATE      blkref 0: rel 1663/16384/16432 blk 1234 (old tuple's page)
                      blkref 1: ... blk 5678 (new tuple's page, if different)
   Btree  INSERT_LEAF blkref 0: rel .../16440 blk 77 (index leaf)
   Transaction COMMIT  xid 48213, timestamp

docs.title: 2.2 The write path
docs.text:
backend                                    WAL writer / any committer
 ---------                                  ------------------------
 modify page in shared_buffers (exclusive content lock)
 XLogInsert(record)  -> copies record into wal_buffers (shared memory ring)
 stamp page->pd_lsn = record LSN            
 mark buffer dirty, release lock
 ...
 COMMIT: XLogInsert(COMMIT record)
         XLogFlush(commit LSN):  write() wal_buffers up to that LSN to the segment file,
                                 then fdatasync()                       <- the durable moment
         wait for sync replicas if synchronous_standby_names is set
         update pg_xact: xid = committed
         return "COMMIT" to client

The dirty data page has not been written. It will be written by the checkpointer, the background writer, or a backend evicting it, and only after XLogFlush(pd_lsn) guarantees the WAL that describes it is already durable. That single invariant (log before page) is what "write-ahead" means.

Settings that shape this path:

Setting Default Meaning wal_level replica minimal (no replication), replica (streaming), logical (logical decoding too) synchronous_commit on off: return before fdatasync (may lose the last few hundred ms of commits on crash, never corrupt); local; remote_write; remote_apply wal_sync_method fdatasync (Linux) how WAL is forced to disk; open_datasync uses O_DSYNC writes wal_buffers 1/32 of shared_buffers, max 16 MB in-memory ring; full ring forces early writes wal_writer_delay 200 ms how often the WAL writer flushes in the background commit_delay / commit_siblings 0 / 5 explicit group-commit tuning (rarely needed) full_page_writes on see 2.4 wal_compression off compress full-page images (pglz, lz4, zstd)

docs.title: 2.3 Checkpoints
docs.text:
A checkpoint is the point from which recovery starts. Doing one means: write every dirty buffer in shared_buffers to its data file, fsync all those files, then write a CHECKPOINT record to WAL and store its redo pointer (the LSN at which the checkpoint began) in $PGDATA/global/pg_control. Everything before the redo pointer is now reflected in the data files, so WAL segments before it can be recycled (renamed and reused as future segments).

Checkpoints are triggered by time (checkpoint_timeout, default 5 min) or WAL volume (max_wal_size, default 1 GB, a soft limit). They are spread out over checkpoint_completion_target (default 0.9) of the interval so the I/O is a steady trickle instead of a burst. log_checkpoints = on (default since 15) logs each one with buffer counts and sync times; read them.

Trade-off: frequent checkpoints mean shorter recovery and less WAL kept, but more page writes and more full-page images (next section). Most production systems raise max_wal_size to several GB and checkpoint_timeout to 15 to 30 minutes.

docs.title: 2.4 Full-page writes and torn pages
docs.text:
An 8 KB page is written as two or more 4 KB OS pages (or sixteen 512-byte sectors). A crash in the middle leaves a torn page: half old, half new. Replaying a delta WAL record ("set byte 40 of tuple 7 to 'A'") onto a torn page produces garbage. Therefore: the first time a page is modified after a checkpoint, the WAL record carries a full-page image (FPI) of the whole page instead of a delta. Recovery restores the image unconditionally, then applies later deltas on top. Subsequent modifications until the next checkpoint log only deltas, because recovery will have restored the page from the FPI first.

Consequences: WAL volume right after a checkpoint spikes (every touched page costs 8 KB); a system that updates many distinct pages generates WAL dominated by FPIs. pg_stat_wal.wal_fpi counts them. Longer checkpoint intervals reduce FPIs. wal_compression = lz4 shrinks them cheaply. full_page_writes = off is only safe on storage that guarantees atomic 8 KB writes (ZFS with matching record size is the usual case).

docs.title: 2.5 Group commit and why WAL makes writes sequential
docs.text:
Each fdatasync costs a device round trip: around 0.1 ms on a datacentre NVMe, 1 to 2 ms on a SATA SSD, 5 to 10 ms on a spinning disk (typical figures). If every commit paid its own fsync, a spinning disk could not exceed about 100 commits per second. Group commit fixes this naturally: XLogFlush(lsn) flushes everything in wal_buffers up to the latest written LSN, so when ten backends commit within the same millisecond, the first one's fsync covers them all, and the others see that the flushed LSN already exceeds theirs and return immediately. Commit throughput becomes (fsyncs per second) x (commits arriving per fsync), which scales with concurrency. commit_delay can add a small sleep to gather more siblings; it rarely helps on SSDs.

The write pattern on disk is therefore: one sequential append stream (WAL) that is fsynced often, plus data pages written in large sorted batches at checkpoint time. Random writes are deferred and batched. That is the whole performance argument for WAL and it is why every transactional store since ARIES does it this way. LSM trees (module 10) push the same idea further by making all writes sequential.

docs.title: 2.6 Crash recovery (redo)
docs.text:
On startup, StartupXLOG() reads pg_control. If the cluster was not shut down cleanly, it takes the redo pointer of the last checkpoint and replays WAL from there to the end:

  1. Read the next record; verify its CRC. A bad CRC or missing record means end of WAL.
  2. For each block reference: if it carries an FPI, overwrite the page with it. Otherwise read the page and apply the delta only if page->pd_lsn < record LSN. This makes redo idempotent: a page that was already written with this change before the crash is not changed twice.
  3. Track transaction status: COMMIT records mark xids committed in pg_xact; xids with no COMMIT record by end of WAL are simply left as in-progress, which MVCC treats as aborted.

Note what is missing: there is no undo phase. PostgreSQL never needs to roll back changes of uncommitted transactions on disk, because MVCC leaves the old row version in place and the new version is invisible unless its xid is committed (module 05). Abort is just "do not record a commit". Oracle, SQL Server and Berkeley DB keep undo information (rollback segments, the log's before-images) and have an undo phase; PostgreSQL's cost for this simplicity is VACUUM.

Recovery time is proportional to WAL since the last checkpoint, which is bounded by max_wal_size. A 4 GB max_wal_size on fast storage replays in well under a minute.

docs.title: 2.7 Replication reuses WAL
docs.text:
Streaming (physical) replication. A standby runs continuous recovery: a walreceiver process connects to the primary's walsender, which streams WAL records as they are written. The standby applies them exactly like crash recovery, forever. With hot_standby = on it also serves read-only queries. The standby is a byte-for-byte copy of the primary, same major version required. synchronous_standby_names makes COMMIT wait until the standby has received (remote_write), flushed (on), or applied (remote_apply) the commit record.

Replication slots make the primary keep WAL until a named consumer has confirmed it. A dead consumer with a slot is the classic cause of pg_wal filling the disk; max_slot_wal_keep_size caps the damage.

Logical replication decodes WAL into row-level changes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE with column values) using wal_level = logical and a plugin (pgoutput for built-in publications, or wal2json, Debezium). It can replicate a subset of tables, across major versions, and into other systems. This is also the mechanism behind change data capture (CDC) cutovers in module 12.

docs.title: 2.8 Point-in-time recovery
docs.text: Take a base backup (pg_basebackup, a copy of the data directory taken while running, with the WAL needed to make it consistent) and archive every WAL segment as it fills (archive_mode = on, archive_command or archive_library). To recover to 14:32:10 yesterday: restore the base backup, set restore_command and recovery_target_time, start. The server replays archived WAL until that time and stops, creating a new timeline (history branches so that WAL after the recovery point is not confused with the new future). This is how you undo a DELETE FROM customers without a WHERE clause: not by rolling back, but by replaying history up to one second before it.

docs.title: 2.9 Berkeley DB's log and transactional subsystem compared
docs.text:
Berkeley DB has the same architecture under different names, which is why your migration source felt familiar:

Concept Berkeley DB PostgreSQL Log files log.0000000001 ... in the environment home pg_wal/0000000100000000000000xx Position DB_LSN {file, offset} 64-bit LSN X/Y Logging style physical undo/redo: records carry before- and after-images redo only; no undo, MVCC provides rollback Enable DB_INIT_LOG | DB_INIT_TXN in DB_ENV->open always on Durability on commit txn->commit(0) fsyncs; DB_TXN_NOSYNC skips; DB_TXN_WRITE_NOSYNC writes without fsync synchronous_commit Checkpoint DB_ENV->txn_checkpoint(kbyte, min, flags), called by you or a thread you create checkpointer process, automatic Recovery you pass DB_RECOVER (normal) or DB_RECOVER_FATAL (catastrophic: replay all archived logs) at env open automatic at startup Log retention db_archive / DB_LOG_AUTO_REMOVE after checkpoint recycled after checkpoint unless slots/archive hold them Replication Berkeley DB HA (replication manager), log-shipping based streaming physical, logical

Two differences worth saying out loud. First, Berkeley DB's undo phase: after a crash it replays forward to redo committed transactions, then rolls back uncommitted ones using the before-images in the log. PostgreSQL skips that step entirely. Second, Berkeley DB leaves the operational discipline to the application: if your server never called txn_checkpoint, the log grew without bound and recovery took forever; if it opened without DB_RECOVER after a crash, it got a corrupt environment. PostgreSQL does both for you. That is a real argument in "why did you migrate", separate from the SQL argument.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m04_wal_inspect.sh runs these from the shell on WSL; here are the pieces.

-- 1. Where is the end of WAL, and which segment file is that?
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn(), pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn());

-- 2. How many WAL bytes does one transaction generate?
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before \gset
UPDATE loan_applications SET status = 'UNDER_REVIEW' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() - :'before'::pg_lsn AS wal_bytes;
-- run it twice: the first run after a checkpoint includes a full-page image (~8 KB),
-- the second only a delta (~100 bytes)

-- 3. Force a checkpoint and watch FPI count rise on the next write
CHECKPOINT;
SELECT wal_records, wal_fpi, wal_bytes FROM pg_stat_wal;
UPDATE loan_applications SET status = 'SUBMITTED' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT wal_records, wal_fpi, wal_bytes FROM pg_stat_wal;

-- 4. The page carries the LSN of its last change
SELECT lsn FROM page_header(get_raw_page('loan_applications', 0));

-- 5. Checkpoint state and settings
SELECT checkpoint_lsn, redo_lsn, timeline_id FROM pg_control_checkpoint();
SHOW checkpoint_timeout;  SHOW max_wal_size;  SHOW checkpoint_completion_target;

-- 6. Checkpoint activity since stats reset (16: pg_stat_bgwriter; 17 splits out pg_stat_checkpointer)
SELECT checkpoints_timed, checkpoints_req, buffers_checkpoint, buffers_backend
FROM pg_stat_bgwriter;

# 7. Decode the WAL records of your last transaction (run as the postgres OS user, or with read access)
SEG=$(psql -Atc "select pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn())" loans)
sudo /usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin/pg_waldump -p /var/lib/postgresql/16/main/pg_wal "$SEG" | tail -20
# expect lines like:
# rmgr: Heap  len (rec/tot): 54/8266, tx: 812, lsn: 0/01A2B3C8, prev 0/01A2B390,
#   desc: UPDATE off 3 xmax 812 flags 0x00 ; new off 9 xmax 0, blkref #0: rel 1663/16384/16432 blk 0 FPW
# rmgr: Transaction len 34/34 ... desc: COMMIT 2026-10-03 ...
# "FPW" marks the full-page image

# 8. Crash test (safe on a dev machine): kill -9 the postmaster mid-transaction and watch redo
psql loans -c "BEGIN; UPDATE loan_applications SET status='X' WHERE id < 100; SELECT pg_sleep(30); COMMIT;" &
sleep 2
sudo kill -9 $(head -1 /var/lib/postgresql/16/main/postmaster.pid)
sudo service postgresql start
sudo tail -30 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-16-main.log
# expect: "database system was interrupted", "redo starts at 0/...", "redo done at 0/...",
# and the uncommitted update is simply not there: no undo pass needed.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Inserting into wal_buffers without a global lock. XLogInsert first reserves space in the WAL stream under a short spinlock (insertpos_lck): it bumps a shared "current insert position" by the record length and gets back its start LSN. It then copies the record into the ring buffer without holding that lock, protected by one of NUM_XLOGINSERT_LOCKS (8) insertion locks that let XLogFlush know when all copies up to a position have finished. This is why many backends can generate WAL concurrently; the serial point is a few dozen instructions.

The WAL writer and the flush horizon. Three shared LSNs matter: insert (reserved), write (handed to write()), flush (fdatasynced). XLogFlush(X) checks if flush >= X; if not, it takes WALWriteLock, writes up to the current write-able position, fsyncs, and advances flush. Everyone waiting for an LSN below the new flush proceeds. That is the whole group-commit mechanism; there is no separate "group commit" code path.

Hint bits and WAL. When a backend reads a tuple and determines its inserting transaction committed, it sets HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED in the tuple header to spare future readers a pg_xact lookup. This dirties the page but writes no WAL record (the information is reconstructible). With data checksums on, however, a torn page with a changed hint bit would fail its checksum, so the engine logs an FPI the first time a page is hint-dirtied after a checkpoint (XLOG_FPI_FOR_HINT). Checksums therefore slightly increase WAL volume. This explains "why did a SELECT generate WAL?"

pg_xact and the commit record. Transaction status lives in pg_xact (formerly pg_clog), 2 bits per xid: in progress, committed, aborted, sub-committed. The COMMIT WAL record is what makes the commit durable; pg_xact pages are themselves written via the buffer manager style SLRU cache and protected by the same WAL-before-page rule. Visibility checks (module 05) consult pg_xact for xids not covered by hint bits.

Replay and the standby's view. The standby applies WAL in LSN order in a single startup process (parallel replay is still not in 16). Hot-standby queries can conflict with replay: a VACUUM record removing tuples the standby query still needs causes max_standby_streaming_delay to pause replay, or cancels the query ("canceling statement due to conflict with recovery"). hot_standby_feedback = on tells the primary which xids the standby still needs, at the cost of bloat on the primary.

What synchronous_commit = off really risks. The WAL writer flushes at least every wal_writer_delay (200 ms) and whenever a page of WAL fills. With off, a crash loses at most the commits of about the last 3 x 200 ms, and clients were told "COMMIT" for those. The data files are never inconsistent, because the WAL-before-page rule still holds; recovery simply ends earlier. For audit logs or idempotent bulk loads it is an acceptable 5x to 10x throughput trade; for a funds transfer it is not.

Timelines. After PITR or promotion, the server increments the timeline id (the first 8 hex digits of segment names). A .history file records the branch point. This prevents a recovered server from reading WAL from a future it did not have, and lets a demoted old primary be re-attached with pg_rewind.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Disk for WAL. Historically a separate spindle for pg_wal (symlink it) because its sequential, fsync-heavy pattern should not compete with random data reads. On NVMe this matters less, but a slow fsync (shared network storage, a VM with a write cache disabled) shows up as WALSync / WALWrite wait events and caps commit rate at a few hundred per second.
  • Checkpoint tuning symptom: checkpoints_req much higher than checkpoints_timed means max_wal_size is too small; the system is checkpointing on WAL volume, generating excess FPIs and I/O bursts. Raise max_wal_size, keep checkpoint_completion_target at 0.9.
  • pg_wal fills the disk (3 AM classic). Causes in order of likelihood: a replication slot whose consumer is dead (SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) FROM pg_replication_slots), archive_command failing (pg_stat_archiver.failed_count), a huge transaction. Fix the cause. Never rm in pg_wal: that is the ledger.
  • Testing recovery is part of having backups. A base backup you have never restored is not a backup. Schedule a monthly restore to a scratch host with recovery_target_time and compare row counts.
  • For the migration story: the Berkeley DB environment needed explicit checkpointing and DB_RECOVER discipline in your server's startup code; PostgreSQL/YugabyteDB handle it. And YugabyteDB (module 11) replaces PostgreSQL's WAL with a per-tablet Raft log, so durability is "a majority of replicas have the entry", not "fdatasync returned on one disk".
  • Synchronous replication latency: synchronous_commit = on with a sync standby adds one network round trip plus the standby's fsync to every commit. Across availability zones that is 1 to 2 ms; across regions 50 ms or more. Decide per transaction with SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off for the non-critical ones.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run snippet 2 twice: once right after CHECKPOINT, once immediately again. Done when you can explain the ~8 KB versus ~100 bytes difference.
  2. (easy) Run pg_waldump on the current segment and identify a Heap UPDATE record, its Btree companion (update an indexed column first), and the COMMIT record. Done when you can read blkref and FPW.
  3. (medium) Perform the kill -9 test in snippet 8. Read the log lines. Done when you can name the redo start LSN, the redo end LSN, and confirm the uncommitted UPDATE is absent with no undo.
  4. (medium) Measure commit throughput: a loop of 2000 single-row inserts each in its own transaction, with synchronous_commit = on then off. Then wrap all 2000 in one transaction. Done when you have three timings and can explain each in terms of fsync count.
  5. (hard) Set up PITR on your WSL instance: archive_mode = on, archive_command = 'cp %p /var/lib/postgresql/wal_archive/%f', take pg_basebackup -D /tmp/base -Fp -Xs, make some changes with timestamps, delete a table, then restore to a second data directory on port 5433 with recovery_target_time set to just before the delete. Done when the table is back in the restored instance and the new timeline id is visible in pg_control_checkpoint().

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is write-ahead logging and what problem does it solve? A: Every change is described in an append-only log record that is forced to disk before the modified data page is allowed to reach disk. After a crash, the log is replayed from the last checkpoint to repair the data files. It solves durability under non-atomic multi-page writes, and it turns random page writes into one sequential log stream plus deferred batched page writes.

Q: What happens between COMMIT and the data being durable? A: The backend writes a COMMIT record into the WAL buffers, then calls XLogFlush, which writes the buffers to the current WAL segment and fdatasyncs it. When that returns, the commit is durable and the client is told COMMIT. The modified heap and index pages are still only in shared buffers; they reach disk later at a checkpoint or on eviction.

Q: What is a checkpoint and why not checkpoint constantly? A: A checkpoint writes all dirty buffers to disk, fsyncs, and records a redo pointer so recovery can start from there and older WAL can be recycled. Checkpointing often shortens recovery and saves WAL space but costs page writes and, more importantly, more full-page images, because the first change to each page after a checkpoint must log the whole page.

Q: What are full-page writes for? A: Protection against torn pages. An 8 KB page write is not atomic, so a crash can leave it half updated; applying a delta onto it would corrupt it. The first modification of a page after each checkpoint logs the entire page, so recovery can restore a known-good image before applying deltas.

Q: How does PostgreSQL roll back an uncommitted transaction after a crash? A: It does not have to. There is no undo log. MVCC keeps the old row versions and the new ones are invisible unless their transaction is marked committed in pg_xact. Recovery only redoes; any transaction with no COMMIT record at the end of WAL is treated as aborted. VACUUM later removes its dead tuples.

Q: How does group commit work? A: XLogFlush flushes WAL up to the latest written position, not just the caller's LSN. When several backends commit concurrently, the first fsync covers all of them and the rest find their LSN already flushed. Commit throughput therefore scales with concurrency rather than being capped at one fsync per commit.

Q: How does replication use WAL? A: Physical streaming replication ships WAL records to a standby that applies them continuously as if in perpetual crash recovery, producing a byte-identical copy. Logical replication decodes the same WAL into row changes so a subset of tables can be replicated across versions or into other systems. Replication slots make the primary retain WAL until the consumer has it.

Q: How did Berkeley DB's logging differ from PostgreSQL's? A: Same write-ahead principle and LSNs, but Berkeley DB logs before- and after-images and runs an undo pass after redo; PostgreSQL logs redo only and relies on MVCC for rollback. Berkeley DB also leaves checkpointing and recovery invocation to the application, which is an operational burden a server database removes.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• WAL is an append-only stream of change records; LSN is a byte position in it.
  • Rule: a dirty page is never written before the WAL describing it is flushed (pd_lsn check).
