  • COMMIT = write COMMIT record + fdatasync WAL. Data pages are written later.
  • Checkpoint = flush all dirty pages, fsync, record redo pointer; recovery starts there.
  • First change to a page after a checkpoint logs a full-page image to beat torn pages.
  • Group commit falls out of flushing to the latest LSN; throughput scales with concurrency.
  • Redo is idempotent via LSN comparison; there is no undo phase thanks to MVCC.
  • Streaming replication is perpetual redo on another machine; logical replication decodes WAL to rows.
  • PITR = base backup + archived WAL + recovery target; creates a new timeline.
  • Berkeley DB: same ideas, undo/redo images, application-driven checkpoint and recovery.

docs.title: 5. Transactions, ACID and MVCC
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A transaction is a group of changes that either all happen or none happen, and that other users either see completely or not at all. The hard part is not the "all or nothing" (WAL and the commit record give you that). The hard part is isolation: hundreds of sessions reading and writing the same rows at once, each one expecting the database to behave as if it were alone.

Old databases did this with locks: a reader locks a row so a writer must wait, and a writer locks a row so readers must wait. That serialises everything. PostgreSQL (and Oracle, and YugabyteDB, and modern SQL Server with snapshot isolation) instead keep multiple versions of each row. A writer creates a new version; readers keep seeing the old version until the writer commits; nobody waits for anyone just to read. This is multi-version concurrency control (MVCC). The price is that old versions pile up and must be cleaned (VACUUM), and that "which version do I see?" becomes a precise question with a precise answer you must be able to state.

The analogy: a shared document with tracked changes. Each editor sees the document as it was when they opened it (their snapshot), plus their own edits. Others' pending edits are invisible until accepted (commit). A periodic cleanup (VACUUM) removes the history nobody can scroll back to anymore.

docs.title: 2.1 ACID, precisely
docs.text:
• Atomicity: all of a transaction's changes commit together or none do. Mechanism: a single COMMIT record in WAL flips all of them from invisible to visible at once; abort leaves no trace to undo because new versions were never marked committed.
  • Consistency: a transaction takes the database from one state satisfying all declared constraints (PK, FK, UNIQUE, CHECK, NOT NULL, triggers) to another. Mechanism: constraints are checked at statement end or, for DEFERRABLE constraints, at commit. Consistency is the property the application mostly owns; the database only checks what you declared.
  • Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate states, to the degree the isolation level promises. Mechanism: MVCC snapshots plus row and predicate locks.
  • Durability: a committed transaction survives crashes. Mechanism: WAL fdatasync before returning COMMIT (module 04); with synchronous replication, also a copy on another machine.

docs.title: 2.2 The anomalies and the isolation levels
docs.text:
Anomaly definitions, each in one line:

Anomaly What you observe Dirty read you read a row version another transaction has written but not committed Non-repeatable read you read a row twice in one transaction and get different values because someone committed in between Phantom read you run the same WHERE twice and the second run returns rows that were not there (or lacks rows that were) Lost update two transactions read the same row, both compute a new value, both write; one write silently overwrites the other Write skew two transactions each read a set of rows, each writes a different row based on what it read, and the combination violates an invariant neither saw broken (the classic: two doctors both go off call because each saw "at least one other doctor is on call")

PostgreSQL's levels and what each prevents:

Level Dirty Non-repeatable Phantom Lost update Write skew Snapshot taken READ UNCOMMITTED prevented (behaves as READ COMMITTED) no no no no per statement READ COMMITTED (default) prevented allowed allowed allowed (unless you lock) allowed per statement REPEATABLE READ prevented prevented prevented (stronger than the SQL standard requires) detected: concurrent update raises serialization_failure allowed at first statement SERIALIZABLE prevented prevented prevented detected detected via SSI, raises serialization_failure at first statement + predicate tracking

Important details for interviews:

  • PostgreSQL never does dirty reads. There is no way to see uncommitted data from another session.
  • READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot for every statement. Within one statement you see a consistent state; between statements you see newer commits. Two SELECTs in one transaction can disagree.
  • READ COMMITTED's UPDATE behaviour: if the row you are updating was changed and committed by someone else after your snapshot, PostgreSQL waits for them, then re-evaluates your WHERE clause on the new version (the "EvalPlanQual" mechanism) and updates that version. This is why UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 7 is safe at READ COMMITTED (the subtraction is applied to the latest version), but SELECT balance; ... UPDATE SET balance = <computed in application> is a lost update unless you SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
  • REPEATABLE READ gives you one snapshot for the whole transaction. If you try to update a row someone else updated after your snapshot, you get ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update (SQLSTATE 40001). Your application must retry.
  • SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL is Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI): snapshot isolation plus tracking of read/write dependencies to detect the patterns that could produce a non-serialisable outcome. It never blocks readers; it aborts one transaction instead. Any transaction at this level must be retryable.
  • Oracle's and YugabyteDB's "SERIALIZABLE" and SQL Server's "SNAPSHOT" are discussed in module 14 because they do not all mean the same thing.

docs.title: 2.3 MVCC in PostgreSQL: xmin, xmax, snapshots
docs.text:
Every tuple version carries (module 02): t_xmin (the transaction that created it), t_xmax (the transaction that deleted or replaced it, or 0), and hint bits in t_infomask. Transaction ids (xids) are 32-bit integers handed out sequentially from a shared counter when a transaction first writes (read-only transactions get no xid). Their commit status is in pg_xact.

A snapshot is three things:

  • xmin: the lowest xid still running when the snapshot was taken. Every xid below it is finished (committed or aborted) and can be judged from pg_xact alone.
  • xmax: one past the highest xid that had been assigned. Every xid at or above it started after the snapshot and is invisible, whatever it later does.
  • xip[]: the list of xids between xmin and xmax that were in progress at snapshot time.

SELECT pg_current_snapshot() prints it as xmin:xmax:xip1,xip2.

An xid X is visible to the snapshot if: X committed, and X < xmax, and X not in xip. (Or X is my own xid and the change was made by an earlier command than the current one; the command id t_cid handles that.)

Tuple visibility rule (HeapTupleSatisfiesMVCC, simplified but faithful):

visible(tuple, snapshot):
    if not visible_xid(tuple.xmin):          # inserter not committed-and-in-past from my view
        return false                           # (uncommitted, aborted, or started after snapshot)
    if tuple.xmax == 0 or xmax is lock-only:  # never deleted (xmax used only for row locks)
        return true
    if visible_xid(tuple.xmax):               # deleter committed and in my past
        return false                           # it is gone for me
    return true                               # deleter is in progress, aborted, or in my future: still there

Worked example. Snapshot 100:105:102. Tuples:

xmin xmax Visible? Why 95 0 yes inserter committed and < xmin; never deleted 95 103 (committed) no deleter 103 is not in xip and < xmax: its delete is in my past 95 102 (committed later) yes 102 was in progress at snapshot time (in xip): its delete is not in my view 104 (committed) 0 yes 104 < xmax and not in xip, committed: visible 106 (committed) 0 no 106 >= xmax: started after my snapshot 101 (aborted) 0 no inserter aborted

This is the single most asked internals question. Practice it until you can do the table in your head.

Two xids are reserved: 1 (bootstrap) and 2 (FrozenTransactionId, "visible to everyone, always").

docs.title: 2.4 VACUUM and bloat
docs.text:
An UPDATE writes a new version and sets xmax on the old one; a DELETE sets xmax. The old version is dead once no snapshot can see it: when its xmax is committed and below every active snapshot's xmin (the oldest xmin horizon). VACUUM:

  1. Scans heap pages not marked all-visible in the VM; collects dead tuple TIDs.
  2. Removes the matching entries from every index on the table (one pass per index, or in parallel workers for big tables).
  3. Marks those heap line pointers LP_UNUSED, compacts pages, updates FSM and VM.
  4. Freezes old tuples: any xmin older than vacuum_freeze_min_age (50 M xids) that is committed gets the HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN bits, meaning "treat as infinitely old". This is what makes wraparound survivable (next section).
  5. Updates pg_class.reltuples/relpages and, if run as VACUUM ANALYZE, the statistics.

VACUUM does not return space to the OS (except trailing empty pages) and does not block reads or writes; it takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, which only conflicts with DDL and other vacuums. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table into a new file (needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, blocks everything, needs 2x disk); use pg_repack for an online rewrite.

Autovacuum launches a worker for a table when dead_tuples > autovacuum_vacuum_threshold (50) + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (0.2) x reltuples. For a 100 M row table that is 20 M dead tuples before it starts: far too lax for hot tables. Set per table: ALTER TABLE app_users SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01). Autovacuum is throttled by autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay (2 ms) and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit (200); raising the limit is the usual first tuning step on busy systems (module 14).

What holds the horizon back (why "VACUUM ran but removed nothing"): any long-running transaction (even an idle BEGIN left open by a connection pool, idle in transaction), a hot standby with hot_standby_feedback, a logical replication slot that is behind, a prepared (2PC) transaction nobody finished. SELECT backend_xmin, xact_start, state, query FROM pg_stat_activity ORDER BY backend_xmin finds the culprit; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout prevents the most common one.

docs.title: 2.5 Transaction id wraparound
docs.text:
Xids are 32-bit and compared circularly: for any xid, the 2 billion xids before it are "in the past" and the 2 billion after are "in the future". If a tuple's xmin is left unfrozen for more than about 2 billion transactions, it suddenly appears to be in the future and becomes invisible: data loss without data loss. Freezing prevents this by marking old tuples as frozen. Safeguards:

  • autovacuum_freeze_max_age (200 M): a table whose oldest unfrozen xid (pg_class.relfrozenxid) is older than this gets an anti-wraparound autovacuum even if autovacuum is disabled for it. These are aggressive vacuums that scan all non-frozen pages.
  • age(relfrozenxid) tells you how far a table is; age(datfrozenxid) the database.
  • At 40 M xids before the limit the server logs warnings; at 3 M it refuses new commands until a vacuum is run. Monitoring age(datfrozenxid) is non-negotiable in production.

Since PostgreSQL 9.4 freezing sets flag bits rather than overwriting xmin with 2, so forensic xmin values survive. PostgreSQL 16 does not have 64-bit xids (an often-discussed change). YugabyteDB does not have this problem at all: DocDB uses hybrid timestamps, not 32-bit xids.

docs.title: 2.6 Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)
docs.text:
Snapshot isolation alone allows write skew because neither transaction writes what the other read. SSI (Cahill, Rohm, Fekete 2008; in PostgreSQL since 9.1) tracks rw-conflicts: T1 read something that T2 later wrote (T1 -> T2, "T1 read the old version"). A result from the paper: a non-serialisable execution requires a transaction with both an incoming and an outgoing rw-conflict edge (a "dangerous structure" of two consecutive edges), where the one at the end committed first. PostgreSQL records reads as SIRead predicate locks on tuples, pages or whole relations (they never block; they are bookkeeping) in a shared memory table sized by max_pred_locks_per_transaction, detects the dangerous structure at commit or on write, and aborts one participant with SQLSTATE 40001. Costs: memory and CPU for tracking, and false positives (aborts of executions that would have been fine) when locks escalate to page or relation level. Benefit: true serialisability with no read blocking, so a SELECT never waits.

Rule for using it: every transaction at SERIALIZABLE must be wrapped in a retry loop on 40001. Read-only transactions can declare READ ONLY DEFERRABLE to wait for a safe snapshot and never be aborted.

docs.title: 2.7 Locks: rows, tables, advisory
docs.text:
Row locks live in the tuple header, not in a lock table: t_xmax is set to the locker's xid with HEAP_XMAX_LOCK_ONLY in the infomask (and a MultiXact id if several transactions hold shared locks on the same row). Waiting for a row lock means waiting for the holder's transaction to end: the waiter takes a lock on the holder's xid in the lock manager (XactLockTableWait), and that is what shows in pg_locks as locktype = transactionid.

Clause Mode Conflicts with Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE strongest all other row locks, UPDATE, DELETE read-modify-write; prevents lost updates FOR NO KEY UPDATE what UPDATE takes when no key column changes FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE FOR SHARE shared FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, UPDATE, DELETE "do not delete this parent while I insert a child" (explicit) FOR KEY SHARE weakest, taken by FK checks on the parent row only FOR UPDATE and key-changing UPDATE/DELETE lets inserts of children not block non-key updates of the parent

NOWAIT errors instead of waiting; SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows, which is how you build a job queue (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10).

Table (heavyweight) locks have eight modes from ACCESS SHARE (any SELECT) to ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (DROP, TRUNCATE, most ALTER TABLE, VACUUM FULL, LOCK TABLE). The conflict matrix is in the manual; the one to memorise: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE conflicts with everything including SELECT, and a request for it queues behind running transactions and blocks everything behind it while it waits. This is how a tiny ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN behind a 10-minute report takes down an application: every new SELECT queues behind the ALTER. Always set lock_timeout before DDL.

Advisory locks are application-defined lock keys (pg_advisory_lock(bigint), pg_try_advisory_lock, pg_advisory_xact_lock) stored in the same lock manager. Use them to serialise an application action ("only one importer for customer 42 at a time") without a row to lock. Session-level ones survive COMMIT and must be released explicitly; prefer the _xact_ forms.

docs.title: 2.8 Deadlocks
docs.text:
A deadlock is a cycle in the waits-for graph: T1 holds row A and wants row B; T2 holds row B and wants row A. PostgreSQL does not prevent deadlocks; it detects them. When a backend has waited deadlock_timeout (1 s) for a lock, it runs the deadlock detector: it walks the lock manager's wait queues building the waits-for graph and looks for a cycle. If one exists, the detecting transaction is aborted with ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01) and the log shows both processes and their statements. The other transaction proceeds.

Prevention is an application discipline: acquire locks in a consistent global order (update accounts in ascending id order; SELECT ... FOR UPDATE ORDER BY id), keep transactions short, avoid user think-time inside transactions, and treat 40P01 like 40001: retry. The two-session scripts in code/m05_deadlock_a.sql and _b.sql produce one on demand.

Note: in Berkeley DB, deadlock detection was also your job (DB_ENV->set_lk_detect or a db_deadlock daemon), and page-level locking made deadlocks far more common than PostgreSQL's row-level MVCC. Both are honest points in the migration story.

docs.title: 3.1 Two-session isolation demos
docs.text:
Open two psql loans windows, A and B, and run code/m05_isolation_session_a.sql and code/m05_isolation_session_b.sql step by step in the numbered order written in the comments. The core of each demo:

-- Demo 1: READ COMMITTED non-repeatable read
-- A1
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;            -- 1000
-- B1
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;   -- autocommit
-- A2
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;            -- 900: new statement, new snapshot
COMMIT;

-- Demo 2: REPEATABLE READ keeps its snapshot, and detects a concurrent update
-- A1
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;            -- 900
-- B1
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;   -- 800 committed
-- A2
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;            -- still 900
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 1;
-- ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
ROLLBACK;

-- Demo 3: lost update at READ COMMITTED, and the FOR UPDATE fix
-- A1
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 2;            -- 500, application computes 500 - 300 = 200
-- B1
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 2;            -- 500, application computes 500 - 400 = 100
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 100 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT;
-- A2
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 200 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT;   -- B's withdrawal is lost: 200
-- Fix: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in A1 and B1; B blocks until A commits, then re-reads 200.

-- Demo 4: write skew, only SERIALIZABLE catches it
-- invariant: at least one doctor on call per shift
-- A1
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
SELECT count(*) FROM on_call WHERE shift = 'night' AND on_duty;   -- 2
-- B1
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
SELECT count(*) FROM on_call WHERE shift = 'night' AND on_duty;   -- 2
-- A2
UPDATE on_call SET on_duty = false WHERE doctor = 'alice' AND shift = 'night';
COMMIT;                                                            -- ok
-- B2
UPDATE on_call SET on_duty = false WHERE doctor = 'bob' AND shift = 'night';
COMMIT;
-- ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
-- At REPEATABLE READ both commit and nobody is on call.

docs.title: 3.2 Seeing MVCC in the tuple headers
docs.text:
-- txid_current() forces an xid to be assigned so you can match it to xmin/xmax
BEGIN;
SELECT pg_current_xact_id();                          -- e.g. 48213
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid,
       (t_infomask & 128) <> 0 AS xmax_lock_only
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('accounts', 0));
-- old version: t_xmax = 48213, t_ctid -> new slot. new version: t_xmin = 48213.
SELECT pg_current_snapshot();                         -- xmin:xmax:xip
COMMIT;

-- Row lock = xmax with LOCK_ONLY, no new version
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, (t_infomask & 128) <> 0 AS xmax_lock_only
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('accounts', 0)) WHERE lp = 1;
COMMIT;

docs.title: 3.3 Who is blocking whom
docs.text:
SELECT a.pid, a.state, a.wait_event_type, a.wait_event,
       pg_blocking_pids(a.pid) AS blocked_by,
       age(now(), a.xact_start) AS xact_age,
       left(a.query, 80) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity a
WHERE a.datname = current_database() AND a.pid <> pg_backend_pid()
ORDER BY a.xact_start;

docs.title: 3.4 A retry loop (what every SERIALIZABLE or REPEATABLE READ client needs)
docs.text:
/* libpq pseudo-code: retry on 40001 (serialization_failure) and 40P01 (deadlock_detected) */
for (int attempt = 0; attempt < 5; ++attempt) {
    PQexec(conn, "BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE");
    PGresult *r = run_business_logic(conn);
    const char *sqlstate = PQresultErrorField(r, PG_DIAG_SQLSTATE);
    if (sqlstate && (strcmp(sqlstate, "40001") == 0 || strcmp(sqlstate, "40P01") == 0)) {
        PQexec(conn, "ROLLBACK");
        backoff_ms(attempt);           /* exponential with jitter, so retries do not collide again */
        continue;
    }
    PQexec(conn, "COMMIT");
    break;
}

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Snapshot construction (GetSnapshotData) scans the shared ProcArray, one entry per backend holding its current xid and xmin. With hundreds of connections this scan is a measurable per-statement cost, which is one reason PostgreSQL 14 reworked it into dense arrays and why connection pooling helps even read-only workloads. The snapshot's xmin also becomes the backend's advertised xmin in the ProcArray, and the minimum of those across all backends is the horizon VACUUM must respect. An idle-in-transaction session with an old snapshot pins that horizon for everyone.

Hint bits and pg_xact. Deciding "did xid 48213 commit?" means reading pg_xact, which is an SLRU cache over files with 2 bits per xid. To avoid doing that for every tuple on every read, the first reader who learns the answer sets HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED or HEAP_XMIN_INVALID (and the XMAX equivalents) in the tuple header. Subsequent visibility checks are then pure bit tests. A freshly bulk-loaded table has no hint bits, so the first full scan after a load is slow and dirties every page; VACUUM (or COPY ... FREEZE in the same transaction that created the table) sets them up front.

Command ids within a transaction. t_cid records which statement in the transaction created or deleted a version, so that statement 3 can see rows inserted by statement 2 but a statement never sees its own partial output (INSERT INTO t SELECT * FROM t does not loop). The combo-cid trick packs both an insert cid and a delete cid into the same field when one transaction both inserts and deletes a tuple.

Subtransactions. SAVEPOINT and PL/pgSQL BEGIN ... EXCEPTION blocks create subtransactions with their own xids, recorded in pg_subtrans as children of the parent. Each backend caches up to 64 subtransaction xids in its ProcArray slot; beyond that (PGPROC_MAX_CACHED_SUBXIDS) every snapshot must consult pg_subtrans on disk, a well-known performance cliff ("subtransaction overflow"). A PL/pgSQL loop with an exception block per iteration over 100,000 rows hits it (module 08).

MultiXacts. When two transactions both hold FOR SHARE or FOR KEY SHARE on a row (common: two inserts of children referencing the same parent), xmax cannot hold both xids, so a MultiXactId is allocated in pg_multixact and stored instead. MultiXacts have their own wraparound and vacuum thresholds (autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age). Heavy FK traffic to a hot parent row is the classic generator.

How a deadlock is actually found. Lock waits are queues in the shared lock table (LOCK/PROCLOCK structures in partitions). The detector (DeadLockCheck) does a depth-first search over "process waits for lock, lock is held by processes" edges, considering that waiters ahead in a queue also block. If a cycle is found it may first try to rearrange the wait queue to break a soft cycle (a case where reordering waiters avoids the deadlock) before aborting. deadlock_timeout is the only cost knob: lower detects faster but runs the check more often.

Why MVCC and not undo-based rollback (as in Oracle). Oracle keeps one current row version in the table and reconstructs older versions from undo segments when a reader needs them (ORA-01555 "snapshot too old" is the undo running out). PostgreSQL keeps all versions in the heap, so reads never reconstruct anything, but the heap bloats and needs VACUUM. SQL Server's row-versioning levels copy old versions into tempdb's version store. Each choice moves the cost: Oracle pays on long readers, PostgreSQL pays on writers and vacuum, SQL Server pays in tempdb. Saying this calmly is what "knows Oracle and SQL Server differences" means (module 14).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The default is READ COMMITTED, and most application code was written assuming it. Changing the default to REPEATABLE READ without adding retry loops turns rare races into user-visible errors. Change it per transaction where it matters.
  • Read-modify-write in application code is the lost-update generator. Either do the arithmetic in SQL (SET balance = balance - $1), or lock the row first (FOR UPDATE), or use an optimistic version column (UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2, check rows affected). Your PL/pgSQL workflow layer should use one of these for every state transition.
  • idle in transaction is the silent killer: it holds row locks and pins the VACUUM horizon. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5min' (or lower) and fix the client that leaves transactions open (usually a pool returning connections mid-transaction after an exception).
  • Table bloat you can measure: pgstattuple, or n_dead_tup in pg_stat_user_tables versus n_live_tup. If last_autovacuum is old on a hot table, check for a horizon holder before touching autovacuum settings.
  • Wraparound alarm: alert at age(datfrozenxid) > 1 billion. If it reaches the shutdown threshold, you are running VACUUM FREEZE on the biggest tables in single-user mode while the bank is down. Nobody wants to explain that.
  • Deadlocks in batch jobs: two batch processes updating overlapping sets in different orders. Sort the ids, or take one advisory lock per logical batch. Log analysis: every deadlock detected message in the server log lists both statements; the fix is almost always ordering.
  • DDL under load: SET lock_timeout = '3s' then ALTER TABLE ...; retry on timeout. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, ADD COLUMN without a volatile default (fast since 11), and ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID followed by VALIDATE CONSTRAINT to avoid long exclusive locks.
  • YugabyteDB implements MVCC with hybrid timestamps in DocDB rather than xmin/xmax in heap tuples, has no VACUUM, defaults to SNAPSHOT (equivalent to REPEATABLE READ) and offers SERIALIZABLE and READ COMMITTED (the last with an explicit flag in older versions). Module 11.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run demos 1 and 2 from the two-session scripts. Done when you have seen the non-repeatable read and the could not serialize error with your own eyes.
  2. (easy) With pageinspect, update a row inside an open transaction and dump the two versions' t_xmin/t_xmax/t_ctid. Done when you can identify which is old, which is new, and what pg_current_snapshot() shows from a second session.
  3. (medium) Build the visibility table from section 2.3 for snapshot 200:210:203,207 and the tuples (xmin 150, xmax 0), (150, 203 committed), (150, 205 committed), (207 committed, 0), (209 aborted, 0), (211 committed, 0). Then verify two of them experimentally by arranging the transactions. Done when all six are right and two are verified.
  4. (medium) Reproduce a deadlock with code/m05_deadlock_a.sql/_b.sql. Read the server log entry. Then fix it by ordering and show it no longer deadlocks. Done when you can quote the log and explain the fix.
  5. (hard) Create a table with 1 M rows, open a BEGIN; SELECT 1; in a second session at REPEATABLE READ and leave it, then update all rows twice in the first session and run VACUUM VERBOSE. Observe "dead row versions cannot be removed yet, oldest xmin: N". Commit the second session, vacuum again. Done when you can explain oldest xmin and its effect on table size.
  6. (hard) Write the retry loop from 3.4 in C with libpq and test it under the write-skew demo running in a loop from two processes at SERIALIZABLE. Done when the invariant is never violated and you can report how many retries happened.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Explain MVCC in PostgreSQL. A: Every row version carries the xid that created it (xmin) and the xid that deleted or replaced it (xmax). A transaction takes a snapshot (lowest running xid, next unassigned xid, list of in-progress xids) and sees a version if its xmin is committed and in the snapshot's past and its xmax is absent, aborted, in progress, or in the snapshot's future. Writers create new versions instead of overwriting, so readers never block writers and vice versa. Dead versions are reclaimed by VACUUM.

Q: What does the default isolation level allow, and what does it prevent? A: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads only. Each statement gets a fresh snapshot, so repeated reads can differ and phantoms can appear, and a read-then-write in application code can lose an update. UPDATE on a concurrently changed row waits and re-evaluates the WHERE on the new version, so arithmetic in SQL is safe.

Q: What is the difference between REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL? A: Both use one snapshot for the whole transaction, so neither has non-repeatable or phantom reads, and both abort on a write to a row changed concurrently. Only SERIALIZABLE detects write skew, where two transactions read overlapping data and write disjoint rows; it does so with SSI, tracking read/write dependencies and aborting a participant when a dangerous structure appears. Both require clients to retry on SQLSTATE 40001.

Q: What is write skew? Give an example. A: Two transactions each read a condition, both find it satisfied, and each writes a different row such that the combination violates the condition. Two doctors each check "at least two on call" and each removes themselves; under snapshot isolation both commit and nobody is on call. Only SERIALIZABLE (SSI) or an explicit lock on the rows read prevents it.

Q: Why is VACUUM necessary and what happens if it falls behind? A: Updates and deletes leave old versions in place; VACUUM removes those no transaction can see, cleans their index entries, updates the free space and visibility maps, and freezes old xids. If it falls behind, tables and indexes bloat, scans read dead space, index-only scans do heap fetches, and eventually the xid wraparound protection forces an emergency vacuum or refuses writes.

Q: What is transaction id wraparound? A: Xids are 32-bit and compared circularly, so a tuple left unfrozen for about 2 billion transactions would appear to be from the future and vanish. VACUUM freezes old tuples (marks them visible to all); autovacuum forces a freeze when a table's relfrozenxid exceeds autovacuum_freeze_max_age, and the server stops accepting commands when a database is 3 M xids from the limit. Monitor age(datfrozenxid).

Q: How does PostgreSQL handle deadlocks? A: It detects rather than prevents. After a backend waits deadlock_timeout for a lock, it searches the waits-for graph in the shared lock table for a cycle and, if found, aborts its own transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01, logging both statements. Applications prevent them by locking rows in a consistent order and keeping transactions short, and retry when they happen.

Q: How do row locks work internally? A: A row lock is recorded in the tuple header: xmax holds the locker's xid with a lock-only flag (or a MultiXact id when several share it). A waiter blocks on the holder's transaction id in the lock manager until that transaction ends. FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE and FOR KEY SHARE are the four strengths; FK checks use FOR KEY SHARE so child inserts do not block non-key parent updates.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• ACID: atomic via one commit record; consistent via constraints; isolated via MVCC + locks; durable via WAL fsync.
  • Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew.
  • READ COMMITTED (default): snapshot per statement; prevents only dirty reads; UPDATE re-evaluates on the new version.
  • REPEATABLE READ: one snapshot; no phantoms in PostgreSQL; concurrent update raises 40001.
  • SERIALIZABLE: SSI, detects write skew with predicate locks, aborts instead of blocking; always retry.
  • Snapshot = xmin, xmax, xip. Visible if xmin committed-in-past and xmax not committed-in-past.
  • VACUUM removes dead versions below the oldest xmin horizon, cleans indexes, sets FSM/VM, freezes.
  • Long transactions and idle-in-transaction sessions hold the horizon and cause bloat.
  • Wraparound: 32-bit circular xids; freeze; monitor age(datfrozenxid).
  • Row locks live in xmax; waits are on the holder's xid; deadlocks are detected after deadlock_timeout and one side is aborted.

docs.title: 6. Query planning and reading EXPLAIN
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
SQL says what you want, not how to get it. For SELECT ... FROM a JOIN b JOIN c WHERE ... there are dozens of ways to execute: which table to read first, whether to use an index, how to join (loop, hash table, or merge sorted streams), when to sort. The planner (optimiser) estimates the cost of many alternatives using statistics about the data and picks the cheapest estimate. EXPLAIN shows you the plan it picked; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and shows what actually happened next to each estimate.

The analogy is a satnav. It does not know the current traffic on every road; it uses a map (statistics: how many rows, how many distinct values, the value distribution) and a cost per kilometre (I/O and CPU cost constants) to choose a route. When the map is out of date (stale statistics) or the costs are wrong for your car (random I/O on SSD is not really 4x sequential), it chooses badly. Reading EXPLAIN is comparing the route it planned against the trip you actually took and spotting where the estimate was off by 1000x.

Every performance problem you will be asked about in an interview reduces to: find the plan node where estimated and actual rows diverge, or where time concentrates, and change the index, the statistics, or the query so the planner can do better.

docs.title: 2.1 What the planner knows: statistics
docs.text:
ANALYZE (run by autovacuum when about 10% of a table changed, or by you) samples 300 x default_statistics_target rows (30,000 at the default target of 100) and stores per column in pg_statistic (readable through the pg_stats view):

Column Meaning Used for null_frac fraction NULL IS NULL, and reducing row estimates avg_width average bytes width in plans, memory estimates for hash and sort n_distinct number of distinct values (negative = fraction of rows, for columns that grow) = selectivity when the value is not in MCVs, GROUP BY estimates, hash sizing most_common_vals / most_common_freqs the top-N values and their frequencies = 'ACTIVE' gets its exact frequency histogram_bounds equal-frequency bucket boundaries for the remaining values ranges <, >, BETWEEN correlation -1 to 1, physical order vs logical order whether an index range scan reads the heap sequentially (cheap) or randomly (expensive)

Selectivity of col = X: if X is in the MCV list, its frequency; else (1 - sum(mcv_freqs)) / (n_distinct - number_of_mcvs). Selectivity of a = X AND b = Y: the planner multiplies, assuming independence. If branch_code and region are correlated (every branch is in one region), the product badly underestimates. Fix with extended statistics: CREATE STATISTICS s (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) ON branch_code, region FROM app_users.

Raise the target for skewed or high-cardinality columns: ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET STATISTICS 1000 (max 10000). More buckets, more MCVs, slower ANALYZE and planning.

Also in pg_class: reltuples and relpages, the base numbers every estimate scales from.

docs.title: 2.2 The cost model
docs.text:
Cost is a dimensionless number built from these constants (defaults):

Parameter Default Meaning seq_page_cost 1.0 one page read in a sequential scan random_page_cost 4.0 one page read at random (index probes); set 1.1 to 1.5 on SSD cpu_tuple_cost 0.01 processing one heap tuple cpu_index_tuple_cost 0.005 processing one index entry cpu_operator_cost 0.0025 one operator or function call effective_cache_size 4 GB how much of the index is assumed cached (lowers index cost); set to ~75% of RAM work_mem 4 MB per sort/hash node budget before spilling; changes plan choice parallel_setup_cost, parallel_tuple_cost 1000, 0.1 when parallel plans are worth it

Each plan node shows cost=startup..total: startup is the cost before the first row can be returned (a Sort or Hash build has high startup; an Index Scan near zero), total is for all rows. A LIMIT 10 prefers low-startup plans, which is why ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 10 loves an index on created_at and hates a Sort.

The planner enumerates join orders exhaustively (dynamic programming) up to join_collapse_limit tables (8), and switches to a genetic search (geqo_threshold, 12) above that. A 15-table join gets a heuristic plan; break it up or use CTEs as optimisation fences (WITH ... AS MATERIALIZED).

docs.title: 2.3 Scan and join methods
docs.text:
Scans (module 03): Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Bitmap Index + Bitmap Heap Scan, plus Parallel Seq Scan under a Gather node, TID Scan (by ctid), Function Scan (generate_series), CTE Scan, Subquery Scan, Values Scan.

Joins:

Method How Cost shape Best when Nested Loop for each outer row, scan inner (ideally an Index Scan parameterised by the outer row's key) outer_rows x inner_cost outer side small (tens to a few thousand rows) and inner has an index on the join key. The only method for inequality joins. Hash Join build a hash table on the smaller input (hashed on the join key), probe with each row of the larger read both once + hash build; needs work_mem, else Batches > 1 spills to temp files equality joins of medium and large sets; the default workhorse Merge Join both inputs sorted on the join key (by index or an explicit Sort), walk them together read both once + sort cost if not pre-sorted both sides already ordered (indexes on join keys), very large joins where hash would spill, or when output order is needed anyway

PostgreSQL 14 added Memoize: a cache in front of the inner side of a nested loop so repeated outer values do not re-probe. You will see it as Memoize with Hits/Misses.

Other nodes: Sort (quicksort in memory, top-N heapsort for LIMIT, external merge on disk), Incremental Sort (input already sorted on a prefix), Aggregate / HashAggregate / GroupAggregate, Unique, Limit, Append (UNION ALL, partitions), Materialize, WindowAgg, Gather/Gather Merge (parallel workers), Result, SetOp, LockRows (FOR UPDATE), ModifyTable (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE).

docs.title: 2.4 Reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) line by line
docs.text:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE off, SETTINGS off, WAL off, FORMAT text)
SELECT c.full_name, a.application_no, a.requested_amount
FROM loan_applications a
JOIN customers c ON c.id = a.customer_id
WHERE a.status = 'SUBMITTED' AND a.submitted_at > now() - interval '7 days'
ORDER BY a.submitted_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

Limit  (cost=0.86..118.42 rows=20 width=52) (actual time=0.061..0.412 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=104
  ->  Nested Loop  (cost=0.86..3121.70 rows=531 width=52) (actual time=0.059..0.405 rows=20 loops=1)
        Buffers: shared hit=104
        ->  Index Scan Backward using la_status_submitted_idx on loan_applications a
                (cost=0.43..1032.21 rows=531 width=31) (actual time=0.031..0.090 rows=20 loops=1)
              Index Cond: ((status = 'SUBMITTED'::text) AND (submitted_at > (now() - '7 days'::interval)))
              Buffers: shared hit=24
        ->  Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c
                (cost=0.43..3.94 rows=1 width=29) (actual time=0.014..0.014 rows=1 loops=20)
              Index Cond: (id = a.customer_id)
              Buffers: shared hit=80
Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=12
Planning Time: 0.410 ms
Execution Time: 0.455 ms

How to read it:

  1. Indentation is the tree; the deepest-indented nodes run first. Children feed parents. Here: the Index Scan Backward produces applications, the inner Index Scan looks up each customer, Nested Loop combines, Limit stops after 20.
  2. cost=a..b: estimated startup..total. rows: estimated rows per loop. width: estimated bytes per row.
  3. actual time=a..b: milliseconds to first row..all rows, per loop. rows: actual rows per loop. loops: how many times the node ran. Total rows = rows x loops; total time = time x loops. The inner Index Scan ran 20 times, 0.014 ms each.
  4. Estimated vs actual rows: the outer scan estimated 531 but stopped at 20 because of LIMIT; that is fine. A mismatch of 100x or more on a node without a LIMIT above it is the usual root cause of a bad plan.
  5. Buffers: shared hit=N read=M dirtied=D written=W: pages from shared_buffers, pages read from the OS (cache or disk), pages dirtied, pages written. temp read/written means sort or hash spilled to disk. read is where your I/O time is; enable track_io_timing to get I/O Timings: read=….
  6. Index Cond is what the index narrowed; Filter is applied to rows after they are fetched, with Rows Removed by Filter telling you how much was wasted. A large Rows Removed by Filter under an Index Scan means the index is not selective enough for this query.
  7. Recheck Cond under a Bitmap Heap Scan means the bitmap went lossy (increase work_mem) or the index is lossy by nature (GIN, BRIN).
  8. Heap Fetches under an Index Only Scan: non-zero means the visibility map is not set; VACUUM.
  9. Sort Method: external merge Disk: 41232kB: work_mem too small for this sort. Hash Batches: 4: same for a hash join.
  10. Planning Time vs Execution Time: a 20 ms planning time on a 0.5 ms query is a sign you want prepared statements or fewer partitions/joins.

Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON) and paste into explain.dalibo.com or explain.depesz.com for big plans; both highlight the node where time or misestimation concentrates.

docs.title: 2.5 Common plan problems and their fixes
docs.text: Symptom in the plan Cause Fix Seq Scan on a big table with Filter and Rows Removed by Filter huge no usable index for the predicate create the index (right column order); or rewrite predicate to be sargable Index exists, Seq Scan chosen, rows estimate far above actual stale statistics, or correlated columns ANALYZE; raise statistics target; CREATE STATISTICS Index exists, Seq Scan chosen, estimate correct low selectivity: index would not help accept it; partial index for the rare value; cover more of the query Filter: (lower(email) = ...) function on the column expression index ON (lower(email)) or store normalised Filter: ((user_code)::bigint = $1) or (id)::text = $1 implicit cast on the column bind the right parameter type Filter: (code ~~ '%abc%') leading-wildcard LIKE GIN with pg_trgm, or full-text Nested Loop with inner Seq Scan, loops=50000 inner side has no index on the join key, planner thought outer was small index the join column; ANALYZE Nested Loop chosen, outer rows=1 estimated but rows=80000 actual misestimate turned a hash join into millions of inner probes fix statistics; extended stats; as a last resort SET enable_nestloop = off for that query to confirm Sort Method: external merge or Hash Batches > 1 work_mem too low for this node SET LOCAL work_mem = '64MB' for that session/statement; add an index providing the order Heap Fetches: 48000 on Index Only Scan VM bits not set VACUUM the table Bitmap Heap Scan with Recheck Cond and lossy= pages bitmap exceeded work_mem raise work_mem Limit over Sort over Seq Scan for ORDER BY x LIMIT n no index on x (in that direction) index on x, or on (filter_col, x) OR across two columns -> Seq Scan one index cannot serve both two indexes (planner can BitmapOr), or rewrite as UNION ALL Many CTE Scan nodes materialised CTEs re-read (pre-12 always; 12+ only when referenced twice or MATERIALIZED) inline with NOT MATERIALIZED or rewrite Gather with Workers Launched: 0 no free parallel workers check max_parallel_workers, concurrency OFFSET 100000 reads and discards 100,000 rows keyset pagination (module 07)

docs.title: 2.6 Prepared statements and "parameter sniffing"
docs.text:
A prepared statement (PREPARE / libpq PQprepare / JDBC PreparedStatement) parses and analyses once and executes many times. The plan question: plan with the actual parameter values (a custom plan, best plan for this value, but costs planning every time) or plan once for any value (a generic plan, plans once, but cannot use value-specific statistics)?

PostgreSQL's rule (plan_cache_mode = auto): the first five executions use custom plans; after that, if the generic plan's estimated cost is not worse than the average custom plan cost, it switches to the generic plan for good. This causes the PostgreSQL version of SQL Server's parameter sniffing: a query that is fast for most values and slow for a skewed value (status = 'ACTIVE' = 98% of rows vs status = 'LOCKED' = 2%) may get a generic plan that is wrong for one of them. Options: SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan for that session or function; rewrite so the skew is not a parameter (partial index, separate statements); or raise statistics so the generic estimate is better. In EXPLAIN you recognise a generic plan by $1 in the conditions instead of a literal. Oracle calls its version bind peeking with adaptive cursor sharing; SQL Server has OPTION (RECOMPILE) and OPTIMIZE FOR. PL/pgSQL caches plans for every SQL statement in a function the same way (module 08).

docs.title: 2.7 Case study: the login query, from Seq Scan to Index Only Scan
docs.text:
Setting: app_users from module 03 (2 M rows, surrogate PK, business codes as columns), originally no index on the codes. The login procedure runs this per attempt.

Step 0: the slow plan.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, password_hash, status, failed_attempts
FROM app_users WHERE branch_code = 'BR0456' AND user_code = 'U00123456';

Gather  (cost=1000.00..38492.33 rows=1 width=49) (actual time=168.211..171.904 rows=1 loops=1)
  Workers Planned: 2
  Workers Launched: 2
  Buffers: shared hit=2112 read=20314
  ->  Parallel Seq Scan on app_users  (cost=0.00..37492.23 rows=1 width=49)
                                      (actual time=112.480..160.337 rows=0 loops=3)
        Filter: ((branch_code = 'BR0456'::text) AND (user_code = 'U00123456'::text))
        Rows Removed by Filter: 666666
        Buffers: shared hit=2112 read=20314
Planning Time: 0.190 ms
Execution Time: 171.960 ms

(Typical output from the demo table on a laptop; your numbers will differ.) Reading it: the estimate (rows=1) is right, so statistics are fine; the problem is structural: there is no access path other than reading all 22,426 pages. 170 ms per login, multiplied by the 4 other lookups in the login path (branch, roles, policy, session insert), and on a cluster each sequential scan fans out to every node. Users saw 1 to 2 second logins.

Step 1: the natural key index.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY app_users_login_idx ON app_users (branch_code, user_code);

Index Scan using app_users_login_idx on app_users  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=1 width=49)
                                                   (actual time=0.038..0.039 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: ((branch_code = 'BR0456'::text) AND (user_code = 'U00123456'::text))
  Buffers: shared hit=5
Execution Time: 0.061 ms

5 buffers: 4 index pages (height 3 plus the meta page is cached; realistically root, internal, leaf) and 1 heap page. 2800x faster.

Step 2: cover the columns the login needs so the heap page is not read either (saves one random I/O when the heap page is cold, and on YugabyteDB saves a second storage read):

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY app_users_login_idx2
    ON app_users (branch_code, user_code) INCLUDE (password_hash, status, failed_attempts);
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY app_users_login_idx;
VACUUM app_users;

Index Only Scan using app_users_login_idx2 on app_users  (cost=0.43..4.45 rows=1 width=49)
                                                         (actual time=0.021..0.022 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: ((branch_code = 'BR0456'::text) AND (user_code = 'U00123456'::text))
  Heap Fetches: 0
  Buffers: shared hit=4

The login still needs id for the session row. It is in the index implicitly? No: the heap TID is, not the id column. Add id to INCLUDE if the SELECT list needs it, or accept the one heap fetch. This is the kind of detail that shows you actually read plans.

Step 3: collapse the round trips. The remaining cost was five statements, five round trips (and on the cluster, five potential cross-node hops). Moving the whole login check into one PL/pgSQL function (module 08) made it one round trip; the function's internal statements each use the indexes above. Measured by pg_stat_statements: mean time of the login path went from hundreds of milliseconds to a few milliseconds. Say the mechanism, not just the number.

Step 4: keep it fast. auto_explain with auto_explain.log_min_duration = '50ms' logs any plan that regresses; the covering index must be extended if the query grows a column; the status column is updated on lock-out so this index is non-HOT for those updates, which is an accepted cost.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m06_slow_vs_fast_queries.sql contains eight paired slow/fast queries over the loan-origination schema with the expected plan shape in comments. Three of them:

-- Pair 1: function on the column vs expression index
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id FROM customers WHERE lower(email) = 'anna.k@example.com';
--   Seq Scan, Filter: (lower(email) = ...)   -- cannot use customers_email_idx
CREATE INDEX customers_email_lower_idx ON customers (lower(email));
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id FROM customers WHERE lower(email) = 'anna.k@example.com';
--   Index Scan using customers_email_lower_idx

-- Pair 2: work queue ORDER BY ... LIMIT with and without a matching index
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, application_no FROM loan_applications
WHERE status = 'SUBMITTED' ORDER BY submitted_at LIMIT 50;
--   Limit -> Sort (top-N heapsort) -> Bitmap Heap Scan ... reads every SUBMITTED row to sort
CREATE INDEX la_status_submitted_idx ON loan_applications (status, submitted_at);
--   Limit -> Index Scan using la_status_submitted_idx: stops after 50 rows, no Sort node

-- Pair 3: a hash join that spills, and the work_mem fix
SET work_mem = '256kB';
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT c.id, count(*) FROM customers c JOIN loan_applications a ON a.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id;
--   Hash Join ... Batches: 16  Memory Usage: 256kB ; temp read=... written=...
SET work_mem = '64MB';
--   Batches: 1, no temp buffers
RESET work_mem;

Also in that file: the statistics views, extended statistics for correlated columns, the prepared-statement generic/custom demonstration, and auto_explain setup:

LOAD 'auto_explain';
SET auto_explain.log_min_duration = '20ms';
SET auto_explain.log_analyze = on;
SET auto_explain.log_buffers = on;
-- now any statement over 20 ms writes its ANALYZE plan to the server log

-- Generic vs custom plans
PREPARE login_q(text, text) AS
  SELECT password_hash, status FROM app_users WHERE branch_code = $1 AND user_code = $2;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) EXECUTE login_q('BR0456', 'U00123456');   -- run 6 times; watch literals turn into $1, $2
SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan;                     -- per session or per function

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Planning pipeline. standard_planner -> subquery_planner (pull up subqueries, flatten joins, simplify constant expressions, convert IN (subquery) to semi-joins) -> query_planner builds RelOptInfo for each base relation with its possible paths (SeqScan path, each usable IndexPath, BitmapHeapPath, TidPath), each with cost and output ordering ("pathkeys"). make_one_rel then joins relations level by level (pairs, then triples) keeping for each set of relations only the cheapest path per distinct ordering and parameterisation (add_path prunes dominated paths). Finally create_plan turns the chosen path tree into Plan nodes. Planning is pure CPU on catalog and statistics; it never touches the table.

Parameterised paths. The reason a Nested Loop can be good: the inner side's Index Scan can take the outer row's join key as a parameter (Index Cond: (id = a.customer_id)), so the inner cost is one probe, not a scan. The planner represents this as a path parameterised by the outer relation. Hash and merge joins have no such option; they read the inner side fully.

Selectivity functions. Each operator in pg_operator names a restriction selectivity function (eqsel, scalarltsel, scalargtsel) and a join selectivity function (eqjoinsel). eqsel is the MCV / n_distinct logic above. eqjoinsel for a.x = b.y compares the MCV lists of both sides and estimates the match fraction. When you write a custom operator or use a function in WHERE, the planner falls back to default selectivities (0.5 for most, 0.005 for = on unknowns), which is why function calls in predicates produce absurd estimates.

Why random_page_cost = 4 is wrong for you. The default encodes spinning disks (one random read costs several sequential ones, less so because of cache). On NVMe with a large OS cache, a random read costs 1.1 to 1.5 sequential reads. Leaving the default makes the planner too afraid of index scans and too fond of sequential and bitmap scans on large tables. Set it to 1.1 to 1.5 for SSD and re-check your top queries' plans; this is one of the few globally correct tuning changes.

Executor memory and spilling. A Sort node collects tuples until work_mem, then switches to external sort: writes sorted runs to temp files (pgsql_tmp), merges them. Hash Join computes the number of batches from estimated inner size / work_mem up front; if the estimate was low it increases batches on the fly, writing tuples to temp files per batch. Both appear as temp read/written in BUFFERS. work_mem is per node per query (and per parallel worker), so a query with four Sort nodes under 20 connections can use 80 x work_mem; hence the low default. PostgreSQL 13+ has hash_mem_multiplier (default 2.0) to let hashes use more than sorts.

JIT. For queries whose total cost exceeds jit_above_cost (100000), PostgreSQL compiles expression evaluation and tuple deforming with LLVM. It helps long analytic scans and hurts short queries with high plan cost estimates (compilation overhead shows as JIT: ... Timing). Turn jit = off on OLTP systems that show JIT time in plans.

On YugabyteDB the same planner runs, but the costs of a Seq Scan include network fan-out and the executor pushes predicates down to DocDB; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST) adds Storage Read Requests and Storage Read Execution Time per node, which is the number to minimise. Module 11.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• pg_stat_statements first, EXPLAIN second. Sort by total_exec_time to find what burns the server, by mean_exec_time to find what users feel, and look at shared_blks_read for I/O-bound statements. Then EXPLAIN the top three. Optimising a query nobody runs is a hobby.
  • Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production-shaped data. A plan on a 1000-row dev table is meaningless; the planner's choices depend on reltuples and distributions. Use a masked copy or pg_stats exported from production.
  • ANALYZE after bulk loads and big deletes. Autovacuum's analyze threshold (10% changed) is fine for drip changes, not for "we loaded 50 M rows at midnight".
  • Plan regressions after upgrades or after ANALYZE itself happen: a new sample tips a borderline estimate. auto_explain gives you the before/after. Pinning plans (Oracle's SQL plan baselines, SQL Server's Query Store forcing) does not exist in PostgreSQL; pg_hint_plan is the extension people use when they must.
  • Misestimates compound through joins. A 10x underestimate on the first table becomes 10x on every join above it and turns a hash join into a nested loop over 100,000 rows. Fix the lowest misestimated node first.
  • statement_timeout in the application connection (say 5 s for OLTP) converts "the whole system is slow because one bad plan holds 50 connections" into "one request failed and we have a log line".
  • 3 AM: everything slow, CPU at 100%, pg_stat_activity full of the same SELECT. Plan flipped: EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan where yesterday's log shows Index Scan. Immediate: ANALYZE the_table; if that does not fix it, check for an implicit cast introduced by a deployment, or a dropped/invalid index (pg_index.indisvalid).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run the case study steps 0 to 2 on app_users from module 03 and save the three plans. Done when you can explain every line of the final Index Only Scan plan.
  2. (easy) Run code/m06_slow_vs_fast_queries.sql pairs 1 to 4. Done when for each pair you can name the node that changed and why.
  3. (medium) Take pg_stats for loan_applications.status: compute by hand the planner's estimated rows for status = 'APPROVED' from most_common_freqs x reltuples, then compare with EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM loan_applications WHERE status = 'APPROVED'. Done when they match within rounding.
  4. (medium) Make the planner choose a nested loop badly: join customers to loan_applications with a predicate on two correlated columns so the estimate is 1 row but the actual is thousands. Then add CREATE STATISTICS and ANALYZE and show the plan changes to a hash join. Done when you can show both plans and the estimate before/after.
  5. (hard) Write the five-statement login path as five separate psql statements and time it with \timing over 100 iterations in a shell loop; then as one PL/pgSQL function call (module 08 has the function). Done when you can explain the difference in terms of round trips, planning, and buffer hits.
  6. (hard) Set random_page_cost = 1.1 and re-run all pairs from the demo file. Note any plan that changed. Done when you can argue for or against the change on your hardware with track_io_timing numbers.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does the PostgreSQL planner choose a plan? A: It builds candidate access paths for each table (sequential, index, bitmap) using per-column statistics (MCVs, histograms, n_distinct) to estimate selectivity, then combines tables with nested loop, hash and merge joins, exploring join orders by dynamic programming up to about 8 tables. Each path gets a cost from constants such as seq_page_cost, random_page_cost and cpu_tuple_cost; the cheapest estimated total (or startup, under LIMIT) wins.

Q: How do you read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan? A: Innermost nodes run first and feed their parents. For each node compare estimated rows with actual rows times loops; a large divergence is the planner's mistake. Look at where actual time concentrates, at Buffers read versus hit for I/O, at Filter rows removed for wasted work, at Sort Method and Hash Batches for memory spills, and at Heap Fetches for index-only scans.

Q: Nested loop versus hash join versus merge join: when is each right? A: Nested loop when the outer side is small and the inner has an index on the join key; it is also the only option for non-equality joins. Hash join for equality joins of larger sets when the smaller side's hash table fits in work_mem. Merge join when both inputs are already sorted on the join key or when the result is needed sorted and the sets are too big to hash.

Q: Your index exists but the planner does a sequential scan. Why? A: Either the predicate is not selective enough for random heap reads to beat a sequential read, which is the correct choice; or the estimate is wrong because statistics are stale or columns are correlated; or the predicate is not sargable: a function or implicit cast wraps the column, or a leading-wildcard LIKE. Check estimated versus actual rows to tell which.

Q: What is parameter sniffing and how does PostgreSQL handle it? A: A plan built for one parameter value being reused for values with very different selectivity. PostgreSQL plans prepared statements with custom plans for the first five executions, then switches to a generic plan if its estimated cost is not worse than the custom average. For skewed columns that can pick the wrong plan; plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan or rewriting the query avoids it.

Q: Describe how you fixed the slow login query. A: EXPLAIN showed a parallel sequential scan with a correct row estimate of 1, so statistics were fine and the issue was the missing access path: the lookup was by natural key with only a surrogate primary key indexed. I added a unique composite index on the natural key, then made it covering with INCLUDE so the plan became an Index Only Scan with zero heap fetches and four buffer hits, and finally collapsed the login's five statements into one function call to remove round trips. On the cluster the index also confined the read to one tablet.

Q: What does work_mem affect and why is the default so low? A: It is the memory budget per sort or hash node before spilling to temp files, and it also influences plan choice because an in-memory hash is cheaper than a batched one. It is per node per query per worker, so a high global value multiplied by concurrency can exhaust RAM; set it per session or per statement for the queries that need it.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• The planner estimates, it does not know; estimates come from pg_statistic sampled by ANALYZE.
  • Selectivity: MCV frequency for common values, 1/n_distinct otherwise, histogram for ranges; AND multiplies (independence).
  • Costs are dimensionless: seq_page 1, random_page 4 (lower it on SSD), cpu_tuple 0.01; LIMIT prefers low startup cost.
  • Joins: nested loop (small outer + indexed inner), hash (equality, fits work_mem), merge (pre-sorted inputs).
  • Read EXPLAIN inside-out; compare estimated vs actual rows x loops; follow the time and the read buffers.
  • Filter vs Index Cond; Rows Removed by Filter; Heap Fetches; Sort Method; Batches; Recheck Cond.
  • Non-sargable predicates (functions, casts, leading wildcards) disable indexes.
  • Prepared statements: 5 custom plans, then possibly generic; plan_cache_mode controls it.
  • Login case study: Seq Scan 170 ms -> Index Only Scan 0.02 ms -> one round trip via a function.
  • pg_stat_statements finds what to fix; auto_explain catches regressions.

docs.title: 7. SQL for backend engineers
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 06

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Most application code treats the database as a slow hash map: fetch one record, look at it, fetch another, loop. That is how you had to work with Berkeley DB, because a cursor was the only tool. SQL is a different tool: you describe the whole result you want (a set of rows) and the engine computes it in one pass, inside the server, next to the data, with a plan chosen for the whole job. One statement that joins, filters and aggregates 50,000 rows is almost always faster than 50,000 round trips doing the same work, and it is often simpler to read.

The analogy: asking a librarian "bring me every overdue book borrowed by members from branch 12, grouped by member" versus walking the shelves yourself, pulling each book, checking the card, walking to the members' file for each. The librarian knows the layout and does it in one trip.

This module is the practical SQL a senior backend engineer is expected to write without looking things up: joins and their traps, CTEs, window functions, upserts, bulk loading, pagination, and the anti-patterns that make interviewers wince.

docs.title: 2.1 Joins, precisely
docs.text:
Join Returns Rows when no match INNER JOIN pairs that satisfy the condition row dropped LEFT [OUTER] JOIN every left row, matched right columns or NULL left kept with NULLs RIGHT JOIN mirror of LEFT (rewrite as LEFT; nobody reads RIGHT) FULL OUTER JOIN all rows from both, NULL-padded both kept CROSS JOIN Cartesian product LATERAL the right side can reference the left row (a correlated subquery as a join) depends on inner semi-join (WHERE EXISTS (...), IN (subquery)) left rows that have at least one match, never duplicated anti-join (WHERE NOT EXISTS (...)) left rows with no match

Traps:

  • Filtering on the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE turns it into an INNER JOIN. LEFT JOIN documents d ON d.application_id = a.id WHERE d.kind = 'ID_PROOF' drops applications with no documents (their d.kind is NULL, and NULL = 'ID_PROOF' is not true). Put the condition in the ON clause, or test d.id IS NULL for anti-join semantics.
  • Fan-out. Joining a parent to two child tables (documents and payments) multiplies rows: 3 documents x 4 payments = 12 rows per application, and SUM(payment.amount) is tripled. Aggregate each child in a subquery first, then join the aggregates.
  • NOT IN (subquery) with NULLs returns no rows if the subquery can produce a NULL. Use NOT EXISTS.
  • DISTINCT to fix duplicates is a smell: it hides a fan-out or a missing join condition and forces a sort or hash of the whole result.

LATERAL is worth knowing by name: "for each customer, their latest 3 applications":

SELECT c.id, c.full_name, la.application_no, la.submitted_at
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT application_no, submitted_at
    FROM loan_applications a
    WHERE a.customer_id = c.id
    ORDER BY submitted_at DESC
    LIMIT 3
) la;
-- plan: Nested Loop with an Index Scan Backward on (customer_id, submitted_at) per customer

docs.title: 2.2 CTEs (WITH) and when they are fences
docs.text:
A common table expression names a subquery so you can read the statement top-down. Since PostgreSQL 12 a CTE referenced once and without side effects is inlined into the main query (the planner can push predicates into it); a CTE referenced more than once, or written AS MATERIALIZED, or containing INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, is computed once into a tuplestore (an "optimisation fence"). AS NOT MATERIALIZED forces inlining.

WITH recent AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
    FROM loan_applications
    WHERE submitted_at > now() - interval '30 days'
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.full_name, r.n
FROM recent r JOIN customers c ON c.id = r.customer_id
WHERE r.n >= 3;

Recursive CTEs walk hierarchies (an org chart, a workflow state graph, bill of materials):

WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
    SELECT id, from_state, to_state, 1 AS depth FROM workflow_transitions WHERE from_state = 'DRAFT'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT t.id, t.from_state, t.to_state, chain.depth + 1
    FROM workflow_transitions t JOIN chain ON t.from_state = chain.to_state
    WHERE chain.depth < 20            -- always bound recursion
)
SELECT * FROM chain;

Data-modifying CTEs let one statement do several things atomically and pass rows along:

WITH moved AS (
    DELETE FROM loan_applications WHERE status = 'WITHDRAWN' AND updated_at < now() - interval '2 years'
    RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO loan_applications_archive SELECT * FROM moved;

docs.title: 2.3 Window functions
docs.text:
A window function computes a value over a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them the way GROUP BY does. Syntax: fn(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... [frame]).

-- running balance per account, row number per customer, and gap to the previous application
SELECT a.customer_id, a.application_no, a.submitted_at, a.requested_amount,
       row_number() OVER w                                   AS nth_for_customer,
       sum(a.requested_amount) OVER (w ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_total,
       lag(a.submitted_at) OVER w                            AS previous_submitted_at,
       a.requested_amount - avg(a.requested_amount) OVER (PARTITION BY a.customer_id) AS vs_customer_avg
FROM loan_applications a
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY a.customer_id ORDER BY a.submitted_at);

Common uses: row_number() to pick "the latest per group" (then filter = 1 in an outer query; DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY customer_id, submitted_at DESC is the shorter PostgreSQL idiom), rank()/dense_rank() for leaderboards, lag()/lead() for deltas between events, sum() OVER (ORDER BY ...) for running totals, ntile() for buckets. Frames: ROWS BETWEEN n PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (moving average), the default frame for ORDER BY is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING which includes peers with equal sort keys (surprising for running totals with ties; use ROWS).

Window functions are evaluated after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING and before ORDER BY/LIMIT; you cannot filter on them in the same SELECT, hence the outer query.

docs.title: 2.4 Upserts
docs.text:
INSERT INTO customers (national_id, full_name, email)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (national_id) DO UPDATE
    SET full_name = EXCLUDED.full_name,
        email     = EXCLUDED.email,
        updated_at = now()
    WHERE customers.email IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.email      -- skip no-op updates (saves WAL and HOT chains)
RETURNING id, (xmax = 0) AS inserted;                           -- xmax = 0 means the row was freshly inserted

ON CONFLICT needs a unique index or constraint matching the conflict target (an arbiter); DO NOTHING is the idempotent-insert form your migration engine used for restartability (module 12). MERGE (PostgreSQL 15+) is the standard-SQL form, supports WHEN MATCHED / NOT MATCHED with DELETE, and does not require a unique index, but it is not safe against concurrent inserts the way ON CONFLICT is (it can raise a unique violation under a race).

docs.title: 2.5 Set-based thinking versus row-at-a-time cursors
docs.text:
Your resume says you moved the application from record-level cursor access to set-based SQL. Here is the shape of that change, so you can show it:

/* Berkeley DB era: for each application in branch X, fetch customer, fetch documents, decide. */
for (ret = cur->get(cur, &key, &val, DB_SET_RANGE); ret == 0; ret = cur->get(cur, &key, &val, DB_NEXT)) {
    app = decode_app(&val);
    if (app.branch != X) break;
    cust = fetch_customer(app.customer_id);          /* one more lookup */
    ndocs = count_documents(app.id);                 /* a cursor over another DB */
    if (cust.kyc_ok && ndocs >= 2) mark_ready(app.id);   /* one write */
}

Ported literally to SQL, that becomes a loop in the application with 3 statements per row: N applications -> 3N round trips. The set-based version is one statement:

UPDATE loan_applications a
SET status = 'READY_FOR_REVIEW', updated_at = now()
FROM customers c
WHERE c.id = a.customer_id
  AND a.branch_code = $1
  AND a.status = 'SUBMITTED'
  AND c.kyc_verified
  AND (SELECT count(*) FROM documents d WHERE d.application_id = a.id) >= 2;

One round trip, one plan, one transaction, and the engine chooses hash joins over the three tables instead of 3N index probes. The rules of thumb for the translation:

Row-at-a-time habit Set-based replacement loop, SELECT by key, decide in code, UPDATE one UPDATE ... FROM ... WHERE with the decision in the WHERE loop, SELECT child count per parent JOIN (SELECT parent_id, count(*) ... GROUP BY parent_id) or LATERAL loop, INSERT one row multi-row INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...), ... or INSERT ... SELECT or COPY loop, "if exists then update else insert" INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE loop, running total in a variable sum() OVER (ORDER BY ...) loop, "latest row per group" DISTINCT ON or row_number() OVER ... = 1 temp arrays of ids, then WHERE id = ? per id WHERE id = ANY($1::bigint[]) with one array parameter, or a VALUES list joined

When a cursor is still right: processing that must call an external system per row (send an email, call a payment gateway), or per-row logic too complex for SQL, or when you must bound memory on the client and the result is huge (use a server-side cursor: DECLARE c CURSOR FOR ...; FETCH 1000 FROM c, which streams instead of materialising the whole result in the client). Even then, fetch in batches of hundreds, not one.

docs.title: 2.6 Batch inserts and COPY
docs.text:
Cost per row, roughly, from cheapest to most expensive: COPY (binary or text, one stream, no per-row parsing of SQL) < multi-row INSERT ... VALUES with hundreds of rows per statement < prepared single-row INSERT in one transaction < single-row autocommit INSERT (one fsync per row). On a laptop SSD, autocommit single rows reach a few hundred to a couple of thousand rows per second; COPY reaches hundreds of thousands (typical, not measured here).

-- From a file on the server (needs superuser or pg_read_server_files)
COPY loan_applications (application_no, customer_id, requested_amount, status)
FROM '/tmp/apps.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true);

-- From the client: psql's \copy streams the client-side file through the connection
\copy loan_applications (application_no, customer_id, requested_amount, status) FROM 'apps.csv' CSV HEADER

-- In libpq: PQputCopyData / PQputCopyEnd. Your migration engine's sink (module 12) should use this.

Bulk-load checklist: load into an unindexed staging table (or drop secondary indexes and recreate after), use COPY, run in few large transactions (one per 10k to 100k rows for restartability), disable triggers if you can prove the data is already valid, ANALYZE afterwards, VACUUM to set visibility bits. COPY ... FREEZE on a table created or truncated in the same transaction writes tuples pre-frozen with hint bits set.

docs.title: 2.7 Pagination
docs.text:
-- OFFSET pagination: page 500 reads and discards 10,000 rows. O(page) per request, and
-- rows shift between pages when data changes.
SELECT * FROM loan_applications ORDER BY submitted_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 9980;

-- Keyset (cursor) pagination: remember the last row's sort key, ask for what comes after.
-- O(log n) with an index on (submitted_at, id); stable under inserts.
SELECT * FROM loan_applications
WHERE (submitted_at, id) < ($1, $2)              -- row comparison: compares lexicographically
ORDER BY submitted_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

The tiebreaker column (id) is mandatory: without it, equal timestamps make pages overlap or skip. The API returns an opaque cursor token encoding (submitted_at, id). Downside: no "jump to page 37"; for that, OFFSET on a bounded range is acceptable, or a precomputed page index.

docs.title: 2.8 Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• N+1 queries: one query for a list, then one per row for details. Replace with a join, a WHERE id = ANY($1) batch fetch, or LATERAL. Detect it in pg_stat_statements as a single-row statement with an enormous calls count.
  • SELECT *: fetches TOASTed columns you do not use, breaks index-only scans, couples code to column order, and makes INSERT INTO ... SELECT * fragile. Name the columns.
  • Implicit casts that break indexes: comparing a text column to an integer parameter (WHERE user_code = 123456) or a varchar to a bigint makes the planner cast the column (or error). Bind parameters with the column's type; in libpq pass paramTypes or use $1::text in the SQL. Likewise timestamptz vs timestamp, numeric vs int, and date_trunc('day', created_at) = $1 (function on the column) instead of created_at >= $1 AND created_at < $1 + interval '1 day'.
  • Functions on indexed columns: WHERE lower(email) = ..., WHERE created_at::date = .... Either an expression index or a rewritten range predicate.
  • Leading wildcard LIKE '%smith': no B-tree can help; pg_trgm GIN index or full-text.
  • OR across columns: often a Seq Scan; rewrite as UNION ALL of two indexable queries.
  • count(*) for "exists": SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ... WHERE ...) stops at the first row.
  • ORDER BY random() on a big table sorts everything; use TABLESAMPLE or a random key range.
  • Unbounded IN (...) lists of thousands of literals: huge parse cost and plans; pass an array parameter (= ANY($1)) or join a VALUES list / temp table.
  • Doing math on money in floating point: numeric(18,2), never double precision.
  • Storing dates as text or epoch integers: timestamptz (module 09).
  • Long transactions around user interaction: see module 05.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m07_sql_patterns.sql has runnable versions of everything above against the loan schema, each with a comment on the expected plan. Highlights:

-- Latest application per customer, two idioms, same plan shape
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id, application_no, submitted_at
FROM loan_applications
ORDER BY customer_id, submitted_at DESC;

SELECT customer_id, application_no, submitted_at
FROM (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY submitted_at DESC) AS rn
      FROM loan_applications) x
WHERE rn = 1;

-- Batch fetch instead of N+1: one statement, one array parameter
PREPARE fetch_apps(bigint[]) AS
SELECT id, application_no, status FROM loan_applications WHERE id = ANY($1);
EXECUTE fetch_apps(ARRAY[1,2,3,4,5]);
-- plan: Index Scan on pkey with Index Cond: (id = ANY ('{1,2,3,4,5}'))

-- Fan-out trap and its fix
-- WRONG: documents x payments multiplies sums
SELECT a.id, count(d.id) AS docs, sum(p.amount) AS paid
FROM loan_applications a
LEFT JOIN documents d ON d.application_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN payments  p ON p.application_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.id;
-- RIGHT: aggregate each child separately
SELECT a.id, coalesce(d.docs, 0) AS docs, coalesce(p.paid, 0) AS paid
FROM loan_applications a
LEFT JOIN (SELECT application_id, count(*) AS docs FROM documents GROUP BY application_id) d ON d.application_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT application_id, sum(amount) AS paid FROM payments GROUP BY application_id) p ON p.application_id = a.id;

-- Row comparison for keyset pagination uses the composite index
EXPLAIN SELECT id, submitted_at FROM loan_applications
WHERE (submitted_at, id) < ('2026-09-01 00:00+00', 500000)
ORDER BY submitted_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
-- plan: Limit -> Index Scan Backward using la_submitted_id_idx, Index Cond: (ROW(submitted_at, id) < ROW(...))

-- Set-based UPDATE replacing a cursor loop
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
UPDATE loan_applications a
SET status = 'READY_FOR_REVIEW', updated_at = now()
FROM customers c
WHERE c.id = a.customer_id AND a.branch_code = 'BR0001' AND a.status = 'SUBMITTED'
  AND c.kyc_verified
  AND (SELECT count(*) FROM documents d WHERE d.application_id = a.id) >= 2;

And the libpq side of COPY, which is what a migration sink should look like:

/* Stream rows into the server without per-row SQL. Text format: tab-separated, \N for NULL. */
PGresult *r = PQexec(conn, "COPY loan_applications (application_no, customer_id, requested_amount, status) FROM STDIN");
if (PQresultStatus(r) != PGRES_COPY_IN) { /* error */ }
PQclear(r);
for (each record) {
    char line[512];
    int n = snprintf(line, sizeof line, "%s\t%lld\t%.2f\t%s\n", app_no, (long long)cust_id, amount, status);
    if (PQputCopyData(conn, line, n) != 1) { /* error */ }
}
if (PQputCopyEnd(conn, NULL) != 1) { /* error */ }
r = PQgetResult(conn);                       /* COPY's final status; check PGRES_COMMAND_OK */

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why set-based wins: the executor runs once. A single statement is parsed, planned, and executed with one pass of the Volcano iterator over a plan optimised for the whole workload: a hash join reads each table once; a nested loop with 50,000 outer rows probes an index 50,000 times but inside one process with hot caches, no protocol framing, no syscalls per row. The application loop pays per row: protocol encode/decode, two syscalls, a context switch, a snapshot (GetSnapshotData), planning or plan-cache lookup, and executor start/stop. At 50 us a round trip that is 2.5 s for 50,000 rows before any real work.

= ANY(array) and arrays as parameters.
