The planner turns col = ANY($1) into an index scan with a ScalarArrayOpExpr, probing the B-tree once per array element in sorted order (since PostgreSQL 9.2 for B-tree; 17 improved it further). Thousands of elements are fine; the cost is linear in elements and logarithmic in table size.

How DISTINCT ON executes. Sort (or Index Scan) on the DISTINCT ON columns plus the ORDER BY columns, then a Unique node that emits the first row of each group. With an index on (customer_id, submitted_at DESC) there is no sort at all.

Window functions execute as WindowAgg over input sorted by PARTITION BY then ORDER BY. All windows with the same partition and order share one sort; windows with different ordering need a separate sort each (you will see stacked WindowAgg -> Sort nodes). Frame evaluation for ROWS BETWEEN is incremental; for RANGE with peers the engine buffers each peer group.

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT internals: speculative insertion (module 03). The heap tuple is inserted with a speculative token, the unique index is probed; on conflict the tuple is "super-deleted" and the DO UPDATE path locks and updates the conflicting row with the same EvalPlanQual re-check as a normal UPDATE. Under READ COMMITTED it is race-free; two sessions upserting the same key serialise correctly.

COPY's fast path. COPY FROM parses the input in bulk, forms tuples, and uses heap_multi_insert to place many tuples on a page under one buffer lock with one WAL record per page (instead of one per row). With FREEZE it writes them with hint bits and frozen flags set. This is why COPY is an order of magnitude cheaper than inserts even inside one transaction.

Row comparison (a, b) < (x, y) is true lexicographic comparison (a < x OR (a = x AND b < y)), and the B-tree AM understands it directly as a boundary condition on a multi-column index, so keyset pagination is a single index descent to the boundary plus a walk.

Cursors on the server. DECLARE ... CURSOR plans with cursor_tuple_fraction (0.1) biasing toward fast-start plans, keeps the executor state open, and FETCH pulls N rows at a time through the protocol. The transaction stays open while the cursor exists (WITH HOLD copies the result to a tuplestore so the transaction can end). This is the right tool for streaming a 50 M row table out of PostgreSQL without 50 M round trips or 50 GB in client RAM.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The N+1 you cannot see hides in ORMs and in "helper" functions that fetch one entity. pg_stat_statements with calls in the millions for a WHERE id = $1 statement is the signature. Batch the ids.
  • Big UPDATE statements and locks. A set-based UPDATE of 10 M rows is one transaction holding 10 M row locks and generating GBs of WAL, blocking everyone touching those rows until it commits. Batch by key range (WHERE id BETWEEN $1 AND $2, 10k to 50k rows per transaction), commit each, and let autovacuum keep up. The same applies to backfills in migrations (module 12).
  • COPY failure semantics: one bad row aborts the whole COPY (no partial load; it is one statement). Load into a staging table with text columns, validate with SQL, then INSERT ... SELECT with casts into the real table. Tooling like pg_bulkload or the 17+ ON_ERROR option can skip rows, but staging is the robust approach.
  • Implicit cast outages are deployment outages. A driver upgrade changed how it binds numeric strings; the login index stopped matching; CPU hit 100%. The plan in auto_explain shows Filter: ((user_code)::bigint = $1). Fix the binding, not the index.
  • Keyset pagination and API design: the token must be opaque and must encode all sort keys; changing the sort order means a new token format. Tell product that "jump to page N" costs O(N) and let them choose.
  • Your PL/pgSQL layer (module 08) is where set-based thinking pays most: a procedure that loops FOR r IN SELECT ... LOOP UPDATE ... END LOOP is a cursor loop with extra steps; write the single UPDATE.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Write the LEFT JOIN trap and its fix on loan_applications and documents. Done when you can show the row counts differ and explain why in terms of NULL comparison.
  2. (easy) Write "latest application per customer" both ways and compare plans with an index on (customer_id, submitted_at DESC). Done when neither plan has a Sort node.
  3. (medium) Implement keyset pagination over loan_applications ordered by (submitted_at DESC, id DESC) and walk 10 pages in psql using the last row of each page as the next cursor. Insert a new row in between pages and show no row is skipped or duplicated. Done when the plan is an Index Scan Backward with a row-comparison Index Cond.
  4. (medium) Load 1 M rows into a staging table three ways: autocommit single-row inserts from a shell loop (stop after 10k and extrapolate), multi-row INSERT of 1000 rows per statement, and \copy. Done when you have three rates and can explain each in terms of round trips, parsing, fsyncs and heap_multi_insert.
  5. (hard) Take the Berkeley DB style loop in 2.5 and write it as (a) a PL/pgSQL FOR loop with three statements per row and (b) a single set-based UPDATE. Time both on 100k applications with \timing. Done when you have both numbers and can explain the ratio.
  6. (hard) Write a recursive CTE over workflow_transitions that lists every reachable state from DRAFT with the shortest path length, and prove with a cycle in the data that your depth bound stops it. Done when it returns correct depths and terminates.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between putting a condition in ON versus WHERE for a LEFT JOIN? A: In ON, the condition decides which right rows match; unmatched left rows survive with NULLs. In WHERE, the condition filters the joined result, and since unmatched rows have NULL in right columns they fail the test, turning the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. Use ON for match conditions and right.id IS NULL in WHERE for anti-joins.

Q: What are window functions and when do you use them instead of GROUP BY? A: They compute an aggregate or ranking over a window of rows related to the current row while keeping every row in the output, whereas GROUP BY collapses rows. Use them for running totals, rankings, "latest per group", and comparing a row to its group's average or to the previous row (lag/lead).

Q: How do you implement an upsert safely under concurrency? A: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (unique_cols) DO UPDATE SET ..., which requires a unique index as arbiter and uses speculative insertion so two concurrent sessions serialise correctly. MERGE is standard SQL and more flexible but can raise a unique violation under a concurrent insert race.

Q: Explain "set-based versus row-at-a-time" and why it mattered in your migration. A: The Berkeley DB application iterated records with cursors and did one lookup per related record, which ported to SQL as N round trips of three statements each. Set-based SQL expresses the whole operation as one UPDATE with joins and subqueries; the engine plans it once, uses hash joins, and does it in one round trip and one transaction. Typical speedups are one to two orders of magnitude, and the code shrinks.

Q: Why is OFFSET pagination slow and what is the alternative? A: OFFSET makes the executor produce and discard all preceding rows, so cost grows linearly with page number, and concurrent inserts shift rows between pages. Keyset pagination uses the last seen sort key in a row comparison, WHERE (ts, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC LIMIT n, which an index satisfies in logarithmic time and which is stable under inserts.

Q: Fastest way to load 10 million rows? A: COPY, into a table without secondary indexes, in a few large transactions, with triggers off if the data is validated, then build indexes, ANALYZE and VACUUM. COPY avoids per-row SQL parsing and uses multi-insert with one WAL record per page; with FREEZE on a freshly created table it also skips later hint-bit and freeze work.

Q: Name three ways a query can fail to use an existing index. A: A function or implicit cast applied to the indexed column, a predicate on a non-leading index column, and a leading-wildcard LIKE. Also low selectivity, where the planner correctly prefers a sequential scan.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• LEFT JOIN filter in WHERE becomes INNER JOIN; aggregate children separately to avoid fan-out; NOT EXISTS over NOT IN.
  • CTEs: inlined when referenced once (12+); MATERIALIZED is a fence; recursive CTEs need a depth bound.
  • Window functions keep rows and add per-partition computations; filter them in an outer query.
  • INSERT ... ON CONFLICT is the race-safe upsert; DO NOTHING gives idempotent inserts.
  • Set-based: one UPDATE ... FROM replaces a loop of SELECT/decide/UPDATE; one array parameter replaces N lookups.
  • COPY > multi-row INSERT > prepared INSERT in a transaction > autocommit INSERT.
  • Keyset pagination with a tiebreaker column and a row comparison; OFFSET is O(page).
  • Anti-patterns: N+1, SELECT *, implicit casts and functions on columns, leading wildcards, OR across columns, floats for money.
  • Batch big UPDATEs by key range to limit locks and WAL.
  • Server-side cursors stream huge results; still fetch in batches.

docs.title: 8. PL/pgSQL stored procedures
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 05, 06, 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
PL/pgSQL is a small procedural language that runs inside the PostgreSQL server. You write a function or procedure once, store it in the database, and call it from any client. Inside it you can run SQL statements, keep local variables, loop, branch, and catch errors, and all of it happens next to the data with no network round trips between steps.

The analogy: instead of phoning the bank clerk five times ("check the password", "check the account is active", "count failed attempts", "record the login", "fetch the roles"), you hand over one form that says "log this user in" and the clerk performs the whole procedure and returns one answer. The procedure is written once, enforced for every caller, and can be changed without redeploying the callers.

You already write PL/pgSQL. This module makes you able to defend every design decision in it: when logic belongs in the database, why EXCEPTION blocks cost more than they look, what plan caching does to your functions, what SECURITY DEFINER risks, and how to test and version procedures like code.

docs.title: 2.1 Functions versus procedures
docs.text:
CREATE FUNCTION CREATE PROCEDURE (PostgreSQL 11+) Called with SELECT fn(...), in expressions, FROM clause CALL proc(...) Returns a value, a row, a set (SETOF, RETURNS TABLE), or void nothing (OUT parameters for results) Transaction control none; runs inside the caller's transaction COMMIT/ROLLBACK allowed when called at top level (not inside a BEGIN block, not from a function) Usable in queries yes no Typical use computations, validations, row producers, triggers multi-step workflows, batch jobs committing per batch

Both are stored in pg_proc; both can be written in PL/pgSQL, SQL, C, or other PLs.

docs.title: 2.2 Structure and control flow
docs.text:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_name(p_arg1 bigint, p_arg2 text DEFAULT 'x')
RETURNS integer
LANGUAGE plpgsql
STABLE                        -- volatility, see 2.6
SECURITY INVOKER              -- default; see 2.5
SET search_path = loans, pg_temp   -- pin the schema resolution for this function
AS $$
DECLARE
    v_count  integer := 0;
    v_row    loan_applications%ROWTYPE;      -- a variable shaped like a table row
    v_status loan_applications.status%TYPE;  -- a variable with a column's type
BEGIN
    SELECT * INTO STRICT v_row FROM loan_applications WHERE id = p_arg1;   -- STRICT: error if 0 or >1 rows

    IF v_row.status = 'DRAFT' THEN
        v_count := 1;
    ELSIF v_row.status IN ('SUBMITTED', 'UNDER_REVIEW') THEN
        v_count := 2;
    ELSE
        v_count := 3;
    END IF;

    v_status := CASE WHEN v_count = 1 THEN 'new' ELSE 'old' END;

    FOR v_row IN SELECT * FROM loan_applications WHERE customer_id = v_row.customer_id LOOP
        CONTINUE WHEN v_row.status = 'WITHDRAWN';
        v_count := v_count + 1;
        EXIT WHEN v_count > 100;
    END LOOP;

    RETURN v_count;
END;
$$;

Naming convention that avoids the most common PL/pgSQL bug: prefix parameters p_ and variables v_ so they never collide with column names. A variable named status in a function that runs WHERE status = status is ambiguous; the default #variable_conflict error makes it fail loudly, which is the setting you want.

Loops over result sets: FOR r IN SELECT ... LOOP, FOR i IN 1..10 LOOP, FOREACH x IN ARRAY arr LOOP, WHILE cond LOOP, and FOR r IN EXECUTE dynamic_sql USING ... LOOP. After any SQL statement: FOUND is true if it affected or returned at least one row; GET DIAGNOSTICS v_n = ROW_COUNT; gives the count.

docs.title: 2.3 Returning sets
docs.text:
-- RETURNS TABLE: the output columns are declared; RETURN NEXT adds a row, RETURN QUERY adds a result set
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_validate_application(p_app_id bigint)
RETURNS TABLE (rule_code text, severity text, message text)
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$
BEGIN
    RETURN QUERY
    SELECT 'DOC_MISSING', 'ERROR', 'At least two supporting documents are required'
    WHERE (SELECT count(*) FROM documents d WHERE d.application_id = p_app_id) < 2;

    RETURN QUERY
    SELECT 'AMOUNT_LIMIT', 'ERROR', format('Requested amount exceeds branch limit of %s', b.max_loan_amount)
    FROM loan_applications a JOIN branches b ON b.code = a.branch_code
    WHERE a.id = p_app_id AND a.requested_amount > b.max_loan_amount;

    RETURN QUERY
    SELECT 'KYC_PENDING', 'WARNING', 'Customer KYC not verified'
    FROM loan_applications a JOIN customers c ON c.id = a.customer_id
    WHERE a.id = p_app_id AND NOT c.kyc_verified;
    -- falling off the end returns the accumulated rows
END;
$$;

SELECT * FROM fn_validate_application(42);

RETURNS SETOF some_table or SETOF record are the older forms. Set-returning functions materialise their whole output in a tuplestore before the caller sees the first row (PL/pgSQL cannot stream), so do not build a 10 M row report this way; write a view or plain SQL.

docs.title: 2.4 Exceptions
docs.text:
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO app_sessions (user_id, token) VALUES (p_user_id, p_token);
EXCEPTION
    WHEN unique_violation THEN
        -- the INSERT's effects are rolled back to the start of this BEGIN block; the function continues
        UPDATE app_sessions SET token = p_token, created_at = now() WHERE user_id = p_user_id;
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
        GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS v_state = RETURNED_SQLSTATE, v_msg = MESSAGE_TEXT, v_ctx = PG_EXCEPTION_CONTEXT;
        INSERT INTO error_log (sqlstate, message, context) VALUES (v_state, v_msg, v_ctx);
        RAISE;                   -- re-raise the original error after logging
END;

Every BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END block is a subtransaction (a savepoint): entering it costs a subtransaction xid allocation on first write, and exiting via an exception rolls back to the savepoint. This is the single most important performance fact about PL/pgSQL: an exception block inside a loop creates one subtransaction per iteration, and past 64 live subtransactions per backend the snapshot code falls off the pg_subtrans cliff (module 05). Put the loop inside the exception block, or avoid exceptions for expected cases (ON CONFLICT, IF EXISTS checks).

Raising your own errors with meaning the application can switch on:

RAISE EXCEPTION 'Transition % -> % not permitted for role %', v_from, p_to, v_role
    USING ERRCODE = 'LN403',                       -- custom 5-char SQLSTATE; class 'LN' is yours
          HINT = 'Request approval from a branch manager',
          DETAIL = format('application_id=%s actor=%s', p_app_id, p_actor_id);

Levels: DEBUG, LOG, INFO, NOTICE, WARNING (continue), EXCEPTION (abort). The client receives SQLSTATE, message, detail and hint as separate fields (PQresultErrorField), so the application maps LN403 to HTTP 403 without parsing text.

docs.title: 2.5 SECURITY DEFINER
docs.text:
A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with the privileges of its owner, like setuid. Use: let an application role call sp_login that reads password_hash, without granting the role SELECT on app_users. Rules that make it safe:

  1. SET search_path = pg_catalog, loans, pg_temp on the function, so a caller cannot create a temp table or function that shadows one you reference (the classic privilege escalation).
  2. REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION ... FROM PUBLIC; GRANT EXECUTE ... TO app_role; because functions are executable by PUBLIC by default.
  3. Schema-qualify everything inside, validate every input, never build SQL by concatenation (format('%I', ...) for identifiers, %L for literals, or EXECUTE ... USING).
  4. Own it by a role with the minimum needed privileges, not a superuser.

docs.title: 2.6 Volatility, strictness, and plan caching
docs.text:
Volatility tells the planner how often it may call the function:

Category Promise Effects VOLATILE (default) may do anything, result can differ per call called once per row, never indexed, gets a fresh snapshot for each statement inside STABLE same inputs + same snapshot -> same result; reads tables but does not modify may be called once per statement for constant args; usable in index conditions; sees the calling statement's snapshot IMMUTABLE pure function of its inputs, never reads tables may be constant-folded at plan time; required for expression indexes and generated columns

Lying is a correctness bug: an IMMUTABLE function that reads a table returns stale results once folded into a plan or an index. Mark every lookup-only function STABLE; it is both faster and honest.

STRICT (RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT): the function is not called at all if any argument is NULL. PARALLEL SAFE lets it run in parallel workers (default UNSAFE). LEAKPROOF matters only for row-level security.

Plan caching. Each SQL statement inside a PL/pgSQL function is prepared on first execution in a session and the plan is cached for the life of the session, with the same custom/generic logic as prepared statements (module 06): five custom plans, then possibly generic. Three consequences:

  • A function statement with a skewed parameter can lock into a bad generic plan. Use SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan on the function (ALTER FUNCTION f SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan), or write the SQL so the skew is not a parameter.
  • EXECUTE 'dynamic sql' USING ... is planned every call: flexible but no caching, and the right tool when the table name or the WHERE shape changes.
  • Cached plans are invalidated when the referenced objects change (DDL); you do not need to reconnect after CREATE INDEX.

Inlining. A LANGUAGE sql function that is a single SELECT and is STABLE/IMMUTABLE and not STRICT-with-nullable-args can be inlined into the calling query, letting the planner see through it. PL/pgSQL functions are never inlined; each call is a black box with a cpu_operator_cost-based default cost (COST 100). For small reusable expressions, prefer SQL functions.

docs.title: 2.7 Transaction control in procedures
docs.text:
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_archive_withdrawn(p_batch_size int DEFAULT 10000)
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
    v_moved int;
BEGIN
    LOOP
        WITH batch AS (
            DELETE FROM loan_applications
            WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM loan_applications
                         WHERE status = 'WITHDRAWN' AND updated_at < now() - interval '2 years'
                         ORDER BY id LIMIT p_batch_size
                         FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
            RETURNING *
        )
        INSERT INTO loan_applications_archive SELECT * FROM batch;
        GET DIAGNOSTICS v_moved = ROW_COUNT;
        COMMIT;                                 -- releases locks, lets VACUUM reclaim, bounds WAL per transaction
        EXIT WHEN v_moved < p_batch_size;
    END LOOP;
END;
$$;
CALL sp_archive_withdrawn(5000);                -- must be called outside an explicit transaction block

After COMMIT inside a procedure a new transaction starts automatically; SET TRANSACTION can change its isolation. Procedures cannot commit if called from a function, from a trigger, or inside BEGIN ... END from the client (the error is "invalid transaction termination").

docs.title: 2.8 Where logic belongs: database or application
docs.text:
Put it in the database when:

  • The rule must hold for every writer (several applications, batch jobs, DBAs): constraints first, then triggers or procedures. "Application status can only change along defined transitions" is such a rule.
  • It is set-oriented and touches many rows: moving it to the application means shipping the rows out and back.
  • It is a multi-statement atomic unit that would otherwise be several round trips in one transaction (your login path; a state transition with audit).
  • Security: the application role should not see raw data (password hashes) but needs a derived answer.

Keep it in the application when:

  • It is CPU-heavy and scales with users (the database is the hardest tier to scale out; a stored procedure that hashes passwords with bcrypt at cost 12 burns the database's CPU).
  • It calls external systems (HTTP, queues) or needs libraries the database lacks.
  • It changes often and is owned by many teams; database deployments are more coupled.
  • Testing and debugging tooling for your application language is far better than for PL/pgSQL, and the logic is complex branching rather than data rules.

The honest answer for your banking server: validation rules, authorisation checks against roles/branches, and workflow transitions with audit went into PL/pgSQL because they are data-integrity rules enforced for all callers and they collapsed many round trips; password hashing and session token generation stayed in C.

docs.title: 2.9 Testing with pgTAP and versioning
docs.text:
pgTAP is a set of SQL assertion functions (CREATE EXTENSION pgtap, package postgresql-16-pgtap on Ubuntu) run with pg_prove. A test is a transaction that is rolled back, so it never dirties the database:

BEGIN;
SELECT plan(5);
SELECT has_function('loans', 'sp_transition_application', ARRAY['bigint','text','bigint','text']);
SELECT lives_ok($$CALL loans.sp_transition_application(1, 'SUBMITTED', 100, 'test')$$, 'DRAFT -> SUBMITTED allowed');
-- the transition exists, but needs CREDIT_OFFICER; user 100 is clerk + branch manager only
SELECT throws_ok($$CALL loans.sp_transition_application(1, 'UNDER_REVIEW', 100, 'test')$$, 'LN403',
                 NULL, 'SUBMITTED -> UNDER_REVIEW blocked without CREDIT_OFFICER');
-- no such edge in the workflow at all: validation failure, checked before the role
SELECT throws_ok($$CALL loans.sp_transition_application(1, 'DISBURSED', 100, 'test')$$, 'LN400',
                 NULL, 'SUBMITTED -> DISBURSED is not a transition');
SELECT is((SELECT status FROM loans.loan_applications WHERE id = 1), 'SUBMITTED', 'status persisted');
SELECT * FROM finish();
ROLLBACK;

Versioning procedures. Treat them as code: one file per function in version control, deployed through the same migration tool as schema changes (Flyway, sqitch, dbmate, or your own numbered SQL scripts with a schema_migrations table). Rules:

  • CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION keeps the OID (callers' cached plans are invalidated, not broken) but cannot change the return type or parameter names; for those you DROP and CREATE, inside one transaction so there is no window without the function.
  • Changing the parameter list creates an overload, leaving the old signature in place. Clean it up explicitly; ambiguous overloads cause "function is not unique" errors.
  • Deploy DDL and procedure changes together in one transaction when the new procedure depends on new columns.
  • Keep the procedures backward compatible across one release when the application and database deploy separately (add parameters with DEFAULTs; add result columns at the end).

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
The example rebuilds your "validation, authorisation and workflow rules" layer for the loan schema. Files: code/plpgsql/m08_functions.sql, m08_procedures.sql, m08_workflow_rules.sql, m08_pgtap_tests.sql. The core procedure:

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_transition_application(
    p_app_id   bigint,
    p_to_state text,
    p_actor_id bigint,
    p_note     text DEFAULT NULL)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
SECURITY DEFINER
SET search_path = pg_catalog, loans, pg_temp
AS $$
DECLARE
    v_from_state text;
    v_required_role text;
    v_violations int;
BEGIN
    -- 1. Lock the application row for the duration: two clerks cannot race a transition.
    SELECT status INTO STRICT v_from_state
    FROM loan_applications WHERE id = p_app_id FOR UPDATE;

    -- 2. Is this transition defined at all? (data, not code: the graph lives in a table)
    SELECT required_role INTO v_required_role
    FROM workflow_transitions WHERE from_state = v_from_state AND to_state = p_to_state;
    IF NOT FOUND THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'No transition % -> %', v_from_state, p_to_state USING ERRCODE = 'LN400';
    END IF;

    -- 3. Authorisation: does the actor hold the required role in the application's branch?
    IF NOT fn_user_has_role(p_actor_id, v_required_role,
                            (SELECT branch_code FROM loan_applications WHERE id = p_app_id)) THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'Transition % -> % requires role %', v_from_state, p_to_state, v_required_role
            USING ERRCODE = 'LN403';
    END IF;

    -- 4. Validation rules: any ERROR-severity violation blocks a submit or approve.
    IF p_to_state IN ('SUBMITTED', 'APPROVED') THEN
        SELECT count(*) INTO v_violations
        FROM fn_validate_application(p_app_id) v WHERE v.severity = 'ERROR';
        IF v_violations > 0 THEN
            RAISE EXCEPTION '% validation error(s) block transition to %', v_violations, p_to_state
                USING ERRCODE = 'LN422', HINT = 'Call fn_validate_application for details';
        END IF;
    END IF;

    -- 5. Apply and audit, in the same transaction as the checks.
    UPDATE loan_applications
    SET status = p_to_state, updated_at = now(), updated_by = p_actor_id
    WHERE id = p_app_id;

    INSERT INTO application_audit (application_id, from_state, to_state, actor_id, note)
    VALUES (p_app_id, v_from_state, p_to_state, p_actor_id, p_note);
END;
$$;
REVOKE EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE sp_transition_application FROM PUBLIC;
GRANT  EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE sp_transition_application TO loans_app;

And the login function that replaced five round trips, returning one row the C server consumes:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_login_check(p_branch_code text, p_user_code text)
RETURNS TABLE (user_id bigint, password_hash text, status text, failed_attempts int, roles text[])
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = pg_catalog, loans, pg_temp
AS $$
BEGIN
    RETURN QUERY
    SELECT u.id, u.password_hash, u.status, u.failed_attempts,
           coalesce(array_agg(r.role_code ORDER BY r.role_code) FILTER (WHERE r.role_code IS NOT NULL), '{}')
    FROM app_users u
    LEFT JOIN user_roles r ON r.user_id = u.id
    WHERE u.branch_code = p_branch_code AND u.user_code = p_user_code      -- hits app_users_login_idx
    GROUP BY u.id;
END;
$$;
-- The password comparison (bcrypt) and session token creation stay in the C server;
-- a second small procedure sp_record_login(p_user_id, p_success) updates failed_attempts and inserts the session.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
How PL/pgSQL executes. On first call in a session the function body is parsed into an AST of PL/pgSQL statements (PLpgSQL_stmt_*) and cached in the session's function cache. Each embedded SQL statement becomes an SPI (Server Programming Interface) prepared plan on its first execution: SPI_prepare -> SPI_execute_plan, with PL/pgSQL variables passed as parameters ($1, $2 ...). Expressions like v_count := v_count + 1 are themselves SQL expressions (SELECT $1 + 1) executed through a fast path for simple expressions, which is why tight arithmetic loops in PL/pgSQL are slow compared to C: each := is an expression evaluation through the executor, not a CPU add.

Subtransactions in detail. Entering a BEGIN ... EXCEPTION block calls BeginInternalSubTransaction; a resource owner and memory context are created; on first write the subtransaction gets its own xid, recorded in pg_subtrans and in the backend's ProcArray cache (64 slots). On error, RollbackAndReleaseCurrentSubTransaction discards the subtransaction's changes (its tuples become invisible: xid aborted) and releases its locks. Cost per block even without an error: a few microseconds of bookkeeping; with a write, an xid. Beyond 64 subxids, every snapshot by any session that must check one of this backend's subxids goes to pg_subtrans on disk (SLRU). A 100k-iteration loop with an exception block per iteration is the canonical way to trigger this on a busy system.

Snapshot behaviour by volatility. A VOLATILE function's statements each take a new snapshot (READ COMMITTED semantics inside the function), so it sees rows committed by other sessions during its own execution. A STABLE or IMMUTABLE function executes with the calling statement's snapshot: everything inside is consistent with the outer query, and it cannot see its own caller's uncommitted modifications made by the same statement. This is why a validation function used in a WHERE clause must be STABLE: with VOLATILE it would be re-evaluated per row with changing snapshots and cost a snapshot each time.

RETURN QUERY and tuplestores. Set-returning PL/pgSQL functions append every result row to a tuplestore (work_mem in memory, then temp file), and the caller reads from it only after the function returns. A function returning 1 M rows therefore holds 1 M rows before the first is delivered; the planner also cannot push a WHERE from the caller into the function. The planner estimates set-returning function output at ROWS 1000 unless you set ROWS n on the function, another source of bad plans in queries that join to functions.

Function call overhead and the COST clause. Each PL/pgSQL call costs tens of microseconds of setup (SPI connect, variable allocation). The planner uses COST (default 100 for PL functions, 1 for C/SQL) to decide evaluation order of predicates: cheaper predicates first. Set it realistically for expensive validation functions so they run after cheap filters.

Triggers are functions with a fixed signature (RETURNS trigger) called by the executor's ModifyTable node per row or per statement with NEW/OLD. Per-row triggers that run SQL turn a set-based UPDATE of 1 M rows into 1 M function calls; statement-level triggers with transition tables (REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS newrows) keep it set-based. Use them for audit and denormalised counters; keep business workflows in explicit procedures where the caller can see them.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Error codes are an API. Define a range of custom SQLSTATEs (LN4xx for client errors, LN5xx for server-side rule failures), document them, and map them in the C server to RPC error codes. Never make the client parse MESSAGE_TEXT.
  • Exception blocks per row in a batch procedure is the most common PL/pgSQL performance bug. Validate with set-based SQL first; use ON CONFLICT; wrap the loop, not the iteration.
  • Lock ordering inside procedures. FOR UPDATE the parent row first, then children, consistently across all procedures that touch the same tables; otherwise two procedures deadlock each other (module 05) and the user sees a 40P01 from a function three calls deep.
  • Long procedures block VACUUM and hold locks. A procedure processing 10 M rows in one transaction is the long transaction from module 05. Commit per batch (2.7).
  • Deploying a new version of a hot function under load: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION needs only a brief lock on the pg_proc row but invalidates cached plans in every session; the first call after deployment re-plans. If the function's dependent table also changed in the same deployment, run both in one transaction.
  • SECURITY DEFINER without search_path is a CVE-class mistake. Lint for it: SELECT proname FROM pg_proc WHERE prosecdef AND NOT coalesce(proconfig::text, '') LIKE '%search_path%'.
  • Debugging: RAISE NOTICE with client_min_messages = notice in psql; auto_explain.log_nested_statements = on to see the plans of statements inside functions; pg_stat_statements.track = all to see them as separate entries; plpgsql_check extension for static analysis (catches typos in column names that only fail at runtime).
  • YugabyteDB: PL/pgSQL runs unchanged on YSQL, but each statement inside may cost a network hop to a tablet leader, so collapsing round trips into procedures matters even more there; and COMMIT inside procedures is supported but each commit is a distributed transaction commit (module 11).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Load code/plpgsql/m08_workflow_rules.sql and the schema. Call sp_transition_application for a valid and an invalid transition from psql; print the SQLSTATE with \errverbose. Done when you see your custom LN403 code.
  2. (easy) Write fn_user_has_role(p_user_id, p_role, p_branch) as a LANGUAGE sql STABLE function and show with EXPLAIN that it is inlined into a calling query (no Function Scan, the join appears in the plan). Done when the plan shows the inlined join.
  3. (medium) Write a batch procedure that inserts 100,000 rows with an EXCEPTION WHEN unique_violation block per row, time it; rewrite with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and no exception block, time it. Done when you can explain the difference in terms of subtransactions.
  4. (medium) Mark fn_validate_application as IMMUTABLE, use it in a query, change the underlying data, and demonstrate a wrong (stale) answer. Done when you can state why STABLE is the correct category.
  5. (hard) Create a SECURITY DEFINER function without SET search_path that calls an unqualified lower(text). As a low-privilege role, create public.lower(text) that logs its argument to a table you control, call the definer function, and show the capture. Then fix the function. Done when the attack works before the fix and fails after.
  6. (hard) Write pgTAP tests for the workflow procedure covering: a permitted transition, a forbidden transition (role), a blocked transition (validation), and the audit row. Run with pg_prove -d loans code/plpgsql/m08_pgtap_tests.sql. Done when all tests pass and the database is unchanged after the run.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Function versus procedure in PostgreSQL? A: A function returns a value or set and is used inside SQL statements, running within the caller's transaction with no transaction control. A procedure is invoked with CALL, returns nothing except OUT parameters, and can COMMIT and ROLLBACK when called at top level, which makes it the right tool for batch jobs that commit per chunk.

Q: What does an EXCEPTION block cost? A: It creates a subtransaction (a savepoint) on entry so that the block's changes can be rolled back independently. That costs bookkeeping and, if the block writes, a subtransaction xid. Inside a loop it creates one per iteration, and beyond 64 live subtransactions per backend snapshot checks fall back to the on-disk pg_subtrans, which can slow the whole server. Wrap the loop, not the iteration, and use ON CONFLICT instead of catching unique violations.

Q: What do STABLE and IMMUTABLE mean and why does lying about them matter? A: STABLE promises the same result for the same inputs within one statement and no writes, so the planner may evaluate it once per statement, use it in index conditions, and run it under the calling statement's snapshot. IMMUTABLE promises a pure function of its inputs, so it can be constant-folded and used in expression indexes. An IMMUTABLE function that reads tables returns stale results from folded plans and indexes.

Q: How does plan caching work inside PL/pgSQL? A: Each SQL statement in a function is prepared through SPI on first execution per session and the plan is cached, following the prepared-statement rule of five custom plans then possibly a generic plan. Skewed parameters can lock in a bad generic plan; force_custom_plan on the function or dynamic EXECUTE avoids it. Plans are invalidated automatically by DDL.

Q: When do you put logic in the database rather than the application? A: When the rule must hold for every writer, when it is set-oriented over many rows, when it is a multi-statement atomic unit that would otherwise be several round trips, or when the application role should not see the raw data. Keep CPU-heavy work, external calls, and frequently changing team-owned logic in the application. In my banking server, validation, authorisation and workflow transitions went into PL/pgSQL; password hashing stayed in C.

Q: What are the risks of SECURITY DEFINER? A: The function runs with the owner's privileges, so an attacker who can influence name resolution can hijack it: without a fixed search_path, a caller's temp schema or public schema function can shadow a referenced function or operator. Mitigate with SET search_path on the function, schema-qualified references, REVOKE EXECUTE FROM PUBLIC, parameterised dynamic SQL, and a non-superuser owner.

Q: How did your login procedure change the latency? A: Five statements in the C server became one function call returning one row with the user's hash, status, attempt count and roles, cutting the round trips from five to one, and the function's statements hit the covering natural-key index, so the whole check became a single index-only read. The password comparison remained in the application.

Q: How do you test and version stored procedures? A: One file per routine under version control, deployed with the same migration tool as schema changes, in one transaction when the routine depends on new DDL. pgTAP tests run inside a transaction that is rolled back, asserting results, raised SQLSTATEs and side effects such as audit rows, and execute in CI via pg_prove against a database built from the migrations.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Functions return values and run in the caller's transaction; procedures use CALL and can COMMIT per batch.
  • Prefix parameters p_, variables v_; #variable_conflict error is your friend.
  • RETURNS TABLE + RETURN QUERY for set results; output is materialised, not streamed.
  • EXCEPTION blocks are subtransactions; never one per loop iteration; use ON CONFLICT.
  • RAISE ... USING ERRCODE = 'LNxxx' makes errors a stable API for the C server.
  • SECURITY DEFINER needs SET search_path, REVOKE FROM PUBLIC, qualified names, format('%I','%L').
  • Volatility: VOLATILE per row, STABLE per statement with the caller's snapshot, IMMUTABLE foldable; never lie.
  • Statements inside functions are cached prepared plans: generic-plan traps apply; EXECUTE replans.
  • Logic in the DB for integrity rules, set operations, atomic multi-step units, data hiding; not for CPU-heavy or external calls.
  • pgTAP in a rolled-back transaction; version routines as code; CREATE OR REPLACE keeps the OID, overloads linger.

docs.title: 9. Schema design and data modelling
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: 03, 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A schema is the set of tables, columns, types and constraints that says what data is allowed to exist. A good schema makes wrong data impossible to store, makes the common queries cheap, and reads like documentation of the business. A bad schema lets the same fact live in three places (and disagree), forces every query through five joins, or stores dates as strings.

The analogy is a set of paper forms designed for a bank branch. If the customer's address is written on the loan form, the account form and the card form, one of them will be wrong after she moves. If the form has a box labelled "status" where clerks write anything, reports break. Normalisation is the discipline of "each fact in exactly one place"; constraints are the printed rules on the form ("tick exactly one"); indexes are the filing order.

This module models the loan-origination domain used by every code example in the course, and explains each decision as you would in a design review.

docs.title: 2.1 Normalisation to 3NF in plain words
docs.text:
• 1NF: every column holds one atomic value; no repeating groups (phone1, phone2, phone3), no comma-separated lists in a text column. Repeating things become rows in a child table.
  • 2NF: every non-key column depends on the whole primary key. Matters for composite keys: in (application_id, document_id, customer_name) the customer name depends only on the application, so it belongs on the application (or the customer), not here.
  • 3NF: every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key: no column depends on another non-key column. branch_code, branch_name on the application row violates it (branch_name depends on branch_code); move branch_name to branches.

In practice: identify the entities (customer, branch, application, document, user), give each a table, store each fact once, and link with foreign keys. Then denormalise deliberately only where measured reads need it (a cached application_count on customers, a current_status copied from the latest audit row), and document how the copy is kept consistent (trigger, or the procedure that owns the write).

Your migration source was the opposite: Berkeley DB records were packed structs with everything inlined (customer name inside the loan record, because joins did not exist). Mapping those records to relational tables is normalisation, and "record-to-relational mapping" on your resume means: decompose each packed record into 3NF entities, choose keys, and keep the reverse mapping for parity checks (module 12).

docs.title: 2.2 Keys: surrogate versus natural
docs.text:
A natural key is a business identifier that already exists (national ID, branch code + user code, application number). A surrogate key is a meaningless identifier the database generates (bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, or a UUID).

Natural key as PK Surrogate key as PK Stability business rules change (codes get renumbered, IDs get reissued); changing a PK cascades through every FK never changes Size often text, 10 to 40 bytes, in every child table and index 8 bytes Joins self-describing child rows one more join to show the code Uniqueness must still be enforced natural key still needs a UNIQUE constraint

The convention that works: surrogate bigint identity as the primary key, natural key as a UNIQUE NOT NULL constraint. Both get an index; both are usable for lookups. Your login bug (module 03) was not caused by having a surrogate key; it was caused by forgetting the unique constraint on the natural key, which would have created the index automatically. Say it that way.

UUIDs as PKs: fine when ids are generated by many clients or must not be guessable; use time-ordered UUIDv7 (or uuid_generate_v1mc) rather than random v4 to avoid B-tree splits everywhere (module 03). 16 bytes versus 8.

Composite primary keys are right for pure link tables (user_roles (user_id, role_id)), where no other table references the row.

docs.title: 2.3 Constraints as documentation
docs.text:
Every constraint is a sentence about the business that the database enforces for every writer, including the DBA with psql at 3 AM:

requested_amount numeric(18,2) NOT NULL CHECK (requested_amount > 0),
term_months      int           NOT NULL CHECK (term_months BETWEEN 6 AND 360),
status           text          NOT NULL REFERENCES workflow_states(code),
CONSTRAINT la_submitted_needs_time CHECK (status = 'DRAFT' OR submitted_at IS NOT NULL),
CONSTRAINT la_app_no_format CHECK (application_no ~ '^LA-[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{6}$'),
-- one active application per customer per product: a partial unique index
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX la_one_active ON loan_applications (customer_id, product_id)
    WHERE status NOT IN ('REJECTED', 'WITHDRAWN', 'CLOSED');
-- no overlapping validity periods for an interest rate: exclusion constraint (GiST)
CONSTRAINT rate_no_overlap EXCLUDE USING gist (product_id WITH =, valid_during WITH &&)

NOT NULL everywhere a value is mandatory; NULL means "unknown", nothing else. DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED on foreign keys only when you must insert circular references in one transaction. Name constraints (CONSTRAINT la_amount_positive CHECK ...) so error messages and migration scripts are readable.

docs.title: 2.4 Foreign keys and their indexes
docs.text:
A foreign key is checked on insert/update of the child (an index lookup on the parent's PK, which exists) and on delete/update of the parent (a scan of the child table for referencing rows, which needs an index you must create). Every FK column that is deleted-through or joined-on gets an index; this is the most common missing-index class in real schemas:

SELECT conrelid::regclass AS child, a.attname AS fk_column
FROM pg_constraint c JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.conrelid AND a.attnum = ANY (c.conkey)
WHERE c.contype = 'f'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_index i
                  WHERE i.indrelid = c.conrelid AND (i.indkey::int2[])[0] = a.attnum);

ON DELETE options: RESTRICT/NO ACTION (default; refuse) for most business data, CASCADE for true children (documents of an application), SET NULL for optional references. Cascading deletes across large child sets happen row by row under locks; prefer soft deletes for anything with history.

docs.title: 2.5 Enums versus lookup tables
docs.text:
CREATE TYPE status AS ENUM (...) lookup table + FK Storage 4 bytes text code (or small int FK) Adding a value ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE (cannot be run inside a transaction block before 12; cannot remove or reorder values) INSERT Attaching data to a value (display name, sort order, who may set it) no yes: columns on the lookup row Portability PostgreSQL-specific standard

Rule: enums for small fixed sets that are truly part of the code ('DEBIT'/'CREDIT'); lookup tables for anything the business will extend or that needs attributes (workflow states, document kinds, rejection reasons). Text codes as FK values (status text REFERENCES workflow_states(code)) keep rows readable without joins and cost a few bytes more than a smallint.

docs.title: 2.6 Soft deletes and audit tables
docs.text:
Soft delete (deleted_at timestamptz NULL) keeps the row for history and FK integrity. Costs: every query needs WHERE deleted_at IS NULL (hide it behind a view or row-level security), unique constraints must become partial (UNIQUE ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL), and "deleted" rows still occupy pages and indexes. Use it for business entities (customers, applications); hard-delete transient data (sessions, tokens).

Audit: two patterns. A per-table history table written by a trigger (loan_applications_history with valid_from/valid_to and the full row image), good for "show me the application as of 1 March"; or an append-only event table (application_audit with from_state, to_state, actor, note, time), good for "who did what". Store the actor from the application (updated_by column or set_config('app.actor_id', ...) read by the trigger), because the database user is the pooled application role, not the clerk. Audit tables are insert-only: REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE from everyone but the owner.

docs.title: 2.7 Time zones
docs.text:
• Use timestamptz ("timestamp with time zone") for every instant. It is stored as 8-byte UTC microseconds; the session TimeZone setting only affects display and parsing. timestamp without time zone is a wall-clock reading with no instant attached: two servers in different zones store different instants for "now".
  • Use date for calendar dates (date of birth, due date). Due dates are business-day concepts: "the 5th" is not an instant.
  • Store the customer's or branch's IANA zone ('Asia/Kolkata') if you need local rendering; never a fixed offset, because offsets change with DST and law.
  • now() is the transaction start time (stable within a transaction); clock_timestamp() is the wall clock. Audit rows should use now() so all rows of one transaction share a timestamp.
  • Monthly scheduling: date_trunc('month', ts AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'), computed in the business zone, not in UTC, or month boundaries land at 05:30.

docs.title: 2.8 Types: the short list
docs.text: bigint for ids and counters (not int: 2.1 billion arrives), numeric(18,2) for money (never float), text (not varchar(n) unless the limit is a business rule; add a CHECK (length(x) <= n) which is easier to change), boolean not char(1), timestamptz, date, uuid, jsonb for genuinely schemaless attachments (with a GIN index when queried), bytea for binary blobs under a few MB (bigger: object storage with a reference). Order columns for alignment (module 02).

docs.title: 2.9 The loan-origination model
docs.text:
branches ---< app_users >--< user_roles >--- roles
    |             |
    |             | (actor)
    |             v
 customers ---< loan_applications ---< documents
    ^               |      |
    |               |      +---< payments
    +-- (kyc)       |
                    +---< application_audit
 loan_products ---< loan_applications
 workflow_states ---< workflow_transitions >--- roles (required_role)
 workflow_states <--- loan_applications.status

Entities and key decisions:

  • branches(code PK text): a natural key is the PK here because branch codes are short, stable, printed on every document, and referenced by name everywhere. One deliberate exception.
  • customers(id identity PK, national_id UNIQUE, email UNIQUE partial where deleted_at IS NULL, kyc_verified, deleted_at).
  • app_users(id PK, branch_code FK, user_code, UNIQUE (branch_code, user_code), password_hash, status, failed_attempts, last_login_at): the login natural key as a unique constraint; see module 03 for the covering index.
  • roles(code PK), user_roles(user_id, role_id, branch_code) PK (user_id, role_id, branch_code).
  • loan_products(id PK, code UNIQUE, max_amount, ...).
  • loan_applications(id PK, application_no UNIQUE, customer_id FK, product_id FK, branch_code FK, status FK workflow_states, requested_amount, term_months, submitted_at, created_at, updated_at, updated_by FK app_users).
  • documents(id PK, application_id FK ON DELETE CASCADE, kind FK document_kinds, storage_key, sha256 bytea, uploaded_at); content in object storage, not in the row.
  • payments(id PK, application_id FK, kind ('DISBURSEMENT','REPAYMENT'), amount, posted_at).
  • workflow_states(code PK, is_terminal), workflow_transitions(from_state, to_state, required_role, PK (from_state, to_state)): the state machine is data, so adding a state is an INSERT, and the procedure in module 08 reads it.
  • application_audit(id PK, application_id FK, from_state, to_state, actor_id, note, at timestamptz default now()): insert-only.
  • accounts and on_call: tiny tables for the isolation demos in module 05.

Index set (beyond PK/UNIQUE): every FK column; (status, submitted_at) for work queues; (customer_id, submitted_at DESC) for "latest per customer"; (submitted_at, id) for keyset pagination; partial unique for one active application per customer and product.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m09_schema.sql creates everything above with comments on each decision; code/m09_seed.sql loads 500 branches, 200k customers, 2 M users (the module 03 table), 1 M applications, documents and payments, using generate_series so it runs in a few minutes on a laptop. Key excerpts:

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS loans;
SET search_path = loans, public;

CREATE TABLE branches (
    code             text PRIMARY KEY CHECK (code ~ '^BR[0-9]{4}$'),   -- natural key, deliberately
    name             text NOT NULL,
    max_loan_amount  numeric(18,2) NOT NULL CHECK (max_loan_amount > 0),
    time_zone        text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Asia/Kolkata'              -- IANA zone, not an offset
);

CREATE TABLE customers (
    id            bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    national_id   text NOT NULL,
    full_name     text NOT NULL,
    email         text,
    date_of_birth date NOT NULL CHECK (date_of_birth > DATE '1900-01-01'),
    kyc_verified  boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
    created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    deleted_at    timestamptz,                                         -- soft delete
    CONSTRAINT customers_national_id_key UNIQUE (national_id)
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_live_key ON customers (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

CREATE TABLE loan_applications (
    id               bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    requested_amount numeric(18,2) NOT NULL CHECK (requested_amount > 0),   -- 8-byte-aligned fields first
    customer_id      bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
    product_id       bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES loan_products(id),
    updated_by       bigint REFERENCES app_users(id),
    submitted_at     timestamptz,
    created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    term_months      int NOT NULL CHECK (term_months BETWEEN 6 AND 360),
    application_no   text NOT NULL,
    branch_code      text NOT NULL REFERENCES branches(code),
    status           text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'DRAFT' REFERENCES workflow_states(code),
    CONSTRAINT la_application_no_key UNIQUE (application_no),
    CONSTRAINT la_application_no_format CHECK (application_no ~ '^LA-[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{6}$'),
    CONSTRAINT la_submitted_needs_time CHECK (status = 'DRAFT' OR submitted_at IS NOT NULL)
);
CREATE INDEX la_customer_submitted_idx ON loan_applications (customer_id, submitted_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX la_status_submitted_idx   ON loan_applications (status, submitted_at);
CREATE INDEX la_submitted_id_idx       ON loan_applications (submitted_at, id);
CREATE INDEX la_product_idx            ON loan_applications (product_id);
CREATE INDEX la_updated_by_idx         ON loan_applications (updated_by);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX la_one_active_key  ON loan_applications (customer_id, product_id)
    WHERE status NOT IN ('REJECTED', 'WITHDRAWN', 'CLOSED');

CREATE TABLE application_audit (
    id             bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    application_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES loan_applications(id),
    actor_id       bigint REFERENCES app_users(id),
    at             timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),                -- transaction time, not clock time
    from_state     text NOT NULL,
    to_state       text NOT NULL,
    note           text
);
CREATE INDEX application_audit_app_idx ON application_audit (application_id, at);
REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON application_audit FROM PUBLIC;

The audit trigger pattern (statement-level, set-based) is also in the schema file:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION trg_touch_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
    NEW.updated_at := now();
    RETURN NEW;
END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER la_touch BEFORE UPDATE ON loan_applications
    FOR EACH ROW WHEN (OLD.* IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.*) EXECUTE FUNCTION trg_touch_updated_at();

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What a constraint costs. NOT NULL and CHECK are evaluated in the executor per row, microseconds. UNIQUE/PRIMARY KEY are B-tree indexes with uniqueness checks at insert time, including waiting on concurrent uncommitted inserters of the same key (module 03). FOREIGN KEY is implemented as system triggers (RI_FKey_check_ins, RI_FKey_noaction_del ...) that run a cached SPI query (SELECT 1 FROM parent WHERE pk = $1 FOR KEY SHARE) per changed row; the FOR KEY SHARE lock on the parent is why heavy inserts of children contend on a hot parent row (MultiXacts, module 05). Statement-level FK checking with transition tables is still not in 16, so a bulk insert of 1 M children runs 1 M parent lookups: fast with the parent's PK index, but not free. Loading with ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER ALL is an option when the data is known good and you accept the responsibility.

Identity and sequences. GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY creates a sequence owned by the column. nextval() is non-transactional: a rolled-back insert leaves a gap. Sequences cache values per session (CACHE 1 default) and are WAL-logged every 32 values, which is why sequence values can jump after a crash. Gaps are normal; never promise gapless numbers from a sequence. For application_no with a per-year gapless counter, use a counter table row updated under a row lock, accepting the serialisation point. On YugabyteDB, sequences are distributed and cache 100 values per node by default, so ids are not monotonic across nodes (module 11).

ALTER TABLE lock classes. ADD COLUMN with no default or a constant default: catalog-only, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for milliseconds. ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT now() (volatile): rewrites the table. ALTER COLUMN TYPE: usually a rewrite plus index rebuilds (except binary-compatible changes such as varchar(50) to text). ADD CONSTRAINT CHECK/FK: scans the table under a lock, unless NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (which takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE). SET NOT NULL: full scan, unless 12+ with an existing valid CHECK (col IS NOT NULL). Knowing which operations rewrite is what lets you promise "zero downtime" for a migration.

Why text and not varchar(n). Both are the same varlena type internally; varchar(n) adds a length check at input. Changing n later on a varchar column is a catalog-only change since 9.2 when growing, but the limit lives in the type, so views, functions and dependent columns inherit it. A CHECK constraint is explicit, named, and droppable.

Partitioning (declarative, 10+): split a huge table by range (created_at by month), list (branch_code), or hash. Benefits: dropping a month is DROP TABLE of a partition instead of a 10 M row delete; partition pruning reads only relevant partitions; smaller indexes per partition. Costs: planning time grows with partition count (hundreds, not thousands), unique constraints must include the partition key, no global indexes. Use it for audit/event tables past a few hundred GB, rarely for core entities.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Migrations that lock. The list above (rewrites, full-scan constraints) is the checklist before every schema change on a hot table. Pattern: add nullable column -> backfill in batches -> add NOT VALID constraint -> VALIDATE -> SET NOT NULL via check constraint. Always with lock_timeout set and a retry.
  • Soft-delete leaks. One query without deleted_at IS NULL and a deleted customer appears in a report. Expose a view (customers_live) and grant the application access to the view, not the table.
  • Audit tables grow forever. Partition by month from day one; archive partitions to cheap storage; keep an index on (application_id, at) only.
  • Natural keys change. The country re-issues national IDs; a branch is merged. Because the PK is the surrogate, this is one UPDATE customers SET national_id = ... instead of a cascade through five tables, and the audit table still points at the same id.
  • Record-to-relational mapping artefacts. Packed records often held "spare" fields, bit flags, and fixed-width codes padded with spaces. Decide per field: drop, normalise into a lookup, or keep in a legacy jsonb column with a sunset date. Trim padding during migration and add a CHECK (code = trim(code)) so it cannot come back.
  • Time zone incidents: month-end batch runs at 00:00 UTC = 05:30 IST and includes the first five and a half hours of the next day. Compute business boundaries in the branch's zone.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Load code/m09_schema.sql and code/m09_seed.sql. Run the "FK without index" query from 2.4. Done when it returns no rows (every FK is indexed) and you can say why each index exists.
  2. (easy) Try to insert an application with status = 'SUBMITTED' and no submitted_at, a negative amount, and an application number in the wrong format. Done when you can name the constraint in each error message.
  3. (medium) Take this denormalised Berkeley DB style record and design its 3NF tables: {loan_no, cust_name, cust_national_id, cust_phone1, cust_phone2, branch_code, branch_name, product_code, product_rate, amount, status_char, officer_code, officer_name}. Write the DDL with keys, FKs and constraints. Done when a reviewer (or you, tomorrow) can find each original field exactly once and every FK has an index.
  4. (medium) Implement a per-year gapless application_no generator as a function using a counter table with FOR UPDATE, and show from two sessions that it serialises correctly and never issues duplicates. Done when 2 x 1000 concurrent calls produce 2000 distinct numbers.
  5. (hard) Convert application_audit into a range-partitioned table by month with 24 partitions and a default partition, migrate the existing rows, and show with EXPLAIN that a query with at BETWEEN ... prunes to one partition. Done when the plan lists one partition and DROP TABLE application_audit_2024_01 removes a month in milliseconds.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Explain 3NF without jargon. A: Each fact is stored once, in the table whose key identifies it. No repeating groups in a row, no column that depends on only part of a composite key, and no column that depends on another non-key column. The payoff is no update anomalies; the cost is joins, which you denormalise deliberately and document when reads demand it.

Q: Surrogate or natural primary key? A: Surrogate bigint identity as the PK for stability and small FKs, plus a UNIQUE NOT NULL constraint on the natural key so it is enforced and indexed. The login bug I fixed was a missing unique constraint on the natural key, not a wrong choice of primary key. Pure link tables use a composite natural PK; stable short codes such as branch codes can be natural PKs by exception.

Q: Why index foreign key columns? A: Deleting or updating a parent row makes the database scan the child table for references; without an index that is a sequential scan under lock per parent delete. Joins through the FK also need it. PostgreSQL does not create the index automatically.

Q: Enum type or lookup table? A: Enums for tiny fixed sets that are part of the code; they are compact but cannot carry attributes and are awkward to change. Lookup tables for anything the business extends or that needs a display name, ordering or permissions, such as workflow states, where adding a state is an INSERT and the procedure reads the graph from the table.

Q: How do you model soft deletes and audit? A: A nullable deleted_at column, partial unique indexes that exclude deleted rows, and a live view for the application. Audit as an insert-only event table with from/to state, actor and transaction timestamp, written in the same transaction as the change, with UPDATE and DELETE revoked, and partitioned by month because it only grows.

Q: timestamp or timestamptz? A: Always timestamptz for instants: it stores UTC and renders in the session zone. Plain timestamp has no instant attached and silently differs between servers in different zones. Use date for calendar concepts, store IANA zone names when you need local rendering, and compute business-day boundaries in the business zone.

Q: Which ALTER TABLE operations are dangerous on a large hot table? A: Anything that rewrites (volatile defaults, most type changes) or scans under a strong lock (adding a validated FK or CHECK, SET NOT NULL). Safe patterns: add nullable columns, backfill in batches, add constraints NOT VALID then VALIDATE, create indexes CONCURRENTLY, and always set lock_timeout before DDL.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• 3NF: one fact, one place; denormalise deliberately and document the synchronisation.
  • Surrogate bigint PK + UNIQUE natural key; composite PK only for link tables.
  • Constraints are enforced documentation: NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE (partial for soft delete), FK, EXCLUDE.
  • Index every FK column; PostgreSQL will not do it for you.
  • Lookup tables over enums for extensible sets; the workflow graph is data.
  • Soft delete with a live view; audit as insert-only, partitioned, written in the same transaction.
  • timestamptz for instants, date for dates, IANA zones, now() for transaction time.
  • Types: bigint, numeric for money, text with CHECK, boolean, jsonb sparingly; align columns.
  • FKs are system triggers with FOR KEY SHARE; sequences have gaps; know which ALTERs rewrite.
  • Record-to-relational mapping is normalisation of packed records with a kept reverse mapping.

docs.title: 10. Berkeley DB and embedded key-value stores
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03, 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
An embedded key-value store is a database with no server: a library you link into your program that stores key -> value pairs in a file and gives you put, get, delete and an ordered cursor. Berkeley DB (1991, Sleepycat, later Oracle) is the classic. SQLite is the embedded relational store. LevelDB (Google, 2011) and RocksDB (Facebook's fork, 2012) are the modern embedded KV stores built on a different structure, the LSM tree, and RocksDB is what sits under YugabyteDB, CockroachDB, TiKV, MyRocks and Kafka Streams.

The analogy: Berkeley DB is a filing cabinet in your own office. Nobody else needs to be hired (no server process), you can reach it instantly (function calls), but you must lock the drawers yourself, keep the ledger yourself, and if you knock it over, you clean it up. PostgreSQL is a records department down the hall with staff.

You spent two years inside Berkeley DB from the application side. This module gives you the vocabulary to describe its architecture precisely, a complete C program you can write from memory, and the comparison with LSM-based stores that explains why YugabyteDB chose RocksDB and why your migration target still had a key-value store at the bottom.

docs.title: 2.1 Berkeley DB architecture
docs.text:
your process                       other process (same DB_ENV)
  +-------------------------------+  +----------------------+
  | application code              |  | application code     |
  |  DB handles, DBC cursors      |  |  DB handles          |
  |  DB_TXN transactions          |  |                      |
  +-------------------------------+  +----------------------+
  | access methods: BTREE HASH    |  | access methods       |
  |                 RECNO QUEUE   |  |                      |
  +-------------------------------+--+----------------------+
  | shared memory region (DB_ENV home: __db.001, __db.002 ...)                   |
  |   mpool   buffer cache of pages, pinned, dirty, LRU-ish                      |
  |   lock    lock table: lockers, objects (page or record), modes, waiters      |
  |   log     in-memory log buffer -> log.0000000001 files on disk               |
  |   txn     transaction table: active txns, their LSNs                          |
  |   mutex   region of shared mutexes                                            |
  +------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | files: mydb.db (one or more databases per file), log.*, __db.* regions      |
  +------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

The four subsystems map one-to-one onto PostgreSQL layers from module 01: mpool = buffer manager, lock = lock manager, log = WAL, txn = transaction manager. They are enabled with flags on DB_ENV->open: DB_INIT_MPOOL, DB_INIT_LOCK, DB_INIT_LOG, DB_INIT_TXN. Without DB_INIT_TXN you have a fast, non-durable, non-isolated store (the "Data Store" product); with all four you have the "Transactional Data Store" (TDS), which is what a banking server needed. All processes that open the same environment home directory share the regions, so the environment, not the process, is the unit of consistency.

Access methods (chosen per database at DB->open):

Method Key Structure Use DB_BTREE arbitrary bytes, ordered by a comparison function (default lexicographic) B+tree with slotted pages, prefix compression on internal pages the default: range scans, ordered cursors, duplicates (DB_DUP, DB_DUPSORT) DB_HASH arbitrary bytes extendible linear hashing pure point lookups on large tables where a B-tree would be deep; no ordering DB_RECNO logical record number (1, 2, 3...) B-tree keyed by record number, optionally over a flat text file line-numbered data, renumbering on delete DB_QUEUE record number fixed-length records in extent files, record-level locking high-concurrency FIFO queues; DB_CONSUME pops atomically

The "B-tree cursor traversal" on your resume: a DB_BTREE database with a packed business key, walked with DB_SET_RANGE to position and DB_NEXT to advance, exactly as the code in section 3 does.

Handles: DB_ENV (the environment), DB (one database = one key space), DBC (a cursor over one DB), DB_TXN (a transaction spanning any number of DBs in the environment). Every operation takes an optional DB_TXN *; NULL means autocommit when DB_AUTO_COMMIT was set, or non-transactional otherwise.

DBT (data-base thunk) is the struct for keys and values:

typedef struct {
    void    *data;     /* pointer to the bytes */
    u_int32_t size;    /* bytes used */
    u_int32_t ulen;    /* bytes available in a user-supplied buffer (DB_DBT_USERMEM) */
    u_int32_t dlen, doff;  /* partial reads/writes (DB_DBT_PARTIAL) */
    u_int32_t flags;   /* DB_DBT_MALLOC (library allocates, you free), DB_DBT_REALLOC, DB_DBT_USERMEM */
} DBT;

Values are opaque bytes: your packed C structs. Berkeley DB never looks inside them, except through callbacks you supply (comparison functions, secondary key extractors). That is the "record-to-relational mapping" problem in one sentence: the schema lived in your #pragma pack headers (module 12).

Secondary indexes: primary->associate(primary, txn, secondary, callback, flags). The callback receives the primary key and value and fills a DBT with the secondary key (or returns DB_DONOTINDEX). Berkeley DB then maintains the secondary database on every put/delete; a secondary->pget() or a cursor on it returns the primary key and value. This is CREATE INDEX done by hand, with you writing the key extractor in C.

Duplicates: DB->set_flags(db, DB_DUP) allows multiple values per key in insertion order; DB_DUPSORT sorts them. Cursors walk duplicates with DB_NEXT_DUP / DB_NEXT_NODUP; DB_GET_BOTH finds a specific key/value pair. Secondaries nearly always need DB_DUPSORT.

docs.title: 2.2 Transactions, locking and logging in Berkeley DB
docs.text:
• Transactions: env->txn_begin(env, parent, &txn, flags), txn->commit(txn, flags), txn->abort(txn). Nested transactions via parent. DB_TXN_NOSYNC / DB_TXN_WRITE_NOSYNC trade durability for speed per transaction or environment-wide; DB_TXN_SNAPSHOT enables MVCC reads (available since 4.5, off by default).
  • Locking: page-level for BTREE/HASH/RECNO, record-level for QUEUE. A reader locks a page in read mode and a writer in write mode, held until transaction end for transactional handles (two-phase locking, 2PL). Readers block writers and writers block readers on the same page, unless you use DB_TXN_SNAPSHOT (MVCC via copy-on-write page versions in mpool) or DB_READ_UNCOMMITTED. Deadlocks are frequent under concurrent writers to nearby keys because two transactions touching different records on one page conflict.
  • Deadlock handling: there is no automatic detector thread unless you configure one: env->set_lk_detect(env, DB_LOCK_DEFAULT) makes the lock manager run detection on every blocked lock request, or you run the db_deadlock utility / env->lock_detect() periodically. A chosen victim's operation returns DB_LOCK_DEADLOCK; the application must abort() the transaction and retry the whole unit of work. Every transactional Berkeley DB program is a retry loop. (You will recognise the shape from module 05's 40001 handling.)
  • Logging: write-ahead, physical undo/redo records with before and after images (module 04); log.NNNNNNNNNN files of set_lg_max bytes (default 10 MB); env->txn_checkpoint() must be called by you (typically a thread every minute or N KB of log); DB_RECOVER at open runs normal recovery, DB_RECOVER_FATAL catastrophic recovery from archived logs; db_archive lists logs that can be removed, or DB_LOG_AUTO_REMOVE deletes them (and kills your ability to do catastrophic recovery). DB_REGISTER lets processes detect that another process died holding the environment and run recovery safely.

Operational truths from the field, phrased for an interview: with Berkeley DB the application owns checkpointing, log archiving, deadlock detection, recovery invocation, and the record schema. Each is a place where a mistake corrupts or loses data without anyone noticing. Moving to a server database transfers all five to the database.

docs.title: 2.3 The C API in one program
docs.text:
code/m10_bdb_cursor_txn.c is complete and compiles on Ubuntu 24.04 with sudo apt install libdb-dev and gcc -Wall -Wextra m10_bdb_cursor_txn.c -o bdbdemo -ldb (libdb 5.3). It opens an environment with all four subsystems, creates a BTREE primary keyed by a packed (branch, user_code) struct, a DUPSORT secondary keyed by branch, inserts records in a transaction, traverses with DB_SET_RANGE/DB_NEXT under a second transaction, updates through the cursor, demonstrates deadlock-retry structure, checkpoints, and closes cleanly. The essential parts:

#include <db.h>
#define CHECK(ret, what) do { if ((ret) != 0) { fprintf(stderr, "%s: %s\n", what, db_strerror(ret)); goto fail; } } while (0)

#pragma pack(push, 1)
struct user_key  { char branch[6]; char user_code[9]; };            /* 15 bytes, big-endian-ish text sorts lexicographically */
struct user_rec  { uint32_t id; uint8_t status; uint16_t failed_attempts; int64_t last_login_epoch; char name[32]; };
#pragma pack(pop)

int main(void) {
    DB_ENV *env = NULL; DB *dbp = NULL, *sdbp = NULL; DBC *cur = NULL; DB_TXN *txn = NULL; int ret;

    CHECK(db_env_create(&env, 0), "db_env_create");
    env->set_errpfx(env, "bdbdemo");
    CHECK(env->set_lk_detect(env, DB_LOCK_DEFAULT), "set_lk_detect");       /* detect deadlocks on each blocked request */
    CHECK(env->open(env, "./bdb_env",
                    DB_CREATE | DB_INIT_MPOOL | DB_INIT_LOCK | DB_INIT_LOG | DB_INIT_TXN | DB_RECOVER | DB_THREAD,
                    0), "env->open");                                          /* DB_RECOVER: always run recovery at startup */

    CHECK(db_create(&dbp, env, 0), "db_create");
    CHECK(dbp->open(dbp, NULL, "users.db", "users", DB_BTREE, DB_CREATE | DB_AUTO_COMMIT | DB_THREAD, 0644), "db->open");

    CHECK(db_create(&sdbp, env, 0), "db_create secondary");
    CHECK(sdbp->set_flags(sdbp, DB_DUPSORT), "set_flags DUPSORT");           /* many users per branch */
    CHECK(sdbp->open(sdbp, NULL, "users.db", "users_by_branch", DB_BTREE, DB_CREATE | DB_AUTO_COMMIT | DB_THREAD, 0644), "sdb->open");
    CHECK(dbp->associate(dbp, NULL, sdbp, branch_key_extractor, DB_AUTO_COMMIT), "associate");

    /* ---- insert in one transaction ---- */
    CHECK(env->txn_begin(env, NULL, &txn, 0), "txn_begin");
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        struct user_key k; struct user_rec r; fill(&k, &r, i);
        DBT key = {0}, val = {0};
        key.data = &k; key.size = sizeof k; val.data = &r; val.size = sizeof r;
        ret = dbp->put(dbp, txn, &key, &val, DB_NOOVERWRITE);                /* NOOVERWRITE: DB_KEYEXIST if present */
        if (ret == DB_KEYEXIST) continue;
        CHECK(ret, "put");
    }
    CHECK(txn->commit(txn, 0), "commit"); txn = NULL;                         /* 0 = fsync the log: durable */

    /* ---- cursor traversal: all users of branch BR0007, in key order ---- */
    CHECK(env->txn_begin(env, NULL, &txn, 0), "txn_begin");
    CHECK(dbp->cursor(dbp, txn, &cur, 0), "cursor");
    struct user_key start = {0}; memcpy(start.branch, "BR0007", 6);
    DBT key = {0}, val = {0};
    key.data = &start; key.size = sizeof start; key.flags = DB_DBT_USERMEM; key.ulen = sizeof start;
    struct user_rec buf; val.data = &buf; val.ulen = sizeof buf; val.flags = DB_DBT_USERMEM;  /* no malloc per record */
    for (ret = cur->get(cur, &key, &val, DB_SET_RANGE);                          /* position at first key >= start */
         ret == 0;
         ret = cur->get(cur, &key, &val, DB_NEXT)) {
        const struct user_key *k = key.data;
        if (memcmp(k->branch, "BR0007", 6) != 0) break;                          /* left the branch: stop */
        struct user_rec r; memcpy(&r, val.data, sizeof r);                       /* copy out: val.data may be unaligned */
        if (r.status == STATUS_LOCKED) {
            r.status = STATUS_ACTIVE; r.failed_attempts = 0;
            val.data = &r; val.size = sizeof r;
            CHECK(cur->put(cur, &key, &val, DB_CURRENT), "cursor put");          /* update the record under the cursor */
        }
    }
    if (ret != DB_NOTFOUND) CHECK(ret, "cursor get");
    CHECK(cur->close(cur), "cursor close"); cur = NULL;                          /* close cursors BEFORE commit */
    CHECK(txn->commit(txn, 0), "commit"); txn = NULL;

    CHECK(env->txn_checkpoint(env, 0, 0, 0), "checkpoint");                       /* your job in Berkeley DB */
    /* close order: cursors, secondary, primary, env */
fail:
    if (cur) cur->close(cur);
    if (txn) txn->abort(txn);
    if (sdbp) sdbp->close(sdbp, 0);
    if (dbp) dbp->close(dbp, 0);
    if (env) env->close(env, 0);
    return ret == 0 ? 0 : 1;
}

The deadlock retry wrapper the full file uses:

/* Run a unit of work; on DB_LOCK_DEADLOCK abort and retry with backoff. Every TDS program needs this. */
static int run_txn(DB_ENV *env, int (*work)(DB_TXN *, void *), void *arg) {
    for (int attempt = 0; attempt < 10; ++attempt) {
        DB_TXN *t = NULL; int ret = env->txn_begin(env, NULL, &t, 0);
        if (ret) return ret;
        ret = work(t, arg);
        if (ret == 0) return t->commit(t, 0);
        t->abort(t);
        if (ret != DB_LOCK_DEADLOCK) return ret;
        usleep(1000u << attempt);                 /* 1 ms, 2 ms, 4 ms ... */
    }
    return DB_LOCK_DEADLOCK;
}

docs.title: 2.4 LSM trees: the other way to build a KV store
docs.text:
A B-tree updates pages in place: every write is a random read-modify-write of a leaf (plus WAL). A log-structured merge tree never modifies a file in place:

  write path                             files on disk (SSTables = sorted string tables, immutable)
  put(k,v) --> WAL append                 L0: [sst][sst][sst][sst]          small, may overlap in key range
           --> memtable (skiplist in RAM)  L1: [  sst  ][  sst  ][  sst  ]   10x bigger, non-overlapping
  memtable full --> flush to L0 SSTable   L2: [ ... 10x bigger again ... ]
                                          L3: ...
  background compaction: merge-sort overlapping SSTables from Ln into Ln+1, dropping overwritten
  and deleted (tombstoned) keys
  • Write: append to WAL (sequential), insert into the memtable (RAM). No random I/O. When the memtable reaches ~64 MB it is frozen and written out as one sorted file. Writes are therefore sequential and batched, which is why LSM stores win on write-heavy workloads and on SSDs (fewer, larger writes also mean less flash wear).
  • Read: check memtable, then each L0 file (they can overlap), then one file per deeper level (binary search on the level's key ranges). Each file has a bloom filter so most non-matching files are skipped without I/O, and a block index. A point read still touches more places than a B-tree's one leaf path; range scans must merge iterators from every level.
  • Compaction: the background merge that keeps levels sorted and bounded.
