Leveled compaction (RocksDB default, LevelDB): each level is 10x the previous, non-overlapping; a key is rewritten about once per level: low space amplification (~1.1x), higher write amplification (~10 to 30x). Tiered / size-tiered / universal: merge files of similar size; lower write amplification, higher space amplification (duplicates across tiers) and more files to check per read.
  • Deletes are tombstones that must propagate down to the bottom level before the space is freed; a table with many deletes reads slowly until compaction catches up (the "tombstone problem", also behind YugabyteDB's and Cassandra's advice about deleting in bulk).

The three amplifications (the RUM conjecture: you cannot minimise Read, Update and Memory overhead at once):

B-tree (PostgreSQL, Berkeley DB) LSM leveled (RocksDB) Write amplification one page rewrite per update (8 KB for a 100 B change) + WAL, + FPIs ~10 to 30x via compaction, but all sequential Read amplification 1 path: height pages, mostly cached memtable + L0 files + 1 per level, bloom filters reduce it Space amplification fragmentation 1.3 to 2x after churn (bloat) ~1.1x leveled; higher tiered; plus temporary space during compaction Latency profile predictable compaction stalls and write stalls when L0 fills (level0_slowdown_writes_trigger) Best for read-heavy OLTP, point and range reads, in-place updates write-heavy, append-heavy, large datasets on SSD, compressible data

RocksDB adds over LevelDB: column families (separate LSM trees sharing one WAL, like tables), multi-threaded compaction and flush, universal compaction, prefix bloom filters, transactions (optimistic and pessimistic), merge operators (read-modify-write without a read), rate limiting, block cache + optional row cache, pluggable comparators and compression per level (LZ4 upper, ZSTD bottom), and DeleteRange. It is a library like Berkeley DB: embedded, no server, your process owns the files.

docs.title: 2.5 Where embedded KV stores are used, and why YugabyteDB is built on RocksDB
docs.text:
Embedded stores appear wherever a process needs durable ordered storage without the cost or operational weight of a server: browsers (Chrome's IndexedDB on LevelDB), mobile apps (SQLite), message brokers' state stores (Kafka Streams on RocksDB), caches with persistence, blockchain nodes (LevelDB/RocksDB), your banking RPC server before the migration, and, crucially, as the per-node storage engine of distributed databases.

A distributed SQL database has to build replication, sharding, distributed transactions and a query layer. It does not want to also reinvent a crash-safe sorted storage engine with compression and caching. So YugabyteDB, CockroachDB (until its own Pebble, an LSM rewrite in Go), TiKV and MyRocks all put RocksDB at the bottom: one RocksDB instance per tablet (shard) per node. RocksDB's properties fit: writes arrive as Raft log entries that are already sequential; replication and recovery are handled above RocksDB by Raft, so RocksDB's own WAL is turned off in YugabyteDB; the LSM's immutable SSTables make snapshots, backups and tablet moves cheap (copy files); MVCC with hybrid timestamps is encoded directly in the key suffix; and the merge operator and prefix bloom filters support the document-key encoding (module 11).

So the honest shape of your migration: from one process-local B-tree key-value store (Berkeley DB) to a SQL layer over a replicated, sharded LSM key-value store (DocDB on RocksDB). The key-value store did not go away; it moved down a layer and gained a schema, a planner, and consensus replication above it.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Build and run code/m10_bdb_cursor_txn.c:

sudo apt install -y libdb-dev
gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 m10_bdb_cursor_txn.c -o bdbdemo -ldb
./bdbdemo
ls -la bdb_env/            # __db.001.. regions, log.0000000001, users.db
db_stat -h bdb_env -c      # lock statistics: see lockers, deadlocks, waits
db_stat -h bdb_env -l      # log statistics
db_stat -h bdb_env -m      # mpool: cache hits, pages created
db_dump -h bdb_env -p users.db | head   # keys and values as printable bytes
db_recover -h bdb_env -v   # run recovery by hand (what DB_RECOVER does)

The file also shows the secondary key extractor signature, which you should be able to write unprompted:

/* Called by the library for every put/delete on the primary: fill `result` with the secondary key. */
static int branch_key_extractor(DB *secondary, const DBT *pkey, const DBT *pdata, DBT *result) {
    (void)secondary; (void)pdata;
    const struct user_key *k = pkey->data;
    memset(result, 0, sizeof *result);
    result->data = (void *)k->branch;       /* points into pkey: valid for the duration of the call */
    result->size = sizeof k->branch;
    return 0;                               /* or DB_DONOTINDEX to skip this record */
}

A minimal RocksDB equivalent, for comparison only (C API, librocksdb-dev):

rocksdb_options_t *o = rocksdb_options_create();
rocksdb_options_set_create_if_missing(o, 1);
rocksdb_t *db = rocksdb_open(o, "./rocks", &err);
rocksdb_put(db, wo, key, klen, val, vlen, &err);                 /* WAL append + memtable insert */
rocksdb_iterator_t *it = rocksdb_create_iterator(db, ro);
for (rocksdb_iter_seek(it, "BR0007", 6); rocksdb_iter_valid(it); rocksdb_iter_next(it)) { ... }  /* merges all levels */

Same shape as the Berkeley DB cursor loop. Under it, totally different physics.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Berkeley DB page locking and why it deadlocks. With default (non-snapshot) TDS, a DB_NEXT cursor read takes a read lock on each leaf page it visits and holds it to transaction end (DB_READ_COMMITTED on the cursor releases it when the cursor moves). A concurrent writer wanting any record on that page blocks. Two transactions each reading page A then writing page B in opposite orders deadlock; the detector picks a victim by policy (DB_LOCK_DEFAULT = youngest, or DB_LOCK_MINWRITE, etc.). PostgreSQL's row-level MVCC never takes read locks, so the same workload simply does not deadlock on reads. If your migration engine read the source with a long-lived transaction while the server kept writing, you fought exactly this; the fix was either DB_TXN_SNAPSHOT (MVCC reads via copy-on-write pages, at the cost of mpool size) or short read transactions with cursor repositioning by last key (which is also the restartable cursor pattern in module 12).

Berkeley DB B-tree internals. Page types: internal (P_IBTREE) holding (key prefix, child pgno, record count), leaf (P_LBTREE) holding key and data items in slots, overflow pages for items larger than a quarter page, duplicate pages (off-page duplicates become their own small B-tree). Keys on internal pages are prefix-compressed by default (bt_prefix). The default comparison is memcmp-like on the bytes: that is why your packed key struct had to be laid out with the most significant field first and in big-endian or text form, or the cursor order would not be the business order. DB->set_bt_compare installs a custom comparator when it is not. Reverse-split (merging under-full pages) is on by default and can be disabled with DB_REVSPLITOFF for append-heavy workloads.

Memory pool and the OS. The mpool region is a shared memory segment (System V or file-backed mmap in the environment home) of set_cachesize bytes (default a few hundred KB, far too small; production used hundreds of MB). Like PostgreSQL's shared_buffers, it double buffers with the OS page cache. DB_DIRECT_DB and DB_DIRECT_LOG use O_DIRECT to avoid that. Pages are checksummed only if DB_CHKSUM is set per database.

Why LSM reads are not as bad as they look. With leveled compaction and 10x fan-out, a 1 TB store has about 7 levels. A point read checks the memtable, the few L0 files, and one file per level, but each file's bloom filter (10 bits per key gives ~1% false positives) is in memory, so only the one file that actually contains the key costs an I/O (plus its index block if not cached). Range scans are worse: a merging iterator must open every level's candidate file and heap-merge them; tombstones in the range are read and skipped. This is the reason YugabyteDB documents that heavy deletes degrade scans until compaction.

Write stalls. When flushes and compactions cannot keep up (L0 file count exceeds level0_slowdown_writes_trigger, or pending compaction bytes exceed a soft limit), RocksDB throttles writers, then stops them. Latency spikes of hundreds of milliseconds during compaction are the LSM's version of PostgreSQL's checkpoint I/O spikes. Both are tuned by spreading background work: max_background_jobs, rate limiter, versus checkpoint_completion_target.

MVCC in the key. RocksDB itself has a sequence number per write; YugabyteDB appends a hybrid timestamp to every key so that multiple versions of a document sub-key are adjacent in the LSM in reverse time order, and a read at timestamp T seeks to the first version <= T. Garbage collection of old versions happens during compaction, bounded by a history retention interval, which is DocDB's VACUUM (module 11).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Berkeley DB environments and process death. A process that dies holding region mutexes leaves the environment unusable until recovery. DB_REGISTER with DB_RECOVER lets the next opener detect and recover automatically; without it, you need an operator to run db_recover. Build this into startup; do not rely on runbooks.
  • Cache size and log size are the two knobs. Too small an mpool means every cursor step is a disk read; too small set_lg_max with no checkpoint thread means thousands of log files. Monitor db_stat -m hit rate and db_stat -l for log growth.
  • Schema drift in packed records. Adding a field to the C struct without a version byte in the record makes old records unreadable. Every record format must carry a version, and the reader must handle every version ever written. Your migration decoder had to (module 12).
  • Choosing an embedded store today. Need SQL and one process: SQLite. Need ordered KV, write heavy, large: RocksDB. Need a tiny dependency and moderate data: LMDB (B+tree, copy-on-write, mmap, read-optimised). Need a server: PostgreSQL. Berkeley DB for new systems is hard to justify (AGPL licence since 6.0, Oracle-owned, declining ecosystem), which is another honest bullet in the migration motivation.
  • RocksDB tuning pitfalls you will meet through YugabyteDB: too few background threads (stalls), block cache too small (every read is an SSD read), bloom filters disabled on a column family (reads check every level), and bulk deletes without compaction (scan latency).
  • 3 AM with Berkeley DB: DB_RUNRECOVERY: Fatal error, run database recovery. Stop all processes, db_recover -h env, restart. If the logs were auto-removed and the database file is corrupt, you restore from the last db_hotbackup and replay nothing. This is why the migration was a risk-reduction project, not only a performance project.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run code/m10_bdb_cursor_txn.c. Run db_stat -h bdb_env -c and -m. Done when you can point at lock requests, deadlocks (0), and cache hit counts.
  2. (easy) Modify the program to insert the same key twice without DB_NOOVERWRITE and with it; observe the return codes. Then add DB_DUPSORT to the primary and insert two values for one key; walk them with DB_NEXT_DUP. Done when you can state what each flag changed.
  3. (medium) Run two instances of the program concurrently that update overlapping keys in long transactions. Make them deadlock (DB_LOCK_DEADLOCK), then show the retry wrapper resolves it. Then open the environment with DB_MULTIVERSION and cursors with DB_TXN_SNAPSHOT and show reads no longer block. Done when you can explain page locking versus snapshot reads.
  4. (medium) Kill the program with kill -9 mid-transaction and restart it. Verify with db_dump that the partial transaction's records are absent, then remove DB_RECOVER from the open flags and kill again: observe the failure mode on restart. Done when you can describe what DB_RECOVER does and why it must always be passed.
  5. (hard) Install librocksdb-dev, write a 60-line C program that inserts 5 M random keys into RocksDB and into a Berkeley DB BTREE with equal cache sizes, timing both, then do 100k random point reads on each. Done when you have the four numbers and can explain them with write and read amplification.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Describe Berkeley DB's architecture. A: An embedded library with four subsystems shared across processes through a shared-memory environment: a memory pool for pages, a lock manager with page-level locking, a write-ahead log with undo and redo images, and a transaction manager. Databases use one of four access methods, B-tree being the usual one, and values are opaque bytes; secondary indexes are maintained through application-supplied key extractor callbacks.

Q: Walk me through a transactional cursor traversal in the C API. A: Open the environment with the four INIT flags plus DB_RECOVER, open the DB handle with DB_AUTO_COMMIT, begin a transaction with txn_begin, open a cursor on the DB within that transaction, position with DB_SET_RANGE on the packed start key, loop with DB_NEXT until the key leaves the range or DB_NOTFOUND, update under the cursor with DB_CURRENT if needed, close the cursor before committing, and wrap the whole unit in a retry loop on DB_LOCK_DEADLOCK.

Q: What did Berkeley DB make the application responsible for that PostgreSQL does not? A: Checkpointing and log archiving, running recovery at startup, deadlock detection configuration and retry, cache sizing, the record format and its versioning, and secondary index maintenance logic. Each is a correctness risk owned by application code; moving to a server database transferred them to the engine.

Q: Explain an LSM tree and compare it with a B-tree. A: Writes go to a WAL and an in-memory memtable, which is flushed as an immutable sorted file; background compaction merges files into larger non-overlapping levels. Writes are sequential and batched, so write throughput and SSD wear are better than a B-tree's in-place page updates, at the cost of read amplification across levels (mitigated by bloom filters), compaction CPU and I/O, and latency spikes during stalls. B-trees give predictable reads and in-place updates with fragmentation and random writes.

Q: What are write, read and space amplification? A: Write amplification is bytes written to storage per byte of user data: a B-tree rewrites whole pages and logs full-page images; a leveled LSM rewrites each key once per level during compaction. Read amplification is storage accesses per logical read: one tree path for a B-tree, several levels for an LSM. Space amplification is disk used over live data: B-tree fragmentation versus LSM duplicate versions awaiting compaction. You can minimise two of the three, not all.

Q: Why is YugabyteDB built on RocksDB? A: A distributed SQL database needs a crash-safe, ordered, compressed, cache-aware local storage engine per shard and should not reinvent one. RocksDB is embedded, write-optimised for the sequential stream of Raft log entries, and its immutable SSTables make snapshots and tablet moves cheap; YugabyteDB disables RocksDB's WAL because Raft provides durability, and encodes MVCC hybrid timestamps in the keys.

Q: When would you choose an embedded store over a server database? A: When a single process owns the data, needs microsecond access without a network, and operational simplicity matters more than multi-client access: local caches, state stores in stream processors, desktop and mobile apps, or as the storage layer inside a larger system. Once several services or people need the data, or you need SQL, replication and managed operations, a server database wins.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Berkeley DB = library + shared-memory environment with mpool, lock, log, txn subsystems.
  • Access methods: BTREE (ordered, cursors, duplicates), HASH, RECNO, QUEUE.
  • Handles: DB_ENV, DB, DBC, DB_TXN; DBT carries opaque bytes; secondaries via associate callbacks.
  • Page-level 2PL locking: readers block writers, deadlocks common; app configures detection and retries.
  • Undo/redo physical logging; the app calls txn_checkpoint and passes DB_RECOVER.
  • Cursor traversal: DB_SET_RANGE then DB_NEXT; close cursors before commit; DB_CURRENT to update.
  • LSM: WAL + memtable + immutable SSTables + compaction; sequential writes, multi-level reads, bloom filters.
  • Leveled compaction: low space, high write amplification; tiered: the reverse.
  • RocksDB = LevelDB + column families, parallel compaction, transactions, merge operators.
  • YugabyteDB puts one RocksDB per tablet under Raft: the KV store moved down a layer, it did not disappear.

docs.title: 11. YugabyteDB and distributed SQL
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 05, 06, 10 (and 08_Networking_Distributed for Raft)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
YugabyteDB is PostgreSQL's upper half (parser, planner, executor, PL/pgSQL, the wire protocol) bolted onto a different lower half: instead of heap files and WAL on one machine, every table is cut into tablets (shards), each tablet is stored in its own RocksDB instance, and each tablet is copied to three nodes that agree on every write using the Raft consensus protocol. The result speaks PostgreSQL, survives a node dying without losing a committed transaction, and spreads data and load across machines.

The analogy: PostgreSQL is one bank branch with one vault. YugabyteDB is a chain of branches where every account's folder is kept in three branches at once; any change is written in all three before it counts, and a chosen branch (the leader) coordinates each folder. Customers still fill in the same forms (SQL), but every form now involves a phone call or two between branches (network hops), and where a folder lives (which branch) is decided by a hash of the account number unless you ask otherwise. That phone call is why a query that was fine on one machine can be slow on the cluster, and why index design changes.

You ran production on YugabyteDB. This module explains what the engine was doing, so that "multi-node cluster" on your resume is a thing you can draw on a whiteboard.

docs.title: 2.1 Architecture
docs.text:
clients (libpq, JDBC ...) --- PostgreSQL wire protocol, port 5433 ---> any node
                                                                           |
  +-------------------------- node 1 ------------------------+   +------ node 2 ------+  +--- node 3 ---+
  | YB-TServer process                                       |   | YB-TServer         |  | YB-TServer   |
  |  +-------------------------------+                       |   |  postgres (YSQL)   |  |  postgres    |
  |  | postgres backend (YSQL layer) |  parser, analyzer,    |   |  DocDB tablets:    |  |  DocDB:      |
  |  |  = modified PostgreSQL        |  planner, executor,   |   |   T1 follower      |  |   T1 follower|
  |  +---------------+---------------+  PL/pgSQL, catalog    |   |   T2 leader        |  |   T2 follower|
  |                  | pggate (RPC to tablet servers)        |   |   T3 follower      |  |   T3 leader  |
  |  +---------------v---------------+                       |   +--------------------+  +--------------+
  |  | DocDB: tablets hosted here    |                       |
  |  |  tablet T1 (leader)  -> Raft log + RocksDB (regular + intents)                   |
  |  |  tablet T2 (follower)-> Raft log + RocksDB                                       |
  |  |  tablet T3 (follower)                                                            |
  |  +-------------------------------+                       |
  +----------------------------------------------------------+
  YB-Master processes (3, Raft group): system catalog location, tablet-to-node map,
  load balancing, DDL coordination, tablet splitting.
  • YB-TServer: one per node; hosts tablets and runs the YSQL (PostgreSQL) processes. Any node accepts connections; the backend that receives your query is the coordinator for it.
  • YSQL: a fork of PostgreSQL (long based on 11.2; recent releases moved to a PostgreSQL 15 base). Same grammar, types, planner, PL/pgSQL, extensions that do not touch storage. The heap access method and B-tree AM are replaced by pggate calls that read and write DocDB.
  • DocDB: the distributed document store. Each tablet is a Raft group with a leader and followers, and each replica is one RocksDB instance (actually two: RegularDB for committed data and IntentsDB for provisional writes of in-flight transactions). RocksDB's own WAL is disabled; the Raft log is the WAL.
  • YB-Master: a small Raft group of three that keeps the catalog of tablets and their locations, runs the load balancer that moves tablet replicas and leaders between nodes, and coordinates DDL.
  • YCQL is a separate Cassandra-compatible API on the same DocDB; ignore it unless asked.

docs.title: 2.2 How a row becomes keys in DocDB
docs.text:
A PostgreSQL row of app_users (id PK, branch_code, user_code, status, ...) is stored as a document keyed by the primary key, with one sub-key per column (recent versions pack all columns of a row into one value, "packed rows", on insert; updates still write per-column entries until compaction repacks):

 DocKey: [hash(id) : 2 bytes][id]                      <- the partition
   SubKey: column_id(branch_code)  @ HT=t1  -> "BR0456"
   SubKey: column_id(user_code)    @ HT=t1  -> "U00123456"
   SubKey: column_id(status)       @ HT=t5  -> "LOCKED"      <- a later update: new version, newer timestamp
   SubKey: column_id(status)       @ HT=t1  -> "ACTIVE"

HT is a hybrid timestamp (physical clock microseconds plus a logical counter), DocDB's transaction time. Multiple versions of a sub-key sit next to each other in the LSM, newest first; a read at time T seeks to the first version <= T. Old versions are garbage-collected during compaction after timestamp_history_retention_interval_sec (default 900 s). That is MVCC without xmin/xmax and without VACUUM. Deletes are tombstones.

A secondary index is its own DocDB table: key = (indexed columns, primary key), value = the INCLUDE columns, if any. An index lookup is therefore one read on the index tablet to get the primary key, then one read on the main table's tablet (possibly on another node) to get the row, unless the index covers the query.

docs.title: 2.3 Tablets and sharding
docs.text:
Every table and index is split into tablets. The split rule is set by the primary key (or index key) definition:

  • Hash sharding (YSQL default for the first PK column): the first column (or an explicit group) is hashed into a 16-bit space [0, 65536), and each tablet owns a contiguous range of hash values. Rows are spread evenly across tablets, so inserts and point lookups scale linearly; but rows with adjacent key values live on different tablets, so a range query on the hash column is a scatter to every tablet and ORDER BY on it needs a sort.
  • Range sharding (ASC/DESC on the first PK column): tablets own key ranges in sort order. Range scans and ordered reads touch few tablets, but a monotonically increasing key (timestamps, sequences) sends every insert to the last tablet: a hotspot.
CREATE TABLE events (                               -- default: hash on the first PK column
    id bigint, at timestamptz, payload jsonb,
    PRIMARY KEY (id HASH)                            -- explicit form of the default
);
CREATE TABLE audit_by_app (                         -- hash on application_id, range within
    application_id bigint, at timestamptz, note text,
    PRIMARY KEY (application_id HASH, at DESC)       -- all of one application's audit on one tablet, newest first
);
CREATE TABLE codes (                                -- range sharded: ordered scans over the whole key space
    code text, name text,
    PRIMARY KEY (code ASC)
) SPLIT AT VALUES (('F'), ('M'), ('T'));             -- pre-split to avoid a single tablet at start

Tablet count: by default a function of cores per node (often 8 per table per node on larger machines, fewer on small ones; ysql_num_shards_per_tserver), with automatic tablet splitting as tablets grow past a size threshold. Too many tablets per node (thousands) costs memory and Raft heartbeat overhead; colocation (below) is the answer for many small tables.

docs.title: 2.4 Replication, leaders, consistency
docs.text:
Each tablet's three replicas (replication factor RF = 3; RF = 5 tolerates two failures) form a Raft group. One is the leader; it serialises all writes to that tablet: append the entry to its Raft log, send it to followers, and once a majority (2 of 3) has written it to their logs, the entry is committed and applied to RocksDB. See 08_Networking_Distributed for the protocol; what matters here:

  • A committed write survives the loss of any one node, with no data loss. There is no asynchronous replica lag to reason about for correctness.
  • A node failure makes the tablets it led unavailable for a few seconds (leader election, raft_heartbeat_interval_ms x leader_failure_max_missed_heartbeat_periods, typically 3 to 6 s by default) and then they continue. Clients see errors or latency for that window and retry.
  • Reads go to the leader by default, so they are strongly consistent (linearisable per tablet). Leaders hold leases so they can serve reads without a Raft round trip. Follower reads (SET yb_read_from_followers = true plus a read-only transaction with yb_follower_read_staleness_ms) trade a bounded staleness for lower latency and load spreading.
  • Replica placement is controlled by cloud/region/zone labels and tablespaces, so RF = 3 across three zones survives a zone outage; across three regions it survives a region but every commit pays an inter-region round trip.

docs.title: 2.5 Distributed transactions
docs.text:
A single-row write whose row lives on one tablet takes a fast path: the leader applies it through Raft, done, ~1 ms in-zone. Anything touching rows on more than one tablet (a multi-row UPDATE, an insert into a table with secondary indexes, a FK check) is a distributed transaction:

  1. The coordinator picks a transaction status tablet and creates a status record.
  2. Writes go to each involved tablet as provisional records (intents) in IntentsDB, with the transaction id; conflicts with other intents or committed data at a newer timestamp are detected here (and, depending on the conflict mode, the transaction waits or fails and retries).
  3. COMMIT: the coordinator writes COMMIT with a commit hybrid timestamp to the status tablet (one Raft commit). The transaction is now durable and visible.
  4. Asynchronously, each participant tablet applies intents into RegularDB with the commit timestamp and removes them.

Readers that meet an intent look up the status tablet to learn whether it committed (and when), so they never see partial transactions. Isolation levels in YSQL:

YSQL level Meaning Notes READ COMMITTED per-statement snapshot, like PostgreSQL only when yb_enable_read_committed_isolation = true; otherwise it is silently treated as snapshot isolation REPEATABLE READ = Snapshot (default) one snapshot per transaction; conflicts abort with 40001 the default differs from PostgreSQL's READ COMMITTED SERIALIZABLE pessimistic: reads take row locks in DocDB so conflicting writers wait or abort not SSI; more aborts, no write skew

Clock skew: hybrid timestamps assume node clocks differ by less than max_clock_skew_usec (default 500 ms); reads whose window overlaps the uncertainty are retried internally. Run NTP or chrony on every node; a node with a bad clock is refused.

docs.title: 2.6 What changes versus single-node PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Topic PostgreSQL YugabyteDB (YSQL) Primary key storage heap + separate B-tree the table is keyed by the PK in DocDB (clustered); no heap, no TID Default PK sharding n/a hash on the first column: WHERE id BETWEEN and ORDER BY id fan out and sort Point lookup cost ~4 page reads, microseconds one RPC to the tablet leader, ~1 ms in-zone, more cross-zone/region Sequential scan one file, OS read-ahead parallel RPCs to every tablet leader, merged at the coordinator; still "fast enough" for small tables, terrible for login paths Secondary index lookup index pages + heap page index tablet RPC + main table RPC (2 hops) unless covering Secondary index write same transaction, same page writes turns a single-row insert into a distributed transaction Sequences per-session CACHE 1, gaps on rollback cached per node (ysql_sequence_cache_minval, default 100): ids are not monotonic across nodes Statistics autovacuum runs ANALYZE historically no autovacuum: run ANALYZE yourself after loads (auto-analyze arrived recently and may be off); without it the planner assumes 1000 rows per table and picks nested loops VACUUM required not needed (compaction GC); VACUUM is a no-op Isolation default READ COMMITTED Snapshot (REPEATABLE READ); client must retry 40001 Large deletes bloat until vacuum tombstones slow scans until compaction; delete in batches, consider partition drop Many small tables fine each is tablets x RF Raft groups: use colocation DDL transactional, fast coordinated through YB-Master, slower, some ALTERs unsupported or non-transactional; CREATE INDEX is online with asynchronous backfill Latency profile sub-millisecond possible per-statement floor of ~1 ms; round trips dominate: batch, use procedures Hotspots rarely matter range-sharded time keys and bigserial with range sharding pile onto one tablet xid wraparound monitor does not exist

Colocated tables: a database created WITH COLOCATION = true puts all its tables (unless opted out) into one tablet, so small reference tables (branches, roles, workflow_states, products) are joined without fan-out and do not multiply Raft groups. Large tables opt out with WITH (COLOCATION = false) and get their own tablets. For your schema: colocate everything except app_users, loan_applications, documents, payments, application_audit.

docs.title: 2.7 Index design on a cluster
docs.text:
Rules that extend module 03:

  1. Choose the sharding of the index explicitly. CREATE INDEX ON app_users (branch_code, user_code) hashes on branch_code by default: a lookup with both columns goes to exactly one tablet (good); a lookup by branch_code alone goes to one tablet (good); a range over user_code within a branch stays on one tablet (good, since the second column is range within the hash). Write it explicitly as (branch_code HASH, user_code ASC) so nobody has to guess. If you need range scans on the first column, use ASC, and accept the hotspot risk.

  2. Cover hot point lookups with INCLUDE: an Index Only Scan is one RPC instead of two, and on a cluster the second RPC may cross a zone. The login index from module 03 is the example:

    CREATE UNIQUE INDEX app_users_login_idx
    ON app_users ((branch_code, user_code) HASH)          -- hash both: even spread, exact match goes to one tablet
    INCLUDE (password_hash, status, failed_attempts);

  3. Every secondary index makes writes distributed. Three indexes on app_users turn a last-login update into a transaction across up to four tablets. Index only what you read. (Updates to non-indexed columns are cheap, the DocDB analogue of HOT.)

  4. Unique indexes cost an extra read at insert time on the index tablet. Needed for correctness; know the cost.
  5. Hash on a low-cardinality column is a hotspot: status HASH puts 98% of rows in the ACTIVE bucket on one tablet. Hash on the high-cardinality column, range on the rest, or use a partial index.
  6. Index backfill is online: CREATE INDEX returns quickly, backfills in the background, and the index is unusable until indisvalid; check pg_index or the master UI before relying on it. A failed backfill leaves an invalid index to drop.
  7. Partial and expression indexes work; GIN exists for jsonb; GiST, BRIN and hash index types do not exist (everything is a DocDB table; the index "type" is the key encoding).

docs.title: 2.8 Reading a multi-node EXPLAIN
docs.text:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST, COSTS OFF)
SELECT password_hash, status FROM app_users WHERE branch_code = 'BR0456' AND user_code = 'U00123456';

 Index Only Scan using app_users_login_idx on app_users (actual time=1.102..1.104 rows=1 loops=1)
   Index Cond: ((branch_code = 'BR0456'::text) AND (user_code = 'U00123456'::text))
   Heap Fetches: 0
   Storage Index Read Requests: 1                 <- one RPC to one tablet leader
   Storage Index Read Execution Time: 0.914 ms    <- time spent in DocDB including network
 Planning Time: 0.090 ms
 Execution Time: 1.150 ms
 Storage Read Requests: 1
 Storage Rows Scanned: 1
 Storage Write Requests: 0
 Catalog Read Requests: 0                         <- non-zero means the catalog cache missed (first call per connection)
 Storage Execution Time: 0.914 ms

Compare the pre-index plan:

 Seq Scan on app_users (actual time=118.414..2410.882 rows=1 loops=1)
   Storage Filter: ((branch_code = 'BR0456'::text) AND (user_code = 'U00123456'::text))
   Storage Table Read Requests: 196                <- paged reads across every tablet
   Storage Table Read Execution Time: 2380.117 ms
   Storage Table Rows Scanned: 2000000

(Shape and magnitudes typical of a small 3-node docker cluster; numbers vary.) What to read: Storage Read Requests (the number of RPC round trips; minimise), Rows Scanned versus rows returned (filter pushdown efficiency: Storage Filter means DocDB applied it, Filter means rows came back to the coordinator first), Catalog Read Requests (schema cache misses; a connection pool with long-lived connections avoids them), and whether the scan is an Index Only Scan (1 hop) or Index Scan (2 hops per row, batched as Storage Table Read Requests). The plan tree itself is PostgreSQL's; the costs are PostgreSQL's constants with YugabyteDB's cost model (yb_enable_base_scans_cost_model in newer versions) adjusting for RPCs.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
Start a cluster: code/docker-compose.yml runs a single-node yugabyted (enough for the API; add nodes for the Raft behaviour), plus PostgreSQL and Redis.

cd code && docker compose up -d yugabyte
docker exec -it yb bin/ysqlsh -h yb            # PostgreSQL-compatible shell, port 5433
# or from WSL with the stock client:
psql -h localhost -p 5433 -U yugabyte -d yugabyte
# web UI: http://localhost:15433 (yugabyted) and http://localhost:7000 (master: tablets, leaders)

code/m11_yugabyte_demo.sql runs on YSQL:

-- 1. Colocated database for the reference tables, with the big tables opted out
CREATE DATABASE loans_yb WITH COLOCATION = true;
\c loans_yb
CREATE TABLE branches (code text PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL);                    -- colocated
CREATE TABLE app_users (
    id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
    branch_code text NOT NULL, user_code text NOT NULL, password_hash text NOT NULL,
    status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE', failed_attempts int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    last_login_at timestamptz,
    PRIMARY KEY (id HASH)
) WITH (COLOCATION = false) SPLIT INTO 6 TABLETS;                                      -- its own tablets

INSERT INTO branches SELECT 'BR' || lpad(g::text, 4, '0'), 'Branch ' || g FROM generate_series(0, 499) g;
INSERT INTO app_users (branch_code, user_code, password_hash)
SELECT 'BR' || lpad((g % 500)::text, 4, '0'), 'U' || lpad(g::text, 8, '0'), md5(g::text)
FROM generate_series(1, 200000) g;                                                     -- keep it small for docker
ANALYZE app_users; ANALYZE branches;                                                   -- you must; nothing does it for you

-- 2. The scatter: no index on the natural key
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST, COSTS OFF)
SELECT password_hash, status FROM app_users WHERE branch_code = 'BR0456' AND user_code = 'U00123456';

-- 3. The fix, with explicit sharding and covering columns
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX app_users_login_idx ON app_users ((branch_code, user_code) HASH)
    INCLUDE (password_hash, status, failed_attempts);
-- wait for backfill: SELECT indisvalid FROM pg_index WHERE indexrelid = 'app_users_login_idx'::regclass;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST, COSTS OFF)
SELECT password_hash, status FROM app_users WHERE branch_code = 'BR0456' AND user_code = 'U00123456';

-- 4. Hash PK means ORDER BY id sorts and ranges fan out
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST, COSTS OFF) SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1100 ORDER BY id;

-- 5. Sequences are cached per node: ids jump
SELECT nextval(pg_get_serial_sequence('app_users', 'id')) FROM generate_series(1, 3);

-- 6. Where are the tablets? (yb_servers lists nodes; the master UI at :7000/tablet-servers shows leaders)
SELECT host, port, zone, region FROM yb_servers();
SELECT * FROM yb_table_properties('app_users'::regclass);                               -- num_tablets, is_colocated

-- 7. Snapshot isolation is the default: watch the error class
BEGIN;  SELECT current_setting('transaction_isolation');  ROLLBACK;                    -- repeatable read
-- in two sessions: both UPDATE the same row -> the second gets 40001 (or waits, depending on conflict mode)

-- 8. Follower reads for a read-only report
BEGIN TRANSACTION READ ONLY;
SET LOCAL yb_read_from_followers = true;
SET LOCAL yb_follower_read_staleness_ms = 30000;
SELECT count(*) FROM app_users;
COMMIT;

Everything from modules 07 and 08 (set-based SQL, PL/pgSQL procedures, ON CONFLICT) runs unchanged on YSQL; only the cost model under it differs.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
The pggate boundary. In the YSQL backend, the heap AM functions (heap_insert, heap_getnext...) and index AM calls are replaced by YBC* functions that build DocDB requests (PgsqlReadRequest, PgsqlWriteRequest protobufs), batch them, and send them to the right tablet leader using the tablet location cache. Predicate pushdown: the executor sends WHERE clauses the storage layer can evaluate (Storage Filter) so rows are filtered at the tablet, and projections so only needed columns cross the network. Reads page through results with a ysql_prefetch_limit (1024 rows per RPC); a Seq Scan on 2 M rows is ~2000 RPCs, which is the Storage Table Read Requests number.

Raft log as WAL, and why fsync still matters. A tablet leader appends the write to its Raft log (fsynced, durable_wal_write = true by default; false is the risky speed knob) and replicates it. Commit requires a majority of durable appends, so the system tolerates one crashed node and a power loss on another only if WAL writes are durable. RocksDB's WAL is off because the Raft log already covers the memtable's contents: on restart, the tablet replays its Raft log from the last flushed index into the memtable, the same redo idea as module 04 one layer up.

Intents, locks and conflict detection. IntentsDB stores, per transaction, the provisional values plus lock intents on rows and prefixes (strong/weak, read/write), encoded as keys. A new write checks IntentsDB for conflicting intents and RegularDB for a committed value newer than its read time. Older versions aborted the newcomer on conflict ("fail on conflict"); newer versions have wait queues so a transaction waits for the holder, like PostgreSQL's row locks, with deadlock detection across tablets. The transaction status tablet records pending/committed/aborted with the commit hybrid time; the apply step rewrites intents into RegularDB with that timestamp and deletes them. A reader hitting an intent whose status is unknown makes an RPC to the status tablet; that is why in-flight hot rows cost readers extra RPCs.

Hybrid logical clocks (HLC). Each node keeps (physical_us, logical); messages carry the sender's HLC and receivers advance to max. A snapshot read at HLC T must be sure no write with timestamp <= T can still arrive: writes with physical time within max_clock_skew of T are in the uncertainty window, and if such a write is found the read is retried at a later time. Tight clocks (chrony, or a cloud provider's clock service) shrink the window; the default 500 ms is loose enough for ordinary NTP. CockroachDB and Spanner solve the same problem differently (Spanner with TrueTime hardware).

Leader leases and read consistency. A leader may only serve a read if it holds a lease whose duration is shorter than the election timeout, so a partitioned old leader cannot serve stale data after a new leader was elected. Leases are renewed with heartbeats. This is how a "read from leader" is linearisable without a Raft round of its own.

Load balancing and tablet moves. YB-Master monitors replica counts per node and moves tablet replicas (remote bootstrap: copy RocksDB SSTables plus Raft log tail) and leaders to even load, respecting placement policy. Immutable SSTables make this a file copy; this is the concrete payoff of the LSM choice from module 10.

Compaction as GC. Full compactions drop versions older than the history retention window and tombstones, and repack per-column entries into packed rows. Scheduled full compactions (scheduled_full_compaction_frequency_hours) are the cluster's "VACUUM"; without them, update- and delete-heavy tables read more entries per row over time.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Latency budget. Every statement is >= 1 network RPC; a 20-statement request is 20+ ms before any real work even in one zone. The login path in module 06 is the model: fewer statements, covering indexes, procedures. On a cluster this is not an optimisation, it is the design.
  • Run ANALYZE. A table loaded by your migration engine and never analysed makes the planner believe it has 1000 rows and nest-loop it against everything. Add ANALYZE to the end of every load job and after large changes. Check pg_class.reltuples.
  • Hotspots are visible in the master UI (per-tablet read/write ops). A range-sharded created_at key or a hash on status shows one tablet carrying the load. Fix the key design; there is no runtime trick.
  • Retry 40001 everywhere. Snapshot isolation by default means concurrent updates of the same row fail one side. The C server needs the retry loop from module 05 around every transaction, with jittered backoff.
  • Connection pooling matters more: each YSQL connection is a PostgreSQL backend plus its catalog cache; the first statement on a fresh connection pays Catalog Read Requests RPCs. Keep long-lived pooled connections; YugabyteDB ships a built-in connection manager in newer versions.
  • Rolling upgrades and node loss are routine: RF = 3 across zones, and the application must tolerate a few seconds of errors for tablets whose leader was on the lost node. Spread leaders (the balancer does) so no single node's failure disturbs every table at once.
  • Backups: distributed snapshots (yb_backup, or the platform's scheduled backups) capture all tablets at one hybrid time; pg_dump works but is a logical, slow, non-consistent-across- tablets-unless-in-one-transaction export. Point-in-time recovery uses the history retention window per database.
  • Honest limits you should mention: no triggers on partitioned tables in older versions, some ALTER TABLE forms rewrite or are unsupported, pg_stat_statements exists but per-node, logical replication/CDC via its own connector (Debezium-based), extensions limited to those that do not touch storage, and version-to-version differences are larger than PostgreSQL's. Check the docs for the version you run.
  • How you phrase the resume bullet: "The login path did sequential scans on hash-sharded tables, fanning out to every tablet across the cluster; I added a covering composite index sharded on the natural key so each login became a single-tablet index-only read, and collapsed the five statements into one PL/pgSQL call, cutting round trips from five to one."

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Bring up the docker cluster, load code/m11_yugabyte_demo.sql steps 1 to 3, and compare the two EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST) outputs. Done when you can read Storage Read Requests and explain the drop.
  2. (easy) Run step 4 and show the Sort node and the fan-out. Recreate app_users with PRIMARY KEY (id ASC) and show the range query now touches one tablet. Done when you can state the trade-off (hotspot on inserts).
  3. (medium) Change the docker compose to 3 yugabyted nodes (the file has the commented block), set RF = 3, load the table, then docker stop one node while running a loop of point reads. Done when you can report the error window length and confirm no committed data was lost after the node returns.
  4. (medium) Create a table with 1000 rows and three secondary indexes. Time 10,000 single-row inserts; drop two indexes; time again. Done when you can explain the difference with distributed transactions and intents.
  5. (hard) Design the tablets and indexes for the full loan schema on a 3-node cluster: which tables colocated, PK sharding for each big table, which indexes hash which columns, and which are covering. Write the DDL and justify every line in a comment. Done when a reviewer could not find a login-style scatter in any of the module 06 queries.
  6. (hard) Reproduce a 40001 under snapshot isolation with two sessions, then implement the retry loop in a small libpq program against port 5433 and show the invariant holds under 1000 concurrent attempts from two processes. Done when the counts reconcile and retries are logged.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Describe YugabyteDB's architecture. A: A PostgreSQL-derived query layer (YSQL) on every node, speaking the PostgreSQL protocol, over DocDB, a distributed document store in which every table and index is split into tablets, each tablet is a Raft group replicated to three nodes, and each replica is a RocksDB instance. A small YB-Master Raft group keeps the tablet map and balances load. Writes commit when a majority of a tablet's replicas have logged them; reads go to the tablet leader.

Q: What changes for the application compared with PostgreSQL? A: Round trips dominate because every statement is a network RPC; the primary key is hash sharded by default so range scans and ORDER BY on it fan out; secondary indexes turn writes into distributed transactions and non-covering lookups into two hops; the default isolation is snapshot, so clients must retry 40001; sequences are cached per node; ANALYZE is manual; VACUUM is unnecessary; small tables should be colocated to avoid tablet explosion.

Q: How does YugabyteDB implement MVCC and transactions without xmin/xmax or VACUUM? A: Each value is stored in RocksDB under a key that ends with a hybrid timestamp, so versions sit adjacent and a read at time T seeks to the newest version at or before T; compaction removes versions older than the retention window. Multi-tablet transactions write provisional intents to each tablet and commit atomically by recording a commit timestamp on a transaction status tablet; readers that meet an intent consult the status tablet, and intents are applied asynchronously.

Q: How did you design indexes differently on the cluster? A: I chose the sharding of each index explicitly, hashing on the natural key columns the lookup always supplies so an exact match goes to one tablet, and included the columns the query reads so the plan is an index-only scan with one storage read request instead of two across nodes. I kept the number of secondary indexes minimal because each one makes every write a distributed transaction, and avoided hashing on low-cardinality columns to prevent hotspots.

Q: What does Storage Read Requests in a YugabyteDB EXPLAIN tell you? A: The number of RPCs the coordinator made to tablet servers for that node. A point lookup should be 1; a sequential scan is one per page of prefetched rows per tablet; an index scan that is not covering adds table read requests. It is the cluster's equivalent of buffer reads and the first number to minimise.

Q: What happens when a node dies? A: Tablets it led lose their leader; followers detect missed heartbeats and elect a new leader within a few seconds; committed data is intact because every commit was on a majority. Tablets it followed continue immediately with two of three replicas. The master later re-replicates under-replicated tablets to healthy nodes if the node stays down.

Q: Why hash sharding by default, and when is it wrong? A: Hashing spreads inserts and point reads evenly across tablets and nodes, which is what most OLTP tables need and what avoids hotspots on increasing keys. It is wrong when the access pattern is range scans or ordered reads on the key, such as time-series or code lookups, where range sharding keeps the scan on one or two tablets; the cost of range sharding is hotspots on sequential inserts, mitigated by pre-splitting or a hash prefix.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• YSQL = PostgreSQL query layer; DocDB = tablets on Raft on RocksDB; YB-Master = tablet map and balancer.
  • Rows are documents keyed by PK with per-column sub-keys and hybrid timestamps; MVCC lives in the key; compaction is GC.
  • Hash sharding by default (16-bit hash space); range sharding for ordered access, with hotspot risk.
  • RF = 3 Raft groups per tablet; majority commit; leader reads with leases; follower reads optional and stale.
  • Single-tablet writes are fast path; multi-tablet operations are distributed transactions with intents and a status tablet.
  • Default isolation is snapshot (REPEATABLE READ); retry 40001; SERIALIZABLE is lock-based here.
  • Every statement is at least one RPC: batch, cover, use procedures; run ANALYZE yourself.
  • Secondary indexes are tables: choose their sharding explicitly, cover hot lookups, index less.
  • Colocate small tables; split big ones; watch the master UI for hotspots and leader distribution.
  • EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST): Storage Read Requests, Rows Scanned, Catalog Read Requests are the numbers that matter.

docs.title: 12. Migrating a key-value store to a relational database
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: 07, 09, 10, 11

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
You have years of business data in a key-value store: packed C structs stored as opaque bytes under packed keys, read and written by one application. You need the same data in relational tables, with a schema, constraints and SQL, served by a cluster, and the business must not stop while you do it. That is a migration, and it is one of the hardest things a backend engineer does, because every mistake is silent: a wrong byte offset turns 3% of balances into garbage and nobody notices until month end.

The analogy is moving a working hospital to a new building. You cannot close for a month. You inventory every ward (the KV layouts), label every item (decode the records), design the new floor plan (the schema), move things in trucks while patients keep arriving (streaming, batching, checkpoints), check every item arrived (parity verification), run both buildings for a while with every new patient registered in both (dual write), and only then lock the old doors (cutover) with a plan to reopen them if the new building floods (rollback).

This module is the methodology, written so you can present your flagship project at senior level: every decision, why, and what you would do differently. The C++17 skeleton in code/ is the engine's shape with a fake source so it compiles and runs without Berkeley DB or libpq.

docs.title: 2.1 Phase 0: inventory the key-value layouts
docs.text:
Before any code: a spreadsheet (really) of every database in the environment, and for each:

  • Access method, key layout (fields, widths, byte order, sort order), value layout (struct, version byte, variable parts), duplicates allowed, secondary databases and their extractors.
  • Record counts and total bytes (db_stat -d), growth rate, and which records are hot.
  • Every writer and reader in the code base (grep for the DB handle). You are about to make every one of them a dual writer or a reader of the new store.
  • Invariants that were enforced in C: "status is one of these 5 chars", "amount is cents, never negative", "customer must exist" (you will turn each into a constraint).
  • Known dirt: records written by old versions, orphans (child records whose parent was deleted), test data in production, padding bytes with garbage. Sample 10,000 records per database and decode them before designing the schema; the dirt decides half the design.

Output: a mapping document per record type: source field -> target table.column, type conversion rule, nullability rule, what to do with invalid values (reject, default, quarantine table). This document is also the specification of the parity checker.

docs.title: 2.2 Phase 1: decoding packed records correctly
docs.text:
The records were written by a C compiler with #pragma pack(1) (or without, with padding!), on a specific architecture, with specific conventions. Reading them back in a different program is where byte-level bugs live.

/* The historical layout. If the original had NO pack pragma, the compiler inserted padding:

 * sizeof may be 40, not 35, and the field offsets depend on the original compiler and ABI. */
#pragma pack(push, 1)
struct loan_rec_v2 {
    uint8_t  version;           /* 2 */
    char     loan_no[12];       /* space-padded, not NUL-terminated */
    uint32_t customer_id;       /* little-endian on x86 */
    int64_t  amount_cents;      /* little-endian */
    char     status;            /* 'D','S','A','R','W' */
    uint8_t  bcd_date[4];       /* YYYYMMDD as packed BCD: 0x20 0x24 0x03 0x15 */
    uint16_t branch_no;         /* big-endian! written by a network-order helper */
    char     officer[3];        /* code */
};                              /* 35 bytes */
#pragma pack(pop)

Rules for the decoder (all of them are in code/m12_packed_record_decode.cpp):

  1. Never cast the buffer to the struct pointer ((struct loan_rec_v2 *)dbt.data). It is undefined behaviour if the buffer is not suitably aligned (Berkeley DB returns arbitrary offsets into a page), and it silently depends on the current compiler's layout matching the original. Read fields with memcpy at explicit offsets, or std::memcpy into a local properly-aligned variable.
  2. Byte order per field. x86 wrote little-endian integers unless the code used htonl-style helpers, in which case big-endian. Decode each with an explicit function: rd_le32, rd_be16. Mixed layouts like the one above happened in real code bases.
  3. Fixed-width strings: not NUL-terminated; trim trailing spaces (and sometimes NULs); decide the character encoding (likely a single-byte code page, convert to UTF-8 explicitly; invalid bytes are a parity-check finding, not a crash).
  4. Dates and amounts: packed BCD, Julian day numbers, days since 1900, cents as integers. Map to date and numeric(18,2); never through double.
  5. Versioned records: read the version byte first, dispatch to the layout for that version, and handle every version ever written. Records with an unknown version go to a quarantine table with the raw bytes (bytea) for later analysis.
  6. Alignment of the output struct is irrelevant: decode into a clean C++ struct with natural types (std::string, int64_t, std::optional<Date>), which is what the mapping and the hash operate on.
  7. Test the decoder against golden records: pick 50 records across versions, hand-verify with db_dump -p and a hex editor, and make them unit tests.

docs.title: 2.3 Phase 2: design the relational schema
docs.text:
Module 09 covers the design rules. Migration-specific points:

  • Keep the natural key as a UNIQUE constraint so the parity checker can find each target row from the source key. Add the surrogate bigint id for the future.
  • Add a source_hash bytea (or bigint) column, or a side table migration_parity(source_db, source_key bytea, hash bigint, migrated_at), so parity can be re-verified without re-decoding.
  • Every invariant found in phase 0 becomes a constraint, but create them NOT VALID during the load and VALIDATE after, or load into staging tables first, so a single dirty record does not abort a 10 M row batch.
  • Decide the fate of denormalised copies: the loan record carried cust_name; the target has it only on customers. The parity rule becomes "loan.cust_name == customers.full_name joined by customer_id", and mismatches are findings about the source data (stale copies), which the business must adjudicate before cutover.
  • For the cluster (module 11): choose sharding and colocation now; the engine's write pattern (batched inserts by source key order) interacts with range-sharded keys (hotspots on the last tablet). Hash sharding on the natural key spreads a bulk load across all tablets.

docs.title: 2.4 Phase 3: the migration engine
docs.text:
+-----------+     +-----------+     +-----------+     +-------------+     +--------------+
 | KV source | --> | decoder   | --> | mapper    | --> | batcher     | --> | relational   |
 | cursor    |     | bytes ->  |     | record -> |     | arena,      |     | sink: COPY / |
 | SET_RANGE |     | typed rec |     | row(s)    |     | N rows/txn  |     | INSERT ...   |
 | NEXT      |     |           |     |           |     |             |     | ON CONFLICT  |
 +-----------+     +-----------+     +-----------+     +------+------+     +------+-------+
       ^                                                      |                   |
       |                 +------------------------------------+                   |
       |                 v                                                        v
       |          +-------------+   after each committed batch              +-----------+
       +--------- | checkpoint  | <----------------------------------------- | parity    |
   resume from    | store       |   (last_key, rows, hash, time)             | hashes    |
   last key       +-------------+                                            +-----------+

Streaming cursor, not a load into memory. The source is read with DB_SET_RANGE from the last checkpointed key and DB_NEXT forward; the engine never holds more than one batch. On the source, use short read transactions (or snapshot reads) per batch to avoid holding page locks against the live application (module 10); reposition by key at each batch.

Batching. A batch of 1,000 to 10,000 source records becomes one target transaction: decoded, mapped, written with COPY into staging or multi-row INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, committed. Batch size trades throughput (per-transaction overhead, fsyncs, on the cluster one distributed commit) against lock duration, WAL/intents per transaction, and the cost of redoing a failed batch. Measure; 5,000 was typical.

Idempotency. Any batch may be retried after a crash, so every write must be safe to repeat: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (natural_key) DO NOTHING for an initial load, or DO UPDATE SET ... WHERE target.source_hash <> EXCLUDED.source_hash when re-running over changed data. Child rows (documents of a loan) are deleted and re-inserted per parent within the batch transaction, or also keyed by a natural key. Never INSERT without a conflict clause in a restartable engine.

Checkpoints and restartability. After each batch commits, write a checkpoint row in the target database, in the same transaction as the batch: (run_id, source_db, last_key bytea, records_done, batch_hash, committed_at). The checkpoint and the data commit atomically, so after a crash the engine reads the last checkpoint and DB_SET_RANGE to last_key, skipping the first record (already done). Also record failed records in a migration_rejects(source_key, reason, raw bytea) table rather than stopping.

Arena allocation per batch. Decoding 5,000 records produces thousands of small strings and rows. Allocating and freeing them individually is slow and fragments the heap over a 12-hour run. Allocate from a per-batch arena (a bump allocator over a few MB) and reset it after the batch commits: O(1) free, no fragmentation, cache-friendly. PostgreSQL does exactly this with memory contexts (module 01). In C++17 this is a std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource with std::pmr::vector/std::pmr::string, or a hand-written bump allocator as in the skeleton.

Parallelism. Partition the key space into ranges (one per worker, by key prefix or by branch), run one engine instance per range with its own checkpoint row. On a hash-sharded target the writes spread; on PostgreSQL, 4 to 8 parallel COPY streams usually saturate the disk.

Throughput controls. synchronous_commit = off for the load session (crash loses at most the last batch, which the checkpoint logic redoes anyway, because checkpoint and data are in the same transaction); indexes created after the load; maintenance_work_mem high for the index builds; ANALYZE at the end; on YugabyteDB, the bulk load path with large batches, and run ANALYZE explicitly.

docs.title: 2.5 Phase 4: data-parity verification
docs.text:
Parity is not "row counts match". It is a regression suite that proves, for every record, the relational form equals the source form under the mapping rules, and keeps proving it while both systems run.

  1. Canonical serialisation and hash per record. Define, in the mapping document, a canonical byte string for each entity: fields in a fixed order, normalised (trimmed, UTF-8, cents as integers, dates as YYYYMMDD, NULL as a sentinel). Hash it (64-bit FNV-1a or xxHash is enough for parity; SHA-256 if someone demands collision resistance). Compute it from the decoded source record in the engine, and recompute it from the target row with a SQL function (fn_parity_hash_loan(application_id)) that applies the same canonicalisation. Store both. Mismatch = a mapping bug or a decoder bug, found per record.
  2. Row counts per entity and per partition (per branch, per status), source versus target, including rejects: source_count = target_count + rejects.
  3. Aggregates that the business already watches: sum of outstanding balances per branch, count of applications per status. If the migration changes the month-end report by one rupee, the business finds it before you do, so find it first.
  4. Sampled deep diff: random sample (and a stratified sample across versions, branches, and edge cases: empty strings, max amounts, oldest dates), decode the source, read the target rows via SQL, compare field by field with a report of every difference. Run it on 0.1% then on 100% if the hardware allows (a full diff of 50 M records at 50k/s is 17 minutes).
  5. Continuous diff during dual write (next section): a daemon that re-hashes records changed in the last N minutes on both sides and alerts on mismatch. This is what makes the dual-write period safe rather than hopeful.
  6. Keep all findings in a table with a status (open, source_bug, mapping_fixed, accepted); the sign-off for cutover is "zero open findings and all accepted ones documented".

The suite runs on every engine change, like unit tests. That is why "regression suite" is the right phrase on your resume.

docs.title: 2.6 Phase 5: cutover strategies
docs.text:
Strategy How Downtime Risk When Big bang stop writes, run final load, verify, switch readers and writers, start hours one shot; rollback = switch back if the old store is untouched small data, tolerable maintenance window, simple dependencies Dual write application writes to both stores (old first, then new) for weeks; reads from old; parity daemon compares; then flip reads; then stop writing old none for reads; a brief write pause at flips application-level complexity; partial failures (old ok, new failed) need reconciliation; both stores must stay consistent your case: single application owns all writes, long verification wanted CDC (change data capture) initial load, then tail the source's change log and apply to target until lag is zero, flip seconds needs a change stream from the source: Berkeley DB has none built in, so you instrument the application's write path (a write-ahead queue table or log) sources with logical replication (PostgreSQL to anything); or when you can hook every write

The strategy for a Berkeley DB source owned by one application server was dual write with an instrumented write path, which is CDC in spirit: every write goes through one function in the C server, so that function wrote to both stores and, on failure of the new store, appended the record key to a replay queue reconciled by the engine. This is the shape to describe.

docs.title: 2.7 Phase 6: rollback plan
docs.text:
Rollback is a plan written before cutover, with a decision owner and a time box. Elements:

  • Keep the old store writable and current until the end of the soak period: dual write continues after reads flip, in reverse (new is primary, old is secondary), so the old store can take over with no data loss.
  • Triggers for rollback, decided in advance: parity findings above a threshold, p99 latency above X for Y minutes, error rate, a failed business report. Not "it feels wrong".
  • Procedure: flip the read switch back (a configuration flag, not a deployment), confirm with a smoke test, open an incident, keep dual writing. The ability to roll back must be tested in staging as a drill.
  • Point of no return: when the application starts using features the old store cannot represent (new columns, new tables) or when the old store is frozen. Announce it; after it, rollback means restoring from backup plus replaying, and the plan says so honestly.

docs.title: 2.8 Zero-downtime cutover runbook
docs.text:
A runbook is a numbered list with an owner, a check, and a rollback step per line. The skeleton:

T-14d  1. Final mapping document and parity suite signed off (owner: you; check: zero open findings)

       2. Target schema deployed with constraints NOT VALID, indexes minimal (owner: DBA)
       3. Dual-write code deployed behind a flag, OFF (owner: app lead; check: flag read in logs)
T-10d  4. Flag dual-write ON (old primary, new secondary). Check: replay queue depth ~0 after 1 h.
          Rollback: flag OFF.
       5. Bulk load of history with the engine, 8 workers, from a snapshot taken at step 4's time.
          Check: checkpoints advance; rejects < threshold. Rollback: none needed (target not read).
       6. Reconcile: engine re-runs over keys changed since snapshot (from the replay/changes log).
          Check: counts match per entity.
T-7d   7. Parity full diff. Check: 0 mismatches; aggregates match month-end report. Fix, re-run.
       8. VALIDATE constraints; build remaining indexes CONCURRENTLY; ANALYZE. Check: plans of the
          top 20 queries (module 06) are index-driven on the cluster (Storage Read Requests small).
       9. Continuous parity daemon ON. Check: alerts wired, test alert fired.
T-3d  10. Shadow reads: application reads from both, serves old, logs differences. Check: 24 h, 0 diffs.
          Rollback: disable shadow reads.
T-0   11. Flip reads to new (flag). Check: latency and error dashboards for 1 h; parity daemon quiet.
          Rollback: flip flag back (tested in staging on T-5d).
      12. Swap dual-write order: new primary, old secondary. Check: replay queue for old ~0.
T+7d  13. Soak. Daily parity, daily business reports compared. Rollback remains one flag.
T+14d 14. Point of no return announced; stop writing old (flag). Old store read-only, backed up,
          retained 1 year. Remove dual-write code in the next release.

Every "flag" is a configuration value read at runtime, so cutover and rollback are not deployments. Every step has a check that is a number, not a feeling.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m12_migration_engine.cpp (C++17, compiles with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread m12_migration_engine.cpp -o migrate) implements the engine shape with abstract interfaces so it runs standalone:

// The four seams. Production swaps FakeKvSource for a Berkeley DB cursor and StubSink for libpq;
// the engine does not change.
struct KvSource {                 // ordered cursor over (key, value) bytes
    virtual bool seek(const Bytes& start_inclusive) = 0;   // DB_SET_RANGE
    virtual bool next(Bytes& key, Bytes& value) = 0;       // DB_NEXT; false at end
    virtual ~KvSource() = default;
};
struct RelationalSink {           // one target transaction at a time
    virtual void begin() = 0;
    virtual void upsert_loans(const std::vector<LoanRow>& rows) = 0;   // INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING / UPDATE
    virtual void write_checkpoint(const Checkpoint& cp) = 0;          // same transaction as the rows
    virtual void write_reject(const Bytes& key, std::string_view reason, const Bytes& raw) = 0;
    virtual void commit() = 0;
    virtual void rollback() = 0;
    virtual std::optional<Checkpoint> last_checkpoint(std::string_view run_id) = 0;
    virtual ~RelationalSink() = default;
};

The batch loop, which is the heart of it:

void MigrationEngine::run() {
    Bytes start = resume_point();                 // last checkpoint's key, or empty for the beginning
    if (!src_.seek(start)) return;
    BatchArena arena(8 << 20);                    // 8 MB bump allocator, reset per batch
    for (;;) {
        arena.reset();
        std::vector<LoanRow> rows; rows.reserve(cfg_.batch_size);
        Bytes key, val, last_key;
        std::size_t n = 0;
        while (n < cfg_.batch_size && src_.next(key, val)) {
            if (n == 0 && key == start && !start.empty()) continue;      // skip the already-committed resume key
            auto decoded = decode_loan(val, arena);                       // memcpy-based, version-dispatched
            if (!decoded) { rejects_.push_back({key, decoded.error(), val}); last_key = key; ++n; continue; }
            LoanRow row = map_to_row(*decoded, arena);                   // mapping document, in code
            row.source_hash = parity_hash(*decoded);                     // canonical bytes -> FNV-1a 64
            rows.push_back(std::move(row));
            last_key = key; ++n;
        }
        if (n == 0) break;
        for (int attempt = 0; ; ++attempt) {                             // retry the whole batch: it is idempotent
            try {
                sink_.begin();
                sink_.upsert_loans(rows);
                for (auto& r : rejects_) sink_.write_reject(r.key, r.reason, r.raw);
                sink_.write_checkpoint({cfg_.run_id, last_key, done_ + n, batch_hash(rows)});
                sink_.commit();
                break;
            } catch (const TransientError& e) {
                sink_.rollback();
                if (attempt >= cfg_.max_retries) throw;
                backoff(attempt);                                        // 40001/40P01/connection loss on the cluster
            }
        }
        done_ += n; rejects_.clear(); start = last_key;
        if (n < cfg_.batch_size) break;
    }
}

Also in the file: FakeKvSource generating versioned packed records (including deliberately corrupt ones), the decoder with rd_le32/rd_be16/bcd_date, the canonical serialiser and FNV-1a hash, StubSink that keeps rows in memory and prints a parity report (source hash == recomputed hash from the "row"), and a #ifdef HAVE_LIBPQ section sketching LibpqSink with COPY ... FROM STDIN into a staging table followed by INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT. code/m12_packed_record_decode.cpp is the byte-level decoder with tests on golden records.

The parity side in SQL, from code/m09_schema.sql's companion functions:

-- Same canonical form as the C++ canonicalise(): fields in fixed order, '|' separated, normalised.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_parity_canonical_loan(p_id bigint) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$
    SELECT concat_ws('|', a.application_no, c.national_id, (a.requested_amount * 100)::bigint,
                     a.status, to_char(a.submitted_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC', 'YYYYMMDD'), a.branch_code)
    FROM loan_applications a JOIN customers c ON c.id = a.customer_id WHERE a.id = p_id
$$;
-- Hash with the same FNV-1a 64 as the engine (implemented in PL/pgSQL in the code file), compare to migration_parity.hash

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why memcpy and not a cast. The C and C++ standards require an object of type T to be accessed through a pointer suitably aligned for T (except via char/unsigned char pointers). *(uint32_t*)(buf + 13) on x86 happens to work (x86 tolerates unaligned loads, with a small penalty across cache lines), but on ARM it may fault or silently load from the rounded address, and the compiler is allowed to assume alignment and emit instructions (SSE movaps) that fault. memcpy(&v, buf + 13, 4) compiles to the same single mov on x86 with no UB, and the compiler knows it. Strict aliasing is the second problem: accessing the same bytes as both char[] and struct loan_rec_v2 is permitted only in one direction (char access to anything is fine; struct access to a char buffer is not). Decode through memcpy; the optimiser removes it.

Endianness in practice. Little-endian stores the least significant byte first; x86 and modern ARM Linux are little-endian; "network order" and many legacy formats are big-endian. A record written with htonl() on x86 has big-endian integers, and a developer reading it back with a plain struct on x86 gets byte-swapped values. Write rd_be32 as (uint32_t)b[0] << 24 | (uint32_t)b[1] << 16 | (uint32_t)b[2] << 8 | b[3] and rd_le32 the other way; cast to the unsigned type before shifting to avoid signed-shift UB.

Alignment pitfalls in the original writer. If the original struct had no pack pragma, the compiler inserted padding (a uint32_t after a char[13] starts at offset 16, not 13) and sizeof was rounded up to the largest alignment. The padding bytes contain whatever was on the stack: so two logically identical records have different bytes, and hashing the raw value for parity is wrong; hash the decoded fields. The offsets are those of the original compiler and ABI (MSVC x86 and GCC x86-64 agree on natural alignment; bitfields and long do not). Your phase 0 inventory must record the original compiler.

Arena allocators and locality. A bump allocator hands out consecutive addresses, so the 5,000 decoded records of a batch are contiguous in memory: fewer cache misses when serialising them, no per-object malloc metadata, no free calls, and no fragmentation growth over a 12-hour run (glibc malloc fragmentation on long-running processes with mixed sizes is real). The cost: you cannot free one object early, and anything that must outlive the batch (rejects queued for the next transaction, the checkpoint) must be copied out. std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource gives this with standard containers; see 02_Modern_CPP for allocators.

What COPY into staging buys on the cluster. On PostgreSQL, COPY avoids per-row parsing and uses multi-insert (module 07). On YugabyteDB, large multi-row inserts are batched into fewer RPCs per tablet (ysql_session_max_batch_size), and the staging-then-INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT pattern turns the idempotency check into one distributed statement per batch instead of per row. Hash-sharded staging tables spread the load.

Checkpoint atomicity. The checkpoint row commits in the same transaction as the batch's rows, so the two possible states after a crash are "batch and checkpoint both committed" or "neither". With synchronous_commit = off the last committed batch may be lost on a database crash, but the checkpoint is lost with it, so the engine redoes the batch: idempotency makes the redo harmless. This is the same argument as PostgreSQL's own redo being idempotent (module 04).

Hashing for parity. FNV-1a 64 is fast and good enough to detect accidental mismatches; it is not collision resistant against an adversary, which is not the threat model. The canonical form must be defined so that two representations that the business considers equal hash equal (trailing spaces, '00' vs 0, time zone of dates); every parity bug you will find is a canonicalisation disagreement between the C++ and the SQL implementations, so test them against each other on golden records first.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The dirty 3%. Every real KV store has records no current code can write: old versions, truncated values from a crash, test data. Design the quarantine path first; a migration that stops on the first bad record never finishes, and one that silently defaults bad fields corrupts the target.
  • Source load. A full cursor scan of the source competes with production for the mpool and takes page read locks. Run with snapshot reads or short transactions, throttle (sleep between batches when the application's latency rises), and schedule the bulk pass off-peak.
  • Target lock and WAL impact. Bulk load generates GBs of WAL and, on PostgreSQL, bloats nothing (inserts only) but forces checkpoints and FPIs; on YugabyteDB it triggers compactions. Watch replication lag (physical standbys must keep up) and disk.
  • Clock and ordering. When reconciling changes made during the load, "changed since" must be judged by the source's own change log sequence, not by wall clock on two machines.
  • Dual-write failure modes: new store down (append to replay queue, alert, keep serving); old store down (that is the old outage, unchanged); both succeed but differ (parity daemon catches it; the usual cause is a code path that bypassed the common write function). Grep for every write site in phase 0 for exactly this reason.
  • Observability: records/s, batches/s, rejects/s, checkpoint lag, parity mismatches, p99 of the application during the load. A migration without a dashboard is a migration run blind.
  • What you would do differently (interviewers ask): start the parity suite before the engine, not after; put the canonicalisation in one shared spec with generated code for both C++ and SQL; use CDC-style change logging from day one so the reconciliation pass is mechanical; rehearse rollback in staging earlier.
  • Numbers to have ready: record count and bytes migrated, batch size, sustained records/s, total bulk-load hours, number of record versions handled, reject rate, parity mismatches found and their root causes, dual-write duration, cutover downtime (zero for reads; seconds for the flag flips). Use your real ones; say "roughly" where memory is approximate.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run code/m12_migration_engine.cpp. Read the parity report. Done when you can explain why every record's source hash equals the recomputed hash, and what the deliberately corrupt records did.
  2. (easy) Build code/m12_packed_record_decode.cpp and run its tests. Change one field to the wrong endianness and watch which test fails. Done when you can explain the failing bytes.
  3. (medium) Add a kill switch to the engine (e.g. throw after batch 3), run it, run it again, and verify with the stub sink's log that no record is written twice and the resume key is correct. Done when the second run starts at the right key and the final counts are exact.
  4. (medium) Implement LibpqSink for real against your WSL PostgreSQL (#define HAVE_LIBPQ, link -lpq), with COPY into a staging table and INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING into loan_applications. Load 1 M fake records and run the SQL parity function over a 1% sample. Done when the sample reports 0 mismatches and migration_checkpoints shows the batches.
  5. (hard) Write the dual-write function for the C server in pseudocode or C: write old, write new, on new-failure enqueue to a replay table, with idempotency keys. Then write the parity daemon's SQL that re-hashes records changed in the last 10 minutes. Done when you can walk a reviewer through every failure branch.
