  6. (hard) Write the complete cutover runbook for the loan schema migration (the 14-step skeleton expanded to your real system's components), with a check and rollback per step, and present it in 10 minutes to someone else. Done when they can find no step without a number to check.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Walk me through how you migrated the Berkeley DB data to YugabyteDB. A: Inventory first: every database, key and record layout, version, writer and reader, with a mapping document per record type that doubled as the parity specification. A decoder that read packed records by explicit offsets with per-field byte order and version dispatch, quarantining unknown versions. A streaming engine: cursor from the last checkpoint, batches of a few thousand records decoded into a per-batch arena, idempotent upserts into the target in one transaction with the checkpoint row, retried on transient errors. A parity suite of per-record canonical hashes, counts and aggregates, sampled deep diffs, and a continuous diff during dual write. Then dual write, shadow reads, a flag flip of reads, a soak, and retiring the old store, with rollback being a flag until the announced point of no return.

Q: How did you make the engine restartable? A: Each batch commits its rows and a checkpoint row (run id, last source key, counts, batch hash) in the same transaction, so after a crash the engine resumes from the last checkpointed key by positioning the cursor with a range seek. All writes are idempotent upserts keyed by the natural key, so redoing a batch whose commit was lost is harmless.

Q: What byte-level problems did decoding packed records raise? A: Unaligned access if you cast the buffer to a struct, so I read fields with memcpy at explicit offsets; mixed byte order where some fields were written in network order; fixed-width space-padded strings in a legacy code page needing explicit trimming and UTF-8 conversion; packed BCD dates and integer cents; and padding bytes with stack garbage in records written by an unpacked struct, which means you must hash decoded fields, never raw bytes, for parity.

Q: How did you prove the data was correct? A: A canonical serialisation per entity defined in the mapping document, hashed in the engine from the decoded source and recomputed in SQL from the target rows; per-partition row counts including rejects; business aggregates compared with existing month-end reports; stratified sampled field-by-field diffs; and a continuous re-hash of recently changed records on both sides during the dual-write period. Findings went into a tracked table and cutover required zero open findings.

Q: Why dual write rather than big bang or CDC? A: The business could not accept hours of downtime, and Berkeley DB has no change stream to tail for CDC, but a single application owned every write through one code path, so instrumenting that path to write both stores with a replay queue for failures gave CDC-like completeness with a long verification window. The cost was application complexity and a reconciliation step, which the parity suite covered.

Q: How was the cutover zero-downtime and how could you roll back? A: Reads and the write order were runtime flags, not deployments. After the bulk load, reconciliation, full parity and shadow reads, we flipped reads to the new store, then made it the primary for writes while still writing the old store, so for the soak period rollback was flipping the read flag back with no data loss. The point of no return was when we stopped writing the old store, announced in advance, after which rollback would have meant restore plus replay.

Q: What would you do differently? A: Build the parity suite before the engine, generate the canonicalisation code for both C++ and SQL from one spec to avoid the disagreements that caused most mismatches, log changes from the first day so reconciliation was mechanical, and rehearse rollback in staging earlier.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Inventory every layout, writer, invariant and dirt sample before designing anything.
  • Decode with memcpy at explicit offsets, per-field byte order, version dispatch, quarantine for unknowns.
  • Schema: natural key UNIQUE, surrogate id, source hash stored, constraints NOT VALID then VALIDATE.
  • Engine: streaming cursor from last key, batches of thousands, per-batch arena, idempotent upserts.
  • Checkpoint row commits with the batch; resume by range seek; retry transient errors; reject table.
  • Parity: canonical hash per record on both sides, counts per partition, aggregates, sampled deep diff, continuous diff.
  • Cutover: big bang vs dual write vs CDC; dual write with a replay queue when the source has no change log.
  • Rollback: flags not deployments, pre-agreed triggers, drilled in staging, announced point of no return.
  • Runbook: numbered steps, each with an owner, a numeric check, and a rollback action.
  • Have your real numbers and your "what I would change" ready.

docs.title: 13. Caching and Redis
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: 05, 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A cache is a copy of data kept somewhere faster than its source, on the bet that it will be asked for again before it changes. The database already has caches (shared buffers, the OS page cache), but they still cost a network round trip, a parse, a plan, and a join. An application cache answers from memory in microseconds and costs no database work at all. The price is the oldest problem in computing: the copy can be wrong. "There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things."

The analogy: a clerk keeps a photocopy of the branch list and the product rate sheet on his desk instead of walking to the filing room for every form. Fast, until head office changes a rate and his copy is stale. Every caching design is a decision about how the clerk learns the copy is stale, how long he is allowed to use it anyway, and what happens when fifty clerks all discover at 9:00 that their copies expired and walk to the filing room at once.

Redis is the standard shared cache: an in-memory data-structure server on a socket, used by every process in a cluster as one cache. This module covers the patterns, the failure modes, Redis's model and persistence, and what your "in-memory caching removing master-table joins" design looks like when done carefully.

docs.title: 2.1 Cache patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Read Write Consistency Use Cache-aside (lazy) app checks cache; on miss reads DB and writes cache app writes DB, then deletes (not updates) the cache key stale until TTL or delete; race windows exist default for read-heavy lookups Read-through cache library loads from DB on miss itself same as aside same when a cache layer wraps the data access Write-through from cache app writes cache and DB synchronously (cache library forwards) cache always has latest written value; DB write still the slow path when reads must see writes immediately and the cache is the system of access Write-behind (write-back) from cache app writes cache; cache flushes to DB asynchronously, batched DB lags; a cache crash loses writes counters, metrics, anything tolerable to loss; never money Refresh-ahead from cache background refresh before TTL expires for hot keys bounded staleness hot reference data

Why delete, not update, on write in cache-aside: two concurrent writers can update the cache in the opposite order to the DB (A writes DB v1, B writes DB v2, B updates cache v2, A updates cache v1: stale forever). Deleting makes the next reader fetch the truth. The remaining race: reader misses, reads DB (old), writer writes DB and deletes cache, reader writes old value to cache. It is narrow (the reader's DB read must straddle the write) and bounded by TTL; if that is not acceptable, use a short TTL plus versioning (below), or lease-based sets (SET key value NX with a lease token).

docs.title: 2.2 TTL and expiry
docs.text: Every cached entry gets a time to live. Short TTL (seconds) bounds staleness for data that changes; long TTL (hours) for reference data with explicit invalidation. Add jitter (TTL ± 10%) so entries loaded together do not expire together. Redis expires keys lazily on access and actively by sampling (default 10 times per second, 20 random keys with TTL each, repeat while more than 25% expired), so memory from expired keys is reclaimed within seconds, not instantly. With maxmemory set, an eviction policy applies when memory is full: allkeys-lru (approximate LRU via sampling), volatile-lru (only keys with TTL), allkeys-lfu (frequency), volatile-ttl, noeviction (errors on write; the default, and wrong for a cache).

docs.title: 2.3 Invalidation strategies
docs.text:
1. TTL only: simplest; staleness up to TTL. Fine for data where a few seconds of lag is invisible (counts, lists).
  2. Delete on write (cache-aside): the writer knows the key. Fails when one DB change affects many keys (a product rate change invalidates every cached quote).
  3. Versioned keys / namespaces: cache product:v{version}:{id} where version is a small value stored in the cache (product_version); bump the version to invalidate the whole family at once; old keys expire by TTL. No scanning of keys.
  4. Event-driven: the writer publishes "product 42 changed" (Redis Pub/Sub, a queue, or PostgreSQL NOTIFY), every cache holder deletes locally. Needed for in-process caches across many servers.
  5. Database-driven: a trigger writes to an outbox table or increments a cache_versions row; cache holders poll it (cheap: one indexed row read per second) or get a NOTIFY. Catches writes that bypass the application (DBA scripts, batch jobs), which pattern 2 cannot.

Rule: invalidate on the data, not on the query. Cache entities by id; compose results in the application; do not cache a 5-table join result keyed by its SQL text unless you can enumerate what changes it.

docs.title: 2.4 Cache stampede (thundering herd, dog-pile)
docs.text:
A hot key expires. 500 concurrent requests miss at once and all run the expensive query; the database, which was idle because of the cache, gets 500 copies of its heaviest query in 10 ms. Defences, combinable:

  • Request coalescing (single flight): in-process, the first miss for a key does the load; others wait on it (a mutex or future per key). Across processes: a Redis lock SET lock:key token NX PX 2000; the winner loads and sets, losers either wait-and-retry or serve stale.
  • Serve stale while revalidating: keep the value past its logical TTL (two TTLs: soft and hard); on soft expiry one request refreshes while others use the old value.
  • Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch): each reader recomputes early with probability rising as expiry approaches (now - delta * beta * ln(rand()) >= expiry), so refreshes spread out and the herd never forms.
  • TTL jitter against synchronised expiry of many keys.
  • Warm-up on deploy: load the hot reference set before taking traffic, and never flush the whole cache in production ("FLUSHALL during the day" is a classic outage).

docs.title: 2.5 Consistency problems you must name
docs.text:
• Read-your-writes: a user updates her address, the next screen shows the old one from cache. Fix: delete on write, and for the writing session bypass the cache or write-through the specific entity.
  • Cross-entity consistency: cache holds customer v2 and application v1 which referenced customer v1; a screen shows an impossible combination. Caches hold entities, not snapshots; if the UI needs a consistent set, read it from the database in one transaction.
  • Negative caching: caching "not found" prevents repeated DB misses for missing keys (lookup of a non-existent user code in a brute-force login attack) but delays the appearance of newly created entities; use a short TTL for negatives.
  • Cache as a source of truth by accident: a counter lives only in Redis; Redis restarts; the counter is gone. Anything you cannot rebuild from the database is not a cache.

docs.title: 2.6 In-process caches versus Redis
docs.text:
In-process (a hash map with TTL in the C server) Redis Latency ~100 ns (a hash lookup) ~100 to 300 us (socket round trip on the same host or LAN) Shared across servers no: each process has its own copy, each warms separately, invalidation must be broadcast yes: one copy, one invalidation Memory per process, counts against the server's RAM separate service with its own limit and eviction Failure modes process restart = cold cache Redis down = every read goes to the DB (must degrade gracefully, with a circuit breaker) Data structures whatever you code strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps, HyperLogLog, geo Atomic operations across clients not applicable INCR, SETNX, Lua scripts, MULTI/EXEC, WATCH Right for small hot reference data (branches, products, roles, states: KBs to a few MB), per-request memoisation sessions, rate limits, shared counters, leaderboards, large hot sets, anything many processes must agree on

Common and correct: both. In-process L1 for reference data with event invalidation; Redis L2 for shared session and per-user state.

docs.title: 2.7 Redis: the model
docs.text:
Redis executes commands on a single thread over an event loop (epoll), one command at a time, each in microseconds, so there are no locks and every command is atomic. Since 6.0, I/O threads can read requests and write replies in parallel, but command execution is still one thread. Consequences: a single slow command (KEYS *, SMEMBERS of a million-member set, a long Lua script, a huge DEL) blocks every client; use SCAN, UNLINK (async free), and keep values small. Throughput is ~100k to over 1 M simple ops per second per instance (Redis's own benchmarks; depends on hardware and pipelining); scale by sharding (Redis Cluster, 16384 hash slots) rather than threads.

Data structures (each with O(1) or O(log n) operations):

Type Commands Cache use String (bytes, up to 512 MB) GET SET SETEX SETNX INCR INCRBY MGET MSET serialised entities (JSON/protobuf), counters, locks Hash HGET HSET HMGET HGETALL HINCRBY an entity's fields individually updatable; small hashes are memory-efficient (listpack) List LPUSH RPUSH LPOP RPOP LRANGE BLPOP queues, recent-items Set SADD SISMEMBER SMEMBERS SINTER membership (roles of a user), tags Sorted set ZADD ZRANGE ZRANGEBYSCORE ZRANK ZINCRBY leaderboards, rate limiters (sliding window by timestamp), scheduled jobs Stream XADD XREADGROUP XACK append-only log with consumer groups: event invalidation fan-out Bitmap / HyperLogLog SETBIT BITCOUNT / PFADD PFCOUNT feature flags per user, approximate distinct counts

Pipelining: send many commands without waiting for each reply; Redis processes them in order and returns all replies. Removes the per-command round trip (the dominant cost): 10,000 GETs pipelined take milliseconds instead of seconds. Not atomic. MULTI/EXEC queues commands and executes them atomically (no interleaving) but without rollback; WATCH gives optimistic check-and-set. Lua scripts (EVAL) run atomically on the server and are the way to express "read, decide, write" safely.

docs.title: 2.8 Persistence: RDB and AOF
docs.text:
A cache does not strictly need persistence, but a cold restart of a large cache is itself an outage (stampede), and Redis is often used for sessions and queues too.

  • RDB: a point-in-time snapshot file (dump.rdb) written by a forked child process (BGSAVE), using the OS's copy-on-write so the parent keeps serving; triggered by save <seconds> <changes> rules. Compact, fast to load, loses everything since the last snapshot. The fork of a 30 GB instance can take hundreds of milliseconds and double memory under heavy writes (every page written by the parent is copied).
  • AOF (append-only file): every write command appended to a log; appendfsync always (durable, slow), everysec (default when enabled: at most one second lost), no (OS decides). The file is rewritten compactly in the background (BGREWRITEAOF); since 7.0 as a multi-part base + incremental files. Slower restarts, better durability.
  • Both can be on (recommended for anything that is not a pure cache); on restart AOF wins. Neither makes Redis a database with transactions and constraints; for money, write to PostgreSQL and cache in Redis.

Replication is asynchronous (replicas may lag; a failover can lose acknowledged writes); Sentinel provides monitoring and automatic failover for a primary/replica set; Redis Cluster shards keys over 16384 slots across primaries each with replicas, with multi-key commands restricted to one slot (hash tags {user:42}:... to co-locate keys).

docs.title: 2.9 Redis as a lock, and why Redlock is debated
docs.text:
The simple lock: SET lock:resource <random-token> NX PX 30000. Acquire succeeds only if the key did not exist; the TTL bounds the lock if the holder dies. Release with a Lua script that deletes only if the value equals your token (so you never delete someone else's lock after your TTL expired). This is fine for efficiency (avoid duplicate work, like stampede protection) and wrong for correctness (mutual exclusion that money depends on), because:

  1. The holder can be paused (GC, VM stall, network partition) past the TTL; the lock expires; another client acquires it; the first resumes and writes, believing it still holds the lock.
  2. With a single Redis, the lock is lost on failover (asynchronous replication): two holders.

Redlock (Antirez's algorithm) acquires the lock on a majority of N independent Redis instances within a time budget and uses the remaining validity time. Martin Kleppmann's 2016 critique: it still depends on bounded clock drift and on the holder not pausing, which a distributed lock cannot assume, and it lacks a fencing token: a monotonically increasing number issued with each lock grant that the protected resource (the database) checks, rejecting writes carrying an older token. The practical conclusion: for correctness, use the database's own locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, advisory locks, unique constraints, or a version column compare-and-set) and let the Redis lock be an optimisation; or use a consensus system (ZooKeeper, etcd, or a Raft-backed store) that issues fencing tokens. Say both sides; interviewers want to hear that you know the lock can be held twice.

docs.title: 2.10 Your design: in-process caching removing master-table joins
docs.text:
The login and transaction paths joined every request to master tables (branches, loan_products, roles, workflow_states, document_kinds): small, almost static, read on every call. Removing those joins by caching them in the C server is right, and here is the version that survives review:

  • What to cache: tables under a few thousand rows that change by administrative action, never per transaction. Keep the join in SQL for anything else (customers, applications).
  • Shape: per table, a hash map from natural key to a decoded struct, built at startup with one SELECT each (not per row), swapped atomically (build a new map, then replace the pointer under a mutex or with an atomic pointer; readers never see a half-built map; see 04_Concurrency for RCU-style swaps).
  • Invalidation: a cache_versions(table_name, version bigint) row bumped by a trigger on each master table; the server polls it every second (one indexed read) or LISTENs to a NOTIFY master_changed from the same trigger, and reloads only the changed table. TTL of a few minutes as a safety net. This catches DBA edits that bypass the application.
  • Consistency boundary: the cached data is used for authorisation and validation decisions, so a stale copy for up to a second after an admin change is acceptable and documented; anything that must be exact at the instant (a product's rate at approval time) is read inside the approving transaction from the database, and the approved rate is stored on the application row.
  • Multi-server: each server instance polls or listens independently; no cross-server coordination needed because the database is the source of truth.
  • Measurement: pg_stat_statements before/after showed the master-table reads disappearing from the top of calls, and p50 latency of the affected RPCs dropping by the round trips saved (have your own numbers ready).
  • What Redis would add: nothing for this data; it would reintroduce a network hop for data that fits in a few MB per process. Redis enters the design for sessions, rate limiting of login attempts (INCR + EXPIRE per user code), and anything shared across servers.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m13_cache_aside.py (Python 3, pip install redis psycopg[binary]) implements cache-aside with stampede protection against your WSL PostgreSQL and the docker Redis:

def get_branch(code: str) -> dict | None:
    key = f"branch:v{VERSION}:{code}"
    raw = r.get(key)
    if raw is not None:
        return None if raw == b"__NONE__" else json.loads(raw)      # negative cache for missing codes
    lock = r.set(f"lock:{key}", TOKEN, nx=True, px=2000)             # single flight across processes
    if not lock:
        time.sleep(0.02)                                              # a loser: brief wait then retry (bounded)
        return get_branch(code) if _retries_left() else load_from_db(code)
    try:
        row = load_from_db(code)                                      # the expensive part, done once
        ttl = int(TTL * random.uniform(0.9, 1.1))                     # jitter against synchronised expiry
        r.set(key, json.dumps(row) if row else b"__NONE__", ex=ttl if row else 30)
        return row
    finally:
        release_if_owner(f"lock:{key}", TOKEN)                        # Lua: DEL only if value == TOKEN

def update_branch(code: str, **fields):
    with pg.transaction():
        pg.execute("UPDATE branches SET ... WHERE code = %s", ...)
    r.delete(f"branch:v{VERSION}:{code}")                             # delete, never set, after commit

code/m13_redis_cli_demo.sh shows the primitives from the shell: SET NX PX, the owner-checked release script, pipelining with --pipe, SCAN versus KEYS, INFO persistence, and a MULTI/EXEC counter with WATCH. The owner-checked release:

-- release.lua: atomic compare-and-delete; never delete a lock you no longer hold
if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
    return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
else
    return 0
end

redis-cli SET lock:branch:BR0001 token123 NX PX 5000
redis-cli EVAL "$(cat release.lua)" 1 lock:branch:BR0001 token123
# pipelining: 100k SETs in one stream
seq 1 100000 | awk '{print "SET k:"$1" v"$1}' | redis-cli --pipe

And the PostgreSQL side of the invalidation signal used by the in-process cache:

CREATE TABLE cache_versions (table_name text PRIMARY KEY, version bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 1, bumped_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION trg_bump_cache_version() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO cache_versions (table_name) VALUES (TG_TABLE_NAME)
    ON CONFLICT (table_name) DO UPDATE SET version = cache_versions.version + 1, bumped_at = now();
    PERFORM pg_notify('master_changed', TG_TABLE_NAME);              -- delivered at COMMIT, to LISTENing sessions
    RETURN NULL;
END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER branches_bump AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON branches
    FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION trg_bump_cache_version();      -- statement-level: one bump per statement

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why single-threaded is fast. Every Redis operation touches a few cache lines in a hash table (dict, incremental rehashing to avoid pauses) and the cost is dominated by the socket syscalls, not the data structure. One thread with epoll_wait over thousands of sockets, batching reads and writes per event-loop iteration, achieves high throughput without any locking or cache-line contention between cores. The I/O threads in 6.0+ exist because read()/write() syscalls and protocol parsing became the bottleneck, not the command execution. Memory allocation uses jemalloc to limit fragmentation (INFO memory shows mem_fragmentation_ratio; above 1.5 is a problem).

Encodings. Small hashes, sets and sorted sets are stored as compact listpacks (contiguous bytes, O(n) operations but n is small and cache-friendly) and converted to hash tables or skip lists above hash-max-listpack-entries (128) etc. A hash with 100 fields costs far less memory than 100 strings. Sorted sets are a skip list plus a hash (O(log n) by score, O(1) by member).

Expiry and memory accounting. Keys with TTL are also indexed in an expires dict. The active expiry cycle runs in the serverCron timer and is bounded in CPU time per cycle; a huge number of keys expiring in the same second causes expiry work to lag and memory to overshoot, which is another reason for TTL jitter. Eviction under maxmemory samples maxmemory-samples (5) keys and evicts the best candidate: approximate LRU/LFU, with an LRU clock per key of 24 bits.

Fork and copy-on-write. BGSAVE and AOF rewrite fork the process; the child walks the data structures and writes the file while the parent serves. Linux shares pages until written; on a write-heavy instance the parent dirties pages and the kernel copies them (4 KB each), so memory grows during the snapshot (INFO persistence: rdb_last_cow_size). Transparent Huge Pages make this far worse (2 MB copies); disable THP on Redis hosts. The fork itself must copy page tables, which for a 50 GB instance is tens to hundreds of milliseconds of pause.

Pub/Sub and Streams semantics. Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget: a subscriber that is disconnected misses messages, so it is fine for "please invalidate" (the subscriber reloads on reconnect anyway) and wrong for anything that must be processed. Streams persist entries and track consumer-group offsets (XACK, pending entries list), giving at-least-once delivery.

PostgreSQL NOTIFY internals. Notifications are queued in a shared-memory SLRU queue at commit and delivered to listening backends, which forward them to clients between statements (libpq PQnotifies() after PQconsumeInput()). Payload up to 8000 bytes; the queue has a size limit (8 GB by default) and a listener that never reads blocks it for everyone (pg_notification_queue_usage()). It is a notification, not a message bus: a disconnected listener misses events, which is why the version row exists as the authoritative signal and NOTIFY is only the wake-up.

Atomic pointer swap for the in-process cache. Build the new map in the loader thread, then std::atomic<Map*>::store(new_map, std::memory_order_release); readers load(acquire) and use the map for the duration of a request. Freeing the old map must wait until no reader uses it: shared_ptr with std::atomic_load/atomic_store (or std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> in C++20) gives this for free at the cost of a refcount increment per read; hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation avoid even that. See 04_Concurrency.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Cache hit ratio is the first metric: INFO stats keyspace_hits / (hits + misses). Under 90% for a read cache means the TTL is too short, the key space too large for maxmemory, or the access pattern is not cacheable.
  • Big keys and hot keys: redis-cli --bigkeys, --hotkeys (with LFU). A 50 MB hash read on every request saturates the network and blocks the event loop; split it or move it in-process.
  • Redis down must not take the application down. Timeouts of tens of milliseconds, a circuit breaker that falls back to the database (and alerts, because the database is now taking the full load and may not survive it: capacity plan the database for a cache outage, or at least for a cache cold start with stampede protection).
  • Never KEYS * or FLUSHALL in production. Rename or disable dangerous commands (rename-command FLUSHALL "").
  • Memory limits: set maxmemory and an eviction policy; without them Redis grows until the OOM killer picks it or the host swaps (and swapping Redis is a slow-motion outage).
  • Persistence on a cache host can still be wanted to avoid a cold start; put RDB on a disk that can absorb the snapshot write, and watch rdb_last_bgsave_status.
  • Serialisation format matters: JSON is convenient and slow; protobuf/msgpack halve the bytes and the CPU. Version the format in the key (v2:) so a deploy that changes the struct does not read garbage from old entries.
  • The login brute-force limiter: INCR login_fail:{branch}:{user} + EXPIRE 900 on failure, check before the DB lookup; this moved the lockout counter off the database row (which was a non-HOT update per failed attempt on an indexed column, module 03) into Redis, with the database remaining the record of the final lock state.
  • 3 AM: database CPU spikes every 15 minutes exactly. A batch of cache keys all have the same 15-minute TTL and expire together; the herd rebuilds them. Add jitter and single-flight; the graph flattens.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Start Redis from code/docker-compose.yml, run code/m13_redis_cli_demo.sh. Done when you can explain each command's output, including why the second SET NX fails.
  2. (easy) Run code/m13_cache_aside.py against the loan schema; call get_branch 1000 times and read INFO stats hits/misses; update a branch and show the next read misses once. Done when hit ratio and the single invalidation are visible.
  3. (medium) Simulate a stampede: delete a hot key and fire 200 concurrent get_branch calls (threads or xargs -P). Count DB queries with pg_stat_statements with and without the lock. Done when the locked version shows 1 (or a handful) of DB loads versus ~200.
  4. (medium) Implement the cache_versions trigger and a LISTEN master_changed loop in a small libpq C program that reloads a branches map on notification. Update a branch from psql and watch the reload. Then kill and restart the listener and show the version row lets it detect what it missed. Done when both paths work.
  5. (hard) Demonstrate the double-holder problem: two processes take the Redis lock with a 2 s TTL; pause the holder with kill -STOP for 3 s; the second acquires; kill -CONT the first and let it write. Then add a fencing token (a PostgreSQL sequence value taken with the lock and checked in the UPDATE ... WHERE token >= $1) and show the stale writer is rejected. Done when you can explain why the database check, not Redis, provided correctness.
  6. (hard) Design the Redis layout for sessions (hash per session with TTL), per-user rate limiting (sorted set sliding window or fixed window counter), and event fan-out (stream with a consumer group per server) for the banking server. Write the commands and the failure analysis for Redis restart, replica failover, and a slow consumer. Done when each failure has a stated consequence and mitigation.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Explain cache-aside and its main race. A: On read, check the cache; on miss, read the database and populate the cache with a TTL. On write, update the database and delete the cache key so the next reader fetches fresh data. The race is a reader that read the old database value before a write, then populates the cache after the writer's delete, leaving a stale entry until TTL; mitigations are short TTLs, versioned keys, or lease-based population.

Q: Why delete rather than update the cache on write? A: Two concurrent writers can apply their cache updates in the opposite order to their database writes, leaving the cache permanently wrong. Deleting forces the next read to fetch the truth; it costs one extra miss and is immune to that reordering.

Q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it? A: Many requests miss the same expired hot key simultaneously and all hit the database with the same expensive query. Prevent it with single-flight (one loader per key, others wait or serve stale, using an in-process mutex or a Redis SET NX lock), serving stale while revalidating, probabilistic early refresh, TTL jitter, and warm-up before taking traffic.

Q: How does Redis achieve high throughput with one thread? A: Every command is a few cache-line touches in a hash table; the cost is socket I/O, which an epoll event loop batches across thousands of connections without locks or cross-core contention. I/O threads since 6.0 parallelise reading and writing sockets; command execution stays single threaded and atomic. The price is that one slow command blocks everyone, so you avoid KEYS, huge collections and long scripts, and shard for more CPU.

Q: RDB versus AOF? A: RDB is a forked point-in-time snapshot: compact, fast to load, loses everything since the last save, and the fork costs memory via copy-on-write under writes. AOF logs every write with fsync policies from always to every second: better durability, larger files, slower restart, periodic rewrite. Use both for anything beyond a pure cache, and neither makes Redis a transactional system of record.

Q: Is a Redis lock safe? A: Safe for efficiency, not for correctness. A holder paused past the TTL or a failover of an asynchronously replicated primary can produce two holders. Redlock reduces the single-node problem but still assumes bounded clock drift and no long pauses and provides no fencing token. For correctness, the protected resource must check a monotonically increasing token, or you use the database's own locks and constraints.

Q: Describe your in-memory caching of master tables. A: Small, administratively changed reference tables such as branches, products, roles and workflow states were loaded once per server into hash maps keyed by natural key and swapped atomically on reload, removing their joins from every request. Invalidation came from a version row bumped by triggers and a NOTIFY wake-up, with a TTL safety net, so DBA edits were caught too. Values that had to be exact at a decision point, like the rate at approval, were read inside the transaction and stored on the row. Redis was reserved for shared state such as sessions and login rate limits.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Cache-aside: read-miss populate, write-then-delete; write-through and write-behind trade durability and latency differently.
  • TTL with jitter; versioned key namespaces for mass invalidation; event or version-row driven invalidation catches out-of-band writes.
  • Stampede defences: single-flight locks, stale-while-revalidate, probabilistic early expiry, warm-up.
  • Caches hold entities, not snapshots; anything you cannot rebuild from the database is not a cache.
  • In-process for small hot reference data; Redis for shared state across processes.
  • Redis: single-threaded command execution over epoll, atomic commands, pipelining removes round trips, Lua for read-decide-write.
  • Data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams; small collections use compact encodings.
  • Persistence: RDB fork snapshot (COW cost), AOF with fsync policy; replication async; Sentinel and Cluster.
  • Redis locks are for efficiency; correctness needs fencing tokens or database locks.
  • Master-table cache: load whole tables, swap atomically, invalidate by version row + NOTIFY, read exact values in-transaction.

docs.title: 14. Performance tuning and operations
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 04, 05, 06

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Modules 01 to 13 explained what the database does with one statement. This module is about keeping a real server healthy while thousands of statements arrive per second, for years: how many connections it can take, how much memory each part gets, how you find the query that is hurting everybody, how dead rows get cleaned up, how you get the data back after a disk dies, and how a second server takes over when the first one goes away.

The analogy is running a bank branch rather than serving one customer. You decide how many counters are open (connections and pooling), how big the filing cabinets on the desks are (memory settings), you watch the queue and ask who is taking so long (monitoring), you send the cleaners in at the right time (VACUUM), you photocopy the ledgers every night and keep the receipts in between (backups and WAL archiving), and you keep a second branch across the road that copies every entry and can open its doors if this one floods (replication and failover).

For an interview this is where "I have used PostgreSQL" becomes "I have run PostgreSQL". The questions are concrete: what does pgbouncer's transaction mode break, how do you size work_mem, why did VACUUM not remove anything, what is your RPO, and what does Oracle call the thing PostgreSQL calls a schema.

docs.title: 2.1 Connections and pooling
docs.text:
PostgreSQL forks one backend process per connection (module 01). Each backend costs memory (typically a few MB of private memory, more once it has touched many catalog entries and cached plans), a slot in the shared ProcArray that every snapshot scans, and lock-table entries. Hundreds of mostly idle connections are therefore not free: snapshot creation gets slower as max_connections grows, and a burst where all of them become active at once oversubscribes the CPUs and makes everything slower, not faster.

The fix is a connection pooler: many client connections share a small number of server connections. pgbouncer is the standard one: a single-threaded, event-driven proxy (the same design as Redis, module 13) that speaks the PostgreSQL protocol on both sides.

Pool mode A server connection is assigned to a client... What breaks Use session for the whole client session nothing; but no multiplexing gain for long sessions legacy apps, tools like psql transaction for one transaction, returned at COMMIT/ROLLBACK any session state: SET (non-LOCAL), session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables kept across transactions, WITH HOLD cursors, protocol-level prepared statements unless pgbouncer 1.21+ with max_prepared_statements set the default for OLTP application servers statement for one statement; multi-statement transactions refused everything transactional rare; autocommit-only workloads

Transaction mode is what gives the large multiplexing gain: 2000 application threads that each spend most of their time outside a transaction can share 40 server connections. It also explains why idle in transaction is so harmful behind a pooler: that client holds a server connection (and a snapshot that blocks VACUUM) while doing nothing.

Sizing. The often-quoted starting point from the PostgreSQL wiki is roughly connections = (2 x CPU cores) + effective spindles of active connections; it is a rule of thumb to start measuring from, not a law. The real answer is the number at which throughput stops rising when you load-test with pgbench. For a 4-core server that is typically in the tens, not the hundreds. Set max_connections a little above the pool size plus admin headroom (superuser_reserved_connections, replication, monitoring).

Your RPC application server already has a connection pool inside the C process. pgbouncer still helps when there are many such processes (each with its own pool), when they run on several machines, or when a deployment restarts them all at once and they reconnect in a storm.

docs.title: 2.2 Memory and WAL settings
docs.text:
The settings that matter, with starting points for a dedicated 16 GB RAM, 4-core, SSD OLTP server. These are conventional starting values used in the community (pgtune-style), not measured optima: change one at a time and measure with the queries in section 3.

Setting What it controls Starting point Notes shared_buffers PostgreSQL's own page cache (module 02) 4GB (~25% of RAM) the OS page cache holds much of the rest; more is not always better (double buffering, checkpoint volume) effective_cache_size the planner's assumption of total cache (shared + OS) 12GB (~75%) allocates nothing; makes index scans look cheaper work_mem per sort/hash node per backend before spilling to temp files 16MB to 64MB multiply by connections x nodes per query; raise per role or per session for reports maintenance_work_mem VACUUM, CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE ADD FK 1GB big index builds and vacuums go faster autovacuum_work_mem dead-tuple memory per autovacuum worker -1 (uses maintenance_work_mem) in 16, at most 1GB is used for the dead-TID array wal_buffers WAL in shared memory before write -1 (auto, 1/32 of shared_buffers, max 16MB) rarely touched max_wal_size WAL between checkpoints before one is forced 4GB to 16GB too small: checkpoints_req dominates, many FPIs (module 04) checkpoint_timeout time between checkpoints 15min longer: fewer FPIs, longer crash recovery checkpoint_completion_target spread checkpoint writes over this fraction 0.9 (default since 14) smooths I/O synchronous_commit wait for WAL flush (and standbys) at commit on off per session for bulk loads: lose at most ~3 x wal_writer_delay of commits on crash, never corruption wal_compression compress full-page images lz4 (or zstd) cuts WAL volume; costs some CPU random_page_cost planner's cost of a random page read 1.1 on SSD (default 4) the default models spinning disks effective_io_concurrency prefetch depth for bitmap heap scans 200 on SSD huge_pages 2 MB pages for shared memory try fewer TLB misses with big shared_buffers (needs OS config) statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout guard rails per role: e.g. 30s, 5s, 60s set on the application role, not globally (it would kill maintenance jobs)

Settings live in postgresql.conf, can be overridden by ALTER SYSTEM (written to postgresql.auto.conf), per database or role (ALTER ROLE loans_app SET work_mem = '32MB'), per session (SET), or per transaction (SET LOCAL). SELECT name, setting, source FROM pg_settings shows which one won. Some need a restart (shared_buffers, max_connections, shared_preload_libraries, wal_level); most need only SELECT pg_reload_conf(); pg_settings.context says which.

docs.title: 2.3 Finding the problem: the observability toolkit
docs.text:
pg_stat_statements (module 06) aggregates every statement by its normalised text (constants replaced by $1): calls, total and mean time, rows, buffers hit and read, temp blocks, WAL bytes. It answers "what is the server spending its time on" and is the first query in every incident. It needs shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements' and a restart.

pg_stat_activity is one row per backend now: state (active, idle, idle in transaction), wait_event_type/wait_event (what it is blocked on: Lock, LWLock, IO, Client), xact_start, query_start, backend_xmin (the snapshot that holds the VACUUM horizon), and the current query text. Sample it every few seconds and you have a poor man's active-session history (Oracle's ASH, section 2.8).

pg_locks is the lock table: one row per held or awaited lock, with granted. Join it to pg_stat_activity, or use pg_blocking_pids(pid) to get the blockers of a waiting backend directly. Row locks appear as waits on a transactionid, because a row lock lives in the tuple's xmax (module 05).

The slow query log writes to the server log (on Ubuntu, /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-16-main.log):

log_min_duration_statement = 250ms     # every statement slower than this, with its duration
log_lock_waits = on                    # any lock wait longer than deadlock_timeout (1s)
log_temp_files = 0                     # every temp file (sorts and hashes spilling)
log_checkpoints = on                   # default on since 15: duration, buffers written, why
log_autovacuum_min_duration = 1s       # autovacuum runs that took longer than this
auto_explain.log_min_duration = 500ms  # the PLAN of slow statements (module 06)
log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d %a ' # time, pid, user, database, application_name

pgBadger turns that log into an HTML report. Set application_name in every client's connection string (your C server: application_name=rpcsrv-node3) so you can tell callers apart.

Cumulative statistics views for trends: pg_stat_user_tables (seq vs index scans, dead tuples, last vacuum), pg_stat_user_indexes (unused indexes), pg_stat_database (commits, rollbacks, deadlocks, temp bytes), pg_stat_bgwriter (checkpoints), pg_stat_wal, pg_stat_replication, pg_stat_progress_vacuum / _create_index / _basebackup. Export them to Prometheus with postgres_exporter and graph rates, not raw counters.

docs.title: 2.4 VACUUM tuning
docs.text:
Module 05 explained why VACUUM exists. Operations is about making it keep up.

When autovacuum starts on a table: n_dead_tup > autovacuum_vacuum_threshold (50) + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (0.2) x reltuples. For app_users with 2 M rows that is 400,050 dead tuples; for a 100 M row table, 20 M. Hot tables need per-table settings:

ALTER TABLE loans.app_users SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01,     -- 1%: ~20k dead rows
                                 autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 1000,
                                 autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.02);
-- Insert-only tables (audit, archive) never get dead tuples; since 13, inserts also trigger
-- vacuum (autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor) so their visibility map and freezing keep up.
ALTER TABLE loans.application_audit SET (autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor = 0.05);

How fast it runs: autovacuum is throttled by a cost budget. Each page hit, miss and dirtied costs points (vacuum_cost_page_hit 1, _miss 2 in 16, _dirty 20); after autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit points (default 200, shared by all workers) it sleeps autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay (2 ms). On modern SSDs the default budget is often too low for a busy system: raising the limit to 1000 to 2000 is the usual first step. autovacuum_max_workers (3) is how many tables are vacuumed at once; more workers share the same cost limit, so raise the limit together with the workers.

What stops VACUUM from removing rows (the "horizon"): the oldest snapshot anywhere. Culprits, in the order you check them: a long or idle in transaction session (pg_stat_activity.backend_xmin), a replication slot that is behind (pg_replication_slots), a hot standby with hot_standby_feedback = on running a long query, an orphaned prepared transaction (pg_prepared_xacts). VACUUM (VERBOSE) prints "N dead row versions cannot be removed yet, oldest xmin: X".

Freezing and wraparound. Transaction ids are 32-bit; tuples older than vacuum_freeze_min_age get frozen so their xid can be reused. Any table whose relfrozenxid age passes autovacuum_freeze_max_age (200 M) gets an aggressive anti-wraparound vacuum that cannot be cancelled by lock conflicts. If ages still approach about 2 billion, the server refuses new xids to protect data. Monitor age(datfrozenxid) (section 3) and alert far below that.

Bloat that VACUUM cannot fix. VACUUM makes space reusable inside the file; it does not shrink it (except trailing empty pages). After a mass delete, VACUUM FULL rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock (an outage); pg_repack does the same online with a trigger-based copy. Indexes: REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY (module 03).

docs.title: 2.5 Backups
docs.text:
Two kinds, with different purposes:

Logical: pg_dump / pg_restore Physical: pg_basebackup + WAL archive What SQL-level dump of one database: DDL + data a copy of the whole cluster's data directory files Consistency one REPEATABLE READ snapshot (module 05) fuzzy copy made consistent by replaying WAL from the backup's start LSN (module 04) Point-in-time recovery no: only the moment of the dump yes, to any moment covered by archived WAL Portability across major versions and architectures; selective (-t, -n) same major version and platform only Speed at scale slow to restore (rebuilds every index) restore = copy files + replay Use upgrades, copying a schema, small databases, extra safety net the real backup of a production cluster 
# Logical: custom (-Fc) or directory (-Fd) format allows parallel and selective restore
pg_dump -d loans -Fd -j 4 -f /backup/loans_$(date +%F)
pg_restore -d loans_restore -j 4 /backup/loans_2026-10-12
pg_dumpall --globals-only > /backup/globals.sql     # roles and tablespaces are not in pg_dump

# Physical base backup, streaming the WAL needed to make it consistent
pg_basebackup -h localhost -U replicator -D /backup/base_$(date +%F) -Ft -z -X stream -P

PITR needs continuous WAL archiving: archive_mode = on and an archive_command (or archive_library) that copies every completed 16 MB WAL segment somewhere safe. Restore = base backup + restore_command + recovery_target_time (module 04 exercise 5). In production use a tool that does archiving, retention, parallelism, compression, encryption and verification: pgBackRest or Barman (WAL-G in cloud setups). Two numbers define the design: RPO (how much data you may lose: the archive lag, or zero with synchronous replication) and RTO (how long recovery may take: base backup size / restore speed + WAL replay time). A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup: schedule restore tests.

docs.title: 2.6 Replication
docs.text:
Streaming (physical) replication. A standby connects to the primary with the replication protocol, receives the WAL byte stream as it is written (walsender on the primary, walreceiver on the standby), and replays it continuously with the same redo code as crash recovery. The standby is a byte-identical copy of the whole cluster and serves read-only queries (hot standby). Key settings and facts:

  • wal_level = replica (default), max_wal_senders, a role with REPLICATION, a pg_hba.conf line for replication.
  • Asynchronous by default: the primary commits without waiting; a crash of the primary can lose the last transactions not yet received (RPO = replication lag, usually milliseconds to seconds). Synchronous: synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 1 (s1, s2)' or 'ANY 1 (...)' and synchronous_commit = on (flush on standby) / remote_apply (visible on standby) / remote_write. Commit latency now includes a network round trip; if every synchronous standby is down, commits wait.
  • Replication slots make the primary keep WAL until the standby has it, so a disconnected standby can catch up instead of needing a rebuild; the price is that a dead standby makes WAL pile up until the disk is full. max_slot_wal_keep_size caps it.
  • Conflicts on the standby: replaying a VACUUM that removes rows a standby query still needs cancels that query (canceling statement due to conflict with recovery) after max_standby_streaming_delay. hot_standby_feedback = on stops the cancellations by holding back VACUUM on the primary (bloat). Pick which pain you prefer, per standby.
  • Lag: pg_stat_replication on the primary (write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag), and pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() on the standby.

Logical replication. The primary decodes WAL into row changes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE per table) with the pgoutput plugin and sends them to subscribers, which apply them as ordinary SQL writes. CREATE PUBLICATION on the source, CREATE SUBSCRIPTION on the target.

Physical streaming Logical Unit WAL bytes, whole cluster row changes, chosen tables Target read-only identical copy writable database with its own indexes and extra tables Versions same major version across major versions (upgrades with near-zero downtime) Not replicated nothing DDL, sequence values (sync them by hand at cutover), large objects; tables need a primary key or REPLICA IDENTITY for UPDATE/DELETE Use HA, read scaling, backups from standby upgrades, CDC, consolidating or splitting databases, feeding analytics

Logical decoding is also how change data capture tools (Debezium) stream PostgreSQL changes to Kafka. That is the "CDC" row of module 12's cutover table, when the source is PostgreSQL.

docs.title: 2.7 Failover and high availability
docs.text:
Replication gives you a copy; failover is the decision and mechanics of making the copy the primary. PostgreSQL itself only provides the mechanics (pg_promote(), pg_ctl promote, timelines, pg_rewind); the decision needs an external manager.

  • Detection and decision: Patroni is the common choice. Each node runs an agent that holds a leader key with a TTL in a distributed configuration store (etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper). The primary's agent renews the key; if it stops (node dead, network partition), a standby's agent acquires the key, promotes its PostgreSQL, and the others re-point to it. The consensus store is what prevents two primaries: only the key holder may be primary, and a primary that cannot renew the key demotes itself.
  • Split brain is the failure to prevent: two nodes accepting writes. Defences are the leader lock above, fencing (the old primary is stopped or isolated before promotion, the "STONITH" idea), and synchronous replication so no acknowledged commit exists only on the old primary.
  • Timelines: every promotion starts a new timeline id; WAL from the old timeline after the fork point is not valid on the new one. The old primary rejoins as a standby after pg_rewind rewinds its divergent pages (needs wal_log_hints = on or data checksums).
  • Routing clients to the primary: a virtual IP, HAProxy health-checking Patroni's REST API, or libpq multi-host connection strings: host=pg1,pg2,pg3 target_session_attrs=read-write (libpq tries each host until it finds a writable one). Your C server's reconnect logic must treat a failover as "connection lost, retry the transaction" (the same retry loop as 40001).
  • What async failover costs: with asynchronous replication, the promoted standby may be missing the last few acknowledged commits. Either accept a small RPO (and say it out loud), or pay commit latency for synchronous replication to at least one standby.

Contrast with YugabyteDB (module 11): every tablet is a Raft group; a leader's failure triggers an election among the tablet's replicas within seconds, automatically, and a write is acknowledged only after a majority has it, so RPO is zero for a single-node loss with no external manager. PostgreSQL HA is assembled from parts; distributed SQL has it built in, and pays for it with consensus latency on every write.

docs.title: 2.8 Oracle, SQL Server and PostgreSQL: an honest comparison
docs.text:
Your resume lists Oracle and SQL Server. In an interview, the safe and senior position is precise knowledge of the differences that change application behaviour, and honesty about the depth of your hands-on use. The table is what you should be able to say without notes.

Terminology and architecture

Concept Oracle SQL Server PostgreSQL Server process model one instance = shared memory (SGA) + background processes; dedicated or shared server processes one process, many threads (SQLOS scheduler) postmaster + one process per connection "Database" the whole set of files; one database per instance traditionally, PDBs inside a CDB since 12c many databases per instance many databases per cluster; no cross-database queries without extensions "Schema" = a user's namespace (user and schema are the same object) namespace inside a database (dbo) namespace inside a database, independent of users Old row versions for readers undo segments; current row in the block, old versions rebuilt from undo (ORA-01555 "snapshot too old") locks by default; with RCSI/SNAPSHOT, row versions in the tempdb version store (or in the user database with Accelerated Database Recovery, 2019+) all versions in the heap itself; VACUUM removes dead ones (module 05) Write-ahead log redo log (online + archived) transaction log (.ldf) WAL (pg_wal) Table organisation heap by default; index-organised tables (IOT) optional usually a clustered index (the table is the B-tree on its key) heap always; CLUSTER reorders once and is not maintained Auto ids sequences; identity columns since 12c IDENTITY; sequences since 2012 GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY over sequences Empty string '' is NULL '' is not NULL '' is not NULL Optimiser hints yes, /*+ INDEX(t idx) */ widely used yes, table hints and OPTION (...); Query Store plan forcing none in core (extension pg_hint_plan) Plans for parameters bind peeking, adaptive cursor sharing plan cache with parameter sniffing (a classic SQL Server incident) custom vs generic plans after 5 executions (module 06) Plan and wait analysis EXPLAIN PLAN, DBMS_XPLAN, AWR / ASH reports actual execution plan, DMVs (sys.dm_exec_query_stats), Query Store EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), pg_stat_statements, pg_stat_activity HA Data Guard (standby), RAC (shared-disk active-active) Always On availability groups, failover cluster instances streaming replication + Patroni Backup RMAN full / differential / log backups pg_basebackup + WAL archive (pgBackRest)

Isolation and concurrency

Oracle SQL Server PostgreSQL Default level READ COMMITTED, with statement-level read consistency from undo READ COMMITTED with shared locks (on-premises default; RCSI is a database option, on by default in Azure SQL Database) READ COMMITTED with a new MVCC snapshot per statement Do readers block writers? no yes under the locking default; no with RCSI no Levels offered READ COMMITTED, SERIALIZABLE (and READ ONLY) READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SNAPSHOT, SERIALIZABLE READ UNCOMMITTED (behaves as RC), READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE What "SERIALIZABLE" really is snapshot isolation: write skew is possible; conflicts raise ORA-08177 true serializable through key-range locks (blocking, deadlock-prone) SSI: snapshot isolation plus dependency tracking; aborts with 40001 instead of blocking (module 05) Snapshot isolation by name (that is its SERIALIZABLE) SNAPSHOT (needs ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION) REPEATABLE READ Deadlock victim error ORA-00060 1205 40P01 Lock escalation none (row locks live in the block) row/page locks escalate to table locks past thresholds none (row locks live in the tuple's xmax)

YugabyteDB YSQL (module 11) supports SERIALIZABLE, REPEATABLE READ (snapshot) and READ COMMITTED, and its default behaves as snapshot isolation unless read-committed support is enabled by a flag; check the version you run before you promise anything.

Procedural languages: PL/SQL, T-SQL, PL/pgSQL

PL/SQL (Oracle) T-SQL (SQL Server) PL/pgSQL (PostgreSQL) Structure blocks; packages (spec + body, package state per session) batches and procedures; no packages functions and procedures; schemas as namespaces, no packages Error handling EXCEPTION WHEN ... THEN; RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20001, ...) BEGIN TRY ... END TRY BEGIN CATCH ... END CATCH, THROW, @@ERROR; SET XACT_ABORT ON to abort the transaction on any error EXCEPTION WHEN ... blocks are subtransactions (cost, module 08); RAISE ... USING ERRCODE Transaction control COMMIT in procedures; autonomous transactions (PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION) for logging that survives rollback COMMIT/ROLLBACK in procedures, nested BEGIN TRAN only counts (@@TRANCOUNT) COMMIT/ROLLBACK only in procedures called at top level; no autonomous transactions (dblink or a second connection) Bulk work BULK COLLECT, FORALL to cut context switches between PL/SQL and SQL engines set-based statements, table variables, #temp tables set-based SQL; RETURN QUERY; no bulk-bind syntax needed Temp tables global temporary tables (definition permanent, data per session) #local and ##global temp tables in tempdb session temp tables created at runtime (catalog churn if overused) Output to caller OUT params, ref cursors, pipelined table functions result sets returned directly from procedures, OUT params RETURNS TABLE / SETOF functions (materialised), OUT params, refcursors Upsert MERGE MERGE (with known race caveats) or UPDATE-then-INSERT with locking hints INSERT ... ON CONFLICT; MERGE since 15

The honest one-liner for an interview: "My deep, daily work is PostgreSQL and PL/pgSQL, and the YugabyteDB migration. I have worked with Oracle and SQL Server, and the differences I watch for when moving code between them are the default isolation and what SERIALIZABLE really means, undo versus heap versioning versus the tempdb version store, empty string as NULL in Oracle, parameter sniffing in SQL Server, and how error handling and transactions behave in PL/SQL, T-SQL and PL/pgSQL." Then answer at the depth you actually have.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m14_monitoring_queries.sql contains the fourteen queries of an incident runbook: settings, top statements, sessions, long transactions, blocking chains, locks, cache hit ratio, dead tuples, autovacuum thresholds and progress, wraparound age, unused indexes, checkpoints, WAL, replication and slots, and sizes. Run it as a whole once, then keep it open during incidents. The three you will use most:

-- What costs the server most (pg_stat_statements)
SELECT left(regexp_replace(query, '\s+', ' ', 'g'), 70) AS query, calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS total_ms, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 3) AS mean_ms,
       shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read AS blocks, rows / greatest(calls, 1) AS rows_per_call,
       temp_blks_written
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 15;

-- Who blocks whom: follow blocking_pid until you reach a session that is not blocked itself
SELECT blocked.pid AS blocked_pid, now() - blocked.query_start AS waiting_for,
       blocking.pid AS blocking_pid, blocking.state AS blocking_state,
       now() - blocking.xact_start AS blocking_xact_age, left(blocking.query, 50) AS blocking_query
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN LATERAL unnest(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) AS b(pid) ON true
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = b.pid;

-- What holds back VACUUM: the oldest snapshots
SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, backend_xmin, left(query, 60)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_xmin IS NOT NULL ORDER BY age(backend_xmin) DESC LIMIT 5;

pgbouncer in front of the WSL PostgreSQL (sudo apt install pgbouncer):

; /etc/pgbouncer/pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
loans = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=loans

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 127.0.0.1
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt
pool_mode = transaction
default_pool_size = 20          ; server connections per (database, user) pair
max_client_conn = 2000          ; client connections pgbouncer accepts
max_prepared_statements = 100   ; 1.21+: protocol-level prepared statements work in transaction mode
server_reset_query =            ; empty in transaction mode (DISCARD ALL is for session mode)

# load test: 200 clients through pgbouncer versus directly (pgbench ships with postgresql-contrib)
pgbench -i -s 20 loans_bench                         # in a separate database
pgbench -h 127.0.0.1 -p 6432 -c 200 -j 4 -T 60 -S loans_bench   # through the pooler
pgbench -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5432 -c 200 -j 4 -T 60 -S loans_bench   # direct (raise max_connections first)
psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 6432 -U $USER pgbouncer -c "SHOW POOLS;"    # cl_active, cl_waiting, sv_active, sv_idle

A streaming replica on the same WSL machine (port 5435; 5433 and 5434 are used by docker):

sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE ROLE replicator WITH REPLICATION LOGIN PASSWORD 'repl'"
echo "host replication replicator 127.0.0.1/32 scram-sha-256" | sudo tee -a /etc/postgresql/16/main/pg_hba.conf
sudo service postgresql reload
sudo pg_createcluster 16 replica --port 5435          # creates config and an empty data directory
sudo rm -rf /var/lib/postgresql/16/replica/*
sudo -u postgres env PGPASSWORD=repl pg_basebackup -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5432 -U replicator \
     -D /var/lib/postgresql/16/replica -R -X stream -C -S replica1 -P
#  -R writes standby.signal and primary_conninfo; -C -S creates and uses replication slot replica1
sudo pg_ctlcluster 16 replica start
psql -p 5432 -c "SELECT application_name, state, sync_state, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication"
psql -p 5435 loans -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(), count(*) FROM loans.branches"   # true, 500
# failover drill
sudo pg_ctlcluster 16 main stop
psql -p 5435 -c "SELECT pg_promote()"
psql -p 5435 -c "SELECT timeline_id FROM pg_control_checkpoint()"                  # 2: a new timeline

Logical replication of the master tables into a reporting database (needs wal_level = logical and a restart):

-- in database loans (publisher)
CREATE PUBLICATION pub_master FOR TABLE loans.branches, loans.loan_products, loans.workflow_states;
-- A subscription to a database in the SAME cluster must use a pre-created slot,
-- otherwise CREATE SUBSCRIPTION waits forever for its own transaction:
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('sub_master', 'pgoutput');

createdb loans_reporting
psql -d loans_reporting -c "CREATE SCHEMA loans"
pg_dump -d loans -s -t 'loans.branches' -t 'loans.loan_products' -t 'loans.workflow_states' \
    | psql -d loans_reporting                                   # DDL is not replicated: copy it first
# Two errors are expected: the cache-version triggers on branches and loan_products refer to a
# function that is not copied. The reporting side does not need them (apply workers do not fire
# ordinary triggers anyway).
psql -d loans_reporting -c "CREATE SUBSCRIPTION sub_master CONNECTION 'dbname=loans'
    PUBLICATION pub_master WITH (create_slot = false, slot_name = 'sub_master')"
psql -d loans -c "UPDATE loans.branches SET name = name || ' *' WHERE code = 'BR0007'"
psql -d loans_reporting -c "SELECT name FROM loans.branches WHERE code = 'BR0007'"   # changed

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why many connections slow down every query. Taking a snapshot (GetSnapshotData) means reading every backend's advertised xid from the shared ProcArray. PostgreSQL 14 made this much cheaper by keeping the xids in a dense array, but the cost still scales with the number of connected backends, and each backend also holds catalog and plan caches in private memory. Context switching between more runnable processes than cores adds latency without adding throughput. A pooler turns "2000 connections, 40 busy" into "40 connections, 40 busy", which is the shape the engine is good at.

pgbouncer's mechanics. One thread, libevent, a state machine per client and per server connection. In transaction mode it watches the ReadyForQuery message's transaction status byte (I idle, T in transaction, E failed): when it returns to I, the server connection goes back to the pool. That is exactly why session state leaks between clients in this mode: the server backend persists, so a SET search_path by client A is seen by client B's next transaction on the same backend. Use SET LOCAL, or set things per role.

shared_buffers versus the OS page cache. A page read by PostgreSQL usually exists twice: in shared_buffers and in the kernel's page cache (PostgreSQL uses buffered I/O, not O_DIRECT, in 16). The clock-sweep replacement in shared buffers protects frequently used pages; the kernel's LRU catches the rest. A huge shared_buffers reduces the useful OS cache, increases the dirty data each checkpoint must write, and makes the buffer mapping table bigger. That is why the conventional starting point is a quarter of RAM rather than most of it.

What a checkpoint costs, precisely. A checkpoint writes every dirty buffer, then fsyncs every touched file, then writes a checkpoint record. After it, the first modification of each page writes a full-page image to WAL (module 04). So frequent checkpoints cost twice: the write storm, and a WAL volume spike from FPIs. checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9 spreads the writes; a larger max_wal_size reduces the frequency; wal_compression shrinks the FPIs.

How streaming replication is wired. The standby's walreceiver connects with replication=true, sends START_REPLICATION SLOT replica1 PHYSICAL 0/3000000, and the primary starts a walsender that reads WAL from pg_wal (or memory) and streams XLogData messages. The standby writes them to its own pg_wal, flushes, and reports positions back (write/flush/apply LSNs), which is where pg_stat_replication's lag columns come from and what synchronous commit waits on. The startup process replays the WAL with the same redo functions used after a crash. Logical replication runs the same walsender but passes WAL through logical decoding, which reassembles each transaction's changes (spilling large ones to disk) and emits them at commit in commit order.

Backups without stopping writes. pg_basebackup calls pg_backup_start, which forces a checkpoint and records its redo LSN, then copies files while they change. The copy is inconsistent (torn pages are possible), and that is fine: recovery replays WAL from the recorded redo LSN, and full-page writes overwrite any torn page with an intact image (module 04). The backup is usable only together with the WAL from its start to its end, which is why -X stream or an archive is mandatory.

Autovacuum's scheduling. The launcher wakes every autovacuum_naptime (1 min) per database and starts workers up to autovacuum_max_workers; each worker picks tables over their thresholds from the statistics system. The cost budget is shared ("balanced") across active workers, so three workers each get a third of autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit unless a table has its own. Anti-wraparound vacuums ignore the lock-conflict cancellation that ordinary autovacuum yields to, which is how an ALTER TABLE can suddenly queue behind a vacuum you cannot cancel.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The connection storm. All application nodes restart after a deploy and each opens its full pool at once: max_connections reached, FATAL: sorry, too many clients already, and the health checks fail too. Fixes: pgbouncer in front, staggered restarts, pools that grow lazily, and superuser_reserved_connections so you can still log in.
  • work_mem out of memory. Someone set work_mem = 1GB globally to fix one report; under load the kernel's OOM killer kills a backend, the postmaster restarts all backends, everyone is disconnected. Set big values per role or per session only.
  • "The database is slow" at 3 AM, in order: pg_stat_activity (what is active, what waits on what), blocking chains, pg_stat_statements deltas since the last snapshot, the slow query log and auto_explain plans, then OS metrics (iostat -x, vmstat, disk full?). Write the timeline as you go; the post-mortem needs it.
  • Idle in transaction behind a pooler. One code path forgot to COMMIT before an RPC to another service. VACUUM stopped removing rows cluster-wide, tables bloated, queries slowed over days. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout on the application role turns this into an error in that one code path.
  • The replication slot that filled the disk. A decommissioned standby or a stopped CDC connector left its slot; WAL accumulated until the primary's disk filled and the primary stopped. Alert on pg_replication_slots retained WAL; set max_slot_wal_keep_size.
  • Backups that do not restore. The archive command returned success while writing to a full disk; nobody tested a restore for months. Use pgBackRest's check and verify, and restore a backup into a scratch server on a schedule.
  • Failover that lost data. Asynchronous replica promoted after the primary died with 2 seconds of lag: those acknowledged payments do not exist on the new primary. Either accept a documented RPO, or run synchronous replication to a standby in another rack and accept the latency. For a banking ledger, the second.
  • Major version upgrades. pg_upgrade --link takes minutes of downtime for any size (it reuses data files); logical replication to a new-version cluster then a switchover takes seconds of downtime but more preparation (DDL freeze, sequences, slots). Run ANALYZE after either, because planner statistics are not carried over by pg_upgrade in 16.
  • Mapping to your system: the RPC server's DB pool size per node x number of nodes must stay under the pooler's max_client_conn; login procedures from module 08 run in transaction mode without session state; the slow query log is where the login regression (module 06) would have shown up first; on YugabyteDB, failover is Raft's job but your client's retry loop is still yours.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Enable pg_stat_statements (README setup), run code/m06_slow_vs_fast_queries.sql, then section 1 of code/m14_monitoring_queries.sql. Done when you can name the top three statements by total time and explain from blocks versus rows_per_call which one lacks an index.
  2. (easy) Start two psql sessions; in one run BEGIN; UPDATE loans.accounts SET balance = balance WHERE id = 1; and leave it. In the other run sections 3, 4 and 5 of the monitoring file. Done when you can point at the idle in transaction session, its backend_xmin, and the lock rows, and end it with pg_terminate_backend.
  3. (medium) Install pgbouncer in transaction mode as in section 3 and run the two pgbench commands with -c 200. Done when you have both TPS numbers, the SHOW POOLS output, and can explain why SET search_path from one client leaks to another in this mode (show it).
  4. (medium) Take a pg_dump -Fd -j 4 of loans, restore it into loans_restore with pg_restore -j 4, and time both. Then create the streaming replica on port 5435, run m09_seed.sql on the primary while watching replay_lag, and promote the replica. Done when you have the restore time, a lag observation, and the new timeline id.
  5. (hard) Make autovacuum fall behind: run a pgbench custom script that updates failed_attempts on random app_users rows at full speed for 5 minutes with default settings, recording n_dead_tup every 30 s. Then apply the per-table settings from section 2.4 and raise autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit to 2000, and repeat. Done when you have two curves of dead tuples over time and can explain the difference with the trigger formula and the cost budget.
  6. (hard) Set up the logical replication of the master tables into loans_reporting, then use it to rehearse a "zero-downtime" cutover: add a publication for loan_applications too, let it catch up, stop writes on the source, check row counts and a parity sample with fn_parity_hash_loan on both sides, and write the five-line runbook you would use. Done when counts and hashes match and the runbook names the sequence-sync step.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why do you need pgbouncer, and what breaks in transaction mode? A: PostgreSQL runs a process per connection, so hundreds of mostly idle connections waste memory, slow snapshot creation and oversubscribe CPUs under bursts. pgbouncer multiplexes many client connections onto a small server pool. In transaction mode a server connection is handed back at every commit, so any session state breaks: session SETs, session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables across transactions, WITH HOLD cursors, and prepared statements unless pgbouncer 1.21+ with max_prepared_statements.

Q: How do you set shared_buffers and work_mem? A: shared_buffers is PostgreSQL's page cache; a quarter of RAM is the conventional start because the OS page cache holds the rest and very large values increase checkpoint work. work_mem is per sort or hash node per backend, so the worst case is connections times nodes times work_mem; keep the global value modest, raise it per role or session for reports, and watch temp_blks_written in pg_stat_statements and log_temp_files to see spills.

Q: VACUUM runs but dead tuples are not removed. Why? A: Something holds back the xmin horizon: a long or idle-in-transaction session, a lagging replication slot, a standby with hot_standby_feedback running a long query, or an orphaned prepared transaction. VACUUM VERBOSE reports "dead row versions cannot be removed yet, oldest xmin"; pg_stat_activity.backend_xmin, pg_replication_slots and pg_prepared_xacts find the culprit.

Q: pg_dump or pg_basebackup? A: pg_dump is a logical, consistent snapshot of one database, portable across versions and selective, but it only restores to the moment of the dump and rebuilds every index on restore. pg_basebackup copies the cluster's files and, with continuous WAL archiving, allows point-in-time recovery to any moment; it is the production backup, ideally through pgBackRest or Barman, with scheduled restore tests to prove RPO and RTO.

Q: Physical versus logical replication? A: Physical streaming ships WAL bytes and produces a read-only, byte-identical copy of the whole cluster on the same major version: HA and read scaling. Logical replication decodes WAL into row changes per table and applies them as SQL on a writable target, across versions: upgrades, CDC, partial copies. Logical does not carry DDL or sequence values, and needs a replica identity (normally the primary key) on each table that receives updates or deletes.

Q: How does failover work for PostgreSQL, and what can go wrong? A: PostgreSQL provides promotion and timelines; a manager such as Patroni decides, using a leader lock in etcd or Consul so only one node may be primary, promotes a standby and re-points the others, while clients find the new primary through a proxy or libpq target_session_attrs. The risks are split brain, which the consensus lock and fencing prevent, and data loss with asynchronous replication, which synchronous replication to at least one standby removes at the cost of commit latency. The old primary rejoins after pg_rewind.

Q: What does "SERIALIZABLE" mean in Oracle, SQL Server and PostgreSQL? A: In Oracle it is snapshot isolation, so write skew is still possible and conflicts raise ORA-08177. In SQL Server it is lock-based serializability with key-range locks, which blocks and deadlocks more. In PostgreSQL it is Serializable Snapshot Isolation: snapshot reads plus read/write dependency tracking that aborts one transaction with 40001 instead of blocking. SQL Server's SNAPSHOT level and PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ are the snapshot isolation equivalents.

Q: Name three behavioural differences that bite when moving code from Oracle or SQL Server to PostgreSQL. A: Oracle treats the empty string as NULL, PostgreSQL does not, so WHERE col = '' and NOT NULL constraints change meaning. SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED takes shared locks so readers block writers, while PostgreSQL never blocks readers, which changes code that relied on blocking for correctness. Error handling differs: a PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION block is a subtransaction with a cost, there are no autonomous transactions for logging, and T-SQL's TRY/CATCH with XACT_ABORT semantics do not map one to one.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Process per connection: pool with pgbouncer; transaction mode multiplexes but forbids session state.
  • shared_buffers ~25% of RAM to start, effective_cache_size is only a planner hint, work_mem is per node per backend.
  • max_wal_size and checkpoint_timeout trade checkpoint frequency (FPIs, write storms) against recovery time.
  • First tools in an incident: pg_stat_activity, pg_blocking_pids, pg_stat_statements, slow log with auto_explain.
  • Autovacuum: per-table scale factors for hot tables, a bigger cost limit, and hunt whatever holds the xmin horizon.
  • Watch xid age; anti-wraparound vacuums cannot be cancelled and the server stops near 2 billion.
  • pg_dump for logical copies and upgrades; pg_basebackup plus WAL archiving for PITR; test restores.
  • Streaming replication = WAL bytes, read-only copy; logical = row changes, writable target, cross-version.
  • Failover needs a manager (Patroni + etcd), fencing against split brain, and an honest RPO.
  • Oracle: undo, '' is NULL, SERIALIZABLE is SI. SQL Server: locking RC by default, tempdb versions, key-range SERIALIZABLE. PostgreSQL: heap MVCC, SSI.

docs.title: Exercises: 07_Databases_Internals
docs.text:
Every exercise from modules 01 to 14 in one place, grouped by module, with difficulty and a hint. The full wording and the exact "done when" condition are in each module's section 6; this list is for planning and for getting unstuck. Before any of them: load code/m09_schema.sql and code/m09_seed.sql (see code/README.md).
