Active closer (A)                       Passive closer (B)
  FIN, seq=m  -->                        B: CLOSE-WAIT    (B's read() returns 0)
  <-- ACK, ack=m+1                       A: FIN-WAIT-2
  ... B may still send data to A ...     (half-close)
  <-- FIN, seq=n                         B: LAST-ACK
  ACK, ack=n+1 -->                       A: TIME-WAIT (2*MSL)   B: CLOSED

Half-close (shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR)): "I am done sending, but I will still read your reply". Useful for a client that sends a request then wants the full response until EOF. close() does both directions and also releases the fd. When the peer sends FIN, your read() returns 0: that is EOF, not an error. Treat 0 as "peer finished sending"; do not loop on it.

RST is the abort path. You receive RST when: you send to a port nobody listens on (ECONNREFUSED at connect), the peer process died and the kernel cleaned up, the peer closed with unread data in its receive buffer, or a firewall/NAT lost the connection state. Your read or write gets ECONNRESET. Writing to a socket that has already received RST gets EPIPE and, unless you disabled it, SIGPIPE kills your process. Every server must ignore SIGPIPE or use MSG_NOSIGNAL (module 03).

docs.title: 2.10 The state machine and what the states mean at 3 AM
docs.text:
+---------+
       passive   | CLOSED  |  active open: send SYN
       open      +---------+----------------------+
         |                                        v
   +-----v-----+                            +-----------+
   |  LISTEN   |                            | SYN-SENT  |
   +-----+-----+                            +-----+-----+
     rcv SYN, send SYN+ACK                  rcv SYN+ACK, send ACK
         v                                        v
   +-----------+   rcv ACK                  +-------------+
   | SYN-RCVD  +--------------------------->| ESTABLISHED |<--+
   +-----------+                            +------+------+   |
                                                   |          |
         app close(): send FIN                     |     rcv FIN: send ACK
                 +---------------------------------+-------------------+
                 v                                                     v
          +------------+                                       +-------------+
          | FIN-WAIT-1 |                                       | CLOSE-WAIT  |  <-- waiting for
          +-----+------+                                       +------+------+      YOUR close()
     rcv ACK    |                                             app close(): send FIN
                v                                                     v
          +------------+                                       +-------------+
          | FIN-WAIT-2 |                                       |  LAST-ACK   |
          +-----+------+                                       +------+------+
     rcv FIN, send ACK                                           rcv ACK
                v                                                     v
          +------------+   2*MSL timer (60 s on Linux)          +---------+
          | TIME-WAIT  +--------------------------------------->| CLOSED  |
          +------------+                                        +---------+

TIME_WAIT is held by whoever closed first (the active closer). It lasts 2 x MSL (maximum segment lifetime), 60 seconds on Linux, 120 s default on Windows (TcpTimedWaitDelay, 30 s minimum). Two reasons: (1) if the final ACK is lost, the peer retransmits FIN and we must still answer; (2) delayed segments from this connection must die before the same 4-tuple is reused, or a new connection could accept stale data.

Lots of TIME_WAIT is normal on a busy server that closes connections, and it costs little (a small kernel structure, no fd). It becomes a problem on a client that opens thousands of short connections per minute to one server: each connection burns an ephemeral port for 60 s, and 28,000 ports / 60 s means about 470 new connections per second before connect fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL. Fixes: connection pooling (the real fix), net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 (safe with timestamps, client side), let the server close first so TIME_WAIT lands on the server, or widen ip_local_port_range. Do not use tcp_tw_recycle (removed in Linux 4.12; broke NAT).

CLOSE_WAIT is the side that received FIN but has not called close() itself. The kernel is waiting for your application. A growing count of CLOSE_WAIT sockets has one meaning: your code leaked a socket. You read 0 from read() and did not close the fd, or an exception path skipped close, or a connection object sits in a pool forever. CLOSE_WAIT never expires on its own (there is no timer in that state). This is the single most useful ss observation in production.

FIN_WAIT_2 piling up on your side means you closed and the peer never sent its FIN: the peer has leaked the socket (their CLOSE_WAIT). Linux times out orphaned FIN_WAIT_2 after tcp_fin_timeout (60 s).

SYN_RECV piling up: accept queue full (your accept loop is stuck or too slow) or SYN flood. Linux SYN cookies mitigate floods.

docs.title: 2.11 Head-of-line blocking
docs.text: Because TCP delivers bytes in order, if segment 5 is lost, segments 6 to 20 sit in the receive buffer and are not delivered to your application until segment 5 is retransmitted and arrives. One lost packet stalls everything behind it for at least one RTT. This is head-of-line (HOL) blocking. It is why multiplexing many independent requests over one TCP connection (HTTP/2) can be worse than several connections on a lossy link, and why QUIC (HTTP/3) runs over UDP with per-stream ordering: a loss on stream A does not stall stream B.

docs.title: 2.12 "TCP is a byte stream, not messages": the number one bug
docs.text:
You call send(fd, "SET a 1\r\n", 9). The receiver calls recv(fd, buf, 4096). Any of these is correct TCP behaviour:

  • recv returns 9 bytes: your whole message. (Common on loopback. This is why the bug hides in testing.)
  • recv returns 3 bytes SET, next call returns 6. (Segment boundaries, small MSS, GRO on/off.)
  • recv returns 18 bytes: your message and the next one you sent 1 ms later. (Nagle, or the receiver was slow and both arrived before it read.)
  • recv returns 1 byte.

TCP has no record boundaries. send boundaries are not preserved. The receiving application must know, from the bytes themselves, where a message ends: a delimiter, a length prefix, or a fixed size. Module 04 is entirely about this. Every time you see code that assumes "one recv equals one message", it is a bug waiting for a slow network or a bigger payload.

The same applies to send: it may write fewer bytes than asked (non-blocking socket, or signal interruption on a blocking one). You must loop (module 03).

docs.title: 2.13 UDP contrast
docs.text:
UDP: 8-byte header (ports, length, checksum). Each sendto is one datagram; each recvfrom returns exactly one whole datagram (or truncates it if your buffer is too small). Message boundaries are preserved. No handshake, no ordering, no retransmission, no flow or congestion control, no connection state in the kernel. Datagrams above the path MTU get fragmented and a single lost fragment loses the whole datagram, so keep UDP payloads under about 1400 bytes.

Use UDP when you can tolerate loss and need low latency or multicast (DNS, metrics like statsd, game state, media). Use TCP for anything where losing data is a bug (RPC, databases, HTTP/1 and /2). QUIC rebuilds reliability over UDP to escape HOL blocking and to evolve faster than kernel TCP.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m02_tcp_options.cpp creates a connected socket pair on loopback and prints and sets the options that this module discussed. Key parts:

// Read an int option. Each getsockopt call is a syscall; fine for a diagnostic tool.
static int get_int_opt(int fd, int level, int opt) {
    int v = 0; socklen_t len = sizeof v;
    if (getsockopt(fd, level, opt, &v, &len) < 0) die("getsockopt");
    return v;
}

// Disable Nagle: every write goes out as soon as possible. Do this on every RPC socket,
// then also build full messages before writing, otherwise you flood the wire with tiny packets.
static void set_nodelay(int fd) {
    int one = 1;
    if (setsockopt(fd, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, &one, sizeof one) < 0) die("TCP_NODELAY");
}

// Keepalive tuned for a server: detect a dead peer within about 60+5*10 = 110 seconds.
static void set_keepalive(int fd, int idle_s, int intvl_s, int cnt) {
    int one = 1;
    if (setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_KEEPALIVE, &one, sizeof one) < 0) die("SO_KEEPALIVE");
    if (setsockopt(fd, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_KEEPIDLE, &idle_s, sizeof idle_s) < 0) die("TCP_KEEPIDLE");
    if (setsockopt(fd, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_KEEPINTVL, &intvl_s, sizeof intvl_s) < 0) die("TCP_KEEPINTVL");
    if (setsockopt(fd, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_KEEPCNT, &cnt, sizeof cnt) < 0) die("TCP_KEEPCNT");
}

Run it and compare the printed SO_RCVBUF with /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_rmem. Note that Linux reports double the value you set for SO_SNDBUF/SO_RCVBUF (it reserves half for bookkeeping).

Shell experiments to pair with the module:

# Watch TIME_WAIT appear and expire. Client closes first => client holds TIME_WAIT.
python3 -m http.server 8000 &
curl -s localhost:8000 >/dev/null; ss -tan | grep 8000      # shows TIME-WAIT on the ephemeral port
sleep 61; ss -tan | grep 8000                                # gone

# Create a CLOSE_WAIT deliberately: server accepts, client closes, server never closes.
python3 -c "
import socket,time; s=socket.socket(); s.bind(('127.0.0.1',7001)); s.listen()
c,_=s.accept(); print(c.recv(10)); time.sleep(300)" &
sleep 0.3; printf 'x' | nc -q0 127.0.0.1 7001
ss -tan | grep 7001       # one CLOSE-WAIT (server side) and one FIN-WAIT-2 (client side)

# Kernel tunables mentioned in this module
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range \
       net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control net.ipv4.tcp_retries2

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Where the bytes live. send() copies from your buffer into kernel sk_buffs on the socket's write queue and returns; the data has not left the machine. TCP later forms segments from the queue up to min(cwnd, rwnd), hands them to IP, and keeps them on the retransmit queue until ACKed. On the receiver, in-order segments are appended to the receive queue; out-of-order ones go to an out-of-order queue until the gap fills. recv() copies from the receive queue to your buffer. So a TCP byte is copied at least twice (user to kernel, kernel to user) plus DMA. Zero-copy paths (sendfile, MSG_ZEROCOPY, io_uring registered buffers) exist for large transfers.

Where the connection lives before accept. Linux keeps two queues per listening socket: the SYN queue (half-open, SYN-RECV) and the accept queue (ESTABLISHED, waiting for accept). The backlog argument to listen caps the accept queue (also capped by net.core.somaxconn, default 4096 on recent kernels). When the accept queue is full, new SYNs are dropped (the client retries after 1 s, then 3 s...) which shows up as "connections randomly take 1 or 3 seconds". Monitor nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows.

RTT estimation. TCP timestamps let the sender measure RTT per ACK. SRTT and RTTVAR are exponentially weighted averages; RTO = SRTT + 4 * RTTVAR, floored at 200 ms. This is why a LAN retransmission still waits 200 ms: the floor dominates. Tail latency spikes of exactly ~200 ms in a LAN service are a strong hint of packet loss and RTO.

Why TIME_WAIT is 2 x MSL. MSL is the longest a segment can survive in the network (TTL-bound; RFC 793 said 2 minutes, Linux uses 30 s so 2 x MSL = 60 s). After the final ACK, the worst case is: our ACK is lost (up to MSL in flight), the peer retransmits FIN (another MSL). After 2 x MSL no segment from this incarnation can still exist, so the 4-tuple is safe to reuse.

Sequence number wrap. 32 bits wrap after 4 GB of data in one direction. At 10 Gbit/s that is 3.4 seconds, less than MSL. TCP timestamps (PAWS: protection against wrapped sequences) solve the ambiguity. This is one reason timestamps are on by default.

SO_LINGER. By default close() returns immediately and the kernel delivers queued data in the background then sends FIN. SO_LINGER with timeout 0 sends RST immediately and discards unsent data, skipping TIME_WAIT. Some load-testing tools do this to avoid port exhaustion. Never do it in a real server: the peer loses data and sees ECONNRESET.

Windows differences. Same protocol, same states (netstat -ano, Get-NetTCPConnection). TIME_WAIT default 120 s via HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters\TcpTimedWaitDelay. Default ephemeral range is 49152 to 65535 (16,384 ports), so port exhaustion arrives sooner than on Linux. Windows has no SIGPIPE; send to a reset connection returns SOCKET_ERROR with WSAECONNRESET or WSAECONNABORTED. Congestion control is CUBIC on modern Windows too. Keepalive defaults are 2 hours idle, 1 s interval, 10 probes.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The 40 ms mystery. An RPC client wrote the header and the body in two send calls. Every call took 40 ms longer than it should. Nagle plus delayed ACK. Fix: one send per message and TCP_NODELAY. If you measure your employer's RPC transport and see a floor near 40 ms on a LAN, this is the first suspect.
  • "Connection reset by peer" after idle. A firewall between branch and data centre dropped idle TCP state after 15 minutes. The next request hit a dead mapping, firewall sent RST. Fix: keepalive at 5 minutes, and the client reconnects on ECONNRESET and retries if the request is idempotent (module 07).
  • CLOSE_WAIT leak. After a release, ss -s on the application server showed CLOSE_WAIT climbing by hundreds per hour. A new error path returned early without closing the client socket. Within a day the process hit the fd limit and accept failed with EMFILE. Lesson: RAII on the socket (module 03) makes this class of bug impossible; and alert on CLOSE_WAIT count.
  • Port exhaustion on a batch client. A migration tool opened a new connection per row. After a minute connect failed with EADDRNOTAVAIL. TIME_WAIT had eaten the ephemeral range. Fix: one connection, or a pool. The Berkeley DB to YugabyteDB migration you worked on used a pool of long-lived connections; this is why that matters.
  • 15-minute hang on a dead host. A database node lost power. Connections to it had data in flight; the kernel retransmitted with exponential backoff for tcp_retries2 rounds, about 15 minutes, while the application thread sat in send. Nothing in the application had a timeout. Fix: SO_SNDTIMEO/SO_RCVTIMEO or poll with timeout (module 05), application-level deadlines, and lower tcp_retries2 on client hosts (around 8 gives about 100 s).
  • Read the capture, not the logs. When two teams blame each other's service, a tcpdump on both sides settles it in minutes: who sent FIN first, who sent RST, were there retransmissions, was the window zero (receiver too slow). Learn to read [F.], [R], win 0 and "TCP Retransmission" in Wireshark.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Using the capture from module 01, identify which side sent FIN first, and with ss confirm that side holds TIME_WAIT. Done when: you can state the rule "active closer holds TIME_WAIT" from evidence.

  2. (easy) Write down the TCP state machine from memory (states and transitions for a normal open and close). Check it against section 2.10. Done when: no state is missing.

  3. (medium) Reproduce the Nagle + delayed ACK stall: write a client that sends a 1-byte header and a 10-byte body in two send calls and waits for a 1-byte reply from a tiny server; time 100 iterations with and without TCP_NODELAY. Done when: you observe a large difference (on loopback Linux may not show it; try with the server in another WSL distro or a VM if needed, and explain why).

  4. (medium) Reproduce CLOSE_WAIT with the Python snippet in section 3, then write the C++ fix: a server that treats read() == 0 by closing. Verify with ss that the state goes to CLOSED. Done when: ss -tan | grep 7001 is empty after the client disconnects.

  5. (hard) Estimate the maximum connection rate a client can sustain to a single server given the default ip_local_port_range and a 60 s TIME_WAIT, then verify by writing a Python loop that opens and closes connections as fast as possible and reports when connect fails. Then enable tcp_tw_reuse and repeat. Done when: your measured limit matches the estimate within a factor of two and you can explain the mechanism.

  6. (hard) Using tc qdisc add dev lo root netem loss 5% delay 20ms, transfer 10 MB over loopback with nc and watch retransmissions in tcpdump/Wireshark. Measure throughput. Remove the qdisc (tc qdisc del dev lo root). Done when: you can point at a fast retransmit and an RTO-triggered retransmit in the capture and explain the throughput drop.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why three packets for the handshake and not two? A: Each side must get its own ISN acknowledged so both know the other can receive. Two packets would leave the server unsure that the client got its SYN-ACK. The third packet (ACK) can already carry data.

Q: You see 30,000 sockets in TIME_WAIT on a server. Is that a problem? A: Usually not on a server: TIME_WAIT costs a small kernel structure and no fd, and is normal when the server closes connections first. It is a problem on a client exhausting ephemeral ports. The fix is pooling; tcp_tw_reuse helps on the client; letting the server close first moves the TIME_WAIT. Never use SO_LINGER 0 to avoid it in production.

Q: You see CLOSE_WAIT growing. What does it mean? A: The peer closed (sent FIN), the kernel ACKed it, and our application has not called close(). It is always an application bug: a leaked fd, an error path skipping close, or ignoring read() == 0. It never times out by itself. RAII wrappers prevent it.

Q: What is the difference between flow control and congestion control? A: Flow control protects the receiver: the advertised window says how much buffer space it has. Congestion control protects the network: the sender's cwnd grows (slow start, then linear) and shrinks on loss. The sender uses the minimum of the two.

Q: What is Nagle's algorithm and when do you disable it? A: It delays small writes while data is unacknowledged, to avoid tiny packets. With delayed ACKs on the peer it causes about 40 ms stalls in write-write-read patterns. Disable with TCP_NODELAY on latency-sensitive request-response protocols, and always coalesce a message into one send.

Q: Why is "one recv equals one message" wrong? A: TCP is a byte stream; segment boundaries and send boundaries are not preserved. recv can return part of a message, several messages, or one byte. The application needs framing (length prefix or delimiter) and an incremental parser.

Q: How does a connection to a crashed machine behave? A: If idle: nothing, it stays ESTABLISHED forever unless keepalive is on. If sending: the kernel retransmits with exponential backoff for tcp_retries2 rounds, about 15 minutes by default, and then returns ETIMEDOUT. If the machine reboots and comes back, it answers with RST and you get ECONNRESET. Application timeouts are mandatory.

Q: What is head-of-line blocking? A: In-order delivery means one lost segment holds back all later bytes until it is retransmitted. Multiplexed streams over one TCP connection all stall together. QUIC avoids it with independent streams over UDP.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK; negotiates MSS, window scale, SACK, timestamps; costs one RTT.
  • Every byte is numbered; ACKs are cumulative; SACK fills holes; lost data is retransmitted by RTO (min 200 ms, doubles) or fast retransmit (3 dup ACKs).
  • Flow control = receiver window; congestion control = cwnd with slow start and CUBIC/BBR; sender uses the minimum.
  • Nagle + delayed ACK = 40 ms stalls; coalesce writes and set TCP_NODELAY.
  • Keepalive detects dead peers; defaults are 2 hours; tune per socket.
  • read() == 0 is EOF (peer FIN). ECONNRESET/EPIPE are RST. Ignore SIGPIPE in servers.
  • TIME_WAIT: active closer, 60 s, normal on servers, a port problem on clients.
  • CLOSE_WAIT: you forgot to close. Never expires. Always an application bug.
  • TCP is a byte stream; frame your messages and loop on partial reads and writes.
  • UDP preserves datagram boundaries but guarantees nothing else.

docs.title: 03. The sockets API and a blocking server
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A socket is a file descriptor that the kernel connects to a network conversation instead of a file on disk. You get one with socket(), you tell the kernel which address you want with bind(), you say "I am a server, queue up callers" with listen(), and every accept() hands you a brand-new socket for one client. On the client side you skip bind and listen and just connect(). After that both sides read() and write() (or recv() and send()) the same way they would on a pipe, and close() when done.

The analogy: a company switchboard. bind picks the phone number, listen turns the switchboard on, accept answers a ringing line and hands it to an operator, and the operator talks on that line until one side hangs up. The switchboard number is still free to ring again.

The hard part is not the calls themselves. The hard part is that each call can fail in many ways, read and write may do less than you asked, and a signal can interrupt any of them. A senior engineer's socket code is 20% happy path and 80% handling exactly these cases. This module gives you a small reusable header that handles them once, so the rest of the course never repeats them.

docs.title: 2.1 The call sequence
docs.text:
Server                                   Client
socket()                                 socket()
setsockopt(SO_REUSEADDR)
bind(addr, port)
listen(backlog)
accept()  --- blocks until ---           connect(addr, port)   (handshake happens here)
  returns new fd
read()/write() on new fd  <----------->  write()/read()
close(new fd)                            close()
(loop back to accept)

docs.title: 2.2 getaddrinfo instead of hand-built sockaddr_in
docs.text:
Old code fills a sockaddr_in with inet_addr("10.1.2.3"). Do not. getaddrinfo does name resolution (DNS, /etc/hosts), handles IPv4 and IPv6 uniformly, parses service names or port numbers, and returns a linked list of candidate addresses you try in order.

addrinfo hints{};
hints.ai_family   = AF_UNSPEC;      // v4 or v6
hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;    // TCP
hints.ai_flags    = AI_PASSIVE;     // for a server: nullptr host means INADDR_ANY / in6addr_any
addrinfo* res = nullptr;
int rc = getaddrinfo(nullptr, "7000", &hints, &res);   // rc != 0: use gai_strerror(rc), NOT errno
for (addrinfo* ai = res; ai; ai = ai->ai_next) { /* socket, bind, listen; break on success */ }
freeaddrinfo(res);

getaddrinfo is a blocking call that can take seconds if DNS is slow. In an event loop (module 06) you call it from a worker thread or use getaddrinfo_a/c-ares.

docs.title: 2.3 SO_REUSEADDR and friends
docs.text: When your server restarts, old connections to its port are still in TIME_WAIT for 60 s. Without SO_REUSEADDR, bind() fails with EADDRINUSE. Set it on every listening socket before bind. It does not let two processes listen on the same port (that is SO_REUSEPORT, used for multi-process accept load balancing). On Windows SO_REUSEADDR has a different, dangerous meaning (it allows hijacking a port already in use); use SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE there and accept the TIME_WAIT bind failure, or set SO_REUSEADDR only on Linux.

docs.title: 2.4 Read and write: the calls that lie to beginners
docs.text:
ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, len) (or recv(fd, buf, len, flags)) returns:

  • n > 0: that many bytes. Any number from 1 to len. Not "the message". Just bytes.
  • n == 0: EOF. The peer sent FIN. It will never send more. You should finish and close.
  • n < 0: error, look at errno.

ssize_t n = write(fd, buf, len) (or send) returns:

  • n == len: all written (into the kernel send buffer; not yet on the wire).
  • 0 < n < len: partial write. Happens on non-blocking sockets when the send buffer fills, and on blocking sockets when a signal arrives after some bytes were copied or SO_SNDTIMEO fires. You must send the rest.
  • n < 0: error.

Therefore every program has these two loops, and the helper header has them once:

// Read exactly len bytes or report EOF/error.
while (got < len) {
    ssize_t n = recv(fd, p + got, len - got, 0);
    if (n < 0) { if (errno == EINTR) continue; return error; }
    if (n == 0) return eof;              // peer closed; if got > 0 this is a truncated message
    got += n;
}
// Write all len bytes.
while (sent < len) {
    ssize_t n = send(fd, p + sent, len - sent, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
    if (n < 0) { if (errno == EINTR) continue; return error; }
    sent += n;
}

"Read exactly N" only works when you know N: a fixed header, or a length prefix (module 04). For delimited text you instead read into a growing buffer and scan for the delimiter.

docs.title: 2.5 errno values you must recognise
docs.text:
errno Where Meaning What to do EINTR any blocking call A signal arrived before the call completed Retry the call. Always. EAGAIN / EWOULDBLOCK read/write/accept Non-blocking socket has nothing to read (or no room to write); or SO_RCVTIMEO expired on a blocking socket Non-blocking: wait for readiness (poll/epoll). Timeout: treat as timeout. ECONNRESET read/write Peer sent RST: crashed, closed with unread data, or a middlebox dropped state Close the connection. Client: reconnect and retry if idempotent. EPIPE write We wrote to a connection the peer already closed/reset. Also raises SIGPIPE unless MSG_NOSIGNAL or SIGPIPE ignored Close. Ignore SIGPIPE process-wide in servers. ECONNREFUSED connect Nothing listens on that port (server got RST) Server down or wrong port. ETIMEDOUT connect/read/write Retransmissions exhausted; host unreachable or black-holed Close. Peer probably dead or firewalled. EADDRINUSE bind Port in use or TIME_WAIT without SO_REUSEADDR Set SO_REUSEADDR; check ss -tlnp. EADDRNOTAVAIL connect Ephemeral ports exhausted (client) Pool connections; tcp_tw_reuse. EMFILE socket/accept Process fd limit hit (ulimit -n) Fix the leak (CLOSE_WAIT!) or raise limit. Back off on accept. ENFILE socket/accept System-wide fd limit Rare; fs.file-max. ECONNABORTED accept Client reset while in the accept queue Ignore and accept again. EHOSTUNREACH / ENETUNREACH connect/write No route Network or routing problem.

SIGPIPE deserves its own line. Default action: terminate the process. A server that writes a response to a client who already disconnected (very common) dies silently. Every server does signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) at startup and/or uses send(..., MSG_NOSIGNAL). Windows has no SIGPIPE.

docs.title: 2.6 Blocking semantics
docs.text:
By default sockets are blocking: accept sleeps until a connection arrives, read sleeps until at least one byte arrives (or EOF or error), write sleeps until all bytes fit in the send buffer, connect sleeps until the handshake completes or fails (up to about 2 minutes for a black hole; set SO_SNDTIMEO or use non-blocking connect with poll to bound it).

A blocking server therefore needs one thread per thing it waits on. This module's server waits on one client at a time; module 05 adds threads; module 06 replaces blocking with readiness notification.

docs.title: 2.7 Shutdown vs close
docs.text:
close(fd): drops this reference to the socket. When the last reference is gone (remember fork and dup copy references), the kernel sends FIN after flushing the send buffer, and the fd number becomes reusable immediately (a later accept may return the same number; this is why storing raw fds in long-lived structures is dangerous).

shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR): send FIN now, keep the fd, keep reading. Lets a client say "request done" and read until the server's EOF. shutdown(fd, SHUT_RD) discards further input. shutdown affects the connection regardless of how many fd references exist, which is how a thread can wake another thread blocked in read on the same socket: shutdown(SHUT_RDWR) makes the blocked read return 0. This is a key graceful-shutdown tool in module 05.

docs.title: 2.8 Winsock differences
docs.text:
POSIX (Linux) Winsock (Windows) Note nothing WSAStartup(MAKEWORD(2,2), &wsa) once per process, WSACleanup() at exit Forgetting it makes every call fail with WSANOTINITIALISED int fd SOCKET s (unsigned, UINT_PTR) Invalid is INVALID_SOCKET, not -1. Never compare to < 0. close(fd) closesocket(s) close on a SOCKET is undefined errno WSAGetLastError() Values are WSAE*: WSAEWOULDBLOCK, WSAECONNRESET, WSAEINTR read/write not for sockets; use recv/send ReadFile works on sockets but mixing is unwise ssize_t return int return, SOCKET_ERROR (-1) on error fcntl(O_NONBLOCK) ioctlsocket(s, FIONBIO, &one) poll WSAPoll (Vista+; had bugs with connect errors before Windows 10) select exists but fd_set is an array, not a bitmap, limited by FD_SETSIZE 64 epoll none; use IOCP (CreateIoCompletionPort, WSARecv overlapped) or WSAEventSelect Module 06 SIGPIPE none send returns WSAECONNRESET/WSAECONNABORTED MSG_NOSIGNAL not needed, does not exist SO_REUSEADDR prevents TIME_WAIT bind failure SO_REUSEADDR allows port hijacking; use SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE Windows does not block bind on TIME_WAIT by default TCP_KEEPIDLE/TCP_KEEPINTVL WSAIoctl(SIO_KEEPALIVE_VALS) (ms units) or the same option names on Windows 10 1709+ getaddrinfo/freeaddrinfo same names, <ws2tcpip.h> inet_pton/inet_ntop same (Vista+) link nothing ws2_32.lib EINTR from signals essentially never happens Winsock blocking calls are not interrupted by signals fork + inherit socket WSADuplicateSocket to pass to another process

A portability layer is a dozen macros and an init function. Your employer's Windows server has one; find it and read it with this table beside you.

docs.title: 3.1 The RAII wrapper (code/m03_socket.hpp)
docs.text:
The core type:

class Fd {
public:
    Fd() noexcept = default;
    explicit Fd(int fd) noexcept : fd_(fd) {}
    ~Fd() { reset(); }                                 // closes on every exit path: no CLOSE_WAIT leaks
    Fd(const Fd&) = delete;                            // two owners would double-close
    Fd& operator=(const Fd&) = delete;
    Fd(Fd&& o) noexcept : fd_(o.fd_) { o.fd_ = -1; }   // move = transfer ownership
    Fd& operator=(Fd&& o) noexcept { if (this != &o) { reset(); fd_ = o.fd_; o.fd_ = -1; } return *this; }
    int  get() const noexcept { return fd_; }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return fd_ >= 0; }
    int  release() noexcept { int f = fd_; fd_ = -1; return f; }
    void reset(int fd = -1) noexcept { if (fd_ >= 0) ::close(fd_); fd_ = fd; }
private:
    int fd_ = -1;
};

Why this matters: the CLOSE_WAIT leak in module 02 cannot happen. Whether the handler returns, throws, or breaks out of a loop, the destructor runs. This is the single biggest robustness gain you get from C++ over C in network code. (In your C server, the equivalent discipline is a single cleanup: label that every error path gotos.)

The I/O loops:

inline size_t read_some(int fd, void* buf, size_t len) {
    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = ::recv(fd, buf, len, 0);
        if (n >= 0) return static_cast<size_t>(n);       // 0 = EOF, caller decides
        if (errno == EINTR) continue;                     // signal: not an error, retry
        throw_errno("recv");                              // ECONNRESET, EAGAIN(timeout), ...
    }
}

inline bool read_exact(int fd, void* buf, size_t len) {
    char* p = static_cast<char*>(buf);
    size_t got = 0;
    while (got < len) {
        size_t n = read_some(fd, p + got, len - got);
        if (n == 0) {
            if (got == 0) return false;                  // clean EOF between messages
            throw std::runtime_error("connection closed mid-message");  // truncated: protocol error
        }
        got += n;
    }
    return true;
}

inline void write_all(int fd, const void* buf, size_t len) {
    const char* p = static_cast<const char*>(buf);
    size_t sent = 0;
    while (sent < len) {
        ssize_t n = ::send(fd, p + sent, len - sent, MSG_NOSIGNAL);   // EPIPE instead of SIGPIPE
        if (n < 0) { if (errno == EINTR) continue; throw_errno("send"); }
        sent += static_cast<size_t>(n);
    }
}

Note the distinction in read_exact: EOF before the first byte is normal (the client finished and closed between requests); EOF in the middle of a message is a protocol violation and is reported differently. Protocol code needs that distinction.

listen_tcp and connect_tcp wrap getaddrinfo, try each address, set SO_REUSEADDR on listeners, and retry connect on EINTR. accept_tcp retries EINTR and ECONNABORTED, and returns an empty Fd when the listener has been closed (that is how module 05 stops the accept loop).

docs.title: 3.2 Echo server (code/m03_echo_server.cpp)
docs.text:
static void serve_one(net::Fd client) {
    net::set_nodelay(client.get());
    char buf[4096];
    try {
        for (;;) {
            size_t n = net::read_some(client.get(), buf, sizeof buf);
            if (n == 0) break;                        // peer FIN: normal end
            net::write_all(client.get(), buf, n);     // echo whatever arrived, however much
        }
    } catch (const std::system_error& e) {
        std::fprintf(stderr, "[!] %s\n", e.what()); // ECONNRESET/EPIPE: client is gone, carry on
    }
}   // client destroyed => close()

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    net::ignore_sigpipe();
    net::Fd listener = net::listen_tcp(nullptr, argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "7000", 128);
    for (;;) {
        net::Fd client = net::accept_tcp(listener.get());
        if (!client) break;
        serve_one(std::move(client));
    }
}

An echo server does not need framing because it does not interpret the bytes. The moment you interpret bytes (module 04), you need framing.

docs.title: 3.3 Echo client (code/m03_echo_client.cpp)
docs.text:
The client sends each stdin line and uses read_exact(line.size()) to get the echo back. It sets SO_RCVTIMEO to 5 s so a hung server cannot hang it, and does shutdown(SHUT_WR) at the end so the server sees EOF and the client holds TIME_WAIT.

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread m03_echo_server.cpp -o echo_server
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread m03_echo_client.cpp -o echo_client
./echo_server 7000 &
seq 1 200000 | ./echo_client 127.0.0.1 7000      # ok: 200000 lines, 1488895 bytes echoed correctly

Run strace -e trace=network,read,write -p $(pidof echo_server) while the bulk test runs. You will see recvfrom return many different sizes. That is section 2.4 in real life.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What socket() allocates. A struct socket plus a protocol-specific struct sock (for TCP, struct tcp_sock, over 2 KB), an fd table entry, and a struct file. The fd is an index into the process's fd table; the kernel object is reference counted. dup/fork add references; close drops one. The TCP connection ends when the last reference closes, which is a classic bug after fork in servers that forget to close the client socket in the parent.

What bind() checks. Port availability per protocol and address family, privilege for ports below 1024 (or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE), and the SO_REUSEADDR rules: can bind if all existing sockets on the port also have SO_REUSEADDR and none is in LISTEN (Linux), or if the existing ones are only in TIME_WAIT.

What listen() does. Transitions the socket to LISTEN state and allocates the SYN queue and accept queue. backlog (clamped by somaxconn) sizes the accept queue. Half-open connections live in the SYN queue (or as SYN cookies under pressure).

What accept() does. Dequeues a fully established connection from the accept queue, allocates a new fd pointing at the already-created struct sock. The handshake happened before, in softirq context, when the ACK arrived. If the queue is empty and the socket is blocking, the thread sleeps on the socket's wait queue and is woken by the softirq that enqueues the next connection.

What recv() does. Takes the socket lock, walks the receive queue of sk_buffs, copies up to len bytes to user space (skb_copy_datagram_iter), frees consumed skbs, updates the receive window (may send a window update ACK), releases the lock. If the queue is empty and the socket is blocking it sleeps with a timeout equal to SO_RCVTIMEO (infinite by default). That is why recv returns whatever is queued: it does not wait for len bytes, only for at least one.

What send() does. Copies user bytes into skbs appended to the write queue up to the send-buffer limit, then calls tcp_push which may transmit immediately (if cwnd/rwnd allow and Nagle allows) or leave the data for the ACK clock to send later. If the send buffer is full the caller sleeps (SO_SNDTIMEO bounds it). A blocking send returning a short count happens when a signal arrives during that sleep after some bytes were already copied.

close() and lingering. Default: close returns at once, the kernel keeps the sock alive ("orphan") until the send queue drains and FIN is ACKed, then TIME_WAIT. Orphans count against tcp_max_orphans. If the receive queue still has unread data when you close, Linux sends RST instead of FIN: the peer sees ECONNRESET. This surprises people who close a socket after a protocol error without draining it.

Thread safety. The kernel socket is thread-safe per call: two threads can send concurrently and bytes will not interleave within one call, but two send calls from two threads can interleave with each other at the message level, corrupting a framed protocol. One writer per socket, or a mutex around whole-message writes (your RPC server likely has exactly this mutex per connection).

Windows: the same shape underneath. Winsock calls go through ws2_32.dll, mswsock.dll, into the AFD driver (afd.sys) and tcpip.sys. recv is a blocking IRP; overlapped I/O (module 06) lets the kernel complete into your buffer asynchronously. closesocket with pending overlapped operations cancels them with WSA_OPERATION_ABORTED.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Partial read bug, classic form. Code that does recv(fd, &header, sizeof header, 0) once and then uses header.length works for months on a LAN. Then a WAN link or a large payload delivers 3 bytes of the 8-byte header, the code reads garbage length (say 2 GB), tries to allocate, and crashes. Every recv that expects a fixed size must be a loop. If your Windows server has a single recv for the header, that is a latent crash; check it this week.
  • Partial write bug, classic form. Non-blocking socket, send returns 1200 of 4096 bytes, code ignores the return value. The peer receives a truncated message and the next message's bytes look like garbage. Symptom: "random protocol errors under load". The fix is write_all or a per-connection output buffer (module 06).
  • SIGPIPE at 3 AM. Server process disappears with no log line and exit status 141 (128 + 13). A client disconnected while a response was being written. Ignore SIGPIPE on day one.
  • EINTR after adding a profiler or a signal-based timer. Code that worked for years starts failing with "Interrupted system call" after someone added SIGALRM-based timeouts or SIGPROF profiling. Every blocking call needs the EINTR retry. (SA_RESTART helps for some calls but not for accept/recv with timeouts, and not for poll.)
  • EMFILE and the accept storm. When the fd limit is hit, accept fails with EMFILE, the listener is still readable, and a naive loop spins at 100% CPU logging errors. Mitigation: on EMFILE, sleep briefly, or keep a spare fd to close-and-accept-and-close to drain the queue politely. The real fix is the fd leak or ulimit -n.
  • Closing with unread data sends RST. A server that detects a protocol error, logs, and closes while the client is still sending sees the client log ECONNRESET, and the client team blames the network. Drain or shutdown(SHUT_WR) then read to EOF before close when you want a clean FIN.
  • Your banking server. The pattern there is the same: a listener thread, accept, hand the socket to a worker. Audit the worker's header read, the write path, the SIGPIPE equivalent (not applicable on Windows), and whether every error path reaches closesocket. Those four checks are the module in one sentence.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run the echo server and client. Run ss -tanp | grep 7000 during a bulk test and after the client exits. Done when: you can name every state you see and which side owns it.

  2. (easy) Remove ignore_sigpipe() and MSG_NOSIGNAL from a copy of the server. Connect with nc, kill nc with kill -9 while the server is mid-echo of a large input (yes | head -c 50000000 | nc ...). Done when: you see the server die with status 141, and you can explain it.

  3. (medium) Make the server print how many bytes each recv returned for one client session. Send seq 1 100000 through the client. Done when: you have seen at least three distinct sizes and can explain why they vary.

  4. (medium) Write connect_with_timeout(host, port, ms) using a non-blocking connect, poll for POLLOUT, then getsockopt(SO_ERROR) to read the result, then switch back to blocking. Test against a black-hole address (10.255.255.1). Done when: it fails within your timeout instead of 2 minutes.

  5. (hard) Write the Winsock version of m03_socket.hpp as m03_socket_win.hpp (you can compile it with MSVC at work): WSAStartup in a static initialiser, SOCKET type, closesocket, WSAGetLastError mapped to a small error enum, ioctlsocket for non-blocking. Done when: the echo client compiles against both headers with #ifdef _WIN32 only in the header.

  6. (hard) Implement a tiny strace-free "recv size histogram": an LD_PRELOAD shared library that wraps recv and read, counts return sizes in buckets, and prints the histogram at exit. Use it on the echo server. Done when: it compiles and shows a distribution.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does recv returning 0 mean, and what should you do? A: The peer closed its sending side (sent FIN). It is EOF, not an error. Finish any response you owe, then close your socket; otherwise you sit in CLOSE_WAIT indefinitely. Never retry recv after 0.

Q: Why must you loop on recv and send? A: TCP is a byte stream. recv returns whatever is in the receive buffer, 1 byte to len. send may copy only part of your buffer when the send buffer is full (non-blocking) or a signal or timeout interrupts (blocking). The loop is the only correct way to read N bytes or write N bytes.

Q: What is EINTR and how do you handle it? A: A signal handler ran while the thread was blocked in a system call; the call returns -1 with EINTR instead of completing. It is not a failure. Retry the call. SA_RESTART reduces but does not eliminate it.

Q: What is SIGPIPE? A: The signal raised when you write to a socket (or pipe) whose peer has closed. Default action kills the process. Servers must signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) or use MSG_NOSIGNAL and handle EPIPE.

Q: What does SO_REUSEADDR do, and is it the same on Windows? A: On Linux it lets bind succeed while old connections on the port are in TIME_WAIT, so a server can restart immediately. It does not allow two listeners. On Windows it allows binding to a port that another socket is actively using, which is a security problem; use SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE there.

Q: close versus shutdown? A: close releases the fd and, when the last reference is gone, sends FIN after flushing. shutdown acts on the connection regardless of references: SHUT_WR sends FIN but keeps the fd open for reading (half-close); SHUT_RDWR also wakes other threads blocked in recv on that socket, which is useful for graceful shutdown.

Q: Why use getaddrinfo instead of filling sockaddr_in? A: It does name resolution, supports IPv4 and IPv6 without separate code paths, returns multiple addresses to try in order, and parses ports and service names. Hand-built sockaddr_in ties you to IPv4 and literal IPs.

Q: How does an RAII fd wrapper prevent a production incident? A: A leaked socket leaves the connection in CLOSE_WAIT forever and eventually exhausts the fd limit so accept fails with EMFILE. With a move-only wrapper whose destructor closes, every return, break and exception path closes the socket, so the leak class disappears.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Server: socket, SO_REUSEADDR, bind, listen, accept loop. Client: socket, connect. Both: recv/send loops, close.
  • Use getaddrinfo; try every returned address; gai_strerror for its errors.
  • recv returns 1..len bytes, 0 on EOF, -1 with errno. send may be short. Loop, always.
  • EINTR: retry. EAGAIN: wait or timeout. ECONNRESET/EPIPE: peer gone, close. EMFILE: you leaked.
  • Ignore SIGPIPE in every server. Use MSG_NOSIGNAL too.
  • shutdown(SHUT_WR) for half-close; shutdown(SHUT_RDWR) to wake a blocked reader.
  • Closing with unread data sends RST, not FIN.
  • One writer per socket at a time, or messages interleave.
  • RAII Fd wrapper: move-only, closes in destructor, kills the CLOSE_WAIT leak class.
  • Winsock: WSAStartup, SOCKET/INVALID_SOCKET, closesocket, WSAGetLastError, no SIGPIPE, SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE, IOCP instead of epoll.

docs.title: 04. Framing and protocol design
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
TCP hands you a river of bytes with no marks in it. Framing is how you put the marks back: a rule that lets the receiver say "this message ends here, the next one starts there" using only the bytes themselves. There are three ways to do it. Put the length first ("the next 57 bytes are one message"). Put a special marker at the end ("a message ends at \r\n"). Or make every message the same size. Everything else in protocol design builds on this choice.

Think of a telegraph operator receiving Morse code all day. Without a convention for where one telegram ends, the operator cannot deliver anything. "STOP" at the end of each telegram is delimiter framing. "This telegram is 12 words" is length-prefix framing.

A protocol is the complete contract on top of framing: what the messages mean, what replies are allowed, what errors look like, and how the two sides stay compatible when one is upgraded. This module designs the tcpkv protocol from scratch, writes a parser that works no matter how TCP chops the bytes, and looks at how Redis does the same.

docs.title: 2.1 Three framing strategies
docs.text:
Length prefix. Each message starts with a fixed-size header that includes the payload length.

| len: 4 bytes | type: 2 | flags: 2 | payload: len bytes |

Pros: binary-safe (payload may contain anything), the receiver knows exactly how much to read, parsing is O(1) to find the boundary, and you can allocate once. Cons: not human-readable on the wire, you must fix the byte order of the header, and a corrupted length desynchronises the stream forever (so always bound it and close on nonsense). This is what almost every RPC transport uses, including, almost certainly, your employer's.

Delimiter. Messages end with a marker, usually or .

GET account:1001

Pros: human-readable, testable with nc and telnet, trivially extensible. Cons: the payload cannot contain the delimiter unless you escape it (escaping is a bug factory), the receiver must scan every byte, and you must cap the line length or an attacker sends 10 GB without a newline. Used by SMTP, HTTP/1.x headers, Redis inline commands, your tcpkv.

Fixed size. Every message is N bytes. Pros: trivial. Cons: wastes space or cannot grow. Used for some legacy financial protocols and sensor data. Headers inside length-prefixed protocols are fixed size, so this strategy is always present at a small scale.

Hybrid (the good answer). A delimited command line that announces the length of any binary part that follows. HTTP does this (Content-Length header, then that many bytes). Redis RESP does it ($5 hello ). tcpkv does it for SET.

docs.title: 2.2 Text vs binary
docs.text:
Text Binary Debugging nc, tcpdump -A, read it by eye Need a decoder or Wireshark dissector Size Larger (digits, spaces, CRLF) Compact Parsing cost Scan and convert digits memcpy and byte swap Extensibility Add a word Add a field; need versioning discipline Numeric precision Decimal strings are exact Fixed widths; floats need IEEE agreement Where used HTTP/1, SMTP, Redis, PostgreSQL startup HTTP/2, gRPC, PostgreSQL data rows, your RPC

For an internal RPC between your own clients and servers, binary wins on throughput and CPU. For a tool people operate by hand, text wins. Many systems do text for control and binary for bulk.

docs.title: 2.3 Endianness
docs.text:
A 32-bit integer 0x01020304 is stored in memory as bytes 04 03 02 01 on x86 and ARM (little-endian) and 01 02 03 04 on big-endian machines. The network standard is big-endian, called network byte order. htonl/htons (host to network, long/short) and ntohl/ntohs convert. On x86 they swap bytes; on a big-endian host they are no-ops.

Rules:

  • Never *(uint32_t*)buf. It violates alignment on some CPUs and strict aliasing in C++. Use memcpy into a uint32_t, then ntohl. The compiler turns memcpy of 4 bytes into one load.
  • Never send a struct with send(fd, &s, sizeof s). Padding, field order and byte order are all compiler and platform dependent. Serialise field by field. (If your employer's protocol does send raw structs, it works only because both ends are the same compiler on the same architecture. That is a known risk worth naming in an interview.)
  • Choose one order for your protocol and write it down. Little-endian is acceptable for an internal protocol (Protocol Buffers and FlatBuffers use little-endian); the point is to fix it.

docs.title: 2.4 Protocol design checklist
docs.text:
1. Framing: how do I find message boundaries? Max sizes for every variable-length part?
  2. Grammar: exact syntax of every request and response. Write it as a BNF-like list.
  3. Error model: machine-readable codes plus human text. The client must distinguish "key not found" (normal) from "server broke" (retry) from "your request is malformed" (do not retry).
  4. Request-response matching: in a strict request-response protocol over one connection, the Nth reply answers the Nth request (pipelining). If replies can be out of order, every request needs an id (module 07).
  5. Versioning: how does a v2 client talk to a v1 server? Options: a version in the handshake, a version in every frame header, "unknown fields are ignored" (protobuf style), or a new port.
  6. Idempotency: which operations can a client safely retry after a timeout? SET k v yes. INCR k no, unless the client attaches a request id the server remembers (module 07).
  7. Limits and defence: max line, max value, max in-flight requests, idle timeout. Anything unbounded is a denial-of-service hole.
  8. Observability: can you tell from a packet capture what is going on? Can you count commands by type?

docs.title: 2.5 The tcpkv protocol
docs.text:
Requests (\r\n terminated; a key is 1 to 256 bytes with no bytes <= 0x20 and no 0x7F):

PING
GET <key>
SET <key> <len>\r\n<len bytes of value>\r\n
DEL <key>
EXISTS <key>
QUIT

Responses:

+OK\r\n                      SET succeeded; also +PONG for PING
$<len>\r\n<bytes>\r\n        GET found: bulk value, binary-safe
$-1\r\n                      GET on missing key: nil
:<n>\r\n                     DEL / EXISTS: integer 0 or 1
-<CODE> <message>\r\n        error. CODE is one of:
                             ERR_SYNTAX       malformed request; do not retry as-is
                             ERR_UNKNOWN_CMD  verb not recognised (maybe version skew)
                             ERR_ARGS         wrong argument count/shape
                             ERR_TOO_LARGE    line or value over the limit; server closes
                             ERR_INTERNAL     server-side failure; safe to retry (all ops idempotent)

Design decisions and why:

  • Text, because the resume line says "text protocol" and because nc localhost 7000 as a client is worth a lot while learning and debugging.
  • The value is length-prefixed, not delimited, so binary values with \r\n inside work and no escaping is needed. This is the hybrid approach.
  • Replies start with one type byte (+ $ : -), so a client can parse the reply without knowing which request it sent. Stolen from Redis.
  • Every command is idempotent (SET, DEL, GET, EXISTS). A client that times out can retry anything. If you later add INCR, you will have to add request ids.
  • Errors have codes that classify retry behaviour. That is the single most useful protocol feature for the client team.
  • Strict request-response, one at a time or pipelined in order. No ids needed.
  • Versioning: a future HELLO <version> as the first command; servers ignore unknown verbs with ERR_UNKNOWN_CMD, so an old server tells a new client exactly what is wrong.
  • Limits: line 1024 bytes, value 1 MiB, enforced by the parser. Exceeding them is fatal to the connection because the server cannot resynchronise safely.

docs.title: 2.6 Incremental parsing with a state machine
docs.text:
A non-incremental parser assumes it has the whole message. It cannot exist over TCP. An incremental parser keeps state between calls: "I have seen GET al so far, waiting for CRLF".

tcpkv needs three states:

            CRLF found, verb != SET          complete command
   +------+ ---------------------------->  emit Command
   | Line |
   +------+ ---- CRLF found, verb == SET, len parsed ----+
      ^                                                   v
      |                                             +---------+   len bytes available
      |                                             | Payload | ---------------------+
      |                                             +---------+                      v
      |                                                                      +-------------+
      +-------------- 2 bytes available, must be CRLF -----------------------| PayloadCrlf |
                       (else fatal: lost sync)                               +-------------+

Rules the implementation follows:

  • feed() only appends. next() only consumes complete units. Never consume a partial line.
  • A std::string buffer plus a read offset, compacted when the consumed prefix is large. Erasing from the front on every message would be O(n^2).
  • Recoverable errors (bad verb, bad args) skip exactly one line and let the stream continue. Fatal errors (line too long, length too large, payload not terminated) mark the error fatal and the caller closes. The distinction: a fatal error means we no longer know where the next message begins.
  • Limits are checked before allocating or buffering. SET k 9999999999 must be rejected at the header, not after trying to read 10 GB.

docs.title: 2.7 Fuzzing the parser
docs.text:
A parser is the most attacked and most bug-prone piece of a server. Two cheap, high-value tests:

  1. Random splits: generate valid command streams, serialise, split the byte string at random points (including one-byte chunks), feed, assert the parsed list equals the input. This is the TCP property made into a test.
  2. Random garbage: feed random bytes from a small alphabet including \r, \n, digits and command letters. The parser may error; it must not crash, loop, or grow its buffer unboundedly.

The test file does both with std::mt19937 and plain assert. Beyond that, libFuzzer (clang++ -fsanitize=fuzzer,address) finds things random testing misses; the parser's feed/next interface is exactly the shape a fuzz target needs. Always run the tests under -fsanitize=address,undefined at least once.

docs.title: 2.8 What Redis RESP does and why
docs.text:
RESP (REdis Serialization Protocol) version 2:

*3
$3
SET
$3
key
$5
hello
      array of 3 bulk strings = SET key hello
+OK
                                              simple string
-ERR unknown command 'FOO'
                       error
:42
                                              integer
$5
hello
                                      bulk string
$-1
                                              null bulk

Why it is designed this way:

  • First byte is the type. The parser branches once and knows the grammar of the rest.
  • Lengths are prefixed as decimal text. Binary-safe and still readable; converting a few digits is cheap compared to a syscall.
  • Requests are arrays of bulk strings, so the command parser never splits on spaces and keys may contain spaces. (Redis also accepts "inline" space-separated commands for telnet users.)
  • No escaping anywhere. Every variable-length thing has an explicit length.
  • Simple to implement in every language; a RESP parser is about 100 lines. RESP3 adds maps, sets, doubles and push messages while keeping the same shape.

tcpkv is "RESP for replies, inline commands with a length-prefixed value for requests". If you ever extend it, moving requests to the RESP array form is the natural step.

docs.title: 3.1 The parser (code/m04_tcpkv_parser.hpp)
docs.text:
Public interface:

enum class Op { Ping, Get, Set, Del, Exists, Quit };
struct Command { Op op; std::string key; std::string value; };
struct ParseError { std::string code, message; bool fatal = false; };
enum class ParseStatus { NeedMore, Ok, Error };

class Parser {
public:
    explicit Parser(size_t max_line = 1024, size_t max_value = 1u << 20);
    void feed(const char* data, size_t len);        // append bytes from recv()
    ParseStatus next(Command& cmd, ParseError& err); // pull one complete command
    size_t buffered() const;
};

The server loop that uses it (module 05 has the full version):

tcpkv::Parser parser;
char buf[4096];
for (;;) {
    size_t n = net::read_some(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
    if (n == 0) break;                                  // EOF
    parser.feed(buf, n);
    for (;;) {                                          // drain: one recv may hold many commands
        tcpkv::Command cmd; tcpkv::ParseError err;
        auto st = parser.next(cmd, err);
        if (st == tcpkv::ParseStatus::NeedMore) break;
        if (st == tcpkv::ParseStatus::Error) {
            net::write_all(fd, tcpkv::fmt_err(err.code, err.message));
            if (err.fatal) return;                      // cannot resync: close
            continue;
        }
        net::write_all(fd, execute(cmd));
    }
}

The heart of next():

case State::Line: {
    size_t nl = avail.find("\r\n");
    if (nl == npos) {
        if (avail.size() > max_line_) { err = {"ERR_TOO_LARGE", "line too long", true}; return Error; }
        return NeedMore;                                 // do not consume a partial line
    }
    std::string_view line = avail.substr(0, nl);
    pos_ += nl + 2;
    ParseStatus st = parse_line(line, cmd, err);        // copies out of `line` before compact()
    compact();
    if (st == NeedMore) continue;                       // SET: fall into Payload state
    return st;
}
case State::Payload: {
    if (avail.size() < payload_len_) return NeedMore;   // wait for the whole value
    pending_.value.assign(avail.data(), payload_len_);
    pos_ += payload_len_; state_ = State::PayloadCrlf;
    continue;
}
case State::PayloadCrlf: {
    if (avail.size() < 2) return NeedMore;
    bool ok = avail[0] == '\r' && avail[1] == '\n';
    pos_ += 2; compact(); state_ = State::Line;
    if (!ok) { err = {"ERR_SYNTAX", "payload not terminated by CRLF", true}; return Error; }
    cmd = std::move(pending_); return Ok;
}

docs.title: 3.2 The tests (code/m04_tcpkv_parser_test.cpp)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread m04_tcpkv_parser_test.cpp -o parser_test && ./parser_test
g++ -std=c++17 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined m04_tcpkv_parser_test.cpp -o parser_test_asan && ./parser_test_asan

The random-split fuzz in one picture:

std::string wire;  std::vector<Command> expected;
for (...) { Command c = random_command(rng); wire += fmt_cmd(c); expected.push_back(c); }
std::vector<size_t> chunks = random_partition(wire.size(), rng);   // many 1-byte chunks
Emitted e = run(wire, chunks);
assert(e.errs.empty() && e.cmds.size() == expected.size());
for (i...) assert(same(e.cmds[i], expected[i]));

docs.title: 3.3 Binary framing (code/m04_framing.cpp)
docs.text:
struct Header { uint32_t length; uint16_t type; uint16_t flags; };   // 8 bytes on the wire

void encode_header(const Header& h, unsigned char out[8]) {
    uint32_t len_be = htonl(h.length); uint16_t type_be = htons(h.type), flags_be = htons(h.flags);
    std::memcpy(out + 0, &len_be, 4);                 // memcpy, never pointer casts
    std::memcpy(out + 4, &type_be, 2);
    std::memcpy(out + 6, &flags_be, 2);
}
Header decode_header(const unsigned char in[8]) { /* memcpy out, ntohl/ntohs */ }

The program writes four frames one byte per send through a socketpair and decodes them with an incremental Decoder that refuses lengths above 16 MiB before allocating. Run it; then change write_all(sv[0], &c, 1) to send the whole wire at once and confirm the decoder does not care.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why the kernel cannot frame for you. TCP's job is a byte stream; it deliberately knows nothing about your messages. The PSH flag was meant as a hint ("deliver now") but Linux sets it on the last segment of every send and readers ignore it. Record-oriented transports exist (SCTP, SOCK_SEQPACKET on Unix sockets) but are not usable across the public internet, so every application protocol frames itself.

Parsing cost. A length-prefixed header is parsed with two or three loads and byte swaps, no scanning: nanoseconds. A delimiter parser must look at every byte (memchr is SIMD-accelerated and runs at tens of GB/s, so this is also cheap in practice). Converting decimal lengths costs a few nanoseconds per digit. None of this matters next to the syscall and the copy; protocol choice is about correctness, debuggability and bandwidth, not CPU, until you reach millions of messages per second per core.

Buffer management. The parser keeps one contiguous std::string per connection and compacts lazily. Alternatives: a ring buffer (no copies, but messages may wrap, which complicates string_view handoff), or a list of received chunks with a "gather" step. For a server with 10,000 idle connections, a 4 KB buffer each is 40 MB; sizing the initial buffer small and growing on demand matters at scale (module 06).

Zero-copy temptation. Returning string_views into the receive buffer avoids copying keys and values, but the view dies on the next feed/compact. The parser copies into Command strings to make ownership simple. For a 1 MiB value that is one extra copy; std::string::assign runs at memory bandwidth. Measure before optimising.

Integer parsing pitfalls. atoi/strtol accept leading whitespace, signs, and overflow silently or saturate. The parser's parse_uint accepts only ASCII digits, at most 10 of them, and nothing else. A length of -1 or 5 or 5x is rejected. Explicit is safer than a library function with a permissive grammar.

Strict aliasing and alignment. *(uint32_t*)(buf + 1) is undefined behaviour in C++ (and C): the compiler may assume a uint32_t* never aliases char storage written through a different type, and on ARM or SPARC the misaligned load traps. memcpy is the sanctioned way and compiles to a single mov on x86.

Windows note. htonl/ntohl live in <winsock2.h>; the semantics are identical. Windows is little-endian on every supported architecture, so the same swaps happen.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The "works on LAN, breaks on WAN" bug. A client parsed the reply with a single recv into a 4 KB buffer and then searched for \r\n. Replies over about 1460 bytes arrived in two segments across a WAN; the first recv had no \r\n, the client reported "protocol error" and disconnected. Fix: incremental parser. Every single time.
  • Desynchronisation. A length-prefixed protocol where the client once sent a payload shorter than its declared length (a bug in a rarely used code path). The server read the next request's header bytes as payload, then interpreted the following payload bytes as a header: a 2 GB length, bad_alloc, crash. Fixes: validate lengths against a sane maximum before allocating; on any framing inconsistency, close the connection rather than guess. The parser's fatal flag is that rule.
  • Escaping disasters. A delimiter protocol allowed values with the delimiter if "escaped". Three different clients implemented escaping three different ways. The fix was a flag day move to length-prefixed values. Design the protocol so escaping is unnecessary.
  • Version skew during rolling upgrade. New clients sent a new command; old servers replied with a generic error the client treated as "retry"; the clients retried in a tight loop and overwhelmed the servers. The fix: an ERR_UNKNOWN_CMD code that clients treat as permanent, and deploying servers before clients. Codes that classify retry behaviour are not optional.
  • Your RPC transport. Look at its header: how many bytes, which field is the length, byte order (probably host order because both ends are x86 Windows), max length check (is there one?), what happens on a bad header (does it close or try to continue?). Being able to describe your own protocol with this module's vocabulary is a strong interview signal.
  • Debugging with nc and tcpdump -A. A text protocol lets you type GET account:1001 into nc and see the reply. With tcpdump -A -i lo port 7000 you see every request and response in ASCII. This is worth real money at 3 AM, and is a legitimate argument for text protocols on internal tools.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run parser_test and framing. Then run parser_test under -fsanitize=address,undefined. Done when: both pass clean.

  2. (easy) Add a KEYS <prefix> request to the grammar (reply: *<n> followed by n bulk strings). Write the grammar lines and the formatting function. Done when: fmt_keys({"a","bb"}) produces *2 $1 a $2 bb .

  3. (medium) Write ReplyParser: an incremental parser for tcpkv replies (+, -, :, $), with the same feed/next shape, and test it with random splits. Done when: a 1000-reply stream fed byte-by-byte parses identically to being fed at once.

  4. (medium) Make the parser tolerant of multiple spaces between tokens and of a bare terminator, without breaking any existing test. Done when: all tests plus three new ones pass, and you can state what ambiguity (if any) the relaxed grammar introduced.

  5. (hard) Write a libFuzzer target LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput for the parser that splits the input at positions derived from the input bytes and feeds the rest. Run it for ten minutes with clang++ -fsanitize=fuzzer,address,undefined. Done when: either no crash, or you fixed one.

  6. (hard) Design a binary version of tcpkv: header {u32 len, u8 version, u8 opcode, u16 flags}, request body for each opcode, reply body including a u16 status. Write the design as a one-page spec with every field's size and byte order, and list what becomes easier and harder compared to the text version. Done when: a colleague could implement a client from the spec alone.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do you know where a message ends when reading from a TCP socket? A: TCP does not tell you; the protocol must. Either a length prefix (read the header, then exactly that many bytes), a delimiter (scan for it, with a maximum length), or fixed-size messages. Most real protocols combine a delimited or fixed header with length-prefixed bodies.

Q: Length prefix or delimiter: when would you pick each? A: Length prefix for binary payloads, high throughput, and when the receiver should allocate once; you must validate the length before using it. Delimiter for human-operable text protocols where nc debugging matters; you must cap the line length and avoid needing to escape the delimiter.

Q: Why must you not send a struct directly with send(&s, sizeof s)? A: Padding, alignment, field order and byte order depend on the compiler and architecture. It works only when both ends are identical builds. Serialise fields explicitly with a fixed byte order using memcpy and htonl/htons, never pointer casts.

Q: What is network byte order and what do htonl/ntohl do? A: Big-endian: most significant byte first. htonl converts a 32-bit host value to that order (byte swap on x86, no-op on big-endian hosts); ntohl converts back. Fix one byte order per protocol and apply it to every multi-byte integer on the wire.

Q: What does an incremental parser need that a normal one does not? A: Explicit state between calls (which part of a message it is in and how many bytes it still needs), a buffer of unconsumed bytes, the rule "never consume a partial unit", and bounded limits checked before allocation. It must produce identical output for any chunking of the same bytes.

Q: How do you handle a malformed request without killing the connection? A: If you still know where the next message starts (bad verb on a complete line), reply with a coded error and continue. If you do not (bad length, missing terminator after a payload, oversize line), reply if you can and close, because guessing risks interpreting payload as headers.

Q: Why does Redis RESP prefix bulk strings with their length if it is a text protocol? A: To be binary-safe without escaping while staying readable. The first byte gives the type, a decimal length gives the size, then raw bytes. A parser is a few dozen lines in any language.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Framing restores message boundaries TCP erased: length prefix, delimiter, fixed size, or hybrid.
  • Binary-safe values need lengths, not delimiters. Avoid escaping by design.
  • Serialise field by field with memcpy and htonl/htons. Never ship raw structs or cast pointers.
  • A protocol spec covers grammar, error codes that classify retryability, request matching, versioning, idempotency, limits.
  • tcpkv: GET/SET/DEL/EXISTS/PING/QUIT, replies typed by first byte (+ $ : -), SET value length-prefixed, all commands idempotent, line 1 KB and value 1 MiB limits.
  • Incremental parser = state machine + unconsumed buffer + "never consume a partial unit" + limits checked before allocation.
  • Recoverable error: skip one line and continue. Fatal error: lost sync, close the connection.
  • Test with random splits (same bytes, any chunking, same result) and random garbage (no crash, bounded memory). Run under ASan/UBSan.
  • RESP: type byte, decimal lengths, no escaping, trivial to implement; tcpkv borrows its replies.

docs.title: 05. Thread-per-connection and thread pools
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 04, and 04_Concurrency modules on threads, mutexes and condition variables

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
The echo server in module 03 serves one client at a time. The second client waits in the accept queue until the first hangs up. To serve many clients you need many "operators". The simplest way is to start a new thread for every connection: each thread runs the same blocking read-parse-write loop and the operating system interleaves them. This is thread-per-connection. It works well up to a few hundred or a few thousand connections and then runs into memory and scheduling costs.

The next step is to hire a fixed staff instead of a new person per caller: a thread pool of N workers and a queue of waiting connections. N bounds your resource use; the queue absorbs bursts; anything beyond that is turned away politely. This is how your employer's RPC server is built (a listener thread plus worker threads), how PostgreSQL works (one process per connection, which is why it needs pgbouncer), and how most Java servers worked for twenty years.

The hard parts are not the threads. They are the edges: a client that connects and never sends, a client that sends and never reads, and stopping the server without cutting off requests mid-flight. This module builds tcpkv v1 with all three handled.

docs.title: 2.1 Thread-per-connection
docs.text:
for (;;) {
    net::Fd c = net::accept_tcp(listener.get());
    std::thread(serve_connection, std::move(c)).detach();   // or keep and join at shutdown
}

Costs per thread on Linux:

  • Stack: 8 MB virtual by default (ulimit -s), but only touched pages are physical, typically tens of KB. 10,000 threads reserve 80 GB of address space, fine on 64-bit, impossible on 32-bit. You can lower it with pthread_attr_setstacksize (not through std::thread).
  • Kernel structures: a task_struct and kernel stack (16 KB), a few KB more.
  • Creation: clone() costs tens of microseconds. Creating a thread per connection for short-lived connections is noticeable; for long-lived connections it is nothing.
  • Scheduling: 10,000 runnable threads make the scheduler work hard; context switches cost about 1 to 5 microseconds each plus cache pollution. 10,000 idle threads blocked in recv cost almost nothing in CPU; they are just memory.

The C10K problem (Dan Kegel, 1999) asked how to serve 10,000 simultaneous connections on one machine. Thread-per-connection was the first answer to break, mainly from memory and scheduler overhead on machines of that time. The solutions were event loops (module 06). Today a 64-bit Linux box handles 10,000 mostly-idle threads without drama, and the practical limit of thread-per-connection is more like "when connections are many and mostly idle, you are wasting memory; when they are few and busy, threads are fine". Say that in an interview rather than "threads do not scale".

docs.title: 2.2 Thread pool + blocking I/O
docs.text:
+-----------+     bounded queue      +----------+
  clients  --->  | acceptor  | ---> [c][c][c][ ] ---> | worker 1 |  blocking read/parse/write
                 |  thread   |                        | worker 2 |
                 +-----------+                        |   ...    |
                       |  queue full?                 | worker N |
                       +--> reply -ERR_BUSY, close    +----------+
  • N workers = N concurrently served connections. For CPU-bound work, N near the core count. For work that blocks on a database, N much higher (hundreds) because most workers are waiting.
  • The queue bounds how many accepted-but-unserved connections wait. Bound it. An unbounded queue turns an overload into a memory and latency disaster; a bounded queue turns it into fast, explicit rejections that the client can retry elsewhere. This is load shedding.
  • Hand-off granularity: this design hands a whole connection to a worker, which then serves all its requests. Alternative: hand each request to the pool (requires an I/O thread that frames requests, which is module 06's design). Connection-per-worker is simpler and is what blocking I/O allows.

docs.title: 2.3 Connection lifecycle
docs.text:
accept -> [queue] -> worker takes it -> set options (NODELAY, timeouts)
  -> loop { wait readable (poll, 1 s tick) ; read ; parse ; execute ; write }
  -> ends on: EOF (client FIN) | QUIT | idle timeout | fatal protocol error | I/O error | shutdown
  -> remove from active set -> close (RAII)

Each exit reason is a counter. Operators look at those counters.

docs.title: 2.4 Timeouts: never block without a bound
docs.text:
A worker blocked forever on one client is a worker lost. Sources of forever:

  • Client connects and sends nothing (half-open, or a port scanner). Idle timeout on read.
  • Client sends half a message and stops. Same idle timeout; the parser just has partial state.
  • Client stops reading replies; our send fills the socket buffer and blocks. Send timeout.
  • The peer host died silently. Keepalive (module 02) or the idle timeout.

Two mechanisms:

  1. SO_RCVTIMEO / SO_SNDTIMEO: the blocking call returns EAGAIN after the timeout. Simple. Downside: the timeout applies per call, you cannot wake the thread early for shutdown, and SO_RCVTIMEO is ignored by some wrappers.
  2. poll(fd, POLLIN, timeout_ms) before each read: returns 0 on timeout without touching the socket. You can use a short tick (1 s) and check a stopping flag and the real deadline on each tick. The server uses this for reads and SO_SNDTIMEO for writes.

Deadlines, not durations: compute deadline = now + idle_timeout once per received byte, compare now >= deadline on each tick. Repeated "sleep 30 s" style logic drifts and makes shutdown slow.

docs.title: 2.5 Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
The sequence that avoids cutting requests in half:

  1. Stop accepting. Close or shutdown() the listener. New connection attempts get RST (ECONNREFUSED), which is a clear signal to a load balancer or retrying client. If a load balancer is in front, first fail the health check and wait for it to stop routing (module 13).
  2. Tell the workers. Set stopping. Idle workers exit. Busy workers finish the current request, then stop at the next tick (they may send a final "shutting down" error to an idle client).
  3. Drain with a deadline (10 to 30 s). Wait for the active-connection count to reach zero.
  4. Force what remains: shutdown(fd, SHUT_RDWR) on each active fd makes its blocked recv return 0 and its blocked send fail, so the worker exits. Then join everything.
  5. Report counters, flush logs, exit 0.

Signal handling in a multithreaded process: block SIGINT/SIGTERM in the main thread before creating any other thread (they inherit the mask), then sigwait in main. No async-signal-safety worries, no volatile sig_atomic_t flags, no self-pipe. This is the cleanest pattern on Linux. (Windows: SetConsoleCtrlHandler or a service control handler sets an event; the main thread waits on it.)

Why shutdown() wakes a blocked reader when close() does not: close() only drops this fd; if another thread is inside recv on it, that thread holds a reference and keeps sleeping (and the fd number can be reused by a new accept, so the sleeping thread now reads from a different connection, which is a nasty bug). shutdown() acts on the socket itself.

docs.title: 2.6 Backlog and somaxconn
docs.text: listen(fd, backlog): the accept queue holds completed handshakes until you call accept. If the acceptor thread is slow (or you have one thread doing accept and serve, like module 03), the queue fills, new SYNs are dropped, clients retry after 1 s and 3 s: "connecting takes exactly 1 or 3 seconds sometimes". Set backlog to 1024 or more on a busy server, and keep the acceptor thread doing nothing but accept and enqueue. The kernel caps it at net.core.somaxconn (4096 on kernels since 5.4; 128 on older ones, which bit many people).

docs.title: 2.7 File descriptor limits
docs.text:
Each connection is an fd. ulimit -n (soft limit, 1024 by default on many systems) caps the process. At the limit, accept fails with EMFILE; the pending connection stays in the accept queue and the listener stays readable, so a naive loop spins. Handle EMFILE by sleeping briefly and logging loudly. Raise the limit with ulimit -n 65536 in the start script, or LimitNOFILE=65536 in a systemd unit, or setrlimit(RLIMIT_NOFILE) at startup up to the hard limit. Also check /proc/sys/fs/file-max (system-wide) and /proc/sys/fs/nr_open.

Windows has no fd limit of this kind; sockets are kernel handles, limited by non-paged pool and the MaxUserPort/dynamic port range for outbound connections.

docs.title: 3.1 tcpkv v1 (code/m05_threadpool_tcpkv_server.cpp)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 m05_threadpool_tcpkv_server.cpp -o tcpkv
./tcpkv 7000 16 &
printf 'SET a 5\r\nhello\r\nGET a\r\nEXISTS a\r\nDEL a\r\nGET a\r\nQUIT\r\n' | nc -q1 127.0.0.1 7000
# +OK  $5 hello  :1  :1  $-1  +OK
