python3 m05_loadtest.py --port 7000 -c 50 -n 2000
python3 m05_loadtest.py --port 7000 -c 50 -n 2000 --pipeline 32     # far higher throughput: why?
kill -TERM %1                                                       # graceful shutdown + report

The store: std::unordered_map behind a std::shared_mutex (readers share, writers exclude).

The worker loop:

void worker_main(Server& srv, int) {
    for (;;) {
        net::Fd conn;
        {
            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(srv.q_mu);
            srv.q_cv.wait(lk, [&] { return srv.stopping.load() || !srv.queue.empty(); });
            if (srv.queue.empty()) return;              // stopping and drained
            conn = std::move(srv.queue.front()); srv.queue.pop_front();
        }
        serve_connection(srv, std::move(conn));
    }
}

Serving one connection, with every wait bounded:

auto deadline = Clock::now() + srv.idle_timeout;
for (;;) {
    if (!net::wait_readable(fd, 1000)) {                 // 1 s tick: re-check flags, no busy loop
        if (srv.stopping) { net::write_all(fd, fmt_err("ERR_SHUTDOWN", "...")); return; }
        if (Clock::now() >= deadline) { ++srv.idle_timeouts; return; }
        continue;
    }
    size_t n = net::read_some(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
    if (n == 0) return;                                  // client FIN
    deadline = Clock::now() + srv.idle_timeout;
    parser.feed(buf, n);
    out.clear();
    for (;;) {                                           // drain all complete commands
        auto st = parser.next(cmd, err);
        if (st == NeedMore) break;
        if (st == Error) { out += fmt_err(err.code, err.message); if (err.fatal) {quit = true; break;} continue; }
        out += execute(srv, cmd);
        if (cmd.op == Op::Quit) { quit = true; break; }
    }
    if (!out.empty()) net::write_all(fd, out);           // ONE send for the whole batch
    if (quit) return;
}

Notice the batching: all replies for one read go out in one send. With --pipeline 32 the load tester shows the effect: fewer syscalls, fewer packets, much higher throughput. This is the cheapest optimisation in network programming and the reason Redis pipelining exists.

The acceptor with load shedding:

std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(srv.q_mu);
if (srv.queue.size() >= srv.queue_cap) {
    lk.unlock(); ++srv.rejected;
    net::write_all(conn.get(), fmt_err("ERR_BUSY", "server overloaded, retry later"));
    continue;                                            // conn closes; client knows why
}
srv.queue.push_back(std::move(conn)); lk.unlock(); srv.q_cv.notify_one();

The shutdown sequence in main is section 2.5 line by line: sigwait, shutdown(listener), join acceptor, stopping = true, notify_all, reject queued connections with a message, drain with a 10 s deadline, shutdown(SHUT_RDWR) the stragglers, join workers, print counters.

docs.title: 3.2 The load tester (code/m05_loadtest.py)
docs.text:
Python with one thread per connection. Each round sends SET k v and GET k, parses the replies with an incremental ReplyParser (yes, the Python client also needs one), and checks the value round-trips. --pipeline N sends N rounds before reading. Reports ops/s and p50/p90/p99.

Experiments worth running:

  • -c 4 -n 5000 vs -c 64 -n 500 with 8 workers: see queueing when connections exceed workers (connections beyond 8 wait in the queue until an earlier one finishes all its rounds).
  • -c 300 with queue_cap 256 and 8 workers: see ERR_BUSY rejections in the error list.
  • Connect with nc and type nothing: watch it get closed after the idle timeout.
  • kill -TERM during a load test: the test reports a few ERR_SHUTDOWN errors, no hangs, no truncated replies.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What a blocked thread costs. A thread in recv is in state S (interruptible sleep) on the socket's wait queue. It consumes no CPU. Its kernel stack (16 KB) and touched user stack pages stay resident. When data arrives, the softirq handler wakes it (wake_up_interruptible), the scheduler puts it on a run queue, and it runs on the next tick or immediately if a CPU is idle. Wake-up latency is typically a few microseconds to tens of microseconds; with thousands of threads waking for small messages, this scheduler work dominates, which is the real C10K cost.

Condition variable hand-off. notify_one wakes one worker; it must re-acquire the mutex, so the acceptor should unlock before notifying (the code does) to avoid the woken thread immediately blocking on the mutex ("hurry up and wait"). With many idle workers and bursts of connections, notify_one per connection is right; notify_all would cause a thundering herd.

shared_mutex trade-off. Reader-writer locks cost more than a plain mutex when the critical section is tiny (a hash lookup) because they touch more atomics. They win when reads are long or heavily concurrent. For a real KV store you shard the map into 16 or 64 stripes each with its own mutex (module 12 at micro scale). Measure with perf before choosing.

False sharing in counters. Six std::atomic<uint64_t> counters declared next to each other share a cache line; every increment from any worker bounces that line between cores. For a learning server it does not matter. In a hot path, pad counters to 64 bytes or keep per-thread counters and sum on read.

Why the 1 s poll tick instead of blocking forever. A thread blocked in recv with no timeout can be woken only by data, a signal, or shutdown() from another thread. Periodic polling costs one syscall per idle connection per second, trivial at thousands of connections, and makes deadlines and shutdown checks local to the thread with no cross-thread signalling. At 100,000 idle connections it becomes measurable and you want epoll with a timer wheel (module 06).

The fd-reuse race. Thread A is blocked in recv(fd 7). Thread B calls close(7). The kernel keeps the socket alive until A's recv returns (it holds a reference), but the number 7 is free and the next accept may return 7 for a new client. If A then wakes and the code uses fd 7 again, it talks to the wrong client. Rules: only the owning thread closes; other threads use shutdown() to wake it; the active-set bookkeeping in the server removes the fd before close runs.

Windows mapping. The same architecture maps directly: a listener thread calling accept, worker threads with recv/send, WSAPoll or select with timeout for the tick, shutdown(SD_BOTH) to wake a blocked reader, an event set by the console control handler for shutdown. Windows also has a built-in thread pool (CreateThreadpoolIo) that integrates with IOCP, which is module 06's territory.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The slow-reader deadlock. Client sends many requests without reading replies. Server replies fill the client's receive buffer, then the server's send buffer; the server's send blocks. The client is blocked in its own send because the server stopped reading (its worker is stuck in send). Both wait forever. This is why the server has a send timeout and why robust clients read and write on separate threads or use non-blocking I/O. Your RPC transport: does the server ever block on send to a client? What bounds it?
  • Worker starvation by idle connections. A monitoring tool opened a connection per check and never closed them. With 16 workers and 16 idle monitors, real clients waited in the queue forever. The idle timeout fixed it; the queue-wait metric found it.
  • Unbounded queue, 40 GB RSS. A server queued incoming requests without limit during a downstream slowdown. Memory climbed until the OOM killer took the process, which dropped every queued request anyway. A bounded queue with fast rejection would have shed 10% of the load and kept 90% working. Bound every queue.
  • Shutdown that took 15 minutes. SIGTERM handler set a flag; workers checked it only between connections, and connections were long-lived. systemd waited 90 s then SIGKILLed, cutting requests in half. The fix is this module's sequence: tick-based checks, drain deadline, forced shutdown() on stragglers.
  • somaxconn 128 on an old kernel. During a traffic spike the accept queue overflowed; clients saw 1 to 3 s connect delays; nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows was climbing. Raising backlog in the code and somaxconn on the host fixed it.
  • ulimit -n 1024 in the systemd unit. A service tested fine, then in production hit EMFILE at 1,000 connections and spun at 100% CPU logging accept errors. LimitNOFILE=65536 and an EMFILE backoff fixed both halves.
  • How this maps to the banking server. Listener thread, worker pool, blocking I/O per connection, a per-connection write mutex: tcpkv v1 is a small version of it. The questions to take back: what is the queue bound, where are the timeouts, what does shutdown do with in-flight loans, and what counters exist.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run tcpkv with 2 workers. Connect three nc sessions. Observe that the third gets no replies until one of the first two quits. Done when: you can explain which queue it sat in and how you would detect this in production.

  2. (easy) Connect with nc, type nothing, wait for the idle timeout (lower it to 5 s for the test). Done when: nc exits and the server's idle_timeouts counter increments at shutdown.

  3. (medium) Add a per-connection max_commands or a per-connection rate limit (module 09 has a token bucket). Done when: a load test with --pipeline 100 gets ERR_BUSY replies for the excess instead of unbounded service.

  4. (medium) Reproduce the slow-reader deadlock: write a Python client that sends 100,000 SET commands without ever reading. Observe the server worker blocked in send, then observe the send timeout free it. Remove set_send_timeout and observe the permanent hang. Done when: you have seen both behaviours in ss -tanp (Send-Q full on both sides).

  5. (hard) Replace connection-per-worker with request-per-worker: one I/O thread per connection that only reads and frames, a shared request queue, a pool that executes and writes replies. Keep replies in order per connection. Done when: the load test passes and you can state what got better and what got more complicated.

  6. (hard) Add SIGHUP handling that re-reads a config file (idle timeout, queue cap) without restarting, and SIGUSR1 that prints the counters. Done when: both work during a load test with no dropped connections.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the C10K problem and does it still matter? A: Serving 10,000 concurrent connections on one machine, which broke thread-per-connection designs in 1999 because of memory and scheduler overhead. Modern 64-bit Linux handles 10,000 mostly-idle threads, but the lesson stands: many idle connections waste memory and wake-up work with threads, and event loops (epoll) are the answer at 100K+ connections.

Q: Thread per connection versus thread pool: when each? A: Thread per connection for few, long-lived, busy connections; it is simple and the OS schedules fairly. Thread pool when you must bound resources and shed load: N workers, bounded queue, explicit rejection beyond that. Both block one thread per active connection; event loops decouple that.

Q: How do you shut down a server gracefully? A: Stop accepting (close the listener, fail the health check first if behind a load balancer), signal workers to finish current requests, drain with a deadline, force-close stragglers with shutdown() so blocked reads return, join threads, flush logs, exit 0. Handle signals via a blocked mask and sigwait in the main thread.

Q: Why shutdown() and not close() to interrupt a thread blocked in recv? A: close only drops the caller's reference; the blocked thread holds another and keeps sleeping, and the fd number can be reused by a new accept, so the sleeper may later read the wrong connection. shutdown acts on the socket and makes the blocked recv return 0 immediately.

Q: What does the backlog argument do? A: Caps the queue of completed connections waiting for accept (also capped by somaxconn). When full, new SYNs are dropped and clients retry after 1 s and 3 s, showing up as sporadic connect delays. Set it high and keep the accept loop fast.

Q: Why bound the work queue? A: An unbounded queue converts overload into unbounded memory growth and latency; eventually everything fails. A bounded queue rejects the excess fast with a clear error, so most requests still succeed and clients can retry elsewhere. Load shedding beats collapse.

Q: Why timeouts on both read and write? A: Read timeout frees workers from idle or half-sending clients. Write timeout frees workers from clients that stopped reading, which otherwise causes a deadlock when both sides are blocked in send. Any unbounded wait is a resource leak waiting for the right client.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Thread-per-connection: simple, fine for hundreds of busy connections; costs stack, kernel structures and scheduler work per thread.
  • Thread pool + bounded queue: N concurrent connections, explicit rejection beyond, load shedding.
  • Connection lifecycle ends on EOF, QUIT, idle timeout, fatal protocol error, I/O error or shutdown; count each.
  • Bound every wait: poll with a tick for reads, SO_SNDTIMEO for writes, deadlines not durations.
  • Graceful shutdown: stop accepting, signal, drain with deadline, shutdown() stragglers, join.
  • Block signals before creating threads and sigwait in main.
  • shutdown() wakes blocked readers; close() does not and invites fd reuse bugs.
  • Backlog and somaxconn size the accept queue; overflow shows as 1 or 3 s connect delays.
  • ulimit -n caps fds; EMFILE needs backoff; fix the leak.
  • Batch replies per read into one send; pipelining multiplies throughput for free.

docs.title: 06. Non-blocking I/O, epoll and event loops
docs.text: Time: ~3.5 hours Prerequisites: 03, 04, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
In module 05 each connection had a thread that sat waiting for it. The thread's stack remembered "where we were" for that connection. An event loop flips this: one thread asks the kernel "which of my 10,000 sockets has something for me right now?", gets a short list, handles each one without ever waiting, and asks again. Because the thread never waits on a single socket, every socket must be non-blocking: a read with no data returns EAGAIN instead of sleeping.

The analogy: a restaurant with one waiter and a board of lights. Instead of standing at each table (thread per connection), the waiter looks at the board, sees which tables lit their lamp, serves exactly those, and looks again. The waiter must never get stuck at one table, and must write down on a notepad anything half-finished (the order that is half taken) because there is no "standing there" to remember it. That notepad is the per-connection state object.

epoll is Linux's board of lights. select and poll are older, slower boards. Windows has a different design, IOCP, where instead of lights the kitchen delivers finished plates to the waiter. This module writes an epoll echo server from scratch, then shows how libuv, Boost.Asio, io_uring and IOCP fit the same two patterns.

docs.title: 2.1 Non-blocking sockets
docs.text:
fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, O_NONBLOCK) or accept4(..., SOCK_NONBLOCK) / socket(..., SOCK_NONBLOCK). Then:

  • recv with nothing buffered returns -1 with EAGAIN (same value as EWOULDBLOCK on Linux).
  • send with a full send buffer writes what fits (possibly 0 bytes, then EAGAIN).
  • accept with an empty queue returns EAGAIN.
  • connect returns -1 with EINPROGRESS; completion is signalled by writability; the result is read with getsockopt(SO_ERROR).

EAGAIN means "not now, ask the readiness API when to try again". It is the normal case, not an error.

docs.title: 2.2 select, poll, epoll
docs.text:
select: pass three bitmaps (read, write, error) of fds and a timeout. O(max fd) to build and scan; FD_SETSIZE is 1024 on glibc. Portable, and on Windows fd_set is an array of 64 sockets. Do not use for servers.

poll: pass an array of pollfd {fd, events, revents}. No 1024 limit, but O(n) in user and kernel space on every call: with 10,000 connections the kernel walks 10,000 entries per call even if one is ready. Fine for a handful of fds (module 05 uses it for one fd with a timeout).

epoll: the kernel keeps the interest list. You register fds once (epoll_ctl ADD), then epoll_wait returns only the ready ones. O(ready), not O(registered). Linux only. BSD/macOS have kqueue with the same idea; Solaris has event ports.

int ep = epoll_create1(EPOLL_CLOEXEC);
epoll_event ev{}; ev.events = EPOLLIN | EPOLLET; ev.data.ptr = conn;    // data is yours: ptr or u64
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fd, &ev);
epoll_event out[256];
int n = epoll_wait(ep, out, 256, timeout_ms);       // -1 = block until something is ready
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) handle(out[i].data.ptr, out[i].events);

Events: EPOLLIN readable (or EOF), EPOLLOUT writable, EPOLLRDHUP peer half-closed, EPOLLERR and EPOLLHUP always reported even if not requested. Modifiers: EPOLLET, EPOLLONESHOT, EPOLLEXCLUSIVE.

docs.title: 2.3 Level-triggered vs edge-triggered
docs.text:
Level-triggered (LT, default): "report this fd as ready as long as it is ready". If data is buffered and you read only some of it, the next epoll_wait reports it again. Forgiving. Like poll. Cost: a readable fd you do not fully drain is reported every iteration; and a thread pool sharing one LT epoll gets thundering-herd wakeups for the same fd.

Edge-triggered (ET, EPOLLET): "report once when the fd becomes ready". If 10 KB arrive and you read 4 KB, you will not be told again until more bytes arrive. Rule: after an ET event, loop reading until EAGAIN. Same for accept: loop until EAGAIN. Same for write: when EPOLLOUT fires, write until EAGAIN or your buffer is empty. Miss the rule and a connection hangs with data in the kernel buffer, forever, with no event: the classic ET bug.

ET gives fewer wakeups and works well with multiple threads on one epoll fd (each edge wakes one waiter). The server in this module uses ET everywhere to make the drain rule a habit.

EPOLLONESHOT: after reporting an fd once, disable it until you EPOLL_CTL_MOD it back on. Use case: a pool of threads calling epoll_wait on the same epoll fd; ONESHOT guarantees one fd is handled by one thread at a time, and the thread re-arms when done. Cost: one epoll_ctl per event.

docs.title: 2.4 The reactor pattern
docs.text:
+--------------------------------------------------+
          |  loop:                                           |
          |    events = epoll_wait()                          |
          |    for each event: dispatch to handler(conn, ev)  |
          +--------------------------------------------------+
 handlers:   on_accept       on_readable       on_writable       on_timer      on_wake(eventfd)
             accept until    recv until        send until        sweep idle    stop
             EAGAIN, add     EAGAIN, parse,    EAGAIN or empty,  conns
             to epoll        queue replies     update interest

A reactor demultiplexes readiness events and calls handlers that perform the I/O themselves. Rules for a correct reactor:

  1. Handlers never block: no blocking I/O, no sleep, no blocking DNS, no long computation. One slow handler stalls every connection. Offload CPU-heavy or blocking work to a thread pool and bring the result back through an eventfd or a pipe.
  2. All per-connection state lives in an object the event's data.ptr points to.
  3. Writes go to a per-connection output buffer first; try to flush immediately; if the kernel buffer is full (EAGAIN), register EPOLLOUT and finish on the writable event. Never block.
  4. Register EPOLLOUT only while you have pending output. A socket is writable almost always, so a permanently registered EPOLLOUT with ET is harmless but with LT spins the loop at 100% CPU.
  5. Backpressure: if a connection's output buffer grows past a high-water mark (the peer is not reading), stop reading from it (remove EPOLLIN). TCP flow control then slows the peer. Resume when the buffer drains below a low-water mark. Without this, one bad client eats all your memory.
  6. Closing inside a handler invalidates the Conn object; any later event in the same batch for that fd must detect this (look it up again) before touching it.

docs.title: 2.5 Per-connection state
docs.text:
struct Conn {
    int fd;
    std::string out;            // what we owe the peer
    tcpkv::Parser parser;       // (for tcpkv) partial request state
    bool peer_closed;           // EOF seen; close after flushing
    bool want_write;            // EPOLLOUT registered
    bool reading_paused;        // EPOLLIN removed for backpressure
    Clock::time_point last_active;
};

This is exactly what the thread's stack held implicitly in module 05: the parser's partial state, the unsent bytes, the deadline. Event loops force you to write it down, which is both the cost (more code) and the benefit (you can inspect it, count it, and hold 100,000 of them in 100 MB).

docs.title: 2.6 eventfd and timerfd
docs.text:
An event loop blocked in epoll_wait can only be woken by an fd. Linux provides fds for things that are not sockets:

  • eventfd: a 64-bit counter. write adds, read returns and zeroes (or decrements with EFD_SEMAPHORE). Signal handlers (write is async-signal-safe) and other threads use it to wake the loop: "shutdown", "a worker finished job 42, pick up the result".
  • timerfd: fires at an absolute or periodic time. Register it in epoll and you have timers without computing epoll_wait timeouts by hand. For many per-connection timeouts you keep a timer wheel or a min-heap of deadlines and arm one timerfd (or the epoll_wait timeout) for the earliest.
  • signalfd: receive signals as fd events; an alternative to the eventfd-from-handler trick.
  • pidfd, inotify, and friends: everything is an fd, so everything fits one loop.

docs.title: 2.7 Multi-threading an event loop
docs.text:
Options, from simple to complex:

  1. One loop, one thread (this module's server, Redis before 6.0, Node.js). Scales to a core's worth of work. CPU work goes to a pool.
  2. One loop per thread, SO_REUSEPORT: N independent loops each with its own listener on the same port; the kernel spreads connections. No sharing between loops (nginx workers, Envoy).
  3. One acceptor loop, N worker loops: acceptor hands fds to workers round-robin via a queue plus eventfd (Netty, Boost.Asio with multiple io_contexts, libuv does not do this natively).
  4. One epoll fd, N threads calling epoll_wait with EPOLLONESHOT or EPOLLEXCLUSIVE: shared state must be locked; rarely worth it.

docs.title: 2.8 When event loops beat thread pools, and when they do not
docs.text:
Event loops win when connections are many and mostly idle (chat, push notifications, long-poll, 100,000 branch terminals with a request a minute): memory per connection is a few KB instead of a thread, and no scheduler work for idle connections. They also win for I/O-bound proxies that shuffle bytes between sockets.

Thread pools win when each request does blocking or CPU-heavy work (a database call through a blocking driver, a loan calculation, decrypting a file) and connections are few hundred. The blocking driver forces a thread anyway, and the code is simpler to read and debug (a stack trace tells the whole story).

The combination is standard: an event loop for network I/O and framing, a thread pool for request execution, eventfd to return results. That is how a modern version of your RPC server would look.

docs.title: 2.9 io_uring
docs.text: epoll tells you readiness; you still do the recv/send syscalls. io_uring (Linux 5.1+) submits operations (recv into this buffer, accept, send) through a shared ring in memory and collects completions from another ring, often with zero syscalls per operation under load. That is a proactor: you ask for the operation and are told when it is done. Benefits: fewer syscalls, batching, true async file I/O (epoll never worked for regular files), zero-copy options. Costs: newer, more complex API (use liburing), security hardening still evolving, kernel-version sensitive. Know what it is and that it is the direction Linux is heading.

docs.title: 2.10 Windows IOCP: proactor from the start
docs.text:
Windows never had a good readiness API (select is limited, WSAPoll arrived late). Its native model is overlapped I/O with I/O completion ports:

CreateIoCompletionPort()                         // the port
CreateIoCompletionPort(socket, port, key, 0)      // associate a socket
WSARecv(socket, &buf, ..., &overlapped, NULL)     // start a receive INTO YOUR BUFFER; returns at once
...
GetQueuedCompletionStatus(port, &bytes, &key, &overlapped, timeout)   // worker threads block here
// => "the receive you started into buffer X completed with N bytes"

Differences from epoll: you hand the kernel the buffer up front (so memory is pinned per pending operation, which is why you keep only one or two receives outstanding per connection); the kernel wakes one of N threads blocked on the port (built-in thread pool integration, with a concurrency limit); you get completions, not readiness. AcceptEx, ConnectEx, TransmitFile are the overlapped versions of accept/connect/sendfile. Your Windows RPC server could be IOCP-based or thread-per-connection with blocking recv; find out which, because IOCP vs blocking changes every answer about its scalability.

Reactor (epoll, kqueue, poll): "tell me when I can do it, I do it". Proactor (IOCP, io_uring): "do it and tell me when it is done".

docs.title: 2.11 libuv and Boost.Asio
docs.text:
libuv (Node.js's loop, written in C): a reactor on Linux (epoll), kqueue on macOS, and IOCP on Windows, exposed with one callback API (uv_read_start(stream, alloc_cb, read_cb)). Internally on Windows it emulates readiness semantics on top of completions. One loop per thread; a thread pool for blocking work (uv_queue_work); uv_async_send is its eventfd.

Boost.Asio (also standalone Asio, and the model behind C++ Networking TS): a proactor interface everywhere. socket.async_read_some(buffer, handler) means "read into this buffer and call the handler with bytes_transferred". On Linux it is implemented over epoll (reactor) by doing the recv for you when the fd is readable; on Windows it maps directly onto IOCP; recent versions can use io_uring. io_context::run() is the loop; strand serialises handlers for one connection when several threads run the context; steady_timer replaces timerfd; post/dispatch replace eventfd. If you write new C++ network code at work, Asio is the default choice; after this module you know what it does underneath.

docs.title: 3.1 The epoll echo server (code/m06_epoll_echo_server.cpp)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 m06_epoll_echo_server.cpp -o epoll_echo
./epoll_echo 7000 &
python3 m05_loadtest.py --echo --port 7000 -c 500 -n 200      # 500 connections, one thread
seq 1 100000 | ./echo_client 127.0.0.1 7000
ss -tanp | grep -c 7000                                        # count connections during the test
kill -INT %1                                                   # eventfd shutdown, prints counters

Accept until EAGAIN (edge-triggered rule):

void on_accept() {
    for (;;) {
        int cfd = accept4(listen_fd, nullptr, nullptr, SOCK_NONBLOCK | SOCK_CLOEXEC);
        if (cfd < 0) {
            if (errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK) return;     // queue drained
            if (errno == EINTR || errno == ECONNABORTED) continue;
            /* EMFILE etc: log, return */
        }
        auto c = std::make_unique<Conn>(); c->fd = cfd; c->last_active = Clock::now();
        epoll_event ev{}; ev.events = EPOLLIN | EPOLLET | EPOLLRDHUP; ev.data.ptr = c.get();
        epoll_ctl(epfd, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, cfd, &ev);
        conns.emplace(cfd, std::move(c));
    }
}

Read until EAGAIN, with backpressure:

void on_readable(Conn& c) {
    char buf[64 * 1024];
    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = recv(c.fd, buf, sizeof buf, 0);
        if (n < 0) { if (errno == EINTR) continue;
                     if (errno == EAGAIN) break;              // drained: wait for the next edge
                     close_conn(c); return; }
        if (n == 0) { c.peer_closed = true; break; }          // EOF: flush, then close
        c.out.append(buf, n);
        if (c.out.size() >= kHighWater) { c.reading_paused = true; epoll_update(c); break; }
    }
    if (!flush(c)) { close_conn(c); return; }
    if (c.peer_closed && c.out.empty()) close_conn(c);
}

Flush, registering EPOLLOUT only while needed:

bool flush(Conn& c) {
    while (!c.out.empty()) {
        ssize_t n = send(c.fd, c.out.data(), c.out.size(), MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        if (n < 0) { if (errno == EINTR) continue;
                     if (errno == EAGAIN) break;              // kernel buffer full: wait for EPOLLOUT
                     return false; }                          // EPIPE / ECONNRESET
        c.out.erase(0, n);
    }
    bool need_out = !c.out.empty();
    bool resume_read = c.reading_paused && c.out.size() < kHighWater / 2;
    if (need_out != c.want_write || resume_read) { c.want_write = need_out; if (resume_read) c.reading_paused = false; epoll_update(c); }
    return true;
}

The shutdown path: SIGINT handler writes 1 to an eventfd; the loop sees it readable and sets running = false. The timerfd fires every second and closes connections idle for 60 s. Both are just more fds in the same epoll.

The dangling-pointer guard in the loop: a Conn closed by the timer or by an earlier event in the same epoll_wait batch may still appear later in that batch. Before using data.ptr, the loop looks up conns.find(fd) and checks the pointer matches.

docs.title: 3.2 From echo to tcpkv on epoll
docs.text: Replace c.out.append(buf, n) with: c.parser.feed(buf, n); drain parser; c.out += replies. The Store from module 05 works as is (single thread: no lock needed). That is the whole change; the parser's feed/next design was made for this.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What epoll keeps. epoll_create allocates an eventpoll with a red-black tree of registered fds (epitems) and a ready list. EPOLL_CTL_ADD inserts into the tree and hooks a callback into the target socket's wait queue. When data arrives, the socket's wakeup callback (ep_poll_callback) runs in softirq context and links the epitem onto the ready list, waking epoll_wait if it is sleeping. epoll_wait copies ready items to user space; in LT mode it re-checks each item's readiness and re-queues it if still ready; in ET mode it does not. That is the entire LT/ET difference, and why ET is cheaper: no re-poll.

Why ET needs the drain loop. The callback fires when the socket state changes (new skb arrives). If you leave data in the buffer and no new segment arrives, nothing fires. With LT, epoll_wait itself re-polls the socket and re-reports.

Readiness is a hint, not a promise. A socket reported readable may return EAGAIN if another thread read it first, or in rare kernel paths (checksum failure after readiness was signalled). Always handle EAGAIN even after an event.

Why EPOLLOUT is almost always true. The send buffer is usually not full, so a registered EPOLLOUT with LT fires on every epoll_wait: the loop spins. Register it only when a send returned EAGAIN, and deregister when the buffer drains. The server does exactly this.

Cost model. epoll_wait returning N events costs one syscall plus O(N). With 100,000 idle connections and 1,000 active, each loop iteration touches 1,000 items; poll would touch 100,000. epoll_ctl is a syscall per modification; ET reduces modifications because interest rarely changes. Measured on commodity hardware, a single epoll thread handles hundreds of thousands of small messages per second; the ceiling is syscall cost (which io_uring attacks) and per-message work, not epoll itself.

Memory per connection. A Conn with an empty std::string and a parser is a few hundred bytes; the kernel's tcp_sock plus socket buffers (autotuned, starting at 16 to 128 KB when data flows, nearly nothing when idle) dominate. 100,000 idle connections fit in a few GB mostly because of kernel structures, which is why tcp_rmem/tcp_wmem minimums matter at that scale.

Thundering herd and EPOLLEXCLUSIVE. Several threads waiting on the same LT epoll fd for a listener all wake on one connection; one wins accept, the rest get EAGAIN. EPOLLEXCLUSIVE (Linux 4.5) wakes only one. SO_REUSEPORT sidesteps it with separate listeners.

IOCP internals. The completion port is a kernel queue; GetQueuedCompletionStatus threads block on it in LIFO order (the most recently active thread is reused: warm cache) and the port enforces a concurrency limit (threads actively running, default = CPUs); a thread that blocks lets another run. The buffer you pass to WSARecv is locked in physical memory until completion, so 10,000 outstanding 64 KB receives pin 640 MB; the standard trick is a zero-byte receive to be told "data is here" and then a normal recv, which turns IOCP back into a readiness model.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The ET hang. A server using EPOLLET read exactly one recv per event. Under load two requests arrived in one segment; the second sat in the kernel buffer with no new event; the client timed out. Reproduced only with pipelining or on a WAN. Rule: drain until EAGAIN.
  • 100% CPU doing nothing. EPOLLOUT registered permanently in LT mode. Every epoll_wait returned immediately with every connection writable. Register EPOLLOUT only with pending output.
  • One slow handler. A handler did a blocking DNS lookup (getaddrinfo) for logging. Each lookup took 5 s when the DNS server was flaky; every connection on the loop froze for 5 s. Never block in a handler; offload to a thread or use an async resolver.
  • Memory explosion from one client. A client sent 1 GB of requests and never read replies. The server buffered 1 GB of replies and was OOM-killed. High-water mark and pause reading: TCP flow control then stops the client at the kernel level.
  • Use-after-free in the event batch. Timer closed an idle connection; a later event in the same batch pointed at the freed Conn. Crash once a week. Fix: look the fd up again before use, or defer destruction to the end of the loop iteration (a "to delete" list).
  • fd reuse within a batch. A Conn is closed and accept returns the same fd number in the same iteration; a stale event for the old connection now matches the new one by fd. The pointer check (it->second.get() != &c) catches it; generation counters are the general solution.
  • Where this meets your work. If the Windows server is blocking thread-per-connection, the IOCP version is the "how would you make it handle 50,000 branch terminals" answer. If it already uses IOCP, map its completion handler and per-connection context to this module's Conn and handlers; you will find the same high-water-mark and dangling-context problems.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run the epoll echo server with the load tester at -c 1000. Compare RSS (ps -o rss) and thread count with the thread-pool server at the same connection count. Done when: you can state the per-connection memory of each design from your measurements.

  2. (easy) Break the ET rule: change on_readable to do exactly one recv. Run the load test with --pipeline 16. Done when: you observe hangs and can explain them from the kernel's point of view. Restore the loop.

  3. (medium) Convert the echo server to tcpkv: add a Parser per Conn, the Store, and reply formatting. Run m05_loadtest.py against it. Done when: the load test passes at -c 500.

  4. (medium) Add a non-blocking connect to the tcpkv client side: start the connect, register EPOLLOUT, read SO_ERROR on the event, then proceed. Test against a black-hole address with a 3 s timer. Done when: it fails cleanly at 3 s instead of hanging.

  5. (hard) Add a thread pool for "slow" commands: a fake SLOW <ms> command that sleeps in a worker and returns +OK. The worker must post the reply back to the loop via an eventfd and a mutex-protected queue, and the reply must be written on the loop thread. Done when: 100 SLOW 1000 requests on 100 connections complete in about 1 s total with 16 workers, while PING on another connection stays instant.

  6. (hard) Rewrite the echo server with Boost.Asio (sudo apt install libboost-dev), using async_read_some / async_write and a single io_context. Compare lines of code and performance. Done when: both pass the load test and you can explain what Asio did for you.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between blocking and non-blocking I/O? A: A blocking recv sleeps until data arrives. A non-blocking one returns EAGAIN immediately if nothing is buffered, so a single thread can service many sockets by asking a readiness API (epoll) which ones have data, and never sleeping on one socket.

Q: Why is epoll faster than poll? A: poll passes the whole fd list on every call and the kernel scans all of it: O(n) per call. epoll keeps the interest list in the kernel and callbacks put ready fds on a list, so epoll_wait is O(ready). With 10,000 connections and 10 active, that is a 1000x difference per iteration.

Q: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered? A: LT reports an fd every time it is ready; ET reports only when it becomes ready. ET requires draining until EAGAIN after each event or you miss data sitting in the buffer. ET has fewer wakeups and suits multi-threaded consumers; LT is forgiving.

Q: What state do you need per connection in an event loop? A: Everything a thread would have kept on its stack: the partial parse state, the output bytes not yet accepted by the kernel, whether the peer half-closed, which epoll interests are registered, and the last-activity time for timeouts.

Q: How do you handle a client that sends but never reads? A: The output buffer grows. At a high-water mark, stop reading (remove EPOLLIN); the receive buffer fills, TCP advertises a zero window and the client's send blocks. Resume at a low-water mark. Also apply a hard limit and close.

Q: Reactor versus proactor? A: Reactor (epoll, kqueue): the loop is told a socket is ready and performs the read or write itself. Proactor (IOCP, io_uring, Asio's interface): the application submits an operation with a buffer and is told when it completed. Asio presents a proactor interface over epoll by doing the read for you on readiness.

Q: How do you wake an event loop from another thread or a signal handler? A: Register an eventfd (or a pipe) in epoll; write to it from the other context (write is async-signal-safe). The loop sees it readable, reads the counter, and processes whatever queue the writer filled. timerfd does the same for time.

Q: When would you not use an event loop? A: When each request does blocking or CPU-heavy work through libraries you cannot make asynchronous (blocking DB drivers, heavy computation) and connections number in the hundreds. A thread pool is simpler, stack traces are readable, and the blocking library forces threads anyway. The hybrid (loop for I/O, pool for work) is the common production answer.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Non-blocking sockets return EAGAIN instead of sleeping; a readiness API says when to retry.
  • select is capped and O(n); poll is O(n); epoll is O(ready) with a kernel-side interest list.
  • LT: reported while ready. ET: reported on change; drain to EAGAIN or hang. EPOLLONESHOT for multi-thread hand-off.
  • Reactor: never block in a handler; per-connection state object; output buffer plus EPOLLOUT only while pending; backpressure via pausing reads; beware dangling Conn within a batch.
  • eventfd wakes the loop from threads and signal handlers; timerfd gives timers as fds.
  • Event loops win for many idle connections and byte shuffling; thread pools win for blocking or CPU-heavy per-request work; hybrids are the norm.
  • io_uring and IOCP are proactors (submit operation, get completion); epoll is a reactor.
  • libuv wraps epoll/kqueue/IOCP as a reactor API; Asio exposes a proactor API over all of them.

docs.title: 07. RPC
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 04, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
RPC (remote procedure call) is the idea that calling a function on another machine should look like calling a function locally: balance = get_balance("ACC-1"). Behind that line, a stub packs the arguments into bytes (serialization), sends them over a connection, the server unpacks them, finds the right function in a table (dispatch), runs it, packs the result, sends it back, and the stub unpacks it and returns. Every RPC system from 1984's Sun RPC to gRPC is this sequence with different choices for each step.

The analogy: ordering from a catalogue by post. You fill in a form (serialize), put your order number on it (request id), post it (transport), the warehouse looks up the item code (dispatch), ships it with your order number on the box (correlation), and you match the box to the order. The post can lose letters, boxes can arrive late, and the warehouse can burn down after charging your card. RPC's real difficulty is that the function call illusion hides all of that: a local call cannot "time out with unknown outcome", a remote one can.

You maintain an RPC-over-TCP server. This module gives you the standard words for what it does, then builds a tiny RPC layer from scratch so each word points at code you wrote.

docs.title: 2.1 Anatomy of an RPC
docs.text:
client code     stub          transport        transport      dispatcher     handler
 ----------      ----          ---------        ---------      ----------     -------
 get_balance  -> encode args -> frame + id  ==>  read frame  -> method 3   ->  lookup account
   <- int64   <- decode      <- frame + id  <==  write frame <- status,ret <-  return 100000
  • Interface definition: which methods exist, their ids, their argument and result types. In protobuf this is a .proto file; in the demo it is namespace methods { constexpr uint16_t ... } plus comments. Both client and server compile against it.
  • Stub (client) and skeleton (server): generated or hand-written code that converts between typed calls and bytes. The demo's BankClient methods are stubs; the lambdas in build_dispatcher are the skeleton.
  • Serialization: typed values to bytes and back, with a fixed byte order and explicit lengths.
  • Framing: module 04. The RPC header is a length-prefixed frame.
  • Dispatch: method_id to handler, a table lookup.
  • Correlation: the response carries the request's id so the client can match them, which is what makes several outstanding calls on one connection possible.

docs.title: 2.2 Serialization choices
docs.text:
Approach Schema Size Speed Evolution Tooling Where Hand-rolled fixed layout (demo) in code and comments smallest fastest manual, fragile none internal, stable protocols Raw C structs on the wire the struct small memcpy none: any field change breaks it; padding/endianness tie you to one compiler none legacy; probably your server JSON none or JSON Schema large (text) slow (parse, allocate) easy, unknown fields ignored universal HTTP APIs, configs Protocol Buffers .proto, codegen compact (varints, tags) fast excellent: tag numbers, optional fields, unknown fields preserved protoc, every language gRPC, Google, most microservices FlatBuffers / Cap'n Proto schema, codegen compact-ish zero-copy read (no parse step) good less common games, low-latency, mmap'd data MessagePack / CBOR self-describing compact fast like JSON many when you want "binary JSON" Apache Thrift / Avro schema compact fast Avro: reader/writer schema resolution Hadoop, Kafka ecosystems data pipelines

Protobuf's key idea for evolution: every field has a number; the wire holds (number, type, value) triples; readers skip unknown numbers and treat missing ones as default. Add fields freely, never reuse a number, never change a field's type. Your hand-rolled format gets evolution only if you build the same discipline: a version byte, optional trailing fields, "ignore what you do not understand".

docs.title: 2.3 Request ids and correlation
docs.text:
In a strict one-at-a-time protocol (tcpkv) the Nth reply matches the Nth request and no id is needed. The moment you want multiple outstanding calls on one connection (multiplexing), or replies that may be out of order (a slow and a fast call in flight), each request needs an id and each reply must carry it. Rules:

  • Ids are unique per connection (a counter is fine), not necessarily globally.
  • The client keeps a map id -> pending call (promise, deadline).
  • A reply with an unknown id (already timed out and removed) is logged and dropped.
  • After a timeout you must either keep the id reserved forever on that connection or close the connection: otherwise a late reply to id 7 could be matched to a new request that reused id 7. The demo client closes.

Correlation ids also appear in logs and traces: the request id (or a globally unique trace id) printed on both client and server lines is how you follow one call through a system (module 09).

docs.title: 2.4 Timeouts, retries and the three outcomes
docs.text:
A remote call has three outcomes, not two: success, failure, and unknown (timeout, or the connection broke after sending). "Unknown" means the server may have executed it. A retry after "unknown" may execute it twice. This is the single most important fact about distributed systems for someone writing a banking server, and it is why module 10 spends time on exactly-once.

Rules that follow:

  • Every call has a deadline. No deadline means a thread waits forever on a dead peer (module 02: 15 minutes of kernel retransmission, or forever if idle). Deadlines propagate: if the client gave you 2 s, give the database 1.5 s.
  • Classify errors so the client knows whether to retry: permanent (bad request, unknown method: never retry), transient (unavailable, overloaded: retry with backoff), unknown (timeout: retry only if idempotent). The Status enum in the demo does this; gRPC's status codes do the same (INVALID_ARGUMENT vs UNAVAILABLE vs DEADLINE_EXCEEDED).
  • Idempotency makes retries safe. Natural idempotency: SET k v, GET, DELETE. Forced idempotency: the client attaches an idempotency key (a unique id for the logical operation, such as a transaction id generated at the branch) and the server stores key -> result; a retried request with a known key returns the stored result without re-executing. The demo's Transfer does this. Stripe, AWS and every payment API work this way. The store of applied keys must be durable and bounded (expire after the client's maximum retry window).
  • Retries need backoff with jitter (module 09) or a hiccup becomes a storm. Cap the attempts. Never retry non-idempotent calls after unknown outcomes without a key.

docs.title: 2.5 Backpressure
docs.text:
If clients can send requests faster than the server handles them, something must give:

  • At the transport: a server that stops reading makes TCP's window close and the client's send blocks (module 05). Crude but automatic.
  • At the protocol: a max in-flight per connection (HTTP/2 SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, gRPC flow-control windows). The client does not send request 65 until one of the 64 outstanding completes.
  • At the application: explicit rejection with Overloaded status when queues are full, so the client backs off or tries another server (load shedding, module 05 and 09).

A server that buffers everything and never pushes back dies first and takes its clients down with it.

docs.title: 2.6 Versioning
docs.text:
Clients and servers are never upgraded at the same instant. Options:

  • Version byte in every frame (demo). Server rejects unknown versions with a clear error.
  • Version negotiated once at connect (HELLO v2), then implied.
  • Method-level: new behaviour gets a new method id; old ids keep old semantics forever.
  • Field-level: protobuf style; add optional fields, never change meaning.

Rule of thumb: servers must accept old clients (backward compatible) for at least one release; deploy servers first, then clients. The error for "I do not understand this" must be distinguishable from "something broke", or clients retry forever (module 04's war story).

docs.title: 2.7 gRPC in one page
docs.text:
gRPC = protobuf for serialization + HTTP/2 for transport + generated stubs in a dozen languages.

  • HTTP/2 gives it framing, multiplexing with stream ids (correlation for free), flow control per stream (backpressure for free), header compression, and TLS integration.
  • Each RPC is one HTTP/2 stream; the method is the path (/bank.Ledger/GetBalance), the body is length-prefixed protobuf messages.
  • Four call shapes: unary (one request, one reply), server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional streaming. Streaming is just many messages on one stream.
  • Deadlines are first-class (grpc-timeout header, propagated to the server which can check context.deadline). Status codes are standard (OK, INVALID_ARGUMENT, NOT_FOUND, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, UNAVAILABLE, UNIMPLEMENTED, ...). Metadata = headers.
  • Costs: HTTP/2 complexity, no browser support without grpc-web, debugging needs grpcurl instead of nc, and head-of-line blocking of all streams on one TCP connection on lossy links.
  • When to use: service-to-service calls where you want codegen, streaming, deadlines and interoperability. When not: a single Windows client and server you control where a 16-byte header does the job and you need no new dependencies.

docs.title: 2.8 Mapping your employer's RPC-over-TCP transport
docs.text:
Go through its code with this checklist and write the answers down; they are your interview answers.

Concept Question to answer about your server Framing Header size? Which field is the length? Is the length validated against a maximum before allocation? Serialization Raw structs? If so, same compiler/arch both ends? Any byte order handling? Strings: fixed arrays or length-prefixed? Dispatch How does the server find the handler: switch on an opcode, table, name lookup? Correlation Is there a request id? Can a client have more than one call outstanding per connection? Timeouts Client side deadline? Server side per-request deadline? What happens on timeout: close or keep waiting? Idempotency Which operations are safe to retry? Is there an idempotency key / transaction id for financial postings? Error model How does a server exception reach the client: status code, error string, connection close? Backpressure Max outstanding per connection? What happens when workers are all busy: queue, reject, block the socket? Versioning How did the last protocol change roll out? Can an old client talk to a new server? Concurrency Who writes to a socket: one thread per connection or a shared mutex around whole-frame writes?

Being able to say "our transport is a length-prefixed binary protocol with a 24-byte header, opcode dispatch, one outstanding request per connection, host byte order because both ends are x86 Windows, and a transaction id that the server uses to deduplicate postings" is a senior answer. Saying "it uses sockets" is not.

docs.title: 3.1 The RPC layer (code/m07_rpc.hpp)
docs.text:
Header, 16 bytes, big-endian:

magic u16 | version u8 | type u8 | request_id u32 | method_id u16 | status u16 | payload_len u32

Serialization primitives:

class Writer { void u8/u16/u32/u64/i64(...); void str(string_view) /* u32 len + bytes */; std::string take(); };
class Reader {                      // every read bounds-checked; throws BadPayload
    uint64_t u64() { uint64_t hi = u32(); return (hi << 32) | u32(); }
    std::string str() { uint32_t n = u32(); need(n); std::string s(p_, n); p_ += n; return s; }
    bool done() const;              // handlers check this to reject trailing bytes (schema skew)
};

Dispatch and error propagation:

using Handler = std::function<Status(Reader& req, Writer& resp)>;

Frame Dispatcher::handle(const Frame& req) const {
    Frame resp; resp.type = Type::Response; resp.request_id = req.request_id;   // correlation
    auto it = table_.find(req.method_id);
    if (it == table_.end()) { resp.status = Status::UnknownMethod; return resp; }  // permanent
    Reader r(req.payload); Writer w;
    try { resp.status = it->second(r, w); resp.payload = w.take(); }
    catch (const BadPayload& e) { resp.status = Status::BadRequest; resp.payload = e.what(); }
    catch (const std::exception& e) { resp.status = Status::Internal; resp.payload = e.what(); }
    return resp;                    // the server never dies because a handler threw
}

Client call with a deadline and the "unknown outcome" rule:

Result Client::call(uint16_t method_id, std::string payload, int timeout_ms) {
    Frame req{Type::Request, next_id_++, method_id, Status::Ok, std::move(payload)};
    write_frame(fd_.get(), req);
    if (!net::wait_readable(fd_.get(), timeout_ms)) {
        fd_.reset();                                  // a late reply must never match a future id
        return {Status::Timeout, "no reply within deadline; outcome unknown"};
    }
    Frame resp; read_frame(fd_.get(), resp);
    return {resp.status, std::move(resp.payload)};
}

docs.title: 3.2 The demo (code/m07_rpc_demo.cpp)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread m07_rpc_demo.cpp -o rpc_demo && ./rpc_demo

It starts a server on an ephemeral loopback port, registers five methods, and runs a client through: a normal call, negative integers surviving the wire, a server exception becoming INTERNAL while the server keeps running, an idempotent Transfer retried with the same key that debits once, a malformed payload becoming BAD_REQUEST, an unknown method, and a timeout that leaves the connection closed so the next call returns UNAVAILABLE.

The idempotency key in the handler:

if (auto done = bank.applied.find(key); done != bank.applied.end()) {
    resp.i64(done->second); return Status::Ok;          // replay: same answer, money moves once
}
... debit, credit ...
bank.applied[key] = bank.balances[from];

In a real system applied is a table in the same database transaction as the balance update, so "money moved" and "key recorded" are atomic. That is how a lending server makes a disbursement safe to retry.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Syscalls per call. Client: one send (header and payload in one buffer: no Nagle stall, no interleaving), one poll, one or two recv (header then payload; read_exact loops). Server: two recv, one send. Six to eight syscalls and two round trips on the wire per RPC, which on loopback is around 20 to 50 microseconds and on a LAN is dominated by the network RTT. Batching several requests per send (pipelining) or readv/writev reduces syscalls; the request id is what makes pipelining safe.

Where time goes in a real RPC stack. Serialization of small messages: tens to hundreds of nanoseconds hand-rolled, about a microsecond for protobuf, tens of microseconds for JSON with allocation. The syscalls and the copy to and from kernel buffers: a few microseconds. The network: tens of microseconds on a LAN, milliseconds across a WAN. Thread hand-off to a worker: a few microseconds. For a banking RPC that then does a database transaction (hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds), the RPC layer is noise. Optimise it only when it is not.

std::function dispatch. The dispatcher's unordered_map<uint16_t, std::function> costs a hash lookup and an indirect call: tens of nanoseconds. A switch or a flat array indexed by method id is faster and what generated code does. It does not matter until millions of calls per second.

Exceptions across the boundary. C++ exceptions cannot cross the wire; the dispatcher converts them into a status and text. On the client, you can choose to throw on non-Ok status to keep the "local call" illusion, but the three-outcome problem means callers must still think about Timeout. Many teams return a result type instead of throwing for exactly this reason.

Thread safety of a connection. One Client object is single-threaded. Sharing a connection across threads needs: a mutex around write_frame, a reader thread that demultiplexes replies by id into per-call promises, and a map of pending calls. That is 100 more lines and is what every production RPC client contains; it is the natural next exercise.

Windows parity. Nothing in the frame format is OS-specific. The transport helpers map to Winsock calls one for one (module 03 table). Your server's equivalent of Dispatcher::handle is probably a switch on an opcode inside the worker thread's loop.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The double disbursement. A branch client timed out on a loan disbursement RPC, retried, and the customer received the amount twice. The first call had succeeded; the reply was lost when a firewall reset the connection. Fix: a transaction id from the client stored with the posting, and the server returning the stored result for a repeated id. Every money-moving RPC needs this.
  • The frozen client. A client with no deadline waited on a server whose worker deadlocked. The branch terminal hung until someone killed it. Every call needs a deadline; every deadline needs an action (close the connection, report, maybe retry).
  • The mismatched reply. A client reused a connection after a timeout. The late reply for the old request was read as the reply to the new one: a balance query returned the result of a different account's query. Close after timeout, or carry ids and discard unknown ones.
  • Struct layout drift. Server rebuilt with a different packing pragma; client not. Every field after the third was misread. Explicit serialization with fixed widths and byte order removes this class of incident entirely; a version byte catches it with a clear error when it happens anyway.
  • Retry storm. A dependency slowed down; clients retried immediately three times; load tripled; the dependency fell over completely. Exponential backoff with jitter and a retry budget (module 09) turn this into graceful degradation.
  • gRPC's UNAVAILABLE after deploys. Rolling restarts caused in-flight calls to fail with UNAVAILABLE; clients without retry logic surfaced errors to users. gRPC's built-in retry policy (for idempotent methods, configured in the service config) fixed it. The same applies to your transport: define which methods are retryable and have the client library honour it.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Add a Ping method (id 6) to the demo with no arguments returning the server's monotonic time in milliseconds. Done when: the client prints it.

  2. (easy) Change kVersion to 2 on the server only. Done when: the client fails with a clear "unsupported version" error rather than garbage, and you can explain which side detected it.

  3. (medium) Make Client support pipelining: send_async(method, payload) -> id, then wait(id, deadline) -> Result, with a map of pending ids. Send 100 Add requests before reading any reply. Done when: all 100 results are correct and arrive in one burst.

  4. (medium) Make the server bound in-flight requests per connection: more than 8 unanswered requests gets Overloaded. Done when: the pipelined client from exercise 3 sees OVERLOADED for the excess and succeeds after backing off.

  5. (hard) Build the multi-threaded client: one writer mutex, one reader thread demultiplexing replies into std::promises keyed by id, per-call deadlines enforced by a timer thread that fails the promise and marks the connection poisoned. Done when: 8 threads each making 1000 calls over one connection get correct results, and a Sleep(5000) call times out without disturbing the others.

  6. (hard) Write the same GetBalance service with gRPC (sudo apt install libgrpc++-dev protobuf-compiler-grpc), measure p50 latency against the hand-rolled version on loopback, and write a half-page on where the difference comes from and when it would matter.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is RPC and what are its parts? A: Making a remote function call look local. Parts: an interface definition, client stub and server skeleton, serialization of arguments and results, framing over a transport, a request id for correlation, a dispatch table on the server, and an error/status model that distinguishes permanent from transient from unknown outcomes.

Q: What are the three outcomes of a remote call and why does it matter? A: Success, failure, and unknown (timeout or broken connection after sending). Unknown means the server may have executed it, so a blind retry can execute it twice. Money-moving calls need idempotency keys; the server stores the result per key and replays it on retry.

Q: Why do you need request ids? A: To match replies to requests when more than one call is outstanding on a connection or replies can be reordered. Also for logs and tracing. After a timeout, either never reuse the id on that connection or close it, or a late reply can be matched to the wrong call.

Q: How do you propagate a server exception to the client? A: Catch it at the dispatch boundary, convert it to a status code the client can classify (bad request vs internal) plus a message in the payload, and keep the server alive. The client maps the status to its own error type or exception. Exceptions never cross the wire.

Q: Protobuf versus hand-rolled structs? A: Protobuf gives schema evolution (numbered fields, unknown fields skipped), codegen in many languages, compact varint encoding, and tooling. Hand-rolled is smallest and fastest and needs no dependency, but every change is manual and risky. Raw C structs on the wire are the worst option: compiler, padding and endianness dependent.

Q: What does gRPC add over your own TCP protocol? A: HTTP/2 transport (multiplexed streams with ids, per-stream flow control, TLS), protobuf codegen in many languages, streaming calls, standard status codes, first-class deadlines and metadata, and an ecosystem (load balancing, retries, tracing). Cost: complexity, HTTP/2 head-of-line blocking, harder manual debugging.

Q: What is backpressure in an RPC system? A: A mechanism that stops a fast producer from overwhelming a slower consumer: TCP windows at the transport, max-in-flight limits at the protocol, explicit "overloaded" rejections at the application. Without it, queues grow until memory or latency fails everything.

Q: Describe your RPC-over-TCP transport. A: (Your answer, from the section 2.8 table.) Framing, serialization, dispatch, correlation, timeouts, idempotency, error model, backpressure, versioning, who writes to the socket.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• RPC = stub, serialization, framing, transport, request id, dispatch, status, skeleton.
  • Serialization: fix byte order and widths; never ship raw structs; protobuf for evolution and codegen; hand-rolled only for small stable internal protocols.
  • Request ids enable multiplexing and correlation; after a timeout close the connection or never reuse the id.
  • Three outcomes: success, failure, unknown. Deadlines everywhere. Classify errors as permanent, transient, unknown.
  • Idempotency keys make retries safe; store key and result atomically with the effect.
  • Backpressure: TCP window, max in-flight, explicit overload rejection.
  • Versioning: version byte or handshake; servers accept old clients; clear "unknown" errors.
  • gRPC = protobuf + HTTP/2 + codegen + deadlines + standard status codes.
  • Describe your own transport with these words; that is the interview answer.

docs.title: 08. HTTP and REST
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
HTTP is a text protocol over TCP where a client sends a request ("GET me the resource at /accounts/1001") and the server sends one response ("200 OK, here are 212 bytes of JSON"). It was built for web pages but became the universal transport for APIs because every language, proxy, firewall and debugging tool understands it. If you can write the tcpkv parser, you can write an HTTP/1.1 parser: a request line, header lines, a blank line, and an optional body whose length is announced by a header.

REST is not a protocol but a style for designing HTTP APIs: things are resources with URLs (/loans/4471), you act on them with the standard methods (GET read, PUT replace, DELETE remove, POST create or do something), the server tells you what happened with standard status codes, and each request carries everything needed to process it (no server-side session state).

This module reads HTTP/1.1 at the byte level, writes a small server by hand in C++17, and then explains what HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and TLS change, and when to stop writing it yourself.

docs.title: 2.1 HTTP/1.1 message format
docs.text:
Request:

GET /kv/greeting HTTP/1.1\r\n            request line: METHOD SP request-target SP version
Host: 127.0.0.1:8080\r\n                 headers: name ":" value, names case-insensitive
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0\r\n
Accept: */*\r\n
\r\n                                     blank line ends the head
                                         body (none for GET)

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n                      status line: version SP code SP reason
Date: Fri, 03 Oct 2026 10:00:00 GMT\r\n
Content-Type: application/json\r\n
Content-Length: 35\r\n                   body length in bytes: this is the framing
Connection: keep-alive\r\n
\r\n
{"key":"greeting","value":"hello"}

Framing of the body, in order of precedence: Transfer-Encoding: chunked (section 2.5), else Content-Length: N, else (responses only) read until the server closes. A request with a body and neither header is invalid (411 Length Required). Content-Length must be validated like any length off the wire: digits only, bounded.

docs.title: 2.2 Methods
docs.text:
Method Meaning Safe Idempotent Body GET read a resource yes yes no HEAD GET without the body (headers only) yes yes no PUT replace the resource at this URL with the body no yes yes DELETE remove the resource no yes no POST create a subordinate resource or trigger an action no no yes PATCH partial update no not necessarily yes OPTIONS what methods are allowed (used by CORS preflight) yes yes no

Safe means no side effects (caches and crawlers may call it freely). Idempotent means repeating has the same effect as doing it once: PUT /kv/a with hello twice leaves one hello; DELETE of a missing resource is still "gone" (return 204 or 404, both acceptable). POST is the non-idempotent one, which is why payment APIs add an Idempotency-Key header to POST (module 07).

docs.title: 2.3 Status codes
docs.text:
• 1xx informational: 100 Continue (client asked Expect: 100-continue before sending a big body).
  • 2xx success: 200 OK, 201 Created (with a Location header), 202 Accepted (async, not done yet), 204 No Content (success, nothing to return, no body allowed).
  • 3xx redirection: 301 permanent, 302/307 temporary, 304 Not Modified (conditional GET hit).
  • 4xx client error (do not retry as-is): 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated), 403 Forbidden (authenticated, not allowed), 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 409 Conflict (version mismatch, duplicate), 413 Payload Too Large, 422 Unprocessable Entity (valid syntax, invalid semantics), 429 Too Many Requests (rate limited; send Retry-After).
  • 5xx server error (may retry with backoff): 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway (proxy got a bad upstream response), 503 Service Unavailable (overloaded or down; Retry-After), 504 Gateway Timeout.

The 4xx/5xx split is the retry classification from module 07 built into the protocol.

docs.title: 2.4 Headers you must know
docs.text:
Host (required in 1.1; virtual hosting), Content-Type (application/json; charset=utf-8), Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, Connection (keep-alive/close), Accept and Accept-Encoding (content negotiation), Content-Encoding (gzip), Cache-Control, ETag and If-None-Match (conditional requests, optimistic concurrency: If-Match: "v7" on PUT returns 412 if the resource changed), Authorization (Bearer <token>), Location, Retry-After, X-Request-Id (correlation; module 09), Date.

Header rules: names are case-insensitive, values may have leading and trailing whitespace trimmed, repeated headers combine with commas (except Set-Cookie), no whitespace between name and colon (a smuggling vector), and you must cap total header size (8 to 64 KB is common).

docs.title: 2.5 Keep-alive, pipelining and chunked encoding
docs.text:
Keep-alive: HTTP/1.0 closed the connection after every response. HTTP/1.1 keeps it open by default; Connection: close ends it. One TCP connection then carries many sequential requests, saving a handshake and slow start each time. Servers apply an idle timeout (5 to 60 s) and clients must handle the server closing an idle connection (retry the request on a new connection if it was idempotent and no bytes of a response were received).

Pipelining: sending the next request before the previous response arrives. Legal in 1.1, responses must come back in order; in practice browsers disabled it (head-of-line blocking, buggy proxies). HTTP/2 multiplexing replaced it. Your server gets it for free if its read loop keeps unconsumed bytes, as the code does.

Chunked transfer encoding: for bodies whose length is unknown when the headers are sent (streaming a generated report). Each chunk is hex-size data , terminated by 0 (optionally with trailers):

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Transfer-Encoding: chunked



7

{"a":1}

8

,{"b":2}

0

A chunked parser is another small state machine (size line, data, CRLF, repeat, trailers). The demo server does not implement it for requests and returns 411; for responses it always knows the length.

docs.title: 2.6 Content negotiation
docs.text: The client says what it can accept (Accept: application/json, Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, Accept-Language: en), the server picks and states its choice (Content-Type, Content-Encoding, Content-Language, plus Vary: Accept-Encoding so caches key on it). If nothing matches: 406 Not Acceptable. Most internal APIs skip this and always speak JSON; public APIs should honour Accept-Encoding: gzip because JSON compresses 5 to 10 times.

docs.title: 2.7 HTTP/2 in a paragraph
docs.text: HTTP/2 (2015) keeps HTTP semantics (methods, status codes, headers) and replaces the text framing with a binary framing layer over one TCP connection: streams identified by ids carry frames (HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, PING, GOAWAY), many streams are multiplexed on one connection so requests and responses interleave without ordering constraints, headers are compressed with HPACK (a shared dynamic table, so repeated Authorization headers cost two bytes), each stream has flow control (per-stream backpressure), and priorities hint at ordering. It eliminates HTTP/1's six-connections-per-host workaround and head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer, but inherits TCP's: one lost packet stalls every stream. It is almost always run over TLS (negotiated via ALPN), and gRPC is built on it. Debug it with curl --http2 -v or Wireshark.

docs.title: 2.8 HTTP/3 in a paragraph
docs.text: HTTP/3 (2022) moves the same HTTP/2 concepts onto QUIC, a transport over UDP that implements its own reliability, congestion control, and per-stream ordering, so a lost packet stalls only the stream it belonged to. QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 into its handshake, giving a 1-RTT (or 0-RTT on resumption) connection setup instead of TCP's handshake plus TLS's. It supports connection migration (a phone switching from Wi-Fi to mobile keeps the connection). Costs: user-space implementations use more CPU than kernel TCP, UDP is sometimes blocked or rate-limited by middleboxes (clients fall back to HTTP/2), and operational tooling is younger. Header compression is QPACK, adapted for out-of-order delivery. Browsers and CDNs use it heavily; internal service-to-service traffic mostly still uses HTTP/2.

docs.title: 2.9 TLS handshake basics
docs.text:
TLS sits between TCP and HTTP (HTTPS = HTTP over TLS, port 443). TLS 1.3 handshake:

Client -> ClientHello: supported versions, cipher suites, key share (ECDHE public key), SNI (host name), ALPN (h2, http/1.1)
Server -> ServerHello: chosen suite, its key share; then (encrypted) Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished
Client -> Finished; application data begins          (1 round trip; 0-RTT possible on resumption)

Both sides derive the same symmetric keys from the ECDHE exchange (forward secrecy: a stolen server private key later cannot decrypt recorded traffic). The certificate, signed by a CA the client trusts, proves the server owns the name in SNI. Mutual TLS adds a client certificate: this is how services authenticate each other inside a data centre. TLS 1.2 took two round trips and allowed weaker options; disable everything below 1.2. In C++ you use OpenSSL (SSL_CTX, SSL_read, SSL_write replace recv/send and handle the record layer), or let a library (Beast, httplib with CPPHTTPLIB_OPENSSL_SUPPORT) do it. Common production failures: expired certificates, missing intermediate certificates in the chain, hostname mismatch, clock skew on the client.

docs.title: 2.10 REST resource design
docs.text:
• Nouns, not verbs, in URLs: /loans/4471, not /getLoan?id=4471. Collections are plural: /customers/88/loans.
  • Use the methods for the verbs: GET /loans/4471, POST /loans (create; reply 201 with Location: /loans/4472), PUT /loans/4472 (full replace), PATCH (partial), DELETE.
  • Actions that do not map to CRUD become sub-resources: POST /loans/4471/disbursements creates a disbursement; its state is GET /loans/4471/disbursements/9. Avoid POST /loans/4471/disburse unless you accept the RPC-ish style (many good APIs do; be consistent).
  • Status codes carry meaning; the body carries detail: {"error":{"code":"INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS", "message":"...","request_id":"..."}}. RFC 9457 "Problem Details" standardises this shape.
  • Idempotency: PUT and DELETE naturally; POST with an Idempotency-Key header.
  • Versioning: /v1/loans in the path (simple, visible) or Accept: application/vnd.bank.v2+json (purer, invisible). Pick path versioning unless you have a reason.
  • Pagination: GET /loans?limit=100&cursor=abc; return next_cursor. Avoid offset for large tables (slow and inconsistent under inserts).
  • Filtering and sorting as query parameters; never put secrets in URLs (they land in logs).
  • Concurrency control: ETag on GET, If-Match on PUT; 412 Precondition Failed on mismatch. This maps directly to an optimistic version column in your database rows.
  • Long operations: 202 Accepted with a Location of a status resource the client polls.

docs.title: 2.11 When to use a library
docs.text:
Writing the parser by hand teaches you the protocol and is fine for an internal tool. For anything that faces other teams or the internet, use a library: the edge cases (chunked requests, Expect: 100-continue, header folding, percent-decoding, request smuggling defences, TLS, HTTP/2) are where hand-written servers get exploited.

  • cpp-httplib: single header, blocking, thread pool, client and server, optional OpenSSL. Ten lines to a working JSON API. Good for internal services and tools. Not for 10K connections.
  • Boost.Beast: HTTP/1 and WebSocket on top of Asio, asynchronous, you control the event loop. More code, more scalability. Pairs with module 06.
  • Drogon, userver, Pistache, Crow: fuller frameworks (routing, JSON, ORM).
  • nghttp2, libcurl (client side; curl is libcurl), gRPC for HTTP/2.
  • Behind a reverse proxy (nginx, Envoy) your server can speak plain HTTP/1.1 and let the proxy do TLS, HTTP/2, compression and rate limiting. This is the common production layout.

docs.title: 3.1 The server (code/m08_http_server.cpp)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 m08_http_server.cpp -o http_server
./http_server 8080 &
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
curl -i -X PUT --data-binary 'hello "world"' http://127.0.0.1:8080/kv/greeting      # 201
curl -i -X PUT --data-binary 'hello again'   http://127.0.0.1:8080/kv/greeting      # 204 (idempotent)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/kv/greeting | python3 -m json.tool
curl -i -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8080/kv/greeting                                 # 204
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/kv/greeting                                           # 404
curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8080/health http://127.0.0.1:8080/stats 2>&1 | grep -E 'Re-using|Connected'  # keep-alive
curl -i --http1.0 http://127.0.0.1:8080/health                                      # Connection: close
printf 'GET /health HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\nGET /stats HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n' | nc -q1 127.0.0.1 8080  # pipelined
printf 'GARBAGE\r\n\r\n' | nc -q1 127.0.0.1 8080                                    # 400, closed

Reading the head, then the body, keeping leftovers for the next request:

while ((head_end = buf.find("\r\n\r\n")) == std::string::npos) {   // head = up to the blank line
    if (buf.size() > kMaxHeaderBytes) { reply 400; return; }         // bounded, like every parser
    size_t n = net::read_some(fd, tmp, sizeof tmp);
    if (n == 0) return;
    buf.append(tmp, n);
}
parse_head(std::string_view(buf).substr(0, head_end), req);
buf.erase(0, head_end + 4);
... validate Content-Length (digits, <= 1 MiB) ...
while (buf.size() < content_length) { read more }
req.body = buf.substr(0, content_length); buf.erase(0, content_length);   // leftovers = next request

Persistence rule, straight from RFC 7230:

if (req.version == "HTTP/1.1") req.keep_alive = conn_v.find("close") == npos;        // default on
else                            req.keep_alive = conn_v.find("keep-alive") != npos;   // 1.0: default off

The response always carries Content-Length (or is 204), so the client knows exactly where it ends and the connection can be reused. On any parse error the server replies and closes, because it no longer knows where the next request starts: the same rule as the tcpkv parser's fatal.

docs.title: 3.2 Testing with curl
docs.text: -i show response headers; -v show request and response headers and connection reuse; -X PUT method; --data-binary @file body from a file; -H 'Content-Type: application/json' header; -s silent; -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' print code and timing; --http1.0; --http2; -k ignore TLS errors (debugging only); --resolve host:443:10.1.2.3 to test a server by IP with the right Host/SNI. curl plus python3 -m json.tool is the REST developer's nc.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why HTTP/1.1 is slow for many small requests. Each request waits for the previous response (no multiplexing), so latency is RTT times the number of sequential requests. Browsers open six connections per host to work around it, which multiplies handshakes and slow-start phases. Request and response headers are repeated verbatim every time (cookies, user agents: hundreds of bytes). HTTP/2 fixes both with multiplexed streams and HPACK; the TCP-level head-of-line blocking remains and HTTP/3 removes it.

Where the server's time goes. For a small JSON response: recv (a few microseconds), parsing (a microsecond with string_view, more if you allocate per header), the handler, formatting (string concatenation: allocation), send. A hand-written server like the demo does roughly 50,000 to 100,000 requests per second per core on loopback with keep-alive (typical for this class of code; measure with wrk or ab), and perhaps 5,000 per second without keep-alive because each request then pays a handshake, a thread creation and a TIME_WAIT. That ratio is the whole argument for keep-alive and connection pooling.
