Date header and strftime. gmtime_r plus strftime costs about a microsecond; nginx caches the formatted date and refreshes it once per second. Small things like this are where "fast HTTP server" work goes.

Request smuggling. When a proxy and a backend disagree on where a request ends (one honours Content-Length, the other Transfer-Encoding; or a header with whitespace before the colon is parsed differently), an attacker can hide a second request inside the first. Defences: reject requests with both length headers, reject malformed header names, normalise before forwarding, close the connection on any ambiguity. The demo's strictness (411 on chunked, digits-only Content-Length, no space before colon) is this defence in miniature.

TLS cost. The 1.3 handshake costs one RTT plus an ECDHE operation (tens of microseconds of CPU) and a signature verification; session resumption skips most of it. Bulk encryption with AES-GCM runs at gigabytes per second with AES-NI. TLS is not a performance excuse in 2026; terminating it at a proxy is about operational convenience (certificates in one place), not speed.

Windows. The same server compiles with Winsock changes from module 03. Windows also has http.sys, a kernel-mode HTTP listener used by IIS and ASP.NET that parses requests in the kernel and can share port 80 among processes by URL prefix; nothing like it exists on Linux.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Missing Content-Length on a keep-alive response. A hand-written server forgot the header on one code path; the client waited for the connection to close to know the body had ended, and with keep-alive it never did: every request on that path "hung" for the idle timeout. Framing is not optional, in either direction.
  • The 15-second idle timeout nobody knew about. A connection pool kept HTTP connections idle longer than the server's keep-alive timeout. The server closed them; the next request hit a closed connection and failed with ECONNRESET. Fix: client idle timeout shorter than the server's, and retry idempotent requests once on a fresh connection when the failure happens before any response byte.
  • GET with side effects. An endpoint GET /loans/4471/approve existed for convenience. A link-prefetching browser extension approved loans. Safe methods must be safe.
  • Retrying POST without a key. A client retried POST /payments on 504 from a gateway; the backend had processed the first one. Idempotency keys on every non-idempotent write, stored with the result, and 409/replay on repeat.
  • Header size attack. A fuzzer sent 10 MB of headers; the server buffered until OOM. Cap head size (the demo: 64 KB) and body size, and reply 431/413 and close.
  • Chunked bodies from a new client library. A rewritten client began sending Transfer-Encoding: chunked for small bodies; the hand-written backend did not support it and silently misparsed. Returning 411 loudly (as the demo does) is better than guessing; supporting chunked is better still, and a library does it for you.
  • Your context. If the lending server ever exposes HTTP (a REST facade for mobile or partner integration), it will sit behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS. Design the resources (loans, customers, disbursements, repayments), use Idempotency-Key on postings, return Problem Details errors with the request id, and use ETag/If-Match to map onto your optimistic row versions.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run the server and every curl line in section 3.1. With tcpdump -A -i lo port 8080 running, confirm the keep-alive test reused one connection. Done when: the capture shows one handshake and two requests.

  2. (easy) Add HEAD support check: curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8080/kv/x must return the same headers as GET with no body. Add ETag (a hash of the value) to GET /kv/<key> and 304 Not Modified when If-None-Match matches. Done when: the second curl with the ETag returns 304.

  3. (medium) Implement chunked request body decoding (state machine: size line, data, CRLF, repeat, terminating 0, optional trailers). Test with curl -H 'Transfer-Encoding: chunked' --data-binary @bigfile -X PUT. Done when: the stored value equals the file.

  4. (medium) Implement If-Match on PUT /kv/<key>: 412 if the current ETag differs. Write a two-client race test in Python that shows one writer winning and one getting 412. Done when: the test is deterministic.

  5. (hard) Port the server onto the module 06 epoll loop: per-connection Request parse state, output buffer, keep-alive. Benchmark with wrk -c 1000 -t 4 -d 10s http://127.0.0.1:8080/health against the thread-per-connection version. Done when: both survive 1000 connections and you can explain the throughput and memory difference.

  6. (hard) Add TLS with OpenSSL: SSL_CTX_new(TLS_server_method()), load a self-signed cert (openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes ...), SSL_accept, SSL_read/SSL_write replacing recv/send. Done when: curl -k https://127.0.0.1:8443/health works and openssl s_client shows TLS 1.3.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does an HTTP/1.1 receiver know where the body ends? A: Transfer-Encoding: chunked (size-prefixed chunks ending with a zero chunk), else Content-Length, else for responses until the connection closes. A request with a body and neither header is a 411. Both headers present is a smuggling risk and should be rejected.

Q: What is keep-alive and why does it matter? A: Reusing one TCP connection for sequential requests, the default in HTTP/1.1. It avoids a handshake, slow start and a TIME_WAIT per request, which is the difference between thousands and tens of thousands of requests per second for small responses. Both sides need idle timeouts and the client must handle the server closing an idle connection.

Q: Idempotent versus safe methods? A: Safe: no side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). Idempotent: repeating has the same effect as once (GET, PUT, DELETE; also HEAD, OPTIONS). POST is neither; make it retry-safe with an idempotency key. Caches, crawlers and retry logic all depend on this classification being honoured.

Q: What does HTTP/2 change and what does it not fix? A: Binary framing, multiplexed streams on one connection, header compression (HPACK), per-stream flow control, server push (deprecated in practice). It keeps HTTP semantics. It does not fix TCP-level head-of-line blocking: one lost segment stalls all streams, which HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes.

Q: Walk through a TLS 1.3 handshake. A: ClientHello with supported suites, an ECDHE key share, SNI and ALPN; ServerHello with its key share and chosen suite, then encrypted Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished; client Finished. One round trip; both derive symmetric keys from ECDHE (forward secrecy); the certificate chain proves identity. Resumption allows 0-RTT data.

Q: How would you design the REST API for loan disbursement? A: POST /loans/{id}/disbursements with an Idempotency-Key header, returning 201 and a Location for the disbursement resource (or 202 if asynchronous, with a status URL). Errors as Problem Details with a machine-readable code and request id. GET for status. Never a GET that disburses.

Q: When would you not write the HTTP server yourself? A: Whenever it faces other teams or the internet: chunked encoding, Expect, smuggling defences, TLS, HTTP/2 and compression are where hand-written servers fail or get exploited. Use cpp-httplib for simple blocking services, Beast on Asio for asynchronous scale, or sit behind nginx/Envoy and speak plain HTTP/1.1.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Request: request line, headers, blank line, body. Response: status line, headers, blank line, body. Body framed by chunked encoding, then Content-Length, else close.
  • Methods: GET/HEAD safe and idempotent; PUT/DELETE idempotent; POST neither (use idempotency keys).
  • 4xx: your fault, do not retry as-is. 5xx: server's fault, retry with backoff. 429/503 carry Retry-After.
  • Keep-alive is default in 1.1; idle timeouts on both sides; keep leftover bytes for pipelining.
  • Chunked: hex size, data, CRLF, repeat, 0\r\n\r\n.
  • HTTP/2: binary frames, multiplexed streams, HPACK, per-stream flow control, TCP HOL remains.
  • HTTP/3: same over QUIC on UDP, per-stream loss recovery, 1-RTT setup with TLS 1.3 built in.
  • TLS 1.3: one-RTT ECDHE handshake, certificate proves identity, forward secrecy; terminate at a proxy for convenience, not speed.
  • REST: resources as nouns, methods as verbs, status codes for outcomes, Problem Details for errors, ETag/If-Match for concurrency, idempotency keys for POST, path versioning, cursors.
  • Hand-write for learning and internal tools; use a library or a proxy for everything else.

docs.title: 09. Client-server architecture and reliability
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 05, 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
One server and one client is easy. Real systems have hundreds of branch clients, several application servers, a load balancer in front, a database cluster behind, and a network that sometimes drops, slows or lies. Reliability engineering is the set of habits that keep the whole thing working when any one piece is misbehaving: give every call a deadline, retry carefully, stop calling things that are failing, keep one bad tenant from hurting the others, say no early when overloaded, and record enough to see what happened.

Think of a bank branch at month-end. Queues form (load), a teller falls ill (server failure), the core system is slow (dependency latency). A well-run branch has a numbered-ticket system (queueing with limits), tells people "come back in an hour" when the queue is too long (load shedding), keeps a separate counter for pensioners so a long business transaction does not block them (bulkheads), and writes everything in a ledger with ticket numbers (observability with correlation ids).

This module names each habit, gives the standard algorithm for it, and ends with the request path of a banking server from branch to database, which is the architecture you already run.

docs.title: 2.1 Stateless vs stateful servers
docs.text:
A stateless server keeps nothing between requests: every request carries what is needed (an auth token, the account id), and any server instance can handle it. Add instances to scale; kill one and nothing is lost. State lives in a database or cache. HTTP APIs are designed this way.

A stateful server remembers the client between requests: a login session, a cursor, a half-built transaction, an open file. Scaling needs sticky sessions (the load balancer routes the same client to the same server) or a shared session store (Redis). Killing an instance loses its sessions. Your RPC server with a long-lived connection per branch and per-connection context is stateful by design; the question to ask is what is lost when a node dies and how the client recovers.

Middle ground: connection state (authenticated identity, protocol version) is fine; business state (the loan being built) should be persisted after each step so a reconnect can resume.

docs.title: 2.2 Sessions
docs.text: Options: server-side session id in a cookie or header with the data in a shared store; a signed token (JWT) that carries the claims so servers verify without a lookup (stateless, but revocation is hard, so keep lifetimes short and use refresh tokens); or a per-connection authenticated context as your RPC server does. Whatever you choose: sessions expire, re-auth is needed, and the logs carry the session or user id for correlation.

docs.title: 2.3 Connection pooling
docs.text:
Establishing a connection costs a TCP handshake, possibly TLS, authentication, and TCP slow start (modules 02, 08). A pool keeps N open connections to a backend and lends them out per request. Rules for a good pool:

  • Bounded size (the backend's capacity, not the client's wish). PostgreSQL and YugabyteDB handle a few hundred connections well; thousands need pgbouncer or the YSQL connection manager.
  • Health-check or validate on borrow (SELECT 1 or a protocol ping) when a connection has been idle longer than the server's idle timeout; discard on any error.
  • Max lifetime (recycle every 30 to 60 minutes) so DNS changes and server restarts are picked up.
  • Acquire timeout: waiting for a free connection is itself a bounded wait; failing fast beats queueing forever.
  • Metrics: in-use, idle, wait time, wait count. Pool exhaustion is the most common "the app is slow but the DB is fine" cause.

docs.title: 2.4 Load balancers: L4 vs L7
docs.text:
branches ---> [ LB ] ---> app1
                       \-> app2
                        \-> app3

L4 (transport layer) balancers forward TCP connections based on IP and port: they see bytes, not requests. Fast, protocol-agnostic, and the natural choice for your RPC-over-TCP: a connection lands on one app server and stays there. Examples: Linux IPVS/keepalived, HAProxy in TCP mode, AWS NLB, F5 in L4 mode. Balancing granularity is per connection, so long-lived connections can be unevenly distributed after a server restarts (everyone reconnected to the survivors).

L7 (application layer) balancers understand HTTP: route by path or header, retry failed requests, terminate TLS, add headers (X-Forwarded-For, X-Request-Id), rate limit, do canary routing by percentage. nginx, HAProxy in HTTP mode, Envoy, AWS ALB. Balancing is per request, so load evens out. Costs: more CPU, HTTP only, a place where request smuggling matters.

Algorithms: round robin, least connections (good for long-lived), weighted (bigger boxes get more), consistent hashing by key (cache affinity, module 12), random-two-choices (pick two at random, send to the less loaded; surprisingly close to optimal with cheap state).

docs.title: 2.5 Health checks
docs.text:
A load balancer removes a backend that fails health checks and adds it back when they pass.

  • Liveness: is the process alive and responding? (GET /health returns 200.) Fail it and the orchestrator restarts you.
  • Readiness: can it serve traffic right now? (Database reachable, caches warm, not shutting down.) Fail it and the LB stops sending traffic without restarting you. This is how graceful shutdown begins behind a load balancer: fail readiness, wait for the LB to notice (its check interval times its failure threshold), then stop accepting (module 05).
  • Depth: a shallow check (process up) is cheap but misses a broken DB connection; a deep check (query the DB) can take down every server at once when the DB hiccups. Common compromise: shallow readiness plus separate dependency metrics with alerts.
  • For an L4 balancer in front of your RPC server, the check is a TCP connect or a protocol-level PING; make sure PING does not need a worker thread, or a busy server looks dead.

docs.title: 2.6 Timeouts everywhere
docs.text:
Every blocking operation has a deadline: connect, each read, the whole request, each database query, the time waiting for a pool connection, the time in a queue. Rules:

  • The caller's deadline bounds the callee's: if the branch gave the app server 5 s, the app server gives the DB at most 4 s and the audit log write 0.5 s. Deadline propagation: pass the remaining time (or an absolute deadline) in the request.
  • Timeouts shorter than the dependency's normal p99 cause false failures; longer than the client's patience are useless. Measure, then set to about p99.9 of healthy latency with headroom.
  • A timeout is an "unknown outcome" (module 07). Decide per operation what happens next.
  • Idle timeouts on servers protect workers; connect timeouts on clients protect threads from black holes (default 2 minutes!).

docs.title: 2.7 Retries with exponential backoff and jitter
docs.text:
A retry turns a transient failure into a success. Done badly it turns a hiccup into an outage: every client retries at once, tripling the load on a server that was already struggling.

Rules:

  1. Retry only transient errors (Unavailable, 503, connection reset before any response byte, timeouts only if idempotent or keyed).
  2. Cap attempts (usually 3 total).
  3. Exponential backoff: wait base * 2^attempt (100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms), capped (say 5 s).
  4. Jitter: randomise the wait so clients do not retry in lockstep. "Full jitter" picks random(0, base * 2^attempt); AWS's analysis found it best for spreading load.
  5. Retry budget: allow retries to be at most, say, 10% of total requests per client; when the budget is exhausted, fail fast. This caps the amplification during an outage.
  6. Retry at one layer only. A client retrying three times, through a proxy that retries three times, onto a server that retries its DB three times, is 27x load.
std::chrono::milliseconds backoff(int attempt, int base_ms = 100, int cap_ms = 5000, std::mt19937& rng) {
    int exp = std::min(cap_ms, base_ms * (1 << attempt));
    return std::chrono::milliseconds(std::uniform_int_distribution<int>(0, exp)(rng));   // full jitter
}

docs.title: 2.8 Circuit breakers
docs.text:
If a dependency is down, every call to it wastes a thread for the full timeout and the failures cascade upward. A circuit breaker tracks recent failures per dependency and, when they cross a threshold, opens: calls fail immediately without touching the dependency. After a cool-down it goes half-open: one trial call; success closes the circuit, failure re-opens it.

   CLOSED --(failure rate > 50% over 20 calls)--> OPEN --(30 s)--> HALF-OPEN --success--> CLOSED
                                                   ^                   |
                                                   +------failure------+

The fast failure protects your own threads and gives the dependency room to recover. Pair it with a fallback where one exists (cached value, degraded response, "try again later" message). Libraries: Resilience4j (Java), Polly (.NET), Envoy outlier detection at the proxy level. In C++ you write it: a mutex, a sliding window of outcomes, a state enum and a timestamp.

docs.title: 2.9 Bulkheads
docs.text: Ships have compartments so one leak does not sink everything. In a server: separate thread pools or connection pools per dependency or per tenant, so a slow reporting query cannot consume every worker that the payment path needs. Also per-client concurrency limits (max in-flight per branch) and separate queues for interactive vs batch work. The cost is lower utilisation; the benefit is that one failure stays in its compartment.

docs.title: 2.10 Rate limiting
docs.text:
Protects a server from a client that sends too much, intentionally or by bug. Algorithms:

  • Token bucket (section 3): burst capacity, sustained rate. The standard. Used by Linux tc, AWS API Gateway, nginx limit_req (a variant: leaky bucket).
  • Leaky bucket: a queue drained at a fixed rate; smooths output rather than policing input.
  • Fixed window counter: "100 per minute" resets at :00; allows 200 in two seconds around the boundary. Simple, flawed.
  • Sliding window log/counter: more accurate, more state.

Where: at the edge (per IP, per API key), per tenant inside the app (per branch code), per dependency (how fast we may call them). Reply 429 or ERR_BUSY with Retry-After so good clients back off. Distributed limiting (many servers, one global limit) uses a shared store (Redis with Lua for atomicity) or per-server limits of global / N with some slack.

docs.title: 2.11 Load shedding and graceful degradation
docs.text: When overloaded, serve some requests well rather than all requests badly. Bounded queues with fast rejection (module 05), priority (health checks and payments before reports), adaptive concurrency limits (lower the in-flight limit when latency rises), and degradation: show cached balances when the live query fails, accept loan applications into a queue when the scoring service is down and process them later, disable a non-essential feature. Each degradation is a product decision made in advance, not at 3 AM.

docs.title: 2.12 Observability: metrics, logs, traces
docs.text:
• Metrics: numbers over time, cheap, aggregated. The RED set per endpoint: Rate (requests per second), Errors (per second, by class), Duration (histogram; p50, p99, p99.9). Plus saturation: queue depth, pool in-use, threads busy, fds open, CLOSE_WAIT count. Prometheus format with Grafana is the de facto standard; on Windows, performance counters or the same Prometheus exporters.
  • Logs: structured (JSON or key=value), one line per event, with a request id on every line so you can grep one request across servers. Log at the boundaries (received, dispatched to DB, replied) with durations. Never log secrets or full card numbers.
  • Traces: a request id that travels with the call (header or RPC field) plus per-hop spans with start, end and parent, assembled into a timeline: "branch -> app (120 ms) -> DB query (95 ms) -> audit write (20 ms)". OpenTelemetry is the standard API; Jaeger and Tempo store traces. Even without tooling, propagating a request id and logging durations per hop gives you 80% of the value.

What to alert on: SLO burn (error rate and latency against the target, module 13), saturation near limits, and nothing else at 3 AM. Everything else is a dashboard.

docs.title: 2.13 The banking server's request path
docs.text:
Branch client (teller UI)
   | RPC over TCP, long-lived connection, request id + branch code + teller id, deadline 10 s
   v
 L4 load balancer / VIP (health check: TCP connect or PING)
   v
 Application server (one of N)
   | acceptor + worker pool (module 05), per-connection auth context
   | per-request: validate, authorise, call business logic
   | DB pool (bounded, validated on borrow, deadline 8 s), circuit breaker per DB cluster
   v
 YugabyteDB (YSQL, RF3): PL/pgSQL procedures, transaction, Raft replication (modules 11-12)
   ^
   | audit/event log write (separate pool: bulkhead), notification queue (async; module 14)

Reliability features to be able to point at in this picture: deadline propagation (10 s at the branch, 8 s for the DB, so the branch always gets an answer before giving up); idempotency key = the branch's transaction id stored with the posting; retries only at the branch client, only for Unavailable, with jitter, never for a timed-out posting without the key; circuit breaker around the DB so a cluster outage fails fast and the branch shows a clear message; a separate pool for audit writes so audit slowness cannot block postings; rate limit per branch to contain a looping client; PING answered off the worker pool so health checks work under load; request id in every log line on both sides. Every one of those is a sentence you can say in an interview, and each maps to something you can check in the real code this week.

docs.title: 3.1 Token bucket (code/m09_token_bucket.cpp)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 m09_token_bucket.cpp -o token_bucket && ./token_bucket

Lazy refill: no timer thread, tokens are computed from elapsed time at each call.

class TokenBucket {
public:
    TokenBucket(double capacity, double rate_per_sec, std::function<TimePoint()> now = Clock::now);
    bool try_acquire(double n = 1.0) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mu_);
        refill();
        if (tokens_ >= n) { tokens_ -= n; return true; }
        return false;
    }
    std::chrono::microseconds time_until(double n = 1.0);   // for Retry-After or a sleep
private:
    void refill() {
        TimePoint t = now_();
        double elapsed = std::chrono::duration<double>(t - last_).count();
        if (elapsed > 0) { tokens_ = std::min(capacity_, tokens_ + elapsed * rate_); last_ = t; }
    }
    double capacity_, rate_, tokens_; std::function<TimePoint()> now_; TimePoint last_; std::mutex mu_;
};

The injectable clock makes the test deterministic (burst of exactly capacity, exactly rate tokens after one second, never above capacity after an hour). The concurrent demo runs 8 threads for one second against burst 50 and rate 100 and checks that about 150 requests were accepted no matter how hard the threads hammer. KeyedLimiter keeps one bucket per key with idle eviction, which is the per-branch limiter from the request path.

docs.title: 3.2 Backoff and circuit breaker sketches
docs.text:
// Full-jitter backoff. attempt starts at 0.
std::chrono::milliseconds backoff_ms(int attempt, std::mt19937& rng, int base = 100, int cap = 5000) {
    int exp = std::min(cap, base * (1 << std::min(attempt, 10)));
    return std::chrono::milliseconds(std::uniform_int_distribution<int>(0, exp)(rng));
}

class CircuitBreaker {
    enum class State { Closed, Open, HalfOpen } state_ = State::Closed;
    int failures_ = 0, window_ = 0; TimePoint opened_at_;
    const int min_calls_ = 20; const double threshold_ = 0.5; const std::chrono::seconds cooldown_{30};
    std::mutex mu_;
public:
    bool allow() {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mu_);
        if (state_ == State::Open) {
            if (Clock::now() - opened_at_ < cooldown_) return false;
            state_ = State::HalfOpen; return true;             // one trial call
        }
        return true;
    }
    void record(bool ok) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mu_);
        if (state_ == State::HalfOpen) { state_ = ok ? State::Closed : State::Open; opened_at_ = Clock::now(); failures_ = window_ = 0; return; }
        ++window_; if (!ok) ++failures_;
        if (window_ >= min_calls_) {
            if (static_cast<double>(failures_) / window_ > threshold_) { state_ = State::Open; opened_at_ = Clock::now(); }
            failures_ = window_ = 0;
        }
    }
};

Exercise 3 turns the sketch into a tested class.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why jitter works. Without it, N clients that failed at the same instant retry at the same instant: the server sees N requests in one burst, which is exactly what overloaded it, repeated at 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms. With full jitter the N retries spread uniformly over the window; the peak load drops by roughly the ratio of window length to request service time. Marc Brooker's AWS analysis (2015) showed full jitter needs the fewest total calls to get all clients through.

Metastable failure. A system can enter a state where load from retries alone keeps it overloaded even after the original trigger is gone: the retries cause timeouts which cause more retries. Recovery needs the clients to back off or the server to shed load below its capacity. Retry budgets and circuit breakers exist to prevent this state; bounded queues and fast rejection end it.

Queueing theory in one line. At utilisation rho, mean wait grows like rho / (1 - rho) times service time (M/M/1). At 50% utilisation you wait one service time; at 90%, nine; at 99%, ninety-nine. This is why p99 latency explodes long before CPU hits 100%, why you provision for 60 to 70% utilisation, and why admission control (reject at a queue depth) keeps latency sane under overload.

Connection pool sizing. Little's law: connections = throughput * latency. 500 queries per second at 20 ms each need 10 connections on average; size for the peak with headroom (say 25), not for the number of application threads (often hundreds). More connections than the database has cores plus disks mostly adds contention. PostgreSQL's advice of "a small pool, around 2 to 4 times the CPU count" comes from this.

Where the token bucket lives. In-process: a mutex and two doubles; contention is negligible below millions of operations per second. Per-key maps need eviction (the demo sweeps on each call after an interval) or a bounded LRU. Distributed: Redis INCR with expiry for fixed windows, or a Lua script implementing the bucket atomically; or let each of N servers enforce limit / N and accept the error.

Health check propagation delay. An LB with a 5 s interval and 3-failure threshold takes up to 15 s to stop sending traffic to a dead backend; during that time those requests fail. Shorter intervals cost load; passive health checks (eject on real request failures, Envoy's outlier detection) react in milliseconds. Graceful shutdown must wait at least the detection window after failing readiness.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Retry storm after a 2-second database stall. All branch clients timed out together and retried immediately, three times. The DB, now healthy, saw 4x normal load and stalled again. The system took 20 minutes to recover from a 2-second event. Jittered backoff and a retry budget would have recovered in seconds. If your clients retry, find out how.
  • Pool exhaustion masquerading as a slow DB. p99 latency jumped to 5 s; DB metrics were flat. The app's pool of 10 connections was fully in use because one slow report query held connections for 30 s each. Pool wait time was not measured. Bulkhead (separate pool for reports) and the wait-time metric fixed diagnosis and cause.
  • Deep health check takes everything down. Readiness checked the database; a 10-second DB failover made every app server fail readiness; the LB had no backends; clients got connection refused for something the app could have partially served (cached reads). Shallow readiness, plus dependency alerting, plus degraded mode.
  • Timeout longer than the caller's. App waited 30 s for the DB; the branch client gave up at 10 s and retried; the app did the work twice and the branch saw a timeout anyway. Deadline propagation: the callee's timeout must be shorter than the caller's remaining time.
  • The looping branch client. A bug made one branch's terminal resend a balance query in a tight loop: 2,000 requests per second from one connection, starving others. Per-connection token bucket (ERR_BUSY) contained it to that branch within seconds.
  • Logs without request ids. An incident where "some" postings failed took two days to reconstruct from unlinked client and server logs. A request id generated at the branch and logged on every line turned the next one into a 20-minute grep.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Add a per-connection TokenBucket to the module 05 tcpkv server (burst 100, rate 50/s). Excess commands get -ERR_BUSY. Done when: m05_loadtest.py --pipeline 200 sees ERR_BUSY and a normal client does not.

  2. (easy) Write backoff_ms and plot (print) the schedule for attempts 0 to 5 for ten different seeds. Done when: you can explain why no two clients retry at the same instant.

  3. (medium) Implement CircuitBreaker as a tested class with an injectable clock: closed to open after 50% failures over 20 calls, half-open after 30 s, one trial. Done when: tests cover every transition.

  4. (medium) Add X-Request-Id handling to the module 08 HTTP server: accept it from the client or generate one, echo it in the response, and log one JSON line per request with method, path, status, duration and the id. Done when: curl -H 'X-Request-Id: abc' produces a log line with abc.

  5. (hard) Build a connection pool for the module 07 RPC client: fixed size, acquire with timeout, validate on borrow if idle more than 10 s (send Echo), discard on error, max lifetime 60 s, metrics for in-use/idle/wait. Done when: 32 threads share 8 connections correctly under the demo server and pool exhaustion produces a clear timeout error rather than a hang.

  6. (hard) Write a one-page reliability review of your employer's request path using section 2.13 as the template: for each hop list the timeout, retry policy, idempotency mechanism, pool bound, breaker, and what the client sees when that hop fails. Mark unknowns. Done when: every row is filled in or marked "find out", and you have three concrete improvements.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Stateless versus stateful servers? A: Stateless servers keep nothing between requests, so any instance can serve any request: easy to scale and replace, state lives in a store. Stateful servers remember clients (sessions, connections, cursors): need sticky routing or shared session stores, and lose state on failure. Keep connection-level state small and persist business state after each step.

Q: L4 versus L7 load balancing? A: L4 forwards TCP connections by IP and port: fast, protocol-agnostic, per-connection granularity, right for RPC-over-TCP. L7 understands HTTP: routes by path and headers, retries, terminates TLS, adds request ids, balances per request. Costs more CPU and only works for HTTP.

Q: How should a client retry? A: Only transient errors, only idempotent (or keyed) operations after timeouts, capped attempts, exponential backoff with full jitter, a retry budget, and at one layer only. Otherwise retries amplify an outage.

Q: What is a circuit breaker and why use one? A: A per-dependency state machine that fails calls fast when the dependency has been failing (open), retries one trial after a cool-down (half-open), and resumes on success (closed). It saves your threads from waiting on timeouts, stops cascading failure, and gives the dependency room to recover. Pair it with a fallback.

Q: Explain the token bucket. A: A bucket of capacity C refills at R tokens per second; each request takes a token; empty means reject or wait. C is the allowed burst, R the sustained rate. Implemented lazily: on each call add elapsed * R capped at C, then try to subtract. One mutex and two doubles.

Q: Why timeouts everywhere, and how do you choose them? A: Any unbounded wait eventually holds a thread forever on a dead peer. Set each timeout from the dependency's healthy p99.9 with headroom, make callee timeouts shorter than the caller's remaining deadline (propagate deadlines), and decide the action for each timeout since the outcome is unknown.

Q: What do you monitor on a server? A: Per endpoint: rate, errors by class, duration histogram (p50/p99/p99.9). Saturation: queue depth, pool in-use and wait time, worker threads busy, fds, CLOSE_WAIT count. Structured logs with a request id on every line; traces or at least per-hop durations. Alert on SLO burn and saturation.

Q: How does graceful shutdown work behind a load balancer? A: Fail the readiness check first, wait for the LB's detection window so it stops sending new connections, then stop accepting, drain in-flight requests with a deadline, force-close stragglers, exit. Skipping the first step causes a burst of connection-refused errors.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Stateless scales by adding instances; stateful needs stickiness or shared state; persist business state after each step.
  • Pools: bounded, validated on borrow, max lifetime, acquire timeout, metrics. Size by Little's law.
  • L4 for TCP protocols, L7 for HTTP features. Health checks: liveness restarts, readiness routes.
  • Timeouts on every wait; propagate deadlines; callee shorter than caller.
  • Retries: transient only, idempotent only after timeouts, capped, exponential backoff with full jitter, retry budget, one layer.
  • Circuit breaker: closed, open, half-open; fail fast; fallback.
  • Bulkheads: separate pools per dependency or tenant.
  • Token bucket: burst C, rate R, lazy refill; per key with eviction; 429/ERR_BUSY with Retry-After.
  • Shed load early with bounded queues; degrade deliberately.
  • Metrics (RED plus saturation), structured logs with request ids, traces across hops.
  • Your request path: branch deadline 10 s, app to DB 8 s, idempotency key = branch txn id, breaker around DB, separate audit pool, per-branch rate limit, PING off the worker pool, ids in every log.

docs.title: 10. Distributed systems fundamentals
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 07, 09; 07_Databases_Internals/05_transactions_acid_mvcc.md

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A distributed system is several computers that cooperate over a network and try to look like one. Your banking server talking to a three-node YugabyteDB cluster is one. The moment there is more than one machine, two new facts rule everything: parts can fail while the rest keeps running, and there is no shared clock to say what happened first. Almost every idea in this module (replication, quorums, consistency models, hybrid clocks) is a way of living with those two facts.

Analogy: three bank branches keep copies of the same ledger and phone each other to stay in sync. The phone line sometimes drops. A clerk sometimes goes home sick without telling anyone. Each branch's wall clock is a few minutes off. Now a customer deposits at branch A and withdraws at branch B two minutes later. Did B see the deposit? Which happened first, by whose clock? If the phone line between A and B is down, should B refuse the withdrawal (safe but unhelpful) or allow it (helpful but maybe wrong)? That last question is CAP, and the rest of the module is the vocabulary for answering the others precisely.

You already know the single-machine version of these problems: threads with no ordering guarantee (see 04_Concurrency/07_atomics_and_the_memory_model.md) and transactions with isolation levels (see 07_Databases_Internals/05_transactions_acid_mvcc.md). Distributed systems are those problems again, with messages that can be lost and machines that can vanish.

docs.title: 2.1 Partial failure and the network you actually have
docs.text:
On one machine, a function call either returns or the whole process crashes. Across a network, a request can:

  1. never arrive (packet lost, peer down, cable cut);
  2. arrive and be processed, but the reply is lost;
  3. arrive and be processed slowly (GC pause, swapping, a disk stall), so the reply is late;
  4. arrive at a node that crashes halfway through.

From the caller's side, cases 1 to 4 look identical: no reply before the timeout. You cannot tell "dead" from "slow" from "did the work but the answer got lost". This is partial failure, and it is the root of every hard problem in this course. Module 07 met it as "timeout with unknown outcome". A distributed database meets it on every replication message.

The eight fallacies of distributed computing (L. Peter Deutsch and others at Sun, 1990s) are the assumptions that break first: the network is reliable; latency is zero; bandwidth is infinite; the network is secure; topology does not change; there is one administrator; transport cost is zero; the network is homogeneous.

System models are how papers state their assumptions. Know the names:

Model Meaning Synchronous Message delay and clock drift have known upper bounds. Easy to reason about; not true of real networks. Asynchronous No bounds at all. A slow node is indistinguishable from a dead one. Partially synchronous Bounds exist most of the time but can be violated for a while. Real systems are designed for this. Raft and Paxos are safe always and make progress when the network behaves. Crash-stop / crash-recovery Nodes fail by stopping (and maybe restarting with their disk). Raft assumes crash-recovery. Byzantine Nodes can lie or be malicious. Needs 3f+1 nodes to tolerate f liars. Blockchains; not databases inside one bank.

FLP impossibility (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985): in a purely asynchronous system, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus if even one node may crash. Practical systems escape it with timeouts (partial synchrony): they stay safe always and are live "when the network is calm enough". That is why Raft uses randomised election timeouts (module 11).

Two Generals problem: two parties communicating over a lossy channel can never be certain they both agree to act, because the last message could always be lost. TCP's handshake does not solve it; it just makes the uncertainty small. Distributed commit protocols (2PC, module 12) live with it by having a durable decision somewhere.

docs.title: 2.2 No global clock
docs.text:
Every machine has its own quartz oscillator, and they drift: typical crystal drift is tens of parts per million, which is a few seconds a day if nobody corrects it. Two kinds of clock:

  • Wall clock (CLOCK_REALTIME, gettimeofday, Windows GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime): seconds since the epoch, synchronised by NTP, and can jump backwards when NTP steps it or an operator changes it.
  • Monotonic clock (CLOCK_MONOTONIC, std::chrono::steady_clock, Windows QueryPerformanceCounter): only goes forward, meaningless across machines. Use it for timeouts and durations, always. Using wall time for a timeout is a classic bug that fires on a leap second or an NTP step.

NTP (Network Time Protocol) estimates the offset to a time server from four timestamps of a request/response, assuming the path is symmetric. On a LAN with a nearby server, typical accuracy is around a millisecond; across the internet, typically tens of milliseconds; under asymmetric routes or a loaded server, worse, and NTP cannot detect asymmetry. chrony (default on Ubuntu and RHEL) converges faster than classic ntpd. NTP slews small offsets (runs the clock slightly fast or slow) and steps large ones (jumps). PTP (IEEE 1588) with hardware timestamping gets to microseconds or better inside a datacenter. Cloud providers offer precise time services (AWS Time Sync, Google's public NTP with leap smearing).

Leap seconds: an extra second inserted at 23:59:60 UTC. Linux used to step backwards; big providers now smear it over many hours instead. Bugs from the 2012 leap second (livelocked threads in futex code on some kernels) are the reason to know the term.

Because clocks disagree, "event A happened at 10:00:00.003 on node 1 and B at 10:00:00.001 on node 2" does not tell you B happened first. You need logical time.

Lamport clocks (Lamport, 1978): each node keeps a counter. Increment before each event; send the counter with each message; on receive set counter = max(local, received) + 1. Guarantee: if A happened-before B (A on the same node earlier, or A is a send and B its receive, or a chain of those), then L(A) < L(B). The converse is false: a smaller number does not prove causality. Lamport timestamps have nothing to do with real time.

Vector clocks: each node keeps a vector of counters, one per node. They capture causality exactly (you can tell "A before B", "B before A" or "concurrent"), at the cost of O(N) size. Dynamo-style stores used them to detect conflicting concurrent writes.

Hybrid logical clocks (HLC) (Kulkarni, Demirbas et al., 2014) combine both: a timestamp (l, c) where l tracks the largest physical time seen and c is a small logical counter. Properties:

  • l is always at least the local physical clock, and never more than the maximum clock skew ahead of it. So HLC values are close to real time and can be compared with wall-clock ranges.
  • If A happened-before B then HLC(A) < HLC(B), like Lamport.
  • It fits in 64 bits.

YugabyteDB's "hybrid time" is an HLC: microseconds of physical time in the high bits and a 12-bit logical counter in the low bits of one uint64. Every Raft message and every RPC between tablet servers carries the sender's hybrid time, and the receiver bumps its own clock past it. MVCC versions are stamped with hybrid time, and a snapshot read "as of time T" means "all versions with hybrid time <= T". CockroachDB uses HLC the same way. Google Spanner instead uses TrueTime: GPS and atomic clocks give each node an interval [earliest, latest] guaranteed to contain true time, and a commit waits out the uncertainty (commit wait) before becoming visible. HLC databases cannot wait out an unknown bound, so they assume one (max_clock_skew_usec in YugabyteDB) and handle the ambiguity on reads (section 4).

docs.title: 2.3 CAP, plainly
docs.text:
CAP (Brewer's conjecture 2000, proved by Gilbert and Lynch 2002): when there is a network partition (some nodes cannot talk to others), a system that replicates data must choose between:

  • Consistency (here it means linearizability, section 2.5): every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were one copy; or
  • Availability: every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response.

It cannot have both during the partition. That is the whole theorem. Things people get wrong:

  • "Pick two of three" is misleading. Partitions are not optional; they happen. The real choice is what you do during a partition: refuse some requests (CP) or answer with possibly stale or conflicting data (AP).
  • C in CAP is not C in ACID. ACID's C means "constraints hold". CAP's C means linearizable.
  • A in CAP is very strict: every non-failed node must answer. A Raft cluster where the majority side keeps serving is "CP" by the definition, yet highly available in everyday language.
  • When there is no partition, CAP says nothing.

Examples:

  • YugabyteDB, CockroachDB, Spanner, etcd, ZooKeeper: CP. A tablet whose Raft group lost its majority refuses writes (and strong reads) until the majority is back. The minority side errors.
  • Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), Riak: AP (tunable). Any replica accepts writes; conflicts are resolved later (last-write-wins by timestamp, or vector clocks, or CRDTs).
  • A single PostgreSQL primary with async standbys: not partition-tolerant in the CAP sense. If the primary is cut off, the clients that can reach it continue; those that cannot get errors. If someone promotes a standby on the other side, you can get two primaries (split brain, section 2.8).

docs.title: 2.4 PACELC
docs.text:
PACELC (Daniel Abadi, 2010): if Partition, choose A or C; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. This is the more useful statement, because the "else" case is 99.99% of your life. Strong consistency costs a round trip to a quorum on every write (and on some reads), even when nothing is broken.

System P: A or C E: L or C Notes YugabyteDB / CockroachDB / Spanner C C Every write waits for a Raft majority. Optional follower reads trade C for L. Cassandra / DynamoDB A L Tunable per request with consistency levels; default favours latency. PostgreSQL + async standby (C on primary) L Commit returns before the standby has the WAL. A failover can lose the last commits. PostgreSQL + synchronous standby C (blocks if standby gone) C Commit waits for the standby's flush. MongoDB (majority write concern) C C With w:1 it is closer to L.

For a bank, the ledger is PC/EC: a wrong balance is worse than a slow one. The customer-facing "recent transactions" screen could be EL (follower read, a second stale) without harm.

docs.title: 2.5 Consistency models with concrete examples
docs.text:
A consistency model is a contract: which values a read is allowed to return given the writes that happened. From strongest to weakest:

Linearizability (atomic consistency). The system behaves as if there is a single copy and each operation takes effect at one instant between its start and its end. Once a write completes, every later read (by anyone, anywhere) sees it or something newer.

  • Example: teller 1 posts a deposit and gets "OK" at 10:00:00. Teller 2 at another branch queries the balance at 10:00:01. Linearizable: teller 2 sees the deposit. Always.
  • Who gives it: Raft-based systems reading from the leader with a valid lease (YugabyteDB default reads), etcd, ZooKeeper sync+read, Spanner.
  • Cost: a quorum round trip per write, and reads must go to (or check with) the leader.

Sequential consistency. All nodes see all operations in one total order that respects each client's own program order, but that order need not match real time.

  • Example: teller 1 posts deposit D at 10:00:00 and gets OK. Teller 2 reads at 10:00:01 and does not see D yet, but will see it later, and every observer agrees D happened before any later operation by teller 1. Allowed under sequential, forbidden under linearizable.
  • Who gives it: ZooKeeper reads without sync (ZooKeeper's actual guarantee is close to this per session).

Causal consistency. Operations that are causally related (one could have influenced the other) are seen by everyone in that order. Concurrent operations may be seen in different orders by different nodes.

  • Example: a customer posts "salary credited" and then their spouse, having seen it, posts "rent paid". Causal: no one sees "rent paid" without "salary credited". Two unrelated deposits at two branches may appear in either order to different readers.
  • Who gives it: MongoDB causal sessions, COPS-style research systems. It is the strongest model that stays available during partitions.

Session guarantees (weaker, but what users notice):

  • Read-your-writes: after you write, you see your write. Violated when your write goes to the leader and your next read goes to a lagging follower. The customer transfers money, the app refreshes from a read replica, and the transfer is "missing". Fix: read from the leader for a while after a write, or carry the write's timestamp and read at or after it.
  • Monotonic reads: you never see time go backwards. Violated when two consecutive reads hit two replicas with different lag: balance shows 900, then 1000 again, then 900. Fix: stick a session to one replica, or carry the last-seen timestamp.
  • Monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads complete the set.

Eventual consistency. If writes stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value. No promise about what you read before that.

  • Example: DNS. Change a record; for up to the TTL, some resolvers return the old address.
  • Who gives it: Cassandra at consistency level ONE, DynamoDB default reads, async read replicas, caches.

How this relates to isolation levels. Isolation (read committed, snapshot, serializable) is about concurrent transactions on the data; consistency models are about replicas and real-time order of single operations. The combination of serializable isolation and linearizability is strict serializability (Spanner calls it external consistency): transactions appear in a serial order that matches real time. YugabyteDB SERIALIZABLE on a single cluster aims at this; snapshot isolation is its default. The Jepsen site's consistency-model map is the best one-page reference.

docs.title: 2.6 Replication topologies
docs.text:
Replication = keeping copies of the same data on several nodes, for fault tolerance (a copy survives a dead node), read scaling, and locality.

Single-leader (primary/replica, master/slave). All writes go to one leader; it ships a log of changes to followers; followers apply it in order. Reads go to the leader (fresh) or followers (maybe stale).

  • PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL replication, MongoDB replica sets, Kafka partitions, and each Raft group (a YugabyteDB tablet is single-leader per tablet).
  • Simple, no write conflicts. The leader is a bottleneck and a single point of failure until failover.

Multi-leader (active-active writes). Several nodes accept writes and replicate to each other asynchronously.

  • Used across datacenters (each DC has a leader), for offline clients (a phone app that syncs later), and for collaborative editing.
  • The hard part is write conflicts: branch A sets the account's address to X while branch B sets it to Y, at the same time, on different leaders. Resolution: last-write-wins by timestamp (silently loses a write), merge functions, CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types; counters and sets that merge mathematically), or application-level resolution.
  • YugabyteDB xCluster bidirectional replication between two clusters is multi-leader with last-writer-wins at the row level; you must design so the same row is not written on both sides.
  • For a ledger, multi-leader on the same accounts is a bad idea. Partition ownership instead: each region owns its accounts.

Leaderless (Dynamo-style). Any replica accepts reads and writes; the client (or a coordinator) sends each write to N replicas and waits for W acknowledgements, and each read to R replicas.

  • Cassandra, Riak, DynamoDB internally, ScyllaDB.
  • Repair mechanisms: read repair (a read that sees a stale replica writes the newer value back), anti-entropy (background Merkle-tree comparison), hinted handoff (if a replica is down, another node holds the write as a "hint" and forwards it later).

docs.title: 2.7 Synchronous vs asynchronous replication
docs.text:
synchronous                                asynchronous
 client -> leader: write                    client -> leader: write
           leader -> follower: log entry              leader: commit locally
           follower: fsync, ack                       leader -> client: OK
           leader: commit                             ... later ...
           leader -> client: OK                       leader -> follower: log entry
  • Synchronous: the client's OK means the change is on more than one machine. Survives the leader dying immediately after OK (RPO = 0). Costs at least one network round trip per commit, and if the synchronous follower is down the leader blocks (unless you have more followers).
  • Asynchronous: OK means "on the leader's disk". Fast, unaffected by follower health. If the leader dies before shipping, the last commits are lost on failover (RPO > 0, typically the replication lag: milliseconds normally, minutes under load).
  • Semi-synchronous / quorum: wait for some followers. PostgreSQL's synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (s1, s2)' waits for any one of two. Raft is quorum replication: the leader waits for a majority (including itself), so with RF3 it waits for one follower, whichever answers first. One slow follower does not slow commits; losing one node loses nothing.

docs.title: 2.8 Failover and split brain
docs.text:
Failover: the leader is detected dead and a follower is promoted. Steps: detect (heartbeats stop for longer than a timeout), choose the new leader (most up-to-date follower), reconfigure clients (VIP move, DNS change, or clients ask "who is leader"), and make sure the old leader stays out.

What goes wrong:

  • False detection: the leader was slow (GC pause, network blip), not dead. Now you fail over unnecessarily, or worse, the old leader comes back believing it is still in charge.
  • Lost writes: with async replication, the promoted follower lacks the last commits. When the old leader returns, its extra writes conflict. GitHub's 2018 incident (a 43-second network partition between US East Coast sites led to a MySQL failover and hours of reconciling writes made on both sides) is the well-known public example.
  • Split brain: two nodes both believe they are the leader and both accept writes. Divergent data that cannot be merged automatically. For a bank: the same money spent twice.

Defences:

  • Quorum / majority: a leader must hold a majority to act. Two disjoint majorities cannot exist, so two leaders cannot both commit. This is Raft's answer (module 11), and why you deploy 3 or 5 nodes, never 2. With 2 nodes, neither side of a partition is a majority; either both stop (safe) or you allow one side to proceed with a tie-breaker (a witness or arbiter node).
  • Fencing tokens: every leadership grant comes with a number that only increases (Raft's term, ZooKeeper's zxid, an epoch). Storage and downstream services reject requests carrying an older token. A zombie leader waking from a 30-second GC pause has an old token and is refused.
  • STONITH ("shoot the other node in the head"): the cluster manager power-cycles or isolates the old leader via IPMI or a cloud API before promoting. Pacemaker clusters do this.
  • Leases: the leader may act only while its lease (a time-bounded grant from a quorum) is valid, and followers will not elect a new leader until the lease could have expired. Leases depend on clocks running at roughly the same rate (not the same time), which is a much weaker assumption.

docs.title: 2.9 Quorums
docs.text:
With N replicas, write to W and read from R. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write (given versions to tell newest from older).

N W R Effect 3 2 2 Classic majority quorum; tolerates 1 failure for both reads and writes. 3 3 1 Fast reads; any one node down blocks writes. 3 1 3 Fast writes; any node down blocks reads; data on one node until replicated. 3 1 1 Eventual consistency; fastest; reads may be stale. 5 3 3 Tolerates 2 failures.

Caveats that interviewers like:

  • R + W > N is not linearizability by itself. With concurrent writes, sloppy quorums, or a write that succeeded on fewer than W nodes before failing, a reader can see a new value and a later reader an old one. Dynamo-style stores are eventually consistent with "usually fresh" reads.
  • Sloppy quorum: if the home replicas are down, write to other nodes (hinted handoff) to stay available. Then R + W > N no longer guarantees overlap.
  • Majority quorum in consensus (Raft, Paxos) is different: N = 2f + 1 tolerates f failures, a leader needs a majority to be elected and to commit, and any two majorities intersect. That intersection is what carries committed data from one leader to the next.

Fault tolerance table to memorise: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2, 7 tolerate 3. 4 nodes still tolerate only 1 (majority of 4 is 3), so even sizes add cost without adding tolerance.

docs.title: 2.10 Exactly-once: the myth and the practice
docs.text:
Delivery guarantees between a sender and a receiver over an unreliable network:

  • At-most-once: send once, never retry. Messages can be lost. ("Fire and forget".)
  • At-least-once: retry until acknowledged. Messages can be duplicated (the ack was lost, not the message).
  • Exactly-once delivery: impossible in general over a lossy network with failing nodes. This is the Two Generals problem again: the sender can never be sure whether the receiver processed the last attempt.

What systems actually provide is exactly-once processing (effect):

 exactly-once effect = at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing (or deduplication)
  • Idempotency key: the client generates a unique id per logical operation (the branch's transaction reference). The server stores it in the same transaction as the effect (a unique constraint on posting.idempotency_key). A retry hits the constraint and returns the stored result instead of posting twice. Module 07 built this vocabulary.
  • Dedup table with expiry: remember processed message ids for longer than the maximum retry window.
  • Naturally idempotent operations: "set balance to 1000" is idempotent; "add 100" is not. Design state changes as "set to" or "apply event #N" where possible.
  • Kafka's exactly-once semantics = idempotent producers (sequence numbers per partition so the broker drops duplicates) plus transactions that atomically write output and commit consumer offsets. It is exactly-once inside Kafka. The moment your consumer calls an external system (sends an SMS, calls a payment API), you are back to at-least-once plus idempotency.

The interview sentence: "There is no exactly-once delivery; there is at-least-once delivery with an idempotent receiver, and I make the dedup check and the side effect atomic."

docs.title: 3.1 Hybrid logical clock simulation (code/m10_hlc.cpp)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 m10_hlc.cpp -o hlc && ./hlc

Three simulated nodes with skewed clocks (B runs 5 ms fast, C runs 8 ms slow) exchange messages with random delays. Halfway through, A's clock is stepped back 20 ms, like an NTP step. The program counts how often raw wall-clock timestamps say a message was received before it was sent (hundreds of times in a typical run), and asserts that the HLC orders every send before its receive, never goes backwards on any node, and never runs ahead of the fastest physical clock.

The whole algorithm is two functions:

struct Hlc { int64_t l = 0; uint32_t c = 0; };   // l: microseconds, c: logical counter

Hlc local_or_send(int64_t true_us) {
    int64_t pt = physical(true_us);                // this node's (skewed) wall clock
    int64_t l_new = std::max(h_.l, pt);
    h_.c = (l_new == h_.l) ? h_.c + 1 : 0;         // physical clock did not advance: bump counter
    h_.l = l_new;
    return h_;
}

Hlc receive(const Hlc& m, int64_t true_us) {
    int64_t pt = physical(true_us);
    int64_t l_new = std::max({h_.l, m.l, pt});
    if (l_new == h_.l && l_new == m.l) h_.c = std::max(h_.c, m.c) + 1;
    else if (l_new == h_.l)            h_.c = h_.c + 1;
    else if (l_new == m.l)             h_.c = m.c + 1;   // sender was ahead: inherit its counter
    else                               h_.c = 0;         // our physical clock is ahead of both
    h_.l = l_new;
    return h_;
}

// YugabyteDB-style packing: one uint64 compare orders two hybrid times.
uint64_t packed() const { return (static_cast<uint64_t>(l) << 12) | c; }

Read the output lines marked [RAW CLOCK WRONG]: the send's physical time is later than the receive's, but the HLC values are correctly ordered because the receiver adopted the sender's l and bumped c.

docs.title: 3.2 An idempotent posting, the SQL half
docs.text:
-- The dedup check and the effect commit together or not at all.
CREATE TABLE posting (
    posting_id      bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
    idempotency_key text   NOT NULL UNIQUE,   -- branch code + branch txn reference
    account_no      text   NOT NULL,
    amount_minor    bigint NOT NULL,
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (posting_id)
);

-- Retry-safe insert: a duplicate returns the original row instead of posting twice.
INSERT INTO posting (idempotency_key, account_no, amount_minor)
VALUES ('BR017-T000981', 'ACC0004242', 50000)
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING posting_id;
-- If RETURNING gave no row, SELECT the existing one by idempotency_key and return it.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why HLC needs a skew bound for reads. A snapshot read at hybrid time T on tablet X wants every write with timestamp <= T. But a write committed on another node whose clock is behind could get a timestamp slightly <= T after our read started, because that node's clock had not caught up. The reader cannot know whether such a write exists. YugabyteDB handles this with an uncertainty window: if a read at T finds a value with timestamp in (T, T + max_clock_skew], it cannot tell whether that write happened before or after the read in real time, so it restarts the read at a later time ("Restart read required" in logs and errors, retried internally where possible). max_clock_skew_usec defaults to 500 ms in YugabyteDB (check your version's docs). If real skew exceeds the configured bound, correctness is no longer guaranteed, which is why YugabyteDB servers refuse to run (crash with a clock-skew error) when they detect their clock is too far off, and why you monitor NTP/chrony on every database node. Spanner avoids the restart by waiting out the uncertainty at commit time instead (commit wait), which needs TrueTime's tight bounds.

HLC counter overflow. The logical counter c grows only while physical time does not advance past l. With microsecond physical time, 12 bits (4096 events per microsecond per node) is plenty. If a node's clock is stepped back a long way, l stays ahead and c carries the ordering until physical time catches up. The demo shows this after the 20 ms step.

What a "linearizable read" costs in Raft. A leader cannot just read its local state: it might have been deposed a moment ago without knowing (a new leader already committed newer writes). Two fixes: (1) ReadIndex: record the commit index, send a heartbeat round to confirm leadership with a majority, wait until the state machine has applied that index, then read. One round trip per read (batched). (2) Leader lease: followers promise not to elect a new leader for a lease period after acknowledging the leader; within the lease the leader reads locally with no round trip. YugabyteDB uses leader leases (default lease around 2 seconds; this is part of why a dead leader's tablets are unavailable for a few seconds before a new one is elected). Leases rely on bounded clock drift rate, not synchronised time.

Replication lag is a queue. Async replication lag = time the follower is behind. It grows when the follower applies slower than the leader writes (single-threaded replay, a long query on the standby holding back replay because of hot_standby_feedback or conflicts, slow disk). PostgreSQL exposes it in pg_stat_replication (write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag). Raft followers expose it as how far their applied index trails the leader's commit index.

Why majorities, mathematically. Two subsets of size > N/2 of an N-set must intersect (their sizes sum to more than N). Any decision made by one majority is therefore seen by at least one member of every future majority. Raft's election vote restriction (module 11) uses that member to guarantee the next leader already has every committed entry.

Timeouts are a guess. Every failure detector in an asynchronous network is either too eager (false positives: needless failovers) or too slow (long unavailability). Production systems use heartbeats every 100 ms to 1 s and declare failure after a few missed ones, and accept that GC pauses and VM stalls occasionally trigger a needless election. The phi accrual detector (Cassandra, Akka) outputs a suspicion level from the observed heartbeat-interval distribution instead of a yes/no.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Read-your-writes on a read replica. A loan officer saves an application; the next screen reads from a replica 300 ms behind and shows "not found"; the officer saves again, creating a duplicate. Fixes: read from the primary for the session's next few seconds, or route reads by "this session wrote recently", or carry the commit timestamp. With YugabyteDB, follower reads are off by default, so the default is safe; turn them on only for screens that tolerate staleness (yb_read_from_followers plus a staleness bound in recent versions).
  • Wall clock used for ordering. Two app servers stamp postings with now() from their own clocks, and a report orders by that column. When one server's clock is 2 seconds fast, postings appear out of order and "balance after" columns look wrong. Fix: take the timestamp from one place (the database's commit time) or use a sequence; never order across machines by local wall time.
  • NTP not running on a database node. A YugabyteDB node with a clock drifting beyond the skew bound triggers read restarts and eventually refuses to start. Always check chronyc tracking (offset, frequency) as part of node health. Alert when offset exceeds a fraction of the bound.
  • Split brain with a two-node active-passive pair. A heartbeat cable failed; both nodes promoted themselves; the VIP flapped between them; writes landed on both. Root cause: no quorum and no fencing. Fix: a third vote (witness), and STONITH or storage fencing.
  • "Exactly once" queue that wasn't. A notification consumer marked messages done after sending the SMS; a crash between sending and marking resent SMS after restart. Customers received the same OTP twice. That is the at-least-once you always have; the fix is a dedup key per message at the SMS gateway or accepting duplicates for messages where they are harmless.
  • Your RPC server is a distributed system already. Branch client, app server and database are three nodes with partial failure between each pair. Every timeout in your logs is a case of section 2.1. When you describe it in an interview, use these words: unknown outcome, idempotency key, quorum-replicated database, failover, fencing.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run m10_hlc. Pick one [RAW CLOCK WRONG] line and explain, with the numbers printed, which branch of the receive rule fired and why the HLC result is correct. Done when: you can explain it without looking at the code.

  2. (easy) On WSL run chronyc tracking (install chrony if needed) or timedatectl timesync-status. Note the current offset and frequency error. Done when: you can say how many microseconds your clock drifts per second at the reported frequency error.

  3. (medium) Add a Lamport clock alongside the HLC in m10_hlc.cpp and print both for every delivered message. Done when: you can show two events where the Lamport clock orders them but the events are concurrent (no happened-before), and explain why HLC has the same limitation.

  4. (medium) For each screen of your banking application (balance inquiry, posting, statement, loan dashboard, end-of-day report), write which consistency model it needs and whether a follower read with 1 s staleness would be acceptable. Done when: every screen has a one-line justification.

  5. (hard) Implement a tiny leaderless store simulation: N=3 replicas as in-memory maps with versioned values, a coordinator doing W-of-N writes and R-of-N reads with read repair, and random node failures. Show a stale read with R=1, W=1 and none with R=2, W=2 (no concurrent writes). Done when: asserts verify both behaviours over 10,000 random operations.

  6. (hard) Write the "unknown outcome" decision table for your employer's posting RPC: for each failure point (before send, during send, after server commit, during reply), what the client sees, what state the server is in, and what a retry does today. Then propose the idempotency change that makes every retry safe. Done when: the table has no "it depends" cell.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is partial failure and why does it make distributed systems hard? A: Some components fail while others keep running, and a caller cannot distinguish a dead node from a slow one or from a lost reply. Every remote call can end in "unknown outcome", so you need timeouts, idempotent retries, and protocols that stay correct when messages are lost or delayed.

Q: State CAP correctly. A: During a network partition, a replicated system must choose between linearizable consistency and availability (every non-failed node answers). Partitions are not optional, so the real choice is behaviour during a partition. YugabyteDB and etcd choose consistency (minority side refuses); Cassandra chooses availability (any replica answers, conflicts resolved later).

Q: What does PACELC add? A: It covers normal operation: even without a partition you trade latency for consistency, because strong consistency needs a quorum round trip per write. Spanner and YugabyteDB are PC/EC; Cassandra is PA/EL; PostgreSQL with async replicas is effectively EL for replicas.

Q: Linearizable versus sequential versus eventual consistency? A: Linearizable: once a write completes, every later read anywhere sees it, as if one copy existed. Sequential: everyone agrees on one order that respects each client's own order, but it may lag real time. Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop, with no promise before that. Example: a deposit confirmed at 10:00:00 must be visible to another branch at 10:00:01 under linearizability only.

Q: Why can't you order events by wall-clock timestamps across machines? A: Clocks drift and are corrected imperfectly (NTP is typically millisecond-accurate on a LAN and can step backwards), so a later event on a slow clock can get an earlier timestamp. Use logical clocks (Lamport, vector) or hybrid logical clocks, which respect causality and stay close to real time.

Q: What is a hybrid logical clock and where is it used? A: A timestamp (physical time, logical counter) that is always at least local physical time, at most the max skew ahead of it, and increases along every causal chain. YugabyteDB and CockroachDB stamp MVCC versions and transactions with it; YugabyteDB packs it into 64 bits with a 12-bit counter and assumes a max clock skew, restarting reads that fall inside the uncertainty window.

Q: Explain R + W > N. A: With N replicas, writing to W and reading from R guarantees the read set overlaps the latest write set when R + W > N, so the reader can see the newest version. It does not by itself give linearizability (concurrent writes, partial failed writes, sloppy quorums break it).

Q: Is exactly-once delivery possible? A: Not over a lossy network with failures: the sender can never know whether the last attempt was processed. Systems provide exactly-once effect: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing or deduplication, with the dedup record committed atomically with the side effect.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Partial failure: dead, slow and "done but reply lost" look the same. Every remote call can end in unknown outcome.
  • Use monotonic clocks for timeouts; wall clocks drift and jump. NTP is typically ms on a LAN.
  • Lamport clocks respect causality; vector clocks detect concurrency; HLC adds closeness to real time. YugabyteDB hybrid time = HLC packed into 64 bits with a 12-bit counter.
  • CAP: during a partition choose linearizable or available. PACELC: otherwise choose latency or consistency. YugabyteDB is PC/EC.
  • Consistency models from strong to weak: linearizable, sequential, causal, session guarantees, eventual. Know one example of each.
  • Replication: single-leader, multi-leader (conflicts), leaderless (quorums, read repair, hints).
  • Sync replication: RPO 0, latency and blocking cost. Async: fast, loses the tail on failover. Raft is majority-quorum replication.
  • Split brain is prevented by majorities, fencing tokens (terms), STONITH, leases. Never 2 nodes.
  • 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2; even sizes add nothing.
  • Exactly-once effect = at-least-once + idempotency key committed with the effect.

docs.title: 11. Consensus: Raft in plain words
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 10

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Consensus is getting several machines to agree on one value, or on one sequence of values, even when some of them crash and messages get lost or delayed. "Agree on a sequence" is the useful form: if every replica agrees on the same ordered log of commands ("debit A 100", "credit B 100") and applies them in that order, every replica ends in the same state. That is called state machine replication, and it is how etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV and YugabyteDB keep copies identical.

Raft (Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout, 2014, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm") is a consensus algorithm designed to be easy to understand. It splits the problem into three parts: elect one leader; the leader replicates its log to the others; and a set of safety rules guarantee that once an entry is committed it is never lost or changed, no matter who becomes leader next.

Analogy: a committee of five keeps the official minutes. One member is chair. Only the chair writes new lines into the minutes and reads them out to the others; a line is official once a majority (three) have copied it into their own books. If the chair stops answering the phone, any member who has waited long enough calls a vote for a new chair for the next "session number". You only vote for someone whose minute-book is at least as complete as yours, and you vote once per session. Because any two majorities of five share at least one member, the new chair always has every official line. That is Raft.

docs.title: 2.1 Roles, terms and the two RPCs
docs.text:
Every node is in one of three roles:

                 times out,                         receives votes from
   +----------+  starts election   +-----------+    a majority           +--------+
   | Follower | -----------------> | Candidate | ----------------------> | Leader |
   +----------+                    +-----------+                         +--------+
        ^  ^   discovers leader or      |  times out: new election           |
        |  +--- higher term ------------+  (term + 1)                        |
        +--------------------------- discovers higher term ------------------+
  • Term: a number that only increases, used as a logical clock and as a fencing token. Each term has at most one leader. Every message carries the sender's term. Seeing a higher term makes any node adopt it and become a follower immediately. A message with a lower term is rejected.
  • RequestVote (candidate to all): "I am candidate for term T; my last log entry is at index i with term t. Vote for me?"
  • AppendEntries (leader to each follower): "For term T: the entry before these is at index p with term pt; here are new entries; my commit index is c." An AppendEntries with no entries is a heartbeat.

Persistent state on every node (must be fsynced before replying to any RPC): currentTerm, votedFor, and the log[]. Volatile: commitIndex, lastApplied; on the leader also nextIndex[] and matchIndex[] per follower.

docs.title: 2.2 Leader election
docs.text:
1. A follower expects heartbeats. If none arrive within its election timeout (randomised, the paper uses 150 to 300 ms), it assumes the leader is gone.
  2. It becomes a candidate: increments its term, votes for itself, resets its timer, and sends RequestVote to everyone.
  3. Each node grants at most one vote per term, first come first served, and only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date as its own (compare last entry's term, then length). Granting a vote also resets the voter's own election timer.
  4. A candidate with votes from a majority becomes leader and immediately sends heartbeats, which stop other elections.
  5. If a candidate receives an AppendEntries from a leader with term >= its own, it steps down.
  6. If nobody wins (split vote), the timers expire again (randomly) and a new term starts.

Why randomised timeouts: if all followers timed out together they would all vote for themselves and split the vote forever. With randomness, one node usually times out first and collects a majority before the others wake up. The paper's rule of thumb:

broadcastTime  <<  electionTimeout  <<  MTBF (mean time between failures)
  (~1 to 20 ms)       (~150 to 300 ms)        (months)

docs.title: 2.3 Log replication
docs.text:
leader (term 3) log:  idx 1   2   3   4   5   6
                       t1  t1  t2  t3  t3  t3
                       x=1 y=2 z=3 a=4 b=5 c=6        commitIndex = 5

 follower A:           t1  t1  t2  t3  t3             matchIndex[A] = 5
 follower B:           t1  t1  t2                     nextIndex[B] = 4 (catching up)
  1. A client sends a command to the leader. The leader appends it to its own log (not yet committed) and sends it in AppendEntries to every follower.
  2. Each AppendEntries carries prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm. The follower accepts only if its own log has an entry at prevLogIndex with term prevLogTerm (consistency check). If not, it rejects and the leader retries with nextIndex - 1 (or a smarter hint) until they find the point where the logs agree; then the follower deletes any conflicting entries after that point and appends the leader's.
  3. When an entry is stored on a majority (the leader counts itself), the leader advances its commit index to it, applies it to its state machine, and replies to the client.
  4. Followers learn the commit index from the next AppendEntries (leaderCommit) and apply up to it.

The Log Matching Property follows by induction from the consistency check: if two logs have an entry with the same index and term, they are identical in every entry up to that index.

docs.title: 2.4 The commit index and the current-term rule
docs.text: An entry is committed when the leader that created it has replicated it to a majority. A committed entry will be present in the log of every future leader. The subtle case (Figure 8 in the paper): a new leader finds entries from older terms in its log that are on a majority. It may not count replicas to commit them directly, because a different future leader could still overwrite them. Rule: a leader only commits entries from its own term by counting replicas; older entries become committed indirectly when a current-term entry after them commits. That is why leaders append a no-op entry at the start of their term: committing it commits everything before it. The simulation in section 3 does this.

docs.title: 2.5 Safety, in five properties
