docs.text:
Property Statement Enforced by Election Safety At most one leader per term. One vote per node per term, majority needed. Leader Append-Only A leader never overwrites or deletes its own entries. Leader only appends. Log Matching Same index and term implies identical prefix. AppendEntries consistency check. Leader Completeness An entry committed in term T is in the log of every leader of a later term. Vote restriction (up-to-date log) + majority intersection + current-term commit rule. State Machine Safety No two nodes apply different commands at the same index. Follows from the above.

Why Leader Completeness holds, in one paragraph: a committed entry is on a majority. A candidate needs votes from a majority. The two majorities share at least one voter. That voter has the entry, and it only votes for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, which (by the comparison rule and Log Matching) means the candidate also has the entry.

What Raft does not promise: that an uncommitted entry survives (a leader that crashes before replicating to a majority loses it, and the client got no OK, so that is fine), or that the client knows the outcome after a timeout (module 07's unknown outcome; real systems add client session ids so a retried command is not applied twice).

docs.title: 2.6 Membership changes
docs.text:
Adding or removing nodes changes what "majority" means. Switching every node from the old configuration to the new at once is unsafe: for a moment, the old majority and the new majority might not intersect, allowing two leaders.

  • Joint consensus (the Raft paper): go through an intermediate configuration C_old,new in which every decision needs a majority of both C_old and C_new. Once that is committed, move to C_new.
  • Single-server changes (Ongaro's thesis, used by most implementations): add or remove one node at a time. Any majority of the old and new configurations then always intersect. To go from 3 to 5 nodes you do two single changes.
  • New nodes join as learners / non-voters first, receive a snapshot and the log, and become voters only once caught up, so a slow new node does not stall commits. YugabyteDB adds a new tablet peer as a PRE_VOTER, bootstraps it from a remote snapshot, then promotes it.
  • Replacing a dead node in RF3: add the new one (temporarily 4 voters) then remove the dead one, or remove first then add. Remove-first leaves you at 2 voters (no fault tolerance) briefly; add-first keeps tolerating one failure throughout. Know why the order matters.

docs.title: 2.7 Practical extensions you will hear about
docs.text:
• Snapshots and log compaction: the log cannot grow forever. Each node snapshots its state machine at some index and discards the log before it. A follower too far behind receives an InstallSnapshot instead of entries. (YugabyteDB: tablet "remote bootstrap" copies RocksDB files.)
  • Pre-vote: before incrementing its term, a would-be candidate asks "would you vote for me?". Prevents a node that was partitioned away (and kept incrementing its term) from forcing a needless election when it rejoins.
  • Check-quorum: a leader that has not heard from a majority for an election timeout steps down, so a minority-side leader stops accepting writes quickly. (The simulation leaves it out on purpose so you can see a stale leader that cannot commit.)
  • Leader leases and ReadIndex: linearizable reads without writing to the log (module 10 section 4).
  • Leadership transfer: the leader brings a chosen follower fully up to date and tells it to start an election immediately. Used for rolling restarts and load balancing leaders.
  • Batching and pipelining: send many entries per AppendEntries and do not wait for one round to finish before starting the next. This is where real throughput comes from.

docs.title: 2.8 Raft per tablet in YugabyteDB
docs.text:
YugabyteDB does not run one Raft group for the whole database. Each table is split into tablets (shards, module 12), and each tablet is its own Raft group with RF replicas ("tablet peers") on different yb-tserver processes. This is called Multi-Raft; CockroachDB (ranges) and TiKV (regions) do the same.

 yb-tserver 1               yb-tserver 2               yb-tserver 3
 +----------------+         +----------------+         +----------------+
 | tablet A  [L]  |         | tablet A  [F]  |         | tablet A  [F]  |
 | tablet B  [F]  |         | tablet B  [L]  |         | tablet B  [F]  |
 | tablet C  [F]  |         | tablet C  [F]  |         | tablet C  [L]  |
 +----------------+         +----------------+         +----------------+
       yb-master (its own Raft group of 3): catalog, tablet placement, load balancing

Consequences you should be able to explain:

  • Leaders are spread: each server leads some tablets and follows others, so write load is spread across the cluster. The master's load balancer moves leaders (leadership transfer) to keep them even, and can pin preferred leaders to a region.
  • Failure is per tablet: when tserver 1 dies, only the tablets it led lose their leader. Their followers wait out the leader lease, elect new leaders in a few seconds (typical), and carry on. Tablets led elsewhere never notice beyond losing one follower.
  • Writes: a write to one row goes to that row's tablet leader, which appends to its Raft log (the WAL), replicates to a majority, applies to its RocksDB-based DocDB storage, and replies. With RF3 the commit waits for the leader plus one follower.
  • Reads: by default from the tablet leader, using the leader lease so no extra round trip is needed. Follower reads are opt-in and return slightly stale data.
  • The WAL is the Raft log. There is no separate database WAL; the Raft log entries are the redo log for the tablet.
  • Thousands of Raft groups on one cluster means heartbeats must be batched per server pair, which YugabyteDB does (one RPC carries heartbeats for many tablets).
  • yb-master is itself a Raft group (usually 3 masters), so losing one master is also tolerated.

docs.title: 2.9 Contrast: PostgreSQL streaming replication is not consensus
docs.text:
PostgreSQL ships WAL from one primary to standbys (physical streaming replication). It is single-leader replication, sync or async (synchronous_commit, synchronous_standby_names with FIRST n or ANY n quorum). What it does not do by itself:

  • Elect a leader. If the primary dies, nothing inside PostgreSQL promotes a standby. A human or an external tool runs pg_ctl promote / pg_promote().
  • Prevent split brain. If the old primary comes back (or was only partitioned), PostgreSQL does not stop it from accepting writes. The tool that promoted must also fence it.
  • Guarantee no loss on failover with async standbys: the promoted standby may lack the last commits. The old primary's extra WAL must be discarded (pg_rewind) before it can rejoin. PostgreSQL marks the fork with a new timeline id.

So HA PostgreSQL setups bolt consensus on from outside: Patroni keeps the leader key in etcd, Consul or ZooKeeper (which run Raft or Zab), and only the node holding the key (with a TTL) may be primary; it demotes itself if it cannot renew the key. pg_auto_failover uses a monitor node. Cloud services do the equivalent internally.

The one-sentence answer to "Why does YugabyteDB need Raft when PostgreSQL does not?": PostgreSQL has one writable node and leaves failover and fencing to external tools, while YugabyteDB has thousands of independently-led shards across nodes and must automatically and safely pick a new leader for each one without losing committed writes, which is exactly what consensus provides.

docs.title: 2.10 Paxos in one page
docs.text:
Paxos (Leslie Lamport; "The Part-Time Parliament", 1998; "Paxos Made Simple", 2001) is the original practical consensus algorithm. Basic (single-decree) Paxos agrees on one value in two phases: a proposer picks a ballot number and asks acceptors to promise to ignore lower ballots (phase 1, prepare/promise); if a majority promise, it asks them to accept a value, choosing the value of the highest-ballot proposal already accepted by any of them if one exists (phase 2, accept/accepted). A value is chosen once a majority accept it.

Multi-Paxos runs Paxos for each log slot and optimises by keeping a stable leader that skips phase 1. It is essentially what Raft is, but the papers left many practical details (leader election, log gaps, membership) to implementers, which is why Raft was written. Raft's terms are Paxos ballots; its election is Paxos phase 1; AppendEntries is phase 2.

Who uses what: Google Chubby and Spanner (Multi-Paxos), Apache ZooKeeper (Zab, a Paxos relative), etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV, YugabyteDB, Kafka KRaft, MongoDB's replica-set protocol (Raft-like) use Raft or variants. Equivalent strength: both tolerate f crash failures with 2f + 1 nodes; neither tolerates Byzantine nodes.

docs.title: 3.1 Raft simulation (code/m11_raft_election_sim.cpp)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 m11_raft_election_sim.cpp -o raft_sim && ./raft_sim

A single process holds five simulated nodes. Time advances in 1 ms ticks. send puts a message in a std::multimap keyed by delivery time (2 to 15 ms later). A crashed node stops ticking and receives nothing; a partition assigns each node a group and drops cross-group messages. Every run with the same seed is identical, which is how serious Raft implementations are tested.

The scripted scenario prints a timeline:

  1. Initial election (one node times out first and wins).
  2. Three client commands committed on all five nodes.
  3. Leader crashes; a new leader is elected with a higher term and commits a new command.
  4. The old leader restarts as a follower and catches up.
  5. The leader and one follower are partitioned away from the other three. The isolated leader still accepts set X=LOST (it does not know it is cut off) but can never commit it. The majority side elects a leader in a higher term and commits set Y=KEPT. Two nodes claim leadership at once, in different terms, which is legal: only one can commit.
  6. The partition heals. The stale leader sees the higher term, steps down, and its uncommitted entry is overwritten by the consistency check.

Then a fuzz loop runs 30 seeds of 20 simulated seconds with random crashes, restarts, partitions and 5% message loss, asserting the safety properties on every tick.

The heart of the vote handler:

case MsgType::RequestVote: {
    // Only vote for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as ours. A winner needs a
    // majority of votes and every committed entry is on a majority, so the winner has them all.
    bool log_ok = m.last_log_term > n.last_term() ||
                  (m.last_log_term == n.last_term() && m.last_log_index >= n.last_index());
    bool grant = m.term == n.term && (n.voted_for == -1 || n.voted_for == m.from) && log_ok;
    if (grant) {
        n.voted_for = m.from;
        reset_election_timer(n);
    }
    ...
}

The follower side of AppendEntries, including conflict truncation:

if (m.prev_index > n.last_index() || n.log[m.prev_index].term != m.prev_term) {
    send(r);                                   // reject: leader will back up nextIndex
    break;
}
int idx = m.prev_index;
for (const Entry& e : m.entries) {
    ++idx;
    if (idx <= n.last_index() && n.log[idx].term != e.term) {
        assert(idx > n.commit_index);          // never truncate a committed entry
        n.log.resize(idx);                     // conflict: drop this entry and all after it
    }
    if (idx > n.last_index()) n.log.push_back(e);
}
n.commit_index = std::max(n.commit_index, std::min(m.leader_commit, idx));

The leader's commit rule with the current-term restriction:

for (int N = n.last_index(); N > n.commit_index; --N) {
    if (n.log[N].term != n.term) break;        // only count replicas for current-term entries
    int count = 0;
    for (int peer = 0; peer < size(); ++peer) if (n.match_index[peer] >= N) ++count;
    if (count > size() / 2) { n.commit_index = N; break; }
}

check_safety() runs after every tick: it records the first entry committed at each index and asserts no node ever commits a different one there (State Machine Safety), and that every leader holds every entry committed in an earlier term (Leader Completeness). become_leader asserts Election Safety with a term -> leader map.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Durability before replying. currentTerm, votedFor and new log entries must be on stable storage before a node replies to RequestVote or AppendEntries. If a node votes, crashes, forgets, and votes again in the same term, two leaders can be elected. Real implementations group-commit: batch many entries into one fsync. The fsync latency of the disk is usually the floor of commit latency: with RF3 the commit time is roughly max(leader fsync, fastest follower's network RTT + fsync). On cloud disks typical fsync is around a millisecond or more; on local NVMe, tens to hundreds of microseconds.

The leader also has to be up to date to serve reads. See module 10 section 4: ReadIndex or leases. Without one of them, a deposed leader in a minority partition serves stale reads.

Why five nodes is not always better. Five nodes tolerate two failures but every commit waits for the third-fastest of five rather than the second-fastest of three, and there is more replication traffic. RF3 is the common default; RF5 for the metadata layer or when you must survive a zone plus a node.

Disruptive servers. A node that is partitioned keeps timing out and incrementing its term. When it rejoins, its higher term forces the current leader to step down, causing a needless election. Pre-vote fixes this. A related problem in the simulation: an ex-leader whose election deadline is stale would time out immediately after stepping down; the code resets its timer when it steps down.

Flexible quorums. Heidi Howard's work (2016) showed that Paxos only needs election quorums and replication quorums to intersect each other, not each to be majorities. Some systems use this to make replication quorums smaller across regions. Raft as specified uses majorities for both.

Raft and the WAL in YugabyteDB. Each tablet's Raft log is stored as WAL segments on the tserver. An entry is "replicated" when it is durable in a majority of WALs. Applying it writes into the tablet's RocksDB memtable; RocksDB's own WAL is disabled because the Raft log already provides durability. On restart a tablet replays its Raft log from the last flushed point ("tablet bootstrap"). Log retention is driven by flushes and by lagging followers (YugabyteDB keeps WAL long enough for followers to catch up, then falls back to remote bootstrap).

Multi-Raft overhead. Each Raft group has its own leader, log and timers. Thousands per node mean heartbeat batching, shared WAL writer threads, and careful per-tablet memory accounting. This is also why tiny tables in YugabyteDB are often colocated into one tablet: fewer Raft groups.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Leader churn from GC or CPU starvation. A tserver under heavy compaction or swap misses heartbeats, its tablets elect new leaders, then it comes back and leadership moves again. Symptom: latency spikes and "leader not ready" errors. Look at leader change counters per tablet, CPU steal on VMs, and disk latency. Fix the starvation; do not just raise timeouts.
  • Two-node clusters. Someone deploys RF2 "to save a node". A single node loss stops all writes (no majority of 2). Always odd numbers: 3 or 5.
  • All replicas in one rack or zone. RF3 with all three tservers on one hypervisor means one host failure loses quorum for everything. YugabyteDB placement policy (cloud.region.zone) must put one replica per zone or per failure domain.
  • Clock problems look like Raft problems. Leases depend on clocks advancing at similar rates; a VM paused for 30 seconds wakes up with a lease it believes is valid only if the code uses the wrong clock. YugabyteDB uses monotonic time for leases and hybrid time for MVCC; still, monitor chrony on every node.
  • PostgreSQL failover runbook: whoever owns HA PostgreSQL must be able to say what fences the old primary. If the answer is "we would notice", it is not fenced.
  • Your migration: when you moved the bank's data from Berkeley DB (a single-process embedded store with no replication) into YugabyteDB RF3, you moved from "durability = one disk" to "durability = a majority of three nodes' Raft logs". That is a sentence worth saying in an interview.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run m11_raft_election_sim with three different seeds. For each, record the time of the first election and the term after the partition heals. Done when: you can explain why the term numbers differ between seeds.

  2. (easy) Change the cluster to 4 nodes and partition it 2-2. Done when: you see that neither side elects a leader and can explain it with the majority rule.

  3. (medium) Set kElectionMin = kElectionMax = 150 (no randomisation) and count elections and terms until a stable leader appears. Done when: you observe split votes and can explain why randomisation fixes them.

  4. (medium) Add check-quorum to the leader: if it has not received a successful AppendEntries reply from a majority within one election timeout, it steps down. Done when: in step 5 of the scenario only one node claims leadership after 1.5 s, and the assertion that expects two leaders is updated.

  5. (hard) Add pre-vote: a candidate first sends PreVote with term + 1 without incrementing its own term, and only starts a real election if a majority would grant it. Done when: a node isolated for 5 seconds rejoins without causing an election (count terms before and after).

  6. (hard) Implement single-server membership change: a ConfigChange log entry that adds node 5 to a 5-node cluster (making 6), taking effect as soon as it is appended. Add node 5 as a learner first and promote it only when its matchIndex reaches the leader's commit index. Done when: the safety fuzz still passes with random add/remove of one node at a time.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Explain Raft leader election. A: Followers expect heartbeats; one whose randomised timeout expires becomes a candidate, increments the term, votes for itself and asks for votes. Each node votes once per term and only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date. A majority makes a leader, which sends heartbeats to suppress further elections. Split votes are retried with new random timeouts.

Q: When is an entry committed in Raft? A: When the leader that created it in its current term has stored it on a majority of nodes; the leader then advances its commit index, applies it and answers the client. Entries from earlier terms are committed indirectly when a current-term entry after them commits, which is why new leaders append a no-op.

Q: Why can't Raft have two leaders in the same term? A: Each node votes at most once per term and persists that vote, and a leader needs a majority. Two majorities of the same cluster always overlap, so two candidates cannot both get a majority in one term. Two nodes may believe they are leader in different terms, but the older one cannot commit because its majority has moved to the higher term.

Q: What is the term used for? A: It is a logical clock and fencing token: every message carries it, higher terms make nodes step down, lower-term messages are rejected. It identifies stale leaders and orders log entries.

Q: How does a lagging or divergent follower catch up? A: The leader's AppendEntries carries the previous index and term; the follower rejects on mismatch; the leader backs up nextIndex until the logs agree, then the follower truncates conflicting entries and appends the leader's. Very far behind followers get a snapshot.

Q: Why does YugabyteDB need Raft when PostgreSQL does not? A: PostgreSQL has a single writable primary and leaves failover and split-brain prevention to external tools like Patroni (which themselves use etcd's Raft). YugabyteDB shards every table into tablets spread across nodes, and each tablet must elect leaders and replicate synchronously and safely on its own, so each tablet is a Raft group.

Q: How do you change cluster membership safely? A: Never switch all nodes at once, because old and new majorities might not intersect. Either joint consensus (decisions need majorities of both configurations) or one server at a time. Add new nodes as non-voting learners until caught up.

Q: Paxos versus Raft? A: Same fault tolerance (2f + 1 nodes for f crash failures) and equivalent core: Raft terms are ballots, election is phase 1, AppendEntries is phase 2. Raft specifies a strong leader, log structure, election and membership in one design, which makes it easier to implement correctly.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Consensus = agree on one ordered log; state machine replication applies it identically everywhere.
  • Roles: follower, candidate, leader. Terms only increase and fence stale leaders.
  • Election: randomised timeout, one persisted vote per term, up-to-date log restriction, majority.
  • Replication: AppendEntries with prevIndex/prevTerm consistency check; truncate conflicts.
  • Committed = on a majority, created in the leader's current term; no-op at term start.
  • Safety: election safety, append-only leader, log matching, leader completeness, state machine safety.
  • Membership: joint consensus or one server at a time; learners first.
  • YugabyteDB: one Raft group per tablet (Multi-Raft), leaders spread, Raft log is the WAL, leader leases for reads, masters are a Raft group too.
  • PostgreSQL streaming replication is replication without consensus; Patroni adds it via etcd.
  • Paxos: same power, older, less prescriptive. Raft is Multi-Paxos made concrete.

docs.title: 12. Sharding, partitioning and distributed SQL
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 10, 11; 07_Databases_Internals/11_yugabytedb_and_distributed_sql.md helps

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Sharding (also called partitioning) splits one big table across many machines so that no single machine has to store all the data or take all the writes. Each piece is a shard (YugabyteDB calls it a tablet, CockroachDB a range, Cassandra a token range). The shard key decides which shard a row lives in. Replication (modules 10 and 11) makes copies of each shard; sharding decides how to cut the data in the first place. Real systems do both: many shards, each replicated three times.

Analogy: a bank's paper archive. One room cannot hold every customer file, so you spread them over ten rooms. You could file by the first letter of the surname (range partitioning: A to C in room 1, and so on), which makes "all customers named B..." easy but leaves the S room overflowing. Or you could compute a number from the customer id and use it to pick a room (hash partitioning), which spreads files evenly but makes "all customers named B..." a visit to every room. Either way, a transfer between two customers in different rooms needs two clerks to coordinate, which is what distributed transactions are about.

Distributed SQL (YugabyteDB, CockroachDB, Spanner, TiDB) is the promise that you keep writing ordinary SQL with ACID transactions while the database does sharding, replication and distributed transactions underneath. The promise mostly holds, but the cost model changes: a query that touched one disk page on PostgreSQL may now touch three machines. This module is about knowing where that cost comes from and designing schemas that avoid it.

docs.title: 2.1 Hash sharding vs range sharding
docs.text:
Hash sharding: compute hash(shard_key), and each shard owns a range of hash values.

  • YugabyteDB YSQL default: the first primary-key column is hashed (PRIMARY KEY (account_no HASH) or just PRIMARY KEY (account_no)). The hash is a 16-bit value in [0x0000, 0xFFFF], and each tablet owns a contiguous slice of that space. A table created with 6 tablets gets slices of about 65536 / 6 hash values each.
  • Pros: even spread of data and writes, even for sequential keys (ACC0000001, ACC0000002 land on different tablets). No hotspot from monotonically increasing ids.
  • Cons: range scans on the shard key are scatter-gather (every tablet); ORDER BY shard_key LIMIT 10 must merge from all tablets.

Range sharding: each shard owns a contiguous range of the key itself.

  • YugabyteDB: PRIMARY KEY (txn_date ASC, txn_id ASC) uses range sharding. CockroachDB, TiDB, Spanner, HBase and Bigtable are range-sharded by default.
  • Pros: range scans and ordered scans hit only the shards covering the range; WHERE txn_date BETWEEN ... is cheap. Natural for time series and prefix queries.
  • Cons: hotspots for monotonically increasing keys: every new row (latest timestamp, next sequence value) goes to the last shard, which takes all the write load.

Compound keys combine both: PRIMARY KEY ((account_no) HASH, txn_ts ASC, txn_id ASC) hashes on the account (spread across tablets) and sorts within the account by time (one account's statement is a single-tablet ordered range scan). This is the most important pattern in this module.

Consistent hashing (section 3) is the third family: shards are points on a hash ring and nodes own arcs. Used by Dynamo and Cassandra, and in caches and load balancers. YugabyteDB does not need it because it moves whole tablets (fixed hash slices) between nodes instead of re-hashing keys; the effect is similar: adding a node moves about 1/N of the data.

Directory-based (lookup table) sharding: a metadata service maps key ranges or tenants to shards explicitly. Flexible (move one big tenant to its own shard) at the cost of a lookup and a metadata service. YugabyteDB's yb-master tablet map is a directory of tablet boundaries; clients cache it.

docs.title: 2.2 Hotspots
docs.text:
A hotspot is a shard that gets much more traffic than its peers. Causes and fixes:

Cause Example Fix Monotonic key with range sharding txn_id from a sequence, created_at timestamp as first key column Hash the first column; or prefix with a hash bucket (bucket = hash(id) % 16) Low-cardinality shard key branch_code with 250 branches, one head office branch doing 30% of volume Shard on a higher-cardinality key (account_no), keep branch as a secondary column or index Celebrity key One merchant's settlement account credited by every card transaction Split the counter: N sub-accounts summed on read; or batch postings and apply periodically Hot range from a batch End-of-day interest job updating accounts in key order Process in hash order or in parallel across shards; throttle Secondary index on a monotonic column Index on created_at Hash-shard the index ((created_at) HASH is useless for ranges) or bucket it

How you see a hotspot: one tablet leader's CPU and RPC queue much higher than others; per-tablet write metrics; latency only on certain keys. In YugabyteDB, the tablet server UI and yb_local_tablets / per-tablet metrics show it.

docs.title: 2.3 Tablet splitting
docs.text:
A table starts with some number of tablets. As it grows, tablets must split, or one will hold gigabytes and be both a hotspot and slow to move.

  • Pre-splitting: decide at creation time. CREATE TABLE ... SPLIT INTO 24 TABLETS (hash) or SPLIT AT VALUES ((...), (...)) (range). Best when you know the size up front, for example before loading a migration. By default YugabyteDB picks a tablet count based on the number of tservers and cores (flags such as ysql_num_shards_per_tserver; check your version).
  • Automatic tablet splitting: YugabyteDB splits a tablet when it passes size thresholds that depend on how many tablets the table already has (small tables split early, big ones later). Enabled by default in recent releases. The split is local and cheap: the tablet's data is not rewritten; the two children initially share the parent's RocksDB files (hard links) and filter by key range, and compaction cleans up later. Each child is a new Raft group.
  • Manual split: yb-admin split_tablet <tablet_id> for an operator-driven split of a known hot tablet.
  • Range tables and splitting: a range-sharded table with a monotonic key will keep splitting its last tablet, but the new last tablet still takes all inserts. Splitting fixes size, not a write hotspot on the latest key.
  • After splits, the load balancer moves tablet replicas and leaders between tservers to even out counts.

docs.title: 2.4 Two-phase commit (2PC)
docs.text:
A transaction that writes rows on two shards (debit account A on tablet 1, credit B on tablet 2) must commit on both or neither. Two-phase commit:

 coordinator                       participant 1              participant 2
     |--- PREPARE ----------------->|                          |
     |--- PREPARE ------------------------------------------->|
     |                    writes data + "prepared" durably, holds locks
     |<-- YES ----------------------|                          |
     |<-- YES -------------------------------------------------|
     | writes COMMIT decision durably  (the commit point)
     |--- COMMIT ------------------>|                          |
     |--- COMMIT --------------------------------------------->|
     |<-- ack ----------------------|<-- ack -------------------|

Rules: a participant that voted YES must be able to commit even after a crash (it made its writes durable), and must wait for the decision; it cannot decide on its own. If any participant votes NO or times out, the coordinator aborts.

The weakness: blocking. If the coordinator crashes after participants voted YES but before they learn the decision, they are stuck holding locks: they cannot commit (maybe someone voted NO) and cannot abort (maybe the coordinator already decided COMMIT and told someone). Classic XA transactions across two different databases have this problem, and operators end up resolving "in-doubt" transactions by hand. Three-phase commit tries to fix it but is not safe under network partitions, so nobody uses it.

The fix used by distributed SQL: make the coordinator's decision record itself replicated by consensus. If the coordinator node dies, the decision is not lost; it is on a majority of the Raft group that stores it, and any node can read it. Spanner runs 2PC across Paxos groups; CockroachDB stores a transaction record in a Raft range; YugabyteDB uses a transaction status tablet.

docs.title: 2.5 YugabyteDB's distributed transactions
docs.text:
For a transaction that touches more than one tablet (the single-tablet case takes a fast path with no status tablet):

  1. Begin: the transaction gets an id and a home transaction status tablet (tablets of a system transactions table, Raft-replicated like any other). A status record PENDING is created there.
  2. Writes: each write goes to the tablet owning the row as a provisional record (an intent), stored in that tablet's separate IntentsDB alongside the transaction id. Intents act as locks: a conflicting transaction sees them. They are replicated via that tablet's Raft group, so they are durable.
  3. Commit: the coordinator (the tserver handling the client session) writes COMMITTED with a commit hybrid time into the status tablet record. That single Raft-replicated write is the commit point. Atomic, because it is one record.
  4. Apply: asynchronously, the participant tablets are told to convert intents into regular versioned records at the commit hybrid time and remove the intents. The client already got OK.
  5. Readers meeting an intent look up the transaction's status record: committed (with time) -> treat as visible if the commit time is within their snapshot; pending -> not visible (or conflict, depending on isolation); aborted -> ignore and clean up.

Why this does not block like classic 2PC: the decision lives in a Raft group, so the loss of any one node (coordinator included) does not lose or hide it. A transaction whose coordinator vanishes before deciding is eventually aborted by heartbeat expiry on the status tablet.

Concurrency control: conflicts between transactions are detected by intents. Older YugabyteDB versions used optimistic "fail-on-conflict" (one transaction gets a serialization error and the client retries, SQLSTATE 40001); newer versions default to wait-on-conflict with distributed deadlock detection, closer to PostgreSQL behaviour. Either way, your application must retry 40001 errors. Default isolation in YSQL is snapshot (REPEATABLE READ); SERIALIZABLE and READ COMMITTED are available (see 07_Databases_Internals/11_yugabytedb_and_distributed_sql.md).

docs.title: 2.6 Distributed indexes
docs.text:
In PostgreSQL an index lives on the same machine as the table. In distributed SQL, a secondary index is its own sharded table, keyed by the indexed columns, with the primary key as the value (or part of the key). Consequences:

  • Writes: inserting a row with two secondary indexes writes three tablets (row, index 1, index 2), probably on three different nodes. That is a distributed transaction (unless everything is colocated). Every extra index makes writes slower, more than on a single node.
  • Reads via index: look up the index tablet, get primary keys, then fetch rows from the main table's tablets: two network hops, possibly to many tablets. A covering index (CREATE INDEX ... ON t (customer_id) INCLUDE (status, amount)) answers from the index alone: one hop (index-only scan).
  • Unique indexes are enforced globally: the index tablet for that value rejects a duplicate, regardless of which shard the row lives in. Works, and costs a distributed transaction.
  • Index sharding matters: an index on created_at should be range-sharded (created_at ASC) if you query ranges, which makes it a write hotspot. Common compromise: hash on a bucket or on a higher-cardinality leading column.
  • Local vs global indexes: some systems (Cassandra, Elasticsearch, partitioned PostgreSQL) have local indexes per shard; queries on them scatter to all shards. YugabyteDB secondary indexes are global.

docs.title: 2.7 Cross-shard joins and their cost
docs.text:
A join between two tables on two sets of tablets means the query layer pulls rows over the network. Cost drivers: number of round trips, rows shipped, and fan-out (how many tablets each step touches).

  • Nested loop with a remote inner side: one round trip per outer row. 10,000 outer rows times 1 ms is 10 seconds. The classic distributed SQL performance bug.
  • Batched nested loop join: send the inner lookups in batches (IN (k1, ..., k1024)). YugabyteDB has this (yb_bnl_batch_size); one round trip per batch.
  • Hash join: pull both sides to the query node and join in memory. Good when both sides are filtered small.
  • Pushdown: filters, projections, aggregates and LIMIT pushed to the tablets so less data crosses the network. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST) in YugabyteDB shows storage read requests and rows per step.
  • Avoid the join's network cost by design:
    • Colocation: put small, frequently joined reference tables (branch master, product codes, currency table, GL chart) into one colocated tablet (CREATE DATABASE ... WITH COLOCATION = true, or per-table options). One Raft group, one hop.
    • Same shard key prefix: account and account_txn both hashed on account_no. Each query becomes "one account", so it touches one tablet per table. Note: YugabyteDB does not guarantee that two tables' tablets for the same hash range live on the same node, so this reduces fan-out, not hops.
    • Denormalise the few columns the hot path needs (branch name on the statement row).

docs.title: 2.8 Choosing shard keys for banking tables
docs.text:
Banking schemas are full of business codes: branch code, product code, customer id, account number, loan application number, GL code. The questions to ask for each table:

  1. What is the most frequent access path? (By account? By customer? By branch and date?)
  2. Is the key's cardinality high enough to spread load? (250 branches: no. 10 million accounts: yes.)
  3. Is it monotonic? (Sequence-generated application numbers: yes. Hash them.)
  4. Which tables are joined on the hot path? (Give them the same leading key.)
  5. Is the table small and static? (Colocate it.)

Worked example:

-- Reference data: small, read everywhere, joined constantly. Colocate.
CREATE TABLE branch (
    branch_code  text PRIMARY KEY,
    branch_name  text NOT NULL,
    region_code  text NOT NULL
);  -- in a colocated database, or WITH (COLOCATION = true)

-- Customers: accessed by customer id. Hash on it.
CREATE TABLE customer (
    customer_id  text,
    branch_code  text NOT NULL,
    full_name    text NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (customer_id HASH)
);

-- Accounts: accessed by account number. Hash on account_no, not branch_code
-- (branch_code is low-cardinality and skewed: head office branches are huge).
CREATE TABLE account (
    account_no     text,
    customer_id    text NOT NULL,
    branch_code    text NOT NULL,
    product_code   text NOT NULL,
    balance_minor  bigint NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (account_no HASH)
);
CREATE INDEX account_by_customer ON account (customer_id HASH) INCLUDE (account_no, product_code);

-- Transactions: the statement query is "one account, newest first". Hash on account,
-- range on time within the account: one tablet, already sorted.
CREATE TABLE account_txn (
    account_no     text,
    txn_ts         timestamptz,
    txn_id         bigint,
    branch_code    text   NOT NULL,   -- denormalised from account for the branch report
    txn_date       date   NOT NULL,   -- business date, not wall-clock date
    amount_minor   bigint NOT NULL,
    narration      text,
    PRIMARY KEY ((account_no) HASH, txn_ts DESC, txn_id DESC)
);

-- Branch end-of-day report needs "all transactions of a branch on a date". Do not make
-- branch_code the shard key of the table for that: use a separate index (or a reporting copy).
-- If one large branch's day makes a single index tablet hot, add a small bucket column
-- (hash(txn_id) % 8) to the hash part of the index and query all 8 buckets.
CREATE INDEX txn_by_branch_day ON account_txn ((branch_code, txn_date) HASH, txn_id);

-- Loan applications: numbers come from a sequence (monotonic). Hash shard so inserts spread.
CREATE TABLE loan_application (
    application_no  bigint,
    branch_code     text NOT NULL,
    status          text NOT NULL,
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (application_no HASH)
);

Notes that show seniority:

  • Sequences in distributed SQL: a sequence is a single row somewhere; every nextval would be a network round trip. YugabyteDB caches sequence values per connection (CACHE clause and a server-side minimum cache). Consequence: values are unique but not gap-free and not in commit order across connections. If a regulator needs gap-free voucher numbers, generate them differently (per-branch counter row updated in the transaction, accepting that it serialises that branch).
  • Money columns: integer minor units (bigint paise) or numeric, never float.
  • Uniqueness of business codes: a unique index on (branch_code, voucher_no) is a global index: correct, but each insert is a distributed transaction.

docs.title: 3.1 Consistent hashing ring (code/m12_consistent_hash.cpp)
docs.text:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -O2 m12_consistent_hash.cpp -o chash && ./chash

The ring is a std::map<uint64_t, std::string> from position to node. Each physical node is inserted vnodes times ("node-3#0", "node-3#1", ...). Lookup is lower_bound with wrap-around:

const std::string& owner(std::string_view key) const {
    auto it = ring_.lower_bound(hash64(key));
    if (it == ring_.end()) it = ring_.begin();   // wrap around the circle
    return it->second;
}

// Replicas: walk clockwise collecting DISTINCT physical nodes (Dynamo's preference list).
std::vector<std::string> replicas(std::string_view key, size_t rf) const;

What the program measures and asserts on 200,000 banking-style keys (BR017-ACC0004242):

  1. Balance vs virtual nodes: with 1 point per node the most loaded node gets well over 1.5 times the mean (in a typical run); with 200 points per node it is within about 20% of the mean. The assert requires under 1.25.
  2. Adding a sixth node moves about 1/6 of keys (asserted between 10% and 25%), and every moved key moves to the new node. The same change with hash % N moves about 5/6 of keys.
  3. Removing a node moves only that node's keys, and they spread over the survivors instead of all landing on one neighbour (a benefit of virtual nodes).
  4. RF=3 preference lists contain three distinct physical nodes, the first being the owner.

The hash is FNV-1a followed by the splitmix64 finalizer. Plain FNV on near-identical strings like node-1#0, node-1#1 clusters badly; a good finalizer matters more than the base hash.

docs.title: 3.2 Seeing sharding in YugabyteDB
docs.text:
-- Which hash value does a key map to? (YugabyteDB function.)
SELECT yb_hash_code('ACC0004242'::text);           -- a number in [0, 65535]

-- Tablet layout of a table (yugabyted / yb-admin), from a shell:
-- yb-admin -master_addresses <m1:7100,...> list_tablets ysql.bankdb account

-- Does this query touch one tablet or all of them?
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST) SELECT * FROM account_txn
WHERE account_no = 'ACC0004242' ORDER BY txn_ts DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Look for one storage read request and an Index Scan on the primary key with no Sort node.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
How a YSQL row becomes a DocDB key. For PRIMARY KEY ((account_no) HASH, txn_ts DESC, txn_id DESC), the DocDB key is [16-bit hash of account_no][account_no][txn_ts desc-encoded] [txn_id desc-encoded][column id] + hybrid time. The 16-bit hash prefix decides the tablet; the rest keeps rows of one account sorted inside the tablet's RocksDB. The hash code is stored in the key, which is why yb_hash_code can be used for parallel full scans by hash range.

Why automatic splitting is cheap. RocksDB SST files are immutable. A split creates two child tablets that reference the parent's files with key-range bounds; no data is copied at split time. Compactions later rewrite each child's files to drop keys outside its range. The expensive part is afterwards: moving one child's replicas to another node, which is a file copy (remote bootstrap).

The cost of a distributed transaction, counted. A two-tablet write with RF3 in one region: two intent writes (each a Raft round: leader fsync plus one follower), one status-tablet write (one more Raft round), then async apply (more Raft rounds, off the critical path). Typical single-region latency for that is a few milliseconds versus around a millisecond for a single-row fast-path write (typical; measure your own). Across regions every Raft round becomes a WAN round trip, which is why geo-distributed deployments place leaders (preferred zones) and use tablespaces to keep a row's replicas close to its users.

2PC atomicity vs isolation. 2PC gives atomicity across shards. Isolation comes from MVCC plus intents plus hybrid-time snapshots: a reader at snapshot time T sees a committed transaction's writes on every tablet or on none, because all of them carry the same commit hybrid time. That is why a distributed snapshot needs a cluster-wide notion of time (HLC, module 10).

Consistent hashing internals. With V virtual nodes per server, the load on a server is the sum of V roughly independent arc lengths, so its relative standard deviation shrinks about as 1/sqrt(V). Memory is O(N V) and lookup O(log(N V)). Alternatives: jump consistent hash (Lamping and Veach, Google, 2014: no memory, perfect balance, but buckets can only be added or removed at the end), rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing (score every node per key, take the top: O(N) per lookup, trivially gives replica lists), and Maglev hashing (Google's load balancer: a lookup table with minimal disruption).

Resharding with a fixed hash space. YugabyteDB and Redis Cluster (16384 slots) avoid re-hashing keys entirely: the hash space is fixed and only the assignment of slices to nodes changes. Moving a slice is a bulk copy plus a cutover of ownership, which is simpler to reason about than re-hashing a ring.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The head-office hotspot. A schema keyed by (branch_code, account_no) with branch_code hashed put the head office's millions of accounts in one tablet's slice. Postings for that branch had high latency while others were fine. Re-keying to account_no HASH (with a secondary index on branch) fixed it. The lesson: never let a skewed business code be the hash key alone.
  • Migration load into too few tablets. A bulk load into a freshly created table with the default tablet count drove a few tablets at a time and kept splitting during the load. Pre-split the table (SPLIT INTO N TABLETS, sized to tservers times cores) before loading, load in hash order or in parallel streams, and create secondary indexes after the bulk load where possible. Your Berkeley DB to YugabyteDB migration engine is exactly this workload.
  • The N+1 query over the network. An ORM loaded 500 accounts and then each account's last transaction in a separate query: 501 round trips, fine on PostgreSQL on localhost, slow on a three-node cluster. Batch (WHERE account_no = ANY($1)) or join.
  • Serialization retries not handled. Moving to distributed SQL surfaced 40001 errors under contention that the old single-node code never saw. The app must retry the whole transaction with backoff (module 09), and the transaction must be idempotent or keyed.
  • Unique constraint on a monotonic business code. UNIQUE (voucher_no) where vouchers are issued sequentially: the unique index is range-hot. Hash it or include a bucket prefix.
  • Cross-region transactions. A table with replicas in two regions and leaders in one: every write from the other region pays a WAN round trip per Raft round. Use leader preference per tablespace so each region's data is led locally.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Build and run m12_consistent_hash. Change vnodes to 1, 5, 20 and 500 and record max/mean. Done when: you have a small table and can explain the 1/sqrt(V) trend.

  2. (easy) For five tables in your employer's schema (or the examples in section 2.8), write the shard key you would choose and one sentence why. Done when: each answer names the access path and the cardinality.

  3. (medium) Add jump consistent hash (int32_t jump(uint64_t key, int32_t buckets), eight lines from the paper) to the program and measure balance and movement when going from 5 to 6 buckets. Done when: you can state when you would use jump hash instead of a ring.

  4. (medium) On a local YugabyteDB (yugabyted start in Docker or WSL, three nodes with --join), create account_txn from section 2.8, load 1 million rows across 10,000 accounts, and compare EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST) for "one account's last 20 transactions" with a version keyed PRIMARY KEY (txn_id HASH). Done when: you can point at the read requests and sort node that differ.

  5. (hard) Write a 2PC simulation: one coordinator, three participants, each with a durable log (vector). Inject coordinator crashes after PREPARE. Show participants blocked holding locks. Then move the decision into a "replicated" status record (reuse the Raft simulation or just a majority-of-three array) and show recovery. Done when: asserts prove atomicity in both versions and the blocking case is visible in the first.

  6. (hard) Design the sharding and colocation plan for a loan-origination schema with 12 tables (applications, applicants, documents, credit checks, approvals, disbursements, reference tables). For each table state shard key, hash or range, colocated or not, secondary indexes, and the hot query each choice serves. Done when: every hot query touches one tablet per table or you have written why it cannot.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Hash versus range sharding? A: Hash sharding spreads keys evenly by hash, which avoids hotspots on sequential keys but makes range scans touch every shard. Range sharding keeps keys sorted so range scans are cheap, but monotonic keys hit the last shard. Compound keys (hash on the entity, range on time within it) get both for the common "one entity's history" query.

Q: What causes hotspots and how do you fix them? A: Monotonic keys under range sharding, low-cardinality or skewed shard keys, celebrity rows, and batch jobs walking keys in order. Fix by hashing or bucketing the key, choosing a higher-cardinality shard key, splitting hot counters into sub-rows, and spreading batch work across shards.

Q: How does consistent hashing work and why use virtual nodes? A: Nodes and keys hash onto a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of keys. Virtual nodes (many points per server) even out arc sizes and spread a dead node's keys over many survivors instead of one neighbour.

Q: Explain two-phase commit and its weakness. A: The coordinator asks all participants to prepare (make writes durable, hold locks, vote); if all vote yes it records commit and tells them, otherwise abort. If the coordinator dies after the votes and before the decision reaches participants, they block holding locks. Distributed SQL fixes this by storing the decision in a consensus-replicated record.

Q: How does YugabyteDB commit a multi-shard transaction? A: Writes go to each tablet as provisional records (intents) replicated by that tablet's Raft group. Commit is a single Raft-replicated write of COMMITTED with a commit hybrid time to the transaction's status tablet. Intents are applied to regular records asynchronously, and readers that meet an intent check the status tablet.

Q: Why are secondary indexes more expensive in distributed SQL? A: Each index is its own sharded table, usually on other nodes, so a write with indexes becomes a distributed transaction across tablets, and a non-covering index read takes two hops. Use covering indexes for hot reads and keep index count low on write-heavy tables.

Q: How would you choose shard keys for a core-banking schema? A: By the hot access path and cardinality: accounts hashed on account number, transactions hashed on account number with time as a range component, customers on customer id, small reference tables colocated. Avoid skewed business codes like branch code as the only hash key, and hash anything sequence-generated.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Sharding splits data; replication copies each shard. Distributed SQL does both under SQL.
  • Hash: even spread, scatter for ranges. Range: cheap scans, hot tail for monotonic keys. Compound (entity) HASH, time covers both for entity histories.
  • YugabyteDB: 16-bit hash space split across tablets; each tablet a Raft group; auto splitting is cheap (shared SST files); pre-split before bulk loads.
  • Consistent hashing moves ~1/N keys on membership change; virtual nodes balance it.
  • 2PC blocks if the coordinator dies; storing the decision in a Raft group removes the blocking.
  • YugabyteDB transactions: intents + status tablet commit record + async apply; retry 40001.
  • Secondary indexes are global sharded tables: writes become distributed, covering indexes save a hop.
  • Cross-shard joins cost round trips: batch, push down, colocate, share shard key prefixes.
  • Banking keys: high-cardinality business codes (account, customer) as hash keys; branch code as a column or index, not the shard key.

docs.title: 13. High availability and operations
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 09, 10, 11, 12

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
High availability (HA) means the system keeps serving when parts of it fail or are being changed. Nothing is up 100% of the time; HA is about agreeing how much downtime and data loss is acceptable, designing so a single failure does not cause either, and practising the recovery so it works at 3 AM. Operations is the day-to-day work that keeps it so: deploying without outages, backing up and actually restoring, testing failure on purpose, and writing down what to do when something breaks.

Analogy: a bank branch. Availability is "the branch is open when customers come". A second teller means one sick teller does not close the branch (redundancy). A generator means a power cut does not close it (no single point of failure). A fire drill means people know where to go (chaos testing and runbooks). Renovating one counter at a time while the others serve customers is a rolling deploy. Moving to a new building over a weekend without customers noticing is a zero-downtime cutover, which is on your resume, and section 5 gives you the words for it.

This module is mostly vocabulary and judgement, with numbers. Interviewers ask about it to see whether you have run systems or only written them.

docs.title: 2.1 SLA, SLO, SLI and error budgets
docs.text:
• SLI (service level indicator): a measured number. "Fraction of posting RPCs that succeeded in under 500 ms over the last 5 minutes." Defined from the user's point of view: success and latency, measured where the user sees it (the client or load balancer, not the server's own log).
  • SLO (service level objective): the target for an SLI. "99.9% of postings succeed within 500 ms, measured over 30 days." Internal, chosen by the team.
  • SLA (service level agreement): a contract with a customer, with penalties (service credits) if missed. Always looser than the SLO so you have warning before you pay. A bank's contract with a core-banking vendor typically has availability during business hours and RTO/RPO clauses.
  • Error budget: 100% minus the SLO. At 99.9% over 30 days you may be "bad" for 43.2 minutes. If the budget is healthy, ship features and take deploy risk; if it is spent, freeze risky changes and fix reliability. It turns "is this reliable enough?" into arithmetic.

The nines, per 30-day month and per year (pure arithmetic):

Availability Downtime per 30 days Downtime per year 99% 7.2 hours 3.65 days 99.9% 43.2 minutes 8.76 hours 99.95% 21.6 minutes 4.38 hours 99.99% 4.32 minutes 52.6 minutes 99.999% 26 seconds 5.26 minutes

Composition. Components in series (request needs all of them) multiply: an app at 99.9% calling a database at 99.9% gives at most 99.8%. Components in parallel (any one suffices) combine as 1 - (1-a)(1-b): two independent 99% instances give 99.99%, if failures are truly independent and failover is instant, which they never fully are. This is why you remove single points of failure and why shared dependencies (one DNS, one config service) quietly cap everything.

docs.title: 2.2 RTO and RPO
docs.text:
• RTO (recovery time objective): how long the service may be down after a disaster. "Back within 15 minutes."
  • RPO (recovery point objective): how much recent data may be lost, measured in time. "At most the last 5 seconds of commits." RPO = 0 means no committed transaction may ever be lost.
   last good backup / replicated point        disaster              service restored
 ---------|-------------------------------------X---------------------------|------>
          |<---------- data at risk (RPO) ----->|<------ downtime (RTO) ---->|

What determines them:

Mechanism Typical RPO Typical RTO Nightly backup, restore to new hardware up to 24 h hours Backup + continuous WAL archiving (PITR) seconds to minutes tens of minutes to hours (restore + replay) Async standby, manual promotion seconds (replication lag) minutes (human in loop) Async standby, automatic failover (Patroni) seconds ~30 s to a few minutes Sync standby / Raft quorum (YugabyteDB RF3) 0 seconds (leader election) Cross-region async (xCluster) for region loss seconds minutes (switch apps to the other cluster)

(Typical figures, not guarantees; measure yours in a drill.) Banks and regulators usually specify both for each system tier. Know your employer's numbers.

docs.title: 2.3 Redundancy patterns: active-passive vs active-active
docs.text:
Active-passive (primary-standby, hot/warm/cold standby): one instance serves; another is ready to take over.

  • Hot standby: running, data replicated continuously, takes over in seconds to minutes.
  • Warm: running, data partly current, needs some steps. Cold: hardware or images only; restore from backup.
  • Pros: simple, no write conflicts. Cons: idle capacity, failover is a rarely-exercised path that breaks when you need it, split-brain risk without fencing (module 10).

Active-active: all instances serve traffic.

  • Stateless tiers (app servers behind a load balancer) are naturally active-active: lose one, the others absorb its load. Requires headroom: N instances at 60% load survive one loss only if the others can take the extra share (N=3 at 60% each becomes 2 at 90%).
  • Stateful tiers are harder. A consensus database (YugabyteDB) is active-active at the tablet level: every node leads some tablets. Multi-leader across regions brings write conflicts (module 10 section 2.6).
  • N+1 / N+2 capacity: size so the loss of one (or two) instances still meets the SLO.

Failure domains: process, host, rack, availability zone, region. Place replicas so that one domain failing never takes out a majority. Three zones with one replica each is the standard RF3 layout.

docs.title: 2.4 Deploying without downtime
docs.text:
Rolling deploy: replace instances one (or a few) at a time. For each: remove from the load balancer (fail readiness, wait the detection window), drain in-flight requests, stop, deploy, start, pass health checks, re-add. Needs: the old and new versions can run side by side (protocol and schema compatibility), and enough spare capacity for one instance being out.

Blue-green deploy: run two complete environments. Blue serves production; deploy to green, test it, then switch traffic (load balancer target, DNS, or VIP) from blue to green in one step. Rollback is switching back. Costs double capacity during the change. The database is usually shared between blue and green, which is the hard part: the schema must work for both.

Canary release: send a small fraction of traffic (1%, then 10%, then 50%) to the new version and compare its error rate and latency against the old. Automatic rollback if the canary is worse. Needs per-request routing (L7) or a subset of instances.

Feature flags: deploy code dark, turn the feature on separately (per branch, per percentage). Decouples deploy from release; rollback is a config change.

Schema changes without downtime: expand and contract.

 1. Expand:   add the new column/table (nullable, no default rewrite). Old code ignores it.
 2. Migrate:  deploy code that writes both old and new; backfill old rows in batches.
 3. Switch:   deploy code that reads the new column.
 4. Contract: after every instance runs the new code (and rollback is no longer needed),
              stop writing the old column, then drop it.

Never rename or drop a column in the same release that stops using it; a rolling deploy has old instances still reading it. In distributed SQL, prefer online index builds (YugabyteDB builds indexes online with backfill; CREATE INDEX NONCONCURRENTLY exists for empty tables).

Your RPC server and rolling deploys: long-lived branch connections make draining slow. Tell clients to reconnect elsewhere (a protocol-level "server going away" message, like HTTP/2 GOAWAY), stop accepting new requests on the connection, finish in-flight ones, then close. Clients must reconnect with jittered backoff (module 09) or every branch reconnects to the same survivor at once.

docs.title: 2.5 Database HA: YugabyteDB RF3 losing a node
docs.text:
Setup: three yb-tservers in three zones, RF3, three yb-masters. Each tablet has three peers, one per node; leaders spread evenly.

What happens when node 2 dies (power loss):

  1. Tablets led by node 2: their followers stop receiving heartbeats. After the leader lease expires (about 2 s by default) and an election timeout, a follower with an up-to-date log wins. Writes and strong reads for those tablets fail or wait for a few seconds (typical), then resume. Clients see errors or retries; YugabyteDB's query layer retries some internally.
  2. Tablets led elsewhere: lose one follower. Commits still need 2 of 3, which the remaining two provide. No visible effect apart from slightly higher tail latency.
  3. Data loss: none. Every committed write was on a majority, so at least one survivor has it and the election rule guarantees it is the new leader's. RPO = 0.
  4. Fault tolerance now: every tablet is down to 2 replicas. A second failure loses quorum for tablets with peers on both dead nodes. You are under-replicated.
  5. Re-replication: if node 2 stays down beyond follower_unavailable_considered_failed_sec (default 900 s; check your version), the masters re-create the missing replicas on other nodes, if there are any (needs a fourth node, or a replacement). With exactly three nodes, nothing can move; you run at reduced tolerance until node 2 or a replacement returns.
  6. Node returns within the window: its peers catch up from the leaders' logs (or remote bootstrap if too far behind). The load balancer moves some leaders back to it.
  7. yb-master on node 2: one of three masters lost; the master Raft group keeps quorum. Catalog operations continue.
  8. Clients: drivers with the node in their connection list get connection errors to it and must use the others. YugabyteDB's smart drivers (cluster-aware) or a load balancer in front of YSQL handle this; a single hard-coded host in your app server's config is a single point of failure that defeats RF3.

Contrast single-region RF3 with zone loss: same as node loss if one node per zone. Region loss needs either a stretched cluster across three regions (every write pays inter-region latency) or xCluster async replication to a second cluster (RPO > 0, failover is an application switch).

PostgreSQL with Patroni: primary dies -> Patroni's leader key in etcd expires (TTL, typically tens of seconds) -> a standby with the least lag is promoted -> the VIP or HAProxy target moves -> old primary, when it returns, is rewound (pg_rewind) and rejoins as standby. With async standbys RPO is the lag at the moment of failure; with synchronous standbys it is 0 at the cost of commit latency.

docs.title: 2.6 Backups
docs.text:
Replication is not a backup. A DELETE without a WHERE, a bad migration, or ransomware is replicated to every copy within milliseconds. Backups protect against logical damage and operator error; replication protects against hardware loss.

  • Types: logical (pg_dump/ysql_dump: portable, slow for big data, consistent snapshot); physical (file or snapshot level: fast, same version); continuous (WAL archiving / point-in-time recovery to any second within a retention window).
  • YugabyteDB: distributed snapshots (consistent across tablets at one hybrid time), exported to object storage; PITR via snapshot schedules plus retained history lets you restore a database to a time before a bad change. Also flashback-style reads at an older time within the history retention.
  • 3-2-1 rule: three copies, two different media, one off-site (now often: one immutable or air-gapped copy, against ransomware).
  • Restore testing: a backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. Schedule restores into a scratch environment, verify row counts and checksums (your parity suite idea), and time it: the restore duration is your real RTO for logical disasters.
  • Retention follows regulation (banks often must keep years of records) and the time it takes to notice a problem (logical corruption is often found days later).

docs.title: 2.7 Chaos testing and game days
docs.text:
Chaos engineering: deliberately inject failures in a controlled way to find weaknesses before they find you. Netflix's Chaos Monkey (randomly terminating instances in production) made it famous. Principles: define steady state (SLIs), hypothesise it holds under a failure, inject the failure with a small blast radius, observe, and fix what breaks.

Failures to inject, from cheap to bold:

  • kill a process (kill -9), reboot a node, stop a container;
  • network: latency, loss, partitions (tc netem, iptables drops) between app and DB, between DB nodes;
  • disk full, slow disk, read-only filesystem;
  • clock skew (step a node's clock; YugabyteDB should refuse or restart reads, module 10);
  • dependency outage (stop the SMS gateway stub; does posting still work?);
  • CPU or memory pressure (stress-ng).

Jepsen (Kyle Kingsbury) is the rigorous version for databases: a test harness that runs operations against a cluster while injecting partitions and clock faults, then checks the history against a consistency model. Its public analyses (including YugabyteDB's in 2019) are excellent reading for how distributed databases fail.

Game day: a scheduled exercise where the team runs a failure scenario (fail over the database, lose a zone) in staging or production, following the runbook, with a time-keeper and a scribe. You find out that the runbook is out of date, the alert went to the wrong channel, and the failover takes 11 minutes instead of 1.

docs.title: 2.8 Runbooks and incident response
docs.text:
A runbook is a step-by-step procedure for a known operational task or alert: what it means, how to confirm, what to do, how to verify, how to roll back, whom to escalate to. Good runbooks:

  • start from the alert name (the on-call engineer arrives from the page);
  • give exact commands with placeholders, not prose ("run yb-admin ... list_tablets");
  • include "how to tell if this made things worse" and a rollback;
  • are tested in game days and updated after every incident.

Incident response basics: one incident commander coordinates (does not debug); one communicator updates stakeholders; others investigate. Mitigate first, root-cause later: roll back, fail over, shed load. Keep a timeline. Afterwards, a blameless postmortem: what happened, impact, timeline, contributing causes (plural), what went well, action items with owners. Module 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/ covers root-cause analysis technique.

Key metrics for HA: MTTD (mean time to detect), MTTR (mean time to recover/repair), MTBF (mean time between failures). Availability is about MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR): you raise it more cheaply by shrinking MTTR (fast detection, practised recovery) than by preventing every failure.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
There is no new program for this module; the operational tools are commands. A practice session on a local three-node YugabyteDB (Docker or WSL; see 07_Databases_Internals/11_yugabytedb_and_distributed_sql.md for setup):

# Three nodes on one machine with yugabyted (loopback aliases 127.0.0.1-3 work on Linux).
yugabyted start --advertise_address=127.0.0.1 --base_dir=/tmp/yb1
yugabyted start --advertise_address=127.0.0.2 --base_dir=/tmp/yb2 --join=127.0.0.1
yugabyted start --advertise_address=127.0.0.3 --base_dir=/tmp/yb3 --join=127.0.0.1
yugabyted status --base_dir=/tmp/yb1

# Steady load: a loop of small transactions with timing (psql via ysqlsh).
ysqlsh -h 127.0.0.1 -c "CREATE TABLE t (k int PRIMARY KEY, v int)"
while true; do
  start=$(date +%s%N)
  ysqlsh -h 127.0.0.1 -qAt -c "INSERT INTO t VALUES ($RANDOM, 1) ON CONFLICT (k) DO UPDATE SET v = t.v + 1" \
    || echo "$(date +%T) ERROR"
  echo "$(date +%T) $(( ($(date +%s%N) - start) / 1000000 )) ms"
  sleep 0.2
done

# In another terminal: kill a node that is not the one the client talks to, and watch the latency
# column for the few-second blip while its tablets elect new leaders.
yugabyted stop --base_dir=/tmp/yb2
# Bring it back and watch it catch up.
yugabyted start --base_dir=/tmp/yb2

The Raft simulation from module 11 (code/m11_raft_election_sim.cpp) shows the same events at the protocol level: crash, election, catch-up after restart.

For application-tier rolling restarts, module 05's tcpkv server already implements graceful shutdown (stop accepting, drain, deadline). Module 09 section 2.5 explains readiness checks.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why failover takes as long as it does. Detection (missed heartbeats times a threshold) plus election or promotion plus client rediscovery (DNS TTL, connection pool eviction, driver retry backoff). In YugabyteDB the leader lease bounds detection from below: followers must not elect a new leader while the old one might still hold a valid lease, or two nodes could serve reads. With Patroni, the etcd key TTL and loop wait set it. On the client side, the slowest part is often a connection pool holding dead connections until each one times out: set TCP keepalive and driver-level timeouts (module 02 and 09) so dead connections are discovered in seconds.

Gray failure. The hardest failures are partial: a node that answers health checks but serves requests slowly, a NIC dropping 2% of packets, a disk with 500 ms tail latency. Health checks say "up", users say "slow". Defences: health checks that measure real work latency, outlier detection on the client side (eject the slowest backend), hedged requests for reads, and SLO alerts measured from the client side.

Correlated failures defeat redundancy math. Two replicas on the same hypervisor, the same bad config pushed everywhere, the same certificate expiring on every node at midnight, the same leap second bug in every kernel. Independence is the hidden assumption in every "two 99% components give 99.99%" calculation. Stagger config rollouts, use different failure domains, and track expiry dates.

Capacity during failure. With RF3 on three nodes each node holds a third of the leaders. Losing one moves its leaders to the two survivors: each now does 50% of the leader work instead of 33%, a 1.5x load increase. If they were at 70% CPU, they are now overloaded and the failure cascades. Size for the failure case (N+1) and test it.

Zero-downtime is a property of the protocol, not just the infrastructure. Old and new versions must interoperate during a rollout: the wire protocol needs versioning (module 07: version byte, optional trailing fields), the schema must be compatible both ways (expand/contract), and serialized data in queues or caches must be readable by both. Most "the deploy caused an outage" incidents are compatibility failures, not infrastructure failures.

docs.title: 5.1 Failure stories to learn from
docs.text:
• Failover that had never been tested. The standby's replication had silently broken weeks earlier (disk full on the standby). When the primary failed, the standby was weeks behind. Monitoring replication lag, and alerting when replication stops rather than only when lag is high, would have caught it.
  • Backups that could not be restored. Nightly dumps succeeded for a year; the first restore attempt found they excluded a schema added later. Restore drills catch this.
  • The rollback that wasn't. A release included a migration that dropped a column; rollback of the binaries brought back code that read the dropped column. Expand/contract would have allowed rollback.
  • Single hard-coded DB host. The app server's connection string pointed at one YugabyteDB node. That node was rebooted for patching; the whole application was down although the cluster was healthy. Use all nodes in the connection string, a cluster-aware driver, or a load balancer.

docs.title: 5.2 Vocabulary for explaining a zero-downtime cutover
docs.text:
Your resume says "zero-downtime cutover to multi-node production". Interviewers will ask "how?", and the answer should use precise terms. The words, each with a one-line meaning:

  • Bulk load (initial load, snapshot copy): copy all existing data to the new store while the old one keeps serving.
  • Change data capture (CDC) / delta sync / catch-up: apply changes made on the old store since the bulk load began, identified by a change log, modification timestamp or sequence number.
  • Dual write: application writes to both stores for a period (risky: partial failures make them diverge; needs reconciliation).
  • Shadow reads / dark reads: read from both and compare results without showing the new one to users.
  • Parity check / reconciliation: compare old and new record by record (counts, checksums, field-level comparison) to prove equivalence. Your data-parity regression suite.
  • Go/no-go criteria: explicit conditions that must hold before the switch (parity zero mismatches, lag under N seconds, smoke tests pass).
  • Freeze / quiesce / brief read-only window: stop writes for the seconds needed to apply the final delta, so old and new are identical at the switch.
  • Cutover (flip, switchover): point the application at the new store (config change, VIP, DNS, connection string), usually via a rolling restart of app servers.
  • Rollback plan: how to switch back, and how to carry writes made on the new store back to the old one if you do. Time-boxed decision point: after it, roll forward only.
  • Hypercare: the period after cutover with extra monitoring and people on call.

A template answer, to be filled with your real numbers (see 11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search/02_telling_your_story.md; never invent figures in an interview):

"We migrated [N] deployments from Berkeley DB to a three-node YugabyteDB cluster, RF3 across [zones/hosts]. The engine did a bulk load while the old system kept running, then a delta pass for records changed since the load, identified by [mechanism]. A parity suite compared old and new field by field; zero mismatches was a go/no-go criterion. The switch itself was [a config change plus rolling restart of the app servers / a short read-only window of N seconds], done in an agreed window with a written runbook and a rollback path that we rehearsed in UAT. Downtime as seen by branches was [none / under N seconds]. Afterwards we monitored [metrics] during hypercare."

Then expect the pushback: "What if a write arrived during the final delta?" (the freeze or read-only window, or CDC that keeps applying until the flip); "What if the parity check found a mismatch on the night?" (no-go, fix, next window); "How would you roll back after branches had posted to the new store?" (reverse sync or replay of the new store's changes, or a defined point-of-no-return after which you only roll forward); "What does RF3 buy you that Berkeley DB did not?" (survives a node loss with RPO 0 and seconds of RTO; module 11).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Compute the monthly error budget in minutes for 99.5%, 99.9% and 99.95%, and the availability of a request path of load balancer (99.99%), app tier (99.95%) and database (99.99%) in series. Done when: the numbers are right and you can say which component to improve first.

  2. (easy) Write the RTO and RPO you believe your employer's banking system has today, and what mechanism provides each. Mark unknowns. Done when: you have a list of questions to ask the operations team.

  3. (medium) Run the three-node yugabyted exercise in section 3. Kill a node under load and measure the longest latency blip and the number of errors. Done when: you can explain the blip with leader leases and elections, and the absence of data loss with Raft majorities.

  4. (medium) Write an expand/contract plan for renaming account.acct_type to account.product_code in a system with four app servers under rolling deploys. Done when: each step lists the code version, the schema state, and why a rollback at that step is safe.

  5. (hard) Write a runbook for "YugabyteDB node down" in your format: alert, impact, confirm (commands), immediate actions, when to replace the node, how to verify re-replication finished, rollback, escalation. Done when: a colleague who has never seen YugabyteDB could follow it.

  6. (hard) Run a small chaos experiment on the module 05 tcpkv server: three instances behind HAProxy in TCP mode, the load tester running, then kill -9 one instance and later add 200 ms latency to another with tc netem. Done when: you have recorded the error count and p99 for each fault and one change that improved it (health check interval, client retry, timeout).

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: SLA, SLO, SLI? A: The SLI is the measured indicator (fraction of requests that succeed within 500 ms); the SLO is the internal target for it (99.9% over 30 days); the SLA is the external contract with penalties, set looser than the SLO. The gap between 100% and the SLO is the error budget that governs release risk.

Q: RTO versus RPO? A: RTO is how long you may be down after a failure; RPO is how much recent data you may lose, measured in time. Synchronous or quorum replication gives RPO 0; async replication gives RPO equal to the lag; backups give RPO equal to the backup interval unless you archive the WAL.

Q: Active-passive versus active-active? A: Active-passive keeps a standby ready to take over: simple, but idle capacity and a rarely exercised failover path with split-brain risk. Active-active serves from all instances: better utilisation and no failover step for stateless tiers, but needs headroom for a loss and, for stateful tiers, either consensus or conflict handling.

Q: Rolling versus blue-green deploys? A: Rolling replaces instances a few at a time, cheap but old and new versions coexist so they must be compatible. Blue-green deploys to a full parallel environment and switches traffic at once, with instant rollback, at double capacity; the shared database still needs compatible schema changes.

Q: What happens when a YugabyteDB RF3 cluster loses one node? A: Tablets led by that node elect new leaders among their two surviving peers after the leader lease expires, so their writes pause for a few seconds; other tablets are unaffected. No committed data is lost because every commit was on a majority. The cluster is under-replicated until the node returns or, after a timeout, replicas are re-created on other nodes if any exist.

Q: Why is replication not a backup? A: Replication copies every change, including mistakes and malicious deletes, to every replica almost instantly. Backups and point-in-time recovery let you return to a state before the damage. Restores must be tested regularly to count.

Q: How do you change a schema with zero downtime? A: Expand and contract: add new structures compatible with old code, deploy code that writes both and backfill, switch reads to the new structure, and only after the old code is gone and rollback is no longer needed, remove the old structure.

Q: How did you achieve a zero-downtime cutover? A: Bulk load while the old system served, delta catch-up of changes since, a parity check as a go/no-go gate, a short quiesce for the final delta, a configuration flip with rolling restarts, a rehearsed rollback plan, and hypercare monitoring. Give your real numbers.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• SLI measures, SLO targets, SLA contracts; error budget = 100% - SLO. 99.9% = 43.2 min/month.
  • Series availabilities multiply; parallel ones help only if failures are independent.
  • RTO = downtime allowed, RPO = data loss allowed. Quorum replication gives RPO 0.
  • Active-passive vs active-active; failure domains; N+1 capacity.
  • Rolling, blue-green, canary, feature flags; expand/contract for schemas; protocol versioning.
  • YugabyteDB RF3 node loss: seconds of unavailability for that node's leaders, no data loss, under-replicated until replaced; never hard-code one DB host.
  • Replication is not backup; test restores; 3-2-1; PITR.
  • Chaos testing and game days find the broken failover before a real failure does.
