  • Runbooks start from the alert and give exact commands; mitigate first; blameless postmortems.
  • Cutover vocabulary: bulk load, delta/CDC, parity check, go/no-go, quiesce, flip, rollback, hypercare.

docs.title: 14. System design interview walkthroughs
docs.text: Time: ~4 hours Prerequisites: all of 01 to 13

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A system design interview is a 45 to 60 minute conversation where you design a service on a whiteboard: "design a key-value store", "design a rate limiter". There is no single right answer. The interviewer is checking whether you can turn vague requirements into concrete ones, pick reasonable components, explain trade-offs with numbers, and go deep where it matters, all while communicating clearly. For a C++ systems role, expect the deep dives to go lower than in a web interview: wire protocols, threading models, storage engines, replication.

Analogy: an architect meeting a client. A good architect does not start drawing the facade. They ask how many people will live there, the budget, the plot, and the must-haves, sketch the floor plan, then go deep on the parts that are risky (the foundation on clay soil). They say "if you want a bigger kitchen, we lose the study" out loud. That is the method below.

This module gives the method once, then five walkthroughs chosen for your profile: a key-value store (your tcpkv project grown into a distributed system), a loan-origination backend (your domain), a rate limiter, a URL shortener, and a notification queue system. Each ends with pushback questions an interviewer is likely to ask, with short answers.

docs.title: 2.1 The method (45 minutes)
docs.text:
Minutes Step What you produce 0 to 5 Requirements Functional (the 3 to 5 operations that matter); non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, security); explicit out-of-scope list. 5 to 10 Estimates Requests per second (average and peak), data size and growth, read/write ratio, bandwidth. Round numbers. 10 to 15 API and data model The calls (RPC or REST) with arguments and results; the main entities and their keys. 15 to 25 High-level design A box diagram: clients, load balancer, services, storage, caches, queues. Walk one request through it. 25 to 40 Deep dives Two or three areas the interviewer cares about or that are risky: storage layout, sharding key, replication and failover, consistency, hot keys, idempotency, concurrency model. 40 to 45 Wrap-up Bottlenecks, failure modes, monitoring, what you would do next with more time.

Habits that score:

  • Ask before assuming, but do not stall: "I'll assume 10,000 requests per second peak and 99.9% availability; tell me if that's off."
  • State trade-offs as sentences: "Async replication gives lower latency but can lose the last few writes on failover; for balances I'll pay for synchronous quorum writes."
  • Use numbers you can defend. Latency figures worth knowing (typical orders of magnitude, from the widely circulated "latency numbers every programmer should know" list and its updates): main memory reference ~100 ns; SSD random read ~tens to ~100 microseconds; round trip within a datacenter ~0.5 ms; fsync on SSD ~0.1 to a few ms; cross-continent round trip ~100 to 150 ms. 1 day = 86,400 s, so 1 million per day is about 12 per second average; peaks are often 2 to 10 times average.
  • Draw the request path and narrate it.
  • Name the failure modes before being asked: what happens when this box dies?
  • Go deep in your strengths: sockets, framing, thread pools, epoll, PostgreSQL/YugabyteDB, C++ memory. Steer deep dives there when the interviewer gives you a choice.

Estimation template:

 users / clients          -> requests per day -> average RPS -> peak RPS (x3 to x10)
 bytes per record         -> records per day  -> storage per year (x replication factor)
 bytes per request        -> bandwidth = peak RPS x bytes
 working set to cache     -> often 20% of data serves 80% of reads (rule of thumb, verify)

docs.title: 2.2 Walkthrough 1: a key-value store, from tcpkv to distributed
docs.text:
Prompt: "Design a key-value store. Start with a single node and evolve it to survive node failures and grow beyond one machine."

Requirements: GET, SET, DEL on string keys up to 256 bytes and values up to 1 MB. Single node first. Then: 1 TB of data, 100,000 ops/s peak, 80% reads, p99 under 10 ms, survive one node loss without losing acknowledged writes. Out of scope: secondary indexes, transactions across keys.

Estimates: 1 TB / 64 GB RAM per node: does not fit in one machine's memory, so disk-backed storage or many nodes. 100,000 ops/s: a well-written epoll server does this on one node for small values, but storage and replication spread it out. With RF3, 3 TB raw.

Stage 1: single node (this is tcpkv)

 clients --TCP, tcpkv text protocol--> [ acceptor | epoll loops or thread pool ] --> in-memory map

                                                                                     + append-only log
  • Protocol: tcpkv from module 04, or a length-prefixed binary protocol for large values.
  • Concurrency: module 05 thread pool (simple) or module 06 epoll loops (scales to many idle connections). Store: sharded unordered_maps each with its own shared_mutex to cut contention (see 04_Concurrency/04_shared_mutex_and_readers_writers.md).
  • Durability: append every write to a log file (write + fdatasync, group-committed every few ms) and replay on start; periodic snapshot to bound replay time. That is a WAL (see 07_Databases_Internals/04_wal_and_crash_recovery.md).
  • Beyond RAM: an LSM tree (memtable, immutable sorted files, compaction) like RocksDB, or a B-tree like Berkeley DB. Writes-heavy: LSM. Read-heavy with range scans: B-tree.

Stage 2: replication for durability and failover

            +-------------------------- Raft group (RF3) --------------------------+
 client --> | leader (node A) --AppendEntries--> follower (node B)                 |
            |                 --AppendEntries--> follower (node C)                 |
            +----------------------------------------------------------------------+
   SET returns OK after the entry is on 2 of 3 logs; GET served by leader under its lease
  • Raft (module 11). The log is the WAL. Clients find the leader (any node redirects with "leader is A").
  • Reads: from leader with lease (linearizable) or from followers (stale OK) per request flag.

Stage 3: sharding for size and throughput

                       +--------------------+
 client (smart, caches |  metadata service  |  (its own Raft group: shard map, placement)
 the shard map) -----> +--------------------+
     |
     | hash(key) -> shard 17 -> leader on node D
     v
 +--------+   +--------+   +--------+   +--------+   +--------+
 | node A |   | node B |   | node C |   | node D |   | node E |
 | s1 L   |   | s1 F   |   | s1 F   |   | s17 L  |   | s17 F  |  ... each shard a Raft group,
 | s17 F  |   | s4 L   |   | s4 F   |   | s4 F   |   | ...    |      leaders spread across nodes
 +--------+   +--------+   +--------+   +--------+   +--------+
  • Fixed hash space split into shards (like YugabyteDB's 16-bit space or Redis Cluster's 16384 slots), or consistent hashing (module 12) if you prefer Dynamo-style.
  • Shards split when large; the metadata service moves replicas and leaders to balance.
  • This is Multi-Raft: YugabyteDB, CockroachDB and TiKV in miniature.

Alternative: leaderless (Dynamo/Cassandra): any replica takes writes, N=3, W=2, R=2, hinted handoff, read repair, last-write-wins or vector clocks. Higher availability under partitions, weaker consistency (module 10). Say which you pick and why: "For a general-purpose store with strong consistency I pick Raft per shard; if the interviewer wants always-writable (shopping cart), Dynamo style."

Pushback questions

  • "What if the leader acknowledges a write and then dies?" It acknowledged only after a majority stored it; the next leader must have it (Raft's vote restriction). No loss.
  • "A client times out on SET. Did it happen?" Unknown. Make SET idempotent (it is, for the same value) or add client request ids that the state machine deduplicates.
  • "One key gets 50% of traffic." Cache it at the client or a proxy for reads (with a short TTL or invalidation); for writes, split the key (sub-keys merged on read) or accept that a shard leader's throughput is the ceiling.
  • "Why not just use consistent hashing without Raft?" Then replicas can diverge on failure and you need conflict resolution; fine for caches, not for a source of truth.
  • "How do you handle a 1 MB value with your text protocol?" Length-prefixed bulk strings (tcpkv's $len) so the parser never scans the value; stream it to disk rather than buffering when large.
  • "How many threads?" One epoll loop per core with connections assigned round-robin; storage fsyncs on a dedicated thread with group commit; Raft per shard driven by the loop owning it.

docs.title: 2.3 Walkthrough 2: a loan-origination backend
docs.text:
Prompt: "Design the backend for a bank's loan-origination system: branch staff and customers submit loan applications, documents are uploaded, credit checks run, approvers approve, the loan is disbursed."

Requirements

  • Functional: create application; attach documents; run checks (credit bureau, KYC, internal limits); multi-level approval workflow by amount; disburse to the core banking system; status tracking; audit trail of every change.
  • Non-functional: 500 branches, about 20,000 applications per day at peak season (assumed), p99 under 1 s for interactive screens, no lost applications, strict audit, data residency in the country, 99.9% during business hours, integrations that are slow and flaky (bureau API: seconds).
  • Out of scope: credit scoring model internals, the core banking ledger itself.

Estimates: 20,000 / day is under 1 per second average; even 10x peak is tiny. Scale is not the problem; correctness, workflow, integrations and audit are. Say that explicitly: it shows judgement. Documents: 10 per application x 500 KB = 100 GB per year (assumed), so object storage, not database rows.

High-level design

 branch UI / customer app
        |  HTTPS (REST/JSON) or RPC over TCP from branch terminals
        v
 +---------------+      +------------------------+
 | API gateway   |----->| Loan application svc   |----> YugabyteDB / PostgreSQL (RF3)
 | authn, rate   |      | state machine, rules,  |        applications, applicants, approvals,
 | limit, audit  |      | idempotency keys       |        outbox table, audit log
 +---------------+      +------------------------+
                            |  (same transaction writes an OUTBOX row)
                            v
                       outbox relay -> message queue (Kafka / RabbitMQ / DB-backed queue)
                            |
         +------------------+------------------+--------------------+
         v                  v                  v                    v
  credit-check worker  KYC worker       notification worker   disbursement worker
  (bureau API,         (KYC vendor)     (SMS/email)           (core banking RPC,
   retries, breaker)                                            idempotent by app no)
         |                  |                                        |
         +--- results posted back to the loan service (API or queue) +
 document upload: client -> pre-signed URL -> object storage (S3-compatible, encrypted);
                  DB stores only the reference + checksum

Data model (core)

 loan_application(application_no PK HASH, branch_code, applicant_id, product_code,
                  amount_minor, status, version, created_at, updated_at)
 application_event(application_no, seq, event_type, payload_json, actor, at)
                  PRIMARY KEY ((application_no) HASH, seq ASC)       -- audit + history
 approval(application_no, level, approver_id, decision, at)
 outbox(id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload, created_at, published_at NULL)

Deep dives

  • Application as a state machine: DRAFT -> SUBMITTED -> CHECKS_PENDING -> CHECKS_DONE -> PENDING_APPROVAL(L1/L2/L3) -> APPROVED -> DISBURSING -> DISBURSED, plus REJECTED, WITHDRAWN. Every transition is a function that validates the current state; illegal transitions are rejected. Store the state plus an append-only event table for audit.
  • Optimistic concurrency: two approvers act at once. UPDATE ... SET status = $new, version = version + 1 WHERE application_no = $1 AND version = $expected; zero rows updated means someone else acted first; reload and show.
  • Transactional outbox: writing the DB row and publishing a message cannot be atomic across two systems (dual write problem). Write the event into an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay process publishes unsent outbox rows and marks them sent. At-least-once publish; consumers deduplicate by event id (module 10).
  • Slow, flaky integrations: never call the credit bureau inside the user's request. Queue it; worker calls with timeout, retries with jittered backoff, circuit breaker, and a dead-letter queue after N failures for manual handling (module 09). The UI shows "checks pending".
  • Disbursement exactly once: the disbursement RPC to core banking carries the application number as the idempotency key; core banking rejects duplicates. State DISBURSING is set before the call; a reconciler queries core banking for applications stuck in DISBURSING to resolve unknown outcomes.
  • Audit: append-only event table, actor and timestamp on every change, no UPDATE/DELETE grants on it for the app user; optionally hash-chained rows for tamper evidence.
  • Database: one YugabyteDB or PostgreSQL cluster is enough for the volume. RF3 for RPO 0. Shard keys per module 12 if distributed.

Pushback questions

  • "Why not microservices for everything?" At this volume a modular monolith plus a few workers is simpler to operate; split out services where the change rate or scaling differs (integrations, notifications). Say what you would split first and why.
  • "The bureau is down for an hour." Breaker opens, applications queue in CHECKS_PENDING, the UI says so, the queue drains when it recovers; alerts fire on queue age, not on each failure.
  • "A message is processed twice." Consumers are idempotent: the check result is stored keyed by (application_no, check_type, request_id); a duplicate is a no-op.
  • "How do you guarantee no lost applications?" The create call is idempotent with a client generated key; the row is committed to an RF3 database before OK; the outbox ensures every committed state change produces its event.
  • "Approver limits differ by branch and product." Rules in configuration tables, versioned, with the rule version recorded on each approval for audit.
  • "How would you migrate the existing system's in-flight applications?" Bulk load plus delta, parity check, cutover window (module 13 vocabulary).

docs.title: 2.4 Walkthrough 3: a rate limiter
docs.text:
Prompt: "Design a rate limiter for an API used by many clients: 100 requests per second per API key with bursts up to 200, across a fleet of 20 API servers."

Requirements: per-key limits (and per-IP for anonymous), configurable per plan; decision latency under 1 ms added; correct within a small tolerance; must not become a single point of failure; return 429 with Retry-After. Out of scope: billing.

Estimates: 1 million keys; 200,000 requests per second total across the fleet (assumed); state per key ~ 16 bytes (tokens + timestamp) + key, so ~100 MB: fits in memory anywhere.

Algorithms (module 09): token bucket (burst + rate, the standard; code/m09_token_bucket.cpp), leaky bucket (smooth output), fixed window (boundary burst problem), sliding window log (exact, memory heavy), sliding window counter (weighted two windows, good approximation).

Where to enforce

 option A: local only                         option B: central store
 client -> LB -> [api-1: bucket per key]      client -> LB -> [api-1] --+
                 [api-2: bucket per key]                    [api-2] --+--> Redis (Lua script:
                 ...                                        ...       |     atomic token bucket)
 each server allows limit / 20                              [api-20]--+    per key, ~0.5 ms RTT

 option C: hybrid
 each server keeps a local bucket and periodically (every 100 ms) syncs usage with the central
 store, or leases a batch of tokens ("give me 50 tokens for key K") and spends them locally.
  • Local only: zero latency, no dependency. Inaccurate when the LB does not spread one key's traffic evenly (sticky connections), and limits change with fleet size.
  • Central (Redis): accurate. Adds a network round trip and a dependency; Redis must be HA (replicas + Sentinel, or Redis Cluster sharded by key). Use a Lua script so read-modify-write is atomic.
  • Hybrid / token leasing: near-local latency, near-global accuracy. The usual production answer for high volume.
  • Failure policy: if the central store is unreachable, fail open (allow, with local fallback limits) for availability, or fail closed for protection of a fragile backend. State the choice per use case.

Pushback questions

  • "Clocks differ between servers; does your bucket break?" Each bucket is refilled using the clock of whoever owns it: the Redis server's time (use TIME in the Lua script) or the local monotonic clock, never mixed wall clocks from different servers.
  • "Hot key: one customer sends 50,000 requests per second." Local pre-check with a local bucket rejects most before touching Redis; only the residual hits the central store.
  • "How do clients know when to retry?" 429 with Retry-After computed from the bucket's time_until; plus RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset headers.
  • "Distributed limit across regions?" Per-region budgets (split the global limit) with occasional rebalancing; exact global limits across regions cost a WAN round trip per request.
  • "Rate limiting vs load shedding?" Rate limiting is per-client fairness by policy; load shedding protects the server by its own capacity, regardless of who is asking. You want both.

docs.title: 2.5 Walkthrough 4: a URL shortener
docs.text:
Prompt: "Design a URL shortener like bit.ly."

Requirements: create short code for a long URL (optional custom alias, optional expiry); redirect short code to long URL; basic click counts. Non-functional: 100 million new URLs per month (assumed), reads 100x writes, redirect p99 under 50 ms, highly available reads, codes not guessable in sequence (soft requirement).

Estimates: 100 M / month ~ 40 writes/s average; reads ~4,000/s average, peaks 10x = 40,000/s. 5 years: 6 billion URLs x ~500 bytes = 3 TB. Code length: base62, 62^7 ~ 3.5 trillion: 7 chars is plenty.

API: POST /urls {long_url, alias?, expires_at?} -> {code}; GET /{code} -> 301/302 Location. Use 302 (or 307) if you need click counting, because browsers cache 301 permanently.

High-level design

 client --> CDN / edge cache --> LB --> redirect service --> cache (Redis / local LRU)
                                              |                   | miss
                                              |                   v
                                              |             KV store: code -> long_url
                                              |             (sharded by code, hash; RF3)
                                              +--> click event --> queue --> analytics aggregator
 client --> LB --> create service --> ID generator --> KV store (insert if absent)

Deep dives

  • Generating codes:
    1. Hash the long URL (MD5/SHA-256) and take 7 base62 chars: same URL gives same code (dedupe for free) but collisions must be checked and resolved (append a salt, retry).
    2. Counter + base62: a unique 64-bit id encoded in base62. No collisions. Ids come from ranges leased to each create server by a coordinator (each server gets 1,000 ids at a time, like YugabyteDB sequence caching), or a Snowflake-style id (timestamp + machine id + sequence). Sequential codes are guessable; scramble with a reversible permutation (e.g. a Feistel network over the 64-bit id) if that matters.
    3. Random 7 chars with insert-if-absent (conditional put): simple; collision probability grows with fill but stays tiny at 3.5 trillion space.
  • Storage: a pure key-value access pattern: hash-sharded by code. Any KV or distributed SQL store. Custom aliases need a uniqueness check: conditional insert on the same key.
  • Caching: read-heavy with a hot head (popular links). CDN for the hottest, Redis for the rest, LRU local cache in each redirect server for the very top. Cache-aside with TTL; codes are immutable so invalidation is rare (only delete/expiry).
  • Analytics: never write to the DB synchronously per click. Emit an event to a queue; batch aggregate counts per code per minute.

Pushback questions

  • "301 or 302?" 301 is cached by browsers and saves load but you lose click data and cannot change the target; 302 keeps every click visible.
  • "How do you prevent abuse (phishing links)?" Rate limit creation per user/IP (walkthrough 3), check against safe-browsing lists asynchronously, allow takedown.
  • "The ID coordinator dies." Servers hold leased ranges and keep working; the coordinator is a small Raft-replicated service or a database row with UPDATE ... RETURNING to lease ranges.
  • "Hot link from a viral post." CDN plus local cache absorbs it; the store sees a handful of requests.
  • "Expiry?" Store expires_at; check on read; background job or TTL feature to delete.

docs.title: 2.6 Walkthrough 5: a notification and queue system
docs.text:
Prompt: "Design a system that sends notifications (SMS, email, push) for events from many services: OTPs, transaction alerts, marketing."

Requirements: services submit notification requests; templates and user preferences (opt-outs, channels, quiet hours); per-channel providers; priorities (OTP within seconds, marketing can wait hours); retries; delivery status; no duplicate OTP if avoidable; audit for regulatory alerts. Assumed scale: 50 million notifications per day, peak 5,000/s during batch campaigns, OTP p99 end-to-end under 5 s.

High-level design

 producer services --RPC/HTTP--> notification API (validate, idempotency key, enqueue)
                                        |
                                        v
                         +----------------------------------+
                         | durable queue, one topic/queue   |
                         | per priority: otp | txn | bulk   |
                         +----------------------------------+
                           |              |              |
                           v              v              v
                 dispatcher workers (pull, render template, apply preferences,
                 dedupe by key, per-provider token bucket, circuit breaker per provider)
                           |              |              |
                           v              v              v
                      SMS provider A/B   email (SMTP/API)   push (APNs/FCM)
                           |
                 delivery receipts (webhooks) --> status store (by notification id)
 failed after N retries --> dead-letter queue --> ops dashboard / replay tool

Deep dives

  • Queue choice: Kafka (partitioned log, consumer offsets, replay, ordering per partition, high throughput) vs RabbitMQ (per-message ack, routing, priorities, delayed redelivery) vs a database-backed queue (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; simple, transactional with your data, fine up to hundreds or low thousands per second, typical). For a bank already on PostgreSQL or YugabyteDB, a DB queue for transaction alerts with the outbox pattern is a defensible start.
  • Priorities and isolation: separate queues and worker pools per priority (bulkheads), so a 10 million message marketing campaign cannot delay OTPs. Do not rely on a single queue with priority fields under load.
  • Delivery semantics: at-least-once from queue to worker. Idempotency key per notification; the worker records "sent" with provider message id before acking; a crash between send and record can still duplicate, so use the provider's own idempotency key if it supports one. For OTPs a duplicate is annoying but harmless; for "your account was debited" alerts, the duplicate is confusing, so dedupe on (event_id, channel).
  • Ordering: usually unnecessary across users; per user, partition by user_id (Kafka key) if ordering matters (e.g. "debited" before "balance low").
  • Backpressure and provider limits: providers have rate limits; per-provider token buckets in the dispatcher; when a provider is slow, the breaker opens and traffic fails over to provider B.
  • Retries: exponential backoff with jitter via delayed queues or a "retry at" column; max attempts by priority (OTP retries quickly then gives up because a late OTP is useless).
  • Scheduling and quiet hours: marketing respects time zones and quiet hours: a scheduled queue keyed by send time.

Pushback questions

  • "Kafka partition count?" Enough for the parallelism you need in consumers (one consumer per partition per group), with headroom since increasing it reshuffles keys; a typical start is tens of partitions per topic.
  • "Consumer crashes mid-batch." Uncommitted offsets are redelivered; idempotency handles the duplicates. Commit offsets after the side effect, not before (that would be at-most-once).
  • "A poison message crashes every worker." Bounded retries, then dead-letter queue; never block the partition forever.
  • "How do you know a message was delivered?" Provider receipt webhooks update status; reconcile missing receipts after a timeout; report delivered/failed/unknown per channel.
  • "Exactly-once?" No: at-least-once with dedupe (module 10). Say it plainly.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
The walkthroughs reuse code from this course. Know where each piece lives so you can say "I built this":

Design element Code Text protocol and incremental parser (KV store stage 1) code/m04_tcpkv_parser.hpp, m04_tcpkv_parser_test.cpp Length-prefixed framing for large values code/m04_framing.cpp Thread-pool server with graceful shutdown code/m05_threadpool_tcpkv_server.cpp Event-loop server code/m06_epoll_echo_server.cpp Binary RPC with request ids and deadlines (loan workers calling core banking) code/m07_rpc.hpp, m07_rpc_demo.cpp HTTP API (URL shortener redirect, notification API) code/m08_http_server.cpp Token bucket (rate limiter, provider limits) code/m09_token_bucket.cpp Hybrid logical clock (timestamps across nodes) code/m10_hlc.cpp Raft election and replication (KV store stage 2) code/m11_raft_election_sim.cpp Consistent hashing (KV store stage 3, cache sharding) code/m12_consistent_hash.cpp The full tcpkv project 10_Capstone_Projects/tcpkv/

A base62 encoder, the kind of five-minute code an interviewer may ask for in the URL shortener:

#include <cstdint>
#include <string>

std::string base62(uint64_t n) {
    static const char* digits = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz";
    if (n == 0) return "0";
    std::string out;
    while (n > 0) {
        out.push_back(digits[n % 62]);
        n /= 62;
    }
    return std::string(out.rbegin(), out.rend());   // most significant digit first
}

And the database-backed queue claim, the core of a simple notification worker:

-- Each worker claims up to 100 due messages without blocking other workers.
WITH next AS (
    SELECT id FROM notification_queue
    WHERE status = 'READY' AND run_at <= now()
    ORDER BY priority, run_at
    LIMIT 100
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE notification_queue q SET status = 'CLAIMED', claimed_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
FROM next WHERE q.id = next.id
RETURNING q.*;

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What separates a senior answer in these interviews is going one layer down when it matters:

  • "How does your server handle 100,000 connections?" epoll, one loop per core, per-connection state machines with buffers, SO_REUSEPORT to spread accepts, file descriptor limits raised, memory per connection estimated (module 06), TCP keepalive or app-level heartbeats to drop dead peers, TIME_WAIT on the side that closes (module 02).
  • "Where does latency go on a write?" Client to LB (~0.1 to 0.5 ms in a DC), parse, queueing in the pool (rises with utilisation, module 09 section 4), the Raft round (leader fsync plus one follower RTT and fsync), apply, reply. The fsync and the queueing usually dominate.
  • "Why not cache everything?" Cache invalidation and consistency: cache-aside with TTL gives stale reads for up to the TTL; write-through costs latency; the thundering herd on a popular key's expiry needs request coalescing or early refresh. See 07_Databases_Internals/13_caching_and_redis.md.
  • "What breaks first at 10x?" Usually the database's hottest shard or a single-threaded component (one Kafka partition, one sequence row, one Redis instance), not the stateless tier.
  • "How do you make it observable?" Request ids end to end, RED metrics per endpoint, queue age (not just length) per queue, per-dependency latency, and SLO burn alerts (module 09 and 13).

Common mistakes interviewers note: jumping to a diagram without requirements; designing for Google scale when the problem is 1 request per second; no numbers; "we'll use Kafka" with no reason; ignoring failure; never stating a trade-off; going silent while thinking. Narrate.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
Everything in these walkthroughs maps to work you have done or can talk about honestly:

  • KV store: you built tcpkv (capstone) and you migrated a Berkeley DB key-value store to YugabyteDB. You can talk about what changes when a KV store becomes distributed from both ends.
  • Loan origination: your employer's domain. The state machine, approvals, audit and integrations are things you know from production; outbox and idempotency keys are the words for patterns you may have implemented with other names.
  • Rate limiter: per-branch limits on your RPC server (module 09 exercise) are a concrete story.
  • Notifications: banks send OTPs and transaction alerts; you know the regulatory side (audit, retention) that most candidates do not.

Practice by saying the walkthroughs out loud with a timer, drawing on paper. Record yourself once. Mock interview scripts are in 11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search/11_mock_interview_scripts.md.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Do the estimates for each of the five walkthroughs from scratch on paper without looking: RPS average and peak, storage per year, bandwidth. Done when: each takes under three minutes and your numbers are within 2x of the module's.

  2. (easy) For the URL shortener, implement base62 and its inverse and assert round trips for 10,000 random 64-bit values. Done when: it compiles with the course flags and passes.

  3. (medium) Run walkthrough 2 (loan origination) aloud in 45 minutes with a timer, drawing the diagram from memory. Then list three questions an interviewer could ask that the module did not answer, and answer them. Done when: you finished all five method steps inside the time.

  4. (medium) Implement the hybrid token-leasing rate limiter in a single process: a "central" TokenBucket (from m09_token_bucket.cpp) and 4 local limiter threads that lease 20 tokens at a time. Done when: under load the total accepted rate stays within 10% of the central limit and the central bucket is called at most 1/20 as often as requests arrive.

  5. (hard) Design a sixth problem on your own: "a distributed job scheduler that runs end-of-day banking batch jobs across a cluster, each job exactly once per business date, with dependencies between jobs". Write requirements, estimates, diagram, three deep dives and five pushback questions with answers. Done when: it fits on two pages and you can present it in 30 minutes.

  6. (hard) Extend m11_raft_election_sim.cpp into the KV store stage 2: commands are SET k v, the state machine is a std::map, and a client retries with a request id that the state machine deduplicates. Done when: the fuzz loop with crashes and partitions shows every acknowledged SET present exactly once and no unacknowledged SET applied twice.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Walk me through how you approach a system design question. A: Clarify functional and non-functional requirements and state assumptions; estimate load and storage; define the API and data model; draw the high-level design and walk a request through it; deep dive into the riskiest parts; finish with bottlenecks, failure modes and monitoring. Trade-offs are stated out loud throughout.

Q: How would you make a single-node key-value store survive a node failure? A: Replicate each write through a consensus log (Raft) to three nodes and acknowledge after a majority stores it; the leader serves linearizable reads under a lease; failover is automatic election. To grow beyond one machine, shard the key space and run a Raft group per shard with a metadata service holding the shard map.

Q: How do you avoid the dual-write problem when a service must update its database and publish an event? A: Transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the state change, and have a relay publish outbox rows and mark them sent. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate by event id.

Q: Local or centralized rate limiting? A: Local is fast and dependency-free but inaccurate when traffic for a key is unevenly spread; central (Redis with an atomic script) is accurate but adds a round trip and a dependency. At scale, lease batches of tokens from the central store and spend locally. Decide fail-open or fail-closed per use case.

Q: How would you generate short codes for a URL shortener? A: Either a unique numeric id from leased ranges or a Snowflake-style generator encoded in base62 (no collisions; optionally scrambled to avoid guessable sequences), or a hash or random code with conditional insert and collision retry. Seven base62 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes.

Q: How do you keep OTP notifications fast while a 10-million-message campaign is running? A: Separate queues and worker pools per priority (bulkheads), per-provider rate limits, and monitoring of queue age per priority. A single shared queue would put OTPs behind the campaign.

Q: Kafka or a database-backed queue? A: A database queue with SKIP LOCKED is transactional with your data and simple to operate, and is enough up to moderate throughput. Kafka gives high throughput, replay, ordering per partition and many independent consumer groups, at the cost of running another distributed system and handling offsets and partitioning yourself.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Method: requirements, estimates, API and data model, high-level design, deep dives, wrap-up.
  • Numbers: 1 M/day is ~12/s; peaks 3 to 10x; DC round trip ~0.5 ms; SSD fsync ~0.1 to a few ms.
  • KV store: tcpkv -> WAL -> Raft group -> sharded Multi-Raft with a metadata service.
  • Loan origination: scale is small; correctness is the design. State machine, optimistic concurrency, outbox, idempotent disbursement, async integrations with breakers, audit.
  • Rate limiter: token bucket; local vs central vs leased tokens; fail-open vs fail-closed.
  • URL shortener: base62 ids from leased ranges, KV store sharded by code, caches and CDN, 302 for analytics, async click events.
  • Notifications: per-priority queues, at-least-once plus dedupe, provider limits and failover, DLQ, receipts.
  • Always state trade-offs and failure modes before being asked. Narrate.

docs.title: 08. Networking and Distributed Systems: all exercises
docs.text:
Every exercise from every module, in one place, with its difficulty and a hint. The full "done when" criteria are in each module's section 6. Work them in module order; within a module, easy first. Suggested minimum before interviews: every easy and medium, plus the hard ones marked with a star (*), which produce something you can show or talk about.

Build everything on WSL Ubuntu 24.04 with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread, or make in code/.

docs.title: Module 01: How the internet moves bytes
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy ip route get for loopback, the WSL gateway and 1.1.1.1; explain each decision Longest-prefix match on the routing table; loopback never leaves the host. 2 easy dig A records, TTLs and a CNAME chain (www.github.com) dig +noall +answer; follow the CNAME until an A record. 3 medium Capture a handshake and a request with tcpdump -w, read it in Wireshark Filter tcp.port == N; MSS is a TCP option in the SYN and SYN-ACK. 4 medium Bandwidth-delay product for 100 Mbit/s at 50 ms RTT vs a 64 KB window Bytes in flight = (bits/s / 8) x RTT; throughput cap = window / RTT. 5 hard Shell script diagnosing DNS, ping and TCP-port failures for a host:port Test layers bottom-up and stop at the first failure; getent, ping -c1 -W1, nc -zv -w2.

docs.title: Module 02: TCP in depth
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Find who sent FIN first and confirm that side holds TIME_WAIT The active closer holds TIME_WAIT; ss -tan state time-wait. 2 easy Draw the TCP state machine from memory Separate the three-way open, active close and passive close paths. 3 medium Reproduce the Nagle plus delayed-ACK stall and fix with TCP_NODELAY Write-write-read pattern with small writes; loopback may hide it. 4 medium Reproduce CLOSE_WAIT, then fix the server to close on read() == 0 CLOSE_WAIT means your code has not called close. 5* hard Estimate and measure the max connection rate under TIME_WAIT, then try tcp_tw_reuse Ports in ip_local_port_range divided by the TIME_WAIT duration. 6 hard tc netem loss and delay on loopback; find fast retransmit and RTO retransmits Fast retransmit follows three duplicate ACKs; RTO shows as a long gap.

docs.title: Module 03: Sockets API and a blocking server
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Run echo server and client, watch ss -tanp during and after Note LISTEN, ESTAB, and who ends in TIME_WAIT. 2 easy Remove SIGPIPE protection and kill the client mid-echo Exit status 141 = 128 + SIGPIPE (13). 3 medium Print each recv size for seq 1 100000 Sizes depend on segment arrival and buffer state, not on the sender's send calls. 4 medium connect_with_timeout with non-blocking connect, poll and SO_ERROR EINPROGRESS is success-so-far; read SO_ERROR when writable. 5 hard Winsock version m03_socket_win.hpp WSAStartup once, SOCKET is unsigned, closesocket, WSAGetLastError. 6 hard LD_PRELOAD library that histograms recv/read sizes dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "recv"); print in a destructor function.

docs.title: Module 04: Framing and protocol design
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Run parser tests and framing under ASan and UBSan Add -fsanitize=address,undefined -g. 2 easy Add KEYS <prefix> to the grammar and its reply formatter Reply is an array header *n followed by n bulk strings. 3 medium Incremental ReplyParser for + - : $ replies, tested with random splits Reuse the request parser's state-machine shape; compare byte-by-byte vs whole. 4 medium Tolerate multiple spaces and bare \n without breaking tests Decide what a bare \n inside a bulk value means before coding. 5 hard libFuzzer target that splits input at data-derived positions Use the first byte(s) of input as split offsets; build with clang. 6* hard One-page spec for a binary tcpkv Specify every field's size, byte order, and the error/status codes.

docs.title: Module 05: Thread-per-connection and thread pools
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Two workers, three nc clients: see the third starve It sits in the accept queue or the task queue, depending on the design. 2 easy Observe the idle timeout firing Lower the timeout constant; check the counter at shutdown. 3 medium Per-connection command limit or token bucket with ERR_BUSY Reuse TokenBucket from m09_token_bucket.cpp. 4 medium Reproduce the slow-reader deadlock and the send timeout freeing it Watch Send-Q and Recv-Q both fill in ss -tanp. 5* hard Request-per-worker with an I/O thread per connection and ordered replies Tag each request with a per-connection sequence number; reorder on output. 6 hard SIGHUP config reload and SIGUSR1 counters dump Use signalfd or a self-pipe; never do real work in a signal handler.

docs.title: Module 06: Non-blocking I/O, epoll and event loops
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Compare RSS and threads of epoll vs thread-pool server at 1000 connections ps -o rss,nlwp -p PID. 2 easy Break the edge-triggered drain rule and observe hangs ET reports a transition once; unread data never re-triggers. 3* medium Convert the epoll echo server into tcpkv One Parser and output buffer per Conn; replies appended to the buffer. 4 medium Non-blocking connect inside the loop with a 3 s timer Register EPOLLOUT, then SO_ERROR; use timerfd for the timeout. 5 hard Worker pool for SLOW commands posting replies back via eventfd Mutex-protected completion queue plus eventfd write to wake the loop. 6 hard Rewrite the echo server with Boost.Asio One io_context, async_read_some then async_write in a loop.

docs.title: Module 07: RPC
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Add a Ping method returning monotonic milliseconds New method id in the dispatch table; steady_clock. 2 easy Bump kVersion on the server only and get a clear error The side that reads the header detects it; reply with a status, not garbage. 3 medium Pipelined client: send_async and wait(id) Map of id to pending result; read replies until yours arrives. 4 medium Server-side in-flight limit per connection returning Overloaded Count outstanding ids per connection; decrement on reply. 5* hard Multi-threaded client with a demux reader thread and promises Writer mutex, one reader thread, timer thread failing promises on deadline. 6 hard Same service in gRPC; compare p50 latency Measure many calls after warm-up; explain HTTP/2 and protobuf costs.

docs.title: Module 08: HTTP and REST
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Confirm keep-alive reuses one connection with tcpdump One SYN for two requests with curl url1 url2. 2 easy HEAD support, ETag and 304 Not Modified ETag = hash of the value; compare with If-None-Match. 3 medium Chunked request body decoding State machine: hex size line, data, CRLF, until size 0, then trailers. 4 medium If-Match on PUT with 412, plus a two-client race test Compare-and-set on the ETag under the store's lock. 5* hard HTTP server on the epoll loop, benchmark with wrk Per-connection parse state survives partial requests across reads. 6 hard TLS with OpenSSL SSL_CTX_new(TLS_server_method()), self-signed cert, SSL_accept.

docs.title: Module 09: Client-server architecture and reliability
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Per-connection token bucket in tcpkv Burst 100, rate 50/s; -ERR_BUSY on empty. 2 easy backoff_ms schedule for ten seeds Full jitter: uniform in [0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)]. 3* medium Tested CircuitBreaker with an injectable clock Test each transition: closed to open, open to half-open, half-open to both. 4 medium X-Request-Id handling and JSON access log in the HTTP server Generate an id if absent; log after the response is written. 5 hard Connection pool for the RPC client Bounded size, acquire timeout, validate-on-borrow after idle, max lifetime. 6* hard Reliability review of your employer's request path One row per hop: timeout, retry, idempotency, pool, breaker, failure UX.

docs.title: Module 10: Distributed systems fundamentals
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Explain one [RAW CLOCK WRONG] line from m10_hlc Identify which of the four receive branches fired from the printed l values. 2 easy Read your clock offset and frequency error from chrony ppm x 1e-6 = seconds of drift per second. 3 medium Add a Lamport clock beside the HLC; find concurrent events it orders Concurrent = neither happened-before the other; Lamport still gives them an order. 4 medium Consistency model needed by each banking screen Ask: what goes wrong if this read is one second stale? 5 hard Leaderless N=3 store with W, R, read repair and random failures Version every value; reader returns the highest version and repairs the others. 6* hard Unknown-outcome decision table for your posting RPC Four failure points times what client sees, server state, retry effect.

docs.title: Module 11: Consensus: Raft in plain words
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Run m11_raft_election_sim with three seeds; compare first election and terms Terms grow with every election attempt, including split votes. 2 easy Four nodes partitioned 2-2 Majority of 4 is 3; neither side has it. 3 medium Remove timeout randomisation; observe split votes Set kElectionMin == kElectionMax; count terms before a stable leader. 4 medium Add check-quorum to the leader Track the last successful reply time per follower; step down without a recent majority. 5 hard Add pre-vote A PreVote round with term + 1 that does not change anyone's persistent state. 6* hard Single-server membership change with learners Configuration takes effect on append; promote a learner when caught up.

docs.title: Module 12: Sharding, partitioning and distributed SQL
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Measure ring balance for 1, 5, 20, 500 virtual nodes Relative imbalance shrinks roughly as 1/sqrt(vnodes). 2 easy Choose shard keys for five tables Name the hot access path and the key's cardinality for each. 3 medium Add jump consistent hash and compare Jump hash needs no memory but only adds/removes buckets at the end. 4* medium YugabyteDB: compare EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST) for two primary-key designs (account_no) HASH, txn_ts DESC vs txn_id HASH for "last 20 of one account". 5 hard 2PC simulation with coordinator crash, then a replicated decision record Participants that voted yes must wait; a majority-replicated decision unblocks them. 6* hard Sharding and colocation plan for a 12-table loan-origination schema Every hot query should touch one tablet per table, or say why not.

docs.title: Module 13: High availability and operations
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Error budgets for 99.5/99.9/99.95% and a series availability 30 days = 43,200 minutes; series availabilities multiply. 2 easy Your employer's RTO and RPO and their mechanisms If you do not know, the mechanism tells you: backup interval, replication mode. 3* medium Kill a yugabyted node under load; measure the blip Expect a few seconds on tablets led by the dead node; zero lost commits. 4 medium Expand/contract plan for renaming a column under rolling deploys Never drop the old column in the release that stops reading it. 5* hard Runbook for "YugabyteDB node down" Start from the alert; exact commands; how to verify re-replication finished. 6 hard Chaos experiment on three tcpkv instances behind HAProxy kill -9 one, tc netem another; record errors and p99 per fault.

docs.title: Module 14: System design interview walkthroughs
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1 easy Redo the estimates for all five walkthroughs on paper 1 M/day is about 12/s; multiply by a peak factor. 2 easy base62 encode and decode with round-trip asserts Divide by 62 repeatedly; decode multiplies and adds. 3* medium Present the loan-origination design aloud in 45 minutes Follow the method table; keep a timer visible. 4 medium Hybrid token-leasing rate limiter in one process Central TokenBucket::try_acquire(20) per lease; local counters spend it. 5 hard Design an exactly-once-per-business-date batch scheduler Exactly-once effect = lease + idempotent job keyed by (job, business date). 6* hard Turn the Raft simulation into a replicated KV store with client dedupe State machine keeps last request id per client; skip duplicates on apply.

docs.title: 08. Networking and Distributed Systems: interview questions
docs.text: 38 questions with model answers, ordered from basic to senior. Answer out loud in 30 to 90 seconds each. The module in brackets has the depth behind the answer.

docs.title: Part A: TCP/IP and sockets
docs.text:
1. What happens in the TCP three-way handshake, and why three messages? [02] The client sends SYN with its initial sequence number; the server replies SYN-ACK with its own ISN and acknowledges the client's; the client ACKs the server's ISN. Three messages are the minimum for both sides to choose a sequence number and confirm the other received it. The server's half-open connections wait in the SYN queue; completed ones wait in the accept queue until accept().

2. What does "TCP is a byte stream" mean for application code? [02, 04] TCP preserves the order and content of bytes, not the boundaries of your send calls. One send can arrive as several recvs and several sends can arrive in one recv. The application must frame messages itself (length prefix or delimiter) and keep a buffer that accumulates bytes until a complete message is present.

3. Length-prefix or delimiter framing: how do you choose? [04] Length prefix makes the receiver know exactly how many bytes to wait for, handles binary payloads, and never scans the body; it needs a maximum length check to stop a hostile 4 GB prefix. Delimiters (like \r\n) are human-readable and easy to debug with nc but need escaping or a length for binary data and require scanning. Text protocols often mix both, as Redis and tcpkv do ($len).

4. recv returned fewer bytes than you asked for. Bug? [03] No, it is normal: recv returns whatever is in the socket buffer, at least one byte. Loop until you have the bytes the frame needs (read_exact), treat 0 as orderly close by the peer, retry on EINTR, and on non-blocking sockets stop on EAGAIN and wait for readiness. The same applies to send: it may write only part of the buffer, so loop (write_all).

5. What are TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT, and what does a pile of each mean? [02] TIME_WAIT is held by the side that closed first, for twice the maximum segment lifetime (60 s on Linux), so late duplicates of the old connection cannot corrupt a new one with the same port pair and the final ACK can be resent. Thousands of them are normal on a busy client and can exhaust ephemeral ports. CLOSE_WAIT means the peer closed and your program has not called close: a pile of them is a file descriptor leak in your code.

6. Why does a server set SO_REUSEADDR? [03] So it can bind its listening port again immediately after a restart while old connections on that port are still in TIME_WAIT. Without it, bind fails with EADDRINUSE for up to a minute. SO_REUSEPORT is different: it lets several sockets listen on the same port and the kernel spreads incoming connections among them.

7. What are Nagle's algorithm and delayed ACKs, and when do you set TCP_NODELAY? [02] Nagle holds small writes while unacknowledged data is in flight, to coalesce them; delayed ACK holds ACKs briefly hoping to piggyback them. Together, a write-write-read pattern can stall for tens of milliseconds. Request/response protocols with small messages set TCP_NODELAY and, better, write each message with a single send.

8. How do you detect a dead peer on an idle TCP connection? [02, 09] TCP sends nothing on an idle connection, so a crashed peer or a dropped NAT mapping goes unnoticed until you write. Use TCP keepalive with short, tuned intervals (TCP_KEEPIDLE, TCP_KEEPINTVL, TCP_KEEPCNT) or, better, application-level heartbeats with a read timeout, which also detect a hung peer process.

9. Why ignore SIGPIPE in a server? [03] Writing to a socket whose peer has reset the connection raises SIGPIPE, whose default action kills the process. Ignore it (or use MSG_NOSIGNAL) and handle the EPIPE error from send by closing that connection.

docs.title: Part B: Server concurrency models
docs.text:
10. Thread-per-connection versus a thread pool versus an event loop? [05, 06] Thread-per-connection is simple but each thread costs memory and scheduling, so it falls over in the thousands of connections. A pool bounds threads but a blocking read on an idle connection still pins a worker. An event loop (epoll) handles many connections per thread by doing only non-blocking I/O when the kernel says a socket is ready; it needs per-connection state machines and must never block, so slow work goes to a separate pool.

11. epoll level-triggered versus edge-triggered? [06] Level-triggered reports a socket as long as it is readable, so reading part of the data is fine; the next epoll_wait reports it again. Edge-triggered reports only when the state changes (new data arrived), so you must read until EAGAIN or you will never be told about the remaining bytes. ET saves wakeups under load and requires non-blocking sockets and careful drain loops.

12. Reactor versus proactor? [06] A reactor tells you when an operation can be done without blocking, and you then do the read or write yourself: epoll, kqueue, poll, libuv on Unix, Asio on Linux. A proactor performs the operation for you and tells you when it has completed: Windows IOCP and Linux io_uring. Asio presents a proactor-style API on top of either.

13. Why must an event-loop thread never block, and how do you run slow work? [06] Every connection on that loop waits while one handler blocks, so latency for all of them jumps. Hand slow work (database calls, CPU-heavy parsing) to a worker pool, and have the worker post the result back to the loop through a queue plus an eventfd wake-up so the reply is written on the loop thread.

14. What is the C10K problem and what solved it? [05, 06] Handling ten thousand concurrent connections on one server, which thread-per-connection and select (O(n) scanning, fd limit 1024) could not do efficiently. Readiness APIs with O(ready) cost (epoll, kqueue, IOCP), non-blocking I/O and event loops solved it; today the question is millions of connections, addressed with the same design plus kernel tuning.

docs.title: Part C: RPC and HTTP
docs.text:
15. What does an RPC framework do for you? [07] It turns a typed function call into bytes and back: the stub serialises arguments, the transport frames and sends them with a request id, the server dispatches by method id, runs the handler and returns a status and result with the same id. It also handles deadlines, errors, versioning and often connection management. gRPC does this over HTTP/2 with protobuf.

16. Why do RPC messages carry a request id? [07] To match replies to requests when several calls are outstanding on one connection or replies come back out of order. After a timeout, you either reserve that id forever or close the connection, so a late reply cannot be matched to a newer request.

17. A call timed out. Should the client retry? [07, 09] Only if the operation is idempotent or carries an idempotency key, because a timeout is an unknown outcome: the server may have done the work. Retry only transient errors, with capped attempts, exponential backoff with full jitter, a retry budget, and at one layer of the stack only.

18. How do you make a non-idempotent operation safe to retry? [07, 10] The client attaches a unique idempotency key per logical operation (for example branch code plus branch transaction number). The server stores the key with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect, and a repeat returns the stored result instead of applying it again.

19. What is HTTP keep-alive and why does it matter? [08] HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default: many requests reuse one TCP connection, avoiding a handshake, TLS negotiation and slow start per request. The server must know where each request body ends (Content-Length or chunked encoding) and should have an idle timeout. HTTP/1.1 still serves one request at a time per connection; HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams on one connection.

20. When would you choose HTTP/REST and when a custom binary RPC over TCP? [07, 08] HTTP/REST for external and cross-team APIs: universal tooling, proxies, caches, browsers, easy debugging. A binary RPC (or gRPC) for internal, high-rate, low-latency calls with typed schemas. A hand-rolled binary protocol is justified only when you control both ends and need the last bit of performance or have a legacy client base, and then it needs versioning and framing discipline.

docs.title: Part D: Reliability
docs.text:
21. Explain exponential backoff with jitter. [09] After each failure wait longer (base times 2 to the attempt, capped), and randomise the wait (full jitter: uniform between 0 and that value) so that many clients that failed together do not retry together and recreate the overload. Combine with a retry budget to cap the extra load.

22. What is a circuit breaker? [09] A per-dependency state machine: closed passes calls and counts failures; when failures cross a threshold it opens and fails calls immediately; after a cool-down it goes half-open and lets a trial call through, closing on success. It saves threads from waiting on a dead dependency and stops failures cascading.

23. How does a token bucket rate limiter work? [09] A bucket of capacity C refills at R tokens per second; each request takes a token or is rejected when empty. C is the burst allowance and R the sustained rate. Implement lazily: on each call add elapsed time times R, capped at C, then try to take a token.

docs.title: Part E: Distributed systems
docs.text:
24. State the CAP theorem correctly. [10] During a network partition a replicated system must choose between linearizable consistency and availability of every non-failed node. Partitions happen regardless, so the choice is how to behave during one: refuse requests on the minority side (CP, like YugabyteDB or etcd) or answer with possibly stale or conflicting data (AP, like Cassandra).

25. What does PACELC add to CAP? [10] Even without a partition there is a trade-off between latency and consistency, because strongly consistent writes wait for a quorum. YugabyteDB and Spanner are PC/EC; Cassandra is PA/EL.

26. Explain linearizable, sequential, causal and eventual consistency with an example. [10] Linearizable: a deposit confirmed at 10:00:00 is visible to any reader anywhere at 10:00:01. Sequential: everyone sees the same order consistent with each client's own order, but it can lag real time. Causal: if "rent paid" was written after seeing "salary credited", nobody sees the first without the second; unrelated writes may appear in different orders. Eventual: replicas converge once writes stop, like DNS after a change.

27. Why can't you order events across machines by wall-clock time? What do you use? [10] Clocks drift and are corrected imperfectly; NTP is typically millisecond-accurate on a LAN and can step backwards, so a later event can carry an earlier timestamp. Use Lamport or vector clocks for causality, or hybrid logical clocks, which respect causality and stay close to physical time; YugabyteDB and CockroachDB timestamp transactions with HLCs.

28. What is split brain and how do you prevent it? [10] Two nodes both believe they are the leader and accept writes, so data diverges. Prevent it with majority quorums (two majorities cannot coexist), fencing tokens such as Raft terms that let downstream reject a stale leader, STONITH, and leases. Never build a two-node cluster without a third vote.

29. Is exactly-once delivery possible? [10] Not over an unreliable network with failures, because the sender can never know whether its last attempt was processed. Systems give exactly-once effect: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing or deduplication committed atomically with the side effect.

docs.title: Part F: Consensus, sharding, distributed SQL
docs.text:
30. Explain Raft leader election. [11] Followers wait for heartbeats; one whose randomised election timeout expires increments the term, votes for itself and requests votes. Each node votes once per term, persisted, and only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. A majority makes a leader, which immediately sends heartbeats; split votes are retried with new random timeouts.

31. How does Raft replicate and commit a log entry? [11] The leader appends the entry and sends AppendEntries with the previous index and term; a follower accepts only if its log matches at that point, otherwise the leader backs up and retries, and the follower truncates conflicts. Once a current-term entry is stored on a majority, the leader advances the commit index, applies it and replies; followers apply up to the commit index they learn from later messages.

32. Why does YugabyteDB use Raft per tablet when PostgreSQL uses streaming replication? [11] PostgreSQL has one writable primary and ships WAL to standbys, leaving leader election and fencing to external tools like Patroni with etcd. YugabyteDB shards tables into tablets led by different nodes, so each tablet needs its own automatic, safe leader election and majority-acknowledged replication; that is a Raft group per tablet, and its Raft log is the tablet's WAL.

33. Hash versus range sharding, and how do you pick a shard key? [12] Hash spreads load evenly and avoids hot tails for sequential keys but makes range scans scatter; range keeps order for cheap scans but monotonic keys hit one shard. Pick the key from the hot access path and cardinality: for banking, hash on account number with transaction time as a range component inside the account, hash sequence-generated numbers, never shard only on a skewed code like branch, and colocate small reference tables.

34. How does consistent hashing work and why use virtual nodes? [12] Nodes and keys hash onto a ring, and each key belongs to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys instead of nearly all with hash % N. Virtual nodes give each server many ring positions, which evens out load and spreads a failed node's keys across many survivors.

35. Explain two-phase commit and how distributed SQL avoids its blocking problem. [12] The coordinator asks every participant to prepare (persist the writes, hold locks, vote); if all vote yes it records commit and tells them, otherwise abort. If the coordinator dies after the votes, participants are stuck holding locks. YugabyteDB records the decision as one Raft-replicated write to a transaction status tablet, with the writes held as replicated intents, so the decision survives any single node failure and readers can resolve intents by looking it up.

docs.title: Part G: High availability and design
docs.text:
36. Define SLO, RTO and RPO, and how replication choices affect RPO. [13] An SLO is the internal target for a user-facing indicator, like 99.9% of postings succeeding within 500 ms over 30 days (43.2 minutes of error budget). RTO is the allowed downtime after a failure; RPO is the allowed data loss, measured in time. Quorum or synchronous replication gives RPO 0; async replication gives RPO equal to the lag; backups alone give RPO equal to the backup interval.

37. What happens when one node of a three-node, RF3 YugabyteDB cluster dies? [13] Tablets it led elect new leaders among their two surviving peers once the leader lease expires, so their writes pause for a few seconds; other tablets just lose a follower. Nothing committed is lost, because every commit was on a majority. The cluster is under-replicated until the node returns or replicas are re-created elsewhere, which needs a spare node.

38. How would you describe a zero-downtime cutover to a new database? [13] Bulk-load while the old system serves, catch up deltas through a change log or timestamps, verify with a field-level parity check as a go/no-go gate, quiesce briefly for the final delta, flip the application's configuration with rolling restarts, keep a rehearsed rollback path with a defined point of no return, and monitor closely afterwards. Use your real numbers for deployments, window length and mismatches found.

docs.title: 09. OOP, Design Patterns and Software Architecture in Modern C++
What this course covers
docs.text:
You already design software. You do it in C: structs that hold state, functions that act on them, function-pointer tables when you need to swap behaviour, and a head full of rules about who free()s what. This course teaches the same job in C++17, with names for the things you already do and tools you do not yet have.

Three layers, in order:

  1. OOP as a tool, not a religion. Classes, invariants, interfaces, virtual dispatch. What each buys you, what each costs (in bytes, cycles, compile time and readability), and when a plain function or a template is the better design.
  2. Design patterns, each shown three ways. The classic class-hierarchy form, the modern C++17 form (std::function, std::variant, templates, value semantics), and the C form you already know (a struct of function pointers, a switch on an enum, a void* context). Patterns click when you see that you have been writing them for 2.5 years.
  3. Architecture. Ownership design, layered server codebases, API design, refactoring legacy C business logic into modules, and the low-level-design (LLD) interview round where you are asked to design a parking lot or a rate limiter on a whiteboard.

Everything targets g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread on WSL Ubuntu 24.04.

docs.title: Why it is on the resume
docs.text:
Your resume says you re-engineered legacy C business logic into a modular layer, that you understand "OOP, design patterns, memory and ownership design", and that you maintain a client-server application server. Interviewers for senior C++ roles will probe all three:

  • "Why did you choose a virtual interface here instead of a template?"
  • "Who owns the connection object? What happens if the client disconnects mid-request?"
  • "Design an LRU cache with TTL. Now make it thread-safe. Now make it testable."

This course is the preparation for those conversations and for the LLD round, which many companies run as a separate 45 to 60 minute interview.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• C at a professional level (you have it).
  • 02_Modern_CPP through classes, constructors, destructors, references and const. Modules here assume you can read a class definition and a range-for loop.
  • 02_Modern_CPP module 05 (at least unique_ptr and shared_ptr basics). Module 03 of this course builds on it.
  • 04_Concurrency for Module 07 (mutex, condition_variable, threads). You can read Module 07 later if you are doing the courses in parallel.

docs.title: 01. OOP for a C Programmer
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: none (C fluency; classes and references from 02_Modern_CPP)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
You already do object-oriented programming. Every time you write a struct that holds state, a set of functions that take a pointer to that struct as the first argument, and a table of function pointers so that callers can swap one implementation for another, you are writing objects, methods and interfaces. C just does not give you a name or a compiler check for any of it.

C++ takes those three habits and makes the compiler enforce them. A class is a struct whose fields you can hide. A member function is a function whose first argument (this) is passed for you. A virtual function is a slot in a function-pointer table that the compiler builds, fills and calls on your behalf, with type checking at every step. That is the whole mechanism. The rest of OOP is a set of design habits about when to use it.

The analogy that works for most C programmers: a class is a .c file with a static state struct and a public .h. The .h is the public section, the .c internals are private, and the compiler now refuses to let other files reach inside. The difference is that you can have many instances of that .c file alive at once, each with its own state.

docs.title: 2.1 From struct + functions to class
docs.text:
/* C */
struct ring_buffer { char* buf; size_t cap, head, tail; };
int  rb_init(struct ring_buffer* rb, size_t cap);
int  rb_push(struct ring_buffer* rb, char c);
int  rb_pop(struct ring_buffer* rb, char* out);
void rb_destroy(struct ring_buffer* rb);

// C++
class RingBuffer {
public:
    explicit RingBuffer(std::size_t cap);     // rb_init, but cannot be forgotten
    ~RingBuffer();                            // rb_destroy, called automatically
    bool push(char c);                        // rb_push; 'this' is the hidden first argument
    std::optional<char> pop();                // rb_pop; return value instead of out-parameter
private:
    char* buf_; std::size_t cap_, head_, tail_;
};

Three concrete gains:

  1. Construction and destruction cannot be skipped. rb_init is a convention; a constructor is a rule. There is no window where a RingBuffer exists but is not initialised, and no path (including exceptions and early returns) where the destructor is not run. This is RAII: Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation. It is the single biggest reason C++ code has fewer leaks than C code of the same size.
  2. The invariant has a boundary. "head_ < cap_ and tail_ < cap_" is enforced by the handful of member functions. In C, any function in any file can write rb->head = 99.
  3. const is enforced for the whole object. std::optional<char> peek() const promises not to mutate; the compiler checks the promise.

docs.title: 2.2 From function-pointer tables to virtual functions
docs.text:
In your RPC server you probably have something like:

struct handler_ops {
    int  (*parse)(void* ctx, const char* buf, size_t len);
    int  (*execute)(void* ctx);
    void (*free)(void* ctx);
};
struct handler { const struct handler_ops* ops; void* ctx; };

That is a vtable and a vptr, hand-made. ops is the vtable: one shared table per implementation. ctx is the object. Every implementation fills its own handler_ops.

In C++:

class Handler {
public:
    virtual ~Handler() = default;
    virtual bool parse(std::string_view bytes) = 0;    // "= 0": pure virtual, must be overridden
    virtual int  execute() = 0;
};
class BalanceEnquiry : public Handler { /* overrides */ };

The compiler emits one vtable per class that has virtual functions and plants a hidden vptr as the first member of every object. h->execute() compiles to roughly:

mov  rax, [rdi]        ; load vptr from object
call [rax + 16]        ; call slot 2 (after dtor slots) -- indirect call

Exactly what h->ops->execute(h->ctx) compiles to in C. The difference: you cannot forget to fill a slot, cannot put the wrong signature in a slot, cannot pass the wrong ctx, and delete h runs the right destructor.

Vocabulary you need to say correctly in interviews:

  • Polymorphism: calling execute() on a Handler& and getting the derived behaviour. Runtime (dynamic) polymorphism uses virtual functions. Compile-time (static) polymorphism uses templates (Section 2.5 and Module 08).
  • Override vs overload: override replaces a virtual function in a derived class; overloading is several functions with the same name and different parameters. Always write the override keyword; it turns a silent signature mismatch into a compile error.
  • Abstract class: has at least one pure virtual function; cannot be instantiated.
  • Interface: an abstract class with only pure virtual functions and a virtual destructor. C++ has no interface keyword; it is a convention.
  • final: on a class, forbids deriving; on a function, forbids overriding further. Lets the compiler devirtualise calls when it knows the exact type.

docs.title: 2.3 Encapsulation and invariants
docs.text:
An invariant is a statement about an object's state that is true between operations. "Balance equals the sum of the ledger." "size_ <= capacity_." "fd_ is either -1 or an open socket."

Encapsulation is not about hiding data for secrecy. It is about shrinking the amount of code that can break an invariant to the member functions of one class, which you can read in one sitting. When a RingBuffer is corrupt, you have 6 functions to read, not 600.

Rules of thumb:

  • Make every data member private unless the type is a plain aggregate (a struct Point { double x, y; } with no invariant should stay a public struct).
  • A getter and setter pair for every field is not encapsulation; it is a struct with extra steps. Expose operations (withdraw, deposit), not fields.
  • const member functions are part of the interface contract. Mark everything that does not mutate.

docs.title: 2.4 What OOP buys you and what it costs
docs.text:
Feature Buys Costs Constructors / destructors (RAII) No leaks, no uninitialised objects, exception safety Almost nothing. Use everywhere. Private members Invariants are enforceable, code is locally reasonable Slightly more typing. Use everywhere there is an invariant. Virtual functions Swap implementations at runtime; plug-in points; test doubles 8 bytes per object (vptr), one indirect call (typically 1 to 5 ns when predicted, 20+ ns on a mispredict), no inlining across the call, heap allocation usually needed to hold "some derived type" Deep inheritance hierarchies Code reuse through base classes Fragile base class problem: a change in the base silently changes every derived class. Hard to test. Prefer composition. Everything-is-an-object style (Java-like) Familiar to Java/C# developers Heap churn, pointer chasing, poor cache behaviour, verbosity. Not idiomatic C++.

The honest summary a senior engineer gives: RAII and encapsulation are almost free and almost always right. Virtual dispatch is a runtime decision mechanism; use it where you need a decision at runtime. Inheritance for code reuse is usually a mistake; use composition.

docs.title: 2.5 When procedural or generic code is better
docs.text:
Three cases where you should not reach for a class hierarchy:

  1. Pure computation over plain data. Parsing an ISO 8583 message, computing an EMI, hashing a key. A free function over a struct is simpler, testable and inlinable. C++ is a multi-paradigm language; "free functions are first-class design tools" is an idiom.
  2. The set of types is fixed and known at compile time. If a request is one of five message types and that list changes once a year, std::variant<A, B, C, D, E> with std::visit gives you exhaustiveness checking (the compiler tells you when you forgot a case) and no heap allocation. Module 06 and Module 08 cover this.
  3. Hot loops where the operation is known at the call site. std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), cmp) with a lambda inlines the comparator; a virtual bool less(a, b) would not. Templates win when performance matters and the type is known when you compile.

The decision question: "Does the choice need to be made at runtime, by configuration or by the client, and is the set of choices open-ended?" Yes to both: virtual interface. No to either: consider templates, std::variant or plain functions first.

docs.title: code/m01_struct_fnptr_vs_virtual.cpp
docs.text:
The same Store abstraction three ways: C struct of function pointers with void* state, C++ virtual interface, and template. Key parts:

// C style: the table and the object are separate things you wire by hand.
struct store_ops {
    int (*put)(void* self, const char* key, const char* value);
    const char* (*get)(void* self, const char* key);
    void (*destroy)(void* self);
};
struct store { const store_ops* ops; void* state; };

// C++: the compiler builds the table, plants the pointer, checks every slot.
class Store {
public:
    virtual ~Store() = default;
    virtual bool put(const std::string& key, const std::string& value) = 0;
    virtual std::optional<std::string> get(const std::string& key) const = 0;
};
class MapStore final : public Store { /* overrides */ };

// Template: the "interface" is whatever exercise<T> calls. No table, no indirect call.
template <class StoreT>
void exercise(StoreT& s) { s.put("acct:1001", "balance=500"); /* ... */ }

Run it and compare sizeof the two MapStore classes: the virtual one is 8 bytes larger on x86-64. That is the vptr.

docs.title: code/m01_invariant_class.cpp
docs.text:
An Account whose balance can never go negative and whose ledger always sums to the balance, an AccountRepository interface, and a transfer() function written against the interface. Note the pattern: the business function depends on an abstract repository, so it can be unit tested with InMemoryAccountRepository and deployed with a database-backed one.

bool transfer(AccountRepository& repo, const std::string& from, const std::string& to,
              Account::Paise amount) {
    Account* src = repo.find(from);     // observer pointer: the repo still owns the object
    Account* dst = repo.find(to);
    if (!src || !dst) return false;
    if (!src->withdraw(amount)) return false;   // invariant protected inside Account
    dst->deposit(amount);
    repo.save(*src); repo.save(*dst);
    return true;
}

One deliberate weakness to notice: find() returns a pointer into a std::vector, and save() could push_back. If save of a new account ran between find and use, the pointer would dangle. Module 03 is about designing so that this cannot happen.

docs.title: Object layout
docs.text:
class Base { virtual void f(); int a; };
class Derived : public Base { int b; void f() override; };

Derived object (x86-64, GCC):            vtable for Derived (read-only data segment):
+0   vptr  --------------------------->  [ offset_to_top = 0      ]
+8   a                                   [ typeinfo* for Derived  ]
+12  b                                   [ &Derived::~Derived (complete) ]
+16  (end; sizeof == 16)                 [ &Derived::~Derived (deleting) ]
                                         [ &Derived::f            ]   <- vptr points here

The vptr points into the table at the first function slot; the two words before it hold the offset-to-top (used for multiple inheritance casts) and the RTTI pointer (used by dynamic_cast and typeid). This is the Itanium C++ ABI, which GCC, Clang and most Unix compilers follow. MSVC's layout differs in details but has the same shape.

A pure virtual slot holds the address of __cxa_pure_virtual, which aborts. That is the "pure virtual function called" crash you can get if a virtual function is invoked from a base class constructor or destructor while the object is still only partly constructed.

docs.title: Cost of a virtual call, precisely
docs.text:
1. Load vptr from the object (1 memory read, usually L1 hit if the object is hot).
  2. Load the function address from the vtable slot (1 memory read, vtable is almost always in cache since it is shared by all instances).
  3. Indirect call. Modern CPUs predict indirect branch targets well if the same call site keeps hitting the same target; a monomorphic call site is nearly free. A call site that alternates between many targets mispredicts, which costs a pipeline flush (typically 15 to 25 cycles on current x86 cores).
  4. Lost optimisation is the real cost: the compiler cannot inline the callee, so it cannot hoist loads, vectorise, or constant-fold across the call. A virtual bool less(int, int) inside std::sort can make the sort 3 to 10 times slower than a lambda; that is the inlining difference, not the indirect call itself.

GCC can devirtualise when it proves the dynamic type: a final class, a local object of known type, or whole-program analysis under -O2 -flto. Speculative devirtualisation adds if (vptr == &Derived::vtable) inline_body(); else indirect_call();.

docs.title: Why virtual destructors matter
docs.text: delete base_ptr on a class without a virtual destructor is undefined behaviour if the dynamic type differs. In practice the derived destructor is skipped (leaks) and operator delete may be called with the wrong size (heap corruption on sized deallocation).
