Rule: any class with a virtual function gets a virtual destructor. GCC warns under -Wall (-Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor).

docs.title: Construction order
docs.text: Base constructors run first, then members in declaration order (not initialiser-list order; GCC warns with -Wreorder), then the constructor body. Destruction is the exact reverse. The vptr is set to the Base vtable while the Base constructor runs and switched to Derived when the Derived constructor starts. That is why a virtual call inside a constructor dispatches to the class being constructed, not the final type.

docs.title: What a member function really is
docs.text: bool Account::withdraw(Paise p) is compiled as a free function withdraw(Account* this, Paise p). Member access balance_ is this->balance_. There is no runtime cost to a non-virtual member function compared to a C function taking a struct pointer. The mangled name encodes the class and parameter types, which is how overloading works at link time.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
Where OOP earns its keep in your server. The places where behaviour genuinely varies at runtime: which storage backend (Berkeley DB vs YugabyteDB), which transport (TCP vs a test harness in memory), which authentication scheme, which message codec. An interface at each of those seams is what lets you unit test the business logic without a database, and swap the database without touching the business logic. Your migration engine almost certainly had an implicit "store interface" with two implementations; naming it and making it a class would have let you test the migration logic against a fake.

Where it hurts. Teams coming from Java build AbstractBaseRequestHandlerFactoryImpl hierarchies five levels deep. Every request becomes six heap allocations and a chain of virtual calls. On a hot path handling tens of thousands of RPCs per second, that is measurable. Flat designs win: a struct Request holding plain data, free functions that process it, one interface at the storage boundary.

War story shape: the partially constructed object. A connection class calls start_reading() from its constructor, which registers a callback with the event loop. The event loop fires before the constructor finishes. The callback does a virtual call that lands in the base class version, which is pure, and the process aborts with "pure virtual method called". Fix: two-phase start (construct, then start()), or a factory function that constructs fully and then registers.

3 AM debugging tips. In a crash dump, a corrupted vptr shows up as a jump to a nonsense address or into the middle of unrelated code. Causes: use-after-free (the memory was reused), writing past the end of the previous object in the heap, or a memcpy of a polymorphic object. -fsanitize=address catches all three in test. In WinDbg/gdb, x/4gx obj and check whether the first word points into the .rodata region of your binary; if not, the object is garbage.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Take the C-style store in m01_struct_fnptr_vs_virtual.cpp and add a third function pointer size. Note every place you had to touch. Then add virtual std::size_t size() const = 0; to the C++ Store and see what the compiler forces you to do. Done when both compile and you can list the differences in failure modes (what happens when you forget to fill the slot in each version).
  2. (easy) Convert a small C module you have written (a ring buffer, a string builder, a config parser) into a C++ class with a constructor, destructor and private state. Done when no caller can break its invariant without going through a member function, and -Wall -Wextra -Werror passes.
  3. (medium) Write a Shape hierarchy (Circle, Rect) with virtual double area(), then the same with std::variant<Circle, Rect> and std::visit. Measure sizeof of each and count heap allocations needed to hold 1000 mixed shapes in a container. Done when you can explain which one you would choose for (a) a plug-in system and (b) a fixed set of geometry types.
  4. (medium) In m01_invariant_class.cpp, find() returns a raw pointer that can dangle if save() reallocates. Fix it in two different ways: (a) make save never invalidate (hint: std::map, or std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Account>>), (b) change the interface so that transfer never holds two pointers across a call that may reallocate. Done when you can explain the trade-off of each.
  5. (hard) Write a 20-line benchmark: a vector of 1 million objects, summed via (a) a virtual value() call where the vector holds unique_ptr<Base> with two derived types alternating, (b) the same with all objects the same derived type, (c) a std::variant, (d) a template. Run with -O2. Done when you can explain the ordering of the results in terms of branch prediction, inlining and cache misses (not just "virtual is slow").

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does the compiler generate for a virtual function call? A: It loads the hidden vptr from the object, loads the function address from the vtable slot for that function, and performs an indirect call. The vtable is one read-only table per class; the vptr is one pointer per object. It is the same mechanism as a C struct of function pointers, generated and type-checked by the compiler.

Q: Why must a base class with virtual functions have a virtual destructor? A: So that delete through a base pointer runs the derived destructor and frees the right size. Without it the behaviour is undefined; in practice derived members leak and sized deallocation can corrupt the heap.

Q: What is the real cost of virtual dispatch? A: Two dependent loads and an indirect call, which is cheap if predicted. The larger cost is that the compiler cannot inline across the call, so it loses constant folding, hoisting and vectorisation. On hot paths with a known type, a template or std::variant lets the optimiser see through.

Q: When would you choose templates over virtual functions? A: When the set of types is known at compile time and the choice does not depend on runtime input or configuration; when the call is on a hot path; when you need the callee inlined. Virtual wins when the choice is a runtime decision, when the set of implementations is open (plug-ins), or when you need to store heterogeneous objects behind one pointer type without knowing all types in one translation unit.

Q: What is an invariant and how does encapsulation help? A: An invariant is a condition that must hold between operations on an object. Encapsulation shrinks the set of code that can violate it to the member functions of one class, so you can verify it by reading one file instead of the whole program.

Q: Why is "inheritance for code reuse" discouraged? A: It creates tight coupling: any change in the base class silently changes every derived class, and derived classes depend on base implementation details. Composition (holding a member of the reused type) gives the same reuse with a narrow, explicit interface.

Q: What happens if you call a virtual function from a constructor? A: It dispatches to the version for the class currently being constructed, not the most derived class, because the vptr is updated as each constructor runs. If that version is pure virtual, the program aborts with "pure virtual method called".

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A class is a struct with an enforced boundary; a member function is a free function with a hidden this; a virtual function is a slot in a compiler-built function-pointer table.
  • RAII (constructor acquires, destructor releases) is the main reason C++ leaks less than C. It cannot be skipped by early returns or exceptions.
  • Encapsulation protects invariants by limiting who can break them to one class's members.
  • Virtual dispatch: 8 bytes per object, two loads and an indirect call, and lost inlining. Use it for decisions made at runtime over an open set of implementations.
  • Always virtual ~Base() = default; in a polymorphic base; always write override.
  • Prefer composition over inheritance for reuse; inherit for interfaces.
  • Plain functions over plain structs, std::variant over fixed type sets, and templates for hot known-type code are all legitimate alternatives to class hierarchies.
  • A vptr pointing outside .rodata in a crash dump means the object is already destroyed or overwritten.

docs.title: 02. SOLID in Plain Words
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 01

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
SOLID is five habits that keep a codebase changeable after it has grown past the point where one person holds it all in their head. Each one answers a question you have already asked while maintaining a legacy server:

  • Single Responsibility: "Why does changing the log format break the parser?"
  • Open/Closed: "Why do I have to edit the 2000-line switch every time we add a message type?"
  • Liskov Substitution: "Why does this subclass crash when passed to code that worked with the base?"
  • Interface Segregation: "Why does my test fake have to implement 14 functions to test one?"
  • Dependency Inversion: "Why can't I unit test this without a running database?"

They are not laws. They are the names of forces. A senior engineer knows each one, knows the cost of applying it (more files, more indirection, more concepts), and applies it where change is expected and skips it where it is not.

docs.title: 2.1 S: Single Responsibility Principle
docs.text:
Definition: a class (or module) should have one reason to change.

"Reason to change" means a stakeholder or concern: wire format, business rule, storage schema, logging policy. If the operations team asks for JSON logs and the product team asks for a new fee rule, those two requests should touch different files.

Bad:

class AccountHandler {
public:
    void handle(int fd) {
        char buf[4096]; read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);       // transport
        auto req = parse_iso8583(buf);                   // protocol
        if (req.amount > limits[req.tier]) reject();     // business rule
        PQexec(conn, build_sql(req).c_str());            // storage
        fprintf(logf, "%s %d\n", req.id, req.amount);    // logging
    }
};

Every concern in one function. A change to any of them risks all of them, and nothing here can be tested without a socket and a database.

Good: the layering from Module 09. Transport reads bytes. Codec turns bytes into a Request struct. AccountService applies rules. AccountRepository talks to storage. A Logger is injected. Each is 50 to 200 lines and has one job.

The trap: SRP taken literally produces one class per function. The unit of "responsibility" is a cohesive set of operations over shared state. Account with deposit, withdraw, balance is one responsibility (account bookkeeping), not three.

docs.title: 2.2 O: Open/Closed Principle
docs.text:
Definition: open for extension, closed for modification. Adding a feature should mean adding code, not editing working code.

Bad:

std::string dispatch(const Request& r) {
    switch (r.type) {
        case MsgType::Balance:   return do_balance(r);
        case MsgType::Transfer:  return do_transfer(r);
        case MsgType::Statement: return do_statement(r);
        // every new type: edit here, re-test everything that goes through here
    }
}

Good:

class Operation { public: virtual ~Operation() = default;
                  virtual std::string apply(Store&, const Request&) = 0; };
std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<Operation>> ops;   // register at startup
auto reply = ops.at(r.op)->apply(store, r);              // dispatch never changes

A new operation is a new class plus one register_op line in the composition root.

The honest counterpoint: a switch over an enum has one property the registry does not. With -Wswitch (in -Wall), the compiler tells you every place you forgot to handle the new enum value. For a closed set of types that rarely changes, the switch (or std::variant + std::visit, Module 06) is the better design because exhaustiveness is checked. OCP is for sets you expect to be open: plug-ins, customer-specific rules, message handlers added by other teams.

docs.title: 2.3 L: Liskov Substitution Principle
docs.text:
Definition: if D derives from B, any code that works correctly with a B& must work correctly with a D&. Subtypes may strengthen what they guarantee and weaken what they require, never the reverse.

Bad (the classic):

class Store { public: virtual void put(key, value) = 0; /* ... */ };
class ReadOnlyStore : public Store {
    void put(key, value) override { throw std::logic_error("read-only"); }  // breaks every caller
};

Every function that takes a Store& and calls put was correct until a ReadOnlyStore was passed. The type system said yes and the runtime said no. Other violations: an override that ignores a parameter, an override that requires a stricter precondition ("key must be non-empty" when the base allowed empty), an override that leaves the object in a state the base's other functions do not expect.

Good: model the difference in the type system. class ReadableStore { get } and `class Store public ReadableStore { put }. Code that only reads takes aReadableStore&, and a read-only backend simply does not implementStore`.

In C you had the same problem in a different costume: a function-pointer slot set to NULL for "not supported", and every caller having to check. LSP says: do not put the slot in the table if some implementations cannot fill it.

The const angle: a const member function in the base is a promise that overrides must keep. An override that mutates through const_cast violates LSP.

docs.title: 2.4 I: Interface Segregation Principle
docs.text:
Definition: clients should not be forced to depend on functions they do not use. Prefer several small interfaces to one large one.

Bad:

class Connection {
public:
    virtual void send(bytes) = 0;      virtual bytes recv() = 0;
    virtual void set_tls(cert) = 0;    virtual Stats stats() = 0;
    virtual void set_keepalive(int) = 0; virtual void close() = 0;
    // ... 9 more
};

Your test fake must implement 15 functions to test a codec that only calls send and recv. Every change to the big interface recompiles every implementor and every user.

Good: class ByteSink { send }, class ByteSource { recv }, class Configurable { set_tls, set_keepalive }. A real socket implements all three; the codec depends on ByteSink and ByteSource; the fake implements two functions.

The cost: more types to name and understand. Apply ISP where you have multiple different clients of an interface or where you need test doubles. A single-user interface can be as large as its single user needs.

docs.title: 2.5 D: Dependency Inversion Principle
docs.text:
Definition: high-level modules (business rules) must not depend on low-level modules (database, sockets, files). Both depend on abstractions. The abstraction is owned by the high-level side: the business layer declares what it needs (AccountRepository), and the database layer implements it.

Bad:

#include <libpq-fe.h>
class LoanService {
    PGconn* conn_;                                   // business logic knows Postgres
public:
    LoanService() { conn_ = PQconnectdb(getenv("DB")); }   // creates its own dependency
    bool approve(LoanId id) { PQexec(conn_, "..."); }
};

You cannot test approve without Postgres. You cannot run two LoanServices against two databases. Changing the database means editing business code.

Good, with constructor injection:

class LoanRepository {           // declared next to LoanService, in the business layer
public:
    virtual ~LoanRepository() = default;
    virtual std::optional<Loan> find(LoanId) = 0;
    virtual void save(const Loan&) = 0;
};

class LoanService {
public:
    explicit LoanService(LoanRepository& repo, Clock& clock) : repo_(repo), clock_(clock) {}
    bool approve(LoanId id);     // uses repo_ and clock_, knows nothing concrete
private:
    LoanRepository& repo_;
    Clock& clock_;
};

// composition root (main or wire()): the only file that knows the concrete types
PgLoanRepository pg(conn_string);
SystemClock clock;
LoanService svc(pg, clock);

In tests: FakeLoanRepository fake; FixedClock clock{2026-10-03}; LoanService svc(fake, clock);. Now approve is tested in microseconds with no I/O.

Why a reference and not shared_ptr? The composition root owns the concrete objects and guarantees they outlive the service. A reference says exactly that. shared_ptr would say "ownership is shared and unclear", which is false here (Module 03).

Why Clock? Anything that makes code non-deterministic (time, randomness, environment variables, network) should be injected so tests can control it. Time is the most common one in banking code: interest accrual, due dates, cut-off times.

docs.title: 2.6 How SOLID maps onto a server codebase
docs.text:
+------------------+   depends on   +-------------------+
  |  transport/      | -------------> |  protocol/        |     (S: each dir = one concern)
  |  TcpListener     |                |  Codec, Request   |
  +------------------+                +-------------------+
                                               |
                                               v
                                      +-------------------+
                                      |  service/         |   declares the interfaces
                                      |  KvService        |   it needs (D):
                                      |  LoanService      |   Store, Clock, Logger
                                      +-------------------+
                                               ^  implements
                                               |
                                      +-------------------+
                                      |  storage/         |   (O: new backend = new file)
                                      |  PgStore, BdbStore|
                                      +-------------------+

Arrows point inward to the service layer. Nothing in service/ includes anything from storage/ or transport/. Module 09 makes this a full directory layout.

docs.title: 2.7 The over-engineering warning
docs.text:
SOLID applied everywhere produces a codebase where every concrete class has an interface, every object is created by a factory, and reading one request path means opening twelve files. That is as unmaintainable as the 2000-line switch, just differently.

Rules for restraint:

  • An interface with exactly one implementation and no test double is probably not needed yet. Add it when the second implementation or the first test arrives (the refactor is cheap).
  • Inject the boundaries (storage, transport, time, external services). Do not inject a StringFormatter.
  • A value type (Money, AccountId, Request) does not need an interface. Interfaces are for behaviour with side effects that varies.
  • If you cannot name a second plausible implementation in ten seconds, do not abstract.

docs.title: code/m02_solid_di.cpp
docs.text:
A minimal key-value service that respects all five principles, plus the test wiring that shows why it matters.

// D: the service receives its dependencies; it does not create them.
class KvService {
public:
    KvService(Store& store, Logger& log) : store_(store), log_(log) {}
    void register_op(std::string name, std::unique_ptr<Operation> op);  // O: extend by adding
    std::string handle(std::string_view line);
private:
    Store& store_;  Logger& log_;  RequestParser parser_;           // S: parsing lives elsewhere
    std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<Operation>> ops_;
};

// I: Logger is one function. Flushable is a separate optional capability.
class Logger    { public: virtual ~Logger() = default; virtual void info(std::string_view) = 0; };
class Flushable { public: virtual ~Flushable() = default; virtual void flush() = 0; };
class StdoutLogger final : public Logger, public Flushable { /* ... */ };

// L: WriteThroughCache IS-A Store and keeps the contract "after put(k,v), get(k)==v".
// The commented-out alternative, a ReadOnlyStore whose put() throws, would not.

// Composition root: the only place that knows concrete types.
InMemoryStore backing;  WriteThroughCache cache(backing);  StdoutLogger logger;
KvService svc(cache, logger);
svc.register_op("GET", std::make_unique<GetOp>());

The test wiring at the end swaps in RecordingLogger and asserts on captured lines. No socket, no database, no stdout.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What dependency inversion costs at the machine level. Each injected interface is a virtual call at the boundary. For boundaries that are already expensive (a database round trip is 100 microseconds or more; a syscall is at least a microsecond) the virtual call (nanoseconds) is noise. That is exactly why DIP is applied at I/O boundaries and not between two tight inner functions: the abstraction cost is proportionally invisible there.

Why abstractions belong to the high-level side. If storage/ defined Store and service/ included storage/store.h, then service/ depends on storage/ at compile time: a change to anything in that header recompiles the service. When service/ owns the header, storage/ includes it and the dependency arrow points the right way. In build terms: the service library has no link dependency on libpq; only the storage library and the executable do. You can see this in a CMakeLists.txt: target_link_libraries(service ...) should never list a database driver.

OCP and link-time behaviour. A registry of operations populated at startup means the linker cannot know which Operation subclasses are used; it keeps all of them. A switch lets the compiler and linker drop dead code and inline small cases. For embedded or size-constrained builds this matters; for a server it does not.

LSP and the compiler. The compiler cannot check LSP; it is a semantic contract. Tools that help: override (signature match), final (prevents further breaking), and contract tests: a single test suite parameterised over every implementation of an interface, asserting the interface's documented behaviour. If WriteThroughCache and PgStore both pass the same StoreContractTest, they are substitutable in practice.

ISP and recompilation. Changing a virtual function signature changes the vtable layout, which changes the offsets compiled into every call site. Every translation unit that calls through the interface must be recompiled, and if the interface is in a shared library, every client binary must be rebuilt (ABI break). Small interfaces change less often and break fewer clients. Module 05 (pimpl) and Module 10 (versioning) continue this.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
Your stored-procedure re-engineering project is a DIP story. Business logic in PL/pgSQL procedures is business logic that depends on the database. Pulling it into a C or C++ layer that talks to the database through a repository interface is dependency inversion: the rules no longer know whether they run against Berkeley DB, YugabyteDB or an in-memory fake. When you tell this story in an interview, use the words: "the business rules were coupled to the storage engine; I introduced a repository boundary so the rules could be tested independently and the backend could change." Module 09 Section 5 gives the full narrative.

The 3 AM version of each principle.

  • SRP violated: a change to log formatting shipped on Friday; on Monday the parser rejects every message with a comma in a field, because the two shared a buffer. You find it by diffing the one giant file.
  • OCP violated: a new message type was added to the switch in four of the five places it needed to go. The fifth is the audit log. Regulators notice three months later.
  • LSP violated: a NullStore used in a staging environment returns success on put and nothing on get. The reconciliation job happily reports zero discrepancies.
  • ISP violated: nobody writes unit tests because every fake is 400 lines. Bugs reach integration test, where each cycle is 40 minutes.
  • DIP violated: the only way to test the interest-calculation fix is against the shared staging database, which someone else is also using. Flaky tests, nobody trusts them.

The anti-pattern to watch for in yourself. Having learned SOLID, engineers go through a phase of abstracting everything. The symptom: IFoo interfaces with one FooImpl each, factories for everything, and no tests actually using the seams. If the seam is not used for a test or a second implementation, it is cost without benefit. Remove it.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) In m02_solid_di.cpp, add a DEL operation without touching KvService. Done when handle("DEL k") returns OK and a subsequent GET k returns NOT_FOUND.
  2. (easy) Write a ReadOnlyStore that throws on put. Pass it to KvService. Observe the failure. Then fix the design: introduce ReadableStore with only get, make Store derive from it, and make GetOp::apply take ReadableStore&. Done when a read-only backend cannot be passed to PutOp at compile time.
  3. (medium) Add a Clock interface with virtual std::int64_t now_ms() = 0; and a TtlStore decorator that expires keys. Write a FixedClock for tests and show a test that advances time without sleep. Done when the test runs in under a millisecond.
  4. (medium) Take one function from your own C codebase that mixes parsing, business rule and storage. Split it on paper into three units and write the interface the business unit needs from storage. Done when you can write a test for the business unit that needs no I/O.
  5. (hard) Write a StoreContractTest function template template <class F> void contract(F make_store) that creates a store via make_store() and asserts the full contract (put-then-get, overwrite, missing key). Run it against InMemoryStore and WriteThroughCache. Done when adding a buggy Store makes the contract test fail with a clear message.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: State the five SOLID principles in one sentence each. A: S: one reason to change per class. O: add behaviour by adding code, not editing it. L: a subtype must be usable wherever its base is, without surprises. I: do not force clients to depend on functions they do not call. D: business logic depends on abstractions it owns, and infrastructure implements them.

Q: How do you implement dependency inversion in C++ without a DI framework? A: Declare an abstract interface in the high-level module, take it by reference or unique_ptr in the constructor of the class that needs it, and wire the concrete object in a composition root (main or a wire() function). No framework is needed; the constructor is the injection point.

Q: Give an example of a Liskov violation and how to fix it. A: A ReadOnlyStore deriving from Store whose put throws. Callers of Store& are now broken by type. Fix: split the interface into ReadableStore and Store, so read-only backends never claim to support put.

Q: When is the Open/Closed principle the wrong choice? A: When the set of variants is closed and small. A switch over an enum or std::visit over a std::variant gives compile-time exhaustiveness checking that a runtime registry cannot. OCP is for open sets: plug-ins, handlers added by other teams.

Q: Why should the interface be declared by the high-level module and not the low-level one? A: So the compile-time and link-time dependency points from infrastructure to business logic, not the reverse. The service library then has no dependency on database drivers, which is what makes it testable and portable.

Q: What does over-applying SOLID look like and how do you avoid it? A: Interfaces with one implementation and no test using them, factories for value types, twelve files per request path. Avoid it by abstracting only at boundaries where you have a second implementation or a test double, and by keeping value types as plain structs.

Q: How does Interface Segregation relate to ABI stability? A: Changing a virtual function changes vtable layout and forces every client to recompile. Small, stable interfaces change less often. For shared libraries, pair ISP with pimpl or a C ABI boundary.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• SOLID names five forces; apply each where change is expected, skip it where it is not.
  • S: split by reason to change (transport, protocol, business, storage, logging).
  • O: registries and interfaces for open sets; switch or std::variant for closed sets.
  • L: subtypes keep the base's contract; model unsupported operations as different types, not as throwing overrides.
  • I: small interfaces, several of them; a test fake should be a few lines.
  • D: business layer declares interfaces, infrastructure implements them, constructor injects them, composition root wires them.
  • Inject the boundaries: storage, transport, time, external services. Not helpers.
  • An abstraction with one implementation and no test is cost without benefit.
  • Your stored-procedure re-engineering is a dependency-inversion story; tell it that way.

docs.title: 03. Ownership and Object Lifetime Design
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01; 02_Modern_CPP module 05 (unique_ptr, shared_ptr basics)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Every object in a running program has exactly one question that must have a clear answer: who is responsible for destroying it, and when? In C you answer this with discipline and comments ("caller frees", "borrowed, do not free"). You already know how that goes at 3 AM: a double free in one place, a leak in another, a use-after-free that only shows up under load.

Ownership design is the practice of answering that question in the type system so the compiler enforces it. std::unique_ptr<T> means "I own this and nobody else does". A plain T& or T* means "I am looking at this, someone else owns it, and they promise it outlives my use". std::shared_ptr<T> means "several of us own it and the last one out turns off the lights", and that is a design statement you should be reluctant to make.

The analogy: in a well-run office every physical key has one person responsible for it. You can lend the key (a reference), but there is never confusion about who returns it at the end of the day. Shared ownership is the key on a hook that everyone uses; eventually nobody knows whether the door was locked.

docs.title: 2.1 The vocabulary
docs.text:
Term Meaning C++ spelling C spelling Owner Responsible for destruction value member, std::unique_ptr<T>, container of values the struct that free()s it Unique ownership Exactly one owner at a time; transferable std::unique_ptr<T>, move semantics "caller takes ownership" comment Shared ownership Several owners; destroyed when last releases std::shared_ptr<T> manual refcount field Observer / borrow Non-owning view, must not outlive owner T&, T*, std::string_view, std::span plain pointer + "do not free" Weak observer Non-owning, can detect that the owner is gone std::weak_ptr<T> generation-checked handle Handle Integer or opaque id resolved by the owner struct ConnId { uint64_t v; } int fd, HANDLE

A lifetime is the span from construction to destruction. A dangling pointer or reference is one whose target's lifetime has ended. Every memory-safety bug in C is a lifetime bug: use before start (uninitialised), use after end (use-after-free), two ends (double free), no end (leak).

docs.title: 2.2 Ownership diagrams
docs.text:
Before writing a class, draw who owns whom. Solid arrows are ownership (unique_ptr or value member), dashed arrows are observation (reference or raw pointer).

   Server
   |-- owns --> Metrics                         (value member, declared first)
   |-- owns --> Listener                        (value member)
   |-- owns --> map<ConnId, unique_ptr<Connection>>
                     |
                     Connection
                     |-- owns --> unique_ptr<Session>     (null until authenticated)
                     |-- owns --> vector<Request>         (values)
                     |-- observes - - -> Metrics&         (Server guarantees lifetime)
                     |-- observes - - -> Store&           (Server guarantees lifetime)

Rules the diagram must satisfy:

  1. It is a tree (or a forest). Every object has exactly one owning path from a root. The roots are main's locals or, rarely, statics.
  2. Every observation arrow points to something whose owner is an ancestor or an earlier-declared sibling. Connection observes Metrics; Metrics is owned by Server, which also owns Connection, and Metrics is declared before the connections map so it is destroyed after. If an observation arrow points to a later sibling or to a descendant of another branch, you have a lifetime risk.
  3. No cycles. If A owns B and B needs to reach A, B gets an observer A& or A*, never a shared_ptr<A>.

Draw this for any class with more than two members holding pointers. It takes two minutes and it finds most lifetime bugs before they are written.

docs.title: 2.3 unique_ptr trees
docs.text:
The default ownership structure for a server, a parser, a UI, anything: a tree of unique_ptrs rooted in one object, usually created in main.

class Server {
    Metrics metrics_;                                            // value: simplest ownership
    std::unique_ptr<Store> store_;                               // unique_ptr because polymorphic
    std::unordered_map<ConnId, std::unique_ptr<Connection>> conns_;  // unique_ptr because
                                                                 // Connection is non-movable
};

When to use a value member vs unique_ptr:

  • Value member when the type is concrete, movable (or never moved), and always present. No heap allocation, no indirection, destroyed automatically.
  • unique_ptr when the member is polymorphic (held through a base class), optional (may be null), non-movable but the container needs to move (a std::vector<Connection> would need Connection to be movable; std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Connection>> does not), or large and rarely present.

Transfer of ownership is a move: std::unique_ptr<Connection> c = acceptor.take_next(); conns_.emplace(id, std::move(c));. The compiler refuses to copy a unique_ptr, so there is no accidental double ownership.

Passing ownership into a function: void adopt(std::unique_ptr<T> t). Caller writes adopt(std::move(t)) and is left with a null pointer; the intent is in the signature.

Passing an object for use without transferring: void process(T& t) or void process(const T& t). Never void process(std::unique_ptr<T>& t) unless the function may reseat the pointer (rare), and never void process(std::shared_ptr<T> t) just to "be safe": it forces every caller into shared ownership and adds an atomic increment per call.

docs.title: 2.4 Shared ownership as a smell
docs.text:
std::shared_ptr is correct when the lifetime of an object is genuinely determined by the last of several independent users, and you cannot know statically which one that will be. Real examples: a cached, immutable configuration snapshot that in-flight requests on several threads are reading while a new one is being installed (Module 07, RCU); an asynchronous operation's completion handler that must keep the connection alive until the callback fires.

It is a smell when it is used because the author could not decide who the owner is. Costs:

  • Two allocations per object (object + control block) unless make_shared; the control block holds two atomic counters.
  • Every copy of the pointer is an atomic increment and decrement, which is a full memory barrier on x86 (lock xadd), roughly 20 cycles uncontended and hundreds under contention from several cores.
  • Cycles leak. A holds shared_ptr<B>, B holds shared_ptr<A>: neither count reaches zero. You need weak_ptr on one side, and now you have to think about which.
  • Destruction happens "somewhere": whichever thread drops the last reference runs the destructor, possibly a thread that should never touch that object's resources.
  • The ownership diagram is no longer a tree; nobody can draw it.

Rule: reach for shared_ptr only after you have tried to draw the tree and proved that no single owner can be identified. In a server, that is usually only the config snapshot and the "keep me alive until my async op completes" case.

docs.title: 2.5 Observer pointers and references
docs.text:
A raw pointer in modern C++ is not a bug. It is the correct spelling for "non-owning, may be null". A reference is "non-owning, never null, cannot be reseated". Use them freely for observation, with one discipline: the observer must not be stored in anything that could outlive the owner.

Safe: a function parameter Store&; a member Metrics& in a Connection owned by the object that owns the Metrics; a local pointer returned by find() used before the next call that could invalidate.

Unsafe: storing a Connection* in a global list of "connections waiting for a reply"; a lambda capturing this and posted to a thread pool; a std::string_view member pointing at a std::string parameter (the string dies at the end of the call).

The invalidation question for every observer: what operations on the owner invalidate this? For a std::vector<T> element pointer: any push_back that reallocates, any erase before it. For a std::map node pointer: only erasing that node. For std::unordered_map: rehash invalidates iterators but not pointers or references to elements (the nodes are stable). std::deque: push_back/push_front keep element references valid but invalidate iterators. Know these for the containers you use.

docs.title: 2.6 Handles vs pointers
docs.text:
A handle is an id that the owner resolves to an object on demand. It is the right tool when an observer must survive across operations that may destroy the target.

struct ConnId { std::uint64_t value; };
Connection* Server::find(ConnId id);   // nullptr if closed

Advantages over a pointer: resolution fails cleanly (nullptr) instead of dereferencing freed memory; handles can cross thread, process and network boundaries; the owner can relocate the object (compact a pool) without updating observers; a handle fits in a log line.

Make the handle hard to reuse by accident: a 64-bit counter never repeats in practice. If you must use a small index (pool slot), pair it with a generation counter that increments every time the slot is reused; find compares generations and rejects stale handles. This is how game engines, kernels (file descriptors plus inode generation) and weak_ptr (the control block's weak count) solve the same problem.

struct SlotHandle { std::uint32_t index; std::uint32_t generation; };

docs.title: 2.7 Lifetimes across threads
docs.text:
A thread is another observer with no synchronised view of your destructor. The three safe patterns:

  1. Structured lifetime: the owner starts the thread and joins it in the owner's destructor, so the thread cannot outlive the objects it uses. std::thread members declared last in the class so they are destroyed (joined) first.
  2. Message passing with values: the thread receives copies or moved values (a Request by value, a std::string, a std::shared_ptr<const Config> snapshot), never a reference to something owned by another thread.
  3. Keep-alive: an async operation holds a shared_ptr to its object until it completes (enable_shared_from_this, the Asio idiom). This is one of the legitimate shared_ptr uses. The cost is that the object's destruction time becomes non-deterministic.

The anti-pattern: thread_pool.post([this] { this->on_timer(); }) followed by delete this (or the owner destroying the object) before the task runs. Module 06 (observer) and 07 cover this bug in detail because it is the most common crash in event-driven servers.

docs.title: 2.8 Object pools and arenas
docs.text:
Allocation is not free: malloc for small sizes is around 20 to 50 ns on glibc with a warm thread cache, more with contention or fragmentation, and every allocation is a potential cache miss on access. Two patterns to control it:

Object pool: pre-construct N objects, lend them out, take them back. Bounded memory, no fragmentation, warm cache lines. Use a unique_ptr with a custom deleter that returns the object, so a forgotten return is impossible. Exhaustion becomes explicit back-pressure (return nullopt, or block with a timeout), which is almost always what you want under overload instead of unbounded heap growth followed by the OOM killer.

Arena (region, bump allocator): one large block; allocation is "round up, bump a pointer"; freeing is "reset the pointer". Perfect for per-request scratch data: parse the message, allocate every field in the arena, process, reset. Hundreds of allocations become one. The constraint: objects in the arena are not individually destroyed, so they must be trivially destructible or you run destructors yourself before reset.

Both exist in C (you have probably written a free-list). The C++ gain is that the return path is enforced by a destructor, and the arena can refuse non-trivial types at compile time with static_assert(std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>).

docs.title: 2.9 Designing ownership in a server: connections, requests, sessions
docs.text:
The concrete design for a TCP application server (the kind you maintain):

main()
  owns Config (value)                               lifetime: whole process
  owns Server (value)
        owns Metrics, Logger (values, declared first)
        owns Store (unique_ptr<Store>, polymorphic)
        owns Acceptor (value, holds listening fd)
        owns WorkerPool (value, declared LAST so threads are joined first)
        owns map<ConnId, unique_ptr<Connection>>
              Connection
                owns fd (RAII wrapper, value)
                owns read/write buffers (values)
                owns unique_ptr<Session>             lifetime: auth .. close
                owns deque<Request>                  lifetime: parse .. reply sent
                observes Store&, Metrics&, Logger&

Decisions and reasons:

  • A Request is a value. It is created by the parser, moved into the connection's queue, moved to a worker, processed, and the reply is moved back. Nothing holds a pointer to it across a thread boundary; the request itself crosses the boundary by move. No shared_ptr<Request>.
  • A Session is owned by its Connection. When the socket closes, the session dies. If sessions must survive reconnects (resume tokens), the Server owns a SessionStore and the connection holds a SessionId handle instead.
  • Workers never hold Connection*. They receive (ConnId, Request) by value and return (ConnId, Reply). The I/O thread resolves ConnId; if the client disconnected meanwhile, the reply is dropped. This single rule eliminates the "client disconnected mid-request" crash class.
  • Store, Metrics, Logger are observed by reference because Server owns them and declares them before the connections and worker pool, so they are destroyed after.
  • Shutdown order is destruction order reversed: workers joined first (no more tasks), then connections closed (fds released), then store flushed, then metrics and logger. This falls out of member declaration order; you do not write a shutdown() function unless you need to run it before destruction.

docs.title: code/m03_ownership_tree.cpp
docs.text:
The server above, single-threaded, with handles. Key parts:

class Server {
    // Declaration order IS destruction order (reversed). metrics_ before conns_,
    // so every ~Connection can still call metrics_.dec_connections().
    Metrics metrics_;
    std::uint64_t next_id_ = 1;
    std::unordered_map<ConnId, std::unique_ptr<Connection>, ConnIdHash> conns_;
public:
    ConnId accept();                 // hands out a handle, never a pointer
    Connection* find(ConnId id);     // observer pointer, valid until the next close()
    void close(ConnId id) { conns_.erase(id); }   // ~Connection runs here
};

Connection deletes its copy operations because its address is handed out as an observer and because it owns a resource with identity (an fd in real code). The main function closes a connection and shows find() returning nullptr where a stored pointer would have dangled.

docs.title: code/m03_object_pool_arena.cpp
docs.text:
A BufferPool whose acquire() returns std::unique_ptr<RequestBuffer, Returner>, so the buffer goes back to the pool at scope exit even on exceptions, and an Arena with bump allocation and a static_assert that rejects non-trivially-destructible types.

struct Returner {
    BufferPool* pool;
    void operator()(RequestBuffer* b) const { pool->release(b); }   // deleter returns, not frees
};
using Handle = std::unique_ptr<RequestBuffer, Returner>;

template <class T, class... Args>
T* Arena::make(Args&&... args) {
    static_assert(std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>, "nothing will call destructors");
    void* p = allocate(sizeof(T), alignof(T));
    return new (p) T(std::forward<Args>(args)...);     // placement new into the arena
}

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
unique_ptr is free. sizeof(std::unique_ptr<T>) == sizeof(T*) with the default deleter (the deleter is an empty class and the empty base optimisation removes it). The destructor is if (p) delete p;, inlined. Moving is two pointer stores. There is no runtime cost over a raw pointer with a manual delete; the only cost is the one you want, which is that the compiler refuses to copy it. With a stateful deleter (the pool Returner holding a BufferPool*) it is 16 bytes.

shared_ptr is not free. sizeof == 2 * sizeof(void*): object pointer plus control block pointer. The control block holds the strong count, the weak count, the deleter and the allocator. make_shared puts the object and the control block in one allocation (faster, one cache line), but then the memory for the object is not released until the weak count also hits zero. Copying does lock xadd on the strong count; in a loop on a shared object across cores, that line bounces between caches and dominates run time.

Why declaration order is destruction order. The compiler generates the destructor body as: user-written body, then destroy members in reverse declaration order, then base classes. That is why "declare what others depend on first" is not a style preference; it is how you guarantee a member is still alive when later members' destructors run.

std::thread in a destructor. A joinable std::thread whose destructor runs calls std::terminate. That is deliberate: it forces you to decide. Declaring the thread (or pool) last and joining in the destructor is the structured pattern. C++20's std::jthread joins automatically; in C++17 you write the join.

Handles and the kernel. A file descriptor is a handle into the process's fd table; the kernel owns the struct file. close(fd) drops the table entry; the struct file is refcounted because dup and fork can share it. The fd number is reused immediately, which is exactly the stale-handle problem Section 2.6 describes, and the cause of the classic "I wrote to the wrong socket" bug when a close races with a write. Generation counters are how you avoid that in your own handle tables.

Arenas and the hardware. A bump allocator hands out consecutive addresses, so objects allocated together are adjacent in memory and prefetch well. malloc returns whatever block fits, scattering related objects across the heap; walking a linked structure then costs one cache miss (60 to 100 ns typical, main memory) per node. This locality, not the saved free() calls, is usually the bigger win.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
Your migration engine. A Berkeley DB cursor, a YugabyteDB connection, a batch of rows in flight, a transformation context. Who owned the row buffer while it was being written? If the answer was "the loop variable, and I free it at the bottom", every continue and every error path was a leak risk. The C++ shape: struct Batch { std::vector<Row> rows; } owned by the loop iteration, a PgConnection RAII wrapper owned by the engine, a BdbCursor RAII wrapper owned by the scan. Zero explicit frees, zero leaks on error paths.

The 3 AM bugs and how ownership design prevents them.

  • Client disconnects mid-request; worker writes reply to freed connection. Prevented by workers holding ConnId, never Connection*.
  • Shutdown crash: logger destroyed before the last worker logs. Prevented by declaring the logger first and the worker pool last.
  • Memory grows until OOM under a burst. Prevented by a bounded pool with explicit back-pressure instead of new per request.
  • Session state leaks after disconnect. Prevented by Connection owning unique_ptr<Session>.
  • Double free of a buffer on an error path. Prevented by the pool's deleter: the compiler will not let you return twice because you cannot copy the unique_ptr.

Debugging lifetime bugs. -fsanitize=address reports use-after-free with the allocation and deallocation stacks; run your test suite under it always. For production crash dumps: a vptr pointing to freed memory, or a string whose length field is a pointer value, means use-after-free. Valgrind's --track-origins=yes for uninitialised reads. gdb with watch -l *ptr to find who writes a location.

Interview framing. When asked "how do you manage memory in a large C++ codebase", the senior answer is not "smart pointers". It is: "I draw the ownership tree first; values and unique_ptr for ownership, references and raw pointers for observation, handles when an observer must outlive its target, shared_ptr only for the two cases where multiple independent lifetimes genuinely decide destruction. Declaration order encodes shutdown order."

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Draw the ownership diagram (solid = owns, dashed = observes) for the RPC server you maintain at work: listener, worker threads, connections, request buffers, database handles, config. Mark every dashed arrow that points to something not owned by an ancestor. Done when you have a list of the lifetime risks in your real codebase.
  2. (easy) In m03_ownership_tree.cpp, swap the declaration order of metrics_ and conns_ in Server. Predict what happens at shutdown; then add a print in ~Metrics and ~Connection to confirm. Done when you can explain the output.
  3. (medium) Add a generation counter to BufferPool so that Handles are indices plus generation, and pool.get(handle) returns nullptr for a stale handle after the buffer was recycled. Done when a test shows a stale handle rejected.
  4. (medium) Make Arena::make support non-trivially-destructible types by recording (void* obj, void (*dtor)(void*)) pairs and running them in reset() in reverse order. Done when a std::string allocated in the arena is destroyed exactly once (verify with AddressSanitizer or a counting type).
  5. (hard) Build a two-thread version of m03_ownership_tree.cpp: an I/O thread owns connections, a worker thread receives (ConnId, Request) through a queue and returns (ConnId, std::string). Close a connection while its request is in flight. Done when the program never touches a freed Connection (run under -fsanitize=address,thread), and you can explain which rule made that impossible.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When do you use unique_ptr, shared_ptr, a raw pointer and a reference? A: unique_ptr for sole ownership of a heap object (polymorphic, optional or non-movable member). shared_ptr only when several independent lifetimes genuinely decide destruction, such as a config snapshot read by in-flight requests or an async keep-alive. Raw pointer for a non-owning, possibly null observer; reference for a non-owning, never-null one. Ownership should form a tree.

Q: Why is shared_ptr a smell? A: It usually means the author did not identify the owner. Costs are atomic refcount traffic, a control block, cycle leaks needing weak_ptr, non-deterministic destruction on whichever thread drops the last reference, and an ownership graph nobody can draw.

Q: How do you design ownership of connections and requests in a server? A: Server owns connections in a map keyed by handle; connection owns its fd, buffers, session and queued requests; requests move by value between threads; workers hold ConnId, not Connection*, and the I/O thread resolves the handle when the reply comes back so a disconnected client's reply is simply dropped.

Q: What is the difference between a handle and a pointer? A: A pointer is an address that is valid only while the object lives; dereferencing a stale one is undefined behaviour. A handle is an id resolved by the owner, so a stale handle fails cleanly. Pair small-index handles with a generation counter to detect slot reuse.

Q: Why does member declaration order matter? A: Members are constructed in declaration order and destroyed in reverse. If member B holds a reference to member A, A must be declared first so it outlives B. Threads and pools go last so they are joined before the resources they use are destroyed.

Q: What does an object pool buy over new/delete per request? A: Bounded memory with explicit back-pressure under overload, no fragmentation, warm cache lines, and no allocator lock contention. With a unique_ptr custom deleter the return path is enforced by the compiler.

Q: When is an arena appropriate and what is its constraint? A: For many short-lived allocations with a common end point, such as everything created while parsing and processing one request. Allocation is a pointer bump and freeing is a reset. The constraint is that objects are not individually destroyed, so they must be trivially destructible or you must run destructors yourself.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Every object has one owner; draw the tree before writing the class.
  • Value members and unique_ptr for ownership; T& and T* for observation; handles when observers must outlive their targets.
  • shared_ptr only when several independent lifetimes genuinely decide destruction; it costs atomics, a control block and clarity.
  • Observation arrows must point to objects owned by an ancestor or an earlier-declared sibling.
  • Declaration order is reverse destruction order; it encodes shutdown.
  • Requests cross thread boundaries by value; workers hold handles, not pointers.
  • Pools give bounded memory and enforced return via custom deleters; arenas give locality and one-shot freeing.
  • -fsanitize=address on every test run; a wild vptr in a dump means use-after-free.

docs.title: 04. Creational Patterns
docs.text: Time: ~2 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Creational patterns answer one question: how does code get an object without knowing, or caring, exactly which class it is and how it was set up? In C you solve this with thing_create(kind, args...) functions that return an opaque pointer, with static globals for "the one logger", and with structs you fill in and then validate. Each of those is a creational pattern with a name.

The reason to name them is the reason to name anything: you can talk about the design in one word instead of a paragraph, and you can recognise when a codebase is using one badly. The most important lesson in this module is about the singleton, which is the pattern C and C++ programmers over-use most, and which you should learn to replace with explicit wiring.

docs.title: 2.1 Factory function
docs.text:
What: a function that returns a new object through an interface, hiding the concrete type. std::unique_ptr<Store> make_store(std::string_view kind, ...).

C equivalent: store* store_create(const char* kind, ...) with a switch inside, or store_ops tables selected by name.

When: the concrete type depends on runtime data (config file, command-line flag, message header) and the caller should not name it. This is 90% of all factory use. It also centralises construction logic that is easy to get wrong (two-phase init, validation).

Cost: one heap allocation per object (you return by unique_ptr because the size is unknown to the caller). Negligible unless called per request on a hot path.

Two refinements:

  • Registry factory: a std::map<std::string, std::function<std::unique_ptr<Store>(...)>> that backends register into at startup. Adding a backend does not edit make_store (Open/ Closed, Module 02). The cost is that the set of backends is invisible to the compiler and you lose dead-code elimination.
  • Static factory function on the class: static std::optional<Date> Date::parse(std::string_view) for constructors that can fail without throwing, or when you need two constructors with the same parameter types (Temperature::from_celsius(double) vs from_kelvin(double)).

docs.title: 2.2 Abstract factory
docs.text:
What: an interface whose methods create a family of related objects that must be consistent with each other. StorageFactory { make_store(); make_locks(); make_wal(); } with FileStorageFactory and MemoryStorageFactory.

C equivalent: a struct of function pointers where every slot is a constructor.

When: you have 2 or more product types that must come from the same "backend" and you switch the whole backend at once (test vs production, Berkeley DB vs Postgres). Mixing a PgStore with BdbLocks must be impossible; one factory object guarantees it.

When not: one product type. Then it is just a factory function with extra ceremony.

docs.title: 2.3 Builder
docs.text:
What: an object that collects the pieces of a complex value step by step and produces the finished, validated value at the end. Usually with a fluent interface (each setter returns *this).

ServerConfig cfg = ServerConfigBuilder{}
    .bind("127.0.0.1", 7000).workers(8).store("file", "/var/lib/tcpkv/data.db").build();

C equivalent: fill a struct config, then call config_validate(&cfg). The difference: with a builder, build() is the only way to obtain a ServerConfig, so every ServerConfig in the program is valid by construction. In C, nothing stops a caller from skipping config_validate.

When: many optional parameters (more than four or so), defaults that must live in one place, validation that spans several fields ("if TLS is on, cert path must be set"), or a value that must be immutable once created.

When not: a struct with three fields and no cross-field constraints. Use aggregate initialisation or designated initialisers (C++20) and skip the builder.

Idiom notes: return Builder& (not Builder) from setters to avoid copying; make build() const so a builder can produce several configs; make the product's fields const or give it only getters if immutability matters.

docs.title: 2.4 Singleton: why mostly avoid
docs.text:
What: a class with exactly one instance, reached through Class::instance().

C equivalent: a static struct logger g_logger; with logger_get().

The one-instance property is often legitimate (one process-wide metrics registry, one connection to a hardware device). The singleton pattern (global access through instance()) is almost always the wrong way to get it, for four reasons:

  1. Hidden dependency. A function that calls Logger::instance() depends on the logger, but its signature does not say so. Readers and tests cannot see the coupling.
  2. Untestable in isolation. Every test shares the same instance. State leaks between tests; tests cannot run in parallel; you cannot substitute a fake without a reset hook.
  3. Lifetime at exit. Function-local statics are destroyed in reverse construction order at exit(). Another static's destructor (or a still-running thread) that uses the singleton after its destruction is a crash in atexit handling, which is miserable to debug. Many codebases "solve" this by leaking the singleton on purpose.
  4. Initialisation order across translation units is unspecified for namespace-scope statics (the "static initialisation order fiasco"). Function-local statics avoid it but introduce point 3.

What to do instead: dependency injection (Module 02). Create the single instance in main (or a wire() function), pass it by reference to everything that needs it. The "single" property is now a fact about your wiring, enforced by the fact that nobody else constructs one, and tests can construct as many as they want.

When a singleton-like thing is acceptable:

  • A process-wide initialisation action (initialise OpenSSL, PQinitSSL, set up a signal handler): use std::call_once with a std::once_flag. It is an action, not an object.
  • Pure, stateless, trivially destructible helpers (a lookup table). No lifetime issue.
  • Deep inside a library where threading an argument through 40 layers is unreasonable and the thing is genuinely process-global (an allocator, a logging sink). Even then, provide a set_instance() hook for tests.

Thread-safe singleton in C++11 and later: the Meyers singleton (static T inst; inside instance()) is guaranteed thread-safe by the standard. The compiler emits a guard variable; the first thread takes a lock (__cxa_guard_acquire), others wait, subsequent calls are a single byte load. You do not need double-checked locking in C++; the compiler does it.

docs.title: 2.5 Prototype
docs.text:
What: create a new object by cloning an existing configured one, via virtual std::unique_ptr<Base> clone() const.

C equivalent: memcpy a template struct, then fix up pointers (deep copy) by hand.

When: construction is expensive (parsing a template, loading a schema) and many similar instances are needed; or you hold objects through a base pointer and need copies without knowing the concrete type (copy constructors are not virtual, so you need clone()).

Modern note: for non-polymorphic types, copying a value is the prototype pattern. ConnectionParams replica = base; replica.host = "..."; There is nothing to name.

docs.title: 2.6 Object pool
docs.text: Covered in Module 03 Section 2.8 from the ownership side. As a creational pattern: a pool creates objects up front and recycles them, which the caller sees as "acquire gives me a ready object". Use for expensive-to-construct objects with a warm-up cost (database connections, large buffers, threads). The unique_ptr custom deleter is the C++ trick that makes the return automatic.

docs.title: 2.7 Choosing
docs.text: Need Use Hide concrete type chosen at runtime Factory function Backends register themselves Registry factory Constructor that can fail, or two constructors with the same parameter types Static named factory function returning optional/expected Several products that must match Abstract factory Many optional fields, cross-field validation, immutable result Builder Exactly one instance Construct once in main, inject by reference One-time initialisation action std::call_once Copy through base pointer Prototype (clone()) Expensive objects, bounded count Object pool

docs.title: code/m04_factory_builder.cpp
docs.text:
Factory function, registry factory, abstract factory and builder on a storage backend example.

std::unique_ptr<Store> make_store(std::string_view kind, std::string_view arg) {
    if (kind == "memory") return std::make_unique<MemoryStore>();
    if (kind == "file")   return std::make_unique<FileStore>(std::string(arg));
    throw std::invalid_argument("unknown store kind: " + std::string(kind));
}

class ServerConfigBuilder {
public:
    ServerConfigBuilder& bind(std::string addr, std::uint16_t port);   // returns *this
    ServerConfigBuilder& workers(int n);
    ServerConfig build() const;         // the ONLY way to get a ServerConfig; validates
private:
    ServerConfig cfg_{"0.0.0.0", 0, 4, std::chrono::milliseconds(30000), 1024, "", ""};  // defaults
};

docs.title: code/m04_singleton_vs_di.cpp
docs.text:
A Meyers singleton MetricsRegistry, a std::call_once initialiser for a legacy C library, and the DI alternative: a plain Metrics class constructed once in main and passed by reference. The test section shows the isolation you get from DI that the singleton cannot give.

static MetricsRegistry& instance() {
    static MetricsRegistry inst;   // thread-safe init guaranteed by C++11
    return inst;
}

std::call_once(flag_, [] { /* init legacy C library exactly once */ });

docs.title: code/m04_prototype_pool.cpp
docs.text: Iso8583Message::clone() as the classic prototype, a value-type copy as the modern form, and a ConnectionPool with a Lease type that returns connections automatically.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Factory functions and allocation. Returning std::unique_ptr<Base> forces a heap allocation because the caller does not know the derived size. If that matters (hot path), alternatives are: return a std::variant<A, B> by value (fixed set, no heap), use a small buffer optimisation type-erasure wrapper (Module 08), or construct in-place into caller-provided storage. Most server code should not care: a request that touches a database costs 10,000 times more than one malloc.

std::function in a registry. Each std::function is typically 32 bytes on GCC (libstdc++), holds small callables inline (up to 16 bytes) and heap-allocates larger ones. Invocation is an indirect call through a stored pointer, same cost class as a virtual call. A capture-less lambda stored in it fits inline.

How the Meyers singleton is compiled. GCC emits a 64-bit guard variable next to the static. The fast path is if ((guard & 1) == 0) { slow path }, one load and one branch, which is cheaper than a mutex. The slow path calls __cxa_guard_acquire, constructs, registers the destructor with __cxa_atexit, then __cxa_guard_release. If the constructor throws, the guard is reset and the next caller retries. __cxa_atexit is why destruction order at exit is reverse construction order, across all translation units.

std::call_once implementation. libstdc++ builds it on pthread_once (older) or on a futex-based state machine (GCC 11 and later). Semantics: if the callable throws, the flag is not set and another caller may retry. Exactly-once applies to successful completion.

Builders and copies. A fluent setter that returns Builder by value copies the whole builder at every step: for a builder holding a few strings that is several allocations per call. Return Builder&. If you want rvalue chaining on a temporary builder to move the contents into build(), you can add &&-qualified overloads; that is an optimisation to apply when measured, not by default.

Prototype and slicing. Base b = derived; copies only the Base subobject and the vptr becomes Base's. This is "slicing" and it is why copying polymorphic objects needs a virtual clone(). A common defence: make the base class's copy constructor protected so only derived classes (in their clone()) can invoke it.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
Config from the environment. A server reads a file, environment variables and command line, in that priority. A builder is the natural shape: three "sources" each call setters, build() validates once. The alternative, a struct that every source mutates and a validate() somebody calls at the end, is how servers end up starting with port 0.

The singleton that bit everyone. A logger singleton with a background flushing thread. At exit(), the static logger is destroyed while the thread is still running; the thread touches the destroyed mutex; the process crashes after main returns, with a stack trace inside exit. Fix: construct the logger in main, join its thread in its destructor, which now runs before main returns. This is also why "declare the thread pool last" from Module 03 matters.

Factories and plug-ins. If backends live in shared libraries (dlopen), each library's initialiser registers its creator into the registry factory. The core never names a backend. This is the real reason to prefer a registry over a switch: the switch cannot name a type that does not exist yet at compile time.

Pools and connection health. A pooled database connection can die while idle (server restart, idle timeout at a firewall). A production pool validates on acquire (cheap ping or PQstatus) or on error, and replaces dead connections. Without this, the first request after a network blip fails with a stale connection, and the second succeeds, which looks like a flaky bug for weeks.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Add a "cached" kind to make_store that wraps a MemoryStore in the WriteThroughCache from Module 02. Done when make_store("cached", "")->name() reports it is a cache over memory.
  2. (easy) Give ServerConfigBuilder a cross-field rule: if store_kind == "file", store_arg must be non-empty. Done when the builder rejects store("file") with a clear message.
  3. (medium) Replace the MetricsRegistry singleton with DI in a small program that has three "modules" (parser, handler, store) all incrementing metrics. Then write a test that runs two scenarios in sequence and asserts counts, and show that the singleton version fails the second assertion (state leaks) while the DI version passes. Done when both programs compile and the behaviour difference is demonstrated.
  4. (medium) Add health-checking to ConnectionPool: a bool DbConnection::alive() that a test can flip to false, and an acquire() that discards dead connections and constructs replacements. Done when a test shows a dead connection replaced transparently.
  5. (hard) Implement a registry factory where backends self-register via a static initialiser object in their own translation unit (static Registrar r{"file", &make_file};). Explain what happens if that translation unit is in a static library and nothing references it (hint: the linker drops it). Done when you can state the fix (--whole-archive, or explicit registration) and why a plain switch does not have this problem.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a factory function and an abstract factory? A: A factory function creates one product of a type chosen at runtime. An abstract factory is an interface that creates a family of related products, guaranteeing they come from the same backend. Use the abstract factory only when there are several products that must match.

Q: Why is the singleton pattern discouraged, and what replaces it? A: It hides dependencies, makes tests share state, and has destruction-order problems at exit. Replace it with one instance created in main and injected by reference; for one-time initialisation actions use std::call_once.

Q: Is a function-local static thread-safe in C++? A: Yes, since C++11. The compiler emits a guard and ensures exactly one thread constructs it while others wait. You do not need double-checked locking.

Q: When do you reach for a builder? A: When a value has many optional fields, defaults that should live in one place, or validation across fields, and when you want every instance to be valid by construction because build() is the only way to make one.

Q: Why does the prototype pattern need a virtual clone()? A: Copy constructors are not virtual; copying through a base pointer slices the object to the base type. clone() dispatches to the derived class, which copies itself fully and returns a base pointer.

Q: What is the cost of returning unique_ptr<Base> from a factory and when does it matter? A: One heap allocation per object because the caller does not know the derived size. It matters on hot paths creating many small objects; alternatives are returning a std::variant by value for a closed set or a small-buffer type-erasure wrapper.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Factory function: hide the concrete type chosen at runtime; the most used creational pattern.
  • Registry factory: open for extension, but the compiler loses sight of the set.
  • Abstract factory: a family of products that must match; skip it for one product.
  • Builder: validated, immutable values with many optional fields; build() is the only exit.
  • Singleton: the one-instance property is fine, the global instance() is not. Construct in main, inject by reference. std::call_once for one-time actions.
  • Meyers singleton is thread-safe by the standard; its problem is exit-time destruction order.
  • Prototype: clone() for polymorphic copies; plain copy for value types.
  • Object pool: bounded, recycled, returned automatically via a custom deleter.

docs.title: 05. Structural Patterns
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Structural patterns are about how objects are composed: how you make two things with different interfaces talk to each other, how you hide a messy subsystem behind one door, how you stack behaviour in layers, and how you keep the inside of a module from leaking into its users. If creational patterns are about birth, structural patterns are about plumbing.

Every one of them exists in C. An adapter is the pq_wrapper.c file you wrote so the rest of the program does not see libpq. A facade is a .h with three functions in front of a subsystem with thirty. An opaque struct conn; in a header is pimpl. The C++ versions add type checking, RAII and the ability to stack them without re-declaring every slot by hand.

docs.title: 2.1 Adapter: making a C API fit your interface
docs.text:
What: a class that implements your interface by calling their API. The rest of the program depends on your interface only.

Why it matters in your world: libpq, Berkeley DB, Win32 sockets, ODBC, OpenSSL. Each has opaque handles, manual free functions, status codes and char* results. Letting those leak into business code means every function has to know the cleanup protocol of three libraries.

The two-step method:

  1. RAII wrapper per handle type. std::unique_ptr<PGconn, decltype(&PQfinish)> or a custom deleter struct. From this point on, no path can leak the handle. This step alone removes a whole class of bugs and is worth doing even without step 2.
  2. The adapter class. Implements your interface (Store), holds the RAII handle, translates each call: your types to their types, their status codes to your optional/exception/expected, their char* to your std::string before the result is freed.
struct ResultDeleter { void operator()(PGresult* r) const { PQclear(r); } };
using ResultPtr = std::unique_ptr<PGresult, ResultDeleter>;

std::optional<std::string> PqStore::get(const std::string& key) const {
    ResultPtr r(PQexecParams(conn_.get(), "SELECT v FROM kv WHERE k = $1", 1, ...));
    if (PQresultStatus(r.get()) != PGRES_TUPLES_OK) throw DbError(PQerrorMessage(conn_.get()));
    if (PQntuples(r.get()) == 0) return std::nullopt;
    return std::string(PQgetvalue(r.get(), 0, 0));   // copy before r goes out of scope
}

Rules: the constructor either produces a usable adapter or throws (no half-open state); the adapter is move-only (it owns a handle with identity); nothing outside the adapter's .cpp includes the C header.

Class adapter vs object adapter: the GoF book distinguishes inheriting from the adaptee (class adapter) from holding it (object adapter). In C++, always hold it. Inheriting from a library type couples you to its layout.

docs.title: 2.2 Facade: one door in front of a subsystem
docs.text:
What: a class (or a header of free functions) that exposes a small, task-oriented interface over a group of classes that callers would otherwise have to orchestrate.

LoanEligibilityFacade::decide(applicant_id) loads the applicant, runs the policy, records the decision and notifies. The RPC handler, the batch job and the test all call one function. If tomorrow the decision also needs a fraud check, one place changes.

C equivalent: the public header of a module. loan.h with loan_decide(); loan.c calling into five other files. Facades are the most C-like pattern; they are just good modules.

Facade vs adapter: an adapter changes the shape of one interface to match another. A facade simplifies access to many. An adapter is a translator; a facade is a receptionist.

Pitfall: a facade that grows into a god class with forty methods and all the business logic inside it. The facade should orchestrate; the rules live in the components.

docs.title: 2.3 Decorator: stacking behaviour around an interface
docs.text:
What: a class that implements interface I, holds another I, and forwards each call while adding something before or after. Decorators stack in any order.

service --> LoggingStore --> MetricsStore --> RetryingStore --> PqStore
             (same Store interface at every arrow)

Why it beats inheritance: with inheritance you would need LoggingPqStore, MetricsPqStore, LoggingMetricsPqStore, and the same again for every backend. With decorators you have one class per concern and compose at wiring time. Order is a deployment decision: metrics outside retry counts attempts; metrics inside retry counts successes.

The forwarding base: write one StoreDecorator that forwards every method, and have each concrete decorator override only what it changes. Without it, every decorator re-types all the forwarding, and adding a method to Store means editing every decorator (that is also a reason to keep interfaces small, Module 02 ISP).

Ownership: the outer decorator owns the inner via unique_ptr. One pointer at the top owns the whole stack; destroying it unwinds the layers.

C equivalent: a store_ops table whose functions call another store_ops held in the context. Works, but you re-declare every slot per layer and the void* context chain is hard to debug.

Cost: one virtual call per layer per operation. Four layers over a database call is nothing; four layers over an in-memory hash lookup on a hot path is measurable. Module 08 shows the template (static) decorator for the hot case.

docs.title: 2.4 Composite: trees where leaf and group share an interface
docs.text:
What: Rule is the component; MinAge is a leaf; AllOf and AnyOf are composites holding vector<unique_ptr<Rule>>. passes(applicant) works on a leaf or on a whole tree.

Use it when callers should not care whether they are holding one thing or a group: rule engines, file systems (file vs directory), UI widget trees, expression trees (a parsed SQL WHERE clause is a composite). Your loan-origination domain is full of these: eligibility policies, fee schedules, document checklists.

Ownership: a unique_ptr tree (Module 03). Composites own children; nobody points upward. If children need their parent, use a Rule* observer set by the parent on add.

Modern alternative for closed sets: std::variant<MinAge, MinScore, AllOf, AnyOf> with recursive std::visit. Harder to write (recursive variants need indirection) but gives exhaustiveness checking and no vtables. For an open set where rules are plug-ins, the virtual composite wins.

docs.title: 2.5 Proxy: controlling access to an object
docs.text:
What: same structure as a decorator (wraps, same interface) with a different intent: a proxy stands in for the real object and controls access. Kinds:

  • Caching proxy: answers reads from memory, writes through, invalidates. The code file builds an LRU proxy in front of a slow store.
  • Lazy (virtual) proxy: creates the expensive object on first use.
  • Remote proxy: looks local, performs an RPC. Your client library's stub objects are remote proxies; the server-side skeleton is the other half.
  • Protection proxy: checks permissions before forwarding.

The caching proxy's contract: after put(k, v) through the proxy, get(k) returns v (write-through plus cache update). What it cannot promise: freshness if someone writes to the backing store around it. State that in the class comment. Every cache has an invalidation story and most cache bugs are about it.

Decorator vs proxy, one sentence: a decorator adds behaviour the caller wants to see; a proxy tries to be invisible.

docs.title: 2.6 Bridge and pimpl: compile firewall and ABI stability
docs.text:
