Bridge (GoF): separate an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary independently, via a pointer from the abstraction to an implementation interface. In practice in C++ this appears as pimpl: a public class holding std::unique_ptr<Impl> where Impl is defined only in the .cpp.

// connection.h -- what clients see
class Connection {
public:
    explicit Connection(std::string host, std::uint16_t port);
    ~Connection();                               // defined in .cpp
    Connection(Connection&&) noexcept;           // declared here, defined in .cpp
    Connection& operator=(Connection&&) noexcept;
    bool send(std::string_view bytes);
private:
    struct Impl;                                 // incomplete here
    std::unique_ptr<Impl> impl_;
};

What you get:

  • Compile firewall. Adding a field to Impl recompiles connection.cpp only. Without pimpl, every file including connection.h recompiles. On a large codebase this is the difference between a 10-second and a 10-minute edit-compile loop.
  • Header hygiene. <winsock2.h>, <libpq-fe.h>, <db.h> stay inside the .cpp. Clients do not inherit their macros and name pollution.
  • ABI stability. sizeof(Connection) is one pointer forever. A shared library can change Impl without clients rebuilding. (Adding virtual functions or changing public signatures still breaks ABI; pimpl protects the data layout only.)

What it costs: one heap allocation per object, one pointer indirection per member access, and the boilerplate of declaring special members in the header and defining them in the .cpp. Do not pimpl small value types or anything on a hot path; pimpl the handful of classes at module boundaries.

C equivalent: struct conn; in the header, struct conn { ... } in the .c, conn_create() / conn_destroy(). That is exactly pimpl. The C++ version adds RAII so the opaque pointer cannot leak, and move semantics so it can be returned by value.

The one rule people get wrong: the destructor (and move operations) must be defined in the .cpp, after Impl is complete. If you write ~Connection() = default; in the header, the compiler instantiates unique_ptr<Impl>::~unique_ptr in client code where Impl is incomplete, and you get "invalid application of sizeof to incomplete type".

docs.title: 2.7 Choosing
docs.text: You want to Pattern Use a C library through your own interface, with RAII Adapter Give callers one simple entry point to a multi-step operation Facade Add logging/metrics/retry around an interface without touching implementations Decorator Treat one item and a group of items the same way Composite Cache, lazy-load, remote-call or permission-check transparently Proxy Hide implementation details from a header; stabilise ABI; cut compile times Pimpl (Bridge)

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
• code/m05_adapter_c_api.cpp: a fake libpq-shaped C library, RAII wrappers for its two handle types, and PqStoreAdapter implementing Store. Shows the "copy the char* before the result is cleared" rule and the "constructor throws on connect failure" rule.
  • code/m05_facade_composite.cpp: a Rule composite (MinAge, MinCreditScore, MaxDebtToIncome, NoExistingDefault, AllOf, AnyOf) that prints itself as an indented tree, and LoanEligibilityFacade::decide() orchestrating repository, policy, log and notifier.
  • code/m05_decorator_store.cpp: StoreDecorator forwarding base; LoggingStore, MetricsStore, RetryingStore; a FlakyStore to exercise retry; two stacking orders to show that order is a design decision.
  • code/m05_proxy_cache.cpp: CachingStoreProxy with LRU eviction (std::list + unordered_map of iterators), write-through, hit/miss counters, compared against the direct store on round-trip count.
  • code/m05_pimpl.cpp: Connection with unique_ptr<Impl>, laid out as header / source / client sections, move-only, with the destructor defined where Impl is complete.

Key lines from the decorator:

class StoreDecorator : public Store {
public:
    explicit StoreDecorator(std::unique_ptr<Store> inner) : inner_(std::move(inner)) {}
    void put(const std::string& k, const std::string& v) override { inner_->put(k, v); }   // forward
    /* get, erase forward too */
protected:
    Store& inner() { return *inner_; }
private:
    std::unique_ptr<Store> inner_;   // outer owns inner; one unique_ptr at the top owns the stack
};

class MetricsStore final : public StoreDecorator {
    using StoreDecorator::StoreDecorator;
    void put(const std::string& k, const std::string& v) override {
        time_it([&] { inner().put(k, v); });  ++c_.puts;
    }
};

Key lines from the proxy:

std::optional<std::string> get(const std::string& k) const override {
    if (auto it = index_.find(k); it != index_.end()) {
        lru_.splice(lru_.begin(), lru_, it->second);   // O(1) move-to-front; iterators stay valid
        return it->second->second;
    }
    auto v = backing_.get(k);
    if (v) insert_or_update(k, *v);
    return v;
}

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Decorator call cost. Each layer is a virtual call: load vptr, load slot, indirect call, and no inlining through it. Four layers add roughly four times 2 to 5 ns when predicted. GCC cannot devirtualise because the inner pointer's dynamic type is a runtime fact. If you need zero-cost layering on a hot path, the template version (Logging<Metrics<MemoryStore>>, Module 08) is inlined completely, at the cost of a distinct type per stack and recompilation when the stack changes.

Why std::list plus unordered_map for LRU. std::list::splice moves a node in O(1) without invalidating any iterator, so the map can store iterators to list nodes and the "move to front" operation touches three pointers. A std::vector would need O(n) shifting; a std::deque invalidates iterators on push. The cost is one heap node per entry and poor cache locality; an intrusive doubly-linked list over a slab of entries is the production version (Module 11, LRU walkthrough).

Pimpl and the ABI. The Itanium ABI defines a class's layout by its members in order with alignment padding. Clients compile sizeof(Connection) and member offsets into their code. Changing a member breaks every client binary; with pimpl, clients only ever see one pointer. Note what pimpl does not protect: adding a virtual function shifts vtable slots; changing a public inline function changes code compiled into clients; changing an exception type thrown changes the contract. Module 10 covers versioning.

Pimpl and const. impl_->x = 1 compiles inside a const member function because the pointer is const, not the pointee. You lose the compiler's help with const-correctness unless you wrap access in const Impl& impl() const and Impl& impl() helpers. The std::experimental::propagate_const wrapper fixes this; most codebases just write the two accessors.

Adapter and exception safety across the C boundary. C code is not exception-aware. If your adapter passes a C++ callback into a C library (qsort comparator, PQnoticeReceiver, DB->set_errcall) and the callback throws, the exception unwinds through C frames compiled without unwind tables, which is undefined behaviour and usually terminates. Catch everything in the callback and translate to a status code or a stored error.

Facade and link-time dependencies. A facade in its own library pulls in every subsystem it orchestrates. If a client only needs one small piece, linking against the facade library drags in all of them. Keep the facade in the application layer, not in a shared foundation library.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
Your Berkeley DB to YugabyteDB migration. Two adapters implementing one Store (or CursorSource and RowSink) interface would have let you write the migration loop once and test it with two in-memory fakes. The adapter for Berkeley DB holds a DB* and a DBC* with custom deleters; the adapter for YugabyteDB holds a PGconn*. The loop never sees either. When telling this story, the phrase is: "I isolated both storage engines behind a common interface so the transformation logic was independently testable."

Decorators are how observability gets into a server without polluting it. Logging, metrics, tracing, retry, circuit breaking, timeout: each is one decorator over the storage interface and one over the transport interface. The business logic has no log(...) calls in it for I/O; they are in the decorators, configured per environment (verbose logging in staging, metrics only in production).

The caching proxy at 3 AM. Symptom: a customer sees an old balance for 30 seconds after a transfer. Cause: a second server instance wrote to the database; this instance's caching proxy served the stale value. Fixes, in order of cost: short TTL; invalidation messages between instances; move the cache to a shared tier (Redis) so there is one cache; or do not cache data that must be read-your-writes across instances. A caching proxy's documentation must say which of these it does.

Pimpl in a shared library you ship to clients. If your bank ships a client SDK (a .so or .dll) to partner systems, every public class should be pimpl'd or behind a C ABI. Otherwise a bug-fix release that adds a field forces every partner to rebuild, which they will not do for months.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) In m05_adapter_c_api.cpp, add erase() to Store and the adapter (the fake library needs a DEL k command). Done when the adapter compiles and erase on a missing key returns false without throwing.
  2. (easy) Add a TimeoutStore decorator that measures each call and logs a warning if it exceeds a threshold. Insert it in both positions relative to RetryingStore and explain the different meaning. Done when both stacks compile and you can state which one you would deploy.
  3. (medium) Extend CachingStoreProxy to cache negative results (key absent) with a short TTL, so repeated lookups of a missing key do not hit the database. Done when a test shows one round trip for five gets of a missing key, and a put of that key is visible immediately after.
  4. (medium) Write a Rule for "applicant age between 21 and 60" two ways: as a new leaf class, and as an AllOf of MinAge and a new MaxAge. Then add a Not composite. Done when Not(NoExistingDefault) reads correctly in describe() and you can argue which of the two age solutions is better and why.
  5. (hard) Convert m05_pimpl.cpp into three real files (connection.h, connection.cpp, main.cpp), compile with -H to see what headers each pulls in, then add a std::vector member to Impl and confirm main.cpp does not recompile (make -n or timestamps). Then move ~Connection() = default; into the header and read the error message. Done when you can explain the error in terms of where unique_ptr<Impl>'s destructor is instantiated.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How would you wrap a C library like libpq in C++? A: First, an RAII wrapper per handle type using unique_ptr with a custom deleter, so no path leaks. Then an adapter class implementing my own interface, translating status codes to optionals or exceptions and copying char* results into std::string before freeing. Nothing outside the adapter includes the C header.

Q: What is the difference between a decorator and a proxy? A: Same structure: wrap an object behind the same interface. Different intent. A decorator adds behaviour the caller wants (logging, metrics, retry) and stacks. A proxy controls access and aims to be transparent (caching, lazy loading, remote access, permissions).

Q: Why use decorators instead of subclasses for logging and metrics? A: Subclassing needs one class per combination of concern and backend. Decorators need one class per concern and compose at wiring time in any order. Order itself becomes a design decision, for example metrics outside or inside retry.

Q: What does pimpl buy and what does it cost? A: It buys a compile firewall (private changes do not recompile clients), header hygiene (platform headers stay in the .cpp), and data-layout ABI stability for shared libraries. It costs a heap allocation, a pointer indirection, and boilerplate; and the destructor and move operations must be defined in the .cpp where Impl is complete.

Q: What can go wrong with a caching proxy? A: Staleness when another writer bypasses it, which needs a TTL, invalidation messages or a shared cache tier. Unbounded growth without eviction. Caching negative results without a TTL so a newly created key stays invisible. Serving a value after a failed write if you update the cache before the backing store.

Q: When would you use a composite, and how do you own the children? A: When callers should treat one item and a group uniformly: rule trees, expression trees, widget trees. Children are owned by vector<unique_ptr<Component>> in the composite; parent links, if needed, are raw observer pointers.

Q: What is the facade pattern in C terms? A: A module's public header: a few task-oriented functions in front of many internal ones. The point is to give callers one entry point and keep the choreography in one place.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Adapter: RAII wrapper per C handle first, then a class implementing your interface over their API; copy results out before freeing.
  • Facade: one simple entry point orchestrating several components; keep rules in the components, not the facade.
  • Decorator: same interface, wraps and forwards, stacks in any order; one class per concern; a forwarding base avoids boilerplate.
  • Composite: leaves and groups share an interface; unique_ptr tree ownership.
  • Proxy: same structure as decorator, intent is access control; caching proxies need a stated invalidation story.
  • Pimpl: unique_ptr<Impl> with special members defined in the .cpp; buys compile firewall and layout ABI stability; costs an allocation and an indirection.
  • Every layer of virtual wrapping is a non-inlinable call; fine around I/O, measurable around in-memory hot paths.
  • Exceptions must never cross into C frames: catch in callbacks and translate.

docs.title: 06. Behavioural Patterns
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 03, 05

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Behavioural patterns are about who does what, in which order, and how they find out. How does a service swap one algorithm for another at runtime? How does one object tell five others that something happened without knowing who they are? How do you turn "do this later" into a thing you can queue? How do you keep a protocol parser from becoming a 600-line switch?

In C you have answered each of these with a function pointer, a callback list, a struct on a queue, and an enum with a switch. Those are the right answers in C, and most of them are still right in C++. This module gives each one its name, shows the class-hierarchy version you will see in older C++ codebases, and then the modern version (std::function, std::variant, lambdas) which is usually shorter and faster.

The single most important idea in this module is in Section 2.2: the observer pattern's lifetime bug. It is the most common crash in event-driven C++ servers and most engineers cannot explain why it happens or how to make it impossible.

docs.title: 2.1 Strategy: std::function vs virtual vs template
docs.text:
What: make an algorithm swappable. A transfer service whose fee rule varies by deployment.

Form When Cost Virtual interface FeePolicy { fee(); name(); } Strategy has several operations, or state with identity, or must be stored by name in a registry 1 heap object, vptr, indirect call std::function<Paise(const Transfer&)> Strategy is one operation; lambdas capture their parameters 32 bytes, indirect call, heap for captures over 16 bytes Template parameter TransferService<Fee> Choice known at compile time; hot path Zero runtime cost, one type per strategy, cannot swap at runtime C: Paise (*fn)(const void* ctx, ...) plus void* ctx C Indirect call, no type safety on ctx

The decision: how many operations and when is the choice made. One operation, runtime choice: std::function. Several operations: interface. Compile-time choice on a hot path: template.

A property of std::function strategies that interfaces lack: they compose trivially. max_of(percent_fee(25, cap), crossbank_fee(300)) is a strategy built from strategies in three lines (see the code file).

docs.title: 2.2 Observer and its lifetime bugs
docs.text:
What: a subject keeps a list of listeners and calls them when an event occurs. Listeners register and (should) deregister.

The bug:

class Subject { std::vector<Observer*> obs_; void notify() { for (auto* o : obs_) o->on_event(); } };

An Observer is destroyed without unsubscribing. The pointer stays in obs_. The next notify() calls a virtual function through a freed object: the vptr is garbage, the jump goes anywhere. Under AddressSanitizer this is caught immediately; in production it is a crash hours later in an unrelated place.

A second bug: a callback subscribes or unsubscribes during notify(), mutating obs_ while it is being iterated. Iterator invalidation; undefined behaviour.

Three fixes, in order of preference:

  1. Subscription token (RAII). subscribe() returns a move-only object whose destructor unsubscribes. The observer stores the token as its last member, so when the observer is destroyed the token goes first and the subject forgets it before any other member dies. Mark subscribe() [[nodiscard]] so dropping the token is a warning. Constraint: the subject must outlive all tokens (it is owned higher in the tree, Module 03), and the subject's notify() iterates over a snapshot of ids so callbacks may mutate the list.
  2. weak_ptr observers. The subject stores std::weak_ptr<Observer> and calls lock() before each call, pruning expired entries. Correct and simple, but forces every observer to be shared_ptr-managed and adds atomics on every notify. Use it when the observers are already shared for other reasons.
  3. Documented manual unsubscribe. The C way. It works until someone forgets, and in a large codebase someone forgets.

Threads make it worse. If notify() runs on thread A while the observer is destroyed on thread B, even the token fix has a window: B's destructor unsubscribes while A is already inside the callback. Full solutions: notify under a lock that the destructor also takes (risk: deadlock if the callback re-enters); or post events to the observer's own thread as values (actor model, Module 07); or the weak_ptr form, where lock() keeps the object alive for the duration of the call. Pick based on whether callbacks may block.

Modern form: the observer list is std::vector<std::function<void(const Event&)>>; no Observer interface. The token mechanism applies identically.

docs.title: 2.3 Command: undo and request queues
docs.text:
What: an operation as an object: what to do and everything needed to do it. Then it can be queued, logged, replayed, undone, or run on another thread.

Two shapes:

  • Undoable commands need an interface with execute() and undo() and state captured at execute time (the previous value), not at construction. A CompositeCommand undoes its parts in reverse order: that is a transaction. A History owns executed commands in a vector<unique_ptr<Command>> and a redo stack.
  • Fire-and-forget commands are just closures: std::function<void()> on a queue. This is what a thread pool's task queue is (Module 07). The closure is the command object; the captures are its arguments.

C equivalent: struct { int type; union { ... } args; } on a queue, with a switch to execute. The C++ form keeps execute and undo next to each other, so they cannot drift apart when someone edits one.

Banking relevance: a reversal is the undo of a posting. Designing postings as commands with a stored inverse is how reversals stay correct when the posting logic changes.

docs.title: 2.4 State machine: connection states, protocol parser
docs.text:
What: behaviour depends on which of a finite set of states the object is in; events cause transitions.

Three implementations:

  1. Enum + switch in each event handler. The C form, and often the best for small machines: the compiler's -Wswitch tells you about a missing case; everything is in one place; no allocations. Grows badly when states carry different data or when there are many events times many states.
  2. State classes (GoF). class State { virtual unique_ptr<State> on_bytes(...) }, one class per state; the context swaps its unique_ptr<State> on transition; on_enter/ on_exit hooks. Each state's data lives in that state object and is destroyed on exit, which is excellent for "buffer being accumulated during this state". Cost: the transition table is spread across classes; one allocation per transition (avoidable with a pool).
  3. std::variant<Connecting, Authenticating, Ready, Closing, Closed> with std::visit. Each state is a plain struct with its own data; transitions return a new variant value; no heap, no vtable, and a missing (state, event) handler is a compile error. This is the form to prefer in new C++17 code (Module 08 has the full example).

The protocol parser is the state machine you already own. A length-prefixed or delimiter-based framing layer is WaitingForHeader -> ReadingBody -> Complete, with the partial buffer as state data. Writing it as an explicit machine (any of the three forms) instead of nested ifs over bytes_so_far is what makes it testable one byte at a time.

docs.title: 2.5 Template method vs NVI
docs.text:
What: a base class fixes the skeleton of an algorithm; subclasses fill in steps.

NVI (Non-Virtual Interface) is the C++ idiom for doing it safely: the public function is non-virtual and calls private virtual hooks.

class Handler {
public:
    std::string handle(const Request& r) {        // public, NON-virtual: the skeleton
        if (!validate(r)) return "ERR";
        log("start"); auto reply = run(r); log("end"); return reply;
    }
private:
    virtual bool validate(const Request&) { return true; }   // hook with default
    virtual std::string run(const Request&) = 0;              // required hook
};

Why private virtual: a derived class can override a private virtual (access and virtuality are independent in C++), but cannot call it, so nobody can invoke run() without the validation and logging around it. The invariant parts (locking, metrics, exception translation) are in one place and cannot be skipped.

Modern alternative: when the varying part is one step, pass a callable to a free function template (handle_with(request, log, [](auto& r) { ... })). No inheritance. Prefer it unless you need several hooks or per-handler state.

docs.title: 2.6 Visitor: std::variant + std::visit as the modern form
docs.text:
The problem visitor solves: you have a closed set of types and an open set of operations. With virtual functions, adding an operation means editing every type. Visitor flips it: adding an operation is one new visitor; adding a type is the expensive change.

Classic form: Message::accept(Visitor&) calls visitor.visit(*this), which overloads on the concrete type. Double dispatch: first on the message's dynamic type (virtual accept), then on the visitor's overload set. Boilerplate: every element type needs accept; every visitor must implement every visit.

Modern form:

using Message = std::variant<Deposit, Withdrawal, Transfer>;   // a type-safe tagged union

template <class... Ts> struct overloaded : Ts... { using Ts::operator()...; };
template <class... Ts> overloaded(Ts...) -> overloaded<Ts...>;

std::string serialise(const Message& m) {
    return std::visit(overloaded{
        [](const Deposit& d)    { /* ... */ },
        [](const Withdrawal& w) { /* ... */ },
        [](const Transfer& t)   { /* ... */ },
    }, m);
}

No base class, no vptr, no heap, no accept. Forget an alternative and it does not compile. A generic lambda [](const auto& x) { return x.amount; } handles "same code for every alternative". A struct with operator() overloads is a stateful visitor.

C equivalent: struct { enum tag; union { ... }; } plus one switch per operation. std::variant is that with the tag maintained for you, the union typed, and the switch checked for exhaustiveness.

docs.title: 2.7 Chain of responsibility: request middleware
docs.text:
What: a request passes through a sequence of handlers; each can answer it, modify it, or pass it on.

Classic: linked handlers with set_next() and a virtual try_handle() returning optional<Response>. Each link owns the next (unique_ptr), so the chain is a list.

Middleware form (what every web framework and most RPC servers use):

using Handler    = std::function<Response(const Request&)>;
using Middleware = std::function<Handler(Handler next)>;   // wraps the rest of the chain
Handler app = compose({logging(log), auth(), rate_limit(2)}, business_handler);

A middleware receives the rest of the chain as next and returns a new handler that does its work before and/or after calling next. Composition is function application from the inside out. Authentication, rate limiting, logging, tracing, timeouts and retries are each 15 lines and independent of each other and of the business handler.

Note the shared_ptr in rate_limit: the counter table must outlive every copy of the closure, and std::function copies closures. That is a legitimate shared-ownership case (Module 03).

docs.title: 2.8 Iterator
docs.text:
In C++ the iterator pattern is not a virtual interface; it is a protocol the language speaks. Provide begin()/end() returning a type with operator*, operator++, operator==, and the five iterator_traits typedefs, and your container works with range-for and every standard algorithm. The code file has a ring buffer with a forward iterator and a paginated database-cursor-style input iterator that fetches pages lazily, so the consumer sees rows and never pages.

Iterator categories you should be able to name: input (single pass), forward, bidirectional, random access. The category tells algorithms what they may do; std::sort requires random access, std::find only input.

docs.title: 2.9 Choosing
docs.text: Problem First choice in C++17 Classic form Swap one operation at runtime std::function Strategy interface Swap several related operations Interface Strategy interface Notify many listeners vector<function> + RAII token Observer interface Queue work / undo Closures / Command with undo Command interface Finite states with per-state data std::variant + visit State classes Fixed skeleton, varying steps NVI, or callable parameter Template method Closed types, open operations std::variant + visit Visitor Request pipeline Middleware functions Chain of handlers Walk a structure begin()/end() protocol Iterator interface

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
• code/m06_strategy_function_vs_virtual.cpp: fee policy as C function pointer, virtual interface, std::function (with composition), and template parameter; prints sizeof of each so the costs are visible.
  • code/m06_observer_lifetime.cpp: the naive observer (bug explained), the RAII Subscription token with snapshot iteration in notify, an AuditLog that is safe by construction (token as last member), and the weak_ptr variant that prunes dead observers.
  • code/m06_command_undo_queue.cpp: SetCommand/EraseCommand capturing previous state at execute time, CompositeCommand as a transaction, History with undo/redo, and a RequestQueue of closures.
  • code/m06_state_machine_connection.cpp: GoF state classes for a connection protocol (Connecting -> Authenticating -> Ready -> Closing -> Closed), transitions by returning the next state, on_enter/on_exit hooks, attempt counter kept in the context.
  • code/m06_template_method_nvi.cpp: Handler::handle as the fixed skeleton with private virtual validate and run, plus the callable-parameter alternative.
  • code/m06_visitor_variant.cpp: classic accept/visit and the std::variant form with overloaded, a stateful Totals visitor and a generic lambda.
  • code/m06_chain_middleware.cpp: linked handlers with NVI, and compose() for std::function middleware with auth, rate limit and access log.
  • code/m06_iterator.cpp: RingBuffer<T, N>::iterator (forward) and RowIterator (input, paginated), used with range-for, std::accumulate, std::max_element, std::find.

The token-based observer, which is the piece to memorise:

class Subject {
public:
    class Subscription {           // move-only RAII token
    public:
        ~Subscription() { reset(); }
        void reset() { if (subject_) { subject_->unsubscribe(id_); subject_ = nullptr; } }
        /* move ctor/assign transfer subject_ and id_ */
    private:
        Subject* subject_ = nullptr;  std::uint64_t id_ = 0;
    };
    [[nodiscard]] Subscription subscribe(Callback cb);   // dropping the token unsubscribes at once
    void notify(const Event& e);                         // iterates a snapshot of ids
};

class AuditLog {
    std::vector<std::string> lines_;
    Subject::Subscription sub_;   // LAST member: destroyed first, so no callback sees dead lines_
};

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
std::function internals (libstdc++). 32 bytes: a 16-byte local buffer, a pointer to a manager function (copy/destroy/type query) and a pointer to an invoker. Callables that fit in 16 bytes and are nothrow-movable are stored inline (a function pointer, a lambda with one or two pointer captures); larger ones are heap-allocated. Invocation: load the invoker pointer and call it indirectly, which then calls the target. Two indirect calls for the heap case, effectively one for the inline case after inlining of the invoker. Copying a std::function copies the callable (and heap-allocates again if it was on the heap). Hence const std::function& parameters, or templates, on hot paths.

std::variant internals. Storage is a union of the alternatives plus an index (unsigned char for small variants, so sizeof(variant<A,B>) is max(sizeof A, sizeof B) rounded up to alignment, plus one byte, padded). std::visit with one variant compiles to a jump table indexed by the index, or to a switch, with each case calling the visitor overload inline. For n variants it builds an n-dimensional table. No heap, no vptr, fully inlinable. The valueless-by-exception state exists if a converting assignment throws mid-way; std::visit throws bad_variant_access then.

Why a private virtual function can be overridden. Access control applies to names at the point of use; virtual dispatch applies to the vtable slot. Derived::run overrides Base::run regardless of either's access specifier. The call inside Base::handle is this->run(), which is legal inside Base. This is the whole trick behind NVI.

Double dispatch cost. Classic visitor: one virtual call (accept), then one more (visit), each a vptr load plus indirect call. Variant visitor: one bounds-checked index load plus one indirect jump through a table, or a direct switch. Both are cheap; the variant form additionally inlines the visitor bodies, which the classic form cannot.

Observer notify and iterator invalidation. std::vector::erase during range-for over the same vector is undefined behaviour; it may appear to work until the vector reallocates. The snapshot-of-ids approach costs an allocation per notify; an alternative is a "notifying" flag plus a deferred removal list, which is what Qt's signals and most GUI toolkits do internally.

State classes and allocation. Each transition make_unique<NextState>() is a malloc and a free. For a connection handling thousands of messages a second this is noise; for a parser running per byte it is not. Fixes: states as std::variant (no allocation), or a per-context pool of state objects.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
The observer crash, as seen in a dump. Stack: Subject::notify -> ??? (). The frame above is at an address that is not in any module, or in the middle of a function. obs_[i] points into freed memory; the first word (vptr) is whatever the allocator wrote there (often a free-list pointer). The fix is architectural (tokens), not a null check.

Middleware in your RPC server. Authentication, per-client throttling, request logging with correlation ids, latency histograms, and panic-to-error-reply translation are each one middleware. The business handlers contain none of it. When the operations team asks for "log every request over 500 ms", that is a ten-line middleware and a config flag, not a change to forty handlers.

State machines and protocol bugs. A connection stuck in Authenticating forever because the timeout event was only handled in Connecting. With state classes, the missing on_timeout override falls back to the base (if you gave it a default), silently. With the variant form and no default in overloaded, the compiler refuses the missing combination. This is the strongest argument for std::variant state machines in protocol code: every (state, event) pair is reviewed because it must be written down.

Commands for audit and replay. If every mutation of the ledger is a Command with a serialisable form, the audit log is the command log, replay into a fresh store is reconstruction, and reversal is undo. This is event sourcing in one sentence, and it falls out of the pattern for free.

Strategy via configuration. A fee schedule that varies per product and per customer tier, loaded from a table at startup and compiled into std::function objects by a factory, lets the product team change pricing without a deploy. The trade-off is that the set of mechanisms (flat, percent, tiered) is still code; only parameters move to data.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) In the strategy file, add a TieredFee as a std::function built from a std::vector<std::pair<Paise, int>> of thresholds and basis points. Done when t2 is charged at the right tier and the lambda captures the table by value.
  2. (easy) In the observer file, make AuditLog unsubscribe itself from inside its own callback (on the third event). Done when notify() survives the mid-iteration unsubscribe and you can explain why the snapshot made that safe.
  3. (medium) Convert m06_state_machine_connection.cpp to an enum + switch form in one function State step(State, Event, Connection&). Compare line counts and list what each form made easier. Then deliberately remove one case and observe -Wswitch. Done when both compile and you can argue for one in a code review.
  4. (medium) Add a Refund alternative to the modern Message variant. Observe every place the compiler stops you. Then add a fourth message type to the classic hierarchy and list what the compiler did and did not catch. Done when you can state the trade-off "open types vs open operations" from the experience.
  5. (hard) Write a timeout(std::chrono::milliseconds) middleware that runs next on a worker thread and returns 504 if it does not finish in time. Then explain the lifetime problem: what does the worker thread touch after the timeout fired and the Request went out of scope? Fix it by passing the request by value into the worker. Done when -fsanitize=thread,address is clean.
  6. (hard) Make RingBuffer::iterator bidirectional (add operator--) and verify std::reverse_copy works. Then explain why it cannot be random-access without changing the representation (hint: operator+ must be O(1) and comparisons must be consistent across the wrap-around).

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When do you use std::function instead of a strategy interface? A: When the strategy is a single operation and lambdas can capture its parameters. std::function composes easily and avoids a class per strategy. When the strategy has several related operations or identity, an interface is clearer. On a hot path with a compile-time known strategy, a template parameter removes the indirection entirely.

Q: Explain the observer pattern's lifetime bug and how you prevent it. A: The subject holds pointers to observers; an observer destroyed without unsubscribing leaves a dangling pointer that the next notify dereferences. Prevent it with an RAII subscription token that unsubscribes in its destructor, stored as the observer's last member; or with weak_ptr observers that the subject locks and prunes. Also iterate over a snapshot so callbacks may subscribe or unsubscribe during notify.

Q: What is NVI and why are the hooks private? A: Non-Virtual Interface: a public non-virtual function implements the fixed algorithm and calls private virtual hooks. Private virtuals can be overridden but not called by derived classes or outsiders, so the skeleton (validation, locking, logging) cannot be bypassed.

Q: Why is std::variant with std::visit considered the modern visitor? A: It gives the visitor's key property, adding operations without editing types, with no accept boilerplate, no base class, no heap, and compile-time exhaustiveness: a missing alternative fails to compile. The trade-off is the same as classic visitor: the set of types is closed.

Q: Compare three ways to implement a state machine in C++. A: Enum plus switch: simplest, exhaustiveness via -Wswitch, but states cannot carry distinct data cleanly. State classes: per-state data and hooks, but the transition table is scattered and each transition allocates. std::variant of state structs with std::visit: per-state data, no allocation, and every (state, event) pair must be written, which the compiler enforces.

Q: What is middleware and how is it chain of responsibility? A: Each middleware is a function that takes the rest of the chain and returns a handler that does work before or after calling it. Composed inside-out, the first listed is outermost. Each link decides whether to answer, modify or pass on the request, which is exactly chain of responsibility expressed with closures instead of linked objects.

Q: What does a type need to work with range-for and standard algorithms? A: begin() and end() returning an iterator type with operator*, operator++, operator==/!=, and the iterator_traits typedefs (category, value_type, difference_type, pointer, reference). The category tells algorithms what operations are allowed.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Strategy: std::function for one operation, interface for several, template for hot and compile-time known.
  • Observer: the lifetime bug is real; fix it with RAII tokens (last member) or weak_ptr, and iterate a snapshot.
  • Command: capture undo state at execute time; a closure on a queue is a command with no undo.
  • State machine: enum+switch, state classes, or std::variant; prefer variant in new code.
  • Template method: public non-virtual skeleton, private virtual hooks (NVI); or a callable parameter.
  • Visitor: closed types, open operations; std::variant + overloaded + std::visit.
  • Chain of responsibility: middleware as Handler(Handler next), composed inside-out.
  • Iterator: a protocol, not an interface; provide begin/end and the typedefs.
  • std::function is 32 bytes with a 16-byte inline buffer; std::variant is a typed union with an index and a jump table.

docs.title: 07. Concurrency Patterns
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 03, 06; 04_Concurrency (mutex, condition_variable, threads, futures)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Every concurrency pattern is an answer to one question: which thread is allowed to touch this state, and how do the others ask it to? There are only a few good answers. Lock the state and let any thread touch it under the lock (monitor). Give the state its own thread and send it requests (active object, actor). Make the state immutable and share it freely (snapshots). Or do not share at all and pass values through queues (producer-consumer).

You maintain a multithreaded RPC server, so you have already met all of these, possibly without names: the connection table under a mutex is a monitor; the worker threads pulling from a request queue are a thread pool over a producer-consumer queue; the config you reload by swapping a pointer is a snapshot. This module names them, shows the idiomatic C++17 spelling of each, and, more importantly, tells you which one to pick for which shape of problem. The mechanics of mutexes and condition variables are in 04_Concurrency; here we talk about structure.

docs.title: 2.1 Monitor object
docs.text:
What: an object whose every public method acquires the object's own mutex. Callers never lock; the invariant is protected at the class boundary. Condition variables inside let methods wait for a state ("not empty") without the caller knowing.

Shape:

class BoundedQueue {
    mutable std::mutex mu_;  std::condition_variable not_empty_, not_full_;  std::deque<T> q_;
public:
    bool push(T);                 // waits while full
    std::optional<T> pop();       // waits while empty; nullopt when closed and drained
    void close();                 // wakes everyone
};

Rules:

  • Wait with a predicate: cv.wait(lk, [&]{ return closed_ || !q_.empty(); }). This handles spurious wakeups and the "notify before wait" race.
  • Unlock before notify when you can; the woken thread can then take the lock immediately instead of blocking on it.
  • Never call out to unknown code (callbacks, virtual functions on foreign objects) while holding the monitor lock. That is how you get deadlocks between two monitors (A's method calls B under A's lock while B's method calls A under B's lock).
  • close() for shutdown: a closed flag plus notify_all, producers get false, consumers drain and get nullopt.

Cost: every call serialises on the mutex. Fine for a queue (operations are tiny). Bad for a hot read-mostly structure (see snapshots).

C equivalent: pthread_mutex_t and pthread_cond_t in the struct, every function does lock/unlock by hand. Same design; the C++ version makes the unlock unforgettable.

docs.title: 2.2 Producer-consumer and bounded queues
docs.text:
What: producers push work, consumers pop it, a queue decouples their rates. The queue is the monitor above.

The bound is the design decision. An unbounded queue lets a burst of requests consume all memory while consumers fall behind; the process dies of OOM an hour later, far from the cause. A bounded queue makes producers block (back-pressure) or fail fast ("server busy"). In a server, fail fast at the edge is almost always right: reject new connections or return a "try later" error while the queue is full, rather than accepting work you cannot finish.

Sizing: bound = consumers times the acceptable queueing delay in units of per-item service time. Eight workers at 1 ms per item and a 50 ms latency budget suggests a bound around 400. Make it configurable; measure.

docs.title: 2.3 Thread pool
docs.text:
What: N worker threads pulling from one task queue; tasks return futures. Fixed N means no thread-per-request explosion and no thread creation cost per request.

Shape: std::future<R> submit(F&& f, Args&&... args) packages the call in a std::packaged_task, pushes a type-erased std::function<void()> onto the queue, returns the future. Exceptions inside the task are stored in the future and rethrown at get().

Rules:

  • Never block a pool thread on work from the same pool. Four workers each submit a child and get() it: all four block waiting for children that can never run. Deadlock. Fixes: separate pools per dependency level, or continuation-style (then) instead of blocking, or ensure children are run inline when called from a pool thread.
  • Capture by value. A task may run long after the submitting scope has ended. [&local] is the most common thread-pool crash.
  • Bound the queue (Section 2.2), and decide what submit does when full: throw, block, or return a failed future.
  • Sizing: CPU-bound work: number of cores. I/O-bound work that blocks (database calls): more, bounded by the downstream's capacity (your database's connection limit), and ideally a separate pool so a slow database does not starve CPU work.
  • Shutdown: stop flag under the lock, notify_all, join all. Decide whether queued tasks are drained or dropped and document it.

C equivalent: pthread_create N times, a mutex/cond queue of {void (*fn)(void*), void* arg}. Results via out-pointers and a separate completion signal; no futures.

docs.title: 2.4 Active object
docs.text:
What: an object with its own thread and a queue of method calls. Callers enqueue closures and receive futures. The object's state is touched by exactly one thread, so it needs no mutex; the queue is the only synchronised structure.

When: state that must be mutated strictly in order (a ledger, a log writer, a device driver), or that would otherwise need a complex lock protocol. Trades lock complexity for one context switch per call and one thread per object.

Monitor vs active object in one line: a monitor runs methods on the caller's thread under a lock; an active object runs them on its own thread from a queue.

Cost: a thread per object (so do not make a thousand of them), latency of a queue hop (microseconds), and the result is asynchronous (a future) even when the caller wanted a plain return value.

docs.title: 2.5 Reactor vs proactor
docs.text:
These describe how an I/O-driven server is organised.

Reactor: one (or a few) event-loop threads block in epoll_wait (Linux) or select/ WaitForMultipleObjects (Windows). When a socket is readable, the loop calls the connection's handler, which performs the non-blocking read itself and parses. Readiness is reported; the application does the I/O. libevent, Node.js, Redis, Nginx are reactors.

Proactor: the application initiates an asynchronous read ("read up to 4 KB into this buffer and tell me when done"); the OS performs the I/O; a completion event is delivered with the data already in the buffer. Completion is reported; the OS did the I/O. Windows IOCP is the canonical proactor; Linux io_uring is one; Boost.Asio presents a proactor interface over both (emulating it on epoll).

Reactor:   epoll_wait -> "fd 7 readable" -> handler calls read(7, buf) -> parse
Proactor:  ReadAsync(fd 7, buf) ... later ... completion(fd 7, 1024 bytes in buf) -> parse

Trade-offs: proactor needs buffers to be committed up front for every pending read (memory proportional to connections); reactor allocates a buffer only when data is ready. Proactor maps better to Windows and to true async disk I/O. Reactor is simpler to reason about and is what Linux servers mostly use. Your Win32 server is very likely IOCP (proactor) or select-based (reactor); know which and why.

Pairing with workers: either model usually hands parsed requests to a thread pool and gets replies back through a queue the loop drains (eventfd/pipe/PostQueuedCompletionStatus to wake the loop). The ownership rule from Module 03 applies: workers hold ConnId, not Connection*.

docs.title: 2.6 Read-copy-update snapshots and immutable messages
docs.text:
Problem: configuration, routing tables, fee schedules: read on every request by every thread, updated rarely. A mutex around reads serialises the hot path for the sake of a once-a-minute write. A reader-writer lock helps but still has shared cache-line traffic.

Solution: readers take a std::shared_ptr<const Config> snapshot (atomic load plus a refcount increment), use it lock-free, drop it. Writers copy the current config, modify the copy, and atomically swap the pointer. Readers holding the old snapshot see a consistent version until they finish; the old object is freed when the last reference drops.

std::shared_ptr<const Config> snapshot() const { return std::atomic_load(&current_); }
void update(F mutate) { lock_guard lk(writer_mu_); Config next = *atomic_load(&current_);
                        mutate(next); atomic_store(&current_, make_shared<const Config>(move(next))); }

Why const: immutability is what makes the sharing safe. A published snapshot is never written again, so any number of threads may read it with no synchronisation. This is also the rule for immutable messages between threads: build the message, then hand it over; never mutate it after sending. Passing by value (move) achieves this trivially; passing shared_ptr<const T> achieves it for large objects.

Relation to kernel RCU: same idea. Readers never block; writers pay a copy; old versions linger until all readers are done (the kernel detects quiescence; shared_ptr counts references).

C++17 detail: std::atomic_load/atomic_store on shared_ptr are free functions (deprecated in C++20 in favour of std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>). They are typically implemented with a small internal spinlock table, so they are not strictly lock-free, but they are uncontended and fast.

docs.title: 2.7 Actor model
docs.text:
What: every actor owns its state, processes one message at a time from its mailbox, and communicates only by sending immutable messages to other actors by address (a name or handle), never by pointer. No shared mutable state means no data races by construction.

Active object is an actor with a typed method interface; the actor model generalises it to untyped messages, dynamic addressing, and supervision (an actor that restarts failed children). Erlang/OTP and Akka are the reference systems.

When in C++: systems with many independent stateful entities and complex interaction protocols: per-account state, per-session state, sagas (multi-step transactions with compensation), simulation. The code file runs a transfer as a saga across two account actors with a coordinator.

Costs: every interaction is asynchronous (a message, not a return value), which makes simple request-reply logic verbose; one thread per actor does not scale past hundreds, so real actor systems schedule actors onto a pool; message ordering is guaranteed only per sender-receiver pair.

docs.title: 2.8 Choosing
docs.text:
State shape Pattern Small shared structure, short operations, any thread Monitor object Work handoff between stages Bounded producer-consumer queue Many independent CPU or I/O tasks Thread pool (bounded queue, by-value captures) State that must be mutated in strict order Active object Read-mostly shared data Immutable snapshots via shared_ptr<const T> Many stateful entities with protocols between them Actors Network I/O multiplexing Reactor (epoll) or proactor (IOCP, io_uring) feeding a pool

The first question in a design review: "which thread owns this state?" If the answer is "any thread, under this lock" you have a monitor and need to check every call path for lock ordering. If the answer is "this one thread" you have an active object or actor and need to check that nothing else touches it. If the answer is "nobody writes it after publication" you have a snapshot and need nothing else.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
• code/m07_active_object.cpp: ActiveLedger with a private worker thread, enqueue() returning futures via packaged_task, strict in-order postings from four client threads, drain-on-destroy.
  • code/m07_monitor_producer_consumer.cpp: BoundedQueue<T> with push, pop, pop_for(timeout), close(); three producers, two consumers, bound of 8 so back-pressure occurs.
  • code/m07_thread_pool.cpp: ThreadPool with submit(f, args...), by-value argument capture through std::apply, bounded queue with rejection, exceptions through futures, the deadlock rule in a comment.
  • code/m07_rcu_snapshot.cpp: ConfigHolder with snapshot() (atomic load) and update() (copy, mutate, atomic store); four readers verify every snapshot is internally consistent while a writer swaps 20 versions.
  • code/m07_actor.cpp: Mailbox, ActorSystem (mailboxes by name), account_actor, coordinator_actor running a debit-then-credit saga with compensation, messages as a std::variant.

The bounded queue's pop is the template for every condition-variable wait you will write:

std::optional<T> pop() {
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(mu_);
    not_empty_.wait(lk, [this] { return closed_ || !q_.empty(); });   // predicate: re-checked on every wake
    if (q_.empty()) return std::nullopt;                               // closed and drained
    T item = std::move(q_.front());  q_.pop_front();
    lk.unlock();                                                       // release before notify
    not_full_.notify_one();
    return item;
}

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What condition_variable::wait does. Atomically releases the mutex and sleeps on a futex (Linux) keyed on the CV's internal word; on wake it re-acquires the mutex before returning. Spurious wakeups are real: the futex can return without a matching notify (signal delivery, timeouts, implementation details), which is why the predicate loop is mandatory. notify_one is a FUTEX_WAKE syscall only if there is a waiter; libstdc++ tracks this to avoid the syscall when nobody is waiting.

Why unlock before notify. If you notify while holding the lock, the woken thread immediately blocks on the mutex you still hold, costing an extra context switch (the "hurry up and wait" problem). Unlocking first lets it proceed. Some argue for notify-under- lock for strict ordering guarantees; for a queue it is unnecessary.

packaged_task and future internals. A shared state object on the heap holds the result or exception, a ready flag and a futex-like waiter. get() blocks on it. The packaged_task is move-only (it owns the promise side); that is why the pool wraps it in a shared_ptr to stuff it into a copyable std::function. Each submit therefore allocates: the shared state, the packaged_task, possibly the std::function target. For a microsecond-level hot path you would use a lock-free queue of fixed-size task structs; for request handling it is irrelevant.

shared_ptr snapshot cost. atomic_load(&sp) is an atomic pointer read plus an atomic increment on the control block (lock xadd). With four readers on four cores all incrementing the same control block, that cache line bounces between cores: tens of nanoseconds per snapshot rather than one. Still far cheaper than a mutex, and readers take one snapshot per request, not per field access. For the very hottest paths, thread-local cached snapshots refreshed by generation counter remove even that.

epoll vs IOCP, mechanically. epoll_wait returns a list of ready fds; the kernel kept a ready-list that network interrupts append to. The application then calls read, copying from the socket buffer into user memory. IOCP: WSARecv posts a user buffer to the kernel; when data arrives the kernel copies directly into it and queues a completion packet; GetQueuedCompletionStatus dequeues it. IOCP also limits the number of concurrently running threads to the number you specify, waking another only when one blocks, which is a built-in thread-pool scheduler. io_uring brings the posted-buffer completion model to Linux with shared submission/completion rings and no syscall per operation in the fast path.

Actor mailboxes and ordering. A mailbox is a monitor queue. Message order is FIFO per mailbox, so messages from A to B arrive in the order A sent them, but messages from A and C to B interleave arbitrarily. Protocol design must not depend on cross-sender order. This is the same constraint as TCP (ordered per connection) and the same mistake people make.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
Your server's worker pool at 3 AM. Requests time out; CPU is idle; the queue is full. All workers are blocked in database calls because the database is slow. Diagnosis: gdb -p or a dump shows every worker in PQexec. Fixes: a separate pool for database-bound work with a size matching the database's capacity; a timeout on the database call; shedding load at the edge (bounded queue, "busy" reply) so clients retry instead of piling up. The underlying design error was one pool for two different resource constraints.

The config reload that crashed. Old design: Config g_config; behind a mutex; reload mutated it in place while a request thread was halfway through reading three related fields and saw a mix of old and new. Fix: snapshots. The reload builds a new Config and swaps the pointer; every request sees exactly one version. This is a one-afternoon change that removes a class of bugs that look like "random" misbehaviour once a day.

The thread-pool capture bug. A handler submits [&request] { ... } and returns; the request lives on the connection's stack frame which is reused; the task reads garbage or writes into the next request. AddressSanitizer catches it in test if the test actually exercises the async path. Rule in code review: every lambda submitted to a pool is checked for & captures and this.

Shutdown ordering. Pool destructor joins workers; workers may be mid-task calling into the store; store must still exist. Declaration order in the owning class (Module 03): store before pool. Also decide: drain or drop queued tasks on shutdown? For a banking server, drain (a posting that was accepted must complete), with a timeout and a log of anything dropped.

Windows note. On your Win32 server the equivalents are CRITICAL_SECTION / SRWLOCK + CONDITION_VARIABLE, IOCP for the reactor/proactor role, and the Windows thread pool API. The patterns are identical; std::thread and friends map onto them in MSVC's standard library.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) In m07_monitor_producer_consumer.cpp, set the bound to 1 and to 1000. Measure total runtime and maximum observed size(). Done when you can explain what the bound trades.
  2. (easy) Add try_push(T) to BoundedQueue that returns false immediately when full instead of blocking. Use it in a producer that counts rejections. Done when you can state when a server should block producers and when it should reject.
  3. (medium) Reproduce the thread-pool self-deadlock: a 2-thread pool, two tasks that each submit a child task and get() it. Observe the hang. Then fix it without changing pool size (hint: run the child inline when std::this_thread::get_id() belongs to the pool). Done when the fixed version completes and you can explain why the detection is needed.
  4. (medium) Convert ConfigHolder to use a std::shared_mutex with readers taking shared_lock. Benchmark 4 readers at -O2 against the snapshot version for one second each. Done when you have numbers and an explanation involving cache lines.
  5. (hard) Extend m07_actor.cpp with a supervisor actor: if an account actor receives a Crash{} message it throws; the supervisor catches the thread's failure (hint: run the actor body in a try, send a Died{name} message), restarts it with the last known balance, and re-sends any messages that were in flight. Done when a transfer survives a crash of one account actor.
  6. (hard) Write a minimal reactor on Linux: epoll on a listening socket plus connections, non-blocking reads into per-connection buffers, echo back. Then add a ThreadPool for "processing" with (ConnId, std::string) messages in both directions and an eventfd to wake the loop when replies are ready. Done when a client disconnecting mid-request causes the reply to be dropped, not a crash.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a monitor object and an active object? A: A monitor runs methods on the caller's thread under the object's mutex; many threads enter one at a time. An active object runs methods on its own thread from a queue of requests; callers get futures. Monitors are simpler and synchronous; active objects remove locking from the object and guarantee ordering at the cost of a thread and asynchronous results.

Q: Why must a condition variable wait use a predicate loop? A: Because wakeups can be spurious, because notify may happen before wait (the notification is lost unless the predicate is checked first), and because another thread may consume the state between the notify and your re-acquiring the lock. The predicate re-check handles all three.

Q: Why should a work queue be bounded? A: An unbounded queue turns overload into unbounded memory growth and an OOM far from the cause. A bound gives back-pressure (producers block) or fast failure (reject at the edge), keeping latency and memory predictable. Rejecting early lets clients retry against a server that is still healthy.

Q: Explain reactor versus proactor. A: Reactor: the event loop waits for readiness (epoll) and the application performs the non-blocking I/O itself. Proactor: the application posts an asynchronous operation with a buffer and is notified on completion with the data already there (IOCP, io_uring). Proactor commits buffers up front; reactor is simpler on Linux. Both typically hand parsed work to a pool.

Q: How do you share a frequently read, rarely updated configuration across threads? A: Publish immutable snapshots: readers take a shared_ptr<const Config> with an atomic load and use it lock-free; writers copy, modify, and atomically swap the pointer. Old versions are freed when the last reader drops them. Readers never block and always see one consistent version.

Q: What is the classic thread-pool deadlock and how do you avoid it? A: A pool task blocks waiting on another task in the same pool; with all workers blocked, the awaited tasks never run. Avoid by never blocking a pool thread on same-pool work: use continuations, separate pools per dependency level, or run child tasks inline when called from a pool thread.

Q: What makes the actor model free of data races? A: Each actor's state is touched only by its own processing loop, and actors communicate only through immutable messages sent to mailboxes by address. There is no shared mutable state to race on; the only synchronised structure is the mailbox queue.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Ask "which thread owns this state?" before choosing a pattern.
  • Monitor: mutex inside the object, predicate waits, no callbacks under the lock.
  • Bounded producer-consumer queues give back-pressure; the bound is a design decision.
  • Thread pool: by-value captures, bounded queue, never block on same-pool work, size by resource.
  • Active object: own thread plus queue; strict ordering, no internal locks, async results.
  • Reactor reports readiness (epoll); proactor reports completion (IOCP, io_uring).
  • Snapshots: shared_ptr<const T>, atomic load/store, copy-on-write; immutability makes sharing safe.
  • Actors: state per actor, messages by address, FIFO per mailbox only.
  • Shutdown is declaration order: pools declared last, resources they use declared first.

docs.title: 08. Modern C++ Alternatives to Classic Patterns
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 05, 06; templates basics from 02_Modern_CPP

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
The classic design patterns were catalogued in 1994 for languages where the only way to vary behaviour was a class hierarchy with virtual functions. C++ today has three more tools: templates (decide at compile time), std::function-style type erasure (decide at runtime without a base class), and std::variant (a closed set of alternatives checked by the compiler). Most patterns from Modules 04 to 06 have a shorter, faster form using one of them.

This module is about the trade. Templates move work from run time to compile time: the program runs faster and the binary and build get bigger. Type erasure gives runtime flexibility without forcing your types to inherit from anything. Variants give exhaustiveness checking. None of them is free, and a senior engineer can say, for a given seam, which one to use and what it costs in nanoseconds, bytes and seconds of compile time.

The C analogy for the whole module: a macro versus a function pointer. The macro is resolved at build time, inlined, fast, and produces one copy per use site. The function pointer is resolved at run time, one copy of the code, slower per call, swappable. Templates are macros with type checking; type erasure is function pointers with type checking.

docs.title: 2.1 Type erasure: std::function, std::any, hand-rolled
docs.text:
Problem: you want to store "anything with put() and get()" behind one type, by value, but the candidate types come from different libraries and share no base class. Inheritance would require editing them.

Mechanism (the thing to be able to draw on a whiteboard):

AnyStore                        heap
+----------------+              +------------------------+
| unique_ptr -------------->    | Model<MapStore>        |  : Concept (abstract)
+----------------+              |  vptr -> Model<MapStore> vtable
                                |  MapStore obj_         |
                                +------------------------+
  • Concept: an abstract class, private to the wrapper, declaring the operations.
  • Model<T>: a template deriving from Concept, holding a T by value, forwarding each operation to obj_.
  • The wrapper holds unique_ptr<Concept> and exposes the operations.

The user's T never inherits from anything. The vtable lives in Model<T>, generated per T when the wrapper is constructed from one. Value semantics (copy via a virtual clone()) are preserved.

The standard examples:

  • std::function<R(Args...)>: erases callables. 32 bytes on libstdc++, 16-byte inline buffer, heap otherwise. Owning.
  • std::any: erases anything copyable; retrieval needs any_cast<T> with the exact type. Rarely the right tool (it is a typed void*); useful for plug-in property bags.
  • std::shared_ptr<void> with a typed deleter erases the deleter type. unique_ptr<T, D> does not (D is part of the type).

function_ref: the non-owning version: two pointers (object, trampoline), no allocation, accepts any callable including capturing lambdas, must not outlive the callable. It is the correct parameter type for "I will call this during my call and not store it". Not in the standard until C++26; the code file hand-rolls it in 15 lines.

Cost: same as virtual dispatch (one indirect call, no inlining) plus, for owning wrappers, a heap allocation unless small-buffer optimised.

When: you need runtime polymorphism over types you do not control, or you want value semantics (copyable, stack-allocatable) for polymorphic objects, or your API should accept lambdas and functors uniformly.

docs.title: 2.2 CRTP for static polymorphism
docs.text:
Mechanism: class Derived : public Base<Derived>. Inside Base, static_cast<Derived&> (*this).step() calls the derived function. The compiler knows the exact type, so the call is direct and inlinable. No vptr, no vtable.

template <class Derived>
class RequestProcessor {
public:
    std::string process(const std::string& in) {           // template method, zero virtual calls
        auto& self = static_cast<Derived&>(*this);
        if (!self.validate(in)) return "ERR";
        return self.run(in);
    }
    bool validate(const std::string& s) const { return !s.empty(); }   // default; Derived may shadow
};
class EchoProcessor : public RequestProcessor<EchoProcessor> { std::string run(const std::string&); };

What you lose: a common base type. RequestProcessor<Echo> and RequestProcessor<Upper> are unrelated types; you cannot put them in one vector<Base*>. If you need that, you need virtual dispatch (or type erasure on top).

Mixins are CRTP's second use: struct Money : Comparable<Money> defines operator< and gets >, <=, >=, ==, != generated as friends. Boost.Operators is this pattern.

When: template-method shaped code on a hot path; mixins that add operators or bookkeeping to many unrelated types; libraries where the user supplies the derived class (Eigen, many serialisation libraries).

docs.title: 2.3 Policy-based design
docs.text:
Mechanism: the host class takes its behavioural pieces as template parameters: PolicyStore<HashedStorage, MutexLock, StdoutLog>. Each policy is a small class with an agreed (duck-typed) interface. The host inherits from or holds them.

It is the decorator stack of Module 05 flattened into one type at compile time: Logging <Metrics<Retry<Memory>>> becomes Store<Memory, Retry, Metrics, Logging> with no virtual calls between layers and every layer inlinable.

Zero-cost layers: a NoLock policy whose Guard has an empty constructor compiles to nothing. A NoLog::log that is an empty static inline function compiles to nothing. The empty base optimisation makes stateless policies take zero bytes in the host. This is how you write one Store that is lock-free in a single-threaded tool and mutex-protected in the server, with no runtime flag.

Cost: one host instantiation per combination; combinations are types, so configuration is a build-time decision; error messages when a policy does not fit are long (C++20 concepts fix this; in C++17, static_assert on the policy's members helps). Readers must understand templates.

When: libraries and infrastructure where the configuration is fixed per build and performance matters: allocators, containers, logging frameworks, serialisers. Not for business logic that product people change weekly.

docs.title: 2.4 Tag dispatch
docs.text:
Mechanism: select an overload by passing an empty struct whose only purpose is its type. std::advance(it, n) calls advance_impl(it, n, iterator_category{}); the random-access overload does it += n, the input-iterator overload loops. Derived tags convert to base tags, so one fallback overload catches a family.

C++17 alternative: if constexpr (std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>) { ... } else { ... }. Prefer if constexpr for short branches inside one function. Prefer tags when the implementations are large, live in different headers, or must be extensible by users adding their own overloads for their own tags (open for extension, at compile time).

docs.title: 2.5 std::variant state machines
docs.text:
Module 06 showed the state-class form; the code file here builds a protocol framer with both states and events as variants and a single overload set of transitions:

using State = std::variant<WaitHeader, ReadBody, Complete, Failed>;
using Event = std::variant<Bytes, Timeout, Reset>;
Step step(State s, const Event& e) {
    return std::visit(overloaded{
        [](WaitHeader st, const Bytes& b) -> Step { /* accumulate 4 bytes, parse length */ },
        [](ReadBody st,   const Bytes& b) -> Step { /* accumulate body */ },
        [](Complete,      const Reset&)   -> Step { return {WaitHeader{}, 0}; },
        [](auto,          const Reset&)   -> Step { return {WaitHeader{}, 0}; },
        [](auto st, const auto&) -> Step { /* loud fallback */ },
    }, std::move(s), e);
}

Properties: every transition in one place; each state carries exactly its data (the partial header, the body so far) and that data is destroyed on transition; no heap; two-dimensional visit builds a (states x events) jump table. The fallback is the one danger: it can hide a forgotten pair, so make it log loudly or omit it and let the compiler complain.

docs.title: 2.6 Ranges-style pipelines
docs.text:
Mechanism: adaptors (filter, map) are small structs that wrap a source and a callable; operator| nests them; nothing executes until a terminal operation iterates. The whole chain is one nested type, so every callable is inlined and the compiler sees a single loop. C++20 <ranges> is the standard version; the code file has a 60-line C++17 model showing the mechanism.

Cost model: zero runtime dispatch; the pipeline object is the size of its captured state (a reference plus empty lambdas is 8 to 16 bytes); but each distinct pipeline is a distinct type with its own instantiated code. Compile time grows with the number of distinct chains. Debugging steps through template machinery.

docs.title: 2.7 When templates beat virtual, with the costs
docs.text:
Dimension Virtual / std::function Template / CRTP / policy Decision time Run time Compile time Call cost 2 loads + indirect call, no inlining Direct, inlined; enables vectorisation and constant folding Per-object size +8 bytes vptr (or 32 bytes for std::function) 0 (empty base optimisation for stateless policies) Heterogeneous containers vector<unique_ptr<Base>> works Not directly; need std::variant or type erasure Open set of implementations (plug-ins, other TUs) Yes No (all types known where instantiated) Binary size One copy of each function One copy per instantiation Compile time Low; implementation in .cpp Higher; implementation in headers, recompiled per TU Error messages Clear Long (improved by static_assert, fixed by C++20 concepts) ABI / shared library boundary Stable if interface stable Templates cannot cross a binary boundary as templates

The decision rule: if the choice depends on runtime data (config, message type, client) or must be made by code you do not compile (plug-ins), use virtual or type erasure. If the choice is fixed at build time and the code is hot or the layering is deep, use templates. If the set of alternatives is closed and small and you want exhaustiveness checking, use std::variant.

Order of magnitude for "hot": a virtual call costs single-digit nanoseconds when predicted. A database round trip costs 100 microseconds or more. Anything that happens once per request around I/O can be virtual with no measurable effect. Anything that happens per byte, per element or per hash-table probe should be a template.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
• code/m08_type_erasure.cpp: AnyStore (Concept/Model/clone, value semantics) holding a MapStore and a VectorStore with no common base; function_ref hand-rolled and used as a callback parameter accepting a capturing lambda; sizeof printed for both.
  • code/m08_crtp_policy.cpp: RequestProcessor<Derived> as a zero-virtual template method, Comparable<Derived> mixin, and PolicyStore<Storage, Lock, Log> with NoLock/MutexLock and NoLog/StdoutLog, including sizeof showing the empty base optimisation.
  • code/m08_variant_state_machine.cpp: the length-prefixed framer with variant states and events, a Framer driver that feeds arbitrary chunk sizes, timeout and bad-length paths.
  • code/m08_tag_dispatch_pipeline.cpp: copy_records dispatching on trivial copyability, my_advance dispatching on iterator category, if constexpr comparison, and a lazy from(c) | filter(...) | map(...) pipeline with to_vector and sum.

The type-erasure core, which is the part to memorise:

class AnyStore {
public:
    template <class T, class = std::enable_if_t<!std::is_same_v<std::decay_t<T>, AnyStore>>>
    AnyStore(T&& obj) : self_(std::make_unique<Model<std::decay_t<T>>>(std::forward<T>(obj))) {}
    AnyStore(const AnyStore& o) : self_(o.self_->clone()) {}
    void put(const std::string& k, const std::string& v) { self_->put(k, v); }
private:
    struct Concept { virtual ~Concept() = default;
                     virtual void put(const std::string&, const std::string&) = 0;
                     virtual std::unique_ptr<Concept> clone() const = 0; };
    template <class T> struct Model final : Concept {
        explicit Model(T obj) : obj_(std::move(obj)) {}
        void put(const std::string& k, const std::string& v) override { obj_.put(k, v); }
        std::unique_ptr<Concept> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<Model>(obj_); }
        T obj_;
    };
    std::unique_ptr<Concept> self_;
};

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What a template instantiation costs the compiler. Each distinct PolicyStore<A, B, C> is parsed, type-checked, and code-generated separately in every translation unit that uses it; the linker then discards the duplicates (COMDAT folding). A header-heavy template codebase can spend most of its build time generating code it throws away. Mitigations: explicit instantiation in one .cpp (template class PolicyStore<...>;) with extern template in the header; keeping non-dependent code out of templates (hoist it into a non-template base); precompiled headers; and simply not templating what does not need it.

Code size. Ten pipelines with different lambdas are ten loops in the binary. Usually small, but instruction-cache pressure is real on hot paths: a tight loop that fits in L1i can be slower when surrounded by many near-duplicate instantiations. Measure with size and perf stat -e L1-icache-load-misses before assuming templates are faster.

Devirtualisation is not nothing. With -O2, GCC devirtualises calls when the dynamic type is provable (final classes, local objects, after inlining a factory). With -flto it does whole-program speculative devirtualisation: if (vptr == &Derived::vtable) inline else call. So the virtual-vs-template gap is sometimes smaller than the table above suggests. The gap is largest when the call site is genuinely polymorphic at run time.

std::visit compiled. For one variant, libstdc++ builds a constexpr array of function pointers indexed by index() and calls through it; for small variants GCC often turns this into a switch and inlines the lambdas. For two variants (states x events) the table is two-dimensional. std::get_if is a compare of the index and a pointer offset.

Empty base optimisation. A base class with no non-static data members occupies zero bytes in the derived object (the standard requires distinct addresses only for distinct subobjects of the same type). That is why PolicyStore<HashedStorage, NoLock, NoLog> is exactly the size of the unordered_map. Policies held as members instead of bases would cost at least one byte each plus padding; C++20's [[no_unique_address]] fixes that for members.

Type erasure's hidden allocation and how to remove it. Owning wrappers allocate for Model<T>. A small-buffer optimisation keeps Model<T> inline when sizeof(T) fits (say, 32 bytes) and heap-allocates otherwise; this is what std::function does with its 16-byte buffer. The implementation uses std::aligned_storage and placement new, with the Concept vtable still in play. Move semantics for the inline case must move the object, not the pointer, which is why std::function's move is not guaranteed noexcept-cheap for every target.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
Where this shows up in a server. The storage interface at the service boundary: virtual (runtime choice of backend, needs a test fake). The framing and parsing of bytes on the socket: templates or std::variant (hot, fixed at build time). Per-request middleware: std::function (configured at startup, called once per request, cost invisible). Metrics and logging inside the hash-table implementation: policy template (called per probe, must compile away when disabled).

A real cost conversation. A team moved a decoder from a virtual Codec interface to a template because a profile showed 12% of CPU in Codec::decode dispatch and lost inlining. Decode time dropped 35%. Build time for the TU went from 4 seconds to 40 because the decoder was now instantiated in nine places. They added explicit instantiation for the three codecs actually used and got back to 9 seconds. Both numbers mattered; the senior decision was to pay the build cost once it was bounded.

The type-erasure trap. std::function members in a hot object (one per callback in a connection class with 50,000 connections): 32 bytes each, plus a heap block each when the captured lambda exceeds 16 bytes. Memory doubled. Fix: function_ref where the callback is only used during a call; a single std::function to a per-connection handler object otherwise; or a plain function pointer plus void* context (the C way is sometimes the right C++ way).

Error messages. A policy that lacks a required member produces a 200-line error from inside the host template. Put static_assert(has_guard_v<Lock>, "Lock policy must define Guard") at the top of the host; the error becomes one line. In C++20 a concept does this natively.

Code review question to ask every time: "Does this decision need to be made at run time?" If the answer is no, the virtual function is a cost without benefit. If the answer is yes, the template is a flexibility you cannot use.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Add a third store type to m08_type_erasure.cpp that is a struct with std::function members for put and get. Store it in the same vector<AnyStore>. Done when it works without modifying AnyStore.
