  2. (easy) In m08_crtp_policy.cpp, write a CountingLog policy that counts calls in a static counter. Compose PolicyStore<OrderedStorage, NoLock, CountingLog>. Done when sizeof is unchanged from NoLog and the count is correct.
  3. (medium) Give AnyStore a small-buffer optimisation: 32 bytes of aligned storage; Model<T> constructed in place if it fits, on the heap otherwise. Done when sizeof(AnyStore) is 40 or 48, MapStore (a std::map, 48 bytes) goes to the heap, and a tiny store stays inline; verify with a counting operator new.
  4. (medium) Add an Escape event and a Paused state to the variant framer. Observe which overloads the compiler asks you to add, and which fell into the fallback. Then remove the fallback and list every (state, event) pair you had to write. Done when the machine compiles without a fallback.
  5. (hard) Benchmark m05_decorator_store.cpp's virtual decorator stack (Logging over Metrics over Memory, with logging to a null sink) against a policy version PolicyStore<HashedStorage, NoLock, NullLog> with a metrics policy, 10 million get calls at -O2. Report ns/call for both and the binary size of each. Done when you can explain the ratio and state when it would and would not matter.
  6. (hard) Compile m08_tag_dispatch_pipeline.cpp with -O2 -S and find the loop that sum(pipeline) became. Confirm there is no call instruction inside it. Then replace the lambdas with std::function objects and find the calls. Done when you can point to the indirect call instruction and the vptr-like load that precedes it.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is type erasure and how does std::function implement it? A: Runtime polymorphism without a common base class. The wrapper holds an internal abstract Concept; a template Model<T> implements it by forwarding to a T it owns; the vtable lives in the wrapper, not in the user's type. std::function adds a 16-byte inline buffer for small callables and heap-allocates larger ones; invocation is an indirect call.

Q: When would you choose CRTP over virtual functions? A: When the derived type is known at compile time and the call is hot: template-method skeletons, mixins that generate operators, library bases where the user supplies the derived type. CRTP gives direct, inlinable calls and no vptr but loses the common base type, so you cannot store mixed derived types in one container.

Q: What is policy-based design and what does it cost? A: The host class takes behavioural pieces as template parameters (storage, locking, logging), composing them at compile time with no virtual calls; stateless policies cost zero bytes via the empty base optimisation. Costs: one instantiation per combination, configuration fixed at build time, longer error messages, and header-only implementation.

Q: Explain the full cost comparison between a virtual call and a template call. A: Virtual: two dependent loads plus an indirect call, cheap when predicted, but no inlining, so the optimiser cannot fold constants, hoist or vectorise across it, and each object carries a vptr. Template: direct call, inlined, optimisable; but one code copy per instantiation (binary size, instruction cache, compile time) and the type must be known at compile time. The right choice depends on whether the decision is a runtime one and how hot the call is.

Q: Why is std::variant a good fit for state machines? A: Each state is a struct carrying exactly its data, destroyed on transition; all transitions can live in one overload set; there is no heap or vtable; and std::visit requires a handler for every combination, so forgotten (state, event) pairs are compile errors unless you add a fallback.

Q: What is tag dispatch and when is if constexpr better? A: Tag dispatch selects an overload by passing an empty tag type (as std::advance does with iterator categories), with derived tags falling back to base overloads. if constexpr is simpler when the branches are short and in one function; tags are better when implementations are large, in different headers, or must be extensible by user-provided overloads.

Q: What is function_ref and when do you use it instead of std::function? A: A non-owning, two-pointer view of a callable: object pointer plus a trampoline that knows the real type. No allocation, accepts capturing lambdas. Use it for callback parameters that are only invoked during the call; never store it, because it does not own the callable.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Type erasure: Concept/Model/wrapper; polymorphism without inheritance; value semantics; one allocation unless small-buffer optimised.
  • function_ref for callback parameters; std::function for stored callbacks; std::any almost never.
  • CRTP: static template method and mixins; loses the common base type.
  • Policy-based design: decorator stacks flattened at compile time; zero-cost disabled policies via empty base optimisation.
  • Tag dispatch for extensible compile-time selection; if constexpr for short local branches.
  • std::variant state machines: one overload set, per-state data, exhaustiveness.
  • Pipelines: lazy, inlined, one type per chain.
  • Templates trade run time for compile time and binary size; virtual trades the reverse. Ask: is the decision made at run time? Is the call hot?
  • Explicit instantiation and static_asserts tame template build cost and error messages.

docs.title: 09. Designing a Server Codebase
docs.text: Time: ~3.5 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03, 05, 06, 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Think of a bank branch. The person at the counter takes your form and hands back a receipt. They do not decide whether you get the loan. The form has a fixed layout, so anyone can read it. The loan officer reads the form and applies the bank's rules. The records room stores the files. The counter clerk never walks into the records room, and the loan officer never cares whether the form came in by hand or by post.

A server codebase works the same way. Transport is the counter: it moves bytes in and out over sockets. Protocol is the form layout: it turns bytes into a request value and a response value back into bytes. Service is the loan officer: business rules. Storage is the records room: a database or an in-memory map. Each layer talks only to the one next to it, and the rules never depend on how the bytes arrived or where the files are kept.

You already work in a server shaped like this, even if nobody drew it. This module gives you the vocabulary and the rules, so you can explain the design in an interview, lay out a new repository (tcpkv) properly, and describe how you moved legacy C business logic into a cleaner layer without breaking a bank's lending flow.

docs.title: 2.1 The four layers
docs.text:
Layer Owns Must not know about Typical types Transport sockets, framing at byte level, timeouts, thread pool, TLS commands, keys, loans Socket, Listener, Connection, ThreadPool Protocol wire grammar, parsing, encoding, protocol versions, limits on message size sockets, databases, business rules Parser, Request (a std::variant), encode_reply() Service business rules, validation, authorisation, workflow, transactions, metrics sockets, wire format, SQL text KvService, LoanService, WorkflowEngine, Rule Storage persistence, SQL, connection pools, caches of tables wire format, sessions MemoryStorage, PgApplicationRepository

Plus two things that are not layers:

  • Common / domain types. Small value types every layer may use: Error, Result<T>, AccountId, Paise, Application. No I/O, no dependencies.
  • The composition root. The one place (usually main) that creates every concrete object and wires them together. It is the only code that knows all the concrete types.

docs.title: 2.2 Dependency direction
docs.text:
Dependency here means "includes the header of" and "links against". The rule:

   transport ---> protocol ---> service <--- storage
                                   ^
                                   |
                         common / domain types (everyone may use)

   app/main (composition root) depends on all of them, nothing depends on app.

Read the arrow from storage carefully: storage depends up on the service, not the other way round. The service declares the interface it needs (a port):

namespace service {
class Storage {                       // declared in service/storage_port.hpp
public:
    virtual ~Storage() = default;
    virtual std::optional<std::string> get(const std::string& key) const = 0;
    virtual void put(const std::string& key, std::string value) = 0;
    virtual bool erase(const std::string& key) = 0;
};
}

and the storage library implements it (an adapter). This is the Dependency Inversion Principle from Module 02 applied at the scale of libraries. The name for the whole shape is ports and adapters, also called hexagonal architecture: business logic in the middle, I/O on the outside, interfaces between them owned by the middle.

Why it matters:

  • You can test every rule with an in-memory fake, no database, in milliseconds.
  • You can replace Berkeley DB with YugabyteDB by writing one new adapter. You have done this migration; in a ports-and-adapters design it is an adapter swap rather than a rewrite.
  • A change in the wire protocol never forces a recompile of storage.

Enforce it with the build, not with discipline. In CMake each layer is a library target, and target_link_libraries lists only what the arrow allows:

add_library(kv_common   INTERFACE)                       # header-only vocabulary types
add_library(kv_service  src/service/kv_service.cpp)
target_link_libraries(kv_service  PUBLIC kv_common)      # no storage, no transport
add_library(kv_storage  src/storage/memory_storage.cpp)
target_link_libraries(kv_storage  PUBLIC kv_service)     # implements service's port
add_library(kv_protocol src/protocol/parser.cpp)
target_link_libraries(kv_protocol PUBLIC kv_common)
add_library(kv_transport src/transport/socket.cpp src/transport/connection.cpp)
target_link_libraries(kv_transport PUBLIC kv_protocol kv_service)
add_executable(tcpkv_server apps/server_main.cpp)        # the composition root
target_link_libraries(tcpkv_server PRIVATE kv_transport kv_storage)

With per-target include directories, #include "storage/..." from inside src/service/ fails to compile. That is the point.

docs.title: 2.3 Interfaces at boundaries, not everywhere
docs.text:
Put a virtual interface (or a template parameter, Module 08) where one of these is true:

  1. It is I/O. Socket, database, file, clock, random numbers, environment. Anything that makes a test slow, flaky or dependent on the machine.
  2. It is a layer boundary. The service's view of storage. The transport's view of the request handler.
  3. There really are two implementations in production (memory store and RocksDB store), or a third is planned.

Do not put an interface in front of every class "for testability". A Parser with an IParser and one implementation is noise: test the real parser, it is pure. Interfaces are not free in reading time: every one is a place where "go to definition" stops working.

Runtime cost is rarely the argument. A virtual call costs a few nanoseconds (typical, when predicted); a recv() syscall costs on the order of a microsecond and a database round trip hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds. One or two virtual calls per request are invisible. Inside a hot loop over millions of keys, the template form is the right tool.

docs.title: 2.4 Directory layout
docs.text:
One directory per layer, one namespace per directory, one CMake target per directory:

tcpkv/
  CMakeLists.txt
  include/tcpkv/            public headers (what the client library exposes)
    client.hpp
  src/
    common/   result.hpp error.hpp log.hpp           namespace tcpkv::common
    config/   config.hpp config.cpp                  namespace tcpkv::config
    protocol/ parser.hpp parser.cpp reply.hpp        namespace tcpkv::protocol
    service/  kv_service.hpp kv_service.cpp          namespace tcpkv::service
              storage_port.hpp                       (the interface storage implements)
    storage/  memory_storage.hpp memory_storage.cpp  namespace tcpkv::storage
    transport/fd.hpp socket.hpp connection.hpp server.hpp thread_pool.hpp
  apps/       server_main.cpp  cli_main.cpp          composition roots
  tests/      one test binary per layer, plus an end-to-end test over a real socket

Private headers live next to their .cpp. Only include/ is installed. Tests link the layer they test plus fakes, never the whole server.

docs.title: 2.5 Configuration
docs.text:
Rules that save you at 3 AM:

  • Read once, at start-up, into a plain struct. Validate everything (ranges, unknown keys, file paths exist). Fail start-up with a clear message. A server that starts with a typo'd key silently ignored is worse than one that refuses to start.
  • Precedence, lowest to highest: compiled defaults, config file, environment variables, command-line flags. Log the effective configuration (minus secrets) at start-up.
  • Immutable after start. Pass const Config& (or the specific sub-struct a component needs, so the dependency is visible). Never call getenv() in the middle of a request: it is a hidden input that a test cannot control, and it is not thread-safe against setenv().
  • Hot reload, if needed, is an RCU-style snapshot: build a new Config, validate it, publish it with an atomic shared_ptr swap; requests take a snapshot at their start (code/m07_rcu_snapshot.cpp). Only reload what is safe to change live (log level, limits), never the port or the thread count.
  • Secrets (DB passwords) come from a secret store or a file with tight permissions, never the command line (visible in ps) and never the log.

docs.title: 2.6 Logging
docs.text:
• Inject a logger interface (or a small set of free functions over a configured sink) so tests can capture output. A global printf to a file cannot be tested and cannot be redirected.
  • Correlation id. Each request gets an id at the transport layer; every log line for that request carries it. Without it, a log from 64 worker threads is unreadable.
  • Levels with meaning. ERROR: someone must act. WARN: unexpected but handled. INFO: one line per significant event (start, stop, config, a connection opened). DEBUG: per request, off in production.
  • Structured fields (req=7f3a op=SET key_len=12 dur_us=85 result=OK) can be parsed by log tools; prose cannot.
  • Never log passwords, full account numbers, Aadhaar or PAN numbers, card data, session tokens. In banking this is an audit finding, not a style issue. Mask at the logging call.
  • Do not log under a lock you care about, and do not let a slow disk block request threads: use an asynchronous logger with a bounded queue that drops and counts (code/m11_logger.cpp).

docs.title: 2.7 Error policy
docs.text:
Decide once, write it down, apply everywhere. A workable policy for a C++ server:

Kind of failure Example Mechanism Programmer bug, invariant broken index out of range, null where impossible assert in debug; in release log and abort the process (a core dump beats corrupt data) Expected, input-related bad key, unknown command, rule failed return a value: Result<T> / std::optional / error enum Environmental, maybe transient DB timeout, connection reset Result with a retryable code, or an exception caught at the service boundary Start-up failure bad config, port in use exception or error return in main, exit non-zero with a message

And these rules:

  • Translate at every boundary. Storage turns PGRES_FATAL_ERROR into Errc::Unavailable or Errc::Internal; the protocol layer turns Errc into wire text in one function (encode_error in the code file). SQL text and file paths never reach a client.
  • Never translate to a different meaning. A timeout is not "not found". If you map it to not-found, a client will create a second copy of something that exists.
  • Exceptions never cross a thread boundary (catch in the worker loop), a C API boundary (callbacks registered with a C library), or a destructor (destructors are noexcept).
  • Log once, where the error is handled, not at every layer it passes through.

docs.title: 2.8 What makes a good module
docs.text:
• Small interface, large implementation ("deep module", the term is from John Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design). KvService has three functions and hides validation, limits, metrics and storage. A module whose interface is as complicated as its body is not hiding anything.
  • One reason to change (Module 02, single responsibility). The protocol module changes when the wire format changes, nothing else.
  • Owns its data. Nobody else reaches into its structs. In C you enforced this with opaque pointers in headers; in C++ with private and, across a library boundary, pimpl (code/m05_pimpl.cpp).
  • No cycles. If A needs B and B needs A, one of them contains a third module trying to get out, or one direction should be an interface owned by the other.
  • No utils dumping ground. A utils directory with string helpers, time helpers and half of the business logic becomes the module everything depends on and nothing can change.

docs.title: 2.9 Full architecture: tcpkv
docs.text:
The spec is 10_Capstone_Projects/tcpkv/00_spec.md. Its components map onto the layers:

 apps/server_main.cpp  (composition root: parse flags -> Config, build Store, Metrics,
         |              Server; install signal handlers; run)
         v
 +------------------------------ transport ------------------------------------+
 |  FileDescriptor  Socket  Server(acceptor loop, wake pipe)  ThreadPool       |
 |  Connection::serve(): poll -> read -> parser.feed -> execute -> write_all   |
 +-------------------------------|---------------------------------------------+
                                 | Request values (std::variant), Reply values
 +------------------------------ protocol -------------------------------------+
 |  Parser (incremental state machine, limits)   reply encoders                |
 +-------------------------------|---------------------------------------------+
                                 | execute_command(Request) -> Reply
 +------------------------------ service --------------------------------------+
 |  command execution: key validation, TTL semantics, STATS                    |
 |  Metrics (atomics, histogram)          port: Store interface (optional)     |
 +-------------------------------|---------------------------------------------+
                                 |
 +------------------------------ storage --------------------------------------+
 |  Store: unordered_map + shared_mutex, lazy expiry + periodic purge          |
 +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 common: log.hpp, limits, error types

Honest note for the interview: tcpkv is small enough that the service layer is thin (execute_command plus metrics), and the spec's Store is concrete rather than behind an interface. That is a defensible choice: there is one store implementation and the store is already fast to test directly. Say so, and say what you would add if a second storage engine arrived (extract the port, keep Store as the first adapter).

docs.title: 2.10 Full architecture: a loan-origination application server
docs.text:
This is the shape of the server you maintain, drawn cleanly. Requests are RPC calls over TCP from branch clients; the backend is a distributed SQL database.

 Branch client (desktop app)         RPC over TCP, length-prefixed binary frames
        |
 +------v--------------------------- transport ---------------------------------+
 | Listener -> Connection (one per client socket)                               |
 | Frame reader (length prefix, max frame size, read timeout)                   |
 | Request pool: bounded queue + worker threads (the "pooled request model")    |
 +------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
        | raw frame
 +------v--------------------------- protocol ----------------------------------+
 | Decode header (msg type, version, session token, request id) and body        |
 | Dispatch table: msg type -> handler (versioned: v1 and v2 decoders co-exist) |
 +------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
        | typed request: CreateApplication, UpdateApplicant, SubmitApplication,
        | ApproveApplication, Disburse, FetchMaster ...
 +------v------------------- cross-cutting middleware --------------------------+
 | authenticate session -> authorise (role x action x branch) -> rate limit     |
 | -> audit "request received" -> start unit of work (DB transaction)           |
 +------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
 +------v--------------------------- service -----------------------------------+
 | ApplicationService  KycService  EligibilityService  SanctionService           |
 | WorkflowEngine (state machine + rules, code/m11_workflow_engine.cpp)          |
 | Rules: FOIR, age, product limits, maker-checker, deviation approvals          |
 | Ports: ApplicationRepository, CustomerRepository, MasterData, Outbox, Clock   |
 +------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
        |
 +------v--------------------------- storage (adapters) ------------------------+
 | Pg/Yugabyte repositories (libpq, prepared statements, stored procedures)     |
 | Connection pool (one connection per worker for the unit of work)             |
 | MasterDataCache: in-memory copy of master tables, refreshed by snapshot swap  |
 | Outbox table: side effects (SMS, CBS posting) committed with the state change |
 +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Points to be able to defend:

  • Unit of work per request. One DB transaction per request: state change, audit row and outbox rows commit together or not at all. Side effects (SMS, posting to core banking) happen afterwards from the outbox, retried until done, so a crash between "approved" and "SMS sent" never loses the SMS or sends it for a rolled-back approval.
  • Where rules live. Validation that needs many rows (limits across a customer's existing loans) is cheaper close to the data (a stored procedure, one round trip). Validation of a single request's fields is cheaper and more testable in the service. Section 2.11 has the trade-off table.
  • Master-data cache. Product, branch and rate tables change rarely and are read on every request. An immutable snapshot (shared_ptr<const MasterData>) refreshed every few minutes removes repeated joins from the hot path; readers never lock. Stale-by-minutes is acceptable for a product list and not for a balance, which is why balances are never cached.
  • Threading. The transport's worker count bounds concurrent DB transactions and so must be no larger than the connection pool. A request holding a DB connection while waiting for another lock is how pools deadlock.
  • Versioning. Branch clients upgrade slowly. The protocol layer keeps old message versions decodable and converts them into the current typed request, so the service has one version of every operation.

docs.title: 2.11 Refactoring legacy C business logic into modules
docs.text:
Your resume line: "Re-engineered legacy C business logic into a modular PL/pgSQL stored-procedure layer that centralises validation, authorisation and workflow rules, cutting application-to-database round trips per transaction." This section gives you the method and the vocabulary to describe it.

The starting point in most legacy servers: one handler function per message type, each hundreds of lines, mixing parsing, validation, several SQL calls, business rules, and response formatting, with globals for shared state. Rules are duplicated across handlers and drift apart. Every rule check that needs data is a separate round trip.

The method (works whether the target is C++ modules or stored procedures):

  1. Inventory. List every entry point (message types, batch jobs) and, for each, the rules it applies and the tables it touches. A spreadsheet is fine. You will find the same rule implemented three slightly different ways; decide which one is correct with the business.
  2. Characterization tests. Before changing anything, record what the old code does: feed it real (masked) inputs and capture outputs, including the wrong ones. These tests pin current behaviour, not desired behaviour. code/m09_layered_server.cpp part 2 does this: old and new must answer byte for byte the same.
  3. Create seams. Extract the SQL calls behind a function or interface (CustomerRepository) so the rules can run without the database. Extract each rule into a pure function (decide(request, customer)). Each extraction is small and covered by step 2.
  4. Move the logic to its new home. In your case, rules that need data moved into procedures: fn_validate_application(app_id) performs all checks in one call and returns every failure, instead of the C code issuing a query per check. Authorisation (role, branch, amount band) and workflow transitions (allowed state changes) became table-driven in the database, so every caller enforces the same rule.
  5. Strangle. Route one message type (or one product) to the new path behind a switch; run old and new side by side in shadow mode where possible; compare; then switch over and delete the old code. Module 10 section 2.10 covers the strangler pattern in detail.
  6. Delete. Refactoring that leaves both versions alive forever doubles maintenance.

Business logic in the application server vs in stored procedures:

Concern In the C, C++ application server In PL/pgSQL procedures Round trips for data-heavy checks one per query unless batched one call for the whole check Unit testing easy with fakes, fast needs a database (pgTAP or tests in a container) Consistency across callers only if every caller uses the same module enforced: every client calls the same procedure Scaling add app servers (stateless) uses database CPU, the hardest tier to scale Deployment and versioning binary release schema migration; must stay compatible with old app versions Debugging debugger, core dumps RAISE NOTICE, logs, EXPLAIN Language full C++, types, libraries SQL-centric; weak for complex algorithms

The honest senior answer: data-intensive validation and invariants that every caller must respect belong close to the data; orchestration, integration with other systems and complex computation belong in the application server. Your project moved the first kind into procedures, which is why it cut round trips.

How to tell it in an interview (situation, task, action, result): the situation (rules spread across C handlers, duplicated, several round trips per transaction), the task (centralise without breaking a live lending flow), the actions (inventory, characterization tests, procedure per business operation returning all failures, table-driven authorisation and workflow, switch-over per message type), the result (fewer round trips per transaction, one place to change a rule). Use your real numbers for round trips before and after; do not invent them.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m09_layered_server.cpp puts a complete layered server in one file so the shape is visible at once: common (Result, Error, Logger interface), config (validated, immutable), service (KvService and the Storage port it owns), storage (MemoryStorage implementing the port), protocol (parse to a std::variant, one error-mapping function), transport (a scripted fake connection), and app::serve gluing them with std::visit. main is the composition root. Part 2 is a legacy C loan handler and its modular replacement, checked by a characterization test.

The composition root, which is the only code that knows every concrete type:

int main() {
    auto cfg = config::parse({{"port", "7400"}, {"max_value_bytes", "8"}});
    assert(cfg.ok());
    storage::MemoryStorage store;                       // concrete: only main sees it
    app::CapturingLogger log;
    service::KvService svc(store, log, cfg.value());    // depends on the PORT, not on MemoryStorage
    transport::ScriptedConnection conn({"PING", "SET a hello", "GET a"});
    app::serve(conn, svc);
}

The service validates and delegates; it never sees sockets or SQL:

common::Result<common::Unit> set(const std::string& key, std::string value) {
    if (auto e = check_key(key)) return *e;
    if (value.size() > cfg_.max_value_bytes)
        return common::Error{common::Errc::TooLarge, "value too large"};
    store_.put(key, std::move(value));
    return common::Unit{};
}

The characterization test (the most useful ten lines in any legacy refactor):

for (const char* in : inputs) {
    char buf[64];
    legacy::process_loan_request(in, buf, sizeof buf);   // old code, untouched
    assert(svc2.handle(in) == std::string(buf));         // new code must agree exactly
}

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What a layer boundary costs at runtime. A virtual call through a port is a load of the vptr, a load of the slot and an indirect call; when the branch predictor has seen it before, a few nanoseconds (typical). It blocks inlining across the boundary, which matters in a tight loop and not at all once per request. Marking adapter classes final lets the compiler devirtualise calls made through the concrete type, and with LTO (-flto) GCC can sometimes devirtualise through the interface when it sees only one implementation in the whole program.

What layers cost at build time. Headers are the real coupling in C++. A service header that includes <libpq-fe.h> makes every file that includes the service recompile when libpq changes, and leaks C symbols into every translation unit. Ports keep heavy includes inside .cpp files of the adapter. Forward declarations (class Socket;) and pimpl cut the include graph further. Tools: -H prints the include tree; include-what-you-use finds unnecessary includes; ninja -d stats and -ftime-trace (Clang) show where compile time goes.

Static libraries and link order. With GNU ld, a static library is searched once, at its position on the command line, for symbols needed so far. If kv_transport uses kv_service, then kv_service must come after it. CMake computes the order from target_link_libraries, which is another reason to declare the graph accurately. A cycle between static libraries needs --start-group; treat needing it as a design bug.

ODR across modules. Two modules defining struct Config in the global namespace with different members is a One Definition Rule violation: no diagnostic required, and in practice one module reads the other's layout and gets garbage. Namespaces per module (tcpkv::config::Config) make this impossible. The same holds for two inline functions or templates with the same name and different bodies.

Symbol visibility. On Linux, every non-static function in a shared library is exported by default. Building with -fvisibility=hidden and exporting only the public API (an EXPORT macro on the classes in include/) shrinks the dynamic symbol table, speeds up loading, lets the compiler optimise internal calls, and makes the ABI surface explicit. This is the Linux equivalent of __declspec(dllexport) that you know from MSVC.

Thread ownership by layer. In the loan server, transport threads own connections, workers own one request each, and the storage pool owns connections to the database. A layer should not create threads that call upward into another layer without a documented contract, because then the caller's locks are held on a thread it did not expect. The outbox worker and the cache refresher are explicit, named threads owned by the composition root.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
Layer skipping. Under deadline pressure someone calls the database from the protocol decoder "just to look up the branch code". Now the decoder cannot be tested without a database and a slow query stalls frame decoding. The build-enforced dependency graph (2.2) turns this into a compile error instead of a code-review argument.

Pass-through layers. The opposite failure: a service layer where every function is return repo_.same_function(args);. That is a layer with no responsibility. Either it gains rules, or delete it and let transport talk to a repository interface directly. Layers are for separating reasons to change, not for symmetry on a diagram.

Error meaning lost in translation. A war story shape common to lending systems: a read from the application table times out under load, the storage layer returns "not found", the service decides the application does not exist and the client is told to create it. The branch user clicks again and now there are two applications for one customer. The fix is an error policy with a distinct Unavailable code and a rule that only a definite answer from the database becomes NotFound.

Config read lazily. A limit read with getenv inside a request handler worked for years until a deployment script changed the environment of only some processes. Half the servers used the old limit. Reading config once and logging the effective values at start-up makes this visible in the first log line.

Logging that takes the server down. A synchronous logger writing to a network share; the share slows down; every worker blocks in fwrite while holding a request; the thread pool is exhausted; the load balancer marks the server dead. Async logging with a bounded, dropping queue (and a counter for drops) turns a disk problem into a gap in the logs instead of an outage.

What to check first at 3 AM. Find the correlation id of one failing request. Grep it across all logs. The layer where the request's log lines stop is the layer to investigate. This only works if every layer logs with that id, which is a design decision made long before the incident.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) In m09_layered_server.cpp, add an EXISTS key command. Touch only the protocol (parse, a new Exists struct) and app::serve; the service gets one new function. Done when the scripted test covers it and no storage code changed.
  2. (easy) Add a RequestIdLogger decorator that prefixes each line with a request id passed through serve. Done when every log line of one request shares an id.
  3. (medium) Replace MemoryStorage with a FlakyStorage decorator (Module 05) that fails every third call with an Unavailable result. Change the port so storage can report failure, and make sure the wire reply is -ERR try again, never $-1. Done when a test proves a storage failure never looks like "not found".
  4. (medium) Draw the CMake target graph for tcpkv (one target per layer) and write the CMakeLists.txt snippet. Done when a deliberate #include "storage/..." from a service file fails to compile.
  5. (hard) Take one real handler from your work (or invent an 80-line one in the legacy style), write characterization tests for it with at least 15 inputs including bad ones, then split it into parse, repository, pure rules and service. Done when the tests pass unchanged before and after.
  6. (hard) Write a one-page architecture for the loan-origination server (2.10) in the design-doc template from Module 12, including the unit-of-work and outbox decisions and a trade-off table for "rules in procedures vs in the server". Done when you can present it in 10 minutes.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How would you structure the codebase of a TCP server? A: Four layers: transport (sockets, framing, threads), protocol (bytes to typed requests and back, pure), service (business rules), storage (persistence), plus common value types and a composition root in main. Dependencies point inward toward the service; the service owns the storage interface, and storage implements it. Each layer is a separate library target so the build enforces the graph.

Q: What is dependency inversion at the architecture level? A: High-level policy (the service) does not depend on low-level detail (the database); both depend on an abstraction, and the abstraction is owned by the high-level side. Concretely the Storage interface lives in the service's directory and the database adapter links against it. That is why rules can be tested with an in-memory fake and why replacing the database is an adapter change.

Q: Where would you put interfaces? A: At I/O (sockets, DB, files, clock), at layer boundaries, and where two real implementations exist. Not in front of pure logic like a parser, which is easier to test directly. The runtime cost of a virtual call per request is negligible next to a syscall; the cost that matters is readability.

Q: What is your error-handling policy in a server? A: Bugs assert or abort; expected failures are values (Result/optional); transient environmental failures are values with a retryable code or exceptions caught at the service boundary. Translate at each boundary into the next layer's vocabulary without changing meaning, map to wire errors in exactly one function, never let exceptions cross threads, C callbacks or destructors, and log once where the error is handled.

Q: How do you handle configuration? A: Load once at start-up with defined precedence (defaults, file, env, flags), validate fully, fail fast on unknown keys or bad values, log the effective config without secrets, and pass it immutable by const&. Hot-reload only safe fields through an atomic snapshot swap.

Q: How would you refactor a 1000-line legacy C handler safely? A: Characterization tests first, capturing current outputs for real inputs. Then create seams by extracting data access behind an interface and rules into pure functions, in small steps each covered by the tests. Route traffic gradually to the new path (strangler), compare in shadow mode, switch over, and delete the old code.

Q: Business logic in stored procedures or in the application server? A: Data-heavy checks and invariants every caller must respect are better near the data: one round trip and impossible to bypass. Orchestration, integrations and complex computation are better in the server: testable, debuggable, scalable horizontally. The cost of procedures is database CPU, harder testing and schema-versioning discipline.

Q: How do you guarantee a side effect (SMS, posting) happens exactly when a state change commits? A: The transactional outbox: write the state change and an outbox row in the same database transaction; a separate worker reads the outbox, performs the side effect with an idempotency key, and marks it done. The side effect may be retried, so it must be idempotent, but it is never lost and never sent for a rolled-back change.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Transport moves bytes, protocol converts bytes to typed values, service applies rules, storage persists. Common types are shared; main is the composition root.
  • Dependencies point toward the service. The service owns the storage port; storage implements it. Enforce the graph with one CMake target per layer.
  • Interfaces at I/O and layer boundaries, not everywhere. A virtual call per request is noise next to a syscall.
  • Config: once, validated, immutable, logged; never getenv mid-request.
  • Logging: injected, levelled, structured, correlated by request id, asynchronous with a bounded dropping queue, never logs secrets or personal identifiers.
  • Errors: bugs abort, expected failures are values, translate at boundaries without changing meaning, map to wire errors in one place.
  • Good modules are deep, own their data, have one reason to change, and form no cycles.
  • Loan server: unit of work per request, outbox for side effects, immutable master-data snapshot, worker count no larger than the DB pool.
  • Legacy refactor: inventory, characterization tests, seams, move, strangle, delete.

docs.title: 10. API Design and Code Quality
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02, 03, 09

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
An API (application programming interface) is the set of functions and types other code is allowed to call: a class's public members, a library's headers, a server's wire protocol. A good API is like a good ATM. There are few buttons, each does one obvious thing, and it is hard to do something dangerous by accident: you cannot take the cash and leave the card in the machine, because the machine returns the card first.

Bad APIs are the source of a large share of production bugs. Not because the implementation is wrong, but because callers use it in ways the author did not expect: arguments swapped, return values ignored, objects used after they are freed, functions called from two threads. In C you defended against this with comments and code review. C++ lets you push much of it into the type system, so the compiler refuses the mistake.

This module is about that, and about the habits that keep a codebase healthy over years: tests that make change safe, code review that catches design problems early, and replacing legacy code gradually instead of in one risky rewrite.

docs.title: 2.1 Easy to use correctly, hard to use incorrectly
docs.text:
Scott Meyers put the whole of API design in one sentence: make interfaces easy to use correctly and hard to use incorrectly. Concretely:

  • Minimal. Every public function is a promise you must keep. If a caller can build it from two existing functions, it probably should not be a member. Fewer functions also means fewer ways to leave the object in a half-updated state.
  • Consistent. Same naming, same argument order, same error style across the whole API. If get() returns optional in one class, do not return a sentinel in another.
  • Obvious at the call site. Readers see calls far more often than declarations. post(txn, true, false) says nothing; post(txn, Posting::DryRun, Notify::No) says it all.
  • Ownership visible in the signature (Module 03):
Parameter Means const T& / T (cheap) borrow for the call / copy T& borrow and modify (prefer returning a value instead) T* borrow, may be null std::unique_ptr<T> the function takes ownership (a sink) std::shared_ptr<T> the function will share ownership (rarely right) std::string_view, pointer plus size read-only view of characters / elements, valid only during the call

docs.title: 2.2 Techniques that make misuse a compile error
docs.text:
1. Strong types instead of raw integers and strings: AccountId, Paise, BranchCode. Section 2.5.
  2. Enums instead of booleans for options. A bool parameter is a puzzle at the call site and silently accepts an int.
  3. Named-field request structs for functions with several same-typed parameters. transfer({.from = a, .to = b, .amount = x}) (C++20 designated initialisers; in C++17 a struct with named members) stops positional swaps.
  4. Make invalid states unrepresentable. A connection that is either Connecting with a retry count or Ready with a session is a std::variant, not a struct with a bool and two fields of which one is meaningless (Module 08).
  5. Parse, don't validate. (The phrase is from an essay by Alexis King.) A type whose only constructor is a parse() that returns optional<T> guarantees that every value of that type in the program is valid. Ifsc::parse("HDFC0001234") in the code file. After the boundary, nobody re-checks.
  6. RAII for paired calls. Lock/unlock, begin/commit, subscribe/unsubscribe: return an object whose destructor does the second half (Module 06's subscription token).
  7. Return values, not out-parameters. std::optional<Customer> find(id) cannot be misused the way int find(int id, Customer* out) can (ignored return, uninitialised out).
  8. Delete what must not happen. = delete the copy constructor of a socket; = delete an overload that would accept a dangerous conversion (void set_timeout(double) = delete; next to set_timeout(std::chrono::milliseconds)).

docs.title: 2.3 const-correctness
docs.text:
• A const member function promises not to change the object's observable state. Mark every member function that does not modify const; the compiler then lets callers holding a const& use it, and stops you from accidentally mutating.
  • Logical vs bitwise constness. A cache inside a const get() or a mutex locked inside a const size() is fine: mark those members mutable. The rule is that observable state does not change.
  • The standard library's convention: const member functions are safe to call concurrently from several threads on the same object. Your classes should keep that promise, which means a mutable cache inside a const function needs a lock or an atomic.
  • Take parameters by const T& (or by value for cheap types). Do not return const T by value: it disables moving from the result.
  • Prefer const local variables. A value that never changes after initialisation is one less thing to track while reading.

docs.title: 2.4 noexcept
docs.text:
noexcept is a promise that the function does not throw. If it throws anyway, std::terminate is called immediately. Use it:

  • On move constructors and move assignment. std::vector moves elements during reallocation only if the move constructor is noexcept (otherwise it copies, to keep the strong exception guarantee). A missing noexcept on a move turns every push_back reallocation into a copy.
  • On swap, destructors (implicitly noexcept already), and simple getters.
  • On functions where throwing would be a bug and you prefer a crash with a clear stack to a half-handled exception.

Do not put it on a function that may reasonably throw later: removing noexcept from a public API is a breaking change for callers that relied on it (for example with std::is_nothrow_move_constructible).

docs.title: 2.5 Strong types
docs.text:
template <class Tag, class Rep>
class Strong {
public:
    constexpr explicit Strong(Rep v) noexcept : v_(v) {}   // explicit: no silent conversion
    constexpr Rep get() const noexcept { return v_; }
    friend constexpr bool operator==(Strong a, Strong b) noexcept { return a.v_ == b.v_; }
private:
    Rep v_;
};
using AccountId = Strong<struct AccountIdTag, std::uint64_t>;
using BranchId  = Strong<struct BranchIdTag,  std::uint32_t>;

AccountId and BranchId are different types, so passing one where the other is expected does not compile. A tag declared inline (struct AccountIdTag) is enough; it is never defined. Give each strong type only the operations that make sense: money adds to money and multiplies by an integer; an id has no arithmetic at all. Money is an integer count of the smallest unit (paise), never double.

docs.title: 2.6 [[nodiscard]]
docs.text:
[[nodiscard]] on a function makes ignoring its return value a warning (an error with -Werror). On a type, it applies to every function returning that type by value.

Put it on:

  • error-returning types (Result, Status): ignoring them is the classic C bug;
  • functions whose only purpose is the return value (parse, empty(), try_lock);
  • factories that return owning handles (subscribe() returning a token that unsubscribes when dropped).

Where you really mean to ignore: (void)f(); or std::ignore = f(); makes it visible.

docs.title: 2.7 Errors in an API
docs.text: Pick one style per API and say it in the header: exceptions, Result<T> (C++23 std::expected), std::optional<T> for "no value" that needs no reason, or error codes with out-parameters (only at C boundaries). Mixing them inside one API forces every caller to handle both. Module 09 section 2.7 has a server-wide policy.

docs.title: 2.8 Documentation that earns its place
docs.text:
The code already says what it does. The header comment should say what the code cannot:

  • Preconditions (key non-empty, at most 256 bytes) and what happens if violated.
  • Postconditions and guarantees (after commit() returns true, the change is durable).
  • Ownership and lifetime (the returned view is valid until the next put).
  • Thread safety (safe to call concurrently / must be externally synchronised).
  • Complexity when it is not obvious (O(n) sweep; amortised O(1)).
  • Errors (which codes, which exceptions).
  • One usage example for anything non-trivial.

docs.title: 2.9 Versioning, API and ABI
docs.text:
• API compatibility: old source still compiles. ABI compatibility: old binaries still link and run against the new library.
  • ABI breaks (old binaries crash or misbehave): adding or reordering data members (size and offsets change), adding a virtual function in the middle (vtable slots shift), changing a function's parameter types (mangled name changes), changing an inline function or template that old binaries compiled into themselves, changing an enum's underlying type.
  • Tools: pimpl keeps data members out of the header, so the class's size never changes (code/m05_pimpl.cpp). Inline namespaces version symbols: namespace api { inline namespace v2 { ... } } lets code compiled against v1 keep its old symbols while new code gets v2 by default (code/m10_api_quality.cpp). [[deprecated("use X")]] warns callers a release before removal.
  • Semantic versioning: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for compatible additions, PATCH for fixes. Applies to wire protocols too: add fields that old readers ignore; never change the meaning of an existing field.

docs.title: 2.10 Seams, fakes and mocks
docs.text:
A seam (term from Michael Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code) is a place where you can change behaviour without editing the code there. In C++:

  • Object seam: an interface parameter (Ledger&, Clock&). The most common.
  • Template seam: a template parameter (Cache<Clock>). Zero cost, compile-time.
  • Link seam: link a different .o that defines the same function (common for C code; swap db_query() with a test version at link time).

Test doubles, named precisely:

Double What it is Assert on Stub returns canned answers the code under test's output Fake a working, simplified implementation (in-memory ledger) resulting state Mock records calls and checks them against expectations the interactions Spy a real or fake object that also records calls both

Prefer fakes. A test that asserts "the balance moved from A to B" survives refactoring; a test that asserts "debit was called before credit exactly once" breaks when you merge them into one post call, even though behaviour is unchanged. Use mocks for effects that have no state to inspect: an SMS sent, an audit event emitted, a metric incremented.

docs.title: 2.11 Code review checklist
docs.text:
Read the change twice: once for design, once for detail.

Design

  • Does it belong in this layer and module? Does it add a dependency in the wrong direction?
  • Is the public API minimal? Could a caller misuse it (swapped args, ignored result, bool flags)?
  • Who owns every new object? Any shared_ptr that could be unique_ptr?
  • Is there a simpler design (a function instead of a class, a value instead of a pointer)?

Correctness

  • Error paths: is every failure handled or propagated, with its meaning intact?
  • Resource cleanup on every path: RAII or a leak on early return?
  • Lifetimes: references or views stored beyond the life of what they refer to?
  • Concurrency: shared data protected? Locks held across callbacks or I/O? Lock order?
  • Integer issues: overflow, signed/unsigned comparison, money in floating point?
  • Input from outside: lengths checked before copying, limits enforced?

Quality

  • Tests for the new behaviour, including a failure case? Do they test behaviour, not implementation?
  • const, noexcept on moves, [[nodiscard]] on results, explicit on single-arg constructors?
  • Names say what, comments say why. Dead code and commented-out code removed.
  • Logs: correct level, correlation id, no personal data.

docs.title: 2.12 Refactoring safely
docs.text:
Refactoring is changing structure without changing behaviour. The safety rules:

  1. Tests first. If there are none, write characterization tests (Module 09, 2.11).
  2. Small steps, each compiling and passing. Rename, extract function, introduce parameter, move function, extract interface: each one alone.
  3. Separate commits for refactoring and for behaviour change. A reviewer can verify a pure refactor mechanically; mixing in a fix hides the fix.
  4. Let the compiler find the call sites. Change a parameter from int to AccountId and fix every error the compiler reports; that is a complete list, unlike a text search.
  5. Run sanitizers (-fsanitize=address,undefined, and thread for concurrent code) on the test suite after each structural change; refactors often change lifetimes.
  6. Keep commits bisectable. If each commit builds and passes, git bisect finds a regression in minutes.

docs.title: 2.13 The strangler fig pattern
docs.text:
Martin Fowler named it after a vine that grows around a tree until it replaces it. Instead of rewriting a legacy system in one big release, you:

  1. Put a router in front of the legacy code: a facade through which every request goes. At first it sends everything to the legacy path.
  2. Build the new implementation for one slice (one message type, one product).
  3. Shadow: send the slice to both, return the legacy answer, compare and count mismatches. Only safe for reads or against a scratch database.
  4. Switch the slice to the new path behind a flag that can be flipped back in seconds.
  5. Repeat slice by slice. Delete the legacy code for each slice once stable.

Branch by abstraction is the same idea inside one codebase: introduce an interface over the old implementation, write the new implementation behind the same interface, switch callers by configuration, delete the old one.

Why it beats the big rewrite: every step is small and reversible, the business keeps running, and you learn the hidden behaviour of the old system one slice at a time instead of all at once on go-live night.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
code/m10_api_quality.cpp builds a small funds-transfer service that uses every technique in this module: Strong<Tag, Rep> and a Paise type with only meaningful arithmetic, static_asserts proving no implicit conversions, an Ifsc type that can only be created by parse(), a [[nodiscard]] TransferResult, a named-field TransferRequest, an enum Posting::DryRun instead of a bool, three seams (Clock, Ledger, Notifier), a fake ledger and a mock notifier, inline-namespace versioning, and a StranglerRouter with legacy, new and shadow routes.

The test shows the difference between a fake and a mock in two lines:

TransferResult r = svc.transfer({a, b, Paise(2'500), "rent"});
assert(*ledger.balance(a) == Paise(7'500));            // FAKE: assert resulting state
assert(notes.calls.size() == 1);                       // MOCK: assert the interaction

The strangler router's shadow mode:

std::string old_answer = legacy_(product, payload);
if (modern_(product, payload) != old_answer) ++mismatches_;   // compare, never serve
return old_answer;

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Strong types cost nothing. A class holding one uint64_t, with a trivial copy constructor and trivial destructor, is passed in a register under the System V x86-64 ABI, exactly like the raw integer. The static_assert(sizeof(AccountId) == sizeof(uint64_t)) in the code file checks the size; compile with -O2 -S and the generated code for a function taking AccountId is identical to one taking uint64_t. A non-trivial destructor or copy constructor changes this: the object is then passed by hidden reference in memory.

const rarely helps the optimiser. const_cast away from a reference to a non-const object is legal, so the compiler cannot assume memory behind a const T& does not change across a call to unknown code. Its value is for humans and for the type checker. The one place it does help: a const object defined as const (not just viewed through a const reference) may be placed in read-only memory and folded.

noexcept and code generation. GCC uses table-based (zero-cost) exceptions: no instructions on the normal path, unwind tables consulted only when something throws. A call to a noexcept function lets the caller omit cleanup landing pads for that call; a noexcept function that does throw goes straight to std::terminate without unwinding further. The big real-world effect is not in the function itself but in library decisions: std::vector uses std::move_if_noexcept during reallocation, and std::is_nothrow_* traits switch algorithms.

[[nodiscard]] is purely a diagnostic. It changes no code generation and no ABI. It can be added to an existing API without breaking binaries, but may break builds that use -Werror, so add it in a minor release with a note.

What an inline namespace does to symbols. api::v2::fee(Paise) mangles as something like _ZN3api2v23feeE5Paise. A binary compiled against the old header that called api::fee when v1 was the inline namespace recorded api::v1::fee, which the new library still exports. Two incompatible versions can therefore be linked into one program without an ODR collision. libstdc++ uses exactly this (std::__cxx11::basic_string) for its C++11 ABI change.

Why ABI breaks are silent. The linker matches names, not layouts. If you add a member to a class whose objects are allocated by an old binary, the old binary allocates the old size and the new library writes past the end. No link error, just heap corruption hours later. This is why shared libraries with C++ classes in their public headers need pimpl or a strict "never change layout" rule, and why C APIs over C++ internals remain popular for plugins.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
The ignored error. db_exec(conn, "UPDATE ..."); with the return value ignored, in C, for years, until the table was locked by a long batch and every update silently failed for an hour. [[nodiscard]] on the C++ wrapper's result type turns this whole class of bug into a build failure. When you wrap a legacy C API (Module 05 adapter), put [[nodiscard]] on everything that can fail.

Boolean traps in banking code. calculate_interest(amount, rate, true, false); the third argument was "compound", the fourth "leap-year aware", and a refactor swapped them in one caller. Enums would have made the swap a compile error.

Mocks that froze the design. A service with 300 tests, each mocking the repository with exact call sequences. Every attempt to batch two queries into one broke 80 tests that were not testing anything the business cared about. The team rewrote them against an in-memory fake repository; the next refactor broke none.

The rewrite that never shipped. The common legacy story: a two-year "rewrite in modern C++" runs in parallel with the old system, which keeps getting features, so the rewrite never catches up. The strangler approach ships value per slice and makes the remaining legacy smaller every month. In an interview, being able to explain why you would not do a big-bang rewrite is a senior signal.

Shadow traffic with side effects. Shadowing a write path against the production database executes the write twice. Shadow only reads, or point the new path at a copy, or make the new path compute a decision without committing it and compare decisions.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Add a BranchId strong type to m10_api_quality.cpp and a function that takes (AccountId, BranchId). Write the call with the arguments swapped and confirm it does not compile. Done when you can paste the compiler error.
  2. (easy) Remove [[nodiscard]] from TransferResult, call svc.transfer(...) without using the result, rebuild, then restore it. Done when you have seen the warning become an error under -Werror.
  3. (medium) Write a ChaosLedger fake that fails post on demand, and test that TransferService returns an error and does not notify. Done when the test passes and the mock shows zero calls.
  4. (medium) Give Strong a std::hash specialisation and use AccountId as an unordered_map key. Done when it compiles without exposing get() at the call site.
  5. (hard) Implement a ShadowAsync route in StranglerRouter that runs the new handler on a separate thread with a timeout, so a slow new implementation never delays the response. Done when a test with a sleeping new handler still returns within 5 ms.
  6. (hard) Pick a function from your work codebase (or legacy::process_loan_request in m09_layered_server.cpp) and write a review using the checklist in 2.11. Done when you have at least one finding in each of the three groups.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What makes an API hard to misuse? A: Types that encode the rules: strong types for ids and money, enums instead of booleans, named-field structs for many parameters, factory functions that validate, RAII for paired operations, [[nodiscard]] on results, and = delete for dangerous conversions. The goal is that the wrong call does not compile, instead of being caught in review.

Q: Why should move constructors be noexcept? A: std::vector reallocates using std::move_if_noexcept: if the move constructor might throw, it copies instead to keep the strong exception guarantee. A missing noexcept turns every reallocation into a full copy, which is a silent performance bug.

Q: What does const on a member function promise, and how do mutexes fit in? A: That observable state does not change, and by standard-library convention that it is safe to call concurrently. A mutex or cache inside it is marked mutable because locking does not change observable state; the cache must itself be thread-safe to keep the concurrency promise.

Q: What is the difference between API and ABI compatibility? A: API compatibility means old source compiles; ABI compatibility means old binaries still work with the new library. Adding a data member or a virtual function keeps the API but breaks the ABI because sizes, offsets and vtable slots change. Pimpl and inline namespaces are the main C++ tools for keeping ABI stable.

Q: Fake or mock: which do you prefer and why? A: Fakes, for most dependencies: tests assert on resulting state, so they survive refactoring. Mocks verify interactions and are right only when the interaction is the observable effect (a notification, an audit event). Over-mocking freezes the implementation.

Q: How do you refactor code that has no tests? A: Write characterization tests that capture current behaviour, then make the smallest structural changes to create seams, extracting functions and interfaces, each step covered by those tests. Separate refactoring commits from behaviour changes so each can be reviewed and reverted independently.

Q: Explain the strangler fig pattern. A: Put a routing facade in front of the legacy system, build the replacement slice by slice behind it, shadow-compare where safe, switch each slice with a reversible flag, and delete legacy code as slices move. It avoids the big-bang rewrite, whose risk is that it never catches up with the moving old system.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Easy to use correctly, hard to use incorrectly. Minimal, consistent, obvious at the call site.
  • Ownership in the signature: reference/pointer borrow, unique_ptr sink, shared_ptr rarely.
  • Strong types, enums for options, named-field requests, parse-don't-validate, RAII pairs.
  • const everywhere it is true; mutable for locks and caches; const means concurrently callable.
  • noexcept on moves and swaps, or vectors copy.
  • [[nodiscard]] on result types and value-only functions.
  • Document preconditions, ownership, thread safety, complexity, errors.
  • ABI breaks are silent; pimpl and inline namespaces protect binaries.
  • Seams: object, template, link. Prefer fakes; mock only effects.
  • Refactor in small, tested, separate commits. Replace legacy with a strangler, not a rewrite.

docs.title: 11. Low-Level Design Interview Walkthroughs
docs.text: Time: ~5 hours Prerequisites: 01 to 08 (06, 07 and 08 especially)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
The low-level design (LLD) round, sometimes called "machine coding" or "object-oriented design", gives you a small system ("design a parking lot", "design a rate limiter") and 45 to 60 minutes. You are expected to ask questions, pick classes and their responsibilities, draw a class diagram, write the core of the code, and discuss how it changes when requirements change: more threads, more types, more scale.

It is not a test of whether you know the "right" answer. There is no right answer. It is a test of whether you work like a senior engineer: you clarify before building, you keep the design as simple as the requirements allow, you name trade-offs out loud, and the code you write compiles and handles the edge cases.

This module gives you a repeatable method and seven complete walkthroughs. Each has a code file in code/ that compiles and checks itself. Practise each one against a 45-minute timer until you can do it without looking.

docs.title: 2.1 The method (use it every time)
docs.text:
0-5 min    1. CLARIFY       functional requirements, scale, concurrency, what is out of scope
 5-10 min   2. ENTITIES      nouns -> classes / value types; verbs -> methods

            3. VARIATION     what will change? -> interface, std::function, or template
 10-15 min  4. DIAGRAM       boxes, ownership (<>-- composition), uses (-->), multiplicity
 15-40 min  5. CODE          core data structures and the 2-3 central methods, compiling
 40-45 min  6. TEST + EXTEND walk one example through; edge cases; threading; scale; trade-offs

1. Clarify. Ask, then write the answers down where the interviewer can see them:

  • What operations? What inputs and outputs? What errors?
  • How many items, requests per second? (Decides data structures.)
  • Single-threaded or concurrent? (Decides locking.)
  • What happens on failure, on full, on duplicate?
  • What is explicitly out of scope (persistence, distribution, UI)?

2. Entities. Underline the nouns. Each becomes a class if it has behaviour or invariants, otherwise a plain struct. Value types (Ticket, Record) are cheap and copyable; entities with identity (Level, ParkingLot) are usually owned in one place.

3. Variation. The interviewer's follow-ups ("now add a new vehicle type", "now a different pricing") target the parts that vary. Put them behind a strategy now, but only those: a FeePolicy, a SpotAllocator, a rate-limit Algorithm. One operation: std::function. Several operations: an interface. Fixed at compile time and hot: template.

4. Diagram. ASCII on the whiteboard or the shared editor:

 +-----------+ 1     * +-------+         <>----->   composition (owns, lifetime bound)
 |   Owner   |<>------>| Part  |         ------->   uses / depends on
 +-----------+         +-------+         ---|>      implements / inherits
 | method()  |
 +-----------+

5. Code. Start with the data structures and the central method. Use the standard library. Show ownership (unique_ptr, references), const, error returns. Leave boilerplate (getters, printing) for the end or skip it with a comment.

6. Test and extend. Walk one example through the code out loud. Then discuss: thread safety (one mutex first, then striping or sharding), scale (what breaks at 10x), testability (injected clock), and the trade-offs of the choices you made.

Things that lose points: coding before clarifying; a class per noun with no behaviour ("Manager" classes that hold one map); inheritance hierarchies three deep for a two-variant problem; global singletons; not handling the full/empty/duplicate case; silence (the interviewer cannot grade what you do not say).

docs.title: 2.2 Walkthrough 1: parking lot
docs.text:
Clarify. Levels with Small/Medium/Large spots. Motorcycle fits any spot, Car fits Medium or Large, Truck only Large. Park returns a ticket or "full"; unpark returns a fee. Fee per hour by vehicle type, first 15 minutes free. Several entry gates (concurrent). Out of scope: payments, reservations, displays.

Entities and variation. Vehicle (value), Spot (identified by level and index), Level (free spots per size), Ticket (value), ParkingLot (facade). Varies: how a spot is chosen (SpotAllocator), how fees are computed (FeePolicy).

 +--------------------+ 1     * +----------------------+
 | ParkingLot         |<>------>| Level                |
 |  park(v, t)        |         |  take(size)          |
 |  unpark(id, t)     |         |  give_back(size, i)  |
 |  free_spots(size)  |         |  free_: set<int>[3]  |
 +--------------------+         +----------------------+
   |  uses        | uses            * active
   v              v                 v
 SpotAllocator  FeePolicy      +-----------+
 (std::function)(std::function)| Ticket    | id, plate, type, spot, size, entry
                               +-----------+

Key code (code/m11_parking_lot.cpp):

// Smallest fitting size first, lowest level first within that size.
std::optional<std::pair<SpotId, SpotSize>>
smallest_fit_lowest_level(std::vector<Level>& levels, VehicleType t) {
    for (auto s = static_cast<std::size_t>(smallest_fit(t)); s < kSizes; ++s)
        for (auto& lvl : levels)
            if (auto spot = lvl.take(static_cast<SpotSize>(s)))
                return std::make_pair(*spot, static_cast<SpotSize>(s));
    return std::nullopt;
}

Each Level keeps a std::set<int> of free spot indices per size, so "nearest free spot" is *begin() in O(log n). The lot keeps active_ tickets by id and a plates_ map so the same car cannot park twice.

Talking points.

  • Why not class Car : public Vehicle? Vehicles have no behaviour here; the only difference is size class. An enum plus one smallest_fit() function is simpler. Use inheritance when types behave differently.
  • Concurrency: one mutex around park/unpark. The critical section is microseconds; gates are a handful of threads. Per-level locks add deadlock risk (a car spilling to the next level needs two) for no measurable gain.
  • Extensions: electric spots with chargers (a new SpotSize or a feature flag on spots and a different allocator); reservations (a Reserved state per spot with expiry); display boards (observer on free-count changes).

docs.title: 2.3 Walkthrough 2: LRU cache with TTL
docs.text:
Clarify. get, put(key, value, ttl), erase. Capacity in entries; evict least recently used when full. Entries expire after their TTL. O(1) operations. Thread-safe. Testable without sleeping.

Design. A doubly linked list in recency order plus a hash map from key to list iterator. Each list node stores key, value and expiry time. Expiry is checked lazily on get and by an O(n) purge_expired() sweep called from a timer.

 +---------------------------+ uses  +-------------+
 | LruTtlCache<K,V>          |------>| Clock       |<|--- SteadyClock, FakeClock
 |  get(k) -> optional<V>    |       +-------------+
 |  put(k, v, ttl?)          |
 |  erase(k), purge_expired()|        index_: unordered_map<K, list<Entry>::iterator>
 +---------------------------+        lru_:   list<Entry>   (front = most recent)
            ^ wraps                   Entry { K key; V value; TimePoint expires; }
 +---------------------------+
 | SyncLruTtlCache (mutex)   |---> ShardedLruTtlCache<K,V,N>: N shards by hash(key)
 +---------------------------+

Key code (code/m11_lru_ttl.cpp):

std::optional<V> get(const K& key) {
    auto it = index_.find(key);
    if (it == index_.end()) { ++stats_.misses; return std::nullopt; }
    auto node = it->second;
    if (is_expired(*node)) { remove(it); ++stats_.expirations; ++stats_.misses; return std::nullopt; }
    lru_.splice(lru_.begin(), lru_, node);   // touch: O(1), no allocation, iterators stay valid
    ++stats_.hits;
    return node->value;                      // a copy: a reference would dangle after eviction
}

Talking points.

  • splice is the key trick: it relinks a node without copying or reallocating, and other iterators in the map stay valid.
  • get mutates (moves the node, updates stats), so a shared_mutex does not help: every call is a writer. To scale, shard by key hash. Sharding makes LRU approximate globally.
  • Lazy expiry alone leaks memory for keys never read again; hence the periodic purge. For millions of entries, keep a min-heap or a timing wheel of expiry times so purging is O(expired) instead of O(n).
  • Time comes from an injected Clock and uses steady_clock, never wall time, which jumps.
  • Alternatives worth naming: CLOCK (second-chance) approximates LRU with a bit per entry and no list reordering, which is cheaper under concurrency; LFU when frequency matters more than recency.

docs.title: 2.4 Walkthrough 3: in-memory KV store with transactions
docs.text:
Clarify. SET, GET, UNSET, COUNT value, BEGIN, ROLLBACK, COMMIT. Transactions nest; ROLLBACK undoes the innermost; COMMIT makes everything permanent. GET and COUNT O(1). Single client (ask!).

Design choice, say it out loud:

Undo log (chosen) Overlay layers Write apply to live map, record before-image once per key per tx write into the top layer only Read O(1), live map O(depth): search layers top-down Rollback replay before-images drop the top layer Commit discard logs (or merge into parent) merge layers down Isolation for other clients none: they see uncommitted writes natural: base untouched until commit 
 +-----------------------------+
 | TxKvStore                   |      data_:   unordered_map<string,string>
 |  set/get/unset/count        |      counts_: unordered_map<string,size_t>  (value -> #keys)
 |  begin/rollback/commit_*    |      txs_:    vector<Tx>   (stack)
 +-----------------------------+      Tx { unordered_map<string, optional<string>> undo; }
          ^ used by
 execute(db, "SET a 10")  -- the protocol layer, kept out of the store

Key code (code/m11_kv_transactions.cpp):

void write(const std::string& k, std::optional<std::string> v) {
    if (!txs_.empty()) txs_.back().undo.emplace(k, get(k));   // first write wins: keeps the ORIGINAL
    raw_write(k, std::move(v));                               // the only function that touches data_
}

[[nodiscard]] bool rollback() {
    if (txs_.empty()) return false;
    Tx tx = std::move(txs_.back());
    txs_.pop_back();
    for (auto& [key, before] : tx.undo) raw_write(key, before);
    return true;
}

Talking points.

  • emplace does not overwrite, so a key written twice in one transaction keeps its value from before the transaction, which is what rollback must restore.
  • COUNT stays O(1) because raw_write maintains counts_; one choke point for the invariant.
  • Nested commit (commit_innermost) merges the child's undo entries into the parent, keeping the parent's own before-image when both touched a key.
  • Multi-client follow-up: overlay layers per transaction give read-committed isolation; conflict detection at commit gives optimistic concurrency; this is how MVCC engines think (see 07_Databases_Internals).

docs.title: 2.5 Walkthrough 4: logger library
docs.text:
Clarify. Levels, runtime minimum level, several sinks, file and line, thread id, timestamps. Asynchronous: request threads must never block on disk. What on overflow: drop and count, or block? (Ask; for a server the answer is usually drop.) Flush on demand and on shutdown.

 LOG(lg, Level::Info) << "loan " << id;      macro: if disabled, nothing to the right is evaluated
        |
        v
 +-----------+  submit(Record)  +--------------------------+  write(Record) +-------------+
 | LogLine   |----------------->| Logger                   |--------------->| Sink        |<|-- Console
 | (RAII:    |                  |  level_ (atomic)         |                |  write()    |<|-- Memory
 | submits in|                  |  queue_ (bounded deque)  |                |  flush()    |<|-- File
 | dtor)     |                  |  worker_ thread          |                +-------------+
 +-----------+                  +--------------------------+

Key code (code/m11_logger.cpp):

#define LOG(lg, lvl) \
    if (!(lg).enabled(lvl)) {} else LogLine((lg), (lvl), __FILE__, __LINE__).stream()

void run() {                                    // the background thread
    std::deque<Record> batch;
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m_);
    for (;;) {
        cv_.wait(lk, [&] { return stopping_ || !queue_.empty(); });
        if (queue_.empty() && stopping_) return;
        batch.swap(queue_);                     // one lock per batch, not per record
        in_flight_ = batch.size();
        lk.unlock();                            // write OUTSIDE the lock: sinks may be slow
        for (auto& r : batch) for (auto& s : sinks_) s->write(r);
        batch.clear();
        lk.lock();
        written_ += in_flight_; in_flight_ = 0;
        drained_cv_.notify_all();               // wakes flush()
    }
}

Talking points.

  • The macro's if (...) {} else shape means a disabled LOG(...) << expensive() costs one relaxed atomic load and a branch; expensive() is never called. It also nests safely inside an unbraced if/else.
  • A Record owns its message (std::string): it crosses threads, so a pointer into the caller's stack would dangle.
  • The worker thread is the last member: constructed after everything it touches, and the destructor stops and joins it before members are destroyed.
  • Bounded queue with drop counting: logging must never take the server down. Expose the drop counter as a metric.
  • Follow-ups: fmt-style formatting done on the background thread (pass arguments, not strings); a lock-free MPSC queue; file rotation; rate-limited logging for repeated errors.

docs.title: 2.6 Walkthrough 5: rate limiter
docs.text:
Clarify. allow(key) per customer or API key. Which algorithm? Burst allowed? Exact or approximate? Memory per key? Distributed across servers (usually: "first single node, then discuss")?

Algorithm State per key Bursts Exactness Notes Token bucket tokens, last refill time up to capacity exact long-run rate default choice Fixed window window index, count 2N at a boundary approximate cheapest Sliding window log timestamps of accepted requests none exact memory O(N) per key Sliding window counter two window counts small approximate (weighted) good compromise 
 +----------------------------+  owns *  +----------------------------+
 | KeyedRateLimiter           |<>------->| Algorithm                  |<|-- TokenBucket
 |  allow(key)                | per key  |  try_acquire(now) -> bool  |<|-- FixedWindow
 |  evict_idle()              |          +----------------------------+<|-- SlidingWindowLog
 |  stripes_[16]: mutex + map |
 |  factory_, now_ (injected) |
 +----------------------------+

Key code (code/m11_rate_limiter.cpp):

bool TokenBucket::try_acquire(TimePoint now) {
    if (now > last_) {                       // lazy refill: no timer thread per key
        const double secs = std::chrono::duration<double>(now - last_).count();
        tokens_ = std::min(capacity_, tokens_ + secs * rate_);
        last_ = now;
    }
    if (tokens_ < 1.0) return false;
    tokens_ -= 1.0;
    return true;
}

Talking points.

  • Algorithms are single-key, single-threaded and take now as a parameter: pure functions of their state, trivial to test. The keyed wrapper adds lookup, locking and eviction.
  • Lock striping (16 mutexes by key hash) means two different customers rarely contend.
  • Idle keys are evicted, or memory grows with every client ever seen.
  • Distributed: a shared store (Redis with an atomic script) for exact global limits at the cost of a network hop per request, or local limits of global / servers with periodic rebalancing, which is approximate but free.
  • Where it sits in a server: as middleware before the service (Module 06, chain of responsibility), returning a "try later" error with a retry-after hint.

docs.title: 2.7 Walkthrough 6: loan-application workflow engine
docs.text:
This one is your home ground. Interviewers at fintech companies ask it in many forms ("design an order workflow", "design a KYC pipeline").
