Clarify. States: Draft, Submitted, UnderReview, Approved, Rejected, Disbursed, Cancelled. Events: Submit, StartReview, Approve, Reject, Disburse, Cancel. Who may trigger what (roles)? Guard rules per transition (KYC done, age range, product limit, FOIR, maker cannot approve own application). Return all failed rules, not just the first. Side effects after success (letters, posting to core banking). Full audit trail.

 Draft --Submit--> Submitted --StartReview--> UnderReview --Approve--> Approved --Disburse--> Disbursed
   |                   |                          |    \--Reject--> Rejected
   +------Cancel-------+-----------Cancel---------+-----------Cancel----+--> Cancelled

 +-------------------------+ owns  +----------------------------------------------+
 | WorkflowEngine          |<>---->| map<(State, Event), Transition>               |
 |  add(from, ev, t)       |       | Transition { to; set<Role>; vector<Rule>;     |
 |  fire(app, ev, actor)   |       |              vector<Action> }                 |
 |  available_events(s)    |       +----------------------------------------------+
 +-------------------------+       Rule   { name; function<optional<string>(app, actor)> }
            | mutates              Action function<void(app&, actor)>
            v
 +-------------------------+ 1  *  +------------+
 | Application             |<>---->| AuditEntry | from, to, event, user, accepted, reasons
 +-------------------------+       +------------+

Key code (code/m11_workflow_engine.cpp):

Outcome fire(Application& app, Event ev, const Actor& actor) const {
    const State from = app.state;
    std::vector<std::string> reasons;
    auto it = table_.find({from, ev});
    if (it == table_.end()) {
        reasons.push_back(std::string("event not allowed in state ") + name(from));
    } else {
        const Transition& t = it->second;
        if (!t.allowed_roles.count(actor.role)) reasons.push_back("role not permitted");
        for (const Rule& r : t.rules)                          // run ALL rules
            if (auto why = r.check(app, actor)) reasons.push_back(r.name + ": " + *why);
    }
    const bool ok = reasons.empty();
    const State to = ok ? it->second.to : from;
    app.audit.push_back(AuditEntry{from, to, ev, actor.user, ok, reasons});
    if (!ok) return Outcome{false, from, std::move(reasons)};
    app.state = to;
    for (const Action& a : it->second.actions) a(app, actor);
    return Outcome{true, to, {}};
}

Talking points.

  • The engine is generic; the loan knowledge is in the table and the rules. A gold-loan product is a different table, not a different engine. The table can be loaded from a database configuration table, which is how lending platforms let operations change a workflow without a release.
  • Rules are small named functions with captured parameters (foir_at_most(5000)), each unit-testable on its own. Money is integer paise; ratios are integer basis points.
  • Why not the GoF state pattern with a class per state? Behaviour per state here is "which transitions exist and which rules guard them", which is data. Classes would scatter the table across seven files.
  • Persistence: state change, audit row and outbox rows for actions commit in one database transaction. Concurrency: two officers acting on one application at once is prevented with optimistic locking (a version column checked in the UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?).
  • Extensions: SLA timers (escalate if UnderReview over 48 hours: the job scheduler below); parallel approvals (a sub-state counting approvals); deviation workflows (a rule failure routes to a higher approver instead of refusing).

docs.title: 2.8 Walkthrough 7: job scheduler
docs.text:
Clarify. Run once at a time; run every period; cancel. Run jobs on a worker pool so a slow job does not delay others. Retry failures with back-off? Missed runs after a pause: run all, run once, or skip? Persistence across restarts (usually out of scope; mention a jobs table)?

Design, the key idea: split pure logic from threads.

 +---------------------------+ owns +-------------------------------+
 | Scheduler (threaded)      |<>--->| SchedulerCore (pure)          |
 |  schedule_after/every     |      |  schedule_at(when, fn, retry) |
 |  cancel(id), stop()       |      |  run_due(now) -> vector<Due>  |
 |  dispatcher_ thread       |      |  report(id, ok, now, backoff) |
 |  workers_ threads         |      |  heap_: min-heap(due,seq,id)  |
 |  ready_ deque             |      |  jobs_, in_flight_: id -> Job |
 +---------------------------+      +-------------------------------+

Key code (code/m11_job_scheduler.cpp):

void dispatch() {                                   // dispatcher thread
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m_);
    while (!stopped_) {
        auto next = core_.next_due();
        if (!next) { cv_.wait(lk); continue; }
        if (cv_.wait_until(lk, *next) == std::cv_status::no_timeout) continue;  // woken: re-check
        for (auto& d : core_.run_due(Clock::now())) ready_.push_back(std::move(d));
        work_cv_.notify_all();
    }
}

Talking points.

  • The core takes now as an argument, so every ordering, cancellation, catch-up and retry rule is tested deterministically without threads or sleeps. The threaded shell is thin.
  • Min-heap keyed by (due time, sequence number): the sequence number gives FIFO order for jobs due at the same instant.
  • Cancellation is lazy: erase from the job map; the heap entry is skipped when it surfaces. Removing from the middle of a binary heap would be O(n).
  • wait_until is woken early by a new job that is due sooner than the current head; the loop re-reads the head after any wake-up (and spurious wake-ups are handled by the same path).
  • Fixed rate (next = previous due + period) does not drift; fixed delay (next = finish + period) never overlaps itself. After a long pause this core runs a missed job once, not once per missed period. Say which you chose.
  • Jobs run outside the lock, and exceptions are caught in the worker so one bad job cannot kill a worker thread.
  • Scale: millions of timers use a hierarchical timing wheel (O(1) insert, as in the Linux kernel's timer wheel and Kafka's purgatory) instead of a heap.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
One file per walkthrough, each with a main() of assert-based checks:

File Contents code/m11_parking_lot.cpp Level with per-size free sets, allocator and fee strategies, ParkingLot facade with a mutex, concurrent-gate test code/m11_lru_ttl.cpp LruTtlCache (list + map + splice), lazy and swept expiry, stats, SyncLruTtlCache, ShardedLruTtlCache, FakeClock code/m11_kv_transactions.cpp TxKvStore with undo log, O(1) COUNT, nested rollback, flat and nested commit, text command interpreter code/m11_logger.cpp Logger (sync/async, bounded dropping queue, flush), Sink interface, LogLine RAII, LOG macro code/m11_rate_limiter.cpp token bucket, fixed window, sliding log, KeyedRateLimiter with lock striping and idle eviction code/m11_workflow_engine.cpp table-driven WorkflowEngine, rules (KYC, age, amount, FOIR, maker-checker), actions to an outbox, audit trail code/m11_job_scheduler.cpp pure SchedulerCore (heap, lazy cancel, catch-up, retry with back-off) and a threaded Scheduler

Build any of them:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -fsanitize=address,undefined -o lld code/m11_lru_ttl.cpp && ./lld
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -fsanitize=thread -o lld code/m11_job_scheduler.cpp && ./lld

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
std::list node cost. Each node is a separate heap allocation holding two pointers plus the element: for Entry<std::string, std::string> on 64-bit libstdc++ that is 16 bytes of links plus two 32-byte strings plus the time point, before malloc overhead. Lookups chase a pointer from the hash bucket to the map node, then to the list node: two likely cache misses per get. High-performance caches use an intrusive list (links inside a slab-allocated entry) or an array-based CLOCK to cut this to one miss.

std::unordered_map in libstdc++ is a vector of buckets, each a pointer into one singly linked list of nodes. reserve(n) sizes the bucket array once, so the hot path never rehashes; a rehash is O(n) and invalidates iterators (but not references or pointers to elements). That is why the LRU stores list iterators in the map and never map iterators anywhere.

std::priority_queue is a binary heap in a std::vector: push and pop are O(log n) with good locality, and there is no way to remove an arbitrary element, which is why the scheduler cancels lazily. A timing wheel is an array of buckets indexed by due / tick % size; insertion is O(1) and the cost moves to the tick.

Condition variables and wait_until. On Linux, std::condition_variable::wait_until with a steady_clock time point uses pthread_cond_clockwait with CLOCK_MONOTONIC (glibc 2.30 and later; libstdc++ uses it when available). Older combinations converted to the system clock, so a wall-clock jump could delay or hasten wake-ups. This is one more reason to keep every deadline on steady_clock.

Floating point in a token bucket. double tokens accumulate rounding error over billions of refills; it does not matter for a rate limiter, but in billing it would. An integer variant stores tokens in micro-tokens or computes refill from integer nanoseconds.

Mutex cost in these designs. An uncontended std::mutex lock/unlock on Linux is a pair of atomic operations in user space (futex fast path), on the order of tens of nanoseconds (typical). Contended, it becomes a futex syscall and a context switch, microseconds. This is why one mutex is fine for a parking lot and striping matters for a rate limiter that sees every request.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
The LRU that ate the heap. A cache keyed by request-supplied strings with no capacity limit, or with capacity counted in entries while values were megabyte-sized documents. Capacity should be in bytes when values vary in size, with the size of each entry computed at put.

Rate limiting the wrong key. Limiting by client IP behind a load balancer that does not pass the original address limits everyone at once. In a branch-banking network, many users share one NAT address; limit by authenticated user or branch id instead.

Logger shutdown order. A global logger destroyed before a global object whose destructor logs: use-after-destruction at exit, visible as a crash in atexit handlers. Owning the logger in main and passing it down (Module 09) makes the order explicit.

Workflow tables changed live. Operations removed a transition from the configuration table while 200 applications were in that state, stranding them. Validate a new table against current data (every non-terminal state with live applications must still have an exit) before activating it.

Scheduler and clock changes. A daily job scheduled with system_clock ran twice on the day the server's clock was corrected backwards by NTP. Use steady_clock for intervals and compute "next civil time" (02:00 IST) explicitly from a time zone each time, never by adding 86,400 seconds.

In the interview room. If the interviewer pushes toward a distributed version, say what changes: state moves to a shared store, operations become idempotent with request ids, locks become leases with expiry, and you now need to discuss what happens during a network partition. Then return to the single-node design they asked for.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Parking lot: add an ElectricCar that must take a spot with a charger. Done when only the allocator and fit rule changed and a test proves it does not take a plain Medium spot.
  2. (easy) KV transactions: add NUMEQUALTO as an alias of COUNT and an END command that stops a script. Done when the script test in main covers both.
  3. (medium) LRU: make capacity count bytes (key.size() + value.size()) instead of entries. Done when one large put evicts several small entries and a value larger than capacity is rejected.
  4. (medium) Rate limiter: implement the sliding window counter (two fixed windows, weighted by overlap) and show it refuses the boundary burst that FixedWindow allows. Done when its test sits next to the fixed-window test.
  5. (hard) Workflow engine: add an SLA. If an application stays UnderReview longer than 48 hours, an Escalate event moves it to a new Escalated state. Use SchedulerCore from m11_job_scheduler.cpp with a fake time to drive it. Done when the test advances time and sees the escalation, and a decision before the deadline cancels the timer.
  6. (hard) Timed practice: for each of the seven problems, start a 45-minute timer, open an empty file, and produce clarifications, a diagram and compiling code. Done when you finish all seven within time, then compare with the code files.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Walk me through how you approach an LLD problem. A: Clarify requirements, scale, concurrency and scope first and write them down. Identify entities and the parts likely to vary, which become strategies. Draw a class diagram with ownership. Code the core data structures and two or three central methods so they compile, then walk an example, cover edge cases, and discuss threading, scale and trade-offs.

Q: Why a list plus a hash map for LRU, and why splice? A: The map gives O(1) lookup of the node, the list keeps recency order with O(1) unlink and relink, and splice moves a node to the front without allocation while keeping all other iterators valid. Storing list iterators in the map is safe because list iterators are never invalidated by operations on other nodes.

Q: How would you make your LRU cache thread-safe and scalable? A: Start with one mutex around the operations; note that get mutates recency so a reader-writer lock does not help. To scale, shard by key hash with an independent cache and lock per shard, accepting approximate global LRU, or move to a CLOCK-style design where hits only set a bit atomically.

Q: Token bucket vs sliding window? A: Token bucket allows controlled bursts up to its capacity and enforces a long-run rate with two numbers of state; it is the usual default. A sliding window log enforces an exact count in any trailing window but stores a timestamp per accepted request; the sliding window counter approximates it with two counters.

Q: Undo log or overlay for transactions in a KV store? A: Undo log keeps reads O(1) and makes rollback replay the before-images, but other clients see uncommitted writes. Overlay layers keep the base untouched until commit, giving isolation at the cost of O(depth) reads. The choice depends on whether multiple clients read concurrently.

Q: How do you design a state machine for a business workflow? A: A table of (state, event) to transition, each with allowed roles, guard rules and actions; a generic engine that runs all guards and reports every failure, records an audit entry for every attempt, changes state, then runs actions. Persist state, audit and outbox in one transaction and use optimistic locking against concurrent edits.

Q: How do you test a scheduler without sleeping? A: Separate a pure core that takes now as a parameter from the thread that waits. All ordering, cancellation and retry logic is tested by calling the core with chosen times; the threaded shell gets a couple of short real-time smoke tests.

Q: In an async logger, what happens when the queue is full? A: Choose explicitly: drop and count (protects request latency; the right default for a server), block (never loses logs, can stall the service), or drop low-severity records first. Expose the drop count as a metric so data loss is visible.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Method: clarify, entities, variation, diagram, code, test and extend. Talk throughout.
  • Make only the varying parts pluggable; std::function for one operation, interfaces for several.
  • Parking lot: enum plus fit rule over a vehicle hierarchy; sets of free indices; one mutex.
  • LRU with TTL: list plus map plus splice; lazy and swept expiry; inject the clock; shard to scale.
  • KV transactions: undo log with first-write-wins before-images; one choke point for counts.
  • Logger: macro that skips disabled work, RAII line, owned records, bounded dropping queue, write outside the lock.
  • Rate limiter: pure single-key algorithms taking now; striped keyed wrapper; idle eviction.
  • Workflow engine: data-driven table, all guards reported, audit always, actions via outbox.
  • Scheduler: pure core plus thin threaded shell; heap with sequence tie-break; lazy cancel.

docs.title: 12. UML and Communicating Design
docs.text: Time: ~1.5 hours Prerequisites: 09, 11

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A design that lives only in your head cannot be reviewed, criticised or improved by anyone else. In an interview it cannot even be graded. Communicating design is a separate skill from having one: choosing what to show, drawing it so it reads in seconds, and explaining the choices before someone asks.

UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a standard set of diagram notations. The full standard is huge; nobody uses all of it. Three diagrams cover almost everything a C++ engineer draws: the class diagram (what the pieces are and who owns whom), the sequence diagram (who calls whom, in what order, for one request), and the state diagram (the states an object moves through). Learn those three well enough to draw them in ASCII on a shared editor, and as PlantUML text that turns into a picture in a design document.

Then learn two formats: a 10-minute spoken design presentation, and a one-to-two page design document with a trade-off table. Those are what senior engineers produce every week.

docs.title: 2.1 Class diagrams: only the notation you need
docs.text:
+----------------------+
 | ClassName            |     name
 +----------------------+
 | - field: Type        |     fields (often omitted on whiteboards)
 +----------------------+     visibility: + public, - private, # protected
 | + method(arg): Ret   |     operations: the important ones only
 +----------------------+

 A <>------> B     composition: A owns B, B dies with A        (C++: B member or unique_ptr<B>)
 A <> - - -> B     aggregation: A refers to B it does not own   (C++: B& / B* / weak_ptr)
 A --------> B     association / uses: A calls or depends on B
 A ------|>  B     generalisation: A inherits from B             (C++: class A : public B)
 A - - - |>  B     realisation: A implements interface B        (C++: B has pure virtuals)
 A - - - - > B     dependency: A uses B transiently (parameter, local)

 Multiplicity at the ends:  1   0..1   *   1..*

Rules for a readable class diagram:

  • Ownership first. For a C++ audience, composition versus reference is the most useful information on the page. Draw every unique_ptr and value member as composition, every reference or observer pointer as aggregation/association.
  • Fewer than about ten boxes. If you need more, draw two diagrams at two levels.
  • Interfaces marked. Write <<interface>> above the name, or name it with the role (Storage, Clock) and draw realisations to it.
  • Leave out getters, setters, constructors and standard library types. Show vector<Level> as a composition with multiplicity *, not as a box for vector.

Example (the KV service from Module 09):

                         +------------------+
                         | <<interface>>    |
                         | Storage          |
                         +------------------+
                         | get/put/erase    |
                         +------------------+
                                  ^
                                  | (realises)
 +-------------+         +--------+--------+       +---------------+
 | KvService   |         | MemoryStorage   |       | <<interface>> |
 | get/set/del |         +-----------------+       | Logger        |
 +-------------+                                   +---------------+
    |     |                                                ^
    |     +-- holds Logger& (not owned) -------------------+
    +-------- holds Storage& (not owned) ---> Storage (above)

The same diagram as PlantUML text (paste into any PlantUML renderer or the VS Code PlantUML extension):

@startuml
interface Storage {
  +get(key): optional<string>
  +put(key, value)
  +erase(key): bool
}
interface Logger {
  +log(level, msg)
}
class KvService {
  +get(key): Result<string>
  +set(key, value): Result<Unit>
  +del(key): Result<bool>
}
class MemoryStorage
Storage <|.. MemoryStorage
KvService o--> Storage : borrows
KvService o--> Logger : borrows
@enduml

PlantUML arrows to remember: <|-- inheritance, <|.. implements, *-- composition, o-- aggregation, --> association, ..> dependency.

docs.title: 2.2 Sequence diagrams: one request, in order
docs.text:
Use one when the order of calls matters: a request through the layers, a handshake, a shutdown. Time flows down; each column is an object; solid arrows are calls, dashed are returns.

ASCII, for SET key value in tcpkv:

 Client     Connection     Parser       KvService      Storage
   |  "SET a 5\nhello\n"     |              |              |
   |---------->|             |              |              |
   |           | feed(bytes) |              |              |
   |           |------------>|              |              |
   |           |  Request{Set}              |              |
   |           |<- - - - - - |              |              |
   |           | set("a","hello")           |              |
   |           |--------------------------->|              |
   |           |             |              | put("a",...) |
   |           |             |              |------------->|
   |           |             |              |<- - - - - - -|
   |           |  Result ok  |              |              |
   |           |<- - - - - - - - - - - - - -|              |
   |  "+OK\n"  |             |              |              |
   |<----------|             |              |              |

PlantUML:

@startuml
actor Client
participant Connection
participant Parser
participant KvService
database Storage
Client -> Connection : "SET a 5\nhello\n"
Connection -> Parser : feed(bytes)
Parser --> Connection : Request{Set}
Connection -> KvService : set("a", "hello")
KvService -> Storage : put("a", "hello")
Storage --> KvService
KvService --> Connection : Result ok
Connection --> Client : "+OK\n"
@enduml

Add alt/else boxes for error paths and loop for repetition, but keep the happy path readable first; draw the error path as a second diagram if it is complicated.

docs.title: 2.3 State diagrams
docs.text:
For anything with a lifecycle: connections, loan applications, orders, jobs.

          Submit             StartReview              Approve              Disburse
 [Draft] -------> [Submitted] ----------> [UnderReview] -------> [Approved] -------> [Disbursed]
    |                 |                     |      |                 |
    |                 |                     |      +---Reject---> [Rejected]
    |                 |                     |                        |
    +-----------------+--------Cancel-------+------------------------+-----> [Cancelled]

 Guard on Approve: [FOIR <= 50% and approver != maker]

PlantUML:

@startuml
[*] --> Draft
Draft --> Submitted : Submit [KYC, age, amount]
Submitted --> UnderReview : StartReview
UnderReview --> Approved : Approve [FOIR, maker-checker]
UnderReview --> Rejected : Reject
Approved --> Disbursed : Disburse
Draft --> Cancelled : Cancel
Submitted --> Cancelled : Cancel
UnderReview --> Cancelled : Cancel
Approved --> Cancelled : Cancel
Disbursed --> [*]
Rejected --> [*]
Cancelled --> [*]
@enduml

Notation: event [guard] / action on each arrow. A state diagram is also the best test plan you will ever get: one test per arrow, one test per guard, and one test per (state, event) pair that is not drawn, which must be refused.

docs.title: 2.4 Other diagrams worth knowing by name
docs.text:
• Component / box-and-arrow diagram: layers and libraries (Module 09's architecture pictures). Not strict UML; the most common diagram in real design documents.
  • Deployment diagram: which process runs on which machine, with which ports. Useful for the loan server: app servers, database nodes, load balancer.
  • Activity diagram: a flowchart with parallel branches. Rarely worth it; a numbered list usually reads better.

The C4 model (context, containers, components, code) is a popular convention for drawing software architecture at four zoom levels; it is worth recognising the name.

docs.title: 2.5 Presenting a design in 10 minutes
docs.text:
The structure that works in interviews and design reviews:

Minute Content 0 to 1 Problem and requirements. One sentence of what, the 3-5 functional requirements, the numbers (scale, latency), what is out of scope. 1 to 3 The big picture. One diagram. Name each box and say its single responsibility. 3 to 6 The core. The central data structure or flow. A sequence diagram for the main request, or the class diagram of the core. Show the one piece of code that matters. 6 to 8 Decisions and trade-offs. Two or three decisions, each with the alternative you rejected and why. The trade-off table. 8 to 9 Failure and scale. What happens when X fails; what breaks first at 10x and what you would do. 9 to 10 Open questions and next steps. What you would build next, what you need decided.

Speaking rules:

  • Lead with the answer. "It is a list plus a hash map, sharded by key" first, then why.
  • Point at the diagram while talking; refer to boxes by the names written on them.
  • Name trade-offs before you are asked. "This makes reads O(depth); I accepted that because transactions are rarely more than two deep." That sentence is the senior signal.
  • Stop for questions at the end of each section instead of racing to the end.
  • Do not defend every choice to the death. "Good point; with that requirement I would switch to X" is the right answer when the requirement changes.

docs.title: 2.6 Design document template
docs.text:
One to two pages for a component, up to about six for a system. Copy this skeleton:

# <Component name>: design

Author: <name>   Reviewers: <names>   Status: draft / in review / accepted   Date: <yyyy-mm-dd>

## 1. Context
Why this exists. The problem in two or three sentences. Links to tickets.

## 2. Goals and non-goals
Goals: numbered, testable ("p99 GET latency under 1 ms at 50k req/s on one node").
Non-goals: what this deliberately does not do, so reviewers do not ask.

## 3. Design
3.1 Overview diagram (component or class).
3.2 Main flow (sequence diagram for the primary request).
3.3 Data model / key data structures.
3.4 Interfaces (public API, wire format, config keys).
3.5 Concurrency and ownership (threads, locks, who owns what).
3.6 Failure handling (what fails, what the system does, what the user sees).

## 4. Alternatives considered
For each: one paragraph and why it was not chosen. Include a trade-off table.

## 5. Testing and rollout
Unit, integration, load tests. Rollout plan: flag, shadow, percentage, rollback.

## 6. Observability
Metrics, logs, alerts that tell you it is working.

## 7. Open questions
Numbered, each with an owner.

Writing rules: state numbers with units and their source ("typical", "measured on staging"). Write decisions as sentences ("We use an undo log because..."), not as bullet fragments. Put the trade-off table where the decision is made, not in an appendix.

docs.title: 2.7 Trade-off tables
docs.text:
A trade-off table compares options against criteria that matter for this problem. It is the fastest way to show you considered alternatives.

Criterion Option A: one mutex Option B: 16 striped mutexes Option C: lock-free map Throughput under contention low high highest Code complexity trivial small high (memory reclamation) Correctness risk very low low (no cross-stripe ops) high Cross-key operations (KEYS, snapshot) easy must lock all stripes in order hard Fits our load (about 2k req/s) yes yes overkill Decision chosen: headroom at small cost

Rules:

  • Criteria first, from the requirements, before you fill cells. Otherwise you choose criteria that favour the option you already like.
  • Words or measured numbers in the cells. "Fast" is not a measurement; "120 ns/op on the staging box, bench/lock_bench" is.
  • Include the option you rejected that a reviewer will suggest. It pre-empts the question.
  • State the decision and the main reason in one line under the table.

Common trade-off axes for C++ design: runtime vs compile-time polymorphism (Module 08), latency vs throughput, memory vs CPU, consistency vs availability, simplicity vs flexibility, build-time cost vs run-time cost.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text:
This module has no code file. Its "code" is the PlantUML above and the diagrams in the headers of the Module 11 files: open code/m11_workflow_engine.cpp, code/m11_job_scheduler.cpp and code/m11_rate_limiter.cpp and compare their ASCII class diagrams to the code beneath. Exercise 2 asks you to turn one into PlantUML.

A compact PlantUML class diagram for the job scheduler, for reference:

@startuml
class Scheduler {
  +schedule_after(d, fn, retries): JobId
  +schedule_every(period, fn): JobId
  +cancel(id): bool
  +stop()
  -dispatch()
  -work()
}
class SchedulerCore {
  +schedule_at(when, fn, retries): JobId
  +run_due(now): vector<Due>
  +report(id, ok, now, backoff)
  +next_due(): optional<TimePoint>
}
class Job
class Entry
Scheduler *-- SchedulerCore
SchedulerCore *-- "*" Job : jobs_ / in_flight_
SchedulerCore *-- "*" Entry : heap_
@enduml

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
How diagram notation maps onto C++ object layout. Composition by value means the part's bytes are inside the whole (sizeof(ParkingLot) includes the std::vector header, and the vector's heap block holds the Levels). Composition by unique_ptr means 8 bytes inside and a separate heap block with its own lifetime bound to the owner. Aggregation by reference means 8 bytes and no lifetime relation, so the diagram must say who does own the target. Generalisation means the derived object starts with its base subobject (and a vptr if the base is polymorphic). A reader who knows this can estimate memory and cache behaviour from a class diagram, which is why ownership arrows matter more to C++ reviewers than to Java reviewers.

Dependency arrows and the build. Each "uses" arrow between components becomes an #include and a link dependency. A cycle on the diagram becomes either a header cycle (fixed with forward declarations) or a static-library cycle (needing --start-group). Draw the component diagram before the CMake file and the two should match.

Sequence diagrams and threads. A plain sequence diagram assumes one thread. When a call crosses threads (enqueue to a pool, condition variable notify), draw it as an asynchronous message (open arrowhead, ->> in PlantUML) and show the queue as its own participant. Many concurrency bugs become visible the moment you draw where each lifeline's thread changes: a callback arriving on a thread that does not hold the lock you assumed.

PlantUML itself is a Java program that parses the text and lays out the graph with Graphviz (for class and component diagrams) or its own layout engine (for sequence diagrams). Because the source is text, diagrams can live in the repository next to the code, be reviewed in pull requests, and be regenerated in CI, unlike a picture pasted into a wiki. Mermaid is a JavaScript alternative with similar syntax that GitHub renders natively in Markdown files.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
The diagram that lied. An architecture diagram on the wiki showed the app server talking only to the database; in reality three handlers also called a credit-bureau service directly with a 30-second timeout. When the bureau slowed down, the worker pool exhausted and the whole server stopped, and the on-call engineer lost an hour because the diagram did not show the dependency. Keep diagrams as text in the repo, next to the code, and update them in the same pull request as the change.

Design reviews that stall. A twelve-page design document with no decision stated up front gets comments on fonts and naming. Put the decision and its trade-off table on page one. Reviewers then argue about the decision, which is what you need.

Sequence diagrams for incidents. In a post-incident review, a sequence diagram of what actually happened (with timestamps from logs on each arrow) is the clearest way to show a race or a timeout chain. It is also the format that convinces a manager to fund the fix.

Explaining your work in interviews. For the resume line on the loan-origination server, prepare one component diagram (Module 09 section 2.10), one sequence diagram for "submit an application", and the state diagram for the application lifecycle. Three pictures, ten minutes, and you can answer most follow-ups by pointing.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Draw the class diagram of code/m11_parking_lot.cpp in ASCII with correct composition and association arrows. Done when every unique_ptr/value member is composition and every reference is aggregation.
  2. (easy) Convert the ASCII class diagram at the top of code/m11_rate_limiter.cpp to PlantUML and render it. Done when the rendered picture matches the code.
  3. (medium) Draw a sequence diagram for tcpkv shutdown (spec section 4.4) including the signal handler, the wake pipe, the acceptor, the thread pool and one busy worker. Mark the asynchronous arrows. Done when every step in the spec appears as an arrow.
  4. (medium) Write a trade-off table for "where should loan eligibility rules live: C++ service, PL/pgSQL procedure, or a rules-engine product" with at least six criteria. Done when it ends with a one-line decision and reason.
  5. (hard) Write a two-page design document using the template for the LRU cache with TTL (Module 11) as if it were going into the loan server as the master-data cache. Present it aloud in 10 minutes with a timer, recording yourself. Done when the recording is under 10 minutes and covers every row of the presentation table.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Which UML diagrams do you actually use? A: Class diagrams for structure and ownership, sequence diagrams for the order of calls in one request or protocol, and state diagrams for lifecycles. Plus informal component diagrams for architecture. The rest of UML rarely pays for itself.

Q: What is the difference between composition and aggregation, in C++ terms? A: Composition means the whole owns the part and the part's lifetime ends with the whole: a value member or a unique_ptr. Aggregation means the whole refers to a part it does not own: a reference, raw observer pointer or weak_ptr, with someone else responsible for keeping it alive.

Q: How would you present a design in ten minutes? A: Problem and requirements in a minute, one big-picture diagram, the core flow or data structure, two or three decisions with rejected alternatives and a trade-off table, failure and scale behaviour, then open questions. Lead with the answer and name trade-offs before being asked.

Q: What goes into a design document? A: Context, goals and non-goals, the design (diagram, main flow, data model, interfaces, concurrency, failure handling), alternatives considered with a trade-off table, testing and rollout, observability, and open questions with owners. Decisions stated as sentences near the top.

Q: How do you build a trade-off table that is not biased? A: Choose criteria from the requirements before filling in options, include the option a reviewer is likely to suggest, use measured numbers or plain words rather than adjectives, and state the decision and its main reason under the table.

Q: Why keep diagrams as text? A: Text diagrams (PlantUML, Mermaid) live in the repository, are reviewed and versioned with the code, and can be updated in the same change that alters the design. Pictures on a wiki drift out of date and mislead people during incidents.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Three diagrams: class (structure and ownership), sequence (order of calls), state (lifecycle).
  • Composition = value member or unique_ptr; aggregation = reference or observer pointer.
  • Fewer than ten boxes per diagram; ownership arrows matter most to C++ readers.
  • PlantUML arrows: <|--, <|.., *--, o--, -->, ..>; async messages ->>.
  • A state diagram is a test plan: one test per arrow, guard and missing arrow.
  • Ten-minute talk: requirements, picture, core, trade-offs, failure and scale, open questions.
  • Design doc: context, goals, design, alternatives with a table, testing, observability, questions.
  • Trade-off tables: criteria first, honest cells, the rejected option included, one-line decision.
  • Keep diagrams as text in the repo and change them with the code.

docs.title: Exercises: 09 OOP, Design Patterns and Architecture
docs.text:
Every exercise from every module, in one place. The full statement and the "done when" condition are in section 6 of each module; this list gives the short form, the difficulty and a hint. Build everything with:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pthread -fsanitize=address,undefined -o ex file.cpp && ./ex

Use -fsanitize=thread (instead of address) for anything with threads.

Suggested path if time is short: do every easy exercise in modules 01, 03, 06, 08, 09 and 11, then the medium ones in 09 and 11, then exercise 11.6 (timed practice) until you can finish each LLD problem in 45 minutes.

docs.title: Module 01: OOP for a C programmer
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 1.1 easy Add size to the C function-pointer store and to the virtual Store; compare failure modes A forgotten C slot is a null call at run time; a missing pure virtual override is a compile error when you instantiate. 1.2 easy Turn one of your C modules into a class with private state Find the invariant first (e.g. head < capacity), then make every mutation a member function that keeps it. 1.3 medium Shape as a hierarchy and as std::variant; compare sizeof and allocations Hierarchy: one heap block per shape plus a vptr each; variant: size of the largest alternative plus a tag, stored inline. 1.4 medium Fix the dangling pointer from find() two ways std::map nodes never move; or look up by id inside transfer after any call that can reallocate. 1.5 hard Benchmark virtual (mixed and uniform types), variant, template Uniform types make the indirect branch perfectly predicted; the remaining gap is lost inlining and pointer chasing.

docs.title: Module 02: SOLID in plain words
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 2.1 easy Add DEL without touching KvService Open/closed: register a new operation object in the table the service reads. 2.2 easy ReadOnlyStore that throws on put; fix with ReadableStore This is Liskov plus interface segregation: split the interface so the read-only type never promises put. 2.3 medium Clock interface and TtlStore decorator tested with FixedClock The decorator stores expiry per key and asks the clock on every get; the test advances the fake clock. 2.4 medium Split one real C function into parse / rule / storage on paper Write the storage interface from the rule's point of view: only the queries the rule needs. 2.5 hard Generic contract(make_store) test template Call it with lambdas returning unique_ptr<Store>; use assert with a message string via && "msg".

docs.title: Module 03: Ownership and object lifetime design
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 3.1 easy Ownership diagram of your work RPC server Every dashed arrow to something not owned by an ancestor is a potential use-after-free; list each one. 3.2 easy Swap member order of metrics_ and conns_ and predict shutdown Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order; a connection's destructor that touches metrics must die first. 3.3 medium Generation counters for BufferPool handles Store a generation per slot, bump it on release, compare in get(). 3.4 medium Arena that runs destructors on reset() Keep a vector of (ptr, dtor) pairs; a captureless lambda converts to void(*)(void*). 3.5 hard Two-thread server: I/O thread owns connections, worker gets ids Workers never hold Connection*; replies carry a ConnId the I/O thread looks up and drops if gone.

docs.title: Module 04: Creational patterns
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 4.1 easy Add a "cached" kind to make_store The factory composes: construct the memory store, then wrap it. 4.2 easy Cross-field validation in ServerConfigBuilder Validate in build(), not in the setters, because the order of setter calls is free. 4.3 medium Replace a MetricsRegistry singleton with DI and show state leaking between tests Run two scenarios in one process; the singleton keeps counts from the first. 4.4 medium Health-checked ConnectionPool::acquire() Loop: pop, check alive(), discard dead ones, construct a new one if the pool runs dry. 4.5 hard Self-registering factory and the static-library trap An unreferenced object file in a .a is never pulled in; fix with --whole-archive or explicit registration calls.

docs.title: Module 05: Structural patterns
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 5.1 easy erase() through the C API adapter Map the C return code to bool; only throw for real failures, not "not found". 5.2 easy TimeoutStore decorator in two stack positions Outside the retry it times the whole retried call; inside it times each attempt. 5.3 medium Negative caching in CachingStoreProxy Cache std::nullopt with a short TTL and invalidate on put of that key. 5.4 medium Age rule as a leaf and as a composite, plus Not Composites win when rules are assembled from configuration; leaves win for clarity of one fixed rule. 5.5 hard Split pimpl into three files and observe rebuilds and the destructor error ~unique_ptr<Impl> needs the complete Impl; define the destructor in the .cpp where Impl is complete.

docs.title: Module 06: Behavioural patterns
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 6.1 easy TieredFee strategy from a threshold table Capture the vector by value in the lambda ([tiers = std::move(t)]). 6.2 easy AuditLog unsubscribes inside its own callback notify() iterates a snapshot of ids and re-checks each id still exists before calling. 6.3 medium Connection state machine as enum + switch Remove a case and compile with -Wall to see -Wswitch name the missing enumerator. 6.4 medium Add Refund to the variant and to the classic visitor Variant: every visit without a generic fallback fails to compile. Classic: only visitors missing the new visit overload fail. 6.5 hard timeout middleware with a worker thread Capture the request by value (or shared_ptr) in the worker; the caller's stack frame is gone after the timeout. 6.6 hard Bidirectional RingBuffer::iterator Store a logical position (0..size) instead of a raw index; wrap only when dereferencing.

docs.title: Module 07: Concurrency patterns
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 7.1 easy Bound of 1 vs 1000 in producer-consumer Small bound: more blocking and context switches; large bound: more memory and latency hidden in the queue. 7.2 easy Non-blocking try_push Same lock, check size() == cap, return false instead of waiting. 7.3 medium Reproduce and fix thread-pool self-deadlock Record worker thread ids at start; if the caller is a worker, run the child task inline. 7.4 medium shared_mutex config vs RCU snapshot benchmark Every shared_lock writes the mutex's reader count: one cache line bouncing between cores. 7.5 hard Supervisor actor that restarts a crashed account actor Wrap the actor loop in try; on exception send Died{name} to the supervisor with the last state. 7.6 hard Minimal epoll reactor plus thread pool and eventfd Replies go through a queue; the worker writes to the eventfd; the loop drains replies and looks up ConnId, dropping unknown ones.

docs.title: Module 08: Modern C++ alternatives to classic patterns
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 8.1 easy Third store type in vector<AnyStore> It only needs put and get members with the right signatures; no base class. 8.2 easy CountingLog policy A stateless policy (static counter) keeps the empty base optimisation, so sizeof does not change. 8.3 medium Small-buffer optimisation for AnyStore alignas(std::max_align_t) unsigned char buf[32], placement new, and a flag or function pointer to know which storage is in use. 8.4 medium Escape event and Paused state in the variant framer Without the fallback overload, the compiler lists each missing (state, event) pair as an error. 8.5 hard Virtual decorator stack vs policy store benchmark Use -O2, a volatile sink for results, and perf stat to see instructions per call; also compare size of both binaries. 8.6 hard Find the pipeline loop in assembly -O2 -S -fverbose-asm; search for the loop label; with std::function look for call *%rax or similar.

docs.title: Module 09: Designing a server codebase
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 9.1 easy Add EXISTS to m09_layered_server.cpp Touch protocol (new variant alternative), serve (new lambda) and one service function; storage already has get. 9.2 easy RequestIdLogger decorator Wrap common::Logger, hold the id, prefix each message; create one per request inside serve. 9.3 medium FlakyStorage that fails as Unavailable, never as "not found" The port must be able to say "failed": return Result<optional<string>> from get, and map Unavailable to -ERR try again. 9.4 medium CMake target graph that forbids service -> storage includes Give each target only its own src/<layer> as an include directory; link only along the allowed arrows. 9.5 hard Characterization tests, then split a legacy handler Capture outputs for at least 15 inputs first, including malformed ones; refactor only while all pass. 9.6 hard One-page architecture for the loan-origination server Use the Module 12 template; the outbox and unit-of-work decisions each need a rejected alternative.

docs.title: Module 10: API design and code quality
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 10.1 easy BranchId strong type and a swapped call that fails to compile Distinct tag types make Strong<A, int> and Strong<B, int> unrelated types. 10.2 easy Observe [[nodiscard]] turning into an error -Werror promotes -Wunused-result; restore the attribute afterwards. 10.3 medium ChaosLedger fake that fails post on demand A public bool fail_next flag in the fake is fine; tests own their doubles. 10.4 medium std::hash for Strong Specialise template <class Tag, class Rep> struct std::hash<Strong<Tag, Rep>> and hash get() inside it. 10.5 hard Asynchronous shadow route with a timeout Run the new handler via std::async or a small pool, never wait for it on the request path; compare results in the background. 10.6 hard Review a real function with the checklist Write findings as "problem, risk, suggested change"; at least one per group (design, correctness, quality).

docs.title: Module 11: Low-level design interview walkthroughs
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 11.1 easy ElectricCar needing a charger spot Model chargers as a separate size class or a per-spot flag; only the fit rule and allocator change. 11.2 easy NUMEQUALTO alias and END command in the KV interpreter Keep the store unchanged; this is protocol-layer work only. 11.3 medium Byte-based capacity in the LRU Track bytes_used_; evict in a loop until the new entry fits; reject entries larger than capacity. 11.4 medium Sliding window counter rate limiter estimate = prev_count * (1 - elapsed_fraction) + curr_count; refuse if estimate >= limit. 11.5 hard SLA escalation in the workflow engine driven by SchedulerCore Schedule an escalation job in the StartReview action; cancel it in the actions of Approve and Reject. 11.6 hard Timed practice: all seven problems in 45 minutes each Write the clarifying questions first, every time; compare your diagram with the one in the code file header.

docs.title: Module 12: UML and communicating design
docs.text: # Level Exercise Hint 12.1 easy ASCII class diagram of m11_parking_lot.cpp vector<Level> is composition with *; the allocator and fee policy are owned std::functions, so also composition. 12.2 easy PlantUML for the rate limiter diagram KeyedRateLimiter *-- "*" Algorithm, Algorithm <|-- TokenBucket, and so on. 12.3 medium Sequence diagram of tcpkv shutdown Signal handler and worker threads are separate lifelines; use ->> for the wake-pipe write and condition variable notify. 12.4 medium Trade-off table: where eligibility rules live Criteria: round trips, testability, consistency across callers, deploy process, scaling tier, who can change rules. 12.5 hard Two-page design doc for a master-data cache, presented in 10 minutes Record yourself; check each row of the presentation table is covered and that the decision appears in the first minute.

docs.title: Interview Questions: OOP, Design Patterns and Architecture in C++
docs.text: 38 questions with model answers, ordered from basic to senior. Answer out loud first, then compare. The module in brackets is where the topic is covered in depth.

docs.title: Basics
docs.text:
1. What does a class give you that a C struct plus functions does not? [01] Access control that enforces invariants (only member functions can change private state), constructors and destructors that run automatically (RAII), and virtual functions for runtime polymorphism without hand-written function-pointer tables. The generated code for a non-virtual member function is the same as a C function taking a struct pointer; the gain is in what the compiler checks for you.

2. How does a virtual call work, and what does it cost? [01] Each object of a polymorphic class holds a vptr to its class's vtable, an array of function pointers. A virtual call loads the vptr, loads the slot, and makes an indirect call: a few nanoseconds when predicted. The bigger cost is that the call cannot be inlined, so the optimiser loses constant folding and vectorisation across it, plus 8 bytes per object.

3. Why must a base class with virtual functions have a virtual destructor? [01] Deleting a derived object through a base pointer calls the base destructor only, unless the destructor is virtual; the derived part is never destroyed, which is undefined behaviour and in practice a leak or corruption. Either make it public virtual or make it protected and non-virtual so deletion through the base is impossible.

4. State the SOLID principles in one sentence each. [02] Single responsibility: a module has one reason to change. Open/closed: add behaviour by adding code, not editing working code. Liskov substitution: a derived type must honour every promise of its base. Interface segregation: clients depend only on the operations they use. Dependency inversion: high-level policy and low-level detail both depend on an abstraction owned by the policy side.

5. Give a Liskov violation and its fix. [02] A ReadOnlyStore deriving from Store and throwing from put(): code written against Store breaks when handed it. Fix by splitting interfaces, a ReadableStore with get and a Store that adds put, so the read-only type never promises what it cannot do.

6. Composition or inheritance? [01, 02] Prefer composition: it couples to a public interface, can be changed at runtime, and does not expose the base's internals. Use public inheritance for a genuine "is-a" with substitutability, mostly to implement an interface. Implementation inheritance for code reuse tends to produce fragile hierarchies where a base change breaks subclasses.

7. What is dependency injection, and why not just use a singleton? [02, 04] Dependency injection means a component receives its collaborators (store, clock, logger) from its creator, usually through the constructor, instead of finding them itself. It makes dependencies visible in the signature and replaceable in tests. A singleton is a hidden global: tests share its state, initialisation and destruction order are hard to control, and every user is coupled to one concrete class.

8. What problems does a singleton cause in C++ specifically? [04] Static initialisation order across translation units is unspecified, so one global may use another before it is constructed; destruction order at exit can leave a logger destroyed before an object that logs in its destructor. Function-local statics fix construction (thread-safe since C++11) but not destruction or test isolation. If one instance is required, create it in main and pass it down.

docs.title: Ownership and lifetime
docs.text:
9. How do you design ownership in a server? [03] Draw a tree: each object has exactly one owner, expressed as a value member or unique_ptr; everything else holds references or observer pointers to things owned by an ancestor, so they outlive the observer. The server owns the listener, pool and store; connections own their sockets and buffers. shared_ptr is reserved for genuinely shared lifetimes, such as an immutable config snapshot read by many requests.

10. Why is shared_ptr everywhere a design smell? [03] It hides who is responsible for an object's lifetime, so destruction happens at an unpredictable time on an unpredictable thread. It costs an atomic increment and decrement per copy and a control block. Cycles leak. Most objects have one clear owner, and saying so with unique_ptr makes the design reviewable.

11. What is the observer lifetime bug and how do you prevent it? [06] The subject keeps raw pointers to observers; an observer is destroyed without unsubscribing, and the next notify calls through a dangling pointer. A second form is a callback that subscribes or unsubscribes during iteration. Fix with an RAII subscription token stored as the observer's last member, and iterate over a snapshot of ids; or store weak_ptrs and lock() before each call. Across threads, the weak_ptr lock or posting events to the observer's own thread is needed, because a token can unsubscribe while a callback runs.

12. When is a raw pointer acceptable in modern C++? [03] As a non-owning, nullable observer of an object whose lifetime is guaranteed by someone else, for example a child pointing to its owner, or a function parameter that may be null. Never as an owner. If it cannot be null, a reference is clearer.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
13. Strategy: std::function, virtual interface, or template parameter? [06] One operation chosen at runtime: std::function, which also accepts lambdas with captures. Several related operations or a strategy with identity: an interface. Choice fixed at compile time on a hot path: a template parameter, which inlines. The question is how many operations and when the choice is made.

14. How does std::variant with std::visit replace the visitor pattern? [06, 08] The variant holds one of a closed set of types with a tag maintained for you; std::visit with an overload set calls the right lambda for the active type. No base class, no accept, no heap, and a missing alternative is a compile error unless you add a generic fallback. It suits closed types with open operations; a virtual hierarchy suits open types with a fixed set of operations.

15. What is NVI and why use it? [06] Non-virtual interface: the public function is non-virtual and calls private virtual hooks. The base class keeps control of the skeleton (validation, locking, logging, exception translation) so derived classes can customise steps but cannot skip the invariant parts, and nobody can call a hook directly.

16. How do you implement undo? [06] The command pattern with execute() and undo(), capturing the previous state at execute time rather than at construction. A history stack owns executed commands; a composite command undoes its parts in reverse, which is a transaction. In banking terms, a reversal is the undo of a posting.

17. How would you implement request middleware? [06] As chain of responsibility in function form: a handler is function<Response(const Request&)> and a middleware is a function taking the next handler and returning a new one. Auth, rate limiting, logging and timeouts each wrap the rest of the chain and are composed in order. State shared across copies of a closure (a counter table) lives in a shared_ptr.

18. What is type erasure? [08] Runtime polymorphism without requiring a common base class: a wrapper holds an internal abstract concept, a template model implements it by forwarding to the stored object, and the wrapper has value semantics. std::function and std::any are examples. It lets unrelated types, including ones you cannot modify, be stored and used through one interface.

19. What is CRTP and when do you use it? [08] The curiously recurring template pattern: class Derived : public Base<Derived>, so the base can call derived functions through a static_cast with no virtual dispatch. Use it for compile-time template methods and mixins (adding operators or counters) on hot paths. You lose a common base type, so different derived types cannot share one container.

20. What is policy-based design? [08] A host class takes its behaviours (storage, locking, logging) as template parameters and composes them at compile time. Disabled policies cost nothing thanks to the empty base optimisation and inlining. Costs: one instantiation per combination, configuration fixed at build time, longer compile times and error messages.

21. Virtual functions vs templates: what is the real cost model? [08] Virtual: an indirect call, no inlining, a vptr per object, one copy of the code, decisions at runtime. Templates: direct inlined calls and full optimisation, but one copy of the code per instantiation (binary size, instruction cache, compile time) and the type must be known at compile time. Ask whether the decision is made at runtime and whether the call is hot.

docs.title: Concurrency patterns
docs.text:
22. Active object vs monitor object? [07] A monitor object protects its state with a lock and runs methods on the caller's thread; simple, but callers block on contention. An active object owns a thread and a queue; calls become messages and return futures, so callers never block on its lock and its state is touched by one thread only, at the cost of a queue hop and asynchronous results.

23. Reactor vs proactor? [07] A reactor waits for readiness (epoll says a socket is readable) and the application then performs the non-blocking read itself. A proactor starts the operation and is notified on completion with the data already transferred (Windows IOCP, io_uring). Linux servers are traditionally reactors; your Win32 background maps to the proactor model.

24. Why should a thread pool's queue be bounded? [07] An unbounded queue turns overload into unbounded memory growth and unbounded latency: every request waits behind everything already queued, and the server dies of memory instead of refusing work. A bounded queue forces a decision at the edge: block the producer, reject with "busy", or shed load, which keeps latency for accepted requests predictable.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
25. Describe a layered architecture for a TCP server. [09] Transport (sockets, framing, threads), protocol (bytes to typed requests and back, pure), service (business rules), storage (persistence), plus common value types and a composition root in main. Dependencies point toward the service; the service owns the storage interface, and storage implements it. One CMake target per layer enforces the graph.

26. What is your error-handling policy in a C++ server? [09] Programmer bugs assert or abort; expected failures are values (Result, optional); transient environmental failures carry a retryable code. Each boundary translates errors into the next layer's vocabulary without changing their meaning, wire errors are produced in one function, exceptions never cross threads, C callbacks or destructors, and each error is logged once where it is handled.

27. How would you refactor legacy C business logic into modules? [09, 10] Inventory entry points and rules, write characterization tests that pin current behaviour, create seams by extracting data access behind interfaces and rules into pure functions, then route slices to the new implementation behind a switch (strangler), shadow-compare, switch over and delete the old code. In my stored-procedure project, data-heavy validation, authorisation and workflow rules moved into procedures that return all failures in one call, which cut round trips per transaction.

28. Business rules in stored procedures or in the application server? [09] Data-heavy checks and invariants every caller must respect are better near the data: one round trip and impossible to bypass. Orchestration, integrations and complex computation are better in the server: testable with fakes, debuggable, and scalable by adding servers. Procedures cost database CPU, which is the hardest tier to scale, and need disciplined schema versioning.

29. What is pimpl and how does it relate to ABI stability? [05, 10] Pointer to implementation: the public class holds only a unique_ptr<Impl> and declares its functions; all data and private helpers live in the .cpp. The class's size and layout never change when the implementation does, so old binaries keep working and clients do not recompile. Costs: one heap allocation and one indirection per call, and the destructor must be defined where Impl is complete.

30. What breaks ABI compatibility? [10] Changing the size or layout of a class used across the boundary (adding or reordering members), adding or reordering virtual functions, changing parameter types (the mangled name changes), changing inline functions or templates compiled into clients, and changing an enum's underlying type. The linker matches names only, so most of these fail silently at run time.

31. How do you make an API hard to misuse? [10] Strong types for ids and money, enums instead of boolean flags, named-field request structs, factory functions that validate (parse, don't validate), RAII for paired calls, [[nodiscard]] on results, explicit constructors, = delete on dangerous overloads, and ownership stated in the signature. The aim is that a wrong call does not compile.

32. Fakes vs mocks? [10] A fake is a working simplified implementation (an in-memory ledger), and tests assert on the resulting state; such tests survive refactoring. A mock records calls and verifies interactions; it is right when the interaction is the only observable effect (an SMS, an audit event). Over-mocking ties tests to the implementation and blocks refactoring.

docs.title: Low-level design
docs.text:
33. How do you approach a low-level design interview? [11] Clarify functional requirements, scale, concurrency and scope, and write them down. Identify entities and the parts likely to change, which become strategies. Draw a class diagram with ownership. Code the core data structures and central methods so they compile. Walk an example, handle edge cases, then discuss thread safety, scale and trade-offs, talking throughout.

34. Design an LRU cache with TTL. Key points? [11] A doubly linked list in recency order plus a hash map from key to list iterator; splice moves a node to the front in O(1) without invalidating other iterators. Each entry stores its expiry from an injected steady clock; expiry is lazy on get plus a periodic sweep. One mutex for thread safety (get mutates, so a reader-writer lock does not help), sharding by key hash to scale.

35. Design a rate limiter. Which algorithm and why? [11] Token bucket by default: two numbers of state per key, lazy refill on each call, bursts up to capacity, exact long-run rate. Sliding window log when an exact count in any window is required, at O(limit) memory per key. Wrap single-key algorithms in a keyed, lock-striped map with idle-key eviction, and inject time so tests do not sleep.

36. How do you design a workflow engine for loan applications? [11] A table of (state, event) to transition, each with allowed roles, guard rules and actions. The generic engine runs every guard and reports all failures, writes an audit entry for every attempt, changes state, then runs actions. Persist state, audit and outbox rows in one transaction, use optimistic locking for concurrent edits, and load the table from configuration so new products need no new code.

37. How would you design and test a job scheduler? [11] A pure core holding a min-heap of (due time, sequence, id) and a job map, with run_due(now) returning due jobs, lazy cancellation and retry with back-off; then a thin threaded shell whose dispatcher sleeps with wait_until on the next due time and hands jobs to workers. All ordering logic is tested by calling the core with chosen times; the threads get a couple of short smoke tests.

38. How do you present a design in ten minutes? [12] One minute of problem and requirements, a big-picture diagram with each box's responsibility, the core flow or data structure, two or three decisions with the rejected alternatives in a trade-off table, failure and scale behaviour, then open questions. Lead with the answer and name the trade-offs before the audience asks.

docs.title: 10. Capstone Projects: build tcpkv (and minidb) so the resume is true
docs.text: Time: tcpkv ~60 hours over 5 weeks; minidb ~50 hours over 4 weeks (optional) Prerequisites: C at a professional level (you have it). Modern C++, concurrency, Linux toolchain and networking are studied in parallel; every step says which modules to read first.

docs.title: 1. What this course is
docs.text:
The other nine courses teach you things. This one makes you ship something.

Your resume lists this project:

tcpkv — Multithreaded TCP Key-Value Server. C++17, Linux, CMake, GoogleTest. - Concurrent TCP server with a fixed thread pool and a text protocol over an in-memory store guarded by shared_mutex; RAII socket and file-descriptor wrappers and move-only connection handles. - Builds clean under -Wall -Wextra -Werror with CMake; GoogleTest suite for protocol parsing and store operations; Valgrind-clean under concurrent load.

Today (2026-10-03) that project does not exist. Every claim in those two bullets is checkable in thirty seconds by anyone with the GitHub link. So the project must exist, be public, and be exactly what the bullets say, before the resume leaves your hands.

The second project, minidb, is optional. It is a durable key-value storage engine with a write-ahead log and a B+tree index. It exists so that when an interviewer asks about WAL, pages, crash recovery or B-trees (all things in 07_Databases_Internals), you can answer from code you wrote rather than from a textbook. Do it only if tcpkv is finished and tagged.

docs.title: 2. The one rule
docs.text:
The repository is public at github.com/khanshaki-r/tcpkv, pinned on your profile, with a green CI badge, before you send the resume to anyone.

Not "almost done". Not "private until I clean it up". A recruiter who clicks a dead link, or a link to a repo whose Actions tab is red, forms an opinion in two seconds and you never hear about it. A senior reviewer who opens the repo and finds // TODO in the server loop forms the same opinion more slowly. The definition of done below is the bar.

docs.title: 3. Why these projects, specifically
docs.text:
• They match the job. Your background is a multithreaded RPC-over-TCP application server in C at a banking vendor. tcpkv is that system reduced to its skeleton, rewritten in modern C++ with the tooling a Linux shop expects (CMake, GoogleTest, sanitizers, CI). An interviewer can draw a straight line from your past work to this code to their job.
  • They are small enough to finish and large enough to be judged. About 3,500 lines including tests. Every design decision (thread pool vs epoll, shared_mutex vs sharded locks, text protocol vs binary) is one you can defend in an interview because you made it.
  • They force the courses to stick. RAII, move semantics, std::shared_mutex, condition variables, poll(), EINTR, partial writes, sanitizers, Valgrind, CMake presets, GitHub Actions: each shows up here as a thing you must get right, not a thing you read about.
