docs.title: minidb specification
docs.text:
Status: the contract for the optional second capstone. 01_build_plan.md builds it in eight steps and gives the key classes in full. If the plan and this document disagree, this document wins and the plan has a bug.

Prerequisites: tcpkv tagged v1.0.0 (README of this course, section 1). 07_Databases_Internals modules 02_storage_engines_pages_and_heap_files.md, 03_btree_indexes_in_depth.md and 04_wal_and_crash_recovery.md read at least once; the build plan points back to them.

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
minidb is a tiny storage engine: a library that stores key-value pairs in one file on disk, finds them quickly through a B+tree, and never loses a write it has acknowledged, even if the process is killed in the middle of writing.

Think of a bank ledger kept in a bound book (the data file) plus a carbon-copy receipt pad (the write-ahead log). Before the clerk changes a page in the book, the full new version of that page goes on the receipt pad, and the pad is put in the safe. If the clerk faints halfway through copying into the book, the next clerk reads the receipts in the safe and redoes the copying. Receipts that were never put in the safe are thrown away. Every so often the book is brought fully up to date and the old receipts are shredded (a checkpoint).

You already know the outside of this from your Berkeley DB to YugabyteDB migration: what a storage engine promises. minidb is the inside: how it keeps the promise. Every interview question about pages, B-trees, WAL, LSNs, checkpoints and recovery can then be answered from code you wrote.

docs.title: 2. Goals and non-goals
docs.text:
Goals:

  • Durable: when put or del returns, the change survives a process crash, and survives a power failure as long as the disk honours fdatasync.
  • Atomic per operation: after any crash, each operation is either fully applied or not at all, including operations that split B+tree pages across several pages.
  • Correct and checkable: a structural checker validates the whole tree; a crash test kills the process mid-write 25 times per run and verifies the result every time.
  • Small: about 1,900 lines of library code (headers included) plus about 600 lines of tests in the reference version. Every line explainable.

Non-goals (and what to say when asked "why not"):

  • Concurrency beyond one mutex. One operation at a time. Latch crabbing and MVCC are the next steps; see section 11.
  • Multi-operation transactions. Each put/del is its own transaction. The commit protocol already supports many pages per transaction, so a WriteBatch is a small extension.
  • Space reclamation. Deletes never merge pages or free them. The file never shrinks.
  • Performance. Every write is one or more full-page log records and an fdatasync. That is correct and slow; group commit and delta records are the known fixes (section 11).
  • SQL, secondary indexes, compression, encryption, replication.

docs.title: 3.1 C++
docs.text:
namespace minidb {

struct Options {
    std::size_t cache_pages = 256;                  // page cache size in 4 KiB frames (1 MiB)
    std::uint64_t checkpoint_wal_bytes = 8u << 20;  // checkpoint when the log exceeds 8 MiB
};

class Db {
public:
    explicit Db(const std::string& path, Options options = {});  // opens or creates, runs recovery
    ~Db();                                                         // checkpoints

    void put(std::string_view key, std::string_view value);       // insert or overwrite; durable on return
    std::optional<std::string> get(std::string_view key);
    bool del(std::string_view key);                                // true if the key existed; durable on return
    std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string>>
        scan(std::string_view start, std::string_view end = {}, std::size_t limit = SIZE_MAX);
    void checkpoint();
    std::size_t check();                                           // full structural check, returns key count
};

}  // namespace minidb
operation semantics put(k, v) insert or overwrite. Durable when it returns. Throws std::invalid_argument for an empty key, a key over 128 bytes or a value over 880 bytes. get(k) the value, or std::nullopt del(k) removes the key; returns whether it existed. Durable when it returns. scan(start, end, limit) keys in [start, end) in ascending byte order, at most limit; an empty end means no upper bound checkpoint() writes all dirty pages, syncs the data file, empties the log check() walks the whole tree, verifies every invariant (section 4.4), returns the key count; throws CorruptionError on a violation

Keys compare bytewise (memcmp order). Errors: CorruptionError (bad checksum, bad magic, impossible structure), DbError (cache exhausted, previous commit failed), std::system_error (I/O failure, with errno).

docs.title: 3.2 Command-line tool (minidb_cli)
docs.text:
minidb_cli <file> put <key> <value>
minidb_cli <file> get <key>
minidb_cli <file> del <key>
minidb_cli <file> scan [start] [end] [limit]
minidb_cli <file> check            # prints the key count, or the first violation
minidb_cli <file> stats            # page count, log size, last recovery statistics

docs.title: 3.3 Limits
docs.text: limit value reason page size 4096 bytes the usual OS page and filesystem block size; one page is one I/O key 1..128 bytes with the value limit, a leaf cell is at most a quarter of a page, which guarantees a split always yields two halves that fit value 0..880 bytes same; larger values would need overflow pages (section 11) pages 2^32 - 1 PageId is 32 bits: 16 TiB of 4 KiB pages

docs.title: 4. On-disk format
docs.text: Two files: the data file <path> and the log <path>-wal. Both use host byte order (little-endian on x86-64 and ARM64 Linux), written and read with memcpy, never pointer casts.

docs.title: 4.1 Data file
docs.text:
Page N occupies bytes [N * 4096, (N + 1) * 4096). Every page starts with a 16-byte header:

offset size field notes 0 4 checksum CRC-32 of bytes [4, 4096). A page of all zeros fails it. 4 2 page type 1 meta, 2 leaf, 3 internal 6 2 reserved zero 8 8 page LSN LSN of the log record that carried this image; 0 = never logged

Page 0, meta: payload u64 magic | u32 version (1) | u32 root page id | u32 page_count. Logged and recovered like any other page.

Leaf page: payload u16 count | u32 next_leaf | count x (u16 key_len | u16 value_len | key | value), cells sorted by key, keys unique. next_leaf = 0 for the last leaf.

Internal page: payload u16 count | u32 child0 | count x (u16 key_len | key | u32 child). key_i is a lower bound (inclusive) for every key under child_i and an upper bound (exclusive) for every key under child_{i-1}.

Page 0 is the meta page, so page id 0 never names a tree node; it doubles as "no page".

docs.title: 4.2 Log file
docs.text:
header (24 bytes): u64 magic | u64 start_lsn | u32 crc32(first 16 bytes) | u32 zero
record (24-byte header + payload), repeated:
    u32 crc32(header bytes [4, 24) + payload)
    u32 payload_len           4096 for PageImage, 8 for Commit
    u64 lsn                   must equal the record's position (below)
    u8  type                  1 PageImage, 2 Commit
    u8[3] zero
    u32 page_id               PageImage only
    payload                   PageImage: the full sealed page; Commit: u64 transaction id

LSN (log sequence number) = start_lsn + (file offset - 24): a byte position in a logical log that never restarts. A checkpoint replaces the file with an empty one whose start_lsn is the old end, so LSNs grow for the life of the database. LSN 0 is reserved for "never logged" (pages written by database creation); a new log starts at LSN 1.

A record is valid if it is complete, its CRC matches, its type and length agree, and its lsn field equals its position. Replay stops at the first invalid record: that is the torn tail of a crash, or bytes left over from before a reset.

docs.title: 4.3 Atomic file creation and replacement
docs.text: Database creation and log reset never write a header in place. They write <name>.tmp, fdatasync it, rename it over the real name, and fsync the directory. rename is atomic on POSIX filesystems, so a crash leaves the old file or the new one, never a mixture. The directory fsync makes the rename itself durable.

docs.title: 4.4 Tree invariants (checked by check())
docs.text:
1. Every leaf is at the same depth.
  2. Keys within a leaf are strictly increasing.
  3. Every key under child_i of an internal node lies in [key_i, key_{i+1}) (open-ended at the ends), recursively.
  4. Internal nodes have exactly count + 1 children, all page ids below page_count.
  5. Following next_leaf from the leftmost leaf visits exactly the leaves of an in-order walk, in the same order, and ends with 0.

docs.title: 5. Architecture
docs.text:
Db  (public API, one mutex, transaction boundaries, commit protocol, checkpoint)
    |
    +--> BPlusTree   get / put / erase / scan / check     (decode page -> modify -> encode)
    |       |
    |       v
    +--> PageCache   fixed frames, pin counts (RAII PageRef), LRU, dirty bits,
    |       |        no-steal for the open transaction, before-images for abort,
    |       |        WAL rule hook before every write-back
    |       v
    +--> Pager       page N at offset N*4096, checksum on write, verify on read
    |       |
    |       v
    |    data file
    |
    +--> Wal         append page images + commit records, fdatasync, replay, reset
    |       |
    |       v
    |    log file
    |
    +--> Recovery    on open: replay log, redo committed page images, cut uncommitted tail
component file responsibility File file.hpp RAII descriptor; pread/pwrite loops with EINTR; fdatasync; atomic rename; directory fsync crc32 crc32.hpp CRC-32 for pages and log records Page, Meta page.hpp the 4 KiB page, its header, checksum seal/verify; meta page encode/decode Pager pager.hpp raw page I/O on the data file; atomic database creation PageCache page_cache.hpp buffer pool: pinning, LRU replacement, dirty tracking, no-steal, abort BPlusTree btree.hpp search, insert with leaf and internal splits, erase, range scan, invariant check Wal wal.hpp log format, append, sync, replay, truncate, reset Recovery recovery.hpp redo-only recovery Db db.hpp wiring, locking, commit protocol, checkpoint policy

docs.title: 6.1 One put, step by step
docs.text:
Db::put(k, v)
  lock mutex
  BPlusTree::put: descend from the root, decode the leaf, insert, encode.
     If the leaf overflows: allocate a page (meta page_count++), split by bytes,
     push the separator up; internal nodes may split the same way; the root may split.
     Every page touched for writing goes through PageRef::write(), which:

        - saves the page's before-image in memory (first write in this transaction only)
        - marks the frame dirty and "in transaction" (no-steal: not evictable)
  commit:
     for every page in the transaction: Wal::append_page (stamps page LSN, seals, buffers)
     Wal::append_commit(txn id)
     Wal::sync()                      <-- fdatasync: the operation is durable from here
     PageCache::commit_txn()          pages become ordinary dirty pages (evictable)
  if the log is larger than checkpoint_wal_bytes: checkpoint
  unlock, return                      <-- the acknowledgement

If anything throws before Wal::sync() returns, PageCache::abort_txn() restores every before-image, drops pages created in the transaction, and Wal::discard_buffer() forgets the buffered records. Memory again matches the last committed state. If fdatasync itself fails, the database refuses further operations until it is reopened (the kernel may have dropped the dirty log pages; PostgreSQL's 2018 "fsyncgate" is the reference story), and recovery on the next open decides what survived.

docs.title: 6.2 Policies, named
docs.text:
• WAL rule (write-ahead): a page is written to the data file only after the log record carrying that page image is durable. Enforced in PageCache::write_back, which calls Wal::ensure_durable(page.lsn()) first.
  • No-steal: pages changed by an uncommitted transaction never reach the data file. So the data file never needs undo, and the log needs no undo records.
  • No-force: commit does not write data pages; it only syncs the log. Data pages are written later, at eviction or checkpoint. Commits cost one sequential log write, not random page writes.
  • Full-page images: the log carries whole pages, not deltas. Redo is then "copy the bytes", which is idempotent, and a page torn by a crash mid-write is repaired by its image. PostgreSQL does the same for the first change to a page after each checkpoint (full_page_writes); minidb does it for every change, which is simpler and costs write volume.

Compared with ARIES (the algorithm behind most commercial engines): ARIES is steal/no-force, so it needs undo as well as redo, compensation log records, and an analysis pass. minidb's no-steal policy removes undo entirely, at the price that a transaction's dirty pages must fit in the cache. For one-operation transactions that is a few pages.

docs.title: 6.3 Read path
docs.text: get and scan take the mutex, descend through the cache (pin, read, decode, unpin) and never touch the log. A cache miss reads the page and verifies its checksum; a mismatch throws CorruptionError rather than returning wrong data.

docs.title: 6.4 Checkpoint
docs.text:
1. PageCache::flush_all()   write every dirty page (WAL rule: their records are durable)
2. Pager::sync()            fdatasync the data file
3. Wal::reset()             replace the log with an empty one starting at the current end LSN

A crash before step 3 completes leaves the old log; replaying it over the newer data file is harmless (section 7). Checkpoints run when the log passes checkpoint_wal_bytes, on open after recovery, and in the destructor, so a clean shutdown leaves an empty log.

docs.title: 7. Recovery
docs.text:
Runs in the Db constructor, before the cache reads any page.

pending = []
for each valid record in the log, in LSN order:
    PageImage -> append (page_id, image) to pending
    Commit    -> for each (page_id, image) in pending:
                     if the data file page is valid and its LSN >= image LSN: skip
                     else write the image to the data file
                 pending = []
                 end = position just after this commit record
discarded = size of pending               (a transaction that never committed)
fdatasync the data file
truncate the log at `end`                 (drop the uncommitted tail and any torn bytes)
then the Db constructor checkpoints

Why it is correct:

  • Nothing committed is lost. A commit was acknowledged only after its records were fdatasynced, so they are in the log. Recovery applies every committed image.
  • Nothing uncommitted appears. No-steal means the data file never contained uncommitted bytes; recovery never applies images without a commit record.
  • Torn pages are repaired. Any page written to the data file since the last checkpoint has its latest committed image in the log. A torn page fails its checksum, so the LSN check cannot skip it, and the image overwrites it.
  • Idempotent. Writing a full image twice gives the same bytes. A crash during recovery is handled by running recovery again.
  • The LSN skip is only an optimisation, and it needs LSN 0 to be reserved: a freshly created page has LSN 0, so if the first record also had LSN 0 the check 0 >= 0 would skip a redo that is needed. (This bug existed in the first draft of the reference code and was caught by Recovery.UncommittedTailIsDiscardedAndNotReplayedLater; tell that story.)
  • Truncating at the last commit is required, not cosmetic. Without it, the orphaned page images of a crashed transaction would sit in front of the next transaction's records, and a later recovery would apply them as part of that next commit.

docs.title: 8. The crash test
docs.text:
tests/crash_test.cpp, run by ctest on every CI job.

  1. fork() a child. The child opens the database with a 16-page cache and a 128 KiB checkpoint threshold (so kills land during evictions and checkpoints too) and runs an infinite, deterministic sequence of operations: operation i is a function of i only (mostly puts of varying sizes over 400 keys, every eleventh a delete). After each operation returns, the child writes i + 1 to a pipe. That write is the acknowledgement.
  2. The parent sleeps a random 20 to 200 ms, sends SIGKILL (cannot be caught: no destructor, no checkpoint, no flush runs), reaps the child, and drains the pipe to find acked, the last acknowledged count.
  3. The parent opens the database (recovery runs), calls check(), and compares the full contents with a std::map model after exactly acked operations, or after acked + 1: the operation in flight may have committed just before the kill, without its acknowledgement reaching the pipe.
  4. 25 rounds, each on a fresh database. The test also fails if nothing was ever acknowledged.

What "acknowledged" means precisely: every operation whose acknowledgement the parent read must be present; no operation after the in-flight one may be visible; the in-flight one is all or nothing.

What it does not simulate: power loss. After SIGKILL the kernel still writes the page cache to disk, so an engine that forgot to fdatasync would pass. Testing that needs a layer that drops unsynced writes: a VM snapshot taken at a random moment, dm-flakey or dm-log-writes in Linux, or a FUSE filesystem like LazyFS. Name these if asked; they are the honest next step.

Unit-level crash tests complement it: a torn data page repaired from the log, a torn log tail ignored, an uncommitted tail discarded and not replayed later, a corrupted byte detected by the checksum.

The reference crash test was checked against a mutant: with redo disabled in Recovery, it fails on the first kill. A crash test that cannot fail proves nothing; try the same mutation on your version.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
A repository that builds and tests in CI, an RAII file class with positioned I/O, a checksum, and the definition of a page. Nothing is stored yet; everything later stands on this.

In plain words: before you can build a library you need the shelves (pages), a way to put a shelf into a numbered slot of the warehouse and take it back out (pwrite/pread at id * 4096), and a seal on every shelf that breaks if the contents change behind your back (the CRC).

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• 4 KiB pages. It is the x86 memory page size, the usual ext4 block size, and the unit the kernel page cache works in. One page is one I/O. Most engines use 4, 8 or 16 KiB.
  • A checksum on every page. Disks, controllers and filesystems occasionally return wrong bytes, and a crash can leave a page half old and half new (a torn write: the drive persists 512-byte or 4 KiB sectors, and a power cut can land between them). Without a checksum you would read garbage as data. With one you detect it, and the log repairs it (step 7).
  • The page LSN in the header. The log sequence number of the log record that last carried this page. Recovery uses it to skip work. Defined now so the format never changes.
  • memcpy, never pointer casts, for fixed-size fields: *(uint32_t*)(p + 4) violates strict aliasing and may be misaligned, which is undefined behaviour that UBSan reports. A 4-byte memcpy compiles to one mov anyway.
  • pread/pwrite, not lseek plus read: no shared file offset (no race if two threads ever share the descriptor), and one syscall instead of two.
  • fdatasync, not fsync: it skips metadata that is not needed to read the data back (the modification time) but still flushes the file size. Cheaper, same durability here.

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)

project(minidb
    VERSION 0.1.0
    DESCRIPTION "Page-based key-value storage engine with a B+tree and a write-ahead log"
    LANGUAGES CXX)

#pragma once

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <stdexcept>

namespace minidb {

using PageId = std::uint32_t;
using Lsn = std::uint64_t;  // log sequence number: byte position in the logical WAL stream

inline constexpr std::size_t kPageSize = 4096;
inline constexpr PageId kMetaPageId = 0;
inline constexpr PageId kNoPage = 0;  // page 0 is the meta page, so 0 never names a tree node

// Chosen so that at least four maximum-size leaf cells fit in one page; that guarantees a
// byte-balanced split always produces two halves that fit (see btree.cpp).
inline constexpr std::size_t kMaxKeySize = 128;
inline constexpr std::size_t kMaxValueSize = 880;

class DbError : public std::runtime_error {
public:
    using std::runtime_error::runtime_error;
};

// The on-disk bytes are not what we wrote: bad checksum, bad magic, impossible field values.
class CorruptionError : public DbError {
public:
    using DbError::DbError;
};

}  // namespace minidb

include/minidb/crc32.hpp and src/crc32.cpp. The table is computed by a constexpr function, so the compiler builds it and it lives in read-only data: no start-up cost and no static-initialisation-order question.

#pragma once

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>

namespace minidb {

// CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3, reflected polynomial 0xEDB88320), the one zlib and Ethernet use.
// Chainable: crc32(b, nb, crc32(a, na)) == crc32(a followed by b).
std::uint32_t crc32(const void* data, std::size_t len, std::uint32_t previous = 0) noexcept;

}  // namespace minidb

#include "minidb/crc32.hpp"

#include <array>

namespace minidb {

namespace {

constexpr std::array<std::uint32_t, 256> make_table() {
    std::array<std::uint32_t, 256> table{};
    for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < 256; ++i) {
        std::uint32_t c = i;
        for (int bit = 0; bit < 8; ++bit) {
            c = (c & 1u) != 0 ? 0xEDB88320u ^ (c >> 1) : c >> 1;
        }
        table[i] = c;
    }
    return table;
}

constexpr std::array<std::uint32_t, 256> kTable = make_table();  // built at compile time

}  // namespace

std::uint32_t crc32(const void* data, std::size_t len, std::uint32_t previous) noexcept {
    const auto* p = static_cast<const unsigned char*>(data);
    std::uint32_t c = previous ^ 0xFFFFFFFFu;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < len; ++i) {
        c = kTable[(c ^ p[i]) & 0xFFu] ^ (c >> 8);
    }
    return c ^ 0xFFFFFFFFu;
}

}  // namespace minidb

include/minidb/file.hpp:

#pragma once

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <string>

namespace minidb {

// RAII wrapper over a POSIX file descriptor with positioned I/O. Move-only.
// Every failure throws std::system_error carrying errno.
class File {
public:
    File() noexcept = default;
    ~File();
    File(File&& other) noexcept;
    File& operator=(File&& other) noexcept;
    File(const File&) = delete;
    File& operator=(const File&) = delete;

    static File open(const std::string& path, bool create);

    // Reads up to len bytes at offset; returns fewer only at end of file. Retries EINTR and
    // short reads.
    std::size_t read_at(std::uint64_t offset, char* buf, std::size_t len) const;
    // Writes all len bytes at offset or throws.
    void write_at(std::uint64_t offset, const char* buf, std::size_t len);
    void sync();  // fdatasync: data plus the metadata needed to read it back (size)
    void truncate(std::uint64_t size);
    std::uint64_t size() const;
    bool valid() const noexcept { return fd_ >= 0; }

private:
    explicit File(int fd) noexcept : fd_(fd) {}
    void close() noexcept;
    int fd_ = -1;
};

bool file_exists(const std::string& path);
void rename_file(const std::string& from, const std::string& to);
// fsync on the directory containing `path`, so a create or rename in it is durable.
void sync_parent_directory(const std::string& path);

}  // namespace minidb

src/file.cpp, outlined. You wrote its twin in tcpkv step 02; the differences:

  • open: ::open(path, O_RDWR | O_CLOEXEC | (create ? O_CREAT : 0), 0644); on failure throw std::system_error(errno, std::generic_category(), "open(" + path + ")").
  • read_at: loop ::pread(fd_, buf + done, len - done, offset + done); retry on EINTR; stop at a return of 0 (end of file) and return the count, so the caller can see a short read.
  • write_at: loop ::pwrite until every byte is written; retry on EINTR.
  • sync: ::fdatasync(fd_). truncate: ::ftruncate. size: ::fstat(...).st_size.
  • Move operations take the descriptor and set the source's to -1; the destructor closes it.
  • rename_file: std::rename, throwing on failure.
  • sync_parent_directory(path): open the directory that contains path with O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY | O_CLOEXEC, fsync it, close it. This is what makes a newly created or renamed file's name durable. Without it a power cut can lose the directory entry even though the file's data was synced.

include/minidb/page.hpp, the format every later step depends on:

#pragma once

#include <array>
#include <cstring>

#include "minidb/common.hpp"
#include "minidb/crc32.hpp"

namespace minidb {

// Fixed-width fields are stored in host byte order with memcpy (never a pointer cast, which
// would break strict aliasing and alignment rules). x86-64 and ARM64 Linux are both
// little-endian; a portable format would convert explicitly.
template <class T>
T read_as(const char* p) noexcept {
    T value;
    std::memcpy(&value, p, sizeof value);
    return value;
}

template <class T>
void write_as(char* p, T value) noexcept {
    std::memcpy(p, &value, sizeof value);
}

enum class PageType : std::uint16_t { Free = 0, Meta = 1, Leaf = 2, Internal = 3 };

// Every page starts with a 16-byte header:
//   [0, 4)   CRC-32 of bytes [4, kPageSize)
//   [4, 6)   PageType
//   [6, 8)   reserved, zero
//   [8, 16)  page LSN: the LSN of the WAL record that carried this page image
inline constexpr std::size_t kPageHeaderSize = 16;
inline constexpr std::size_t kPagePayloadSize = kPageSize - kPageHeaderSize;

struct Page {
    alignas(64) std::array<char, kPageSize> bytes{};

    PageType type() const noexcept { return static_cast<PageType>(read_as<std::uint16_t>(bytes.data() + 4)); }
    void set_type(PageType type) noexcept { write_as(bytes.data() + 4, static_cast<std::uint16_t>(type)); }
    Lsn lsn() const noexcept { return read_as<Lsn>(bytes.data() + 8); }
    void set_lsn(Lsn lsn) noexcept { write_as(bytes.data() + 8, lsn); }

    char* payload() noexcept { return bytes.data() + kPageHeaderSize; }
    const char* payload() const noexcept { return bytes.data() + kPageHeaderSize; }
    void clear_payload() noexcept { std::memset(payload(), 0, kPagePayloadSize); }

    // Computes and stores the checksum. Call after the last modification, before any write.
    void seal() noexcept { write_as(bytes.data(), crc32(bytes.data() + 4, kPageSize - 4)); }
    // A page of all zeros (never written, or a hole) fails this check: crc32 of zeros is not 0.
    bool verify() const noexcept {
        return read_as<std::uint32_t>(bytes.data()) == crc32(bytes.data() + 4, kPageSize - 4);
    }
};

// Page 0. Logged and recovered like every other page.
//   payload: u64 magic | u32 version | u32 root | u32 page_count
struct Meta {
    static constexpr std::uint64_t kMagic = 0x3142444E494D2121ULL;  // arbitrary, fixed forever
    static constexpr std::uint32_t kVersion = 1;

    PageId root = kNoPage;
    std::uint32_t page_count = 0;  // pages allocated so far, including page 0

    static Meta decode(const Page& page) {
        const char* p = page.payload();
        if (page.type() != PageType::Meta || read_as<std::uint64_t>(p) != kMagic) {
            throw CorruptionError("meta page: bad type or magic (not a minidb file?)");
        }
        if (read_as<std::uint32_t>(p + 8) != kVersion) {
            throw CorruptionError("meta page: unsupported format version");
        }
        Meta meta;
        meta.root = read_as<std::uint32_t>(p + 12);
        meta.page_count = read_as<std::uint32_t>(p + 16);
        if (meta.root == kNoPage || meta.root >= meta.page_count) {
            throw CorruptionError("meta page: root page out of range");
        }
        return meta;
    }

    void encode(Page& page) const noexcept {
        page.set_type(PageType::Meta);
        page.clear_payload();
        char* p = page.payload();
        write_as(p, kMagic);
        write_as(p + 8, kVersion);
        write_as(p + 12, root);
        write_as(p + 16, page_count);
    }
};

}  // namespace minidb

static_cast<PageType> of an arbitrary uint16_t read from disk is well defined because the enum has a fixed underlying type; an unknown value matches no enumerator and the tree code rejects it. alignas(64) starts each page on a cache-line boundary; it is a nicety, not a correctness requirement.

docs.title: What to say in an interview
docs.text: "Every page is 4 KiB with a 16-byte header: a CRC-32 over the rest of the page, the page type, and the page LSN, the log sequence number of the last log record that carried this page. The checksum is how the engine notices a torn or corrupted page instead of returning garbage; the LSN lets recovery skip pages that are already up to date. Fields go through memcpy, which avoids strict-aliasing and alignment undefined behaviour and costs nothing after optimisation."

docs.title: Step 2. Pager: pages on disk, checksums, atomic creation
docs.text: Time: ~5 hours Week: 6 Read first: 07_Databases_Internals/02_storage_engines_pages_and_heap_files.md (page addressing, torn pages). 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps/01_linux_for_a_windows_developer.md (the page cache, fsync). 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/04_the_catalogue_of_memory_bugs.md (why every length read from disk must be bounds-checked).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Read and write page N of the data file, checksummed, and create a new database file so that a crash during creation can never leave a half-initialised database.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Page N at offset N * 4096. No indirection. The meta page (page 0) holds the root page id and the page count.
  • Seal on write, verify on read. write() computes the CRC; read() throws CorruptionError on a mismatch or a short read.
  • read_if_valid() for recovery. During recovery a missing or torn page is an expected state, not an error: it is about to be overwritten. A separate function says so in its name.
  • Atomic creation: write <path>.tmp, fdatasync it, rename it over <path>, fsync the directory. rename(2) replaces the name atomically, so after a crash there is either no database or a complete one.
  • No caching, no policy. The Pager does raw I/O; deciding when to write is the cache's job. One class, one responsibility, testable alone.

docs.text:
#pragma once

#include <string>
#include <vector>

#include "minidb/file.hpp"
#include "minidb/page.hpp"

namespace minidb {

// Raw page I/O on the single data file: page N lives at byte offset N * kPageSize.
// Checksums are applied on write and verified on read. No caching, no policy: that is the
// PageCache's job. Not thread-safe; the Db serialises access.
class Pager {
public:
    // Opens an existing data file. Throws std::system_error if it does not exist.
    explicit Pager(const std::string& path);

    // Creates a new data file atomically: writes `pages` (page i at index i) to path + ".tmp",
    // fsyncs it, renames it over `path`, fsyncs the directory. A crash leaves either no file
    // or a complete one, never a half-initialised database.
    static void create(const std::string& path, std::vector<Page> pages);

    // Reads and verifies page `id`. Throws CorruptionError on a short read or bad checksum.
    void read(PageId id, Page& out) const;

    // Recovery helper: like read(), but reports a missing or torn page as `false` instead
    // of throwing, because during redo that is an expected state, not corruption.
    bool read_if_valid(PageId id, Page& out) const;

    // Seals (checksums) the page and writes it in place. Not durable until sync().
    void write(PageId id, Page& page);

    void sync() { file_.sync(); }

    // Pages physically present in the file (may be fewer than Meta::page_count after a
    // crash: allocated pages are only written at eviction or checkpoint).
    PageId file_page_count() const;

    const std::string& path() const noexcept { return path_; }

private:
    std::string path_;
    File file_;
};

}  // namespace minidb

#include "minidb/pager.hpp"

#include <string>
#include <utility>

namespace minidb {

namespace {

std::uint64_t offset_of(PageId id) noexcept { return static_cast<std::uint64_t>(id) * kPageSize; }

}  // namespace

// The file size need not be a multiple of kPageSize: a crash while extending the file can
// leave a partial last page. Such a page was written at eviction or checkpoint, so its
// committed image is in the WAL; read_if_valid() reports it as missing and redo rewrites it.
Pager::Pager(const std::string& path) : path_(path), file_(File::open(path, /*create=*/false)) {}

void Pager::create(const std::string& path, std::vector<Page> pages) {
    const std::string tmp = path + ".tmp";
    {
        File file = File::open(tmp, /*create=*/true);
        file.truncate(0);  // a leftover .tmp from an earlier crashed create
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < pages.size(); ++i) {
            pages[i].seal();
            file.write_at(offset_of(static_cast<PageId>(i)), pages[i].bytes.data(), kPageSize);
        }
        file.sync();
    }
    rename_file(tmp, path);
    sync_parent_directory(path);
}

void Pager::read(PageId id, Page& out) const {
    const std::size_t n = file_.read_at(offset_of(id), out.bytes.data(), kPageSize);
    if (n != kPageSize) {
        throw CorruptionError("page " + std::to_string(id) + ": short read (beyond end of file)");
    }
    if (!out.verify()) {
        throw CorruptionError("page " + std::to_string(id) + ": checksum mismatch");
    }
}

bool Pager::read_if_valid(PageId id, Page& out) const {
    const std::size_t n = file_.read_at(offset_of(id), out.bytes.data(), kPageSize);
    return n == kPageSize && out.verify();
}

void Pager::write(PageId id, Page& page) {
    page.seal();
    file_.write_at(offset_of(id), page.bytes.data(), kPageSize);
}

PageId Pager::file_page_count() const { return static_cast<PageId>(file_.size() / kPageSize); }

}  // namespace minidb

Why file.truncate(0) in create: a .tmp left by an earlier crashed creation may be longer than the new one; without the truncate, stale pages would survive past the new content.

TEST(Pager, CreateWriteReadRoundTrip) {
    TempDir dir;
    const std::string path = dir.file("db");
    Pager::create(path, BPlusTree::initial_pages());
    Pager pager(path);
    EXPECT_EQ(pager.file_page_count(), 2u);

    Page out = page_with_byte('x');
    pager.write(5, out);  // beyond the end: the file grows, pages 2..4 are holes
    pager.sync();
    Page in;
    pager.read(5, in);
    EXPECT_EQ(std::memcmp(in.bytes.data(), out.bytes.data(), kPageSize), 0);
    EXPECT_EQ(pager.file_page_count(), 6u);
    EXPECT_THROW(pager.read(3, in), CorruptionError);  // a hole is all zeros: checksum fails
    EXPECT_FALSE(pager.read_if_valid(3, in));
    EXPECT_FALSE(pager.read_if_valid(100, in));  // beyond EOF
}

TEST(Pager, DetectsCorruptedPage) {
    TempDir dir;
    const std::string path = dir.file("db");
    Pager::create(path, BPlusTree::initial_pages());
    {
        File f = File::open(path, false);
        const char junk = 0x5A;
        f.write_at(kPageSize + 100, &junk, 1);  // flip a byte inside page 1
    }
    Pager pager(path);
    Page page;
    EXPECT_THROW(pager.read(1, page), CorruptionError);
    EXPECT_NO_THROW(pager.read(0, page));
}

CreateWriteReadRoundTrip also documents a Linux fact worth knowing: writing page 5 of a two-page file creates a hole (pages 2 to 4) that reads back as zeros and takes no disk space. Zeros fail the checksum, so a hole can never be mistaken for a valid page.

docs.title: What to say in an interview
docs.text: "Creating the database file is atomic: write a temporary file, fdatasync it, rename it into place, fsync the directory. Rename is atomic on POSIX filesystems, and the directory sync makes the rename itself durable, which people forget: without it a power cut can lose the directory entry of a file whose data was synced. Every page read is verified against its CRC, so corruption becomes an exception, never wrong data."

docs.title: Step 3. PageCache: pinning, LRU, dirty pages, no-steal
docs.text: Time: ~7 hours Week: 7 Read first: 07_Databases_Internals/02_storage_engines_pages_and_heap_files.md (buffer pool) and 04_wal_and_crash_recovery.md (steal/no-steal, force/no-force). 02_Modern_CPP: 05_smart_pointers_and_ownership.md (RAII handles), 06_stl_containers_deep_dive.md (std::list iterator stability, unordered_map). 04_Concurrency is not needed: the cache is single-threaded by design; the Db mutex protects it.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
A fixed pool of page frames in front of the Pager, with the four properties the rest of the engine relies on: a pinned page never moves; a dirty page is written back before its frame is reused; the write-ahead rule is enforced at that moment; pages changed by an uncommitted transaction never reach the disk.

In plain words: the cache is a desk with room for N open books. You may only put a book back on the shelf if nobody is reading it (pin count zero), you put back the one used least recently first (LRU), and if you wrote in it you must first copy your notes into the safe (the log, the WAL rule). Books you are in the middle of editing stay on the desk until the change is signed off (no-steal).

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Frames and a page table. A std::vector<Frame> sized once, so references into it stay valid, plus unordered_map<PageId, frame index>.
  • PageRef, an RAII pin. fetch() pins; the PageRef destructor unpins. Move-only. An exception anywhere in the tree code cannot leak a pin, so it cannot slowly make every frame unevictable. tcpkv's FileDescriptor idea, applied to a buffer-pool pin.
  • read() versus write() on the handle. write() must be called before modifying the page: it saves the before-image (the first time in this transaction), marks the frame dirty and joins it to the transaction. Making it the only way to get a mutable reference means you cannot forget.
  • LRU over unpinned frames with a std::list and stored iterators: O(1) touch, O(1) evict. Real engines use CLOCK (a cheaper approximation) or LRU-K / 2Q (resistant to one big scan flushing the hot set); plain LRU is the clear version.
  • The WAL-rule hook. The cache knows nothing about the log. It receives a std::function<void(Lsn)> that must make the log durable up to an LSN, and calls it before every write-back. Dependency inversion in one line, and it lets this step's tests run with a no-op hook.
  • No-steal and abort. Frames in the open transaction are skipped by eviction. abort_txn() restores before-images and drops pages created in the transaction (the meta page's before-image undoes the allocation). In-memory undo is all a no-steal engine needs.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: include/minidb/page_cache.hpp, src/page_cache.cpp.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
#pragma once

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <functional>
#include <list>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

#include "minidb/page.hpp"
#include "minidb/pager.hpp"

namespace minidb {

// Fixed-size buffer pool in front of the Pager.
//
//  * Pinning: fetch()/create() return a PageRef that pins the frame; a pinned frame is never
//    evicted. The PageRef unpins in its destructor (RAII), so an exception cannot leak a pin.
//  * Replacement: least recently unpinned frame first (LRU over unpinned frames).
//  * WAL rule: before a dirty page is written to the data file, wal_flush(page.lsn()) is
//    called so the log record carrying that image is durable first.
//  * No-steal: a page modified by the current transaction is never written to the data file
//    before commit_txn(). On abort_txn() its before-image is restored from memory. This is
//    what makes a redo-only WAL sufficient: the data file never contains uncommitted bytes.
//
// Not thread-safe; the Db holds one mutex around every operation.
class PageCache {
public:
    using WalFlush = std::function<void(Lsn)>;

    PageCache(Pager& pager, std::size_t capacity, WalFlush wal_flush);
    PageCache(const PageCache&) = delete;
    PageCache& operator=(const PageCache&) = delete;

    class PageRef {
    public:
        PageRef() noexcept = default;
        PageRef(PageRef&& other) noexcept : cache_(other.cache_), frame_(other.frame_) { other.cache_ = nullptr; }
        PageRef& operator=(PageRef&& other) noexcept {
            if (this != &other) {
                release();
                cache_ = other.cache_;
                frame_ = other.frame_;
                other.cache_ = nullptr;
            }
            return *this;
        }
        PageRef(const PageRef&) = delete;
        PageRef& operator=(const PageRef&) = delete;
        ~PageRef() { release(); }

        PageId id() const noexcept { return cache_->frames_[frame_].id; }
        const Page& read() const noexcept { return cache_->frames_[frame_].page; }
        // Joins the page to the current transaction (saving its before-image the first time)
        // and returns it for modification. Always call write() *before* changing bytes.
        Page& write() { return cache_->begin_write(frame_); }

    private:
        friend class PageCache;
        PageRef(PageCache* cache, std::size_t frame) noexcept : cache_(cache), frame_(frame) {}
        void release() noexcept {
            if (cache_ != nullptr) {
                cache_->unpin(frame_);
                cache_ = nullptr;
            }
        }
        PageCache* cache_ = nullptr;
        std::size_t frame_ = 0;
    };

    PageRef fetch(PageId id);   // pins; reads (and verifies) from disk on a miss
    PageRef create(PageId id);  // pins a zeroed frame for a newly allocated page id

    // Transaction support. A transaction is implicit: it starts with the first write() and
    // ends with commit_txn() or abort_txn().
    void for_each_txn_page(const std::function<void(PageId, Page&)>& fn);
    void commit_txn() noexcept;
    void abort_txn() noexcept;
    bool in_txn() const noexcept { return !txn_frames_.empty(); }

    // Writes every dirty, committed page. The caller then calls Pager::sync().
    void flush_all();

    struct Stats {
        std::uint64_t hits = 0;
        std::uint64_t misses = 0;
        std::uint64_t evictions = 0;
        std::uint64_t writebacks = 0;
    };
    const Stats& stats() const noexcept { return stats_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const noexcept { return frames_.size(); }

private:
    struct Frame {
        PageId id = 0;
        Page page;
        int pins = 0;
        bool used = false;
        bool dirty = false;
        bool in_txn = false;
        bool created_in_txn = false;
        bool in_lru = false;
        std::list<std::size_t>::iterator lru_pos;
    };
    struct BeforeImage {
        Page page;
        bool was_dirty = false;
    };

    std::size_t obtain_frame();  // a free frame, or an evicted one; throws if none
    void write_back(Frame& frame);
    void pin(std::size_t frame);
    void unpin(std::size_t frame) noexcept;
    Page& begin_write(std::size_t frame);
    void drop_frame(std::size_t frame) noexcept;

    Pager& pager_;
    WalFlush wal_flush_;
    std::vector<Frame> frames_;                      // never resized: references stay valid
    std::unordered_map<PageId, std::size_t> table_;  // page id -> frame index
    std::list<std::size_t> lru_;                     // unpinned frames, least recent at front
    std::vector<std::size_t> free_;                  // frames holding no page
    std::vector<std::size_t> txn_frames_;            // frames written by the current transaction
    std::unordered_map<PageId, BeforeImage> before_images_;
    Stats stats_;
};

}  // namespace minidb

#include "minidb/page_cache.hpp"

#include <string>
#include <utility>

namespace minidb {

PageCache::PageCache(Pager& pager, std::size_t capacity, WalFlush wal_flush)
    : pager_(pager), wal_flush_(std::move(wal_flush)), frames_(capacity) {
    if (capacity < 16) {
        // A put pins one page per tree level and a split creates up to one new page per level
        // plus a new root; 16 frames covers trees far deeper than 4 KiB pages ever produce.
        throw DbError("page cache needs at least 16 frames");
    }
    free_.reserve(capacity);
    for (std::size_t i = capacity; i > 0; --i) {
        free_.push_back(i - 1);
    }
}

PageCache::PageRef PageCache::fetch(PageId id) {
    const auto it = table_.find(id);
    if (it != table_.end()) {
        ++stats_.hits;
        pin(it->second);
        return PageRef(this, it->second);
    }
    ++stats_.misses;
    const std::size_t index = obtain_frame();
    Frame& frame = frames_[index];
    try {
        pager_.read(id, frame.page);
    } catch (...) {
        free_.push_back(index);  // frame was not registered yet; just give it back
        throw;
    }
    frame.id = id;
    frame.used = true;
    frame.dirty = false;
    table_.emplace(id, index);
    pin(index);
    return PageRef(this, index);
}

PageCache::PageRef PageCache::create(PageId id) {
    if (table_.count(id) != 0) {
        throw DbError("page " + std::to_string(id) + " already cached; allocated twice?");
    }
    const std::size_t index = obtain_frame();
    Frame& frame = frames_[index];
    frame.page = Page{};
    frame.id = id;
    frame.used = true;
    frame.dirty = true;
    frame.in_txn = true;
    frame.created_in_txn = true;  // abort removes it; there is no before-image to restore
    txn_frames_.push_back(index);
    table_.emplace(id, index);
    pin(index);
    return PageRef(this, index);
}

Page& PageCache::begin_write(std::size_t index) {
    Frame& frame = frames_[index];
    if (!frame.in_txn) {
        before_images_.emplace(frame.id, BeforeImage{frame.page, frame.dirty});
        frame.in_txn = true;
        txn_frames_.push_back(index);
    }
    frame.dirty = true;
    return frame.page;
}

void PageCache::for_each_txn_page(const std::function<void(PageId, Page&)>& fn) {
    for (const std::size_t index : txn_frames_) {
        fn(frames_[index].id, frames_[index].page);
    }
}

void PageCache::commit_txn() noexcept {
    for (const std::size_t index : txn_frames_) {
        frames_[index].in_txn = false;
        frames_[index].created_in_txn = false;  // now an ordinary dirty, committed page
    }
    txn_frames_.clear();
    before_images_.clear();
}

void PageCache::abort_txn() noexcept {
    for (const std::size_t index : txn_frames_) {
        Frame& frame = frames_[index];
        if (frame.created_in_txn) {
            drop_frame(index);  // the allocation is undone by the meta page's before-image
            continue;
        }
        const auto it = before_images_.find(frame.id);
        if (it != before_images_.end()) {
            frame.page = it->second.page;
            frame.dirty = it->second.was_dirty;
        }
        frame.in_txn = false;
    }
    txn_frames_.clear();
    before_images_.clear();
}

void PageCache::flush_all() {
    for (Frame& frame : frames_) {
        if (frame.used && frame.dirty && !frame.in_txn) {
            write_back(frame);
        }
    }
}

std::size_t PageCache::obtain_frame() {
    if (!free_.empty()) {
        const std::size_t index = free_.back();
        free_.pop_back();
        return index;
    }
    for (auto it = lru_.begin(); it != lru_.end(); ++it) {
        Frame& frame = frames_[*it];
        if (frame.in_txn) {
            continue;  // no-steal: uncommitted bytes never reach the data file
        }
        if (frame.dirty) {
            write_back(frame);  // may throw; the frame stays cached and consistent
        }
        const std::size_t index = *it;
        lru_.erase(it);
        frame.in_lru = false;
        table_.erase(frame.id);
        frame.used = false;
        ++stats_.evictions;
        return index;
    }
    throw DbError("page cache exhausted: every frame is pinned or part of the open transaction");
}

void PageCache::write_back(Frame& frame) {
    wal_flush_(frame.page.lsn());  // the WAL rule: log record durable before the page
    pager_.write(frame.id, frame.page);
    frame.dirty = false;
    ++stats_.writebacks;
}

void PageCache::pin(std::size_t index) {
    Frame& frame = frames_[index];
    if (frame.in_lru) {
        lru_.erase(frame.lru_pos);
        frame.in_lru = false;
    }
    ++frame.pins;
}

void PageCache::unpin(std::size_t index) noexcept {
    Frame& frame = frames_[index];
    if (--frame.pins == 0 && frame.used) {
        frame.lru_pos = lru_.insert(lru_.end(), index);  // most recently used at the back
        frame.in_lru = true;
    }
}

void PageCache::drop_frame(std::size_t index) noexcept {
    Frame& frame = frames_[index];
    if (frame.in_lru) {
        lru_.erase(frame.lru_pos);
        frame.in_lru = false;
    }
    table_.erase(frame.id);
    frame.used = false;
    frame.dirty = false;
    frame.in_txn = false;
    frame.created_in_txn = false;
    if (frame.pins == 0) {
        free_.push_back(index);
    }
    // A dropped frame that is still pinned would be a bug in the caller (abort while a
    // PageRef is alive); it then leaks one frame rather than corrupting another page.
}

}  // namespace minidb

Two details to be able to explain:

  • In fetch(), if the disk read throws, the frame goes back to the free list before it was entered in the page table, so a failed read leaves the cache exactly as it was.
  • In obtain_frame(), a dirty victim is written back before it leaves the table. If the write throws, the page is still cached and still dirty: nothing is lost.

TEST(PageCache, EvictsLeastRecentlyUsedAndWritesBackDirtyPages) {
    TempDir dir;
    const std::string path = dir.file("db");
    std::vector<Page> pages(20);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < pages.size(); ++i) {
        pages[i] = page_with_byte(static_cast<char>('a' + i));
    }
    Pager::create(path, pages);
    Pager pager(path);
    std::vector<Lsn> flushed;
    PageCache cache(pager, 16, [&](Lsn lsn) { flushed.push_back(lsn); });

    {
        PageCache::PageRef ref = cache.fetch(3);
        ref.write().payload()[0] = 'Z';  // dirty, inside a "transaction"
    }
    cache.commit_txn();  // now an ordinary dirty page: evictable
    for (PageId id = 4; id < 20; ++id) {
        cache.fetch(id);  // 16 more pages through a 16-frame cache: page 3 must be evicted
    }
    EXPECT_GE(cache.stats().evictions, 1u);
    EXPECT_EQ(flushed.size(), 1u);  // the WAL rule hook ran before the write-back
    Page on_disk;
    pager.read(3, on_disk);
    EXPECT_EQ(on_disk.payload()[0], 'Z');
}

TEST(PageCache, NoStealAndAbortRestoresBeforeImage) {
    TempDir dir;
    const std::string path = dir.file("db");
    std::vector<Page> pages(20);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < pages.size(); ++i) {
        pages[i] = page_with_byte('a');
    }
    Pager::create(path, pages);
    Pager pager(path);
    PageCache cache(pager, 16, [](Lsn) {});

    {
        PageCache::PageRef ref = cache.fetch(2);
        ref.write().payload()[0] = 'U';  // uncommitted
    }
    for (PageId id = 3; id < 20; ++id) {
        cache.fetch(id);  // pressure: 17 other pages through the 15 remaining frames
    }
    Page on_disk;
    pager.read(2, on_disk);
    EXPECT_EQ(on_disk.payload()[0], 'a');  // no-steal: the uncommitted byte never hit the file

    cache.abort_txn();
    EXPECT_EQ(cache.fetch(2).read().payload()[0], 'a');  // before-image restored
}

TEST(PageCache, ThrowsWhenEveryFrameIsPinned) {
    TempDir dir;
    const std::string path = dir.file("db");
    std::vector<Page> pages(20, page_with_byte('a'));
    Pager::create(path, pages);
    Pager pager(path);
    PageCache cache(pager, 16, [](Lsn) {});
    std::vector<PageCache::PageRef> pins;
    for (PageId id = 0; id < 16; ++id) {
        pins.push_back(cache.fetch(id));
    }
    EXPECT_THROW(cache.fetch(16), DbError);
    pins.pop_back();  // unpin one
    EXPECT_NO_THROW(cache.fetch(16));
}

docs.title: What to say in an interview
docs.text: "The buffer pool pins pages through a move-only RAII handle, so an exception cannot leak a pin. Before a dirty page is written back, the cache calls a hook that makes the log durable up to that page's LSN: the write-ahead rule, enforced in exactly one place. Pages modified by the open transaction are never evicted, which is the no-steal policy; the data file therefore never holds uncommitted bytes, so recovery needs redo but never undo. I did not use mmap, because the engine has to control when a page reaches the disk to keep the WAL rule, and with mmap the kernel writes dirty pages back whenever it likes. The CIDR 2022 paper 'Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your Database Management System?' makes that argument in detail."

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
A B+tree stored in pages: get, insert, overwrite, leaf splits, internal splits, root splits, every leaf at the same depth, and a checker that proves it after any sequence of operations.

In plain words: a library card catalogue. The top drawer says "A to F: drawer 2, G to M: drawer 3". Drawer 3 says "G to H: card box 17, ...". The card box holds the cards in order. When a card box overflows you split it into two and add one line to the drawer above it. When a drawer overflows you split it and add a line to the one above that. When the top drawer overflows you build a new top drawer above it: the only way the catalogue gets taller, which is why every card box is always the same number of drawers from the top.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Decode, modify, encode. Each operation decodes a page into a small struct of vectors, changes it, and encodes it back. Real engines edit slotted pages in place; this is slower but far easier to get right, and the on-disk format is identical.
  • Separators. In an internal node, key_i is the smallest key that may appear under child_i. The child for a search key is the number of separators <= the key, which is std::upper_bound.
  • Split by bytes, not by count. Cells range from 5 to 1,012 bytes. Splitting at the middle cell can leave one half overfull; splitting at the middle byte cannot. Because a cell is at most a quarter of a page, the left half is at most about 5/8 of a page and the right at most about 7/8. Redo that arithmetic on a whiteboard: total after the insert is at most one page plus one cell; the left half stops at or before half of that; the right half is the rest, at most half plus one cell.
  • A leaf split copies the separator up (the first key of the right leaf stays in the leaf); an internal split moves it up (the middle separator leaves the node). That difference is the B+tree in one sentence.
  • Leaves are chained through next_leaf for range scans (step 5).
  • Allocation is "increment page_count in the meta page", done through the cache, so it is part of the transaction: an aborted insert also un-allocates.
  • The checker (check()) walks the whole tree and verifies every invariant in 00_spec.md section 4.4. Write it in this step, not later: it is the test oracle for every split you are about to debug.
  • Fan-out, for interviews. With 16-byte keys an internal entry is 22 bytes, so an internal page holds about 185 children. With 100-byte values a leaf cell is 120 bytes, so a leaf holds about 34. One million keys need roughly 30,000 leaves (more, since split leaves are partly empty) and two internal levels above them: height 3. Three page reads per lookup, and the top two levels stay in the cache.

#pragma once

#include <cstddef>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

#include "minidb/page_cache.hpp"

namespace minidb {

// B+tree over pages from the PageCache. Keys and values are byte strings; keys are compared
// with std::string_view::compare (bytewise, like memcmp).
//
//   internal page: child0 | key1 child1 | key2 child2 | ...   key_i = smallest key in child_i
//   leaf page:     next_leaf | key1 value1 | key2 value2 | ...  sorted, unique keys
//
// Every leaf is at the same depth. Leaves are chained left to right through next_leaf, so a
// range scan descends once and then walks sideways.
//
// Simplification (documented, deliberate): erase() never merges or rebalances. A leaf may
// become empty; it stays in the chain and is skipped by scans. Space is reclaimed only by
// rebuilding the file. Many production B-trees also delete lazily for the same reason:
// merges are complex and rarely pay for themselves.
//
// Mutating calls must run inside a PageCache transaction (the Db does this). Not thread-safe.
class BPlusTree {
public:
    explicit BPlusTree(PageCache& cache) : cache_(cache) {}

    // Pages for a brand-new database: page 0 = meta (root = 1, page_count = 2), page 1 = empty leaf.
    static std::vector<Page> initial_pages();

    std::optional<std::string> get(std::string_view key);
    void put(std::string_view key, std::string_view value);
    bool erase(std::string_view key);

    // Keys in [start, end), ascending, at most `limit`. An empty `end` means "no upper bound".
    std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string>> scan(std::string_view start, std::string_view end,
                                                          std::size_t limit);

    // Walks the whole tree and checks every structural invariant (key order, separator
    // bounds, equal leaf depth, leaf chain matches in-order leaves). Throws CorruptionError on
    // the first violation; returns the number of keys. Used by tests and after recovery.
    std::size_t check();

private:
    struct Split {
        std::string separator;  // smallest key of the new right sibling
        PageId right = kNoPage;
    };

    std::optional<Split> insert(PageId id, std::string_view key, std::string_view value, int depth);
    PageId find_leaf(std::string_view key);
    PageId allocate_page();
    PageId root();
    void set_root(PageId root);

    PageCache& cache_;
};

}  // namespace minidb

src/btree.cpp, part 1: node codecs, search, insert and splits.

#include "minidb/btree.hpp"

#include <algorithm>
#include <iterator>
#include <string>

namespace minidb {

namespace {

constexpr int kMaxDepth = 32;  // a 4 KiB-page tree of any realistic size is under 6 levels

// Decoded node forms. We decode a page, change the vectors, and encode it back. Real engines
// edit slotted pages in place; decode/encode costs some CPU but is far easier to get right,
// and the on-disk format is identical either way.
struct LeafNode {
    PageId next = kNoPage;
    std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string>> cells;  // sorted by key, unique
};

struct InternalNode {
    std::vector<std::string> keys;  // separators, strictly increasing
    std::vector<PageId> children;   // keys.size() + 1 entries
};

// Leaf payload:     u16 count | u32 next | count x (u16 klen | u16 vlen | key | value)
// Internal payload: u16 count | u32 child0 | count x (u16 klen | key | u32 child)
constexpr std::size_t kNodeHeader = 2 + 4;

std::size_t leaf_cell_size(const std::pair<std::string, std::string>& cell) noexcept {
    return 4 + cell.first.size() + cell.second.size();
}

std::size_t internal_entry_size(const std::string& key) noexcept { return 2 + key.size() + 4; }

std::size_t leaf_size(const LeafNode& node) noexcept {
    std::size_t size = kNodeHeader;
    for (const auto& cell : node.cells) {
        size += leaf_cell_size(cell);
    }
    return size;
}

std::size_t internal_size(const InternalNode& node) noexcept {
    std::size_t size = kNodeHeader;
    for (const auto& key : node.keys) {
        size += internal_entry_size(key);
    }
    return size;
}

// Bounds-checked decoding: a corrupt length can never read past the page.
class Reader {
public:
    explicit Reader(const char* p) noexcept : p_(p), left_(kPagePayloadSize) {}
    template <class T>
    T get() {
        need(sizeof(T));
        const T value = read_as<T>(p_);
        p_ += sizeof(T);
        left_ -= sizeof(T);
        return value;
    }
    std::string bytes(std::size_t n) {
        need(n);
        std::string out(p_, n);
        p_ += n;
        left_ -= n;
        return out;
    }

private:
    void need(std::size_t n) const {
        if (n > left_) {
            throw CorruptionError("b+tree node overruns its page");
        }
    }
    const char* p_;
    std::size_t left_;
};

class Writer {
public:
    explicit Writer(char* p) noexcept : p_(p) {}
    template <class T>
    void put(T value) noexcept {
        write_as(p_, value);
        p_ += sizeof(T);
    }
    void bytes(const std::string& s) noexcept {
        std::memcpy(p_, s.data(), s.size());
        p_ += s.size();
    }

private:
    char* p_;
};

LeafNode decode_leaf(const Page& page) {
    if (page.type() != PageType::Leaf) {
        throw CorruptionError("expected a leaf page");
    }
    Reader r(page.payload());
    LeafNode node;
    const auto count = r.get<std::uint16_t>();
    node.next = r.get<PageId>();
    node.cells.reserve(count);
    for (std::uint16_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        const auto klen = r.get<std::uint16_t>();
        const auto vlen = r.get<std::uint16_t>();
        std::string key = r.bytes(klen);
        std::string value = r.bytes(vlen);
        node.cells.emplace_back(std::move(key), std::move(value));
    }
    return node;
}

// Precondition: leaf_size(node) <= kPagePayloadSize (callers check before encoding).
void encode_leaf(const LeafNode& node, Page& page) {
    page.set_type(PageType::Leaf);
    page.clear_payload();
    Writer w(page.payload());
    w.put(static_cast<std::uint16_t>(node.cells.size()));
    w.put(node.next);
    for (const auto& [key, value] : node.cells) {
        w.put(static_cast<std::uint16_t>(key.size()));
        w.put(static_cast<std::uint16_t>(value.size()));
        w.bytes(key);
        w.bytes(value);
    }
}

InternalNode decode_internal(const Page& page) {
    if (page.type() != PageType::Internal) {
        throw CorruptionError("expected an internal page");
    }
    Reader r(page.payload());
    InternalNode node;
    const auto count = r.get<std::uint16_t>();
    node.keys.reserve(count);
    node.children.reserve(count + 1u);
    node.children.push_back(r.get<PageId>());
    for (std::uint16_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        const auto klen = r.get<std::uint16_t>();
        node.keys.push_back(r.bytes(klen));
        node.children.push_back(r.get<PageId>());
    }
    return node;
}

void encode_internal(const InternalNode& node, Page& page) {
    page.set_type(PageType::Internal);
    page.clear_payload();
    Writer w(page.payload());
    w.put(static_cast<std::uint16_t>(node.keys.size()));
    w.put(node.children.front());
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < node.keys.size(); ++i) {
        w.put(static_cast<std::uint16_t>(node.keys[i].size()));
        w.bytes(node.keys[i]);
        w.put(node.children[i + 1]);
    }
}

// Index of the child whose subtree may contain `key`: the number of separators <= key.
std::size_t child_index(const InternalNode& node, std::string_view key) {
    const auto it = std::upper_bound(node.keys.begin(), node.keys.end(), key,
                                     [](std::string_view k, const std::string& sep) { return k.compare(sep) < 0; });
    return static_cast<std::size_t>(it - node.keys.begin());
}

auto leaf_lower_bound(LeafNode& node, std::string_view key) {
    return std::lower_bound(node.cells.begin(), node.cells.end(), key,
                            [](const auto& cell, std::string_view k) { return std::string_view(cell.first).compare(k) < 0; });
}

}  // namespace

std::vector<Page> BPlusTree::initial_pages() {
    std::vector<Page> pages(2);
    Meta meta;
    meta.root = 1;
    meta.page_count = 2;
    meta.encode(pages[0]);
    encode_leaf(LeafNode{}, pages[1]);
    return pages;
}

PageId BPlusTree::root() {
    PageCache::PageRef meta_ref = cache_.fetch(kMetaPageId);
    return Meta::decode(meta_ref.read()).root;
}

void BPlusTree::set_root(PageId new_root) {
    PageCache::PageRef meta_ref = cache_.fetch(kMetaPageId);
    Meta meta = Meta::decode(meta_ref.read());
    meta.root = new_root;
    meta.encode(meta_ref.write());
}

PageId BPlusTree::allocate_page() {
    PageCache::PageRef meta_ref = cache_.fetch(kMetaPageId);
    Meta meta = Meta::decode(meta_ref.read());
    if (meta.page_count == UINT32_MAX) {
        throw DbError("database full: page id space exhausted");
    }
    const PageId id = meta.page_count++;
    meta.encode(meta_ref.write());  // logged with the transaction; undone by abort
    return id;
}

PageId BPlusTree::find_leaf(std::string_view key) {
    PageId id = root();
    for (int depth = 0; depth <= kMaxDepth; ++depth) {
        PageCache::PageRef ref = cache_.fetch(id);
        const Page& page = ref.read();
        if (page.type() == PageType::Leaf) {
            return id;
        }
        const InternalNode node = decode_internal(page);
        id = node.children[child_index(node, key)];
    }
    throw CorruptionError("b+tree deeper than possible (cycle?)");
}

std::optional<std::string> BPlusTree::get(std::string_view key) {
    PageCache::PageRef ref = cache_.fetch(find_leaf(key));
    LeafNode leaf = decode_leaf(ref.read());
    const auto it = leaf_lower_bound(leaf, key);
    if (it == leaf.cells.end() || it->first != key) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    return std::move(it->second);
}

void BPlusTree::put(std::string_view key, std::string_view value) {
    const PageId old_root = root();
    std::optional<Split> split = insert(old_root, key, value, 0);
    if (!split) {
        return;
    }
    // The root split: the tree grows by one level, at the top. This is the only way a
    // B+tree gets taller, which is why all leaves stay at the same depth.
    InternalNode node;
    node.keys.push_back(std::move(split->separator));
    node.children = {old_root, split->right};
    const PageId new_root = allocate_page();
    PageCache::PageRef ref = cache_.create(new_root);
    encode_internal(node, ref.write());
    set_root(new_root);
}

std::optional<BPlusTree::Split> BPlusTree::insert(PageId id, std::string_view key, std::string_view value,
                                                  int depth) {
    if (depth > kMaxDepth) {
        throw CorruptionError("b+tree deeper than possible (cycle?)");
    }
    PageCache::PageRef ref = cache_.fetch(id);

    if (ref.read().type() == PageType::Leaf) {
        LeafNode leaf = decode_leaf(ref.read());
        const auto it = leaf_lower_bound(leaf, key);
        if (it != leaf.cells.end() && it->first == key) {
            it->second.assign(value.data(), value.size());
        } else {
            leaf.cells.emplace(it, std::string(key), std::string(value));
        }
        if (leaf_size(leaf) <= kPagePayloadSize) {
            encode_leaf(leaf, ref.write());
            return std::nullopt;
        }

        // Leaf split, balanced by bytes rather than by count, so that a few large values
        // cannot leave one half overfull. Because one cell is at most a quarter of a page
        // (kMaxKeySize, kMaxValueSize), both halves are guaranteed to fit.
        std::size_t total = 0;
        for (const auto& cell : leaf.cells) {
            total += leaf_cell_size(cell);
        }
        std::size_t mid = 0;
        std::size_t left_bytes = 0;
        while (mid + 1 < leaf.cells.size() && left_bytes + leaf_cell_size(leaf.cells[mid]) <= total / 2) {
            left_bytes += leaf_cell_size(leaf.cells[mid]);
            ++mid;
        }
        mid = std::max<std::size_t>(mid, 1);

        LeafNode right;
        right.cells.assign(std::make_move_iterator(leaf.cells.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(mid)),
                           std::make_move_iterator(leaf.cells.end()));
        leaf.cells.resize(mid);

        const PageId right_id = allocate_page();
        right.next = leaf.next;  // splice the new leaf into the sibling chain
        leaf.next = right_id;
        PageCache::PageRef right_ref = cache_.create(right_id);
        encode_leaf(right, right_ref.write());
        encode_leaf(leaf, ref.write());
        return Split{right.cells.front().first, right_id};
    }

    InternalNode node = decode_internal(ref.read());
    const std::size_t index = child_index(node, key);
    std::optional<Split> child_split = insert(node.children[index], key, value, depth + 1);
    if (!child_split) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    node.keys.insert(node.keys.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(index), std::move(child_split->separator));
    node.children.insert(node.children.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(index) + 1, child_split->right);
    if (internal_size(node) <= kPagePayloadSize) {
        encode_internal(node, ref.write());
        return std::nullopt;
    }

    // Internal split: keys[mid] moves *up* to the parent (unlike a leaf split, which copies
    // the first right key up and keeps it in the leaf).
    std::size_t total = 0;
    for (const auto& k : node.keys) {
        total += internal_entry_size(k);
    }
    std::size_t mid = 0;
    std::size_t left_bytes = 0;
    while (mid + 2 < node.keys.size() && left_bytes + internal_entry_size(node.keys[mid]) <= total / 2) {
        left_bytes += internal_entry_size(node.keys[mid]);
        ++mid;
    }
    mid = std::max<std::size_t>(mid, 1);

    InternalNode right;
    right.keys.assign(std::make_move_iterator(node.keys.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(mid) + 1),
                      std::make_move_iterator(node.keys.end()));
    right.children.assign(node.children.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(mid) + 1, node.children.end());
    std::string promoted = std::move(node.keys[mid]);
    node.keys.resize(mid);
    node.children.resize(mid + 1);

    const PageId right_id = allocate_page();
    PageCache::PageRef right_ref = cache_.create(right_id);
    encode_internal(right, right_ref.write());
    encode_internal(node, ref.write());
    return Split{std::move(promoted), right_id};
}

src/btree.cpp, part 2 (end of file): the invariant checker.

std::size_t BPlusTree::check() {
    struct Checker {
        explicit Checker(PageCache& c) : cache(c) {}
        PageCache& cache;
        std::uint32_t page_count = 0;
        int leaf_depth = -1;
        std::size_t keys = 0;
        std::vector<PageId> leaves;  // in key order

        void visit(PageId id, const std::string* lo, const std::string* hi, int depth) {
            if (depth > kMaxDepth || id == kNoPage || id >= page_count) {
                throw CorruptionError("check: bad child pointer or depth");
            }
            PageCache::PageRef ref = cache.fetch(id);
            if (ref.read().type() == PageType::Leaf) {
                const LeafNode leaf = decode_leaf(ref.read());
                if (leaf_depth == -1) {
                    leaf_depth = depth;
                } else if (leaf_depth != depth) {
                    throw CorruptionError("check: leaves at different depths");
                }
                for (std::size_t i = 0; i < leaf.cells.size(); ++i) {
                    const std::string& key = leaf.cells[i].first;
                    if (i > 0 && !(leaf.cells[i - 1].first < key)) {
                        throw CorruptionError("check: leaf keys not strictly increasing");
                    }
                    if ((lo != nullptr && key < *lo) || (hi != nullptr && !(key < *hi))) {
                        throw CorruptionError("check: leaf key outside its separator bounds");
                    }
                }
                keys += leaf.cells.size();
                leaves.push_back(id);
                return;
            }
            const InternalNode node = decode_internal(ref.read());
            ref = PageCache::PageRef();  // unpin before descending: pins stay O(1), not O(depth)
            if (node.children.size() != node.keys.size() + 1) {
                throw CorruptionError("check: internal node child count");
            }
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < node.keys.size(); ++i) {
                if ((i > 0 && !(node.keys[i - 1] < node.keys[i])) || (lo != nullptr && node.keys[i] < *lo) ||
                    (hi != nullptr && !(node.keys[i] < *hi))) {
                    throw CorruptionError("check: separators out of order or out of bounds");
                }
            }
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < node.children.size(); ++i) {
                const std::string* child_lo = i == 0 ? lo : &node.keys[i - 1];
                const std::string* child_hi = i == node.keys.size() ? hi : &node.keys[i];
                visit(node.children[i], child_lo, child_hi, depth + 1);
            }
        }
    };

    Checker checker(cache_);
    {
        PageCache::PageRef meta_ref = cache_.fetch(kMetaPageId);
        checker.page_count = Meta::decode(meta_ref.read()).page_count;
    }
    checker.visit(root(), nullptr, nullptr, 0);

    // The sibling chain must visit exactly the leaves the tree walk found, in the same order.
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < checker.leaves.size(); ++i) {
        PageCache::PageRef ref = cache_.fetch(checker.leaves[i]);
        const PageId expected_next = i + 1 < checker.leaves.size() ? checker.leaves[i + 1] : kNoPage;
        if (decode_leaf(ref.read()).next != expected_next) {
            throw CorruptionError("check: leaf chain does not match tree order");
        }
    }
    return checker.keys;
}

}  // namespace minidb

Points that come up in review:

  • insert keeps the parent pinned while it recurses into the child, so pins grow with the tree height (3 or 4), far below the 16-frame minimum. check unpins a node before visiting its children, so it holds O(1) pins however large the tree.
  • find_leaf and insert stop after 32 levels and throw CorruptionError: a corrupted child pointer that forms a cycle must not hang the process.
  • Reader bounds-checks every length read from a page, so a corrupt count or klen can never read past the 4 KiB buffer. This is exactly the class of bug ASan finds in parsers.

tests/btree_test.cpp: the tree on a Pager and a PageCache with a no-op WAL hook, committing each operation in the cache directly, so tree bugs show up here and not in recovery. In step 4, leave out the erase helper of the fixture.

// BPlusTree on a Pager + PageCache with no log: each operation is committed in the cache
// straight away. Isolates the tree from the WAL so tree bugs show up here, not in recovery.

#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <random>
#include <string>

#include <gtest/gtest.h>

#include "minidb/btree.hpp"
#include "test_util.hpp"

using namespace minidb;

namespace {

std::string key_of(int i) {
    char buf[16];
    std::snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "k%08d", i);
    return buf;
}

std::string create_database(const TempDir& dir) {
    const std::string path = dir.file("db");
    Pager::create(path, BPlusTree::initial_pages());
    return path;
}

class TreeFixture : public ::testing::Test {
protected:
    TreeFixture()
        : path_(create_database(dir_)),
          pager_(path_),
          cache_(pager_, 32, [](Lsn) {}),  // no WAL in this test: nothing to make durable
          tree_(cache_) {}

    void put(const std::string& k, const std::string& v) {
        tree_.put(k, v);
        cache_.commit_txn();  // what Db::commit does after logging
    }
    bool erase(const std::string& k) {
        const bool removed = tree_.erase(k);
        cache_.commit_txn();
        return removed;
    }

    TempDir dir_;
    std::string path_;
    Pager pager_;
    PageCache cache_;
    BPlusTree tree_;
};

}  // namespace

TEST_F(TreeFixture, MaximumSizeCellsAlwaysSplitIntoFittingHalves) {
    // Worst case for the split rule: every cell at the maximum size, inserted in reverse.
    for (int i = 300; i > 0; --i) {
        std::string key = key_of(i);
        key.resize(kMaxKeySize, 'k');
        put(key, std::string(kMaxValueSize, 'v'));
    }
    EXPECT_EQ(tree_.check(), 300u);
}

This is the adversarial case for the split rule: every cell at the maximum size, inserted in descending order so every insert goes to the leftmost leaf. If the byte-balanced split or the size limits were wrong, encode_leaf would be asked to write more than a page, which the checker or ASan would catch.

docs.title: What to say in an interview
docs.text: "It is a B+tree: values only in leaves, leaves chained for range scans, internal nodes holding separators. Splits are balanced by bytes rather than by count, because cells vary in size, and the key and value limits guarantee that a cell is at most a quarter of a page, so both halves of a split always fit. A leaf split copies the first key of the new leaf up; an internal split moves its middle key up. The tree only grows by splitting the root, which is why every leaf is at the same depth. With 4 KiB pages and 16-byte keys the fan-out is about 185, so a million keys is three levels. And there is a check() that verifies every invariant; every test calls it."

docs.title: Step 5. BPlusTree II: erase, range scan, model-based test
docs.text: Time: ~5 hours Week: 8 Read first: 07_Databases_Internals/03_btree_indexes_in_depth.md (deletion, merges, range scans). 03_Data_Structures_Algorithms: std::map as an ordered reference model.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Delete keys, scan ranges through the leaf chain, and prove the whole tree against std::map under tens of thousands of random operations.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Erase without merge. Remove the cell from its leaf; never merge or redistribute. Leaves may become empty; they stay in the chain and scans skip them. Separators in internal nodes may then name keys that no longer exist, which is harmless: they are still valid bounds. Merging is where most B-tree bugs live, and many production engines also delete lazily and reclaim space by rebuilding. Say it as a decision, with the cost: the file never shrinks.
  • Range scan. Descend once to the leaf that would contain start, then follow next_leaf, stopping at end or limit. One descent plus sequential leaf reads, which is why B+trees (not plain B-trees) are the standard index structure.
  • Model-based testing. Run the same random operations against the tree and against a std::map, compare results as you go, compare full contents at the end, and call check() periodically. It finds the bugs you did not think to write a test for.
