# tcpkv

A multithreaded TCP key-value server in C++17. Work in progress; v1.0.0 is the first release.

## Build

    cmake --preset debug && cmake --build --preset debug && ctest --preset debug

docs.title: 4. Build and run
docs.text:
cmake --preset debug
cmake --build --preset debug
ctest --preset debug

Expected: the configure step clones googletest (one time, ~20 s), the build produces build/debug/hello_test, and ctest prints 100% tests passed, 0 tests failed out of 2.

Then prove the sanitizer path works too:

cmake --preset asan && cmake --build --preset asan && ctest --preset asan

docs.title: 5. Test
docs.text:
The test here is the pipeline itself:

  1. Break something on purpose: change EXPECT_EQ(1 + 1, 2) to 3, rebuild, run ctest. You must see the failure named Hello.ToolchainWorks with file and line. Revert.
  2. Add an unused variable int x; to the test. The build must fail with error: unused variable 'x' [-Werror=unused-variable]. That is -Werror doing its job. Revert.

docs.title: 6. Commit and push
docs.text:
git add -A
git commit -m "Project skeleton: CMake, presets, GoogleTest via FetchContent, CI


- C++17, -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Werror on a shared INTERFACE target
- CMakePresets for debug/release/relwithdebinfo/asan/tsan/ubsan
- GitHub Actions: debug and asan jobs on ubuntu-24.04
- hello_test proves the toolchain end to end"
git push -u origin main

Open https://github.com/khanshaki-r/tcpkv/actions. Wait for both jobs to go green. If a job is red, read the log, fix, push again. Do not move to step 02 with a red CI; the habit of "CI is always green on main" is the whole point of setting it up first.

docs.title: 7. What you learned, and what to say in an interview
docs.text:
• CMake targets, not variables. Flags live on targets (tcpkv_warnings) and propagate through target_link_libraries. That is how you keep -Werror off third-party code.
  • Presets make "configure with TSan" a single reproducible command for humans and CI.
  • Sanitizers must be applied to everything that ends up in the same process.
  • Pinned dependencies (GIT_TAG v1.14.0) are what makes a build reproducible a year later.

Interview sentence: "I set the repo up so that from the first commit every build was -Werror clean and every push ran the tests under AddressSanitizer in CI. Adding a feature was always just adding a file and a test; the infrastructure never changed after week one."

docs.title: Step 02. RAII FileDescriptor and Socket wrappers (move-only), with unit tests
docs.text: Time: ~7 hours Week: 1 (Oct 6 – Oct 12) Read first: 02_Modern_CPP: RAII, destructors, the rule of five, move semantics and std::move, noexcept, explicit, deleted functions, exceptions and std::system_error. 08_Networking_Distributed: the BSD socket API (socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, read, send, poll), getaddrinfo, EINTR, partial writes, SO_REUSEADDR, TCP_NODELAY. 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps: file descriptors, O_CLOEXEC, strace.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
Two classes that make it impossible to leak a file descriptor or to forget the three things every C network programmer has forgotten at least once: retrying on EINTR, looping on partial writes, and closing on every exit path.

In plain words: in a C server you write close(fd) in every error branch and hoped you did not miss one. In C++ you write the close once, in a destructor, and the compiler calls it for you on every path including exceptions. That is RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization): a resource is owned by an object, and the object's lifetime is the resource's lifetime.

docs.title: 2. Design
docs.text:
FileDescriptor                      Socket
  int fd_ = -1                        FileDescriptor fd_
  explicit FileDescriptor(int)        static listen_tcp(host, port, backlog)
  ~FileDescriptor() -> close          static connect_tcp(host, port)
  copy: deleted                       accept() -> Socket
  move: transfers, source = -1        read_some(buf, len) -> 0 on EOF
  get(), valid(), release(), reset()  write_all(data, len)   loops partial sends
                                      wait_readable(timeout) poll()
                                      shutdown_both(), local_port(), peer_address()

Decisions worth remembering:

  • Move-only. Two objects owning the same descriptor would close it twice; the second close might hit a descriptor the kernel has just handed to another thread. Deleting the copy constructor makes that a compile error.
  • close() is not retried on EINTR. On Linux, if close returns EINTR the descriptor is already gone. Retrying could close somebody else's new descriptor. (This is the opposite of read/write, and it is a classic interview question.)
  • write_all uses send(..., MSG_NOSIGNAL). Writing to a socket whose peer has gone away raises SIGPIPE, which kills the process by default. MSG_NOSIGNAL turns that into EPIPE, which we can handle per connection.
  • Errors are exceptions (std::system_error carrying errno). Inside a constructor you cannot return an error code, and a Socket that failed to connect must not exist.
  • accept4/SOCK_CLOEXEC/pipe2(O_CLOEXEC): descriptors are created close-on-exec atomically, so a fork() in another thread can never leak them to a child.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/fd.hpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/include/tcpkv/fd.hpp:

#pragma once

#include <utility>

namespace tcpkv {

// Throws std::system_error built from an errno value.
// Every wrapper that talks to the kernel uses this so error reporting is uniform.
[[noreturn]] void throw_system_error(int err, const char* what);

// Owning handle for one POSIX file descriptor.
//
// Rules:
//   * exactly one owner: copying is deleted, moving transfers ownership
//   * the destructor closes the descriptor exactly once; a moved-from handle holds -1
//   * close() is NOT retried on EINTR: on Linux the descriptor is already released
//     when close() returns EINTR, and retrying could close a descriptor that another
//     thread has just been handed by the kernel
class FileDescriptor {
public:
    FileDescriptor() noexcept = default;
    explicit FileDescriptor(int fd) noexcept : fd_(fd) {}
    ~FileDescriptor() { reset(); }

    FileDescriptor(const FileDescriptor&) = delete;
    FileDescriptor& operator=(const FileDescriptor&) = delete;

    FileDescriptor(FileDescriptor&& other) noexcept : fd_(other.release()) {}
    FileDescriptor& operator=(FileDescriptor&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            reset(other.release());
        }
        return *this;
    }

    int get() const noexcept { return fd_; }
    bool valid() const noexcept { return fd_ >= 0; }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return valid(); }

    // Gives up ownership without closing. The caller now owns the raw descriptor.
    int release() noexcept {
        const int fd = fd_;
        fd_ = -1;
        return fd;
    }

    // Closes the current descriptor (if any) and takes ownership of `fd`.
    void reset(int fd = -1) noexcept;

    friend void swap(FileDescriptor& a, FileDescriptor& b) noexcept { std::swap(a.fd_, b.fd_); }

private:
    int fd_ = -1;
};

// Creates a pipe with O_CLOEXEC on both ends. Returns {read_end, write_end}.
// Throws std::system_error on failure.
std::pair<FileDescriptor, FileDescriptor> make_pipe();

// Sets or clears O_NONBLOCK on a descriptor. Throws std::system_error on failure.
void set_nonblocking(int fd, bool enabled);

}  // namespace tcpkv

Line-by-line, the parts that matter:

  • explicit FileDescriptor(int): without explicit, FileDescriptor fd = 3; would compile and silently adopt descriptor 3. Adopting a descriptor is a deliberate act.
  • The move constructor calls other.release(), so the source is left holding -1 and its destructor does nothing. That is what "transfer ownership" means mechanically.
  • Move assignment guards this != &other. Self-move-assignment is rare but legal, and reset(release()) on the same object would close the descriptor and then adopt the closed value.
  • Everything is noexcept. Containers (std::vector<Socket>) only move elements during reallocation if the move constructor is noexcept; otherwise they copy, and here copying is deleted, so without noexcept the vector would not compile.

docs.title: src/fd.cpp
docs.text:
#include "tcpkv/fd.hpp"

#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#include <cerrno>
#include <system_error>

namespace tcpkv {

void throw_system_error(int err, const char* what) {
    // generic_category() is the category for POSIX errno values; its messages come from strerror.
    throw std::system_error(err, std::generic_category(), what);
}

void FileDescriptor::reset(int fd) noexcept {
    if (fd_ >= 0 && fd_ != fd) {
        // The return value is deliberately ignored. There is nothing useful to do with an
        // error from close() in a destructor, and on Linux the descriptor is gone either way.
        ::close(fd_);
    }
    fd_ = fd;
}

std::pair<FileDescriptor, FileDescriptor> make_pipe() {
    int fds[2] = {-1, -1};
    // pipe2 with O_CLOEXEC is atomic: no window in which a fork()ed child inherits the ends.
    if (::pipe2(fds, O_CLOEXEC) != 0) {
        throw_system_error(errno, "pipe2");
    }
    return {FileDescriptor(fds[0]), FileDescriptor(fds[1])};
}

void set_nonblocking(int fd, bool enabled) {
    const int flags = ::fcntl(fd, F_GETFL);
    if (flags < 0) {
        throw_system_error(errno, "fcntl(F_GETFL)");
    }
    const int wanted = enabled ? (flags | O_NONBLOCK) : (flags & ~O_NONBLOCK);
    if (wanted != flags && ::fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, wanted) < 0) {
        throw_system_error(errno, "fcntl(F_SETFL)");
    }
}

}  // namespace tcpkv

docs.title: include/tcpkv/socket.hpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/include/tcpkv/socket.hpp.

#pragma once

#include <chrono>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <utility>

#include "tcpkv/fd.hpp"

namespace tcpkv {

// A TCP socket built on FileDescriptor. Move-only, like the descriptor it owns.
//
// Every blocking call retries on EINTR. write_all() loops until every byte is
// handed to the kernel, because send() on a stream socket may accept fewer bytes
// than asked. All failures are reported as std::system_error carrying errno.
class Socket {
public:
    Socket() noexcept = default;
    explicit Socket(FileDescriptor fd) noexcept : fd_(std::move(fd)) {}

    Socket(const Socket&) = delete;
    Socket& operator=(const Socket&) = delete;
    Socket(Socket&&) noexcept = default;
    Socket& operator=(Socket&&) noexcept = default;
    ~Socket() = default;

    // Resolves `host` (empty means "any address"), binds, listens. `port` 0 picks a free port.
    static Socket listen_tcp(const std::string& host, std::uint16_t port, int backlog);

    // Resolves and connects. Tries every address returned by getaddrinfo in order.
    static Socket connect_tcp(const std::string& host, std::uint16_t port);

    // Blocks until a client connects (unless the listener is non-blocking, in which case
    // it throws std::system_error with EAGAIN when nothing is pending).
    Socket accept();

    // Returns the number of bytes read; 0 means the peer closed its side.
    std::size_t read_some(char* buf, std::size_t len);

    // Writes all bytes or throws. Uses MSG_NOSIGNAL so a dead peer gives EPIPE, not SIGPIPE.
    void write_all(const char* data, std::size_t len);
    void write_all(std::string_view data) { write_all(data.data(), data.size()); }

    // Waits up to `timeout` for the socket to become readable (data, EOF or error).
    // Returns false on timeout. EINTR is reported as a timeout so callers re-check their state.
    bool wait_readable(std::chrono::milliseconds timeout);

    // shutdown(SHUT_RDWR). Errors (e.g. ENOTCONN) are ignored: this is a courtesy to the peer.
    void shutdown_both() noexcept;

    std::uint16_t local_port() const;
    std::string peer_address() const noexcept;  // "ip:port", or "?" if it cannot be determined

    void set_nodelay(bool enabled);
    void set_nonblocking(bool enabled);

    int fd() const noexcept { return fd_.get(); }
    bool valid() const noexcept { return fd_.valid(); }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return valid(); }

private:
    FileDescriptor fd_;
};

}  // namespace tcpkv

Notice that Socket has no user-written destructor, move constructor or move assignment. It contains one FileDescriptor, and the compiler-generated versions do the right thing by composing it. This is the rule of zero: if every member manages itself, the class needs no special member functions. Socket only deletes copying so the intent is explicit.

docs.title: src/socket.cpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/src/socket.cpp (about 230 lines). Type it in from there. The parts to understand deeply:

// RAII for the linked list returned by getaddrinfo(). Move-only: a copy would free twice.
struct AddrInfoList {
    addrinfo* head = nullptr;

    AddrInfoList() = default;
    AddrInfoList(const AddrInfoList&) = delete;
    AddrInfoList& operator=(const AddrInfoList&) = delete;
    AddrInfoList(AddrInfoList&& other) noexcept : head(other.head) { other.head = nullptr; }
    AddrInfoList& operator=(AddrInfoList&&) = delete;
    ~AddrInfoList() {
        if (head != nullptr) {
            ::freeaddrinfo(head);
        }
    }
};

Even a helper that lives for ten lines gets a destructor. The getaddrinfo result is a heap list; any throw between the call and freeaddrinfo would leak it. With this struct it cannot.

std::size_t Socket::read_some(char* buf, std::size_t len) {
    for (;;) {
        const ssize_t n = ::read(fd_.get(), buf, len);
        if (n >= 0) {
            return static_cast<std::size_t>(n);
        }
        if (errno == EINTR) {
            continue;
        }
        throw_system_error(errno, "read");
    }
}

void Socket::write_all(const char* data, std::size_t len) {
    std::size_t offset = 0;
    while (offset < len) {
        const ssize_t n = ::send(fd_.get(), data + offset, len - offset, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        if (n < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) {
                continue;
            }
            throw_system_error(errno, "send");
        }
        offset += static_cast<std::size_t>(n);
    }
}

read returns 0 only at EOF; send on a blocking socket can return less than len when the socket buffer is nearly full. The 4 MiB test below exists to force that path.

std::uint16_t Socket::local_port() const {
    sockaddr_storage storage{};
    socklen_t len = sizeof storage;
    if (::getsockname(fd_.get(), reinterpret_cast<sockaddr*>(&storage), &len) != 0) {
        throw_system_error(errno, "getsockname");
    }
    // memcpy instead of a pointer cast: sockaddr_storage and sockaddr_in are different types
    // and reading one through a pointer to the other is undefined behaviour.
    if (storage.ss_family == AF_INET) {
        sockaddr_in in4{};
        std::memcpy(&in4, &storage, sizeof in4);
        return ntohs(in4.sin_port);
    }
    ...

The reinterpret_cast<sockaddr*> into the syscall is the API's sanctioned use; reading the port back through ((sockaddr_in*)&storage)->sin_port is a strict-aliasing violation that UBSan and optimising compilers will eventually punish. memcpy is free after optimisation.

docs.title: tests/fd_test.cpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/tests/fd_test.cpp. The core idea: ask the kernel whether a descriptor is open.

// fcntl(F_GETFD) is the cheapest way to ask the kernel "is this descriptor still open?".
bool fd_is_open(int fd) { return ::fcntl(fd, F_GETFD) != -1; }

TEST(FileDescriptor, ClosesOnDestruction) {
    int raw = -1;
    {
        const std::pair<FileDescriptor, FileDescriptor> ends = tcpkv::make_pipe();
        raw = ends.first.get();
        ASSERT_TRUE(fd_is_open(raw));
    }
    EXPECT_FALSE(fd_is_open(raw));
}

Other tests: move constructor leaves the source invalid and the descriptor open; move assignment closes the old descriptor; release does not close; reset closes and adopts; pipe ends have FD_CLOEXEC; set_nonblocking toggles O_NONBLOCK; listen on port 0 gives a real port; echo over loopback; read_some returns 0 after peer shutdown; wait_readable times out and then wakes; a 4 MiB write arrives intact (with a reader thread, or both sides would block); connecting to a closed port throws; non-blocking accept with no client throws EAGAIN.

docs.title: 7. What you learned, and what to say in an interview
docs.text:
• RAII turns "remember to close on every path" into "cannot forget". The destructor runs on return, on break, on throw, on scope exit after a moved-from object.
  • Move-only types encode "exactly one owner" in the type system. The compiler, not a code review, catches the double close.
  • Rule of zero: Socket has no special members because FileDescriptor already behaves.
  • noexcept on moves is not decoration; standard containers check it.
  • The three syscall gotchas: EINTR on read/accept/poll (retry), partial send (loop), close after EINTR (do not retry). Plus SIGPIPE (MSG_NOSIGNAL), SO_REUSEADDR (restart during TIME_WAIT), and CLOEXEC (atomic, not a separate fcntl).
  • Strict aliasing: memcpy into the right sockaddr_* type instead of casting pointers.

Interview sentence: "Every descriptor in tcpkv is owned by a FileDescriptor; there is one close() call in the whole codebase, in its reset(). The test for it asks the kernel via fcntl(F_GETFD) whether the descriptor is really gone after the destructor runs."

docs.title: Step 03. Protocol parser: incremental state machine, with malformed-input tests
docs.text: Time: ~8 hours Week: 2 (Oct 13 – Oct 19) Read first: 02_Modern_CPP: std::string_view, std::optional, std::variant and std::get_if, std::from_chars, enums with enum class, inline constexpr, namespaces. 08_Networking_Distributed: why TCP is a byte stream (message boundaries do not exist; one read() may return half a command or three commands).

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
A Parser that you feed whatever bytes read() returned and that hands back complete commands, one at a time, never blocking and never touching a socket. Plus the encoders for requests and replies, and the limits from 00_spec.md section 3.5. Plus a test for every malformed input the spec lists.

In plain words: TCP gives you a hose of bytes with no markers. The parser is the thing that cuts the hose into commands. Because it only ever sees bytes, you can test every nasty case (a command split at every possible byte, a 2 GB length, a missing newline) in microseconds without a network.

docs.title: 2. Design
docs.text:
feed(bytes)                         next()
  socket ----------->  buffer_ [pos_ ....]  ----------> Command | ParseError | nullopt (need more)

  State machine:
    Line  --"SET k n" header-->  Value  --n bytes + '\n'-->  Line   (emit Command)
    Line  --any other line---->  Line   (emit Command or non-fatal ParseError)
    any   --fatal error------>  Dead   (emit fatal ParseError once; then nullopt forever)
  • feed() only appends. next() does all the work and is called in a loop until it returns nullopt. This separation is what makes pipelining free: one read() of "PING\nPING\nGET a\n" yields three commands.
  • The buffer is a std::string plus a read offset pos_. Consumed bytes are erased lazily (compact()), only when the offset is large or everything is consumed, so the common case is amortised O(1) per byte.
  • Errors are data (ParseError{message, fatal}), not exceptions. A bad command from a client is a normal event, not an exceptional one, and the server must keep running.
  • fatal splits the errors the spec lists: after an unknown command we know the next line starts a new request; after SET k 999999999999 we do not know where the next request is.
  • The SET length token is consumed by the parser and not passed on in args; the executor gets args = {key} and value. One less thing for the executor to parse.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/protocol.hpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/include/tcpkv/protocol.hpp. Key parts:

namespace limits {
inline constexpr std::size_t kMaxKeyLength = 256;
inline constexpr std::size_t kMaxValueLength = 1024 * 1024;  // 1 MiB
inline constexpr std::size_t kMaxLineLength = 4096;
inline constexpr std::size_t kMaxArgs = 64;
}  // namespace limits

enum class CommandType { Ping, Get, Set, Del, Exists, Keys, Expire, Ttl, Stats, Quit };

struct Command {
    CommandType type = CommandType::Ping;
    std::vector<std::string> args;  // everything after the command name, SET's length excluded
    std::string value;              // SET only
};

struct ParseError {
    std::string message;
    bool fatal = false;
};

using ParseEvent = std::variant<Command, ParseError>;

class Parser {
public:
    void feed(const char* data, std::size_t len);
    void feed(std::string_view data) { feed(data.data(), data.size()); }
    std::optional<ParseEvent> next();
    std::size_t buffered() const noexcept { return buffer_.size() - pos_; }
    bool dead() const noexcept { return state_ == State::Dead; }

private:
    enum class State { Line, Value, Dead };
    std::optional<ParseEvent> parse_line(std::string_view line);
    std::optional<ParseEvent> fail(std::string message, bool fatal);
    void compact();

    State state_ = State::Line;
    std::string buffer_;
    std::size_t pos_ = 0;
    Command pending_;
    std::size_t value_len_ = 0;
};

inline constexpr (C++17) lets a constant live in a header with one definition across all translation units. std::variant is a type-safe union: an event is either a command or an error, and std::get_if makes the caller handle both.

All ten command types are recognised now, including EXPIRE, TTL and STATS, even though the store does not implement TTL until step 09. The parser is the protocol; it should be complete and tested in one go. The executor will answer -ERR not implemented yet for them until step 09.

docs.title: src/protocol.cpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/src/protocol.cpp (about 330 lines). The heart of it:

std::optional<ParseEvent> Parser::next() {
    for (;;) {
        switch (state_) {
            case State::Dead:
                return std::nullopt;

            case State::Line: {
                const std::size_t newline = buffer_.find('\n', pos_);
                if (newline == std::string::npos) {
                    if (buffered() > limits::kMaxLineLength) {
                        return fail("line too long", /*fatal=*/true);
                    }
                    compact();
                    return std::nullopt;
                }
                std::string_view line(buffer_.data() + pos_, newline - pos_);
                if (!line.empty() && line.back() == '\r') {
                    line.remove_suffix(1);
                }
                pos_ = newline + 1;
                if (line.size() > limits::kMaxLineLength) {
                    return fail("line too long", /*fatal=*/true);
                }
                if (auto event = parse_line(line)) {
                    return event;
                }
                break;  // blank line or SET header: loop and look at the next thing
            }

            case State::Value: {
                const std::size_t available = buffer_.size() - pos_;
                if (available < value_len_ + 1) {
                    compact();
                    return std::nullopt;
                }
                const char* data = buffer_.data() + pos_;
                std::size_t consumed = 0;
                if (data[value_len_] == '\n') {
                    consumed = value_len_ + 1;
                } else if (data[value_len_] == '\r') {
                    if (available < value_len_ + 2) {
                        compact();
                        return std::nullopt;
                    }
                    if (data[value_len_ + 1] != '\n') {
                        return fail("value not terminated by newline", /*fatal=*/true);
                    }
                    consumed = value_len_ + 2;
                } else {
                    return fail("value not terminated by newline", /*fatal=*/true);
                }
                pending_.value.assign(data, value_len_);
                pos_ += consumed;
                state_ = State::Line;
                Command command = std::move(pending_);
                pending_ = Command{};
                return ParseEvent(std::move(command));
            }
        }
    }
}

Things to notice:

  • line is a string_view into buffer_. That is only safe because nothing modifies buffer_ between creating the view and finishing parse_line (which copies the tokens into Command::args). compact() runs only on the "need more" path, after the view is dead.
  • The for (;;) with break inside the switch is how a blank line or a SET header continues to the next line without recursion.
  • pending_ = Command{}; after the move: a moved-from std::string is valid but unspecified; resetting it keeps the next SET from inheriting stale state.

Integer parsing uses std::from_chars:

bool parse_unsigned(std::string_view text, std::uint64_t& out) {
    if (text.empty()) {
        return false;
    }
    const char* begin = text.data();
    const char* end = begin + text.size();
    // from_chars rejects leading '+', whitespace and (for unsigned types) '-': exactly the
    // strictness a wire protocol wants.
    const auto result = std::from_chars(begin, end, out);
    return result.ec == std::errc() && result.ptr == end;
}

Why not std::stoul or atoi? atoi("12abc") returns 12; stoul("-1") returns a huge number; both accept leading whitespace and +. from_chars does none of that, does not allocate, does not throw, and reports overflow. Checking ptr == end rejects trailing junk.

docs.title: tests/protocol_test.cpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/tests/protocol_test.cpp (about 330 lines, 36 tests). The pattern:

std::optional<Command> next_command(Parser& parser) {
    std::optional<ParseEvent> event = parser.next();
    if (!event) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    if (Command* command = std::get_if<Command>(&*event)) {
        return std::move(*command);
    }
    return std::nullopt;
}

TEST(Parser, ByteByByteFeedingProducesExactlyOneCommand) {
    Parser parser;
    const std::string wire = "SET key 5\nhello\n";
    int commands = 0;
    for (const char c : wire) {
        parser.feed(&c, 1);
        while (auto cmd = next_command(parser)) {
            ++commands;
            EXPECT_EQ(cmd->type, CommandType::Set);
            EXPECT_EQ(cmd->args[0], "key");
            EXPECT_EQ(cmd->value, "hello");
        }
    }
    EXPECT_EQ(commands, 1);
}

The byte-by-byte test is the most important one in the file. It simulates the worst TCP can do (every read() returns one byte) and proves the state machine resumes correctly from every possible split point.

The malformed-input section covers each error from the spec: unknown command (non-fatal, parsing continues with the next line), every wrong arity, invalid keys (too long, control character, UTF-8), bad SET lengths (abc, -1, +5, 5x), oversized value (fatal; parser dead; further input ignored), 4097 bytes without newline (fatal) vs exactly 4096 (not fatal, just waiting), value not followed by newline (fatal), 65 arguments, non-integer EXPIRE seconds. Plus the encoders round-tripping binary data through the parser.

docs.title: 7. What you learned, and what to say in an interview
docs.text:
• TCP is a stream. A parser for a TCP protocol must be resumable at any byte. The byte-by-byte test is how you prove it.
  • Separate parsing from I/O. The parser never sees a socket, so 36 tests run in milliseconds with no ports, no threads, no flakiness.
  • Errors as values for expected failures (bad client input); exceptions for unexpected ones (the kernel refused a syscall).
  • Fatal vs recoverable is a protocol design decision: can the server resynchronise?
  • Length prefix beats escaping for binary safety, O(1) framing and pipelining.
  • from_chars is the correct way to parse integers off the wire; atoi is a bug.

Interview sentence: "The parser is a three-state machine over a byte buffer. I tested it by feeding a SET command one byte at a time and asserting exactly one command comes out, and by feeding every malformed input the spec names and asserting the exact error and whether the connection survives it."

docs.title: Step 04. Store with std::shared_mutex: single-thread tests, then multi-thread stress
docs.text: Time: ~6 hours Week: 2 (Oct 13 – Oct 19) Read first: 04_Concurrency: data races and the C++ memory model (what "undefined behaviour" means for a torn read), std::mutex, std::lock_guard/std::unique_lock, std::shared_mutex and std::shared_lock, std::atomic, std::thread and join, ThreadSanitizer. 02_Modern_CPP: std::unordered_map, std::optional, pass-by-value and std::move for sink parameters, const member functions and mutable.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
The in-memory table, safe to use from any number of threads at once. This step builds the version without TTL (expiry arrives in step 09); the API is designed so step 09 only adds methods.

In plain words: an unordered_map<string, string> with a lock around it. The interesting part is which lock. A plain mutex lets one thread in at a time; a shared_mutex lets any number of readers in together but gives a writer the room to itself. A key-value server is read-heavy, so this is the standard choice, and you should be able to say when it is the wrong one (see section 7).

docs.title: 2. Design
docs.text:
GET / EXISTS / KEYS / size            SET / DEL
                 |                                  |
          shared_lock (many at once)       unique_lock (one, excludes readers)
                 |                                  |
                 +------------> std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string> <------+
  • One std::shared_mutex, declared mutable so const readers can lock it.
  • Readers copy the value out under the lock and return the copy. Returning a reference or a string_view into the map would be a use-after-free the moment a writer runs.
  • set takes std::string key, std::string value by value and moves them in. Callers that have a temporary pay nothing; callers with an lvalue pay one copy, which they would have paid anyway.
  • keys() collects under the shared lock and sorts after releasing it. Never do more work under a lock than you must.
  • Nothing is static, nothing is global: tests can create ten Stores.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/store.hpp (step-04 version)
docs.text:
#pragma once

#include <cstddef>
#include <optional>
#include <shared_mutex>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

namespace tcpkv {

// In-memory key/value store.
//
// Concurrency: one std::shared_mutex. Readers (GET, EXISTS, KEYS) take a shared lock and run
// in parallel; writers (SET, DEL) take an exclusive lock. The map is never touched without
// the lock, so every method is safe to call from any thread.
class Store {
public:
    Store() = default;
    Store(const Store&) = delete;
    Store& operator=(const Store&) = delete;

    std::optional<std::string> get(const std::string& key) const;
    void set(std::string key, std::string value);
    bool del(const std::string& key);  // true if the key existed
    bool exists(const std::string& key) const;

    // Keys starting with `prefix` (empty prefix = all keys), sorted ascending.
    std::vector<std::string> keys(std::string_view prefix = {}) const;

    std::size_t size() const;

private:
    mutable std::shared_mutex mutex_;
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string> map_;
};

}  // namespace tcpkv

docs.title: src/store.cpp (step-04 version)
docs.text:
#include "tcpkv/store.hpp"

#include <algorithm>
#include <mutex>
#include <utility>

namespace tcpkv {

std::optional<std::string> Store::get(const std::string& key) const {
    std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    const auto it = map_.find(key);
    if (it == map_.end()) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    return it->second;  // copy made under the lock; the caller owns it afterwards
}

void Store::set(std::string key, std::string value) {
    std::unique_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    map_[std::move(key)] = std::move(value);
}

bool Store::del(const std::string& key) {
    std::unique_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    return map_.erase(key) > 0;
}

bool Store::exists(const std::string& key) const {
    std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    return map_.find(key) != map_.end();
}

std::vector<std::string> Store::keys(std::string_view prefix) const {
    std::vector<std::string> out;
    {
        std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
        for (const auto& [key, value] : map_) {
            (void)value;
            if (key.size() >= prefix.size() && key.compare(0, prefix.size(), prefix) == 0) {
                out.push_back(key);
            }
        }
    }
    std::sort(out.begin(), out.end());  // sort after releasing the lock
    return out;
}

std::size_t Store::size() const {
    std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    return map_.size();
}

}  // namespace tcpkv

map_[std::move(key)] = std::move(value) does an insert-or-assign in one hash lookup. The (void)value; silences the unused-binding warning for the structured binding; step 09 uses value and removes it.

docs.title: tests/store_test.cpp (step-04 version)
docs.text:
#include <atomic>
#include <string>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

#include <gtest/gtest.h>

#include "tcpkv/store.hpp"

using tcpkv::Store;

// ------------------------------------------------------------------ single-threaded semantics

TEST(Store, GetMissingKeyReturnsNullopt) {
    Store store;
    EXPECT_FALSE(store.get("nope").has_value());
    EXPECT_EQ(store.size(), 0u);
}

TEST(Store, SetThenGet) {
    Store store;
    store.set("k", "v");
    const auto value = store.get("k");
    ASSERT_TRUE(value.has_value());
    EXPECT_EQ(*value, "v");
    EXPECT_EQ(store.size(), 1u);
}

TEST(Store, SetOverwrites) {
    Store store;
    store.set("k", "one");
    store.set("k", "two");
    EXPECT_EQ(store.get("k").value_or(""), "two");
    EXPECT_EQ(store.size(), 1u);
}

TEST(Store, EmptyAndBinaryValuesRoundTrip) {
    Store store;
    store.set("empty", "");
    const std::string binary("\x00\x01\xff\n", 4);
    store.set("bin", binary);
    ASSERT_TRUE(store.get("empty").has_value());
    EXPECT_TRUE(store.get("empty")->empty());
    EXPECT_EQ(store.get("bin").value_or(""), binary);
}

TEST(Store, DelReportsWhetherKeyExisted) {
    Store store;
    store.set("k", "v");
    EXPECT_TRUE(store.del("k"));
    EXPECT_FALSE(store.del("k"));
    EXPECT_FALSE(store.get("k").has_value());
}

TEST(Store, Exists) {
    Store store;
    EXPECT_FALSE(store.exists("k"));
    store.set("k", "v");
    EXPECT_TRUE(store.exists("k"));
}

TEST(Store, KeysAreSortedAndFilteredByPrefix) {
    Store store;
    store.set("user:2", "");
    store.set("user:1", "");
    store.set("order:9", "");

    const std::vector<std::string> all = {"order:9", "user:1", "user:2"};
    EXPECT_EQ(store.keys(), all);
    const std::vector<std::string> users = {"user:1", "user:2"};
    EXPECT_EQ(store.keys("user:"), users);
    EXPECT_TRUE(store.keys("zzz").empty());
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------ multi-threaded stress
//
// These tests cannot prove the absence of races, but under ThreadSanitizer (cmake --preset tsan)
// any access to the map outside the lock is reported. Without TSan they still catch torn
// values and crashes.

namespace {

constexpr int kKeys = 32;
constexpr int kIterations = 20000;

std::string key_for(int i) { return "k" + std::to_string(i % kKeys); }

// Writer `id` always stores a run of one repeated letter, so a reader can detect a torn value.
std::string value_for(int writer, int i) {
    return std::string(static_cast<std::size_t>(1 + i % 64), static_cast<char>('a' + writer));
}

bool looks_valid(const std::string& value, int writers) {
    if (value.empty() || value.size() > 64) {
        return false;
    }
    const char c = value.front();
    if (c < 'a' || c >= 'a' + writers) {
        return false;
    }
    for (const char x : value) {
        if (x != c) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

}  // namespace

TEST(StoreStress, ConcurrentReadersAndWriters) {
    constexpr int kWriters = 4;
    constexpr int kReaders = 4;

    Store store;
    std::atomic<int> torn{0};
    std::atomic<bool> go{false};
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;

    for (int w = 0; w < kWriters; ++w) {
        threads.emplace_back([&, w] {
            while (!go.load()) {
                std::this_thread::yield();
            }
            for (int i = 0; i < kIterations; ++i) {
                store.set(key_for(i), value_for(w, i));
            }
        });
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < kReaders; ++r) {
        threads.emplace_back([&, r] {
            while (!go.load()) {
                std::this_thread::yield();
            }
            for (int i = 0; i < kIterations; ++i) {
                const auto value = store.get(key_for(i + r));
                if (value && !looks_valid(*value, kWriters)) {
                    ++torn;
                }
                if (i % 1000 == 0) {
                    EXPECT_LE(store.keys("k").size(), static_cast<std::size_t>(kKeys));
                    (void)store.exists(key_for(i));
                }
            }
        });
    }
    go.store(true);
    for (std::thread& t : threads) {
        t.join();
    }

    EXPECT_EQ(torn.load(), 0);
    EXPECT_EQ(store.size(), static_cast<std::size_t>(kKeys));
    for (int i = 0; i < kKeys; ++i) {
        const auto value = store.get(key_for(i));
        ASSERT_TRUE(value.has_value());
        EXPECT_TRUE(looks_valid(*value, kWriters));
    }
}

TEST(StoreStress, SetAndDeleteRace) {
    constexpr int kWriters = 3;

    Store store;
    std::atomic<int> torn{0};
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;

    for (int w = 0; w < kWriters; ++w) {
        threads.emplace_back([&, w] {
            for (int i = 0; i < kIterations; ++i) {
                store.set(key_for(i), value_for(w, i));
            }
        });
    }
    threads.emplace_back([&] {
        for (int i = 0; i < kIterations; ++i) {
            store.del(key_for(i * 7));
        }
    });
    threads.emplace_back([&] {
        for (int i = 0; i < kIterations; ++i) {
            const auto value = store.get(key_for(i));
            if (value && !looks_valid(*value, kWriters)) {
                ++torn;
            }
        }
    });
    for (std::thread& t : threads) {
        t.join();
    }

    EXPECT_EQ(torn.load(), 0);
    // Whatever interleaving happened, the store must still be fully usable.
    for (int i = 0; i < kKeys; ++i) {
        store.set(key_for(i), "final");
    }
    EXPECT_EQ(store.size(), static_cast<std::size_t>(kKeys));
    for (int i = 0; i < kKeys; ++i) {
        EXPECT_EQ(store.get(key_for(i)).value_or(""), "final");
    }
}

The stress tests are designed to maximise interleavings: many threads, a tiny key space (32 keys), no sleeps, and a go flag so all threads start together. The "repeated letter" trick means a torn read (half of one writer's value, half of another's) is detectable by content.

docs.title: 5. Prove the test can fail
docs.text:
This is the most valuable twenty minutes of the step. Comment out the lock in Store::set:

void Store::set(std::string key, std::string value) {
    // std::unique_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    map_[std::move(key)] = std::move(value);
}

Rebuild and run the stress tests three ways:

  1. ctest --preset debug: likely a crash (unordered_map rehash while another thread reads) or torn > 0, but possibly a pass. Races are not deterministic.
  2. ctest --preset asan: probably a heap-use-after-free report from a reader holding a pointer into a bucket that a writer freed.
  3. ctest --preset tsan: a deterministic report naming both threads, both stacks and the two accesses: "WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race ... Write of size 8 by thread T1 ... Previous read of size 8 by thread T5".

Put the lock back. You now know what each tool does and does not promise, which is exactly the question an interviewer asks after "you say it's thread-safe; how do you know?".

docs.title: 7. What you learned, and what to say in an interview
docs.text:
• A data race (two threads, one writes, no synchronisation) is undefined behaviour in C++, not "sometimes wrong". The compiler may assume it does not happen.
  • shared_mutex fits read-heavy workloads. It is not free: it has more internal state than a mutex, writers can starve or be starved depending on the implementation (glibc's pthread_rwlock prefers readers by default), and for very short critical sections a plain mutex is often faster because of less bookkeeping. Measure before choosing.
  • Alternatives you can name: sharded locks (N maps, N mutexes, pick by hash) to cut writer contention; a single std::mutex for simplicity; lock-free hash maps (much harder, rarely worth it); RCU-style copy-on-write for read-mostly data.
  • Never return a reference into a locked structure. Copy under the lock.
  • Testing concurrency: stress tests find crashes; TSan finds races. Both, always.

Interview sentence: "The store is one unordered_map behind one shared_mutex; readers share, writers exclude. I verified it by removing the lock and watching TSan name the race, then putting it back. If profiling showed writer contention I would shard by key hash into sixteen maps with sixteen locks before considering anything lock-free."

docs.title: Step 05. A blocking single-threaded server, tested by hand with nc
docs.text: Time: ~5 hours Week: 3 (Oct 20 – Oct 26) Read first: 08_Networking_Distributed: the accept loop, nc/netcat, ss -tlnp, tcpdump -i lo, what ECONNRESET and EPIPE mean. 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps: strace -f, signals (SIGINT, SIGPIPE). 02_Modern_CPP: fold expressions (used in the logger), std::ostringstream.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
The first thing a client can talk to. One listener, an accept loop, and one Connection object that reads bytes, runs them through the parser, executes commands against the store, and writes replies. Single-threaded and blocking: it serves one client at a time. That is deliberate. Get the request/response path right in the simplest possible shape, then add concurrency in step 06 without changing it.

In plain words: wire the parser (step 03) to the store (step 04) through a socket (step 02).

docs.title: 2. Design
docs.text:
main: listen_tcp(port) -> loop { Socket c = accept(); Connection(c, store).serve(); }

Connection::serve():
   loop:
     n = socket.read_some(buf)        0 -> peer closed -> return
     parser.feed(buf, n)
     out = ""
     for each event in parser:        Command -> out += execute_command(cmd, store)
                                      ParseError -> out += "-ERR ..."; fatal -> close after write
     socket.write_all(out)            one write per read(), so pipelined requests get one reply segment

execute_command is a free function (Command, Store&) -> std::string so it can be tested without a socket and reused by anything else later (it is the only place that knows what a command does). It takes the Command by value so SET can move the key and value into the store without copying a 1 MiB payload.

A tiny logger goes in now too, because a server that prints nothing is undebuggable. It is final: step 09 does not change it.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/log.hpp and src/log.cpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/include/tcpkv/log.hpp and code/src/log.cpp. The interesting bit is the variadic format:

template <class... Args>
std::string format(const Args&... args) {
    std::ostringstream os;
    (os << ... << args);   // C++17 fold expression: os << a << b << c ...
    return os.str();
}

template <class... Args>
void info(const Args&... args) {
    if (level() <= Level::Info) write(Level::Info, format(args...));
}

No format strings means no %s/%d mismatches, which -Wformat cannot catch for std::string arguments anyway. write() builds the whole line, then takes a mutex and emits it with one fwrite, so lines from different threads never interleave. The thread id printed is the kernel tid (gettid()), the same number top -H and gdb show.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/connection.hpp (step-05 version)
docs.text:
#pragma once

#include <string>

#include "tcpkv/protocol.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/socket.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/store.hpp"

namespace tcpkv {

// Runs one parsed command against the store and returns the encoded reply.
// Takes the Command by value so SET can move the key and value into the store without copying.
// Free function so it can be unit-tested without a socket.
std::string execute_command(Command command, Store& store);

// One client connection. Move-only: it owns the Socket.
class Connection {
public:
    Connection(Socket socket, Store& store) noexcept;

    Connection(const Connection&) = delete;
    Connection& operator=(const Connection&) = delete;
    Connection(Connection&&) noexcept = default;
    Connection& operator=(Connection&&) noexcept = default;
    ~Connection() = default;

    // Blocks until the peer disconnects, sends QUIT, or triggers a fatal protocol error.
    void serve();

private:
    // Drains every complete event from the parser into `out`. Returns false when the
    // connection must close after `out` has been sent.
    bool process_events(Parser& parser, std::string& out);

    Socket socket_;
    Store* store_;  // pointer, not reference, so the class stays move-assignable
};

}  // namespace tcpkv

docs.title: src/connection.cpp (step-05 version)
docs.text:
#include "tcpkv/connection.hpp"

#include <optional>
#include <string_view>
#include <system_error>
#include <utility>
#include <variant>
#include <vector>

#include "tcpkv/log.hpp"

namespace tcpkv {

std::string execute_command(Command command, Store& store) {
    switch (command.type) {
        case CommandType::Ping:
            return reply::status("PONG");

        case CommandType::Get: {
            const std::optional<std::string> value = store.get(command.args[0]);
            return value ? reply::bulk(*value) : reply::null();
        }

        case CommandType::Set:
            store.set(std::move(command.args[0]), std::move(command.value));
            return reply::status("OK");

        case CommandType::Del: {
            long long removed = 0;
            for (const std::string& key : command.args) {
                removed += store.del(key) ? 1 : 0;
            }
            return reply::integer(removed);
        }

        case CommandType::Exists: {
            long long present = 0;
            for (const std::string& key : command.args) {
                present += store.exists(key) ? 1 : 0;
            }
            return reply::integer(present);
        }

        case CommandType::Keys:
            return reply::array(store.keys(command.args.empty() ? std::string_view{}
                                                                : std::string_view{command.args[0]}));

        case CommandType::Expire:
        case CommandType::Ttl:
        case CommandType::Stats:
            return reply::error("not implemented yet");  // step 09

        case CommandType::Quit:
            return reply::status("BYE");
    }
    return reply::error("internal error: unhandled command");  // unreachable; keeps -Wreturn-type quiet
}

Connection::Connection(Socket socket, Store& store) noexcept
    : socket_(std::move(socket)), store_(&store) {}

void Connection::serve() {
    const std::string peer = socket_.peer_address();
    log::info("connection from ", peer);

    Parser parser;
    std::vector<char> buffer(16 * 1024);
    std::string out;

    try {
        for (;;) {
            const std::size_t n = socket_.read_some(buffer.data(), buffer.size());
            if (n == 0) {
                break;  // peer closed its side
            }
            parser.feed(buffer.data(), n);

            out.clear();
            const bool keep_open = process_events(parser, out);
            if (!out.empty()) {
                // One write for every reply produced by this read: pipelined clients get
                // one segment back instead of one per command.
                socket_.write_all(out);
            }
            if (!keep_open) {
                break;
            }
        }
    } catch (const std::system_error& e) {
        // ECONNRESET and EPIPE are normal here: the client went away mid-conversation.
        log::info("connection ", peer, " error: ", e.what());
    }

    socket_.shutdown_both();
    log::info("connection ", peer, " closed");
}

bool Connection::process_events(Parser& parser, std::string& out) {
    while (std::optional<ParseEvent> event = parser.next()) {
        if (const ParseError* error = std::get_if<ParseError>(&*event)) {
            out += reply::error(error->message);
            if (error->fatal) {
                return false;
            }
            continue;
        }

        Command& command = std::get<Command>(*event);
        const bool quit = command.type == CommandType::Quit;
        out += execute_command(std::move(command), *store_);
        if (quit) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

}  // namespace tcpkv

Why a switch with every enumerator and no default: GCC's -Wswitch (in -Wall) then warns when a new CommandType is added and not handled. A default: would silence that safety net. The return after the switch exists because the compiler cannot prove the switch is exhaustive for an enum class with an out-of-range value.

docs.title: apps/tcpkv_server.cpp (step-05 version)
docs.text:
// tcpkv_server, step 05: single-threaded, blocking. One client at a time.

#include <charconv>
#include <csignal>
#include <cstdint>
#include <exception>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>
#include <system_error>
#include <utility>

#include "tcpkv/connection.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/log.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/socket.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/store.hpp"

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    std::uint16_t port = 7379;
    if (argc == 3 && std::string_view(argv[1]) == "--port") {
        const std::string_view text = argv[2];
        unsigned value = 0;
        const auto result = std::from_chars(text.data(), text.data() + text.size(), value);
        if (result.ec != std::errc() || result.ptr != text.data() + text.size() || value > 65535) {
            std::cerr << "invalid port\n";
            return 2;
        }
        port = static_cast<std::uint16_t>(value);
    } else if (argc != 1) {
        std::cerr << "usage: tcpkv_server [--port N]\n";
        return 2;
    }

    // A write to a socket whose peer vanished would otherwise kill the process.
    std::signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);

    try {
        tcpkv::Store store;
        tcpkv::Socket listener = tcpkv::Socket::listen_tcp("0.0.0.0", port, 128);
        tcpkv::log::info("tcpkv (single-threaded) listening on port ", listener.local_port());

        for (;;) {
            tcpkv::Socket client = listener.accept();
            tcpkv::Connection connection(std::move(client), store);
            connection.serve();  // blocks until this client leaves: one at a time (fixed in step 06)
        }
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        tcpkv::log::error("fatal: ", e.what());
        return 1;
    }
}

docs.title: 5. Test by hand
docs.text:
In a second terminal:

nc localhost 7379

Type (each line followed by Enter):

PING
SET greeting 11
hello world
GET greeting
GET missing
DEL greeting missing
KEYS
FOO
SET k 2
abc

Expected replies: +PONG, +OK, $11 + hello world, $-1, :1, *0, -ERR unknown command 'FOO', then -ERR value not terminated by newline and nc exits because the server closed the connection (fatal error). The server log shows the connection open and close.

Now the limits of this step, on purpose:

  1. Open two nc sessions. The second one connects (the kernel accepts into the backlog) but gets no reply until the first one quits. That is the single thread. Step 06 fixes it.
  2. Press Ctrl-C on the server. It dies immediately, mid-connection, and nc reports the connection closed. Not graceful. Step 06 fixes that too.
  3. Run strace -f -e trace=accept4,read,sendto,close -p $(pgrep tcpkv_server) while using nc. Watch one read, one sendto per command. Pipelining check: paste three lines at once into nc; you should see one read and one sendto with all three replies.
  4. ss -tlnp | grep 7379 shows the listener; ss -tnp | grep 7379 shows connections.

Optional: python3 -c "import socket; s=socket.create_connection(('127.0.0.1',7379)); s.sendall(b'SET k 3\nabc\nGET k\n'); print(s.recv(100))" gives b'+OK\n$3\nabc\n'.

docs.title: 7. What you learned, and what to say in an interview
docs.text:
• The request/response loop of every TCP server: read, parse incrementally, execute, batch replies, write, repeat; EOF ends it; any socket error ends it.
  • Pipelining falls out of an incremental parser plus "one write per read".
  • Separation: the parser knows bytes, execute_command knows semantics, Connection knows the socket. Each is testable alone.
  • SIGPIPE is the classic way a server dies without a stack trace; ignore it or use MSG_NOSIGNAL. tcpkv does both.
  • Exhaustive switch without default turns "forgot to handle the new command" into a compiler error under -Werror.

Interview sentence: "I built the server single-threaded first so the request path could be verified with nc and strace before any concurrency was added. The connection handler did not change shape afterwards; the thread pool just runs many of them."

docs.title: Step 06. Thread pool, move-only Connection handles, graceful shutdown
docs.text: Time: ~10 hours Week: 3 (Oct 20 – Oct 26) Read first: 04_Concurrency: std::condition_variable and the wait-with-predicate idiom, spurious wakeups, producer/consumer queues, std::atomic<bool> and memory orders (relaxed vs acquire/release), std::thread lifetime rules (a joinable thread's destructor terminates), thread pools, lost wakeups. 02_Modern_CPP: type erasure, std::unique_ptr, lambdas with init-capture ([c = std::move(conn)]), mutable lambdas, SFINAE with std::enable_if_t. 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps: signals and sigaction, async-signal-safe functions, the self-pipe trick. 08_Networking_Distributed: poll() on multiple descriptors.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
Make the server concurrent and make it stop cleanly.

  • A ThreadPool with N worker threads and one queue.
  • A Connection that can be handed to the pool by moving it into a task, and that notices a shutdown flag within a bounded time.
  • A Server class that owns the accept loop and can be stopped from a signal handler.
  • Integration tests that start a real server on an ephemeral port.

In plain words: in step 05 one waiter served the whole restaurant. Now there are N waiters (the pool) and a host at the door (the acceptor) who hands each new table to a free waiter. And when the manager says "we're closing" (SIGINT), the host stops seating, each waiter finishes the order in hand, and everyone goes home. Nobody is left mid-sentence.

docs.title: 2.1 The thread pool
docs.text:
submit(task) --> [ queue (deque<Task>) ] --> worker 1..N: wait(cv) ; pop ; run ; repeat
                        |                       |
                   mutex + work_cv         idle_cv for drain()

Three subtleties that separate a toy pool from a usable one:

  1. The task type must be move-only. std::function requires copyable callables, and a lambda that captured a Connection is not copyable. So MoveOnlyFunction (40 lines of type erasure) is the task type. C++23 has std::move_only_function; we are on C++17.
  2. Stop semantics are explicit. stop() rejects new tasks, drops queued ones (their destructors run, closing sockets), and lets running tasks finish. The destructor calls stop() and joins. For a server this is what you want: queued connections that were never served are closed, not served after shutdown began.
  3. A task that throws must not kill the worker. The worker catches, logs, continues. An uncaught exception in a std::thread calls std::terminate.

docs.title: 2.2 The connection, revisited
docs.text: The step-05 Connection blocked in read() forever. A blocked thread cannot notice a flag. So the loop becomes: poll(fd, 250 ms); on timeout re-check the stop flag; on readable, read(). Shutdown latency is bounded by the poll interval; 250 ms is invisible to humans and costs four wakeups per second per idle connection.

docs.title: 2.3 The server and the self-pipe
docs.text:
signal handler  -->  Server::request_stop():  stop_.store(true); write(wake_pipe, 1 byte)
acceptor loop   -->  poll({listener, wake_pipe_read})  -->  returns at once  -->  loop ends

A signal handler may only call async-signal-safe functions: no malloc, no mutex, no std::cout, no condition_variable::notify. write(2) on a pipe and a lock-free atomic store are allowed. The acceptor polls the pipe's read end alongside the listener, so one byte wakes it immediately instead of after its next timeout. This is the self-pipe trick, older than Linux and still the right answer.

docs.title: 2.4 Ownership through the pipeline
docs.text:
accept()  ->  Socket (acceptor thread)
          ->  Connection{Socket, &store, &stop_flag, config}   (acceptor thread)
          ->  lambda [conn = std::move(connection)]() mutable { conn.serve(); }
          ->  MoveOnlyFunction  ->  queue  ->  worker: task()  ->  ~lambda  ->  ~Connection  ->  ~Socket  ->  close()

The socket is created on one thread and closed on another; no shared_ptr, no reference counting, no manual close. The compiler enforces single ownership at every arrow.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/thread_pool.hpp and src/thread_pool.cpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/include/tcpkv/thread_pool.hpp and code/src/thread_pool.cpp. The two pieces to understand completely:

class MoveOnlyFunction {
public:
    MoveOnlyFunction() noexcept = default;

    template <class F, class = std::enable_if_t<!std::is_same_v<std::decay_t<F>, MoveOnlyFunction> &&
                                                std::is_invocable_r_v<void, std::decay_t<F>&>>>
    MoveOnlyFunction(F&& f)
        : impl_(std::make_unique<Impl<std::decay_t<F>>>(std::forward<F>(f))) {}

    MoveOnlyFunction(MoveOnlyFunction&&) noexcept = default;
    MoveOnlyFunction& operator=(MoveOnlyFunction&&) noexcept = default;
    MoveOnlyFunction(const MoveOnlyFunction&) = delete;
    MoveOnlyFunction& operator=(const MoveOnlyFunction&) = delete;

    void operator()() { impl_->call(); }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return impl_ != nullptr; }

private:
    struct Base {
        virtual ~Base() = default;
        virtual void call() = 0;
    };
    template <class F>
    struct Impl final : Base {
        template <class G>
        explicit Impl(G&& g) : f(std::forward<G>(g)) {}
        void call() override { f(); }
        F f;
    };
    std::unique_ptr<Base> impl_;
};

This is type erasure: any callable F is stored inside an Impl<F> behind a Base pointer, so the pool's queue holds one concrete type. The enable_if stops the template constructor from hijacking the move constructor (is_same check) and from accepting things that are not callable with no arguments.

void ThreadPool::worker_loop() {
    for (;;) {
        Task task;
        {
            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
            work_cv_.wait(lock, [this] { return stopped_ || !queue_.empty(); });
            if (stopped_) {
                return;
            }
            task = std::move(queue_.front());
            queue_.pop_front();
            ++active_;
        }
        try {
            task();
        } catch (const std::exception& e) {
            log::error("task threw: ", e.what());
        } catch (...) {
            log::error("task threw a non-std exception");
        }
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
            --active_;
            if (queue_.empty() && active_ == 0) {
                idle_cv_.notify_all();
            }
        }
    }
}

wait(lock, predicate) is the only correct way to wait on a condition variable: it handles spurious wakeups and the lost-wakeup race (the predicate is checked under the lock before sleeping). The task runs outside the lock, or there would be no concurrency.

Note also the constructor: if creating thread number 5 of 8 throws (EAGAIN), the first four are already running. The constructor catches, stops, joins and rethrows, because otherwise the destructor never runs (the object was never fully constructed) and std::thread's destructor on a joinable thread calls std::terminate.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/connection.hpp (step-06 version)
docs.text:
#pragma once

#include <atomic>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstddef>
#include <string>

#include "tcpkv/protocol.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/socket.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/store.hpp"

namespace tcpkv {

struct ConnectionConfig {
    // How often a blocked handler wakes up to check the shutdown flag. Bounds shutdown latency.
    std::chrono::milliseconds poll_interval{250};
    // Close a connection that has sent nothing for this long. 0 disables the idle timeout.
    std::chrono::seconds idle_timeout{0};
    std::size_t read_buffer_size = 16 * 1024;
};

std::string execute_command(Command command, Store& store);

// One client connection, served by one worker thread for its whole lifetime.
//
// Move-only: it owns the Socket. Dependencies are held as pointers (not references) so the
// class stays move-assignable; a moved-from Connection holds an invalid socket and must not be
// served.
class Connection {
public:
    Connection(Socket socket, Store& store, const std::atomic<bool>& stop_flag,
               ConnectionConfig config) noexcept;

    Connection(const Connection&) = delete;
    Connection& operator=(const Connection&) = delete;
    Connection(Connection&&) noexcept = default;
    Connection& operator=(Connection&&) noexcept = default;
    ~Connection() = default;

    // Blocks until the peer disconnects, sends QUIT, triggers a fatal protocol error,
    // exceeds the idle timeout, or the server asks everyone to stop.
    void serve();

private:
    bool process_events(Parser& parser, std::string& out);

    Socket socket_;
    Store* store_;
    const std::atomic<bool>* stop_;
    ConnectionConfig config_;
};

}  // namespace tcpkv

docs.title: src/connection.cpp (step-06 version)
docs.text:
execute_command is unchanged from step 05. Replace the constructor and serve():

Connection::Connection(Socket socket, Store& store, const std::atomic<bool>& stop_flag,
                       ConnectionConfig config) noexcept
    : socket_(std::move(socket)), store_(&store), stop_(&stop_flag), config_(config) {}

void Connection::serve() {
    using Clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;

    const std::string peer = socket_.peer_address();
    log::debug("connection from ", peer);

    Parser parser;
    std::vector<char> buffer(config_.read_buffer_size);
    std::string out;
    auto last_activity = Clock::now();

    try {
        while (!stop_->load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
            if (!socket_.wait_readable(config_.poll_interval)) {
                if (config_.idle_timeout.count() > 0 &&
                    Clock::now() - last_activity >= config_.idle_timeout) {
                    log::debug("connection ", peer, " idle timeout");
                    break;
                }
                continue;  // timed out: loop re-checks the stop flag
            }

            const std::size_t n = socket_.read_some(buffer.data(), buffer.size());
            if (n == 0) {
                break;  // peer closed its side
            }
            last_activity = Clock::now();
            parser.feed(buffer.data(), n);

            out.clear();
            const bool keep_open = process_events(parser, out);
            if (!out.empty()) {
                socket_.write_all(out);
            }
            if (!keep_open) {
                break;
            }
        }
    } catch (const std::system_error& e) {
        log::debug("connection ", peer, " error: ", e.what());
    }

    socket_.shutdown_both();
    log::debug("connection ", peer, " closed");
}

(process_events is unchanged from step 05. Add #include <chrono> at the top.)

memory_order_relaxed is enough for the stop flag: we only need to eventually see the store, and nothing else is published through it. Connection events moved to debug level so a busy server does not log thousands of lines a second.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/server.hpp (step-06 version)
docs.text:
#pragma once

#include <atomic>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <string>

#include "tcpkv/connection.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/fd.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/socket.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/store.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/thread_pool.hpp"

namespace tcpkv {

struct ServerConfig {
    std::string host = "0.0.0.0";
    std::uint16_t port = 7379;  // 0 = let the kernel choose (tests use this)
    std::size_t threads = 4;
    int backlog = 128;
    // Connections accepted while every worker is busy wait in the pool queue. Beyond this
    // many waiting, new connections get "-ERR server busy" and are closed immediately.
    std::size_t max_pending_connections = 1024;
    ConnectionConfig connection;
};

// Acceptor + fixed thread pool.
//
//   run() thread:        poll(listener, wake_pipe) -> accept -> pool.submit(Connection)
//   worker threads:      Connection::serve() until the client leaves or stop is requested
//   any thread/signal:   request_stop() sets the flag and writes to the wake pipe
//
// The constructor binds and listens, so port() is valid immediately after construction.
class Server {
public:
    Server(ServerConfig config, Store& store);
    ~Server() = default;

    // Not movable: a signal handler may hold a pointer to this object.
    Server(const Server&) = delete;
    Server& operator=(const Server&) = delete;

    // Blocks until request_stop() is called. Workers are joined before it returns.
    void run();

    // Async-signal-safe: an atomic store and one write(2) on a non-blocking pipe.
    void request_stop() noexcept;
    bool stop_requested() const noexcept { return stop_.load(std::memory_order_acquire); }

    std::uint16_t port() const { return listener_.local_port(); }

private:
    void accept_one(ThreadPool& pool);

    ServerConfig config_;
    Store& store_;
    Socket listener_;
    FileDescriptor wake_read_;
    FileDescriptor wake_write_;
    std::atomic<bool> stop_{false};
};

}  // namespace tcpkv

docs.title: src/server.cpp (step-06 version)
docs.text:
#include "tcpkv/server.hpp"

#include <poll.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#include <cerrno>
#include <chrono>
#include <system_error>
#include <thread>
#include <utility>

#include "tcpkv/log.hpp"

namespace tcpkv {

Server::Server(ServerConfig config, Store& store)
    : config_(std::move(config)),
      store_(store),
      listener_(Socket::listen_tcp(config_.host, config_.port, config_.backlog)) {
    // Non-blocking listener: poll() can report readable for a connection that is reset before
    // we call accept(); with a blocking socket that accept() would hang the acceptor thread.
    listener_.set_nonblocking(true);

    std::pair<FileDescriptor, FileDescriptor> wake_pipe = make_pipe();
    wake_read_ = std::move(wake_pipe.first);
    wake_write_ = std::move(wake_pipe.second);
    // The write end must never block: request_stop() may run inside a signal handler.
    set_nonblocking(wake_write_.get(), true);
    set_nonblocking(wake_read_.get(), true);
}

void Server::request_stop() noexcept {
    stop_.store(true, std::memory_order_release);
    const char byte = 1;
    // write(2) is on the async-signal-safe list. If the pipe is full (stop requested many
    // times) the write fails with EAGAIN, which is fine: one byte is enough to wake poll().
    const ssize_t rc = ::write(wake_write_.get(), &byte, 1);
    (void)rc;
}

void Server::run() {
    ThreadPool pool(config_.threads);

    pollfd fds[2]{};
    fds[0].fd = listener_.fd();
    fds[0].events = POLLIN;
    fds[1].fd = wake_read_.get();
    fds[1].events = POLLIN;

    log::info("tcpkv listening on ", config_.host, ":", port(), " with ", pool.size(),
              " worker threads");

    while (!stop_requested()) {
        const int rc = ::poll(fds, 2, 1000);
        if (rc < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) {
                continue;  // a signal arrived; the loop condition sees the stop flag
            }
            throw_system_error(errno, "poll(listener)");
        }
        if (rc > 0 && (fds[0].revents & POLLIN) != 0) {
            accept_one(pool);
        }
        // fds[1] (the wake pipe) needs no handling: stop_ is already set when it fires.
    }

    log::info("shutdown requested: ", pool.pending(), " connections queued");
    // Leaving this scope destroys `pool`: queued connections are dropped (their sockets close),
    // workers return as soon as their Connection::serve() loop observes stop_, then are joined.
}

void Server::accept_one(ThreadPool& pool) {
    Socket client;
    try {
        client = listener_.accept();
    } catch (const std::system_error& e) {
        const int code = e.code().value();
        if (code == EAGAIN || code == EWOULDBLOCK || code == ECONNABORTED) {
            return;  // nothing to accept after all
        }
        if (code == EMFILE || code == ENFILE || code == ENOBUFS || code == ENOMEM) {
            // Out of descriptors or memory. Back off briefly; closing a connection frees one.
            log::warn("accept failed (", e.what(), "); backing off 100 ms");
            std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(100));
            return;
        }
        throw;  // anything else is a bug or a dead listener
    }

    if (pool.pending() >= config_.max_pending_connections) {
        log::warn("rejecting ", client.peer_address(), ": ", pool.pending(), " connections queued");
        try {
            client.write_all(reply::error("server busy, try again later"));
        } catch (const std::system_error&) {
            // The client is gone; nothing to do.
        }
        return;  // `client` closes here
    }

    Connection connection(std::move(client), store_, stop_, config_.connection);
    if (!pool.submit([conn = std::move(connection)]() mutable { conn.serve(); })) {
        log::warn("pool stopped; dropping new connection");
    }
}

}  // namespace tcpkv

Why EMFILE gets a sleep: when the process is out of descriptors, accept fails but the connection stays in the kernel's queue, so poll returns readable immediately, accept fails again, and the acceptor spins at 100% CPU. Sleeping 100 ms turns a spin into a graceful slowdown while connections close and free descriptors. This is a well-known production failure mode (Nginx, HAProxy and Redis all handle it).

docs.title: apps/tcpkv_server.cpp (step-06 version)
docs.text:
Identical to code/apps/tcpkv_server.cpp except: no Metrics, Server server(options.server, store); with two arguments, and no --stats-interval flag (the Options struct, --port, --threads, --host, --idle-timeout, --max-pending, --log-level, --help are all as in the final version). The signal handling is the essential part:

// The only global: the signal handler needs to find the server. An atomic pointer load is
// async-signal-safe (lock-free atomics are allowed in handlers).
std::atomic<tcpkv::Server*> g_server{nullptr};

void on_signal(int /*signum*/) {
    if (tcpkv::Server* server = g_server.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {
        server->request_stop();  // atomic store + write(2): both async-signal-safe
    }
}

void install_signal_handlers() {
    struct sigaction action {};
    action.sa_handler = on_signal;
    ::sigemptyset(&action.sa_mask);
    action.sa_flags = 0;  // no SA_RESTART: let poll() return EINTR so loops re-check the flag
    ::sigaction(SIGINT, &action, nullptr);
    ::sigaction(SIGTERM, &action, nullptr);
    std::signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);
}

and in main:

        tcpkv::Store store;
        tcpkv::Server server(options.server, store);

        g_server.store(&server, std::memory_order_release);
        install_signal_handlers();

        server.run();

        g_server.store(nullptr, std::memory_order_release);
        tcpkv::log::info("tcpkv stopped cleanly");
        return 0;

sigaction, not signal(): signal()'s semantics (one-shot or not, SA_RESTART or not) vary between systems; sigaction says exactly what you get.
