docs.text:
// End-to-end tests: a real Server on an ephemeral port, real sockets, real threads.

#include <algorithm>
#include <atomic>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdint>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <system_error>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

#include <gtest/gtest.h>

#include "tcpkv/log.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/protocol.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/server.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/socket.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/store.hpp"

using tcpkv::Server;
using tcpkv::ServerConfig;
using tcpkv::Socket;
using tcpkv::Store;
namespace reply = tcpkv::reply;

namespace {

constexpr std::size_t kWorkers = 4;

std::string read_exactly(Socket& socket, std::size_t count) {
    std::string out;
    char buf[4096];
    while (out.size() < count) {
        const std::size_t n = socket.read_some(buf, std::min(sizeof buf, count - out.size()));
        if (n == 0) {
            break;
        }
        out.append(buf, n);
    }
    return out;
}

std::string read_until_eof(Socket& socket) {
    std::string out;
    char buf[4096];
    for (;;) {
        std::size_t n = 0;
        try {
            n = socket.read_some(buf, sizeof buf);
        } catch (const std::system_error&) {
            break;  // ECONNRESET counts as "closed" for our purposes
        }
        if (n == 0) {
            break;
        }
        out.append(buf, n);
    }
    return out;
}

// Sends `request` and reads back exactly `expected` bytes; returns what was read.
std::string roundtrip(Socket& socket, const std::string& request, const std::string& expected) {
    socket.write_all(request);
    return read_exactly(socket, expected.size());
}

class ServerFixture : public ::testing::Test {
protected:
    void SetUp() override {
        tcpkv::log::set_level(tcpkv::log::Level::Warn);
        ServerConfig config;
        config.host = "127.0.0.1";
        config.port = 0;  // ephemeral: tests can run in parallel
        config.threads = kWorkers;
        config.connection.poll_interval = std::chrono::milliseconds(20);
        server_ = std::make_unique<Server>(config, store_);
        thread_ = std::thread([this] { server_->run(); });
    }

    void TearDown() override {
        server_->request_stop();
        thread_.join();
    }

    std::uint16_t port() const { return server_->port(); }
    Socket connect() { return Socket::connect_tcp("127.0.0.1", port()); }

    Store store_;
    std::unique_ptr<Server> server_;
    std::thread thread_;
};

}  // namespace

TEST_F(ServerFixture, PingPong) {
    Socket s = connect();
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "PING\n", "+PONG\n"), "+PONG\n");
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, SetGetDelRoundTrip) {
    Socket s = connect();
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "GET k\n", "$-1\n"), "$-1\n");
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, tcpkv::encode_set("k", "hello"), "+OK\n"), "+OK\n");
    const std::string bulk = reply::bulk("hello");
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "GET k\n", bulk), bulk);
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "EXISTS k missing\n", ":1\n"), ":1\n");
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "DEL k missing\n", ":1\n"), ":1\n");
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "GET k\n", "$-1\n"), "$-1\n");
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, ValuesAreBinarySafe) {
    Socket s = connect();
    const std::string value("line one\nline two\r\n\x00\xff tail", 26);
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, tcpkv::encode_set("bin", value), "+OK\n"), "+OK\n");
    const std::string bulk = reply::bulk(value);
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "GET bin\n", bulk), bulk);

    const std::string big(tcpkv::limits::kMaxValueLength, 'B');
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, tcpkv::encode_set("big", big), "+OK\n"), "+OK\n");
    const std::string big_bulk = reply::bulk(big);
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "GET big\n", big_bulk), big_bulk);
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, KeysWithPrefix) {
    Socket s = connect();
    roundtrip(s, tcpkv::encode_set("user:1", "a"), "+OK\n");
    roundtrip(s, tcpkv::encode_set("user:2", "b"), "+OK\n");
    roundtrip(s, tcpkv::encode_set("order:1", "c"), "+OK\n");
    const std::string users = reply::array({"user:1", "user:2"});
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "KEYS user:\n", users), users);
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, UnknownCommandIsAnErrorButKeepsTheConnection) {
    Socket s = connect();
    const std::string error = "-ERR unknown command 'FROB'\n";
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "FROB x\n", error), error);
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "PING\n", "+PONG\n"), "+PONG\n");  // same connection still works
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, NotYetImplementedCommandsReplyWithError) {
    Socket s = connect();
    const std::string error = "-ERR not implemented yet\n";
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "TTL k\n", error), error);
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, OversizedSetHeaderIsFatalForTheConnection) {
    Socket s = connect();
    s.write_all("SET big " + std::to_string(tcpkv::limits::kMaxValueLength + 1) + "\n");
    EXPECT_EQ(read_until_eof(s), "-ERR value too large\n");
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, QuitClosesTheConnection) {
    Socket s = connect();
    s.write_all("QUIT\n");
    EXPECT_EQ(read_until_eof(s), "+BYE\n");
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, PipelinedCommandsGetPipelinedReplies) {
    Socket s = connect();
    const std::string expected = "+PONG\n+OK\n$1\nx\n$-1\n:1\n";
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "PING\nSET a 1\nx\nGET a\nGET nope\nDEL a\n", expected), expected);
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, BlankLinesAndCrLfAreTolerated) {
    Socket s = connect();
    EXPECT_EQ(roundtrip(s, "\r\n\nping\r\n", "+PONG\n"), "+PONG\n");
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, ManyConcurrentClientsSeeTheirOwnWrites) {
    constexpr int kClients = 16;  // more clients than workers: some wait in the pool queue
    constexpr int kOps = 100;
    std::atomic<int> failures{0};
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int c = 0; c < kClients; ++c) {
        threads.emplace_back([&, c] {
            try {
                Socket s = connect();
                for (int i = 0; i < kOps; ++i) {
                    const std::string key = "t" + std::to_string(c) + ":k" + std::to_string(i);
                    const std::string value = "v" + std::to_string(c * 1000 + i);
                    if (roundtrip(s, tcpkv::encode_set(key, value), "+OK\n") != "+OK\n") {
                        ++failures;
                    }
                    const std::string bulk = reply::bulk(value);
                    if (roundtrip(s, "GET " + key + "\n", bulk) != bulk) {
                        ++failures;
                    }
                }
                s.write_all("QUIT\n");
                read_until_eof(s);
            } catch (const std::exception&) {
                ++failures;
            }
        });
    }
    for (std::thread& t : threads) {
        t.join();
    }
    EXPECT_EQ(failures.load(), 0);
    EXPECT_EQ(store_.size(), static_cast<std::size_t>(kClients * kOps));
}

TEST(ServerShutdown, RequestStopUnblocksRunAndClosesClients) {
    tcpkv::log::set_level(tcpkv::log::Level::Warn);
    Store store;
    ServerConfig config;
    config.host = "127.0.0.1";
    config.port = 0;
    config.threads = 2;
    config.connection.poll_interval = std::chrono::milliseconds(20);
    Server server(config, store);
    std::thread runner([&] { server.run(); });

    Socket idle_client = Socket::connect_tcp("127.0.0.1", server.port());
    Socket busy_client = Socket::connect_tcp("127.0.0.1", server.port());
    ASSERT_EQ(roundtrip(busy_client, "PING\n", "+PONG\n"), "+PONG\n");

    const auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    server.request_stop();
    runner.join();  // must return promptly: the wake pipe interrupts poll(), workers see the flag
    const auto elapsed = std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - t0;
    EXPECT_LT(elapsed, std::chrono::seconds(2));
    EXPECT_TRUE(server.stop_requested());

    // Both clients were closed by the server.
    EXPECT_EQ(read_until_eof(idle_client), "");
    EXPECT_EQ(read_until_eof(busy_client), "");
}

TEST(ServerShutdown, RequestStopBeforeRunReturnsImmediately) {
    tcpkv::log::set_level(tcpkv::log::Level::Warn);
    Store store;
    ServerConfig config;
    config.host = "127.0.0.1";
    config.port = 0;
    Server server(config, store);
    server.request_stop();
    server.run();  // loop condition is false on entry
    EXPECT_TRUE(server.stop_requested());
}

1. Two nc sessions at once: both get replies immediately. Four workers, so a fifth nc waits until one of the first four quits (--threads 2 makes this easy to see).
  2. With a session open, press Ctrl-C on the server. Expected log: shutdown requested: 0 connections queued, then tcpkv stopped cleanly; nc reports the connection closed within a quarter of a second. Nothing is killed.

docs.title: 7. What you learned, and what to say in an interview
docs.text:
• Condition variables need a mutex, a predicate and a loop (wait(lock, pred)), or you get lost wakeups and spurious wakeups.
  • std::function needs copyable callables. Type erasure in 40 lines fixes that; so does std::move_only_function in C++23.
  • A blocked thread cannot be told to stop. Bound every blocking call (poll with a timeout) or have a way to wake it (the self-pipe).
  • Signal handlers may only do async-signal-safe things. Atomic store + write. Never lock a mutex, never allocate, never log from one.
  • Shutdown order matters: stop accepting, drop never-served work, let in-flight work finish, join. The scope of pool inside run() encodes that order.
  • Thread-per-connection is a real design with a real limit (N concurrent connections). You know what the next step is (epoll) and why you did not start there.
  • EMFILE on accept is a production incident waiting to happen; back off, do not spin.

Interview sentence: "A Connection is created on the acceptor thread, moved into a lambda, queued, and executed on a worker; the socket closes on whichever thread destroys it, with no reference counting. Shutdown is a self-pipe write from the signal handler; the acceptor leaves its loop, the pool drops queued connections and joins workers that each notice the flag within one poll interval. The integration test asserts that takes under two seconds with clients connected; in practice it is about 20 milliseconds."

docs.title: Step 07. Client library and tcpkv_cli
docs.text: Time: ~6 hours Week: 4 (Oct 27 – Nov 02) Read first: 08_Networking_Distributed: 04_framing_and_protocol_design.md (length-prefixed framing, why a reader needs a buffer), 02_tcp_in_depth.md (Nagle's algorithm, delayed ACK, TCP_NODELAY, "TCP is a byte stream, not a message stream"). 02_Modern_CPP: 10_error_handling_exceptions_optional_expected.md (std::optional for "absent" vs an exception for "failed"), 04_value_semantics_copy_move.md (defaulted move operations), 13_cpp17_features_tour.md (std::from_chars, std::string_view). 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps: 07_debugging_and_profiling_tools_on_linux.md (strace -e trace=network).

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
Give tcpkv a proper client side.

  • A Client class in the library: connect, send a command, parse the reply into a typed Reply, with one method per command (get, set, del, keys, ...).
  • tcpkv_cli, an interactive shell and one-shot tool in the spirit of redis-cli.
  • The integration tests rewritten on top of Client, so they read like the protocol table instead of like byte arithmetic. Raw sockets stay only where a test needs to send something a well-behaved client never would.

In plain words: until now you talked to the server with nc, counting bytes for SET by hand. Now you write the phone handset, not just the exchange. The client is also the code that load_gen (step 08) uses to hammer the server, so it has to be correct before it can be fast.

docs.title: 2.1 The reply model
docs.text:
The server sends six kinds of reply (spec section 3.2). The client turns each into one Reply value:

'+' text      -> Kind::Status   text
"-ERR " text  -> Kind::Error    text  (the "ERR " prefix stripped)
':' n         -> Kind::Integer  integer
'$' len bytes -> Kind::Bulk     text  (binary safe: may hold '\n' and '\0')
"$-1"         -> Kind::Null
'*' n {bulk}  -> Kind::Array    array

A plain struct with a kind tag, not a std::variant. The CLI needs to print every kind and the typed helpers need to check one kind; a tag and three fields make both a one-line switch. A variant would be equally correct and slightly more ceremony at every use.

docs.title: 2.2 Two layers of API, two ways to fail
docs.text:
typed helpers      get() set() del() exists() keys() expire() ttl() stats() quit()
                       |  throw ClientError on "-ERR" or on the wrong reply kind
                       v
execute(tokens) / send_raw(bytes)   -> Reply      (errors are data, never thrown)
                       |
read_reply()  read_line()  read_bulk()  fill()    (buffer_ holds unconsumed bytes)
                       |
Socket::write_all / read_some                     (std::system_error on transport failure)
  • execute() returns error replies as data. The CLI wants to print (error) unknown command 'FOO' and carry on. Throwing for that would be using exceptions for control flow.
  • Typed helpers throw ClientError. A program that calls client.set(k, v) and gets -ERR back has a bug or a broken server; returning a status it will forget to check is how C code loses errors. Your Extrieve code checks every return code by hand; here the type system does it.
  • std::optional for "not found". GET on a missing key is not an error, it is an answer. std::optional<std::string> says that in the signature.
  • Transport failures stay std::system_error from the Socket layer, carrying errno. The caller can tell "the server said no" (ClientError) from "the network broke" (system_error). The CLI uses that difference: the first keeps the session, the second ends it.

docs.title: 2.3 Why the client needs its own buffer
docs.text: TCP delivers a byte stream. One read() may return half a reply, or one and a half replies (if the server batched them). So the client keeps buffer_: bytes received but not yet consumed. read_line() looks for \n in the buffer and only reads from the socket if there is none. read_bulk(n) makes sure n + 1 bytes are buffered, then takes them. Bytes left over after one reply stay in buffer_ for the next. This is the same idea as the server's Parser, simpler because the client always knows what it is waiting for.

docs.title: 2.4 Nagle and TCP_NODELAY
docs.text: The constructor calls socket_.set_nodelay(true). Without it, a request/response client can stall for tens of milliseconds per command. The mechanism: Nagle's algorithm holds back a small segment while earlier data is unacknowledged; the receiver's delayed-ACK timer holds back the ACK hoping to piggyback it on data. Each side waits for the other. Linux's delayed ACK is typically up to 40 ms; on other stacks it is often 200 ms (see 08_Networking_Distributed/02_tcp_in_depth.md). SET with a big value is the classic victim: the client writes the header and value as one buffer here (encode_set builds one string), but any client that does two writes per request will hit it. TCP_NODELAY turns Nagle off. The cost is more small packets, which is what a request/response protocol sends anyway.

docs.title: 2.5 The CLI
docs.text:
tcpkv_cli                       interactive: "tcpkv> " prompt, one command per line
tcpkv_cli -p 7400 set k hello   one-shot: runs one command, prints the reply, exits
  • Inline commands are split on whitespace and sent with execute().
  • SET key value... is special: everything after the key, spaces included, is the value, and it goes through client.set() so the length prefix is computed for you. You never count bytes again.
  • Replies are printed the way redis-cli prints them: (integer) 3, (nil), (error) ..., bulk strings quoted with \n, \t and \xNN escapes so binary values cannot wreck your terminal.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/client.hpp
docs.text:
Final version; it does not change in later steps.

#pragma once

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <optional>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

#include "tcpkv/socket.hpp"

namespace tcpkv {

// Thrown for "-ERR ..." replies and for malformed or unexpected replies.
// Transport failures surface as std::system_error from the Socket layer.
class ClientError : public std::runtime_error {
public:
    using std::runtime_error::runtime_error;
};

struct Reply {
    enum class Kind { Status, Error, Integer, Bulk, Null, Array };
    Kind kind = Kind::Null;
    std::string text;                // Status, Error, Bulk
    long long integer = 0;           // Integer
    std::vector<std::string> array;  // Array
};

// Blocking, single-connection client. Not thread-safe: one Client per thread.
class Client {
public:
    Client(const std::string& host, std::uint16_t port);

    Client(const Client&) = delete;
    Client& operator=(const Client&) = delete;
    Client(Client&&) noexcept = default;
    Client& operator=(Client&&) noexcept = default;
    ~Client() = default;

    std::string ping();
    std::optional<std::string> get(const std::string& key);
    void set(const std::string& key, std::string_view value);
    long long del(const std::vector<std::string>& keys);
    long long exists(const std::vector<std::string>& keys);
    std::vector<std::string> keys(std::string_view prefix = {});
    bool expire(const std::string& key, long long seconds);
    long long ttl(const std::string& key);
    std::string stats();
    void quit();

    // Sends an inline command ("GET key") and returns whatever the server replied,
    // including error replies. Used by the CLI.
    Reply execute(const std::vector<std::string>& tokens);

    // Sends pre-encoded bytes and reads one reply.
    Reply send_raw(std::string_view wire);

private:
    Reply read_reply();
    std::string read_line();
    std::string read_bulk(std::size_t length);
    void fill(std::size_t needed);  // read from the socket until buffer_ holds >= needed bytes
    static Reply expect(Reply reply, Reply::Kind kind);

    Socket socket_;
    std::string buffer_;  // bytes received but not yet consumed
};

}  // namespace tcpkv

Points to be able to defend:

  • Move-only, like Socket. A Client owns a connection. Copying it would mean two objects reading the same byte stream, each consuming the other's replies. The defaulted move operations are noexcept because Socket's and std::string's are, which lets a std::vector<Client> move rather than copy when it grows.
  • expire, ttl and stats are declared now even though the server answers -ERR not implemented yet until step 09. The client is the protocol's other half; like the parser in step 03 it is written complete once. Until step 09 those three helpers throw ClientError, which is the honest behaviour.
  • "Not thread-safe: one Client per thread" is a design decision, not laziness. Sharing one connection between threads needs either a lock around each request/response pair or request ids to match replies. A connection per thread is what load_gen does, and it is what connection pools in real client libraries hand out.

docs.title: src/client.cpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/src/client.cpp. The pieces to understand line by line:

#include "tcpkv/client.hpp"

#include <charconv>
#include <system_error>
#include <utility>

#include "tcpkv/protocol.hpp"

namespace tcpkv {

namespace {

long long parse_integer_or_throw(std::string_view text) {
    long long value = 0;
    const char* begin = text.data();
    const char* end = begin + text.size();
    const auto result = std::from_chars(begin, end, value);
    if (result.ec != std::errc() || result.ptr != end) {
        throw ClientError("malformed integer in reply: '" + std::string(text) + "'");
    }
    return value;
}

}  // namespace

Client::Client(const std::string& host, std::uint16_t port)
    : socket_(Socket::connect_tcp(host, port)) {
    // Request/response protocol: every command is a small write that must leave immediately.
    socket_.set_nodelay(true);
}

std::from_chars rather than atoll or stoll: no locale, no exceptions, no silent acceptance of "12abc" (the result.ptr != end check rejects trailing junk), and no undefined behaviour on overflow (it reports errc::result_out_of_range). The server's parser uses the same function for the same reasons.

The typed helpers are one line each. Two examples:

std::optional<std::string> Client::get(const std::string& key) {
    Reply reply = execute({"GET", key});
    if (reply.kind == Reply::Kind::Null) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    return expect(std::move(reply), Reply::Kind::Bulk).text;
}

void Client::set(const std::string& key, std::string_view value) {
    expect(send_raw(encode_set(key, value)), Reply::Kind::Status);
}

set reuses encode_set from protocol.hpp (step 03), the same function the protocol tests round-trip through the parser. One encoder, tested once, used by both sides.

The reply parser:

Reply Client::read_reply() {
    const std::string line = read_line();
    if (line.empty()) {
        throw ClientError("empty reply line");
    }
    const std::string_view payload(line.data() + 1, line.size() - 1);

    Reply reply;
    switch (line[0]) {
        case '+':
            reply.kind = Reply::Kind::Status;
            reply.text = payload;
            break;
        case '-':
            reply.kind = Reply::Kind::Error;
            // Strip the "ERR " prefix so callers see just the message.
            reply.text = payload.substr(0, 4) == "ERR " ? payload.substr(4) : payload;
            break;
        case ':':
            reply.kind = Reply::Kind::Integer;
            reply.integer = parse_integer_or_throw(payload);
            break;
        case '$': {
            const long long length = parse_integer_or_throw(payload);
            if (length < 0) {
                reply.kind = Reply::Kind::Null;
            } else {
                reply.kind = Reply::Kind::Bulk;
                reply.text = read_bulk(static_cast<std::size_t>(length));
            }
            break;
        }
        case '*': {
            const long long count = parse_integer_or_throw(payload);
            if (count < 0) {
                throw ClientError("negative array length in reply");
            }
            reply.kind = Reply::Kind::Array;
            reply.array.reserve(static_cast<std::size_t>(count));
            for (long long i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
                const std::string header = read_line();
                if (header.empty() || header[0] != '$') {
                    throw ClientError("array element is not a bulk string");
                }
                const long long length =
                    parse_integer_or_throw(std::string_view(header).substr(1));
                if (length < 0) {
                    throw ClientError("null element inside array reply");
                }
                reply.array.push_back(read_bulk(static_cast<std::size_t>(length)));
            }
            break;
        }
        default:
            throw ClientError("malformed reply: '" + line + "'");
    }
    return reply;
}

payload is a string_view into line, which lives until the end of the function, so the view never dangles. Every branch that copies out of it (reply.text = payload) copies before line dies.

The buffer management:

std::string Client::read_line() {
    for (;;) {
        const std::size_t newline = buffer_.find('\n');
        if (newline != std::string::npos) {
            std::string line = buffer_.substr(0, newline);
            buffer_.erase(0, newline + 1);
            if (!line.empty() && line.back() == '\r') {
                line.pop_back();
            }
            return line;
        }
        if (buffer_.size() > limits::kMaxLineLength) {
            throw ClientError("reply line too long");
        }
        fill(buffer_.size() + 1);
    }
}

std::string Client::read_bulk(std::size_t length) {
    if (length > limits::kMaxValueLength) {
        throw ClientError("bulk reply larger than protocol limit");
    }
    fill(length + 1);
    if (buffer_[length] != '\n') {
        throw ClientError("bulk reply not terminated by newline");
    }
    std::string value = buffer_.substr(0, length);
    buffer_.erase(0, length + 1);
    return value;
}

void Client::fill(std::size_t needed) {
    char chunk[16 * 1024];
    while (buffer_.size() < needed) {
        const std::size_t n = socket_.read_some(chunk, sizeof chunk);
        if (n == 0) {
            throw ClientError("connection closed by server");
        }
        buffer_.append(chunk, n);
    }
}

Reply Client::expect(Reply reply, Reply::Kind kind) {
    if (reply.kind == Reply::Kind::Error) {
        throw ClientError(reply.text);
    }
    if (reply.kind != kind) {
        throw ClientError("unexpected reply type from server");
    }
    return reply;
}

Three defensive limits mirror the server's: a reply line longer than 4096 bytes, a bulk longer than 1 MiB, and a bulk not followed by \n are all rejected. A client is also a network parser and also faces untrusted input (a buggy or hostile server, or the wrong port: point the CLI at an HTTP server and see what happens). Without the line limit, read_line would grow buffer_ forever against a peer that never sends \n.

fill(buffer_.size() + 1) means "at least one more byte than I have". It may get far more; the extra stays buffered.

buffer_.erase(0, n) is O(remaining bytes). For a client that reads one reply at a time the remainder is usually empty, so this is fine. The server's Parser uses a read offset and compacts occasionally because it may hold many pipelined requests; know the difference.

docs.title: apps/tcpkv_cli.cpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/apps/tcpkv_cli.cpp. The important parts:

// Prints bytes the way redis-cli does: quoted, with escapes for anything that is not printable.
std::string quoted(std::string_view bytes) {
    static const char kHex[] = "0123456789abcdef";
    std::string out = "\"";
    for (const char c : bytes) {
        const auto u = static_cast<unsigned char>(c);
        switch (c) {
            case '\\': out += "\\\\"; break;
            case '"': out += "\\\""; break;
            case '\n': out += "\\n"; break;
            case '\r': out += "\\r"; break;
            case '\t': out += "\\t"; break;
            default:
                if (u >= 0x20 && u < 0x7F) {
                    out += c;
                } else {
                    out += "\\x";
                    out += kHex[u >> 4];
                    out += kHex[u & 0x0F];
                }
        }
    }
    out += '"';
    return out;
}

The static_cast<unsigned char> matters. char is signed on x86 Linux, so byte 0xFF is -1 as a char; -1 >> 4 is -1 and kHex[-1] reads before the array. The same cast appears in upper() because std::toupper with a negative argument other than EOF is undefined behaviour. This is a C trap you already know; C++ inherited it unchanged.

// Executes one line. Returns false when the session should end.
bool run_line(tcpkv::Client& client, const std::string& line, std::ostream& os) {
    std::istringstream in(line);
    std::string command;
    if (!(in >> command)) {
        return true;  // blank line
    }
    const std::string name = upper(command);
    if (name == "EXIT") {
        try {
            client.quit();
        } catch (const std::exception&) {
            // Leaving anyway.
        }
        return false;
    }

    try {
        if (name == "SET") {
            std::string key;
            if (!(in >> key)) {
                os << "(error) usage: SET key value\n";
                return true;
            }
            std::string value;
            std::getline(in, value);  // the rest of the line, starting with the separating space
            if (!value.empty() && value.front() == ' ') {
                value.erase(0, 1);
            }
            client.set(key, value);
            os << "OK\n";
            return true;
        }

        std::vector<std::string> tokens = split(line);
        tokens[0] = name;
        const tcpkv::Reply reply = client.execute(tokens);
        print_reply(reply, os);
        return !(name == "QUIT" && reply.kind == tcpkv::Reply::Kind::Status);
    } catch (const tcpkv::ClientError& e) {
        os << "(error) " << e.what() << '\n';
        return true;
    } catch (const std::system_error& e) {
        os << "(connection error) " << e.what() << '\n';
        return false;
    }
}

The two catch clauses are the two failure classes from section 2.2: ClientError keeps the session, std::system_error ends it. run_line takes an std::ostream& rather than writing to std::cout directly so it could be unit-tested with an std::ostringstream (exercise 3).

In main, the option loop stops at the first non-option argument, and one-shot mode glues the remaining argv back into one line, so tcpkv_cli set greeting hello world stores hello world:

        if (i < argc) {
            // One-shot mode: rebuild the command line so SET's value keeps its spaces.
            std::string line;
            for (int j = i; j < argc; ++j) {
                if (j != i) {
                    line += ' ';
                }
                line += argv[j];
            }
            run_line(client, line, std::cout);
            return 0;
        }

Port parsing uses std::from_chars into an unsigned and rejects values above 65535 before narrowing to std::uint16_t. Narrowing first would turn -p 70000 into port 4464 silently.

docs.title: tests/integration_test.cpp (step-07 version: Client instead of raw sockets)
docs.text:
The server still takes (config, store); Metrics arrives in step 09. Raw sockets remain for the tests that must send bytes a correct client never sends (oversized header, pipelining, \r\n and blank lines) or must observe the connection closing.

// End-to-end tests: a real Server on an ephemeral port, real sockets, real threads.

#include <algorithm>
#include <atomic>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdint>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <system_error>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

#include <gtest/gtest.h>

#include "tcpkv/client.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/log.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/protocol.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/server.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/socket.hpp"
#include "tcpkv/store.hpp"

using tcpkv::Client;
using tcpkv::ClientError;
using tcpkv::Reply;
using tcpkv::Server;
using tcpkv::ServerConfig;
using tcpkv::Socket;
using tcpkv::Store;

namespace {

constexpr std::size_t kWorkers = 4;

std::string read_exactly(Socket& socket, std::size_t count) {
    std::string out;
    char buf[4096];
    while (out.size() < count) {
        const std::size_t n = socket.read_some(buf, std::min(sizeof buf, count - out.size()));
        if (n == 0) {
            break;
        }
        out.append(buf, n);
    }
    return out;
}

std::string read_until_eof(Socket& socket) {
    std::string out;
    char buf[4096];
    for (;;) {
        std::size_t n = 0;
        try {
            n = socket.read_some(buf, sizeof buf);
        } catch (const std::system_error&) {
            break;  // ECONNRESET counts as "closed" for our purposes
        }
        if (n == 0) {
            break;
        }
        out.append(buf, n);
    }
    return out;
}

class ServerFixture : public ::testing::Test {
protected:
    void SetUp() override {
        tcpkv::log::set_level(tcpkv::log::Level::Warn);
        ServerConfig config;
        config.host = "127.0.0.1";
        config.port = 0;  // ephemeral: tests can run in parallel
        config.threads = kWorkers;
        config.connection.poll_interval = std::chrono::milliseconds(20);
        server_ = std::make_unique<Server>(config, store_);
        thread_ = std::thread([this] { server_->run(); });
    }

    void TearDown() override {
        server_->request_stop();
        thread_.join();
    }

    std::uint16_t port() const { return server_->port(); }
    Client connect() { return Client("127.0.0.1", port()); }
    Socket raw_connect() { return Socket::connect_tcp("127.0.0.1", port()); }

    Store store_;
    std::unique_ptr<Server> server_;
    std::thread thread_;
};

}  // namespace

TEST_F(ServerFixture, PingPong) {
    Client client = connect();
    EXPECT_EQ(client.ping(), "PONG");
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, SetGetDelRoundTrip) {
    Client client = connect();
    EXPECT_FALSE(client.get("k").has_value());
    client.set("k", "hello");
    EXPECT_EQ(client.get("k").value_or(""), "hello");
    EXPECT_EQ(client.exists({"k", "missing"}), 1);
    EXPECT_EQ(client.del({"k", "missing"}), 1);
    EXPECT_FALSE(client.get("k").has_value());
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, ValuesAreBinarySafe) {
    Client client = connect();
    const std::string value("line one\nline two\r\n\x00\xff tail", 26);
    client.set("bin", value);
    EXPECT_EQ(client.get("bin").value_or(""), value);

    const std::string big(tcpkv::limits::kMaxValueLength, 'B');
    client.set("big", big);
    EXPECT_EQ(client.get("big").value_or(""), big);
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, KeysWithPrefix) {
    Client client = connect();
    client.set("user:1", "a");
    client.set("user:2", "b");
    client.set("order:1", "c");
    const std::vector<std::string> users = {"user:1", "user:2"};
    EXPECT_EQ(client.keys("user:"), users);
    EXPECT_EQ(client.keys().size(), 3u);
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, UnknownCommandIsAnErrorButKeepsTheConnection) {
    Client client = connect();
    const Reply reply = client.execute({"FROB", "x"});
    EXPECT_EQ(reply.kind, Reply::Kind::Error);
    EXPECT_NE(reply.text.find("unknown command"), std::string::npos);
    EXPECT_EQ(client.ping(), "PONG");  // same connection still works
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, ErrorRepliesSurfaceAsClientError) {
    Client client = connect();
    // execute() hands back error replies as data; the typed helpers turn them into exceptions.
    EXPECT_EQ(client.execute({"GET"}).kind, Reply::Kind::Error);  // wrong arity
    EXPECT_THROW(client.ttl("has space"), ClientError);           // becomes "TTL has space": arity error
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, NotYetImplementedCommandsReplyWithError) {  // deleted in step 09
    Client client = connect();
    const Reply reply = client.execute({"TTL", "k"});
    EXPECT_EQ(reply.kind, Reply::Kind::Error);
    EXPECT_EQ(reply.text, "not implemented yet");
    EXPECT_THROW(client.stats(), ClientError);
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, OversizedSetHeaderIsFatalForTheConnection) {
    Socket raw = raw_connect();
    raw.write_all("SET big " + std::to_string(tcpkv::limits::kMaxValueLength + 1) + "\n");
    EXPECT_EQ(read_until_eof(raw), "-ERR value too large\n");
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, QuitClosesTheConnection) {
    Socket raw = raw_connect();
    raw.write_all("QUIT\n");
    EXPECT_EQ(read_until_eof(raw), "+BYE\n");
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, PipelinedCommandsGetPipelinedReplies) {
    Socket raw = raw_connect();
    raw.write_all("PING\nSET a 1\nx\nGET a\nGET nope\nDEL a\n");
    const std::string expected = "+PONG\n+OK\n$1\nx\n$-1\n:1\n";
    EXPECT_EQ(read_exactly(raw, expected.size()), expected);
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, BlankLinesAndCrLfAreTolerated) {
    Socket raw = raw_connect();
    raw.write_all("\r\n\nping\r\n");
    EXPECT_EQ(read_exactly(raw, 6), "+PONG\n");
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, ManyConcurrentClientsSeeTheirOwnWrites) {
    constexpr int kClients = 16;  // more clients than workers: some wait in the pool queue
    constexpr int kOps = 100;
    std::atomic<int> failures{0};
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int c = 0; c < kClients; ++c) {
        threads.emplace_back([&, c] {
            try {
                Client client = connect();
                for (int i = 0; i < kOps; ++i) {
                    const std::string key = "t" + std::to_string(c) + ":k" + std::to_string(i);
                    const std::string value = "v" + std::to_string(c * 1000 + i);
                    client.set(key, value);
                    if (client.get(key).value_or("") != value) {
                        ++failures;
                    }
                }
                client.quit();
            } catch (const std::exception&) {
                ++failures;
            }
        });
    }
    for (std::thread& t : threads) {
        t.join();
    }
    EXPECT_EQ(failures.load(), 0);
    EXPECT_EQ(store_.size(), static_cast<std::size_t>(kClients * kOps));
}

TEST(ServerShutdown, RequestStopUnblocksRunAndClosesClients) {
    tcpkv::log::set_level(tcpkv::log::Level::Warn);
    Store store;
    ServerConfig config;
    config.host = "127.0.0.1";
    config.port = 0;
    config.threads = 2;
    config.connection.poll_interval = std::chrono::milliseconds(20);
    Server server(config, store);
    std::thread runner([&] { server.run(); });

    Socket idle_client = Socket::connect_tcp("127.0.0.1", server.port());
    Socket busy_client = Socket::connect_tcp("127.0.0.1", server.port());
    busy_client.write_all("PING\n");
    ASSERT_EQ(read_exactly(busy_client, 6), "+PONG\n");

    const auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    server.request_stop();
    runner.join();  // must return promptly: the wake pipe interrupts poll(), workers see the flag
    const auto elapsed = std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - t0;
    EXPECT_LT(elapsed, std::chrono::seconds(2));
    EXPECT_TRUE(server.stop_requested());

    // Both clients were closed by the server.
    EXPECT_EQ(read_until_eof(idle_client), "");
    EXPECT_EQ(read_until_eof(busy_client), "");
}

TEST(ServerShutdown, RequestStopBeforeRunReturnsImmediately) {
    tcpkv::log::set_level(tcpkv::log::Level::Warn);
    Store store;
    ServerConfig config;
    config.host = "127.0.0.1";
    config.port = 0;
    Server server(config, store);
    server.request_stop();
    server.run();  // loop condition is false on entry
    EXPECT_TRUE(server.stop_requested());
}

Why Client connect() can return by value: Client is move-only and C++17 guarantees copy elision for a returned prvalue, so Client client = connect(); constructs once, in place. That is the same guarantee that lets Socket::connect_tcp return a Socket.

The ManyConcurrentClientsSeeTheirOwnWrites test is now also a test of the client: sixteen Clients on sixteen threads, each with its own buffer, none shared. If you ever make Client share state between instances (a static buffer, say), this test fails under TSan.

Add src/client.cpp to the tcpkv library sources, and the CLI executable:

docs.title: 5. Test by hand
docs.text:
1. Interactive session. Expected output, exactly:

    tcpkv> set greeting hello world
OK
tcpkv> get greeting
"hello world"
tcpkv> get nope
(nil)
tcpkv> exists greeting nope
(integer) 1
tcpkv> keys gr
1) "greeting"
tcpkv> frob
(error) unknown command 'FROB'
tcpkv> ttl greeting
(error) not implemented yet
tcpkv> quit
BYE

  2. Binary value from nc, displayed by the CLI: printf 'SET bin 5\na\tb\x01c\n' | nc -q1 127.0.0.1 7379, then ./build/debug/tcpkv_cli get bin prints "a\tb\x01c".

  3. Nagle off: strace -f -e trace=setsockopt ./build/debug/tcpkv_cli ping shows setsockopt(3, SOL_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, [1], 4) = 0.
  4. One write per command: strace -f -e trace=sendto,read ./build/debug/tcpkv_cli set k v shows one sendto carrying "SET k 1\nv\n" (glibc implements send() with the sendto syscall) and one read on the socket returning "+OK\n" (read_some uses plain read).
  5. Server dies mid-session: start the CLI, Ctrl-C the server, type ping. Expected: (error) connection closed by server (the read saw EOF) or (connection error) ... (the write saw EPIPE/ECONNRESET), depending on timing. Know why both are possible: the first write after the peer closed usually succeeds into the local send buffer, and only the next read or write learns about the RST.
  6. Wrong port: ./build/debug/tcpkv_cli -p 1 ping prints could not connect to 127.0.0.1:1: ...Connection refused and exits 1.

docs.title: 6. Commit
docs.text:
git add -A
git commit -m "Add blocking Client library and tcpkv_cli; port integration tests to Client


- Client: typed helpers per command (optional for GET, ClientError on -ERR), execute() and
  send_raw() return replies as data; buffered reply parser with protocol limits;
  TCP_NODELAY; move-only
- tcpkv_cli: interactive and one-shot modes, SET takes the rest of the line as the value,
  redis-cli style output with escaped binary
- integration tests use Client; raw sockets only for malformed input and close semantics"
git push

docs.title: 7. What you learned, and what to say in an interview
docs.text:
• TCP is a byte stream. Both ends need a buffer and a framing rule. The client keeps unconsumed bytes between replies exactly as the server's parser does.
  • Two failure classes deserve two types. Protocol errors (ClientError) and transport errors (std::system_error) need different handling; one exception type would force string matching.
  • std::optional for absence, exceptions for failure, data for the CLI. Each API layer picks the error style that fits its caller.
  • TCP_NODELAY for request/response protocols, and you can explain the Nagle + delayed-ACK stall from first principles.
  • A client is a parser of untrusted input too. Limits on line and bulk length are not optional on either side.
  • static_cast<unsigned char> before toupper and table lookups because char is signed on x86.

Interview sentence: "The client library is the protocol's other half: a buffered reply parser with the same limits as the server, typed helpers that return std::optional for a missing key and throw ClientError for an error reply, and a lower execute() layer that returns errors as data, which is what the CLI and the load generator use. It is move-only because it owns a connection, not thread-safe by design (one client per thread, like a pool), and it sets TCP_NODELAY because a request/response protocol over Nagle and delayed ACK can stall for the delayed-ACK timeout on every request."

docs.title: Step 08. Load generator, ASan, TSan, UBSan and Valgrind: clean under concurrent load
docs.text: Time: ~8 hours Week: 4 (Oct 27 – Nov 02) Read first: 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA: 08_valgrind_and_sanitizers.md (how each tool works), 04_the_catalogue_of_memory_bugs.md, 09_leaks_and_memory_growth.md, 10_concurrency_crashes_and_heisenbugs.md. 04_Concurrency: 02_data_races_and_why_they_are_ub.md, 07_atomics_and_the_memory_model.md (happens-before), 12_debugging_concurrency_bugs.md. 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps: 03_gcc_and_clang_flags_that_matter.md (-fsanitize=, -fno-omit-frame-pointer), 09_ci_cd_github_actions_and_azure_devops.md (matrix jobs). 02_Modern_CPP: 13_cpp17_features_tour.md (std::from_chars).

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
Make the resume line "Valgrind-clean under concurrent load" true, and provable by anyone in one command.

  • load_gen, a C++ load generator that is also a correctness checker: every GET is verified against the last value that client wrote.
  • tools/load_gen.py, the same contract in 220 lines of Python with no build step.
  • tools/valgrind_check.sh: run the server under Valgrind memcheck, drive it with load_gen, stop it with SIGINT, fail on any error or leak.
  • CI grows from debug, asan (step 01) to debug, release, asan, tsan, ubsan plus a Valgrind job. All green, every push.
  • Zero findings from all four tools. Not "zero findings I could not explain away". Zero.

In plain words: so far the tests show the server does the right thing when you ask it nicely, one thing at a time. This step makes sixteen clients shout at once for ten seconds while three different X-ray machines watch the memory and the threads. If anything is read after it was freed, read before it was written, or touched by two threads without a lock, one of the machines lights up with a stack trace.

docs.title: 2.1 Four tools, four kinds of bug
docs.text:
tool how it works catches typical cost (source) ASan (-fsanitize=address) compiler adds a check before every load/store against shadow memory (1 shadow byte per 8 bytes of app memory); malloc is replaced to add poisoned redzones around blocks and to quarantine freed blocks heap/stack/global buffer overflow, use-after-free, use-after-scope, double free; with LSan (on by default on x86-64 Linux) leaks at exit ~2x CPU (AddressSanitizer docs) TSan (-fsanitize=thread) every memory access and every sync operation (mutex, atomic, thread create/join) is recorded; per-thread vector clocks compute happens-before; two accesses to the same address, at least one a write, with no happens-before between them = data race data races, lock-order inversions (potential deadlock), unsafe calls in signal handlers, destroyed locked mutex 5x–15x CPU, 5x–10x memory (ThreadSanitizer docs) UBSan (-fsanitize=undefined) compiler adds a check at each operation that can be UB signed overflow, shift out of range, misaligned pointer, null deref through a reference, invalid bool/enum load, out-of-bounds index on a fixed array small; usually under 2x Valgrind memcheck runs the unmodified binary on a synthetic CPU (dynamic binary translation); tracks a validity bit for every bit of memory and an addressability bit for every byte invalid reads/writes on the heap, use of uninitialised values (ASan cannot), bad syscall arguments, leaks, open descriptors at exit (--track-fds=yes) "typically 10–50 times slower" (Valgrind manual)

Rules that follow from the mechanisms:

  • ASan and TSan cannot be combined. Both own the shadow memory layout and both replace malloc. Hence separate presets and separate CI jobs.
  • Valgrind cannot run a sanitizer build. Both intercept malloc; run Valgrind on a plain build (relwithdebinfo).
  • Valgrind and ASan overlap but are not redundant. Valgrind sees uninitialised reads and checks the binary you would ship. ASan sees stack and global overflows, which memcheck cannot (it only knows heap block boundaries), and is fast enough to run the whole test suite.
  • TSan only sees races that happen in the run. It does not prove absence. That is why the stress tests and load_gen use a small key space and no sleeps: maximise interleavings.
  • Leak checks happen at exit. Only a clean exit makes "definitely lost" meaningful. A server killed with SIGKILL reports nothing. That is one more reason graceful shutdown (step 06) was not optional.

docs.title: 2.2 load_gen: a benchmark that is also a test
docs.text:
A load generator that only counts replies will happily measure a server that returns the wrong value. So:

client i owns keys  "lg:<run_id>:<i>:0" .. "lg:<run_id>:<i>:<keyspace-1>"
versions[k] = last version client i wrote to key k   (0 = never written)

SET:  version = versions[k] + 1 ; value = "<i>:<k>:<version>:xxxx...x" ; versions[k] = version
GET:  versions[k] == 0  -> reply must be nil
      otherwise         -> reply must equal make_value(i, k, versions[k])
  • Disjoint key ranges mean no other client can legitimately change your keys, so a mismatch is a server bug, never a test race. Shared-key workloads are possible but then you can only check "value is one of the values someone wrote", which is much weaker.
  • The run id (time XOR random_device) makes key names unique per invocation. Without it, a second run against the same server would find the first run's values and count mismatches.
  • The value encodes who wrote it and which version, so a torn read or a stale read is detected and points to the culprit.
  • Exit status 1 on any error or mismatch makes it usable from scripts and CI.

Latency is recorded per operation into a LatencyHistogram (the same lock-free histogram the server uses for STATS in step 09), one per worker thread, merged at the end. Percentiles are bucket upper bounds, so the output says p99<=200 us, which is honest: the histogram cannot know more precisely than its bucket.

docs.title: 2.3 Why the Valgrind check is a script, not a test
docs.text: It needs a real server process (Valgrind wraps the process), a real load (a test with one client exercises one worker), and a real SIGINT (so the shutdown and leak check run). A shell script is the simplest thing that does all three. It uses --error-exitcode=42 so "Valgrind found something" is distinguishable from "the server crashed" (non-zero, not 42) and from "the server was fine but load_gen saw a mismatch".

docs.title: include/tcpkv/metrics.hpp and src/metrics.cpp (step-08 version: the histogram only)
docs.text:
load_gen needs the histogram now; the server's Metrics struct and STATS come in step 09 and are added to these same files. Step-08 header:

#pragma once

#include <array>
#include <atomic>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>

namespace tcpkv {

// Lock-free latency histogram with fixed log-scale buckets in microseconds.
// record() is a single relaxed fetch_add on one counter, so it is cheap enough to call per
// command from every worker thread. Percentiles are bucket upper bounds, i.e. "p99 <= X us".
class LatencyHistogram {
public:
    static constexpr std::size_t kBucketCount = 16;
    // Bucket i (i < 15) counts latencies in (bounds[i-1], bounds[i]] microseconds;
    // the last bucket counts everything above bounds[14].
    static constexpr std::array<std::uint64_t, kBucketCount - 1> kBoundsUs = {
        50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000, 100000, 200000, 500000,
        1000000, 5000000};

    struct Snapshot {
        std::uint64_t count = 0;
        std::uint64_t total_us = 0;
        std::array<std::uint64_t, kBucketCount> buckets{};

        double mean_us() const noexcept;
        // p in (0, 1], e.g. 0.99. Returns the upper bound of the bucket holding that rank.
        std::uint64_t percentile_us(double p) const noexcept;
        void merge(const Snapshot& other) noexcept;
    };

    LatencyHistogram() = default;
    LatencyHistogram(const LatencyHistogram&) = delete;
    LatencyHistogram& operator=(const LatencyHistogram&) = delete;

    void record(std::chrono::nanoseconds latency) noexcept;
    Snapshot snapshot() const noexcept;

private:
    std::array<std::atomic<std::uint64_t>, kBucketCount> buckets_{};
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> count_{0};
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> total_us_{0};
};

}  // namespace tcpkv

src/metrics.cpp for this step is code/src/metrics.cpp without Metrics::render() and without #include <sstream>. The implementation is explained in step 09.

Add src/metrics.cpp to the tcpkv library in CMakeLists.txt.

docs.title: tools/load_gen.cpp
docs.text:
Identical to code/tools/load_gen.cpp. The heart of it:

void run_worker(unsigned id, std::uint64_t run_id, const Options& options,
                std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point deadline, WorkerResult& result) {
    using Clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;

    tcpkv::LatencyHistogram get_hist;
    tcpkv::LatencyHistogram set_hist;
    std::vector<std::uint32_t> versions(options.keyspace, 0);  // 0 = never written
    std::mt19937_64 rng(run_id ^ (static_cast<std::uint64_t>(id) * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15ULL));
    std::uniform_int_distribution<unsigned> key_dist(0, options.keyspace - 1);
    std::uniform_real_distribution<double> op_dist(0.0, 1.0);
    const std::string key_prefix = "lg:" + std::to_string(run_id) + ":" + std::to_string(id) + ":";

    try {
        tcpkv::Client client(options.host, options.port);
        while (Clock::now() < deadline) {
            const unsigned k = key_dist(rng);
            const std::string key = key_prefix + std::to_string(k);

            if (op_dist(rng) < options.read_ratio) {
                const auto t0 = Clock::now();
                const std::optional<std::string> value = client.get(key);
                get_hist.record(Clock::now() - t0);
                ++result.gets;
                if (versions[k] == 0) {
                    if (value.has_value()) {
                        ++result.mismatches;  // we never wrote it; nobody else may have
                    }
                } else if (!value.has_value() ||
                           *value != make_value(id, k, versions[k], options.value_size)) {
                    ++result.mismatches;
                }
            } else {
                const std::uint32_t version = versions[k] + 1;
                const std::string value = make_value(id, k, version, options.value_size);
                const auto t0 = Clock::now();
                client.set(key, value);
                set_hist.record(Clock::now() - t0);
                versions[k] = version;
                ++result.sets;
            }
        }
        client.quit();
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        ++result.errors;
        result.fatal = e.what();
    }
    result.get_latency = get_hist.snapshot();
    result.set_latency = set_hist.snapshot();
}

Things a reviewer will check:

  • Each thread writes only its own WorkerResult (passed by std::ref(results[i])), and main reads them only after join(). join is a synchronisation point (happens-before), so no atomics are needed. TSan agrees.
  • Each thread has its own Client, RNG and histograms. Nothing shared, nothing locked in the measurement loop. A shared std::mt19937_64 would be a data race; a shared one behind a mutex would measure the mutex.
  • The seed mixes the run id with the thread id times the 64-bit golden-ratio constant, so threads do not walk the same key sequence.
  • steady_clock, never system_clock, for intervals. system_clock can jump (NTP).
  • The latency includes the client's own parsing, which is what a user of the server experiences. That is why the README says "client-observed round trip".

main parses options with std::from_chars (with range checks: --clients > 0, --value-size <= 1 MiB, --read-ratio in [0, 1]), starts the threads, joins them, merges, and prints:

tcpkv load_gen: 16 clients, 10 s, keyspace 10000 per client, value 64 B, read ratio 0.80, target 127.0.0.1:7379
total  <N> ops in 10.00 s  ->  <N/10> ops/s
GET    n=<...>  mean=<...> us  p50<=<...> us  p99<=<...> us  p99.9<=<...> us
SET    n=<...>  mean=<...> us  p50<=<...> us  p99<=<...> us  p99.9<=<...> us
errors 0, mismatches 0

docs.title: tools/load_gen.py
docs.text:
Identical to code/tools/load_gen.py. Same contract (disjoint keys, versions, exit 1 on mismatch), its own 80-line client:

    def set(self, key: str, value: bytes) -> None:
        self.sock.sendall(f"SET {key} {len(value)}\n".encode() + value + b"\n")
        kind, payload = self._read_reply()
        if kind != b"+" or payload != b"OK":
            raise ProtocolError(f"unexpected reply to SET: {kind!r} {payload!r}")

Why have it at all: it proves the protocol is easy to speak from another language (an interviewer may ask "how would a Python service use this?"), it needs no build, and it is an independent implementation of the client, so a bug shared by Client and the server (both using encode_set, say) cannot hide from it. It is not a benchmark: CPython's GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so its ops/s measures Python. Its percentiles are exact (it keeps every sample) where the C++ tool's are bucketed.

docs.title: tools/valgrind_check.sh
docs.text:
Identical to code/tools/valgrind_check.sh except that in step 08 the server line has no --stats-interval 0 (that flag arrives in step 09; add it then, to keep the log quiet):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Runs tcpkv_server under Valgrind memcheck, drives it with load_gen, stops it with SIGINT and
# fails if memcheck reported any error or any definite/indirect leak.
#
#   bash tools/valgrind_check.sh build/relwithdebinfo
#
# Build with RelWithDebInfo: optimised enough to finish in CI, with symbols for readable reports.
set -euo pipefail

BUILD_DIR=${1:-build/relwithdebinfo}
PORT=${PORT:-7400}
CLIENTS=${CLIENTS:-8}
DURATION=${DURATION:-5}
VALGRIND_EXIT=42

if ! command -v valgrind >/dev/null; then
    echo "valgrind not installed (sudo apt install valgrind)" >&2
    exit 2
fi

valgrind \
    --quiet \
    --error-exitcode=$VALGRIND_EXIT \
    --leak-check=full \
    --show-leak-kinds=definite,indirect \
    --errors-for-leak-kinds=definite,indirect \
    "$BUILD_DIR/tcpkv_server" --port "$PORT" --threads 4 &
SERVER_PID=$!

# Wait until the server answers PING (Valgrind makes start-up slow).
for _ in $(seq 1 100); do
    if "$BUILD_DIR/tcpkv_cli" -p "$PORT" ping >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        break
    fi
    sleep 0.2
done

if ! "$BUILD_DIR/tcpkv_cli" -p "$PORT" ping >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "server did not come up on port $PORT" >&2
    kill -TERM "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
    wait "$SERVER_PID" || true
    exit 1
fi

set +e
"$BUILD_DIR/load_gen" --port "$PORT" --clients "$CLIENTS" --duration "$DURATION" --keyspace 1000
LOAD_STATUS=$?
set -e

kill -INT "$SERVER_PID"
set +e
wait "$SERVER_PID"
SERVER_STATUS=$?
set -e

echo "load_gen exit: $LOAD_STATUS, server exit: $SERVER_STATUS"
if [ "$SERVER_STATUS" -eq "$VALGRIND_EXIT" ]; then
    echo "valgrind reported errors" >&2
    exit 1
fi
if [ "$SERVER_STATUS" -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "server exited abnormally" >&2
    exit 1
fi
if [ "$LOAD_STATUS" -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "load generator reported errors or mismatches" >&2
    exit 1
fi
echo "valgrind: clean"

Line by line, the parts that matter:

  • set -euo pipefail: stop on the first failing command, on an unset variable, and on a failure anywhere in a pipeline. The script turns -e off (set +e) exactly around the two commands whose exit status it wants to inspect rather than die on.
  • --show-leak-kinds=definite,indirect --errors-for-leak-kinds=definite,indirect: only memory with no pointer to it at exit ("definitely lost") and memory reachable only from such blocks ("indirectly lost") fail the run. "Still reachable" (a global still points at it, as libstdc++ and glibc do for some one-time allocations) and "possibly lost" (an interior pointer exists) are not leaks of your server in the sense the resume means. If "possibly lost" ever shows up with a pthread_create frame, it means a thread was not joined: treat that as a bug anyway.
  • The readiness loop polls with the CLI because Valgrind start-up takes seconds; a fixed sleep would be either flaky or slow.
  • kill -INT then wait gives the server's exit status, which under Valgrind is 42 if memcheck found anything.
  • Clients versus threads. A connection holds a worker for its whole life and a load_gen client stays connected until its deadline. The script starts 4 workers and 8 clients, so 4 clients are served for the whole run and the other 4 wait in the pool queue and do their first operation only at the end. That is still a useful test (it exercises the queue and the queued-connection path at shutdown), but the true concurrency is 4. If you want "8 concurrent clients" to be literally true, change the server line to --threads "$CLIENTS". Everywhere in this course: N concurrent load_gen clients need --threads N or more.

docs.text:
Add the tools option and target:

option(TCPKV_BUILD_TOOLS "Build the load generator" ON)
...
