docs.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml (final version)
docs.text:
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ["v*"]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    name: ${{ matrix.preset }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        preset: [debug, release, asan, tsan, ubsan]
    steps:

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4


      - name: Install toolchain
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ninja-build g++


      - name: Lower ASLR entropy for ThreadSanitizer
        # TSan in GCC 13's runtime aborts with "unexpected memory mapping" on kernels that use
        # 32 bits of mmap randomisation (6.x). 28 bits is the documented workaround.
        if: matrix.preset == 'tsan'
        run: sudo sysctl -w vm.mmap_rnd_bits=28


      - name: Configure
        run: cmake --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}


      - name: Build
        run: cmake --build --preset ${{ matrix.preset }} --parallel


      - name: Test
        run: ctest --preset ${{ matrix.preset }} --parallel 2

  valgrind:
    name: valgrind (memcheck under load)
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4


      - name: Install toolchain
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ninja-build g++ valgrind


      - name: Configure and build (RelWithDebInfo, no tests)
        run: |
          cmake --preset relwithdebinfo -DTCPKV_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
          cmake --build --preset relwithdebinfo --parallel


      - name: Run the server under memcheck while load_gen hammers it
        run: bash tools/valgrind_check.sh build/relwithdebinfo

  format:
    name: clang-format (advisory)
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    # Advisory until the whole tree has been formatted once (step 10 of the build guide
    # removes this line and makes formatting a hard requirement).
    continue-on-error: true
    steps:

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install clang-format
        run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends clang-format
      - name: Check formatting
        run: |
          find include src apps tools tests -name '*.hpp' -o -name '*.cpp' \
            | xargs clang-format --dry-run --Werror
  • fail-fast: false: if TSan fails you still want to know whether ASan passed.
  • The tsan preset is RelWithDebInfo, not Debug: TSan's overhead on an -O0 build makes the stress tests slow enough to hit the 300 s per-test timeout on a CI runner.
  • The test presets set halt_on_error=1 for every sanitizer, so the first report fails the test instead of scrolling past in a log nobody reads.
  • tags: ["v*"] makes the v1.0.0 tag (step 10) run CI too, so the release has a green run.

docs.title: 4. Build and run (WSL Ubuntu 24.04): the exact commands
docs.text: Install once: sudo apt install -y valgrind python3 (Valgrind 3.22 on Ubuntu 24.04).

docs.title: 4.1 Unit and integration tests under each sanitizer
docs.text:
cd ~/dev/tcpkv
cmake --preset asan  && cmake --build --preset asan  && ctest --preset asan
cmake --preset ubsan && cmake --build --preset ubsan && ctest --preset ubsan
cmake --preset tsan  && cmake --build --preset tsan  && ctest --preset tsan

If every TSan test dies at start-up with FATAL: ThreadSanitizer: unexpected memory mapping, your kernel uses more mmap randomisation than GCC 13's TSan runtime supports. Same fix as CI:

sudo sysctl -w vm.mmap_rnd_bits=28   # until the next WSL restart (wsl --shutdown)

Without sudo, turn address-space randomisation off for one command instead. This also covers cmake --build, because gtest_discover_tests runs each test binary at build time to list its tests, and a TSan binary that aborts there fails the build:

setarch $(uname -m) -R cmake --build --preset tsan
setarch $(uname -m) -R ctest --preset tsan

This failure is intermittent (it depends on where the kernel happens to place mappings), so "it passed once" does not mean the setting is right. It is the WSL2 kernel's default of 32 random bits that triggers it, the same as on the GitHub runner.

To re-run only the stress tests many times (races are probabilistic):

ctest --preset tsan -R 'Stress|Concurrent' --repeat until-fail:20

docs.title: 4.2 The whole server under a sanitizer, driven by load_gen
docs.text:
The tests exercise the code paths; this exercises them with sixteen clients at once.

cmake --preset release && cmake --build --preset release      # an uninstrumented load_gen

# ThreadSanitizer server (drop the setarch prefix if you ran the sysctl above)
TSAN_OPTIONS="halt_on_error=1 second_deadlock_stack=1" \
    setarch $(uname -m) -R ./build/tsan/tcpkv_server --port 7400 --threads 16 &
./build/release/load_gen --port 7400 --clients 16 --duration 10 --keyspace 100
kill -INT %1; wait %1; echo "server exit: $?"

# AddressSanitizer + LeakSanitizer server
ASAN_OPTIONS="detect_leaks=1 halt_on_error=1 detect_stack_use_after_return=1" \
    ./build/asan/tcpkv_server --port 7400 --threads 16 &
./build/release/load_gen --port 7400 --clients 16 --duration 10 --value-size 64
kill -INT %1; wait %1; echo "server exit: $?"

# UBSan server
UBSAN_OPTIONS="halt_on_error=1 print_stacktrace=1" \
    ./build/ubsan/tcpkv_server --port 7400 --threads 8 &
./build/release/load_gen --port 7400 --clients 8 --duration 10
kill -INT %1; wait %1; echo "server exit: $?"

Expected each time: load_gen prints errors 0, mismatches 0, the server logs tcpkv stopped cleanly, server exit: 0, and no sanitizer report on stderr. --keyspace 100 for TSan concentrates traffic on few hash buckets; --value-size 64 for ASan makes values heap-allocated (short strings live inside the std::string object, the small-string optimisation, and a use-after-free on them may not touch the heap at all).

docs.title: 4.3 Valgrind
docs.text:
cmake --preset relwithdebinfo && cmake --build --preset relwithdebinfo
bash tools/valgrind_check.sh build/relwithdebinfo
# ... load_gen output ...
# load_gen exit: 0, server exit: 0
# valgrind: clean

Longer and harder: CLIENTS=16 DURATION=30 bash tools/valgrind_check.sh build/relwithdebinfo.

Descriptor leaks are invisible to ASan. Check them by hand once:

valgrind --track-fds=yes --leak-check=full ./build/relwithdebinfo/tcpkv_server --port 7400 --threads 8 &
./build/relwithdebinfo/load_gen --port 7400 --clients 8 --duration 5
kill -INT %1; wait %1

At exit the FILE DESCRIPTORS: N open summary must list only 0, 1, 2 (stdin, stdout, stderr) and, depending on the Valgrind version, Valgrind's own log descriptor. A socket in that list is a leak. While the server runs, ls -l /proc/$(pgrep -f tcpkv_server)/fd | wc -l should return to its idle value after load_gen finishes.

Optional: valgrind --tool=helgrind and --tool=drd are Valgrind's race detectors. They understand pthread mutexes and rwlocks (which std::mutex and std::shared_mutex wrap on glibc) but not C++ atomics, so they report false races on the atomic stop flag and metrics. TSan is the race detector of record for this project; know that the Valgrind ones exist.

docs.title: 4.4 Python load generator
docs.text: python3 tools/load_gen.py --port 7379 --clients 8 --duration 10

docs.title: 5.1 The green path
docs.text:
1. All six presets pass: debug, release, asan, tsan, ubsan via ctest, and valgrind_check.sh prints valgrind: clean.
  2. load_gen against the debug server and the release server: mismatches 0 both times. Note the ops/s difference; you will put release numbers in the README in step 10.
  3. Push. All six CI jobs green. The format job may be red; it is advisory until step 10.

docs.title: 5.2 What sanitizers find in a server like this, and the fix
docs.text:
Every item below is a bug that real thread-per-connection servers ship with. Most are bugs the tcpkv design already avoids; know which line avoids each, because "how did you get it Valgrind-clean?" is a standard follow-up. The reports are abridged to their shape.

1. A plain bool stop flag (TSan: data race).

WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=...)
  Write of size 1 at 0x7b0c... by main thread:
    #0 tcpkv::Server::request_stop() src/server.cpp:...
  Previous read of size 1 at 0x7b0c... by thread T3:
    #0 tcpkv::Connection::serve() src/connection.cpp:...

A non-atomic flag written by one thread and read by another is a data race, which is undefined behaviour, not just "might see a stale value": the compiler may hoist the load out of the loop and spin forever. Fix: std::atomic<bool> (what Server::stop_ is). Relaxed loads are enough for the flag itself (step 06).

2. Returning a reference or string_view into the map (ASan: heap-use-after-free).

const std::string& Store::get_ref(const std::string& key) const {   // WRONG
    std::shared_lock lock(mutex_);
    return map_.at(key).value;
}   // lock released here; the caller still holds a reference into the map

Another worker's SET on the same key assigns a new value (freeing the old buffer), or a DEL erases the node outright. (A rehash alone would not hurt: unordered_map never moves its nodes, so references survive rehashing. Erasure and reassignment are the killers.) The caller's later read hits freed memory:

ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x6060... READ of size 64
    #0 __interceptor_memcpy
    #1 std::string::string(const std::string&)
    #2 tcpkv::execute_command(...)
freed by thread T2 here:
    #0 operator delete(void*)
    #1 tcpkv::Store::set(...)

Fix: copy under the lock and return by value (std::optional<std::string>), which is what Store::get does. This is also why the ASan run uses 64-byte values: with SSO, a 10-byte value is stored inside the std::string object and the bug can go unreported.

3. Capturing the connection by reference in the task (ASan: stack-use-after-return).

Connection connection(std::move(client), ...);
pool.submit([&connection] { connection.serve(); });   // WRONG: accept_one() returns first

The worker runs after accept_one has returned and its stack frame is reused. With detect_stack_use_after_return=1, ASan reports stack-use-after-return; without it you get random crashes. Fix: init-capture by move, [conn = std::move(connection)]() mutable, which is why MoveOnlyFunction exists.

4. Raw new for per-connection state (LSan: direct leak).

ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks
Direct leak of 96 byte(s) in 3 object(s) allocated from:
    #0 operator new(unsigned long)
    #1 tcpkv::Server::accept_one(...)

A path that returns early (busy rejection, an exception from peer_address(), shutdown dropping queued tasks) skips the delete. Fix: no raw new; values and unique_ptr only. The dropped-queued-task path is exactly what ThreadPool::stop() exercises, and the Probe test in thread_pool_test.cpp checks the destructors run.

5. A leaked descriptor (Valgrind --track-fds=yes; ASan is blind to it). A close() missing from one error path of a C-style accept loop. Over days the process reaches ulimit -n and accept fails with EMFILE. Fix: FileDescriptor owns every descriptor (step 02); there is no close() outside FileDescriptor::reset. SOCK_CLOEXEC, accept4 and pipe2(O_CLOEXEC) also stop descriptors leaking into a fork()ed child.

6. Logging from the signal handler (TSan: signal-unsafe call; in production: deadlock).

WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: signal-unsafe call inside of a signal
    #0 malloc
    #1 tcpkv::log::format(...)
    #2 on_signal(int)

If the signal lands while the interrupted thread holds the malloc lock or the log mutex, the handler waits for a lock its own thread holds: a hang on Ctrl-C, once a month. Fix: the handler does an atomic store and one write(2) to the self-pipe (step 06), nothing else.

7. Uninitialised values (Valgrind: "Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s)", or "Syscall param ... points to uninitialised byte(s)"). Typical sources: a member without a default initialiser (bool stopped_;, read by a worker before the constructor body sets it) or a socklen_t len; passed to getpeername without setting it to sizeof storage. ASan does not report these; Valgrind does. Fix: default member initialisers everywhere (bool stopped_ = false;, std::atomic<bool> stop_{false};) and value-initialisation for C structs (sockaddr_storage storage{};, pollfd fds[2]{};).

8. Erasing while iterating (ASan: heap-use-after-free).

for (auto it = map_.begin(); it != map_.end(); ++it) {
    if (is_expired(it->second, now)) map_.erase(it);   // WRONG: ++it on an erased node
}

Fix: it = map_.erase(it); and increment only in the else branch, as in Store::purge_expired (step 09).

9. Signed overflow in number parsing and time arithmetic (UBSan). A hand-written len = len * 10 + (c - '0') overflows on SET k 99999999999999999999 before any range check can run. Fix: std::from_chars, which reports result_out_of_range instead. The same class of bug hides in std::chrono: converting a huge seconds value to the clock's nanoseconds multiplies by 10^9 in a signed 64-bit integer. Step 09 shows the one place in tcpkv where this can happen, the UBSan report it produces, and the fix.

10. Lock-order inversion (TSan: "lock-order-inversion (potential deadlock)"). Thread A takes the store lock then a metrics mutex; thread B (handling STATS) takes the metrics mutex then reads the store. TSan reports it even if the deadlock never happens in the run, because it records lock acquisition order. tcpkv avoids the class entirely: Metrics is atomics only, and no code path holds two locks at once. Say that sentence in interviews.

11. Destroying a joinable std::thread (not a sanitizer finding: std::terminate). If ThreadPool's constructor throws after starting some workers and does not join them, the std::thread destructors call std::terminate and you get terminate called without an active exception and a core dump. Fix: the constructor's catch block stops and joins before rethrowing (step 06). In gdb, bt on the core shows std::thread::~thread.

12. Shutdown races (TSan: data race on a destroyed object, or ASan: use-after-free). The signal handler calls request_stop() on a Server that main has already destroyed. Fix: g_server is cleared (store(nullptr)) before server goes out of scope, and the Server is not movable so the pointer cannot dangle by relocation.

docs.title: 5.3 Break it on purpose (do at least three)
docs.text:
You do not really know a tool until you have seen it catch something you planted. Use a throwaway branch: git switch -c break-it.

  1. Race: in src/connection.cpp add a global std::uint64_t g_commands = 0; in the anonymous namespace and ++g_commands; in process_events next to the command execution. Run ctest --preset tsan -R ManyConcurrentClients. Read the report: the two conflicting accesses with their stacks, the "Location is global 'g_commands'" line, and the stacks that created the two threads. Then make it std::atomic<std::uint64_t> and watch the report disappear. (Test names in ctest are the gtest names, Suite.Test, so -R matches on those, not on file names.)
  2. Use-after-free: add get_ref from item 2 to Store and use it in the GET branch of execute_command. Run the ASan server with load_gen --keyspace 10 --value-size 64 --read-ratio 0.5. Expected: a report within seconds.
  3. Leak: in accept_one, replace the move-capture with auto* conn = new Connection(std::move(connection)); pool.submit([conn] { conn->serve(); });. Run ctest --preset asan -R 'ServerFixture|ServerShutdown' and read the LSan summary. Then add delete conn; after serve(): the tests pass, but the program still leaks whenever a queued task is dropped at shutdown, because a dropped task never runs its body. Prove it: ASan server with --threads 1, three nc sessions, Ctrl-C. That is the argument for RAII, demonstrated.
  4. Uninitialised read: remove = false from bool stopped_ = false; in thread_pool.hpp and run bash tools/valgrind_check.sh build/relwithdebinfo. The pool lives on run()'s stack, so stopped_ starts as stack garbage: memcheck reports "Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s)" in worker_loop. If the garbage happened to be non-zero, the workers also exit immediately and load_gen fails: the same bug, seen from the outside. Neither -Wall -Wextra nor ASan says anything.
  5. Valgrind error exit: confirm the script really fails: plant item 2 in a relwithdebinfo build and run the script. Expected: valgrind reported errors, exit 1.

git switch main && git branch -D break-it when done.

docs.title: 6. Commit
docs.text:
git add -A
git commit -m "Add load generators, Valgrind check and full sanitizer CI


- LatencyHistogram: lock-free log-scale histogram (relaxed atomics), snapshot/merge/percentile
- load_gen: N client threads with disjoint key ranges; verifies every GET against the last
  SET; per-op latency histograms; exit 1 on any error or mismatch
- load_gen.py: same contract in Python, independent client implementation
- valgrind_check.sh: memcheck on the server under load, SIGINT shutdown, fails on errors
  or definite/indirect leaks
- CI: debug/release/asan/tsan/ubsan matrix (tsan with vm.mmap_rnd_bits=28) + valgrind job"
git push

docs.title: 7. What you learned, and what to say in an interview
docs.text:
• Each tool has a mechanism, and the mechanism tells you its blind spots. ASan: shadow memory and redzones, no uninitialised reads, no descriptor leaks. TSan: happens-before over the accesses that actually happened. Valgrind: synthetic CPU, slow, sees uninitialised values and syscall arguments, cannot see stack overflows. UBSan: per-operation checks.
  • They do not combine, so CI runs a matrix. Sanitize the whole build tree, gtest included.
  • A load generator must verify, not just count. Disjoint key ranges plus versioned values turn a benchmark into a correctness test.
  • Leak checking needs a clean exit, which makes graceful shutdown a testability requirement, not a nicety.
  • Most findings in a server come from five patterns: non-atomic flags, references into shared containers, lambda captures by reference into async work, raw new on early-return paths, and unsafe work in signal handlers. tcpkv avoids each by construction, and you can point to the line.

Interview sentence: "Every push runs the full test suite under ASan with LeakSanitizer, TSan and UBSan, and a separate job runs the release-with-debug-info server under Valgrind memcheck while load-generator clients hammer it for five seconds, then stops it with SIGINT so the leak check runs; any error fails the build. The load generator gives each client a disjoint key range and versions every value, so it verifies every GET rather than just counting replies. I planted the classic bugs on a branch (a plain bool stop flag, a reference returned from the store, a raw new in the accept path) to make sure each tool catches them the way I expect."

docs.title: Step 09. Metrics, logging, STATS, TTL, and KEYS revisited
docs.text: Time: ~7 hours Week: 5 (Nov 03 – Nov 09) Read first: 04_Concurrency: 07_atomics_and_the_memory_model.md (memory_order_relaxed and when it is enough), 10_cache_lines_false_sharing_performance.md, 04_shared_mutex_and_readers_writers.md (writer starvation, long readers). 02_Modern_CPP: 13_cpp17_features_tour.md (std::optional, structured bindings), 03_raii_the_core_idea.md (RAII for things that are not memory: a counter guard). 07_Databases_Internals: 13_caching_and_redis.md (TTL, lazy and active expiry, why KEYS is banned in production Redis). 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA: 08_valgrind_and_sanitizers.md (UBSan). 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps: 07_debugging_and_profiling_tools_on_linux.md.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
Make the server observable and finish the protocol.

  • Metrics: atomic counters for connections, commands, bytes, and a latency histogram of command execution time.
  • STATS returns them; the acceptor logs one throughput line every 10 seconds (--stats-interval).
  • EXPIRE and TTL: per-key time-to-live with lazy expiry on read plus a once-a-second purge.
  • connections_active that is correct on every exit path, via a small RAII guard.
  • Revisit the two pieces that already exist: the logger (step 05) and KEYS prefix (steps 04 and 05), this time with their production costs.
  • The -ERR not implemented yet branch disappears. The protocol in 00_spec.md is now fully implemented.

In plain words: a server you cannot see into is a server you cannot run. At 3 AM the first three questions are "is it up, how busy is it, how slow is it", and STATS plus one log line every ten seconds answer all three without a debugger. TTL is the feature that turns a map into a cache: "keep this for 60 seconds, then forget it".

docs.title: 2.1 Metrics: relaxed atomics, no locks
docs.text:
worker threads (N)                      acceptor thread              any client
  ++commands_total  (relaxed)             every 10 s: read           STATS: render()
  ++bytes_in / bytes_out                  commands_total, diff,        reads every counter
  histogram.record(latency)               log ops/s and p99            (relaxed loads)
  connections_active +1 / -1 (guard)
  • Every counter is independent. Nobody needs commands_total ordered relative to bytes_out, and no other data is published through a counter. So memory_order_relaxed is correct: each fetch_add is still atomic (no lost increments), it just does not act as a fence. On x86-64, a relaxed fetch_add and a seq_cst one compile to the same lock xadd; the difference is what the compiler may reorder around it, and on ARM it is a real difference in barriers.
  • No mutex anywhere in Metrics. That rules out a whole bug class: no lock-order inversion with the store lock, no contention between STATS and workers.
  • A STATS snapshot is not atomic as a whole. Counters may move between two loads, so connections_active and commands_total in one reply are not from one instant. For monitoring that is fine; say so rather than pretending otherwise.
  • False sharing, honestly. All counters sit next to each other in one struct, so every worker's fetch_add pulls the same 64-byte cache line into its core in exclusive state. With 4 to 16 workers doing one network round trip per command, the syscalls dominate and this does not show up in a profile. If it ever did, the fixes are alignas(64) per hot counter, or per-thread counters summed on read (what the Linux kernel does with per-CPU counters). Measure first (see 04_Concurrency/10_cache_lines_false_sharing_performance.md).

docs.title: 2.2 The latency histogram
docs.text:
Sixteen buckets on a roughly logarithmic scale, upper bounds in microseconds:

<=50 <=100 <=200 <=500 <=1ms <=2ms <=5ms <=10ms <=20ms <=50ms <=100ms <=200ms <=500ms <=1s <=5s  >5s
  • record() finds the bucket with a linear scan of 15 constants (cheaper than it sounds: the array is 120 bytes, one or two cache lines) and does three relaxed fetch_adds.
  • percentile_us(p) walks the cumulative counts to the bucket holding rank ceil(p * count) and returns its upper bound. So "p99 = 100 us" means "99% of commands took at most 100 us". You cannot report finer than the bucket, and you should not pretend to.
  • Why not store every sample and sort? Memory grows without bound, and a sort under load is not free. HdrHistogram (used by many load tools) is the production-grade version of this idea with configurable precision; ours is the 60-line version.
  • What is measured: server-side execution of the store operation only, from just before execute_command to just after. It excludes parsing, the socket write and network time. Small numbers here and large numbers in load_gen mean the time is in the network, the kernel or the queue for a worker, not in the store. That split is the point of measuring both.

docs.title: 2.3 TTL: lazy expiry plus a periodic purge
docs.text:
struct Entry {
    std::string value;
    std::optional<Clock::time_point> expires_at;   // nullopt = lives forever
};
  • steady_clock, not system_clock. A TTL is an interval. If NTP moves the wall clock back an hour, system_clock would make every key live an hour longer.
  • Lazy expiry: every reader checks is_expired(entry, now) and reports "not found". Readers hold only a shared lock, so they cannot erase; they just do not see the entry.
  • Active expiry: the acceptor calls store.purge_expired() once a second. It takes the exclusive lock and erases every expired entry. Without it, keys that are never read again stay in memory forever.
  • SET clears the TTL (like Redis). EXPIRE k 0 or negative deletes at once. DEL on an expired-but-unpurged key erases it and returns 0 (it was not live).
  • TTL rounds up (std::chrono::ceil), so a key with 0.3 s left reports 1, not 0. 0 would read as "expires now" and is easy to confuse with "no TTL".
  • Clock read outside the lock. Clock::now() is a vDSO call, cheap but not free; doing it before taking the lock keeps the critical section to the hash lookup.

The trade-off to be able to state: purge_expired() is O(total keys) under the exclusive lock, once a second. With a million keys that is a pause of the order of milliseconds during which no writer or reader runs (measure it on your machine before quoting a number). Two better designs:

  1. Sampling (what Redis does): keep a separate set of keys that have a TTL; each cycle, test a small random sample and erase the expired ones; repeat if a large fraction was expired. Bounded work per cycle, probabilistic memory bound.
  2. An expiry index: a min-heap or std::multimap<time_point, key>; purge pops from the front while front <= now. O(expired * log n) per cycle, at the cost of extra memory and of keeping the index in sync on SET/DEL/EXPIRE.

v1.0.0 uses the simple full scan because it is obviously correct and the key counts in the benchmarks are small. Say exactly that.

docs.title: 2.4 KEYS prefix, revisited
docs.text:
KEYS has been there since step 04 (store) and step 05 (command): collect matching keys under a shared lock, release, sort. Two production problems:

  • It is O(n) in the total number of keys, not in the number of matches. An unordered_map has no order, so a prefix query must look at every key.
  • It holds the shared lock for the whole scan. Other readers are unaffected, but every writer waits for the full scan. And libstdc++'s std::shared_mutex on Linux wraps pthread_rwlock_t with glibc's default reader-preferring policy (04_Concurrency/04_shared_mutex_and_readers_writers.md): a steady stream of GETs and KEYS overlapping each other can keep the reader count above zero indefinitely, and a SET waits until there is a gap. Long readers plus reader preference is how writer starvation happens.

This is why Redis documentation warns against KEYS in production and provides SCAN. If asked how you would fix it, in order of effort:

  1. Cap the reply (KEYS prefix LIMIT n) and document it. Cheap, honest.
  2. SCAN cursor [MATCH prefix] [COUNT n]: return up to n keys and a cursor; the client loops. With an unordered_map the cursor can be a bucket index (iterate bucket(i)), which is stable across calls unless a rehash happens; Redis solves that with reverse-binary cursor iteration. Each call holds the lock for a bounded time.
  3. A second, ordered index (std::map<std::string, ...> or a trie) so a prefix query is lower_bound(prefix) then walk while the prefix matches: O(log n + matches). Costs memory and a second structure to update on every write.

docs.title: 2.5 Logging, revisited
docs.text:
The logger arrived in step 05. What matters now that the server is concurrent and long-lived:

  • One line, one fwrite, under one mutex. write() formats the whole line first, then locks only for the fwrite + fflush. Lines from different threads never interleave, and the critical section does no formatting.
  • The level check happens before formatting. log::debug(...) with the level at info costs one relaxed atomic load and a compare; the arguments are never streamed. That is why per-connection events are at debug: a busy server would otherwise spend measurable time formatting and writing thousands of lines a second.
  • localtime_r, not localtime. localtime returns a pointer to a static buffer shared by all threads: a data race TSan would report.
  • gettid() in the line: the kernel thread id, the same number top -H, ps -L and gdb's info threads show. When a worker is stuck, the log tells you which LWP to attach to.
  • stderr, not a file. The process does not manage log files, rotation or disk-full. Under systemd, stderr goes to the journal; in a container, to the container runtime's log driver. This is the twelve-factor convention, and it is what you want in production.
  • Not async-signal-safe. It allocates and locks. Never call it from a signal handler (step 08, item 6).

docs.title: include/tcpkv/metrics.hpp (final version)
docs.text:
Step 08 created the file with LatencyHistogram. Add #include <string> and the Metrics struct below the histogram:

// All server counters live here. Plain atomics with relaxed ordering: each counter is
// independent and we never need one to be ordered relative to another.
struct Metrics {
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> connections_accepted{0};
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> connections_active{0};
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> connections_rejected{0};  // "server busy": queue was full
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> commands_total{0};
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> commands_failed{0};  // parse errors
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> bytes_in{0};
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> bytes_out{0};
    LatencyHistogram command_latency;  // execution time of the store operation, server side
    std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point started_at = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    // "name value\n" per line. This is what the STATS command returns.
    std::string render() const;
};

Metrics is not copyable (atomics and the histogram are not), which is right: there is one set of counters per server, passed by reference.

docs.title: src/metrics.cpp (final version)
docs.text:
#include "tcpkv/metrics.hpp"

#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <sstream>

namespace tcpkv {

double LatencyHistogram::Snapshot::mean_us() const noexcept {
    return count == 0 ? 0.0 : static_cast<double>(total_us) / static_cast<double>(count);
}

std::uint64_t LatencyHistogram::Snapshot::percentile_us(double p) const noexcept {
    if (count == 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    const double clamped = std::min(std::max(p, 0.0), 1.0);
    const auto target = std::max<std::uint64_t>(
        1, static_cast<std::uint64_t>(std::ceil(clamped * static_cast<double>(count))));
    std::uint64_t cumulative = 0;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < kBucketCount; ++i) {
        cumulative += buckets[i];
        if (cumulative >= target) {
            return i < kBoundsUs.size() ? kBoundsUs[i] : kBoundsUs.back();
        }
    }
    return kBoundsUs.back();
}

void LatencyHistogram::Snapshot::merge(const Snapshot& other) noexcept {
    count += other.count;
    total_us += other.total_us;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < kBucketCount; ++i) {
        buckets[i] += other.buckets[i];
    }
}

void LatencyHistogram::record(std::chrono::nanoseconds latency) noexcept {
    const auto signed_us = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds>(latency).count();
    const std::uint64_t us = signed_us < 0 ? 0 : static_cast<std::uint64_t>(signed_us);
    std::size_t index = 0;
    while (index < kBoundsUs.size() && us > kBoundsUs[index]) {
        ++index;
    }
    buckets_[index].fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    count_.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    total_us_.fetch_add(us, std::memory_order_relaxed);
}

LatencyHistogram::Snapshot LatencyHistogram::snapshot() const noexcept {
    // Not atomic as a whole: counters may move between loads. For monitoring that is fine.
    Snapshot s;
    s.count = count_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    s.total_us = total_us_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < kBucketCount; ++i) {
        s.buckets[i] = buckets_[i].load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    }
    return s;
}

std::string Metrics::render() const {
    const auto uptime = std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - started_at;
    const auto latency = command_latency.snapshot();
    std::ostringstream os;
    os << "uptime_seconds " << std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::seconds>(uptime).count()
       << '\n';
    os << "connections_accepted " << connections_accepted.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) << '\n';
    os << "connections_active " << connections_active.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) << '\n';
    os << "connections_rejected " << connections_rejected.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) << '\n';
    os << "commands_total " << commands_total.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) << '\n';
    os << "commands_failed " << commands_failed.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) << '\n';
    os << "bytes_in " << bytes_in.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) << '\n';
    os << "bytes_out " << bytes_out.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) << '\n';
    os << "latency_count " << latency.count << '\n';
    os << "latency_mean_us " << static_cast<std::uint64_t>(latency.mean_us()) << '\n';
    os << "latency_p50_us " << latency.percentile_us(0.50) << '\n';
    os << "latency_p99_us " << latency.percentile_us(0.99) << '\n';
    os << "latency_p999_us " << latency.percentile_us(0.999) << '\n';
    return os.str();
}

}  // namespace tcpkv

Details worth a sentence each:

  • std::max<std::uint64_t>(1, ...) makes percentile_us(0.0) mean "the smallest sample" rather than rank 0, which does not exist.
  • duration_cast<microseconds> truncates: a 49.9 us command lands in the <=50 bucket. Negative durations (impossible with steady_clock, but cheap to guard) clamp to 0.
  • total_us can in theory overflow uint64_t (max about 1.8 x 10^19). At one million commands per second averaging 100 us, it grows by 10^8 per second and wraps after about 5,800 years. Unsigned overflow is defined (it wraps), so even then the mean is wrong, not undefined. Do this arithmetic out loud if asked; it is the kind of check seniors make.
  • render() uses ostringstream because STATS is rare and readability wins. Format is Prometheus-like (name value) so a scraper could be written in ten lines.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/store.hpp and src/store.cpp (final versions)
docs.text:
Identical to code/include/tcpkv/store.hpp and code/src/store.cpp. Compared with step 04: the value type becomes Entry, three methods are added, and every reader checks expiry.

    // ttl <= 0 deletes the key. Returns false if the key does not exist.
    // Takes Clock::duration (not seconds) so tests can use short TTLs; std::chrono::seconds
    // converts implicitly.
    bool expire(const std::string& key, Clock::duration ttl);

    // -2: key does not exist, -1: exists without expiry, otherwise seconds left (rounded up).
    long long ttl(const std::string& key) const;

    std::size_t size() const;  // includes expired-but-not-yet-purged entries

    // Erases expired entries; returns how many were removed.
    std::size_t purge_expired();

private:
    struct Entry {
        std::string value;
        std::optional<Clock::time_point> expires_at;
    };

    static bool is_expired(const Entry& entry, Clock::time_point now) noexcept {
        return entry.expires_at.has_value() && *entry.expires_at <= now;
    }

    mutable std::shared_mutex mutex_;
    std::unordered_map<std::string, Entry> map_;

The new and changed methods:

std::optional<std::string> Store::get(const std::string& key) const {
    const auto now = Clock::now();  // read the clock outside the lock: it is not free
    std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    const auto it = map_.find(key);
    if (it == map_.end() || is_expired(it->second, now)) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    return it->second.value;  // copy made under the lock; the caller owns it afterwards
}

void Store::set(std::string key, std::string value) {
    std::unique_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    Entry& entry = map_[std::move(key)];
    entry.value = std::move(value);
    entry.expires_at.reset();  // like Redis: SET makes the key persistent again
}

bool Store::del(const std::string& key) {
    const auto now = Clock::now();
    std::unique_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    const auto it = map_.find(key);
    if (it == map_.end()) {
        return false;
    }
    const bool was_live = !is_expired(it->second, now);
    map_.erase(it);
    return was_live;
}

bool Store::expire(const std::string& key, Clock::duration ttl) {
    const auto now = Clock::now();
    std::unique_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    const auto it = map_.find(key);
    if (it == map_.end() || is_expired(it->second, now)) {
        return false;
    }
    if (ttl.count() <= 0) {
        map_.erase(it);
        return true;
    }
    it->second.expires_at = now + ttl;
    return true;
}

long long Store::ttl(const std::string& key) const {
    const auto now = Clock::now();
    std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    const auto it = map_.find(key);
    if (it == map_.end() || is_expired(it->second, now)) {
        return -2;
    }
    if (!it->second.expires_at) {
        return -1;
    }
    const auto remaining = *it->second.expires_at - now;
    return std::chrono::ceil<std::chrono::seconds>(remaining).count();
}

std::size_t Store::purge_expired() {
    const auto now = Clock::now();
    std::unique_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(mutex_);
    std::size_t removed = 0;
    for (auto it = map_.begin(); it != map_.end();) {
        if (is_expired(it->second, now)) {
            it = map_.erase(it);  // erase() returns the next valid iterator
            ++removed;
        } else {
            ++it;
        }
    }
    return removed;
}

exists and keys gain the same is_expired check; in keys the structured binding becomes [key, entry] and the step-04 (void)value; goes away. size() deliberately counts expired-but-unpurged entries: it reports memory, not logical contents, and the tests rely on that to observe the purge.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/connection.hpp and src/connection.cpp (final versions)
docs.text:
Identical to the files in code/. execute_command and Connection take a Metrics&:

std::string execute_command(Command command, Store& store, Metrics& metrics);

    Connection(Socket socket, Store& store, Metrics& metrics, const std::atomic<bool>& stop_flag,
               ConnectionConfig config) noexcept;
    ...
    Metrics* metrics_;

The three branches that replace -ERR not implemented yet:

        case CommandType::Expire: {
            const auto ttl = std::chrono::seconds(parse_seconds(command.args[1]));
            return reply::integer(store.expire(command.args[0], ttl) ? 1 : 0);
        }

        case CommandType::Ttl:
            return reply::integer(store.ttl(command.args[0]));

        case CommandType::Stats:
            return reply::bulk(metrics.render());

The active-connection guard, in the anonymous namespace:

// Increments connections_active for the lifetime of serve(), whatever path leaves it.
class ActiveConnectionGuard {
public:
    explicit ActiveConnectionGuard(Metrics& metrics) noexcept : metrics_(metrics) {
        metrics_.connections_active.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    }
    ~ActiveConnectionGuard() { metrics_.connections_active.fetch_sub(1, std::memory_order_relaxed); }
    ActiveConnectionGuard(const ActiveConnectionGuard&) = delete;
    ActiveConnectionGuard& operator=(const ActiveConnectionGuard&) = delete;

private:
    Metrics& metrics_;
};

serve() starts with const ActiveConnectionGuard active_guard(*metrics_);. serve() has five ways out (EOF, QUIT, fatal parse error, idle timeout, stop flag) plus any exception. A manual --active at the end would be wrong on at least one of them. This is RAII for a counter instead of memory, and the ActiveConnectionsDropToZeroAfterClientsLeave test proves it. In C you would write goto out; and hope every path reaches it.

serve() also adds bytes_in after each read and bytes_out after each write. process_events counts parse errors and times each command:

        Command& command = std::get<Command>(*event);
        const bool quit = command.type == CommandType::Quit;
        const auto start = Clock::now();
        out += execute_command(std::move(command), *store_, *metrics_);
        metrics_->command_latency.record(Clock::now() - start);
        metrics_->commands_total.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);

Note quit is read before std::move(command). Reading a moved-from object's members is legal but its value is unspecified for the moved parts; reading first removes the question.

docs.title: include/tcpkv/server.hpp and src/server.cpp (final versions)
docs.text:
Identical to the files in code/. ServerConfig gains:

    // Log a one-line throughput summary this often. 0 disables.
    std::chrono::seconds stats_log_interval{10};

and the constructor becomes Server(ServerConfig config, Store& store, Metrics& metrics). accept_one increments connections_accepted after a successful accept and connections_rejected on the busy path, and passes metrics_ to the Connection. The run loop gains periodic maintenance after the accept:

        const auto now = Clock::now();
        if (now - last_purge >= std::chrono::seconds(1)) {
            const std::size_t purged = store_.purge_expired();
            if (purged > 0) {
                log::debug("purged ", purged, " expired keys");
            }
            last_purge = now;
        }
        if (config_.stats_log_interval.count() > 0 && now - last_stats >= config_.stats_log_interval) {
            log_throughput(now, last_stats, last_commands);
        }

The acceptor's poll has a 1000 ms timeout, so the loop runs at least once a second even with no new connections; that is what makes it a usable timer without a timer thread. Under a flood of connections it runs more often, and the >= checks keep the cadence right.

void Server::log_throughput(std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point now,
                            std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point& last_time,
                            std::uint64_t& last_commands) const {
    const std::uint64_t commands = metrics_.commands_total.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    const double seconds = std::chrono::duration<double>(now - last_time).count();
    const std::uint64_t delta = commands - last_commands;
    const auto rate = seconds > 0 ? static_cast<std::uint64_t>(static_cast<double>(delta) / seconds) : 0;
    log::info("stats: ", delta, " commands in last ", static_cast<std::uint64_t>(seconds), " s (",
              rate, " ops/s), active connections ",
              metrics_.connections_active.load(std::memory_order_relaxed), ", p99 ",
              metrics_.command_latency.snapshot().percentile_us(0.99), " us");
    last_time = now;
    last_commands = commands;
}

The rate is computed from deltas, so it is "ops/s over the last interval", not since start. The p99 is since start (the histogram is cumulative). Know that difference if asked; a windowed p99 would need a histogram per interval, swapped and reset by the acceptor.

The shutdown log line now reports active connections as well as queued ones.

docs.title: apps/tcpkv_server.cpp (final version)
docs.text:
Identical to code/apps/tcpkv_server.cpp. Compared with step 06: a tcpkv::Metrics metrics; next to the Store, Server server(options.server, store, metrics);, the --stats-interval <s> option, and the final log line includes the command count:

        tcpkv::log::info("tcpkv stopped cleanly; ", metrics.commands_total.load(), " commands served");

Declaration order in main matters: store and metrics are declared before server, so they are destroyed after it (reverse order), and every worker that touches them has been joined by then. This is spec section 4.3 in three lines.

docs.text: Add --stats-interval 0 to the server's command line, as in code/. With Valgrind slowing the server, the 10-second line would otherwise appear mid-run and clutter the CI log.

docs.title: tests/store_test.cpp
docs.text:
Add the TTL tests from code/tests/store_test.cpp: ExpireOnMissingKeyReturnsFalse, TtlSemantics, SetClearsTtl, ExpireWithZeroOrNegativeDeletesImmediately, ExpiredKeyIsInvisibleUntilPurged, DelOnExpiredKeyReturnsFalseAndRemovesIt, SetAfterExpiryRevivesKey, and the stress test StoreStress.SetDeleteAndExpireRace. The one that pins down lazy expiry:

TEST(Store, ExpiredKeyIsInvisibleUntilPurged) {
    Store store;
    store.set("k", "v");
    ASSERT_TRUE(store.expire("k", std::chrono::milliseconds(20)));
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(60));

    // Logically gone...
    EXPECT_FALSE(store.get("k").has_value());
    EXPECT_FALSE(store.exists("k"));
    EXPECT_TRUE(store.keys().empty());
    EXPECT_EQ(store.ttl("k"), -2);
    EXPECT_FALSE(store.expire("k", std::chrono::seconds(5)));
    // ...but physically still there until purge runs.
    EXPECT_EQ(store.size(), 1u);
    EXPECT_EQ(store.purge_expired(), 1u);
    EXPECT_EQ(store.size(), 0u);
}

This is why expire takes Clock::duration and not seconds: a 20 ms TTL keeps the test fast. The sleeps are three times the TTL so a slow CI runner does not make it flaky.

docs.title: tests/integration_test.cpp (final version)
docs.text:
Identical to code/tests/integration_test.cpp. Changes from step 07:

  • #include "tcpkv/metrics.hpp", a Metrics metrics_; member in the fixture, config.stats_log_interval = std::chrono::seconds(0); and std::make_unique<Server>(config, store_, metrics_). The two ServerShutdown tests get their own Metrics the same way.
  • Delete NotYetImplementedCommandsReplyWithError.
  • ManyConcurrentClientsSeeTheirOwnWrites also asserts metrics_.connections_accepted == kClients.
  • Three new tests:
TEST_F(ServerFixture, ExpireAndTtl) {
    Client client = connect();
    client.set("tmp", "v");
    EXPECT_TRUE(client.expire("tmp", 1));
    EXPECT_EQ(client.ttl("tmp"), 1);
    EXPECT_EQ(client.ttl("missing"), -2);
    client.set("forever", "v");
    EXPECT_EQ(client.ttl("forever"), -1);
    EXPECT_FALSE(client.expire("missing", 5));

    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(1200));
    EXPECT_FALSE(client.get("tmp").has_value());
    EXPECT_EQ(client.ttl("tmp"), -2);
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, StatsReportsCounters) {
    Client client = connect();
    client.ping();
    client.set("k", "v");
    const std::string stats = client.stats();
    EXPECT_NE(stats.find("commands_total"), std::string::npos);
    EXPECT_NE(stats.find("connections_active 1\n"), std::string::npos);
    EXPECT_GE(metrics_.commands_total.load(), 3u);
    EXPECT_EQ(metrics_.connections_accepted.load(), 1u);
}

TEST_F(ServerFixture, ActiveConnectionsDropToZeroAfterClientsLeave) {
    {
        Client a = connect();
        Client b = connect();
        a.ping();
        b.ping();
        EXPECT_EQ(metrics_.connections_active.load(), 2u);
    }
    // Workers notice EOF on their next poll (<= 20 ms); give them a moment.
    for (int i = 0; i < 100 && metrics_.connections_active.load() != 0; ++i) {
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(10));
    }
    EXPECT_EQ(metrics_.connections_active.load(), 0u);
}

EXPECT_GE(commands_total, 3u), not EQ: STATS itself is counted after its reply is rendered, so the counter may read 2 inside the reply and 3 afterwards. Asserting the exact value would test a timing detail, not behaviour. The last test polls rather than sleeping a fixed time: it passes in 20 ms normally and still passes on a slow TSan runner.

docs.title: A real UBSan finding: EXPIRE with a huge number of seconds
docs.text:
The parser accepts any long long for seconds. execute_command builds std::chrono::seconds(n), and Store::expire takes Clock::duration, which on Linux is nanoseconds in a signed 64-bit integer. The implicit conversion multiplies by 10^9. Any n above about 9.2 x 10^9 (roughly 292 years) overflows: signed overflow, undefined behaviour, triggered by one line from any client. A minimal reproduction of the same conversion, built with -fsanitize=undefined on GCC 13 in WSL, reports:

/usr/include/c++/13/bits/chrono.h:225:38: runtime error: signed integer overflow:
10000000000 * 1000000000 cannot be represented in type 'long long int'
    #0 ... std::chrono::__duration_cast_impl<...>::__cast<long, std::ratio<1l, 1l> >(...)
    #1 ... std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::duration<long, std::ratio<1l, 1000000000l> >, ...>
    #2 ... std::chrono::duration<long, std::ratio<1l, 1000000000l> >::duration<long, std::ratio<1l, 1l>, void>(...)

Reproduce it against the server: run ./build/ubsan/tcpkv_server --port 7400, then ./build/ubsan/tcpkv_cli -p 7400 set k v and ./build/ubsan/tcpkv_cli -p 7400 expire k 10000000000. Negative values overflow the same way (expire k -10000000000), before the ttl <= 0 check can run, because the conversion happens at the call.

None of the tests send such a value, so every CI job is green with this bug present. That is the lesson: sanitizers only judge the inputs you give them. If the parser in your copy of code/ does not already reject these values, fix it in your repo:

// include/tcpkv/protocol.hpp, in namespace limits
// 100 years. Converted to steady_clock's nanoseconds this is ~3.2e18, below INT64_MAX (~9.2e18),
// and adding it to steady_clock::now() (time since boot) cannot overflow either.
inline constexpr long long kMaxExpireSeconds = 100LL * 365 * 24 * 3600;

// src/protocol.cpp, in the CommandType::Expire validation
            long long seconds = 0;
            if (!parse_signed(cmd.args[1], seconds) || seconds > limits::kMaxExpireSeconds ||
                seconds < -limits::kMaxExpireSeconds) {
                return fail("invalid expire seconds", false);
            }

// tests/protocol_test.cpp
// Uses the next_error / next_command helpers already at the top of protocol_test.cpp.
TEST(Parser, ExpireSecondsOutOfRangeIsNonFatal) {
    Parser parser;
    parser.feed("EXPIRE k 10000000000\nEXPIRE k -10000000000\nEXPIRE k 3153600000\nPING\n");
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; ++i) {
        const auto error = next_error(parser);
        ASSERT_TRUE(error.has_value());
        EXPECT_EQ(error->message, "invalid expire seconds");
        EXPECT_FALSE(error->fatal);
    }
    const auto at_limit = next_command(parser);  // exactly 100 years: accepted
    ASSERT_TRUE(at_limit.has_value());
    EXPECT_EQ(at_limit->type, CommandType::Expire);
    const auto ping = next_command(parser);  // the stream is still in sync
    ASSERT_TRUE(ping.has_value());
    EXPECT_EQ(ping->type, CommandType::Ping);
}

Add a row for the limit to docs/PROTOCOL.md and the limits table in your README. Rejecting is better than clamping: a client that sends 10^10 seconds has a bug, and an error tells it so.

Keep this story. "Our sanitizer jobs were green and the server still had UB on one input; here is how I found it and the test that pins it" is a better interview answer than "it is sanitizer-clean".

docs.title: 5. Test by hand
docs.text:
1. TTL from the CLI:

    tcpkv> set session abc
OK
tcpkv> expire session 5
(integer) 1
tcpkv> ttl session
(integer) 5
tcpkv> ttl nope
(integer) -2

    Wait six seconds: get session prints (nil), ttl session prints (integer) -2.

  2. SET clears TTL: expire k 100, set k again, ttl k prints (integer) -1.

  3. Purge: start the server with --log-level debug, run for i in $(seq 1 1000); do echo "SET t$i 1"; echo x; echo "EXPIRE t$i 1"; done | nc -q1 127.0.0.1 7379 >/dev/null. Within two seconds the log shows purged 1000 expired keys (possibly split across two purge cycles).
  4. Throughput log: with --stats-interval 2, run ./build/release/load_gen --port 7379 --clients 8 --duration 10. Every two seconds: stats: <n> commands in last 2 s (<rate> ops/s), active connections 8, p99 <x> us. (connections_active counts connections being served, inside serve(). Start the server with fewer threads than clients and it reports the thread count, not the client count: the rest are queued, not active.) After load_gen ends: active connections 0.
  5. ./build/release/tcpkv_cli stats prints the counters as one quoted bulk string with \n escapes. printf 'STATS\n' | nc -q1 127.0.0.1 7379 shows the raw lines. Run it before and after a load_gen --clients 8 run: connections_accepted grows by the 8 load clients plus one for each of your own STATS connections.
  6. Busy rejection is counted: restart with --threads 1 --max-pending 1. Open three nc sessions in three terminals. The first is served, the second waits in the queue, the third gets -ERR server busy, try again later and is closed. Type QUIT in the first; the second is now served; type STATS in it: connections_rejected 1. (Note that --max-pending 0 would reject every connection, because the check is pending >= max_pending; that is a sharp edge worth a sentence in --help.)
  7. The UBSan finding above: reproduce it, fix it, see the new parser test pass and the expire k 10000000000 command answer (error) invalid expire seconds.

docs.title: 6. Commit
docs.text:
Two commits, because they are two changes and a reviewer should be able to read each:

git add -A
git commit -m "Add Metrics, STATS, TTL and periodic maintenance


- Metrics: relaxed atomic counters (connections, commands, bytes) and a lock-free latency
  histogram of command execution time; STATS renders them as 'name value' lines
- Store: per-key expiry on steady_clock; lazy expiry on read, purge_expired() once a second
  from the acceptor; SET clears TTL; EXPIRE <= 0 deletes; TTL rounds up
- Connection: ActiveConnectionGuard keeps connections_active right on every exit path;
  bytes in/out and per-command latency recorded
- Server: accepted/rejected counters; throughput log line every --stats-interval seconds
- tests: TTL semantics and expire/purge race; integration tests for EXPIRE/TTL, STATS and
  active-connection accounting"

git add -A
git commit -m "Reject EXPIRE seconds beyond 100 years

std::chrono::seconds -> steady_clock::duration multiplies by 1e9 in int64; values above
~9.2e9 overflowed (UBSan: signed integer overflow in chrono.h). Bound the argument in the
parser so it is a non-fatal 'invalid expire seconds' error; add a parser test."
git push

docs.title: 7. Optional extensions (design notes only; not in v1.0.0)
docs.text:
Do none of these before v1.0.0 is tagged. If you do one after, it is a v1.1.0 with its own tests and README section. Each is a good "what would you do next" answer even if never built.

  • SCAN cursor [MATCH prefix] [COUNT n] (section 2.4). Cursor = bucket index; hold the shared lock per call, not per scan; document that keys inserted during a scan may or may not be returned and that a rehash can cause duplicates (Redis's reverse-binary cursor avoids misses across a rehash; read about it before claiming you would implement it).
  • maxmemory with LRU eviction. Account key.size() + value.size() + overhead per entry (overhead: node, hash, std::string headers; estimate it as a constant and say so). Exact LRU needs an intrusive list updated on every GET, which turns reads into writes and kills the shared lock's benefit. Redis uses approximated LRU by sampling; that is the version compatible with a reader lock.
  • Sharded store. N Store shards, shard = hash(key) % N, each with its own shared_mutex. Writers on different shards stop contending. Costs: KEYS and purge must visit every shard (and cannot give a consistent cross-shard snapshot); multi-key DEL takes several locks (lock in shard order to avoid deadlock). Do it only with a benchmark showing writer contention first (perf, off-cpu time in futex).
  • Prometheus endpoint. A second listener that answers GET /metrics with the render() text plus # TYPE lines. Ten lines of HTTP, and the server plugs into every monitoring stack.
  • Windowed percentiles. Two histograms; the acceptor swaps them every interval and logs the old one's p99, so the log line describes the last 10 seconds, not all time.

docs.title: 8. What you learned, and what to say in an interview
docs.text:
• Relaxed atomics are correct for independent counters, and you can say why (no data is published through them) and what they cost (a lock-prefixed instruction on x86, plus cache-line traffic if they share a line).
  • Histograms, not averages. Means hide the tail; p99 is what users feel. Bucketed percentiles are upper bounds; say so.
  • Lazy plus active expiry is the standard TTL design; a full-scan purge is the simple version; sampling or an expiry index is the scalable one.
  • KEYS is O(n) under a lock and stalls writers; SCAN or an ordered index is the fix.
  • RAII for counters: the active-connection guard is correct on every exit path by construction.
  • Green sanitizers prove nothing about inputs you never sent. The EXPIRE overflow passed every CI job until one test sent a big number.

Interview sentence: "Observability is a Metrics struct of relaxed atomics, no locks, and a 16-bucket log-scale latency histogram of command execution time; STATS renders it and the acceptor logs ops/s and p99 every ten seconds. TTL is lazy expiry on read under the shared lock plus a once-a-second purge under the exclusive lock; I know the purge is O(n) and would move to Redis-style sampling or an expiry heap at scale. And one honest story: UBSan in CI was green, but EXPIRE with ten billion seconds overflowed the chrono conversion to nanoseconds; I found it by feeding the UBSan build hostile input by hand, bounded it in the parser, and pinned it with a test."

Read first: 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps: 06_git_properly.md (annotated tags, clean history, what never to commit), 09_ci_cd_github_actions_and_azure_devops.md (badges, release triggers), 07_debugging_and_profiling_tools_on_linux.md (perf stat, taskset). 11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search: 08_resume_linkedin_github.md (projects section, pinned repos), 02_telling_your_story.md. 08_Networking_Distributed: 05_thread_per_connection_and_thread_pools.md (so you can explain the shape of your numbers).

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
Turn a working repository into evidence.

  • A README a reviewer understands in 30 seconds and can verify in 5 minutes: badges, demo, architecture diagram, protocol table, build commands, your benchmark numbers with the machine they came from, "what I would do next".
  • docs/PROTOCOL.md complete; formatting enforced in CI; version 1.0.0 in CMake.
  • An annotated tag v1.0.0 and a GitHub release with notes.
  • The repository public at github.com/khanshaki-r/tcpkv, with a description and topics, pinned on your profile.
  • Resume bullets rewritten so every word is true of the tagged code, with the ops/s and p99 numbers filled in from your own benchmark.

In plain words: steps 01 to 09 built the thing. This step is the shop window and the price tag. A recruiter gives the repo two seconds (is it real? is CI green?), a hiring engineer gives it five minutes (does the README make sense? do the tests exist? is the code clean?), and an interviewer gives it an hour of questions. This step is for all three.

time who what they look at what must be true 2 s recruiter repo exists, pinned, green badge, description public, CI green on main, one-line description 30 s engineer README top: what it is, demo, diagram first screen explains the project without scrolling 5 min engineer src/server.cpp, src/store.cpp, tests/, .github/workflows/ci.yml, commit history no TODO in hot paths, tests named after behaviour, sanitizer jobs real, commits with messages 1 h interviewer any line they pick you can explain why that line exists

docs.title: 3.1 README.md (final)
docs.text:
Start from code/README.md; it follows the outline in 00_spec.md section 9. Keep its structure, rewrite the prose in your own words (an interviewer may quote it back to you), and fill in the benchmark section from section 4 below. The parts that carry the most weight:

Badges (line 3 onwards). The CI badge URL is derived from the workflow file name, so it works as soon as the repo is public:

[![CI](https://github.com/khanshaki-r/tcpkv/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/khanshaki-r/tcpkv/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
![C++17](https://img.shields.io/badge/C%2B%2B-17-informational)
![Platform: Linux](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Linux-lightgrey)

The CI badge shows the status of the latest run on the default branch. A red badge on a pinned repo is worse than no badge. If CI goes red after you are public, fixing it is the first task of the day.

Demo session directly under the description: ten lines of tcpkv_cli output, copied from a real run (not typed from memory; the output format must match the code).

Architecture diagram. ASCII, so it renders everywhere and diffs in git:

                 +-----------------------------------------------------------+
   clients       |                      tcpkv_server                         |
                 |                                                           |
  nc / cli ----->|  acceptor thread                    worker pool (N)       |
  load_gen ----->|  poll(listener, wake_pipe)          +-----------------+   |
  Client lib --->|    accept4()                        | Connection      |   |
                 |    Connection{Socket}  --submit-->  |  poll/read      |   |
                 |    pool.submit(move)                |  Parser.feed    |   |
                 |                                     |  execute -------+---+---> Store
                 |  every 1 s: store.purge_expired()   |  write_all      |   |     unordered_map
                 |  every 10 s: log ops/s, p99         +-----------------+   |     + shared_mutex
                 |                                                           |
   SIGINT/TERM ->|  request_stop(): atomic flag + write(wake_pipe)           |
                 +-----------------------------------------------------------+

followed by the five design bullets (one connection per worker, shared_mutex store, RAII, MoveOnlyFunction, self-pipe shutdown). Each bullet names a trade-off, not just a feature: "simple, debuggable, fast enough for a few thousand connections; epoll would be next".

Protocol table and a link to docs/PROTOCOL.md. If you added the EXPIRE bound from step 09, add it to the limits sentence.

Build, test, sanitizers, Valgrind: copy-pasteable commands, exactly the ones CI runs.

Benchmark: section 4 of this step.

What I would do next: epoll event loop, persistence (point to minidb if it exists by then; otherwise say "append-only log with snapshots"), replication, sharded locks if profiling shows writer contention. Four bullets, each one a conversation you are ready to have (see INTERVIEW_TALKING_POINTS.md).

docs.title: 3.2 docs/PROTOCOL.md
docs.text: Identical to code/docs/PROTOCOL.md: transport, encoding, request grammar, every command with its reply, error list split into fatal and non-fatal, limits, a session example. Read it once against src/protocol.cpp line by line. Every error message string in the doc must appear verbatim in the code and in a test. A protocol document that disagrees with the code is worse than none.

docs.title: 3.3 CMakeLists.txt
docs.text:
project(tcpkv
    VERSION 1.0.0
    DESCRIPTION "Multithreaded TCP key-value server"
    LANGUAGES CXX)

docs.title: 3.4 .github/workflows/ci.yml: formatting becomes required
docs.text:
Format the whole tree once, commit that alone, then delete the continue-on-error: true line (and the comment above it) from the format job:

find include src apps tools tests -name '*.hpp' -o -name '*.cpp' | xargs clang-format -i
git diff --stat            # whitespace only; read it anyway
cmake --build --preset debug && ctest --preset debug
git commit -am "Apply clang-format to the whole tree (no functional change)"

A formatting-only commit keeps git blame useful: reviewers can skip it (git blame --ignore-rev <sha>), and it never hides a logic change.

docs.title: 3.5 Check the repository for things that must not be public
docs.text:
Before the visibility switch, not after:

git log --all --oneline | wc -l                         # history you are about to publish
git log --all -p | grep -inE 'password|secret|token|api[_-]?key|BEGIN (RSA|OPENSSH)' | head
git log --all --format='%an <%ae>' | sort -u            # author identities
git ls-files | grep -vE '^(include|src|apps|tools|tests|docs|\.github)/|^(CMakeLists.txt|CMakePresets.json|README.md|LICENSE|\.gitignore|\.clang-format)$'
  • Nothing from your employer. No Extrieve code, file names, table names, client names, hostnames or log excerpts, not even in a commit message or a test fixture. tcpkv is written from scratch; keep it provably so. This is also a contractual point: read your employment agreement's IP clause, and if in doubt keep the repo strictly generic (it is).
  • Author identity. Commits should carry the name and email you want recruiters to see (git config user.name, git config user.email). GitHub can hide your email with the @users.noreply.github.com address (Settings, Emails).
  • The last command lists tracked files outside the expected layout: build directories, core dumps, .vscode/ or vgcore.* files must not be there (.gitignore from step 01 covers them; check anyway).

If a secret ever was committed, deleting it in a new commit is not enough: rewrite history (git filter-repo) and rotate the secret. For this project there should be nothing to find.

docs.title: 4. Benchmark: the procedure and the table
docs.text: Numbers on a resume must be reproducible by you on demand and labelled with where they came from. The procedure below is what you will describe if asked "how did you measure that?".

docs.title: 4.1 Record the machine
docs.text:
lscpu | grep -E 'Model name|^CPU\(s\)|Thread|Core|Socket'
nproc
free -h | head -2
uname -r                      # a "-microsoft-standard-WSL2" suffix means WSL2
cat /etc/os-release | grep PRETTY_NAME
g++ --version | head -1

Your WSL is limited to 4 CPUs and 3 GB by .wslconfig. Say so in the README: "WSL2 on Windows 11, 4 vCPUs (Intel/AMD ), 3 GB RAM, kernel , GCC 13.3, release build". Numbers from a VM on a laptop are fine for a portfolio as long as they are labelled; they are wrong only when presented as something else.

docs.title: 4.2 Run
docs.text:
cd ~/dev/tcpkv
cmake --preset release && cmake --build --preset release

# Terminal 1: server on cores 0-1, logging quiet
taskset -c 0,1 ./build/release/tcpkv_server --port 7379 --threads 8 --stats-interval 0 --log-level warn

# Terminal 2: load generator on cores 2-3; 5 s warm-up run first, discard it
taskset -c 2,3 ./build/release/load_gen --port 7379 --clients 8 --duration 5
for run in 1 2 3; do
  taskset -c 2,3 ./build/release/load_gen --port 7379 --clients 8 --duration 20 \
      --value-size 64 --read-ratio 0.8 | tee -a bench_8c_4t_64b.txt
done
./build/release/tcpkv_cli stats           # server-side latency, for the note under the table
  • taskset gives server and load generator separate cores. On 4 vCPUs, sharing cores means the load generator steals CPU from the server and you measure both. Note the split in the README.
  • Three runs, report the median of ops/s and of each percentile. If the three differ by more than about 10%, something else is running (Windows Update, the IDE indexer); find it and rerun.
  • Repeat for each row of the table, restarting the server with that row's --threads (the commands above are for the 8 clients / 8 threads row). Restarting also resets STATS to that row. For 8 or 16 threads on a 2-core server allocation, say so: more threads than cores is a legitimate configuration for a blocking server (threads mostly wait on I/O), but the reader should know.
  • Do not tune for the benchmark. No -march=native, no special flags beyond the release preset. The point is "this is what the code does".

docs.title: 4.3 The table (template)
docs.text:
Copy into the README and fill from your runs. Leave a row out rather than invent it.

## Benchmark

Measured on: WSL2 on Windows 11, <CPU model>, 4 vCPUs, 3 GB RAM, kernel <uname -r>, GCC 13.3,
`release` preset. Server pinned to 2 vCPUs, `load_gen` to the other 2, loopback TCP.
Each row is the median of three 20-second runs after a 5-second warm-up. Value size 64 B
unless stated. Latencies are client-observed round trips from `load_gen`, reported as
histogram bucket upper bounds ("p99 <= X us").

| clients | server threads | value size | read ratio | ops/s | GET p50 | GET p99 | SET p99 |
|--------:|---------------:|-----------:|-----------:|------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|
|       1 |              4 |       64 B |       0.80 |       |         |         |         |
|       4 |              4 |       64 B |       0.80 |       |         |         |         |
|       8 |              8 |       64 B |       0.80 |       |         |         |         |
|      16 |             16 |       64 B |       0.80 |       |         |         |         |
|      16 |             16 |      4 KiB |       0.80 |       |         |         |         |
|      64 |              8 |       64 B |       0.50 |       |         |         |         |

Server-side command execution time (`STATS`, row 4): p50 <= <x> us, p99 <= <y> us.
The last row deliberately has more clients than worker threads; see the note below the table.

Why clients <= threads in every row but the last. A connection holds a worker for its whole life, and a load_gen client stays connected until its deadline. With 16 clients on 8 threads, 8 clients would sit in the pool queue for the entire run and the row would really measure 8 clients. (The benchmark template in code/README.md has 16 clients / 8 threads rows; replace them with the rows above.) The same applies to every load_gen run in this course: when you want N truly concurrent clients, start the server with --threads N or more.

How to read your own numbers, because you will be asked:

  • Row 1 is latency-bound. One client waits for each reply before sending the next (closed loop), so ops/s is roughly 1 / round-trip time. It measures loopback plus two syscalls each way plus the store, not throughput.
  • Rows 2 to 4 should scale with clients until the server's cores saturate. If they do not, the bottleneck is elsewhere: the load generator's cores, or the store lock under writes. perf top -p $(pgrep tcpkv_server) tells you which.
  • Row 6 has more clients than threads. With 64 clients and 8 workers, 56 connections wait in the pool queue. Their connect succeeds (the kernel completed the handshake and the acceptor accepted them) but no worker reads from them. And a load_gen client never leaves before its deadline, so a worker frees up only when one of the first 8 clients finishes at the end of the run. Predict the result before you run it: ops/s about the same as 8 clients, and most of the 56 queued clients completing exactly one operation, at the very end, after waiting roughly the whole run, which puts the tail percentiles in the top buckets. That row is the honest demonstration of the thread-per-connection limit, and the reason epoll is first in "what I would do next". Do not delete it because it looks bad; it is the most interesting row. (If your numbers do not match the prediction, find out why before publishing.)
  • Server p99 tiny, client p99 large means the time is in the network stack, scheduling and queueing, not in Store. Say that sentence with your numbers in it.
  • Closed-loop load hides queueing delay (coordinated omission): a slow reply delays the next request, so the slow period is under-sampled. Open-loop generators (wrk2-style, constant arrival rate) avoid this. Knowing the term is a senior signal.

docs.title: 4.4 The two numbers for the resume
docs.text:
Pick one configuration and use its numbers everywhere (resume, LinkedIn, interviews): the 16-client, 16-thread, 64-byte, 80%-read row is a good default. You need:

  • ops/s: the median from that row. Round down to two significant figures (e.g. 41,730 becomes "~41k"). Never round up.
  • p99: the GET p99 bucket bound from the same row, "p99 <= 200 us" style. If you prefer a single p99 for all operations, run load_gen with the same settings and use the larger of the GET and SET p99 values.

Write them, with the machine description, into a file in your notes, not just the README: when an interviewer asks in March, you want the exact numbers and conditions.

docs.title: 5.1 Tag and release
docs.text:
git switch main && git pull
git status                                    # clean
cmake --preset release && cmake --build --preset release && ctest --preset release

git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "tcpkv 1.0.0

Multithreaded TCP key-value server in C++17.

- Text protocol with length-prefixed values: PING GET SET DEL EXISTS KEYS EXPIRE TTL STATS QUIT
- Fixed thread pool, move-only Connection handles, graceful SIGINT/SIGTERM shutdown
- In-memory store behind std::shared_mutex with lazy + periodic TTL expiry
- Client library, tcpkv_cli, load_gen (C++ and Python) with per-GET verification
- GoogleTest suites; CI: debug, release, ASan, TSan, UBSan, Valgrind memcheck under load"
git push origin v1.0.0

An annotated tag (-a) stores the tagger, date and message; a lightweight tag is just a name for a commit. Releases use annotated tags. The tags: ["v*"] trigger from step 08 runs CI on the tag. Wait for it to be green, then create the release:

gh auth status                                # once: gh auth login
cat > /tmp/release_notes.md <<'EOF'
First stable release. See README for architecture, protocol and benchmark numbers
(<CPU>, WSL2, 4 vCPUs): ~<N> ops/s with 16 clients, GET p99 <= <X> us.

Build: cmake --preset release && cmake --build --preset release
EOF
gh release create v1.0.0 --title "tcpkv 1.0.0" --notes-file /tmp/release_notes.md

(Use a mktemp file instead of /tmp/release_notes.md if you prefer; delete it afterwards.)

If you find a bug after tagging, do not move the tag. Fix it on main and tag v1.0.1. Moving a published tag breaks everyone who fetched it, and it looks like hiding something.

docs.title: 5.2 Make it public, describe it, pin it
docs.text:
gh repo edit khanshaki-r/tcpkv --visibility public --accept-visibility-change-consequences
gh repo edit khanshaki-r/tcpkv \
  --description "Multithreaded TCP key-value server in C++17: thread pool, shared_mutex store, RAII sockets, GoogleTest, ASan/TSan/UBSan/Valgrind CI" \
  --add-topic cpp17 --add-topic tcp-server --add-topic key-value-store \
  --add-topic multithreading --add-topic linux --add-topic cmake --add-topic googletest

(The web route: repo Settings, General, Danger Zone, "Change repository visibility".)

Pinning has no gh command. On github.com: your profile page, "Customize your pins", tick tcpkv, save. Put it first. Then open your profile in a private browser window, logged out, and check what a stranger sees: the pin, the description, the green badge on the README.

docs.title: 5.3 Fresh-clone check
docs.text:
The ultimate test of "builds clean": a clone on a machine state that is not yours.

dir=$(mktemp -d) && cd "$dir"
git clone https://github.com/khanshaki-r/tcpkv && cd tcpkv
git checkout v1.0.0
cmake --preset release && cmake --build --preset release && ctest --preset release
./build/release/tcpkv_server --port 7390 & sleep 1
./build/release/load_gen --port 7390 --clients 4 --duration 3
kill -INT %1; wait

If this fails, the repo depends on something only your machine has (an untracked file, a locally installed package). Fix and tag v1.0.1.

docs.title: 6. The resume bullets: true, specific, checkable
6.1 The rule
docs.text: Every noun in a bullet must point at code on main at the tag. Every number must come from section 4 with its conditions written down. Anything else is a claim the interviewer can disprove in thirty seconds, and after that every other line on the resume is in doubt too.

docs.title: 6.2 Check the current bullets against the repo
docs.text: claim on the resume (from the course README) where it is true verdict Concurrent TCP server with a fixed thread pool ThreadPool, Server::run true text protocol Parser, docs/PROTOCOL.md true in-memory store guarded by shared_mutex Store true RAII socket and file-descriptor wrappers FileDescriptor, Socket true move-only connection handles Connection, MoveOnlyFunction true Builds clean under -Wall -Wextra -Werror with CMake tcpkv_warnings, every CI job true (and stricter: also -Wpedantic -Wshadow) GoogleTest suite for protocol parsing and store operations tests/protocol_test.cpp, tests/store_test.cpp true (understated: also fd, thread pool, integration) Valgrind-clean under concurrent load tools/valgrind_check.sh, CI valgrind job true

docs.title: 6.3 Claims you must not make about v1.0.0
docs.text:
Other parts of this curriculum sketch a bigger tcpkv. In particular 11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search/02_telling_your_story.md and 08_resume_linkedin_github.md mention sharded locking / lock striping, an append-only log with replay, LRU eviction with a memory cap, and an epoll variant. None of those is in v1.0.0. Until one is merged, tested and tagged (v1.1.0 and later), it does not go on the resume, the LinkedIn profile, or into your spoken story. Edit your copy of those story paragraphs to match what you built. In an interview they become "what I would do next", which is a strong answer when you can explain the design and its trade-offs.

Also avoid: "high-performance" (compared to what?), "production-ready" (it has no persistence, auth or TLS), "Redis-compatible" (the protocol is RESP-like, not RESP), "lock-free store" (the histogram is lock-free; the store is not).

docs.title: 6.4 The bullets
docs.text:
Project heading line:

tcpkv — Multithreaded TCP Key-Value Server · C++17, Linux, CMake, GoogleTest · github.com/khanshaki-r/tcpkv

Bullets (fill the brackets from section 4.4; delete the bracket text if you have no number):

  • Concurrent TCP server with a fixed thread pool and a length-prefixed text protocol over an in-memory store guarded by std::shared_mutex, with per-key TTL; RAII socket and file-descriptor wrappers, move-only connection handles, and graceful SIGINT/SIGTERM shutdown via the self-pipe trick.
  • Sustains ~[N]k ops/s with 16 concurrent clients at GET p99 <= [X] µs (80% reads, 64 B values, 4-vCPU WSL2 VM, loopback), measured with a load generator that verifies every read against the last write.
  • Builds clean under -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror with CMake; GoogleTest suites for protocol parsing, store operations, the thread pool and end-to-end server behaviour; CI runs them under ASan, TSan and UBSan and runs the server Valgrind-clean under concurrent load.

Why each change from the original two bullets:

  • The metric bullet is new and carries the numbers. It states the conditions in the same line, so it cannot be read as a production claim.
  • "length-prefixed" and "per-key TTL" are true and are better interview hooks than "text protocol" alone: each invites a question you have a good answer to.
  • The CI clause names the three sanitizers, which are exactly the keywords Linux C++ job descriptions use, and each is backed by a green job anyone can click.

Three bullets is the maximum for a side project on a 2.5-years-experience resume. If space is tight, merge the first and third and keep the metric bullet.

LinkedIn "Projects" entry: the same three bullets plus the repo link. GitHub profile README (optional): one line, "tcpkv: multithreaded TCP KV server in C++17, [N]k ops/s, ASan/TSan/ Valgrind-clean CI", linking to the repo.
