docs.text:
cd ~/dev/tcpkv
# 1. everything green locally
for p in debug release asan ubsan; do cmake --preset $p && cmake --build --preset $p && ctest --preset $p || break; done
setarch $(uname -m) -R cmake --preset tsan && setarch $(uname -m) -R cmake --build --preset tsan && setarch $(uname -m) -R ctest --preset tsan

# 9. fresh-clone check; 10. resume bullets

docs.title: 8. Test by hand
docs.text:
1. Logged-out browser: profile shows tcpkv pinned first with description; README badge green; the Actions tab shows the tag run green; the Releases sidebar shows v1.0.0.
  2. Click every link in the README (LICENSE, PROTOCOL.md, badges). None 404s.
  3. Fresh-clone check (section 5.3) passes.
  4. Read the README aloud. Every sentence is something you can defend for two minutes.
  5. Give the 2-minute pitch from INTERVIEW_TALKING_POINTS.md to someone (or a recording) with the README open and no notes. Time it.
  6. Ask a friend who programs to clone and run it from the README alone. Where they hesitate, the README is wrong.

docs.title: 9. Commit
docs.text:
git add -A
git commit -m "Release 1.0.0: README with architecture and benchmarks, protocol doc, required format check


- README: badges, demo, architecture diagram, protocol table, build/sanitizer/Valgrind
  commands, benchmark table with machine description, what I would do next
- docs/PROTOCOL.md checked against the parser and tests
- CMake project version 1.0.0
- CI: clang-format job is now required"
git push

(The formatting commit from section 3.4 comes before this one, on its own.)

docs.title: 10. What you learned, and what to say in an interview
docs.text:
• A portfolio project is evidence, not code. Public, pinned, green, documented, reproducible, honestly labelled numbers.
  • Benchmarks need conditions. Machine, build, pinning, warm-up, repetitions, what the latency includes. Without them a number is noise.
  • Closed-loop vs open-loop load, and why your p99 under closed loop is optimistic.
  • Annotated tags and immutable releases. Fix forward with a patch version.
  • Resume claims are a contract. Every one maps to a file and a test; the ones that do not exist yet are "what I would do next".

Interview sentence: "It is public at github.com/khanshaki-r/tcpkv, tagged 1.0.0. On a 4-vCPU WSL2 VM with the server and load generator pinned to separate cores, it does about [N] thousand operations a second with sixteen clients at a GET p99 of [X] microseconds, and the load generator checks every read, so that is correct operations per second. Server-side execution is [Y] microseconds at p99, so nearly all the latency is the network stack and scheduling, not the store. With 64 clients on 8 threads you can see the thread-per-connection limit in the tail, which is why epoll is the first item in my next-steps list."

docs.title: tcpkv: interview talking points
docs.text: Use: read this after step 10, then practise out loud until you can give the 2-minute and 15-minute versions without notes, with the repo open on a screen share. Every claim below is true of v1.0.0 as built in steps 01 to 10. Replace every [N], [X], [Y] with your own benchmark numbers (step 10, section 4) before you say them.

docs.title: 1. In plain words: what an interviewer wants from a project discussion
docs.text:
They are not checking whether tcpkv is impressive. They are checking three things:

  1. Did you build it? (You can go to any line and say why it exists.)
  2. Do you understand the trade-offs? (You know what you chose, what you rejected, and when your choice stops being right.)
  3. Can you reason about what you did not build? (Asked "how would you add X", you design out loud instead of reciting.)

So the talk is structured as: what it is, how a request flows, the three or four decisions that matter, how you know it is correct, what the numbers are, and what you would do next. Lead with the request flow; it gives the interviewer a map to hang questions on.

docs.title: 2. The 2-minute version
docs.text:
Say this at roughly 140 words a minute. It is about 280 words. Practise with a timer.

"tcpkv is a multithreaded TCP key-value server I wrote in C++17 on Linux to move my production C experience onto modern C++. At work I maintain a multithreaded RPC-over-TCP server in C on Windows; tcpkv is that kind of system reduced to its skeleton and done with the tooling a Linux team expects.

A client sends text commands, like SET, GET, DEL, EXPIRE. Values are length-prefixed, so they are binary-safe and the parser never has to scan for escapes. One acceptor thread polls the listening socket, accepts, wraps the descriptor in a move-only Connection, and moves it into a fixed thread pool. A worker owns that connection for its lifetime: it reads, feeds an incremental parser, executes against an in-memory store, and writes all replies for that read in one write. The store is an unordered_map behind a std::shared_mutex, so reads run in parallel and writes are exclusive.

Every resource is RAII: file descriptors, sockets, the connection. There is no close call outside one destructor. Shutdown on SIGINT uses the self-pipe trick: the handler sets an atomic flag and writes one byte to a pipe the acceptor polls; workers notice within one poll interval and the pool joins them.

For correctness, there are GoogleTest suites for the parser, store, thread pool and end-to-end server, and CI runs them under AddressSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer and UBSan, plus a job that runs the server under Valgrind while a load generator hammers it. The load generator verifies every read. On a 4-vCPU WSL2 VM it does about [N] thousand operations a second with sixteen clients at a GET p99 of [X] microseconds.

The main limit is thread-per-connection: concurrent clients are bounded by the thread count. The next step would be an epoll event loop."

Then stop and let them choose where to dig. Do not keep talking.

docs.title: 3. The 15-minute walkthrough
docs.text: Screen-share the repo. Each block lists what to say and what to have open. Times are targets.

docs.title: 0:00–1:30 The pitch and the README
docs.text: The 2-minute version, slightly shorter, with the README's architecture diagram on screen. Point at the diagram as you describe the request flow.

docs.title: 1:30–4:00 The protocol (docs/PROTOCOL.md, src/protocol.cpp)
docs.text:
• Show the grammar and one SET on the wire: SET k 5\nhello\n.
  • Why length-prefix (spec section 3.1): binary-safe, O(1) to find the end, pipelining is free, still typeable in nc. Quoting would mean an escape layer, the classic source of parser bugs. Binary framing would be faster to parse but useless with nc.
  • The parser is an incremental state machine (Line, Value, Dead): feed it whatever read() returned, call next() until it says "need more". It never touches the socket, which is why it has about thirty unit tests (31 in protocol_test.cpp at v1.0.0, count yours) including byte-by-byte feeding.
  • Fatal vs non-fatal errors: an unknown command skips one line; an oversized value or a missing terminator is fatal, because after that you cannot know where the next request starts. That split is the most important protocol decision; say it clearly.
  • Limits: 256-byte keys, 1 MiB values, 4 KiB lines, 64 args. Each bounds memory per connection against a hostile client.

docs.title: 4:00–7:00 Concurrency (src/server.cpp, src/thread_pool.cpp, src/connection.cpp)
docs.text:
• Server::run: poll on the listener and the wake pipe; accept4 with SOCK_CLOEXEC; EMFILE back-off (100 ms sleep instead of a 100% CPU spin); busy rejection above max_pending_connections.
  • The ownership pipeline (step 06 section 2.4): socket created on the acceptor, moved into Connection, moved into a lambda, into MoveOnlyFunction, into the queue, out by a worker. Closed on whichever thread destroys it. No shared_ptr.
  • Why MoveOnlyFunction: std::function requires a copyable callable; a lambda holding a move-only Connection is not copyable. Forty lines of type erasure; C++23 has std::move_only_function.
  • Worker loop: wait(lock, predicate); task runs outside the lock; exceptions caught so a task cannot kill a worker.
  • Connection loop: poll with a 250 ms timeout so the stop flag is seen; one write per read, so pipelined requests get one batched reply.
  • Store: shared_lock for GET/EXISTS/KEYS/TTL, unique_lock for writes; values copied out under the lock, never a reference.

docs.title: 7:00–9:00 Shutdown (apps/tcpkv_server.cpp, Server::request_stop)
docs.text:
• Signal handler: one atomic pointer load, one atomic store, one write(2). All async-signal-safe. Why not log or notify a condition variable from the handler (deadlock on a lock the interrupted thread holds).
  • sigaction without SA_RESTART, so poll returns EINTR and loops re-check the flag.
  • Order: stop accepting, drop queued connections (their sockets close in destructors), let in-flight commands finish, join. The scope of ThreadPool pool inside run() encodes it.
  • Show ServerShutdown.RequestStopUnblocksRunAndClosesClients: asserts under 2 s with clients connected.

docs.title: 9:00–11:30 Correctness evidence (tests/, .github/workflows/ci.yml, tools/)
docs.text:
• Four test layers (spec section 6): pure unit, unit with real descriptors, integration on an ephemeral port, system tests with the load generator.
  • CI matrix: debug, release, ASan, TSan, UBSan; plus Valgrind on the server under load. Why separate jobs: ASan and TSan cannot be combined; Valgrind cannot run a sanitizer build.
  • load_gen verifies every GET: disjoint key ranges per client, versioned values.
  • The EXPIRE overflow story (step 09): every sanitizer job green, yet UB on one hostile input; found by hand with the UBSan build, fixed in the parser, pinned by a test. Tell it as "what sanitizers do not do for you".

docs.title: 11:30–13:00 Numbers (README benchmark table)
docs.text:
• Machine, pinning, warm-up, median of three, closed-loop clients.
  • Server-side p99 ([Y] us) vs client p99 ([X] us): the store is not the bottleneck; the network stack and scheduling are.
  • The 64-clients-on-8-threads row: the thread-per-connection limit made visible.

docs.title: 13:00–15:00 What I would do next, and questions
docs.text: Epoll, persistence, replication (section 5). Then stop and invite questions.

docs.title: 4. Design decisions and the alternatives
docs.text: For each: what you chose, why, what it costs, and when you would switch. That last part is what makes the answer senior.

docs.title: 4.1 Thread pool (thread per connection) vs epoll event loop
docs.text:
fixed pool, one connection per worker (tcpkv) epoll event loop(s), non-blocking sockets concurrency limit N connections served at once; the rest queue thousands to millions of connections per thread per-connection cost a whole thread: stack reservation (glibc default is 8 MiB of virtual address space, committed lazily), a kernel task, scheduler work a small state object (buffers, parser) code shape straight-line: read, parse, execute, write state machine per connection; partial reads and partial writes must be resumed; EPOLLOUT handling; output buffering idle cost each idle connection wakes every 250 ms (our poll interval) zero latency for few active clients good: no event dispatch comparable debuggability a stack trace shows the whole request the request is spread across callbacks

Why I chose the pool: it is the design closest to the server I maintain at work, it is easy to make correct, and it put the effort where the resume claims are (RAII, move-only ownership, a correct pool, clean shutdown). It is a real production design for moderate connection counts with short-lived or busy connections (many database connection handlers and RPC servers work this way).

When it stops being right: many mostly-idle connections (chat, push, IoT, long-poll), or connection counts above a few thousand. Then threads cost memory and scheduler time for doing nothing, and N bounds concurrency.

What epoll would look like here: K event-loop threads (K = cores), each with its own epoll instance; the listener either in one loop that hands accepted sockets round-robin to the others, or SO_REUSEPORT with a listener per loop so the kernel balances. Each connection: non-blocking socket, the existing Parser, an output buffer. Edge-triggered: read until EAGAIN; write until EAGAIN, then arm EPOLLOUT and resume when writable. Backpressure: stop reading from a connection whose output buffer exceeds a limit. The Store and protocol code do not change, which is the payoff of keeping the parser free of I/O. Shutdown: an eventfd per loop instead of the self-pipe.

docs.title: 4.2 One std::shared_mutex vs a plain mutex vs sharded locks vs lock-free
docs.text:
• Plain std::mutex: simplest; but readers serialise, and a KV store is read-heavy.
  • One std::shared_mutex (tcpkv): readers in parallel. Costs: acquiring even a shared lock is an atomic read-modify-write on one shared word, so under many cores that cache line bounces between them; at high read rates a shared lock can be slower than you hope. On glibc it is reader-preferring, so continuous readers can starve writers (04_Concurrency/04_shared_mutex_and_readers_writers.md). Critical sections are one hash lookup plus a copy, which keeps both effects small at this scale.
  • Sharded (striped) locks: S independent {shared_mutex, unordered_map} shards chosen by hash(key) % S. Writers to different shards stop contending, and the lock word stops being one hot line. Costs: KEYS and purge visit every shard and give no consistent snapshot; multi-key DEL must lock shards in a fixed order to avoid deadlock; more memory. When: after a profile shows time in futex waits on the store lock, not before.
  • Lock-free / RCU-style maps: readers take no lock at all. Costs: memory reclamation (hazard pointers, epochs), much harder to get right, harder to review. Not justified without a measured need.

Say: "I would shard when the profile says so; with my numbers, the server-side p99 is [Y] microseconds while the client sees [X], so the lock is not where the time goes."

docs.title: 4.3 Text protocol with length-prefixed values vs binary vs RESP
docs.text:
• Text inline commands for debuggability: nc and telnet work, logs are readable.
  • Length-prefixed values for correctness: binary-safe, no escaping, O(1) framing, pipelining for free. It is the same idea as RESP bulk strings.
  • Not exact RESP: RESP requests are arrays of bulk strings (*2 $3 GET ...), which are harder to type by hand. tcpkv's replies are RESP-like (+, -, :, $, *), so a RESP reader would mostly parse them, but tcpkv is not Redis-compatible and should never be described that way.
  • Binary framing (fixed header with opcode and lengths, like memcached's binary protocol or a protobuf-over-length-prefix scheme) parses faster and is smaller on the wire. It costs the ability to debug by eye. For a service-to-service API with a generated client, binary (or gRPC) is the better default.

docs.title: 4.4 Bounded poll timeout in workers vs other wake-up mechanisms
docs.text: Workers block in poll(fd, 250 ms) and re-check an atomic flag. Alternatives: shutdown(fd, SHUT_RDWR) on every client socket from the acceptor (needs a registry of live sockets and a lock); pthread_kill with a signal per worker (fragile); an eventfd polled alongside each socket (one more descriptor per connection, or one shared eventfd). The timeout costs four wake-ups a second per idle connection and bounds shutdown latency to 250 ms. Simple, and the cost is visible and bounded. With epoll the answer becomes "one eventfd per loop".

docs.title: 4.5 Error handling style
docs.text:
• Network input errors are expected, so the parser returns ParseError values; no exceptions on the per-request path.
  • System call failures are exceptional: std::system_error with errno, caught at the connection boundary (a client vanishing is logged at debug and the connection ends).
  • std::optional for "not found" in the store and the client.
  • Startup failures (cannot bind) propagate to main, which logs and exits 1.

docs.title: 4.6 Smaller decisions worth one sentence each
docs.text:
• unordered_map, not map: O(1) average lookups; ordering is only needed by KEYS, which sorts its (usually small) result instead.
  • std::from_chars everywhere: no locale, no exceptions, explicit overflow reporting.
  • MSG_NOSIGNAL on every send and SIGPIPE ignored: a dead peer becomes EPIPE.
  • memcpy from sockaddr_storage instead of pointer casts: avoids strict-aliasing UB.
  • Warnings as an INTERFACE target so GoogleTest's code is not compiled with -Werror.
  • Sanitizer flags applied to the whole tree so the library, tests and gtest agree.
  • Relaxed atomics for metrics: independent counters, nothing published through them.

docs.title: 5. What next, and how you would design it
5.1 Epoll
docs.text: Section 4.1. Add: measure first and after. The expected result is that idle connections stop costing threads and the 64-clients row stops queueing; the per-request latency for a few busy clients may not improve at all. Saying that shows you understand what epoll buys.

docs.title: 5.2 Persistence
docs.text:
Two classic options, both of which Redis offers:

  • Append-only log (AOF): after executing a write, append the command to a log file; on start, replay it. Durability is set by the fsync policy: every write (safe, slow: each write waits for the disk), every second (lose up to about a second on power loss), or never (leave it to the OS). The log grows forever, so it needs rewriting: write a compact log from the current state and swap it in atomically (rename).
  • Snapshots: periodically write the whole map. Redis uses fork() and copy-on-write so the child writes a consistent image while the parent keeps serving. In a multithreaded C++ server fork is dangerous (only the forking thread survives in the child, and any lock another thread held stays locked forever), so you would instead copy under the lock (pause) or iterate shard by shard (no consistent snapshot without versioning).

Order of operations for the log, to be able to state: apply to memory and append to the log under the same ordering, reply to the client only after the append (and after fsync if the policy demands it). Replying first is how acknowledged writes get lost. minidb is where you built the real version of this: WAL before data, LSNs, checkpoints, recovery.

docs.title: 5.3 Replication
docs.text:
• Leader/follower with log shipping: followers connect to the leader and receive the same append-only stream; they apply it in order. Reads can go to followers if stale reads are acceptable.
  • Asynchronous (reply after local apply): fast, but a leader crash loses writes not yet shipped. Synchronous to a majority (reply after a quorum acknowledges): no acknowledged write lost while a majority survives, at the cost of a network round trip per write.
  • Failover needs agreement on who is leader, which is a consensus problem: Raft is the standard answer, and it also gives you the replicated log itself. Do not claim you would "just add Raft"; say you would use the Raft paper's design or an existing library, and that the hard parts are membership changes, snapshots, and testing with fault injection.

docs.title: 5.4 Other good answers
docs.text: Sharded locks (4.2); SCAN instead of KEYS; maxmemory with sampled LRU; a Prometheus endpoint; open-loop load generation to measure without coordinated omission; TLS via a library such as OpenSSL with non-blocking handshakes (much easier with an event loop); authentication (a shared secret per connection at minimum).

docs.title: 6. Likely questions, with answers
docs.text: Grouped by topic, roughly easy to hard within each group. Answers are what you say, in two to six sentences. Practise them aloud.

docs.title: Protocol and parsing
docs.text:
1. Why a text protocol and not binary? Debuggability: I can test with nc and read traffic in tcpdump. Values are length-prefixed, so the protocol is still binary-safe and framing is O(1). For a high-volume internal API with generated clients I would choose binary or gRPC; for a tool people poke at by hand, text wins.

2. How does the parser handle a request split across two read() calls? It is incremental: it buffers bytes and keeps a state (Line or Value). next() returns an event only when a complete line, or a complete value of the declared length plus its terminator, is buffered; otherwise it returns "need more" and the connection reads again. There is a test that feeds a SET one byte at a time and expects exactly one command.

3. What happens if a client sends 10 GB without a newline? After 4096 bytes without \n, the parser emits a fatal line too long error, the server replies and closes. Memory per connection is bounded by the line limit plus one value (1 MiB) plus the read buffer. Without the limit, one client could exhaust server memory.

4. Why are some errors fatal and others not? A non-fatal error (unknown command, wrong arity) is confined to one line, so the parser can skip it and stay in sync. A fatal one (value too large, bad terminator) means the parser can no longer know where the next request begins, so continuing could interpret value bytes as commands. Closing is the only safe action.

5. How does pipelining work? The client may send many requests before reading replies. The worker parses every complete request in its buffer, appends each reply to one output string, and sends it with one write_all. Replies come back in order because one connection is handled by one thread.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
6. Why shared_mutex and not mutex? The workload is read-heavy and reads do not conflict, so a reader-writer lock lets GETs run in parallel. I would revisit it if profiling showed the shared lock's own atomic operations or writer starvation mattering; then sharding is the next step.

7. Can a GET return a torn value? No. The value is copied out while the shared lock is held, and writers need the exclusive lock to modify it, so a copy sees either the old or the new value completely. The stress tests use values that are runs of one repeated letter so a torn read would be detectable, and they run under TSan in CI.

8. Why does the pool need MoveOnlyFunction? std::function requires its target to be copy-constructible, and a lambda capturing a move-only Connection is not. MoveOnlyFunction is type erasure (a virtual call on a heap-allocated Impl<F>) with copying deleted. C++23 adds std::move_only_function for exactly this reason.

9. Walk me through wait on a condition variable. Why the predicate? wait(lock, pred) loops: check the predicate under the mutex; if false, atomically release the mutex and sleep; on wake, re-acquire and check again. The predicate handles spurious wakeups and the case where another worker already took the task. Checking under the same mutex the producer uses to push prevents the lost-wakeup race.

10. What memory order is your stop flag, and why is that enough? The worker's load is relaxed: it only needs to eventually see true, and no other data is published through the flag. The store in request_stop is release and stop_requested() uses acquire, which costs nothing on x86 and documents intent. What makes the shutdown correct is the join, which is a full synchronisation point.

11. What happens to a connection that is queued when shutdown starts? ThreadPool::stop() moves the queued tasks out and destroys them outside the pool lock. The lambda's destructor destroys the Connection, whose Socket closes the descriptor. The client sees the connection close without a reply. There is a test with a Probe type that counts destructions to prove dropped tasks are destroyed.

12. What is the maximum number of concurrent clients? --threads clients are served at once. Up to --max-pending more wait in the pool queue; beyond that new connections get -ERR server busy and are closed. That limit is the main weakness of the design and the reason epoll is next.

13. Why can't the signal handler just log "shutting down" and notify a condition variable? Both may take locks or allocate. If the signal interrupts a thread that holds the same lock (the log mutex, the malloc arena lock), the handler waits for a lock its own thread holds, forever. Only async-signal-safe functions are allowed: a lock-free atomic store and write(2) are; malloc, printf and pthread_cond_signal are not.

docs.title: Resources and system calls
docs.text:
14. How do you guarantee no descriptor leaks? One class, FileDescriptor, owns every descriptor and closes it in its destructor; it is move-only so ownership is unique. Socket and Connection hold it by value. There is no close call anywhere else in the code. Descriptors are created with SOCK_CLOEXEC / O_CLOEXEC so they do not leak into child processes either. Valgrind's --track-fds=yes confirms only stdin, stdout and stderr are open at exit.

15. What does write_all handle that a single send does not? send on a stream socket may accept fewer bytes than asked (the socket buffer is full), so write_all loops until every byte is sent. It retries on EINTR. It uses MSG_NOSIGNAL so writing to a closed peer returns EPIPE instead of killing the process with SIGPIPE. There is a test that writes 4 MiB to force partial sends.

16. What happens when the process runs out of file descriptors? accept fails with EMFILE, but the pending connection stays in the kernel's accept queue, so poll immediately reports the listener readable again: a busy loop at 100% CPU. The acceptor logs and sleeps 100 ms instead, so existing connections can finish and free descriptors.

17. Why TCP_NODELAY in the client? Nagle's algorithm delays small sends while data is unacknowledged, and the peer's delayed ACK delays the acknowledgement, so a request/response exchange can stall for the delayed-ACK timeout. Disabling Nagle makes each request leave immediately, which is what a request/response protocol wants.

docs.title: Testing and tooling
docs.text:
18. How do you know there are no data races? I do not know there are none; I know TSan has not found any in the runs CI does, which are designed to maximise interleavings (many threads, a small key space, no sleeps). TSan proves the presence of races, not their absence. The design also keeps shared state minimal: the store behind one lock, metrics as atomics, the pool queue behind its mutex, and nothing else.

19. Why both Valgrind and ASan? They catch different things. ASan is fast enough for the whole test suite and finds stack and global overflows that memcheck cannot. Valgrind needs no special build, checks the binary as shipped, and finds reads of uninitialised memory, which ASan does not. They cannot run together, so they are separate CI jobs.

20. Tell me about a bug the tools found. The best one is the one they missed. EXPIRE key 10000000000 converted std::chrono::seconds to the steady clock's nanoseconds, multiplying by 10^9 in a signed 64-bit integer: signed overflow, undefined behaviour from one line of client input. Every CI job was green because no test sent a big number. I found it by sending hostile inputs to the UBSan build by hand, bounded the argument in the parser, and added a test. (Replace or supplement this with whatever you actually hit while building; a real story you lived beats a good one you read.)

21. How did you test graceful shutdown? An integration test starts the server in a thread with an idle client and a busy one, calls request_stop, and asserts run() returns within two seconds and both clients see the connection closed. A second test calls request_stop before run and expects an immediate return. Manually: Ctrl-C under Valgrind, which also proves the shutdown path frees everything.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
22. What is your throughput and what limits it? About [N] thousand operations a second with sixteen clients on sixteen worker threads, on a 4-vCPU WSL2 VM with the server and load generator pinned to separate cores. Server-side execution is [Y] us at p99 while clients see [X] us, so the time is in syscalls, loopback TCP and scheduling, not the store. One request per round trip per client is the real limit; pipelining in the client or more connections would raise throughput.

23. Is your p99 trustworthy? It is a bucket upper bound from a closed-loop load generator. Closed loop under-samples slow periods (coordinated omission): a stalled request delays that client's next request, so the stall is counted once instead of for every request that would have arrived. For a stricter number I would use an open-loop generator with a fixed arrival rate.

24. Where would you look first if latency spiked in production? STATS for server-side p99 versus what clients report: if the server-side number is flat, the time is outside the store (queueing for a worker, network, GC-like pauses in clients). Then connections_active against --threads (all workers busy means requests queue), top -H for a hot thread, perf top for where CPU goes, and off-CPU analysis for time spent waiting in futex on the store lock. A large KEYS or the per-second purge holding the exclusive lock is a prime suspect.

docs.title: Design and C++
docs.text:
25. Why is Connection move-only? Why not shared_ptr<Connection>? A connection has exactly one owner at a time: the acceptor, then the queue, then a worker. Move-only makes the compiler enforce that and makes the close happen exactly once, on whichever thread destroys it. shared_ptr would add atomic reference counting and hide the question of who closes the socket.

26. Why does Connection hold pointers to Store and the stop flag, not references? Reference members delete the assignment operators, so the class would not be move-assignable. Pointers keep it a regular movable value. The lifetimes are guaranteed by scope in main and run(): the store outlives the server, which outlives the pool, which outlives every connection.

27. Why is Server not movable? The signal handler holds a pointer to it (g_server). If it could move, the pointer could dangle. Deleting copy and not declaring move operations makes it immovable, and main clears g_server before the server is destroyed.

28. Exceptions in a server: where do you throw and where do you catch? System call failures throw std::system_error; they are caught at the connection boundary, so one broken client cannot affect others, and in the worker loop as a backstop, so an exception can never terminate a worker thread. Protocol errors are values, because bad input from the network is normal, not exceptional.

29. How would you make KEYS safe on a million keys? Today it scans every key under the shared lock, blocking writers for the whole scan. I would add SCAN with a cursor and a count, so each call holds the lock briefly, or keep an ordered index so a prefix query is a lower_bound plus a walk. Redis documents KEYS as unsafe in production for exactly this reason.

30. If you rewrote it tomorrow, what would you change? I would start with the event loop design so the connection limit goes away, keep the parser and store as they are (they are I/O-free and well tested), and add a windowed latency histogram so the periodic log line describes the last interval rather than all time. I would also write the hostile-input tests (huge numbers, every limit plus one) on day one rather than discovering the EXPIRE overflow late.

docs.title: 7. Weaknesses to state before they are found
docs.text:
Saying these first is a strength. Have each one ready in one sentence.

  • Thread per connection: concurrency bounded by --threads; idle connections cost threads.
  • No persistence, no replication, no auth, no TLS. Memory only, single node.
  • KEYS and the TTL purge are O(n) under a lock.
  • One shared_mutex for the whole store.
  • The p99 in the log is since start, not windowed; percentiles are bucket bounds.
  • Benchmarks are on a WSL2 VM over loopback; no cross-machine numbers.

docs.title: 8. Mapping to your experience at work
docs.text:
When asked "how does this relate to what you do?":

  • The application server at work is a multithreaded RPC-over-TCP server in C on Win32; tcpkv is the same architecture with RAII instead of goto cleanup, move-only ownership instead of conventions about who frees what, and sanitizers instead of finding the bug in a crash dump at a bank.
  • The crash-dump and RCA work maps to step 08: the bug classes ASan and TSan catch are the ones you have diagnosed after the fact in WinDbg. Now you can say how you prevent them.
  • The Berkeley DB to YugabyteDB migration maps to minidb and to the persistence answer in section 5.2: you know what a storage engine promises because you moved data between two.

Keep the employer's code, data and client names out of every example. Talk about the shape of the problems, never the specifics.

docs.title: 9. Recap: ten sentences to know cold
docs.text:
1. One acceptor, a fixed pool, one connection per worker for its lifetime.
  2. Length-prefixed values: binary-safe, O(1) framing, typeable in nc.
  3. Incremental parser with fatal and non-fatal errors; limits on every buffer.
  4. unordered_map behind one shared_mutex; values copied out under the lock.
  5. RAII for every descriptor; Connection is move-only and travels by move into the pool.
  6. Self-pipe shutdown: atomic flag plus one write from the handler; bounded poll in workers.
  7. Tests in four layers; CI under ASan, TSan, UBSan and Valgrind under load.
  8. A load generator that verifies every read.
  9. [N]k ops/s at GET p99 <= [X] us, with the conditions.
  10. The limit is thread-per-connection; next is epoll, then persistence, then replication.

docs.title: 12. C programming: the language under everything else
What this course covers
docs.text:
C from the ground up to senior and interview depth. It starts with what a C compiler and linker actually do with your files, then rebuilds the fundamentals one at a time: integer types and the conversion rules, pointers drawn as memory, storage duration and lifetime, strings and buffers, struct layout, function pointers and callbacks, and the preprocessor. The second half is about writing C that survives production: undefined behaviour and what the optimiser does with it, error handling and cleanup, data structures and allocators written in C, files and sockets, threads, working safely in legacy code, and a final module for C interview rounds.

Every module explains each idea in plain words first, then goes down to what the compiler, the linker, the C library and the CPU really do, then to how the idea shows up in a multithreaded banking server at 3 AM. Every module has complete programs in code/ that build with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror and check themselves with assert.

docs.title: Why it is on the resume
docs.text:
Your resume says "Languages: C, C++17". For 2.5 years your C work has been maintenance: analysing and fixing bugs in an existing multithreaded Win32 server, rather than designing C code from an empty file. That is real and valuable experience, but it can leave gaps in the fundamentals: you fix what is in front of you without always being able to say why the language behaves that way. Interviewers for C, C++ systems roles probe exactly those fundamentals:

  • "What does -1 < 1u evaluate to?" "Why is signed overflow undefined?" (module 02)
  • "What is the difference between an array and a pointer?" (module 03)
  • "What happens if realloc fails?" "Write strlcpy." (modules 04, 05)
  • "Why is this struct 24 bytes?" "Is union type punning legal?" (module 06)
  • "Why do { } while (0)?" (module 08)
  • "The compiler deleted my NULL check. Why?" (module 09)

This course turns 2.5 years of fixing C into the ability to explain C, write it from scratch, and defend every C line on the resume:

"Languages: C, C++17"

"multithreaded server-side C"

"C migration engine ... arena allocator with explicit ownership contracts"

"memory corruption & leak investigation"

docs.title: How to study it: a parallel track
docs.text:
This course is not studied in one block. It runs as the C track next to the main weekly plan in 00_START_HERE.md: two modules a week, one every three or four days, in the weekday lunch slot or on the weekend. Most of it consolidates what you already do at work, so it moves faster than a new subject.

Week (00_START_HERE.md) C track modules 1 (Oct 6 - 12) 01, 02 2 (Oct 13 - 19) 03, 04 3 (Oct 20 - 26) 05, 06 4 (Oct 27 - Nov 2) 07, 08 5 (Nov 3 - 9) 09, 10 6 (Nov 10 - 16) 11, 12 7 (Nov 17 - 23) 13, 14 8 (Nov 24 - 30) 15, 16

It is also the revision source before any C interview round: see "Revising before a C round" below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• None beyond having written some C. You have far more than that.
  • The WSL setup from 01_Environment_Setup (Ubuntu 24.04, GCC 13, gdb, Valgrind). Optional: sudo apt install dwarves for pahole (struct layout, module 06) and clang for a second compiler.
  • Modules list their own prerequisites. Modules 01 to 08 assume only the modules before them.

docs.title: Building the code
docs.text:
All code targets C17 on WSL Ubuntu 24.04 with GCC 13. Work on a copy in the Linux file system, not under /mnt/d (01_Environment_Setup explains why: file system speed and permissions):

mkdir -p ~/dev && cp -r /mnt/d/Cpp_DSA/LEARNING_PATH/12_C_Programming/code ~/dev/c12 && cd ~/dev/c12

# one program
gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g m03_pointer_basics.c -o m03_pointer_basics
./m03_pointer_basics

# every C program in the folder (-pthread is needed only by the threading modules, harmless elsewhere)
for f in m*.c; do
    gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -pthread "$f" -o "${f%.c}" || echo "BUILD FAILED: $f"
done

# the same with sanitizers: the best way to run the exercises
gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined m05_string_traps.c -o m05_string_traps_asan

Conventions used by every file in code/:

  • Named mNN_short_name.c, where NN is the module number.
  • main() checks its own results with assert and prints a short report; exit status 0 means every check passed. The module text shows the real output, captured from these builds.
  • The first comment gives the exact build line, and any extra flags or arguments the file needs.
  • Files that deliberately contain undefined behaviour say so in that first comment, and give the build line (without -Werror where GCC would refuse). In modules 01 to 08 these are m02_overflow.c (one call overflows int on purpose), m04_returning_buffers.c (with -DSHOW_BUG) and m06_unions_and_punning.c (with -DSHOW_ALIASING_UB).
  • Windows: the portable files also build with MSVC (cl /std:c17 /W4 file.c), which is a useful exercise for module 01's "MSVC versus GCC" section. GCC-only features (__builtin_*, __attribute__) are pointed out where they are used.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
# File Topic Hours 01 01_how_c_really_works.md The abstract machine, translation units, preprocess/compile/assemble/link, declarations versus definitions, linkage, object files and symbols, C89 to C23, MSVC C versus GCC C 2.5 02 02_types_integers_and_conversions.md Data models (LP64 versus Windows LLP64), two's complement, integer promotions, usual arithmetic conversions, signed/unsigned bugs, overflow, size_t, <stdint.h>, printf specifiers, floating point and why money is never a double, endianness 3 03 03_pointers_from_the_ground_up.md Addresses, * and &, pointer arithmetic, arrays versus pointers and decay, sizeof traps, pointer-to-pointer, const placement, void *, NULL, 2-D arrays, restrict 3 04 04_memory_storage_scope_and_lifetime.md Storage durations, scope versus lifetime, static/extern, stack frames, malloc/calloc/realloc/free contracts, the realloc-leak idiom, ownership comments, alignment, VLAs and alloca, an arena allocator 3 05 05_strings_and_buffers.md NUL-terminated strings, <string.h> traps, strncpy, snprintf, memcpy versus memmove, strtol versus atoi, sscanf, strtok_r, UTF-8, safe helpers, buffer overflows 3 06 06_structs_unions_enums_and_layout.md Layout and padding, offsetof, packing, bit-fields, unions and type punning, strict aliasing, flexible array members, designated initializers, opaque types, explicit binary formats 3 07 07_functions_function_pointers_and_callbacks.md Pass by value, out-parameters, function pointer syntax, callbacks with void * context, qsort/bsearch, dispatch tables, state machines, variadic functions, format-string bugs, static inline 2.5 08 08_the_preprocessor_and_macros.md #include, include guards, macro traps, do { } while (0), # and ##, X-macros, platform conditionals, _Static_assert, _Generic, logging macros 2.5 09 09_undefined_behaviour_and_the_optimizer.md Implementation-defined, unspecified and undefined; the UB catalogue; how the optimiser deletes overflow and NULL checks; strict aliasing; -fwrapv and friends; UBSan and ASan 3 10 10_error_handling_and_resource_cleanup.md How C reports failure, the rules of errno, goto-cleanup and single exit, ownership, assert versus runtime checks, a library error model in the Berkeley DB style, fault injection 3 11 11_data_structures_in_c.md Dynamic arrays, singly and intrusive linked lists with container_of, an open-addressing hash table, ring buffer, binary heap, three ways to be generic in C 3 12 12_memory_allocators_arena_pool_and_malloc.md Why custom allocators, alignment math, the arena and its ownership contract, a fixed-size pool, a teaching malloc with splitting and coalescing, a debug allocator with guards and leak reports 3 13 13_files_io_and_posix_system_calls.md stdio buffering, open/read/write with partial transfers and EINTR, durability (fsync, atomic replace), binary formats read through mmap, a TCP echo server in C, Win32 equivalents 3 14 14_multithreading_in_c_pthreads_and_c11.md pthreads, mutexes, condition variables, read-write locks, pthread_once, C11 <threads.h> and <stdatomic.h>, thread-safe versus reentrant versus async-signal-safe, a thread pool, TSan 3 15 15_reading_debugging_and_changing_legacy_c.md Navigating an unfamiliar code base, global state, reproducing bugs, characterisation tests, the smallest safe fix, diagnostics, blame/log/bisect, reviewing and refactoring C, describing maintenance work in interviews 3 16 16_modern_c_and_the_c_interview_playbook.md C standards in one table, C versus C++ differences, classic conceptual and coding questions with edge cases, how C interview rounds run 3

Total: about 47 hours of study plus exercises.

Modules 01 to 08 are the language model: after them you can predict what any line of C does and why. Modules 09 to 12 are robust C: the rules and techniques that keep a long-running server alive. Modules 13 to 16 are systems C and the job: I/O, threads, legacy code, and interviews.

docs.title: How this course connects to the others
docs.text:
• 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA is the other side of the same coin: modules 03, 04, 05 and 09 here explain the bugs whose crash dumps that course teaches you to read. Do modules 01 to 06 here before 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA modules 03 and 04.
  • 02_Modern_CPP shows how C++ encodes what C leaves to discipline: RAII instead of goto-cleanup (module 10 here), smart pointers instead of ownership comments (module 04 here), templates instead of void * and macros (modules 07 and 08 here).
  • 04_Concurrency teaches threads with C++17; module 14 here is the same material in C with pthreads and C11 <threads.h>, which is closer to your Win32 server.
  • 07_Databases_Internals/12_migrating_a_kv_store_to_relational.md applies module 06 (decoding packed records) and module 02 (amounts as integers) to your migration work.
  • 08_Networking_Distributed/04_framing_and_protocol_design.md applies modules 02, 06 and 07 (byte order, explicit wire formats, state-machine parsers).
  • 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps/02_how_a_cpp_program_is_built.md and 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps/03_gcc_and_clang_flags_that_matter.md go deeper into the linker and the warning flags used in module 01 and throughout; module 13 here pairs with 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps/11_linux_systems_programming_essentials.md.

docs.title: Revising before a C round
docs.text:
The evening before an interview that includes C:

  1. Read section 8 (Recap) of all sixteen modules aloud. About an hour.
  2. Answer section 7 (Interview questions) of modules 02, 03, 04, 05, 06 and 09 aloud without looking, then check. These six cover most of what C rounds ask.
  3. Do module 16's questions on paper, with a timer.
  4. Pick two programs from code/, predict their output line by line, then run them.

docs.title: You are done when you can...
docs.text:
• Explain what the preprocessor, compiler, assembler and linker each do, read nm output, and tell an "undefined reference" from a "multiple definition" and fix both.
  • Name the differences between MSVC C and GCC C that break ported code (long, VLAs, _snprintf, _s functions, Debug fill patterns).
  • Predict the result of any mixed signed/unsigned expression, on Linux and on Windows, using the promotion and conversion rules.
  • Write overflow-checked addition and multiplication, and explain why x + 1 < x gets deleted.
  • Explain why money is never a double and implement interest in integer paise with explicit rounding.
  • Draw any pointer, array, pointer-to-pointer or 2-D array situation as memory, and explain array decay and every sizeof trap.
  • State the four storage durations, the exact contracts of malloc/calloc/realloc/free, write the realloc idiom, and document ownership of every pointer in an API.
  • Write an arena allocator with alignment and explain its ownership contract.
  • Explain why strncpy, strcat, sprintf, atoi and strtok are traps, and write a safe copy, a safe builder on snprintf, and a fully checked strtol wrapper.
  • Predict any struct's size and offsets, decide when packing is acceptable, use unions and memcpy without breaking strict aliasing, and design a versioned binary record format.
  • Read and write any function pointer declaration, build a dispatch table and a state-machine parser, and write a printf-like function with the format attribute.
  • Write macros that survive every classic trap, an X-macro table, _Static_assert checks and a logging macro with file, line and function.
  • Recognise the main kinds of undefined behaviour and catch them with UBSan and ASan.
  • Write C functions that release every resource on every error path.
  • Implement a vector, a hash table and a thread pool in C, and explain how each would look in C++.
  • Walk into a C interview round and answer the questions in module 16 without notes.

docs.title: Resume lines this course backs up
docs.text:
"Languages: C, C++17"

The C half of that line: all sixteen modules, and module 16 for the interview itself.

"multithreaded server-side C"

Module 07 (callbacks, dispatch tables, state machines: how a server routes requests), module 10 (cleanup on every path), module 14 (threads in C) and module 15 (working safely in an existing server code base).

"C migration engine ... arena allocator with explicit ownership contracts"

Module 04 (storage, ownership comments, a first arena), module 06 (decoding packed records, explicit formats), module 12 (allocators in depth), module 13 (binary files and I/O), with module 02 for amounts and byte order.

"memory corruption & leak investigation"

Modules 03, 04, 05 and 09 (how corruption and leaks happen in C, and how to make them impossible or detectable), module 12 (a debug allocator with guard bytes and leak reports), together with 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA for the debugging tools and the RCA side.

docs.title: 01. How C really works: from source files to a running program
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: none (you have written and fixed C before)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A C program is a set of text files. The compiler never sees "the program". It sees one .c file at a time, after the preprocessor has pasted every #included header into it. It turns that one file into an object file: machine code with holes in it wherever the code mentions something defined in another file. The linker then takes all the object files plus the libraries, fills every hole with a real address, and writes the executable.

Analogy: a book written by several authors. Each author (a .c file) writes one chapter alone, with only a shared glossary (the headers) to know what the other chapters contain. A translator (the compiler) translates each chapter separately and leaves notes like "see chapter 7, page ?" wherever a chapter refers to another. The editor (the linker) binds the chapters together and fills in every "page ?". If chapter 3 refers to a section that nobody wrote, the editor, not the translator, is the one who complains: that is your "unresolved external symbol".

The C standard does not describe your CPU. It describes an imaginary abstract machine and says which results your program must produce. The compiler may generate any machine code that gives the same observable results. That freedom is why optimised code is fast, and why code that breaks the rules (undefined behaviour) can "work in Debug and crash in Release". Your maintenance work on the Win32 server has almost certainly hit bugs of exactly these kinds: link errors after a header change, a global defined twice, a crash that only appears in the optimised build. This module gives you the model that explains all of them.

docs.title: 2.1 The abstract machine and the as-if rule
docs.text:
The standard (ISO/IEC 9899) defines the meaning of a program in terms of an abstract machine that executes every expression exactly as written. A real compiler must only preserve the observable behaviour of that machine (C17 5.1.2.3):

  • accesses to volatile objects happen exactly as written, in order;
  • data written to files is what the abstract machine would have written when the program ends;
  • input and output on interactive devices happens in the right order.

Everything else is fair game: the compiler may keep variables in registers, delete stores nobody reads, reorder independent computations, inline functions, or compute a loop's result at compile time. This is the as-if rule. It is why a debugger shows "optimised out" for a variable at -O2, and why stepping through Release code jumps around.

The standard sorts "not fully specified" behaviour into four buckets. Interviewers ask for the difference, with examples:

Kind Meaning Examples Implementation-defined The compiler picks, and must document its choice sizeof(int), whether plain char is signed, result of -8 >> 1, converting an out-of-range value to a signed type Unspecified The compiler picks among allowed options, need not document, may differ call to call order of evaluation of function arguments and of the operands of + Undefined (UB) The standard places no requirement at all signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, null dereference, use after free, data race, i = i++ + 1 Locale-specific Depends on the runtime locale what isalpha(0xE9) returns

Undefined behaviour is not "random". It means the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens and optimise on that assumption. Module 02 shows GCC deleting an overflow check because signed overflow "cannot happen". Module 09 of this course, 09_undefined_behaviour_and_the_optimizer.md, is dedicated to UB.

docs.title: 2.2 Sequencing: when side effects happen
docs.text:
A side effect is a change to an object (assignment, ++, writing a file). C11 replaced the old term "sequence point" with sequenced before: if one evaluation is sequenced before another, its side effects are complete before the other starts. The guarantees you rely on:

  • &&, ||, ?: and the comma operator: the left operand is fully evaluated (side effects included) before the right one. && and || skip the right side when the result is known.
  • A full expression (a statement's expression, an if condition, each part of a for) is complete before the next one starts.
  • All arguments are evaluated before the function body runs. Their order among themselves is unspecified. Two function calls never interleave.

If two side effects on the same object are unsequenced (or a side effect and a read of the same object), the behaviour is undefined. GCC catches the obvious cases with -Wall:

w5.c:1:25: warning: operation on 'i' may be undefined [-Wsequence-point]
    1 | int k(int i) { return i = i++ + 1; }

docs.title: 2.3 The four stages of a build
docs.text:
foo.c ──► [preprocessor] ──► foo.i ──► [compiler] ──► foo.s ──► [assembler] ──► foo.o ─┐
 bar.c ──► ...                                                          bar.o ─┤
                                         libc.so / libm.a / your .a ───────────┤
                                                                               ▼
                                                                         [linker] ──► prog
Stage What it does GCC MSVC Preprocess runs #include, #define, #if; strips comments; output is one big C file gcc -E foo.c (or -save-temps keeps foo.i) cl /P foo.c (writes foo.i) Compile parses C, type-checks, optimises, emits assembly gcc -S foo.c cl /FA foo.c (listing) Assemble assembly to an object file with a symbol table and relocations gcc -c foo.c cl /c foo.c (gives foo.obj) Link joins objects and libraries, resolves symbols, writes the executable gcc foo.o bar.o -o prog link foo.obj bar.obj

gcc -save-temps -c m01_eval_order.c leaves all the intermediate files, so you can look at each:

m01_eval_order.c
m01_eval_order.i
m01_eval_order.o
m01_eval_order.s

docs.title: 2.4 Translation units
docs.text:
A translation unit (TU) is one .c file after preprocessing: the file itself plus every header it includes, recursively. The compiler handles exactly one TU at a time and knows nothing about the others. Everything it needs to know about a function or global defined elsewhere must come from a declaration in this TU, usually from a header.

m01_eval_order.c is 63 lines. After preprocessing it is 788 lines (317 without the line markers), almost all of it from <assert.h>, <stdio.h> and <string.h>. gcc -H prints the include tree, one dot per nesting level:

. /usr/include/assert.h
.. /usr/include/features.h
... /usr/include/features-time64.h
. /usr/include/stdio.h
.. /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/bits/libc-header-start.h
.. /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/13/include/stddef.h

This is why a change to a widely included header rebuilds the whole project, and why MSVC projects use precompiled headers (stdafx.h, pch.h).

docs.title: 2.5 Declarations and definitions
docs.text:
• A declaration introduces a name and its type: "there is an int called g_requests somewhere", "there is a function next_id taking nothing and returning int".
  • A definition is a declaration that also creates the thing: it reserves storage for an object, or provides the body of a function.
extern int g_requests;     /* declaration only: no storage */
int next_id(void);         /* declaration (a prototype): no body */

int g_requests = 0;        /* definition: storage reserved here */
int next_id(void) { ... }  /* definition: the body */

The rule (C17 6.9p5): every object or function with external linkage that the program uses must have exactly one definition in the whole program. Declarations can repeat as often as you like, as long as they agree.

Tentative definitions. At file scope, int counter; with no initializer and no extern is a tentative definition. Within one TU it becomes a real definition (zero-initialised) if no other definition appears. Across TUs, two files that both say int counter; used to be merged silently by the linker as "common" symbols. GCC 10 and later (and Clang 11 and later) default to -fno-common, so the same code now fails:

/usr/bin/ld: /tmp/ccsbNaen.o:(.bss+0x0): multiple definition of `counter'; /tmp/ccauhZNV.o:(.bss+0x0): first defined here
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

With -fcommon it links again. Legacy C written for older compilers (and for MSVC, which still accepts the pattern for C) often contains this. The fix is the proper pattern: extern int counter; in the header and int counter; in exactly one .c file.

docs.title: 2.6 Headers versus source files
docs.text:
A header is a contract that several TUs include. Put in it only things that may appear in many TUs without creating duplicate definitions:

In a header In a .c file function prototypes function definitions extern declarations of globals the one definition of each global struct, union, enum, typedef definitions static helpers and static file-scope data macros anything that is private to this file static inline functions (each TU gets its own copy)

Two rules that prevent most header pain:

  1. Every header is self-contained: it includes what it uses, so it compiles when it is the first and only include. Check it by making foo.h the first #include in foo.c.
  2. Every header has an include guard (module 08), so including it twice in one TU is harmless.

docs.title: 2.7 Linkage
docs.text:
Linkage decides whether the same name in different places refers to the same thing.

Linkage Meaning How you get it external the name refers to the same object or function across all TUs file-scope declaration without static; extern internal the name is private to its TU; another TU can reuse the name for something else static at file scope none each declaration is a separate entity locals, function parameters, typedef names

static means two unrelated things depending on where it is (module 04 covers both in full):

  • at file scope: internal linkage (private to the file);
  • at block scope: static storage duration (one object that lives for the whole program).

Make every file-scope function and global static unless another file really needs it. Fewer external names means fewer clashes, faster links, and better optimisation (the compiler knows every caller of a static function, so it can inline it or drop it).

docs.title: 2.8 Object files and symbols
docs.text:
An object file contains machine code with relocations: placeholders that say "put the address of symbol X here". It also has a symbol table listing what it defines and what it needs. nm prints the table (dumpbin /symbols on Windows). From the split build in section 3:

unit_a.o:
0000000000000000 t bump
0000000000000000 B g_requests
000000000000001d T next_id
0000000000000000 d s_next
0000000000000045 T unit_a_name

unit_b.o:
0000000000000065 r __PRETTY_FUNCTION__.0
                 U __assert_fail
                 U g_requests
0000000000000000 T main
                 U next_id
                 U printf
                 U unit_a_name
Letter Meaning T / t defined in .text (code). Upper case = external linkage, lower case = internal (static) D / d defined in .data (initialised data) B / b defined in .bss (zero-initialised data: takes no space in the file) R / r defined in .rodata (read-only data) U undefined here: used by this object, must be defined by another object or a library

Notice g_requests = 0 is in .bss, not .data: zero-initialised data costs nothing in the file. Notice also that bump and s_next are lower case: static turned them into internal symbols that the linker will never match against another file.

Two link errors you will meet forever, in both toolchains:

Problem GNU ld MSVC link.exe a name is used but never defined undefined reference to 'next_id' LNK2019: unresolved external symbol a name is defined in two objects multiple definition of 'counter' LNK2005: already defined in foo.obj

The linker works on names only. In C a symbol carries no type information, so if one file declares extern long g_requests; and another defines int g_requests;, nothing complains; the first file simply reads 8 bytes from a 4-byte object. (C++ mangles function parameter types into the symbol name, which catches the function case; see 02_Modern_CPP/01_from_c_to_cpp.md.) For libraries, shared objects, link order and the dynamic loader, see 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps/02_how_a_cpp_program_is_built.md: the mechanics are identical for C.

docs.title: 2.9 The C standards
docs.text:
Standard __STDC_VERSION__ What it added that you use daily C89 / C90 (not defined) prototypes, void, const, volatile, the standard library C95 199409L wide-character functions, digraphs C99 199901L // comments, declarations anywhere, for (int i...), long long, <stdint.h>, <stdbool.h>, inline, restrict, designated initializers, compound literals, flexible array members, variadic macros, snprintf, __func__, VLAs C11 201112L _Generic, _Static_assert, _Alignas/_Alignof, _Noreturn, _Thread_local, <threads.h>, <stdatomic.h> and a memory model, anonymous structs and unions, aligned_alloc; VLAs became optional; gets removed C17 201710L bug fixes only, no new features. This course targets C17. C23 202311L nullptr, bool/true/false/static_assert as keywords, typeof, constexpr objects, [[attributes]], #embed, binary literals, <stdckdint.h> (checked arithmetic), strdup in the standard, two's complement required, () now means "no parameters"

GCC 13 defaults to -std=gnu17 (C17 plus GNU extensions). Use -std=c17 -Wpedantic to stay inside the standard; that is what every program in this course is built with.

docs.title: 2.10 MSVC C versus GCC C: the differences you will hit
docs.text:
You have spent 2.5 years in MSVC. These are the differences that bite when the same C code moves to GCC on Linux, or when you explain your Windows experience in an interview:

Topic MSVC GCC on Linux Standard support historically C89 plus selected C99 library pieces. /std:c11 and /std:c17 since VS 2019 16.8; recent VS 2022 releases added <threads.h> and experimental atomics full C17, most of C23 by GCC 14 __STDC_VERSION__ defined only with /std:c11 or later always (C99 and later) VLAs never supported (__STDC_NO_VLA__) supported long 32 bits (LLP64) 64 bits (LP64). Module 02. snprintf real C99 snprintf only since VS 2015. Before that, _snprintf, which does not NUL-terminate on truncation and returns -1 standard printf("%zu") supported since VS 2015 (UCRT); older code uses %Iu standard "Safe" functions strcpy_s, strtok_s, localtime_s, and warning C4996 for strcpy unless _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS glibc does not provide them Same name, different signature MSVC localtime_s(struct tm *, const time_t *) vs C11 Annex K localtime_s(const time_t *, struct tm *); MSVC strtok_s has 3 parameters, Annex K has 4 POSIX localtime_r, strtok_r POSIX names strdup deprecated in favour of _strdup, fileno as _fileno standard POSIX names .c vs .cpp .c compiled as C unless /TP. Many "C" Windows code bases are really compiled as C++ by extension, same idea Debug fill patterns Debug CRT fills new heap blocks with 0xCD, freed blocks with 0xDD, guard bytes with 0xFD; /RTC1 fills uninitialised stack with 0xCC no fill unless you ask (-ftrivial-auto-var-init=pattern, GCC 12+) Missing prototype warning C4013 GCC 13: warning (-Wimplicit-function-declaration); GCC 14: error Extensions __int64, __declspec(...), __stdcall, #pragma comment(lib, ...) __attribute__((...)), __builtin_*, statement expressions

The debug fill patterns matter a lot for "works in Debug, fails in Release" (section 5).

docs.title: 3.1 One file, two translation units: code/m01_two_units.c
docs.text:
The file contains a "header" part (declarations), a unit A part (definitions) and a unit B part (main). Built normally, both halves are switched on and it is one TU. Built with -DUNIT_A and -DUNIT_B separately, it becomes two TUs that only meet in the linker.

#if !defined(UNIT_A) && !defined(UNIT_B)
#define UNIT_A
#define UNIT_B
#endif

/* ---- What a header would contain: DECLARATIONS both units agree on. No storage here. ---- */
extern int g_requests;          /* declaration: "an int called g_requests exists somewhere" */
int next_id(void);              /* declaration (prototype) of a function defined in unit A */
const char *unit_a_name(void);

#ifdef UNIT_A
int g_requests = 0;             /* definition: storage is reserved here, external linkage */
static int s_next = 1000;       /* internal linkage: unit B cannot name this object */

static int bump(int *p)         /* internal linkage function: invisible outside this unit */
{
    return (*p)++;
}

int next_id(void)
{
    ++g_requests;
    return bump(&s_next);
}

const char *unit_a_name(void) { return "unit A"; }
#endif

#ifdef UNIT_B
#include <assert.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int a = next_id();
    int b = next_id();
    assert(a == 1000 && b == 1001);
    assert(g_requests == 2);
    printf("ids %d and %d came from %s; g_requests = %d\n", a, b, unit_a_name(), g_requests);
    return 0;
}
#endif

Split build:

gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -DUNIT_A -c m01_two_units.c -o unit_a.o
gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -DUNIT_B -c m01_two_units.c -o unit_b.o
gcc unit_a.o unit_b.o -o m01_split && ./m01_split

ids 1000 and 1001 came from unit A; g_requests = 2

nm unit_a.o unit_b.o gives the table shown in section 2.8. Now link unit_b.o alone (gcc unit_b.o -o broken). The compiler was perfectly happy with unit B; the linker is the one that fails (two linker warnings about text relocations trimmed):

/usr/bin/ld: unit_b.o: in function `main':
/home/shakir/dev/c12.v9Oc/m01_two_units.c:55:(.text+0xe): undefined reference to `next_id'
/usr/bin/ld: /home/shakir/dev/c12.v9Oc/m01_two_units.c:56:(.text+0x16): undefined reference to `next_id'
/usr/bin/ld: /home/shakir/dev/c12.v9Oc/m01_two_units.c:58:(.text+0x59): undefined reference to `g_requests'
/usr/bin/ld: /home/shakir/dev/c12.v9Oc/m01_two_units.c:59:(.text+0x8c): undefined reference to `g_requests'
/usr/bin/ld: /home/shakir/dev/c12.v9Oc/m01_two_units.c:59:(.text+0x91): undefined reference to `unit_a_name'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

The .text+0xe style offsets are the positions of the holes (relocations) the linker could not fill.

docs.title: 3.2 Which standard am I really compiling? code/m01_compiler_and_standard.c
docs.text:
#if defined(__STDC_VERSION__)
    long v = __STDC_VERSION__;
#else
    long v = 0L;                 /* C90 did not define the macro at all */
#endif
    printf("__STDC_VERSION__ = %ldL -> %s\n", v, std_name(v));

#if defined(_MSC_VER)
    printf("compiler: MSVC, _MSC_VER = %d\n", _MSC_VER);
#elif defined(__clang__)
    printf("compiler: clang %d.%d\n", __clang_major__, __clang_minor__);
#elif defined(__GNUC__)
    printf("compiler: gcc %d.%d\n", __GNUC__, __GNUC_MINOR__);
#endif

#ifdef __STDC_NO_VLA__
    puts("variable length arrays: NOT supported");
#else
    puts("variable length arrays: supported (optional since C11; MSVC never had them)");
#endif

Output with the course flags:

__STDC_VERSION__ = 201710L -> C17
__STDC_HOSTED__  = 1 (1 = full standard library available)
compiler: gcc 13.3
variable length arrays: supported (optional since C11; MSVC never had them)
<threads.h>: available
<stdatomic.h>: available
double is IEEE 754 binary64 (__STDC_IEC_559__ defined)

First line with other -std= values (the C99 and C11 builds stop at the final assert on purpose):

-std=gnu17:  __STDC_VERSION__ = 201710L -> C17
-std=c2x:    __STDC_VERSION__ = 202000L -> C2x draft (what GCC 13 reports for -std=c2x)
-std=c11:    m01_compiler_and_standard.c:65: main: Assertion `v >= 201710L' failed.

Note __clang__ is tested before __GNUC__: Clang also defines __GNUC__ for compatibility, so the order of the tests matters.

docs.title: 3.3 What order is guaranteed: code/m01_eval_order.c
docs.text:
note() appends a letter to a trace each time it is called, so the program can print the order in which the compiler chose to evaluate things:

    int sum = note('a', 1) + note('b', 2);              /* order of the two calls: unspecified */
    int packed = three(note('x', 1), note('y', 2), note('z', 3));   /* argument order: unspecified */
    int r = note('p', 0) && note('q', 1);               /* &&: left first; right only if needed */
    r = (note('s', 1), note('t', 2));                   /* comma operator: s, then t; value of t */

note(a) + note(b)     called in order "ab", value 3
three(x, y, z)        called in order "zyx", value 123
p && q                called "p", value 0
m || n                called "m", value 1
(s, t)                called "st", value 2
c ? d : e             called "cd", value 10
all guaranteed orderings held

GCC 13 on x86-64 evaluated the three arguments right to left ("zyx") but the operands of + left to right. Neither is promised. Code that depends on argument order (for example printf("%d %d", next(), next())) is a latent bug that appears when the compiler, the flags or the platform change.

docs.title: What the preprocessor hands the compiler
docs.text:
gcc -E output starts with line markers so that error messages can point back to your file:

# 0 "m01_eval_order.c"
# 0 "<built-in>"
# 0 "<command-line>"
# 1 "/usr/include/stdc-predef.h" 1 3 4
# 0 "<command-line>" 2
# 1 "m01_eval_order.c"
# 11 "m01_eval_order.c"
# 1 "/usr/include/assert.h" 1 3 4

# 1 "/usr/include/assert.h" 1 3 4 means "now at line 1 of assert.h; flag 1 = entering a new file, 3 = system header (warnings suppressed), 4 = treat as extern "C"". When a macro or a header does something surprising, gcc -E (MSVC: cl /P) shows you exactly what the compiler saw. This is the first tool to reach for when a build behaves differently from what the source appears to say.

docs.title: What the compiler does with a TU
docs.text:
GCC parses the TU into a tree, lowers it to GIMPLE (three-address code in SSA form, where every variable is assigned once), runs hundreds of optimisation passes on it, lowers to RTL (close to machine instructions), allocates registers and emits assembly. The UB-based optimisations you will see in this course happen in those passes: GCC treats "x + 1 > x for signed x" as always true because overflow is undefined. Here is GCC 13 -O2 on two small functions (the endbr64 instructions that -fcf-protection adds are removed for readability):

int naive_increment_overflows(int x) { return x + 1 < x; }
int checked(int x) { return x == 2147483647; }

naive_increment_overflows:
    xorl    %eax, %eax          # return 0: the comparison was deleted
    ret
checked:
    xorl    %eax, %eax
    cmpl    $2147483647, %edi   # the correct check survives
    sete    %al
    ret

docs.title: Relocations: the holes in an object file
docs.text:
objdump -dr unit_b.o shows the holes the linker has to fill:

   d:   e8 00 00 00 00          call   12 <main+0x12>
            e: R_X86_64_PLT32   next_id-0x4
  57:   8b 05 00 00 00 00       mov    0x0(%rip),%eax        # 5d <main+0x5d>
            59: R_X86_64_PC32   g_requests-0x4

The call instruction's target is 00 00 00 00. The relocation record says: "at offset 0xe, write the distance from here to next_id, minus 4". The linker computes every such value once it has placed all sections in memory. R_X86_64_PC32 is a PC-relative data reference; that is how x86-64 code reaches globals without absolute addresses, which is what makes position-independent executables (and ASLR) cheap.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
objdump -h unit_a.o (trimmed):

  0 .text         00000056   ...  2**0
  1 .data         00000004   ...  2**2
  2 .bss          00000004   ...  2**2
  3 .rodata       00000007   ...  2**0

.data holds s_next = 1000 (4 bytes), .bss holds g_requests (4 bytes of zeros that are not stored in the file), .rodata holds the string "unit A" plus its NUL (7 bytes). At load time the OS maps .text and .rodata read-only, .data read-write from the file, and .bss as fresh zero pages. That is why writing to a string literal crashes: it lives in a read-only page. The full process layout is in 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/01_process_memory_layout.md.

docs.title: Static initialisation needs no code
docs.text: C requires initialisers of static-duration objects to be constant expressions. The compiler writes the bytes straight into .data, so nothing runs before main to set them up. (C++ allows dynamic initialisation of globals, and therefore has the "static initialisation order fiasco"; C does not.) Before main, the C runtime's _start sets up the stack, argc/argv, stdio and atexit handlers, and calls main; when main returns, exit flushes stdio buffers and runs the handlers.

docs.title: Why missing prototypes crash only on 64-bit
docs.text:
In C89, calling a function with no declaration in scope made the compiler assume it returns int. GCC 13 still accepts this with a warning:

imp.c:1:28: warning: implicit declaration of function 'make' [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
imp.c:1:28: warning: initialization of 'char *' from 'int' makes pointer from integer without a cast [-Wint-conversion]

On a 32-bit target int and pointers have the same size and the code works by accident. On x86-64 the caller reads only the low 32 bits of the returned 64-bit pointer (eax instead of rax) and sign-extends it. Heap addresses on 64-bit Linux are above 4 GiB, so the truncated pointer is garbage and the first dereference crashes. The classic case is calling malloc without #include <stdlib.h>. Treat -Wimplicit-function-declaration as an error (GCC 14 does).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• "Works in Debug, crashes in Release." The usual causes, in order of frequency: an uninitialised variable (MSVC Debug fills stack with 0xCC and heap with 0xCD, so a pointer is never accidentally NULL or valid in Debug; Release gets whatever was there); undefined behaviour that the optimiser exploits (deleted checks, reordered stores); and timing changes that expose a data race. When a crash moves or vanishes with optimisation level, think "UB" first, and build with sanitizers (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/08_valgrind_and_sanitizers.md).
  • LNK2019 after a refactor. A function was declared in a header but its .c file is not in the project, or it was made static in its file, or the C function is being called from a C++ file without extern "C" (the C++ side looks for a mangled name the C object does not have). dumpbin /symbols foo.obj | findstr name on Windows, nm -A *.o | grep name on Linux: look for U on one side and the missing T on the other.
  • LNK2005 / multiple definition. Someone put int g_debug_level = 0; in a header. Every TU that includes it defines it. Fix: extern in the header, definition in one .c file.
  • A header that changes layout depending on who includes it. #pragma pack(1) without a matching pop at the end of a header leaks into every struct declared after it in each TU that includes it. Two TUs can then disagree about the size and offsets of the same struct, and neither compiler nor linker notices. Symptoms are fields that read as garbage only when the struct crosses a module boundary. Module 06 shows the safe push/pop form.
  • Mismatched declarations across files. extern int g_count; in one file and long g_count; in another, or a prototype in a header that no longer matches the definition. Prevent it by making every .c file include its own header, so the compiler sees declaration and definition together.
  • 3 AM tools. gcc -E / cl /P for "what did the compiler actually see"; gcc -H / cl /showIncludes for "which header got pulled in from where"; nm / dumpbin /symbols for "who defines this symbol"; objdump -dr / dumpbin /disasm /relocations for "what is this instruction really calling".

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Do the split build of m01_two_units.c and run nm on both objects. Done when you can say, for every line of the nm output, which line of source created it and why its letter is upper or lower case.
  2. (easy) Remove static from s_next in unit A and add a definition int s_next = 5; to unit B. Rebuild split. Done when you have the multiple definition error, can explain it, and can fix it two ways (make either one static).
  3. (medium) In the unit B part only, change the declaration to extern long g_requests; (wrap it in #ifdef UNIT_B). Build split. Done when it links with no error and you can explain why the linker cannot notice, and what main now reads.
  4. (medium) Run gcc -std=c17 -save-temps -c m01_eval_order.c. Open the .i file and find your own code at the bottom; open the .s file and find the call order of note('x'...), note('y'...), note('z'...). Done when you can point at the instructions that prove the right-to-left order.
  5. (hard) Write make.c with char *make(void) { return malloc(16); } and main.c that calls make() with no prototype. Build with gcc -std=c89 -w and run. Done when you see it crash (or print a truncated pointer) and can explain the eax versus rax mechanism; then add the prototype and see it work.
  6. (hard) If you have Visual Studio, build m01_compiler_and_standard.c with cl /std:c17 and with plain cl (no /std). Done when you have both outputs side by side and can explain every difference from the GCC output above.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What happens between gcc main.c util.c and a running program? The preprocessor expands includes and macros for each file, producing one translation unit per .c. The compiler turns each TU into assembly and the assembler into an object file with a symbol table and relocations. The linker resolves every undefined symbol against the other objects and libraries, lays out sections and patches the relocations. At run time the loader maps the sections, the C runtime sets up and calls main.

Q: What is the difference between a declaration and a definition? A declaration introduces a name and its type; a definition also creates the entity, reserving storage for an object or supplying a function body. You can declare many times but must define an externally linked entity exactly once in the program. extern int x; is a declaration; int x = 0; at file scope is a definition.

Q: What does static mean at file scope and inside a function? At file scope it gives internal linkage: the name is private to that translation unit. Inside a function it gives static storage duration: one object, initialised once before main, that keeps its value between calls. They are two different features that share a keyword.

Q: Explain undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined behaviour with an example of each. Implementation-defined: the compiler chooses and documents it, such as sizeof(long) or the signedness of char. Unspecified: the compiler chooses among valid options without documenting it, such as the order in which function arguments are evaluated. Undefined: no requirements at all, such as signed overflow or reading past an array; the optimiser may assume it never happens.

Q: "undefined reference" versus "multiple definition": which tool reports them and why? Both come from the linker, because only the linker sees all object files together. "Undefined reference" means some object uses a symbol that no object or library defines; "multiple definition" means two objects define the same external symbol. The compiler cannot report either because it sees one translation unit at a time.

Q: Why can a type mismatch between extern declarations in two C files go undetected? C symbols are just names; the object file records no type. Each TU is compiled against its own declaration, and the linker matches names only. The defence is to include a module's own header in its .c file so the compiler checks the declaration against the definition.

Q: What does the as-if rule allow? Any transformation that preserves observable behaviour: volatile accesses, file output and interactive I/O. The compiler may keep values in registers, remove dead stores, reorder and inline code. It is why debugging optimised code is hard and why UB can make an apparently unrelated check disappear.
