Q: Which differences between MSVC and GCC have you had to deal with in C code? long is 32 bits on Windows and 64 on Linux; MSVC has no VLAs; old MSVC _snprintf does not terminate on truncation; MSVC _s functions are not available in glibc and some differ from Annex K in argument order; POSIX names like strdup and strtok_r have _strdup and strtok_s equivalents. Also MSVC Debug builds fill memory with 0xCC/0xCD, which hides uninitialised variable bugs until Release.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• The compiler sees one translation unit at a time; the linker joins them by symbol name.
  • Four stages: preprocess (-E), compile (-S), assemble (-c), link. You can stop after each.
  • Declaration = name and type; definition = also creates it. Exactly one definition per external name; GCC 10+ rejects duplicate tentative definitions (-fno-common).
  • Headers hold declarations, types, macros and static inline functions; never definitions of globals or non-inline functions.
  • Linkage: external (shared), internal (static at file scope), none (locals).
  • nm: T/D/B defined, U needed from elsewhere, lower case = static.
  • "Undefined reference" and "multiple definition" are linker errors; C symbols carry no types.
  • The as-if rule lets the optimiser do anything that keeps observable behaviour; UB breaks the contract and the optimiser exploits it.
  • Order of evaluation of + operands and function arguments is unspecified; &&, ||, ?: and comma are ordered.
  • MSVC C differs from GCC C in long size, VLAs, _snprintf, _s functions and Debug fill patterns; know them before you port Windows code.

docs.title: 02. Types, integers and conversions
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Every value in C has a type, and the type fixes two things: how many bytes the value occupies, and how its bits are read (as a signed number, an unsigned number, a floating-point number). So far so simple. The trouble is that C converts types silently in almost every expression. Small types grow into int before any arithmetic. When a signed value meets an unsigned one, the signed one is turned into unsigned. A negative number becomes a huge positive one. No warning, no exception: just a different number.

Analogy: a bank where every counter quietly exchanges your money into its own currency. Most counters use rupees, so nobody notices. But one counter (unsigned arithmetic) has no concept of debt: hand it minus one rupee and it gives you 4,294,967,295. A length check that should reject a corrupt negative length now passes, and memcpy copies 18 quintillion bytes.

Many C bugs that end up as CVEs (published security vulnerabilities) start here: a wrong size, a sign flip, an overflow in a length calculation. And in banking code there is a second, quieter trap: storing money in a double, which cannot represent 0.10 exactly. This module covers the rules precisely enough that you can predict every one of these results before running the code.

docs.title: 2.1 Sizes and the data model
docs.text:
The standard fixes only minimum ranges and an ordering: char at least 8 bits, short and int at least 16, long at least 32, long long at least 64, and sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long) <= sizeof(long long). sizeof(char) is 1 by definition. Everything else is the platform's choice, summarised as a data model:

Data model int long long long pointer Where ILP32 32 32 64 32 32-bit Windows and Linux LP64 32 64 64 64 64-bit Linux, macOS, BSD LLP64 32 32 64 64 64-bit Windows (MSVC and MinGW)

The only difference between Linux and Windows is long, and it is enough to break code. On Windows, long cannot hold a pointer, a file size above 2 GiB, or an amount above 21,474,836.47 rupees counted in paise (INT32_MAX paise). Code that casts a pointer to long works on 64-bit Linux and truncates on 64-bit Windows. Use intptr_t/uintptr_t for pointers-as-integers, and the fixed-width types from <stdint.h> whenever the size matters. Win32 has its own names for the same idea: DWORD is a 32-bit unsigned long, while DWORD_PTR, ULONG_PTR and SIZE_T are pointer-sized.

On WSL Ubuntu 24.04 (code/m02_data_model.c):

sizes on this platform:
  char          1 bytes
  short         2 bytes
  int           4 bytes
  long          8 bytes
  long long     8 bytes
  void *        8 bytes
  size_t        8 bytes
  ptrdiff_t     8 bytes
  float         4 bytes
  double        8 bytes
  long double  16 bytes
data model: LP64 (64-bit Linux, macOS)
CHAR_BIT = 8, plain char is signed

long double is 16 bytes of storage holding the x87 80-bit extended format on x86-64 Linux. On MSVC it is just a double (8 bytes). Plain char is signed on x86 with both GCC and MSVC, and unsigned on ARM Linux: never rely on it.

docs.title: 2.2 Two's complement
docs.text:
Every mainstream CPU stores signed integers in two's complement: the top bit has weight -2^(N-1) instead of +2^(N-1). C23 finally requires it; before C23 the standard also allowed sign-magnitude and ones' complement, which no one ships.

 8-bit pattern    unsigned    signed (two's complement)
 0000 0000             0         0
 0000 0001             1         1
 0111 1111           127       127   <- INT8_MAX
 1000 0000           128      -128   <- INT8_MIN (no positive partner)
 1111 1110           254        -2
 1111 1111           255        -1   <- "all ones" is -1

Consequences you need to know cold:

  • The range is asymmetric: INT_MIN is -2147483648 but INT_MAX is 2147483647. So -INT_MIN, abs(INT_MIN) and INT_MIN / -1 all overflow.
  • The CPU's add instruction is the same for signed and unsigned. Only the interpretation of the result (and of the overflow flags) differs.
  • Converting signed to unsigned is defined by the standard as "add or subtract 2^N until it fits", which on two's complement is just "keep the bits": (unsigned)-1 == UINT_MAX.
  • Converting an unsigned or wider value to a signed type that cannot hold it is implementation-defined (GCC and MSVC keep the low bits). Case 9 in section 3 shows 5000000000 becoming 705032704.

docs.title: 2.3 Integer promotions
docs.text:
Before any arithmetic, every operand whose type is narrower than int (char, signed char, unsigned char, short, unsigned short, _Bool, bit-fields) is converted to int, or to unsigned int if int cannot hold all its values. This is the integer promotion. It is why:

  • uint8_t a = 200, b = 100; a + b is 300, an int. It wraps to 44 only if you store it back into a uint8_t.
  • ~(uint8_t)0x0F is ~(int)15 = -16, not 0xF0. if (~mask == 0xF0) is always false; GCC warns: comparison of promoted bitwise complement of an unsigned value with constant.
  • uint8_t x = 0x80; x << 24 is computed in int, and 0x80 << 24 overflows int: undefined. Cast first: (uint32_t)x << 24.
  • A char holding byte 0xE9 promotes to -23 on x86. Used as an array index (counts[c]), it indexes before the array. Use unsigned char for bytes.

docs.title: 2.4 The usual arithmetic conversions
docs.text:
When a binary operator (+ - * / % < > == & | ^ ?:) gets two operands of different types, after promotion, C converts them to a common type with this algorithm:

  1. If either is long double, double or float, convert the other to that floating type.
  2. Otherwise both are integers. If they have the same signedness, convert to the one with greater rank (long long > long > int).
  3. If the unsigned one has rank greater than or equal to the signed one, convert the signed one to the unsigned type. (int meets unsigned int: both become unsigned int.)
  4. If the signed one has greater rank and can represent every value of the unsigned type, convert to the signed type. (long meets unsigned int on LP64: both become long.)
  5. Otherwise convert both to the unsigned version of the signed type.

Rule 4 versus rule 5 is a portability bomb: the same expression gives different answers on Linux and Windows.

Expression LP64 (Linux) LLP64 (Windows) -1 < 1u int vs unsigned: rule 3, -1 becomes 4294967295: false same: false -1L < 1u long (64) can hold every unsigned (32): rule 4, true long (32) cannot: rule 5, both unsigned long: false -1 < (size_t)3 size_t is unsigned long: rule 3, false size_t is unsigned long long: false

docs.title: 2.5 The signed/unsigned bugs, catalogued
docs.text:
These are the real-world patterns. Each is in code/m02_promotions_and_conversions.c.

/* 1. The negative length that passes the check */
int len = read_len_from_wire();             /* -5 from a corrupt packet */
if (len > (int)sizeof buf) return ERR;      /* -5 > 64 is false: check passes */
memcpy(buf, src, len);                      /* len converts to size_t: 18446744073709551611 */

/* 2. Subtracting sizes */
if (strlen(a) - strlen(b) > 0)              /* size_t never goes negative: true unless equal */

/* 3. Counting down with an unsigned index */
for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; --i)         /* i >= 0 is always true: infinite loop, then crash */

GCC catches the third with -Wextra:

loop.c:2:57: warning: comparison of unsigned expression in '>= 0' is always true [-Wtype-limits]

The correct count-down idiom is for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; ): the test happens before the decrement, so the body sees n-1 ... 0 and the loop stops after 0. For the length check, validate before converting: reject len < 0 explicitly, or read the length as unsigned from the start.

docs.title: 2.6 Overflow: undefined for signed, wrapping for unsigned
docs.text:
• Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo 2^N. UINT_MAX + 1u == 0. This is not an error as far as C is concerned, which is exactly why malloc(count * size) with a wrapped product allocates a tiny buffer and the following loop overflows it.
  • Signed overflow is undefined behaviour. The compiler assumes it never happens. GCC folds x + 1 < x to false even at -O0, so the "overflow check" disappears.
  • Other integer UB: dividing by zero; INT_MIN / -1 and INT_MIN % -1; shifting by a negative count or by >= the width of the (promoted) type; left-shifting a negative value or shifting a 1 into the sign bit (1 << 31 on 32-bit int).
  • Implementation-defined: right shift of a negative value (-8 >> 1 is -4 on GCC and MSVC: an arithmetic shift).
  • Defined but surprising: integer division truncates toward zero since C99, so -7 / 2 == -3 and -7 % 2 == -1.

Checking correctly means testing before the operation, using only operations that cannot overflow:

static bool add_i64_checked(int64_t a, int64_t b, int64_t *out)
{
    if ((b > 0 && a > INT64_MAX - b) || (b < 0 && a < INT64_MIN - b))
        return false;
    *out = a + b;
    return true;
}

static bool mul_size_checked(size_t a, size_t b, size_t *out)
{
    if (a != 0 && b > SIZE_MAX / a)
        return false;
    *out = a * b;
    return true;
}

GCC and Clang also provide __builtin_add_overflow(a, b, &result) (and _sub_, _mul_), which compile to the arithmetic instruction plus a jump on the overflow flag. C23 standardises them as ckd_add, ckd_sub, ckd_mul in <stdckdint.h>. MSVC has neither; use the portable form.

Compiler switches that change the rules: -fwrapv makes signed overflow wrap (defined), at some optimisation cost; -ftrapv aborts on signed overflow; -fsanitize=undefined reports it at run time (section 3.3 shows the report).

docs.title: 2.7 size_t, ptrdiff_t and friends
docs.text:
Type Header What it is Print with size_t <stddef.h> unsigned; type of sizeof, every size and count in the library %zu ptrdiff_t <stddef.h> signed; type of p - q for pointers into the same array %td ssize_t <sys/types.h> (POSIX, not ISO C) signed size_t; read/write return it, -1 on error %zd intptr_t, uintptr_t <stdint.h> integers wide enough to hold a pointer PRIdPTR, PRIuPTR intmax_t <stdint.h> widest signed integer %jd

Whether to index with int or size_t is a style debate. The senior answer: the bugs come from mixing them. Pick one per interface, keep comparisons between same-signedness values, and turn on -Wsign-compare (in -Wextra) so the compiler shows you every mix.

docs.title: 2.8 <stdint.h>: say how big you mean
docs.text:
• Exact width: int8_t, int16_t, int32_t, int64_t and the uint versions. Use them for anything stored on disk, sent over the network, or holding money.
  • At least / fastest: int_least32_t, int_fast32_t. Rarely needed.
  • Literal macros: INT64_C(5000000000), UINT32_C(1). They append the right suffix (L on Linux, LL on Windows), so UINT64_C(1) << 40 works everywhere while 1 << 40 is UB.
  • Limits: INT64_MAX, UINT32_MAX, SIZE_MAX.

docs.title: 2.9 printf and scanf format specifiers
docs.text:
A mismatch between the format and the argument's type is undefined behaviour, and on 64-bit it really breaks: printf("%d", some_size_t) reads 4 bytes of an 8-byte argument. GCC checks literal formats with -Wformat (in -Wall).

Type printf scanf int / unsigned %d / %u, %x same long / unsigned long %ld / %lu same long long %lld / %llu same size_t / ptrdiff_t %zu / %td same int64_t / uint64_t "%" PRId64 / "%" PRIu64, PRIx64 "%" SCNd64 int32_t / uint32_t PRId32 / PRIu32 SCNd32 void * %p rarely double %f, %g, %.17g for round-trip %lf (scanf needs the l)

int64_t is long on Linux and long long on Windows, so no single %ld or %lld is right everywhere. That is what the PRId64 macros from <inttypes.h> solve. Legacy MSVC code uses %I64d; it still works on Windows but is not portable.

docs.title: 2.10 Floating point basics, and why money is never a double
docs.text:
A double is IEEE 754 binary64: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, 52 fraction bits. It holds about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits and represents numbers as fraction x 2^exponent. Any value that is not a sum of powers of two, such as 0.1, is stored as the nearest representable binary value:

  • 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false.
  • Addition is not associative: (0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3 is 0.60000000000000009 but 0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3) is 0.59999999999999998. Two systems that sum the same transactions in a different order get different totals.
  • printf("%.2f", 2.675) prints 2.67, because the stored value is slightly below 2.675.
  • Every integer up to 2^53 (9,007,199,254,740,992) is exact; above that, only even numbers are. A float is exact only up to 2^24 = 16,777,216: 16777217.0f prints as 16777216.0.
  • NaN != NaN, and 0.0 == -0.0 is true although the bits differ.

For money this is unacceptable. Rules for banking code:

  1. Store amounts as integers of the smallest unit: int64_t paise or cents. An int64_t holds about 92 quadrillion rupees in paise, so range is not the issue. Some currencies have three decimals (Kuwaiti dinar, 1000 fils), so a multi-currency system stores the scale per currency.
  2. Or use a decimal type where one exists: PostgreSQL and YugabyteDB NUMERIC(18,2), COBOL packed decimal, Java BigDecimal. Never convert through double on the way in or out (07_Databases_Internals/12_migrating_a_kv_store_to_relational.md, decoding rule 4).
  3. Make rounding explicit: where it happens (per transaction, per day, at the end), and which rule (half-up, or half-even "banker's rounding", which rounds ties to the even digit to avoid systematic bias). Write it in the code and the specification.
  4. Interest = principal x rate x time involves division, so it needs rounding. Do it in integers with the rate in basis points (1 bp = 0.01 %), multiply first, check for overflow, and round once at the end. Section 3.4 shows it.

docs.title: 2.11 Endianness
docs.text:
A multi-byte integer is stored at several consecutive addresses. Little-endian puts the least significant byte at the lowest address (x86, x86-64, and ARM as configured by every mainstream OS). Big-endian puts the most significant byte first (network protocols, "network byte order"; older SPARC, POWER/AIX and mainframe systems).

value 0x11223344 at address A:
                 A     A+1   A+2   A+3
little-endian:  44    33    22    11      (x86: what memcpy into a uint32_t gives you)
big-endian:     11    22    33    44      (network byte order)

Endianness matters whenever bytes cross a boundary: a socket, a file, a database record, a memory-mapped device. Within one process it never matters, as long as you do not reinterpret memory. The portable way to read or write a multi-byte field from a byte buffer is to assemble it with shifts; it works on any host, needs no #ifdef, and the compiler turns it into one instruction (section 4). htonl/ntohl (from <arpa/inet.h>, or <winsock2.h> on Windows) do the same for 16 and 32 bits.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: Build any file with gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g file.c -o file.

docs.title: 3.1 Data model and portable printing: code/m02_data_model.c
docs.text:
int64_t   balance_paise = INT64_C(-123456789012);
uint32_t  account_no    = UINT32_C(4000000000);
printf("int64_t   via PRId64: %" PRId64 "\n", balance_paise);
printf("uint32_t  via PRIu32: %" PRIu32 "\n", account_no);
printf("size_t    via %%zu  : %zu\n", n);
printf("ptrdiff_t via %%td  : %td\n", gap);

Output after the size table in section 2.1:

INT_MAX  = 2147483647
LONG_MAX = 9223372036854775807
SIZE_MAX = 18446744073709551615
int64_t   via PRId64: -123456789012
uint32_t  via PRIu32: 4000000000
size_t    via %zu  : 10
ptrdiff_t via %td  : 5
intmax_t  via %jd  : 9223372036854775807

docs.title: 3.2 Promotions and conversions: code/m02_promotions_and_conversions.c
docs.text:
Nine cases, each with an assert. Two of them compare signed with unsigned on purpose; GCC rejects that under -Werror (-Wsign-compare, part of -Wextra; MSVC warning C4018), so the file turns the warning off for those lines only:

#pragma GCC diagnostic push
#pragma GCC diagnostic ignored "-Wsign-compare"
    int lt = (minus_one < one);            /* -1 becomes 4294967295u, so this is FALSE */
#pragma GCC diagnostic pop

That pragma is for teaching. In real code the warning is telling you to fix the types.

    char buf[64];
    int len = -5;                          /* e.g. a corrupt length field read from the wire */
    int passes_check = (len <= (int)sizeof buf);            /* -5 <= 64: true, check passes */
    size_t what_memcpy_sees = (size_t)len;                  /* 18446744073709551611 */

Output:

1. uint8_t 200 + 100 = 300 in int, 44 when stored back into uint8_t
2. ~(uint8_t)0x0F = -16 as int, 0xF0 after casting back to uint8_t
3. char holding 0xE9 -> -23 as int, 233 via unsigned char
4. (-1 < 1u) is false
5. len=-5 passes 'len <= sizeof buf': yes; memcpy would copy 18446744073709551611 bytes
6. strlen("abc") - strlen("abcdef") = 18446744073709551613
7. (-1 < (size_t)3) is false
8. UINT32_C(1) << 31 = 2147483648, UINT64_C(1) << 40 = 1099511627776
9. int64_t 5000000000 squeezed into int32_t = 705032704

docs.title: 3.3 Overflow: code/m02_overflow.c
docs.text:
This file contains deliberate undefined behaviour (it says so in its header): it calls naive_increment_overflows(INT_MAX), which evaluates INT_MAX + 1. It still compiles cleanly with -Werror, which is the frightening part: no warning at all.

/* UB when x == INT_MAX. GCC folds "x + 1 < x" to 0 (false) even at -O0. */
static int naive_increment_overflows(int x) { return x + 1 < x; }

Output:

naive_increment_overflows(INT_MAX) = 0   <- UB: 0 means the check was deleted
UINT_MAX + 1u = 0                       <- defined: unsigned arithmetic wraps
add_i64_checked(INT64_MAX - 10, 50)   -> rejected, would overflow
__builtin_add_overflow(LLONG_MAX, 1)  -> overflow detected
mul_size_checked(2^62, 8)             -> rejected, would wrap to 0
unchecked (size_t)2^62 * 8            =  0
INT_MIN = -2147483648 has no positive partner: INT_MAX = 2147483647

The first line is 0 at -O0 and at -O2. With -fwrapv it becomes 1 (signed overflow is then defined to wrap). Built with gcc -std=c17 -g -fsanitize=undefined m02_overflow.c, UBSan reports the overflow at run time, and its instrumentation also stops the folding:

m02_overflow.c:21:56: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'
naive_increment_overflows(INT_MAX) = 1   <- UB: 0 means the check was deleted

docs.title: 3.4 Money: code/m02_money_and_float.c
docs.text:
typedef int64_t paise_t;

/* Simple interest for `days` at `rate_bp` basis points a year (1 bp = 0.01 %), ACT/365,

 * rounded half-up to the paisa. Every step is integer arithmetic with an overflow check. */
static bool simple_interest(paise_t principal, int64_t rate_bp, int64_t days, paise_t *out)
{
    if (principal < 0 || rate_bp < 0 || days < 0) return false;
    if (rate_bp != 0 && principal > INT64_MAX / rate_bp) return false;
    int64_t t = principal * rate_bp;
    if (days != 0 && t > INT64_MAX / days) return false;
    t *= days;
    const int64_t denom = 10000 * 365;
    if (t > INT64_MAX - denom / 2) return false;
    *out = (t + denom / 2) / denom;           /* add half the divisor, then truncate: half-up */
    return true;
}

The formatter computes the magnitude as uint64_t so that even INT64_MIN prints correctly (negating INT64_MIN as a signed value would overflow):

uint64_t mag = v < 0 ? (uint64_t)0 - (uint64_t)v : (uint64_t)v;

Output:

0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004, equal to 0.3? no
one million x 0.10: double = 100000.0000013329, int64 paise = 100000.00
printf("%.2f", 2.675) = 2.67 (you expected 2.68)
int64 9007199254740993 -> double -> int64 9007199254740992
interest on 1000000.00 at 7.25% for 30 days = 5958.90
INT64_MIN paise formats as -92233720368547758.08

docs.title: 3.5 Endianness: code/m02_endianness.c
docs.text:
/* The (uint32_t) casts matter: p[0] << 24 alone promotes p[0] to int, and 0x80 << 24 overflows int. */
static uint32_t load_be32(const unsigned char *p)
{
    return (uint32_t)p[0] << 24 | (uint32_t)p[1] << 16 | (uint32_t)p[2] << 8 | (uint32_t)p[3];
}

Output:

this host is little-endian
0x11223344 as stored in memory:    44 33 22 11
store_be32 (network byte order):   11 22 33 44
store_le32:                        44 33 22 11
length 256 sent big-endian: memcpy reads 65536, load_be32 reads 256

The last line is a real protocol bug in one line: a peer sends the length 256 in network order and the x86 receiver memcpys it into a uint32_t, getting 65536.

docs.title: One adder, two interpretations
docs.text: x86 add produces the same bits for signed and unsigned operands and sets two flags: CF (carry, meaning unsigned overflow) and OF (overflow, meaning signed overflow). C exposes neither, which is why checked arithmetic is either a pre-test or a compiler builtin. __builtin_add_overflow on signed operands compiles to add followed by jo (jump if OF); on unsigned, add then jc. Unsigned wrap costs nothing because it is literally what the hardware does.

docs.title: Why signed overflow is undefined: loop optimisation
docs.text: Consider for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i) a[i] = 0; on x86-64. Because signed overflow cannot happen, the compiler may assume the loop runs exactly n + 1 times, keep i in a 64-bit register (no sign-extension on every array access), and vectorise. With an unsigned 32-bit index it must preserve wrap-around at 2^32, which can block both. This is the performance argument the standard committee accepted, and it is also why "obviously harmless" overflow can produce very non-obvious code.

docs.title: Promotions in machine code
docs.text: x86 has 8- and 16-bit registers, but C semantics are defined in int. Loading a char produces movsx (sign-extend, because char is signed); loading an unsigned char produces movzx (zero-extend). When you see a byte value that came out as 0xFFFFFFE9 in a debugger, a movsx on a signed char is why.

docs.title: What the endian helpers compile to
docs.text:
GCC 13 at -O2 recognises the shift-and-or pattern and emits one load, plus bswap for the foreign byte order:

load_be32:
    movl    (%rdi), %eax
    bswap   %eax
    ret
load_le32:
    movl    (%rdi), %eax
    ret

So the portable code costs nothing. There is no reason to cast a buffer to uint32_t *, which is both an alignment hazard and a strict-aliasing violation (module 06).

docs.title: Excess precision: Debug and Release disagree on floating point
docs.text: On 32-bit x86 with the old x87 FPU (gcc -m32 -mfpmath=387, old MSVC /arch:IA32), intermediate results are kept in 80-bit registers and only rounded to 64 bits when stored to memory. Whether a value is spilled to memory depends on optimisation and register pressure, so the same calculation can give different last digits in Debug and Release. FLT_EVAL_METHOD in <float.h> tells you which mode applies (0 on x86-64, where SSE2 is used). One more reason money stays in integers.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The 21-lakh-rupee overflow. A balance or a batch total kept as long paise on Windows, or as int anywhere, overflows at INT32_MAX = 2,147,483,647 paise = 21,474,836.47 rupees. A single large corporate payment or a daily branch total crosses it. Symptoms: totals that turn negative, or reconciliation reports that are off by exactly 2^32 paise. Use int64_t for every amount and every sum of amounts.
  • Windows to Linux port. Code that used long as "the 32-bit type" now has 64-bit values in structs that are written to disk or sent over sockets: record sizes change and old files no longer parse. Code that used long to hold a pointer worked on Linux and truncates on Windows. Use <stdint.h> types in every on-disk and on-wire structure.
  • MSVC C4267 and C4018. conversion from 'size_t' to 'int', possible loss of data and signed/unsigned mismatch appear by the hundred in old code bases and get disabled. Each one is a candidate for the bugs in section 2.5. When a crash involves a length or an index, grep the build log for these warnings on the lines involved.
  • Length fields from the network or from files must be validated as the type you will use them as: reject negative values and values above the buffer size before any conversion. Section 2.5 bug 1 is the root cause of many buffer overflows; see 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/04_the_catalogue_of_memory_bugs.md (integer overflow leading to a bad size).
  • Reconciliation mismatches. Two systems compute the same interest or fee, one in double and one in decimal, and differ by a paisa on some accounts. The fix is to agree on integer or decimal arithmetic and on the rounding rule, not to add a tolerance.
  • Finding these bugs. -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion are noisy but show every silent narrowing (conversion from 'int64_t' to 'int32_t' may change value); turn them on per file when investigating. Run tests with -fsanitize=undefined. On MSVC, /W4 and do not suppress C4244, C4267, C4018.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Without running anything, write down what m02_data_model.c prints on 64-bit Windows. Done when you have the full size table and the data model line, and can name the one line that differs from Linux.
  2. (easy) Before running m02_promotions_and_conversions.c, predict all nine output lines. Done when you can explain each wrong prediction using the rule from section 2.3 or 2.4.
  3. (medium) Write bool mul_i64_checked(int64_t a, int64_t b, int64_t *out) without builtins, covering all sign combinations and INT64_MIN * -1. Done when a loop of 100,000 random pairs (include the edge values 0, 1, -1, INT64_MAX, INT64_MIN) agrees with __builtin_mul_overflow on every pair.
  4. (medium) Write three correct versions of "visit indices n-1 down to 0" with a size_t index, and one deliberately broken version. Done when the broken one triggers -Wtype-limits and the three correct ones handle n == 0 without touching the array.
  5. (medium) Monthly compound interest: 1,00,000.00 rupees at 9 % a year for 12 months, rounding to the paisa every month. Implement it once with double and once with int64_t paise using half-even rounding. Done when you print both results side by side and can explain any difference, and your integer version matches a hand calculation for month 1.
  6. (hard) Write load_be64, store_be64, and a parser for a 16-byte header (u32 magic, u16 version, u16 opcode, u64 length, all big-endian). Compile with -O2 -S. Done when you can show the bswap (or movbe with -march=native on a CPU that has it) in the assembly and your test round-trips 1000 random headers.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between LP64 and LLP64, and why does it matter? LP64 (Linux, macOS) has 64-bit long and pointers; LLP64 (64-bit Windows) keeps long at 32 bits and makes only long long and pointers 64-bit. Code that stores pointers, file sizes or large amounts in long works on one and truncates on the other, and struct layouts written to disk change. Use <stdint.h> fixed-width types and intptr_t where the size matters.

Q: What are the integer promotions? What is (uint8_t)200 + (uint8_t)100? Operands narrower than int are converted to int (or unsigned int if int cannot hold them) before arithmetic. So the sum is the int 300; it only becomes 44 if stored back into a uint8_t. The same rule makes ~ on a uint8_t produce a negative int.

Q: What does -1 < 1u evaluate to, and why? False. Under the usual arithmetic conversions, int meeting unsigned int converts the int to unsigned int, so -1 becomes UINT_MAX. The same happens with size_t, which is why comparing a signed length with sizeof is dangerous, and why -Wsign-compare exists.

Q: Why is signed overflow undefined while unsigned overflow is defined? How do you check for it? Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo 2^N, matching the hardware. Signed overflow is undefined so the compiler can assume it does not happen, which enables loop and range optimisations; as a result checks written as a + b < a are deleted. Check before the operation with comparisons that cannot overflow (a > INT64_MAX - b), or use __builtin_add_overflow / C23 ckd_add.

Q: How do you print an int64_t and a size_t portably? printf("%" PRId64, x) using the macro from <inttypes.h>, because int64_t is long on Linux and long long on Windows; and %zu for size_t. A mismatched specifier is undefined behaviour and on 64-bit platforms prints garbage.

Q: Why should money never be stored in a double, and what do you use instead? Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift, rounding at display differs from expectations, and summing in a different order gives different totals. Use integers of the smallest unit (int64_t paise) or a decimal type such as SQL NUMERIC, and define the rounding rule explicitly.

Q: How do you read a big-endian 32-bit integer from a byte buffer portably? Assemble it with shifts on uint32_t-cast bytes: (uint32_t)p[0] << 24 | (uint32_t)p[1] << 16 | (uint32_t)p[2] << 8 | p[3]. It is independent of host byte order and alignment, avoids strict-aliasing problems, and compilers turn it into a single load plus bswap.

Q: What is wrong with for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; --i)? i >= 0 is always true for an unsigned type, so after 0 the index wraps to SIZE_MAX and the loop reads far out of bounds; it also misbehaves for n == 0. Use for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; ).

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Only minimum ranges are guaranteed; the data model decides the rest. Linux is LP64, Windows is LLP64: long is the difference.
  • Two's complement: -1 is all ones, the range is asymmetric, INT_MIN has no positive partner.
  • Integer promotion: anything narrower than int becomes int before arithmetic.
  • Usual arithmetic conversions: signed meets unsigned of equal or higher rank, the signed value becomes unsigned; -1 < 1u is false; -1L < 1u differs between Linux and Windows.
  • Signed overflow is UB and checks after the fact get deleted; unsigned wraps. Check before you compute, or use the builtins / C23 ckd_*.
  • size_t for sizes (%zu), ptrdiff_t for pointer differences (%td), PRId64 for int64_t; a wrong format specifier is UB.
  • Use <stdint.h> exact-width types for disk, network and money.
  • Money is int64_t minor units or a decimal type, with an explicit rounding rule; never double.
  • Endianness only matters at boundaries; read and write multi-byte fields with shifts, which cost one instruction after optimisation.

docs.title: 03. Pointers from the ground up
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 02

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Memory is a very long street of numbered houses. Each house holds one byte. The house number is the address. A variable is a group of neighbouring houses with a name: an int occupies four houses, a double eight.

A pointer is a slip of paper with a house number written on it. The slip itself also lives in some houses (eight of them on a 64-bit machine). Two operators move you between the slip and the house:

  • &x asks "what is the house number of x?" and gives you a slip.
  • *p says "go to the house written on slip p" and lets you read or change what lives there.

The pointer's type tells C how many houses the thing at that address occupies and how to read them. That is why p + 1 on an int * moves four houses, not one: it moves to the next int.

Everything confusing about pointers comes from a handful of rules: arrays are not pointers but turn into one at the slightest touch; sizeof sees the difference and nothing else does; const can apply to the slip or to the house; a pointer to a pointer is a slip that tells you where another slip is kept. This module draws each of these as memory, because when you read a crash dump, memory is all you get.

docs.title: 2.1 Objects, addresses and pointer variables
docs.text:
int x = 7;
int *p = &x;

On a 64-bit little-endian machine (addresses invented for the picture):

 address    bytes                       name   type
 0x1000     07 00 00 00                 x      int        (4 bytes)
 0x1004     .. .. .. ..                 (padding or something else)
 0x1008     00 10 00 00 00 00 00 00     p      int *      (8 bytes, holds 0x1000)

   p ──────────────► x
 [0x1000]           [7]
  • p is an object like any other. It has its own address (&p is 0x1008, of type int **).
  • *p is an lvalue (something with a location) referring to x. *p = 8; changes x.
  • C has no references. "Pass by reference" in C means passing a pointer by value (set_to_42(&x) in section 3.1).

Declaration syntax mirrors use: int *p reads "*p is an int". The * binds to the name, not the type, which is why this declares one pointer and one int:

int* a, b;     /* a is int *, b is int. Write one declaration per line, star next to the name. */

docs.title: 2.2 Pointer arithmetic
docs.text:
Adding n to a pointer moves it by n * sizeof(*p) bytes. Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them, as a ptrdiff_t.

int ia[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40};          (int is 4 bytes)

 address   0x2000  0x2004  0x2008  0x200C  0x2010
           [ 10 ]  [ 20 ]  [ 30 ]  [ 40 ]  (one past the end)
             ^       ^                       ^
            ia      ia+1                    ia+4  may be formed and compared, never dereferenced

 &ia[3] - &ia[0] == 3 elements == 12 bytes

a[i] is defined as *(a + i). Addition commutes, so i[a] is legal and means the same thing; you will only ever see it in quiz questions.

The rules that matter in production:

  • You may form pointers to every element of an array and to one past the last element. Computing any other out-of-range pointer is undefined, even if you never dereference it (p - 1 when p points at element 0 is already UB).
  • Subtracting or comparing (<, >) pointers is only defined within the same array (or object). == and != are fine between any two pointers.
  • A plain object counts as an array of one element for these rules.

docs.title: 2.3 Arrays are not pointers: decay
docs.text:
An array is a block of N elements. Its name is not a variable holding an address: there is no pointer stored anywhere. But in almost every expression, an array is converted ("decays") into a pointer to its first element. The three exceptions:

  1. operand of sizeof: sizeof arr is the size of the whole array;
  2. operand of unary &: &arr has type "pointer to array of N", same address, different type;
  3. a string literal used to initialise a char array: char s[] = "hello"; copies the bytes.
char s1[] = "hello";          char *s2 = "hello";   (better: const char *)

 s1: [h][e][l][l][o][\0]       s2: [0x4010] ─────► [h][e][l][l][o][\0]   (read-only page)
     6 bytes, writable             8-byte pointer   string literal, shared, not writable
 sizeof s1 == 6                sizeof s2 == 8

Because of decay, a function can never receive an array. These three parameter declarations are identical: all three declare int *a.

void f(int a[10]);    void f(int a[]);    void f(int *a);

GCC warns if you take sizeof of such a parameter:

w1.c:2:46: warning: 'sizeof' on array function parameter 'arr' will return size of 'int *' [-Wsizeof-array-argument]
    2 | static size_t f(int arr[10]) { return sizeof arr; }

So every function that takes an array must also take its length, or use a sentinel such as the terminating NUL of a string.

The extern trap. One file defines int table[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; and another declares extern int *table;. It links (symbols have no types, module 01). The second file now reads the first 8 bytes of the array, 01 00 00 00 02 00 00 00, as a pointer (0x0000000200000001) and dereferences it. The declaration must match: extern int table[];.

docs.title: 2.4 sizeof traps
docs.text:
Expression Value on x86-64 Why sizeof arr where int arr[10] 40 whole array sizeof arr inside f(int arr[10]) 8 it is a pointer sizeof p where char *p = "hello" 8 size of the pointer sizeof "hello" 6 array of 6 chars, NUL included strlen("hello") 5 characters before the NUL sizeof *p where struct account *p size of the struct does not dereference: sizeof does not evaluate its operand

Two allocation idioms remove a whole class of bugs:

struct account *a = malloc(sizeof *a);          /* not sizeof(struct account): stays right if the type changes */
int *v = malloc(n * sizeof *v);                  /* not sizeof(int *), not sizeof v */
memset(a, 0, sizeof *a);                         /* not sizeof a: that is 8 bytes */

malloc(sizeof p) instead of malloc(sizeof *p) allocates 8 bytes for a struct of 64, and every write after the eighth byte corrupts the heap. -Wall does not catch it.

#define ARRAY_LEN(a) (sizeof(a) / sizeof((a)[0])) works only on real arrays; on a pointer it silently returns 8 / sizeof(element).

docs.title: 2.5 Pointers to pointers
docs.text:
A T ** points at a T *. You need one when a function must change the caller's pointer:

struct node *head = NULL;          push_front(&head, 7);

 main's frame                      push_front's frame
 head: [NULL] ◄──────────────────  head: [&main.head]       (struct node **)
                                   *head = n;  writes into main's variable
 after:
 head: [0x5000] ───► node@0x5000 { value 7, next NULL }

Without the extra level, push_front(head, 7) would receive a copy of NULL, change the copy, and leak the node.

The same idea gives the cleanest linked-list removal. Instead of tracking "previous node" and special-casing the head, walk with a pointer to the link that leads to the current node:

 head ──► [7| ]──► [4| ]──► [7| ]──► NULL
  ^          ^
  link       link after one step = &first_node->next
 if (*link)->value matches:  *link = (*link)->next  rewires whichever pointer led here

remove_all in section 3.3 is six lines and has no head special case.

Other common ** uses: char **argv (an array of string pointers), out-parameters that return an allocated object (int make_greeting(const char *name, char **out)), and jagged 2-D arrays.

docs.title: 2.6 const placement
docs.text:
Read the declaration from the name outwards, right to left:

Declaration Read as Change the pointer? Change the pointee? const int *p p is a pointer to const int yes no int const *p same as above yes no int *const p p is a const pointer to int no yes const int *const p const pointer to const int no no

In an API, const on the pointee is a promise: size_t strlen(const char *s) promises not to write through s. Use it on every parameter you only read. It documents the contract and lets the compiler reject accidental writes.

Two rules people get wrong:

  • char ** does not convert implicitly to const char **. If it did, you could store a pointer to a truly const string into the const char **, then write through the original char **. C++ does allow the safe version, char ** to const char *const *, implicitly; C does not, so C code needs a cast even there.
  • Casting away const is legal; writing to an object that was defined const (or to a string literal) is undefined behaviour and usually a crash, because such objects live in read-only pages.

docs.title: 2.7 void * and NULL
docs.text:
void * is the generic object pointer. Any object pointer converts to void * and back implicitly in C (C++ requires a cast, which is why code bases compiled as C++ cast the result of malloc). What you cannot do with a void *:

  • dereference it (there is no type to read);
  • do arithmetic on it (GCC allows it as an extension and treats it as char *; -Wpedantic flags it). Convert to unsigned char * to walk bytes;
  • convert a function pointer to it, in ISO C. POSIX requires it to work because dlsym returns void *, and on all mainstream platforms it does.

qsort, bsearch, memcpy and every generic container in C are built on void * plus an element size plus a callback; section 3.5 shows the pattern.

NULL is a null pointer constant (0 or ((void *)0)). A null pointer compares unequal to every pointer to an object. Dereferencing it is undefined. On Linux and Windows the first pages of the address space are never mapped, so it faults: SIGSEGV on Linux, access violation 0xC0000005 on Windows. Note that p->field with p == NULL faults at address offsetof(field), not 0: a struct field at offset 0x20 faults at 0x20. C23 adds nullptr.

docs.title: 2.8 Two-dimensional arrays
docs.text:
int grid[3][4] is an array of 3 elements, each of which is an array of 4 ints, stored row-major (one row after another):

grid[0][0] grid[0][1] grid[0][2] grid[0][3] grid[1][0] ... grid[2][3]
[   0    ][   1    ][   2    ][   3    ][   10   ] ... [   23   ]
 \_____________ row 0 ______________/ \___ row 1 ...
 grid decays to int (*)[4]: a pointer to a whole row; +1 skips 16 bytes

A function that takes it must know the column count: int sum(const int (*m)[4], int rows) (or int m[][4]). Three ways to have a 2-D structure at run time:

 contiguous (one malloc):   int (*m)[COLS] = malloc(rows * sizeof *m);
   m ──► [r0c0 r0c1 r0c2 r0c3 | r1c0 ... ]          m[r][c]: one load, address = m + r*16 + c*4

 flat (one malloc, manual index):   int *m = malloc(rows * cols * sizeof *m);   m[r * cols + c]

 jagged (array of row pointers):   int **m;
   m ──► [ptr0][ptr1][ptr2]
           │     │     └──► [r2c0 r2c1]
           │     └────────► [r1c0 r1c1 r1c2]
           └──────────────► [r0c0]                  m[r][c]: TWO loads, rows can differ in length

The jagged form uses the same m[r][c] syntax for completely different memory, and int ** is not compatible with int (*)[4]. Passing one where the other is expected (with a cast to silence the compiler) reads row pointers as if they were integers. C99 also allows variably-modified parameters, void f(int rows, int cols, int m[rows][cols]); GCC supports them, MSVC does not (they are VLA types).

docs.title: 2.9 Returning pointers
docs.text: A function may return a pointer to: a static object, heap memory, or memory the caller passed in. It must never return the address of one of its own local variables, because that storage is reused by the next function call. Module 04 shows all four options and the bug. Whenever a function returns a pointer, its comment must say who owns the memory and how long it stays valid.

docs.title: 2.10 restrict
docs.text: restrict (C99) on a pointer parameter is a promise: during this call, the object it points to is accessed only through this pointer. The compiler may then keep values in registers across writes through other pointers, and vectorise loops. memcpy is declared with restrict parameters; that is the formal reason overlapping copies must use memmove. Breaking the promise is undefined behaviour, and the compiler will not warn you. Section 4 shows the generated code.

docs.title: 3.1 Basics and arithmetic: code/m03_pointer_basics.c

docs.title: 3.3 const and pointer-to-pointer: code/m03_const_and_double_pointers.c
docs.text:
/* Pointer-to-pointer removal: `link` points at whichever pointer leads to the current node

 * (the head variable, or some node's next field), so the head needs no special case. */
static void remove_all(struct node **link, int value)
{
    while (*link != NULL) {
        if ((*link)->value == value) {
            struct node *dead = *link;
            *link = dead->next;
            free(dead);
        } else {
            link = &(*link)->next;
        }
    }
}

/* Out-parameter allocation. On success returns 0 and *out owns a malloc'd string (caller frees).

 * On failure returns -1 and *out is untouched. */

/* Linear search over any array: base address, count, element size, and an equality callback.

 * This is the same shape as the standard qsort and bsearch. */
static void *find_any(const void *base, size_t n, size_t size, const void *key,
                      int (*equal)(const void *elem, const void *key))
{
    const unsigned char *p = base;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i, p += size)
        if (equal(p, key)) return (void *)p;     /* like bsearch: returns non-const */
    return NULL;
}

docs.title: What pointer operations compile to
docs.text:
A pointer is an address held in a register; *p is a load or a store. x86-64 addressing modes compute base + index * scale + displacement in one instruction, with scale 1, 2, 4 or 8, which is exactly C's pointer arithmetic. GCC 13 -O2 (CET instructions removed):

int get(const int *a, long i) { return a[i]; }
long long bal(const struct account *p) { return p->balance; }   /* balance at offset 8 */
int get2d(int (*m)[4], long r, long c) { return m[r][c]; }
int getjag(int **m, long r, long c) { return m[r][c]; }

get:
    movl    (%rdi,%rsi,4), %eax      # a + i*4: one load
    ret
bal:
    movq    8(%rdi), %rax            # p + 8: field offset is a displacement
    ret
get2d:
    salq    $4, %rsi                 # r * 16 (one row = 16 bytes)
    addq    %rsi, %rdi
    movl    (%rdi,%rdx,4), %eax      # one load of data
    ret
getjag:
    movq    (%rdi,%rsi,8), %rax      # FIRST load: the row pointer m[r]
    movl    (%rax,%rdx,4), %eax      # SECOND load: the element
    ret

The jagged version needs two dependent loads, and each row may be anywhere in the heap, which costs cache misses. Contiguous storage is the default for performance; jagged is for rows of different lengths.

docs.title: Arrays have no pointer object
docs.text: For a local int a[10], the compiler knows a as "rsp + some offset"; for a global, as a symbol address. There is no memory cell holding "the address of a". That is why &a and a have the same value, and why the extern int *table mismatch is so destructive: the code generated for a pointer loads 8 bytes from the symbol and uses them as an address, while the code for an array uses the symbol's address directly.

docs.title: Virtual addresses and what a bad pointer does
docs.text:
A pointer holds a virtual address. The MMU translates it through page tables on every access (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/01_process_memory_layout.md). On x86-64 only 48 bits of address are used (57 with 5-level paging); the upper bits must be copies of bit 47 ("canonical" addresses). So a bad pointer fails in one of three ways:

Pointer value What happens Linux report unmapped page (NULL, small offsets, freed and unmapped) page fault, no mapping SIGSEGV, si_addr = the address mapped page you may not write (literal, code) page fault, protection SIGSEGV, si_addr = the address non-canonical (garbage like 0x4141414141414141) general protection fault SIGSEGV, si_code 128 (SI_KERNEL), si_addr 0

Verified on WSL with gdb's $_siginfo: dereferencing 0x4141414141414141 gives si_code = 128 and si_addr = 0x0, while p->field with p == NULL and field at offset 0x20 gives si_addr = 0x20. So a "fault at address 0" can actually be a garbage pointer, not a NULL: look at the register used by the faulting instruction before concluding.

The most dangerous bad pointer is the one that points into mapped, writable memory: a dangling pointer into the heap or a wild pointer into another object. It does not fault. It corrupts, and the crash happens later somewhere else (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/04_the_catalogue_of_memory_bugs.md).

docs.title: restrict in the generated code
docs.text:
update_twice:
    movl    $1, (%rdi)
    movl    $2, (%rsi)
    movl    (%rdi), %eax        # must reload *a: b might point to the same int
    ret
update_twice_restrict:
    movl    $1, (%rdi)
    movl    $1, %eax            # returns the constant: the promise says *a was not changed
    movl    $2, (%rsi)
    ret

Call the second function with two pointers to the same int and it returns 1 while the int holds 2. That is what "undefined behaviour" looks like in practice: the code does exactly what the promise allowed, not what you meant.

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text: Every type has an alignment requirement (_Alignof(int) is 4, _Alignof(double) 8 on x86-64). Dereferencing a misaligned pointer is undefined. x86 hardware tolerates most misaligned scalar loads, so the bug hides there, but ARM may fault, and even on x86 the compiler may emit aligned SSE instructions (movaps) that do fault when it assumes alignment. Casting a char buffer at an odd offset to int * is therefore a real bug even on Intel. Use memcpy (module 06).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Reading pointer values in a crash dump. The value of the bad pointer is evidence. On Windows Debug builds and debug heaps, these patterns are classic:

    Value Usual meaning 0x00000000 plus a small offset NULL pointer, faulting on a field at that offset 0xCCCCCCCC uninitialised stack variable (MSVC /RTC1) 0xCDCDCDCD uninitialised heap memory (MSVC Debug CRT) 0xDDDDDDDD memory already freed (MSVC Debug CRT) 0xFDFDFDFD guard bytes just outside a Debug CRT block: an overflow by a few bytes 0xFEEEFEEE memory freed by HeapFree with heap debugging on non-canonical, ASCII-looking (0x4141...) a string overwrote a pointer: buffer overflow

    glibc has no fill by default; MALLOC_PERTURB_=165 makes it fill allocated and freed memory so the same bugs show up on Linux. See 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/07_windbg_and_windows_crash_dumps.md.

  • sizeof of the wrong thing. memset(req, 0, sizeof req) clears 8 bytes of a 400-byte request; the rest keeps the previous request's data. This is a classic in server code that reuses buffers: one client sees fields of another. Always sizeof *req.
  • Array length lost at a function boundary. A helper written for a fixed array is later called with a shorter buffer and uses ARRAY_LEN on its parameter (8 / 4 = 2 elements) or a hard-coded size. Pass lengths explicitly; never compute them from a parameter.
  • Off-by-one in pointer loops. for (p = buf; p <= buf + len; ++p) touches one element past the end. Use < with one-past-the-end and say so in a comment.
  • Pointers into a buffer that moves. A pointer into a growable buffer is invalid after the buffer is realloced. In a server that parses a request in place while still receiving bytes, a pointer kept from before the buffer grew points into freed memory. Store offsets, not pointers, into growable buffers.
  • extern mismatches between a definition and a hand-written declaration in another file (array versus pointer, int versus long). Every global should be declared in exactly one header that the defining file also includes.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) For int x = 5; int *p = &x; int **pp = &p; draw the memory with invented addresses, then verify in gdb with p &x, p p, p &p, p *pp, p **pp and x/4xb &x. Done when your drawing matches gdb exactly (apart from the actual address values).
  2. (easy) Predict, then check: sizeof of int a[5], &a, *&a, a + 0, "abc", (char *)"abc", a[0], and of a struct { char c; double d; }. Done when all eight predictions are right or you can explain each miss.
  3. (medium) Implement remove_all twice: once with a prev pointer and an explicit head case, once with the pointer-to-pointer technique. Done when both pass the same test (remove from head, middle, tail, all nodes, no nodes) and Valgrind reports no leaks.
  4. (medium) Write int **matrix_new(int rows, int cols) that makes a jagged-looking matrix with one malloc: the row-pointer array followed by the data, with row pointers pointing into the data part. Done when m[r][c] works, a single free(m) releases everything, and you have checked the alignment of the data part.
  5. (medium) Reproduce the extern trap: a.c defines int table[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};, b.c declares extern int *table; and prints table[0]. Done when you have the crash, the faulting address from gdb, and can explain why that address is 0x200000001.
  6. (hard) Write a generic void isort(void *base, size_t n, size_t size, int (*cmp)(const void *, const void *)) (insertion sort, same contract as qsort) using only unsigned char * arithmetic and memcpy through a temporary buffer. Done when it sorts ints, doubles and a 40-byte struct correctly and matches qsort on 1000 random arrays.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between an array and a pointer? An array is a block of elements; a pointer is a variable holding an address. In most expressions an array decays to a pointer to its first element, which is why they look alike. They differ under sizeof (whole array versus pointer size), under & (pointer to array versus pointer to pointer), in assignability, and in how an extern declaration is compiled.

Q: When does an array not decay to a pointer? As the operand of sizeof, as the operand of unary &, and when a string literal initialises a char array. Also, function parameters declared as arrays are adjusted to pointers, so inside the function sizeof gives the pointer size.

Q: What is the difference between const int *p and int *const p? const int *p is a pointer to a const int: you can move p but not write *p. int *const p is a const pointer to an int: you can write *p but not change p. Read the declaration right to left from the name.

Q: Why would a function take a T **? To modify the caller's pointer: allocate and return an object through an out-parameter, insert at the head of a list, or advance a caller's parsing position. It is also the type of an array of pointers, such as argv. The pointer-to-link technique uses it to remove list nodes without a head special case.

Q: What can you not do with a void *? Dereference it or do arithmetic on it in standard C; you convert it to a concrete pointer type first (unsigned char * for bytes). ISO C also does not allow converting function pointers to void *, although POSIX requires it for dlsym. In C, void * converts implicitly to any object pointer, unlike C++.

Q: What does restrict do? It promises the compiler that, for the duration of the call, the pointed-to object is accessed only through that pointer. The compiler can then avoid reloading values after writes through other pointers and can vectorise. Violating the promise is undefined behaviour; memcpy has restrict parameters, which is why overlapping copies need memmove.

Q: What does p + 1 do for int *p versus char *p? It moves by sizeof(*p) bytes: 4 for an int * on common platforms, 1 for a char *. Pointer subtraction similarly returns a count of elements, as ptrdiff_t.

Q: A Windows crash dump shows the faulting pointer is 0xDDDDDDDD. What does that tell you? In a Debug build, the Debug CRT fills freed heap blocks with 0xDD, so the code read a pointer out of an object that was already freed: a use-after-free. 0xCDCDCDCD would point to uninitialised heap memory and 0xCCCCCCCC to an uninitialised stack variable.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A pointer is an object holding an address; & takes an address, * follows one.
  • p + n moves n * sizeof *p bytes; pointer subtraction counts elements (ptrdiff_t).
  • Valid pointers: into an object or one past its end; anything else is UB even without dereferencing.
  • Arrays decay to pointers except under sizeof, & and string-literal initialisation; array parameters are pointers.
  • malloc(n * sizeof *p), memset(p, 0, sizeof *p): size the pointee, never the pointer.
  • Use T ** to change the caller's pointer; the pointer-to-link trick simplifies list removal.
  • const left of * protects the pointee; right of * protects the pointer.
  • void * is generic, converts implicitly in C, has no arithmetic and no dereference.
  • Contiguous 2-D arrays need one load per access; jagged int ** needs two.
  • restrict is a promise the compiler will exploit; break it and you get wrong results silently.
  • In a dump, the pointer value itself (0x0+offset, 0xCD..., 0xDD..., non-canonical) tells you the bug class.

docs.title: 04. Memory: storage duration, scope and lifetime
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 01, 03

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Every object in C has a lifetime: the period during which it exists and its memory is reserved for it. Separately, every name has a scope: the region of source code where the name can be used. The two are easy to confuse, and most memory bugs live in the gap between them.

Analogy: a hotel. The storage duration is how the room is booked. An automatic variable gets a room until the function checks out. A static variable is a permanent resident for the life of the program. Heap memory from malloc is booked until someone explicitly checks out with free. A thread-local variable is one room per guest thread. The scope is only whose name is on the door directory. A dangling pointer is a room key kept after checkout: the key still opens the door, but the room now belongs to someone else, and what you find (or break) in there is not yours.

C gives you no automatic cleanup (C++ has destructors: 02_Modern_CPP/03_raii_the_core_idea.md). So in C the question "who frees this, and when?" must be answered by convention, written down in comments. This module covers the rules of each storage duration, the exact contracts of malloc, calloc, realloc and free, how to write ownership down, and the arena allocator: the pattern behind the "arena allocator with explicit ownership contracts" line on your resume.

docs.title: 2.1 The four storage durations
docs.text:
Duration How you get it Starts Ends Initial value Where it lives automatic local variable, parameter, compound literal in a block entry to its block exit from its block indeterminate (garbage) unless initialised stack, or only in registers static file-scope variable, or static local before main program exit zero, or the constant initialiser .data (initialised), .bss (zero) allocated malloc, calloc, realloc, aligned_alloc the call free (or realloc that moves it) indeterminate (calloc: zero) heap thread _Thread_local (C11; thread_local in C23) thread start thread exit zero, or the constant initialiser per-thread TLS block

Two details people miss:

  • An automatic object's lifetime ends at the end of its block, not its function. A pointer to a variable declared inside an if or a loop body is dangling once that block ends.
  • Static objects are initialised before main, with constant expressions only. A static local is not "initialised on first call" as in C++; it already has its value when the program starts.

docs.title: 2.2 Scope, lifetime and linkage are three different things
docs.text:
Declaration Scope (where the name works) Lifetime (when the object exists) Linkage int x; inside a function the block the block's execution none static int x; inside a function the block the whole program none static int x; at file scope rest of the file the whole program internal int x; at file scope rest of the file (other files via extern) the whole program external malloc(n) no name at all until free n/a

A static local is the case that shows the difference best: its name is visible only inside the function, but the object outlives every call. That is why a function can safely return a pointer to a static local (with the caveats in section 3.4) but never to an automatic one.

docs.title: 2.3 Every meaning of static and extern
docs.text:
Where Keyword Meaning file scope, object or function static internal linkage: private to this translation unit block scope, object static static storage duration: one object for the whole program file or block scope extern declaration only; the definition is elsewhere (external linkage) array parameter static void f(int a[static 10]) (C99): caller promises at least 10 elements, and that a is not NULL

The last one is rare but it is a fair interview curiosity, and GCC 13 uses it to check callers: passing a 4-element array gives 'sum10' reading 40 bytes from a region of size 16 [-Wstringop-overread], and passing NULL gives argument 1 to 'int[static 10]' is null where non-null expected [-Wnonnull].

docs.title: 2.4 Stack frames
docs.text:
Each function call pushes a frame on the calling thread's stack: the return address, saved registers, and space for locals that do not fit in registers. Returning pops it, and the next call reuses the same memory.

 higher addresses
 ┌──────────────────────────┐
 │ main's frame             │
 │   int n = 1              │
 │   char out[16]           │
 ├──────────────────────────┤ ◄── frame of format_id_bug() while it runs
 │ return address into main │
 │ saved rbp                │
 │ char buf[16] "ACC-000005"│ ◄── the function returns &buf[0] ...
 ├──────────────────────────┤
 │ (free stack)             │     ... and after the return this region is
 └──────────────────────────┘         reused by the next call (printf, say)
 lower addresses (the stack grows down on x86-64)

Stack sizes are small and fixed: 8 MiB for the main thread on Linux (ulimit -s prints 8192 on WSL) and, by default, for threads created by glibc; 1 MiB by default on Windows, for the main thread and for CreateThread, unless the linker option /STACK or the dwStackSize argument says otherwise. A 64 KiB local buffer in a function that is three levels deep in a recursive parser is how Windows servers die with exception 0xC00000FD (stack overflow). Frame layout and calling conventions in detail: 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/02_stack_frames_and_calling_conventions.md.

docs.title: 2.5 The heap API: exact contracts
docs.text: Function Contract void *malloc(size_t n) Returns uninitialised memory aligned for any type (_Alignof(max_align_t), 16 on x86-64 glibc), or NULL. malloc(0) returns NULL or a unique pointer (glibc: non-NULL) that you must still free. void *calloc(size_t count, size_t size) Like malloc(count * size) but zero-filled and checks the multiplication for overflow (returns NULL). void *realloc(void *p, size_t n) Resizes. May move the block: contents up to the smaller size are copied, the old block is freed, and every old pointer into it is now dangling. On failure returns NULL and leaves the old block untouched and still yours. realloc(NULL, n) is malloc(n). realloc(p, 0) is implementation-defined in C17 and undefined in C23: never use it. void free(void *p) p must come from this allocator and not be freed yet. free(NULL) does nothing. After free, the pointer's value is indeterminate: even comparing it is formally undefined. void *aligned_alloc(size_t align, size_t n) C11, for alignments above 16 (cache lines, pages). Not provided by MSVC: use _aligned_malloc and _aligned_free there (and they must be paired). POSIX alternative: posix_memalign.

docs.title: 2.6 The realloc-leak idiom
docs.text:
/* WRONG */
b->data = realloc(b->data, cap);   /* on failure: NULL overwrites the only pointer to the old block */

/* RIGHT */
char *p = realloc(b->data, cap);
if (p == NULL) return -1;          /* b->data is still valid and still owned */
b->data = p;

The wrong version leaks the old block and leaves the struct claiming len bytes of data at a NULL pointer, so the next access crashes. It only misbehaves when realloc fails, which is why it survives code review and testing and then appears under memory pressure in production.

Also check the size arithmetic before calling: n * size can wrap (module 02), and doubling a capacity can wrap. calloc checks its own multiplication; malloc and realloc do not.

docs.title: 2.7 Writing ownership down
docs.text:
C has no destructor and no smart pointer, so every pointer in an interface needs a sentence saying who owns the memory. Use the same small vocabulary everywhere:

Phrase in the comment Meaning Returns an owned pointer; free with x_free() caller must release it, with exactly that function Borrows p callee uses it during the call only; does not keep it, does not free it Borrowed result, valid until ... caller must not free it; say what invalidates it (next call, x_reset, x_free(parent)) Takes ownership of p callee will free it; caller must not touch it afterwards. Say what happens on failure: does the callee still free it? Caller provides buf, bufsz no ownership transfer at all; usually the best API

Paired functions make the rules mechanical:

  • x_new() / x_free() for objects the library allocates (opaque types, module 06);
  • x_init(&x) / x_destroy(&x) for objects the caller allocates (on the stack, or inside another struct) but that own resources inside.

x_free(NULL) should do nothing, like free(NULL), so that cleanup paths stay simple. After freeing a pointer that lives on in a struct, set it to NULL so a second cleanup is harmless. Module 10 of this course (10_error_handling_and_resource_cleanup.md) builds error handling and goto-cleanup on top of these rules. How C++ encodes the same contracts in types is in 02_Modern_CPP/05_smart_pointers_and_ownership.md and 09_OOP_Design_Patterns_Architecture/03_ownership_and_object_lifetime_design.md.

docs.title: 2.8 Alignment
docs.text:
Every type has an alignment: its address must be a multiple of _Alignof(T) (alignof with <stdalign.h>). A struct's alignment is the largest alignment of its members. malloc returns memory aligned for max_align_t, so it is good for any standard type. When you carve your own allocations out of a big block (an arena, a pool, a buffer), you must align each one yourself:

/* round x up to a multiple of a, where a is a power of two */
uintptr_t aligned = (x + (a - 1)) & ~(uintptr_t)(a - 1);

_Alignas(64) char buf[256]; over-aligns an object (for example to a cache line, to avoid false sharing: 04_Concurrency/10_cache_lines_false_sharing_performance.md).

docs.title: 2.9 VLAs and alloca: avoid
docs.text:
int vla[n]; (a variable length array, C99) and alloca(n) both allocate n-dependent space on the stack. In server code they are a liability:

  • There is no failure path. If n is too big, the program does not get NULL: it runs off the end of the stack and crashes, or worse, jumps over the guard page into other memory.
  • If n comes from a request (a length field), an attacker chooses your stack usage.
  • MSVC never supported VLAs; C11 made them optional; alloca is not standard at all.

Use a fixed-size local buffer for the common small case and fall back to malloc for the rare large case. GCC's -Wvla flags every VLA (ISO C90 forbids variable length array 'vla').

docs.title: 2.10 Returning the address of a local
docs.text:
static char *format_id_bug(int id)
{
    char buf[16];
    snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "ACC-%06d", id);
    return buf;                 /* buf's lifetime ends here */
}

GCC warns even without -Wall:

m04_returning_buffers.c:60:12: warning: function returns address of local variable [-Wreturn-local-addr]

And GCC 13 then compiles the function to return NULL, so the bug becomes a clean crash at the first use. Other compilers return the real stack address, the caller reads the string successfully (the bytes are still there), and the program "works" until the next function call overwrites that stack region. Section 3.4 shows the four correct alternatives.

docs.title: 3.1 Storage durations side by side: code/m04_storage_durations.c
docs.text:
int g_total_calls;                  /* static storage, file scope, EXTERNAL linkage, starts at 0 */
static int s_module_calls;          /* static storage, file scope, INTERNAL linkage, starts at 0 */
static _Thread_local int t_calls;   /* thread storage: every thread gets its own copy, starts at 0 */

static int next_sequence(void)
{
    static int seq = 100;           /* static storage, BLOCK scope: initialised once, before main,
                                       and keeps its value between calls */
    ++g_total_calls;
    ++s_module_calls;
    return seq++;
}

static int worker(void *arg)
{
    int n = *(const int *)arg;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        ++t_calls;                  /* no lock: no other thread can see this thread's t_calls */
    return t_calls;
}

It uses C11 <threads.h> (thrd_create, thrd_join); glibc 2.34 and later need no -pthread.

static: seq continued 100 -> 101, g_total_calls = 2, s_module_calls = 2
automatic: automatic_demo() returned 6 twice (fresh local each call)
allocated: block freed, and the copy of its address is now dangling
thread: A counted 1000, B counted 250, main's own t_calls is still 0

docs.title: 3.2 Heap contracts and a growable buffer: code/m04_malloc_contracts.c
docs.text:
/* A growable byte buffer.

 * OWNERSHIP: a struct buf owns `data`. Release with buf_free(). Copying the struct by value
 * creates two owners of one block: do not do it. */
struct buf {
    char  *data;
    size_t len;
    size_t cap;
};

/* Ensures cap >= need. On failure returns -1 and leaves *b UNCHANGED and still valid. */
static int buf_reserve(struct buf *b, size_t need)
{
    if (need <= b->cap) return 0;
    size_t cap = b->cap ? b->cap : 16;
    while (cap < need) {
        if (cap > SIZE_MAX / 2) return -1;          /* doubling would wrap */
        cap *= 2;
    }
    char *p = realloc(b->data, cap);
    if (p == NULL) return -1;                       /* b->data still points to the old block */
    b->data = p;                                    /* the block may have MOVED */
    b->cap = cap;
    return 0;
}

static void buf_free(struct buf *b)
{
    free(b->data);                                  /* free(NULL) is fine: no check needed */
    b->data = NULL;                                 /* a second buf_free is now harmless */
    b->len = b->cap = 0;
}

calloc(SIZE_MAX / 2, 4) -> NULL (overflow detected)
appended 10000 bytes; capacity is 16384 after 11 reallocations (doubling)
all allocations released

valgrind --leak-check=full -q ./m04_malloc_contracts prints nothing beyond the program's own output: no leaks, no invalid accesses.

docs.title: 3.3 An arena allocator with an ownership contract: code/m04_arena_allocator.c
docs.text:
An arena (also called a bump or region allocator) grabs one big block up front and hands out pieces by moving a pointer forward. Individual pieces are never freed; the whole arena is reset at once. It fits work that has a natural "batch" or "request" boundary: parse a request, build the response, reset; or decode a batch of records, write them out, reset.

/* OWNERSHIP CONTRACT (the comment every arena-using module should carry):

 *   1. The arena OWNS one block from malloc. Every pointer handed out by arena_alloc() is
 *      BORROWED from the arena; callers never free() it.
 *   2. A borrowed pointer is valid until the next arena_reset() or arena_destroy() of THAT arena.
 *      Storing it anywhere that outlives the reset is a use-after-free waiting to happen.
 *   3. Allocation failure returns NULL; the arena stays valid.
 *   4. Not thread-safe. One arena per thread, or per request.
 */

/* align must be a power of two. Rounds the current position up to a multiple of align. */
static void *arena_alloc(arena *a, size_t size, size_t align)
{
    assert(align != 0 && (align & (align - 1)) == 0);
    uintptr_t cur = (uintptr_t)(a->base + a->used);
    uintptr_t aligned = (cur + (align - 1)) & ~(uintptr_t)(align - 1);
    size_t pad = (size_t)(aligned - cur);
    /* Written as subtractions so that a huge `size` cannot wrap the check. */
    if (pad > a->cap - a->used || size > a->cap - a->used - pad) return NULL;
    a->used += pad + size;
    if (a->used > a->high_water) a->high_water = a->used;
    return (void *)aligned;
}

#define ARENA_NEW(a, T) ((T *)arena_alloc((a), sizeof(T), alignof(T)))

static void arena_reset(arena *a) { a->used = 0; }     /* frees EVERYTHING at once, O(1) */

1-byte alloc, then customer (size 24, align 8) placed at offset 8; used = 32
customer 42 "R. Kumar" at 725 bp; used = 41
request 1 used 240 bytes
request 2 used 480 bytes
request 3 used 720 bytes
high-water mark: 720 of 4096 bytes
arena destroyed: every borrowed pointer is now invalid

The first line shows alignment at work: after a 1-byte allocation, the 8-byte-aligned customer starts at offset 8, not 1, and 7 bytes are padding. The high-water mark tells you how big the arena really needs to be. Module 12 of this course (12_memory_allocators_arena_pool_and_malloc.md) goes further with arenas, pools and a debugging allocator.

docs.title: 3.4 Four ways to return a string, and the bug: code/m04_returning_buffers.c
docs.text:
/* 1. Caller provides the buffer. Best default: no allocation, thread-safe. */
static int format_id(char *out, size_t outsz, int id);

/* 2. Static buffer. NOT thread-safe and overwritten by the next call

 *    (strerror, inet_ntoa, asctime and localtime work this way, hence their _r versions). */
static const char *format_id_static(int id);

/* 3. Heap. OWNERSHIP: the caller owns the result and must free() it. NULL on failure. */
static char *format_id_alloc(int id);

/* 4. Return a struct by value: the array travels inside the struct as a copy. */
static struct id_text format_id_value(int id);

1. caller buffer : ACC-000042
2. static buffer : ACC-000001 and ACC-000001   <- same text twice
3. heap          : ACC-000007 (caller frees)
4. struct value  : ACC-000009

Line 2 is the static-buffer trap in one printf: both arguments are the same pointer, so both print whichever call ran last. In a multithreaded server the same thing happens between threads, silently.

The file also contains the bug, compiled only with -DSHOW_BUG (deliberate undefined behaviour; build without -Werror because GCC warns):

gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -g -DSHOW_BUG m04_returning_buffers.c -o m04_bug && ./m04_bug

m04_returning_buffers.c: In function 'format_id_bug':
m04_returning_buffers.c:60:12: warning: function returns address of local variable [-Wreturn-local-addr]
   60 |     return buf;
      |            ^~~

1. caller buffer : ACC-000042
2. static buffer : ACC-000001 and ACC-000001   <- same text twice
3. heap          : ACC-000007 (caller frees)
4. struct value  : ACC-000009
BUG: format_id_bug returned (nil)

docs.title: Where each duration physically lives
docs.text:
• Static: in .data or .bss, addressed relative to the instruction pointer: movl s_calls(%rip), %eax. The address is fixed once the program is loaded.
  • Automatic: at an offset from rsp (or rbp), or only in a register. An automatic variable whose address is never taken may never touch memory at all, which is why gdb says "optimized out" in Release builds.
  • Allocated: in heap memory that glibc's malloc obtains from the kernel with brk (small blocks, the main arena) or mmap (large blocks, by default 128 KiB and above, adjusted dynamically). Each block has a 16-byte header just before the pointer you receive, which records its size: that is how free knows how much to release, and why free of a pointer that did not come from malloc aborts with free(): invalid pointer. Details: 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/03_the_heap_malloc_internals.md.
  • Thread: in a per-thread block that the fs segment register points at on x86-64 Linux (gs and the TEB on Windows x64). GCC 13 -O2 for ++t_calls in an executable:
bump_tls:
    movl    %fs:t_calls@tpoff, %eax     # fixed offset from this thread's TLS base
    addl    $1, %eax
    movl    %eax, %fs:t_calls@tpoff
    ret

In a shared library (-fPIC) the same access becomes a call to __tls_get_addr, because the library's TLS block offset is not known until load time. Thread-local variables in hot paths of a .so can therefore cost a function call per access.

docs.title: Why use-after-return often "works"
docs.text: Returning from a function only moves rsp; nothing erases the old frame. The dangling pointer still points at the old bytes, which stay intact until the next call reuses that region. So the bug shows up as "the string is correct in the log line but corrupted in the next one", depending on which function ran in between. AddressSanitizer catches it with ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1.

docs.title: What realloc really does
docs.text: glibc first tries to grow the block in place (if the next chunk is free or the block is at the top of the heap). Otherwise it allocates a new block, copies, and frees the old one. For blocks that were mmaped, it uses mremap, which moves the pages without copying their contents. Doubling the capacity makes the total copying cost O(n) over n appends (amortised O(1) per append): 10,000 appended bytes needed only 11 reallocations in section 3.2.

docs.title: Why free does not shrink the process
docs.text: Freed blocks go back to glibc's free lists, not to the kernel, unless they were mmaped or sit at the top of the heap. So a server's RSS (resident memory) stays high after a burst even with no leak. Telling a leak from growth and fragmentation is the subject of 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/09_leaks_and_memory_growth.md. Arenas sidestep fragmentation entirely: one block in, one block out.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Cross-module free on Windows. Each DLL linked with a different C runtime, or statically with /MT, has its own heap. Memory allocated by malloc in one DLL and freed by free in another goes to the wrong heap: heap corruption, reported later and elsewhere (often in ntdll!RtlpFreeHeap). The rule: the module that allocates also frees. Export x_free() next to every function that returns owned memory.
  • Stack overflow in worker threads. Windows threads get 1 MiB by default. A large local buffer (say char row[65536]) in a function called from a recursive parser or a deep call chain blows it under one particular input: exception 0xC00000FD. On Linux it is SIGSEGV on the guard page below the stack. Move big buffers to the heap or to per-thread storage allocated once.
  • Static buffers in a multithreaded server. strtok, strerror, inet_ntoa, asctime, localtime and any function of yours with a static char buf[] are data races when two worker threads call them. Use strtok_r/strtok_s, strerror_r/strerror_s, inet_ntop, localtime_r/localtime_s, or a caller-provided buffer. See 04_Concurrency/02_data_races_and_why_they_are_ub.md.
  • Ownership ambiguity on error paths. A function "takes ownership" of a buffer, fails halfway, and frees it; the caller, seeing the failure, also frees it: double free. Or neither frees it: leak. Every "takes ownership" comment must say what happens on failure, and the tests must cover the failure path (fault injection: make the Nth allocation fail).
  • Callback contexts that die first. A function registers &local_ctx as the context of an asynchronous callback and returns. The callback fires later and writes into a stack frame that now belongs to someone else. Contexts for asynchronous callbacks must be heap-allocated (or static) and freed when the callback is unregistered.
  • Arena pointers that escape.
