In a batch job using an arena per batch (for example a migration engine decoding records), a pointer to a decoded field is stored in a long-lived cache or a "last error" global. After arena_reset it points into the next batch's data: wrong values, no crash. The contract in section 3.3 is what reviewers check: nothing allocated from the arena may be stored anywhere that outlives the reset; copy it out instead.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Annotate every object in m04_storage_durations.c with its storage duration, scope and linkage. Done when your table has no blank cells and you can say when each object is created and destroyed.
  2. (easy) Build m04_returning_buffers.c with -DSHOW_BUG, then rewrite format_id_bug into each of the four correct forms in turn. Done when each version passes the existing asserts and you can name one disadvantage of each.
  3. (medium) Fault injection: write void *test_realloc(void *p, size_t n) that fails on the Nth call (N from an environment variable) and use it in buf_reserve. Show with Valgrind that the WRONG idiom leaks and leaves data == NULL when the failure hits, and the RIGHT one does not. Done when you have both Valgrind reports.
  4. (medium) Extend the arena with size_t arena_mark(arena *) and void arena_release_to(arena *, size_t mark) (stack-like nested scopes), and an arena_calloc(a, count, size, align) with an overflow check. Done when a test allocates in a nested scope, releases to the mark, and gets the same addresses again.
  5. (medium) Write the header comment block for a small API: cust_parse(const char *line) returning a record, cust_name(const cust *), cust_free(cust *), and cust_set_name(cust *, char *name) which takes ownership of name. Done when every pointer parameter and return value uses a phrase from the table in section 2.7, including what happens to name if cust_set_name fails.
  6. (hard) Write a recursive function with a 4 KiB local array and find the recursion depth at which it crashes in the main thread (8 MiB stack) and in a thread created with pthread_attr_setstacksize of 256 KiB. Done when both measured depths match your calculation within 10 % and you can explain the difference (frame overhead, guard page).

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What are the four storage durations in C? Automatic (locals: from block entry to block exit, indeterminate initial value), static (globals and static locals: the whole program, zero or constant-initialised before main), allocated (malloc to free), and thread (_Thread_local: one instance per thread, for the thread's lifetime).

Q: What is the difference between scope and lifetime? Scope is the region of source where a name can be used; lifetime is the period during execution when the object exists. A static local has block scope but program lifetime; a malloced block has a lifetime but no name at all. Dangling pointers are pointers used after the lifetime ended, regardless of scope.

Q: What happens if realloc fails? Show the correct way to call it. It returns NULL and leaves the original block allocated and unchanged. Assigning the result directly to the only pointer (p = realloc(p, n)) leaks the block and loses the data. Assign to a temporary, check it, then replace the pointer; also check the size calculation for overflow first.

Q: malloc versus calloc? malloc(n) returns uninitialised memory. calloc(count, size) returns zeroed memory and checks count * size for overflow, returning NULL instead of a short block. For large blocks glibc's calloc can skip the zeroing because fresh pages from mmap are already zero.

Q: Why is returning the address of a local variable wrong, and why does it sometimes appear to work? The local's lifetime ends when the function returns, and its stack memory is reused by the next call. Nothing erases the bytes on return, so an immediate read often sees the old value, and the corruption appears later. GCC warns and in fact returns NULL; ASan detects it with detect_stack_use_after_return.

Q: Why avoid VLAs and alloca in server code? They allocate on a small fixed-size stack with no failure path: a large size crashes instead of returning NULL, and if the size comes from input, an attacker controls your stack usage. MSVC does not support VLAs. Use a fixed buffer for the common case and fall back to the heap.

Q: What is an arena allocator, and what is its ownership contract? It allocates one large block and hands out aligned pieces by bumping an offset; nothing is freed individually and a reset releases everything in O(1). The contract: the arena owns the memory, callers only borrow pieces, and every piece is invalid after the next reset or destroy, so nothing allocated from it may be stored beyond that point. It fits per-request or per-batch work and removes per-object free calls, fragmentation and most leak opportunities.

Q: How do you document ownership in a C API? Say for every pointer whether the caller owns the result (and which function frees it), whether the callee borrows a parameter (and for how long a borrowed result stays valid), or whether the callee takes ownership (including on failure). Pair x_new/x_free and x_init/x_destroy, make x_free(NULL) a no-op, and prefer caller-provided buffers, which need no transfer at all.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Four storage durations: automatic, static, allocated, thread. Know when each starts, ends and what its initial value is.
  • Scope is about names, lifetime about objects; automatic lifetime ends at the end of the block.
  • static at file scope = internal linkage; static in a block = static storage duration.
  • Stacks are small (8 MiB Linux, 1 MiB Windows threads by default); big locals and VLAs crash servers.
  • realloc may move the block and on failure leaves the old one intact: assign to a temporary.
  • calloc zeroes and checks overflow; free(NULL) is a no-op; never realloc(p, 0).
  • Write ownership down: owns, borrows (until when), takes ownership (and on failure?).
  • Align carved allocations with (x + a - 1) & ~(a - 1).
  • Never return the address of a local; use a caller buffer, a static (not thread-safe), the heap, or a struct by value.
  • An arena owns one block, lends pieces, and invalidates them all at reset; nothing from it may outlive the reset.

docs.title: 05. Strings and buffers
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03, 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
C has no string type. A "string" is a convention: some bytes in a char array, ending at the first byte whose value is zero (the NUL character, written '\0'). Every string function walks the bytes until it finds that zero. Everything else in this module follows from that one fact:

  • The length of a string (bytes before the NUL) and the size of the array holding it are different numbers, and C tracks neither for you.
  • A string of length 5 needs 6 bytes. Forget the + 1 and you write one byte past the end.
  • If the NUL is missing, functions keep walking into whatever memory comes next.

Analogy: a train whose only end marker is the red caboose. The platform (the buffer) has a fixed length. The train (the string) must fit on the platform including the caboose. Someone who counts carriages walks until they see the caboose; if it fell off, they keep walking onto the next train's track. A buffer overflow is a train longer than its platform: the extra carriages crash into whatever is parked next to it, which in memory is another variable, a heap header, or the return address of the current function.

For a maintenance engineer this module is the highest return on time: string handling is where the largest share of crashes, corrupted log lines and security bugs in old C servers comes from. You will learn which standard functions are traps, how to build strings safely with snprintf, how to parse numbers without atoi, and what UTF-8 means for "length".

docs.title: 2.1 The representation
docs.text:
char buf[8] = "hi";

 index:   0     1     2     3     4     5     6     7
 buf:   ['h'] ['i'] [\0]  [\0]  [\0]  [\0]  [\0]  [\0]    sizeof buf == 8, strlen(buf) == 2
                     ^ the string ends here; the rest is spare capacity
  • '\0' is the character with value 0. '0' is the digit zero (value 48). NULL is a null pointer. Three different things.
  • A string literal "hi" has type char[3] (NUL included) and lives in read-only memory. Writing to it is undefined behaviour and in practice a crash.
  • Any function that writes a string needs to know the capacity of the destination; any function that reads one relies on the terminator. Bugs come from violating one or the other.

docs.title: 2.2 <string.h>: what each function really promises
docs.text:
Function Bounds Traps strlen(s) none O(n) every call; reads past the end if s is not terminated strcpy(d, s) none overflows d if strlen(s) + 1 > sizeof d strcat(d, s) none same, plus re-scans d from the start each call: a loop of strcats is O(n squared) strncpy(d, s, n) writes exactly n no terminator when strlen(s) >= n; zero-pads when shorter (section 2.3) strncat(d, s, n) appends at most n chars, then a NUL n is the append limit, not the size of d. Correct n is sizeof d - strlen(d) - 1 strcmp(a, b) none returns <0, 0, >0 (not -1/0/1); 0 means equal, so if (strcmp(a, b)) means "different" strncmp(a, b, n) compares at most n handy for prefixes: strncmp(s, "GET ", 4) == 0 strchr, strrchr, strstr none return a pointer into the string, or NULL: check it strspn, strcspn none lengths of the leading run of characters in (or not in) a set: the basis of safe tokenising memcpy(d, s, n) exactly n d and s must not overlap memmove(d, s, n) exactly n handles overlap memset, memcmp, memchr exactly n no NUL handling at all: work on bytes strdup(s) allocates POSIX (and C23); caller frees; MSVC spells it _strdup

And two comparisons people get wrong: if (s == "PAID") compares addresses (GCC warns, -Waddress), and two arrays with equal contents are never ==. Use strcmp.

docs.title: 2.3 Why strncpy is not a safe strcpy
docs.text:
strncpy was designed in early Unix for fixed-width, NUL-padded fields (14-byte file names in directory entries), not as a bounded copy. From code/m05_string_traps.c, copying into char dst[8] that was pre-filled with #:

strncpy(dst[8], src):           a  b  c \0 \0 \0 \0 \0
  NUL-terminated?              yes
strncpy(dst[8], src):           A  B  C  D  E  F  G  H
  NUL-terminated?              NO - strlen(dst) would read past the end

Two surprises:

  1. When the source is as long as n or longer, no terminator is written. The next strlen, printf("%s") or strcpy on dst runs off the end.
  2. When the source is shorter, it pads the rest with zeros, always writing all n bytes. strncpy(buf, "x", 65536) writes 64 KiB.

GCC recognises the trap when it can see the sizes (-Wstringop-truncation, part of -Wall):

warning: '__builtin_strncpy' output truncated before terminating nul copying as many bytes from a string as its length [-Wstringop-truncation]

Safer options: snprintf(d, sizeof d, "%s", s); a strlcpy-style helper (BSD; in glibc since 2.38; section 3.2 writes one); on Windows strcpy_s or strncpy_s(d, sizeof d, s, _TRUNCATE). The one legitimate use of strncpy is its original one: filling a fixed-width field that is defined as "NUL-padded, not necessarily terminated".

docs.title: 2.4 snprintf: the safe string builder
docs.text:
int n = snprintf(dst, size, fmt, ...);

The contract (C99 and later):

  • Writes at most size - 1 characters and always a terminating NUL, when size > 0.
  • Returns the number of characters it would have written with unlimited space (not counting the NUL), or a negative value on an encoding error.
  • So truncation happened if and only if n < 0 || (size_t)n >= size.

The append pattern keeps an offset and stops on the first truncation:

size_t used = 0;
int n = snprintf(buf + used, sizeof buf - used, "acct=%s ", acct);
if (n < 0 || (size_t)n >= sizeof buf - used) goto truncated;
used += (size_t)n;

vsnprintf is the same with a va_list, which is how you build your own printf-style helpers (section 3.2, and module 07). Two cautions: before Visual Studio 2015, MSVC had only _snprintf, which does not terminate on truncation and returns -1, and old Windows code still calls it; and the format must be a literal you wrote, never data you received (module 07).

docs.title: 2.5 memcpy versus memmove
docs.text:
memcpy is declared with restrict pointers (module 03): source and destination must not overlap. memmove behaves as if it copied through a temporary buffer, so overlap is fine; in practice it chooses the copy direction. Shifting elements inside one array (insert at the front, remove from the middle, compact a receive buffer after consuming a message) always overlaps:

memmove(&q[1], &q[0], used * sizeof q[0]);   /* shift right by one: overlapping, so memmove */

Calling memcpy on overlapping buffers is undefined behaviour, and it does break: in 2010 a glibc optimisation made memcpy copy backwards on some CPUs, and programs that had been passing overlapping buffers for years (Adobe Flash among them) started producing corrupted output. If in doubt, use memmove; the cost difference is negligible.

docs.title: 2.6 Parsing numbers: never atoi
docs.text:
atoi("12abc") is 12, atoi("abc") is 0, atoi("1O0") (letter O) is 1, and an out-of-range input is undefined behaviour. There is no way to tell "zero" from "not a number". In banking code that is how a malformed amount field becomes a zero-amount transaction.

Use the strto* family (strtol, strtoll, strtoul, strtoull, strtod), and check all four failure modes:

char *end;
errno = 0;                                   /* 1. strtoll SETS errno on error, never clears it */
long long v = strtoll(s, &end, 10);          /* 2. always give the base: base 0 reads "010" as octal 8 */
if (end == s)          -> not a number       /* 3. no digits consumed */
if (errno == ERANGE)   -> out of range       /*    v is LLONG_MAX or LLONG_MIN */
if (*end != '\0')      -> trailing garbage   /* 4. "12abc" */

More traps:

  • strtoul("-1", ...) succeeds and returns ULONG_MAX: the unsigned functions accept a minus sign and negate. Reject the - yourself.
  • strtol skips leading whitespace; trailing whitespace is up to you (allow it if input comes from fgets, which keeps the \n).
  • Base 0 auto-detects 0x (hex) and a leading 0 (octal): strtol("010", NULL, 0) is 8. Account numbers and branch codes with leading zeros must be parsed with base 10.
  • Range-check against the type you will store into (strtol into long then cast to int silently truncates on Linux).
  • strtod honours the current locale's decimal point. A program that calls setlocale(LC_ALL, "") on a machine with a comma locale parses "12.50" as 12.

docs.title: 2.7 sscanf pitfalls
docs.text:
sscanf looks convenient and has five traps:

  1. It returns the number of successful conversions. sscanf("12 abc", "%d %d", &a, &b) returns 1 and leaves b unchanged. Always compare the return value with the number you expected.
  2. %s and %[...] with no width are as dangerous as gets. The width is the maximum number of characters, so for char name[8] write %7s.
  3. %d on a number that does not fit in an int is undefined behaviour. For untrusted input, extract the digits and use strtol.
  4. Trailing garbage is silently ignored: "250xyz" matches %d. Use %n to learn how many characters were consumed, then check that you are at the end.
  5. Most conversions skip leading whitespace, but %c and %[ do not.

docs.title: 2.8 strtok versus strtok_r
docs.text:
strtok(s, delims) splits a string in place. It has three problems:

  • It modifies the input: every delimiter it passes becomes '\0'. You cannot tokenise a string literal or a buffer you still need.
  • It keeps its position in one hidden static variable for the whole process. Nested tokenising (split records on ;, then each record on =) destroys the outer position, and two threads using it at once corrupt each other.
  • It treats a run of delimiters as one, so "a,,b" gives two tokens; CSV needs three, with an empty middle field.

strtok_r(s, delims, &saveptr) (POSIX) keeps the position in a variable you own, so nesting and threads are fine. On Windows the equivalent is strtok_s(s, delims, &context) with the same three parameters. Beware: C11 Annex K also defines a strtok_s, with four parameters and different semantics; it is not the same function. For fields that may be empty, use strcspn to find each delimiter without modifying anything (section 3.4), or strsep (BSD and glibc), which keeps empty fields but still modifies the input.

docs.title: 2.9 UTF-8 basics
docs.text:
Text from outside your program (customer names, addresses, narration fields) is increasingly UTF-8. UTF-8 encodes each Unicode code point in 1 to 4 bytes:

Code points Bytes Pattern U+0000 to U+007F 1 0xxxxxxx (plain ASCII) U+0080 to U+07FF 2 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx U+0800 to U+FFFF 3 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx U+10000 to U+10FFFF 4 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx

Consequences:

  • ASCII is valid UTF-8, and no multi-byte sequence contains a zero byte, so NUL-terminated functions work on UTF-8 as bytes.
  • strlen counts bytes. The rupee sign U+20B9 is 3 bytes (E2 82 B9), so strlen("₹100") is 6 while a person counts 4 characters. Column widths, field limits and truncation must be defined in bytes or in code points, and the code must agree with the database.
  • Continuation bytes always look like 10xxxxxx. Count code points by counting bytes that are not continuation bytes. Truncate by backing up to a byte that is not a continuation byte, or you produce invalid UTF-8 that the database rejects.
  • Validation must reject overlong encodings (C0 AF for /, a classic filter-bypass trick), UTF-16 surrogates (U+D800 to U+DFFF), values above U+10FFFF, and truncated sequences.
  • <ctype.h> functions (isalpha, toupper) take an int that must be EOF or an unsigned char value. Passing a plain char holding a byte >= 0x80 (negative on x86) is undefined behaviour: cast to unsigned char. They classify single bytes in the current locale; they cannot upper-case a multi-byte character.
  • Windows uses UTF-16 internally (wchar_t is 2 bytes; the ...W Win32 APIs), Linux uses UTF-8 (wchar_t is 4 bytes). Convert at the boundary with MultiByteToWideChar(CP_UTF8, ...) and WideCharToMultiByte. Old banking data is often in a single-byte code page such as Windows-1252; convert it explicitly before it reaches a UTF-8 database (07_Databases_Internals/12_migrating_a_kv_store_to_relational.md, rule 3).

docs.title: 2.10 Rules for your own string helpers
docs.text:
Every helper that writes into a buffer should follow the same contract, so callers never have to remember which one is which:

  1. Take the destination and its size, as char *dst, size_t dstsz.
  2. Always terminate when dstsz > 0, even on truncation.
  3. Report truncation: return the length that was needed (the snprintf/strlcpy convention) or an explicit status. Never truncate silently.
  4. Treat non-terminated input (fixed-width record fields) with a separate function that takes the field width, so nobody ever calls strlen on such a field.

docs.title: 3.1 The traps, demonstrated safely: code/m05_string_traps.c
docs.text:
Two demos hand their input through a function parameter. If GCC could see the literals it would refuse to compile (-Wstringop-truncation, -Wformat-truncation): the compiler knows these traps and catches the cases it can prove at compile time. In real code the data comes from outside, so it cannot.

1. sizeof p = 8, sizeof a = 32, strlen = 5
strncpy(dst[8], src):           a  b  c \0 \0 \0 \0 \0
  NUL-terminated?              yes
strncpy(dst[8], src):           A  B  C  D  E  F  G  H
  NUL-terminated?              NO - strlen(dst) would read past the end
3. strncat with the right n: "/var/log/server" (15 chars, fits in 16)
4. strcmp("abc","abd") < 0, strcmp("abc","abc") == 0 is true
5. two "PAID" arrays: == says different, strcmp says equal
6. snprintf wanted 13 chars, buffer holds 7: got "TXN-123" -> TRUNCATED
7. "IFSC0001" needs 9 bytes, not 8

docs.title: 3.2 Safe helpers: code/m05_safe_string_helpers.c
docs.text:
/* Copy with the strlcpy contract: always NUL-terminates when dstsz > 0 and returns strlen(src).

 * Truncation happened if and only if the return value >= dstsz. */
static size_t str_copy(char *dst, size_t dstsz, const char *src)
{
    size_t srclen = strlen(src);
    if (dstsz > 0) {
        size_t n = srclen < dstsz - 1 ? srclen : dstsz - 1;
        memcpy(dst, src, n);
        dst[n] = '\0';
    }
    return srclen;
}

/* Fixed-width record fields are space-padded and NOT NUL-terminated.

 * Turn one into a C string, trimming trailing spaces. */
static size_t field_to_cstr(char *dst, size_t dstsz, const char *field, size_t width);

/* A string builder over a caller-supplied buffer. Once anything is cut off, `truncated` stays

 * true so the caller checks once at the end. */
__attribute__((format(printf, 2, 3)))           /* lets -Wformat check every call site */
static void sb_printf(strbuf *sb, const char *fmt, ...)
{
    if (sb->truncated) return;
    va_list ap;
    va_start(ap, fmt);
    int n = vsnprintf(sb->buf + sb->len, sb->cap - sb->len, fmt, ap);
    va_end(ap);
    if (n < 0 || (size_t)n >= sb->cap - sb->len) {
        sb->truncated = true;
        sb->len = sb->cap - 1;                  /* vsnprintf filled and terminated the rest */
    } else {
        sb->len += (size_t)n;
    }
}

str_copy into 8 bytes: "ACCOUNT", needed 15 -> truncated
str_append: "/srv/bank/ledger.dat" (20 chars, fits)
field_to_cstr: "LN0042" (6 chars)
strbuf: "acct=ACC-000042 amount=1234.05 " truncated=no
strbuf: "acct=ACC-000042 amount=1234.05 status=S" truncated=yes

str_append uses strnlen, which is POSIX (and C23), so the file defines _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L before its first #include: with -std=c17, glibc hides everything that is not ISO C unless you ask for it.

docs.title: 3.3 Parsing numbers: code/m05_parse_numbers.c
docs.text:
static parse_status parse_i64(const char *s, int64_t *out)
{
    if (s == NULL || *s == '\0') return PARSE_EMPTY;
    char *end;
    errno = 0;                                   /* strtoll SETS errno on error, never clears it */
    long long v = strtoll(s, &end, 10);
    if (end == s) return PARSE_NOT_A_NUMBER;     /* not a single digit was consumed */
    if (errno == ERANGE) return PARSE_OUT_OF_RANGE;   /* v is LLONG_MAX or LLONG_MIN */
    while (isspace((unsigned char)*end)) ++end;  /* allow "42\n" from fgets */
    if (*end != '\0') return PARSE_TRAILING_GARBAGE;
    *out = (int64_t)v;
    return PARSE_OK;
}

atoi("12abc") = 12, atoi("abc") = 0, atoi("1O0") = 1   (letter O)
parse_i64("42"                     -> 42
parse_i64("  -17\n"                -> -17
parse_i64(""                       -> error: empty
parse_i64("abc"                    -> error: not a number
parse_i64("12abc"                  -> error: trailing garbage
parse_i64("99999999999999999999"   -> error: out of range
parse_i64("1O0"                    -> error: trailing garbage
strtoul("-1") = 18446744073709551615 with no error; parse_u32("-1") -> out of range
sscanf("12 abc", "%d %d") returned 1; b is still -1
sscanf("SBIN0001234", "%7s") -> "SBIN000" (bounded)
sscanf("250xyz", "%d%n") -> value 250, stopped at offset 3 ("xyz" left over)

docs.title: 3.4 Tokenising and moving bytes: code/m05_tokenize_and_memmove.c
docs.text:
/* Nested strtok: the inner loop clobbers the ONE hidden position the outer loop relies on. */
for (char *item = strtok(s, ";"); item != NULL; item = strtok(NULL, ";")) {
    char *key = strtok(item, "=");
    char *val = strtok(NULL, "=");
    ...
}

/* A non-destructive splitter that KEEPS empty fields. */
for (;;) {
    size_t n = strcspn(s, set);             /* length up to the next delimiter or the end */
    cb(s, n, ctx);
    if (s[n] == '\0') break;
    s += n + 1;
}

nested strtok   found 1 pair(s)
nested strtok_r found 3 pair(s)
after strtok, the input buffer reads "a" (it was modified in place)
strtok on "ACC1,,250.00," sees 2 fields; split_keep_empty sees: [ACC1] [] [250.00] []  (4 fields)
after memmove insert at front: 10 20 30 40 50

printf("%.*s", (int)n, f) prints exactly n bytes of a field that is not terminated: the standard way to print a slice of a buffer.

docs.title: 3.5 UTF-8: code/m05_utf8_basics.c
docs.text:
Non-ASCII text is written with \x escapes ("\xE2\x82\xB9" for the rupee sign) so the source file is pure ASCII and compiles identically with GCC and MSVC (MSVC assumes the local code page for source files unless you pass /utf-8).

/* Copy at most dstsz - 1 bytes without cutting a multi-byte character in half. */
static size_t utf8_truncate_copy(char *dst, size_t dstsz, const char *src)
{
    size_t n = strlen(src);
    if (n >= dstsz) {
        n = dstsz - 1;
        while (n > 0 && ((unsigned char)src[n] & 0xC0) == 0x80) --n;   /* back off to a lead byte */
    }
    memcpy(dst, src, n);
    dst[n] = '\0';
    return n;
}

"₹100": strlen = 6 bytes, 4 code points
"José": 5 bytes, 4 code points
invalid (overlong '/') rejected: yes
invalid (truncated) rejected: yes
invalid (surrogate) rejected: yes
invalid (above U+10FFFF) rejected: yes
invalid (stray continuation) rejected: yes
truncate "₹100" to 3 bytes -> "₹" (3 bytes, the rupee sign kept whole)
truncate to 2 bytes -> "" (0 bytes: cutting inside the sign is not allowed)
isalpha((unsigned char)0xC3) in the "C" locale -> false

docs.title: How strlen is really implemented
docs.text: A byte-at-a-time loop is far too slow for glibc. The classic word-at-a-time trick tests 8 bytes at once: for a 64-bit word x, (x - 0x0101010101010101) & ~x & 0x8080808080808080 is non-zero exactly when some byte of x is zero. Modern glibc goes further with SSE2/AVX2 (compare 16 or 32 bytes against zero in one instruction, pmovmskb to get a bit mask, tzcnt/bsf to find the first set bit). These versions read aligned blocks and may read a few bytes past the terminator. That is safe because an aligned block never crosses a page boundary, so it can never touch an unmapped page; but it is formally out of bounds, which is why Valgrind replaces the string functions with its own versions instead of checking glibc's.

docs.title: How memcpy and memmove are implemented
docs.text: glibc picks an implementation at load time for your CPU (through an IFUNC resolver). Small copies use a couple of possibly overlapping unaligned loads and stores; medium ones use vector registers; large ones use rep movsb on CPUs with fast string instructions; very large ones may use non-temporal stores that bypass the cache. memmove is the same code plus a direction check. Since the overlap check is a pair of comparisons, memmove costs almost nothing extra.

docs.title: Where string literals live
docs.text: Literals go into .rodata and identical ones are usually merged (-fmerge-constants), so two "PAID" literals in different functions may have the same address. That is why if (status == "PAID") sometimes "works" in testing and fails when the string comes from a buffer.

docs.title: What catches overflows at run time, and how
docs.text:
• Stack protector (-fstack-protector-strong, on by default on Ubuntu): the compiler puts a random "canary" value between local buffers and the saved return address, and checks it before returning. Overflowing a local buffer far enough to reach the return address changes the canary: *** stack smashing detected ***: terminated, then abort.
  • FORTIFY_SOURCE: with optimisation enabled, strcpy, memcpy, sprintf and friends are replaced by checking versions (__strcpy_chk) whenever the compiler knows the destination size (__builtin_object_size). Ubuntu 24.04's GCC defines _FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 by default at -O1 and above. Overflowing char buf[8] with strcpy(buf, argv[1]) then aborts with *** buffer overflow detected ***: terminated before any damage. It cannot help when the size is unknown (a pointer into the heap passed through several functions). The course builds use -g without -O, so FORTIFY is off there; build with -O2 to see it.
  • AddressSanitizer finds overflows of any buffer, stack, heap or global, at the exact instruction: 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/08_valgrind_and_sanitizers.md.

docs.title: What an overflow destroys
docs.text: On the stack, the bytes past a local array are other locals, then the saved frame pointer and the return address: a long string controls where the function returns to (the classic exploit). On the heap, the bytes past a block are the next chunk's header; glibc notices the damage only when that chunk is freed or merged, with messages like free(): invalid next size (fast), often long after and far from the overflowing code (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/04_the_catalogue_of_memory_bugs.md).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Unterminated strings in logs. A field copied with strncpy (or legacy _snprintf) into an exactly-sized buffer has no terminator, and the next printf("%s") prints it plus whatever follows in memory. Symptoms: log lines with garbage tails, or worse, response messages that leak another customer's data from an adjacent buffer. The fix is a helper that always terminates.
  • strtok in a multithreaded request parser. Works in testing, corrupts fields under load when two worker threads parse at once. Grep the code base for strtok( and replace with strtok_s (Windows) or strtok_r (POSIX).
  • atoi on amounts and account numbers. An empty field becomes 0, "1,250.00" becomes 1, "0123" parsed with base 0 becomes 83. Each produces a valid-looking but wrong transaction. Every numeric field from a file, a socket or a database string goes through a checked parser like parse_i64, and a parse failure is a rejected record, never a zero.
  • Silent truncation. A narration, address or reference field longer than the buffer gets cut, and two different references now look the same. Use the snprintf return value; decide per field whether truncation is an error.
  • Encoding errors during migration. Names in a Windows-1252 code page sent to a UTF-8 PostgreSQL or YugabyteDB fail with errors such as invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0xe9, or worse, get inserted mis-converted. Validate UTF-8 (section 3.5) and convert code pages explicitly at the boundary; count invalid records instead of crashing on them.
  • Finding these in an old code base. Grep for strcpy, strcat, sprintf, strncpy, _snprintf, strtok(, atoi, gets, scanf("%s". Many teams keep a "banned functions" header that turns these into compile errors (Microsoft's banned.h, and Git's banned.h, do exactly this). Build tests with ASan and fuzz every parser, as in 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/13_defensive_design_to_prevent_the_bugs.md.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) For char d[6], predict the 6 bytes after strncpy(d, s, sizeof d) for s = "", "abc", "abcde", "abcdef", "abcdefgh". Done when all five predictions match a program that dumps the bytes, and you can say which ones are terminated.
  2. (easy) Rewrite sprintf(buf, "%s-%06d-%s", branch, seq, suffix) into a function that uses snprintf, returns an error on truncation, and never leaves buf unterminated. Done when a test with a 10-byte buffer reports truncation and a 64-byte buffer succeeds.
  3. (medium) Write int parse_amount_paise(const char *s, int64_t *out) for inputs like "1234.50", "-0.75", "12", using no floating point. Reject more than two decimals, empty input, stray characters, and anything that overflows int64_t. Done when a table of at least 15 cases (including ".", "1.", "-", "9223372036854775807") passes.
  4. (medium) Write a non-destructive CSV splitter that handles quoted fields containing commas and doubled quotes (a,"b,c","d""e" gives a, b,c, d"e). Done when it passes 10 cases and never writes into the input.
  5. (medium) Write int utf8_next(const char **s, uint32_t *cp) that decodes one code point and advances, returning an error for every invalid case in section 2.9. Done when it agrees with utf8_valid on 100,000 random byte strings.
  6. (hard) Write a program with a char buf[16] overflowed by strcpy from argv[1]. Run it built with -O2 (FORTIFY on), with -O0 -fstack-protector-strong, and with -fsanitize=address. Done when you have all three reports and can explain why FORTIFY stops a strcpy into a stack array but not into a heap buffer whose size the compiler cannot see.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why is strncpy not a safe strcpy? It does not write a terminator when the source is at least n bytes long, so the result may not be a string at all, and it zero-pads the rest of the buffer when the source is shorter, which wastes time. It was designed for fixed-width NUL-padded fields. Use snprintf(d, sizeof d, "%s", s) or a strlcpy-style function that always terminates and reports truncation.

Q: How do you detect truncation with snprintf? It returns the length it would have written given unlimited space. If the return value is negative or greater than or equal to the buffer size, the output was truncated (it is still terminated when the size is non-zero). Old MSVC _snprintf is different: no terminator on truncation and a return of -1.

Q: What is the difference between memcpy and memmove? memcpy requires that source and destination do not overlap (its parameters are restrict); overlapping use is undefined and has broken real programs when glibc changed its copy direction. memmove handles overlap correctly, typically by choosing the copy direction. Shifting elements within one array needs memmove.

Q: Why is atoi dangerous, and how do you use strtol correctly? atoi cannot report errors: a non-number returns 0 and overflow is undefined. With strtol, set errno = 0 first, pass an explicit base, check that end != s (some digits), that errno is not ERANGE, that *end is the terminator (no trailing garbage), and that the value fits the target type. Reject a minus sign yourself for the unsigned variants.

Q: What is wrong with strtok? It modifies its input, merges consecutive delimiters so empty fields disappear, and keeps its position in a single static variable, which breaks nested tokenising and is a data race between threads. Use strtok_r (POSIX) or strtok_s (MSVC, three arguments), or a non-destructive strcspn loop.

Q: What does strlen return for a UTF-8 string, and why does it matter? The number of bytes before the NUL, not characters; the rupee sign alone is 3 bytes. Buffer sizes and database column limits must be agreed in bytes or code points, and truncation must not split a multi-byte sequence, or the result is invalid UTF-8.

Q: What happens when you write past the end of a stack buffer? A heap buffer? On the stack you overwrite neighbouring locals, the saved frame pointer and the return address; the stack protector detects canary damage at function return and aborts. On the heap you overwrite the next chunk's metadata or another object; glibc detects it only when that chunk is freed or merged, often much later, which is why heap overflows are found with ASan or Valgrind rather than from the crash site.

Q: Write a strlcpy-style function. Compute srclen = strlen(src); if dstsz > 0, copy min(srclen, dstsz - 1) bytes with memcpy and write a NUL after them; return srclen. The caller detects truncation with return value >= dstsz.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A C string is bytes up to the first NUL; length (strlen) and capacity (sizeof) are different, and length n needs n + 1 bytes.
  • strcpy, strcat, sprintf, gets have no bounds; strncpy may not terminate; strncat's n is an append limit.
  • snprintf always terminates and returns the needed length: truncated iff n < 0 || n >= size.
  • memcpy for non-overlapping buffers, memmove when they might overlap.
  • Never atoi. strtol with errno = 0, explicit base, end checks, range check; strtoul accepts "-1".
  • sscanf: check the return value, always give %s a width, use %n for trailing garbage.
  • strtok is destructive, merges delimiters and is not thread-safe: use strtok_r / strtok_s.
  • UTF-8: strlen counts bytes; truncate on code point boundaries; cast to unsigned char for <ctype.h>.
  • Write helpers that take a size, always terminate, and report truncation.
  • Stack protector, FORTIFY_SOURCE and ASan catch overflows at run time; heap overflows surface late.

docs.title: 06. Structs, unions, enums and memory layout
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: 02, 03, 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A struct is a paper form with labelled boxes printed in a fixed order. The compiler decides where on the sheet each box goes, and it is allowed to leave blank gaps between boxes so that each box starts at a position its type likes (an 8-byte number likes to start at a multiple of 8). Those gaps are padding. You do not see them in the source, but they are in memory, in sizeof, and in every byte you write to a file or a socket.

A union is one box that can hold one of several kinds of things, all starting at the same place: writing one kind overwrites the others. An enum is a set of named integer constants.

Why spend three hours on this? Because the layout is what you actually see in a crash dump (raw bytes, not field names); because decoding records written by another program (the Berkeley DB records in your migration work) is entirely about layout; and because "write the struct to disk with fwrite" is one of the most common and most damaging shortcuts in old C code. By the end you will be able to predict every offset, know when packing is acceptable, use unions without undefined behaviour, hide a struct's layout behind an opaque pointer, and design a byte format that survives compilers, platforms and versions.

docs.title: 2.1 The layout rules
docs.text:
For an ordinary struct, every mainstream C compiler follows the same rules:

  1. Members are placed in declaration order. The compiler never reorders them.
  2. The first member is at offset 0, so a pointer to a struct, converted, points to its first member.
  3. Each member is placed at the next offset that is a multiple of its alignment; any gap before it is padding.
  4. The struct's alignment is the largest alignment of its members.
  5. The struct's size is rounded up to a multiple of its alignment (trailing padding), so that in an array every element is correctly aligned.

From code/m06_layout_and_padding.c (x86-64):

struct txn_bad {           /* declared in "logical" order */
    char    type;          /* 'D' or 'W' */
    int64_t amount_paise;
    char    channel;       /* 'B'ranch, 'A'TM, 'N'et */
    int32_t branch;
};

offset: 0    1 ... 7    8 ............ 15   16   17 18 19   20 ...... 23
        [type][ pad 7 ][  amount_paise   ][chan][ pad 3 ][   branch    ]     sizeof = 24

The same fields, largest first:

offset: 0 ............ 7    8 ...... 11   12     13     14 15
        [  amount_paise   ][   branch    ][type ][chan ][pad 2]               sizeof = 16

struct txn_bad:  sizeof 24, alignof 8
  type           offset  0 size 1
  amount_paise   offset  8 size 8
  channel        offset 16 size 1
  branch         offset 20 size 4
struct txn_good: sizeof 16, alignof 8
  amount_paise   offset  0 size 8
  branch         offset  8 size 4
  type           offset 12 size 1
  channel        offset 13 size 1
array stride = 16 bytes

A third smaller for free. For a struct held a million times in memory (a cache of accounts), or sent a million times a day, that matters. The tool pahole (from the dwarves package) prints every hole in every struct of a binary built with -g.

docs.title: 2.2 offsetof and container_of
docs.text:
offsetof(type, member) from <stddef.h> gives a member's byte offset as a size_t. Its most important use is the reverse direction: given a pointer to a member, get back the enclosing struct. The Linux kernel calls this container_of:

#define container_of(ptr, type, member) ((type *)((char *)(ptr) - offsetof(type, member)))

struct link { struct link *next; };
struct item { int id; struct link node; };   /* the link lives INSIDE the item */

struct link *l = ...;                        /* found by walking a generic list */
struct item *it = container_of(l, struct item, node);

This is how intrusive data structures work: the list or tree code knows only struct link, the node memory is part of your object (no separate allocation per node), and one object can sit in several lists through several link members. Module 11 of this course (11_data_structures_in_c.md) builds containers in C.

docs.title: 2.3 Padding bytes have unspecified values
docs.text:
The standard says padding bytes take unspecified values whenever a member is stored. In practice they hold whatever was in that memory before. Consequences:

  • memcmp(&a, &b, sizeof a) can report two structs with equal fields as different. The program pre-fills x with 0xAA and y with 0x00, then assigns the same field values to both:
fields equal: yes, memcmp equal: no
x bytes:  44 AA AA AA AA AA AA AA  F0 49 02 00 00 00 00 00  41 AA AA AA 07 00 00 00
y bytes:  44 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  F0 49 02 00 00 00 00 00  41 00 00 00 07 00 00 00
  • Hashing a struct's bytes, or using them as a cache key, has the same problem.
  • Writing a struct's bytes to a socket or a file leaks whatever was in the padding: fragments of previous requests, stack contents, other customers' data. Operating system kernels have shipped exactly this information-leak bug many times.

If the raw bytes of a struct ever matter, memset it to zero before filling it, and compare field by field. Better still, never use raw struct bytes outside the process (section 2.9).

docs.title: 2.4 Packing
docs.text:
Packing tells the compiler to drop padding, so members sit at unaligned offsets:

#pragma pack(push, 1)        /* MSVC, GCC and Clang all accept this form */
struct rec_pragma { uint8_t version; uint32_t customer_id; int64_t amount_paise; uint16_t branch; };
#pragma pack(pop)            /* restore: without it the packing leaks into every later struct */

struct rec_attr { uint8_t version; uint32_t customer_id; int64_t amount_paise; uint16_t branch; }
    __attribute__((packed)); /* GCC and Clang only */

natural: sizeof 24, amount_paise at offset 8
pragma : sizeof 15, amount_paise at offset 5
attr   : sizeof 15, amount_paise at offset 5

What packing costs:

  • Unaligned access. Accessing a packed member by name is safe: the compiler knows it may be misaligned. On x86-64 an unaligned load inside one cache line costs about the same as an aligned one, but one that straddles two 64-byte cache lines or two pages is slower. On strict-alignment CPUs (some ARM, SPARC, older MIPS) the compiler must emit byte loads and shifts.
  • Pointers to packed members are wrong. int64_t *p = &r.amount_paise; creates an int64_t * that is not 8-byte aligned, which is undefined behaviour; code that receives it assumes alignment. GCC 13 warns for __attribute__((packed)) structs (taking address of packed member of 'struct rec_attr' may result in an unaligned pointer value [-Waddress-of-packed-member]) but, verified on this toolchain, says nothing for the #pragma pack version: the Windows-style code is the silent one.
  • Atomic operations on misaligned fields are not atomic, or on x86 become "split locks" that stall the whole memory bus; recent Linux kernels can detect and throttle processes that do it.

Packing is acceptable for describing an external byte format that you cannot change. Even then the robust way to read such data is not to overlay a packed struct on the buffer, but to decode each field from its offset (section 2.9 and 07_Databases_Internals/12_migrating_a_kv_store_to_relational.md).

docs.title: 2.5 Bit-fields
docs.text:
struct acct_flags {
    unsigned int active    : 1;
    unsigned int frozen    : 1;
    unsigned int kyc_level : 3;   /* 0..7 */
    unsigned int reserved  : 27;
};

Compact and readable, and almost everything about their layout is implementation-defined:

  • the order of fields within the storage unit (GCC and MSVC on x86 fill from the least significant bit; big-endian ABIs typically fill from the most significant);
  • whether a field may straddle two units;
  • whether a plain int bit-field is signed (GCC: yes, so int x : 3 holding 7 reads back as -1);
  • which types are allowed besides int, unsigned int and _Bool, and how mixing them packs. struct { unsigned char a : 4; unsigned short b : 4; } is 2 bytes with GCC; MSVC starts a new storage unit whenever the declared type's size changes, giving 4.

And one rule that is not about layout: a bit-field is not a separately addressable object. Writing one field is a read-modify-write of the whole unit, and the C11 memory model treats adjacent bit-fields as one memory location. Two threads updating active and frozen of the same struct, each under its own lock (or none), race and lose updates.

So: bit-fields are fine for in-memory flags owned by one thread. For anything stored, sent, or shared between threads, use a fixed-width integer with explicit masks:

#define ACCT_ACTIVE      (UINT32_C(1) << 0)
#define ACCT_FROZEN      (UINT32_C(1) << 1)
#define ACCT_KYC_SHIFT   2
#define ACCT_KYC_MASK    (UINT32_C(0x7) << ACCT_KYC_SHIFT)

bitfield struct: sizeof 4, active=1 kyc=5 stored as 0x00000015 (GCC on x86: first field in the lowest bit)
mask version   : 0x00000015, active=1 frozen=0 kyc=5

docs.title: 2.6 Unions, type punning and the strict aliasing rule
docs.text:
A union's members all start at offset 0; its size is the largest member's size, rounded up to the union's alignment. The safe everyday use is the tagged union (a variant): a struct with an enum tag saying which member is currently valid, and a switch on the tag everywhere it is read.

struct value {
    enum value_kind kind;
    union {
        int64_t i;
        char    text[16];
        int64_t paise;
    } as;
};

Type punning means reading the bytes of an object as a different type, for example the bits of a float as a uint32_t. There are three ways to write it:

Code C C++ memcpy(&u, &f, sizeof u); correct correct union { float f; uint32_t u; } x = {.f = f}; return x.u; correct (C11 6.5.2.3, footnote 95) undefined return *(uint32_t *)&f; undefined (strict aliasing) undefined

The strict aliasing rule (C17 6.5p7): an object may be accessed only through an lvalue of its own type (or a compatible type, a signed/unsigned variant, a qualified version, an aggregate or union containing it) or through a character type. Because of it, the compiler may assume that an int * and a float * never point to the same memory, and optimise accordingly (section 4). Reading any object's bytes through unsigned char * is always allowed, which is why every hex dump in this course uses it.

The memcpy form is not slow: GCC compiles it to one register move (section 4). Prefer it in code that may one day be compiled as C++.

docs.title: 2.7 Enums
docs.text:
• Enumeration constants have type int in C17. The enum type is compatible with some integer type the compiler picks (usually int or unsigned int; -fshort-enums makes GCC pick the smallest). So sizeof(enum x) is not portable; never put an enum in a byte format.
  • An enum variable can hold any value of its underlying type, not just the listed ones. Validate enums read from outside.
  • switch on an enum without a default gets a -Wswitch warning (in -Wall) when an enumerator is not handled. That is a feature: leave default out where you want the compiler to tell you about new enum values, and handle "unknown" after the switch.
  • Use a ..._COUNT last enumerator to size tables, and designated initializers to index them (section 2.9).
  • C23 adds a fixed underlying type: enum opcode : uint8_t { ... };.

docs.title: 2.8 Flexible array members
docs.text:
A struct whose last member is an array of unspecified size (C99):

struct message {
    uint32_t      type;
    uint32_t      len;
    unsigned char payload[];      /* must be last; contributes nothing to sizeof */
};

struct message *m = malloc(sizeof *m + len);     /* header and payload in ONE allocation */

One malloc, one free, header and data adjacent in memory (good for the cache and for sending). Rules: it must be the last member; the struct cannot be an array element or a member of another struct (except as the last member, as a GCC extension); and struct assignment copies only the header.

Older code uses the "struct hack", unsigned char payload[1]; (or GNU payload[0]), and indexes past the end. Formally that is undefined, and it now bites: GCC 13's -fstrict-flex-arrays and _FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 can treat [1] as a real one-element array and abort on access to element 1. Convert struct hacks to [] when you touch them.

docs.title: 2.9 Designated initializers and compound literals
docs.text:
static const struct server_config k_defaults = {
    .bind_addr = "0.0.0.0",
    .port = 7000,
    .max_connections = 256,
    .timeout_ms = 5000,           /* .tls is not named: it is zero, i.e. false */
};

static const char *const k_level_names[LOG_LEVEL_COUNT] = {
    [LOG_ERROR] = "ERROR",        /* index by enum: reordering the enum cannot misalign names */
    [LOG_WARN] = "WARN",
    [LOG_INFO] = "INFO",
    [LOG_DEBUG] = "DEBUG",
};

print_config(&(struct server_config){.bind_addr = "127.0.0.1", .port = 7001});   /* compound literal */

Members you do not name are zero-initialised. Adding a field to the struct never shifts the meaning of an initializer, which positional initializers ({"0.0.0.0", 7000, 256, 5000}) cannot promise. A compound literal is an unnamed object whose lifetime is the enclosing block (static if at file scope). MSVC has supported both for C since Visual Studio 2013.

docs.title: 2.10 Opaque types: encapsulation in C
docs.text:
Put only an incomplete declaration in the header:

/* account.h */
typedef struct account account;          /* fields unknown to callers */
account *account_open(const char *id, int64_t opening_paise);
int      account_deposit(account *a, int64_t paise);
int64_t  account_balance(const account *a);
void     account_close(account *a);

and the full struct account { ... }; only in account.c. Callers can hold and pass account * but cannot read fields, allocate one, or take sizeof. Benefits: invariants are enforced in one file; you can add, remove or reorder fields without recompiling callers (a stable ABI for a shared library); callers cannot depend on internals. Costs: every object is heap-allocated by the library, and every field access is a function call (no inlining across the boundary unless you use LTO). FILE * and Win32 HANDLE are opaque types you use daily. This is C's version of a class with private members (09_OOP_Design_Patterns_Architecture/01_oop_for_a_c_programmer.md).

docs.title: 2.11 Why you never fwrite a raw struct
docs.text:
fwrite(&rec, sizeof rec, 1, f) (or send(sock, &rec, sizeof rec, 0)) ties the file format to:

  1. Padding: the size and offsets depend on the compiler, the flags and #pragma pack state; the padding bytes themselves are garbage, or leaked data.
  2. Type sizes: long is 4 bytes on Windows and 8 on Linux; enums vary; bool varies in old code.
  3. Endianness: the bytes are in host order; a big-endian reader gets nonsense.
  4. No version: the day you add a field, every old file becomes unreadable, and nothing in the file tells the reader which layout it has.
  5. Pointers: a pointer member is a meaningless number in another process.

The fix is an explicit wire format: a version byte first, fixed-width fields at documented offsets, a defined byte order, a length for variable parts, and an encoder and decoder that move one field at a time with shifts (module 02). The decoder validates everything and rejects unknown versions. This is exactly what decoding the packed Berkeley DB records requires (07_Databases_Internals/12_migrating_a_kv_store_to_relational.md, section 2.2: never cast the buffer to the struct, decode per field, per-field byte order, versioned records) and what every network protocol needs (08_Networking_Distributed/04_framing_and_protocol_design.md).

docs.title: 3.1 Layout and padding: code/m06_layout_and_padding.c
docs.text:
The full output is in sections 2.1 and 2.3. The macro that prints each field uses offsetof and a sizeof on a member of a null pointer, which is fine because sizeof never evaluates its operand:

#define SHOW_FIELD(T, f) \
    printf("  %-14s offset %2zu size %zu\n", #f, offsetof(T, f), sizeof(((T *)0)->f))

docs.title: 3.2 Packing and bit-fields: code/m06_packed_and_bitfields.c
docs.text:
struct rec_pragma r = {2, 1001, -250000, 7};
    int64_t amount;
    memcpy(&amount, (const unsigned char *)&r + offsetof(struct rec_pragma, amount_paise), sizeof amount);

natural: sizeof 24, amount_paise at offset 8
pragma : sizeof 15, amount_paise at offset 5
attr   : sizeof 15, amount_paise at offset 5
packed amount read via member = -250000, via memcpy = -250000
bitfield struct: sizeof 4, active=1 kyc=5 stored as 0x00000015 (GCC on x86: first field in the lowest bit)
mask version   : 0x00000015, active=1 frozen=0 kyc=5

docs.title: 3.3 Unions and punning: code/m06_unions_and_punning.c
docs.text:
static uint32_t bits_memcpy(float f)        /* always correct, in C and C++; compiles to one mov */
{
    uint32_t u;
    memcpy(&u, &f, sizeof u);
    return u;
}

static uint32_t bits_union(float f)         /* defined in C (C11 6.5.2.3 footnote 95), UB in C++ */
{
    union { float f; uint32_t u; } x = {.f = f};
    return x.u;
}

sizeof(struct value) = 24 (tag + padding + largest member)
int 42
text "NEFT"
amount 12345.05
bits of 1     = 0x3F800000 (memcpy) 0x3F800000 (union)
bits of -0    = 0x80000000 (memcpy) 0x80000000 (union)
bits of 0.1   = 0x3DCCCCCD (memcpy) 0x3DCCCCCD (union)
first byte of 0xA1B2C3D4 in memory: 0xD4

The file also contains a strict-aliasing violation, compiled only with -DSHOW_ALIASING_UB (deliberate undefined behaviour, documented in the file header):

static int alias_demo(int *i, float *f)
{
    *i = 1;
    *f = 2.0f;           /* GCC -O2 assumes this cannot change *i (different types) */
    return *i;           /* ...so it returns the constant 1 without reloading */
}
    int target = 0;
    int r = alias_demo(&target, (float *)&target);

gcc -std=c17 -O2 -Wall -DSHOW_ALIASING_UB m06_unions_and_punning.c -o m06_alias && ./m06_alias

UB: alias_demo returned 1, but target now holds 0x40000000 (the float 2.0f)

At -O0 the same program returns 1073741824 (the reloaded bits of 2.0f): the result depends on the optimisation level, the signature of undefined behaviour.

docs.title: 3.4 Flexible arrays, designated initializers, opaque types: code/m06_flexible_array_and_opaque.c
docs.text:
sizeof(struct message) = 8, offsetof payload = 8, this message uses 22 bytes
payload: BAL?ACC-000042
config 0.0.0.0:7000 max=256 timeout=5000ms tls=off
config 0.0.0.0:9000 max=256 timeout=5000ms tls=on
config 127.0.0.1:7001 max=0 timeout=0ms tls=off
k_level_names[LOG_WARN] = WARN
opaque account balance: 125050 paise

The third config line is a reminder of how designated initializers work: unnamed members of the compound literal are zero, not copied from k_defaults. To override a few fields of the defaults, copy the defaults and assign (the second line).

docs.title: 3.5 An explicit, versioned record format: code/m06_serialize_record.c
docs.text:
/* On the wire / on disk, version 1. Little-endian, no padding, every offset written down:

 *   off  0  u8   version (= 1)
 *   off  1  u8   type
 *   off  2  u16  branch
 *   off  4  u32  account_id
 *   off  8  i64  amount_paise (two's complement)
 *   total 16 bytes                                                                         */

static int txn_decode(const unsigned char *in, size_t insz, struct txn *t)
{
    if (insz < 1) return -1;
    if (in[0] != TXN_V1) return -1;                 /* unknown version: quarantine, do not guess */
    if (insz < TXN_V1_SIZE) return -1;
    if (in[1] != 'D' && in[1] != 'C') return -1;
    t->type = (char)in[1];
    t->branch = get_u16(in + 2);
    t->account_id = get_u32(in + 4);
    t->amount_paise = u64_to_i64(get_u64(in + 8));
    return 0;
}

sizeof(struct txn) = 24, wire size = 16
raw struct bytes:      44 AA AA AA AA AA AA AA  25 2F FC FF FF FF FF FF  01 28 6B EE 01 02 AA AA
encoded v1:            01 44 01 02 01 28 6B EE  25 2F FC FF FF FF FF FF
decoded: type=D amount=-250075 account=4000000001 branch=513
decode of version 9 -> rejected

The raw struct line is what fwrite(&t, sizeof t, 1, f) would have written: 24 bytes, 9 of them padding (AA, which in a real program would be leftover memory). The encoded record is 16 bytes, all meaningful, in a documented order. The encoder writes at offset 1 of its buffer on purpose: because it moves bytes, alignment never matters. u64_to_i64 converts the decoded bits back to a negative amount without relying on implementation-defined conversion.

docs.title: Strict aliasing in the generated code
docs.text:
GCC 13 -O2 for alias_demo (and for the memcpy punning function):

alias:
    movl    $1, (%rdi)            # *i = 1
    movl    $1, %eax              # return value decided NOW: *f cannot alias *i
    movl    $0x40000000, (%rsi)   # *f = 2.0f
    ret
bits:
    movd    %xmm0, %eax           # the whole memcpy: one register move
    ret

The Linux kernel and some other large C code bases build with -fno-strict-aliasing to switch this assumption off, trading some optimisation for safety with legacy casts. Know the flag exists; do not rely on it in new code.

docs.title: Unaligned access in hardware
docs.text: x86-64 handles unaligned scalar loads in hardware. The cost appears when an access straddles a 64-byte cache line (two lines must be fetched) or a 4 KiB page (two address translations). Locked instructions (lock cmpxchg, used for atomics) on a line-straddling address become split locks, which lock the memory bus for all cores. On ARMv8 Linux, ordinary unaligned loads work, but exclusive and atomic instructions on unaligned addresses fault. For data you control, natural alignment is free performance; packing is for formats you do not control.

docs.title: How bit-field access compiles
docs.text: Reading f.kyc_level is: load the 32-bit unit, shift right by 2, AND with 7. Writing it is: load the unit, clear bits 2 to 4, OR in the new value shifted left, store the unit. That load-modify-store sequence is why two threads writing different bit-fields of one unit lose each other's updates: each writes back a stale copy of the other's bits.

docs.title: Structs across function calls
docs.text: On the System V x86-64 ABI (Linux), a struct of up to 16 bytes made of integer fields is passed and returned in registers (rdi/rsi, returned in rax/rdx); larger ones are copied to the stack, and the caller passes a hidden pointer for the return value. On Windows x64 only structs of exactly 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes travel in a register; everything else goes by hidden pointer. So returning a small struct by value (module 07) is cheap on both. Details: 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/02_stack_frames_and_calling_conventions.md.

docs.title: Reading layouts in a debugger
docs.text: In gdb, ptype /o struct txn_bad prints every member with its offset and size and marks the holes, just like pahole. In WinDbg, dt module!txn_bad prints offsets, and dt module!txn_bad <address> decodes a struct at an address in a dump. When a field "looks wrong" in a dump, compare the offsets your debugger shows with the offsets the writing code was compiled with: a #pragma pack mismatch between two modules shows up exactly here.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Decoding legacy records. Records written by C code with #pragma pack(1) (or without it, with whatever padding that compiler chose) are the input of every migration. Casting (struct rec *)dbt.data is undefined behaviour (alignment) and silently depends on today's compiler matching the writer's. Decode each field from its offset, per-field byte order, version byte first, and test against hand-verified golden records (07_Databases_Internals/12_migrating_a_kv_store_to_relational.md).
  • Pack state leaking across modules. A header that does #pragma pack(1) without pop makes the same struct 15 bytes in one DLL and 24 in another. Fields after the first padding read as garbage only when the struct crosses that module boundary. Use push/pop in every header, and add _Static_assert(sizeof(struct x) == N, "...") next to every struct that crosses a boundary (module 08).
  • Information leak through padding. A response struct sent with send(s, &resp, sizeof resp, 0) carries uninitialised padding: bytes of earlier requests, possibly account numbers. Encode explicitly, or at minimum memset the struct first.
  • Lost flag updates. A connection struct has unsigned closing : 1; unsigned authenticated : 1; set by different threads. Occasionally a connection "forgets" it was authenticated. Bit-fields in the same unit are one memory location; use separate bool/byte fields or atomic masks.
  • Change detection with memcmp. "Has the record changed?" implemented as memcmp of two structs reports spurious changes because of padding, causing needless writes or replication traffic. Compare fields.
  • Adding a field to a persisted struct. If the struct is written raw, every old file is now unreadable and nothing detects it: reads succeed and return shifted fields. With a versioned wire format, the decoder handles v1 and v2 and rejects unknown versions loudly.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Predict sizeof and every offsetof for: struct { char a; double b; char c; }, struct { char a; char c; double b; }, struct { int a; char b[3]; }, struct { short s; struct { char c; int i; } in; }. Done when a program using offsetof confirms all of them, or you can explain each miss.
  2. (easy) Take a struct with nine fields of mixed sizes, reorder it for minimum size, and lock the result in with _Static_assert(sizeof(...) == N, ...). Done when the assert compiles and fails if you swap two fields back.
  3. (medium) Implement container_of and an intrusive doubly linked list (struct dlink { struct dlink *prev, *next; }). Put one struct account into two lists at once (by branch and by status). Done when removing it from one list leaves it in the other, with no extra allocation per list node.
  4. (medium) Write a decoder for the 35-byte loan_rec_v2 layout shown in 07_Databases_Internals/12_migrating_a_kv_store_to_relational.md (little-endian ids and amount, big-endian branch, BCD date, space-padded fixed-width strings) using only byte offsets, no packed struct. Done when it decodes three hand-built golden records correctly and rejects a record with a wrong version or a short length.
  5. (medium) Bit-field race: a struct with unsigned a : 1; unsigned b : 1;. Thread 1 toggles a one million times, thread 2 toggles b one million times, each counting its own toggles. Done when you observe a final state inconsistent with the counts (run it several times, or under TSan), then fix it by making a and b separate unsigned char fields and can explain why that fixes it.
  6. (hard) Add version 2 to the format in m06_serialize_record.c with a 3-letter currency code. The decoder must accept v1 (currency defaults to "INR") and v2; the encoder writes v2. Then fuzz txn_decode with random buffers of random length for one minute under ASan and UBSan. Done when both versions round-trip in tests and the fuzzer finds nothing.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why is sizeof a struct often larger than the sum of its members? The compiler inserts padding so that each member starts at a multiple of its alignment, and pads the end so that the size is a multiple of the struct's alignment, which keeps array elements aligned. Order matters: the same fields sorted largest first usually need much less padding.

Q: What is offsetof used for, and what is container_of? offsetof gives a member's byte offset in a struct. container_of subtracts that offset from a pointer to the member to recover a pointer to the enclosing struct; it is how intrusive lists and trees (the Linux kernel's, for example) link objects without separate node allocations.

Q: What does #pragma pack(1) do and what does it cost? It removes padding, placing members at unaligned offsets. Member access by name stays correct but can be slower, especially across cache-line boundaries and on strict-alignment CPUs; pointers to packed members are misaligned and dangerous; atomics on them are not atomic. Use it only to describe external formats, always with push/pop, and prefer field-by-field decoding.

Q: Are bit-fields portable? Are they thread-safe? Their layout (bit order, straddling, allowed types, signedness of plain int fields) is implementation-defined, and MSVC and GCC differ for mixed types, so they must not define file or wire formats. Adjacent bit-fields form one memory location, so concurrent writes to different fields of the same unit race. Use masks on fixed-width integers for portable or shared flags.

Q: How do you reinterpret a float's bits as a uint32_t without undefined behaviour? memcpy into a uint32_t, which is correct in C and C++ and compiles to one register move. A union also works in C (not C++). Casting (uint32_t *)&f violates the strict aliasing rule: the compiler assumes pointers to different types do not alias and may produce stale results.

Q: What is a flexible array member, and how does it differ from the "struct hack"? A last member declared T data[]; sizeof ignores it and you allocate sizeof(struct) + n. The old hack declared data[1] and indexed past the end, which is undefined behaviour and is now caught by -fstrict-flex-arrays and _FORTIFY_SOURCE=3. Both give a single allocation for header and payload.

Q: What is an opaque type and why use one? A struct declared but not defined in the public header, used only through pointers and functions. It hides the layout, enforces invariants in one file, and lets you change the struct without recompiling callers (stable ABI). The cost is a heap allocation per object and a function call per access. FILE * is the classic example.

Q: Why should you never fwrite a struct to a file or a socket? Its bytes include padding (garbage or leaked data), depend on the compiler's type sizes and packing, are in host byte order, and carry no version. Use an explicit format: version byte, fixed-width fields at documented offsets, defined endianness, encoded and decoded field by field with validation.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Members stay in declaration order; each is aligned to its type; the struct is aligned to its largest member and padded at the end.
  • Order fields largest first to remove padding; pahole or ptype /o shows the holes.
  • offsetof gives offsets; container_of turns a member pointer back into the struct pointer.
  • Padding bytes are unspecified: no memcmp, no hashing, no raw writes of structs.
  • #pragma pack(push, 1)/pop for external formats only; never take the address of a packed member (GCC warns for the attribute form, not for the pragma).
  • Bit-field layout is implementation-defined and adjacent bit-fields are one memory location; use masks for anything stored, sent or shared.
  • Tagged unions for variants; memcpy for type punning; casts that break strict aliasing are UB.
  • Enums are int constants with a compiler-chosen size; keep them out of byte formats.
  • Flexible array members give one allocation for header plus payload; replace struct hacks.
  • Opaque types are C's encapsulation; designated initializers keep initialisation robust.
  • On disk and on the wire: version byte, fixed-width fields, explicit endianness, field-by-field encode and decode.

docs.title: 07. Functions, function pointers and callbacks
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 03, 04

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
When you call a C function, C copies every argument into the function. The function works on its own copies. If you want a function to change something of yours, you give it the address of that thing (module 03). That is the whole story of "pass by value" in C, and it explains out-parameters, the "return a status code, deliver results through pointers" style of every C API you have used (Win32, POSIX, Berkeley DB), and why passing a big struct by value is a quiet performance bug.

A function pointer is a phone number for a function. You can write it in a table, hand it to someone else, and they can call it later. Handing someone your number so they can call you when something happens is a callback. Because the caller does not know anything about you, you also hand over a note saying who you are and what you were doing: that is the void * context argument you see in CreateThread, pthread_create, qsort_r and every event library.

Analogy: the reception desk of your bank's head office. A directory maps request types to extension numbers (a dispatch table: opcode to handler function). The receptionist does not know how to handle a loan query; she looks up the extension and transfers the call. Your RPC server does exactly this with every request it reads from a socket. This module covers that machinery, state machines built from function pointers, qsort/bsearch, variadic functions such as printf, and the format-string vulnerability that comes with them.

docs.title: 2.1 Pass by value, always
docs.text:
• Scalars and pointers: the value is copied. Changing the parameter changes the copy.
  • Arrays: cannot be passed; the array decays to a pointer to its first element, and the pointer is copied. So the callee can change the caller's elements, which makes arrays look like "by reference". They are not; the pointer was passed by value.
  • Structs: the whole struct is copied. A 4000-byte struct passed by value copies 4000 bytes per call (section 3.1). Pass large structs as const struct x *; return small structs by value freely (it is cheap and clear, see module 06 section 4 for the ABI).

docs.title: 2.2 Out-parameters and the status-code convention
docs.text:
The dominant shape of a C API: the return value is a status, results go out through pointers.

/* Contract: *new_balance is written only when the result is ST_OK. */
static status withdraw(struct account *acct, int64_t paise, int64_t *new_balance);

Decide, and document, one of two policies for out-parameters on failure: "untouched" (as above) or "always set to a defined value (0, NULL) at entry". Callers that read an out-parameter after a failure are reading garbage under the first policy, so the comment matters.

The conventions you meet in practice:

API family Success / failure Where the error detail is POSIX system calls -1 (or NULL) on failure errno (thread-local) pthreads 0 on success the return value is the error number; errno is not set Win32 BOOL FALSE or invalid HANDLE GetLastError() (thread-local) COM HRESULT (SUCCEEDED(hr)) the value itself Berkeley DB 0 on success return value (DB_NOTFOUND, ...), db_strerror() your own an enum status the value, plus a log line

10_error_handling_and_resource_cleanup.md is dedicated to error handling, errno and cleanup paths.

docs.title: 2.3 Prototypes and () versus (void)
docs.text:
In C17, int f(); declares a function with unspecified parameters, not "no parameters". The compiler checks nothing at call sites. This compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra:

int f();
int g(void) { return f(1, 2, 3); }   /* no diagnostic */
int f(int a) { return a; }           /* the real definition takes one int: undefined behaviour */

Always write int f(void) for "no parameters", and -Wstrict-prototypes will find the old style. C23 finally changes () to mean (void).

docs.title: 2.4 Function pointer syntax
docs.text:
int add(int a, int b);

int (*op)(int, int) = add;     /* op is a pointer to a function (int, int) returning int */
int *op2(int, int);            /* WITHOUT the parentheses: a function returning int *     */

op = &add;                     /* & is optional: a function name decays to a pointer */
int r1 = op(2, 3);             /* call */
int r2 = (*op)(2, 3);          /* identical */

Typedefs make everything else readable. Two styles, both common:

typedef int (*binop_fn)(int, int);    /* a pointer type:   binop_fn op;   */
typedef int binop(int, int);          /* a function type:  binop *op;     */

Reading hard declarations: start at the name, go right while you can, then left, and jump out of each parenthesis level. The classic test is the standard signal function:

void (*signal(int sig, void (*func)(int)))(int);
/* signal is a function taking (int, pointer to function(int) returning void)
   that returns a pointer to function(int) returning void. With a typedef:   */
typedef void (*sig_handler)(int);
sig_handler signal(int sig, sig_handler func);

A function pointer can be NULL; calling a NULL function pointer jumps to address 0 and faults with the instruction pointer at 0 (in a crash dump: rip = 0, often with a garbage stack trace, because the call pushed a return address and nothing else ran). ISO C does not allow converting function pointers to void * (module 03); converting between different function pointer types is allowed, but calling through the wrong type is undefined.

docs.title: 2.5 Callbacks with a void * context
docs.text:
A callback needs state. Globals work until there are two users or two threads. The C solution is a void * that the registering code passes in and the library hands back untouched:

typedef void (*txn_visitor)(const struct txn *t, void *ctx);

static void for_each_txn(const struct txn *arr, size_t n, txn_visitor fn, void *ctx)
{
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) fn(&arr[i], ctx);
}

static void accumulate(const struct txn *t, void *ctx)
{
    struct totals *tot = ctx;    /* the caller promised ctx is a struct totals * */
    ...
}

for_each_txn(book, n, accumulate, &tot);

The price of void * is type safety: nothing checks that ctx really is a struct totals *. Keep the registering call and the callback next to each other in the code, and remember the lifetime rule from module 04: the context must outlive every call to the callback.

qsort has no context parameter, which is why every platform added one, incompatibly:

Function Comparator signature Where qsort_r(base, n, size, cmp, arg) int cmp(const void *a, const void *b, void *arg) glibc qsort_r(base, n, size, arg, cmp) int cmp(void *arg, const void *a, const void *b) BSD, macOS qsort_s(base, n, size, cmp, ctx) int cmp(void *ctx, const void *a, const void *b) MSVC qsort_s(base, n, size, cmp, ctx) int cmp(const void *a, const void *b, void *ctx) C11 Annex K (not in glibc)

Portable code wraps one of them behind an #ifdef (module 08), or ships its own sort.

docs.title: 2.6 qsort and bsearch
docs.text:
The comparator contract: return a negative value, zero or a positive value, and be a consistent total order (if a < b and b < c then a < c; the same pair always gives the same answer). Breaking it is undefined behaviour for qsort, not just "a wrong order": in 2024 a memory-corruption bug was reported in glibc's qsort that an inconsistent comparator could trigger.

The classic broken comparator subtracts:

return (int)(x->amount_paise - y->amount_paise);   /* WRONG: truncates to int, can flip sign;
                                                      with int fields the subtraction itself can overflow */
return (x->amount_paise > y->amount_paise) - (x->amount_paise < y->amount_paise);   /* RIGHT */

Other rules:

  • qsort is not stable: equal elements may change their relative order. Sort by a tie-breaker key (an id) if order matters.
  • The comparator receives pointers to elements. For an array of char *, each argument is a char **; passing them straight to strcmp compares pointer bytes as text.
  • bsearch(key, base, n, size, cmp) needs the array sorted by the same key, calls cmp(key, element) (key first), and the key need not have the element's type: search a struct txn[] with a uint32_t id.

docs.title: 2.7 Dispatch tables
docs.text:
An array of function pointers indexed by a small integer replaces a long switch and makes the mapping data instead of code:

typedef void (*handler_fn)(const struct request *req, struct response *resp);

static const handler_fn k_handlers[OP_MAX] = {
    [OP_BALANCE] = h_balance,
    [OP_DEPOSIT] = h_deposit,
    [OP_WITHDRAW] = h_withdraw,
};

static void dispatch(const struct request *req, struct response *resp)
{
    if (req->opcode >= OP_MAX || k_handlers[req->opcode] == NULL) {   /* from the network: check */
        resp->status = 1;
        snprintf(resp->text, sizeof resp->text, "unknown opcode %u", (unsigned)req->opcode);
        return;
    }
    k_handlers[req->opcode](req, resp);
}

Three rules: bounds-check the index (it came from a socket), NULL-check the entry (gaps in the table are NULL), and make the table const so it lives in read-only memory. A writable table of function pointers is a favourite exploitation target: one heap overflow that reaches it turns into control of the instruction pointer. For sparse or large opcode spaces use a sorted array of {opcode, handler} and bsearch.

docs.title: 2.8 State machines with function pointers
docs.text:
A parser that receives bytes from TCP never gets a whole message at once (08_Networking_Distributed/04_framing_and_protocol_design.md). It must remember where it was between reads: that memory is its state. A clean C design gives each state a handler function and keeps a table from state to handler:

typedef enum { ST_LENGTH, ST_PAYLOAD, ST_COMMA, ST_ERROR, ST_COUNT } state_id;
typedef state_id (*state_fn)(struct parser *p, unsigned char c);

static const state_fn k_states[ST_COUNT] = {
    [ST_LENGTH] = on_length,
    [ST_PAYLOAD] = on_payload,
    [ST_COMMA] = on_comma,
    [ST_ERROR] = on_error,
};

static int parser_feed(struct parser *p, const char *data, size_t n)
{
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n && p->state != ST_ERROR; ++i)
        p->state = k_states[p->state](p, (unsigned char)data[i]);
    return p->state == ST_ERROR ? -1 : 0;
}

Each handler consumes one byte and returns the next state. Limits live in the handlers (maximum length digits, maximum payload), so a hostile peer cannot make the parser allocate or loop without bound. The error state is sticky: once the stream is invalid, the connection must be closed, because there is no reliable way to find the next message boundary.

An alternative design makes the state itself a function pointer. A function cannot return its own type in C, so you wrap it: struct state { struct state (*fn)(struct parser *, unsigned char); };. The table-driven version is easier to log ("state 2"), test and extend.

docs.title: 2.9 Variadic functions
docs.text:
printf takes a variable number of arguments through <stdarg.h>:

static int64_t sum_i64(int count, ...)
{
    va_list ap;
    va_start(ap, count);              /* start after the last named parameter */
    int64_t s = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; ++i) s += va_arg(ap, int64_t);   /* you state the type */
    va_end(ap);                       /* every va_start needs a va_end */
    return s;
}

The function receives no information about how many arguments there are or their types. Caller and callee must agree by convention: a count (sum_i64), a sentinel (a trailing NULL), or a format string (printf). If they disagree, the behaviour is undefined and the compiler cannot tell:

  • sum_i64(3, 100, 250, -50) passes three ints while the function reads three int64_ts. GCC 13 gives no warning. Write INT64_C(100) or cast.
  • Default argument promotions apply to the ... part: float becomes double, char and short become int. So va_arg(ap, float) or va_arg(ap, char) is undefined: read double or int.
