  • A sentinel must be a pointer: NULL may be the plain integer 0, which is 4 bytes where a pointer is 8. Pass (char *)NULL. GCC's __attribute__((sentinel)) checks it.
  • A va_list can be walked once. To walk twice (measure with vsnprintf(NULL, 0, ...), then format), va_copy it first.
  • To forward arguments, call the v version (vprintf, vsnprintf, vfprintf) with your va_list. You cannot pass ... on to another variadic function.
  • Mark printf-like functions with __attribute__((format(printf, fmt_index, first_arg_index))) so -Wformat checks every call site exactly like printf. (MSVC has _Printf_format_string_ for its code analysis instead.)

Prefer non-variadic APIs where you can: an array plus a count is type-checked; ... is not.

docs.title: 2.10 The format-string vulnerability
docs.text:
printf(user_text);          /* WRONG: the data is used as the format */
printf("%s", user_text);    /* RIGHT: the data is an argument */

If user_text contains conversion specifiers, printf reads arguments that were never passed: %x prints stack contents (leaking pointers and data), %s dereferences stack garbage (crash), and %n writes the count of printed characters to an address taken from the stack, which is how format-string bugs become arbitrary memory writes. The same applies to fprintf, snprintf, syslog, and to every logging wrapper you write. Ubuntu's GCC enables -Wformat-security by default, even without -Wall:

fs.c:2:1: warning: format not a string literal and no format arguments [-Wformat-security]
    2 | void p(const char *user) { printf(user); }

docs.title: 2.11 static, inline and static inline
docs.text:
• static on a function: internal linkage. The compiler knows every call site, so it can inline it, specialise it, or delete it if unused. Make every helper static.
  • inline in C99 does not mean what it means in C++. A plain inline function defined in a header is an inline definition only; if the compiler decides not to inline a call (for example at -O0), it emits a call to an external symbol that must be defined in exactly one .c file with extern inline. Verified with GCC 13: the same program links at -O2 and fails at -O0:
a.c:(.text+0xe): undefined reference to `twice'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
  • The simple rule for headers: static inline. Each translation unit gets its own private copy if one is needed; there is nothing to link.
  • _Noreturn (C11; [[noreturn]] in C23) marks functions like a fatal() that calls abort, which helps both warnings and code generation.

docs.title: 3.1 Pass by value and out-parameters: code/m07_pass_by_value_and_out_params.c
docs.text:
after try_to_change: 1, after change(&n): 99
sum_by_value == sum_by_pointer == 499500 (sizeof(struct big) = 4000 bytes copied by value)
split_amount(123456) -> 1234 rupees 56 paise
withdraw 200.00 -> status 0, new balance 30000
withdraw 999.99 -> status 2 (insufficient funds), out-param untouched: -1

split_amount returns a small struct by value (two results, no out-parameters), the same idea as the standard div() returning a div_t.

docs.title: 3.2 Syntax and an RPC dispatch table: code/m07_function_pointers.c
docs.text:
/* A function RETURNING a function pointer.

 * Without typedef:  int (*pick(char c))(int, int)
 * With typedef:     binop_fn pick(char c)                                                     */
static binop_fn pick(char c)
{
    switch (c) {
    case '+': return add;
    case '-': return sub;
    case '*': return mul;
    default:  return NULL;
    }
}

table[i](6, 3) = 9 3 18
opcode   1 -> status 0, "balance of ACC-000042 is 1500.00"
opcode   2 -> status 0, "deposited 250000 paise"
opcode   3 -> status 2, "insufficient funds"
opcode   7 -> status 1, "unknown opcode 7"
opcode 500 -> status 1, "unknown opcode 500"

Opcode 7 is inside the table but has no handler (NULL entry); opcode 500 is outside it. Both are rejected without crashing.

docs.title: 3.3 Comparators, bsearch, context callbacks: code/m07_qsort_bsearch_callbacks.c
docs.text:
/* Sorting an array of char *: the comparator receives POINTERS TO the elements, i.e. char **. */
static int cmp_str(const void *a, const void *b)
{
    const char *const *x = a;
    const char *const *y = b;
    return strcmp(*x, *y);
}

cmp_amount_bad(30000000.00, 0) = -1294967296  (negative: claims big < zero)
cmp_amount    (30000000.00, 0) = 1
by amount: -120000 -9900 0 500000 3000000000
bsearch id 105 -> amount -9900
sorted codes: IMPS NEFT RTGS UPI
debits -129900, credits 3000500000, 3 over the 1000.00 limit

The first line is the subtraction bug: an amount of 30,000,000.00 rupees (3,000,000,000 paise) compared with 0 gives a difference that does not fit in an int, and the truncated value is negative. A sort using it would put the largest transaction first.

docs.title: 3.4 A table-driven state machine: code/m07_state_machine.c
docs.text:
The parser reads netstrings (<length>:<payload>,, for example 5:hello,), fed in deliberately awkward chunks:

fed 5:he                 -> frames so far 0
fed llo,1                -> frames so far 1
fed 2:BAL?ACC-0042,0     -> frames so far 2
fed :,                   -> frames so far 3
payloads: hello|BAL?ACC-0042|
bad input 5:hello;   -> rc -1, error: missing ',' after payload
bad input 99999:x    -> rc -1, error: length has too many digits
bad input 2:ab,x:    -> rc -1, error: bad character in length

The second frame's length (12) is split across two reads, and the third frame is empty (0:,). 99999:x is rejected at the fifth digit, before any memory is committed: limits belong in the parser, not after it.

docs.title: 3.5 Variadic functions: code/m07_variadic_functions.c
docs.text:
__attribute__((format(printf, 1, 2)))
static char *format_alloc(const char *fmt, ...)
{
    va_list ap, ap2;
    va_start(ap, fmt);
    va_copy(ap2, ap);                         /* a va_list can be walked ONCE: copy it first */
    int n = vsnprintf(NULL, 0, fmt, ap);      /* pass 1: measure */
    va_end(ap);
    char *s = NULL;
    if (n >= 0 && (s = malloc((size_t)n + 1)) != NULL)
        vsnprintf(s, (size_t)n + 1, fmt, ap2);  /* pass 2: format */
    va_end(ap2);
    return s;                                 /* caller frees */
}

sum_i64(3, 100, 250, -50) = 300
join_words -> "NEFT batch 07 settled"
format_alloc -> "acct=ACC-000042 amount=1234.05" (31 bytes allocated)
[INFO] server listening on port 7000
100% done %s %n
[WARN] 100% done %s %n

The last two lines print hostile-looking text (%s %n) safely, because it is passed as an argument to "%s".

docs.title: Calling conventions
docs.text: On Linux x86-64 (System V ABI) the first six integer or pointer arguments travel in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9, floating-point ones in xmm0 to xmm7, and the result comes back in rax (or xmm0). On Windows x64 the first four go in rcx, rdx, r8, r9 (or xmm0 to xmm3), and the caller must reserve 32 bytes of "shadow space" on the stack. 32-bit Windows had several conventions (__cdecl, __stdcall, __fastcall): a callback declared with the wrong one (missing CALLBACK/WINAPI) corrupted the stack pointer on return. On x64 there is one convention, so that class of bug disappeared. Full detail and how debuggers use it: 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/02_stack_frames_and_calling_conventions.md.

docs.title: Indirect calls
docs.text: A call through a function pointer compiles to call *%rax, and a table dispatch to something like call *k_handlers(,%rax,8). The CPU predicts the target with its branch target buffer; a dispatch that always goes to the same few handlers predicts well. Two security features make indirect calls more expensive or stricter: Spectre v2 mitigations (retpolines, -mindirect-branch=thunk) on some builds, and on Windows Control Flow Guard (/guard:cf), which checks every indirect call target against a bitmap of valid function starts. With CFG on, a corrupted function pointer does not jump into the weeds; the process is terminated with a fast-fail (exception code 0xC0000409), which is a clue worth recognising in a dump.

docs.title: How va_list works
docs.text: On System V x86-64, a variadic callee cannot know which registers hold its arguments, so its prologue saves all six integer argument registers (and, if the caller set al non-zero, the vector registers) into a "register save area". va_list is a small struct (offsets into that area plus a pointer to the stack-passed arguments), declared as an array of one struct. That is why you cannot copy a va_list with = (use va_copy) and why a va_list passed to another function is consumed by it. On Windows x64, va_list is just a char * walking the stack, because the caller always spills arguments into the shadow space; code that "worked" by copying va_lists on Windows breaks on Linux.

docs.title: Why qsort is slower than std::sort
docs.text: qsort calls the comparator through a pointer for every comparison and moves elements with a size-generic copy. C++ std::sort with a lambda is a template instantiated for the exact type: the comparison is inlined and elements are moved as their real type. The algorithm is similar; the abstraction cost is not (02_Modern_CPP/07_stl_algorithms_lambdas_iterators.md). In C, if a sort is hot, write a type-specific sort or use a macro-generated one.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Unchecked opcode dispatch. handlers[msg->opcode](msg) with an opcode from the wire and no bounds check reads a "function pointer" from beyond the table and calls it. In a dump: the instruction pointer is garbage or a data address, and the previous frame is the dispatcher. Always bounds-check and NULL-check, and keep the table const.
  • Callbacks under a lock. A library calls a user callback while holding its internal mutex; the callback calls back into the library, which takes the same mutex: deadlock (or, with a recursive lock, corrupted internal state). Rule: release internal locks before invoking callbacks, or document that callbacks must not re-enter (04_Concurrency/06_deadlocks_livelocks_starvation.md).
  • Dangling callback context. register_timer(cb, &local_state) followed by the function returning; the timer fires later and writes into a dead stack frame. Heap-allocate contexts and free them on unregister (module 04).
  • Wrong comparator. Subtraction comparators work in tests with small values and misorder large amounts in production. Grep for return a - b style comparators.
  • Logging wrappers without the format attribute. log_msg("%d", amount_int64) prints garbage on Windows (where int64_t is wider than int), and log_msg(customer_name) is a format-string vulnerability. Add __attribute__((format(printf, ...))) to every printf-like function and fix every warning it produces.
  • Out-parameters read after failure. A function fails early without writing its out-parameter; the caller logs it anyway and prints stack garbage, or uses it as a pointer. Initialise out-parameters at the top of the function or initialise the variable at the call site.
  • Win32 thread start routines. CreateThread(NULL, 0, worker, ctx, 0, &tid) follows exactly the callback-with-context pattern; the same lifetime and ownership rules apply to ctx.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Write each declaration in English, then rewrite it with typedefs: int (*f[4])(double), char *(*g)(const char *), void (*signal(int, void (*)(int)))(int), int (*(*h)(int))(int). Done when a test program declares each one, assigns a real function to it and calls it.
  2. (easy) Add OP_TRANSFER with a handler to m07_function_pointers.c and tests for opcode 0, OP_MAX - 1 and OP_MAX. Done when all unknown opcodes produce status 1 and the program never calls through NULL.
  3. (medium) Write void sort_ctx(void *base, size_t n, size_t size, int (*cmp)(const void *, const void *, void *), void *ctx) that uses qsort_r on glibc, qsort_s on MSVC (adapting the argument order with a small trampoline), and your own merge sort elsewhere. Done when the same test (sort accounts by a field chosen at run time through ctx) passes on WSL, and the MSVC branch at least compiles in your head line by line.
  4. (medium) Re-implement the netstring parser with the alternative design, where the state is a struct state { struct state (*fn)(struct parser *, unsigned char); }. Done when it passes the same chunked and bad-input tests, and you have written three sentences comparing the two designs.
  5. (medium) Write log_msg(int level, const char *fmt, ...) with the format attribute. Pass an int64_t with %d and read the compile error; fix it with PRId64. Then call log_msg(LOG_INFO, user) and read the -Wformat-security warning. Done when your wrapper compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra -Wformat=2 -Werror.
  6. (hard) Build an event dispatcher: subscribe(event_type, cb, ctx) returns a handle, unsubscribe(handle), publish(event_type, data) calls every subscriber. A callback may unsubscribe itself or another subscriber during publish. Done when a test that unsubscribes during dispatch runs clean under ASan, and you can explain your deferred-removal design.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Does C have pass by reference? No. Every argument is passed by value; to let a function modify an object you pass its address, which is itself copied. Arrays look like they are passed by reference only because they decay to a pointer; structs are copied whole, so large ones should be passed as const pointers.

Q: Declare a pointer to a function that takes an int and returns a char *, and an array of four of them. char *(*fp)(int); and char *(*table[4])(int);. With a typedef: typedef char *(*fn_t)(int); fn_t table[4];. The parentheses around *fp are what make it a pointer to a function rather than a function returning a pointer.

Q: Why do C callback APIs take a void * context? So the callback can reach caller-specific state without globals, which would break with multiple users or threads. The library stores the pointer and hands it back unchanged; the callback casts it to the real type. The costs are lost type checking and a lifetime obligation: the context must outlive all callback invocations.

Q: What is wrong with return a - b; in a qsort comparator? The subtraction can overflow (undefined for signed int) or, for wider types, be truncated to int, flipping the sign, so the comparator is no longer a consistent order. Use (a > b) - (a < b). An inconsistent comparator is undefined behaviour for qsort.

Q: How does a variadic function know how many arguments it got? It does not; the caller and callee must agree through a convention such as a count, a sentinel or a format string. The callee also states each argument's type in va_arg, and default argument promotions apply (float to double, char/short to int), so reading the wrong type is undefined behaviour. The format and sentinel attributes let GCC check call sites.

Q: What is a format-string vulnerability? Passing untrusted data as the format argument of a printf-family function. Conversion specifiers in the data make the function read nonexistent arguments: %x leaks stack memory, %s crashes, %n writes memory. Always pass data as an argument to a literal format such as "%s", and compile with -Wformat-security.

Q: What should you put in a header: inline, static, or static inline? static inline. In C99, a plain inline definition in a header requires one external definition elsewhere; when the compiler does not inline a call (often at -O0) the link fails with an undefined reference. static inline gives each translation unit its own copy, and unused copies are discarded.

Q: In C17, what is the difference between int f(); and int f(void);? int f(void) declares a function with no parameters and the compiler checks calls. int f(); is an old-style declaration with unspecified parameters, so calls with any arguments compile without a diagnostic and a mismatch with the definition is undefined behaviour. C23 makes () mean (void).

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• C passes everything by value; pass addresses to modify, const pointers for large read-only structs, return small structs by value.
  • Return a status and deliver results through out-parameters; document what out-parameters hold on failure.
  • int f(void), never int f(), before C23.
  • int (*fp)(int, int): parentheses make it a pointer; typedefs make the rest readable.
  • Callbacks take a void * context; it must outlive every callback call. qsort_r/qsort_s differ per platform.
  • Comparators: consistent total order, (a > b) - (a < b), element pointers (not elements) as arguments; qsort is not stable.
  • Dispatch tables: const, bounds-checked, NULL-checked.
  • State machines: one handler per state, limits inside the handlers, sticky error state.
  • Variadic: no count or types are passed; promotions apply; (char *)NULL sentinels; va_copy to walk twice; format attribute on printf-like functions.
  • Never pass data as a format string. Use static inline in headers.

docs.title: 08. The preprocessor and macros
docs.text: Time: ~2.5 hours Prerequisites: 01, 07

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Before the compiler sees your code, a text-processing robot runs over it: the preprocessor. It does three jobs. It pastes files into other files (#include). It replaces names with text (#define). And it deletes chunks of code depending on conditions (#if, #ifdef). It knows nothing about types, variables, scopes or functions; it works on tokens (words, numbers, punctuation). Its output is a single long C file, the translation unit of module 01.

Analogy: find-and-replace across a document before it goes to the translator. Find-and-replace is powerful and completely literal. Replace x with a + b, and the sentence 2 * x becomes 2 * a + b, which is not what anybody meant. Nearly every macro bug is that sentence in some disguise.

You will never write a large C program without the preprocessor: headers, platform differences (_WIN32 versus POSIX), logging with file and line numbers, and error-code tables all depend on it. The skill is knowing its traps well enough to use it only where a function or a constant cannot do the job, and to read the macro-heavy code that legacy servers are full of.

docs.title: 2.1 #include mechanics
docs.text:
#include pastes the named file's text in place of the directive. The two spellings differ only in where the preprocessor looks first:

Form Search order (GCC) #include "foo.h" the directory of the file containing the #include, then -iquote dirs, then the <...> list #include <foo.h> -I directories in command-line order, then system directories (/usr/include, the compiler's own)

MSVC is similar (/I for both). gcc -H prints every header opened (module 01), cl /showIncludes does the same on Windows. Two habits keep include graphs healthy: include what you use (every header includes the headers it needs, nothing more), and use a forward declaration (struct account;) instead of an include when a header only needs a pointer to the type.

docs.title: 2.2 Include guards versus #pragma once
docs.text:
A header included twice in one TU would define its structs twice: an error. Two ways to prevent it:

/* bank_account.h */
#ifndef BANK_ACCOUNT_H
#define BANK_ACCOUNT_H
/* ... declarations ... */
#endif /* BANK_ACCOUNT_H */

#pragma once
/* ... declarations ... */
Include guard #pragma once Standard yes no, but GCC, Clang and MSVC all support it Failure mode two headers that accidentally use the same guard name (copy-pasted header): the second is silently skipped the same file reached through two different paths (symlinks, network shares, a copied file) may be included twice, or two identical files treated as one Speed GCC and Clang recognise the guard idiom and skip re-opening the file, so no real difference fast

Use either, consistently. Name guards after the project and path (BANK_CORE_ACCOUNT_H). Do not start them with an underscore followed by a capital letter (_ACCOUNT_H): those identifiers are reserved for the implementation.

docs.title: 2.3 Object-like and function-like macros
docs.text:
#define MAX_CONN 256                    /* object-like */
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))           /* function-like: NO space before the ( */
  • A function-like macro's arguments are token sequences, split on top-level commas. Commas inside parentheses are protected; commas inside braces are not, so M({1, 2}) passes two arguments, {1 and 2}.
  • After substitution the result is rescanned for more macros, but a macro is never expanded inside its own expansion, so macros cannot recurse.
  • Predefined macros you will use: __FILE__, __LINE__, __DATE__, __TIME__ (these two make builds non-reproducible), __STDC_VERSION__, and the platform and compiler macros in section 2.8. __func__ looks similar but is not a macro: it is a predefined static const char array inside each function. So "in " __func__ does not compile (string-literal concatenation happens at the token level, and __func__ is not a literal); pass it as an argument instead.
  • gcc -dM -E file.c dumps every macro defined at the end of preprocessing. Compile with -g3 and gdb can macro expand LOG(LOG_INFO, "x") and info macro LOG.

docs.title: 2.4 The classic macro traps
docs.text:
All of these are in code/m08_macro_traps.c, each next to its fix.

Precedence. Parenthesise every use of a parameter and the whole body:

#define SQUARE_BAD(x) x * x          /* SQUARE_BAD(2 + 3) -> 2 + 3 * 2 + 3 = 11 */
#define SQUARE(x)     ((x) * (x))    /* 25 */
#define DOUBLE_BAD(x) (x) + (x)      /* 10 * DOUBLE_BAD(3) -> 10 * (3) + (3) = 33 */

Double evaluation. The argument's text is pasted wherever the parameter appears, so side effects happen as many times:

#define MAX_BAD(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))
int m = MAX_BAD(i++, 3);   /* ((i++) > (3) ? (i++) : (3)): i++ runs twice, m == 6, i == 7 */

Same with function calls: MAX(read_balance(acct), limit) reads the balance twice, possibly getting two different values from another thread. A static inline function evaluates each argument once.

Multi-statement bodies.

#define BUMP_BOTH_BAD(a, b) (a)++; (b)++
if (enabled)
    BUMP_BOTH_BAD(a, b);     /* expands to: if (enabled) (a)++; (b)++;  -- b changes anyway */

GCC 7 and later warn (-Wmultistatement-macros, in -Wall); MSVC and older compilers say nothing.

Name capture. A macro's local variable can collide with the caller's:

#define SWAP(a, b) do { int tmp = (a); (a) = (b); (b) = tmp; } while (0)
SWAP(tmp, x);                /* int tmp = (tmp); ...  -- the caller's tmp is shadowed */

Scope blindness. Macros ignore scope and namespaces. <windows.h> defines min and max as macros (define NOMINMAX before including it) and wingdi.h defines ERROR as 0, which breaks any enum or function of yours named ERROR (define NOGDI if you do not need GDI). Prefix your macro names (BANK_) and use upper case so macros are recognisable.

Debuggability. A macro has no symbol, you cannot step into it, and compiler errors point into the expansion.

docs.title: 2.5 Why do { ... } while (0)
docs.text:
A multi-statement macro must behave like one statement that needs exactly one semicolon. Braces alone are not enough:

#define SWAP_BRACES(a, b) { int t = (a); (a) = (b); (b) = t; }
if (x) SWAP_BRACES(a, b); else other();
/* expands to:  if (x) { ... } ; else other();   -> "else without a previous if" */

do { ... } while (0) is a single statement, requires the trailing semicolon the caller writes, and the optimiser removes the loop entirely. Every multi-statement macro in this course uses it.

docs.title: 2.6 #, ## and variadic macros
docs.text:
#define STR(x)    #x            /* stringise the argument's tokens */
#define XSTR(x)   STR(x)        /* expand first, then stringise */
#define CAT(a, b) a##b          /* paste two tokens into one */

STR(__LINE__)    /* "__LINE__" : # applies to the argument BEFORE it is expanded */
XSTR(__LINE__)   /* "78"       : XSTR's argument is expanded, then passed to STR */
CAT(counter_, debit)   /* counter_debit */

Arguments are normally macro-expanded before substitution, except where the parameter is used with # or ##. That is why stringising the value of a macro needs the two-level XSTR.

Variadic macros (C99) use ... and __VA_ARGS__. In C17 the ... must receive at least one argument; with -Wpedantic, GCC rejects a call that passes none:

error: ISO C99 requires at least one argument for the "..." in a variadic macro [-Werror]

GCC's , ##__VA_ARGS__ extension swallows the comma; C23 adds __VA_OPT__(,) for the same job. The portable C17 solution is to make the format string part of __VA_ARGS__: #define LOG(lvl, ...) log_write((lvl), __FILE__, __LINE__, __func__, __VA_ARGS__). A call always has at least the format, so there is never an empty ....

docs.title: 2.7 X-macros
docs.text:
An X-macro is a list written once as a macro that takes another macro as a parameter. Each time you need the list in a different shape, you define X to produce that shape and expand the list:

#define ERROR_TABLE(X)                                                    \
    X(ERR_OK,                 0, "success")                               \
    X(ERR_NOT_FOUND,          1, "account not found")                     \
    X(ERR_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS, 2, "insufficient funds")                    \
    X(ERR_ACCOUNT_FROZEN,     3, "account is frozen")                     \
    X(ERR_DB_UNAVAILABLE,     4, "database unavailable, retry later")     \
    X(ERR_PROTOCOL,           5, "malformed request")

enum err_code {
#define X(name, value, text) name = value,
    ERROR_TABLE(X)
#undef X
};

static const char *err_name(enum err_code e)
{
    switch (e) {
#define X(name, value, text) case name: return #name;
        ERROR_TABLE(X)
#undef X
    }
    return "ERR_UNKNOWN";
}

The enum, the symbolic names for logs, the human messages, a count, and even struct definitions with matching debug printers all come from one table and can never drift apart. Adding an error is one line. The cost is readability for people who have not seen the idiom; a comment pointing to the table fixes that. Note that the table's continuation lines end in \ and contain no // comment: see section 4 for why.

docs.title: 2.8 Conditional compilation and platform macros
docs.text:
#if defined(_WIN32)          /* defined on 32- AND 64-bit Windows; _WIN64 only on 64-bit */
#  define WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN
#  include <windows.h>
#elif defined(__linux__) || defined(__APPLE__) || defined(__unix__)
#  include <unistd.h>
#else
#  error "unsupported platform: add a branch to the portability layer"
#endif
Macro Meaning _WIN32, _WIN64 Windows target (any compiler, including MinGW) __linux__, __APPLE__, __unix__ Linux, macOS, Unix-like _MSC_VER MSVC, with its version (1938 for VS 2022 17.8) __clang__ Clang (test before __GNUC__, which Clang also defines) __GNUC__, __GNUC_MINOR__ GCC (and compatible compilers) __x86_64__ / _M_X64, __aarch64__ / _M_ARM64 CPU architecture, GCC/Clang spelling and MSVC spelling __BYTE_ORDER__ == __ORDER_LITTLE_ENDIAN__ byte order (GCC, Clang)

Feature-test macros go the other way: you define them, before the first #include, to ask the C library for more than ISO C. _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L exposes POSIX functions (strtok_r, strnlen, nanosleep) when compiling with -std=c17; _GNU_SOURCE exposes everything glibc has. On Windows, WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN trims <windows.h>, NOMINMAX removes min/max, _WIN32_WINNT selects the minimum Windows version whose APIs are declared.

Rules for platform code:

  • Keep #ifdefs in one small portability layer (plat_sleep_ms, plat_mutex_lock); the rest of the code calls those functions and never names a platform (section 3.5).
  • A misspelled macro in #if silently evaluates to 0. -Wundef catches it: warning: "ENABLE_AUDIT_LOGS" is not defined, evaluates to 0 [-Wundef].
  • Use #if 0 ... #endif to disable a block; /* */ comments do not nest.
  • Code in a branch that your CI never compiles rots. Build every platform you ship, every time.

docs.title: 2.9 _Static_assert
docs.text:
A compile-time check (C11). If the constant expression is zero, compilation fails with your message:

_Static_assert(sizeof(struct wire_header) == 12, "wire_header must be exactly 12 bytes");
_Static_assert(offsetof(struct wire_header, length) == 8, "length must be at offset 8");
_Static_assert((PAGE_SIZE & (PAGE_SIZE - 1)) == 0, "PAGE_SIZE must be a power of two");
_Static_assert(ERR_COUNT == 6, "error table changed: update the client documentation");

Put one next to every struct that crosses a process boundary, every table that must match an enum, and every assumption about type sizes. <assert.h> also defines the spelling static_assert (a keyword in C23, where the message becomes optional). Legacy code uses the pre-C11 trick of a typedef with a negative array size, typedef char check_x[(cond) ? 1 : -1];; Windows headers wrap the same trick as C_ASSERT(cond).

docs.title: 2.10 _Generic
docs.text:
_Generic(expr, type1: result1, type2: result2, default: result3) chooses one result by the type of expr, at compile time. The controlling expression is not evaluated. Uses:

  • type-generic interfaces such as <tgmath.h> (sqrt picks sqrtf, sqrt or sqrtl);
  • a MAX(a, b) that dispatches to a real function per type, so each argument is evaluated once;
  • type-safe print or serialise macros.

Things it teaches you about C types (from code/m08_generic_and_static_assert.c):

TYPE_NAME('a')                  = int   (character constants are int in C, char in C++)
TYPE_NAME(sizeof(int))          = unsigned long   (size_t on LP64)
TYPE_NAME(small + small)        = int   (uint8_t promoted)

A trap: on Linux int64_t is long, so a _Generic that lists both is an error there and fine on Windows (where int64_t is long long):

error: '_Generic' specifies two compatible types

List the basic types (long, long long) and let the typedefs fall into them.

docs.title: 2.11 Logging macros with __FILE__, __LINE__, __func__
docs.text:
Location information must be captured at the call site, which only a macro can do. A production shape:

#define LOG(lvl, ...)                                                                   \
    do {                                                                                \
        if ((lvl) >= LOG_COMPILED_MIN && (lvl) >= g_runtime_min)                        \
            log_write((lvl), __FILE__, __LINE__, __func__, __VA_ARGS__);                \
    } while (0)
  • The level test comes before the arguments are evaluated, so a disabled debug line costs one comparison, not a snprintf of its arguments.
  • LOG_COMPILED_MIN is a constant, so lines below it are removed by the compiler entirely (build with -DLOG_COMPILED_MIN=1 to drop debug logging from a release binary).
  • log_write carries __attribute__((format(printf, 5, 6))), so every LOG call is format-checked.
  • log_write formats the whole line into one buffer and emits it with one call, so lines from different threads do not interleave mid-line.
  • __FILE__ is the path as given to the compiler, which may be a long build-machine path. Strip it at run time (as the example does), use GCC 12+'s __FILE_NAME__ (just the file name), or -fmacro-prefix-map=/build/dir/= to rewrite it at compile time.

docs.title: 2.12 When to prefer static inline functions and constants
docs.text:
Use a function (static inline in a header) whenever it can do the job: arguments are type-checked and evaluated once, it has a symbol you can break on, it respects scope. Use an enum for integer constants that need to be constant expressions. Note the C-specific catch: static const int N = 16; is not a constant expression in C (it is in C++), so it cannot size a file-scope array or be a case label:

error: variably modified 'table' at file scope
error: case label does not reduce to an integer constant

Use enum { N = 16 }; or #define N 16 for those.

Macros remain the right tool only for what functions cannot do: capturing __FILE__/__LINE__/ __func__ at the call site; stringising and token pasting (#, ##, X-macros); conditional compilation; constants used in #if; type-generic selection (_Generic); and control flow at the call site (return or goto cleanup inside a CHECK macro).

docs.title: 3.1 The traps: code/m08_macro_traps.c
docs.text:
One trap (the multi-statement macro) is caught by GCC, so the file silences that warning around that single statement with #pragma GCC diagnostic, with a comment saying why. Run gcc -std=c17 -E -P m08_macro_traps.c | tail -60 to see every expansion.

SQUARE_BAD(2 + 3) = 11, SQUARE(2 + 3) = 25
10 * DOUBLE_BAD(3) = 33, 10 * DOUBLE(3) = 60
MAX_BAD(i++, 3) = 6 and i is now 7   (i was incremented twice)
max_int(i++, 3) = 5 and i is now 6
BUMP_BOTH_BAD under a false if: a = 0, b = 1   (b changed anyway)
STR(__LINE__) = __LINE__, XSTR(__LINE__) = 78
CAT(counter_, debit) -> counter_debit = 2

docs.title: 3.2 X-macro error codes and struct printer: code/m08_xmacro_error_codes.c
docs.text:
#define TXN_FIELDS(X)                       \
    X(uint32_t, id,           PRIu32)       \
    X(int64_t,  amount_paise, PRId64)       \
    X(uint32_t, branch,       PRIu32)

struct txn {
#define X(type, name, fmt) type name;
    TXN_FIELDS(X)
#undef X
};

static void txn_print(const struct txn *t)
{
#define X(type, name, fmt) printf("  %-13s = %" fmt "\n", #name, t->name);
    TXN_FIELDS(X)
#undef X
}

6 error codes:
  0 ERR_OK                   success
  1 ERR_NOT_FOUND            account not found
  2 ERR_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS   insufficient funds
  3 ERR_ACCOUNT_FROZEN       account is frozen
  4 ERR_DB_UNAVAILABLE       database unavailable, retry later
  5 ERR_PROTOCOL             malformed request
txn:
  id            = 9001
  amount_paise  = -250075
  branch        = 7

The count is computed by expanding the table with X defined as +1, and a _Static_assert on it forces whoever adds an error to look at the documentation.

docs.title: 3.3 _Generic and _Static_assert: code/m08_generic_and_static_assert.c
docs.text:
static int    max_i(int a, int b)       { return a > b ? a : b; }
static long   max_l(long a, long b)     { return a > b ? a : b; }
static double max_d(double a, double b) { return a > b ? a : b; }
#define MAX(a, b) _Generic((a) + (b), int: max_i, long: max_l, double: max_d)((a), (b))

TYPE_NAME('a')                  = int   (character constants are int in C, char in C++)
TYPE_NAME(sizeof(int))          = unsigned long   (size_t on LP64)
TYPE_NAME(small + small)        = int   (uint8_t promoted)
TYPE_NAME(1.0f * 2)             = float
TYPE_NAME("abc")                = char *
TYPE_NAME(1u + 1L)              = long
TYPE_NAME((struct wire_header){0}) = something else
MAX(i++, 2) evaluated i++ once; MAX(2.5, 1.0) = 2.5; MAX(10L, 20L) = 20

"abc" is char *, not const char *: in C a string literal has type char[4] (modifying it is still undefined). 1u + 1L is long on LP64 by the usual arithmetic conversions (module 02, rule 4); on Windows it would be unsigned long. The file also shows that a side effect must never be placed inside assert(): with NDEBUG defined (Release builds) the whole expression disappears.

docs.title: 3.4 Logging and CHECK macros: code/m08_logging_and_check_macros.c
docs.text:
/* CHECK: on failure, record the code, log the failing expression as text, jump to cleanup.

 * Requires a local `int rc` and a `cleanup:` label in the calling function. */
#define CHECK(cond, code)                                                               \
    do {                                                                                \
        if (!(cond)) {                                                                  \
            rc = (code);                                                                \
            LOG_ERRORF("check failed: %s -> rc=%d", #cond, rc);                         \
            goto cleanup;                                                               \
        }                                                                               \
    } while (0)

static int load_customer_file(const char *path, size_t want_bytes)
{
    int rc = 0;
    FILE *f = NULL;
    char *buf = NULL;

    LOG_INFOF("loading %s (%zu bytes)", path, want_bytes);
    buf = malloc(want_bytes);
    CHECK(buf != NULL, -1);
    f = fopen(path, "rb");
    CHECK(f != NULL, -2);
    CHECK(fread(buf, 1, want_bytes, f) == want_bytes, -3);
    LOG_INFOF("loaded %s", path);

cleanup:
    if (f != NULL) fclose(f);
    free(buf);
    return rc;
}

INFO  m08_logging_and_check_macros.c:94 main(): server starting, pid file /run/bank.pid
DEBUG m08_logging_and_check_macros.c:96 main(): debug now visible, 8 workers
INFO  m08_logging_and_check_macros.c:77 load_customer_file(): loading /nonexistent/customers.dat (64 bytes)
ERROR m08_logging_and_check_macros.c:81 load_customer_file(): check failed: f != NULL -> rc=-2
load_customer_file returned -2; 4 log lines written

#cond turns the failing expression into the text f != NULL in the log: at 3 AM that tells you which check failed without opening the source. The first LOG_DEBUGF in main is filtered at run time and its arguments are never evaluated. Built with -DLOG_COMPILED_MIN=1, the debug line vanishes from the binary and the program prints 3 log lines (its final assert adapts). Verified: strings finds the text "debug now visible" once in the default build and zero times in the -DLOG_COMPILED_MIN=1 build, at both -O0 and -O2.

docs.title: 3.5 One source, two platforms: code/m08_platform_conditionals.c
docs.text:
#if defined(_WIN32)
#  define WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN
#  include <windows.h>
#  define PLAT_NAME "Windows"
#  define PLAT_PATH_SEP '\\'
static void plat_sleep_ms(unsigned ms) { Sleep(ms); }
static unsigned long plat_pid(void) { return (unsigned long)GetCurrentProcessId(); }
#elif defined(__linux__) || defined(__APPLE__) || defined(__unix__)
#  include <time.h>
#  include <unistd.h>
#  define PLAT_NAME "POSIX"
#  define PLAT_PATH_SEP '/'
static void plat_sleep_ms(unsigned ms)
{
    struct timespec ts = {(time_t)(ms / 1000), (long)(ms % 1000) * 1000000L};
    while (nanosleep(&ts, &ts) != 0 && errno == EINTR) { /* signal: sleep the remainder */ }
}
static unsigned long plat_pid(void) { return (unsigned long)getpid(); }
#else
#  error "unsupported platform: add a branch to the portability layer"
#endif

[plat] platform: POSIX, path separator '/'
[plat] long is 64-bit (LP64)
[plat] <threads.h> available: yes
[plat] pid is positive: yes
[plat] slept 20 ms through the portability layer

The data-model line comes from #if LONG_MAX == 2147483647L: limits from <limits.h> can be tested by the preprocessor, sizeof cannot (the preprocessor does not know types). __has_include(<threads.h>) is standard in C23 and an extension in GCC and Clang, so the file first checks #if defined(__has_include).

docs.title: Translation phases: why a backslash ends your comment
docs.text:
The standard describes eight translation phases. The first four are the preprocessor's, and their order explains several surprises:

  1. Map source characters (and, before C23, trigraphs like ??/).
  2. Line splicing: every backslash immediately followed by a newline is deleted, joining the two lines. This is how multi-line macros work.
  3. Tokenise; replace each comment by one space.
  4. Execute directives and expand macros.

Because splicing (phase 2) happens before comments are removed (phase 3), a // comment that ends with a backslash swallows the next line:

    int x = 1;
    // add one to x, see C:\temp\
    x = x + 1;
    printf("%d\n", x);     /* prints 1: the increment became part of the comment */

GCC warns (warning: multi-line comment [-Wcomment], in -Wall) and MSVC has warning C4010 (single-line comment contains line-continuation character), but only if someone reads the warnings. Windows paths in comments are exactly where trailing backslashes appear. This is also why the continuation lines of the X-macro tables in this course contain no // comments.

docs.title: How macro expansion really works
docs.text: For a function-like macro, the preprocessor collects the arguments, fully macro-expands each argument on its own (unless the parameter is an operand of # or ##), substitutes, then rescans the result together with the rest of the file. During rescanning, the name of a macro being expanded is "painted blue" and not expanded again, which is why macros cannot recurse and why #define foo foo + 1 is harmless. The # exception to argument pre-expansion is the whole reason XSTR needs two levels.

docs.title: The multiple-include optimisation
docs.text: When GCC or Clang preprocess a header whose entire content is wrapped in #ifndef X / #define X / ... / #endif, they remember the file and the guard macro. A later #include of the same file, with X still defined, is skipped without even opening the file. So include guards cost nothing at build time, and #pragma once is not faster on these compilers.

docs.title: _Generic and lvalue conversion
docs.text: The controlling expression undergoes lvalue conversion: arrays decay to pointers, functions to function pointers, and top-level qualifiers are dropped (const int x selects int). Qualifiers below the top level remain, so const char * and char * are different associations. Since the expression is not evaluated, _Generic(i++, ...) does not increment i; only the chosen branch's code runs.

docs.title: Seeing what the preprocessor did
docs.text:
• gcc -E file.c (MSVC cl /P file.c): the full translation unit with line markers.
  • gcc -E -P file.c: without line markers, easier to read.
  • gcc -dM -E file.c: every macro defined at the end; echo | gcc -dM -E - lists only predefined ones (that is how you find __BYTE_ORDER__ or check _FORTIFY_SOURCE).
  • -g3 keeps macro definitions in the debug info: gdb info macro NAME and macro expand EXPR.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Side effects inside assert. assert(init_audit_log() == 0); works in the Debug build and silently skips initialisation in the Release build, where NDEBUG removes the whole expression. The audit log then fails much later. Call the function, store the result, assert on the variable.
  • Windows header macros. min/max from <windows.h> break code that uses those names (NOMINMAX); ERROR from wingdi.h breaks enums (NOGDI); <windows.h> included before <winsock2.h> drags in the old winsock.h and produces redefinition errors (define WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN, or include winsock2.h first).
  • Double evaluation with real side effects. MAX(next_sequence(), floor) consumes two sequence numbers; ABS(read_sensor()) reads twice. Found by reading macro definitions whenever a value is "occasionally off by one step". Replace with static inline functions.
  • The #ifdef branch nobody builds. The Linux branch of the portability layer was written once and never compiled again; the first Linux build of the server fails in forty places. Build all supported platforms in CI on every change.
  • Silent #if typos. #if ENABLE_AUDIT_LOG where the build defines ENABLE_AUDIT_LOGS: auditing is off and nothing says so. Compile with -Wundef and prefer #if defined(X) plus #error for impossible combinations.
  • Expensive disabled logging. A logging macro that formats its arguments before checking the level spends real CPU on lines nobody sees. Profile shows vsnprintf high in a server that "logs nothing". Check the level first.
  • Build paths in binaries. __FILE__ embeds the build machine's absolute paths in every log line and in the binary. Use __FILE_NAME__ or -fmacro-prefix-map to keep logs short and builds reproducible.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. (easy) Run gcc -std=c17 -E -P m08_macro_traps.c and find the expansion of every macro use in main. Done when you can point at the exact text that makes MAX_BAD(i++, 3) increment twice and BUMP_BOTH_BAD escape the if.
  2. (easy) Write a SWAP macro with an internal tmp, then break it with SWAP(tmp, x). Fix it twice: with GCC's __typeof__ and a less collision-prone name, and with a static inline function per type. Done when you can argue which fix you would ship and why.
  3. (medium) Combine this module with module 07: write one X-macro table of opcodes (X(OP_BALANCE, 1, h_balance, "balance")) that generates the opcode enum, the name strings for logs, and the const dispatch table. Done when adding an opcode is one line and a _Static_assert fails if the table and an OP_COUNT disagree.
  4. (medium) Extend the logging macro: add a monotonic timestamp and the thread id, build the whole line in one buffer, and emit it with a single fwrite. Done when building with -DLOG_COMPILED_MIN=1 leaves no debug format strings in the binary (check with strings ./prog | grep debug).
  5. (medium) Add plat_mutex (CRITICAL_SECTION on Windows, pthread_mutex_t on POSIX) and plat_thread_create to m08_platform_conditionals.c, using the callback-with-context shape of module 07. Done when the POSIX branch compiles with -Werror and is exercised by a two-thread counter test, and you have checked every Windows call against its documentation.
  6. (hard) Write PRINT(x) with _Generic covering int, unsigned, long, unsigned long, long long, unsigned long long, double, char * and const char *. Then try to add int64_t and read the error. Done when the macro compiles on LP64, you can explain why it would also compile on LLP64, and you have a test that prints one value of each type.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does the preprocessor do, and when does it run? It runs before compilation proper, on tokens: it splices continued lines, removes comments, executes directives (#include pastes files, #define sets up text replacement, #if removes code) and expands macros. Its output is one translation unit per source file. It knows nothing about types or scopes, which is the source of most macro bugs.

Q: Include guards or #pragma once? Both prevent double inclusion. Guards are standard but fail if two headers share a guard name; #pragma once is supported by all major compilers but can be confused by the same file reached via different paths. GCC and Clang optimise guards so speed is equal. Pick one and be consistent.

Q: Why are multi-statement macros wrapped in do { } while (0)? So the macro is a single statement that requires exactly one trailing semicolon. Without a wrapper only the first statement is controlled by an if; with bare braces, MACRO(); else becomes {...}; else, a syntax error. The loop runs once and is optimised away.

Q: What are the dangers of function-like macros, and when would you use a static inline function instead? Missing parentheses change precedence, arguments with side effects are evaluated multiple times, local names can capture the caller's names, there is no type checking, and macros cannot be debugged. Use static inline functions for computations; keep macros for call-site information (__FILE__, __LINE__), stringising and pasting, conditional compilation and type dispatch.

Q: What is an X-macro? A list defined once as a macro taking another macro, expanded several times with different definitions of that macro to generate parallel artefacts: an enum, its name strings, messages, dispatch tables, struct fields and printers. It keeps them in sync by construction.

Q: What do # and ## do, and why does stringising a macro's value need two levels? # turns an argument into a string literal, ## pastes two tokens. Arguments are expanded before substitution except when used with # or ##, so STR(__LINE__) gives "__LINE__"; an outer XSTR(x) expands x first and then calls STR.

Q: Give uses of _Static_assert. Checking the size and field offsets of structs that are written to disk or the network, that a table has as many entries as its enum, that a constant is a power of two, and assumptions such as sizeof(void *) == 8. The build fails with a message instead of the program failing at run time.

Q: What is the type of 'a' in C, and how would you show it? int (in C++ it is char). _Generic('a', char: "char", int: "int") selects "int", and sizeof 'a' is 4 on common platforms.

Q: How do you write a logging macro that records file, line and function? A variadic macro that passes __FILE__, __LINE__ and __func__ plus __VA_ARGS__ (with the format inside it) to a printf-like function marked with the format attribute, wrapped in do { } while (0), with the level check before the call so disabled lines do not evaluate their arguments, and a compile-time minimum level so debug lines can be removed entirely.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• The preprocessor works on tokens before compilation: #include pastes, #define replaces, #if removes. gcc -E shows its output.
  • Include guards or #pragma once, consistently; self-contained headers.
  • Parenthesise macro parameters and bodies; beware double evaluation; wrap statements in do { } while (0).
  • # stringises, ## pastes; use two levels to stringise a macro's value; keep the format inside __VA_ARGS__ for portable variadic macros.
  • X-macros generate enums, names, messages and tables from one list.
  • Confine platform #ifdefs to a small portability layer; _WIN32 is defined on 64-bit Windows too; test __clang__ before __GNUC__; use -Wundef.
  • _Static_assert locks layouts and table sizes at compile time.
  • _Generic selects by type without evaluating; 'a' is int; int64_t is long on Linux.
  • Logging macros capture __FILE__/__LINE__/__func__, check the level first, and call a format-checked function.
  • Prefer static inline functions and enum constants; static const int is not a constant expression in C.
  • Never end a // comment with a backslash: line splicing happens before comments are removed.

docs.title: 09. Undefined behaviour and the optimizer
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: modules 01 (how C works), 02 (integers and conversions), 03 (pointers)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
The C standard is a contract between you and the compiler. You promise to follow its rules. The compiler promises that your program behaves as written, but only for runs that follow the rules. When a run breaks a rule, for example a signed int overflows or a null pointer is dereferenced, the standard says the behaviour is undefined. It does not mean "the hardware does whatever it does". It means the contract is void. The compiler owes you nothing for that run.

The surprise is not that broken code crashes. The surprise is that the compiler uses the rules as facts while optimising. If you dereference p, the compiler concludes "p is not null, or the programmer broke the contract", and it deletes your later if (p == NULL) check. If you write a + b < a, it concludes "signed addition cannot overflow", and it folds the whole check to false. Your safety check disappears from the binary without a warning.

An analogy: a bank teller who is told "customers never present forged cheques". She does not check for forgery, because she was told it cannot happen. Every rule you break is a forged cheque the system was told it would never see. Usually nothing happens. Then one day, after a compiler upgrade, it does, and only in the release build.

This module teaches the categories, the catalogue of undefined behaviour (UB), real GCC 13 examples you can reproduce, and the flags, warnings and sanitizers that defend you.

docs.title: 2.1 Three kinds of "the standard does not say exactly"
docs.text:
Kind Meaning Must the compiler document it? Examples Implementation-defined The compiler picks one behaviour and documents it Yes sizeof(int), whether plain char is signed, right shift of a negative int, converting an out-of-range value to a signed type Unspecified One of several allowed behaviours, chosen silently, may differ per call No order of evaluation of function arguments (f(a(), b())), whether two identical string literals share memory, the value of padding bytes Undefined No requirements at all, for the whole run No signed overflow, null dereference, out-of-bounds access, data race

The difference matters. Implementation-defined code is portable if you check the documented choice (GCC documents its choices in the "C Implementation-Defined Behavior" chapter of its manual). Unspecified code is fine as long as every allowed outcome is acceptable to you. Undefined code is never fine, even when it "works".

Two more facts that interviewers like:

  • UB is a property of a run, not of the source file. a + b is perfectly defined for a = 1, b = 2. It is undefined only for the inputs that overflow.
  • UB can travel backwards in time. Because the compiler may assume UB never happens, it can reason "the code after this point would be UB if x were 0, so x is not 0", and that conclusion can change code that runs before the bad operation. You cannot rely on "it printed my log line before crashing, so everything before the crash ran as written".

docs.title: 2.2 The catalogue
docs.text:
These are the classes you must be able to name, show a one-line example of, and say how to catch.

UB One-line example What the optimiser does with it Catch it with Signed integer overflow INT_MAX + 1, x * 2 assumes it never happens: folds overflow checks, widens loop counters UBSan signed-integer-overflow, -ftrapv, -fwrapv to define it Null pointer dereference int n = p->len; with p == NULL concludes p != NULL afterwards, deletes later null checks UBSan null, ASan, the crash itself Out-of-bounds access a[4] for int a[4]; also forming p + 5 for a 4-element array assumes indexes stay in range: may delete loop exits or return constants ASan, UBSan bounds, -Warray-bounds Reading an uninitialised local int v; if (c) v = 1; return v; picks whatever value is convenient (often the other branch's value) Valgrind, MSan (clang), -Wmaybe-uninitialized (not reliable) Strict-aliasing violation *(float *)&some_int = 0.0f; assumes an int * and a float * never point to the same object, keeps stale values in registers -Wstrict-aliasing (at -O2), -fno-strict-aliasing to switch the assumption off Shift too wide or negative 1u << 32, 1 << -1, -1 << 1 assumes the count is in range UBSan shift, -Wshift-count-overflow for constants Unsequenced modification i = i++ + 1;, a[i] = i++; any order, or both, or neither -Wsequence-point (in -Wall) Data race two threads, one writes, no lock and no atomic assumes no other thread writes: hoists loads out of loops, merges stores TSan Division by zero, INT_MIN / -1 x / 0 assumes the divisor is valid UBSan integer-divide-by-zero, SIGFPE on x86 Misaligned access *(int *)(buf + 1) may emit instructions that require alignment (SSE, ARM) UBSan alignment Use after the lifetime ends using freed memory, a dangling pointer to a local anything (see 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/04_the_catalogue_of_memory_bugs.md) ASan, Valgrind Bad arguments to library functions memcpy(dst, NULL, 0), overlapping memcpy uses glibc's nonnull attributes as facts UBSan nonnull-attribute, ASan Modifying a string literal char *s = "abc"; s[0] = 'X'; literal is in read-only memory: SIGSEGV the crash; declare const char *

The last few are covered in modules 03, 04 and 05 of this course; this module concentrates on the ones where the optimiser turns a latent bug into a different program.

docs.title: 2.3 How the optimiser uses UB, step by step
docs.text:
Compilers do not hunt for UB in order to punish you. They run ordinary optimisations that are only correct if the rules hold:

  1. Value-range reasoning. For signed x, x + 1 > x is "always true" in a world without overflow. GCC's constant folder rewrites it to 1. With overflow defined as wrapping (-fwrapv) it cannot.
  2. Facts from dereferences and attributes. After *p or after passing p to a parameter declared nonnull, the compiler records "p is not null" and deletes any later test of it. GCC's flag for this is -fdelete-null-pointer-checks, on by default at -O2.
  3. Type-based alias analysis (TBAA). The strict aliasing rule (C17 6.5p7) says an object may only be accessed through its own type, a compatible type, a signed or unsigned variant, or a character type. So a store through float * cannot change an int, and the compiler keeps the int in a register across it.
  4. Loop analysis. A loop for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) with a signed counter cannot wrap, so it runs exactly n + 1 times and i can be promoted to a 64-bit register without sign-extension on every iteration. With unsigned i the compiler must allow for wraparound. This is the legitimate performance reason signed overflow is UB.

None of these is a bug in the compiler. All of them turn your bug into surprising machine code.

docs.title: 2.4 The flags that change the contract
docs.text:
Flag Effect Cost -fwrapv Signed overflow wraps (two's complement) and is no longer UB Loses some loop optimisations -ftrapv Signed overflow aborts at run time Slow; GCC's implementation is incomplete; prefer UBSan -fno-strict-aliasing Disables TBAA; any pointer may alias any object Fewer values kept in registers; often a few percent in hot loops (typical, measure yours) -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks Keeps null checks after dereferences Tiny -fno-strict-overflow In current GCC, the same as -fwrapv plus pointer wrapping As -fwrapv

The Linux kernel builds with -fno-strict-aliasing, -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks and -fno-strict-overflow: kernel code does type punning and low-address tricks on purpose, and its maintainers decided the safety was worth the speed. These flags are a safety net for legacy code, not a licence to write new UB. Code that needs them is still non-portable: MSVC and Clang have their own, different sets of switches.

docs.title: 2.5 Tools: warnings first, sanitizers second
docs.text:
Warnings catch the forms that are visible in one function. This is real GCC 13 output for a file with four classic mistakes (gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -c w1.c):

w1.c:2:22: warning: operation on 'i' may be undefined [-Wsequence-point]
    2 | int unseq(int i) { i = i++ + 1; return i; }
w1.c:3:41: warning: 'sizeof' on array function parameter 'a' will return size of 'int *' [-Wsizeof-array-argument]
    3 | size_t param(int a[10]) { return sizeof a; }
w1.c:4:28: warning: dereferencing type-punned pointer will break strict-aliasing rules [-Wstrict-aliasing]
    4 | float pun(int x) { return *(float *)&x; }

The fourth mistake was int maybe(int c) { int v; if (c) v = 1; return v; }. GCC 13 printed no warning for it at -O2: the optimiser had already decided that v is 1 on both paths (it is allowed to, because reading the uninitialised v is UB) and then had nothing left to warn about. Lesson: -Wmaybe-uninitialized is useful but not a proof. Valgrind and MSan are the tools for uninitialised reads.

Sanitizers check at run time, on the inputs you actually run:

Sanitizer Flag Catches Overhead (typical) UBSan -fsanitize=undefined overflow, shifts, null, bounds (static arrays), alignment, bad nonnull args, invalid bool/enum loads small, usable in test builds ASan -fsanitize=address out-of-bounds heap/stack/global, use-after-free, double free, leaks about 2x CPU, 2-3x memory TSan -fsanitize=thread data races, some lock-order problems 5-15x CPU MSan -fsanitize=memory (clang only) uninitialised reads about 3x

Make UBSan fatal in CI with -fno-sanitize-recover=all, otherwise it prints and carries on and a test that "passed" may have hit UB. The deep dive on all sanitizers is 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/08_valgrind_and_sanitizers.md; the flag reference is 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps/03_gcc_and_clang_flags_that_matter.md.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: Four programs in code/. Each says in its header comment that it contains deliberate UB, gives the exact build line, and still compiles cleanly with gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror. The UB functions are marked __attribute__((noinline)) and fed through volatile variables so the optimiser cannot fold the whole demo at compile time.

docs.title: 3.1 The overflow check that disappears (m09_overflow_check.c)
docs.text:
/* WRONG: by the time we compare, the overflow (UB) has already happened. */
__attribute__((noinline)) bool naive_add_overflows(int a, int b)
{
    return b > 0 && a + b < a;
}

/* RIGHT 1: compare against the limit BEFORE adding. Works on every compiler. */
static bool add_overflows_precheck(int a, int b)
{
    if (b > 0) return a > INT_MAX - b;   /* INT_MAX - b cannot overflow when b > 0 */
    if (b < 0) return a < INT_MIN - b;   /* INT_MIN - b cannot overflow when b < 0 */
    return false;
}

/* RIGHT 2: let the compiler do it. C23 standardises this as ckd_add() (GCC 14+). */
static bool add_overflows_builtin(int a, int b, int *sum)
{
    return __builtin_add_overflow(a, b, sum);
}

/* RIGHT 4: the size_t check you need before every malloc(count * size). */
static bool mul_size_overflows(size_t count, size_t size)
{
    return size != 0 && count > SIZE_MAX / size;
}

Real results for naive_add_overflows(INT_MAX, 1) with GCC 13.3 on x86-64:

Build Result Why -O0 0 folded even without optimisation: GCC's front end rewrites a + b < a to b < 0 -O2 0 same, and the function body becomes xorl %eax,%eax; ret -O2 -fwrapv 1 overflow is now defined as wrapping, so the fold is not allowed -O0 -g -fsanitize=undefined 1 plus a report UBSan instruments the add, which blocks the fold

The -O2 assembly, from gcc -std=c17 -O2 -S -o - m09_overflow_check.c:

naive_add_overflows:
    endbr64
    xorl    %eax, %eax
    ret

The UBSan report:

m09_overflow_check.c:30:23: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'

The point to remember: "it fails at -O2 but works at -O0" is a common sign of UB, but not a reliable test. Here even -O0 was affected.

docs.title: 3.2 The null check that disappears (m09_null_check_deleted.c)
docs.text:
/* The CVE-2009-1897 shape (Linux tun driver): use the pointer first, check it later. */
__attribute__((noinline)) int record_len(const struct record *r)
{
    int n = r->len;            /* line A: if r were NULL, this is already UB ... */
    if (r == NULL)             /* line B: ... so GCC deletes this at -O2         */
        return -1;
    return n;
}

/* A version whose deletion you can SEE at run time without crashing. */
__attribute__((noinline)) int copy_then_check(char *dst, const char *src, size_t n)
{
    memcpy(dst, src, n);       /* UB if src == NULL, even with n == 0 */
    if (src == NULL)           /* GCC: "src went to a nonnull parameter, so it is not NULL" */
        return -1;
    return 0;
}

The assembly of record_len at -O2, then with -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks:

record_len:                         record_len:
    endbr64                             endbr64
    movl    (%rdi), %eax                testq   %rdi, %rdi
    ret                                 movl    $-1, %eax
                                        cmovne  (%rdi), %eax
                                        ret

copy_then_check(dst, NULL, 0) at run time:

Build Result -O0 -1 (check survived) -O2 0 (check deleted) -O2 -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks -1 UBSan -1, plus runtime error: null pointer passed as argument 2, which is declared to never be null

memcpy(dst, NULL, 0) "works" on every C library you will meet, which is exactly why this bug survives code review. The fix is boring: validate first, and skip the call when n == 0.

docs.title: 3.3 Strict aliasing (m09_strict_aliasing.c)
docs.text:
__attribute__((noinline)) int store_both(int *i, float *f)
{
    *i = 1;
    *f = 0.0f;       /* a float store "cannot" change an int ... */
    return *i;       /* ... so at -O2 this returns the cached 1 */
}

Called as store_both(&x, (float *)&x):

-O0                       store_both returned 0, x now holds bits 0x00000000
-O2                       store_both returned 1, x now holds bits 0x00000000
-O2 -fno-strict-aliasing  store_both returned 0, x now holds bits 0x00000000

At -O2 the function returns 1 while memory holds 0. That is the shape of the real bug: a value in a register disagrees with memory. The three legal ways to reinterpret bytes:

uint32_t u; memcpy(&u, &f, sizeof u);                    /* 1. memcpy: compiles to one move */
union { float f; uint32_t u; } pun = { .f = f };         /* 2. union: legal in C, not in C++ */
unsigned char first = *(const unsigned char *)&one;      /* 3. character types may alias anything */

The same file parses a wire header that sits at an odd offset in a buffer with memcpy into a local struct, which is also the cure for misaligned access.

docs.title: 3.4 Let UBSan name each class (m09_ubsan_catalogue.c)
docs.text:
With no argument it runs only safe helpers (checked_add, safe_shl, safe_div, safe_get). With an argument it triggers one class. Real output of the UBSan build (gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -O0 -g -fsanitize=undefined ..., then ./m09_ubsan_catalogue_ub all):

--- add
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:34:56: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'
    returned -2147483648
--- mul
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:35:56: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 * 2 cannot be represented in type 'int'
    returned -2
--- negate
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:36:46: runtime error: negation of -2147483648 cannot be represented in type 'int'; cast to an unsigned type to negate this value to itself
    returned -2147483648
--- shift_wide
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:37:53: runtime error: shift exponent 32 is too large for 32-bit type 'unsigned int'
    returned 1
--- shift_neg
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:38:48: runtime error: shift exponent -1 is negative
    returned -2147483648
--- shift_lneg
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:39:55: runtime error: left shift of negative value -1
    returned -2
--- bounds
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:43:15: runtime error: index 4 out of bounds for type 'int [4]'
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:43:15: runtime error: load of address 0x7fff75a10040 with insufficient space for an object of type 'int'
    returned 1973485664
--- misaligned
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:49:12: runtime error: load of misaligned address 0x7fff75a10051 for type 'int', which requires 4 byte alignment
    returned 0

(The hex-dump lines UBSan prints under the bounds and alignment reports are left out; addresses and the garbage value from bounds change from run to run.)

Look at shift_wide: 1u << 32 returned 1, not 0. The x86 shl instruction masks the count to 5 bits, so the hardware computed 1 << 0. Another CPU, or a constant the compiler folds, gives 0. "What the hardware does" is not a definition. The cases that trap after the report:

$ ./m09_ubsan_catalogue_ub null
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:54:12: runtime error: load of null pointer of type 'int'
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
$ ./m09_ubsan_catalogue_ub div0
m09_ubsan_catalogue.c:56:49: runtime error: division by zero
Floating point exception (core dumped)

Build with -fno-sanitize-recover=all and the first report ends the run with exit status 1, which is what a CI job needs.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Where in GCC each example happened. The overflow fold is done by fold-const.cc while the front end builds the expression tree, which is why it appears even at -O0. The null-check deletion is value-range propagation (the tree-vrp and related passes) using "non-null" facts derived from dereferences and from __attribute__((nonnull)) on glibc's memcpy declaration. GCC goes further with -fisolate-erroneous-paths-dereference (on at -O2): if a path is certain to dereference null, it replaces that path with a trap instruction (ud2), so you get SIGILL instead of SIGSEGV. The aliasing result comes from type-based alias analysis: every type gets an alias set, and loads and stores from disjoint sets are allowed to be reordered or forwarded. char, signed char and unsigned char have alias set 0, which conflicts with everything.

Why int loop counters are faster. On x86-64 an int index must be sign-extended to 64 bits before it can be used in an address. If i could wrap, the compiler would have to redo that extension every iteration. Because signed overflow is UB, GCC can compute the index in a 64-bit register once ("induction variable widening") and vectorise the loop knowing its exact trip count. With -fwrapv or an unsigned counter that can wrap, some of these transformations are lost. This is the honest argument for why the language keeps signed overflow undefined.

How UBSan works. It is compile-time instrumentation, not a library trick. For a + b with -fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow, GCC emits the add with an overflow-flag check and, on overflow, calls __ubsan_handle_add_overflow with a static descriptor holding the file, line, column and type. That is why the report is so precise, and why instrumented code is not folded the same way: the instrumentation itself uses the result. -fsanitize-trap=undefined replaces the handler calls with a trap instruction and needs no runtime library, which makes it usable in constrained environments.

LLVM's model, for completeness. Clang represents "this value came from UB" as poison. Poison propagates through arithmetic and only becomes true UB when it reaches something that matters (a branch, a memory address, a call). That model explains why a compiler can delete code before the bad operation: the branch that depends on poison may be resolved either way.

The data-race rule is the same idea. C11 5.1.2.4 makes a data race UB so the compiler may keep a shared variable in a register inside a loop. A while (!stop) {} loop on a plain int stop may legally become an infinite loop that never reloads stop. volatile stops that particular reload problem but still leaves a race; _Atomic is the fix (module 14).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• MSVC to GCC ports expose UB that "worked for years". MSVC does not perform type-based alias analysis, so code that casts char buffers to struct pointers or punns int and float usually behaves as written there. Built with GCC or Clang at -O2 on Linux, the same code can read stale values. If you port parts of a Win32 server to Linux, either fix the punning with memcpy or build those files with -fno-strict-aliasing until you have.
  • Compiler upgrades are a risk event. Each GCC release learns new facts to use. A length check like if (offset + len < offset) on signed values can pass review and testing for years and silently vanish after an upgrade. Run the test suite under UBSan before and after any compiler change, and keep -Wall -Wextra -Werror on.
  • "Only fails in the release build" playbook. (1) Rebuild the release flags plus -fsanitize=undefined,address and rerun the failing case. (2) If that is clean, toggle the contract flags one at a time: if -fno-strict-aliasing makes it disappear, hunt for punning; if -fwrapv does, hunt for overflow; if -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks does, look for a check after a use. (3) Bisect the optimisation level per file (#pragma GCC optimize or per-object flags) to find which translation unit is affected. Record the finding in the RCA as "latent UB exposed by optimisation", not "compiler bug": it almost never is the compiler.
  • Untrusted lengths make UB a security problem. In a banking server, lengths come from network messages and files. Signed overflow in a length check, or a size multiplication that wraps, is the first step of a remotely triggered memory corruption. Do size arithmetic in size_t with the SIZE_MAX / size check from 3.1, or with __builtin_mul_overflow.
  • Do not "fix" UB with volatile or by lowering the optimisation level. That hides the symptom on today's compiler. Fix the operation, then add the UBSan run to CI so it stays fixed.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - classify. For each, say implementation-defined, unspecified or undefined, with one line of reasoning: sizeof(long); f(g(), h()) call order; -1 >> 1; INT_MAX + 1; (int)3000000000u; char *s = "hi"; s[0] = 'H';. Done when all six are classified and you can name the clause of the contract each one breaks or relies on.
  2. Easy - reproduce. Build m09_overflow_check.c four ways (-O0, -O2, -O2 -fwrapv, UBSan) and fill in the table from 3.1 yourself. Done when your numbers match and you can explain the -O0 result.
  3. Medium - see the deletion. Generate assembly for m09_null_check_deleted.c at -O2 with and without -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks. Done when you can point at the instruction that holds the null check in one listing and say why it is missing from the other.
  4. Medium - aliasing in a parser. Write uint32_t read_be32(const unsigned char *p) three ways: pointer cast plus ntohl, memcpy plus ntohl, and shifts. Call each on buf + 1. Build with -O2 -fsanitize=undefined. Done when you can say which version UBSan reports and why, and which one is portable without ntohl.
  5. Hard - the loop that never ends. Write a loop for (int i = 1; i > 0; i += i) that counts iterations. Build at -O0 and -O2, run each with timeout 2. Explain the difference using section 2.3. Done when you have the two outputs (or the timeout) and a three-sentence explanation.
  6. Hard - audit legacy code. Take any C file you know from work (or m15_legacy_report.c) and build it with -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wstrict-aliasing=2 -fsanitize=undefined. Run its tests. Done when you have a list of every warning and report with a one-line verdict each: real UB, false positive, or implementation-defined.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined behaviour? A: Implementation-defined behaviour is a choice the compiler must document, such as the size of int or whether char is signed. Unspecified behaviour is one of several allowed outcomes chosen without documentation, such as the order in which function arguments are evaluated. Undefined behaviour has no requirements at all: the standard places no constraint on the whole run, and the optimiser may assume it never happens.

Q: Why might if (a + b < a) fail to detect overflow? A: For signed int, overflow is undefined, so the compiler may assume a + b does not overflow and simplify a + b < a to b < 0. With b > 0 the check becomes constant false; GCC 13 does this even at -O0. Check before adding (a > INT_MAX - b) or use __builtin_add_overflow or C23 ckd_add.

Q: How can the compiler remove a null check? A: If the pointer was already dereferenced, or passed to a function whose parameter is declared nonnull such as glibc's memcpy, then a null value would already have caused UB, so the compiler infers the pointer is non-null and deletes later tests. This was the root of the 2009 Linux tun driver exploit. Check before use, or build legacy code with -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks.

Q: What is the strict aliasing rule and how do you type-pun legally? A: An object may only be accessed through an lvalue of its own (compatible) type, a signed or unsigned variant, a qualified version, an aggregate containing it, or a character type. Writing an int through a float * breaks it, and GCC at -O2 may keep the old int in a register. Pun with memcpy (portable, compiles to a register move), with a union in C (not in C++), or read the bytes through unsigned char *.

Q: Your service works in debug and fails in release. How do you investigate? A: Treat it as likely UB or a race exposed by optimisation. Rebuild release flags with UBSan and ASan and rerun the failing input; for threads, run TSan. If the sanitizers are quiet, toggle -fno-strict-aliasing, -fwrapv and -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks one at a time to find the class, then narrow the translation unit by building files at different optimisation levels.

Q: Is volatile a fix for undefined behaviour? A: No. volatile forces every access to happen in memory, which suppresses some optimisations, but it does not make signed overflow, aliasing violations or data races defined. It is meant for memory-mapped hardware and for volatile sig_atomic_t flags set by signal handlers. Fix the operation instead.

Q: What does -fsanitize=undefined do, and why add -fno-sanitize-recover=all in CI? A: It instruments operations such as signed arithmetic, shifts, array indexing and pointer alignment with checks that call a runtime handler on failure and print the exact file, line and values. By default it prints and continues, so a test can pass while hitting UB; -fno-sanitize-recover=all makes the first report abort the run so CI fails.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Implementation-defined = documented choice; unspecified = undocumented choice among allowed outcomes; undefined = no requirements for the whole run.
  • The optimiser treats the rules as facts: no signed overflow, no null dereference, no out-of-bounds access, no aliasing across unrelated types, no data races.
  • Real GCC 13 results: the naive overflow check folds to false (even at -O0); a null check after memcpy(dst, NULL, 0) is deleted at -O2; an int written through float * reads back stale at -O2.
  • Correct overflow checks compare against the limit before the operation, or use __builtin_add_overflow / C23 ckd_add; size products use count > SIZE_MAX / size.
  • Pun types with memcpy, a union (C only) or unsigned char *; never by casting pointers.
  • -fwrapv, -fno-strict-aliasing and -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks change the contract; they are a safety net for legacy code, not a fix.
  • Warnings catch local forms (-Wsequence-point, -Wstrict-aliasing, -Wsizeof-array-argument), but they are not proof; GCC 13 did not warn on an obvious uninitialised read.
  • UBSan for arithmetic and pointer UB, ASan for memory, TSan for races, Valgrind or MSan for uninitialised reads; -fno-sanitize-recover=all in CI.
  • A compiler upgrade or an MSVC-to-GCC port can turn latent UB into a production incident.

docs.title: 10. Error handling and resource cleanup
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: modules 04 (memory, storage and lifetime), 05 (strings), 09

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
C has no exceptions and no destructors. A function that can fail tells you so through its return value, and every resource you acquire (memory, a file, a socket, a lock, a database handle) you must release yourself, on every path out of the function: the normal path and each error path.

That second part is where mature C servers keep most of their bugs. The normal path runs a million times a day and is well tested. The path where the third malloc fails, or the second fopen fails, runs almost never, so nobody notices that it leaks the first buffer or closes a file twice. Then a disk fills up at a customer site, every request takes the error path, and the process leaks itself to death.

Think of closing a bank branch at night. Whatever was opened during the day (vault, safe, cash drawer, lights) must be closed in the reverse order, whether the staff leave at six as usual or at three because the fire alarm went off. The goto-cleanup idiom in this module is that checklist written in code: one place at the bottom of the function, closing things in reverse, reached from every exit.

This module covers how C reports errors (return codes, errno), how to clean up correctly, who owns what, when to use assert, how to log an error so that someone can act on it, and how to design the error model of a C library the way Berkeley DB did.

docs.title: 2.1 The ways C code reports failure
docs.text:
