Convention Example How you check Trap -1 (or NULL) plus errno POSIX open, read, fopen, malloc if (fd < 0) { use errno } errno is only valid right after the failure Negative errno as return value Linux kernel: return -ENOMEM; if (ret < 0) mixing it with the -1 style in one codebase Positive error number as return value pthread_*, Berkeley DB, getaddrinfo (its own codes) if (rc != 0) perror is wrong here: errno was not set Sentinel value EOF from fgetc, NULL from strchr, 0 from fread compare, then ask why (ferror, feof) 0 from fread can be EOF or an error Out-parameter error object struct err *e filled by the callee inspect after the call forgetting to initialise it Per-thread "last error" errno, Win32 GetLastError(), WSAGetLastError() read immediately any other call in between may overwrite it

Pick one convention per library or module and write it in the header. Most bugs here come from a caller assuming one convention while the callee uses another, for example calling perror after pthread_mutex_lock fails (pthreads return the error number and leave errno alone).

docs.title: 2.2 The rules of errno
docs.text:
errno is a per-thread integer (C11 and POSIX make it thread-local; glibc defines it as (*__errno_location())). Its rules are stricter than most people remember:

  1. It is meaningful only when the function's return value said "failed".
  2. No library function ever sets it to 0. A successful call may still change it (glibc's printf can leave ENOTTY behind the first time it probes whether stdout is a terminal).
  3. Any call between the failure and your read of errno may overwrite it. Logging is the usual culprit: your logger calls fopen, write or localtime, and the reason is lost.
  4. strtol, strtoll and friends are the exception that needs errno = 0 before the call, because they report overflow only through errno == ERANGE.
  5. strerror(e) returns text but is not guaranteed thread-safe. Use strerror_r. Careful: with _POSIX_C_SOURCE you get the XSI version that returns int and fills your buffer; with _GNU_SOURCE you get the GNU version that returns a char * that may not be your buffer.

On Windows the equivalent is GetLastError(), with the same overwrite problem, plus WSAGetLastError() for Winsock. FormatMessage turns the number into text.

docs.title: 2.3 The goto-cleanup idiom
docs.text:
Without goto, a function that acquires three resources needs either deeply nested ifs (the "arrow" shape) or copies of the cleanup code at every return, and the copies drift apart. With goto, every failure jumps forward to a cleanup block at the bottom. Two shapes are common.

Shape 1, Linux kernel style: one label per resource, in reverse order of acquisition.

in = fopen(src, "rb");
if (!in) { err = errno; goto out; }
out = fopen(dst, "wb");
if (!out) { err = errno; goto close_in; }
buf = malloc(N);
if (!buf) { err = ENOMEM; goto close_out; }
/* ... work ... */
free_buf:
    free(buf);
close_out:
    if (fclose(out) != 0 && err == 0) err = errno;
close_in:
    fclose(in);
out:
    return err;

A failure jumps to the label that releases exactly what has been acquired so far, and falls through the rest. The labels read like a stack being unwound.

Shape 2: one cleanup: label, every resource starts as NULL.

FILE *f = NULL;
char *line = NULL;
struct table *t = NULL;
/* ... every failure: err = ...; goto cleanup; ... */
*out = t;      /* success: ownership moves to the caller ... */
t = NULL;      /* ... so cleanup must not free it */
cleanup:
    table_free(t);         /* accepts NULL, like free() */
    free(line);
    if (f) fclose(f);      /* fclose(NULL) is UB: guard it */
    return err;

Shape 2 is easier to keep correct when code is edited later, because the order of labels cannot get out of step with the order of acquisition. It needs release functions that accept NULL, or a guard for the ones that do not: fclose(NULL) is undefined, close(-1) merely fails with EBADF, and Win32 CloseHandle on an invalid handle fails (and raises an exception under a debugger).

Why goto is accepted here: the jumps go only forward and only to cleanup, so the control flow stays readable. The Linux kernel coding style recommends it, and the SEI CERT C rule MEM12-C ("consider using a goto chain when leaving a function on error when using and releasing resources") describes it. The alternatives have their own costs: do { ... } while (0) with break works for one level only; GCC and Clang's __attribute__((cleanup(fn))) (used by systemd's _cleanup_free_) runs a function when a variable leaves scope, which is close to RAII but not portable to MSVC.

docs.title: 2.4 Single exit discipline
docs.text:
"One return at the bottom" makes cleanup and logging easy to verify and is required by some standards (MISRA C 2012 rule 15.5 is advisory). Enforced dogmatically, it produces flag variables and deep nesting. The pragmatic rule most senior C programmers use:

  • Early returns are fine before you have acquired anything (argument validation).
  • After the first acquisition, every exit goes through the cleanup block.
  • Never return from the middle of a function that holds a lock.

docs.title: 2.5 Ownership, written down
docs.text:
C has no type that says "I own this". So you say it in names and in comments, and you keep the same convention everywhere:

Convention Meaning x_create() / x_destroy(), x_open() / x_close(), x_init() / x_fini() pairs: whoever called the first calls the second "Returns a pointer the caller must free with x_free()" ownership transferred to the caller "Returns a pointer into t, valid until the next call that modifies t" borrowed; do not free, do not keep const char * parameter the function reads it and does not keep it after returning "Takes ownership of buf" after the call, the caller must not touch or free buf Out-parameter "set only on success" on failure the caller's variable keeps its previous value

The idiom *out = t; t = NULL; before the cleanup label is how ownership transfer looks in code: the cleanup frees whatever the function still owns, and after the transfer it owns nothing. free(NULL) being a no-op is what makes this pattern cheap. Setting a pointer to NULL after freeing it turns a later double free into a harmless no-op and a later use into an immediate, easy-to-diagnose null dereference.

docs.title: 2.6 assert versus runtime checks
docs.text:
assert(cond) runtime check For conditions that can only be false if the program is wrong (invariants, preconditions between your own functions) conditions that depend on input or environment (user data, files, network, memory, disk) In release builds removed when NDEBUG is defined always present On failure prints the expression, file, line, then abort() (core dump) returns an error the caller handles Example assert(acc != NULL) in an internal function if (amount > balance) return WD_INSUFFICIENT;

Rules that follow:

  • Never put work inside assert: assert(fd = open(...)) disappears in release builds.
  • Never use assert to validate input. A malformed message must not kill a banking server.
  • _Static_assert (C11) checks layout assumptions at compile time for free: _Static_assert(sizeof(struct hdr) == 16, "wire header layout");.
  • Some server teams keep asserts on in production on purpose: if an internal invariant is broken, stopping with a core dump is better than continuing and writing wrong balances. That is a deliberate decision; write it down, and still never assert on input.

docs.title: 2.7 Logging an error so someone can act on it
docs.text:
A useful error line answers five questions: what was being attempted, on which object, what went wrong (code and text), where in the code, and which request it belonged to.

ERROR m10_error_model.c:261 main(): loading accounts for branch 42: No such file or directory (code 2)

Two rules keep logs useful at scale:

  • Log once, at the layer that decides what to do. Lower layers return the code plus a detail string; the request handler logs it with the request id. If every layer logs, one failure becomes five lines and nobody can count incidents.
  • Save the error code before calling the logger. The logger itself may change errno or GetLastError() (section 2.2 and the real bug in m10_errno_conventions.c).

docs.title: 2.8 Designing a C library's error model, Berkeley DB style
docs.text:
Berkeley DB, which you meet in 07_Databases_Internals/10_berkeley_db_and_embedded_kv_stores.md, has a clean model worth copying:

  1. Every function returns int; 0 is success.
  2. Positive values are system errno codes passed through unchanged (ENOENT, ENOMEM).
  3. Negative values in a reserved range are the library's own codes (DB_NOTFOUND, DB_KEYEXIST, DB_LOCK_DEADLOCK, ...), chosen far from zero (near -30000) so they never collide with an errno.
  4. One function, db_strerror(int), turns any of them into text.
  5. Expected outcomes are not errors. DB_NOTFOUND from a get is a normal answer. It is returned quietly, not logged.
  6. Detailed messages go to an application-supplied callback (DB_ENV->set_errcall) with a prefix (set_errpfx), so the application decides where messages are written.

m10_error_model.c implements the same model for a tiny key-value store and adds two habits: the handle keeps the detailed message for the last failure (like sqlite3_errmsg(db) in SQLite), and out-parameters are written only on success. Other well-known models: SQLite returns SQLITE_OK or a code and keeps a per-connection message; OpenSSL keeps a per-thread queue of errors. Whatever you choose, a library must never call exit() or abort() on a runtime error: that decision belongs to the application.

docs.title: 2.9 What C++ changes (and what it does not)
docs.text: In C++, destructors run on every exit path, including exceptions, so the goto chain becomes a set of RAII objects and the cleanup code disappears (02_Modern_CPP/03_raii_the_core_idea.md). Errors can travel as exceptions or as values (std::optional, std::expected in C++23; see 02_Modern_CPP/10_error_handling_exceptions_optional_expected.md). But as soon as C++ calls a C library (POSIX, Win32, Berkeley DB, libpq), the C conventions of this module are back: you check the return code, read errno or GetLastError() immediately, and usually wrap the handle in a small RAII class whose destructor calls the C close function.

docs.title: 3.1 Both cleanup shapes, proved by fault injection (m10_goto_cleanup.c)
docs.text:
The file wraps malloc, realloc, free, fopen and fclose in counting wrappers. Setting g_fail_at = N makes the Nth wrapped call fail. The test first runs a function successfully and counts its calls, then reruns it once per call with that call failing, and after each run checks that no allocation is live and no file is open:

static void *t_malloc(size_t n)
{
    if (should_fail()) return NULL;
    void *p = malloc(n);
    if (p) g_live_allocs++;
    return p;
}

/* in main(): */
for (int n = 1; n <= load_points; n++) {
    struct account_table *never = (struct account_table *)&never;   /* sentinel */
    reset_injection(n);
    int err = load_accounts(acc, &never, NULL);
    assert(err == ENOMEM || err == EMFILE);
    assert(never == (struct account_table *)&never);   /* *out untouched on failure */
    assert(g_live_allocs == 0 && g_open_files == 0);
}

Real output:

copy_file: 3 failure points injected, 0 leaks, 0 open files
load_accounts: 6 failure points injected, 0 leaks, 0 open files
load_accounts(bad file): Invalid argument at line 3
load_accounts(missing file): No such file or directory
all checks passed

Six failure points for load_accounts: the fopen, two mallocs and the three reallocs that grow the table from 4 to 8 to 16 entries. Every one of them is now a tested path. This technique is how you test error handling that never happens on a developer machine; it works the same for Win32 (HeapAlloc, CreateFileW) wrappers.

Note the realloc handling inside load_accounts:

struct account *grown = t_realloc(t->items, ncap * sizeof *grown);
if (!grown) {                    /* t->items is still valid and is freed below */
    err = ENOMEM;
    goto cleanup;
}
t->items = grown;

Writing t->items = realloc(t->items, ...) directly would overwrite the only pointer to the old block with NULL on failure: a leak that only happens when memory is already short.

docs.title: 3.2 A library error model (m10_error_model.c)
docs.text:
#define KV_OK        0
#define KV_NOTFOUND  (-30500)   /* key not present: a normal outcome, not a failure */
#define KV_KEYEXIST  (-30501)
#define KV_FULL      (-30502)
#define KV_BADARG    (-30503)
#define KV_CORRUPT   (-30504)

typedef struct kv kv_t;         /* opaque: callers never see the fields */

const char *kv_strerror(int err)
{
    switch (err) {
    case KV_NOTFOUND: return "KV_NOTFOUND: key not found";
    /* ... */
    }
    if (err > 0)
        return strerror(err);   /* system error passed through */
    return "KV: unknown error code";
}

/* Records a contextual message on the handle, reports it through the callback, and

 * returns err so call sites can write: return kv_fail(kv, KV_FULL, "...", ...); */
static int kv_fail(kv_t *kv, int err, const char *fmt, ...);

Real output (the first three lines come from the application's error callback, the fourth from the LOG_ERR macro that adds file, line and function):

[kv-test] kv_put: key 'ACC-1': KV_KEYEXIST: key already exists
[kv-test] kv_put: key 'ACC-3', capacity 2: KV_FULL: store is full
[kv-test] kv_load: open '/no/such/file.kv': No such file or directory
ERROR m10_error_model.c:261 main(): loading accounts for branch 42: No such file or directory (code 2)
all checks passed

The test also checks that kv_get of a missing key returns KV_NOTFOUND without calling the error callback, and that a failed kv_open leaves the caller's pointer untouched.

docs.title: 3.3 errno done right and done wrong (m10_errno_conventions.c)
docs.text:
static int parse_long(const char *s, long *out)
{
    char *end;
    errno = 0;                         /* strtol sets errno only on failure; clear it first */
    long v = strtol(s, &end, 10);
    if (end == s)       return EINVAL; /* no digits */
    if (errno == ERANGE) return ERANGE;
    /* ... skip trailing spaces ... */
    if (*end != '\0')   return EINVAL; /* "12abc": atoi would silently return 12 */
    *out = v;
    return 0;
}

static int open_for_write_buggy(const char *path)
{
    int fd = open(path, O_WRONLY);
    if (fd < 0) {
        log_to_file("open failed\n");  /* BUG: clobbers errno before the caller reads it */
        return -1;
    }
    return fd;
}

Real output. Opening the directory / for writing fails with EISDIR; the buggy version's logger tries to open a log file in a missing directory, and that ENOENT is what reaches the caller:

parse_long("12abc") -> Invalid argument; atoi("12abc") -> 12
buggy: errno says 'No such file or directory'
fixed: errno says 'Is a directory'
all checks passed

Imagine that second line in a production log. The support engineer spends a day looking for a missing file. The real problem was a path that pointed at a directory.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What goto compiles to. Nothing special: a jump. GCC produces essentially the same machine code for the goto chain as for the equivalent nested ifs. The cleanup block is ordinary code that the optimiser can share between paths. With __builtin_expect (or the kernel's unlikely() macro) on the failure tests, GCC lays out the error blocks away from the hot path, and with -freorder-blocks-and-partition (on by default at -O2 on x86) it moves blocks it believes are cold, from __builtin_expect or profile data, to a separate .text.unlikely section, so error handling costs almost nothing in instruction-cache space.

Why C has no exceptions, and what setjmp/longjmp really do. setjmp saves the callee-saved registers, stack pointer and program counter into a jmp_buf; longjmp restores them, which makes setjmp appear to return a second time. Nothing in between is unwound: no free, no fclose, no pthread_mutex_unlock. Local variables modified after setjmp have indeterminate values after the jump unless they are volatile. That is why longjmp is used only in narrow places (some parsers, Lua's error handling, libpng's error callback) and why C++ exceptions needed compiler-generated unwind tables (.eh_frame) to run destructors.

How errno is per-thread. glibc declares extern int *__errno_location(void) and defines errno as (*__errno_location()). The function returns the address of a thread-local variable (in the TLS block that the %fs register points to on x86-64). A system call wrapper stores the negated kernel return value there when the kernel returns a value in the range -4095 to -1. So errno is cheap to read, but every library call is free to write it.

__attribute__((cleanup)). GCC and Clang call the named function with a pointer to the variable when the variable goes out of scope, by any path (return, break, goto), but not on longjmp. It is the closest C gets to RAII, and code like systemd relies on it heavily. MSVC does not support it, which rules it out for a Win32 codebase.

Fault injection at scale. The wrapper technique in 3.1 needs source changes. Alternatives: an LD_PRELOAD library that replaces malloc and fails the Nth call (no recompilation), the Linux kernel's fault-injection framework (failslab, fail_page_alloc) for kernel code, and on Windows Application Verifier's low-resource simulation. Running the full test suite with each injected failure point is expensive; teams usually run it nightly rather than per commit.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Error-path leaks are slow incidents. A leak in the error path of request parsing costs nothing until a misbehaving client sends a burst of bad requests. Memory then grows by (leak size x bad requests) and the process is eventually killed. The RSS graph shows steps that line up with error-log bursts, which is the clue (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/09_leaks_and_memory_growth.md).
  • Win32 handles are resources too. CreateFileW, CreateEventW, OpenProcess and RegOpenKeyExW return handles that must be closed (CloseHandle, RegCloseKey) on every path. Task Manager's "Handles" column growing over hours is the Windows version of an fd leak. Note the inconsistent failure values: CreateFileW returns INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE (-1), while CreateEventW returns NULL.
  • Half-updated state is worse than a leak. If a function updates two fields of a shared structure and fails between them, the next request sees an inconsistent object. Either validate everything first and mutate last, or build the new state on the side and swap it in at the end. In money-moving code this rule is not optional.
  • Map internal errors to wire errors at the boundary. A client of the RPC server should get a stable error code ("insufficient funds", "invalid account", "internal error, reference REQ-81723"), not strerror text or a file path. Log the internal detail with the same reference so support can join the two.
  • Out of memory is real on Windows. Linux usually overcommits, so malloc rarely returns NULL and the OOM killer acts later. Windows commits memory at allocation time, so a 32-bit or commit-limited process sees NULL from malloc or HeapAlloc under load. Code that never checks crashes at a random dereference far from the cause.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - spot the bug. Find three errors in this code and fix them: char *buf = malloc(n); FILE *f = fopen(p, "r"); if (!f) { perror("fopen"); return -1; } if (fread(buf, 1, n, f) != n) return -1; fclose(f); return 0;. Done when your version has no leak on any path and reports which call failed.
  2. Easy - errno discipline. Write int read_int_file(const char *path, long *out) that returns 0 or a positive errno, uses strtol correctly, and leaves *out untouched on failure. Test it on a missing file, an empty file, "12abc" and "99999999999999999999". Done when all four return the right code.
  3. Medium - convert a nested function. Rewrite a function with four nested if levels that opens two files and allocates two buffers into shape 2 of the goto idiom. Add the fault injection wrappers from m10_goto_cleanup.c. Done when the injection loop reports N failure points and zero leaks.
  4. Medium - extend the error model. Add kv_del and a KV_READONLY code to m10_error_model.c, plus a kv_set_readonly(kv, 1). Done when kv_put on a read-only store returns KV_READONLY, the callback prints a contextual message, and kv_strerror knows the new code.
  5. Hard - LD_PRELOAD fault injection. Write failmalloc.c that defines malloc and fails the Nth call (read N from an environment variable; call the real one via dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "malloc")). Run an unmodified program under it for N = 1..20. Done when you can name every N where the program crashes instead of reporting an error.
  6. Hard - Win32 version. Port copy_file from m10_goto_cleanup.c to Win32 with CreateFileW, ReadFile, WriteFile, CloseHandle, returning a DWORD from GetLastError(). Done when it compiles with MSVC /W4 /WX and every handle is closed on every path.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do you handle errors and cleanup in C without exceptions? A: Each function returns a status (0 or an error code, or -1 with errno), and callers check every call. Resources are released through a single cleanup section at the end of the function, reached with forward gotos from each failure point, releasing in reverse order of acquisition. Ownership of returned resources is documented and transferred explicitly.

Q: Why is goto acceptable for cleanup? A: The jumps only go forward to one cleanup block, so control flow stays readable, and the alternative is either deep nesting or duplicated cleanup code that drifts out of sync. The Linux kernel coding style recommends it and CERT C rule MEM12-C describes it. It is the C equivalent of a destructor running on every exit path.

Q: What are the pitfalls of errno? A: It is only meaningful immediately after a call that reported failure; successful calls may change it and nothing resets it to 0; any intervening call, especially logging, can overwrite it, so save it at once. strtol needs errno = 0 before the call. pthreads and many libraries return the error number instead of setting errno.

Q: When do you use assert and when a runtime check? A: assert is for conditions that can only fail if the program itself is wrong, such as an internal invariant or a precondition between your own functions; it is removed with NDEBUG, so it must have no side effects. Anything that depends on input, files, network or resources gets a runtime check that returns an error, in every build.

Q: How would you design the error model for a C library? A: Return int from every function, 0 for success, positive values for passed-through errno codes and negative library-specific codes in a reserved range, like Berkeley DB. Provide one lib_strerror, keep a detailed per-handle message and an optional error callback, treat expected outcomes such as "not found" as quiet return values, write out-parameters only on success, and never call exit or abort from the library.

Q: What goes wrong with p = realloc(p, n)? A: If realloc fails it returns NULL and leaves the old block allocated, so the assignment loses the only pointer to it: a leak that only happens under memory pressure. Assign to a temporary, check it, then update p.

Q: How do you test error paths that almost never run? A: Fault injection: wrap allocation and I/O functions so the Nth call fails, count the calls on a successful run, then rerun once per call with that call failing and assert no leaks, no open handles and a correct error code. Without source changes, an LD_PRELOAD failing malloc or Windows Application Verifier can do the same.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• C reports errors through return values; pick one convention per module and document it.
  • errno is valid only right after a reported failure; save it before calling anything else, set it to 0 before strtol; pthreads return the error number instead.
  • The goto-cleanup idiom releases resources in reverse order from one place; shape 2 (NULL-initialised resources, one label) is the easiest to keep correct.
  • Transfer ownership with *out = t; t = NULL;; write out-parameters only on success; release functions should accept NULL.
  • Never p = realloc(p, n); never put work inside assert.
  • assert for program bugs, runtime checks for input and environment; _Static_assert for layout assumptions.
  • Log once, at the layer that decides, with what/which/code/where/request id.
  • Berkeley DB model: 0 ok, positive errno passthrough, negative library codes, one strerror, "not found" is not an error, an error callback for detail.
  • Fault injection turns rare error paths into tested paths; m10_goto_cleanup.c exercises 9 failure points.
  • C++ RAII removes the cleanup code, but C conventions return at every C API boundary.

docs.title: 11. Data structures in C
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: modules 03 (pointers), 04 (memory, storage and lifetime), 06 (structs and layout), 07 (function pointers), 10

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
C gives you three building blocks: arrays, structs and pointers. There is no vector, no map, no list. Every C codebase of any size therefore contains its own growable array, its own linked list, its own hash table, and usually a ring buffer and a priority queue. In an old server you will find several versions of each, written by different people over the years.

Writing them is not hard. Writing them so they are correct under every edge case, safe when sizes come from outside, and usable for more than one element type is the senior part. Two questions decide the design of every C container:

  1. Who owns the memory? Does the container copy the element, or keep a pointer to something the caller owns? When does a pointer you got from the container stop being valid?
  2. How is it generic? C has no templates. You choose between void * plus an element size plus a comparator (the qsort way), macros that generate a typed version per element type, or intrusive links embedded in your own structs (the Linux kernel way).

Think of a warehouse. A dynamic array is one long shelf that you replace with a longer shelf when it fills (and everything moves). A linked list is boxes chained with string: easy to insert anywhere, slow to walk. An intrusive list is boxes with the hook already built into the box. A hash table is a wall of numbered pigeonholes. A ring buffer is a carousel. A heap is the "most urgent first" tray.

docs.title: 2.1 Dynamic array
docs.text:
State: a pointer, a length, a capacity, and for the generic version the element size.

  • Growth. When full, multiply capacity by a constant factor (2 here; 1.5 is also common) and realloc. Geometric growth makes push amortised O(1): the total copying over n pushes is at most about 2n element copies. Growing by a constant (+16) makes it O(n) per push on average.
  • Overflow. cap * elem_size must not wrap. Check ncap > SIZE_MAX / elem_size before multiplying. A wrapped size gives a tiny allocation followed by a heap overflow.
  • realloc may move the block. Every pointer into the array is invalid after a push that reallocates. This is the C version of "iterator invalidation" and a common use-after-free.
  • Removal in the middle shifts the tail with memmove (not memcpy: the regions overlap). If order does not matter, move the last element into the hole instead: O(1).
  • Failure must leave the array usable. Assign realloc's result to a temporary first.

docs.title: 2.2 Singly linked list and the pointer-to-pointer trick
docs.text:
Most people write list deletion with a special case for the head. Using a pointer to "the link that points at the current node" removes the special case:

struct snode **pp = head;              /* first: the address of the head variable */
while (*pp) {
    if ((*pp)->value == value) {
        struct snode *dead = *pp;
        *pp = dead->next;              /* relinks the head OR a previous node's next */
        free(dead);
    } else {
        pp = &(*pp)->next;             /* now: the address of this node's next field */
    }
}

Two more rules: read next before you free a node, and remember that a list costs a cache miss per node, so walking a long list is much slower than scanning an array of the same length. Lists win when you need O(1) insertion or removal at a known position, stable element addresses, or splicing whole lists together.

docs.title: 2.3 Intrusive doubly linked lists and container_of
docs.text:
A normal ("non-intrusive") list allocates a node that points to your data: two allocations per element and an extra pointer hop. An intrusive list puts the links inside your struct:

struct list_head { struct list_head *next, *prev; };

struct session {
    int              id;
    char             user[16];
    struct list_head all_link;    /* on the list of all sessions */
    struct list_head lru_link;    /* and, at the same time, on the LRU list */
};

The list code only ever sees struct list_head *. To get back from a link to the object that contains it, subtract the link's offset inside the struct:

#define container_of(ptr, type, member) \
    ((type *)(void *)((char *)(ptr) - offsetof(type, member)))

Design points of the Linux kernel's list_head that m11_lists.c copies:

  • Circular with a sentinel head. An empty list's head points at itself. Insertion and removal never test for NULL, which removes a whole class of edge-case bugs.
  • One object, many lists, zero allocations. Adding a session to the LRU list costs four pointer writes and no malloc. Removing it, given only the object, is O(1).
  • list_for_each_safe reads the next pointer before the loop body runs, so the body may remove (and free) the current element.

Windows has the same idea: LIST_ENTRY and the CONTAINING_RECORD macro (both in winnt.h), plus InsertTailList and RemoveEntryList in the driver kit headers, are list_head, container_of, list_add_tail and list_del under other names.

docs.title: 2.4 Open-addressing hash table
docs.text:
All entries live in one array of slots. To insert, hash the key, take hash & (cap - 1) (cap is a power of two) and probe forward until you find the key or an empty slot (linear probing).

cap = 8, keys A (hash -> 3), B (hash -> 3), C (hash -> 4)

slot:  0     1     2     3     4     5     6     7
      [   ] [   ] [   ] [ A ] [ B ] [ C ] [   ] [   ]
                         ^home of A and B; B probed to 4; C's home 4 taken, probed to 5
  • Deletion needs tombstones. If you delete B by marking slot 4 empty, a lookup for C starts at 4, sees "empty" and stops: C is lost. Mark it TOMB instead: lookups skip it, inserts may reuse it.
  • Load factor. Keep (live + tombstones) / cap below about 0.7. Above that, probe chains get long fast. Rebuilding (rehashing into a new array) drops all tombstones; if most slots are tombstones, rebuild at the same size instead of growing.
  • Store the full hash in the slot. A mismatch is then usually rejected by comparing two integers, without touching the key string in another cache line.
  • Own the keys. Copy the key on insert, or document that the caller must keep it alive. A key pointing into a request buffer that is later freed is a classic dangling-pointer bug.
  • Hash function. FNV-1a is simple and fine for trusted keys. When an attacker chooses the keys (HTTP headers, account ids in requests) they can force every key to collide and turn O(1) into O(n) per operation (hash flooding). Use a keyed hash such as SipHash with a random seed.

Separate chaining (an array of linked lists) is the other design; it tolerates high load and simple deletion, but costs an allocation and a pointer hop per entry. 03_Data_Structures_Algorithms/04_hashing_hash_tables.md compares the two in depth.

docs.title: 2.5 Ring buffer
docs.text:
A fixed array used as a FIFO queue. The classic implementation keeps head and tail indexes and wastes one slot to tell "full" from "empty". The cleaner version keeps free-running unsigned counters and a power-of-two capacity:

count = head - tail;                     /* correct even after head wraps past UINT_MAX */
buf[head & (cap - 1)] = v; head++;       /* push */
v = buf[tail & (cap - 1)]; tail++;       /* pop  */

Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2^N, so head - tail is the element count even when head has wrapped and tail has not. (With signed counters this would be UB, module 09.) A single-producer single-consumer version with atomics for head and tail is the basis of lock-free queues between two threads (04_Concurrency/08_lock_free_basics.md).

docs.title: 2.6 Binary heap
docs.text:
A complete binary tree stored in an array. For index i: parent (i - 1) / 2, children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. The root holds the minimum (for a min-heap).

  • push: append at the end, then sift up (swap with the parent while smaller): O(log n).
  • pop: take the root, move the last element to the root, sift down (swap with the smaller child while larger): O(log n).
  • heapify an existing array bottom-up: O(n), not O(n log n).
  • Top-k from a stream: keep a min-heap of size k; replace the root when a bigger item arrives. O(n log k) time, O(k) memory.

Servers use heaps for timers (the next timeout is at the root) and schedulers.

docs.title: 2.7 Three ways to be generic in C
docs.text:
Approach Example Type safety Speed Cost void * + element size + function pointers qsort, bsearch, struct vec in m11_vec.c, struct heap in m11_ring_heap.c none: a wrong cast compiles memcpy of a runtime size per element; comparator is an indirect call that usually cannot be inlined one copy of the code Macros that stamp out typed code DEFINE_VEC(T, name) in m11_vec.c; BSD <sys/queue.h>; klib's khash.h full as fast as hand-written code bloat, unreadable compiler errors, debugger steps into macros Intrusive links list_head + container_of (Linux), LIST_ENTRY + CONTAINING_RECORD (Windows) partial (the container_of type is trusted) best: no extra allocation or indirection the object's struct must know which lists it can be on

The comparator rule for the void * approach: never return a - b;. For ints, 2000000000 - (-2000000000) overflows (UB) and gives the wrong sign. Write return (a > b) - (a < b);.

C++ templates are the third row done properly: the compiler generates typed code, type-checks it and can inline the comparator. That is why std::sort with a lambda is usually faster than qsort on the same data.

docs.title: 3.1 m11_vec.c: generic vector and macro-generated typed vector
docs.text:
static int vec_reserve(struct vec *v, size_t want)
{
    if (want <= v->cap)
        return 0;
    size_t ncap = v->cap ? v->cap : 8;
    while (ncap < want) {
        if (ncap > SIZE_MAX / 2)
            return ENOMEM;
        ncap *= 2;
    }
    if (ncap > SIZE_MAX / v->elem_size)
        return ENOMEM;
    void *p = realloc(v->data, ncap * v->elem_size);
    if (!p)
        return ENOMEM;        /* v->data is still valid: nothing lost, nothing dangling */
    v->data = p;
    v->cap = ncap;
    v->reallocs++;
    return 0;
}

#define DEFINE_VEC(T, name)                                                     \
    struct name { T *data; size_t len; size_t cap; };                           \
    static inline int name##_push(struct name *v, T x) { /* grow, then */      \
        /* ... */ v->data[v->len++] = x; return 0; }

DEFINE_VEC(double, dvec)            /* no ';' after it: -Wpedantic rejects a stray one */
DEFINE_VEC(struct txn, txnvec)

(The macro above is shortened; the file has the full body.) Real output:

1000 pushes: capacity 1024, 8 reallocations
all checks passed

Eight reallocations for 1000 pushes: capacities 8, 16, 32, ..., 1024. The test also sorts struct txn records with a two-key comparator, uses bsearch, removes with memmove, and shows that 2000000000 - (-2000000000) does not fit in an int.

docs.title: 3.2 m11_lists.c: pointer-to-pointer singly list, and an intrusive LRU
docs.text:
The session table keeps every session on two intrusive lists at once and evicts from the tail of the LRU list:

static void session_touch(struct session_table *t, struct session *s)
{
    list_del(&s->lru_link);
    list_add(&s->lru_link, &t->lru);      /* O(1) move to front: no search */
}

static struct session *session_evict_lru(struct session_table *t)
{
    if (list_empty(&t->lru))
        return NULL;
    struct session *s = list_entry(t->lru.prev, struct session, lru_link);
    list_del(&s->lru_link);
    list_del(&s->all_link);               /* O(1) removal from the other list too */
    t->count--;
    return s;                             /* caller owns it now */
}

Real output:

evicted session 101 (bilal); container_of recovered it from &lru_link
offsetof(struct session, lru_link) = 40
all checks passed

offsetof is 40 because id (4 bytes) + user (16 bytes) + 4 bytes of padding + all_link (16 bytes) come first. container_of subtracts exactly that from the address of lru_link. Add a hash table from session id to struct session * and you have the classic O(1) LRU cache.

docs.title: 3.3 m11_hash_table.c: linear probing with tombstones
docs.text:
static struct slot *ht_probe(const struct htab *t, const char *key, uint64_t h, int for_insert)
{
    size_t mask = t->cap - 1;
    struct slot *first_tomb = NULL;
    for (size_t i = (size_t)h & mask;; i = (i + 1) & mask) {
        struct slot *s = &t->slots[i];
        if (s->state == SLOT_EMPTY)
            return for_insert ? (first_tomb ? first_tomb : s) : NULL;
        if (s->state == SLOT_TOMB) {
            if (!first_tomb)
                first_tomb = s;
        } else if (s->hash == h && strcmp(s->key, key) == 0) {
            return s;
        }
    }
}

The loop has no exit condition of its own: it terminates because the load rule guarantees at least one EMPTY slot. That invariant is the kind of thing you write next to the code. Real output:

after 10000 inserts: cap=16384 live=10000 load=0.61 rebuilds=11
after 200000 put/del pairs: cap=16384 live=5000 tombs=4600 rebuilds=28
all checks passed

The churn test inserts and deletes 200 000 temporary keys. Tombstones pile up, a same-size rebuild clears them 17 times, and the capacity never grows: memory stays flat under a workload of short-lived keys, such as sessions that log in and out.

docs.title: 3.4 m11_ring_heap.c: ring buffer across the wrap point, generic heap, top-k
docs.text:
The ring test starts both counters at UINT_MAX - 3 so the head wraps during the test, and the heap is checked against qsort on 1000 values and then used for a top-3 query over 10 000 transactions:

ring: counters wrapped (head=4 tail=4), FIFO order kept
top-3 amounts: 999745 999730 999678
all checks passed

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What realloc really costs. glibc first tries to grow the block in place (if the next chunk is free or it is the top chunk). Blocks above the mmap threshold (128 KiB by default, adjusted dynamically) live in their own mmap mapping, and growing them uses mremap, which moves page-table entries instead of copying bytes. So a vector of a few MiB grows cheaply, while a vector of 64 KiB records in a fragmented heap copies. Either way, your pointers into it are invalid. See 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/03_the_heap_malloc_internals.md.

Cache behaviour decides more than big-O. A cache line is 64 bytes on current x86 CPUs. An array of 8-byte values gives eight elements per miss, and the hardware prefetcher hides most misses on a sequential scan. A linked list gives one element per miss and the prefetcher cannot guess the next address. Linear probing works well for the same reason: the next probe is usually in the same or the next cache line. A binary heap's children are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, next to each other, so a sift-down touches one line per level.

void * genericity in machine code. qsort calls your comparator through a function pointer for every comparison: an indirect call the compiler cannot inline, and it copies elements with a runtime-sized loop. A typed macro version or a C++ template sees the element type and the comparator at compile time, inlines both, and can vectorise. With link-time optimisation (-flto) GCC can sometimes specialise a static generic function for a constant comparator, but you should not rely on it.

container_of and the standard. It subtracts an offset from a pointer to a member to get a pointer to the enclosing struct. This relies on the member really being inside a struct of that type; if you pass a list_head that is not embedded in a struct session, the result points at garbage and nothing checks it. The kernel's version adds a compile-time type check using typeof, a GNU extension (standard in C23). The conversion through char * is what keeps the arithmetic byte-exact.

Tombstones and latency. Without same-size rebuilds, a table under insert/delete churn fills with tombstones until every miss scans the whole array. The rebuild itself is O(n) and happens on some unlucky insert: a latency spike. Production tables either rebuild incrementally (move a few slots per operation) or use a deletion scheme that needs no tombstones, such as backward-shift deletion in Robin Hood hashing.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The dangling element pointer. struct conn *c = vec_at(&conns, i); followed later by vec_push(&conns, &new_conn); and then c->state = .... If the push reallocated, c points into freed memory. In a server this shows up as a corrupted connection object only under load (when the vector grows). Rule: store indexes or ids, not pointers into growable arrays; or use an intrusive list or a pool so addresses are stable (module 12).
  • A server's core structures are this module. A connection table keyed by socket or session id (hash table), a request queue between the acceptor and the workers (ring buffer or intrusive list protected by a lock, module 14), timers for idle connections (heap), and an LRU cache of account records (hash table plus intrusive list). Knowing how each one fails is most of debugging a C server.
  • Unbounded growth. Every container needs a maximum, enforced at insert, with a clear error. A queue with no bound turns a slow database into an out-of-memory crash instead of back-pressure.
  • Hash flooding. If request fields become hash keys, an attacker can send keys that all collide. With a public, unkeyed hash such as FNV-1a, CPU goes to 100% on one thread. Use a keyed hash with a per-process random seed for anything derived from input.
  • Old codebases have several hand-written lists. Before fixing a bug in one, check whether the others have the same bug (grep for the same idiom). That is often where the second and third production incidents are hiding.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - shrink policy. Add vec_shrink_to_fit to m11_vec.c, and make vec_pop halve the capacity when the length drops below a quarter of it. Done when a test that pushes 1000 and pops 990 ends with a capacity of at most 64 and no reallocation ping-pong when you then alternate one push and one pop.
  2. Easy - reverse and find the middle. Add slist_reverse and slist_middle to the singly list in m11_lists.c using the pointer techniques from module 16. Done when both pass on lists of length 0, 1, 2 and 5.
  3. Medium - O(1) LRU cache. Combine m11_hash_table.c (key: account id, value: pointer to a struct session) with the intrusive LRU list from m11_lists.c into lru_get and lru_put with a fixed capacity. Done when every operation is O(1) and a test with capacity 3 evicts in the right order. Compare with 03_Data_Structures_Algorithms/05_linked_lists.md.
  4. Medium - typed heap by macro. Write DEFINE_HEAP(T, name, less) that generates a typed heap where less is a macro or inline function. Benchmark it against the generic heap on 1 000 000 ints. Done when you have both timings and can explain the difference with section 4.
  5. Hard - backward-shift deletion. Replace tombstones in m11_hash_table.c with backward-shift deletion (after removing a slot, shift following entries back if that moves them closer to their home slot). Done when the churn test passes with zero tombstones and no same-size rebuilds.
  6. Hard - lock-free SPSC ring. Make the ring buffer safe for exactly one producer thread and one consumer thread using _Atomic unsigned head and tail with release/acquire ordering. Done when a 10 000 000-item test passes and TSan is clean (module 14).

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does a dynamic array achieve amortised O(1) append? A: It grows its capacity geometrically, usually by a factor of 1.5 or 2, so each reallocation copies all elements but happens after a number of pushes proportional to the current size. Over n pushes the total copying is O(n), so each push is O(1) on average. Growing by a constant amount would make the total copying O(n squared).

Q: What is an intrusive list and why does the Linux kernel use it? A: The link fields live inside the object (struct list_head embedded in the struct) instead of in a separately allocated node that points to the object. Adding to or removing from a list then needs no allocation, an object can be on several lists at once, and removal given the object is O(1). container_of recovers the object from the link by subtracting the member's offsetof.

Q: Why does open addressing need tombstones, and what is their cost? A: A lookup stops at the first empty slot, so deleting an entry by emptying its slot would break the probe chain for keys inserted after it. A tombstone marks the slot as deleted: lookups skip it and inserts may reuse it. Tombstones lengthen probes and count toward the load factor, so the table must periodically rebuild to drop them.

Q: How do you write a generic container in C? A: Either store elements as bytes with void *, an element size and function pointers for comparison (like qsort), which is one copy of code but has no type safety and an indirect call per comparison; or generate typed code per element type with macros, which is type-safe and fast but bloats code and is hard to debug; or embed intrusive links in the element type. C++ templates do the macro approach with type checking.

Q: Why is return a - b; a bad comparator? A: For signed integers the subtraction can overflow, which is undefined behaviour and in practice gives the wrong sign, so the sort silently produces a wrong order. Use return (a > b) - (a < b);, which yields -1, 0 or 1 without arithmetic overflow.

Q: How do you tell "full" from "empty" in a ring buffer? A: Either waste one slot (full when (head + 1) % cap == tail), keep a separate count, or use free-running unsigned head and tail counters with a power-of-two capacity, where head - tail is the count even after wraparound because unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition.

Q: You store a pointer to a vector element and later the program crashes reading it. Why? A: A later append reallocated the array to a new address and freed the old block, so the stored pointer dangles into freed memory. Store an index or id, reserve the final capacity up front, or use a structure with stable addresses such as a pool or an intrusive list.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Every C container design answers two questions: who owns the memory, and how it is generic.
  • Dynamic array: geometric growth for amortised O(1), overflow-checked sizes, realloc into a temporary, and pointers into it die on growth.
  • Singly list: the pointer-to-pointer walk removes the head special case; read next before free.
  • Intrusive lists embed list_head in the object; container_of uses offsetof; circular with a sentinel means no NULL checks; Windows calls it LIST_ENTRY and CONTAINING_RECORD.
  • Open addressing: power-of-two capacity and a mask, stored hashes, tombstones on delete, rebuild below about 70% load, keyed hashes for untrusted keys.
  • Ring buffer: free-running unsigned counters; head - tail is the count.
  • Heap: array layout (i-1)/2, 2i+1, 2i+2; push and pop O(log n); top-k with a min-heap of size k.
  • Generic C: void * + size + comparator, typed macros, or intrusive; never return a - b.
  • Cache behaviour (arrays and probing good, pointer chasing bad) matters as much as big-O.

docs.title: 12. Memory allocators: arena, pool and a teaching malloc
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: modules 04 (memory, storage and lifetime), 06 (structs and layout), 10, 11; 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/03_the_heap_malloc_internals.md (sections 1 and 2)

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
malloc is a general-purpose allocator. It accepts any size, any order of free calls, from any thread, and it must never lose track of a byte. That generality has a price: a header in front of every block, locks or per-thread caches, searching for a block that fits, fragmentation over time, and latency that varies from call to call. And when your code misuses memory, malloc usually notices much later, somewhere else, or never.

When you know how your program allocates, a special-purpose allocator is simpler, faster and safer:

  • Arena (bump) allocator. You allocate many objects that all die at the same moment (one request, one batch, one parse). Allocation is "move a pointer forward"; freeing is "reset the pointer". No per-object free, so no per-object leaks or double frees.
  • Pool allocator. You allocate many objects of the same size and free them in any order (connections, request records, list nodes). Every slot is the same size, so there is no searching and no fragmentation.

A restaurant analogy: malloc is the a la carte kitchen that can cook anything in any order. An arena is the buffet tray: fill it during the event, then wash the whole tray at once. A pool is an egg carton: identical slots, take one, put one back.

This module builds both, then builds a small but real malloc so that glibc's internals and its error messages make sense, and finishes with a debug allocator that catches overflows, double frees, use after free and leaks with the file and line of the allocation.

docs.title: 2.1 Why write your own allocator
docs.text:
Goal How a custom allocator gets it Speed Bump-pointer or free-list pop: a few instructions, no lock, no search Predictable latency No coalescing or searching at random moments; important on hot paths No fragmentation Same-size slots (pool) or whole-region reset (arena) Fewer lifetime bugs One reset instead of thousands of frees; nothing to forget Memory accounting "This batch used 3.2 MiB" is one counter, not a heap profile Debugging Guard bytes, fill patterns, allocation tags with file and line

The costs are real too: you must state the lifetime rules and everyone must follow them, and a custom allocator hides misuse from ASan and Valgrind unless you tell them about it (section 5).

docs.title: 2.2 Alignment math
docs.text:
Every type has an alignment: its address must be a multiple of alignof(T). On x86-64, alignof(double) is 8 and alignof(max_align_t) is 16, which is why malloc returns 16-byte aligned memory on glibc. A misaligned access is undefined behaviour in C (module 09); on x86 it is usually just slower, on other CPUs and with SSE or atomic instructions it can fault.

Alignments are powers of two, which makes rounding up a bit trick:

align_up(x, a) = (x + (a - 1)) & ~(a - 1)        a must be a power of two

x = 13, a = 8:   13 + 7 = 20 = 0b10100
                 ~(8 - 1)    = ...11111000
                 20 & ~7     = 0b10000 = 16      13 rounded up to 16
x = 16, a = 8:   16 + 7 = 23, 23 & ~7 = 16       already aligned: unchanged
is_power_of_two(a) = a != 0 && (a & (a - 1)) == 0

Rules that follow for allocator writers: every header must be a multiple of the largest alignment you promise (or the payload after it is misaligned); a block's size should be a multiple of that alignment too, so the next block starts aligned; and C11 gives you alignof, alignas and aligned_alloc(alignment, size) (size must be a multiple of the alignment).

docs.title: 2.3 Arena allocator and its ownership contract
docs.text:
chunk (newest)                              chunk (older)
+------+---------------------------------+  +------+-------------------------------+
| prev | cap | used | [obj][pad][obj] ... |->| prev | cap | used | [obj][obj]....... |-> NULL
+------+---------------------------------+  +------+-------------------------------+
                         ^ next allocation = align_up(data + used)
  • Allocate: round the current offset up to the requested alignment; if the object fits, advance used and return the address. If not, allocate a new chunk (big enough for this request even if it is larger than the usual chunk size) and push it on the chunk stack.
  • Mark and rewind: save (chunk, used), allocate temporaries, then rewind to the mark. This turns an arena into a scratch stack for one function.
  • Reset: free everything at once. m12_arena.c keeps one chunk sized to the high-water mark, so a workload that repeats (batch after batch) settles into zero malloc calls.
  • No individual free. realloc can only grow the most recent allocation in place.

The ownership contract, which is the part that prevents bugs. Put it in the header:

  1. Memory from the arena is owned by the arena. Never free() it.
  2. It stays valid until arena_reset, a rewind past it, or arena_destroy.
  3. Nothing allocated from an arena may be stored in a structure that outlives the arena's next reset (a global cache, another thread's queue). Copy it out instead.
  4. An arena is not thread-safe. Use one per thread or one per batch.

Where arenas fit. Anything batch- or request-scoped: an RPC request whose decoded fields and response buffers all die when the response is sent; a parser building a tree that is thrown away after evaluation; and a data-migration job that reads N rows from a source store (for example a Berkeley DB cursor), converts them into structs, strings and SQL parameter buffers, writes them to the target (for example YugabyteDB), and then needs none of it. One arena per batch, reset after each commit, gives constant memory per batch and makes leaks impossible by construction.

docs.title: 2.4 Fixed-size pool with an embedded free list
docs.text:
one malloc:  [ slot 0 ][ slot 1 ][ slot 2 ][ slot 3 ] ... [ slot N-1 ]
free list:   head -> slot 2 -> slot 0 -> slot 3 -> NULL
             (a free slot's first 8 bytes hold the pointer to the next free slot)
  • alloc pops the head, free pushes the slot back: O(1), no header per object.
  • LIFO reuse: the slot freed last is handed out next, and it is probably still in cache.
  • Slot size = max(object size, sizeof(void *)), rounded up to the alignment you promise.
  • Debug checks that cost almost nothing: is the pointer inside the pool, on a slot boundary, and currently allocated? That catches foreign pointers, interior pointers and double frees.
  • A slab allocator (the Linux kernel's kmem_cache, and the core of jemalloc, tcmalloc and mimalloc) is a set of pools, one per size class, that grows by adding pages.

docs.title: 2.5 A teaching malloc: headers, free list, splitting, coalescing
docs.text:
m12_teaching_malloc.c manages one 64 KiB region. Every block carries its size in a header and a footer (a "boundary tag"). Sizes are multiples of 16, so the low 4 bits are free for flags; bit 0 means "in use".

   0       8          16         24        32
   | pad   | prologue | prologue | header  | payload (16-aligned) ... | footer | ... | epilogue |
           | 16 | 1   | 16 | 1   | size|u  |                          | size|u |     |  0 | 1   |

free block payload: [ next free ][ prev free ] ......
minimum block: header 8 + next 8 + prev 8 + footer 8 = 32 bytes
  • malloc(n): block size = align_up(n + 16, 16), at least 32. Walk the explicit free list (only free blocks are linked) and take the first fit.
  • Splitting: if the free block is at least 32 bytes bigger than needed, cut it in two and put the tail back on the free list. Otherwise hand out the whole block (the waste inside is internal fragmentation).
  • free(p): mark the block free, then coalesce: if the next block is free (its header says so), merge; if the previous block is free (its footer, just before our header, says so), merge. The footer is what makes "is my left neighbour free?" an O(1) question.
  • Prologue and epilogue blocks are permanently "in use", so coalescing never needs bounds checks.
  • A heap checker (tm_check) walks every block and verifies alignment, header equals footer, no two adjacent free blocks, and that the free list matches the heap. You write this first; it turns allocator bugs into immediate assertion failures.

External fragmentation is the problem no first-fit allocator escapes: plenty of free bytes, but in pieces too small for the request. The test fills the heap with 48-byte requests, frees every other one, and asks for 100 bytes (section 3.3).

From here to glibc (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/03_the_heap_malloc_internals.md): glibc's chunk header has the same size-plus-flag-bits design (PREV_INUSE, IS_MMAPPED, NON_MAIN_ARENA), and it uses the previous chunk's size field the way our footer works. Instead of one free list it has many: per-thread tcache bins and fastbins for small sizes (not coalesced immediately), an unsorted bin, and sorted small and large bins. It grows the heap with brk, serves big requests with mmap, and keeps several arenas so threads do not fight over one lock. The error messages you see in crash logs, such as free(): invalid next size or double free or corruption (!prev), are glibc's versions of the checks in tm_check.

docs.title: 2.6 Debug allocators: guards, canaries, fill patterns, quarantine
docs.text:
A debug allocator wraps every block with extra bytes and bookkeeping:

[ header: magic, size, file, line, live-list links ][ front guard 0xFD x16 ][ user bytes ][ back guard 0xFD x16 ]
Technique Catches When Guard bytes (red zones) with a known pattern overflow and underflow at free, or on a periodic check Header magic (canary) freeing a pointer you never returned; double free at free Fill new memory with 0xCD reading before writing: values look like 0xCDCDCDCD in the debugger Fill freed memory with 0xDD and quarantine it use after free (writes break the pattern; reads see 0xDD) when the block leaves quarantine Live list with file and line leaks at exit or on demand

The byte values are the ones the MSVC debug CRT uses, so they will look familiar in a Windows crash dump: 0xCD clean (allocated, never written), 0xDD dead (freed), 0xFD "no man's land" (guards). Related platform tools: the MSVC debug heap (_CrtSetDbgFlag, _CrtCheckMemory); PageHeap (gflags /p /enable app.exe /full), which puts every allocation at the end of a page followed by an inaccessible guard page so an overflow faults on the exact instruction; and on glibc, MALLOC_PERTURB_ (fill patterns) and MALLOC_CHECK_=3 (since glibc 2.34 it needs LD_PRELOAD=libc_malloc_debug.so.0). ASan is the industrial version: red zones and quarantine, with shadow memory checked on every access instead of only at free (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/08_valgrind_and_sanitizers.md).

docs.title: 3.1 m12_arena.c
docs.text:
static void *chunk_take(struct chunk *c, size_t size, size_t align)
{
    uintptr_t base = (uintptr_t)c->data;
    uintptr_t p = align_up(base + c->used, align);
    size_t offset = (size_t)(p - base);
    if (offset > c->cap || size > c->cap - offset)   /* written so nothing can overflow */
        return NULL;
    c->used = offset + size;
    return (void *)p;
}

#define ARENA_NEW(a, T)        ((T *)arena_alloc((a), sizeof(T), alignof(T)))
#define ARENA_ARRAY(a, T, n)   ((T *)arena_alloc_array((a), (n), sizeof(T), alignof(T)))

Note the bounds check: size > c->cap - offset instead of offset + size > c->cap, because the addition could wrap for a huge size. The batch test converts 1000 rows per batch (a pointer array, a struct row and a string per row) and resets after each batch. Real output:

batch 1: 3 malloc calls; batches 2-51: 0 malloc calls in total
all checks passed

The first batch needed three 16 KiB chunks. arena_reset replaced them with one chunk of the combined size, and the next 50 batches ran without a single malloc.

docs.title: 3.2 m12_pool.c
docs.text:
static void *pool_alloc(struct pool *p)
{
    void *slot = p->free_list;
    if (!slot)
        return NULL;                                   /* exhausted: caller decides */
    memcpy(&p->free_list, slot, sizeof(void *));       /* free_list = slot->next */
    p->state[((unsigned char *)slot - p->mem) / p->slot_size] = 1;
    p->in_use++;
    return slot;
}

memcpy reads and writes the embedded next pointer without any alignment or aliasing assumptions. Real output:

sizeof(struct request)=40, slot_size=48, slots=64
double free -> 3, foreign pointer -> 1, interior pointer -> 2 (all rejected)
all checks passed

A 40-byte object gets a 48-byte slot because slots are rounded to alignof(max_align_t) = 16. The file then runs a million alloc/free pairs with no malloc involved.

docs.title: 3.3 m12_teaching_malloc.c
docs.text:
static void tm_free(void *ptr)
{
    /* ... validity and double-free check ... */
    size_t size = tag_size(hdr(bp));
    byte *next = next_blk(bp);
    int prev_used = tag_used(prev_ftr(bp));    /* the boundary tag makes this O(1) */
    int next_used = tag_used(hdr(next));

    if (!next_used) {                          /* merge with the following block */
        list_remove(next);
        size += tag_size(hdr(next));
    }
    if (!prev_used) {                          /* merge with the preceding block */
        byte *prev = prev_blk(bp);
        list_remove(prev);
        size += tag_size(hdr(prev));
        bp = prev;
    }
    set_block(bp, size, 0);
    list_insert(bp);
}

All header and footer access goes through memcpy-based helpers, and the region comes from aligned_alloc rather than a static unsigned char array, so the allocator itself has no aliasing or alignment UB. Real output:

after freeing a, b, c: 1 free block of 65504 bytes (fully coalesced)
stress: 20000 random ops, heap valid after each, 2 out-of-memory results
fragmented: 32800 bytes free in 512 blocks, largest 96 -> malloc(100) FAILED
all checks passed

The last line is external fragmentation made visible: 32 800 bytes free, but no single block can hold a 100-byte request (which needs a 128-byte block).

docs.title: 3.4 m12_debug_alloc.c
docs.text:
#define DMALLOC(n) dbg_malloc((n), __FILE__, __LINE__)
#define DFREE(p)   dbg_free((p), __FILE__, __LINE__)

char *s = DMALLOC(8);
memcpy(s, "ACC-1001", 9);            /* 8 chars + NUL = 9 bytes into an 8-byte block */
assert(dbg_check_all() == 1);        /* found before free, by the periodic checker */
r = DFREE(s);
assert(r == DBG_OVERFLOW);

Real output:

uninitialised int read from a fresh block: 0xCDCDCDCD
dbg: OVERFLOW past 8-byte block from m12_debug_alloc.c:191, detected at free m12_debug_alloc.c:194
dbg: UNDERFLOW before 16-byte block from m12_debug_alloc.c:198, detected at free m12_debug_alloc.c:200
dbg: DOUBLE FREE at m12_debug_alloc.c:207 of block allocated at m12_debug_alloc.c:204
dbg: WRITE AFTER FREE into 40-byte block from m12_debug_alloc.c:211
dbg: LEAK 7 bytes allocated at m12_debug_alloc.c:220
dbg: LEAK 100 bytes allocated at m12_debug_alloc.c:219
all checks passed

The off-by-one in the overflow case is the most common C string bug there is: forgetting the byte for the terminating NUL. Every deliberate "bug" in the test stays inside memory the debug allocator owns, so the test itself is defined behaviour and runs clean under ASan and Valgrind.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
How glibc gets and gives back memory. The main arena grows the heap with brk; requests above the mmap threshold (128 KiB initially, raised dynamically up to 32 MiB on 64-bit) get their own mmap mapping and are unmapped on free. Memory freed inside the brk heap returns to the OS only when the free space at the top exceeds M_TRIM_THRESHOLD, or when you call malloc_trim(0). That is why RSS often stays high after a burst even with no leak.

Per-allocation overhead. On 64-bit glibc the smallest chunk is 32 bytes, so malloc(1) and malloc(24) cost the same 32 bytes; each chunk carries an 8-byte size field. A pool slot has no header at all, and an arena object has only alignment padding. For millions of small objects that difference is the size of the process.

Threads. glibc gives each thread a tcache (up to 7 cached chunks per size, for sizes up to 1032 bytes by default) that needs no lock, and creates extra arenas (up to 8 x the number of cores on 64-bit) when threads contend. Memory freed by one thread into another arena's bins is the reason multithreaded servers sometimes show RSS far above their live data; MALLOC_ARENA_MAX caps the number of arenas. jemalloc, tcmalloc and mimalloc are built from size-class slabs plus thread caches, which is section 2.4 scaled up.

Locality. A bump allocator returns consecutive addresses, so objects created together sit together in cache lines and pages: walking a batch of rows allocated from an arena touches far fewer pages than walking the same rows scattered across the general heap. A pool returns the most recently freed slot first for the same reason. The flip side: a pool shared by threads hands out neighbouring slots to different threads, which can put two hot objects in one cache line (false sharing, 04_Concurrency/10_cache_lines_false_sharing_performance.md).

Why a custom allocator blinds ASan. ASan instruments malloc and free. If your arena takes one 16 KiB chunk from malloc and carves objects out of it, ASan sees one valid 16 KiB block: overflowing one object into the next, or using an object after arena_reset, is invisible. Fix it with the manual poisoning API (ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION and ASAN_UNPOISON_MEMORY_REGION from <sanitizer/asan_interface.h>) on reset and between objects, or with a build switch that routes every arena allocation to plain malloc in sanitizer builds.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The classic arena bug is a broken contract, not a broken allocator. Someone stores a pointer to an arena-allocated string in a long-lived cache "to save a copy". After the next reset the cache points at memory now holding the next batch's data: no crash, just wrong values, which in a banking system means wrong account data. Defend the contract in code review, in the header comment, and with the sanitizer build switch from section 4.
  • Pools need a sizing policy. A pool that returns NULL when exhausted must be sized for the peak, or allowed to grow by adding blocks. Expose in_use and capacity as metrics; a pool at 95% is an early warning that a matching free is missing somewhere (a leak in pool form).
  • Windows has arenas built in. HeapCreate gives a private heap; HeapDestroy frees everything in it at once, which is an arena with a general allocator inside. A per-subsystem heap also makes heap corruption easier to localise in a dump: the corrupted heap tells you which subsystem did it. The Low Fragmentation Heap (LFH) is Windows' size-class pool layer.
  • Use the debug allocator to catch the bug where it happens. Heap corruption in a C server usually crashes far from the bug, in an innocent malloc. Turning on guard-byte checking in a test environment, or calling a check_all function from a debug command or a timer, moves the detection close to the culprit. On Windows, enable full PageHeap for the process in a test environment and the first overflowing write faults with the guilty stack.
  • Measure before replacing malloc. glibc's allocator is good for general workloads. Custom allocators pay off for clear patterns: per-request or per-batch lifetimes, millions of same-size objects, or hard latency limits. Profile first (perf, heaptrack).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - alignment by hand. Without running code, compute align_up(x, a) for (1, 8), (8, 8), (9, 16), (100, 64), (0, 32), and explain why align_up(5, 12) is meaningless. Done when you check your answers with a five-line C program.
  2. Easy - arena_realloc. Add arena_realloc(a, p, old, new) that grows in place when p is the most recent allocation and there is room, and otherwise allocates and copies. Done when a test shows the in-place case returns the same pointer and the other case copies correctly.
  3. Medium - best fit. Change tm_malloc in m12_teaching_malloc.c to best fit and rerun the stress and fragmentation tests. Done when you can report the out-of-memory count and the largest free block for both policies and explain the difference.
  4. Medium - tm_realloc. Implement tm_realloc that grows in place by absorbing a free next block (and splitting off the excess), shrinks in place by splitting, and otherwise falls back to malloc-copy-free. Done when tm_check passes after every call in a random test.
  5. Hard - ASan-aware arena. Add ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION calls to m12_arena.c so that the unused tail of each chunk and everything released by arena_rewind and arena_reset is poisoned. Build with -fsanitize=address and write a test that reads an object after reset. Done when ASan reports use-after-poison on that read and the normal tests still pass.
  6. Hard - thread-local pools. Give each worker thread its own pool through a _Thread_local pointer, with a fallback to a shared, mutex-protected pool when the local one is empty. Done when a 4-thread test runs clean under TSan and you have measured it against plain malloc.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When would you use an arena allocator instead of malloc? A: When many objects share one lifetime, such as everything for one request, one parse or one batch. Allocation becomes a pointer bump, there is no per-object free to forget or repeat, and the whole region is released in one operation. It is wrong for objects with independent lifetimes, because nothing can be freed individually.

Q: How does a fixed-size pool allocator work? A: It allocates one large block divided into equal slots and threads a singly linked free list through the free slots themselves, so it needs no extra memory. Allocation pops the list head and free pushes the slot back, both O(1) with no searching and no fragmentation. Debug builds can check that a freed pointer lies inside the pool, on a slot boundary, and is currently allocated.

Q: How do you round a size or address up to an alignment? A: For a power-of-two alignment a, (x + a - 1) & ~(a - 1). Adding a - 1 moves x past the next boundary unless it is already on one, and masking clears the low bits. Headers and block sizes in an allocator must be multiples of the maximum alignment it promises, so every payload stays aligned.

Q: What are boundary tags and why does malloc need them? A: A footer at the end of each block that repeats its size and in-use flag. When a block is freed, the allocator reads the footer just before the block's header to learn in O(1) whether the previous block is free and how big it is, so it can coalesce in both directions. glibc stores the previous chunk's size for the same purpose, valid only while that chunk is free.

Q: Internal versus external fragmentation? A: Internal fragmentation is waste inside an allocated block, from rounding up to an alignment or size class. External fragmentation is free memory split into pieces too small for a request, so allocation fails or grows the heap although enough total memory is free. Pools remove external fragmentation for one size; arenas avoid it by freeing whole regions.

Q: How does a debug allocator detect overflows and use after free? A: It surrounds each block with guard bytes holding a known pattern and checks them on free or on demand, which catches overflow and underflow. It fills freed memory with a pattern and keeps it in a quarantine instead of reusing it, so a write after free changes the pattern and a double free finds the block already marked dead. ASan does the same with shadow memory, checked on every access.

Q: Why might a custom allocator make memory bugs harder to find? A: ASan and Valgrind only see the large blocks the custom allocator takes from malloc, so overflows between objects inside a block, or uses after an arena reset, look like valid accesses. You need manual poisoning, a sanitizer build that bypasses the custom allocator, or the allocator's own guard checks.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• malloc is general and pays for it in headers, locking, searching, fragmentation and late error detection; a known allocation pattern deserves a matching allocator.
  • align_up(x, a) = (x + a - 1) & ~(a - 1) for power-of-two a; headers and block sizes must be multiples of the promised alignment (16 on x86-64).
  • Arena: bump pointer, mark/rewind, reset; the ownership contract (no free, valid until reset, never store in longer-lived structures, one per thread) is what makes it safe.
  • Resetting to one chunk at the high-water mark gave 0 malloc calls for batches 2 to 51.
  • Pool: equal slots, embedded free list, O(1), LIFO reuse; cheap debug checks catch double free, foreign and interior pointers.
  • Teaching malloc: header and footer tags, explicit free list, first fit, split, coalesce both ways, prologue/epilogue, and a heap checker written first.
  • glibc adds tcache, fastbins, sorted bins, arenas per thread, brk and mmap; its abort messages are failed consistency checks like tm_check.
  • Debug allocators: guards (0xFD), fill patterns (0xCD new, 0xDD freed), header magic, quarantine, leak list with file and line; PageHeap and ASan are the industrial versions.
  • Custom allocators hide bugs from ASan unless you poison memory manually or bypass them in sanitizer builds.

docs.title: 13. Files, I/O and POSIX system calls
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: modules 05 (strings), 06 (structs and layout), 10; 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps/11_linux_systems_programming_essentials.md (sections 2.1 to 2.4) is a useful companion

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
There are two layers for doing I/O in C on Linux, and most I/O bugs come from not knowing which layer you are in.

  • stdio (FILE *, fopen, fprintf, fread) is the portable C library layer. It keeps a buffer in your process and only calls the kernel when the buffer fills, when you flush, or at certain characters (a newline, for a terminal).
  • System calls (open, read, write, close) work on file descriptors, small integers that index the kernel's table of open files. Every call goes to the kernel, and the kernel is allowed to do less than you asked: read may return fewer bytes than requested, write may write fewer, and either may be interrupted by a signal.

Below both layers, the kernel has its own buffer (the page cache). When write returns, your data is in kernel memory, not on the disk. A power cut can still lose it.

A shopping analogy. stdio is a basket: you collect items and go to the till once. write() is paying at the till for each item separately. And the till's receipt (write returned) is not the bank statement (fsync returned): only the statement proves the money really moved.

This module shows each of these facts with a program you can run, then covers binary file formats, mmap, a minimal TCP server and client in plain C, and the Win32 equivalents.

docs.title: 2.1 The layers
docs.text:
your code      fprintf(f, ...)                  write(fd, buf, n)
                    |                                  |
stdio buffer   [ in your process, ~4 KiB ]             |
                    | fflush / buffer full / '\n'      |
                    v                                  v
system call    write(fd, ...)  ----------------------> kernel
                                                       |
page cache     [ dirty pages in kernel memory ]  <-----+
                    | writeback (seconds later) or fsync
                    v
disk           [ durable ]

fileno(f) gives the descriptor under a FILE *; fdopen(fd, mode) wraps a descriptor in a FILE *. Mixing the two layers on the same file without fflush reorders output (section 3.1).

docs.title: 2.2 stdio buffering
docs.text:
Mode Set with Flushes when Default for Full (_IOFBF) setvbuf(f, NULL, _IOFBF, size) buffer full, fflush, fclose, normal exit files, pipes, and stdout when it is not a terminal Line (_IOLBF) setvbuf(f, NULL, _IOLBF, size) also at every '\n' stdout when it is a terminal None (_IONBF) setvbuf(f, NULL, _IONBF, 0) every call stderr

Consequences you will meet:

  • setvbuf must be called before any other I/O on the stream.
  • printf debugging "loses" the last lines when a program crashes with output redirected to a file: stdout was fully buffered and the buffer died with the process. Write diagnostics to stderr, or fflush(stdout).
  • fclose writes the last buffer, so fclose can fail (disk full, quota, network filesystem). For an output file, check its return value.
  • fork() copies the process including unflushed stdio buffers; both copies write them later, so the output appears twice. fflush(NULL) before fork, and use _exit in a child that does not exec.
  • exit() flushes stdio; _exit() and a crash do not.

docs.title: 2.3 open, read, write, close
docs.text:
int fd = open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC | O_CLOEXEC, 0644);

Flags worth knowing: O_CREAT with a mode (filtered by the process umask), O_TRUNC, O_EXCL (fail if it exists: safe creation of lock or temp files), O_APPEND (every write goes to the current end of file atomically with respect to other writers: what log files need when several processes write), O_CLOEXEC (close on exec, so child processes do not inherit the descriptor), O_NONBLOCK (calls fail with EAGAIN instead of waiting).

Return values that do less than you asked. read returns the number of bytes read (possibly fewer than requested), 0 at end of file, or -1 with errno. write returns the number written (possibly fewer), or -1. Short transfers are normal for pipes, sockets and terminals, and happen on regular files at EOF, when a signal arrives, or when the disk fills. So every read or write of a known amount is a loop:

static ssize_t read_full(int fd, void *buf, size_t n)
{
    size_t done = 0;
    while (done < n) {
        ssize_t r = read(fd, (char *)buf + done, n - done);
        if (r < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR)
                continue;                /* interrupted before any data: just retry */
            return -1;
        }
        if (r == 0)
            break;                       /* EOF: the other side closed */
        done += (size_t)r;
    }
    return (ssize_t)done;
}

EINTR. If a signal handler runs while a thread is blocked in a slow system call (reading a pipe, socket or terminal, wait, accept), the call fails with EINTR unless the handler was installed with SA_RESTART, in which case most calls restart automatically. Some never restart regardless (select, poll, epoll_wait, nanosleep). Library code cannot know how the application installed its handlers, so it always retries on EINTR.

docs.title: 2.4 Durability: write is not "saved"
docs.text:
write returns when the data is in the page cache. The kernel writes dirty pages to disk later (by default within about 30 seconds on Linux, controlled by vm.dirty_expire_centisecs). To make data survive a power cut:

  • fsync(fd) flushes the file's data and metadata (size, timestamps) to stable storage and asks the drive to flush its own cache. fdatasync(fd) skips metadata that is not needed to read the data back.
  • Opening with O_SYNC or O_DSYNC makes every write behave like write plus sync.
