  • Replacing a file safely is four steps: write a temp file in the same directory, fsync it, rename it over the old name (atomic on POSIX within one filesystem), then fsync the directory so the rename itself is durable. After a crash you see the old file or the new one, never a mix. That is durable_replace in m13_robust_io.c.
  • A failed fsync is not retryable. In 2018 PostgreSQL developers found that after fsync reports an error on Linux, the kernel may already have dropped the dirty pages, and a second fsync can then succeed even though the data never reached disk ("fsyncgate"). PostgreSQL now treats an fsync failure as fatal and recovers from its write-ahead log. The lesson for your code: on fsync failure, assume the data is lost and fail loudly.

Databases are built on exactly these primitives: see 07_Databases_Internals/04_wal_and_crash_recovery.md.

docs.title: 2.5 Binary file formats
docs.text:
fwrite(&record, sizeof record, 1, f) writes the in-memory bytes of a struct, which depend on the compiler (padding), the CPU (byte order) and the platform (sizeof(long) is 4 on Windows and 8 on 64-bit Linux). A file written by the Windows server and read by a Linux tool is then garbage, silently. A format meant to last is encoded field by field:

  • Fixed-width types (uint32_t, int64_t) and one documented byte order. Shifts are endian-independent: p[0] = v; p[1] = v >> 8; ... writes little-endian on any CPU.
  • A magic number at offset 0 (so a wrong file is detected at once) and a version.
  • A header-size field, so a newer writer can append header fields that an older reader skips.
  • A checksum (CRC-32 here) over the payload, so corruption and truncation are detected rather than decoded.
  • Length-prefixed variable fields, and a decoder that checks every length against the bytes actually present. The file is input; input can be truncated, corrupted or hostile.

This is the same discipline as a network protocol (08_Networking_Distributed/04_framing_and_protocol_design.md).

docs.title: 2.6 mmap
docs.text:
mmap(NULL, len, PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0) maps a file into your address space. Reading the memory triggers page faults that load pages from the page cache; there is no read call and no copy into a user buffer.

  • Good for: large files read randomly, read-only data shared between processes, and formats you can parse in place.
  • MAP_SHARED + PROT_WRITE: writes go to the page cache and other mappers see them; msync(addr, len, MS_SYNC) is the fsync of a mapping.
  • Pitfalls: if another process truncates the file, touching the missing pages raises SIGBUS, which kills the process unless handled; I/O errors also arrive as signals instead of return codes; and the mapping stays valid after close(fd) until munmap.

On Windows the same idea is CreateFileMappingW plus MapViewOfFile.

docs.title: 2.7 A TCP echo server and client in C
docs.text:
The call sequence, in plain C (the C++ RAII version and the details are in 08_Networking_Distributed/03_sockets_api_blocking_server.md):

server: getaddrinfo -> socket -> setsockopt(SO_REUSEADDR) -> bind -> listen -> accept (loop) -> read/write -> close
client: getaddrinfo -> socket -> connect -> write -> shutdown(SHUT_WR) -> read until 0 -> close
  • getaddrinfo handles IPv4 and IPv6 and name resolution; its errors come back as its return value and are printed with gai_strerror, not errno.
  • SO_REUSEADDR lets a restarted server bind while old connections sit in TIME_WAIT.
  • shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR) sends FIN ("I have finished sending") while still allowing reads. The server sees read return 0 and knows the request is complete.
  • Writing to a socket whose peer has gone raises SIGPIPE, whose default action kills the process. Servers set signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) (or pass MSG_NOSIGNAL to send) and handle EPIPE.
  • A TCP stream has no message boundaries: one write of 32 KiB may arrive as several reads, and two writes may arrive in one read. That is why both sides loop.

docs.title: 2.8 Win32 equivalents
docs.text: POSIX / C Win32 Notes open CreateFileW returns INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE on failure; share modes decide whether others may open the file read / write ReadFile / WriteFile byte counts come back through a DWORD * out-parameter; also partial for pipes and sockets close CloseHandle sockets use closesocket instead fsync FlushFileBuffers also flushes the drive cache rename (atomic replace) MoveFileExW(..., MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING \| MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH) or ReplaceFileW renaming over a file that someone has open usually fails on Windows mmap CreateFileMappingW + MapViewOfFile UnmapViewOfFile to release errno / strerror GetLastError / FormatMessageW sockets: WSAGetLastError sockets setup WSAStartup(MAKEWORD(2, 2), &wsa) once per process, WSACleanup at exit without WSAStartup, every socket call fails with WSANOTINITIALISED socket, bind, listen, accept, connect same names in Winsock2 SOCKET is an unsigned handle: test against INVALID_SOCKET, not < 0 read / write on a socket recv / send Winsock sockets are not file descriptors fopen(path, "w") fopen(path, "wb") text mode translates \n to \r\n on Windows: always use "rb"/"wb" for binary data SIGPIPE none Winsock returns WSAECONNRESET or WSAECONNABORTED instead

docs.title: 3.1 m13_stdio_buffering.c: watch the buffer with stat
docs.text:
The program checks the file size on disk after each step. Real output:

full buffering : after fputs 0 bytes on disk, after fflush 6
full buffering : 5006 bytes written, 4102 on disk (st_blksize = 4096)
line buffering : before newline 0 bytes, after newline 4
no buffering   : after fputs("abc") 3 bytes
mixing layers  : wrote A then B, file contains "BA"
fork with pending : file contains "xx"
fork after fflush  : file contains "x"
all checks passed

The second line: glibc sized the buffer from the filesystem block size (4096), flushed one full buffer (4096 bytes on top of the 6 already flushed) and kept the remaining 904 bytes in memory. strace -e trace=write ./m13_stdio_buffering shows the system calls behind the first five lines:

write(3, "hello\n", 6)                  = 6
write(3, "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"..., 4096) = 4096
write(3, "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"..., 904) = 904
write(3, "abc\n", 4)                    = 4
write(3, "abc", 3)                      = 3
write(3, "B", 1)                        = 1
write(3, "A", 1)                        = 1

5000 fputc calls became two system calls. And "A" was written by the program before "B", but reached the kernel after it, because it waited in the stdio buffer while write(fileno(f), "B", 1) went straight through.

The fork case:

f = open_fresh(-1);
fputs("x", f);                   /* sits in the user-space buffer */
fflush(stdout);
pid_t pid = fork();
if (pid == 0)
    exit(0);                     /* exit() flushes the child's copy of the buffer */
waitpid(pid, &status, 0);
fclose(f);                       /* the parent flushes its own copy: "xx" */

docs.title: 3.2 m13_robust_io.c: partial reads, EINTR and durable replace
docs.text:
A child process writes a 46-byte message into a pipe in five pieces, 60 ms apart. Meanwhile the parent has a 20 ms interval timer whose SIGALRM handler was installed without SA_RESTART, so the blocking read keeps failing with EINTR:

struct sigaction sa;
memset(&sa, 0, sizeof sa);
sa.sa_handler = on_alarm;
sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
sa.sa_flags = 0;                    /* no SA_RESTART: blocking read() fails with EINTR */
sigaction(SIGALRM, &sa, NULL);
struct itimerval every20ms = { { 0, 20000 }, { 0, 20000 } };
setitimer(ITIMER_REAL, &every20ms, NULL);

ssize_t got = read_full(p[0], buf, len);

Real output:

read_full: 46 bytes intact; short reads=4 or more, EINTR retries=1 or more
durable_replace: new contents visible, no temp file left
all checks passed

A naive single read would have returned the first 10 bytes, or -1 with EINTR, and a naive caller would have treated either as the whole message or as a fatal error.

docs.title: 3.3 m13_binary_format_mmap.c: an explicit format, read back through mmap
docs.text:
static void put_u32(uint8_t *p, uint32_t v) { for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) p[i] = (uint8_t)(v >> (8 * i)); }

static int64_t u64_to_i64(uint64_t u)      /* no implementation-defined conversion */
{
    if (u <= (uint64_t)INT64_MAX)
        return (int64_t)u;
    return -(int64_t)(UINT64_MAX - u) - 1;
}

Real output, with the header decoded by hand underneath:

file is 93 bytes; first 48:
00000000  41 43 43 54 01 00 10 00 03 00 00 00 96 a8 ce 98
00000010  e9 03 00 00 00 00 00 00 40 78 7d 01 00 00 00 00
00000020  08 41 73 68 61 20 52 61 6f ea 03 00 00 00 00 00
  id=1001 balance=25000000 name=Asha Rao
  id=1002 balance=-150 name=Bilal Khan
  id=1003 balance=9223372036854775807 name=Treasury
corrupt, truncated, wrong-magic and wrong-version inputs all rejected
all checks passed

41 43 43 54   "ACCT"                     magic
01 00         version 1                  little-endian
10 00         header size 16
03 00 00 00   3 records
96 a8 ce 98   CRC-32 of the payload      = 0x98cea896
e9 03 00 00 00 00 00 00   id 1001        (0x3e9)
40 78 7d 01 00 00 00 00   25000000 paise (0x017d7840)
08            name length 8, then "Asha Rao"

The test flips one bit, truncates the file, breaks the magic and bumps the version, and each is rejected with a specific code instead of being decoded into garbage.

docs.title: 3.4 m13_tcp_echo.c: server and client in plain C
docs.text:
static long echo_connection(int cfd)
{
    char buf[4096];
    long total = 0;
    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = read(cfd, buf, sizeof buf);
        if (n < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) continue;
            return -1;
        }
        if (n == 0)
            return total;                /* orderly shutdown from the client */
        if (write_full(cfd, buf, (size_t)n) != 0)
            return -1;
        total += n;
    }
}

With no arguments the program binds 127.0.0.1 port 0 (the kernel picks a free port), forks a server child and runs two round trips as the client. Real output (the port changes each run):

echo of "PING ACC-1001": 13 bytes back on port 35189
echo of 32768 bytes: intact
all checks passed

It also runs as a real server and client in two terminals: ./m13_tcp_echo server 9000 and ./m13_tcp_echo client 127.0.0.1 9000 "hello".

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What a read costs. The syscall instruction switches to kernel mode; the kernel looks up the descriptor in the process's file table, goes through the VFS to the filesystem, finds the pages in the page cache (or starts disk I/O and sleeps), and copies the bytes to your buffer with copy_to_user. A system call costs on the order of 100 ns or more on current hardware (typical; more with mitigations for speculative-execution attacks). That fixed cost is why stdio buffers: 5000 one-byte writes become two write calls.

Where the stdio buffer comes from. glibc allocates it on the first I/O, sized by st_blksize from fstat (4096 here), which is why the strace shows 4096-byte writes. setvbuf after the first I/O is too late because the buffer already exists.

Writeback. Dirty pages are written by kernel flusher threads when they are older than vm.dirty_expire_centisecs (3000, that is 30 s, by default) or when dirty memory exceeds vm.dirty_background_ratio; past vm.dirty_ratio, writers are throttled inside write. fsync writes the file's dirty pages, waits for them, commits the filesystem journal for its metadata, and issues a cache-flush command to the device. On an SSD that is commonly hundreds of microseconds to a few milliseconds (typical; it depends heavily on the device). This cost is why databases batch commits ("group commit").

rename atomicity. On ext4, XFS and other POSIX filesystems, rename replaces the directory entry atomically: a concurrent reader opens either the old inode or the new one. Durability of the rename is a separate question, answered by fsync on the directory. (ext4 has a heuristic, auto_da_alloc, that forces data out before a rename-over-existing, which hides missing fsync calls on ext4 and not elsewhere: do not depend on it.)

EINTR mechanics. A thread blocked in an interruptible sleep receives a signal; the kernel interrupts the wait and arranges to run the handler on the way back to user space. If no data has been transferred, the system call returns -ERESTARTSYS internally, which becomes either an automatic restart (SA_RESTART) or EINTR. If some data was transferred, the call returns the partial count instead, which is one of the ways a short read happens.

mmap faults. The first touch of each page is a page fault: the kernel finds the page in the page cache (minor fault) or reads it from disk (major fault) and maps it. Sequential access triggers readahead. For a file you read once from start to end, read into a reused buffer is often as fast and has simpler error handling; mmap shines for random access and sharing.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• The last log lines before a crash are missing. The log was written with fprintf to a fully buffered FILE * and the crash destroyed the buffer. Make the logger line-buffered or unbuffered, or have it format into a local buffer and call write once per line (which is also atomic with O_APPEND for lines up to PIPE_BUF on pipes, and in practice for small writes to local files). Do not call fflush from a crash handler: stdio is not async-signal-safe.
  • Disk full. ENOSPC can come from write, from fsync, or from close (network filesystems report deferred errors at close). A server that ignores these keeps "writing" an audit log that is not there. Check all three and alert.
  • Descriptor leaks. A descriptor not closed on an error path (module 10) leaks one fd per bad request until accept or open fails with EMFILE. Watch ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l or lsof -p <pid>, and open with O_CLOEXEC so child processes do not inherit them.
  • Binary files on Windows. fopen(path, "w") in text mode turns every 0x0A byte into 0x0D 0x0A. A binary file written that way decodes fine on Windows (the read side translates back) and is corrupt everywhere else. Use "rb" and "wb" for anything that is not text.
  • Partial writes on sockets are real under load. With non-blocking sockets or a full send buffer, send returns less than requested. A server that ignores the count sends truncated responses only under load: exactly the bug that never reproduces on a developer machine.
  • Config and state files are replaced, not overwritten. Truncating and rewriting a file in place leaves an empty or half-written file if the process dies in between. Use the temp-fsync-rename-fsync recipe (on Windows, MoveFileExW with MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH or ReplaceFileW).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - predict the output. Without running it, predict what printf("a "); write(1, "b ", 2); printf("c "); prints on a terminal and when piped to cat. Then run it both ways. Done when you can explain why the two orders differ, using section 2.2.
  2. Easy - strace. Run strace -e trace=openat,read,write,close ./m13_binary_format_mmap. Done when you can point at the write of 93 bytes and explain why there is no read of the file afterwards.
  3. Medium - write_full under pressure. Make the pipe writer in m13_robust_io.c the parent and the reader a slow child, and write 1 MiB with O_NONBLOCK on the write end. Count how many partial writes and EAGAIN errors occur and add poll to wait for writability. Done when 1 MiB arrives intact and you can report both counts.
  4. Medium - format version 2. Add a u32 branch_code field to each record and bump the version to 2. Make the reader accept both versions. Done when a version 1 file and a version 2 file both decode, and a version 3 file is rejected.
  5. Hard - crash-test durable_replace. Write a loop that calls durable_replace with alternating contents A and B while a second script kill -9s it at random moments. Check the file after each kill. Done when 1000 kills always leave exactly A or exactly B. Then remove the fsync calls and explain why the test on WSL may still pass (hint: a process kill is not a power cut).
  6. Hard - Win32 port. Port m13_tcp_echo.c to Winsock2 (WSAStartup, SOCKET, closesocket, recv, send, WSAGetLastError) and build it with MSVC /W4 /WX. Done when the Windows client talks to the Linux server running in WSL.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a FILE * and a file descriptor? A: A file descriptor is a small integer that indexes the kernel's per-process table of open files; read and write on it are system calls with no user-space buffering. A FILE * is a C library object that wraps a descriptor with a buffer and formatting functions, so many small writes become few system calls. Mixing both on one file without fflush reorders data.

Q: Why must read and write be called in a loop? A: Both may transfer fewer bytes than requested: on pipes, sockets and terminals routinely, and on any file when a signal arrives or near EOF or a full disk. They can also fail with EINTR when a signal interrupts a blocking call. A correct helper loops until the full count is transferred, EOF is reached, or a real error occurs.

Q: Does write returning success mean the data is on disk? A: No. It means the data is in the kernel page cache; the kernel writes it later. Use fsync or fdatasync (or O_SYNC/O_DSYNC) for durability. To replace a file atomically and durably, write a temp file, fsync it, rename it over the target, and fsync the directory.

Q: What does fork do to unflushed stdio buffers? A: The child gets a copy of the parent's memory, including any unflushed buffer, so both processes eventually write the same data and the output appears twice. Call fflush(NULL) before fork, and use _exit in a child that does not exec so it does not flush the copied buffers.

Q: Why not fwrite a struct to a file? A: The bytes depend on padding, byte order and type sizes, which differ between compilers and platforms (long is 4 bytes on Windows and 8 on Linux), so another program or platform reads garbage. Encode each field with fixed-width types in a documented byte order, add a magic number, a version and a checksum, and bounds-check every length when decoding.

Q: When would you use mmap instead of read? A: For large files accessed randomly, data shared between processes, or formats parsed in place, because it avoids system calls and copies. The costs are page-fault overhead, errors arriving as signals (SIGBUS if the file is truncated), and more complex durability (msync). For one sequential pass, read into a reused buffer is usually as fast and simpler.

Q: What is SIGPIPE and how does a server deal with it? A: Writing to a socket or pipe whose reading end is closed raises SIGPIPE, whose default action terminates the process. Servers ignore it (signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN)) or pass MSG_NOSIGNAL to send, and handle the resulting EPIPE error by closing that connection.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Two layers: stdio buffers in your process; system calls go to the kernel; below both, the page cache.
  • Buffering: full for files and pipes, line for a terminal stdout, none for stderr; setvbuf first; fclose can fail; fork duplicates unflushed buffers.
  • read and write may do less than asked and may fail with EINTR: loop with read_full/write_full.
  • write success is not durability: fsync the file, rename atomically, fsync the directory; a failed fsync means the data is lost.
  • Binary formats: fixed widths, explicit byte order, magic, version, header size, CRC, and bounds-checked decoding.
  • mmap avoids copies and calls; beware SIGBUS and signal-based errors.
  • TCP: getaddrinfo, SO_REUSEADDR, shutdown(SHUT_WR) for a clean end of request, ignore SIGPIPE, loop on every transfer.
  • Win32: CreateFileW/ReadFile/WriteFile/CloseHandle, FlushFileBuffers, MoveFileExW, WSAStartup before any socket call, and "rb"/"wb" for binary files.

docs.title: 14. Multithreading in C: pthreads and C11
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: modules 07 (function pointers), 09, 10; 04_Concurrency modules 01 to 03 (sections 1 and 2) for the concepts

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Threads in one process share everything: globals, the heap, open files. That is what makes them fast to communicate and dangerous to combine. The one rule that matters: if one thread writes a variable and another thread reads or writes it, every access must be protected, either by a lock that both threads take, or by making the variable atomic. Break the rule and you have a data race, which in C is undefined behaviour (module 09), not just "a wrong number sometimes".

Picture a bank branch with one shared ledger.

  • A mutex is the single pen chained to the ledger. Whoever holds the pen may write; everyone else waits.
  • A condition variable is the waiting room with a bell. A clerk who needs "a customer in the queue" sits down and releases the pen; whoever adds a customer rings the bell. The clerk wakes up, takes the pen back, and checks the queue again before acting, because someone else may have served that customer first.
  • A read-write lock is the reading room: many people may read the rate sheet at once, but updating it needs the room empty.
  • An atomic is a counter that clicks forward in one indivisible step, so two clerks pressing it together still count two.

You maintain a multithreaded Win32 server, so you have seen CRITICAL_SECTION and friends. This module is the same ideas in the POSIX and C11 APIs that Linux systems interviews expect, with a Win32 mapping table, and it ends with ThreadSanitizer, the tool that finds races for you.

docs.title: 2.1 Creating and joining threads
docs.text:
int pthread_create(pthread_t *thread, const pthread_attr_t *attr,
                   void *(*start)(void *), void *arg);
int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **retval);
int pthread_detach(pthread_t thread);
  • Arguments in: pass a pointer to a struct that lives at least as long as the thread uses it. The classic bug is for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) pthread_create(&t[i], NULL, f, &i);: all four threads read the same i, which keeps changing and dies when the loop ends. Give each thread its own struct (an array of job structs indexed by thread).
  • Results out: write them into the caller-owned job struct, or return a heap pointer from the thread function, which pthread_join hands back and the joiner frees.
  • Join waits for the thread and also makes everything it wrote visible to the joiner.
  • Detach says "nobody will join this thread"; its resources are freed when it exits. A detached thread must signal completion some other way (a semaphore, a condition variable) and must not touch anything that the rest of the program may free first, which makes them a shutdown hazard.
  • Every joinable thread must be joined or detached, or its stack and descriptor leak.
  • pthread functions return an error number (0 on success) and do not set errno. Use strerror(rc), not perror.

docs.title: 2.2 Mutexes
docs.text:
static pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
balance += amount;            /* the critical section: as short as possible */
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
  • Default mutexes are not recursive: locking twice in one thread deadlocks. Win32's CRITICAL_SECTION is recursive, which hides design problems that appear when code is ported.
  • PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK (set with pthread_mutexattr_settype) returns EDEADLK on a relock and EPERM on unlock by a non-owner. Use it in debug builds of code you are not sure about.
  • Lock ordering prevents deadlock: if any code path holds A while taking B, then no path may hold B while taking A. Document the order next to the lock declarations.
  • Never hold a lock across blocking I/O (a socket read, a database call, a log write to a slow disk). Copy what you need, unlock, then do the I/O.

docs.title: 2.3 Condition variables and the predicate loop
docs.text:
pthread_mutex_lock(&q->mu);
while (q->count == 0 && !q->closed)               /* WHILE, never if */
    pthread_cond_wait(&q->not_empty, &q->mu);     /* atomically: unlock, sleep, relock */
/* here: the predicate is true and we hold the lock */
  • pthread_cond_wait must be called with the mutex held. It releases the mutex and sleeps as one atomic step, so a signal sent between "check" and "sleep" cannot be lost, and it reacquires the mutex before returning.
  • Why while, not if. POSIX allows spurious wakeups (returning with no signal), and even a real wakeup can be stolen: another thread takes the item between the signal and your wakeup. Re-checking the predicate handles both.
  • The predicate lives in shared state protected by the mutex. A condition variable has no memory; signalling when nobody waits does nothing. A "flag only" design that waits without checking state loses wakeups.
  • pthread_cond_signal wakes at least one waiter; pthread_cond_broadcast wakes all. Use broadcast when the state change may let several threads proceed, and always for shutdown.
  • Timed waits take an absolute deadline. By default it is measured on CLOCK_REALTIME, which jumps when NTP or an administrator changes the clock; set CLOCK_MONOTONIC with pthread_condattr_setclock and compute the deadline from clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC).
  • Shutdown: set a closed flag under the lock and broadcast; every wait loop checks the flag.

docs.title: 2.4 Read-write locks
docs.text: pthread_rwlock_rdlock lets many readers in together; pthread_rwlock_wrlock waits until there are none. Worth it only for read-mostly data with critical sections long enough to amortise the more expensive lock; for tiny critical sections a plain mutex is often faster. Watch for writer starvation: glibc's default rwlock prefers readers, so a steady stream of readers can keep a writer waiting indefinitely (glibc offers PTHREAD_RWLOCK_PREFER_WRITER_NONRECURSIVE_NP as an option).

docs.title: 2.5 One-time initialisation
docs.text: pthread_once(&once, init_fn) runs init_fn exactly once even if many threads call it together, and every caller returns only after it has finished, with its writes visible. It is the correct form of "lazy global init", which written by hand with a flag is a data race (and the classic broken double-checked locking).

docs.title: 2.6 C11 <threads.h> and <stdatomic.h>
docs.text:
Purpose pthreads C11 Win32 create / wait pthread_create / pthread_join thrd_create / thrd_join _beginthreadex / WaitForSingleObject + CloseHandle thread function void *f(void *) int f(void *) unsigned __stdcall f(void *) mutex pthread_mutex_t mtx_t (mtx_plain, mtx_recursive, mtx_timed) CRITICAL_SECTION, SRWLOCK condition variable pthread_cond_t cnd_t CONDITION_VARIABLE + SleepConditionVariableCS/SRW read-write lock pthread_rwlock_t none SRWLOCK (shared / exclusive) once pthread_once call_once InitOnceExecuteOnce thread-local pthread_key_create or _Thread_local tss_create, thread_local TlsAlloc, __declspec(thread) atomic add _Atomic / GCC builtins atomic_fetch_add InterlockedIncrement, InterlockedAdd semaphore sem_t (POSIX, separate header) none CreateSemaphoreW

The full Win32 reference, with code, is 04_Concurrency/13_win32_concurrency_reference.md.

C11 threads are portable but thinner: no read-write lock, no thread attributes (stack size), and timed waits only against TIME_UTC (wall clock). glibc has shipped them since 2.28 and MSVC since Visual Studio 2022 17.8.

<stdatomic.h> is the part of C11 everyone uses:

static atomic_long hits;
atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&hits, 1, memory_order_relaxed);        /* a pure counter */

g_msg.amount = 250000;                                             /* plain data ...       */
atomic_store_explicit(&ready, 1, memory_order_release);            /* ... then publish     */
while (!atomic_load_explicit(&ready, memory_order_acquire)) ;      /* reader: see the flag */
use(g_msg.amount);                                                  /* ... then the data    */
  • memory_order_relaxed: the operation is atomic, nothing else is ordered. Right for counters.
  • release on a store and acquire on the load that reads it: everything written before the release is visible after the acquire. This is how one thread hands data to another without a lock.
  • seq_cst (the default of the non-_explicit functions): one global order of all such operations. Safest, sometimes slower.
  • atomic_flag is the one type guaranteed lock-free: enough to build a spinlock.

The theory, with diagrams, is 04_Concurrency/07_atomics_and_the_memory_model.md. The practical rule: use a mutex unless you can say exactly which memory order you need and why.

docs.title: 2.7 Thread-safe, reentrant, async-signal-safe
docs.text:
Property Meaning Example Thread-safe correct when called from several threads at once malloc, printf (it locks the FILE) Reentrant correct when called again before the previous call finished in the same thread (nested, recursive, from a handler) strtok_r, localtime_r, anything with only arguments and locals Async-signal-safe may be called from a signal handler write, _exit, sem_post; not printf, malloc

Functions with hidden static state are neither thread-safe nor reentrant, and POSIX gives most of them an _r twin: strtok -> strtok_r, localtime / gmtime / ctime -> localtime_r / gmtime_r / ctime_r, rand -> rand_r, strerror -> strerror_r, getpwnam -> getpwnam_r; gethostbyname and inet_ntoa are replaced by getaddrinfo and inet_ntop. Moving a static result buffer to _Thread_local makes a function thread-safe but still not reentrant: two calls in one printf still overwrite each other (m14_reentrant.c proves both). errno itself is thread-local, which is why it works at all in threaded code.

docs.title: 2.8 A thread pool in C
docs.text:
A fixed set of worker threads takes tasks (a function pointer plus an argument) from a queue:

submit(fn, arg) -> [ lock | append task | pending++ | signal has_work | unlock ]
worker loop     -> [ lock | while (no task && !stopping) wait(has_work) | pop | unlock ]
                   run fn(arg) WITHOUT the lock
                   [ lock | pending-- | if 0: broadcast idle | unlock ]
wait_idle()     -> [ lock | while (pending > 0) wait(idle) | unlock ]
destroy()       -> [ lock | stopping = 1 | broadcast has_work | unlock ] then join every worker

The design decisions: the task runs outside the lock; pending counts queued plus running tasks so wait_idle is exact; shutdown drains the queue before workers exit; and pool_create joins the threads it already started if a later pthread_create fails. Sizing and queue policies are in 04_Concurrency/09_thread_pools_and_task_queues.md.

docs.title: 2.9 ThreadSanitizer
docs.text:
Build with -fsanitize=thread -g -O1 and run. TSan records which thread accessed each memory location under which locks, and reports two accesses that are not ordered by any synchronisation (a "happens-before" relation). This tiny racy program (counter++ from two threads, no lock) is the canonical example:

static long counter;
static void *work(void *arg) { (void)arg; for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) counter++; return NULL; }

Built with plain -O2 it printed counter = 200000 on both runs: GCC turned the loop into a single counter += 100000, so the lost updates you expect did not appear. The race is still there and the next compiler may expose it. TSan reports it regardless (real output, paths shortened):

WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=1554)
  Read of size 8 at 0x555555558018 by thread T2:
    #0 work race.c:4 (race_t+0x1263)

  Previous write of size 8 at 0x555555558018 by thread T1:
    #0 work race.c:4 (race_t+0x128d)

  Location is global 'counter' of size 8 at 0x555555558018 (race_t+0x4018)
  ...
SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: data race race.c:4 in work

On this WSL kernel TSan binaries sometimes abort with "unexpected memory mapping"; run them as setarch $(uname -m) -R ./prog (it disables address randomisation for that run).

A verified TSan limitation. With GCC 13.3 and clang 18.1 on glibc 2.39, a TSan build that uses glibc's <threads.h> crashes at start-up:

ThreadSanitizer:DEADLYSIGNAL
==1530==ERROR: ThreadSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000018 (pc 0x7ffff6eb3f90 ...)

glibc's thrd_create, mtx_lock and cnd_wait call glibc's internal pthread functions directly, so TSan's interceptors (which hook the public pthread_* symbols) never see the new thread or the locks. m14_c11_threads_atomics.c therefore has a small -DUSE_PTHREADS shim that maps the C11 names onto pthreads for the TSan build. That is worth knowing before you choose C11 threads for a codebase you want to race-check.

docs.title: 3. Code
docs.text: All five programs build with -pthread, pass their self-checks, and run clean under TSan using the command in each file's TSan: header line.

docs.title: 3.1 m14_pthreads_basics.c
docs.text:
Arguments in through per-thread job structs, a result returned as a heap pointer, a mutex counter, pthread_once, a read-write lock with an invariant check, and a detached thread that reports through a semaphore. Real output:

parallel sum over 4 threads: 2999997
mutex counter: 400000 (expected 400000)
rwlock: 60000 reads during 200 updates, torn reads = 0
all checks passed

The rwlock test is the useful pattern: the writer updates four fields that must stay equal, and the readers count how often they see them unequal. Zero torn reads is the evidence that the lock protects the invariant, not just the individual fields.

docs.title: 3.2 m14_bounded_queue.c
docs.text:
One mutex, two condition variables (not_empty, not_full), predicate loops, a timed pop on CLOCK_MONOTONIC, and bq_close that broadcasts. Four producers push 20 000 values each through a 16-slot queue to four consumers:

4 producers -> 4 consumers: 80000 items, sum 800040000 (expected 800040000)
timed pop on empty queue: ETIMEDOUT, waited at least 45 ms
all checks passed

The deadline arithmetic is a classic bug site, so it is worth reading:

struct timespec deadline;
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &deadline);     /* absolute deadline, computed once */
deadline.tv_sec += timeout_ms / 1000;
deadline.tv_nsec += (timeout_ms % 1000) * 1000000L;
if (deadline.tv_nsec >= 1000000000L) {         /* normalise, or timedwait fails with EINVAL */
    deadline.tv_sec++;
    deadline.tv_nsec -= 1000000000L;
}

Computing the deadline once, before the loop, means spurious wakeups do not extend the total wait.

docs.title: 3.3 m14_thread_pool.c
docs.text:
static void *worker_main(void *arg)
{
    struct pool *p = arg;
    for (;;) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&p->mu);
        while (!p->head && !p->stopping)
            pthread_cond_wait(&p->has_work, &p->mu);
        if (!p->head) {                     /* stopping and nothing left */
            pthread_mutex_unlock(&p->mu);
            return NULL;
        }
        struct task *t = p->head;
        p->head = t->next;
        if (!p->head)
            p->tail = NULL;
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&p->mu);

        t->fn(t->arg);                      /* run WITHOUT the lock: tasks may be slow */
        free(t);

        pthread_mutex_lock(&p->mu);
        if (--p->pending == 0)
            pthread_cond_broadcast(&p->idle);
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&p->mu);
    }
}

Real output:

10000 square tasks done on 4 workers
50000 counter tasks drained at shutdown: hits = 50000
all checks passed

Compare it line by line with the C++ pool in 04_Concurrency/code/m09_thread_pool.hpp: the logic is the same, and most of the extra C lines are cleanup that destructors would do.

docs.title: 3.4 m14_c11_threads_atomics.c
docs.text:
thrd_create, mtx_t, cnd_t with a predicate loop and call_once; a relaxed atomic counter; a spinlock from atomic_flag; release/acquire message passing; and thread_local:

atomic counter = 400000, spinlock counter = 400000
message passed with release/acquire: account 1001 amount 250000
all checks passed

docs.title: 3.5 m14_reentrant.c
docs.text:
/* Count "key=value" pairs in "a=1;b=2;c=3". The inner strtok call resets the hidden cursor,

 * so the outer loop loses its place after the first pair. */
for (char *item = strtok(s, ";"); item; item = strtok(NULL, ";")) {
    char *key = strtok(item, "=");
    char *val = strtok(NULL, "=");
    if (key && val)
        pairs++;
}

Real output:

pairs counted with strtok: 1, with strtok_r: 3
errno per thread: 22 and 12 survived each other
all checks passed

The strtok bug needs no threads at all: a nested call in one thread is enough. That is the difference between "not reentrant" and "not thread-safe". The file also shows that localtime() returns the same pointer on every call and that a _Thread_local buffer gives each thread its own copy.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
A mutex is a futex. glibc's pthread_mutex_t (40 bytes on x86-64) holds an integer state. An uncontended lock is one atomic compare-and-swap in user space: no system call. Only when the CAS fails does the thread call futex(FUTEX_WAIT) to sleep in the kernel on that address, and unlock calls futex(FUTEX_WAKE) only if someone is waiting. That is why uncontended locks cost tens of nanoseconds and contended ones cost microseconds (typical figures): the expensive part is contention, not locking. Condition variables are built on futexes too, with sequence counters so that wakeups are not lost between the unlock and the sleep.

What pthread_create does. glibc mmaps a stack (8 MiB by default, from ulimit -s) with a guard page below it, sets up the thread's TLS block and its thread control block, and calls clone with flags that share the address space, files, filesystem info and signal handlers (CLONE_VM | CLONE_FS | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD | ...). To the kernel a thread is a task that happens to share memory. _Thread_local variables live in the TLS block, addressed through the %fs segment register on x86-64; errno is one of them.

Memory ordering on x86. x86-64 is close to sequentially consistent ("total store order"): the only reordering the hardware does is a later load passing an earlier store to a different address. So acquire loads and release stores compile to plain mov instructions; the memory_order still matters because it stops the compiler from reordering. A seq_cst store needs xchg (or mov plus mfence). On ARM, which reorders much more, acquire and release become ldar and stlr. Code that "works on x86" with the wrong order can fail on an ARM server.

Why spinlocks are rarely right in user space. A spinning thread burns its time slice; if the lock holder was preempted, every waiter spins until the holder runs again. A futex mutex spins briefly (glibc's adaptive mutex type) and then sleeps. Spinlocks fit kernels with preemption disabled, not application servers. The atomic_flag spinlock in m14_c11_threads_atomics.c is there to teach acquire and release, and it yields instead of spinning hard.

How TSan works. Every memory access is instrumented; for each 8-byte word TSan keeps shadow cells recording the last few accesses with the thread id and a vector clock. Locks, atomics, thread create and join update the clocks. Two accesses to one word, at least one a write, where neither clock happens-before the other, form a race. The shadow memory is why TSan needs a fixed address-space layout (hence the setarch -R workaround) and costs about 5 to 15 times in CPU (typical).

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Locks held across I/O are the top latency bug. A thread takes the session-table lock, then writes a log line to a slow disk or calls the database. Every other request queues behind it. In a dump, many threads are blocked in EnterCriticalSection or futex_wait on the same lock, and one thread holding it is in WriteFile or recv. Fix: copy what you need under the lock, release, then do I/O.
  • Lock-order inversion. Path one locks the connection table, then a session; path two locks a session, then the connection table to remove itself. Under load they deadlock. In gdb: thread apply all bt shows two threads each waiting for the lock the other holds; in WinDbg, !locks and ~*kb. The fix is a documented order (04_Concurrency/06_deadlocks_livelocks_starvation.md).
  • if instead of while around a wait. Works for months, then a second consumer thread is added and the queue pop crashes on an empty queue once a week. Grep every pthread_cond_wait and SleepConditionVariable* call for a surrounding while.
  • Non-reentrant library calls in a threaded server. localtime, strtok, inet_ntoa and gethostbyname used from worker threads give log lines with another request's timestamp or a corrupted token. They are easy to find with grep and easy to replace with the _r versions. On MSVC the CRT makes many of these per-thread, so code ported to Linux can break.
  • Shutdown races. At exit, main frees globals while a detached thread still uses them, or a worker is still running a task when the pool's memory is freed. Make shutdown explicit: set the stop flag, wake everyone, join every thread, then free.
  • Run TSan on the test suite. It finds races that never reproduced under a debugger. Add a TSan build to CI for any component with threads, and treat every report as a bug (04_Concurrency/12_debugging_concurrency_bugs.md).

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - the loop-variable bug. Write a program that passes &i from a for loop to four threads that print it. Run it a few times, then run it under TSan. Fix it with an array of ints. Done when you can explain the original output and TSan's report.
  2. Easy - error numbers. Lock a default mutex twice from one thread with a 1-second pthread_mutex_timedlock, then repeat with an ERRORCHECK mutex and plain lock. Done when you can show ETIMEDOUT in the first case and EDEADLK in the second, printed with strerror.
  3. Medium - break the queue. Change one while in m14_bounded_queue.c to if and run the test 200 times in a loop, then under TSan. Done when you either catch a failure or can explain why it is still wrong even though you did not.
  4. Medium - priority pool. Give m14_thread_pool.c two priority levels (two queues; workers always drain the high queue first). Done when a test with a slow low-priority flood shows high-priority tasks still finish quickly, and TSan is clean.
  5. Hard - rwlock versus mutex. Benchmark the rate table from m14_pthreads_basics.c with a read-write lock and with a mutex, for 1, 2, 4 and 8 reader threads and a critical section of 10 ns and 1 microsecond (busy loop). Done when you have a table and can explain where the rwlock starts to win.
  6. Hard - Win32 port. Port m14_bounded_queue.c to Win32 with SRWLOCK and CONDITION_VARIABLE (SleepConditionVariableSRW, WakeConditionVariable, WakeAllConditionVariable). Done when it passes the same test on Windows; compare with 04_Concurrency/code/m13_win32_srwlock_condvar.c.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why must pthread_cond_wait be called in a while loop? A: POSIX allows spurious wakeups, and even a real wakeup can find the condition false again because another thread consumed the state between the signal and this thread reacquiring the mutex. Re-checking the predicate under the mutex after every wakeup handles both cases. The predicate must be shared state protected by the same mutex.

Q: What does pthread_cond_wait do with the mutex? A: It must be called with the mutex held. It atomically releases the mutex and puts the thread to sleep, so no signal can slip in between the check and the sleep, and it reacquires the mutex before returning, so the caller can safely re-check the predicate.

Q: What is the difference between thread-safe and reentrant? A: Thread-safe means correct when called concurrently from several threads, possibly using locks or per-thread state. Reentrant means correct when re-entered before a previous call in the same thread has finished, as with recursion, nested calls or signal handlers, which requires no hidden shared state. strtok is neither; a version with a thread-local cursor would be thread-safe but still not reentrant; strtok_r is both.

Q: When do you use an atomic instead of a mutex? A: For a single variable updated with a simple operation, such as a counter, a flag or a pointer swap, where an atomic read-modify-write is enough. As soon as an invariant spans several variables, use a mutex. Atomics also require choosing a memory order; relaxed suffices for a pure counter, release/acquire for publishing data.

Q: Is volatile enough for a flag shared between threads? A: No. volatile forces the compiler to load and store the variable each time, but it gives no atomicity and no ordering with respect to other memory, and a concurrent non-atomic access is still a data race and therefore undefined. Use _Atomic (for example atomic_bool with release/acquire) or a mutex.

Q: How do you shut down a thread pool cleanly? A: Under the queue lock set a stopping flag and broadcast the condition variable so every idle worker wakes. Workers finish (or drain) the queue, see the flag with an empty queue and return. The owner joins every worker before freeing the pool, so no thread touches freed memory.

Q: How does a futex-based mutex avoid system calls? A: The lock word lives in user memory; an uncontended lock or unlock is a single atomic instruction. Only on contention does a thread call the futex system call to sleep on that address, and unlock wakes a sleeper through futex only if the state shows there are waiters.

Q: How do you find a data race? A: Build with ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread -g -O1) and run the tests or a load test; it reports both conflicting accesses with stacks and the threads' creation points. Races rarely show up in a debugger because breakpoints change timing, so TSan, Helgrind and careful review of which lock protects each shared field are the main tools.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• A variable written by one thread and accessed by another needs a lock or an atomic; anything else is a data race and undefined behaviour.
  • pthread_create takes a void *(*)(void *); give each thread its own argument struct; join or detach every thread; pthread calls return error numbers, not errno.
  • Mutex: short critical sections, a documented lock order, never across blocking I/O.
  • Condition variable: wait in a while on a predicate protected by the mutex; broadcast for shutdown; absolute deadlines on CLOCK_MONOTONIC.
  • rwlock for read-mostly data with non-trivial critical sections; watch writer starvation.
  • pthread_once / call_once for one-time init; never a hand-rolled flag.
  • C11: thrd_t, mtx_t, cnd_t, call_once, thread_local, and <stdatomic.h> with relaxed, release/acquire and seq_cst orders.
  • Thread-safe is not reentrant: static buffers break both; _Thread_local fixes only the first; use the _r functions.
  • A thread pool: queue under one mutex, tasks run unlocked, pending counter for wait-idle, drain and join on shutdown.
  • TSan finds races that tests and debuggers miss; on this setup it needs setarch -R, and it cannot see glibc's <threads.h>, so race-check C11 threads code through pthreads.

docs.title: 15. Reading, debugging and changing legacy C
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours Prerequisites: modules 09, 10, 14; 05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/05_gdb_from_zero_to_fluent.md; 06_Linux_Toolchain_DevOps/06_git_properly.md

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
Most professional C work is not writing new programs. It is changing old ones without breaking them: code you did not write, often without tests, written by people who have left, running at customers who cannot accept downtime. Banks, telecoms, embedded products, databases and operating systems all run on C that is ten or twenty years old, and every one of those organisations needs engineers who can work in it safely.

That is a distinct, senior skill set: find your way around a large unfamiliar codebase, understand what a piece of code really does (including the parts nobody documented), reproduce a bug, fix it with the smallest safe change, prove nothing else changed, and explain what happened. Your 2.5 years of analysing and fixing bugs in an existing multithreaded server are experience in exactly this. This module gives that experience a method and a vocabulary, and the last part of section 2 shows how to present it honestly and strongly in interviews, without claiming to have built things you did not build.

An analogy: a surgeon, not a robot builder. The surgeon does not redesign the patient. She studies the scans first, makes the smallest incision that fixes the problem, monitors the patient before, during and after, and writes up exactly what she did. A careless surgeon who "cleans up" healthy organs on the way is not more senior; she is more dangerous.

docs.title: 2.1 Navigating a large unfamiliar C codebase
docs.text:
Step 0: build it yourself. Until you can build and run it, you are reading fiction. While building, produce a compilation database (compile_commands.json), the file every modern C tool reads to know each file's flags and include paths:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON     # CMake projects
bear -- make -j8                                            # Makefile projects (sudo apt install bear)

Step 1: a code index. With compile_commands.json, clangd (the VS Code clangd extension) gives go-to-definition, find-references and a call hierarchy that understands macros and include paths. For terminals and very old code, the classic tools still work:

ctags -R .                    # universal-ctags: jump to definitions from vim/emacs
cscope -Rbq                   # build the cscope database
cscope -dL1 kv_put            # where is kv_put defined?
cscope -dL3 kv_put            # who calls kv_put?
cscope -dL2 kv_put            # what does kv_put call?

On Windows, Visual Studio's "Find All References" and "View Call Hierarchy" do the same for an MSVC project.

Step 2: grep, precisely. ripgrep (rg) recipes that answer real questions:

rg -n '\bprocess_line\s*\('                     # every call and the definition
rg -n 'g_txn_count\s*([-+*/]?=|\+\+|--)'        # every WRITE to a global
rg -n '\.handler\s*=|->handler\s*='             # where a function pointer is assigned
rg -n 'pthread_create|_beginthreadex|CreateThread'   # thread entry points
rg -n 'signal\(|sigaction\('                    # signal handlers
rg -n '^static [a-z_ ]+\*?[a-z_]+\[?' --type c  # file-scope statics: hidden state

Step 3: find the entry points. A server rarely flows from main in a straight line. List main, every thread start routine, signal handlers, atexit handlers, Windows service entry points (ServiceMain) and DllMain, and above all the dispatch tables: arrays of function pointers indexed by message type or opcode. In an RPC server, the dispatch table is the map of the whole application.

Step 4: follow one request end to end. Pick one operation (a login, a balance enquiry) and trace it: accept, read the frame, decode, dispatch, handler, database call, response, logging. Use the debugger with a breakpoint in the handler and bt to see the real call chain, or perf record -g and strace -f to see what it does at run time. Write a one-page map. Then the next request is twice as fast to understand.

Step 5: read the data structures before the code. The structs and globals tell you what the program believes about the world. Fred Brooks put it as "show me your tables, and I won't usually need your flowchart".

docs.title: 2.2 Global state and hidden coupling
docs.text:
Legacy C couples distant code through shared state that no function signature mentions:

Hidden channel Example How to find it Globals and file-scope statics int g_txn_count; updated in five files nm obj.o \| grep -E ' [BbDd] ' (B/b = bss, D/d = data); the rg write-pattern above Function-local statics and static result buffers char *fmt_amount(long) returning static char buf[] rg -n 'static char .*\[' Library calls with hidden state strtok, localtime, rand, setlocale module 14's list of non-reentrant calls Order of initialisation a config global read before load_config() ran breakpoints on the first reads Process-wide settings umask, current directory, signal dispositions, environment variables rg -n 'chdir|umask|setenv|getenv' Files and shared memory two processes that "communicate" through a temp file strace -f -e trace=file

Each of these causes "action at a distance": a change in one module breaks another that shares the hidden state. Before changing a function, list what global state it reads and writes. That list is also its thread-safety story.

docs.title: 2.3 Reproducing a bug
docs.text:
1. Collect facts before theories. Exact version and build, configuration, input, time, log lines around the failure, the crash dump. Ask "what changed?" (deploy, configuration, data volume, operating system patch).
  2. Reproduce in the smallest setting you can. A unit-level call with the captured input is best; a single request replayed against a test server is next; a full system test is last. Capture the exact bytes of the failing request (a log hex dump, tcpdump) so you can replay it.
  3. Make it deterministic. For timing bugs: stress (many threads, many iterations), sanitizers (TSan finds races without the race having to happen), and record-and-replay debuggers: rr on Linux records a run and lets you step backwards through it; WinDbg's Time Travel Debugging does the same on Windows.
  4. Write the reproduction down as a failing test before fixing. It proves you found the bug, and it stays in the suite so the bug cannot return silently.

docs.title: 2.4 Characterisation tests before changing code
docs.text:
A characterisation test pins down what the code does today, right or wrong. The term comes from Michael Feathers' Working Effectively with Legacy Code (2004), which defines legacy code as code without tests. The recipe:

  1. Pick the function you need to change.
  2. Call it with many inputs, including edge cases (zero, negative, maximum, empty, malformed).
  3. Record the outputs from the running code (a --print mode that prints table rows works well), and paste them in as expected values. Do not "correct" them: a known bug is recorded as it is, with a comment.
  4. Now refactor. Any difference is a behaviour change you must justify.

C has few natural places to cut code apart for testing. Feathers calls those places seams:

Seam How it works in C Link seam Compile the test with fake_db.c instead of db.c; same function names, test behaviour --wrap seam GNU ld -Wl,--wrap=send sends calls to send to your __wrap_send; __real_send reaches the original Preprocessor seam #ifdef UNIT_TEST or #define fopen test_fopen in a test-only header Function-pointer seam the code calls through a pointer (ops->send) that the test replaces

The fault-injection wrappers in m10_goto_cleanup.c are a seam of the last two kinds.

docs.title: 2.5 The smallest safe fix
docs.text:
• Fix the root cause at the right layer, with the smallest diff that does it. A NULL check that hides a lifetime bug is not a fix; a rewrite of the module to fix a one-line bug is not safe.
  • Separate refactoring commits from behaviour changes. Reviewers can check a pure refactor against the characterisation tests and a small fix by reasoning. Mixed together, neither is checkable.
  • Check every caller. rg for the function and for every place its output is used. A changed return value or error code ripples.
  • Look for siblings. The same mistake is usually copied elsewhere (the same realloc misuse, the same missing while around a wait). Fix or ticket them all.
  • Preserve compatibility. Wire formats, file formats, configuration keys, error codes, log formats that monitoring parses, struct layouts shared with other binaries. In banking, a client's batch files may depend on a lenient parser that you consider a bug.
  • Guard risky changes. A configuration switch that restores the old behaviour lets operations roll back without a redeploy.

docs.title: 2.6 Adding diagnostics
docs.text:
When you cannot attach a debugger (a customer machine, an intermittent fault), add evidence:

  • Contextual log lines at decision points: request id, account, sizes, error codes, and the file and line (m15_diagnostics.c).
  • A trace ring: a fixed in-memory array of the last N events per thread, cheap enough to leave on in production and dumped when something goes wrong. It answers "what happened just before?", which a single error line cannot.
  • Soft asserts (CHECK) that log the violated condition with context and return an error, instead of aborting a production server.
  • Hex dumps of bad input, so the exact bytes reach the bug report.
  • Counters (requests, errors by code, pool usage) exposed in a status command.

Two cautions. Logging changes timing, so a race may disappear when you add logs (a "heisenbug"); prefer the trace ring, which is just memory writes. And rate-limit error logging, or the first bad client fills the disk.

docs.title: 2.7 History as evidence: blame, log and bisect
docs.text:
git blame -w -C -C -C file.c                 # ignore whitespace, follow code moved between files
git log -L :process_line:legacy.c            # the full history of one function
git log -S 'atol(' --oneline -- src/         # commits that added or removed this string
git log -G 'fee.*1000' --oneline             # commits whose diff matches a regex
git bisect start BAD GOOD; git bisect run ./test.sh   # binary search for the breaking commit

The commit message and its ticket number often explain why strange code exists ("customer X sends amounts with trailing spaces"). Read them before deleting anything. git bisect run needs a test script that exits 0 for good, 1 to 127 (except 125) for bad, and 125 for "cannot test, skip" (for example a commit that does not compile). With n commits it needs about log2(n) builds. Older codebases may live in SVN or TFS; svn blame and svn log answer the same questions.

docs.title: 2.8 Reviewing C changes
docs.text:
A checklist that catches most of what reaches production:

  • Every new acquisition is released on every path, including errors (module 10).
  • Every return value is checked; errno is saved before any other call.
  • Size arithmetic cannot overflow; buffer lengths include the NUL; snprintf truncation is handled.
  • Ownership of every pointer passed or returned is documented.
  • New globals or statics are thread-safe, or documented as single-threaded.
  • Locks: taken in the documented order, never held across blocking I/O, released on every path.
  • No undefined behaviour: signed overflow, aliasing casts, uninitialised reads (module 09).
  • Format strings match their arguments; no user data used as a format string.
  • Signed/unsigned comparisons and narrowing conversions are deliberate.
  • Behaviour changes are called out; characterisation or regression tests are included.
  • Wire, file and struct-layout compatibility is preserved, or the version is bumped.

docs.title: 2.9 Refactoring legacy C safely
docs.text:
Behaviour-preserving steps, each small and each behind the characterisation tests:

  1. Extract function: pull a block out of a 600-line function into a named function with explicit parameters. The name documents intent; the parameters expose hidden inputs.
  2. Introduce a struct: replace a cluster of globals with a struct passed by pointer (struct ledger *lg). State becomes explicit and two instances become possible (tests!).
  3. Replace static result buffers with caller-provided buffers (fmt_amount_r(v, buf, n)), and keep the old function as a thin wrapper so old callers still compile.
  4. Opaque types: the header declares typedef struct ledger ledger_t; and functions; only the .c file knows the fields. Callers can no longer reach inside, so the layout can change.
  5. Make it const-correct from the leaves upward; the compiler then finds unintended writes.
  6. Strangler approach: build the new implementation behind the old interface, move callers over one at a time, and delete the old code when nothing calls it. The system works at every step. (The name comes from Martin Fowler's "strangler fig" pattern.)
  7. Ratchet the warnings: record today's warning count per file in CI and fail the build if it rises; turn on -Wall -Wextra for each file as it is cleaned.

m15_refactored_report.c performs steps 1 to 4 on the legacy code, then fixes a bug in a separate, final step.

docs.title: 2.10 Static and dynamic analysis on old code
2.11 Describing maintenance work in interviews
docs.text:
Interviewers for systems roles respect maintenance experience when it is described precisely, because it is what most of the job is. The two mistakes are underselling it ("I just fixed bugs") and overselling it (claiming to have designed or built what you maintained). Both get found out: the first in the screen, the second in the follow-up questions.

Use verbs that match what you did. Diagnosed, root-caused, reproduced, fixed, hardened, added tests for, reduced, extended, maintained, analysed crash dumps of. Use "designed" or "built" only for what you designed or built.

Lead with impact and root cause, not activity. For each story have: the symptom and its cost (crashes per week, escalations, a stuck batch), how you found the cause (dump, logs, reproduction, bisect), the root-cause class in precise words (use-after-free in connection teardown, lock-order inversion between the session table and the connection table, signed overflow in a length check), the fix, and how you prevented a recurrence (a test, a sanitizer run, a review rule). Use only numbers you can defend if asked how you measured them; if you do not have one, describe the scale in words instead of inventing a figure.

Resume bullets, before and after (fill in your real facts):

Weak:    Worked on bug fixing for the core-banking application server.
Strong:  Diagnosed and fixed [N] production defects in a multithreaded C (Win32/MSVC) RPC server
         used by [bank customers], including [use-after-free / deadlock / memory leak] root causes
         found through crash-dump analysis in WinDbg.

Weak:    Responsible for maintenance of the migration engine.
Strong:  Maintained and extended a C data-migration engine (Berkeley DB to YugabyteDB):
         root-caused [a data-loss / performance] issue in [batch handling], added regression
         tests that [caught X before release].

A STAR answer shape for "tell me about a hard bug":

Situation  The server crashed [how often] at [a customer]; no reproduction in house.
Task       I owned the RCA and the fix.
Action     From the dump: crash in [function], freed memory being read. I read the teardown
           path and found two threads could release the same connection. Reproduced it with
           [a stress test that closes connections during requests]. Fixed the ownership so only
           [one thread] frees, kept the change to [N lines], and added [a regression test / an
           ASan run] so it cannot come back.
Result     [No recurrence since], RCA shared with support; I added the pattern to our review
           checklist and found [one more] instance elsewhere.

When asked "have you built something like this from scratch?" answer straight: "Not in production. At work my role has been maintaining and fixing a large existing server, which taught me [X and Y]. To build design experience I built tcpkv from scratch; here is how its thread pool and protocol parser work." The capstone in 10_Capstone_Projects exists precisely so that this answer has a strong second half. Align the stories in 11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search/02_telling_your_story.md with the same rule: each story should use the verbs that match your actual role in it.

docs.title: 3.1 m15_legacy_report.c: pinning current behaviour
docs.text:
The legacy code, as found (abridged):

char g_last_error[128];
int  g_txn_count;
long g_total_paise;

char *fmt_amount(long paise)
{
    static char buf[40];
    long rupees = paise / 100;
    long frac = paise % 100;
    if (frac < 0)
        frac = -frac;
    sprintf(buf, "%ld.%02ld", rupees, frac);   /* BUG #4711: -50 -> rupees 0 -> "0.50" */
    return buf;
}

The sign is lost for amounts between -0.99 and -0.01 because -50 / 100 is 0 in C (division truncates toward zero) and 0 has no sign. Running ./m15_legacy_report --print prints the current behaviour as table rows (real output):

FMT_CASES:
    { 0, "0.00" },
    { 5, "0.05" },
    { 100, "1.00" },
    { 123456, "1234.56" },
    { -250, "-2.50" },
    { -50, "0.50" },
    { -1, "0.01" },
    { 9223372036854775807, "92233720368547758.07" },
    { -9223372036854775808, "-92233720368547758.08" },
LINE_CASES:
    { line 0: ret 0, count 1, total 2500, error "" },
    { line 1: ret 0, count 2, total 1500, error "" },
    { line 2: ret 0, count 3, total 1488, error "" },
    { line 3: ret -1, count 3, total 1488, error "bad type REFUND" },
    { line 4: ret -1, count 3, total 1488, error "bad format" },
    { line 5: ret -1, count 3, total 1488, error "bad format" },
    { line 6: ret 0, count 4, total 1488, error "bad format" },

Those rows became the expected values, with the two wrong rows marked KNOWN BUG #4711. Other surprises the table pins down rather than "fixes": "DEBIT|ACC-1001|12abc" is accepted as 12 paise (atol), "CREDIT||500" is a format error because strtok merges empty fields, and a successful line does not clear the previous error message. Each of these may be relied on by someone. Normal run:

9 fmt cases, 7 line cases, 0 failures
all checks passed

docs.title: 3.2 m15_refactored_report.c: refactor, then fix
docs.text:
struct ledger {                         /* step 1: the globals, made explicit */
    int  txn_count;
    long total_paise;
    char last_error[128];
};

/* step 3 + step 5: caller buffer, and the sign handled separately */
static int fmt_amount_r(long paise, char *buf, size_t n)
{
    unsigned long mag = paise < 0 ? 0UL - (unsigned long)paise : (unsigned long)paise;
    int w = snprintf(buf, n, "%s%lu.%02lu", paise < 0 ? "-" : "", mag / 100, mag % 100);
    return (w < 0 || (size_t)w >= n) ? -1 : w;
}

/* step 4: the old API kept for old callers (thread-safe now, still not reentrant) */
static char *fmt_amount(long paise)
{
    static _Thread_local char buf[32];
    fmt_amount_r(paise, buf, sizeof buf);
    return buf;
}

0UL - (unsigned long)paise is the safe way to get the magnitude: -LONG_MIN would overflow. The same tables run against the new code, with exactly two rows changed by the fix, each marked in the table:

9 fmt cases, 7 line cases, 0 failures (2 fmt rows changed by the #4711 fix)
all checks passed

The parser still uses atol: tightening it to reject "12abc" is a behaviour change that needs a product decision (a customer's batch file may contain such amounts), so it is deliberately not part of a refactor.

docs.title: 3.3 m15_diagnostics.c: log, trace ring, soft assert, hex dump
docs.text:
#define CHECK(cond, ...) \
    ((cond) ? 1 : (check_failed(#cond, __FILE__, __LINE__, __func__, __VA_ARGS__), 0))

static int process_message(const unsigned char *msg, size_t len)
{
    TRACE("recv", len, msg[0]);
    if (!CHECK(len >= 3, "len=%zu", len))
        return -1;
    size_t declared = (size_t)msg[1] | ((size_t)msg[2] << 8);
    TRACE("header", msg[0], declared);
    if (!CHECK(declared == len - 3, "type=%u declared=%zu actual=%zu", msg[0], declared, len - 3)) {
        hexdump(g_log, msg, len);
        return -1;
    }
    TRACE("ok", msg[0], declared);
    return 0;
}

Real output (your timestamps will differ):

2026-10-13T15:38:50.402Z INFO  t1 m15_diagnostics.c:163 main(): server starting, 4 workers
2026-10-13T15:38:50.402Z ERROR t1 m15_diagnostics.c:148 process_message(): check failed: declared == len - 3 (type=2 declared=255 actual=8)
  last 8 trace events of t1 (oldest first):
    #0 recv       a=7 b=1
    #1 header     a=1 b=4
    #2 ok         a=1 b=4
    #3 recv       a=5 b=1
    #4 header     a=1 b=2
    #5 ok         a=1 b=2
    #6 recv       a=11 b=2
    #7 header     a=2 b=255
  00000000  02 ff 00 41 43 43 2d 31 30 30 31                 |...ACC-1001|
all checks passed

One error produced the violated condition, the values involved, the two good messages that came before, and the exact bytes of the bad one: enough to write the reproduction test without another round trip to the customer.

A true story from writing this file: the first draft defined #define TRACE(what, a, b) and wrote ev_->what = (what); in the body. The preprocessor replaced the member names too (ev_->"recv"), and the build failed with expected identifier before string constant. Macro parameters are substituted everywhere in the body, including after ->. The fix, now in the file, is parameter names that cannot collide (what_, a_, b_). Module 08's rules on macro hygiene exist because of exactly this.

docs.title: 3.4 m15_bisect_demo.sh: let git find the guilty commit
docs.text:
The script builds a throwaway repository with eight commits; commit 5, titled "avoid overflow in fee formula", changes (amount_paise * 5) / 1000 to amount_paise / 1000 * 5, which divides first and loses precision. Real output (hashes differ on every run):

== history (newest first)
6ecc8b7 v8: release 2.3.1
b7ec1b8 v7: update banner
cdfa196 v6: tidy includes
0ec5311 v5: avoid overflow in fee formula
b8e3d8c v4: bump version string
8fd833e v3: parenthesise for readability
0247ed6 v2: add usage comment
0a9bd79 v1: initial fee calculation
== bisect
running '/tmp/tmp.Ejl77rsl9D/test.sh'
running '/tmp/tmp.Ejl77rsl9D/test.sh'
running '/tmp/tmp.Ejl77rsl9D/test.sh'
0ec531191d14d405afff3cba8b61628f659160e2 is the first bad commit
    v5: avoid overflow in fee formula
== the guilty change
0ec5311 v5: avoid overflow in fee formula
-long fee_paise(long amount_paise) { return (amount_paise * 5) / 1000; }
+long fee_paise(long amount_paise) { return amount_paise / 1000 * 5; }

Three test runs to search eight commits. The commit message sounded harmless, which is normal: the message describes the intent, the diff shows the effect.

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
Why changing old C is risky: implicit contracts. C interfaces carry contracts the compiler never sees: who frees, how long a pointer stays valid, which lock must be held, what a return value of 0 means, whether a buffer is NUL-terminated. Old code also has binary contracts: a struct written to a file or shared memory, sent on the wire, or compiled into another module or plugin that is not rebuilt with yours. Adding a field to such a struct changes its size and offsets and silently breaks the other side. Before touching a struct, rg for sizeof(struct name), fwrite, send, memcpy and shared-memory mappings that involve it.

How --wrap and interposition work. With -Wl,--wrap=send, the GNU linker resolves every undefined reference to send in the objects being linked to __wrap_send, and references to __real_send to the original. It only affects objects linked in that step, which makes it a precise test seam. LD_PRELOAD works at load time instead: the dynamic linker searches the preloaded library first, so its malloc or send wins for every library in the process.

How static analysers find a leak. -fanalyzer and the Clang static analyzer perform path-sensitive symbolic execution: they walk each path through a function with abstract values ("buf points to a fresh heap region; f may be NULL") and report a state where the last reference to an allocation is lost. They do not run the code, so they are limited by how far they follow calls and loops, which produces both false positives and missed bugs. That is why their findings are triaged, not blindly fixed, and why they complement sanitizers, which see only the paths you actually execute.

Record and replay. rr records a run by capturing the results of every system call and other nondeterministic event, running the program on one core so thread interleaving is fixed. Replaying reproduces the run exactly, and gdb can then run it backwards (reverse-continue), so you can set a watchpoint on a corrupted field and run backwards to the write that corrupted it. WinDbg's Time Travel Debugging records at the instruction level and offers the same on Windows. Both turn "it happened once" into "it happens every time I replay".

Bisect complexity. Bisect halves the candidate range each step, so 1000 commits need about 10 builds. It assumes the property is monotonic (good, then bad). Flaky tests break that assumption: make the test script run the scenario several times and fail if any run fails, or skip (125) commits where the build is broken.

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• Restore service first, then diagnose, and preserve evidence. At 3 AM the order is: keep the crash dump and logs, restart or fail over, disable the triggering feature if a switch exists, and only then debug. A restart that deletes the core file loses the only evidence (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/11_production_incident_triage.md).
  • "Works at customer A, fails at B" is usually configuration or data. Diff the configuration files, the data volumes, the operating system and runtime versions, and the time zone and locale. Legacy C is full of fixed-size buffers that only overflow with one customer's longest branch name.
  • Hotfixes go to old versions. A bank may run a release two years old. The fix is written on the main branch with its test, then cherry-picked to each maintenance branch, rebuilt and retested there. Keep fixes small precisely so that they backport cleanly.
  • Production data is sensitive. Reproducing with real account data is usually not allowed. Build the reproduction from the shape of the data (lengths, character sets, counts), or use a masked extract.
  • Every fix gets a regression test and every incident gets an RCA. The RCA states the root cause, why it was not caught earlier, and what now prevents the class of bug (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA/12_writing_a_formal_rca.md). Over two or three years, that list of RCAs is your strongest interview material.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - map an unfamiliar codebase. Clone a real C project (SQLite's amalgamation is one file; Redis is a server like yours). Find main, the event loop and the function that handles one command (for Redis, GET). Done when you have written the call chain from socket read to reply in ten lines or fewer, with file names.
  2. Easy - read history. In any git repository you use, run git log -L on one function and git log -S on one string. Done when you can name the commit that introduced the current behaviour and the reason given in its message.
  3. Medium - characterise. Pick a function at work or in an open-source project that has no tests. Write a --print mode that prints its outputs for 20 inputs including edge cases, then turn that into a test table. Done when the test passes and you have marked any output you think is a bug instead of changing it.
  4. Medium - analyse. Install cppcheck (sudo apt install cppcheck) and run it, clang-tidy and gcc -fanalyzer on m15_legacy_report.c and on one real legacy file. Done when you have a table of every finding with a verdict: real bug, risky but intended, or false positive.
  5. Hard - seam with --wrap. Write a function that calls send in a loop, then test it without a network: link the test with -Wl,--wrap=send and make __wrap_send return short writes and EINTR. Done when the test proves the function handles partial sends and EINTR.
  6. Hard - your stories. Write three STAR stories from your real work using section 2.11: one crash or memory bug, one concurrency bug, one change that needed backward compatibility. Use only numbers you can defend. Done when each fits in two minutes spoken and a friend can repeat the root cause after hearing it once.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: You join a team with a 500 000-line C codebase. How do you get productive? A: Build and run it first, generating compile_commands.json so clangd or ctags/cscope can index it. Read the main data structures and find the entry points: main, thread start routines and the dispatch table. Then trace one real request end to end with a debugger and write a short map. Fixing a small bug early is the fastest way to learn the build, test and release process.

Q: How do you change code that has no tests? A: Write characterisation tests first: call the code with many inputs, record what it does today (including known bugs) and make that the expected output. Use seams such as link substitution, --wrap or function pointers to isolate it. Then refactor in small behaviour-preserving steps and make behaviour changes in separate commits with their own tests.

Q: What is the smallest safe fix, and why does it matter? A: The minimal change that removes the root cause at the right layer, without unrelated cleanups. It is easy to review, easy to backport to maintenance branches, and limits the risk of regressions in code nobody fully understands. Refactoring and improvements come in separate, test-protected changes.

Q: How do you find which commit introduced a bug? A: Write a script that builds and tests one commit and exits 0 for good, 1 for bad and 125 to skip unbuildable commits, then run git bisect start BAD GOOD and git bisect run script. It finds the commit in about log2(n) steps. git log -S, git log -L and git blame -w -C narrow the search when you already suspect a function or string.

Q: What hidden coupling do you look for in legacy C? A: Globals and file-scope statics written in several files, functions returning static buffers, library calls with hidden state such as strtok and localtime, initialisation order, and process-wide settings like the current directory, umask and signal handlers. Each one lets a change in one place break code elsewhere, and each one is a thread-safety question.

Q: Which static analysis tools would you run on old C code, and how do you deal with the noise? A: GCC's -fanalyzer, clang-tidy with the analyzer, bugprone and CERT checks, cppcheck, and MSVC /analyze on Windows, plus ASan, UBSan and Valgrind runs of the tests. The first run produces many findings, so record a baseline, fix by bug class starting with leaks and memory errors, and fail CI only on new findings.

Q: Most of your experience is maintenance. Why should we hire you for a role building systems? A: Maintenance at depth means I have debugged the failure modes that new systems must design out: use-after-free in teardown paths, lock-order deadlocks, leaks on error paths, and compatibility breaks. I can name the root causes I fixed and the tests I added to prevent them. I have also built a server from scratch (tcpkv) to practise the design side, and I can walk you through its decisions.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Legacy work is a senior skill: navigate, understand, reproduce, fix minimally, prove, explain.
  • Build first; generate compile_commands.json; use clangd or ctags/cscope; grep precisely for writes, function-pointer assignments and thread entry points.
  • Find entry points and dispatch tables; trace one request end to end; read data structures first.
  • Hidden coupling: globals, statics, static buffers, non-reentrant library calls, init order, process-wide settings.
  • Reproduce with facts, the smallest setting, deterministic tools (sanitizers, rr, TTD), and a failing test.
  • Characterisation tests pin current behaviour, bugs included; seams in C are link, --wrap, preprocessor and function pointers.
  • Smallest safe fix; refactors and behaviour changes in separate commits; check callers and siblings; keep compatibility.
  • Diagnostics: contextual logs, per-thread trace rings, soft asserts, hex dumps, counters.
