  • git blame -w -C, git log -L, git log -S, git bisect run turn history into evidence.
  • Run several analysers (-fanalyzer found a FILE leak clang-tidy missed); baseline the noise.
  • In interviews: precise verbs, root causes, impact you can defend, prevention; never claim to have built what you maintained; tcpkv covers the build-from-scratch question.

docs.title: 16. Modern C and the C interview playbook
docs.text: Time: ~3 hours (plus practice: write every coding answer twice on paper) Prerequisites: modules 01 to 15

docs.title: 1. In plain words
docs.text:
A C interview tests three things. First, precise knowledge of the language: what static means in each place, why volatile is not for threads, what sizeof gives for an array parameter. Second, writing small correct functions without a library: strlen, memmove, atoi, reversing a list. Third, care: do you mention the empty string, the NULL pointer, the overflow, the overlap, before the interviewer has to ask?

Think of a driving test. Everyone can drive in a straight line. The examiner is watching whether you check the mirrors at every turn. In a C interview the mirrors are the edge cases and the undefined behaviour, and saying them out loud is how the interviewer knows you checked.

This module is the reference sheet for that day: what each C standard added (including C23), the C versus C++ differences interviewers like, the classic conceptual questions with model answers, the classic coding questions with complete tested solutions in code/, and how C rounds are run at embedded, systems and product companies.

docs.title: 2.1 The C standards in one table
2.2 C versus C++: the differences interviewers ask about
2.3 Classic conceptual questions
docs.text:
static in three contexts.

  1. Inside a function: the variable has static storage duration: it is initialised once, before main, and keeps its value between calls (not thread-safe without a lock or atomic).
  2. At file scope, on a function or variable: internal linkage: the name is invisible to other .c files, so two files can each have a private helper() without a link clash.
  3. In an array parameter (C99): void f(int a[static 4]) promises the caller passes at least 4 valid elements, so the compiler may optimise and can warn on violations.

const int *p, int *const p, const int *const p. Read right to left from the name: p is a pointer to a const int (you cannot write *p, you can change p); p is a const pointer to an int (you can write *p, not p); both const. int const *p means the same as const int *p. A const on the pointer itself is top-level and is dropped when the value is copied, which is why _Generic sees int *const cpi as int * (m16_modern_c_features.c checks it).

volatile, and why it is not for threads. volatile tells the compiler that every read and write of the object is a visible side effect: it must not cache the value in a register, merge or remove accesses. That is what memory-mapped hardware registers need, and what a volatile sig_atomic_t flag set by a signal handler needs (the only object type a handler may portably write). It does not make a read-modify-write atomic, it does not order other memory accesses around it, and a concurrent non-atomic access from two threads is still a data race, which is undefined behaviour. Use _Atomic or a mutex (module 14). (MSVC historically gave volatile acquire/release semantics on x86 as an extension, /volatile:ms; code relying on it breaks on other compilers and on ARM.)

sizeof of an array parameter. An array parameter is adjusted to a pointer, so void f(int a[10]) is void f(int *a) and sizeof a is 8 on a 64-bit system. GCC warns:

warning: 'sizeof' on array function parameter 'a' will return size of 'int *' [-Wsizeof-array-argument]

Pass the length separately (f(int *a, size_t n)), or pass a pointer to the array (void f(int (*a)[10]), where sizeof *a is 40).

Array versus pointer. char a[] = "hi"; is a 3-byte array you may modify; sizeof a is 3. char *p = "hi"; is a pointer to a string literal, which you must not modify (it is usually in read-only memory); sizeof p is 8. An array name decays to a pointer to its first element in most expressions, except as the operand of sizeof, &, or as a string literal initialising an array.

More you should answer in two sentences each: i++ + ++i (unsequenced modifications: UB); -1 < 1u is false (the -1 is converted to unsigned int, a huge value); unsigned char arithmetic is done in int (integer promotion); malloc versus calloc (zeroed, and checks the n * size overflow) versus realloc (may move; keep the old pointer until it succeeds); free(NULL) is a no-op; macros versus static inline functions (MAX(a++, b) evaluates a++ twice); why do { ... } while (0) in macros (one statement, safe after if without braces); header guards versus #pragma once; extern declarations versus definitions; what runs before main (section 4).

docs.title: 2.4 Classic coding questions: approach and edge cases
docs.text:
All of these are implemented and tested in code/m16_string_questions.c and code/m16_classic_questions.c. For each, say the edge cases before you write code.

Question Approach Edge cases to say out loud strlen walk to the NUL, return the pointer difference empty string; NULL is the caller's bug (the standard function does not check) strcpy copy including the NUL; return dst overlap is UB; caller must size dst; prefer a bounded copy strncpy trap does not NUL-terminate when the source is too long, and pads with zeros why strlcpy (or snprintf(dst, n, "%s", src)) is the safe answer strcmp compare as unsigned char until a difference or NUL bytes above 127; return sign only memcpy byte loop; restrict says no overlap overlap is UB; n == 0 memmove copy forwards if dst < src, backwards if dst > src both overlap directions; equal pointers; comparing unrelated pointers atoi with overflow skip spaces, sign, digits; check before acc * 10 + d INT_MIN (magnitude one more than INT_MAX), "+", "-", "", trailing junk Reverse a string in place two indices moving inward empty, one character, even and odd lengths Reverse a linked list three pointers: prev, cur, next empty list, one node; recursive version uses O(n) stack Detect a loop Floyd: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; they meet inside the loop loop at the head, self-loop, no loop Find where the loop starts after meeting, move one pointer to the head; step both by 1 whole list is the loop Endianness look at the first byte of uint32_t 1 through unsigned char * or a union say "union punning is legal in C, not in C++" Count set bits v &= v - 1 clears the lowest set bit; loop count = bits 0, all ones; __builtin_popcount Power of two x != 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0 zero is not a power of two Stack array + length + capacity, grow by doubling pop on empty returns an error, never UB Tokenizer strspn to skip delimiters, strcspn to find the end empty fields (a CSV needs them; strtok drops them), state in the caller Rotate an array right by k reverse all, reverse first k, reverse the rest k >= n (use k % n), n == 0

Four of them in full, because they are asked most:

/* memmove: overlap allowed. If dst is after src, copy backwards so we never read a byte we

 * already overwrote. Comparing pointers into DIFFERENT objects with < is undefined in C, so
 * compare their integer values (implementation-defined, correct on flat-memory platforms). */
void *my_memmove(void *dst, const void *src, size_t n)
{
    unsigned char *d = dst;
    const unsigned char *s = src;
    if ((uintptr_t)d < (uintptr_t)s) {
        while (n--)
            *d++ = *s++;
    } else if ((uintptr_t)d > (uintptr_t)s) {
        d += n;
        s += n;
        while (n--)
            *--d = *--s;
    }
    return dst;
}

/* atoi with overflow detection: accumulate in unsigned so INT_MIN's magnitude fits. */
int my_atoi(const char *s, int *out, const char **end)
{
    while (isspace((unsigned char)*s))       /* cast: isspace(negative char) is UB */
        s++;
    int neg = 0;
    if (*s == '+' || *s == '-')
        neg = (*s++ == '-');
    if (!isdigit((unsigned char)*s)) {
        if (end) *end = s;
        return ATOI_NO_DIGITS;
    }
    unsigned limit = neg ? (unsigned)INT_MAX + 1u : (unsigned)INT_MAX;
    unsigned acc = 0;
    for (; isdigit((unsigned char)*s); s++) {
        unsigned d = (unsigned)(*s - '0');
        if (acc > (limit - d) / 10) {         /* acc * 10 + d would exceed limit */
            *out = neg ? INT_MIN : INT_MAX;   /* clamp, like strtol */
            while (isdigit((unsigned char)*s))
                s++;
            if (end) *end = s;
            return ATOI_OVERFLOW;
        }
        acc = acc * 10 + d;
    }
    if (neg)
        *out = acc == (unsigned)INT_MAX + 1u ? INT_MIN : -(int)acc;
    else
        *out = (int)acc;
    if (end) *end = s;
    return ATOI_OK;
}

/* Reverse a singly linked list: each step turns one arrow around. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
static struct node *reverse_iter(struct node *head)
{
    struct node *prev = NULL;
    while (head) {
        struct node *next = head->next;
        head->next = prev;
        prev = head;
        head = next;
    }
    return prev;
}

/* Floyd's cycle detection, plus the start of the loop. */
static const struct node *loop_start(const struct node *head)
{
    const struct node *slow = head, *fast = head;
    while (fast && fast->next) {
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;
        if (slow == fast) {
            for (slow = head; slow != fast; slow = slow->next, fast = fast->next)
                ;
            return slow;
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

Why the loop start works: let the distance from the head to the loop start be a, and the meeting point be b steps into a loop of length L. Fast travelled twice as far as slow: 2(a + b) = a + b + kL, so a = kL - b. Walking a steps from the head and a steps from the meeting point therefore lands both pointers on the loop start.

The overflow check in my_atoi deserves one sentence in the interview: "I check before multiplying, because once acc * 10 + d has overflowed it is too late to detect it", which links straight back to module 09.

docs.title: 2.5 How C interview rounds run
docs.text:
The format varies by company type more than by country. Typical patterns:

  • Embedded and firmware (automotive, semiconductors, devices). A written or online test with "what does this print" snippets (operator precedence, integer promotion, sizeof, pointer arithmetic, static), bit manipulation (set, clear, toggle a bit; count bits; swap nibbles), volatile and interrupt service routines (keep them short, no malloc, no printf), memory-mapped registers, struct packing and alignment, endianness, fixed-point arithmetic, and RTOS questions (mutex versus semaphore, priority inversion). Coding without dynamic memory is common.
  • Systems (operating systems, networking, storage, databases, infrastructure). Pointers and memory layout, writing an allocator or a hash table in C, concurrency (a bounded queue, a race to spot), system calls (fork/exec, read/write loops, sockets, mmap), and a debugging discussion: "this server crashes once a day; here is the stack; what do you do?" Your RCA and crash-dump experience is the strongest card here (05_Memory_Debugging_RCA, 11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search/06_debugging_and_rca_round.md).
  • Product companies hiring for C, C++ backend roles. One or two data-structures rounds where you usually may choose C++ (use it: the STL saves time; 03_Data_Structures_Algorithms/16_interview_coding_playbook.md), a language round that mixes C and C++ (manual memory versus RAII, extern "C", undefined behaviour), and a design round (11_Interview_Prep_Job_Search/01_how_cpp_systems_interviews_work.md).

How to answer a C coding question, every time:

  1. Repeat the problem and ask about the contract: can the input be NULL? Can buffers overlap? What should happen on overflow: clamp, error, or is it the caller's problem?
  2. List the edge cases out loud (table in 2.4).
  3. Write the code, small and plain: no clever tricks you cannot explain.
  4. Walk through it by hand with one normal case and two edge cases.
  5. State complexity, and name any undefined behaviour you avoided ("I compare as unsigned char", "I check before multiplying").

docs.title: 3.1 m16_string_questions.c
docs.text:
my_strlen, my_strcmp, my_strcpy, my_strlcpy, my_memcpy, my_memmove, my_atoi, reverse_in_place, my_strtok_r and a non-destructive next_field, each tested against the C library or a table. The tests include both overlap directions for memmove, every atoi boundary ("2147483647", "2147483648", "-2147483648", "-2147483649", "-", "", " -17xyz"), and a CSV line where strtok loses the empty fields that next_field keeps:

const char *csv = "TXN,,ACC-1001,";
const char *cur = csv, *f;
size_t flen, nf = 0;
size_t lens[] = { 3, 0, 8, 0 };
while (next_field(&cur, ',', &f, &flen))
    assert(nf < 4 && flen == lens[nf++]);
assert(nf == 4);

It also runs clean under ASan and UBSan: gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -O1 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -o m16_strings_asan m16_string_questions.c.

docs.title: 3.2 m16_classic_questions.c
docs.text:
Lists (iterative and recursive reverse, Floyd, loop start, middle), bits (endianness, byte swap, three popcounts cross-checked on 100 000 values, power of two), a growable stack with a balanced-brackets checker, rotation checked against a naive version for every n up to 7 and every k up to 2n + 1, the XOR swap and its aliasing trap, and sizeof through a pointer to an array. Real output:

endianness: little; popcount(0x9E3779B9) = 20
all checks passed

The XOR swap is in the file to show why it is a bad answer: xor_swap(&a, &a) sets a to 0 unless you guard against equal pointers, and it is slower than a temporary on modern CPUs.

docs.title: 3.3 m16_modern_c_features.c
docs.text:
C99 and C11 features with checks: designated initialisers (struct and array), compound literals, a flexible array member, _Static_assert (including sizeof('a') == sizeof(int)), _Generic, bool conversion, PRId64, alignas, VLAs, integer division, static in all three contexts, const pointer forms, volatile sig_atomic_t set by a real signal handler, and _Noreturn. Real output:

__STDC_VERSION__ = 201710L, TYPE_NAME(cpi) = int *, __func__ = main
all checks passed

#define TYPE_NAME(x) _Generic((x),                                              \
    int: "int", unsigned: "unsigned", long: "long", double: "double",           \
    char *: "char *", const char *: "const char *", int *: "int *",              \
    const int *: "const int *", default: "other")

char c1 = 'a', c2 = 'b';
assert(strcmp(TYPE_NAME(c1 + c2), "int") == 0);     /* integer promotion, made visible */

docs.title: 4. Under the hood (senior-level)
docs.text:
What happens before and after main. The kernel starts the program at _start (from crt1.o), which calls glibc's __libc_start_main. That sets up the C library (TLS, stdio, atexit machinery), runs the functions in .init_array (constructors: GCC __attribute__((constructor)), and C++ static initialisers), then calls main(argc, argv, envp). When main returns, its value goes to exit, which runs atexit handlers and .fini_array destructors in reverse order, flushes and closes stdio streams, and calls _exit. A crash, abort or _exit skips all of that, which is why buffered output is lost (module 13).

How glibc's memcpy and strlen are really written. They are not the byte loops above. glibc selects an implementation at load time through an IFUNC resolver based on the CPU (SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512, rep movsb with ERMS). Small copies use overlapping unaligned loads and stores instead of loops. strlen reads a whole word or vector at a time and detects a zero byte with a bit trick: for 32-bit words, (x - 0x01010101) & ~x & 0x80808080 is non-zero exactly when some byte of x is zero. Reading a full aligned word may read past the terminator, which would be undefined in C but is safe in hand-written assembly because an aligned word never crosses a page boundary. Mentioning that in an interview, after writing the simple loop, is a good senior signal.

The 2010 memcpy story. In 2010 glibc changed its x86-64 memcpy so that, on some CPUs, it copied backwards. Programs that had (incorrectly) used memcpy on overlapping buffers started producing corrupt output; Adobe's Flash plugin on Fedora was the famous case. The programs had always had undefined behaviour; a faster library exposed it. It is the clearest real example of why "memcpy for non-overlapping, memmove for overlapping" is a rule, not a style preference.

popcount in hardware. With -mpopcnt or -march=native, __builtin_popcount becomes one POPCNT instruction; without it GCC emits a short bit-twiddling sequence or a library call. Many compilers also recognise the Kernighan loop and replace it with POPCNT. Interviewers like hearing both the loop and the builtin.

Reading C++ mangled names. c++filt _Z8kv_closeP2kv prints kv_close(kv*). When a mixed C and C++ build fails with undefined reference to 'kv_close(kv*)', the demangled signature in the error tells you at once that a C function was declared without extern "C".

docs.title: 5. In production
docs.text:
• strncpy in old code. It was designed for fixed-width fields in old Unix directory entries, not as a "safe strcpy". Production code that uses it to copy into a buffer and then prints the buffer has a missing-terminator bug waiting for a long enough input. When you see strncpy(dst, src, sizeof dst) without dst[sizeof dst - 1] = '\0', you have found a bug.
  • atoi on input. atoi("12abc") is 12 and atoi("abc") is 0, with no error. In a banking message parser that turns a corrupted amount into a valid one. Use strtol with the checks from module 10 or a parser like my_atoi that reports errors.
  • Mixed C and C++ builds. When a C++ service links a C library (Berkeley DB, libpq, OpenSSL), missing extern "C" produces link errors, and mismatched struct definitions between the C and C++ sides produce memory corruption. Include the library's own header; never re-declare its structs.
  • Interview answers become code review comments. Every edge case in the table in 2.4 is a real review comment you will write on a colleague's patch: "this compares char as signed", "this memcpy overlaps", "this atoi accepts garbage". Practising the questions is practising the job.

docs.title: 6. Try it
docs.text:
1. Easy - five from memory. On paper, with no references, write strlen, strcmp, memmove, reverse_iter and is_power_of_two. Type them in, add them to a copy of the test files, and run. Done when all tests pass on the first compile, or you know exactly which edge case you missed.
  2. Easy - what does this print? Predict, then run: printf("%zu %zu ", sizeof("abc"), strlen("abc"));, printf("%d ", -1 < 1u);, unsigned char c = 200; printf("%d ", c + c);, int a[5]; printf("%td ", &a[4] - &a[0]);. Done when every prediction matches and you can give the rule behind each.
  3. Medium - strtod-free parser. Write parse_amount("1234.56", &paise) that accepts an optional sign, digits, and an optional point with exactly two digits, and rejects everything else (including overflow of long long). Done when a table test of 20 inputs passes under UBSan.
  4. Medium - C23 tour. Rewrite m16_modern_c_features.c for -std=c2x: bool without the header, nullptr, constexpr, typeof, [[nodiscard]] on a function whose result you then ignore (read the warning), static_assert without a message. Done when it builds with GCC 13 -std=c2x -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic and you have listed which C23 features GCC 13 lacks.
  5. Hard - word-at-a-time strlen. Implement strlen that first walks byte by byte to an 8-byte boundary, then reads uint64_t words with memcpy and uses the zero-byte bit trick. Done when it matches strlen on every length from 0 to 100 at every starting alignment 0 to 7, and you can explain why the C version must not read past the buffer while glibc's assembly may.
  6. Hard - mock interview. Have someone pick five questions from section 2.3 and three coding questions from 2.4, 45 minutes in total, coding in a plain editor without compiling. Done when you have done it twice and written down every edge case you forgot to say out loud.

docs.title: 7. Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does static mean in C? A: Inside a function it gives a local variable static storage duration: initialised once and kept between calls. At file scope it gives a function or variable internal linkage, hiding it from other translation units. In an array parameter, int a[static 4] promises that the argument points to at least four elements.

Q: Why is volatile not suitable for sharing data between threads? A: It only stops the compiler from caching or removing accesses; it provides no atomicity for read-modify-write operations and no ordering relative to other memory, and a concurrent non-atomic access is still a data race, which is undefined. Use C11 atomics or a mutex. volatile is for memory-mapped I/O and volatile sig_atomic_t signal-handler flags.

Q: What is the difference between const int *p and int *const p? A: In const int *p the pointed-to int is read-only through p but p can be re-pointed. In int *const p the pointer itself is fixed but the int can be modified through it. const int *const p fixes both. Reading the declaration from the name outward, right to left, gives the meaning.

Q: What does sizeof return for an array parameter, and why? A: The size of a pointer, because a parameter declared as an array is adjusted to a pointer to its element type; the array's length is not passed. GCC warns with -Wsizeof-array-argument. Pass the length as a separate argument or pass a pointer to an array of known size.

Q: Write memmove. How is it different from memcpy? A: memmove must work when source and destination overlap, so it copies forwards when the destination is before the source and backwards when it is after, so it never reads a byte it has already overwritten. memcpy may assume no overlap (its parameters are restrict), which allows faster copying; using it on overlapping buffers is undefined behaviour.

Q: How do you detect overflow in atoi? A: Accumulate the magnitude in an unsigned type and, before each acc * 10 + digit, check acc > (limit - digit) / 10, where the limit is INT_MAX for positive numbers and INT_MAX + 1 for negative ones so that INT_MIN parses. Checking after the multiplication is too late, since signed overflow is undefined. Report where parsing stopped so trailing junk can be rejected.

Q: Why does C++ need extern "C" to call C functions? A: C++ mangles function names to encode parameter types, so int kv_close(struct kv *) becomes _Z8kv_closeP2kv, while the C library exports plain kv_close. extern "C" tells the C++ compiler to use C linkage and the unmangled name. C headers wrap their declarations in #ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { ... }.

Q: Name three differences between C and C++ that can change the meaning of the same code. A: sizeof('a') is sizeof(int) in C and 1 in C++; reading a different union member than the one last written is defined in C and undefined in C++; and void f() declares a function with unspecified parameters in C before C23 but no parameters in C++. Also, const int n = 10; is a constant expression in C++ but not in C, where int a[n] inside a function creates a VLA.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• C99 gave most of modern C (stdint, bool, inline, restrict, VLAs, designated initialisers, compound literals, flexible arrays); C11 added _Generic, _Static_assert, alignment, threads and atomics; C17 fixed defects; C23 adds nullptr, constexpr, typeof, attributes, ckd_add, #embed and makes bool a keyword.
  • GCC 13 supports most of C23 with -std=c2x, but not <stdckdint.h> (GCC 14) or #embed (GCC 15).
  • C versus C++: implicit void * conversion, struct tags, const and constant expressions, sizeof('a'), union punning, void f(), VLAs, designated initialisers, C99 inline.
  • C++ mangles names (_Z8kv_closeP2kv); C headers need extern "C" guards.
  • static: storage duration inside a function, internal linkage at file scope, minimum size in array parameters.
  • volatile is for hardware registers and signal flags, never for thread synchronisation.
  • An array parameter is a pointer; sizeof gives 8; pass the length.
  • Coding answers: state the contract and edge cases first, write plain code, trace two edge cases by hand, state complexity and the UB you avoided.
  • memmove copies backwards when the destination is after the source; atoi checks before multiplying and parses INT_MIN; Floyd finds loops and their start.
  • Embedded rounds stress bits, volatile and no-malloc code; systems rounds stress memory, concurrency, syscalls and debugging; product rounds mix DSA (use C++) with C and C++ language questions.

docs.title: 12_C_Programming — all exercises
docs.text:
Every exercise from section 6 ("Try it") of modules 01 to 16, in one place: 96 exercises, each with a difficulty, a short "done when" and a hint. The full statement (exact inputs, file names, flags) is in the module; it is shortened here so you can tick exercises off without opening the module.

How to use this file:

  • Do every easy exercise as you finish each module. Most take 10 to 30 minutes.
  • Do at least two medium exercises per module. Writing the code yourself is where the rules stop being things you have read and become things you can predict.
  • Pick the hard exercises that back a resume line or an interview story (see the minimum path at the end). Each one is something you can talk about for five minutes in an interview.
  • Read a hint only after ten minutes of being stuck. Hints point at the mechanism; they do not give the answer.
  • Work on a copy in the Linux file system (~/dev/c12, see README.md "Building the code"). Build every program twice: gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g, and again with -fsanitize=address,undefined. For Valgrind runs (3.3, 4.3, 10.3) build without sanitizers: ASan and Valgrind do not work together.
  • Windows exercises (1.6, 10.6, 13.6, 14.6, and the MSVC branches of 7.3 and 8.5) need Visual Studio's "Developer Command Prompt". Build with cl /std:c17 /W4 /WX.

TSan note for WSL Ubuntu 24.04 (exercises 6.5, 11.6, 12.6 and module 14): if a TSan binary dies immediately with FATAL: ThreadSanitizer: unexpected memory mapping, the kernel's ASLR entropy is higher than TSan expects. Run it as setarch $(uname -m) -R ./prog, or once per boot sudo sysctl vm.mmap_rnd_bits=28. This is an environment issue, not a bug in your code.

Legend: E = easy, M = medium, H = hard.

docs.title: Module 01 — How C really works (01_how_c_really_works.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 1.1 E Split-build m01_two_units.c (-DUNIT_A, -DUNIT_B) and run nm on both objects. You can name, for every nm line, the source line that produced it and why its letter is upper or lower case. The letter gives the section (text, data, bss, undefined) and the case gives the linkage. Check which names carry static, and notice that a zero initialiser and a non-zero one land in different sections. 1.2 E Make s_next non-static in unit A, add int s_next = 5; to unit B, rebuild split. You have the multiple definition error, can explain it, and have fixed it two ways. Both objects now export the same initialised symbol. Only the linker sees both objects, and either side can withdraw from external linkage. 1.3 M In unit B only, declare extern long g_requests; (inside #ifdef UNIT_B) and build split. It links with no error, and you can explain why the linker cannot notice and what main now reads. Keep the shared extern int declaration out of unit B, or the compiler sees both and refuses. Then ask what an object file records about a symbol besides its name, and how many bytes a long load reads. 1.4 M gcc -std=c17 -save-temps -c m01_eval_order.c; find your code in the .i and the call order of note('x'), note('y'), note('z') in the .s. You can point at the instructions that prove the right-to-left order. Your code is at the very bottom of the .i, after the expanded headers. In the .s, the characters appear as $120, $121, $122 (ASCII x, y, z) loaded into %edi before each call note. 1.5 H Call char *make(void) (returns malloc(16)) from another file with no prototype; build with gcc -std=c89 -w; then add the prototype. You have seen the crash or truncated pointer, can explain eax versus rax, and the prototype fixes it. Without a prototype C89 assumes the function returns int. Compare the instruction right after call make in the two -S listings: one of them keeps only 32 bits. 1.6 H Build m01_compiler_and_standard.c with cl /std:c17 and with plain cl. Both outputs side by side, and every difference from the GCC output explained. Without /std, MSVC compiles its older default C dialect. Compare which standard macros (__STDC__, __STDC_VERSION__) each build defines, then sizeof(long).

docs.title: Module 02 — Types, integers and conversions (02_types_integers_and_conversions.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 2.1 E Predict the full output of m02_data_model.c on 64-bit Windows without running it. You have the size table and the data-model line, and can name the one line that differs from Linux. Look up what the letters in "LP64" and "LLP64" stand for: the name lists exactly which types are 64 bits. 2.2 E Predict all nine lines of m02_promotions_and_conversions.c, then run it. Every wrong prediction is explained with the rule from section 2.3 or 2.4. Two steps, in order, for each expression: promote anything narrower than int, then apply the usual arithmetic conversions. When a signed and an unsigned type of the same rank meet, ask which one changes. 2.3 M bool mul_i64_checked(int64_t a, int64_t b, int64_t *out) without builtins, covering all sign combinations and INT64_MIN * -1. 100,000 random pairs plus the edge values (0, 1, -1, INT64_MAX, INT64_MIN) agree with __builtin_mul_overflow. Split by the signs of a and b, and compare against a limit divided by b before multiplying. Handle b == 0 and b == -1 first: dividing by them is undefined or overflows itself. 2.4 M Three correct "visit n-1 down to 0" loops with a size_t index, and one deliberately broken one. The broken one triggers -Wtype-limits; the three correct ones touch nothing when n == 0. An unsigned value is always >= 0. Test before you decrement, or count something that can legitimately reach zero. -Wtype-limits is part of -Wextra. 2.5 M Monthly compound interest on 1,00,000.00 rupees at 9 % a year for 12 months, rounded to the paisa monthly: once with double, once with int64_t paise and half-even rounding. Both results printed side by side, any difference explained, and month 1 of the integer version matches a hand calculation. 9 % a year is exactly 75 basis points a month. Multiply first, then divide by 10,000 and round the remainder yourself. Month 1 divides exactly; month 2 is the first month where the rounding rule matters. 2.6 H load_be64, store_be64 and a parser for a 16-byte big-endian header (u32 magic, u16 version, u16 opcode, u64 length). The -O2 -S output shows bswap (or movbe), and 1000 random headers round-trip. Cast each byte to the wide type before shifting: shifting a promoted int by 32 or more is undefined. Search the assembly for bswap.

docs.title: Module 03 — Pointers from the ground up (03_pointers_from_the_ground_up.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 3.1 E Draw memory for int x = 5; int *p = &x; int **pp = &p; with invented addresses, then check in gdb. Your drawing matches p &x, p p, p &p, p *pp, p **pp and x/4xb &x (apart from the real address values). Every variable is a box with an address and contents; a pointer's contents is another box's address. x/4xb shows the int's bytes lowest address first. 3.2 E Predict sizeof of int a[5], &a, *&a, a + 0, "abc", (char *)"abc", a[0] and struct { char c; double d; }. All eight right, or every miss explained. For each operand ask: is it still an array (arrays do not decay under sizeof) or already a pointer? A string literal is an array that includes its NUL. 3.3 M remove_all twice: with a prev pointer and an explicit head case, and with the pointer-to-pointer technique. Both pass the head, middle, tail, all-nodes and empty-list tests, and Valgrind reports no leaks. In the second version, walk the links (the head pointer and every next field) rather than the nodes; then the head stops being a special case. 3.4 M int **matrix_new(int rows, int cols) with one malloc: row pointers followed by the data. m[r][c] works, one free(m) releases everything, and the data part is correctly aligned. Total size = row-pointer array + data, with the pointer-array size rounded up to the data's alignment. Check rows * cols for overflow before computing it. 3.5 M The extern trap: a.c defines int table[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};, b.c declares extern int *table; and prints table[0]. You have the crash, the faulting address from gdb, and can explain why it is 0x200000001. b.c believes the symbol's storage holds a pointer, so it loads 8 bytes from there and dereferences them. Write out the first 8 bytes of the array in little-endian order. 3.6 H Generic isort(void *base, size_t n, size_t size, cmp) with the qsort contract, using only unsigned char * arithmetic and memcpy. It sorts ints, doubles and a 40-byte struct, and matches qsort on 1000 random arrays. Element i starts at (unsigned char *)base + i * size. You need one element-sized temporary; shift the sorted part with memmove, never through a typed pointer.

docs.title: Module 04 — Memory, storage, scope and lifetime (04_memory_storage_scope_and_lifetime.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 4.1 E Annotate every object in m04_storage_durations.c with its storage duration, scope and linkage. No blank cells, and you can say when each object is created and destroyed. Three independent questions per object: where can the name be used, how long does the object live, and can another file name it? A static local answers them in an unusual combination. 4.2 E Build m04_returning_buffers.c with -DSHOW_BUG, then rewrite format_id_bug into each of the four correct forms. Each version passes the existing asserts, and you can name one disadvantage of each. The four forms differ in who provides the storage. For each, ask: who frees it, is it safe from two threads, and is it safe to call twice inside one printf? 4.3 M void *test_realloc(void *p, size_t n) that fails on the Nth call (N from an environment variable), used in buf_reserve. Two Valgrind reports: the WRONG idiom leaks and leaves data == NULL, the RIGHT one does not. Read N once with getenv and strtol, count calls in a static counter, and return NULL without calling realloc when the count reaches N. 4.4 M arena_mark, arena_release_to and an overflow-checked arena_calloc(a, count, size, align). A test allocates in a nested scope, releases to the mark, and gets the same addresses again. A mark is just the current offset. The overflow check must happen before count * size is computed: compare count against SIZE_MAX / size. 4.5 M Ownership header comments for cust_parse, cust_name, cust_free and cust_set_name (which takes ownership of name). Every pointer parameter and return value uses a phrase from the table in section 2.7, including what happens to name if cust_set_name fails. For each pointer ask: who frees it, until when is it valid, and does ownership move? The failure case of a "takes ownership" function is the one people forget to write down. 4.6 H Recursive function with a 4 KiB local array: find the crash depth on the main thread (8 MiB stack) and in a thread with a 256 KiB pthread_attr_setstacksize. Both measured depths are within 10 % of your calculation, and you can explain the difference. Build at -O0, make sure the array is really used, and print the depth to stderr (unbuffered) as you go. Each frame costs more than 4096 bytes, and a thread stack ends in a guard page.

docs.title: Module 05 — Strings and buffers (05_strings_and_buffers.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 5.1 E For char d[6], predict the 6 bytes after strncpy(d, s, sizeof d) for "", "abc", "abcde", "abcdef", "abcdefgh". All five predictions match a program that dumps the bytes, and you can say which results are terminated. Read the contract word by word: strncpy always writes exactly n bytes, and copies at most n bytes from the source. 5.2 E Rewrite sprintf(buf, "%s-%06d-%s", branch, seq, suffix) as a function on snprintf that reports truncation. A 10-byte buffer reports truncation, a 64-byte buffer succeeds, and buf is never left unterminated. snprintf returns the length it wanted to write. Check for a negative return as well as for "too long", and convert carefully before comparing with a size_t. 5.3 M int parse_amount_paise(const char *s, int64_t *out) for "1234.50", "-0.75", "12", with no floating point. A table of at least 15 cases passes, including ".", "1.", "-" and "9223372036854775807". Parse sign, integer part and fraction separately into an unsigned accumulator. Decide up front what "1." and "1.5" mean, and check for overflow before every multiply-and-add. 5.4 M Non-destructive CSV splitter with quoted fields and doubled quotes. a,"b,c","d""e" gives a, b,c, d"e; 10 cases pass; the input is never written. Model it as a small state machine (outside quotes, inside quotes, quote seen inside quotes). Return each field as pointer plus length, and unescape into a separate buffer. 5.5 M int utf8_next(const char **s, uint32_t *cp) that decodes one code point, advances, and rejects every invalid case in section 2.9. It agrees with utf8_valid on 100,000 random byte strings. Check in a fixed order: lead-byte class, enough bytes left, each continuation byte is 10xxxxxx, then the decoded value (overlong form, surrogate range, above U+10FFFF). 5.6 H A char buf[16] overflowed by strcpy from argv[1], run with -O2 (FORTIFY), with -O0 -fstack-protector-strong, and with -fsanitize=address. You have all three reports and can explain why FORTIFY stops a strcpy into a stack array but not into a heap buffer of unknown size. Ubuntu's GCC turns _FORTIFY_SOURCE on whenever you optimise. FORTIFY swaps strcpy for a checking version only when the compiler can work out the destination's size at that call.

docs.title: Module 06 — Structs, unions, enums and layout (06_structs_unions_enums_and_layout.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 6.1 E Predict sizeof and every offsetof for {char a; double b; char c;}, {char a; char c; double b;}, {int a; char b[3];} and {short s; struct {char c; int i;} in;}. A program using offsetof confirms all of them, or you can explain each miss. Each member goes at the next multiple of its own alignment; the total rounds up to the largest alignment inside; a nested struct brings its own alignment and size. 6.2 E Reorder a nine-field struct of mixed sizes for minimum size and lock it with _Static_assert(sizeof(...) == N, ...). The assert compiles, and fails if you swap two fields back. Sort by alignment, largest first, then see whether the tail padding can be filled by moving the smallest members. 6.3 M container_of plus an intrusive doubly linked list (struct dlink); one struct account in two lists at once (by branch, by status). Removing it from one list leaves it in the other, with no allocation per list node. Give the account one struct dlink member per list. A circular list with a sentinel head removes every NULL special case. 6.4 M Decoder for the 35-byte loan_rec_v2 record from 07_Databases_Internals/12_migrating_a_kv_store_to_relational.md, by byte offsets only (no packed struct). Three hand-built golden records decode correctly; a wrong version and a short record are rejected. Write tiny helpers (get_le32(p, off), get_be16(p, off), a BCD digit pair) and validate length and version before reading any field. Trim the padding only after copying. 6.5 M Bit-field race: two threads toggle unsigned a : 1 and unsigned b : 1 one million times each; then fix with separate unsigned char fields. You have seen a final state inconsistent with the counts (or a TSan report), and can explain why the fix works. Look at the assembly for one bit-field toggle: how many bytes are loaded and stored? Then look up "memory location" in the C11 standard (section 3.14). 6.6 H Version 2 of the format in m06_serialize_record.c with a 3-letter currency code; v1 still decodes (currency "INR"); fuzz txn_decode for a minute under ASan and UBSan. Both versions round-trip in tests and the fuzzer finds nothing. Check the version before any field and derive the expected length from it. A loop feeding random bytes of random length until a time limit is a sufficient fuzzer; save any input that crashes.

docs.title: Module 07 — Functions, function pointers and callbacks (07_functions_function_pointers_and_callbacks.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 7.1 E Say in English, then rewrite with typedefs: int (*f[4])(double), char *(*g)(const char *), void (*signal(int, void (*)(int)))(int), int (*(*h)(int))(int). A test program declares each one, assigns a real function to it and calls it. Start at the name and work outward: postfix [] and () bind tighter than prefix *, and parentheses override that. Typedef the innermost function type first. 7.2 E Add OP_TRANSFER with a handler to m07_function_pointers.c, with tests for opcode 0, OP_MAX - 1 and OP_MAX. Every unknown opcode gives status 1 and the program never calls through NULL. Range-check the opcode as an unsigned value before indexing, then check the slot for NULL. A designated initialiser [OP_TRANSFER] = h_transfer keeps the table aligned with the enum. 7.3 M sort_ctx(base, n, size, cmp(a, b, ctx), ctx) on qsort_r (glibc), qsort_s (MSVC, via a trampoline), and your own merge sort elsewhere. A sort by a field chosen at run time through ctx passes on WSL, and the MSVC branch compiles in your head line by line. glibc's comparator is (a, b, ctx), MSVC's qsort_s comparator is (ctx, a, b), and BSD's qsort_r differs again. glibc needs _GNU_SOURCE defined before the first #include. 7.4 M Re-implement the netstring parser with struct state { struct state (*fn)(struct parser *, unsigned char); }. The same chunked and bad-input tests pass, and three sentences compare the two designs. C cannot directly spell "a function that returns a pointer to a function of its own type"; wrapping the pointer in a struct breaks that recursion. Each state function returns the next state. 7.5 M log_msg(int level, const char *fmt, ...) with the format attribute; trigger and fix the %d-for-int64_t error and the -Wformat-security warning. The wrapper compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra -Wformat=2 -Werror. In format(printf, M, N), M is the position of the format and N of the first variadic argument. Forward with a va_list and vfprintf; never pass data as the format. 7.6 H Event dispatcher: subscribe(type, cb, ctx) returns a handle, unsubscribe(handle), publish(type, data); callbacks may unsubscribe themselves or others during publish. A test that unsubscribes during dispatch runs clean under ASan, and you can explain your deferred-removal design. Never free or shift the subscriber array while iterating it. Mark entries dead and clean up when the outermost publish returns: publishes can nest.

docs.title: Module 08 — The preprocessor and macros (08_the_preprocessor_and_macros.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 8.1 E gcc -std=c17 -E -P m08_macro_traps.c; find the expansion of every macro use in main. You can point at the exact text that makes MAX_BAD(i++, 3) increment twice and BUMP_BOTH_BAD escape the if. Search the output for i++ and count the occurrences. For the if, add the braces the compiler actually sees and check which statement it controls. 8.2 E A SWAP macro with an internal tmp, broken by SWAP(tmp, x); fix it with __typeof__ and a safer name, and with a static inline function per type. You can argue which fix you would ship and why. After textual substitution the caller's tmp and the macro's tmp are the same name. Weigh type checking, debuggability and portability to MSVC. 8.3 M One X-macro opcode table (X(OP_BALANCE, 1, h_balance, "balance")) generating the enum, the log names and a const dispatch table. Adding an opcode is one line, and a _Static_assert fails if the table and OP_COUNT disagree. Define the list once as #define OPCODES(X) ... and expand it three times with different X definitions. sizeof table / sizeof table[0] gives the count to assert on. 8.4 M Logging macro with a monotonic timestamp and the thread id, built into one buffer and emitted with a single fwrite. With -DLOG_COMPILED_MIN=1, strings finds no debug format strings in the binary. clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) and gettid() (glibc 2.30 and later, needs _GNU_SOURCE). Compare the level against a compile-time constant inside the macro so the compiler can drop the call and its format string. 8.5 M plat_mutex (CRITICAL_SECTION or pthread_mutex_t) and plat_thread_create in m08_platform_conditionals.c. The POSIX branch compiles with -Werror and passes a two-thread counter test; every Windows call is checked against its documentation. The two thread entry points have different signatures (void *(*)(void *) and DWORD WINAPI (*)(LPVOID)). Hide that behind a small heap struct holding your callback and context, passed to a per-platform trampoline. 8.6 H PRINT(x) with _Generic over int, unsigned, long, unsigned long, long long, unsigned long long, double, char *, const char *; then try adding int64_t. It compiles on LP64, you can explain why it would also compile on LLP64, and a test prints one value of each type. Look up what int64_t is a typedef for in glibc's <stdint.h> and in MSVC's. _Generic rejects two associations with compatible types.

docs.title: Module 09 — Undefined behaviour and the optimiser (09_undefined_behaviour_and_the_optimizer.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 9.1 E Classify sizeof(long); f(g(), h()) call order; -1 >> 1; INT_MAX + 1; (int)3000000000u; char *s = "hi"; s[0] = 'H';. All six classified as implementation-defined, unspecified or undefined, with one line of reasoning each. Does the standard require the compiler to document the choice, allow a choice without documentation, or impose no requirement? Converting an out-of-range value is not the same as overflowing during arithmetic. 9.2 E Build m09_overflow_check.c at -O0, -O2, -O2 -fwrapv and with UBSan; fill in the table from section 3.1 yourself. Your numbers match, and you can explain the -O0 result. Look for an add instruction in naive_add_overflows in the -O0 assembly. If it is missing, ask which part of the compiler removed it. 9.3 M Assembly for m09_null_check_deleted.c at -O2, with and without -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks. You can point at the null-check instruction in one listing and say why it is missing from the other. Look for a test of the pointer register followed by a conditional jump. Then ask what the compiler had already learnt about that pointer before the check. 9.4 M uint32_t read_be32(const unsigned char *p) three ways (pointer cast plus ntohl, memcpy plus ntohl, shifts), each called on buf + 1, built with -O2 -fsanitize=undefined. You can say which version UBSan reports and why, and which one is portable without ntohl. buf + 1 is not 4-byte aligned. Which versions perform a 4-byte load through a uint32_t *, and which only ever load bytes? 9.5 H for (int i = 1; i > 0; i += i) counting iterations, built at -O0 and -O2, each run under timeout 2. You have both outputs (or the timeout) and a three-sentence explanation based on section 2.3. Ask what the compiler may conclude about i > 0 when i starts positive and only positive values are ever added, given that overflow "cannot happen". 9.6 H Build a legacy file (from work, or m15_legacy_report.c) with -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wstrict-aliasing=2 -fsanitize=undefined and run its tests. Every warning and report listed with a one-line verdict: real UB, false positive, or implementation-defined. Change nothing yet. Run with UBSAN_OPTIONS=print_stacktrace=1 and record the exact line and the operand values each report prints.

docs.title: Module 10 — Error handling and resource cleanup (10_error_handling_and_resource_cleanup.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 10.1 E Find and fix the three errors in the module's malloc + fopen + fread snippet. Your version has no leak on any path and reports which call failed. At every return, list what is still allocated or open. Also ask what happens when malloc itself fails, and what a short fread can mean. 10.2 E int read_int_file(const char *path, long *out): returns 0 or a positive errno, uses strtol correctly, leaves *out untouched on failure. A missing file, an empty file, "12abc" and "99999999999999999999" each return the right code. Save errno before any other call, including fclose and logging. Pick a code for "no digits" and "trailing junk" (EINVAL is the usual choice) and write *out as the very last step. 10.3 M Rewrite a four-level nested function (two files, two buffers) into the goto-cleanup shape, with the fault-injection wrappers from m10_goto_cleanup.c. The injection loop reports N failure points and zero leaks. Initialise every resource variable to NULL at the top so one cleanup block can release whatever exists, in reverse order. Run once with no injection to learn N. 10.4 M Add kv_del, a KV_READONLY code and kv_set_readonly(kv, 1) to m10_error_model.c. kv_put on a read-only store returns KV_READONLY, the callback prints a contextual message, and kv_strerror knows the new code. Put the new code in the library's reserved negative range and add it to kv_strerror in the same change. Decide whether deleting a missing key is an error or a quiet "not found". 10.5 H failmalloc.c: an LD_PRELOAD malloc that fails the Nth call (real one via dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "malloc")); run an unmodified program for N = 1..20. You can name every N at which the program crashes instead of reporting an error. Build with -shared -fPIC (plus -ldl on glibc older than 2.34). dlsym can itself allocate on first use, so guard against recursion with a flag and a small static buffer. 10.6 H Port copy_file from m10_goto_cleanup.c to Win32 (CreateFileW, ReadFile, WriteFile, CloseHandle), returning a DWORD from GetLastError(). It compiles with MSVC /W4 /WX and every handle is closed on every path. CreateFileW fails with INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, not NULL, so initialise handles to that. Save GetLastError() immediately, before CloseHandle can overwrite it.

docs.title: Module 11 — Data structures in C (11_data_structures_in_c.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 11.1 E vec_shrink_to_fit, and vec_pop halving the capacity when the length drops below a quarter of it. Push 1000 then pop 990 ends with capacity at most 64, and alternating push and pop then causes no reallocation ping-pong. Count reallocations in the test. The gap between the grow threshold (full) and the shrink threshold (a quarter) is what prevents thrashing; keep a minimum capacity. 11.2 E slist_reverse and slist_middle for the singly linked list in m11_lists.c. Both pass on lists of length 0, 1, 2 and 5. Reversal turns one arrow around per step and must remember where it was going next. For the middle, use two pointers moving at different speeds, and decide which node is "the middle" of an even-length list. 11.3 M O(1) LRU cache from m11_hash_table.c (account id to struct session *) plus the intrusive LRU list from m11_lists.c. Every operation is O(1), and a capacity-3 test evicts in the right order. The hash value points to the object that embeds the list link, so a hit can unlink and re-insert at the head without searching. Eviction must remove the tail from both structures. 11.4 M DEFINE_HEAP(T, name, less) generating a typed heap; benchmark it against the generic heap on 1,000,000 ints. You have both timings and can explain the difference with section 4. Paste names with ## to generate static inline functions per type. Time at -O2 with clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC), and think about indirect calls and byte-wise swaps. 11.5 H Replace tombstones in m11_hash_table.c with backward-shift deletion. The churn test passes with zero tombstones and no same-size rebuilds. Walk forward from the hole until an empty slot. Move an entry back into the hole only if that does not put it before its home slot, and remember that the table wraps around. 11.6 H Make the ring buffer safe for one producer and one consumer thread with _Atomic unsigned head and tail and release/acquire ordering. A 10,000,000-item test passes and TSan is clean. Each index has exactly one writer. For each, decide which slot access its release store must publish, and where the other side's acquire load must go.

docs.title: Module 12 — Memory allocators: arena, pool and malloc (12_memory_allocators_arena_pool_and_malloc.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 12.1 E By hand: align_up(x, a) for (1, 8), (8, 8), (9, 16), (100, 64), (0, 32); explain why align_up(5, 12) is meaningless. Your answers match a five-line C program. Use the formula from section 2.2 and write a - 1 in binary. What does it look like when a is a power of two, and when a is 12? 12.2 E arena_realloc(a, p, old, new): grow in place when p is the most recent allocation and there is room, otherwise allocate and copy. A test shows the same pointer in the in-place case and correct copying in the other. p is the most recent allocation exactly when p + old equals the arena's current bump position. Do not forget the shrink case. 12.3 M Switch tm_malloc in m12_teaching_malloc.c to best fit and rerun the stress and fragmentation tests. You report the out-of-memory count and the largest free block for both policies and explain the difference. Best fit scans the whole free list and keeps the smallest block that fits (stop early on an exact fit). Use the same random seed for both runs. 12.4 M tm_realloc: grow in place by absorbing a free next block (splitting off the excess), shrink in place by splitting, otherwise malloc-copy-free. tm_check passes after every call in a random test. The next block's header says whether it is free and how big it is. After merging, split off any excess of at least the minimum block size, and update both header and footer. 12.5 H ASan-aware m12_arena.c: poison each chunk's unused tail and everything released by arena_rewind and arena_reset. ASan reports use-after-poison on a read after reset, and the normal tests still pass. <sanitizer/asan_interface.h> turns the poisoning macros into no-ops when ASan is off, so the normal build is unaffected. Unpoison exactly the bytes you hand out; poisoning works at 8-byte granularity. 12.6 H Per-thread pools through a _Thread_local pointer, falling back to a shared, mutex-protected pool when the local one is empty. A 4-thread test runs clean under TSan and you have measured it against plain malloc. The fast path must touch only thread-local state and take no lock. Decide what happens when thread A frees a block that came from thread B's pool.

docs.title: Module 13 — Files, I/O and POSIX system calls (13_files_io_and_posix_system_calls.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 13.1 E Predict printf("a "); write(1, "b ", 2); printf("c "); on a terminal and piped to cat, then run both. You can explain why the two orders differ, using section 2.2. For each destination ask when stdio hands its buffer to the kernel; write bypasses that buffer entirely. 13.2 E strace -e trace=openat,read,write,close ./m13_binary_format_mmap. You can point at the write of 93 bytes and explain why no read of the file follows. Add mmap to the trace list and look at what follows the openat that reads the file back. 13.3 M Parent writes 1 MiB through a pipe with O_NONBLOCK to a slow child; count partial writes and EAGAIN; then add poll. 1 MiB arrives intact and you report both counts. A Linux pipe holds 64 KiB by default. Wait for POLLOUT instead of spinning, and verify the data on the reader side with a pattern or checksum. 13.4 M Add a u32 branch_code to each record, bump the format to version 2, make the reader accept both. A v1 file and a v2 file both decode; a v3 file is rejected. The record size now depends on the version, so read and check the version before computing any offset. Keep a v1 file as a test fixture. 13.5 H Crash-test durable_replace: alternate contents A and B while another script kill -9s it at random; then remove the fsync calls. 1000 kills always leave exactly A or exactly B, and you can explain why the no-fsync version may still pass on WSL. Make A and B large enough to need several write calls, and compare the whole content, not just the size. Ask what survives a process kill versus a power cut. 13.6 H Port m13_tcp_echo.c to Winsock2 (WSAStartup, SOCKET, closesocket, WSAGetLastError) and build with MSVC /W4 /WX. The Windows client talks to the Linux server running in WSL. Link ws2_32.lib, compare against INVALID_SOCKET and SOCKET_ERROR instead of -1, and read errors with WSAGetLastError. WSL2 forwards localhost ports to Windows by default.

docs.title: Module 14 — Multithreading in C: pthreads and C11 (14_multithreading_in_c_pthreads_and_c11.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 14.1 E Pass &i from a for loop to four threads that print it; run it, run it under TSan, fix it with an array of ints. You can explain the original output and TSan's report. Count how many i objects exist, and who writes it while the threads read it. TSan's two stacks name the writer and the reader. 14.2 E Lock a default mutex twice from one thread with a 1-second pthread_mutex_timedlock; then an ERRORCHECK mutex with plain lock. ETIMEDOUT in the first case and EDEADLK in the second, printed with strerror. pthread functions return the error number instead of setting errno. The timeout is an absolute CLOCK_REALTIME time, and the mutex type is set with pthread_mutexattr_settype. 14.3 M Change one while to if in m14_bounded_queue.c; run the test 200 times, then under TSan. You catch a failure, or can explain why it is still wrong even though you did not. The bug needs two waiters woken for one item, or a spurious wakeup, so a light test may never show it. Write the interleaving down instead of relying on luck. 14.4 M Two priority levels in m14_thread_pool.c (two queues; workers always drain the high one first). Under a slow low-priority flood, high-priority tasks still finish quickly, and TSan is clean. Keep one mutex and one condition ("either queue non-empty, or stopping"), and check the high queue first under that lock. Measure latency from submit to start. 14.5 H Benchmark the rate table from m14_pthreads_basics.c with a rwlock and with a mutex: 1, 2, 4, 8 readers; 10 ns and 1 microsecond critical sections. A table of results, and an explanation of where the rwlock starts to win. Taking a read lock still writes a shared counter, so tiny critical sections can favour the mutex. Calibrate the busy loop against clock_gettime rather than guessing an iteration count. 14.6 H Port m14_bounded_queue.c to Win32 SRWLOCK and CONDITION_VARIABLE. It passes the same test on Windows; you have compared it with 04_Concurrency/code/m13_win32_srwlock_condvar.c. SleepConditionVariableSRW takes a timeout (INFINITE) and a flags argument (0 for exclusive mode), and still needs the while loop. SRWLOCK and CONDITION_VARIABLE need no destroy call.

docs.title: Module 15 — Reading, debugging and changing legacy C (15_reading_debugging_and_changing_legacy_c.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 15.1 E Map a real C project (SQLite's amalgamation, or Redis): find main, the event loop, and the function that handles one command. The call chain from socket read to reply, in ten lines or fewer, with file names. Start from main and find where the event loop starts; then grep the command table for the command's name. In Redis, processCommand is a good waypoint. 15.2 E git log -L on one function and git log -S on one string, in any repository you use. You can name the commit that introduced the current behaviour and the reason given in its message. git log -L :function_name:file.c follows one function through history; -S finds the commits that changed how many times a string appears. 15.3 M Characterise an untested function: a --print mode for 20 inputs including edge cases, turned into a test table. The test passes, and outputs you think are bugs are marked rather than changed. Record what the code does today, including outputs that look wrong. Mark those with a comment and a ticket instead of "fixing" the expected value. 15.4 M Run cppcheck, clang-tidy and gcc -fanalyzer on m15_legacy_report.c and on one real legacy file. A table of every finding with a verdict: real bug, risky but intended, or false positive. Give clang-tidy the same flags as the build (a compile_commands.json, or -- followed by the flags). Record tool, location, check name and verdict for each row. 15.5 H Test a function that calls send in a loop without a network: link with -Wl,--wrap=send and a scripted __wrap_send. The test proves the function handles partial sends and EINTR. With --wrap=send, calls to send from your objects go to __wrap_send, and __real_send reaches the real one. Drive the wrapper from a static array of planned return values and errnos. 15.6 H Three STAR stories from real work: a crash or memory bug, a concurrency bug, a change that needed backward compatibility. Each fits in two minutes spoken, uses only numbers you can defend, and a listener can repeat the root cause after hearing it once. Keep Situation and Task to two sentences. Spend most of the time on how you found the root cause, and end with the result and what now prevents a recurrence.

docs.title: Module 16 — Modern C and the C interview playbook (16_modern_c_and_the_c_interview_playbook.md)
docs.text: # Diff Exercise Done when Hint 16.1 E On paper, no references: strlen, strcmp, memmove, reverse_iter, is_power_of_two; then type them in and run the tests. All tests pass on the first compile, or you know exactly which edge case you missed. Say the edge cases before writing: the empty string, bytes above 127, both overlap directions, the empty list, zero. 16.2 E Predict: sizeof("abc") and strlen("abc"); -1 < 1u; c + c for unsigned char c = 200; &a[4] - &a[0] for int a[5]. Every prediction matches and you can give the rule behind each. One rule each: what sizeof sees for a string literal, the usual arithmetic conversions, integer promotion, and the unit of pointer subtraction. 16.3 M parse_amount("1234.56", &paise) without strtod: optional sign, digits, optional point with exactly two digits; reject everything else, including long long overflow. A 20-input table test passes under UBSan. Accumulate the magnitude in unsigned long long and check before each acc * 10 + d. The negative limit's magnitude is one larger than the positive limit. 16.4 M Rewrite m16_modern_c_features.c for -std=c2x: bool, nullptr, constexpr, typeof, [[nodiscard]], static_assert without a message. It builds with GCC 13 -std=c2x -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic, and you have listed which C23 features GCC 13 lacks. Ignore a [[nodiscard]] result on purpose and read the warning. For missing features, try #include <stdckdint.h> and #embed, and read the GCC 13 release notes. 16.5 H Word-at-a-time strlen: byte by byte to an 8-byte boundary, then uint64_t words read with memcpy and the zero-byte bit trick. It matches strlen for every length 0 to 100 at every start alignment 0 to 7, and you can explain why the C version must not over-read while glibc's assembly may. Look up the "has zero byte" trick (subtract 1 from every byte, then test the high bits). Then ask whether an aligned 8-byte load can ever cross a page boundary. 16.6 H Mock interview: five questions from section 2.3 and three coding questions from 2.4, 45 minutes, plain editor, no compiling. Done twice, with every edge case you forgot to say out loud written down. State the contract and the edge cases before coding, and walk one normal and two edge inputs through by hand at the end.

docs.title: Suggested minimum path if you are short of time
docs.text:
C interview rounds (module 16, section 2.5) are built from three things: "what does this print" questions, small functions written without a compiler, and a discussion of a real bug. Spend your time in that order.

  1. Prediction drills (about two hours in total). 2.2, 3.2, 5.1, 6.1, 9.1, 13.1, 16.2. These are exactly the snippet questions of written tests and language rounds: promotions, sizeof, strncpy, padding, UB classes, buffering.
  2. Functions you must be able to write on paper (about four hours). 16.1, 5.2, 10.2, 2.3, 3.3, 11.2, 6.3. Between them: strlen/strcmp/memmove, a truncation-safe copy, strtol with errno checked properly, overflow-checked arithmetic, pointer-to-pointer list edits, list reversal and container_of.
  3. Robust C you will be asked to reason about (about four hours). 4.3 (the realloc leak, proven with Valgrind), 10.3 (goto cleanup with fault injection), 9.3 (the deleted null check), 8.3 (X-macro dispatch table), 14.1 and 14.3 (the two classic pthread bugs), 13.3 (partial writes).
  4. One hard exercise per resume line. 6.4 for the migration engine (decoding packed records), 12.5 for "arena allocator with explicit ownership contracts", 15.6 for "memory corruption & leak investigation" and the behavioural round, and 16.6 (twice) in the last week before interviews.

If you have a single evening before a C round: 16.2, 16.1, 2.2, 3.2, 5.2 and 10.2, then rehearse the stories from 15.6 aloud.

docs.title: 12_C_Programming — interview questions and model answers
docs.text:
40 questions, ordered from basic to senior. Each answer is what you would say out loud in 30 to 60 seconds. The module that covers the topic in depth is given in brackets. Five questions (6, 9, 14, 24 and 33) are "what does this print / what is wrong with this code" snippets of the kind used in written tests and language rounds; their outputs were checked with GCC 13.3 and glibc 2.39 on Ubuntu 24.04.

Answers describe GCC 13 and glibc on x86-64 Linux. Where MSVC or Windows behaves differently in a way that breaks ported code, the answer says so: for a Linux role, knowing both is a strength, and it is the honest way to connect your Win32 server work to the question.

Practise by covering the answer, saying yours aloud, then comparing. If yours is longer than the model answer, cut it. The coding questions (strlen, memmove, atoi, list reversal, loop detection) are in module 16, section 2.4, and in exercise 16.1.

docs.title: Part A — Building and linking
docs.text:
1. What happens between gcc main.c util.c and a running program, and which tool reports "undefined reference" and "multiple definition"? [01] The preprocessor expands #includes and macros in each .c file, giving one translation unit per file; the compiler turns each unit into assembly and the assembler into an object file holding machine code, a symbol table and relocations. The linker resolves every undefined symbol against the other objects and libraries, lays out the sections and patches the addresses; at run time the loader maps the program and the C runtime calls main. Both errors come from the linker, because only the linker sees all objects together: "undefined reference" means a symbol is used but no object or library defines it, "multiple definition" means two objects define the same external symbol. MSVC reports the same two situations as LNK2019 and LNK2005.

2. Two .c files both contain int counter; at file scope, and a third declares extern long counter;. What happens? [01] int counter; without an initialiser is a tentative definition. GCC 9 and older emitted it as a "common" symbol and the linker silently merged the two copies; since GCC 10 the default is -fno-common, so GCC 13 fails with "multiple definition of counter". The extern long file links anyway, because object files record names, not types, so on Linux it reads 8 bytes where only 4 exist (on Windows long is 4 bytes, so the same bug hides there). C has no cross-file check like C++'s one-definition rule; the defence is one header declaring extern int counter;, included by every user and by the one .c file that defines it, so the compiler compares declaration and definition. Everything that does not need to be shared should be static.

3. What does static mean in C? Give all three contexts. [01, 04, 16] On a local variable it gives static storage duration: one object, initialised once before main (with a constant expression only), that keeps its value between calls and is shared by every thread, so concurrent use needs a lock or an atomic. At file scope, on a variable or a function, it gives internal linkage: the name is invisible to other translation units, so two files can each have a private helper() without a link clash. In an array parameter, void f(int a[static 4]) promises that the argument points to at least four elements, which lets the compiler optimise and warn about a NULL or too-short argument. The first two share a keyword but are unrelated features.

docs.title: Part B — Types and integers
docs.text:
4. What is the difference between LP64 and LLP64, and why does it matter? [02] They are the two common 64-bit data models: on LP64 (Linux, macOS) long and pointers are 64 bits; on LLP64 (64-bit Windows) long stays 32 bits and only long long and pointers are 64 bits. int is 32 bits on both. Code written on one breaks on the other: a pointer or file offset stored in a long is truncated on Windows, %ld is the wrong specifier for int64_t on one of them, and a struct containing long changes size and layout, so a file written on one platform is misread on the other. Use <stdint.h> types for anything with a required width, size_t for sizes, intptr_t/uintptr_t for pointers stored as integers, and the PRId64 family for printing.

5. What are the integer promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions, and how do they cause signed/unsigned bugs? [02] Before arithmetic, every type narrower than int (char, short, uint8_t, small bit-fields) is promoted to int, so (uint8_t)200 + (uint8_t)100 is the int 300, and ~(uint8_t)0 is the int -1. Then the two operands are converted to a common type, and when a signed and an unsigned type of the same rank meet, the signed one becomes unsigned: -1 < 1u is false because -1 becomes UINT_MAX. That is why a negative int length compares as huge against a sizeof (a size_t), or turns into a huge count when passed to memcpy. The rules also depend on the data model: -1L < 1u is true on Linux (a 64-bit long holds every unsigned int) and false on 64-bit Windows (both become unsigned long). Build with -Wsign-compare (in -Wextra for C) and -Wconversion, or /W4 on MSVC.

6. What does this print on x86-64 Linux? [02] 

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    unsigned char a = 200, b = 100;
    int sum = a + b;
    unsigned char wrapped = a + b;
    int len = -1;

    printf("%d %d\n", sum, wrapped);
    if (len < sizeof(int))
        puts("small");
    else
        puts("huge");
    printf("%d\n", -1L < 1u);
    return 0;
}
It prints 300 44, then huge, then 1. a + b is computed in int after promotion, so sum is 300; storing 300 into an unsigned char reduces it modulo 256, giving 44, which is well defined because the target is unsigned. len < sizeof(int) compares an int with a size_t, so -1 is converted to SIZE_MAX and the test is false; GCC warns with -Wsign-compare under -Wextra. The last line prints 1 on Linux and 0 on 64-bit Windows, for the data-model reason in question 5.

7. Why is signed overflow undefined, and how do you check for it? [02, 09] Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2^N, but signed overflow is undefined, so the compiler may assume it never happens: it can treat i + 1 > i as always true and widen a 32-bit loop counter to 64 bits without re-checking it. The price is that after-the-fact checks are folded away: GCC 13 turns b > 0 && a + b < a into constant false, even at -O0. Check before the operation with comparisons that cannot overflow (b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b), or use __builtin_add_overflow and __builtin_mul_overflow (C23 standardises them as ckd_add and ckd_mul in <stdckdint.h>, available from GCC 14). MSVC has no such builtins in C, so Windows code uses hand-written pre-checks or <intsafe.h> helpers such as SizeTMult. For legacy code, -fwrapv makes wrapping defined, and UBSan finds the overflows at run time.

docs.title: Part C — Pointers, memory and lifetime
docs.text:
8. What is the difference between an array and a pointer, and what is decay? [03] An array is a contiguous block of elements whose length is part of its type; a pointer is a variable that holds an address. In most expressions an array name is converted ("decays") to a pointer to its first element, which is why a[i] and p[i] look the same (a[i] is defined as *(a + i)). It does not decay as the operand of sizeof (you get the whole array's size), of unary & (&a has type int (*)[N]: same address, different type), or when a string literal initialises a char array. Arrays cannot be assigned or returned, and char a[] = "hi" is a modifiable 3-byte copy while char *p = "hi" points at a read-only literal. The difference also shows across files: extern int *table; for an object defined as int table[4] reads the array's first bytes as an address and crashes.

9. What is wrong with this code? [03, 16] 

#include <string.h>

void clear_balances(long balances[16])
{
    memset(balances, 0, sizeof balances);
}

int main(void)
{
    long b[16];
    clear_balances(b);      /* most of b still holds garbage */
    return 0;
}
A parameter declared as an array is adjusted to a pointer, so balances is a long * and sizeof balances is 8 on x86-64: only the first 8 bytes are cleared, which is one long on Linux and two on Windows. The 16 in the parameter is ignored and nothing checks it. GCC 13 warns twice: -Wsizeof-array-argument (on by default) and -Wsizeof-pointer-memaccess (in -Wall). Pass the count (void clear_balances(long *b, size_t n) with memset(b, 0, n * sizeof *b)), or pass a pointer to the array, long (*b)[16], where sizeof *b is the full size.

10. What is the difference between const int *p and int *const p? [03, 16] Read the declaration from the name outward, right to left. const int *p (the same as int const *p) is a pointer to a const int: you can re-point p, but cannot write *p. int *const p is a const pointer to an int: *p = 5 is fine, p = &other is an error; const int *const p fixes both. A const on the pointee is a promise in an API ("I will not modify your buffer", as in strlen(const char *)), not a guarantee that the object never changes, because other non-const pointers may still modify it. C does not convert char ** to const char ** implicitly, because that would let you store the address of a const object into a plain char *.

11. What can you do with a void *, and what can you not? [03] void * is the generic object pointer: any object pointer converts to it and back without a cast and without loss, which is why malloc returns it and qsort and callback APIs take it. You cannot dereference it, and standard C does not allow arithmetic on it: GCC allows void * arithmetic as an extension (-Wpointer-arith warns), MSVC rejects it, so convert to unsigned char * for bytes. It carries no type information, so casting it to the wrong type in a callback is silent undefined behaviour. In C, int *p = malloc(n); needs no cast (in C++ it does), and function pointers are not object pointers: converting them to void * is not ISO C, although POSIX requires it to work for dlsym.

12. What does restrict mean, and how does it relate to memcpy versus memmove? [03, 05] restrict on a pointer parameter promises that, for the duration of the call, the object it points to is accessed only through that pointer (or pointers derived from it). The compiler can then keep values in registers across stores made through other pointers, and vectorise loops without run-time overlap checks; breaking the promise is undefined behaviour. memcpy's parameters are restrict, so overlapping source and destination is UB, and real programs broke when glibc changed its copy direction; memmove must handle overlap, typically by choosing the copy direction. C++ has no restrict; GCC, Clang and MSVC all accept __restrict as an extension there.

13. What are the four storage durations, and what is the difference between scope and lifetime? [04] Automatic: locals and parameters, alive from block entry to block exit, indeterminate unless initialised. Static: globals and static locals, alive for the whole run, zero- or constant-initialised before main. Allocated: from malloc, calloc or realloc until free. Thread: _Thread_local objects, one instance per thread for that thread's lifetime. Scope is the part of the source where a name is visible; lifetime is when the object exists at run time, so a static local has block scope but program lifetime, and a heap block has a lifetime but no name. A dangling pointer is a pointer used after the lifetime of its object has ended, whatever its scope.

14. What is wrong with this code, and what does it print when built with GCC 13? [04] 

#include <stdio.h>

const char *format_account(int id)
{
    char buf[16];
    snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "ACC-%06d", id);
    return buf;
}

int main(void)
{
    const char *a = format_account(42);
    const char *b = format_account(7);
    printf("%s %s\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
buf has automatic storage, so its lifetime ends at return and both pointers dangle. GCC 13 warns (-Wreturn-local-addr, on by default) and deliberately compiles the return as NULL, so the program prints (null) (null) (glibc's text for a NULL %s) at every optimisation level. MSVC warns (C4172) but returns the real stack address; the bytes are often still there, so such code "works" until another call reuses that stack: here the second call overwrites the first result, and printf's own frame can overwrite both. Fix it with a caller-provided buffer (int format_account(char *out, size_t outsz, int id)), a heap result the caller frees, or a struct returned by value; a static buffer stops the crash but is neither thread-safe nor safe to call twice in one printf.

15. State the contracts of malloc, calloc, realloc and free. What is the realloc leak? [04, 10] malloc(n) returns uninitialised memory aligned for any type, or NULL; malloc(0) may return NULL or a unique pointer (glibc returns a pointer), which must still be freed. calloc(count, size) returns zeroed memory and checks count * size for overflow, which malloc(count * size) does not. realloc(p, n) may move the block: on success the old pointer is invalid; on failure it returns NULL and leaves the old block allocated and unchanged, so p = realloc(p, n) leaks the block and loses your data exactly when memory is short. The idiom is void *tmp = realloc(p, n); if (!tmp) return ERR; p = tmp;, after checking the size calculation for overflow. free(NULL) is a no-op, a double free is UB, realloc(p, 0) is implementation-defined in C17 and undefined in C23, and on Windows a block must be freed by the same CRT that allocated it (a classic DLL-boundary bug).

docs.title: Part D — Strings
docs.text:
16. Why is strncpy not a safe strcpy, and what do you use instead? [05] strncpy(d, s, n) was designed for fixed-width, NUL-padded record fields: it always writes exactly n bytes, padding with zeros when s is shorter, and writes no terminator at all when s has n or more characters, so the result may not be a string. snprintf(d, sizeof d, "%s", s) always terminates (when the size is non-zero) and returns the length it wanted to write, so ret < 0 || (size_t)ret >= sizeof d detects truncation.
